## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III;** a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; embellished with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with those possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately evident to the reader which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of each biblical book, and in which places in their works they have done so.

A most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, and the low price; above all, this collection is a single, methodical, and chronological compilation of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the universal library of the clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold in 1,200 volumes for 1,000 francs; the Greek-Latin edition in 1,300 volumes for 800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of the Lord 882  
## Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims

# Prolegomena to Hincmar’s Works

[Col. 0009]

## Historical Notice

*(From Cave, Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers.)*

[Col. 0009A] Hincmar, born among the nobility of Gaul, was educated from childhood in the monastery of Saint-Denis near Paris under Abbot Hilduin; [Note: [Col. 0009C] Flodoard, *History of Reims*, book III, throughout.] there he made remarkable progress both in learning and in piety. Since he possessed a fortunate and penetrating intellect, he acquired considerable favor at the court of Emperor Louis.

When Hilduin was exiled to Saxony in 830, Hincmar himself, with the bishop’s permission, accompanied him into exile and provided him, during his banishment, with assistance that was not unwelcome. After Ebbō was deposed in 835 on the charge of treason, the see of Reims had already been vacant for nearly ten years when, at the beginning of 845, Hincmar was ordained archbishop of Reims at the Council of Beauvais, with the votes of both clergy and people united and with the support of King Charles. The bishops assembled at Paris the following year again confirmed his election by their votes; at that time King Charles also restored to the Church of Reims the possessions which the royal officials had plundered while the see was vacant.

In 848 he took part in the Council of Quierzy, and in the synodal decrees against Gottschalk—whether made here or [Col. 0009B] elsewhere—he played almost everywhere the leading role. [Note: [Col. 0009C] Councils, vol. VIII, p. 79.] In 853 the Council of Soissons was held, as the acts of that council testify, although Flodoard reports that it was held in the seventh year of Hincmar’s episcopate. At this council Hincmar secured the reconfirmation of his ordination and caused Wulfad and the other priests ordained by Ebbō after his deposition in 840 to be removed from their dignity.

In 855 the decrees passed seven years earlier at the Council of Quierzy through Hincmar’s efforts were annulled at the Council of Valence. [Note: [Col. 0009C] Ibid., p. 137; in the cited place, pp. 673–674.] The decrees of the Council of Valence were confirmed in 859 by the Councils of Langres and Toul; their chapters, presented to King Charles, were given by the king to Hincmar to refute. He performed this task in a distinguished written work.

In 860 he attended the two Councils of Aachen, [Note: [Col. 0010C] Ibid., p. 696.] where Theutberga confessed that she had had intercourse with her brother Hucbert, whether compelled by force or by the truth of the matter, and the Fathers decreed that she was to be repudiated by King Lothair and subjected to public penance. This provided Hincmar with an excellent opportunity for much activity in writing and [Col. 0009C] in other matters. In the same year he subscribed to the Second Council of Toul and, the following year, to the Third Council of Aachen.

In 863 he was present at the Council of Metz, [Note: [Col. 0010C] Ibid., p. 764.] at which the marriage of King Lothair with Waldrada, contracted after Theutberga’s repudiation, was declared valid. This council, however, was soon condemned by Pope Nicholas at a Roman synod.

In the same year, after obtaining confirmation of the privileges of the Church of Reims, Hincmar caused Rothad, bishop of Soissons, who was unwilling to resign, to be deposed at a council held at Senlis and, after another had been [Col. 0010A] substituted in his place, to be confined in a monastery. When Rothad appealed to the Apostolic See—the booklet of his Appeal is extant in Baronius under the year 863, no. 81, and in the Councils, vol. VIII, p. 785—Hincmar condemned him again.

Although Pope Nicholas intervened and Hincmar released Rothad from prison, he by no means permitted him to go to Rome, even though the pontiff had ordered that he be sent there to reopen the case. Nor, when admonished for a third time by Nicholas, did he wish to abandon his purpose. Although daily threats were made that letters of excommunication would be sent from Rome, he nevertheless defended himself against everything by the authority of the canons, as is abundantly clear from his apologetic letter to Nicholas.

In 865, at the Roman Council, Rothad was restored to his see, and Hincmar’s two judgments were annulled. [Note: [Col. 0010C] Councils, ibid., p. 808, etc.] In 866 he presided over the Third Council of Soissons, at which Wulfad and his fellow priests, by order of Pope Nicholas, recovered their former dignity. The following year, at the Council of Troyes, which he presided over, he examined the same case more carefully.

In 869 Hincmar, bishop of [Col. 0010B] Laon, his nephew, accused of many crimes at the Synod of Verberie, was himself condemned by Hincmar of Reims, who was more hostile to him than anyone else. Hence arose serious enmity between uncle and nephew, and abundant material for major controversies.

In 882, when the Normans broke into Gaul, Hincmar abandoned Reims and, taking with him the body of Saint Remigius, sought the wooded country beyond the Marne. There, at Sparnacum, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, he ended his life and was buried in the monastery of Saint Remigius.

It is not for me to pass judgment on so great a man, whom Rabanus Maurus, who knew him exceptionally well, calls “a most reverend and deeply mourned man, and one rightly to be venerated by all Catholics for his orthodox faith and sound profession.” Lupus of Ferrières says: “The nobility of his birth is adorned by salutary learning; the dignity of his office is commended by the religion of his profession.” [Letter 42.]

In theological studies, as Baronius himself admits, he was extremely accomplished, and [Col. 0010C] many consulted him on various questions. [Baronius, under the year 882, no. 17.] In knowledge of the canons he was most learned, although at times excessively favorable to them, exalting them even above the decrees of the Apostolic See. Indeed, no one understood the laws and rights of the Church better, and no one defended them more vigorously.

His works, filled with much learning, doctrine, and piety, wonderfully illuminate the history of the Gallican Church. Sirmond rightly says of them that there is none which lacks usefulness, and none in which the author’s outstanding judgment does not shine forth together with the abundance of his knowledge.

[Col. 0011]

## Second Historical Notice, Composed in French

*(Literary History of France, vol. V, p. 544.)*

[Col. 0011A] Hincmar, the prelate who among all those of his time played the greatest role in the Church of France, was born in the first years of the ninth century, apparently in 806, although his birthplace has not yet been discovered. [Note: [Col. 0011C] Flodoard, book III, chapters 1 and 25, pp. 547, 586.]

He was French by nationality, descended from an ancient noble family, and related to Bernard II, count of Toulouse, and Bertrand, count of Tardenois. He had a sister settled in the Boulonnais, who became the mother of Hincmar, later bishop of Laon. This is all that is known about the parents of our archbishop.

[Note: [Col. 0011C] Ibid., chapter 1, pp. 547–548; Councils, vol. VIII, p. 1912.] From childhood he was placed in the monastery of Saint-Denis near Paris, to be instructed in piety and liberal learning under Abbot Hilduin, whom he always afterward honored as his teacher. Since the abbey had by then fallen into laxity, the young Hincmar at first took only the habit of a canon. After some time he was removed from it because of the excellence of his mind and the eminence of his birth, and placed at the court of Emperor Louis the [Col. 0011B] Pious. The prince admitted him to his friendship; but Hincmar used this favor only to persuade the emperor to restore monastic discipline at Saint-Denis. The plan was devised at the Council of Paris in 829 and carried out shortly afterward.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXX, no. 27; Baluze, *Capitularies*, vol. I, p. 676; Flodoard, ibid., p. 548; Councils, ibid., pp. 1912–1913; Astronomus, under the year 830; Thegan, chapter 16.] Hincmar was the first to reform himself. He left the court, assumed the monastic habit, embraced the full rigor of the rule, and remained in this condition for a long time, without hope or desire of an episcopate or any other prelacy.

When Hilduin, his abbot, fell out of the emperor’s favor and was consequently exiled to Saxony in 830, Hincmar followed him into exile with the permission of his bishop and the blessing of his brethren. He did still more for him. He used his influence with the prince and the lords of the court so effectively that, as early as the following year, he obtained Hilduin’s recall and the restoration of two of his abbeys.

Later, when Pope Gregory IV came to [Col. 0011C] France to support Lothair’s party against Emperor Louis, Hilduin tried to involve Hincmar in the same party, but in vain. Hincmar remained peacefully in his monastery until the same prince recalled him to court, to which he went out of obedience. After the emperor’s death, it seems that Hincmar returned once more to Saint-Denis, where he was entrusted with the office of treasurer, or guardian of the relics.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Flodoard, ibid., chapters 1 and 18, pp. 548, 568; Mabillon, ibid., book XXXIII, no. 15.] Charles the Bald then wished to have him in his service, and, in order to attach him more closely to himself, gave him the monasteries of Notre-Dame and Saint-Germain at Compiègne, together with that of Saint-Germer-de-Fly. He also added an estate, which Hincmar ceded to the infirmary of Saint-Denis after he had become archbishop. [Note: [Col. 0011D] Councils, ibid., p. 1913.]

[Col. 0012A] One of his principal functions at court was to serve the bishops in their assemblies. [Note: [Col. 0011D] Vol. VII, p. 1805.] In 844 he attended the assembly held at Verneuil in December. If he had not yet received priestly ordination, [Note: [Col. 0011D] pp. 1811–1812; Flodoard, ibid., chapters 1 and 5, pp. 547, 550; [Col. 0012C] Labbe, *New Library*, vol. I, p. 359; Hincmar, vol. II, pp. 272–273, 303.] he had certainly received it by the following year, in April, when he attended in that capacity the Council of Beauvais, composed of the bishops of the two provinces, Reims and Sens.

The former province had been without a metropolitan for ten years, since Ebbō’s deposition in 835. The bishops, convinced that it was necessary to provide one, took the precautions appropriate to the case; and Hincmar was elected by the clergy and people of Reims to occupy the see. His election, made with the consent of his community and the approval of King Charles, was applauded by the bishops of the province and approved by the archbishop of Sens, the bishop of Paris, and the abbot of Saint-Denis, his superiors. Accordingly, Hincmar was ordained on the third day of May of that same year by Rothad, bishop of Soissons.

[Col. 0012B] [Note: [Col. 0012D] Councils, ibid., p. 1813; vol. VIII, pp. 38–39; Flodoard, ibid., chapter 2, p. 548.] As early as the following June he attended the Council of Meaux, and afterward the Council of Paris in February 847. At the latter his ordination was confirmed, which Emperor Lothair had attempted to disturb by restoring Ebbō to the see of Reims.

After that, scarcely any council was held this side of the Loire at which Hincmar was not personally present, and at which he did not also play the leading role, serving as its soul or even its president. In this way he acquired very great authority throughout the Church of France, among reigning princes, and even at Rome. This authority, combined with his profound learning, especially in canon law, made him the arbiter of most delicate and important affairs.

He was, as it were, the bishop of the court and was almost always in its train. No ceremony of importance took place there at which he did not appear prominently. [Note: [Col. 0012D] Baluze, ibid., vol. II, p. 310; Bertinian Annals, under the year 856.] It was he who at Verberie in 856 [Col. 0012C] performed the marriage ceremony of Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, with Æthelwulf, king of the West Saxons, and the coronation ceremony of that princess. [Note: [Col. 0012D] Councils, vol. VIII, pp. 832, 836.]

In 866 he also occupied the first place at the coronation of Queen Hermentrude, held at the Council of Soissons. [Note: [Col. 0012D] Baluze, ibid., pp. 302, 306.] Three years later he likewise crowned Charles the Bald at Metz as king of the territories of his nephew Lothair; and in December 877 he crowned Louis the Stammerer at Compiègne. [Note: [Col. 0012D] Ibid., p. 137.]

At Coblentz, where the reigning princes had assembled in 860 to make peace among themselves, Hincmar stood at the head of the thirteen prelates whom they chose, together with thirty-three nobles, to draft the oath they were mutually to sign and the articles their subjects were to observe.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Flodoard, ibid., chapters 17, 18, and 26, pp. 567, 587, 586; Baluze, ibid., p. 68.] Charles the Bald held [Col. 0013A] our prelate in high esteem and derived great benefits from his services. Accordingly, he undertook nothing important, whether in ecclesiastical affairs or in his purely temporal enterprises, without consulting him either by letter or in person.

Knowing Hincmar’s zeal for good order, Charles made him one of his envoys or commissioners to supervise the execution of his ordinances. Nevertheless, the prince gave him his confidence only up to a certain point—that is, when he was certain that Hincmar had no personal interest in deceiving him. [Note: [Col. 0013D] Councils, ibid., pp. 811, 31–32; vol. IX, pp. 291–294; Hincmar, ibid., pp. 834–837; Baluze, ibid., p. 264, no. 12.]

The affair of Wulfad had shown him that Hincmar was not a slave to his word. Charles also knew that Emperor Lothair, with whom he was almost always at odds despite being his brother, counted on the devotion of our prelate. All this, together with the suspicion that Hincmar had favored the invasion of France by Louis, king of Germany, led Charles the Bald to demand from him privately, at the Council of Ponthion, a new oath of fidelity.

Hincmar swore it; but his [Col. 0013B] self-respect suffered greatly from this, as appears from one of his writings on the subject. Nevertheless, when Charles departed in 877 on his final journey to Italy, he did not fail to name Hincmar first among his testamentary executors.

Five popes governed the Roman Church during Hincmar’s episcopate, and all of them, on various occasions, gave him signs of the high esteem they held for his merits. [Note: [Col. 0013D] Flodoard, book X, chapter 10, p. 552.] Leo IV granted him the use of the pallium, with the singular privilege of wearing it every day. It was in consideration of his learning and piety that the pontiff granted him this favor, which no other archbishop had yet received. [Note: [Col. 0013D] Councils, vols. VIII and IX, passim.]

A later pope made a kind of crime of this against our prelate, who defended himself by assuring him that he had used it only twice a year, at Easter and Christmas. At Hincmar’s request, Benedict III, delighted by his zeal for maintaining ecclesiastical discipline, confirmed the acts of the second [Col. 0013C] Council of Soissons, which was important for Hincmar.

It is true that, in doing so, the pope declared that this was only on the condition that the facts were as they had been reported to him; a condition that later had unfortunate consequences for the archbishop of Reims.

Nicholas I, the pope who had the closest relations with Hincmar and knew him best, certainly valued his learning and his other great talents, but he did not flatter him when occasions arose. No one more forcefully pointed out what was blameworthy in the conduct of this prelate.

Adrian II and John VIII were two of his greatest admirers, and they always held him in an esteem and friendship that would not permit them to refuse him anything.

Four celebrated events that occurred in the Church of France during Hincmar’s time, and in which he played the principal role, especially revealed his mind, genius, skill, and [Col. 0013D] ability. The first was the great affair of Gottschalk.

Our prelate, having too readily embraced the unfortunate prejudices of Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, against that unhappy monk, employed every means to force him to renounce his earlier convictions. Forgetting, according to the fine observation of Saint Remigius of Lyon, that truth is persuaded and not commanded, [Note: [Col. 0013D] Remigius, *On the Three Epistles*, chapter 25, p. 680; Bertinian Annals, under the year 849.] he had him treated in a horrible manner. Afterward he confined him in the prison of Hautvillers, where he allowed him to die without any spiritual assistance.

We shall not repeat here everything that occurred during [Col. 0014A] the captivity of this poor prisoner, which lasted about twenty years. It will suffice to say that, after Hincmar had exhausted all his ingenuity and the initial strength of his pen, and felt himself too weak to sustain the burden of the dispute alone, he solicited assistance from abroad.

Rabanus, who had drawn him into the affair, as has been said, refused to lend him any. Saint Prudentius of Troyes, to whom Hincmar appealed, far from supporting his views, believed himself obliged to oppose him, fearing that the doctrine of Saint Augustine might be implicated in what Hincmar and his supporters presented as errors.

Lupus, abbot of Ferrières (*Letter* 129), to whom it appears that our archbishop also appealed, answered him in such a way as to convince him that Lupus thought no differently on the questions at issue than Gottschalk himself.

Pardulus of Laon, the deacon Amalarius, and John Scotus Eriugena were more accommodating and considered it a distinction to come to Hincmar’s support. But their efforts were soon overturned both [Col. 0014B] by the arguments of Saint Prudentius and Florus, deacon of Lyon, and by the writings of Lupus and Ratramnus, monk of Corbie.

Hincmar next appealed to Amolo, archbishop of Lyon, who indeed condemned the errors presented to him, but took care to attach to his response a writing with which our prelate could not be pleased, since it agreed with Gottschalk’s doctrine. [Note: [Col. 0014D] Flodoard, ibid., p. 570, 2; Agobard, vol. II, appendix, pp. 149–171, 179–186.]

This apparently prevented Hincmar from invoking Amolo’s authority in his great work on predestination, where he cites other writers who appear less favorable to him. He was not discouraged, however, and tried a second time to win this archbishop over to his party. But it was in vain; and this second effort had consequences still more fatal to his cause than the first.

It in fact gave Remigius, Amolo’s successor, the opportunity to refute Hincmar’s writing and those of his associates with considerable effect. [Note: [Col. 0014D] Remigius, ibid., preface.] The Councils of Valence and Langres did not [Col. 0014C] delay in declaring against the same doctrine and confirmed by their canons what these great theologians had established in their learned works, in agreement with Scripture and the writings of the Fathers of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0014D] Councils, ibid., pp. 134–139, 690–691.]

Pope Nicholas did the same, or at least it was firmly believed by Hincmar himself and by one of his most zealous panegyrists that the pontiff had approved the views of Hincmar’s opponents. [Note: [Col. 0014D] Hincmar, ibid., p. 292; Bertinian Annals, under the year 859.]

Thus this famous dispute showed all who wished to open their eyes that our prelate, although otherwise highly skilled, did not understand theological matters. He was no more successful in trying to prohibit the singing of the stanza “You, Triune God” (*Te trina Deitas*).

The dispute over predestination was still at its height when another affair arose for Hincmar, greatly perplexing him and bringing him considerable distress. [Note: [Col. 0014D] Flodoard, ibid., chapter 11, p. 553; Councils, ibid., passim.]

He believed that he ought to depose—and in fact did depose—at the second Council of [Col. 0014D] Soissons in 853 Wulfad and the other clerics ordained by his predecessor Ebbō. These men appealed to the Holy See, while King Charles the Bald protected them out of regard for Wulfad. Their case was therefore examined again at another Council of Soissons, held in 866 and attended by Hincmar.

There the prelate employed all his ingenuity to prevent his first sentence from being overturned. Nevertheless, the council referred the decision of the case to Pope Nicholas, who pronounced in favor of the clerics. Hincmar was not finished with this contradiction.

After examining the [Col. 0015A] documents of the trial, the Roman pontiff believed that he had discovered that Hincmar had employed every kind of trickery and artifice. He reproached him bitterly, portraying Hincmar as a chameleon or a Proteus who feigned every sort of character according to his purposes and interests.

Charles the Bald was scarcely more pleased with the conduct of the archbishop of Reims in this affair. Likewise, the prelates who made up the Council of Soissons in 866 were so scandalized by the contents of the fourth memorandum he presented there on the same subject that they could not endure hearing it read to the end.

The manner in which Hincmar conducted himself in the affair of Rothad, bishop of Soissons, his own ordainer, was no more honorable, whatever the Annalist of Saint-Bertin, his panegyrist, may say. [Note: [Col. 0015D] Bertinian Annals, under the years 861 and 863; Councils, ibid., pp. 736, 761, 775, 785, 791.]

When Rothad, in accordance with the canons, punished one of his priests who had been convicted of a capital crime, Hincmar—who had long been hostile to Rothad—deprived him of episcopal communion under the pretext of [Col. 0015B] disobedience to the rules of the Church, because Rothad refused to reinstate the priest whom the metropolitan had undertaken to defend.

This occurred in 861 at the Council of Soissons. At Hincmar’s instigation the council confirmed the sentence, and Rothad appealed to the Holy See. But the archbishop of Reims, having found a way to prevent him from going to Rome, had him deposed from the episcopate and confined in a monastery.

Pope Nicholas, however, informed of this injustice, removed the obstacles that held Rothad back and had him brought to Rome. Finally, after vainly urging Hincmar to appear, he restored the unfortunate prelate to his former dignity.

[Note: [Col. 0015D] Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXXVIII, no. 62.] According to the opinion of some writers, Hincmar on this occasion abused the influence he possessed with King Charles the Bald; and he made no better use of it in the great affair of Hincmar of Laon, his nephew, in which our archbishop was very far from allowing mercy to prevail over [Col. 0015C] severity.

On the contrary, he displayed much harshness and other passions that suited neither a metropolitan nor an uncle. The feelings of nature and the honor of the episcopate will always protest against the conduct he maintained on this occasion.

It is true that he did not have his nephew’s eyes put out, as some have accused him of doing; but there is no reason to doubt that, if he had wished to use his influence with the king to soften that prince’s disposition, he would have spared this other unfortunate prelate so inhuman a punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0015D] Councils, ibid., pp. 1913, 1917.] So many distressing experiences and so many hardships encountered during his episcopate sometimes made him regret the peace and tranquility he had formerly enjoyed in his cloister.

To use his own language, he regarded it as a punishment for his sins that, when the anchor cable which perhaps had attached him too carelessly to that safe harbor was broken, he found himself cast into the storms of a turbulent [Col. 0015D] sea under the specious pretext of saving others.

On the other hand, the multitude of needs of Church and State, and the entanglement of secular affairs from which he could not withdraw, caused him to lament that he so often found himself far from his own flock. He admitted that, if he had known well the sorrows and dangers inseparable from the episcopate, he would certainly have taken care not to accept it.

Nevertheless, justice requires us to acknowledge that, despite [Col. 0016A] all these great distractions, he did not neglect the spiritual or temporal welfare of his Church. From the enumeration of his writings one will see the care he took to instruct properly the clergy and people of his diocese. [Note: [Col. 0015D] Flodoard, ibid., chapter 23, p. 580; Baluze, ibid., p. 1241.]

He was no less attentive to maintaining the rights of his see, preserving the lands and estates left to it by his predecessors, and reclaiming those that had been either plundered or alienated.

He extended his beneficial care even to the monastery of Saint-Remi, of which he was abbot although archbishop of Reims. [Note: [Col. 0015D] Flodoard, book I, chapter 21; book III, chapter 9; Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXXIII, no. 24; book XXXIV, no. 42.]

After enlarging its church, he had a magnificent vault of admirable workmanship constructed there in 852, and transferred the body of the patron saint there with a solemn ceremony. He wished further to mark his devotion and respect for the saint with verses of his own composition, with which he adorned the site and the silk cloths in which this precious treasure was wrapped.

[Col. 0016B] [Note: [Col. 0015D] Flodoard, book III, chapter 5, p. 550.] Ten years later, having completed the beautiful nave of his cathedral church, begun by his predecessor Ebbō, he magnificently embellished it and then carried out its dedication, attended by King Charles the Bald and a large number of prelates.

Nothing, it seems, escaped Hincmar’s solicitude. He took care not to neglect the maintenance of studies among his clergy, though he himself was continually engaged in writing and thereby gave them an example of cultivating learning. [Note: [Col. 0016D] Mabillon, ibid., book XXXVIII, no. 62.]

Two schools had previously been established, one for the canons of the cathedral and the other for the remaining clergy of the diocese. Hincmar took care to support them and likewise watched over Saint-Remi so that ignorance should not enter there.

With this aim he gave the monastery and his cathedral church several books on which he ordered his name to be written. [Note: [Col. 0016D] Flodoard, ibid., chapters 5, 21, and 23, pp. 550, 572, 579; Lupus, letter 76; Hincmar, *Instruction for the King*, p. 201.]

Besides the books he composed every day, he took great care to collect the works of the ancients. He carried this care so far as to gather [Col. 0016C] apocryphal works as well as the others. But what is extremely astonishing is to learn that a prelate occupied with so many important affairs could still find leisure to copy the writings of others himself. [Note: [Col. 0016D] Flodoard, ibid., chapters 23 and 25, p. 580, 1; 583, 2; Councils, ibid., p. 1917.]

This multitude of occupations not only enables us to understand how industrious this archbishop was; it also helps us recognize what his piety was like. [Note: [Col. 0016D] Councils, vol. IX, p. 337.] For despite all the various difficulties they caused him, he did not cease to think seriously about death.

From the final years of Nicholas I’s pontificate, he regarded death as near and already felt the infirmities of old age. Nevertheless, he lived for more than fifteen years thereafter.

After presiding over the council that he convened at Fismes at the beginning of April 881, he spent the remainder of the year in relative tranquility [Note: [Col. 0016D] Flod. ib., c. 30, p. 592. 2; Mab. ib.]. But during the course of the following year, as the Normans continued [Col. 0016D] their ravages around Champagne, and since the city of Reims still lacked defensive walls, this prudent prelate thought he ought to provide for the safety of Saint Remigius’s body, in order to save it from the fury of these barbarians. He therefore took this precious deposit with him and withdrew beyond the Marne, to the town of Épernay. There, after some time, sensing that his final day was approaching, he wished, before dying, to give yet another sign of his zeal for the Church by writing to the bishops [Col. 0017A] his colleagues, exhorting them to flee simony, to devote themselves to the study of the canons, and to instruct the peoples entrusted to their care. In these dispositions this great archbishop died—the most illustrious and learned of the successors of the apostle of the Franks. His body was immediately carried back to Reims and buried behind the tomb of Saint Remigius, with the following epitaph, which he had taken care to have engraved during his lifetime on a copper plate that can still be seen to the left of the high altar. The day of his death is variously recorded in the ancient necrologies: in some, on 21 December; in others, on the 23rd of the same month. This difference, moreover, apparently arises only from the precise day on which he died at Épernay and the day on which he was buried at Saint-Remi. As for the year, it is recorded, together with the duration of his episcopate, in the addition made to his epitaph.

## EPITAPH

[Col. 0017B]

**Nomine non merito, praesul Hincmarus, ab antro,**  
**Te, Lector, tituli, quaeso, memento mei.**

Hincmar, a prelate in name but not in merit, from the tomb,  
I beg you, reader of this inscription, remember me.

**Quem grege pastorem proprio Dionysius olim**  
**Rhemorum populis, ut petiere dedit.**

Him, as shepherd of his own flock, Dionysius once gave  
To the people of Reims, who had requested him.

**Quisque humilis magnae Rhemensis regmina plebis**  
**Rexi pro modulo, hic modo verme voror.**

Humbly, according to my measure, I ruled  
The government of the great people of Reims; now here I am devoured by worms.

**Ergo animae requiem nunc, et cum carne resumpta,**  
**[Col. 0018A] Gaudia plena mihi haec quoque posce simul.**

Therefore now ask for rest for my soul, and, when it has taken up its flesh again,  
Ask also, at the same time, that full joys may be granted me.

**Christe, tui clemens famuli miserere fidelis:**  
**Sis pia cultori, sancta Maria, tuo.**

Christ, mercifully have pity on your faithful servant;  
Holy Mary, be gracious to your worshiper.

**Dulcis Remigii sibimet devotio prosit,**  
**Qua te dilexit pectore, et ore, manu.**

May his devotion to gentle Remigius benefit him,  
The devotion with which he loved him in heart, speech, and deed.

**Quare hic suppetiis supplex sua membra locari,**  
**Ut bene complacuit: denique sic obiit.**

For this reason, suppliant, he asked that his body be laid here with aid,  
As seemed good to him; and thus at last he died.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 882, and in the thirty-seventh year of his episcopate, in the seventh month and on the fourth day.

[Note: [Col. 0017B] Mabill. ibid.]

Those who have applied themselves most diligently to studying the history of this learned prelate agree that he was irreproachable in his morals and that he had acquired a very great reputation; but they also acknowledge that it was not without blemish. There was scarcely, in his time, any prelate of a certain distinction in France with whom he was not in correspondence. He was even, as it were, the oracle of most of them, and was consulted from all sorts of places by princes, princesses, great lords, abbots, and other persons of distinction. Besides the ties he [Col. 0018B] maintained with the popes [Note: [Col. 0018B] Flod. ib., c. 21, 33; Hinc. t. II, p. 824.], he also formed relationships with learned men of foreign countries, such as Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church. Thus, since the earliest centuries of the Church, few bishops more famous than Hincmar had appeared in France. Until his death he maintained abstinence from meat, which he had vowed when professing the Rule of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 0017]

## BIBLIOGRAPHICAL NOTICE

*(From the same Literary History.)*

### § I.—Extant Writings of Hincmar

[Col. 0017C]

The brief account of Hincmar’s history has shown that this prelate wrote a great deal. Unfortunately, however, the centuries that followed him were not careful to preserve all the productions of his pen. We shall first enumerate those that remain, beginning with the collection published by the learned Father Sirmond. We shall then add those discovered since, and finally provide a notice of those that are lost but of which some knowledge has been preserved. We would wish to follow the chronological order here, but the last editor did not follow it himself, because he considered that impossible. Nevertheless, we shall take care to assign each work its true date insofar as we are able to discover it.

**1.** At the beginning of the edition placed before the reader stands the dedicatory epistle of a work [Col. 0017D] that is lost. We shall return to this piece later, and begin the catalogue of Hincmar’s writings with his major treatise on predestination, with which the collection published by Father Sirmond properly begins. It is entitled *Last Dissertation on the Predestination of God and Free Will*, and is divided into thirty-eight chapters, most of them very prolix, not counting the dedicatory epistle that serves as its preface and the epilogue, which contains six substantial chapters. It is called the “last dissertation,” or “last treatise,” because other writings on the same subject preceded it. Father Sirmond counts only one other; but it will appear below that the author composed at least three or four works on these matters, not counting simple letters to various persons.

Hincmar undertook it after June of the year 859 and completed it as he was able to steal a few hours from his other occupations: *furatis horulis a diversis occupationum distensionibus*—“having stolen little hours from the various distractions of his occupations.” This expression suggests that he took a considerable time to finish it. He had completed it at least by 863, since he then sent it to Rome to Pope Nicholas through Odo, bishop of Beauvais, who was traveling there on other business. At the beginning is a preface devoted almost entirely to reporting extraneous documents: the Sermon of Florus, deacon of Lyon; the second canon and the five following canons of the Council of Valence; several sentences of the Fathers drawn from the writing of Lyon, which Hincmar places between the sixth and seventh canons; the eighth canon of the Council of Langres and another drawn from elsewhere; the four famous articles of Quierzy; and finally Saint Prudentius’s letter to the assembly of Sens. The author dedicates his work to King Charles the Bald and pursues two principal aims: first, to show that Gottschalk had revived the supposed heresy of the Predestinarians; second, to defend the four famous articles of Quierzy against the censure directed against them by the Fathers of the Third Council of Valence. He dwells particularly on this second aim, and the examination of the first six or seven canons of that council forms the body of the work. Hincmar thereby shows that the first writing he had published several years earlier on predestination, in which he had already attacked these same canons, had been judged weak and insufficient to prove what he claimed. The work under discussion here has no greater force. Its author displays more erudition than judgment and soundness of mind, and has really succeeded only in showing that he was not a theologian.

The very erudition of which he makes a display is indiscriminate and uncritical. He takes Hilary, who was a layman and whose letter to Saint Augustine he cites, for Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles. He assumes that the council of that same city, at which the priest Lucidus retracted his views, was held by order of Pope Saint Celestine, [Col. 0019A] who had died more than forty years before that council. He maintains that the *Hypognosticon* is a work of Saint Augustine and that the treatise on the Hardening of Pharaoh is a work of Saint Jerome. Since he suspected that the seventh canon of Valence, concerning the irregular ordination of bishops, had been maliciously directed against him, he discusses it at length and takes the opportunity to report the history of his own ordination and the Acts of the Council of Soissons, at which it had been confirmed. Flodoard, in enumerating Hincmar’s works, explicitly attributes this one to him, carefully distinguishing it from the others on the same subjects, and reports its dedicatory epistle in full.

**2.** The same author also records in his catalogue the writing that Hincmar composed from passages of the Fathers to show that one must not use the expression *Trina Deitas*—“Triune Godhead”—against the blasphemies of Gottschalk, to use his own expression. This work, whose title is phrased in almost the same terms used here by Flodoard, is printed after the preceding one. Hincmar addresses it to the children of the Catholic Church and to his colleagues in the sacred ministry. Father Sirmond dates it to 857. The occasion for it was what Ratramnus and Gottschalk had published in defense of the stanza of the famous hymn of the martyrs, *Te trina Deitas*—“You, Triune Godhead”—which Hincmar had altered to *Te sancta Deitas*—“You, holy Godhead”—on the pretext that *Trina* implied three gods in the mystery of the Trinity. Irritated at being contradicted in this alteration, he undertook to answer his opponents in the work in question. Although he attacks Ratramnus there, he cites nothing from his writing. He focuses especially on Gottschalk’s work and, in replying to it, follows the same method Saint Prudentius had already followed in refuting John Scotus’s treatise on predestination. Undertaking to answer it point by point, he reports his adversary’s text in sections, marking it with an obelus, and then [Col. 0019C] adds his own response, marked with a chrismon, so that it may be more clearly distinguished from the adversary’s text.

This work displays much erudition and just as much subtlety. But it rests entirely on a false inference, which Gottschalk forestalls at the beginning of his writing by declaring that *Trina* applies only to the persons and not at all to the divine essence or nature. As for the accusations Hincmar levels against Ratramnus, he is content to assert them without undertaking to prove them, however serious they may be. The author’s style is vehement and almost everywhere reveals his ill humor toward Gottschalk. In any case, the Church did not find his arguments very conclusive, since it continued to sing *Te Trina Deitas*. At the end of the work are twenty-six verses from Gottschalk’s letter to Ratramnus.

**3.** Hincmar’s writing on the divorce of King Lothair and Queen Theutberga, which follows the preceding work, consists of thirty questions proposed to the author on two different occasions concerning this subject, together with his answers and a preface addressed to reigning princes, bishops, and all the faithful, since all had an interest in the matter. He proves this in his preface, where he also attempts to protect his readers against the scandal that the facts reported in the questions might cause them. Hincmar worked on this treatise between the years 860 and 863. He establishes excellent principles in it, but he also says various things that are neither interesting nor well supported. Such are his statements concerning trial by hot water. In answering the fifteenth question, he shows that he believed there were sorcerers. There is both good and bad in what he says concerning the twenty-ninth question, which is the sixth of the final seven. He rightly establishes that a king has no one above him except God alone, but he seems to say that he is king only insofar as he performs his duty, and that one ought not to obey a criminal prince.

**4.** Following this work comes the collection of our prelate’s capitularies, reprinted in the general collection of the Councils. The first capitulary, divided into seventeen articles, was published in a synod on 1 November 852. Hincmar recommends that every priest of his diocese thoroughly learn the explanations of the Lord’s Prayer and the Apostles’ Creed, so as to be able to teach them to others; learn by heart the preface of the Canon and the Creed attributed to Saint Athanasius; understand their meaning well enough to explain it to the people; apply himself to reading the Gospel, the Epistles, and the Psalms distinctly and correctly; possess the forty homilies of Saint Gregory and understand them well; know by heart the same pope’s sermon on the seventy-two disciples of the Savior, after whose model, he says, priests were established in the ecclesiastical ministry; [Col. 0020B] and finally acquire a perfect knowledge of the computus, or necessary calculation, and of chant. From this one can see how concerned Hincmar was to banish ignorance from his clergy. Among the other disciplinary matters prescribed by this capitulary, one finds holy water and blessed bread for every Sunday, more or less as this is still practiced today in parishes.

The second capitulary comprises twenty-seven articles, the last of which is very prolix and may be regarded as a kind of brief penitential, since it concerns the penances to be imposed on priests and deacons. The other articles are instructions for rural deans and others charged with supervising the parish churches and chapels of the diocese. Hincmar urges them to give him every year, on the first day of July, a faithful report of what they have observed, in accordance with the instructions prescribed here.

[Col. 0020C] The third capitulary, divided into three articles, is properly an addition made to the first in June 857, the twelfth year of Hincmar’s episcopate. By the first article, which is important, parish priests are charged to watch over public sinners, to persuade them to submit to public penance, and to report to the bishop how they conduct themselves in this regard.

The fourth capitulary comprises five articles, which Hincmar gave to his parish priests in a synod held in July 874. In the same year, according to Fathers Cossart and Labbe, or only three years later according to Father Sirmond, our prelate composed another capitulary, the fifth and last in the collection. In thirteen articles it contains an instruction for the priests Gontaire and Odelhard, whom he was appointing archdeacons, and in particular seeks to dissuade them, during their visitations, from sordid exactions, which perhaps were only too common in other dioceses. [Col. 0020D] All these capitularies testify to Hincmar’s pastoral concern for the observance of exact discipline.

**5.** After them, in the edition that serves as our guide, come the coronations of the kings and queens in which Hincmar played the greatest part—that is, the collection of speeches, blessings, and prayers pronounced in ceremonies of this kind. These coronations are those of Charles the Bald, as king of Lorraine; of Hermentrude, his wife; of Louis the Stammerer, their eldest son; and of Judith, their daughter, as queen of the Western Saxons.

**6.** The first volume of this edition concludes with the prose explanation of a verse work that Hincmar had addressed to King Charles the Bald under the title *Ferculum Salomonis*, “Solomon’s table service” or “Solomon’s dish,” and that is no longer extant. This explanation is a fabric of [Col. 0021A] mysticisms, from which we nevertheless learn that by this Dish of Solomon the author means the Church, which is the mystical body of Jesus Christ, and that, while establishing the doctrine of human free will, he also takes care to establish that of prevenient grace for willing and practicing the good. Hincmar reports, under the name of Saint Ambrose, fourteen hexameter verses on the ternary number, and concludes his explanation with fourteen further verses of his own, extremely flat and in varying meter.

**7.** At the beginning of the second volume stands a treatise entitled *De regis persona et regio ministerio*, “On the Person of the King and Royal Service.” Flodoard, who lists this work among those of our prelate, gives a reasonably accurate summary by saying that it is drawn from Scripture and the Fathers of the Church, and that its author pursues three principal aims, which he discusses in thirty-three chapters: the qualities and duties of a king in relation [Col. 0021B] to the state; the discretion he ought to exercise in the benefits and favors he grants; and the vengeance he ought to exact from certain individuals. Hincmar prescribes in it very fine and useful maxims for ruling successfully. The work is addressed to Charles the Bald by a short preface in which the author explains his purpose.

**8.** Another treatise follows, more prolix than the preceding one and addressed to the same prince. It is entitled “The Vices to Be Avoided and the Virtues to Be Practiced,” a title apparently taken from Flodoard, who entered it under these same terms in the catalogue of our archbishop’s works and speaks of it as a very useful instruction. It is so indeed; and after setting out in the preceding work the duties of a prince as sovereign, the author treats at great length here of the virtues he ought to practice as a Christian. This too is a collection of passages from Scripture and [Col. 0021C] the Fathers, arranged under twelve very long chapters, the second of which consists of Pope Saint Gregory’s letter to Reccared, king of the Visigoths in Spain. Charles the Bald had requested this letter from Hincmar, and that apparently gave him the occasion to compose this work, in which he discusses almost all the duties of Christian piety.

**9.** The treatise that follows, “On the Nature of the Soul,” bears no author’s name in the manuscripts. It is there entitled “A Collection by a Certain Sage, Drawn from Saint Augustine’s Books on the Nature of the Soul.” Flodoard likewise does not count it among Hincmar’s other writings. Father Sirmond was nevertheless convinced that it belonged to him, and that what the author says in the preface could apply only to Charles the Bald, to whom he consequently addressed it. This is how it was represented in the edition made of it. The treatise consists of eight chapters, in [Col. 0021D] which Hincmar discusses eight questions concerning the soul, apart from the preface, from which it appears that Charles the Bald himself had proposed the eight questions. In answering them, the author establishes in the first ones that the soul is spiritual, that it is not in place in the manner of bodies, and that it likewise does not move locally, although it changes its will and dispositions. The final question is devoted to discussing whether the righteous, after the resurrection, will see God with the eyes of the body or only with those of the spirit. The entire treatise is a chain of passages from Scripture and the Fathers, in which little use is made of reasoning. At the end, a list was printed of other passages drawn from Saint Augustine, and several from Saint Jerome, to prove that the soul is in the body. This list is found, exactly as it is given here, in an ancient manuscript following the treatise.

**10.** Continuing the examination of our prelate’s letters and minor works, we encounter the long and fine letter written to Louis, king of Germany, in the name of the bishops of the province of Reims and of that of Rouen, as the title states in the general collection of the Councils and in the collection of the capitularies of our kings, where this letter is inserted. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that it was produced by Hincmar’s pen, whose entire genius can be recognized in it. It contains excellent advice in fifteen articles; but the fable of Charles Martel’s damnation in body and soul, which is read in the seventh section, serves only to show the author’s excessive credulity. Some scholars [Note: [Col. 0021D] Boll. 20 Feb. p. 213–215.] even believe it to have been invented by Hincmar; and its natural-sized representation can be seen in the church of Saint-Remi at Reims, opposite the high altar, on the Epistle side. Hincmar sent Charles the Bald, through his nephew, a complete copy of the [Col. 0022B] letter, and later, on another occasion, warned him that the advice it contained applied even more to him than to King Louis, his brother.

**11.** It is in the following letter, addressed to Charles, that Hincmar informs us of this circumstance. He wrote it to that prince when, in 859, Charles was setting out with his army to avenge the invasion that the king of Germany had made in France the previous year. The author’s principal aim is to urge Charles to prevent his soldiers from engaging in plunder, as is expressed in the letter’s title. Hincmar also mixes in several other counsels for the king.

**12.** The following letter, which constitutes the sixth minor work in the collection, concerns the same subject. It is written to the clergy of the court who accompanied the king and queen. Since their servants committed the same crimes as the soldiers, Hincmar points out to these clerics that they are [Col. 0022C] responsible for their servants’ sins, and that they must not only abstain from evil but also turn others away from it.

**13.** The seventh minor work is a mandate for suppressing plunder. It was composed in the same year, 859, and addressed to the parish priests of the diocese of Reims, with orders that it be published at Mass after the Epistle. It was then Lent, and Hincmar takes occasion from this holy season to urge his diocesan people to abstain from such crimes and from others that would render them unworthy of Easter Communion. This leads him to speak of the dispositions necessary to avoid receiving Communion unworthily. He also sent this mandate to Charles the Bald, so that it might from time to time be read to the officers and soldiers of his army.

**14.** Hincmar devotes the eighth minor work to explaining the seventeenth verse of Psalm 103: *Herodii domus dux est eorum*—“The house of the heron is their leader,” or, as he renders it, “The stork’s nest is like the first and chief of the others.” [Col. 0022D] For this purpose he has recourse to the Hebrew text as Saint Jerome interprets it, to the different versions of the text reported by the same Father, and to the other Fathers who wrote on the Psalms, namely Saint Augustine, Saint Prosper, and Cassiodorus. This explanation is addressed to Louis, king of Germany, who, in asking Hincmar and Bishop Altfrid other questions about other difficulties in Scripture, gave rise to the question at issue here. The author ends it with six elegiac verses containing wishes for the prince’s prosperity.

**15.** The ninth minor work was composed concerning the same king. It is a long letter in forty-two articles, addressed to the bishops and lords of the province of Reims. The former, having learned that Louis was to enter France with an armed force in order to compel King Charles, his brother, to [Col. 0023A] leave Italy, where he had gone to claim the succession of Emperor Louis, their nephew, consulted Hincmar, their archbishop, about the conduct they ought to adopt on this occasion. Hincmar replied to them in this letter, which, in accordance with his customary method, is almost entirely filled with authorities from the Fathers. What he says amounts to advising them to remain faithful to Charles the Bald, without nevertheless breaking communion with King Louis, to whom they should merely represent his obligations arising from the faithfulness owed under the treaties made with his brother the king. The letter is from the year 875, as the title carefully indicates.

**16.** Hincmar’s tenth minor work is a letter to Louis the Stammerer, written almost immediately after that prince’s coronation, which took place in December 877. Flodoard lists it among our prelate’s other writings; in it he gives the young king wise advice for the good government of his states.

**17.** The title of the eleventh minor work [Col. 0023B] gives a fairly accurate idea of its contents. It is a letter to Charles the Fat, emperor, urging him to supervise the education of the young kings Louis and Carloman and to provide them with good counselors so that they might rule successfully. It apparently dates from the beginning of their reign, in April or May of the following year, 879.

**18.** The twelfth minor work is a letter to King Louis, son of Louis the Stammerer, asking him to leave free the election of a bishop at Beauvais. At the death of Odo, at the beginning of 881, the clergy and people of that Church elected as his successor a cleric named Odacre, whom the court protected but whom the Council of Fismes, held in April of the same year, judged unworthy of the episcopate. The council therefore sent a delegation to the king and wrote to him explaining the reasons for its refusal. The court took offense, and the king sent Hincmar a letter insisting in favor of Odacre. Hincmar wrote the letter in question in reply, to justify the council’s conduct. [Col. 0023C] It is truly episcopal in character and highly important with regard to the election of bishops and the role played by princes in those times.

**19.** This letter drew from the king a threatening reply, to which our prelate responded with an answer even more vigorous than the preceding one. This forms his thirteenth minor work, which contains interesting material concerning the two powers, spiritual and temporal. Its author displays unshakable firmness and an ardent zeal, even to the point of giving his life in defense of the rights of the Church. But his expressions are neither sufficiently respectful nor sufficiently restrained.

**20.** The following minor work, the most substantial of all Hincmar’s, is an instruction that he drafted in 882 at the request of the lords of western France, for the guidance of their young king Carloman. The principal part of this writing is taken from the treatise that Saint Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, had composed [Col. 0023D] concerning the ordering of the palace.

**21.** Hincmar devotes the fifteenth minor work once again to giving counsel for the conduct of the same prince. He addresses it to the bishops, and almost everything he says is drawn from Scripture and the Fathers. Goldast printed it under the title *De potestate regia et pontificia*—“On Royal and Pontifical Power.”

**22.** Hincmar drew from the same sources his sixteenth minor work, against the abductors of widows, girls, and virgins consecrated to God. It is issued in the name of the bishops of Gaul and Germany and addressed to the king, who appears to be Louis, Carloman’s brother. It was consequently composed before the two preceding minor works. At the end, the author added an unordered list of passages taken from the canons of several imperial edicts, and especially from the Decretals of the popes that concern the same subject.

**23.** The seventeenth minor work is a long letter [Col. 0024A] to Pope Nicholas I, in reply to one that the pontiff had written to him toward the end of 863 through Odo, bishop of Beauvais; it therefore dates from the following year, 864. Flodoard considered it so important that he inserted it in full into the history of our prelate. Hincmar pursues four different aims in it. First, in a few words, he explains why the see of Cambrai had been vacant for ten months. He then speaks to him of the affair of Count Baldwin and Queen Judith, the widow of Æthelwulf, on which he passes rather lightly. What occupies him more is, on the one hand, the deposition of Rothad, bishop of Soissons, and, on the other, the case of Gottschalk. Rothad had departed for Rome to pursue his appeal to the Holy See. Hincmar leaves nothing undone to justify this prelate’s deposition and to dissuade the pope from considering his restoration; in this he did not succeed. But to judge this part of our archbishop’s letter soundly, it must be compared with the petition that Rothad presented to the [Col. 0024B] same pope. As for Gottschalk, Hincmar first complains that the Roman pontiff had not deigned to send him even a word in reply concerning the writings he had sent him through Odo of Beauvais against the errors of which this unfortunate monk was accused. Then, after accusing himself of not having attended the Council of Metz, where his case was to be examined, he gives, in his own manner, an abridgment of his life and a detailed account of the errors laid to his charge. Yet throughout everything Hincmar says here about his prisoner, he lets it be seen that the pope had received different information and that, consequently, he retained some goodwill toward Gottschalk. For this reason, our prelate insinuates that he did not fail to show him consideration.

**24.** Hincmar’s eighteenth minor work is the first of the four memoranda that he presented to the archbishops and bishops assembled in council at Soissons in 866 concerning Vulfade and the other [Col. 0024C] clerics ordained by Ebbo of Reims. It seeks to show that these clerics had been deposed by the bishops of five provinces; that their deposition had been confirmed by two popes; but that, nevertheless, since Nicholas I, one of the popes, wished the matter to be judged anew, Hincmar consented and desired the restoration of these clerics, while asking that he be shown in what respect the first judgment pronounced against them was contrary to the canons; otherwise, he maintained, the pope’s intention was not that the matter should be reopened.

**25.** In the second memorandum, which forms the nineteenth minor work, Hincmar establishes the evidence for the deposition of Ebbo, his predecessor, and refutes the reasons offered to invalidate it. Afterward he demonstrates the regularity of his own ordination, performed at the Council of Beauvais in 845.

**26.** He devotes his third memorandum, the twentieth minor work in the collection, to setting out the reasons or grounds that might permit the clerics in question to be received and promoted to higher orders. The grounds he indicates are the pope’s indulgence and authority; but he declares that whatever is done on this occasion will have no consequence for the future. He therefore adds that he gives his consent to the rehabilitation of the clerics.

**27.** The fourth memorandum, and the twenty-first minor work, is directed against Vulfade in particular. Hincmar portrays his conduct in such dark colors that the bishops could not endure its reading. These four memoranda of our prelate form part of the Acts of the Third Council of Soissons, among which they are printed. They were first published in Father Sirmond’s collection of the Councils of France. Whoever, moreover, wishes to become thoroughly informed about what took place in the deposition of Ebbo and of the clerics whom he had ordained must not confine himself to Hincmar’s four memoranda; one must also [Col. 0025A] read the account of these clerics, drawn up by one of them, which Du Chesne published from an Arras manuscript. It is written with great candor and, it would seem, ought to have found a place in the collection of the Councils. One must also read Charles the Bald’s letter to Pope Nicholas I on the same subject and add the two letters that this pontiff wrote to Hincmar after the Council of Soissons was held in 866, which Hincmar did not receive until the following year.

28. The twenty-second opusculum is a letter from our archbishop to the same Pope, to whom he sent it through Egilo, archbishop of Sens, who had been deputed to Rome by the council just mentioned in order to carry the acts of the assembly there. In this letter, which was reprinted at the end of the eighth volume of the Councils and is dated 1 September of the same year, 866, Hincmar sets out the reasons he had for not restoring Vulfade and his associates by his own authority. Nevertheless, he assures the Pope that he will take as much joy in their restoration as he had sorrow in their deposition [Col. 0025B]—something that would be very difficult to reconcile with the conduct he displayed throughout this affair. For the rest, he refers the Roman Pontiff to the bearer of his letter, who would inform him of everything orally.

29. So that Egilo might be able to discharge this commission to Hincmar’s satisfaction, Hincmar took care to give him his instructions and omitted nothing that might win him over to his interests. He did this in a letter that constitutes the twenty-third opusculum in the collection of his works and that was printed in the collection of the Councils immediately after the preceding letter. Hincmar begins by telling Egilo that he is speaking to him in confidence, as to another self. Whatever he may say in his letter to the Pope about the joy he would feel at the restoration of the deposed clerics, he shows at the end of this one that he did not desire it as strongly as he wished to persuade the Pope.

The author ends his letter with two noteworthy points. He asks Egilo to take care to read the letters [Col. 0025C] that the Pope would have dispatched concerning the matter in question before they were sent to France, lest, he says, the secretaries commit some fraud in them, as they are accused of doing. Finally, he asks him to bring the *Gesta* of the popes from the pontificate of Sergius up to the year in which Hincmar was writing his letter. As for those of the other popes, he tells him that he already had them. Here we see our archbishop’s zeal for collecting materials for ecclesiastical history. It seems likely that these *Gesta* were a kind of annals of what took place under each pontificate, rather than Lives of the Popes.

30. The following opusculum, twenty-fourth in the order of the collection, is another letter or instruction addressed to Egilo on his departure for Rome. Hincmar wrote it after learning that Gottschalk had found a way to send his appeal to the Pope, a development that seems to have greatly perplexed him. He gives Egilo a brief account of the errors with which he continued constantly [Col. 0025D] to charge Gottschalk, and confidentially asks him, if he should be questioned about the prisoner’s condition, to say that great care was taken to provide him not only with everything necessary but even with comforts, such as a bath. It is in this letter that Hincmar tells us that Saint Prudentius of Troyes had composed Annals in which he stated that Pope Nicholas had confirmed the truth of the two predestinations and the other doctrinal points then under dispute. Egilo was asked to keep this letter secret.

31. Hincmar added another letter, which Egilo could show, and which constitutes his twenty-fifth opusculum. This letter is devoted entirely to setting out at length the errors of which he had given only a brief summary in the preceding one.

32. The twenty-sixth opusculum is a long letter to Pope Nicholas, written in response to the two letters that Egilo, [Col. 0026A] on his return from Rome, had delivered to Hincmar on behalf of that pontiff on 20 May 867. In this letter, written the following July, Hincmar undertakes to justify himself against the vehement reproaches the Pope had directed at him in his letters, where he portrayed him as a proud man who acted only through tricks, cunning, dissimulation, and the like. Thus this letter is an apology for Hincmar’s conduct, but differs from the one he was later obliged to address to Pope John VIII. The letter under discussion here was inserted into the general collection of the councils.

33. Another letter from our prelate was also included there, constituting the twenty-seventh of his opuscula. It too is addressed to the same Pope Nicholas and concerns the same subject as the preceding letter, of which it is for the most part merely a repetition. For this reason, the editors printed only what is not found in the other letter, which consists almost entirely of Hincmar’s excuses to the Pope [Col. 0026B] for not having sent him all the writings from both sides concerning this great affair, as he had requested. It is difficult to understand how our archbishop could have written, one immediately after the other, two letters to the same person so similar in subject. Perhaps his desire to justify himself to the Pope led him to fear that his first letter might not reach him, and he therefore sent him a second by a route that seemed more secure.

34. The twenty-eighth opusculum in the collection is a brief instruction to the monks of Hautvillers concerning the conduct they were to maintain toward Gottschalk at the time of his death and after it.

35. The twenty-ninth is a long letter to Charles the Bald in favor of Hincmar, bishop of Laon. After the king had received complaints concerning him and publicly reprimanded him, Hincmar [Col. 0026C] responded with such hauteur that the prince could not help addressing harsh words to him. The quarrel went so far that the property of the bishopric of Laon was seized. This gave rise to the letter in question. Hincmar of Reims believed that he ought to come to the aid of his nephew by representing to the king that what he had done against the bishop was contrary to the laws of the emperors, the decrees of the popes, and the decisions of the councils; in support of this, as was his custom, he cites several texts.

The editor admits that the manuscript from which he supplied the letter did not permit him to print it correctly or in its entirety. This led M. de la Lande, who had recovered a better manuscript in the abbey of Ripoll, to include it in his *Supplement to the Councils of France*. Father Cellot had already given it in full at the end of the Acts of the Council of Douzy, as will be said below.

36. Next, in the edition of our archbishop’s Works [Col. 0026D], come two short letters to Hincmar, his nephew, together with the latter’s replies. They are counted as the thirtieth and thirty-first opuscula. One concerns Nivin and Bertric, and the other supports the priest Hadulphe, whom Hincmar of Laon had excommunicated—one of the sources of the disagreement between uncle and nephew.

37. Hincmar’s thirty-second opusculum is a letter written to the bishops of the province of Lyon at the beginning of March 871. After briefly informing them of Carloman’s revolt against his father the king, and of the acts of brigandage that he and those of his faction had committed particularly in the province of Reims, without being deterred by Hincmar’s repeated exhortations and remonstrances, he announces to them the punishment with which he believed he ought to punish these crimes, so that the bishops to whom he was writing might conform to it when [Col. 0027A] occasion arose.

Since Father Sirmond had given this letter only imperfectly, the editor of the *Supplement to the Councils of France* had it reprinted in full from a manuscript belonging to M. Petau, which at that time belonged to Queen Christina.

38. Of all the pieces that make up the body of Hincmar’s opuscula, none is more prolix than his treatise against Hincmar of Laon, comprising fifty-five chapters, not counting the preface and the verse piece placed at the beginning. This work responds to two memoranda that Hincmar, our prelate’s nephew, had supplied in support of his appeal to the Holy See. Just as the author is intent on rebutting the reproaches of the bishop of Laon, so he is equally attentive to retaliating, which he most often does bitterly.

The most interesting part of this long work is the section in which Hincmar discusses in some detail the rights of metropolitans and councils, the authority of their canons, and the letters of the Popes.

[Note: [Col. 0027D] Turrien and several other authors cite, under Hincmar’s name, a treatise *On Councils*, which appears to be none other than chapters 20 and 21 and the following four chapters [Col. 0028D] of the work of fifty-five chapters.]

This work is filled with learning. The author cites [Col. 0027B] secular writers as well as others. Yet it contains even less criticism than his other writings. Hincmar of Laon took care to reply to it.

39. The thirty-fourth opusculum of our archbishop is a response to what his nephew had communicated to him orally, through Heddon, provost of the church of Laon, concerning certain grievances that had given him cause for complaint since the events at Attigny.

40. The following opusculum, extracted from chapter 22 of Book III of Flodoard’s *History*, does not appear to be complete. It is a fabric of sharp and bitter reproaches against Hincmar of Laon, among which are mixed several replies to the writings of that prelate that followed the work of fifty-five chapters.

41. In the same Flodoard there are excerpts from another work, which have been made into the thirty-sixth [Col. 0027C] opusculum of our archbishop. In it he continues his reproaches against his nephew. Thus, if Flodoard had not distinguished it from the preceding work, one would take it for a natural continuation of it.

42. Hincmar’s thirty-seventh opusculum forms part of the Council of Douzy. It is an instruction addressed to the archbishops of Bourges and Bordeaux, Rodulf and Frotaire, concerning the marriage that a lord of the court had contracted with the daughter of Count Raymond [Col. 0027C], and whose dissolution the contracting party sought for fear of becoming guilty of incest.

43. The thirty-eighth opusculum, which was reprinted in the general Collection of the Councils, is a response to Gunther, archbishop of Cologne, who had consulted Hincmar on behalf of his provincial council, to which the response is addressed. Ingeltrude, wife of Count Boso of the province of Milan, who had left her husband and withdrawn [Col. 0027D] into the diocese of Cologne after being excommunicated by a council held at Milan, is the subject of the consultation.

Gunther asks how he ought to conduct himself in this affair. Hincmar responds with equal wisdom and clarity, while referring him to other decisions he had already issued concerning similar difficulties. He specifically names the twenty-second and the twenty-eighth. He apparently refers here to his major work on the divorce of Lothair and Theutberga.

44. We have already seen that our archbishop declared himself in favor of trial by hot water. His thirty-ninth opusculum is intended to establish trial by cold water. He addresses it to Hildegar, bishop of Meaux, who [Col. 0028A] had asked him to state his opinion of the work Raban had composed on the same subject.

Almost everything Hincmar adduces here in support of his position is drawn from Scripture, which he applies as he pleases, without accuracy and often contrary to the natural meaning of the text.

45. The fortieth opusculum is remarkable for its singularity. It is an absolution by letter, addressed to Hildebold, bishop of Soissons, who, being dangerously ill, had sent his confession to Hincmar and asked him for letters of absolution. But, as the theologians observe, it is less a sacramental absolution [Note: [Col. 0028D] *Mor.*, *De sacramento paenitentiae*, Book VIII, chapter 25, no. 45.] than a kind of indulgence and blessing. This is apparent from Hincmar’s own words, in which he warns Hildebold to take care to confess himself in detail to a priest.

46. We have something even more interesting in the forty-first opusculum, which is a vigorous letter in reply to Pope Adrian II. [Col. 0028B] It belongs to the year 870, and two parts may be distinguished in it.

The first is devoted to answering the letter Hincmar had received from Adrian on 19 October of the same year. Among other grievances, the Pontiff complained that Hincmar had not dissuaded Charles the Bald from usurping Lothair’s kingdom, and that consequently he had made himself an accomplice, indeed even the author, of this usurpation. He ordered Hincmar to separate himself from communion with that prince if he wished to remain in communion with the Pope, should the king nevertheless persist in his disobedience.

To all these complaints and threats Hincmar responds with great clarity and with a firmness worthy of a French bishop, though he puts into the mouths of others what seemed too harsh for him to say in his own. This part of his response contains several fine observations concerning the two powers and the rights of each, as well as concerning excommunication. It is in this response that Hincmar [Col. 0028C] says that the Pope cannot be both king and bishop. Cardinal Baronius, departing from his customary moderation, took this as an occasion to inveigh so vehemently against our prelate that M. Baluze felt obliged to defend him.

In the second part of the letter, Hincmar responds to what the Pope had written to him the previous year in favor of Hincmar of Laon. Adrian had asked him to send the latter to Rome, together with three other bishops deputed in the name of all the bishops of Charles the Bald’s kingdom. The archbishop represents to him that he has no power to send a bishop—even one from his own province—to Rome or elsewhere without the king’s order, nor to leave the kingdom himself without the king’s permission.

47. The forty-second opusculum of our archbishop is none other than King Charles the Bald’s second letter to Pope Adrian II. Hincmar wrote it in the prince’s name. In the edition [Col. 0028D] of Hincmar’s works, this opusculum is counted as the forty-third, although it is actually only the forty-second. The error affected only the following opusculum and was corrected in the one immediately after it, which appears under the number appropriate to it.

The forty-third, which for the reason just given is marked forty-fourth, is a letter addressed to Advence, bishop of Metz, in which Hincmar gives an interesting account of the ceremony of ordaining archbishops and bishops.

48. The forty-fourth opusculum contains a treatise concerning the rights of metropolitans, addressed to all the bishops. Hincmar composed it on the occasion of Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens, whom [Col. 0029A] Pope John VIII had appointed in 876 as his vicar in Gaul and Germany. The purpose of the work is to show that the new claims of these papal vicars must not prejudice the ancient rights of metropolitans. The author does not forget to exalt those of the Church of Reims.

49. The following opusculum is a response to a bishop’s consultation concerning the translation of Actard, bishop of Nantes, to the metropolitan see of Tours. Although Hincmar had consented to it at the Council of Douzy and had written accordingly to Pope Adrian, he nevertheless opposes it in the work under discussion, in which he first gives reasons against translations in general from one see to another.

50. The forty-sixth opusculum may be regarded as one of our prelate’s most useful writings, although it is fairly brief. It is a treatise on the duties of a bishop, both with respect to temporal and spiritual matters, in which he also discusses the usurpation [Col. 0029B] of ecclesiastical property.

What he says near the end concerning the church of Beauvais shows that it still had no legitimate bishop, and that this treatise was written after Odo’s death, in 881, at the time of Odacre’s intrusion.

51. The forty-seventh opusculum is a long letter to Pope John VIII concerning the appeals of bishops and priests to the Holy See, which had then become very frequent in the kingdom. The letter is written in the name of Charles the Bald, then emperor.

52. In the following opusculum, entitled *On Criminal Priests*, and so forth, Hincmar gives us a collection of ecclesiastical and civil laws, beginning with the capitularies of our kings, concerning the accusations and judgments of these priests. He discusses the persons who may accuse them; the character and number of the witnesses; the judge before whom the accusation may be brought; the matters on which [Col. 0029C] it may be based; and the manner in which these priests must clear themselves when there are neither evidence nor witnesses against them.

He demonstrates the falsity of a decree drawn from the Acts of Pope Saint Sylvester, which seeks to establish that a cleric cannot be accused by a layman, nor a superior cleric by an inferior cleric. In the forty-ninth opusculum, he applies to a particular case the general principles he had established in the preceding opusculum. The question there is how the case of a priest named Theutfrid, who had stolen church ornaments, ought to be examined and finally judged.

53.
