Of the twelve opuscula of Hincmar that remain for us to discuss, which together with the preceding works bring the total to sixty-one, most are very short letters containing nothing especially interesting. The fiftieth contains the story of a vision experienced by a man named Bernold, of the diocese of Reims, after a life-threatening illness, some time after [Col. 0029D] the death of Charles the Bald. Bernold recounted it to his confessor, from whom Hincmar learned of it. Hincmar sends the account to all the faithful, exhorting them always during this life to remain fearful concerning their condition after death and not to neglect the remedies God has prepared for us. This vision, moreover, is of approximately the same kind as that of Wettin of Reichenau.

The letter following the account of this vision was written to persuade Odo, bishop of Beauvais, to respond to the reproaches of the schismatic Greeks. The fifty-second opusculum contains the sentence of excommunication that Hincmar pronounced against Odacre when his intrusion into the see of Beauvais had already lasted more than a year.

The fifty-eighth opusculum concerns mystical interpretations drawn from numbers, intended to explain why Hincmar had described the Council of Nicaea as mystical in one of his writings. It is astonishing [Col. 0030A] that so occupied a prelate should have amused himself with such minutiae, and no less astonishing that he should have applied this description to the council on the grounds he adduces.

The following opusculum is more serious. Hincmar gives his opinion concerning the penance that ought to be imposed on Pepin, son of Pepin, king of Aquitaine, and nephew of Charles the Bald, who, although a monk, had joined the Normans and adopted their religion. Two of the preceding opuscula, which are synodal letters—the first very short—were reprinted in the general collection of the Councils.

At the end of Hincmar’s opuscula, his editor published a letter that Pardulus, bishop of Laon, wrote to congratulate him on the recovery of his health. It is curious for the detail with which the author discusses the foods he prescribes for maintaining it. Nothing else remains to us, so far as we know, concerning Pardulus except fragments of another letter to Amolo of Lyon, quoted and refuted [Col. 0030B] by Saint Remigius, his successor.

Father Sirmond concludes the edition of Hincmar’s Works with several substantial fragments from letters he wrote to different persons, supplied by the historian Flodoard. Having given a detailed account of all the pieces contained in this edition, it is now our purpose to discuss those that are not found in it but belong to our prelate.

54. In the general Collection of the Councils there is a letter by him on Baptism, addressed to the priests of his diocese, to instruct them concerning this sacrament and the ceremonies accompanying it. It is a treatise roughly similar to those that had appeared under Charlemagne in response to the questions posed by that prince on the same subject.

55. There is no doubt that the long synodal letter of the Council of Douzy, held in 860, is Hincmar’s work. It is addressed to all the faithful, to [Col. 0030C] instruct them concerning the nature of goods consecrated to God; to turn them away from the usurpations then being committed against such goods in so many ways; and to inspire in them horror of every kind of plunder in general.

56. It is conjectured that the letter written to Pope Nicholas I in the name of Charles the Bald, in which he recounts the deposition of Ebbo of Reims and its consequences, was composed by Hincmar. The conjecture is based on Father Sirmond’s assurance that he found it following several works by this prelate in two manuscripts, one from Notre-Dame of Laon and the other from Saint Lawrence of Liège.

But, apart from the fact that Hincmar’s style is not recognizable in it, it is beyond doubt that he would not have expressed himself about Ebbo’s affair in the manner used by the actual author of the letter.

57. Several writings by Hincmar of Reims against Hincmar of Laon, his nephew, have already been enumerated. Here are others that he published in the [Col. 0030D] course of the same affair:

1. A long petition in which he sets out his complaints and grievances against that unfortunate prelate, presented and read at the Council of Douzy in 871. It comprises thirty-five chapters, not counting the conclusion, in which the author shows that, despite the appeal lodged with the Holy See, judgment may still be rendered and a definitive sentence pronounced.

2. The synodal letter of the same council to Pope Adrian II, in which one sees all the genius of our archbishop, president of the council, whose sentence against his nephew is also his work.

3. A private letter to the same Pope, in which he first announces to him, in order to court his favor, that he has consented to Actard’s translation to the metropolitan see of Tours, and then gives him an account of the case of Hincmar, his nephew.

There is considerable reason to believe that the complaint Charles the Bald presented at the same council against this bishop was also composed by our prelate. At least its style is very similar [Col. 0031A] to that of his other writings. All these pieces form the principal part of the Acts of the Council of Douzy.

58. There are also four opuscula or memoranda by our archbishop presented to King Charles the Bald on the occasion of the seizure of the property of the bishopric of Laon. The first of these memoranda is none other than Hincmar of Reims’s twenty-first opusculum, of which we gave a sufficient account under item 35 in the enumeration of his writings. The following three support the first, and all four concern Hincmar of Laon’s dispute with the king.

As early as 1658, Father Cellot printed them, together with two other short pieces by the bishop of Laon on the same subject, at the end of the Acts of the Council of Douzy. The whole is furnished with notes by the editor and was reprinted in the same form in the general Collection of the Councils. One year before Father Cellot, Dom Luc d’Achery had published the fourth memorandum under the title of a letter to King Charles.

59. [Col. 0031B] Following these memoranda, the same collection published eight letters by our archbishop, almost all very prolix, which had escaped the searches of his editors. They were taken from a Vatican manuscript through the efforts of M. Holstenius and may help us better to understand what took place at the councils of Verberie, Attigny, and Douzy concerning the great affair of the two Hincmars.

The first four, two of which are addressed to the clergy of Laon, concern the interdict imposed there by the bishop and its consequences. The others are written to that prelate, to whom the uncle addresses sharp reproaches in the final four, especially in the eighth, which is the longest of all and is a reply to another letter from the nephew that appears to have deeply irritated the uncle. Various things are found in them that do honor neither to uncle nor nephew.

The seventh may be of some use for the history of the church of Laon; it gives the succession of its [Col. 0031C] bishops from Genebaud to Hincmar. These eight letters were written during the years 869 and 870. To them was added an account of what took place between uncle and nephew from the time of our archbishop’s work comprising fifty-five chapters, mentioned above, until 18 July 870, as it appears in the Vatican manuscript following those same chapters. The author of this account is unknown.

M. Eccard, believing that these eight letters had never been printed, published them as anecdotes in the second volume of his *Corpus of Historians*, pp. 375–430.

60. Father Sirmond, in his learned dissertation on the election and ordination of bishops in those times, printed after the writings just enumerated, gives us five letters by Hincmar on the same subject, already published by M. des Cordes. The one concerning the ordination of Hedenulf, bishop, addressed to the clergy and people of that church, dated to the year 877 and signed by [Col. 0031D] seven suffragans of Reims, is substantial and deserves to be read. M. Baluze had the first four reprinted after the capitularies of our kings.

61. The Acts of the Council of Fismes, held in 881, must also be counted among Hincmar’s writings. Besides the fact that our archbishop presided over that assembly, what remains of it bears all the marks of his learning and genius.

62. Surius gave us, under Hincmar’s name, a very extensive Life of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, together with the history of two of his translations. Our prelate is named with his customary titles at the head of the preface, which he addresses to the parish priests of his diocese. Flodoard mentions one of his letters to Louis, king of Germany, concerning this Life and the miracles [Col. 0032A] it contains.

Sigebert and the Anonymous of Melk acknowledge that Hincmar was the author of a Life of the same saint, and what the former tells us about this work shows that it is the same one found in Surius. In addition to the abridgment of the ancient Life of Saint Remigius by Fortunatus of Poitiers, on which, Sigebert says, Hincmar worked, he also incorporated into his own version not only everything supplied on the subject by earlier histories and various private records, but also what the tradition of his own time was reporting.

All skilled critics agree that this work by Hincmar in no way lives up to his reputation. It is a long succession of words that say nothing particularly solid. The facts, which are the essential element of history, are rare and uncertain, or rather for the most part suspect, because of the distance separating the author from the events. Digressions are frequent, and citations even more so, and almost always irrelevant.

A subject so rich treated in so imperfect a manner shows that Hincmar, despite all his learning, possessed neither the genius nor the talent necessary for writing history.

63. In addition to the preceding work, Mosander, the continuator of Surius, published a eulogy of Saint Remigius by Hincmar, which is properly nothing more than a fabric of moralizations and applications of Scripture, whose dominant quality is not accuracy. This piece seems to us to be the same one that Surius says he read in certain manuscripts following the Life just mentioned, but which he did not think fit to print. It even seems originally to have formed part of that same Life. At least its beginning presupposes that it is a continuation of some work.

Bollandus published nothing of these two pieces on 13 January, the day of Saint Remigius’s death. Father Sirmond likewise included nothing in the collection of our archbishop’s Works.

64. [Note: [Col. 0031D] Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, pp. 59–62.]

A famous letter [Col. 0032C] to Charles the Bald is also produced under Hincmar’s name, concerning the Life of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, allegedly written in Greek by Methodius and translated into Latin by Anastasius the Librarian. It has been claimed that this letter dates from 876 or 877, since it gives Charles the Bald the title of emperor.

The author’s purpose is to support Hilduin’s opinion concerning the Areopagite identity of Saint Dionysius, bishop of Paris—a view that, despite that abbot’s writings in its support, encountered opposition. The proofs he adduces to confirm this opinion are taken from Methodius’s recent work and from the Acts of Saint Sanctinus, which, according to this writer, openly favored it.

To lend greater force to his claims, he says that he was sending the king these Acts, which he had formerly copied and corrected with his own hand. On this occasion he tells us that they had been unearthed in the small abbey of Saint Sanctinus by Wandelmar, who, after learning chant under Teugarius at Saint-Denis, had taught it in the church [Col. 0032D] of Meaux, and to whom Bishop Hucbert had granted this small abbey as a benefice.

But scholars are now persuaded that this letter is spurious, and M. l’Abbé Le Beuf offers several proofs of this.

Dom Mabillon, who regarded it as Hincmar’s and believed that it had not been brought out of obscurity, had it printed in two places in his works. It is true that it is not found in the collections of Hincmar’s writings, but Surius had published it under 9 October, and, following him, M. de Launoy published it after his judgment on Hilduin’s Areopagitica, with critical observations of his own.

Nevertheless, Dom Mabillon’s reprinted edition is not useless. From it one learns that the letter ends with the words: *magis splendescit in lucem*—“shines forth more brightly into the light.” The remainder, [Col. 0033A] which is read in Surius and in M. de Launoy, is an addition made by some other partisan of the Areopagite identity of Saint Dionysius.

It is chiefly this addition that M. de Launoy censures, and on it that the purported history of Saint Sanctinus is based. It is impossible to say precisely where the author obtained what he relates there—whether from the Acts of the saint that he was sending to Charles the Bald, or from some other monument. But one may assert, on the basis of the impression the impostor himself gives us, that this addition is not the same thing as those Acts.

65. M. Baluze, having recovered a letter from Hincmar that had escaped all his editors, published it in the seventh volume of his *Miscellanea*. It is written to King Louis, son of Louis the Stammerer, both in the name of our archbishop and of the other prelates then assembled at the Council of Fismes, concerning the election of a bishop to fill the see of Beauvais.

In the first part of this letter, which is a reply to one of the king’s letters, Hincmar points out the heresy into which [Col. 0033B] the scribe of the letter had fallen, perhaps inadvertently, by admitting two persons in Jesus Christ.

66. To omit nothing that remains to us among Hincmar’s writings, we shall add to all those whose catalogue has just been given the profession of faith that he made at his ordination and subsequently sent to Rome in order to obtain the pallium. Although brief, it contains everything that could be required of a metropolitan in such a case. Dom Marlot included it in the *History of our Prelate*.

67. It has been said that Hincmar occasionally occupied himself with versification, and the poems composed by him that are attached to his prose writings have already been mentioned. Besides those, there are still several other short pieces of verse belonging to him: 1. the epitaph of Saint Remigius, in thirty-two elegiac verses, found in Flodoard and Surius, following the Life of that same saint by our prelate; 2. the epitaph [Col. 0033C] of Archbishop Tilpin; 3. his own epitaph, as we have given it after drawing it from Flodoard; 4. several heroic and elegiac verses to adorn the altar of the Virgin, which he had had renewed in his cathedral; 5. several other verses engraved near the tomb of Saint Remigius. None of these short poems differs in any respect from the other pieces of that period.

68. Two modern scholars—M. le Beuf, in his *Dissertations and Clarifications on the History of France*, and the Bishop of La Ravalière, in a work printed in the *Mercure* of December 1736 and in two letters published in the following years, 1737 and 1738—maintain that Hincmar was the author of the final part of the *Annals* known as those of Saint-Bertin; that is, of the section which resumes the history in the year 861 and carries it through to the end of 882. It must be admitted that they succeeded fairly well in making one recognize there the character and genius of this prelate; and we would willingly adopt their opinion [Col. 0033D] if we were not held back by various difficulties that deserve attention.

Indeed, one cannot attribute this continuation of the *Annals* to Hincmar without supposing in him two atrocious vices: an implacable hatred of pious bishops, whom he would have publicly slandered, and excessive self-love, which would have led him to praise himself while disparaging his adversaries. The evidence for this is drawn from the work itself. The author deliberately begins it with the death of Saint Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, in order to have an opportunity to portray him as an excessive defender of the heresy with which Gottschalk was charged, as a prelate full of gall and hostility toward his fellow bishops, and finally as an author who had composed nothing but works full of contradictions and contrary to the common faith of the Church. These calumnies were all the more atrocious because they were less well founded, and all the more [Col. 0034A] scandalous because they fell so directly upon a holy bishop already judged by the supreme Judge. From Saint Prudentius the annalist passes to Rothad, bishop of Soissons, whom he depicts as the most insane of men, *singularis amentiae*—“of singular madness”—as another Pharaoh in his hardness of heart; in short, as a savage beast rather than a man. Yet it is certain, as we have seen, that Rothad was completely vindicated at Rome, without Hincmar, his accuser and judge, daring either to appear there or to send anyone to support his accusations, and that he was afterward restored with honor to his see. After this horrifying beginning, the annalist is perpetually intent on bringing Hincmar onto the stage and exalting his slightest actions. It seems that he undertook his work for no other purpose.

That is not all. It is beyond dispute that what is read under the year 882, and which concludes these *Annals* as Duchesne published them, is by the same hand as the preceding articles, [Col. 0034B] without the slightest indication of an addition made afterward. Yet it is certain that this final article contains events that occurred only after Hincmar’s death. Such is the extraordinary protection that God granted the city of Rheims, preserving it from the fury of the Normans, whose threat had caused Hincmar to flee to the place where he died; such is the advantage that King Carloman gained over these barbarians; and such, finally, is their withdrawal after the agreements made with them, which are reported in detail by the annalist of Metz under the year 884.

Moreover, the author in question, when announcing our archbishop’s flight to Épernay, speaks of that town with the same indifference with which another continuator of the same *Annals* speaks of the abbey of Saint-Bertin, *in quadam villa*—“in a certain village.” Would Hincmar have expressed himself in this way when speaking of a place where he was ill for some time and where he died? Let us add one final reflection that supports the preceding ones. Is it credible [Col. 0034C] that a man compelled to flee precipitately, and already stricken with the illness of which he was to die, would, in such extremities—when he had so many other and much more important things to do—think of recording these minutiae in *Annals*, as they are found in those under discussion here?

These are the difficulties that seem sufficient to us for denying Hincmar this portion of the work. But the difficulties will disappear, and everything will be reconciled, if the work is attributed to one of his pupils and most zealous partisans: a man otherwise capable and as well versed as his master in canon law, who undertook and carried out this continuation of the *Annals* in the form it has in order to court the favor of that prelate, and who, having failed during his lifetime to obtain from him what he expected, neglected—or even disdained—to record his death.

Casimir Oudin and Cave, following him, wished to transfer to Hincmar the honor of a short poem entitled [Col. 0034D] *De fonte vitae*—“On the Source of Life”—published by the former of these two scholars. But this work belongs to Audrade, chorepiscopus of Sens, to whom they claim that Hincmar addressed it.

## § II. — Lost Writings

However numerous the writings of Hincmar that remain to us may be, those that people have neglected to preserve for us, or that have not yet been brought out of the obscurity of libraries, are still more numerous. The enumeration that follows of the works belonging to this class of which we have some knowledge will demonstrate this.

1. Of all the works he composed against the doctrine of Gottschalk, we do not possess the one he addressed to Gottschalk himself concerning several passages of the Fathers—especially Saint Prosper—which, Hincmar claimed, Gottschalk did not understand, and which Hincmar explained in his own way by means of other passages [Col. 0035A] from Saint Augustine and other Fathers [Note: [Col. 0035D] Flodoard, book III, chapter 28]. In addition to this discussion, the author undertook to establish in it the unity of predestination with respect to the good alone, and to show that God merely foresees the wicked without predestining them. These subjects, treated by an author as prolix as Hincmar was, must have produced a large volume.

2. Our prelate, seeing that despite all his efforts several people were taking Gottschalk’s side, wrote a treatise to the recluses of his diocese to put them on their guard against his doctrine. He began it toward the end of 849 or at the beginning of 850; and already in March of the latter year he sent it to Raban, archbishop of Mainz. He appended the writings that had by then been published against their views: those of Saint Prudentius of Troyes, Ratramnus, and Gottschalk’s fuller profession of faith. This treatise by Hincmar to the recluses has not come down to us.

3. We also lack the letter that accompanied it, [Col. 0035B] and that appears to have been of some length [Note: [Col. 0035D] Flodoard, in the same place, chapter 21], since he used part of it to report passages from several Fathers concerning the mysteries of the Trinity and predestination, on which he asked Raban to provide him with explanations. Raban replied in another very long letter, which had a happier fate than Hincmar’s. Among other things, our archbishop informed us in his letter that Raban was then the only one of Alcuin’s disciples still living.

4. Several other letters concerning Gottschalk and his doctrine have also been lost—letters that Hincmar had written to Raban himself and to Amolo, archbishop of Lyon, as well as to Rothad, bishop of Soissons, and Saint Prudentius of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0035D] The same, in the same place]. All that remains of them is the brief notice given by Flodoard and what is found in the refutation that Saint Remigius of Lyon made of the letter to Amolo, his predecessor.

5. In addition to the preceding treatises and the individual letters [Col. 0035C] that were as substantial as complete treatises, Hincmar composed a large work, *volumen ingens*—“a huge volume”—divided into three books and dedicated to Charles the Bald [Note: [Col. 0035D] The same, in the same place, chapter 15]. Of this work, in which the author discussed predestination and free will against his adversaries, particularly once again Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, nothing remains except the dedicatory epistle preserved for us by Flodoard, which Father Sirmond had reprinted at the beginning of the edition of Hincmar’s works. This epistle, together with the one by which the author addressed the other surviving work on the same subject to the same prince, tells us when and on what occasion the work under discussion here was composed.

After the Council of Valence in 855, Remigius, archbishop of Lyon, who had presided over it, carried its canons to the emperor Lothair, to whom the city of Lyon was subject. He added the nineteen articles of John Scotus condemned at that council and the two treatises that John had written—one against the three letters, the other *On the Truth of Scripture*—and asked Lothair to send all these writings to Charles the Bald, his brother. Charles, having received them at Verberie from Ebbo, bishop of Grenoble, whom Lothair had entrusted with them before his death, handed them over to Hincmar in September 856, when they were at Neaufle, a residence of the archbishop of Rouen. Thus it was in order to answer them, and also to refute Ratramnus’s treatise on the same subject, as Flodoard informs us, that our prelate undertook the work in question.

The manner in which he executed it, and which he himself explains, led M. l’abbé Fleury, that wise and judicious historian, to judge that Hincmar had employed more artifice than good faith [Note: [Col. 0036D] Flodoard, in the same place]. He claims, in fact, that until then he had had no knowledge of John Scotus’s nineteen articles and had not even been able to discover their author. Yet it is evident that he himself, together with Pardulus of Laon, had encouraged this writer to take up his pen, and that the latter dedicated his work to them.

Speaking of the canons of the Council of Valence, Hincmar calls them synodal decrees and regards them as the work of an assembly of archbishops and bishops distinguished by their merit—an undertaking in which Ebbo of Grenoble, against whom he appears irritated and whose history he discusses at some length, had played the principal part. Nevertheless, he conceals from himself the fact that these canons really belonged to the Council of Valence. This leads him to say that, not knowing with whom he was dealing, he addressed his reply to King Charles, who had handed him the writings he was undertaking to refute. He does admit that this council had condemned his four articles of Quierzy; but he complains that they had not been inserted into the council’s decree and that he had been condemned without being heard.

[Col. 0036B] 6. Hincmar also discussed grace and predestination in a poem that Flodoard calls an excellent work, *opus quoddam egregium*. In it he also treated what concerns the mystery of the Eucharist, the vision of God, the origin of the soul, and faith in the Trinity. The poem was entitled *The Dish of Solomon*, *Ferculum Salomonis*, and was dedicated to King Charles the Bald. After giving Pardulus a reading of it, the author subsequently wrote to him to ask for his opinion before presenting it to the prince. It contained 446 elegiac verses, not counting the preface, which contained twenty-four. Of the entire work, only twelve verses remain, quoted by Durand, abbot of Troarn, and reprinted among the fragments of our prelate; in them he clearly establishes the doctrines of the real presence and transubstantiation. The mystical explanation that he gave of this poem, and which concludes the first volume of his works, has been discussed above.

[Col. 0036C] 7. Besides the treatise on the *Trina Deitas*—“Triune Deity”—that remains to us and has also been mentioned, Hincmar composed another work on the same subject [Note: [Col. 0036D] Flodoard, in the same place, chapter 15]. This one was dedicated to Charles the Bald, but people neglected to preserve it for us.

8. Among the works transmitted to us, mention has been made of an apologetic letter from Hincmar to Pope Nicholas I, intended to justify his conduct. He also addressed another work to the same pontiff, which we no longer possess and know only through Flodoard. In it our prelate made his profession of faith and his defense against the error he attributed to Gottschalk, and devoted himself to showing that the preservation of orthodox faith depended upon this matter.

9. These apologetic writings must not be confused with another work that Hincmar composed after the Council of Troyes to justify himself against the accusations brought against him before Pope John VIII, because he rejected the authority of the decretals [Note: [Col. 0036D] The same, in the same place, chapter 21]. In it he showed, as he had already explained at that council, that he accepted them with the appropriate qualification—that is, insofar as they had been received and approved by councils. He also discussed what had occurred in the great affair of Hincmar of Laon: how he had been deposed and then restored; how Hedenulf had been ordained in his place and confirmed by the pope.

In the same work Hincmar also defended himself against the slander circulated before the same pope, as though he had claimed that the dignity of the Roman Pontiff was not superior to his own. To all this he added certain explanations [Col. 0037A] concerning Carloman and various other matters that had served as pretexts for accusing him. He ended this great work by declaring that it would be equally easy for him to clear himself of all the other calumnies with which he was covered; but that he refused to do so, lest he appear to repel insults with other insults, being persuaded that there was more glory in despising his slanderers than in defeating them by his replies.

10. Among the six or seven letters of our archbishop to Pope Leo IV that have been lost, there was an important consultation [Note: [Col. 0037D] The same, in the same place, chapter 10]. It concerned chorepiscopi, who presumed to administer confirmation and, upon the death of the bishop, performed all the other episcopal functions—something Hincmar regarded as a series of abuses. In the same work he also spoke to the pope about the clerics whom Ebbo, his predecessor, had ordained.

11. He sent Charles the Bald a collection in which he had assembled a large number of authorities concerning churches and chapels, in order to oppose what Saint Prudentius of Troyes had established on this subject [Note: [Col. 0037D] The same, in the same place, chapter 18].

[Col. 0037B] 12. Hincmar also composed, for the instruction of the same prince, a treatise entitled *On the Twelve Abuses*. It was a fabric of passages from the Fathers and of constitutions promulgated by the kings, his predecessors. In this work he took care to remind the prince of the promises he had made before the ceremony of his coronation, both to the great men of the kingdom and to the bishops. Among the works falsely attributed to Saint Cyprian and Saint Augustine, we possess a treatise bearing the same title. But it is certainly not Hincmar’s. Besides the fact that it shows none of his diffuse manner of writing, its author employs only the authority of the sacred books.

13. As we have seen, several other instructions remain to us that our prelate composed for reigning princes. But some others have been lost that appear to have been substantial, judging from [Col. 0037C] the impression given to us of them [Note: [Col. 0037D] The same, in the same place]. We do not possess the one he addressed to Charles the Bald, in which, after informing him what his brother, the Emperor Lothair, was doing at Rome and when he would return to France, he prescribed the conduct the king should observe toward God and toward human beings. He also gave the queen salutary advice, so that she might encourage the prince, her husband, to lead a blameless life worthy of a king.

14. Nor do we possess the instruction he composed for Louis the Stammerer immediately after the death of the Emperor Charles, his father; it is different from the one we discussed elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0037D] The same, in the same place, chapter 19]. In it he prescribed to the prince how he should conduct himself in order to begin his reign well, setting before him the examples of his predecessors and giving him, point by point, advice on good government, the respect he owed the Church, and various other matters of importance to him and to the state.

[Col. 0037D] 15. Another instruction by Hincmar to Louis, son and successor of Louis the Stammerer, is also missing [Note: [Col. 0037D] The same, in the same place]. It concerned the nature and constitution of the council that a king ought to form for his own advantage; the manner of administering justice and delivering judgments; the benefits produced by observing the rules he prescribed on this subject; and the harms caused by neglecting to put them into practice.

16. Among several letters that Hincmar wrote to Louis, king of Germany, there was one that could be regarded [Col. 0038A] as a treatise on the manner of praying and the qualities prayer ought to possess [Note: [Col. 0037D] The same, in the same place, chapter 20]. It was written in response to a letter from that prince, in which he urged Hincmar to pray and to have as many people as possible pray for the repose of the soul of the emperor, his father, who had appeared to him in a dream and implored him to deliver him from the punishments he was suffering.

17. The work Hincmar composed on the calculation used to determine the day on which the feast of Easter should be celebrated deserves mention [Note: [Col. 0038D] The same, in the same place, chapter 23]. In this work he made several observations on a similar treatise composed by the abbot Saint Adalhard.

18. Hincmar wrote several letters to Eberard, or Evrard, count of Friuli, among which there was one that might be regarded as a treatise on piety [Note: [Col. 0038D] The same, in the same place, chapter 26]. After praising this lord’s thoroughly Christian conduct, the author established in it the necessity of advancing from virtue to virtue in order to fortify oneself against the natural inclination that leads human beings to vice. [Col. 0038B] He gave him as a principle the search for ways to please God in all things; the effort to bring peace to the Church; the refusal to be content merely to exhort the princes over whom he had influence to practice goodness, instead urging them effectively to do so; the contribution of his power toward establishing public tranquility; the protection of good people; resistance to the wicked; and careful watchfulness over himself through the practice of temperance, justice, and Christian piety.

19. The long letter that our prelate wrote to Roric, one of the leaders of the Normans, after he had converted to the faith and received holy baptism, may also be regarded as another treatise on piety, or a Christian instruction [Note: [Col. 0038D] The same, in the same place].

20. At the request of his fellow bishops, Hincmar had also composed a treatise on the veneration of images, both those of the Savior and those of the saints [Note: [Col. 0038D] The same, in the same place, chapter 29]. The epilogue to this treatise was in verse.

[Col. 0038C] 21. He had composed another work [Note: [Col. 0038D] The same, in the same place] in response to the question of a certain person who had asked him why baptized people who were neither priests nor deacons, and who had the misfortune to fall into apostasy, received a second imposition of the bishop’s hands when they came to penance.

22. Besides what he said about the principal mysteries of our redemption in his poem *Ferculum Salomonis*, he wrote a separate prose work on the same subject, which he addressed to an archbishop who was his friend.

23. Flodoard, who gives extensive details about the lost writings of our archbishop, makes no mention of the one he addressed to the Church of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0038D] Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 65]. But we know from another source that it still existed in the eleventh century and was well known to Sigebert of Gembloux, who makes particular mention of it. The work was a response to the letter that the clergy of that Church had written to Charles the Bald concerning clerical clothing, and which M. des Cordes printed among Hincmar’s minor works.

24. To abbreviate what concerns the lost or still-hidden writings of this prelate, we shall observe in general that Flodoard, who appears to have had them all before his eyes, gives an enumeration in which more than four hundred are counted, including most of those mentioned in this section and several from the preceding one. [Col. 0039A] Even this writer takes care to warn us that he has omitted several, as may be observed in the catalogue we have given of those that remain to us. He devoted particular attention to making Hincmar’s letters known to us, since he regarded them as important. They were indeed important for the most part, judging from the impression he has left us of them. And if it were possible to recover them, one would find in them a wealth of material of interest for the history of that period, both ecclesiastical and civil; for knowledge of the customs and practices then observed; for discipline concerning penance, the elections of bishops, appointments to parishes, presentation to benefices, the form of ecclesiastical judgments, and so forth.

In some of those that remain to us there are various observations concerning the duties of bishops; but there would be many more in seven or eight of those that are lost. Such was the letter he wrote [Col. 0039B] to Bertulf, archbishop of Trier, at the beginning of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 0039D] Flodoard, book III, chapter 21], to instruct him in the manner of governing his diocese and his metropolitan church. Such was the one he addressed to Hincmar of Laon, his own nephew, immediately after his ordination, to prescribe the rules of wise government to him. He also gave salutary advice in another letter to Ercanrad, bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne, concerning whom unfavorable reports had been made to him. The one addressed to Guillebert, his predecessor’s successor, also contained excellent instructions for a successor of the apostles. The reply he made to Wala, or Walon, bishop of Metz, who had asked him for advice on the conduct of a pastor, appears likewise to have been a substantial work on the same subject. In another, he entered into detail concerning the conduct a bishop ought to maintain toward the rural parishes [Note: [Col. 0039D] Flodoard, in the same place, chapters 22–23].

## § III. — *On Hincmar’s Genius, Learning, Doctrine, and Manner of Writing*

[Col. 0039C]

What has already been said about Hincmar in the history of his life and in the reasoned catalogue of his writings might suffice to make his genius known. But one will form a more accurate idea of it by bringing together the various features that have been presented separately. The reader may have observed in him a mixture of good and bad qualities. This led Cardinal Bona to say that it would be difficult to determine what prevailed in him, good or evil: *dubio vitiorum ac virtutum temperamento*—“with an uncertain balance of vices and virtues.” Indeed, he cannot be properly known except by considering these two aspects of him.

At first one perceives in him a lively, subtle, penetrating, and expansive mind, capable of the greatest things; a superiority of knowledge and regularity of morals which, joined to the eminence of his dignity, made him shine among the other prelates of his century and attracted the respect of popes and kings, as well as of others. But at the same time one discovers in him a proud, inflexible, imperious, cunning, partial, secretive, artful, and enterprising character; a political spirit that skillfully led him to employ every means to accomplish his aims and undertakings. No other proofs are needed to establish this judgment than those already read in the course of his history. It was this political spirit that led him to reject the decretals when they were contrary to his designs, as Pope Nicholas I reproached him before his fellow bishops, and to accept them when they favored him.

Lupus of Ferrières, a great admirer of Hincmar, [Col. 0040A] represents him (*Epistle* 42) as a generous prelate, benevolent toward everyone, in whom nobility of sentiment kept pace with eminent wisdom. This truly was the character of that archbishop toward those to whom he was attached; but with regard to those whom he did not like, or from whom he believed he had received some cause for displeasure, he placed limits on his indignation only for political reasons. Besides the various examples already cited, one may also offer that of Saint Prudentius of Troyes. Certainly this bishop was very far from the errors of John Scotus; nevertheless Hincmar, who was not pleased with him, did not hesitate to try to make him appear an accomplice in the excesses of that sophist [Note: [Col. 0040D] See *Book on Predestination*, chapter 31, pp. 231–232].

One of the excellent qualities of our archbishop, which all his defects could never eclipse, was his firmness in defending the rights of the Church in general and those of the Gallican Church in particular. It was on these occasions that he knew no respect of persons and showed that he feared God alone. Among the many events in which he displayed this episcopal firmness, the intrusion of Odacre into the diocese of Beauvais would by itself suffice to reveal it in all its brilliance. The court persisted in supporting the intruder against the judgment that the bishops had pronounced in full council. Hincmar continually opposed this injustice with a zeal of pure fire, extending even to a willingness to shed his blood in defense of the cause. Likewise, when the Empress Richildis expelled the legitimate abbess from Aurigni in order to favor the intrusion of an ambitious woman, our prelate wrote to her with a vigor capable of withstanding everything.

We have seen how he made King Charles the Bald speak in the letters he wrote to the popes in that prince’s name, whenever it was a question of maintaining the rights of the monarchy and the liberties of the Church of France against the claims of the court [Col. 0040C] of Rome. Hincmar spoke no less vigorously on these same occasions when writing in his own name. We have unequivocal evidence of this in his forceful reply to Pope Hadrian II, who wanted to persuade him to withdraw from communion with King Charles, his sovereign. This apostolic vigor appears equally clearly in the letter to the same pope against frequent appeals to the Holy See, and in the treatise defending the rights of metropolitans against the privilege that Rome had granted to Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens [Note: [Col. 0040D] Marca, *Councils*, book IV, chapters 6 and 12]. This same vigor, reinforced in Hincmar by the authority he had acquired in France, by his skill in canon law, and by his seniority in the episcopate, brought upon him the displeasure of the Roman court, which held him responsible for all the vigorous resolutions formed by the bishops of France in their councils against the Roman rescripts they did not approve [Col. 0040D]. Perhaps this was also partly the source of Pope Nicholas’s unfavorable disposition toward our archbishop, a disposition inherited in later times by certain Roman writers, particularly Cardinal Baronius.

Hincmar knew a great deal, but his learning was far from universal. Scripture appears to have been very familiar to him, and he cites it frequently and without constraint in his works. But he had not penetrated deeply into its mysteries and possessed it only by memory. This is shown by his manner of applying it: he did so according to his fancy, without precision, and often against the natural meaning of the sacred text. He had read most of the Fathers and made fairly frequent [Col. 0041A] use of their authority [Note: [Col. 0041D] Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXXVIII, no. 62]; but he had not studied, or had been unable to appreciate, the views of Saint Augustine or those of the other Fathers who thought like that holy teacher.

The favorite and dominant field of our prelate’s learning was the discipline of the Church, which he had drawn from the canons and other writings of the councils through serious and daily study. He willingly wrote on this class of subjects, which forms the object of most of his works, and found it difficult to stop when treating them, so full was he of the valuable knowledge he had acquired through this study. He did in fact succeed in introducing into his writings an infinity of excellent rules and authorities concerning the government of the Church [Note: [Col. 0041D] Dupin, *Ecclesiastical History*, ninth century]. There is no ancient author in whom one finds such a large number of them, so well established, or from whom one can learn more ecclesiastical law. Hincmar also made use of his learning to write on subjects of morality and piety. [Col. 0041B] The numerous instructions he composed for crowned heads, archbishops, and bishops bear witness to this; and it may be said that he succeeded reasonably well in this respect for the time in which he wrote.

It is nevertheless surprising to see a prelate who knew so many good things and was so occupied amuse himself by treating fairly useless questions seriously. We mean what he wrote about ordeals by cold water and hot water. It is no less surprising to see him fall into insipid mysticism and visions, some of which have the flavor of the crudest fable. Such, on the one hand, are the writings he composed to explain his *Ferculum Salomonis*, and the mystical designation he had given to the Council of Nicaea. Such, on the other, is the fable of the damnation of Charles Martel in body and soul.

These provide evidence that Hincmar’s learning lacked taste. It also had all the other defects [Col. 0041C] of the learning of his century. It was raw, undiscriminating, and uncritical. Most of his works are heaps—compilations of authorities without order or arrangement—in which, through his continual desire to display a great memory, he left few signs of judgment or intellectual precision. He reveals his ignorance of criticism not only by attributing the famous *Hypognosticon* to Saint Augustine, the work *On the Hardening of Pharaoh* and a sermon on the bodily and spiritual Assumption of the Blessed Virgin to Saint Jerome, but also by rejecting the writings of Saint Fulgentius as apocryphal because he assumed that they had been declared so by the decree of Pope Gelasius, which preceded by several years the origin of that Father’s works. We shall pass over the other features of the same kind that we have reported elsewhere, in order to speak of what concerns the False Decretals. Hincmar knew that they were of very recent date and unknown to the preceding centuries. Yet he could never discern their spuriousness, although he sensed it very well. It would have been necessary to examine whether they truly came from the ancient popes to whom their honor was purportedly attributed. But since he was ignorant of the rules of criticism, he could not enter into that investigation.

This defect in criticism caused him to confuse good and bad authors, and on this defective basis he constructed a system of religion that could not be accurate. We have seen how the councils and theologians of his time censured the opinions he had adopted concerning grace, predestination, and free will. Although in his writings he nevertheless granted much to the latter, he does not fail [Col. 0042A] to acknowledge in them the necessity of prevenient grace, grace that gives both willing and doing, according to God’s good pleasure. But he is not content to teach that free will has a share in the proper use of this grace; he places the two agents on an equal footing. This may be one of the reasons that led him to reject the writings of Saint Fulgentius and prevented him from appreciating those of Saint Augustine, whom he nevertheless often cites without understanding him.

For the rest, Hincmar appears to have held sound views concerning the other dogmas of the Catholic faith. He wrote little on these subjects, which he had not studied with sufficient seriousness. The small portion that remains of his *Ferculum Salomonis*, in which he treated some of them, shows that he clearly established the real presence and the transubstantiation of the Eucharist. From some of his other writings one can see that he had a correct idea of the nature of the soul and of kingship, above which he placed God alone. It is true that in this passage he seems to advance an [Col. 0042B] somewhat inaccurate opinion concerning a king who would not perform his duty.

The principles he lays down for regulating morals in the various instructions that have come down from him tend to establish an evangelical morality and a piety that is both solid and enlightened. Everything he wrote on discipline conforms to the canons, of which he had particular knowledge, since they had been the principal object of his study. When one reads his works on this subject, one readily perceives that it was not his fault if, in his time, the Church’s rules concerning penance, the administration of the other sacraments, elections, the ordination of ministers of the altar, the form of ecclesiastical judgments, and so forth, were not observed. Likewise, one discovers much insight and wisdom in his replies to consultations from those who addressed themselves to him. If he did not always follow himself, in his own case, what he prescribed for others, that is an error of fact, [Col. 0042C] which should not be treated as consequential.

There is clarity and a certain precision in his manner of writing, but it is excessively diffuse, and one finds in it neither elegance nor refinement. Thus, it is observed [Note: [Col. 0042D] Dupin, same place.] that it is more suitable for memoranda and instructions than for works of doctrine and eloquence. It is no more suited to the historical genre; and the lengthy legend that Hincmar left us, composed in his own manner, about Saint Remigius shows all who read it that its author possessed neither taste, genius, nor talent for writing history, however capable he may otherwise have been. The other characteristics of his manner of writing become apparent from the variety of his works. Those that he composed in his own cause reveal touches of subtlety and a certain skill in turning the authorities he employs to his own advantage. On the other hand, in those he composed against his adversaries, one sees a vehement style, full of harshness, bitterness, and often invective. In other words, when he [Col. 0042D] seeks to make himself feared, to assert his influence, and to defend his rights and the prerogatives of his dignity, he speaks in a lofty, proud, imperious tone. When, on the contrary, there is some reason for him to fear for himself, he lowers his tone, assumes an air of timidity, and at times becomes servile. This can be observed in most of his letters to the popes and in those addressed to Archbishop Egilo.

§ IV. — On the Editions of Hincmar’s Works

Until the year 1602, nothing of Hincmar’s works had appeared publicly except what Flodoard reports in the third book of his *History of Reims* [Note: [Col. 0042D] *Bibl. Teller.*, p. 26.]. At that time Jean Buséc, a Jesuit, published nine [Col. 0043A] minor works together with other ancient monuments and notes of his own. This collection, in quarto, was printed at Mainz by Jean Albin. The writings of Hincmar that it contains are the same as opuscula 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 44, and 47, together with the following two works from the latest edition, which will be discussed below.

Thirteen years later, Jean des Cordes, a canon of Limoges Cathedral, having recovered approximately twenty other minor works, both among the manuscripts in the library of M. de Thou and through his friend François Pithou, published them in a quarto volume that appeared in Paris at the press of Nivelle in 1615. The editor had included several other pieces by ancient authors that did not belong to Hincmar, among which we shall mention only the letter of Otfrid to Liutbert, Archbishop of Mainz; the *Dialogue on the State of the Church*; the treatise of Jesse of Amiens on Baptism; the Constitution of Riculf of Soissons; and several letters of Pope Nicholas I.

The principal writings of our archbishop collected [Col. 0043B] in this volume are the large work divided into fifty-five chapters against Hincmar of Laon; the treatise on the divorce of King Lothair and Queen Teutberga; the reply to the consultation of Gunthar of Cologne; and several letters to Popes Nicholas and Adrian, both in Hincmar’s name and in the name of Charles the Bald. It seems to have been the editor’s intention to append to the newly discovered writings of our prelate those that Buséc had already published; but he did not do so. Nor did he think it appropriate to add notes, for fear, as he says in his dedicatory epistle to M. de Thou, of prejudicing the judgment of his readers. He merely placed at the beginning of his edition the passages of Hincmar cited by Yves of Chartres and Gratian in his *Decree*, together with an extract from the history of Trier concerning Lothair’s divorce.

Father Sirmond, while conducting research for his edition of the Councils of Gaul, subsequently recovered [Col. 0044A] other writings of Hincmar. He incorporated some of them into the Acts of the councils to which they belong and referred others to the end of his third volume. Having afterward discovered an even greater number, he formed the intention of joining them to those that had already been printed and producing a complete edition. He carried this out in two folio volumes, which appeared in Paris at the press of Sébastien Cramoisy in 1645. This edition served as our guide in the reasoned catalogue we have made of Hincmar’s writings, and it provides a correct idea of them. We shall add only that Father Sirmond, like the preceding editor, left his author’s text without any notes, limiting himself to placing at the beginning a very brief notice and a chronological summary indicating approximately the time at which each work he published was composed. It was observed above that Father Sirmond did not consider it appropriate to include in his edition what Surius had already printed [Col. 0044B] from Hincmar concerning Saint Remigius, Bishop of Reims, and Saint Denis of Paris. He likewise refused this honor to several letters of our prelate concerning the election and ordination of various bishops, although he had inserted them in his dissertation on the same subject and M. des Cordes had included them in his edition.

After Father Sirmond’s edition, Father Cellot, his confrère, discovered on his own some writings of our archbishop that had escaped the searches of the earlier editors, and published them in 1658 together with the Acts of the Council of Douzy. Fathers Cossart and Labbe subsequently found still more and incorporated them into the eighth volume of their general collection of the Councils, as we have already noted elsewhere. Duchesne also inserted several selected minor works of Hincmar in the second volume of his *French Historians*.

[Col. 0043]

## TESTIMONIES OF ANCIENT WRITERS CONCERNING HINCMAR

Rabanus, Archbishop of Mainz, in the heading of his letter to Hincmar:

[Col. 0043C]

“To the most reverend and most beloved brother, deservedly and rightly venerated by all Catholics for his sound faith and orthodox profession, Hincmar, bishop: Rabanus, servant of the servants of God, wishes eternal salvation in the Lord.”

Lupus, Abbot of Ferrières, Letter 42, to Hincmar, Bishop of Reims.

[Col. 0044C]

“I am not unaware that, since you abound in so many gifts of divine grace, you spontaneously consider that you have received from God, in the presence of the prince, the ability to assist the good, so that they may possess in you what they do not possess in themselves and may provide an occasion for rewarding your diligence. [Col. 0045A] The nobility of your lineage is adorned by salutary learning; the dignity of your office is commended by the piety of your profession. I have written these things to your exalted person, not through the fault of arrogance but out of friendship, so that, since nobility and wisdom have come together in you, [Col. 0046A] the power of this union may stand out even to those unwilling to acknowledge it—those who strive even to obscure the very lights of the Church.”

[Col. 0045]

## SIRMOND’S PREFACE

Reader, we have gathered Hincmar of Reims’s works into these two volumes—not, to be sure, all of them, for who would dare promise or hope for that?—but precisely those that we have been able to investigate and obtain, whether already published or still hidden. While more may present themselves, when God wills, I trust that this addition of so many of his books will not be unwelcome to you and to others who take pleasure in the labors of so great a man. There will also be those who consider that noble dissertation against the Predestinarians, now appearing for the first time, is timely and especially well suited to refuting them. Although none of Hincmar’s works is without its usefulness, and in none does the author’s outstanding judgment fail to shine forth together with his abundance of knowledge, the fact remains that in arranging and organizing these works, the circumstances did not allow us to maintain everywhere the chronological sequence we had in view. We have therefore prepared for your assistance a chronological synopsis, extending from Hincmar’s ordination to the end of his life, which indicates, for nearly every year, the events and dates to which each item should chiefly be referred. Enjoy it, Reader, and farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0045D] We adapt this to our edition by interspersing the text, as is our custom, with bold numerals [Col. 0046D] that indicate the pages of Sirmond’s edition for the Reader.] [Note: [Col. 0046D] In this synopsis, page numbers refer to numbers printed in the text in bold type.] **CHRONOLOGICAL SYNOPSIS**, arranged for the understanding of both volumes.

[Col. 0045B] **(844)** Hincmar, ten years after the deposition of Ebo, is ordained Archbishop of Reims at the Council of Beauvais, under King Charles and Pope Sergius. Vol. II, Letter 19, p. 272.

**(847)** Pope Sergius dies on 27 January, and Leo IV is elected in his place.

The Synod of Mainz under Archbishop Rabanus, at which the monk Gottschalk, holding erroneous views concerning God’s predestination, was condemned and sent to Hincmar, his metropolitan. Vol. I, p. 20; Vol. II, p. 262.

The Synod at the palace of Quierzy, at which Gottschalk was again condemned, deprived of the rank of priest, and confined in the prison of the monastery at Hautvillers; and four chapters opposing Gottschalk’s chapters were established. Vol. I, p. 20, and chapter 16 and following.

**(851)** Ebo, formerly Bishop of Reims, dies on 20 March. Vol. II, p. 313.

**(852)** Hincmar’s Chapters are given to the priests of the Diocese of Reims [Col. 0045C] on 1 November. Vol. I, pp. 710, 716.

**(853)** The Council of Soissons of five provinces, at which the case of Wulfad and the other clerics ordained by Ebo after his deposition was considered, as well as the legitimacy of Hincmar’s election as his successor. Vol. II, pp. 282 and 306.

The ordination of Aeneas, Bishop of Paris, on which occasion Prudentius of Troyes wrote the letter concerning which Hincmar speaks near the end of his preface and in chapter 5 of *On Predestination*. Vol. I, p. 26.

**(855)** The Council of Valence of three provinces, whose first canons oppose the chapters of Hincmar of Quierzy in their criticism. In the letter to King Charles, at the beginning of Vol. I.

Pope Leo IV dies in August and is succeeded by Benedict III.

**(856)** Judith, daughter of King Charles, betrothed to King Æthelwulf of the English, is crowned by Hincmar [Col. 0045D] at Verberie on 1 October. Vol. I, p. 750.

Hincmar writes three books to King Charles on God’s predestination and free will, against his critics, especially Gottschalk and Ratramnus. Of this work there remains only the preface’s letter, mentioned above, at the beginning of Vol. I.

[Col. 0046B] **(857)** Hincmar’s Chapters are supplemented by additional chapters in the twelfth year of his episcopate. Vol. I, p. 730.

Hincmar’s *Collection from Sacred Scripture and the Sayings of the Orthodox*: that the Godhead should be spoken of as one and not three, against Gottschalk. Vol. I, p. 415.

**(858)** Nicholas succeeds Pope Benedict, who has died.

The bishops of two provinces write an admonition to Louis, King of Germany, when he invaded the kingdom of his brother Charles. Vol. II, p. 126.

**(859)** While Charles was departing with his army to repel the attack of his brother Louis, Hincmar sent him and the clerics of the palace a letter concerning the restraint of soldiers’ plundering. Letters 5, 6, and 7, Vol. II, p. 142, etc.

The Synod of Langres, at which the decrees of the Council of Valence were confirmed by Remigius of Lyon and other bishops.

The Council of Toul of twelve provinces at [Col. 0046C] Savonnières, where the chapters of Langres were reread and soon presented to the king, who gave them to Hincmar for his response. Vol. I, pp. 2, 3.

Hincmar publishes a second notable volume on predestination against Gottschalk and the other Predestinarians. Vol. I, p. 1, etc.

**(860)** The twofold Synod of Aachen concerning Teutberga, wife of King Lothair, at which they condemned her to public penance. When Hincmar learned of this, he wrote a book entitled *On the Divorce of Lothair and Queen Teutberga*. Vol. I, p. 561.

Consulted by Gunthar, Hincmar replies to his questions concerning Ingeltrude, wife of Count Boso, who had fled after leaving her husband. Vol. II, Letter 28, p. 669.

The Second Council of Toul of fourteen provinces at Tusey, by whose mandate Hincmar wrote to Bishops Rudolf and Frothar concerning the marriage of Stephen and the daughter of Regimund. Vol. II, p. 647.

[Col. 0046D] **(862)** The Third Synod of Aachen, at the end of April, at which Lothair was permitted to contract another marriage.

Count Baldwin abducts the daughter of King Charles to marry her. Vol. II, p. 244.

**(863)** The Council of Metz, at which Waldrada’s marriage to [Col. 0047A] Lothair was approved; it was soon condemned at the Roman Council, and its authors, Gunthar and Theutgaud, were deposed. Vol. II, pp. 261–262.

Pope Nicholas orders that Rothad, Bishop of Soissons, recently deposed at the Council of Silvanectum at Hincmar’s instigation, be sent to Rome to have the judgment reopened. Vol. II, pp. 246 and 260.

At Pope Nicholas’s request, King Charles permits his daughter Judith to be lawfully joined in marriage to Baldwin. Vol. II, p. 246.

**(865)** The Roman Council, at which Rothad was restored to his former honor and Hincmar’s judgment was annulled. Vol. II, pp. 399, 401.

**(866)** The Third Council of Soissons, convened by order of Pope Nicholas for the case of Wulfad and his associates, in order to restore them to their ranks, on 18 August. Hincmar’s Letters 18, 19, 20, and 21 are addressed to the bishops of this synod. Vol. II, p. 265, etc. Letters 22, p. 282; 23, p. 285; 24, p. 290; and 25, p. 298 also belong here.

[Col. 0047B] Queen Hermentrude is crowned at Soissons in the basilica of Saint Medard by Hincmar and other bishops, at the request of King Charles. Vol. I, p. 752.

After the death of Bishop Rudolf, the Church of Bourges is entrusted by King Charles to Wulfad. Vol. II, p. 285.

**(867)** Pope Nicholas sends the objections of the Greeks to Gaul for refutation. Vol. II, p. 809.

The Council of Troyes of six provinces, celebrated on 25 October by the bishops who had attended the Council of Soissons. Its acts, sent through Bishop Actard to Nicholas but delivered to his successor Adrian, accurately set out the entire case of Ebo and of the clerics ordained by him. Vol. II, pp. 406 and 824.

**(868)** Pope Nicholas dies on 13 December and is succeeded by Adrian II.

King Charles summons Hincmar of Laon before a secular tribunal and proscribes him. Vol. II, [Col. 0047C] Letter 29, pp. 316–317.

**(869)** The Council at Verberie on 24 April, at which Hincmar of Laon, accused for the first time, appealed to the Apostolic See. Vol. II, pp. 351, 604, 605.

Hincmar of Laon compiled a twofold Collection of ancient decretals for his defense. First, a monstrous book, to which he himself subscribed and required his supporters to subscribe. Vol. II, pp. 526, 599. Then another, prefaced with verses, which was returned to Hincmar at Gundulf’s estate by Wenilo, Archbishop of Sens; it is found in Vol. II, p. 355 and following. Both are mentioned in Letter 35, pp. 599–600.

King Lothair dies in Italy on 8 August; King Charles obtains his kingdom and is crowned at Metz by Hincmar on 9 September. Vol. I, p. 741, etc.

[Col. 0047D] **(870)** The Council at Attigny of ten provinces, in May, at which Hincmar of Laon, accused again, chose three judges and gave his profession of faith to the king and his metropolitan; afterward, having fled, he appealed to the Apostolic See. The rebellion of Carloman, the king’s son, was also considered at the same council. Vol. II, pp. 350, 604, 644. Letter 30, p. 334, and Letter 31, p. 359, were also written in this year but before the council.

Hincmar’s volume of fifty-five chapters, presented to his nephew Hincmar at Attigny, in which he responds to both of his Collections and to all his other writings. Vol. II, Letter 33, p. 377 and p. 600. Letters 34, 35, and 36, together with the lengthy letter of Hincmar’s nephew inserted between them, pp. 608 and following, also belong to this period, as do Letters 41 and 42, p. 689, etc.

**(871)** The associates of Carloman are excommunicated by Hincmar unless they reform by 11 March. Vol. II, p. 353.

The Synod of Douzy in August, at which Hincmar [Col. 0048A] of Laon was removed from office. Its acts were sent to Rome through Bishop Actard.

**(872)** Actard, Bishop of Nantes, is transferred to the Church of Tours. Vol. II, p. 741.

Pope Adrian dies and is succeeded by John VII on 14 December.

**(873)** The Council of Silvanectum, at which Carloman, son of King Charles, a cleric and deacon, was deprived of his rank and restored to lay communion.

Hincmar’s letter concerning the purification of the priest Hunold. Vol. II, p. 819.

**(874)** Hincmar’s Chapters are promulgated at a synod in Reims in July. Vol. I, p. 732.

**(875)** While King Charles was traveling to Rome, his brother Louis again invaded his kingdom. Vol. II, pp. 157 and 834.

After the Emperor Louis dies, Charles is crowned emperor at Rome by Pope John at the end of the year.

Hildebold, Bishop of Soissons, near death, sends Hincmar a brief confession of his faith and is absolved by him. Vol. II, [Col. 0048B] p. 686.

**(876)** John delegates his authority in Gaul and Germany to Ansegisus of Sens on 2 January. Vol. II, Letter 44, p. 719.

The Council of Pontion in June, at which Pope John’s letter concerning Ansegisus’s primacy was read, together with the oath exacted from Hincmar, concerning which see Vol. II, p. 834.

Frothar of Bordeaux is transferred to the Church of Bourges on 28 October because of the devastation caused by the pagans.

Hincmar writes from the estate of Novilliacum. Vol. II, p. 832.

**(877)** Chapters given by Hincmar to the archdeacons and priests Gunthar and Odelhard. Vol. I, p. 738.

Emperor Charles writes to Pope John concerning the judgments and appeals of bishops and priests. Vol. II, p. 768.

[Col. 0048C] **LOUIS THE STAMMERER** succeeds his father Charles after his death and is crowned by Hincmar at Compiègne on 8 December. Vol. I, p. 747.

Hincmar sends King Louis, at his request, a letter on the proper administration of the kingdom. Vol. II, p. 179.

Letter 46, *What a Bishop Ought to Carry Out*, was also written at this time. Vol. II, p. 762. So too was Letter 50, concerning the vision of Bernold. Vol. II, p. 811.

**(878)** The Council of Troyes under John VIII, at which Hincmar of Laon protested against Hincmar of Reims and the others.

**(879)** King Louis dies at Compiègne on Good Friday, 10 April. His sons Louis and Carloman succeed him, and Ansegisus crowns them at Ferrières.

After the Synod of Reims on 22 April, Hincmar writes two letters concerning the deposition of the priest Godbald and the excommunication of Fulcher and Hardoisa for incestuous marriage. Vol. II, p. 821.

[Col. 0048D] **(880)** Louis and Carloman divide the kingdom between themselves at Amiens, so that Louis receives Francia and Neustria, while Carloman receives Aquitaine and Burgundy.

Charles the Fat is crowned emperor at Rome by Pope John on Christmas Day.

**(881)** The Synod at Saint-Macre on 2 April. The bishops of this synod write to King Louis concerning a free election in the Church of Beauvais. Vol. II, Letter 12, p. 188. Hincmar also writes a private letter to the same king, Letter 13, concerning Odacre, the intruder in that Church. Letter 52, containing Odacre’s excommunication, should also be referred to this period. P. 811.

**(882)** King Louis dies in August at Saint-Denis. Hincmar writes Letter 14 to the nobles of the kingdom concerning the establishment of King Carloman. Vol. II, p. 201; and Letter 15 to the bishops of the kingdom, p. 216.

Hincmar dies on 23 December.

# THE COMPLETE WORKS OF HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS, ARRANGED IN TWO VOLUMES

Edited and prepared by JACQUES SIRMOND, priest of the Society of Jesus.

# HINCMAR’S *ON PREDESTINATION* AGAINST GOTTSCHALK

[Note: [Col. 0049B] Flodoard, Book III of the *History of Reims*, chapter 15, concerning the books composed by Hincmar: “He composed a massive volume containing several books on the predestination of God and free will, against certain of his critics among the bishops, especially against Gottschalk and Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, addressed to King Charles.” The same author, in chapter 16: “He also published another notable volume addressed to the same king, against the aforementioned Gottschalk and the other Predestinarians.”]

[Col. 0049]

## TO THE READER: On Hincmar’s Earlier Work against the Predestinarians

Hincmar’s labor against the Predestinarians was twofold. One work consisted of three books, defending his Chapters of Quierzy against Gottschalk, which the men of Lyon had attacked in their writings. The other was not divided into books but into thirty-eight chapters, written when the men of Lyon again rose up against Hincmar. This latter work is the Dissertation that we present here in its entirety, from a manuscript of Saint Remigius of Reims—or rather, of Hincmar, as the inscription shows, by whom the book was given to that monastery. Of the earlier work, as far as I know, only the letter or preface to King Charles remains in Flodoard. As a consolation for its loss, it seemed worthwhile to present it here.

[Col. 0049]

# HINCMAR’S LETTER TO KING CHARLES

Prefixed to his Earlier Work against the Predestinarians

[Col. 0049A]

“To the glorious lord King Charles: Hincmar, in name but not in merit Bishop of Reims and servant of God’s people, together with my fellow bishops, my venerable lords and brothers, devoted petitioners for your salvation and prosperity.

“We give thanks to God, who has kindled your heart with love for him and inflamed it with knowledge of the truth and with knowledge and diligence for the orthodox faith. He has also divinely inspired you with prudence and understanding in the writings he has inspired, and, through your meditation upon and practice of them, insofar as the affairs of the state permit you, he advances the zeal of your devotion day by day for the benefit of his holy Church.

“Moreover, we have reviewed the synodal chapters of our venerable fellow bishops—namely, of the three provinces—[Col. 0049B] which were brought to you, as they are contained there and will be found written below. In accordance with the command of Scripture, ‘Ask the priests about my law’ (Haggai 2:12)—for we also read that it is the law of faith—you gave them to us, following the custom of former kings, to be read and debated out of a desire to learn the truth. In them, although our names are not mentioned, we found ourselves, by the designation of their effects, criticized as though we were not Catholics and despised without fraternal regard. We also found that the chapters we had excerpted from the opinions and words of the Catholic Fathers, because of a necessity that is known to you and will become known below, had been rejected and condemned as useless, indeed harmful. [Col. 0050A] These chapters, just as we had excerpted them, they did not wish to incorporate into their own writings, lest they be read by those into whose hands their chapters might come. Instead, they touched upon some of the matters contained in the chapters excerpted by us, but in another sense and with other words, so as to make those matters appear detestable. They suppressed others, and remembered them in such a way as to suggest that we had held opinions contrary to the teaching of the holy Fathers at the African and Orange synods.

“Concerning one particular chapter—that God wills all human beings to be saved, although not all are saved—they were completely silent, as we shall demonstrate more clearly later, when the Lord says: ‘See, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and tear down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant’ (Jeremiah 1:10). [Col. 0050B] First, if they trusted in the integrity of their understanding, they ought to have set before their readers the things they were trying to destroy, just as they had received them in their entirety, showing them those things in which what was to be uprooted and demolished could be recognized. Then, after destroying and dispersing them by authority, they ought rationally and orderly to have planted their own positions and raised them up by building them on high.

“Concerning another chapter, as though some mockery could exist in the sacred mysteries, they wrote in such a way that readers might understand that we had said this, although nothing of the sort had been mentioned by us. Why we said nothing about it, and in whose writings we later found it after we had written those chapters, [Col. 0051A] we shall explain in its proper place.

“They also inserted in those same writings certain sixteen chapters, as though they ought to be charged to us. We had heard or seen nothing of them before the venerable Ebo, Bishop of Grenoble, brought them to you at the palace of Verberie, as though they had been sent by your brother, of blessed memory, Lothair. We found no author of these chapters identified there, nor, although we searched diligently, were we able to discover one. We therefore thought that they had been compiled out of someone’s envy to discredit another’s reputation, as we often read has happened.

“To mention a few examples out of many: there was a letter of chapters which the venerable Bishop Ibas denied at a synod to be his own; and there was what certain rivals did with the words of blessed Augustine during his lifetime—[Col. 0051B] words which he cleverly and catholically repudiated when the matter came to his attention. After his death, certain envious persons undertook to collect from his writings, chapter by chapter, including material related to the matter now under discussion, in order to degrade his orthodox and most useful teaching out of hatred for his person and to turn devout readers away from loving, reading, and necessarily believing him. Saint Prosper, acting at the delegation of the holy Roman See through Pope Celestine, demonstrated in a Catholic and prudent style that these lies of his rivals were false and imprudently alleged, and he most clearly proved that the teaching of this distinguished and memorable man was orthodox.

“Thus it may also be that these chapters, which were brought or sent to you in the name of our fellow bishops by persons other than those bishops themselves, [Col. 0051C] were not composed in this manner to disparage us. Rather, at the devil’s instigation, amid the other evils now multiplying in this world, they may have been fabricated to introduce discord among the Lord’s priests. The devil fears and envies charity intensely in us, when he sees us preserving on earth among earthly human beings the charity that he, as an angelic spirit, lost in heaven by refusing to preserve it.

“For how could it be that our brothers should judge us in such an inflammatory manner and with contempt amounting to annihilation, when they constantly have before their eyes and daily put into practice the Lord’s rule concerning how each person should admonish his fellow? For they know that it is written: ‘Before you question anyone, do not reproach him; and when you have questioned him, rebuke him justly’ (Sirach 11:7).”

[Col. 0051D] For Saint Augustine received with the greatest kindness the writings of heretics and of those who criticized him, whenever he found something well said in them, and he worked to interpret many passages in accordance with correct meanings; but he never attempted to incline anything from a correct meaning toward a perverse one. How, then, could our brothers have acted in such a way before questioning us about the matter according to the evangelical rule, either orally or in their writings—so that, if they wished to speak, they might teach us, or, if they thought us mistaken and unwilling to return to the path of truth and faith, might admonish us fraternally and repeatedly, set before us the writings of divine authority and of the holy Fathers, and invite us with gentleness and mildness to come together as one—knowing that a bishop ought to come to a synod of fellow priests in order either to learn or to teach?

For some among us received kind and fraternal letters from some of them, and we sent our replies to them; yet we have neither seen, heard, understood, sensed, nor been able to perceive anything of this sort concerning their father. But if they wrote such things—if, perhaps, they did write them—in order to display their own wisdom through our foolishness, and to seek more eagerly the praise of boasting than, through charity, to make their own whatever good things we had or had said, if there were any; and if they found that we had said anything otherwise, and preferred to publicize it rather than correct us fraternally, we marvel at such things from men so great and of such standing, archbishops and leading bishops—especially from Ebo, who, as we have heard, is a religious man. For he was raised from almost the cradle under religious discipline and in the regular habit in the monastery of the Church of Rheims, where Saint Remigius rests.

[Col. 0052A] In that religious place he spent his life until, by Lord Ebo his uncle, then archbishop of Rheims, he was consecrated a deacon there and, by episcopal appointment, was ordained abbot of the monks to observe and govern the regular order. We have learned that he was so formed in the practice of humility, and taught to seek and retain the place of humility, that the following was written to him and to everyone: “If the spirit of one who has authority rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccles. 10:4).

[Col. 0052B] For “the spirit of one who has authority” is the spirit of pride, whereas our place is humility. It is this place that the true fortified place and tower of strength commands us to learn from him: “Learn from me,” he says, “because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:19).

[Col. 0052C] We have heard, and firmly believe, that the aforesaid religious man earnestly wished to hold this place as a secure position against the spirit of self-exaltation and boasting. For that reason we do not believe that these chapters were composed by him: his name alone, omitting the names of the other fellow priests, has been ostentatiously expressed there alongside those of the archbishops, as some think; and it is made to seem, as it were, that he collaborated in this matter more than anyone else, and that in the judgment he was greater and more learned than the other archbishops.

We find nothing of this sort concerning Saint Augustine, who surpassed the others in knowledge, labor, and vigilance in the African councils.
