For Saint Augustine not only did not place himself before his fellow bishops, seeking private glory, nor allow himself to be placed before them; he actually subordinated himself to others, although he labored more than the others, as anyone who wishes to read the letters written to Saint Pope Innocent and to other prelates of the apostolic see will be able to find.

[Col. 0052D] Nor do we read that any bishop was treated in this way in any council, unless perhaps an apostolic letter, for an evident reason, decided that one of the fellow bishops should be designated by name for this business together with his archbishop, as we read concerning the bishop of Autun in the letters of blessed Gregory. How much less, then, would this religious and prudent man have wished to put himself forward or to be preferred in such a way, disregarding and passing over his fellow bishops?

[Col. 0053A] Moreover, our brothers and fellow priests ought not to have passed over in silence the admonition of Solomon if they had secretly received from us, whether by word or in writing, something sinister, so as to proclaim it prematurely in public, driven by whatever agitation against us—something of which we ourselves are unaware—and thereby provoke contentions and quarrels. For he says: “What your eyes have seen, do not bring hastily into a quarrel, lest afterward you be unable to correct it, when you have dishonored your friend” (Prov. 25:8).

Yet we know that there are some who, while striving to know more than they ought to know, recoil from peace with their neighbors because they despise them as dull and foolish. Therefore Truth itself admonishes us, saying: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). Whoever strives to possess the salt of wisdom must necessarily take care never to depart from the peace of concord.

[Col. 0053B] Hence Paul gives a fearful admonition: “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. 12:10). Above all, we must preserve and pursue it—that is, follow it perfectly—we who ought daily to sacrifice to God. Truth itself specially commands us, as though by an explicit injunction, that if we offer our gift at the altar and there remember that our brother has something against us, we should leave our gift there before the altar, go first to be reconciled with our brother, and then come and offer our gift (Matt. 15:23).

[Col. 0053C] Behold: our leader and teacher does not wish to receive sacrifice from those who are at odds; he refuses to accept a burnt offering. We must therefore consider how great the evil of discord is, on account of which even that by which guilt is released is not accepted. We do not have anything against our brothers if they wrote such things against us before the conference. But we must believe that, if they had written them, they would have sent them to us, against whom they had written them. How, then, can we write back to them when we do not know whether they wrote them?

Nevertheless, so that your lordship may not remain without an answer, we intend to reply to you—from whose hand we received these things—with heart, mouth, and pen, without fearing the reproach of those who criticize us. First, we shall send what is said to have been written by these same brothers of ours at the synod, although it appears to have been written earlier than the other material. But since these texts are known to have been composed as an attack upon us and against the chapters excerpted by us, we judged it appropriate to place them first. Although they bear a greater name, they do not possess greater authority—for they are in part untrue—yet, because of their synodal title, we considered them worthy of serious attention.

[Col. 0053D] Next we shall present what we received from several people, through the hands of others, concerning several of these matters: the necessity for which, as we have said, we undertook to excerpt those four chapters from the thoughts and words of the Catholic Fathers, on the condition that from the writings of individual Fathers we should set down certain passages from the individual statements contained in the chapters excerpted by us, as we judge necessary.

After this we shall present the chapters excerpted by us from the thoughts and words of the Fathers, exactly as we excerpted them. If we can demonstrate that the meaning expressed by us in those chapters agrees with the divine and authoritative Scriptures, with the faith of the Catholic and apostolic Church and of the holy Roman see, and with the thoughts of the orthodox Fathers who presided over that holy mother Church and whose writings the same apostolic Roman see has given us in the canon to receive, we shall strive to act truthfully, humbly, and devotedly.

[Col. 0054A] We have neither wished to accept nor to put forward the opinions of others as supporting evidence for our Catholic understanding, since it is clear that whatever that mother of all Churches, the universal Church, has judged worthy of approval is true and Catholic. Even if some have been called teachers, we neither accept nor put forward their opinions to prove the sincerity of the faith, except those whose opinions the Catholic mother Church herself has decreed to be acceptable.

[Col. 0054B] If, moreover, any emerged who occupied a teaching chair after the canon of sacred Scripture and of the Catholic teachers had been given by that holy see to all the faithful, and who thought otherwise than those whom the Catholic mother Church received, embraces, and cherishes in her orthodox bosom had understood and taught, we ought neither, nor need, to invoke their opinions as authority; nor do we wish to advance or accept them, since in these Fathers and through them we have enough for salvation.

If anyone has taught, or presumed to teach as doctrine, something other than what these authorities taught should be held on the basis of a more mature and sounder instruction, we regard as contrary to faith and salvation everything that is demonstrably different from their salutary teaching.

[Col. 0054C] We likewise embrace, with equal reverence, the opinions of those who, by divine favor, flourished in the Church in Catholic understanding, doctrine, and holiness of life after blessed Gelasius himself had composed the canon, and who wrote or taught nothing discordant with, or different from, the faithful—that is, Catholic—doctrine of those orthodox Fathers recorded in that same canon.

Such are the venerable Bede the priest, instructed in the Catholic faith by disciples of Saint Pope Gregory and taught to no small degree by Saint Theodore the archbishop, learned in both languages, Greek and Latin, who had been sent by the holy Roman Church to the English for their instruction after the disciples of blessed Gregory; and Paulinus, patriarch of the province of Aquileia, of venerable memory; and Alcuin, a religious and learned man.

[Col. 0054D] The Roman apostolic see not only most graciously accepted their faith and teaching but also exalted them with many praises, as we find in the writings of that holy see, which our Church received from that mother of Churches during the reign of the emperor Charles of blessed memory, when a synod was held concerning the known infidelity of Felix and its acts were sent to the Roman Church, as to the summit of the Churches. Whoever reads their writings also understands how worthy they are of praise and acceptance.

Finally, if we cannot demonstrate that the chapters we have excerpted agree with the opinions of such men, as we have said, we are prepared to listen to more learned and Catholic men, to submit our understanding, and without contention to subject ourselves to their teaching.

[Col. 0055A] And because we received from the archive of your brother Lothair of blessed memory a little book without the author’s name, in which the chapters excerpted by us are set out individually in their respective places and have been criticized and condemned with the approval of whoever he may have been, we shall also include his criticisms when we undertake, if possible, to confirm our chapters from the sayings of the Catholic Fathers, and we shall strive, insofar as the Lord grants, to refute them.

Then we shall set out the fifth chapter of our fellow brothers, by which they struck us, as it were, silently and from the side: the material that we found in the writings of Gottschalk after we had excerpted the four often-mentioned chapters. We shall say, with the Lord’s inspiration, what we think about it.

[Col. 0056A] Finally, we shall append the sixteen chapters for which our brothers have decided, through the Scots’ porridge, to feed us in this particular matter, though without any fault of ours; and from the thoughts of the Catholic Fathers we shall show what we think about those chapters.

[Col. 0055]

# Preface of Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, to the Following Work

[Col. 0055B] We humbly and devoutly ask, through the bonds of charity, all into whose hands this little work of our labor may come: because, at the urgent request of our lord King Charles, we had it transcribed quickly from the notaries’ sheets before correction, and because this made it necessary to erase and correct certain passages in many places, if some rival, taking the opportunity, has erased what was correct here and perhaps written something corrupt over it, or if the ignorance of scribes has caused it to be transcribed differently, let them not impute another’s error to us.

Rather, when they examine here the testimonies of the Catholics, whose doctrine we follow in understanding, speech, and writing insofar as the Lord grants, let them uproot and gather up the weeds sown by the enemy among the wheat. Or, if they have been willing to devote sufficient effort to the matter, let them make these matters known to us in a few letters, through whomever they prefer, and endeavor to resolve from the archive of the Church of Rheims whatever they have doubted.

[Col. 0055C] And let whoever is pleased, by whose favor the following material has been transcribed, also arrange for this request to be copied. We say and ask these things because we have learned from records exposing the matter that formerly Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, and Macarius, bishop of Antioch, erased and corrupted certain passages from authoritative Scriptures and the sayings of the saints.

We likewise learned from the report of those who were present at the council that when our lord Charles of blessed memory discovered Felix, the unfortunate bishop of the city of Urgell, proved and condemned as a heretic by synodal decree, he also found that Felix had been refuted because, having bribed a junior librarian of the palace at Aix, he scraped the book of blessed Hilary and changed the wording where it said, “The humility of the flesh is adored in the Son of God,” inserting, “The humility of the flesh is adopted.”

[Col. 0055D] And, as the reader will soon discover, we believe on reliable evidence that the sermon of Florus on predestination, recently published, has been corrupted.

[Col. 0056B] At the head of the index of the following work we have judged it worthwhile to place in full the sermon of Florus which, when Heribold, formerly the venerable bishop of Auxerre, lent it to us, we transcribed at the synodal assembly at Bonneuil; and which, after our return from the turmoil at Brienne, a certain cleric offered us from the archive of Ebo, the venerable bishop of Grenoble, as he himself said.

We do this because the sermon proceeds cautiously both in its construction and in the truth of its meaning, except in two places where we do not believe that he said what we find in the copy that we received from the archive of the venerable Ebo, since in other passages he spoke so Catholicly, as will be clear to readers. This is especially significant because in the same writing which we received through the hands of the aforesaid Heribold—as we understood it had been sent to him by the aforementioned Florus—we found the text differently from the copy that we received later. For this reason we suspect that these passages were altered by someone.

[Col. 0056C] Before we begin to write that sermon, we shall identify the places specifically. Where it says:

> “But those whom he foreknew and foresaw would become evil and impious through their own fault, he himself predestined to eternal damnation by a just judgment,”

the little copy we received from Heribold reads:

> “But because he foreknew and foresaw that they would become evil and impious through their own fault, he predestined them to eternal damnation, by which they would be punished through a just judgment.”

And where it is written:

> “For he did not predestine anyone to be evil, but truly predestined every evil person not to remain unpunished,”

we find in the copy received from the aforesaid Heribold:

> “But truly he predestined punishment, so that no evil person would remain unpunished.”

[Col. 0056D] He himself demonstrates this in what follows when he says:

> “He both foreknew their punishment, because he is God, and predestined it, because he is just.”

We leave the rest to the judgment of the Catholic reader. We considered it necessary to include this sermon in full because its fabricator, in the two immediately following chapters on foreknowledge and predestination, endeavored to compile material in a confused and inverted order and with an entirely false meaning, as anyone who reads both this sermon and those chapters will clearly understand.

# Sermon of Florus on Predestination, as Taken from the Archive of Ebo

[Col. 0057A] Almighty God, because he is most truly the true and only God, foreknew everything in his eternal and unchangeable knowledge before it came to be, as Scripture testifies, saying: “Eternal God, knower of hidden things, you know all things before they come to be” (Dan. 13:42).

Therefore, without doubt, he foreknew both the good things that the good would do and the evil things that the wicked would commit. Yet in the case of good people, he himself by his grace made them good; in the case of evil people, he did not himself make them evil—God forbid—but merely foreknew that they would become such through their own fault.

The foreknowledge of God did not impose necessity upon them so that they could not be anything else. Rather, God, in his omnipotent majesty, foresaw as God what they would become of their own will. Hence Scripture, impressing upon us his undefiled justice, says of him: “He commanded no one to act impiously, and he gave no one room to sin.”

[Col. 0057B] Therefore, the impious and wicked are responsible for the evil they commit, as well as for turning the time of this present life, which God gave them for doing good, toward the practice of evil. The fault is not God’s but theirs, and therefore they are rightly condemned by his justice.

The same almighty God also foreknew their eternal damnation, but on account of their merit, since he foresaw that they would persist in their own wickedness—not on account of any iniquity of his, God forbid—for he established nothing unjustly and will repay each according to his works: eternal good things to those who act well and everlasting evils to those who act wickedly.

Thus he entirely foreknew the good as destined to become good through his grace and to receive eternal rewards through the same grace: that is, to live well in the present age and to be happily rewarded in the age to come. Both, however, come from God’s gift of mercy. Hence the Apostle calls them “vessels of his mercy,” saying: “That he might show the riches of his grace upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Rom. 9:23).

[Col. 0057C] Conversely, he foreknew that the wicked would become wicked through their own wickedness, and he foreknew that through his justice they would be condemned to eternal punishment. Thus he foreknew concerning Judas the traitor that he would betray him, as the Gospel says, although he was one of the Twelve (John 6:72). He also foreknew his eternal damnation when he said: “Woe to that man by whom the Son of Man will be betrayed. It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Mark 14:21).

Similarly, he undoubtedly foreknew the future impiety of the wicked Jews, concerning which he foretold in the Psalm: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22). He also foreknew their subsequent damnation, concerning which he added in the same Psalm: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written among the righteous” (ibid., 29).

In these people and in all the wicked, the first belongs to their own depravity, while the second follows from divine equity.

[Col. 0057D] The same must be understood entirely concerning God’s predestination. In the case of the good, he predestined both the goodness they would have in the future, from the gift of his grace, and their eternal reward for that same goodness, so that by his gift they would become good and by his gift they would be rewarded.

Hence the Apostle says: “He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, in him” (Eph. 1:5); and elsewhere: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8:29).

He therefore predestined his chosen ones both to be adopted now as sons of God through the grace of baptism and, in the future, to be conformed to the image of the Son of God, renewed and glorified according to his image by the same grace of God.

[Col. 0058A] He certainly predestined them to be good here—not from themselves but from him—and blessed there—not through themselves but through him. In both cases, therefore, he foreknew and predestined the good things that would come to be in and through them.

But in the case of the wicked and impious, almighty God did not predestine wickedness and impiety—that is, he did not predestine them to be wicked and impious so that they could not be anything else. Rather, those whom he foreknew and foresaw would become evil and impious through their own fault, he himself predestined to eternal damnation by a just judgment—not because they could not have been otherwise, but because they did not wish to be otherwise.

They themselves, therefore, became the cause of their own destruction; God is the just judge and just disposer of that damnation. He did not predestine anything unjust but something just. Yet he predestined both crowns for the righteous and punishments for the unrighteous, because both are just.

Commending this justice to us, the Apostle says: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath? Certainly not” (Rom. 3:5).

And because God now grants everyone patience so that they may turn to repentance, while those who perish perish through their own contempt and hardness because they despised such great goodness of God, the Apostle says again elsewhere: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and longsuffering, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will repay each according to his works” (Rom. 2:4).

[Col. 0058B] Another Scripture likewise testifies, saying: “God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living. But the impious summoned it by their hands and words; considering it a friend, they wasted away and made a covenant with it, because they are worthy to belong to it” (Wis. 1:13).

Almighty God, therefore, is not the cause of death or destruction for anyone. Rather, the wicked themselves summon death and destruction upon themselves by their hands and words: by acting wickedly, and by persuading others to act more wickedly, they bring damnation upon themselves and others. Loving the way of iniquity and destruction, they turn aside from the straight path and hasten toward everlasting damnation, as though joining right hands with one another, by a common agreement in wickedness, as if by a pledge and covenant—confederates of death and enemies of eternal life.

According to their hardness and impenitent heart, they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath. On that day of God’s just judgment, since each person receives according to his works, no one is condemned by a prejudgment of God but by the merit of his own iniquity.

[Col. 0058C] For he did not predestine anyone to be evil, but truly predestined every evil person not to remain unpunished. Every just law, likewise, commits no crime, lest it be unjust, and yet it punishes the criminal, so that it may truly be just.

Whoever therefore says that those who perish were predestined to destruction and therefore could not turn out otherwise must say the same concerning the righteous—that they are saved because they were predestined to salvation and could not be anything else.

Whoever speaks so confusedly and foolishly removes from those who perish the merit of damnation and from those who are saved the merit of salvation. What else does he thereby do except impose upon those who perish the necessity of destruction and upon those who are saved the necessity of salvation? Thus the former would not be justly condemned, because they could not be righteous, and the latter would not be justly rewarded, because they could not be anything other than righteous.

[Col. 0058D] In both cases, therefore, destruction and salvation would result not from the judgment of one’s own action but from the prejudgment of divine predetermination. Where, then, would be the statement, “He will repay each according to his works” (Rom. 2:4)? And again: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath? Certainly not” (Rom. 3:5).

For the cause of the destruction of those who perish would plainly be attributed to God if he predestined them to destruction in such a way that they could not be anything else. To think or say this is horrible blasphemy.

But the faith of the Catholic Church, whose children and followers we ought to be, firmly instructs us to hold what we briefly set out above according to the authority of sacred Scripture: almighty God foreknew the wickedness of the wicked because it comes from them, but did not predestine it because it does not come from him. He foreknew their punishment because he is God, and predestined it because he is just, so that in them there might be the merit of their damnation and in him the power and judgment of the one who justly condemns.

God predestines only what he himself is going to do; but he foreknows many things that he himself is not going to do, such as all evil things, which the wicked certainly do, not he.

[Col. 0059A] The wicked themselves do not perish because they could not be good, but because they did not wish to be good. Through their own fault they persisted as vessels of wrath fitted for destruction and remained in the mass of damnation, whether by original or actual merit.

In the case of the good, as has been sufficiently shown above, almighty God both foreknew and predestined them to be good in the present life through his grace and also blessed in the future. He himself is the author and giver of both their goods, that is, both the present and the future; and therefore he is undoubtedly the foreknower and predestiner of both.

For they themselves, before being made righteous from the wicked by him who justifies the ungodly, not only could have been otherwise but actually were otherwise.

[Col. 0059B] Whether in those who are saved or in those who perish, their own will is rewarded and their own will is condemned. In those who are saved, because it has been healed by the grace of the Lord Savior so that from evil and perverse it became good and upright, it is deservedly crowned. In those who perish, because they refuse through the Savior to receive healing, it will most justly experience everlasting damnation through the same judge.

This, briefly, is everything that must be held concerning free choice according to the truth of the Catholic faith. God created every human being with free choice. But because through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned, free choice in the whole human race was so impaired and corrupted by the guilt of that transgression, and so blinded and weakened, that it is sufficient for a person to do evil—that is, to fall into iniquity—and can be free for this alone.

[Col. 0059C] But for doing good—that is, for the practice of virtue and the fruit of good works—it cannot rise or recover strength in any way unless it is restored, illumined, and healed through faith in the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, and through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The Savior himself promises this in the Gospel, saying: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36). And the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

Through this grace of Christ and the Spirit of Christ, therefore, human free choice, liberated, illumined, and healed, may gratefully say the words of the Psalmist: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 26:1).

Whoever desires to receive this grace of freedom, so as to become truly free for living well and piously, should not presume upon his own powers. Rather, let him faithfully entrust himself to the one by whom he must be healed and strengthened, of whom the same Psalmist says: “The steps of a man will be directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way” (Ps. 36:23).

[Col. 0059D] Let him pray to him and entreat him, saying: “Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Ps. 118:133); and again: “Lord, lead me in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Ps. 5:9), and other similar prayers.

I have written these things briefly in reply to what you ordered. Now I faithfully beg and exhort you: grounded in the simplicity and sincerity of true faith, close your ears against the wicked tongue of that most vain and miserable man who, being ready for contention and obstinate against the truth, preferred—unhappy man, puffed up by a diabolical spirit—to separate himself from the Church of Christ and its priests rather than abandon his profane and empty words.

# Here Ends the Work of Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, Addressed—With Its Author’s Name Suppressed—to Nearly All the Bishops of That Time, Both of Gaul and of Other Provinces, against Gottschalk

Gottschalk was at that time confined by Hincmar himself in the monastery at Hautvillers; he had previously been a monk in the monastery at Orbais.

These chapters, first reread in the synod of the territory of Toul and rejected by certain brothers, have subsequently been more fully refuted in the following work by Catholic teaching. The divergence of the fourth and fifth chapters from the perversity of the others is explained consecutively in the subsequent little work, in chapters twenty-two and thirty-five.

[Col. 0060A]

## I. 

We faithfully hold, and it pleases us to hold, that God eternally foreknew both the good things that the good would do and the evil things that the wicked would commit, since we possess the voice of Scripture, which says: “Eternal God, who are the knower of hidden things, you know all things before they come to be” (Dan. 13:42).

We hold that he entirely foreknew the good as destined to become good through his grace and to receive eternal rewards through the same grace. He foreknew the wicked as destined to become wicked through their own wickedness and to be condemned to eternal punishment through his justice, so that, according to the Psalmist, “because power belongs to God, and mercy belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 61:12–13), he may repay each according to his works.

As apostolic teaching declares: “To those who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption: eternal life; but to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth, yet obey iniquity: wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress upon every soul of a human being who works evil” (Rom. 2:7–9).

[Col. 0060B] The same Apostle says elsewhere in the same sense: “At the revelation of our Lord from heaven, with the angels of his power, in a flame of fire inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our God, who will pay eternal penalties in destruction, when he comes to be glorified in his saints and made wonderful in all who have believed” (2 Thess. 1:7).

Nor did God’s foreknowledge impose necessity upon any wicked person, so that he could not be anything else. Rather, what that person would become through his own will, God, who knows all things before they come to be, foreknew in his omnipotent and unchangeable majesty.

We believe that no one is condemned by God’s prejudgment but by the merit of his own iniquity. The wicked do not perish because they could not be good, but because they did not wish to be good, and through their own fault they remained in the mass of damnation, whether by original merit or also by actual merit.

[Col. 0060C]

## II. 

Concerning God’s predestination also, it has pleased us and continues faithfully to please us to hold, according to apostolic authority, which says: “Does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:21). Immediately afterward it adds: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted or prepared for destruction, so that he might show the riches of his grace upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (ibid., 22–23), we confidently confess the predestination of the elect to life and the predestination of the impious to death.

In the election of those who are to be saved, however, God’s mercy precedes good merit; in the damnation of those who perish, evil merit precedes God’s just judgment.

[Col. 0060D] By predestination God established only what he himself would do either by free mercy or by just judgment, according to Scripture, which says: “He made the things that are to be.”

In the wicked, however, he foreknew their wickedness because it comes from them, but did not predestine it because it does not come from him. He certainly foreknew the punishment that follows evil merit, as God who foresees all things, and predestined it because he is just.

With him, as Saint Augustine says, there is concerning all things altogether a sentence as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain.

To this the saying of the Wise One also applies: “Judgments are prepared for scoffers, and hammers to strike the bodies of fools” (Prov. 19:29).

[Col. 0061A] Concerning the immutability of God’s foreknowledge and predestination, by which future things are already accomplished before him, Ecclesiastes is also rightly understood to say: “I have learned that all the works that God has made endure forever; we cannot add to them or take away from them, for God has acted so that he may be feared” (Eccles. 3:14).

But we do not merely fail to believe that some have been predestined to evil by divine power—that is, predestined so that they are unable to be anything else; we also pronounce anathema, with complete detestation, against anyone who wishes to believe such an evil thing, just as the Council of Orange did.

### III. On the Redemption by Christ’s Blood

Because of the excessive error that has arisen concerning this matter—so that certain people, as their writings indicate, even define Christ’s blood as having been poured out for those ungodly persons who, from the beginning of the world until the Lord’s Passion, died in their ungodliness and were punished with eternal condemnation—contrary to that prophetic passage, “I will be your death, O Death; I will be your sting, O Hell” (Hos. XIII, 14), it pleases us to hold and teach simply and faithfully, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic truth, that this price was given for those of whom our Lord himself says:

> “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John III, 14);

and the Apostle says:

> “Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many” (Heb. IX, 28).

Moreover, the nineteen chapters most ineptly and falsely concluded by a certain Scot in syllogisms—wherein there appears not an argument of faith but rather a contrivance of perfidy, constructed by no philosophical art at all, as some arrogantly proclaim, but confused through empty sophistry and the most unskilled deception—we utterly reject from the devout hearing of the faithful. And so that such things and the like may be avoided in every respect, we forbid them by the authority of the Holy Spirit; we also judge that those who introduce novelties ought to be chastised, lest they be struck more severely.

### IV.

Likewise, we firmly believe that the entire multitude of the faithful, regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit and thereby truly incorporated into the Church, and, in accordance with apostolic teaching, baptized into Christ’s death, has been washed from its sins in his blood. For there could not have been true regeneration in them unless there had also been true redemption, since in the sacraments of the Church nothing is empty, nothing deceptive, but everything is entirely true and supported by its own truth and sincerity.

Yet from this same multitude of the faithful and redeemed, some are saved with eternal salvation, because they faithfully remain in their redemption through God’s grace, carrying in their hearts the voice of their Lord: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22). Others, however, who did not wish to remain in the salvation of the faith that they received at the beginning, and who chose rather to nullify the grace of redemption through wicked teaching or life than to preserve it, will in no way attain the fullness of salvation or the reception of eternal blessedness.

In both respects we have the teaching of the devout teacher:

> “All who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Rom. VI, 3);

and:

> “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III, 27);

and again:

> “Let us draw near with a true heart in the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water; let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering” (Heb. X, 22);

and again:

> “Anyone who sets aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will the one deserve who has trampled upon the Son of God, regarded as unclean the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (ibid., 28).

### V.

Likewise, concerning the grace by which believers are saved, and without which no rational creature has ever lived blessedly, and concerning free will, weakened by sin in the first man but restored and healed in the Lord Jesus’ faithful through grace, we most steadfastly and with full faith confess precisely what the most holy Fathers left us to hold on the authority of the sacred Scriptures; what the African and Arausican synods professed; and what the most blessed pontiffs of the Apostolic See held in the Catholic faith. We likewise presume in no way to deviate toward another position concerning nature and grace.

But we wholly reject the inept little questions and almost childish fables, and the Scots’ porridge, which nauseate the purity of the faith—matters that, in these most dangerous and grievous times, have lamentably and tearfully grown to increase our burdens, even to the breaking of charity—in order that Christian minds may not be corrupted by them and fall away from the simplicity and purity of the faith that is in Christ Jesus. We admonish fraternal charity, for love of the Lord Christ, to discipline its hearing by avoiding such things.

Let the brotherhood remember that it is being crushed by the world’s grievous evils, by an abundant harvest of the wicked, and that it is being most harshly suffocated by the chaff of frivolous men. Let it burn to overcome these things and labor to correct them, and let it not burden the assembly of those who piously grieve and groan with superfluities. Rather, let it embrace with firm and true faith what the holy Fathers have sufficiently set forth concerning these and similar matters.

### Opinions of the Holy Fathers on Grace and Free Will

1. In Adam’s transgression, all human beings lost natural possibility and innocence, and no one can rise by free will from the depth of that ruin unless the grace of the merciful God raises him up.

2. No one uses free will well except through Christ.

3. All the endeavors, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to God’s glory and praise, because no one pleases God for any other reason than that which he himself has granted.

4. God works in human hearts and in free will itself in such a way that holy thought, devout counsel, and every movement of good will come from God, because through him we can do something good, and without him we can do nothing.

5. We profess God to be the author of all endeavors and all virtues by which one turns toward God from the beginning of faith. We do not doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we both begin to will and to do something good.

By this help and mercy of God, free will is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes healthy, and what was imprudent becomes prudent. For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wishes our merits to be his gifts, and for what he has bestowed he will grant eternal rewards. For he acts in us so that we may both will and do what he wills.

6. We confess that God’s grace and help are given even for individual acts, and that this grace is not given according to our merits, so that it may truly be grace—that is, freely given through the mercy of the one who said: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion” (Rom. IX, 15).

7. We confess that free will exists, even though it needs divine assistance.

8. Free will, weakened in the first man, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism.

9. The will’s freedom is truly free when it does not serve vices and sins. Such freedom was certainly given by God to the first man; once lost, it could not be restored except by the one from whom it could have been given. Hence the Truth says: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John VIII, 36).

### VI.

And because, through our sins, bishops are appointed throughout the cities who have not been examined or tested, who are almost ignorant of literary learning, and who approach the apostolic prescription too little—an occasion by which ecclesiastical vigor is especially diminished—it has pleased us that, whenever the bishop of any city departs at the Lord’s call, a petition should be made to the most glorious princes that they deign to permit a canonical election by the clergy and people of that city. Thus a person approved and worthy of office should be sought either among the clergy, or among the people, or certainly in the diocese itself, and, if necessary, in its vicinity; once found, that person should be placed in honor over the city with the consent of the entire clergy and people.

But if any cleric comes from the service of our pious princes so that he may be appointed bishop over some city, he must first be carefully examined, with holy fear, as to what sort of life he leads, and then as to what sort of learning he possesses. The metropolitan must act in this matter with ecclesiastical vigor under the eyes of almighty God, while the other bishops, as God’s ministers, provide assistance, so that no bishop who leads a stained life, is puffed up with worldly display, and polluted by the Simoniac heresy may be placed over the humble and pure members of Christ and of the Church. Nor should he presume to place over the people an unlearned man blinded by unlawful greed, who will have to render an account of his action to God.

If that same metropolitan sees that it is necessary, lest he be forced to commit so great an evil as giving an honor owed only to the worthy, he should instruct the people and educate the Church. Rather, he should approach the clemency of the kings, and himself, together with whatever fellow bishops he can enlist, should approach them by whatever means possible, so that the glorious kings may honor God’s Church with a worthy minister.

But if the metropolitan, shamefully overcome by any greed or deceived by some gift, has negligently and unwillingly carried out so great a duty, let him not doubt that he has incurred the judgment of the all-seeing God, and let him know that he is also to be condemned by ecclesiastical judgment.

That those who are to be ordained may be ordained according to ecclesiastical order and the institution of the holy Fathers—that is, that they may be advanced to ecclesiastical authority by the judgment of the metropolitans and of the bishops who are situated all around them—from excerpts of Martin:

> “It is not permitted to make the election of those who are being called to the priesthood; rather, the judgment belongs to the bishops, so that they themselves may test the one who is to be ordained, whether he has been instructed in speech, in faith, and in episcopal life.”

Likewise, concerning the judgment by which those who have neglected the statutes of the holy Fathers in ordaining bishops are to be punished, from the decrees of Pope Leo:

> “If any bishops consecrate as a priest one who may not lawfully be such, even if they somehow escape damage to their own honor, they shall nevertheless have no right to ordain another, nor shall they ever participate in that sacrament which, having neglected God’s judgment, they unjustly conferred.”

The following four chapters were established at Carisiacum against the Predestinarians. After the preceding material had been read, they were reread at the aforementioned synod, and in the subsequent work they were also confirmed by testimonies from the Scriptures and from orthodox writers.

### I.

Almighty God created human beings upright and without sin, with free will, and placed them in paradise, where he wished them to remain in the holiness of righteousness. Human beings, using free will badly, sinned and fell, and became a mass of perdition for the entire human race.

But the good and just God chose from that same mass of perdition, according to his foreknowledge, those whom he predestined by grace for life, and predestined eternal life for them. As for the others, whom by the judgment of his justice he left in the mass of perdition, he foreknew that they would perish, but he did not predestine them to perish; rather, because he is just, he predestined eternal punishment for them.

Accordingly, we speak of only one predestination of God, which concerns either the gift of grace or the retribution of justice.

### II.

We lost freedom of will in the first man, and received it again through Christ our Lord. We have free will for good when grace precedes and assists us, and we have free will for evil when grace abandons us. We have free will because grace has liberated it, and grace has healed it from corruption.

### III.

Almighty God wishes all human beings without exception to be saved, although not all are saved. The fact that some are saved is the gift of the one who saves; the fact that some perish is the merit of those who perish.

### IV.

Christ Jesus our Lord: just as there is no human being—none who is, has been, or will be—whose nature has not been assumed in him, so there is no human being—none who is, has been, or will be—for whom he has not suffered, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion.

That not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion does not concern the greatness and abundance of the price, but concerns the part of unbelievers and of those who do not believe with the faith that works through love. For the cup of human salvation, prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed possess within itself what benefits everyone; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.

### Letter of Prudentius, Bishop of the City of Tricasses

The letter of Prudentius, bishop of the city of Tricasses, follows. It is frequently mentioned in the course of the work that follows and is shown to disagree with the faith and teaching of the Catholics.

To the venerable Father and to the other fathers and brothers most sincerely worthy of love, and to the reverend fellow bishops, Prudentius sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

As far as the merit of my sins is concerned, I am prevented by the most just judgment of God; but, as far as his undeserved and unfailing mercies are concerned, by his most merciful gift, I am weighed down by almost every known infirmity and forbidden to be present at your holy and desirable assembly.

Nevertheless, through this letter and through Arnold, the priest and envoy of our Church, I offer the presence of my agreement to the extent that, if the man who is to be ordained is willing to subscribe by confessing, and to confess by subscribing, to all the institutions of the Apostolic See and to the writings and sayings of the blessed Fathers—Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Sixtus, Leo, Gelasius, Celestine, Gregory, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Isidore, Primasius, Fulgentius, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Bede, and other equally Catholic and orthodox men—and especially to the four chapters by which the entire Catholic Church fought against Pelagius and the followers of his heresy and conquered, and which it committed to writing for the memory of posterity, writings full of authority and truth, then I declare myself in agreement with his ordination. Otherwise, I neither agree nor advise Christ’s faithful to agree.

Although I do not doubt that your wisdom is much more vividly acquainted with the sequence of the four chapters set forth above than is my weakness, I nevertheless judged it necessary to append them briefly, so that your blessedness might more easily recognize what I think and to what truth I assent:

First, that he should confess that free will, lost in Adam through the merit of disobedience, has been restored and liberated for us through our Lord Jesus Christ—meanwhile in hope, but afterward in reality—as the Apostle says, “For in hope we were saved” (Rom. VIII, 24). Yet we must always need the grace of almighty God for every good work: whether for thinking, beginning, doing, or bringing it perseveringly to completion. We must know that without this grace we are in no way able even to think, will, or perform anything good.

Second, that he should believe and confess that, by the highest and hidden counsel of almighty God, some were predestined by God’s gratuitous mercy before all ages to life, and some were predestined by inscrutable justice to punishment—namely, that in those who are saved and in those who are condemned he predestined what he had foreknown he would do in judgment, as the prophet says: “He who made the things that are to be.”

Third, that he should believe and confess with all Catholics that the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ was poured out for all human beings throughout the world who believe in him, but not for those who have never believed in him, do not believe in him even today, and will never believe in him, as the Lord himself says: “For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Matt. XXI, 28).

Fourth, that he should believe and confess that almighty God wills to save all whomsoever he wills, and that no one can in any way be saved unless he himself saves that person; and that all whom he himself wills to save are saved. Accordingly, whoever is not saved is in no way the object of his will to be saved, as the Prophet says: “The Lord has done whatever he willed, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Ps. CXXXIV, 6).

Although there are other matters concerning which the universal Church agreed, labored, and subscribed in the condemnation of Pelagius, these particular points, extracted and vindicated against him and his accomplices by the Apostolic See through the diligence of the blessed Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and Augustine, together with three hundred and fourteen other bishops, and published throughout the world in many letters and books, the Church even today rejoices in, confesses, proclaims, and holds—and will continue to hold.

May heavenly grace deign perpetually to preserve your praiseworthy fatherhood and brotherhood, agreeing in every respect with these matters, invincible and most powerful, and rejoicing in its own gift.

As for the many tortuous and poisonous opinions of Gottschalk, whom in the following work we frequently mention with the condemnation he deserves, and the destructive struggles of his accomplices, we have not thought it necessary to set them forth here in advance. Although their pestilential teaching divides itself along several divergent paths, they are nevertheless known to agree concerning the predestination of the reprobate to destruction, concerning the claim that God does not wish all human beings to be saved but only those who are saved, and concerning the claim that Christ did not suffer for everyone. The following work sufficiently demonstrates the Catholic teaching on these matters. We have already devoted labor against them individually in other booklets composed before this one, as will be evident to anyone to whom the Lord grants or permits it to become clear.

---

## HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS: A LATER TREATISE ON GOD’S PREDESTINATION AND FREE WILL

### Against Gottschalk and the Other Predestinarians

## 1. Letter to the King

To the glorious lord King Charles, Hincmar, bishop of Rheims in name but not in merit, and servant of God’s people, together with my fellow lords and most venerable brothers, the bishops, devoted ambassadors of your salvation and prosperity.

Last June, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 859, you gave us certain chapters, as you told our humility, which the most reverend Remigius, archbishop of Lyons, had presented to your Highness. You commanded us, at a suitable time, to return you an answer concerning them, namely, whether we agreed unanimously and with one voice with the meaning of those chapters, or whether, because they seemed to you in certain respects to dissent from the ancient faith of the Fathers, our judgment—which you believed did not deviate from the Catholic path—differed from them in any way. In this we followed both the command of the Lord and the Christian custom of your predecessors.

For divine laws have provided, and it has been customary according to the ancient practice of earlier rulers, that whenever anything new arises concerning the Catholic faith or divine religion, it should be referred by the sovereign’s decision to the consultation of the bishops. Whatever they determine should be believed, followed, held, and proclaimed according to their judgment, the authority of the holy Scriptures, the teaching of orthodox teachers, canonical authority, and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs—vicars of Christ our God and prelates of the holy Church—should be believed by all in the heart for righteousness, confessed by the mouth for salvation, followed for vocation, held for the crown, and proclaimed for gain.

These chapters were read at a gathering of bishops held in the territory of Toul, in a village called Saponaria, two days before they were presented to you. The lord Remigius, archbishop of Lyons, brought them forward and submitted them to the synod. As he said, and as is contained in the inscription of those same chapters, he and the bishops of his province had published them in that same year, on the Kalends also recorded there, and in the suburb of the city of Langres, for the instruction of the Lord’s people.

On the following day certain other chapters, about which we shall speak later, were reread, and, as it seemed to some of the brothers, the minds of certain people were disturbed by them. For, to speak truthfully—and we too acknowledge it—when the chapters that, as we have said, Archbishop Remigius had presented to the synod were read, recalling the traditions of Catholic teachers to memory, our consciences were shaken not a little.

Therefore some of our men, inflamed by zeal for the Christian faith, wished to bring certain matters before the synod. But our agitation was calmly settled by the same venerable Remigius, archbishop of Lyons. He spoke with reverence, urging that if the judgment of any among us were disturbed by dissenting in some respect from the chapters that had been brought forward, each of us should take care to bring the books of Catholic teachers to the next synod, and that thereafter we should all unanimously hold what we found together to accord best with Catholic and apostolic teaching.

In view of his devotion and that of his fellow bishops of the same diocese—whose Catholic mind and teaching, even before his ordination, we have known, as you also know—we have understood, so far as we dare give credence to the judgment of our weakness, that these chapters were not brought forward by them, not to say through them, at the synod.

Therefore, although some wished to mark them with a gentle hiss because Saint Celestine rebuked the Gallic bishops, saying (letter 8):

> “What hope is there,” he says, “where, while the teachers are silent, those speak who, if this is so, have not been their disciples? I fear that this silence is itself a restraint; I fear that those who permit them to speak in such a manner are themselves speaking through them. In such matters silence is not free from suspicion, because truth would come forward if falsehood were displeasing. The matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by silence.”

Nevertheless, since many of us know their faith, teaching, and prudence, and since we were less acquainted with these matters, we proposed to them, concerning the disagreement over baptism, the judgment about blessed Cyprian that Saint Augustine repeatedly praised and set forth in the second book *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 4:

> “How could this matter, wrapped in such clouds of dispute, have been brought to the clear illumination and confirmation of a plenary council unless it had first been established through lengthy treatment in many discussions and conferences among bishops throughout the regions of the world, on both sides? The health of peace does this: when obscure matters are investigated for a long time and, because of the difficulty of discovering the truth, produce different judgments in fraternal debate, the bond of unity remains until the truth becomes clear, lest the wound of error remain incurable in a severed part. And therefore, often something is revealed less to the more learned, so that their patient and humble charity, in which there is greater fruit, may be tested—either how they preserve unity while holding different opinions on obscure matters, or how they accept the truth when they learn that what they thought has been declared otherwise.”

Those same venerable Catholic and learned men knew that this pestilential teaching had again been stirred up in many regions and provinces. Therefore they did not wish to impose silence on error in their provinces as readily as they perhaps could have, until the question, having come to the knowledge of many, might be quieted by the judgment of many. For, as Saint Celestine says in his letter to Nestorius (letter 5, at the end):

> “All must know what is being dealt with whenever the matter of all is under discussion,”

namely, so that, when the deliberation of all has been settled in the proposition of one, the solution may spread from all to all.

You can easily recall that, three years ago, when we were stationed on guard against the invasion of the Northmen in the village belonging to the bishopric of Rouen called Nielfa, you gave us these same chapters, written under the title of having supposedly been composed at the Council of Valence, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 855, under Emperor Lothair. You asked us to respond to them as seemed Catholic according to the teaching of the orthodox, together with whatever writings of others had reached your notice from this quarter.

We received some of those writings, but did not wish to publish them, concerned to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. IV, 3), until we could speak familiarly with those who had sent them to you and, if in any way we were able, with the Lord’s cooperation, recall them from this perverse intention to the unity of the Catholic faith.

But because we were hindered partly by our duties and partly because we were obeyed less than necessary in our fraternal admonitions, we were unable to recall those whom we intended to warn from their intention. Therefore, since, as the Apostle says, “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, while others follow after them. In the same way, good deeds are manifest, and those that are otherwise cannot remain hidden” (1 Tim. V, 24–25), the dissent of certain people grew so greatly that this discord reached your notice. Then, by synodal decree, out of zeal for the faith and love of unanimity, before you entrusted these matters to us for investigation, you required four chapters to be collected from the sayings of the Catholic Fathers by episcopal determination and confirmed by the hands of each bishop.

Afterward, the folly of some of those who had subscribed to the same chapters, as well as of others, increased to such an extent that it became necessary, both because of your urgent command and because of our obedience in carrying it out, to respond in writing to the writings and propositions of those whom we have mentioned above. Among these, we also responded, according to the capacity of our small intellect and yet with some hesitation, to the chapters that you recently gave us.

We did not believe that our brothers and fellow bishops ought to have written such things against us contrary to ecclesiastical regulations, especially since they knew that the institutions of the Lord and the laws promulgated by the Holy Spirit had prescribed how they should summon us and then, by synodal judgment, expel us and our opinions from their communion if we spoke against the aforesaid articles of faith.

Now, however, because we are certain to whose composition we must respond concerning the frequently mentioned questions, while preserving the explanations of our reports against those to whom, by your authority, we were commanded to render an account as part of the ministry imposed upon us, we shall strive to respond simply to these chapters alone, insofar as it lies with us, while remaining at peace with everyone, on the authority of the holy Scriptures and the judgments of the Catholic Fathers.

Thus anyone who perhaps has neither been able nor wished to read all those materials may here find concise responses to the chapters for the present. Snatching brief hours from the distractions of various duties—we who have no leisure for our thoughts—we have endeavored to commit these responses to sheets in hurried language, as we received them from the judgments of the holy Fathers, lest we be marked by your Christian devotion for sluggishness or disobedience.

For, provoked in the reports mentioned above by the manifold inferences of many people, and by manifold and numerous comparisons, we have labored to respond in three books with diffuse language—not without, as we know and confess, the reader’s weariness, but nevertheless with a Catholic mind. Yet in this especially we think we satisfy the kindly reader: we have always set down the individual opinions one by one and have endeavored to respond separately to each objection and resistance to the faith.

In this alone we trust that we shall win every devoted reader to our side: when he has weighed our labor according to his own judgment, he will hold us excused before him.

But whoever composed these chapters, to whom we are compelled to respond as though to a new opponent, will reveal himself when he is necessarily pressed to come into the light of truth. For the worker of dark deeds—among which the Apostle also counts heresies—hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his deeds be exposed. But everyone who does what is good—and among good things the Apostle also counts faith—comes to the light, so that his deeds may be revealed, because they have been done in God.

Yet whoever he may be, if he comes to the light and consents to the truth from the heart, he can become a son of light. But if he stubbornly contradicts the truth, he will impose upon himself the name of heretic through his unbelief and the folly of his contentiousness. For what is ignorantly judged different from the faith is not immediately heretical, unless it becomes heretical through stubborn contention.

## CHAPTER ONE

### When, where, and from what origin this Predestinarian heresy first arose, and by whom and in what manner it was refuted and suppressed

We have now judged that it must be explained when, where, and on what occasion this heresy first arose. Approximately four hundred and thirty years ago, and somewhat more, this heresy arose in the time of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, during the episcopate of Saint Celestine. It was at the same time that the Nestorian heresy also boiled over among the Greeks in the city of Constantinople, with Nestorius as its author, as the end of Saint Augustine’s temporal life was approaching, as Prosper demonstrates in his *Chronicle*, saying:

> “In the consulship of Theodosius XI and Valentinian: and at that time Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, began to introduce a new error into the Churches. And again: In the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, Augustine, bishop, outstanding in every respect, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, responding to the books of Julian amid the attacks of the besieging Vandals at the very end of his days, and persevering gloriously in defense of Christian grace.”

And Bede says in his *Chronicle*:

> “Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, reigned for twenty-six years. Valentinian the Younger, son of Constantius, was made emperor at Ravenna.”

And shortly afterward:

> “But blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo and the outstanding teacher of all the Churches, lest he should see the ruin of his own city, departed to the Lord in the third month of its siege, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, having lived seventy-six years and having completed almost forty years in the clerical office.”

That blessed Augustine, at the very end of his days, wrote the book *On Heresies* to the deacon Quodvultdeus, among his responses to the aforementioned books of Julian, which Prosper had mentioned. Augustine himself recalls this in his letter to the aforesaid deacon:

> “When, he says, an opportunity for writing these things was offered to me through the presbyter of Fussala, whom I commend to your charity, I reread your letter, in which you ask me to write something about the heresies that could have arisen from the time when the Lord’s coming in the flesh began to be announced. I did this to see whether I ought now to undertake the work itself and send you something from it, in which you would observe that it was all the more difficult because you wanted it to be shorter.

> “But I could not even do this, being hindered by such cares as had come upon me, from which I could not altogether withdraw. For they also turned me away from what I had in hand. That work was my response to the books of Julian, who published eight after those four to which I had previously responded. When our brother Alypius received these at Rome, he had not yet transcribed them all when he did not wish to let the opportunity pass by; through it he sent me five, promising that he would soon send the other three, and pressing me greatly not to delay my response.

> “Compelled by his urgency, I was always forced to proceed more slowly with what I was doing, so that I would not fail either work—one by day and the other by night—to the extent that I could spare time from other occupations continually coming upon me from every side.

> “I was engaged in a very necessary task: I was revising my own short works, and, if anything in them displeased me or could displease others, I was working out what could and should be read, partly by criticizing and partly by defending it. I had already completed two volumes, having revised all my books, whose number I had not known; I discovered that there were two hundred and thirty-two. The letters remained, along with the popular treatises that the Greeks call homilies.”

These books of Julian, as is clear, are not the same ones that he mentions in the books of the *Retractions*.

But the same remarkable teacher Augustine also wrote about eighty-eight heresies, adding the Pelagian heresy as the latest. Thereupon Gennadius of Massilia, a very learned priest, who also wrote about illustrious men—beginning at the point where Saint Jerome brought his account of illustrious writers to an end and commemorating famous writers down to his own time with due praise—inserted this Predestinarian heresy as the ninetieth heresy of the Pelagian sect, saying:

> “There are,” he says, “those who maintain that God does not create all human beings for the purpose that all may be saved, but so that the world may be adorned by the multitude of human beings,”

and the rest of what he continues, which we shall demonstrate in due course. Next he places Nestorianism as the ninety-first, and then Eutychianism, and after this Timotheanism. Hyginus also, in compiling a catalogue of heresies, places Nestorianism as the eighty-ninth heresy and this Predestinarianism as the ninetieth, together with a little book composed by those same Predestinarians, saying:

> “The ninetieth heresy,” he says, “which in our preface we said had falsely claimed to derive its name from Bishop Augustine, took the name of the Predestinarians.”

Blessed Augustine also says in the preface to his *Retractations* concerning his own minor works:

> “For the statement that has been written, ‘You will not escape sin through much speaking’ (Prov. 10:19), greatly terrifies me—not because I have written much, or because many things that were not dictated were nevertheless written down as things spoken by me; far be it from me that it should be counted as much speaking when necessary things are said, however great the multitude of words in which they are said. But I fear this statement of Holy Scripture for the following reason: from so many of my discussions many things can undoubtedly be gathered which, even if they are not false, may nevertheless appear—or may even be proved—not to have been necessary.”

And a little earlier:

> “No one except an impudent person will dare to criticize me because I criticize my own errors. But if someone says that I ought not to have said things that later displeased even me, he speaks the truth and agrees with me. For he is criticizing the very things of which I too am a critic. Nor ought I to criticize them if I ought to have said them.”

For this heresy first began in the African and Gallic regions, while blessed Augustine was still alive. Accordingly, he himself wrote a book, *On Rebuke and Grace*, to Valentinus and the monks with him, as Prosper demonstrates in his letter addressed to that same Augustine, saying:

> “Many servants of Christ who reside in the city of Massilia think that whatever you discussed in your writings composed against the Pelagian heretics concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s purpose is contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to ecclesiastical understanding. For some time they preferred to blame their own slowness rather than criticize what they did not understand; and when some of them wished to request a clearer and more explicit explanation from Your Blessedness on this matter, it came about, by God’s merciful ordering, that when certain people in Africa had raised similar questions, you issued the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, full of divine authority. When it was conveyed to our knowledge at an unexpected and opportune moment, we thought that all the complaints of those who resisted would be silenced, because all the questions on which your Holiness was to be consulted have been answered there so fully and conclusively, as though you had made it your particular aim to settle what had been disturbed among us.””

Blessed Augustine placed this book last in the sequence of his *Retractations*. In the preface to those books he says:

> “Therefore, whoever is going to read these works should not imitate me in my error, but should imitate me as I advance toward what is better. For whoever reads my minor works in the order in which they were written will perhaps discover how I progressed through writing. In order that this may be possible, I shall take care in this work, insofar as I can, that he may know that same order.”

Concerning this book Prosper added the following later in the aforementioned letter:

> “After this book of Your Blessedness had been reviewed, just as those who had previously followed the holy and apostolic authority of your teaching became much more discerning and better instructed, so those who had been obstructed by the obscurity of their own persuasion withdrew more hostile than before. Their extremely abrupt dissent must first be feared on their own account, lest the spirit of Pelagian impiety deceive men so distinguished and outstanding in their pursuit of every virtue; and lest the simpler people, among whom these men enjoy great respect because of their reputation for probity, consider it most secure for themselves to hear those whose authority they follow without judgment asserting such things.”

And near the end of that letter:

> “It is necessary and useful,” he says, “to write again what has been written, lest something be considered insignificant because it is not frequently criticized.”

For this reason Hilary, Bishop of Arles, also sent a letter to that same holy Augustine, in which he says:

> “These, then, are the matters being discussed at Massilia and also in certain places in Gaul,”

and other things. Again, near the end of his letter, he says:

> “When the books have been published which you are preparing concerning the whole matter, I beg that we may be deemed worthy to possess them, especially so that, by their authority, if anything in your writings displeases us, we may no longer hesitate to separate ourselves from it without detracting from the dignity of your name.”

[Col. 0072B] Accordingly Saint Augustine wrote two books to the aforementioned bishops, Prosper and Hilary: one *On the Predestination of the Saints*, the other *On the Gift of Perseverance*. In these books he used the term “predestination” in its proper sense, as it seemed to him appropriate, although previously he had used it indiscriminately in some of his other books; and in the book *On Rebuke and Grace* he had also corrected it definitively.

In these books he also makes frequent mention of these new heretics, as anyone who reads them recognizes; we present the matter briefly to the reader’s view. For in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance* (chapter 19) he says:

> “Moreover, if they knew that God gives these things in such a way that they did not fail to understand that he had foreknown himself as going to give them, and that he could not have been unaware to whom he would give them, undoubtedly they knew the predestination which, preached through the Apostles, we defend against the new heretics with greater effort and care.”

And again (chapter 20):

> “What compelled the passages of Scripture in which predestination is commended to be defended more fully and more clearly by this labor of ours, except that the Pelagians say that God’s grace is given according to our merits?”

And elsewhere (chapter 23):

> “For concerning this matter, which we are now compelled not merely to mention but plainly to protect and defend against the new heretics”; and again: “Which is now defended with more diligent care against the new heretics”; and again: “And consequently the Church of Christ has never lacked faith in this predestination, which is now defended against the new heretics with renewed concern.”

There are also those who say that blessed Augustine wished to revise the term “predestination” in no other way than he had used it in his other books. Let them therefore know that, after all the books he mentions in the books of his *Retractations*, he composed these two books, which he produced in the place of a *Retractation*. Nevertheless, in them he refers to those same books of the *Retractations*, as the reader can easily recognize. For in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints* (chapter 4) he says:

> “I spoke about the first of those two books in the second book of the *Retractations*.”

And again, in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance* (chapter 11):

> “Finally, in the first book of the *Retractations*, a work that you have not yet read, when I had come to revise those same books,”

and the rest.

In the book *Hypomnesticon* he shows that he had been slandered by his opponents, saying (book 6):

> “You reproach us for believing or preaching that, when we speak of predestination together with the law of God and the prophets, with the Gospel of Christ and his Apostles, we mean that God predestines certain human beings to the life of the heavenly kingdom in such a way that, even if they do not wish to pray and fast, or to remain vigilant in every divine work, they cannot possibly perish.”

And a little later:

> “We are not surprised that you can fabricate falsehoods about us—that is, human beings about human beings—when we see that you have been so bewitched by the devil that you strive to alter the holy and truthful Scriptures to fit the understanding of your own will,”

and the rest, which he sets out at length.

Concerning this book, the *Hypomnesticon*, some argue that Saint Augustine did not compose it, because it very clearly contradicts their errors. They say that the holy bishop who appended a list containing the names of all his books to his *Life* did not record it. It should therefore be understood that we possess many of his books that are not included in that same little index, such as the book *On Christian Discipline*, and also the book entitled *On Christian Doctrine*. We likewise possess *On the Predestination of Grace*, *On Heresies*, addressed to the deacon Quodvultdeus, *On the Unity of the Trinity*, and a book *On Penance*, which he mentions in his letter to the monk Consentius (Letter 146, near the end), as well as the book entitled *On the Words of the Lord*, and others which we consider it unnecessary to mention.

For Saint Augustine himself says at the end of the *Retractations*:

> “I recall that I dictated these works—nine hundred and three in two hundred and thirty-two books—when I revised them, not knowing whether I would dictate any more. I published the revision itself in two books, urged on by the brethren, before I began to revise my letters and sermons to the people, some dictated by others and some spoken by me.”

The same holy bishop who compiled that index of his books or letters adds at the end of the index:

> “In all, the books, treatises, and letters which the aforementioned holy Augustine, moved by the divine Spirit, produced in the holy Catholic Church for the instruction of souls number one thousand and thirty, excluding those that cannot be counted because he did not specify their number.”

The holy bishop who recorded these things said that his treatises and letters could not be counted; yet some assert that, at the end of that very work, he carefully appended the total number of all his books or letters. They themselves can see in the same index whether the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance* are recorded there—books which no one either wishes or is able to deny belong to Saint Augustine.

We have also heard some argue that, because they had not read those blessed Augustine’s books intelligently, the index states that they are *Book One, Reply to Hilary’s Objections*. This can readily be shown to be false by those known to possess the same books. For the Hilary to whom a reply was made in one book was a Syracusan monk, whereas this Hilary was Bishop of Arles, to whom, together with Prosper, he sent the books we are now discussing.

If anyone does not possess these books, let him consult the collection of the venerable priest Bede concerning Saint Augustine’s minor works on the Apostle; there he will be able to learn what he previously did not know.

The holy bishops of the province of Africa likewise mention these books in their synodal letter, saying:

> “To our holy brothers, greatly beloved in the grace of God, John the priest and archimandrite, Venerius the deacon, and the faithful men whose signatures are contained in your letter: Datianus, Fortunatus, Boethus, Victor, Scholasticus, Orontius, Vindicianus, Victor, Januarius, Victorianus, Pontius, Quodvultdeus, servants of Christ, greeting in the Lord.”

And in the same letter, at the relevant point:

> “Present the books of Saint Augustine, which he wrote to Prosper and Hilary, for the aforementioned brothers to read. The blessed Hormisdas, the glorious bishop of the Apostolic See, inserted a mention of them with great praise of Catholic teaching in the letter that he wrote in reply to our holy brother and fellow priest Possessor, who had consulted him. His words are these (Letter 67):
>
> ‘Although what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and preserves concerning free choice and God’s grace can be abundantly recognized in the various books of blessed Augustine, and especially in those addressed to Hilary and Prosper, nevertheless the ecclesiastical archives also contain explicit chapters on the matter.’”

In the same letter the aforementioned holy bishops set out, in order to refute the heretics, Saint Augustine’s own words from the book *Hypomnesticon*, in his response to the third question.

Blessed Augustine himself, in the book addressed to Dulcitius, *On Eight Questions*, which he answered in writing after returning from Carthage, mentions the books in which he had written about these same questions; at the end of that work he refers to the same book *Hypomnesticon*, saying:

> “It is especially necessary to add this to the present work, so that your calumny, which you are accustomed to bring against us, may be defeated—or rather refuted—through the illumination of the Savior’s grace, and the integrity of our faith may be proved.
