For you reproach us for believing or preaching that, when we speak of predestination together with the law of God and the prophets, with the Gospel of Christ and his Apostles,”

and the rest, which the reader will find there in full, together with the solution of the sixth question, from the book *Hypomnesticon*.

They make a similar effort concerning the book entitled, under the name of Saint Jerome, *On the Hardening of Pharaoh’s Heart*, because it contradicts their understanding, striving very hard to establish that it is not his. But rejecting it does them no good, since that same Saint Jerome, together with the other Catholic teachers, proves that they hold an erroneous view in precisely the sense in which that book burns up their tares.

[Col. 0075A] Concerning his own criticism, which we mentioned earlier, the same Augustine says against his detractors at the end of the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*:

> “But those who think that I am in error should consider very carefully what has been said, lest perhaps they themselves be in error.”

Blessed Coelestine also demonstrates this in a decretal letter to Venerius and the other Gallic bishops, even after Augustine’s death (Letter 8), saying:

> “Let such men be avoided—men who labor to sow throughout the earth something other than what our farmer commanded. Yet we cannot be surprised if they now dare to attempt such things against the living, since they strive even to scatter the memory of brothers who have died. We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion because of his life and merits, and never did even a rumor of sinister suspicion touch him. We remember that he was once a man of such great learning that even my predecessors always counted him among the best teachers. All therefore formed a good common judgment of him, since everywhere he was both loved and honored by all.
>
> “Therefore, let us resist such men, whom we see growing in evil. It is impious for religious souls to suffer these things; and because they are our members, their affliction must also cause us to be afflicted. Nevertheless, the blessedness promised remains for all who are proved by enduring persecution for righteousness; what the Lord promises them in the future is declared by the following statement. This is not the concern of those alone who are acting, when the universal Church is shaken by any novelty. Let us understand that the very things displeasing to us displease you also. We shall be able to prove this only if, after the wicked have been silenced, complaint about this matter ceases in the future.”

Saint Prosper likewise says in his letter to Rufinus:

> “These stratagems by which the sons of darkness wished to transform themselves into the likeness of the sons of light—the judgments of the Eastern bishops, the authority of the Apostolic See, and the vigilance of the African councils detected them. Blessed Augustine too, unquestionably a principal portion of the Lord’s priests in this age, demolished them fully and beautifully in many discussions contained in his volumes. Among the many gifts of God with which the Spirit of truth filled him most abundantly, he also possessed this power of knowledge and wisdom arising from God’s love: not only did he strike down this heresy, still struggling in its mutilated remains, but he also defeated many earlier heresies with the invincible sword of his word.
>
> “Yet, amid so many palms of combat and so many crowns of triumph, for the illumination of the Church and the glory of Christ, by whom he himself was brilliantly illumined, some of our people—something that should greatly grieve us—slander him in secret murmurs, not unknown to us. Whenever they find ears susceptible and well disposed to them, they defame his writings in which the error of the Pelagians is attacked, saying that he entirely removes free choice and preaches fatal necessity under the name of grace. They even add that he wishes two masses of the human race and two natures to be believed, so that the impiety of the Pagans and Manichaeans may be attributed to so pious a man.
>
> “If these charges are true, why are they themselves so negligent—not to say impious—that they do not drive such a precipitous destruction from the Church, resist such insane preaching, or at least confront in writing the man from whom such a doctrine proceeds? They would have done the human race great honor if they had recalled Augustine from error. Unless perhaps these modest men and new censors mercifully and respectfully spare an old man of such great prior merit, and rest secure because no one anywhere accepts his books.
>
> “Yet let them know—or rather, they do know—that not only the Roman and African Church but throughout all the regions of the world all the children of the promise agree with him, both in the whole faith and in the confession of grace according to the teaching of this man. Moreover, even in those very places where complaint against him is being stirred up, by God’s favor there are many who are being imbued with the saving disputations of his writings for the reception of evangelical and apostolic teaching, and who are daily being extended among the members of Christ’s body, insofar as he himself multiplies them.”

Again the same Prosper, in the book he published against the book of Cassian, formerly an abbot, entitled *On the Protection of God*, speaks of those who criticized Saint Augustine’s books—namely, *On Rebuke and Grace*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, which he had published toward the end—in the following words, after reporting Coelestine’s praise of blessed Augustine:

> “Against the trumpet of this most illustrious praise, against the dignity of this most sacred testimony, does anyone dare to utter the murmur of a malicious interpretation and to cast a cloud of crooked ambiguity over a clear and most sincere statement? Is it so that, because the title of the books under consideration was not stated in the pope’s letter, it should therefore appear that they were not approved, and that this praise of Saint Augustine was bestowed for the merits of his earlier writings?”

And a little later:

> “For the Apostolic See approves, together with what it already knows, what does not differ from what it already knows; and what it joins to its judgment, it does not separate from its praise.” Therefore, those who reject these recently published books should accept the earlier ones and agree with what was first written in defense of Christian grace. But they do not do so. For they know that all those writings are contrary to the Pelagians, and that they can claim nothing for the resolution of what follows if they admit that the truth remains in the earlier works.
>
> “Therefore, resistance must be offered to the perversity of such men not so much by the effort of debate as by the privilege of authority, so that no member of a dogma long ago overthrown may be allowed to rise again. For it is known that the stratagems of this falsehood are such that, if it is permitted, under the pretext of correction, to preserve for itself some shoot of its root that finds support, it can restore itself in its entirety from a small part of itself. Where the whole is no more than a portion, it is not devotion to have surrendered nearly everything, but fraud to have restored even the smallest part.
>
> “To prevent this from being achieved by the plots of hypocrites, we trust that, by the Lord’s protection, what he accomplished through Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Coelestine, he will also accomplish through Xystus. May this be reserved as part of the glory of this shepherd in guarding the Lord’s flock: just as those men drove away open wolves, so may he drive away hidden ones. Let the speech of that most learned old man resound in his ears, by which he encouraged his fellow laborer, saying:
>
> “‘There are some who think that impieties justly condemned should still be defended more freely; and there are some who enter houses more secretly and do not cease to sow in private what they already fear to proclaim openly. There are also those who have remained entirely silent, constrained by great fear, but who still retain in their hearts what they no longer dare to utter with their mouths. Nevertheless, they can be recognized by their brothers from their earlier defense of that doctrine. Therefore, some must be restrained more severely, others must be investigated more vigilantly, and others must indeed be treated more gently but must not on that account be taught with less diligence, so that, even if they are not feared lest they be lost, they may not be neglected lest they perish.’”

It has been sufficiently demonstrated, I think, that the critics of Saint Augustine make empty accusations, attack what is right, defend what is wrong, and, taking up the weapons of the condemned to stir up internal war, rebel against divine and human decrees. Nevertheless, since they have not yet been separated from fraternal fellowship, their intention should be tolerated rather than their correction despaired of. Until the Lord, through the leaders of the Church and the lawful ministers of his judgments, sets right what has been disturbed through the pride of a few and the ignorance of some, our task, with God’s help, is to repay hatred with love through calm and modest patience, to avoid conflicts with foolish people, not to abandon the truth, not to contend with falsehood, and always to ask God that in all our thoughts, all our wills, all our words, and all our actions, he himself may hold the first place—he who declared himself to be the beginning. For from him, through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory forever. Amen.

Again, Prosper, writing to Camillus and Theodore, presbyters of the Genoese, says:

> “In the books of blessed memory, Bishop Augustine, whose title is *On the Predestination of the Saints*, certain things have moved Your Holiness, whether because they are unfamiliar or because they are less clear. You sent me extracts from them taken from the course of the discussion, so that you might learn with what understanding and by what judgment I receive them,”

and the rest.

Again, in the book entitled *Against the Ungrateful*, written against the Pelagians and other heretics whose names are specified there, he writes:

> “Against Augustine, it is said, a certain writer is creeping,
>
> whom consuming envy long ago scorched.
>
> Among the many things that the heresiarch handed down to his followers,
>
> he says that you recognize the nature that was made good
>
> as being created in no one at all together with any vices,
>
> and that the guilt of the first parent harmed no one,
>
> and that, since people are now also born such as
>
> the father of our race was before his transgression,
>
> a human being can pass through life without sin,
>
> if he wishes, just as the first man was able
>
> by his freedom to commit no offense.
>
> Surely you admit that these teachings were condemned
>
> by councils and by the authority of the world.
>
> The same author also connects the claim
>
> that the law once sent the saints into the kingdom of heaven
>
> in the same way that grace now sends them.
>
> You know that this too was destroyed by holy judgment.
>
> Another charge was brought forward: that the same teacher had said
>
> that Christ’s grace is bestowed according to human merits,
>
> in proportion as each person makes himself suitable
>
> for God’s gifts.
>
> But seeing that this was exceedingly contrary
>
> and exceedingly opposed to the faith,
>
> he said that he did not believe this,
>
> and that those whose mind held such a view
>
> deserved condemnation.”

In the preface to his *Objections and Responses against the Gauls Who Think Wrongly*, he likewise demonstrates the same point, saying:

> “The teaching which Bishop Augustine, of blessed memory, asserted apostolically against the Pelagians, the enemies of Christ’s grace and the destroyers of free choice, over many years and committed to writing, some people have seemed to criticize it either through not understanding it or through unwillingness to understand it. They offered this as a kind of abridgment of knowledge to those who were led by their judgment, publishing in brief lists of chapters the things they boasted of having found condemnable in the books of the aforementioned man. By such a contrivance they both secured the detestation of the man whom they attacked and, by frightening the reader, diverted his attention from the things they had defamed.
>
> “Therefore, lest anyone rashly accept this persuasion and suppose that the Catholic teacher’s writings contain the meaning which those who falsely slander him display, I answer each of the chapters they prefixed with the title of condemnation by a brief and unambiguous profession, departing in no respect from the path of those definitions contained in the holy man’s discussions. Thus even an observer of modest diligence may readily perceive with what unjust reproaches the memory of the Catholic preacher is assailed, and into what sin those fall who, moved by another’s instigation, are more ready to blame a writer of the highest renown than to know him.”

[Col. 0078C] These matters, then, which were brought forward by Saint Coelestine and blessed Prosper in the refutation and suppression of this new heresy through the words of blessed Augustine, took place after the death of that most learned and Catholic man, in the second year after his death. As Prosper demonstrates in his *Chronicle*, a synod of more than two hundred priests was convened at Ephesus, and Nestorius was condemned together with the heresy that took its name from him and with many Pelagians who supported a doctrine related to their own error.

Saint Liberatus also, archdeacon of the sixth ecclesiastical region of Carthage, says at the relevant point in his *Brief Account of the Affair of the Nestorians and Eutychians* (chapter 4):

> “Cyril, through his deacon Posidonius, reported to Pope Coelestine concerning Nestorius and informed him by letter what was being done at Constantinople.”

And a little later (chapter 5):

> “The emperor wrote to blessed Augustine, Bishop of Hippo Regius, through Ebagnius the *Magisterianus*, asking him to attend the council in person. When Ebagnius came to Carthage, he heard from Capreolus, the bishop of that city, that blessed Augustine had departed from this world to the Lord. After receiving from him a letter to the emperor speaking of blessed Augustine’s death, he returned to Constantinople, from which he had come.
>
> “But because of the attacks of the Vandals, who were besieging the African regions, Archbishop Capreolus was unable to convene a universal council; therefore he sent his deacon Vesula to the council at Ephesus as his legate. Pope Coelestine of Rome wrote a letter of rebuke to Nestorius,”

and what follows.

The aforementioned letter of Capreolus, which is possessed by us and by many others, also testifies that these things occurred as described, just as the account itself confirms for those who read it.

Against this heresy Augustine, of revered memory, was unable, because death intervened, to engage in a special labor of opposition, as he had been accustomed to do against other heresies. Perhaps this was also because it certainly did not come to his knowledge. If he had clearly recognized it, one may believe, from the zeal of his ardor for the purity of the faith, that he would not have failed to undertake a written refutation of it—just as he did against this heresy, which had arisen among the Gauls and became known to him through Prosper and Hilary, and whose earlier agitation in the African regions he did not fail to recognize. He did not give it the name it later acquired, because it was not completely silenced even after being suppressed in his lifetime.

But after his death, by the authority of the Apostolic See, through blessed Coelestine, at the urging of Saint Prosper and by delegation from that holy universal Church, it was refuted, convicted, and silenced by synodal judgment, using the words of the aforementioned venerable Augustine, as blessed Coelestine demonstrates in the letter mentioned above (Letter 8), saying:

> “To our most beloved brothers Venerius, Marinus, Leontius, Ausonius, Arcadius, Filtanius, and the other bishops of Gaul: Coelestine.”

And at the relevant point:

> “Our sons Prosper and Hilary, whose concern for our God is worthy of praise, have reported to us that, I know not by what permission, certain priests there are being allowed to do so much—men who are devoted to the dissension of the churches—that, bringing undisciplined questions forward, they are said stubbornly to preach things contrary to the truth. But we more justly attribute this to your Belovedness, since they have such opportunity to debate above you.”

And again:

> “Take this treatise, dearest brothers, as undertaken for the peace of the Catholic people. Let them know—if indeed they are considered to possess the dignity of the priesthood—that they are subject to you; let all who teach wrongly know that it is more appropriate for them to learn than to teach. For what are you doing in the churches if they hold the highest authority to preach?”

At his command the aforementioned bishops of Gaul held a synod. Those who thought wrongly in this manner they either received back in an orderly fashion, after they had come to their senses through ecclesiastical compassion, or, if they persisted in their madness and perverse opinions, they separated them from the fellowship of the faithful by episcopal, Catholic, and Apostolic authority. This is openly demonstrated by the friendly letter of Faustus to the priest Lucidus and by the little book of that same priest Lucidus, presented to the bishops at the synod. Since both documents—the letter and the book of correction—provide clear evidence of the matter, and since we are not seeking to establish the truth by means of a falsehood, we have judged it necessary to insert them here.

## Faustus’s Letter to the Priest Lucidus
“Faustus to Lucidus the presbyter, a most devoted lord and brother whom I specially honor and welcome with affection.”

It is a great charity, through God’s grace and assistance, to desire rather to cure the error of a brother who is insufficiently cautious than, as the highest prelates are considering, to suspend him from unity. How can I discuss this understanding with you in writing, as you wish, in unanimity with you, when, though present with you, I was never able to draw you toward the way of truth through much gentle and humble conversation? [Col. 0080A]

Speaking, then, about God’s grace and human obedience, we must establish this in every way: that, neither inclined toward the left nor excessively pressing toward the right, we should walk rather along the royal road. But I was astonished that your Reverence said that no one under a religious profession had ever written or preached anything against the Catholic faith, when very many men, though they boasted in the Christian name, believed that their manifold and profane errors should also be inserted into written records.

I shall therefore say briefly, insofar as I can speak with one who is absent, what you ought to believe together with the Catholic Church. Namely, that, while always joining the work of the baptized servant to the grace of the Lord, you should detest, together with the Pelagian doctrine, the person who asserts predestination while excluding human labor.

Anathema, therefore, to the one who, among the other impieties of Pelagius, rashly and condemnably contends that a human being is born without sin and can be saved through labor alone, and to the one who believes that a human being can be freed without the grace of God.

Likewise, anathema to the one who asserts that a person solemnly baptized with a faithful confession, professing the Catholic faith, and afterward having fallen through the various delights and temptations of this world, perished in Adam and in original sin.

Likewise, anathema to the one who says that through God’s foreknowledge a human being is driven down into death.

Likewise, anathema to the one who says that the person who perished did not receive the possibility of being saved.

Likewise, anathema to the one who says that a vessel made for dishonor cannot rise to become a vessel made for honor.

Likewise, anathema to the one who says that Christ did not die for all, nor desire all human beings to be saved. [Col. 0080C]

When, however, you come to us in Christ’s name, or when you have been summoned by holy priests, then, if the Lord commands, we shall bring forward in their proper places the relevant testimonies, by which what is Catholic may be made evident and what is contrary to Catholic teaching destroyed.

For our part, through Christ’s illumination, we truthfully and confidently assert both that the person who perished through fault could have been saved through grace, had he not denied obedience to the labor of grace itself, and that the person who, through grace and obedient service, reached the goal of good perfection could have fallen through negligence and perished through fault.

We, therefore, walking midway under Christ’s guidance, assert, after grace—without which we are nothing—the labor of dutiful service; but we entirely exclude the arrogance and presumption of labor, so that, striving with all our strength lest grace be made void in us, whatever we have received from the hand of the Lord we may declare to be a gift, not a payment. We know that the fruit of that labor is a matter of duty, not of merit, saying with the Evangelist: ‘We are worthless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’ (Luke 17:10).

Let your unanimity reply in a renewed exchange whether you accept or reject these matters, which have been briefly recalled because of the letter’s brevity. Moreover, whoever does not follow this measure of truth, with grace preceding and human effort rising to meet it, will be worthy of being barred from the sacred thresholds.

Nevertheless, I retain your goodness as inseparably joined to me in the full embrace of sincere kindness, and I desire that you remain within the womb of Mother Church after rejecting this error. If it is quickly rejected, it will appear to have arisen from ignorance; but if it is defended stubbornly, it will be judged blasphemy.

For we turn serious blame upon the author if we say that he did not wish to give the possibility of attaining salvation to the one who perished, since we can by no means deny that he will condemn the transgressor of the commandment in the examination of his judgment. For one who is not liable concerning what he received—I do not know how he could be liable concerning what he lost. Thus, sinning against God, whose grace we asserted too incautiously at the outset, we shall in the end appear to attack his justice.

I retain a copy of this letter with me, to be produced at the assembly of the holy prelates, if that should be necessary. If your fraternity thinks it should be accepted, either return it immediately signed in your own hand, or reply in a subsequent letter that you have altogether rejected it. But if you refuse to return it signed, as I have said, by that very silence you will openly confirm that you still persist in error; consequently, you will already compel me to expose your person in public assemblies.

Therefore write back in accordance with these matters I have directed to you, so that, without circumlocution, you may either acknowledge or reject them.

Written in another hand: ‘I, Faustus, have reread and signed the copy of my letter.’”

## Likewise, the copy of the petition of Lucidus the presbyter

“To the most blessed lords and most reverend fathers in Christ: Eufronius, Viventius, Verianus, Paulus, Eutropius, Marcellus, Claudius, Leontius, Mamertus, Auxanius, Megetius, Leontius, Crocus, Ursicinus, Fonteius, Patientius, Faustus, Graecus, Claudius, Basilius, Praetextatus, Pragmatius, Viventius, Bishop John, Theoplastus, Julianus, Opilio, Leocadius, Amicalis, and Licinius the presbyters—Lucidus.

Your correction is public salvation, and your judgment is medicine. Therefore I regard it as the supreme remedy that, by accusing my former errors, I may excuse myself and cleanse myself through a life-giving profession of faith.

Accordingly, in agreement with the council’s recent statutes concerning preaching, I condemn with you the opinion that says human obedience and labor must not be joined to divine grace; the opinion that says that, after the first human being’s fall, free choice of the will was altogether extinguished; the opinion that says that Christ the Lord and our Savior did not undergo death for the salvation of all; the opinion that says that God’s foreknowledge violently compels a human being to death, or that those who perish perish by God’s will; the opinion that says that anyone who sins after legitimately receiving baptism dies in Adam; the opinion that says that some are appointed to death and others predestined to life; the opinion that says that from Adam until Christ no one from the nations was saved through God’s first grace—that is, through the law of nature—in anticipation of Christ’s coming, on the grounds that they had lost free choice entirely in their first parent; the opinion that says that the patriarchs and prophets, or any of the greatest saints, even before the time of redemption, lived in the habitation of paradise; and the opinion that says that there are no fires or hells. [Col. 0082A]

I condemn all these as impious and filled with sacrilege.

I assert God’s grace in such a way that I always join human striving and effort to grace; I declare that human freedom of the will has not been extinguished, but weakened and impaired; and I affirm that the person who is saved may be endangered and that the person who perished could have been saved.

I also affirm that Christ, our God and Savior, insofar as concerns the riches of his goodness, offered the price of death for all human beings, and that he does not wish anyone to perish, being the Savior of all human beings, especially of believers, and rich toward all who call upon him.

Since, however, in such important matters one must satisfy the conscience, I remember that I previously said that Christ came only for those whom he foreknew would believe, following the Lord’s statements in which he says: ‘The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many’ (Matthew 20:28). And this: ‘This is the cup of my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins’ (Matthew 26:28). Or the Apostle’s statement: ‘Just as it has been appointed once for human beings to die, so Christ also was offered once to exhaust the sins of many’ (Hebrews 9:27).

But now, on the authority of sacred testimonies, which are abundantly found throughout the expanses of divine Scripture, and in accordance with the reasoning disclosed by the teaching of the elders, I willingly confess that Christ also came for the lost, who perished against his will. For it is not right to confine the immense riches of goodness and divine benefits only to those who appear to have been saved.

For if we say that Christ brought remedies only to those who have been redeemed, we shall seem to absolve the unredeemed, whom it is established are punished because they despised redemption. [Col. 0082C]

I also affirm that, according to the order and succession of the ages, some were saved under the law of grace, others under the law of Moses, and others under the law of nature, which God wrote in the hearts of all, in hope of Christ’s coming; yet no one from the beginning of the world was released from the bond of original sin except through the intercession of the sacred blood.

I also profess that eternal fires and infernal flames have been prepared for capital offenses, because divine judgment justly follows human sins when people persevere in them to the end; those who have not believed these things with their whole heart justly incur that judgment.

Pray for me, holy and apostolic lords and fathers.

I, Lucidus the presbyter, have signed this letter with my own hand, and I affirm what is asserted in it, while I condemn what has been condemned.”

We have thought it worthwhile to insert these documents here so that it may become clear that certain things said by these modern Predestinarians had also been said earlier by the ancient heretics. These men, who would arise and come much later, were overcome and condemned in advance by Catholic and apostolic authority, as Prosper says at the relevant point in the book published against the book of the abbot Cassian:

“Coelestine, pontiff of venerable memory, to whom the Lord granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church, knowing that the condemned are owed not an examination at trial but only the remedy of a sentence, ordered Celestius, who was seeking a hearing as though his case had not been investigated, to be expelled from the whole territory of Italy. [Col. 0083A]

He considered the statutes of his predecessors and the decrees of synods so inviolably binding that he would by no means permit the matter of one who had once deserved to be cut off to be reopened.

Nor did he free Britain from this same disease with less care. When he discovered certain enemies of grace, occupying only their own place of origin, even beyond that remote and secluded ocean, he excluded them; and, having appointed a bishop for the Scots, while striving to preserve the Roman island as Catholic, he also made it Christian though barbarous.

Through this man the Eastern Churches were also cleansed of a twofold plague. When Cyril, bishop of Alexandria and most glorious defender of the Catholic faith, was waging war against Nestorian impiety, he assisted him with the apostolic sword; by that same sword the Pelagians, while joining themselves to related errors, were again overthrown.

Through this man, within Gaul itself, freedom of malicious speech was taken away from those very men who criticize the writings of Augustine of holy memory. When he had received the action of those who consulted him and had praised with devotion the books displeasing to the erring, he made clear through holy speech what ought to be thought about their authority, expressly declaring how much he disliked the novelty of this presumption, by which certain men dared insolently to rise against ancient teachers and, through undisciplined slander, obstruct the preaching of truth:

‘Augustine,’ he said, ‘a man of holy remembrance, we have always held in our communion, on account of his life and his merits,’”

and what follows, as we have set out above from the letter of that same pope.

That these matters, confused in the regions of Gaul, were nevertheless set in order through a commission from the Apostolic See, just as Coelestine also showed in the aforementioned letter, the same Prosper demonstrates in the preface to the objections of Vincentius, saying:

“Certain people, forgetful of Christian and fraternal charity, strive by every means to injure our reputation so greatly that, in their desire to harm us, they do not see that they are overthrowing their own. For they weave together, and gather into whatever statements they can, the monstrous falsehoods of certain utterly senseless blasphemies, and publicly and privately circulate them for many people to see and absorb, asserting that our view contains things such as are found in a diabolical little catalogue.

We could easily and sufficiently prove that these things are falsely spread against us to arouse hatred by subscribing a single anathema, were it not that the malice of those who think themselves harmed if people think well of us would regard the very brevity of our subscription with suspicion.

Therefore, lest an occasion for this complaint be found, we have judged it necessary and appropriate—whether to calm the minds of our slanderers or to instruct those whose ears have heard anything of the kind—to explain fully and clearly, insofar as the Lord enables us, what judgment we hold concerning these perverse definitions.

Accordingly, after setting out the sixteen chapters one by one, we shall place beneath each one the words expressing our own understanding and the faith which, by the authority of the Apostolic See, we defend against the Pelagians, so that those who deign to devote even a little time to reading these matters may clearly recognize that no trace of impious or profane opinions has adhered to our hearts, and may judge that the blasphemies which they see condemned by our profession ought to be punished in their authors.”

Thus these matters were stirred up, suppressed, and settled in those times.

## CHAPTER II  
### Through whom and in what manner this same heresy, like a false shoot from the trunk of bitterness, has sprouted again in the present time

In the present period, a certain Gothescalcus, a monk in the monastery of the metropolitan Church of Rheims called Orbais—monkish in habit but savage in mind, unable to tolerate quiet, and conspicuous among his own people for harmful restlessness—selected for himself four chapters from all the perversely held opinions he had learned at that time. These contained within themselves the foul and muddy dregs of almost all those perversions, so that he might corrupt the minds of the simple and devout, usurp for himself the name of teacher, draw disciples after him, and improperly preside over religious life and Catholic doctrine—since he could not do so legitimately—over those who, with itching ears, strive to heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires.

He made as many accomplices as he could, desiring only that they become known—men who, since they could not be known for their rectitude, would at least become known for their perversity.

After leaving the monastery irregularly and traveling through many regions, he attended a synod held in the city of Mainz and presented a written statement of his error to Archbishop Rabanus. He was condemned and sent back to the metropolitan see of Rheims with the synodal letters. We have reasonably thought it appropriate to insert a copy of those letters here. They read as follows:

“To our most reverend brother and fellow priest, Hincmar, archbishop, Rabanus, servant of Christ and of his servants, sends greetings in the Lord.

Let your affection know that a certain wandering monk named Gothescalc, who claims that he was ordained a priest in your diocese, has come to us at Mainz from Italy, introducing new superstitions and a harmful doctrine concerning God’s predestination and leading peoples into error. He says that God’s predestination applies to evil as well as to good, and that there are in this world certain people who, because of God’s predestination—which compels them to go to death—cannot correct themselves from error and sin, as though God had made them incorrigible from the beginning and destined to go to destruction, liable to punishment.

After hearing this opinion from him recently at the synod held at Mainz and finding him incorrigible, with the consent and command of our most pious king Louis, we have decreed that he should be sent to you, condemned together with his harmful doctrine. You are to confine him within your diocese, from which he first departed disorderly; you must not allow him to teach error any longer or to lead the Christian people astray, since, as I have heard, he already has many who have been deceived and who are less devoted to their salvation. They say: ‘What benefit will it be for me to labor in the service of God? For if I am predestined to death, I shall never escape it; but if I do evil and am predestined to life, I shall go to eternal rest without any doubt.’

We have written these matters briefly to you, informing you what sort of doctrine we found in him. You will also be able to hear more fully from his own mouth what he thinks and to decide justly what ought to be done about it.

May almighty God deign to preserve your holiness in good health and praying for us forever.”

After this, he was again heard by the bishops at the synodal assembly in the palace of Quierzy, together with many other ecclesiastical and religious men who attended that synod: namely, Wenilo, archbishop of Sens; Hincmar, bishop of Rheims; Folcuinus, bishop of Thérouanne; Theuderic, bishop of Cambrai; Rothadus, bishop of Soissons; Ragenarius, bishop of Amiens; Immo, bishop of Noyon; Erpoinus, bishop of Senlis; Lupus, bishop of Châlons; Yrminfridus, bishop of Beauvais; Pardulus, bishop of Laon; Teutboldus, bishop of the province of Lyon and of the city of Langres; Gernobrius, bishop of the province of Tours; Rigbaldus, chorepiscopus of Rheims; Wita, chorepiscopus of Cambrai; and others who, by God’s grace, are now ordained bishops but at that time had attended the aforesaid synod with their bishops according to ecclesiastical custom.

Wenilo was then with his father Ragenarius and is now archbishop of Rouen; Aeneas was a notary of the sacred palace and is now bishop of Paris; Isaac was Pardulus’s deacon and is now bishop of the city of Langres.

The venerable abbots also attended that synod: Ratbertus of Corbie, Bavo of Orbais, and Halduinus of the monastery of Hautvillers, together with other lordly priests and deacons. Wlfadus, treasurer of the metropolitan see of Rheims, and Rodoaldus, archdeacon, were also present with the other succeeding orders of the clergy.

In their presence, the same Gothescalcus was found to be heretical and incorrigible, just as he had been at Mainz. He was stripped of the priestly honor which he had usurped rather than received through Rigbaldus, chorepiscopus of Rheims, when he was a monk of the diocese of Soissons, without the knowledge of his own bishop. Because of his irrevocable contumacy, in accordance with the laws, the canons of Agde, and the rule of Saint Benedict, he was beaten with rods as a wicked man, as the bishops of the German provinces had decreed, and was confined in a prison lest he harm others, since he did not wish to benefit himself. [Col. 0085D]

But, lest he alone perish, those who agreed with him began to arise from every quarter and to spread in word and writing the perverse doctrine derived from him. From this adulterous seed these chapters sprang, to which you command us to respond.

Therefore it must first be understood that, concerning the aforementioned four chapters which Gothescalc initially adopted for himself, and concerning a fifth which he later added presumptuously, certain heretics of ancient times said one thing, while Gothescalc, the first leader of the new Predestinarians and head of the school of perversity, says something else.

Yet, as it is written, ‘Like straw gathered together is the assembly of sinners, and their end is a flame of fire’ (Sirach 21:10), that old gathering and this new combination are equal in error, although they make different professions.

For this reason we have thought it necessary to set down chapter by chapter what each group said and what these men say—men who contradict the teaching of the Catholics and of the Apostolic See, and who tear apart chapters excerpted by us from orthodox authors’ words. By setting out the statements of the teachers of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, and showing how those teachers understood them, we shall, with the Lord inspiring and cooperating, endeavor to demonstrate whether the definitions of those orthodox teachers support our fellowship or their division, when we begin to respond to the pestilential sect according to Catholic understanding and to give an account of the chapters excerpted by us.”

## CHAPTER III  
### Concerning Fulgentius, from whose books the Predestinarians produce examples to support their opinion

We therefore warn every reader not to cling to the opinions of the wicked when he finds testimonies from the books of Fulgentius placed in their writings, namely, that the reprobate are predestined not to evil but to destruction—a point which he repeats frequently in the book addressed to Monimus, supposedly in defense of blessed Augustine.

It is therefore unnecessary for Catholics to accept from him this defense of blessed Augustine, because blessed Augustine himself sufficiently and more than sufficiently defended himself in this matter and, by retracting, vindicated his position.

The blessed Prosper, legate of the Roman Church and its faithful interpreter, whose books Saint Gelasius mentions among those to be received into the catalogue of orthodox authors, says among other things:

‘Likewise, the little works of blessed Prosper, a most religious man, satisfy us most fully on his behalf.’

And since we must neither say nor believe that God predestined the reprobate to destruction, but that he predestined punishment for the reprobate, Prosper teaches us this most clearly to believe and teach.

Nevertheless, we do not reject the venerable Fulgentius in every respect because of this statement; nor, on this point—namely, that the reprobate ought to be believed or said to have been predestined by God to destruction—do we follow him as we do Augustine, and Augustine only in what he said on this matter in the books mentioned above: *On Rebuke and Grace*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, *On the Good of Perseverance*, *The Hypomnesticon of Six Questions against the Pelagians and Coelestians*, and the book *On the Predestination of Grace*, which he wrote against his opponents on this matter. In this we follow blessed Prosper—indeed, the holy Mother and Apostolic See.

But concerning the venerable Fulgentius we speak as Hilary of Arles speaks in his letter to Saint Augustine on this very matter, concerning those who criticized his works:

“‘But plainly,’ he says, ‘I must not conceal the fact that they say they admire your holiness in all your deeds and words, except for this one matter.’”

We know that Saint Cyprian held a different opinion concerning the baptism of heretics from that held by Saint Stephen, pontiff of the Roman Church, and from that now held by the holy Church; nevertheless, Cyprian is counted among Catholic teachers.

Saint Augustine shows in the sixth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter ten, that he understood certain matters differently from Saint Hilary, although he wishes the same position to be held. Saint Leo, in confirming the Council of Chalcedon, counts the testimonies of that same blessed Hilary among the examples of Catholic teachers, indeed among the first. Blessed Gelasius likewise counts him, along with Saint Augustine, Prosper, Cyprian, Leo, and Jerome, among the most widely received authors in the catalogue of ecclesiastical and illustrious writers.

It is also said of him, as is well known, by a very famous authority: ‘Hilary, bishop of the Romans, the morning star, the lamp of the Churches, and the precious torch, speaks of everything with beautiful and golden lips.’

Saint Augustine understood certain matters differently from blessed Jerome; likewise, Saint Jerome understood certain matters differently from blessed Augustine, and both continue among the Catholic teachers.

Blessed Gregory, whose mind was filled above all with the flowers of the teaching of those who preceded him, like a honeycomb overflowing with abundant sweetness, understood certain matters differently from Saint Jerome, and explained certain matters differently from the way Saint Augustine had explained or corrected them. Yet the Church embraces both as orthodox and venerates both as teachers.

For, as blessed Augustine says in the second book of *On Baptism*, chapter 5:

‘Sometimes, therefore, less is revealed to more learned men, so that their patient and humble charity, in which there is greater fruit, may be proved; or so that it may be shown how they preserve unity while holding different opinions in obscure matters, or how they receive the truth when they learn that what they thought has been clarified against their former understanding.’

Knowing that divine Scripture is a precious pearl which can be pierced from every side, they explain many things in various styles, though not with different faith, so that they may become known to many—not only beneficially but also delightfully.

Furthermore, in the catalogue of the Apostolic See, where Saint Gelasius listed and designated Catholic teachers, we do not find the same venerable Fulgentius recognized. Yet neither, because we find him designated in the list of those to be rejected, do we judge him altogether unacceptable.

For during the reign of Anastasius, in whose time blessed Gelasius published the list of orthodox and illustrious men, as is made clear by his letters addressed to that emperor, Trasamundus, king of the Vandals, held power in Africa, as we find in other Chronicles and also in the *Chronicle* of the venerable presbyter Bede.

Fulgentius flourished in Africa during Trasamundus’s reign. He wrote a reply against certain propositions of Trasamundus and composed three books against his perfidy: the first, *On the Mystery of the Mediator*; the second, *On the Immensity of the Divinity of the Son of God*; and the third, *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Passion*.

Yet Saint Gelasius did not number him among ecclesiastical writers, as he did blessed Prosper, who survived into the time of Pope Gelasius.

From Adam up to the time of the Emperor Justin, and the death of Pope John, the fourth after blessed Gelasius, and the end of the consulship of Symmachus and Boethius—at which time Hilderic, the successor of Trasamundus, ruled the Vandals, and, after the slaughter of the saints and countless disasters, ended an unworthy life by a worthy death—the same blessed Prosper composed a *Chronicle* with remarkable truthfulness.

In it he identified men of different regions distinguished in holiness and wisdom, as well as heretics who had arisen, assigning to each a reputation appropriate to him; yet he did not name the same venerable Fulgentius.

The venerable presbyter Bede, too, although he described many other illustrious men in his *Chronicle*, did not mention the aforesaid Fulgentius at all.

Nor is he found listed among the orthodox teachers summoned to confirm the Catholic faith by the fifth synod, which was assembled at Constantinople in the time of Pope Vigilius, the eleventh after Gelasius, under Justinian, against Theodore and other heretics.

Indeed, at the sixth universal synod, held at Constantinople in the time of Agatho, the thirty-first pope after blessed Gelasius, under the emperor Constantine, no mention of his books is found among the testimonies of Catholic teachers used to confirm the Catholic faith—especially since many who flourished in the Church after Fulgentius are found summoned as witnesses for that purpose.

Therefore, if he spoke about God’s predestination differently from the way Saint Augustine corrected his responses to the objections raised against him in the books mentioned above, and differently also from the way blessed Prosper defined it by delegation of the Apostolic See and by order of Saint Coelestine, and differently from the way the holy Apostolic See itself received and wished those statements to be made, let him take responsibility for it.

We, too, cannot fail to know what he said about the matter, since it is evident to all who read.

## CHAPTER IV  
### Concerning the Apostolic See, whose teaching we must follow and whose authority we must rely upon

We follow what the holy Roman Church, Catholic and Apostolic, teaches us—the Church that brought us forth in the faith, nourished us with Catholic milk, fed us at breasts full of heaven until we reached solid food, brought us to the mature human being through orthodox discipline, trained us by its own testing to instruct others, and, with the Lord supporting and assisting, established us in the teaching chair by elevating us.

Thus Saint Innocent writes to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, saying (letter 29, at the beginning):

“Who, indeed, is unaware, or who fails to perceive, that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, the prince of the apostles, and has been preserved to the present day, ought to be observed by all, and that nothing should be added or introduced which either lacks authority or appears to derive its example from elsewhere?

This is especially so since it is evident that throughout Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one established Churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Let them read and see whether any other apostle is found or reported to have taught in these provinces.

If they do not read this, because they find it nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves, since there is no doubt that they received their beginning from it. Otherwise, while striving after foreign assertions, they may appear to lose the source of their institutions.”

## CHAPTER V  
### Concerning the practice of Gothescalcus and his accomplices, and their books, from which certain excerpts are presented here

We also warn that it is the practice of Gothescalcus and his accomplices to mutilate excerpts from Catholic testimonies while putting forward the names of teachers and books, and to try to bend them to their own opinions, just as they bend the statements of Scripture, so that, if their hearers are insufficiently cautious, they may succeed in winning their minds over to themselves.

Therefore, anyone rereading their writings should remember what is said:

“Flee from here, boys: a cold snake lurks in the grass.”

And:

“Gather the grape-cluster; beware the thorn.”

Accordingly, following the Apostle’s instruction to test everything and retain what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21), readers should compare what these men say and what they try to confirm by examples from authors. They should examine in the authors’ books, from which the testimonies are said to have been taken, whether the passages they produce, mutilated or compiled to support their opinion, have been excerpted with unadulterated truth.

Thus, by believing incautiously what has been presented, they will not be plunged into the abyss of unbelief along paths that appear good but whose end leads to destruction. Instead, let them do as they have been commanded: “Stand upon the roads, ask which is the good way, and walk in it” (Jeremiah 6:16).

With these matters prefaced, let us set out what Gothescalcus, standard-bearer, guide, and modern reviver of this perverse doctrine, writes about the first chapter—the matter presently under discussion—in the book of his poisonous composition presented to Archbishop Rabanus. He says:

“At last,” he says, “I read your book, venerable pontiff, in which I found it stated that the impious, or reprobate, have not been divinely predestined to damnation.”

And after a little:

“He foreknew,” I said, “that they would have the worst origin and a worse end; but he predestined them to undergo perpetual torment and everlasting destruction.”

And again, after a little:

“For truly, just as he predestined all the elect to life through the gratuitous benefit of his grace alone, as the pages of the Old and New Testaments provide a most evident indication to those who consider them carefully and soberly, so he most certainly predestined all the reprobate to the punishment of eternal death, through the utterly just judgment of his unchangeable justice.”

In his written profession addressed to the same Bishop Rabanus he likewise says:

“I, Gothescalcus, believe and confess, profess and testify, and affirm and approve before God and his saints, that there is a twofold predestination: of the elect to rest and of the reprobate to death. For just as the unchangeable God, before the foundation of the world, unchangeably predestined all his elect to eternal life through his gratuitous grace, so, in precisely the same way, that same unchangeable God, through his just judgment, unchangeably predestined all the reprobate, who will be condemned on the day of judgment because of their evil merits, to a death that is deservedly everlasting.”

And Lord Prudentius, in the letter which your Reverence delivered to us through the venerable Aeneas, bishop of Paris, and which Prudentius himself sent to his archbishop Wenilo and the other fellow bishops concerning Aeneas’s ordination—so that, if the man to be ordained held a contrary opinion, Prudentius himself should in no way consent to his ordination—says:

“Secondly, that he should believe and confess that, by the highest and hidden counsel of almighty God, some were predestined to life through God’s gratuitous mercy before all ages, while others were predestined to punishment through inscrutable justice: namely, that God predestined in those who are saved and in those who are condemned what he foreknew he would do in judging, as the prophet says: ‘He made the things that are to come.’”

Ratramnus, likewise a monk of the monastery of Corbie, presented two little books which you gave us to examine. They were composed with the intention of showing that, just as the elect are predestined by God to life, so the reprobate are predestined by God to death.

Passing over other authors whose names we do not think it necessary to recite here, since they all converge upon one opinion, and since in the three books mentioned above we have already responded as far as we could from the authority of Catholic writers, let us come to the chapters which, at your command, we have undertaken to circumcise with stone knives, as is read in the ancient law (Joshua 5:4). We shall endeavor to cut away their harmful and superfluous sharpness with the edge of Catholic teaching.

## CHAPTER VI  
### The beginning of the chapters under discussion, and the source from which their compiler attempted to assemble them
For, after prefacing their argument with the fables of their commendations, they say in the second chapter:

> “We believe and faithfully hold it right to hold that God eternally foreknows and foreknew both the good things [27] that the good would do and the evil things that the wicked would commit, since we have the voice of Scripture, which says: ‘O eternal God, knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to be’ (Dan. 13:4). We faithfully hold, and are pleased to hold, [Col. 0090D] that he altogether foreknew, by his grace, that the good would be good and that, by that same grace, they would receive eternal rewards; and that he foreknew that the wicked would become wicked through their own wickedness and would be condemned by his justice to eternal punishment. Thus, according to the Psalmist, ‘For power belongs to God, and to the Lord is mercy’ (Ps. 61:12), he will render to each according to his works (Rom. 2:6). And as apostolic teaching has it: ‘To those who, by perseverance in good works, seek glory and honor and incorruption, eternal life; but to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth, yet believe in iniquity, wrath and indignation. Tribulation and distress upon every human soul that works evil’ (ibid., 8–9).

“In the same sense [Col. 0091A] he says elsewhere:

> ‘At the revelation of our Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our God. They will suffer eternal destruction when he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be marveled at in all who have believed’ (2 Thess. 1:7–10).

“God’s foreknowledge certainly did not impose necessity on any wicked person, so that he could not be otherwise; rather, whatever that person was going to be by his own will, God, who knows all things before they come to be, foreknew by his omnipotence and unchangeable majesty. We believe that no one is condemned as a result of God’s prejudgment, but on account of the merit of his own iniquity. Nor do the wicked perish because they could not be good, but because they did not wish to be good, and by their own fault they remained in the mass of condemnation, whether through original or even actual merit.” [Col. 0091B]

We found this chapter, for the most part, excerpted—as we established by comparison—from the writing of Florus, a minister of the Church of Lyons, which we once received at Bonoil from Heribold, of venerable memory, bishop of Auxerre. For that reason, however one considers it, it is not found to be wholly alien to reason. For it does not speak against the Catholic faith concerning God’s foreknowledge. But the foolish excerptor omitted what he had found in the same passage: an example concerning the elect, who are brought to eternal life by the gift of grace. He wished to add certain things from his own wisdom, and therefore took care to heap together examples of what is to be rendered to the wicked by the retribution of justice.

For, while saying that God altogether foreknew, by his grace, that the good would be good and that, by that same grace, they would receive eternal rewards [Col. 0091C], he passed over corresponding merits and omitted examples of the gift of grace. Then, following upon this, he added that God foreknew the wicked as destined through their own wickedness to become wicked and, by his justice, to be condemned to eternal punishment. Thus he set in disordered sequence the examples which he had found collected through another’s labor.

Then, after he had disorderly placed what he had received in an orderly form from another’s mouth—‘Nor do the wicked perish because they could not be good, but because they did not wish to be good, and by their own fault they remained in the mass of condemnation, whether through original or even actual merit’—he added without any intervening material in the third chapter:

> “It has also pleased us, and faithfully continues to please us, concerning God’s predestination [28], in accordance with apostolic authority, which says: ‘Does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor [Col. 0091D] and another for dishonor?’ (Rom. 9:21). Immediately afterward he adds: ‘But if God, wishing to show wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted or prepared for destruction, so that he might show the riches of his grace in the vessels of mercy which he prepared for glory’ (ibid., 22), we confidently confess the predestination of the elect to life and the predestination of the wicked to death.”

As was said long before us, he gives voice without understanding. A little earlier he had said that the wicked remain in the mass of condemnation by their own fault, whether through original merit or also through actual merit; and immediately afterward he added that it had pleased him, continued faithfully to please him, and that he confidently confessed the predestination of the elect to life and the predestination [Col. 0092A] of the wicked to death. We cannot see how both propositions can hold together: namely, that they remain abandoned in the mass of condemnation and yet that those same persons are predestined by God, through his predestination, to death.

If he had set forth the matter with the same consistent meaning with which Florus expressed it in his discourse—the source from which this man compiled it—everyone would understand it well, because it would stand correctly. For, as we have heard and as is evident, that learned man says almost at the beginning of his writing:

> “God therefore undoubtedly foreknew both the good things that the good would do and the evil things that the wicked would commit. But in the case of the good, he himself acted by his grace so that they would be good; in the case of the wicked, he himself did not make them wicked—far be that thought—but merely foreknew that they would become such through their own fault. For God’s foreknowledge did not impose necessity [Col. 0092B] upon them, so that they could not be otherwise; rather, God foresaw, in his omnipotent majesty, only what they were going to be by their own will.”

And a little later:

> “No one is condemned as a result of God’s prejudgment, but on account of the merit of his own iniquity.”

And again, much earlier, before he reached this point:

> “In the case of the wicked and ungodly, almighty God did not predestine their wickedness and ungodliness—that is, that they should be wicked and ungodly and unable to be otherwise. Rather, those whom he foreknew and foresaw as destined to become wicked and ungodly through their own fault, he predestined to eternal condemnation, by which they would be punished according to just judgment—not because they could not be otherwise, but because they did not wish to be otherwise.”

We reread this judgment in this form in the roll received from Heribold. But in the roll which we received through a certain person from the archive of Ebo, bishop of Grenoble [Col. 0092C], we found it to stand differently. We do not at all disbelieve that it was falsified, since in these two chapters we find the writing of that religious and learned man mingled, confused, and mutilated by their compiler. For in Heribold’s roll, as stated above, we reread the wording already given; but in the roll received, as stated, from Ebo’s archive, we found written: ‘He himself predestined them to eternal condemnation by a just judgment,’ whereas this man placed at the end of the chapter: ‘And by their own fault they remained in the mass of condemnation, whether through original or even actual merit.’ [29]

The former stated it better—indeed, he stated it correctly—because the latter stated it badly. Florus says that almighty God foreknew the wickedness of the wicked because it comes from them, but did not predestine it [Col. 0092D] because it does not come from him; as for their punishment, he both foreknew it because he is God and predestined it because he is just.

This part of the sentence the compiler reserved from the sequence of what preceded it for the present chapter. In Florus’s writing it is joined to the statement that they have the merit of their own condemnation, while God possesses the power and judgment of the one who justly condemns. For God predestines only what he himself was going to do; but he foreknows many things that he himself is not going to do, such as all evil things, which the wicked certainly do, not he. The wicked do not perish because they could not be good, but because they did not wish to be good; and through their own fault they persevered as vessels of wrath fitted for destruction.

This the compiler stole from the middle. Knowing that he was going to introduce this apostolic [Col. 0093A] example, he joined it to the other chapter so that he would not immediately be refuted by all who read it, adding that they had remained through their own fault in the mass of condemnation, whether by original or actual merit.

As we observed these things, what Macarius, bishop of Antioch, said came to our assistance. He was reproved at the Sixth Synod before the emperor Constantine because he had mutilated testimonies of Catholic writers, which he had been proved to have stolen from a certain pamphlet and compared with authentic books. For, when asked why he had done this, he replied: “I did it in order that I might establish my position.”

So this man knowingly set down badly the composed writings of that learned man for the same purpose: to confirm his own perverse understanding by falsehood, since he could not confirm it by truth. He hastened to display false things so that he could steal away true ones—either unknowingly or forgetfully—although painters are accustomed to paint an error with wings but without feet [Col. 0093B], because it cannot stand for long. Such is the unstable snare, resembling a spider’s web, which those who think perversely, and those who are careless and inconsiderate, are accustomed to spread. But, as it is written: “In vain is the net spread before the eyes of the winged” (Prov. 1:17).

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the apostolic example which the compiler of the chapters adduces to confirm his position

Finally, the compiler of the chapters adduces an example from the blessed apostle Paul, saying that just as the elect are predestined to life, so also the wicked are predestined by God to death:

> “Does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:21).

Therefore it must be considered whether the vessels of wrath have been fitted or prepared by God—that is, by his predestination—for destruction [Col. 0093C]. If so, God is unjust, since he inflicts wrath by punishing those whom he predestined to be such. But surely there is no injustice with God—far be it.

If, however, the vessels of wrath were not fitted or prepared for destruction by God’s predestination, how does this example help him confirm his position, in which he says that the wicked have been predestined by God to death?

The Predestinatiani also brought forward this example to confirm their position, as Hyginus says in the pamphlet of theirs mentioned above. But the blessed Augustine explains it in another sense in his letter to the presbyter Sixtus, saying (Epistle 105):

> “But if they are vessels of wrath, which have been perfected for destruction—the punishment due to them being rendered to them—let them attribute this to themselves, since they were made from that mass which, on account of the sin of one man in whom all sinned, God justly and deservedly [Col. 0093D] condemned. But if they are vessels of mercy, to whom, though made from the same mass, he did not wish to render the punishment due, let them not exalt themselves, but glorify him who bestowed on them mercy that was not due.”

And somewhat earlier:

> “Therefore, he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18). “To such people, then, let us say with the Apostle—for we cannot find anything better to say than what he said—‘O man, who are you to answer back to God?’ (ibid., 10). We seek the merit of hardening, and we find it: the entire mass was condemned by the merit of sin. God does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by not [Col. 0094A] imparting mercy. Those to whom mercy is not imparted are neither worthy nor deserving of it; rather, they are worthy of not receiving it and deserve not to receive it. But we seek the merit of mercy and do not find it, lest grace be emptied of its meaning if it is not freely given but rendered according to merits.”

The holy Gregory likewise, in the thirty-fourth book of the *Moralia* (chapter 17), speaks of the rebellious spirit by an apt comparison:

> “He was made so that he feared no one” (Job 40:24). By nature he was indeed made in such a way that he ought to have feared his Creator chastely, with a sober and secure fear—not with the fear that charity casts out, but with the fear that remains forever and ever. Yet through his perversity he became such that he feared no one. Abandoning the one who could truly have been sufficient for him, he judged that he could be sufficient for [Col. 0094B] himself; and the more he raised himself against the glory of his Creator, the farther he fell beneath himself.”

Thus also the vessels which are in the mass of the human race—Adam being the good vessel, in whom we were all made good by the good God—would have remained good if Adam himself had remained in the condition in which he had been made upright. But when he perished through the devil’s suggestion and his own fault, in which we all perished, we became vessels of wrath, prepared or fitted, or perfected, for destruction.

If no one were rescued from that condition, God’s judgment would be beyond reproach. But since many are rescued, this is an inexpressible gift of God’s grace.

Again, the blessed Gregory says in the twenty-ninth book of the *Moralia* (chapter 6):

> “The devil or man fell from the state of his proper condition through an exalted mind: the one saying, ‘I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most [Col. 0094C] High’ (Isa. 14:14), and the other, on hearing, ‘Your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods’ (Gen. 3:5), believing it. Each therefore fell because he desired to be like God—not through righteousness, but through power. But man, freed by grace, who had fallen by perversely desiring God’s likeness, recognizes in the guilt of his sin that he is far inferior to God and cries out, ‘Lord, who is like you?’ (Ps. 34:10). The devil, however, justly abandoned in the fall of his sin, did not remain within the measure of his fall. The longer he remained without the grace of almighty God, the more he accumulated the guilt of his sin. For he fell because he perversely wished to be like God, and he was brought to such a point that, when Antichrist comes, he will disdain even to appear like God and, condemned, will regard as beneath him the one whom [Col. 0094D], in his pride, he could not have as his equal.”

So also, concerning the vessels of wrath perfected for destruction by their own iniquity: whoever cleanses himself by God’s grace from the things by which he is defiled, as Paul says, will be a vessel for honor (2 Tim. 2:21). But whoever chooses to remain in iniquity, or has already grown so deeply into iniquity that, with God as judge, he cannot return from it by the retribution of justice, will be a vessel for dishonor and perfected for destruction—like Pharaoh, who is said to have been hardened because he was not softened by grace, and like those who were handed over to a debased mind because they were not freed by grace.

Whoever is not rescued from that destruction will suffer eternal torment, just as God’s judgment is beyond reproach, so also the torment will be inexcusable and irrefragable. For the vessels of wrath are fitted for destruction in the same way as the Apostle likewise calls them “by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2:3) [Col. 0095A]—not according to the nature in which the first man was created, but according to the nature in which, after his sin, each person was generated from the accursed seed.

Thus only those are saved who are made safe by the grace of the Savior. The Psalm says: “I have become like a discarded vessel” (Ps. 30:13), which Jerome explains as meaning: a human being lost through sin.

## CHAPTER VIII. Whence the Predestinatiani took the authority—or rather the opinion—of this kind of exposition of the apostolic passage, which will not profit them because they took it from falsehood

Moreover, it is not hidden from us where the compiler of the chapters obtained this interpretation of the apostolic teaching and confidently [Col. 0095B] assumed it in order to establish his own error and that of his accomplices: namely, from the words of Fulgentius, who, as we stated above, had written to Monimus concerning those predestined to destruction (Book I, chapter 3), almost under the protection of Saint Augustine, explaining the words Augustine had spoken in his book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*:

> “‘While reading,’ you say, ‘the book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, and rereading in sequence the testimony of the prophet, I cautiously reconsidered it little by little as I listened, and so forth,’ until the blessed Augustine says in that same place: ‘but in that class of human beings which has been predestined to destruction.’”

Here Fulgentius, having concluded the words of Saint Augustine and directing the purpose of his letter to me, says:

> “You say that you wonder why I repeat these things again, namely, that I now understand why you repeat these things: namely, because I so often resist your contention that predestination is spoken of not only in relation to good but also in relation to evil [Col. 0095C].”

Afterward he brings forward testimony from Saint Augustine’s second book *On the Baptism of Infants*, addressed to Marcellinus, in order to confirm his own position that there are people predestined to punishment. In that book, while treating this apostolic testimony, Augustine says (ibid., chapter 26):

> “Because a human being had the cause of his iniquity in his own will, the blessed Paul therefore asserts that God endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction” (Rom. 9:22).

And a little later:

> “God therefore fitted these vessels for the thing to which he predestined them—that is, for destruction: the destruction, namely, which Paul shows will suddenly overtake the wicked when he says, ‘When they say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them’” [Col. 0095D] (1 Thess. 5:3).

After this, in the same book, he added the following concerning the blessed Augustine (chapter 29):

> “And so that our assertion may be supported by a clearer indication of his words, something must be set before us from the book he wrote *On the Predestination of the Saints*. In it he more clearly shows that foreknowledge can exist without predestination, whereas predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge.”

And a little later (chapter 30):

> “You are not unaware that, in a former period, certain Gauls objected to that most illustrious work of the blessed Augustine which he wrote *On the Predestination of the Saints*: they claimed that, in asserting divine predestination, the blessed Augustine said that sinners were predestined not only to judgment but also [Col. 0096A] to sin. Because Augustine himself was overtaken by an early death, the learned and holy Prosper defended his statements with right faith and copious discourse [variant: ‘defended them rightly with faithful and copious discourse’].

“To avoid setting forth many of the Gallic objections here—for the necessity of disputing compels this pamphlet to be lengthy, and I do not wish my intention to make it even longer—we have decided to insert two passages containing responses.

“The fourteenth objection of the Gauls is stated as follows:

> ‘That those who do not believe the evangelical preaching do not believe by God’s predestination; and that God had so decreed that whoever does not believe does not believe by his own ordinance.’

“To this depravity, which was objected to the statements of the blessed Augustine not from truth but from ill will, Prosper replied in these words:

> ‘The unbelief of those who do not believe the [Col. 0096B] Gospel is in no way generated by God’s predestination. God is the author of good things, not of evil ones. God’s predestination, therefore, is always directed toward the good, whether it pertains to the retribution of justice or to the bestowal of grace. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). Accordingly, the unbelief of those who do not believe must be referred not to God’s decree but to his foreknowledge, which did not impose the necessity of unbelief merely because it could not be deceived about the unbelief that was going to occur.’

“The fifteenth objection is likewise inserted in these words:

> ‘That foreknowledge and predestination are the same thing.’

“To this Prosper replied:

> ‘Whoever in no respect distinguishes God’s foreknowledge from his predestination attempts to ascribe to God, in the case of evil things, what must be attributed to him in the case of good things [Col. 0096C]. But since good things must be referred to God as their giver and co-worker, while evil things must be referred to the voluntary wickedness of rational creation, there is no doubt that, without any [33] temporal difference, God both foreknew and predestined those things which were to be done with him as their author, or which were to be repaid to evil merits by a just judgment. But he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, those things which were not going to have their cause of action from him.’” 33

We therefore preferred, dearest brother, to insert these few passages for the time being from the books of Saint Augustine and from Prosper’s responses, so that everyone might know what they ought to think concerning the predestination of the saints and of the wicked.

These passages are taken from the book of Fulgentius.

## CHAPTER IX. That they also bring Isidore forward as a witness to confirm their position, and produce certain passages from the books of the blessed Augustine, by which that distinguished man refutes them, while Fulgentius himself plainly dissolves the authority which they derive from him

[Col. 0096D]

They also bring forward Isidore of Seville as a witness, a learned man who was of great benefit to readers in many matters. In his *Book of Sentences* he says that there is a twofold predestination: that of the elect to rest, and that of the reprobate to death. Whoever this compiler may have taken this opinion from—whether, as readers seem to find, from the words of Saint Gregory in the twenty-ninth or twenty-fifth book of the *Morals*, or from the sayings of Saint Augustine, or from somewhere else—he compiled it in his second book, chapter 6: [Col. 0097A] but he did not extract it in that manner, as anyone can very clearly recognize by reading the same book, according to the meaning of blessed Gregory. Hence one may suppose that this Isidore, learned in other matters, retained in this opinion some remnant of the Gauls in Spain through successive transmission. Concerning them Prosper wrote to blessed Augustine in his letter, sending word to him in this passage:

> Finally, we ask you to show how, through this preaching of God’s purpose—by which those ordained to eternal life become believers—none of those who must be exhorted may be hindered, nor acquire an occasion for negligence if they despair that they are predestined. We also ask you to show patiently, bearing with our ignorance, how the following objection is to be resolved: when the opinions of earlier writers on this subject are reviewed, almost all are found to have one common and unanimous view, by which they accepted God’s purpose and predestination according to his foreknowledge, so that God made some vessels of honor and others of dishonor because he foresaw the end of each person, and, under the assistance of grace, foresaw the will and action that each would have. Once all these matters have been disentangled, and many further points belonging to this issue have been examined—points that you are able to see more deeply—we believe and hope not only that our weakness will be strengthened by the support of your discussions, but also that those very men whose distinction in merits and honors is obscured by the darkness of this opinion will receive the clearest light of grace.

> For let your blessedness know that one of them, a man of exceptional authority and spiritual learning, Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles, is in all other matters an admirer and follower of your teaching. Concerning the matter about which he raises his complaint, he has for some time wished to communicate his view to your holiness by letter. But since it is uncertain whether he will do this, or for what purpose he will do it, and since, by God’s grace and providence in this present age, the weariness of us all finds relief in the strength of your charity and learning, add instruction to the humble and add rebuke to the proud. It is necessary and useful to write what has already been written, lest what is not frequently reproved be considered insignificant.
