For they think that what does not hurt is healthy, and they do not feel the wound covered over by skin; but let them understand that what has a persistent swelling will eventually come to the surgeon’s knife. [Col. 0097C]

In response to these men, Prosper and Hilary, Saint Augustine, as was stated above, sent his books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. But whoever examines Isidore’s words, with which he follows the aforesaid opinion concerning a twofold predestination, saying:

> Both are governed by divine judgment: he always causes the elect to follow heavenly and inward things, and always permits the reprobate, abandoning them, to take pleasure in things low and outward, in such a way that human beings do not know the boundary between light and darkness, or what the end of either thing will be,

and the other words that follow, and rereads the passage of blessed Gregory’s words in the aforesaid book of the *Morals*, where he says:

> Tell me, if you know all things, in what way light dwells, and what place belongs to darkness, so that you may lead each thing to its boundaries and understand the paths of its house (Job 38:18),

plainly sees that blessed Gregory did not wish it to be understood that the reprobate had been predestined by God to death, just as the elect had been predestined by him to life. For, among other things that the reader will find more fully in their proper places, he says in book 29, chapter 9:

> “And understand,” he says, “the paths of its house”: that is, consider and distinguish either to whom a persevering good action grants an eternal dwelling in the kingdom, or whom a wicked action, binding him until his appointed end, condemns to eternal punishment.

And again:

> Woe to us wretched people, who have not yet learned any word of God concerning our election, and already grow sluggish in idleness, as though secure. There ought indeed to be security in hope, but also fear in one’s manner of life, so that the former may encourage those who struggle, and the latter prick those who grow sluggish. Hence it is rightly said through the Prophet: “Those who fear the Lord, hope in the Lord” (Psalm 113:11); as though he plainly said: He presumes in vain upon hope who refuses to fear God in his actions. [Col. 0098B]

And again:

> Woe even to the praiseworthy life of human beings if it is judged without mercy, since, when it is strictly examined, the very thing by which it supposes that it pleases is what overwhelms it before the eyes of the Judge. Hence it is rightly said to the Lord through the Prophet: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2).

And shortly afterward:

> Again it is said through Solomon: “Who among human beings can understand his own way?” (Proverbs 20:24). Certainly, whoever does good or evil knows this with the testimony of conscience. But it is said that a person’s way is unknown to human beings because, even if each person understands that he is performing righteous works, he nevertheless does not know, under strict examination, toward what end he is proceeding. [Col. 0098C]

And in the same book, chapter 33, while explaining the statement, “Do you know the order of heaven, and can you establish its rule on earth?” (Job 38:33), he shows the modes of heavenly judgments in the elect and the reprobate in a different sense from that which Isidore gathers in the aforesaid opinion. We shall speak of these in their proper place.

For whoever takes care to read through all the books of blessed Gregory with attentive consideration will find that he neither said nor understood a twofold predestination in such a way that, just as the elect are predestined to life, so the reprobate are predestined by God to death. Rather, as Saint Augustine says in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and Prosper says against the Gauls, God’s predestination, which is always directed toward the good—because it either pertains to the gift of grace or to the recompense of justice—is plainly confirmed in God’s works, which are always good. Among these works are counted the salvation of the elect through unmerited grace and the punishment of the reprobate through deserved justice, as we shall demonstrate in what follows. [Col. 0098D]

Nevertheless, the modern Predestinarians bring forward, to confirm their opinion, the fact that the priest Saint Bede, as he plainly demonstrates in his works, understood and maintained something different from the words of Saint Augustine in a certain passage of his book on the *Hexameron*, and that the venerable Alcuin, in his abridgment of the commentary on the Evangelist John—which Saint Augustine expounded at great length in sermons to the people—placed among the predestined those destined for destruction, just as they had found it stated there. [Col. 0099A] For if they had set down in their excerpts anything different from what they found in the treatises of the aforementioned men, they would not be extractors of other men’s words, but rather compilers of their own from other men’s writings, instead of authors.

Therefore, let them accept not our words, but those that they themselves read together with us. The Lord said to the Jews: “I do not accuse you; there is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope” (John 5:45). Likewise, blessed Augustine—who used the term “predestination” without strict discrimination, sometimes saying “predestined to destruction” in books he had written before those mentioned above, in which he had explained predestination in its proper sense—rebukes them by the response with which, in book 12 of *On the Gift of Perseverance*, he undertook to answer those who opposed his later position, drawing on his books *On Free Choice*:

> “It is therefore pointless,” he says, “to appeal against me on the basis of the antiquity of that book of mine, and so forth. No one, I think, would be so unjust and envious as to prevent me from making progress.” [Col. 0099B]

And again, in the same book, chapter 21:

> Although I do not wish anyone to embrace all my writings in such a way as to follow me, except in those matters in which he recognizes that I have not erred. For this reason I am now composing books in which I undertake to revise my shorter works, so that I may show that I have not always followed even myself. I consider that, through God’s mercy, I have written while making progress, though I did not begin from perfection. For if I now say that, at this age, I have reached the point of writing perfectly and without any error, I would be speaking more arrogantly than truthfully. Yet it matters how much one errs, in what matters one errs, how readily one corrects oneself, and with how much obstinacy one attempts to defend one’s error.

> A person is of good hope if the final day of this life finds him making such progress that what was lacking in him as he advanced is added to him, and he is judged more as one to be perfected than as one to be punished. Therefore, if I do not wish to prove ungrateful to those who loved me because some benefit of my labor reached them before they loved me, how much more must I avoid ingratitude toward God, whom we would not love unless he had first loved us and made us lovers of him, because love is from him (1 John 4:7), as those whom he made great have said—not only those who love him, but also those who proclaim him? [Col. 0099C]

But even if they wish to produce examples from Fulgentius in support of their opinion, we shall object that, in the aforesaid book addressed to Monimus, Fulgentius praises the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and the responses of Prosper, because Prosper, a learned man of upright faith and abundant eloquence, opposed the critics of blessed Augustine. Therefore, let them hear what blessed Augustine says concerning the aforementioned testimony of the Apostle in the book praised by them, Augustine’s *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 8:

> “But why he does not teach all,” he says, “the Apostle disclosed as much as he judged should be disclosed: ‘Wishing to show wrath and to make his power known, he endured with much patience the vessels of wrath that were made complete for destruction, and in order to make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy that he prepared for glory’ (Romans 9:22–23). Hence it is that ‘the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God’ (1 Corinthians 1:18).” [Col. 0100A]

And after a little further:

> Faith, therefore, both begun and perfected, is a gift of God. Let no one who does not wish to contradict the clearest sacred writings doubt that this gift is given to some and not given to others. But why it is not given to all should not trouble the believer who believes that, in one person, all went into condemnation—without any doubt, a condemnation most just—so that there would have been no just accusation against God even if no one had been delivered from it.

> Hence it is clear that great is the grace by which many are delivered, and that those who are not delivered recognize what was owed to them, so that the one who boasts may boast not in his own merits, which he sees to be equal to those of the condemned, but in the Lord. “Why he delivers this person rather than that one” are “his unsearchable judgments, and his ways are past finding out” (Romans 11:33). For it is better that here also we hear or say: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20), than that we should dare to say, as though we knew what he wished to remain hidden, that he could nevertheless have wished something unjust. [Col. 0100B]

And again, in his letter to the priest Sixtus, letter 105:

> In the vessels made complete for destruction—which is owed to the condemned mass—let the vessels made from the same mass for honor recognize what divine mercy has freely bestowed upon them.

And shortly afterward:

> Finally, he concludes concerning both: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18). This occurs with one in whom there is no injustice. He therefore has mercy through a free gift, but hardens through the most just merit.

And somewhat earlier:

> For we seek the merit of hardening and we find it: the entire mass was condemned on account of the merit of sin. God does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by not imparting mercy. Those to whom he does not impart it are neither worthy nor deserving of it; rather, they are worthy of and deserve that it not be imparted to them. But we seek the merit of mercy and do not find it, because there is none; otherwise grace would be emptied of its meaning if it were not given freely but repaid according to merits. [Col. 0100C]

The same Saint Augustine also says in his book *On the Predestination of Grace*, chapter 2:

> The question arises why some of these perish, although the Almighty “wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” Then again, why does he harden some while having mercy on others, or how does he will all people to be saved when he himself hardens some so that they may not be saved?

And after a little further, chapter 3:

> If, then, as has been shown, we are all born indebted from the seed of the transgressor, because “all sinned in him,” as the Apostle says (Romans 3:12), and if the mass from which we descend was already condemned at the beginning, let no one dare complain of his hardness, and let no one complain of the punishment that is owed even in the absence of personal sins, solely by the condition of birth. But the fact that God bestows unmerited mercy on some who are converted through a free calling must be attributed, in accordance with the truth, not to injustice on the part of the steward but to the supremely merciful generosity of the giver. [Col. 0100D]

And shortly afterward, chapter 4:

> Accordingly, from the earlier part of this statement, in which he says, “He has mercy on whom he wills” (Romans 9:18), I think that no one who is unworthy of mercy should dare dispute. But in what follows, “He hardens whom he wills,” the attention of the human mind is somewhat confused by the novelty of the expression. It must not be understood as though God produced in a person the hardness of heart that had not existed. For what else is hardness than resistance to God’s commands? [Col. 0101A]

And after a few words:

> Therefore, whatever punishment a human being born after that transgression suffers must be acknowledged to be justly and deservedly inflicted. God is said to harden the one whom he does not wish to soften; likewise he is said to blind the one whom he does not wish to illuminate, and to reject the one whom he does not wish to call. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Romans 8:29).

And after a little further, chapter 6:

> These things, insofar as they accord with the rule of faith, should be piously spoken with the Lord’s illumination. But I already see what slanderous perversity can object even here. It follows that, if those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, then those who were neither predestined nor called, and therefore were not justified, ought to be innocent of all guilt, and that it is unjust for punishments to be demanded from them on the day of judgment for the wicked life they have led.

> Let the Apostle Paul say to such people, “Is there injustice with God?” (Romans 9:14), and let him immediately answer, “Certainly not.” When this has been firmly established in a sound human mind through pious belief—that there is no injustice with God—let him understand “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” as though it were said: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and on whom he does not will he does not have mercy.” Let him likewise understand this in the following way: “He gives to whom he wills, and from whom he wills he demands what is owed.”

> Whoever persists in calling this unjust should hear from the Apostle: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). The apostolic authority appropriately strikes down this kind of impiety, imposing such weight through the force of its expressions when it says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? O man, to God; clay, to the potter?” For the same Apostle adds: “Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” [Col. 0101C]

And after what follows, chapters 13–14:

> Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Word of the Father, equal and coeternal with the Father, emptied himself by taking the form of a servant. Although he himself was without sin, he became sin by taking flesh, so that, once the sin of the flesh had been healed in the human being, he might condemn sin in the flesh. He came to seek what had been lost, to heal what was sick, to raise up what was lying prostrate, possessing the power to forgive sins—which he did not owe to give, but which was owed to him to forgive. Having erased all the stains of the former guilt, he restored the nature that he had made.

> From those whom severity had justly decreed for punishment, according to the ineffable mercy of a hidden ordering, he chose vessels to make for honor. Some he absolved from the coming wrath by the gift of a free calling; others he abandoned and reserved for the judgment of equality. Yet he took away from no one the capacity to acknowledge the truth. Thus the fullness of divine foreknowledge was completed, with justice flowing into some and grace overflowing into others, so that the Church, spread throughout the whole world, might be enlarged through those whom God had foreknown to perish and those whom, in his secret election, he had foreknown to be saved.

> Therefore rejoice, whoever you are who have been enlightened, and acknowledge the grace you did not deserve. Mourn, whoever you are who have been hardened, and confess justice. Say, whoever you are who boast that you have been washed from original contagion by the bath of grace: “The Lord is merciful and gracious, patient and abundant in mercy; he has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities” (Psalm 102:10).

> And whoever you are who are condemned, say: “You are just, O Lord, in all the things that you have done to us, and all your judgments are true” (Daniel 3:27), because in truth and judgment you have brought all these things upon us on account of our sins. [Col. 0102A]

And again, in the same work, chapter 6:

> “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exodus 4:21). What does “I will harden” mean except “I will not soften”? It is evident that the statement of Scripture was fulfilled: justice flowed into some and grace overflowed into others. God says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I have raised you up, to show my power in you and to proclaim my name throughout all the earth” (Exodus 9:16).

> Since God makes good use even of evil people—through Pharaoh’s hardening, the plagues of Egypt, and the many great miracles accomplished all together in that nation—what else was done except that God’s power, great in itself and complete in itself, might reach the knowledge of the human race? These things would benefit not God, but those who read them again and come to believe. [Col. 0102B]

And after a few words, chapter 7:

> Blessed Paul also displayed this judgment of divine power in the election of human beings through very powerful examples when, speaking of Rebecca’s offspring while they were still in the womb, he referred everything to God’s grace. For he says: “But Rebecca also conceived by one man, Isaac our father. For when the children had not yet been born and had done nothing either good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from him who calls—it was said: ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’ as it is written, ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Romans 9:10–13). Immediately he added: “What shall we say? Is there injustice with God?” and he answered by denying it: “Certainly not.” [Col. 0102C]

And after a little further, as the reader will find more fully in its proper place, chapter 8:

> Jacob, therefore, was predestined as a vessel for honor, but not from works, because it was said not from works but from him who calls: “The elder shall serve the younger.” And lest the vessels predestined for honor should deny glory to the Creator by attributing something to their own powers, the Apostle elsewhere calls them “vessels of mercy,” so that they might recognize that whatever they were, they were according to mercy. [Col. 0102D]

And after a few words:

> Behold: in the former, iniquity is justly punished; in the latter, no justice is rewarded freely.

And again, chapter 10:

> This distribution, then, by which we have said that human beings are called by God when no merits exist, and that those who are called need God’s assistance in order to perform anything good, the Apostle demonstrates by an example taken from the ancient writings. After referring the election of the two twins—excluding every praise of merits—to God’s grace and judgment, he saw what impious chatter might blasphemously say and declared, “Is there injustice with God?” and the answer follows, “Certainly not.”

> And as though he were asked, “From where do you prove this?”, he considered the authority of his teaching insufficient unless he also taught his opinion by the example of the Law. Thus he wished what Moses had said—“I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I am merciful” (Exodus 33:19)—to be understood as meaning that we should believe that the first mercy from God is granted to human beings through calling. This alone is not sufficient for right living if the one who called abandons them.

> For this reason the addition is made: “And I will show mercy to whom I am merciful,” so that it may be clear that even the works of mercy themselves are received from God. When we seem to perform them, we earn God’s mercy. [Col. 0103A]

And shortly afterward:

> If anyone is troubled that not all—even among those who have already been called—deserve to reach the second grace, that is, the gift of living rightly, let him understand from this what sort of thing is being defended against God’s grace by the person who takes comfort in his free choice, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22:14).

> For all who, having abandoned the gift of divine calling, have again fallen away into impious unbelief find their free choice sufficient to accomplish what they wish, because God’s grace itself has abandoned them. [Col. 0103B]

And again, after a little further, chapters 14–15:

> Pharaoh therefore did not receive this mercy, and for that reason his free choice was sufficient for his destruction. No one so ignorant of the divine Scriptures will dare to say that he suffered all those things unjustly. Or perhaps, if we think piously about God as we ought, we may find that mercy was given even to Pharaoh.

> For God’s patience ought to have served him for salvation. By delaying the just and deserved punishment, God repeatedly intensified the blows of the miracles. Could Pharaoh not, just as he expelled the people when yielding to the blows, recognize God as possessing such great power by believing in the miracles?

> If it is said that Pharaoh could no longer be changed because God had foreknown that he would not be changed, the answer is that God’s foreknowledge does not compel a human being to be such as God foreknew him to be. Rather, God foreknows that he will be such as he will be, although God did not make him so. For if foreknowledge compelled him to be so, it would compel what is not. But if God had foreknown that what is not would come to be, that would not be foreknowledge.

> Anyone who uses this as a flattering excuse for his sins, because God foreknew that he would become a sinner, should consider how impiously this is said of God. [Col. 0103C]

Perhaps someone may nevertheless say that the way to salvation would be less suitable if a person were scourged without first being inwardly stirred by a calling. How, then, did Nebuchadnezzar attain fruitful repentance? Did he not repent after being scourged following countless impieties, and receive again the kingdom he had lost?

But Pharaoh became harder through those very scourges and perished. Let the person who judges the divine plan with an excessively lofty mind give me an explanation: why did the medicine prepared by one physician bring death to one person and salvation to another, unless it is because “the good odor of Christ” is “to some an odor of life unto life, and to others an odor of death unto death” (2 Corinthians 2:15–16)?

In nature, both were human beings; in rank, both were kings; in circumstance, both possessed God’s captive people; in punishment, both were mercifully admonished by scourges. What, then, made their ends different except that one, feeling the hand of God, groaned in remembrance of his own iniquity, while the other fought by free choice against God’s most merciful truth?

Whoever answers here that divine assistance was present for the first so that he might be changed, but absent for the second so that he might be hardened, and who argues that this was unjust—thereby placing the ends of these matters in God’s will, as the Apostle says, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18)—and as the Lord also says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), should understand that all these things are either accomplished with the Lord’s help or permitted when he abandons a person, yet should also recognize that nothing at all is admitted against his will. [Col. 0104B]

And after a few words, chapter 16:

> But now, when just punishment is given to the condemned and unmerited grace is given to the saved, who is so forgetful of the human condition that he would examine the secrets of the divine mind and, having deserved the punishment itself, complain that another received grace that was not owed to him?

And again, Saint Augustine in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 11:

> For there is no injustice with God, but his judgments are unsearchable and his ways are past finding out (Romans 11:33); and all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Psalm 24:10). His mercy, therefore, is unsearchable: by it he has mercy on whom he wills, without any preceding merits of theirs. His truth is also unsearchable: by it he hardens whom he wills, indeed according to their preceding merits, but often according to merits shared with the one on whom he has mercy.

> Thus, in the case of two twins, one of whom is taken and the other left behind, the outcome is different though their merits are shared. Yet in these two, one is delivered through God’s great goodness without the other being condemned through any injustice on God’s part. Is there injustice with God? Certainly not; but his ways are unsearchable.

> Therefore, let us acknowledge without doubt his mercy in those who are delivered and his truth in those who are punished, and let us not attempt to search out what is unsearchable or investigate what is past finding out.

> For from the mouth of infants and nursing children he perfects his praise (Psalm 8:3), so that, when we see in those whose deliverance is preceded by no good merits, and in those whose condemnation is preceded only by original conditions shared by both, what occurs, we should by no means hesitate to believe that the same thing happens in adults. That is, we should not think either that grace is given to anyone according to his merits, or that anyone is punished except according to his merits—whether those who are delivered and those who are punished have equal causes, or whether they have different evil causes.

> Thus, “let the one who seems to stand take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12), and let the one who boasts boast not in himself but in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31). [Col. 0104D]

Again, Augustine says in book 4 *Against the Pelagians*, chapter 5:

> “He endured with much patience the vessels of wrath that were made complete for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy that he prepared for glory.” Wrath is not returned except when it is deserved, lest there be injustice with God; but mercy, even when given without being deserved, does not involve injustice with God.

> From this the vessels of mercy understand how freely mercy is given to them: with the vessels of wrath, with which they share the common mass that is the cause of destruction, deserved and just wrath is repaid. [Col. 0105A]

And again Augustine had said in his letter to Optatus, letter 57:

> Like a potter with clay, from the same mass he makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor. It would indeed seem unjust that vessels of wrath are made for destruction if the entire mass had not been condemned in Adam.

> That they become vessels of wrath by being born belongs to deserved punishment; that they become vessels of mercy by being born again belongs to unmerited grace.

> God therefore displays his wrath—not, of course, as a disturbance of mind such as the anger of human beings is called, but as a just and fixed vengeance—because the offspring of sin and punishment is derived from the stock of disobedience, and because a human being born of woman, as it is written in the book of Job, has a short life and is full of trouble (Job 14:1). He is a vessel of that with which he is filled; hence they are called vessels of wrath.

> He also displays his power, by which he makes good use even of the wicked, granting them many natural and temporal goods and employing their wickedness to exercise the good and to admonish the good by comparison, so that through them the good may learn to give thanks to God because they have been distinguished from them not by their own merits—which were equal in the same mass—but by God’s mercy. [Col. 0105B]

Concerning such vessels Gregory says in his twenty-first homily on Ezekiel:

> When Paul was still inexperienced in the calling of the faith, because he had already received the Lord’s words and was full of heavenly grace, he is called a vessel of election, when it is said: “He is a vessel of election for me” (Acts 9:15).

> Hence the prophet admonishes pastors and teachers, saying: “Cleanse yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52:11). For those who, by teaching, sustain the life of the faithful carry, as it were, the vessels of the Lord’s table, so that eventually they may bring it to the Lord as a holocaust and sacrifice. [Col. 0105C]

Following these statements, Florus—whose writing this deceitful compiler, whoever he may be, has chewed up and spat out while assembling these chapters—wrote in the same place:

> Hence the Apostle calls them “his vessels of mercy” (Romans 9:20), to show the riches of his grace, which he prepared for glory.

> On the other hand, God foreknew that the wicked would become wicked through their own malice, and he foreknew that they would be condemned to eternal punishment by his justice. Thus he foreknew concerning Judas the traitor that he would betray him, as the Gospel says, although he was one of the twelve (John 6:72). He also foreknew his eternal condemnation when he said: “Woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed; it would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matthew 26:24).

> Likewise, the wicked do not perish because they were unable to be good, but because they wished to be wicked. Through their own fault they remained fitted as vessels of wrath for destruction, and they remained in the mass of perdition, whether by original or by actual merit. [Col. 0105D]

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the testimonies of Scripture that Gothescalcus and his accomplices, by an alien interpretation, most irreverently misuse against the Catholic faith and the teaching of the orthodox.

[Col. 0106A]

It must also be understood that, under this interpretation by which that compiler used the Apostle’s testimony, Gothescalcus and his disciples also employ other testimonies in asserting their error: “The Lord has made all things for himself, even the wicked for the day of evil” (Prov. 16:4); and from Ecclesiasticus: “He who turns from righteousness to sin, God has prepared him for the sword” (Ecclus. 26:27). Concerning these, Catholics hold the following view: the Lord made the wicked for the day of evil, and prepared the one who turns from righteousness to sin for the sword, because the person whom he foresaw would become wicked and transgressor [Col. 0106B] he did not predestine to reach the evil day appointed for him or the sword—that is, the deserved punishment of vengeance—but permitted him to become wicked by his own fault and a transgressor by his own choice, and condemned him by a just judgment. He did not become wicked, nor did he transgress, because God foresaw that he would become wicked and a transgressor; rather, God foresaw him as wicked and a transgressor because he was going to become wicked and a transgressor by his own fault.

Therefore, whoever reads this testimony of the Apostle, placed in the third chapter of this compiler, ought to understand more soundly, according to the teaching of the Catholic Fathers, what the Apostle said: “Vessels of wrath made ready or prepared for destruction” (Rom. 9:22)—made so by the sin of the first transgression; and [Col. 0106C] what he says, “God makes a vessel for honor,” namely, by grace and predestination, whereas he makes a vessel for dishonor not by working it, but by abandoning it with the greatest justice, as the volumes of the orthodox are full of this interpretation.

That is, because he hardened Pharaoh’s heart by a just judgment, since he did not soften it through grace; he gave him over to a depraved mind as a retribution of justice, because this is both sin and the punishment of sin. He often handed sinners over to one sin after another because grace did not free them; justice blinded them because grace did not enlighten them; he made them a vessel for dishonor because he justly left them in the mass of perdition and condemnation, and did not make them an honorable vessel by predestining them through grace.

Thus he also “shut” because he did not open; he destroyed because he did not build; he despised the one whom he did not regard. The one who turns from righteousness to [Col. 0106D] iniquity, God prepared for the sword as a retribution of justice. He permitted the nations to enter their own ways, and left a human being in the power of his own counsel. By justly abandoning them he dissolved the kings’ girdle; by permitting it, he girded their loins with a rope. As a retribution of justice he leads into temptation, since he justly permits a person to be led into it.

And in Job: “God deprived him of wisdom” (Job 39:17), since he justly did not give it to him. Concerning those of whom it is written that “they could not hear, because God wished to kill them” (1 Sam. 2:25), the meaning is that they deserved this, so that justice might render what grace does not forgive.

Hence Prosper, drawing on the words of Saint Augustine in his response to the fifteenth objection of the Vincentians, shows that just as God deprives no one of the path of correction, so he [Col. 0107A] deprives no one of the possibility of doing good: for whoever turns himself away from God has himself taken away from himself both the will and the ability to do what is good. It does not therefore follow that, when God has not given certain people repentance, he has taken away their conversion; nor that, when he has not lifted certain people up, he has cast them down. For it is one thing to lead an innocent person into crime, which is foreign to God, and another thing not to grant forgiveness to a criminal, which arises from the sinner’s own merit.

These are the two lots and the two measured cords—one for killing and one for giving life—mentioned from the Scriptures in the book of Lord Prudentius, to confirm the opinion that the reprobate are predestined by God to death, just as the elect are predestined to life. But Prosper, as we have said, drawing on the words of Saint Augustine, has more accurately, and more truly, explained how such expressions of Sacred Scripture [Col. 0107B] ought to be understood in a Catholic manner. Namely, whatever God does mercifully and justly belongs either to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice—he who made the things that were to come. For, as Saint Augustine says in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, nothing happens except what God himself either does or permits to be done. And in *On Grace and Free Choice*, addressed to Valentinus and the monks with him (chap. 21), he says:

> “This must be fixed and immovable in your hearts: there is no iniquity with God. Therefore, when you read in the writings of truth that people are led astray by God, or that their hearts are dulled or hardened, do not doubt that their evil merits came first, so that they might justly suffer these things. Otherwise you will fall into that proverb of Solomon: ‘The folly of a man distorts his ways, but in his heart he blames God’ (Prov. 19:3).”

And in the same work, a little later (chap. 23):

> “When, therefore, you hear the Lord saying, ‘I, the Lord, have led that prophet astray’ (Ezek. 14:9), and what the Apostle says, ‘He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills’ (Rom. 9:18), faithfully and without doubt recognize, in the one whom he permits to be led astray or hardened, his evil merits; but in the one on whom he [Col. 0107C] has mercy, recognize the grace of God, who does not repay evil with evil but good with evil. Nor should you therefore take free choice away from Pharaoh because God says in many places, ‘I hardened Pharaoh,’ or ‘I have hardened’ or ‘I will harden Pharaoh’s heart.’ For this does not mean that Pharaoh himself did not harden his heart. Indeed, this too is read concerning him when the dog-flies were removed from the Egyptians, as Scripture says: ‘And Pharaoh hardened his heart at this time also and [Col. 0107D] would not let the people go’ (Exod. 8). Thus God hardened him by a just judgment, and Pharaoh himself hardened his heart by free choice.”

Bede also demonstrates the manner of this expression in the second book of his commentary on Luke the Evangelist, explaining the Lord’s saying, whether “to save a soul or to destroy it”—that is, whether to heal a person or not:

> “This is the same as what he had said earlier: whether to do good or evil. This does not mean that God, who is supremely good, can be the author of evil or destruction for us; rather, in accordance with the customary language of Scripture, his not saving is called destroying, just as he is said to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart—not because he hardened what was soft, but because he did not mercifully soften what had been hardened by preceding merits. And when we pray, ‘Do not lead us into temptation,’ immediately [Col. 0108A] adding, ‘But deliver us from evil’ (Matt. 6:13), we are clearly taught that his leading us into temptation means nothing other than his not delivering us from evil; and that his destroying a soul means his not saving it from destruction.”

Saint Gregory likewise says in the twenty-ninth book of the *Moralia* (chap. 15):

> “The Lord is said to bring forth this frost—not because he himself forms the minds of the wicked for guilt, but because he does not free them from guilt. Thus it is written, ‘I will harden Pharaoh’s heart’ (Exod. 4 and 7): because he did not mercifully soften it, he plainly declared that he would strictly harden it.”

Hence Saint Augustine says on Psalm 35:

> “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to do what is unfitting” (Rom. 1:28). “If God does this, so that they do what is unfitting, what did they themselves do? [Col. 0108B] There was therefore a desire which they were unwilling to overcome, so that by God’s judgment they might be handed over to it, if they were judged worthy to be handed over.”

And on Psalm 28:

> “Some were saying, ‘He is good’; others, ‘No.’ He transferred some into his love and left others in their wickedness.”

And on Psalm 6:

> “God gave them over to a depraved mind. For that is the blindness of the mind. Whoever is given over to it is excluded from the inner light of God, though not yet completely while he is in this life. For there is an outer darkness, which is understood to belong more particularly to the day of judgment, so that whoever, while there is still time, has been unwilling to be corrected may be wholly outside God.”

And on Psalm 5:

> “When God punishes sinners, he does not inflict his own evil upon them; he abandons them to their own evils.”

And on Psalm 7:

> “To be is related to light; not to be, to [Col. 0108C] darkness. Therefore, whoever abandons the one by whom he was made and inclines toward that from which he was made—that is, toward nothingness—is held in darkness by this sin. Yet he does not perish completely, but is ordered among the lowest things.”

From these testimonies of the Catholics, let the compiler of these chapters recognize that Fulgentius cannot assist him at all in interpreting this apostolic testimony according to his own meaning. Let us therefore proceed to examine the remaining parts of the chapter.

## CHAPTER XI. On examining the remains of the following chapter

Finally, our author, a most hostile persecutor of the truth according to his own understanding, says:

> “In the election of those who are to be saved, however, God’s mercy precedes good merit; but in the condemnation of those who perish, evil merit precedes God’s just judgment.”

This compiler did not set these words down as Florus carefully presented them in his own work; and to the extent that he altered them in wording, to that same extent he distorted their proper meaning. Florus said:

> “Whether in those who are saved or in those who perish, their own will is rewarded, and their own will is condemned. But in the former, because it has been healed through the grace of the Lord Savior, so that from bad and perverse it might become good and upright, it is unquestionably crowned most deservedly. In the latter, however, because it does not consent to receive healing through the Savior, it will most justly experience eternal condemnation through the same judge.”

And above he said:

> “Therefore he wholly foresaw [Col. 0109A] the good, both that they would become good through his grace and that through the same grace they would receive eternal rewards—that is, that they would live well in the present age and be happily rewarded in the future. Yet both come from the gift of God’s mercy. Hence the Apostle calls them his vessels of mercy, saying: ‘That he might show the riches of his grace in the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory’ (Rom. 9:23). Conversely, he foresaw the wicked as becoming wicked through their own wickedness, and foresaw them as destined to be condemned to eternal punishment by his justice.”

The compiler altered words that had been properly composed and transferred their sound meaning into a perverse one. If he had said, “In the salvation of the elect, God’s mercy precedes good merit,” the statement could in some way be understood as coherent. But [Col. 0109B] because he preferred to say, “In the election of those who are to be saved, God’s mercy precedes good merit,” he departed from the consequence of the correct meaning.

For concerning the election of those who are to be saved it is written: “God chose us in him”—that is, in Christ—“before the foundation of the world, predestining us for adoption as sons” (Eph. 1:4). Hence Augustine says in *On the Predestination of the Saints* (chap. 10):

> “If it is asked from what source anyone is made worthy, there are those who say, ‘By human will’; we say, ‘By grace or divine predestination.’”

And predestination, which cannot exist without foreknowledge, is itself election, as the Apostle teaches:

> “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8:29).

And again:

> “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; those he predestined, he also called; those he called, he also justified; those he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. [Col. 0109C] 8:30).

Saint Augustine opposes the phrase “and not others” to each of these stages (chap. 17). And election by grace is itself mercy. Let him therefore say what other mercy precedes good merit in the election of those who are to be saved, if mercy precedes in their election. Thus mercy would precede mercy, and there would be two mercies by which those who are to be saved are elected.

Yet God’s mercy is to be understood in two ways not in the election of those who are to be saved, but in the salvation of the elect: namely, as his freely given grace. Therefore, if he wishes to recognize the distinction between the first and the second mercy—that is, between gratuitous grace and the other—let him read Saint Augustine’s book *On the Predestination of Grace*, where he says at the relevant passage (chap. 10):

> “‘I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will show mercy [Col. 0109D] to whom I will show mercy’ (Exod. 33:19), so that we may believe that God first grants mercy to human beings by calling them. This alone is not sufficient for right living if the one who called abandons them. Therefore it was added, ‘And I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy,’ so that it might be clear that even the works of mercy themselves are received from God; for when we seem to exercise them, we earn God’s mercy. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy’ (Matt. 5:7). If the Apostle had not understood this in this way, he would never have taken care to insert this testimony into his argument as a proof. If anyone is troubled by the fact that not all, even among those who have already been called, deserve to reach the second grace—that is, the gift of [Col. 0110A] living rightly—as the Lord says in the Gospel, ‘Many are called, but few are chosen’ (Matt. 22:14), let him understand from this what sort of thing the person is trying to defend against God’s grace who takes pride in his own free choice. For all who, abandoning the gift of the divine calling, have again fallen away into impious unbelief, have enough free choice to accomplish what they wished, since they themselves have abandoned God’s grace.”

And the heavenly preacher develops the rest of this at greater length and with greater eloquence in the same place.

Hence Prosper, in his book *Sentences in Epigrams*, which he briefly noted from the sayings of Saint Augustine (chap. 130), says:

> “Just as there are two functions of medicine, one by which illness is healed and another by which health is preserved, so there are two gifts of grace: one that removes the desire of the flesh, and another [Col. 0110B] that makes the virtue of the mind persevere.”

By these statements of the teachers, let him learn and understand that he did not speak correctly when he said that, in the election of those who are to be saved, God’s mercy precedes good merit. For the first grace is such that no second grace precedes it in the election and calling of those who are to be saved; it precedes every good merit. Indeed, even thinking and willing what is good, and faith—the beginning of every good work, which works through love and without which it is impossible to please God—come from this grace, as Scripture testifies:

> “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5).

And:

> “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

And:

> “To one is given faith in the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:8).

Hence Augustine says in *On the Predestination of the Saints* [Col. 0110C] (chap. 18):

> “God chose his members in Christ before the foundation of the world; and how could he choose those who did not yet exist, except by predestining them?”

And a little later:

> “Therefore God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, predestining us for adoption as sons—not because we were going to be holy and blameless through ourselves, but he chose us and predestined us to be so.”

Otherwise grace is no longer grace if it has not been given freely.

The second mercy, however, or grace of right living, is that to which those who were foreknown and predestined, chosen and called, deserve to attain by the gift of grace. Having been justified by this grace, they will be glorified in the future, receiving grace for grace—that is, the grace of blessed recompense in return for the grace of good works—as Saint Augustine wrote in *On the Gift of [Col. 0110D] Perseverance*.

## CHAPTER XII. Saint Augustine’s definition of the predestination of the saints, from which the compiler of these chapters is known to disagree in every respect; by circuitous arguments he weakens and perverts faith in divine predestination and bends the words of truth toward falsehood as far as he can. Catholic teaching therefore refutes him with open truth and, if it does not turn him from his obstinacy back to the path of truth, at least proves him contrary to the truth in his falsehood

> “This is the predestination of the saints,” he says: “nothing other than the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are liberated are most certainly liberated.”

And again in the same work (chap. 7):

> “After [Col. 0111A] the fall of humanity, God willed that a person’s approach to him should belong to his grace alone; and he likewise willed that a person’s not departing from him should belong to his grace alone. He placed this grace in the one in whom we obtained our lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things. Thus, just as he works so that we approach, so he works that we may not depart.”

And in the book mentioned above, *On the Predestination of the Saints* (chap. 10):

> “If the question is examined and it is asked from what source anyone is made worthy, there are those who say, ‘By human will’; but we say, ‘By grace or divine predestination.’ The only difference between grace and predestination is that predestination is the preparation for grace, whereas grace is the gift itself already bestowed. Thus, when the [Col. 0111B] Apostle says, ‘Not from works, lest anyone should boast; for we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works’ (Eph. 2:9), this refers to grace. But what follows—‘which God prepared so that we might walk in them’—refers to predestination, which cannot exist without foreknowledge.”

But this reviser, altering Florus’s words and meaning—although Florus had followed Augustine’s meaning—may be compared to the saying:

> “In the darkness the cat caught a magpie instead of a mouse.”

We suppose that when he said, [Col. 0111C] “In the election of those who are to be saved, God’s mercy precedes good merit, but in the condemnation of those who perish, evil merit precedes God’s just judgment,” he intended to say what Saint Augustine states most correctly and plainly in *On the Gift of Perseverance* (chap. 11):

> “From the mouth of infants and nursing children God has perfected his praise” (Ps. 8:3), so that in those whose liberation—that is, whose election—we see, no good merits precede; and in those whose condemnation we see, let us not hesitate to say that each is punished only for his own merits, whether those who are liberated and those who are punished have equal or different evil causes.”

They are called elect because, from the mass of perdition, they were chosen by grace, possessing no merit before they were chosen. Their election itself is God’s mercy. Thus in the Council of Orange, over which blessed Caesarius presided as delegate of the apostolic see, and whose chapters directed by the apostolic see he presented for all to [Col. 0111D] subscribe and uphold, chapter 14 says:

> “No wretched person is delivered from whatever misery except one who is preceded by God’s mercy, as the Psalmist says: ‘Let your mercy, O Lord, quickly go before us’ (Ps. 78:8); and again: ‘My God, his mercy will go before me’ (Ps. 58:11).”

And chapter 18:

> “Reward is owed to good works if they are performed, but grace, which is not owed, precedes them so that they may be performed.”

This is gratuitous election, which precedes good works. This is the mercy by which the wretched are delivered when they are chosen from the mass of perdition—that is, chosen freely. [Col. 0108D] No other mercy precedes this mercy, namely, this election before the ages, God’s eternal predestination.

By this mercy [Col. 0112A] the wretched are chosen so that the good may be made from the wicked. To those who have been chosen by the same mercy are given faith and prepared good works; in these works, having been preceded and assisted by grace, walking in them and then supported so that they may persevere, they reach life—that is, eternal grace.

But if what he added—“in the condemnation of those who perish, evil merit precedes God’s just judgment”—is meant to call God’s predestination itself the judgment of God, and if he means that this judgment of God, that is, predestination, is preceded by the evil merit of the reprobate, on account of which, according to his foreknowledge, he predestined the reprobate to destruction, since God foresaw their evil merit and predestined them to destruction, then he should recognize how badly he speaks.

For God condemns no one before he sins, because he [Col. 0112B] abandons no one before that person abandons him, as the Catholic teachers say. Saint Augustine, in *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, opposes this view at the greatest length, most frequently, and in the most Catholic manner, with examples from Sacred Scripture and exceedingly sound arguments. The words of those who held this error expressed such ignorance and demonstrated such folly.

But if he wishes it to be understood as meaning that God’s just judgment precedes the evil merit of those who perish, and that punishment has been predestined for them as a retribution of justice, then he appears to destroy with certainty the position which he is attempting to establish when he says that they were predestined to destruction. For the two things cannot both be true: that they were predestined and that they were left behind—that is, that they were prepared by grace and that they were left in the mass of perdition, to which [Col. 0112C] punishment was predestined, by a retribution of justice.

Our Catholic teachers confirm this by their judgment: God created the human being whom he willed to stand unto eternity, and did not predestine him to perish. But he foresaw that he would perish—the one who became the mass of perdition of the entire human race. From this mass of perdition he foresaw and predestined certain people, before all ages, to life, and predestined eternal life for them, as the Apostle says: “The grace of God is eternal life” (Rom. 6:23). In the Gospel this is called the kingdom prepared—that is, predestined—for the elect, who were predestined from the foundation of the world.

Then he adds and says:

> “By predestination God established only those things which he himself was going to do either by gratuitous mercy or by a just judgment, according to [Col. 0112D] the Scripture that says, ‘He made the things that were to come’ (Isa. 65, according to the Septuagint). But in the wicked he foresaw their wickedness, because it comes from them, and did not predestine it, because it does not come from him. He certainly foresaw and predestined the punishment that follows their evil merit, since God foresees all things and predestined it because he is just.”

Florus, from whose work this compiler confusedly cut and extracted these words, is read to have set them down in a more orderly fashion. He says:

> “The omnipotent God foresaw their wickedness in the wicked, because it comes from them, and did not predestine it, because it does not come from him. But he both foresaw their punishment, because he is God, and predestined it, because he is just, so that in them there might be the merit of their condemnation, and in him the power and judgment [Col. 0113A] of the one who justly condemns. For God predestines only what he himself is going to do; but he foreknows many things which he himself is not going to do, such as all evils, which the wicked certainly do, not he.”

Hence Prosper says in his fifteenth response against the Gauls:

> “Whoever in no respect distinguishes God’s foreknowledge from his predestination attempts to ascribe to God, in the case of evils also, what must be ascribed to him in the case of good things. But since good things are to be referred to God as their giver and co-worker, while evils are to be referred to the voluntary wickedness of rational creation, there is no doubt that, without any temporal distinction, God both [Col. 0113B] foreknew and predestined those things which were to be done with him as their author, or which were to be repaid to evil merits by a just judgment. But he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, those things whose operative cause was not to come from him. Foreknowledge can therefore exist without predestination, but predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge.”

However this confused compiler may have arranged these matters, we think that we can understand what he says:

> “By predestination God established only those things which he himself was going to do either by gratuitous mercy or by a just judgment, according to the Scripture that says, ‘He made the things that were to come.’ But in the wicked he foresaw their wickedness, because it comes from them, and did not predestine it, because it does not come from him. He certainly foresaw and predestined the punishment that follows their evil merit, since God foresees all things and predestined it because he is just.”

For blessed Augustine says, and Prosper makes perfectly clear from his words, that God’s [Col. 0113C] predestination is either directed toward the gift of grace by which the elect are delivered, or toward the retribution of justice by which the unjust are punished. He rightly wrote—although he did not understand what he took from another’s words—that by predestination God established what he himself was going to do either by gratuitous mercy or by a just judgment: by mercy he established the deliverance of the elect; by judgment he predestined punishment for the unjust. This is all God’s predestination, which is directed either toward the gift of grace or toward the retribution of justice.

Let him now explain how God predestined those who perish to destruction, since in the second chapter he said that they “remained in the mass of condemnation either by original or even by actual desert”; and in the third chapter he boldly confessed “the predestination of the elect to life, and the predestination [Col. 0113D] of the wicked to death”; and afterward he said, “The elect are saved by mercy; punishment is predestined for the unjust by judgment.”

His composition expresses precisely this meaning. How, then, can the unjust now again be understood as predestined by God to punishment? For if they are predestined by God to destruction, they undoubtedly perish by God’s predestination, just as those predestined to salvation are saved by God’s predestination. And if the reprobate perish by God’s predestination, let them say who is the author of their destruction.

Hence Prosper says in his sixteenth response against the Vincentians:

> “Those who will not persevere—that is, those who will perish—fall away not by God’s work but by their own will, although they are foreknown as destined to [Col. 0114A] fall and depart from the one who cannot be deceived.”

In these two chapters, this disorderly composer said that the reprobate were left in the mass of perdition and again predestined to destruction. After this he said that the same people, first left behind and afterward predestined to destruction, were foreknown in their evils but not predestined, while their punishment was predestined. A monstrous concoction, formed by transformation from the mountain of Lycia:

> “First a lion, last a dragon, and in the middle the Chimaera itself.”

Why does he seek hiding places? Truth has no corners. Why does it adapt itself to everything by evasive argument? It says what the Catholics say—or rather, it eagerly adapts itself to those things—and it asserts with all its strength what the heretics say. Like the chameleon, which is said immediately to change itself into whatever colors it sees, and like the fable told of Aesop’s [Col. 0114B] beard, in which the deceitful servant’s master could always find whatever statement he made about it, so this man adjusts his position in such a way that, accommodating himself both to Catholics and to the unruly, while presenting himself to both sides, he agrees with neither.

After saying, “He certainly foresaw and predestined the punishment that follows their evil merit, since God foresees all things and predestined it because he is just,” he added:

> “With him, as Saint Augustine says, there is concerning absolutely all things a decree as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain.”

What Saint Augustine most appropriately set down is true, but this disorderly composer has used it here most inappropriately. God foreknows nothing that [Col. 0114C] is not altogether going to happen; nor can anything be going to happen that God has not foreknown. Yet those who perish do not perish because God foreknows that they will perish; rather, God foreknows them as going to perish because they are going to perish.

As Prosper says in his thirteenth response against the Vincentians:

> “Although from eternal foreknowledge he has known in advance what he will repay to each person according to his merits, nevertheless by this fact—that he cannot be deceived—he has imposed on no one either a necessity or a will to sin. If, therefore, anyone falls away from justice and piety, he is carried headlong by his own choice, drawn by his own desire, and deceived by his own persuasion. There the Father does nothing, the Son does nothing, and the Holy Spirit does nothing; nor does anything of the divine will intervene in such an affair. By [Col. 0114D] his work we know that many are held back lest they fall, but none are driven to fall.”

And in the fifteenth response:

> “If, therefore, one lives in holiness, advances in virtue, and perseveres in good pursuits, this is plainly God’s gift, without which no fruit of any good work is acquired. But if one withdraws from these things and turns to vices and sins, God puts no evil temptation there; he does not abandon the one who is about to depart before that person abandons him, and he often causes him not to depart, or, even if he has departed, to return. But why he retains one person and does not retain another cannot be comprehended, nor is it lawful to investigate, when it is enough to know that the standing comes from him, while the falling does not come from him.”

And Prosper says in his book *Sentences* (chap. 379): [Col. 0115A]

> “God compels no one to sin; yet he foresees those who will sin by their own will. Why, then, should the just one not avenge what, although foreknowing it, he does not compel?”

Therefore it is true that this excerptor inserted here from Florus’s work, though in disordered sequence, when he said:

> “But in the wicked he foresaw their wickedness, because it comes from them, and did not predestine it, because it does not come from him. He certainly foresaw and predestined the punishment that follows their evil merit, since God foresees all things and predestined it because he is just.”

As for Augustine’s statement which he appended—“Concerning absolutely all things, his decree is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain”—Saint Prosper, in the aforementioned book (chap. 157), explains that Augustine did not say it in the sense in which this compiler of the chapter inserted it, wishing to prove from it that the [Col. 0115B] reprobate were predestined to destruction just as the elect were predestined to life. Prosper says:

> “God’s anger is not a disturbance in him, but the judgment by which punishment is inflicted for sin. His thinking and rethinking of changing things is an unchangeable order. For God, unlike a human being, does not repent of any action of his; for concerning all things his decree is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain.”

Prosper explains the final part of this statement in the same book (chap. 291), saying:

> “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills” (Ps. 110:2). “He foresees that the good will be good and creates them; he foresees that the wicked will be wicked and creates them, offering himself to the good for enjoyment, bestowing many of his gifts even upon the wicked, mercifully forgiving and justly avenging. Again, he mercifully avenges and justly [Col. 0115C] forgives, fearing nothing from anyone’s wickedness, needing nothing from anyone’s justice, seeking nothing for himself from the works of the good, and providing even for the good through the punishments of the wicked.”

And again (chap. 140):

> “God would not have created any angel or human being whom he had foreknown would become evil unless he had likewise known for what useful purposes among the good he would commend them; and thus he adorned the order of the ages as a most beautiful poem, even from certain antitheses.”

The God who foreknows and predestines all good things does these things: he foreknows but does not predestine all evils. With him, concerning absolutely all things, his decree is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain, because nothing else and nothing otherwise will occur except what—and as—he [Col. 0115D] foreknows; and God foreknew beforehand what would occur and in what manner it would occur. Yet his foreknowledge did not compel evils to happen. Rather, he foreknew beforehand the things that were going to happen, as it is written:

> “Eternal God, knower of hidden things, who know all things before they happen” (Dan. 13:42).

The compiler’s further addition in the chapter is also suited to this meaning:

> “Judgments are prepared for scoffers, and hammers striking the bodies of fools” (Prov. 19:29).

This can appropriately be understood in the sense in which he wrote that God “foresaw and predestined the punishment that follows their evil merit, since he foresees all things and predestined it because he is just.” We do not fail to understand why he placed it there; nevertheless [Col. 0116A], so that the statement may in some way stand together, we wish to interpret it.

Concerning this testimony, the venerable priest Bede, following the opinions of the Fathers, says in book 11 of his commentary on Proverbs: [Col. 0116B]

> “‘Judgments are prepared for scoffers, and hammers striking the bodies of fools.’ Even if the reprobate,” he says, “as has been foretold, scoff at the judgment of the divine command or threat, judgments of condemnation nevertheless await them, which will strike them without end in the furnace of Gehenna as hammers strike heated iron.”

Hence Saint Gregory says in the fifteenth book of the *Moralia*:

> “The justice of the Almighty, foreknowing the future, created from the very beginning of the world a fire which would begin to exist once for the punishment of the reprobate, but which would never bring its burning to an end, even without wood.”

And Saint Jerome, in the tenth book of his commentary on the prophet Isaiah:

> “From yesterday, and from former time, Topheth has been prepared by the king and lord—that is, broad and spacious Gehenna—which will burn them, that is, the impious, with eternal fires.”

What immediately follows concerning the immutability of God’s foreknowledge and predestination, by which future things are already done for him, is also well understood as having been said in Ecclesiastes:

> “I know that all the works which God has made endure forever; we cannot add anything to them or take anything away from them, which God has made so that he may be feared” (Eccl. 3:14).

It must be examined in the treatises of the Doctors how this example supports his opinion, by which he attempts to assert that, just as the elect are predestined by God to life, so also the reprobate are predestined by God to punishment. For Jerome says in his exposition of Ecclesiastes (ch. 31):

> “I have understood,” he says, “that all the things which God has made will themselves endure forever: nothing can be added to them, and nothing can be taken away from them; and God has made them so that they may fear before him.”

“There is nothing,” he says, “in the world that is new. The course of the sun, the changes of the moon, and the dryness or greenness of the earth and of the trees were born and created together with the world itself. And therefore God has ordered all things according to a fixed rational plan, and has commanded the elements to serve human uses, so that, seeing these things, human beings may understand that there is providence, and may fear before God, while from the equality, course, order, and constancy of things they understand the Creator. For his invisible attributes are clearly perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made, as are his eternal power and divinity (Rom. I, 20).

“But if we wish to read the preceding sense as complete, almost from the beginning—‘And God made them so that they may fear before him’—the meaning is this: God made all these things so that human beings might fear to deviate from what God once established. He has beautifully tempered the expression by saying, ‘so that they may fear before him.’ For the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

And Alcuin, in his explanation of the same book, addressed to his disciples Onias the priest, Candidus the presbyter, and Nathanael the deacon, says:

> “I have learned that all the works which God has made endure forever. We cannot add anything to them, nor take away anything from what God has made, so that he may be feared” (Eccl. III, 14).

“There is nothing,” he says, “in the world that is new. The course of the sun, the changes of the moon, and the dryness or greenness of the earth and of the trees were born and created together with the world itself. And therefore God has ordered all things according to a fixed rational plan, and has commanded the elements to serve human uses, so that, seeing these things, human beings may understand that there is the providence of God, and may fear before God, while from the equality, course, order, and constancy of things they understand the Creator.”

And since we have demonstrated by the opinions of the Doctors how this testimony from Ecclesiastes accords with his support for his position—namely, that it does not accord with it at all—let Prosper answer him from Book II, chapter 33, of *The Calling of the Nations*, on the basis of what he had prefaced: “Concerning this immutability of God’s foreknowledge and predestination, through which future things are already accomplished in his sight”:

> “There is,” he says, “in God no accidental movement, no new will, no temporal deliberation, nor does his thought vary with the inequality of mutable things. Rather, he comprehends all times and temporal things together in an eternal and stable vision, and he has already assigned to all people all things, since he has already made the things that are to be future. Hence comes that saying of the blessed Apostle Paul, writing to the Ephesians: ‘Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight in love; he predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, in himself, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace’ (Eph. I, 3), and so forth”—as every devout or inquisitive reader may find there more fully and at greater length—“which he connects under the preaching of the same meaning, teaching that the gift and work of grace have always remained in the eternal counsel of God, and that all the sons of adoption were chosen not only at the time when, already existing, they were called, but also before the world was established.

“In this election, no human being who has not been foreknown in Christ will be joined to him for any reason. For all who are to come to the kingdom of God from the calling of whatever age have been marked out in this adoption, which preceded all ages. And just as no unbeliever has been numbered among this company, so no devout person has been separated from this blessing. For from the fullness of the members of Christ’s body, the foreknowledge of God—which cannot be deceived—loses nothing and cannot be diminished by any loss. The whole has been foreknown and chosen beforehand in Christ before the eternal ages. As the Apostle writes to Timothy: ‘Labor with the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with his holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us before eternal times’ (II Tim. I, 8).”

And Saint Augustine, in *On the Predestination of the Saints* (ch. 18), says:

> “This is the immutable truth of predestination and grace, as the Apostle says: ‘He chose us in him before the foundation of the world’ (Eph. I, 4). God therefore chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, predestining us for adoption as sons—not because we were going to be holy and blameless through ourselves, but he chose and predestined us in order that we might be so. He did this according to the good pleasure of his will, so that no one might glory in his own will toward God, but in God’s will toward him.

“He did this according to the riches of his glory, according to his good will, which he set forth in his beloved Son. In him we have obtained a share, having been predestined according to a purpose—not our purpose, but that of him who works all things—so completely that he himself works in us even the willing. He works according to the counsel of his will, so that we may be to the praise of his glory.”

And again, chapter 17:

> “From this purpose of his comes that particular calling of the elect, for whom all things work together for good, who are called according to his purpose; and the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.”

And again:

> “He therefore chose them from the world while he was living here in the flesh, but they had already been chosen in himself before the foundation of the world.”

Such is the orthodox faith concerning the predestination of the saints. Let the compiler of these chapters make the effort and say that God predestined the reprobate, the impious, the unjust, and those destined to perish, before the foundation of the world, to destruction, perdition, and punishment. We do not dare to say this, because the Apostle did not say it, nor did the Lord Jesus Christ, speaking through him. Nor did the blessed Augustine, correcting his writings with a more carefully revised style and a censor’s pen, command us to preach such things from those same writings.

The same blessed Augustine says in the same book (the same chapter):

> “They were therefore chosen—indeed, predestined—before the foundation of the world by that predestination in which God foreknew his future works as already accomplished. They were chosen from the world by that calling through which God fulfilled what he predestined. For those whom he predestined, he also called, namely, with the calling according to his purpose. Therefore he called not others, but those whom he predestined; nor did he justify others, but those whom he called in this way; and those whom he predestined, called, and justified, he also glorified—at that end which has no end.”

And again (ch. 18):

> “God chose,” he says, “his members in Christ before the foundation of the world. And how could he choose those who did not yet exist, except by predestining them? He therefore chose us by predestining us. Would he choose the impious and the unclean? For if the question were posed whether he chooses these or rather the holy and blameless, who would seek to know what answer should be given, rather than immediately pronounce judgment in favor of the holy and blameless?”

And again in *On the Predestination of the Saints* (ch. 15):

> “There is also,” he says, “a most splendid light of predestination and grace: the Savior himself, the Mediator himself between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.”

And again in the same work:

> “This, then, is the predestination of the saints, which was supremely manifested in the Holy of Holies. Who among those rightly understanding the words of truth could deny it? For we have also learned that the Lord of glory himself, insofar as he was made human, was predestined as the Son of God. The Doctor of the Nations cries out at the beginning of his Epistles: ‘Paul, servant of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle’ (Rom. I, 1), and so forth, until he says: ‘who was predestined as the Son of God in power.’”

And again in the same book:

> “Therefore, just as that one was predestined to be our head, so we, the many, have been predestined to be his members.”

And again (ch. 16):

> “For God calls many predestined people his sons, so that he may make them members of his one predestined Son.”

And at the end of *On the Gift of Perseverance* (ch. 24):

> “There is no more illustrious example of predestination,” he says, “than Jesus himself. I have already discussed this in the first book, and at the end of this one I have chosen to commend it. There is, I say, no more illustrious example of predestination than the Mediator himself. Whoever among the faithful wishes to understand it properly should attend to him and find himself in him. I mean the faithful person who believes and confesses that he possesses a true human nature—our nature—which, although uniquely assumed by God the Word, has been exalted into the one Son of God, so that he who assumed and that which he assumed might be one person in the Trinity.”

Behold the head; behold the light of the predestined; behold the example of predestination. Therefore, let those who say that the reprobate were predestined to destruction say by whom they were predestined. Let them produce an example of their predestination; let them show the head of such predestined people; let them demonstrate their light, since they cannot demonstrate light, but only their darkness.

Against those who say that the reprobate were predestined to destruction, Saint Prosper says in his *Response to the Twelve Objections of the Vincentians*:

> “Those of whom it is said, ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us’ (I John II, 19), went out by their will and fell by their will. And because they were foreknown as destined to fall, they were not predestined. They would have been predestined if they had been destined to return and remain in holiness and truth. Thus God’s predestination is for many a cause of standing; it is the cause of falling for no one.”

And Saint Augustine, in *On the Gift of Perseverance* (ch. 8), says:

> “Why perseverance to the end is given to one of two devout people and not given to the other—God’s judgments in this matter are inscrutable. Yet this ought to be absolutely certain to the faithful: the one is among the predestined, the other is not. For if they had been of us,” said one of the predestined, who had drunk this secret from the Lord’s breast, “they would certainly have remained with us.”

“What does ‘they were not of us’ mean, I ask, except ‘if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us’? Were not both created by God, both born from Adam, both made from the earth, and did they not receive souls of one and the same nature from him who said, ‘I have made every breath’ (Isa. LVII, 18)? Finally, had not both been called, and followed the one who called them? Were not both justified from the impious, and both renewed through the washing of regeneration?”

According to all these respects, they were of us. And shortly afterward:

> “They were not predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things.”

Consider what the blessed Augustine says: this one is among the predestined, that one is not. Why did he not say, “this one is among those predestined to life, and that one among those predestined to destruction”?

And Prosper, in his recapitulation of the tenth objection of the Gauls, says:

> “The one who has been predestined therefore lives by the faith given to him; the one who has not been predestined perishes through voluntary, not compelled, unbelief.”

And in his *Book of Sentences* (ch. 28):
