> “If we consider all of them together—some of whom are saved by mercy, while others are condemned by truth—the universal ways of the Lord, that is, mercy and truth, are separated in their outcome.”

Finally, the compiler of the chapters concludes by saying:

> “But that some have been predestined to evil by divine power, namely, so that they supposedly could not be anything else, we not only do not believe; if there are people who wish to believe such a great evil, we also pronounce an anathema against them with complete abhorrence, just as the Synod of Orange did.”

Let him do as he promised. Let him read that entire synod and see whether he can find that the holy synod said in any way that people were predestined to destruction. If he finds this there, let him say what that synod said. But if he does not find what he has said there, let him say what he said in such a way that he says nothing other than the truth, since he professed that he would say what that synod said. For if he says something else or adds anything contrary to the faith, it is clear that, in pronouncing an anathema against those who hold the contrary view, he is not speaking as that synod spoke, since that synod deviated in no respect from the catholic faith.

And since Scripture calls “evil” not only sin but also the punishment of the sinner, let him examine the opinions of Catholics to determine whether a human being should be understood as predestined neither to the evil of sin nor to the punishment due for sin, but rather whether punishment should be understood as predestined, by the retribution of justice, for the person who voluntarily sins, as something owed by the just Judge.

In Scripture, evil is indeed called affliction, as it is written: “Sufficient for the day is its evil” (Matt. VI, 34), which the Doctors interpret as referring to affliction. Likewise, a day is called evil, not because it is evil, but because it is evil for those who do evil. So too eternal fire is evil for the sinners who are tormented by it, namely, for evil angels and human beings—not in the good nature of the divine works by which angels, human beings, and the fire of Gehenna itself were created, but through the operation of evil. The beginning of that operation is unbelief, namely, abandonment of the truth, just as the beginning of salvation is recognized to be faith, given by the grace of the giver.

The same fire, which could not harm the angels and human beings who stood firm, punishes the transgression of those who fell through the retribution of justice. Likewise, the flame of the Babylonian furnace burned the bonds of the innocent and did not scorch even one of their hairs, but, spreading around the furnace, it burned the servants of the king whom it found there and who had heated it. The fire of the dreadful judgment, which goes before the Judge who is to come, will kindle his enemies all around, and it will be passable for the saints who go to meet him.

This visible sun also illuminates the world and harms diseased eyes—not from itself, but because of the afflictions of the eyes. It does not itself act differently in different cases when it melts wax and hardens clay. Bread strengthens the life of the strong but kills the little ones; a gentle hiss calms horses but incites puppies; poison is death to a human being and life to a serpent.

Thus, in Egypt, one operation of God’s signs softened the hearts of believers and hardened unbelievers, because, according to their hardness and unrepentant heart, they stored up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath from these miracles, which they saw being performed but did not believe. The word of preachers is for some an aroma of life leading to life, and for others an aroma of death leading to death.

So also, through its operation, eternal fire becomes evil for the fugitive spirits and reprobate human beings, while through divine creation it is good.

Nor has a human being been predestined by God to this evil—namely, death without death—any more than to the death of the soul or of the body. Adam, as is well known, through sin incurred the death of the soul together with his entire offspring. Of this it is written: “God did not make death” (Wis. I, 13). Therefore he received death from the just Judge who exacts punishment—that is, in the separation of soul and body—and, unless he has been freed by the grace of God before that separation, he receives eternal torment of soul and body.

This is the death in which, when the soul departs, the flesh alone dies and the soul is tortured by punishments, until, returning to the flesh, it is punished eternally in and with that same flesh in which it sinned. Thus, with the flesh with which it shared in the death of sin—which God’s goodness forbade human beings—it shares also in the death of punishment, which divine justice prepared for the sinner.

Of this death our Savior says: “Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28). Of it also it is written: “Death and life are from the Lord God” (Ecclus. XI, 14), as Augustine explains: life is from the giver, and death from the avenger.

And as Prosper says in his *Book of Sentences* (ch. 295):

> “It is the just judgment of God that each person should perish through his own sin, since God does not make sin, just as he did not make death; yet he kills the one whom he judges worthy of death. Hence we read, ‘God did not make death’ (Wis. I, 13), and, ‘Death and life are from God’ (Ecclus. XI, 14). Whoever distinguishes divine judgments from divine works does not see that these two statements are certainly contrary to one another. For it is one thing not to have established mortality by creating, and another thing to punish the sinner by judging.”

And again (ch. 296):

> “God indeed made the world and absolutely all bodies; but that the corruptible body should weigh down the soul and the flesh lust against the spirit was not the prior nature of the human being who was created, but the punishment of the one who was condemned.”

And again, *Against the Gauls* (ch. 14):

> “God’s predestination is that which, in the elect and the reprobate, pertains either to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice.”

Paul confirms this when he says: “The wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life” (Rom. VI, 23). Thus the good and merciful God eternally crowns in a human being what has been rightly done in time, because a person who, through God’s grace preceding, accompanying, and following him, guarded himself from sins by his will and right intention, insofar as human frailty permits—or withdrew from sins or unbelief before death—and persevered in right faith and good works until the end of bodily life, would always have wished to live for God, if he had been able always to live in the body without the intervention of death.

Conversely, through the wages of sin, namely eternal death, the eternal and just God eternally avenges what was done wickedly by the human being in time, because the person who willingly persevered in unbelief and sins until the end of bodily life would always have wished to sin, if he had been able always to live according to his own desire.

Hence Prosper says in his *Book of Sentences* (ch. 276):

> “It is natural for us to wish to live; but to live wickedly is no longer a matter of nature, but of a perverse will, which punishment justly follows.”

But because, just as a human being is not predestined to the evil of sin, so neither is he predestined to the evil of death, Augustine demonstrates this in Book IV of *The Trinity*, saying (ch. 12):

> “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Rom. V, 12). The devil was the mediator of this way, the persuader to sin and the one who plunged us into death. For, in bringing about our double death, he brought his own single death. Having died in spirit through impiety, he did not die in the flesh. But he persuaded us to impiety as well, and on account of it caused us to become deserving of coming into the death of the flesh.

“We therefore desired one thing through an evil persuasion, and the other followed us through a just condemnation. For this reason it is written, ‘God did not make death’ (Wis. I, 13), because he himself was not the cause of death. Yet, through his retribution, the most just death was inflicted on the sinner, just as a judge inflicts punishment on the accused; the cause of the punishment, however, is not the judge’s justice but the merit of the crime.

“Therefore, to the death to which the mediator of death led us, although he himself did not come—namely, the death of the flesh—our Lord God inserted for us the medicine of correction, which he did not merit, through the hidden and exceedingly secret ordering of divine and profound justice.

“Thus, just as death came through one human being, so the resurrection of the dead might come through one human being, because human beings feared more what they could not avoid—the death of the flesh—than the death of the spirit; that is, they feared punishment more than the merit of punishment. For not sinning is either not cared about or cared about very little, whereas not dying, although it cannot be attained, is earnestly pursued.

“The Mediator of life therefore showed that death should not be feared, since through human condition it can no longer be avoided, but rather impiety, which can be guarded against through faith.”

And the rest, which he develops there.

Prosper says in his *Book of Sentences* (ch. 251):

> “The human being had been made immortal; God willed him to be divine. He did not lose what he was as a human being, but he lost what he was as an immortal, and from the disobedience of pride punishment was contracted by nature.”

Behold, these catholic Doctors show that a human being is predestined by God neither to the evil of sin nor to the evil of punishment, but that, through the retribution of justice, just as the death of the body, so also destruction has been assigned to him as the due consequence of just vengeance and punishment.

## CHAPTER XIII. On what Fulgentius wrote in his book addressed to Monimus: that God’s predestination is spoken of not only in relation to good but also in relation to evil

Now let us examine what Fulgentius said in the book mentioned above, addressed to Monimus: that God’s predestination is spoken of not only in relation to good but also in relation to evil.

Let the blessed Augustine answer him from *On the Predestination of the Saints*, a work which Fulgentius himself had praised, as it deserves to be praised. For he says (ch. 10):

> “Therefore God’s predestination, which is directed toward good, is, as I have said, the preparation of grace, while grace is the effect of that predestination itself.”

Let Fulgentius himself take care to be healed by the remedy which he proposed. For, as we have already stated, he says in the aforementioned book (*Book I, addressed to Monimus*, ch. 30):

> “To this depravity, which was brought forward against the statements of the blessed Augustine not from truth but from envy, Prosper replied in the following words: ‘The unbelief of those who do not believe the Gospel is in no way generated by God’s predestination; for God is the author of good things, not of evil things. God’s predestination, therefore, is always directed toward good, whether it pertains to the retribution of justice or to the gift of grace. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth’ (Ps. XXIV, 10).”

[Col. 0123B] Again, with pardon to lord Fulgentius, let us point out another matter that troubles us in his words. In the book cited above, as we have shown (the same chapter), he says:

> “You are not unaware,” he says, “that in the past some Gauls also brought an accusation against that brilliant work of the holy Augustine, which he wrote on the predestination of the saints: namely, that in asserting divine predestination the blessed Augustine said that sinners were predestined not only to judgment but also to sin. Because Augustine himself was quickly overtaken by death, Prosper, an educated and holy man, defended his statements in the right faith [variant: ‘defended them rightly in faithful fashion’] and at length. Of the chapters of these Gauls, so as not to set out many here—for fear that the necessity which compels us to make this little book lengthy by discussion might appear to make it still longer by choice—we have decided to insert two passages of the responses.”

Leaving aside those responses, which contradict him more openly, although these themselves also openly resist him, and which Prosper gave in answer to the objections collected from the same books, he turns to other passages, saying:

> “The fourteenth objection of the Gauls is stated as follows: that those who do not believe the evangelical preaching do not believe through God’s predestination, and that God has determined it in such a way that whoever does not believe does not believe by God’s own ordinance.”

To this depravity, which was brought forward against the statements of the blessed Augustine not from truth but from envy, Prosper replied in the following words:

> “The unbelief of those who do not believe the Gospel is in no way generated by God’s predestination; for God is the author of good things, not of evil things. God’s predestination, therefore, is always directed toward good, whether it pertains to the retribution of justice or to the gift of grace. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10).

> “Therefore the unbelief of those who do not believe is to be referred not to God’s constitution but to his foreknowledge. His foreknowledge did not impose the necessity of not believing, because it could not be deceived concerning the unbelief that was going to occur.”

The fifteenth objection is also inserted in these words:

> “That foreknowledge is the same thing as predestination.”

Prosper answered it as follows:

> “Whoever does not distinguish God’s foreknowledge in any respect from his predestination attempts to ascribe to God, in the case of evil things, what ought to be attributed to him in the case of good things. But since good things are to be referred to God, their giver and co-worker, while evil things are to be referred to the voluntary wickedness of the rational creature, there is no doubt that, without any temporal distinction, God simultaneously foreknew and predestined those things which were to be done with him as their author, or which were to be repaid by a just judgment for evil merits.

“But he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, those things which were not going to have from him the cause of their operation.”

After this, he brought the book to an end.

But why he abandoned Prosper’s clearer responses, to which he had appealed, and inserted these instead, let him see for himself. We, however, because Fulgentius has appealed to them, have judged it appropriate to set forth the objections and responses mentioned by Fulgentius from the aforementioned books of the blessed Augustine, so that, if they should perhaps refuse to listen to us, they may hear the counsel of Fulgentius, whom they themselves call their supporter, which we shall produce hereafter.

For the blessed Prosper says to Camillus and Theodotus, presbyters of the city of Genoa:

> “In the books of blessed memory Augustine, whose title is *On the Predestination of the Saints*, certain things have disturbed your holiness, whether because they are unfamiliar or because they are less clear.”

Proceeding through seven objections and responses, he reaches the eighth, in which it is said:

> “Next follows what is found in the second book: ‘Will anyone dare to say that God did not foreknow to whom he was going to give the gift of believing, or whom he was going to give to his Son, so that he would lose none of them? If he foreknew these things, he certainly foreknew his benefits, by which he graciously deigns to free us. This is the predestination of the saints: nothing else but the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are freed are most certainly freed. But where are the others left except in the mass of perdition, by a just divine judgment? Where were the Tyrians and Sidonians left, who could also have believed if they had seen those marvelous signs of Christ? (Matt. XI, 21.) But since it had not been given to them to believe, even the means by which they might believe was denied them.’”

To this Saint Prosper responded—him whom Fulgentius praised for his faith and extensive discourse:

> “Those who resist these statements are shown most clearly to hold that faith is not a gift of God, that grace does not precede free will but follows it, and that God’s grace is given according to our merits.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Truly, those who think in this way have not received faith, or they have lost the faith they had received.”

And again, after a little:

> “Let us therefore understand wisely and confess devoutly that God immutably foreknew to whom he would give the gift of believing, or whom he would give to his Son so that he would lose none of them. If he foreknew these things, he foreknew his benefits, by which he graciously deigns to free us; and this is the predestination of the saints, namely, the predestination and preparation of God’s benefits by which all who are freed are most certainly freed.

“As for the others, whom grace did not rescue from the general perdition of the human race, let us know that they were not rescued by a just judgment, and let us learn from them what has been remitted to us, since we cannot complain about their condemnation. For there is no injustice with God (Rom. IX, 14), nor does anyone innocent perish under his judgment (Job IV, 7).”

And the rest, which we have omitted here for the sake of brevity, and which anyone who reads with diligence or curiosity will be able to find in its proper places.

Now let those who rely upon the statements of Fulgentius hear his own counsel. For in the aforementioned book, as though addressing their little synagogue in *To Monimus* (Book I, near the end), he says:

> “For this reason, dearest brother, we have preferred to insert these few passages for the present from the books of Saint Augustine and from Prosper’s responses, so that everyone may know what they ought to think concerning the predestination of the saints and of the impious.”

What all ought to think on this matter according to his counsel, he himself explains at the beginning of the following book, addressed to the same Monimus (Book II, ch. 1):

> “The preceding discussion, dearest Monimus, has, as I think, sufficiently treated and resolved the question of the difference between the predestination of the just and that of the wicked—that is, between those whom God’s gratuitous mercy, coming beforehand, converts by justifying them and will glorify once converted, and those whom God’s just severity leaves in their sins in order to punish them when they are condemned—insofar as the Lord has deigned to assist our weakness.

“Thus, although many are accustomed to be seriously disturbed by this question, they can easily be instructed both by the testimonies of the divine books and by the books of Saint Augustine and the responses of the most learned man Prosper. From these they may recognize that God’s predestination is nothing other than the preparation of his works, which in his eternal disposition he foreknew he would accomplish either mercifully or justly.

“And because neither mercy nor justice is found in sins, the entire evil will of the wicked, by which they sin, was foreknown by God but was not predestined by God. They would not have possessed that evil will in any other way except by departing from the Lord. God did not predestine the human being’s departure from himself, since the cause of that departure was solely the sinner’s voluntary turning away. Because God was not unaware that this would occur, the evil will found in his eternal foreknowledge the punishment of just retribution prepared for itself.”

## CHAPTER XIV. An exhortation here follows to the unruly school of Gottschalk

Now hear, from Gottschalk’s school, whatever he may have said previously, the counsel of Fulgentius, and believe the statements of Augustine and Prosper which the same Fulgentius set forth shortly before:

> “God’s predestination,” he says, “is always directed toward good, whether it pertains to the retribution of justice or to the gift of grace. It is the predestination and preparation of God’s grace by which all who are freed are most certainly freed. As for the others, whom grace did not rescue from the general perdition of the human race, let us know that they were not rescued by a just judgment.

“And confess that the elect—that is, those elected by grace from the general mass of perdition (from *lego*, “I gather,” as in “you who gather flowers”)—are predestined, that is, prepared by grace for life. As for the others, let us confess that they were justly left in the mass of perdition; for them punishment has been predestined through the retribution of justice by the just Judge, just as eternal life has been given to the elect as a gift of grace by the most merciful Giver.

“For the Apostle also testifies to both things when he says: ‘The wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life’ (Rom. VI, 23).”

## CHAPTER XV. From whose words and from which scriptural statements the four chapters formerly excerpted by us against the re-emergent Predestinarians were collected and excerpted, and what the ancient Predestinarians said from them, and what modern heretics, delirious with these teachings, say

And since, concerning two chapters—whose source we do not know, but which were excerpted from the writing of Florus on the foreknowledge and predestination of God—we have responded individually to the statements set forth above, drawing on the words and meanings of orthodox writers according to the modest capacity of our understanding, we have judged it necessary, so that we may demonstrate more appropriately from whose words we collected the chapters excerpted by us and criticized by the compiler of the aforementioned chapters, to attach them in four bundles for the burning of the tares which the ancient Predestinarians sowed in the midst of the Lord’s wheat.

They composed their exceedingly pernicious doctrine concerning God’s foreknowledge and predestination with various wording but related and equal impiety. Augustine and Prosper refuted them most sufficiently in their writings, and the blessed Coelestine decreed against them.

The first of these propositions is that, according to foreknowledge, God condemns human beings on account of the merits of a life which they did not possess because they were overtaken by death, but which they would have possessed if they had lived.

The second is that, among those who are not predestined to life, the grace received in baptism does not remove original sin; and that, even if they have lived piously and justly, this benefits them nothing, but they are preserved only until they fall and perish.

It is also claimed that free will in the human being is nothing, but that God’s predestination operates in human beings either toward good or toward evil, because God fashions in human beings a will such as that of the demons, which by its own movement can will nothing other than evil.

The third proposition is that foreknowledge is the same thing as predestination.

The fourth is that they do not deny the predestination of the elect to life, but confess the predestination of the reprobate to destruction; and, just as they say that the reprobate were predestined by God to destruction, so also they say that they were predestined to sin.

The modern Predestinarians do not touch the first of these, leap over the second, evade the third, and alter the fourth by changing its appearance; yet they betray their understanding through the odor and flavor of their doctrine. For they say: “God predestined the reprobate to destruction, not to sin,” although no one can reach destruction except through sin.

These four heresies blessed Augustine and Prosper—and, later in time but earlier in place, Saint Gregory—dissolve by judging them equal in character and condemning them equally. For blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints* (ch. 13):

> “I cannot say how deeply I am distressed that what the Pelagians recognized as utterly false and absurd was not recognized by these men, who, together with us, condemn the error of those heretics by Catholic authority. Cyprian wrote his book *On Mortality* (ch. 14), commendably known to many, indeed almost all, who love ecclesiastical writings; in it he says that death is not merely not harmful to the faithful, but is even found to be beneficial, because it removes a person from the dangers of sinning and establishes him in security from sinning. But what does that profit him if even future sins that have not been committed are punished? Yet he says, most fully and excellently, that the dangers of sinning neither fail to be present in this life nor remain after this life. There he also cites the testimony from the Book of Wisdom: ‘He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding’ (Wis. 4:11). You have said that these brothers rejected this testimony when I cited it, as though it had not been taken from a Catholic book. [Col. 0127A] As though, apart from the testimony of this book, the matter itself—which we wish to establish from it—were not clear!

> “For what Christian would dare deny that a righteous person, if overtaken by death, will be in a place of refreshment? Whatever person said this, what person of sound faith would think that it ought to be resisted? Likewise, if someone says that a righteous person, after withdrawing from his righteousness in which he lived for a long time, and dying in the ungodliness in which he lived—not merely for one year, but for one day—will go from here to the punishments due to the wicked, and that his former righteousness will profit him nothing, what believer contradicts this evident truth? Moreover, if we are asked whether, had he died at the time when he was righteous, he would have found punishment or rest, shall we hesitate to answer ‘rest’? This is the whole reason why it was said, by whomever it was said: ‘He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding’ (Wis. 4:11). [Col. 0127B] For it was said with reference to the dangers of this life, not with reference to the foreknowledge of God, who foreknew what would be future, not what would not be future—that is, he foreknew that he would grant him an untimely death so that he might be removed from the uncertainty of temptations, not that he would sin, since he would not remain in temptation.”

And a little later:

> “For if people were judged according to the merits of their life, which they did not have because they were overtaken by death, but would have had if they had lived, then it would profit nothing either the person who was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding, or those who die after falling, if they had died earlier—which no Christian will dare say. Therefore our brothers ought not to assert what, I should think, no one would believe, indeed no one would even dream: namely, that each of the dead is judged according to what he would have done had he lived for a longer time.”

And Saint Gregory says in the twenty-seventh book of the *Moralia* (ch. 2):

> “Well is it said through Solomon: ‘As you do not know what is the way of the spirit, or how bones are formed in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all things’ (Ecclus. 11:5). To speak of one instance among many: two infants come into this light, but to one it is granted to return to redemption through baptism, while the other is taken away before the regenerating water has washed him; often the child of the faithful is taken away without faith, and often the child of unbelievers is renewed through the sacrament of faith that has been granted. But perhaps someone may say that God knew that this person would act wickedly even after baptism, and therefore did not bring him to the grace of baptism. [Col. 0128A] If that is so, then without doubt the sins of some are punished before they have been committed. And who, knowing what is right, would say that the almighty God, who frees some from crimes already committed, condemns in others crimes that have not even been committed? His judgments, therefore, are hidden; and to the extent that they cannot be seen because of their profound obscurity, to that same extent they must be revered with humility.”

Prosper, in his work *Against the Gauls* (ch. 11), demonstrates concerning a second point:

> “All sins are forgiven in the baptism of Christ; but whoever withdraws from Christ after baptism and ends this life alienated from grace is condemned not because of those things that were forgiven him in baptism, but because of the crimes that he afterward committed. When he fell into these and died without repentance, he did not have the necessity of perishing because he was not predestined; rather, he was not predestined because God foreknew that he would be such through voluntary transgression. [Col. 0128B] He says that free choice exists in man (ch. 6), but that before the illumination of faith man remains in darkness and in the shadow of death, until he is freed by God’s grace from the dominion of the devil. In good actions, therefore, the will is to be understood as deriving from grace; in evil actions, the will is to be understood as existing without grace.”

Concerning the third point the same Prosper says (ch. 15):

> “There is no doubt that, without any temporal distinction, God both foreknew and predestined those things which were to be done with him as their author, or which were to be repaid to evil merits by a just judgment; but he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, those things that were not to derive from him the cause of their being done. [Col. 0128C] Foreknowledge, therefore, can exist without predestination, but predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge.”

Concerning the fourth point as well, blessed Prosper dissolves and rejects the argument, drawing on the words of Saint Augustine from the book entitled *On the Good of Perseverance*, in his eighth response against the Januenses (ch. 9), from the book entitled *On the Good of Perseverance*:

> “Let us wisely recognize and piously confess that God unchangeably foreknew those to whom he would give the gift of believing, or those whom he would give to his Son so that he would lose none of them. And if he foreknew these things, he also foreknew the benefits by which he graciously deigns to free us; and this is the predestination of the saints, namely, the predestination and preparation of God’s grace, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. As for the rest, whom grace did not remove from the general perdition of the human race, let us understand that they were not removed by a just judgment; [Col. 0128D]”

And in his explanation of the third objection of the Gauls he says concerning the passage:

> “Those, therefore, who, having fallen into such evils, died without correction through repentance did not have the necessity of perishing because they were not predestined; rather, they were not predestined because they were foreknown as destined to be such through voluntary transgression.”

And shortly afterward:

> “They were not abandoned by God so that they might abandon God; rather, they abandoned him and were abandoned, and by their own will were changed from good to evil. Therefore, although they had been reborn and justified, they were nevertheless not predestined by the one who foreknew that they would be such.”

[Col. 0129A] The ancient Predestinarians also devised two further arguments, so that they might more forcefully confirm their opinion: that God predestined the reprobate both to sin and to destruction—namely, because he does not wish all human beings to be saved, but only a fixed number of the predestined, even if all wished to be saved; and that the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world, since it is certain that he wishes all human beings to be saved, as the Apostle says (1 Tim. 2:4), and died for all (1 Pet. 3:18), as Peter says, he clearly wishes no one to perish and must not be believed to have predestined anyone to destruction.

Against these four chapters, compelled by the attack of the new Predestinarians, we have once again been forced to extract four chapters from the sayings and opinions of the Catholic Fathers. Each of these, [Col. 0129B] just as we found them written in the chapters previously given to us three years ago by Your Lordship and held at the Council of Valence, was rejected, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, through the critic’s condemnation—as it pleased him, not God, to say. Therefore it is necessary for us to show whose words we carefully extracted them from, so that it may become more evident whether those men ought to be believed to have spoken by the Holy Spirit, whose words every reader will find in the chapters excerpted by us.

When this has been established, no one will doubt that the rejecter of these chapters belonged to the number of those of whom it is written: “They prophesied from their own heart, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ when the Lord had not spoken” (Ezek. 13:2, 11). Likewise, as the Lord says through the prophet concerning a wall built or plastered without proper mixture: “Go and say to that wall that it will fall,” while he pronounces woe upon its builders. [Col. 0129C] And elsewhere the Lord again says to the prophet: “See, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and tear down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant” (Jer. 1:10).

Since the wall built upon sand has been struck and overturned because it did not have Christ, the power and wisdom of God, as its foundation; and since it has been scattered because it did not have apostles and apostolic men as its builders, it is fitting for us to build upon the true foundation, from living stones—that is, from Catholic opinions—a fortress for the simple and faithful against the smoky assaults of heretics. [Col. 0129D] And since the truthful saying has been fulfilled, “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13), we ought to plant faithful shoots bearing fruit—that is, faithful understandings—for this is the purpose for which, by the grace of God, we have been planted in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.

## CHAPTER XVI

The text of the first chapter excerpted by us is set out below, with its sources indicated piece by piece.

This is the text of the first chapter:

> “Almighty God created man upright, without sin and with free choice, and placed him in paradise, wishing him to remain in the holiness of righteousness. Man, using free choice badly, sinned and fell, and became a mass of perdition for the entire human race. But God, being good and just, chose from that same mass of perdition, according to his foreknowledge, those whom by grace he predestined to life, and predestined eternal life for them. As for the rest, whom by the judgment of his justice he left in the mass of perdition, he foreknew that they would perish, but did not predestine them to perish; yet, because he is just, he predestined eternal punishment for them. Accordingly, we speak of only one predestination of God: that which pertains either to the gift of grace or to the recompense of justice.”

This is the chapter that, against Gottschalk and his erroneous school, we were compelled by necessity and driven by the earnest request of the principal devotee to extract, according to the course of the holy Scriptures, from the words of blessed Augustine and Prosper and from the opinions of the other Catholic teachers. Since the most hostile critic abominates it, together with the other three chapters excerpted by us, as though it disagreed with the teaching and faith of the Catholic Fathers, it is necessary for us to demonstrate, word by word, how it agrees everywhere not only with their meaning and teaching but also with the words of the orthodox Fathers.

We wrote at the beginning of the chapter: “Almighty God,” just as it is written in the Heptateuch that the Lord said to Moses: “I, the Lord God; this is my memorial name for ever, throughout generations and descendants” (Exod. 3:15). [Col. 0130A] And Hilary says in his commentary on Psalm 129:

> “It is the devout confession of human weakness to know this only about God: that he is God.”

And Ambrose says in his *Epistle to the Galatians*:

> “God is the name of nature and of power.”

And in the Song of Exodus:

> “Almighty is his name.”

Therefore, from the Apostles’ Creed, and from the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds, according to the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic voices, we believe, confess, and proclaim God almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist: to him be glory for ever and ever.

We next wrote: “He created man upright, without sin and with free choice.” In Genesis it is written: “And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him” (Gen. 1:27). [Col. 0130B] It is established, and no believer doubts or denies, that the holy and righteous God, who is without sin, created upright and without sin the one whom he created in his own image. And in the Book of Ecclesiasticus:

> “God created man, and made him according to his own image” (Ecclus. 17:1).

And again:

> “He turned him back to himself and clothed him with strength like his own” (ibid., 2).

And again:

> “From the beginning God made man, and left him in the hand of his own counsel” (Ecclus. 15:14).

And in Ecclesiastes:

> “This alone I have found: that God made man upright, but he himself became involved in countless questions” (Eccl. 7:30).

Accordingly, Alcuin says in his explanation of this chapter:

> “We were created good by God, but because we were left to free choice, through our own fault we slide toward worse things while seeking greater ones and thinking various thoughts beyond our strength.”

And blessed Augustine says in his book *On Correction and Grace* concerning this passage (ch. 12):

> “To the first man, therefore, who in the good in which he had been made upright had received the ability not to sin, the ability not to die, and the ability not to abandon that very good…”

And somewhat earlier in the same book (ch. 10):

> “Therefore we most beneficially confess what we most rightly believe: that God, the Lord of all things, who created all things very good, foreknew that evil would arise from good, and knew that it belonged more to his almighty goodness to bring good even out of evil than not to permit evil to exist. He therefore ordered the life of angels and human beings in such a way that he would first show what their free choice could accomplish, and afterward what could be accomplished by the benefit of his grace and the judgment of his justice.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Thus also he made man with free choice.”

Likewise, in his book *On Nature and Grace* (ch. 67):

> “When we speak of the free will to do what is right, we are speaking of that will in which man was created.”

Next we added: “And placed him in paradise,” which the reading of Genesis also teaches:

> “God planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed” (Gen. 2:8).

We continued: “Whom he wished to remain in the holiness of righteousness.” Accordingly, blessed Gregory says in his homily on the Gospel passage, “Tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus,” concerning this point (*Homily 34 on the Gospels*):

> “The Lord created the nature of angels and human beings to know him. Since he wished it to endure for eternity, he undoubtedly created it in his own likeness.”

Man would have remained in that eternity if he had persevered in the holiness of righteousness, as Saint Augustine says in the aforementioned book *On Correction and Grace* (ch. 10):

> “In that upright and faultless state, if man had wished to remain through his own free choice, he would certainly have received, without any experience of death or unhappiness, the fullness of blessedness deserved by such perseverance—the blessedness enjoyed by the holy angels: namely, that he could no longer fall and would know this with complete certainty. For how could he himself be blessed even in paradise—or rather, how would he not be there, where it would be unfitting to be miserable—if foreknowledge and fear of so great a fall made him miserable?”

Likewise blessed Gregory says in the eighth book of the *Moralia on Job* (ch. 6):

> “For this purpose man had been created: that, standing firm in mind, he might raise himself to the citadel of contemplation, and that no corruption might turn him away from the love of his Creator.”

Again, in the same work (ch. 10):

> “Man had been created for contemplating the Creator, so that he might always seek his appearance and dwell in the solemnity of his love. But, cast outside himself through disobedience, he lost the place of his mind; scattered along dark paths, he withdrew from the dwelling of the true light.”

Again, in book seventeen (ch. 18):

> “Man was created for life in the freedom of his own will, but by his own choice he made himself a debtor to death.”

Again, in book nineteen (ch. 24):

> “Having contemplated the inward joys of the vision of God and the fellowship of the angels who remained standing, he turned his eyes downward. He saw where he lay, though he had been created for the purpose of being able to stand in the heavenly places.”

Again, in book twenty (ch. 16):

> “The human race, therefore, abandoned by the just judgment of God to its own pleasures, and through those same pleasures handed over to voluntary tribulations, is drunk with wormwood.”

And in his seventeenth homily:

> “What else should I call human souls except the food of the Lord? They were created for this purpose: to be transferred into his body, that is, to advance toward the increase of the eternal Church.”

And Ambrose says in his commentary on Psalm 118:

> “Hence the Apostle says: toward those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness. For if they had not fallen, they too would certainly have enjoyed God’s goodness.”

And Saint Augustine says in the thirteenth book of *The Trinity* (ch. 12):

> “By a certain justice of God, the human race was handed over to the power of the devil through the sin of the first man, which passed originally into all who are born through the union of the two sexes, binding all descendants by the debt of their first parents. This handing-over was first signified in Genesis. When it had been said to the serpent, ‘You shall eat earth,’ it was said to the man, ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go’ (Gen. 3:14, 19). In the words ‘To earth you shall go,’ the death of the body was foretold, for he would not have experienced even that if he had remained upright as he had been made.”

And a little farther on:

> “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3). Therefore all human beings from their origin are under the ruler of the power of the air, who works in the children of unbelief. When I said ‘from their origin,’ I meant what the Apostle says by ‘nature,’ and that he himself had been like the rest: by nature, that is, as nature has been corrupted by sin, not as it was created upright in the beginning.”

And Jerome says in the second book of his commentary on the prophet Micah:

> “For God created man so that he would not perish, and he did not make death.”

And blessed Gregory says in the fourth book of the *Moralia* (ch. 28):

> “For if no corruption of sin had infected our first parent, he would by no means have begotten children of Gehenna from himself; rather, those alone who are now to be saved through redemption would have been born chosen by him.”

And Saint Ambrose, when expounding the words, “Give me understanding, and I shall live” (Ps. 118:144), says:

> “If Adam had asked as David asked, he would by no means have fallen into those inextricable snares of error by which all his inheritance is strangled. Therefore he died—and what is more serious than bodily death, he died the death of sin—because he first presumed to know before he had received the understanding by which he would be made alive.”

Next we added:

> “Man, using free choice badly, sinned and fell, and became a mass of perdition for the entire human race.”

Hence the Apostle says:

> “Through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12).

And again:

> “Judgment from one offense resulted in condemnation, and through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings” (ibid., 16).

For this reason Saint Ambrose says in his exposition of Luke:

> “Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him we all perished.”

And blessed Augustine says:

> “Because man abandoned God through free choice, he experienced God’s just judgment, so that he was condemned together with his entire race, which was still wholly present in him and had sinned wholly together with him.”

Finally we added:

> “But God, being good and just, chose from that same mass of perdition, according to his foreknowledge, those whom by grace he predestined to life, and predestined eternal life for them.”

Hence the prince of the apostles:

> “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the elect exiles according to the foreknowledge of God the Father” (1 Pet. 1:1).

And the Apostle Paul:

> “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8:29).

And Augustine, in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and Prosper, using his words, against the objections of the querulous ignorance or deceitful envy of Augustine’s opponents:

> “Predestination, they say, is the preparation of grace; it cannot exist without foreknowledge, but foreknowledge can exist without predestination. Those things which we possess as a gift from God and which are said to be foreknown cannot fail to be predestined; and whatever is called predestined cannot fail to be foreknown. The Lord also says in the Gospel: ‘Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom that has been prepared—that is, predestined—for you from the foundation of the world’ (Matt. 25:34). And Paul likewise says: ‘The grace of God is eternal life’ (Rom. 6:23).”

Hence Augustine says in the aforementioned book *On the Predestination of the Saints*:

> “Grace is itself already the gift of life.”

And again:

> “Accordingly, God’s predestination, which is directed toward good, is, as I have said, the preparation of grace, while grace is the effect of that very predestination.”

Next we joined to this:

> “As for the rest, whom by the judgment of his justice he left in the mass of perdition, he foreknew that they would perish, but did not predestine them to perish; yet, because he is just, he predestined eternal punishment for them.”

And Prosper, in his third action against the Vincentians:

> “God is indeed the creator of all human beings, but no one was created by him for the purpose of perishing.”

And blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Good, or Gift, of Perseverance* concerning this passage (ch. 14):

> “Will anyone dare say that God did not foreknow to whom he would give the gift of believing, or whom he would give to his Son so that he would lose none of them? If he foreknew these things, he certainly foreknew the benefits by which he graciously deigns to free us. This is the predestination of the saints, and nothing else: namely, the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. But where else are the rest left except in the mass of perdition, by the just divine judgment?”

Hence Saint Prosper, in his explanation of the eighth objection against the Januenses:

> “Let us therefore wisely recognize and piously confess that God unchangeably foreknew those to whom he would give the gift of believing, or those whom he would give to his Son so that he would lose none of them. And if he foreknew these things, he foreknew the benefits by which he graciously deigns to free us; and this is the predestination of the saints, namely, the predestination and preparation of God’s grace, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. As for the rest, whom grace did not remove from the general perdition of the human race, let us understand that they were not removed by a just judgment, and let us learn from them what has been forgiven us, since we cannot complain about their condemnation.”

And Gregory says in the twenty-fifth book of the *Moralia* (ch. 7):

> “It is clear to everyone that at the final reckoning the almighty God will conduct a public examination, so that he may consign some to punishments and admit others to participation in the heavenly kingdom. But even now, by a secret judgment, what will then be displayed publicly is daily taking place. For, justly and mercifully examining or disposing the hearts of individuals, he rejects some toward outward things and draws others toward inward things; he kindles in these the desire for inward things, while he abandons those to think about outward things according to their pleasures.”

And Augustine says in the aforementioned book *On Correction and Grace* (ch. 10):

> “All who are freed from this stock—the stock of the first man—by God’s grace are certainly freed from condemnation, to which they were already bound. Even if no one were freed, no one could justly criticize God’s judgment. Therefore, although few are freed in comparison with those who perish, many are freed in their own number; this is done freely, and thanks must be given for grace, because it is done so that no one may exalt himself as though on the basis of his own merits, but every mouth may be stopped, and whoever boasts may boast in the Lord.”

And in the book *On the Grace of Christ, Free Choice, and Original Sin*, which he called the *Hypomnesticon*, he says in his explanation of the sixth question concerning predestination (book 6, at the beginning):

> “Predestination is so called from foreseeing, anticipating, or preordaining something future. Therefore God, for whom foreknowledge was not an accident but has always been and is his essence, predestines whatever he foreknows before it exists; and he predestines it because he foreknows what it will be. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined’ (Rom. 8:29). But he does not predestine everything that he foreknows. For he foreknows evil things only, whereas he both foreknows and predestines good things. What is good, therefore, foreknowledge predestines—that is, it preordains before it exists in reality. Once it begins to exist with him as its author, he calls, orders, and arranges it. Hence what follows: ‘Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified’ (ibid.).

> “Let us now explain more openly what we are saying: how God, in whom there is no iniquity, makes use of his foreknowledge and predestination concerning the human race. The mass of the human race, made condemnable and mortal by the transgression of Adam and Eve, owes the punishment and torment of Gehenna not to divine creation in general, but as a debt; pardon, however, is bestowed not as a merit but through the generosity of the mercy of God, the just judge. Since God is just and merciful, and foreknows the future, from this condemnable mass he prepares—by gratuitous mercy, not by respect for persons but by the irreproachable, indeed incomprehensible, judgment of his equity—those whom he foreknows for eternal life; that is, he predestines them to eternal life. As for the rest, he punishes them with the punishment due to them, as I have said. He punishes them because he foreknew what they would be, but he himself neither made nor predestined them to be punished; rather, as I have said, he merely foreknew them in the condemnable mass.

> “If you ask me to know why God does these two things differently, if he is not a respecter of persons—since in general justice must either punish or mercy must free—contend with Paul; or, if you dare, accuse Paul, who said, with Christ speaking in him: ‘O man, who are you to answer back to God?’ (Rom. 9:10).”

And other matters that the reader can find there in ample sufficiency. For the present, it is enough for us to demonstrate how our chapters were excerpted from the words and opinions of the Catholic Fathers.

And after much more, blessed Augustine says in the same book:

> “We must therefore return to what we began to discuss above. We said that from the condemnable mass of the human race God foreknew, and by mercy rather than merits predestined through the election of grace to life, those whom he predestined; but he merely foreknew the rest, who by the judgment of his justice were made strangers to this grace, as destined to perish through their own fault, and did not predestine them to perish. Yet, as I have said, those whom he foreknew as destined for works of ungodliness and death he did not preordain or compel. These, provoking God to anger, either refuse to receive the faith of salvation preached to them, or, under God’s judgment, cannot receive it, or misuse what they have received; and for this reason they are handed over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting (Rom. 1:28). We rightly confess that punishment has been predestined for such people.”

And Saint Prosper, in the first response to the first objection of the Gauls, says concerning this passage:

> “The faith of predestination is supported by the authority of many holy Scriptures. It is in no way permissible to ascribe to it the evil things done by human beings; those came from the transgression of the first father. No one is freed from the punishment of that transgression except through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, prepared and predestined in God’s eternal counsel before the foundation of the world.”

And Augustine says in the fourth book of *The Trinity* (ch. 12):

> “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). “The devil was the mediator of this way, the persuader to sin and the precipitant into death. For, in bringing about our twofold death, he brought his own single death. Through ungodliness he was dead in spirit, though he was not dead in the flesh; but he persuaded us to ungodliness and thereby brought it about that we deserved to come to the death of the flesh. We therefore desired one thing through an evil persuasion, and another followed us through a just condemnation.

> “For this reason it is written, ‘God did not make death’ (Wis. 1:13), because he himself was not the cause of death; nevertheless, through his most just retribution, death was inflicted upon the sinner. Just as a judge inflicts punishment upon the accused, but the justice of the judge is not the cause of the punishment—the merit of the crime is—so the mediator of death led us where he himself did not come, namely, to the death of the flesh. There our Lord God inserted for us the medicine of correction, which he did not deserve, by the hidden and exceedingly mysterious ordering of divine and profound justice.

> “Thus, just as death came through one man, so the resurrection of the dead might come through one man, because human beings feared more what they could not avoid—the death of the flesh—than the death of the spirit; that is, they feared punishment more than the merit of punishment. For not sinning is either not cared about or cared about little, whereas not dying, although it cannot be attained, is pursued with great eagerness. The mediator of life therefore showed that death is not to be feared, since through human condition it can no longer be avoided, but rather ungodliness, which can be guarded against through faith.”

Likewise Augustine says in the thirteenth book of *The Trinity* (ch. 11):

> “The Father did not spare his Son for our sake; he himself delivered him up to death for us” (Rom. 8:32). But I see that the Father loved us even earlier—not merely before the Son died for us, but before he created the world—the Apostle himself bearing witness, for he says: ‘He chose us in him before the foundation of the world’” (Eph. 1:4).

And Saint Cyprian, in his book *On the Lapsed*, says, because punishment has been established for the reprobate:

> “The Lord,” he says, “in the Gospel, teacher in his words and perfecter in his deeds, teaching what was to be done and doing whatever he had taught—did he not beforehand warn us of everything that is now happening and will happen? Did he not also beforehand establish eternal punishments for those who deny, and saving rewards for those who confess?”

And in *On Mortality* he says:

> “No one considers the fear of things to come, the day of the Lord and the wrath of God, the punishments about to come upon unbelievers, and the eternal torments established for the faithless; no one considers them.”

Likewise, in *On Jealousy and Envy*:

> “He who hates his brother,” he says, “walks in darkness and does not know where he is going. For, unknowingly, he departs into Gehenna; ignorant and blind, he is hurled into punishment, departing, that is, from the light of Christ, who warns and says: ‘I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life’ (John 8:12).”

Likewise, in his book *To Demetrianus*:

> “Therefore, when plagues strike, the scourges and blows of God are not absent. Since they accomplish nothing here, and do not turn individuals to God through so great a terror of calamities, an eternal prison, an unceasing flame, and everlasting punishment remain hereafter. There the groaning of those who plead will not be heard, because here also the terror of the forgiving God was not heard.”

And again:

> “God made you upright; and while all the other animals are bowed forward and pressed down, their posture inclining toward the earth, you have an elevated stance and a face raised toward heaven and toward your God. Look there; raise your eyes there. Seek the Lord on high, so that you may be able to avoid the underworld. Preserve the loftiness in which you were born; remain such as the Lord made you.”

And again:

> “Believe in him who will inflict eternal punishments upon unbelievers from the fires of Gehenna.”

Likewise, in his epistle *To the Romans*:

> “For God, just as he is forgiving, is also an exacting enforcer of his commandments. Indeed, just as he invites people to the banquet, so he casts outside the assembly of the saints the one who does not have a wedding garment, bound hand and foot. He prepared heaven, but he also prepared Tartarus; he prepared places of refreshment, but he also prepared eternal punishments; he prepared inaccessible light, but he also prepared the vast and everlasting darkness of perpetual night.”

And Saint Hilary, in his exposition of Psalm 118, on the verse “My soul has desired”:

> “Since we shall have to give an account for every idle word, would we desire the day of judgment, on which we must undergo that unwearied fire, in which those grievous punishments for the purification of the soul from sins must be endured?”

Because no one perishes by God’s predestination, and God abandons no one before he is abandoned, Cyprian says in *On the Lapsed*:

> “What force,” he says, “can he allege by which he may purge his crime, when he himself rather used force so that the man might perish?”

And thus he presents from the book of Chronicles [Col. 0137B] (Cyprian, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, Epistle to Fortunatus, chapter 8):

> “The Lord is with you as long as you are with him; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you” (2 Chronicles 15:2).

Teaching that God’s foreknowledge, not his predestination, pertains to punishment, he presents an example from the book of Maccabees, saying (chapter 15):

> “The fifth, besides trampling underfoot the king’s executioners and harsh and various tortures through the strength of his faith, also, inspired by the spirit of divinity with foreknowledge and knowledge of future things, prophesied to the king God’s indignation and the vengeance that would swiftly follow: ‘You have power among human beings’ (2 Maccabees 7:16),” and the rest that he continues.

And shortly afterward:

> “Nor is it worth gaining the brief moments of this life at the cost of offending God and incurring eternal punishments.”

By this example it is shown that a human being is not predestined by God to punishment, but incurs punishment through his own iniquity. Elsewhere, in *On the Good of Patience*, explaining the Apostle’s words, “You are storing up wrath for yourself” (Romans 2:5), and what follows, he said that God’s judgment is just because it is delayed, because it is postponed for a long time and at length, so that God’s long patience may provide for a human being’s life. And then punishment is brought upon the impious and the sinner, when repentance can no longer benefit the sinner.

And Saint Ambrose, when expounding Psalm 118, “Let your mercy come, that it may comfort me,” commending the grace of God, says:

> “For God says to Moses: ‘I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whomever I show mercy’ (Exodus 33:19). Therefore it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Romans 9:16). Are we therefore not to will or to run? Yet God is accustomed to abandon the negligent. He does not say this, then; let us consider what he does say. The perseverance of a human being is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs. For it is not in human power; rather, it is of God who shows mercy, so that you may complete what you have begun. Finally, he says again: ‘For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you’ (Exodus 9:16). It follows, therefore, that exhortation is to be attributed to divine mercy. Hence what follows is: ‘Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills’ (Romans 9:17–18): he exhorts the one on whom he has had mercy; the other, having cursed him, he does not call back.”

Likewise, because God did not predestine a human being to fire and to become the companion of the devil, but a person becomes his companion—or rather, the devil’s portion—by his own iniquity, Ambrose, treating the verse “I have practiced judgment and righteousness” (Psalm 118:121), says:

> “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” (1 Timothy 6:9).

And again:

> “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5). “For in these things we do the devil’s will and carry out his power; through the desires of this flesh he works the stimulus of his deceit. Therefore, whoever he finds in possession of his vices, he claims as subject to his authority. Whoever commits adultery, practices debauchery, or seizes what belongs to another is the devil’s portion; but the chaste, self-controlled, and merciful person is Christ’s portion. The devil cannot claim Christ’s servant for himself unless perhaps he finds him fallen into vices. Even then he does not claim him, but demands that he be handed over to him as his own.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The devil places his throne above the stars when he deceives the elect, when he ensnares the righteous, whose works shine like stars in heaven.”

Did not Judas the betrayer also hear, among the others, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14)? Did not the devil extinguish his light? Indeed, those whom he could not ensnare, he slanders out of envy of the glory of the heavenly kingdom, so that those whom he could not separate from Christ by his enticements, he may try to deprive, through his slanders, of the fruit of their due honor.

And Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, whose examples the apostolic see, together with other luminaries of the world, and blessed Augustine repeatedly employ authoritatively in *Against Julian* and in his other works, like a most powerful hammer for crushing the heads of heretics and the hairy crowns of those who walk in their sins, says in his book *On the Restoration of the Fallen*:

> “For this reason,” he says, “God created us and brought into being those who did not exist, so that he might confer eternal goods upon us and grant us the kingdoms of heaven. He did not make us for this purpose, that he might hand us over to Gehenna and everlasting fire. The kingdom of heaven was made for us; Gehenna was made for the devil. And I shall prove from the Gospels that this is so. For the Lord himself says to those who are at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’ (Matthew 25:34). But to those who are at his left he says: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which was prepared’—he did not say ‘for you,’ but ‘for the devil and his angels’ (Matthew 25:41). If, therefore, the fire of Gehenna was prepared for the devil, and the kingdom of heaven for human beings from the foundation of the world, let us take care only not to exclude ourselves from the entrance into these good things by stubbornly persisting in evil. For as long as we are in this life, whatever sins may befall us, it is possible for all of them to be absolved through repentance. But when we have been taken away from this world, then we shall indeed repent there; we shall repent greatly, but repentance will be of no use. And although there will be gnashing of teeth, although there will be wailing and weeping,”

and the rest that he continues.

This example of a most catholic man, as also of any of the others whom we have cited and shall cite, could have sufficed for correct understanding and authority, if, among those who contradict, right agreement had been able to carry greater weight than perverse contention. In the synod, and also in his writings, the condemned Gothescalcus criticized this great man. But Augustine, an upright man, very frequently adopted him in support of his own positions; and we, following him, embrace Augustine, who grasped the divine knowledge and the Catholic faith by the grace of God.

And lest any stubborn people, increasing the faith of their contentions by cords with which they may be bound more tightly to their own destruction, boast that we have said that punishment was predestined for the reprobate, and lest they demonstrate from this testimony that eternal fire was prepared not for human beings but for the devil, let them listen more attentively to what this holy man continues:

> “The only matter at issue is that we must not stubbornly exclude ourselves from entering into good things by persisting in evil: that is, ceasing to be what we were made, we begin, through our own fault, to be what we are forbidden to become, as the divine word says: ‘When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them’ (Psalm 48:13).”

Hence Saint Ambrose, when treating the verse of Psalm 118, “Your hands made me and fashioned me,” says:

> “For Scripture,” he says, “calls him a human being who is according to the image and likeness of God. But it customarily calls the sinner not a human being, but a serpent, or a horse neighing after females, or a little fox, or a beast of burden. ‘Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding. Restrain their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not draw near to you’ (Psalm 31:9–10). And, ‘Say to that fox’ (Luke 13:32), he says concerning Herod. ‘Brood of vipers’ (Luke 3:7) is what John calls the people of human beings. You are therefore a great work of God, O human being; great is what God has given you. Take care lest you lose what God has granted you; lest you lose that great gift by which you are made according to the image of God, and lest this be punished more severely in you. For God does not punish his likeness, but punishes the one who, having been made according to the likeness of God, was unable to preserve what he received. He therefore punishes that which ceases to be according to the likeness of God, namely, your sin. For God does not condemn his own image, nor does he cast it into that eternal fire; rather, he avenges the image against the one who wronged that image, so that through malice you might cease to be what you were and become, from a human being, a mule. The image is therefore avenged, not condemned; it is avenged as though expelled, not condemned as though guilty. For after you sinned, you began to be something else; you ceased to be what you were. How, then, is that which is not found in you punished in you? For if the image and likeness of God is found in you, you do not begin to be worthy of punishment but of reward. Thus that image, according to which you were made in the image and likeness of God, is not condemned but crowned. You are condemned, however, in that by which you yourself have been changed, so that from a human being you became a serpent, a mule, a horse, or a little fox. Scripture has already condemned us by these names: stripped of the adornment of the heavenly image, we even lose the name of human being, because we do not retain the grace of humanity.”

And Saint Augustine, in his sermon *On the Creed to the Neophytes*:

> “Remember to believe in the omnipotent God in such a way that there is absolutely no nature which he himself did not create; and therefore he punishes sin, which he did not make, because through it the nature which he made is defiled.”

Here one must carefully consider how harmoniously these holy teachers, filled with one Spirit, spoke through different mouths to various peoples. Hence apostolic teaching also salutarily admonishes us to be re-formed according to the image of God, in which we were created, to be renewed in the spirit of our mind (Romans 12:2; Ephesians 4:23), and to judge ourselves, so that we may not be judged and condemned along with this world.

And Saint Gregory, in the fourteenth book of *The Morals on Job* (chapter 11), because human beings are not predestined by God to punishment as the elect are to glory, but the devil, together with his body, is predestined by God to punishment as a matter of just retribution, says:

> “All who,” he says, “have been born from his—that is, Antichrist’s—perverse persuasion in evil actions will be struck with eternal destruction, together with their own head, at the revelation of the Lord’s coming.”

Likewise:

> “These are the tents of the wicked”—indicating, namely, that the one who is now exalted through ignorance will then reach his own tents, when his iniquity plunges him into punishments.

Likewise, in the fifteenth book (chapter 5):

> “The hands of that man therefore return pain to him, because he will receive just condemnation from his iniquitous action. It is rightly said not that they will give, but that they will return, because his perverse actions will pay him eternal punishment as a kind of debt.”

Likewise (chapter 17):

> “A fire that is not kindled will devour him” (Job 20:26). “In a very remarkable manner, the fire of Gehenna has been expressed in a few words. For corporeal fire, in order to be fire, requires corporeal fuel. Since it must be preserved, it is undoubtedly nourished by piled-up wood; it cannot exist unless it is kindled and unless it is replenished. But, by contrast, the fire of Gehenna, although incorporeal and corporeally burning those cast into it, is neither kindled by human effort nor nourished by wood. Rather, once created, it endures unquenchable; it does not need kindling and does not lack heat. He therefore rightly says of this wicked person, ‘A fire that is not kindled will devour him,’ because the justice of the Almighty, foreknowing future things, created the fire of Gehenna from the very beginning of the world, so that it would begin once to exist in the punishment of the reprobate, but would never end its burning, even without wood.”

And Saint Jerome, in the tenth book of his commentary on the prophet Isaiah:

> “From yesterday and from times past Topheth has been prepared by the King, the Lord” (Isaiah 30:33)—that is, broad and spacious Gehenna, which burns them, that is, the reprobate, with eternal fires.

Likewise, the same author, in the third book on the prophet Amos:

> “We must understand God’s repentance in Scripture in the same way as sleep and anger: not as though God repents and changes his decision—he who speaks through the prophet, ‘I am God and I do not change’ (Malachi 3:6), and to whom we say, ‘But you are the same, and your years will not fail’ (Psalm 101:28)—but in the sense that, when we turn toward better things, he himself is said to repent of his decision, so that he neither gives the rewards he promised to the righteous person if that person turns toward iniquity, nor inflicts upon the sinner the punishments he threatened if the sinner turns toward salvation.”

And again:

> “You, children of Israel, I will cleanse and choose, as though shaken and tossed in a sieve, so that the one who is a little stone and has been strengthened through repentance may not fall from my sieve; but the one who falls to the ground like dust may be struck with the sword and die: the sinners of my people—not because they sinned previously, but because they persevered in sins until death.”

Likewise, where it says, “Behold, I will cleanse,” when he explains Jeremiah’s testimony, “I will take up and speak concerning a nation,” and what follows:

> “God is not therefore changed, since he is always unchangeable. Rather, when we change our conduct, he rages, grows angry, threatens, and says that he will inflict punishments; if we do penance, he too is said to repent of his decision.”

And Saint Augustine, on Psalm 7:

> “Let us not suppose that the tranquility and ineffable light of God brings forth from itself the means by which sins are punished; rather, let us understand that it orders sins themselves in such a way that what were delights to the sinning human being become instruments for the punishing Lord.”

And on Psalm 28:

> “When the Lord comes bearing in his hand the retributions—condemnations for the impious, a kingdom for the righteous, companionship with the devil for the wicked, and companionship with Christ for the faithful—”

And on Psalm 40:

> “For the Devil desired to destroy Christ, and Judas wished to kill Christ; but when Christ had been killed and had risen, we were brought to life. Yet the Devil and Judas receive the evil reward of their evil will, not the reward of our salvation. Know that each person must be judged according to his heart, for the recompense either of reward or of punishment.”

We concluded the chapter by adding:

> “And therefore we say that there is one predestination of God, which pertains either to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice.”

And blessed Augustine, in *On the Good—or Gift—of Perseverance* (chapter 14):

> “Because it has been given to you,” he says, “to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given, one of these pertains to the mercy and the other to the judgment of him to whom our soul says: ‘I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord’ (Psalm 100:1).”

And much earlier (chapter 12):

> “Since, therefore, he gives grace to some and does not give it to others, why do they refuse to sing to the Lord, ‘mercy and judgment’? But why it is given to these rather than to those—who has known the mind of the Lord? Who could search out his unsearchable judgments? Who could investigate what cannot be investigated? It is therefore established that God’s grace is not given according to the merits of those who receive it, but according to the good pleasure of his will, for the praise and glory of his grace, so that whoever glories may in no way glory in himself but in the Lord. He gives to human beings whom he wills, because he is merciful; and even if he does not give, he is just. He does not give to those whom he does not will, so that he may make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy. By giving to some what they do not deserve, he clearly wished his grace to be gratuitous and therefore true. By not giving to all, he shows what all deserve: good in the benefit bestowed upon some, just in the punishment of others; and good in all, because it is good when what is owed is repaid; and just in all, because it is just when what is not owed is given without defrauding anyone.”

And in his book *Against Pelagius and Coelestius, On the Grace of Christ, Free Will, and Original Sin*, at the relevant passage (the sixth book of the *Hypomnesticon*):

> “O human being, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me this way?’ Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:20–21).

I say what I have said: whatever God does, he does mercifully, justly, and holily, because he alone knows through foreknowledge what a human being, through ignorance, does not know.

> “For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him? Or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, so that he might be repaid? Or who says to him, ‘Why did you make me this way?’ God cannot be called merely just or merely merciful, but just and merciful. Thus we read; thus we believe. Therefore, when with David we sing mercy and judgment to him, we do not question in fear what his will may be, by disputing about judgment and mercy.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For if we wish to search out God’s secret, which is known only to his justice, we cannot comprehend it, and what is written is fulfilled in us: ‘Those who search have failed in their searching’ (Psalm 63:6). Why? Because, he says, ‘the human being approached the deep heart, and God will be exalted’ (ibid., 7). But perhaps, although you are blameworthy, you boast that the judgments of God are comprehensible to you—surely pleasing God better than the Apostle Paul, who proclaimed through the Holy Spirit that they are incomprehensible.”

And after a little more:

> “Behold: in all the things that we have brought forward on divine authority, you have mercy and judgment.”

And Saint Prosper, in the fourteenth response to the objection of the Gauls, says:

> “The predestination of God, therefore, is always directed toward good; it pertains either to the retribution of justice or to the gift of grace. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10).

And Saint Jerome, in his exposition of the prophet Hosea:

> “They turned their silver and gold, whatever they could naturally possess of speech and understanding, into idols which they fashioned from their own heart.
