They turned them not in order to perish, but because they turned them, they perished. For they did not act for the purpose of perishing; but because they acted, they therefore perished.”

Agreeing with the words of blessed Jerome, we say that they did not perish because they were predestined by God to perish; rather, they were not predestined by God to be saved because he foreknew that they would perish through their own fault, and to them, as a matter of the retribution of justice, he predestined eternal punishment.

And Prosper, in the resolution of the third objection of the Gauls:

> “That such people,” he says, “having fallen into these evils, perished without correction through repentance, did not thereby have a necessity of perishing because they were not predestined; rather, they were not predestined because they were foreknown as going to become such through voluntary transgression.”

And again:

> “They were not abandoned by God so that they might abandon God; rather, they abandoned him and were abandoned, and they were changed from good to evil by their own will. They were not predestined by him who foreknew that they would become such.”

And again, in the resolution of the twelfth objection:

> “He did not therefore take away from anyone the strength of obedience because he did not predestine that person; rather, he did not predestine him because he foresaw that he would withdraw from that very obedience.”

And in the resolution of the thirteenth objection against the Vincentians:

> “Although God possesses in his eternal knowledge the foreknowledge of what he will repay to each person according to that person’s merits, nevertheless, by the fact that he cannot be deceived, he has imposed upon no one either a necessity or a will to sin.”

Likewise Jerome, on the prophet Amos:

> “Those who come to an evil day prepare an evil day for themselves by their own fault—not because any day is evil, but because each person prepares evil for himself, in accordance with what we read in Ecclesiastes: ‘Do not say, “The former days were better for me than these,” for it is not in wisdom that you ask about this’ (Ecclesiastes 7:11). For it is foolish to attribute the matter to times, when it lies within our power either to make a good day for ourselves or an evil one. Likewise, in the prophet Nahum, at the beginning of the chapter: ‘Where is the dwelling place of the lions?’ (Nahum 2:11). Jeremiah also speaks of sinners: ‘The lion from the forest has struck them’ (Jeremiah 5:6).”

And shortly afterward:

> “All who go out from them—that is, from the cities—will be captured. Observe in this that no one is captured unless he has gone out from the cities of God. Finally, Judas belonged to Christ’s sheepfold, and, seized by the lion, was strangled by hanging. Likewise, the prophet whom the Lord had commanded not to eat bread in that region, where there were golden calves and a false religion, was struck by a lion because he ate (1 Kings 13:24). All of this pertains to the retribution of divine justice.”

Hence Saint Gregory, in the tenth book of *The Morals on Job* (chapter 8), because the reprobate are not predestined by God to punishment as the elect are to glory, but are left in the mass of perdition or in their sins by a just judgment, as a matter of the retribution of justice, says:

> “If he overturns everything, who will contradict him?” (Job 11:10). “Often the heart is lifted up in pride when it is strengthened in virtue by happy successes. But when the Creator sees the hidden movements of boldness concealed in thought, he abandons the person to himself by showing him what he is, so that the abandoned mind may discover what it is, although it had rejoiced in wrongful security.”

Likewise, in the eleventh book (chapter 2):

> “It must be understood that one thing is what the omnipotent God mercifully bestows, and another is what, in anger, he permits a person to possess. For what plunderers do perversely, the most equitable dispenser permits only justly.”

Likewise (Job 12:14; chapter 5):

> “If he destroys, no one can build; if he shuts a person in, no one can open” (Job 12:14). “The omnipotent God destroys the human heart when he abandons it; he builds it when he fills it. For he does not destroy the human mind by conquering it, but by withdrawing from it, because a mind left to itself is sufficient for its own destruction.”

Likewise:

> “If he shuts a person in, there is no one who can open, because just as no one resists the generosity of the one who calls, so no one opposes the justice of the one who abandons. To shut in, therefore, is God’s not opening to those who have been shut in. Hence it is said to Moses concerning Pharaoh: ‘I will harden his heart’ (Exodus 4:21). He is said to harden through justice when he does not soften a reprobate heart through grace. He therefore shuts in the person whom he leaves in the darkness of his own works.”

Likewise (chapter 7):

> “He knows the deceiver, because he abandons him, left in the hand of his own works, so that he may rush into worse things, as it is written: ‘Let the one who does harm do harm still; and let the one who is filthy be filthy still’ (Revelation 22:11). He also knows the one who is deceived, because human beings often commit evils that they know, and for that reason they are permitted to be deceived, so that they may also fall into evils that they do not know. Yet this happens to the deceived sometimes for purification, and sometimes as the beginning of vengeance.”

Behold how God’s predestination either pertains to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice.

Likewise, the same author in the same work (Job 12:18; chapter 8):

> “He loosens the belt of kings.” When the mind is touched by pride concerning its very self-restraint, the omnipotent God often abandons its pride and permits it to fall into an impure act. He therefore loosens the belt of kings when, in those who seemed to govern their members well, he destroys the girdle of chastity because of the fault of pride.

Likewise (chapter 9):

> “He overthrows nobles” (Job 12:19), because when he abandons the mind of rulers by a just judgment, that mind does not seek the eternal reward of retribution.

Likewise, in the thirteenth book (chapter 11):

> “This is not said as though the omnipotent and merciful God places the human heart far from discipline, but because he permits what has fallen of its own accord to remain where it fell, judging it accordingly; just as in prayer we also say: ‘Do not lead us into temptation’ (Matthew 6:13), that is, ‘Do not permit us to be led into it.’”

Likewise, in the fifteenth book:

> “God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (Romans 1:28). “Because they did not wish to glorify the one whom they knew, they were handed over to a reprobate mind and left for this purpose: that they should no longer know how to weigh the evils they were doing.”

Likewise, in the twentieth book (chapter 16):

> “The human race, therefore, left by the just judgment of God to its own pleasures and handed over through those same pleasures to voluntary tribulations, is drunk with wormwood.”

And Saint Augustine, in his *Annotations on the Epistle to the Romans*:

> “When he says ‘he handed them over,’ this is understood as ‘he abandoned them to the desires of their hearts.’”

And Cassiodorus, on Psalm 82:

> “It follows: ‘Let them be put to shame and perish.’ The meaning is the same as what he said above: those who are destined for eternal punishment do not progress by being put to shame there, but perish through their obstinacy, not through divine predestination, as he immediately adds: ‘And let them know that you alone are named the Lord, the Most High over all the earth’ (Psalm 82:19). ‘Let them know’ refers to both classes of sinners: whether those who are going to perish through their obstinacy, or those who are liberated after having made satisfaction. For all will know the omnipotence of the Lord, because he alone is the Most High, when they themselves recognize that he both spares those who have converted and condemns the hardened to eternal vengeance.”

And on Psalm 88:

> “You dissolved him from purification and struck his throne upon the earth. Divinity frequently purifies those whom it scourges, so that, once cleansed, it may receive the one whom it had rejected as filthy through sins. But those whom it dissolves from purification—that is, removes from it—it has already decided to condemn. Here, therefore, he signifies the Jews, who preferred to reject Christ through the obstinacy of their minds. Their throne was also struck upon the earth when, having rejected the Lord Christ the Savior as king, they no longer deserved to have a ruler from their own nation. For ‘throne’ is used in place of ‘kingdom.’”

And again, in the same work:

> “This is Christ’s transformation, by which he abandoned the obstinate and admitted the faithful through the gift of his mercy.”

And on Psalm 108:

> “Or rather, that one generation must be understood as the generation in which we are born in sins; and therefore he asks that they may not reach the second generation, that is, regeneration. Yet those who are rejected in predestination are rejected so that they may perish in the first filth of their sins and may not escape the snare of death through the benefit of the second birth. But these and similar words are spoken concerning those who will be condemned in the Lord’s judgment.”

And because there is one predestination, Saint Augustine says in the frequently mentioned book *Hypomnesticon against Pelagius and Coelestius, On the Grace of Christ, Free Will, and Original Sin*, as we have recalled, as follows (Book VI, at the beginning):

> “Predestination is so called from foreseeing and going before, or from preordaining something future; and therefore God, for whom foreknowledge is not something accidental but has always been and is essential, [Col. 0145C] foreknows and predestines whatever is going to exist before it exists, and for this reason predestines it because He foreknows what it will be. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘For those whom He foreknew, He also predestined’ (Rom. VIII, 29).”

And in the book *On the Good of Perseverance* (chap. 14):

> “This is the predestination of the saints: nothing other than the foreknowledge, namely, and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered.”

And in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*:

> “This,” he says, “is the predestination of the saints, which shone forth most fully in the Holy of holies. Who, among those rightly understanding the utterances of truth, can deny it? For we have learned that the Lord of glory Himself, insofar as He became man, was predestined to be the Son of God.”

And again in the same book (chap. 10):

> “There is only this difference between grace and predestination: [Col. 0145D] **82** predestination is the preparation of grace, whereas grace is the gift itself.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge; foreknowledge, however, can exist without predestination. By predestination God foreknows those things which He Himself was going to do, whence it is said: ‘He made the things that were to be.’ But He is also able to foreknow things which He Himself does, such as every sin. For although there are certain things which are sins in such a way that they are also punishments of sins—whence it is said: ‘God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting’ (Rom. I, 28)—there is not God’s sin in that, but judgment. Accordingly, God’s predestination, which is directed toward the good, is, as I have said, the preparation of grace; whereas grace is the effect of that [Col. 0146A] predestination.””

And again in the same book (chap. 8):

> “Why, then, does He not teach everyone to come to Christ, unless because He teaches all whom He teaches through mercy, while those whom He does not teach He does not teach through judgment? For ‘He has mercy on whom He wills, and He hardens whom He wills’; but He has mercy by granting what is good, and He hardens by requiting what is deserved.”

And likewise Saint Augustine, in the book *On the Predestination of Grace* (chapters 4–5):

> “Therefore, whatever punishment a human being born after that transgression suffers, it must be acknowledged to be justly and deservedly imposed. For God is said to harden the one whom He does not wish to soften. Likewise, He is said to blind the one whom He does not wish to illuminate. Likewise, He is said to repel the one whom He does not wish to call. For those whom He predestined, He also called; those whom He called, He also justified. For He Himself gave us existence; He Himself gave us the ability to be good. [Col. 0146B] His divinity foreknew us, His wisdom created us, His justice condemned us, and His grace delivered us.

> “Although the world began in time, from the moment it was made, it could have no beginning in that light of the divine foreknowledge in which it was to be made. And however many human beings have been born from Adam up to the present day, or will be born by the succession of generations after our age, in God they have already been born and have passed through the whole course of their lives, remaining nevertheless in the light of that divine gaze. For God, who is confined neither by place nor anticipated by time, is full of the memory of all past things and the knowledge of things that are imminent. He is not turned backward by remembering into the past, nor stretched forward by hoping into the future. And whatever things exist at all, which are agitated by the movements of time, [Col. 0146C] from that beginning in which ‘the Word was,’ and ‘the Word was with God,’ and ‘God was the Word,’ to the end of all ages—for concerning that end blessed Moses said: ‘Lord, who reigns for ever and ever, and beyond’—are neither hoped for as future nor have they passed away as past, but are always seen in the present light of the divine presence.”

And again, after some intervening material (chap. 13):

> “From those for whom severity had justly decreed punishment, according to the ineffable mercy of a hidden disposition, He chose vessels to make for honor; and from the coming wrath He absolved some by the gift of gratuitous calling, while leaving others and reserving them for an equal judgment. Yet He took away from no one the ability to recognize the truth. Thus the fullness of divine foreknowledge was completed, with justice flowing upon some and grace pouring upon others, [Col. 0146D] **83** so that the Church, spread throughout the whole world, might be multiplied both through those whom God had foreknown would perish and through those whom, in His secret election, He had foreknown would be saved.”

And shortly afterward (chapters 14–15):

> “If we think piously about God, as is necessary, we find that mercy was given even to Pharaoh. For God’s patience ought to have benefited him unto salvation, since, by delaying the just and deserved punishment, He increased the repeated blows of the miracles. Could he not, just as he expelled the people when yielding to the scourges, have recognized God as possessing such great power by believing in the miracles? But it is said that Pharaoh could no longer be changed because God had foreknown that he would not be changed. The answer is that God’s foreknowledge does not compel [Col. 0147A] a human being to be such as God foreknew him to be; rather, it foreknows that he will be such as he will be, although God did not make him so. For if it compelled him to be, it would certainly compel him to be what he is not. But if God had foreknown that what is not would come to be, that would not be foreknowledge. Anyone who flatters himself in his sins on the grounds that God foreknew he would become a sinner perceives how impiously this would be said of God.”

Behold from whose words we have excerpted this chapter. Let our critics and opponents approach—indeed, opponents but not conquerors of the right faith—and let them bring the sharpest claws together with the finest needles. Let them stretch out the chapter in the manner of women doing embroidery, and attempt to diversify and discolor [Col. 0147B] it with the various colors of their perverse interpretations. Wherever they find anything contrary or divergent, even in a single word, and all the more in its meaning, from the faith of orthodoxy and the teaching of the catholic Fathers, let them pierce it through stitch by stitch. But if they cannot find such a thing, let them understand that, pierced through by the blade of their own malice, confounded by the victory of truth, and covered with the blush of shame by the refutation of blessed Augustine and Prosper—whose words they boastfully claimed to have conquered—they should cease attacking us and yield their hands to sound understanding.

But if they still refuse to do this, let Saint Gregory come and strike them—not with the club of Hercules, but with ecclesiastical authority, handed down to blessed Peter, first of the apostles, by the Judge of the living and the dead—so that their sorrow may turn upon their own heads, their bow may be broken, and their iniquity [Col. 0147C] may descend upon their own crown. We, meanwhile, shall confess the Lord in His justice.

For in the seventeenth *Homily on the Gospel* he says:

> “Into whatever house,” he says, “you enter, first say: ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon it; but if not, it will return to you” (Luke X, 5). The peace brought from the preacher’s mouth either rests in the house, if a son of peace is in it, or returns to that same preacher. For either someone will be predestined to life and will follow the heavenly word that he hears, or, if no one wishes to hear, the preacher himself will not be without fruit, because the peace will return to him: for the Lord repays him with a reward for the labor of his work.”

**84** Let the critics of this chapter attend and weigh the matter: they wish those who are [Col. 0147D] predestined by God to destruction to be believed and called predestined in the same way as the faithful are believed and called predestined to life and elect, while the reprobate are not predestined but left to destruction. Why, then, did Saint Gregory not say: “And someone will be predestined to destruction and will not follow the word that he hears,” just as he said: “Someone will be predestined to life and will follow the heavenly word that he hears”? Concerning one predestined to life he said that he would follow the word; concerning those who are not predestined but left in the mass of perdition, he said: “If no one wishes to hear,” when the preacher comes.

But if they cannot perceive the truth from this, let them hear what he says in the thirteenth *Homily on the Prophet Ezekiel*:

> “Our Redeemer,” he says, “[Col. 0148A] “because He graciously granted that the words He spoke should also be written through the diligence of teachers, held a measuring reed in His hand. It is called a reed of measurement because the very efforts of teachers are restrained under a certain dispensation of hidden judgment, so that they may benefit some who read and be unable to benefit others who read. Hence, when the holy apostles sought a teacher who would speak the truth to them more openly and asked why He spoke to the crowds in parables, they heard: ‘To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not’ (Matt. XIII, 11).

> “Or certainly, the reed of measurement is so called because, in His sacred utterance written down for us, we recognize that His dispensations are hidden. For by His incomprehensible judgment, one person is measured within the measure of the elect, while another is left outside, so that he may in no way deserve to belong to the number [Col. 0148B] of the elect.” He therefore has a cord; he has in his hand a measuring reed. For one who measures a place with a cord draws the cord in one place, pulls it back from another, and brings it here while withdrawing it from elsewhere. Thus, plainly, our Redeemer acts in the gathering of human beings: He draws some away from their iniquities, while leaving others in their iniquity. In those whom He has deigned to gather, He has drawn the cord of hidden measurement; and from those whom He judged ought to be left behind, what else did He do but draw back the cord? Thus the good are held within the measure of the heavenly structure, while the wicked remain outside the structure, as though without measure, since the good things attributed to them are not found in them.

> “Our Redeemer held this cord and measuring reed in His hand when He deigned to admonish the apostle Paul through [Col. 0148C] the apparition of a Macedonian man, so that this same Macedonian said: ‘Cross over and help us’ (Acts XVI, 9). Yet when the apostles wished to go to Asia to preach, the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them. What does it mean that the holy apostles are called to go where perhaps they had not been planning to go, while they are said to be prevented from going where they desired, unless the cord of hidden judgment and the measuring reed are held in the hand, so that some may hear the words of life while others may in no way deserve to hear them? The cord, therefore, is a cord of measurement, drawn in one direction and pulled back in another.

> “We have also learned from the testimony of the holy Gospel that someone came and said: ‘Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.’ He was answered: ‘Foxes have dens, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His [Col. 0148D] head’ (Matt. VIII, 19–20). Another came and said: ‘Teacher, allow me first to go and bury my father.’ He was told: ‘Let the dead bury their dead; but you, follow me and announce the kingdom of God’ (Matt. VIII, 21–22). What does it mean that the former promises to go and is rejected, while the latter wishes to return home and yet is commanded to follow? The former is not received, while the latter is not released from obedience even for an hour? The cord and measuring reed are therefore directed by an inner and hidden judgment: by it this one is drawn and that one left behind, so that the heavenly structure may be built neither without pious nor without just examination.”

And likewise Saint Gregory, in the twenty-fifth book of the *Moralia* (chap. 8):

> “‘I mingled my drink with weeping’ (Ps. CI, 10). Drink is drawn inward [Col. 0149A] from external things, whereas weeping flows outward from internal things. Therefore, to mingle the Lord’s drink with weeping is to draw some inward from external things and to reject others from within toward external things. For ‘He will crush many and innumerable ones, and will cause others to stand in their place’ (Job XXXIV, 24).”

And shortly afterward (in the same place):

> “When he said, ‘He will crush many,’ and immediately added ‘innumerable,’ he either wished to express the multitude of the reprobate, which surpasses the number that human reason can calculate, or certainly wished to indicate that all who perish are not included within the number of the elect. Thus they are innumerable because they run outside the number.”

And a little later (in the same chapter):

> “But because, as the multitude in the Church increases, the reprobate are also gathered in, it is appropriately added”—for he had said a little earlier that it had been foretold through the prophet [Col. 0149B] Jeremiah: “The city shall be built for the Lord, from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate, and shall go beyond the line of measurement” (Jer. XXXI, 38)—“‘It shall go beyond the line of measurement,’ because it extends even to those who, crossing beyond the rule of justice, are not within the number of heavenly measurement. Hence through Isaiah also it is said to that same Church: ‘For you shall spread out to the right and to the left, and your seed shall inherit the nations’ (Isa. LIV, 3). As the multitude of the nations enters, it spreads to the right by receiving some who are to be justified; it also spreads to the left by admitting to itself some who will nevertheless remain in iniquity. Because of this multitude, which lies outside the number of the elect, the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Many are called, but few are [Col. 0149C] elect’ (Matt. XX, 16). But the fact that some elect persons are crushed while others are preserved is due to the merit of the one who suffers, not to iniquity on the part of the one who punishes. For God is not unjust when He inflicts wrath.”

And shortly afterward (chap. 9):

> “‘Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness’ (Matt. XXII, 13). He is then compelled to be sent into the outer darkness because now he voluntarily blinds himself in the inner darkness.”

And likewise Saint Gregory, in the thirty-third book of the *Moralia on Job* (chap. 20):

> “‘I will not raise him up as though I were cruel’ (Job XLI, 1)—namely, Leviathan. And as though the question of reason were immediately raised against us: ‘How do you not raise him up as though you were cruel, when we know that You permit him to attack and devour so many?’ he immediately added: ‘For who can resist My face, and who has first given to Me, that I should repay him?’ (ibid., 1–2). [Col. 0149D] In these two verses He fulfilled both the power of His might and the whole weight of His reasoning. For the sake of power He said: ‘Who can resist My face?’; and for the sake of reason He added: ‘Who has first given to Me, that I should repay him?’ As though He were saying: ‘I do not raise him up as though I were cruel, because from his [Leviathan’s] might I powerfully rescue My elect, and again condemn the reprobate not unjustly but reasonably’; that is, I can wonderfully rescue those whom I kindly choose, and I do not unjustly abandon those whom I reject.”

And shortly afterward:

> “In a wondrous manner the Creator, equally just toward all, both chose some beforehand and justly left others in their reprobate ways. Nor does He then show mercy to His elect without justice, since here He presses them with harsh [Col. 0150A] afflictions; nor does He exercise justice toward the reprobate without mercy, since here He patiently tolerates those whom He will one day condemn eternally. If, then, the elect follow the grace that precedes them, and the reprobate receive according to what they deserve, the elect find in mercy something for which they give praise, while the reprobate have nothing in justice that they can accuse. It is therefore rightly said: ‘Who has first given to Me, that I should repay him?’ As though it were plainly said: ‘I am compelled by no reason to spare the reprobate, because I am not held as their debtor on account of their conduct.’”

Let the critics of this chapter say—let them say—why blessed Augustine, in the book [Col. 0150B] *On the Good or Gift of Perseverance*, which he wrote together with the book *On the Predestination of the Saints* as a kind of retraction in response to the slanders of this objection, said (chap. 14):

> “This is the predestination of the saints: nothing other than the foreknowledge, namely, and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. But the others—where are they left except in the mass of perdition, by the just judgment of God?”

As we have already stated from his words, if no one were delivered, God’s judgment would nevertheless be beyond reproach. Why did he not define the predestination of the reprobate to destruction in the same way as the predestination of the saints to deliverance through the benefit of divine grace? For he said:

> “Predestination is the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. But the others—where are they left except in the mass of perdition, by the just judgment of God?”

Let those subtle men say who these “others” are. And if they dare, let them contend with Augustine [Col. 0150C] at this point and say that they are predestined to destruction, as you, Augustine, had said earlier. We, however, in accordance with the more accurate words of Saint Augustine, say:

> “The saints are predestined to life by the benefit of God’s grace; they are not found holy but made holy by grace. The others, that is, the reprobate, are left in the mass of perdition by the retribution of justice.”

Let them also read what we have set forth from the book *Hypomnesticon* (Book VI) of that same blessed Augustine against Pelagius and Coelestius, *On the Grace of Christ, Free Will, and Original Sin*, and let them not err like blind men groping at midday. For this is, as the prophet says, the straight way, “so that fools shall not go astray upon it” (Isa. XXXII, 2).

> “The mass, therefore, of the human race, which through the transgression of Adam and Eve was made damnable and mortal, [Col. 0150D] **87** is owed the punishment and torment of Gehenna not generally by divine appointment, but as a debt. Forgiveness, however, is conferred not as something deserved, but through the generosity of the mercy of God, the just Judge. Since God is just and merciful and foreknows the future, from this damnable mass He foreknows and prepares— that is, predestines to life—those whom, not through respect of persons but by the unassailable, indeed incomprehensible, judgment of His equity, free mercy chooses. But the others He punishes with the punishment owed, as I have said. He punishes them because He foreknew what they would be; yet He Himself did not make them or predestine them to be punished. Rather, as I have said, He merely foreknew them in the damnable mass.”

What could he have said more plainly, more certainly? And blessed Gregory, [Col. 0151A] as we quoted above:

> “Thus, plainly, our Redeemer acts in the gathering of human beings, drawing some away from their iniquities and leaving others in their iniquity.”

What could he have said more clearly or openly? And again, in the fourth *Homily on the Gospel*, he says:

> “The Lord first wished to be preached to Judea alone and afterward to all the nations, so that, when that people refused the call to conversion, the holy preachers might proceed in due order to the calling of the nations, and what was done to Judea as a testimony might become an increase of grace for the nations. Even then there were some who were to be called from Judea and some from the nations who were not to be called. For in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts II, IV, XVI), while Peter was preaching, we read that first three thousand Hebrews believed and afterward five thousand. And when the apostles wished [Col. 0151B] to preach to the nations in Asia, they are said to have been forbidden by the Spirit. Yet that same Spirit, who first forbade the preaching, afterward poured it into the hearts of the Asians. Therefore He first forbade what He afterward did because at that time there were among them some who were not to be saved. At that time there were among them those who did not yet deserve to be restored to life, although they were not thereby to be judged more severely for rejecting the preaching.

> “Thus by a subtle and hidden judgment the holy preaching is withdrawn from the ears of some because they do not deserve to be saved by grace. Hence the Psalmist says: ‘Come and see the works of the Lord: how terrible He is in His counsels concerning the sons of men’ (Ps. LXIII, 5). For he saw that one person was mercifully called and another repelled as justice demanded; and because the Lord orders some things by sparing and others by anger, he was terrified at what [Col. 0151C] he could not penetrate. Since he saw Him not only as unsearchable in certain judgments but also as unbending, he declared Him terrible in His counsels.”

And elsewhere in the Gospel we read concerning those who were called to the dinner but did not wish to come, that those who had been invited were not worthy (Matt. XXII, 8). For some are called by the word of preaching but are not worthy to come in obedience; others come but are not worthy to remain in the calling; and some are not even worthy to be called, as this outstanding teacher said in the aforementioned homily on the Gospel.

But in the thirty-fifth *Homily on the Gospel*, concerning those who are called and do not wish to come, he also says:

> “Just as those who were called and did not wish to come were sinners, so too are those sinners who are invited and come. But proud sinners are [Col. 0151D] rejected, so that humble sinners may be chosen.”

**88** Concerning those who come when called but do not remain in the calling, it is likewise written that “they believe for a time, and in the time of temptation fall away.” The Lord clearly demonstrates this in the Gospel concerning those who hear the word but do not produce fruit, speaking of the seed that fell beside the road, on the ground, and among thorns (Luke VIII). Yet none of them will escape the judgment of punishment, because none will be able to offer an excuse.

Concerning those who were not worthy to hear the word of preaching, Paul says:

> “For whoever sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Rom. II, 12).

For the invisible things of God, as well as His eternal [Col. 0152A] power and divinity, are perceived and seen from the creation of the world through the things that have been made, so that they are without excuse (Rom. I, 20).

Concerning those who heard but did not obey, it is written again:

> “I called, and you refused; you despised all my counsel. I also will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. I, 24–25).

And concerning those who heard the word, believed, but did not remain in right faith and good works, the Gospel says:

> “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX, 62).

And concerning those who hear, believe, and persevere, he says that the seed fell on good soil and produced fruit (Luke VIII, 8). And:

> “Whoever hears my words and keeps them is like a man who built his house upon a rock” (Matt. VII, 24).

And again:

> “Whoever has my words and keeps them is the one who loves me; and whoever [Col. 0152B] loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV, 21).

And:

> “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV, 13).

And again the same blessed Gregory speaks briefly of the elect and the reprobate in the eighth homily:

> “The world is registered at the birth of the Lord, because He appeared in the flesh who would register His elect in eternity. In contrast, concerning the reprobate the Prophet says: ‘Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous’ (Ps. LXVIII, 29).”

But if they still wish to hear something from blessed Augustine that we have not yet set forth, let them receive what he said in the aforementioned book *On the Good or Gift of Perseverance*, speaking about the Tyrians and Sidonians left in the mass of perdition (chap. 14):

> “From this,” he says, “[Col. 0152C] it is evident that some possess by natural endowment itself a divine gift of understanding, by which they may be moved toward faith if they either hear words suited to their minds or see signs suited to them. Yet if, by God’s deeper judgment, they have not been separated from the mass of perdition by the predestination of grace, neither the divine words nor the divine deeds by which they might believe are presented to them.”

And shortly afterward:

> “But it did not benefit them that they were able to believe, because they were not predestined by Him whose judgments are inscrutable and whose ways are unsearchable. Nor would it have harmed these others that they were unable to believe—for concerning them it was said through the Prophet: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart’ (Isa. VI; John XII)—if they had been predestined in such a way that God would illuminate them though blind and wish to take away the heart of stone from them though hardened.”

Hence shortly afterward [Col. 0152D] there follows what we quoted above, of which one part pertains to mercy and the other to the judgment of Him to whom our soul says:

> “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C, 1).

**89** Concerning what we placed near the end of this chapter—“But He predestined eternal punishment for them,” namely, for those left in the mass of perdition—let them hear what blessed Augustine says in the frequently mentioned book *On the Good or Gift of Perseverance* (chap. 12):

> “Since what is written—‘Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings’ (Rom. V, 12)—cannot rightly be understood in any other way, no one, small or great, is delivered from perpetual [Col. 0153A] death, which was most justly requited for sin, except the one who died to remit both our original and our personal sins, without any original or personal sin of His own. But why these rather than those? Again and again we say—and we are not weary of saying it—‘O man, who are you to answer back to God?’ (Rom. IX, 20). His judgments are inscrutable and His ways unsearchable (Rom. XI, 33). Let us add this also: ‘Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you’ (Ecclus. III, 22).”

But if these passages and the others are not enough—the passages we have set forth from the frequently mentioned book against Pelagius and Coelestius—we shall add from the same work what that most discerning man himself discussed there, which we have not yet presented (*Hypomn.*, Book VI):

> “But that what we have said is true, although it has been fully [Col. 0153B] argued—namely, that punishment has been predestined for those who are to perish—hear the apostle Peter, when he says that there will be false prophets, deceitful teachers, and apostates in the Church, just as there were among the ancient people (II Peter II, 1): ‘For whom judgment from long ago is not idle, and their destruction does not sleep.’ Likewise the apostle Jude says: ‘Certain men have slipped in, who long ago were designated for this judgment, ungodly men who turn the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ into sensuality and deny the only God and Lord Jesus Christ’ (Jude 4).

> “And in the Gospel the Lord says to sinners: ‘Go into the eternal fire, which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels’; but to those predestined He says: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’ (Matt. XXV, 41, 34), that is [Col. 0153C] predestined.”

> “Therefore we must hold firmly to the unshaken rule of this discussion, by which it has become clear through divine testimonies that sinners, in their own evils, were foreknown before they existed in the world, but were not predestined; whereas punishment was predestined for them according to the fact that they were foreknown.”

And Prosper, in the resolution of the tenth objection against the Vincentians:

> “God predestined this—that is, His judgment, by which He will repay each person according to what he has done, whether good or evil.”

Let our detractors say what discordant, contrary, or divergent element they have found in these statements of the saints Augustine, Gregory, and Prosper within the chapter excerpted by us. And if they cannot say, it is clear that they preferred to utter curses rather than speak the truth.

Let them also receive an example of blessed Augustine harmonious and consonant with the preceding [Col. 0153D] **90** statements, from the often-mentioned book entitled *On the Good or Gift of Perseverance*. Certain people abuse this example and attempt to bend it toward their own interpretations, but they cannot, because the most manifest truth in this very example and in the preceding and subsequent passages of the same book resists their efforts with the greatest force.

For, speaking against those who object to the sincerity of the truth—as anyone who wishes may easily recognize from reading the same book—he says at the relevant point (chap. 11):

> “Therefore, as the Apostle says: ‘It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy’ (Rom. IX, 16). He comes to the aid even of little ones [Col. 0154A] whom He wills, even when they neither will nor run; those whom He chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, intending to give them grace freely, that is, with none of the merits of their faith or works preceding it. He also comes to the aid of adults whom He foresaw would believe in His miracles if those miracles had been performed among them. Those whom He does not wish to help, [Col. 0154B] He does not help; concerning them, in His predestination, He secretly but justly made another judgment.”

For our detractors attempt to confirm their own position by this example, twisting what he said—“concerning them, in His predestination, He secretly but justly made another judgment”—as though Saint Augustine wished it to be understood that “He made another judgment” means “He predestined them to destruction.” How absurd this is appears from the clearest indications.

For he says: “Those whom He does not wish to help, He does not help,” namely, because those whom He does help He helps through predestination, that is, through the preparation of grace. But concerning those whom He does not help, “He secretly but justly made another judgment in His predestination.” And what He judged he states most openly in what follows:

> “‘For there is no iniquity with God; but His judgments are inscrutable and His ways unsearchable’ (Rom. IX, 33); ‘all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth’ (Ps. XXIV, 10). Therefore mercy is unsearchable, because He has mercy on whom He wills, with none of his preceding merits; and truth is unsearchable, because He hardens whom He wills, indeed according to preceding merits, but often shared with the one on whom He has mercy, as in the case of two twins, one of whom is taken and one left.”

Behold what that “other” judgment [Col. 0154C] was which the Lord made in His predestination.

Hence, finally, there follow the words of Augustine himself in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*:

> “The outcome is different, the merits common; yet in such a way is one of them delivered by the great goodness of God that the other is not condemned by any injustice of his. For is there injustice with God? Certainly not. But his ways are inscrutable. Therefore, let us undoubtedly believe that there is mercy in those who are delivered and truth in those who are punished, and let us not attempt to scrutinize what is inscrutable or investigate what is unsearchable. For ‘from the mouth of infants and nursing children’ he perfects his praise (Ps. VIII, 3), so that, when we see what occurs in these persons, whose deliverance is preceded by no good merits, and in those whose condemnation is preceded only by the original sins common to both [Col. 0154D], we should in no way hesitate to believe that the same thing also occurs among adults: that is, we should not suppose either that grace is given to anyone according to his merits, or that anyone is punished except according to his merits—whether the persons delivered and punished have equal or unequal evil causes—so that ‘he who seems to stand may take heed lest he fall’ (I Cor. X, 12), and ‘he who glories may glory not in himself but in the Lord’ (I Cor. I, 31).”

And after a little further on in the same book he continues, saying (chapter 17):

> “Therefore, whatever gifts of his God bestows on anyone, he undoubtedly foreknew that he would bestow them and prepared them in his foreknowledge. Thus, those whom he predestined, he also called with that calling which I am never weary of mentioning, concerning which it is said: ‘The gifts and calling of God are without repentance’ [Col. 0155A] (Rom. XI, 29). For to dispose in his foreknowledge—which cannot be deceived or changed—his future works is nothing other than to predestine.”

And a little further on:

> “When we have said these and many other things which it is tiresome to repeat, and have shown that both the beginning of faith and perseverance to the end are gifts of God, and that God could not fail to foreknow any future gifts of his—both which gifts were to be given and to whom they were to be given—it follows that those whom he liberates and crowns were predestined by him.”

And somewhat earlier:

> “Or perhaps they do not even say that these themselves are gifts of God, predestined? Then they are not given by God, or he did not know that he would give them. But if they are both given and he foreknew that he would give them, then he certainly predestined them.”

And Saint Jerome, in his interpretation of Ecclesiastes:

> “Not everything new under the sun is to be called new” (Eccl. I, 10), since through the foreknowledge and predestination of God those things which are future have already been accomplished. For those who were chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world already existed in the earlier ages.

And Saint Augustine, in the book *On Correction and Grace* (chapter 9):

> “The prophet Isaiah also says of him: ‘He made the things that are to be’ [Col. 0155B]. Therefore, all who in God’s most provident ordering have been foreknown, predestined, called, justified, and glorified—I do not say merely those not yet reborn, but even those not yet born—are already children of God and absolutely cannot perish.”

And Prosper, in the fifteenth *Answer to the Objection of the Gauls*:

> “There is no doubt,” he says, “that, without any temporal distinction, God simultaneously foreknew and predestined those things which, with him as their author, were to be done, or which were to be repaid to evil merits by a just judgment. But he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, those things which were not going to have their cause of operation from him. Foreknowledge, therefore, can exist without predestination, but predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge.”

And likewise in the fifteenth *Recapitulation*:

> “For the things we have from God’s gift, and which are said to have been foreknown, cannot fail to have been predestined; and the things called predestined cannot fail to have been foreknown.”

And in the fifteenth *Answer to the Objection against the Vincentians*:

> “God did not prepare any soul that would live wickedly and disgracefully in order that it might live in that manner; but he was not ignorant that it would be such, and he foreknew that he would judge such a person justly. Thus nothing else can be referred to his predestination except what pertains either to the due repayment of justice or to the undue generosity of grace.”

Let our critics and the condemners of the chapter we have excerpted see from these statements how harmoniously the sense excerpted by us in this same chapter from the words of blessed Augustine, Prosper, and other teachers agrees with these statements that the same holy man Augustine set forth against his calumniators, as well as with other statements issued through the proclamation of the Holy Spirit by them.

I shall also add certain passages, as though by way of supererogation, from the letter of blessed Augustine to the presbyter Xystus (Letter 105). Nothing would need to be added from it if the plurality of the other testimonies did not require this:

> “Those who think that they believe God to be a respecter of persons—indeed, the authors and disseminators of this perverse doctrine—if they believe that, without any preceding merits, God has mercy on whom he wills, calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whom he wills, pay little attention to the fact that the deserved punishment is repaid to the condemned, while undeserved grace is given to the one delivered. Let us therefore give thanks to the Savior, since we see that what was not repaid to us would nevertheless have been owed to us in the condemnation of those like us. For if both were delivered, what sin deserved through justice would remain hidden; and if no one were delivered, what grace could bestow would remain hidden. ‘Mercy and truth have met one another,’ so that neither mercy impedes the truth by which the worthy person is punished, nor truth the mercy by which the unworthy person is delivered [Col. 0156B]. Therefore, ‘he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.’ For we seek the merit of hardening and find it: the entire mass was condemned deservedly on account of sin; and God does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by not imparting mercy. For those to whom he does not impart it are neither worthy nor deserving of it; rather, they are worthy and deserving that it not be imparted to them.

> “But we seek the merit of mercy and do not find it, because there is none. Otherwise grace would be emptied if it were not given freely but repaid according to merits. What merit, then, does a human being possess before grace, by which merit he may receive grace, when every good merit of ours is produced in us only by grace, and when, as God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing other than his own gifts? ‘The wages of sin,’ he says, ‘is death, but the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord’ (Rom. VI, 23).

> “But if they are vessels of wrath, made complete for destruction, let them attribute to themselves the punishment repaid to them as their due, because they were made from that mass which God deservedly and justly condemned on account of the sin of the one in whom all sinned. But if they are vessels of mercy, made from the same mass, to whom he did not wish to repay the punishment they deserved, let them not inflate themselves, but glorify him who bestowed on them mercy that was not owed. Therefore, let them not oppose the gratuitous mercy of God with the most obstinate madness. Let them allow the Son of Man, at whatever age, to seek and save what had perished.

> “Nor should they dare to judge his inscrutable judgments: why, in one and the same case, his mercy comes upon one person while his wrath remains upon another. For who are these people that they should answer God, when he said of Rebecca, our father Isaac’s wife, who had conceived twins from a single intercourse, while they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, so that his purpose according to election might remain—namely, the election of grace, not of what was owed, the election by which he himself makes, rather than finds, those to be chosen—that the elder would serve the younger, ‘not on the basis of works but of him who calls’ (Gen. XXV; Rom. IX)?

> “Therefore, ‘he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.’ He does this with one in whom there is no injustice: he has mercy by a free gift, but hardens by a most just merit. Let the vessels, therefore, that have been made for honor from the same mass acknowledge what divine mercy has granted them.”

[Col. 0157A] Saint Augustine likewise says in the fifth book *Against Julian* (chapter 3):

> “Finally, after saying here, ‘All things work together for good for those who are called according to his purpose,’ he immediately added: ‘For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified’ (Rom. VIII, 28–30). These are those called according to the purpose. They are therefore the elect, and this before the foundation of the world, by him who calls things that are not as though they were; but they were elected through the election of grace.

> “Hence the same teacher also says concerning Israel: ‘The remnant has been saved through the election of grace’ (Rom. XI, 3). And lest they perhaps be thought to have been elected before the foundation of the world on the basis of foreknown works, he continued and added: ‘But if by grace, then it is not by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace’ (ibid., 6).

> “From this number of the elect and predestined, even those who have led the worst kind of life are brought by God’s goodness to repentance. Through his patience they were not removed from this life in the very midst of their crimes, so that it might be shown both to them and to their fellow heirs how deep an evil God’s grace can rescue a person from. None of these perishes, whatever age he may die at. For far be it from us to believe that one predestined to life is permitted to end this life without the sacrament of the Mediator.

> “For their sake the Lord says: ‘This is the will of him who sent me, the Father, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me’ (John VI, 39). But the other mortals who are not of this number, although they are from the same mass from which these also come, have been made vessels of wrath and are born for the benefit of these. For God does not create any of them rashly or by chance, nor is he ignorant of what good he might accomplish through them: indeed, he accomplishes this very good, that he creates human nature in them and adorns the order of the present age through them.

> “He brings none of these to saving and spiritual repentance, by which a human being is reconciled to God in Christ, whether he grants them greater patience or patience no less than that granted to others. Although, therefore, all from the same mass of perdition and condemnation, according to the hardness of their heart and their unrepentant heart, insofar as it depends on them, store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, when each person is repaid according to his works, God nevertheless brings some of them to repentance by merciful goodness, while by just judgment he does not bring others.”

And other things which he continues in the same passage. Concerning this chapter, Saint Prosper has discussed the matter sufficiently and in a Catholic manner against the thirteenth objection of the Gauls.

Likewise, Saint Augustine says in the third book *Against Julian* (chapter 17):

> “What Christian could be ignorant that he who made the first human being from dust fashions all human beings from seed—but from seed already corrupted and condemned? Of these, some remain in punishment through truth, while others are delivered from evil through mercy.”

Likewise, in the third book:

> “God is good; God is just. He can deliver some without good merits, because he is good; he cannot condemn anyone without evil merits, because he is just.”

And in the fifth book (chapter 18):

> “Therefore, concerning this evil of lust, when faithful married people make good use of it, having been freed from its guilt by the gift of the Savior, whoever are born from it are, by the gift of the Creator, not—as you charge us—prepared for the kingdom of the devil, but are rather to be rescued by him and transferred into the kingdom of the Only-Begotten.”

Likewise, in the same book:

> “For absolutely no one can avoid suffering these things while living here, in no way and for no reason. Yet whether a person is oppressed by the greatest or the smallest evils, it is not permissible for him to say to the one who formed him, though he is almighty, just, and good: ‘Why have you made me thus?’ And no one delivers us from the heavy yoke that lies upon the children of the first Adam except the second Adam.”

And a little later:

> “Although they themselves do not know this, until, if they belong to the number of the predestined, they receive the Spirit who is from God, so that they may know the things granted to them by God.”

And likewise in the same book:

> “If you perceive this to be deeper than can be discovered by you, let the question why God wishes to help one and does not wish to help another, both among the greater and among the lesser, be equally deep for both of us. Nevertheless, let us hold this certain and immovable: there is no injustice with God by which he condemns anyone without evil merits, and there is goodness with God by which he delivers many without good merits. In those whom he condemns, he demonstrates what is owed to all, so that from this those whom he delivers may learn what deserved punishment is remitted to them and what undeserved grace is bestowed upon them.”

And likewise in the fifth book:

> “Or perhaps, because the life he obtained by being born was too little, he added mercy as well, so that he would not naturally remain a son of wrath like the others, and would not become a vessel of wrath rather than a vessel of mercy.”

And in the sixth book (chapter 1):

> “Grace, through the blood of the Mediator, can rescue them from this great evil. But how could they have fallen into such great evil if, by divine judgment, no punishment were owed to a corrupted origin?”

Likewise in the same book (chapter 4):

> “In them, therefore, as we have often said, he makes known, according to the Apostle, in the vessels of wrath, the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy, so that they may not glory as though on account of the merits of their life, when they recognize that what they see repaid to their equal companions in death could most justly have been repaid to them as well.”

And likewise in the same book (chapter 5):

> “Certainly here, where there is neither the immobility of fate, nor the randomness of fortune, nor the dignity of persons, what remains except the depth of mercy and truth? Thus we may know, and from this incomprehensible matter comprehend, that, in accordance with the two human beings—one through whom sin entered the world, the other who takes away the sin of the world—all children of carnal desire, wherever they are born, belong deservedly to the heavy yoke of the children of Adam; while from among them all the children of spiritual grace, wherever they are born, arrive without merit at the easy yoke of the children of God.”

And likewise in the same book (chapter 8):

> “Why do we think that it is contrary to his works that those who are born from a corrupted origin, and are therefore condemnable, should be born through him who creates them, since he is the Creator of all, and that those regenerated through the Mediator should be freed from deserved condemnation by gratuitous and undeserved mercy? He chose them before the foundation of the world through the election of grace, not on the basis of works, whether past, present, or future. Otherwise grace is no longer grace.”

Let the reader consider all these examples and see whether they support the chapter excerpted by us, in which it is written:

> “The human being, using free will badly, sinned and fell, and became a mass of perdition for the whole human race. But the good and just God chose from this same mass of perdition, according to his foreknowledge, those whom he predestined to life through grace, and predestined eternal life for them. But the others, whom by the judgment of his justice he left in the mass of perdition, he foreknew would perish, but did not predestine them to perish; yet, because he is just, he predestined eternal punishment for them.”

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the fact that Gothescalcus used an example from the book of blessed Augustine, whose authorship his associates deny, to confirm his own view, and on other statements of the saints set forth in support of the position of the chapter excerpted by us

[Col. 0159B]

Finally, from Augustine’s book *Hypomnesticon*, Gothescalcus, among other things, set down the following example to confirm his view that the reprobate were predestined by God to punishment. Speaking of Judas, he says:

> “If he had been made such,” blessed Augustine says, “he would have been without guilt, and it would have been attributed to God’s workmanship, not to Judas. His condemnation would also have been unjustly imposed upon him. Likewise Peter: ‘For them judgment from long ago is not idle, and their destruction does not sleep’ (II Pet. II, 3). And Judas: ‘Certain men have slipped in, who long ago were designated for this judgment as ungodly’ (Jude 4).”

His blindness seems not so much to be marveled at as exposed, since, abandoning such manifest and weighty examples as we have produced from the same book, he clipped these three examples alone and shamelessly bent them to his own meaning. For, speaking in the same book about the predestination of the elect and the abandonment of the reprobate, blessed Augustine says as follows (*Hypomn.*, book VI):

> “For we have said that, from the condemnable mass of the human race, God foreknew—through mercy, not through merits—those whom he also predestined to life by the election of grace. But the others, who by the judgment of his justice are made without this grace, he merely foreknew would perish through their own fault; he did not predestine them to perish.”

And a little later:

> “We rightly confess that punishment was predestined for these. To prove this, I think Judas alone is sufficient as an example. For when God had foreknown that he would be exceedingly wicked through the vices of his own will—that is, that he would abuse the discipleship graciously bestowed by Christ, and, burning with avarice, would hand the Lord over to the Jews for money—he predestined punishment for him according to his merit.”

After confirming this very fully with examples from Scripture, he reached the passage which Gothescalcus did not fear to appropriate after mutilating it:

> “Therefore, when the Holy Spirit recalls in the Psalms his evil works, before he existed he was foreknown, not made, to be such as he would be in the future against the Son of God. For if he had been made such, he would have been without guilt, and it would have been attributed to God’s workmanship, not to Judas. His condemnation would also have been unjustly imposed upon him. But far be this from the supremely good Judge, the God who is the author of all good things but the condemner of all evils. As I have said, he foreknew the evil Judas but did not make him evil; nevertheless, in the things he foreknew, he permitted him to fulfill them, handing him over to a reprobate mind by a just judgment. And he permitted this because, through the Holy Spirit, he had foretold beforehand that Judas would perish.”

And a little later:

> “Such, therefore, is the cause of all who perish, although the guilt differs from guilt. But although what we have said has been discussed fully—namely, that punishment was predestined for those who perish—hear the Apostle Peter, when he says that there would be false prophets, lying teachers, and apostates in the Church, just as there had been among the ancient people: ‘For them,’ he indicates, ‘judgment from long ago does not cease, and their destruction does not sleep’ (II Pet. II, 3). Likewise the Apostle Jude says: ‘Certain men have slipped in, who long ago were designated for this judgment as ungodly, transferring the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ into licentiousness and denying the only God and Lord Jesus Christ’ (Jude 4).

> “And in the Gospel the Lord says to sinners: ‘Go into the eternal fire which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels’; but to the predestined: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’ (Matt. XXV, 41, 34)—that is, predestined.”

[Col. 0160C]

For this reason, we have judged that nothing should be said against this same Gothescalcus, since Saint Augustine himself speaks clearly enough against him on his own behalf. Saint John Chrysostom agrees with his meaning and words concerning the kingdom prepared for the saints and the punishments prepared for the reprobate, with one spirit, one mind, and one voice, in the book *On the Restoration of the Fallen*, as we set forth above. From evangelical truth he demonstrates that the glory of the kingdom of heaven was made for human beings, while Gehenna was also made for the devil.

But concerning Judas, the same Saint John says in the same book:

> “Therefore,” he says, “the enemy finally snatched Judas away from this life, lest, because he knew that there was a return to salvation, he should restore his fall through repentance. For my part, even if what I say seems astonishing, I would not say that even Judas’s sin exceeded the power of repentance.”

Hence Saint Ambrose, when expounding the verse of Psalm CXVIII, “Sinners have laid a snare for me,” says:

> “And lest you think this snare a minor one, this snare strangled the apostle Judas. Miserable man, when he had been ensnared in order to betray the Lord, and perceived how great a crime had been committed, he hanged himself with the snare. But that snare was also the devil’s, so that he would not repent but would suffocate himself with the snare. For God is merciful even toward the betrayers themselves, so that they may be summoned to repentance, turned back from their shameful purpose, and recover their senses from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to do his will.

> “It is no longer a misfortune to have fallen into the snare, but a crime: they not only gave themselves to be captured, but are also held bound to the devil’s will, although they could say: ‘Let us break their bonds.’ For divine Scripture has given you the means not only to beware of the devil’s snare but also, through repentance, to break his bonds.”

How greatly God accepts and loves the repentance of every sinner—he who does not wish the sinner’s death but rather that he should turn and live—he himself demonstrates in the evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic Scriptures. Seeing the sinful city, he wept over it, saying: “If you too had known” (Luke XIX, 42), with “you would have wept with tears of repentance” understood; for “there is joy over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV, 7). Repentance is frequently preached, as in: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. III, 1).

And in Mark’s Gospel:

> “Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God and saying: ‘The time has been fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has drawn near; repent and believe the Gospel’” (Mark I, 14).

And John the Baptist says:

> “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III, 8).

And Peter:

> “Repent and turn back, so that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts III, 19).

And Scripture likewise says:

> “You have mercy on all, Lord, and hate nothing that you have made, overlooking the sins of human beings for the sake of repentance” (Wis. XI, 24–25).

Whoever flees from practicing repentance does not perish through God’s predestination, but plunges himself into destruction. The Lord attests this in Luke’s Gospel, when certain people reported to him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. He answered them:

> “‘Do you think that these Galileans were greater sinners than all the other Galileans because they suffered such things? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. Or those eighteen upon whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them—do you think that they were debtors beyond all the people dwelling in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but if you do not repent, you will all likewise perish’” (Luke XIII, 1–5).

Hence Bede says:

> “These Jerusalemites, like those Galileans, were not the only sinners, but they were punished as a warning to the others. Overwhelmed by the tower’s collapse, they foretell that all who refuse to repent will perish.”

Paul laments such people, saying:

> “That I may mourn many of those who sinned before and did not repent” (II Cor. XII, 11).

And concerning such people the Lord says:

> “I called, saying, ‘Repent,’ and you refused; I extended my hand, and there was no one who looked. You despised all my counsel and neglected my reproofs” (Prov. I, 24).

Therefore he will punish such people with the predestined judgment, concerning which it follows in the same passage:

> “I also will laugh at your destruction and mock when what you feared comes upon you; when sudden calamity falls upon you, and judgment or condemnation rushes upon you like a storm; when tribulation and distress come upon you” (Prov. I, 26–27).

Paul addresses such people:

> “Do you despise the riches of God’s goodness, patience, and forbearance? Do you not know that God’s goodness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each according to his works: eternal life to those who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption; but wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress upon every human soul that works evil—upon the one who is contentious and does not obey the truth but obeys iniquity” (Rom. II, 4–9).

Concerning such people the Psalmist says:

> “They set their eyes on turning toward the earth; and behold, those who distance themselves from you, Lord, will perish” (Ps. XVI, 11).

And:

> “You have destroyed all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. LXXII, 27).

The Lord invites them, saying:

> “Hear, my people, and I will testify to you; Israel, if you will listen to me. There shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god. For I am the Lord your God” (Ps. LXXX, 9–11).

And concerning them he complains again, saying:

> “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not heed me. Therefore I abandoned them according to the desires of their heart; they shall walk in their own inventions. If my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways, perhaps I would swiftly have humbled their enemies and laid my hand upon those who afflicted them. The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time shall be forever” (ibid., 12–16).

Luke’s Gospel also exhorts them in the singular:

> “When you go with your adversary to the magistrate, while you are on the way, make an effort to be freed from him, lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison” (Luke XII, 58).

Bede says:

> “Our adversary on the way is the word of God, which is contrary to our carnal desires in the present life. The one who humbly submits to its commands is freed from it. Otherwise, the adversary will hand him over to the judge, and the judge to the officer: for the guilty sinner will be held accountable in the judge’s examination on account of his having despised the Lord’s word. The judge will hand him over to the officer because he will permit him to be dragged by an evil spirit to punishment, so that the spirit may exact from the body for punishment the soul that had willingly consented to it for guilt.

> “The officer throws him into prison because, through the evil spirit, he is thrust into hell until the day of judgment, from which point the spirit itself will also be tormented together with him in the fires of hell. ‘I tell you, you will not come out from there until you have paid even the last penny’—that is, until you have paid even for the smallest sins. Since you will always be able to pay them by suffering punishments, but never to pay them off by obtaining forgiveness—for there will be no place for forgiveness there—you will never come out from there, where you will suffer the perpetual punishments of your deeds, by the predestined judgment arising from the repayment of justice.”

And because we are compelled to answer those who are more obstinate in understanding than perceptive, and more curious than studious, let us say to them what Saint Augustine replied to his detractors in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*:

> “We have said many things,” he says, “and perhaps long ago we were able to persuade them of what we wish, yet we continue to speak to minds so good as though they were dull, to whom even what is excessive is not enough. But let them forgive us: a new question has compelled us to do this.”

Hence let the detractor—or indeed whoever they may be from the school of the modern Gothescalcian Predestinarians—since they have heard what blessed Augustine and Saint Prosper wrote against the Gauls, receive what the same blessed Augustine wrote against the African Predestinarians in the book *On Correction and Grace*. Concerning this book Saint Prosper says to blessed Augustine, in a letter sent to him for this very matter:

> “It came about through the ordering of God’s mercy that, when certain people within Africa had raised similar questions, like those which you yourself had described among people resident in the city of Massilia, you issued the book *On Correction and Grace*, full of divine authority. Concerning this book, as also concerning the other books we have mentioned, it is more appropriate to set forth examples by which he himself wished to refute those same errors, rather than to use passages from those whom he certainly labored to correct in these books.

> “In the chapter mentioned above, as has been stated earlier, we said: ‘The good and just God chose from the same mass of perdition, according to his foreknowledge, those whom he predestined to life through grace, and predestined eternal life for them. But the others, whom by a just judgment he left in the mass of perdition, he foreknew would perish, but did not predestine them to perish; yet, because he is just, he predestined eternal punishment for them.’”

And blessed Augustine, in the aforementioned book *On Correction and Grace* (chapter 7):

> “Those who will not persevere, and who will fall away from the Christian faith and manner of life in such a way that the end of this life finds them in that condition, are certainly not to be counted among the predestined, even at the time when they live well and piously. For they have not been separated from that mass of perdition by God’s foreknowledge and predestination.”

And likewise (chapter 9):

> “Nor should it disturb us that God does not grant this perseverance to some of his children. For it would be impossible for this to be so if they were among those predestined and called according to his purpose, who truly are children of promise. For while they live piously, they are called children of God; but since they will live wickedly and die in that same wickedness, God’s foreknowledge does not call them children of God.”

Observe why here he did not say, as the Predestinarians say, “God’s predestination to destruction,” but, speaking of the elect, he mentioned predestination, while concerning the reprobate he mentioned foreknowledge.

And shortly afterward:

> “Those who are truly sons have been foreknown and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, and they have been called according to his purpose so that they might be elect. For it is not the son of promise who perishes, but the son of perdition. These, therefore, belonged to the multitude of the called, but not to the small number of the elect. Therefore God did not fail to give perseverance to his predestined children. They would have had it if they had belonged to that number of children. They are the predestined—those predestined and called according to his purpose—none of whom perishes.”

And likewise:

> “Already in that predestination they are his children.”

And after a little further:

> “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son; those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; those whom he justified, he also glorified. All these things have already occurred: he foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and glorified, because all the foreknown and predestined have already been foreknown and predestined, and many have already been called and justified.

> “But what he placed at the end—‘he also glorified them’—if that glory is to be understood here of which he likewise says, ‘When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory’ (Col. III, 4), has not yet occurred. Although those two things also—‘he called’ and ‘he justified’—have not occurred in all of those about whom they were said, for many are still to be called and justified until the end of the age, nevertheless he used past-tense verbs concerning future things as though God had already done what he had already disposed from eternity to occur.

> “Therefore the prophet Isaiah also says of him: ‘He made the things that are to be.’ Whoever, then, in God’s most provident ordering have been foreknown, predestined, justified, and glorified—I do not say merely those not yet reborn, but even those not yet born—are already children of God and absolutely cannot perish.”

And after a little further (chapter 10):

> “For if this person has been called according to the purpose, then undoubtedly God also cooperates for good in the very correction he receives. But since the one who corrects does not know whether this is that calling, let him do with charity what he knows ought to be done. For he knows that by correcting such a person God will bring about either mercy or judgment: mercy, if the one being corrected has been separated from the mass of perdition by the generosity of grace and is not among the vessels of wrath, which are made complete for destruction, but among the vessels of mercy, which he has prepared for glory.”

Therefore the same blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Predestination of Grace* (ch. 5):

> “From him, then, who is eternal and foreknowing, who is both just and merciful, who both exercises the severity that is due and displays the mercy that is not due, and who possesses power over the creation and election of human beings, as a potter has power over clay, some vessels were made for honor, but others for dishonor. Before he made us, he foreknew us, and in that very foreknowledge he chose us when he had not yet made us. But by whom could this have been done except by him who calls things that are not as though they were (Rom. IV, 17)? For the Apostle says: ‘He chose us before the foundation of the world’ (Eph. I, 4). We were made within the world, and chosen before the world; and thus, in one and the same continuous moment—or, if it can be said in some other way, though it can indeed be said so—with God there is no passing or future moment, but simultaneously foreknowing, making, and choosing; and, while his foreknowledge remains unchangeable, choosing to be made those whom he was going to make by choosing them.””

And again, in the same book (ch. 16):

> “Moses showed that this divine election is not given to human beings as a repayment of merits, but bestowed solely through the generosity of the will, when he was teaching a people that was still carnal. For in Deuteronomy he says to the people: ‘Behold, the heaven and the heaven of heavens belong to the Lord your God, the earth and all that is in it. Nevertheless, the Lord chose your fathers, to love them, and he chose their descendants after them, namely you, above all the nations’ (Deut. X, 14). And he added: ‘Circumcise, therefore, the hardness of your heart, and do not harden your neck any further’ (ibid., 16). But that this hardness of heart nevertheless remained in them, as I have already said above, blessed Stephen showed when he rebuked the Jews. For in the Acts of the Apostles he says: ‘Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit’ (Acts VII, 51). How, then, could there be a stiff neck in that people which was chosen from the world?”

And somewhat later:
