> “When such matters are asked about together with the Apostle, let us marvel; and while the judgment remains that there is no injustice with God, if anything should exceed the measure of our understanding and our intellect should not be deemed worthy to remain within the narrow limits of our thought, let us nevertheless confess, with unshaken equity, that the fullness of divine justice, mercy, and foreknowledge remains intact.”

And again, somewhat earlier in the same book (ch. 13):

> “He chose vessels to make for honor, and by the gift of a gracious calling he freed them from the coming wrath, while abandoning others and reserving them for the judgment of equality; yet he deprived no one of the ability to recognize the truth. Thus the fullness of divine foreknowledge was completed, with justice remaining upon some and grace pouring forth upon others.””

Likewise, blessed Augustine says in his book *On Rebuke and Grace* (ch. 12):

> “He himself, therefore, makes those persevere in the good whom he makes good; but those who fall and perish were not among the number of the predestined.”

Let Gothescalcus, chief of storytellers and reviver of this wicked fiction, hear with his school what Saint Augustine says:

> “‘They were not among the number of the predestined.’ If he had wished, and if it had been appropriate, he could have said: ‘Those who fall and perish were predestined to destruction, and therefore they fell and perished.’”

And again Saint Augustine says in the aforementioned book, at the same place (ch. 13):

> “I speak of those who are predestined to the kingdom of God, whose number is so certain that no one is added to them and no one is taken away from them—not of those who, when the message had been announced and proclaimed, became more numerous than the number.”

And again, in the same book:

> “Those, however, who do not belong to this number of the predestined—whom the grace of God brings to the kingdom, whether they do not yet possess any free choice of their will, or possess the choice of the will but are free because they have been liberated through that very grace—those, then, who do not belong to this most certain and elect number are judged with complete justice according to their merits.”

And again:

> “If the person who is being rebuked belongs to the number of the predestined, let the rebuke be a salutary medicine for him; but if he does not belong to it, let the rebuke be a punitive torment for him.”

And again (ch. 15):

> “As far as we are concerned, at the time when we preach, a person begins to be a son of peace when he obeys this Gospel and, justified by faith, begins to have peace with God; but according to God’s predestination, he was already a son of peace. For it was not said: ‘Upon whomever your peace rests, he will become a son of peace’; rather, he says: ‘Where there is a son of peace, your peace will rest upon that house’ (Luke X, 6).”

And again:

> “Therefore, as far as we are concerned, we are unable to distinguish the predestined from the non-predestined.”

Here we must observe why Saint Augustine did not say, “We are unable to distinguish those predestined to life from those predestined to destruction.”

And what we have already cited from the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*:

> “God grants perseverance to the end. God foreknew that he would do this; this is the predestination of the saints, whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, so that they might be holy and blameless in his sight in love, predestining them for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ.”

And again:

> “Nevertheless, this must be utterly certain to the faithful: that this person belongs to the predestined, and that other person does not.”

Cassiodorus says on Psalm XIV:

> “In truth,” he says, “the inheritance was restored to the one to whom it had been granted in predestination before the creation of things.”

And again:

> “The inheritance of Christ is the predestined multitude of the saints.”

And on Psalm XLIX:

> “Remember that through these allusions he signifies that the number of the predestined is completed not from the synagogue of the Jews alone, but from all the nations.”

And on Psalm LXXVII:

> “‘You have prepared in your sweetness for the poor, O God.’ ‘You have prepared’ signifies the predestined, who from the beginning of the world were prepared by his mercy.”

And on Psalm LXXXVIII:

> “‘Let your right hand be exalted.’ Let the number of the predestined be glorified, the number that is to be placed at the right hand.”

And on Psalm XC:

> “Those who are already known to have been predestined among the number of the blessed cannot fall from the Lord’s side or from his right hand. But this is rightly said of the presumptuous, who believe that they will obtain what they have in no way deserved.”

And on Psalm XCI:

> “When ‘planting’ is mentioned, the Lord’s predestination is signified, because unless someone has been planted in it, he will not have the most blessed growth.”

And on Psalm XCV:

> “For this house—that is, the universal Church, in which Christ dwells—is continually built with living stones, because every day it receives an increase of its structure from those who confess the faith. It does not cease to be built until the number of the predestined is fulfilled at the end of the age.”

And on Psalm CIII:

> “And the cedars of Lebanon which you planted—that is, those whom by your predestination you established in the most beautiful paradise of religion.”

And again, in the same place:

> “Whenever a just person desires that God’s Church be increased, he undoubtedly wishes sinners to be converted, especially when he knows that the desirable coming of the Lord can be delayed until the number of the predestined is complete.”

And on Psalm CXVIII:

> “Not inappropriately, the four corners of the world are understood to indicate the Catholic Church, which is still being formed in this world, while it remains incomplete until it suitably acquires the number of the predestined.”

And on Psalm CXLIII:

> “You count him, of course, among your sheep, in the number of the predestined.”

From these statements of the holy teachers it can be observed that no one perishes by God’s predestination; neither did Judas perish, nor will even the supreme Antichrist perish by it. Rather, all who perish perish through unbelief and persistent wickedness, because God abandons no one before that person abandons him. Nevertheless, God foreknew before all ages, just as he foreknew Judas, all who perish and all who are going to perish, in accordance with what is written: “For Jesus knew who were unbelieving and who would betray him” (John VI, 65).

And since Saint Augustine has spoken at length about the fixed number of the predestined, lest anyone, interpreting the Scriptures wickedly like the devil, should say that the number of the predestined is fixed, that those who perish were not among the predestined, and that those predestined to life cannot perish whatever they may do, however negligently they may live—for this too was said by the ancient Predestinarians—let them hear the same blessed Augustine speaking against his detractors in the book *Hypomnesticon* (book I):

> “You reproach us for believing or preaching that, when together with the Law and the Prophets, with the Gospel of Christ and his Apostles, we speak of predestination, we mean that God predestines certain human beings to the life of the heavenly kingdom in such a way that, even if they do not wish to pray and fast or to remain watchful in every divine work, they cannot perish at all and need have no concern for themselves, since God, because he willed it, once and for all chose and predestined them to life; while he predestines others to the punishment of hell in such a way that, even if they wish to believe and subject themselves to fasts, prayers, and every divine will, God does not delight in them and eternal life cannot be given to them at all—so that they are predestined by election to perish. You claim that by acting in this manner we say God is a respecter of persons.

> “We are not surprised that you, human beings speaking about human beings, can falsely fabricate charges against us, when we see that you have been so bewitched by the devil that you strive to alter the holy and truthful Scriptures to suit your own interpretation, to overthrow the faith founded on the Apostles’ preaching, and to put your false doctrine before the truth. This is why you cannot recognize the truth. Indeed, this is why you have become corrupt and abominable in your desires.”

And again, at the same place:

> “You bring an accusation against us, as though we prohibited the performance of good works and insisted that we ought not to be solicitous about God’s purpose. On the contrary, we exhort those who recognize that they belong, by the gift of grace, to God’s mercy to devote themselves to prayers, supplications, fasts, vigils, and every work of the divine will.

> “The Apostles were predestined, yet what Christ says to them is universal: Christ was predestined according to the flesh from the seed of David, but predestines according to the power of God the Father together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He says: ‘Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation’ (Matt. XXVI, 41). Likewise: ‘Watch at all times, praying that you may be worthy to escape all these things that are about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man’ (Luke XXI, 36). Likewise: ‘Strive to enter through the narrow gate’ (Luke XIII, 24). Likewise: ‘You are my friends if you do what I command you’ (John XV, 24). And there are many other such passages, which would take too long to recount.

> “But, as I said above, the one who told them, ‘Without me you can do nothing,’ enables them through himself to do what they are commanded. The Apostle says that God’s elect are in Christ in this manner: ‘In whom we were predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes all things’ (Eph. I, 11). Understand the expression ‘who accomplishes all things,’ and believe that the works of those who walk according to God’s purpose are God’s work.

> “Those who are without the grace of predestination—that is, strangers to God’s purpose—and persist in evil works: if they should depart from this life while still doing so, we do not say, as you suppose, that they were ordered by God, the maker of human beings, to perish, as though he himself had created their wicked way of life and himself compelled them, against their will, to every work of death. Far be this from the divine purpose. For God does not will iniquity; he has not commanded anyone to act wickedly, nor given anyone license to sin.

> “He made all things to exist, and the nations of the world to be capable of healing. But through the envy of the devil death entered the world. Therefore those who belong to his portion imitate him.

> “Nor do we say, as you invent, that if they wish to believe or devote themselves to God’s good works, God does not wish to grant this to them, since such willing is itself God’s gift. If, therefore, what they will is from God, God wills that what he has granted should be brought to perfection. But if it is not from God, but is also the boastfulness of a self-directed will by which they think they can earn God’s favor through their merits, they plainly cannot obtain what they desire, because, as the Apostle says, ‘it is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy’ (Rom. IX, 16).

> “And because a human being cannot do anything from himself unless it has been given to him from above, the supremely good God does not act here through malice but through justice—not through respect of persons, but through the discernment of hidden causes.”

And again, in the same work, *On the Gift of Perseverance* (ch. 22):

> “You ought also to hope for perseverance in obedience from the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends (James I, 17), and to ask for it in daily prayers. By doing this, trust that you are not strangers to the predestination of his people, because he himself grants that you do this.

> “But far be it from you to despair of yourselves because you are commanded to place your hope in him, not in yourselves. For ‘cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being’ (Jer. XVII, 5), and ‘it is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in a human being’ (Ps. CXVII, 8), because blessed are all who trust in him.

> “Holding fast to this hope, serve the Lord in fear and rejoice in him with trembling (Ps. II, 13, 11), because concerning the eternal life which God, who cannot lie, promised to the children of the promise before eternal times, no one can be secure until this life—which is a trial upon the earth—has been brought to its completion. But may he cause us to hope in him until the end of this life, to whom we say each day: ‘Do not lead us into temptation’ (Matt. VI, 13).”

And again, somewhat later (ch. 23):

> “Let them therefore consider how those are deceived who think that it is from us, rather than given to us, that we ask, seek, and knock; and who say that our merit precedes grace, so that grace follows when we receive after asking, find after seeking, and the door is opened to those who knock. They are unwilling to understand that it is also a gift of God that we pray—that is, that we ask, seek, and knock. For ‘we have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father”’ (Rom. VIII, 15).

> “Blessed Ambrose also understood this. For he says (*Commentary on Isaiah*): ‘To pray to God is likewise a gift of spiritual grace; as it is written: No one says “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit.’

> “Therefore, these things which the Church asks from the Lord, and has always asked from the time she began to exist, God foreknew that he would give to his called ones in such a way that he had already given them in predestination. The Apostle declares this without ambiguity. For, writing to Timothy, he says: ‘Work together for the Gospel according to the power of God, who saves us and calls us with his holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times, but has now been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ’ (II Tim. I, 8).”

And again, in the same work, *On Rebuke and Grace*:

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Fixed Number of the Predestined

[Col. 0169B]

> “That the number of the elect is fixed, neither to be increased nor diminished, is signified also by John the Baptist when he says: ‘Therefore produce worthy fruit of repentance, and do not say among yourselves, “We have Abraham as our father.” For God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones’ (Matt. III, 8). This shows that they are to be cut off if they do not produce fruit, so that the number promised to Abraham may nevertheless not fail. Yet it is said more openly in the Apocalypse: ‘Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown’ (Rev. III). For if another will not receive it unless this person has lost it, the number of the elect is fixed.

> “But since these things are said even to the saints who will persevere as though it were uncertain whether they will persevere, those for whom it is beneficial not to think highly of themselves but to fear ought to hear them in no other way. For who, among the multitude of the faithful, so long as life is lived in this mortality, would presume that he belongs to the number of the predestined? This must be kept hidden here, where exaltation must be so carefully avoided that even so great an Apostle was buffeted by an angel of Satan lest he be exalted.

> “Thus it was said to the Apostles: ‘If you remain in me,’ by the one who certainly knew that they would remain; and through the prophet: ‘If you are willing and obey me,’ although he himself knew in whom he was working the will; and many similar things are said.”

This statement must be read repeatedly and held firmly against those who say: “Whatever one predestined to life does, he will reach the everlasting kingdom; and whatever one predestined to destruction does, he will go to eternal death.” The rivals of Saint Augustine said this too, as Prosper clearly demonstrates in his *Objections of the Calumniators*, which he refuted according to orthodox teaching; and we have recalled it to the best of our limited ability. For this reason, in the letters that the same Prosper and Hilary of Arles had sent to blessed Augustine, they had also complained about these matters, and blessed Augustine had written his reply to them.

And again, at the same place in the same book, he says:

> “The number of the saints predestined by God’s grace to God’s kingdom, having been granted perseverance to the end, will be led there complete, and there, already made perfectly whole, will be kept blessed without end, with the mercy of their Savior remaining with them—whether when they are converted, when they struggle, or when they are crowned. For Holy Scripture testifies that even then they need God’s mercy, when the saint says to the Lord his God concerning his soul: ‘He crowns you with compassion and mercy’ (Ps. CII).”

Yet even then mercy will be bestowed by a just judgment according to the merits of good works. Blessed Gregory, that distinguished ornament of the first and holy Roman See, understood this when he said in the first book of the *Dialogues* (ch. 8):

> “The predestination of the everlasting kingdom,” he says, “has been arranged by almighty God in such a way that the elect reach it through labor, so that by asking they may merit to receive what almighty God arranged before the ages to give them.”

Hence, as is also read in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, he took care to enrich the secret rites of the heavenly sacraments:

> “That he may order our days in his peace, rescue us from eternal condemnation, and command that we be numbered among his elect, through Christ our Lord, God and Father of that same Lord of ours Jesus Christ, to whom the sacred canons command that priests offer prayers at the altar, through the same Son of his, our Lord, with whom in the unity of the Holy Spirit there is glory, power, and dominion, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XIX. How One Predestination of God Can Faithfully Be Called Twofold, and How Gothescalcus and His Synagogue of Sinners Labor Anxiously and Destructively by Thinking and Interpreting Wrongly

[Col. 0170C]

Gothescalcus’s argument nevertheless labors to establish a twofold predestination in such a way that, just as the elect are predestined by God to life, so the reprobate are predestined by God to death. We have now judged it appropriate to answer him in this matter with the words and reasoning of the Catholic Fathers.

Blessed Gregory says in the twentieth book of the *Moralia* (ch. 23):

> “God is called jealous, he is called angry, he is called repentant, he is called merciful, he is called foreknowing, although in God there can be neither jealousy, nor anger, nor repentance, nor mercy in the proper sense, nor foreknowledge. For all these expressions have been transferred to him from human qualities. In him neither past nor future things can be found; rather, all mutable things endure immutably, and things that cannot exist simultaneously in themselves are all present to him at once.

> “For when certain prosperous and adverse circumstances vary around us, we suspect that his attitude toward us has changed, because we ourselves are changed by them. Yet he remains unchangeable in himself and is perceived differently in human thought according to the quality of our merits.”

Accordingly, as far as the proper meaning of the names and the divine essence are concerned, we have shown from blessed Gregory’s words that we cannot say that there is foreknowledge in God, for whom being and knowing are not different, but knowing is being; nothing past happens to him and nothing future arrives, but being is always in him. In him there is neither change nor shadow caused by alteration, and to him it is truthfully said: “But you are always the same” (Ps. CI, 28). Nor can we properly say that he foreknows, to whom it is again said: “But you, Lord, know all things before they happen” (Dan. XIII, 42), and of whom it is written: “He made the things that are to be.”

Nevertheless, Holy Scripture, which cannot show us its excellence in any other way than by adapting itself to us, accommodates itself to such expressions as can draw and raise us toward its understanding. It has adopted expressions proper to us in order to teach us what is proper to itself, so that through improper expressions we may recognize, insofar as mortals are able, what is proper.

Thus Saint Gregory says in the twenty-ninth book of the *Moralia* (ch. 1):

> “Our Lord God Jesus Christ, insofar as he is the power and wisdom of God, was born from the Father before the ages—or rather, because he neither began to be born nor ceases to be born, let us more truly say that he is always born. We cannot say ‘he is always being born,’ lest he appear imperfect. But so that he may be designated eternal and perfect, let us say both ‘always’ and ‘born,’ so that ‘born’ may refer to perfection and ‘always’ to eternity: so that, in whatever manner that timeless essence can be designated by temporal speech, it may be designated.

> “Although by the very fact that we call it perfect we deviate greatly from expressing that truth, since what has not been made cannot be called perfect. Yet the Lord, adapting himself to the words of our weakness, says: ‘Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect’ (Matt. V, 5).”

We have drawn this from the root and carry it in the branches: we need to be taught through expressions of this sort and in this manner, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind occupied with many thoughts” (Wis. IX, 15); and as long as we are in this body, “we are away from the Lord and groan under our burden, longing to put on the dwelling that is from heaven.” But when this corruptible body has put on incorruption, and this mortal body has put on immortality, what the divine essence now teaches us in part through improper expressions, as though in a figure and riddle—the one who teaches human beings knowledge, from whose face come knowledge and understanding—when the perfect has come and what is partial has been abolished, we shall contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face in the bright and transparent city, which is like pure gold and pure glass, and whose lamp is the Lamb. Then all of us shall be his children, taught by the Lord; we shall no longer need to be taught what is proper through what is proper.

Nevertheless, without prejudice to the understanding of faith, it is entirely correct to speak of God’s foreknowledge and predestination. These do not arise in him as temporal accidents, but are his essence, for whom being always is, and knowing is being. And just as the same God is eternally, always, and essentially good, so his foreknowledge and predestination are coeternal and good: they were and always are not an accident but his essence.

Hence Augustine, in his exposition of the Gospel of John, comments on the words, “I judge as I hear” (John V, 30). He hears, that is, through unity of substance and the property of knowledge. From the one by whom he is begotten comes his understanding; from him, certainly, comes his knowledge; from him, therefore, comes his hearing, which is nothing other than knowledge.

And just as the one God is essentially, not accidentally, good and just, so his predestination—which cannot exist without foreknowledge—is one, good, and just. It pertains either to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice, as Saint Augustine says in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*:

> “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance. For to arrange in his foreknowledge, which can neither be deceived nor changed, the works that he is going to perform is precisely, and nothing else than, to predestine.”

And in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*:

> “By predestination God foreknew the things that he himself was going to do; hence it was said: ‘He made the things that are to be.’”

For, as he himself says in the third book of *On the Trinity*:

> “In that supreme essence nothing is born or dies, nothing begins to be or ceases to be.”

And in the book *Hypomnesticon* (book VI, at the beginning):

> “God, for whom foreknowledge was not an accident but has always been and is his essence, foreknows and predestines whatever is to exist before it exists; and he predestines it because he foreknows what it will be. But he does not predestine everything that he foreknows. For he merely foreknows evils, whereas he both foreknows and predestines good things. Therefore, what is good, foreknowledge predestines—that is, it orders beforehand, before it exists in reality; and when it begins to exist together with its author, he calls, orders, and arranges it.”

By this foreknowledge and predestination, the good and just God foreknew and predestined without time whatever he made in time, and time itself—he who made the things that are to be—because before all times he intended to make the human being with free will. But he foreknew, without predestining him, that this same human being would fall through that free will and become the mass of perdition of the whole human race.

He also foreknew and predestined without time—that is, before all times—that from this same mass he would restore some by grace to the same eternal life to which he had first intended the original human being to attain; and before all times he foreknew and predestined that he would make that human being in his own image and likeness. By the same grace he foreknew and predestined before the times of the world that he would grant this same eternal life to those whom he had foreknown and predestined.

But he foreknew, without predestining them, that some would remain in the same mass of death and reach the second death, which is eternal. Yet for those who, persisting in iniquity, would reach eternal death, he predestined that he would repay them with punishment according to their deserts.

For just as before all times he foreknew, but did not predestine, that the human being would sin and through sin incur death, so he—who is not the author of death but the condemner of life and death, who is not the death of those who die but the life of those who live, who said, “God is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matt. XXII, 32)—foreknew, but did not predestine, the human being for death, although he had intended him to remain in eternity. In that human being all would have remained had he himself persisted, just as all sinned in him when he sinned, as it is written: “In whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12).

He did not predestine to punishment the human being whom he created with honor for glory. No, I say, he did not predestine him; rather, he foreknew the human being for punishment, to which one reaches through works worthy of punishment. For unbelief too is a work deserving punishment, just as faith is a work of salvation, as the Lord says: “This is his work: that you believe in him whom he sent” (John VI, 29).

Thus whoever goes to punishment while remaining in unbelief through original or actual sin—whether by not believing or by evil works, denying God, as the Apostle says—does not reach it by God’s predestination. Otherwise it would be reckoned as his workmanship, just as it is reckoned as his workmanship when those predestined to life reach everlasting life.

Nor did the first human being sin or incur death through God’s predestination, because God predestines only those things that are to be done with him as their author. The same must be understood concerning God’s foreknowledge. Just as the first human being sinned and fell not through God’s foreknowledge but through his own fault, so no descendant of his is compelled by God’s foreknowledge to remain in the mass of sin or to reach punishment. The first human being did not sin because God foreknew that he would sin; rather, because the first human being was going to sin, God foreknew it.

Likewise, the reprobate do not remain reprobate because God foreknew this; rather, because they were going to remain reprobate, God foreknew it—but he did not predestine it. For God cannot fail to foreknow what is going to happen, just as what God foreknows cannot fail to happen. It is neither otherwise nor different except as God foreknows it; nor does God foreknow it otherwise or differently than it certainly is going to be.

Therefore, in evil things there is God’s foreknowledge without his predestination, whereas in good things there are both God’s foreknowledge and predestination. God’s predestination is always directed toward the good. As has been said, it pertains either to the giving of grace or to the retribution of justice. Those who are foreknown and predestined reach life by the gift of grace, and eternal life is given to them. Those who are foreknown only and not predestined reach punishment, and by the retribution of justice the punishment foreknown and predestined for them is imposed eternally.

Consequently, there is one predestination of God, which is always directed toward the good. There is predestination by God of the elect to life, but there is no predestination by God of the reprobate to death.

Yet, as the venerable presbyter Bede says in his *Commentary on the Gospel of Luke*:

> “There is no false doctrine that does not mix in some truth.”

And Saint Cyril says to the presbyter Eulogius, near the beginning of his letter:

> “Not everything that heretics say should be fled from and rejected. For they confess many things just as we do. For example, when the Arians say that the Father is the Creator and Lord of all, should we therefore flee from confessions of this kind? Likewise in the case of Nestorius: although he speaks of two natures, indicating the distinction between flesh and the Word—for one nature is that of the Word and the other that of the flesh—he nevertheless does not confess unity with us. We, however, uniting these things into one, confess one Christ, one Son, the same one, and one God.”

And again, at the place cited above, the memorable presbyter Bede says:

> “In heretics and wicked Catholics we must detest and prohibit not the common sacraments which they share with us and which are not against us, but the division contrary to peace and truth, by which they are against us and do not follow the Lord together with us.”

Since Gothescalcus and his accomplices assert a twofold predestination, we must not reject the whole of what they say in every respect. Rather, the sons of the Catholic faith must abominate and anathematize the sense contrary to Catholic faith in the statement by which they assert that God’s predestination is twofold.

For, as we have already stated, they say that just as the elect are predestined by God to life, so the reprobate are predestined by God to death. They must be avoided by the Church to such an extent that, if possible, like the lepers who signify heretics, standing at a greater distance, they should call upon Christ with a loud cry and not press in together with the other crowds; of these it is written that they “stood at a distance” (Luke XVII, 12).

But whoever, placed in the bosom of the Catholic mother Church, wishes to call God’s predestination twofold while understanding correctly the effect of God’s works—he who made the things that are to be—namely, by acknowledging that the gift of grace belongs to the elect and, according to the preceding account, that retribution of justice belongs to the reprobate, so that the elect are predestined to life by the gift of grace and eternal life is predestined for them, whereas the reprobate are not predestined by God to punishment, but eternal punishment is predestined for them by the retribution of justice—does not depart from the truth if he calls this predestination of God twofold in the same way that Catholic teachers call charity twofold.

Charity is one, yet it is called twofold because of the two commandments: love of God and love of neighbor. The charity by which one loves one’s neighbor is not different from the charity by which one loves God. Although God is one thing and one’s neighbor another, God and one’s neighbor are to be loved with one charity.

And just as there is one Spirit and two gifts, so there is one predestination of God, which pertains either to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice. For, as blessed Gregory says in Homily 17 on the prophet Ezekiel, near the middle:

> “God does not help the just by one thought and condemn the unjust by another, but by one and the same power of his singular nature, ever unlike nothing else and never unlike itself, he arranges unlike things.

> “Why should we marvel at this concerning the Creator’s power, when we see traces of his power even in creation? The nature of clay is one thing and the nature of wax another, but the sun’s ray is not different. Yet, although it is not different, the things it works in clay and wax are different, because by the same heat of its fire it hardens clay and melts wax.

> “But perhaps this is a feature of the nature of clay or wax, not of the sun’s substance itself, which appears to work differently in different natures. Almighty God, however, possesses in himself the ability, without change, to arrange mutable things; without diversity in himself, to perform diverse works; and without any alternation of thoughts, to shape unlike things.

> “Therefore God, who is never unlike himself, works in wholly different ways upon different things: he who is everywhere and is wholly present everywhere.”

And as Paul says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God in every place, both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” [Col. 0175A] (II Cor. 2:15): by one and the same good odor some are saved, while others perish. Those who are saved are saved and crowned by the gift of grace; those who perish perish through their own iniquity and are punished by the retribution of justice.

And, as blessed Gregory says in his treatise on the prophet Ezekiel, as well as in the *Moralia on Job*: “Bread strengthens the life of the strong but kills the little ones; and a gentle whistling calms horses but incites puppies.”

Blessed Augustine, expounding the seventh Psalm near its end, says:

“But since he said that the Lord had prepared not only arrows but also vessels of death in his bow, it may be asked what the vessels of death are. Perhaps the heretics? For they too leap forth from the same bow—that is, from the same Scriptures—into souls, to inflame them with love, but to destroy them with the poison of death; and this occurs only according to their merits. Therefore even this arrangement must be attributed to divine Providence—not because it makes sinners, but because it orders them after they have sinned. For those who read with an evil desire are compelled by sin to understand wrongly, so that this itself becomes the punishment of sin. Yet through their death the sons of the Catholic Church are roused from sleep, as though by certain thorns, so that they may advance toward understanding the divine Scriptures. For there must also be heresies, so that, as he says, ‘those who are approved may become manifest among you’ (I Cor. 11:19)—that is, among human beings, though they are manifest to God.

“Or perhaps he appointed the same arrows and vessels of death for the destruction of unbelievers, while he fashioned them burning, or for the burning, for the exercise of the faithful? For what the Apostle says is not false: ‘To some we are the odor of life unto life, and to others the odor of death unto death’ [Col. 0175C] (II Cor. 2:16). And who is sufficient for these things? Therefore it is not surprising if the same apostles are vessels of death to those by whom they suffered persecution, and fiery arrows for inflaming the hearts of believers.

“After this dispensation, just judgment will come. He speaks of it in such a way that we understand punishment to be made for each person and iniquity itself to be converted into punishment for him. Let us not suppose that God’s tranquility and ineffable light itself produces something from which sins are punished; rather, it orders sins themselves so that what had been delights to the person sinning may become instruments for the Lord who punishes.”

And in Psalm 44:

“Those who followed the good odor. The bride herself loved the friend of her bridegroom, saying in the Song of Songs: ‘We shall run after the odor of your perfumes’ [Col. 0175D] (Song 1:3). But the others, the more they saw him—namely Paul—in the glory of preaching the Gospel and in blameless life, the more they were tortured by envy and were killed by the good odor.”

And likewise Saint Augustine, in his book *On the Predestination of Grace* (ch. 15):

“Nevertheless, perhaps someone may say that the way to salvation would be less suitable if someone were scourged without being inwardly summoned by any calling. How did Nebuchadnezzar merit fruitful repentance? Was he not scourged after countless acts of impiety, repented, and received again the kingdom he had lost? Pharaoh, however, became harder through those very scourges and perished. Let the person who judges the divine counsel with a heart of excessive wisdom give me an explanation: why did the medicine prepared by one physician benefit one person unto destruction and another unto salvation, unless it is because Christ’s good odor is to some ‘the odor of life unto life,’ and to others ‘the odor of death unto death’ (II Cor. 2:15)?

“As regards nature, both were human beings; as regards dignity, both were kings; as regards their situation, both possessed God’s captive people in the same cause; as regards punishment, both were mercifully admonished by scourges. What, then, made their ends different, except that one, sensing God’s hand, groaned in remembrance of his own iniquity, while the other fought back with free will against God’s most merciful truth?

“If someone replies that divine assistance was present for the one so that he might be changed, but absent for the other so that he might be hardened, and claims this to be unjust—on account of which he establishes the ends of these matters in God’s will, saying with the Apostle, ‘He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens’ (Rom. 9:18), while the Lord says, ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5)—let him understand that all these things are either accomplished with God’s help or permitted when he withdraws it.”

And Prosper, in the *Book of Epigrams*, ch. 28, on the twofold work of God:

“If we consider all human beings together, some of whom are saved by mercy and others condemned by truth, all the ways of the Lord—that is, mercy and truth—are distinguished by their respective ends. But if we look only upon the saints, these ways are not distinguished. For there truth is inseparable from mercy, and mercy from truth, since the blessedness of the saints comes both from the gift of grace and from the retribution of justice.

[Col. 0176C]

In all things the Almighty’s work is twofold:

Whatever he does is either justice or mercy.

Both descend together upon the earth from the citadel of light,

So that neither good may be lacking to any portion.

And since we all need the help of the merciful one,

Grace always precedes justice,

Condemning the proud and saving those who have been justified,

Whom God increases both by gifts and by merits.”

And likewise, in the same book, ch. 16, on Justice and Grace:

“There are two retributions of justice: when either good is rendered for good or evil for evil. There is a third retribution, that of grace, when through regeneration evils are forgiven and good things are repaid. Thus it is made clear that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. God does not know that retribution of the wicked by which they return evil for good; for if he did not repay good for evil, there would be no one to whom he could repay good for good.

[Col. 0176D]

The reward of justice is twofold, when either good

Is rightly restored to the upright, or deserved evil to the wicked.

But Christ’s grace, the salvation of all,

Without weighing merit, wipes away every evil.

Renewing all who believe through holy baptism,

It grants good things so that it may give better things in return for good works.”

And likewise Saint Augustine, in *On the Gift of Perseverance* (ch. 6):

“But everyone abandons God by his own will, so that he may deservedly be abandoned by God—who would deny this? Yet for this reason we ask that we not be led into temptation, so that this may not happen. For nothing happens unless either he himself does it or he himself permits it to happen.”

Hence Saint Hilary says in his *Commentary on Matthew* (canon 26):

“As in the time of the Flood, so in the very course of our life, while all are acting and doing what they do, that great day will come. Indeed, he shows that there will be a distinction in the taking up of the faithful, when, with two persons in the field, one is taken and the other left; with two women grinding, one is rejected and the other chosen; and of two who are in bed, one adheres while the other is abandoned. For he teaches the distinction between unbelievers and believers by leaving some and taking others.

“As the wrath of God grows heavier, the saints, as the Prophet says, will be stored in storehouses, while the faithless will be left as material for heavenly fire. Thus the day of the Lord will find two in the field—that is, two peoples, of the faithful and of the unbelieving, in the world, as though engaged in the work of this life. Yet they will be separated, one being left and the other taken.

“The same principle applies to the women grinding. The mill is the work of the Law. But because part of the Jews believed through the apostles and will likewise believe through Elijah, and will be justified through faith, one woman will be taken through that same faith for good work, while the other will be left in the fruitless work of the Law, grinding in vain and not making the bread of heavenly food.

“But there are two in bed, proclaiming the same rest of the Lord’s Passion, concerning which there is one and the same confession among heretics and Catholics. But because the truth of the Catholics proclaimed the unity of the Father and the Son, and their common *theoteia*—which we call divinity—while the falsehood of the heretics attacked the same doctrine with many insults, therefore of the two in bed one will be left and the other taken. For the judgment of divine decision will confirm the faith of both confessions by taking one and leaving the other.”

[Col. 0177C]

From the examples given above it is therefore demonstrated most clearly that this predestination of God may rightly be called twofold—not because the reprobate are predestined to destruction by that same predestination in the way the elect are predestined to life, but because grace gives the elect what their wickedness does not merit, while equity renders to those who are left what their iniquity merits.

But charity is one, because God is charity; and, like every good gift and every perfect gift descending from the Father of lights, it is called not only twofold by blessed Gregory, but he also writes of it:

“Just as many branches of a tree proceed from one root,” he says, “so from one charity many virtues are generated. And although the Holy Spirit is one, there are two gifts of that same Holy Spirit. When the praise of wisdom is described in the book entitled *Wisdom*, after it has been said, ‘The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world’ (Wis. 1:7), it is added: ‘For in her there is a spirit of wisdom, an understanding spirit, a spirit that is unique, manifold, subtle, mobile, human, steadfast’ (Wis. 7:22). Yet there is no doubt that he is one. He is called unique because undivided, but manifold because he is multiform in the effects of the virtues.

“And in the prophecy of Isaiah, which the Lord showed in the Gospel to have been fulfilled in himself, it is said: ‘The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord’ (Isa. 11:2; Luke 4:21). The Church celebrates and continually observes these gifts of the Holy Spirit, bestowing them from heaven through the laying on of the bishop’s hand and the signing with sacred chrism in the confirmation of the faithful.”

Hence blessed Ambrose says in the third book of *On the Sacraments* (ch. 1):

“Then follows the spiritual seal, which you heard read today, because after the font it remains that perfection should be completed. For at the invocation of the priest the Holy Spirit is poured in: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the Holy Spirit of fear. There are, as it were, seven virtues, and all virtues indeed belong to the Spirit; but these seven are, as it were, cardinal and principal virtues, which you receive when you are signed.

“For, as the holy Apostle says that the wisdom of our Lord is manifold, and the wisdom of God is manifold (Eph. 3:10), so the Holy Spirit is manifold, possessing diverse and varied virtues. Hence he is called the God of virtues, which can be applied to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

And Saint Gregory, in book XXXV of the *Moralia* (ch. 7):

“John wrote in the Apocalypse to seven churches (Rev. 1:4), through which he wished the universal Church to be understood. Now, so that this universal Church might be marked as full of the sevenfold Spirit of grace, Elisha is described as having yawned seven times over the dead boy. For when the Lord comes upon an extinguished people, he yawns, as it were, seven times, because he mercifully breathes into them the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit of grace.

“And heretics and those who likewise stand outside the Church do not receive absolution from their guilt unless they are joined by the Spirit of sevenfold grace to the universal peace from which they had been cut off.”

Blessed Paul also says: “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge,” and so forth, until he says: “But all these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (I Cor. 12:8–11).

For just as faith is the work of God, according to the Gospel truth that says, “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent” (John 6:29), so the remaining virtues are also divine works belonging to the gifts of grace. They are then shown by the effects of their works to proceed from God’s predestination, when, in the abundance of the goodness of his riches—he who is rich in all things—they are distributed to human beings according to his mercy and will for the benefit of believers, as the Apostle says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” [Col. 0178D] (I Cor. 12:7). All these effects of divine work are therefore recognized as belonging to the gift of grace.

## CHAPTER XX  
How it should be understood that blessed Gregory spoke of predestinations in the plural

Blessed Gregory also named the effects of God’s predestination in the plural—namely, dispositions and predestinations—in book XXVIII of the *Moralia* (ch. 18), saying:

“To know the order of heaven is to see the hidden predestinations of heavenly dispositions; but to place its reasoning upon the earth is to disclose before human hearts the causes of such mysteries.”

A little later he counts many effects of the divine work, all of which either belong to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice. For he says:

“Who can understand what the reason of these mysteries may be: that often a righteous man returns from judgment not only without being avenged but even punished?” This belongs to the gift of grace, as it is written: “Let the holy person be holy still” (Rev. 22:11). Thus the saints of God were scourged in councils and synagogues and brought before kings and governors, where they were condemned. For, in order to save us by the gift of grace, for us human beings and for our salvation, Jesus also stood before the governor; struck with blows and insults, he departed from judgment unjustly judged, and he will come in his own majesty and that of the Father and the holy angels to judge the living and the dead justly.

Saint Gregory’s words continue:

“And that his wicked adversary departs not only unpunished but even victorious?” This belongs to the retribution of justice, so that “the one who does harm may do harm still,” while “the righteous may be justified still.”

He continues:

“Who can understand why one person lives while plotting the deaths of his neighbors?” This belongs to the retribution of justice, so that “the one who is filthy may become filthy still.”

Likewise:

“And why does another die who would have benefited the lives of many?” This belongs to the gift of grace, as it is written: “He was taken away lest wickedness change his understanding” (Wis. 4:11).

Hence Augustine, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*:

“This was said with regard to the dangers of this life, not with regard to God’s foreknowledge: he was taken away from the uncertainty of temptations, not because he would have sinned, but because he would not remain in temptation.”

He continues:

“Another attains the height of power who desires only to harm.” This belongs to the retribution of justice, as it is written: “They passed over into the desire of their heart.”

“Another desires only to defend those who have been harmed, and yet lies himself oppressed.” This belongs to the gift of grace, because some people often guard themselves more cautiously in subjection but sin in positions of authority, as we learn from David’s deeds. The Lord mercifully governs him, lest one who stumbles on level ground perhaps place his foot upon a precipice, as the same Saint Gregory demonstrates in the *Pastoral Rule*. And as it is written, “Let the holy person be holy still” (Rev. 22:11), as happened with Tobias and the other elect in captivity.

“Another desires to be free from affairs but is entangled in countless business matters; another desires to be entangled in business but is compelled to be free.” These things often belong to the gift of grace and often to the retribution of justice, as the same Saint Gregory demonstrates both in the books of the *Moralia* and in the *Pastoral Rule*.

“Another, beginning badly, advances toward worse things until the end of his life.” This belongs to the retribution of justice, as we find many very clear examples of it throughout the Scriptures. Paul says in the Epistle to the Romans, concerning those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God: “Therefore God handed them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1:28), as is read concerning Pharaoh.

“Another, beginning well, advances through the length of time toward an increase of merits.” There is no doubt that this belongs to the gift of grace, as it is written: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83:6); and, as Paul says, “he is renewed day by day” (II Cor. 4:16). The Psalm also says: “They will still multiply in abundant old age” (Ps. 91:15), because those multiply in abundant old age whose strength, while their life is prolonged, is always extended toward what is better, and whose gains in merit also grow with the passage of time.

Conversely:

“Another, living badly, is preserved for a long time so that he may be corrected.” This belongs to the gift of grace, as Paul says: “The saying is trustworthy: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I received mercy, because I was formerly a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man, so that in me first Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example to those who would believe in him for eternal life” (I Tim. 1:15).

“Another appears indeed to live well, but remains in this life until he breaks out into perversity.” This happens by God’s hidden but not unjust judgment, in whom there is no iniquity. Concerning such people it is written: “They believe for a time, but in the time of temptation they fall away” (Luke 8:13). Thus Balaam, after prophecy and tears, and Judas, after his apostleship and signs of miracles, reached everlasting torments because he refused to extinguish the fire of covetousness. This belongs to the retribution of justice.

“Another, born in the error of unbelief, dies in error.” This belongs to the retribution of justice, because what rotted at the root withered in the branch. Concerning such people it is written: “They have gone astray from the womb” (Ps. 57:4), as Esau was rejected while still in the womb.

“Another, born in the uprightness of the Catholic faith, is brought to completion in the uprightness of the Catholic faith.” This belongs to the gift of grace, as with Jeremiah and John, who were called from the womb and sanctified in the womb, and Isaac, designated before he was conceived, and Jacob, chosen by calling.

Conversely:

“Another, born from the womb of a Catholic mother, is devoured near the end of life by the abyss of error.” This belongs to the retribution of justice, because, although he knew God, as Paul says, he did not honor him as God (Rom. 1:21). And concerning the devil, the head of such people, it is written that he “did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44)—in which he had undoubtedly been, but in which he did not remain. For, swollen with pride because of God’s gift of grace and his lofty excellence, he fell through the retribution of justice to the lowest depths of misery.

“Another, however, completes his life in Catholic devotion, although, born in unbelief, he had drunk in the poison of error with his mother’s milk.” This belongs to the gift of grace, as it is written: “By grace you have been saved, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Eph. 2:8).

“Another both desires and is able to strive toward the height of living well.” This belongs to the gift of grace, as Paul says: “It is God who gives us both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good will” (Phil. 2:13).

“Another neither wills nor is able; another wills but is not able; another is able but does not will.” These belong to the retribution of justice, since, even without the additional burden of our iniquity, the general mass of perdition merited this. Concerning it, as Augustine says, if no one were delivered, God’s justice would be as incomprehensible as it would be irreproachable.

No one ascends to know the recesses of these secret judgments. The craftsman and skilled builder knows, in his secret counsel, where he should draw or withdraw the plumb line: which stone he should draw from within to outside in the wall of Jerusalem, which is built as a city, and which he should draw from outside to within; where he should place each stone in the work of its construction; and which he should leave out of the arrangement of that city itself. This is accomplished by one and the same predestination, either through the gift of grace or through the retribution of justice.

Hence Saint Gregory says in homily 13 on the prophet Ezekiel:

“That power of divinity, which is not led into motion and change by diversity, gives life to the afflicted and penitent by that very light of justice by which it strikes the proud and obstinate.”

And in homily 17:

“Almighty God, because he is not unlike himself, sees by the power by which he hears, and creates by the power by which he judges created things. His seeing all things is at once his administering them, and his administering them is his perceiving them. He does not help the righteous by one thought and condemn the unrighteous by another, but by one and the same power of his singular nature, ever unlike no other and always unchanged from itself, he disposes unlike things.”

Regarding this terrible matter of the counsels concerning the sons of men, Paul exclaims:

“O the depth,” he says, “of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 2:13).

Although he changes times, he does not change his counsel, because his counsel remains forever, and the thoughts of his heart endure from age to age.

This is the predestination of God: he predestines those things that are from him, or those things that he was going to do himself. Predestining means preparing the elect, the approved, and the righteous by grace for the kingdom and eternal life—that is, for grace, which is the effect of predestination. He punishes those who have been left behind, the reprobate and the unrighteous; this is the effect of just retribution.

Thus, as blessed Prosper confesses in these very words, and as other Catholic teachers acknowledge with one accord, and as Sacred Scripture and the Catholic Church believe and teach, God’s predestination is always directed toward good, either belonging to the retribution of justice or to the gift of grace.

For this reason we have endeavored to show how these many variations and effects of divine predestination, counted by blessed Gregory, belong either to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice. Some people, as we demonstrated in the books mentioned above, have inferred from the words of Saint Gregory predestinations in the plural, so as to teach from this a twofold predestination by which the saints are predestined to life and, as they say, the reprobate are predestined to death.

Now let us proceed to give an account of the second chapter.

## CHAPTER XXI  
How the ancient Predestinarians understood the second chapter, excerpted by us against the Predestinarians, concerning grace and free will; from whose words we took what we set down; and concerning the transposition of that chapter, which some are evidently said to have made disorderly

[Col. 0182A]

We excerpted the second chapter, concerning grace and free will, from the sayings of the holy Fathers at the synod held at Quierzy. Concerning it, the ancient Predestinarians said that free will in human beings is nothing, but that, whether toward good or toward evil, God’s predestination operates in human beings, because God fashions in human beings a will such as that of demons, which by its own motion can will nothing except evil.

For this reason the modern Predestinarian Gottschalk, in his little book addressed to Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, says in this passage:

“Regarding this free will, what the Church of Christ ought to hold and believe has been clearly discussed, thanks be to God, by the other Catholic Fathers, but especially against the Pelagians and Coelestians it is known to have been more fully and abundantly inculcated by blessed Augustine in various short works, and most of all in the *Hypomnesticon*. Therefore I would much rather have relied upon the incomparably fruitful assertions of that same most Catholic teacher than upon the erroneous opinions of Gennadius of Massilia, who in many places presumed to resist both the Catholic faith and the invincible authorities of the blessed Fathers, following the excessively pernicious dogma of the unhappy Cassian.”

Against this we wrote in the aforementioned synod:

“We lost the freedom of will in the first human being, but through Christ our Lord we have received it again. We have free will toward good, preceded and assisted by grace, and we have free will toward evil, abandoned by grace. We have free will because it has been freed by grace and healed by grace from its corruption.”

With the other three chapters concerning which the matter is being discussed, this chapter was subscribed at the gathering of bishops by Lord Prudentius.

Afterward, in a letter sent to Wenilo, his archbishop, concerning the ordination of Aeneas as bishop of Paris, he set out four chapters and says the following about this first one:

“Let it be confessed that free will, lost in Adam by the merit of disobedience, has been restored and liberated for us through our Lord Jesus Christ—meanwhile in hope, but afterward in reality—as the Apostle says: ‘For in hope we were saved’ (Rom. 8:24). Nevertheless, let us know that we always need the grace of almighty God for every good work, whether for thinking, beginning, doing, or bringing it perseveringly to completion, and that without it we are in no way able either to think, will, or perform anything good.”

We therefore wonder why, after subscribing at the aforementioned synod to the chapters mentioned above, and possessing sufficient knowledge of the canonical decrees and the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see through his synodal subscription and profession, he sent such a document so thoughtlessly and unusually, without a credible comparison and contrary to the institutions of the rules, to his archbishop and fellow bishops as consent for the ordination of his fellow bishop.

Or, since in the often-mentioned chapters the second place is held by the chapter concerning grace and free will, why did he place that chapter first in this letter of his? More appropriately, the chapter in which he speaks of God’s predestination—which exists before all ages and times—should be placed before the chapter in which he speaks of free will, which human beings did not entirely or completely lose in this world and in time, but weakened.

Finally, in the volume entrusted to us by your lordship for our response, we find the following in the sixth chapter:

“Likewise, concerning the grace by which believers are saved, and without which no rational creature has ever lived blessedly, and concerning free will, weakened by sin in the first human being but restored and healed for Christ’s faithful through the grace of the Lord Jesus: we most steadfastly and with full faith confess the very thing that the most holy Fathers left to us to hold on the authority of the sacred Scriptures; that the African Synod and the Synod of Orange professed; that the most blessed pontiffs of the apostolic see held in Catholic faith. Nor do we dare to turn in any way toward another position concerning nature and grace.”

We are also surprised by the compiler of these chapters. Why, after all the chapters concerning which the revived controversy is being debated, did he place last the chapter on grace and free will, when it could more suitably have been placed before the third and fourth chapters, as anyone of sound judgment can discern from the sequence of the reasoning?

But this is not surprising. When a crafty person wishes to display snares to the unwary and incautious, he strives to conceal the same trap by mixing it with a manifold confusion of straw or whatever refuse he can, just as he also tried to act in the previously cited chapter concerning the words and opinions of Florus.

Therefore it is necessary for us to set down again the integrity of the chapter excerpted by us and to show the words of the Catholics from which we excerpted it.

Here is the text of the second chapter:

“We lost the freedom of will in the first human being, but through Christ our Lord we have received it again, and we have free will toward good, preceded and assisted by grace; and we have free will toward evil, abandoned by grace. We have free will because it has been freed by grace and healed by grace from its corruption.”

Therefore Augustine, in *On the Gift of Perseverance* (ch. 7), speaking of the freedom of will that existed in the first human being, says:

“It existed,” he says, “in the human being before he fell; yet how powerful that freedom of will was in the excellence of that first condition became apparent in the angels.”

We lost this freedom in that first human being, as the same teacher says in *On Rebuke and Grace* (ch. 12):

“But now, after that great freedom was lost by the merit of sin, the infirmity remained to be assisted by greater gifts.”

And somewhat earlier (ch. 11):

“This is so much greater that it is little for a human being, through it, to restore the freedom that was lost.”

We followed with the words, “which we have received through Christ our Lord.” The freedom of will that we received through Christ is precisely the freedom that we lost in the first human being—not another freedom. The first human being possessed free will either to sin or not to sin, and he incurred offense through nothing other than that by which he was able to resist the one persuading him, so as not to sin.

Therefore, the one who, through the ability to do good, was able to conquer the will to evil lost the ability to do good through willing evil.

Hence, after the fall of our first parent, the human will, before it is liberated from the domination of the devil by God’s grace, lies in that abyss into which it plunged itself by its own freedom. Thus, apart from grace, in all evils the will is to be understood as free in the exercise of choice, but enslaved to sin.

When grace approaches, that same free will, which by its own freedom was perverse, is made upright by the action of the Spirit of God. Thus, in all good things, free will is to be understood as proceeding from grace. This is the freedom of will that we received through Christ, who with the Father gave us the pledge of the Spirit. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom,” and, as it is written, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36). Christ liberated us by this freedom.

Hence Saint Augustine says in *On Rebuke and Grace* (ch. 12):

“Why, then, should no flesh—that is, no human being—glory before him except in his merits? He could indeed have had merits, but he lost them; and by that through which he could have had them, he lost them—that is, by free will. Therefore nothing remains for those who are to be liberated except the grace of the one who liberates.”

And likewise in book III of the *Hypomnesticon*, near the beginning:

“When free will was corrupted, the whole human being was corrupted; through it, without the help of grace, he is neither able to begin nor sufficient to complete what pleases God.”

And somewhat earlier:

“It was therefore called free will because it is placed in its own power, possessing the power to do what it wills; this is the movement of a living and rational soul. But such was the condition, as I have already said, of the first-formed human being, when he remained unharmed before sin. For he incurred offense through nothing other than that by which he was able to resist the one persuading him, so as not to sin.

“By willing evil, therefore, he rightly lost the ability to do good, although by the ability to do good he had been able to conquer the will to evil. God justly handed him over, now captive to sin, to his depraved will, so that what had been sufficient for every good work he wished to perform, had he always obeyed God, might become his punishment in his inability to do what he wished.”

And likewise:

“The Catholic Church believes that the salvation of the human being comes from God, who is Christ; by his wound our wounded free will is healed and restored.”

And again, in the same work:

“When he has received the Spirit of the Lord, there will be freedom in him for undertaking the Lord’s commandments, because where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”

Then we added: “And we have free will for the good when preceded and assisted by grace, and we have free will for evil when abandoned by grace.” And Augustine, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*: “It is therefore in the power of the wicked to sin; but that, by sinning, they should do this or that evil deed is not in their power, but in the power of God, who divides the darkness and orders it.”

And likewise Augustine, in Book III of the *Hypomnesticon*, near the middle [Col. 0185A]:

> “There is therefore free will; whoever denies that it exists is not a Catholic, and whoever says that it exists in such a way that, without God, it can neither begin nor complete a good work—that is, a work belonging to his holy purpose—is a Catholic.”

And likewise, in the same work, near the beginning:

> “When free will has been corrupted, the whole human being has been corrupted: by means of it, without the assistance of God’s grace, a person can neither begin nor sufficiently complete what pleases God. But the remedy—that is, Christ’s grace—precedes, so that the will corrupted in him may be healed and restored and may be prepared; always needing assistance, and illuminated by the grace of the Savior, it can both know God and live according to his will.”

And likewise:

> “A human being, therefore, with his will still limping through the corruption of free will, does not precede God in order to know and seek him, as though he were going to receive grace as a reward for merits. Rather, as we have said, God in his most merciful grace precedes human beings who are ignorant and do not yet seek him by the will of free choice, so that he may make them know and seek him, as the apostle John says in his Epistle: ‘We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son. He is the true God and eternal life’ (1 John 5:20).”

Let every reader, whether kindly or hostile, also hear what this same Catholic teacher thinks about free will preceded and assisted by grace, and about that same free will abandoned by grace:

> “We confess,” he says (Book III, near the beginning), “that free will exists in all human beings, possessing indeed the judgment of reason—not by which it is capable, without God, of beginning or certainly accomplishing things that pertain to God, but only in the works of the present life, both good and evil. By good I mean those things that arise from the good of nature: wishing to work in the field, wishing to eat and drink, wishing to have a friend,”

and so forth, as he continues there. All these things do not exist without divine governance; rather, they are from him and through him, or began to exist through him. By evil I mean such things as wishing to worship an idol, wishing to commit murder, and the other examples that he continues to give in the same Book of the *Hypomnesticon*.

As for what we added in conclusion, saying, “But we have free will because it has been liberated by grace and healed by grace from corruption,” Saint Augustine develops the point in *On Rebuke and Grace* (chapter 13) [Col. 0185D]:

> “Those, however, who do not belong to this number of the predestined—those whom the grace of God leads to the kingdom, whether they do not yet possess any free will of their own, or possess a will that is free precisely because it has been liberated by that grace—those, therefore, who do not belong to this most certain and faithful number, are judged with the utmost justice according to their merits. For either they lie beneath the sin that they originally acquired by generation and depart from this life with that hereditary debt, which has not been forgiven through regeneration; or by free will they have added further sins: free will, I say, but not liberated—free from righteousness, but a slave of sin—by which they are rolled through various harmful desires, some more, some less, but all evil, and according to this diversity they are to be judged with diverse punishments.”

Concerning the meaning and context of the whole chapter, the same blessed Augustine says in *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*:

> “It is true what his detractor says: that God, being both good and just, made such a human being as would have been capable of being free from the evil of sin, if he had wished. For who does not know that he was made sound and blameless, and established with free will and free power to live justly? But now the discussion concerns the man whom robbers left half-dead on the road. Wounded and pierced by grievous injuries, he cannot ascend to the summit of righteousness in the same way that he was able to descend from it; and even if he is already in the inn, he is being healed. God therefore does not command the impossible, but by commanding he admonishes a person both to do what he can and to ask for what he cannot.”

And in Letter 46 to Valentinus:

> “At first, the Lord Jesus, as it is written in the Gospel of the apostle John, ‘did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him’ (John 3:17). But afterward, as the apostle Paul writes, ‘God will judge the world’ (Romans 3:6), and he will come, as the whole Church confesses in the Creed, to judge the living and the dead. If, then, there is no grace of God, how does he save the world? And if there is no free will, how does he judge the world? Accordingly, understand the book or letter of mine that the persons mentioned above brought with them to you according to this faith, so that you neither deny God’s grace nor defend free will in such a way as to separate it from God’s grace, as though without that grace we could in any way either think or act according to God—which we absolutely cannot do.”

And a little later:

> “Believe the divine utterances, because both human free will is free and there is the grace of God, without whose assistance free will can neither be converted to God nor make progress toward God. And pray that what you piously believe you may also understand wisely. For this very purpose—that is, so that we may understand wisely—there is surely free will. For unless we understood and possessed wisdom through free will, Scripture would not command us, saying: ‘Understand, you who are foolish among the people, and at last become wise, you fools’ (Psalm 99:8). By the very fact that we are commanded and ordered to understand and become wise, our obedience is required; and this cannot exist without free will. But if this very act—understanding and becoming wise—could take place through free will without the assistance of God’s grace, it would not be said to God: ‘Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments’ (Psalm 118:73); nor would it be written in the Gospel: ‘Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures’ (Luke 24:45); nor would the apostle James say: ‘If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him’ (James 1:5).”

And again, in another letter to the same Valentinus (Letter 47):

> “As far as we have been able, we have dealt with these brothers of yours and ours so that they may persevere in the sound Catholic faith, which neither denies free will—whether toward an evil life or toward a good one—nor attributes so much to it that it can accomplish anything without God’s grace: whether to be converted from evil to good, to make persevering progress in good, or to attain eternal good, where it will no longer fear falling away.”

And a little later:

> “Consider in these words of Holy Scripture, brothers, that if there were no free will, it would not be said: ‘Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways; do not turn to the right or to the left’ (Proverbs 4:27). Yet if this could be done without God’s grace, it would not afterward be said: ‘He himself will make your paths straight and lead your journeys in peace.’”

And a little later:

> “For this reason I told you not to turn to the right or to the left—that is, neither defend free will in such a way as to attribute good works to it without God’s grace, nor defend grace in such a way that, as though secure because of it, you love evil works. May the grace of God itself turn this away from you.”

And likewise, to the same Valentinus, in *On Grace and Free Will* (chapter 4):

> “Therefore, so that this word, which is not understood by everyone, may be understood by some, free will is also a gift of God.”

And likewise (chapter 5):

> “We urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Corinthians 6:1). “For why does he urge them, if they received grace in such a way that they lost their own will? Yet, lest the will itself be thought capable of doing anything good without God’s grace, immediately after saying, ‘His grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored more than all of them,’ he added: ‘Yet not I, but the grace of God with me’ (1 Corinthians 15:10)—that is, not I alone, but the grace of God with me. Consequently, it is neither the grace of God alone nor he alone, but the grace of God with him.”

And likewise (chapter 6):

> “By such divine testimonies it is proved that God’s grace is not given according to our merits, since we see that it has been given, and is daily given, not only when no good merits precede, but even when many evil merits precede. But once it has been given, our good merits also begin to exist—through it, nevertheless. For if it withdraws itself, a human being falls, not raised up but thrown down by free will.”

And likewise, in the same book (chapter 14):

> “I have said these things so that, in the words of the apostle, I might deter your free will from evil and exhort it to good. Yet for that very reason you ought not to glory in a human being—that is, in yourselves—but in the Lord.”

And likewise:

> “Human free will is summoned when it is said: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts’ (Psalm 94:8). But unless God could also remove the hardness of the heart, he would not say through the prophet: ‘I will take from them their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh’ (Ezekiel 2:19; 36:26).”

And likewise (chapter 15):

> “The will within us is always free, but it is not always good. For it is either free from righteousness when it serves sin, and then it is evil; or it is free from sin when it serves righteousness, and then it is good. God’s grace, however, is always good, and through it a person who was previously of evil will becomes a person of good will. It is useful to will when we are able, and it is useful to be able when we will. For what benefit is there if we will what we cannot do, or do not will what we can do?”

And likewise (chapter 17):

> “Therefore, in order that we may will, he works without us; but when we will, and will in such a way that we act, he cooperates with us. Nevertheless, without him—whether working so that we may will or cooperating when we will—we are capable of nothing in works of good devotion.”

And likewise, in Book III of the *Hypomnesticon*, toward the end, he says:

> “Grace and free will,” he says, “undoubtedly complete the journey of faith. Free will does so when the Christian performs God’s commandments, but not—as I said above—without grace directing or governing. Therefore he says in the Psalms: ‘Direct my way in your sight’ (Psalm 5:9), and, ‘The steps of a person are directed by the Lord’ (Psalm 36:23). Thus neither does grace without free will cause a person to possess blessed life, nor does free will without grace. Nevertheless, grace causes little children to possess blessed life without the exercise of free will; but those who are already capable of reason it precedes and teaches, so that they may will and be able to do good.”

And likewise:

> “Let no one be sluggish or negligent in serving God, nor rely on grace in such a way as to suppose that, because of the free will that God restored through the death of his Son and prepared for himself, he requires no works.”

And likewise:
