> “We do not condemn the good works of free will that are prepared to be done through the preceding action of grace, without any merits of free will, and that grace itself brings about, governs, and perfects, so that they may abound in free will. For by these or similar works human beings have been justified, are justified, and will be justified in Christ. But we condemn by divine authority those works of free will that are placed before grace and by which people are exalted as though they were justified in Christ on the basis of merits. For ‘who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid?’”

And likewise:

> “Listen and understand, if indeed you have ears to hear and your heart has not been hardened against understanding. Because of free will, by which human beings perform good and evil deeds, it was said that each person would be repaid according to his works. A person has evil merit when, having already been baptized, he turns away from the good through his own fault and does evil—that is, when he abandons God and loves the world, as the Apostle testifies that Demas did (2 Timothy 4:9), and Hermogenes (2 Timothy 1:15); or when, even while placing his hope wholly in various images, he refuses to acknowledge the true God, whom he has the power to know in this world. If the Most High God should will, he can save the ungodly through the gratuitous grace by which he justifies, just as, when a person turns away, he can justly hand him over to a reprobate mind and reserve him for the future punishment of Gehenna, so that he may repay him according to his works. A person also has good merit when, in all things, he does not resist the grace of God working good in him, but becomes its fellow worker.”

And likewise:

> “But you say to me that, with your eyes clouded by heretical grief, you cannot direct them toward the light of truth, and that there is absolutely no merit belonging to one’s own will. There is, if you distinguish between will and grace. Hear, then, briefly: the merit of one’s own will is good when the gift of grace precedes each person’s will and works so that a human being acquires merit through his own will.”

And Gregory, in Book XVI, chapter 10 of the *Moralia*:

> “If someone is believed to be saved by the purity of his hands in such a way that he becomes innocent through his own strength, there is undoubtedly error. For if heavenly grace does not precede the guilty person, it will certainly never find anyone whom it may reward as innocent. Hence it is said in the words of truthful Moses: ‘No one is innocent before you by himself’ (Exodus 34). Heavenly goodness therefore first acts in us without us, so that, when our free will subsequently follows, it may act with us in the good that we already desire. Yet through the grace it has generously bestowed, it rewards this good in us at the final judgment as though it had proceeded from us alone. Because divine goodness precedes us in order to make us innocent, Paul says: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am’ (1 Corinthians 15:10). And because our free will follows that same grace, he adds: ‘His grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored more abundantly than all of them.’ Since he saw that of himself he was nothing, he said, ‘Yet not I’; but because he found that, with grace, he was something, he added, ‘but the grace of God with me.’ Thus he will be saved innocent through the purity of his hands, because the one who is preceded here by the gift that makes him innocent is rewarded according to merit when he is brought to judgment.”

And in Book XXXIII:

> “No one has first contributed anything to God so that divine grace might follow him. For if we precede God by doing good, where is what the prophet says: ‘His mercy will precede me’ (Psalm 58:11)? If we have offered some good work so as to merit his grace, where is what the apostle Paul says: ‘You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works’ (Ephesians 2:8)? If our love precedes God, where is what the apostle John says: ‘Not because we loved God, but because he first loved us’ (1 John 4:10)? Where is what the Lord says through Hosea: ‘I will love them freely’ (Hosea 14:5)? If we follow God by our own strength, without his gift, where is what the Truth declares through the Gospel, saying: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5)? Where is what he says: ‘No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him’ (John 6:44)? Where is what he says again: ‘You did not choose me, but I chose you’ (John 15:18)? If at least we precede the gifts of good works by thinking well through our own strength, where is what is said so beneficially through Paul, cutting away from the very root of the heart every human confidence in itself: ‘Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God’ (2 Corinthians 3:5)? No one, therefore, precedes God by merits, so as to be able to hold him as though he were a debtor.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For this reason the reprobate do not receive the eternal rewards of the heavenly homeland: they despised them now, when they were able to merit them, through free will. This free will is formed in the good among the elect, when their mind, with grace breathing upon it, is lifted away from earthly desires. The good that we do belongs both to God and to us: to God through preceding grace, and to us through the free will that follows. For if it does not belong to God, why do we give him eternal thanks? Again, if it does not belong to us, why do we hope that rewards will be repaid to us? Since, therefore, we rightly give thanks, we know that we are preceded by his gift; and since, again, we rightly seek repayment, we know that, with free will following, we chose the good things that we would do.”

And in Homily 37 on the Gospel:

> “‘You did not choose me, but I chose you, and appointed you to go and bear fruit’ (John 15:16). ‘I appointed you’: I planted you in grace, so that you might go by willing and bear fruit by working. He said, ‘Go by willing,’ because to will to do something is already to go in the mind. What kind of fruit they ought to bear is added: ‘and that your fruit should remain.’ There, therefore—that is, after death—the repayment begins where this life ends.”

And in Homily 9, at the beginning, on the prophet Ezekiel:

> “‘And the Spirit entered into me after he had spoken to me, and set me upon my feet’ (Ezekiel 2:2). Behold, the divine voice commanded the prophet, who was lying down, to rise; but he could not rise at all unless the Spirit of the almighty God had entered him. For by the grace of almighty God we can indeed strive toward good works, but we cannot accomplish them if he himself does not help who commands. Thus Paul, when exhorting the disciples, said: ‘Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling’ (Philippians 2:12–13); immediately he added who would work these very good things in them, saying: ‘For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure.’ Hence the Truth itself says to the disciples: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5).

> “But in these matters we must consider this: if our good works are so entirely gifts of almighty God that nothing of ours is in them, why do we seek eternal repayment as though for merits? On the other hand, if they are ours in such a way that they are not gifts of almighty God, why do we give thanks for them to almighty God? We must therefore know that our evil deeds belong solely to us, whereas our good deeds belong both to almighty God and to us. He precedes us by inspiring us to will, and then follows us by assisting us, so that we do not will in vain but can fulfill what we will. Thus, with grace preceding and good will following, what is the gift of almighty God becomes our merit.”

Paul explains this well in a brief statement [Col. 0190D], saying:

> “He labored more than all of them” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

But lest he seem to have attributed what he had done to his own strength, he added:

> “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.”

Because he had been preceded by a heavenly gift, he acknowledged himself as alien to his own good work, saying, “Yet not I.” But because preceding grace had made free will good within him, and by that free will he had followed the same grace in his work, he added, “but the grace of God with me”—as though he were saying: “I labored in the good work—not I, but also I. Insofar as I was preceded by the Lord’s gift alone, it was not I; but insofar as I followed the gift by my will, it was also I.” Having said these brief things against Pelagius and Coelestius [Col. 0191A], let us return to the order of exposition.

And Prosper, in his letter to Rufinus *On Grace and Free Will*:

> “Who would doubt,” he says, “that free will obeys the exhortation of the one who calls when the grace of God has generated in it the disposition to believe and obey?”

And likewise:

> “Those who believe are moved by the Spirit of God; those who do not believe turn away through free will.”

And likewise:

> “Everything that is not from faith is sin, so that you may understand that the righteousness of unbelievers is not righteousness, because nature without grace is sullied. For after natural innocence had been lost, the human being, an exile and ruined, walking without a path, entered into ever deeper errors. But after being sought, found, and carried back, he was brought into the way that is truth and life, and was recognized through love of God—who loved him first, when he did not love God.”

And likewise [Col. 0191B]:

> “The grace of God, therefore, makes all whom it justifies not better from good people, but good from evil people; afterward, through progress, it makes them better from good people—not by taking away free will, but by liberating it. For as long as it was alone, without God, it was dead to righteousness and lived for sin; but when the mercy of Christ illuminated it, it was snatched from the kingdom of the devil and made the kingdom of God. Yet in order that it may remain in that kingdom, it is not sufficient for itself even with the capacity it has received, unless it receives perseverance from the one from whom it received diligence.”

And likewise Saint Augustine, in Book III of the *Hypomnesticon*:

> “If you attend to the sin of the first human beings, through which the mass of the human race deserved condemnation—for, according to the testimony of the apostle Paul, ‘from one all came into condemnation’ (Romans 5:16)—you will be able to recognize that the judgments of God are most just. For this reason there is evil merit in all, both in little children and in adults, preceding the judgments of God, so that they may be punished by his just judgment.”

And likewise:

> “Hear still more explicitly [the reading *calcatius* is uncertain], so that we may return to the purpose of the preceding discussion: the human being is wounded in free will through Adam’s sin; without God’s grace, by himself alone, he cannot heal himself, nor can he voluntarily return to paradise and be joined to the number of the saints, nor can he receive grace on the basis of any merits. Rather, God accomplishes the whole through his mercy.”

And speaking there, according to the evangelical parable, about the wounded and half-dead man who was left behind (Luke 10:30), the same Saint Augustine adds:

> “He was rightly called half-dead. For he possessed a vital movement—that is, wounded free will—which by itself was not sufficient for him to return to eternal life, which he had lost.”

And likewise:

> “When he has received the Spirit of the Lord, there will be freedom in him for undertaking the Lord’s commandments, because where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”

And a little later:

> “For when, with God’s mercy preceding him, a person also acts sufficiently through free will so that he may be cleansed, yet if he presumes on his own will alone, he cannot be cleansed.”

And likewise:

> “To whom are the words spoken in the Psalms—unless to those who possess free will? ‘Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord’ (Psalm 33:12). And how would each person be repaid according to his works on the day of judgment unless free will existed? [Col. 0192A] Therefore there is no partiality with God. In every holy work, therefore, God’s will comes first and free will afterward: God works, and the human being cooperates.”

There are many other passages; whoever wishes to know them more fully should reread the same book in order, in which he will be able either to learn or to recognize again many remarkable and astonishing things.

And Saint Coelestine, in the *Decretals*, from the words of Pope Innocent, after Letter 8:

> “For the first human being, having suffered free will, fell because he used his own goods too rashly and, sinking into the depths of transgression, found no way by which he could rise thereafter. Deceived in his freedom for ever, he would have remained crushed beneath this ruin, unless the coming of Christ had afterward raised him up through his grace [Col. 0192B]; through the purification of a new regeneration, Christ cleansed every past fault by the washing of his baptism.”

Likewise:

> “Understand at last, perverse doctrine of perverse minds, that freedom itself deceived the first human being, so that, while he used its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression. He could not be rescued from it unless the coming of Christ the Lord, through the providence of regeneration, restored in him the condition of his former freedom.”

And a little later:

> “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God, so that we may neither sense that our free will is absent nor doubt that, in each movement of human will toward good, the assistance of God is more powerful.”

And a little later:

> “By this assistance and gift of God, free will is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark may become bright, what was crooked straight, what was weak sound, and what was imprudent prudent.”

And likewise Saint Prosper, in his letter to Rufinus:

> “And so that it might be demonstrated more fully,” he says, “that free will can accomplish nothing without grace, the one to whom it had been said, ‘Strengthen your brothers, and pray that you do not enter into temptation’ (Luke 22:32), and who had answered, certainly from free will, ‘Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death,’ is told that before the cock crows he will deny the Lord three times. What else does this mean than that he would fail in faith?”

And likewise:

> “It is said by opponents with excessive foolishness and extreme thoughtlessness that through this grace of God nothing at all is left to free will.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Accordingly, the human being who was evil through free will was made good in that same free will: evil through himself, good through God. God reformed him to that original honor by another beginning, so that he not only forgave him the guilt of evil will and action, but also granted him the ability to will and do good and to persevere in it.”

And likewise:

> “From one mass, which is the flesh of the first human being, we know that the nature of all human beings was created and is being created; and that this same nature, through the free will of that first human being in whom all sinned, was cast down and in no way freed from the debt of eternal death, unless the grace of Christ, through a second creation, reformed it according to the image of God and, by acting, breathing upon, and assisting its free will, preserved it by going before it all the way to the end.”

And likewise, in the same letter:

> “Now that same free will has been converted, not overthrown, and has been granted the ability to will, understand, and act differently, and to place its safety not in itself but in the physician. For it does not yet enjoy such perfect health that the things that harmed it can no longer harm it, or that it can already govern itself by its own strength in wholesome things.”

And in the sixth response against the Gauls:

> “It is wrongly said either that free will is nothing or that it does not exist. But it is not wrongly denied that, before the illumination of faith, it acts in darkness—that is, in the shadow of death—because, before it is liberated from the dominion of the devil by God’s grace, it lies in that abyss into which it plunged itself by its freedom.”

And shortly afterward, after Letter 8:

> “Thus what has been begun in it through the grace of Christ may also be increased through the diligence of free will, while God’s assistance is never removed, without which no one can make progress or persevere in the good.”

And Cassiodorus, on Psalm 117:

> “There is indeed a freedom of will that is accursed in the evil direction, by which the transgressor abandons the Creator and turns toward wicked vices. But in the good direction we lost free will when Adam sinned; and we cannot return to it except through the grace of Christ, as the Apostle says: ‘For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure.’ Therefore we must pray continually that a perverse will may not carry us away, but that divine inspiration may possess us, because whatever we think from ourselves, we stir up by deadly audacity against ourselves. Rightly, therefore, he forbade trust in a human being, since by himself he cannot provide a remedy either for another or for himself.”

Behold how we lost the freedom of will in Adam, how we received it again through Christ, and how we have free will for good when preceded and assisted by grace. Hence Prosper added:

> “When the will is directed toward good things, it must be understood as arising from grace; and we have free will for evil when abandoned by grace.”

Immediately afterward the same author adds:

> “In evil things, however, the will must be understood as existing without grace.”

And Saint Augustine, in *On Rebuke and Grace*:

> “Free will is sufficient for evil, but for good it is insufficient unless it is helped by the omnipotent Good.”

Let the reader also hear that, as we stated in the conclusion of the chapter, we have free will because it has been liberated by grace. Hence Prosper, in the recapitulation of his tenth response:

> “The grace of God does not abolish human free will but cultivates it, and recalls and leads it back from error into the way, so that what was crooked through its freedom may become straight through the Spirit of God acting upon it.”

And Saint Coelestine, as we said above:

> “By the assistance and gift of God, free will is not taken away but liberated.”

Let the reader learn from Prosper’s fourteenth response how and through whom we lost it, and from whom we receive what we had lost:

> “For the one who lost what he had received—that is, free will—does not recover it from the source through which he lost it, but receives it from the one from whom he had received what he lost.”

And in the fifth response against the Vincentians:

> “God is not therefore the author of any sin, but the creator of nature. Although nature possessed the power not to sin, it sinned voluntarily and, by its own will, subjected itself to its deceiver. It is not moved in vice by a natural movement but by a captive movement, until it dies to sin and lives to God. It cannot do this without the grace of God, because the freedom that it lost through freedom it does not receive again unless Christ liberates it.”

Behold, reader, you have it: the freedom which we lost through freedom itself we in no way recover unless Christ liberates us; and, liberated by Christ’s grace, we possess it for the good, while without Christ’s grace we are turned toward evil by a captive movement. And Saint Coelestine, as we wrote above, says:

“Freedom itself so deceived the first man that, while he used its reins too indulgently, he fell into the transgression of presumption; nor could he be rescued from this unless the coming of Christ the Lord, through the providence of regeneration, restored to him the condition of his former freedom.” [Col. 0194B]

Let the person who composed those chapters, which you gave us so that we might answer you concerning them, therefore see whether the chapter—excerpted by our modest ability from these and also from the words of other teachers—departs from the Catholic faith. For in the sixth chapter, as though we were departing from it, he wished to write as follows:

“Likewise, concerning the grace by which believers are saved, and without which a rational creature has never lived in blessedness, and concerning free will, weakened by sin in the first man but restored and healed in the Lord Jesus’ faithful by grace: we confess most steadfastly and with full faith that same doctrine which the holiest Fathers, by the authority of the sacred Scriptures, left for us to hold; which the African Synod and the Synod of Arausio professed; and which the most blessed pontiffs of the Apostolic See held in the Catholic faith. But, also, we presume in no way to incline to either side concerning nature and grace.”

In truth, as we have shown above, we have held and continue to hold, and have written and continue to write in Catholic language, concerning grace and free will, what the holiest Fathers, by the authority of the sacred Scriptures, left for us to hold, and what the most blessed pontiffs of the Apostolic See held in the Catholic faith. But where the compiler of the chapters wrote, with an omission, “presuming in no way to incline to either side concerning nature and grace,” we supply the missing words and add that we most firmly believe [Col. 0194C] and hold precisely what they believed and held.

Thus Saint Augustine also wrote in his book *On Nature and Grace*, and says in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*:

“Are there, then, two human natures? Far be it from us. If there were two natures, there would be no grace. For no gratuitous liberation would be granted if what was owed to nature were restored. Human beings, however, suppose that all who appear to be good believers ought to receive perseverance to the end. But God judged it better that some who would not persevere should be mingled with the fixed number of his saints, so that those for whom security in the temptation of this life is not advantageous might not be secure. For many are restrained from a destructive pride by what the Apostle says: ‘Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands see to it that he does not fall.’ He who falls falls by his own will, and he who stands stands by God’s will. For God is able to make him stand. Therefore it is not he himself, but God. Nevertheless, it is good not to think highly of oneself, but to fear. In his own thought each person either falls or stands. As the Apostle says—and I recalled this in the preceding book: ‘We are not competent to think anything as from ourselves, but our competence is from God’ (2 Cor. 3:5).”

Following him, the blessed Ambrose also dares to say:

“For our heart and our thoughts are not in our own power.”

Everyone who is humbly and truly devout recognizes this as entirely true.

Let the compiler of the chapters reread what we have written and see whether, in them, he can find—as he wrote in the aforesaid [Col. 0195A] sixth chapter—silly little questions, almost old-womanish tales, and Scottish porridge nauseating to the purity of the faith. These things, in the most dangerous and grievous times, have lamentably and tearfully grown, adding to the burden of our labors, even to the rending of charity, lest Christian minds be corrupted by them and fall away from the simplicity and purity of the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

Let him also see whether Christian minds are corrupted and fall away from the simplicity and purity of the faith that is in Christ Jesus by the two chapters mentioned above, and by two others also to be written in what follows, which we excerpted from the words of Catholics; or rather by those inventions which he excerpted together with the modern Predestinarians and the anathematized Predestinarians of former times, in order to revive the heresy that had been crushed and utterly extinguished. That heresy, to increase the burden of our labors in the most dangerous and grievous times, is lamentably and tearfully being removed even to the sundering of unanimous brotherhood.

### CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the person who, concealing his name, composed a booklet to criticize these chapters, and concerning the synodal statements collected by the compiler of the chapters given to us by the royal highness, wishing to show that we had disagreed with them

Finally, the compiler of the chapters given by your highness to our humility also appended statements of the holy Fathers, written out chapter by chapter, clearly proclaiming that, since the chapters excerpted by us disagreed with that faith, every faithful person should faithfully hold what he had supposedly recovered from the hidden writings of the Fathers out of the same zeal for piety, and had supposedly established by promulgating it.

A certain rustic in speech, foolish in understanding, and, according to the measure of his knowledge, perverse in judgment, inserted these statements into a booklet which he composed, though he concealed his name and produced it in a sufficiently disorderly fashion. In it he tried, as far as he could, to tear apart and demonstrate as heretical the four chapters excerpted by us, so that, growing from something small, he might become great from something lesser, and, since he could not obtain favor through praise of his own [work], might in some way purchase it through blasphemies against us.

It is related that a certain young man, seeking useless notoriety, set fire to the great temple of Diana at Ephesus. When he was seized and asked why he had dared such a thing, he is said to have replied: “Because I could not become known through good deeds, I would at least become known through evil ones.” Indeed, the same man who wrote the aforesaid booklet against us would, so far as can be understood, have willingly become a heretic if he had known the means by which he could bring his desire to the result he wanted, so that he might become known.

But, contracted by lack of knowledge and distracted by boastfulness, he neither prevailed in teaching the errors he wished to teach, nor, swollen with arrogance and goaded by boastfulness as by certain spurs, and as though pressed down by a press, could he restrain himself within the bounds of silence without making some sound. In the booklets mentioned above we answered him, together with the other Predestinarians recently arisen again, insofar as the giver of all grace deigned to grant us the ability.

But since the compiler of these chapters now before us made mention of the African and Arausian Synods and appended their written statements to his chapters, lest we seem to evade the objections in his response by passing them over, and lest anyone say that we did not wish to answer him but were unable to do so, and lest anyone be secretly led to suspect that a chapter excerpted by us disagrees with these statements of the Fathers, let us compare, in accordance with the straight line of the faith, the chapters excerpted by us with these statements of the Fathers. Let the reader see whether they can agree.

We shall first set out the synods of which he made mention, and then the statements of the Fathers which he appended to his chapter; and we shall take care to compare the meaning of those statements with the chapters excerpted by us. [Col. 0195D]

Saint Coelestine, writing to Venerius and the other Gallican bishops in his Decretal Letter, says in this passage:

“What the rulers of the Roman Church judged concerning the heresy that had arisen in their times, and what they determined should be thought concerning the grace of God against the most pernicious defenders of free will, we set forth in such a way that we also joined certain statements of the African councils, which the apostolic bishops approved by making them their own. Therefore, so that those who are in any doubt may be instructed more fully, we make known the constitutions of the holy Fathers in a brief list. If anyone is not excessively contentious, he will recognize that the entire connection of the disputations depends upon this brief summary of the authorities set out below, and that no basis for contradiction remains if he believes and says with Catholics” (chapter 1):

“That Adam injured all human beings, and that no one can be saved except by the grace of Christ.”

We said the same thing in the first chapter, stating:

“Man sinned by using free will badly and fell, and became a mass of perdition for the entire human race.”

Saint Coelestine continued, saying (chapter 2):

“That no one is good by his own powers, except through participation in him who alone is good.”

Following his teaching, we too said:

“The good and just God chose from that same mass of perdition those whom he predestined to life by grace, and predestined eternal life for them.” [Col. 0196D–0197A]

Then Saint Coelestine added (chapter 3):

“That unless we are continually aided by the grace of God, we cannot overcome the snares of the devil; that through Christ we make good use of free will; that all the merits of the saints are gifts of God; that every holy thought and movement of a devout will is from God; and that the grace of God not only forgives sins but also helps us not to commit them.”

Following his teaching, we wrote that “we lost the freedom of free will in the first man, which we received through Christ our Lord.” We did not, however, lose free will itself utterly in the first man, but the freedom of that free will, which we received through Christ.

“And we possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace.” [Col. 0197B]

That is, we possess it so that we may use it well for every pursuit, every work, every holy merit, every holy thought, and every movement of a devout will; so that we may will and be able to do what is good, ask for it, merit it, and obtain not only the forgiveness of past sins but also the precaution of not committing future ones.

Saint Coelestine then continues (chapter 4):

“That, in addition to the statutes of the Apostolic See, all the prayers of the Church resound with the grace of Christ, by which the human race is restored from eternal condemnation; and that the established purification of those to be baptized also testifies to the grace of God, since unclean spirits are driven away from them by exorcisms and exsufflations.”

Instructed by his teaching, we said:

“The good and just God chose from the mass of perdition those whom he predestined by grace—that is, whom grace prepared—for life.” [Col. 0197C]

And whatever takes place in holy prayers and ecclesiastical mysteries is God’s predestination, since the preparation of grace belongs to God, through which the ministries of the sacraments bring those predestined to life to the eternal life predestined for them.

We also set out Saint Coelestine’s understanding concerning that free will in the second chapter excerpted by us (at the end of the same passage), saying:

“But we have free will because it has been liberated by grace and healed from corruption by grace.”

For he himself says:

“Certainly, by God’s help and gift free will is not taken away but liberated, so that from being dark it may become bright, from crooked straight, from weak sound, and from imprudent provident. For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wills our merits to be his gifts.” [Col. 0197D]

Behold how we do not dissent from the meaning of the African Synod, how we have written nothing contrary to that holy synod, and how we do not oppose the glorious Roman Church.

Now let us see whether we disagree in anything with the holy Synod of Arausio, over which Saint Caesarius presided by delegation of the Apostolic See.

Its first chapter is:

“If anyone says that, through Adam’s transgression, man was not wholly changed for the worse—that is, according to both body and soul—but believes that the freedom of the soul remained unharmed while only the body was subject to corruption.”

Second:

“If anyone asserts that Adam alone was harmed by his transgression and not his offspring, or testifies that only bodily death, which is the punishment of sin, but not sin itself, which is the death of the soul, passed through one man into the entire human race.” [Col. 0198A]

Third:

“If anyone says that the grace of God can be conferred at human invocation, but does not acknowledge that grace itself causes us to invoke it.”

Fourth:

“If anyone contends that God awaits our will in order that we may be cleansed from sin, and does not confess that, so that we may also will to be cleansed, this comes about in us through the infusion and operation of the Holy Spirit.”

Fifth:

“If anyone says that both the increase and the beginning of faith, and the very affection of belief—by which we believe in him who justifies the ungodly and come to the regeneration of holy baptism—come not through the gift of grace, that is, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit correcting our will from unbelief to faith, and the other matters which it pursues there.”

Sixth:

“If anyone says that, without the grace of God, mercy is divinely conferred upon those who believe and will, but does not acknowledge that grace is given so that we may believe, will, and so forth.”

Seventh:

“If anyone affirms that, by the strength of nature, he can think as is fitting of anything good pertaining to the salvation of eternal life, or choose it, or consent to saving—that is, evangelical—preaching without the illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit.”

Eighth:

“If anyone contends that some come to the grace of baptism through mercy, while others come through free will—which, in all who are born from the transgression of the first man, is acknowledged to have been corrupted.”

Ninth, concerning God’s help:

“It is God’s gift when we think rightly and restrain our feet from falsehood and injustice.” [Col. 0198B–C]

Tenth, concerning God’s help:

“God’s help must always be implored by those who have been reborn and healed.”

If anyone wishes to consider all these chapters with a kindly disposition and devout zeal, he will find that we have dealt with them in our two chapters, in which we said:

“Man sinned by using free will badly and fell, and became a mass of perdition for the entire human race. But the good and just God chose from that same mass those whom he predestined to life by grace”;

and:

“We possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace.”

Therefore, if we did not fear being branded as arrogant and wearying the reader—lest someone say that we arrogantly claimed this as though it had been given uniquely to us, so that others reading these things could not understand them unless we demonstrated each point individually in separate statements—we would undertake to show, by setting the statements of these two chapters alongside each individual chapter, how they agree.

Now let us give a more detailed account of the eleventh chapter and the other chapters that follow, which are taken chiefly from Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*, in which he briefly recorded sayings of Saint Augustine, just as certain of the matters we mentioned earlier were also taken from it.

The eleventh chapter is “Concerning the Obligation of Vows”:

“No one rightly vows anything to the Lord unless he has received it from him.”

We too said:

“We possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace.”

The twelfth: “What Sort of People Does God Love?”

“God loves us as we shall be by his gift, not as we are by our merit.”

This is precisely what we wrote:

“Those whom he predestined to life by grace.”

The thirteenth:

“The freedom of the will,” says the synod, “having been weakened in the first man, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism; and what was lost cannot be restored except by the one from whom it was able to be given.”

We said:

“We lost the freedom of free will in the first man, which we received through Christ our Lord.”

The fourteenth:

“No wretched person is freed from any misery except one who is preceded by God’s mercy.”

We said:

“And we possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace.”

The fifteenth:

“Adam was changed from what God formed him to be, but for the worse through his iniquity; the faithful person is changed from what iniquity has wrought in him, but for the better through the grace of God.”

We said:

“Man sinned by using free will badly and fell, and became a mass of perdition for the entire human race. But the good God chose those whom he predestined by grace—that is, whom grace prepared—for life.”

The sixteenth:

“Let no one glory in what he appears to have, as though he had not received it,” and so forth.

We said:

“We possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace.”

The seventeenth:

“Worldly desire makes the strength of the Gentiles; the love of God makes the strength of Christians,” and so forth.

And since love is grace, it precedes our will and makes and preserves our strength; this love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, as the Psalmist also demonstrates, saying:

“I will love you, O Lord, my strength,”

and:

“I will preserve my strength from you.”

We did not keep silent concerning this when we said:

“Grace precedes our free will,”

writing:

“We possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace.” [Col. 0199B–C]

The eighteenth:

“Reward is owed to good works if they are performed; but grace, which is not owed, precedes them so that they may be performed.”

It can be understood that we said this with complete clarity, since:

“We possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace.”

The nineteenth:

“Human nature, even if it remained in that integrity in which it was created, could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator. Therefore, since it could not preserve without grace the salvation which it received, how could it restore without God’s grace what it lost?”

For this reason we stated that:

“Man sinned by using free will badly and fell; and the freedom of free will, which we lost in the first man, we received through Christ our Lord; and we possess free will, preceded and aided by grace.”

The twentieth:

“Man can do nothing good without God. God does many good things in man which man does not do; but man does no good thing which God does not enable man to do.”

Therefore we said:

“We possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace,”

because without it we can do nothing, whereas with it we can do what he himself deigns to grant, who said:

“Without me you can do nothing.” [Col. 0199D–0200A]

The twenty-first, “Concerning Nature and Grace”:

“As the Apostle most truthfully says to those who, wishing to be justified by the law, have fallen away from grace: ‘If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing.’ And if righteousness is through nature, then Christ died for nothing.”

Christ did not therefore die for nothing among us, because we said what we believe, as it is written:

“I believed, and therefore I spoke,”

and:

“We also believe, and therefore we speak.”

“Man sinned by using free will badly, and fell, and became a mass of perdition for the entire human race. But the good God chose those whom he predestined to life by grace.”

The twenty-second, “Concerning What Belongs Properly to Man”:

“No one has anything of his own except falsehood and sin.”

Therefore we said:

“We possess free will for evil, grace having abandoned [it].” [Col. 0200B]

The twenty-third, “Concerning the Will of God and Man”:

“Human beings do their own will, not God’s, when they do what displeases God. But when they act according to their will in such a way that they serve the divine will, although they willingly do what they do, nevertheless it is the will of the one by whom what they will is both prepared and commanded.”

For, as we said:

“We possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace,”

and:

“We possess free will for evil, grace having abandoned [it].”

The twenty-fourth, “Concerning the Branches of the Vine”:

“The branches are in the vine in such a way that they contribute nothing to the vine, but receive from it the means by which they live,” and so forth.

For, as the Apostle says:

“By the grace of God I am what I am.”

And from the mass of perdition, as we wrote, God chose those whom he predestined to life by grace. [Col. 0200C]

The twenty-fifth:

“The love with which we love God is wholly God’s gift,” and so forth.

We said:

“We possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace.”

And what follows in the same chapter we also believe according to the Catholic faith: that, once the grace received through baptism has been granted, all the baptized, with Christ helping and cooperating, can and ought faithfully to labor for what pertains to the salvation of the soul, and, if they wish, to fulfill it, because, as we said:

“We possess free will for the good, preceded and aided by grace.”

And concerning what follows:

“That some have been predestined to evil by divine power,”

we not only do not believe this; but if there are people who wish to believe so great an evil, we pronounce anathema upon them with complete abhorrence. Accordingly, in the explanation already given concerning the first chapter, we wrote the same thing above.

And we too, together with the holy synod, must pronounce anathema upon the Predestinarians who say that, just as the elect have been predestined by God to life, so also the reprobate have been predestined to destruction, and upon those who confess that some have been predestined to evil by divine power—unless they correct themselves and return, through appropriate satisfaction, to the unity of the Catholic faith and the bosom of holy Mother Church.

From this point, let anyone who looks with the eye of a dove at what our holy Fathers proposed and what we have followed—and who does not seek, with the talons of a hawk, to tear apart fraternal and innocent simplicity—see what we have woven together, although in shorter words, because of the dullness of those less capable and less diligent, from the venerable, revered, and Catholic fullness of such great teachers. He will see that we have deviated in no respect. For it is clear that anyone who prefers, without cause, to gnaw at us with a poisonous tooth will prove himself malicious, rather than proving that we are non-Catholics.

Now let us examine the statements mentioned, which the compiler of the chapters had annotated.

“1. That in Adam’s transgression all human beings lost natural ability and innocence, and that no one can rise from the depth of that ruin through free choice unless the grace of the merciful God has raised him up.”

Nor did we deny that in Adam’s transgression all human beings lost natural ability and innocence, when we said: “In the first human being we lost the freedom of choice.” Thus also Saint Augustine said in his book *On Rebuke and Grace* (chapter 12):

“Now, he says, after that great freedom was lost through the desert of sin, the weakness that remained had to be assisted even by greater gifts.”

And again:

“It is little enough for a human being to restore through that [grace] the freedom he had lost.”

Let him himself explain what he called “lost freedom.” For in the book *Hypomnesticon* (book III, not far from the beginning) he says:

“Thus, through sin, the human free choice lost the good of possibility, but not its name and nature.”

And again (after the middle):

“What else, moreover, do we show in that one lost sheep out of a hundred sheep, except that free choice, through the good of possibility having been lost by the fault of the first human being, wandered away from the company of the righteous?”

And again:

“By willing evil, therefore, he rightly lost the ability to do good, who through the ability to do good had been able to overcome the willing of evil.”

And again:

“But the one to whom he had freely granted the ability both to will and not to will first taught him to will and not to will; and while using that ability badly, in his heedlessness he voluntarily offered consent to the serpent persuading him and transgressed the Lord’s command. Having lost the good of possibility, wounded, he retained only the power to will.”

And Saint Celestine says, drawing on the words of Saint Innocent, which he had written to the Council of Carthage:

“The first human being, he says, having experienced free choice, while using his own goods too heedlessly fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression, and found nothing by which he could rise from there; deceived forever by his own freedom.”

And for this reason we wrote: “In the first human being we lost the freedom of choice.”

2. He added: “That no one can use free choice well except through Christ.” We likewise said this, setting down:

“We have received that freedom through Christ our Lord, and we have free choice for good, anticipated and assisted by grace.”

We have free choice, however, because it has been liberated by grace and healed by grace from its corruption. And Saint Celestine, from the words of Innocent, had prefaced this:

“The first human being, deceived in his freedom forever, would have remained subjected to and overwhelmed by this ruin, unless Christ’s coming, in accordance with his grace, had afterward raised him up.”

And Saint Prosper, in his letter to Rufinus:

“Having lost natural innocence, the human being, an exile and one who had perished, walking without a path, entered into ever deeper errors. But he was sought, found, and carried back; he was brought into the way which is truth and life, and was recognized through love for God, who first loved the one who loves him.”

And a little later:

“Free choice was not taken away, but liberated. As long as it was alone, without God, it was dead to righteousness and lived for sin. But when the mercy of Christ enlightened it, it was torn from the kingdom of the devil and made the kingdom of God. Yet, so that it may be able to remain in that kingdom, it is not sufficient for itself even with that ability, unless it receives perseverance from the same source from which it received diligence.”

And again:

“Unless the grace of Christ reforms his free choice by acting, breathing into it, assisting it, and preserving it by going before it even to the end.”

And *Against the Gauls*:

“For before it is liberated from the dominion of the devil through God’s grace, it lies in that depth into which the human choice plunged itself through its own freedom.”

And Saint Augustine:

“Therefore nothing remains for those who are to be liberated except the grace of the one who liberates.”

For this reason we said:

“We have free choice, because it has been liberated by grace and healed by grace from corruption.”

3. Next he proposed:

“That all the endeavors, works, and merits of the saints are to be referred to God’s glory and praise, because no one pleases him from any other source except from what he himself has bestowed.

4. That God works in human hearts and in free choice itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will come from God, because through him we are able to do something good, without whom we can do nothing.”

We too do not deny these things; indeed, we confess them, saying:

“We have free choice for good, anticipated and assisted by grace.”

We expressly used “for good” so that by “good” we might understand every good thing, whatever is good. If endeavor is good, if holy work is good, if holy merit is good, if what we think holily is good, if pious counsel is good, if being moved toward any good thing and toward any good will is good—in all these matters our free choice, anticipated and assisted by God’s grace, we both believe, affirm, and have confirmed in writing.

Believing that all these things come from God, we said so when we wrote: “Our free choice for good, anticipated and assisted by God’s grace.” We also professed that God works within our very free choice holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will, when we said:

“We have free choice, anticipated”—that is, before we think good thoughts—“and assisted by grace,” so that we may think well, act well, and persevere in good things.

In these two chapters, then, thanks be to God, we have deviated in no respect from the Catholic meaning or from the words of Catholics.

5. He proposed:

“We profess God to be the author of all endeavors and of all virtues by which one moves toward God from the beginning of faith, and we do not doubt that all human merits are anticipated by his grace, through which it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good. By this assistance and mercy of God free choice is not taken away, but liberated, so that what was dark may become bright, what was crooked straight, what was sickly healthy, and what was imprudent prudent. For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wills our merits to be what are his gifts, and for what he has bestowed he will bestow eternal rewards. For he acts within us so that we may both will and do what he wills.”

Here, without omitting our response but interrupting it for a little while, let us address the compiler of these chapters. See, brother—whether you wish it or not, our brother—how long you have said, whether truly or falsely, “Our Father,” to the Lord. For it is written: “Say to those who alienate themselves, ‘You are our brothers’” (Isaiah 66:5). Let Saint Celestine, who remains in the One before whom all things are naked and open, and to whom the thought of the human heart confesses, and who therefore sees and hears all our affairs, not hear from you, uncorrected as you are, that you abused this testimony of his. Let him say to you:

“By your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant.”

When you read, wrote down, and caused these words—which were to be believed, held, and preached—to reach royal hands, you said, filled with the Holy Spirit and speaking truthfully:

“God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wills our merits to be what are his gifts.”

Accordingly, it is utterly certain that God, according to the Apostles Paul and Peter, wills all human beings to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4) and wills no one to perish (2 Peter 3:9). Why, then, did you say in the chapter written above that he predestined certain people to destruction?

For it is entirely certain that, as I said—and as you abusively wrote—God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wills our merits to be what are his gifts. Hence what you said, that God predestined certain people to destruction, is certainly and utterly false. For he who wills all human beings to be saved and no one to perish must not be believed to have predestined anyone to perdition.

Thus our fellow soldiers and fellow ministers, holding to the apostolic teaching above, are known to have instructed us. And if you come to his judgment with such an opinion, know for certain that you will receive on the head a blow—not from the club of Hercules, but from an apostolic rod weighing even more heavily—such that you will scarcely, or perhaps never, rise again afterward.

We have answered this chapter sufficiently in what was said above. And lest some associate of the compiler of the chapter say that we have not answered everything fully, since in the chapter excerpted by us from Saint Celestine’s words we included only two statements concerning free choice, when we said:

“We have free choice because it has been liberated by grace and healed by grace from corruption,”

let us add what Saint Celestine said about the other matters.

For he said:

“‘What was dark may become bright’: when it was dark, it was undoubtedly corrupt; when it received light, it received healing. ‘What was crooked may become straight’: when it was crooked, it was undoubtedly corrupt; when it was restored by God’s grace, it undoubtedly received healing. ‘What was sickly may become healthy’: when it was sickly, it was without doubt corrupt; when it received healing, it was healed and therefore undoubtedly healthy.”

And because “healthy” is one thing and “healed” another, just as “able to be healed” is one thing and “healthy” another, and “able to be restored” one thing and “restored” another, Prosper demonstrates this in the second book *On the Calling of the Nations*, saying:

“Not everything capable of being restored has been restored, nor is everything capable of being healed healthy; for ‘capable of being restored’ and ‘capable of being healed’ belong to nature, whereas to have been restored and healed belongs to grace. Therefore it must be gathered and understood that free choice was indeed healthy in the first human being, having been given to that first human being, by which he possessed both the freedom and the possibility of willing and being able to do good, and by which, through willing evil, he lost the ability to do good—he who, through the ability to do good, had been able to overcome the willing of evil.

“After this, however, free choice in the human being was not healthy but capable of being healed—yet capable of being healed by the One for whom nothing is impossible. It is healthy in those who are healed by him and through him whose grace it is: liberated by grace from slavery to sin, endowed with freedom by grace, and restored to freedom by grace. Thus in his elect God’s grace heals it from corruption and grants it the health of wholeness: now in hope, but in the future life truly healthy, given and to be given without any interruption or defilement of corruption.”

And for this reason we said:

“We have free choice healed by grace from corruption.”

Saint Celestine continues:

“Let what was imprudent become prudent.”

Nor is this excluded from what we said about being healed from corruption. For, to pass over for the sake of brevity what Augustine, Prosper, Saint Gregory, and Ambrose say about it, Saint Celestine says in the words of Saint Innocent:

“He would have been plunged into the depths of transgression and would have lain oppressed beneath this ruin, unless Christ’s coming had afterward raised him up by his grace. For, plunged into the depths of transgression, free choice corrupted free choice; and, lying oppressed beneath the ruin, what useful thing could he have prudently provided for himself unless Christ’s grace had raised him up, healed him, and enlightened him, and made what was imprudent prudent?”

In this too, thanks be to eternal grace, we have deviated in no respect from the Catholic meaning or from the words of Catholics.

6. He added:

“We confess that God’s grace and assistance are given even for individual acts, and that they are not given according to our merits, so that grace may truly be grace—that is, freely given through the mercy of him who said: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.’”

He joined these two chapters, the seventh and eighth, into one, taking them from what was said against Pelagius by the Council of Palestine. Perhaps, overcome by a lethargic illness or intoxicated from a Silenian cup, he forgot, with his memory deadened, that he had already written these things in the third and fourth chapters of blessed Celestine. We have shown that we did not disagree with those chapters.

7. “We confess that there is free choice, even if it needs divine assistance.”

He also arranged to insert this chapter, the tenth of the Council of Palestine. Concerning it we have confessed that:

“We have free choice for good, anticipated and assisted by grace, and we have free choice because it has been liberated by grace and healed by grace from corruption.”

To these statements, and to those which he adds, we respond freely because we have already responded to them; yet we do not refuse to respond further, since it is written:

“Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return.”

Saint Celestine in no way forbids us to draw out further lessons from these matters. Therefore, he says, so that those who are in any doubt may be more fully instructed, we briefly display the constitutions of the holy Fathers. If anyone is not excessively contentious, let him recognize that the connection of all the arguments depends upon the brevity of the authorities set out below, and that no reason for contradiction remains for him if he believes and speaks with Catholics—namely, in accordance with what we have stated above from his words.

But since perhaps the compiler of these chapters is excessively contentious, and neither believes nor says with Catholics what Catholics believed and said, and prefers to be an Aristodemus opposed and hostile to the Apostle John rather than a disciple of the Apostle John and of the apostolic Celestine, let him receive our tunic—the tunic woven by the labor of the Fathers—that is, a faithful garment by which he himself may, through God’s grace, be raised again to faith, so that in this way we may perhaps remove his anger against us, who are faithful.

For this reason we shall still respond to him concerning the two following chapters.

8. “The choice of the will, weakened in the first human being, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism.”

He also took this from the thirteenth chapter of the Council of Orange. Concerning it we said:

“We have received the freedom of choice”—that is, the possibility of the free choice of the will—“through Christ our Lord. And we have free choice because it has been liberated by grace,” as it is written:

“Then you will truly be free, when the Son has set you free” (John 8:36).

This takes place when we are reborn in the same Spirit in whom Christ our Redeemer and Savior was born for us from the undefiled flesh of the Virgin.

9. “The choice of the will is truly free when it does not serve vices and sins. Such a choice was certainly given by God to the first human being; once lost, it could not be restored except by the One by whom it had been able to be given. Hence the Truth says: ‘If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.’”

As in the preceding case he jointly set down two chapters from the Council of Palestine, and inserted them superfluously—as though what the apostolic see had issued sufficiently were not enough—so now he divided the thirteenth chapter of the Council of Orange into two and, by cutting it apart, composed it differently from the way the council itself had presented it.

The Council of Orange in fact took this chapter in part from Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*, chapter 150, and said:

“The choice of the will, weakened in the first human being, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism; once lost, it cannot be restored except by the One by whom it had been able to be given. Hence the Truth himself says: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free’” (John 8:36).

But this man, as we stated above, constructed his eighth chapter from half of this conciliar chapter, writing:

“The choice of the will, weakened in the first human being, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism.”

And he constructed the ninth from Prosper’s statement, in which, drawing on the words of Saint Augustine, he says:

“The choice of the will is truly free when it does not serve vices. Such a choice was given by God to the first human being. Once lost, it cannot be restored except by the One by whom it was able to be given. Hence the Truth says: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.’”

The holy council, however, weaving and arranging the chapter that must be held both Catholicly and sufficiently, commended it to us, its successors. Our writing has deviated in no respect from its agreement—or, in truth, from Prosper’s statement—as we demonstrated above.

Even if, for some reason, the compiler of these chapters had distilled the meaning of this chapter, what he did would not have been unreasonable. But since the words and meaning of the chapter remain intact, he divided and compiled it with less necessity than was appropriate.

For the holy Caesarius, who presided over this Council of Orange by delegation of the apostolic see, knew well what Saint Augustine had said in the book *On Rebuke and Grace* concerning the free choice given to the first human being. He also knew what Augustine recalled in his books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, written to his predecessor Hilary. His equal and companion, Saint Prosper, does not conceal that he possessed that same book, in his letter to Augustine, saying:

“You would issue the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, full of divine authority. When it was brought to our knowledge at an unexpected and opportune moment”—and so forth.

And it must be believed that Saint Prosper did not withhold from Hilary, his close friend and companion, the same book which he said he possessed. Hence blessed Caesarius, succeeding Saint Hilary in his office, was not unaware of what Saint Augustine had said there.

Saint Augustine says in the aforementioned book (chapter 11, toward the end):

“Through this grace of God, in receiving the good and holding it perseveringly, there comes about in us not only the ability to do what we will but also the willing of what we are able to do. This was not the case in the first human being: one of these two was present in him, the other was not. He did not need grace in order to receive the good, because he had not yet lost it; but in order to remain in it he needed the assistance of grace, without which he could not do so at all.

“He had received the ability, if he wished, which descended from free choice so that he might not wish. At that time his free choice was such that he could will good and evil. What, then, will be freer than free choice when it cannot serve sin? This was to be the reward of merit for the human being, just as it was made so for the holy angels. But now, after the good merit has been lost through sin, in those who are liberated grace has become the gift that was to be the reward of merit.”

And shortly afterward:

“Are we perhaps to say: ‘He who had such free choice could not sin’? Or: ‘He to whom it was said, “If you sin, you shall die,” could not die’? Or: ‘He could not abandon the good,’ when by sinning he did abandon it, and therefore died?”

And again (chapter 11):

“But he abandoned it and was abandoned. For the assistance was such that he could abandon it if he wished, and in which he would remain if he wished—not such that it would make him wish. This is the first grace, which was given to the first Adam; but this grace is more powerful in the second Adam. The first grace makes it possible for a human being to possess righteousness if he wishes; the second is therefore more powerful, since it also makes him wish, and wish so greatly and love with such ardor that the will of the spirit overcomes the will of the flesh, which desires what is contrary.”

And again Saint Augustine, in the same book *On Rebuke and Grace* (chapter 11, at the beginning):

“What, then, did Adam not have God’s grace? On the contrary, he had great grace, but of a different kind. He was among the good things which he had received from the goodness of his Creator. For he had not acquired those good things by his own merits; in them he suffered absolutely no evil.

“But the saints in this life, to whom this grace of liberation belongs, are in evils, from which they cry out to the Lord: ‘Deliver us from evil’ (Matthew 6:13). He did not need Christ’s death for those good things; these people are absolved from both inherited and personal guilt by the blood of that Lamb.

“He did not need the assistance which these people implore when they say: ‘I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Romans 7:23–25).

“For in them the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; and, laboring and endangered in such a struggle, they ask through Christ’s grace that the power to fight and conquer be given to them. But he, tempted and disturbed by no such conflict within himself against himself, enjoyed his own peace with himself in that place of blessedness.

“Therefore, although in the meantime they do not need a happier grace, they nevertheless now need a more powerful grace. And what is more powerful than God’s only-begotten Son, equal to the Father and coeternal with him, made human for their sake and crucified by sinful human beings, though without any sin of his own, whether original or personal?

“Although he rose on the third day, never again to die, he nevertheless endured death for mortals—the one who granted life to the dead—so that, redeemed by his blood and having received so great and such a pledge, they might say: ‘If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things?’ (Romans 8:31–32).

“Through this mediator God shows that those whom he redeemed by his blood he makes eternally good thereafter from their evils. He received him in such a way that he would never be evil, and that, having never been made from evil, he would always be good.

“The first human being did not have this grace, through which he would never wish to be evil. Yet he certainly had the grace by which, if he wished to remain in it, he would never be evil.”

And blessed Augustine likewise says:

“The first freedom of the will was the ability not to sin; the final freedom will be much greater, the inability to sin. This was to be the reward of merit for the human being, just as it was made so for the holy angels.”

## CHAPTER XXIII

The refutation of the compiler himself follows, from the words of blessed Augustine and the other teachers.

From these words of Saint Augustine it is perfectly clear that the holy council composed its chapter more rationally than this man divided it. For what the council said:

“The choice of the will, weakened in the first human being, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism; once lost, it cannot be restored except by the One by whom it had been able to be given,”

contains everything that we need thereafter to know and believe.

For it is made clear in this statement that the choice of the will had been given healthy to the first human being, that it was weakened in him, and that what was lost cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism. Through baptism the faithful are reborn in the same Spirit in whom our Creator and Restorer was born, and the same choice of the will is restored to the faithful by him as had been given to the first human being.

Full and perfect health, and complete freedom, are now restored to the faithful in hope; in the future, when death—the last enemy—has finally been destroyed, they will be restored in reality, as it is written: “We were saved in hope.”

For as long as we live here in mortality, we struggle with death, where the corruptible body weighs down the soul and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind occupied with many thoughts. There the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do whatever we wish.

There are times when we have abandoned God and are therefore justly abandoned by grace: free choice is free from righteousness but enslaved to sin, as the Apostle demonstrates when he says:

“When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death” (Romans 6:20–21).

At other times, having been anticipated and assisted by grace, we have free choice liberated from sin and enslaved to righteousness, as the same Apostle again demonstrates:

“Now, having been liberated from sin and made slaves of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life” (ibid., 22).

But when this mortal has put on immortality, and this corruptible has put on incorruption, and what is perfect has come, and what is partial has been abolished, then we shall possess the choice of free will perfectly: namely, the inability to will sin, the inability to sin, the inability to die, and the inability to abandon the good.

In all these matters the mercy of our Savior will remain with us, as blessed Augustine says in the often-mentioned book *On Rebuke and Grace*, concerning the predestined: whether they are converted, whether they fight, or whether they are crowned. For even then Holy Scripture testifies that they need God’s mercy, when the holy person says to the Lord God concerning his own soul:

“He crowns you with compassion and mercy” (Psalm 102:4).

The first human being would have possessed this free choice if he had used in the way he could have the free choice he had received, as we stated above from Saint Augustine’s words (chapter 11):

“What,” he says, “will be freer than free choice when it will be unable to serve sin? This was to be the reward of merit for the human being, just as it was made so for the holy angels.”

But let anyone who wishes compare, with a kindly disposition, the chapter of the holy Council of Orange with the chapter excerpted by us according to its meaning—for at that time we did not have the book at hand, when we were compelled to dictate this chapter from the statements of the orthodox—and let him see whether, in dictating it, we deviated in any respect from the Catholic faith or from the council’s exposition.

The council says:

“The choice of the will, weakened in the first human being, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism; once lost, it cannot be restored except by the One by whom it had been able to be given. Hence the Truth himself says: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.’”

And we said:

“In the first human being we lost the freedom of choice, which we received through Christ our Lord. And we have free choice for good, anticipated and assisted by grace; and we have free choice for evil, abandoned by grace. We have free choice, however, because it has been liberated by grace and healed by grace from corruption.”

Having thus answered the critic of this chapter excerpted by us, we have decided briefly to mention, as if incidentally, the following matter. For it has come to our attention that those scoundrels who still do not dare to publish openly all that they perversely think are secretly composing a book against us, while taking care that it should not reach our knowledge or be brought to our reading, even though they are writing against us.

In that book, as someone reported to us who had tried to bring us a transcript of it but lost it, along with his other possessions, in the violent turmoil that recently occurred in this kingdom, our rivals say that we assert, write, and preach that free choice was utterly lost in the first human being when he sinned.

Therefore we have decided briefly to record what we think about free choice, so that anyone who happens to encounter their folly may find here without difficulty what our mind—seasoned with the salt of Catholic wisdom—holds.

The first human being was created immortal with free choice in such a way that he could refrain from sinning if he wished and could sin if he wished. He would not die if he did not sin, but he would die if he sinned; and he would not sin if he did not wish to do so.

And if he had persisted in free choice in such a way that he did not wish to sin, he would have received that great permanence of merit, so that he could neither sin nor wish to sin, just as the holy angels received it as a gift—a reward of merit that was to be given to the human being also.

This was the great and first freedom of the free choice of the first human being. Through that freedom he sinned by his will, and by sinning through his will he incurred the death that God had foretold to him, so that he might not incur it by sinning. Through willing evil he lost the ability to do good, although through the ability to do good he had been able to overcome the willing of evil.

And just as the human being, created immortal—as we said—because God willed him to be so, lost what made him immortal while what made him human remained, so after the fall he retained free choice: free from righteousness but enslaved to sin, sufficient by itself for evil but weak and powerless for every good, until through Christ’s coming, by the action of God’s Spirit, it was made upright and enlightened by the grace of faith—although by its own freedom it had been crooked and dark.

He did not receive this from the source from which he had lost it; rather, he received from the One who gave him what he now has what he had lost. For after the fall of the first human being, God willed that the human being’s approach to him and his not departing from him should belong solely to God’s grace, as it is written:

“Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself, and we shall not depart from you” (Psalm 79:18).

This is the second Adam, through whom we approach God and in whom we do not depart from God. For in the first Adam we departed from God; in him that greatest freedom of the free choice was lost, and nothing remained except weakness.

Therefore nothing remains for those who are to be liberated except the grace of the one who liberates.

We received that freedom of choice so that we might not only will and be able to do good, but also not wish to depart from the good and be able to persevere in the good: not with grace abolishing free choice, but with grace nourishing it—free choice liberated by grace and healed by grace from corruption.

This is the second grace, and the freedom of free choice recovered through God’s grace.

When, however, in the elect death—the last enemy—has finally been destroyed, and this mortal has put on immortality, and this corruptible has put on incorruption, this will be for the honor of life, not for the duration of punishment. For sinners too will put on incorruption, but for the duration of punishment, not for the honor of life.

When the unquenchable fire receives them, it will not extinguish or destroy them; rather, it will preserve them forever intact for their punishment.

Then, through the grace of our Creator, Restorer, and Crown-giver, who crowns us with mercy and compassion, if we are judged worthy of being changed when we rise with the elect, we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed. We shall receive that perfect and greatest freedom, so that we can neither sin nor be able or willing to depart from eternity.

The holy angels received this freedom as a gift. It was the reward of merit belonging to free choice, without the intervening condition of death, which would also have been given to the human being if he had not sinned.

The first human being did not possess this freedom of choice, because, in order that he might reach it as he could, he used the freedom of choice he had received too heedlessly, turned aside onto the left-hand path, and was abandoned by God’s grace, although he himself had first abandoned God.

But because God will not cast away forever or forget to have mercy, this grace will be given to the human being in the future, when he will be like the holy angels in heaven: now saved in hope in this age, but then saved in reality for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXIV

An account begins to be rendered concerning the third chapter excerpted by us, which the compiler of the chapters given to us by royal majesty sharply criticized, together with the claims that the Predestinarians derive from it to confirm their own opinion, and how Catholics contradict their erroneous statements from the teachings of Scripture.

Having completed, as the Lord granted, two chapters, and having given our answer to their sifters—but not their consumers—we now approach the third chapter with complete confidence, not presuming upon ourselves but trusting in the One who said:

“I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:15).

We believe with absolute certainty and without any hesitation in faith that the One who began the work will himself complete it. To him be glory, power, and dominion throughout the eternal ages.

Concerning this chapter, as Saint Prosper demonstrates from the objections of the Gauls and the Vincentians, and from the responses by which, through delegation of the apostolic see, he dissolved the inventions of those people and their like, the ancient Predestinarians made the following statements.

The eighth objection of the Gauls says:

“That God does not will all human beings to be saved, but only a fixed number of the predestined.”

And the second objection of the Vincentians says:

“That God does not wish to save all, even if all wish to be saved.”

And the modern Predestinarian Gothescalcus, in his book to Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, says:

“All whom God wills to be saved are saved without doubt; nor can anyone be saved except those whom God wills to be saved. Nor is there anyone whom God wills to be saved who is not saved. For our God has done all that he willed. Therefore all whom he wills to be saved are saved.”

And Lord Prudentius, in his letter to his archbishop Wenilo concerning the ordination of Aeneas as bishop of Paris, says in the fourth chapter:

“That he should believe and confess that almighty God saves all whomsoever he wills, and that no one can in any way be saved except the one whom he himself has saved. All whomsoever he himself wills to save are saved; and consequently, whoever are not saved are entirely outside his will to be saved, the Prophet saying: ‘The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses’” (Psalm 134:6).

Leo briefly demonstrates in the letter to Flavian that these men are convicted of falsehood and that they wrongly hand down Holy Scripture. He says (letter 12, before the middle):

“There was need,” he says, “of the dispensation of a hidden plan, so that the unchangeable God, whose will cannot be deprived of its goodness, might fulfill his first disposition of mercy toward us through a more hidden sacrament, and so that the human being, driven into guilt by the devil’s deceitful wickedness, might not perish contrary to God’s purpose. Therefore the Son of God enters the lowliness of this world.”

The compiler of these chapters—which you gave us so that we might answer them—said nothing more explicitly, as we think, because he realized that he had inserted words of Saint Celestine which he had written in the fourth chapter, where he says:

“God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wills our merits to be what are his gifts.”

We, however, against both the ancient and the modern Predestinarians, excerpted this chapter from Prosper’s words and from the judgments of Prosper himself and of other Catholic teachers, saying:
