“Almighty God wills all human beings without exception to be saved, although not all are saved. That some are saved is the gift of the one who saves; that some perish is the merit of those who perish.”

[Col. 0211D] Let us first satisfy our readers, since we inserted the words of the Apostle and of Prosper without qualification for this reason: Gottschalk, the foremost of the new Predestinarians, had written in his aforementioned little book to Rabanus:

“‘All’ and ‘all’ must be understood to mean all who are saved, concerning whom the Apostle says, ‘Who wills all human beings to be saved’ (1 Tim. 2:4), and all who are not saved, whom God does not will to save.”

Thus, by this perverse interpretation, he distorted both the apostolic words and Prosper’s statements before his hearers. It is therefore necessary for us to show, from the writings of the orthodox, whether this chapter extracted by us accords with the Catholic faith.

Above all, let us consult the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, which is also the mother of all the churches throughout the world. Jerusalem, honored according to the sacred canons of Nicaea, once called “the city of righteousness” and “the mother of cities,” lost this privilege through its unbelief and denial of the Son of God, calling him the son of Joseph and the son of a carpenter, and saying to him, “Though you are a man, you make yourself God, and you have a demon”; and of him, “We have no king but Caesar,” and, “According to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.” The Roman Church obtained that privilege through the confession of blessed Peter, who said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16), and through Paul’s testimony, affirming that Christ Jesus became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross; “therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:8 ff.).

Therefore, just as it was once said of Jerusalem through the Prophet, “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God. Zion shall be called ‘a man,’ and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:3), so this city was glorified by the presence of the great Peter, prince of the apostles. To him it was said by the true Son of God and truly Son of man—one Jesus Christ subsisting in two natures and substances, or operations, namely divine and human, in the unity of person, not in the unity of substance; wholly in those things which he possesses equally and indivisibly with the Father and the Holy Spirit, with whom he has one coeternal and indivisible substance; and wholly in those things in which he belongs to our race, that is, a rational soul and human flesh without any contagion of sin, flesh from the immaculate flesh of the Virgin Mother, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, which the Creator formed in us from the beginning and which he undertook to restore—then still passible and mortal, but now, having conquered death, glorified by the victory over suffering, remaining in the glory of God the Father, destined to judge the age and reigning without end—to him, I say, it was said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18).

And just as that former Jerusalem, the holy city, was fortified by the guardianship of angels until, because of its unbelief and hardness of heart, it heard from them, “Let us depart from these dwellings” [Col. 0212D], and from its Savior, if it had been willing to hear him, “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate,” so this city, illuminated and preserved, remains protected by the prayers of the teacher of the nations, who says: “God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I make remembrance of you in my prayers” (Rom. 1:9).

This holy see, like Peter and Paul in their apostolate, received primacy over all cities not from a human being or through a human being, but through the Lord Jesus Christ. Thus the holy Anacletus, third bishop of the Roman see after blessed Peter, ordained presbyter by that same prince of the apostles, says in his letter (Letter 3, near the beginning):

“Other principal cities, which we send you described in a certain volume, received their foremost preachers from the holy apostles, from blessed Clement, or from us. But this holy Roman and Apostolic Church received its primacy not from the apostles but from the Lord himself, our Savior, just as he said to blessed Peter the Apostle: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it’; and, ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. 16:18–19).

“The fellowship of the most blessed Apostle Paul, the vessel of election, was also added in that same city of Rome. On one day and at one time, struggling under Nero, he was crowned with a glorious death together with Peter; and both consecrated the holy Roman Church and placed it before the other cities throughout the world by their presence and venerable triumph.”

And Saint Innocent writes to Decentius, bishop of Eugubium, saying (Letter 29, at the beginning):

“For who could be unaware, or fail to perceive, that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, prince of the apostles, and has been preserved to the present time, ought to be observed by all, and that nothing should be added or introduced which either lacks authority or appears to take its example from elsewhere? Especially since it is evident that throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one founded churches except those whom the venerable Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Let them read whether in these provinces any other apostle is either said or found to have taught. If they do not read this, because nowhere do they find it, they ought to follow what the Roman Church observes, from which there is no doubt that they received their beginning, lest, while striving after foreign assertions, they appear to lose the source of their institutions.”

Since these things are so, and since Pope Saint Coelestine, during whose time this heresy first arose, states in his Decretal Letter (after Coelestine’s Letter 8) to Venerius and the other Gallican bishops what we ought to believe, hold, and preach in a Catholic manner (chapter 11):

“Let us consider the mysteries of priestly supplications, which, handed down from the apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in the whole Catholic Church, so that the law of prayer may establish the law of belief.”

He himself explains in the same chapter what the law of prayer is. The Church, especially on the day of the crucifixion of our Lord Jesus Christ, shows for whom he was crucified and whom he wills to be saved: she demonstrates this by supplication and groaning, praying for all human beings, individually and distinctly for every order, every rank, and every dignity; for schismatics and heretics, for Jews and pagans, so that no one is believed to be excluded, pleading before divine clemency the cause of the whole human race.

Accordingly, he says in that passage: “O God, who wills all to be saved and no one to perish, although some perish through their own iniquity and hardness.”

For it is the truth that said: “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn back from his way and live. Turn back from your most evil ways; and why will you die, house of Israel? Do I desire, desiring it, the death of the wicked? says the Lord God” (Ezek. 33:11).

The Lord swears this so that no one may despair beneath the weight of his crimes, because he does not desire the death of the wicked, but that he turn back from his way and live. The Predestinarians, however, perjure themselves when they say that, for those who are not saved, it is in no way the Lord’s will that they be saved.

Again, the Lord says in the Gospel: “I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7). And if the angels rejoice over one repentant person, will they not rejoice much more if all repent and believe—those holy angels who see in him the reason for their joy, namely the joy from him from whom they received everlasting joy?

Therefore, as Saint Coelestine commands, let the law of prayer establish for us the law of belief. Since the whole Catholic Church entreats God for all, let us believe that God wills all human beings to be saved, although not all are saved; and that the salvation of some is the gift of the one who saves, whereas the perdition of others is the merit of those who perish.

For the pious, devout, and Catholic, this ought to be sufficient: what the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, the mother of all churches, teaches. For as a mother she gave us birth for Christ, nourished us in religion, and instructed us in doctrine. Having received us from Christ, the firm rock, in holy Peter, she appointed teachers for us; having nourished us with Catholic milk and brought us to maturity, she formed us to teach others, saying through Paul that “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15).

Let the Predestinarians say whom they can exclude as not a sinner, except him who came without sin—neither another’s nor his own—to seek and save what had perished. Let them say who did not perish, since the same Apostle says that from one all came under condemnation (Rom. 5:16). If we all perished, he came to seek us all; if he came to seek us all, he willed us all to be saved.

It is likewise written: “Through the envy of the devil, death entered the world” (Wis. 2:24). And the apostle John says: “For this purpose the Son of God appeared, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8).

Hence Bede says:

“All sinners are born from the devil insofar as they are sinners. For this reason Christ came as a human being: to destroy human sins. Therefore, if he came for this reason, he came to save sinners; and because, according to the Apostle, all were sinners—for, as he said, through sin came death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Rom. 5:12)—he who came to seek what had perished came to seek all and willed all to be saved. Paul again says through him by whom Christ himself spoke: ‘Who wills all human beings to be saved’ (1 Tim. 2:4); and Peter: ‘He wills no one to perish, but all to turn to repentance’ (2 Pet. 3:9).”

[Col. 0215A] Why, then, are not all saved? Let the Truth itself answer through the evangelist John: “This is the judgment: that light has come into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light, for their works were evil” (John 3:19).

Hence Saint Augustine says (Tractate 12 on John):

“How did some do a good work so that they might come to the light, that is, to Christ, and how did some love darkness? If he found all sinners and heals all from sin, and if that serpent in which the Lord’s death was prefigured heals those who had been bitten—and the serpent was lifted up because of the serpent’s bites, that is, the Lord’s death because of mortal human beings whom he found unrighteous—how is this understood: ‘This is the judgment, that light has come into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light, for their works were evil’? What does this mean? Whose works were evil? Did you not come to justify the ungodly? But they loved darkness rather than light, he says. There he placed the force of the matter. For many loved their sins.

“He who confesses his sins and accuses his sins is already acting with God. God accuses your sins; if you also accuse them, you are joined to God. There are, as it were, two things: the human being and the sinner. When you hear ‘human being,’ God made that; when you hear ‘sinner,’ the human being himself made that. Destroy what you made, so that God may save what he made. You must hate in yourself your own work and love in yourself the work of God.

“But when what you have done begins to displease you, your good works begin there, because you accuse your evil works. The beginning of good works is confession of evil works. You practice truth and come to the light. What does ‘you practice truth’ mean? You do not flatter yourself, you do not indulge yourself, you do not cajole yourself, you do not say, ‘I am righteous,’ when you are unrighteous; thus you begin to practice truth.

“You come to the light so that your works may be revealed, because they have been done in God. For even this—that your sin displeased you—would not displease you unless God were shining upon you and his truth were being shown to you.”

But if one of the Predestinarians reads these words, he may perhaps say according to his own interpretation what certain people said at that time: “The one who opened the eyes of the man born blind—could he not have made it so that this man would not die?” And the Predestinarian replies: “Just as God gave light to the one whom he willed to be saved, so he would also have given light to this man, so that he might be saved, if he had willed him to be saved.”

For God is omnipotent, as the Catholic Church also confesses in the Creed: he has done everything whatsoever he willed.

Let the evangelist Mark answer: “He could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief” (Mark 6:5).

Hence Bede says in his fourth chapter on the Gospel of Luke: “He loved his fellow citizens; but they themselves, through their envy, deprived themselves of their countryman’s love.”

And when the man who said to him, “If you can do anything, help us and have mercy on us” (Mark 9:22), received the reply, “If you can believe, all things are possible to the one who believes.”

Saint Gregory likewise says in Homily 31:

“When Jesus saw this bent woman, he called her to himself,” and so forth. “He calls her,” Saint Gregory says, “but he does not raise her up; for by his grace we are enlightened, but because of the demands of our merits we cannot be helped.”

This concerns the Omnipotent, of whom Paul also says: “If we deny him, he will deny us; if we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself” (2 Tim. 2:12).

As Augustine demonstrates, this inability belongs especially to omnipotence. He remains faithful; he cannot deny himself.

Hence the same outstanding teacher says in his Sermon on the Creed to the Neophytes:

“The Omnipotent first made all things from nothing, together with the material from which he made them. Thus the material of heaven and earth, just as these were created in the beginning, was created together with them. There was nothing from which the things God made in the beginning could be made, and yet the things the Omnipotent made were made; having been made, he composed, filled, and adorned them.

“For if he made from nothing the things he made in the beginning, then from the things he made he is also able to make whatever he wills, because he is omnipotent. Let the wicked not therefore believe that God is not omnipotent because they do many things against his will. For even when they do what he does not will, he will do to them what he wills.

“In no way, therefore, do they alter or overcome the will of the Omnipotent: whether a person is justly condemned or mercifully freed, the will of the Omnipotent is fulfilled. The only thing the Omnipotent does not will, and therefore cannot do, is what he does not will.

“He therefore makes use of evil things, not according to their perverse will, but according to his own righteous will. For just as evil people misuse their good nature—that is, God’s good work—so he, being good, makes good use even of their evil works, lest the will of the Omnipotent be defeated in any respect.

“If he had no just and good purpose to accomplish through evil people, he would in no way allow them either to be born or to live. He did not make them evil, because he made them human beings; for he created not sins, which are contrary to nature, but nature itself. Yet, since he foreknew that they would become evil, he could not be ignorant of this. And just as he knew what evils they would do, so he also knew what good he would bring about through them.”

A little later he says:

“But since I have said that the Omnipotent cannot do what he does not will, lest anyone think that I rashly said that the Omnipotent cannot do something, blessed Paul also said this: ‘If we do not believe, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself.’ For justice cannot will to do what is unjust, nor wisdom will what is foolish, nor truth will what is false.

“Thus we are reminded that God the Omnipotent cannot do not only what the Apostle says—he cannot deny himself—but many things. Behold, I too say, and I dare to say it by his truth, what I cannot deny: God the Omnipotent cannot die, cannot change, cannot be deceived, cannot become wretched, cannot be conquered. Far be it from the Omnipotent to be able to do such things.

“Accordingly, the Truth not only shows that the Omnipotent is omnipotent because he cannot do these things; it also compels us to understand that one who could do them would not be omnipotent. For God is whatever he is by will. He is therefore eternal, unchangeable, truthful, blessed, and unconquerable by will. If he can be what he does not will, he is not omnipotent. But he is omnipotent; therefore he can do whatever he wills. Of him the Psalm also says: ‘In heaven and on earth he has done whatever he willed’ (Ps. 113:3).”

And likewise in his book On Nature and Grace (chapter 49):

“Far be it from us to say that God can sin. For he is not, as fools suppose, therefore not omnipotent because he cannot die and cannot deny himself.”

Similarly, because he remains just, of whom the apostle John says, “He is faithful and just” (1 John 1:9), he cannot be unjust by saving those who refuse to turn or return to him. For, as Gregory says, “He waits a long time for sinners to turn, but condemns them more severely when they do not turn.” Through the Prophet he says: “Am I a God who is near, and not a God who is far away?” (Jer. 23:23). And again through the same Prophet: “Sins separate between me and you.”

Hence John of Constantinople says in his book On the Restoration of the Fallen:

“If, then, sins are what separate us from God, let us remove this obstacle, and there is nothing to prevent us from being joined to God.”

The same author says in the same book:

“When the truth’s definition shows that the divine nature is impassible, we must understand that even if God punishes and inflicts penalties, he does not do so with passible anger, but with ineffable clemency, with the disposition of one who heals, not one who destroys. Therefore he receives the penitent very willingly.

“If the medicine of repentance, coming beforehand, heals the soul, it does not allow him to reach the punishment of anger for the things he committed against God. For, as we have said, God does not punish the sinner for his own sake, as though avenging an injury against himself. The divine nature receives nothing of this kind within itself; rather, he does everything for our benefit. For our benefit he brings correction and punishments, not to avenge himself but to amend us.

“But if someone persists in hardness, just as the one who turns his eyes away from the light does no harm to the light but condemns himself to darkness, so also the one who, through an impenitent heart, thinks he can despise God’s power makes himself alien to salvation.”

And it is written in the Gospel of Mark: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but is guilty of an eternal offense” (Mark 3:29).

Hence Bede says in his forty-first chapter on Luke:

“Whoever, therefore, clearly understands the works of God, yet, unable to deny their power, driven by envy slanders Christ and the Word of God and says that the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub—this person will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.

“This does not mean that we deny that, if he should wish to repent, he could be forgiven by him who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Rather, trusting in the Judge and giver of forgiveness, who says both that he will always receive repentance and that this blasphemy will never be forgiven, we believe that this blasphemer, because of the demands of his merits, will reach neither forgiveness nor even the worthy fruits of repentance.

“This accords with what the Evangelist John most truly wrote concerning some who were blinded because of the merit of their blasphemy: ‘Therefore they could not believe’ (John 12:39), because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn, and I heal them’ (Isa. 6:10).”

This must be greatly feared in the case of heretics, who mutilate the statements of holy Scripture and the clearest sayings of Catholics, violently bending them to their own interpretations and attempting to establish from them the wicked doctrines they disseminate against their own conscience.

Hence Bede again says in his twelfth chapter on Luke:

“Only blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—by which someone, in the likeness of the devil and his angels, does not hesitate to attack the majesty of the Godhead against his own conscience—has no forgiveness forever, but he will be guilty of an eternal offense, as the evangelist Mark clearly explains. After setting down this testimony of the Lord, he added and said, ‘Because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit”’ (Mark 3:30).”

Blessed Gelasius explains this prophetic statement, “Blind the heart of this people” (Isa. 6:10), and what follows, in his volume On the Anathema of Acacius, as anyone who reads it will be able to discover.

Bede likewise says in his twelfth chapter on Luke concerning those who perish inexcusably, although God wills all to be saved:

“Why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? He shows that they, as rational creatures, even if they do not know letters, can nevertheless discern by natural understanding either that the one who performed works in himself which no other could perform must be understood to be above humanity and therefore believed to be God, or that, after so many injustices in this age, the just judgment of the Creator will come.

“Therefore, on the basis of what was said above—namely, that the servant who did not know his master’s will would be beaten with few blows—let no one presume, while sinning, to claim the excuse of ignorance concerning the remedy. For, to say nothing else, simply because he is human, he cannot be ignorant either of the evils he ought to avoid or of the goods he ought to desire.”

Hence Paul also says in the Epistle to the Romans: “What can be known of God is manifest among them” (Rom. 1:19).

Ambrose accordingly says:

“The knowledge of God has been manifested through the structure of the world. Since God, invisible by nature, can also be known through visible things, he made a work which would manifest its maker by its own visibility, so that the unknown might be known through what is certain, and so that the one who made this work, which is accessible to all, might be believed to be God of all. For God manifested it to them. God manifested himself when he made the work through which he could be recognized. ‘His invisible attributes have been understood and seen through the things that have been made since the creation of the world’ (Rom. 1:20),” together with the following words, which the remarkable Paul and his expositor Ambrose develop in that passage.

Leo likewise demonstrates this when speaking of Eutyches in his Tome to Flavian (Letter 10, chapter 2):

“But if he could not hear a sound understanding of this from the purest source of the Christian faith, it was because, by his own blindness, he had darkened for himself the brightness of evident truth,” and so forth.

What has been said concerning a particular case must be understood generally. Thus Saint Gregory says in Book XVI of the Moralia (chapter 24):

“God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting” (Rom. 1:28). “Because they did not wish to glorify the one whom they knew, having been handed over to a reprobate mind, they were left to this end: that they no longer knew how to weigh the evils they were doing.”

And again in Book VIII (chapter 9):

“Now every sinner does not fear God and yet lives; he blasphemes and prospers. For the merciful Creator, whom by waiting he wishes to correct, does not wish to punish by looking upon him, as it is written: ‘You overlook the sins of human beings for the sake of repentance’” (Wis. 2:24).

And in Book XVI (chapter 18):

“Thus his soul did whatever it willed, so that even through that by which his will appeared to be resisted, he might fulfill his own will.”

For, as Augustine says in his book On the Gift of Perseverance:

“Nothing happens unless he either does it himself or permits it to happen.”

Hence Saint Gregory says in Book II of the Moralia (chapter 14):

“Because God, without change, sees all things together and comprehends them without succession—both the good things which he assists and the evil things which he judges, both those which, after assisting, he rewards and those which, after judging, he condemns—in these things, though he orders them differently, he himself is not different.”

And Jerome, in his letter to Philemon, against what Gottschalk and Prudentius say—“For those who are not saved, it is in no way God’s will that they be saved”—writes as follows:

“If, then, God is good voluntarily and not by necessity, when he made the human being in his own image and likeness he ought to have made him such that he too would be good voluntarily and not by necessity, just as God himself is good voluntarily and not by necessity.

“Those who assert that the human being ought to have been made so that he could not receive evil are saying this: he ought to have been made such that he would be good by necessity and not by will. But if he had been made such that he accomplished good not by will but by necessity, he would not be like God, who is good because he wills it, not because he is compelled.”

And Saint Prosper says in his Book of Sentences (chapter 168):

“No one does good unwillingly, even if what he does is good, because the spirit of fear is of no benefit where the spirit of charity is absent.”

Saint John Chrysostom, in his book to Demetrius On Compunction of Heart, likewise says:

“We can even furnish the heretics with pretexts if we say that the apostles and all the saints became admirable not through their own purpose and labor but through the grace of God alone. For they will say, ‘What prevents everyone from becoming such? If the grace of God requires nothing from us, but is itself what makes each person perfect, why is it not poured equally upon everyone, so that all suddenly become perfect? For God is not a respecter of persons.’

“But since the grace of God does not accomplish this by itself alone, it follows that we too must fulfill what lies within our purpose and strength. Therefore God’s grace indeed comes to each person, but it remains with those who worthily fulfill what lies within them; from those who act less worthily it soon departs; and to those who have not yet begun to turn to God it does not come at all. For it loves upright minds and an unfeigned purpose.

“This is also apparent in Paul. Although he seemed still to be traveling by another road, because he was acting with an upright purpose and zeal for God, the Lord says of him: ‘He is a vessel of election for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and all the people of Israel’ (Acts 9:15).”

And in his second homily on Psalm 50:

“God’s mercy is immeasurable and without end; it cannot be comprehended. It surpasses every understanding and exceeds every thought. Yet because the Lord’s mercy is such, God nevertheless seeks something from us, so that those who have obtained mercy may not become more negligent.

“He has mercy, but he does not have mercy indiscriminately. He summons us and says: ‘You too give something’—for example: ‘You have committed a thousand crimes; you bear a burden of sins. I wish to lighten your load. You too give me your hand—not because I need anything from you, but because I wish you also to contribute something to your salvation.’

“How, then, was the thief saved, and how did he pay for so many sins? Know that he was summoned by mercy and used his faith as an aid when he said: ‘Remember me, Lord, in your kingdom’ (Luke 23:42).

“What did God contribute to his salvation? The forgiveness of sins. What did the thief contribute? The indication of his salvation, the faith of his confession. What kind of confession? Great and exceedingly exalted, touching heaven.

“How so? I shall explain. The Jews saw the dead raised and the other miracles that had been recounted. The thief, he says, saw none of these things, but he looked upon one filled with spittle, crucified, given vinegar and gall. Although he saw all these things, he was not scandalized; rather, he confessed him to be the King of heaven.

“Do you see that he did not obtain mercy without reason, because he too brought faith toward his salvation?

“Likewise, how was the tax collector saved, who unjustly took what belonged to others? As Christ passed by, he said to him, ‘Come, follow me.’ Immediately he rose and followed him (Matt. 9:9). Just as the thief brought confession, so the tax collector brought his obedience, and he deserved to be placed among the apostles.

“For just as, when someone is afflicted with a severe illness and needs medicines of many kinds, and has been weakened by expenses, if a physician enters and says to the sick man, ‘Several ingredients will be needed to prepare the medicine,’ and the sick man replies, ‘I have no means to purchase so many ingredients; I am held down by poverty,’ the physician says to him, ‘Give me this ingredient and that one only; I shall provide the rest from my own supplies.’

“For this reason David asks to be washed greatly from his iniquity. What gift, then, did he bring for this? He said: ‘Have mercy on me,’ and, ‘Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin, for I know my iniquity’ (Ps. 50:4).

“There is an exchange: God gives, and the guilty person gives what can bring salvation. The Lord gave his mercy, and the one who had sinned gave the confession of his sins—little indeed, but what he possessed.

“What will you give, David, so that you may be saved and the medicine may be compounded? ‘For I know my iniquity,’ he says” (Ps. 50:4).

And again, in his work to Demetrius On Compunction of Heart:

“Therefore the cause of our perdition is nothing other than our own negligence and indolence.”

And in his homily On Spiritual Warfare:

“Know that the nature of the body will not conquer you, nor will it strangle you against your will, nor will it make you subject, from being free, except through a voluntary turning aside.”

And again in his homily On the Father and the Two Sons:

“In these events the freedom which God the Creator implanted in the rational soul is described and clearly displayed. Consider how this father neither restrains the one who wishes to depart nor removes the power of free choice. Nor does he compel the other, who wishes to remain, to leave, lest he appear to be the author of the evils that later came upon them through their own fault, if he had cut away from them the freedom of their own will.

“Thus he gives to the one who asks, because the cause of our poverty and offense proceeds from us, not from God. ‘The younger son, having received his portion, went abroad,’ it says, ‘and departed into a distant country’ (Luke 15:13).

“When it says ‘distant,’ it expresses not distance of place but a turning aside of the mind. For whoever has fallen into forgetfulness of God is truly said to be wandering from God. Conversely, worldly conduct makes a person not only a wanderer but alien to God.

“To put it briefly: just as those who wander from the world are presented before the Lord, so those who remain in earthly matters are exiled from heavenly things.

“Thus Cain also went out from the presence of the Lord and became distant—not because there was some place outside God’s sight, but because, divided in his mind, he had departed from the Lord’s regard and, through murder, had separated himself from God.”

And again in his book On the Instruction of Discipline:

“Sin is indeed less serious for the one who sins before he recognizes the Lord’s discipline. But there is no forgiveness for one who sins after recognizing the Lord, unless he returns in repentance; for God did not make death and does not desire the death of the dying, but rather that he return and live. Let him not be a wandering spirit and not return; the condemnation of such people is just.”

And in his second homily on Psalm 50:

“You have perished, but you can be saved; you have committed fornication, but you can become chaste; you have committed adultery, but you can be freed; you rushed to the spectacles, but you can withdraw your foot; you associated with evil people, but you can depart and be with the good. In either direction you possess free choice.”

And in the homily on Judas’s betrayal:

> “What, then? He who was able to change the ways of prostitutes could not retain a disciple? He was indeed, I say, and without hesitation, able to retain him; but he did not want to accomplish good by compulsion, nor did he take care to drag him to himself by force. ‘Then he went away,’ it says—not invited by the chief priests, constrained by no necessity, but proceeding of his own accord, and by his own malignity forming a plot of his wicked mind without summoning any accomplice.” [Col. 0221D]

And shortly afterward:

> “For those things which are shown to be insulting actually declare the Lord’s mercy and clemency: he who enlarged his betrayer, a criminal thief, with such great benefits, and endured him with his customary admonitions right up to the very time of the betrayal. For he admonished him, urged him, and took every possible care to heal him. But if he rejected the exhortation, if he despised the words of so great a teacher, Christ is the charge against him, and the prostitute is the witness, since she was concerned for her own liberation. Therefore, when you see the prostitute, do not despair of your own liberation; but when you consider Judas, you must not be secure either. Both confidence and despair are dangerous. Confidence casts down the one who is standing, while despair, after the fall, does not allow one to rise again. And therefore Paul exhorts us, saying: ‘Let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall’ (1 Cor. X, 11). You have an example of both persons. The disciple fell when he thought that he was standing; the prostitute rose when she thought that she had fallen.” [Col. 0222A]

And again in the same homily:

> “But neither did he openly proclaim him to everyone, lest he make him more shameless; nor did he pass him over entirely in silence, lest, thinking that he was concealed, he should hasten boldly to the betrayal. And therefore, by frequent admonition, he cries out: ‘One of you will betray me’ (Matt. XXVI, 21). Yet the most loving Teacher did not publicly identify him. He also spoke very frequently about Gehenna and continually treated of the kingdom of heaven. He often taught the merit of each: what has been appointed for sinners and what has been prepared for those who do not sin. But that cruel man despised all these things, and God did not drag him unwillingly. And because God placed good and evil within our power, he granted the freedom of choice: he does not retain the unwilling, but embraces those who are willing. For one who is not good by choice does not abandon his wickedness. And therefore Judas, driven headlong by the heat of excessive greed and deceived by a kind of blind heedlessness, sold his soul and became the merchant of his own salvation, saying: ‘What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?’ (Matt. XXVI, 15). [Col. 0222B–C]

> “And so that you may recognize Christ’s power even in this matter: when they had come to seize him, they could not endure his voice at all, but all of them, terrified, fell down. And since they nevertheless persisted in their shamelessness, he himself voluntarily gave himself up; he himself surrendered himself. We have said these things so that no one may accuse Christ, asking why he did not change Judas’s hostile purpose. But if someone should say this, he will hear the question: In what way could Judas have been corrected—willingly or unwillingly? If unwillingly, there is no correction, for the wickedness of the mind is not removed by compulsion. If willingly, it is clear that he had heard everything that could improve the soul. And if he rejected the remedy, the fault lies not with the physician but with the sick man.

> “And so that you may know that the crime of the betrayal was his, not the Teacher’s, God had often foretold the betrayal, instructed him by the command and discourse of the whole philosophy, and demonstrated it through deeds. He had given him power over demons, shown him the torments of Gehenna, promised him the kingdoms of heaven, foretold the secrets of his mind without making them public, washed his feet along with those of the others, made him a participant at the table, and omitted absolutely nothing. Yet he voluntarily persisted in wickedness and, rejecting all admonitions, emerged as a malicious betrayer. [Col. 0222D]

> “And so that you may recognize that he was able to change but did not want to be corrected: after he had betrayed him, he threw down the thirty pieces of silver and said: ‘I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.’ What is this? When miracles were being performed by him, you did not say, ‘I have sinned by betraying righteous blood,’ but rather, ‘What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?’ Only after the wicked deed, after the crime had been committed, after the betrayal had been completed, after the sin had been consummated, did you recognize the sin. [Col. 0223A]

> “From this, beloved brothers, we are taught that admonition cannot easily benefit the negligent and sluggish, whereas even when admonition ceases, it brings great advantage to the diligent. For this man was not moved when the Teacher admonished him; but when no one admonished him, his conscience was aroused, he recognized the crime he had committed, and he threw down the thirty pieces of silver.”

And likewise in the book *That No One Is Harmed Except by Himself*, after the labors of Paul have been enumerated:

> “‘Did Paul,’ he says, ‘not always remain the same Paul, and was he not the same man called an apostle? Judas, on the other hand, was one man, and he too was one of the Twelve, and he was called an apostle. But neither the fact that he was one of the Twelve nor the fact that he was called an apostle could benefit him in any way, since he did not possess a mind devoted to virtue. [Col. 0223B]

> “‘Paul, indeed, ran his course, which leads to heaven, amid poverty and blows. But that man, although he had first been called to the apostleship, had been endowed with grace like the others, had been taught the heavenly philosophy, had become a participant in Christ’s sacred table and venerable sacrament, and had even received the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that he raised the dead, healed lepers, and drove out demons—and although he had been taught contempt for worldly affairs, had clung to Christ’s side, and had been entrusted with the care and distribution for the needy, in order that the hidden vice of greed in him might thereby be healed—for he was a thief—nevertheless, even then he could not progress toward what was better, although so many and such great provisions were being employed for his sake.

> “‘For Christ knew that Judas was greedy and would perish for love of money; and not only did he fail to rebuke him for this vice, but he also wanted to heal him by hidden remedies, entrusting him with the administration of the money, so that, having in his hands what he desired, the destructive passion might cease once his desire had been satisfied—so that he would not fall into that pit of death, but might restrain greater evils by means of lesser ones. [Col. 0223C]

> “‘Thus, among all who have not harmed themselves, no one else can harm them; and again, whoever has refused to correct and amend himself, and to accomplish what lies within him and within his power, will receive no benefit from anyone outside himself.’”

Therefore Saint Augustine also says in the book *Hypomnesticon*, at the relevant passage:

> “To establish this, I think Judas alone is sufficient as an example. For although God had foreknown that he would be utterly wicked through the vices of his own will—that is, that he would misuse the discipleship graciously bestowed on him by Christ and, burning with greed, would betray the Lord to the Jews for a price—he predestined punishment for him according to his merit. The Holy Spirit says through David: ‘O God, do not be silent about my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man have been opened against me’ (Ps. CVIII, 1)—that is, the mouth of Judas, or of the Jews, against Christ. Judas says: ‘What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?’ (Matt. XXVI, 15); and after the promise of money, he gives the sign of the betrayal: ‘Whomever I kiss,’ he says, ‘that is he; seize him.’ Therefore he says, ‘it has been opened against me.’ For when he gave the sign, he opened with a deceitful mouth the identity of the one whom they were to seize. [Col. 0223D–0224A] The Jews also, wishing to destroy him by deceit, as the Gospel relates, cried out, saying: ‘Crucify, crucify!’”

Hence the aforesaid John also says in the mentioned book:

> “As that Judas, he says, fell away not only without anyone inwardly impelling him, but, on the contrary, although aided by many remedies, was unable to stand. Do you want me to teach this not only through individual deeds but also through peoples? How great was the care of divine providence for the people of the Jews! Were not, so to speak, all creatures prepared to serve their correction? Were not new and magnificent institutions of life handed down to them above all other human beings? And after everything, he says, divine gifts were bestowed on them. [Col. 0224B]

> “And yet, after all these manifest signs of divine power and after all the glory that had been given to them above all mortals, they became faithless and ungrateful. For they worshiped the head of a calf and sought to have other gods made for themselves, although some of God’s great and wonderful powers were still before their eyes, while others preserved in their hearts the fresh memory of what had recently been done.

> “But the people of the Ninevites, foreigners and barbarians, unaccustomed beforehand to any benefits of divine providence, enlightened by no laws, miracles, commandments, or works, saw a man shipwrecked in appearance and foreign in face, previously unknown to them, saying at his very first entrance: ‘In three days Nineveh will be overturned.’ By these words alone they were converted to the fear of God; immediately casting aside the evils of their former life, they turned to virtue and justice through repentance. [Col. 0224C]

> “You see that the one who is inwardly present and watchful, who remembers himself, can not only not be harmed by human beings but also repel the wrath threatening from heaven; whereas the one who betrays and harms himself, even if he is supported inwardly by a thousand divine benefits, will not find them sufficient for salvation. For neither did such great miracles bestowed upon the Jews benefit them, nor did the fact that the foreigners had obtained none of these things harm them; rather, because they gave themselves to God with a right purpose of mind, they made immense progress from a small opportunity.” [Col. 0224D]

Therefore, as Saint Gregory says in the thirteenth homily on the Gospel:

> “God is despised and waits; he sees himself scorned and calls back; he suffers injury from the contempt shown toward him, and yet at some time he even promises rewards to those who return.”

He also says, as Augustine states in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*: “They too believed because they wished to.” And Gregory likewise says:

> “Let no one neglect his long-suffering, for he exercises a stricter justice in judgment in proportion to the longer patience he has previously shown before judgment.”

For this reason Paul says:

> “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment” (Rom. II, 4).

And concerning them Augustine says in the aforesaid book: “Because they did not wish to believe, they did not believe.” And if perhaps they did believe, they belonged to the number of those about whom the Apostle also says: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I, 6). [Col. 0225A]

Finally, let us set forth the testimonies of orthodox and most highly approved men in the Church, and let the devout reader see whether they bear witness to us and to the chapter excerpted here from their understandings and words—that we are sons of the Catholic Church and faithful stewards of the word of God by his grace.

## CHAPTER XXV

### The words of the orthodox follow, by which it may be known how thereafter the catholic doctors of the holy Church thought

Dionysius also, whom the blessed Gregory calls the Areopagite, an ancient and venerable Father—who, as it is read, was enlightened by the grace of God through the Apostle Paul and baptized, and who, together with blessed Peter and James, the Lord’s brother, and many other most holy disciples of Christ, was present at Jerusalem near the tomb of the Prince of Life in a synod, as he himself relates in the book *On the Divine Names*, and both heard their discussions about the incarnation of the Son of God and formally stated his own position before them—says in his letter to Demophilus, concerning the statement that God wills all human beings to be saved:

> “Surely it belongs to Christ Jesus, the Son of God, in his paternal and suprarational goodness—the goodness which gives being to existing things and brought all things themselves into being—always to will all human beings to become like himself and to share in what belongs to him, according to the suitability of each one. [Col. 0225B]

> “But what is this? He eagerly joins himself even to those who flee, strives with them, does not disdain to be disdained by those who desire him, and tolerates those who reject him and accuse him without cause, while he himself makes excuses for them. Rather, he promises to heal them, and in these matters they themselves hold back. Yet he runs ahead to those who approach and meets them, embracing all of them entirely and kissing them; he does not accuse them concerning the past but loves what is present, celebrates a feast, and summons his friends—that is, the kindly angels—so that there may be a dwelling for all who rejoice.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Should not the benevolent one delight in the salvation of the lost and in the life of those who had been put to death, and without delay have the one turning back from error carried upon his shoulders, and stir up the kindly angels to the banquet? He is kind toward the ungrateful, and makes his sun rise upon the evil and the good, and gives his own soul for those who flee.” [Col. 0225C–D]

And again, at the passage, “Heaven was horrified at this”:

> “I too was horrified, because Demophilus supposes that God is not benevolent and humane toward all human beings, nor that they need one who shows mercy or saves, even though priests worthy by their ordination offer the people’s ignorance to benevolence, understanding well that they themselves are also subject to weakness.”

And shortly afterward:

> “He rebukes the disciples as well (Luke IX, 55), because they think it worthy, without mercy, to judge the Samaritans who were persecuting him. This has been read ten thousand times in our not reckless letter: ‘We do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses’ (Heb. IV, 15). He is also innocent and merciful; he will not break out or cry aloud; he himself is gentle and the propitiation for our sins. [Col. 0226A]

> “Therefore we will not accept your impetuous zeal, even if ten thousand times you bring forward Phinehas and Elijah, hearing from the disciples—who at that time shared in a gentle and benevolent spirit—the very things that did not please Jesus. Let Christ be benevolent in our minds; let him seek the one who has gone astray, call to the one who flees, and carry upon his shoulders the one whom he has scarcely found.

> “I do not implore this, nor should we devise evil counsel against ourselves or drive the sword against ourselves. For whoever begins to act wickedly, and whoever, on the contrary, begins to act well, associates with himself the angels whose will he carries out, either through wickedness or through benevolence. The latter, disciples and companions of the benevolent angels, both here and there attaining most blessed ends in the everlasting age, with every sacred gift and freedom from all evils, will always be with God, which is the greatest of all good things. The former, however, will fall away alike from divine and everlasting peace, and both here and after death will be with their familiar demons. [Col. 0226B]

> “Therefore should we not hasten greatly to become benevolent with the benevolent God, to be always with the Lord, and to separate ourselves from evil among those who justify us, enduring according to the worthiness that comes from ourselves?”

And in the second chapter of the book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> “Each of the hierarchs, by assimilation to God and because he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, proclaims true Gospels to everyone. ‘To as many as received him,’ he says, ‘he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name’ (John I, 12). Therefore, if anyone departs from the true light, or, by a voluntary choice of wicked desire, shuts himself off from the intellectual virtues naturally implanted in him so that they might be enlightened, he destroys himself.” [Col. 0226C]

Cyprian also, a marvelous teacher and glorious martyr, says in the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*:

> “For since the disciples are no longer called earthly by him but ‘the salt of the earth’ (Matt. XV, 13), and since the Apostle calls the first man one from the earth’s clay but the second one from heaven (1 Cor. XV, 47), we too, who ought to be like God the Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust, thus instructed by Christ, pray and ask that we make prayer for the salvation of all: so that, just as in heaven—that is, in us—God’s will has been accomplished through our faith, so that we might be from heaven, so also on earth—that is, in those who believe—God’s will may be done, so that those who are still earthly by their first birth may begin to be heavenly, born of water and Spirit.” [Col. 0226D–0227A]

And again:

> “Peter, ascending at the sixth hour to the upper roof (Acts IX, 10), was instructed by a sign and by the voice of God’s warning alike to admit everyone to the grace of salvation, although previously he had doubted concerning the cleansing of the Gentiles.”

And in his letter to Antonianus:

> “Certainly, he says, the Lord would not exhort people to repentance unless he promised pardon to those who repent. For since it is written: ‘The Lord did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living’ (Wis. I, 13), surely he who wishes no one to perish desires sinners to repent and through repentance return again to life.” [Col. 0227A]

Likewise, in his letter *Against the Jews*, he says:

> “The Lord rose on the third day, opened the New Testament, and said: ‘Come, foreign nations, my heirs, for Israel did not obey. Therefore go, disciples, even to the farthest earth, and preach throughout the world these words: Come from everywhere, nations of every land; enter into the eternal inheritance, for Israel was unwilling.

> “‘Let no one doubt: there is no exception here—neither of nobility, nor dignity, nor condition, nor position, nor appearance, nor age. Whether magnificent in dignity, noble, old, young, poor or rich, good or evil, masters or servants, enter without distinction and equally into the inheritance. Even if you are weak and captive, deformed in body, marked by an ugly blemish, defective in the head, or deprived of your eyes, everyone is freely permitted to recline at the banquet and feast at the Bridegroom’s wedding. Let no one be ashamed—neither of age, humility, health, nor condition. [Col. 0227B]

> “‘For the Lord is accustomed to support such people: he restored eyes to the blind, enabled the lame to walk, returned speech to the mute, cleansed the blemished, and raised the dead. And do not fear, you who have sinned; come first to life. Nor should the one who has committed murder be afraid because he committed it; nor should the one who stole another’s property despair because he stole it; nor should the tax collector fear because he extorted. For the forgiveness of sins has been established for all.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “The Lord addressed them gently with these words: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. For my yoke is gentle and my burden very light’ (Matt. XI, 28). And they replied: ‘We will not listen.’ But the Gentiles listened and believed the saving word.” [Col. 0227C]

And shortly afterward:

> “He whom you killed lives, impious Jerusalem, and yet the Lord did not deny all hope. For he granted the pardon of repentance, if in any way you are able to repent. Who is so good? Who is so devout? Who is so merciful? ‘Receive salvation,’ he says, ‘although you killed me; be an heir together with the virgin. Although you do not deserve it, I forgive you if you repent.’”

Blessed Hilary, the catholic teacher, who on account of his outstanding learning is called the “light-bearer of the Romans,” explaining the verse of Psalm CXVIII which says, “With my whole heart I have sought you; do not reject me from your commandments” (in *Beth*, Ps. CXVIII, 10), says:

> “It does not seem consistent with God’s goodness that he should reject anyone from his commandments; but the addition of the words and the force of the expressions, arranged according to the reasoning of perfect and heavenly doctrine, contain nothing doubtful and nothing contradictory. Therefore, if according to the prophet he prefers the repentance of sinners to death, should he be thought to reject anyone from his commandments? Far be such a thought. Nor did the prophet mean this here, especially since he sought God with his whole heart. [Col. 0227D–0228A]

> “But the resolution of the difficulties must be sought precisely in the things from which the difficulty appears to arise. For what the prophet meant is readily known. We read in Jeremiah: ‘Cursed is the one who performs the works of God negligently’ (Jer. XLVIII, 10). We also read in the Gospels: ‘To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away’ (Matt. XXV, 29). Therefore the one who has will abound. The prophet is not subject to the condition of the curse, because he performed God’s works not negligently, seeking him with his whole heart.

> “Then he confidently asks not to be rejected from God’s commandments, because he seeks him with his whole heart. According to the Gospels, more will be given to the one who has, while from the one who does not have even what he has will be taken away. God therefore takes away only from the one who does not have, just as he rejects only the negligent. Yet he is so full of goodness that he rewards the one who has with an abundance of gifts; and he so truly does not wish anyone to be without possession that, even from the one who does not have, he takes away the very thing that he has. He rejects no one except the one who resists, and casts out no one except the negligent. [Col. 0228B]

> “The prophet therefore stated this as the reason why he asked not to be rejected from God’s commandments: he had sought the Lord not partially or through sloth, but with his whole heart. From this we understand that the one who is rejected from the commandments is he who, through great negligence, has become unworthy of admission; and that what arises from the fault of the unworthy has nothing to do with the envy of the one who prohibits.”

And again the same writer, in the same psalm (in *Heth*, Ps. CXVIII, 64):

> “‘The earth is full of your mercy, O Lord.’ The earth, he says, is full of God’s mercy—the earth that has been polluted, corrupted, irreligious, faithless, and ruined. And if someone should perhaps dare, with an impious mouth, to accuse the prophet of falsehood, as though he thought that God’s mercy had not been spread throughout the whole earth, let him recall that God said in the Gospels: ‘Be good, like your Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust’ (Matt. V, 45). For God, patient and merciful, preferring the repentance of sinners to death, bestows his gifts upon the just and the unjust alike, granting each one, through the patience of his long forbearance, time for repentance.” [Col. 0228C]

And again the same writer (in *Lamed*, Ps. CXVIII, 89):

> “‘Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven.’ For the word of God remains as if in heaven in those in whom this word is not offended by anger, drunkenness, hatred, faithlessness, or wantonness. For even if it sometimes remains in us, it does not endure these insults of its dwelling so as to remain always within us. If, however, these vices just mentioned are always in us, it will not even deign to enter polluted dwellings of the body.

> “Yet it is near to everyone, as has been said. The word of God stands at the door and knocks at the door of our soul, saying: ‘Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens the door for me, I will enter in to him’ (Rev. III, 20). He therefore always wishes to enter, but we exclude him from entering. Through these bodily vices we close the entrance to our soul. If it begins to lie open after all things have been cleansed, he will enter like the sun, which is prevented from entering when the shutters of the windows are closed, but pours itself in completely when they are open. He himself is always ready to illuminate, but the house itself excludes the light by blocking its entrances. For the word of God is the Sun of Justice, standing beside each person so that it may enter, and it does not delay when it finds entrances.” [Col. 0228D–0229A]

And again he himself, in the same psalm (in *Samekh*, Ps. CXVIII, 115): “Depart from me, evildoers.”

> “It is our task,” he says, “to love both the evil and the good, and to teach the good toward goodness, according to the one who invites everyone to himself rather than away from himself, saying: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matt. XI, 28).”

And again: “You have despised all who depart from your justifications” (Ps. CXVIII, 118).

> “Here too,” he says, “the same principle has been preserved, so that it does not say, ‘You have despised all sinners,’ but, ‘You have despised all who depart.’ For if God despised sinners, he would despise everyone, since no one is without sin; but he despises those who depart from him, whom they call apostates. Nor does it matter whether someone was ever among God’s justifications. Whoever has departed must be despised by God, because the merit of remaining is preserved by the completion of perseverance. [Col. 0229B]

> “Departure differs from sin, because forgiveness is reserved for the sinner through repentance; but departure condemns itself along with repentance, and arises when the will of those who are going to depart is wicked.”

And again in the same psalm (in *Tau*, Ps. CXVIII, 174):

> “‘I have desired your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation.’ This man stretches his whole self toward the coming of Jesus, that is, of the Savior, so that through his Savior and eternal Shepherd he may testify that he has been received in heaven into eternal joys among the angels. For the Son of Man came to save what had perished, the Lord Jesus Christ, who was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and who is blessed forever. Amen.” [Col. 0229C]

Likewise the same writer, in his treatise on Psalm LI, says of the people of Israel:

> “He cursed Moses, abhorred God, vowed his sons as offerings to demons, killed the prophets, and even raised against the cross the very God and Lord who had been born a man for his sake, after betraying him to the governor; and thus, glorying in wickedness throughout the whole day of his life, although he was powerful, he nevertheless remained powerful in wickedness.” [Col. 0229C–D]

And in the same work:

> “The Lord condemns this disposition toward deliberate wickedness in the Gospel, saying: ‘This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than the light’ (John III, 19). Therefore the people for whose redemption from sins the Word became flesh and God was born man, so that through the justification of faith they might be free from the curse of the law, while preferring to serve the curse in transgression of the law, handed over that very God of theirs to punishment, taking his blood upon themselves so that the governor might be innocent; and in doing these things they reverse the customary order of nature. For they love wickedness more than benevolence and turn love away from good things toward the worst. They also preferred to love injustice rather than speak justice.”

Likewise in the same work:

> “‘I will raise up David’s fallen tabernacle’ (Amos IX, 11). That holy and venerable body of God, born from the Virgin, and the temple, namely, in which the one who has believed will dwell as a participant in the Lord’s flesh. Every unbeliever, however, will be torn away and driven out from this kinship with the body that was not believed—that is, from God’s tabernacle—unworthy of dwelling in this spiritual tabernacle. [Col. 0230A]

> “The Lord is understood to signify this when he says: ‘I am the true vine, and you are the branches. My Father is the farmer. Every branch in me that does not remain and bear fruit will be cut off. And every branch in me that remains, my Father will cleanse so that it may bear more fruit’ (John XV, 1).

> “Therefore, if some through faith in the embodied God are deemed worthy to remain in the nature of the body assumed by God, they are cleansed for the eternal fruits that they are to produce from themselves; for it is necessary that the branch, remaining within the vine, retain the nature of the true vine.

> “But whoever is born unbelieving in the body of God, or, even if he remains believing, lacks the fruits of his faith, will be cut off—either because of unbelief or because of the uselessness of denied fruits. The Son of God, born of the Virgin, was not first the Son of God when he became the Son of Man; rather, in the Son of God he was also the Son of Man, so that the Son of Man might also be the Son of God. He assumed in himself the nature of all flesh, through which, having become the true vine, he contains in himself the race of every branch. [Col. 0230B]

> “Therefore, if any branch is unbelieving or fruitless, it presents itself to be cut off: remaining by nature, it is torn away through unbelief or uselessness. From this tabernacle, then, as from the true vine, that wicked Doeg is both torn away and driven out—remaining by nature both in the tabernacle and in the vine, but, through unbelief, worthy to be torn away. Once torn from the tabernacle, he will be uprooted from the land of the living.

> “For the one who does not remain in Christ will not be an inhabitant of Christ’s kingdom. He will not be one—not because habitation was not open to him. It is open to everyone to become a participant in the body and kingdom of God, because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, assuming in himself the nature of the whole human race. But each person, according to his merit, presents himself to be torn from the tabernacle and uprooted from the land of the living. He was never prohibited from being within it, since through the assumption of nature he was received as an inhabitant; but he will be uprooted because, through the crime of unbelief, he proves unworthy of participation in that nature. [Col. 0230C]

> “He is therefore uprooted from the land of the living, which is prepared in the blessed region where the saints are gathered to the Lord. The Lord himself mentions it in the Gospel, saying: ‘Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth’ (Matt. V, 4). And the same prophet says: ‘I will please the Lord in the land of the living’ (Ps. CXIV, 9).”

And again:

> “For confession of sins exists only during the time of this age, while each person is permitted to follow his own will and possesses, through the freedom of life, the choice of confession. For when we depart from life, we depart at the same time from the right of the will. Then, according to the merit of the will previously exercised, the already established law receives the will of those departing from the body, either into rest or into punishment.

> “The Prophet shows that the will at that time is no longer free but necessary when he says: ‘For there will be no will for me in those days,’ for free wills cease, and even if there is any will, the effect of the will will cease. The rich man, wishing to pass over to Abraham, is not permitted because of the chasm between them, although through the freedom of his will he could have been in Abraham’s bosom.

> “The freedom of the will is therefore shut off, because there is no confession for the dead, according to what is written: ‘Who in the underworld will confess to you?’ (Ps. VI, 6).” [Col. 0230D–0231A]

Likewise, in Psalm LII:

> “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX, 13), because they are unwilling to believe what they cannot deny.

Likewise, in Psalm LVII:

> “‘Sinners have been estranged from the womb’ (Ps. LVII, 4). Thus Esau was estranged from the womb, when it was announced, even before he existed, that the elder would serve the younger—God knowing the future will, although the falsity of speech and the error of life arise from the womb, since he himself knew this rather than some necessity imposed upon one born with a nature of sin. [Col. 0231A]

> “And lest the vice be attributed to origin, he reproaches them for the crime of a will hardened toward obedience, saying: ‘Their fury is like the fury of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers, though they employ remedies administered by a wise man.’

> “No supposed natural necessity is excused in the crime. For the serpent could have been innocent, although its ears are stopped so as to be deaf and it does not hear the voice of the charmer, failing to perceive the remedies administered by the wise man. Nor does he here refer to the chants of the Marsi or to hissing that lulls vipers, since these are rendered numb with far greater force through faith in the name and power of God. [Col. 0231B]

> “Rather, he teaches the obstinate and insolent disobedience of the ancient serpent, which grows deaf to the songs of the saints and to the remedies prepared by the wise man. Although it is commanded daily, even under an invocation of the divine name, not to deceive, not to creep in secretly, and not to bite, nevertheless it rages with its hearing blocked. Hence those who do not obey the Gospel are born as ‘broods of vipers.’” [Col. 0231C]

In Psalm LXVIII:

> “This table of teaching, or this word of living food, is a snare, a capture, a recompense, and a stumbling block when it is shown by us that the God of Jacob is the one who was crucified by them. For this is the recompense for such great impiety: what is the power of God for us is a stumbling block for them.

> “For although they have been ensnared and captured by the Scriptures, they nevertheless lack the sense of understanding. And therefore their eyes have been darkened so that they may not see—that is, so that they may not behold the light of understanding—because, according to the Gospel, ‘to everyone who has, more will be given, but whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him’ (Matt. XXV, 29).

> “They were plainly unworthy to receive the sense and light of understanding, and therefore, having failed to obtain the knowledge of evangelical freedom, they remain perpetually weighed down by the burden of the law, so that they bear what they cannot endure.” [Col. 0231D]

Likewise, in Psalm CXXI:

> “That Israel, rescued by the Lord from Pharaoh, carried away through the sea, fed in the desert with the food of angels, instructed in the law, rebuked through the prophets, received by the Lord at his birth through sharing in his body, saved at the cross if it had believed, and glorified at the resurrection if it had confessed—believed none of these things to be its own and wished none of these things to remain its own.”

In Psalm 128:

> “According to the ruler of the power of this air, the spirit which now works in the sons of disobedience. These spiritual wickednesses therefore work in those who are disobedient to God’s law; they choose such people as laborers for their own will, intending to use them in their affairs through the service of another’s intervention.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Judas also, in the Lord’s Passion, was the devil’s instrument, and through him he carried out the purpose of his own will, as the Evangelist testifies.”

Again, in the same work:

> “The Lord is just, patient, namely, for the time of vengeance, postponing punishment until the time for repentance. He is not ready to punish at the beginning of human wickedness, but waits for sinners’ belated willingness to cease from their crimes. Then he will cut down their necks, when they are fashioned without any intention of ceasing, when sins are prolonged, when all the time for the mercy of the one who is patient has already been exhausted.”

In Psalm 132:

> “Therefore, since the gifts and blessings of God, with which he first blessed all things when they were created and made, afterward, because of Adam’s sin, stood under a curse, it is pleasing to God that they should return and descend again to the place of sanctification. For man was blessed, but after the blessing he sinned and immediately became impious. Yet he who prefers the sinner’s repentance to death wishes the dew of his blessing to descend from Hermon to Zion—that is, to pass from the seat of impiety into the place of sanctification. For by dew all things grow green, are nourished, and increase; so by that principal blessing of God man is begotten, breathes, and grows. It is therefore good and joyful that, descending from pagan error—that is, from the profane veneration of Hermon—he should pass to Zion, that is, to the house of eternal blessedness, and delight him who rejoices in the salvation of all.”

In Psalm 134:

> “For he would have preferred that his people, whom he had chosen in their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, should not be judged—the people for whose sake he had afflicted Egypt with various plagues, for whose sake he had stood in the pillar of fire and cloud, for whose sake he had divided the sea, brought water from the rock, sent manna from heaven, established the law, granted pardon for so many sacrileges, overthrown so many kingdoms of irreligious people, sent prophets, and wished his only-begotten Son to be born as a man. But the people, ungrateful for so many and such great benefits, the first chosen tenant of the vineyard, lifted parricidal hands against the lord of the vineyard himself, killing God, so far as depended on them, by putting him to death in human form. But servants were chosen, to whom the vineyard would be entrusted as they rendered its fruit, and through whom the Lord, having judged his people, would console the loss suffered by his mercy.”

In Psalm 137, “For you have magnified your holy name above all things” (Psalm 137:2):

> “Not only is the name of God’s only-begotten Son known; it has been magnified above all things, and the gentleness of holiness has extended itself to everyone. No barbarian, no Scythian, no slave, no free person, no woman, no man, no age is excluded. For the name of God has been magnified above all things.”

And likewise, in the first book *On the Faith* (Book I of *The Trinity*, at the beginning):

> “To be sons of God is not a necessity but a possibility, because, although God’s gift is offered to everyone, sonship is not conferred by the nature of those who beget, but the will receives its reward. And lest the fact that each person has from God the Son the possibility of being a son of God should in any way hinder the weakness of a trembling faith—for what is more earnestly hoped for is most difficult to believe because of its difficulty—the Word, God, became flesh, so that through the Word of God made flesh, flesh might advance toward the Word of God. And lest the Word made flesh should either be something other than God the Word or the flesh should not be flesh of our body, he dwelt among us: so that, while dwelling among us, he might remain nothing other than God, and, while he dwelt in us, God made flesh might be nothing other than the flesh of our flesh.” Through the condescension of the flesh he assumed, he was not deprived of his own, since, as the only-begotten Son from the Father, he is full of grace and truth; he is perfect in what is his own and true in what is ours.”

Again, in the second book (Book II of *The Trinity*, toward the middle):

> “For the sake of the human race, the Son of God was born from a Virgin and from the Holy Spirit, the Spirit himself ministering to him in this work. By his divine power overshadowing her, he sowed in himself the beginnings of a body and established the origins of flesh, so that, having become man from the Virgin, he might receive in himself the nature of flesh, and, through the fellowship of this union, the body of the whole human race might exist sanctified in him. Thus, just as all might be created in him through the fact that he willed himself to be corporeal, so he might again be brought into all through what is invisible in him.”

And shortly afterward:

> “He did not need to become man, through whom man was made; rather, we needed God to become flesh and dwell in us—that is, by assuming one flesh, to inhabit the members of all flesh.”

And again:

> “An angel announces to the shepherds that Christ the Lord, the salvation of all, has been born.”

And again:

> “The Lord was speaking with the Samaritan woman; for the redemption of all had come.”

And again:

> “The gift that is in Christ is one, open to everyone, and present everywhere. It is given to the extent that anyone wishes to receive it; it remains to the extent that anyone wishes to deserve it.”

In the third book (Book III, at the beginning):

> “Therefore, since the Son of God was concerned for the human race, he first became man so that he might be believed, so that he might be a witness to us of divine things from among our own people, and through the weakness of the flesh might proclaim God the Father to us, who are weak and carnal, accomplishing in him the will of God the Father, as he says: ‘I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me’ (John 6:38).”

Saint Athanasius of Alexandria likewise says this in his letter to Bishop Epictetus:

> “When the Savior truly became man, the salvation of the whole human being was accomplished. Not of the body alone, but truly the salvation of the whole human soul and body was accomplished in the Word himself. The Savior’s body was human by nature, from Mary, according to the divine Scriptures, and it was truly a body. It was truly so because it was like ours. For Mary was our sister, since we all come from Adam.”

Saint Ambrose, whose statements concerning the faith, the Church, and all the virtues are firmest pillars, and who by God’s grace enlightened Saint Augustine with faith, consecrated him in baptism, and instructed him in the teaching of piety, says the following in his book *On Paradise*:

> “Let them therefore learn that the command was neither superfluous nor unjust, even though it was given to a transgressor. For the Lord Jesus himself chose Judas, whom he knew to be a betrayer. If they think that he was chosen through ignorance, they detract from divine power. But they cannot maintain this, since Scripture says that Jesus knew who would betray him (John 13:11). Let them also understand for what reason the Son of God either gave a command to one who would transgress or chose a betrayer. The Lord Jesus had come to save all sinners; he ought also to demonstrate his will toward the ungodly. Therefore he ought not to pass over even the betrayer, so that all might recognize that, in choosing even his betrayer, he set forth a notable sign of the salvation of all.

> “Nor was Adam harmed because he received a command, nor Judas because he was chosen. For God imposed neither the necessity of transgression on the one nor of betrayal on the other, since either of them could have abstained from sin if he had kept what he had received. In the end, he knew that not all the Jews would believe, and yet he said: ‘I have not come except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel’ (Matthew 15:24). Therefore the fault is not in the one who gives the command, but the sin is in the one who transgresses. And what depended on God he displayed to all: that he wished to free everyone.

> “Yet I do not say that he was unaware that the transgression would occur—rather, I affirm that he knew it—but for that reason he ought not to have brought upon himself the hatred directed at the betrayer who was perishing, so that it might be attributed to him that both had fallen. Now both are rebuked and convicted: the one because he received a command not to fall, and the other because he was even called to the apostolic office, so that he might be recalled from his inclination to betrayal by God’s benefit, and so that the means by which the wicked are refuted might at the same time benefit everyone.”

And, explaining in Psalm 118 the verse, “You have dealt well with your servant, Lord, according to your word” (Psalm 118:69), he says:
