> “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart! Therefore he is good to all, because he wishes everyone to be upright in heart. But whoever turns his heart aside himself turns away from himself the grace of divine goodness. God is always good; therefore Paul says: ‘See, then, the goodness and severity of God’ (Romans 11:22). Goodness is toward all, severity toward a few. Finally, the same Apostle adds: ‘Severity indeed toward those who fell, but toward you goodness.’ For if they had not fallen, they too would certainly have enjoyed God’s goodness. He is good to you because you remain. But if you do not remain in goodness, you too will be cut off.

> “God will not therefore cease to be good because you have fallen and require severity, provided that, so that God’s severity may return to goodness, each person who has been chastened turns his foot back from sins and returns to the path of the virtues and to a good way of life. Finally, the Apostle teaches concerning those who fell that, if they do not remain in unbelief, they will be grafted in. For God is able to graft them in again, so that, like abandoned branches, human beings too, grafted as though into the stocks of virtue, may bear the fruits of good deeds.”

Again, where he explains, “Those who persecute me have drawn near to iniquity” (Psalm 118:150):

> “It penetrates the soul,” he says, “and, like the brightness of eternal light, illuminates it. Although it is spread widely among all, in all, and above all by its power, because the one born of the Virgin has arisen for everyone, both good and wicked, just as he commands his sun to rise upon the good and the wicked, nevertheless it cherishes the one who draws near to it.

> “For just as the person who shuts the windows of his house and chooses a dark place in which to live excludes the sun’s radiance from himself, so the person who turns away from the sun of righteousness cannot behold its splendor, because he walks in darkness and, amid the light of all, is himself the cause of his blindness. Open your windows, therefore, so that your whole house may shine with the radiance of the true sun. Open your eyes, so that you may see the sun of righteousness rising for you.

> “The Word of God is knocking at your door: ‘If anyone opens to me,’ he says, ‘I will enter’ (Revelation 3:20). If someone does not open, is the fault not rather that of the one who does not open than of the one who does not enter? Nothing is barred to God; nothing is closed to eternal light. But he disdains to open the doors of wickedness and does not wish to enter the rooms of iniquity. Or, when the vigor of our soul rejects the rotting portion of the body, so that corrupted limbs cannot feel its grace, does God likewise disdain to dwell in certain limbs of a corrupted soul?

> “Yet the vigor of the soul is diffused throughout the whole body: whether hand, foot, or finger, each shares in sensation. Can God’s wisdom be absent anywhere? Can his majesty be absent anywhere? Certainly, he does not hold back those who flee, nor compel the unwilling, but neither does he despise those who draw near. His power and his Word, God himself, are near to everyone. For all things subsist in him, and he is the head of the body, the Church, in whom all fullness dwells.

> “But sins separate many from him, concerning whom it is said: ‘Behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish.’ Hence the Psalmist says: ‘But for me, it is good to cling to God’ (Psalm 72:27). And the Apostle says that God is not far from each one of us: ‘In him,’ he says, ‘we live and move and exist’ (Acts 17:27). For, supplying vital grace to all, he is present to all by the gift of his goodness; but he is nearer to those who are contrite in heart.”

Again, where he explains, “Your mercies are many, Lord” (Psalm 118:156):

> “Even if salvation is far from sinners,” he says, “let no one despair, because the Lord’s mercies are many. Those who perish through their own sin are saved by the Lord’s mercy. ‘I will have mercy,’ he says, ‘on whom I have mercy’ (Exodus 33:19). He appeared openly to those who were not seeking him, called those who were fleeing, and gathered those who were ignorant.”

And again, where he explains, “Salvation is far from sinners” (Psalm 118:155):

> “For those whose judgment is late, salvation is far away,” he says. “But they themselves are the authors of their danger, because they did not draw near to the Lord. Therefore they became far away, because by their own will they separated themselves from the grace of salvation. Salvation does not flee from them; they flee from salvation, having distanced themselves.

> “He came to the Jews, but they did not receive salvation. How did they not receive it? Listen. Jesus is salvation; Jesus was called the Son of Man. The Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished. But the Jews asked that the robber be released to them and rejected Jesus.”

And again: “Do not cast me away from your commandments” (Psalm 113:10):

> “If God casts away each person whom he considers worthy of being cast away, let us see whether he thereby gives an excuse to the one who wishes to follow God but has been rejected. First, let us consider how God, who is good, rejects the one who follows him—unless that person deserves to be rejected—as the Lord himself says: ‘Foxes have dens’ (Matthew 8:20), and therefore, as though he were a fox, he rejects him.”

Again, where he explains, “Reveal my eyes” (Psalm 118:18):

> “The Gospel reading that has just been recited rightly gave this warning. In it, the leper who said, ‘If you are willing, you can cleanse me’ (Matthew 8:2), was healed, placing the exercise of power in the Lord’s will. He answered him in the same way: ‘I am willing; be cleansed.’ The piety of the will came first; the authority of power followed.

> “Jesus says to everyone, ‘I am willing,’ for he does not will that sin should exist. Christ’s willing is common to all; being cleansed belongs to the faith of the one who believes in Christ. ‘And he touched him.’ He touches those whose faith touches him. Finally, he says: ‘Someone touched me; I feel power going out from me.’”

And again: “Take away from me reproach and contempt” (Psalm 118:22):

> “They spoke against me,” he says. “I had come as their redeemer; I had come to cleanse the sins of all, to recover those who were lost, to restore to holy Jacob the inheritance of paradise, and they spoke against me.”

Again: “Forever, Lord, your word remains” (Psalm 118:89):

> “Enlarge your heart,” he says, “meet the Sun of eternal light, who enlightens every human being. That true light shines upon everyone; but if anyone closes his windows, he deprives himself of eternal light. Christ too is excluded if you close the door of your mind. Although he is able to enter, he does not wish to force his way in uninvited, nor does he wish to compel the unwilling.

> “Born of the Virgin, he came forth from the womb, illuminating the whole world, so that he might shine upon all human beings. Those who desire it receive the splendor of perpetual radiance, which no night interrupts.”

And again, when he was explaining, “My soul is always in your hands” (Psalm 118:109), he said:

> “For this reason the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head: although he was rich, he became poor. Nor did he seek the glory of this age, because he had come not to help the human race in part, but in its entirety, saying: ‘Are you angry with me because I made the whole human being well on the Sabbath?’ (John 7:23). This is what ‘whole’ means—not that he should enrich people by bestowing possessions, or heap upon them distinctions of honor, or increase worldly glory, for these things do not possess the fullness of blessedness and grace, but that he should embrace the whole length of eternal life.”

Again, in the same Psalm:

> “The devil sets his throne above the stars when he deceives the chosen, when he ensnares the righteous, whose works shine like stars in heaven.

> “Did not Judas the betrayer also hear, among the others: ‘You are the light of the world’ (Matthew 5:14)? Did the devil not extinguish his light? He even slanders those whom he has been unable to surround, begrudging them the glory of the heavenly kingdom, so that he may attempt to deprive those whom he could not separate from Christ by his enticements of the fruit of their deserved honor.

> “Behold, the hand of the Lord is ready to guard and protect you as you flee from your adversaries. Pharaoh held you in your ancestors—proud and ruthless. You fled from him; the hand of the Lord received you and freed you from dangers. Pharaoh would not have let you go unless you had fled for refuge to the Lord. Pharaoh said: ‘I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go’ (Exodus 5:2). You see how proud he was. Therefore the one who flees from evil is rightly received into what is good.

> “God does not permit us to remain in evil; he receives us into what is good. Nor does he permit his own to be subjected to slander. Why, then, are not all saved? He explains this in the same Psalm. Wisdom says: ‘The wicked seek me and will not find me.’ This is not because the Lord did not wish to be found by human beings—for he offered himself even to those who were not seeking him—but because he was sought through such deeds that they were unworthy to seek and find him.

> “Otherwise, Simon, who did not know him, found him; Andrew found him; Philip told Nathanael that he had found him.”

And again, in the book *On Joseph*:

> “But as concerns the moral interpretation, because the Lord our God wishes all to be saved, he also gave through Joseph consolation to those who are in servitude.”

Again, in the first book *On Repentance* (chapter 3):

> “‘God will not cast off forever, nor will God forget to show mercy’ (Psalm 76:8, 10), the prophet cries out, and there are some who introduce a kind of forgetfulness into divine mercy. But they say that they assert this so as not to appear to make God changeable if he forgives those with whom he has been angry. What then? Shall we reject the divine oracles and follow these people’s opinions? God must be judged not by the assertions of others but by his own words.”

And somewhat later (chapter 4):

> “You, Lord, desire to heal everyone, but not everyone wishes to be healed.”

And again, somewhat later (chapter 12):

> “Let the one who did not deny forgiveness even to those who did not keep his commandments teach you this, as you have in the body of the Psalm: ‘If they profane my ordinances’ (Psalm 88:32), and what follows. Therefore he promises mercy to everyone.”

Again, in the second book (chapter 4):

> “Therefore return to the Church, if any of you have wickedly separated yourselves from it. For he promises forgiveness to all who turn back, because it is written: ‘Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved’ (Romans 10:13).”

And again (chapter 5):

> “But if they do not turn back, then at least you return—you who have fallen through various lapses from the lofty height of innocence and faith. We have a good Lord, who wishes to grant forgiveness to everyone.”

And somewhat later (chapter 6):

> “The Lord himself wept over Jerusalem, so that, because she did not wish to weep herself, she might be brought to forgiveness through the Lord’s tears. He himself wishes us to weep so that we may escape, as it is written in the Gospel: ‘Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves’ (Luke 23:28).”

And again, in the same author’s sermon based on the Apostle’s statement:

> “‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’ (Galatians 2:6). Finally, the Apostle says: ‘Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you’ (Galatians 5:2)—not because he is unable to benefit you, but because he judges those who abandon his ways to be unworthy of his benefits.”

And again, in the sermon on the Gospel in which Jesus, passing by, saw a man blind from birth (John 9:1):

> “A woman accused of adultery had been brought before the Lord Jesus by the scribes and Pharisees. They had brought her through this stratagem so that, if he acquitted her, he would appear to annul the law, but, if he condemned her, he would seem to alter the purpose of his coming, since he had come to forgive the sins of all.”

And again, in the same sermon:

> “See, reader, the divine mysteries and the clemency of Christ. When the woman is accused, Christ bows his head; but he raises it when the accuser has disappeared. Thus he wishes no one to be condemned; he acquits everyone.”

Now, since the time and order have come to introduce Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, who, because of the sweetness of his salutary and flavorful eloquence, was most worthily called by the Greeks *Chrysostom*, that is, “Golden Mouth,” we have judged it fitting to use the words of Saint Augustine, by which he summoned John as a witness for his case against Julian.

> “Enter, Saint John,” he says, “enter and sit with your brothers, from whom no argument and no temptation has separated you. Your judgment too is needed.”

In his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews* he says:

> “‘To make atonement for our sins.’ Why did he not say ‘for the world,’ but ‘for the people’? For he bore the sins of all, but meanwhile the discussion concerned them. The angel also said to Joseph: ‘You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people’ (Matthew 1:12). This first had to happen, and for this reason he came: to save these people, and then through them the others, although the opposite occurred.

> “From the very beginning the Apostles also said this: ‘For you, raising up his Son, he sent him to bless you’ (Acts 3:26). And again: ‘The word of salvation has been sent to you; but because you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles’ (Acts 13:46). Here he displays the nobility of the Jewish people, saying that he makes atonement for the sins of the people.”

Again he said:

> “Who is he? He is the one who forgives the sins of all. He made this manifest in the paralytic when he said: ‘Your sins are forgiven you’ (Mark 5). And in baptism also. For he said to his disciples: ‘Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matthew 28:19).”

And again:

> “For the beatitudes spoken by Christ were not spoken only for monks; otherwise the whole world would perish, and we would accuse God of cruelty. But if the beatitudes were given only to monks, while it is impossible for a secular person to fulfill them, then he himself commanded marriage, and he himself destroyed everyone. For if people cannot fulfill the things belonging to monks while married, they have perished and are corrupted, and the things belonging to virtue have been confined within a narrow enclosure; how can those things be honorable that hinder us so greatly?

> “What, then, is impossible? It is entirely possible, even for those who have wives, to pursue virtue if we wish. How? By living as though we did not have them; by not rejoicing in the things we possess; by using the world as though we were not using it.

> “If some have been hindered by marriage, let them know that marriage was not their hindrance, but the will that makes bad use of marriage. For wine does not produce drunkenness either; the will and excess beyond moderation do. Use marriage with moderation, and you will be first in the kingdom and will enjoy all good things.”

And again:

> “‘Rejected and near to a curse’ (Hebrews 6:8). Oh, how much consolation this statement contains! He says ‘near to a curse,’ not ‘a curse.’ Whoever has not yet fallen under the curse but is near to it can also become far from it. He did not console us only in this respect, but also in what follows. He did not say: ‘Rejected and near to a curse, which will be burned.’ What then? ‘Whose end is for burning.’ That is, ‘if it remains until the end.’ Therefore, if we cut off and burn the thorns, we shall be able to enjoy a thousand good things, become approved, and share in blessing.”

And again:

> “Tell me, what is more difficult than carrying a pole on one’s forehead and bearing upon it a child who performs many thousands of figures there, delighting the spectators? What is more difficult than playing with swords as though they were balls? What is more difficult than walking on a stretched rope as though on level ground, and, while walking, putting on and taking off one’s clothes, as though sitting on a bed?

> “Does this not seem to us a wondrous and terrifying spectacle, so that we do not even wish to watch it, but fear and tremble at the sight itself? What is more arduous, tell me, than exploring the depths of the sea, or than the ten thousand other arts that one could name?

> “If virtue is easier than all these things, then, if we wish, we may even ascend to heaven. Here only willingness is required, and everything follows. You cannot say, ‘I cannot,’ nor can you accuse the Creator. For if he made us incapable and then gave commands, the accusation would fall upon him.

> “How, then,” he says, “are many unable?” Say instead: how are many unwilling? For if they wish, all will be able. For this reason Paul also says: ‘I wish all people to be as I myself am’ (1 Corinthians 7:7), because he knew that all could be as he was. He would certainly not have said this if it were impossible.

> “Do you wish to become so? Grasp only the beginning. Tell me: in all the arts, when we wish to become perfect in them, is it enough for us to wish, or do we also undertake the activities themselves? For example, someone wishes to become a pilot: he does not say only ‘I wish,’ and consider that sufficient, but also undertakes the activity itself. Someone wishes to become a merchant: he does not merely say ‘I wish,’ but undertakes the activity. Thus, in everything, wishing alone is not sufficient; action must also be added.

> “But someone who wishes to ascend to heaven says only, ‘I wish.’ How then,” he says, “did you say that wishing is sufficient?” It is wishing while undertaking the work, and accomplishing the task through labor. For we have God as our fellow worker and helper. Let us only take up the task, let us only approach the work as though to an undertaking, let us only take care, let us only place it in our minds, and everything will follow.

> “But if we sleep and hope, snoring, to enter heaven, when will we be able to grasp the heavenly inheritance? Let us desire these things, then, I beg you; let us desire them. Why do we conduct all our business for the present life, which we shall leave tomorrow? Let us therefore take up virtue, which will suffice for us forever, in which we shall always exist and enjoy eternal blessings.”

And again:

> “After he had previously spoken of those great and exceedingly pitiable things, he now speaks also of what is beautiful, arising from the concern he has for human beings. Although that universal reality contains everything, this is nevertheless much more universal: that all should believe, insofar as it depends on him.

> “For John also says: ‘There was life.’ But, again revealing his providence, he says that he is light. ‘Through him,’ he says, ‘making purification for our sins, he sits at the right hand of Majesty in the heights.’ In this passage he signifies two especially important things: that he cares for us, and that he has purified our sins by himself. In many places you will find him glorying especially in this—not only that we have turned to God, but also that this was accomplished through the Son.”

And again:

> “I do not think there is any weakness in the fact that he said the Father would be indignant over the things he endured undeservedly. Rather, this demonstrates the Father’s great love and honor toward the Son. For the one who is indignant on his behalf—how can he be judged to be a stranger to him? The same is also said in another Psalm: ‘He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them. Then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his wrath he will trouble them’ (Psalm 2:4).”

And again he himself said:

> “‘But bring here those who did not wish me to reign over them, and kill them in my presence.’ Because these words truly belong to him, listen to what he says elsewhere: ‘How often I wished to gather your children, and you did not wish it? Behold, your house will be left to you desolate’ (Luke 13:34). And again: ‘The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.’”

And again:

> “We are seen to be like God in this respect: if we love everyone and love even our enemies, not if we perform signs or miracles. For we do indeed admire God himself when he performs miracles, but we admire him even more when he shows mercy and patiently endures. If this is more worthy of admiration even in God, how much more in a human being?”

And again:

> “For if your fathers,” he says, “because they did not hope as they ought to have hoped, suffered these things, you will suffer much more. This word was spoken concerning them.

> “‘Today’ is always present, as long as the world endures. Therefore console one another each day, while it is called ‘today’; that is, build one another up, correct one another, lest similar things happen to you, lest any of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.

> “Do you observe that unbelief produces sin? For just as unbelief gives birth to an evil life, so also, when the soul has descended into the depths of evils, it becomes contemptuous. Once contemptuous, it does not even permit itself to believe so as to free itself from fear. For it says: ‘The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand’ (Psalm 93:7).”

And again:

> “Some, when they heard, became embittered, but not all who came out of Egypt through Moses. With whom was he angry for forty years? Was it not with the sinners whose bodies fell in the wilderness? To whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, if not to the unbelieving? And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief.”

And shortly afterward:

> “When he mentions those who were hardened, does he not mean the Jews?”

What he says is this:

> “They also heard,” he says, “just as we heard, but it did not benefit them at all. Therefore do not think that you are helped merely by hearing the preaching, because they too heard, but gained no benefit, since they did not believe.

> “Caleb and Jesus, however, because they did not agree with the unbelieving, escaped the punishment inflicted upon them. And observe how remarkably he expresses it. He did not say that they ‘did not agree,’ but that they ‘were not united with them’; that is, they dissented without rebellion, while all the others held one and the same opinion.”

And again:

> “‘On the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them,’ says the Lord (Jeremiah 31:32).”

> “Observe that the evils begin with us. ‘They themselves,’ he says, ‘did not remain first.’ The negligence comes from us.”

And likewise: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can be” (Rom. VIII, 7). “What then,” he says, “is this not a crime? Indeed, it is a very great crime. For a wicked man, so long as he is wicked, is not subject to it; yet he can be changed and become good. Let us therefore cast away carnal understandings. What, then, are carnal things? Whatever makes the body flourish and indulge itself, but corrupts the soul.”

Some, however, offer as an example the Apostle’s statement concerning Esau: “For he found no place for repentance, although he sought it earnestly with tears” (Hebr. XII, 17), wishing to show that God does not will all to be saved, even if they wish to be saved. Therefore this teacher says in the same work:

“What shall we say here? Does Paul exclude repentance? By no means. How, then, does he say that he did not find a place for repentance? For if he blamed himself, if he groaned with great lamentation, why did he not deserve to find a place for repentance? Because that was not repentance. Just as Cain’s sorrow did not arise from patience, as the killing of his brother revealed: so here too those words were not words of repentance. For here also he is convicted by the murder of his brother, since, so far as it depended on him, he himself too inflicted death upon his brother Jacob. For he said: ‘The days of the mourning for my father are approaching, and I will kill my brother’ (Gen. XXVII, 41).

“Thus tears alone were not sufficient to grant him repentance. Nor did he say simply that he sought through repentance, but that ‘with tears he sought a place of repentance and did not find it.’ What, then, shall we say except that he did not repent as was fitting? For this is repentance: that it be carried out appropriately. Otherwise, if the Apostle condemns repentance, how does he again admonish and exhort those who are, as it were, sluggish? How does he invite the lame, the relaxed, and the loosened—conditions that are the beginning of collapse—to rise up?

“It seems to me, however, that he is indicating that there were some adulterers among them whom he did not wish to accuse publicly. Instead, he pretends ignorance; but if they persist, then he finds it appropriate to rebuke them, lest, if you wish to accuse them beforehand, you make them shameless and insolent. Moses did the same in the case of Zimri and Cozbi.

“‘He found no place for repentance.’ This may also be understood in another way: he committed a sin greater than repentance. For there are sins that surpass repentance—as if he were saying: ‘Let us not fall into an incurable ruin.’ While someone is limping, he can easily be made straight or restored to health; but if he is utterly overthrown, what can follow? Accordingly, he says this to those who had not yet fallen, in order to overwhelm them with fear—as if he were saying that one who has fallen will no longer be able to deserve any consolation.

“Here, therefore, he admonished these people in one way, so that they would not fall; but elsewhere, when he speaks to those who had already fallen, so that they would not fall into despair, he says the opposite: ‘My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you’ (Gal. IV, 19). Elsewhere he said to them: ‘You who are being justified by the law have fallen away from grace’ (Gal. V, 4). There he himself testifies that they had fallen.

“Therefore, one who stands and hears that the fallen person cannot obtain pardon will stand more firmly and more cautiously. But if you use similar severity toward the one who has fallen, he is reduced to such a state that he can never rise again. What hope of conversion, or what fruits, can he receive? ‘He not only shed tears,’ he says, ‘but also sought earnestly.’ He appears indeed to exclude repentance; but he makes them more cautious and more attentive, lest they be carried headlong into ruin on every side.

“Therefore, let all who do not believe that Gehenna exists recall these things; and let all who think that sins remain unpunished consider why Esau was unable to obtain pardon: namely, because he did not repent as he ought.

“Do you wish to see complete repentance? Consider Peter, and how he repented after denying Christ. For when the evangelist relates his story to us, he says: ‘And going out, he wept bitterly’ (Matt. XXVI, 75). His great sin was forgiven because he practiced repentance as he ought. Judas too repented, but badly: for he hanged himself.

“Esau also repented, as I have already said; but rather, he did not repent. Those tears were not tears of repentance, but of a violent spirit and inward indignation, as his deeds make clear.

“The blessed David also repented: ‘Every night I wash my bed; I drench my couch with my tears’ (Ps. VI, 6–7). He mourned the sin that he had committed long before, after so many years and so many generations, as though it had been committed only recently. One who repents ought not to be indignant or exasperated, but rather to restrain himself, as one condemned, without confidence, and as one who desires to be saved by mercy.”

And likewise:

“For this is the cause of all good things, if spiritual grace perseveres in us. For it leads us back by the straight road to everything, just as, whenever we depart from it, we perish and are deprived of every good. Let us therefore not repel it. It is also within us whether it remains in us or departs from us. The former happens when we meditate on heavenly things; the latter, when we turn aside toward worldly things.”

Likewise, in the first homily on Psalm 50:

“I write for this reason, so that all may know both the wound and the remedies. I do not fear shame, because I desire my salvation. Paul does the same: he makes his sins public, saying: ‘I give thanks to him who strengthened me, Christ Jesus, because he considered me faithful, although previously I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; and now he made me faithful’ (I Tim. I, 12).

“For this reason,” he says, “I make myself public, so that if someone is a blasphemer, an abuser, and subject to many evils, he may not despair of salvation. Let him only turn away from evil and do good, and let him have hope of salvation, because the Lord says: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he turn and live’” [Col. 0243B].

Likewise, in the homily on the Canaanite woman:

“‘As he passed by, Jesus saw Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and said to him: Follow me’ (Matt. IX, 9). O power of the word! It entered like a hook of a kind, made a captive soldier, and fashioned gold out of clay. The hook came, and immediately he rose and followed him.

“He was in the depths of wickedness, yet he climbed to the summit of virtue, so that he might teach us that no one ought to despair of salvation, because wickedness is not natural. For God created us with free will, so that by our own will, with God’s help, we may do what we wish.

“If you are a tax collector, you can become an evangelist. If you are a blasphemer, you can become an apostle. If you are a robber, you can become an inhabitant of paradise. If you are a magician, you can come to worship. There is no wickedness that repentance cannot undo.

“And for this reason Christ chose people who were, as it were, the beginnings of wickedness, so that no one might despise himself to the end. Do not say to me: ‘I have perished,’ because you already have a physician who is much stronger than you and more powerful than your sickness. You have your own will as a physician: if you will, it is corrective, powerful, and willing.””

Likewise, in the homily on the Turtledove:

“‘The sun rises and the sun sets, and returns to its place.’ For the sun of righteousness, Christ, has risen for us, born according to the flesh from holy Mary; ‘Dawn’ is his name. He sets when, after the cross, he descended to the lower world. ‘The sun rises and the sun sets, and returns to its place,’ as he himself says: ‘When I am lifted up, I shall draw all people to myself’ (John XII, 32).

“Isaiah also proclaims concerning this sun of righteousness, saying: ‘In those days the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings’ (Mal. IV, 2). For when the sun of righteousness, Christ, came, the fountain of the issue of blood was dried up at the touch of the fringe of his garment.

“‘I am black but beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem.’ If any soul here has been blackened by sins, let it not fear; let it only do penance and say: ‘I am black, yet beautiful.’ And even if it is at its final breath, and, so to speak, placed at the last gasp, let it not be afraid; let it only repent with tears and confess with a contrite heart. ‘For weeping will remain for the evening, and joy for the morning.’

“Imitate King Hezekiah,” and what follows.

And in the book On the Restoration of the Fallen:

“Finally, consider either what is reported about God at the beginning of Jeremiah, or what is found among the other prophets. Even when he was despised and scorned by the people, he nevertheless returned to them again, and, bound by love for them, pursued even those who had turned away from him.

“This is what the Lord himself indicates in the Gospels when he says: ‘Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you: how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling?’ (Matt. XXIII, 37).

“Paul also says, writing to the Corinthians, that ‘God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore, we act as ambassadors for Christ; as though God were appealing through us, we entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God’ (II Cor. V, 19–20).

“Let us think that these words are also spoken to us. For it is not only unbelief but also a polluted way of life that creates these accursed hostilities between God and humanity. Thus the Apostle says: ‘The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God’ (Rom. VIII, 7). Come, then: let us destroy this wall of hostility and make for ourselves a way of reconciliation with God, so that we may again become pleasing and beloved by him.”

“But we, who are certain of the end and clearly know that, if we do not will it, we cannot suffer either shipwrecks of the soul or losses—how is it that we do not again take up our former exercises and repair the concerns that we negligently lost, but lie supine and idle, folding our inactive hands upon our breast—if only inactive, and not working our destruction! This is surely manifest madness.”

And likewise:

“For if God had made us for this purpose, to punish us, you would rightly despair and doubt your salvation. But if he made us solely through his goodness, so that we might enjoy his eternal goods and gifts, and if everything that he does from the beginning of the world until the present time he does for this purpose, and admonishes us for this purpose, that his mercy may save us, what ground remains for our despair or doubt?”

And a little later, showing how lovingly he receives the sinner’s conversion, he says:

“‘Who will give them such a heart that they may fear me and keep my commandments all the days of their life, so that it may be well with them and with their children forever?’

“Moses too, wishing to teach the people what God requires of everyone, says: ‘And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all his ways, and love him with all your heart and with all your soul?’ (Deut. X, 12).

“God desires to be loved by us, and does everything for this purpose. He does not even spare his only-begotten Son for our salvation and love. He desires, so to speak, that by whatever means and at whatever time we may be reconciled to him. How, then, will he not gladly receive and love as children those who repent and turn back to him?”

And so forth, which any reader will be able to find more fully and extensively in the statements of his cited works.

In his Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew he also says:

“‘Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you’ (Matt. XXIII, 37). The Lord, foreseeing all future events, also foresaw the ruin of that city and the blow that was to come upon that people from the Romans. Therefore, raising a lament, he mourned for it, saying: ‘Jerusalem, Jerusalem.’

“He remembered the blood of his saints that had been shed by them and that was afterward still to be shed. But he did not grieve only over the insult done to his saints, knowing what glory he had prepared for them in exchange for bodily death; he wept over their destruction, and over the worse things involved in it.

“For just as, when we do good, we do not benefit God but ourselves, while God rejoices not in his own gain but in our salvation, so, when we sin, we do not harm God but ourselves, while God is grieved not by an injury to himself but by our ruin.

“Just as a kind king, hearing of criminal persons, himself indeed pronounces the sentence of death against them according to the law; yet, stirred by mercy, sheds tears over them and wishes to help them but cannot, because justice contradicts him.

“For mercy is then true mercy if it is practiced in such a way that justice is not condemned by it. But if mercy is observed while justice is disregarded, that mercy is not mercy but folly. Likewise, justice is not true justice unless it contains mercy within itself. Justice without mercy is not justice but cruelty; and mercy without justice is not mercy but folly.

“So also the Lord himself pronounced the sentence of death upon the Jews, saying: ‘Behold, I send you prophets, and some of them you will kill, so that all righteous blood may come upon you’ (Matt. XXIII, 34); yet he himself mourned them with a pitiable lament, saying: ‘Jerusalem, Jerusalem.’

“For God is compelled, against his will and with great grief, to condemn sinners. He does not grieve because he himself is offended by them, but because he is, as it were, forcibly compelled to destroy someone, though he desires to save all.

“For how can it be contrary to nature for you to do good? But someone may say: Since God has the power to destroy and to save, who compels him against his will to condemn, if he does not wish to?

“You do, who do not desire God’s mercy. For just as the person who denies mercy to one who desires it is cruel, so the person who grants mercy to one who does not desire it is unjust.

“But you say: Who is there who does not desire the mercy of God?

“You are the one who persists in sins. To desire God’s mercy is to turn back to God. The one who fears his anger desires God’s mercy. The person who does not turn back to the God who made him does not desire God’s mercy but despises it.

“‘Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who until now have struggled against my mercy through your sins, but now you have overcome. For I wish to show mercy to you, but I have no strength left to exercise mercy, nor can I bear you any longer. Through your unceasing iniquities my mercy, as though already exhausted, has failed in its purpose.

“‘You who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you. I sent Isaiah to you, and you sawed him apart; I sent Jeremiah to you, and you stoned him; I sent Ezekiel, and you dragged him over a stone and smashed his skull. How can you be healed, when you allow no physician to come to you? How can you cure your sickness, when you trample every medicine?

“‘I did not spare my saints so that I might spare you, sinful woman. I disregarded their life so that I would not see your death. All the spiritual physicians have failed in your case, and you have not been cured: your incurable affliction has overcome divine skill.

“‘If I had rejoiced at your death, I would never have sent prophets to you. If I had wished to destroy you, I would never have come to you myself. What can I do for you, if you yourself do not wish to live? How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling?

“‘When Pharaoh pursued you in Egypt like a bloodthirsty hawk, I sent Moses and Aaron over you as two very soft wings of mercy. Having freed you from his claws, I snatched you away into the desert; and you were unwilling, making for yourselves a calf at Horeb, so that you might serve a dead idol rather than the living God. How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling?

“‘If you wish, run through the judgment: how often they sinned, and God handed them over, and again delivered them.’”

And Saint Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria:

“The witness to this matter is the one who says: ‘All have turned aside; together they have become worthless’ (Ps. XIII, 3). And the prophets, imploring Christ’s help, say: ‘Lord, bow the heavens and come down’ (Ps. CXLIII, 5)—not that he might change places, but that, for our salvation, he might assume flesh of human frailty.”

[Col. 0246C] And Saint Jerome, most skilled in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages, who is said to have deserved, by investigating the Holy Scriptures under the inspiration of the Lord, to penetrate their marrow and very inner parts as one breaking a nut beside its kernel, says this in his exposition of the prophet Ezekiel:

“‘Is the death of the impious my desire,’ says the Lord God, ‘and not rather that he should turn from his ways and live?’ (Ezek. XVIII, 23.) Therefore it is the Lord’s desire that all be saved and come to knowledge of the truth. Wherever God’s judgment appears severe and savage, it condemns not human beings but sins.”

And likewise above:

“The word is addressed to those who wish to practice repentance and erase their sins through righteousness, so that they may turn back with confidence and practice repentance wholeheartedly. Here, however, he speaks to those who, because of the greatness of their sins—or rather, of their impieties—despair of salvation.”

And shortly afterward:

“To them God replies that he does not desire the death of the impious, but that he should turn back and live. And so that we may know who the impious are to whom he speaks, the following statement demonstrates it: ‘Why will you die, house of Israel?’ (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

“Life and death in this passage do not signify the life by which we all live under the common law of nature with the beasts, or by which we are dissolved in death; rather, they signify the life of which it is written: ‘I shall please the Lord in the land of the living’ (Ps. CXIV, 9), and: ‘The soul that sins shall itself die’ (Ezek. XVIII, 20).

“From the particular admonition with which he was speaking to the house of Israel, he passes to a general discussion: the righteous person’s former righteousness does not save him if he has been seized by new crimes; and the sinner or impious person’s former sins do not destroy him if he has corrected his old errors through works of righteousness. In both cases God judges not the past but the present.

“‘If I say to the righteous,’ he says, ‘You shall surely live,’ and promise him the rewards of righteousness, but he, trusting in this, sins, all his former righteousness will be consigned to oblivion; he will die in his present iniquity. Nor has my judgment changed, since I cannot give to the sinful person in the same man what I promised to the righteous.

“‘Conversely, if I threaten a sinful and impious person and say: “In three more days Nineveh will be overthrown,” and he practices repentance, corrects his error through good works, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust, will he not have life, for whom Christ is life and not death? The threat against the sinner ought not to punish the righteous.’”

And in the prophet Hosea:

“‘When I wished to heal Israel’ (Hos. VII, 1): ‘I, who prefer the sinner’s repentance to his death, and who afterward say in the Gospel, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke V, 31), attempted to heal the wounds of my people. And while I was treating these things with every skill, so that the wretched people might be healed, suddenly Jeroboam arose from the tribe of Ephraim, making golden calves, and the wickedness of Samaria was revealed.

“The meaning is this: when I wished to erase the former sins of my people on account of their ancient idolatry, Ephraim and Samaria found new idols. But this may also be said: when the Lord Savior, after the shedding of his blood and the gathering of the Church from both Jews and Gentiles, wished to heal the sins of the people and lead them back to repentance, suddenly Ephraim—those who promise an abundance of false doctrines—and the people of Samaria, who claim to keep God’s commands, arose and fashioned an idol of false doctrines. Through them the thief and robber, the devil, entered the Church; or the doctrine of the heretics entered like a thief and a brigand.

“Concerning them the Savior also says in the Gospel: ‘All who came before me were thieves and robbers’ (John X, 8).”

Likewise:

“‘They have not returned to the Lord their God, and they have not sought him amid all these things’ (Hos. VII, 10). If they had returned to the Lord, they would certainly have heard the Lord speaking through Jeremiah: ‘Return to me, and I will return to you.’ Yet, after doing so many things, they did not seek the one whom they had lost through their own fault.”

Likewise:

“‘Ephraim has surrounded me with falsehood’ (Hos. XI, 12). Ephraim, the house of Israel, and Judah have surrounded God with falsehood and impiety. Yet God is so great in clemency that he does not cut off their hope of salvation, but forgives them and is ready to call holy people and the people of God those who are now perverted by impiety.

“According to the tropological sense, the Lord also wills heretics, ecclesiastical sinners, and all people to be saved and to be called by his name.”

And likewise:

“‘I shall heal their wounds’ (Hos. XIV, 5). This can be referred both to heretics and Jews, and to the Gentiles and every perverse doctrine, so that, when they practice repentance, they may obtain pardon.”

Likewise, in the prophecy of Amos:

“‘For three crimes of Gaza’ (Amos I, 6). This, then, is what he says: ‘I waited a long time for them to practice repentance, and therefore I did not wish to punish the sinners, so that at some point, having turned back, they might receive healing.’”

And likewise:

“‘The Lord God does nothing unless he has revealed it’ (Amos III, 7). Observe that the merciful and kind God always foretells what is future, lest he be compelled to inflict punishments. The one who foretells does not wish to punish sinners.”

And likewise:

“‘The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob’ (Amos VIII, 7), so that the one who practices repentance may ascend with the rising river, while the one who persists in sins may descend like the river of Egypt and, entering the sea, be swallowed up. By this he shows that the pride of Jacob, against which God swears, is to be devoured by eternal punishments.”

And likewise:

“‘If that nation turns from its evils, I too shall repent of the things I had planned to do to it’ (Jer. XVIII, 8). God therefore is not changed, for he is always immutable. Rather, when we change our conduct, he rages, becomes angry, threatens, and says that he will inflict punishments. If we practice repentance, he too will repent of his sentence.”

And likewise in the prophecy of Jonah (Jonah IV, 2):

“‘For the Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and of great mercy.’ Yet he does not abandon those who cling to vanities; he does not detest them, but waits for them to return. They, however, voluntarily abandon such great mercy, which offers itself freely.”

And likewise:

“‘Jonah was afflicted’ (Jonah IV, 1). Appropriately, then, the dove—this is what Jonah means—is afflicted with pain, and his soul is sorrowful unto death, because, so far as it depended on him, Christ endured many things so that the Jewish people would not perish.”

And likewise:

“He answered confidently and said: ‘I am right to be angry, or to grieve, even unto death.’ For I did not wish to save some in such a way that others would perish; I did not wish to gain strangers in such a way that I would lose my own. And truly, to the present day Christ mourns Jerusalem, and mourns even unto death—not his own death, but that of the Jews—so that they may die while denying, and rise again while confessing the Son of God.”

And in the prophet Micah:

“‘They divided before them’ (Mic. II, 13): because the angels—or the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—divided what appeared to obstruct the way and made a path for those who wished to enter.”

And likewise:

“‘I shall show you, O human being, what is good’ (Mic. VI, 8). Because you are in doubt, O people of Israel—or rather, the whole human race, for I am not speaking to the Jewish people but generally to every human being—about how you can appease God for your sins, if you do not possess sacrifices by which your impiety may be compensated, I shall answer you concerning what God seeks.”

And likewise, in the same author’s Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians:

“We human beings often wish to do things by deliberation, but the result by no means follows. No one, however, can resist God—he does everything that he wishes. He wishes what is full of reason and deliberation. He wishes all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

“But since no one is saved without his own will—for we possess free will—he wishes us to will the good, so that, when we have willed it, he himself may also wish to fulfill his plan in us.”

And likewise:

“‘Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God’ (Eph. IV, 30). The grief of the Holy Spirit is to be understood in the same way as the anger of God, his sleep, and the other passions expressed in human likeness. This does not mean that the Spirit is grieved or that the divinity experiences any disturbance; rather, from these words we learn God’s dispositions: that he grieves whenever we sin and mourns over sinners.

“For the Savior too, while present in the body, wept over Jerusalem, and in the prophet he laments the whole human race, saying: ‘Woe is me, for the devout person has perished from the earth, and there is no one upright among human beings. All lie in wait for blood’ (Mic. VII, 2).”

[Col. 0249B] And likewise, in the eleventh homily on the Gospel according to Luke:

“‘This was the first enrollment, when Quirinius was governor of Syria’ (Luke II, 2). O Evangelist, you appear to indicate that Christ too had to be enrolled in the census of the whole world, so that, being written together with all, he might sanctify all; and, being registered with the world in the census, he might grant the world a share in himself. After this enrollment, he might also enroll with himself those from the world in the book of the living, so that whoever had believed in him might afterward be written with his saints in heaven.”

And in the twelfth:

“For this reason the angel descended from heaven and said: ‘I announce to you great joy’ (Luke II, 10), and what follows. I think this should also be understood generally of all human beings. Two angels attend each person: one of righteousness and one of iniquity. If good things are in our heart, the angel of the Lord speaks to us. But if evil things have been active in our heart, the angel of the devil speaks to us. The same applies to each province.”

Likewise, in the thirteenth:

“When they had done everything”—namely, the angels—“that was within their power so that human beings might be healed, and those people were unwilling to receive healing, they saw the one who was able to heal being glorified.”

Likewise, in the fifteenth:

“Seeing that the little child whom he carried had come to release the bound, and that he himself was to be freed from the bonds of the body, Simeon knew that no one could release anyone from the prison-house of the body with hope of the future life except the one whom he held in his arms. Therefore he says to him: ‘Now you release your servant in peace’ (Luke II, 29).

“This should be understood not only of Simeon but of the whole human race. If anyone is released from the prison-house of those in bonds so that he may go to Christ, let him take Jesus in his hands, encircle him with his arms, and hold him wholly in his bosom; then, rejoicing, he will be able to go wherever he desires.”

And likewise, in the twenty-first:

“It must be said that at the baptism of Jesus heaven was opened, and that the heavens were opened and the Holy Spirit descended for the dispensation of the forgiveness of sins—not for the forgiveness of the one who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found, but for the whole world. And after the Lord ascended and led captivity captive on high, he granted us the Spirit who had come from him. He also gave it at the time of the resurrection, saying: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’”

Let these testimonies from Saint Jerome suffice. For if we were to set down all the testimonies that can be gathered from all the books of his that we possess, we would exceed not only what is sufficient but even the measure of sufficiency.

And Saint Cyril, to Nestorius (Epistle 2):

“Therefore, he who was begotten from the Father before all ages is also said to have been bodily born from a woman. This is not because his divine nature took its beginning from the Virgin, nor because he himself needed to be born a second time after that birth which he had from the Father. For it is foolish and senseless to say that he who is co-eternal with the Father before all ages needed a second birth in order to begin to exist.

“Rather, because for our sake and for our salvation he joined a human nature to himself and came forth from a woman, he is therefore said to have been born bodily.”

Saint Augustine, a man of exceptionally keen and learned intellect, repeatedly and in various ways expounded against the heretics these words of the Apostle, in which he says that God wills all human beings to be saved. He discussed the matter at length in the *Enchiridion*, and also in his books *Against Julian*, *On Rebuke and Grace*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. Accordingly, in more explicit and emphatic terms, in *On the Spirit and the Letter* (ch. 33), he says:

> “Again, it must be feared that unbelievers and ungodly people may seem, not without justification, to excuse themselves as though they were justified in not believing because God did not wish to give them this will. For the statement, ‘It is God who works in you both to will and to work for the good will’ (Phil. 2:13), refers already to grace, which faith obtains, so that there may be good works belonging to human beings—works which faith, acting through love, produces, and which love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.
>
> “But we believe in order to obtain this grace, and certainly we believe by the will. Concerning this will, the question will be asked: From where does it come to us? If it comes from nature, why does it not come to everyone, since the same God is the Creator of all? If it comes as a gift of God, why does this also not come to everyone, since he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth?
>
> “Let us therefore first state the following and see whether it satisfies this question: free choice, naturally bestowed by the Creator upon the rational soul, is that intermediate power which can either be directed toward the goal or inclined toward unbelief. And therefore it cannot be said that a person possesses this will by which he believes in God without having received it, since, when God calls, it arises from free choice, which he received naturally when he was created.
>
> “God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Yet he does not will this in such a way as to take away from them free choice, by the proper use of which—whether for good or for evil—they are most justly judged. When this happens, unbelievers act against God’s will when they do not believe his Gospel. Yet they do not thereby overcome that will; rather, they deprive themselves of a great and supreme good and involve themselves in punitive evils. They will learn in their punishments the power of the one whose mercy in his gifts they despised. [Col. 0251A]
>
> “Thus the will of God is always unconquered. It would, however, be conquered if he did not find what to do with those who despise him, or if they could in any way escape what he has determined concerning such people. For example, someone may say: ‘I want all these servants of mine to work in the vineyard and, after their labor, to rest and feast, so that whoever among them refuses this may grind continually in the mill.’ Anyone who despises his master’s will would appear to act against it; but he would overcome it only if, while also despising the mill, he escaped it—which cannot happen in any way under God’s power.
>
> “Hence it is written: ‘God has spoken once’ (Ps. 61:12), that is, unchangeably—although this may also be understood of a single word. Then, adding what he has spoken unchangeably, he says: ‘Two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy, for you repay each according to his works.’ He, therefore, will be guilty and condemned under the power of the one who despises his mercy by refusing to believe. But whoever believes in him, and does not despise him when he offers to absolve that person from all sins, heal all vices, and kindle and enlighten him with his warmth and light, will possess good works through his grace. Through them he will also be redeemed in body from the corruption of death, crowned, and satisfied with good things—not temporal but eternal—beyond what we ask or understand.
>
> “If this discussion is sufficient to resolve that question, let it suffice. But if the reply is that care must be taken lest anyone think that God should be credited with the sin committed through free choice—if, in the statement ‘What do you have that you did not receive?’ the will by which we believe is therefore also attributed to God’s gift because it arises from free choice, which we received when we were created—then let him attend and see that this will is not to be attributed to the divine gift only because it comes from free choice, which was naturally created with us, but also because God acts through the persuasions of things seen, so that we may will and believe.
>
> “He acts either outwardly, through evangelical exhortations—where the commandments of the Law also accomplish something, if they admonish a person of his weakness so that he may flee in faith to justifying grace—or inwardly, where no one has power over what comes into his mind, but consenting or dissenting belongs to his own will.
>
> “Therefore, when God acts with the rational soul so that it may believe in him—for it cannot believe just anything by free choice if there is no persuasion or calling to which it may believe—God himself certainly works in the human being even the will to believe, and in all things his mercy goes before us. To consent to God’s calling or dissent from it, as we have said, belongs to one’s own will.
>
> “This fact not only does not weaken the statement, ‘What do you have that you did not receive?’ but also confirms it. For the soul cannot receive and possess the gifts about which it hears this statement except by consenting. Thus, what it has and what it receives belong to God; but receiving and possessing belong, of course, to the one who receives and possesses.
>
> “Now, if someone presses us to investigate that profound question—why one person is persuaded in such a way that he is convinced, while another is not—two answers alone occur to me for the present: ‘O the depth of riches!’ and ‘Is there injustice with God?’ Let anyone who dislikes this answer seek out more learned authorities, but let him beware lest he find people who are presumptuous.”

And in Book V (ch. 3), *Against Julian*:

> “Have you forgotten what that same teacher says: ‘Perhaps God may grant them repentance for the knowledge of the truth, and they may recover from the snares of the devil’ (2 Tim. 2:25)? But his judgments are like a great abyss. Certainly, if we permitted those over whom we have authority to commit crimes before our eyes, we would be guilty along with them. Yet how innumerable are the things he permits to be done before his eyes (ch. 26)—things which, if he had not wished them, he would certainly not permit in any way? And yet he is just and good, and by showing patience he gives room for repentance, not wishing anyone to perish.” [Col. 0252B]

And in the book *On Instructing Beginners*, in which, however he may have expounded this statement against the heretics, he clearly shows how it should be handed on to those being instructed in the faith and retained by those already instructed, saying:

> “Truly, brother, that is the great and genuine blessedness which is promised to the saints in the age to come. All visible things pass away, and all the splendor, pleasures, and curiosities of this age will perish, dragging their lovers with them to destruction. From this destruction—that is, from eternal punishments—the merciful God wishes to free human beings, provided they are not enemies to themselves and do not resist the mercy of their Creator. Therefore he sent his only-begotten Son, that is, his Word, equal to himself, through whom he created all things. Remaining in his divinity, not departing from the Father, and not changed in any respect, he nevertheless assumed humanity and appeared to human beings in mortal flesh. He came to human beings so that, just as through one human being, the first who was made, namely Adam, death entered the human race because he consented to his wife, who had been deceived by the devil, so that they might transgress God’s commandment, so through one human being who is also God—the Son of God, Jesus Christ—all who believe in him might enter eternal life, with all former sins blotted out.” [Col. 0252C]

And in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance* (ch. 23):

> “Would that those who are slow of heart and weak, who cannot understand the Scriptures or their expositions, might so listen to—or not dare to engage in—our discussions on this question that they would look more attentively to their own prayers, which the Church has always had and will have from her beginning until this age is ended.
>
> “For concerning this matter, which we are now compelled to recall, and not merely recall but plainly uphold and defend against the new heretics (ch. 24), the Church has never been silent in her prayers, even though at some time she did not think it necessary to develop the matter in sermons when no adversary was pressing her.
>
> “For when has prayer not been offered in the Church for unbelievers and for her enemies, that they might believe? When has any believer had a friend, neighbor, or spouse who was an unbeliever and not asked the Lord to give that person an obedient mind in the Christian faith? Who has ever failed to pray for himself, that he might remain in the Lord? Or who, when he heard a priest invoking the Lord over unbelievers and saying, ‘Grant them, Lord, to hope in you to the end,’ has dared to criticize him—not only with his voice, but even in thought—instead of responding to such a blessing with a believing mouth and a confessing heart: ‘Amen’?” [Col. 0253A]

Behold how Saint Augustine agrees with and confirms what the holy Pope Coelestine had said: “The law of prayer should establish the law of belief.”

But why are not all saved, since God wills all to be saved? He himself says in *On the Predestination of the Saints* (ch. 6):

> “Many hear the word of truth, but some believe and others contradict it. These, then, wish to believe, while those do not wish to believe. Who is unaware of this? Who would deny it? But since in some the will is prepared by the Lord and in others it is not prepared, we must certainly distinguish what proceeds from his mercy and what from his judgment.
>
> “What Israel was seeking, the Apostle says, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it, while the rest were blinded, as it is written: ‘God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they might not see, and ears so that they might not hear, to this very day’ (Isa. 6; Rom. 11:8). And David says: ‘Let their table become a snare, and a retribution, and a stumbling block for them. Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and keep their back bent’ (Ps. 68:23).
>
> “Behold mercy and judgment: mercy in the election that obtained the righteousness of God, but judgment upon the rest who were hardened. And yet the former believed because they wished to believe, while the latter did not believe because they did not wish to believe. Thus mercy and judgment have taken place in the very wills.” [Col. 0253B]

And again:

> “It is therefore within the power of the wicked to sin. But that, by sinning, they should commit this or that evil is not within their power; it belongs to God, who divides the darkness and orders it, so that even what they do against God’s will is fulfilled only as God wills.”

And in *On the Gift of Perseverance* (ch. 6):

> “We ask that we not be led into temptation; and if we are heard, then certainly it does not happen, because God does not permit it to happen. For nothing happens unless he himself either does it or permits it to happen.”

And in the book *On the Predestination of Grace* (ch. 2):

> “Let us investigate, as far as we can with the Lord’s gift, the hidden depths of this question, which the blessed Apostle Paul presents to earnest investigators in various passages, not even always using identical words, and through them speaks to them by the truth itself.
>
> “Concluding the statement established in his broadest and strongest discussion of preceding grace, he says: ‘Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills’; while in another letter he himself says concerning divine benevolence: ‘He wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth’ (1 Tim. 2:4).
>
> “For the question arises why some of them perish, since the Almighty wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; and then why he again hardens some while showing mercy to others, or how he wills all human beings to be saved when he hardens some so that they may not be saved.
>
> “As far as human justice is concerned, this appears unjust. But who would be so foolish—or rather, who would blaspheme so greatly—as to say that God’s justice should be discussed according to the rule of human justice? If human justice is opposed to God’s justice, it is unjust. For it is evident that everything which is just in any way proceeds from him who is supremely just.
>
> “Who, then, would weigh the wisdom of God—which remains unchangeable and creates, governs, and preserves all things—by the judgment of human wisdom, of which the same Apostle says: ‘The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God’ (Rom. 8:7), and elsewhere: ‘The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God’ (1 Cor. 3:19)? The majesty of divine wisdom must not therefore be debated according to the judgment of human vanity.” [Col. 0254A]

And shortly afterward (ch. 3):

> “Therefore, whoever is troubled by this diversity in the administration of divine glory and considers it unjust that one person should be denied what another has received should understand how the Psalmist spoke divinely: ‘All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth’ (Ps. 24:10); and should recognize that God governs human affairs by such a judgment that he either justly inflicts punishments that are due or mercifully remits them.”

And somewhat further below:

> “‘Through one human being,’ he says, ‘sin entered the world, and through sin, death, and thus death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Rom. 5:12). Death could not enter unless sin entered; and since death is not a condition of nature but the punishment of sin, it necessarily follows that punishment follows sin.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Since all sinned in him—that is, in the first human being—as the Apostle says, and since the condemned mass from which we descend was already present at the beginning, let no one dare complain about his hardness, and let no one complain about the punishment which is due even without personal sins, solely by the condition of birth.
>
> “But when God, through a gratuitous calling, grants to some who are converted a mercy they did not deserve, this must be referred not to injustice on the part of the administrator but, in accordance with the truth, to the most merciful generosity of the giver.” [Col. 0254C]

And again shortly afterward (ch. 4):

> “Therefore, from the earlier part of this statement, where he says, ‘He has mercy on whom he wills’ (Rom. 9:18), I think that no one except one unworthy of mercy would dare to argue. But in what follows—‘he hardens whom he wills’—the attention of the human mind is briefly confused by the novelty of the expression.
>
> “It is not, however, to be understood as though God works in a human being the hardness of heart that was not already there. For what else is hardness than opposition to God’s commandments? Hence blessed Stephen said to the people: ‘You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit’ (Acts 7:51).
>
> “Let whoever thinks that this hardness is produced by God, because it is said, ‘he hardens whom he wills,’ look to the beginning of the transgression itself and consider, when God grants the commandment, how the guilt of transgression was worked in the heart. Yet even by the tempter he could not have been compelled if he had refused consent.
>
> “Therefore, whatever punishment a human being born after that transgression suffers, let him acknowledge that it is justly and deservedly inflicted. For God is said to harden the one whom he has not wished to soften (ch. 6); likewise, he is said to blind the one whom he has not wished to enlighten, and to repel the one whom he has not wished to call.” [Col. 0254D]

And after some intervening material:

> “But whoever, in pious inquiry, desires to discover something should reread that passage of the same Scripture where fire appeared to Moses in the bush and kindled his heart with the heat of divine love, so that, in the presence of kings, he would speak of God’s testimonies without shame, as David says. There he will find that everything Scripture first states about God hardening Pharaoh’s heart pertains not to God’s action but to his foreknowledge.
>
> “For, speaking from the bush, the Lord says: ‘I know that Pharaoh, king of Egypt, will not let you go except by a mighty hand’ (Exod. 3). ‘But I will stretch out my hand and strike the Egyptians with all the wonders that I shall perform, and afterward he will let you go.’
>
> “This is the first utterance of God, in which he indicated Pharaoh’s future will as he had foreseen it. Then, amid the very downpour of miracles, he is subsequently read to have said: ‘But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that he will not let the people go’ (Exod. 4:21).
>
> “Here it is plainly understood that he repeated the first statement. For what is ‘I will harden’ except ‘I will not soften’? It is apparent that the statement of Scripture was fulfilled: while justice flowed upon some and grace poured forth upon others, God said to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I have raised you up, to show my power in you and to proclaim my name throughout all the earth’ (Exod. 9:16).
>
> “Since God makes good use even of the wicked—through Pharaoh’s hardening, the plagues of Egypt, and the many great miracles completed together and in succession among that people—what else was accomplished except that God’s power, great in itself and complete in itself, might come to the knowledge of the human race, benefiting not God but those who would read and believe?
>
> “God foresaw, in that profound light of his providence, that Pharaoh would not be changed, nor that entire nation which, after so many blows, had scarcely allowed God’s people to escape and was still attempting to pursue them with arms and in war. But he willed the destruction of those who were destined to perish to become an argument for the salvation of the vessels of mercy whom he had predestined, and he used the perdition of some for the salvation of others.” [Col. 0255C]

And after much intervening material (ch. 13):

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Word of the Father, equal and coeternal with the Father, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Although he himself was not sin, having assumed flesh he was made sin, so that, by healing the human being from the sin of the flesh, he might condemn sin in the flesh.
>
> “He came to seek what had been lost, to heal what was sick, to raise up what was lying fallen, possessing the power to forgive sins, to grant what he was not obliged to grant, to pardon what was owed to him, and, having erased all the stains of the ancient guilt, to restore the nature that he had made.
>
> “From among those for whom just severity had decreed punishment, according to the ineffable mercy of his hidden arrangement, he chose vessels to make for honor. He freed some from the coming wrath through the gift of a gratuitous calling, while leaving others and reserving them for an equal judgment. Yet he took away from no one the capacity to recognize the truth.
>
> “Thus the fullness of divine foreknowledge was completed, with justice flowing upon some and grace pouring forth upon others, so that the Church, spread throughout the whole world, might be multiplied through those whom God had foreknown to be destined to perish and those whom, in his secret election, he had foreknown to be destined for salvation.” [Col. 0256A]

The same author, in Psalm 32:

> “The Lord says in the Gospel: ‘I do not judge anyone; the word that I have spoken to them will judge them on the last day’ (John 8:15). Let no one who refuses to hear excuse himself, as though nothing were required of him. That very thing is required of him, because he was unwilling to receive it when it was offered. It is one thing to be unable to receive, and another to be unwilling.”

And in Psalm 35:

> “‘The unjust person said within himself that he would sin; there is no fear of God before his eyes’ (Ps. 35:2). He does not speak of one person but of a race of unjust people, who oppose themselves by failing to understand how to live well—not because they cannot, but because they do not wish to.” [Col. 0256A]

Prosper also, a man of great learning and profound religious devotion, says the following in Book I of *On the Calling of All Nations* (ch. 2):

> “We believe and piously confess that the care of divine providence has never been absent from the whole human race. Although it directed the people it had specially chosen toward piety through particular institutions, it nevertheless deprived no human nation of the gifts of its goodness, so that they might be convicted of having received the prophetic utterances and legal commandments through the service and testimony of the elements.
>
> “Thus they became without excuse, because they made gods for themselves out of God’s gifts and worshiped as objects of veneration what had been created for their use.
>
> “Even that nation which the Lord separated from all other nations would have entirely fallen into this impiety, unless he had extended the purpose of his mercy to sustain the falls of the elect. For the pages of the Old Testament are full of accounts of Israel’s apostasy, so that it plainly appears always to have been the work of divine grace that not the entire people departed from the Lord.
>
> “Thus human nature, corrupted by the transgression of the first human being, is always more inclined toward an outward will even amid God’s benefits, commandments, and helps; and to entrust it to that will is nothing other than to abandon it.” [Col. 0256C]

And after some intervening material (ch. 3):

> “For what is surprising if some do not come to the sacraments of life, when many who seemed to have come depart? Of such people it is said: ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “Such people do not call upon the name of the Lord because they do not possess the Spirit of the adoption of sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ No one can say ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit; and whoever is led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. They reach God through God, and those who wish to be saved are altogether saved, because they conceive the very desire for salvation through God’s inspiration and, through the enlightenment of the one who calls, come to the knowledge of the truth.” [Col. 0256D]

And again after some intervening material (ch. 4):

> “When those who love contentious disputes read or hear these things, they will say that by such discussions we contradict the Apostle, who declares that Almighty God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
>
> “We receive this portion of the Apostle’s words so completely and fully that we subtract nothing from what precedes or follows and pertains to it. For, setting aside the other testimonies of the divine utterances, this passage alone is sufficient both to nullify what they object to calumniously and to defend what they impiously deny.
>
> “Thus, writing to Timothy, Paul the Apostle, the teacher of the nations, says: ‘Therefore, first of all, I urge that entreaties, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all human beings, for kings, and for all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity’ (1 Tim. 2:1).
>
> “‘For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for all.’
>
> “Concerning this rule of apostolic teaching, by which the universal Church is instructed, let us not wander into a divergent interpretation according to our own judgment; let us ask what the universal Church herself believes. For there can be no doubt about the commandment when obedience is united in its observance.
>
> “The Apostle therefore commanded—or rather, through the Apostle, the Lord who was speaking in the Apostle commanded—that entreaties, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all human beings, for kings, and for those who are in positions of authority.
>
> “The devotion of all priests and all the faithful observes this law of supplication so harmoniously that there is no part of the world in which Christian peoples do not offer such prayers.
>
> “Everywhere, therefore, the Church supplicates God not only for the saints and those already reborn in Christ, but also for all unbelievers and enemies of the cross of Christ, for all worshipers of idols, for all who persecute Christ in his members, for the Jews, upon whose blindness the light of the Gospel does not shine, and for heretics and schismatics, who are alienated from the unity of faith and charity.
>
> “But what does she ask for these people except that, abandoning their errors, they may turn to God, receive faith, receive the truth, and, freed from the darkness of ignorance, come to the knowledge of the truth?
>
> “Because they cannot accomplish this for themselves, weighed down by the burden of evil habit and bound by the chains of the devil, nor can they overcome the deceptions to which they have clung so stubbornly—loving falsehood as much as truth ought to be loved—the merciful and just Lord wills that supplication be made to him for all these people.
>
> “Thus, when we see countless people rescued from such profound evils, let us not doubt that God has granted what he was asked to grant. Giving thanks for those who have been saved, let us also hope that those who have not yet been enlightened will, through the same work of divine grace, be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God before they depart this life.
>
