> “But if, as we see happen, saving grace passes some people by and the Church’s prayer is not accepted on their behalf, this must be referred to the hidden judgments of divine justice, and we must recognize that the depth of this secret cannot be opened to us in this life.
>
> “For we know in part and prophesy in part, and now we see through a mirror, in an enigma. Nor are we wiser or more knowledgeable than the blessed Apostle, who, when he was discussing the power of grace and had entered into the secret of great mysteries, faltered before recounting what could not be explained.” [Col. 0257D]

And after a short interval (ch. 5):

> “The assertion of the teacher set forth above gave rise to a many-sided question: among so many peoples and ages, the cause of grace was sought, namely, why in earlier ages all the nations were allowed to go their own ways, with only Israel, instructed by the divine utterances and chosen for knowledge of the truth, excepted.
>
> “Did Israel’s unbelief finally make room for the salvation of the nations, as though, if one people remained in the faith of its own race, God’s mercy could not extend itself to the other nations?
>
> “Why, finally, are those whose diminution is the salvation of the nations not freed from their blindness before the fullness of the nations enters—as though those who are to be saved when the total number of the nations has been gathered could not be enlightened together with all the others?
>
> “Or how will all Israel be saved once its blindness has been removed, when an innumerable multitude of it, falling away in its unbelief, does not reach the times promised for salvation?
>
> “Or how is the fullness of the nations—whose calling did not previously occur—now said to enter, when so many thousands of people of every age and condition, among all the nations beneath heaven, die without Christ’s justification?
>
> “But the pious and learned teacher preferred to suspend the causes of these mysteries and judgments upon the depth of God’s riches, wisdom, and knowledge, rather than rashly investigate the secret withheld from human understanding by the most just truth and the most merciful goodness.
>
> “He omitted nothing that ought not to be unknown, and he touched upon nothing that may not be known. For many things in the administration of divine works have causes that remain hidden while their effects alone are shown, so that what is done is evident although why it is done is not.
>
> “The matter is brought into the open while its rationale is withdrawn into secrecy, so that, concerning the same matter, presumptuousness about what cannot be searched out may be restrained and falsehood concerning what is manifest may be refuted.” [Col. 0258C]

And after much intervening material (ch. 7):

> “But if it is asked why the Savior of all human beings has not given all people the understanding by which they might know the true God and be—that is, remain—in his true Son, although we believe that the help of grace has not been entirely withdrawn from any human beings, concerning which we shall discuss more fully in what follows, perhaps this too has been veiled in the same way as that hidden matter: why, when all the nations were passed over, he chose for himself one people to instruct in the knowledge of the truth.
>
> “If there is no complaint to be made about that judgment of God, still less should there be murmuring about what is done through the election of all the nations. What God has willed to be hidden must not be investigated; what he has made manifest must not be neglected.” [Col. 0258D]

And in Book II (chapter 1): “Although the Gospel was directed toward the calling of all human beings, and although the Lord wished all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, he had not thereby deprived himself of authority over his dispensations, so that the course of his plan might proceed otherwise than he had determined by a hidden and just judgment. Hence there is no place for the complaints and murmurs of the obstinate, since it is evident that what God willed to happen could not have happened otherwise than he willed.” [Col. 0259A]

And shortly afterward: “But not even in past ages was the world deprived of this same grace, which after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ was spread everywhere, and of which it is written: ‘Your flashes illumined the world’ (Psalm 76:19).” And a little later: “Yet the eternal goodness of the Creator did not turn itself away from those people in such a way that it failed to admonish them by any signs whatsoever to know and fear him.” And a little later: “Therefore, as the Prophet says, ‘The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord’ (Psalm 32:5); this mercy was never absent in any age or generation. He has always bestowed that providence by which he governs and sustains the whole universe, continually bestowing it upon created natures, to govern and nourish them, having determined from the eternity of his unchangeable plan at what times he would distribute each thing and by what gifts and sacraments he would vary the inscrutable and unsearchable measures of his manifold grace.” [Col. 0259B]

And again, after some intervening material (chapter 3): “For many authorities of the divine utterances have made this clear, and the continuous experience of all ages has taught that God’s justice is merciful and his mercy just, and that he has never failed either to nourish human bodies or to teach, assist, and enlighten human minds. For he has always rained upon the good and the evil, and has always caused his sun to rise upon the just and the unjust.” And, recalling at length very many gifts of divine mercy, he continues extensively.

And after some intervening material (chapter 7): “Although what is devoutly believed concerning God’s goodness—that he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth—ought to be understood as perpetual and eternal, according to those measures by which God knows how to heap general gifts upon particular benefits, so that those who have been deprived of grace may be convicted of their wickedness, while those who have shone in his light may glory not in their own merit but in the Lord.” [Col. 0259C]

And after some intervening material (chapter 8): “Therefore, whether we contemplate the final ages or the intervening ones, it is reasonably and piously believed that God always has willed, and always wills, all human beings to be saved. This is demonstrated from nothing other than those benefits that God’s providence bestows commonly and impartially upon every generation. These general gifts have been and are of such a kind that, by their testimony, human beings could be helped to seek the true God; and while these gifts proclaim their author throughout all ages, the abundance of special grace has been poured over them. Although this grace is now bestowed more abundantly than before, the Lord has nevertheless kept the reasons for its distributions within his own knowledge and concealed them in the secrecy of his most powerful will. If these gifts flowed equally to everyone, they would not be hidden; and just as there would be no ambiguity concerning general benevolence, so there would be nothing extraordinary concerning special mercy. Consequently, the latter would be grace, but the former would not. Yet it pleased God both to bestow this grace upon many and to withhold that general gift from no one, so that from both it might be evident that what was bestowed upon a portion was not denied to the whole: rather, that grace prevailed in some, while nature recoiled in others. For we believe and desire this more abundant grace to be so powerful that we in no way consider it violence when everything that is done in the salvation of human beings is accomplished solely by God’s will, since even infants are assisted through the service of another’s will.” [Col. 0259D]

And again (chapter 9): “Therefore, just as those who have believed are assisted so that they may remain in faith, so those who have not yet believed are assisted so that they may believe. And just as those have it in their own power not to come [the reference is unclear], it becomes evident that God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth in diverse and innumerable ways: those who come are directed by God’s help, while those who do not come resist through their own obstinacy.” [Col. 0260A]

And against the Gauls (thesis 8): “Likewise, the person who says that God does not wish all human beings to be saved, but only a fixed number of the predestined, speaks more harshly than one ought to speak about the depth of God’s inscrutable grace. For he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and he fulfills the purpose of his will in those whom he foreknew and predestined, predestined and called, called and justified, justified and glorified.” [Col. 0260B]

And shortly afterward: “As for what God has promised, he is able also to accomplish it: those who are saved are saved because God willed them to be saved, while those who perish perish because they deserved to perish.” [Col. 0260C]

Hence, in Book II (chapter 10), *On the Calling of the Nations*: “There must be no murmuring, since the just and good arbiter is neither unjust in will nor uncertain in discrimination, so that under his immeasurable mercy and justice we should suppose that anyone perishes who ought not to perish.”

And concerning the objection of the Vincentians (objection 2), that God does not wish to save all, even if all wish to be saved: “Since the Truth says, ‘If you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?’ (Matthew 7:11), how can it be that God, who even saves those of whom it cannot be said that they wish to be saved, should not wish to save some who do wish to be saved—unless there exist certain causes which, although they are unknown to us, he nevertheless judges them well—and it cannot otherwise be said of him that he ought to have done anything other than what he did? Once this discrimination, which divine knowledge holds within the secrecy of its justice, has been set aside, we must most sincerely believe and confess that God wills all human beings to be saved. [Col. 0260D] For the Apostle, whose statement this is, most earnestly commands—and this is piously observed in all the churches—that supplication be made to God for all human beings. Of the many who perish, their own merit is the cause; of the many who are saved, the gift belongs to the one who saves. That the guilty person is condemned is the unimpeachable justice of God; that the guilty person is justified is the ineffable grace of God.”

And Saint Coelestine, establishing for us by the law of supplication the law of belief expressed in the promulgated sentence—namely, that because the Catholic Church prays for all, we should believe that God wills all human beings to be saved—confirms this in his conclusion, saying (after Letter 8): “So great is God’s goodness toward all human beings that he wishes our merits to be his gifts, and for the things he has bestowed he will bestow eternal rewards.” [Col. 0261A]

Saint Leo also, a most devout and learned man, exceedingly rich in the eloquence of honorable expression—since this heresy had arisen shortly before the time of his ordination—it is most carefully necessary to observe how great and what sort of arguments he brings against it. For he says in his letter to Leo Augustus: “Just as it could not be denied, when the Evangelist says that ‘the Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14), so it cannot be denied, when the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims, that ‘God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself’ (2 Corinthians 5:19). What reconciliation could there have been by which God might be made propitious to the human race, unless the mediator of God and human beings assumed flesh for the sake of all?” [Col. 0261B]

And again: “In order to restore the life of all, he undertook the cause of all and, by paying on behalf of all the force of the former bond, which he alone among all did not owe, cancelled it, so that just as through the guilt of one all had been made sinners, so through the innocence of one all might become innocent, with righteousness flowing from there into all, wherever human nature had been assumed.”

And in his letter to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople (Letter 10, chapter 2): “The same eternal Only-Begotten of the everlasting Father, himself eternal, was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. This temporal birth diminished nothing and contributed nothing to that divine and eternal birth; rather, he devoted his whole self to restoring the human being who had been deceived, so that he might conquer death and by his power destroy the devil, who held dominion over death. For we could not overcome the author of sin and death unless he had assumed our nature and made it his own—a nature which neither sin could contaminate nor death retain.” [Col. 0261C]

And again in the same letter (chapter 3): “Therefore, while the distinct property of each nature and substance was preserved and they came together in one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by strength, mortality by eternity. And, in order to discharge the debt of our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that one and the same mediator between God and human beings, the human Christ Jesus, could both die by virtue of one nature and could not die by virtue of the other.” [Col. 0261D]

And again in the same work: “Since the devil was boasting that the human being, deceived by his fraud, had been deprived of divine gifts, stripped of the endowment of immortality, and subjected to the harsh sentence of death, and that he himself had found a kind of consolation in his evils through the fellowship of the transgressor, the devil was also boasting that God, justice requiring it, had changed his original sentence concerning the human being whom he had created with such great honor. Therefore, through the dispensation of a hidden plan, the unchangeable God, whose will cannot be deprived of his goodness, had to fulfill his first disposition of kindness toward us in a more secret sacrament, so that the human being, driven into guilt by the devil’s wicked cunning, would not perish contrary to God’s purpose.” [Col. 0262A]

The same author, in his homily on the Epiphany (Homily 1, chapter 1): “The salvation of all human beings is concerned in the fact that the infancy of the mediator between God and human beings was already being declared to the whole world, while he was still confined to a small town.”

Again, in his sermon on the same feast (Sermon 3, chapter 1): “The providence of God’s mercy, having determined to assist the perishing world in the final times, predetermined the salvation of all nations in Christ. For since impious error had long before turned all nations away from the worship of the true God, and the particular people of God, Israel, had almost entirely fallen away from the institutions of the Law, he had mercy on all, having shut all under sin.” [Col. 0262B]

And again (in the same sermon, chapter 3): “Let all peoples, represented by the three Magi, adore the Author of the universe; and let God be known not only in Judaea but throughout the whole world, so that his name may be great everywhere, as it is in Israel. For just as unbelief proves the dignity of the chosen race degenerate in its descendants, so faith makes it common to all.” [Col. 0262C]

Again (Sermon 5, chapter 2): “What those three men, representing all the nations, attained by worshiping the Lord, the whole world attains in its peoples through the faith that justifies the ungodly.”

Saint Felix, pope, in a decretal letter sent through the various provinces, at the relevant passage: “But because the same Lord and Savior is most merciful, and wishes no one to perish, it is fitting that they should lie in repentance until the end of their life, if they come to their senses.” [Col. 0262D]

And Saint Gregory, in Book VIII (chapter 6) of the *Moralia*: “For this purpose the human being had been created: to raise himself with an upright mind into the citadel of contemplation, and to allow no corruption to turn him away from the love of his Creator.”

And again (chapter 9): “Now every sinner does not fear God and yet lives, blasphemes and yet prospers, because the merciful Creator, whom by waiting he wishes to correct, does not wish to punish merely by looking upon him, as it is written: ‘You overlook the sins of human beings for the sake of repentance’ (Wisdom 11:24).”

And again (chapter 10): “The human being had been created to contemplate the Creator, so that he might always seek his appearance and dwell in the solemnity of his love. But, cast outside himself through disobedience, he lost the place of his mind, because, scattered along dark paths, he withdrew from the indwelling of the true light.”

And again (chapter 20): “Why do you despise the human being as though he were opposed to you, when I know for certain that you do not wish even the one whom you believe you ought to despise to perish?” [Col. 0263A]

And in Book XVII (chapter 4): “God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it in pride. Whoever sins and lives is tolerated by the divine dispensation in his iniquity for this reason: that he may be restrained from iniquity. But the person who is tolerated for a longer time and nevertheless is not restrained from iniquity receives the gift of heavenly patience, yet through that very gift binds himself more tightly in the chains of his guilt.”

And in the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 37: “‘The house of Israel has become dross to me. All these are bronze, tin, iron, and lead in the midst of the furnace’ (Ezekiel 22:18). It is as though he were openly saying: ‘I wished to purify them by the fire of tribulation and sought to make them silver or gold; but in the furnace they became bronze, tin, iron, and lead for me, because even in tribulation they burst forth not into virtue but into vices.’”

And again in Book XVII: “Those who perish, like the first human being, perish not by God’s will but by their own iniquity. ‘The human being,’ he says, ‘was created for life in the freedom of his own will; by his own choice he made himself liable to death.’” [Col. 0263B]

And again in Book VIII (chapter 20): “God made the human being opposed to himself when the human being abandoned God by sinning. But the just Creator made him opposed to himself because he counted him as an enemy through his pride.”

And again: “There are many who, even after receiving the assistance of redemption, fall into the darkness of despair and perish all the more wickedly because they despise the remedies of mercy that have been offered.”

And again: “Certainly God orders all things wondrously, and justly does what the evil spirit unjustly desires to do; and he permits this to happen only justly.” [Col. 0263C]

And in Book XVIII (chapter 10): “In this matter it must be asked why it is said that the wicked receive this portion and inheritance of theirs from the Almighty. But, if it is rightly considered, it is clear that although they had from themselves the will to act unjustly, nevertheless the equity of heaven is able to judge justly the things they have done unjustly, so that the divine sentence may assign to punishment those whom their disordered action has drawn into guilt.”

And again: “For God, who does good and orders it, does not himself do evil, but, arranging what has been done by the wicked so that it may not occur disorderly, considers the end of all things, patiently tolerates everything, and beholds the end of the elect, by which they are changed from evil to good. He also beholds the end of the reprobate, by which they draw themselves from an evil deed toward a punishment worthy of them.” [Col. 0263D]

And again in Book XVI (chapter 18): “His soul did whatever it wished. Thus his soul did whatever it wished in such a way that he fulfills his own will even through that by which his will seemed to be resisted.”

The same author, in Book XXV (chapter 13): “Sometimes it is God’s doing to permit, in anger, what he forbids to be done.”

And in the same work: “Let no one inquire why, while the Jewish people formerly stood in unbelief, the Gentiles lay there, and why, when the Gentiles rose to faith, the Jewish people was cast down in the guilt of unbelief. Let no one inquire why one is drawn by gift and another repelled by merit. For if you marvel that the Gentiles have been received, who is there to condemn when he himself has granted peace? If you are astonished that Judaea has been lost, who is there to contemplate him since he has hidden his face? Therefore, let the plan of the highest and hidden power be the satisfaction of manifest reason.”

Again in Book XXVI (chapter 22): “‘If they hear and serve him, they shall complete their days in goodness and their years in glory; but if they do not hear, they shall pass through the sword and perish in folly’ (Job 36:11). ‘Goodness’ signifies right action, while ‘glory’ signifies heavenly recompense. Those who strive to obey the heavenly commandments complete their days in goodness and their years in glory, because they bring both the course of the present time to completion in upright work and their consummation in a blessed recompense. But if they do not hear, they shall pass through the sword and perish in folly, because punishment strikes them in tribulation and their end closes in stupidity. For there are some whom not even torments restrain from their ruined ways; concerning them the Prophet says: ‘You struck them, and they did not grieve; you scourged them, and they refused to accept correction’ (Jeremiah 5:3), and concerning them it is said under the figure of Babylon: ‘We treated Babylon, but she was not healed’ (Jeremiah 51:9). And again concerning them it is said: ‘I struck and destroyed my people’ (Jeremiah 15:7), and yet they did not turn back from their ways. Such people sometimes become worse through the blow, because, struck by suffering, they become either harder through obstinate perversity or—what is worse—even break out into the frenzy of blasphemy.” [Col. 0264A]

Again in Book XXVII: “Just as you do not know what the way of the spirit is, or how bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all things (Ecclesiastes 2:5). To speak of one instance among many (chapter 2): two infants come into this light, but to one it is granted to return to redemption through baptism, while the other is taken away before the regenerating water bathes him. Often the son of the faithful is taken away without faith, and often the son of the unfaithful is renewed through the sacrament of faith that has been granted. But perhaps someone may say that God knew this child would act wickedly even after baptism, and therefore did not bring him to the grace of baptism. If this is so, then without doubt the sins of some are punished before they have been committed. And who, knowing what is right, would say that the almighty God, who frees some from crimes already committed, condemns in others crimes not even committed? His judgments, therefore, are hidden; and to the degree that they cannot be seen because of their great obscurity, they must be venerated with equal humility.” [Col. 0264B]

In Book XXIX (chapter 2): “Since the mystery of the divine work is carried out by mercy in such a way that anger also accompanies it, the hidden arbiter, looking upon some, redeems them, while abandoning others, he destroys them.”

And in the same work: “‘Their light shall be taken away from the wicked’ (Job 38:25), because, while they refuse to believe the truth, they lose forever the understanding of the Law; and while they grow proud over the Law they have received, they are blinded by the glory of their knowledge. For it is written: ‘Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see’; and again it is written: ‘Blind the heart of this people and make their ears heavy’ (Psalm 68:24). And again it is written: ‘For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind’; and because they raised themselves against the Lawgiver through the works of the Law, it is appropriately added: ‘and the exalted arm shall be broken’ (John 9:39).” [Col. 0264C]

In Book XXXI: “The security of a just man is rightly compared with a lion. When he sees various people rising against him, he returns to the confidence of his mind and knows that he overcomes all his adversaries, because he loves him alone, whom he by no means loses against his will.” [Col. 0264D]

In Book XXXII (chapter 7): “For by a just judgment the Lord hides the proud and impious in the dust, because he has permitted their hearts to be oppressed by earthly concerns, the very things they choose after scorning the love of the Creator.”

Again in Book XXXIII (chapter 10): “Everywhere heavenly medicine meets us, because he gave the human being commandments, so that he might not sin, and yet, when he sinned, he gave remedies, so that he might not despair. Therefore, one must take the greatest care lest anyone be carried away by the mouth of this Leviathan through the delight of sin; yet, if he is carried away, let him not despair, because, if he mourns his sin perfectly, he still finds a hole in its jaw through which he may escape. He is already being ground by its teeth; but if a way of escape is still sought, a hole is found in its jaw. Even the captive has a way out, though he had been unwilling to take precautions lest he be captured.” [Col. 0265A]

And shortly afterward (in the same chapter): “For mercy and anger come from him. Divine kindness, therefore, piercing the jaw of this Behemoth everywhere meets the human race both mercifully and powerfully, because it neither withheld from the free person a warning to take precautions nor withdrew from the captive a remedy for escape.”

Again in Book XXXIII (chapter 20): “I am compelled by no reason to spare the reprobate, since by their own action I am not held as their debtor. For this reason they then receive no eternal rewards in the heavenly homeland: because, while they could have earned them by free choice, they despised them.” [Col. 0265B]

And again (in the same chapter): “This Leviathan indeed lost my blessedness, but he did not escape my dominion, because even those powers that oppose me by their wicked actions serve me.”

And again in the same work (chapter 24): “Therefore, while the Lord was repaying them according to their evil works, he gave them the labor of their own hearts as a shield. For by a just judgment he showed them to be proudly hardened against him by the very thing through which he himself labored for us in the weakness of the flesh. They rejected from themselves the words of the preachers, because they disdained in the Lord the weakness of his sufferings.” [Col. 0265C]

Again in Book XXXIV (chapter 10): “‘The archer did not drive him away.’ Therefore, rightly angered by preceding sins, the Lord says through the Prophet concerning those whom he abandons in the hand of the ancient enemy: ‘I will send among you venomous serpents against which there is no incantation’ (Jeremiah 8:17). It is as though he were saying: ‘By a just judgment I will hand you over to such unclean spirits that they cannot be driven from you by the exhortation of preachers, as though by the speech of enchanters.’” [Col. 0265D]

And shortly afterward (in the same chapter): “But what wonder is it if he despises human strength, when he also scorns the eternal torments of the heavenly judgment imposed upon him?”

Again in the same book (chapter 15): “Almighty God, because he is compassionate, does not feed upon the torment of the miserable; but because he is just, he is not forever appeased apart from the vengeance of the wicked. All the wicked, however, are punished with eternal punishment, and indeed punished for their own iniquity; yet they are burned for a purpose: so that all the just may see, in the Lord, the joys they receive, and the unjust may behold the punishments from which they escaped. Thus they may recognize themselves to be eternal debtors to divine grace all the more clearly, the more eternally they see the evils punished that they could have avoided with his help.”

And in the first homily on the Gospel: “Our Lord and Redeemer, wishing to find us prepared, announces what evils will follow upon the world as it grows old.” [Col. 0266A]

And again in the same homily: “They will see in power and majesty the one whom they refused to hear when he was placed in humility, so that they may then feel his power all the more sternly, the more now they bend the neck of their heart before his patience.”

And the venerable presbyter Bede, in his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles: “Peter himself understood that all human beings were equally summoned to the Gospel of Christ and that no one is polluted by nature.”

And again: “‘For the heart of this people has grown dull, and they have heard with difficulty in their ears’ (Acts 28:27). Lest we suppose that the dullness of the heart and the heaviness of the ears belong to nature rather than to the will, he adds the guilt of free choice and says: ‘They have closed their eyes, lest they should see with their eyes.’ That is, by their preceding merits they themselves were the cause that God closed their eyes. Or this may be joined to what comes before, where the Lord says to the prophet: ‘Go to this people and reproach them for the sins by which they deserved blindness, if perhaps even so they may deign to hear and turn to me.’” [Col. 0266B]

And again the same author, in his exposition of the Gospel of the evangelist Mark (Book I, chapter 3): “Whoever, therefore, clearly understands the works of God and, since he cannot deny their power, slanders them, driven by envy, and says that Christ, the Word of God, and the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub—this person will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come. This does not mean that we deny that, if he should wish to repent, he could be forgiven by the one who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Rather, because we believe the judge and giver of forgiveness, who says both that he will always receive the penitent and that this blasphemy will never be forgiven, we believe that this blasphemer, by the demands of his merits, will reach neither forgiveness nor even the worthy fruits of repentance. This agrees with what the evangelist John most truthfully wrote concerning certain people blinded because of the merit of their blasphemy: ‘Therefore they could not believe’ (John 12:39–40), because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them.’” [Col. 0266C]

And again (in the commentary on Mark, Book I, chapter 4): “‘These are those beside the path where the word is sown; and when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that was sown in their hearts,’ and so forth. In this opposition of the Lord, the difference among all those who were able to hear the words of salvation but cannot attain salvation is comprehended. For there are some who do not deign to receive the word they hear with any faith, understanding, or even the opportunity to test its usefulness. In their undisciplined and hardened hearts, the word that has been planted is immediately snatched away by the unclean spirit, like seed by birds from a well-trodden path.” [Col. 0266D]

And again: “‘He could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands upon a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief.’ This does not mean that he could not perform many miracles even for those unbelievers, but that, by performing many miracles, he would have condemned the unbelieving citizens.”

And again (in the same work, Book I, chapter 10): “‘To sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared’ (Mark 10:40). This should be understood to mean that the kingdom of heaven does not belong to the giver but to the receiver. For there is no partiality with God; but whoever presents himself as worthy of the kingdom of heaven will receive what has been prepared not for a person but for a life. If, therefore, you are such as may attain the kingdom of heaven—which my Father has prepared for those who triumph and conquer—you too will receive it.” [Col. 0267A]

And again: “You, therefore, if you do not wish to hear Christ say to you in judgment, ‘Depart from me, accursed one, into eternal fire,’ beware of being a barren tree in this life. Rather, offer to poor and hungry Christ the fruit of compassion that he needs.”

And again: “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations’ (Mark 11:17): ‘For all nations,’ he says—not for the one nation of the Jews, nor in one place within the city of Jerusalem, but throughout the whole world.” [Col. 0267B]

Again, in the commentary on the Gospel of Luke: “For just as those skilled in hunting, when they have learned where wild animals, fish, and birds are most abundant, spread their nets there above all, so the Lord always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews gathered, wishing all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

And again: “‘You have taken away the key of knowledge.’ This is the humility of the faith of Christ, by which you could have reached the knowledge of his divinity; you preferred to despise and cast it away.”

And again (in the same work, Book IV, chapter 11): “For if what is asked is given, what is sought is found, and to the one who knocks it will be opened, then concerning the person to whom it is not given, who does not find, and to whom it is not opened, it is evident that he did not ask, seek, or knock properly.” [Col. 0267C]

And again: “But he who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth does not cease, now speaking to them and now speaking to his disciples while they listen, to bestow generously the gifts of his customary compassion.”

And again (Book V, chapter 19): “‘For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost.’ This is what he says elsewhere: ‘I have not come to call the righteous but sinners.’ Truly a compassionate teacher, who does not disdain to explain his mysteries to the murmuring crowds—so entirely does he refuse to reject the repentance of sinners—that for the sake of seeking it above all, the Son of God himself was sent to earth. And, to impress upon us the dispensation of his compassion, he very often calls himself the Son of Man, carefully commending to us what he graciously became for our sake.”

And again: “The impiety of the Jews, or of all the reprobate who are unwilling to be converted to Christ, is signified as destined to be punished on the day of judgment.”

And again: “Because it did not at all recognize the time of its visitation, it is handed over at the end of its life to those enemies with whom it is joined in the fellowship of its condemnation at the eternal judgment.”

And again: “God is always said to hesitate, so that free will may be preserved for the human being.” [Col. 0267D]

And Cassiodorus, on Psalm 55: “This means ‘on whatever day,’ because the Lord, in merciful patience, awaits whatever time may be granted for our conversion. Therefore he tolerates the guilty and waits for those who err, saying: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.’ The only thing necessary is that in this life we confess every sin, in which we offend through human frailty.”

And on Psalm 68: “It was added as a retribution, because that table, having been withdrawn and given to the nations, was a recompense for evils. For when they were unwilling to feast at it, they are rightly seen to be excluded from it.”

And on Psalm 73: “In the present psalm the overthrow of the city is lamented, so that the exceedingly hard spirit of the Jews might be frightened by the calamities of the city itself. The good physician did everything, if the sick person had been willing to regain health.”

And on Psalm 75: “Therefore they also lost this, those who were altogether unwilling to believe in his majesty.”

And on Psalm 81: “And he blessed them as sheep—not, however, sheep, because by refusing to believe they became goats.”

And on Psalm 77: “A perverse generation, because they were unwilling to receive the truth.” [Col. 0268A]

And again in the same psalm: “He abandoned the wickedness of the human being in his indignation, anger, and tribulation, so that those who disdain to obey divine commands might be afflicted by their own perversities.”

And on Psalm 94: “For when the Lord fasted for forty days, corresponding to the mystical number, and then spent another forty days with the apostles after the resurrection so that the whole world might believe, the obstinate Jews were found resisting. They were unwilling to accept the benefits of forty years. Their ruin is therefore prepared as greater, because long-standing pride grows within them.” [Col. 0268B]

And again: “Therefore, whoever has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, just as God rested from his. This signifies the time of that blessedness when the just, after the struggle of this age, enjoy eternal rest. It will certainly not be given to the impious, who have become hardened through their own unworthiness.”

And on Psalm 95: “Here this was said to the homeland of the nations, so that no native, no resident, and no foreigner would be excluded.”

And on Psalm 113: “No kind of human being who believes in him is shown to be excluded or alienated from his gifts.” [Col. 0268C]

And in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans he says many things agreeing with these, which we omit for the sake of brevity.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Recapitulation of the argument made after the names of the saints have been indicated, concerning the third chapter.

Here is what men filled with the Holy Spirit of God understood from this chapter. Furthermore, the chapters excerpted by us from the holy Fathers, which the venerable bishop Prudentius criticized, he established and confirmed together with us. Later, in the letter of which we are speaking, he so confused and disordered them that, by altering the wording, reversing the meaning, and changing the order, he destroyed them as far as he could. He found no further way to tear them apart: he changed the words, introduced the opposite meaning, and so thoroughly disrupted the order that he made the second first and the third fourth. If he could have found a fourth method by which to scatter them, it is clear that he would have done so intentionally.

Nevertheless, whatever he may have done, this legitimate order of presentation will remain. First should be set forth, by anyone wishing to describe these matters chapter by chapter, the foreknowledge and predestination of the elect, and the foreknowledge and abandonment of the reprobate, which existed before all ages. Next comes free choice, which man received in time and weakened through his own fault by the devil’s persuasion; and then the grace of God, without which the elect, lost in the first man, are not restored, and by which those abandoned in the general mass of perdition are not liberated.

Then, since human free choice, although through the merit of the first fault it lost freedom—that is, the capacity for good—nevertheless did not lose its name and nature, God, who created man in his own image and likeness and willed him to endure unto eternity, came as the true physician to heal by grace the man wounded by mortal injuries, struck down and left half-dead by robbers; and the good shepherd came freely to seek and save the lost sheep.

Thus one must set forth what the apostle John says: “What we have seen and testify to is that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world” (1 John 1:14); who, according to Paul, “wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4); and, according to Peter, “does not wish anyone to perish, but all to turn to repentance” (2 Pet. 3:9).

And finally what John again says: “By this we know the love of God, that he laid down his life for us” (1 John 3:16); who, as Peter says, “died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous” (1 Pet. 3:18). For the saying is faithful: as Paul says, “Christ came into this world to save sinners,” so that “everyone who believes in him should not perish” (1 Tim. 1:15), as the Gospel proclaims, “but have eternal life” (John 3:15).

Therefore the same Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him, commanded his disciples: “Go and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:14). Those who believed were baptized and, made safe through the grace of God, believed because they wished to do so. Those who did not believe were not baptized and were not saved, because they did not wish to believe, and therefore they perished.

“He who does not believe,” he says, “has already been judged” (John 3:18)—that is, he has already been condemned by God’s foreknowledge. Why? Because he did not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. “This is the judgment,” namely, “that light has come into the world, and men loved darkness more than light.” He subsequently explains what the darkness is, saying: “For their works were evil.”

Faith, too, which works through love, is light, as it is likewise written: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works” (Matt. 5:16). Without faith these cannot be good, because they are not pleasing to God. “Without faith it is impossible to please God.” The one who does good comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed as having been done in God. He who came as light into the world said: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness” (John 8:12).

This darkness is hated by him who hates none of the things he has made; those who perished loved it persistently. And those who, loving iniquity and hating their own souls, hate what the righteous Lord loves—for the righteous Lord loves righteous deeds—therefore perished.

Accordingly, the compassionate and merciful one, lamenting the misery of the city that was destined to perish, says to Jerusalem: “How often I wanted to gather your children, just as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Luke 13:34). It is as though he openly said: “What I wanted, you did not want, and therefore you perished.” So also he who says to all, “Watch,” says through Solomon to everyone:

“I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked. You rejected all my counsel and neglected my reproofs. I too will laugh at your destruction and mock you when what you feared has come. When sudden calamity falls, and destruction rushes upon you like a storm, when tribulation and anguish come upon you, then they will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise early, and they will not find me” (Prov. 1:24).

For there the one who asks can no longer earn anything from God, because here he refused to hear what God commanded.

If, then, as these modern Predestinarians say, there is no one whom God wishes to save who is not saved; if all who are not saved are entirely outside his will to be saved; if those who are saved have salvation imposed upon them as a necessity, and those who perish have perdition imposed upon them as a necessity; and therefore neither are those justly condemned who could not be saved, nor are these justly rewarded, since they could not be anything other than saved—then in both cases neither perdition nor salvation would arise from the judgment of one’s own action, but from the prior determination of divine preordination. For free choice of the will would be entirely removed from both groups, although it is written of God: “You will repay each one according to his works” (Ps. 61:13). And again: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath? By no means” (Rom. 3:5).

The venerable presbyter Bede, explaining this saying in a homily on the Gospel, says:

“‘When he comes, the Holy Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment’ (John 16:8). It is clear that the Son of God himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, while he was in the world, convicted the world—that is, the followers of the world—concerning the sin of their unbelief. He convicted it concerning righteousness, because they were unwilling to imitate the righteousness of the faithful; and concerning judgment, namely, why they followed the devil, who had already been judged and condemned.

“But he does not say without reason that the Spirit will do this when he comes. For the courage of the disciples was certainly to be strengthened through his inspiration, so that they would not be afraid to convict the world, which was raging against them. The Lord, explaining his meaning, added: ‘Concerning sin, because they did not believe in me.’ He identified the sin of unbelief as something special, because just as faith is the origin of the virtues, so persistence in unbelief is the foundation of vices. The Lord bears terrible witness to this when he says: ‘Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he did not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.’ On the contrary, ‘the righteous lives by faith.’”

A little later he says:

“The righteousness of the other faithful, who did not see the Lord in the flesh, consists in this: although they never saw him with bodily sight, they believe and love him in their hearts as the true God and man. By this righteousness of faith unbelievers are certainly convicted: why, when they likewise heard the word of life, were they unwilling to believe unto righteousness? For the wickedness of the evil is shown to be worthy of condemnation not only by its own force but also by comparison with the upright” [Col. 0271A].

Saint Augustine likewise says in *The Christian Combat* (ch. 27), concerning this saying of the Gospel: “‘Whoever does not believe has already been judged’—by the foreknowledge of God, who knows what awaits unbelievers.”

Here too it becomes clear that the disorderly school of the Predestinarians lies when it struggles to assert from this Gospel saying that people were predestined by God to destruction.

The venerable presbyter Bede, likewise, following the interpretations of blessed Augustine and the other orthodox Fathers in his Commentary on the Gospel of Luke, says:

“‘To everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away’ (Matt. 13:11). This saying looks back to what preceded. It teaches that even one who has may lose God’s gift, if he has it without truly possessing it—that is, if he does not use it—and that it is increased in the one who, having it, possesses it, that is, uses it well.”

A little earlier he says:

“He rightly loses the grace bestowed on him because he neglected to communicate it by preaching to others, so that it may be increased in the one who labored through it. Accordingly, it is said to the angel of the church of Ephesus: ‘I will remove his lampstand from its place, unless he repents’ (Rev. 2:5). And when Saul lost the royal anointing through pride, David earned it through obedience: ‘The Spirit of the Lord,’ it says, ‘departed from Saul and was directed to David from that day onward.’”

The Predestinarians also produce, in support of their position that it is not at all the Lord’s will that those who are not saved should be saved, testimonies from the Psalms: “Our God is in heaven; he has done whatever he willed” (Ps. 113:11). And: “The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. 134:8). But Catholic teachers explain these passages in a very different sense.

Before setting forth the interpretations of the saints, we wish to ask them whether the angels fell from heaven and human beings fell in paradise by God’s will. If they say that they fell by the Lord’s will, the whole people will stone them; for it follows that they must say that God was the author of their fall. Everyone knows that Saint Gregory truthfully says in Homily 34:

“The Lord created the nature of angels and human beings so that it might know him. Since he willed it to endure unto eternity, he unquestionably created it in his own likeness.”

But if, compelled by the truth, they say that the angels and human beings fell not by God’s will but through their own fault, it is manifest that the testimonies they themselves produce work not with them but against them.

For just as the first two human beings fell not by God’s will but through their own fault—and, as we believe from the statements of blessed Augustine and the other saints, returned through repentance to salvation in the blood of Christ by the grace of God—so, among all those lost in the sin of the first man and generated in that same state of perdition, whoever are saved are saved by the grace of God, who wills all men to be saved; and whoever perish perish not by God’s will but by the merit of their deserved destruction.

For just as the Creator willed human nature—that is, the first man, since Eve is also Adam—to endure unto eternity, because he is eternally good; just as he justly condemned him when he fell against his will, because he is just; and just as he restored him to salvation by grace, because he is merciful—so the just Redeemer in all his ways and holy in all his works wills all those born from the general mass of perdition to be saved, because he is good. Yet he abandons some in that same mass of perdition by judgment, because he is just, while he frees others from the destruction owed to all by the gift of grace, because he is merciful.

And lest those hostile to the right faith mock us by saying that God is just because he abandons some in the mass of perdition—for otherwise he could not be just—let them read the Psalm in which, among other things, it is sung:

“He struck down great kings and killed mighty kings, and gave their land as an inheritance to his people; for he remembered us in our humiliation and redeemed us from our enemies—for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 135:17).

He is just in all things, good in all things: when he punishes the wicked, when he frees sinners, and when by grace he crowns the righteous.

As for the first testimony they set forth, Saint Augustine says in his exposition of Psalm 112 (at the end of the exposition of Ps. 113:11):

“‘Our God is in heaven above.’ In heaven above—that is, in what transcends all heavenly and earthly bodies—‘in heaven and on earth he has done whatever he willed.’ Nor does he need his works as though he were placed in them in order to remain; rather, he persists in his own eternity, and, remaining in it, he has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth. Therefore, where he is present as though in need, he contains them; he is not contained by them as though he were in need.

“Or it may be understood in this way: ‘In heaven and on earth he has done whatever he willed’—whether among higher or lower peoples, he established his voluntary grace, so that no one might glory in the merits of works.”

Saint Jerome says:

“‘Our God is in heaven; he has done whatever he willed.’ ‘God is in heaven above,’ the saints say to those unbelievers who worship idols. ‘You touch your gods with your hands and see them with bodily eyes; but our God is in heaven above. In heaven and on earth he has done whatever he willed.’ In those who live a heavenly life while still enclosed in earthly flesh, he will fulfill his purposes.”

Concerning the other testimony, from Psalm 134, Saint Jerome likewise says:

“‘He has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses’ (Ps. 134:6). By the will of his goodness, it pleased God to perform wonders in lofty souls, in arid minds, amid the waves of the world, and in the depths of wickedness.”

Saint Augustine explains it in this way:

“‘The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses.’ Who can comprehend these things? Although we cannot comprehend everything, we must nevertheless believe and hold firmly to everything, because whatever creature exists in the heavens, on earth, and in all the abysses was made by the Lord.

“He was not compelled to make everything he made; his will is the cause of everything he made. Necessity compelled you to make a house, clothing, and other things.”

A little later he says:

“We find something that we do by free choice when, by loving God himself, we praise him. It is not from necessity, but because it pleases us. Thus God pleased the righteous and holy, even when he scourged them.”

And again:

“‘God has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth.’ May he himself give you grace, so that you may do in yourself what you will. For unless he helps you, you will not even do in yourself what you will, because ‘the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh,’ so that you do not do whatever you wish.”

A little later:

“Because he did not fulfill what he wished, not only in his house or in his field but in his flesh and in his spirit, he cried out to God, who has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, and said: ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?’ (Rom. 7:24). And that good, that sweet one, as though answering him immediately, added: ‘The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.’ Love this sweetness, then; praise this sweetness. Understand that God, who has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, will himself do in you what you will. With his help you will fulfill your will; but you cannot yet. When you can, confess; give thanks; lying prostrate, cry out; when raised up, do not become proud.”

If the modern Predestinarians should here vomit forth their old poison, saying that those whom God does not wish to be saved—since he has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth—he does not make willing, does not make confessing, and does not raise when fallen because he predestined them to eternal death; and therefore, after they have fallen, God so disposes them that they can neither be freed by repentance nor wish to be freed, Prosper should answer them with what he replied to the Vincentians in the fifteenth action, by delegation of the apostolic see:

“This is said neither truthfully nor wisely. For those who have fallen away from faith and holiness do not rise again by their will, just as they fell by their will, and they willingly endure the domination of the desires to which they submitted. But if some lament their captivity and, judging themselves, flee to God’s mercy with a changed heart, they do this not without the Spirit’s divine visitation.

“For this is the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High: he gives repentance to countless fallen people, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will. God denies no one the way of correction, nor does he strip anyone of the possibility of good, because whoever turns himself away from God has himself taken away from himself both the will and the ability to do what is good.

“Therefore, it does not follow, as those who raise such objections think, that when God has not given some repentance, he has taken away their recovery; or that, when he has not raised some, he has cast them down. For it is one thing for an innocent person to commit a crime, which is foreign to God; it is another thing not to grant forgiveness to a criminal, which arises from the sinner’s merit.”

The Predestinarians nevertheless claim for themselves the saying from the book of blessed Job, in order to display what they think is a plausible falsehood: “His soul does whatever it wills” (Job 23:13). Blessed Gregory explains this in the *Moralia* (book 16, ch. 18):

“His soul therefore does whatever it wills, so that by this very fact he fulfills his will even when his will appears to be resisted.”

And again:

“Sometimes it is God’s action to permit, in anger, what he forbids to be done.”

Saint Augustine says in *The Gift of Perseverance* (ch. 6):

“Nothing happens unless God either does it or permits it to happen.”

Let those who contend with these men read further, if this is not enough, the testimony we cited from Saint Augustine’s book *On the Spirit and the Letter*.

For the sake of their dispute, the saying from the Gospel of Luke must also be explained to the simple-minded: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate, because many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able” (Luke 13:24).

Bede says on Luke, chapter 13:

“They seek to enter, stirred by love of salvation, but they will not be able, deterred by the harshness of the journey. They seek this because of the ambition for rewards, but soon withdraw from it through fear of the labors—not because the Lord’s yoke is harsh and his burden heavy, but because they do not wish to learn from him that he is gentle and humble in heart, so that they may find rest for their souls. For this reason the gate by which one enters into life is narrow.”

A little later:

“To stand outside and knock at the door is to plead in vain for mercy from God, having been separated from the lot of the blessed because of the mercy they neglected. And he will answer you: ‘I do not know where you are from.’ For then God abandons as strangers those whom, because of the merit of their life, he does not now acknowledge as his own.”

Gregory says in Homily 13 on the Gospels:

“For this reason Paul says: ‘Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment’ (Rom. 2:4). For this reason the Psalmist says: ‘God is a righteous judge, strong and patient’ (Ps. 7:12). In saying that he is patient, he first called him righteous, so that when you see him patiently enduring the sins of sinners for a long time, you may know that he will at some point judge strictly.

“For this reason it is said through a certain wise man: ‘The Most High is a patient repayer’ (Ecclus. 5:4). He is called a patient repayer because he bears with the sins of human beings and repays them. For those whom he tolerates for a long time so that they may be converted, he condemns more severely if they are not converted. He wishes to be appeased by prayers, knowing that he cannot be endured when angry. While he still delays his coming, he accepts an embassy of peace. He would already have come, if he wished, and slaughtered all his enemies. Yet he indicates how terrifyingly he will come, and nevertheless delays his coming, because he does not wish to find people whom he will punish—he who came to seek and save what had perished, who wills all men to be saved and wishes no one to perish, who has deigned to invite all to salvation: ‘Come to me,’ he says, ‘all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matt. 11:28).”

Hence Bede says in his exposition of the Gospel of Luke:

“In the moral sense, the Lord invites all; he rejects no one who is willing, nor binds anyone unwilling; he neither casts out those who come nor is absent from those who ask. He is near to all who call upon him in truth, God who searches hearts and reins. To him, together with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, all honor and worship are due throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. The explanation of the fourth chapter begins: the chapter that we excerpted against the Predestinarians, and which the compiler of the chapters you gave us marked with excessive error, bringing forward, to magnify the charge of our criticism, the Antichrist and the wicked who died in their wickedness and were condemned to eternal fire before Christ’s coming

As we approach the explanation to be given of the fourth chapter, we beseech the grace of Christ our Lord, so that, with sound understanding of the faith, the authority of the holy Scriptures, and the testimonies of the orthodox, he may redeem us from the merchandise of our detractors—those who seek to purchase for themselves a reputation for praise through our defamation—he who redeemed Israel from all his iniquities. May he always and everywhere be for us a protecting God and a fortified place, so that he may save us from the deceptive snares of heretical perversity.

Concerning the meaning of this chapter, the ancient Predestinarians said, as Yginus writes and Saint Prosper demonstrates in the ninth objection of the Gauls, that the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world. Likewise, in the first objection of the Vincentians: “Because our Lord Jesus Christ suffered not for the salvation and redemption of all human beings.”

And Gothescalc, the standard-bearer of the new Predestinarians, says in his little book to Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, concerning this passage:

“All those impious and sinful people whom the Son of God came to redeem by pouring out his own blood—the goodness of almighty God wills that these alone, predestined to life, be irreversibly saved. And again, all those impious and sinful people for whom that same Son of God neither assumed a body nor offered a prayer—not to mention shedding his blood—and for whom he was in no way crucified, since he foreknew that they would become extremely wicked and had most justly determined that they would be cast into eternal torments: God absolutely and perpetually does not wish these to be saved.”

He wrote many other things in the same sense, repeating them in various forms. We have thought it superfluous to include them here, since from this anyone can sufficiently understand his position.

The venerable Prudentius also wrote in the frequently mentioned letter to his archbishop Wenilo, concerning the ordination of Aeneas as bishop of Paris, in chapter 3:

“He should believe and confess, together with all Catholics, that the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ was shed for all human beings throughout the whole world who believe in him; but not for those who have never believed in him, do not believe in him even today, and will never believe, since the Lord himself says: ‘For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many’ (Matt. 20:28).”

The compiler of those chapters to which you ordered us to respond says in the fourth chapter:

“Likewise, concerning the redemption by Christ’s blood, because an excessive error has arisen on this matter, so that some, as their writings indicate, even define that it was shed for those impious people who, from the beginning of the world until the Lord’s Passion, died in their wickedness and were punished by eternal condemnation—contrary to the prophetic saying: ‘I will be your death, O Death; I will be your sting, O hell’ (Hos. 13:14).”

We are astonished that the compiler of these chapters omitted the fact that some, in order to refute us because we had not rightly said that Christ suffered for all, although not all have been redeemed by the mystery of his Passion, customarily add to the impious and sinners who, from the beginning of the world, were plunged into hell for their crimes and are to be tormented eternally, the devil with his apostate angels and the Antichrist.

Boethius laments these people, together with others ruined by folly, in *The Consolation of Philosophy* (part 1, ch. 9), saying: “Alas, how miserable are those whom ignorance leads astray along wandering paths!”

Saint Gregory says of such people in the *Pastoral Rule* that arrogance does in the mind what a white film does in the eye. When it attributes to itself the brightness of justice or wisdom, it excludes itself from the light of heavenly knowledge; and the more it exalts itself through arrogance in its own estimation, the less it penetrates the radiance of the true light. As it is said of certain people: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1:22).

A certain madman whom we mentioned above wrote against us as follows:

“Concerning the second definition, by which it was defined in those chapters that there is no human being for whom Christ did not suffer—whether he is, was, or will be—what else can we answer except first to question carefully those who defined this and warn them to take care, attentively and faithfully, lest perhaps, through insufficient consideration of what ought to have been said, they have spoken and written such things against their own faith and conscience?

“For, to say nothing of those who exist now or who will exist until the end of the age, among whom the Antichrist will certainly be found, what are we to say about that innumerable multitude of wicked people who existed from the beginning of the world until the Lord’s coming, died in their wickedness, and have been condemned to eternal punishments? We do not think that even those who said this believe that the Lord should be understood to have suffered for these people, who died in their wickedness and have already been condemned by eternal judgment. For if it is believed that he suffered for them, why should it not likewise be believed that he suffered for the devil and his angels?”

To him we can appropriately respond with the Lord’s words from the Gospel: “You are mistaken, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.” The apostle Paul says: “For he nowhere takes hold of angels” (Heb. 2:16), but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham.

Hence John Chrysostom says:

“Because he did not take hold of any of the angels—that is, he did not assume the nature of any angel—but took hold of the seed of Abraham. For such dignity was not granted to angels that the Son of God should be joined to their nature in one person. Rather, God the Son granted this honor and dignity to human nature, so that God and man might be one person.

“Why did he say ‘he took hold’? Because he pursued and took hold of us as we were withdrawing from him and fleeing far away, and he adapted the nature of our weakness to himself in one person. Therefore, he had to redeem what he assumed.”

As blessed Gregory says in book 9, chapter 28, of the *Moralia*:

“The spirits of angels sinned irreparably because they were able to stand all the more firmly since no mixture with flesh restrained them. Man, however, merited forgiveness after his fault because through a fleshly body he received something by which he was lesser than himself. Hence, in the judgment of the Judge, this same weakness of the flesh is an argument for mercy.”

[Col. 0277B] There is also another reason why the spirits who fled perished irreparably, whereas humanity merited restoration by grace: namely, because the devil perished through his own iniquity, while humanity did so also through diabolical persuasion, as Alcuin demonstrates in his *Book of Responses on Genesis to Sigulfus*. Hence Saint Ambrose says in Psalm 118:

“Perhaps you will say: For what reason is it not written, ‘The heaven is full of the Lord’s mercy,’ since there are also spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places? But those wickednesses do not belong to the common gift of his indulgence and the remission of sins, for which eternal fire is reserved.”

And Saint Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, says in his second synodal letter:

“But why do we recall these things, when Origen burst into such folly, indeed madness, that he imputes another crime to the Savior, saying that he must also be crucified above for demons and spiritual wickednesses, without understanding into what abyss and chasm of impiety he falls? For if Christ suffered for human beings and became human, as the utterances of Scripture testify, it will follow that Origen must say: ‘He will suffer for demons and become a demon.’ For he will necessarily have to draw this conclusion, lest he appear to depart from what he began, as though he were contradicting himself. For they too spoke similarly about Christ: ‘You have a demon’ (Matt. XI, 18); and, ‘By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, you cast out demons’ (Matt. XII, 24). But far be it that Christ suffered for demons, lest he himself also become a demon.

“And those who believe this crucify the Son of God again and hold him up to ridicule, not understanding that, just as he took hold of the seed of Abraham, he will in no way also assume the nature of demons, so as to be crucified for them as well. Nor will the demons, seeing God in his Passion, cry out with the prophet, ‘This one bore our sins and suffers for us’; nor will they say with Isaiah, ‘By his bruise we were healed’ (Isa. LIII, 5). Nor, for demons as for the human race, will Christ be led like a sheep to sacrifice; nor will it be said for their salvation, ‘He did not spare his own Son.’ For the demons will not cry out, ‘He was delivered up for our sins and rose again for our justification.’ Paul plainly writes: ‘For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures’ (I Cor. XV), calling those Scriptures as witnesses and wishing by their authority to establish what is doubtful.

“Origen, however, without any testimony from the divine voice, attempts to do violence to the truth and to find it after extinguishing the lamp. A supporter of demons, not of human beings, he assails the Son of God with repeated slanders and crucifies him again, not understanding into what deep and dreadful pit of impiety he is dragged. For it follows that whoever accepts the earlier propositions must accept what follows as well: whoever says that Christ is crucified for demons must also admit that it must be said to them, ‘Take and eat; this is my body. And take and drink; this is my blood’ (Mark XXVI, 26). If he is crucified for demons as the advocate of new doctrines asserts, what privilege or what reason would there be for human beings alone to share in his body and blood, and not the demons also, for whom he shed his blood in his Passion?

“But the demons will not hear, ‘Take and eat,’ or, ‘Take and drink’; nor will the Lord abolish his own commands, he who says to his disciples, ‘Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine, lest they perhaps trample them under their feet, and then turn and tear you apart’ (Matt. V, 6). For when the Apostle writes, ‘I do not want you to become participants with demons’ (I Cor. X, 2)—‘You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons’—he demonstrates that it is impossible for demons to drink from the Lord’s cup and share in his table.

“The devil’s food is those who deny God, as Habakkuk says: ‘His chosen foods’ (Hab. I, 16). But the food of all the impious is the accursed devil himself, as the prophet’s prophecy resounds: ‘You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia’ (Ps. LXXI, 14). From all these considerations it is proved that Christ cannot be crucified for demons, lest demons become participants in his body and blood.

“Since, then, the Apostle also says of the Savior, ‘For he did this once, offering himself’ (Heb. VII, 27), while Origen so boldly contradicts that statement, it is time to apply the words: ‘Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord; write this man down as rejected’ (Jer. XXII). For what hell can receive these evils? What Tartarus can conceive of such things? What madness of giants has proved so rebellious and built such a tower of impiety? What wanton desire, wasting away in love of demons, has so spread the legs of its mind before every passing doctrine? Who drank so deeply from the vineyard of Sodom that, drunk with its wine of fury, he fell with all his heart? Who was so irrigated by the torrents of Babylon that he abandoned the living springs of Israel? Who, going out from Jerusalem and imitating Jeroboam son of Nebat, built so many altars of error and kindled profane incense upon the shrines? Why will Dathan and Abiram, who committed lesser sins, not come before Christ’s tribunal to condemn by comparison with themselves the man who, outside the Savior’s Church, filled censers of various doctrines with the devil’s fire?

“For the Lord, who speaks through the prophet, ‘I multiplied visions, and I was represented in the hands of the prophets’ (Hos. XI, 10), did not teach him to utter adulterous doctrines, nor did those who from the beginning saw him and were ministers of the word of God. Nor did the choir of prophets, who were once called ‘seers,’ instruct him in these things. Rather, serving the demons’ fury by the judgment of his own mind and deceived by the seductive error of his thoughts, he released throughout the world into the minds of the unlearned a flock—or, so to speak, a swarm—of perverse doctrines.

“This is the man who opened his mouth to the rivers of Assyria and Babylon; who attempted to overwhelm the ship of the Church, full of the good merchandise of saving doctrine, with waves, while he is lifted up by the praise of the ignorant and, explaining the meaning of Scripture otherwise than truth requires, glories in confusion.

“For who wrote books so innumerable, so talkative, and so full of verbosity and ignorance, and joined days and nights in tireless labor, so that, leaving monuments of error, he deserved to hear: ‘You have been deceived by your many journeys’? He used popular applause as his worst guide; and, after composing very many volumes of false knowledge, fighting against God with a rebellious mind, he mingled a kind of pus and the stench of his own foulness into the ointment of heavenly doctrines, so that it might again be said to his soul: ‘Unclean, infamous, and exceedingly wicked.’

“For he did not wish to hear the prophet’s warning: ‘Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?’ (Ps. IV, 3). He crucifies Christ for demons, so that he may become mediator not only of God and human beings, but also of demons. But far be it that we should believe such monstrous impiety about the Savior: that, being about to lose the temple of his body which he deigned to raise up for us, he should affix to himself another temple of demonic nature and, having assumed their likeness as well, undergo the cross for them.

“I beg you, beloved brothers, to forgive my grief as I resist impious doctrines. For while we strive to repel the shamelessness of his followers, we have brought into the open the structure of his breastplate and the frauds of his poisonous heart, so that this too might be fulfilled in him: ‘I will reveal your disgrace and display it to your lovers’ (Ezek. XVI, 37).”

Concerning Antichrist, Saint Gregory says in Book XXXI of the *Moralia* (chapter 2):

“Since transgression is expressed by the number eleven, the eleventh horn of this beast is judged to be the author of transgression himself. It arises as a little horn because he is born a mere human being, but it grows monstrously because it advances to the power of angelic strength joined to it.”

And again (chapter 18):

“Behemoth is called the beginning of God’s ways, because, when he was creating all things, he formed this one first and made him more eminent than the other angels.”

And again (chapter 12):

“What else is the tail of this Behemoth except the extremity of the ancient enemy, when it enters its own vessel, that lost human being who is specially called Antichrist?”

And again in the same chapter:

“Then Antichrist, temporally possessing the glory of the world, surpasses human measures both in the summit of honor and in the power of signs. For there is in him the spirit who, having been created among the higher beings, did not lose the power of his nature even when cast down.”

And again in the edict addressed to the Roman citizens (Book XI, Letter 3):

“It has come to my attention that certain priests, men of a perverse spirit, have sown among you things that are corrupt and contrary to the holy faith, so that they prohibited the performance of any work on the Sabbath day. What else should I call them but preachers of Antichrist? For when he comes, he will cause both the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day to be kept free from every work. Since he will pretend to die and rise again, he wishes the Lord’s Day to be held in veneration; and since he will compel the people to Judaize, restoring the external observance of the Law and subjecting them to the Jews’ unbelief, he wishes the Sabbath to be honored.”

And Bede says in his *Chronicle*:

“And I saw a beast rising from the sea, and the dragon gave it his power and great authority. That is: I saw a man of exceedingly savage character, born from the tumultuous stock of the impious. As soon as he was born, and had been imbued through magical arts by the worst teachers, the devil joined himself to him and brought, as his inseparable companion, the whole power of his strength, by which he would accomplish greater magical deeds than all others. ‘And authority was given to him to act for forty-two months,’ that is, three years and a half.

“But when that son of perdition has been struck down—whether by the Lord himself or by the archangel Michael, as some teach—and condemned to eternal vengeance, it should not immediately be believed that the days of judgment will follow. Otherwise, the people of that age could know the time of judgment if it followed immediately after the three and a half years from the beginning of Antichrist’s persecution.”

And Saint Jerome, explaining Daniel’s prophecy:

“Blessed are those who, after Antichrist has been slain, await beyond 1,220 days—that is, three and a half years and forty-five days—within which the Lord and Savior will come in his majesty.”

And again Gregory in Book XXXII of the *Moralia* (chapter 12):

“What is added through Daniel, ‘He will be shattered without human hand’ (Dan. VIII, 15), is expressed through Paul: ‘The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming’ (II Thess. I, 8). He will be shattered without human hand, because he will be struck with eternal death not by a battle of angels or a conflict of the saints, but at the Judge’s coming, by the breath of his mouth alone.”

And again (chapter 13):

“But since we have heard what the head of the wicked is like, let us now recognize what members adhere to this head. Whoever is exalted in pride, whoever is tormented by desires of avarice, whoever is dissolved in the pleasures of lust, whoever burns in the lashes of unjust and immoderate anger—what else is he than a witness of Antichrist? And it is written in the letter of the Apostle John: ‘And just as you heard that Antichrist is coming, so now there are many antichrists’ (I John XII, 18).”

Hence the venerable presbyter Bede says:

“He calls heretics antichrists, but also those who destroy by perverse actions the catholic faith which they confess. Thus it is evident that Antichrist is called one who is contrary to Christ. All such people bear witness to the great Antichrist who will come at the end of the age, as to their head. As Paul also says, ‘The mystery of iniquity is already at work’ (II Thess. II, 7).
