Concerning his heralds it is written again: ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us’ (I John II, 19). For none go out except Antichrists.

“Hence it is also written concerning Judas, the chief Antichrist throughout the whole period until that greatest Antichrist comes: ‘The devil put it into the heart of Judas to betray him,’ and after the morsel, ‘Satan entered into him, and he went out immediately’ (Luke XXII, 3). He was called the son of perdition, just as the great Antichrist will be.”

And again:

“Judas the antichrist betrayed him who is truly called Christ and is worshiped as God, who is blessed above all forever. But that other one, in his own time, will oppose and exalt himself above everything called God or worshiped, so that he will sit in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he himself were God.”

Concerning this man—that is, Judas—Saint Augustine says after much else in the *Hypomnesticon*:

“Such is the cause of all those who perish, although the guilt differs from one guilt to another.”

And concerning him and his body Saint Gregory says in Book XXXIII of the *Moralia* (chapter 19):

“And he will be cast down while all are looking on. For he will be cast down while all are looking on, because when the eternal Judge appears terribly, when legions of angels stand by, when the ministry of the heavenly powers is present, and when all the elect have been brought to this spectacle, that cruel and mighty beast will be led captive into the midst and, together with his body—that is, with all the reprobate—will be consigned to the eternal fires of Gehenna, when it is said: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Matt. XXV, 45).”

Therefore, since he will be a reprobate human being and the head of the reprobate—that is, of those and all the others who, from the beginning of the world until the Lord’s coming, were handed over to eternal punishments, whom the compiler of these chapters introduced as witnesses in order to attack us, as well as of those who, after the Lord’s coming until the end of the world, will belong to his fellowship through unbelief and persistent iniquity—we shall shortly write what catholic teachers think about these same reprobates.

Let any one of our slanderers who wishes place himself before us and see whether he can refute us for having written falsely about Antichrist. If we cannot find catholic teachers as defenders and assistants against him, let him triumph over us with rejoicing.

As we have already stated, Saint Paul, Saint Gregory, and all the other teachers say that he will be a human being, and we believe the same; nor will any of our critics wish to deny it. And if he will be human, although filled with the devil as his companion, then insofar as he is human, however reprobate, he will die. The Lord Jesus, as it is written, “will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming,” when the coming of the Son, who is God and man, will be like lightning that goes out from the east and appears in the west.

And because he will die, he will rise again, as it is likewise written: “To you all flesh will come” (Ps. LXIV, 3), and “all flesh will see the salvation of God” (Luke III, 6)—which will not happen without the soul in the resurrection. At his coming, according to the catholic faith, all human beings must rise again with their bodies. If all, then also that human being under discussion, who, as it is written, will come in his own name as Antichrist.

And if Christ’s Passion conferred something upon the other reprobates, namely, his members, it did not deny it to the head either, as we shall demonstrate by the statements of catholic authorities. First, however, we shall answer the compiler of the chapters under discussion concerning whatever God grants regarding this chapter, and then, with his favor, we shall proceed in order to answer what follows.

We did not write in the manner in which this compiler composed it; let him consider for himself why he was unwilling to set out the chapters excerpted from our work as they were written. We nevertheless believe that he has already seen painters place black color beneath white, so that what was bright might appear brighter by comparison with darkness. For this reason he did not wish to combine the truth, which we took from truthful authorities, with the darkness of his falsehood, lest he be less able to deceive the unwary and lest he be more readily recognized by the faithful as a liar.

For, drawing on Prosper’s words and on the understanding of Prosper himself and other orthodox writers, we wrote in chapter 4:

“Christ Jesus our Lord, just as there is no human being, was, or will be whose nature was not assumed in him, so there is no human being, was, or will be for whom he did not suffer, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion. But the fact that not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion does not concern the greatness and abundance of the price; rather, it concerns the portion belonging to unbelievers and to those who do not believe with the faith that works through love. For the cup of human salvation, which was prepared from our weakness and divine power, certainly possesses within itself the capacity to benefit everyone; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.”

It is evident that, when he said this, we did not write against the prophetic statement, “I will be your death, O Death; I will be your sting, O Hell” (Hos. XIII, 14), by saying: “But the fact that not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion does not concern the greatness and abundance of the price; rather, it concerns the portion belonging to unbelievers and to those who do not believe with the faith that works through love.”

For we were not unaware that Saint Gregory, in Homily 22, when we wrote these things, had said:

“Through this, the elect, who, although held in the bosom of tranquility, were nevertheless confined within the gates of hell, were brought back to the delights of paradise. What Christ said before his Passion, ‘And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself’ (John XII, 32), he fulfilled in his resurrection. For he drew all things, since he left none of his elect among the dead. He took away all things—certainly the elect. For he did not restore unbelievers, who had been consigned to eternal punishments for their sins, to forgiveness by rising again; rather, he snatched from the prison of hell those whom he recognized as his own in faith and deeds.”

Hence we said that, in the case of those who are not redeemed, the matter concerns not the abundance of the price but the portion belonging to unbelievers.

Saint Gregory continues:

“Therefore he rightly also says through Hosea, ‘I will be your death, O Death.’ As though he openly said: ‘Because I utterly destroy you in my elect, I will be your sting, O Hell, because after removing them I pierce you in part.’”

Hence we said: “There is no human being for whom Christ did not suffer, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion.”

But when we wrote these things, we were also not unaware that Saint Augustine, in the *Catalogue of Heresies* written to the deacon Quodvultdeus, described, in the eightieth place, the heresy which he says:

“This is a heresy which says that, when Christ descended to hell, the unbelievers believed and were all subsequently liberated.”

And we read that the venerable presbyter Bede wrote in his exposition of the First Epistle of Peter (chapter 3):

“Someone interpreted this passage in this way: that the saints resting in hell desired that consolation of which the Lord says to the apostles, ‘Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it’ (Matt. XIII, 17); concerning which the Psalmist also says, ‘My eyes have failed at your word, saying, “When will you comfort me?”’ (Ps. CXVIII, 82). He said that this consolation was preached when the Lord descended into hell even to those who were in prison and had formerly been unbelieving in the days of Noah.

“But the catholic faith holds that, when the Lord descended into hell, he brought out from there not the unbelievers but only his own faithful, and led them with him to the heavenly kingdoms. He does not demonstrate the ways of life to souls stripped of their bodies and confined in the prison of hell for their crimes, but in this life, either through himself or through the examples and words of his faithful, he demonstrates them daily.”

Therefore we said:

“Christ suffered for all, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion; and because not all are redeemed, the matter concerns not the greatness of the price but the portion belonging to those who do not believe.”

And since, in the course of the argument to be given concerning this chapter, we shall endeavor to demonstrate from the statements of catholic authorities what we wrote in a catholic manner—namely, that Christ suffered for all, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion—we mean both those who existed before his coming and those whom his Passion found living in the flesh.

### CHAPTER XXVIII. How the Catholics Understood the Impious Who Died in Their Impiety, and That the Lord Suffered Also for Them, Although They Were Not Redeemed for Eternal Salvation by the Mystery of His Passion

We shall also demonstrate, concerning those who arose and will arise after his Passion and resurrection until the end of the age, that we do not fear the slanders of our detractor. What did the catholic authorities think and write about the reprobates whom he brought forward in his fourth chapter to refute us? Did Christ’s Passion and resurrection confer anything upon them, even if, because of their guilt, it benefited them nothing for salvation? Let us show this.

For it is certain that, if the Lord’s Passion conferred anything upon them, the Lord also suffered for them. Since his Passion did not benefit them for salvation, the matter concerns, as Saint Prosper says—and as we wrote from his words—the portion belonging to unbelievers, not the power of the sacrament.

Let Paul speak, and let Ambrose explain, what Christ’s Passion conferred generally upon all, faithful and unfaithful alike, although it benefited only the faithful for salvation. For Paul says:

“As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (I Cor. XV, 22).

Hence Saint Ambrose writes in his commentary on that Epistle:

“He says this because, just as Adam, by sinning, found and retained death, so that all who derive their origin from him might be dissolved, so also Christ, without sinning and therefore conquering death—for whoever does not sin conquers death, since death arises from sin—acquired life, that is, resurrection, for all who belong to his body.

“Although, therefore, he granted a general resurrection to all, so that just as in Adam all—both just and unjust—die, so in Christ all—both believers and unbelievers—rise again, nevertheless some rise for punishment. The unbelievers, however, appear to be made alive because they receive their bodies, no longer to die but to suffer punishment in them without end, because they refused to believe.”

And blessed John Chrysostom says in his book *On the Restoration of the Fallen*:

“Scripture says that sinners too will put on incorruption—not for the honor of life, but for the duration of punishment.”

And Saint Hilary says in his exposition of Psalm 118 (verse 22):

“For he reproves the proud and accursed, asking why they thought that nothing of the benefit of his blood and death belonged to them, when he was born, suffered, and died for our sake.”

And again the same Saint Hilary, agreeing with Saint Ambrose, says in Psalm 55 (verse 8):

“‘As they awaited my soul, you will save them for nothing; in wrath you will bring down the peoples.’ This is a new saying of the prophet: that God should save for nothing those who await his soul. And although ‘for nothing’ is one thing and ‘to be saved’ another, the salvation that will come upon them is now said to be for nothing.

“There is, then, something that is saved for nothing—plainly, whatever, having been granted resurrection, is not worthy of transformation. For although all flesh has been redeemed in Christ so that it may rise, and although all must stand before his tribunal, nevertheless the glory and honor of rising again are not distributed equally to all. Those, therefore, to whom resurrection alone, and not transformation, has been granted are saved for nothing. In wrath these peoples will be brought down, for whom the salvation of resurrection has been established for the experience of punishment.

“From that wrath the Apostle promises that we shall be rescued when he says: ‘For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, having been justified by his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath’ (Rom. V, 8). Therefore he died for sinners for the salvation of resurrection, but he will save those sanctified by his blood from wrath.”

And Saint Ambrose says in his Epistle to the Corinthians:

“What does it mean to be guilty except to undergo the punishments of the Lord’s death? For he was killed for those who render his benefit void.”

And Saint Hilary says in Book III of *On the Faith* (*On the Trinity*, Book III):

“The Son of God is crucified, but on the cross God conquers human death. Christ, the Son of God, dies, but all flesh is made alive.”

And Saint Augustine says in Book XX of *The City of God*, chapter 6, concerning this passage:

“And here he made no distinction between the good and the evil. For it is good for all to hear his voice and live, passing over to the life of piety from the death of impiety. Concerning this death the Apostle Paul says: ‘Therefore all died, and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and rose again’ (II Cor. III, 14).

“Therefore all were dead in sins, absolutely no one excepted, whether through original sins or through those added by the will, either through ignorance or through knowing and not doing what is just. And for all the dead, the one living man died—that is, the one who was wholly without sin—so that those who live through the remission of sins might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for all because of our sins and rose again because of our justification.

“Thus, believing in him who justifies the impious, and having been justified from impiety, as though made alive from death, we may belong to the first resurrection, which exists now. For those who will be blessed eternally belong to this first resurrection; to the second, of which he spoke immediately afterward, he will teach that both the blessed and the miserable belong. The one is mercy, the other judgment. For this reason it is written in the Psalm: ‘I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord’ (Ps. C, 1).”

From all these people, whether they will belong to mercy or to judgment, let any one of our slanderers who wishes exclude, if he can, the Antichrist about whom we have written above.

Therefore we too wrote from Prosper’s words:

“Christ suffered for all, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion; but because not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion, the matter concerns not the greatness of the price but the portion belonging to those who do not believe.”

Hence Saint Gregory says in Homily 9 on Ezekiel:

“It should be noted that, after he had spoken about the evils of deceased parents, he sent the prophet to their sons, saying: ‘Perhaps they themselves will hear, and perhaps they will cease’ (Ezek. III, 11). What does ‘they themselves’ mean except that their fathers, who died in guilt, refused to hear?”

And Prosper says against the Gauls, action 9:

“The Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world, and the world did not wish to be redeemed, because the darkness did not receive the light. But the darkness received it, to which the Apostle says: ‘You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord’ (Eph. V, 8).”

And this is what that compiler continued by adding in his chapter, though not with the correct meaning:

“It pleases us to hold and teach simply and faithfully, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic truth, that we should regard the price as given for those concerning whom our Lord himself says: ‘Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life. For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life’ (John III, 14).

“Although this requires no explanation, since the Lord so plainly stated everything he wished all to observe that it can be understood by everyone, and no sound-minded person can fail to understand most clearly that the Son of Man was lifted up on the cross for all, and that the only-begotten Son of God was given for the world, so that salvation might be prepared for all in him, yet that everyone who believes in him might not perish—nevertheless, Saint Pope Leo, in his letter to Leo Augustus (Letter 97, chapter 2), briefly and clearly explains the meaning of these testimonies from the holy Gospel, saying:

“‘The shedding of Christ’s blood, the righteous one for the unrighteous, was so rich as a price that, if the entire community of captives believed in its Redeemer, no one would remain held by the devil’s chains.’”

But the Apostle demonstrates what “the entire community of captives” is when he says: “From one came condemnation upon all, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 16). For what captivity can be greater than for the sons of God to become sons of the devil, and for the inhabitants of paradise to become liable to eternal destruction?

[Col. 0286B] The apostolic testimony which the compiler of the chapters appended to confirm his own opinion—that Christ did not suffer for all, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion—helps him in no way, unless the saying applies: “Like a thorn in a drunkard’s hand, so is a parable in the mouth of fools” (Prov. 26:9). For it first wounds the man himself. If he had wished to present a truly sound interpretation to his readers, he would more appropriately have placed these two sentences from Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews in their proper order, just as he took care to set down the Gospel testimonies in the order in which the Evangelist placed them. For the Apostle says in Hebrews: “By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone” (Heb. 2:9). And later: “He was offered once to take away the sins of many” (Heb. 9:28).

Let us therefore see how Saint John Chrysostom—whose testimonies the Apostolic See, and also Saint Augustine, frequently employ in their books to refute heretics—interpreted these two statements. Concerning the first he says:

> “He suffered these things because of the grace of God that was given to us. ‘He did not spare his own Son,’ he says, ‘but delivered him up for us all.’ For what reason? These things were not owed to us; grace accomplished this.”

And a little later:

> “He himself died for all. But what if not all believe? He fulfilled what belonged to him.”

And again, concerning the other testimony:

> “‘He was offered once to take away the sins of many.’ Why ‘of many,’ and not ‘of all’? Because not all believed. He died for all—that is, insofar as it depended upon him; that death has the same efficacy as the perdition of all. But he did not take away the sins of all, because they were unwilling.”

Saint Augustine likewise says in his exposition of Psalm 43:

> “The cross itself was also made for those who were persecuting him. From them afterward came the saints who believed in him whom they had killed.”

And again, in book 6, chapter 1, Against Julian:

> “‘One died for all; therefore all died,’ he says, showing that it could not have happened that he died except for the dead. For by this he proved that all were dead: one died for all. I press the point, insist upon it, force it upon the one who refuses. Receive it; it is salutary. I do not want you to die. One died for all; therefore all died. See that he wished it to follow that all should be understood as dead if he died for all. Since they are not dead in the body, it remains that all are dead in sin, if Christ died for all. Let no one deny it, let no one doubt it, who does not deny or doubt that he is a Christian.”

Saint Dionysius also says in book 3 of *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> “For the divine beatitude proceeds toward all, through divine benevolence, to the communion of those who participate in its divine things; yet it does not become external according to the substance of immovable station and stability.”

Saint Cyprian, in his book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, says:

> “What did he teach concerning unity? He wished one person to pray for all, just as he himself bore all in one.”

[Col. 0287B] Saint Jerome, in book 14 of his commentary on the prophet Isaiah, says:

> “Christ was reckoned among the wicked so that he might redeem the wicked from sin and become all things to all, so that he might save all.”

Augustine likewise, in *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 16 toward the end:

> “Who loved the weak more than he who became weak for all and was crucified in that very weakness for all?”

Ambrose likewise, on Psalm 118:

> “This visible sun rises daily over all. But that mystical sun of righteousness has risen for all, has come for all; he suffered for all and rose again for all. He suffered in order to take away the sin of the world. If anyone does not believe in Christ, he has deprived himself of the universal benefit. But what belongs to the sun preserves its privilege; what belongs to the imprudent excludes from itself the common grace of light.”

Saint Basil of Cappadocia, in his sermon on Psalm 59, says:

> “Moses had sealed the Israelite doorposts with the blood of a lamb; but you have given us a sign: the blood itself of the true and spotless Lamb, who was offered as a sacrifice for the salvation of the whole world.”

Saint Leo likewise, in his letter to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem (Epistle 72):

> “The true generation of Christ is therefore confirmed by the true cross.”

And shortly afterward:

> “In order to restore the life of all, he took up the cause of all and, by paying for all what only he among all did not owe, annulled the force of the ancient bond, so that just as through the guilt of one all had been made sinners, so through the innocence of one all might be made innocent. Righteousness therefore flows into all, wherever human nature has been assumed.”

Saint Gregory, in book 14 of the *Moralia*, chapter 22:

> “‘Fools also despised me.’ As though it were said openly: They themselves also despised me, for whose healing I assumed the foolishness of preaching—that is, so that they might be healed through the flesh of the Word. I was despised by those for whom I did not fear being considered foolish.”

And in book 35, chapter 9:

> “The Lord found no one to console him in his Passion, for, in contempt of death, he endured even those enemies for whom he came to death.”

Saint Cyril, in his third letter to Nestorius, says:

> “In order to overcome death by ineffable power, to become through his flesh the firstborn from the dead, and to make a way for human nature to return to incorruption as the firstfruits of those who sleep, he, as was said above, by the grace of God tasted death for all; and, rising on the third day, he stripped hell.”

The venerable presbyter Bede, in his exposition of the Gospel of Mark:

> “He alone prays for all, just as he alone suffers for everyone; and just as he was made a curse of the cross for us, scourged, and crucified, so he is crucified as though guilty for the salvation of all.”

And in his exposition of the First Epistle of Peter, chapter 1, toward the end:

> “Therefore, just as incorruptible is the price of the Lord’s Passion by which we have been redeemed, so also incorruptible is the sacrament of the sacred font by which we are reborn. These are so joined to one another that one cannot confer salvation upon us without the other. For the Lord redeemed us all together by his sacred blood at the time of his incarnation, so that we too, in our own time, must attain individually, through the regeneration of baptism, participation in that same regeneration.”

Saint Prosper, *Against the Gauls*, ninth recapitulation:

> “He who says that the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world looks not to the power of the sacrament but to the lot of unbelievers, since the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world. Those are excluded from that price who either, delighted by captivity, did not wish to be redeemed, or after redemption returned to the same slavery.”

And in *Against the Vincentians*, first disputation:

> “Since, therefore, because of the one nature of all and the one cause of all, truly assumed by our Lord, all are rightly said to have been redeemed, yet not all have been brought out of captivity, the proper effect of redemption is undoubtedly found among those from whom the prince of this world has been cast out, and who are now not vessels of the devil but members of Christ. His death was not expended upon the human race in such a way that even those who were not to be regenerated belonged to its redemption; rather, what was accomplished through one unique example for all was celebrated in each through a singular sacrament. For the cup of immortality, prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed contain what benefits all; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.”

From these words of Saint Prosper and from the opinions of the Catholic writers cited above, we have extracted the fourth chapter, which is now under discussion, as any reader who wishes to compare them will easily be able to discover. For the present, it is enough to have set down these few testimonies—few in number but powerful in force—to demonstrate the explanation of one Gospel testimony and two apostolic testimonies, until we append further testimonies of orthodox writers, no less strong.

## CHAPTER XXIX. An account is given of two things that, compelled by necessity, we inserted in the words of blessed Prosper in this fourth chapter.

There are two things which, compelled by necessity, we expressed more fully, and concerning which we wish to give an account. The first is this:

> “Just as there is no human being, was none, or will be none whose nature was not assumed in him, so there is no human being, was none, or will be none for whom Christ did not suffer, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion.”

It would have been entirely sufficient to say what Prosper said *Against the Gauls*, in his ninth disputation:

> “There is absolutely no one among all human beings whose nature was not assumed by Christ our Lord.”

And again, in the same work:

> “Since, therefore, the Savior is most rightly said to have been crucified for the redemption of the whole world, because of the true assumption of human nature and because of the common perdition of all in the first man.”

And *Against the Vincentians* (response 1):

> “Since, therefore, because of the one nature of all and the one cause of all, truly assumed by our Lord, all are rightly said to have been redeemed, yet not all have been brought out of captivity.”

We shall explain what necessity there was for our fuller wording. As we stated above, Gothescalcus wrote in his little book to Archbishop Rabanus:

> “Again, all those impious and sinful people for whom that same Son of God neither assumed a body nor poured out prayer, not to mention blood, nor was in any way crucified.”

After this chapter had been written, a certain rustic from his school wrote a booklet against these chapters, [p. 0289A] in which he inserted the following:

> “For if it is carefully considered, we do not know whether it can even be said of every human being that he assumed the nature of all human beings by being born.”

We heard these things said by certain ill-disposed persons from Gothescalcus’s school. Therefore, although our wording does not disagree with Prosper’s words or with the Catholic understanding of orthodox writers, we wrote it more explicitly. We humbly render an account of where we took this wording to all devout persons.

Saint Athanasius, in his letter to Epictetus, did not hesitate to say:

> “In the very Word there was truly and naturally, from Mary and according to the divine Scriptures, what was human; and truly there was the Savior’s body. It was truly so because it was like ours. For Mary was our sister, since we all are from Adam; and no one has ever doubted this.”

Saint Augustine, explaining Psalm 29, says in the preface to his second exposition:

> “‘I will exalt you, Lord, because you have received me.’ Every human being in Christ is one human being, and the unity of Christians is one human being.”

And on Psalm 34:

> “Mary and Adam: Adam died because of sin, and the Lord’s flesh from Mary died because sins were to be destroyed.”

And on Psalm 35:

> “We are born from Adam in order to die; we rise through Christ in order to live forever. When we bear the image of the earthly man, we are human beings; when we bear the image of the heavenly man, we are sons of man, because Christ was called the Son of Man. Adam indeed was a man, but he was not the Son of Man. Therefore those belong to Adam who desire carnal goods. We exhort them to be sons of men and to desire the mercy that is in heaven.”

And on Psalm 37:

> “He assumed our flesh, or rather flesh from us, that is, from the human race.”

Saint Leo, in his letter to Leo Augustus (Epistle 97, chapter 2):

> “What reconciliation could there be by which God might be appeased toward the human race, unless the mediator between God and human beings assumed the cause of all in flesh?”

And again:

> “In order to restore the life of all, he took up the cause of all.”

Saint Hilary, in book 2 of *On the Faith*:

> “For the sake of the human race the Son of God was born from a Virgin and the Holy Spirit. With the latter serving him in this work and his own divine power overshadowing him, he sowed in himself the beginnings of a body and established the origins of flesh, so that, having become man from the Virgin, he might receive in himself the nature of flesh, and through the fellowship of this union the body of the entire human race might exist sanctified in him.”

Saint Ambrose, in *On Paradise*, chapter 10:

> “‘She will be saved,’ he says, ‘through the bearing of children’ (1 Tim. 2:15), among whom she bore Christ. Nor is it without purpose that the woman was made not from the same earth from which Adam was formed, but from Adam’s own rib: so that we might know that man and woman have one bodily nature and one source of the human race.”

And in the hymn frequently used according to ecclesiastical custom, he says to Christ:

> “You are the everlasting Son of the Father.  
> You, intending to assume humanity in order to set it free, did not shrink from the Virgin’s womb.  
> You, having conquered the sting of death, opened the kingdoms of heaven to believers.”

How what Saint Ambrose said—“You, intending to assume humanity in order to set it free”—should be understood is explained by Augustine at the beginning of his book *On the Good of Marriage*. For, as we have heard from our predecessors, when blessed Ambrose composed this hymn at the time of Saint Augustine’s baptism, Augustine composed it with him. Augustine says:

> “Since every human being is a part of the human race, and human nature is a kind of social reality, possessing a great and natural good, namely the power of friendship, God wished all human beings to be created from one person so that they might be held together in fellowship not only by the likeness of their race but also by the bond of kinship.”

This hymn also explains that Christ assumed the nature of all in order to liberate all, but opened the kingdoms of heaven to believers.

Saint Augustine says in *On the Predestination of the Saints*:

> “Why is grace different where nature is common?”

There are many other passages, which we collected in the booklets mentioned above against the same people.

These things have been said concerning the first expression, which was seemingly unnecessary but not unreasonable. The second matter is what we added more explicitly when, in the fourth chapter, we wrote:

> “But because not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion, this does not pertain to the greatness and abundance of the price, but to the lot of unbelievers and of those who do not believe with the faith that works through love.”

We added to Prosper’s words the phrase “of those who do not believe with the faith that works through love.” We added this because Gothescalcus wrote in his aforementioned booklet to Archbishop Rabanus:

> “Therefore, what I most faithfully believe, I speak with complete confidence, and with the utmost certainty and benefit I confess, and I proclaim most truly: that our almighty God, creator and maker of all creatures, has deigned to be the gracious restorer and refreshment of all the elect alone; but he willed eternally to be the Savior, Redeemer, and Crown-giver of none of the reprobate.”

And to a certain accomplice of his:

> “Far be it from me even to dream, much less once to whisper, that the ancient serpent could carry away with him to perish eternally any of those for whose redemption the blood of his Son, our Lord God, so precious to God the Father, was poured out. Amen.”

When we read these words, we understood the meaning of that devilish man, who wished to empty the abundance of Christ’s blood, that is, the price of our redemption. Hence he also wrote to the same accomplice:

> “For he purchased them by the sacrament of baptism, but he did not undergo the cross for them, nor endure death, nor shed blood.”

Therefore, we truly and faithfully rejected the blame—which he falsely and perniciously wished to turn against the abundant redemption accomplished by Christ’s blood—upon the scantiness and uncertainty, indeed the unbelief, of unbelievers and of those who do not believe, supported by the authority of the sacred Scriptures and Catholic writers. For this reason we inserted:

> “It pertains to the lot of unbelievers and of those who do not believe with the faith that works through love.”

That is, because this alone is the faith by which believers are saved. But demons also believe and tremble; and an unbeliever is not without faith, as Saint Gregory says in book 4 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 21:

> “I say boldly that without faith not even an unbeliever lives.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Unbelievers also have faith—but would that they had faith in God; if they did, they would not be unbelievers.”

The venerable presbyter Bede, in his exposition of the Epistle of James, chapter 2, says:

> “Thus faith also, if it does not have works, is dead in itself, if it is not enlivened by works of love by which it may live again. Nor is the Lord’s statement contrary to this: ‘Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved’ (Matt. 16:16). For it must be understood there that only the person truly believes who practices through works what he believes.”

Hence Saint Gregory says in his twenty-ninth homily on the Gospel:

> “‘Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature: whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.’ Perhaps, he says, each person may say to himself: ‘I have already believed; I shall be saved.’ He speaks truly if he holds the faith by works.”

He proceeds with the remaining matters there, which are well known to many.

There is also a corresponding testimony which this opponent of ours composed in order to reproach us, saying:

> “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16).

For true faith is, as Gregory says in the aforementioned homily, “the faith that does not contradict in conduct what it says in words.” Hence Paul says of certain false believers:

> “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. 1:16).

Concerning the Gospel testimony proposed by our opponent:

> “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:14),

the venerable presbyter Bede says in homily 56:

> “Just as those who looked upon the bronze serpent lifted up as a sign were healed for a time from temporal death, and from the wound inflicted by the bite of the serpents, so those who behold the mystery of the Lord’s Passion by believing, confessing, and sincerely imitating it are saved forever from every death which they had incurred in soul and body alike by sinning.”

Hence it is rightly added:

> “So that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”

The meaning of this statement is clear: whoever believes in Christ not only escapes the destruction of punishments but also receives eternal life, as Gregory says in the aforementioned homily:

> “Then we are truly faithful if we fulfill by our works what we promise in words.”

Hence John says:

> “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4).

Prosper likewise says in chapter 324 of the *Sentences*:

> “Therefore, you who rejoice in receiving baptism, live in the holiness of the new man; and, holding the faith that works through love, possess the good that you do not yet have, so that what you have may benefit you.”

Bede likewise, in his exposition of the Epistle of James:

> “‘You believe that God is one. You do well; even the demons believe and tremble.’ Do not suppose that you are doing something great by believing that there is one God. The demons do this too: they believe not only in God the Father but also in the Son of God.”

Hence Luke says:

> “Demons also came out of many, crying out and saying, ‘You are the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.”

And a little later:

> “Only those who love God know how to believe in God; they are not Christians in name only, but also in deeds and life. For without love faith is empty; with love it is the faith of a Christian, without love it is the faith of a demon.”

He continues with the matters that follow there.

The venerable presbyter Bede also explains, in his homily on the Gospel—homily 1, *On the Saints*—how the faithful and the unbelieving understand baptism. He discusses the passage more fully and in a Catholic manner concerning “a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus,” and says:

> “Only this mother, the Church, which gives birth, knows. To the eyes of the foolish, however, the person who emerges from the font seems to be just as he entered it, and the whole ceremony appears to be mere play.”

The blessed apostle Peter says:

> “Baptism, corresponding to this, now saves you—not as a removal of dirt from the flesh, but as an appeal to God for a good conscience” (1 Pet. 3:21).

From this statement Bede says, in his exposition of the First Epistle of Peter, chapter 3:

> “For where is there a good conscience unless there is also an unfeigned faith? The Apostle Paul teaches that the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5).

And again, in his exposition of the Epistle of John, chapter 4:

> “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God” (1 John 4:2).

He says:

> “Here he requires not only confession of Catholic faith but also of good works, which are performed through love. Otherwise, some heretics, many schismatics, and many false Catholics confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, but deny their confession by their deeds, because they do not have love. Love brought the Son of God into the flesh; therefore whoever does not have love denies that he came in the flesh. Such a person is shown not to have the Spirit from God.”

And again:

> “‘This is the victory that conquers the world, our faith’ (1 John 5:4)—namely, the faith that works through love.”

Bede likewise, in his exposition of the Epistle of James, chapter 2:

> “Even in the present time, if someone who has recently come to the faith receives baptism and, intending with all his heart to keep God’s commandments, immediately departs from this life, he departs justified by faith without works, because, by God’s providence, he did not have the time for doing works by which to prove his faith. But those who, after receiving the sacraments, live on for a long time and do not take care to persist in good works must be reminded of what blessed James, having proposed the example of Abraham’s faith together with his works, immediately adds: ‘You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone’ (Jas. 2:24).”

What he calls “by works” signifies “by works of faith,” because no one can possess perfect works without faith; many, however, may possess faith without works if they have no time for works. Concerning such people it is said:

> “He was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding or deceit should beguile his soul” (Wis. 4:11).

But even in such persons faith itself is a work, as it is written in the Gospel:

> “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent” (John 6:29).

The person who believes in him performs this work, because this very act of believing is true faith, which works through love: believing in the one who justifies the ungodly, whose every work is in faith. Without this faith no one approaches the sacrament of baptism in such a way as to be renewed by the sacrament, because the Holy Spirit, by whom we are adopted as sons of discipline, flees what is false and withdraws from thoughts that lack understanding.

Hence Saint Ambrose says in his Epistle to the Galatians:

> “For without the Spirit the name of sons was not complete.”

And again, in his book *On the Sacraments*:

> “In baptism the Spirit renews the mind; the water contributes to the washing; the blood pertains to the price. The water of the sacred font cleanses us, the Lord’s blood redeems us, and the Spirit makes us sons of God through adoption.”

Concerning this, Saint Gregory says in homily 30 on the Gospel:

> “The Holy Spirit himself is love. Hence John says: ‘God is love’ (1 John 4:8). Therefore whoever desires God with an undivided mind already possesses the one whom he loves. No one could love God if he did not possess the one whom he loves.”

Behold how, even in baptism, both in little ones and in adults, the faith that works through love is active, as Saint Augustine says in book 4 *Against Julian*:

> “But perhaps you say: ‘Then infants who do not believe—or, as you have put it, who do not possess the faith that works through love—are not reborn in Christ, nor renewed in Christ through faith in Christ’s blood in baptism, nor incorporated into Christ.’ Answer us, if you please: are they carried by their parents to the church through faith or unbelief? Are they offered by their parents to their sponsors through love of salvation or hatred of perdition? Are they likewise offered by the sponsors to the priests, and exsufflated and exorcized by the priests, so that they may be rescued from the power of the devil? Are they baptized into Christ’s death so that, planted in the likeness of his death, they may certainly die to sin? Whether you wish it or not, you will answer under the greatest constraint that all these things are done by the faith that works through love, unless you decide presumptuously to lie with an impudent face.”

And again, in book 6, chapter 4:

> “For how does it benefit him to enter the kingdom of God if each person receives what he has done, unless what was done by another—that is, believed by another—also belongs to the infant? Therefore, just as what he believes belongs to him so that he may receive the good, namely, the kingdom of God, so also, even if he has not believed, the judgment of condemnation belongs to him, because the Gospel itself declares: ‘Whoever does not believe will be condemned’ (Mark 16:16).”

And shortly afterward:

> “It is another’s work when he believes through another, just as it was another’s work when he sinned in another. We do not doubt that every sin is cleansed in baptism, but each person is cleansed by being reborn. Therefore what only regeneration removes, generation does not cease to transmit.”

The venerable presbyter Bede likewise, in his exposition of the Gospel of Mark:

> “We should certainly observe how much each person’s own faith will avail before God, since another’s faith availed so much that the whole man—namely, inwardly and outwardly already saved—rose at once, and the sins of some were forgiven through the merit of others.”

For this reason we also set down several examples in the booklets so often mentioned, against our detractors; we now consider it superfluous to heap them together here. Especially since anyone who deigns to read those books will be able to recognize their contents quickly and without difficulty, gathered together as though in little bundles.

## CHAPTER XXX. Except for these two almost syllabic statements, we placed nothing in this chapter except what we excerpted from the words of blessed Prosper.

Now, setting aside these two additions, concerning which we have given an account, let us see whether, as the saying goes, we have deviated by a crosswise fingernail from the meaning of blessed Prosper in our composition of the fourth chapter.

Prosper says in the eighth disputation, response 9, *Against the Gauls*:

> “There is absolutely no one among all human beings whose nature was not assumed by Christ our Lord.”

And again, Prosper *Against the Gauls*:

> “Since, therefore, the Savior is most rightly said to have been crucified for the redemption of the whole world, because of the true assumption of human nature and because of the common perdition of all in the first man.”

And *Against the Vincentians*, response 1:

> “Yet not all human beings have been brought out of captivity.”

We wrote:

> “Thus there is no human being for whom he did not suffer, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion.”

Prosper, in the ninth recapitulation *Against the Gauls*, sentence 9:

> “He who says that the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world looks not to the power of the sacrament but to the lot of unbelievers, since the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world.”

We wrote:

> “But because not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion, this does not pertain to the greatness and abundance of the price, but to the lot of unbelievers.”

Prosper, in the first disputation *Against the Vincentians*, response 1:

> “For the cup of immortality, prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed contain what benefits all; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.”

We wrote:

> “For the cup of human salvation, prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed contain what benefits all; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.”

If in these words we altered any syllable, but not the meaning, it happened neither through deliberate intent nor through arrogance, but because we did not have the book of that same blessed Prosper at hand. Nor, as you yourselves know better, could we obtain sufficient time for it to be brought, because of the urgency imposed by your Christian devotion and by our venerable lord, the glorious King Charles. Thus we were compelled by a most worthy constraint, following the example from Jerome’s book *On the Best Kind of Translation*: you were seeking not so much the words of another’s composition as the Catholic proofs of a sincere and episcopal conscience.

After the foregoing, concerning which we have given an account, the compiler of the chapters added in order:

> “Moreover, we utterly reject from the pious hearing of the faithful the nineteen chapters concluded by a certain Scot with utterly inept and mendacious syllogisms. In them not an argument of faith but rather a fabrication of perfidy is evident. They were constructed by no philosophical art whatsoever, as some arrogantly boast, but were confused through empty deceit and the most incompetent deception. And, so that such things and similar things may be avoided, we forbid them in every respect by the authority of the Holy Spirit.”

We find that some material was removed from this chapter from what you entrusted to us three years ago, as we mentioned above, at the village of Nielfa in the diocese of Rouen. For there it is written:

> “Moreover, the four chapters which, through the counsel of our brothers, were accepted with insufficient foresight, because of their uselessness, or even harmfulness, and their error contrary to the truth; and also the nineteen other chapters concluded with utterly inept and mendacious syllogisms…”

The rest is as this compiler has now arranged it here.

We therefore wonder: if this compiler participated in assembling those chapters, why did he then remove from this one what he had inserted into them so diligently? And if this compiler did not participate in those chapters, how did he deviate from or alter them so consistently—more consistently than anywhere else except in this passage and in the following chapter, from which he removed an apostolic statement, as we shall show in its proper place—without straying by even a hair’s breadth from their harmonious meaning?

If he confidently believes that he can and ought justly and reasonably to rebuke us, remembering that Paul resisted Peter to his face (Gal. 2:11), he should bring forward the fullness of his writings and authoritatively resist what we had said incorrectly. But if, with his conscience reproaching him, he wished to correct an error and therefore erased these things from the middle, then he ought also to have completely removed his earlier errors and our subsequent unjust accusations.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the nineteen chapters which the compiler of the chapters given to us by royal authority mentions in reproach of us, and concerning other chapters, whether those which we found written here and there or those which we heard had been invented by questioning certain frivolous persons.

Concerning the nineteen chapters which he mentions, we now refrain from writing, having been called away to other occupations. Since we have heard that those who criticized them are writing against them, we await the outcome, until we see whether anyone attempts to defend them or what he will attempt to assert while writing against them.

Nevertheless, we received other chapters, seventy-seven in number, from someone who offered them to us. Their heading is as follows:

> “Recapitulation of the entire work. The first chapter is as follows:
>
> ‘You say that every question can be solved by the fourfold division of the four rules of the whole of philosophy. We answer that neither that fourfold division nor any opinions of worldly wisdom are sufficient for solving every question without the grace of God and faith, which works through love, together with sincere zeal and knowledge of the holy Scriptures.
>
> “The last one:
>
> ‘You say that you anathematize those who speak of a twofold predestination or express predestinations in the plural. We answer that this is more fitting for you, since you attack for so long the truth of God’s judgments, deny the faith of truthful statements, utterly corrupt the most faithful teachings of the Fathers, who are worthy of all reverence, and furthermore proclaim as a new inventor of falsehoods things which no one before is found ever to have said or written.’”

Many claim that their authors—or rather their fellow combatants, and in certain matters opponents of the truth—are Bishop Prudentius and John Scotus Eriugena. But we neither wish to believe nor to affirm what we cannot demonstrate by more certain evidence.

For the present, however, we have not wished to involve ourselves in their disputes, until we learn more clearly to what end, whoever they may be, they have carried their contention, remembering the proverb of the Wise One:

> “Like one who seizes a dog by the ears is one who meddles in another person’s quarrel” (Prov. 26:17).

There are also others who, delighting in novel expressions and thereby procuring for themselves empty little rumors, speak against the truth of the Catholic faith. Namely, they say that the Deity is threefold; that the sacraments of the altar are not the true body and true blood of the Lord, but only a memorial of his true body and blood; that angels are bodily by nature; that the human soul is not in the body; and that there are no infernal punishments other than the tormenting memory of sins in the conscience.

Perhaps those who do not take care to see the Lord after the universal judgment has ended are disputing with biting contentiousness how he ought to be seen. And there are many other matters against which it will be necessary for the orthodox rulers of the Catholic Church to keep watch with diligent attention.

But also in the aforementioned synod, among the chapters that you gave us, we found seven appended in the little booklets of one of our fellow priests—not rules in truth, but in name. For, as we find written there, they are not rules of faith, but nets stretched out toward unbelief for the simple; and they are believed to belong to the same author whose chapters were given to our humility by your loftiness, because their words and meanings agree. Their beginning is as follows:

> “First of all, and with greater insistence, insofar as it now occurs to the memory of our littleness, we believe that seven certain rules of faith must be set forth and commended. They proceed from the authority of the divine Scriptures and have been most diligently commended by holy and orthodox Fathers: namely, concerning divine foreknowledge and predestination. Every Catholic must hold them with complete fidelity, and whoever thinks contrary to them must be shown not to think catholically.”

And thus, through those seven—not true rules, but fabricated little rules, like fortune-tellers are accustomed to put honey at the mouth of a vessel and poisons in its lower parts—he places before us mutilated words of the orthodox and reduces the conclusion of his understanding to this proposition: that just as the elect are predestined to life, so also the reprobate are predestined by God to death; and that, according to his foreknowledge, God condemned those whom he foreknew would persevere in iniquity and ungodliness, and predestined those same people to perish.

In attempting to imitate Isidore, who extracted seven rules from the sacred Scriptures concerning Tichonius and other wise men, he babbled rather tastelessly and implausibly, asking what he might say who, unable to speak, could not keep silent. We have considered it superfluous to write about these matters, because the first, second, and third, or fourth, webs of spiders—as though more specifically—are shown by Saint Augustine, in *On Rebuke and Grace* and in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, and by Saint Prosper against the Januarians, to be utterly without force. Blessed Augustine, in *On the Predestination of the Saints* against the ancient Predestinarians, and Saint Gregory, in the twenty-fifth book of the *Moralia on Job*, completely and altogether annihilate the fifth of these absurdities and the seventh rule. The sixth, as it is called, blessed Augustine blows away like the smoke of porridge, among other places in his books *On Grace and Free Will*, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, *On the Predestination of Grace*, and *To the Presbyter Sixtus*, and makes it wholly disappear.

Our own mediocrity has shown, in the three preceding little books and in this one, on the authority of the holy Fathers, that these inventions are utterly false. What is true concerning the foreknowledge and predestination of God we have sufficiently gathered both there and here from the judgments of the Catholic Fathers; so much so that this collection ought to suffice for anyone who desires the truth. But for those whom so great a compilation does not satisfy, it is certain that even more will not benefit them, and that they are eager to entrust themselves more to falsehoods than to truths.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the conclusion of the compiler’s chapter, and on the three matters that we have undertaken to append to this chapter; one of them is that the crowds who preceded the Lord’s coming and those who follow it proclaim with one and the same faith, “Hosanna,” because we believe that we are saved by the grace of God just as they were

[Col. 0298A]

Finally, in this conclusion, the contriver of these chapters brought the present chapter to an end, saying:

> “We also judge that the introducers of new doctrines must be chastised, lest they be struck more severely.”

And we likewise agree. Saint Augustine took care to chastise the ancient Predestinarians—the introducers, that is, of new doctrines—most sufficiently, faithfully, and fatherly in his books *On Rebuke and Grace*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, as well as in the book *Hypomnesticon* and in *On the Predestination of Grace*. Then Saint Coelestine, by apostolic authority, at the urging of Saint Prosper and by synodal judgment, rebuked and restrained them. Now too, the reintroducers of these new expressions must be chastised, rebuked, and restrained by that same authority of the holy Scriptures and by the judgments produced by Catholic and ancient Fathers.

Therefore we shall append three matters to this chapter. One is that the crowds who preceded the Lord’s coming and those who follow it (*Homily* 17) proclaim with one and the same faith, saying: “Hosanna,” that is, as Saint Gregory explains in his treatise on Ezekiel, “Save us in the highest.” For, as Peter says, “We believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord, just as they were” (Acts XV, 11).

Next, we shall show how Catholic men teach, on the authority of the holy Scriptures, that Christ suffered generally for all. From this we shall explain how orthodox and ancient teachers demonstrate from authentic Scriptures that we must understand the matter discriminately: although Christ suffered for all, not all have been redeemed for eternal salvation by the price of the world—that is, by the mystery of his passion. Those are strangers to this price who either, delighting in captivity, were unwilling to be redeemed, or, after redemption, returned to the same servitude.

So too our present critic, without a complete understanding, placed in this chapter concerning those who were unwilling to be redeemed:

> “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John III, 16).

For, as the venerable presbyter Bede explains:

> “The same Lord and our Redeemer, existing as the Son of God before the ages, was made the Son of Man at the end of the ages, so that he who by the power of his divinity had created us to enjoy the blessedness of life might himself, through the frailty of our humanity, restore us to receive the life that we had lost.”

Blessed Augustine likewise says in Psalm 36, sermon 3:

> “The Lord himself, in his body, which is the Church, was younger in the earliest times, and behold, he has now grown old. You know, recognize, and understand that you have been placed in this body, and that you have believed in this way: Christ is our head; we are the body of that head. Are we alone to have Christ as our head, and not also those who existed before us—all the righteous who have existed from the beginning of the world? They believed that he would come, whom we now believe has come, and they too were saved in faith in him, in whom we are saved. Thus he might be the head of the entire city of Jerusalem, with all the faithful counted together from beginning to end, together also with the legions and armies of angels, so that there might be one city under one king and one province under one emperor: happy and in perpetual peace and salvation, praising God without end, blessed without end.”

And the venerable presbyter Bede, in his *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke* (chapter 2), says:

> “You see that the righteous not only of the New Testament but also of the Old Testament desired to be released from the body in hope of future life.”

And shortly afterward:

> “By these words he plainly reveals how great a consolation at the end he hopes to receive amid present calamities. He desires that end to come in the meantime, saying: ‘For my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples’ (Luke II, 31). He says: ‘What you foresaw and prepared so that all nations, peoples, and languages might afterward behold it in mind and faith, and seek it in hope and love, I now, after long desiring it, behold as your salvation with the eyes both of flesh and of the heart.’ The light of God’s salvation for both peoples—that is, Christ—is prepared by God the Father. Yet he is more especially the glory of Israel, to whom, long awaited and announced from the beginning, he came. For the Gentiles he is called a revelation, since he deigned to visit, reveal, and illuminate the eyes of their minds, already sunk into profound blindness and raised by no hope toward the Lord’s coming.”

And again:

> “I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke X, 24). Abraham rejoiced that he might see Christ’s day; he saw it and was glad. Isaiah and Micah also, and many other prophets, saw the glory of the Lord; therefore they were called ‘Seers.’”

And in his homily on the same Evangelist:

> “There is a common and most joyful promise for all believers, whether those who preceded the time of his incarnation by their birth, or those who saw him in the flesh, or we who believe after his ascension. He says: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’” (Matthew V, 8).

And Saint Gregory, in Homily 18:

> “For the Lord, in order to instruct his people, as though cultivating his vineyard, never ceased to send workers at any time. First through the Fathers, afterward through the teachers of the Law and the prophets, and finally through the apostles, while cultivating the conduct of his people, he labored as though through workers in the cultivation of his vineyard. The worker of the morning, the third hour, the sixth, and the ninth signifies that ancient Hebrew people which, in its elect, from the very beginning of the world, while striving to worship God with right faith, did not cease, as it were, to labor in the cultivation of the vineyard. Yet whoever, in whatever degree or measure, stood forth with right faith and good action was a worker of this vineyard.”

And again:

> “How many Fathers existed before the Law, and how many under the Law? Yet those who were called at the Lord’s coming reached the kingdom of heaven without any delay. Therefore those who labored at the eleventh hour received the same denarius that those received who had waited with their whole desire and had labored from the first hour, because those who came to the Lord at the end of the world obtained an equal reward of eternal life with those who had been called from the beginning of the world.”

And again:

> “But because the ancient Fathers, however justly they lived until the Lord’s coming, were not led into the kingdom unless he descended who, by the intervention of his death, would open the gates of paradise to human beings, their very murmuring consisted in this: that they had lived rightly in order to receive the kingdom, and yet had been delayed for a long time from receiving it. For those whom the places of hell, although tranquil, received after they had completed their righteousness, it was certainly both laboring in the vineyard and murmuring. Thus, after their murmuring, those receive the denarius who, after long periods in hell, reached the joys of the kingdom. But we who came at the eleventh hour do not murmur after our labor, and we receive the denarius, because, coming into this world after the Mediator’s arrival, we are led into the kingdom as soon as we depart from the body, and without delay receive what the ancient Fathers merited to receive only after a great delay.”

And Saint Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved, just as they were” (Acts XV, 11).

Hence Bede:

> “If, then, they—that is, the Fathers—believed that they were saved through the grace of the Lord, unable to bear the yoke of the ancient Law, it is evident that this is the grace that caused the ancient righteous to live, because ‘the righteous person lives by faith.’ Therefore the sacraments could be different according to the diversity of times, yet they returned most harmoniously to the unity of the same faith.”

And in the First Epistle of Peter (chapter 1):

> “Through those who preached the Gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven” (1 Peter I, 12).

He had said above that the prophets foretold by the Spirit of Christ his sufferings and the glories that would follow; now he says that the apostles announce the same things to them by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Hence it is clear that the same Spirit of Christ was formerly in the prophets and afterward in the apostles. Therefore they preached to both peoples the same faith in Christ’s passion and subsequent glory: the former that it was still to come, the latter that it had already come. Accordingly, there is one Church, one part of which preceded the Lord’s coming in the flesh and the other followed it.

And again (chapter 2):

> “Honor to you who believe; but to those who do not believe, ‘the stone that the builders rejected’” (1 Peter II, 7).

Just as they rejected him when they were building their deeds, unwilling to place him in the foundation of their hearts, so they too may be rejected by him at his coming, since he will not then wish to receive into the building of his house, which is in heaven, those who rejected him. This distinction between the honor of believers and the rejection of unbelievers extends this far.

And again (chapter 5):

> “In which he came in the spirit and preached to those who were imprisoned in the flesh, who had once been unbelieving” (1 Peter III, 19).

He who in our times came in the flesh and preached the way of life to the world also, before the Flood, came in the spirit and preached to those who were then unbelieving and had lived according to the flesh. For he was in Noah and the other saints who existed then through the Holy Spirit, and through their good conduct he preached to the wicked people of that age, so that they might turn to better things. He calls them imprisoned because they were heavily burdened by carnal desires. Hence Scripture says of them: “For all flesh had corrupted its way.”

When he says “in which,” he signifies “in that which he had said previously,” namely, “to offer us to God.” For even then, if any had wished to believe the Lord’s preaching, which he displayed through the life of the faithful, he rejoiced to offer them also to God the Father.

Behold, concerning the peoples who preceded the Lord’s incarnation, those who did not believe are without excuse, because they were not without preaching of salvation, nor without the sacraments of salvation by which they might be saved. By these Abel was saved, offering Christ in the lamb; Enoch, believing through the sole invocation of faith; Noah, who both preached in the construction of the ark and offered sacrifices. The ark bore the type of the Church, and the water of the Flood was a figure of baptism.

Hence it is also written in the same epistle:

> “Those who were once unbelieving, when the patience of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being constructed” (1 Peter III, 20).

For the very patience of God was his preaching, when Noah, devoting himself to the work of the ark for a hundred years, showed by the daily execution of his work what was going to happen to the world. Hence Paul says:

> “Or do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Romans II, 4).

In this ark, “a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water.” The baptism that now saves you is of corresponding form. He says that the form of baptism corresponds to the ark and the waters of the Flood: when the whole world perished, a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water, because compared with those who perish, the number of the elect is much smaller.

Therefore, because the water of the Flood did not save those placed outside the ark but killed them, it undoubtedly prefigured every heretic who, although possessing the sacrament of baptism, is plunged into hell by those very waters—not by other waters—by which the ark is lifted toward heaven.

Abraham sacrificed Christ in his son. Melchizedek, in the figure of the bread of eternal life and the cup of perpetual salvation, offered bread and wine. Moses sacrificed the paschal lamb, for “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.” Aaron entered the Holy Place once a year with the blood of a calf. Hence Paul says:

> “Christ, appearing as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by hand, entered once into the Holy Place through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption” (Hebrews IX, 11).

Hence Ambrose, in book I of *On the Holy Spirit*, in the preface, explaining the statement in the Book of Judges concerning Gideon, says that Christ was prefigured by the calf:

> “He himself also sacrificed another seven-year-old calf to God. By this act he most clearly revealed that after the Lord’s coming all the sacrifices of paganism would have to be abolished, and that only the sacrifice of the Lord’s passion should be offered to God as the religion of the people. For that calf was a type of Christ, in whom dwelt the fullness of the seven spiritual virtues, as Isaiah says. Abraham also offered this calf when he saw the Lord’s day and rejoiced. This is the one who was offered now under the type of a kid, now of a sheep, now of a calf: of a kid because it is a sacrifice for sins; of a sheep because it is a voluntary victim; of a calf because it is an immaculate victim.”

And:

> “All our fathers were baptized in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink.”

Hence Augustine, in his exposition of the Gospel according to John (tractate 26):

> “‘Your fathers ate manna and died’ (John VI, 49). Moses and Aaron, and the other holy people who were among the people, ate manna and did not die, because they understood the visible food spiritually and hungered spiritually. Others, however, ate and remained in unbelief. So the Jews heard Christ speaking, but they did not understand his words spiritually. Therefore he said to them: ‘Your fathers ate manna in the desert and died.’ By what death, if not the death of unbelief? For the saints who were among them also died the common death. Thus the Lord signified spiritual death, not bodily death, in these words: ‘Your fathers ate manna and died’—not because the manna was evil, but because they ate it evilly. ‘This is the bread that came down from heaven’ (John VI, 50). The manna signified this bread; the sacraments of God’s altar signify this bread.”

And behold, we have spoken of the people who preceded the Lord’s coming. Let us speak of the people who follow his coming.

Likewise, in the First Epistle of Peter:

> “Knowing that you were redeemed from your futile way of life inherited from your fathers, not with perishable gold or silver, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Peter I, 18).

Hence Bede, on the First Epistle of Peter (chapter 2):

> “The greater the price by which you were redeemed from the corruption of carnal life, the more you ought to fear lest, by returning to the corruption of vices, you offend the minds of your Redeemer. You have been reborn not from corruptible seed but from incorruptible, through the word of the living and everlasting God. The same is found in the Gospel of John concerning those who believe in his name: ‘They were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God’ (John I, 13). Therefore, just as the price of the Lord’s passion by which we were redeemed is incorruptible, so also the sacrament of the sacred font by which we are reborn is incorruptible. These are so joined to one another that one cannot confer salvation on us without the other, because the Lord redeemed us all at the time of his incarnation by his sacred blood in such a way that we too, in our own time, must individually attain participation in that same rebirth through baptismal regeneration. From this it follows that just as flesh that will perish is born from corruptible seed, so through water consecrated by the word of God a life that knows no end is bestowed upon us.”

And again (chapter 2):

> “So that, by learning well, you may reach the nourishment of the living bread that came down from heaven—that is, through the sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation, by which you were reborn and by which you were nourished, you may reach the contemplation of the divine majesty.”

But since there are some who, after the Lord’s coming, have existed before us and will exist afterward, who do not receive what they hear, it is likewise written there:

> “To those who stumble at the word and do not believe in that for which they were appointed.”

They stumble at the word who, precisely because they have happened to hear the word of God, are offended in mind, since they are unwilling to believe what they hear. To magnify their folly, he added: “and do not believe in that for which they were appointed,” because human beings were appointed for this—that is, were naturally made for this—that they should believe God and obey his will, as Solomon testifies when he says: “Fear God and observe his commandments, for this is the whole human being” (Ecclesiastes XII, 13). That is, every human being was naturally made for this: to fear God and obey his commandments.

Some, however, do not preserve the gift that they receive. Hence in the same Epistle the Apostle admonishes them, saying:

> “Beloved, I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Peter II, 11).

Bede, in the same place:

> “Up to this point blessed Peter has instructed the Church generally, explaining either the benefits by which divine mercy deigned to call us to salvation, or the gifts by which it once deigned to honor the Jews and now honors us. From this point he carefully exhorts various kinds of believers not to make themselves unworthy of so great a grace of the Spirit by living according to the flesh, lest those who have been distinguished by the royal and priestly name, overcome by the evils of vices, degenerate from the glory of the nobility granted or promised to them.”

And again:

> “You have been called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Galatians V, 13). We are rightly called free because through baptism we have been released from the bonds of sins, redeemed from demonic servitude, and made children of God. Yet we have not received, as a gift of freedom, a greater ability or license to sin. Rather, if we sin, freedom is immediately lost and we become servants of sin. Whoever thinks that he received freedom from the Lord for the purpose of sinning more freely turns his freedom into a covering for wickedness.”

And again it is written in the same Epistle:

> “For you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing” (1 Peter III, 9).

And yet, among those called to blessing, among the redeemed and justified, people perish every day. Hence Paul also says to the Corinthians:

> “And the weak person will perish through your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died” (1 Corinthians VIII, 11).

Hence Saint Ambrose:

> “The weak person will perish if, in your conscience, he eats what has been sacrificed contrary to faith in the one God. That is, your knowledge kills him when he sees you doing what he understands otherwise; and you will be the occasion of the death of the brother whom Christ allowed himself to be crucified in order to redeem.”

But just as some of the Fathers ate manna and were saved from spiritual death, while others ate and died, so, as Paul says to the Corinthians, it happened after the Lord’s passion, happens every day, and will continue to happen: some approach the Lord’s table unworthily, while others approach devoutly; some eat and drink judgment upon themselves, while others receive it for their salvation.

Concerning the earlier people, the venerable presbyter Bede says in Homily 8:

> “Because circumcision under the Law performed the same saving remedy against the wound of original sin that baptism now performs in the time of revealed grace—except that they could not yet enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom until he came who gave the blessing, he who gave the Law, so that God of gods might be seen in Zion—they waited happily in hope for entry into the peace above, consoled after death by blessed rest in Abraham’s bosom.”

Therefore both purifications—the circumcision under the Law and baptism in the Gospel—were established by grace for the removal of the first transgression. And lest the gifts of heavenly concern be lacking to anyone in any age of the passing world, those also who, from the beginning of the world until the time when circumcision was given, or after circumcision had been given, pleased God among other nations, commended their own souls and those of their people to the Creator either by offerings of sacrifices or by the virtue of faith alone, and took care to be released from the bonds of the first guilt.

“For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews XI, 6); and, as it is written elsewhere, “The righteous shall live by faith” (Romans I, 17).

And again, in Homily 13, concerning the people who followed the Lord’s passion until the end of the age:

> “He loved us,” he says, “and washed us from our sins in his blood.” He not only washed us from our sins in his blood when he gave his blood for us on the cross, or when one of us was washed in the waters of baptism into the mystery of his most holy passion; rather, he also takes away the sins of the world daily and washes us from our daily sins in his blood, when the remembrance of that blessed passion is repeated at the altar, when the substance of bread and wine is transferred into the sacrament of his body and blood by the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit. Thus his body and blood are not poured out and slain by the hands of unbelievers to their destruction, but are received by the mouths of the faithful for their salvation.
