> “The paschal lamb under the Law rightly displayed a figure of this. Once freeing the people from Egyptian servitude, it used to sanctify that same people every year by its sacrifice in memory of that liberation, until he came to whom such a victim bore witness. Offered to the Father for us as a sacrifice and an offering of sweet fragrance, he transferred the mystery of his passion, after the lamb had been removed, into the substance of bread and wine, having become a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. His blood opened the gates of the kingdom to the ancient elect.”

And Leo, in Homily 3 on the Nativity of the Lord:

> “The truth of redemption had to be added for mortal beings, and the origin corrupted from the beginning had to be reborn through new beginnings. A victim had to be offered for reconciliation, one that would both share our race and be free from our contamination, so that this purpose of God—by which it pleased him to destroy the sin of the world through the birth and passion of Jesus Christ—might extend to the ages of all generations. The mysteries, varied according to the order of the times, ought not to disturb us but rather strengthen us, since the faith by which we live has been different in no age.

> “Let the complaints of those, therefore, cease who, reviling the divine dispensations with impious murmuring, complain of the lateness of the Lord’s birth, as though what was accomplished in the final age of the world had not been bestowed in former times. For the incarnation of the Word conferred, when it was to be accomplished, what it conferred when accomplished, and the sacrament of human salvation never ceased in any antiquity. What the apostles preached, the prophets had also announced; what had always been believed was not fulfilled late.

> “The wisdom and goodness of God, and the delay of the saving work, made us more capable of his calling, so that what had been announced through so many signs, voices, and mysteries over so many ages would not be obscure in the days of the Gospel. The Savior’s birth, which would surpass every miracle and every measure of human understanding, would produce a more steadfast faith in us because its proclamation had preceded it both earlier and more frequently.

> “God therefore did not provide for human affairs by a new plan or by late compassion, but from the foundation of the world established one and the same cause of salvation for all. For the grace by which the entire company of the saints has always been justified was increased when Christ was born; it did not begin then. And this sacrament of great piety, by which the whole world has now been filled, was so powerful even in its signs that those who believed it promised received no less through it than those who received it as a gift.”

And Saint Augustine, in *On Nature and Grace* (chapter 43):

> “The faith that saved the ancient righteous saves us also: faith in the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus; faith in his blood, faith in his cross, faith in his death and resurrection. Therefore, possessing the same spirit of faith, we too believe, and therefore we speak.”

And the venerable presbyter Bede, in his exposition of Luke’s Gospel (chapter 1):

> “To turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children and the unbelieving toward the prudence of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people.”

To turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children is to pour the spiritual knowledge of the ancient saints into the peoples by preaching. The prudence of the righteous is not to presume upon righteousness from works of the Law, but to seek salvation from faith, so that although they fulfill the commands of the Law while placed under the Law, they may nevertheless understand that they are to be saved by the grace of God through Christ. “The righteous shall live by faith.”

And Peter, concerning the yoke of the Law, says:

> “A yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear, but through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved, just as they were” (Acts XV, 10–11).

And in the *Treatise on the Acts of the Apostles*, from the words of Saint Leo the Pope (chapter 4 on Acts):

> “There is salvation in no one else.” If salvation of the world is in no one else but Christ alone, then the Fathers of the Old Testament were also saved by the incarnation and passion of that same Redeemer, by which we believe and hope to be saved. Although the sacraments differ according to the order of the times, the faith nevertheless agrees as one and the same, because what we have learned through the apostles to have been accomplished, they learned through the prophets to be going to come as Christ’s dispensation. For there is no redemption of human captivity except in the blood of him who gave himself as a redemption for all.

And again the venerable presbyter Bede, in the First Epistle of Peter (chapter 1):

> “Above he had said that the prophets foretold by the Spirit of Christ his sufferings and the glories that would follow; now he says that the apostles announce the same things to them by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Hence it is clear that the same Spirit of Christ was formerly in the prophets and afterward in the apostles. Therefore they preached to both peoples the same faith in Christ’s passion and subsequent glory: to the former that it was still to come, to the latter that it had already come. Accordingly, there is one Church, one part of which preceded the Lord’s coming in the flesh and the other followed it.”

As Saint Gregory likewise says in Homily 15 on Ezekiel:

> “Indeed, the passion of the Church began already with the blood of Abel, and there is one Church of the elect who preceded and those who followed.”

And in Homily 17:

> “Those who went before and those who followed cried out, ‘Hosanna.’ The Jewish people went before; the Gentile people followed. And because all the elect—whether those who could be found in Judea or those who now exist in the Church—believed and believe in the mediator between God and human beings, both those who go before and those who follow cry out, ‘Hosanna.’ ‘Hosanna’ is said in Latin as ‘Save us.’ From him the earlier people sought salvation, the present people seek it, and they confess him who comes in the name of the Lord to be blessed, because there is one hope and one faith of the peoples who preceded and those who followed. For just as they were saved by the passion and resurrection that they awaited, so we are saved by his past passion and resurrection, which endures forever.”

Concerning those who are not saved, the same author says in Homily 9:

> “It should be noted that after he had spoken of the evils of deceased parents, he sent the Prophet to their children and said: ‘Perhaps they themselves will listen, and perhaps they will cease.’ What does ‘they themselves’ mean except that their fathers, who died in guilt, were unwilling to listen?”

And shortly afterward:

> “We too still follow our parents into iniquity and are not changed by the pride that we have seen in them. They sinned amid joys, whereas we, which is more serious, sin amid scourges. But behold, almighty God, judging iniquities, has already removed our predecessors and already summoned them to judgment; he still waits for us to repent and sustains us so that we may return. He who has already exercised judgment upon them extends to us the long patience of his forbearance, lest he destroy us together with our predecessors, saying: ‘Perhaps they themselves will listen, and perhaps they will cease, for it is a provoking house’” (Ezekiel II, 5).

Therefore, all who are saved, both those who preceded and those who followed, are saved through his redemption. Those of the later people who do not believe and perish so as not to be redeemed perish through unbelief; and those who perish after redemption through wicked conduct and sinful works perish through their own unbelief and iniquity.

Likewise, among the ancient people, all who were lost perished through unbelief and iniquity, as the sacred pages of the Old Testament clearly demonstrate, from the reprobate Cain to Annas and Caiaphas. All who were saved, believing in him who was to come, just as we believe in him who has already come, were saved through the redemption that is in his blood, just as we are saved through the same redemption; and all who are to be saved will undoubtedly be saved.

Hence the venerable presbyter Bede says in Homily 24 on the Gospel:

> “The crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying: ‘Hosanna to the Son of David’ (Matthew XXI, 9). With one and the same voice of confession and praise, those who go before and those who follow exalt the Lord, because there is plainly one faith among those who were approved before the Lord’s incarnation and those who came afterward, although they possessed different sacraments according to the order of the times, as Peter testifies when he says: ‘But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved, just as they were’” (Acts XV, 11).

And Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians:

> “This little heir, who differs in nothing from a slave although he is lord of all, but is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the father, signifies the whole human race until Christ’s coming, and, to say more, until the consummation of the world. For just as all who had not yet been born die in the first-formed Adam, so all who were born before Christ’s coming are made alive in the second Adam. Thus it comes about that we served the Law in the fathers, and that they are saved by grace in the children. This understanding agrees with the Catholic Church, which asserts one providence for both the Old and New Testaments and does not distinguish in time those whom their condition has joined together.”

Thus Saint Augustine also says to Marcellinus in Book II of *On Baptism* (chapter 34), concerning the redemption of the first human beings, which is in the blood of Christ:

“It is not surprising that bodily death would not have come to humanity unless sin had preceded it, and that such a punishment would have followed from it; nor is it surprising that, after the remission of sins, death should still befall the faithful, so that the strength of righteousness might be exercised in conquering its fear. For the flesh that was first made was not sinful flesh, and in it humanity was unwilling to preserve righteousness amid the delights of paradise. Therefore God decreed that, after its sin, sinful flesh—once propagated—should strive through labors and hardships to receive righteousness. For this reason also, after Adam had been expelled from paradise, he dwelt opposite Eden, that is, opposite the seat of delights, so that it might signify that sinful flesh, which had not preserved obedience amid delights before it became sinful flesh, was to be instructed through labors, which are contrary to delights.

“Therefore, just as those first human beings, afterward living righteously, and thus reasonably believed to have been liberated through the Lord’s blood from the final punishment, nevertheless did not, in that life, merit being restored to paradise, so also sinful flesh—even if, after his sins have been remitted, a person has lived righteously in it—does not immediately merit escaping that death which it drew from the propagation of sin.

“Something of this sort has been indicated to us concerning the patriarch David in the Book of Kings. When the prophet had been sent to him and threatened him, on account of the sin he had committed, with evils that would come upon him through God’s anger, he earned forgiveness by confessing his sin, when the prophet replied that his crime and offense had been forgiven him. Nevertheless, the consequences that God had threatened followed, so that he might be humbled by his son. Why, then, is it not said here also: If God had threatened these things on account of that sin, why did he fulfill what he had threatened after the sin had been forgiven? The answer is that the forgiveness of that sin was granted so that the man would not be prevented from attaining eternal life. The consequence of the threat, however, followed so that the man’s devotion might be exercised and tested in that humility. Thus God both inflicted bodily death on humanity because of sin and, after the remission of sins, did not remove it, for the exercise of righteousness.”

244. Hence Saint Gregory, in his letter to Eulogius of Alexandria and Anastasius, bishop of Antioch (Book VI, Letter 31), says:

“We say that Adam’s soul was dead in sin, not with respect to the substance of living, but with respect to the quality of living. Since substance is one thing and quality another, the soul was not dead in such a way that it did not exist, but dead in such a way that it was not blessed. Yet afterward Adam returned to life through repentance.”

And Saint Ambrose, in *On Paradise* (chapter 10), says:

“But if you consider that God cares for the whole universe, you will find that what contained the cause of the universe ought to have pleased the Lord more than what contained the cause of sin ought to have been condemned. Therefore, since the propagation of the human race could not come from the man alone, the Lord declared that it was not good for the man to be alone. For God preferred that there should be many whom he could save and to whom he could grant forgiveness of sin, rather than one Adam alone who would be free from guilt.

“Finally, since the same author is responsible for both works, he came into this world to save sinners. Indeed, he did not allow even Cain, who was guilty of fratricide, to perish before he had begotten children. Therefore, for the propagation of the succession of the human race, the woman had to be added to the man.

“Finally, the very words spoken by God make this clear: that it is not good for the man to be alone. For even if the woman was the first to sin, she ought not, since she was to bear redemption for herself, to have been excluded from the operation of divine action. Although Adam was not deceived, while the woman was deceived and was in transgression, nevertheless, he says, she will be saved through the bearing of children, among whom she bore Christ.”

And Saint Augustine, in the aforementioned book addressed to Marcellinus (Book II, chapter 25), says:

“Such a people, as I have said, instructed in the kingdom of heaven through the two Testaments, the Old and the New, turning neither to the right through proud presumption of righteousness nor to the left through carefree love of sin, enters the promised land. There we shall no longer wish that sins be forgiven us, nor fear that they be punished in us, having been liberated by that Redeemer who, though not sold under sin, redeemed Israel from all its iniquities, whether committed in anyone’s individual life or inherited originally.”

Hence it is clear, as Saint Ambrose explains when treating the Apostle’s statement, “And the brother who is weak will perish through your knowledge, for whom Christ died” (1 Corinthians 8:11), that is, “Your knowledge has killed him, and you will be the occasion of the death of a brother whom Christ allowed himself to be crucified in order to redeem.”

A person who has already received the gift of redemption can perish—namely, because he perished by abusing the gift. Why, then, should it not also be said that Christ suffered for those who did not wish to be redeemed, who, if they had believed, would certainly have been redeemed, just as those who believed were redeemed? Prosper also demonstrates this in the first objection against the Vincentians, saying:

“Against the wound of original sin, by which the nature of all human beings was corrupted and killed in Adam, and from which the disease of desires grew, the true, powerful, and unique remedy is the death of the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, who, free from the debt of death and alone without sin, died for sinners and those indebted to death.

“As regards the greatness and power of the price, and as regards the one cause that concerns the human race, the blood of Christ is the redemption of the whole world. But those who pass through this age without faith in Christ and without the sacrament of regeneration are alien from redemption.”

And because the crowds that preceded and those that followed were saved by one and the same faith, it follows that, although their sacraments were different, the crowds that preceded and those that followed perish through similar unbelief and iniquity. The Apostle also demonstrates that, through one and the same good fragrance, some are saved and others perish, saying: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.”

And Ambrose, explaining the Apostle’s discourse on the Lord’s Supper in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, says the following concerning those who receive salvation from it:

“For it is a spiritual medicine which, when tasted with reverence, purifies the person devoted to it. For it is the remembrance of our redemption, so that, remembering the Redeemer, we may merit to obtain greater things from him.”

Then, concerning those who through their own fault receive judgment for themselves from it:

“It will happen,” he says, “that, just as each person approaches, he will give an account on the day of the Lord Jesus Christ—for those who approach without the discipline of tradition and conduct are guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But what does it mean to be guilty, except to suffer the punishments of the Lord’s death? For he was killed even for those who nullify his benefit.”

Behold: he is said to have suffered for those who are not saved by his suffering. This is demonstrated most clearly in the Gospel according to Luke, where it says:

“And having taken bread, he gave thanks and broke it, and gave it to them, saying: ‘This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which will be poured out for you’” (Luke 22:19).

And Judas was there among the apostles, although one of the leading Catholic teachers says otherwise. But John Chrysostom, in his homily on Judas’s betrayal; Saint Augustine, in his exposition of the tenth psalm; and Leo, in his third homily on the Lord’s Passion, demonstrate that the same traitor was there. Immediately after the Gospel words quoted above, it follows in the same place:

“Nevertheless, behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table” (John 13:11).

It is written concerning him:

“And no one perished except the son of perdition”—the one whom he already knew would betray him, as it is written: “For he himself knew who would betray him; therefore he said: ‘You are not all clean.’”

And here it is truly written:

“This is my body, which is given for you.”

And:

“This is the cup of the new covenant in my blood, which will be poured out for you.”

Let every contradictor answer this question: was it for those alone who had received those sacred things from his hand, or for those who were present there, or also for others—namely, for us, who were going to believe in him? We know that he will readily answer: “And for all who believe in him,” because it is written:

“Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19).

Therefore, because the crowds that preceded and those that followed cried out, saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” just as we believe that the later ones are saved by the grace of God, so also, as Peter says, we believe that the earlier ones are saved “in the same way as they” (Acts 15:10).

Let him not hesitate now to answer a second question: when he said, “This is my body, which is given for you,” and, “This is the cup which will be poured out for you,” since he did not exclude Judas, will he dare to exclude him? We know that, however much he may presume, he will not dare to say that the Lord lied.

And if the Lord did not exclude him from redemption, but Judas himself, although unworthy, received it and made himself alien from it, what fault is there in Catholic teachers who say: “Christ suffered for all, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion”—he who assumed the nature of all, wishes all to be saved, and wishes no one to perish, as Paul and Peter say, although not all are saved?

And what contrary to the Catholic faith have we said, when, setting forth both their meaning and their words, we wrote: “Christ suffered for all, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion”? For the fact that all are not redeemed by the mystery of his Passion does not pertain to the greatness of the price, but to the lot of unbelievers. The cup of human salvation, which has been prepared from our weakness and divine power, certainly contains within itself what can benefit everyone; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.

The saints in the Old Testament drank it spiritually and were saved, as the Apostle testifies: “They drank from the spiritual rock” (1 Corinthians 10:4). So now the devout drink in the New Testament and are saved. Unbelievers in the Old Testament drank, although with an unequal devotion of faith compared with the saints, and were condemned, just as they ate manna and died.

How did Judas eat and drink, and not only die temporally but also die eternally?

And as the Apostle says of certain people who ate and drank irreverently: “For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep” (1 Corinthians 11:30).

Since, in the words of Saint Augustine above, we have shown this concerning the manna, let us speak about the spiritual drink—from which the Apostle said, “And all drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Corinthians 10:4)—in the words of Saint Ambrose from the book *On the Sacraments* (chapter 1):

“When the Jewish people were thirsty and murmured because they could not find water, God commanded Moses to strike the rock with the rod. He struck the rock, and the rock poured forth a very great stream, as the Apostle says: ‘They were drinking from the rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.’ It was not an immovable rock that followed the people. You too, drink, so that Christ may follow you.”

And Saint Augustine, in his *Exposition of the Gospel of John*, said shortly before:

“Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54),

and now he says:

“The flesh profits nothing” (ibid., 6:63), that is, if you wish to understand it carnally.

Accordingly, in the Old Testament, spiritual people, understanding spiritually, drank the spiritual drink and were saved from sins and punishments, until that true Lamb came who takes away the sins of the world. In the figure of that Lamb, through the sacrifice of the ancient Passover lamb, they were redeemed from Egyptian slavery.

By his blood, as we have shown above from the words of Saints Augustine and Ambrose, the first human beings were redeemed, and he opened the gate of the heavenly kingdom to all who believe in the mystery of his Incarnation and Passion. But for those who refused to believe, who understood and lived carnally, and who persevered in unbelief and iniquity, that spiritual food and drink, and the blood of the true Lamb, become a judgment of condemnation.

The same is known to occur after his Passion among those who do not believe, or who come together to receive this sacred mystery for judgment, as the Apostle says. And just as Saint Gregory says concerning the persecutors of the saints—a statement that must equally be understood of those who end their lives in an unworthy manner—in his thirty-eighth homily:

“For they do not even come into our remembrance, or into the number of the dead.”

So too those spiritual men in the Old Testament are believed to have understood this concerning the reprobate of their own time. How much more ought our opponent to have believed that we should understand this, since, through the manifestly revealed teaching of the Lord, his apostles, and the Catholic teachers, we know what happened to them in figure and in veiled mystery, as the Apostle says.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
From this point follows how Catholic men teach, on the authority of the holy Scriptures, that Christ suffered generally for all.

It is clear from the testimonies set forth above that Christ Jesus, the redemption of human captivity, was to come to all before his Incarnation and Passion. Whoever wished to believe and strove to live through works corresponding to faith were redeemed and saved through the mystery of his Passion. But those who did not wish to believe and did not strive to live through works worthy of faith made themselves, as they did in his Passion and after his Passion, and as they will do, alien from the redemption that had been offered.

And just as his Passion is now of no benefit, but will become a judgment, to those who depart from this world in unbelief or evil works, so neither did it benefit those people; rather, his Passion was, is, and will be a judgment against those who could have been redeemed through it if they had wished, just as those who believed in him who was to come were redeemed and merited to be saved through his Passion.

Thus Saint Augustine also says, as we have already stated, concerning those who ate the manna:

“Moses and Aaron and the other saints who were among the people ate manna and did not die, because they understood the visible food spiritually and hungered spiritually. Others ate and persisted in unbelief, and they died—not only bodily death but also spiritual death.”

The same must clearly be understood concerning the baptism with which they were baptized, as we have shown above from the testimony of blessed Peter concerning the ark and the flood.

Now that it is evident that they have falsely accused us, claiming that we said what we did not say—that the Lord suffered for those impious people who, from the beginning of the world until the Lord’s Passion, died in their impiety and were punished with eternal damnation, as though they had been redeemed by the shedding of his blood—we clarify that we said salvation was made available to all who lived before his Incarnation, just as it was made available to those who were born, and who would be born, after his Passion: provided only that they believe with the faith that works through love, just as those believed who were saved, those who are now being saved, and those who will be saved.

They were saved from original sin from the beginning of the world until the time when circumcision was given; or, after circumcision had been given, those from other nations who pleased God were saved either through the offering of sacrifices or, certainly, through the sole power of faith, commending their own souls and those of their people to the Creator.

Likewise, after the time when circumcision was given, those who were to be circumcised according to the law were purified by circumcision from the wound of original sin and saved through faith in the Mediator who was then to come and who has now been received by the faithful.

And because the compiler of these chapters introduced an apostolic testimony by which, as it seems to us, he wished to demonstrate that Christ did not suffer for all, although not all—as we wrote—are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion, whether already redeemed or yet to be redeemed, he writes:

“Christ, he says, was offered once to exhaust the sins of many” (Hebrews 9:28).

And the lord Prudentius, from the Gospel and other holy Scriptures, sets forth several examples in support of this assertion. In the aforementioned letter, chapter 3, he says:

“So that the person to be ordained may believe and confess, together with all Catholics, that the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ was poured out for all human beings throughout the whole world who believe in him, but not for those who have never believed in him, do not believe in him even today, and will never believe in him, since the Lord himself says: ‘For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many’” (Matthew 20:28).

But Gothescalcus also comes to this conclusion:

“Let us leave these absurdities—or rather, blasphemies—for the time being, and let us take care to demonstrate what the Catholic Fathers thought concerning the mystery of the Lord’s Passion: whether he suffered for all, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion, or only for those who are redeemed and saved by the outpouring of his blood. We shall designate the names of each individual and set forth their statements one by one.”

Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, in *The Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 15:

“Concerning perceptible fire, it may be said that it comes into all and through all without mixture, surpasses all, and, while shining upon all, is at the same time hidden; unknown, it does not display its own activity to the matter lying before it; it is innumerable, invisible, and intangible, transforming all in whom it comes to be toward its own activity, distributing itself to all who draw near to it.”

Likewise, in Book III of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

“For the divine, supreme blessedness is for all, even if through divine goodness it proceeds to the communion of those who participate in its divine gifts; yet it does not come to be outside itself, according to the immovable position and stability of its substance.”

Saint Cyprian, in the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, says:

“This had already been foretold through the prophet Isaiah, when, full of the Holy Spirit, he spoke concerning God’s gracious favor and compassion: ‘A word completing and shortening in righteousness, because God will make a shortened word throughout the whole world’ (Isaiah 10; Romans 9).

“For when the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, came for all, gathering together the learned and the unlearned alike, and issuing the commands of salvation to every sex and age, he made a great summary of his commands, so that the memory of those learning the heavenly discipline would not labor, but would quickly learn what was necessary for simple faith.”

And again, in the same book:

“He who taught unity wished one person to pray for all in the same way that he himself bore all in one.”

Saint Hilary, in Book II of *On the Faith*, says:

“For the sake of the human race, the Son of God was born from the Virgin and the Holy Spirit, the latter serving him in this work, while his own divine power overshadowed her. He sowed within himself the beginnings of a body and established the origins of flesh, so that, having become human from the Virgin, he might receive in himself the nature of flesh, and through the fellowship of this union the body of the whole human race might exist sanctified in him. Thus, just as all were established in him through that by which he willed to be bodily, so again he might be extended into all through that which is invisible in him.”

And in Psalm 118:

“‘Take away from me reproach and contempt.’ Sins are worthy of reproach, and therefore sinners will rise to eternal reproach. That all sins are worthy of reproach, let us learn from the Gospels, when the Lord began to reproach those cities in which more of his mighty works had been performed, yet they had not repented—Chorazin and Bethsaida.

“What began with them must necessarily become applicable to all who are their equals in crime. Then he reproaches the human race that does not repent and does not proceed on the Gospel way with what is contained in the psalm: ‘What profit is there in my blood, when I go down into corruption?’ (Psalm 29:10).

“For he reproaches the proud and the accursed: why did they think that there was no benefit in the mystery of his blood and death, when he was both born and suffered and died for our sake?”

Likewise, in Psalm 59:

“Therefore the inscription of the title is written for those who will be changed, to the glory of his death, who died for all.”

And a little later:

“Thus mercy followed anger, while, in place of the loss of earthly things, a great recompense of eternal things was repaid. These things, moreover, are fitted no more to Israel than to the whole human race, because from one person the sentence of death and the labor of life went forth upon all, when it was said: ‘Cursed is the earth in your works’ (Genesis 3:17).

“But now, through one person, the grace of the justification of life has abounded for all, so that those whose earth was cursed may now have bodies conformed to God; and that which had been shaken by fear, disturbed by ignorance, and saddened by labor—and pierced by that very drink of wine that brings joy—may now, through the secure power of the sign it has received, escape the power of future wrath.”

Likewise, in Psalm 61:

“After he has recognized that the Spirit of God, the power of God, the wisdom of God, the Son of God, and God the Only-Begotten was born as a human being for the remission of sin and the condemnation of sin in the flesh, and that, having undergone the lot of human sufferings, he died in order to condemn in himself the impious temptations of heavenly wickedness, so that he might bring eternity to all who were dying through the law of sin dwelling in our flesh, then, having received this mystery of piety and having been placed, after the night of ignorance, in the light of knowledge, he says: ‘Will not my soul be subject to God?’”

Likewise, in Psalm 64:

“We also have prepared food. And what is this food? That food, certainly, by which we are prepared for fellowship with God, through communion in the holy body, to be placed thereafter in communion with the holy body.

“For the present psalm signifies this by saying: ‘You have prepared their food, for thus is your preparation.’ For although we are saved in the present through that food, we are nevertheless prepared for the future.”

Likewise, in Psalm 67:

“First, it can certainly not appear foreign to the mercy and goodness of God that he should restore life to all in himself from the dead.”

Likewise, in Psalm 68:

“This was the expectation of the saints: that all flesh might be redeemed in Christ, so that in him the firstfruits of the eternal resurrection might exist.”

And again, in the same psalm:

“For this is well pleasing in the abundance of mercy: the time when God, in his compassion, would restore the life of all human beings in himself, so that, as a merciful God, he might give life to the dead.”

Again, in the same psalm:

“When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is finished’ (John 19:30). He had come to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and, while seeking one who would console and grieve with him, he found none. This was not because he needed consolation, since he willingly chose to suffer and die, but because he sought someone who would grieve with him over the impiety of the whole people, and who would console him, grieving with him, through the salvation of those who would be saved, so that, for all who had undergone such a great crime, he might at least receive consolation in those who were saved, according to the saying: ‘And in his servants he will be consoled’ (2 Maccabees 7:6).”

Likewise, in Psalm 129:

“For with you there is propitiation. For the only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, is our redemption and our peace; in his blood we have been reconciled to God. He is the one who came to take away the sins of the world, who, fastening the bond of the law to the cross, erased the decree of the ancient condemnation.”

And a little later:

“Because he is merciful, because abundant redemption is with him, because he will redeem all from their iniquities.”

Likewise, in Psalm 135:

“He redeemed us through his blood, through his Passion, through his resurrection. These are the great prices of our life. For, as the Apostle says, ‘You were bought with a great price’ (1 Corinthians 6:20), and redeemed from enemies: from the devil, from his angels, from the son of perdition, from the princes of the air, from the powers of the world, and from hostile death.

“And he redeemed us by giving food to all flesh. He who gives food to all flesh—that is, to the flesh that has been redeemed—gives the incorruptible and eternal food of the living bread, the heavenly bread.

“And in each of these things, the reason why we have been redeemed and why all the flesh of the redeemed receives food is that his mercy endures forever. Whatever heaven, earth, and the other things are, and that very thing which we are, although we did not exist; whatever we will be, although we are not yet so—the cause is nothing other than the mercy of God, who, because he is good, wished us to be born for participation in his good things: our Lord Jesus Christ.”

And Saint Athanasius, in his letter to Epictetus:

“Because the Word, remaining God by nature, is impassible, he himself was incorporeal within a passible body, while the body had within itself the impassible Word, destroying the body’s weaknesses. He both did this and experienced it, so that, taking what was ours and offering it as a sacrifice, he might destroy it, and, now clothing us with what is his, cause the Apostle to say: ‘This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality’ (1 Corinthians 15:53).

“Let it be far from us that these things occurred figuratively, as some again suppose; rather, since the Savior truly became human, the salvation of the whole human being was accomplished.”

And again:

“If, because the Savior is said in the Scriptures to be from Mary and to have a human body, they think that a quaternity is spoken of in place of the Trinity, they greatly err by equating what has been made with its maker. They suppose that the Godhead can receive some addition, and they do not understand that the Word became flesh not because of an addition to the Godhead, but so that flesh might rise again. Nor did the Word proceed from Mary in order to be improved, but in order to liberate the human race.”

Gregory Nazianzen, in the book *Apology*, says:

“For this reason God was joined to the body through the mediation of the soul: to unite what had been separated and to restore discordant things to harmony and peace, recalling all things into unity, both to himself and through himself.

“He received the soul first brought forth from the one father of our race, because of the flesh disobedient to the soul, because of its evil obedience, for which it too had been condemned together with it, so that, just as condemnation had occurred in flesh and soul, salvation might likewise occur in flesh and soul.

“Therefore Christ is introduced for Adam, for the one who was made under sin, the one who was without sin; the new is introduced for the old, so that, through this one’s voluntary suffering, the one who had suffered unwillingly might be healed. Thus, for each of us, that which is above us might be restored.”

Likewise, in his sermon on the Nativity of the Lord:

“This is that solemnity; this is the great and glorious festival of this day. We celebrate the Lord’s coming among human beings, so that we may advance toward God—or rather, so that we may return to God.

“For it is more correctly said in this way: having laid aside the old person, let us put on the new; and just as we all died in Adam, so let us be crucified with Christ and buried with him in death, so that we may also rise with him to life (Romans 6:4).

“For it is necessary that we undergo this useful and necessary exchange: just as we have fallen from good things into sad things, so may we be restored from sad things to better ones. ‘Where sin abounded, grace abounded even more’ (Romans 5:20), so that those whom the taste of the forbidden tree condemned, the cross of Christ might justify with more abundant grace.”

And again, in the same sermon:

“But what do these calumniators say to us here, who come before us as exceedingly severe examiners of the Godhead, accusing things worthy of all reverence and honor? They are dark even in the light, unlearned concerning wisdom, those for whom Christ died freely; ungrateful creatures against their Creator, works of the devil, reproaching God for his benefits. Is he therefore lesser because he is humble for your sake?”

Likewise, in his sermon on the Epiphany:

“Since our enemy had presumed that his sophistical art could not be defeated, just as he himself had deceived us through hope by saying, concerning the promised divinity, ‘You will be like gods’ (Genesis 3:5), so now he himself is deceived by the presentation of flesh. Like a fish caught by bait covering the hook, he desires to devour the carnal nature of Adam, but finds God hidden within it.

“Thus this new Adam restores the old, and the condemnation of the first is absolved: flesh is restored in place of flesh, and death is repaid in place of death—or rather, through death the very author of death is punished.”

And again, in the same sermon:

“Nor should the mercy of Jesus cause you shame, for he took our weaknesses and bore our diseases (Isaiah 53:4); he came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Mark 2:17); he desires mercy more than sacrifice (Matthew 9:13); and he wishes sins to be forgiven the repentant seventy times seven (Matthew 18:22).”

Likewise, in his sermon of intercession for a certain person addressed to the emperor:

“I bring Christ himself before you, who emptied himself in order to speak with us human beings. I bring before you his sufferings, although he himself is impassible; I offer you for intercession his cross and the nails with which his most holy hands were fastened, the blood which he poured out for the salvation of the whole world, his burial, resurrection, and ascension into heaven.

“I bring before you this altar, to which we all approach together, on which, with this very mouth with which I now entreat you, we celebrate the figure of our salvation. Together with me I bring those most sacred mysteries by which we are joined to the heavenly powers, in order to soften you.”

And Saint Basil of Cappadocia, in his sermon on Psalm 59:

“‘The end’ is said because it is fitted to the end of the age, at its completion. For this reason the psalm is also said to be written ‘for those who will be changed,’ which, to say everything at once, must be understood of the whole human race. For the meaning of the psalm ought to reach everyone.”

And a little later:

“‘Therefore, O God,’ he says, ‘you have rejected us’ (Psalm 107:12). Whom? Those who have made ourselves far from him. Therefore, because of sins and because of the iniquities intervening between us and God, God is said to have rejected us. For another prophet also says: ‘Sins separate between you and God’ (Isaiah 59:2).”

And shortly afterward:

“Moses had sealed the Israelite doorposts with the blood of a lamb (Exodus 12:7); but you have given us a sign: the blood itself of the true immaculate Lamb, who was offered as a victim for the salvation of the whole world.”

253 Blessed Ambrose likewise, in Psalm 118, where he says, “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord”:

“How is the earth full of the mercy of the Lord, unless through the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ? Foreseeing it as something still to come, the prophet celebrates it as though it had been promised. The earth is therefore full of the mercy of the Lord, because forgiveness of sins has been given to all. The sun is commanded to rise over all, and this sun indeed rises daily over all (Matt. 5:45); but that mystical sun of righteousness has risen for all, has come for all, has suffered for all, and has risen again for all. He suffered for this reason: to take away the sin of the world. But if someone does not believe in Christ, he has deprived himself of the universal benefit. Yet what belongs to the sun preserves its privilege; what belongs to the foolish person excludes from himself the common grace of the light. Rain falls upon all.”

Likewise, where he says, “The beginning of your words is truth” (Ps. 118:160):

“I believe that there is one God, not several gods. When you begin to read that the Lord Jesus, the Son of God, came in the flesh for the redemption of the whole world, understand wisely that there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things and we through him.”

Likewise, where he explains, “I have hated iniquity” (ibid., 163):

“He who is daily our advocate with the Father, so that for those toward whom, during the days of his flesh, he showed compassionate affection, he may work daily forgiveness of sins for them. For what other hope is there for the human race except that the offenses of all the living may be forgiven?”

Likewise, where he explains, “Your mercies are many, O Lord” (ibid., 156):

“And although salvation is far from sinners” (ibid., 155), he says, “nevertheless no one should despair, because the Lord’s mercies are many: those who perish through their own sin are delivered by the Lord’s mercy. ‘I will have mercy,’ he says, ‘on whom I have mercy’ (Exod. 33:19). He appeared openly to those who were not seeking him; he called those who were fleeing; he gathered the ignorant; he offered himself to suffering on behalf of all. Is he not therefore very merciful? Human mercy extends to one’s neighbor; the Lord’s mercy extends to all flesh, so that all flesh might ascend to God, granted this by the Lord’s compassion. Finally, he who acquitted Susanna while she was silent offered himself to death: in that case, so that no one might despair; in this, so that he might not refuse the sacrifice for the redemption of the whole universe.”

Likewise:

“Who is it who distances himself from the Lord, except the one who does not seek his righteousness? But whoever seeks his righteousness is near and clings to God. Therefore the Apostle says to those who seek God’s righteousness: ‘You who were far away have been brought near in the blood of Christ’ (Eph. 2:13). The blood of Christ is righteousness. Finally, he himself says to John: ‘Let us fulfill all righteousness’ (Matt. 3:15).”

Likewise, where he explains, “Repay your servant” (Ps. 118:17):

“Christ also answers, he says: ‘Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved’ (Song 1). Because the Church had understood the mystery and was proclaiming the Lord Jesus crucified for the redemption of the whole world, she deserved to hear: ‘Behold, you are beautiful,’ because the Lord Jesus came to save the world, not to destroy it. Therefore he forgets the injury and remembers grace.”

Likewise, where he explains, “Take away from me reproach and contempt” (Ps. 118:22):

“They were slandering me,” he says. “I had come as their redeemer; I had come to cleanse the sins of all, to recover the lost, to restore to holy Jacob the inheritance of paradise—and they were slandering me” (Ps. 118:58).

Likewise, where he explains, “Have mercy on me according to your word”:

“What is the righteousness of the cross,” he says, “except that when our Lord Jesus Christ ascended that gibbet, he nailed the record of our sins to the cross (Col. 2:14), and cleansed the sin of the whole world with his blood?”

And likewise:

“The evil succession of Eve devoured the whole human being; the glorious inheritance of Christ set the whole human being free. Jesus wrote his testament not for one person or a few, but for all. We are all written as heirs, not in proportionate shares but as a whole. The inheritance of all is common to everyone, and each possesses it fully. Individuals approach the New Testament, and all possess it; whatever is claimed by co-heirs does not diminish the heir’s portion. The benefit remains entire, and it increases for each person all the more the more widely it has been acquired. The inheritance of Christ is the resurrection. Would anyone regard as his loss what, in one person, has found the name of a common grace? For Christ, rising again, rose again for all, since through a human being comes the resurrection of the dead. Can what is the reformation of the whole body and of the human race be a loss to each individual?”

Likewise, when treating the fifteenth Hebrew letter, he said:

“But because the Savior’s passion redeemed all, it is not absurd to understand that these people shook their heads in the way that that leader of the Synagogue prophesied: ‘It is expedient that one man should die for the people’ (John 18:14).”

Likewise, when treating “I am young and despised” (Ps. 118:141), he said:

“That harsh king, the devil, is indignant and grows angry because the young women were singing, since the son of harshness deceived a few, whereas Christ redeemed the whole world.”

Likewise, when treating “Tribulation and distress have found me” (Ps. 118:143):

“Do not sin again after baptism,” he says. “Christ died once for all collectively, and he dies once for each individual, not repeatedly.”

Likewise:

“The Lord’s cup is the forgiveness of sins; his blood will be poured out, and it has redeemed the sins of the whole world.”

Likewise, in his treatise on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 3:

“For Christ lived, died, and rose again for this reason: so that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead. Through Christ the Lord the creature was made which, because of sin, had been estranged and taken captive by its creator. God the Father, so that his work might not perish, sent the Son from heaven to earth and taught it what it should do to escape the hands of the pirates. For this reason he also allowed himself to be killed by his enemies, so that, descending to the lower world, because he had been killed though innocent, he might condemn sin, and release from the lower world those whom sin held. Since, therefore, he showed the living the way of salvation and offered himself for them, while he freed the dead from the underworld, he is Lord both of the living and of the dead. For from those who had been lost he re-formed them for himself as servants.”

And likewise, in the same chapter:

“For whoever serves Christ in this matter pleases God, because Christ redeemed us. Therefore,” he says, “whoever serves Christ in this matter—why? Because he himself sent Christ to redeem the human race.”

Likewise, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1:

“For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing” (1 Cor. 1:18). “It is clear that those for whom the cross of Christ is foolishness are in destruction; they have not been rescued from infernal death. But to those who are being saved it is the power of God” (ibid.). “It is not obscure: for those who believe, it is the power of God. For they believe that the cross of Christ is not weakness but power, understanding that death was conquered on the cross; those who bear its sign are saved and cannot be held by death.”

Chapter 6: “‘You are not your own, for you were bought with a price’ (1 Cor. 6:19). It is clear that the one who has been bought is not free to choose for himself, but belongs to the one by whom he was bought, so that he should do not his own will but that person’s. And because we were bought at a great price, we ought to serve God more devotedly, lest, if he is offended, he return us to the death from which he redeemed us. For at how precious a price did he purchase us, so that he might give his blood for us?”

And likewise, chapter 9:

“Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things” (1 Cor. 9:25)—“in all those things which the same discipline teaches must be avoided, since they know that one person is to be crowned. How much more must we observe discipline, when the promise has been made to all?”

And likewise, chapter 10:

“You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons.” “For this reason was Christ crucified: because he destroyed the works of the devil? Whoever therefore does the works of the devil opposes Christ.”

And likewise, chapter 11:

“He will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27). “What does it mean to be guilty, except to suffer the penalties of the Lord’s death? For he was killed even for those who render his benefit void.”

And again, chapter 5:

“The love of Christ urges us,” judging this: “that if one died for all” (2 Cor. 5:14), “then Christ, loving the human race, gave himself over to death in order to redeem them.”

And likewise:

“Therefore all were dead, and he died for all. Because all must die on account of Adam, Christ died for all, in order to free them from the second death. Therefore those who live in the body, knowing that Christ died for them, should be subject to him and confess him as Lord. For those whom his death benefits bear witness to his resurrection.”

Likewise, in the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 4, “But speaking the truth in love, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ” (Eph. 4:15):

“He says that this is the truth: that, considering the love of Christ with which he loved us and gave himself for us, we should all submit to him, knowing that he is the author of everyone’s life, so that, as members are subject to the head, we may be subject to him. If some people, through error or ill will, do not confess that Christ is the head of all because all things were made by him according to the Father’s will, nevertheless we who cling to the catholic faith must act with complete devotion and care so that we bring gain, not loss, to this faith, persisting in this assertion so that the conversations of perverse minds armed against the truth may be silenced.”

Likewise, in the Epistle to Timothy, chapter 11, “Who gave himself as a redemption for all” (1 Tim. 2:6):

“Since the human being, now reconciled to God, was subject to infernal death and could not ascend to the one to whom he had been reconciled, the Savior, in order to bring his own purpose to fulfillment, allowed himself to die contrary to the law, so that, descending to the lower world, he might condemn death for the impiety it had committed against him, taking away from it those whom it held. Thus, thereafter, whoever bore his sign could not be held by death. He displayed testimony to this when he rose again. For the destruction of death is the resurrection of the dead.”

The same holy Augustine, in the book *On the Holy Spirit* (in the preface to book 1), explaining the passage in the Book of Judges concerning Gideon (Judg. 6), says:

“When Gideon heard that, although the thousands of peoples were failing, the Lord would deliver his people from their enemies through one man, he offered a young goat. According to the angel’s instructions, he placed its flesh and unleavened cakes upon a rock and poured broth over them. As soon as the tip of the staff carried by the angel of God touched them, fire burst forth from the rock, and the sacrifice that was being offered was consumed. By this sign it appears to have been declared that that rock prefigured the body of Christ, because it is written: ‘They drank from the rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ’ (1 Cor. 10:4). This was referred not to his divinity but to his flesh, which flooded the thirsting hearts of the peoples with the perpetual stream of its blood.

“Already then, therefore, it was declared in a mystery that the Lord Jesus would abolish, by being crucified in his flesh, the sins of the whole world—not only the sins of deeds but also the desires of souls. For the flesh of the young goat refers to guilt incurred; the broth to the allurements of desires, as it is written: ‘The people desired an evil desire, and they said, “Who will feed us with meat?”’ (Num. 11). What the angel therefore did when he stretched out the staff and touched the rock from which fire came showed that the Lord’s flesh, filled with the divine Spirit, would burn away all the sins of human nature. Hence the Lord also says: ‘I have come to cast fire upon the earth’ (Luke 12:49).”

And likewise:

“As you yourself said, Lord, to those who follow you: ‘You will be able to tread upon serpents and scorpions’ (Luke 10:19). You redeemed the world; redeem the soul of one sinner. This is the particular privilege of your mercy, by which you redeemed the whole world in each individual.”

And in the book *The Apology of David*:

“It is not clear that he wished also to test the holy David, noble in faith, outstanding in gentleness, and strong in hand—how he might conceal a fault and correct a lapse—so that he might not teach us how we can cover an admitted sin. Unless perhaps someone thinks it a trivial matter that such a great prophet should have gone astray for our correction, when Christ, though he knew no sin, took upon himself our weaknesses and was made sin for us for the redemption of all. Nor is it plausible to believe that David incurred the reproach of a single fall for the benefit of posterity, when the Lord himself was made reproach for us, as he says: ‘But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people’ (Ps. 21:7). And elsewhere: ‘The reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me’ (Ps. 68:10).”

And likewise:

“In the figure, the bronze serpent was fastened as though to a cross, because the one who was truly to be crucified was being announced to the human race: he would empty the poisons of the serpent, the devil. In the figure he was accursed, but in reality he was the one who would erase the curses of the whole world.”

And likewise:

“He fittingly added that he did not spare him. For Christ did not spare himself, so that he might help all.”

And likewise, in the book *On Joseph*, chapter 7:

“Buy Christ for yourself, therefore—not with what a few possess, but with what all possess. All possess him by nature; few offer him through fear. What Christ demands from you belongs to him. He himself gave life to all; he himself offered his death for all. Pay for the author what you will pay by law.”

And in the book *On the Patriarchs*, chapter 4:

“From the seed, my son, you have ascended, because, like a shrub of the earth, he germinated in the Virgin’s womb and, like a flower of good fragrance, was sent forth from his mother’s womb in the splendor of new light, to redeem the whole world.”

And likewise, chapter 4:

“He will wash his garment in wine,” he says (Gen. 49:11). “The garment is good: it is the flesh of Christ, which covered the sins of all, took upon itself the offenses of all, and concealed the errors of all. Good is the garment that clothed everyone in a robe of joy.”

And likewise, chapter 11:

“‘The firstborn of the bull is his beauty, having horns like a unicorn, with which he will scatter the nations.’ And rightly a bull, like a victim for offenses and the sacrifice of the whole world, so that he might reconcile all things.”

And likewise, in book 1 of *On Repentance*, chapter 15:

“For ‘Christ our Passover has been sacrificed’ (1 Cor. 5:7)—that is, the Lord’s passion has gone before all and granted redemption to sinners who repented of the crime they had committed.”

And likewise, in book 2, chapter 3:

“For whenever we receive the Lord’s blood, we proclaim the Lord’s death. Therefore, just as he was sacrificed once for all, so whenever sins are forgiven we receive the sacrament of his body, so that forgiveness of sins may come through his blood.”

And likewise:

“Whoever rejoices in another’s fall rejoices in the devil’s victory. Therefore we ought to grieve more when we hear that a human being has perished, for whom Christ died.”

And in book 1 of *On the Death of a Brother*:

“For this reason Christ died according to the flesh for all, so that we might learn not to live only for ourselves.”

And likewise, in book 2:

“For Christ came, as we read, ‘to save what had perished’ (Matt. 18:11), and so that he might be Lord not only of the living but also of the dead. I fell in Adam; in Adam I was expelled from paradise; in Adam I died. Who will recall me unless he finds me in Adam?—so that, just as in Adam I am liable to guilt and subject to death, so in Christ I may be justified.”

And likewise:

“By the death of one, the world was redeemed. For our Christ could have avoided death if he had wished. But he did not consider death something to be avoided as cowardly, nor could he have saved us better than by dying. Thus his death is the life of all: just as through a human being came death, so through a human being came the resurrection of the dead. Therefore a human being rose again, because a human being died; a human being was raised, but God raised him. Then he was human according to the flesh; now in every respect he is God. For now we no longer know Christ according to the flesh, but we hold the grace of the flesh, so that we may know him as the firstfruits of those who sleep and the firstborn from the dead.

“The firstfruits are of the same kind and nature as the remaining fruits, whose abundant yield brings the first offerings to God: a sacred offering for all, as it were, certain first portions of a restored nature. Christ is therefore the firstfruits of those who sleep—but is he the firstfruits of his own who sleep, who are held in a kind of gentle sleep as though innocent of death, or of all the dead? Yet just as all die in Adam, so all are made alive in Christ. Therefore, just as death has its firstfruits in Adam, so resurrection also has its firstfruits in Christ.

“All rise again, but no one should despair, and no righteous person should grieve over the common fellowship of rising again, while awaiting the special fruit of virtue. All indeed rise again, but each one, as the Apostle says, ‘in his own order’ (1 Cor. 15). The fruit of divine clemency is common, but the order of merits is distinct. Day shines for all; the sun warms all peoples, and rain falls upon all lands. We all rise again, but in each case the grace either of living or of coming back to life is different, and the condition is diverse.

“In the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed (ibid.). Indeed, even in death some rest while others live. Rest is good, but life is better. Finally, Paul awakens the one who is resting to life, saying: ‘Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you’ (Eph. 5:14). Therefore he is awakened here so that he may live, so that he may be like Paul, so that he may be able to say: ‘We who live shall not precede those who have fallen asleep’ (1 Thess. 4:14). For he is not speaking of the common practice of living here, or of the fellowship of breathing, but of the merit of rising again. For after saying, ‘The dead who are in Christ will rise first,’ he added: ‘Then we who are alive, together with them, will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air’ (1 Thess. 4:15–16). Paul certainly died, and through a venerable passion exchanged the life of the body for immortal glory. He therefore did not deceive when he wrote that he, living, would be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ,” and so forth.

Likewise, in the same work:

“We recognize how grave a sacrilege it is not to believe in the resurrection. For if we do not rise again, then Christ died in vain; then Christ did not rise again. If he did not rise again for us, certainly he did not rise again—for why would he need to rise again for himself? In him the world rose again; in him heaven rose again; in him the earth rose again, for there will be a new heaven and a new earth. But where was resurrection necessary for him, whom the bonds of death did not hold? For even if he died as a human being, nevertheless among the dead he was free, as it says: ‘I became like a man without help, free among the dead’ (Ps. 87:5).”

And after some intervening material:

“But these mysteries belong not only to individuals but also to the whole universe. Observe, then, according to the type of the Law, the order of grace. When the first trumpet sounds, it gathers the eastern peoples, as the foremost and chosen. With the second, those of comparable merit who, like Lebanon, abandoned the mockeries of the nations. With the third, those who, as though tossed upon the sea, wavered amid the waves of this world’s strait. With the fourth, those whose hardness of mind could not be sufficiently softened by the command of spiritual teaching. Therefore they were called from the north, for according to Solomon the north wind is harsh.

“Thus, although all are raised in an instant, all are nevertheless raised according to the order of their merits. The first to rise are those who, coming forth in the maturity of devotion and in a kind of dawn of faith, received the rays of the eternal Sun. I may rightly understand this either of the patriarchs according to the succession of the Old Testament or of the apostles according to the Gospel. The second are those who, abandoning the rites of the nations, passed from sacrilegious error into the discipline of the Church. Therefore the former are first from the fathers, the latter second from the nations. From the former the light of faith began; in the latter it will endure until the setting of the world.

“The third are raised who are from the south and from the north. By these four regions the earth is distinguished; by these four the year is enclosed; by these four the world is filled; by these four the Church is gathered. For all who are joined to the holy Church and are reckoned under the name of the divine Name will obtain the privilege of resurrection and the grace of eternal joy, because they will come from the east and the west, and from the north and the south, and will recline in the kingdom of God.

“For Christ does not embrace his world with a small light, since ‘his going forth is from the end of heaven, and his circuit reaches to its end, and there is no one who can hide from his heat’ (Ps. 18:7). He kindly illumines all. He does not wish to reject the weak but to correct them; nor does the Church wish to exclude the hardened but to soften them. Therefore the Church in the Song of Songs, and Christ in the Gospel, invite them, saying: ‘Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart’ (Matt. 11:28–29).”

And likewise, in his sermon on the Apostle, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law” (Gal. 3:13):

“You were redeemed,” he says, “with precious blood—not that of a lamb, but of the one who came in gentleness and humility like a lamb and freed the whole world by the single sacrifice of his body, as he himself says: ‘I was led like a lamb to be sacrificed.’ Hence John also says: ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world’ (John 1:29).”

And in the book *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 6:

“You have therefore learned that he offered a sacrifice to our God. For what was the reason for the Incarnation except that the flesh which had sinned might be redeemed through him? What had sinned was therefore redeemed. The divinity of the Word was not sacrificed, for the divinity of the Word had not sinned.”

And likewise, chapter 7:

“He therefore took upon himself that which was in greater danger in us. But what benefit would it be to me if he had not redeemed me wholly? Yet he redeemed me wholly, who said: ‘You are angry with me because I made the whole person well on the Sabbath’ (John 7:23). He redeemed the whole person, because in the perfect human being the faithful person rises again, not in part but wholly.”

There are also many more testimonies in the books of this teacher—namely, in *On Abraham*, *On the Flight from the World*, *On Isaac and the Soul*, *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, *On the Good of Death*, and his other works. We have postponed including them here for the sake of brevity, lest they become tedious to the reader, since the reader can more readily find them in their proper places.

But Saint John Chrysostom says the following in his treatise on the Epistle to the Hebrews:

“Then he shows,” he says, “that the cross is glory and honor, just as he always calls it, saying: ‘That the Son of Man may be glorified’ (John 11:14). If he calls glorious the things he suffered for servants, how much more should you call glorious the things you suffer for the Lord? Do you see how great the fruit of the cross is? Do I fear this matter? It seems grievous to you, but it produces ten thousand blessings.

“He also demonstrates from this the usefulness of temptation, saying in this way that, by the grace of God, he tasted death for all. ‘How,’ he says, ‘by the grace of God?’ He suffered these things because of God’s grace, which was given to us. ‘He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all’ (Rom. 8:32). For what reason? These things were not owed to us; grace accomplished this. And again he said: ‘Much more abundantly did the grace of God and the gift of the one man Jesus Christ overflow to many’ (Rom. 5:15): by the grace of God he tasted death for all—not only for the faithful, but for the whole world. He indeed died for all. But what if not all believe? He fulfilled what belonged to him. And he said precisely: ‘He tasted death for all.’ He did not say, ‘So that he might die’; for truly, just as one who tastes makes only a brief contact with something, so he immediately rose again.”

And likewise:

“‘Whom he appointed heir of all things’: this signifies the flesh. As it is also said in the second psalm: ‘Ask of me,’ he says, ‘and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.’ The Lord’s portion is no longer only Jacob, nor Israel his share, but immediately all the nations; that is, he appointed the Son Lord of all. Peter also speaks this way in Acts, saying: ‘God made him both Lord and Christ’ (Acts 2:36).”

And likewise:

“Since, therefore, we have such a high priest, let us imitate him and follow in his footsteps. There is no other sacrifice: this one purified us; after it come fire and Gehenna.”

And likewise:

“He became our mediator with the Father and persuaded him. And how, then, did he become mediator? He conveyed and brought messages to us from the Father through intermediaries. He also added death. We were under accusation; we ought to have died. He died for us and made us worthy of the testament. In this way the testament was made firm.

“Were we not already made worthy? At the very beginning, as a father, he made a testament for his sons. But because we became unworthy, we no longer needed a testament but punishment. Why then do you boast in the Law? It placed us under such great sin that we could never have been saved unless the Lord died for us; the Law would have been powerless, since it is weak.

“He confirms this not merely from common custom but especially from what occurred in the Old Testament, introducing them through those examples. No one there failed to die. How, then, is the testament made firm? ‘In the same manner,’ he says. Just as there was blood there, so there is blood here. But if Christ’s blood was not present there, do not be surprised; it was a type. Hence he said: ‘Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.’ What does ‘was inaugurated’ mean? It was made firm and strengthened. What he said, ‘therefore,’ means the same as if he had said: ‘For this reason the solemnity of the testament also had to be completed through death.’

“Now,” he says, “once, at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the destruction of sin through his sacrifice. And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after that comes judgment. Then he says: ‘And having died once’—because redemption was accomplished through that death, he says that human beings were appointed to die. Thus he died once for all.

“What then? Do we no longer die that death? We do die, but we do not remain in it; and that is no longer truly death. For the tyranny of death—and death in the true sense—is that the dead are never permitted to return to life. But when one is to live after death, and to live a better life, that is not death but sleep.

“Since death was going to hold everyone, he died in order to free us. So also Christ, he says, ‘was offered once.’ By whom was he offered? Clearly, by himself. Here he calls him not only the priest but also the victim and the sacrifice offered by himself. ‘He was offered once to take away the sins of many.’ Why ‘of many,’ and not ‘of all’? Because not all believed. He died for all, that is, as far as depended on him: that death has the same magnitude as the destruction of all. But he did not take away the sins of all because they did not wish it.

“What does ‘he took away sins’ mean? Just as in the offering we bring sins upward and say, ‘Whether willingly or unwillingly, we have sinned; forgive us’—that is, we first mention them and then ask for forgiveness—so it is clear that the same happened here. And where did Christ do this? Hear him saying: ‘For their sake I sanctify myself’ (John 17:19). Behold, he offered the sins; he took them from human beings and offered them upward to the Father, not so that he might issue any judgment against them, but so that he might forgive them.

“‘He will appear a second time without sin to those awaiting him for salvation.’ What does ‘without sin’ mean? As though he were not a sinner. He did not die as one liable to death, nor because of sin. But how will he appear? ‘Punishing,’ he says. Yet he did not say this; rather, he said what is joyful and welcome: ‘He will appear without sin to those awaiting him for salvation,’ so that thereafter they would no longer need a sacrifice in order to be saved, but would accomplish this through their works themselves.”

And likewise:

“‘Let no one among you be lacking the grace of God.’ What does he mean by the grace of God? Future blessings, evangelical faith, and excellent conduct. For everything belongs to the grace of God. Do not say to me that there is one person who will perish. Indeed, Christ died for one person. Do you therefore neglect the one for whom Christ deemed it worthy to die?”

Likewise, in the first homily on Psalm 50:

“When he again says, ‘They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones’ (Ps. 21:17), he certainly does not announce his own sufferings, but foretells the Lord’s cross, the sacrifice of the whole earth, and salvation for the human race.”

Likewise, in the homily on the betrayal of Judas:

“They gave the price of blood that had no price. What did you receive, Judas? Thirty pieces of silver. Christ came freely, intending to pour out his blood for the common salvation, and you make cruel sins out of his blood?”

And likewise, in the same homily:

“Christ was placed there to be killed, and let us see why he was killed: so that he might reconcile the heavenly things, reconcile all things on earth, make you a friend of the angels, and unite you to God who holds power over all.”

Likewise, in the homily on the Cross:

“For this reason he did not suffer under a roof, nor in the Jewish temple, lest the Jews take away the sacrifice and claim it for themselves, and lest you think that it was offered only for that people. For this reason he suffered outside the city, outside the walls, so that you might know that the sacrifice is common: an offering of the whole earth and a common lamentation, not belonging to one part, as was customary among the Jews.

“For this reason God commanded the Jews to leave the whole earth and celebrate sacrifice and offering in one place: at that time the whole earth was unclean, polluted by the smoke, stench, and foreign contamination arising from the sacrifices celebrated by the nations. But for us, because Christ came and cleansed the whole earth, every place is free for prayer. Therefore Paul exhorts us with complete confidence, saying: ‘I wish men to pray in every place, lifting holy hands’ (1 Tim. 2:8).

“Behold, the whole world has been cleansed; the elements have been purified, so that everywhere we may proclaim God, and the whole earth is holier than that place which at that time was called the Holy of Holies. There an irrational animal was offered; here a spiritual victim has been sacrificed. And the sacrifice is so much greater as the holiness brought forth from the sacrament is greater.”

And likewise, in the same homily:

“They were saying, ‘If you are the Son of God, save yourself’ (Matt. 27:49); but he endured everything in order to save those who crucified him.”

Likewise, in the third homily on the Cross:

“If Christ endured anything, then, it was not for himself or for his Father, but so that through the cross he might save the human race.”

And likewise, in the same homily:

“When he saw the human race overcome by the devil’s wickedness, he wished to assume his creature and clothe himself, as it were, with one human being, and fasten him to the cross, so that through the wood of the cross salvation might arise for the whole human race.”

And likewise, in the homily on Pentecost:

“For this reason,” Christ says, “I became human; for this reason I put on flesh, so that I might save the whole world.”

And likewise, in the homily on the Nativity of the Lord:

“On earth a perfect human being is born, a complete human being, so that he might save the whole world.”

And in the homily on the Nativity of Christ and John the Baptist:

“He remembered that Christ alone would be the true priest, to whom the Father had said: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’ (Ps. 109:4), who alone offers to God a propitiatory sacrifice for the sins of all.”

And likewise, in the same homily:

“For the one priest was coming, who would offer to God, for the sins of all, a sacrifice from the one lamb, his own immaculate offering. Therefore John displayed him to the Jews: ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world’ (John 1:29).”

Likewise, in the homily on the Father and the two sons:

“He also added a fattened calf to the banquet that was to be prepared—clearly our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the Father gave as a victim for our salvation. He calls him a calf because of the sacrifice of his immaculate body; and he rightly calls him fattened, because he is rich and abundant, so much so that he is sufficient to send up to God, for the salvation of the whole world, the fragrance of sweetness and the odor of sacrifice, and to intercede for all.”

And in the book addressed to Stelechius, *On Compunction of Heart*:

“This is the disposition of a faithful servant: to regard the benefits of his lord, which have been given commonly to all, as though they had been granted to him alone, and to consider himself alone the debtor for all, as though he alone were held liable for everyone. Paul did this too. He says that the death of our Lord and Savior, which was expended for the whole world, was bestowed upon him alone. For, speaking as though of himself alone, he writes: ‘The life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who gave himself for me.’

“He said this not because he wished to narrow the exceedingly great gifts of Christ, spread throughout the whole world, but—as we have said—as one who considered himself alone liable for all. And truly, what difference does it make if he bestowed it upon others also, when what has been bestowed upon you is so complete as though nothing from it had been bestowed upon anyone else? Therefore even that parable of the good shepherd does not say that he came to seek many sheep, but one. It is one because the divine benefits are bestowed upon all as upon one.”
