[Col. 0328A] Jerome, in the twelfth book on Isaiah, commenting on “And there is no Savior besides me” (Isa. 43:11), says: “He shows that in the Father the Son saves all things; of him the same prophet testifies: ‘And the Lord will send them a Savior, and he will save them’ (Isa. 19:20).” Again, in the thirteenth book, on “Hear me, and you shall eat good things” (Isa. 1:19): “And he announced not only good things, but salvation to all—the salvation provided by him who says to Zion, that is, to the Church, ‘Your God shall reign’ (Isa. 62:7).” Again, in the fourteenth book: “Christ was counted among the wicked so that he might redeem the wicked from sin and become all things to all, in order to save all.” Again, in the same prophecy: “Because he knew that the peoples of the nations, who did not believe them, would believe, he passes to the Gentiles and says that he sent his Son as the witness or testimony of all the nations [Col. 0328B], to announce his precepts and commandments to the peoples. He himself speaks of this when he says: ‘This Gospel must be preached throughout the whole world, as a testimony to all nations.’ Concerning this the Apostle Paul writes to Timothy: ‘There is one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all’ (1 Tim. 2:5).”

Again, in the same prophecy: “He said: ‘I will not always be angry, nor will I be indignant forever, because I strike in order to correct; therefore I kill in order to make alive. For I have mercy on my creature, and those whom I myself created I will not allow to perish forever. Since my spirit proceeds from me, and by my breath and inspiration all things are enlivened and live, it is not right that those who are sustained by my breath and spirit should perish forever.’”

Again, in the prophecy of Hosea, book three: “I loved them so greatly and was such a merciful shepherd that I myself carried the diseased sheep upon my shoulders. Yet they did not recognize me when I healed them by my suffering; and I, who love all, drew them with the bonds of love.”

Again, in the same prophecy: 264 “I shall deliver them from the hand of death. He calls the works by which death kills ‘the hand of death,’ in accordance with what is written: ‘In the power of the tongue are death and life’ (Prov. 18:21). The Lord delivers all and redeemed them through the suffering of the cross and the shedding of his blood, when his soul descended into hell, while his flesh did not see corruption; and he spoke to death itself and to hell: ‘I shall be your death, O death’ (Hos. 13:14). For this reason I died, so that you might die through my death. ‘I shall be your sting, O hell,’ which devoured all with your jaws [Col. 0328D].”

Again: “I shall deliver them from the hand of death, so that what was then represented in part may now be experienced in its fullness, and Israel, together with the entire human race, may be delivered and redeemed.”

Again, in his prophecy of Jonah, on “Jonah was afflicted”: “Beautifully, he who is called Jonah, ‘the grieving one,’ is afflicted with grief, and his soul is sorrowful unto death, because, so far as it depended on him, Christ endured many sufferings so that what had been lost might not perish.”

Again, in the same author’s commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians: “Therefore the Father handed over the Son, and the Son himself handed himself over; Judas and the priests, together with the rulers, handed him over; and finally Pilate himself handed over the one entrusted to him. But the Father handed him over in order to save the lost world; Jesus himself handed himself over in order to accomplish the will of the Father and his own.”

Again: “Do not suppose that this was said merely from my own judgment. Scripture bears witness that Christ, by the grace of God—as certain copies read, apart from God—died for all. But if he died for all, then also for Moses and for all the prophets, none of whom could erase the ancient bond written against us and affix it to the cross (Col. 2:14). ‘All have sinned and lack the glory of God’ (Rom. 3:23).”

And in his Epistle to the Ephesians, on “In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” (Eph. 1:3): “The one who was captured and came under the power of enemies ceases to be free—that is the one who is redeemed. Some therefore say that we too are captives in this world, held under rulers and authorities beneath the yoke of slavery, unable to free our hands from their chains or raise our eyes upward until the Redeemer comes. But who, they ask, is so great and so powerful that he could redeem the whole world at his price? Jesus Christ, the Son of God, gave his own blood, and, rescuing us from slavery, granted us freedom. Indeed, if we believe the histories of the pagans—that Codrus, Curtius, and the Decii Mures [variant: *mures*] checked the pestilences of their cities, famine, and wars by their deaths—how much more should this be judged possible in the Son of God, who by his blood cleansed not one city but the whole world?”

In the fourteenth homily on the Gospel according to Luke: “Such also was the pair of turtledoves. Those birds were not like these birds that fly through the air, but something divine and more august than human contemplation appeared under the form of a dove and a turtledove. Thus the one who was born for the whole world and was destined to suffer was cleansed before the Lord not by sacrifices such as all human beings offer, but, since his dispensation made all things new, he also had new sacrifices, according to the will of almighty God.”

And Saint Augustine, in his book *On Rebuke and Grace* (chapter 16): 265 “Far be it from us to believe, while babbling such things, that we ought to remain secure in this negligence. For it is true that no one perished except the son of perdition. Yet God says through the prophet Ezekiel: ‘He will indeed die in his sin, but I will require his blood from the hand of the watchman’ (Ezek. 33:6). Therefore, insofar as it concerns us—we cannot distinguish the predestined from the non-predestined, and for that reason we ought to wish all to be saved—we must apply severe correction medicinally to all, lest they perish or cause others to perish [Col. 0329D]. It belongs to God to make that correction beneficial to those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.

“For the Apostle says: ‘Reprove sinners in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear’ (1 Tim. 5:20). This must be understood of sins that are not hidden, lest he appear to have spoken contrary to the Lord’s command. For the Lord says: ‘If your brother sins against you, reprove him between yourself and him alone’ (Matt. 18:15). Yet he himself carries the severity of correction so far as to say: ‘If he will not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector’ (Matt. 18:17).

“And who loved the weak more than the one who became weak for all and was crucified for all in that very weakness [Col. 0330A]? Since this is so, grace neither forbids correction nor does correction deny grace. Therefore righteousness must be commanded in such a way that grace from God—by which the commanded righteousness may be accomplished—is sought through faithful prayer. Both must be done in such a way that righteous correction is not neglected, while all these things are done with love, because love neither commits sin nor fails to cover a multitude of sins.”

Again, Saint Augustine, in the twentieth book of *The City of God*, under title 6, from a sermon of the Apostle (chapter 6), on “He died for all” (2 Cor. 5:14): “‘It is good for all,’ he says, ‘to hear the voice of the Son of God and live.’ We must pass from the death of ungodliness to the life of piety. Concerning this death the Apostle says: ‘Therefore all have died, and he died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and rose again’ (2 Cor. 5:15).

“Thus all were dead in sins, absolutely no one excepted, whether through original sins or through those added by the will, whether through ignorance or knowledge, by failing to do what is just. And for all the dead, the one who was alive died—one who had absolutely no sin—so that those who live through the forgiveness of sins might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for all on account of our sins and rose again for our justification.”

Again, in book four of *On the Trinity* (chapter 13): “Christ was killed innocent, so that he might justly and most fairly overcome the devil and, by his just blood unjustly shed, redeem from captivity on account of sin the bond of death and sinners who were to be justified [Col. 0330C]. Hence the devil still deceives his own, opposing himself as a false mediator to those whom he pretends to cleanse by his sacred rites, or rather to bind and plunge into them. He very easily persuades the proud to mock and despise the death of Christ; and the farther he himself is from that death, the holier and more divine he is believed by them to be. Yet very few remained with him, once the nations acknowledged their price, drank it in pious humility, and, trusting in it, abandoned their enemy and hastened to their Redeemer.”

And in the 120th sermon on the Gospel of John: “He makes all those his sheep for whom he suffered, because, in order to suffer for all, he became a sheep.”

Again, Saint Augustine, on Psalm 43: “For even the cross itself was made for those who were persecuting him; afterward those who believed in the one whom they had killed were healed through it.”

And on Psalm 45: “‘Struck to the heart,’ they said, ‘What shall we do?’ (Acts 2:37), as though in profound despair: He is so great, and we are the ones who killed him—where shall we be? And Peter said: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, and your sins shall be forgiven’ (Acts 2:38). They could imagine nothing more serious than this sin. What sin is more serious for a sick person than killing the physician? What more serious thing can a sick person do than kill his physician? When this is forgiven, what will not be forgiven?

“From him, therefore, to whom it was said, ‘You are my refuge and strength,’ they received great assurance: ‘Let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.’ You are baptized in the name of the one whom you killed, and your sins are forgiven. You have come to know the physician afterward; now drink without fear the blood that you shed.”

Again, on Psalm 46: “‘All you nations, clap your hands, for God is king over all the earth.’ It was not enough for him to have one nation under him. Therefore he gave so great a price from his side, so that he might purchase the whole world.”

Again, on Psalm 49: “He called the earth, and he called the whole earth; he called as much earth as he fashioned. Why do false Christs and false prophets rise up against me? Why do they try to entangle me with deceptive words, saying: ‘Behold, here is the Christ; behold, there’? I do not listen to those who point out portions. The God of gods showed me the whole, who called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting; he redeemed the whole, but condemned those who make false claims for particular parts.”

Again, Saint Augustine, in *On Rebuke and Grace* (chapter 11): “The only-begotten Son of God, equal and coeternal with the Father, became human for human beings; without any sin of his own, whether original or personal, he was crucified by sinful human beings. Although he rose on the third day, never again to die, he nevertheless endured death for mortals; by dying he bestowed life, so that those redeemed by his blood, having received so great and such a pledge, might say: ‘If God is for us, who can be against us? He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all’ (Rom. 8:31–32).”

And in book six *Against Julian* (chapter 1): “You also say that Christ died for sinners; I say that he died only for sinners, so that you are compelled to answer: if infants are bound by no sin, then he did not die for infants. For the Apostle says to the Corinthians: ‘Since one died for all, therefore all died, and he died for all’ (2 Cor. 5:14). You are not permitted in any way to deny here that Jesus died only for those who were dead.

“Whom, then, do you understand to be the dead spoken of here? Surely those who have departed from the body? Who could be so foolish as to think that? We therefore understand the dead for whom Christ, one, died for all in the way he says elsewhere: ‘And when you were dead in offenses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him’ (Col. 2:13). And by this, he says, ‘one died for all; therefore all died,’ showing that it could not happen that he died except for the dead. For he proved that all were dead by the fact that one died for all the dead.

“I press this upon the one who refuses; I repeat it; I force it upon him. Accept it—it is salutary. I do not want you to die: one died for all; therefore all died. See that he wanted it to follow that all are understood to be dead if he died for all. Therefore, since they are not dead in the body, it remains that all are dead in sin if Christ died for all. Let no one deny it, let no one doubt it, who does not deny or doubt that he is a Christian.”

Again, in the same book (chapter 11): “One died for all; therefore all died. With what heart, with what mouth, with what face do you deny that infants are dead, when you do not deny that Christ died for them? If Christ did not die for them, why are they baptized? For all who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.

“But if he also died for those for whom the one who died for all died, then all died—and these with all. And because they died in sin, they die to sin, so that they may live to God when they are reborn from God. If I cannot explain how the living gives birth to the dead—for one who is dead to sin and alive to God nevertheless gives birth to one dead in sin, unless he too dies to sin through regeneration and lives to God—is it therefore false because it cannot be explained in words, or can be explained only with great difficulty? Deny it, if you dare: a dead person has been born, for whom you do not deny that Christ died.

“For one died for all; therefore all died” (2 Cor. 5:14). These are apostolic words, but they are our weapons. If you do not wish to resist them, you understand what must be believed without hesitation, even if you do not understand it” (chapter 3).

“We heard from our elders, who said that they knew and had seen it, that Fundanius, the rhetorician of Carthage, though he himself was one-eyed because of an accidental defect, fathered a one-eyed son. By this example your assertion is overturned, in which you say that natural characteristics are not transferred through an accident. For what was accidental in the father became natural in the son.

“Your other assertion—that parents cannot transmit to their children what they themselves do not possess—is overturned by another son of Fundanius, who, as happens most commonly, was born with two eyes from a one-eyed father, and by innumerable people who are born sighted from blind parents. By transmitting to those whom they beget what they themselves do not possess, they demonstrate that you, rather than their sons, resemble themselves, since you have been so blind in your definitions.”

Again, in the same book (the same chapter): “For what things come from parents, and whether there are also other forms of the contagion of sins, we are free to investigate, whether it be easy, difficult, or impossible to discover. Nevertheless, let us not think it permissible to understand otherwise than that through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death, and thus passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. We must believe that all were dead in the sin of the first human being, for whom Christ died, and that all who are baptized in Christ die to sin” [Col. 0332D]. 268

Again, in the same book (chapter 4): “For if you did not wish to twist the right meaning into your crooked interpretation, you would hear the Apostle explaining this briefly. He said that there was one in whom all sinned. In that one all died, so that another one might die for all. For one died for all; therefore all died, for whom Christ died.

“Do you hear, Julian? These are the Apostle’s words, not mine. Why do you ask me how it happened, when you see that it happened somehow? If you believe the Apostle in any way, he could in no way have lied about Christ and about those for whom Christ died.”

Again, in the same chapter: “Therefore those who do not have life are rightly understood to be dead, for whom Christ died. For one died for all; therefore all died. He died, as it is read in the Epistle to the Hebrews, ‘so that through death he might destroy the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil.’”

Again, in chapter 5: “For this reason, I say, infants are found dead under the bond of death—not by that most familiar death which separates soul from body, but by the death by which all those were held for whom Christ died. For we know, as the Apostle says—a statement that must be repeated by us very often—‘that one died for all; therefore all died, and Christ died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves but for him who died for all and rose again’ (2 Cor. 5:14).

“Those, therefore, live for whom the one who was living died, so that they might live. This is expressed more clearly in the following way: Those are freed from the bonds of death for whom the one free among the dead died; or, more clearly still: Those are freed from sin for whom the one who had never been in sin died. Although he died once, he nevertheless dies for each person when that person, whatever his age, is baptized into his death. That is, his death benefits a person when that person is baptized into his death, provided that he too has died to sin—he who had been dead in sin.”

Again: “The human race is freed from the most just condemnation of death through the one mediator between God and human beings—not merely from bodily death, but from the death in which those were dead for whom one died; therefore all died.”

And in book one (chapter 11): “Finally, Saint John says—the one whom you honorably mentioned, whom you praised as holy and learned, whom you said had received testimony and glory from fellowship with the truth—that he too says that Adam sinned in such a grave way that he condemned the whole human race collectively.”

And shortly afterward: “He says that the Jew denies that the world can be saved by the power of the one Christ.”

Again, in book three (chapter 12): “What Christian, however, is unaware that the one who first made the human being from dust fashions all human beings from seed? But it is seed already corrupted and condemned, of which some remain in punishment by justice, while others are freed from evil through mercy. Thus, contrary to what you think and conclude, the assertion of natural sin is not strangled by any of your snares. Nature, corrupted by the will of the first transgressor, is not cleansed by your empty defense through your novel doctrine, but by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Again, in book six (chapter 14): “For one died for all; therefore all died, and he died for all. No one can live for whom he did not die, because the living one died for the dead. In denying this, resisting it, and attempting to tear it down, you dare to shatter the defenses of the Catholic faith and the very sinews of Christian religion and true piety. Moreover, you dare to say that you have undertaken war against the impious, although you arm yourself with the weapons of impiety against the mother who spiritually gave birth to you” [Col. 0334A].

And in book four of *Christian Doctrine* (chapter 21), Saint Ambrose also, although treating a great subject concerning the Holy Spirit, in order to demonstrate that he is equal to the Father and the Son, nevertheless uses a restrained manner of speech, since the matter undertaken requires not verbal ornament, nor emotional appeals for moving the mind, but proofs of the facts. Therefore, at the beginning of this work, among other things, he says:

“Gideon, moved by the divine oracle (Judg. 6:21), when he had heard that, although the thousands of peoples were failing, the Lord would deliver his people from their enemies through one man, offered a young goat. According to the angel’s command, he placed its flesh and unleavened bread upon a rock and poured broth over them. As soon as the tip of the staff carried by the angel of God touched them, fire burst from the rock, and thus the sacrifice that had been offered was consumed.

“By this sign it appears to have been declared that the rock represented the type of Christ’s body, because it is written: ‘They drank from the rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ’ (1 Cor. 7:10). This was certainly referred not to his divinity but to his flesh, which flooded the thirsty hearts of the peoples with the perpetual stream of its blood.

“Already, therefore, the mystery had made clear that the Lord Jesus, crucified in his flesh, would abolish the sins of the whole world—not only sins of deeds but also the desires of souls. The flesh of the young goat refers to guilt incurred; the broth refers to the allurements of desire, as it is written: ‘The people desired a most evil desire, and they said, Who will give us meat to eat?’ (Num. 11:18).

“Thus, when the angel extended the staff and touched the rock from which fire came forth, he showed that the Lord’s flesh, filled with the divine Spirit, would burn away all the sins of the human condition. Hence the Lord also says: ‘I have come to cast fire upon the earth’ (Luke 12:49), and so forth.”

Saint Prosper likewise says in book one of *The Calling of the Nations* (chapter 19): “‘And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people for the forgiveness of their sins, because of the merciful compassion of our God, by which the rising from on high has visited us, to shine upon those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, to direct our feet into the way of peace’ (Luke 1:76ff.).”

Chapter 20 [Col. 0334D]: “The Lord bestowed this merciful compassion not for the redemption of one people only, but for the salvation of all nations. The Evangelist says that Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:51–52).

“This is what that voice of the Lord says—a voice resounding throughout the whole world like a trumpet of compassion, inviting and summoning all human beings. For after he had said, ‘I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you,’ he added: ‘All things have been handed over to me by my Father; and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him.’ Then he added: ‘Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light’ (Matt. 11:25–29).

“John the Baptist, in the Gospel of John, testifies with prophetic spirit, saying: ‘He who comes from heaven is above all; what he has seen and heard, this he testifies, and no one accepts his testimony. Whoever accepts his testimony has certified that God is true’ (John 3:31–33).

“Therefore, as regards the blindness of the human race, contracted through the long night of ignorance and pride, the Creator of the world came into the world, and the world did not know him (John 1:10). ‘The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it’ [Col. 0335B] (ibid., 5). He who is above all testifies to what he has seen and heard, and no one accepts his testimony.

“But because the Son of God did not come into the world without purpose, and gave himself for all, and afterward died—not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God—and says to all, ‘Come to me, all who labor and are burdened,’ while preserving for himself the inscrutable freedom of election and giving knowledge of his Father to those to whom he wishes to reveal it, all the children of light, children of promise, children of Abraham, children of God, a chosen race, a royal priesthood, Israelite men foreknown and predestined for the kingdom of God, whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles (Rom. 9:24), receive the testimony of him who came from heaven. They certify that God is true [Col. 0335C], explicitly signifying in their salvation that God is true, fulfilling and perfecting what he promised to Abraham, the father of all nations.

“When God promised that Abraham would be heir of the world, he did not waver through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God and being fully convinced that what he had promised he was able also to do (Rom. 4:20). Who, then, is so alien to the faith of Abraham, so degenerate from the father of all nations, as to say that the promise either will not be fulfilled or will be fulfilled by someone other than the one who made it?

“That one will be a liar, but God is true; and everyone who accepts his testimony certifies and indicates this: that through the illuminating light he has become seeing, obedient, and understanding, as the Evangelist John testifies: ‘We know that the whole world lies in the power of the evil one, and we know that the Son of God has come and given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and be in his true Son’ (1 John 5:19).”

Chapter 21: “But if it is asked why the Savior of all human beings did not give all people one understanding, so that they might know the true God and be—that is, remain—in his true Son, although we believe that the help of grace was not wholly withdrawn from any human beings, perhaps this has been veiled in the same way as it is hidden why, passing over all the nations, he chose one people for himself to instruct in the knowledge of the truth.

“If that judgment of God is not to be investigated, much less should we murmur about this work carried out with the election of all nations. What God wished to remain hidden must not be investigated; what he made manifest must not be denied.”

Again, in the same chapter: “Since it is not expedient to fight an enemy without a protector—for one is engaged in combat with the one by whom one was once overcome—let no one trust in his own strength. Even when those strengths were intact, they did not stand. Instead, let him seek vengeance through the one who alone was not conquered and conquered all.

“And if he seeks, let him not doubt that he received from the one whom he seeks the desire to seek him. Nor, because he is moved by the Spirit of God, should he think that he does not possess free will. He did not lose it even when he surrendered himself to the will of the devil, by whom the judgment of the will was corrupted, not removed.”

Again, in book two (chapter 16): “There is therefore no reason to doubt that Jesus Christ our Lord died for the ungodly and sinners. If anyone from their number has been found free, Christ did not die for all. But he died absolutely for all. No human being, therefore, before the reconciliation accomplished through Christ’s blood, was not either a sinner or ungodly, as the Apostle says: ‘For while we were still weak, at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly. Indeed, scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps for a good person someone might dare to die’ (Rom. 5:6–7), so that those who live may no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them.

“God demonstrates his love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, having now been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life (ibid., 8–10).

“The same Apostle says in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: ‘The love of Christ urges us, judging this: that if one died for all, therefore all died, and he died for all, and rose again’ (2 Cor. 5:14).

“Let us hear what he declares about himself: ‘The saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I received mercy, so that in me first Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example to those who would believe in him for eternal life’ (1 Tim. 1:15ff.).

“Whether circumcision or uncircumcision, all were universally shut up under sin; one guilt had bound everyone, and among the more and less ungodly there was no one who could be saved without Christ’s redemption. This redemption extended itself to the whole world and was made known indiscriminately to all human beings” [Col. 0336D]. 272

And in the ninth objection against the Gauls: “There is absolutely no human being whose nature was not assumed by Christ the Lord, although he was born in the likeness of sinful flesh, whereas every human being is born in sinful flesh. Thus God the Son, sharing in human mortality without sin, bestowed this upon sinners and mortals: that those who became sharers in his birth might escape the bondage of sin and death.

“Just as being born a human being, Jesus Christ, is not sufficient for the renewal of human beings unless they are reborn in that same Spirit from which he himself was born, so being crucified, the Lord Jesus Christ, is not sufficient for the redemption of human beings unless they die and are buried with him in baptism.

“Otherwise, once the Savior had been born in the flesh of our substance and crucified for us all, it would not have been necessary for us to be reborn and planted together in the likeness of his death. But since no human being obtains eternal life without this sacrament, the one who has not been crucified in Christ has not been saved by the cross of Christ. And no one is crucified in Christ who is not a member of Christ’s body; nor is anyone a member of Christ’s body who has not put on Christ through water and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0337B]. For this reason he underwent fellowship with death in our weakness, so that in his power we might share in the resurrection.

“Therefore, although it is entirely correct to say that the Savior was crucified for the redemption of the whole world, because he truly assumed human nature and because all were lost in the first human being, it can nevertheless be said that he was crucified only for those whom his death benefited.

“For the Evangelist says that Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:51–52). ‘He came to his own, and his own did not receive him; but to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God’ (John 1:11, 13).

“The lot of those who are counted among them is therefore different from that of those concerning whom it is said: ‘The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it’ (ibid., 5). Accordingly, it can be said: ‘The Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world, and the world did not wish to be redeemed,’ because the darkness did not receive the light. But the darkness received it—the light—namely those to whom the Apostle says: ‘You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord’ (Eph. 5:8).

“The Lord Jesus himself, who said that he had come to seek and save what had perished, says: ‘I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel’ (Matt. 10:6). But let the Apostle Paul explain which sheep these are of the house of Israel: ‘Not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor, because they are Abraham’s offspring, are they all children, but “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. 21:12), that is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of promise are counted as offspring’ (Rom. 9:6, 8).

“Among these, therefore, are those of whom we recalled above that it was said: ‘Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God.’ For through him who calls into being things that do not exist as though they existed, and who gathers the scattered of Israel, the children of God and children of promise are gathered into one Church, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, so that what was promised to Abraham might be fulfilled: that in his offspring all the tribes of the earth would be blessed (Gen. 12:3).”

And in the first objection against the Vincentians: “Against the wound of original sin, by which the nature of all human beings was corrupted and killed in Adam, and from which the disease of all desires grew, there is one true, powerful, and singular remedy: the death of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who, free from the debt of death and alone without sin, died for sinners and those liable to death.

“As regards the greatness and power of the price, and as regards the one cause affecting the human race, Christ’s blood is the redemption of the whole world. But those who pass through this age without faith in Christ and without the sacrament of regeneration are alienated from redemption.

“Therefore, because of the one nature of all, truly assumed by our Lord, it is rightly said that all have been redeemed; nevertheless, not all have been rescued from captivity. The particular reality of redemption undoubtedly belongs to those from whom the ruler of this world has been cast out, who are no longer vessels of the devil but members of Christ.

“His death was not expended upon the human race in such a way that even those who were not going to be regenerated belonged to its redemption; rather, it was expended in such a way that what was accomplished through one example for all might be celebrated in each person through a singular sacrament. For the cup of immortality, which was prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed possess within itself the capacity to benefit all; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.”

And Saint Cyril, in his synodal letter to Nestorius, says (Council of Ephesus, Part I, ch. 26):

> “We confess also,” he says, “that the very one who was born from God the Father, the only-begotten Son, God, although according to his own nature he was incapable of suffering, nevertheless suffered in the flesh for us according to the Scriptures, and, in the crucified body of his own flesh, impassibly made its suffering his own. Yet by the grace of God he tasted death for everyone, giving up his own body, although by nature he himself is life and the resurrection of the dead. For in order to trample down death by his ineffable power, to become the firstborn from the dead in his own flesh, and to make a way for human nature to return to incorruption, he, by the grace of God, as was said above, tasted death for everyone; and, rising on the third day, he stripped hell.”

Likewise, in his letter to the presbyters and deacons, the fathers of the monks, and to those who had embraced the solitary life and remained steadfast in the faith of God, at the same place (ibid., ch. 2):

> “It is sufficient, I think, even for faith, that the most holy Paul testifies, saying: ‘What then shall we say? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how will he not also, together with him, give us all things?’ (Rom. 8:31–32). Therefore tell me: how is Christ, who is from the holy Virgin, understood and called God’s own Son? For just as what is generated from a human being according to nature is properly his own, and likewise what is generated from each of the other animals, so what is from God’s substance is understood and called God’s own. How, then, is Christ named God’s own Son? He who was handed over by God and the Father for the sake of the salvation and life of all was handed over because of our sins,”

and so forth. Likewise, in the same letter:

> “Thus also he laid down his soul for us: because his death was salutary for the world, he endured the cross.”

And likewise:

> “The one, worthy of compensation for all, died for all, so that by his own blood he might redeem whatever is under heaven and offer to God and the Father those who dwell throughout the whole earth.”

And likewise:

> “The one, therefore, who was more worthy than all, laid down his soul for all.”

And likewise:

> “For just as it says in Adam, ‘Death came,’ so it also fell in Christ; and he ascended for us and on our behalf to the Father and God who is in heaven, in order to show heaven as accessible to those who are on earth.”

The great Leo, moreover—clearly not inferior to the dignity of the Roman see—in his letter to Emperor Leo says [Col. 0339B] (letter, ch. 11):

> “For just as it cannot be denied, as the Evangelist says, that ‘the Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14), so it cannot be denied, as the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims, that ‘God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself’ (2 Cor. 5:19). What reconciliation could there be by which God might be made favorable to the human race, unless the Mediator between God and human beings, for the sake of all, assumed flesh? And how could he fulfill the truth of his mediation unless he who, in the form of God, was equal to the Father, in the form of a servant also became a participant in us, and the bond of death contracted through one transgression were released by the death of one who alone owed nothing to death? For the pouring out of Christ’s blood, the just one for the unjust, was so rich as a price that, if the whole company of captives believed in their Redeemer, no one would remain held by the bonds of the devil; for, as the Apostle says, ‘where sin abounded, grace abounded even more’ (Rom. 5:20). And although those born under the sentence of sin received the power to be reborn into righteousness, the gift of freedom became stronger than the debt of servitude.”

And likewise:

> “What sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true and eternal high priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh? Although the death of many saints was precious in the sight of the Lord (Ps. 115:15), no killing of an innocent person was the redemption of the world. The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. The courage of the faithful provides examples of patience, not gifts of righteousness. Their deaths were individual deaths, each belonging to the individual; no one paid another’s debt by his own end. Among the children of human beings, only our Lord Jesus Christ truly existed as the spotless Lamb. In him all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised—the people of whom he himself said: ‘When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself’ (John 12:32). For true faith, which justifies the ungodly and creates the righteous, draws human beings into participation in his humanity and obtains salvation in him, in whom alone a human being finds himself innocent. By God’s grace, he is free to glory in the power of the one who, in the humility of our flesh, engaged the enemy of the human race and granted his vengeance to those in whose body he triumphed.”

And likewise, in the same letter:

> “But if heretical obstinacy does not abandon its darkness in the midst of so great a light of truth, let them show from where they promise themselves hope of eternal life, which cannot be reached except through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. For, as the blessed Apostle Peter says, ‘there is no other name given among human beings under heaven by which we must be saved’ (Acts 4:12). Nor is there any redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him who gave himself as a redemption for all, and who, as the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father’ (Phil. 2:6–11).”

And in his letter to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem (letter 72, ch. 3):

> “The true generation of Christ is therefore confirmed by the true cross, because he who is crucified in our flesh is himself born in our flesh. Without the intervention of sin, he could not have been mortal unless he belonged to our race. In order to restore the life of all, he assumed the cause of all and, by paying on behalf of all the force of the ancient bond, which he alone among all did not owe, canceled it. Thus, just as through the guilt of one all had been made sinners, so through the innocence of one all might become innocent, with righteousness flowing from there into all, where human nature had been assumed.”

And in his letter to Flavianus (letter 10):

> “From the very beginning of the human race, Christ was announced to all human beings as one who would come in the flesh. In that flesh, as it is said, ‘the two shall be one flesh’ (Gen. 2:24)—namely, God and human being, Christ and the Church, which came forth from the Bridegroom’s flesh when, from the side of the crucified man, blood and water flowed and she received the sacrament of regeneration and redemption.”

And likewise in his homily on the Nativity of the Lord (homily 1):

> “Our Savior, beloved, was born today; let us rejoice. For there is no place for sadness where the birthday of Life is celebrated—of that Life which, having consumed the fear of mortality, brings us joy concerning the promised eternity. No one is excluded from participation in his gladness; the reason for joy is common to all, because our Lord, the destroyer of sin and death, just as he found no one free from guilt, so he came to liberate everyone.”

And likewise in another homily (homily 2):

> “For the pride of the ancient enemy had not unjustly claimed tyrannical authority over all human beings, nor did he oppress them by an unlawful dominion, since they had neglected God’s command and voluntarily allowed themselves to be drawn into obedience to his will. Therefore he would not justly have lost the servitude of the human race originally held captive unless he were defeated by the very thing he had subjugated. When, therefore, the merciful and almighty Savior so ordered the beginning of his assumption of humanity that he concealed the power of the divinity inseparable from his human being beneath the veil of our weakness, the enemy’s confident cunning was deceived. He thought that the birth of the child produced for the salvation of the human race was subject to him no less than the birth of every other human being.”

And shortly afterward (ch. 4):

> “Nature, cleansed from its ancient defilements, returns to its honor; death is destroyed by death; birth is restored by birth. For at the same time redemption removes servitude, regeneration changes our origin, and faith justifies the sinner.”

And shortly afterward (ch. 5):

> “To you, once cast away and expelled from the dwelling places of paradise; to you, dying through long exile; to you, dissolved into ash and dust, for whom no hope of living remained—to you, through the incarnation of the Word, power has been given to return from afar to your creator, to recognize your parent, to become free from being a slave, and to be advanced from a stranger into a son. Thus, though you were born from corruptible flesh, you may be reborn from the Spirit of God and obtain by grace what you do not possess by nature.”

And likewise in the fourth homily (ch. 2):

> “Let the hearts of believers therefore exult in praise of God, and let the children of human beings confess his wonders. For in this work of God above all, our humility recognizes how highly its Creator valued it: although he had granted much to human origin by making us in his image, he bestowed far more upon our restoration when the Lord himself adapted himself to the form of a servant. Although everything that the Creator bestows upon creation proceeds from one and the same goodness, it is nevertheless less astonishing for a human being to advance toward divine things than for God to descend toward human things. But unless the Almighty had deigned to do this, no appearance of justice and no form of wisdom could have rescued anyone from the captivity of the devil and the depths of eternal death.”

And in the homily on the Epiphany (homily 5, ch. 2):

> “The Jews who wished to remain outside the kingdom of Christ are still, in a certain manner, under the rule of Herod; while the enemy of the Savior dominates them, they serve a foreign power. But what those three men, representing the universal person of the nations, achieved by faith among their peoples when they worshiped the Lord, the whole world attains through the faith that justifies the ungodly. The adopted receive the inheritance of God prepared before the ages, while those who seemed to be legitimate lose it.”

And likewise in the same homily (ch. 4):

> “Meanwhile, the goodness of God remains above all things and denies his mercy to no one, since he indiscriminately bestows many good things upon everyone. To those whom he might justly subject to punishments, he prefers to invite them by benefits. The postponement of vengeance gives room for repentance; nor can it be said that there is no vengeance where there is no conversion. For a hard and ungrateful mind is already punishment for itself, and in its own conscience it suffers whatever is postponed by God’s goodness. Let sinners not be so delighted by their sins that the end of this life finds them in their deeds; for there is no correction in hell, and no remedy of satisfaction is granted where no exercise of the will remains.”

Likewise, in the homily on the Passion of the Lord (homily 1, ch. 5):

> “These deeds therefore possess divine power. But the fact that the Lord restrains the power of his majesty and allows the persecutor to use force against him arises from that will by which he loved us and handed himself over for us, with the Father cooperating in this very act, who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us. The Father and the Son have one will, just as they have one divinity. Of the effect of this disposition, you, Jews, owe us no thanks, nor do you, Judas. For our salvation, although you did not wish it, your impiety served, and through you came to pass whatever the hand and counsel of God had determined should happen. Christ’s death therefore frees us and accuses you. Rightly you alone do not possess what you wished all to lose; yet so great is the goodness of our Redeemer that you too may obtain pardon if, by confessing Christ as the Son of God, you abandon that parricidal wickedness. For the Lord did not pray on the cross in vain: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23:34). This remedy would not have passed you by, Judas, if you had fled to the repentance that would have brought you back to Christ, not to that which drove you toward the noose. But when you said, ‘I have sinned by betraying innocent blood’ (Matt. 27:4), you persisted in the perversity of your impiety, believing Jesus, even amid the extreme dangers of your own death, to be not God, the Son of God, but merely a human being of our condition. You would have bent his mercy to you if you had not denied his omnipotence.”

And in the third homily on the Passion of the Lord (ch. 2):

> “Whatever mockery and insult, whatever harassment and punishment the fury of the impious inflicted upon the Lord was endured not from necessity but by his will. For ‘the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost’ (Matt. 18:11), and he used the malice of his persecutors for the redemption of all in such a way that, through the sacrament of his death and resurrection, his killers too could be saved if they believed. Therefore you proved more criminal than all and more wretched than all, Judas, whom repentance did not bring back to the Lord but despair dragged to the noose. You should have awaited the completion of your crime and postponed your hanging until Christ’s blood had been poured out for all the weak. When so many miracles of the Lord, so many gifts, and even those sacraments received at the Paschal supper—when you had already been exposed by the sign of divine knowledge because of your treachery—might have recalled you from your plunge, why did you despair of his goodness? He did not exclude you from communion in his body and blood; he did not deny you the kiss of peace when you came with the crowds and the armed cohort to seize him. But you, a man incapable of conversion, a spirit that went away and did not return, followed the frenzy of your heart. While the devil stood at your right hand, you turned back upon your own head the wickedness which you had armed against the head of all the saints. Since your crime had exceeded every measure of vengeance, your impiety had you as its judge, and your punishment endured you as its executioner.

> “When, therefore, God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, and the Creator himself bore the creature in order to reform it according to the image of its creator, after completing the miracles of divine works that the prophetic Spirit had formerly foretold would take place—‘Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall speak clearly’ (Isa. 35:5–6)—Jesus, knowing that the time had come to fulfill his glorious Passion, said: ‘My soul is sorrowful unto death’ (Matt. 26:38); and again: ‘Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me’ (ibid., 39). By these words, which expressed a certain fear, he cared for us by sharing the feeling of our weakness and dispelled the fear of painful experience by undergoing it. The Lord therefore trembled in us with our fear, and by assuming our weakness clothed himself in it, so that he might clothe our instability with the solidity of his power.”

Likewise, in the fourth homily on the Passion of the Lord (ch. 1):

> “When everything had been accomplished that the divinity, moderated by the veil of flesh, permitted to take place, Jesus, the Son of God, was fastened to the cross that he himself had carried. Two robbers were likewise crucified, one on his right and the other on his left, so that even in the appearance of the gibbet that distinction might be shown which will be made in his judgment among all human beings: the faith of the believing robber expressing the figure of those who are to be saved, and the impiety of the blaspheming robber foreshadowing the condition of those who are to be condemned.

> “The Passion of Christ therefore contains the sacrament of our salvation, and from the instrument that the iniquity of the Jews prepared for punishment, the power of the Redeemer made a step toward glory. The Lord Jesus undertook it for the salvation of all human beings in such a way that, amid the nails by which he was fastened to the wood, he pleaded the Father’s clemency for his killers and said: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23:34). But the chief priests, for whom the Savior was asking pardon, sharpened the punishment of the cross with the barbs of mockery. Against the one upon whom they could no longer rage with their hands, they hurled the weapons of their tongues, saying: ‘He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the king of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him’ (Matt. 27:42).”

Likewise, in the fifth homily on the Passion of the Lord (ch. 3):

> “In all the insults and insolence that the madness of the populace and the priests inflicted upon him, our stains were washed away and our offenses expiated, because the nature that had always been guilty and captive in us suffered innocent and free in him. Thus, in order to take away the sin of the world, the Lamb offered himself as a sacrifice—the one whose bodily substance joined him to all, while his spiritual origin distinguished him from all.”

Likewise, in the sixth homily (ch. 1):

> “The blindness of the Jews achieved nothing except to destroy themselves by their own impiety; but the patience of Christ brought this about, that he saved all by his Passion.”

And likewise in the same homily (ch. 4):

> “When Pilate yielded to the seditious cries of the Jews, Christ was crucified at the place called Golgotha. Through the wood, the one who had fallen by the wood was raised up; by the taste of gall and vinegar, the food of sin was dissolved. The Lord had rightly said before he was handed over: ‘When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself’ (John 12:32)—that is, I will deal with the entire cause of the human race and restore the nature once lost to wholeness; in me every weakness will be abolished, in me every wound will be healed.

> “That Jesus, when lifted up, drew all things to himself was shown not only by the suffering of our substance but also by the disturbance of the whole world. While the Creator hung upon the gibbet, all creation groaned together, and all the elements simultaneously felt the nails of the cross. Nothing was free from that punishment. By it he drew both earth and heaven into participation in himself; by it he split rocks, opened tombs, unlocked the regions below, and hid the rays of the sun amid the horror of thick darkness. The world owed this testimony to its author, so that at the setting of its Creator all things might desire to come to an end. But God’s patience preserves order among things and times, and instead invites us toward this disposition: that we should seek the salvation of those whose crime we shudder at.

> “By so great a price and so great a sacrament, we have been rescued from the power of darkness and released from the bonds of ancient captivity.”

And in the eighth homily (ch. 1):

> “He set before the devil, raging through the agency of the Jews, the form of a servant who had no sin, so that through him the cause of all might be accomplished, in whom alone the nature of all was without guilt. The children of darkness therefore rushed upon the true light, and, using torches and lanterns, they did not escape the night of their unbelief because they did not understand the author of light. They seized him who was ready to be seized and dragged him who wished to be dragged. If he had wished to resist, their impious hands could have done nothing against him; but the world’s redemption would have been delayed, and no one would have been saved by the one who was destined to die for the salvation of all.”

And likewise (ch. 5):

> “Our Passover, as the Apostle says, has been sacrificed: Christ (1 Cor. 5:7). Offering himself to the Father as the new and true sacrifice of reconciliation, he was crucified not in the temple, whose reverence had already come to an end, nor within the boundaries of the city, which were destined to be destroyed because of its crime, but outside, beyond the camp. Thus, with the mystery of the ancient victims brought to an end, a new victim was placed upon a new altar, and the cross of Christ was not the altar of a temple but of the world.”

And likewise in the same homily:

> “You have drawn all things to yourself, Lord, so that what was enacted in the one temple of Judea under shadowy signs might be celebrated throughout the world by the devotion of all nations through a full and open sacrament. Now, with the variety of bodily signs brought to an end, the one offering of your body and blood fulfills every distinction among sacrifices, because you are the true Lamb who takes away the sin of the world. Thus you complete all mysteries in yourself: just as there is one sacrifice for every victim, so there is one kingdom from every nation.

> “Let us therefore confess, beloved, what Paul, the teacher of the nations, confessed in a glorious voice: ‘The saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners’ (1 Tim. 1:15). Here, then, God’s mercy toward us is even more wonderful: Christ died not for the righteous or the holy, but for the wicked and impious. And although the nature of divinity could not receive the sting of death, by being born from us he nevertheless assumed what he could offer for us.”

In the ninth homily (ch. 2):

> “Let the carnal Jew mourn, but let the spiritual Christian rejoice; and let the festival that was turned into night for them shine upon us as light, because the cross of Christ is both the glory of believers and the punishment of unbelievers.”

And likewise in the same homily (same chapter):

> “If, at Israel’s departure from Egypt, the blood of the lamb was the restoration of freedom, and a most sacred festival was established because the sacrifice of an animal had turned away the destroyer’s anger, what joy ought the Christian peoples to conceive, for whom the almighty Father did not spare his only-begotten Son but handed him over for us all? Through Christ’s killing, the Passover might be true—not one people being rescued from Pharaoh’s domination, but the whole world from the captivity of the devil.”

In the homily for Lent:

> “The wisdom of God made the devil’s prudence foolish, so that the proud enemy, seeing the human being whom he had once overcome, would not fear to persecute the one who had to be killed for all.”

In the homily on the Passion of the Lord:

> “The traitor Judas could not attain this pardon, because the son of perdition, with the devil standing at his right hand, passed into despair before Christ fulfilled the sacrament of universal redemption. For when the Lord had died for all the impious, even he might perhaps have obtained a remedy if he had not hurried to the noose.”

In another homily:

> “That universal bond of our sale has been canceled, and the agreement of captivity has passed into the jurisdiction of the Redeemer.”

In the homily for Holy Saturday:

> “From this,” he says, “the beginning of resurrection was made for us in Christ: that in him who died for all, the pattern of all our hope went before us.”

Blessed Gregory likewise says in his sixteenth homily:

> “It is therefore not unworthy of our Redeemer that he wished to be tempted, since he had come to be killed. For it was just that he should conquer our temptations by his temptations, just as he had come to overcome our death by his death.”

And in his twenty-seventh homily:

> “The Lord had come to die even for his enemies, yet he said that he would lay down his life for his friends, clearly showing us that, when by loving we can gain profit from our enemies, even those who persecute us are friends.”

And in the fourteenth book of the *Moralia* (ch. 22):

> “‘Even fools despised me’ (Job 19:18), as if it were plainly said: They too despised me, for whose healing I assumed the foolishness of preaching—that is, so that they might be healed through the flesh of the Word—and I was despised by those for whom I was not afraid to be considered foolish.”

Likewise, in the twenty-first book (ch. 5):

> “The Lord appeared in the flesh for this purpose: to awaken human life by admonition, kindle it by providing examples, redeem it by dying, and restore it by rising again.”

Likewise, in the twenty-second book (ch. 13):

> “For the only-begotten Son to intercede for a human being is to show himself as a human being before the co-eternal Father; and to have asked for human nature is to have assumed that same nature in the exalted dignity of his divinity.”

Likewise, in the twenty-fourth book (ch. 2):

> “Through that by which he showed himself like us, he speaks to the Father on our behalf. For his speaking, or interceding, is to show himself to be a human being on behalf of all.”

In the thirtieth book (ch. 15):

> “For this reason he became human among us: not only to redeem us by the shedding of his blood, but also to change us by the example he displayed. In our manner of life, therefore, by coming he found one pattern and by living he taught another. All those born from proud Adam’s stock were eager to seek the prosperity of the present life, avoid adversity, flee reproach, and pursue glory. The incarnate Lord came among them seeking adversity, scorning prosperity, embracing reproach, and fleeing glory. When the Jews wished to make him their king, he refused to become king; but when they sought to kill him, he came willingly to the gibbet of the cross. He therefore fled what all seek and sought what all flee; he did what all would marvel at, so that he himself, after dying, might rise again and by his death raise others from death.”

In the thirty-first book (ch. 19):

> “For who are the jagged rocks except those strongest choirs of angels who, although not remaining whole, nevertheless stayed fixed in their proper state when the devil fell with his angels? They are jagged because part of them fell and part remained. They stand whole in the quality of their merit, but are jagged in the quantity of their number. The Mediator came to restore this broken condition, so that, once the human race had been redeemed, he might repair the loss among the angels and perhaps enrich the measure of the heavenly homeland even more. Because of this broken condition it is said of the Father: ‘He purposed in him, when the fullness of times had come, to restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth’ (Eph. 1:10). In him the things on earth are restored when sinners are converted to righteousness; in him the things in heaven are restored when humbled human beings return there, from where the proud apostate angels fell.”

In the thirty-fourth book (ch. 8):

> “For it was fitting that the death of sinners who were dying justly should be released by the death of the just one who was dying unjustly.”

Likewise, in the thirty-fifth book (ch. 9):

> “‘I waited for one who would grieve together with me, and there was none; I sought someone to console me, and found none’ (Ps. 68:21). He found no one to console him in his Passion because, by despising death, he endured even his enemies, for whom he had come to death.”

And in the thirty-sixth homily:

> “To wipe away the disgust of your minds, that unique Lamb was slain for you at God’s supper. But what are we to do, when we see many still doing what follows? ‘They all began together to make excuses’ (Luke 14:18). God offers what ought to have been requested; unasked, he wishes to give what could scarcely have been hoped for, namely, that he would deign to bestow it when asked. Yet he announces the delights of eternal refreshment prepared for those who despise them, and still they all make excuses.”

And somewhat later:

> “For he says: ‘I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper’ (ibid., 24). Behold, he calls by himself, he calls through angels, he calls through prophets, he calls through apostles, and he also calls through us. Often he calls through miracles; often through scourges; sometimes through the prosperity of this world; sometimes through adversity. Let no one despise him, lest, while making excuses when called, he be unable to enter when he wishes. Hear what Wisdom says through Solomon: ‘Then they will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise early, and will not find me’ (Prov. 1:28). Hence the foolish virgins, arriving late, cry out: ‘Lord, Lord, open to us’; but then the answer is given to those seeking entry: ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you’ (Matt. 25:11–12).”

The same author says in his twelfth homily:

> “There, the one who refused to hear what God commanded here can no longer merit from God what he asks. The one who squandered the time suitable for repentance comes in vain with prayers before the gate of the kingdom. Hence the Lord says through Solomon: ‘I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked; you despised all my counsel and neglected my reproaches. I too will laugh at your destruction and mock you when what you feared comes upon you—when sudden calamity falls upon you and destruction rushes upon you like a storm, when tribulation and distress come upon you. Then they will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise early, and will not find me’ (Prov. 1:24–27).”

And somewhat earlier:

> “Then the gate of the kingdom is closed to those who mourn, although now it is opened daily to those who repent.”

The venerable presbyter Bede also says in his exposition of the Acts of the Apostles:

> “The Apostle soothes the minds of the Jews in order to make them more ready to believe, saying that the Savior of the whole world had chosen them to visit and bless them first: ‘For you first,’ he says, ‘God, having raised up his Son’ (Acts 3:26).”

And likewise:

> “It was very fitting that Cornelius should be heard, since by continuing his earnest prayer for three hours he extended it from the sixth hour to the ninth—the time when the Lord himself, whom he was imploring, prayed with outstretched hands upon the cross for the salvation of the whole world.”

And in his exposition of the Gospel of the evangelist Mark, at the relevant passage:

> “In a deeper sense: it is easier for Christ to suffer for those who love the world than for those who love the world to be converted to Christ.”

And likewise:

> “About to suffer for the whole world and redeem all nations by his blood, he remains in Bethany, in the house of obedience.”

And likewise:

> “A man carrying a jar of water meets them, to show that the mystery of this Passover was to be celebrated for the perfect cleansing of the whole world. Water signifies the washing of grace; the jar signifies the fragility of those through whom that same grace was to be administered to the world.”

And likewise:

> “The names of the water-carrier and of the master of the house have deliberately been omitted, so that permission might be signified for all who wish to celebrate the true Passover—that is, to be instructed in Christ’s sacraments and to receive him as a guest in the dwelling of their minds.”

And again:

> “He alone prays for all, just as he alone suffers for all; and just as for us he became the curse of the cross, was scourged, and was crucified, so for the salvation of all he is crucified as though he were guilty.”

And in his Commentary on Luke:

> “The Pharisees and the experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves, not having been baptized by him. The phrase ‘for themselves,’ or ‘against themselves,’ signifies either that the one who rejects God’s grace acts against himself, or that, as foolish and ungrateful people, they criticized God’s purpose sent to them and refused to receive it. God’s purpose is therefore that by the Passion and death of the Lord Jesus he determined to save the world.”

Likewise:

> “The calf is rightly called fattened, because its flesh is so rich in spiritual power that it is sufficient for the salvation of the whole world, sending up to God the fragrance of sweetness—that is, the scent of sacrifice—and interceding for all.”

And likewise:

> “He who was called king of the Jews on earth is lord of the angels in heaven. But because Christ, in the flesh, shone forth as the propitiation of the whole world, of both human beings and angels, the heavenly and earthly realms fittingly sing together in his praise.”

And likewise, from the words of Ambrose:

> “‘Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?’ (Luke 22:48). ‘The Son of Man,’ he says, ‘you betray,’ because it is flesh, not divinity, that is seized. Yet what more thoroughly condemns the ungrateful man is that he betrayed the one who, although he was the Son of God, nevertheless for our sake wished to be the Son of Man—as if he were saying: ‘For your sake, ungrateful man, I assumed what you are betraying.’ It should certainly be pronounced as a question, as though he were reproving the betrayer with the affection of one who loves: ‘Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?’ That is: do you inflict a wound under the pledge of love, shed blood through the duty of charity, inflict death through the instrument of peace? A servant betrays his master, a disciple his teacher, the chosen one his author?”

And likewise, from the words of Jerome:

> “And just as for us he became the curse of the cross, was scourged, and was crucified, so for the salvation of all he is crucified as though guilty among the guilty, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound even more.”

And Cassiodorus, on Psalm 20:

> “He alone is the one who earnestly desired to die, when he offered himself to be slain for the salvation of all, so that his precious blood might redeem the world, lest the devil should still ravage it through his wicked presumption.”

And likewise, in the same work:

> “For, without knowing the truth, they said: ‘It was necessary for one to die for all.’”

And likewise, on Psalm 21:

> “Let us therefore hear the voice of the members from the mouth of the head, and understand that he spoke in our person, rightly, who offered himself as a victim for the salvation of all.”

And likewise [Col. 0348D], in the same work:

> “Therefore we are no longer afraid to say that God suffered in the flesh, that God died for the salvation of all.”

And likewise, in the same work:

> “For since he had come to suffer for the salvation of all, whom among them would he not call his brother?”

And on Psalm 30:

> “Being about to say many things concerning his passion, he most mercifully reminds us of it by frequent recollection—the passion which he undertook for the salvation of all.”

And on Psalm 44:

> “All these things befit the flesh, to which the most devoted Word was united for the salvation of all.”

And on Psalm 63, “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy”:

> “He does not ask that he should in no way die for the salvation of all. Hence he rebukes Peter, who said, ‘Be favorable to yourself, Lord; this shall certainly not happen to you’ (Matt. XVI, 22). Rather, he asks that, once his soul has been delivered from fear of the persecuting people [Col. 0349A], he may complete the passion of his holy dispensation.”

And on Psalm 70:

> “When I say that the Word of the Father made heaven and earth and all that is in them, I have praised the Lord with perfect devotion. But when I add that he became incarnate for the salvation of all, I have added a crowning element to praises that are complete.”

And on Psalm 73:

> “Asaph truly became understanding, since he asks for such things that the whole world could thereby be absolved.”

And on Psalm 74:

> “In order to be freed from guilt, he neglected to invoke the Redeemer of all.”

And on Psalm 84:

> “To the sick the physician came; to those filled with pestilence, the author of salvation came. This must be understood not merely with reference to one nation, but as applying to the benefit of the whole world.”

And on Psalm 115:

> “For he who deigned to suffer for the salvation of all ought rightly to be praised publicly” [Col. 0349B].

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Now follows the third point that we mentioned above: how orthodox and ancient teachers demonstrate from authoritative Scriptures that the matter must be understood with distinction. Although Christ suffered for all, nevertheless not all have been redeemed for eternal salvation by the price paid for the world—that is, by the mystery of his passion. Those are strangers to this price who either, delighted by their captivity, did not wish to be redeemed, or, after redemption, returned to the same slavery of captivity.

Behold how the holy teachers understood and wrote that Christ Jesus our Lord—the redemption, namely, of the whole world—suffered for all, although not all have been redeemed by the mystery of his passion. For if we say that Christ brought remedies only to those who have been redeemed [Col. 0349C], we will seem to absolve the unredeemed, although it is clear that they are punished because they despised redemption. Thus Saint Augustine says in his sermon *On the Creed to the Newly Baptized*, from the Gospel:

> “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28). “And they will see him in the form of a man in whom they believed, and him whom they despised. But they will not see the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father. For the wicked will be taken away, lest they see the glory of the Lord, while blessed are the pure in heart, because they will see God.”

And the Lord says:

> “Preach the Gospel to every creature,” that is, to every human being. “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark XVI, 15–16).

And:

> “Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. This is the judgment: that light has come into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light, for their works were evil” (John III, 18–19).

And:

> “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will convict the world”—that is, the inhabitants and lovers of the world—“concerning sin, because they do not believe in me” (John XVI, 8).

For:

> “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John I, 5),

not because it could not, but because it did not wish to. For the darkness also received those to whom it is said:

> “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8);

and:

> “To all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I, 12) [Col. 0350A].

Therefore, if—as the Predestinarians say—the Lord suffered only for those who have been redeemed by the mystery of his passion, and if the salvation of those who are not saved is not the will of God, against which no one can resist, so that they may be saved completely, then God is unjust in bringing wrath. Against this the Apostle says: “By no means!” For, as the Catholic teachers acknowledge, there is the grace of God for saving, and there is free will for voluntarily offering sacrifice to God. No one does good unwillingly, even when what he does is good, because the spirit of fear is of no benefit where the spirit of charity is absent.

Therefore the Catholic Church sings to the Lord of mercy and judgment. He did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Yet, as it confesses in the Creed, he will come to judge the living and the dead. If, then, as Augustine says, there is no grace of God, how does he save the world? And if there is no free will, how does he judge the world?

The Lord therefore suffered for all, although not all have been redeemed by the mystery of his passion, so that everyone who believes in him might not perish but have eternal life. He invites all to this life, saying:

> “Come to me, all of you, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI, 29),

and he wills all people to be saved, since he wishes no one to perish, although not all are saved.

That some are saved is the gift of the one who saves; that others perish is the merit of those who perish, because Adam perished, and in him we all perished. From this mass of perdition, some are chosen by grace for life, while some are abandoned within it by judgment. They are not predestined by God to death, since he does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live (Ezek. XVIII, 23).

For he himself is the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in him, even if he has died, will live, and whoever lives and believes in him will never die (John XI, 25–26). He is the living life that comes from the living bread which descended from heaven and gives life to the world; he gave this bread on the cross for the redemption of all, as he himself says:

> “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI, 52).

The Psalmist invites everyone to eat of him, saying:

> “Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Ps. XXXIII, 6);

and:

> “Taste and see how gracious the Lord is; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (ibid., 9).

And concerning him he says again:

> “Those who distance themselves from you will perish” (Ps. LXXII, 27),

because, as the Lord himself says:

> “Whoever does not believe”—namely, in the salvation promised and prepared for all—“will be condemned” (Mark XVI, 16).

And Paul—or rather Christ himself through Paul—says that believers are saved by that faith alone which works through love, while his fellow apostle affirms that faith is of no benefit if a person has no works.

[286] For those whose examples we have set forth, whom we have identified individually by name, are known and manifest throughout the whole world. We rely upon their teaching, and whoever disagrees with their doctrine and understanding cannot be numbered among Catholics. Whether they shone in the preaching of Catholic truth in the Hebrew, Greek, or Latin languages, from their writings peace and manifold instruction are offered to sound-minded people who seek in devotion. Just as this instruction destroyed other heresies, so too it has cut off this error, now sprouting again.

These modern Predestinarians are known to avoid, with great imprudence and extreme ineptitude, the reading—or rather the true understanding of the reading—of these teachers. Thus the Prophet’s words may be applied to the singular agreement of their perverse conspiracy:

> “He refused to understand, so that he might do good; he meditated iniquity upon his bed” (Ps. XXXV, 45).

What is more unjust, as Leo writes, than to think impiously and refuse to believe wiser and more learned men? Yet those who, when some obscurity obstructs them in their attempt to know the truth, turn not to prophetic utterances, apostolic writings, or evangelical authorities, but to themselves, fall into this folly. They become teachers of error because they were not disciples of truth.

The Lord’s saying has already been cited:

> “This Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world” (Matt. XXIV, 14),

in accordance with the prophetic prediction:

> “The sound of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI, 19),

that is, the preaching of the Gospel throughout the world. He also says:

> “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15),

and:

> “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5).
