They continue to go forth even today. These are the Catholic Fathers whom we have described. Through the Prophet the Lord said to them—and continues to say today, while their teaching governs the Church in right faith and good works:

> “Set your hearts upon its strength”—that is, upon the strength of the city Jerusalem, which is the Church—“and distribute its houses, so that you may declare it to the generation to come, for he is our God” (Ps. XLVII, 14).

That is: do not possess merely the appearance of piety while denying its power; rather, set your hearts upon its strength, which is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. By this ordering of your preaching, distribute the houses of my city, namely, of the great King, joined together in true love at the corner of the Gospel, so that you may declare to the generation to come:

> “For I am God, remaining with you all days until the consummation of the age, who will give you who govern my Church—against which the gates of hell shall not prevail—a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict” [Col. 0351D].

These orthodox teachers, I say, in Asia, Europe, and Libya—which is also called Africa—and in the four parts of the world, East, West, North, and South, were enlightened by him who is truly the light of the world and enlightens every person coming into this world (John I, 9). Whoever is enlightened, whether by natural ability or by instruction in wisdom, was also taught by the perfect number of the apostles, three times four; and, perfected [287] in faith in the Trinity, in teaching, and in evangelical life, they sat among the eleven regions of the world lying in darkness and the shadow of death—namely, Italy, Gaul, Africa, Spain, Illyricum, Thrace, Asia, the East, Pontus, Egypt, and Britain [Col. 0352A].

Just as these regions, exceeding the number ten but not reaching twelve, were imperfect in number, so too they were imperfect in merit before being perfected by evangelical faith and teaching. From the writings of these teachers we have gathered the following teachings, among other declarations of right faith, according to the equally mystical number of one hundred and thirteen provinces.

Whoever, in the three aforementioned divisions of the world—Europe, Asia, and Africa—and in the four parts of the world, as well as in the eleven regions and these one hundred and thirteen provinces, has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; whoever observes the Decalogue in life and conduct through the grace of evangelical preaching, persevering in love of God and neighbor and in the unity of the Catholic Church, will reach eternal life—which is signified by the number one hundred, transferred from the left to the right—with Christ as author and helper.

By his authority these Fathers, through the apostolic arrangement that assigned them the land—that is, the field of the Church—in measured allotments, undertook the houses assigned to them for governance. They handed these on to their successors, to be governed by the faith and teaching with which they had been instructed from heaven, and then departed for the heavenly kingdoms.

Thus Basil says in his sermon on Psalm 59:

> “Now, then,” he says, “I will call this principal and, as it were, private inheritance to division, and I will make it common with all the others. But when the testament has been divided among all, and all its usefulness has begun to be shared by everyone, while God provides something better for all of us, then the valley of the tents will also be measured out—that is, the entire world, which is called the valley of tents because of the dwellings of bodies. Divided and measured out as if by lot, it will be distinguished place by place among the parishes and settlements of the Churches of God. Then he who makes peace through his blood will gather into the unity of faith the things that have been divided, whether those on earth or those in heaven, and he who, by removing the intervening wall of the enclosure, makes both one (Eph. II, 14).”

From these measured allotments these Catholic teachers received such parishes to govern: in the city of Rome, the head of the world, and from there throughout the whole world [Col. 0352D], Innocent, Celestine, Leo, and Gregory. They taught not only concerning this chapter, in which evangelical and apostolic authority teaches that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, that he died for the ungodly, the just one for the unjust, and that if one died for all, then all died, and he died for all; they also taught, as we have stated, concerning the foreknowledge and predestination of God, grace and free will, and the fact that God wills all people to be saved and wishes no one to perish.

In Italy, likewise, in the province of Liguria and the other eighteen provinces of the Italian region, Saint Ambrose taught. In the seventeen provinces of Gaul, Saint Hilary and Prosper taught as we have written. In the six provinces of Africa, Cyprian, archbishop of Carthage, and Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, taught in this Catholic manner. The same blessed Augustine also sent a preparation of an antidote, wonderfully effective against this and many other illnesses, to those suffering from this disease in Gaul near the end of his life.

The seven provinces of Spain were likewise illuminated by this Catholic teaching through Saint Hilary and Prosper. In the nineteen provinces of Illyricum, founded by Paul’s preaching, and in the six provinces of Thrace, where Constantinople is located, Gregory Nazianzen, a man of the highest reputation in faith and teaching, ruled episcopally for twelve years, crushed the heads of the heretics, and erased them from those provinces with the razor of the Catholic tongue [Col. 0353B].

Moreover, Dionysius the Areopagite, an ancient and venerable Father, taught apostolically, as we have written; and John Chrysostom preached in the manner shown by his testimonies. In the twelve provinces of Asia, as John Chrysostom himself demonstrates in his writings, he taught in this manner, although he was exiled through the faction of heretics and the envy of certain others.

In Syria of Cilicia, where Antioch is located—namely, in ten provinces—John Chrysostom is shown to have taught this doctrine before he was taken from Antioch and ordained bishop at Constantinople, as Liberatus, archdeacon of Carthage, writes. Blessed Jerome in Syria-Palestine, where the city of Jerusalem and the town of Bethlehem are located, is shown to have held and taught this understanding, as the testimonies from his writings that we have set forth make clear [Col. 0353C].

In the eight provinces of Pontus, one of which is Cappadocia, Basil of Cappadocia, a great and orthodox teacher, taught in this Catholic manner. In Egypt, where Alexandria is located, Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril taught in six provinces, as we have written. In Britain, comprising five provinces, Bede the presbyter, as we have shown, left these Catholic records to his successors, on the authority of the holy Scriptures and the teaching of the holy Fathers.

Thus, while the Catholic Church—illuminated by Christ, founded by the apostles, and spread throughout the whole world—continued through the preaching of such men, these modern Predestinarians, who, as far as we can discover, are of different orders and habits and different professions, and have not reached the number ten, have arisen in only three provinces against the teaching of so many. As it is written, they are like mice emerging from their holes; like pustules formed by the accumulation of harmful moisture, they break out from place to place upon the body; and, like decayed and corrupt scars, they attempt to defile the members of the Church. Yet they call themselves Catholics, and, through their little chapters—or rather, their lice—presume to mark or disgrace the bishops of the churches, appointed with excessive error and without examination or scrutiny, because they do not approach the apostolic form [Col. 0353D].

But this is not new, just as the heresy they exalt is not new. For, as blessed Augustine says both in his treatises on the Psalms, in his little works *On Shepherds and Sheep*, and in his other books:

> “The Donatists boasted that the Catholic Church had remained only among themselves in Africa. Among other passages, they falsely applied to their cause the scriptural example that says: ‘God will come from the southwest wind, and the Holy One from the densely wooded and shadowy mountain’ (Hab. III, 3).”

The same blessed Augustine laid bare, rejected, and defeated their falsehood most clearly.

If there are more modern Predestinarians than the number we have mentioned, we have not yet been able to discover them. Although their hearts boil over into madness through a perverse understanding, they nevertheless do not dare to express openly the evil things they think. Thus we clearly see fulfilled what is written:

> “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin” (Ps. XXXII, 7).

The water of the sea has been gathered as in a wineskin when the bitter knowledge of heretics compresses in the heart what it perversely believes and does not dare to say openly [Col. 0354B].

And rightly, as we have said, these newly chattering people remain, as far as we can determine, at the number nine and do not reach ten—just as the nine lepers remained ungrateful to the Lord when one returned to give thanks. So too these, separating the smallness of their worthlessness from the unity of the Church that remains in Catholic faith, must, if they wish to be saved, take care to return to the unity of the Catholic faith.

The nine therefore need the one, so that they may be joined together in a form of unity and become ten. But the one does not need them in order to preserve unity. When one is added to nine, a certain image of unity is completed, producing such a totality that it does not proceed beyond that point; and by this rule it is preserved throughout the infinity of number [Col. 0354C]. Those who, made reprobate by the perversity of their own understanding, have been excluded from the fellowship of unity will remain in the number nine, like imperfect beings, unless they return; and on the day of the great judgment they will be condemned among the unknown, to whom the Lord says:

> “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV; Luke XIII).

But if these people, who produce testimonies from certain teachers whom we have identified by name in order to support their error, would carefully read the judgment of the book *Apology* by blessed Gregory Nazianzen and diligently strive to apply it to themselves, they would advance more skillfully and beneficially through reading and teaching, and through hearing the teaching of those same Fathers. They would present their testimonies to their hearers with due consideration.

If we too store that teaching devotedly in our minds, attend to it vigilantly, and read the Scriptures and the treatises of the teachers with a more penetrating understanding, we will strive to ruminate upon it with a simple tooth, to taste it beforehand on the palate of the heart, and to receive it with sincere faith, sober understanding, and a pure heart. We will also strive to place a door and bolts upon our mouths, to set a balance before our words, and to impose restraint upon them, so that we may be able to distribute to our hearers, at the proper time, a measure of wheat, as it is written (Luke XII, 42).

For the Lord says through the Prophet to the choir of preachers:

> “Hearing, you shall announce to them from me” (Ezek. III, 17),

that is, from me, not from yourself. He openly admonishes all of us to conform our understanding to the words of Scripture and of the Catholics, and to offer to our hearers what we gather from them, with the Lord’s inspiration, as though from a pure press, unadulterated. We must not presume to bend Catholic teachings toward our own perverse understanding.

For the aforementioned illustrious teacher Gregory says in the book we mentioned, namely, the *Apology*:

> “There is a threefold danger for those who speak in the Church: danger arising from understanding, from speech, and from hearing. It can very easily happen that one slips in at least one of these, if not in all. Either the understanding is insufficiently enlightened, or adequate speech is lacking for explanation, or the hearing, being duller, does not receive what has been well expressed. From any one of these circumstances danger to the truth arises in everything.
>
> “In other studies and teachings, what is said is easily either expressed or received. In our schools, however, the very expectation of the hearers creates danger for the one who is about to speak. For since they are about to hear about God and receive a word concerning the highest hope and salvation of all, the more clever they have been in matters of faith, the more attentive and scrupulous they become in listening. Thus, if the speaker’s words sound in any place otherwise than they should, they do not consider it a slip of the tongue, but condemn it as a betrayal of faith and piety; and they judge everything not according to the teacher’s reasoning, but according to their own understanding.
>
> “They preserve not the doctrines that they hear in the Church, but those that they bring with them from home; not what they have learned rationally, but what they have retained from an unapproved custom.
>
> “Even this, I say, is not yet a very serious fault in wicked people. Although they do not hold the rule of truth, they nevertheless seem to endure these matters religiously and to possess zeal for God, though not according to knowledge. Therefore perhaps they should not be condemned too severely, since they will not be beaten very much, being ignorant of the Lord’s will and consequently not doing it. Perhaps they may at some time be corrected and amended.
>
> “A religious mind, however, is healed as promptly and easily as it is quickly offended. If an appropriate and suitable word should strike its heart, immediately, like flint struck against iron, it kindles the lamps of truth from the spark of light naturally present within it.
>
> “But what shall we say about those who seek the glory of boasting and delight in ruling over peoples, and who speak iniquity on high? Like certain Jannes and Jambres, they resist not so much Moses as the truth, and raise the weapons of words against sound teaching.
>
> “There is also a third kind, consisting of those who contradict through ignorance. Ignorance is necessarily accompanied by insolence, and they meet every word—unless it is one they themselves have uttered—with hostility and arrogance. From such people, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, the pearls of truth are trampled underfoot in the manner of swine.
>
> “There are others who bring no opinion of their own understanding and possess no particular conception of the faith of God, whether good or bad. Rather, they surrender themselves to every teacher and accept every discourse, as though they were going to choose what is best and most correct from among them all. They do not realize that they have chosen themselves as judges who are not good judges of the truth; they think that they can judge for themselves matters that they admit they do not know.
>
> “Then, frequently turning and changing from one position to another on the basis of probabilities, now agreeing with every word and shortly afterward resisting it again, they change both teachers and studies, and, like dust driven by the wind, are easily carried elsewhere.
>
> “Finally they produce the fruit of their folly. Wearied, as it were, by listening to different people and overcome by boredom, they reject everything at once. As though emptied and left without substance in all the things they had believed, they immediately begin also to despise and mock us, as though our faith contained nothing rational. They suffer what commonly happens to those whose eyes hurt and who blame the light of the sun, or to those who complain that human voices are not sufficiently clear.
>
> “Therefore it is much more beneficial for the soul to receive simply and purely the first elements of truth and, like wax not yet marked, to inscribe them upon it, rather than to write over things that have previously been badly written—that is, to force the word of faith and truth upon an evil teaching and perverse doctrines—and thus confuse the last things with the first.”

And a little later:

> “I will cultivate more successfully that soul which has not yet been violated by the plow of a malicious cultivator and has not been occupied beforehand by the worst seed. Otherwise our labor will be doubled, since it will first be necessary to drive out the forms of evil already conceived; then, afterward, to reform upon the wax of the virtues the image of goodness in varied patterns. Just as the forms of corruption in the soul had been many and diverse, so many and diverse must be the forms of restoration.”

Moreover, concerning what Lord Prudentius says in his little book, which he composed for certain brothers before sending the letter mentioned above to Wenilo, his archbishop:

> “For when, as the holy Evangelists—the truest witnesses and writers of his words and deeds—testify, while dining he set forth the mysteries of his death, which he voluntarily underwent though it was wholly undeserved, and of our redemption, he made known for whom he would suffer.
>
> “Matthew says: ‘And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: Drink from it, all of you. For this is my blood of the new testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins’ (Matt. XXVI, 27–28).
>
> “Mark, however, says: ‘And taking the cup and giving thanks, he gave it to them, and they all drank from it. And he said to them: This is my blood of the new testament, which will be poured out for many’ (Mark XIV, 23–24).
>
> “Luke says: ‘And taking bread, he gave thanks and broke it and gave it to them, saying: This is my body, which will be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me. Likewise the cup, after he had supped, saying: This cup is the new testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you’ (Luke XXII, 19–20).
>
> “If what the Evangelist Luke says is to be understood by us only in this way, so that we understand it in no other manner than ‘which will be given for you’ and ‘which will be poured out for you’—that is, for those who were present there—then in what Matthew and Mark said we may have some hope. For we may be among those many.
>
> “But in what Luke said there will be no hope of salvation for us, nor will any faith remain, because Luke said only ‘for you.’ And if the truth, as it truly speaks, has spoken truly—because this body will be given for you and this cup will be poured out for you—then, since Judas was present there and received the sacraments with the other disciples, it remains for us to understand that the Lord also suffered for them, as the Catholic teachers showed us above, although they are not redeemed for eternal salvation by the mystery of his passion” [Col. 0357A].

Since Judas too had been present at the Lord’s supper, as the truth of the Gospel shows, the Lord says that he will pour out his blood for him, although Judas was not redeemed for salvation. Saint John Chrysostom also testifies to this in his homily on Judas’s betrayal:

> “You see,” he says, “that their unleavened bread is unclean, that their festival is unlawful, that it is not the Jewish Passover, but that it has been removed and annulled by the arrival of the spiritual Passover, which Christ handed down.
>
> “For, he says, while they were eating and drinking, he took bread and broke it and said: ‘This is my body, which will be given for you.’ Those who have been consecrated to the divine mysteries understand what I am saying.
>
> “And again: ‘He took the cup and said: This is my blood, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.’
>
> “Judas was present while Christ said these things. This is the blood, say, Judas, which you sold for thirty pieces of silver. This is the blood concerning which you made an agreement with the Pharisees.
>
> “O mercy of Christ! O madness of Judas! He was making an agreement for thirty pieces of silver in order to sell him, and Christ was offering him the blood that he had sold, so that he might have forgiveness of sins—if only he had not wished to remain wicked.
>
> “For Judas was present and was deemed worthy to share in that sacrifice; and Christ washed his feet when he washed the feet of the other disciples, so that Judas would have no excuse for his wickedness. Yet he was devising the detestable plots of his mind” [Col. 0357C].

And Saint Leo, in his third homily on the Lord’s Passion:

> “Why, Judas, do you distrust his goodness, which did not drive you away from participation in his body and blood?”

Blessed Augustine likewise says in his exposition of Psalm 10, speaking against heretics:

> “What has Christ done to you? He endured his betrayer with such patience that he gave him the first Eucharist, prepared by his own hands and commended by his own mouth, just as he gave it to the other apostles. What has Christ done to you? He sent the same betrayer, whom he called the devil, and who even before the Lord’s betrayal could not demonstrate faithfulness concerning the Lord’s purse, with the other disciples to preach the kingdom of heaven, so that he might show that the gifts of God reach those who receive them in faith, even if the person through whom they receive them is like Judas” [Col. 0357D].

And on Psalm 34:

> “He saw his betrayer and chose him for the necessary work; through that man’s evil he brought about a great good. Yet he was chosen among the twelve, so that the number twelve itself would not be so small as to exist without an evil person.
>
> “This was given as an example of our patience. Since it was necessary for us to live among the wicked, and necessary for us to tolerate the wicked, whether knowingly or unknowingly, he offered an example of patience, lest you fail when you begin to live among the wicked.
>
> “And since that school of Christ did not fail because of one wicked man among the twelve, how much stronger ought we to be, since the great Church is filled with what was foretold concerning the mingling of the wicked?” [Col. 0358A].

And on Psalm 47:

> “All Christians who receive the sacrament of Christ’s baptism are called Christians, but not all live worthily of that sacrament. For there are some of whom the Apostle says: ‘They have the appearance of piety, but they deny its power’ (2 Tim. III, 5).”

And a little later:

> “There are therefore evil daughters, and among them is the lily in the midst of thorns. Thus they possess the sacraments but do not possess good morals; they are called God’s and not God’s, his and alien: his because of the sacrament itself, alien because of their vice.”

This Catholicly discriminating understanding—that Christ Jesus our Lord suffered for all, although not all have been redeemed by the mystery of his Passion—is also demonstrated by blessed Ambrose in his Second Epistle to the Corinthians, where he says (chap. 5):

> “But if one died for all, then all died. For Christ, loving the human race, gave himself over to death in order to redeem them; and because all must die on account of Adam, Christ died for all, so that he might free them from the second death.”

And in the First Epistle (chap. 11):

> “They are guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. For he was slain even for those who render his benefit void.”

And in the Epistle to the Romans (chap. 5):

> “Through one man sin entered this world, and through sin, death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). “Because one Adam—that is, Eve also, since woman too is Adam—sinned in all, so one Christ, the Son of God, conquered sin in all. And because he revealed God’s purpose of grace toward the human race, so as to disclose the very beginnings of sin, he began with Adam, who first sinned, in order to teach that, by the providence of the one God, he had restored through one what had fallen and been dragged into death through one.”

And again:

> “Adam, however, is therefore a type of the one to come, because God had already decreed, in the mystery, to amend through one Christ what had been made sinful through one Adam, just as the apostle John says in the Apocalypse: ‘The Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world’” (Rev. 13:8).

These statements concern God’s general purpose for all, because Christ suffered for all. But because, through their own fault, not all will be saved by the mystery of his Passion, he says again in the same epistle (the same chapter):

> “Just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification unto life came upon all” (Rom. 5:16). “That is: just as through the offense of one all were likewise in condemnation as sinners, so through the righteousness of one all who believe are justified. Just as some suppose that this condemnation is general, they similarly understand justification as general; but this is not true, because not all believe.”

And in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (chap. 15):

> “For I delivered to you first of all that Christ died for our sins” (1 Cor. 15:3).

And Moses concerning his cross:

> “Then you shall see your life hanging before your eyes, and you shall not believe” (Deut. 28:66).

And concerning the general benefit, because he suffered for all and rose again—for he says that he rose on the third day (1 Cor. 15:4):

> “No believer denies that all have risen in Christ, just as they died in Adam.”

And again:

> “Through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:21). “Thus, because death was discovered through human sin, Christ’s righteousness deserved the resurrection of the dead.”

And again, because not all are saved by the mystery of Christ’s Passion, he says in the same epistle who are saved (Second Epistle, chap. 6):

> “‘At an acceptable time I heard you’” (2 Cor. 6:2). “For God decreed that he would make his mercy abound, so that he might bestow help upon those who ask in Christ’s name.”

And again, concerning the benefit of his Passion, generally offered to all (the same epistle, chap. 5):

> “For Christ,” he says, “after the cross descended into hell, death having been conquered. And because he knew no sin, he could not be held by death, because death had made sin and hell powerless, so that the death of the righteous might benefit sinners, and so that from then on death might be unable to hold those who bear the sign of the cross.”

Again (chap. 6), concerning those who are saved by the mystery of the cross, he says in the Epistle to the Romans:

> “For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be united with his resurrection” (Rom. 6:5).

> “He says that we can then rise happily if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death—that is, if in baptism we lay aside all vices and, transferred into a new life, no longer sin thereafter. Through this we shall likewise be made like his resurrection, because the likeness of death will produce a corresponding resurrection. For there would be no likeness if the one made like him differed in no respect: he will be like him in the glory of the body, not in the nature of divinity.”

And again (chap. 15), he demonstrates the distinction concerning the general benefit in the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22).

> “He acquired life—that is, resurrection—for all who belong to his body. Although, therefore, he grants a general resurrection, so that just as in Adam all—both righteous and unrighteous—die, so also in Christ all—both believers and unbelievers—may rise, nevertheless the unbelievers appear to be made alive for punishment, because they will receive their bodies, no longer to die, but to suffer in them without end the punishment of what they refused to believe.”

Again (chap. 1), that the salvation generally offered to all through the cross operates in individuals, he says in the same epistle:

> “For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing” (1 Cor. 1:18).

> “It is clear that those for whom the cross of Christ is foolishness are in perdition, for they have not been rescued from the death of hell. But to those who are being saved it is the power of God” (ibid.). “It is not obscure: for those who believe, it is the power of God. They believe that the cross of Christ is not weakness but power, understanding that death was conquered on the cross. Those who bear its sign are saved, because they cannot be held by that death.”

Because salvation is generally offered to all, he says again (chap. 9) in the same epistle:

> “Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things” (1 Cor. 9:25).

> “He exercises self-control in all those things which the same discipline teaches must be avoided, knowing that one is to be crowned. How much more, then, must we observe this, since salvation has been promised to all?”

How, however, each person defrauds himself of this general benefit, he himself demonstrates in the same epistle, saying (First Epistle, chap. 2):

> “The spiritual person judges all things” (1 Cor. 2:15).

> “Since it is established that all enemies of the faith hold false things as true, their accusation has already been rendered void, condemned by the judgment of truth, because, as the Lord says, ‘The one who does not believe has already been judged’” (John 3:18). “But even a believer and redeemed person, if he does not remain in what he believed and in the redemption he received, deprives himself of the general benefit.”

Again, the same author says in the same epistle (chap. 6):

> “You were bought with a price” (1 Cor. 6:20).

> “And because we were bought with a price in the flesh, we ought to serve our Lord more earnestly, lest, if he is offended, he return us to the death from which he redeemed us.”

And that even such people will not perish if they do not persist in unbelief or iniquity, he demonstrates in the same work, saying (chap. 3):

> “I could not speak to you as spiritual people” (1 Cor. 3:1).

> “The Holy Spirit then remains in the one into whom he has poured himself if that person remains in the purpose of regeneration; otherwise, he departs, yet in such a way that, if the human being reforms himself, he returns to him. For he is always ready for what is good and loves repentance.”

What this Catholic teacher says here concerning the Holy Spirit must be understood also of the Father and the Son together with the same Holy Spirit, whose will and operation are one.

This Catholicly discriminating understanding concerning the redemption of the human race through the Lord’s Passion was held by Saint Jerome, who says in his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> “This must be judged possible in the Son of God: that by his blood he cleanses not one city but the whole world.”

And in his Commentary on Matthew:

> “‘The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many’” (Matt. 20:28). “He did not say ‘for all,’ but ‘for many,’ that is, for those who were willing to believe.”

So also Bede, in the thirteenth homily on the Gospel:

> “‘Baptizing in the Holy Spirit’—indeed, Christ is able to remove sins not only from Israel but also from the whole world, if it is willing to believe in him.”

Saint Hilary likewise held and taught this, saying in his exposition of Psalm 118:

> “Then he reproaches the human race that does not repent and does not proceed along the evangelical way with what is contained in the psalm: ‘What benefit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?’” (Ps. 29:20). “For he reproaches the proud and accursed, asking why they have thought that there is no benefit for them in the mystery of his blood and death, although he was born, suffered, and died for our sake.”

Saint John Chrysostom likewise understood and taught this. In the Epistle to the Hebrews he says that, by the grace of God, Christ tasted death for all—not only for the faithful but for the whole world. And it is said of him: “to take away the sins of many” (Heb. 9:28). He himself indeed died for all. But what if not all believe, while he fulfilled what was his to fulfill?

Saint Augustine likewise understood and taught this, saying in his book *On Rebuke and Grace*:

> “Who loved the weak more than he who became weak for all and was crucified for all in that very weakness?”

And in Book Six *Against Julian*:

> “Those have been freed from sin for whom he died who had never been in sin. Although he died once, he nevertheless dies for each one at the time when that person, whatever his age, is baptized into his death. That is, his death benefits the one who had been in sin when, baptized into his death, he too dies to sin—the one who had died in sin.”

Saint Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, held and preached this, saying at the beginning of his Third Paschal Epistle:

> “Even now the living Wisdom of God calls us to celebrate the holy Passover, desiring all to share in it.”

And in his First Synodical Letter:

> “For this reason,” he says, “the living Word of God came to our aid on earth for all who had been led astray by error, for those nations that did not know the worship of God and were anxious concerning the truth. The witness to this is the one who says: ‘All have sinned; together they have become worthless’” (Rom. 3:12).

And again in his Second:

> “Making ourselves worthy of communion in the body and blood of Christ. For thus we shall merit receiving the kingdoms of heaven in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

And Saint Leo, in his epistle to Leo Augustus:

> “For the pouring out of Christ’s blood—the blood of the righteous for the unrighteous—was so rich as a price that, if the whole company of captives believed in their Redeemer, none would remain held by the devil’s chains.”

And Ambrose, on Psalm 118:

> “Christ died; he died once. He died once for all in common, and he dies once for individuals, not repeatedly.”

Saint Gregory likewise held and preached this in Book Fourteen of the *Moralia*, saying (chap. 22):

> “‘Fools also despised me’”—as though it were said openly: “They themselves also despised me, for whose healing I assumed the foolishness of preaching, that is, so that they might be healed through the flesh of the Word. I was despised by those for whom I did not fear being considered foolish.”

And in his Second Homily on the Prophet Ezekiel:

> “Holy preachers love their persecutors. But the author and Redeemer of all, placed in his Passion, intercedes for his persecutors, saying: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’” (Luke 23:34). “They offer their own members in the Passion for their brothers; but for the life of the elect, the author of life handed himself over even to death.”

And in his Twentieth Gospel Homily:

> “John the Baptist came to preach him who came to preach some from Judea and many from the nations.”

And in Book Twenty of the *Moralia*:

> “The Redeemer offered to suffering the body which he had assumed for the elect.”

And again:

> “The Lord intercedes for us, not by voice but by compassion, because, by assuming what he did not wish to be condemned in the elect, he set it free.”

And Prosper, by delegation from the Apostolic See, explained this Catholic understanding, saying *Against the Gauls*, in the ninth recapitulation:

> “He who says that the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world looks not to the power of the sacrament but to the portion of unbelievers, since the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world.”

The holy Apostolic See itself retains this teaching in the secrets of the heavenly mysteries, received from the tradition of the apostles, saying:

> “May this offering, we beseech you, O Lord, cleanse our offenses; sacrificed upon the altar of the cross, it bore away the offense of the whole world.”

And again:

> “Grant us, O Lord, that this offering may benefit the soul of your servant Leo—an offering which, by its immolation, you granted to release the sins of the whole world.”

And:

> “Look, almighty and merciful God, upon this family of yours, for which our Lord Jesus Christ did not hesitate to be handed over into the hands of the wicked and to undergo the torment of the cross.”

Hence, as blessed Celestine writes, the rule of prayer establishes the rule of belief.

Our Catholic fathers drew this distinction of orthodox understanding from the fountains of the Savior, who says:

> “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who made a marriage feast for his son and sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding, but they were unwilling to come” (Matt. 22:2–3).

And later:

> “I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper” (Luke 14:24).

Many, however, who were called from the roads and hedges came, and the wedding feast was filled with those reclining at table. One of those who came did not have a wedding garment, and after his hands and feet were bound he was cast into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

This wedding feast was prepared from the very beginnings of the world; the calling to this wedding feast has existed from the origin of the human race. As Saint Jerome says in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians:

> “This heir, while still a child, who differs in no respect from a slave although he is lord of all, but is under guardians until the time predetermined by the father, signifies the whole human race from its origin until the coming of Christ—and, to say more, until the consummation of the world. For just as all who had not yet been born die in the first-formed man Adam, so all those who were born before the coming of Christ are made alive in the second Adam. Thus it comes about that we served the law in our fathers, while they are saved by grace in their children.”

And since, as blessed Augustine says in Book Eight of *On the Gift of Perseverance*, “Are there perhaps two human natures? Far be it from us. If there were two natures, there would be no grace. Hence it is clear that there is one nature, but grace is diverse.” Although there is one common merit in the general mass of perdition, there is nevertheless great diversity among human beings, from the beginning to the consummation of the age, in morals and actions.

Through the likeness of one human being and the diversity of one vineyard, and through the distinction of two readings, the Savior demonstrates this, saying:

> “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20:1).

When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his steward:

> “Call the laborers and pay them their wages” (ibid., 8).

Hence Saint Gregory says (Homily 19):

> “The Lord never ceased sending laborers to instruct his people, as though to cultivate his vineyard, because first through the Fathers, then through the teachers of the Law and the prophets, and finally through the apostles, while he cultivated the conduct of his people, he worked, as it were, through laborers in the cultivation of the vineyard. Whoever, in whatever degree or measure, existed with right faith and good works was a laborer of this vineyard.”

And again:

> “A man planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, dug a winepress, built a tower, and sent a servant to the tenants at the proper time, so that he might receive from the tenants some of the fruit of the vineyard” (Mark 12:1), and so forth.

Hence Bede:

> “He rightly says ‘the time of fruits,’ not ‘the yield.’ For no fruit came from the stubborn people; no produce of this vineyard was found, although it was sought frequently and diligently. So it was with the first, second, and third servants mentioned above, continuing until the coming of the Son, concerning whom it is said: ‘Perhaps they will respect my son’” (Matt. 21:37). “The fact that God is said to doubt does not arise from ignorance, but so that free will might be preserved for the human being.”

And the Son came—he who came to seek and save what had perished—saying:

> “‘Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’” (Matt. 11:28), “who did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.”

And the tenants seized and killed the Son. What, then, will the owner of the vineyard do to those tenants? The answer was:

> “He will put those wicked men to a miserable death” (ibid., 41),

because:

> “The one who does not believe has already been judged”—that is, already condemned, because he did not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.

This is the judgment—namely, the condemnation:

> “The light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil.”

After those tenants had been judged, that is, condemned, the owner leased his vineyard to other tenants who would render him its fruit at the proper seasons, because, as that same author explained in Matthew:

> “Therefore I tell you: the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21:43).

For:

> “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16).

And blessed Peter says:

> “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, but waits for you, not wishing anyone to perish, but all to return to repentance” (2 Pet. 3:9).

And Saint Paul:

> “He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

And:

> “If one died for all, then all died” (2 Cor. 5:14).

And he died for all—he who gave himself for all and, by the grace of God, tasted death for all—because, as Isaiah says:

> “We all have gone astray like sheep” (Isa. 53:6). “Each one has turned aside to his own way, and the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all.”

But because not all have been redeemed by the mystery of his Passion, although he suffered for all, he makes this clear again through Isaiah, saying:

> “By his knowledge he himself will justify his many servants” (Isa. 53:11).

And again:

> “He himself bore the sins of many” (ibid.).

And again:

> “This one will sprinkle many nations” (Isa. 52:15).

And in the Gospel:

> “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Matt. 20:28).

And the Apostle:

> “Through the obedience of one, many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5:19).

And again:

> “So that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. 8:29).

And again:

> “He who had brought many sons into glory” (Heb. 2:10).

And again:

> “Christ suffered once to take away the sins of many” (Heb. 9:28).

And again:

> “Christ loved the Church and handed himself over for her” (Eph. 5:25).

Matthew, Mark, and Luke also say that the Lord and Savior declared—not “for all,” but “for many” and “for you”:

> “My body will be handed over, and my blood will be poured out”—

because, although he suffered for all, not all have been redeemed by the mystery of his Passion. And because not all for whom he suffered have been redeemed, this concerns the portion of unbelievers, not the power of the price, since the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world.

It is also clear that, according to the Apostle:

> “All who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Rom. 6:3).

And, as the same Apostle says:

> “We were bought with a great price” (1 Cor. 6:20).

And blessed Peter says:

> “You were redeemed from your futile conduct, inherited from your fathers, not with perishable gold or silver but with precious blood, as of a spotless and immaculate lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 1:18–19).

And yet, although Gottschalk most obstinately denies that anyone redeemed by Christ’s blood can perish, some do perish—either having returned to unbelief or having died in iniquity—as the same blessed Peter demonstrates, saying:

> “There were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will introduce destructive sects, even denying the Lord who bought them, and bringing upon themselves swift destruction” (2 Pet. 2:1).

Hence Bede:

> “Concerning this time Paul also says: ‘You were bought with a great price; glorify and bear the Lord in your body.’ They rightly bring swift destruction upon themselves who, denying their Redeemer, refuse to glorify him by rightly confessing him and to bear him in their body by doing good. All heretics do this.”

And Saint Paul says in the Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27).

Hence Ambrose:

> “What does it mean to be guilty except to suffer the penalties of the Lord’s death? For he was slain even for those who render his benefit void.”

And again:

> “Through your knowledge the brother for whom Christ died will perish” (1 Cor. 8:11).

Here Saint Ambrose says:

> “You too will be the occasion of the death of the brother whom Christ allowed himself to be crucified in order to redeem.”

And the Lord says:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21).

And:

> “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them: ‘I do not know you; depart from me, accursed ones’” (ibid., 22–23).

And Paul:

> “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

This can also be proved by very many other testimonies.

Therefore, if some of those who are to be redeemed perish through their own fault, having returned to unbelief or persevering in iniquity, while it is not denied that Christ suffered for them, why should it not also be believed and said that he suffered for those who, delighting in their captivity, either were unwilling or are unwilling to receive the faith, or were unwilling or are unwilling to abandon iniquity? This is especially so since the Lord openly says to the disciples:

> “Preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:15–16).

And again:

> “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20).

And what Gottschalk says—that the cross of Christ is made void if it is said that Christ suffered for all, while not all for whom he wished to suffer are redeemed—is not surprising, since he explains the cross of Christ as being made void in this way, having presumed to make void the sacrament of baptism while explaining the Apostle Peter’s statement:

> “Denying the Lord who bought them” (2 Pet. 2:1).

> “He bought them,” he says, “by the sacrament of baptism; nevertheless he did not undergo the cross for them, nor endure death, nor shed blood.”

But how the Apostle’s statement, “Let the cross of Christ not be made void” (1 Cor. 1:17), is to be understood is well known from the Catholic exposition. For the sake of brevity, we give only Augustine’s words from *On Nature and Grace* (chap. 7):

> “The cross of Christ is made void if it is said that, in some way apart from his sacrament, one can attain righteousness and eternal life.”

We touch very briefly upon this: just as the faith of Christ is not made void if not all believe, and the sacrament of baptism—which is to be preached to all—is not made void if not all believers are baptized,

> “For,” says Prosper, citing the Apostle (*Response to the Gauls*, ninth sentence), “the word of God has not failed, nor has the redemption of the world been made void. For even if the world did not know God in the vessels of wrath, the world nevertheless knew God in the vessels of mercy.”

So the Passion of the Redeemer is not made void if not all those to whom the cup of human salvation—prepared by divine power and offered to our weakness—has been given refuse to drink it, or if, by living perversely in wicked morals and an evil way of life, they deliver the true, righteous blood of Christ our God into judgment and condemnation through their own sinful members, even if they do not deliver it, as Judas did, to sinful Jews.

For, as Ambrose says, it is a spiritual medicine which, tasted with reverence, purifies the one devoted to it; it is the memorial of our redemption. Hence the Apostle teaches that one must approach communion with devotion and fear, so that the mind may know that it owes reverence to him whose body it approaches to receive.

For a person must judge within himself that he is Lord, whose blood he drinks in the mystery, and that he is a witness to God’s benefit. If we receive him with discipline, we shall not be unworthy of the body and blood of the Lord. For grace will be shown to the Redeemer.

> “Whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27),

because those who approach without the discipline of tradition and conduct are guilty of the body and blood—that is, they will suffer the penalties of the Lord’s death.

For, as Saint Gregory says in his Tenth Homily on the Prophet Ezekiel, there is one hope and one faith of the peoples who preceded and those who followed. Just as they were saved by awaiting the Passion and resurrection of the Son of God, so we are saved by his completed Passion and his resurrection, which endures forever.

And Saint Jerome, in his Epistle to the Galatians:

> “Christ, by the grace of God—or, as it is read in certain copies, ‘apart from God’—died for all” (2 Cor. 5:15).

> “But if for all, then also for Moses and for all the prophets, none of whom was able to erase the ancient bond written against us and fasten it to the cross. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23).

And concerning those who have not been saved, Saint Gregory says in his Ninth Homily on Ezekiel:

> “It should be noted that, after he had spoken of the evils of deceased parents, he sent the prophet to their children, saying: ‘Perhaps even they will listen, and perhaps they will cease’” (Ezek. 2:5). “What does ‘even they’ mean except that their fathers, who died in guilt, were unwilling to listen?”

And Ambrose, in his Epistle to the Romans:

> “‘Have they stumbled so as to fall?’ Certainly not” (Rom. 11:11).

> “This says what I mentioned above: they did not despair in such a way that they could never believe; that is, they were not so blinded by their unbelief that they could not be healed, as we read that the devil fell.”

We have said these things so that we would not now leave unexamined the error of the man who falsely said that we had erred concerning the impious punished before Christ’s Passion.

For we did not write:

> “Christ Jesus our Lord, just as there is no human being, has been or will be whose nature was not assumed in him, so there is no human being, has been or will be, whom Christ, by suffering, did not redeem for eternal salvation.”

Rather, we wrote:

> “Christ Jesus our Lord, just as there is no human being, has been or will be, whose nature was not assumed in him, so there is no human being, has been or will be, for whom Christ did not suffer, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion.”

Why, however, not all are redeemed, although Christ suffered for all, was not concealed by the chapter excerpted by us, as anyone who wishes to read it will be able to discover.

Moreover, from the time of the Lord’s Passion, let us repeat this again: it is absolutely certain that, just as the Truth truly says,

> “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5),

so the same Truth truly says:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54),

and likewise the Truth itself truly says:

> “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16),

because, according to the Apostle:

> “All who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Rom. 6:3);

and:

> “All who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27).

No less true is that statement which the same Truth truly declares:

> “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57).

And if Christ is truly believed to have suffered for the baptized and for those who participate in the heavenly sacraments, as we have demonstrated from Scripture and the words of the Catholics, why should it not also be believed that he suffered for those who perish after relapsing persistently either into unbelief or into an evil life? For the fact that they do not believe proceeds from the hardening of free will, not from God’s action—God who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4).

For our God is the God of salvation. Whoever perishes, perishes through voluntary, not compelled, unbelief, through his own iniquity, not through the will of the Lord, who invites all to salvation, saying:

> “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

But among the humble there is what is written in the Gospel:

> “Those who do not see may see” (John 9:39),

and among the presumptuous:

> “Those who see may become blind” (ibid.)—

not so that they may see, but because they think they see, or rather pretend to see.

Therefore it is safer for all of us to hear the advice which blessed Jerome gives while expounding the same Gospel in his Nineteenth Homily on the Gospel of Luke:

> “You,” he says, “whenever you read the Scriptures, seek their meaning with a certain grief and anguish—not as though you thought that the Scriptures had erred or contained anything improper, but because they possess inwardly the truth of their words and arguments, while you are unable to discover what is true. This is what is meant by: ‘Grieving, we sought you’” (Luke 2:48).

Thus Saint Prosper also sought, as legate of the Holy Apostolic See and as a pupil of the Catholic mother, the truth of the redemption through Christ’s blood in these statements; and he found both the understanding of the truth and the discrimination of understanding.

Hence he said *Against the Gauls*, in the ninth objection:

> “Although, therefore, it is stated with complete correctness that the Savior was crucified for the redemption of the whole world, because he truly assumed human nature and because all shared in the perdition of the first man, he can nevertheless be said to have been crucified only for those whom his death benefited, as the evangelist says: ‘Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad’” (John 11:51–52).

> “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him; but to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:11, 13).

> “The lot of those who are counted among them is therefore different from that of those concerning whom it is said: ‘The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it’” (ibid., 5). “Accordingly, it can be said: The Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world, and the world was unwilling to be redeemed, because the darkness did not receive the light. And there are darknesses which received the light, to whom the Apostle says: ‘You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord’” (Eph. 5:8).

And *Against the Vincentians* (first response):

> “Although, therefore, because of the one nature of all and the one cause of all, truly assumed by our Lord, all are rightly said to have been redeemed, nevertheless not all have been released from captivity. The proper effect of redemption unquestionably belongs to those from whom the ruler of the world has been cast out, and who are no longer vessels of the devil but members of Christ.”

> “His death was not expended upon the human race in such a way that those who were not to be regenerated also belonged to its redemption, but in such a way that what was accomplished through one example for all might be celebrated through a particular sacrament in individuals. For the cup of immortality, prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed possess within itself the capacity to benefit all; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.”

And again *Against the Gauls*, in the ninth recapitulation:

> “He who says that the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world looks not to the power of the sacrament but to the portion of unbelievers, since the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world. Those are strangers to that price who, delighting in captivity, were unwilling to be redeemed, or who, after redemption, returned to the same slavery.”

> “Yet the word of God has not failed, nor has the redemption of the world been made void. For even if the world did not know God in the vessels of wrath, the world nevertheless knew God in the vessels of mercy, which God, without any preceding merits of their own, rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of his love.”

Whoever wishes faithfully to hold this understanding will neither deviate from the correct sense nor disagree with the Catholic teachers; he will neither think that the holy Scriptures are diverse or opposed to one another, nor strive to serve contentious disputes.

Concerning the words of that holy man Prosper, then, to confess simply and truthfully to all readers: compelled by the urgent devotion of our lord and most Christian prince Charles, although we did not have his book before us, our humble understanding has excerpted this chapter insofar as it came to our memory and as the brevity of time and the sudden pressure permitted. But whoever wishes to consider the matter with a kindly and straightforward intention will see that we have departed from nothing in his meaning and scarcely at all from his words. Let him reread both the chapter we excerpted and the words of Saint Prosper that we presented just above, and see whether what we say is true. And lest it be burdensome for any reader to search so far above for the chapter we excerpted, we have thought it appropriate to place it here. This, then, is the chapter excerpted by us:

> “Christ Jesus our Lord, just as there is no human being who is, was, or will be, whose nature was not assumed in him, so there is no human being who is, was, or will be, for whom he did not suffer, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his passion. Since, however, not all are redeemed by the mystery of his passion, this is not due to the greatness and abundance of the price, but concerns the portion of the unbelieving and of those who do not believe with that faith which works through love. For the cup of human salvation, which was prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed contain within itself the capacity to benefit all; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.”

For the Eucharist of the Redeemer and Savior of the world is offered to all, but it gives salvation to the faithful, which is in that same Lord of ours Jesus Christ, who, according to the Apostle, is “the Savior of all human beings, especially of those who believe”; for “there is no other name given under heaven among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). To him, together with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory, power and dominion, before all ages, through all ages, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXXV

The answer concerning the fifth chapter follows. It is as though, adding pain to our wounds, our most bitter accuser wished to spit upon us as a reproach.

[Col. 0369B]

In the fifth chapter this most bitter accuser of ours likewise says:

> “We believe that it must be held with the greatest firmness that the entire multitude of the faithful, regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit and thereby truly incorporated into the Church, and, in accordance with apostolic teaching, baptized into the death of Christ, has been cleansed from sins in his blood.”

Proceeding with what follows in the same order, just as it is contained in the chapter that you formerly gave us—except that, as we stated above, he removed this one apostolic testimony found there: “If we sin deliberately after receiving knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Heb. 10:26)—we do not greatly concern ourselves with why he did this. Although this chapter unjustly thrusts that charge upon us, it cannot wound us, because we have written nothing on that subject and have thought or think nothing contrary to the faith. We also took care to answer concerning it in our earlier books against our detractors. Whoever among them reads their fabrications and rereads our defense will know that we were unjustly criticized here, and that, driven more by a compilation of spite than by any consideration of truth, whoever they were, they wove their spiderwebs against us through futile labor.

Therefore let every devoted reader know that no indication of suspicion whatsoever proceeded from us, or from anything belonging to us, as to why such things should have been written against us or about us. But we have found this written in a memorandum of Gottschalk, which he had composed for a certain monk. We shall set it down here so that we may demonstrate to all who wish to read what he said and how we hold the Catholic position. And although, for those to whom sufficient things can suffice, we had taken care to collect sufficient material in the fourth chapter of this work, nevertheless, because of the shamelessness of those who press us importunately, we are still striving to add certain matters that seem to pertain more specifically to this issue.

The ancient Predestinarians therefore said that, among those who are not predestined to life, the grace of baptism received does not take away original sin; and that those not predestined to life, even if they have been regenerated in Christ through baptism and have lived piously and justly, gain no benefit from it, but are kept so long as to fall and perish, and are not taken from this life before this happens to them. They also said that God does not give perseverance to certain of his children whom he regenerated in Christ and to whom he gave faith, hope, and love, because they were not distinguished from the mass of perdition by God’s foreknowledge and predestination.

Gottschalk, however, after the testimonies cited from Scripture that the Lord suffered for all, speaks as follows:

> “But whoever,” he says, “on account of these testimonies or others like them, says that the Lord suffered generally for the salvation and redemption of all—that is, both of the elect and of the reprobate—contradicts God the Father,”

and so on, until he reaches the following:

> “Nevertheless, because the elect and the reprobate, on account of original sin and, in addition, every actual sin, were, are, and will be held captive under the devil until they were, are, and will be divinely redeemed through the grace of baptism, whenever and whoever among us was baptized in the name of the Trinity, then without doubt we were commonly redeemed, whether elect or reprobate—that is, snatched and freed from the dominion of demonic power. And whenever anyone is baptized, and whoever will be baptized thereafter until the day of judgment, then they are and will be redeemed from diabolical captivity altogether—that is, they are and will be snatched away and freed.

> “Hence there is the statement of the Apostle Peter concerning lying teachers who introduce destructive sects and bring swift destruction upon themselves: ‘Denying the Lord who bought them’ (2 Pet. 2:1). He bought them through the sacrament of baptism, yet he did not undergo the cross for them, nor suffer death, nor shed blood. That the reception of baptism is called redemption is plainly confessed by the Teacher of the Gentiles: ‘Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption’ (Eph. 4:30). And earlier in the same Epistle to the Ephesians: ‘In whom, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise’ (Eph. 1:13).

> “Saint Jerome also asserts this, saying that he found the redemption of ancient sins in the waters of baptism; but this kind of redemption, which is common to the elect and the reprobate, redeemed only from past sins.”

These, then, are the words of Gottschalk. Against them Saint Augustine says in his letter to Boniface (Epistle 106):

> “Thus,” he says, “may the Lord Christ present to himself on that day a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, which he now cleanses by the washing of water with the word; for nothing remains in baptism that is not forgiven of all past sins, provided that baptism itself is not held outwardly in vain, but is either given inwardly, or, if it is already given outwardly, one does not remain outwardly with it. And whatever faults are contracted through human weakness by those who live here after receiving baptism are forgiven on account of that very washing.”

And in the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (chapter 33):

> “For this must be understood,” he says, “in what the same Apostle says: ‘Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the glorious Church to himself, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind’ (Eph. 5:25). This, I say, must be understood in such a way that by the same washing of regeneration and the word of sanctification all the evils of regenerated human beings are entirely cleansed and healed—not only sins, all of which are now forgiven in baptism, but also those contracted afterward through human ignorance or weakness.

> “This does not mean that baptism is to be repeated as often as one sins, but that, because it is given once, forgiveness of every kind of sin is obtained for the faithful not only for sins committed beforehand but also afterward. For what benefit would repentance before baptism have if baptism did not follow, or repentance afterward if baptism had not preceded it? In the Lord’s Prayer itself, which is our daily cleansing, with what benefit and effect would we say, ‘Forgive us our debts,’ unless it were said by those who have been baptized? Likewise, however great the generosity and kindness of almsgiving, to whom would it benefit for the forgiveness of his sins if he had not been baptized?

> “Finally, whose will be the happiness of the kingdom of heaven itself, where the Church will not have spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, where there will be nothing blameworthy and nothing feigned, where there will be not only no guilt but no concupiscence of sin—whose will it be, except that of the baptized? Consequently, not only all sins but absolutely all evils of human beings are removed by the holiness of Christian washing, by which Christ cleanses his Church so that he may present it to himself, not in this age but in the age to come, without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind.

> “For those who now say that she is such, and yet are themselves in her—since they also confess that they have sins—if they speak the truth, then, because they are not cleansed from sins, the Church has a spot in them. But if they speak falsely, because they speak with a double heart, the Church has a wrinkle in them. If they say that they possess these things but that the Church herself does not, let them therefore confess that they are not her members and do not belong to her body, so that they may be condemned even by their own confession.”

And Bede, in the first Epistle of John (chapter 1):

> “And the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from every sin.”

> “For the sacrament of the Lord’s passion has equally released us from all past sins in baptism, and the grace of that same Redeemer forgives whatever we have committed after baptism through daily frailty. This is especially so when, among the works of light that we perform, we humbly confess our errors to him every day; when we receive the sacraments of his blood; when, forgiving our debtors, we pray that our debts also may be forgiven; and when, mindful of his passion, we willingly endure adversity as well.”

Then Gottschalk continues in his aforementioned blasphemies:

> “But that redemption which is proper and particular to all the elect alone, which the Redeemer of them, in his goodness, bestowed upon them alone by being crucified, redeemed all the elect alike—those born and those to be born, the living and the dead—from past as well as present sins; he rescued them and washed them from sins. They themselves, absolutely they themselves, are the world for which the Lord suffered, as he himself said: ‘The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world’ (John 6:51).”

And elsewhere the same Gottschalk writes:

> “Far be it from me even to dream, much less once to whisper, that the ancient serpent could ever seize away and cause any of those to perish eternally with him for whose redemption the blood of the precious Son of our Lord God was poured out to God the Father. Amen.”

And, speaking to God:

> “It is therefore plainly clear that no one belonging to you perishes if he has been redeemed through the blood of your cross.”

Thus, by setting forth many examples from Scripture and the Fathers, which he bends to his own interpretations by distorting them through manifest falsehood, he attempts to strengthen his opinion. This heresy was, among other things, an invention of the Predestinarians.

Accordingly, a certain Paulinus writes to Faustus—whose little works the Apostolic See took care to classify among the apocryphal, because, along with other tares of unsound teaching, he also spread erroneous opinions concerning final repentance, as his writings demonstrate; Saint Celestine refuted them in writing to the Gallican bishops, as is found in his decretal letter—saying:

> “Ignorant as I am, I desire to know how an immortal soul can be tormented for mortal sins, whether soul and spirit are the same or how they are distinguished, so that I may understand. For the aforementioned man Marinus so terrified me, even with the intervention of an oath, that he who has fallen through bodily sins can obtain no forgiveness, but is preserved in the same punishments even at the resurrection, nor can the infernal torments cleanse what he had contracted by being long burdened with bodily sins.

> “Nevertheless, in my wretchedness I believe that if the sign of the divine name, once received, and the character of our Lord, impressed upon the forehead, are never violated by one conscious of no evil or by a deceitful falsifier, then, after lightly endured torments for the expiation of error, he may bring forth a pure, airy understanding and the fire of a simple soul, long consumed. For if we exempt sinners from all these things with which my lord Marinus threatens us, I do not know what greater punishment the ungodly could deserve.”

And somewhat earlier:

> “This is my opinion: if the Christian is exempt from all these things, then the Arian can receive nothing.”

[Col. 0372D]

Saint Augustine also demonstrates that this was an invention of the Predestinarians. He resisted them in another error as well: namely, that some people were condemned according to foreknowledge even before they were born, and that, according to what God foreknew they would become, they were to be condemned according to foreknowledge even if they were taken from the world before they manifested themselves as unjust. In his book *On the Predestination of the Saints* (chapter 14), he says:

> “For who,” he says, “would dare deny that a Christian who is overtaken by death will be in refreshment if he is just? Whoever says this, what person of sound faith would think that he ought to be resisted? Likewise, if someone says that a just person, if he departs from the justice in which he lived for a long time and dies in the impiety in which he lived—not merely for one year but for one day—will go from here to the punishments due to the wicked, and that his former justice will profit him nothing, who among the faithful contradicts this evident truth?

> “Moreover, if we are asked whether, had he died at the time when he was just, he would have found punishment or rest, shall we hesitate to answer ‘rest’? This is the entire reason why it was said, whoever may have said it: ‘He was taken away, lest wickedness should alter his understanding’ (Wis. 4:11). It was said with reference to the dangers of this life, not to the foreknowledge of God, who foreknew what was going to happen, not what was not going to happen. That is, he foreknew that he would grant him an untimely death so that he might be removed from the uncertainty of temptations, not that he would sin, since he would not remain in temptation.”

Against these and many other impious statements of the Predestinarians, that most discerning teacher spoke. We have not undertaken to collect many of them, because those who share certain differences with Gottschalk against Catholic teaching, as we showed above, also resist these perversities of his.

But, following the teaching of the Catholic and apostolic Church, we oppose Gottschalk and his perverse doctrine. With dread and indignation toward all who think wrongly, and with the heart, mouth, and pen of blessed Leo, bishop of the Apostolic See, sounding forth, we cry out (Epistle 4 to the bishops of Sicily, chapter 3):

> “Although those things that pertain to Christ’s humility and those that pertain to his glory come together in one and the same person, and everything in him that belongs both to divine power and to human weakness is directed toward our restoration, nevertheless, properly in the death of the one crucified and in the resurrection of the one who died, the power of baptism creates a new creature from the old. Thus, in those who are reborn, both the death and the life of Christ may operate, as blessed Paul the Apostle says: ‘Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection’ (Rom. 6:3).

> “And the rest of what the Teacher of the Gentiles discussed at greater length in order to commend the sacrament of baptism: so that it might become clear, from the spirit of this teaching, that the day and time were chosen for the regeneration and adoption of the children of human beings as children of God in which, through the likeness and form of the mystery, the things performed in the members might correspond to those performed in the head himself. For in the rule of baptism, death intervenes through the killing of sin; the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial; and the raising from the waters is an image of the one rising from the tomb.”

And the same author likewise says:

> “He established in himself the sacrament of his baptism, because, holding primacy in all things, he showed himself to be the beginning. He then sanctioned the power of regeneration when blood of redemption and water of baptism flowed from his side. The Lord himself demonstrates this when he says in the Gospel according to Luke: ‘I have a baptism with which to be baptized’ (Luke 12:50).”

Hence Bede says:

> “I must first be drenched with the coloring of my own blood, and thus inflame the hearts of believers with the fire of the Spirit, by which they may despise—or rather hate—both all earthly things and their own soul. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. This is the victory of the passion, concerning which he says elsewhere: ‘Can you drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?’ (Mark 10:38).”

And Leo, in his letter to the Constantinopolitans (Epistle 23), says:

> “This is a great sacrament; I mean Christ and the Church. From the very beginning of the human race, Christ was announced to all human beings as one who would come in the flesh. In that flesh, as it has been said, ‘the two shall be one flesh’: namely, God and human being, Christ and the Church, which came forth from the bridegroom’s flesh when, from the side of the crucified, blood and water flowed and she received the sacrament of redemption and regeneration.

> “For she is the new condition of creation, which in baptism is stripped not of the clothing of true flesh but of the contagion of condemned antiquity, so that a human being may become the body of Christ, because Christ too is the body of the human being.”

Hence Saint Siricius to Himerius, chapter 3:

> “It has also been reported that certain Christians, passing into apostasy—which it is unlawful even to say—have been defiled by the worship of idols and the pollution of sacrifices. We order that they be cut off from the body and blood of Christ, by which they had previously been redeemed through rebirth.”

And Athanasius, in the Creed, says that, after the preceding articles, he believes in Christ, who was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father; “from there we await him to judge the living and the dead, obtaining forgiveness of sins through his death and blood.”

And Saint Gregory, in Book 33 of the *Moralia* (chapter 6):

> “He will swallow the river and not be astonished, and he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job 40:18). Who are designated by the name of the Jordan except those who have already been imbued with the sacrament of baptism? Because our Redeemer graciously chose to be baptized in this river, all the baptized ought to be designated by his name, in whom the sacrament of baptism itself happened to begin.

> “But because, even after the Mediator’s coming, it seizes certain believers who neglect to live rightly, and trusts that it can swallow certain others who have been marked with the sacraments of baptism, it devours some who bear the name of Christianity because it trips them up in the very error of their faith. Others it does not turn away from the correctness of the faith, but inclines them toward the practice of evil.”

And shortly afterward:

> “It is exceedingly terrifying that it receives many with open mouth even after they have known the Redeemer; that after the washing of the font it pollutes them; and that after the heavenly sacraments it drags them into the depths of hell.”

And Saint Ambrose, in the second book *On the Sacraments* (chapter 2):
