> “See where you are baptized, and from where baptism comes: is it not from the cross of Christ, from the death of Christ? There is the whole mystery, because he suffered for you; in him you are redeemed, in him you are saved.”

Again, in the same work (chapter 7):

> “The Apostle therefore cries out, as you heard in the present reading, that whoever is baptized is baptized into the death of Jesus. What does ‘into death’ mean? So that, just as Christ died, you too may taste death; just as Christ died to sin and lives to God, so you too may, through the sacrament of baptism, die to your former enticements to sin and rise through the grace of Christ.

> “It is therefore death, but not in the reality of bodily death; rather, it is in likeness. For when you are immersed, you receive the likeness of death and burial; you receive the sacrament of that cross on which Christ hung and his body was fastened with nails. When you are crucified, therefore, you cling to Christ; you cling to the nails of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the devil may not be able to pull you away.”

Again, in Book 5:

> “Then one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and water and blood flowed from his side. Why water? Why blood? Water, to cleanse; blood, to redeem.”

And Saint John Chrysostom, in his homily to the newly baptized:

> “Do you wish to investigate another power of this blood? I want you to begin from where it first flowed and from what fountain it came. It first proceeded from the cross itself; the Lord’s side was its beginning. For when Jesus had died, and while he was still hanging on the cross, a soldier approached, struck his side with a spear, and from it water and blood flowed.

> “The one was a symbol of baptism, the other of the sacrament. He did not say, ‘Blood and water came out,’ but ‘Water first and blood came out,’ because first we are washed by baptism and afterward dedicated through the mystery. The soldier opened his side and disclosed the wall of the holy temple.

> “And I have found a splendid treasure, and I rejoice to discover shining riches. The same thing happened with that lamb: the Jews slaughtered a sheep, and I recognized the fruit of the sacrament; blood and water came forth from the side. I do not want you, listener, to pass so easily over such great secrets of the mystery. A mystical and secret discourse is more valuable to me.

> “I said that the symbol of baptism and the water of the mysteries are shown by that water and blood. For from these the holy Church was founded, through the washing of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit. Through baptism, he says, and through the mysteries that appear to have come forth from the side.

> “From his side, therefore, Christ built the Church, just as Eve, his wife, was brought forth from Adam’s side. For this reason Paul also testifies, saying: ‘We are of his body and of his bones’ (Eph. 5:30), signifying that side. For just as from that side God caused the woman to be created, so also from his own side Christ gave us water and blood, from which the Church might be restored.

> “And just as, during the sleep of Adam who was resting, God opened the members of his side, so now, after his death, he gave us water and blood. That sleep is now death, so that you may learn that death cannot be distinguished from sleep by any separation.

> “See how Christ joined the bride to himself; see with what food of satiety he nourishes you. He himself is the substance and nourishment of our food. For just as a woman, compelled by the nature of her affection, hastens to nourish the child she has borne with the abundance of her milk, so Christ continually nourishes with his blood those whom he himself regenerates.”

And in the first homily on Psalm 50:

> “Among the wealthy, the nurse who has become a mother is ashamed to act as a nurse. But Christ is not so: he is our nourisher. Therefore he feeds us with his own flesh as food, and gives us his blood as drink.”

And in the homily on the beginnings of Mark:

> “Great is the mercy of him who had committed no sins yet was baptized as a sinner. In the Lord’s baptism all sins are forgiven. But the Savior’s baptism is as a prelude; the true forgiveness of sins, however, is in Christ’s blood, in the mystery of the Trinity.”

And in the sermon on the Apostle’s words:

> “‘Do you not know, brothers,’ he says, ‘that all of us who have been baptized in Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death’ (Rom. 6:3). What does ‘we were baptized into his death’ mean? It means that we too should die as he did.

> “For baptism is a cross. What the cross and tomb were for Christ, baptism has become for us—although not in those very things themselves. He died and was buried in the flesh; we die and are buried in sin. Therefore he did not say that we were planted together with his death, but with the likeness of his death. Death applies to both this and that, but not to the same things: the one to Christ’s flesh, ours to sin. Thus, just as that death was real, so is this.”

And the great Pope Leo, in the *Tome of the Catholic Faith* to Flavian (Epistle 10, chapter 5):

> “If, therefore, he has embraced the Christian faith and has not turned his hearing away from the preaching of his Gospel, let him see what nature hung, transfixed by nails, upon the wood of the cross. And when the side of the crucified was opened by the soldier’s spear, let him understand from where the blood and water flowed, so that the Church of God might be watered both by the washing and by the cup.

> “Let him hear the blessed Apostle Peter preaching that sanctification occurs through the sprinkling of Christ’s blood. Let him not read casually the words of that same apostle: ‘Knowing that you were redeemed from your empty way of life inherited from your ancestors, not with perishable silver and gold, but with precious blood, as of a spotless and undefiled lamb, Jesus Christ’ (1 Pet. 1:18).

> “Nor should he resist the testimony of the blessed Apostle John, who says: ‘The blood of Jesus, the Son of God, cleanses us from every sin’ (1 John 1:7). And again: ‘This is the victory that conquers the world, our faith. Who is it that conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies that Christ is truth, because there are three who testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and the three are one’ (1 John 5:4).

> “The Spirit, certainly, is the Spirit of sanctification; the blood, of redemption; and the water, of baptism. These three are one and remain indivisible, and none of them is separated from its connection with the others, because the Catholic Church lives and advances by this faith: that in Christ Jesus there is neither humanity without true divinity nor divinity without true humanity.”

And in his letter to Turibius, bishop of Astorga (chapter 10), he says:

> “No one can be freed from the condition of the old human being except through the sacrament of Christ’s baptism, in which there is no distinction among those reborn, as the Apostle says: ‘For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus’ (Gal. 3:27).”

And Saint Augustine, in Book 6 *Against Julian* (chapter 8):

> “If a person forgets that he has sinned and his conscience is not pricked, where will that guilt be, which you allow to remain after the sin has passed until it is forgiven? Certainly it is not in the body, because it is not among those accidents that occur to the body. It is not in the mind, because forgetfulness has erased its memory. And yet it exists.

> “Where, then, does it exist, when a person is already living well and committing nothing of that kind, and it cannot be said that the guilt of sins he remembers remains while that of sins he has forgotten does not remain? It remains until they are forgiven. Where, then, does it remain except in the hidden laws of God, which have in a certain way been written in the minds of the angels, so that no iniquity may go unpunished unless the blood of the Mediator has expiated it?

> “By the sign of whose cross the water of baptism is consecrated, so that the guilt, as though written in a legal document in the awareness of spiritual powers through which the punishment for sins is exacted, may be washed away. All who are born carnally in the flesh from flesh are born liable to this document; they must be freed from this debt by the blood of him who was indeed born in the flesh and from the flesh, but not carnally, rather spiritually. For he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary: of the Holy Spirit, so that there might not be in him sinful flesh; but from the Virgin Mary, so that there might be in him the likeness of sinful flesh. Therefore he did not become liable to that document, and he released those who were liable to it.”

Again, in the same book:

> “All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. 6:3). By saying “all,” he certainly did not exclude infants. But what is it to be baptized into Christ’s death except to die to sin? Hence, in another place, he says of Christ himself: “For the one who died died to sin once for all” (Rom. 6:10).

> “This was said on account of the likeness of sinful flesh, on account of which the great mystery of his cross also exists, where our old human being was crucified together with him so that the body of sin might be destroyed. If, therefore, infants are baptized in Christ, they are baptized into his death. Planted together in the likeness of his death, they certainly die to sin.

> “For ‘the one who died died to sin once for all; but the one who lives lives to God’ (Rom. 6:5). And what is it to be planted together in the likeness of his death except what follows: ‘So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus’?

> “Are we going to say that God died to sin, which he never had? Far be it from us. And yet it is said that the one who died died to sin once for all. For his death signified our sin, on account of which that death itself occurred, and to that death he died. That is, so that he might no longer be mortal, he is said to have died to sin.

> “What he signified, therefore, in the likeness of sinful flesh, we accomplish by his grace in sinful flesh: just as he, by dying in the likeness of sin, is proclaimed to have died to sin, so whoever has been baptized in him should die—that is, to sin. But in Christ there was a likeness; we truly die to the same reality of which that was the likeness. And just as there was a true death in his true flesh, so in true sin there may be true forgiveness.”

Again, in the same book, chapter 3:

> “Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death—not without infants, since all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death—so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, so shall we also be in the likeness of his resurrection.

> “Here too infants have been planted together in the likeness of his death. For this applies to all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus. We know this because our old human being was crucified together with him. Whose old human being is this, except that of all of us who have been baptized into Christ?”

Again, in Book 3 (chapter 21):

> “The fact that you were born pertains to God’s creation and your parents’ fertility. But the fact that you fight against it because you have been reborn pertains to the transgression that the devil’s cunning sowed. Christ’s grace freed you from this, so that formerly you might use that evil well in your spouse, but now oppose it in yourself.

> “You are no longer guilty on account of it as you were when born, but you have not been freed from that same guilt except by being reborn, so that you may be able to reign, redeemed, with Christ—provided that this heresy does not make you perish with the devil. Rather, and this is what we prefer, confess the evil against which you wage war, so that, once it has not been separated from you as though it were something else, but you have been healed in every respect, you may rejoice in perpetual peace.”

And again in the same work (chapter 5):

> “Nor will you be forced to say impious and absurd things: either that infants ought not to be baptized—which perhaps you will say later—or that so great a sacrament is a mockery in them, so that they are baptized in the Savior but are not saved; redeemed by the Liberator but not liberated; washed by the washing of regeneration but not cleansed; exorcised and exsufflated but not rescued from the power of darkness; that their price is the blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins, yet they are cleansed by the forgiveness of no sin.”

And again (chapter 3):

> “For the rest, I ask you: how can this redemption be understood unless it is redemption from evil by the one who redeemed Israel from all his iniquities? For wherever redemption is mentioned, a price is understood. And what is this except the precious blood of Christ Jesus, the spotless Lamb?

> “But concerning this price—why it was poured out—why should we ask anyone else? Let the Redeemer himself answer; let the merchant himself say: ‘This is my blood, which will be poured out for many, for the forgiveness of sins’ (Matt. 26:28).

> “Go on, go on further, and, as you say, say also this: They are baptized in the Savior’s sacrament but are not saved; they are redeemed but not liberated; they are washed but not cleansed; they are exorcised and exsufflated but are not rescued from the power of the devil. Likewise say: Blood is poured out for them for the forgiveness of sins, but they are cleansed by the forgiveness of no sin.

> “Marvelous are the things you say; new are the things you say. We are astonished at the marvelous things, we avoid the new things, and we prove them false.”

[Col. 0379A] Bede likewise, in his First Epistle of John, says: “He who came through water and blood”—namely, through the water of the laver and the blood of his passion. “Not in water only, but in water and blood.” He did not merely deign to be baptized for our cleansing, in order to consecrate and hand over to us the sacrament of baptism; rather, he also gave his blood for us, when he redeemed us through his passion, so that we might always be nourished for salvation by the refreshment of this sacrament. Again: “There are three who bear witness to the truth, and these three are one” (1 John 5:7). For these remain undivided; none of them is separated from its connection with the others, since humanity cannot be believed to exist without true divinity, nor divinity without true humanity. Yet in us also these are one, not by nature, but through the operation of the same mystery.”

For, as blessed Ambrose says: “The Spirit renews the mind, the water serves the laver, and the blood pertains to the price. The Spirit made us children of God by adoption; the water of the sacred font washed us; the Lord’s blood redeemed us. Thus the one invisible and the other visible testimony follows from the spiritual sacrament.”

And in the consecration of the baptismal water the Catholic Church says: “I bless you through Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, our Lord, who brought you forth together with blood from his side and commanded his disciples that believers should be baptized in you, saying: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’” (Matthew 28:19). Again: “Let the power of your Spirit descend into the fullness of this font, and let it make the whole substance of this water fruitful with the effect of regeneration.” And shortly afterward: “So that every person who enters this sacrament of regeneration may be reborn through our Lord Jesus Christ into the new infancy of true innocence.”

Here the holy Catholic mother Church believes, professes, and proclaims to all Catholics who have been baptized the undivided sacraments of the blood of redemption, the Spirit of sanctification, and the water of baptism. Therefore, as Saint Celestine says, “the law of believing should establish the law of praying.”

Bede likewise, in his treatise on the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 1), says: “After we have been buried with Christ through baptism into death, as though we had crossed by way of the Red Sea, we necessarily have the Lord as our guide in this wilderness, leading us to the heavenly kingdoms.”

[Col. 0379D] Again (chapter 8): “And just as a lamb before its shearer is without a voice, so he redeemed us not only by his blood but also covered us with his wool.”

Hence the same author, in the twelfth homily on the Gospel, says: “How he takes away the sins of the world, and by what order he justifies the ungodly, the apostle Peter shows when he says: ‘You were not redeemed from your futile manner of life inherited from your fathers with perishable silver or gold, but with the precious blood, as of a spotless and undefiled lamb, Jesus Christ’” (1 Peter 1:18). And in the Apocalypse the apostle John says: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Revelation 1:5).

“He not only washed us from our sins in his blood when he gave his blood for us on the cross, or when each one of us was washed by the waters of baptism into the mystery of his most holy passion; rather, he also takes away the sins of the world daily and washes us from our sins in his blood, when the memory of that blessed passion is recalled at the altar, when the created elements of bread and wine are transferred into the sacrament of his body and blood through the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit. Thus his body and blood are not poured out and slain by the hands of unbelievers to their destruction, but are received by the mouths of the faithful for their salvation.”

And the same author, in his treatise on the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 10), says: “It is especially fitting that we be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, because, as the Apostle says: ‘All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death’” (Romans 6:3).

[Col. 0380B] But since those redeemed by the blood of Christ in baptism can perish through unbelief or persistent iniquity, Saint Ambrose, against Gothescalcus, says in his letter to the Vercellenses:

“Paul says to the Ephesians: ‘Fornication, and every impurity and greed, must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints’ (Ephesians 5:3). And below: ‘For know this: no immoral person, or impure person, or greedy person—which is idolatry—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.’

“It is clear that this was said about the baptized. For those who are baptized into Christ’s death and buried with him so that they may rise with him receive the inheritance. Therefore they are heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ: heirs of God because God’s grace is transferred to them; co-heirs of Christ because they are renewed into his life; and heirs of Christ because through his death, as that of a testator, an inheritance is given to them. These people, therefore, should take greater care of themselves, since they have something they can lose, than those who have nothing.”

Again, in the same letter: “What, then, do those people intend who try to corrupt those whom the Apostle acquired, whom Christ redeemed with his blood, when they maintain that the baptized ought not to direct themselves to the disciplines of virtue?”—and the rest.

The same author, in his Letter to the Corinthians, says: “And because we were bought with a price, we ought to serve our Lord all the more earnestly, lest, offended, he hand us over to death—that Lord who bought us at so great a price, giving his blood for us.” Again, in the same letter: “And the weak person will perish because of your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died” (1 Corinthians 8:11). That is, your expertise kills him when he sees you doing something that he understands differently; and you will be the occasion of the death of the brother for whom Christ allowed himself to be crucified in order to redeem him.”

And Saint Prosper, against the Gauls: “The sacrament of baptism, by which all sins absolutely are wiped away, is true even in those who will not remain in the truth.” Again: “The blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world. Those who are strangers to that price are the ones who either, delighted with captivity, did not wish to be redeemed, or, after redemption, returned to the same slavery.”

Bede, in his Epistle of Jude, says: “He who did not spare the angels when they sinned will not spare arrogant human beings either. They did not preserve their principality—that is, the one by which they had become children of God through the grace of adoption—but abandoned their dwelling, namely, the unity of the Church in which they had been reborn for God; or certainly the seats of the heavenly kingdom, which they would have received if they had kept the faith. He will condemn them severely before the judgment, and even more severely in the universal judgment.”

And Peter, in his Second Epistle: “Therefore, brothers, make every effort to make your calling and election certain through good works” (2 Peter 1:10). Hence Bede says:

“Many are called, but few are chosen. The calling of all who come to the faith is certain. But those who steadfastly join good works to the sacraments of the faith they have received make their election, together with their calling, certain to those who observe them. Conversely, those who return to crimes after their calling, when they depart this life in such conduct, make it clear to everyone that they are reprobate.”

Again, in the same letter: “There were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will introduce destructive sects, even denying the Lord who bought them, and will bring swift destruction upon themselves” (2 Peter 2:1). Hence Bede (chapter 2): “Paul also speaks of this buyer: ‘You were bought with a great price; glorify and bear God in your body’” (1 Corinthians 6:20). They rightly bring swift destruction upon themselves, for they deny their Redeemer and refuse to glorify him by rightly confessing him and to bear him in their body by doing good—something all heretics do.

And Peter, in his First Epistle: “Baptism, corresponding to this, now saves you also” (1 Peter 3:21). Hence Bede says:

“Therefore, the fact that the water of the flood did not save those who were outside the ark but killed them undoubtedly prefigured that every heretic, even if he possesses the sacrament of baptism, will be plunged into hell by those very waters—not by others—by which the ark is lifted toward heaven.

“Here we could set forth many examples, and exceedingly numerous ones, but we have considered it unnecessary, since those very people who, as we have said, banded together against the unanimity of the Church’s teaching and resist this perversity themselves gather and heap up many testimonies from many persons. Saint Leo, in his letter to Leo Augustus (letter 97, chapter 4), according to his promise, sent not so much the testimonies of many authors as those of the most renowned authors, and not so many testimonies as strong ones gathered from those same authors, in support of his—indeed, orthodox—opinion. For it is not the number but the authority of the testimonies that matters.

“From these things it is shown that Gothescalcus, through a little leaven, corrupted, insofar as depended on him, the whole mass of the Church. Let these things therefore suffice for the devout; but for the impious, these and still more will not suffice for the satisfaction that leads to salvation. For whoever has received the Lord’s words with a devout mind will not lend an ear to such trivial inventions as Gothescalcus and his associates put forward—words by which the Lord commands us to pray, saying: ‘Thus you shall pray,’ and shortly afterward: ‘Lead us not into temptation.’

“For when, abandoning God, we are justly abandoned by God, we are led into temptation—that is, we suffer ourselves to be overcome by temptation. Against this the Lord again commands: ‘Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation’ (Matthew 26:42). And: ‘Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath’ (Matthew 24:20), that is, so that while the opportunity remains, each person may do whatever good he can, lest anyone then begin to wish to do good when it will no longer be possible to perform good works in any manner.

“For this reason the Lord willed the hour of our departure to be uncertain, so that it might always be feared and so that we might always be ready for the Judge’s arrival, before whose judgment-seat we shall not be able to hide. He does not wish to find people whom he may condemn. Therefore, in the greatest mercy, he warns everyone, saying: ‘What I say to you I say to all: Watch’ (Mark 13:37). And he says: ‘You also must be ready, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. And if he comes in the first, second, or third watch, be like servants waiting for their lord to return from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him. For you do not know at what hour your Lord will come’” (Luke 12:36).

“But this is certain: whoever perseveres to the end—in the right faith, namely, and in good works, which, according to the Apostle, are faith working through love, and love from a pure heart (Galatians 5:6; 1 Timothy 1:5), so that he is not defiled by participation in any heresy, and a good conscience, so that he is not mixed with the confusion of evil, and a sincere faith, so that it is not joined by agreement with the faithless or the wicked—this person will be saved by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“It is beyond doubt that he is the author of good works and spiritual devotion: he stirs their minds, assists their actions, gives perseverance to those who persevere, and crowns those who are to be crowned in mercy and compassion. To him, with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI

The apology for our denunciation follows, because the son of Ephraim, aiming his bow against us, sent arrows; but perhaps he will find his bow crooked. His own sword, turned against him, will not provide assistance to him on the day of battle.

After those six chapters to which we gave a response, you appended a seventh to us in the aforesaid villa of Nielfa, because—so it says—“through the action of our sins, bishops are ordained throughout the cities without having been heard or examined, almost entirely ignorant of literary knowledge, and falling short of the apostolic command; for this reason ecclesiastical vigor has especially perished.” But in the volume that you recently gave us, the compiler of these chapters inserted certain other matters among them, with the result that what had been seventh among those chapters is counted as the tenth among these.

As far as we have been able to understand, this chapter has been placed both there and here so that readers might more easily be persuaded that it is not surprising if we teach perversely, since we approached the order of teaching perversely, inconsiderately, and improperly. For, as Leo says, whoever has had a bad beginning will scarcely have a good course; and if we are suspect in the faith, which is the foundation of all good things, good works will not stand without a right foundation—indeed, they will not even be good.

Therefore, as Saint Gregory teaches, it remains that when the life of those who preach is despised, their preaching is also held in contempt; and when the shepherd proceeds over precipitous paths, the flock follows him to destruction. Hence it is necessary for us to demonstrate to all who wish to know how and in what manner, so far as human eyes can judge, we entered the ecclesiastical order: first concerning the metropolitan bishop of Rheims, and then concerning the suffragans of his diocese.

And because this chapter concerns not us specifically but all bishops generally, with the sole exception of the person who composed it, let us set out the chapter in its entirety, so that we may not appear concerned only about our own defamation. Let everyone who reads it see whether he has ever heard so monstrous an accusation brought and directed generally against all bishops, cities, peoples, archbishops, and princes.

The text of this chapter is as follows:

“And because bishops are ordained throughout the cities without having been heard or examined, almost entirely ignorant of literary knowledge, and falling short of the apostolic command, through the action of our sins, ecclesiastical vigor has especially perished, it has been decided that whenever the bishop of any city departs at the Lord’s calling, the most glorious princes should be petitioned to grant the clergy and people of that city permission to conduct a canonical election. Thus a person proven and worthy of office should be sought either among the clergy, or among the people, or certainly in that diocese itself, or, if necessary, in its vicinity; and once found, that person should be placed over the city, with the consent of the entire clergy and people, for the honor of God.

“Moreover, if one of the clerics of our pious princes should come in order to be placed as bishop over some city, let him be carefully examined with holy fear—first, as to what sort of life he leads, and then as to what knowledge he possesses. Let the metropolitan act in this matter under the eyes of almighty God, while the other bishops assist him as ministers of God, lest a bishop whose life is stained, who is puffed up by worldly pomp, and who is polluted by the Simoniacal heresy, be placed over the humble and pure members of Christ and over the Church.

“Let him not presume to place over the people an unlearned man blinded by unlawful greed, since he will have to render an account of his action to God. But if that metropolitan sees that it is necessary, lest he be compelled to commit so great an evil as to grant the honor owed only to the good to one who is unworthy, let him instruct the people and inform the Church. Rather, let him approach the mercy of the kings, and let him himself, together with his fellow bishops, approach them by whatever means he can, so that the glorious kings may honor the Church of God with a worthy minister.

“But if the metropolitan, shamefully overcome by any sort of greed or deceived by some gift, should negligently and reluctantly carry out so important a task, let him not doubt that he will incur the judgment of God, who sees all things; and let him know that he will also be condemned by ecclesiastical judgment.”

[Col. 0384A] This is the censorious pronouncement of the compiler of the chapters, as though what the canons decree here were insufficient. Therefore let us say with Boethius: “Alas, how deeply sunk in precipitous ruin is the mind dulled!”—namely, the mind of the compiler of this chapter, so that he is unable to understand either what he says or even itself.

For it is written: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23), and: “By your own words I judge you” (Luke 19:22). Let him see how he himself reached the sacred order, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another. For the Truth says: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber. I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10:1, 9).

It is therefore clear that whoever does not enter the sheepfold through him—that is, whoever has not been advanced to govern the Church—is not a shepherd of the sheep but a thief and a robber. He will not be saved but condemned.

How one must enter through the door, namely through Christ, into the sheepfold—that is, how one must assume ecclesiastical governance—the same Christ, the door of the sheep, the way, the truth, and the life, demonstrates when he speaks of his Spirit: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father will teach you everything and will remind you of everything that I have said to you” (John 14:26). “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

Those through whom that same Spirit spoke, as Saint Leo says, still live with us in their constitutions, because God is not the God of the dead but of the living. Therefore, whoever is advanced to govern the Church contrary to the sacred canons, established by the Spirit of God through its instruments and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, does not enter the sheepfold through the door but climbs in by another way, and therefore is a thief and a robber.

Of such people the Psalmist says to the Lord: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Psalm 72:18). For the one who is cast down when he is lifted up is the person who advances in honors but declines in morals. Concerning such people the Lord complains through the prophet: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hosea 8:4).

Those who, inflamed by their own desire, seize the height of governance rather than attain it, reign from themselves and not by the decision of the supreme ruler. Yet the inner Judge both raises them up and does not know them, because those whom he tolerates by permitting them, he certainly does not acknowledge through the judgment of rejection. In the promotion of such men, as Leo says, it is not a matter of caring for the people but of harming them, nor of providing governance but of increasing danger.

Let our detractor, then, return to his own conscience. He departed from the Church in which he had been tonsured and ordained, fled to other provinces, and, bound by canonical excommunication, irregularly usurped governance, since the word of the Lord is not bound. Thus he increased the danger for himself, for those who ordained him, and for his subjects, as Pope Leo demonstrates.

It should also be noted that he omitted certain decrees concerning the appointment of a bishop over a city, whether seized by forgetfulness or prompted by conscience. Among other provisions, the sacred canons have decreed that when someone is requested or taken from another Church to be ordained bishop, he must not be ordained without the approval or letters of the bishop whose cleric he had been—except that the Church of Carthage was granted permission in a specifically noted necessity.

Let the holy brotherhood reread the councils and decrees celebrated and promulgated by the Roman pontiffs; let it review the decrees of councils held in the Greek regions; let it investigate the synods held in the Italian, Gallic, German, and Belgian provinces; and let it see whether, under this heaven, the pontiff of the apostolic see has ever given or sent such a chapter to the consideration of a provincial, much less a general, synod; whether any emperor has ever directed it by his sanction to a synod assembled for that purpose; whether any synod has ever issued it; or whether any bishop has ever presumed to present it to a synod, anywhere or at any time.

The holy brotherhood should know with certainty and truth that we are not saying these things because of any special injury to ourselves. We know and firmly believe that it was by no means written by our brothers—namely, Remigius, the venerable archbishop, and our honorable fellow priests of the province of Lyon—for almost all of them have known us from our youth, and, as familiar associates, have learned intimately our modest learning and our way of life. They could not have been ignorant, as members of our household, from which Churches and orders and in what manner we were raised by divine grace to the highest priesthood. Nor do we wish or are we able to conceal from them how we conduct ourselves in governance, life, conduct, knowledge, and teaching.

In these men, as spiritual persons, we have the greatest confidence, since we know both their religious life, their Catholic teaching, and their canonical ordination.

The compiler of this chapter says:

“Because bishops are ordained throughout the cities without having been heard or examined, almost entirely ignorant of literary knowledge, and falling short of the apostolic command, through the action of our sins, ecclesiastical vigor has especially perished.”

At the beginning of this chapter its compiler teaches that those whom he called bishops are not bishops, when he says: “Because bishops are ordained without being heard or examined.” For in the first chapter of the Council of Carthage it is also written (Council IV): “He who is to be ordained bishop must first be examined,” and so forth.

It is therefore clear that one who appears to have been ordained contrary to the canons ought not to be considered a bishop, as Innocent, Celestine, and Leo, among others, demonstrate. For when he says “without being heard,” it follows that it is uncertain whether they are Catholic in faith or reprobate concerning the faith. When he says “without being examined,” it follows that they are not approved in life and conduct. When he says “almost entirely ignorant of literary knowledge,” we may recall Saint Jerome: “Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of God.” And the Apostle says: “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14:38).

How, then, will those who are themselves unknown be regarded as mediators or intercessors before God for their own sins and those of the people? Even if they say, “Lord, in your name we prophesied” (Matthew 7:22), and “We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets” (Luke 13:26), they will hear: “Depart from me; I do not know who you are.”

Let us add further: how will they be able to say, “In your name we prophesied,” and “In our streets”—that is, in the broad extent of the people entrusted to us—“you taught through us,” when, ignorant of the light of knowledge, they are blind guides and mute heralds?

What follows—“and falling short of the apostolic command”—means plainly: therefore they are strangers to good merit and unworthy of ordination. When he says, “Bishops are ordained throughout the cities, for which reason ecclesiastical vigor has especially perished,” he should have said not that bishops are ordained throughout the cities, but that invaders of cities, usurpers of another’s ministry, thieves and robbers—not to mention hirelings—are appointed, through whom ecclesiastical vigor perishes. They ought instead to have been placed in office so that, if ecclesiastical vigor had declined in any respect, it might have been restored through them and, remaining in its proper state, might have been firmly established.

And although Saint Gregory, in the seventeenth homily on the Gospel, made himself one of those whose particular sin he had said was responsible for the destruction of the people of that time, and complained of a general sin, he did not thereby accuse the priesthood as a whole of specific crimes, lack of merit, ignorance, and unlawful ordination. Even when he rebuked certain people without naming them for Simoniacal heresy, saying, “For I speak with mourning to you priests, because we have learned that some of you perform ordinations for rewards,” he did not, although he was pontiff of the first see throughout the whole world, strike everyone with a general attack, inserting the qualification “some,” as this man has struck them with a schoolmaster’s rod, without any exception.

In the chapter of this compiler, let the reader see what portion of the Lord’s people has not been trampled, what city has not been dishonored, what bishop has not merely been bitten but annihilated, what prince has not been reproved, and what archbishop has not been confuted. For he says:

“Bishops are ordained throughout the cities without being heard or examined, almost entirely ignorant of literary knowledge, and falling short of the apostolic command. It has therefore been decided that whenever the bishop of any city departs at the Lord’s calling, the most glorious princes should be petitioned,”

and so forth, as he continues. It is as though he were saying that the princes had not previously granted such things.

Then, concerning the archbishops, he says: “But if the metropolitan, shamefully overcome by any sort of greed or deceived by some gift, should negligently and reluctantly carry out so important a task, let him not doubt that he will incur the judgment of God, who sees all things. And let him know that he will also be condemned by ecclesiastical judgment.”

[Col. 0386D] Behold what sort of princes he has denounced; behold what sort of archbishops he has described—overcome by greed and deceived by gifts; behold what sort of bishops he has asserted are ordained throughout the cities.

We read in the canons, and have learned from the teaching of Saint Gregory, that the sacred canons condemn the Simoniacal heresy and command that those who seek payment for conferring orders be deprived of the priesthood. Our Redeemer overturns their chairs and destroys their priesthood; and whoever gives or receives a gift for the laying on of hands makes himself anathema.

For we know that in spiritual matters we must avoid a gift from the hand, a gift from the tongue, and a gift from service. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “He who shakes his hands free from every gift will dwell on the heights” (Isaiah 33:15).

Therefore, according to the admonition of Saint Gregory, we must consider what sort of person he will be in governance who is promoted for the purpose of becoming a heretic. If the princes are such, if the archbishops are such, and if the bishops ordained throughout the cities are such, woe to those lands which such men not only occupy as unfruitful but also harmful fig trees, but certainly oppress.

Woe to the sinful cities in which such plagues sit. Woe to the wretched peoples who, without any obstacle, lie exposed not only to the teeth but also to the gaping throats of wolves; who sit in darkness without any light of the word of God; who, without the bread of God’s word or spiritual nourishment, waste away from hunger and approach death—and, more grievously, eternal death.

“The children ask for bread, and there is no one to break it for them”—bread in which even the hirelings abound in the house of this great Father who has described us as miserable bishops. Thus, from the people entrusted to them alone, we might say, if indeed we may say it: “They called blessed the people to whom such things belong” (Psalm 144:15)—namely, the things he bestows; blessed is the people whose ruler, without comparison, is this one alone.

As it is said of Job’s messengers, “He alone escaped to tell” the Church what sort of men it endures—not rulers but subverters. But let him hear the Lord answering him, who said to Elijah with a different feeling than this man expressed in his complaint: “I alone have remained.” The Lord replied: “I have left seven thousand men for myself who have not bent the knee before Baal” (1 Kings 18:19).

Therefore the Lord, through the free gift of his everlasting mercy, has many bishops appointed throughout the cities in a different manner and has archbishops who ordain differently, as well as princes who, by his concession, do not strive through contempt to depart from the divine rules.

The first son of Adam, this compiler of the chapters, knowing that he was going to write perverse things, counted the names of bishops in the preface to those same chapters, wishing to hide himself among the trees of paradise so that he would not be recognized as a sinner. And, as though covered with a covering of precious stones and cloaked in dense foliage so that he might appear more glorious than the rest, he displayed himself in this chapter, as also in those chapters which he labeled by the name of the Synod of Valence, in which he described himself as having collaborated most extensively by name.

But if he decided to direct a general accusation specifically against us, so that we would not perceive it as such, we shall ensure—not to refute him, but to satisfy those who perhaps do not know our path into the sacred orders—that the truth of the matter may become known to all readers and to all who wish to know.

The question concerning the metropolitan of the metropolitan Church of Rheims had already arisen, as anyone who wishes may discover more fully in the records of the synods.

When the venerable bishops were seated in synod in the name of the Lord—Hincmar, archbishop of the Church of Rheims; Wenilo, archbishop of Sens; Amalric, archbishop of Tours; Theodoric, bishop of Cambrai; Hrothad, bishop of the city of Soissons; Lupus, bishop of Châlons; Immo, bishop of Noyon; Erpuin, bishop of Senlis; Yrminfrid, bishop of Beauvais; Pardulus, bishop of Laon; Hilmerad, bishop of Amiens; Hubert, bishop of Meaux; Aio, bishop of Orléans; Prudentius, bishop of the city of Troyes; Herimann, bishop of Nevers; Jona, bishop of Autun; Godelsad, bishop of Chalon; Dodo, bishop of Angers; Guntbert, bishop of Évreux; Hildebrand, bishop of Sées; Erloinus, bishop of the city of Coutances; Baltfrid, bishop of the Church of Bayeux; Heirard, bishop of the Church of Lisieux; Ansegaud, bishop of the city of Avranches; Teutbold, bishop of the city of Langres; Breiding, bishop of the Church of Mâcon; Launo, bishop of the city of Aequoles; Ricbold, chorepiscopus of Rheims—

and when priests and abbots were also seated, including Dodo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Sabinus; Lupus, abbot of the monastery of Bethlehem, which is called Ferrières; Bernard, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, which is called Fleury; Hodo, abbot from the monastery of Corbie; Henry, abbot from the monastery of Corbion; Bavo, abbot from the monastery of Orbais; and very many other priests and abbots; and when deacons were standing by, together with the clergy of the remaining orders; and when the glorious King Charles was also seated in the midst of the assembly of bishops, having deigned to offer his presence to that holy synod—

at the city of Soissons, in the monastery of Saint Medard, confessor of Christ, situated in the suburb of that city, in the church consecrated in honor of the Holy Trinity, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 853, and in the thirteenth year of the aforesaid prince Charles, in the first indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May—

while certain ecclesiastical and very necessary matters were being debated and decided in that synod, consideration was given to the ordination of Hincmar, metropolitan bishop of Rheims. Since Ebo, who had been archbishop of that see, was still alive, some said that Hincmar had been ordained contrary to the canonical rules.

His ordainers therefore gave the following response. Theodoric, bishop of Cambrai, presented a written statement and brought forward the following:

“Pope Leo, in his decrees to the bishops established throughout Caesarean Mauretania, commands that a person who has either been convicted or has certainly confessed must submit to judgment, saying” (Letter 87, chapter 2):

“It has also been added that this man is known to have been rashly substituted for him; he ought not to have been ordained before Lupicinus, who was present, could justly submit to judgment after either being convicted or certainly confessing, so that the one who was being consecrated might receive the vacant place in the manner required by ecclesiastical discipline.”

[Col. 0389A] It is already clear how someone must be accused and convicted: he must be accused by written document or by witnesses, as is written concerning bishops and clerics in the Theodosian law, in the fifth book (chapter 5) of the Sentences of Paul: “No one can be convicted in judgment without witnesses or written evidence.”

That Roman laws are approved in this matter by canonical authority is also written in the eleventh chapter of the Council of Toledo (Council of Toledo VI, canon 11), that no one should be condemned without a legitimate accuser:

“It is fitting that the life of an innocent person not be stained by the ruin caused by accusers. Therefore, whenever anyone accuses another, both the accused and the accuser must be presented, and the judgments of the laws and canons must be sought.”

It is therefore clear that divine and human laws adjudge or condemn no one unless he has either openly confessed or been openly convicted [Col. 0389B]; and it has been specified how an accused person ought to be accused and convicted. We must now examine to what class of judges or condemnors Ebo belonged, since it is manifest that he had been deposed.

After he had mounted the ambo in the church of Saint Stephen at the city of Mediomatricum, he publicly denounced himself before the bishops, the emperor, the clergy, and the people who were present, because he had falsely accused that same emperor Louis and, after unjustly deposing him from the imperial throne, had subjected him to public penance. Concerning these matters he also handed the same emperor a written statement signed in his own hand. Anyone who seeks it will be able to find it in the archive of that Church of Metz.

Accordingly, when he was accused by that Augustus himself at the general synod held in the palace at the estate of Thionville [Col. 0389C], he asked for a postponement and, in accordance with canonical institution, chose for himself, with the consent of the synod, bishops as judges of his sins—those whom the canons call “chosen judges.” Concerning these the African council, chapter 63, states that no appeal may be made from chosen judges. He gave the synod a written statement, confirmed by his own hand, containing the following:

> I, EBO, an unworthy bishop, recognizing my frailty and the weight of my sins, have appointed as judges of my offenses my confessors, namely Archbishop Aiulf, Bishop Badarad, and Bishop Modoin. To them I have given a pure confession, seeking a remedy through penance and the salvation of my soul, so that I might withdraw from the episcopal office and ministry, for which I acknowledge myself unworthy. I make myself alien from it on account of my offenses, in which I have confessed privately to them that I sinned, in such a way that they may be witnesses to the appointment, consecration, and substitution of another in my place—one who can worthily preside over and benefit the Church over which I have hitherto presided unworthily. And so that thereafter I may have no ability, by canonical authority, to make any further claim or appeal, I have confirmed this by subscribing with my own hand. + I, Ebo, formerly bishop, have subscribed.

When this document had been produced and confirmed before the synod, he himself confessed orally and supplied other witnesses besides the judges: Archbishop Nothon, Bishop Theodoric, and Bishop Achard. Thus he received sentence from all the bishops who were present at that council [Col. 0390A], all saying in turn: “According to your confession, withdraw from the ministry.”

Then, in his presence, at the synod’s command and hearing, this statement was dictated by Jonas, bishop of Orléans, to the priest Helias, later bishop of Chartres, and was subscribed and appended to the aforesaid page containing his confession in these words:

> This profession of Ebo was made and strengthened by his own handwritten subscription at the general synodal assembly held at the estate of Thionville, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 835, likewise in the twenty-third year of the reign of the glorious Caesar Louis, in the thirteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Nones of March.

These are the bishops who heard the confession confirmed by his own hand, in which it was stated [Col. 0390B] that Ebo himself, on account of certain crimes that he had confessed to his confessors—Archbishop Aiulf, Bishop Badarad, Bishop Modoin, Bishop Achard, Bishop Theodoric, and Archbishop Nothon—ought in no way to exercise the episcopal office.

Indeed, these same witnesses, at Ebo’s request and with him standing before them, testified orally in the sight of all who were present, both bishops and the other priests, that he had confessed to them such a sin that he was not worthy thereafter to exercise the episcopal ministry. These same witnesses and confessors also added that, if he had committed that sin before his ordination, he ought in no way to have been ordained bishop.

For this reason Ebo himself, following their counsel, said before everyone that he was unworthy of the episcopal ministry, that he ought to withdraw from it, and that he wished, in the manner of penance, to make the Lord favorable toward him. The bishops, therefore, on the basis of his confession confirmed by his own hand and the testimony of his confessors, decreed that he should withdraw from the episcopal ministry and, by serving the Lord in other offices of prayer and vigils, make Him favorable toward him.

These are the names of those bishops:

Drogo, archbishop; Hetti, archbishop; Otgarius, archbishop; Ragnoardus, archbishop; Landrannus, archbishop; Aldricus, archbishop; Nothon, archbishop; Aiulf, archbishop; Ratoldus, bishop; Jonas, bishop; Frotarius, bishop; Erchanradus, bishop; Raganarius, bishop; Wlfinus, bishop; Theodoric, bishop; Achard, bishop [Col. 0390D]; Rothadus, bishop; Batradus, bishop; Modoin, bishop.

Also Theodoric, bishop; Walocharius, bishop; Godolricus, bishop; Godofridus, bishop; Teutmundus, bishop; Ermbertus, bishop; Hubertus, bishop; Erardus, bishop; Albericus, bishop; Freculfus, bishop; Joannes, bishop; Hildemannus, bishop; Hildi, bishop; Christianus, bishop; Sisagutus, bishop.

Also Raganarius, bishop; Crispio, bishop; Teutgandus, bishop; Bonus, bishop; Favo, bishop; Ado, bishop; Teutbertus, bishop; Wiladus, bishop; Morbertus, bishop.

After all these matters had been carried out and the synod had rendered judgment, this document was given by Drogo, who presided over the synod together with Hetti, bishop of Trier, to Fulco, who had been designated as Ebo’s successor in the see of Reims [Col. 0391A].

Anyone who reads the history of the lord Emperor Louis in the Annals for the year 835 of the Lord’s Incarnation will discover by an unmistakable reading that what we say is true. Moreover, as we stated above, concerning the subscription of one person on behalf of all, just as Bishop Jonas, at everyone’s request, acted before everyone and on behalf of everyone through the hand of the synodal notary, anyone who reads the African council, chapters 52 and 60, will find sufficient confirmation.

That, through a written confession of this sort—which must be followed by a subscription in one’s own hand—a bishop burdened by bodily or spiritual infirmity, so that he ought not or cannot rise to the sacred ministry, should be removed from the episcopal see and priesthood and another substituted and ordained in his place is found very frequently in the decretal letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see. Blessed Gregory also states this many times in his letters: in his letter to John, archbishop of Prima Justiniana, concerning Paul; to Marianus, bishop of Ravenna; to the clergy and people of Ariminum; likewise to the deacon Anatolius, to Bishop Aetherius, and to Queen Brunechild concerning an infirm bishop; and Zosimus concerning Proculus. It is also found in the letters of Pope John concerning a bishop who had committed an outrage. The Gallican canons concerning Potamius, archbishop of Braga, and the Council of Valence likewise recognize it clearly.

Leo also demonstrates this clearly concerning such a confession in his decretal letter to all the bishops throughout Campania, Samnium [Col. 0391C], and Picenum (letter 1), as anyone who wishes to read it will be able to see.

After all this, the same Ebo, formerly bishop, issued a written statement of penance in which he set out in writing the crimes that he had previously confessed to his judges and witnesses, and in which he recorded that he had performed seven years of penance for them. He publicly recited this statement of satisfaction in the Church of Reims, where the diligence of the Reims archives still preserves it among the other records.

In this condition, after his deposition, he approached the apostolic see and Pope Sergius. Before him, as anyone may find in the Papal Acts, he obtained the following. For the passage there reads:

> After these things had been completed, they asked the aforesaid pontiff that all the Roman primates should promise fidelity by oath to King Louis [Col. 0391D]. The most prudent bishop by no means consented to this, and thus began to speak to them: “If you wish them to make this oath only to the lord Lothair, the great emperor, I consent and permit it. But that it be made to Louis, his son, neither I nor the nobility of the Romans consents.”
>
> Then at last, seated together in that same Church—the most blessed pontiff, the great king, and all the archbishops and bishops, while the remaining priests and the nobles of the Romans and Franks stood by—they promised fidelity to Lothair, the great emperor, forever Augustus.
>
> After this, however, the archbishops Ebo and Bartholomew, who had been deprived of their honor on account of their crimes and expelled from the Church, asked the most holy pontiff [Col. 0392A] to deign to reconcile them and grant them the pallium.

The same bishop replied that they were not worthy even to receive communion among the clergy, but that they should have permission only to communicate among the common people.

When ten years had passed after Ebo’s deposition, the bishops of the diocese of Reims assembled in a synod at the city of Beauvais. With the consent of the glorious lord King Charles, they obtained from the archbishop and bishop of the city itself, as well as from the other co-bishops of that province, a certain man from the diocese of Sens and the parish of Paris: Hincmar, monk of the venerable monastery of Saint Denis and his companions, whom they ordained bishop of that metropolitan church by canonical decree of the clergy and people of the Church of Reims [Col. 0392B].

The bishops of the diocese of Reims strove to demonstrate this with the clearest and most regular documents at the aforesaid synod: for, as Saint Gregory says in his letter to the clergy and people residing at Naples (Book of Letters), it has been established by canonical regulations that, when a shepherd has died or been removed, a city ought not to remain deprived of a priest for long.

As for the other bishops of the diocese of Reims: if we have been taken from the canonical habit and, by divine will, assumed to the episcopal rank, we have been ordained from distinguished churches, according to the procedure prescribed by the sacred regulations, without the intervention of an improper payment. And if we have been selected from monastic discipline, then, according to the teaching of the blessed Siricius and Gelasius and in accordance with the regulations promulgated by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0392C], we have reached the episcopal order by divine grace, in the presence and through the ordination of the archbishop.

Together with that same archbishop of ours, to whom, according to chapter 4 of the Council of Nicaea, the authority over what is done in each province has been assigned as metropolitan bishop, we are able to demonstrate these things by canonical writings.

Our prince also, humbly subject to ecclesiastical regulations, most devotedly assents to the just and reasonable petitions of the priests. He himself works sufficiently to ensure that bishops are ordained regularly and according to the rule, and that they perform their ministry in a manner pleasing to God, by showing favor, giving admonition, and providing assistance.

For it is written: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him”; and immediately afterward it is written: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself” (Proverbs 16:4). Whoever distinguishes rationally between the time, place, person, and cause will be able to observe both sayings.

Whoever has written such things against the true faith—as we have shown above by refuting them through the teaching of Catholics—whoever has presumed so greatly against episcopal authority and has expressed such unworthy claims concerning the dignity of a prince, should set himself before himself, consider the paths of his steps from the very beginnings of infancy, and carefully examine by what route he reached the position he now holds. He should take counsel for himself while he can, lest, after striving willingly or unwillingly in an inconvenient manner, he should no longer be able to do so conveniently.

We, however, mindful of the Scripture that says, “The fool pours out his whole spirit, but the wise person delays and reserves it for the future” (Proverbs 29:11), do not wish to identify anyone by name or manifest reproof [Col. 0393A], knowing that the Lord corrected the betrayer by signs rather than by open denunciations, so that the guilty man might undertake penance.

Therefore, as the Apostle says, “Lest perhaps God grant repentance to this person of whom we speak, so that he may recover his senses” (2 Timothy 2:24), and lest afterward conscience bite us, in accordance with Solomon’s command—“What your eyes have seen, do not bring forth hastily in a quarrel, lest afterward you be unable to correct it, when you have dishonored your friend” (Proverbs 25:8)—we do not wish to mark him by name. We would have corrected him privately and with others brought in, according to the Lord’s command, if the cause portrayed in so many and such great matters had not for so long been very well known [Col. 0393B].

Concerning this matter, we could connect the divine laws by adding the exception of the matter of faith. But it is superfluous to gather laws when no one is yet attempting to identify the person more precisely.

We have been compelled, unwillingly and reluctantly, to respond to this seventh chapter, not boasting as though seized by empty glory, nor as though angered and digesting the rancor of our spirit against anyone like the bitterness of bile. For there is no one at whom we ought to be angry. In this matter, the testimony not only of a sincere conscience but also the certain knowledge of many faithful people is sufficient for us.

It is better to show compassion toward one who speaks presumptuously than to grow angry with the innocent on account of such an imputation. Yet we have responded to these matters out of zeal for, and necessity of, truth and faith, lest, when someone reads this chapter, he should think that it was spoken about us and that it had been fulfilled in us, and should believe that, just as we were irregularly ordained, so we are polluted by doubtful and heretical perversity in the sincerity of the faith [Col. 0393C].

Therefore, when our reprehensible critic perhaps reads that he has been criticized by us, let him not grow angry with us because of his own criticism, nor reject the truth of the faith on account of our name. Let him remember the chief of the apostles, who, because the necessity of the truth of the Gospel required it, was criticized by blessed Paul even before everyone; and let him remember that the kindly Peter praised the letters of his critic in which he read that he himself had been criticized.

If he wishes to prove himself harmonious who is now called our discordant opponent, he will thus glory in himself and not in another, when he measures himself against his own cause.

**329 CHAPTER XXXVII.** Since the heresy recently raised, as we have shown, was formerly refuted among the ancient heretics, we have taken care to append, in twelve chapters, what ecclesiastical authority decrees concerning those who hold such perverse opinions.

[Col. 0393D]

But concerning what we know with certainty, and what we cannot conceal in silence because many know it without danger, and what, on account of the ministry imposed upon us, we are admonished by ecclesiastical authority to add to what we have set forth above, we undertake to set these matters forth, at suitable and unsuitable times, to willing and unwilling hearers.

That is: concerning these four chapters, as we have already shown above, a heresy arose near the end of the temporal life of blessed Augustine. It was again refuted, rejected, or suppressed by the authority of holy Pope Celestine, through the insistence of blessed Prosper, on the basis of the statements of that same blessed Augustine and the teaching of the other catholic masters. We have therefore judged it necessary and worthy to append, in chapters, what was decreed by the apostolic see and by apostolic men concerning a heresy once refuted and trampled down, and also concerning those who have chosen either to revive it or to remain in it.

**I. That once a heresy has been condemned, it must not afterward be debated.**

Gelasius, in the volume explaining how Acacius was rightly condemned by the apostolic see (Gelasius, Letter 11, at the beginning), writes:

> Gelasius to all his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Dardania.

And shortly afterward:

> Rejecting, he says, the folly of empty complaints, you ought to go back to the blessed apostles themselves and wisely consider that our fathers—namely, catholic and learned pontiffs—whenever a heresy was raised at any time, once they had assembled and, according to the course of the Scriptures and the preaching of their predecessors, decreed anything concerning faith, truth, and catholic and apostolic communion, wished it thereafter to remain unshaken and firm. They did not permit what had been established in the same matter to be reconsidered again through any fresh presumption.
>
> They saw most wisely that, if anyone were allowed to repeat decrees that had been salutarily issued, no ecclesiastical ordinance would remain stable against each individual error, and every complete definition would continually be disturbed by the recurrence of the same madnesses.
>
> For if, after limits had once been fixed by the established synodal rules, defeated plagues do not cease to raise themselves against the foundation of truth by renewing their struggles and to strike simple hearts, what would happen if the faithless were repeatedly permitted to convene a council? However evident any truth might be, pernicious falsehood would never fail to produce something, even if lacking in reason or authority, provided only that it did not yield in its determination.
>
> Our fathers, seeing this by divine inspiration, necessarily took precautions: they would not allow what a synod had once promulgated concerning faith, communion, and catholic and apostolic truth against each heresy to be mutilated by subsequent new reconsiderations, lest an opportunity be given to the wicked to attack what had been established as medicine [Col. 0394D].

Hence the great Pope Leo, in his letter sent to Emperor Leo Augustus through Philoxenus, agent in affairs (Letter 84), writes:

> Let your piety, venerable emperor, know in advance that those whom I promise to send will not depart from the apostolic see to fight with the enemies of the faith or to contend against them, because concerning matters defined at Nicaea and at Chalcedon, as was pleasing to God, we dare to enter into no discussion, as though those things were doubtful or weak which such authority, through the Holy Spirit, established so firmly.
>
> We do not deny the support of our ministry to the instruction of our little ones, who, after the nourishment of milk, desire to be satisfied with more solid food. Just as we do not despise the simpler among them [Col. 0395A], so we abstain from rebellious heretics, mindful of the Lord’s command: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7:6).
>
> It is exceedingly unworthy and unjust to admit to the freedom of debate those of whom the Holy Spirit says through the prophet: “Foreign sons have lied to me.” Even if they did not resist the Gospel, they would nevertheless show themselves to belong to those of whom it is written: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him.”

The same writer, in his letter to Emperor Marcian (heading 1, Letter 45), likewise writes:

> By our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is the author and ruler of your kingdom, I implore and beg your clemency not to permit the faith which our blessed fathers proclaimed as handed down to them from the apostles to be reconsidered in the present synod as though it were doubtful, nor to permit what was once condemned by the authority of our predecessors to be revived now by renewed efforts.

Likewise, in his letter to Emperor Leo (Letter 84):

> These gifts of God will finally be granted to us from heaven if we are not found ungrateful for what has been bestowed, seeking instead what is contrary as though we had acquired nothing. For to seek what has been revealed, to reconsider what has been perfected, and to tear down what has been defined—what else is this than to fail to give thanks for what has been received and to extend the wicked desires of deadly covetousness toward the food of the forbidden tree?

Likewise, in his letter to the Council of Chalcedon (Letter 49):

> Therefore, dearest brothers, let the empty unbelief of those who err be utterly rejected in its audacity to debate against the divinely inspired faith; and let it not be permitted to defend what it is not permitted to believe.

For this reason the decrees are also found expressed in the plural.

**II. That once the author of a heresy has been condemned, all who fall back into the same heresy are to be regarded as condemned.**

The same Gelasius, in the volume explaining how Acacius was rightly condemned by the apostolic see (Letter 11 to the Dardanians, at the beginning), writes:

> Once the author of any madness, together with the error itself, had been condemned, they judged it sufficient that anyone who had at any time become a participant in that error should be bound by the principal sentence of his condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized either by his own profession or by his communion.
>
> To pass over earlier matters, which a diligent investigator can easily search out: the synod condemned Sabellius, and it was not necessary afterward to condemn his followers individually by holding separate synods for each person. Rather, according to the force of the ancient constitution, the universal Church judged all who had participated either in that depravity or in his communion to be rejected.
>
> Thus, on account of the blasphemies of Arius, the form of the catholic faith and communion promulgated by the assembly at Nicaea enclosed without contradiction all Arians, and everyone who had fallen into that plague either by consent or by communion.
>
> Thus, once the synod had condemned Eunomius, Macedonius, and Nestorius, it did not allow those who had fallen into these blasphemies in any manner to come to new councils, but rejected them within the synodal boundary entrusted to it. Nor is it ever rightly evident that, under whatever necessity, anyone has dared through new attempts to violate what had been salutarily established.
>
> We are not unaware that, during the persecution of the Arians, many pontiffs, breathing again after peace had been restored from their exiles, assembled with their brothers in various provinces and brought disturbed Churches into order. Yet they did not do this to alter anything that the Council of Nicaea had defined concerning the faith and catholic communion, nor to strike anyone with a new condemnation for his lapse. Rather, in accordance with that decree, they judged him condemned unless he repented; and it followed that, unless he corrected himself, he would certainly be subject to condemnation.

And later in the same work:

> Since the same error, once condemned together with its author, bears within every participant who has become involved in its depraved communion its own execration and punishment [Col. 0396B].

Likewise, in his letter to Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople (Letter 9):

> You still ask, he says, when Acacius was condemned, as though, even if no one had condemned him previously, he would not have deserved to be excluded from participation in the orthodox and apostolic communion, whose traitor and deserter he was. In the same way, anyone who was previously catholic, if he communicates with any heresy, is rightly judged to be removed from our fellowship; or, if he dies in such a condition, he is in no way counted among the names of Catholics.

The same writer, in the Commonitorium given to Faustus the Master and Irenaeus while they were carrying out an embassy to Constantinople, says:

> I am astonished if Euphemius does not himself perceive his ignorance when he says that Acacius could not be condemned by one person. Does he not perceive that, according to the form of the Council of Chalcedon, Acacius was condemned? Does he not know that council—or does he pretend not to know it—in which, by the numerous sentence of the priests, the authors of this error are established as having been condemned, just as it is manifestly shown by the course of events that this has both happened and continues to happen in every heresy from the beginning of the Christian religion?

Leo, in his letter to Emperor Leo (Letter 81, at the beginning), likewise writes:

> For when, with holy and spiritual zeal, you fortify the universal peace of the Church, and nothing is more fitting for defending the faith than to adhere to what, with the Holy Spirit instructing in every respect, has been irreprehensibly defined, we ourselves would seem to be tearing down what has been well established and, at the demand of heresy, weakening the authorities embraced by the universal Church. Thus we would place no limit on the collision of Churches, but, once permission had been given to wage war, would prolong rather than quiet the conflicts [Col. 0396D].

**III. Concerning the accomplices of one who communicates with heresy.**

The same writer, in the volume explaining how Acacius was rightly condemned by the apostolic see, addressed to all the bishops established throughout Dardania (Letter 2, near the end), writes:

> Because they had chosen to communicate with the successors of those heretics, they were in no way in agreement with the apostolic see. Because they had fallen into the lot of the traitor Acacius, and plainly saw that they were consequently bound by his sentence, they did not wish him to appear condemned, since they recognized that they themselves were condemned in the same treachery, in which they remain even today.
>
> But just as those bound under a similar condition cannot judge their accomplice to have been rightly condemned, nor can the guilty competently absolve the guilty, so, when that traitor has been justly condemned, these men too lie prostrate under an equal condemnation. They cannot be wholly absolved from it unless they repent, because just as the transgression of all who had fallen into the same action of faithlessness was published through one person who wrote, so the transgression of all was punished in one and the same person who had written on behalf of everyone, or who, by writing, had betrayed the wishes of all [Col. 0397A].

The same writer also says in his letter to Emperor Anastasius (Letter 10):

> Therefore, just as, when a participant in perversity has been accepted, perversity itself cannot not likewise be approved, so perversity cannot be rejected when its accomplice and follower is admitted.
>
> Certainly, under your laws, the same judicial penalty binds those conscious of crimes and those who follow robbers; nor is one considered free from the crime who, although he did not commit it himself, nevertheless received the perpetrators into familiarity and alliance.
>
> Accordingly, the holy Council of Chalcedon, which was held for the communion of catholic faith and apostolic truth, condemned Eutyches, the author of detestable madness, but did not consider this sufficient unless it likewise struck his associate Dioscorus and the others.
>
> In this way, as it is always established or beyond doubt that it has happened in every heresy, the Church likewise struck down their successors—Timothy, Peter, and the other Peter of Antioch—not individually through a new council held for each person, but consequently by the rule of the synod once conducted.
>
> How, then, is it not plainly evident that all who were their communicants and accomplices are likewise bound in the same manner and are deservedly separated altogether from catholic and apostolic communion?

The same writer, in the volume concerning the bond of anathema attached by Pope Felix to Acacius, likewise writes:

> For just as error, insofar as it is error, never ceases to be error, so it will never be released from a sentence once established. For an error recognized as condemned remains bound by that same condemnation for as long as it remains error.
>
> Therefore, those who are in that error are bound by the sentence against the error, and as long as they remain in it they are in no way absolved, just as the error itself in which they are is not absolved. Error itself never merits pardon; rather, pardon belongs to the person who has truly abandoned it and withdrawn from participation in it.
>
> As long as error is in them, therefore, they retain its condemnation, and it is never removed, because error always deserves punishment. Its participants, however, either remain participants in its punishment if they do not cease to persist in it, or, if they withdraw from it, then, to the extent that they have become alienated from the error and separated from participation in it, they will consequently be alienated from its punishment.
>
> When punishment is assigned to the one who errs, as long as he remains in error he is bound by that same punishment, because one cannot be in error without the punishment of error. This punishment is perpetual and can never be removed as long as he persists in being in error.
>
> If he ceases to be in error, however, the punishment assigned perpetually to the one who errs cannot be perpetual for one who no longer errs—that is, for one who has become other than the person to whom it was assigned. Indeed, it cannot even any longer be punishment, for he is not the person to whom it was assigned.

Leo, in his letter to the Empress Pulcheria concerning Eutyches (Letter 18), likewise writes:

> When he saw that the meaning of his foolishness displeased catholic ears, he ought to have withdrawn from his opinion and not so disturbed the rulers of the Church as to deserve to receive a sentence of condemnation. If he chooses to remain in his opinion, no one will be able to release him from that sentence.

And in the same letter:

> The moderation of the apostolic see maintains this temperance: it acts more severely with the obstinate and desires to grant pardon to those who have corrected themselves.
