**IV. That if bishops have assented to a heresy formerly condemned, or have communicated with one who communicates with heresy, a synod ought not to be held with them by Catholics.**

The same Gelasius, in the aforesaid volume addressed to all the bishops established throughout Dardania (Letter 11), writes:

> Let us suppose, nevertheless, that no synod had preceded, for which the apostolic see would rightly act as executor: with whom would a synod concerning Acacius have been held? Surely with those who were already held as participants with Acacius, who, after catholic priests throughout the entire East had been violently excluded and driven into various exiles, were plainly their associates in an alien communion, transferring themselves to this fellowship before consulting the decisions of the apostolic see?
>
> With whom, then, was a synod to be held? The catholic pontiffs had already been driven out everywhere, and only the associates of the faithless remained, with whom it was no longer permissible to hold an assembly, as the Psalm says: “I did not sit in the council of vanity, and I will not enter in with those who act unjustly” (Psalm 1).
>
> Nor is it the custom of the Church to mix a council with those who have polluted communion and mingled themselves with the faithless. Rightly, therefore, this treachery was rejected according to the form of the Council of Chalcedon, before proceeding to a council that was neither necessary after the first synod nor permissible with such people.

### V

And since this heresy was formerly overcome and suppressed by the Apostolic See through the authority of the blessed Pope Celestine, through the diligence of Saint Prosper, and through the testimony of Sacred Scripture and orthodox teachers, and since in our own time it has been removed—not, I will not say, by men of authority, but by men of the lightest weight and almost no importance or learning—what ought to be done with those who remove it and, as it were, blow cold ashes back into their own eyes, the same holy Gelasius says in the aforementioned *Commonitorium* delivered to the legates of the Apostolic See sent to Constantinople:

> “According to the form of the Council of Chalcedon, Acacius is clearly shown to have been condemned, just as it is plainly demonstrated that this has been done, and is done, in every heresy from the beginning of the Christian religion; and that my predecessor was the executor of an old decree, not the author of a new constitution. This is permitted not only to the apostolic bishop, but also to any bishop, namely, that he may separate anyone from Catholic communion according to the rule of the heresy itself, which had already been condemned. For Acacius was not the inventor of a new or personal error, so that new decrees should be issued against him; rather, he joined himself by his communion to another’s crime. Therefore it was necessary that he should fall under the just sentence which the author of the error, together with his successors, had incurred through the synodal decision.”

Saint Leo likewise impresses this upon all the bishops established throughout the various provinces (*Epistle* 2, to the bishops of Italy), saying in this passage:

> “For we cannot govern those entrusted to us in any other way unless, with zeal for the Lord’s faith, we pursue those who are destroyers and destroyed, and cut them off from sound minds with whatever severity we can, lest this plague spread more widely. Therefore I exhort, entreat, and admonish Your Dilection to remain vigilant with whatever care you ought and can, in order to seek them out, and not to leave them any opportunity to conceal themselves. For just as the one who diligently carries out what benefits the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive from God a great reward, so whoever is unwilling to protect his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will be unable to excuse himself before the Lord’s tribunal from the guilt of negligence.”

Saint Ambrose likewise says in his treatise on the Epistle to the Galatians (chapter 1):

> “He asserts the Gospel that he had preached to them to be so firm and true that he teaches that even they themselves—that is, the apostles—should not be heeded if they should happen to preach otherwise after being changed, although their reputation as apostles of Christ had certainly spread everywhere. Or if the devil, pretending to be an angel of God so that he might easily be heard, should appear from heaven preaching contrary to these things, he would be recognized as opposed to them and regarded as an abomination. If, therefore, he commanded that the apostles of Christ, whose eminent reputation was displayed in the working of signs and wonders, and even an angel from heaven, whom spiritual reasoning might commend, should be anathematized if they taught otherwise than they had been taught by the Apostle Paul, how much more should those be anathematized whom no testimony can commend for the purpose of seducing others?”

Likewise, in Celestine’s letter to Nestorius (Celestine, *Epistle* 5):

> “If you despise it as though it were familiar, understand that you will be inexcusable when the One who continually expects His profit from this holy investment through us asks you to account for the talent entrusted to you. Consider what punishment awaits the one who hides what he has received, who at least returns intact what he received. From this clearly recognize what and how great a danger it is not to have returned even what you received. Will you say to the Lord: ‘Those whom you gave me I have guarded’? When we hear that His Church is being torn into parts, with what conscience do you live, almost deserted by everyone in this city? I had wished that they had then been as cautious as they now are when they desire assistance for themselves.”

And again:

> “Therefore, although your brother Cyril asserts in his second letters that you have been summoned, I want you to understand that, after his first and second letters and this correction of ours—which is clearly already the third—you have been completely separated from the whole assembly and fellowship of Christians, unless the things wrongly said are immediately corrected, unless you return to that way which Christ testifies Himself to be. You wrongly turned the weapons of desperation against the one who had previously allowed you to be appointed over His household as a faithful and prudent servant. The blessedness promised to you in place of this office has perished, since you not only fail to give food at the proper time, but even infect with poison those whom He acquired by His blood and death.”

And again, in his letter to the Constantinopolitans (Celestine, *Epistle* 4):

> “Let him hear Ezekiel and recognize what threatens him: ‘I will stretch out my hand against the prophets who see lies and speak empty things. They shall not be among the discipline of my people, nor shall they be written in the writing of the house of Israel, and they shall not enter the land of Israel, because they have deceived my people’ (Ezek. 13:9).”

And again:

> “Such people must always be cut off: they disturb the mind of the Christian people and, at their own will, overturn the Gospels; they cannot bear fruit for God. The vineyard that acknowledges the owner’s right must be cultivated.”

And again:

> “All these people have been and remain in our communion up to the present, because no one who hesitated while preaching such things was able either to depose or remove anyone.”

And again:

> “There is often a kind of piety from which impiety arises, when affection for the flesh prevails and bodily affection is preferred to that charity which is God, for God is charity.”

Saint Ambrose likewise says in Psalm 118:

> “There is, therefore, a just mercy, but there is also an unjust mercy. Thus, in the Law it is written concerning a certain person: ‘You shall not pity him’ (Deut. 19). And in the Books of Kings we read that Saul incurred offense for this reason: he pitied Agag, the king of the enemies, whom the divine sentence had forbidden to be spared (1 Kings 15). If someone, moved by the entreaties of a robber’s children and softened by the tears of his wife, should think that the robber ought to be released, although the desire to continue robbing still burned within him, would he not hand over the innocent to destruction—the one who frees a man contemplating the destruction of many? Certainly, if he restrains the sword, loosens the chains, and relaxes the exile, why does he not, by whatever more merciful means he can, take away the opportunity for robbery, since he could not extort the will to rob?  
> 
> “Again, when judgment is to be rendered between two men—that is, between an accuser and an accused—over their lives, with equal danger to each, one if he has not proved his charge, the other if he has been convicted by the accuser, the judge does not follow what justice requires but, while pitying the accused, condemns the one who has proved his case, or, while favoring an accuser who cannot prove his charge, condemns the innocent. This, therefore, cannot be called just mercy.  
> 
> “In the Church itself, where it is especially fitting to show mercy, the rule of justice must be observed most carefully, lest someone who has been excluded from communion’s fellowship extort from a priest’s leniency, by a brief tear or a display of tears prepared for the moment—or even by more abundant weeping—the communion that he ought to request for a very long time. Does he not, by indulging one unworthy person, provoke many others toward the contagion of falling away? Leniency gives an incentive to sin.  
> 
> “This has been said so that we may know that mercy must be dispensed to debtors according to the word of God and according to reason. If a physician finds beneath the surface a scar from a serpent’s wound, and although he ought to cut out the disease of the ulcer lest it spread farther, is nevertheless moved by the sick man’s tears to abandon his purpose of cutting and burning, and covers with medicines what ought to have been opened with the knife, would this not be useless mercy, if, because of the brief pain of incision or cautery, the whole body should waste away and the use of life perish?  
> 
> “Therefore a priest, like a good physician, ought rightly to cut off a serious wound from the whole body of the Church lest it spread farther, and expose the hidden poison of the crime rather than foster it, lest, by judging one person unworthy of exclusion, he make many others worthy of being excluded from the Church. Rightly, therefore, the Apostle exhorts us by a divine example, saying: ‘See, then, the goodness and severity of God’ (Rom. 11): severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness.  
> 
> “He shows that the people of the Jews were rightly separated from the body of the Church, lest the poison of unbelief contaminate the Church, while the people of the Gentiles were received through the Lord’s goodness and glory in the gift of obedience. Therefore divine goodness rightly supports the one who remains in divine goodness; but if he too should defect, he will be condemned according to the nature of his crime.  
> 
> “For what reason is God described as both light and fire? So that He may shine as a lamp for the one walking in darkness, lest the one who seeks the brightness of light be able to wander longer. But to the one who has produced many works that ought not to remain but to burn, the Lord is fire, so that He may consume the hay and stubble of our work and make us safe through a beneficial loss.”

Since it is also recognized that the sacred canons have made provision for this, as the Council of Toledo teaches—that in necessary matters the judgments of laws and canons should be sought—we must set forth what the emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius the Augusti decreed in Book 16 of the Theodosian Code under the title “On the Catholic Faith” (Theod. Code, *On the Catholic Faith*, law 2), in an edict addressed to the people of the city of Constantinople:

> “Following this law, we command that the name of Catholic Christians be embraced; but we judge the others to be demented and insane, and command that they bear the disgrace of heretical doctrine. Their assemblies shall not receive the name of churches; they shall first be punished by divine vengeance and afterward by the retaliation of our authority, which we shall assume by heavenly judgment.”

Likewise, in the same book (title 4, law 2), under the title “On Those Who Dispute Concerning Religion”:

> “The emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius Augusti to Tatianus, prefect of the praetorium. Let no opportunity be open for anyone to go out into public to dispute about religion, discuss it, or bring forward any proposal. If thereafter anyone should believe that he ought to violate such a law with grave and punishable audacity, or should dare to persist through the movement of a pestilential obstinacy, let him be restrained by a suitable penalty and deserved punishment.”

Likewise, in the same book (title 5, law 6), under the title “On Heretics”:

> “The emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius Augusti to Eutropius, prefect of the praetorium. Let no place or opportunity be open to heretics for practicing the madness of a more stubborn mind. Let everyone know that, even if something has been obtained from a special rescript fraudulently elicited from such a class of men, it is invalid. The crowds of all heretics are to be barred from unlawful gatherings.”

Likewise, in the same book and title (law 62):

> “But action must be taken especially against those who, through wicked persuasions, suspend themselves from communion with the venerable pope, by whose schism the rest of the people are also corrupted. After prior notice, we grant them a delay of twenty days; within that period, unless they return to the unity of communion, they shall be expelled and made to languish in the solitude they have chosen, up to the hundredth milestone.”

And likewise in the rescript of the Council of Chalcedon addressed to Palladius, prefect of the praetorium:

> “If hereafter any followers of this sacrilege should be found anywhere, or should again utter speech concerning the condemned perversity, let them be dragged by anyone who apprehends them before the competent judge. Whether cleric or layperson, anyone shall have the power to report them and to prosecute them without any procedural limitation. We therefore order that, when found, they be apprehended by anyone, brought before a public hearing, and accused indiscriminately by all, so that once the crime has been proved, the public record may pursue it, while they themselves are condemned to implacable exile.”

And likewise in Book 16 of the Theodosian law, chapter 4 (title 5, law 1):

> “The privileges granted in consideration of religion ought to benefit only those who observe the Catholic law. We wish heretics and schismatics not only to be excluded from these privileges, but also to be bound and subjected to various obligations.”

And likewise concerning all heretics (title 5, law 60)—whose error and name we abhor, that is, the Eunomians, Arians, Macedonians, and all the others whose sects it is wearisome to include in the most pious sanction—we command that the provisions established by the divine grandfather and father of Our Clemency be observed for all alike. Let everyone know that, if they persist in the same madness, they will be liable to unlimited punishment.

Likewise, in the imperial letter to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage:

> “By a recent sanction we have also decreed that if anyone, knowing that such people are hiding in any part of the provinces, should delay either driving them out or exposing them, he shall be subject as a participant to the prescribed penalties. Above all, however, the obstinacy of certain bishops must be corrected: they either support their wicked arguments by silent consent or fail to destroy them by public opposition. Therefore let Your Religion cause everyone to be warned by appropriate writings, so that they may know that, by the decision of your holiness, this determination has been written against them: whoever, through impious obstinacy, neglects to subscribe to the condemnation of the aforementioned persons wherever a pure mind can do so, shall be punished by loss of the episcopate, expelled forever under prohibition, and deprived of communion.”

And the holy Council of Chalcedon, in its fifth session:

> “Since all these matters have been established by us on every side with complete deliberation and diligence, this holy and universal council decreed that no one may produce, write, overturn, hold, or transmit another faith. Those who dare either to compose another faith, or to produce or teach one, or to transmit another creed to those wishing to turn to the knowledge of the truth from paganism, Judaism, or any heresy whatsoever—if they are bishops or clerics—shall be alienated from the episcopate and the clergy respectively. If they are monks or laypersons, they shall be anathematized.”

Let those who not only discuss creeds or conferences verbally in assemblies, but also compose books and chapters as though they were synodal writings and set them forth, as truth to be held, for the simple, consider whether they can prevail in claiming exemption from this condemnation.

For the Creed was first written by the apostles, and then by the Council of Nicaea, the Council of Ephesus, the Council of Constantinople, the Council of Chalcedon, and all the other universal councils; yet they did not produce another creed, because no creed discordant with the truth exists. Therefore, whatever is written in the form of a creed but is alien to the truth is another creed than that which the Catholic Church has written. It is worthy of anathema together with its writers and must be struck down by the public laws.

Accordingly, the emperor Marcian says in an edict addressed to Palladius:

> “Severity of sanctions ought to be abundant where there is frequent license for offenses. Moreover, the care of the orthodox faith ought to be applied by My Serenity with all the greater diligence because divine matters precede human affairs.”

And in the same place, concerning heretics:

> “They shall have no power to make a will or establish a last disposition, nor shall they receive what has been left to them by anyone’s will; nor shall they obtain anything by any gift. But if anything has been conferred upon them, whether through the generosity of a living person or by the will of one who is dying, it shall immediately be assigned to Our treasury. Nor shall they transfer anything from their possessions to anyone under the title or right of gift. They shall not be permitted to create or retain bishops, priests, or other clerics.”

The reader will be able to find the remaining provisions there in sufficient detail.

And since the Catholic Mother Church favors these Christians through the laws of Christian emperors, as Saint Gelasius also demonstrates in his decree to the bishops of Sicily (Gelasius, *Epistle* 7), saying in this passage:

> “For the authority of our sons, the emperors, has likewise issued in this manner.”

And Saint Gregory repeatedly does the same in the *Commonitoria* (Book 11, Epistle 54), addressed to John the Defender as he was going to Spain; these *Commonitoria* consist entirely of imperial laws, which he judged to be ecclesiastical.

The great Pope Leo likewise says in his letter to all the bishops established throughout the various provinces:

> “Certain people have plunged themselves so deeply that no remedy offered by anyone can assist them. Subjected to the laws, according to the constitutions of Christian rulers, they have been consigned by public judges to perpetual exile, lest they pollute the holy flock with their contagion.”

The same pope likewise says in his letter to Pulcheria Augusta (*Epistle* 47):

> “Concerning Eutyches, the author of every scandal and perversity, let Your Clemency command that he be transferred farther away from the place where he is excessively near the city of Constantinople, lest he make use of more frequent assistance from those whom he has drawn into his impiety. Command also that a Catholic abbot be placed over his monastery, which he presided over perniciously and unworthily, so that he may both free that congregation of God’s servants from wicked doctrine and instruct it in the institutions of truth.”

The same pope says in his letter to Leo Augustus (*Epistle* 75):

> “For this evil, which pestilently obscures the purity of the Church of Constantinople, ought also to arouse Your Piety’s priestly and apostolic spirit to the justice of punishment. Certain clerics are found there who agree with the opinion of the heretics and, within the very entrails of the Catholics, assist the party of the heretics through their assertions. If my brother Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, is found too slow in removing them because he spares them with excessive kindness, deign, for the sake of your faith, to provide this medicine to the Church also, so that such men may be driven not only from the clerical order but also from residence in the city, lest the holy people of God be polluted any longer by the contagion of perverse men.”

And likewise in his letter to the bishop of Aquileia (*Epistle* 3):

> “Let Your Dilection not doubt that, if the things we decree for the protection of the canons and the integrity of the faith have been neglected—which we do not believe—our anger will be aroused all the more strongly, since the faults of those in lower orders are attributable to no one more than to sluggish and negligent rulers, who often nourish a great pestilence while neglecting to apply the necessary remedy.”

And in his letter to Turibius, bishop of Astorga:

> “Whoever does not recall others from error demonstrates that he himself is in error” (*Epistle* 93).

### VI

We have also thought it worthy to set forth what ecclesiastical laws decree concerning those who hold such perverse opinions. For it is written in the constitution of the Council of Chalcedon (Session 5, Chalcedon):

> “Aetius, archdeacon of Constantinople, New Rome, read aloud: ‘The holy, great, and universal council, which by the grace and ordinances of the pious and Christian emperors Valentinian and Marcian Augustus has assembled at Chalcedon, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, in the martyr-shrine of the holy martyr Euphemia, has decreed the matters appended below. Our Lord and Savior Christ, confirming the knowledge of the faith to his disciples, said: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you” (John 14:27), so that no one may disagree with his neighbor in the doctrine of piety, but may show forth the truth by uniformity of preaching.’”

And near the end:

> “Since, therefore, these matters have been determined by us on every side with all truth, diligence, and care, the holy and universal council decrees that it is permitted to no one to produce, write, compose, or teach another faith differently. But those who have dared to compose another faith, or to produce, teach, or transmit another creed to persons wishing either to be converted or to come to the knowledge of the truth from the Gentiles, Jews, or any heresy whatsoever—if they are bishops or clerics—are to be deprived, bishops of their episcopate and clerics of their clergy; but if they are monks or laypersons, they are to be anathematized. Nor should those think themselves exempt from this sentence who are not ashamed to contradict the creed—that is, the exposition—of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, set forth from the authority of the holy Scriptures and the teaching of orthodox masters for belief, observance, and instruction.”

Likewise, in the aforesaid Council of Chalcedon (canon 4 of the synod), chapter 3, it is written:

> “Those who truly and sincerely pursue the solitary life are to be accorded fitting honor. But since some, using the habit of monks, disturb ecclesiastical and civil affairs …”

And shortly afterward:

> “Monks in every city or district are to be subject to the bishop, to love quiet, and to devote themselves solely to fasting and prayer, remaining in the places in which they have renounced the world. They are not to participate in either ecclesiastical or secular business, nor cause trouble in any matter by leaving their own monasteries, unless perhaps the bishop of the city orders this because of a necessary work. We decree that anyone transgressing this definition of ours shall be excommunicated.”

Likewise, in the Council of Agde (canon 38), chapter 38:

> “Among monks also let the rule of the present sentence be observed. If rebuke by words does not correct them, we decree that they be restrained even by blows.”

### VII

We have now thought it right to set forth, from ecclesiastical rules, how those who come to their senses are to be received. For the great Pope Leo says in a letter to Anatolius sent through the deacon Patricius (*Epistle* 83):

> “I entrusted to the judgment of Your Dilection the inquiry whether the presbyter Atticus, whom I had learned had dared such things, should be excluded from the grace of communion unless he had cleared himself by complete satisfaction and had condemned the heretics not only by word but also by the subscription of his own hand.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Moreover, in order that the aforesaid man may appear free from every suspicion of opposition, let him show clearly what he anathematizes and condemns in Eutyches, and let him subscribe to the condemnation of the specified error, with every doubt removed; let him profess that he will observe in every respect the definition of faith of the Council of Chalcedon, to which Your Dilection also assented by subscribing and which the authority of the Apostolic See confirmed. Let the subscription of his own hand be added and read in church in the presence of the Christian people, so that neither we may be regarded as negligent on behalf of the Catholic faith nor he remain further under suspicion. But if, persisting in the same perversity, he is unwilling to obey the salutary command, let him receive the sentence of the Council of Chalcedon, against whose definitions he protests.”

And in his letter to Pulcheria Augusta concerning Eutyches, the author of the heresy (*Epistle* 15, at the end):

> “If he himself who has fallen into this temptation comes to his senses, so as to condemn by his own voice and subscription what he had wrongly thought, communion in his order is to be restored to him. Let Your Clemency know that I have written this also to my brother and fellow bishop Flavian, and have instructed those whom we sent that pardon be granted if the error is abolished.”

And in his letter to the Constantinopolitans (*Epistle* 25):

> “Let no one dare flatter himself concerning priestly rank if he can be convicted of the impiety of an accursed opinion. For if ignorance is scarcely tolerable in laypeople, how much more among those who preside is it worthy neither of excuse nor pardon, especially when they even presume to defend the inventions of perverse opinions and draw into agreement with themselves, by error or favor, all whom they render incurable? Let such persons be separated from the sound members of Christ’s body, and let not Catholic freedom permit the yoke of unbelievers to be imposed upon it.”

And in his letter to Theodosius (*Epistle* 14):

> “Since there can be no doubt what the integrity of Christian confession is, let the perversity of every error be condemned; and if one who has strayed comes to his senses and asks pardon, let priestly goodwill assist him.”

And in his letter to Julian (*Epistle* 19):

> “If a condemned presbyter is corrected by full satisfaction, let the sentence by which he is bound be relaxed. But if he chooses to lie in the same mire of his folly, let the decrees stand and let him share the lot of those whose error he has followed.”

And in his letter to Flavian (*Epistle* 22):

> “But if, putting aside the vanity of their ignorance, they come to their senses and, having condemned every error, embrace the true and unique faith, let episcopal goodwill not deny them mercy—while the preceding judgment remains in force if impiety, justly condemned, persists in its perversity.”

Indeed, in his letter to the Constantinopolitans (*Epistle* 41, to Pulcheria):

> “Both are marks of Christian devotion: that just truth restrains the obstinate, and that charity does not reject those who have turned back.”

And in his letter to Anatolius (*Epistle* 42):

> “Let those who condemn their misdeeds by complete satisfactions, and choose rather to accuse than defend themselves, rejoice in the unity of our peace and communion, provided that they first condemn with a fitting anathema the things accepted against the Catholic faith.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For our kindness cannot be reproached in any respect when we receive those who make satisfaction and whom we grieved to see deceived. Therefore the grace of our communion is neither to be denied harshly nor granted rashly: for as it is wholly pious to restore the Lord’s charity to the oppressed, so it is just to impute everything to the authors of disturbance.”

And shortly afterward:

> “They ought either to be struck down for faithlessness or to labor for pardon.”

And Saint Innocent, in his letter to the Council of Milevis (*Epistle* 32, near the end):

> “We decree, by the authority of apostolic vigor, that the inventors of new expressions—which, as the Apostle said, are accustomed to produce not edification but rather utterly empty disputes—are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion.”

And a little later:

> “We command, since Christ our Lord expressly declared that He does not wish the death of the dying, but only that he return and live, that if they should ever recover to soundness after abandoning the error of their wicked doctrine, and should condemn the things by whose transgression they themselves have condemned themselves, the Church must not deny them the customary medicine—that is, her place of refuge. Otherwise, while perhaps preventing them from returning, we may leave them truly outside the fold to be swallowed by the jaws of the waiting and raging enemy, whom they armed within themselves with the darts of wicked disputation.”

And Saint Gregory, to Quiricus and the other Catholic bishops in Ireland (Book 10, Epistle 61):

> “All who return from the perverse error of Nestorius must confess before the holy assembly of Your Fraternity, anathematizing Nestorius himself with all his followers and the remaining heresies. They must also promise to receive and venerate the venerable councils which the universal Church accepts; and, once this has been done, let Your Holiness receive them into your assembly without hesitation, preserving their proper orders.”

And in the canons collected by the blessed Martin, chapter 36, “On Purging the Opinion of Heresy”:

> “If any bishop, or priest or deacon of any bishop, should have fallen into the opinion of any heresy and for this reason have been excommunicated, no bishop shall receive him into communion unless he first satisfies everyone in a common council by presenting a written statement of his faith, and thereby establishes his purification as free and complete. The same decree shall apply to faithful laypersons if they have been accused of holding an opinion of heresy.”

The formularies of these statements of reception also show this procedure: first, the statement which Pope Damasus sent to Paulinus of Antioch (*Epistle* 4), by subscribing to which the Macedonians, Eunomians, and Apollinarists were to be received; second, the statement which Leo sent to the Council of Chalcedon (*Epistle* 49), by subscribing to which Nestorians and Eutychians were to be received; third, the statement whose subscribers, in the time of Celestine, were to be received as Predestinarians, the text of which we set forth above as Lucidus the presbyter presented it in the Gallican synod; fourth, the statement issued by Saint Gregory (Book 10, Epistle 30), by subscribing to which schismatics were to be received.

### VIII

Under what condition those who repent and restore themselves to the unity of the Church by a written satisfaction ought to be received, the blessed Leo likewise determines in his letter to Bishop Januarius (*Epistle* 3 to the bishops of Aquileia), concerning heretics and schismatics, saying:

> “We have deemed it necessary to admonish Your Dilection, indicating that it concerns the danger of the soul if anyone who has fallen from us into the sect of heretics or schismatics and has in some way stained himself with the contagion of heretical communion, after repenting, is retained in Catholic communion without a lawful profession of satisfaction.  
> 
> “For it is most salutary and completely filled with the benefit of spiritual medicine that presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, or clerics of any order who wish to appear corrected and seek to return to the Catholic faith which they previously lost should first confess without ambiguity that they condemn both their own error and the authors of their error. Once their perverse opinions have been put to death, no opportunity for aspiring should remain, lest any member be violated by association with such men, since their own profession will have become wholly opposed to them.  
> 
> “Concerning these men we command that the canonical constitution be observed, so that they may regard it as a great benefit if, after every hope of promotion has been taken away, they remain permanently in the order in which they are found—provided they have not been polluted by the sacrilege of a second baptism. For the person who judges that someone of this kind should be promoted to the sacred orders incurs no slight offense before the Lord. If this is granted only after strict examination to those without fault, much less ought it to be permitted to the suspect.  
> 
> “Therefore let Your Dilection, whose devotion gives us joy, join its care to our arrangements and see that the measures commendably proposed and salutarily ordered for the safety of the whole Church are carried out carefully and swiftly. Let Your Dilection not doubt that, if the things we decree for the protection of the canons and the integrity of the faith have been neglected—which we do not believe—our anger will be aroused all the more strongly, since the faults of those in lower orders are attributable to no one more than to sluggish and negligent rulers, who often nourish a great pestilence while pretending not to apply the necessary remedy.”

Likewise, in his letter to Marcian concerning the bishop of Constantinople (*Epistle* 1.11):

> “We shall not be able to show him brotherly charity in any other way than by requiring him to prove that he execrates the enemies of the Catholic faith and cuts off from himself the fellowship of the one whom he rightly rejected. Even if that man had been cleansed by great satisfaction, after returning from a doubtful error he ought nevertheless to have been placed below Catholic deacons, not above them.”

And in his letter to Pulcheria Augusta (*Epistle* 53):

> “If Your Clemency deigns to consider my purpose, it will recognize that I conducted everything with this intention: that, without harm to anyone’s soul, the extinction of heresy alone might be achieved. For this reason I diminished something of the customary severity toward the authors of the most savage storms, so that some tardiness on their part might be stirred by repentance to seek pardon. Although, after that judgment of theirs, both impious and unjust, they are not as honorable in the Catholic fellowship as they once were, they still retain their sees and enjoy the dignity of their episcopate. Either they will recover the peace of the Church through true and necessary satisfaction, or, if—God forbid—they defend the heresy, they will rightly be judged according to their profession.”

Attention must be paid to these statements: those returning from heresy must be received through written satisfaction together with a Catholic profession, but they must not be promoted beyond the order in which they were found; indeed, they are shown to be held in less honor than those who have persevered in Catholic faith.

### IX

Likewise, concerning those who have subscribed to the Catholic faith after presenting a written statement in a synod and who later have fallen into perverse opinions, or who have subscribed to definitions or doctrines contrary to the teaching of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, it is written in the Council of Carthage, chapter 13 (Council of Carthage II, canon 13):

> “If anyone in any matter acts against his own profession or subscription, he shall deprive himself of his honor.”

### X.

And because, as is shown by the decrees of blessed Celestine, this Predestinarian heresy was defeated and suppressed by his authority, if anyone subscribed in synod to definitions agreeing with his judgment and afterward turned aside into deviant views, or even, without subscribing, held opinions contrary to the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, let him read what blessed Leo decreed in his decretal letter (Letter 1) to all the bishops established throughout Campania, Picenum, Tuscany, and all the provinces, chapter 5:

> “Our admonition therefore declares that if any of the brethren should attempt to contravene these decrees, and should dare to admit what has been forbidden, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and will not be a participant in our communion—he who was unwilling to be a partner in discipline. But lest anything be thought to have been inadvertently omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions both of blessed memory, Innocent, and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons, be so carefully observed by Your Love that, if anyone should violate them, he must know that pardon will henceforth be denied him.”

For when he referred to the constitutions of all his predecessors, he by no means excluded Celestine, whose successor was Sixtus, nor Sixtus, whose successor was Leo. And when he added “concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons,” he did not omit the rule of faith. The Council of Chalcedon likewise, favoring this same principle, wrote as follows (canon 1): “We decree that the rules established by the holy Fathers in each of the councils down to the present retain their proper force.” 345

Blessed Gelasius likewise sought to strengthen what the Council of Carthage had decreed, together with other synodal definitions, saying in chapter 9 that the apostolic see, with pious zeal and devoted care, observes the canons of the Fathers:

> “Since we desire to undertake nothing rashly against the reverence due to salutary rules, and since the apostolic see, with the Lord’s favor, endeavors with pious and devoted purpose to uphold all that has been established by the canons of the Fathers, it is exceedingly unworthy that anyone—whether bishops or those belonging to the subsequent orders—should reject this observance, which he sees the See of blessed Peter both following and teaching. It is altogether fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree with itself in this observance, which it sees prevailing there where the Lord placed the primacy of the whole Church.”

And Leo, in his letter to Maximus of Antioch (Letter 66), says:

> “Since the tranquility of universal peace cannot otherwise be preserved unless the reverence due to the canons is maintained inviolate. For whatever disagrees with their rules and constitution can never obtain the consent of the apostolic see.”

### XI.

Moreover, concerning those who, after subscribing to the orthodox faith, subscribed to erroneous doctrines, if they repent and, having presented a written profession of the correct faith bearing their own signature, return devotedly to the holy Catholic and apostolic mother Church, ecclesiastical compassion should extend mercy to them and receive them in their own ranks. Saint Hilary demonstrates this in his book *On the Synods*, saying:

> “You ought not to think it strange, dearest brothers, that the faith has begun to be set forth so frequently: heretical fury explains this necessity. For the danger to the Eastern Churches is so great that it is rare to find either priests or people who possess this faith—which it is for you to judge what kind it is. Authority has indeed been wrongly granted to impiety through certain men. During the exiles of the bishops, whose case you know, the strength of the profane was increased. I am not speaking of foreign matters, nor am I writing of things unknown. I have heard and seen the faults of those presently living—not of laymen, but of bishops. For, apart from Bishop Eleusius and the few who were with him, the ten provinces of Asia, for the most part, within which I reside, truly do not know God—and would that they did not know him at all. They would have been ignorant with a readier pardon than they have been slanderous. But the grief of these bishops, unable to contain itself within silence, seeks the unity of this faith, which it lost long ago through others.

> “For at that first synod at which a statement of faith was presented, this faith encountered the necessity of the situation, when at Sirmium, through Hosius—forgetful of his deeds and words—the doctrine of a new, yet already long-festering, impiety broke forth. But I say nothing about him, who was preserved for this reason: so that human judgment might not remain ignorant of what kind of life he had previously led. Everywhere there are scandals, everywhere schisms, everywhere faithlessness. Hence it happened that some of those who had previously subscribed to something else were compelled to subscribe to a profession of the faith. Nor do I complain about the most patient Eastern bishops, for whom at least a compelled profession after their willingness to blaspheme is sufficient. Indeed, amid such heretical obstinacy on the part of blaspheming bishops, it seems cause for rejoicing that one of them should be received as a penitent.

> “But amid these things, blessed and glorious in the Lord are you, who, retaining the perfect and apostolic faith through a profession of conscience, do not yet know written professions of faith. You had no need of a letter, since you abounded in the Spirit; nor did you desire the hand’s service of writing, since you confessed with your mouth for salvation what you believed in your heart. You had no need for a bishop to read what you, reborn as neophytes, already held; but necessity introduced the practice of setting forth the faith and subscribing to what had been set forth. For where the judgment of conscience is endangered, there a written document is demanded; and certainly what is salutary to confess is not hindered by being subscribed.”

And holy Pope Celestine, in his letter to Cyril, bishop of Alexandria (Letter 10), says:

> “We therefore briefly return an answer to Your Holiness. For you ask whether the holy synod ought to receive a man who condemns what he himself has proclaimed, or whether, since the period of the truce has elapsed, the sentence formerly issued should remain in force. Concerning this, let us both consult our common Lord through a common deliberation. Does he not immediately answer us through the prophet that he does not desire the death of the one who dies (Ezekiel 33), and through the apostle Paul that he desires every human being to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2)? Is correction ever displeasing to God when it is promptly made in anyone? Let it belong to Your Holiness, or to the venerable council of the brethren, to suppress the disturbances that have arisen in the Church, and, with God’s help, let us learn through a desired correction that the matter has been brought to an end.”

And again:

> “We desire even priests to be corrected, although this is contrary to what is lawful; for we shall either advise them after a prior conference, or, if they abuse our salutary admonition, we must confirm against them a sentence of condemnation. This, however, will be the full evidence of correction after the condemnation of the evil doctrine: if they recall to the Church all those who appear to have been excluded on account of Christ, its Head. Unless what we say is done, the one who must be expelled will be expelled, even though those whom we know to have been such are in our communion.”

And Leo, in his letter to the emperor Theodosius (Letter 35), says:

> “When he recognizes that what will benefit him is being sought and desired from him, let him wholeheartedly consent to the judgments of the Catholics, so that he may declare, before all the clergy and the entire people, a sincere profession of the common faith by an entirely complete subscription, and let it be made public to the apostolic see, to all the Lord’s priests, and to the Churches.”

The same Leo likewise says in his letter to the empress Pulcheria (Letter 53):

> “Although we detest the heresy that is unchangeably most hostile to the Christian religion, nevertheless, if those persons are corrected without doubt and purify themselves by worthy satisfaction, we do not judge them alien from the ineffable mercy of our God. 347 Rather, we groan with those who groan and weep with those who weep, and we use the justice of correction in such a way that we do not lose the remedies of charity. As Your Piety recognizes, this is promised not merely by words but also demonstrated by deeds. For nearly all those who had either been led or compelled to consent to the leaders in that Ephesian assembly—which was not a judgment but a robbery—by rescinding what they had decreed and condemning what they had written, obtained perpetual abolition of their guilt and the grace of apostolic peace. If Your Clemency deigns to consider my purpose, it will approve that I acted throughout with this intention: that, without injury to anyone’s soul, only the extinction of the heresy might be accomplished.”

It should be understood that these judgments, written in this eleventh chapter concerning those who have transgressed so repeatedly and so grievously, belong to that form of the canons by which, according to the character of reason and time, certain things are sometimes allowed either for the benefit of the Church or for the unity of peace and concord, without prejudicing the statutes of the Fathers; they do not belong to that form by which matters are established as laws to be held irrevocably.

Hence Leo says to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 95):

> “Since certain questions seem to exceed the proper measure of diligence, I understand that they are more suitable for conversation than for writing; for just as there are certain matters that cannot be overturned by any reasoning, so there are others that ought to be tempered either out of consideration for ages or because of the necessities of circumstances. This condition must always be preserved: in matters that are doubtful or obscure, we must know to follow what is found to be contrary neither to the evangelical commandments nor to the decrees of the holy Fathers.”

Saint Paul also demonstrates these several distinct forms individually in his letter to the Corinthians, saying: “I say this by way of concession, not by command,” and elsewhere: “To those who are joined in marriage I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:6), and what follows.

The African Council likewise, in one chapter concerning the Donatists, says (canon 35):

> “For the peace and benefit of the Church, so that even those Donatist clerics who, having corrected their judgment, wish to pass over to Catholic unity may be received in their honors, according to the will and counsel of each Catholic bishop who governs the Church in that place, if this should seem beneficial to Christian peace, as is clearly shown to have been done in the earlier periods of that division. This is not so that the council held in the transmarine regions concerning this matter should be dissolved, but so that it may remain in force regarding those who thus wish to pass over to the Catholics, so that no compensation for unity may be procured through them.”

And other matters that he develops there.

Saint Innocent, in two letters—namely, to Bishop Marcian and to the bishops of Macedonia (Letters 28 and 29)—demonstrates both forms. Specifically, those whom Bonosus had ordained while still in heresy, before his condemnation, are to be received in their orders if they decide to pass over to the Catholic Church. But those whom he ordained from the Catholic Church even after his condemnation are to be removed from the ecclesiastical order. 348

Leo also sets forth both forms concerning one and the same matter in a single chapter addressed to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, saying (chapter 1):

> “No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the bishops of the province with the metropolitan’s judgment. Therefore, since the question of an improperly assumed honor often arises, who can doubt that what is not shown to have been conferred ought by no means to be granted to such men? But if any clerics were ordained by these pseudo-bishops in Churches belonging to their proper bishops, and their ordination was carried out with the consent and judgment of the presiding bishops, it may be considered valid, so that they may remain in those Churches. Otherwise, the consecration must be regarded as void, since it was founded neither in the proper place nor supported by authority.”

And again, to the same man in the same letter (chapter 10):

> “If, while still a young man, under the pressure either of fear of death or of the danger of captivity, he undertook penance, and afterward, fearing a lapse into youthful incontinence, chose marriage lest he incur the crime of fornication, he appears to have done something pardonable, provided that he knew no woman at all besides his wife. Nevertheless, we are not establishing a rule in this matter, but are judging what is more tolerable. For according to true understanding, nothing is more appropriate for one who has undertaken penance than persevering chastity of both mind and body.”

Thus Innocent likewise writes concerning both forms to the bishops of Macedonia (Letter 10):

> “Let Your Love therefore carefully observe that such things have gone so far, and understand that what necessity—as you say—certainly compelled must not be presumed upon in Churches already established in peace. But, as often happens, whenever a people or crowd sins, because punishment cannot be exacted from everyone on account of their number, the matter commonly passes without penalty. I therefore say that the earlier matters must be left to God’s judgment, while for the future the greatest care must be taken to prevent them.”

And somewhat earlier:

> “Therefore, it is clear that what was established as a remedy and because of the necessity of the time did not exist at first, and that there were ancient rules which the Roman Church, handed down by the apostles or apostolic men, observes and commands to be observed by those accustomed to hear her. But the necessity of the time urgently demanded that this be done. Therefore, when the necessity has ceased, what necessity discovered as a remedy must likewise cease, because one thing is the legitimate order, and another is the usurpation which present circumstances compel for a time.”

And holy Gelasius, to all the bishops (Letter 6), speaks in chapter 2 concerning ecclesiastical institutions arranged with moderation according to the character of the times:

> “Therefore, while the ancient constitutions remain in force because of their own reverence, they ought, where no pressing difficulty of circumstances or times exists, properly to be observed.”

And what follows.

Both these forms are also shown in this eleventh chapter, when the following words of blessed Celestine are brought forward from his letter to Nestorius, near the end:

> “We desire even priests to be corrected, although this is contrary to what is lawful; and just as we advise them through the correction already mentioned, so, if they abuse our salutary admonition, we must necessarily confirm against them a sentence of condemnation.” 349

As for the forms of the canons, which some, failing to consider them carefully, claim to be in disagreement with one another, and as for what and how many they are, and what judgments each individual canon contains: since the perceptive and diligent have no need of this, if the Lord grants us time and leisure, we intend, as grace reveals to us and as we have received from the teaching of our masters, to write these matters in due course for the devoted and simple. Then any reader will easily be able to recognize that there is nothing discordant or mutually contradictory in the sacred canons.

Rather, according to the variety of times and causes, and according to the treatment of diseases, through different instruments—as though all these things were uttered by one Spirit in manifold ways—he will find everything harmonious and everything suited to the circumstances of time, necessity, and weakness. For just as the inequality of needs and times demands an appropriate adaptation to circumstances, so different kinds of diseases compel us to discover different experiments in medicines, as is well known.

### XII.

That the person who, after subscribing to an evil error, refuses to subscribe to the orthodox faith is also condemned by his own judgment, the same holy Celestine demonstrates in the same letter to the same Bishop Cyril (Letter 10):

> “I am concerned for the peace of the Catholic Church; I am concerned for the salvation of one who is perishing, provided that he is willing to acknowledge his sickness. We say this so that we may not perhaps seem to be lacking toward one who wishes to correct himself. For if, while we endure the sour grape, he adds thorns to himself, let the earlier statutes remain in force, let him gather the fruit of his own judgment, and let him reap what he has sown in a demonic furrow—not through our counsel, but with himself as the author of his destruction. Let him prove that we do not have swift feet for shedding blood, when he recognizes that a remedy has also been offered to him.”

And Bede, in his exposition of the Gospel of Luke, says (Luke 3:14):

> “Go,” he says, “show yourselves to the priests.” The Lord is found to have sent none of those to whom he granted these bodily benefits to a priest except lepers. For whoever, whether through heretical perversity, pagan superstition, Jewish faithlessness, or even fraternal schism, has been freed by the Lord’s grace from a condition marked by various colors, must come to the Church and show the true color of the faith that he has received.

And again:

> “The nine therefore need the one, so that they may be joined together in a certain form of unity and become ten. But the one does not need them in order to preserve unity. Therefore, just as the one who gave thanks was approved and praised as a sign of the one Church, so those nine who did not give thanks, having been made reprobate, were excluded from the fellowship of unity. For this reason they will remain as an imperfect group in the number nine; and deservedly the Savior seeks them, as ungrateful, in the place where they are. To know God is to choose him; not to know him is to reject him.”

And because good works are of no benefit to such a person, Prosper, drawing on the words of Saint Augustine in the *Book of Sentences*, chapter 124, says:

> “There are no good works except those performed through faith and love, because either one without the other produces the fruit of no virtue.” 350

Concerning baptism also, Bede says in his exposition of the Epistle of Peter:

> “Therefore, because the water of the Flood did not save those placed outside the ark but killed them, it undoubtedly prefigured every heretic who, even though he possesses the sacrament of baptism, is to be plunged into hell by those very waters, not by others, by which the ark is lifted toward heaven.”

And Prosper, in the *Book of Sentences*, chapter 324:

> “Those who do not preserve the gifts of the grace of regeneration do not diminish it, just as filthy places do not pollute the brightness of light. Therefore, you who rejoice in receiving baptism, live in the holiness of the new man; and, holding the faith that works through love, possess the good that you do not yet possess, so that the good you possess may benefit you.”

For the sacrifice also is not salutary for such a person. The same Prosper, in the same book, chapter 15, says:

> “Whoever rightly considers what he should vow to God and what vows he should fulfill should vow and render himself: this is demanded, this is owed. Let Caesar’s image be rendered to Caesar, and God’s image to God. But just as one must consider what one offers, so one must also consider where one offers it, because there is no place for a true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church.”

Because participation in the body and blood of Christ benefits such a person not for salvation but for judgment, the same Prosper says in the same book, chapter 338:

> “The flesh of Christ is the life of the faithful, if they do not neglect to be his body. Let them therefore become the body of Christ, if they wish to live by the Spirit of Christ.”

And again, chapter 339:

> “He receives the food of life and drinks the cup of eternity who remains in Christ and whose dwelling is Christ. For one who is at variance with Christ neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he daily and without discernment receives the sacrament of so great a reality for the judgment of his presumption.”

And again, chapter 69:

> “The unworthy person takes the sacrament of supreme piety for his own judgment. What is good cannot be good for one who receives it badly.”

Because martyrdom also does not benefit such a person for salvation, Saint Gregory, in the eighteenth book of the *Moralia* (chapter 14), says:

> “There is a place where gold is smelted. For, in accordance with what has already been said both by us and before us, ‘Whoever suffers outside the unity of the Church may suffer punishments, but cannot become a martyr, because there is a place where gold is smelted.’”

And Saint Gregory, in his letter to Secundinus, a recluse and servant of God (Book VII, Letter 52):

> “There is a place with me, and you will stand upon the rock.” What place is not in God, since all things are contained by him through whom they were created? Yet there is a place with him—namely, the unity of the holy Church—in which one stands upon the rock while holding firmly and beneficially to the solidity of its confession. Concerning this place it is added: “Then you shall see my back” (Exodus 33:23). For when we stand upon the rock, that is, in the holy Church, we see God’s back when we contemplate the joys of the heavenly homeland promised at the end.

And Ambrose, in the first book *On the Death of His Brother*, speaking of that man, says:

> “He summoned a bishop to himself, and considered no grace genuine except that of the true faith. He asked him whether he agreed with the Catholic bishops, that is, with the Roman Church. Perhaps the Church in that region belonged to Lucifer while he was in schism. For Lucifer had separated himself from our communion at that time. And although he had gone into exile for the faith and had left heirs to his faith, he nevertheless did not consider faith to exist in schism. For even if they held faith toward God, they did not hold it toward the Church of God, whose limbs they suffered to be divided and whose members to be torn apart. Since Christ suffered for the sake of the Church, and the Church is Christ’s body, it does not appear that those people offer faith to Christ by whom his suffering is emptied of meaning and his body is torn apart.”

Hence the Council of Laodicea says in chapter 6:

> “Heretics who remain in heresy must not be permitted to enter the house of God.”

Moreover, concerning those who live without life in this manner, Prosper says in the aforementioned book, chapter 364:

> “They are branches in the vine in such a way that they contribute nothing to the vine, but receive from it the source of their life; for the vine is in the branches in such a way that it supplies them with vital nourishment and does not receive it from them. Thus, for the disciples, both to have Christ remaining in them and to remain in Christ is beneficial to them, not to Christ. For when a branch is cut off, another may sprout from the living root; but the branch that has been cut off cannot live without the root.”

For he is dead in the sight of God, even if he appears to human beings to perform virtuous deeds, just as in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 19:14) the sons of Sceva appeared to cast out demons, and the apostle Judas is reported to have performed many signs among the other apostles while possessing a traitor’s heart.

As Bede likewise says in his exposition of the Gospel of Luke:

> “Whoever, after baptism, is seized either by heretical perversity or by worldly desire will immediately be thrown down into the depths of every vice. Hence those worse spirits are rightly said to have entered him, because he will possess not only those seven vices that are opposed to the seven spiritual virtues, but will also pretend through hypocrisy that he possesses the virtues themselves.”

And because conversation with such a person must be avoided, the Apostle says:

> “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a one is perverted and condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3:10).

And Saint Jerome, in his exposition of Psalm 5, says:

> “Here, when he says, ‘You will destroy all who speak falsehood’ (Psalm 5:7), we can understand from what follows in the psalm and from its very order that he is speaking about heretics. For the one who commits iniquity kills only his own soul; but the one who is a heretic and speaks falsehood kills as many as he leads astray.”

The zeal with which our fathers avoided conversations with heretics is demonstrated by Polycarp, the disciple of the apostle John. When Marcion pressed him to answer and said to him, “Do you recognize me?” he replied, “I recognize the firstborn of Satan.” And it is read concerning the apostle John that he left the bath without washing, saying:

> “Flee, lest the bathhouse also collapse where Cerinthus is bathing.”

And Prosper, in the aforementioned book, chapter 265:

> “The more eloquence flows from a foolish person, the more he must be avoided, because the more the listener delights in those things that are useless to hear from him, the more, hearing him speak in an orderly fashion, he assumes that he is also speaking truthfully.” 352

For this reason the Lord also imposed silence on demons when they confessed him, lest anyone, while hearing them preach, follow them in their error.

Therefore, in the synod presided over by Flavian of holy memory, concerning the condemnation of Eutyches, the following is written in the relevant passage (Council of Chalcedon, Act 1, from Action 7 of the Constantinopolitan council of Flavian):

> “The holy synod rose and acclaimed, saying: ‘Anathema to him.’ After this Bishop Flavian said: ‘Let the holy synod state what the man present here deserves, who neither confesses the true faith nor wishes to agree with the present synod, but persists in his perversity and savage malevolence.’ Bishop Seleucus said: ‘He is indeed worthy of condemnation, but the matter rests upon the humanity of Your Holiness.’ Bishop Flavian said: ‘If, confessing his own sin, he were to anathematize his own doctrine and agree with us as we follow the traditions of the holy Fathers, he would rightly be worthy of pardon. But because he persists in the same wickedness, he will be subject to the punishments of the canons.’ And Bishop Flavian said again: ‘Eutyches, formerly presbyter and archimandrite.’ And after some further words:”

> “Therefore, grieving over his complete destruction, we have decreed through the Lord Jesus Christ, whom he has blasphemed, that he be a stranger to every priestly office, to our communion, and to the primacy of the monastery. We know and announce to those who afterward converse with him and visit him that they too will be liable to the penalty of excommunication if they do not avoid his conversations.”

Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, subscribed this judgment, and the others subscribed in the same manner.

The names of such people—that is, of those who remain in heresy—are also to be erased from the sacred diptychs and entirely silenced in the Church, as is prescribed by the authority divinely promulgated concerning those condemned forever.

Pope Gelasius demonstrates this in his letter to Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople (Letter 9), saying:

> “You still ask when Acacius was condemned, as though, even if no one had condemned him previously, he would not have deserved to be excluded from participation in the orthodox and apostolic communion, of which he was a transgressor and deserter. Likewise, anyone who was previously Catholic but communicates with any heresy is deservedly judged to be removed from our fellowship; or, if he dies in such a condition, he is in no way to be counted among the names of Catholics.

> “Yet we are astonished that you make such statements: namely, that you profess to receive the Council of Chalcedon for the Catholic faith, while at the same time you do not consider that those whom it condemned—the communicants of the sectarians—were likewise and universally condemned. Show, then, which synod in any heresy did not condemn all at once, together with the errors, their successors, all who communicate with them, and their accomplices.”

And again, somewhat earlier in the same letter:

> “You therefore asked by letters sent through the deacon Simplicius that we provide, without difficulty, a remedy prepared according to the tradition of our predecessors, and especially suited to the concern of your regions, concerning those whom Acacius ordained. How much farther do you wish us to yield to you? Why are you silent? Why are you ashamed to express in words what you carry in your heart? That very shame ought at least to have warned you how unjust the request is. Or perhaps you want us to agree that the names of heretics, condemned persons, and those who communicate with them or with their successors should be admitted? This is not yielding in order to provide help, but plainly being plunged into hell. Spare, I beg you, both us and yourselves,”

and what follows.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 0417D]

There follows at last a brief epilogue, composed from the four chapters into which the entire matter has been arranged. The fifth chapter, concerning baptism, is contained in this fourth chapter, concerning Christ’s Redemption. It has been made concise so that it should not weary readers, with the rambling response of the opponents of the true faith removed. Its purpose is to heal the one whom it depicts in the thirty-eighth chapter as though he had lain sick for thirty-eight years—namely, the company of those who think wrongly—who are two short of the number forty, the number completed by the Decalogue of the Law through the four books of the holy Gospel, and who go about empty of the love of God and neighbor, which the text of both the Law and the Gospel equally commends.

Although they are many in the company, if they agree to submit to the truth, they will recover health as one person in the unity of faith. For outside the unity of the Catholic Church no place of salvation is open to anyone; whoever differs from this unity can in no way attain the salvation that comes from the One.

## EPILOGUE, CHAPTER I
For we showed much earlier when, where, and from what source this Predestinarian heresy first arose, and by whom and how it was refuted; and we demonstrated by the authority of Scripture and the Catholic writers that the chapters recently reread in the Synod near the city of the Leuci had been falsely compiled against the truth. We likewise showed, on the same authority, that the four chapters newly directed against the Predestinarians who have recently re-emerged—chapters to which, apart from this little work in which we have gathered these materials, we responded in three books—are consistent with the orthodox faith, having collected them from the statements of the Fathers. We also established from divinely promulgated decrees that every heresy, once refuted, is perpetually condemned together with its authors and adherents; that it must not be taken up for discussion individually, but trampled down as soon as it raises its head with a hiss, and that its very breath must be restrained; and we gathered how those who turn back from any heresy are to be received, or, if they persist in folly, anathematized.

354 All these matters may perhaps seem to some too extensive for reading and, if anyone wishes to copy them, excessive, just as the four chapters mentioned above, collected in concise form, seemed contemptible to certain opponents. Finally, in the manner of an epilogue, and for the convenience of readers and copyists, we have taken care to gather briefly, in chapters, certain points from what precedes, so that they may be familiar to the simple without being burdensome to the learned. Through them the reader may easily recognize what the truth is concerning God’s foreknowledge and predestination, grace and free will, the fact that God, according to the Apostle, wills all people to be saved, although not all are saved, and the fact that Christ suffered for all, although not all are saved through the mystery of his Passion.

Therefore, whoever desires fuller treatment should read everything above. But if what follows seems sufficient and satisfies them, let them conform their faith in these matters to the truth proclaimed by these men and to Catholic sincerity. If anyone, however, thinking otherwise, refuses—according to the rule contained in the chapters just set out, on the authority of the Church and with episcopal agreement or synodal decree, while preserving in every respect the privilege of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church and of its pontiff, the first see throughout the whole world—to agree and to receive or subscribe together with the holy Catholic and Apostolic unity, that person separates himself from the bond and communion of that unity whose discipline he has refused to share.

For the whole Catholic Church has always held that those who agree in one communion are bound by one doctrine, one charity, and one consent. Just as communion, formed from all who offer, becomes one and returns as one in all—not corporeally, but by divine power—so unanimity extends through all who communicate in it. This is represented by the Savior’s tunic, which was seamless, woven from above throughout. The soldiers divided the other garments into four parts, according to their number, and cast lots for the tunic.

The Lord’s fourfold garment signified his fourfold Church, spread throughout the whole world, which consists of four regions, and distributed equally—that is, harmoniously—through all those regions. But the tunic for which they cast lots signifies the unanimity of all the regions, held together by the bond of charity. For if charity, according to the Apostle, is the more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and stands above all commandments, the garment that signifies it is rightly said to have been woven from above throughout.

And what else is commended by the casting of lots but the grace of God? In this way it comes to all in one, when the lot was pleasing to all; for God’s grace also comes to all in unity, and when the lot is cast, the outcome is assigned not according to anyone’s person or merits, but according to God’s hidden judgment. For if one communion is not a sign of one agreement, what is mystically celebrated for confessing the harmony of the whole Church, when we ask God the almighty Father through our Lord Jesus Christ that the holy, undefiled sacrifices offered for the holy Catholic Church may be accepted and consecrated, so that it may be pacified, guarded, united, and governed throughout the whole world, and for all who offer them while in communion?

Nor should anyone suppose that he recognizes Christ, just as those men did not recognize him whose eyes were held so that they would not know him until the breaking of the bread, if he is not a participant in his body—that is, in the Church, whose unity the Apostle commends in the sacrament of the bread when he says: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (1 Cor. 10:17). When he therefore gave them the blessed bread, their eyes were opened so that they recognized him: opened, plainly, to the knowledge of him, once the impediment by which they were prevented from recognizing him had been removed.

We may not improperly understand this impediment in their eyes to have come from Satan, so that Christ would not be recognized. Nevertheless, the impediment was allowed by Christ until the sacrament of the bread, so that it might be understood that, once participation in his body had taken place, the enemy’s impediment was removed and Christ could be recognized. His flesh is truly food, and his blood is truly drink. Since, when seeking food and drink, people seek not to hunger or thirst, this is truly accomplished only by that food and drink which makes those who receive it immortal and incorruptible—that is, by the fellowship of the saints, where there will be full and perfect peace and unity.

For this reason, as men of God before us also understood, our Lord Jesus Christ commended his body and blood through those things that are brought together into one from many. One thing is made into one from many grains, and another flows together into one from many grapes. Finally, he now explains how what he is saying occurs, and what it means to eat his body and drink his blood: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

Therefore, to eat that food and drink that drink means to remain in Christ and to have him remaining in oneself. Consequently, whoever does not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain, unquestionably does not eat his spiritual flesh, even if bodily and visibly he presses the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood with his teeth. Rather, he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a reality to his own judgment, because an unclean person presumes to approach Christ’s sacraments, which no one receives worthily except one who is clean. Of such people it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Nor are such people absolved by this sacrifice, nor do they become participants in it without judgment, since they are opposed to what so many holy priests have proclaimed by divine inspiration and confirmed in writing. Likewise, the whole assembly cannot be absolved if it says and does contrary things, confessing that it knows God but denying him by its deeds, even if it communicates with a priest whose preaching and subscription it rejects.

Thus, for these people who think wrongly, it will not profit them to receive ecclesiastical ranks according to ecclesiastical tradition, except for condemnation, while opposing the faith of ecclesiastical tradition. For just as the mouth and hand are members of one and the same body, so the ordainers and the ordained, priests and people, are members of one and the same Church—whether Catholics together with Catholics, or unbelievers together with unbelievers.

This is why, at the end of the age, the Lord commands the weeds to be gathered from among the wheat and tied into bundles to be burned. This is why, as the holy prophet Ezekiel testifies, if a priest does not distinguish matters for the people, the people themselves will die in their sin, but the Lord will require their life from the priest’s hand. He does not say that the priest will not die because he is outside the people’s sin; rather, he says that the people will die in their sin, while their life will be required from the priest’s hand. The people will die for themselves alone, but the priest will die also for the people.

This is why, if a blind person leads a blind person, not only the one who leads falls into the pit, but both fall into it. This is why the holy Leo declares to bishops established throughout all the provinces:

“If any of the brethren attempts to act against the statutes and dares to admit what has been prohibited, let him know that he is to be removed from his office, and that he who refused to be a partner in discipline will not be a participant in ecclesiastical communion. Whoever has presumed to deviate from the decrees of all his predecessors, promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, should know that pardon will henceforth be denied him.”

But, as the holy Cyprian once said, we patiently and gently preserve charity of spirit, the honor of the College, the bond of faith, and the harmony of the priesthood; and, insofar as it depends on us, we desire to have peace with all people, even with those who hate peace. Let each person, however, be confronted by his own conscience, and let no one separate himself from ecclesiastical peace—which we do not desire.

## EPILOGUE, CHAPTER II  
### What is the difference between grace and predestination, and between foreknowledge and predestination

[Col. 0421A]

Augustine says in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints* (chap. 10):

“If it is examined and asked from what source each person is worthy, there are those who say, ‘By the human will’; but we say, ‘By divine grace or predestination.’ The only difference between grace and predestination is that predestination is the preparation for grace, while grace is the gift itself already bestowed.

Thus, when the Apostle says, ‘Not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works’ (Eph. 2:9), this refers to grace. But what follows—‘which God prepared so that we might walk in them’—refers to predestination. Predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge, but foreknowledge can exist without predestination. Through predestination God foreknew what he himself was going to do; hence it is said, ‘He made the things that were to be.’ But he can also foreknow what he himself does not do, such as all sins.

For although there are certain things that are sins and are also punishments for sins—hence it is said, ‘God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting’ (Rom. 1:28)—the sin there is not God’s, but his judgment. Accordingly, God’s predestination, which is directed toward good, is, as I have said, the preparation for grace, while grace is the effect of predestination itself.”

And Prosper says in *Against the Gauls*, disputation 15:
