“There is no doubt that, without any temporal distinction, God simultaneously foreknew and predestined those things which, with him as their author, were to be done, or which were to be repaid to evil persons by a just judgment. But he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, those things which were not going to have their cause of operation from him. Foreknowledge, therefore, can exist without predestination, but predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge.”

And in the recapitulation of *Against the Gauls*, section 15:

“For the things that we possess as gifts from God and that are said to have been foreknown cannot fail to have been predestined; and the things called predestined cannot fail to have been foreknown. But in our evil works only God’s foreknowledge is to be understood. For just as he foreknew and predestined what he himself did, and gave us to do, so he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, what he neither did himself nor required us to do.”

And in the *Book of Sentences*, chapter 379:

“God compels no one to sin, but he foresees those who will sin by their own will. Why, then, should the just one not punish what he foreknows but does not compel? Just as no one by his memory compels past deeds to have happened, so God by his foreknowledge does not compel future things to happen. And just as a person remembers certain things he has done, but has not done everything he remembers, so God foreknows all things of which he himself is the author, but he is not the author of everything he foreknows. Of those things whose evil author he is not, he is the just avenger.”

No one, therefore, perishes through God’s foreknowledge, any more than through his predestination. Rather, the one who was going to perish through persistent unbelief or iniquity, and from whom nothing escapes God’s essential knowledge, God foreknew as one who would perish. He does not perish because God foreknew that he would perish; he perishes because he was going to perish, and God, who knows all things even before they occur, foreknew that he would perish. And just as God foreknows nothing except what will certainly occur, so what he foreknows cannot fail to occur.

Modern heretics contradict this clear truth, asserting that the reprobate were not only foreknown by God but also predestined by him to destruction. The ancient Predestinarians thought the opposite, saying that God condemns those who will perish according to his foreknowledge. Against them, Saint Augustine, in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, explains the meaning of Scripture as follows:

“He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding” (Wis. 4:11). This, he says, was spoken with reference to the dangers of this life, not to the foreknowledge of God, who foreknew what was going to happen, not what was not going to happen—that is, he foreknew that he would grant him premature death so that he might be removed from the uncertainty of temptations, not that the one who would not remain in temptation would perish. For of this life it is written in the book of Job: ‘Is not human life a temptation upon the earth?’ (Job 1:7).”

He also says:

“For if people were judged according to the merits of the life that they did not have because death overtook them, but would have had if they had lived, then it would have profited nothing the one who was taken away lest wickedness change his understanding; nor would it have profited those who die after falling, if they had died earlier. No Christian will dare say this.”

The most eloquent teacher speaks at greater length in the same work to destroy this destructive error of those who go astray.

Saint Gregory, later in time but earlier in rank, shows most clearly in the twenty-ninth book of the *Moralia* (chap. 10) that God’s predestination—which cannot exist without foreknowledge and is always directed toward good, since it pertains either to the gift of grace or to the repayment of justice—is present in the divine works, which are always good. Among these works are the salvation of the elect through undeserved grace and the punishment of the reprobate through deserved justice. He says:

“God, who has always existed without beginning, foreknew that which, at the beginning of his earthly life, he assumed from the Virgin’s womb; and because he foreknew it, he ordained it. Because he ordained it, he plainly endured nothing in human form without his will. Let a human being, then, be convicted of complaining about his scourges, since he could not foreknow the origin or course of his own life, if even he who foreknowing its origin and course ordained it also prepared himself among human beings for scourges.”

And again (*Moralia*, book 29, chap. 7):

“The dark gates” (Job 38:17) the Lord saw when, penetrating the barriers of hell, he struck the cruel spirits and, by dying, condemned the rulers of death. This is said not of the future but already of the past because what he was going to do in his work he had already done in predestination.”

And shortly afterward:

“For when he sought the anguish of death, he extended his faith among the nations.”

These words clearly show us that his penetrating the barriers of hell, striking the cruel spirits, and condemning the rulers of death by dying—something he had already done in predestination and afterward did in his work—pertains to the repayment of justice. But when he sought the anguish of death and extended his faith among the nations, something he had already done in predestination and afterward did in his work, this undoubtedly pertains to the gift of grace.

And later in the same book (chap. 15):

“Thus,” he says, “Moses, who knew that he would speak both powerful things to the strong and earthly things to the weak, said: ‘Let my speech be expected like rain, and let my words descend like dew’ (Deut. 32:2). But behold, we have heard by what gift the Gentile people are called; let us now hear with what strictness Judea is rejected. We have heard how he raises up the deserted and pours moisture upon the parched; let us now hear how he casts away those things that appear, as it were, to be inward. For he does not gather the elect in such a way that he does not also judge the reprobate, nor does he forgive the faults of some in such a way that he does not also strike others. For it is written: ‘For mercy and wrath are with him’ (Sir. 5:7).”

359 Recently, moreover, like worms stirred by the fury of an impious hunger, the revived Predestinarians—[reading uncertain: *rescatentes*]—and sharpening their tongues like serpents and spitting the poison of asps from beneath their lips, contend that God’s predestination is twofold. They veil the abominable sense of their perverse understanding by not rejecting the term altogether.

For, as the venerable priest Bede says in his *Commentary on the Gospel of Luke*: “There is no false doctrine that does not mingle in some truths.”

And Saint Cyril, writing to the priest Eulogius (letter 37), says:

“Not everything that heretics say should be fled from and rejected. For they confess many things just as we confess them. For example, when the Arians say that the Father is the Creator and Lord of all, is it therefore necessary to flee from such confessions? Likewise, even if Nestorius says ‘two natures,’ signifying the distinction between flesh and Word—for one nature is that of the Word and another that of the flesh—nevertheless he by no means confesses the union as we do. We, however, uniting these things into one, confess one Christ, one Son, the same one God.”

And again, in the place cited above, the venerable priest Bede, drawing on Augustine’s words:

“In heretics and evil Catholics we must detest and prohibit not the sacraments we share with them, in which they are with us and not against us, but the division contrary to peace and truth by which they are against us and do not follow God with us.

Therefore, since Gottschalk and his associates speak of a twofold predestination, we should not reject this statement in every respect or in its entirety. Rather, the children of the Catholic faith must abhor and anathematize the meaning contrary to the Catholic faith in the assertion by which they establish a twofold predestination of God.

For they say—as we set out at length above—that just as the elect are predestined by God to life, so the reprobate are predestined by God to death. They must be avoided by the Church to such an extent that, if possible, like the lepers who signify heretics—as we read—they should stand at a distance and appeal to Christ with a loud cry, without pressing in among the other crowds. Of such people it is written: ‘They stood at a distance’ (Luke 17:12).

But if someone placed in the bosom of the Catholic mother Church wishes to speak of God’s predestination as twofold in such a way that he understands correctly, in the effect of God’s works—he who made the things that were to be—the following truth: namely, that the gift of grace pertains to the elect, and, according to the foregoing explanation, the repayment of justice pertains to the reprobate; so that the elect are predestined to life by the gift of grace, and eternal life is predestined for them, while the reprobate are not predestined by God to punishment, but eternal punishment is predestined for them by the repayment of justice—then it does not depart from the truth if he calls this predestination of God twofold in the same way that Catholic teachers call charity twofold. Charity is one, but it is called twofold in the two commandments, namely love of God and love of neighbor.

And just as there is one Spirit and two gifts, so there is one predestination of God, which pertains either to the gift of grace or to the repayment of justice. And just as Paul says, ‘We are the good aroma of Christ to God in those who are saved and in those who perish’ (2 Cor. 2:15), so by one and the same good aroma some are saved and others perish. Those who are saved are saved and crowned by the gift of grace; those who perish perish through their own iniquity and are punished by the repayment of justice.”

And as blessed Gregory says in his *Treatise on the Prophet Ezekiel* and also in the *Moralia on Job*:

“Bread strengthens the life of the strong but kills the little ones; a gentle hiss calms horses but provokes puppies; and one and the same sun melts wax and hardens clay.”

Likewise, blessed Augustine, explaining the seventh psalm, says:

“But because he said that the Lord had prepared not only arrows but also vessels of death in the bow, it may be asked what the vessels of death are—perhaps heretics? For they too leap from the same bow, that is, from the same Scriptures, upon souls not to be inflamed with charity but to be destroyed by the poison of death. This does not occur except because of merits. Therefore even this arrangement must be attributed to divine Providence—not because Providence makes sinners, but because it orders them after they have sinned.

For, reading with an evil desire because of sin, they are compelled to understand wrongly, so that this itself becomes the punishment of sin. Nevertheless, through their death the children of the Catholic Church are awakened from sleep, as though by thorns, so that they may advance toward understanding the divine Scriptures. For heresies must exist, so that, as the Apostle says, those who are approved may become manifest among you, when they are already manifest to God.

Or did he perhaps arrange those same arrows and vessels of death for the destruction of unbelievers, while he made them burning—or made them instruments of burning—for the exercise of the faithful? For what the Apostle says is not false: ‘To some we are an aroma of life unto life, to others an aroma of death unto death.’ And who is sufficient for these things?

It is therefore not surprising if the same apostles are vessels of death to those from whom they suffered persecution, and fiery arrows for inflaming the hearts of believers. After this dispensation, however, a just judgment will come. Concerning it he speaks in such a way that we understand each person’s punishment to arise from his own sin, and his iniquity to be turned into punishment.

Let us not suppose that God’s tranquility and ineffable light itself brings forth the source from which sins are punished. Rather, it orders sins themselves in such a way that what was a pleasure to the person who sinned becomes an instrument for the Lord who punishes.”

And Prosper, in the twenty-eighth chapter of his *Book of Epigrams*, “On the Twofold Work of God”:

“If we consider all human beings together, some of whom are saved by mercy and others condemned by truth, all the ways of the Lord—that is, mercy and truth—are distinguished by their outcome. But if we look only upon the saints, these ways are not distinguished. For there mercy is inseparable from truth, and truth from mercy, because the blessedness of the saints comes both from the gift of grace and from the repayment of justice.

### Epigram

In all things the work of the Almighty is twofold:

Everything he does is either justice or mercy.

These descend together upon the earth from the citadel of light,

So that neither good may be lacking to any part.

And since we all need the help of the merciful one,

Grace always goes before justice,

Condemning the proud, saving the justified,

Whom God has increased both by gifts and by merits.”

And again, in the same book, chapter 16, “On Justice and Grace, by Which God’s Predestination Is Constituted”:

“There are two repayments of justice: when either good things are rendered for good things or evil things for evil things. There is a third repayment, that of grace, when evils are forgiven through regeneration and good things are repaid. Thus it is made clear that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.

But God does not know that repayment of the ungodly by which they return evil for good. For if he did not repay good for evil, there would be no one to whom he could repay good for good.

### Epigram

The reward of justice is twofold, when it fittingly restores either good things

To the upright, or evil things to the wicked.

But Christ’s grace, which saves all,

Without weighing merit, washes away every evil,

Renewing all who believe through holy baptism,

And gives good things, so that in return for good things he may give better things.”

But Saint Gregory sets out predestinations—that is, the effects of the divine work—in the plural in the twenty-ninth book of the *Moralia*. In the preceding sections of this little work we have sufficiently shown, according to the measure of our understanding and from the teaching of Gregory himself and of other teachers of the Church, in what sense he said this and how it is to be understood according to the truth.

## EPILOGUE, CHAPTER III  
### That there is a predestination of the saints; that those elected by God are predestined to life, and that eternal life is predestined for them; but that the reprobate are not predestined by God, but foreknown and left to punishment, and that eternal punishment is predestined for them by the repayment of justice

[Col. 0425D]

Saint Augustine says in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance* (chap. 14):

“This is the predestination of the saints: nothing else, namely, the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits by which all who are liberated are most certainly liberated. But where else are the rest left except in the mass of perdition, by the just judgment of God?”

And Prosper, in disputation 8 (response 9), addressed to the Januensian priests Camillus and Theodotus:

“Let us therefore acknowledge wisely and confess devoutly that God unchangeably foreknew those to whom he would give the gift of believing, or those whom he would give to his Son so that he would lose none of them. And if he foreknew these things, he also foreknew the benefits by which he deigns to liberate us.

This is the predestination of the saints: the predestination and preparation of God’s grace by which all who are liberated are most certainly liberated. Let us know that the others, whom grace did not remove from the general perdition of the human race, were not removed by a just judgment, so that from them we may learn what has been forgiven to us, since we cannot complain about their condemnation. For there is no iniquity with God, nor does anyone innocent perish under his judgment.”

And likewise in his book *Against the Ungrateful*, against the Pelagians:

*[The supplied text marks a lacuna here.]*

All have one

Nature, and alike they cannot will good or evil.

Yet from these merciful grace chooses some,

And, born again through baptism, transfers them

Into the eternal kingdom, leaving many in death.

And again:

But those who, rescued from darkness, live in the light,

Rejoice, and from those who pay what they owe

They learn how much has been forgiven them

Through the goodness of the one who calls.

And again, blessed Augustine says in the *Hypomnesticon* (book 6, at the beginning):

“First, then, let us explain what the name ‘predestination’ indicates; afterward we shall prove by the authority of the divine Scriptures that predestination exists with God, who shows no partiality.

Predestination is so called from foreseeing, anticipating, or preordaining something future. Therefore God, for whom foreknowledge is not accidental but has always been and is his essence, foreknows and predestines whatever he foreknows in this way before it exists; and he predestines it because he foreknows what it will be. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined’ (Rom. 8:29).

But he does not predestine everything he foreknows. He foreknows evil things alone; good things he both foreknows and predestines. Therefore foreknowledge predestines what is good—that is, it preordains it before it exists in reality. When it begins to exist with its author himself, he calls, orders, and disposes it. Hence the passage continues: ‘Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.’

Let us now discuss more openly what we are saying: how God, who is without iniquity, uses his foreknowledge and predestination generally with respect to the human race.

The mass of the human race, made liable to condemnation and mortal through the transgression of Adam and Eve, is subject—not by a general divine ordinance, but by what is owed—to the punishment and torment of Gehenna. Forgiveness, however, is bestowed not according to merit, but through the generosity of the mercy of God, the just judge.

Because God is just, merciful, and foreknowing of future things, from this condemnable mass, not through partiality toward persons but by the irreproachable—indeed incomprehensible—judgment of his equity, he foreknows and prepares, that is, predestines to eternal life, those whom his gratuitous mercy foreknows. But he punishes the others with the punishment they deserve, as I have said. He punishes them because he foreknew what they would be; nevertheless, he did not make or predestine them to be punished, but, as I have said, merely foreknew them in the condemnable mass.”

And after a little further:

“We must therefore return to the matters whose discussion we began above. We said that, from the condemnable mass of the human race, God foreknew by mercy, not by merits, those whom he predestined to life by the election of grace. But the others, who by his judgment of justice are deprived of this grace, he merely foreknew as destined to perish through their own fault; he did not predestine them to perish.

But, as I have said, those whom he foreknew in works of ungodliness and death he did not preordain or compel. These are people who provoke God to anger, either unwilling to accept the faith of salvation preached to them, or unable to do so under God’s judgment, or who misuse what they have accepted. For this reason they are handed over to a reprobate mind, so that they do not do what is fitting. We rightly confess that punishment has been predestined for such people.”

[Col. 0427B] We have also thought it necessary to recall that the revived adherents of these opinions, upon which the Predestinarians long ago buried beneath ancient ashes had relied, abuse the apostolic testimonies in order to confirm their own position: “He endured with much patience vessels of wrath, perfected—or fitted or prepared—for destruction; and he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” Against them blessed Augustine explained those words in this way in *On the Predestination of the Saints* (ch. 9):

“He brought forth in much patience vessels of wrath”—and so forth up to “he prepared for glory”: “Faith,” he says, “both begun and perfected, is a gift of God; and that this gift is given to some and not given to others is something one who does not wish to contradict the most manifest sacred Scriptures does not doubt at all. But why it is not given to all ought not to trouble the believer who [Col. 0427C] believes that all proceeded from one person into a condemnation that was without doubt most just, so that there would be no just accusation against God even if no one were delivered from it. Hence it is clear that it is a great grace that very many are delivered, and that those who are not delivered recognize what was owed to them.”

And in his letter to the presbyter Sixtus (Letter 105): “In the vessels that are fitted for destruction—which is owed to the condemned mass—let the vessels made for honor from the same mass recognize what divine mercy has bestowed upon them.”

And in his letter to Optatus (Letter 157): “The Apostle had said, namely, that the potter makes from the same lump of clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor. It would rightly seem unjust that vessels of wrath are made for destruction if the entire mass itself had not been condemned in Adam. Therefore, the fact that they are made vessels of wrath by being born belongs to the punishment that is owed; but the fact that they are made vessels of mercy by being born again belongs to grace that is not owed. Thus God displays his wrath—not, certainly, an agitation of spirit such as is called human anger, but a just and fixed retribution—because from the stock of disobedience there is derived a succession of sin and punishment. And a human being born of woman, as it is written in the book of Job, is short-lived and full of wrath (Job XIV, 1). For he is the vessel of that with which he is filled. Hence they are called vessels of wrath.” And a little later, concerning the elect: “so that in them—that is, in those who were left behind—they may learn to give thanks to God, because they were separated from them not by their own merits, which were equal in the same mass, but by his mercy.”

And in Book II of *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (ch. 3): “For by whatever a person is overcome, says Scripture, by that he is also made a slave. And no one except through the grace of the liberator is released from this bond of slavery, from which no human being is exempt. For through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. Thus God is the creator of those who are born in such a way that all proceed from one into condemnation, unless the deliverer of those who are born again intervenes. He himself is called the potter, making from the same mass one vessel for honor according to mercy and another for dishonor according to judgment; to him the Church sings, ‘mercy and judgment’ (Psalm C).”

And in *On the Gift of Perseverance* (ch. 11), concerning what is written, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills”: “For there is no injustice with God—far from it. But his judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. His mercy, therefore, is unsearchable, because he has mercy on whom he wills without any preceding merits; and his truth is unsearchable, because he hardens whom he wills on account of preceding merits of that person, though those merits are often shared with the one on whom he has mercy. So it is with two twins, one of whom is taken and the other left: their outcome is unequal, but their merits are shared. Yet one of them is delivered by God’s great goodness in such a way that the other is not condemned by any injustice of his.”

And in his letter to the presbyter Sixtus (Letter 105): “For we seek the merit of hardening [Col. 0428C] and find it: the entire mass was indeed condemned on account of the merit of sin. God does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by not imparting mercy. Those to whom he does not impart it are neither worthy nor deserving of it; rather, they are worthy of, and deserve, its not being imparted. But we seek the merit of mercy and do not find it, because there is none; otherwise grace would be emptied of its meaning if it were not freely given but repaid according to merits.”

And in *On the Predestination of Grace* (ch. 2): “For the question arises why some of these perish, since the Almighty wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Then again, why does he harden some while having mercy on others, or how does he will all human beings to be saved when he himself hardens some so that they may not be saved?”

And a little later (ch. 3): “If, then, as has appeared, we are all born from the seed of the transgressor as debtors, since in him all sinned, as the Apostle says (Rom. V), and since the mass from which we descend was already condemned at the beginning, let no one dare complain about his hardness, and let no one complain about the punishment owed even in the absence of personal sins, solely by the condition of birth. But the fact that God bestows on others, converted by a gratuitous calling, a mercy that is not owed must be attributed—not to injustice on the part of the steward, but, in accordance with truth, to the most merciful generosity of the giver.”

And a little later (ch. 4): “Therefore, from the earlier part of this statement, in which he says, ‘He has mercy on whom he wills,’ I think that no one except one unworthy of mercy would dare argue. But in what follows—‘he hardens whom he wills’—the attention of the human mind is for a little while confused by the novelty of the expression. Yet it must not be understood as though God worked in a human being a hardness of heart that did not already exist. For what else is hardness than opposing the commands of God? Therefore, whatever punishment a human being born after that transgression suffers, let it be acknowledged as justly and deservedly repaid. For God is said to harden the one whom he has not wished to soften; so also he is said to blind the one whom he has not wished to illuminate; and likewise to repel the one whom he has not wished to call.”

What we have demonstrated through the words of that eminent teacher concerning the preparation of the vessels for destruction or their hardening is plainly all accomplished by retributive justice. For we are all naturally children of wrath: not created by God in Adam as such, but conceived in iniquities and born in sins from Adam’s seed, corrupted through sin and, according to Scripture, accursed. But those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified. This is wholly a gift of grace, because we were not born from Adam, but, so that we might receive the adoption of sons—which we lost in Adam, from whom we are mortal—we were reborn in Christ and made children of God through the grace of adoption.

The statements in the Acts of the Apostles concerning justice toward those left behind and grace toward the elect—statements that the Predestinarians also abuse—likewise demonstrate this. Paul says: “We too are mortal, announcing to you that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, who in past generations allowed all the nations to go their own ways” (Acts XIV, 14). And he did so not without testimony—namely, testimony by which they could recognize that he is God—as he also demonstrates in the Epistle to the Romans. He did indeed permit them, that is, he left them, as Scripture says elsewhere of God: “He left the human being in the hand of his own counsel.” This is the result of retributive justice: deservedly, he condemns the mass that is liable to destruction.

And again, concerning the elect, it is written in the same Acts of the Apostles: “All who were appointed to eternal life believed” (Acts III, 48). For the mass of perdition of the whole human race, when Adam sinned, was cast down from the order of its first creation into the destruction of condemnation. From this eternal condemnation—from the beginning of the world condemned through the sin of the first human being, as we have said, and foreknown by God before all ages but not predestined—those whom God predestined before all ages to eternal life are rescued throughout the ages, one by one, all who are counted among the flock of the elect: that is, those chosen by grace from the mass of perdition, predestined through Christ our Lord, the head and light of the predestined.

And this election—that is, the choosing by grace from the mass of perdition [*lectio*, “choice,” from *lego*, “I choose,” as in the supplied wordplay]—is not the election by which Saul and Judas are said in Scripture to have been chosen. For it is written concerning Saul: “Chosen and good, and there was no man among the children of Israel better than he.” And concerning Judas, who was chosen but not gathered into the election of the elect: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” The Lord also distinguished him elsewhere from this election—that is, from the choosing of grace—saying: “I do not speak of all of you; I know whom I have chosen.” For he knew who would betray him. Therefore he said: “You are not all clean.”

[Col. 0430A] Hence blessed Augustine says in *On Correction and Grace* (ch. 7): “They were chosen”—namely, the eleven apostles—“to reign with Christ, not in the manner in which Judas was chosen for the work suited to him. For he was chosen by the one who knows how to make good use even of evil things, so that through his damnable work the venerable work for which he himself had come might be accomplished. Therefore, when we hear, ‘Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?’ (John VI), we ought to understand them as chosen through mercy, and him through judgment. He chose them to obtain his kingdom, and him to pour out his blood.” Rightly the statement concerning the kingdom of the elect follows: “If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things?”

For this reason holy Ambrose also says in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans (ch. 8): “Those whom he foreknew and predestined: those whom he foreknew as destined to be devoted to him, he chose to obtain the promised rewards, so that those who appear to believe but do not remain in the faith they began may be denied as chosen by God, because those whom God chose remain with him. For there is one who is chosen for a time, such as Saul and Judas—not from foreknowledge, but according to present justice. ‘To be conformed to the image of his Son.’ He says this because they are predestined for the future age so that they may become like the Son of God.”

By these words of Scripture and the teachers, the falsehood of the Predestinarians is destroyed. Because Saul and Judas are read to have been chosen by God, they attempt to establish that the reprobate were predestined and chosen for destruction. Yet, as we find in the sacred Scriptures, if Saul had joined his tears with Samuel’s tears shed on his behalf, he would not have been rejected by the Lord forever. And if Judas had shown repentance before Jesus, the merciful judge, as he had shown it before the wicked Jews, he would not have perished eternally.

Judas therefore perished through his own iniquity, not through God’s election, as the Predestinarians whisper, wrongly interpreting the words of blessed Augustine, just as their ancient fathers did—“eating the sour grape,” from which their teeth remain numb to this day. To their hearers they put it this way: “Listen,” they say, “to what Augustine says: ‘He chose them to obtain his kingdom, and he chose this man to pour out his blood.’ For Judas could not otherwise have perished except by doing what caused him to perish, because he was predestined for destruction.” By such a statement they proclaim God the author of evil, while declaring Judas free of evil, since he could not have acted otherwise than by betraying the Lord and going to the destruction for which he had been predestined.

They do not wish to read the books that blessed Augustine wrote against them, in which, as we have often said, he repeatedly teaches that the elect are predestined, while the reprobate are left in the mass of perdition. If they read those books, they either neglect to understand them or, insofar as they are able, distort them by their perverse interpretation. Every wise person with sound understanding recognizes how contemptible and refutable their doctrine is.

For the name “elect,” or “election,” as found in Scripture, does not always refer to God’s election of the elect before the ages, just as “left” or “leaving” does not refer always to the condemnation of the reprobate. It is written in the Book of Kings, where Elijah says: “I alone have been left” (3 Kings XIX, 18). And the Lord says: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (Rom. XI, 4). Concerning this leaving the Apostle says: “The remnant will be saved through election” (Rom. III). And Jeremiah in the Lamentations: “The Lord has removed all my great ones from among me. He summoned a time against me to crush my chosen ones” (Lam. I, 15). And in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen among thousands” (Song V, 20). He is called by the Apostle “the predestined Son of God in power according to the spirit of holiness” (Rom. I, 4).

But also in this passage, from whose words of blessed Augustine they attempt to establish their wicked position concerning Judas as one chosen, it must be shown how perversely they understand him. That same remarkable teacher says: “They were chosen”—namely, the eleven apostles—“to reign with Christ, not in the manner in which Judas was chosen for the work suited to him.”

He says this because Judas was such a person that he was worthy to be the means by which that most damnable work, directed against Christ, his companions, and the devil who persuaded him, and yet venerable to all believers, might be accomplished. It was necessary that this work take place, because otherwise the human race, sold under sin, could not be redeemed from the death it deserved except by the death of the one who had come to be killed without his own sin, as it is written: “Thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to enter into his glory.”

And because it was necessary that this happen, Scripture likewise says: “It is necessary that scandals come” (Matt. XVIII, 7). Luke says: “It is impossible that scandals should not come. But woe to him through whom they come” (Luke XXXVII, 1). And the Apostle says: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. XI, 19).

Therefore, as the teachers explain, in this world, which is full of errors and afflictions, it is impossible that scandals should not very often arise. But woe to the one who, through his own fault, causes what cannot fail to come to come through him—as Judas did, when he prepared his mind for betrayal. Concerning him it is written, “Then he went away,” as though it said: voluntarily, without being sought; and he asked the chief priests: “What will you give me, and I will deliver him to you?” (Matt. XXVI, 14).

For he was inflamed not only by burning greed, but also, being vehemently inflamed by that same vice, he was a thief and, having the money box, he carried away what was put into it. Therefore, as blessed Augustine says, “He was chosen through judgment by the one who knows how to make good use even of evil things, for the work suited to him, so that through his damnable work the venerable work for which he himself had come might be accomplished.”

Saul the king was likewise chosen by the Lord, who causes a hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people, and who says: “They have made kings, but not by me; they have appointed princes, and I did not know it, for their contempt, to avenge the stubbornness of the people” (Hos. VIII, 4).

Nor did Scripture keep silent about this, saying: “Then the Lord said to Samuel: ‘Listen to the voice of the people. For they have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them. Nevertheless, proclaim to them the law of the king’” (1 Kings VIII, 7). And a little later Samuel says to the people: “You will cry out on that day because of your king whom you have chosen for yourselves, and the Lord will not hear you on that day.”

Thus Saul and Judas were chosen for the works suited to them, as blessed Augustine also says in *On Grace and Free Will* (ch. 23): “When you hear the Lord saying, ‘I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet’ (Ezek. XIV), and what the Apostle says, ‘He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills,’ and ‘he handed them over to a reprobate mind’ (Rom. IX), do not doubt that their evil merits preceded this. Thus Saul too was chosen to carry out against a stiff-necked and ungovernable people those things that the Lord commanded Samuel to announce to them.”

By contrast, it is written concerning Moses in the book of Ecclesiasticus: “He chose him from all flesh.” And shortly afterward it states for what God chose him: “To teach Jacob the covenant and Israel his judgments” (Ecclus. XLV, 4, 6).

And if Judas was chosen to betray the Lord, who had come to be killed for the redemption of all, then, insofar as a comparison can be made between a servant and the Lord, holy Gregory relates in Book III, chapter 37, of the *Dialogues* the story of a Lombard who offered himself to death in place of the religious presbyter Sanctulus, who had been condemned to be beheaded.

He says: “The man of God was brought into the midst, and from among all the brave men one was chosen, of whom there could be no doubt that with a single blow he would cut off his head.” And a little farther on: “The chosen executioner kicked him with his foot so that he would rise.” And below: “Then the chosen executioner, holding his drawn sword”—and concerning those from whom this chosen man was selected he says above: “All the Lombards who were found in that place gathered together; since they were exceedingly cruel, they rejoiced at the spectacle of death.”

And Judas, the son of perdition, was chosen from among all the members of Antichrist, the son of perdition, to betray Christ by reason of his own iniquity, so that through his damnable work, as Augustine says, the venerable work for which Christ had come might be accomplished.

It must also be considered how the words of blessed Ambrose agree here with the words of Saint Augustine. Ambrose says: “There is one who is chosen for a time, such as Saul and Judas, not from foreknowledge but according to present justice.”

And Saint Augustine says in *On Correction and Grace* (ch. 1): “Those who will not persevere, and who will fall away from the Christian faith and manner of life so that the end of this life finds them in such a condition, are without doubt not to be counted among the elect even at the time when they live well and devoutly. For they have not been separated from that mass of perdition by God’s foreknowledge and predestination. Therefore they were not called according to the purpose, and consequently they were not elect, but were among those who were called, concerning whom it is said, ‘Many are called,’ not among those concerning whom it is said, ‘But few are elect’ (Matt. XXI, 14).

“And yet who would deny that they are elect when they believe and are baptized and live according to God? Clearly they are called elect by those who do not know what they will be, not by the one who knows that they will lack the perseverance that leads the elect to blessed life. He knows that they stand in such a way that he has foreknown them as destined to fall.”

It should also be noted that from this opinion, together with certain other statements of blessed Augustine, the ancient Predestinarians established a heresy: namely, that the grace of baptism received by those who are not predestined to life does not take away original sin; and that even if those who are not predestined have been reborn in Christ and have lived devoutly and justly, this benefits them nothing, but they are preserved only until they fall and perish, nor are they removed from this life before that happens to them.

Prosper refuted them (*Against the Gauls*, ch. 3), saying: “Every human being who, by believing in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is reborn in baptism is absolved both from his own sins, which he contracted through evil will and action, [Col. 0433B] and from original sin, which he drew from his parents. But if, having departed from Christ and become alienated from grace, he ends this life by falling into perdition, he does not fall back into what was remitted, nor will he be condemned for original sin; rather, because of his final crimes he will suffer the death that was owed on account of what was remitted.

“And those who abandoned God and were themselves abandoned, and who by their own will changed from good to evil, although they were reborn and justified, were nevertheless not predestined by the one who foreknew them as such. God’s foreknowledge was neither ignorant nor deceived concerning what they would become. Therefore he never chose such people, never predestined them, and never separated those who would perish from eternal condemnation.”

Saint Gregory clearly demonstrates in Book IV of the *Moralia* (ch. 28) that the first human being, created for life, would not, if he had not sinned, have generated children of hell from himself, but those who are now to be saved through redemption:

“God foreknew the one who would sin but did not predestine him; rather, as it is written, he left him in the hand of his own counsel (Ecclus. XV, 14). But, left to the freedom of his own will, he made himself and all those born from the transmission of his seed liable to destruction and destined for condemnation.

“God, however, from the same mass of perdition of the whole human race, according to his foreknowledge, as Peter says at the beginning of his First Epistle, chose some (1 Pet. I, 2)—that is, chose them beforehand by grace before any merit and predestined them—that is, prepared them by grace. For the chosen are the same as those predestined to life, and he predestined eternal life for them.

“As the Apostle says: ‘He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight in love, predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he has favored us in his beloved Son. In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which has abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, for the arrangement of the fullness of times: to restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth, in him. In him we have also obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we may be to the praise of his glory’” (Rom. VI, 23).

And the Gospel says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom that has been prepared—that is, predestined—for you from the foundation of the world.”

And again the Apostle says: “The grace of God is eternal life” (Rom. VI, 28).

But those whom he foreknew and did not predestine, he justly left for punishment; and through retributive justice he predestined—that is, prepared—eternal punishment for them.”

The same man—the pontiff of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman See, namely, the mother and teacher of all the Churches throughout the whole world—says in Homily 34 on the Gospels: “The Lord created the nature of angels and human beings to know him; and when he willed it to endure unto eternity, he undoubtedly created it in his own likeness.”

And in Homily XVII on the Gospels: “What else should I call human souls except the Lord’s food? They were created for this purpose, so that they might be transferred into his body—that is, so that they might grow into the increase of the eternal Church.”

And in Book XVII of the *Moralia*: “For human beings were created for life, but by the freedom of their own will they voluntarily became debtors to death.”

And again in Book XX of the *Moralia*: “Therefore the human race, by the right judgment of God left to itself in its pleasures and through those same pleasures handed over to voluntary tribulations, is drunk with wormwood.”

And again in Book XXV: “The first human being was created in such a way that, when he died, the ages would pass away, but he himself would not pass away with the ages. For as the moments ran on, since he was not advancing toward the end of life through the increase of days, he stood all the more firmly the more closely he clung to the one who always stands. But when he touched what was forbidden, immediately, having offended the Creator, he began to move along with time. Having lost the state of immortality, he was swallowed up by the course of mortality.

“Since, as we have said, the first human being abused the freedom of his will, sinned, and became the mass of perdition of the whole human race, some from that same mass of condemnation—those who have been saved, are being saved, and will be saved through the redemption of Christ’s blood, since, as the chief of the apostles says, ‘There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved’ (Acts IV, 12)—were foreknown before the ages of the world and chosen or predestined by grace for life; but others, foreknown but not predestined, were left in that same mass for punishment by just judgment.”

As the same Gregory, the outstanding teacher, says in Book XXV (ch. 8) of the *Moralia*: “The Apostle Paul, impressing this fear of the heavenly judgments upon the hearts of his disciples, says: ‘Let the one who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall’ (1 Cor. X, 12). And when he says, ‘He will crush many,’ he immediately adds, ‘innumerable’ (Job XXXIV, 24). Either he sought to express the multitude of the reprobate, which exceeds the number comprehensible by human reason, or certainly he wished to indicate that all who perish are not counted among the elect, so that they are innumerable because they run outside the number.

“Therefore the Prophet, seeing so many apparently believing during the time of the Church—so many, indeed, that it is certain they exceed the fixed number and total of the elect—says: ‘They have multiplied beyond number’ (Psalm XXXIX, 6), as though he said: Although many enter the Church, even those come apparently to faith in the kingdom who are excluded from the heavenly number, because by their multiplication they exceed the sum of the elect.

“Thus through Isaiah also it is said to that same Church: ‘For you will spread out to the right and to the left, and your seed will inherit the nations’ (Isa. LIV, 3). When the multitude of the nations enters, it is extended to the right when it receives some who are to be justified; and it is extended to the left when it admits to itself some who also remain in iniquity, apart from that multitude which lies outside the number of the elect.”

And a little earlier (the same chapter): “It must be noted that, while some fall, others are said to be strengthened so as to stand; the fixed number of the elect is thereby revealed. Hence also it is said to the Church of Philadelphia through the angel: ‘Hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown.’

“By this statement, which recounts that some are raised up while the good life of others is crushed, the hope of the humble is nourished and the pride of the arrogant is restrained: those may lose the good things of which they are proud, while these may receive what they are despised for not possessing.”

And again, somewhat earlier (ch. 7): “In both classes of human beings it often happens that those who appear, according to human judgment, to stand are already lying before the sight of the eternal Judge, while those who now lie before human beings stand before the sight of the eternal Judge. For who could have estimated that Judas would lose the lot of his life after his apostolic ministry, while the thief would find eternal rewards at the moment of death? But the hidden Judge, presiding and discerning the hearts of both, established one in piety and justly crushed the other; he sternly rejected the one outwardly and mercifully drew the other inwardly.”

And again in Book XXIX (ch. 15), on “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm XXXV, 7): “Therefore let no one desire to investigate why one is rejected while another is chosen, or why when one is chosen another is rejected, because the surface of the abyss is confined, and, as Paul testifies, ‘His judgments are unsearchable and his ways are inscrutable’” (Rom. II, 33).

The same writer says again in Book XXIX (the same chapter): “The Lord says: ‘Heaven is my throne’; and, ‘The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom.’ The soul of the just is certainly heaven; Abraham was heaven. For when Caiaphas was born from Abraham, what else proceeded from heaven except ice? Yet the Lord says that he himself generated that ice because, through their wickedness and by just judgment, he permitted the Jews—whom he himself had naturally created good—to depart from him cold.

“For the Lord is the creator of nature, not of guilt. Thus, by creating, he naturally generated those whom he permitted, through patient endurance, to live as wicked people.”

And again in the same book (ch. 19): “Hence Paul says: ‘Because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, therefore God will send upon them a working of error, so that they may believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity.’ Therefore evening would not have risen over them if they had wished to be children of heaven.”

And again in Book XXV (chs. 8–9): “This—that some of the elect are crushed by others—is due to the merit of the one who suffers, not to the iniquity of the one who punishes. For God is not unjust when he inflicts wrath. Hence it is aptly added: ‘For he knows their works, and therefore he brings on the night, and they are crushed’” (Job XXXIV, 25).

And because God’s foreknowledge can exist without predestination, as in all those things that were not going to have the cause of their action from him, yet cannot be hidden from him who knows all things even before they occur, the reprobate are foreknown but not predestined by God for punishment. For they perish not with him as author, but because iniquity—whether inherited or personal—demands it; they are justly left by God’s judgment.

Those who are both foreknown and predestined, however, are saved with him as author through the gift of grace, because his mercy goes before us so that we may will what is good; he is our helper in times of need and tribulation, to whom we say, “You are my helper; to you I will sing psalms,” and, “Help us, God our Savior.” He helps us so that we may be able to do good, and his mercy will follow us all the days of our life, so that we may persevere in goodness. He himself crowns us with mercy and compassion, he who satisfies our desire with good things. For we shall be satisfied when his glory is revealed.

This great teacher demonstrates the point in Book XXXIV of the *Moralia* (ch. 13), saying: “Perhaps someone may wonder why the merciful God permits this to happen, so that this Leviathan—whether now through cunning suggestions or then through that condemned one whom he fills, or whether he subjects to himself the rays of the sun, that is, learned and wise men, or gold, that is, men radiant with the splendor of holiness, and stains them with vices as though spreading them beneath himself like mud.

“But we answer more quickly that whoever could be spread like mud by his wicked persuasions was never gold before the eyes of God. For those who can at some time be led astray and not return appear to human eyes to lose a holiness they possessed, but before God’s eyes they never possessed it. For a human being is often secretly entangled in many sins and appears great in one particular virtue. That virtue itself, however, withers and fails, because when it becomes known to human beings it is undoubtedly praised, and its praise is eagerly desired. Thus it happens that the virtue itself is not virtue before God’s eyes, since it conceals what displeases him and displays what pleases him.”

And a little later: “Let this Leviathan therefore go forth, subject the rays of the sun to himself, and spread gold beneath him like mud. Almighty God knows how to make good use of the evil of the reprobate for the consolation of his elect, since those who are destined to reach him both advance toward him through their own merits and are often corrected by the falls of others in the very matter about which they arrogantly think themselves wise.”

And because punishment has been prepared by God for the reprobate, but eternal life for the elect, a little later he continues: “For Truth itself says: ‘These will go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life’” (Matt. XXV).

And again, a little later (ch. 16), he adds: “‘But,’ they say, ‘a fault with an end ought not to be punished without end.’ The Almighty God is certainly just, and what was not committed as an eternal sin ought not to be punished with eternal torment.”

“We answer them more quickly that they would be speaking rightly if the just and strict Judge who comes weighed not the hearts of human beings but their deeds. The wicked transgressed with an end because they lived with an end. For they would have wished to live without end so that they might be able to remain in their iniquities without end. Indeed, they desire sin more than life, and therefore they wish always to live here, so that, while they live, they may never cease to sin.

“It therefore belongs to the strict justice of the Judge that those should never be without punishment whose mind in this life never wished to be without sin, and that no limit of vengeance be given to the wicked person who, as long as he was able to have one, did not wish to have an end to his crimes.”

[Col. 0437B] Since the inventors of the theories concerning predestination—those who blow again upon them, scrape perverse notions into the ears, and have an itching tongue—say that we proclaim God’s will to be changeable and a new plan of his, if he condemns those whom before the ages he by no means predestined to death and damnation, let them accept, read, hear, and understand that we follow the teaching of the Catholic Fathers and say—as we said above, and do not hesitate to repeat—that God predestined many by grace to glory, but predestined no one to damnation and punishment; rather, he justly abandoned them. Those whom he foreknew before the ages would persevere in impiety and wickedness, without predestining them to do so, he predestined to be condemned by the recompense of justice; and he likewise predestined the judgment by which they would be punished most justly. Saint Augustine shows this most clearly at the beginning of his *Commentary on the Gospel of John*:

> “The creature was made in time, but in the eternal wisdom of the Creator it had always been determined when and of what kind it would be created. This is what he says: ‘What was made in him was life’—that is, whatever appeared as having been made in time, whether living or lacking life, all of it had, as it were, always lived and lives in the spiritual conception of its Maker. This is not because what he created is coeternal with the Creator, but because the conception of his will is coeternal with him; in that conception, from eternity, he had and has knowledge of what he would create and when, how he would govern what was created so that it might endure, and to what end he would bring each thing that he created.”

And Saint Gregory says in the twenty-fifth book of the *Moralia* (chapter 7):

> “It is clear to all that at that final examination Almighty God will conduct a public judgment, so that he may abandon some to punishments and admit others to participation in the heavenly kingdom. Yet what will then be made public is already carried out daily in secret judgment. For, justly and mercifully examining or disposing of the hearts of individuals, he rejects some into the outer realm and draws others toward what is within; he kindles in these a desire for inward things, while he abandons those, because of their pleasures, to think about outward things.”

Likewise Saint Augustine says in the fifth chapter of *On the Predestination of Grace*, commenting on the passage, “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Rom. VIII):

> “He himself gave us existence; he himself gave us the ability to be good. His divinity foreknew us; his wisdom created us; his justice condemned us; his grace freed us. For although the world began when it was made, it could have no beginning in that light of divine foreknowledge in which it was to be made. And however many people have been born from Adam up to the present day, or will be born by descent after [374] our age, with God they have already been born and have already passed through the whole course of their life, nevertheless remaining in the light of the divine gaze. [376] For God, who is confined neither by place nor anticipated by time, is full of the memory of all past things and the knowledge of things that are imminent. He does not, by remembering, turn toward the past, nor by hoping stretch toward the future. And whatever things exist and are stirred by the movements of time have existed from that beginning in which ‘the Word was,’ and ‘the Word was with God,’ and ‘God was the Word,’ all the way to the end of the ages. Concerning that end blessed Moses said: ‘Lord, you who reign for age and age.’ Even now future things are neither merely hoped for, nor have past things passed away; rather, they are always seen in the present light of the divine presence. From him, therefore, who is eternal and foreknowing, both just and merciful, who exercises the severity that is due and displays the mercy that is not due, and who has power over the creation and election of human beings as a potter has power over clay, some vessels were made for honor and others for dishonor. Before he made us, he foreknew us; and in that very foreknowledge, while he had not yet made us, he chose us. But by whom could this have been done except by him who calls things that are not as though they were? For the Apostle says: ‘He chose us before the foundation of the world’ (Rom. IV; Eph. III, 1). We were made within the world, and we were chosen before the world. Thus, in one and the same time—which neither passes away nor lies in the future, but is continuous, or however else it may be expressed, if it can be expressed—foreknowledge, making, and choosing are present with God. And while his foreknowledge remains unchangeable, he had chosen those to be made whom he was going to make as the chosen.”

And Prosper says in the fifty-eighth epigram of the *Book of Epigrams*, “On God’s Timeless Work”:

> The order of time in God’s eternal wisdom is without time,  
> nor are there any new things with him who made what is to come.
>
> In the supreme Artificer the order of time exists without time,  
> and in God the sequence of things does not change.
>
> With the eternal Author all things are always present together,  
> with whom whatever will be is present in the order of things made.

## EPILOGUE, CHAPTER IV  
### How the Catholic Church holds the doctrine of grace and free will

Saint Innocent, in his letter to Aurelius and the Council of Carthage, and likewise Saint Celestine to Venery and the other Gallic bishops (Innocent, letter 31; Celestine, letter 8), says:

> “Free will, formerly possessed by that man—that is, the first man—while he used his own goods too incautiously, fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression. He found no way by which he could rise from them; deceived by his own liberty, he would have lain oppressed forever beneath this ruin, unless the coming of Christ had afterward raised him up through his grace. Through the cleansing of the new regeneration, Christ purged every past fault by the washing of his baptism; and, strengthening his condition, by which he might proceed more rightly and steadfastly, he nevertheless did not deny him his grace for the future. For although he redeemed the human being from former sins, yet, knowing that he could sin again, he reserved many means for his restoration, by which he might correct him even after these things, granting him daily remedies. Unless we rely and depend upon these as we strive, we can by no means overcome human errors. For it is necessary that by him whose help enables us to conquer, we should again be conquered when he does not help us. Therefore, of all good affections and works, of all endeavors and all virtues by which from the beginning of faith one tends toward God, let us profess God to be the author; and let us not doubt that every human merit is anticipated by his grace, through whom we begin both to will and to do something good. Certainly, by this help and gift of God free will is not taken away but set free, so that from dark it becomes bright, from crooked straight, from feeble sound, from imprudent provident.”

And Saint Augustine says, in the resolution of the third question against the Pelagians and Celestians, in the *Hypomnesticon* (book III, near the beginning):

> “Therefore we believe with certain faith, and unhesitatingly proclaim, that human beings possess free will. It must be briefly explained why it is called free will. I think that *arbitrium* takes its name from judging by rational consideration, or from discerning what it chooses and what it rejects; or it is called free because it is placed in its own power, having the capacity to do what it wills—which is a movement of the living and rational soul. But such free will, as I have already said, existed unimpaired in the first-formed human being before sin. For he incurred offense through nothing other than that by which he was able, in order not to sin, to resist the persuader. Therefore, by willing evil he justly lost the ability to do good—he who, through the ability to do good, could have overcome the will to do evil. God justly left him, now captive through sin, to his depraved will, so that this might be his punishment: not to do what he wills, though, had he always obeyed God, it could have sufficed for every good thing that he willed. Thus he conceived the willing of evil not from the good condition of his nature, as though from an inborn evil, as the Manichaean believes, but from an accidental corrupt desire.”

Against this is the exposition of the Scriptural statement which the same doctor explained in the second book of *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (book II, chapter 13): “For their race is evil and their natural wickedness; and because their thought could not be changed forever. For their seed was cursed from the beginning” (Wisdom XII, 10).

> “Surely,” he says, “whoever these people may be of whom he says this, he speaks of human beings. How then is the wickedness of any human being natural, and the seed cursed from the beginning, unless reference is made to that which says: ‘Through one human being sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Rom. V, 12)? And whose evil thought cannot be changed forever except because it cannot change itself, but only if divine grace comes to its aid? When that grace does not come to its aid, what are human beings but what the apostle Peter calls ‘like mute animals, naturally brought forth for captivity and destruction’ (II Pet. II, 12)? Hence the apostle Paul, mentioning in one place both the wrath of God with which we are born and the grace by which we are freed, says: ‘We too all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of the affections, and we were by nature children of wrath, as were the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace we are saved’ (Eph. II, 3). What then are the natural wickedness of the human being, the seed cursed from the beginning, those naturally brought forth for captivity and destruction, and children of wrath by nature? Was this nature so created in Adam? Far be it. But because it was corrupted in him, it has thus run and now runs naturally through all, so that nothing frees us from this destruction except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

And again in the *Hypomnesticon* (book III, near the middle):

> “There is therefore free will: whoever denies that it exists is not a Catholic; and whoever says that it exists in such a way that, without God, it cannot either begin or complete a good work—that is, one pertaining to his holy purpose—is a Catholic.”

And again: “Listen, heretic, foolish enemy of the truth of faith:

> “We do not condemn the good works of free will, which are prepared to be done by the prevenience of grace—not by any merits of free will, but by grace itself acting, governing, and bringing them forward—so that they may abound in free will; for by these or such works human beings of God have been justified, are justified, and will be justified in Christ. But by divine authority we condemn works of free will which are preferred to grace and by which people boast that they are justified in Christ as though by merits.”

And again, in *On Grace and Free Will* (chapter 15):

> “Will is always free in us, but it is not always good. For it is either free from righteousness when it serves sin, and then it is evil; or free from sin when it serves righteousness, and then it is good. But God’s grace is always good, and through it a human being who previously had an evil will comes to have a good will. Through it also that good will which has already begun to exist is increased and becomes so great that, when it wills very fully and perfectly, it can fulfill the divine commands that it wills. For this is the force of what is written: ‘If you will, you shall keep the commandments’: that the person who wills but cannot may recognize that he does not yet will fully, and pray that he may have a will great enough to fulfill the commandments. Thus he is helped to do what he is commanded. For then willing is useful when we can, and then being able is useful when we will.”

And Saint Gregory, in the twenty-fourth book of the *Moralia*, says:

> “He delivered his soul so that it should not go on to destruction. Because, when divine grace has gone before in a good work, our free will follows, we ourselves are said to free ourselves, because we consent to the Lord who frees us. Hence, when Paul said, ‘I labored more abundantly than all of them,’ [377] lest he seem to have attributed his labors to himself, he added: ‘Yet not I, but the grace of God with me’ (I Cor. XV, 10). Because he himself had followed God’s prevenient grace also by free will, he aptly added ‘with me,’ so that he might not be ungrateful to the divine gift and yet might not remain a stranger to the merit of free will.”

And again, in the thirty-third book (chapter 20):

> “‘Who has first given to me, that I should repay him?’ As though it were said openly: ‘I am compelled by no reason to spare the reprobate, because I am not bound to them as a debtor by their own action.’ For this reason they by no means receive the eternal rewards of the heavenly homeland: because, when they could have deserved them, they despised them through free will. This free will works for good in the elect when their mind is lifted, by the inspiration of grace, above earthly desires. For the good that we do is both God’s and ours: God’s through prevenient grace, ours through obedient free will. For if it is not God’s, why do we give him eternal thanks? But again, if it is not ours, why do we hope for rewards to be given us? Therefore, because we do not give thanks without cause, we know that we are anticipated by his gift; and again, because we do not seek recompense without cause, we know that, with free will following, we chose the good things that we would do.”

The venerable Alcuin, in his little work of questions on the book of Genesis, addressed to the priest Sigulf, when asked why the human being was made with free will, replied:

> “Because the Creator did not wish to create as a slave anyone whom he made in his own image, so that through voluntary good he might appear praiseworthy, or through an appetite for evil condemnable.”

And when asked why God permitted the human being to be tempted when he foreknew that he would consent, he replied:

> “Because there would not be great praise if the human being had not sinned merely because he had been unable to do wrong. For even today, without interruption, human beings throughout the whole human race are tempted by the devil’s snares, so that the virtue of the tempted may thereby be tested, and the palm of the one who does not consent may appear more glorious.”

And on the question how the words “His desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it” are to be understood, he replied:

> “Because you possess free will, sin does not have dominion over you; rather, you have dominion over it, and it is in your power either, with God’s grace, to restrain it or, by your own appetite, to desire it.”

And when asked what true liberty is, he replied:

> “This is the greatest liberty: to serve righteousness and to be free from sin.”

And Prosper, against the Gauls (response 6), says:

> “It is wrongly said that free will is nothing or does not exist; but it cannot rightly be denied that before the illumination of faith it acts in darkness—that is, in the shadow of death—because, before it is freed from the devil’s dominion by God’s grace, it lies in that abyss into which it plunged itself by its own liberty. For God’s grace does not abolish human choice, but nourishes it, and calls and brings it back from error to the way, so that what was crooked by its own liberty may become straight through the working of God’s Spirit.”

And again, in *On the Ungrateful*, against the Pelagians:

> Just as a branch cannot bear any fruit
>
> unless it remains in the vine, which, serving from its root,
>
> sends sap into its branches and fills the grapes with must,
>
> so those barren of virtues and lacking their fruit
>
> will be the food of everlasting fire: they who, having left the vine,
>
> dare to rely upon the spreading tresses of liberty,
>
> lest they be fruitful through Christ’s abundance.
>
> And they believe that they can excel more by their own powers
>
> than if God were the author of the virtues that please him.

And a little later:

> There is nothing except sin by which
>
> freedom is tormented, to which evil deeds alone have recourse.
>
> Yet when we direct our mind toward holy acts,
>
> when a chaste mind resists the desires of the flesh,
>
> when we do not yield to the tempter and, afflicted by bitter punishments,
>
> remain with our heart unharmed,
>
> we act by freedom, but by redeemed freedom,
>
> of which God is the ruler.

And again in the same work (chapter 15):

> And we hold these things concerning the goodness
>
> [Col. 0442B] and power of God: unless he cherish and govern
>
> those whom he calls and keep them safe from every sin,
>
> no one’s own prudence will preserve him, nor will anyone perfect himself
>
> by the powers of nature alone.
>
> But because in us now both willing and not willing have been created,
>
> and summoned freedom can direct the movements of its choice
>
> where it wills, and through the ear
>
> the purpose by which God proposed in his counsel to save the world
>
> has been opened to the judgment of the heart,
>
> let the awakened mind shake off its long sleep,
>
> submit and fit itself to him,
>
> who may lead it, eager and faithful, into the joys he has promised.

And in *On Divine Providence*:

> [lacuna]
>
> The best Creator gave this special honor to the human being. And when he created all things by a word, he created this one by hands; a double substance is joined, and opposites come together into one life.
>
> For the soul, like the rest, is brought forth from nothing, free from destruction, except that it is answerable to the Lord alone; and, being guilty, it can bear punishment under the name of death. Entering its earthly home, it gives life to its companion and together with it draws in the divine breath.
>
>
> [Col. 0442C] Nor, because the natures of the two things are unlike, is their condition unequal: one end awaits both, whether the inferior be subjected to the right of the superior, or the weaker be matched with the strength of the greater.
>
> For both can be conquered and can conquer, can advance and diminish, can reign and lose their kingdom.
>
> It is not because at the origin or cause of birth they brought to anyone more or less, or because any external force presses upon those created and drives them, unaware, into differing moral conditions;
>
> but because the human being is free and wise, able to distinguish wrong from right, having within himself the distinctions between things and the right of will by which the mind governs choice.

## EPILOGUE, CHAPTER V  
### That God wills all human beings to be saved, although not all are saved; that some are saved by the gift of the Savior, and that some perish by the merit of those who perish

Saint Celestine, to Venery and the other Gallic bishops (after letter 8):

> “Let us consider the sacraments of priestly prayers, which, handed down by the Apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the whole world and in the entire Catholic Church, so that the law of praying may establish the law of believing. For when the bishops of holy peoples carry out the mission entrusted to them, they plead the cause of the human race before the divine clemency. With the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith may be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters may be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, when the veil of the heart has been removed from the Jews, the light of truth may appear to them; that heretics may recover to receive the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be conferred upon the fallen; and finally that, when catechumens have been led to the sacraments of regeneration, the hall of heavenly mercy may be opened to them.”

For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wills our merits to be his gifts, and for the things he has bestowed he will grant eternal rewards.

And John Chrysostom says in Homily 25 on the Gospel of Matthew:

> “For this reason the priest, standing at the altar, commands us to give thanks to God for the whole world, for those absent and present, for those who lived before us, and for those who will come after us, with that sacrifice set before him. For this both frees us from the earth and transfers us to heaven, and makes angels out of human beings.”

Saint Dionysius the Areopagite says in the second chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> “Each of the hierarchs, desiring that all human beings be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth in likeness to God, proclaims the true Gospels to all: ‘To as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name’ (John I, 12). Therefore, if anyone departs from the true light, shutting off by spontaneous choice, through desire for wickedness, the intellectual virtues naturally sown within him so that they might be enlightened, he destroys himself.”

[380] And Saint Cyprian says in his book *On the Lord’s Prayer*:

> “For when the disciples are no longer called earthly by him, but ‘the salt of the earth’; when the Apostle calls the first human being one from the earth’s clay and the second one from heaven; and when we ought to be like God the Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust, so, at Christ’s instruction, we pray and ask that we make our prayer for the salvation of all: that just as in heaven—that is, in us—God’s will has been accomplished through our faith, so that we might be from heaven, likewise on earth—that is, among those who believe—God’s will may be accomplished, so that those who are still earthly by their first birth may begin to be heavenly, born from water and the Spirit.”

And Saint Hilary says in the second book *On the Faith* (*On the Trinity*, book II, after the middle):

> “For the sake of the human race the Son of God was born from a virgin. The Holy Spirit himself served him in this work, while his divine power overshadowed him; he formed for himself the beginnings of a body and established the origins of flesh, so that, having become human from a virgin, he might receive human nature in himself, and through the fellowship of this union the body of the whole human race might exist sanctified in him. Thus, just as all were established in him through that by which he willed to be bodily, so again he might be brought into all through that which is invisible in him.”

And again:

> “The gift that is in Christ is one and open to all; and wherever it is not absent, it is given to the extent that someone wishes to receive it, and it remains to the extent that someone wishes to merit it.”

Saint Ambrose, explaining the verse, “You have dealt kindly with your servant, Lord,” in Psalm 118, says:

> “‘How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!’ (Ps. LXXII, 1). Therefore he is good to all, because he wills all to be upright in heart. But whoever turns aside in heart turns away from himself the grace of divine goodness. God is always good.”

And Saint John Chrysostom says in his book *On the Restoration of the Fallen*:

> “If God had made us for the purpose of punishing us, you would rightly despair and doubt your salvation. But if he made us solely because of his goodness, so that we might enjoy his eternal blessings and gifts; and if everything he has done from the beginning of the world to the present he has done for this reason, and for this reason admonishes us, namely, that he may save us by his mercy, what ground for despair or doubt will remain for us?”
