And Saint Jerome, in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, on “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Eph. IV, 30):

> “The grief of the Holy Spirit is to be understood in the same way as the anger of God, sleep, and the other passions expressed in human likeness. It does not mean that the Spirit is grieved or that the Divinity experiences any disturbance; rather, from our words we learn God’s dispositions: that he grieves whenever we sin and mourns over sinners. The Savior too, while present in the body, wept over Jerusalem; and through the prophet he mourns over the whole human race, saying: ‘Woe is me, my soul, for the reverent one has perished from the earth, and there is no one who corrects among human beings; all are judged in blood.’”

And Saint Augustine says in the thirty-third chapter of *On the Letter and the Spirit*:

> “God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; yet not in such a way as to take away their free will, by which, whether using it well or badly, they are judged most justly. When this happens, unbelievers act against God’s will when they do not believe his Gospel; yet they do not thereby overcome it. Rather, they deprive themselves of the great and highest good and entangle themselves in punishments, destined to experience in torments the power of the one whose mercy in gifts they despised. Thus God’s will is always unconquered. It would be conquered if it found nothing to do with those who despise it, or if they could in any way escape what he has determined concerning such people.”

And in his book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*:

> “Truly, brother, that great and genuine blessedness which is promised to the saints in the age to come is blessedness indeed. All visible things pass away, and all the splendor, pleasures, and curiosity of this age will perish, dragging their lovers with them to destruction. From this destruction—that is, from eternal punishments—merciful God wishes to free all human beings, provided they are not enemies to themselves and do not resist the mercy of their Creator. For this reason he sent his only-begotten Son, that is, his Word equal to himself, through whom he established all things. Remaining in his divinity and not departing from the Father, changed in nothing, yet by assuming humanity and appearing to human beings in mortal flesh, he came to human beings. Thus, just as through one human being, the first who was made, namely Adam, death entered the human race because he consented to his wife, who had been deceived by the devil, so that they might transgress God’s command, so through one human being who is also God, the Son of God, Jesus Christ, all who believe in him, with all past sins erased, might enter eternal life.”

And Prosper says in his response against the Vincentians:

> “We must believe and profess with complete sincerity that God wills all human beings to be saved. For the Apostle, whose statement this is, most earnestly commands what is devoutly observed in all the churches: that supplication be made to God for all human beings. That many perish is the merit of those who perish; that many are saved is the gift of the one who saves. For God’s justice is without blame when the guilty person is condemned; but when the guilty person is justified, it is the ineffable grace of God.”

And again, in his book *On Divine Providence*:

> But lest we delay too long over these matters,
>
> which have been set forth in various ways through the ages,
>
> and lest anyone deny in the whole what is present in a part,
>
> while divided affairs conceal the Lord’s solid care
>
> and nothing that appears rare is accepted,
>
> say what people, in what remote region of the world,
>
> or what human beings, of what race or condition,
>
> God has neglected to save: man, woman, slave,
>
> free person, Jew, Greek, Scythian, barbarian—we are all one in Christ.

[382] For this was held by the Law, by the revered volumes of the prophets, and by the sure hope of the patriarchs:

> When the world’s final age was running close to its end,
>
> God would come to earthly realms, who, death having been destroyed,
>
> would loosen the laws of hell
>
> and raise up the long ruin of the human race
>
> through a better birth.

And in his book *Against Eutyches* (*On Providence*):

> Just as grace once embraced only those of the past
>
> who saw Christ by faith, so in our time
>
> Christ renews no one unless he is received in the heart.
>
> Behold, human being, how great a power has been freely bestowed upon you:
>
> if you wish, you can become a child of God.

And in his book *Against Nestorius*:

> Is God’s love now understood, and his care,
>
> poured out upon all, now plainly revealed,
>
> and is salvation known to stand before everyone?
>
> Yet, alas, again you wage war with complaining words,
>
> chattering human being, and pierce your own flesh with your weapons:
>
> “Why am I not good?” You do not will this.
>
> “Why am I evil?” You will this.
>
> “Why do I will what is evil,
>
> and why do I not will what is good?”
>
> You are free, and though you can distinguish right from wrong,
>
> you choose what is worse.

And in his book *Against the Mathematicians*:

> Pursue this work of goodness; cautiously flee that of wickedness.
>
> From the one blessed life is born; from the other death is produced.
>
> Before you stand saving water and consuming fire.
>
> Stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish: equal ability lies open.

And shortly afterward:

> The fires of heaven do not give birth to them,
>
> nor does fire flow from the ether;
>
> it rises from our hearts themselves,
>
> and freedom itself stirs the war,
>
> while we are shaken by civil arms.
>
> When sluggish will, embracing soft idleness,
>
> refuses to travel the difficult road.

And in his book *Against the Epicureans*:

> If, amid the many offenses of their former conduct,
>
> the unrelenting severity of wrath had punished them too soon,
>
> the time of a better life would have been cut off,
>
> and the fallen would not have been allowed
>
> to regain the strength to stand.

> “I do not desire the death of the sinner,” says the Lord,
>
> “nor is there any gain from one who perishes.
>
> Let him return instead, and, changed,
>
> let him be brought back to the path he abandoned,
>
> and let him enjoy life.”

> And because he wills those whom he created
>
> to be like himself in virtues, he says:
>
> “Leave vengeance to me; I will repay
>
> with a judgment worthy of me. Let there be room for wrath.”

> Thus, while the punishment of many wicked people is delayed,
>
> some are often recalled to honorable conduct,
>
> [383] and each person becomes his own judge and severe avenger,
>
> destroying what he had been before and rising as another.

> But those who persist in clinging to prolonged error,
>
> although they grow old unpunished amid many vices,
>
> will come to a savage end, where there will be no hope of pardon.

And after a little:

> For just as no one becomes saved unwillingly
>
> and while sunk in deep sleep,
>
> nor is one who has voluntarily departed compelled by force,
>
> so the gates of life stand open to those who return when summoned,
>
> and heaven’s senate receives the citizens who have been saved.

[Col. 0446A] And Saint Leo, in the *Tome to Flavian* (letter 10, chapter 3):

> “It was necessary that, through the dispensation of a hidden plan, the unchangeable God—whose will cannot be deprived of its goodness—should complete his original ordering of mercy toward us through a more hidden sacrament, so that the human being, driven into guilt by the cunning of the devil’s wickedness, might not perish contrary to God’s purpose. Therefore the Son of God enters the lowly regions of this world.”

Likewise Pope Saint Leo, in his letter to Emperor Leo:

> “In order to restore the life of all, he took up the cause of all, and, paying on behalf of all the force of the ancient bond, which he alone among all did not owe, he rendered it void.”

And Saint Gregory, in the eighth book of the *Moralia* (chapter 20):

> “Why do you despise as though he were opposed to you the human being whom you believe you despise, when I know for certain that you do not wish even the one whom you seem to despise to perish?”

And again, in book XXXI (chapter 14):

> “The security of a just man is rightly compared to a lion. When he sees anyone rising against him, he returns to the confidence of his mind, and knows that he overcomes all who oppose him, because he loves only the one whom, even against his will, he cannot lose. For whoever seeks outward things, which are taken away even from those unwilling to surrender them, willingly subjects himself to foreign fear.”

And John Chrysostom, in the twenty-fifth homily on the Gospel of Matthew:

> “‘This Gospel will be preached in the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.’ Which nations? Clearly those who do not obey and do not consent to the Gospel. For lest anyone say, ‘Why is it preached to all, if not all are going to believe?’—he says: ‘So that it may be clear that I have done everything I ought to do, and that afterward no one can blame me.’”

Hence Prosper too says in his *Book of Epigrams*:

> “A human being can lose temporal goods unwillingly, but never loses eternal goods except willingly.
>
> Every good joined to the world and produced in time
>
> can be lost under any circumstance.
>
> Although a person carefully resists losses,
>
> he is nevertheless often stripped of his own possessions.
>
> But the goods that are truly good, and are not held only temporarily,
>
> whoever always desires to possess them always possesses.
>
> [384] Nor can a will supported by Christ be overpowered by force;
>
> in him, love, persisting, conquers all things.”

And the venerable presbyter Bede, in his treatise on the Acts of the Apostles:

> “Peter himself thus understood that all human beings alike are summoned to Christ’s Gospel, and that no one is polluted by nature. [Col. 0446D] So too the Lord, through the prophet and in the Gospel, cries out to everyone, saying: ‘Who is the man who desires life and loves to see good days? Let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it’ (Psalm 33:13); and: ‘Draw near to him and be enlightened’; and he says: ‘Come, children, listen to me’ (ibid. 6, 12). And: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matthew 11:28).
>
> “For it is certain that the one who calls everyone to salvation, both in the Old and in the New Testament, wishes everyone to be saved. He is not a liar or deceiver, of whom Scripture says, ‘God is truthful’ (Romans 3:4), and, ‘No deceit was found in his mouth’ (1 Peter 2:22), so that he would invite to salvation those whom he did not wish to be saved.
>
> “Therefore, among all those who are called, whoever comes to him according to his command is certainly enlightened and refreshed. [Col. 0447A] But whoever, invited to this Lord’s banquet—that is, to the refreshment of eternal salvation, in which that fattened calf, sufficient to provide the fullest refreshment of salvation for all human beings without exception, provided only that they believe in him faithfully and firmly, and that singular and true Lamb, who takes away the sins of the world, was slain for all who wished to feast—either does not come of his own will, like the elder son returning from the field and declining, even when asked by his father, to enter his father’s banquet so that he might feast with his younger and prodigal brother who had returned, thereby portraying those who, though invited to this same meal, did not wish to come; or, having come, withdraws from this will before he is filled with the complete joy of refreshment.
>
> “If he did not withdraw from it before the perfection of refreshment and joy by acting courageously and enduring the Lord, he would in no way wish, indeed would not be able, to withdraw thereafter. [Col. 0447B] Just as each person does not come by God’s will but by his own, and withdraws not by God’s will but by his own, so each person perishes not by God’s will but through his own contempt, his own unbelief, or his persevering iniquity, whether original or actual. For the Truth himself truly says: ‘I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but that he should turn back and live.’
>
> “Otherwise God would be unjust, bringing wrath and punishing those who could not be saved for the reason that he did not wish them to be saved—he whose will no one can resist. But far be this from us. For salvation was proposed and prepared for everyone: the humble received it humbly, and God the Father revealed it to them by his grace; the proud, judging himself unworthy of eternal life, proudly rejected it, and divine justice, by the merit of sin and the strictness of judgment, hid it from him to whom grace did not reveal it, as is often found in Scripture. [Col. 0447C]
>
> “Thus, under the name of the ostrich, it is written concerning the hypocrite: ‘God deprived him of wisdom and did not give him understanding’ (Job 39:17).”

Hence Saint Gregory, in the thirty-second book of the *Moralia* (chapter 9), says:

> “Although [385] ‘to deprive’ is one thing and ‘not to give’ another, nevertheless, by adding ‘he did not give’ he repeated what he had first said with ‘he deprived.’ It is as though he said: in saying ‘he deprived,’ he did not unjustly take wisdom away, but justly did not give it. Hence the Lord is also described as having hardened Pharaoh’s heart—not because he conferred hardness upon it, but because, in response to Pharaoh’s deserving, he did not soften it from above by any perceptible infusion of fear.” [Col. 0447D]

And Saint Augustine, in the book *On Grace and Free Choice* (chapter 21), addressing Valentinus and the monks with him:

> “This must be fixed and immovable in your hearts: there is no injustice with God. Therefore, when you read in the writings of truth that human beings are led astray by God, or dulled, or that their hearts are hardened, do not doubt that their evil merits preceded this, so that they might justly suffer these things. Otherwise you will fall into Solomon’s proverb: ‘The folly of a man perverts his ways, and he blames God in his heart.’”

And in the same work, somewhat later (chapter 23):

> “When, then, you hear the Lord saying, ‘I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet’ (Ezekiel 14), and what the Apostle says, ‘He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens’ [Col. 0448A] (Romans 9), faithfully and without doubt recognize, in the one whom he permits to be led astray or hardened, his evil merits; but in the one on whom he has mercy, recognize the grace of God, who does not repay evils with evils but good for evils.
>
> “Do not therefore take free choice away from Pharaoh because God says in many places, ‘I hardened Pharaoh,’ or ‘I have hardened’ or ‘I will harden Pharaoh’s heart.’ For that reason Pharaoh himself did not fail to harden his own heart. Indeed, this too is read concerning him, when the swarm of flies was removed from the Egyptians, for Scripture says: ‘And Pharaoh hardened his heart, both at this time, and he was unwilling to let the people go’ (Exodus 8). Thus God hardened him through just judgment, and Pharaoh himself through free choice.”

And in the thirty-fifth Psalm:

> “‘God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to do what is unseemly’ (Romans 1:28). If God does this, so that they do what is unseemly, what did they themselves do? There was therefore a desire which they were unwilling to conquer—not one to which they were handed over by God’s judgment, but one by which they were judged worthy to be handed over.” [Col. 0448B]

And in the fifth Psalm:

> “When God punishes sinners, he does not inflict his own evil upon them, but leaves them to their evils.”

Accordingly, since, as the same venerable Augustine says in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, nothing happens except what God either does or permits to happen, Cassiodorus writes on Psalm 103:

> “Nothing can be done by anyone except what God himself, by a secret judgment, has permitted to be done either for testing or for punishment. Thus other authors also say, by this manner of expression, that those who are not enlightened by grace are deservedly blinded by God; that those who are abandoned by just judgment are handed over; and that those who are not established are struck down.” [Col. 0448C]

Many other such passages are found in the works of Saints Gregory, Ambrose, and Jerome, and in the blessed Augustine’s aforementioned book *On Grace and Free Choice*, in the book *On the Predestination of Grace*, in the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, and in his letter to Sixtus, presbyter of the Roman Church and later bishop of that holy see, as we showed [386] above when we were speaking of the vessels of wrath made ready for destruction: vessels of wrath prepared for destruction not by God’s predestination but by paternal or personal transgression.

Thus the same blessed Augustine says in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints* (chapter 8):

> “Why does he not teach all? The Apostle disclosed as much as he judged should be disclosed: ‘Wishing to show his wrath and to make known his power, he endured with much patience the vessels of wrath that had been made ready for destruction, and in order to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory’ (Romans 9:22–23). Hence the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God.” [Col. 0448D]

And somewhat later (chapter 9):

> “Why, then, it is not given to all should not disturb the faithful person who believes that all proceeded from one person into a condemnation that was unquestionably most just, so that there would be no just reproach against God even if no one were delivered from it. Hence it is clear that the grace is great by which many are delivered.”

And in his letter to the aforementioned presbyter Sixtus (Letter 105):

> “In the vessels made ready for destruction, which is the punishment owed to the condemned mass, let the vessels made from the same mass for honor recognize what divine mercy has bestowed upon them.” [Col. 0449A]

And shortly afterward he concludes concerning both:

> “Therefore, ‘he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.’ He does this in whose presence there is no injustice. He has mercy, therefore, by a gratuitous gift, but he hardens by a most just merit.”

And again:

> “For we seek the merit of hardening, and we find it: the whole mass was condemned because of the merit of sin. God does not harden by imparting evil, but by not imparting mercy. Those to whom he does not impart it are neither worthy nor deserving; rather, they are worthy and deserving that it not be imparted to them. But we seek the merit of mercy and do not find it, because there is none. Grace would be emptied if it were not given freely but repaid according to merits.” [Col. 0449B]

And because the Predestinarians cry out, “The Lord has done whatever he willed. If he wished all to be saved, then all would certainly be saved,” they say that those referred to as “all” by the Apostle—“God wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4)—are only those who are saved; whereas those who are not saved are in no way included in God’s will as desiring their salvation.

Saint Jerome, refuting them in his commentary on the Letter to Philemon, says:

> “If, as he says, God is good voluntarily and not by necessity, then, when he made the human being in his own image and likeness, he ought to have made him good voluntarily—that is, so that he would be voluntarily good, just as God himself is voluntarily and not necessarily good. If he had been made such that he accomplished the good not by will but by necessity, he would not be like God, who is good because he wills it, not because he is compelled. Nothing can be called good unless it is voluntary; but what is good by necessity is not good.
>
> “Therefore, leaving us to our own free choice, he made us more in his own image and likeness. To be like God is, plainly, good.” [Col. 0449C]

Saint Gregory demonstrates the same in the seventh book of his letters, letter 6, under the second indiction, addressing Bishop Januarius concerning the Jews, who were subjected to force so that they might believe:

[387]

> “We should use greater gentleness toward them, so that they may be drawn to wish to possess rather than to resist—not so that they may be brought in against their will. For it is written: ‘I will sacrifice to you voluntarily’ (Psalm 53:8), and, ‘I will confess to him of my own will’ (Psalm 27:7).” [Col. 0449D]

And Saint Augustine, addressing Valentinus and the brothers who are with him:

> “First, as it is written in the Gospel of the Apostle John, the Lord Jesus ‘did not come to judge the world but that the world might be saved through him’ (John 12:47). Later, however, as the Apostle Paul writes, ‘God will judge the world’ when he comes (Romans 3:6), just as the whole Church confesses in the Creed: ‘to judge the living and the dead.’ If, then, there is no grace of God, how does he save the world? And if there is no free choice, how does he judge the world?”

Accordingly, as the holy teachers demonstrate from Scripture, those who could have been saved by God’s grace, had they followed that same grace by free choice—free in relation to righteousness but enslaved to sin—are justly punished. [Col. 0450A] For, as the extraordinary Paul says in writing to the Hebrews, “By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:9). Our Lord Jesus, as it is written, came freely, “not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy” (Titus 3:5), which is also grace, to seek and save what had perished.

For the saying is trustworthy: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners. “All have sinned and lack the glory of God.” Even those who, according to the Apostle Paul, could understand God’s invisible attributes—his eternal power and divinity—through the things that have been made (Romans 1:20), are without excuse, as Ambrose explains this statement.

Hence Bede the presbyter says in his commentary on the Gospel of Luke:

> “‘Why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?’—thereby showing that they, as rational creatures, even if they did not know the written letters, could nevertheless by natural intelligence discern either that the one who had performed works in himself that no other had performed was to be understood as above humanity and therefore believed to be God, or that after so many injustices in this age the just judgment of the Creator would come. [Col. 0450B]
>
> “Let no one, therefore, presume to interpret, on the basis of what was said above about the servant who did not know his master’s will being beaten with few blows, that ignorance provides a remedy. To say nothing else, simply because he is human, no one can be ignorant either of the evils he ought to avoid or of the goods he ought to desire.”

And Augustine, in the book *On Nature and Grace* (chapter 7):

> “Such examples show what certain people were at a particular time, not that they could not have been something else. Hence they are rightly found guilty. For if they were such because they could not have been otherwise, they would be free from guilt.” [Col. 0450C]

Therefore everyone will be without excuse, because they refuse salvation by free choice—free in relation to righteousness but enslaved to sin. For at the second coming, the Lord will come terrible and exalted to judge the world, that is, those who have dwelt in the world; at his first coming he came appeased and humble to save the world by grace.

Since salvation was proposed to everyone—namely, the salvation of our God [388] prepared before the face of all peoples—some rejected it by free choice and will therefore rightly be condemned, while others received it by free choice and will therefore be saved by grace. Scripture demonstrates this, saying:

> “Life was the light of human beings, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:4); and, “This is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light” (John 3:19); and, “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). [Col. 0450D]

Concerning those who receive him it is said:

> “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20).

And:

> “As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12).

And:

> “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

Again Paul says concerning those who despise him:

> “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, God will send them an operation of error so that they may believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (2 Thessalonians 2:10–12). [Col. 0451A]

And, writing concerning those who receive the truth, he says:

> “We give thanks to God without ceasing, because when you received from us the word of the hearing of God, you accepted it not as the word of human beings but, as it truly is, the word of God, which also works in you who have believed” (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

And Cassiodorus, on Psalm 77:

> “‘He sent upon them the anger of his indignation, indignation, anger, and tribulation, an immission through evil angels.’ The order of vengeance is recounted with the utmost accuracy. First, the Lord becomes angry with our sins when we do not turn with any compunction; then, in his indignation, anger, and tribulation, he abandons human wickedness to itself, so that those who scorn to obey divine commands may be afflicted by their own perversities.” [Col. 0451B]

And Augustine, in the book *On Grace and Free Choice* (chapter 3):

> “Those, therefore, who know the divine commandments are deprived of the excuse that people commonly have from ignorance. But even those who do not know God’s law will not be without punishment. ‘Those who have sinned without the law will perish without the law, and those who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law’ (Romans 2:12).
>
> “It does not seem to me that the Apostle said this as though he meant that those who do not know the law will suffer something worse in their sins than those who know it. For it seems worse to perish than to be judged. But since he was speaking about Gentiles and Jews—because the former are without the law, while the latter received the law—who would dare say that Jews who sin under the law will not perish because they did not believe in Christ, when it was said concerning them that they would be judged by the law? No one can be delivered without faith in Christ, and therefore they will be judged in such a way that they perish. [Col. 0451C]
>
> “For if the condition of those who do not know God’s law is worse than that of those who know it, how will what the Lord says in the Gospel be true? ‘The servant who does not know his master’s will and does things deserving blows will receive few blows; but the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do what is deserving will receive many blows’ (Luke 12:47–48). There he shows that the person who knows sins more gravely than the one who does not know.
>
> “Nevertheless, one must not therefore flee into the darkness of ignorance and seek an excuse there. Not to have known is one thing; not to have wished to know is another. The will [389] is accused in the one of whom it is said: ‘He did not wish to understand, so as to act well’ (Psalm 35:4).
>
> “But even that ignorance which belongs not to those who do not wish to know but to those who simply do not know does not excuse anyone so completely that he will not burn in everlasting fire if he did not believe because he had not heard at all what he should believe—though perhaps he may burn more mildly. For it was not said without reason: ‘Pour out your wrath upon the nations that do not know you’ (Psalm 78:6). And the Apostle says: ‘When he comes in a flame of fire to inflict vengeance upon those who do not know God’ (2 Thessalonians 1:8). [Col. 0451D]
>
> “Nevertheless, so that we may possess knowledge itself and no one may say, ‘I did not know, I did not hear, I did not understand,’ the human will is summoned where it is said: ‘Do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding’ (Psalm 32). Yet even worse appears to be the one of whom it is said: ‘A stubborn servant will not be corrected by words; for even if he understands, he will not obey.’”

Many other passages of this kind are found in the writings divinely inspired.

For just as, according to Scripture, “the Lord has done whatever he willed” (Psalm 113:3), so he made all things good as he willed. For he is not good accidentally but essentially, and, being omnipotent and unable to deny himself, he could neither will otherwise nor wish to be able otherwise. As the blessed Augustine says in his sermon *On the Creed* addressed to the newly baptized:

> “If, as I say, God made the things he made in the beginning from nothing, then from the things he made he is able to make whatever he wills, because he is omnipotent. Nor should the unrighteous therefore believe that God is not omnipotent because they do many things against his will. Whether a person is justly condemned or mercifully delivered, the will of the Omnipotent is fulfilled. The only thing the Omnipotent does not will, and therefore cannot do, is what he does not will. He therefore uses evil things, not according to their perverse will, but according to his own righteous will.” [Col. 0452A]

And shortly afterward:

> “Let no one think that I have rashly said that the Omnipotent cannot do something. The blessed Apostle also said this: ‘If we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself’ (2 Timothy 2:13). But because he does not will it, he cannot; and he cannot will it because he cannot will.
>
> “For justice cannot will to do what is unjust, wisdom cannot will what is foolish, and truth cannot will what is false. Thus we are warned that the omnipotent God cannot do not only what the Apostle says—deny himself—but many other things.
>
> “I say this myself, and I dare say it by his truth, which I dare not deny: God the Omnipotent cannot die, cannot change, cannot be deceived, cannot become miserable, and cannot be conquered. Far be it from us to say that the Omnipotent can do these or similar things. Truth therefore shows not only that he is omnipotent because he cannot do them, but also compels us to conclude that he would not be omnipotent if he could do them.
>
> “God voluntarily is what he is. He is therefore eternal, unchangeable, truthful, blessed, and unconquerable. If, then, something he does not will could exist, he would not be omnipotent. But he is omnipotent; therefore he can do whatever he wills. Accordingly, what he does not will to exist cannot exist, and he is called omnipotent precisely because he can do whatever he wills. Of him the Psalm also says: ‘In heaven and on earth he has done whatever he willed’ (Psalm 113:3).” [390] [Col. 0452B–D]

And in the book *On Nature and Grace* (chapter 49):

> “Far be it from us to say that God can sin. For, as fools suppose, he is not omnipotent because he cannot die and cannot deny himself.”

Let Catholics see how badly the heretics interpret the statement, “The Lord has done whatever he willed,” when they say: “Those who are not saved are in no way included in God’s will as desiring their salvation.” It is established, however, that those who do not follow the will of the Lord inviting them to salvation—because “the righteous Lord has loved righteousness; his face has seen equity” (Psalm 11:7)—experience, in the retribution of justice, the will of the Lord taking vengeance in punishment. [Col. 0453A]

“And God saw,” Scripture says, “all that he had made, and it was very good.” And again: “God made the human being in his own image and likeness” (Genesis 1:31, 26). To be in the image and likeness of God is unquestionably good.

Again it is written:

> “God established the human being from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel” (Sirach 15:14).

But what counsel he used—or rather abused—and which counselor he obeyed is apparent in his offspring, while the prophet cries out:

> “We have all gone astray; we were conceived in iniquities and born in sins.”

Thus no one is clean, nor is there anyone whose life is even a single day upon the earth, before him in whose sight no living person is justified, with whom no one is innocent by himself, because “there is no one on earth who does good and does not sin.” The same divine Apostle declares that all proceeded from one person into condemnation. [Col. 0453B]

For the first Adam, earthly and from the earth, perished, and in him we all perished. The second Adam, heavenly and from heaven, came—not losing what he was, but assuming what he was not—in the unity of his person, not in a unity of substance. Therefore it was also said:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

He came to seek and save what had perished. We all perished; he came to seek and save us all.

That some are saved is the gift of the one who saves; that some perish is the merit of those who perish, not the desire of the Savior, who came to seek and save what had perished. If no one were delivered from this universal ruin, God’s judgment would be beyond reproach; but because many are delivered, his gift of grace is ineffable. [Col. 0453C]

He who wishes all to be saved said to everyone:

> “If you listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land”—that is, of the land of the living—“but if you are unwilling to hear me and provoke me to anger, the sword shall devour you” (Isaiah 1:19–20).

In that land—that is, in the kingdom of God—blessed is the one who will eat the bread of eternal life and drink the drink of perpetual salvation, and will not thirst again for anything else, except that, once satisfied, he may drink continually and eternally.

By this sword, all who hear, on account of their barrenness in good works and the retribution of their sins, will be cut off from the fellowship of the righteous:

> “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

When the wicked have been separated from the midst of the righteous by this sword, the righteous will be led into the fellowship and joy of the angels, where they will sing the mercies of the Lord forever. [Col. 0453D] By his grace they deserved to believe in him, follow him, and persevere in doing what he commanded. The impious, however, scorned to follow him by believing and to remain [391] in him through right faith and good works.

According to the teaching of the Apostles Peter, Paul, and John:

> “The Son of God appeared for this purpose: to destroy the works of the devil,”

at whose suggestion the first human being had perished. Therefore the same Son of God graciously assumed, for the redemption of human beings, the nature—not the guilt—of that human being, as we have said. He desires all human beings to be saved and desires no one to perish.

## CHAPTER VI OF THE EPILOGUE

That Christ suffered for all human beings, although not all are redeemed to eternal salvation through the mystery of his passion; and because not all are redeemed through the mystery of his passion, this pertains not to the power of the sacrament but to the part of unbelievers: for the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world, but those are strangers to that price who either, delighted by their captivity, did not wish to be redeemed, or, after redemption, returned to the same slavery through persevering unbelief or iniquity.

The great Leo, pontiff of the Catholic and apostolic Church—that is, of the holy Roman see—says in his letter to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem (Letter 78):

> “The true cross therefore confirms Christ’s true generation, because the one who is born in our flesh is the one who is crucified in our flesh. Without the intervention of sin, that flesh could not have been mortal unless it had belonged to our race. [Col. 0454B]
>
> “In order to restore the life of all, he took up the cause of all and canceled the force of the ancient bond, which he alone among all did not owe, by paying it on behalf of all. Thus, just as through the guilt of one all had been made sinners, so through the innocence of one all might become innocent, with righteousness flowing from him into human beings, since human nature had been assumed.”

And again, in his letter to the Emperor Leo (Letter 97, chapter 2):

> “The pouring out of Christ’s blood, the righteous one for the unrighteous, was so rich as a price that, if the whole multitude of captives believed in their Redeemer, no one would remain held by the bonds of the devil. For, as the Apostle says: ‘Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more’ (Romans 5:20). And although those born under the sentence of sin had received the power to be reborn into righteousness, the gift of freedom became stronger than the debt of slavery.” [Col. 0454C]

And Saint Augustine, in the book *On Correction and Grace* (chapter 16; *City of God*, book XX, chapter 6):

> “Who loved the weak more than the one who became weak for all and died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and rose again?
>
> “All were therefore dead in sins, absolutely no one excepted, whether through original sins or through sins added by the will, whether through ignorance or knowledge, by failing to do what is just. [392] For all the dead, one living person died—that is, one who had absolutely no sin—so that those who live through the forgiveness of sins might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for all because of our sins and rose again for our justification.” [Col. 0454D]

And because the Predestinarians, newly arisen, loudly proclaim their error—if Christ is believed and said to have suffered for all, they bring forward to support their opinion the impious who were eternally condemned to the punishments of hell for their crimes before the Lord’s passion, even from the beginning of the world, and, after the triumph of the life-giving cross, Antichrist and the other sons of perdition, for whom they say Christ should not be believed to have suffered—we have judged it appropriate to demonstrate more briefly, by repeating certain points from above, the following.

There was one faith and the same hope of salvation before the Lord’s passion, and after his passion there is one faith and the same hope of salvation for all the saints, in the shedding of the blood of the same God and mediator between God and human beings. [Col. 0455A]

Next, what did the passion of the Redeemer confer upon all the righteous and impious whom the Predestinarians set before us, who died in their impiety?

We say that the righteous were not justified by their own powers but by the grace of the one who, righteous, died for the unrighteous. We say that the impious were not evil by the nature of their condition, nor made impious by the one who justifies many of the impious and, as Paul writes to the Romans, died for the impious. Rather, they were born from the good Adam, who had been made by the good God, but who had lost the freedom of choice; and they died in original or personal impiety without faith in that redemption. He alone among the dead, free from the debt of death, died for all who were debtors to death.

Afterward, the Savior’s death benefited believers particularly for salvation; but for unbelievers the grace of his passion, despised by them, became judgment and condemnation. [Col. 0455B]

Then we shall explain how and with what distinction orthodox teachers understood and taught from Scripture that Christ suffered for all, although not all are redeemed to eternal salvation through the mystery of his passion. Let us now proceed by reviewing each point.

There was one faith and the same hope of salvation before the Lord’s passion, and after his passion there is one faith and the same hope of salvation for all the saints, in the shedding of the blood of the same God and human mediator. The Apostle Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “Through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we shall be saved, just as they also were” (Acts 15:12).

Hence Bede:

> “If they too—that is, the Fathers—believed that they would be saved through the grace of the Lord, since they were unable to bear the yoke of the old law, it is clear that this is the grace that made the ancient righteous live, because ‘the righteous person lives by faith.’ Therefore the sacraments could be different according to the variation of times, yet they returned in complete harmony to the unity of the same faith.” [Col. 0455C]

And Augustine, on Psalm 36:

> “Are we alone, and not also those who existed before us—all the righteous who existed from the beginning of the world—to have Christ as their head? They believed that he would come, whereas we believe that he has come. They too were born in his faith, in which we also [393] were born, so that he might be the head of the entire city of Jerusalem, with all the faithful counted together from beginning to end, including the legions and armies of angels. Thus there may be one city under one king and one province under one emperor, happy in perpetual peace and salvation, praising God without end and blessed without end.” [Col. 0455D]

And Saint Ambrose, in the first book of *On the Holy Spirit*, in the preface, explaining a passage from the book of Judges, says:

> “The Lord’s passion alone is the sacrifice to be offered to God in the religious worship of the people. For, he says, that calf is a type of Christ, in whom dwells the fullness of the seven spiritual virtues, as Isaiah said. Abraham also saw this calf when he saw the Lord’s day and rejoiced. This is the one who was offered under the type of a young goat, now of a sheep, now of a calf: a young goat because it is a sacrifice for sins; a sheep because it is a voluntary victim; a calf because it is an immaculate victim.”

And again Saint Augustine, in the book *On Nature and Grace* (chapter 44):

> “The faith that saved the ancient righteous also saves us: the faith of the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus; faith in his blood, faith in his cross, faith in his death and resurrection. Since we have the same spirit of faith, we too believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Corinthians 4:13). [Col. 0456A]

And Saint Gregory, in his fifteenth homily on Ezekiel, says:

> “Indeed, from the blood of Abel the passion of the Church already began, and there is one Church of the elect who came before and those who follow.”

And Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Paul’s Letter to the Galatians:

> “This little heir, who differs in nothing from a servant although he is lord of all, is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the Father. He signifies the whole human race until Christ’s coming, and, to say more, until the end of the world.
>
> “For just as all die in the first-created Adam before they are even born, so all—even those who were born before Christ’s coming—are made alive in the second Adam. Thus it comes about that we served the law in our fathers, while they are saved by grace in their children.” [Col. 0456B]

This is the one Church that exists from the beginning of the world to its end. Concerning it Saint Gregory says in his seventeenth homily on Ezekiel:

> “‘Those who went before and those who followed cried out, “Hosanna”’ (Matthew 21:9). *Hosanna* means in the Latin language, ‘Save us.’ From him the former sought salvation, the present seek it, and they confess him who comes in the name of the Lord to be blessed, because there is one hope and one faith of the peoples who came before and those who follow.
>
> “For just as they were healed by awaiting his passion and resurrection, so we are saved by his past passion and his resurrection that endures forever.” [Col. 0456C]

The unity of this Church, which is won for the Lord no less through repentance for folly already committed than through diligent pursuit of the wisdom that must be learned—as the venerable priest Bede shows, from the sayings of the earlier Fathers, in his *Commentary on the Gospel of Luke*—is gathered from two groups: namely, those who do not know how to sin and those who cease from sinning. For repentance abolishes sin, while wisdom guards against it.

Of these matters, [p. 394] one example drawn from the whole should suffice for the reader: namely, the scriptural practice by which something spoken at a particular time to one person or to a few is understood as spoken to the whole community and to all successive generations. Thus there is the statement which Moses alone heard in the bush, and which the Lord recapitulates in the Gospel, saying: “But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken by God when he says to you?” (Matt. XXII, 31); and: “What I say to you I say to all” (Mark XIII, 37); and: “Moses is read to this day” (II Cor. III, 15); and: “This is what God says in the prophets” (Heb. I, 1). [Col. 0456D] What he had said at that time, Jesus says today and forever to his disciples.

Just as at that time, when very large crowds gathered and hurried to Jesus from the cities, he described through the parable of the sower the labor and various results of the seed, so also in this our mournful time, through rare sowers, intervals of time, and a broad field, some seed falls beside the road, some among thorns, some upon rock, and little upon good soil. [Col. 0457A] For—what is said not without sorrow—there are many who come to Jesus, confessing him with their words but denying him by their deeds, and returning in their hearts to Egypt; indeed, they associate with those who dwell in Kedar. Yet few, while very many perish, are preserved within the ark of true faith amid the flood of many iniquities.

Thus Abel the righteous, who by wisdom abstained from sins under the law of nature, awaited for himself the opening of the entrance into the heavenly kingdom by him whom, while offering a lamb, he contemplated with the eyes of faith. Adam and Eve blotted out their sin through repentance, as Saint Augustine demonstrates to Marcellinus in Book II of *On the Baptism of Infants* (chapter 34), saying:

“As, therefore, those first human beings afterward lived justly—for which reason they are rightly believed to have been delivered from the final punishment through the blood of the Lord—yet in that life they did not merit to be restored to paradise.” [Col. 0457B]

Cassiodorus likewise says in his exposition of Psalm 102 (Ps. CII, 17):

“‘But the mercy of the Lord is from age to age.’ Hence, he says, it seems appropriate to observe that Adam, as many of the Fathers have said, was recalled to the grace of the Lord when he himself was the first in the world. So too Abel, Noah, Abraham, and the other Fathers, who were indeed in the world but were not from the world. Cain, however, through his unbelief and iniquity, was banished and alien from this Church, in which salvation is offered to all: neither did he abstain from sin through wisdom, nor, even when admonished, did he take care to erase his sin through repentance.” [Col. 0457C]

Under the Law were Zechariah and Elizabeth, of whom it is written: “They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord”; and Simeon the righteous, who himself was awaiting the redemption of Israel (Luke I, 6), that is, the salvation of God prepared before the face of all peoples. Anna too did not depart from the temple, serving the Lord with fastings and prayers night and day. Through wisdom they abstained from sins.

David erased his sins through repentance, awaiting to be made whiter than snow through the sprinkling of Christ’s blood, which is signified by hyssop—that is, by the humility of his incarnation. Saul, unrepentant, was not cleansed even by Samuel’s tears. Although, because of the great merit of his being heard, he is displayed by the Lord, almost singly with Moses, as an example, nevertheless, after the many things he had received from God, he ended an unworthy life by a deserved death, as he had heard from the ventriloquist whom, in his distress, he had sought while neglecting the Lord. [Col. 0457D]

Under grace, James, who was called “the Just,” the first bishop of Jerusalem, is extolled with what praise because he did not know how to sin through wisdom, the divine writings bear witness. And, in order to honor with silence the tears of the great Peter—tears which, God willing, we may proclaim by our example—the thief on the cross repented, confessed, and heard from the fountain of mercy: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43). The other, however, struck by the same punishment and seeing the same fountain of mercy but refusing to drink from it, representing the character of those who despise it, was corrected neither by the punishment nor converted by the example.

This holy Church has always had lambs, among whom goats have mingled and will continue to mingle until that time when the Son of Man will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him; and the wicked will be separated from the good, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. [Col. 0458A] He will place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left, and he will repay each according to his works.

This holy Church likewise always possessed, in the one faith of salvation, sacraments differing according to the variety of times. Namely, from the beginning of the world until the time when circumcision was given, they took care to commend their own souls and those of their people to the Creator and to free them from the bonds of the first guilt either through the offerings of sacrifices or certainly through the sole power of faith. They did the same for other nations while circumcision—the sign of faith—was in force among the Hebrew people. [Col. 0458B]

“For without faith it is impossible to please God,” and, as it is written elsewhere, “The righteous person lives by faith.” After circumcision had been given, that same circumcision in the Law provided the same help of saving healing against the wound of original sin which baptism now provides in the time of revealed grace. The difference was that they could not yet enter the door of the heavenly kingdom, until the one who had given the Law came and bestowed the blessing, so that God, the God of gods, might be seen in Zion. After death they were consoled only by blessed rest in Abraham’s bosom, and in hope they awaited, happy, entry into the peace above.

Yet, as Saint Paul says: “Our fathers were all baptized in the cloud and in the sea” (I Cor. X, 2). This was in the form of Christ’s baptism, which was signified at the very beginnings of the world, when the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters, so that nature might already conceive the power of the sanctification of the waters; it was also clearly signified in the very outpouring of the Flood. [Col. 0458C]

In that baptism—namely, of the cloud and of the sea—not all who were baptized were saved, because not all understood, believed, and preserved its spiritual meaning; just as in the Flood no one was saved except those whom the ark, clearly signifying the holy Church, is known to have contained. So too, among those baptized with Christ’s baptism, some are saved, persevering in right faith and good works through grace, while others perish. For although the baptism in them is true, by which all sins whatsoever are completely erased, they nevertheless do not remain in the truth, and therefore perish, as the blessed Apostle Peter demonstrates, saying:

“In the days of Noah, while the ark was being constructed, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water, baptism, corresponding to this figure, now saves you also” (I Pet. III, 20). [Col. 0458D]

Hence Bede says:

“What, therefore, the water of the Flood did not save when they were outside the ark, but killed, undoubtedly prefigured that every heretic, even though possessing the sacrament of baptism, is to be plunged into hell by the very waters—not by other waters—by which the ark is lifted toward heaven.”

And since, as the Lord says, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John III, 5)—the earlier baptisms having been proclamations of this rebirth—so he likewise declares:

“Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 54). [Col. 0459A]

And again:

“I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John VI, 51).

The figures of this were the tree of life planted in the midst of paradise and granted to Adam for food before the sin, when he was told: “You may eat from every tree of paradise, but you shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. II, 16). After the sin, however, when the Lord said, “See that he does not perhaps take from the tree of life and live forever” (Gen. III, 22), it was altogether forbidden until the one who had been prefigured should come. Of him it was also said: “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her”—namely, Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God. [Col. 0459B]

Again, the mysteries of that same living bread and of the chalice of the true vine were signified by figures. Concerning them Paul likewise says: “All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; but God was not pleased with most of them” (I Cor. X, 3–5). Saint Augustine demonstrates this from the words of the holy Gospel, saying:

“‘Your fathers ate manna and died’ (John VI, 49). Moses and Aaron and the other saints who were among the people ate manna, and they did not die, because they understood the visible food spiritually and hungered spiritually. Others, however, ate and remained in unbelief, just as the Jews heard Christ speaking but did not understand his words spiritually. Therefore he said to them: ‘Your fathers ate manna in the desert and died.’ What death could this be except that of unbelief? For the saints who were among them also died the common death.” [Col. 0459C]

Concerning the New Testament, Paul shows, from the bread of eternal life and the chalice of everlasting salvation, and Ambrose explains in his commentary on the Epistle to the Corinthians:

“Whoever eats this bread and drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (I Cor. XI, 27).

Ambrose says:

“There will be a judgment, so that each person, according to the manner in which he approaches, may render an account on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. For those who approach without discipline in tradition and conduct are guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But what is it to be guilty except to suffer the penalties of the Lord’s death? For he was killed for those who nullify his benefit. Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (ibid., 28–29). [Col. 0459D]

Ambrose says further:

“He teaches that one must approach communion with a devoted spirit and with fear, so that the mind may know that it owes reverence to the one whose body it approaches to receive. For it ought to judge within itself that he is the Lord, whose body it eats and whose blood it drinks in the mystery, he who is witness to God’s benefit. If we receive him with discipline, we will not be unworthy of the body and blood of the Lord; for grace will be shown to the Redeemer.”

And again:

“For it is a spiritual medicine which, when tasted with reverence, purifies the devoted recipient.”

And again:

“Therefore many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep. To prove that there will be an examination concerning the reception of the Lord’s body, he already displays here an image of the judgment upon those who had received the Lord’s body carelessly, while they were struck by fevers and illnesses, and many were dying.” [Col. 0460A]

Finally, Pope Leo says in his third homily on the Nativity of the Lord:

“Let the complaints of those who, with impious murmuring, oppose the divine dispensations and complain about the lateness of the Lord’s birth cease, as though what was accomplished in the final age of the world had not been provided in former times. The incarnation of the Word bestowed the same benefit before it was accomplished as it did after it had been accomplished, and the sacrament of human salvation never ceased in any age. What the apostles preached, the prophets also proclaimed; nor was what had always been believed fulfilled late. God therefore did not provide for human affairs by a new plan or by a tardy act of mercy, but from the foundation of the world he established one and the same cause of salvation for all.” [Col. 0460B]

What, then, did the passion of the Redeemer confer upon all the righteous and wicked generally—those whom the Predestinarians set before us, dead in their impiety? Let Paul say, and let Ambrose explain in his commentary on that epistle:

“He says this because, just as Adam, by sinning, found death and held it, so that all from his origin might be dissolved—‘For as in Adam all die’ (I Cor. XV, 22)—so Christ, who did not sin and therefore conquered death—for whoever does not sin conquers death, since death arises from sin—acquired life, that is, resurrection, for all from his body. Although, therefore, he granted resurrection generally, so that just as in Adam all, whether righteous or unrighteous, die, so in Christ all, both believers and unbelievers, rise again, though for punishment, nevertheless unbelievers seem to be made alive because they receive their bodies, no longer to die but to suffer punishment in them without end, because they were unwilling to believe.” [Col. 0460C]

And again, in the Epistle to the Corinthians:

“Because he rose on the third day” (I Cor. XV, 4). “For no believer denies that all rose again in Christ, just as they died in Adam.”

And again:

“By a man came death, and by a man the resurrection of the dead” (ibid., 21), so that, because death was found through the sin of man, Christ’s righteousness merited the resurrection of the dead.

The blessed John Chrysostom likewise says in his book *On the Restoration of the Fallen*:

“Scripture says that sinners too will put on incorruption—not for the honor of life, but to serve the enduringness of punishment.” [Col. 0460D]

Saint Hilary, in his exposition of Psalm 118, says:

“For he reproaches the proud and the accursed: why did they think that nothing useful for them existed in the sacrament of his blood and death, when he was born, suffered, and died for our sake?” [Col. 0461A]

The same Saint Hilary, agreeing with Saint Ambrose, says in his exposition of Psalm 55:

“‘You will save them for nothing; in anger you will bring down the peoples’ (Ps. LV, 8). This is a new saying of the prophet: that God should save for nothing those who await their own soul for nothing, and that, while ‘for nothing’ is one thing and ‘to be saved’ another, the salvation which will come upon them should now be ‘for nothing.’ There is, therefore, something that can be saved for nothing—indeed, whatever is not worthy, after the resurrection has been granted, of being changed. For since all flesh has been redeemed in Christ so that it may rise, and all must stand before his tribunal, resurrection is nevertheless not granted equally to all with glory and honor. Those, therefore, to whom resurrection but not transformation has been granted are saved for nothing. In anger these peoples will be brought down, for whom the salvation of resurrection has been established for the experience of punishment.” [Col. 0461B]

Bede, in his commentary on Luke, drawing on Augustine, says:

“In a deeper sense, however, it is easier for Christ to suffer for the lovers of the world than for the lovers of the world to be converted to Christ.”

Saint Ambrose says in his Epistle to the Corinthians:

“What is it to be guilty except to suffer the penalties of the Lord’s death? For he was killed for those who nullify his benefit.”

Saint Hilary likewise says in Book III of *On the Faith*:

“The Son of God is crucified, but on the cross God conquers the death of man. Christ, the Son of God, dies, but all flesh is made alive in Christ.” [Col. 0461C]

Saint Augustine says in Book XX, chapter 6, of *The City of God*:

“Therefore all were dead in sins, without exception, whether in original sins or in those added by the will, either through ignorance or through knowledge, by failing to do what is just; and for all the dead, one living person died—namely, one who had absolutely no sin.” [Col. 0461D]

Concerning Antichrist, through whom, together with his body—that is, all the reprobate—the Predestinarians think they can enclose us, let them hear what Saint Gregory says in Book XXXII, chapter 12, of the *Moralia*:

“Since transgression is expressed through the number eleven, the eleventh horn of this beast indicates the author of transgression himself. It arises as a little horn because he is born a mere man; but he grows monstrously, advancing until he is joined to the power of angelic strength.” [Col. 0462A]

And again, chapter 18:

“Behemoth is called ‘the beginning of the ways of God,’ because, when he was creating all things, he first created him and made him more eminent than the other angels.”

And again, chapter 12:

“What else is called the tail of this Behemoth except the extremity of the ancient enemy, when he enters his own vessel, that lost man who is specially called Antichrist?”

And again, in the same chapter:

“Then Antichrist, possessing the glory of the world temporarily, surpasses human measures both in the height of honor and in the power of signs. For the spirit in him is one who, having been created among the heights, did not lose the power of his nature even when cast down.” [Col. 0462B]

And again, in the edict addressed to the Roman citizens (Book XI, Letter 3):

“It has come to my attention that certain priests—perverse men, to be sure—have sown among you various things that are wrong and contrary to the holy faith, to the extent that they forbade people to perform any work on the Sabbath. What else should I call them except preachers of Antichrist, who, when he comes, will cause both the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day to be kept from all work? Since he will pretend that he has died and risen again, he wishes the Lord’s Day to be held in veneration; and since he will compel the people to Judaize, restoring the external observance of the Law and subjecting the faithlessness of the Jews to himself, he wishes the Sabbath to be worshiped.”

Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Daniel, confirms from the prophecy of Isaiah that Antichrist will come as far as the summit of the Mount of Olives and will perish there. This will happen, as Catholic teachers commonly say, because, insofar as falsehood can imitate truth, he will resemble Christ our God. Christ, having defeated the prince of darkness, ascended the mountain of light and anointing, and from there, entering the heights of heaven, sent the Holy Spirit, whose anointing teaches us about all things. After this man of perdition has falsely claimed to have risen from the dead, he will be filled with the same ruler of darkness whom Christ had defeated through the triumph of the cross and the victory of the resurrection. He will ascend the Mount of Olives, but he will be killed by the spirit of the mouth of the Lord Jesus and destroyed by the brightness of his coming. [Col. 0462C]

So too Simon Magus, falsely claiming to have risen from the dead and promising that he would ascend to the heavens, was released from the demons who carried him by the prayers and command of the apostles Peter and Paul, and fell upon a stone. And, having yielded at “Aretium” [reading materially uncertain], as the truthful historian Hegesippus wrote in a notably useful history, he died from the breaking of his legs.

The blessed Jerome says of him in his *Commentary on Matthew*:

“Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and they will lead many astray” (Matt. XXIV, 5). “One of these was Simon the Samaritan, whom we read about in the Acts of the Apostles. He said that he was a great power (Acts VIII, 10), and left these statements, among others, written in his books: ‘I am the Word of God; I am the Beautiful One; I am the Paraclete; I am the Almighty; I am all things of God.’ The apostle John also says in his epistle: ‘You have heard that Antichrist is coming; now there are many antichrists’ (I John II, 18).” [Col. 0462D]

Bede says in his *Commentary on Luke*:

“And they will say to you, ‘Look here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There he is’; do not go and do not follow them.” This statement can be understood not only of a time but also of a person. Of a time, indeed, because there have been some who, calculating the courses of the ages, claimed that they had discovered the exact year, day, and hour of the end of the world, contrary to the Lord’s authority: “It is not for you to know times or seasons” (Acts I, 7). Of a person, because many have come and many heretics will come against the Church, asserting that they are christs. The first of these was Simon Magus; the last, and greater than the rest, is Antichrist.

Gregory says in Book XI of the *Moralia*:

“What is added through Daniel—‘He will be broken without a hand’ (Dan. VIII, 25)—is expressed by Paul: ‘The Lord Jesus will kill him with the spirit of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming’ (II Thess. II, 8). He will be broken without a hand because he will be struck with eternal death not by the warfare of angels or by the struggle of the saints, but by the spirit of his mouth alone at the coming of the Judge.” [Col. 0463A]

And again:

“Since we have heard what the head of the wicked is like, let us now recognize which members cling to this head. Whoever is lifted up in pride, whoever is tormented by desires for greed, whoever is dissolved in the pleasures of lust, whoever burns with the scourges of unjust and immoderate anger—what else is each of these than a witness of Antichrist?”

And in Book XXIX, chapter 6:

“Although he did not see the time of Antichrist, Cain was nevertheless a member of Antichrist by his deserts. Judas did not know the savagery of his persecution, yet, persuaded by greed, he succumbed to the power of his cruelty. Simon existed long before the times of Antichrist, yet by perversely seeking the power of miracles he joined himself to his pride. Thus the wicked body is joined to its head, and members to members, when they do not know one another in time yet are joined together by wicked action.

“For Pergamum (Rev. II, 14) had not known Balaam’s books or words, yet, following his wickedness, it heard the voices of heavenly rebuke. There you have those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication.

“Time and place separated the Church of Thyatira from Jezebel’s knowledge and presence; but because she had bound it to herself through the guilt of its life, Jezebel is said to be present in it and to persist in wicked deeds, as the angel testifies when he says: ‘I have this against you, that you allow the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants to commit fornication and to eat food sacrificed to idols’ (Rev. II, 20).

“See how people could be found who followed Jezebel’s corrupt life by their actions. Jezebel is said to have been found there because, clearly, shared conduct makes a wicked body one, even if places or times divide it. Hence it comes about that in its perverse imitators there remains each wicked person who has already passed away, and in its own agents the author of the wicked appears, although he has not yet come.

“Hence John says: ‘Now there are many antichrists’ (I John II), because all the wicked are already his members; by their perverse deeds they have anticipated their head through evil living. Hence Paul says: ‘So that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work’ (II Thess. II). It is as though he said: ‘Then Antichrist will be seen openly; for now he already works secretly in the hearts of the wicked.’” [Col. 0463B]

Concerning his preachers it is written again: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” For none go out except antichrists. Concerning Judas, therefore, the chief member of Antichrist, we read that the devil put it into Judas’s heart to betray him, and after the morsel Satan entered into him, and he went out immediately. He was called the son of perdition, as Antichrist also is.

Judas, an antichrist, betrayed him who is truly called Christ and worshiped as God, who is blessed above all forever. But that other, in his own time, will oppose and exalt himself above everything called God or worshiped, so that he will sit in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God. [Col. 0463C]

Concerning this man—that is, Judas—Saint Augustine says after much else in the book *Hypomnesticon*:

“Such is the cause of all who perish, although the fault is not the same in every case.”

Concerning him and his body, Saint Gregory says in Book XXXIII, chapter 19, of the *Moralia*:

“And he will be cast down in the sight of all” (Job XL, 18). He will be cast down in the sight of all because, when the eternal Judge then appears in terror, with legions of angels standing by, the ministry of the heavenly powers attending, and all the elect brought together for this spectacle, this cruel and powerful beast will be led captive into the midst. Together with his body—that is, with all the reprobate—he will be handed over to the eternal fires of Gehenna, when it is said: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). [Col. 0464A]

Therefore, since he will be a reprobate man and the head of all the reprobate—both of those who, from the beginning of the world until the Lord’s coming, and of those who after the Lord’s coming will belong to his fellowship through unbelief and persistent iniquity—the Predestinarians should place this before themselves and read it again, because Saint Paul, Saint Gregory, and all the other teachers say that this man will be human, and they themselves cannot deny it.

And if he will be human, although filled with the devil as his companion, then, insofar as he is human, though reprobate, he will die in the flesh. “Who,” it says, “is the man who will live and not see death?” The Lord Jesus, as it is written, “will kill him with the spirit of his mouth” (II Thess. II, 8; Ps. LXIV, 3). [Col. 0464B]

And because he will die and rise again, as it is likewise written, “All flesh will come to you,” and “all flesh will see the salvation of God” (Luke III, 6)—which will not happen without the soul in the resurrection—according to the Catholic faith all human beings will rise at his coming with their bodies. If all, then Antichrist also.

And if the death of the Redeemer conferred upon the other reprobates—his members, as we have shown from the teaching of Catholics—the resurrection of the flesh, though not for the honor of life but for the duration of punishment, neither did it deny this to their head. And since by his death he bestowed the resurrection of the flesh upon them, he undoubtedly suffered for them—not because they were redeemed for eternal salvation through the mystery of his passion, for, in accordance with what they were foreknown to be, they will be punished with the due penalty predestined for them because they despised redemption, but, in the manner we have stated, we confess with the Catholics that Christ also suffered for the wicked. [Col. 0464C]

And those for whom he willed to suffer he by no means predestined to death. For since, as God, he could be ignorant of nothing, he was not ignorant that they would perish. Yet they did not perish because they were foreknown by God as destined to perish; rather, because they were going to be such, they were foreknown by God as destined to perish.

They are therefore in error who say that Antichrist, together with his members, was predestined by God for destruction. For God predestines nothing except what was to be done with God himself as its author, or what was to be repaid to evil persons by a just judgment on account of their merits. [Col. 0464D] God merely foreknew what would not have its cause of action from him; he did not predestine it.

Therefore, whoever says that human beings were predestined by God for destruction must go on to say that they perish by predestination—that is, by his operation—just as those predestined for life are saved by predestination, that is, by his operation, as the Apostle testifies: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. II, 13). And again: “He who began it will himself complete it.”

Since faith is the beginning of salvation, it is written concerning it: “To another is given faith,” and the rest, “which one and the same Spirit brings about in all” (I Cor. XII, 9–11). Again it is written: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 29–30). [Col. 0465A]

And again: “He chose us before the ages, predestining us”—that is, preparing us—“to be holy and without blemish” (Eph. I, 4).

From this it is known that whoever, as this conditional definition demonstrates, says—or strives by whispering insinuations to imply—that Antichrist or any of the reprobate has from God the cause of his destruction, or perishes through his operation, is not a Catholic but a madman; and if he prefers to persist incorrigibly, he should be driven even from the conversation of the faithful.

For God is an avenger, not the author of evil, and he does not will iniquity, as it is written (Ps. V, 5). To all who are saved he is the cause of salvation; to no one is he the cause of destruction, since he wills all to be saved and wills no one to perish. [Col. 0465B]

Those who despise the will of the Lord when it invites them will experience the will of the Lord when it avenges, because he removes from no one the way of correction, nor deprives anyone of the possibility of good. But the person who turns away from him has himself deprived himself—not God—of willing and being able to do what is good.

It does not therefore follow that, when God has not given certain people repentance, he has taken away their amendment; or that, when he has not raised them up, he has cast them down. For one thing is to lead an innocent person into a crime by which punishment is reached—something foreign to God—and another is not to grant forgiveness to a criminal, which arises from the sinner’s merit and is exacted by the judgment of the just Judge as a retribution of justice. [Col. 0465C]

For if we say that Christ brought remedies only to those who were redeemed, we will seem to absolve the unredeemed, who are known to be punished for despising redemption. For if, as the blessed Gregory writes in his thirty-fifth homily, the death of the righteous is help to the good but testimony against the wicked—so that the wicked perish without excuse through the very means from which the elect receive an example by which to live—then much more must the death of our Redeemer, who died for all, be believed to be salvation for believers and the devoted, but testimony of condemnation for unbelievers and despisers.

We must therefore follow what Prosper says most correctly in *Against the Gauls*:

“Since the blood of Christ is the redemption of the whole world, those who are outside that price are those who either, delighted by captivity, did not wish to be redeemed, or, after redemption, returned to the same slavery. Christ therefore suffered for all, although not all have been redeemed through the mystery of his passion.” [Col. 0465D]

Because, however, the Savior’s death specifically benefited believers for salvation, while the grace of his passion, despised by unbelievers, became for them judgment and condemnation, Saint Hilary says in his exposition of Psalm 55:

“These peoples will be led down in anger, for whom the salvation of resurrection has been established for the experience of punishment. From this anger the Apostle promises that we will be rescued, saying: ‘If, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, having been justified by his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath’ (Rom. V, 9). He therefore died for sinners for the salvation of resurrection; but he will save those sanctified in his blood from wrath.” [Col. 0466A]

Saint Augustine says in Book XX, chapter 26, of *The City of God*:

“For all the dead, one living person died—one who had no sin at all—so that those who live through the remission of sins might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for all because of our sins and rose again because of our justification. Thus, believing in him who justifies the ungodly, we may be justified from ungodliness and, as though brought to life from death, belong to the first resurrection, which is now. For only those who will be blessed forever belong to this first resurrection; to the second, of which he spoke immediately afterward, he will teach that both the blessed and the wretched belong. This is the resurrection of mercy; that is the resurrection of judgment. Therefore it is written in the psalm: ‘I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord’ (Ps. C, 1).” [Col. 0466B]

Ambrose says in his Epistle to the Corinthians:

“For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (I Cor. XV, 22): “Therefore he acquired life—that is, resurrection—for all who are from his body, although he granted resurrection generally.”

And again in the same epistle:

“For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing” (I Cor. I, 18): “It is clear that those for whom the cross of Christ is foolishness are in perdition, for they have not been rescued from infernal death. But for those who are being saved it is the power of God. It is not obscure: for those who believe, the power of God is the cross. They believe that the cross of Christ is not weakness but power, understanding that death was conquered on the cross. Those who bear its sign are saved, because they cannot be held by that death.” [Col. 0466C]

Bede, in his commentary on Luke, on the words “It will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke XIV, 14), says:
