“He calls it the resurrection of the righteous because, although all rise again, it is not improperly called their own, since they do not doubt that they will be blessed in this resurrection.”

Prosper says in the ninth disputation of *Against the Gauls*:

“The Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world, and the world did not wish to be redeemed, because the darkness did not receive the light. Yet the darkness received it, to which the Apostle says: ‘You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord’ (Eph. V, 8). And the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life’ (John III, 16). And: ‘This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil’ (ibid., 19).

“Hence it is established that Christ suffered for all, but gives salvation to believers.”

Finally, let us consider with what distinction the orthodox understood from Scripture and the teachers taught that Christ suffered for all, although not all are redeemed for eternal salvation through the mystery of his Passion. Peter says:

> “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some consider slowness, but he waits for you, not wishing anyone to perish, but all to return to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).

And Paul says:

> “He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32).

And:

> “If one died for all, therefore all died; and he died for all” (2 Corinthians 5:14), “who gave himself as a redemption for all” (1 Timothy 2:6).

And:

> “By the grace of God he tasted death for all” (Hebrews 2:9).

For, as Isaiah says:

> “We all went astray like sheep; each one turned to his own way, and the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

But that not all were redeemed through the mystery of his Passion, although he suffered for all, he makes clear again through Isaiah, saying:

> “By his knowledge he himself will justify his many servants” (Isaiah 53:11).

And again:

> “He himself bore the sins of many” (ibid.).

And again:

> “This one will sprinkle many nations” (Isaiah 52:15).

And in the Gospel:

> “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Matthew 20:28).

And the Apostle:

> “Through the obedience of one, many will be constituted righteous” (Romans 5:19).

And again:

> “So that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29).

And again:

> “He who had brought many sons into glory” (Hebrews 2:10).

And again:

> “Christ suffered to take away the sins of many” (Hebrews 9:28).

And again:

> “Christ loved the Church and handed himself over for her” (Ephesians 5:25).

In each of these statements it must be understood that “for many,” rather than “for all,” is said because not all believed, as we shall demonstrate below through the words of the Fathers. Matthew, Mark, and Luke likewise say that the Lord and Savior declared—not “for all,” but “for many” and “for you”—that his body would be handed over and his blood poured out, because although Christ suffered for all, not all were redeemed through the mystery of his Passion.

And because not all for whom he suffered are redeemed, this concerns the part belonging to unbelievers, not the power of the price, since the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world. For, after the coming in the flesh of this same Mediator between God and human beings, those who do not believe in him, Jesus—as the Catholic Church holds and teaches him to be the Savior of the world—were not saved, are not saved, and will not be saved; nor will those be saved who confess him with their words but deny him by their deeds, because they do not believe with the faith that works through love. For even the demons believe and tremble. Scripture says:

> “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18),

because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.

And James says:

> “What benefit is it, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? Surely faith cannot save him?” (James 2:14).

And the Lord says:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father” (Matthew 7:21).

Likewise, those who did not believe in him before his coming in the flesh—that is, in Jesus, the blessed King of Israel who was to come in the name of the Lord to save the nations—or who, although possessing a form of godliness, denied its power by their deeds, perished through persistent unbelief and iniquity.

Therefore, in addition to the passages given above, blessed Augustine says in the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (chapter 11):

> “The male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day—his soul shall perish from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Genesis 17:14). Let this man say, if he can, how that eight-day-old child broke God’s covenant, since, so far as he himself is concerned, he was an innocent infant. Yet God or Holy Scripture would in no way say this falsely. He therefore broke God’s covenant—not the covenant concerning the commanded circumcision, but the one concerning the prohibition of the tree—when through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Romans 5:12). This was signified as being cleansed by the circumcision of the eighth day, that is, by the sacrament of the Mediator who was to come in the flesh. For by the same faith in Christ, who was to come in the flesh, die for us, and rise on the third day—which was to be the eighth day after the seventh day, the Sabbath—the ancient righteous were also saved. For he was handed over because of our offenses and rose because of our justification.

> Once circumcision was instituted among the people of God, as it was then the seal of the righteousness of faith (Romans 4:11), it served to signify the cleansing of infants from original and ancient sin, just as baptism began from its institution to serve for the renewal of the human being. This does not mean that before circumcision there was no righteousness of faith. For while he was still uncircumcised, Abraham himself was justified by faith, the father of the nations that were to follow his faith. But in earlier times the sacrament of justification by faith remained entirely hidden.

> Nevertheless, the same faith in the Mediator made the ancient righteous—little and great—safe: not the Old Testament, which gives birth to slavery (Galatians 4:24); not the law, which was not given in such a way that it could give life (ibid. 3:21); but the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Romans 7:25). For just as we believe that Christ came in the flesh, so they believed that he would come; just as we believe that he died, so they believed that he would die; just as we believe that he rose, so they believed that he would rise; and both we and they believe that he will come to judge the dead and the living.

> Therefore this man, by wrongly defending human nature, does not prevent it from being saved, because we are all born under sin and are freed through the one who alone was born without sin,”

namely, through the faith that works through love, in those who believe both before and after the Lord’s coming, and who will believe from that time until the end of the age.

But those who have not wished, do not wish, and will not wish to believe with this same faith have themselves been, are, and will be the cause of their death. For, as Prosper says (*Response to the Objections of Vincent*, response 1):

> “The cup of immortality, prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed contain what can benefit everyone; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.”

This Catholicly discriminating understanding—that Christ Jesus our Lord suffered for all, although not all are redeemed through the mystery of his Passion—is also demonstrated by blessed Ambrose, who says in his *Letter to the Corinthians* (chapter 5):

> “If one died for all, therefore all died” (2 Corinthians 5:15). Since Christ, loving the human race, gave himself over to death in order to redeem them; and since, because of Adam, all must die, Christ died for all, so that he might free them from the second death.

And in the First Epistle (chapter 11):

> “They are guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” For he was killed on behalf of those who nullify his benefit.

And in his *Epistle to the Romans*:

> “As through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one righteousness came justification of life upon all human beings” (Romans 5:16). That is, just as through the offense of one all human beings, sinning in the same way, deserved condemnation, so through the righteousness of one all are justified who believe. But if anyone thinks that this condemnation is universal, he will likewise receive a universal justification. This is not true, because not all believe.

Saint Jerome held this view, saying in his *Exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians*:

> “This must be judged possible in the Son of God: by his blood he cleanses not one city but the entire world.”

And in his commentary on Matthew:

> “He alone prays for all, just as he alone suffers for all.”

And again in the same work:

> “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Matthew 20:28). He did not say “for all,” but “for many,” that is, for those who wished to believe.

And Bede, in the thirteenth homily on the Gospel:

> “Baptizing in the Holy Spirit”—that is, Christ—is capable of taking away the sins not only of Israel but also of the whole world, if it wishes to believe in him.

Saint Hilary understood it in this way, saying in his *Exposition of Psalm 118*:

> “Then the human race, which does not believe and does not proceed along the Gospel way, will be reproached with what is contained in the psalm: ‘What benefit is there in my blood, while I descend into corruption?’ For he reproaches the proud and the accursed: why did they think that there was no benefit for them in the sacrament of his blood and death, when he was born, suffered, and died for our sake?”

Saint John Chrysostom likewise held and taught this, saying in his *Epistle to the Hebrews* that:

> “By the grace of God he tasted death for all,” not only for the faithful but for the entire world. And therefore it is said, “to take away the sins of many.” He indeed died for all. But what if not all believe? He fulfilled what belonged to him.

And in the second homily on the evangelist Matthew:

> “This,” he says, “the prophet Isaiah announces beforehand to you. For, proclaiming his Passion and his very great and most pious care for the whole world, he marveled,”

and so forth.

And again in the fourth homily:

> “He did not say, ‘She will give birth to you,’ but placed that word in the middle and suspended it. For she did not give birth to Christ for him, but for the entire world.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Through him he declares that good things are to be bestowed upon the whole world.”

And again in the fifteenth homily:

> “‘You are the salt of the earth’ (Matthew 5:13). By this he shows how necessary these instructions are. For this teaching,” he says, “is entrusted to you not only for your own salvation but for the entire world. I do not send you to two cities, or ten, or twenty, nor to one nation, as he sent the prophets, but to the whole earth and sea, to the entire world, oppressed by various crimes.”

And because not all are saved to whom the word of salvation has been sent, nor are all redeemed through the mystery of his Passion, although he underwent the Passion of the cross for all, salvation having been prepared for all, the same Catholic teacher says in the seventh homily on the same evangelist:

> “Not all who are from Israel are Israelites, but those who have been born through faith in the promise. If he does not rule over all, the fault belongs to those who were called, not to the one who called.”

And again:

> “Paul certainly says this too: ‘It was necessary that the word of God be announced to you first; but since you judged yourselves unworthy, we turn to the Gentiles’” (Acts 13:46). “Although they had previously remained unbelieving, after they had also heard of him from the Magi, they ought immediately to have hastened to Christ. But they did not wish to, and therefore, while these slept, those others came to him.”

And again in the sixth homily:

> “Why,” he says, “did he not reveal this to all the Magi? Because, evidently, not all would have believed.”

And again in the tenth homily:

> “Therefore he added, ‘as a testimony to all the nations’ (Matthew 24:14), showing that he would not wait for all to believe first and then come, as he had foretold. For what he says, ‘as a testimony to all the nations,’ means ‘as an accusation and refutation of those who refused to believe the Gospel.’”

Saint Augustine preached in this way in his book *On Rebuke and Grace* (chapter 16):

> “Who loved the weak more than he who became weak for all and was crucified in weakness for all?”

And in the sixth book *Against Julian* (chapter 5):

> “They are freed from sin for whom he died who had never been in sin. Although he died once, he dies for each person at the time when that person, whatever his age, is baptized into his death. That is, his death benefits the one who was in sin when, baptized into his death, that person himself dies to sin.”

Thus the roar of the great Leo—namely, the pope of the Roman city, which is the head of all the churches and of the whole world—resounds throughout the entire world, as we stated above (*Epistle* 97, chapter 2):

> “The outpouring of Christ’s blood, the righteous one for the unrighteous, was so rich as a price that, if the whole company of captives believed in their Redeemer, no one would be held by the devil’s bonds.”

Saint Gregory likewise held and preached this. In the fourteenth book of the *Moralia* (chapter 22), he says:

> “‘Fools despised me’ (Job 19:18). As though it were plainly said: They themselves also despised me, for whose healing I assumed the foolishness of preaching—that is, so that they might be healed through the flesh of the Word—and I was despised by those for whom I was not afraid to be considered foolish.”

And in his homily on the prophet Ezekiel:

> “For the life of the elect, the author of life handed himself over even unto death.”

And in the twentieth homily on the Gospel:

> “John the Baptist came to preach the one who was coming to save some from Judea and many from the Gentiles.”

And in the twentieth book of the *Moralia*:

> “The Redeemer offered to suffering the body which he had assumed for the elect.”

And again:

> “The Lord intercedes for us, not by voice but by mercy, because, by assuming what he did not wish to be condemned in the elect, he set it free.”

And in the twenty-fourth book of the *Moralia* (chapter 11):

> “Since, therefore, the Lord was truly born, truly died, and truly rose again, yet in all things differs from us by the greatness of his power, while he agrees with us only in the truth of his nature, it is rightly said that for our sake this angel speaks of one among those who are like him (Job 33:23). For although in all his works he surpasses us by immeasurable power, in one respect—that is, in the variety of form—he does not differ from us. Through this he speaks to the Father for us: he shows himself like us. For his speaking or interceding consists in demonstrating that he himself became human for all.”

How we may understand more clearly what is meant by his demonstrating himself to be “for all,” evangelical truth shows when it says:

> “So that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:15);

but:

> “Whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16),

as that teacher says in the thirty-sixth book of the *Moralia*:

> “But all the wicked are punished with eternal punishment, indeed punished for their own iniquity, and yet they are burned for a purpose: namely, so that all the righteous may see in God the joys they receive and behold in these people the punishments which they escaped.”

The venerable presbyter Bede also understood and held this discriminating understanding of redemption through the blood of Christ, which must be understood and maintained with the Catholic teachers cited above. In his exposition of Luke’s Gospel he says:

> “His sweat became like drops of blood falling upon the earth” (Luke 22:44), so that by his innocent death he might raise to heavenly life the whole wide world, dead in sins.

And again:

> “He is clothed in a white garment, giving an indication of his immaculate Passion, because the immaculate Lamb of God was to take away the sins of the whole world.”

And:

> “When he had touched his ear, he healed him” (ibid., 51), mystically teaching that even those who have been wounded by their agreement with his death can be healed if they turn back.

And again:

> “After they came to the place called Calvary, there they crucified him” (Luke 23:33). The Lord was crucified there so that, where previously there had been the ark of the condemned, the banners of martyrdom might be raised. And just as for our sake he became a curse of the cross, was scourged, and was crucified, so for the salvation of all he is crucified as though guilty among the guilty, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound still more.

And again:

> “Whether they wish it or not, the Jews, the entire kingdom of the world, all worldly wisdom, and all the mysteries of divine law testify that Jesus is King of the Jews—that is, the ruler of those who believe and confess God.”

And again:

> “When the disciples were preparing the Passover, a man carrying a jar of water appropriately met them, so that it might be shown that the mystery of this Passover was to be celebrated for the complete absolution of the whole world.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The names of both the water-carrier and the master of the house have deliberately been omitted, so that an opportunity might be indicated for all who wish to celebrate the Passover—that is, to be instructed in Christ’s sacraments and to receive Christ as a guest in the lodging of their minds.”

Cassiodorus likewise understood and held this, saying on Psalm 149:

> “‘Praise him in the firmament of his power.’ The firmness of his power is this: by undertaking destruction for the salvation of all, he overcame death itself, together with its most wicked author, through the power of his might.”

And on Psalm 142:

> “No one sought his life, while no consolation was offered him; but he alone was left to the Passion, he who was to die for the salvation of all.”

And again:

> “For if that wondrous summit of his divinity had not inclined itself through the reality of the body he assumed, how could he have been crucified for the salvation of all?”

And on Psalm 110:

> “He proclaimed to his people”—that is, to the Christian people whom he redeemed with his precious blood—“the power of his works.”

And on Psalm 129:

> “With him there is abundant redemption,” so that that precious blood was so exceedingly rich in abundance that it might redeem the sins of the whole world and, as if by a salutary flood, cleanse the earth from its stains.

And again on Psalm 147:

> “What measure could there be to that joy: to behold the Lord of all things, who is believed to have died here for the salvation of everyone?”

And on Psalm 118:

> “‘Judge my judgment and redeem me.’ Whom could he redeem except one who believes? Or for whom would he pour out the blood of redemption most especially, if he had not been a faithful servant?” He added:

> “‘Give me life according to your word’—namely, the word in which he promises: ‘Whoever believes in me will not die, but will have eternal life.’”

The same applies to the prophet’s complaint to the Lord concerning certain people:

> “‘You struck them,’ he says, ‘and they refused to accept correction’” (Jeremiah 5:3);

and:

> “‘We healed Babylon, but she was not healed’” (Jeremiah 51:9).

And the Lord says:

> “I killed and destroyed the righteous people, yet they did not turn back from their ways” (Jeremiah 15:7).

And again:

> “The people did not return to the one who struck them” (Isaiah 9:13).

And:

> “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it” (John 1:5);

and the Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world, but the world did not wish to be redeemed.

And again it is written:

> “Do not fear, poor one, shaken by the storm, because in the furnace of poverty I refined you” (Isaiah 54:11).

And again:

> “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem and call to her,”

until it says:

> “She has received double from the hand of the Lord for all her sins” (ibid. 40:2).

And again it is written:

> “The bruise of a wound wipes away evil, and blows reach the innermost parts of the belly” (Proverbs 20:30).

And the Apostle says:

> “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8),

because the darkness, receiving the light, was illumined, and those who believed were redeemed for salvation by the price of the world.

Prosper, acting under the authority of the Apostolic See, likewise demonstrates this Catholic understanding against the Gauls in the ninth recapitulation:

> “Whoever says that the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world is considering not the power of the sacrament but the part belonging to unbelievers, since the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world.”

The holy Apostolic See itself retains this teaching in the secret rites of the heavenly mysteries, according to the tradition of the apostles, saying:

> “May this offering, we beseech you, Lord, cleanse our offenses: offered upon the altar of the cross, it bore away the offense of the whole world.”

And again:

> “Grant us, Lord, that this offering may benefit the soul of your servant Leo, by offering which you granted remission of the sins of the whole world.”

And:

> “Look, almighty and merciful God, upon this family of yours, for whom our Lord Jesus Christ did not hesitate to be handed over into the hands of the guilty and to undergo the torment of the cross.”

Therefore, as blessed Celestine writes to Venerius and the Gallican bishops:

> “The law of praying should establish the law of believing.”

And again Prosper, in the first book of *The Calling of the Nations* (chapter 20):

> “Thus, as regards the blindness of the human race, contracted through a long night of ignorance and pride, the Creator of the world came into the world, and the world did not know him” (John 1:10); “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it” (ibid., 5). “The one who is above all testifies to what he has seen and heard, and no one accepts his testimony” (John 3:31–32). But because God the Son did not come into the world in vain, and gave himself for all and died for all—not only for one nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who had been scattered (John 11:52)—he says to everyone: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matthew 11:28).

> While reserving to himself the inscrutable freedom of election, he gives knowledge of himself and of his Father to those to whom he wishes to reveal it. All the children of light, children of promise, children of Abraham, children of God, an elect race, a royal priesthood, true Israelites, foreknown and predestined for the kingdom of God by the one who called them—not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles (Romans 9:24)—receive the testimony of the one who came from heaven, “sealing” that God is truthful; that is, clearly signifying in their salvation that God is truthful, fulfilling and completing what he promised to Abraham, the father of all nations.

> When God promised that he would be heir of the world, Abraham did not waver through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God and being fully convinced that what God had promised, he was able also to accomplish (Romans 4:20–21).

And again, against the Vincentians and the Gauls (response 1):

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ, free from the debt of death and alone without sin, died for sinners and for those indebted to death. Therefore, as regards the greatness and power of the price, and as regards the one cause shared by the human race, the blood of Christ is the redemption of the whole world.”

(*Against the Gallican Chapters*, the sentence cited above, section 9.)

Those who are strangers to this price are the ones who either, delighted by their captivity, refused to be redeemed, or, after redemption, persistently returned to the same slavery. May he deign to rescue us from that captivity and from the eternal punishments owed to and prepared for that slavery by the just Judge, and to protect and preserve us unharmed—he who by the blood of that Mediator and our Redeemer rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.

To whom, with him, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, be honor, glory, and dominion, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0473]

## 413. Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims: A Collection from Holy Scripture and the Sayings of the Orthodox Concerning One Deity and Not a Threefold Deity—That Is, the Unity of the Holy and Inseparable Trinity

To repel the blasphemies of Gottschalk and refute his ravings.

[Note: Flodoard, book 3 of the *History of Rheims*, chapter 15: “Moreover, Hincmar wrote a book compiled from the sayings of the orthodox Fathers, addressed to the sons of his Church, stating that the deity of the divine Trinity should not be called threefold, since it is the supreme unity of the Trinity, in order to repel the blasphemies of Gottschalk.”]

## Prologue

[Col. 0473C] Hincmar, in name though not in merit bishop of Rheims, and servant of the people of God, to the beloved sons of the Catholic Church and our fellow ministers.

It is a long time since certain people, taking an opportunity from the ending of a hymn whose author is entirely unknown, in which it says:

> “We beseech you, threefold and one Deity,”

began, delighting in novel expressions and striving to make themselves known, to argue that just as God is threefold and one, so “threefold Deity” and “one Deity” both ought to be said and can properly be said in Catholic usage. Accordingly, various people have written according to their limited abilities.

Among them was Ratramnus, a monk of the monastery of Corbie. Drawing passages from the books of blessed Hilary and Augustine, mutilating their statements and twisting them incongruously toward his own perverse meaning—as we read that Macarius, bishop of Antioch, did with many Catholic books at the Sixth Synod—he compiled from this material a volume of considerable size for Hildegarius, bishop of Meaux. Anyone who reads it will clearly see that the collection itself, when compared with authoritative writings, exposes and refutes its author’s perverse understanding as a falsehood.

When Gottschalk heard this—he was a pseudomonk of the Orbaise monastery belonging to the Church of Rheims—he was motivated both by his envy of me, whom he had heard had forbidden the singing of “threefold deity” in the Church, and by his customary disposition. From the beginning of his defective character he had delighted in devising and proclaiming novelties, things previously unheard of and contrary to the ancient understanding of the orthodox, and he remained committed to this pursuit. He therefore arranged to write many things on the subject and send them to as many people as he could: first secretly, and afterward openly, as far as he was able.

Most recently, in these days, he composed the following attached document, which came to us through his accomplices and agents. In accordance with your good desires, it pleased me to include it intact in this work and afterward answer each point with Catholic authorities. Thus, once his own propositions on this matter have been slain by the mouths of Catholics—by the spiritual sword, as it were—the deceitful lips of the others who follow his opinion may be silenced, and, with the Lord’s help, every iniquity may close its mouth.

The words of blessed Gregory from his *Homily on the Gospel* (homily 8) were proposed to me:

> “What does it mean,” he says, “that an angel appears to shepherds who are keeping watch, and that the glory of God shines around them, except that those who are diligently placed over faithful flocks deserve, more than others, to see sublime things? While they themselves watch piously over the flock, divine grace shines more abundantly upon them.”

And he explains from the *Song of Songs*:

> “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon” (Song of Songs 7:4),

because the discernment of those set over others must be fortified by vigilance and must stand upon the height of life: it must not lie in the valley of weak conduct; it must see the attacks of evil spirits from far away; and through its foresight it must make the souls entrusted to it cautious. Thus, in accordance with blessed Peter’s words, we may sanctify the Lord Jesus Christ in our hearts and always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason concerning the hope that is in us (1 Peter 3:15).

Therefore, through the divine favor, I have been assigned this ministry despite my unworthiness. I have been invited—and indeed compelled—not only by your requests but also by this responsibility and concern. To the extent that the Deity itself, which is the unity of the Trinity, grants me ability, and to the extent that my many occupations, together with the obstinacy and sluggishness of my mind, permit, I shall undertake to carry out what you ask.

I shall place in this little work Gottschalk’s documents in their entirety. Beside each of his propositions, following the practice of the ancients, we shall place an obelus (÷), that is, a reclining stroke, so that, as with a spear, it may pierce his false statements. But beside those statements which are set against his propositions from the sayings of the orthodox, we shall place the figure ΧΡ, called *chresimon*, so that by it the Catholic testimonies that resist his poisonous opinions may be indicated, and a sound and truly Christian understanding—handed down, as is fitting, by Christ against antichrists—may be clearly shown to simple and devout minds.

Along with the other pestilential, or rather deadly, poisons that Gottschalk proposes for those who cannot endure sound doctrine, who delight in novel expressions, and who have itching ears—people who, according to their own desires, hasten to heap up teachers for themselves, so that they may finally become teachers of error, having refused to become disciples of truth—he thinks and speaks iniquity on high, sets his mouth against heaven, and says the following:

## Gottschalk’s Document: That One May Speak of a Threefold Deity

[Col. 0475]

[Col. 0475C] “Whoever it is who says that the Godhead cannot in any way be called threefold in a catholic manner, but that there is only one Godhead, ought to be carefully asked how he calls it one, or in what sense—namely, whether naturally or personally. If he answers and says that one Godhead is to be believed and confessed personally, unless he quickly corrects his own opinion, he truly deserves to hear, together with Sabellius, the anathema pronounced here and now, and deserves also to suffer it perpetually by right. For this reason the heretics were called and named Sabellians, and also Patripassians, because they neither wished nor were altogether able to deny that God the Father suffered, since they imagined God to be one personally—not as the holy catholic and apostolic Church believes and confesses God to be one naturally [Col. 0476C] and three personally.

“But if, fearing to be properly struck by the anathema and to suffer that punishment with the Patripassians, he says that the Godhead is one naturally, he must consequently believe and confess, if indeed he wishes to merit pardon, that it is altogether three personally [Col. 0476D], just as it is unquestionably established that God, one naturally, is three personally. Accordingly, just as in hymns and in the books of the holy Fathers, where ‘threefold and one God’ is said, it cannot be changed to ‘holy and one God,’ so likewise it cannot be changed without mortal peril where ‘threefold and one Godhead’ is said, so that ‘holy and one Godhead’ might be said there. Indeed, this cannot at all be done even where ‘Godhead’ alone is said, without the addition ‘and one,’ but only ‘threefold Godhead’ [Col. 0477A]; much less can it be done where ‘threefold and one Godhead’ is said. For then it would immediately be said to the simple—as indeed it is said: ‘See, it is now clear that the Godhead could not and cannot truly be called threefold, but only one.’

“But surely now the time has come for those who believe and say that the Godhead cannot authoritatively or truly be called threefold to look and read in the book concerning the holy Synod, which was written in Greek at Constantinople under the younger Constantine, that the Arians who worshipped τριθεοτείας—that is, ‘three godheads’—were rightly condemned and anathematized by one hundred and fifty Fathers. Yet in that very volume it is subsequently contained, in Constantine’s edict, that the threefold Godhead is to be glorified; and it was not necessary to add ‘one’ there, because, when ‘threefold Godhead’ is said under a singular number, ‘one’ is nevertheless understood at the same time, although it is not stated.

“Thus Prosper loved the expression ‘threefold majesty,’ Prudentius ‘threefold piety,’ and Arator ‘threefold power’ twice over; likewise, among the Greeks, τρισάγιον, and among the Latins, quite properly, regularly, and catholically, ‘threefold holiness’ is said. Accordingly, just as τριθεοτεία is said by them in a thoroughly catholic manner, so by us ‘threefold Godhead’ is said in a thoroughly catholic manner. Nevertheless, both they and the Latins, by equal agreement, have condemned and do condemn, anathematized and do anathematize, the Arians, who worship three majesties, three pieties, three powers, three gods, and three godheads.

“Likewise, it is established and clear—if not even more so—that the Sabellians, likewise called Patripassians, are rightly condemned and must be condemned. They worship, after the Jewish poverty of understanding, a majesty, piety, power, holiness, and godhead that is singularly solitary and personally one. For the Father alone is God in such a way that he is not from God but has begotten God; the Son alone is God in such a way that he has been begotten by God; and the Holy Spirit alone is God in such a way that he proceeds from God, both unbegotten and begotten. It is therefore entirely clear that God is one naturally and three personally.

“Likewise, while God the Father is an unbegotten, unborn, and unoriginated Godhead; God the Son a begotten, born, and originated Godhead; and God the Holy Spirit is a Godhead neither unbegotten, unborn, and unoriginated, nor begotten, born, and originated, [Col. 0477D] but proceeding from the unbegotten, unborn, and unoriginated Godhead and from the begotten, born, and originated Godhead—it is entirely clear that ἁγία τριὰς, that is, ‘holy Trinity,’ just as it is one essentially and naturally, is without doubt a threefold Godhead personally. Thus majesty, piety, and power are altogether one and three, because each person separately is the first power, as is clearly said of God the Son of God in the prophet Micah: ‘And you, tower of the flock, misty daughter of Jerusalem, to you shall come, and to you shall come the first power’ (Mic. IV, 8).

“Therefore, because the Father is not greater than the Son, nor the Son greater than the Holy Spirit, but all three persons are entirely equal and coeternal with one another, God the Trinity is therefore truly the first power. Accordingly, not, God forbid, three powers as the Arians teach, nor, God forbid, a power personally one as the Sabellians dream, but, according to the catholics, power is one naturally and three personally.

“It remains, therefore, and it follows, that those who are grammarians, if they do not wish to be heretics as well, should not presume to confess in the Church of the true God, the real God, that τριθεοτεία, that is, ‘threefold Godhead,’ exists in any way as a plural number, since it is plainly singular—as all who have even moderate knowledge of grammatical art understand. For just as God the Trinity is singular in number according to the words, ‘Blessed be the holy Trinity,’ so τριθεοτεία, ‘threefold Godhead,’ is also singular in number; whereas, by contrast, the plural-number form τριθεοτείας, that is, ‘three godheads,’ is clearly that of the Arians, who have rightly been condemned by catholics.

“Therefore, rightly, under the singular number, we humbly and suitably say to the threefold and one Godhead:

> We beseech you, threefold and one Godhead,  
> That you wash away our sins and remove what is harmful,  
> Give peace to your servants, and also give us glory  
> Throughout all the ages. Amen.

“For we do not say, as the Arians do, ‘You three godheads, we beseech you to wash away our sins, remove what is harmful, give peace to us, and also give us glory to you.’ O Godhead, keep watch—you who are called, believed, affirmed, recognized, and proved to be threefold and one; come to the aid of your own needy servants in all things.

“Let him to whom the threefold and one Godhead, always to be adored, cultivated, and feared, gives what his piety inspires and grants to be inserted here, attend to this, weigh it, and ponder it in his mind. Namely, just as every catholic believes and confesses each person of the Trinity to be wholly, fully, and perfectly God, so let him believe, confess, and affirm that each person possesses his own proper Godhead, wholly, fully, and perfectly; and let him thereafter, according to the abilities given and to be given by God, convict all who contradict this.

“For it is clearer than daylight and brighter than the sun that each person possesses his own proper godhead and divinity. For it was certainly not the whole Trinity, God forbid, that assumed humanity in any way, but only the Godhead of the Son [Col. 0478D]. This is the ever-unconquered and victorious truth of catholic faith concerning the threefold and one Godhead.

“Thus, as it was before the ages, so throughout the ages and unto the ages, blessed be the threefold and one Godhead, majesty, power, piety, truth, and charity; and thus may praise, glory, and brightness always belong to it alone. Amen.

“Grant, O true and living God, one naturally and three personally, that your chosen may clearly believe, understand, confess, and affirm that, just as you, God—whose name is interpreted as ‘fear’—and you, God—whose name is interpreted as ‘love’—when you are called personally threefold fear and threefold love, are not, God forbid, three fears and three loves naturally, but naturally one fear and one love, so likewise, when you are called τριθεοτεία, ‘threefold Godhead,’ and ‘threefold charity,’ you are not, God forbid, three godheads and three charities naturally, but naturally one Godhead and only one charity.

“This we can plainly prove through the preacher of truth and teacher of the nations in faith and truth, who said most truly: ‘We can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth’ (II Cor. XIII, 8). For when we are baptized—that is, dipped—we are unquestionably plunged three times; yet for that reason the threefold plunging and the threefold baptism, that is, the threefold dipping, are not, God forbid, three plungings, three dippings, or three baptisms, but there is generally one plunging and one dipping, that is, one baptism, as the Apostle says: ‘One Lord, one faith, one baptism’ (Eph. IV, 5).

“Likewise, when ‘threefold’ or ‘ternary faith’ is said, as in the words of your faithful poet Sedulius:

> ‘This man embraces a threefold faith, but that one does not embrace one,’

there are not, God forbid, three faiths, but one faith, as the Apostle says: ‘One faith.’

“Therefore, those who do not wish to have eternal fellowship with the heretics, the Sabellians, should, as catholics with catholics, believe, confess, worship, and sing τριθεοτείαν, ‘threefold Godhead’; τρισάγιον, ‘threefold holiness’; threefold life, wisdom, glory, fear, love, charity, light, salvation, virtue, peace, brightness; and threefold majesty, power, and piety. For we must also embrace a ternary or threefold faith, which the perverse Sabellians deny through their faithless impiety.

“That all things are as I have said can be plainly proved by only two nouns of the singular number, namely, ‘light’ and ‘peace.’ For unbegotten light and peace, begotten light and peace, and proceeding light and peace are not permitted by grammatical art to be called three lights or three peaces in the plural; nor are they three naturally, as the Arian heresy barks; nor personally one, as the Sabellian heresy dreams. Rather, unquestionably, light and peace are one naturally and three personally, as one who embraces the threefold and one faith, and therefore believes, confesses, worships, and sings the threefold and one light and peace, majesty, power, piety, and threefold and one Godhead.

“But the great, holy, catholic Church believes and confesses one and threefold God, to whom the grace of God has been freely given, is given, and will be given; and therefore, in return, praise, honor, and glory are rightly and humbly given, are given, and will be given by it to the threefold and one Godhead, both throughout the ages and together unto the ages. Amen.

“According to that saying: ‘They give me wisdom; I shall give glory.’ Amen.

“Let the person full of virtues come unwillingly to rule; let the person empty of virtues approach even if compelled.”

ΧΡ. Up to this point the words belong to the heresy; from here onward begin the words of Gothescalcus himself.

The devil, splitting himself away from the unity of charity, devised the deadly poison of this heresy—namely, the idolatry of a mother in which many gods, indeed demons, are worshipped in images—by wrongly interpreting, as is his custom, the words of God: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 16). Through the envy by which death entered the world, he offered this poison to the first human beings in the sap of the fruit of the forbidden tree, saying: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. III, 5).

Yet God, who is the holy Trinity, as Athanasius shows in his book on the proper Persons and on the united name of the Godhead, and as Hilary and Ambrose show in their books on the Faith, and Augustine in his books on the Trinity, said at the creation of the first human being: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” By saying “in the image and likeness” in the singular number, he showed that the nature—that is, the Godhead—in whose image man was to be made was not threefold but one. The holy Trinity, one God, made him in its own image, as Sacred Scripture plainly demonstrates.

But by saying in the plural, “Let us make” and “our,” he showed that the God in whose image man was being made was not one person but three persons.

Likewise, when the Lord had said in the Gospel, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30), that same devil, speaking through vessels suited to him, taught through Sabellius a union in the Trinity of persons; in the word “are,” he closed the eyes of the mind against it. Through Arius he divided the substance of the one Godhead; and, lying to him as to the first human beings, he opened his eyes to knowledge of evil and closed them to knowledge of good and truth in the word “one,” lest there be a distinction of power.

Inspired by him, Gothescalcus, following Arius in his understanding—although he detests him verbally—after the discovery of the punishment for that monstrous crime, so clearly and justly manifested in Arius himself, does not fear to teach a threefold Godhead.

Against these men—namely, Arius and Gothescalcus, the son not merely of Arius but of the devil himself—blessed Ambrose, inspired by the Holy Spirit, explains the Apostle in his book On the Holy Spirit (ch. 13): “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the charity of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (II Cor. XV, 13):

> “We observe,” he says, “that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit dwell in one and the same temple through the unity of the same nature. Therefore the one who dwells in the temple possesses divine power. For just as we are the temple of the Father and of the Son, so also we are the temple of the Holy Spirit—not many temples, but one temple, which belongs to one power. Wherever one Godhead is understood” (ch. 14), “one God is said, because there is one God, one divinity, and unity of power. We do not assert three gods but deny them, because plurality is produced not by unity but by division of power. For how does the unity of divinity admit plurality, since plurality belongs to number, while divine nature does not admit number?”

From this it is evident that, just as unity has no number, so the threefold designation, or “Trinity,” has number. Therefore, in the holy and inseparable Trinity of the Godhead, it is not unity that admits what is called “trine” or “threefold,” terms which have number, but the distinct property of the persons.

The perverse interpreter, the devil, continuing, also added, while speaking to the first human beings, “knowing good and evil” (Gen. III, 35), so that, just as he himself, through the advance of greed, aspiring beyond measure to loftiness, fell when he said, “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14), so man too might fall through an immoderate ambition for sublimity, as indeed he did. For when he improperly desired divinity, he justly lost immortality.

“According to Augustine, ‘the devil stood as the mediator of this way for man, the persuader of sin and the precipitant into death, as we have said. God did not make this death, as it is written, because he himself was not the cause of death; but through his most just recompense, death—of which it is written, “Death and life are from the Lord God” (Wis. I, 13)—was inflicted upon the sinner, just as a judge inflicts punishment upon the guilty. The cause of punishment, however, is not the judge’s injustice but the merit of the crime.

“‘The devil made man miserable and mortal by his persuasion. Having seduced him through his consent, he possessed him as though by a legitimate right; and although the devil himself was not enclosed by any corruption of flesh and blood, he ruled over man, weakened through the fragility of his body and all the more wretched because the devil was, as it were, richer and stronger. Like a ragged and afflicted man, he ruled over him even in his posterity, because through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. He caused himself to be worshipped in images—namely, in various supposed divinities—throughout the world, which by a certain justice of God had been handed over to him, in comparison with the lost, with a few elect excepted, until the coming of the Lord.

“‘At the Lord’s coming, when he saw the temples of demons being deserted and the human race hastening toward the name of the liberating Mediator, he stirred up heretics who, under the Christian name, would resist Christian teaching, as though they could be tolerated indiscriminately, without any correction, in the city of God, just as the city of confusion indiscriminately tolerated philosophers who held mutually diverse and opposing views.

“‘Those, therefore, who in the Church of Christ hold some sick or perverse opinion, if, when corrected so that they may think what is sound and right, they resist obstinately and refuse to amend their pestilential and deadly doctrines but persist in defending them, become heretics. They are a clever kind of people—not through the spirit of wisdom but through impatience, by which the beginnings of heresies are accustomed to seethe and disturb the peace of the saints.’”

We have often experienced these words of blessed Augustine in Gothescalcus, who was agitated and rather filled with a diabolical spirit. But, as the same blessed Augustine says, this serves the purposes of those who make progress, according to the Apostle’s saying: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. II, 19).

Hence it is also written: “An instructed son will be wise, but he will use an imprudent servant.”

For while many matters belonging to the catholic faith are agitated by the sharp restlessness of heretics, so that they may be defended against them, they are considered more carefully, understood more clearly, and preached more earnestly. Many who could excellently discern and handle the Scriptures remained hidden among the people of God and did not set forth solutions to difficult questions when no accuser was pressing them.

Was the doctrine of the Trinity ever treated perfectly before the Arians began to bark? Was the doctrine of penance ever treated perfectly before the Novatians resisted? Likewise, the doctrine of baptism was not treated perfectly before the rebaptizers, standing outside, contradicted it; nor was the unity of Christ itself explained distinctly until that separation began to press upon the weaker brethren.

Many meanings of the holy Scriptures remain hidden and are known only to a few who are more intelligent; they are not brought forth more suitably and acceptably unless concern to answer heretics impels this. Then even those who neglect the studies of doctrine, shaken from their sleep, are roused to attentive hearing so that the adversaries may be repelled.

Finally, how many meanings of the sacred Scriptures concerning Christ as God were asserted against Photinus? How many concerning Christ as man against Manichaeus? How many concerning the Trinity against Sabellius? How many concerning the unity of the Trinity against the Arians, Eunomians, and Macedonians? How many concerning the catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, and concerning the mixture of the wicked with the good until the end of the age—since the wicked do not harm the good in their fellowship in the sacraments—against the Donatists and others, if there are any who dissent from the truth through a similar error?

For we have learned that each heresy has brought its own questions into the Church. Divine Scripture would not have been defended against them so carefully if no such necessity had compelled it.

What compelled those passages of Scripture in which predestination is commended to be defended more fully and distinctly through our labor, except that the Pelagians say that God’s grace is given according to our merits? Therefore, so that this opinion, displeasing to God and hostile to the free gifts of God by which we are delivered, may be destroyed, we defend, according to the Scriptures, that both the beginning of faith and perseverance in it unto the end are gifts of God, concerning which we have already said much.

In this faith, many against the aforementioned heretics and against the other heretics—whose enumeration or mention would be excessive and unnecessary for the present work, although their approved defenders of these doctrines would either have remained entirely hidden or would not have stood out so prominently—made their assertions. The contradictions of the proud caused those who knew how to handle and resolve these matters to bring forth obscure matters of the law into public view, lest the weak perish, troubled by the questions and impious speeches of their opponents.

Hence the Apostle, as we also stated earlier, says: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. II, 19). They must be corrected by their superiors with corrections proceeding from charity, and likewise subordinate brothers must be corrected according to the diversity of their faults, by corrections either lesser or greater. For even that which is called condemnation—the punishment imposed by episcopal judgment, than which there is no greater punishment in the Church—can, if God wills, become and contribute to a most salutary correction.

For we do not know what may happen on the following day, nor should anyone be despaired of before the end of this life. Nor can God be resisted, lest he receive someone, grant repentance, and, once he has accepted the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and contrite heart, absolve him from guilt, however just the condemnation, and not himself condemn the condemned person.

Pastoral necessity, however, requires that, lest dreadful contagions spread among many, the sick sheep be separated from the healthy—perhaps to be healed by that very separation by him for whom nothing is impossible.

Since we do not know who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not, we ought to be moved by such charity that we wish all to be saved. This happens when, one by one, as they come before us and with whom we are able to undertake this work, we strive to turn them toward this end: that, having been justified by faith, they may have peace with God. The Apostle preached this even when he said: “Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us; we beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (II Cor. 5, 20).

Whoever has been separated from the catholic Church, however laudably he may think he lives, will not have life because of this one crime—that he has been severed from the unity of Christ—but the wrath of God remains upon him. Whoever has lived well in this Church is not harmed by the sins of others, because “each person will bear his own burden” (Gal. VI, 5), as the Apostle says. And whoever in it eats the body of Christ and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

When he says, “He eats judgment upon himself” (I Cor. II, 19), he sufficiently shows that he does not eat judgment upon another but upon himself. For fellowship with the wicked does not defile someone through participation in the sacraments, but through consent to their deeds. If someone does not consent to them in their evil deeds, the wicked person bears his own cause, and his own person does not prejudice another who has no partnership in the crime through confession of the evil deed.

Let these things, said for the moment in the preface from the words and thoughts of the holy Fathers, suffice. From here onward, with the favor of the one and inseparable Godhead, we shall begin to answer individually, one by one, the deadly words of Gothescalcus with the assertions of these same and many other catholics.

Just as magicians and sorceresses customarily place honey at the mouth of a vessel concealing poison, so Gothescalcus, at the beginning of the compilation written above, sets forth the errors of heretics and rejects them verbally, so that, by pretending more credibly to be catholic, he may deceive the simple and make himself appear praiseworthy. Thus, speaking as a heretic against heretics, wishing to cover himself as a wolf with a sheep’s skin, he says:

I.

÷ “But if, fearing to be properly struck by the anathema and to suffer that punishment with the Patripassians, he says that the Godhead is one naturally, he must consequently confess, if indeed he wishes to merit pardon, that the Godhead is altogether three personally, just as it is established that God is one naturally and unquestionably three personally.”

And shortly afterward:

“Just as every catholic believes and confesses each person of the Trinity to be wholly, fully, and perfectly God, so let him believe, confess, and affirm that each person possesses his own proper Godhead, wholly, fully, and perfectly.”

[Col. 0484A] XL. This is the sum of all his blasphemy, which from this point he elaborated in a lengthy discourse. In it, like a fish, bird, or any other animal twisting about in agitation, he entangled himself still further in the worst stains and tighter knots of blasphemy. He wishes to argue from assertions of his own opinion, without testimonies from Scripture and without the judgments of catholics, that just as God is naturally one and personally three, so the Godhead ought to be called naturally one and personally three.

But when he says that God is personally three and naturally one, he speaks the truth. When, however, he says that one must confess the Godhead to be personally three in the same way as it is naturally one, he certainly lies. For the Godhead itself is a nature without plurality or number. In this nature, or Godhead, the holy and inseparable Trinity, as it is written, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4)—namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is one God naturally and three personally.

Hence the Son of God says: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30). He does not say, “We are one,” but “We are one thing,” which demonstrates the unity of nature or Godhead.

Hence he also says: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John X, 38); and, “The Father, abiding in me, himself does the works” (John XIV, 10); and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9).

And concerning the Holy Spirit: “When the Paraclete comes,” he says, “whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John XV, 26). And: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you. All things whatsoever the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John XVI, 13).

He spoke of those things that pertain to the very divinity of the Father, in which the Son is equal to him by possessing all that the Father has. For the Holy Spirit was not to receive from a creature subject to the Father and the Son what he says, “He will receive from what is mine,” but certainly from the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds and from whom the Son was born.

Therefore the nature—that is, the Godhead—of the Father is the nature of the Son and the nature of the Holy Spirit, who proceeds equally from the Father and the Son and is an ineffable communion of the Father and the Son. He proceeds wholly from the Father and wholly from the Son; he remains wholly in the Father and wholly in the Son. He remains in such a way that he proceeds, and proceeds in such a way that he remains.

Therefore, naturally, he possesses with the Father and the Son the fullness of unity and the unity of fullness, so that he wholly possesses the Father and wholly possesses the Son, while he himself is wholly possessed by the Father and wholly possessed by the Son. He is also given equally by the Father and the Son—indeed, he is given by himself, as the Son says of him: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John III, 8).

Thus, just as the Father and the Son are full and perfect God—indeed, one God with the Father and the Son—and there is one substance, one Godhead, one divinity, one essence, and one nature, which, as Athanasius and Ambrose say in agreement, cannot be divided among the persons, according to the truth of the Lord’s words: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

He says “in the name,” not “in the names,” both to show one God through the undivided name of the divine essence and to teach that the distinction of the persons is demonstrated by their proper characteristics.

And Saint Athanasius, in the eighth book On the Unity of the Faith (book X), says:

> “Whoever introduces three powers confesses three gods. But we believe in three persons, one Godhead. If we introduce three gods, we are like the nations; but we confess the Father in the Son, and the Son in the Father, with the Holy Spirit. Unity is not separated; the Godhead is not divided.”

And this same catholic teacher, who, while still a deacon, attended the holy Council of Nicaea with his archbishop Alexander, wrote and defined this throughout the eight books he composed against the Arians—not only on every page, but, so to speak, in every verse and period.

Therefore there is not a threefold nature or threefold Godhead, but one nature and one Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and this Trinity is one God alone, good, great, eternal, and almighty. He himself is unity, Godhead, greatness, goodness, omnipotence, and whatever is substantially predicated of him.

These things must not be understood or said in the same way with relative terms. For the Father cannot be called father to himself, nor the Son son to himself, nor the Holy Spirit the Holy Spirit to himself; rather, these relative terms must certainly be referred to another person.

Since the Lord says, “If you separate the precious from the worthless, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. XV, 18), by the Lord’s own words and by the judgments of catholics, the falsehood has been separated and driven far away—and, if it cannot be driven farther, it will nevertheless, with the assent of him who opens the mute mouth, makes infants’ tongues eloquent, and says, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX, 11), be driven still farther.

The falsehood of Gothescalcus, which he has disorderly mixed with truth, will be exposed like that of a leper who has various colors mingled together on one body. For, as the teachers of the Church explain, lepers aptly signify heretics, who do not possess the knowledge of true faith and bring forth various doctrines of error.

They do not conceal their ignorance but bring it into the light as the highest expertise and display the vanity of their speech. There is absolutely no false doctrine that does not mix some truth into it. Thus truths mixed disorderly with falsehoods, appearing together in one disputation or account of a human being, like colors on a single body, signify leprosy, as colors in true and false places vary and stain human bodies.

Such people must be avoided by the Church so carefully that, if possible, they should stand at a distance and call out to Christ with a loud cry, as we read about the lepers: “They stood at a distance and lifted up their voice” (Luke XVII, 13).

It is also necessary for the leaders of the Church and for all the faithful not only to resist openly the enemies of Christ with strength, but also prudently to observe and avoid ravenous wolves who cover themselves with sheep’s skins, lest they be able to deceive them. Such was Gothescalcus, who for a time concealed himself not only under the religious habit of a monk but also under the reputation of false learning and deceived many, until what he had cherished in his heart burst forth openly as a basilisk.

The catholic teachers strip away his sheep’s skin, since he did not cover himself with it properly, and show him to be a naked wolf and an open enemy of the Lord’s fold, which is the Church.

In this way Athanasius says in the first book On the Trinity:

> “This is the substance of the formula in the clash with heretics, and this is the victory of the title in the acquittal of catholics, which the principal commandment of God signifies: ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. XXVIII, 19). Hear in this the wondrous and royal decree, in which the whole sacrament is contained together in the Godhead of the Trinity. He who said ‘in the name’ clearly declared that one Godhead exists in the Trinity; and by what he added, ‘of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,’ he distinguished that individual persons exist under the individual names.”

And Hilary says in the book On the Synods:

> “Therefore, brothers, likeness of nature is free from the suspicion of insult. Nor can the Son be thought not to exist in the proper nature of the Father on the ground that he is like him, since likeness exists only from equality of nature. Equality of nature cannot exist unless there is one nature—one, however, not through unity of person but of kind. This is the devout faith, this the religious conscience, this the saving confession: not to deny that the Father and the Son have one substance because the Son is like the Father, but to proclaim him like for this reason, that they are one.”

That the same must be understood concerning the Holy Spirit he also demonstrates at the end of the twelfth book On the Faith (Hilary, book XII On the Trinity), praying:

> “Grant me,” he says, “this utterance of my conscience, so that what I professed when I was baptized in the symbol of my regeneration, in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, I may always retain: namely, that I may worship you as our Father, your Son together with you, and may merit your Holy Spirit, who is from you through your only-begotten Son.”

And in the beautiful evangelical hymn he himself composed, he says: “The perfect Spirit of God, bond of the Trinity.”

Gregory of Nazianzus, whose words blessed Augustine cites as testimony in the book On the Gift of Perseverance (ch. 19), says:

> “I ask you, confess the Trinity of one Godhead; but if you wish otherwise, say that it is of one nature.”

And Saint Ambrose says in a catholic hymn:

[Col. 0486D]

> You, unity of the Trinity,
“[You who] powerfully rule the globe”—which blessed Augustine, as though explaining its meaning, expounds in the first book of *On the Trinity* (ch. 8): “Divinity—or, to express it more precisely, deity—which is not a creature but the incorporeal and unchangeable unity of the Trinity, consubstantial with itself and coeternal in nature.” Likewise, Saint Ambrose says in the first book of *On the Faith* (ch. 2):

“We speak of one God, not two or three gods, as the impious heresy of the Arians incurs while being accused. For the person who separates the divinity of the Trinity speaks of three gods, whereas the Lord, when he says, ‘Go, baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28), showed that the Trinity possesses one power. We confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that in the perfect Trinity there is both the fullness of divinity and the unity of power. ‘Every kingdom divided against itself will quickly be destroyed’ (Matt. 12:25), says the Lord. Therefore the kingdom of the Trinity is not divided. But if it is not divided, it is one; for whatever is not one is divided. They therefore wish the kingdom of the Trinity to be such that it may easily be destroyed by its division—indeed, because it cannot be destroyed, it is evident that it is not divided. For the Trinity is neither divided nor split apart, and therefore it is neither subject to corruption nor to age.”

And again, in the same chapter:

“Difference produces plurality; the unity of power excludes numerical quantity, because unity is not a number but itself the beginning of all things.” [Col. 0487B]

Augustine likewise says in Book VIII of *On the Trinity*: “We speak of three persons of the same essence, or of three persons as one essence.” And again, in Book V (ch. 8):

“Whatever is said of God in relation to himself, and is said similarly of each person—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is also said of the Trinity itself, not in the plural but in the singular. Since, in fact, for God to be is not one thing and to be great another, but being and greatness are the same for him, just as we do not speak of three essences, so we do not speak of three greatnesses, but of one greatness and one essence. I say ‘essence,’ which in Greek is called *ousia* (οὐσία), and which we more commonly call ‘substance.’”

We nevertheless confess three persons. And Saint Jerome, writing to Pope Damasus (Epistle 57), says:

“Let it suffice for us to say: one substance, three subsisting, perfect, equal, coeternal persons. Let the term ‘three hypostases’ be silent, if you please, and let one be retained.” And again: “If, however, someone, understanding *hypostasis* as *ousia*, says that there is one hypostasis rather than three persons, he is alien from Christ.”

It must also be understood that essence, which the Greeks call *ousia*, and hypostasis, which is translated as “substance,” as well as nature, divinity, and deity, mean one and the same thing among the Latins in the holy and inseparable Trinity, as the catholic teachers demonstrate.

For Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, says in his Paschal Letter (Epistle 1, at the end):

“May we receive rewards in heaven with those who confess the one divinity of the Trinity.” [Col. 0487D]

And again, in another Paschal Letter (Epistle 9, at the end):

“Let piety toward God be preserved with the full fear of the heart; and, cursing the number of gods, let us confess the one and undivided substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. In this substance we have received eternal life through baptism, and, if the mercy of God grants it, we shall be worthy to celebrate the Lord’s Passover with the angels.”

And again, in the third Paschal Letter (Epistle 3, near the end):

“Let us seek the possessions of chastity and holiness, worshiping the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

And Saint Pope Celestine, in his letter to the Eastern bishops (Epistle 6 to John of Antioch), says:

“We would indeed wish that, just as there is one essence of deity, so among all human beings everywhere there might be held one truth of the right faith.” [Col. 0488A]

And Pope Leo the Great and the holy synod that convened in the city of Rome, in their letter to Emperor Theodosius (Epistle 27), say:

“We beseech you before the inseparable Trinity of the one deity, which is injured by such an act.”

And in the letter to the Palestinians (Epistle 87):

“The nature of the Only-Begotten is the nature of the Father, and the nature of the Holy Spirit; it is at once impassible and at once unchangeable: the undivided unity and consubstantial equality of the everlasting Trinity.”

And in the letter to Leo, bishop of Ravenna (Epistle 39):

“While apostolic doctrine protests, which proclaims to us one deity in the Trinity, one confession in the faith, and one sacrament in baptism.”

And the glorious Pope Gregory, in the eighteenth homily on the Gospels, says: [Col. 0488B]

“Abraham saw the day of the Lord when, as a figure of the highest Trinity, he received three angels as guests. Having received them, he spoke to the three as though to one, because although there is a number of persons in the Trinity, there is unity of divinity in nature.”

And in the twenty-fourth homily:

“He perceives the operation of the Spirit who acknowledges the faith of the Trinity, so that he believes the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be of one power and confesses them to be of one substance.”

And a little later:

“Our true rest is present when we already acknowledge that very glory of the Trinity which we firmly hold to exist in the unity of divinity.”

And in the sixteenth homily on Ezekiel:

“That same faith and that same merit,” he says, “held the hearts of those who came before, and filled the hearts of those who came after, who were placed under the New Testament, just as it is also said through Paul: ‘But having the same spirit of faith, as it is written: I believed, and therefore I spoke; we also believe, and therefore we speak’ (2 Cor. 4).

“For those spiritual fathers believed that the omnipotent God is the Trinity in the same way that the fathers of the New Testament openly proclaimed that same Trinity. For Isaiah heard the angelic hosts crying out in heaven: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts’ (Isa. 6:3). In order to show the Trinity of persons, ‘holy’ is said three times; but so that the Trinity’s one substance might be evident, it is not said ‘Lords of hosts’ but ‘Lord of hosts.’ David likewise, holding the same understanding, says: ‘May God bless us, our God; may God bless us’ (Ps. 66:8). Although he had said ‘God’ three times, so as to show that this God is one, he added: ‘And may all the ends of the earth fear him.’ [Col. 0488D]

“Paul likewise says: ‘For from him and through him and in him are all things’ (Rom. 11:36)—from him, namely from the Father; through him, through the Son; and in him, in the Holy Spirit. Having said ‘him’ three times, he added: ‘To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.’ For by not saying ‘to them’ but ‘to him,’ he distinguished the persons by saying ‘him’ three times, and by adding ‘to him be glory’ he did not divide the substance.”

Saint Prosper says in his *Book of Epigrams*:

“Almighty Father, Son, and life-giving Spirit—  
one deity, equal in three persons.”

And again:

“One is the deity of the three; one is their essence.” [Col. 0489A]

And the venerable presbyter Bede says in a homily:

“The apostles then knew that Christ was in the Father through the unity of the undivided Trinity.”

And a little later:

“There must be no doubt that those to whom the glory of the Son will be revealed will also be permitted to behold the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because those whose divinity is one likewise have one and inseparable vision.”

And somewhat earlier:

“Ten days after his assumption—that is, on this day—the Spirit bestowed heavenly chrism upon them. No one doubts that Christ himself came to them there who recognizes that the nature, power, and operation of the holy Trinity are inseparable.”

And in the thirty-second homily:

“What he added, ‘because you love me’ (John 16:27), must be understood according to the same reasoning, because whoever rightly loves the Son loves him together with the Father and the Spirit of both, ‘since those whose nature of divinity is inseparable have one and the same gifts of power.’”

By these testimonies of the orthodox—who confirmed their opinions by evangelical truth, apostolic authority, and the oracles of the Law and the Prophets, as anyone who wishes can readily find in the books mentioned above—it is most clearly demonstrated that the deity which is the unity of the Trinity must not be understood, believed, or called threefold personally, as Gothescalc blasphemes. For if deity is personally threefold, just as there are three persons in the holy Trinity, then—God forbid—it will be divided among those three persons, and there will no longer be an undivided Trinity, which, because of the one and same indivisible deity—that is, substance and nature—is to be understood as inseparable even in the persons, as Augustine and the other orthodox teachers say. Catholic faith therefore most firmly proclaims that the unity of deity in the Trinity and the Trinity of persons in the unity of deity must be venerated.

For just as Christian truth compels us to confess each person individually as the one full and perfect God and Lord, and to confess of each whatever can be said substantially of God, because of the one and same deity, which is wholly present in each person, so catholic religion forbids us to speak of three gods or three lords, because of the one and same deity—namely, the unity of the holy Trinity—which is wholly, undividedly, and inseparably present at once in the three persons of the holy Trinity. [Col. 0489D]

We could collect here many more testimonies both of these and of other catholic teachers, unless we believed that these alone were sufficient to demonstrate the truth. For even Leo, pontiff of the holy catholic and apostolic see, believed that the few testimonies of those who preceded him in time, though not necessarily in place or merit, testimonies great in authority and in the spirit of right faith, were sufficient to be sent to Emperor Leo for the confirmation of the catholic faith (Epistle 97).

Therefore Gothescalc’s opinion—whether he does not understand what he says or knowingly errs, and whether he is openly contradicting himself by saying that deity is naturally one and personally threefold, just as God is naturally one and personally threefold—is conclusively shown to be utterly false by the authority of so many and such witnesses. Hence, according to the sacred African canons, he ought no longer to be admitted to put forward other false statements or to have any of his false opinions heard, especially since it is written: “Every word must be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matt. 18:16).

The sacred Nicene canons (Council of Nicaea, canon 2) likewise prescribe that a neophyte bishop, if any offense of the soul concerning such a person is discovered, must, after being reproved by two or three witnesses according to the Apostle, abstain from the clergy. Much more, then, must the mouth of a heretic—whom the Apostle commands to be avoided after a first and second correction (Tit. 3:10)—be closed by every means.

For this was established by the sacred Council of Nicaea not by human invention but by divine inspiration and authority. All the holy councils held afterward—namely, the councils of Antioch, Sardica, the First Council of Ephesus, Chalcedon, and all the councils of the province of Africa—confirmed it. The statements of all catholic interpreters of the sacred Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments likewise bear witness to it from those same Scriptures, so that whoever wishes to be saved must believe and confess the three persons of the holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—*homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), that is, of the same essence, substance, deity, divinity, or nature—or one inseparable and indivisible essence, substance, deity, divinity, or nature. He must believe and confess each person individually to be the true, full, and perfect God, and all three persons together to be one true, full, and perfect God, because the deity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one, and this is the unity of the Trinity.

By this unity—that is, by the deity, which cannot be threefold because it lacks the plurality and number that belong to the persons—one God, the holy Trinity, is to be understood as inseparable even in the distinction of persons. In this faith, according to the Lord’s tradition, all who baptize baptize faithfully, and the faithful are baptized and become Christians throughout the whole world.

Only the false synod of Ariminum, following the madness of Arius, deceitfully rejected this consubstantiality of the Trinity, and for that reason it has deserved a sentence of condemnation from then and now and forever.

Therefore, since, as Saint Celestine says, “the matter does not concern only those who are acting,” and since the whole Church is shaken by whatever innovation, a sentence of eternal judgment must be pronounced also against those who, with renewed fury, attempt to revive this most ancient and most destructive heresy—conquered by the sweat of many powerful warriors and slain by the heavenly sword—by teaching a threefold deity.
