This sentence is not new but belongs to the eternal deity, which is the unity of the Trinity: it is the sentence of the first chapter of the eighth session of the Fifth Synod, comprising one hundred and fifty-three bishops, held at Constantinople under Emperor Justinian and Pope Vigilius against Theodore and all heretics.

At the beginning of the eighteen chapters subscribed by them, they decreed as follows (Fifth Synod, session 8, chapter 1): [Col. 0491A]

“If anyone does not confess one nature or substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and one power and authority, the consubstantial Trinity, one deity to be worshiped in three subsistences or persons, let him be anathema. For there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things.”

And in the letter of Saint Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, to Sergius, bishop of Constantinople, which was most fully received by the Sixth Synod (Sixth Synod, session 11), it is written:

“We therefore believe the Trinity in unity, and we glorify unity in the Trinity. We speak of Trinity because of the three subsistences, but of unity because of the singularity of the deity. Just as the holy Trinity is numerable in its personal subsistences, so the holy unity is beyond every number. The former has an indivisible division and an unconfused conjunction.

“For when it is divided into numerable subsistences and numbered according to personal distinctions, it is joined by the identity of essence and nature and admits no partition of any kind. For singular and uncountable unity avoids every numerical division according to essence. We earnestly believe in one God because we fervently proclaim one deity, although we recognize it in the Trinity of persons; and we proclaim one Lord because we firmly acknowledge one lordship, although it is manifested in three subsistences.

“Nor, because God is one and deity is one, is it divisible and to be partitioned into three gods, or to be extended into three deities. Nor, because the Lord is one, is he separate and to be expanded into three lords or enlarged into three lordships. This is the impiety of the Arians, who cut one God into unequal gods, divide one deity into dissimilar deities, and distinguish one lordship into three lordships of different kinds.” [Col. 0491C]

And again:

“Just as we have learned to understand one God, so we have learned to confess one deity; and just as we have learned to entreat three subsistences, so we are instructed to glorify three persons. Recognizing no other one God besides the three persons, and no other persons besides the three consubstantial persons of the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—we acknowledge no others besides the one God.

“Therefore we proclaim these three, in whom the deity exists, as one; and we announce the one, whose deity they possess, as three—or, to say what is more precise and clearer, we announce what God is and is known to be. This same reality is believed to be one, proclaimed as three, and truthfully announced as one. Neither is the one, insofar as it is one, received as three, nor are the three, insofar as they are three, understood as one. This is both marvelous and certainly full of all wonder.

“For this same reality is numerable and avoids number: numerable in its three subsistences, but avoiding number through the singularity of its deity. The unity of its essence and nature absolutely refuses to be numbered, so that it may not introduce a difference of deity and thereby make the plurality of essence, nature, and gods arise from one principle.” [Col. 0492A]

And again:

“The Father is God, the Son is God, and likewise the Holy Spirit is God, because these three persons are indivisibly and undiminishedly filled with one deity, and in each of them it is wholly present. For deity does not tolerate division, and it is fully and perfectly present in the three persons—not filling those persons in parts or partially, but existing in each one: remaining most full and one, although it is manifested in three persons, and not extending into a multitude of gods, although it exists in three subsistences. Thus it does not undergo any bodily division, for it is certainly impassible and incorporeal and knows nothing of what belongs properly to a creature [the printed *et pari* is uncertain].” [Col. 0492B]

Concerning this letter, the holy Sixth Council says in its thirteenth session:

“We examined,” it says, “the synodical letter of the venerable former archbishop of the holy city of God, Jerusalem, and, finding it consistent with the true faith and equal to the apostolic teachings of the holy and approved Fathers, we received it as orthodox and accepted it as salutary for the holy catholic and apostolic Church. We judged it right that his name should be inserted in the holy diptychs of the holy Churches.”

Likewise, in the letter of Pope Agatho sent to the younger Emperor Constantine (Sixth Synod, session 4), it is written:

“So that we may briefly make known to your divinely established piety what the strength of our apostolic faith contains—a faith which we have received through the apostolic tradition of the apostles’ successors and through the sacred five general councils, by which the foundations of Christ’s catholic Church have been strengthened and established—this, then, is the standing and regular tradition of our evangelical and apostolic faith:

“Confessing the holy and inseparable Trinity, that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to be of one deity, one nature and substance or essence, we proclaim it to possess one natural will, power, operation, dominion, majesty, authority, and glory. Whatever is said essentially of this same holy Trinity, we understand according to the rule established for us in the singular number, as of one nature of three consubstantial persons.” [Col. 0492D]

Moreover, in the synodical letter of that same Pope Agatho, confirmed in the Roman synod by one hundred and twenty-five bishops and sent through his representatives to the Sixth Synod of one hundred and fifty bishops at Constantinople (Sixth Synod, session 4), it is written:

“Our faith alone is our substance,” he says, “with which it is our highest glory to live and for which it is eternal gain to die. This is our perfect knowledge: that we preserve with the full vigilance of our minds the boundaries of the catholic and apostolic faith, which the apostolic see has until now both held with us and handed down.

“We believe in God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible; and in his only-begotten Son, who was born from him before all ages, true God from true God, light from light, begotten not made, consubstantial with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things in heaven and on earth were made; and in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son.

“We believe in Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity: unity of essence, but Trinity of persons or subsistences. We confess God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit—not three gods but one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; not the subsistence of three names, but one substance of three subsistences.

“Their essence, substance, or nature—that is, their one deity—is one: one eternity, one power, one dominion, one glory, one worship, one essential will and operation of the holy and inseparable Trinity, which created, governs, and sustains all things.”

These doctrines, to use the words of the Sixth Synod itself, were received with high acclaim together with the five holy councils previously held, and were confirmed in session 18 as doctrines to be proclaimed, believed, and held without refutation:

“Therefore,” says the Sixth Synod (Sixth Synod, session 18), “Christ our God raised up a most faithful emperor, finding a new David, a man after his own heart, who did not give sleep to his eyes or slumber to his eyelids, as it is written (Ps. 131:4), until through this sacred assembly, gathered by God, he found the perfect proclamation of the right faith, according to the word spoken by the Lord: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them’ (Matt. 18:20).

“This present holy and universal synod faithfully received and embraced with open hands the petition presented by the most holy and most blessed Agatho, of ancient Rome, to our most pious and most faithful Emperor Constantine. That petition specifically rejected those who taught or proclaimed, as stated above, one will and one operation in the dispensation of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God.

“The synod likewise embraced the other synodical petition sent by the sacred council of one hundred and twenty-five bishops, beloved of God, assembled under the same most holy pope, to his tranquility instructed by God. For this petition agreed with the holy Council of Chalcedon and with the Tome of the most sacred and most blessed Pope Leo of that same ancient Rome, which was sent to Saint Flavian and which this synod called the pillar of right faith.

“Further, it agreed with the synodical letters written by blessed Cyril against the impious Nestorius and to the Eastern bishops. Having also followed the five holy universal councils and the holy and approved Fathers, we define and confess in harmony that our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, is one of the holy, consubstantial Trinity, which gives origin to life; perfect in deity and the same perfect in humanity; truly God and the same truly man, consisting of a rational soul and a body; consubstantial with the Father according to deity and consubstantial with us according to humanity.” [Col. 0494A]

And thus, continuing their catholic discourse to the end, the one hundred and fifty bishops confirmed it and subscribed, saying:

“Having therefore formulated these things with every care and diligence on every side, we define that no one may present, write, compose, believe, or teach any other faith. If anyone presumes either to compose, present, teach, or hand down another faith, or to offer a creed to those who wish to turn from paganism, Judaism, or any heresy to the knowledge of the truth, or to introduce any novelty of expression or invention of speech for the subversion of what has now been determined by us, then, if they are bishops or clerics, the bishops shall be deprived of their episcopate and the clerics of their clergy; if they are monks or laypeople, they shall also be anathematized.” [Col. 0494B]

And the subscriptions:

“Theodore, humble presbyter of the holy Roman Church, representing Agatho, thrice most blessed universal pope of the city of Rome, have subscribed.”

And thereafter, each one in order.

Then, according to their custom, by acclamation—as we also read in the other councils—they anathematized all heretics and all who supported heretics. Among all those anathematized were the Predestinarians, whose heresy, by the authority of Pope Celestine and on his commission, was refuted in Gaul by Saint Prosper (Sixth Synod, session 18).

And in the edict of Emperor Constantine, which he issued and confirmed at the request of the bishops for the confirmation of this Sixth Synod, it is written:

“We believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity, one substance in three subsistences. Unity because of natural union and dominion; Trinity because of the perfection of the three subsistences and the riches of the transcendent goodness.

“For unity is truly Trinity, because the deity is united; and Trinity is truly unity, distinguished by properties but not divided by eternity. For it is coeternal with itself, and its essence is of equal honor. There was never an age when the Son was not with the Father, whose name would rightly be ‘Father’ if the Son had not been with him simultaneously and without beginning. Nor was there ever a time when the Holy Spirit was not with both.

“Therefore these three are one God. They are understood as distinct from one another only by individual difference, which inseparably distinguishes each person within the community of essence. The Father alone is Father, the Son alone is Son, and the Holy Spirit alone is Holy Spirit. These distinctions are not interchangeable with one another.

“Thus they are inseparably divided according to these distinctions, but they share in the unity of essence: a simple, undivided, and uncompounded Trinity. From three perfect persons there is one nature and deity, perfect in itself and superperfect, and one will and one operation to be glorified. For those who have one nature also have one will and one operation, as Basil, the worshiper of God, taught us.” [Col. 0495A]

And at the end of that edict:

“One Lord, one faith, one baptism; now there is one Church in God. Therefore, if anyone is a lover of Christ, fears the Lord, and desires the salvation he longs for, let him hold this orthodox faith. For he will not be saved by another faith.

“But if any person shows favor to human persons and does not demonstrate himself to be a champion of love for God, and does not receive this present pious constitution of ours, then, if he is a bishop, cleric, or clothed in the monastic habit, he shall pay the penalty of deposition. If he is enrolled among the orders of dignities, he shall be punished with proscription and deprived of his belt of office. But if he is of ordinary status, he shall be consigned to foreigners, banished from this imperial city and indeed from every city; and, in addition to all these penalties, he shall not escape the torment of the dreadful and inexpiable judgment.”

Therefore, concerning those things which Gothescalcus—namely, another Simon Magus, in his own measure—frequently set down in his writings, driven on by a frenzied spirit, with an exalted heart and lifted eyes, falsely promising himself that he would walk upon wonders, asking that three vats be prepared for him: one vat full of boiling fat, another full of boiling oil, and a third full of seething pitch; and that, after entering each of the three vats in turn up to his neck and emerging unharmed from them, everyone should believe his assertion to be utterly true—namely, that, besides this blasphemy, the Godhead is personally threefold just as it is naturally one; that just as God predestined the elect to eternal kingdom, so he predestined the reprobate to eternal destruction; that he does not will all human beings to be saved, but only those who are saved; and that Christ suffered only for the elect, and no one for whom Christ’s blood was shed will perish—no faithful and sober-minded person ought to accommodate himself to such claims, especially since the Lord, both by word and by example, said in his encounter with the devil: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matt. 4:7). For although, as omnipotent, he could have done what the devil demanded, this man cannot fulfill what he falsely and shamelessly fabricates.

Rather, inflamed with apostolic zeal, against such deadly suggestions he ought to bring forth, as a wholesome antidote, in heart and mouth:

“If anyone,” he says, “preaches another gospel contrary to what was evangelized by the Holy Spirit through the mouths of the aforementioned teachers and holy bishops in the six councils specified above, concerning the unity of the Godhead, which is the unity of the Trinity, and concerning all the articles specifically belonging to the orthodox faith that the catholic and apostolic Church proclaims and holds, let him be anathema.”

Regarding those matters that have been defined according to the course of Scripture and the tradition of the elders, no one ought to presume to enter into controversy against Gothescalcus or against anyone else. Rather, once condemned, like an illegitimate calf separated from the very root of bitterness, whether by exile or by imprisonment, and removed from the fellowship of the faithful lest he be able to harm others while refusing to benefit himself, he ought, while obstinately maintaining his evil opinion without retraction, to be confined and remain perpetually bound in that exile or confinement—unless, perhaps, God in his mercy looks upon him and he repents of the devil’s snare by which he is held captive, according to the will of that most merciful and almighty Lord.

We have learned this from the authority of the letter of the great Pope Leo to the Empress Pulcheria (Epistle 47), in which it is written:

“Concerning Eutyches,” he says, “the author of all the scandal and wickedness, let your Clemency decree that he be transferred farther away from the place which is too near the city of Constantinople, lest he enjoy the more frequent consolations of those whom he has drawn into his impiety. Moreover, order a catholic abbot to be placed over his monastery, which he presided over perniciously and unworthily, so that he may both free that congregation of God’s servants from its perverse doctrine and instruct it in the principles of truth.”

Since, however, we ought not to dispute about such matters as though they were doubtful, the same Leo says to the Emperor Marcian (Epistle 45):

“By our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is the author and ruler of your kingdom, I appeal and earnestly beseech your Clemency not to permit the faith which our blessed Fathers proclaimed as handed down to them from the apostles to be reconsidered in the present synod as though it were doubtful. Do not permit those things which were once condemned by the authority of the elders to be revived now by renewed efforts. Rather, order that the ancient decrees of the Council of Nicaea remain in force, with heretical interpretation removed.”

Likewise, in a letter to the Emperor Leo (Leo, Epistle 84), he says:

“Let your piety, venerable Emperor, know beforehand that those whom I promise will be sent from the apostolic see will not be going to fight against the enemies of the faith, nor to contend with them. We do not dare to enter into any discussion concerning matters defined at Nicaea and Chalcedon, as God has willed, as though those things were doubtful or insecure which such great authority, through the Holy Spirit, has established. We do not refuse the support of our ministry for the instruction of our little ones, who, after the nourishment of milk, desire to be satisfied with more solid food. Just as we do not despise the more simple, so we avoid rebellious heretics, mindful of the Lord’s command: ‘Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine’ (Matt. 7:6).

“For it is exceedingly unworthy and unjust that those whom the Holy Spirit signifies through the Prophet, saying, ‘The sons of strangers have lied to me’ (Ps. 17:46), should be admitted to the freedom of debate. Even if they did not resist the Gospel, they would nevertheless show themselves to belong among those of whom it is written: ‘They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him.’”

To the same emperor he also says:

“To seek what has been revealed, to reconsider what has been completed, and to overthrow what has been defined—what else is this than to fail to give thanks for the grace received and to stretch out the wicked desires of deadly greed toward the food of the forbidden tree?”

Blessed Ambrose likewise, in the first book of *The Faith* addressed to the Emperor Gratian; Saint Augustine in his book *Against Five Kinds of Enemies*; Pope Agatho; and Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, held the same opinion. Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, says:

“Let us flee the turbulent and muddy streams of deceit, the sects that attack God—I mean the madness of Arius, who divides the indivisible Trinity,”

[the printed text adds “writing in the Fifth Synod”; its syntactical connection is uncertain]. Saint Athanasius likewise demonstrates in his books that Arius and his accomplices, condemned in the holy Council of Nicaea, held what Gothescalcus learned: namely, that just as God is personally threefold, so the Godhead is personally threefold. All the catholic councils condemned and continue to condemn them, together with all who presume to think contrary to the Nicene Creed.

Thus Saint Gelasius, writing to all the bishops established throughout Dardania (Epistle 11, at the beginning), says:

“Our fathers, catholic and learned bishops, whenever any heresy arose, decreed once and for all, after assembling according to the course of Scripture and the teaching of the elders, whatever they had established for the faith, for truth, and for catholic and apostolic communion. They wanted these decisions thereafter to remain unshaken and firm, and did not permit what had been determined in the same matter to be reconsidered through any recent presumption. They wisely perceived that, if anyone were freely permitted to repeat salutary decrees, no ecclesiastical settlement against any particular error would remain stable, and every complete definition would continually be disturbed by renewed outbreaks of the same madness.

“For if, even after synodal rules have once been established with fixed boundaries, defeated plagues do not cease to raise themselves up in renewed struggles against the foundation of truth and to strike simple hearts, what would happen if it were continually lawful for the faithless to convene a council? However evident the truth might be, pernicious falsehood would never lack something to bring forth, even if it lacked both reason and authority, provided that it did not yield in intention.

“Our elders, seeing this by divine inspiration, necessarily took precautions so that what a synod had once promulgated for the communion of faith and for catholic and apostolic truth would not afterward be mutilated by new reconsiderations. They did not wish to provide the wicked with an opportunity to attack what had been established as a remedy. Rather, once the author of any madness and the error itself had been condemned, they judged it sufficient that whoever afterward became a participant in such an error should be bound by the original sentence of its condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized either by his profession or by his communion.”

And a little later:

“Since the same error, condemned together with its author, carries its own execration and punishment against every participant who embraces wicked communion.”

From these authorities of the apostolic see it is clear that this matter, like every heresy previously defeated and condemned together with its followers, ought not to be disputed again, nor should Gothescalcus, canonically condemned, be recalled for judgment.

Even if he had not been condemned in the case of a presbyter or deacon by a fixed and decreed number of bishops, but had been condemned by his own bishop alone for manifest heresy, judgment concerning him ought not to be reopened. Thus Pope Gelasius, in his *Memorial* addressed to Faustus, master of the soldiers serving as an envoy to Constantinople, reasonably shows that Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, had been condemned by Pope Felix. He says:

“My predecessor,” he says, “was the executor of an ancient decree, not the author of a new constitution. This is lawful not only for an apostolic bishop but for any bishop.”

And, as the Council of Nicaea says, the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes such presumptuous persons.

The Council of Constantinople likewise declared that the faith of the 318 Fathers who had assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia must not be violated, that it must remain firm and stable, and that every heresy must be anathematized.

The holy Council of Chalcedon likewise decreed (Council of Chalcedon, session 5, near the end):

“The holy and universal synod has decreed that no one may present, write, compose, hold, or teach another faith. Those who dare to compose another faith, or to present, teach, or transmit another creed to those who wish either to be converted, or to come from paganism to knowledge of the truth, or from Judaism, or from any heresy—if they are bishops or clerics, they are to be removed: bishops from the episcopate and clerics from the clergy; but if they are monks or laypeople, they are to be anathematized.”

All these things have therefore come upon the head of Gothescalcus, yet even so he has not returned to himself after being struck by them.

Our venerable brothers, the monks and religious men, will therefore act well if, in accordance with what is written in the rule of blessed Benedict, which they have professed under oath that they will observe, they render obedience to that most holy Father—or rather, to the Holy Spirit who spoke through him—and, abandoning the unnecessary compositions of the superstitious, use in their daily and nightly praises the hymns of Saint Ambrose, as Saint Benedict himself commanded, or those of the most famous and orthodox authors. They possess enough of these hymns, in which the catholic faith shines forth, the prayers are devout, and the composition is admirable.

They should avoid, on account of such matters, causing scandal in the Church—which is already shaken and troubled by many disturbances—through the ending of the hymn whose beginning is *Sanctorum meritis inclyta gaudia*, a hymn whose composer we have so far been unable to discover, where some sing, or rather blaspheme, “You threefold God” (*te trina deitas*), whether knowingly or unknowingly.

They should know what punishment is deserved by one who through his own fault causes one of the little ones who believe to stumble, as Paul teaches:

“When you thus sin against the brothers and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ” (1 Cor. 8:12).

They must therefore be struck with canonical severity, in accordance with what the great Council of Chalcedon, consisting of 630 bishops and more, defined concerning such matters. Those who ought to devote themselves to silence and quiet sometimes, even though they possess zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, stir up ecclesiastical or civil affairs.

Moreover, the sacred authority of the canons themselves, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, commanded in the African Council of 208 bishops, in its seventy-first chapter, that no other prayers be celebrated except those which had been examined together in council with the more prudent, lest—God forbid—something contrary to the faith be uttered in those same prayers by which each believer ought to be reconciled to God, thereby causing scandal to those who hear.

Let them also read, during the hours regularly assigned to them for reading, the books of the orthodox. In them they will find that everyone contradicts the claim that the Godhead is threefold and that such a claim should ever be believed or plausibly uttered by a faithful person.

Nevertheless, they will also find that among the statements of catholics the ignorant have foolishly taken as authority the claim that, just as God is called threefold, so the Godhead should be called threefold.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are called one God because the Godhead is one: it is the unity of the Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The holy catholic and apostolic Church briefly confirms and explains this through blessed and great Pope Leo, in his letter to Turibius, bishop of Astorga (Leo, Epistle, chapter 1), saying:

“This is the confession of the catholic faith: it confesses the Trinity of the Godhead as *ὁμοούσιον*—consubstantial—in such a way that it believes the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be, without confusion, undivided; without time, everlasting; and without difference, equal, because unity in the Trinity is fulfilled not by the same person but by the same essence.”

Those who say, not only absurdly but also impiously, that the Godhead ought to be called threefold because each of the three persons is God—the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God—and therefore that in the Father, who is fully and perfectly God, there is a full and perfect Godhead; in the Son, who is fully and perfectly God, there is a full and perfect Godhead; and in the Holy Spirit, who is fully and perfectly God, there is a full and perfect Godhead—let them see, if they can, by what name that threefold Godhead can be called one.

If they say that the Godhead is threefold in persons but one in Godhead, this does not stand. If they say that the Godhead is threefold in persons but one in substance, essence, divinity, or nature, it is likewise most certainly clear that this does not stand. For in God, nature, substance, essence, divinity, and Godhead are one and the same.

They must therefore confess that God is called threefold in persons and one in Godhead; and they must confess that the Godhead is not threefold but one, since it is the unity of the Trinity.

Thus Saint Ambrose, as he says more fully in his books, says briefly in his hymn:

> You are the unity of the Trinity,  
> who mightily rule the world.

And in another hymn:

> O blessed light of the Trinity,  
> and principal unity.

Explaining this as it were, Augustine says in the first book of *On the Holy Trinity* (chapter 8):

“For the unity of the Trinity is the incorporeal and unchangeable Godhead, consubstantial with itself and an eternal nature.”

Athanasius likewise declared this to be the catholic faith: that it is believed that “the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; but the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, their glory equal and their majesty coeternal.”

Saint Ambrose therefore also clearly shows in another hymn how the triune and the one God ought to be believed and understood, saying:

> Most high God of mercy,  
> creator of the world’s structure,  
> one in power,  
> threefold in person.

Augustine explains “one in power” as “substantially.”

Saint Gregory likewise says in his *Homily on Ezekiel* (Homily 16):

“He acknowledges that the spiritual fathers of the Old and New Testaments believed and preached that the persons of the Holy Trinity are of one Godhead, and that the angelic hosts in heaven cry this out without ceasing.”

Having weighed these matters, let our honorable brothers, the monks, discern whether it is better to blaspheme with Gothescalcus and Ratramnus by saying “You threefold God” in a hymn whose author they do not know, or to believe and sing with the highest powers of heaven, with the blessed spirits, and with all holy catholic men that in three persons there is one substance of the Godhead—that is, one Godhead.

Let them also see whether they ought to follow the blasphemies of Gothescalcus, which he most falsely uttered from his own heart, or rather under the inspiration of an evil spirit, and the fabrications of Ratramnus, which he falsely composed from the books of blessed Hilary and Saint Augustine, attacking the truth so that the Godhead might be called threefold; or whether they ought to follow the truth of the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the holy prophets, the apostles, and the successors of the apostles, saying and confirming that there are three persons of the Holy Trinity and one Godhead, which is the unity of the Trinity.

For Saint Augustine, in the first book of *On the Trinity*, as though specifically refuting Ratramnus, who wished to strengthen his falsehood—that the Godhead ought to be called threefold—by compiling it from Augustine’s books, set down the very stone of faith upon which Christ, strong-handed, founded his Church and with which he struck the devil, represented by Goliath, on the forehead. All the antichrists—that is, the heretics—speak filled with the devil’s madness. Augustine, speaking on behalf of himself and all catholics whose books on the faith of the Holy Trinity he had read, says against this man (Book 1, chapter 4):

“All those whom I have been able to read who wrote about the Trinity that is God before me—catholic interpreters of the divine books, both Old and New—intended to teach, according to the Scriptures, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit signify the divine unity by an inseparable equality of one and the same substance, and therefore that there are not three gods but one God.”

Let our venerable brothers, the monks and religious men, therefore attend to what the same blessed Augustine says in Book 9 of *On the Trinity* (chapter 1):

“Let us have no unbelieving doubt concerning what must be believed; concerning what must be understood, let us make no rash assertion. In the former, authority must be held; in the latter, truth must be sought.”

Let them therefore seek through catholic teachers how they ought to understand this truth concerning the Godhead of the Trinity, namely, concerning the unity of the Holy Trinity. Let them hold catholic authority and not follow the perversity of those who think wrongly. Nor should they stubbornly defend anything which thus far they have not held faithfully. Rather, let them hear and heed blessed Augustine, who admonishes each of us in his exposition of Psalm 130:

“If perhaps you are in error about something, why do you not return to your mother’s milk? For if you are not lifted up, if you do not exalt your heart, if you do not enter into things too wonderful for you, but preserve humility, God will reveal to you that you think otherwise. But if you wish to defend precisely what you think otherwise, and stubbornly maintain it against the peace of the Church, then this curse spoken over the mother will be yours while you are with her: you will be separated outside from the milk, and outside from your mother’s womb you will die of hunger.

“But if you persevere in catholic peace, and perhaps think otherwise than you ought to think, God will reveal it to you in your humility. Why? Because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

Since thereafter they will not be able to err unknowingly, let them fear what the same distinguished teacher says in the fourth book (chapter 5) *On Baptism*:

“Since it is evident that one who sins knowingly sins much more grievously than one who sins unknowingly, I would like someone to tell me: if one person falls into heresy without knowing how great an evil it is, while another knowingly does not withdraw from avarice, which of them is worse? I can also put the question this way: if one person, unknowingly, rushes into heresy, while another knowingly does not withdraw from idolatry—for the Apostle also says, ‘Avarice, which is the service of idols’ (Eph. 5:5)—which sins more grievously: the one who unknowingly falls into heresy, or the one who knowingly has not withdrawn from avarice, that is, from idolatry?

“According to the rule by which the sins of those who know are placed above the sins of ignorance, the avaricious person knowingly prevails in wickedness. But perhaps the greatness of the crime in heresy produces what the knowingly committed avarice produces, so that the heretic who is ignorant may be equated with the avaricious person who knows, their sins being weighed equally: the blasphemy of the ignorant person and the idolatry of the knowing person being judged by the same sentence.

“Should one who, while seeking Christ, falls into a plausible discourse of falsehood, and one who unknowingly resists Christ speaking through the Apostle—‘No fornicator, or impure person, or avaricious person, who is a servant of idols, has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God’ (Eph. 5:5)—be judged by the same sentence?”

Therefore, let no catholic dare to contend against authority, and let no peaceable person dare to contend against the peace of the Church, lest he be found a schismatic rather than a catholic and be separated from Christ’s body.

The subjects must therefore be admonished by the rulers of the holy Church to understand correctly the words of the sacred law. If they cannot understand them by themselves, then, according to the command of divine authority, let them ask their fathers, “and they will announce it to them,” and their elders, “and they will tell them” (Deut. 32:7).

Those who do not correctly understand the words of the sacred law must be admonished, according to the pastoral rule of blessed Gregory (Part 3, chapter 25):

“Let them consider that they turn the most wholesome drink of wine into a cup of poison for themselves, and strike themselves with a mortal wound through a medicinal instrument, when by the very means through which they ought beneficially to cut away what is wounded, they destroy what is sound within themselves. Let them be admonished to consider that Holy Scripture has been placed for us in the night of the present life like a lamp. Yet when they do not understand its words correctly, they darken themselves by the light. A perverse intention would not drag them into a corrupt understanding unless pride had first inflated them.

“For when they consider themselves wiser than others, they disdain to follow others toward a better understanding. In order to wrest from the ignorant crowd for themselves the name of learning, they strive with all their might both to destroy what others have rightly understood and to strengthen their own perversities. Thus it is rightly said through the Prophet: ‘They cut open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their own boundary’ (Amos 1:15).

“Gilead is interpreted as ‘a heap of testimony.’ Since the whole congregation of the Church, through confession, serves as a testimony to the truth, Gilead appropriately signifies the Church, which through the mouth of all the faithful bears witness to whatever is true concerning God.

“The pregnant women of Gilead are souls that conceive an understanding of the word from divine love and, when they come to the proper time, are about to give birth to the understanding they have conceived through the manifestation of their works. To enlarge one’s boundary means to extend the reputation of one’s opinion.

“Thus they cut open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their boundary, because heretics destroy by perverse preaching the minds of the faithful that have already conceived something of the understanding of truth, while extending their own reputation for learning. They cut the hearts of the little ones, already pregnant with the conception of the word, with the sword of error, and thereby establish for themselves a reputation for teaching.

“When, therefore, we try to instruct such people so that they may not think perversely, we must first admonish them not to seek empty glory. For if the root of pride is cut away, the branches of perverse assertion consequently wither.

“They must also be admonished not to turn the law of God into a sacrifice to Satan by generating discord through error, although that law was given precisely to prohibit sacrifices to Satan. Therefore the Lord complains through the Prophet, saying: ‘I gave them grain, wine, and oil; I multiplied silver for them, and gold, which they made into Baal’ (Hos. 2:8).

“We receive grain from the Lord when, in more obscure statements, the covering of the letter having been removed, we perceive the inner things of the law through the marrow of the spirit. The Lord gives us his wine when, through attentive preaching of his Scripture, he makes us drunk. He also gives us his oil when, through clearer commandments, he orders our life with gentle kindness. He multiplies silver when he supplies us with words full of the light of truth. He enriches us with gold when he illuminates our heart with the understanding of supreme radiance.

“Heretics offer all these things to Baal, because they corruptly understand everything and pervert it in the hearts of their hearers. From God’s grain, oil, silver, and gold they offer sacrifice to Satan, because they bend words of peace toward the error of discord. They must therefore be admonished to consider that, when by a perverse mind they create discord out of peace for those deceived, by God’s just judgment they themselves die from words of life.”

They must also be taught neither to be ignorant of nor to despise the decrees of the great Pope Leo addressed to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch (Epistle 62, chapter 6, to Maximus of Antioch), in which he wrote what he established by the authority of the apostolic and general synod:

“It is fitting,” he says, “that your Dilection take care to prevent anyone except the Lord’s priests from daring to claim for himself the right to teach and preach, whether he is a monk or a layman who boasts in the name of some learning. For although it is desirable that all the children of the Church should understand what is right and sound, it must nevertheless not be permitted that anyone outside the priestly order assume for himself the office of preacher, since everything in the Church of God ought to be ordered so that, in the one body of Christ, the more excellent members fulfill their office and the inferior do not resist the superior.”

Our brothers and sons, therefore, the monks and religious men, must attend to the rule of their profession, in which it is written:

“The eighth degree of humility is if a monk does nothing except what the common rule of the monastery or the examples of the elders encourage.

“The ninth degree of humility is if a monk restrains his tongue from speaking and, practicing silence, does not speak until he is questioned.”

If, however, the necessity of instructing a parish should require that the word be spoken to the people through priestly monks, the bishop must test in them soundness of understanding, catholic faith, the discipline of religion, the virtue of humility, and the stability of holy conduct, and only then summon them to the office of teaching.

Those who have not been summoned must not in any way assume what has not been assigned to them. If they are found either teaching perversely, displaying harmful things, or showing pride in any aspect of their teaching, they must be removed from that office until they are found to have been corrected through humble satisfaction.

For the Holy Spirit, speaking through the mouth of blessed Benedict in the rule established by him, gives a similar instruction concerning craftsmen of every art in a monastery. And if, God forbid, any are found—for, as it is written, wickedness was found even in the angels—who, through contempt of their fault, preferred to be bound by a deliberate plan, they must be admonished from the pastoral rule of blessed Gregory (Part 3, chapter 33):

“Let them carefully consider that, when they do evil deliberately, they kindle a stricter judgment against themselves, so that the harsher sentence strikes them in proportion as the bonds of deliberation bind them more tightly in guilt.

“They might perhaps wash away their offenses more quickly through repentance if they had fallen into them through mere haste. For a sin is dissolved more slowly when it is solidified by deliberation. Unless the mind utterly despised eternal things, it would not perish in guilt through deliberate judgment.

“Those who have fallen through haste and perish through deliberation delay their ruin. For when such people fall from the state of righteousness by sinning, they often fall at the same time into the snare of despair and are entirely torn away from the root of hope.

“Therefore the Lord, through the Prophet, reproves not so much the perversity of haste as the deliberate pursuit of sins, saying: ‘Lest my indignation go forth like fire and burn, with no one to extinguish it, because of the wickedness of your pursuits’ (Jer. 4:4). Again, in anger, he says: ‘I will visit upon you according to the fruit of your pursuits’ (Jer. 21:14).

“Since, therefore, sins committed deliberately differ from other sins, the Lord pursues not so much the evil deeds as the deliberate pursuit of wickedness. In deeds one often sins through weakness, often through negligence; in deliberate pursuits, however, one always sins with a malicious intention.

“Against this, it is rightly said of the blessed man through the Prophet: ‘He did not sit in the seat of pestilence’ (Ps. 1:1). The seat is ordinarily that of a judge or of one presiding. To sit in the seat of pestilence is to commit evil through judgment, to discern evil through reason, and nevertheless to carry it out deliberately.

“He sits, as it were, in the seat of perverse counsel who is lifted up by such great pride of iniquity that he endeavors to accomplish evil even through deliberation. Just as among the crowds attending the exalted there are those who are supported by the honor of the seat, so the sins of those who fall through haste are surpassed by sins deliberately sought out.

“They must therefore be admonished to gather from this how great a vengeance awaits those who bind themselves in guilt even through deliberation—those who now become not merely companions but leaders of the wicked.”

Finally, if—God forbid—anyone among our brothers should henceforth, on account of the ending of the hymn from which this obstinate controversy arose without any necessity, defend the threefold Godhead; or should argue concerning the predestination of the saints and the abandonment of the reprobate; or should maintain that God does not will all human beings to be saved and that Christ did not suffer for all, although the Apostle Paul says, “God wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4), and Peter says that he wills no one to perish; and although the Lord himself says through the Prophet, “As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner”; since, according to the Apostle, all have sinned; and since the Lord says to Jerusalem, “How often I desired to gather your children, and you were unwilling?” (Matt. 23:37); and since Paul likewise says:

“If Christ died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for all” (2 Cor. 5:14);

or should think contrary to apostolic teaching concerning the sacrament of baptism, in which there is no distinction among those who are reborn; or should think contrary to the catholic faith and to the teaching of blessed Augustine in *Correction and Grace*, *The Predestination of the Saints*, *The Gift of Perseverance*, and the *Hypomnesticon*; or contrary to the decrees of Saint Pope Celestine, through whose delegation blessed Prosper defeated and suppressed in Gaul the heresy that had arisen there by the authority of Scripture and the teaching of blessed Augustine; or should think contrary to the tradition of the other orthodox authorities; or should henceforth presume to dogmatize concerning anything defined by the authority of the apostolic see and the six general synods and remain irreverently obstinate in his position, he will be subject to canonical punishment.

Let no one therefore claim to be wiser than he ought to be, since it is written:

“Just as eating much honey is not good for him, so whoever investigates majesty is overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25:27).

And:

“Unless you believe, you will not understand.”

Since it is exceedingly difficult, as blessed Gregory explains, for us mortals to understand every sacred utterance and penetrate all its mystery, it remains that whatever we cannot penetrate concerning the mystery of the divine word we should humbly reserve to the power of the Holy Spirit. No one should presumptuously dare either to despise or to condemn what he does not understand; rather, he should consign it to the fire when he reserves it for the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, as Augustine explains, let him believe without doubt what the divine word says, even though his understanding is insufficient to penetrate its mystery. For, as blessed Celestine says in his decrees (after Epistle 8, at the end):

“Although we do not dare to despise the deeper and more difficult parts of the questions that arise, which those who resisted the heretics have treated at greater length, neither are we obliged to establish them.”

But if anyone should refuse to obey this admonition of ours, supported by the authority of the Scriptures and of the orthodox leaders of the Church [Col. 0505B], since the sacred canons of Antioch, created by the Spirit of God and, as Leo says, consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, decree that “a council is complete when the metropolitan is present together with his suffragans,” and since Saint Leo likewise writes to Maximus, bishop of Antioch (Epistle 66, near the end):

> “Whatever is brought before episcopal judgment apart from the particular cases of synodal councils may properly be adjudicated, provided that nothing concerning it has been defined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. For whatever disagrees with their rules and constitution can never obtain the consent of the Apostolic See.”

And the sacred canons of Nicaea, followed by those of Antioch and Chalcedon, order that questions of this kind, which arise throughout the provinces, be [Col. 0505C] examined, and that, if any should perhaps emerge in provincial synods, each one be corrected.

The Council of Agde, in its thirty-eighth chapter (canon 31), decreed, saying:

> “We determine that monks whom verbal reproof has not corrected shall also be restrained by beatings.”

The holy Rule, promulgated through the mouth of blessed Benedict by the same Holy Spirit by whom the sacred canons were established in the venerable councils, likewise commands in its second chapter that the undisciplined and restless be rebuked more severely, and that the wicked, hard-hearted, proud, or disobedient be restrained at the very beginning of their sin by blows or bodily punishment, as it is written: “A fool is not corrected by words,” and, “Strike your son with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death.”

Therefore, mindful of their promise, let them follow the teaching of our common father, blessed Benedict, who says in the sixth chapter of the Rule, citing the prophet:

> “If,” he says, “one must sometimes remain silent concerning good words because of silence, how much more must one refrain from evil words because of the punishment of sin?”

For what worse thing can be said than to violate and tear apart, most pestilently, obstinately, and deliberately, the creed of the faith handed down by Christ, preached by the apostles and their successors, and confirmed at the great Council of Nicaea by the mystical number of priests, when Scripture says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God”?

And because, in so great a matter—which is that rock of the great Peter’s true confession upon which the Lord founded his Church, to which he gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0506A], and which is the foundation of every good thing—one cannot offend through ignorance, if thereafter anyone should offend through contempt, then, though we say this most unwillingly, whoever words have not corrected shall receive blows. He shall be condemned, with deprivation of rank and separation from the body and blood of Christ, to exile or confinement in prison, just as the most obstinate Gottschalk was condemned. Thus, as the decrees of the Apostolic See determine, whoever attempts to hold contrary to the statutes, and dares to admit what has been forbidden, must know that he is to be removed from his office; and whoever did not wish to be a companion of discipline shall not be a sharer in our communion, but shall have his portion with the one whose error he chose to follow.

The rule of the holy profession of monks also decrees in its twenty-sixth chapter [Col. 0506B] that anyone who rashly associates himself with such persons in any way shall incur the punishment of excommunication.

Therefore every faithful person must know with certainty that, even if—whether remaining hidden from the knowledge of the Church’s leaders, evading their sloth or negligence, mocking them, or in any manner eluding their authority—he should escape before human eyes the judicial sentences decreed by the Holy Spirit, who searches even the depths of God and fills the world, nevertheless, in the sight of God, before whose eyes everything is naked and open, and who made the things that are to come, he will depart from this world bound by his obstinacy. These judgments are rendered through those to whom he said: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20); and, “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:22). They reign with him in heaven and shine forth in miracles on earth; and, as blessed Leo writes, they still live with us in their constitutions. He will depart bound by his obstinacy unless, through worthy fruits of repentance, he is restored to ecclesiastical communion by episcopal authority.

The pontifical authority, the royal power, and all the leaders of the Church—that is, the priests and rulers of monasteries—certainly know, as we believe, from sacred reading, where among other things they read how the negligence of Eli the priest toward his sinful sons was terribly punished. They also find written concerning a certain king: “Because you have released”—that is, without the deserved punishment—“a man deserving death, your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people” [Col. 0506D] (1 Kings 20:42).

As Saint Gregory writes to Archbishop Eusebius (Book 7, Epistle 6):

> “Whoever does not correct what must be cut away commits it.”

Saint Augustine likewise explains, in a sermon on the words of the Gospel (Sermon 18), the judgment of the blessed apostle Paul, who says: “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, expose them” (Eph. 5:11):

> “Do not,” he says, “be negligent in correcting your own people—that is, those who in any way belong to your care—by warning, teaching, exhorting, and frightening them. Use every means available to you, lest, when you find in Scripture and in the examples of the saints—whether those who lived before or those who lived after the coming of Christ—that the wicked do not defile the good within unity, you become sluggish in correcting the wicked.  
>   
> “The wicked person does not defile you in two ways: if you do not consent and if you rebuke him. This means: do not participate and do not consent. But because it would be too little not to consent if negligence of discipline followed, he says, ‘Rather, expose them.’ Therefore do not consent to the wicked, so as to approve them; do not be negligent, so as not to rebuke them; and do not be proud, so as to rebuke them insultingly.”

Again, in a sermon on the words of the Gospel, explaining the apostle’s statement, “Therefore go out from their midst and separate yourselves, says the Lord” (2 Cor. 6:17), he says:

> “What does it mean to go out from there, except to do what belongs to the correction of the wicked, insofar as it can be done for each person’s rank and status without violating peace? You were displeased that someone had sinned; you did not touch the unclean thing; you exposed, corrected, warned, and, if the matter required it, applied suitable discipline that did not violate unity. You have gone out from there.”

And in his sermon on the universality of almsgiving—beginning, “There are some who think”—explaining the statement, “Give to the merciful, and do not receive a sinner” (Ecclus. 12:4), he says:

> “These two designations are not uttered without reason when we say, ‘a sinful man.’ Because he is a sinner, correct him; because he is a human being, have mercy on him. You will not wholly free the human being unless you pursue the sinner in him. Every form of discipline watches over this duty, as it is fitting and appropriate to each ruler—not only the bishop who rules his people, but also the poor man who rules his household, the husband who rules his wife, the father who rules his children [Col. 0507C], the judge who rules his province, and the king who rules his nation.  
>   
> “All these, when they are good, certainly desire the good of those whom they govern. And servants, according to the authority bestowed by the Lord of all, who also governs rulers, take care that those whom they govern both remain human beings and perish as sinners. Thus they fulfill what is written: ‘Give to the merciful, and do not receive a sinner,’ lest they wish to preserve in him that which makes him a sinner. ‘Repay the impious and sinners with punishment.’ And let the very fact that they are impious and sinners be destroyed in them. ‘Do good to the humble’ because he is humble, and do not give to the impious because he is impious, since the Most High also hates sinners and will repay the impious with punishment.  
>   
> “Yet because they are not only sinners and impious but also human beings, he makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust. Thus mercy must be closed to no human being, but the sins of no sinner may be released without punishment.”

And in his exposition of Psalm 129:

> “Whoever consents to a sinner is burdened not by another’s sins but by his own. For you consent, and another’s sin becomes your sin; there is therefore no reason for you to complain that another’s sins weigh upon you: they weigh upon you, but they are yours.”

And in the book *On Correction and Grace*:

> “See that no one repays evil for evil. Here we should understand evil being repaid for evil especially when the person who ought to be corrected is not corrected but is neglected through a wicked concealment. For he says: ‘Rebuke sinners in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear’ [Col. 0508A] (1 Tim. 5:20). This must be understood of sins that are not hidden, lest he be thought to have spoken contrary to the Lord’s judgment. For he says: ‘If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone’ (Matt. 18:15). Nevertheless, he carries the severity of correction so far as to say: ‘If he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector.’”

Pastoral necessity requires that, lest dreadful contagions spread among the many, the diseased sheep be separated from the healthy, perhaps to be healed by that very separation by him for whom nothing is impossible.

For this reason Saint Leo, writing to Leo Augustus (Epistle 81), also sets forth the proper model for royal power:

> “Since the Lord has enriched your Clemency with so great an illumination of his sacrament, you must recognize without hesitation that royal power has been bestowed upon you not merely for the governance of the world, but especially for the protection of the Church, so that by suppressing wicked attempts you may defend what has been rightly established and restore true peace to what has been disturbed.  
>   
> “For this evil, which pestilently obscures the purity of the Church of Constantinople, where certain clerics are found to agree with the opinions of heretics and, within the very entrails of the Catholics, to assist heretics by their assertions, ought also to stir the priestly and apostolic spirit of your piety toward the execution of justice. If my brother Anatolius is found too sluggish because he spares them with excessive kindness, deign, for the sake of your faith, to provide this medicine for the Church as well, so that such men may be expelled not only from the clerical order [Col. 0508C] but also from residence in the city, lest the holy people of God be further polluted by the contagion of perverse men.”

We too, pastors and teachers of the peoples entrusted to us, bishops and governors of the Church, and rulers of monasteries, who are called abbots, must return to ourselves and consider carefully that, if the sword of God has been made drunk in heaven, and if, as the great Peter says, “God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them into Tartarus, drawing them down with the chains of hell to be tormented and reserved for judgment” (2 Pet. 2:4), he will not spare us when we apostatize from him in faith and deeds. Nor did the sacred councils spare bishops of even the most renowned sees, as we can read in them: those of Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, Constantinople, and Nicomedia [Col. 0508D].

Moreover, they anathematized Honorius, pope of great Rome, after his death, because he was discovered and most clearly proved to have held an opinion contrary to the faith and to have consented to those who held an evil opinion, as is found in the Sixth Synod (Act 13). In this, when the guilt was made manifest in this world, they agreed with the just judgment of God, which had already acted in secret.

For if Honorius had not deserved this in the present world, and if he had not rightly departed from this world with that fate, then those who hurled curses would have harmed themselves rather than him—not by a judgment of justice but through envy or rashness. This is just as good deeds performed for the dead benefit those who perform them more than those for whom they are performed, provided that the dead themselves did not merit in this life that the good deeds of their living people should be able to benefit them in the life to come [Col. 0509A].

Read blessed Augustine’s exposition of the apostle’s Epistle to the Thessalonians, and Saint Gregory, who discusses this matter apostolically:

> “But the pious mother Church offers the true and singular sacrifice for all who rest in Christ—that is, in the unity of Catholic peace and faith and in communion with the body and blood of our Redeemer and Savior. She does not tolerate their disparagement, as Saint Coelestine writes to the Gallican bishops (Epistle 8), saying: ‘It is impious that these religious souls should suffer such things. Since they are our members, their affliction ought also to make us suffer, although the blessedness promised to those who are proved to endure persecution for righteousness remains in store for them.’”

The following statement explains what the Lord promises them: “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Thus it is clear, as Pope Felix says, and as we learn from Saint Augustine’s letter to Boniface, that “it is dangerous to judge the merits of those who have already gone before us to the Lord, except when their crimes or their apostasy from the true faith—that is, their departure from God—and their perseverance in it to the end are manifest.”

Only that person will be followed by an anathema—even if he is not judged by a human being—that is, alienation from God, who perseveringly remains an apostate in this life by faith or by works.

Therefore, attending to the statements of sacred Scripture, which say, “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:27), and, “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” [Col. 0509C] (Rom. 2:21), “You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?”, let us beware—we who must correct and teach others—that we do not interpret the sacred Scriptures sacrilegiously, as Arius, Macedonius, Nestorius, and Eutyches presumed to do. For this reason, by divine vengeance and canonical judgment, Arius at Nicaea, Macedonius at Constantinople, Nestorius at the First Council of Ephesus, and Eutyches at Chalcedon were condemned, together with all their associates and supporters.

Let us beware that we do not mutilate the Scriptures or insert anything into them, against the Catholic faith, in order to compose and confirm a lie and establish our own opinion, so that we are found, contrary to the apostle Paul, adulterating the word of God.

Let us also fear lest what the apostle John says in the Apocalypse come upon us:

> “I testify,” he says, “to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share from the book of life and from the holy city and from the things written in this book” (Rev. 22:18).

He said this concerning falsifiers, not concerning those who simply state what they think without in any way mutilating or corrupting the prophecy.

For Catholic teachers maintain that the Apocalypse of Jesus Christ is the recapitulation and conclusion of the whole of sacred Scripture, and therefore that by this name the entire canonical Scripture must be understood. Likewise, they interpret what is written there concerning “the testimony of Jesus” as referring to the spirit of prophecy of the Old and New Testaments [Col. 0510A].

Whatever the spirit of prophecy has spoken is a testimony to Jesus, who, as it is written, has testimony from the Law and the Prophets. He himself says to the apostles—and therefore to all apostolic men who bear witness to him by word, writing, upright action, or suffering for his name:

> “And you,” he says, “will bear witness to me, because you have been with me from the beginning” (John 15:17).

His truthful promise concerning all his own must likewise be rightly understood: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

Theodore at the Fifth Synod and Macarius at the Sixth Synod were found and convicted as detractors from the testimony of Jesus—that is, from the explanations of sacred Scripture and from the interpreters themselves—and as those who had added falsehoods. They were deposed from the episcopal rank, condemned together with their associates, and sent into perpetual exile [Col. 0510B].

Let us also fear the sentence of Saint Coelestine, pope, written to Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople (Epistle 5), in which he said:

> “Therefore, although your brother Cyril already declares in his letters that he has summoned you, I wish you to understand that, after his first and second letters and after this correction of ours—which is clearly already the third—you are to be understood as entirely separated from the whole fellowship and assembly of Christians, unless the things that have been condemned are immediately corrected and unless you return to that way which Christ declares himself to be.  
>   
> “You have wickedly raised the weapons of despair against the one who had permitted you to be placed over his household as a faithful and wise servant. The blessedness promised for this office has perished for you: you not only fail to give food at the proper time, but even kill with poison those whom he acquired by his own blood and death.”

Let this suffice concerning these matters.

There remain, however, many more things concerning the blasphemies of Gottschalk. Against them we have collected, not in the manner of a disputant but for the assistance of the simple, just as the preceding material, so also what follows from the sayings of the Catholic Fathers, lest we should seem, to those who do not know, to have failed to respond to all of Gottschalk’s ravings. For Saint Peter commands us to be ready, however we may be assailed, to give satisfaction to everyone who asks.

Finally, after his blasphemies against God, to which we have responded above from the judgments of Catholic teachers and general councils, Gottschalk added the following, saying:

## II.

÷ “Let those who believe and say that one can speak of a threefold deity neither authoritatively nor truly look and read in the book *On the Holy Synod*, which was written in Greek at Constantinople under the younger Constantine, that the Arians who worshipped τριθεοτείας (*tritheoteias*), that is, three deities, were rightly condemned and anathematized by one hundred and fifty Fathers. Yet in that very volume it is subsequently stated, in Constantine’s edict, that the threefold deity is to be co-glorified.””

ΧΡ. Here he refutes himself and shows himself to be a compiler, because he appears to say, as though it were acceptable, that the very same book both rejects three deities and professes that a threefold deity is to be glorified.

For in the letter of Pope Agatho (Sixth Synod, Act 4), addressed to the aforementioned Constantine and his imperial colleagues and read aloud at that same synod, it is written:

> “This, therefore, is the position of our evangelical and apostolic faith and its rule of tradition: that, while confessing the holy and inseparable Trinity—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—to be of one deity, one nature and substance or essence, we proclaim it to have one natural will, power, operation, dominion, majesty, authority, and glory; and whatever is said essentially of that same holy Trinity, we comprehend in the singular number, as of one nature of three consubstantial persons, in accordance with the rule established for this purpose.”

Again, in another letter of the same pope (Sixth Synod, Act 4), in the corresponding passage, it is written:

> “We confess the Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity: unity of essence, but Trinity of persons or subsistences. We confess God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit—not three Gods, but one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; not the substances of three names, but one substance of three subsistences. Their essence, substance, or nature is one: one deity, one eternity, one power, one dominion, one glory, one adoration, one essential will and operation of the same holy and inseparable Trinity, which created, governs, and sustains all things.”

And in the letter of Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem (Sixth Synod, Act 11), which was most fully accepted by the Apostolic See and by that synod:

> “We believe in the Trinity in unity, and we glorify unity in Trinity: Trinity because of the three subsistences, but unity because of the singularity of the deity.”

Again:

> “Therefore it has rightly been established by the divine speakers that we should understand unity according to one and singular deity and the identity of essential and natural dominion, but Trinity according to three unconfused subsistences and the diversity of the personal alternation counted threefold.”

A little later he says:

> “For this very thing is both one and is believed to be three, is proclaimed to be three, and is truly announced to be one. Neither is the one, insofar as it is one, received as three, nor is the three, insofar as it is three, understood as one.”

In this way the same Catholic teacher explained the matter plurally elsewhere in the same letter.

And in the edict of the aforementioned Constantine, which Gottschalk recalled to confirm his own opinion, it is written as follows (Sixth Synod, Act 18):

> “We believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity; one substance in three subsistences—unity because of natural union and dominion, but Trinity because of the perfection and riches of the three subsistences of the transcendent goodness.  
>   
> “Unity is truly Trinity, because it is united in deity; and Trinity is truly unity, divided by properties but not separated by eternity. For it is coeternal with itself, and equal in essence and honor. There was never an age when the Son was not with the Father. Whose Father, indeed, would he be if the Son, without beginning, did not exist together with him? Nor was the Holy Spirit absent from both of them.  
>   
> “These three, therefore, are one God, because, when they are understood in relation to one another, the sole difference that individually distinguishes each person within the community of essence distinguishes them inseparably. Thus the Father alone is Father, the Son alone is Son, and the Holy Spirit alone is the Holy Spirit. Through these distinctions they are not converted into one another; rather, they are inseparably divided according to these distinctions, while they share in the unity of essence.  
>   
> “The Trinity is simple, undivided, and uncompounded, consisting of three perfect persons; perfect and superperfect from itself, one nature and deity, and possessing one will and one operation, is to be glorified. Therefore, those whose nature is one have one will and one operation, as Basil, the worshiper of God, taught us.”

After several further passages of that edict, the following is written in the new manuscript:

> “We embrace the holy and universal five synods, including the one at Nicaea of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers who assembled against the madness of Arius and who, with the cooperation of the threefold and co-glorifiable deity, defined the sacred creed of the faith.””

We believe that this feminine, mobile adjective *trina* (“threefold”), which is inserted here, was corrupted by Gottschalk when the aforementioned book was copied in the monastery of Hautvillers, where he was staying, from the authentic copy that Peter, bishop of Arezzo, had lent me [Col. 0512C], just as we have often read that other heretics did.

For elsewhere we find *ter conglorificanda deitate* (“the deity to be co-glorified threefold”), which has the same meaning as if one said *Trinitatis conglorificanda deitate* (“the deity of the Trinity to be co-glorified”), as is also demonstrated in the earlier portions of this book.

The following also gives us a certain indication that Gottschalk falsified this book: at the same time when this manuscript was written in the monastery of Hautvillers, Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, as we said much earlier, compiled a volume of considerable size for Hildegarius, bishop of Meaux, from the books of Saints Hilary and Augustine on the Trinity—the Augustinian book itself having been falsified—with the intention of asserting that there is a threefold deity. His compilation clearly demonstrates the falsehood of its compiler.

Moreover, the book of Saint Augustine *Against Five Kinds of Enemies*, as he himself says in that book—that is, against pagans, Jews, Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians—was at that time given to a certain king by someone who apparently argued that “threefold deity” could be said in a Catholic manner. We discovered that it had been falsified in the following way.

One day, while we were speaking about the unity of the deity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, among other things we said that blessed Augustine repeatedly states in Book 5 *On the Trinity*:

> “Whatever is said of God in relation to himself—that is, substantially—is to be expressed in the singular number both of the individual persons and of the three persons together.”

In response, one of those with whom we were discussing this matter, not contentiously but perhaps thinking that Augustine had indeed said it, produced this book as evidence. He said that *truth* is an essential name, since the Lord says, “I am the truth.” Hence, he said, Augustine wrote, “one and threefold truth.”

When I heard this, I obtained from him the book that had been given to the lord king. Reading it through, I found that, from the place in the book where Saint Augustine says, “Thanks be to you, God, Power; thanks be to you, God the Father, who both showed me your Son and gave me a teacher,” someone who had adulterated it had inserted the following:

> “Thanks be to you, God; thanks be to you, true and one Trinity, one and threefold truth, threefold and one unity.”

After this, Augustine’s statement had been placed again:

> “Thanks be to you, God the Father, who both showed me your Son and gave me a teacher.”

When I read this, I was greatly astonished, since I had found no such expressions in that book, nor anywhere in the work of any Catholic, and certainly not in the work of blessed Augustine [Col. 0513B].

For this reason I had the most ancient manuscripts from many cities and monasteries brought together in one place. Through them I most clearly detected the sacrilege of the falsehood and the sacrilegious falsifier. Among these very ancient books, newly written quires were also brought to me from certain monasteries. In them I found this falsehood inserted, and after investigating more carefully and diligently I discovered that all those quires had been copied from the same muddy source from which the falsified book given to the lord king had been transcribed, and that they had flowed from it through a fraudulent stream.

Since a synod of five provinces was soon to be held—namely, of Reims, Rouen, Tours, Sens, and Lyon—at the city of Soissons, in the presence of the glorious lord King Charles [Col. 0513C] and the bishops who had assembled for that same synod, I brought forward both the falsified book and the authentic, true, and most ancient manuscripts. I gave an authentic book for examination to each bishop, and also to the man who had innocently given the falsified manuscript to the king. I had this document read aloud before everyone at the same synod, as follows:

Augustine says in Book 3 of *On Christian Doctrine* (chapters 1–2):

> “When the proper words make a passage ambiguous, we must first see whether we have improperly distinguished or pronounced it. When careful attention has perceived that it is uncertain how it should be distinguished or pronounced, let it consult the rule of faith, which it has received from the clearer passages of Scripture and from the authority of the Church.  
>   
> “But if both parts of the ambiguity, or even all of them if there are more, sound according to the faith, then the text of the discourse itself must be consulted through the preceding and following passages that placed the ambiguity in the middle, so that we may see to which of the several meanings that present themselves it gives its support and allows to be woven into itself.”

Let us therefore obey the counsel and teaching of blessed Augustine. First let us see what has been inserted here in this book, and only then let us examine what precedes and follows.

The inserted passage is:

> “Thanks be to you, true and one Trinity, one and threefold truth, threefold and one unity.”

In the preceding material it is written:

> “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people—not to those who divide the holy unity, but to people of good will.”

And again:

> “Eternity is one, and substance is one. I say that the Father and the Son are God; I say that they are one: duality in offspring, unity in deity. The one birth makes another; but divinity shows one. When I say ‘Son,’ he is another; when I say ‘God,’ he is one. Be ashamed, Arians. The executioners of Pilate did not dare to tear apart the tunic of the man already judged and hanging on the cross, yet you attempt to divide the love of God who sits in heaven—or rather, to divide love itself, which is God. But try, as much as you can; try! You have rushed into hell; you will not tear it apart now.”

And in the following material it is written:

> “This man has just come, he has overturned the world, and he divides the unity of the faith and separates the Trinity.”

And again:

> “Whoever separates the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in eternity, substance, or communion, and denies that he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, is full of an unclean spirit and empty of the Holy Spirit. For this reason God is called love: not because he divides unity into parts, but because he ineffably binds together the Trinity. For the Trinity itself is one God, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy, who protects those who believe in him.”

These preceding and following words of the Catholic blessed Augustine, concordant with all Catholics and with the orthodox faith, clearly show that the words inserted here were not uttered by Augustine, but were fraudulently introduced here by someone corrupting the word of God and the Catholic faith.
