And again, following the counsel and teaching of that same blessed Augustine, let us consult the rule of faith. Athanasius says:

> “This is the Catholic faith: that we venerate one God in a Trinity of persons, and a Trinity of persons in the unity of the Godhead; neither confusing the persons, so that there are not three, nor separating the substance, so that it is threefold. For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; but the divinity—that is, the Godhead—of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. As the same Athanasius, Ambrose, and Augustine say, it is the unity of the Trinity.”

Let us also inquire, in accordance with the emperors’ edicts, through the earlier and more truthful witnesses whom you hold in your hands, whether any ambiguity remains concerning this most certain matter. Since the law says—and the Lord confirms this in the Gospel—that “every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” [Col. 0514D], and since the Apostle likewise requires the same number of witnesses in an accusation against a presbyter, and the Council of Nicaea, following apostolic teaching, seeks witnesses of the same number against a novice bishop, while the law of public affairs demands seven until we produce more, let us accept the words of blessed Augustine set forth above on the testimony not merely of seven but of more than fourteen ancient and earlier witnesses. None of these contains anything concerning the falsehood inserted above under the name of blessed Augustine. Once the truth has been disclosed, let us therefore believe that he is innocent of this blemish of falsification.

After this document had been read through, and the genuine and most ancient books—which were found to contain nothing of this falsification—had been examined, it was proved that the book of blessed Augustine mentioned above had been corrupted. Then the same man who had given the falsified book to the king said: “You will patiently hear what I say”; and he brought forward a testimony of blessed Ambrose concerning the divinity of the Trinity, to confirm the imposture discovered in the book of blessed Augustine. This thoroughly Catholic testimony most clearly contradicted that imposture, and we were all astonished that he had produced such a testimony: it not only failed to confirm the same opinion, but actually weakened the falsity by the truth.

Then he said that in the book of blessed Augustine lent to him, entitled *On the Words of the Lord*, he had found the heading of his sermon “On the One Trinity and the Threefold Unity.” We were likewise astonished that he had paid attention only to the heading and had not intelligently read what followed, said in a Catholic manner by blessed Augustine in the same sermon. For, speaking popularly against the Sabellians and Arians, he says in that sermon (*On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 63, chapters 1–2):

> “We have,” he says, “a distinct Trinity; and if we consider the places, I dare to say—although I say it fearfully—nevertheless I dare to say that the Trinity is, as it were, separable.”

A little later (chapter 2):

> “These three are separated, as it were, by places; they are separated by offices; they are separated by works.”

Thus, whether in this manner or in this sense, by that figure of speech called *metonymy*, that is, transference of name, the title of this sermon reads “On the One Trinity and the Threefold Unity.”

After the foregoing, blessed Augustine immediately added in the same sermon:

> “Let someone say to me: Show me the inseparable Trinity.”

And shortly afterward (the same chapter):

> “Nevertheless, by the faith itself we most rightly and firmly hold that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are an inseparable Trinity, one God, not three gods. Yet one God in such a way that the Son is not the Father, the Father is not the Son, and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. We therefore know this ineffable divinity, remaining in itself, renewing all things, creating, recreating, sending, recalling, judging, and liberating, as both ineffable and inseparable.”

Again, in the same chapter:

> “Where is the inseparable Trinity? When, therefore, I draw this meaning from many things and gather it into one God, the inseparable Trinity, so that I may see something to say.”

And after much more (chapter 5):

> “Divinity is beyond bodily places: let no one seek it as though it were in space. It is invisibly and inseparably present everywhere, neither greater in one part nor smaller in another, but wholly everywhere and divided nowhere. Who sees this? Who comprehends this? Let us restrain ourselves and remember from whom and about what we are speaking. Whatever that is which God is, let it be piously believed, holily contemplated, and, insofar as it is granted and possible, ineffably understood.”

Again, after some further discussion (chapter 7):

> “These three things are in you, which you can count but cannot separate. Observe, then, these three—memory, understanding, and will—which, I say, are pronounced separately but operate inseparably.”

Again, after much more (chapter 10):

> “I believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit can, through certain visible signs and through certain forms of assumed creation, be demonstrated separately and operate inseparably. This is enough. I do not say that the Father is memory, the Son understanding, and the Spirit will; I do not dare to say that this should be understood in any such way. Let us reserve greater matters for the wise; being weak, what can we do for the weak? I do not say these things as though they were to be equated with that Trinity, as though they were to be directed toward an analogy—that is, toward some principle of comparison. I do not say this; but what do I say? Behold, in you I have found three things demonstrated inseparably and operating inseparably, and each one of these three has become a name made from the three, though it belongs not to three things but to one thing among these three.”

Behold, in this sense blessed Augustine shows that the heading of his sermon, entitled “On the One Trinity and the Threefold Unity,” must be understood.

In a similar sense, while still a presbyter, he also wrote in the book *On Two Souls*:

> “The threefold unity which the Catholic Church venerates,”

meaning—as he himself understood it—that there is unity in substance and Trinity in persons.

He records in the fourteenth place of his *Revisions* that he wrote this book; and in the twenty-fifth place he shows that he dealt with the book *On Eighty-Three Various Questions*. Then, in the forty-first place, he shows that he wrote the book *On the Trinity*, which he composed over a long period, with great labor and much examination.

Therefore, in *On Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter 24, concerning the Trinity of substance and divinity, he says what seemed to him more probable and safer to say. But concerning this question also, in the aforesaid book of the *Revisions*, he writes that he later treated it better in the book *On the Trinity*. There he says, in chapter 4 of book 1:

> “All Catholic writers,” he says, “have aimed to teach, according to the Scriptures, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit manifest the divine unity by an inseparable equality of one substance; and therefore there are not three gods but one.”

This he confirms most openly and consistently, in every respect and in all his writings, without any retraction. In the preface to his *Revisions* he says:

> “Therefore, whoever will read these works should not imitate me in my errors, but in my progress toward better things. For whoever reads my little works in the order in which they were written will perhaps discover how I progressed through writing. So that he may do this, I shall take care in this work, insofar as I can, to make that order known to him.”

In this same sense Pelagius, bishop of the city of Rome, in the sermon on the faith addressed to King Childebert at the king’s request, made through the magnificent man Rufinus, that Pelagius might write to him whether he would receive the *Tome* of Pope Leo of blessed memory and clear himself of the scandal of suspicion that had been spread about him throughout Gaul (Pelagius, letter 16), speaks of the threefold unity and the one Trinity in this way:

> “I believe,” he says, “in one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

And shortly afterward:

> “These are three persons, or three subsistences, of one essence or nature, of one power, one operation, one blessedness, and one authority, so that the unity is threefold and the Trinity is one, in accordance with the truth of the Lord’s saying: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matthew 28:19). He says ‘in the name,’ not ‘in the names,’ so that he might show one God through the undivided name of the divine essence, and might teach the distinction of the persons demonstrated by their proper characteristics. For since there is one name of divinity for the three, the equality of the persons is shown; and again, the equality of the persons permits nothing foreign or accidental to be understood in them. Thus each one of them is true and perfect God, and all three together are one true and perfect God: namely, from the fullness of divinity, nothing less is to be understood in each individual, and nothing more in the three.”

From these words, as also from the foregoing statements of blessed Augustine, it is most clearly evident that the divinity, which is the unity of the Trinity, ought not to be believed or called threefold. Rather, because of the inseparability and equality of the three persons, who are one in divinity, it should be believed and called inseparable, wholly full and perfect in each individual person. Accordingly, the heading of the sermon of Saint Augustine should be understood in the sense stated above, as he himself explained it.

And because heretics have appeared to find scandals in these words—which Catholics both understand and utter in a Catholic manner—as they have also done with many words of sacred Scripture, the orthodox teachers and masters of the Church wished entirely to avoid the expression “threefold unity,” just as they avoided “threefold divinity” and “three substances” among the Latins. They spoke in this way:

> “That is called a Trinity from which a whole is made out of certain three things, as it were a Trinity—that is, a unity of three things—such as memory, understanding, and will, in which the mind possesses within itself a certain image of the divine Trinity. For although they are three, they are one, because each remains in itself and all are in all. Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are Trinity and unity. The same thing is one and three: one because of the communion of majesty, three because of the distinct property of the persons. For the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; yet the one is another person, not another thing, because they are equally simple, equally immutable, good, and coeternal.

> “The Father alone is not from another and therefore alone is called unbegotten. The Son alone is born from the Father and therefore alone is called begotten. The Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son and therefore alone is called the Spirit of both.

> “In this Trinity some names are appellative and others proper. The proper names are essential, such as God, Lord, Almighty, Immutable, and Immortal. They are proper because they signify the substance itself, since they are one. The appellative names, however, are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as well as unbegotten, begotten, and proceeding. These are also relative, because they refer to one another. When ‘God’ is said, it is essence, because it is said with reference to himself; but when ‘Father,’ ‘Son,’ and ‘Holy Spirit’ are said, they are said relatively, because they refer to one another. The Father is not called Father with reference to himself but relatively to the Son, because the Son is his Son. Likewise the Son is called Son relatively, because he has the Father. Likewise the Holy Spirit is called Spirit relatively, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. These appellations signify that they refer to one another.

> “The substance itself, by which they are one, is therefore Trinity in the relative names of the persons. The divinity is not tripled but exists in singularity; for if it were tripled, we would introduce a plurality of gods.

> “The name ‘gods’ is applied in the plural to angels and holy human beings because they are not equal in merit. Concerning them the Psalm says: ‘I said, You are gods’ (Psalm 81:6). But concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of their one and equal divinity, it is shown that the name is not ‘gods’ but ‘God,’ as the Apostle says: ‘For us, however, there is one God’ (1 Corinthians 8:6); or as the divine voice says: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God’ (Deuteronomy 6:4), so that there is both a Trinity and one Lord God.

> “Among the Greeks the faith concerning the Trinity is expressed in this way: μία οὐσία (*mia ousia*), that is, one nature or one essence, three hypostases. This is rendered in Latin either as three persons or three substances. For Latin usage properly speaks of God only in terms of essence; it does not properly speak of substance but does so abusively, since among the Greeks substance properly means person, not nature.”

For this reason Saint Jerome, writing to Pope Damasus, says (letter 57):

> “Let it be enough for us to say ‘one substance, three subsisting persons,’ perfect, equal, and coeternal. If you wish, let the term ‘three hypostases’ be left unmentioned and let one expression be retained; it is not a sign of good suspicion when words disagree though the meaning is the same. Let the faith which we have stated be sufficient. Or, if you think that we ought to say ‘three hypostases’ together with their interpretations, we do not deny it; but believe me, poison lies beneath honey. Satan’s angel has transformed himself into an angel of light.”

A little earlier he says:

> “And how does God claim for himself as proper the common name ‘essence’? But because that nature alone is perfect, and the one divinity subsists in three persons, which truly exists and is one nature, whoever says that there are three—that is, three hypostases, or *ousiai*—attempts under the name of piety to assert three natures. And if that is so, why do we separate ourselves from Arius in our walls while being joined to him in faithlessness? Let Ursicinus be joined to your blessedness, and let Auxentius be associated with Ambrose. May this be far from the Roman faith; may the religious hearts of the peoples not drink in so great a sacrilege.”

Again, somewhat earlier:

> “We proclaim: If anyone confesses three hypostases, or three *enhypostata*, that is, three subsisting persons, let him be anathema; and because we do not learn the terminology, we are judged heretics. But if anyone, understanding *hypostasis* as *ousia*, does not say one hypostasis in three persons, he is alien from Christ; and under this confession we are likewise branded with the same mark of union. Distinguish, if you please—I beg you, I shall not fear to say ‘three hypostases.’ If you order it, let a new faith be composed after Nicaea, and let us orthodox Christians confess with the Arians in similar words. The entire school of secular literature knows no meaning for *hypostasis* other than *ousia*; and who, I ask, will proclaim three substances with sacrilegious lips?

> “There is one nature of God, and it alone truly exists, for that which subsists does not have its existence from elsewhere but is its own. Other things that have been created, even if they seem to exist, do not truly exist, because at one time they were not, and what once was not can again cease to be. God alone, who is eternal—that is, who has no beginning—truly bears the name of essence. Therefore he speaks to Moses from the bush: ‘I am who I am’ (Exodus 3:14), and again: ‘He who is has sent me’ (ibid.).”

Hilary, in the book *On the Synods*, says:

> “I fear these likenesses, which do not arise from unity of nature. For I fear, brothers, the heresies of the East, sprouting up at particular times. In their avoidance of the madness of Arius, Catholic men did not wish the unity to be called threefold by anyone, but spoke instead of the one divinity, Godhead, nature, essence, and substance of the Holy Trinity.”

In this statement also, in which one substance is proclaimed, the Sabellians laid a snare, as Saint Hilary likewise demonstrates in the aforementioned book *On the Synods*:

> “Many among us, dearest brothers, proclaim one substance of the Father and the Son in such a way that they may seem to proclaim it not so much piously as impiously. For this expression contains both the consciousness of faith and a prepared fraud.

> “If, according to the proper character of nature and likeness—so that likeness does not merely present an appearance but preserves a genus—we piously proclaim one substance, provided that by ‘one substance’ we understand a likeness of property, so that the fact that they are one does not signify singularity but equality—by ‘equality’ I mean the absence of difference in likeness, so that likeness is understood as equality—then one is said to be one because he is equal. But ‘one,’ in which equality is signified, must not be claimed to mean one solitary individual.

> “Therefore ‘one substance,’ if it does not destroy the subsisting person and does not divide one substance shared between two, may be piously proclaimed, since by the proper character of birth and by the likeness of nature it is so without difference that it is called one. But if the Father and Son are called of one substance for this reason: that the one subsisting under the meaning of two names is one and alone, then, although we confess one substance, we do not retain in our consciousness the Son confessed by name, if we say that he is uniquely and singly both Father and Son.”

After some further discussion:

> “The likeness of nature is therefore free, brothers, from the suspicion of insult. Nor can the Son be thought not to possess the proper character of the Father’s nature because he is similar, since there is no likeness except from equality of nature; and equality of nature cannot exist unless there is unity—not unity of person, but of kind.

> “This is the pious faith, this is the religious consciousness, this is the saving doctrine: not to deny one substance of the Father and the Son because he is similar, but to proclaim him similar because they are one.

> “Dearest brothers, having set forth with faithful and pious understanding the one substance, called in Greek ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*), and the like substance, called ὁμοιούσιον (*homoiousion*), and having most fully exposed the errors that might arise from the deceptive brevity or dangerous nakedness of the words, I must direct the remainder of my discourse to the holy Eastern bishops, so that, since no suspicion concerning our faith remains among us, those things which still give rise to suspicion because of the words may be cleared away.”

Because of these frauds and scandalous snares, which the Arians, detracting from the unity of the divinity in the Holy Trinity, and the Sabellians, detracting from the distinct property of the persons, were placing in the path of right understanding, our fathers and teachers—Catholic men, doctors, and rulers of the Church—because, as it is written, “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Daniel 12:4), preferred to say and write “one God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,” namely the Trinity, ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*), that is, of one substance or consubstantial, inseparable and indivisible, rather than “threefold unity” and “one Trinity.” They handed this down for their successors to say and write by their decision [Col. 0520B].

Their purpose was to prevent anyone, by saying “threefold unity” and adding to that unity a number which belongs to the threefold expression, from making the same unity countable and from seeming, like the Arians, to divide the divinity—that is, the unity of the Trinity. This can be gathered from the foregoing words of Saint Jerome and, in this work, from the letter of Pope Gregory to Leander, bishop of Spalatum (book 1, letter 41), part of which the discerning reader will find placed in its proper location. Likewise, by saying “one Trinity,” they wished to prevent the distinct property of the three persons in that holy and inseparable Trinity from being removed, lest the Sabellians bring accusations, as anyone attentive to the preceding words of Saint Hilary can understand.

Therefore blessed Augustine himself, whose sermon is said to bear the title “On the One Trinity and the Threefold Unity,” writes in book 7 of *On the Trinity*, as though with a censor’s fingernail, as he had done concerning many other matters (chapter 6):

> “Nor do we speak of the Trinity as three persons or subsistences, one essence and one God, as though three things subsisted from one matter, even if whatever that thing is were unfolded in these three. For nothing else belongs to that essence apart from this Trinity. Nevertheless, we say three persons of the same essence, or three persons who are one essence; but we do not say three persons from the same essence, as though there were one thing there which is essence and another which is person.”

And in book 15 (chapter 7):

> “Can we say that there is a Trinity in God in such a way that something belonging to God is not itself God? Certainly not. But that Trinity in its entirety is nothing other than God; in its entirety it is nothing other than the Trinity; nor does anything belong to the nature of God which does not belong to that Trinity.”

Those three persons are therefore of one substance and of one essence. We must hold and follow the royal and safest path in the true understanding of this Holy Trinity amid the snares of those robbers, namely the Arians and Sabellians.

As we showed above, blessed Athanasius, and Saint Augustine in the book addressed to Pope Laurence concerning the Creed, most aptly demonstrates this, saying:

> “This is the Trinity,” he says, “hidden everywhere and appearing everywhere, distinguished by names and persons, yet the inseparable substance of the divinity.”

And in the sermon on the Holy Spirit, that he is of the same substance and divinity as the Father and the Son:

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, when, after being glorified, he rose from the dead and was about to ascend into heaven to the Father, left this sacrament of faith to his disciples, that is, to the apostles. For he said: ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you’ (Matthew 28:19–20). The effect of the things themselves dictates that we believe in the power of three persons in one divinity.”

And in the sermon on the mystery of baptism:

> “When anyone hears ‘Father,’ ‘Son,’ or ‘Holy Spirit,’ let no one think that we confess three gods. May such sacrilege be far from our faith, for we know by his own testimony that there is one God: ‘I am God, and there is no other besides me; a just God and a Savior, there is none besides me. Turn to me and you shall be saved, for I am God from the end of the earth, and there is no other besides me’ (Isaiah 45:21–22). And in another book: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God’ (Deuteronomy 6:4). And again: ‘The Lord is God in heaven above and on earth beneath, and there is no other besides him’ (Deuteronomy 4:39).

> “We therefore hold and believe three persons, that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of one power, one substance, one eternity, one will, and also one divinity; and we venerate the whole Trinity under the name of one God. To believe in several gods is the impiety of the pagans.”

Again:

> “Not to believe that the three persons are of one substance in one divinity, and equal or coeternal, is heretical madness, since this authority of Christ, which we have cited, is manifest: ‘Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’”

Augustine likewise says in book 5 of *On the Trinity* (chapter 8):

> “This must especially be held: whatever is said with reference to itself of that most excellent and divine sublimity is said substantially; but whatever is said with reference to something is said not substantially but relatively. Such is the force of the same substance in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that whatever is said of each with reference to itself is understood not in the plural collectively but in the singular.”

Again, in book 5 (chapter 10):

> “Nothing is greater than God. Therefore he is great with that greatness which he himself is, since he is that very greatness; and therefore, just as we do not say three essences, so neither do we say three greatnesses. The same must be said of the goodness, eternity, and omnipotence of God, and of every category that can be predicated of God, when it is said with reference to himself.”

And in book 6 (chapter 4):

> “For God, to be is the same as to be almighty, or just, or wise; and the same applies to whatever you say concerning that simple multiplicity and multiple simplicity by which his substance is signified.”

And in book 8:

> “The Father and Son are therefore one essence, one greatness, one truth, and one wisdom; and the Holy Spirit is not separated from them. Concerning him the Son says in the Gospel: ‘I shall ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth’ (John 14:16). And the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘I am the truth’ (ibid., 14:6). In God, therefore, ‘truth’ is a substantial name. And who is greater, as Augustine says in book 5 of *On the Trinity* (chapter 2), than the one who said to his servant: ‘I am who I am,’ and, ‘You shall say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you’ (Exodus 3:14)?”

Therefore there is not “threefold truth,” as the impostor fraudulently inserted into the words of blessed Augustine, but one truth: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because substance cannot be divided.

As the same blessed Augustine says in the same book, against the five kinds of enemies:

> “Eternity is one and substance.”

And in book 6 of *On the Trinity* (chapter 7):

> “The goodness of God is the same as his wisdom and greatness, and the same truth is all those things; in him it is not one thing to be blessed and another to be great, wise, true, or good, or simply to be. Therefore, just as there is not a threefold essence or a threefold nature, so there is neither a threefold divinity nor a threefold truth.”

Boethius, in the book addressed to John, Roman deacon and afterward bishop, whom blessed Gregory shows in the *Dialogues* to have been glorified by martyrdom during the persecution of the Arian king Theodoric, says, as he himself acknowledges, from the words of blessed Augustine:

> “There is therefore one substance of the three. It cannot in any way be separated or divided, nor is it joined together into one as though from parts; rather, it is simply one. Whatever, therefore, is predicated of the divine substance must be common to the three.”

A little later:

> “If, therefore, their one divinity is one substance, the name ‘God’ may be predicated substantially of the divinity. Thus the Father is truth, the Son is truth, and the Holy Spirit is truth; the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three truths but one truth. If, therefore, there is one substance in them and one truth, truth must necessarily be predicated substantially of goodness, immutability, justice, omnipotence, and all the other things which we predicate individually both of each one and of all together. It is clear that these are said substantially.”

Again:

> “For the one who is Father does not transmit this name to the Son or to the Holy Spirit. Consequently, this name is not a substantial one. For if it were substantial, as ‘God,’ ‘truth,’ ‘justice,’ and ‘substance’ itself are, it would be said of the others as well. Likewise, the Son alone receives this name; for he is not joined with the others in it, as he is in the other things mentioned above. The Holy Spirit also is not the same as the Father and the Son. From this, therefore, we understand that ‘Father,’ ‘Son,’ and ‘Holy Spirit’ are not said substantially of the divinity itself, but in another manner. For if they were predicated substantially, they would be said both of each individually and of all together. It is clear that these are said with reference to something.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The Trinity consists in the plurality of persons, while unity consists in the simplicity of substance.”

Again:

> “The Trinity therefore does not belong to substance. Consequently, neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the Trinity is predicated substantially of God, but, as has been said, relatively. ‘God,’ ‘truth,’ ‘justice,’ ‘goodness,’ ‘omnipotence,’ ‘substance,’ ‘immutability,’ ‘power,’ ‘wisdom,’ and whatever else of this kind can be conceived are said substantially of the divinity.”

Again, concerning the Trinity (*To Symmachus*):

> “Substance contains unity; relation multiplies the Trinity.”

Again:

> “Since the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and God has no differences by which he differs from God, none of them differs from another. Where differences are absent, plurality is absent; where plurality is absent, unity is present.”

Again:

> “Where there is no difference, there is absolutely no plurality; therefore there is no number, but only unity.”

Again:

> “Therefore, if ‘God’ is predicated three times of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the threefold predication does not thereby produce a number. This threatens those who establish a difference of merits among them. But among Catholics, who establish nothing in difference and posit the form as it is, believing that what is is nothing other than what it is, the repetition of the same thing rather than an enumeration of different things rightly seems to be present when we say: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, and this Trinity is one God.”

Ambrose, in book 1 of *On the Holy Spirit* (chapter 15), says:

> “Christ is truth; the Spirit is truth. For you have in the letter of John: ‘Because the Spirit is truth’ (1 John 5:6). Therefore the Spirit is called not only of truth but also truth itself, just as the Son is proclaimed to be truth, who says: ‘I am the way, and the truth, and the life’ (John 14:6). The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are therefore one; there is one name of the Trinity and one inseparable essence.”

And in book 1 of *On the Faith* (chapter 7):

> “Believe that the Son came forth from God, as he himself testifies, saying: ‘I proceeded from God and came’ (John 8:42). And elsewhere: ‘I came forth from God’ (John 16:27). He who proceeded from God and came forth from God can possess nothing other than what belongs to God. Therefore he is not only God but true God, true from true, and so true that he himself is truth. Thus, if we seek the name, he is truth; if we seek the natural majesty, the Son is true God to such a degree that he is also proper to the Father. For it is written: ‘He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all’ (Romans 8:32). He handed him over, certainly, according to the flesh. The proper character of divinity is the truth of property, the mercy of piety, and the offering of security.”

Therefore what was deceitfully and falsely inserted into the words of blessed Augustine—“threefold truth”—cannot stand, as Boethius likewise demonstrates in the aforesaid book, saying (to the deacon John):

> “Substance contains unity; relation multiplies the Trinity.”

Ambrose shows this substance of the Trinity when he sings in the Catholic hymn:

> “You, Unity of the Trinity.”

And Augustine, as though explaining it, says in book 1 of *On the Trinity*:

> “The divinity which is the unity of the Trinity.”

Blessed Ambrose also agrees with this in another hymn, saying:

> “O blessed light of the Trinity,”

And the principal unity.

But that statement inserted into the same compilation—“a threefold and one unity”—cannot stand, as blessed Ambrose demonstrates in Book I of *On the Faith*, chapter 2, where he says:

> “There is a fullness of divinity in the Father, and there is a fullness of divinity in the Son; yet it is not a divergent but one divinity, nor is what is one confused, nor is what is undifferentiated multiple. For if, as it is written, the soul and heart of all believers were one (Acts 4:32); if everyone who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17); if, as the Apostle said, a man and his wife are one flesh (Matt. 19:5); if all human beings, insofar as nature is concerned, are of one substance; if Scripture says this of human beings: ‘For many are one’ (1 Cor. 10:17)—and none of these can be compared with divine things—how much more are the Father and the Son one in divinity, where there is no difference whatsoever either of substance or of will? For otherwise, how do we say that there is one God? Difference produces plurality; the unity of power excludes numerical quantity, because unity is not a number, but is the principle of all things.”

And Boethius, in the aforementioned book (*On the Trinity*, addressed to Symmachus), says:

> “Where there is no difference, there is no plurality at all; therefore there is no number, but unity alone.”

And again:

> “For one is the thing itself; unity is that by which we call something one.”

The arithmeticians likewise say:

> “One is the seed of number, not a number; and the simple numbers, which have no other part except unity alone—for example, three has only its third part, five only its fifth, and seven only its seventh—have one part alone.”

Ambrose likewise says in the aforementioned first book, chapter 2:

> “The Arians must necessarily deny either the divinity of the Father or that of the Son, unless they believe the unity of the same divinity.”

And again:

> “The unity of operation does not make divinity plural.”

And again:

> “For what other judgment can there be where there is unity of divinity?”

And again:

> “He was present in the form of an angel, guarding it, so that in the number of the Trinity there might be one praise of power.”

Many other testimonies are found in the same books, showing that one cannot speak, in Catholic fashion, of a threefold unity in God, or a threefold divinity, a threefold nature, or a threefold substance. For unity, divinity, nature, and substance in God lack both plurality and the number implied by “threefold” and by “Trinity.”

And the expression “one unity,” which occurs in the same false insertion, destroys what is there called “threefold truth” and “threefold unity.” For when one says “one” or “unity,” without specifying what is one or what is unity, one must understand “one substance”; and the unity of substance has no plurality, and therefore no number, which is implied by “threefold” and by “Trinity.”

Accordingly, Augustine, explaining the Apostle’s statement in his exposition of Psalm 38, “But one thing I do, forgetting what lies behind” (Phil. 3:13), says:

> “‘One thing,’ he says—that one thing is this: ‘Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us’ (John 14:8). ‘One thing,’ which is also called ‘one’ in another psalm: ‘One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life’ (Ps. 26:4). Why? ‘That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord.’”

And in the book *Against Maximinus* we read:

> “‘He who plants and he who waters are one’ (1 Cor. 3:8); but both were human beings, and they were of the same substance, not different substances.”

Again we read, with Christ himself saying:

> “‘That they may be one, just as we are one’ (John 17:21). He did not say, ‘that they and we may be one,’ but ‘that they may be one’ in their own nature and in their own substance, united and joined together, in a certain way, by the quality of concord. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one because of their undivided and identical nature.”

For “they are one” is one thing, “we are one” another, and “he is one” another. When one says “they are one,” even if one does not state what they are one in, one substance is understood. When one says “he is one” of two different substances, one must ask, “one in what respect?” For example, soul and body are different substances, yet they constitute one human being; the spirit of a human being and the Spirit of God are different substances, yet when a person cleaves to the Lord, he is one spirit. The Apostle added “spirit”; he did not say “they are one.” But where it says “they are one,” one substance is signified.

So too when the Apostle says: “We know that an idol is nothing” (1 Cor. 8:4), and: “There is no God but one.” For although there are those who are called many gods and many lords, whether in heaven or on earth, for us there is nevertheless one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we for him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him (ibid., 4–6). He adds “who” or “what” is one. When he says “one God, the Father,” and “one Lord, Jesus,” he distinguishes the persons by naming the Father and the Son, while he indicates one substance by saying “God.”

Elsewhere, therefore, speaking of the Trinity of persons, he demonstrates the unity of one divinity when he says: “From him”—that is, from the Father—“and through him”—through the Son—“and in him”—that is, in the Holy Spirit—“are all things; to him be glory” (Rom. 11:36). He did not add “to them be glory,” because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; but unity is believed and proclaimed in the divinity, because the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, their glory equal, and their majesty coeternal.

But the impostor of falsehood, and the insulter of the words of Saint Augustine—whoever he may have been—not daring to insert openly “a threefold and one divinity,” lest he be detected, introduced an expression of equivalent force. By means of the substantive term “truth,” he said “threefold and one truth,” even though, as Augustine says, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three truths, nor a threefold truth, but one truth, just as they are one essence and one life. By adding “threefold and one unity,” he could thus prove that one ought to say “threefold and one divinity.”

He did not want to insert the words of Gothescalc, namely, that “divinity is threefold personally and one naturally,” lest he be recognized and rejected on that account. Yet he inserted, without qualification, “threefold and one unity,” so that his words would not differ in meaning from Gothescalc’s words.

But, as it is written, “In vain is the net spread in the sight of the birds” (Prov. 1:17). The sacrilegious fraud is evident, as has been plainly shown and will be shown further, because this insertion is destroyed not only by reason and authority, but also by its own argument.

It is destroyed by reason because, as Augustine says, “the divinity of the Trinity is unity,” and the unity by which the three persons are one cannot be threefold. In nature—that is, in divinity, or essence—the three persons are one, that is, one God; they are not one person, namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

It is destroyed by authority because, as Boethius says in his book *On the Trinity*:

> “In the number by which we count, the repetition of units produces plurality; but in the number of things, the repetition of units does not produce plurality, as when the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three times declared to be God.”

And again:

> “One is the thing itself; unity is that by which we call something one.”

Ambrose likewise says in Book I of *On the Faith*, chapter 2:

> “Unity is not a number, but is itself the principle of all things.”

This insertion is also destroyed by its own argument when it says “a threefold and one unity,” because unity, insofar as it is one, cannot be threefold, just as the Trinity, insofar as it is threefold, cannot be one.

The Trinity, namely, cannot be one in respect of the persons, as Sabellius wanted; nor can the unity of the Trinity, that is, the divinity, be threefold, as Arius taught. Catholic faith, however, is—as Athanasius teaches and the unanimous agreement of Catholics confirms—that we venerate one God in the Trinity of persons, against Sabellius, and the Trinity of persons in the unity of divinity, against Arius: neither confusing the persons, as Sabellius did, as though there were not three, nor separating the substance, as Arius did, as though it were threefold.

Therefore, if the expression improperly placed by the impostor, “one unity,” is understood in this way—even though it cannot otherwise be rightly understood—then, since it is above all those things of which unity can be predicated, the three persons of the holy Trinity, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, have one, that is, singular, unity, and their divinity is one. Or, if it is expressed more clearly as “divinity,” it destroys what was placed earlier, namely, that unity should be threefold: that is, the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which is the unity of the Trinity.

The perverse doctrine must therefore be eradicated, and what the Catholics teach must be followed: the Trinity—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is spoken of relatively, that is, relationally; hence plurality exists in the persons. But “truth,” “essence,” and “divinity”—which, as Augustine says, “is the unity of the Trinity”—are said of God in himself, that is, substantially and therefore singularly. Thus the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. They are not called “one” in the respect in which they are three, nor “three” in the respect in which they are one.

But, as blessed Ambrose sings:

> “One in power,” that is, substantially, as Augustine says, “and three personally.”

It has therefore become clear and has been demonstrated that the book of blessed Augustine *Against the Five Kinds of Enemies* was compiled, adulterated, and falsified, and that this heretical perversity was inserted by some falsifier. The vigilance of Catholics discovered a similar practice at the Fifth Synod: certain testimonies from Catholic books had been mutilated by heretics to confirm their own perversity, while certain false passages had been inserted into Catholic works using the words of Catholics.

Thus, we read that Macarius, bishop of Antioch, was detected in this manner at the Sixth Synod. So too Donatus, as Augustine says in the book of his *Retractations*, removed from the statement, “He who washes after touching a dead person and again touches him, what does his washing profit him?” (Ecclus. 34:30), the words “and again touches him,” in order to confirm his heresy. The Arians likewise erased from the Gospel what the Savior says: “For God is Spirit” (John 4:24). They did not wish to believe that the Holy Spirit was God almighty.

Similarly, those who were not from God and who, by their perverse doctrine, wanted to separate Christ’s divinity from the dispensation of his humanity erased from John’s Epistle the verse that says: “Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God” (1 John 4:3), lest they be convicted of their error by its authority.

Finally, Nestorius showed that he did not know that this statement had been included in the authentic copies; therefore he did not fear dissolving Jesus, thereby making himself an outsider in this matter. He said that the blessed virgin Mary was the mother not of God but only of a human being. Thus he made one person belong to humanity and another to divinity, refusing to believe that there is one Christ in the Word of God, the flesh, and the soul, but proclaiming separately one Son of God and another son of man.

And Felix, formerly bishop of the city of Urgell—unfortunate Felix—in the book of blessed Hilary, where that saint had said, “The humility of the flesh is adored,” adulterated every copy he was able to seize in the time of the emperor Charlemagne, changing it to “the humility of the flesh is adopted,” so that, since he could not support his opinion by truth, he might support it by falsehood.

So too this adulterator of the words of blessed Augustine, in accordance with what is written, “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John 7:18), inserted his own falsehood into the truth, so that he might boast against the truth. In this way Gothescalc, insofar as it depended on him, changed truth into falsehood by substituting “threefold [divinity]” for “three times” or “the divinity of the Trinity” in the decree of the Sixth Synod.

Even if the decree contained the expression in the form in which we believe he adulterated it, on the basis of a Greek interpretation, or even if some claim that it appears in this form in certain other ancient books, Gothescalc’s invention, or that of his associates, would still derive no support from it. For the Greek language, by the idiom of its own speech, can correctly express certain things that the Latin language does not accept, especially in matters pertaining to the faith.

Thus, in speaking of the holy Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the Greeks say “one essence” and “three substances severally” (*tres suatim substantias*), meaning subsistences, that is, persons. The Latin language does not accept this usage. A word-for-word translation, just as it often loses the proper harmony of a language, can also lack understanding and disturb the meaning of the faith. It may therefore be that the translator of that decree, translating word for word, did not translate its sound meaning.

We, however, should follow what Leo writes to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (*Epistle* 95, in the preface): we must recognize as authoritative what is found neither contrary to the evangelical commands nor opposed to the decrees of the saints. From these we have learned that we must believe and confess one and the same divinity, full and perfect, in the three persons of the holy and inseparable Trinity.

Accordingly, we have no doubt that Gothescalc incurred and must endure the condemnation pronounced by that same holy Sixth Synod, which, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, imposed it upon all who held opinions contrary to what it had divinely inspired and decreed (*Acts of the Sixth Synod*, act 18, at the end):

> “Having formed these definitions among ourselves with every caution and diligence on every side, we decree that no one may bring forward, write, compose, hold, or teach any other faith. But if anyone should presume either to compose, bring forward, teach, or transmit another faith, or a creed for those wishing to be converted to the knowledge of the truth from paganism, Judaism, or any heresy, or should introduce a novelty of speech or an invention of language to subvert what has now been determined by us, then, if they are bishops or clerics, the bishops are to be deprived of the episcopate and the clerics of the clergy; but if they are monks or laypeople, they are to be anathematized. And one hundred and fifty bishops subscribed.”

Gothescalc then continues:

### III

> “For Prosper has spoken of a threefold majesty, Prudentius of a threefold piety, and Arator of a twice-threefold power; likewise, in Greek, *τρισάγιον* (*trisagion*), and in Latin, quite properly, regularly, and catholically, ‘threefold holiness.’ Therefore, just as the Greeks say most catholically *τριθεοτεία* (*tritheoteia*), so we too may say most catholically ‘threefold divinity.’”

### χρ.

As evidence for his assertion he says that Arator and Prudentius speak of “threefold power” and “threefold piety” because of the necessities of meter, which do not prejudice the free simplicity of the faith. Augustine, Athanasius, and Boethius, however, as the reader will find from their statements in this work, contradict him.

Prudentius himself also writes:

> “Through your begotten Christ, supreme Father,  
> Through whom are your splendor, honor, praise, wisdom,  
> Majesty, goodness, and piety,  
> He maintains the kingdom by a threefold divine power”—  
> or, as it is found in certain manuscripts, “with threefold name.”

Saint Ambrose refutes this at the beginning of Book I, chapter 1, of *On the Faith*, because neither *numen* (“divine power”) nor *nomen* (“name”) should be called threefold or triple in God, who is three in persons and one in divinity. He says:

> “The Lord and God is so called either because he rules all things, or because he watches over all things and is feared by everyone. If, therefore, there is one God, there is one name, one power, and one Trinity. Accordingly, he says: ‘Go, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28:19)—in the name, certainly, not in the names—in order to show that the Trinity has one power.”

And again, in chapter 2:

> “We confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in such a way that in the perfect Trinity there is both the fullness of divinity and the unity of power.”

This has the same force as though he had said, “the unity of divine power.”

Saint Augustine likewise says in Book VI, chapter 8, of *On the Trinity*:

> “Although the Father alone, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone, is as great as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, he must by no means be called triple, because that perfection has no means by which it can increase. The Father is perfect, the Son is perfect, and the Holy Spirit is perfect; therefore one should speak of a Trinity rather than of something triple.”

Prudentius himself, perhaps compelled by the law of meter, elsewhere writes, to demonstrate three persons of one substance:

> “God is the three supreme realities, a threefold form, one power.”

But since, as Priscian says, *specimen* (“form” or “appearance”) is derived from *species* (“form” or “kind”), one cannot speak catholically of a “threefold form” in God. Augustine says in Book VII, chapter 6, of *On the Trinity*:

> “For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three forms of one essence.”

Gothescalc also produced against himself a testimony of blessed Jerome, taken from his *Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew*, in order to confirm the statements of his compilation. He says:

> “They interpret this woman as the Church, which has mixed three measures of flour with the leaven of human faith—the belief in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and, when it has been fermented into one, it leads us not to knowledge of a triple God but to knowledge of one divinity. The three measures of flour likewise, since their nature is not different in each, draw us toward unity of substance.”

And again:

> “They are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that, since they have one divinity, there may be one gift and one name; for the Trinity is one God.”

In the books of blessed Prosper we likewise very frequently read of the one divinity, essence, substance, and nature of the Trinity, as well as of one majesty, one power, one light, and one principle.

For in the *Book of Sentences* (sentence 324) he says:

> “What the Father does with Christ, Christ does; and what Christ does with the Father, the Father does. The inseparable charity, majesty, and power do nothing separately, as the Lord himself says: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30).”

And again, in sentence 227:

> “In the divine Trinity the unity of substance is so great that it maintains equality and admits no plurality.”

And again:

> “In the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there remains an eternal and unchangeable unity, where the undifferentiated Trinity is one God, one light, and one principle.”

In the *Book of Epigrams* (epigram 3) he says:

> “There is no true eternity and no true immortality except in the divinity of the Trinity, for in it perfect being is what it is to be.
>
> This is the Father, this the Father’s Word, and this the life-giving Spirit,
>
> Whose nature is one and the same in the three.”

And again, in epigram 55:

> “There is no difference in the divinity of the Trinity, because whatever is less than God is not God.
>
> One is the omnipotent nature that created all things,
>
> And properly gave being to all that exists.
>
> Whatever is less than God is not God. The Word born from the Father,
>
> And the Spirit who is of them both, is God,
>
> For the essence of the three is one and the same,
>
> And can never be either greater or less.”

And again, in epigram 64:

> “The omnipotent begetter, the begotten, and the life-giving Spirit:
>
> One divinity, equal in the three persons.”

And in the final epigram:

> “One is the divinity of the three, one the essence; from the One
>
> Comes the same Spirit, both of the Word and of the Father.”

What he says—that the Greek term *τρισάγιον* (*trisagion*) is properly, regularly, and catholically interpreted as “threefold holiness,” and that consequently “threefold divinity” should be said catholically in the same way as “threefold holiness”—is not true.

For Saint Quintianus, bishop of Asculum, speaking to Peter of Antioch concerning the holy Trinity, interpreted *τρισάγιον* not as “threefold holy” but as “holy three times.” And in the offertory of the Greek Mass composed by blessed Basil, in which *τρισάγιον ὕμνον* occurs, learned interpreters translated it not as “a threefold holy hymn” but as “a thrice-holy hymn.”

A little farther on, Gothescalc adds one wrong thing to another and says:

### IV

> “It is altogether clear that *ἁγία τριάς* (*hagia trias*), that is, ‘holy Trinity,’ just as it is one essentially and naturally, is beyond doubt a threefold divinity personally, just as holiness, majesty, piety, and power are.”

### χρ.

What was said by God at the creation of the first human being—“Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26)—the devil interpreted wrongly, and, using a parable, said to our first parents: “You will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). Arius followed him, introducing degrees into the holy Trinity contrary to the Lord’s command in the Law: “You shall not go up by steps to my altar” (Exod. 20:26), and teaching three divinities in the holy Trinity.

Now Gothescalc, in the opposite direction, divides the one divinity among the three persons of the holy Trinity, saying:

> “Just as the holy Trinity is one essentially and naturally, so undoubtedly it is a threefold divinity personally.”

But, as the Catholic teachers say—and as is true—the Trinity is the unity of divinity, by which naturally the one God is Trinity. If this divinity were personally threefold, the unity of the Trinity would have been divided or partitioned among the three persons. That cannot be, because what is one, insofar as it is one, does not admit division.

Boethius, using the words of blessed Augustine—as he himself admits—says:

> “One is the thing; unity is that by which we call something one. And where there is no difference, there is no plurality at all; therefore there is no number, but unity alone. For when God is named three times, as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are named, three units do not produce numerical plurality in that which they are themselves, namely, in divinity, essence, and nature.”

Ambrose likewise says in Book I, chapter 2, of *On the Faith*:

> “Difference makes plurality; the unity of power excludes numerical quantity, because unity is not a number, but is itself the principle of all things.”

Thus Arius and Gothescalc are, in the poet’s words:

> “Equal in error, although they speak differently.”

For if this new augur—or perhaps one more pernicious than any augur—had said, “Just as the holy Trinity is one essentially and naturally, so undoubtedly it is threefold personally,” the statement would have been coherent. But by adding “divinity is threefold personally,” he not only contradicts the Catholic faith; he also attacks what he had stated previously, just as the subsequent statements destroy what had preceded them.

For what he said, “Just as the holy Trinity is one essentially and naturally,” if it is understood as it ought to be understood—namely, that the Trinity is one essence and nature, that is, divinity, the unity of the Trinity—then divinity cannot be threefold personally. Consequently, what he placed first, “the holy Trinity is one essentially and naturally,” destroys what he added afterward, “divinity is threefold personally.” This cannot be, since divinity is the same as substance and nature, which is always one and cannot be threefold, because, as Athanasius, Ambrose, and Augustine say, divinity is the unity of the Trinity.

What he added, “divinity is threefold personally,” also attacks what he had stated earlier, “the Trinity is one essentially and naturally.” For the Trinity cannot be threefold in the respect in which it is one—that is, in essence and nature—as Arius derangedly taught. Nor, in the respect in which the Trinity is called one God or threefold—that is, in the distinct property of the persons—is it one person, as Sabellius blasphemed; rather, it is “one,” as Christ says in the Gospel.

Against them Ambrose sings:

> “One God in power, and three personally.”

And Athanasius says:

> “This is the Catholic faith: that we venerate one God in the Trinity of persons, and the Trinity of persons in the unity of divinity, neither confusing the persons, so that they are not three, nor separating the substance, so that it is threefold. For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; but the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, their glory equal, and their majesty coeternal.”

Augustine likewise says in Book VII, chapter 6, of *On the Trinity*:

> “Just as the substance of the Father is the Father himself—not insofar as he is Father, but insofar as he is—so the person of the Father is nothing other than the Father himself. ‘Person’ is said of himself, not in relation to the Son or to the Holy Spirit, just as ‘God,’ ‘great,’ ‘good,’ and ‘just,’ and anything else of this kind, are said of himself. And just as for him being is the same as being God, being great, and being good, so for him being is the same as being a person.
>
> “Nor, when someone hears ‘the Father alone is God,’ should he separate the Son or the Holy Spirit from that statement. God is alone with the one with whom he is also one God. Likewise, when we hear that the Son alone is God, we must understand this without any separation from the Father and the Holy Spirit, as it is written in the Gospel: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30). He said both ‘one’ and ‘we are’: ‘one’ according to essence, since they are the same God; ‘we are’ according to relation, since one is the Father and the other the Son.”

For this reason they also admit a plural number. Why, then, do we not call these three together one person, just as we call them one essence and one God, but call them three persons, while we do not call them three gods or three essences? It is because we want one term to serve the signification by which the Trinity is understood, so that, when asked what the three are, we would not be entirely silent, even though we confess that they are three. In the holy Trinity, “three persons” is said relationally; essentially, that is, naturally, they are one, not one person. For the *deitas* (“divinity”), *divinitas* (“divinity”), essence, substance, and nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, not three.

This is the Catholic faith: that we venerate one God in the Trinity of persons and the Trinity of persons in the unity of divinity, neither confusing the persons, so that they are not three, nor separating the substance, so that it is threefold. That one substance—that is, the divinity which is the unity of the Trinity—cannot be divided among the persons, and by its own inseparability shows that the three persons of the inseparable Trinity exist and cannot be separated from one another, because the name of any one person always refers to another person.

If you say “Father,” you indicate the Son; if you name the Son, you proclaim the Father; if you call him the Holy Spirit, you must understand that he is the Spirit of someone, namely, of the Father and the Son. Their substance is one and the same—that is, their divinity, which is the unity of the Trinity—and it is wholly present in each of the persons and wholly present in all three persons together.

Or, if it is expressed more correctly, lest anyone think that the persons in the holy Trinity are one thing and divinity another, the divinity is wholly and perfectly each individual person of the holy Trinity, and the divinity is wholly and perfectly the three persons together in the holy Trinity.

Therefore the holy Trinity must be understood as inseparable even in the persons, although in speech it has names that are separable, because it admits no plural number in the names of nature. The Trinity consists in the persons; in the nature—that is, in the divinity—there is unity, which cannot be divided, because the nature, that is, the divinity, is the unity of the Trinity.

That alone is properly called inseparable which cannot in any way admit separation. For what is not separated but can be separated is not inseparable.

The holy Trinity, therefore, must be understood as inseparable even in the persons, because the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not threefold but one, their glory equal and their majesty coeternal.

Gothescalc therefore lies, as is his custom, when he says:

### V

> “For just as the holy Trinity is one essentially and naturally, so undoubtedly it is a threefold divinity personally, just as majesty, piety, and power are.”

ΧΡ. This is refuted by the catholic faith, which, speaking through the mouths of all the orthodox, proclaims and confirms that “Trinity” refers to the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, while “unity” pertains to the nature of the eternal Godhead. Hence Augustine says in Book Seven, chapter 6, of *On the Trinity* [Col. 0532D]:

> “For to be God is the same as to subsist; and therefore, if there is one essence, there is also one substance. For this reason it is more suitably said that there are three persons than three substances. For to God, being is not one thing and being a person another, but they are altogether the same: ‘being’ is said absolutely, whereas ‘person’ is said relatively—namely, the Father in relation to the Son, the Son in relation to the Father, and the Holy Spirit in relation to the Father and the Son, whose Spirit he is, as the same teacher explains.”

And in Book Fifteen, chapter 22:

> “Trinity itself is one thing; the image of the Trinity in another thing is another.”

For such is the inseparability within it that it is both called and truly is one God; the Trinity is not in one God as something distinct, but is one God. Therefore the Godhead is not “triple” in respect of persons; rather, the one substance of the three persons to whom the Trinity refers [Col. 0533A] is the Godhead. As Augustine says in the first book of *On the Trinity*, this is the unity of the Trinity—namely, by which the Trinity is inseparable—for the whole of it is in each individual person and the whole of it is in the three persons together.

It must therefore be said, as Augustine says, “one essence and one substance, three persons,” or “the Trinity is substantially one God,” not, as Gothescalcus says without qualification, “the Trinity is essentially and naturally one,” lest this be taken to imply a confusion of the persons. We have already set this forth above as far as the matter required. Nor is Gothescalcus to be followed in this respect either, so that one should believe or say that the Godhead is triple in respect of persons. For whoever believes and says that the Godhead is personally triple differs in no respect from Arius. To refute his perverse understanding, the holy catholic Fathers, not by human invention but by divine inspiration, decreed at the holy Council of Nicaea that the term ὁμοούσιον—that is, consubstantiality, namely one substance, essence, nature, and Godhead of the three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—must be believed and held with the utmost firmness; and they anathematized those who deviated from this rule.

Gothescalcus, however, wishing to eat more honey than is sufficient—that is, to know more than it is proper to know—and searching into majesty beyond the capacity of his weakness, appears, by this statement of doctrine, to run knowingly and unwillingly, like one who closes his eyes before a fire, into the opinions of those who think perversely—namely, Sabellius and Arius, whom he detests when he names them but follows in his reasoning. He appears to run with his associates toward the judgments concerning whom it is written: “Let them descend alive into hell”—that is, “let them knowingly fall into the sin of blasphemy” [Col. 0533C].

For if the Godhead is triple in respect of persons, there will be three Godheads and consequently three gods; or one Godhead will be divided among three persons, and the Trinity will no longer be inseparable but separated. Just as it would then be numerable in respect of persons, so also it would be numerable in respect of substance; and the Godhead would not be perfect in any of the three persons. Thus God would be imperfect—a thing both foolish and impious to say.

For this reason we do not count it irrelevant to reckon that we hear through his mouth the very same spirit who hissed to our first parents through the serpent: “You will be like gods.” Against this impiety Saint Augustine says, among other things, in Book Seven, chapter 6, *On the Holy Trinity* [Col. 0533D]:

> “We do not therefore say ‘three persons’ or ‘subsistences,’ one essence and one God, as though three things subsisted from one matter, even if whatever that matter is were unfolded in these three. For there is nothing else belonging to its essence apart from this Trinity. Nevertheless, we say ‘three persons of the same essence,’ or ‘three persons, one essence’; but we do not say ‘three persons from the same essence,’ as though there were one thing there which is essence and another which is persons, as we can say ‘three statues from the same gold.’ For being gold is one thing for them, and being statues another. And when three human beings are said to be one nature, or three human beings of the same nature, they can also be called three human beings from the same nature, because other human beings of the same nature can exist from that same nature. In the essence of the Trinity, however, no other person can in any way exist from that same essence. For the essence of the Father and Son together is not greater than that of the Father alone or the Son alone; rather, those three subsistences together—or persons, if they are to be called that—are equal to each individually. The animal man does not perceive this.”

And the same most discerning teacher explains the rest at greater length in that place [p. 472]. In the thirty-sixth sermon on the Gospel according to John he says:

> “The Trinity is one God; the Trinity is one eternity, one power, one majesty. What, then, are the three? For if he says ‘three,’ you must say what the three are. I answer: Father, Son, and Spirit. For that which the Father is in himself is God; that which he is in relation to the Son is Father; that which the Son is in himself is God; that which he is in relation to the Father is Son.”

And shortly afterward:

> “There is nothing I can say are the three except the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one God, one almighty being, therefore one principle.”

And in the thirty-seventh sermon:

> “For if, as few understand, the nature of truth is simple, then for the Son to be is the same as to know.”

And in the forty-fourth sermon:

> “The Arians say, ‘The Father is one thing, the Son another,’ as though the Father and Son were not of the same substance.”

In the forty-fifth sermon:

> “If we understand ‘hand’ as power, the power of the Father and the Son is one, because the Godhead is one.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore no one snatches them from the hand of my Father—that is, no one snatches them from me.”

In the seventy-fourth sermon:

> “Since the Trinity is altogether inseparable, the Trinity would never be known as Trinity if it were always taught as inseparable. For when we say ‘Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,’ we would certainly not be saying them together if they could ever be anything other than together.”

In the eighty-eighth sermon:

> “For Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is not three gods but one God, of whom it is written: ‘Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wondrous works’ (Psalm 71:18).”

In the ninety-first sermon:

> “Wherever any one of them is—the Father, namely, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit—there is the Trinity, one God. Yet the Trinity had to be made known in such a way that, although there was no diversity of substance, the distinction of persons nevertheless began to be perceived individually; and those who believe rightly can never see a separation of the natures.”

Likewise, in the ninety-second sermon:

> “We have often said that the works of the Trinity are inseparable, but that the persons had to be presented individually, so that both unity and Trinity might be understood, not only without separation but also without confusion.”

And Pope Leo the Great, speaking against the heretics to Turibius, bishop of Astorga, says, chapter 5:

> “For what is from God the Father is what he himself is, and it is no other than the Son and the Holy Spirit. Apart from this one consubstantial, eternal, and unchangeable Godhead of the supreme Trinity, there is nothing among all created things that was not created from nothing at its beginning.”

And again, chapter 17:

> “By these same heretics, he says, against the true worship of the true God, the Trinity of the Godhead is confused by denying the distinct property of the persons.”

And Saint Gregory, in his sixteenth homily on Ezekiel, says [Col. 0535A]:

> “Isaiah, he says, heard the angelic hosts in heaven crying: ‘Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts’ (Isaiah 6). Thus, to show the Trinity of persons, ‘Holy’ is said three times; but, to make clear that the substance of the Trinity is one, it is not ‘Lord of hosts’ but ‘Lord’ that is proclaimed. David, likewise holding this understanding, says: ‘May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us’ (Psalm 66). Although he had said ‘God’ three times, to show that this is one, he added: ‘And may all the ends of the earth fear him.’ Paul likewise speaks, saying: ‘From him and through him and in him are all things’ (Romans 11). ‘From him,’ namely from the Father; ‘through him,’ through the Son; ‘in him,’ in the Holy Spirit. When he had thus said ‘him’ three times, he added: ‘To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.’ For in not saying ‘to them’ but ‘to him,’ by saying ‘him’ three times he distinguished the persons, and by adding ‘to him be glory’ he did not divide the substance.”

And blessed Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, says in his book against Felix:

> “The holy catholic and apostolic Church, which, although spread throughout the entire world, is nevertheless the one beloved, intimate, and dove-like bride of the Bridegroom, shining with the beauty of sacred discourse on silvered wings and gleaming in the golden brightness of its latter parts through the purity of right faith, confesses the holy and ineffable Trinity in unity. While preserving without confusion the distinct property of the persons, it confesses an inseparable substance. Thus, indeed, the Father is believed to be one because he is Father, who begot the Son, coeternal with himself, without time and without any beginning; the Son is believed to be another because he is Son, begotten without beginning from the Father, not figuratively but truly; and the Holy Spirit is believed to be another because he is the Holy Spirit and proceeds from the Father and the Son. Yet the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; rather, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are inseparably one. Not one person but one being, because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; but the majesty of the ineffable divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, equal, consubstantial, and coeternal, because there is one God. For we confess unity in essence, but proclaim Trinity in the distinction of persons.”

[Col. 0535D] And Saint Alcuin, drawing on the words of blessed Augustine, says to the emperor Charles the Great in Book One of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8:

> “Whatever is said of God in relation to himself, and is said of the individual persons—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and likewise of the Trinity itself, must be said not in the plural but in the singular. Since, then, for God to be is not one thing and to be great another, nor to be one thing and to be good another, but for him being and being great, and being and being good, are the same, therefore, just as we do not say ‘three gods’ or ‘three essences,’ so we do not say ‘three greatnesses’ or ‘three goodnesses,’ but one God, one essence, one greatness, and one goodness.”

And when the Apostle calls Christ “the power of God” and “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), this is not to be understood as though the Father could not also be called power or wisdom, just as he cannot be called Son or Word, because the latter are relative names, whereas the former—power and wisdom—are substantial names. Therefore the Father is power and wisdom, the Son is power and wisdom, and the Holy Spirit is power and wisdom; yet there are not three powers or three wisdoms, but one power and wisdom—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—just as there is one substance and one omnipotence [Col. 0536A], and likewise with the other things said substantially of the divine nature [p. 474].

Thus the Son is to be understood as the wisdom of the Father in the same way as he is called the light of the Father: just as light is from light, and both are one light, so wisdom is to be understood as being from wisdom, and both are one wisdom. For in the simplicity of the divine nature, to know is not one thing and to be another, nor to be one thing and to be able another, nor to be able one thing and to live another. There wisdom and essence are the same, life and essence are the same; all these are one, and God is one.

The same must be understood and confessed concerning majesty, piety, power, and everything else that is said substantially of God. And again Gothescalcus has woven together the following depraved and perverse statements.

VI.

÷ “For just as God the Trinity is a number in the singular, according to the phrase ‘Blessed be the Holy Trinity,’ so also it is a number in the singular, and τριθεοτεία—‘triple godhead’—is triple godhead.”

ΧΡ. Here the book of the Sixth Synod, by which Gothescalcus falsely won back his position and attempted to confirm his false opinion, refutes him as a liar and proves him a falsifier in his false interpretation. For, wishing to utter what he had not swallowed, he interpreted τριθεοτεία as “triple godhead.” But the element *tri* in the unity of the Godhead, which is the unity of the Trinity, does not admit number, nor any addition that indicates plurality.

Victorinus, the rhetor of the city of Rome and teacher of blessed Jerome, did not understand it in the way Gothescalcus interprets it. Victorinus wrote to Candidus the Arian, who was attempting to confirm his heresy through the conclusions and expansions of dialectical and rhetorical discipline—disciplines that are in a certain sense related—refuting and destroying his impiety by means of the meanings of the Greek words concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Among other things he says:

> “Thus the one divinity of these three, who exist as one and the same, is not a many-faceted majesty; and the three are one, and the one is three, and three times one are three, and the same is both one and alone.”

The true interpreters of the Greek language, when translating the letter of Saint Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem—a letter most fully received by the apostolic faith and by the aforementioned holy Sixth Synod, as we have said—translated the term not as “triple” but as “three times.” They anathematize those who do not understand that “three times” correctly and who say “triple godhead,” as the same Sixth Synod contains:

> “The blessed Trinity is therefore not numbered by essences, natures, or different godheads, nor by three dominions—far be it!—as the Arians rave, and as the new barkers of τριθεοτεία, that is, of ‘three-times godhead,’ rave: three essences, three natures, three dominions, and likewise three godheads.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The holy Trinity is divided and yet undivided, and is again joined while divided. For, having division in the persons, it remains undivided; and it is inseparable in essence and nature, and likewise in the Godhead.”

And Boethius, in his book *On the Trinity*, drawing on the writings of blessed Augustine, as he himself acknowledges, says:

> “In the number by which we count, the repetition of units produces plurality; but in the number of things, the repetition of units does not produce plurality. For example, if I say of the same thing, ‘one sword, one blade, one weapon,’ one sword can be recognized under so many names. This repetition of units is repetition rather than counting. Thus, if we say ‘weapon, blade, sword,’ it is a repetition of the same thing, not a counting of different things. Likewise, if I say ‘sun, sun, sun,’ I have not made three suns, but have said of one sun the same thing repeatedly. Therefore, if ‘God’ is said three times of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, this does not for that reason make a triple counting or produce a number.”

This is because the Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, and this is the unity of the Trinity.

In the distinct property of the persons of the holy and inseparable Trinity, when the Father is related to the Son, the Son to the Father, and the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son, it is said relatively and in a certain sense separately among the Greeks as *trias*—“Trinity.” Thus, if one asks, “To what does ‘Trinity’ refer?” the answer is “to the persons,” or “in relation to the persons.” For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are called “Trinity” by catholics because the whole is made one from certain three, as though it were *Triunity*—that is, “three-times unity”—and not “triple unity.” It consists of three numerable persons of one Godhead, which is as free from division as from plurality and number; for where there is no difference, there is no plurality at all, as Boethius says, and therefore no number. Thus there is unity alone, and unity cannot be triple in itself.
