For this reason catholic and true interpreters have always understood that, in the holy and inseparable Trinity, the Greek term τρίς should be translated into Latin as *ter*, “three times.” For the triple repetition of the one God, when the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are named, does not produce plurality in the essence; rather, one God is proclaimed so many times in respect of persons.

But the number by which we count, in which we show plurality—such as τριπλόος, “triple”; τρίγωνος, “triangular”; τριάκοντα, “thirty”; τριακόσια, “three hundred”; τριετία, “a period of three years”; τριέτης, “three-year-old,” masculine or feminine; τριετηρικός, “triennial”—and many similar forms, are applied to things and seek the names of the things to which they are applied. When they are applied to material things, they signify and show a variety or multitude of accidents which exists distinctly in countable things through the diversity or plurality they contain; they also indicate in the things to which they are applied a certain plurality and numerical distinction. For example: “a three-year-old calf,” “a three-year-old heifer,” “a triple cord,” “a triangular stone,” “thirty men,” “three hundred shields.”

From these statements of the orthodox and from the true interpretation of the Greek language, it is perfectly clear that Gothescalcus lied in his interpretation and exposition. For us Latins, who are ignorant of the Greek language, there is no need to labor over this further, since in the books of the orthodox, who were skilled in both languages, we find sufficient evidence of how, according to the catholic faith, we ought to believe, confess, hold, and proclaim the Trinity of the one and inseparable Godhead [p. 476].

Nor should any scruple arise in us from the words of Gothescalcus and other ignorant men who thought wrongly and were entirely unfamiliar with the Greek language, since in the writings of our forebears we read that many who arrogated to themselves the interpretation of Greek speech did not understand how greatly the force of its signs and punctuation—and even of the accents placed above the letters—was said to contribute to removing ambiguity, which among the Greeks arises from certain of their letters, and to understanding expressions and distinguishing pronunciation. They consequently erred, translating one thing for another: for example, “mountain” for “vision,” “pig” for “son,” “triple” for “three times,” and similar cases; and at times translating singular forms as plurals and plurals as singulars.

After the foregoing, Gothescalcus spews forth the poison of that most ancient writer, cursed and condemned by the holy Fathers, at the Council of Nicaea, at other catholic councils, and in orthodox writings, saying:

VII.

> “Just as every catholic believes and confesses each one of the persons of the Trinity to be wholly, fully, and perfectly God, so let him believe, confess, and assert that each person possesses his own proper Godhead, wholly, fully, and perfectly; and henceforth, with whatever strength he has or can acquire by divine aid, let him refute all who contradict this. For it is clearer than daylight and more evident than the brightness of the sun that each person possesses his own proper Godhead and divinity, because it was certainly not the whole Trinity—but only the Godhead of the Son—that assumed humanity, God forbid.”

ΧΡ. From this, let every sensible person perceive how great is the vice of arrogance, which does not allow a man whom it has seized to recognize not only the truth but even himself. Hence the Lord, speaking to Moses (Leviticus 21:20), commanded, among other things, that a man who had a white spot in his eye should not offer bread to his God or approach his ministry.

As Gregory explains (*Pastoral Care*, Part One, chapter 2), a person has a white spot in his eye “who is prevented from seeing the light of truth because he is blinded by arrogance concerning wisdom or righteousness. The black pupil of the eye sees; one suffering from a white spot sees nothing. For when the sense of human thought understands itself to be foolish and sinful, it grasps the knowledge of inner brightness. But when it attributes to itself the whiteness of righteousness or wisdom, it excludes itself from the light of heavenly knowledge. The more it exalts itself before itself through arrogance, the less it penetrates the brilliance of the true light. Thus it is said of certain people—and may rightly be understood of this singularly mad man: ‘Claiming to be wise, they became fools’ (Romans 1:22).”

For shortly before this he divided the one Godhead according to nature, saying that it was triple in respect of persons. Then, as it is written under the figure of a harlot woman (Proverbs 7:11)—which catholic men interpret as referring to heresy, because it cannot stand on its own feet without falling from bad to worse—he forgot himself and said that each person in the Holy Trinity must be believed, asserted, and defended as possessing his own Godhead, wholly, fully, and perfectly, and consequently three Godheads, a doctrine rightly condemned by catholics [p. 477].

Concerning him the prophet Isaiah says, according to the Septuagint translation [Col. 0539B]:

> “The fool speaks foolish things, and his heart understands vain things, and he completes what is hostile; he speaks error to God, to destroy hungry souls and leave thirsty souls empty. For they have devised wicked counsels to destroy the humble with wicked words and to scatter the words of the humble in judgment. But the pious have devised wisdom, and this counsel will endure.”

Namely, this is the counsel by which the Apostle Paul, rebuking and refuting him, wrote to the Corinthians:

> “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:13).

Here “the love of God” is to be understood as the love of the Father, of whom the Apostle John says: “God is love” (1 John 4:9). “In this the love of God was manifested among us, because God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him” (1 John 4:16).

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ” refers to Christ of whom the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:9).

“The communion of the Holy Spirit,” as Augustine says, is to be understood “because he exists in the same unity of substance and equality with the Father and the Son. Whether he is the unity of both, or holiness, or love, or unity because he is love and love because he is holiness, he is in no way lesser than those from whom he proceeds. He remains as he proceeds, and proceeds as he remains. Therefore he proceeds wholly from the Father and wholly from the Son; he remains wholly in the Father and wholly in the Son. For this reason he naturally possesses with the Father and the Son the fullness of unity and the unity of fullness, so that he wholly possesses the Father and wholly possesses the Son, and he himself is wholly possessed by the Father and wholly possessed by the Son. He is likewise given equally by the Father and the Son—or rather, he is given by himself as well” [Col. 0539D].

And Athanasius, explaining this statement of the Apostle, says at the beginning of Book Four:

> “Did he not clearly distinguish by the individual names that individual persons are present? The individual names are perfectly manifested only in the persons; through these same names the unity of the substance of the Godhead is indicated. Thus the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father; but the Holy Spirit is the conjunction of the Godhead, the power and unity of the Trinity. Whoever introduces three powers confesses three gods. We, however, believe in three persons and one Godhead; we confess the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, together with the Holy Spirit. The unity is not separated; the Godhead is not divided: God from God, not two gods; power from power, but one power; light from light, truth from truth, but one light and one truth.”

And again, explaining the Apostle’s statement “All things are from him and through him and in him” (Romans 11:36), he says in the latter part of Book Four:

> “‘From him’ is said of the Father, ‘through him’ of the Son, and ‘in him’ of the Holy Spirit; and in him it is brought together as one. Therefore, because he says ‘from him’ and ‘in him,’ since this same divinity belongs to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, all things are made from him, through him, and in him. To that Trinity, united in ineffable unity, be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen” [p. 478].

And Ambrose, in Book Three of *On the Holy Spirit*, says:

> “He remains with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Hence the Apostle joined the grace of Jesus Christ and the love of God with the communion of the Holy Spirit, saying: ‘The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, be with you all’ (2 Corinthians 13:13).”

We therefore observe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit remain in one and the same temple through the unity of the same nature.

For if, as Gothescalcus says—and as the catholic faith contradicts—each person possesses his own particular and special Godhead, and the Trinity is not the one Godhead common to the three persons together, then there are three Godheads, just as there are three persons, each of whom possesses a special property.

It is proper to the Father, who is from no one, that he is Father; it is proper to the Son, who is begotten from the substance of the Father, that he is Son; and it is proper to the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, that he is the Spirit of both, namely the Father and the Son. And if—God forbid—there are three proper Godheads belonging to the persons, so that each person has his own, that is, his special, Godhead, there will be three gods. The Trinity will no longer be inseparable, since the Godhead that is the unity of the Trinity, and by which the Trinity is inseparable, will be separable—or rather, separated. And he says:

VIII.

÷ “It remains, then, that those who are grammarians, if they do not wish to be heretics as well, must not presume to confess in the Church of the true God, of the God of truth, of the true God, that τριθεοτεία—that is, triple godhead—exists in any respect as a plural number, since, as is plainly evident, it is singular, just as all who are even moderately skilled in the art of grammar know.”

### ΧΡ.

Having forgotten—or rather, because of his arrogance, being unable to see—the elementary principles of grammar, that is, Donatus’s teaching, which little boys learn in school like the alphabet, namely the beginnings of the elements, where it is written, with Donatus himself teaching it:

“There are certain nouns singular in sound but plural in meaning, such as *gens* [nation], *populus* [people], *concio* [assembly], *plebs* [the common people], and *multitudo* [multitude]. There are also certain inflected and adjectival nouns that are singular in sound but contain plurality in their meaning, and, when attached to fixed nouns of the singular number, indicate plurality—for example, *tertia*, *trina*, *trima*, *trigama*, and other expressions of this kind. We give some of them by way of example: *tertia hora* [the third hour], *trina repetitio* [a threefold repetition], *trima juvenca* [a three-year-old heifer], *trigama mulier* [a woman married to three men]. In all these expressions, a certain plurality is demonstrated through adjectival words that themselves contain plurality, when they are joined to fixed nouns.

“For when we say ‘the third hour,’ a multiplication of hours is indicated; when we say ‘a threefold repetition,’ we show a plurality of repetitions; when we say ‘a three-year-old heifer,’ we signify a plurality of years in it; when we say ‘a woman married to three men,’ we make it clear that she has had several husbands.”

One also finds Augustine saying in his books *On the Trinity*: “a trinity of rings,” “a trinity of persons,” and “a trinity in the mind of man,” where he was made in the image of God. Therefore, as we think, it may not improperly be said even that there is a “threefold Trinity.”

But when Gothescalcus improperly says “a threefold deity”—a plurality and number, which, as Boethius says, arise from difference—he imposes this upon that simple and indivisible nature in which there is no difference whatsoever among the persons. Moreover, plurality is contained both in this inflected and adjectival word *trina* [threefold] and in the fixed noun to which it is attached, namely *Trinitas* [Trinity]; yet deity does not receive plurality into itself.

For this reason, “threefold deity” has been declared not to be understood, believed, or spoken by any Catholic, as Boethius says in his book addressed to John:

> “If, then, I ask whether the one who is called the Father is substance, the answer is that he is substance. If I ask whether the Son is substance, the same answer is given. No one will doubt that the Holy Spirit also is substance. And when I again collect together the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, there appears to be not several substances but one substance. Therefore there is one substance of the three. It cannot in any way be separated or divided, nor is it joined together as though from parts; rather, it is simply one.

> “Whatever, therefore, is predicated of the divine substance must be common to the three. If we say, ‘The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God,’ then the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. If, therefore, their deity is one, their substance is one.”

And in his book *On the Trinity*:

> “The fact that God is named three times when the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are named does not make three unities into a plurality in that which they themselves are—that is, in the deity, which is nature and essence, and which is called essence from the word *to be*.”

Therefore, the same Boethius says in the same book, earlier:

> “If God is predicated three times of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, this does not for that reason make the predicate threefold or produce a number. This applies to those who introduce a difference of merits among them. But for Catholics, who establish their complete indifference and posit the very form of being as it is, judging that what is itself is nothing other than what it is, the repetition of the same thing rather than the enumeration of different things is rightly understood when it is said: ‘God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit.’ And this Trinity is one God, just as sword, blade, and sabre are one sword, or as ‘sun, sun, sun’ is one sun.

> “Let this meanwhile be said with the meaning and purpose of showing that not every repetition of unities produces a number and plurality. Yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not spoken of in this way as though they were a collection of homonyms. For blade and sword are one and the same thing; whereas the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are indeed the same, but they are not one and the same person.”

From this it is evident that Gothescalcus does not speak the truth when he says:

> “Just as God the Trinity is of the singular number, according to the words, ‘Blessed be the holy Trinity,’ so also the threefold deity is of the singular number.”

For *trina* [threefold] and *Trinitas* [Trinity] are singular in sound but plural in meaning. Deity, however, by which we call the Father God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God, is singular both in sound and in meaning; it does not admit an addition signifying plurality. For the Trinity is understood and called holy and inseparable with respect to the persons, while unity is understood and called so with respect to substance, essence, nature, divinity, and deity, because the deity of the Trinity is unity.

Thus all Catholic teachers—and Boethius also, in the aforementioned book *On the Trinity*, as we have already stated—say:

> “Where there is no difference, there is no plurality at all; therefore there is no number, but only unity. For the fact that God is repeated three times when the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are named does not make three unities into a numerical plurality in that which they themselves are,”

that is, in essence, namely deity.

Hence God said to Moses:

> “I am who I am,”

and:

> “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14).

Accordingly, the rule of faith, according to the authority of sacred Scripture—in which we read, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3); and, “May God have mercy on us and bless us; may God, our God, bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. 66:8); and, “From him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory” (Rom. 11:36)—is expressed in Catholic fashion:

> “Blessed be the holy Trinity and undivided unity; we shall confess him, because he has shown us his mercy.”

But just as it is said in Catholic fashion, “Blessed be the holy Trinity,” namely of the persons, “and undivided unity,” which is understood as the deity that is the unity of the Trinity, so it cannot be said in Catholic fashion, as Gothescalcus raves, “threefold deity.” For, as Augustine says above, this deity is “the unity of the Trinity,” of which Ambrose says:

> “You are the unity of the Trinity, who powerfully rule the world.”

And Athanasius, in the sixth book *On the Faith*, says:

> “God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit. You see the indication of the Trinity in the three persons, and that these three persons are distinguished only by their names. Therefore neither can unity be shown without the persons, nor can these persons be shown without the united name of deity.”

This, as Augustine says, the natural man does not perceive. Gothescalcus is unable to see it, because, as we read in divinely inspired writings, there are four kinds of arrogant people: when an arrogant person reckons that what he has either comes from himself, or has been given to him on account of his merits, or pretends to have what he does not have, or arrogates to himself what he has in a singular manner above others. In this man we plainly see the latter two kinds.

As for the first two kinds of arrogant people, let him see to them himself. But those who knew him from childhood, and plainly see and have seen him, testify that the latter two have been and still are present in him. He cannot endure hearing anything that does not agree with his own judgment, and still less can he endure being taught by anyone. He considers everyone else’s understanding incomparable with his own, thinks that no one is his equal in knowledge, and does not take care to conform his own understanding to the Scriptures but bends the Scriptures to his own understanding. Because he reads them with an evil intention, he is unable to see the truth in them.

For, as it is written, “His wickedness blinded him” (Wis. 1:21), and, “Wisdom shall not enter into a malicious soul” (Wis. 1:4), and “the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of discipline, by whom the Scriptures themselves were inspired, flees deceit and withdraws from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1:5). For it rests upon the humble and quiet person; and, as the holy Gregory says, truth flees the mind in which it does not find humility.

Of him and others like him the blessed Gregory likewise says (*Moralia*, book VIII, chapter 2):

> “Heretics in their inquiries do not strive to attain the truth but to appear victorious. When they desire to display wisdom outwardly, inwardly they are bound by the chains of their own foolish pride. Hence they seek the contests of disputation, and, although God is our peace, they do not know how to speak peacefully about him; indeed, from the business of peace they become inventors of quarrels. To them Paul rightly says: ‘If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor the Church of God’” (1 Cor. 11:16).

Therefore it is not surprising that, like the Pharisee, he is rightly regarded as unjust after being expelled from the temple of the Lord, that is, from the holy Church. He had remained there for a long time, perniciously wicked, by his depraved conduct and teaching, by which he unjustified many. And, as the holy Hilary says of Hosius, he has been preserved for this reason: so that human judgment might not fail to know what kind of life he had previously led.

Against his deadly poisons, by which he spews forth the claim that each person has a deity of his own, complete, full, and perfect, and that only the deity of the Son assumed humanity, Saint Athanasius says in the first chapter of the first book *On the Trinity*:

> “You are one God, the Father, and the only-begotten Son of God, God the Holy Spirit, who have revealed to us one deity, and disclosed the undivided glory of the sacred divinity alone, and demonstrated the perfect glory of the Trinity, your eternal fullness. Therefore I considered it best that your truth should shine forth clearly once it had been revealed, and that the exposed blindness of the heretics should become known.”

And, weaving this Catholic teaching throughout the whole book, he says at one point, concerning the united name of the Trinity:

> “Although many meanings have been expressed at this point, they have nevertheless been approved more clearly with respect to the united divinity of the Trinity.”

A little later he says:

> “Do you not know that the Father is one God, that the Son is one God, and that the Holy Spirit is one God? Is there not one God, since the name is united in the nature of the *ousia* [essence]? So also there is one Spirit, because his deity is united. For if, according to the individual names of the persons, you have designated the united name ‘Spirit’ three times, ought you therefore to say that there are three spirits? Certainly not. If this could be said, then it would also have to be introduced into the confession that three gods should be named in the plural, so that there would no longer be in these persons a united nature of divinity, but each would exist in his own or a different nature—which God forbid.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let us know that we confess the unity of the deity in the Trinity as unity, not as plurality.”

Again:

> “Therefore there is one God, because the deity is united, just as it is written concerning the individual persons. And because there is no God except one, there is also this: ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God’” (Deut. 6:4).

Again:

> “Remember that the name of divinity is united in the individual persons.”

He confirms this by the authority of Scripture in the same book and, after those testimonies, says:

> “You see that in these persons the name of the Trinity is united in nature.”

Again, after several further testimonies from Scripture:

> “Do you see that through the individual designations—that is, the persons—the united name of deity is indicated three times?”

And a little later:

> “It is written: ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name,’ and he continued, ‘of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’” (Matt. 28:19). “Therefore, in these persons, the united name exists in every respect in the deity of divinity, and through these names only the persons of the Trinity are distinguished.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Thus, in baptism, you first confess the united name of divinity, so that you may deserve to obtain remission of sins through these persons.”

Again:

> “You see that in deity and in the substance of fullness they are one in every respect, while in the names of the persons there are three.”

And in the second book, concerning the individual persons and the united name of divinity—“I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14:16)—he says:

> “Know that one differs from another, or one from the other, only in person and not in the united fullness of the divinity of the *ousia*. For if, according to the individual names of the persons, one may undoubtedly be said to be in the other, can one likewise be proclaimed ‘another God’—the Father—as though he were different in nature from the Son? Can the Son be called another God from the Father, as though he were another in deity? Can the Holy Spirit be confessed as another God, as though he differed in substance from the Father and the Son? Certainly not. For the united name exists in them in one true nature, and therefore there is one true God.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Since their deity is united, this God cannot verbally be called another God from that other God, because the name is united, both in the fullness of divinity; and therefore there is one God.”

Again:

> “Moreover, where neither number nor any difference is found in the united fullness of the deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one is contained distinctly in the divine name of the other and yet is contained in unity.”

**Question.** Explain to me, then, how three are one, or how one is three.

**Answer.** Remember that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three who are one, because they subsist in the nature of the Trinity. Therefore three are one, or one is three.

**Question.** Is this Trinity divided or undivided? Tell me.

**Answer.** It is plainly divided only in the names of the persons; in deity it is undivided.

**Question.** Tell me how unity is interpreted.

**Answer.** Do you not know that the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one?

**Question.** What is signified or understood here by “nature”?

**Answer.** That which is understood: truth and deity (*dealitas*), or substance—what the Greeks call *ousia* [essence]—which is plainly the united fullness of divinity.

**Question.** What is one Trinity?

**Answer.** Certainly, because the fullness of divinity is one in that very Trinity, the name of the unity of nature is likewise declared to subsist in unity within the Trinity, and within that Trinity the Trinity itself is equally and perfectly demonstrated through the individual names of the persons.

Saint Hilary, in his *Commentary on Matthew* (canon 26), says:

> “There are two in the bed, proclaiming the same rest of the Lord’s Passion; and concerning this there is the same and one confession among heretics and Catholics. But because the truth of the Catholics will proclaim the unity of the Father and the Son and their common *theoteia*—which we call deity—and because the falsehood of the heretics will again attack this same doctrine with many insults, therefore, from the two in the bed, one is left and the other is taken, because the judgment of divine decision will approve the faith of both confessions in taking one and leaving the other.”

Ambrose, in the first book *On the Faith* (book I, chapter 1), says:

> “It is written: ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God’” (Deut. 6:4). “For ‘God’ and ‘Lord’ are names of magnificence, names of power, as he himself says: ‘The Lord God is my name’; and as the prophet asserts elsewhere: ‘The Lord God Almighty is his name’” (Exod. 15:3). “Thus ‘Lord’ and ‘God’ signify either that he rules over all, or that he observes all and is feared by all. If, therefore, there is one God, one name, and one power, there is one Trinity.

> “Finally, he says: ‘Go, baptizing in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’” (Matt. 28:19). “He says ‘in the name,’ certainly not ‘in the names.’ He also says: ‘I and the Father are one’” (John 10:30). “He said ‘one,’ so that there might be no division of power; he added ‘are,’ so that you might recognize the Father and the Son, believing that the perfect Father begot the perfect Son, and that the Father and the Son are one—not through confusion of persons, but through unity of nature.”

And again, in chapter 2:

> “We therefore speak of one God, not two or three gods, as the impious heresy of the Arians incurs while it brings its accusation. For the one who separates the divinity of the Trinity speaks of three gods.”

Augustine, in his book *Against Five Heresies*, says:

> “Speak, my teacher, holy Paul; teach, divine jurist, friend of the Bridegroom. This man has now come, overturned the world, torn apart the unity of the faith, and divided the Trinity.”

And again, a little later:

> “We have said what we could about the Father and the Son, and as much as we could—if indeed we were able to say anything worthily—we have remained silent about the Holy Spirit, but we have not separated him. Whatever we have said about the Father and the Son, we have also said about the Holy Spirit. For he is in them and with them, equal, one God, neither lesser nor third.

> “What more can I say, exhausted as I am? Whoever separates the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in eternity, substance, or communion, and whoever denies that the Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, is full of an unclean spirit and empty of the Holy Spirit. For God is called love precisely because he does not divide unity into parts but ineffably joins the Trinity together. For this is the Trinity, one God, the tower of strength against the enemy, who keeps those who believe in him forever and ever.”

And again, the same Saint Augustine, in his sermon *On the Faith against the Heretics*:

> “Let us say something from the Scriptures, following not reasoning but the authority of the Lord and Savior. Christ, about to ascend into heaven, speaks to the apostles, to whom he preaches as teacher and Lord. No one knows how to speak about his own nature as does the one who is himself God. Let it be enough for us to know about the Trinity what the Lord has deigned to explain.

> “What, then, does he say to the apostles? ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’” (Matt. 28:19). “I hear three names, yet one name is spoken. For he did not say ‘in the names,’ but ‘in the name.’ He speaks of three names, and how does he present them as one: ‘in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’? The name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, but it is the name of the Trinity.

> “What is said ‘in the name of God the Father,’ ‘in the name of God the Son,’ and ‘in the name of God the Holy Spirit’ is one name of divinity: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one name. But you ask me how three are called by one name. I do not know, and I freely confess that I do not know what Christ did not wish to disclose. I know only this—and in this I am a Christian—that I confess one God in the Trinity.

> “But if I say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one person, I shall be called a Sabellian, and I shall begin to be not a Christian but a Jew. For the Jew says there is one God, and because he does not acknowledge the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he does not grasp the mystery of the Trinity.

> “Therefore, if we say ‘one God’ in such a way as to exclude the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit from the mystery of the Trinity, we become Jews. I freely say—not from myself but according to the Savior’s judgment—that the stumbling block arises in the listener’s mind: how three are one, and how the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not divided in divinity but distinguished in the quality of their persons.

> “Whenever I speak of persons, I ask you not to think that I mean human persons. I do not speak of persons in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as though they were human persons. I speak of the person of the Father because he is Father, of the person of the Son because he is Son, and of the person of the Holy Spirit because he is the Holy Spirit. The Father is not the Son, nor is the Son the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son. They are divided by their properties but joined in nature.”

Again, in another sermon *On the Faith against the Arians and Sabellians*:

> “There is absolutely no rank in the Trinity, nothing that can be called lower or more particular. The whole deity is so equal in its perfection that, except for the names that indicate the properties of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most worthily be understood of the three.

> “Just as, in refuting Arius, we say that the Trinity has one and the same substance and confess one God in three persons, so, in avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish the three persons as expressly marked by their own properties. We do not say that the Father is himself the Son, or himself the Holy Spirit, but that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another.

> “We confess not merely names but also the property of the names, that is, the persons. The Father never excludes the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, nor does the Son or the Holy Spirit in turn receive the name and person of the Father. The Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance and distinguished in persons and names.”

And again, Saint Augustine, in book I, chapter 4, *On the Trinity*:

> “All those whom I have been able to read who wrote before me about the Trinity, which is God—the Catholic interpreters of the divine books, both ancient and new—intended to teach according to the Scriptures that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, being of one and the same substance and inseparably equal, disclose the divine unity. Therefore they are not three gods but one God.

> “Yet the Father begot the Son, and therefore the Son is not the Father; the Son was begotten by the Father, and therefore the Father is not the Son; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but solely the Spirit of the Father and the Son, himself also coequal with the Father and the Son and belonging to the unity of the Trinity.”

Saint Sophronius, in his Catholic letter, which the Sixth Synod produced for the confirmation of the Catholic faith (Sixth Synod, act 11), says:

> “We know one principle of one deity, one dominion, one power, one operation, one counsel, one will, one sovereignty, one movement—both creative and providential, stabilizing and preserving, of all things that come after it—one dominion, one eternity, and whatever other such singular and uncompounded attributes belong to one essence and nature in three personal subsistences.

> “We neither confuse the subsistences by reducing them to one subsistence, nor divide the same one essence and tear it apart into three essences, thereby dividing the one deity. Rather, there is one God, one deity, shining forth in three subsistences, and the three subsistences and persons are recognized in the one deity.

> “Therefore the Father is perfect God, the Son is perfect God, and the Holy Spirit is perfect God, because each person possesses the one and same deity—inseparable, undiminished, and perfect. And insofar as each is God, each is the same thing when considered separately, with the intellect separating what is not separable, so that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit may nevertheless be called ‘another, and another, and another.’

> “For this reason those capable of understanding God proclaim these as ‘God, and God, and God,’ but these three are one God. The Father is not another God, nor is the Son another God, nor again is the Holy Spirit another God, because the Father is not of one nature, the Son of another nature, or the Holy Spirit of yet another nature.

> “For this would also produce many and different gods and generate many varied deities. But the Father is God, the Son is God, and likewise the Holy Spirit is God, because the same three persons are filled with one undivided and undiminished deity, and in each of them it exists wholly.

> “For deity does not endure division; it exists fully and perfectly in the three persons—not filling those persons in parts or partially, but existing in each as complete, while remaining one, although it is shown in three persons and extends toward a plurality of gods, although it exists in three subsistences. Thus it does not undergo any bodily division, since it is impassible and incorporeal and cannot suffer, qualities proper to creatures.”

These things the Holy Spirit speaks through the holy Athanasius, Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine. But the unclean spirit exhales through the most unclean Gothescalcus, saying:

> “Just as every Catholic believes and confesses each one of the persons of the Trinity to be wholly, fully, and perfectly God, so let him believe and confess that each person possesses his own deity, wholly, fully, and perfectly.”

Yet, as Saint Ambrose writes (*On the Faith*, book I, chapter 2):

> “By saying, ‘Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’” (Matt. 28:19), “the Lord showed that the Trinity possesses one power. We confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in such a way that in the perfect Trinity there is both the fullness of divinity and the unity of power.

> “Every kingdom divided against itself will quickly be destroyed, the Lord says. The kingdom of the Trinity, therefore, is not divided. If it is not divided, it is one. For what is not one is divided. They wish the kingdom of the Trinity to be such that it may easily be destroyed by its division. Rather, since it cannot be destroyed, it is clear that it is not divided. Unity is not divided or torn apart.”

And a little later, in the same chapter:

> “There is a fullness of divinity in the Father, and there is a fullness of divinity in the Son—not a differing fullness, but one divinity; nor is what is one confused, nor what is undifferentiated multiple.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The Arians must deny either the divinity of the Father or that of the Son unless they believe in the unity of the same divinity.”

Again:

> “To prove that the deity and dominion of the Father and the Son are one, and to prevent us from falling into the error of Gentile or Jewish impiety, the Apostle, foreseeing what we ought to follow, showed it by saying: ‘One God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him’” (1 Cor. 8:6).

And shortly afterward, in the same chapter:

> “What other judgment can there be where there is unity of deity?”

And in book I *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 13:

> “Is there one offense against the Son and another against the Holy Spirit? For just as there is one divinity, so there is one injury. If, therefore, there is one peace, one grace, one love, and one communion of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, there is certainly one operation; and where there is one operation, the power cannot be divided between the two, nor can the substance be distinguished.

> “For it is written: ‘Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’” (Matt. 28:19). “He said ‘in the name,’ not ‘in the names.’ Therefore the name of the Father is not one, the name of the Son another, and the name of the Holy Spirit another. There is one God, not several names; there are not two gods or three gods.

> “And to make clear that one divinity is one majesty, because the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, and that the Son did not come in one name and the Holy Spirit in another, the Lord himself says: ‘I have come in my Father’s name’” (John 5:43).

And shortly afterward, in the same chapter:

> “It is written: ‘But the Paraclete, the Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything’” (John 14:26). “Since he who comes in the name of the Son certainly also comes in the name of the Father, the name of the Father and the Son is one. Thus the name of the Father and the Son is one, and so is the name of the Holy Spirit. For there is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved. He thereby taught that the unity of the divine name must be believed, not disparity.”

And in book III, chapter 14:

> “Where one deity is understood, one God is named. But let us excuse you from ignorance, even if we do not excuse you from guilt. For according to our judgment, since there is one God and one divinity, the unity of power is understood. Just as we say one God and confess the Father under the name of the true deity, without denying the Son, so we do not exclude the Holy Spirit from the unity of deity. We do not assert three gods but deny them, because plurality is produced not by unity but by division of power.

> “For how can the unity of divinity receive plurality, when plurality belongs to number, while divine nature does not receive number?”

And in chapter 15:

> “There is therefore one God, while the majesty of the eternal Trinity remains unharmed, as the example proposed makes clear. Nor is it only in that passage that we see the Trinity expressed by the name of divinity, but also in many places, as we have said above, especially in the letters that the Apostle wrote to the Thessalonians.”

Again, in chapter 17:

> “Therefore, just as the Father is God and the Son is Lord, so the Son is God and the Father is Lord. The pious designation is reciprocal, but the divine nature is not reciprocal; grace remains unchanged. For these are not comparative expressions of generosity but the decrees of natural love, because unity also possesses property, and property possesses unity.”

Again, in chapter 19:

> “Let them say, then, what they confess the deity to be without the Father and the Son.”

Saint Augustine, in book IV, chapter 21, *On the Trinity*, says:

> “In their own substance, in which they exist, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, without any temporal movement, above every creature, themselves without any intervals of times or places, simultaneously one and the same from eternity to eternity, as the very eternity—which does not exist without truth and love.

> “But in my words the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are separated; they cannot be spoken simultaneously, and in visible letters they occupy separate spaces according to place.”

And in his book *On True Religion* (chapter 55):

> “Therefore we ought to worship and hold the very gift of God, together with the Father and the Son, as equally unchangeable: the Trinity of one substance.”

And in his book *Against Maximinus* (book III, chapter 10):

> “For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, and these three, because they are of one substance, are one—indeed supremely one—where there is no diversity of natures and no diversity of wills. If they were one in nature but not in agreement, they would not be supremely one. If they were different in nature, they would not be one. These three, therefore, because they are one through the ineffable union of deity by which they are ineffably joined, are one God.”

And again, from his book *Against Maximinus* (book III, at the end):

> “It is sufficiently clear that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one power, one substance, one deity, one majesty, and one glory; through these the Trinity itself is one Lord our God, of whom it was said: ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God’” (Deut. 6:4).

And Leo, in his letter to Turibius, bishop of Astorga (letter 4, chapter 1):

> “The Catholic faith confesses the Trinity of the deity as *homoousios* [consubstantial], believing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be undivided without confusion, eternal without time, and equal without difference, because unity in the Trinity is fulfilled not by the same person but by the same essence.”

And Saint Gregory repeatedly writes in his books on the Trinity of the one deity, just as we showed above that he said in the sixteenth homily on the prophet Ezekiel. Likewise Prosper and the other Catholic teachers, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, thought and spoke in this way, and handed these things down to us in their writings to be read and held immutably.

Hence Saint Athanasius, in his book *Profession of the Catholic Faith* against Gothescalcus and his associates—these statements appear in Book VI—says:

> “Cursed is he who does not confess that the substance of the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one and eternal. So be it, so be it.

> “Cursed is he who confesses that there are three different substances in these three persons. So be it, so be it.

> “Cursed is he who does not confess that the name is united according to the deity of the Trinity. So be it, so be it.

> “Cursed is he who does not confess the undivided deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. So be it, so be it.

> “Cursed is he who professes that the united deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exists only through the love of concord, and not rather through this very united divinity. So be it, so be it.

> “Cursed is he who does not confess that the united deity exists in these three persons. So be it, so be it.

> “Cursed is he who does not confess that the unity or fullness of the divine Trinity is undivided. So be it, so be it.”

A thousand testimonies from the sacred Scriptures and from the writings of the orthodox could be offered on this point. Indeed, it is never found or stated otherwise anywhere in the sacred Scriptures or in the words of the orthodox except that in the holy Trinity there are three persons and one divinity, deity, nature, essence, and substance.

But against what that same Gothescalcus, more demented—or rather, utterly insane—says:

### IX.

> “In this it is clearer than daylight and more evident than the brightness of the sun that each person possesses his own deity and divinity, because in truth the whole Trinity did not assume humanity in any way—God forbid—but only the deity of the Son assumed it.”

ΧΡ. Raising its voice, the Catholic Church—more powerfully than thunder and more sonorously than a trumpet—exposes Gothescalc’s falsehood as darker than night and more obscure than darkness. It says [Col. 0551A] that, contrary to the way that liar falsely claims, there is not in each person his own, that is, particular, deity and divinity; rather, the deity and substance of the three persons together are one and the same. By this one deity, all three persons together are one true and perfect God, from the fullness of that one and the same divinity, in which nothing less is understood to be in each individual person and nothing more in the three. Hence the holy Trinity is called indivisible and inseparable.

Thus Leo, from Rome—the head of the world—not only against him but throughout the whole world against all heretics, thunders in a sweet-toned roar, writing to Turibius, bishop of Astorga (Letter 4, chapter 1): “Because unity in the Trinity is effected not by the same person but by the same essence.” And Augustine, explaining Ambrose when he says, “You, unity of the Trinity,” says: “The divinity—or, if it can be expressed more clearly, the deity—which is the unity of the Trinity.” Athanasius, explaining what “unity” means, says that the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. Therefore it is not, as Gothescalcus says, the deity of the Son alone, but the person of the Son alone who assumed humanity, as blessed Augustine says in the sermon on faith against the Sabellians and Arians mentioned above:

“Although,” he says, “properly speaking the person of the Son, that is, the Word of God, assumed a passible human being, nevertheless, through his indwelling, according to his substance the deity of the Word suffered nothing, so that the whole Trinity—which must be confessed to be impassible—did not suffer.”

Concerning the unity of substance of this Trinity, namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the same blessed Augustine says in *Against Pascentius* (Letter 178) [Col. 0551C]:

“Behold, we rightly prove that *ὁμοούσιον* [*homoousion*, ‘of the same substance’] has been correctly placed and, as an affirmation of the faith by which the Trinity is believed by Catholics to be unity, was spoken by the Greek Fathers.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore *ὁμοούσιος* is explained as meaning: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance.”

Again, in the same book:

“It is therefore not absurd that in the councils of the Fathers the one substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit was established by a Greek word, since at the beginning, upon the apostles, the variety of languages was poured out through the particular generosity of the Holy Spirit.”

And a little later:

“For just as in Greek the word *ὁμοούσιον* is said or believed by the faithful to mean that the substance of the Trinity is altogether one, so by all Latins and barbarians one nature of the one God is asked to have mercy.”

This whole holy Trinity, which is of one substance and whose operation is inseparable, as are its deity and will, fashioned ineffably and incomprehensibly in the womb of the perpetual virgin, blessed and glorious Mary, the humanity which the Son of God, one person of that same holy Trinity, assumed in the unity of his person. Thus Saint Athanasius says in his book on faith (Book XI, midway through):

“That which is greater in the whole creation—the body of the Lord—is believed to be from the Holy Spirit, as the evangelist Matthew relates: ‘The generation of Christ was thus. When Mary his mother had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to have conceived in the womb from the Holy Spirit. But Joseph her husband, being a just man and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly. While he was considering this, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said to him: Son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife, for what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. I, 18).

“And although the Wisdom of Solomon says in Proverbs concerning the Savior’s body, ‘Wisdom built herself a house’ (Prov. IX, 1), and here it confesses that the Only-Begotten himself created his body, nevertheless the angel said that this body was from the Holy Spirit; and thus every Christian believes when instructed. For Scripture does not disagree concerning the Trinity, everywhere teaching that its operation is one and the same.

“Finally, when the blessed Virgin Mary was about to give birth to God, after hearing Gabriel say, ‘Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus,’ and the rest, and after asking, ‘How will this be, since I do not know a man?’ (Luke I, 31), she was immediately instructed by him, who said: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.’

“But if the power of the Most High is the Only-Begotten, according to Paul, who says, ‘Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God’ (I Cor. I, 24), while the Holy Spirit is the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, and, when these overshadowed her, Mary gave birth to God and the Lord’s temple was created; and if the angel said that he was created from the Holy Spirit, why are we not taught that this is the operation of the Trinity?”

Saint Ambrose likewise says in Book II, chapter 8, *On the Holy Spirit*:

“For, as we read that the Father created the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, so we also read that the Holy Spirit created it; and likewise we read that Christ himself created his own body. The Father created it, according to what is written: ‘The Lord created me’ (Gal. IV, 4). And elsewhere: ‘God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law’ (Matt. I, 18). The Spirit also created that entire mystery, according to what we read: ‘Mary was found to have conceived in the womb from the Holy Spirit.’ You have it that the Father created; the Holy Spirit also created. Accept that the Son of God also created, when Solomon says: ‘Wisdom made herself a house’ (Prov. IX, 1).”

Blessed Augustine likewise confirms these same things with testimonies from Scripture in his sermon on the Trinity.

And the memorable Alcuin, in his book on faith addressed to the great emperor Charles, compiled from Saint Augustine’s first book *On the Trinity* and from the sayings and judgments of other Catholic Fathers—whose words anyone who reads them in their proper places will be able to recognize in this work—says as follows (Book III, *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity*, chapter 10):

“Although the nature of the holy Trinity is one, nevertheless the whole Trinity was not incarnate, but the person of the Son alone mercifully assumed human nature. Yet the Son of God was not so incarnate that there was in him one nature of divinity and flesh. For divinity could not be what flesh is, nor flesh what divinity is, since each nature—that is, the divine and the human—remained in its own distinct property.

“Therefore we confess that human nature, that is, flesh and a rational soul, was assumed not by the whole Trinity but by the Son alone, into the unity of person, not into the unity of nature. The person of the Son is certainly not the same as that of the Father or of the Holy Spirit. Thus the unity of person, while the distinct property of each substance remains, just as did not make Christ a double person, likewise did not make the assumption of human nature common to the holy Trinity.

“For that assumption of servile form belongs only to the person of God the Word; yet the assumption of humanity removed nothing from the fullness of divinity and deprived Christ of none of his dominion. Hence, in one and the same Christ, the reality of human nature shone forth and the unchangeability of divine nature remained eternal.

“Nevertheless, this must be understood: although the whole Trinity made this servile form, which the Son of God alone assumed, it is certain that, having been made by the whole holy Trinity, it belongs only to the person of the Son of God. For neither the Father assumed flesh nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone, so that he who was the Son of God the Father in divinity might himself become the son of the Virgin Mother in humanity, lest the name ‘son’ pass to another person who would not be a son by birth.

“Thus the Son of God became the Son of man, born according to the truth of nature from God as the Son of God, and according to the truth of nature from man as the son of man—being in both natures truly the Son of God, not merely by designation or adoption.”

Therefore there are not two sons of Christ, nor two sons, but one Christ and one Son, God and man; for the Son of God assumed human nature, not a human person, receiving eternally the person of divinity and temporally the substance of humanity. Man passed into God, not by a changeability of nature but because of the unity of the divine person, lest there be a quaternity rather than a Trinity in the holy Trinity.

Behold how the Catholics show that the heretic Gothescalcus lied: not as he said does each person in the holy Trinity possess his own deity and divinity, but the three persons in the holy Trinity belong to one and the same substance of deity and divinity, that is, to one nature or essence. For if each person in the holy Trinity possessed his own, that is, particular, deity—as we have said above and must always assert in contradicting heretics—the holy Trinity would not be indivisible and inseparable, and there would be three gods.

And not, as that same son in imitation of his father the devil, who is a liar and the father of lies, falsely says, did the deity of the Son alone assume flesh. Rather, the person of the Son alone assumed flesh: it is proper to him that, as the coeternal Son born from the substance of the Father without any beginning, he is of one and the same substance—that is, deity, which is the unity of the Trinity—with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The flesh which he assumed was fashioned together in the womb of the ever-Virgin by the whole holy Trinity, coessential, coeternal, and co-omnipotent with itself.

Finally, he adds:

## X.

÷ “Indeed, when we are baptized—that is, immersed—we are unquestionably plunged three times; nevertheless, because of this, the triple immersion and the threefold baptism, that is, the triple dipping, are not, God forbid, three immersions and three dippings, or three baptisms. Rather, there is one immersion in general and one dipping, that is, one baptism, as the Apostle says: ‘One Lord, one faith, one baptism’ (Eph. IV, 5).”

ΧΡ. As is his custom, he has invented novelties of expression, in which he has always delighted and which he has sought in order to appear wise while evading the simplicity of the faith; in this matter too, he devised them so that he might confirm his perverse opinion.

To support what he had said—that Judas, Simon Magus, the false brothers of whom the Apostle speaks, and all those baptized with Christ’s baptism who are not to be saved were not redeemed by Christ’s blood—when the saying of the Apostle Peter was shown to him concerning heretics, “Denying the Lord who bought them” (II Pet. II, 1), he was pressed by difficulty and devised his own interpretation of that same passage. He taught that there are two redemptions: one by which those who are not to be saved were redeemed, although they were not baptized in Christ’s blood, and another by which those who are to be saved were baptized in Christ’s blood. He said that no one who had been redeemed by Christ’s blood could perish, failing to see what Paul, Peter’s fellow apostle, says: “All who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Rom. VI, 5); and, “Through your knowledge the brother for whom Christ died will perish” (I Cor. VIII, 11).

What he says is astonishing; what he says is novel. Therefore, as Augustine says in writing against Julian: “We are astonished at the astonishing, we avoid the novel, and we prove the false.” In another book, which we have compiled from authoritative Scriptures and the sayings of the orthodox against his perverse statements and those of his accomplices, we prove that he spoke falsely, as is evident to all wise people.

But concerning his claim that the threefold immersion and threefold baptism, that is, the threefold dipping, are not, God forbid, three immersions and three dippings—that is, three baptisms—but one immersion in general and one dipping, that is, one baptism, with the Apostle saying, “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV, 5), let the Catholic faith say to him: “By your own words I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke XIX, 22).

If you believe and confess that the three immersions in the name of the holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are one baptism, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, of one essence, one deity, and one nature, and because Catholic baptism is celebrated in his name, why are you so witless as to divide the unity of the deity by asserting a threefold deity—the deity by which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God?

And because, following the custom of your father the devil, you mix falsehoods with truths and poison with honey, so that from truth and the sweetness of honey you may commend false and deadly things, in what you said—that the three immersions or dippings are one baptism because there is one Lord and one faith—we approve you. But because you also said that there are not three immersions and three dippings in baptism, we reject you and prove that you are lying.

Nevertheless, we wish to ask you why those three immersions and three dippings are not three baptisms but one baptism. If you remain silent, we say that the three immersions are one baptism because it is celebrated Catholicly in the united—indeed, one—name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whose deity, divinity, and substance are one.

Thus Athanasius says in his book *On the Individual Persons and the United Name of the Divinity* (Book II, near the end):

“John,” he says, “testifies concerning the Lord: ‘He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God’ (John I, 11).

“Learn, therefore, that this united name is everlasting in the deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

Likewise there is one baptism of faith, which grants eternal life to believers. For just as the name is united in the nature of the Trinity, so there is also one gift through the baptism of divinity. The Apostle says: “One faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV, 5).

Therefore, as the name of the Father is in the divinity, so the name of the Son is in the nature of the deity; likewise this name belongs also to the Holy Spirit in the substance of glory. For there are three, as the Apostle John says, who bear witness: spirit, water, and blood, and these three are one (I John V, 7).

“The spirit,” says Leo, “of sanctification, the blood of redemption, and the water of baptism—these three are one and remain indivisible, and none of them is separated from its connection.”

For, as Augustine says, and Leo after him in his letters, neither humanity exists without true divinity, nor divinity is to be believed without true humanity.

These things are also one in us, not by nature but through the same operation of the mystery. For, as blessed Ambrose says, the Spirit renews the mind, the water benefits for washing, and the blood pertains to the price. The Spirit made us children of God by adoption, the water of the sacred font washed us, and the Lord’s blood redeemed us.

As for what he adds—that there is one immersion in general and one dipping, that is, one baptism—he himself does not know what he is saying, but the Catholic teachers clearly show that he is lying.

Those three immersions are individually three, and there is not one immersion in general, just as the three persons in the holy Trinity are distinct, subsisting according to their own properties, and inseparable; there is not one person in general. There are indeed three immersions individually because of the distinct properties of the persons of the holy Trinity, but there is one baptism because there is one God, namely, of one essence, one deity, and one nature, and therefore one name—God—which is the holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In this name we are baptized and made children of God by grace, having been reborn, although we were children of the devil, generated through the transmission of accursed seed.

And just as the inner man, created in the image of the holy Trinity, must be restored to that image through faith in the holy Trinity, so the outer man must be washed by a threefold immersion, so that what the Spirit invisibly accomplishes in the soul the priest may visibly imitate in the water.

For original sin was committed in three ways: by delight (*delectatione*), consent, and deed. Thus every sin is committed either in thought, word, or action. Therefore a threefold washing appears suited to the threefold kind of sin—whether because of original sin, which brings infants to perdition, or because of those sins added in people of more advanced age by will, word, or deed.

And rightly, the human being who was created in the image of the holy Trinity is restored to that same image through the invocation of the holy Trinity, so that the one who fell into death by sinning in a threefold degree may, being raised three times from the font, rise through grace to life.

Hence Saint Jerome, in Book II of his exposition of the Epistle of Saint Paul to the Ephesians, explaining the saying “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV), speaks as follows concerning the threefold immersion and one baptism:

“For if, as the Arians believe, God the Father alone is God, then by the same reasoning Jesus Christ alone will be Lord, and neither will the Father be Lord nor the Son God. But far be it from us to say that there is not divinity in lordship or lordship in divinity. There is one Lord and one God, because the lordship of the Father and Son is one divinity.

“Therefore faith is also called one, because we believe similarly in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and baptism is one. For we are baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in the same way, and we are immersed three times, so that the sacrament of the Trinity may appear as one.

“And we are not baptized in the names of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but in one name, which is understood to mean God. I am astonished by what reasoning Arius, Macedonius, and Eunomius suspect a diversity of nature in one word, the same act, and the same sacrament. In agreement only in impiety, while holding a muddy fountain of creaturehood concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit, they have led out different streams of heresies.

“One baptism also stands against Valentinus, who maintains that there are two baptisms, and against all heretics, so that they may know that they do not possess baptism, but that the life-giving font is in the one Church of Christ.

“One baptism can also be said in this way: although we are baptized three times because of the mystery of the holy Trinity, nevertheless the baptism is reckoned as one. There is also one baptism in water, Spirit, and fire, and the baptism of which the Lord speaks: ‘I have a baptism with which I must be baptized’ (Luke XII, 50); and elsewhere: ‘With the baptism with which I am baptized you will be baptized’ (Mark X, 39).”

[Col. 0556D] By these words of the holy Jerome, Athanasius, and the other teachers—especially Ambrose, Augustine, Leo, and Gregory, from whose sayings we have excerpted what follows—it is clearly shown that Gothescalcus did not speak truly when he said that the three immersions are one immersion in general.

Rather, the truth is that, just as in the holy Trinity there are three inseparable persons, subsisting according to their own properties, and one deity, nature, will, power, and operation, so in the Lord Jesus Christ there are, conversely, two natures, divinity and humanity, and one person.

He, as the Apostle John says, “came by water and blood, not by water only, but by water and blood” (I John V, 6), so that his body, which is the Church, might be watered by the washing and the cup.

Thus in the one baptism which is celebrated for the remission of sins in the Catholic Church—under three immersions against the fraud of the Sabellians, just as in certain provinces it is celebrated under one immersion in the name of the holy Trinity against the fraud of the Arians, according to the Church’s faithful tradition—because within one faith a differing custom does no harm to the holy Church, there are three who bear witness: spirit, water, and blood. These three are one, not by nature but by the mystery and indivisible sacrament, and none of them is separated from its connection.

And just as we must undoubtedly believe that whatever is read as performed by the individual persons of the holy Trinity is performed inseparably by the holy Trinity itself, whose substance and deity are inseparable, so it is entirely certain that the Father alone said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17); that the Son alone is the one upon whom the voice of the Father alone sounded when the same Only-Begotten God, who alone assumed flesh, was baptized according to his humanity in the Jordan; and that the Holy Spirit alone, belonging to the Father and the Son, descended in the form of a dove upon him as he rose from the water after being baptized, and, on the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection, came and filled the faithful gathered in one place in the appearance of fiery tongues.

Nevertheless, we must most truly believe that the voice by which God the Father alone spoke, the flesh by which the Only-Begotten God alone became man, the dove in whose form the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ, and the fiery tongues in whose appearance he filled the faithful assembled in one place were works of the whole holy Trinity—that is, of the one God who made visible and invisible things in heaven and on earth.

Thus, in the one Catholic baptism, although the Spirit renews the human mind, the blood pertains to the price, and the water benefits for washing—not merely cleansing the flesh by removing dirt, but cleansing all the filth of sins through faith and the appeal of a good conscience toward God—nevertheless redemption by the blood does not occur without the sanctification of the Spirit or the washing of the life-giving font; nor does sanctification by the Spirit occur without redemption by the life-giving blood and cleansing by the regenerating water; nor does the washing of the water sanctified by the Word occur without the redemption of the blood and the sanctification of the regenerating Spirit.

When the Word is added to the element, it becomes a sacrament.

And Pope Leo, writing to all the bishops established throughout Sicily (Letter 5, chapter 3), says concerning the threefold immersion and one baptism—as the reader will find more fully in its proper place:

“The rule of baptism includes death through the destruction of sin, and the threefold immersion imitates a three-day burial; the raising from the waters represents the one rising from the tomb” (Book I, Letter 41).

Saint Gregory likewise writes in his letter to Leander, bishop of Spalato:

“Concerning the threefold immersion of baptism, nothing truer can be answered than what you yourselves have understood: in one faith a differing custom does no harm to the holy Church.

“We immerse three times to signify the sacrament of the three-day burial, so that, when the infant is raised from the waters three times, the resurrection of the three-day period may be expressed.

“But if someone should perhaps think that it is also done out of supreme reverence for the Trinity, this likewise presents no obstacle to immersing the one being baptized once in the water. Since there is one substance in three subsistences, it cannot in any way be blameworthy to immerse an infant in baptism either three times or once: in the three immersions the trinity of persons may be signified, and in the one immersion the singularity of the divinity.

“But if until now the infant has been immersed three times in baptism by heretics, I do not think this should be done among you, lest, while they count the immersions, they divide the divinity, and, while you do what they did, they boast that they have overcome your custom.”

Because the Lord had commanded his disciples, “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19), Saint Athanasius exposed this fraud of the heretics of that time in Book VII, saying:

“Why, after removing this name of the divinity—of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—do you baptize by saying, ‘I baptize you in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit,’ and not in one name? In this way you can cunningly remain silent about, or secretly fail to name or deny, the united name in the deity, while wishing to assign the names only to the persons.

“For if baptism were to be celebrated in this way, the assertion of the Arians would prevail. They think that wherever the names are indicated as persons, there, together with those names, individual or different substances are also to be declared in the names themselves, so that they assign unity only to an agreement of love and not rather to the united fullness of divinity.

“And what more can be said about this? They should perhaps also profess that the name of the unity of God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—has recently appeared as if adopted, so that this name might seem to be from nothing, or from something else, or from time. Far be it from us! For when they name the true name of the deity, they assign it by these words to the person of the Father alone, so that they may divide the true unity of the divinity.

“Where they ought to distinguish only the names according to the persons, there they simultaneously distinguish three natures along with those names. Far be it from us to admit this blasphemy, since we accept the one name of the deity, spoken in unity in the Trinity, through which we receive the remission of sins effected in baptism, while we perfectly distinguish the individual names only according to the persons.

“I ask: where is the bond of faith among them if the name of the unity of substance is not maintained in the Trinity? I ask: how are the three one if there is a different nature of divinity in the two? I ask: how do they deserve to obtain this sevenfold Spirit—the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord—if they do not confess him to consist of the united fullness of divinity?

“When the Lord says, ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. XXVIII, 19), I am truly astonished at this and, remaining longer intent in amazement of mind, praise the fact that such glory of the most sacred Trinity has been briefly set forth in precisely twelve words of distinctions or syllables” (Book VIII, at the beginning).

“Truly, in this command the united name of the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit has been sent forth. Truly, in this most sacred Trinity the names are distinguished only according to the persons. Truly, neither the Law nor the Prophets revealed this hidden mystery so explicitly.

“Above every divinely established ordinance, this above all must be guarded. Truly, nothing can be added to it, and nothing can be taken away from it. Truly, in this gift of baptism it is blasphemous to add to or subtract from the command. Why is unity proclaimed if in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there is not one and the same equal fullness of divinity?” (Book II, after the middle, toward the end.)

And in Book II he says that the apostles were sent to baptize all nations in the united or common name of the divinity: “Go, baptize all nations in the name,” and then he continued through the individual persons: “of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

“Can baptism be celebrated perfectly in the Church against the rule of evangelical tradition if the person of the Holy Spirit is removed or omitted from this united name of the Trinity? Far be it! Learn, therefore, that this united name is everlasting in the deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

Likewise, baptism of faith is one, granting eternal life to believers, because just as the name is united in the nature of the Trinity, so there is one gift through the baptism of divinity. The Apostle says: “One faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV, 5). Therefore, as the name of the Father is in the divinity, so the name of the Son is in the nature of the deity; likewise, this name belongs to the Holy Spirit in the substance of glory.

The reader will find these matters, collected here briefly, more fully in their proper places.

By these words and judgments of the Catholic teachers it is proved that Gothescalcus’s testimony is not valid. Speaking from himself, seeking his own glory, and not drawing from the Catholic Scriptures to confirm his opinion, he said: “The threefold immersion and threefold baptism, that is, the threefold dipping, is one immersion in general and one dipping, that is, one baptism.” For Catholic baptism, as blessed Gregory has shown, may be performed with one immersion, but in the name of the holy Trinity.

Hence Athanasius says in his first book *On Faith* (*On the United Name of the Trinity*):

“Are the nations, for whom the entrance of the gate stands open to believers unto eternal life, baptized only into the person of the Father and not into the three whose names are distinguished according to their persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—to whom belongs one nature of divinity, as it is written: ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name,’ and then he continued, ‘of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. XXVIII, 19)?

“Therefore, in these persons the name is united in every respect in the deity of divinity, and through these names only the persons of the Trinity are distinguished.”

And a little later:

“This is the hope of our faith: that in baptism you first confess the united name of the divinity, so that you may deserve to obtain the remission of sins in these persons.”

As for what we read in the sacred history of the Acts of the Apostles—that the apostles commanded the Gentiles to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ—the same Athanasius explains it in Book X:

“For it is not written” (Book XI, after the middle), he says, “that they baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but only in the name of Jesus; yet they did not transgress—far be it! For although only the name of the Son is mentioned, it nevertheless contains the Father and the Holy Spirit as proclaimed, as we prove from the holy Scriptures.

“Thus the Holy Spirit is also called ‘Sabaoth,’ and he is worshiped together with God and the Son by the Seraphim. For this reason they said three times: ‘Holy, holy, holy,’ in order to proclaim the Trinity.”

And blessed Ambrose says in his book *On Faith* that the mystery is fulfilled through the unity of the name:

“Whether you say ‘Christ,’ you have indicated God the Father by whom the Son was anointed, the Son himself who was anointed, and the Spirit by whom he was anointed. For it is written: ‘Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit’ (Acts X, 38). Or whether you say ‘Father,’ you have likewise indicated his Son and the Spirit of his mouth, provided that you also comprehend this in your heart.”

The reader will find these matters more fully in their proper places.

Now the Catholic Church, blocking the tunnels of the heretics, pronounces the very words of the Lord the Savior—of whom it is written, “For he is the one who baptizes”—in the consecration of holy baptism, believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation.

At last Gothescalcus adds:

## XI.

÷ “Likewise, when a threefold or triple faith is mentioned, as in that saying of Sedulius, your faithful poet:

> ‘This man embraces a threefold faith, but that one does not embrace one,’

there are not, God forbid, three faiths, but one faith, as the Apostle says: ‘One faith.’”

ΧΡ. Concerning this point, which he wished to present to us as though it were something novel—and thus presumably something at which we should marvel—the holy Hilary, an ancient and venerable Father, showed us in his book *On the Synods*, with sound understanding, what this man has displayed with the most perverse presumption. “Nothing,” says Saint Hilary, “ought to seem marvelous to you, dearest brothers, because the faiths began frequently to be expounded. Heretical madness imposed this necessity.” Because of the several writings composed by Saint Hilary, *faiths* is said in the plural, and because of the plurality of writings, not because of any division of belief; for, as Jerome says in the second book of his *Commentary on the Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians* [Col. 0560D]: “For this reason faith is also called one, because we believe alike in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

And Augustine, in the thirteenth book of *On the Trinity* (chapter 11), says: “Faith is not one in number, but in kind. Nevertheless, because of the likeness and the absence of any difference, we call it one rather than many; and yet when one says, ‘Woman, great is your faith’ (Matthew 15:28), and to another, ‘O you of little faith, why did you doubt?’ (Matthew 14:31), he indicates that each has her own faith. But it is called the same faith, one faith, in the same way that the will of those who will is called one will.
