And Saint Gregory says in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* (chapter 2) that without faith not even the unbeliever lives.”

The faith of which the Apostle says, “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5), is catholic; from it the one dove of God—namely, the holy Church—is called catholic, that is, universal. This is the one house concerning which the Lord commands through Moses that nothing be taken out of the paschal lamb (Exodus 12:46), but that it be eaten within it; and it is the ark, outside which no one found during the time of the Flood could live.

This, I say, is the one faith—not one in number, but general in kind, belonging generally to all who remain in the unity of the holy Church. As it is contained in the apostolic Creed, it was handed down by Christ to the holy Apostles and, through their successors—apostolic men, that is—was proclaimed in the six general synods: the Nicene Synod, in the time of Saint Pope Sylvester and Constantine; the Constantinopolitan, in the times of Damasus and Gratian; the Ephesian, under Celestine and Theodosius [Col. 0561B]; the Chalcedonian, in the times of Leo and Marcian; the second Constantinopolitan, under Vigilius and Justinian; and the third Constantinopolitan, under Agatho and the younger Constantine; as well as in the other catholic synods confirmed by the Apostolic See. Unless each person preserves it whole and inviolate, he cannot be saved, but will perish eternally.

Hence Saint Augustine says in his *Commentary on the Epistle of John*: “Faith with love is the faith of a Christian; faith without love is the faith of a demon. Those who do not believe are worse than demons. Someone does not wish to believe in Christ: he does not yet even imitate the demons. Now he believes in Christ, but he hates Christ. He possesses a confession of faith through fear of punishment, not through love of the crown. Add love to this faith, so that it may become the faith of which the Apostle Paul says, ‘Faith working through love’ (Galatians 5:6): you have found a Christian; you have found a citizen of Jerusalem.”

And in the Gospel of John: “Who is soundly faithful except one who has that faith which works through love?” Prosper, drawing on Augustine’s words, likewise says: “Good works are only those which are performed through faith and love, because either one without the other produces the fruit of no virtue.”

For this reason Gothescalcus the heretic, who verbally preaches one faith according to the Apostle, demonstrates that he does not possess true faith in his writings cited above, because the Apostle Paul says: “Faith working through love.” Love is called *dilectio* in Latin and *charity* (*charitas*) in Greek. Concerning it the same Apostle Paul says: “If I hand over my body to be burned but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

Hence Saint Gregory says in the eighteenth book of the *Moralia* (chapter 14): “Some hold perverse opinions about God; others retain right opinions about their Creator, but do not maintain unity with their brothers. The former are divided by error in faith, the latter by the perpetration of schism. Therefore, in the very first part of the Decalogue, the faults of both parties are restrained, when the divine voice says, ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength’ (Deuteronomy 6:5), and immediately adds, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’ (Matthew 22:36; 28:39). Whoever thinks perversely about God clearly does not love God. Whoever, while thinking rightly about God, is divided from the unity of the holy Church plainly does not love his neighbor, whom he refuses to have as a companion. Therefore, whoever is separated from this unity of his mother Church—whether by thinking perversely about God through heresy, or by failing to love his neighbor through the error of schism—is deprived of this grace of charity.”

And the aforesaid Apostle says: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4). Hence Augustine says: “Christ is called the end because Christ is God, the end of the commandment of charity; and God is charity, through which the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one.”

We also wonder why, when he cited Sedulius concerning *ternary faith*, he neglected to cite Arator concerning *triune faith*, since Arator, speaking figuratively in the first book, says:

> Triune faith calls this one, by whose name he is washed in the font.

And concerning the *triune name* he says in the second book:

> … Our faith does not compel this man to go again to the water,
>
> who [is] by a threefold name.

And again, speaking figuratively of faith in the first book:

> It was then more nearly the ninth hour, when more rightly the hour
>
> would already bring forth triune faith and the third, simple one.

When he summoned him as a witness to confirm his opinion, saying that Arator had spoken of a *triune power*, just as Prudentius had spoken of *triune piety*—to which we gave some answer above, where it would have been more appropriate to place what we shall add here concerning Sedulius, Arator, and Prosper—he did so because we were concerned to set against each of his evasions and disorderly repetitions suitable statements from the writings of teachers of the simple and catholic faith.

Finally, concerning what Arator said, compelled by metrical necessity:

> Triune faith calls this one, by whose name he is washed in the font.

And:

> … It does not compel him to go again to the water,
>
> our faith, because under a triune name
>
> wicked doctrines draw him along.

Catholic teachers, both in what precedes and in what follows, state with complete sufficiency that the name of the one God is not triune but one. In that name they are commanded by the Lord to be baptized in the unity of the catholic faith; and believers are baptized by Catholics with the one baptism of Christ, in which alone the remission of all sins takes place.

Hence Ambrose, in Book I of *On the Faith* (Book I, chapter 1) [Col. 0562D], says: “If there is one God, one name, one power, there is one Trinity. Finally, he says, ‘Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matthew 28:1). He says ‘in the name,’ certainly, not ‘in the names.’ He also says, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30). He said ‘one,’ so that there might be no division of power; he added ‘are,’ so that you might recognize the Father and the Son, and believe that the perfect Father begot a perfect Son, and that the Father and the Son are one—not by confusion of person, but by unity.”

What Arator said in the second book:

> He himself—namely, John—remembering the way, [foretelling] a baptism destined for all
>
> after another which is rightly given, which the triune power
>
> is accustomed to illuminate …

And in the first book, speaking figuratively and likewise because of metrical necessity:

> … For the triune power
>
> gathers this offspring, dividing the number equally.

All catholic writers demonstrate most plainly from the sacred Scriptures that the holy and inseparable Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—has not a divided but one and indivisible operation, and one and inseparable power. Thus Ambrose, in Book I, chapter 6 [Col. 0563A], says: “Since the Son performs the same works that the Father performs, and the Son gives life to those whom he wills, as it is written, without differing in power and free in will, unity is likewise preserved, because the power of God resides in the property of divinity, and freedom consists not in any difference but in the unity of the Trinity.”

And again, in Book II, chapter 4: “We have learned that the Father and the Son have one image, one likeness, one sanctification; we have learned that they have one operation, one glory, and likewise one divinity. Therefore there is one and only one God, because it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve’ (Matthew 4). One God—not that he himself is Father and Son, as the impious Sabellius asserts, but because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one divinity. Where there is one divinity, there is one will and one command. Finally, so that you may know that the Father exists, that the Son exists, and that the Father and Son have one work, follow the Apostle, who said: ‘But may God our Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you’ (1 Thessalonians 3:11). He speaks of the Father and he speaks of the Son, but the direction is one, because the power is one.”

That same Arator also shows more clearly that in this matter he was speaking not literally but figuratively. In the same book, chapter 10, he says:

> … God, judge of the world,
>
> exists in three persons, in whom there is one power together.

And in chapter 9:

> Behold, so many throngs begin to possess one heart,
>
> and the people acquire one soul.
>
> Who could doubt the mysteries of doctrine—that God is one,
>
> three persons—when thousands of the populace
>
> come together with one mind and in great numbers,
>
> bearing the cross and faithfully following the Lord?

And in chapter 3:

> The third hour shone forth with starry utterances.
>
> The one God has this number, simple in substance,
>
> distinguished in three persons …

And again, in chapter 21 [Col. 0563D]:

> Three times the Lord’s voice sounded, which was spoken for salvation.
>
> This the Father, the Son, and the holy Spirit accomplished together:
>
> hence the combative Arius falls, denying
>
> that the three persons are one; Sabellius, denying
>
> that the one is three persons.

Prosper likewise says in his book *Promises and Predictions*: “Led by grace, let us follow the love of God—the unity of the threefold majesty—as the way surpassing all others.”

And because he used the expression *triune majesty* improperly, he himself demonstrates this in the same book, saying (concerning the glory of the Saints, chapter 8): “The Apostle Paul says: ‘Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face’ (1 Corinthians 13:12), indicating how the saints see God, the Trinity: the Father and the Son; the Son in the Father; and the Holy Spirit in the Father and the Son.”

Therefore, if the Son is in the Father and the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son, because they are one God, then there is also one majesty belonging to them, as the same Prosper says in the book of *Sentences* (Sentence 324): “What the Father does with Christ, Christ does; and what Christ does with the Father, the Father does. Inseparable love, majesty, and power do nothing separately, just as the Lord himself says: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30).”

There are also several very celebrated verses of blessed Ambrose concerning the excellence of the number three, in which he says:

> All things flourish threefold beneath the majesty of the Thunderer:
>
> the Father, the Word, and the holy Spirit—three, yet one.

In many places—indeed, everywhere he speaks on this subject—he says that the majesty of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one. We have therefore thought it worthwhile to set down here a few examples. For in Book III of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 22 [Col. 0564A], he says: “Now it is possible to recognize the unity of majesty in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” And shortly afterward: “Therefore there is one vision, one command, one majesty.”

And Athanasius says: “The divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one; their glory is equal, their majesty coeternal.”

Augustine also says this very frequently in his books *On the Trinity*. For when the venerable Sedulius, compelled by metrical necessity, likewise placed *triune faith* in the same work *Paschale*, saying:

> What is simple he makes threefold, and what can be made threefold he makes simple,

blessed Augustine rejects this in Book VI of *On the Trinity* (chapter 8), saying: “In God himself, therefore, when the Son, equal to the Father, adheres to the equal Father, or when the Holy Spirit, equal to the Father and the Son, adheres to them, God does not become greater than each of them individually, because that perfection of the supreme Trinity has no room to increase. The Father is perfect, the Son is perfect, and the Holy Spirit is perfect; and the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are perfect God. Therefore it should be called a Trinity rather than a threefold entity.”

Consequently, the testimony of the faithful poet Sedulius does not assist Gothescalcus’s perverse understanding: Sedulius constrained the correct meaning of the faith by the law of meter, which does not prejudice the simplicity of the true faith. This faith, moreover, subjected emperors to itself not through orators but through fishermen.

Since Gothescalcus neither wished nor was able, the devout reader should understand that the expressions used by Sedulius, Arator, and Prosper were tropic, by metonymy—that is, by transnomination, of which there are many species. This figure is found not only in meter, secular literature, and common speech, but also frequently in the authoritative sacred Scriptures and in the writings of catholic authors, whether for ornament or from necessity. We have therefore not thought it necessary to set down here testimonies for each instance.

It is enough to say this: in the expressions *threefold piety*, *threefold power*, and *threefold majesty*, Prudentius, Arator, and Prosper employed the substantial names *piety*, *power*, and *majesty* for the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who are spoken of relatively within the holy Trinity. These names are properly said not in the plural but always in the singular, both of each person individually and of the three persons together: theirs is one piety, one power, and one majesty. The same applies to whatever is said substantially of God, that is, of what pertains to God himself, as those very authors demonstrate in the same little works.

Concerning this figurative or transferred manner of speaking, Saint Athanasius says in Book I of *On the Trinity* (*On the Unity of the Name of the Trinity*): “Therefore, I ask you, reader, who are reading this confession of the catholic faith in my writing, not to seek from it superfluous or diffuse words, but to compare the things said concisely and intelligibly—or rather, spiritually, with the utmost attention—to the style of sacred Scripture, and to weigh them according to the equity of the rule, with justice as your guide.

“Therefore, accept now not eloquent but powerful words; not earthly fabrications but true heavenly teachings; not the wicked and heretical inventions of philosophers but the perfect apostolic mysteries; not grammatical learning, which is superfluous to wisdom’s teaching, but divine commandments from the evangelical Scriptures, sweeter and better than honey and the honeycomb. Learn, then, that the sophists of this world were made foolish or mute in this matter, because they did not recognize true wisdom, and therefore were rejected.”

It is evident from his own writings that the wicked and most obstinate Gothescalcus had read these things. But just as Saint Hilary says that the perverse people behaved toward Christ’s resurrection—“Lying Judea saw these things; having seen them, it denies them”—so Gothescalcus either entirely omitted what he had read here, denied it by interpreting it perversely, or, as heretics are accustomed to do, because he read what he read with an evil intention, was unable by the retribution of justice to understand it rightly. Bending it toward the perversity of his own understanding, he presented it as he wished.

But what he plainly saw to have been well said, although he saw it with the eye of the body, he did not wish to see with the eye of the mind; and therefore, as though he had not seen it, he passed over it, according to the Gothic proverb: “Capra lusca hortum videt, sepem nusquam” (“The one-eyed goat sees the garden, but nowhere the fence”).

And in his conclusion—or rather, in his assault upon right faith—Gothescalcus says:

### XII.

÷ “Therefore, those who do not wish to have fellowship eternally with the heretics who are Sabellians should believe, confess, worship, and sing with catholic Catholics: *tritheism*, the triune deity; the *trisagion*; triune holiness; triune life, wisdom, and glory; triune fear, triune love, triune charity; triune light, salvation, virtue, peace, and brightness; triune majesty, power, and piety. For indeed we ought also to embrace a ternary or triune faith, which the perverse Sabellians deny through their faithless impiety.”

### CHR.

To whom we first reply: according to his wisdom—not given to him by God, but either inspired in him by an evil spirit or foolishly invented by himself—he ought to have recognized that there is a difference between *ternus* and *trinus*. But, while claiming to be wise, he became a fool.

It is well known that number is of two kinds. One kind is that in which the repetition of units produces plurality and therefore number; the other consists in countable things, in which the repetition and plurality of units does not produce a numerical diversity of countable things. And *ternus* is reckoned by those who discuss numbers not among composite numbers, but among the simple numbers, which have no other part except unity alone. It does not come from the number by which we count when we say “three,” but from the adverbial form when we say *ter*, “three times,” and it has a collective meaning.

Thus Bede says in his discussion of computus: “The four Ides take three each.” And Hilary says in a hymn: “And he returns the fragments of the meal in three groups of four baskets.” When we say *semel, bis, ter, quater*—“once, twice, three times, four times”—we express motion. When we say *unum, duo, tria, quatuor*—“one, two, three, four”—we do not express motion, but by the repetition of units we indicate plurality.

From *ter*, expressed adverbially, come *terna* and the other forms of this kind, just as *quaterna* comes from *quater*. But from the number by which we count when we say *tres* or *tria*, “three,” comes *trinus*. Hence God is called *trinus* with respect to the persons, while in deity he is one. From that same number from which *trinus* is derived, *trina* is also derived through the repetition of units, just as *trinus* is, expressing a plurality that the unity of deity does not admit.

Furthermore, because “three,” or “three things,” is the first odd number, by which the Trinity is signified as consisting of the monad and the first even number, this number is indicated because whoever strives here to preserve love of God and neighbor will attain eternal life, and all our perfection will consist in contemplation of that one true God who is the holy Trinity. In the vision of him, nothing lacking in salvation or joy will remain for us.

Thus a certain division is shown in the word *trina*, which comes from the number by which three things are counted; yet the unity of deity—wholly present in each person and wholly present together in the three persons of the holy Trinity—does not permit any division or plurality. It is therefore perfectly clear that one cannot speak of “a triple deity” (*trina deitas*) in a Catholic manner.

Let anyone who wishes read what we have said about number in the writings of Saints Augustine, Gregory, Boethius, and Bede. Saint Augustine, speaking about the divinity in the thirty-sixth sermon on the Gospel of John, says:

> “There is there,” he says, “something ineffable that cannot be explained in words: that there is number, and yet there is not number. For consider whether the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the Trinity, do not appear, as it were, to constitute a number. If there are three, what are the three? Number fails. Thus God is number departing from number, and is not grasped by number; for they are three, as though a number. But if you ask what the three are, there is no number. Hence it is said: ‘Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number’ (Psalm 146:5). They are indicated by number only insofar as they are related to one another, not insofar as they are related to themselves.”

Saint Gregory, in the thirtieth book of his *Moralia on Job*, commenting on the saying of the Gospel of John (chapter 5), says:

> “I will openly announce to you concerning the Father” (John 16:25). He says that he will openly announce concerning the Father because he then reveals the appearance of his majesty: how he himself is begotten without being unequal to the one who begets him, and how the Spirit of both proceeds, coeternal with both. Then we shall clearly see how that which is to be born does not come after the one from whom it is born, and how he who is produced by procession is not preceded by those who produce him. Then we shall clearly see how the one is divisibly three, and the three indivisibly one. The brightness of God, who raises us up, will then be seen as the tongue of the one who narrates.

And Saint Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, whose thoroughly Catholic letter was held in the highest esteem at the Sixth Synod, says in that letter, in the relevant passage (Sixth Synod, act 9):

> “The one, insofar as it is one, is not received as three; nor is the three, insofar as it is three, understood as one. This is marvelous and certainly full of every kind of astonishment. For this very reality is both countable and flees number: countable in its three subsistences, but fleeing number through the singularity of its deity. The unity of its essence and nature absolutely does not permit itself to be counted, lest it introduce a difference in deity and thereby make one principle out of a multitude of essence, nature, and gods. Every number therefore has difference as its companion, and every difference and distinction brings number upon itself as something inherent. The blessed Trinity is therefore counted neither in essences, nor in natures, nor in diverse deities or lordships of threefold form. Far be it—as the Arians rave, and the new barkers of tritheism, that is, of triple deity.”

Blessed Ambrose, in the second book *On the Holy Spirit*, showing that *trina* possesses a plurality which deity does not admit, says among other things (chapter 11):

> “Because the figure repeated three times expressed the operation of the Trinity, therefore in the mysteries a threefold questioning is delivered, and a threefold confirmation is celebrated.”

And in the second book *On the Faith*:

> “What does the threefold repetition under the one name of holiness mean? If there is a threefold repetition, why is there one praise? If there is one praise, why is there a threefold repetition? Why is there a threefold repetition, unless because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one in holiness?”

He says again:

> “Because the unity of deity does not admit the division that *trina* demonstrates, as he says many times in the second book *On the Holy Spirit*: Abraham saw three and worshiped one, because there is one God, one Lord, and one Spirit; and therefore there is unity of honor because there is unity of power.”

And again:

> “For how does the unity of divinity admit plurality, since plurality belongs to number, while divine nature does not admit number?”

For this reason we think that the venerable Sedulius wished to place not a *trina* but a *terna* faith within the requirements of meter, so that he might indicate, as it were, a certain inseparable but non-local movement—one that is expressed by *terna*, derived from *ter*: that the Son was born from the Father, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Each person, individually, is fully and perfectly God, and together they are one full and perfect God: three persons of one deity in this holy Trinity. Sabellius denied these persons, saying: “The same God is Father when he wishes, Son when he wishes, and Holy Spirit when he wishes”; yet he is one and the same.

Sedulius did not wish to say *trina fides*, “triple faith,” lest, by signifying plurality, he make numerable the one deity of the undivided and inseparable Trinity, which Arius denied. Against them he wrote in his Easter hymn.

Because of the one and same deity, which is wholly in each person and wholly in the three persons together, the holy Trinity is called undivided and inseparable. That alone is truly called inseparable which cannot in any way admit separation. For what is not separated but can be separated is not inseparable.

If anyone thinks that the three persons of one deity can be separated—that one deity which cannot be separated among the three persons—then the reality should not be called an inseparable Trinity, but a unity. Yet let no one perhaps become angry with me because I said that Sedulius wished to demonstrate, by the phrase *terna* rather than *trina* faith, that the Son was begotten from God the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father and the Son by a non-local movement. I shall satisfy my reader by explaining that I understood this from what I said about non-local movement.

The Lord says: “He who sent me is truthful” (John 8:26). As Augustine says, it is as though he were saying:

> “I speak the truth because I am the truth of the truthful one. The Father is truthful; the Son is truth. Just as the Son is from the Father, so truth is from the truthful one. And this is what is meant by ‘He who sent me.’”

For sacred Scripture could not disclose to us the height of its profundity if it had not adapted itself to us in such a way as to raise us to its understanding and reveal its inner meaning through things familiar to us and by speaking according to our manner—as when a cultivated and learned person, flattering and encouraging a little child, deliberately softens his words and, so to speak, stammers by breaking them up.

Thus, when Scripture says “sent,” a kind of movement appears to be indicated. But this must not be understood as local movement, any more than in the statement that the Father “gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26), which means that he begot the Son as having life in himself. The mission of the Holy Spirit is itself his procession, by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son together, as all Catholic teachers most clearly teach from the holy Scriptures.

Even less than *terna*, and indeed in no way properly, should faith be understood as *trina* in God. Rather, as the Apostle says: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5). For although, as blessed Gregory says, no unbeliever lives without some faith, only the Catholic faith sanctifies the human race, and only it gives life.

And although there are various baptisms and the washings of heretics—which, just as under the Law, according to the Apostle, could not make the one serving perfect, so now cannot advance toward perfect purification—nevertheless there is one Catholic baptism. It alone is celebrated in the Catholic Church, and when conferred and received in the one faith, it benefits believers unto perfect purification.

As Saint Ambrose says in the first book *On the Holy Spirit* (chapter 3):

> “There is one baptism. Where the full sacrament of baptism is absent, neither the beginning nor any form of baptism is to be considered present. It is full, however, if you confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; if you deny one, you overthrow the whole. And just as, if you include one in your statement—whether the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—but in faith deny neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, the sacrament of faith is full, so also, although you name the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, if you diminish the power of either the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, the entire mystery is empty.”

And shortly afterward:

> “There is one work, because there is one mystery; one baptism, because there is one death for the world. Therefore there is unity of operation and unity of preaching, which cannot be separated.”

Therefore, believing in one God and three persons of one deity, holding one Catholic faith—which alone sanctifies and alone gives life—and possessing and celebrating one baptism, in which alone the sacrament of faith is complete, we shall not obey Gothescalcus by believing and saying “triple deity,” “triple holiness,” “triple light,” and the other expressions he gave above, lest we share a portion with heretics.

Rather, we urge him that, if he does not wish to have eternal fellowship with the Arian heretics, he should, as a Catholic, believe, confess, worship, and sing with Catholics: that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, the holy and inseparable Trinity—are one God, of one and the same deity, and therefore one deity, one holiness, one life, one wisdom, one glory, one fear, one love, one charity, one light, one salvation, one power, one peace, one majesty, one authority, and one piety.

As Athanasius says at the beginning of the eighth book *On the Unity of the Faith*:

> “This is the faith of the one substance of the Trinity: of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, without beginning of time, beyond every sense, word, and spirit—one power, one God, but three names and one authority.”

All this is so because, as Augustine and the other Catholic teachers say—whose words and meanings the venerable Alcuin gathered together in the book mentioned above (*On the Faith of the Holy Trinity*, book I, chapter 13):

> “There is one nature, essence, substance, divinity, and deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. All names that signify the substance, power, or essence of God, or whatever is properly said of God in relation to himself, apply equally to all the persons: ‘great,’ ‘good,’ ‘eternal,’ ‘almighty,’ ‘holy,’ and all things naturally said of God. There is therefore no name of nature that can apply to the Father in such a way that it cannot apply equally to the Son and the Holy Spirit” (chapter 15).

> “Properly speaking, God is one supreme and ineffable substance, which is always what it is, in which nothing accidental or incidental can exist, which is always what it is because it is always unchangeable. God is called great not by any greatness other than that by which he himself is great and immeasurable. He is therefore great by the greatness that he himself is; and he is good by the goodness that he himself is. For God, being is not one thing, being great another, and being good another; rather, by that by which he is, he is great and good. Therefore it is not lawful to say of God that there are three substances, three great ones, or three good ones” (book II, chapter 2).

> “He is supreme existence, supreme understanding, and supreme life, from whom all life, all understanding, and all existence come. For in God power, substance, and deity are the very same thing, and all these are one, so that this one is simple” (chapter 13).

> “There is one work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, while the distinct property of the persons is shown. Therefore the unity of inseparable nature cannot have separable persons. The nature of the supreme Trinity and undivided unity alone is wholly everywhere; just as it has everywhere an inseparable unity of nature and work, so it cannot admit separation among the persons.

> “The operation of God—that is, of the holy Trinity—is the will of God, and the will of God is simple and always at rest in blessedness. For God’s working is not one thing and his willing another; rather, willing and working are the same for him, because the will of God is effective power. For God, being is not one thing and willing another, but one and the same thing, wholly simple, wholly Unity, wholly Trinity, wholly *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον, consubstantial); because substantial being is one in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and their action is one, just as their will is one” (chapter 14).

What the Apostle says—that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24)—must not be understood as though the Father could not be called power or wisdom, just as he cannot be called Son or Word. The latter are relative names, as was said above; power and wisdom, however, are substantial names.

Therefore the Father is power and wisdom, the Son is power and wisdom, and the Holy Spirit is power and wisdom; yet there are not three powers or three wisdoms, but one power and one wisdom: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. So too there is one substance, one omnipotence, and all the other things said of the substance of deity.

The Son is therefore understood as the wisdom of the Father in the same way that he is called the light of the Father: just as light comes from light and both are one light, so wisdom is from wisdom and both are one wisdom. For in the simplicity of the divine nature, knowing or being wise is not something other than being; being is not something other than having power; and having power is not something other than living. There is the same wisdom as essence, the same life as essence, and all these are one, and one God (chapter 15).

Just as the Father is life, so the Son is life, and the Holy Spirit is life, because the work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, just as their substance and essence are one. The Father is life in himself, not from another; the Son is life in himself, but from the Father, who begot him such that he should have life in himself.

For it is said, as the Son himself says: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26)—that is, he begot the Son as having life in himself.

The only difference is that the Father is life without being born, while the Son is life through being born; the Father is from no father, while the Son is from God the Father. The Father is Father because of the Son; the Son is Son because of the Father, and what he is is from the Father and from life. The Father, who is life in himself, begot the Son so that he would be life in himself.

Therefore the Son himself says: “As the Father lives, so I live because of the Father” (John 6:58). This is not said as though the Son did not possess life in himself, but had life by participating in the Father’s life, like a bodily eye that receives light by participating in another light—light which it would not have in itself unless it had borrowed it from elsewhere. Rather, the Son was begotten by the Father precisely as one who would live in himself.

Just as the Father does not lack life, so the Son does not need another life in order to exist. The Father is life, and so is the Son; yet both are one life, not two, because there is one God, not two gods (chapter 18).

The same must be understood of the Holy Spirit: he has life in himself, proceeding from the Father and the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son.

And wherever “God alone” is read in holy Scripture, it is not to be understood of one particular person in the holy Trinity, but of the whole holy Trinity, which performs equally all the works that it judges ought to be performed. The holy Trinity is one, alone, blessed, powerful, invisible, and true God, because the power of the whole holy Trinity is one.

For the Son himself, speaking elsewhere in the voice of Wisdom—for he is the Wisdom of God who says, “I alone have compassed the circuit of heaven” (Ecclesiasticus 24:8)—did not separate the Father from himself. How much less, then, is it necessary to understand as referring only to the Father, apart from the Son or the Holy Spirit, what is said: “He alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Timothy 6:16, chapter 20)?

The Holy Spirit, who is called in Scripture the gift of God, the Paraclete, or the charity of God, exists in the same unity of substance and equality with the Father and the Son. Whether he is called the unity of both, or holiness, or charity—or whether he is called unity because he is charity, and charity because he is holiness—he is in no way inferior to those from whom he proceeds.

This is the highest charity: that the one begotten is loved by the one who begets, and that he loves his begetter. Therefore there are no more than three: one who loves the one who is from him; one who loves the one from whom he is; and love itself, of which it is said that God is charity.

This supreme and ineffable Trinity should not be said to belong to one God, but should be said to be one God (chapter 21). And this charity is possessed only in the unity of Christ’s Church; those who separate themselves from the unity of Catholic peace do not possess it.”

We have set forth these things, gathered by Alcuin into one collection from the sayings of the Catholic Fathers.

To remove every scruple from those who read, by using the words of blessed Athanasius, let us add the following:

> “I shall clarify briefly,” he says, “while proving in many ways that this name of unity is most truly the name of the Trinity. Yet it is referred to the manifold wisdom of God, which exists as one in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. If you speak of the deity of wisdom and the wisdom of deity, is this not itself the unity of wisdom, which is also the divinity of the Trinity?

> “Therefore, to state the matter concisely: whether it is called the glory of wisdom, or the deity of glory, or sublimity, or dominion, or dignity, or brightness, or majesty, or sovereignty, or power, although these are expressed in many ways, are they not nevertheless declared as one with respect to the incomparable, unified deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? Or do you suppose that as many meanings as are spoken of the glory of deity, so many forms of diversity also exist? Far from it. All these expressions are referred to one substance.

> “For if this one and same thing is the manifold and prophetic wisdom of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—one power, one form of greatness and equality, one majesty, one brightness, all of which are gathered together here into this unified deity according to the rule of Scripture—could we, contrary to the Scriptures, speak in the plurality of the same Trinitarian deity of three wisdoms, three powers, three images, three substances, three brightnesses, three plenitudes of deity, or anything else of this kind, after the manner of the Ariomanites? Far from it.

> “Just as you, Hosius, now advanced in age, were, even in your earliest beginnings, a Catholic authority at the Synod of Sirmium, where you nullified the faith that you had written at Nicaea while serving royal power. Moreover, when you were exceedingly near death, you fell into the noose of the abyss of the pit, so that you were cut off as one dead in heart and said: ‘Who does not know that the Father is greater in honor, dignity, brightness, and majesty?’—as though there were two or certainly three brightnesses or majesties in each of the persons, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Far from it.

> “For if their blasphemy were truly as they say, why do they not also call them three gods in the plural, and openly assert this concerning their own or diverse substances? Far from it, since the perfectly unified name of deity, although expressed in many ways, exists as one in the Trinity.”

Saint Ambrose, in the second and third books *On the Holy Spirit*, clearly demonstrates from the authority of Scripture—as a devoted reader will easily be able to find—that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one power; that the counsel of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one; that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one life; that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the creator of all things; that the kingdom of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one; that the will of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one; that their vision and command are one; and that their majesty, omnipotence, and holiness are one.

For it is written: “A fool utters all his spirit, but a wise person delays and reserves something for the future” (Proverbs 29:11). Thus, so that Gothescalcus might display his foolishness more fully, he wished to reserve nothing, but to pour forth the whole spirit of his folly. Hence he added the following almost as a conclusion to what had been said:

### XIII.

> ÷“All things,” he says, “are just as I have said, as can be clearly proved by two nouns of singular number, namely, *light* and *peace*. For unbegotten light and peace, begotten light and peace, and also proceeding light and peace are not permitted by the art of grammar to be called three lights or three peaces in the plural. Nor are they three naturally, as the Arian heresy barks, nor one personally, as the Sabellian heresy dreams. Rather, without doubt, light and peace are one naturally and three personally, just as he embraces a triple and one faith; and therefore he believes, confesses, worships, and sings of triple and one light, peace, majesty, authority, piety, and triple and one deity,”

and the other things he pursued there.

### CHR.

We have judged it appropriate to turn briefly to address him.

Foolish, impious, cruel tyrant of God: what not only meaning but even the art of grammar wholly denies, you yourself previously deny in accordance with the art, since the letter of the art contains no error and its letters are without fault. Why, by perversely interpreting the meaning, do you stain the light and peace with the crime of a perverse understanding, saying that they are naturally one and personally three in God?

The Psalmist contradicts your impiety concerning the light when he says: “With you, Lord, is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10).

> “In your light,” says Jerome, “we shall see light. The light of the Father is Christ. In the light of Christ the Father we shall see the light, the Holy Spirit. And your light, Christ, is the Father, whose will you came to accomplish, to illuminate the hidden things of darkness, so that in you, who are the light of the world, we might deserve to see that light in the grace of a pure mind.

> “Thus he says to Philip: ‘Whoever sees me sees the Father also’ (John 14:9). In his light—that is, in Christ—we shall see light, that is, the Holy Spirit, who appeared upon the apostles in the form of illuminating fire. And ‘in your light we shall see light’: that is, we shall be illuminated by Christ, as it says in the Gospel: ‘He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world’ (John 1:9).”

The Apostolic See, exalted by Peter’s confession and adorned by Paul’s preaching, and the Catholic Church itself, through its tradition, recognizing on the sacred vigil of Pentecost that this verse is better obtained and commended to others by praying than by explaining it, instituted the following prayer to be sung during the sacred celebration of Mass:

> “Grant, we ask, almighty and merciful God, that the splendor of your brightness may shine upon us, and that the light of your light may, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, strengthen the hearts of those who have been reborn by your grace.”

If you recall, heretic, what is written—“For you who fear God the Sun of righteousness shall rise” (Malachi 4:2); and again, “Who, being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Hebrews 1:3); and again, “He is the brightness of eternal light” (Wisdom 7:26)—then you will understand why he himself says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also, because I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:9).

It is also written: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:23). If, by the grace of God, you cleanse the eye of your mind from the dust or whiteness of arrogance, you will be able to perceive this Catholic prayer with understanding.

And since it is written: “The invisible things of God are understood and seen through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world, as are his eternal power and divinity” (Romans 1:20), look at the sun and, if you can, somehow separate from it its brightness or heat. When you see three inseparable things in one created substance, understand light and peace: just as in the art of grammar they are singular in number, so understand in meaning that light and peace are one, not triple—the creator of all things, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

For just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, yet they are not three gods but one God, so the Father is light, the Son is light, and the Holy Spirit is light; and they are not three lights or a triple light, but one light: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

And just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are said to be *trinus* in persons and one God in power and deity, as blessed Ambrose says:

> God of supreme mercy,  
> Maker of the world’s structure,  
> One in power,  
> And threefold in person—

it cannot be said in a Catholic manner, as you rave, that light, peace, and deity are naturally one and personally three.

Therefore Ambrose says the same thing in another hymn:

> You are the unity of the Trinity,
You who rule the world mightily; [Col. 0574B] concerning which he did not say, “one potentially and three personally,” because in God these terms are said with reference to himself—that is, essentially and naturally—just as divinity and substance, light and peace and life, power, and other things of this kind are said, and not relatively; and therefore they are expressed in the singular and neither admit nor can possess plurality or number. The persons, however, which constitute the holy and inseparable Trinity of the one divinity, are said relatively to one another, and for that reason possess plurality—that is, number—which the essential names “divinity,” “peace,” and “light” cannot possess; this light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world, is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For just as the substance, that is, the divinity, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is inseparable, so too the works of that same holy [Col. 0574C] and undivided Trinity are inseparable; and whatever we read that is performed by the individual persons must be understood to have been performed inseparably.

Although it is absolutely certain that the Father alone is in the person of fatherhood—he who said, “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17)—and that the Son alone is Son, over whom the Father’s voice alone sounded when that same only-begotten God was baptized according to his humanity in the Jordan, he who alone assumed flesh; and that the Holy Spirit alone, personally, is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, who descended in the form of a dove upon that same baptized man as he came up from the water, and who, on the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection, came upon and filled the faithful gathered in one place in the appearance of fiery tongues, through whom all the faithful have remission of all sins, whether in baptism or in repentance—nevertheless, that voice through which God the Father alone spoke, that flesh through which the only-begotten God alone became man, that dove in whose form the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ, and those fiery tongues in whose appearance he filled the faithful gathered in one place, through which remission of sins is given to believers, must be believed most truly to be works of the whole holy Trinity, that is, of the one God who made visible and invisible things in heaven and on earth.

Regarding peace, then, about which you boast of preaching, as though wisely and conclusively, together with light, and in fact blaspheme most destructively, saying, “unbegotten peace, begotten peace, and proceeding peace, naturally one, personally three,” just as above you said concerning divinity: those things that we have shown above at greater length from the words of the Catholics about all things that are said substantially of God ought to have been sufficient for anyone whom they satisfy. But lest you say that in these two names you have trapped us and that we have failed in our answer, according to the ancient proverb, we oppose your knot of an evil tree with the strongest wedge—on the authority of Saint Ambrose and with the reasoning of truth itself.

For truth speaks through Ambrose, and through the Apostle it says: “He himself is our peace” (Eph. II, 14); and, “God is light” (I John I, 5). What else, then, is to be understood except that what God is is itself peace and light? For that simple nature which is God cannot have anything in itself except what it itself is; for knowing is the same for it as being able, and being able is the same as being and knowing. Hence this exalted name of peace and light is most suitably applied to the holy Trinity—plainly because each consists of three letters and, like “God,” does not recognize the number of plurality. When we say *pax* (“peace”) or *lux* (“light”), through the three letters the three persons in God are understood; and because “peace,” just as “light,” does not admit the plural number, through the singular number the substance, that is, his divinity as the one God, is understood.

Thus Saint Ambrose says in the first book *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter twelve:

> “One peace, one grace of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Finally, it is written: ‘Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ’ (Gal. I, 3). You have here that the grace of the Father and of the Son is one, and that the peace of the Father and of the Son is one. But grace and peace are also the fruit of the Spirit, as the Apostle himself taught, saying: ‘The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience’ (Gal. V, 22). And peace is good and necessary, so that no one may be disturbed by the uncertainty of disputes [variant: *incertis*, “uncertain things”], nor shaken by the storm of bodily sufferings, but that, in the simplicity of faith and tranquility of mind, the devoted soul may persevere in the worship of God.”

And shortly afterward:

> “If, therefore, the peace is one, the grace one, the love one, and the communion one of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, then certainly the operation is one; and where the operation is one, the power cannot be divided, nor the substance separated. For how could the grace of the same operation be harmonious?”

And in chapter thirteen:

> “Who, then, would dare to separate the unity of the name when he sees the unity of the operation? But why do I establish the unity of the name by arguments, when there is clear testimony from the divine voice? There is one name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For it is written: ‘Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. XXVIII, 19). He said ‘in the name,’ not ‘in the names.’ Therefore the name of the Father is not one, the name of the Son another, and the name of the Holy Spirit another, because the one God has not many names, since there are not two gods, nor three gods. And to make clear that there is one divinity and one majesty, because there is one name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—”

—and so forth.

And in chapter fourteen:

> “For God is light, as John said: ‘God is light, and in him there are no darknesses at all’ (John I, 5). Light is also the Son, because ‘the life was the light of human beings’ (John I, 4). And to show that the evangelist was speaking of the Son of God, he says concerning John the Baptist: ‘He was not that light, but came to bear witness to the light. He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world’ (John I, 8–9). Therefore, because God is light, and the true light is the Son of God, without doubt the Son of God is true God. You have elsewhere also that God is light: ‘The people who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death saw a great light’ (Isa. IX, 2). What could be clearer than what he says: ‘For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light’ (Ps. XXXV, 10)? This means: with you is God the almighty Father, who are the fountain of life; in your light, the Son, we shall see light. We shall see the light of the Holy Spirit, as the Lord himself shows when he says: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John XX, 22), and elsewhere: ‘Power went out from him.’

“Who could doubt that the Father himself is light, when it has been read concerning his Son that he is ‘the brightness of eternal light’ (Heb. I, 3)? For whose brightness is the Son except the Father’s, since he is always with the Father and shines with the same, not a different, splendor? Isaiah signifies that the Holy Spirit is not only light but also fire when he says: ‘And Israel’s light will become fire’ (Isa. X, 17). Thus the prophets called him burning fire, because in these three kinds we more clearly perceive the majesty of divinity: for sanctifying belongs to divinity, illuminating to light and fire; and it is customary for the divine nature to be expressed or seen in the form of fire, for ‘God is a consuming fire,’ as Moses says (Deut. IV, 24).”

There you have it: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three personally but one naturally and essentially—one peace and one light. Therefore, just as concerning divinity and all things that are said substantially of God, you have been refuted as a liar, Gothescalcus, because such things must be expressed in the singular, not the plural, both of the individual persons and of the three persons (chapter 8).

Likewise Saint Augustine, in the fifth book of *On the Trinity*, contradicts your lie when he says:

> “This must be held above all: whatever that most exalted and divine majesty says concerning itself is said substantially; and such is the force of the same substance in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that whatever is said of the individual persons in relation to themselves is taken not plurally in the totality but singularly.”

But whatever is said in relation to something else is said not substantially but relatively, and therefore plurally.

We could have set forth many more testimonies of these and other orthodox writers, which the reader will be able to find in their proper places. But we know that however many we might produce, even if we could overcome the envy of our rivals and the perfidy of Gothescalcus by reason and authority, we would not be able completely to quiet it. Therefore we also bring against him the sacred Council of Nicaea, at which, together with Arius, his like-minded follower was condemned, although in words he detests the one whom he follows in understanding.

The council’s inviolable confession and irrefragable decree taught that our Lord Jesus Christ, born from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, must be believed and confessed with the Holy Spirit as one light, not two lights, to such a degree that it decreed that those who thought otherwise were to be anathematized by the Catholic Church.

Let these statements against him suffice. Now let us return to the order of the narrative concerning his other statements.

In another compilation of his, in which he falsely presents numerous testimonies under the names of Catholics, while completely concealing the names of the books from which he took them, and inserts some passages known to us, perversely interpreting them in his customary manner against himself—passages which, as he thinks, strongly support his own statements but which in fact strongly and catholically destroy them—he also presents a testimony from the letter of Peter, bishop of Nicomedia, which Peter submitted at the Sixth Council so that he might not be condemned. Gothescalcus boasts that in this letter a “threefold light” was set forth and approved by the bishops at that council.

He does not know that the idiom of a language often introduces doubt or difficulty of understanding in a translation made word for word, as blessed Augustine clearly demonstrates. Nor does he know that at a council, because of the many obligations involved and because the words and opinions of many people intervene, certain matters that are not especially relevant are often necessarily passed over with less examination—especially matters that are not being specifically discussed—and that a council is more intent on settling the wavering than on pursuing a brother’s deposition.

Thus Leo, to give one example out of many, writes to Flavian, saying (letter 12):

> “I marvel that so absurd and so faithless a profession of his—of Eutyches, that is—was passed over without any rebuke from the judges, and that a speech so foolish and so blasphemous was omitted as though nothing offensive had been heard, when he is said to have asserted so impiously that the only-begotten Son of God possessed two natures before the incarnation, and so wickedly that, after the Word became flesh, he affirmed that there was in him a single nature—something that Eutyches considers rightly or tolerably said because no judgment of yours refuted it.”

Although these matters stand thus, we nevertheless considered it necessary to show plainly that Gothescalcus did not speak truth. For nowhere in the entire libellus of satisfaction of Peter, bishop of Nicomedia, is anything found about a threefold light; rather, the unity of the divinity is demonstrated in it most clearly and catholically. It begins as follows (Sixth Council, act 10, near the end):

> “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who was born from the Father before all ages, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, through whom all things were made. And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son: the consubstantial Trinity, one divinity, essence, power and authority, dominion, one God. When he contemplates him singularly, distinguishing in thought what is undivided, he worships the unity in the Trinity and the Trinity in the unity: the unity according to the account of essence or divinity, but the Trinity according to subsistences or persons.”

There is, to be sure, something about three lights in the profession submitted to the council by Macarius, the heretic and bishop of Antioch, who did not hold the Catholic faith concerning the two wills and operations in the one Lord Jesus Christ and who was convicted of falsifying the statements of the orthodox and was deposed. After other matters already mentioned, he says as follows (Sixth Council, act 8):

> “The Trinity is not divided in perfect glory, authority, and counsel; it is one divinity and one dominion. For there is nothing servile or subject in the Trinity, nor anything introduced as though it had not previously existed but had later been brought in. For the Son was not lacking to the Father, nor the Spirit to the Son; rather, our holy Trinity is always unchangeable and consubstantial. When I say ‘true God,’ I am enlightened by one light. And [I am enlightened] by three according to properties, or subsistences and persons; but by one according to the account of essence, that is, divinity. It is divided indivisibly, so to speak, and joined divisibly. For divinity itself is one in the three, and the three themselves are one, in which divinity is—or, to say it more expressly, which is divinity.” And let us neither make the unity itself confusion nor the division itself separation.”

Hence Saint Augustine, in the seventh book of *On the Trinity* (chapter 3), says:

> “The Father is light, the Son is light, the Holy Spirit is light; together they are not three lights but one light.”

And blessed Ambrose demonstrates in his evening hymn that the holy Trinity is one light according to the unity of the divinity—not according to Gothescalcus’s perversity but according to the universal belief and confession of the Catholic faith. Gothescalcus sang this hymn with monastic lips from the earliest beginnings of childhood, in the monastery of monks in which he had been offered and tonsured according to the rule and where he remained until adulthood; but he could not grasp its meaning in his heart, because wisdom does not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sins. The hymn begins:

> “O blessed light of the Trinity, and principal unity,
>
> Now the fiery sun withdraws; pour light into our hearts.”

At last, after Gothescalcus had completed on this sheet his blasphemies against God, he placed, for the disparagement of the Lord’s priests—so that we might be recognized as unequal to him in knowledge and merits, and therefore marked as unworthy of the priesthood—the words of blessed Gregory, with his familiar seal of blasphemies, in his usual manner, and after his customary “Amen” he signed them, so that Gregory’s words, hurled as an accusation against us who abhor Gothescalcus’s doctrines, might be thought to have greater force. He wrote:

**XI.**

÷ “Let one who is full of virtues come unwillingly to rule; let one who is empty of virtues not approach, even when compelled.”

**ΧΡ.** We reverently receive these statements of blessed Gregory as promulgated by the Holy Spirit, but we do not reverence them when uttered by Gothescalcus with evil intent. For it is not the heretic Gothescalcus who judges, but, as it is written: “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” (I Cor. II, 15). That is, as blessed Augustine says, he is judged by no human being but only by the law itself, according to which he judges all things.

For this too was said with complete truth: “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (II Cor. V, 10). He judges all things because he is above all, when he is with God. He is with him when he understands with complete purity and loves with complete charity what he understands. Thus, as far as he is able, he himself also becomes the law according to which he judges all things.

No one can judge that law, especially none of those concerning whom blessed Augustine likewise says:

> “For many, not only among Catholics but also in various heresies, if persecution should arise and they hand over their bodies to the flames with us for the faith which they confess together with us, nevertheless, because they do these things while separated, not enduring one another in love and not striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, since they do not have charity, they cannot reach eternal salvation with all those things that profit them nothing, because apart from unity even one who performs miracles is nothing. Apart from unity were Pharaoh’s magicians, and they did things similar to Moses. And the disciples, boasting, said to the Lord: ‘Behold, even the demons are subject to us in your name’ (Luke X, 17). They confessed well enough and paid honor to the name of Christ; and yet he said to them: ‘Do not rejoice in this, that the demons are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven’ (Luke X, 20).

“Peter drives out demons; some old widow, some unknown person, whatever sort of layman, possessing charity and holding the integrity of faith, does not do this. Peter is an eye in the body; that person is a finger in the body. Yet he is in the same body in which Peter is. And although the finger has less power than the eye, it has not nevertheless been cut off from the body. It is better to be a finger and remain in the body than to be an eye and be torn from the body.”

Thanks be to God: whatever sort of priests we are, placed in ecclesiastical government and preserving the Catholic faith in the body of Christ, from which Gothescalcus has been torn, we are not entirely empty of virtues. For, as the same blessed Augustine says, virtue is either right or perfect reason. And this is truly perfect virtue: reason arriving at its end, which the blessed life follows.

That vision itself is the understanding that exists in the soul; the soul’s act of looking is reason. But because it does not follow that everyone who looks actually sees, the upright and perfect act of looking is the one followed by vision, and it is called virtue. Even if we have not yet attained it perfectly, because we have not yet reached the summit of perfection, nevertheless on the way of God we daily labor to place our steps in holy desire.

Therefore, as blessed Gregory says, Truth consoles us when it says through the Psalmist: “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and in your book all shall be written” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 16). Our imperfection will not be wholly harmful to us if, established on God’s road, we neither look back toward what has passed nor fail to hasten onward toward what remains. For he who graciously kindles the desires of the imperfect strengthens them in some way toward perfection through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with him lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

And since that same Gothescalcus compiled several sheets of his blasphemies, to all of which it would have been lengthy for us to respond because of our many obligations, we have decided to write only about those matters concerning which we have learned that certain people were scandalized. Among other things, he wrote in one of his sheets of dirges:

**XV.**

[Col. 0580B] ÷ “Indeed, the term ‘person’ is used of God because it is one in itself. Therefore, since the nature of God is nothing other than the general, common, and universal substance of all three, and each person in the Trinity is nothing other than the proper, particular, and individual substance and essence of each, the difference between the one nature of God and the three persons has been revealed, thanks be to God, more clearly than light: namely, in the nature the substantial generality, commonality, universality, and unity of all three are demonstrated; but in the persons the individual particularity and property of each are declared. Consequently, the Trinity is also made manifest in them; and just as above there is one nature, so in these there is a threefold divinity.”

**ΧΡ.** In opposition to this, blessed Augustine says in the seventh book of *On the Trinity*, as we cited above:

> “Nor do we speak of the Trinity as three persons or subsistences, one essence and one God, as though three things subsisted from one material, even if whatever that material is were unfolded in these three. For there is nothing else belonging to that essence besides this Trinity. Nevertheless, we say three persons of the same essence, or three persons who are one essence; but we do not say three persons from the same essence as though something there were the essence and something else the persons, as we can say three statues from the same gold. For there it is one thing to be gold and another to be statues.

“And when three human beings are said to be one nature, or three human beings of the same nature, they may also be called three human beings from the same nature, because from the same nature other such human beings can exist. In that essence of the Trinity, however, no other person whatsoever can exist from the same essence. For the Father and Son together are not a greater essence than the Father or the Son alone; rather, those three subsistences, or persons, if they must be called that, are equal to each one individually—something the natural man does not perceive.”

And in the thirty-sixth sermon on the Gospel of John:

> “The Trinity is one God; the Trinity is one eternity, one power, one majesty. What, then, are the three? For if he says ‘three,’ you must say what three. I answer: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. That which the Father is in himself is God; that which he is in relation to the Son is Father. That which the Son is in himself is God; that which he is in relation to the Father is Son.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Because it is divinity, there is in it something ineffable that cannot be expressed in words, so that there is number and there is not number. See whether the Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit does not appear, as it were, to be number. If there are three, what are the three? Number fails. Thus God, who is number, withdraws from number and is not grasped by number. For they are three as though they were a number; but if you ask what the three are, there is no number. Hence it is said: ‘Great is the Lord our God, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number’ (Ps. CXLVI, 5).”

And again shortly afterward:

> “Only that which they are in relation to one another indicates number, not that which they are in relation to themselves.”

From these words of blessed Augustine it is demonstrated that Gothescalcus, as usual, speaks against the Catholic faith when he proclaims a threefold divinity. From these same words of Saint Augustine he is also proved to teach falsely in what follows in the same compilation, saying:

**XVI.**

÷ “It is also clear, and shines without any cloud, that personal names are in no way relative but rather essential or substantial, just as natural names are. They differ among themselves only in this: natural names are equally common or general to all three persons, whereas personal names are shown to belong properly or particularly to the individual persons. For example, when ‘the nature of God’ is said, the common essence of the whole Trinity is understood; but when ‘person’ is said, it is recognized as the particular substance of only one of the Trinity. Indeed, the natural name ‘God,’ when used generally, embraces all three persons equally, whereas the personal name applies only to the individual persons.”

**ΧΡ.** Let us repeat each point and answer distinctly and individually, in accordance with the statements and understanding of the Catholics, these detestable blasphemies.

“It is clear,” he says, “that personal names are in no way relative but rather essential or substantial, like natural names.” We ask him, therefore, what the personal names in the holy Trinity are. If he says—since he has nothing else to say—that they are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, Saint Augustine proves him a liar when he says that personal names are not relative but natural. He does so in many places, especially in the fifth and seventh books of *On the Trinity* (book V, chapter 8), where he shows that natural names in God are said in relation to himself, that is, substantially, whereas personal names are said in relation to something, that is, relatively: the Father in relation to the Son, the Son in relation to the Father, and the Holy Spirit in relation to the Father and the Son, whose Spirit the Holy Spirit is.

He confirms that this must be held above all: whatever that most exalted and divine majesty says in relation to itself is said substantially, and whatever is said of the individual persons in relation to themselves is taken not plurally in the totality but singularly. But whatever is said in relation to something is said not substantially but relatively.

Hence Boethius, as though explaining blessed Augustine, says in his book addressed to John, Roman deacon and later bishop:

> “Let us understand that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not said substantially of the divinity itself but in some other way. For if they were predicated substantially, they would be said singularly both of the individual persons and of all together; but it is clear that these are said in relation to something.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The Trinity consists in the plurality of persons, whereas unity consists in the simplicity of substance.”

And again:

> “The Trinity, therefore, does not pertain to substance. It follows that neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the Trinity is predicated substantially of God, but, as has been said, in relation to something. God, however, truth, justice, goodness, omnipotence, substance, immutability, power, wisdom, and whatever of this sort can be conceived are said substantially of the divinity.”

And again the same author says in his book *On the Trinity*:

> “Substance contains unity; relation multiplies the Trinity.”

Therefore, if there were in the holy Trinity, as Gothescalcus falsely claims, three natural names that were personal, there would be in the holy Trinity a threefold nature—that is, a threefold divinity—and each nature would have its proper name, just as each person has a certain property of its own within this one and same divinity common to the holy Trinity.

The Father’s property is that he is from no other and therefore alone in the person of fatherhood, though not alone in the essence of divinity. The property of the only-begotten Son of God is that he alone is begotten consubstantially and coessentially from the one source, that is, from the Father; and in this lies the property of his person: that he is alone in the person of the Son, but not alone in the substance of divinity. The property of the Holy Spirit is that he proceeds equally from the Father and the Son and is the Spirit of both, of the same substance and eternity as the Father and the Son.

If, I say, there were three natural names in the holy Trinity, there would certainly be three natures, and there would be a threefold divinity, just as Gothescalcus falsely strives to establish that it is three personally; and consequently there would be three gods. Against this falsehood, uttered through Gothescalcus by the devil who said to the first human beings, “You will be like gods,” the Lord speaks when he says: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

Hence Athanasius says in the first book *On the Faith*:

> “He who said ‘in the name’ clearly declared that one divinity exists in the Trinity; and by adding ‘of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,’ he distinguished that individual persons are present through the individual names. In this statement he also showed that the name of the one God is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and, as a thoroughly Catholic writer, he distinguished through the individual names that individual persons are present, since the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another, although the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. Rather, the Father is the very same as the Son and the Holy Spirit; but the Father is not himself the same person as the Son or the Holy Spirit.”

As blessed Ambrose says in the first book of *On the Faith* (chapter 1):

> “If, therefore, there is one God, there is one name, one power, and one Trinity. Finally, the Lord says: ‘Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. XXVIII, 19)—in the name, he says, not in the names.”

And Athanasius likewise, in agreement with this, says:

> “In the name, he says, not in the names, so that he might show both one God through the undivided name of the divine essence and the distinction of the persons through their own properties.”

Next Gothescalcus continues:

> “They differ among themselves only in this: natural names are equally common or general to all three persons, whereas personal names are shown to belong properly or particularly to the individual persons.”

Let us see how contrary to himself and foolishly he speaks—like a heresy of which it is written that it cannot stand on its own feet. A little earlier he said that personal names are in no way relative but natural; immediately afterward he adds that natural names are common and general to the Trinity, while personal names belong properly to the individual persons.

We have not thought it necessary to write at greater length against these statements, since it is obvious how contrary he speaks to the Catholic faith, to the words of the Catholics, and to himself. Moreover, this work contains many testimonies of Catholics that refute his falsehood, although he does not believe them unless they say what agrees with his perverse understanding. For, as it is written, “A fool does not receive the words of wisdom unless you say what is in his heart.”

Furthermore, he criticizes without any reverence everyone who disagrees with his doctrine. In this same compilation, for example, he criticizes Paul because Paul did not say in the proper order, “Faith, hope, and charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (I Cor. XIII, 13). Gothescalcus says that Paul ought to have said, “the greatest of these,” and he censures Priscian, asserting that this grammatical rule escaped him. He also attacks Jerome, Augustine, and Bede, with his whole mouth and enormously puffed-out cheeks, wherever it seems good to him.

Nevertheless, Augustine—whom he very often calls his own—he accuses of thinking wrongly in this cunning compilation of his, saying:

> “It must be known that certain things are said substantially of God, such as ‘God,’ ‘great,’ ‘almighty,’ and whatever is said in relation to himself, signifying the substance of divinity. Certain things, therefore, are said relatively, such as the Father in relation to the Son, the Son in relation to the Father, and the Holy Spirit relatively in relation to the Father and the Son; but in relation to himself, the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit is said.”

And again:

> “Whatever, therefore, is said in relation to himself of the Father and the Son is not said of one without the other—that is, whatever is said of them that displays their substance is said of both together. If this is so, then the Father is not God without the Son, nor the Son God without the Father. That is, the Father is not called God as though the Son were not God, nor is the Son called God as though the Father were not God; rather, both together are God, and one God.

“Therefore, whatever can be said of them according to substance or eternity belongs to both together. Although it is said of the Son, ‘God from God, light from light,’ both are God and both together are light; but the Father is not ‘God from God’ or ‘light from light.’ Rather, the Son is God from God and light from light. Nevertheless, both together and always together are one God and one light.

“The same must be said of the other names that are spoken according to substance: whatever they are together must be said of them together. The sole exception is what cannot be said of one with respect to the other when they are not both the same thing together. Thus ‘Word from Word’ cannot be said, because both are not Word together, but the Son alone; nor can ‘image from image,’ ‘Son from Son,’ or ‘Father from Father’ be said.”

And again:

> “For just as the Father and the Son are said relatively, so the Holy Spirit is also said in some way relatively to the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. But the relation of the Holy Spirit cannot be turned back reciprocally in the same way as that of the Father and the Son. We can indeed say ‘the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son,’ but in the reverse order we cannot say ‘the Father of the Holy Spirit,’ as we say ‘the Father of the Son,’ lest two Sons be thought to exist in the holy Trinity. Likewise, we cannot say ‘the Son of the Holy Spirit,’ as we say ‘the Son of the Father,’ lest two Fathers be understood to exist in the holy Trinity. Thus we say ‘the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son’ without reciprocal reversal of the relative names.”
