As for the etymology or definition of “person,” Boethius, although in his book *Against Eutyches and Nestorius* he brought forth in many ways the understanding of the learned of both languages, Greek namely and Latin, did not find one such as Gothescalcus has here invented:

“Therefore,” he says, “in God a person is said to be such because it is one in itself. Since the three persons of the one Godhead in the holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are mutually spoken of not substantially but relatively, as we have shown from the words of blessed Augustine. For the Father is spoken of relatively to the Son, because he is called Father by virtue of having a Son; the Son is spoken of relatively to the Father, because he is called Son by virtue of having a Father. The Holy Spirit, the third person in the holy Trinity, is spoken of in a certain manner relatively, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, and is called by catholic teachers the charity, holiness, unity, and bond of the Trinity, belonging to both, namely the Father and the Son. Thus the Trinity refers to the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; unity belongs to the nature of the eternal Godhead.

“And each person in the holy Trinity has something proper to it—not as Gothescalcus says, that in God a person is said to be such because it is one in itself, but as Augustine says, because they display in themselves some property with inseparable equality. The Father alone is Father, the Son alone is Son, and the Holy Spirit alone is Holy Spirit. The Father has this proper to him: that of all things that are, he alone is from no other; hence he alone is in the person of fatherhood, not alone in the essence of Godhead. The only-begotten Son of God has this proper to him: that he alone is begotten consubstantially and coessentially from one alone, that is, from the Father; and in this lies the property of his person. The Holy Spirit has this proper to him: that he proceeds equally from the Father and the Son and is the Spirit of both, of the same substance and eternity as the Father and the Son.

“Yet these three are truly also three—ineffably three and essentially three—having their own properties; and these three are one, truly one, and this one is three; but they are not three Fathers, nor three Sons, nor three Holy Spirits, but three persons. One Father, one Son, one Holy Spirit; and these three, namely the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are one in nature, omnipotence, Godhead, and eternity.

“Let the judgment of the catholic reader therefore compare the words of Gothescalcus, who says, ‘Therefore in God a person is said to be such because it is one in itself,’ with the words of blessed Augustine, who says, ‘Each person in the holy Trinity has something proper to it, by which, with inseparable equality, they display some property in themselves’; and let him say: ‘As far as the east is from the west,’ so far may the Lord remove Gothescalcus’s perverse understanding from our catholic understandings. For, together with Gothescalcus, we do not say that in God a person is called such because it is one in itself; rather, with Saint Augustine and the other orthodox teachers, we believe and confess that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God.

“Thus the unity of the inseparable nature cannot have separable persons. The Father alone, of all things that are, exists from no other, which is proper to him; and he alone is in the person of fatherhood, but he is not alone in the essence of Godhead. The only-begotten Son of God is begotten from the Father alone, consubstantially and coessentially, and this is proper to his person; but he is not by himself alone and singly one in the essence of Godhead. The Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and the Son, and this is proper to his person. Hence he is not by himself alone and singly one in the essence of Godhead, but is the Spirit of both, namely of the Father and the Son, of the same substance and eternity as the Father and the Son. Therefore the holy Trinity must be understood as inseparable even in its persons, although in speech it has names that are separable, because it admits no plural number in the names of its nature.

“Indeed, this too shows that the persons cannot be divided in the holy Trinity: the name of any one person always looks toward another person. If you say ‘Father,’ you indicate the Son; if you name the Son, you proclaim the Father; if you call him the Holy Spirit, you must understand that he is the Spirit of someone.”

Therefore, contrary to Gothescalcus’s blasphemy, it is not said that there is a person in God because it is one in itself—as he habitually does, that is, in the manner of heretics, seeking profane novelties of expression. For, as blessed Gregory says, when such men desire to be praised as possessing exceptional intellect, they bring forth things that are supposedly new, which are not found in the ancient books of the Fathers. Thus, while they desire to appear wise, they scatter seeds of folly among their wretched hearers.

Boethius, then, more correctly than Gothescalcus—or rather, Boethius correctly, since Gothescalcus is incorrect—gave us the definition of “person” from the opinions of the learned, saying:

“‘Persona’ is said from *personando*, with the penultimate syllable circumflexed. But if the antepenultimate is accented, it will most clearly be seen to derive from *sonus* [sound].”

And again:

“Let this meanwhile be established: we have already said that nature and person differ, because nature is the specific property of any substance, whereas person is the individual subsistence of a rational nature. Therefore, it is not—as Gothescalcus has falsely invented—that a person is said to be in God because it is one in itself. Let him explain what he wishes to add when he says ‘because it is one in itself.’ And if he repeats—even though it is absurd—‘one person in itself,’ so that the Father is Father in himself, the Son Son in himself, and the Holy Spirit Holy Spirit in himself, his claim will not stand. For although the Father alone is in the person of fatherhood, the Son alone is from the Father—that is, born from the substance of the Father—and the Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son, nevertheless the Father is spoken of relatively to the Son, the Son to the Father, and the Holy Spirit because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son.”

Hence Saint Augustine, in the sixth book of *On the Trinity* [book VI, chapter 7], says:

“It cannot be discovered how one could say either ‘the Father alone’ or ‘the Son alone,’ since always and inseparably the one is with the Son and the other with the Father—not that both are Father or both Son, but because they are always mutually present, neither is alone.”

The same must be understood of the Holy Spirit. If he should say, “A person is said to be in God because the Godhead or substance, or something of that kind, is one in itself,” the catholic faith does not accept this, since the one and the same Godhead—which is the unity of the Trinity—is wholly in each person and wholly in the three persons together.

He therefore ought not to have said, in explaining why a person is called a person, “in itself,” but rather “with reference to itself,” in the sense in which Augustine says in the seventh book of *On the Trinity*: namely, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are spoken of relatively in the Trinity, whereas the person of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit is spoken of with reference to itself.

“‘To be God,’ Augustine says in the aforementioned book [book VII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6], ‘is not one thing and to be a person another, but they are altogether the same. For “to be” is said with reference to oneself, whereas “person” is said relatively, namely when one says Father, Son, or Holy Spirit. And just as the substance of the Father is the Father himself—not insofar as he is Father, but insofar as he is—so also the person of the Father is nothing other than the Father himself. A person is spoken of with reference to itself, not to the Son or to the Holy Spirit, just as God, great, good, and just are spoken of with reference to themselves, and anything else of this kind. And just as for him “to be” is the same as “to be God,” “to be great,” or “to be good,” so for him “to be” is the same as “to be a person.”

“‘Why, then, do we not call these three together one person, as we call them one essence and one God, but call them three persons, while we do not call them three gods or three essences? It is because we wish some one term to serve the signification by which the Trinity is understood, so that we would not remain entirely silent when asked what the three are, while confessing that they are three.

“‘Nor, when someone hears “the Father alone is God,” should he separate the Son or the Holy Spirit from him. For God alone is with him with whom he is also one God. Likewise, when we hear “the Son,” we must understand “the one God” without any separation of the Father or the Holy Spirit. Thus he should say “one essence” without supposing that one is different from another, greater, better, or in any respect different.

“‘Yet this is not to say that the Father himself is the Son and the Holy Spirit, or that whatever else is spoken of individually in relation to one another is identical—for example, “Word,” which is said only of the Son, or “gift,” which is said only of the Holy Spirit. For this reason they also admit the plural number, as it is written in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He said “one” according to essence, because they are the same God; and “are” according to relation, because the one is Father and the other Son.

“And in the fifteenth book [book XV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 17]:

“‘The Holy Spirit, according to the holy Scriptures, is neither the Father’s alone nor the Son’s alone, but belongs to both; and therefore he communicates to us the charity they share, by which the Father and the Son love one another. And just as wisdom is said of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and all together are not three wisdoms but one wisdom, so charity is said of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and all together are one charity. For the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and all together are one God.’”

Hence the holy Trinity must be understood as inseparable even in its persons. And the one who deceitfully invented this etymology of “person” will perhaps, as is his custom, perversely interpret Boethius’s words in his book *On the Trinity*:

“‘The repetition of units does not produce plurality in the number of things. For example, if I say of the same thing, “one sword, one blade, one weapon”; or if I say “sun, sun, sun,” I have not thereby made three suns, but have spoken repeatedly of one. Therefore, if “God” is said three times of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the threefold predication does not for that reason produce number. And, as he has collected concerning “person,” he says: “Just as God is said to be three and one, so the Godhead may and ought, in catholic usage, to be called three and one.”’

Perhaps he will say: “God is called threefold as though three times one, and the Godhead is called threefold, that is, three times one.”

Against him, Boethius himself defends both himself and us, immediately continuing without any interruption:

“‘Therefore, if “God” is said three times of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the threefold predication does not for that reason produce number. This threatens those who, as has been said, introduce a difference of merits among them.’

“And a little earlier:

“‘Where there is no difference, there is no plurality at all, and therefore no number; consequently there is unity alone. For when “God” is repeated three times, while the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are named, the three units do not produce a plurality of number in that which they are—that is, in the Godhead—as he demonstrates a little later, saying:

“‘“But for Catholics, who establish no difference and posit the very form of being as it is, judging that what is itself is nothing other than what it is, repetition of the same appears more appropriate than enumeration of different things when one says, ‘God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit,’ and ‘This Trinity is one God,’ just as blade, weapon, and sword are one sword, or sun, sun, sun are one sun.

“‘“Yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not spoken of as though they were something multivocal. For blade, weapon, and sword are both themselves and the same; whereas the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are indeed the same, but not themselves in the same way. There is therefore no difference among them in reality; consequently number does not enter, since, as was explained above, number is formed from the diversity of subjects.”

“And the Lord himself demonstrates this same thing in the Gospel, as all catholic teachers transmit it in this sense, when he says: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matthew 28:19). He does not say ‘in the names,’ but ‘in the name,’ because Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the one name of the one God, of whom it is written: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God’ (Deuteronomy 6:5).

“Therefore, although God may be called threefold in the persons, as it were in some manner ‘three times one,’ because the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, of the one and same essence of the Godhead—which is the unity of the Trinity—wholly in each person and wholly in the three persons together, nevertheless the Godhead cannot in catholic usage be called threefold as though three times one. For the one and undivided nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not threefold, or triple, or three times one in each person; nor is it threefold, triple, or three times one in the three persons. Rather, it is one and the same, always wholly full and perfect in each person, and wholly full and perfect in the three persons together. It contains no number in itself, nor any difference in the persons in which the Trinity is spoken of relatively. For ‘triple’ and ‘trinity’ either possess or signify number, as we have shown above from the words of the catholic teachers.

“Thus, when we offer the hymn ‘Holy’ three times and, together with the heavenly and celestial powers, glorify the Godhead that is to be worshiped with threefold adoration, saying ‘Holy, Holy, Holy,’ we follow it with ‘The Lord God of hosts,’ not ‘the Lords God of hosts’; and ‘The heavens and the earth are full of your glory,’ not ‘your glories.’ Believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation, we sing.”

Thus taught and wrote Dionysius the Areopagite and Cyprian; Basil of Cappadocia; Gregory of Nazianzus; Gregory of Nyssa; John of Constantinople; Timothy and Cyril, bishops of Alexandria; Epiphanius of Cyprus; Hilary and Augustine; Jerome and Prosper; Leo and Saint Gregory, Roman pontiffs; and Bede, the distinguished teacher. We wished to set down here all their testimonies, together with certain others that we could gather from their books, but because of their number and length we have omitted them, knowing that those whom these testimonies do not satisfy will not be helped by more.

Nor is it surprising that the man mentioned above speaks in such a way, since from his earliest age he has always sought, and still seeks, novelties of expression, so that by saying things no one else says he might become known, whether for good things or for the worst.

Among his other heretical statements he also says:

## XVII.

÷ “When,” he says, “we speak individually to each one of the persons of the Trinity, we are not then speaking at all to the whole Trinity. For example, to God the Father, who is light, we say: ‘In your light we shall see light’—that is, in your Son, the Holy Spirit. Likewise to the Son: ‘God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness.’ Likewise to the Holy Spirit: ‘Now, Holy Spirit, be for us the one Spirit of the Father with the Son.’

“Therefore, when we supplicate one person individually and separately in this way, and know, perceive, or believe that we have obtained, are obtaining, or will obtain what we ask, we ought submissively to say to the very person to whom we then prayed and are praying: ‘Thanks be to you, God’; and together with that person, equally to the other two: ‘Thanks be to you [plural], God.’ For plurality is properly admissible in the pronouns and verbs concerning these three persons. This is proved by the Father’s statement: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ He did not say ‘Let me make,’ because the Father is not alone, now Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit, as the Sabellians dream. Nor did he say ‘in our images and likenesses,’ because there are not three gods, as the Arians bark; rather: ‘Let us make him in our image and likeness,’ because truly our Lord God is three and one, as Catholics—true Christians, that is—believe and confess.

“Furthermore, a plural number is spoken by God the Son concerning two persons of the Trinity: ‘I and the Father are one’; and: ‘That they may be one, as we also are one’; and: ‘That they too may be in us.’

“For this reason I have also repeatedly said to the Holy Spirit: ‘Come, blessed God, Lord Paraclete; come, sent by the blessed God, the Lord Paraclete; in the name of the blessed God, the Lord Paraclete’; and: ‘May all honor, praise, and glory rightly be forever rendered to you, blessed God, Lord Paraclete, three and one, and likewise to your blessed name and divinity. Amen.’”

ΧΡ. We have never heard the ancient serpent hiss such things through the tongue of any heretic except through the mouth of Gothescalcus; nowhere have we read them except in his own writings. We shudder, utterly astonished at his blindness, because from the Scriptures and the sayings of the Catholics he affirms the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, setting down: “In your light we shall see light”; and: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness,” by which the Holy Spirit is signified; and, quoting the words of Saint Ambrose:

“Now, Holy Spirit, be for us the one Spirit of the Father with the Son.”

And immediately he adds:

“Therefore, when we supplicate individually and separately one person of the Trinity, we ought submissively to say to the very person to whom we then prayed and are praying: ‘Thanks be to you, God’; and together with that person, equally to the other two: ‘Thanks be to you [plural], God.’”

To him must therefore be applied what the Apostle says concerning such people: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1:22). For what is more foolish than to utter things that he has found nowhere uttered and has never heard said by anyone?

And what is especially foolish is that, in order to confirm his opinion, he has produced such testimonies from Scripture as plainly destroy his own opinion; like a madman, he carries the rope by which he may be bound and offers the sword by which he may be killed. “The sword,” says the Apostle, “of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17).

The holy Scriptures sometimes speak only of the Father, as: “How great are your works, O Lord!” (Psalm 91:6); sometimes only of the Son, who is the power and wisdom of God, which says: “I have traversed the circuit of heaven alone” (Ecclesiasticus 24:8); sometimes of the Holy Spirit, as: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7); sometimes only of the Father and the Son, as: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24); and: “With you is the fountain of life” (Psalm 25:10); and: “Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation. For he himself is my God and my savior” (Psalm 61:2); and he says: “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:28); and: “I proceeded from God” (John 8:42); and again the psalm: “In God is my salvation and my glory” (Psalm 61:8).

Likewise the Son himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38); and: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

At other times the Holy Spirit is also mentioned, as: “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10), that is, in your Son, the Holy Spirit, who proceeds wholly and equally from the Father, proceeds wholly from the Son, remains wholly in the Father, remains wholly in the Son, and is the Spirit of both, a kind of communion of the Father and the Son.

And again, in the Psalms he names the whole holy and inseparable Trinity individually and most clearly: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6). Here the Trinity is declared most plainly: the Lord, the Word, and the Spirit of the Lord the Father and of the Word. The whole Trinity is one God, as the Lord also demonstrates in the Gospel when he says: “Go, baptizing in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). He says “in the name,” not “in the names,” showing both that there is one God through the undivided name of the divine essence and that the distinction of the persons is demonstrated by their proper characteristics.

Thus blessed David, full of the Holy Spirit, distinguished the persons but did not separate in Godhead the inseparable persons, when, after speaking to the Father—“How great are your works, O Lord!” (Psalm 91:6)—he also mentioned the Son, saying: “You have made all things in wisdom,” and, adding, “the earth is filled with your possession” (Psalm 108:24). He did not, in the manner of Gothescalcus, add any plurality to the singularity of the holy and inseparable Godhead, nor did he fear being ungrateful to the person whom he had not named.

Similarly, when he said: “In your light we shall see light; extend your mercy to those who know you” (Psalm 35:10), he added the singular number, not the plural “extend.” And when he said: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6), speaking of the same Trinity he used the singular rather than the plural number, adding: “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin” (Psalm 32:7).

The Lord—namely, the holy and inseparable Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whose operation is one just as their divinity is one—gathers the waters of the sea as in a wineskin, restraining with wondrous governance the threats of carnal people, shut up in their own hearts, while he orders all things. A wineskin signifies carnal thought. The waters of the sea are therefore gathered in a wineskin when the bitterness of a perverse mind does not burst forth externally in the voice of wicked freedom.

So too blessed Ambrose, many times in his hymns addressing at one time the person of the Father, at another the person of the Son, at another the person of the Holy Spirit, and at another the three persons of the holy Trinity, always demonstrates that the holy Trinity is one God of one Godhead. The Father is not to be understood, believed, or proclaimed without the Son and the Holy Spirit; nor the Son without the Father and the Holy Spirit; nor the Holy Spirit without the Father and the Son.

To give a few examples from many, we ask the reader not to be angry with me if he finds the words of Ambrose or of other catholic writers repeated often in this little work of our service, since he will find the same in the writings of very famous men. Blessed Ambrose says:

“Refreshed in our limbs by sleep, we rise, having spurned the bed.”

We ask you, Father, to be present for us as we sing; and throughout that entire hymn he entreats the person of the Father, but not without the Son and the Holy Spirit. Again, throughout another hymn he speaks to the person of the Son, saying:

“Christ, who are light and day, you disclose the darkness of night.”

And again he addresses the person of the Holy Spirit, showing that he is not without the Father and the Son, when he says:

“Now, Holy Spirit, be for us the one Spirit of the Father with the Son.”

At another time, mentioning only the persons of the Father and the Son, he says:

“May the dawn advance its course; may the whole dawn emerge.”

“The whole Son is in the Father, and the whole Father is in the Word.”

And again:

“Partner of the Father’s light, yourself the light and day of light.”

“We have shattered the night by singing; be present to those who ask.”

At another time he indicates the persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit, saying:

“May Christ be our food, and may faith be our drink,”

“Let us drink joyfully and soberly with the intoxication of the Spirit.”

And again:

“Christ, Lord of powers, not from human seed,”

“of the one Godhead, and partner of the Holy Spirit.”

At another time, bringing forward all three persons of the holy Trinity individually, he shows that the Trinity is holy and one in Godhead, saying:

“Radiance of the Father’s glory, bringing forth light from light,

light of light and source of light, illuminating day with day.

And may the true sun descend, shining with perpetual splendor,

and pour the radiance of the Holy Spirit into our senses.

Let us call upon you in our vows as Father, Father of eternal glory,

Father of mighty grace, banish slippery guilt.”

Whether he speaks to the person of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, he always uses the singular number. He does not fear, like Gothescalcus, being ungrateful to the other persons, nor does he say to the other persons, “Thanks be to you [plural], God”; rather, he says:

“We offer everlasting praises to God the Father with the Son,

God, who was called out of Egypt through his servants.

Born again through the Holy Spirit, we see the light of the gift.

Following you, Lord, we shall be saved forever.”

And again:

“Let us ask Christ, and the Father of Christ, and the Spirit of the Father.

Nourish us, O powerful Trinity, one through all things, as we pray.”

And in the first book of *On the Faith* [book I, chapter 5], he says:

“Let reverence join the Son to the Father, whom divinity has joined; let impiety not separate him whom the property of generation has united.”

And in book I of *On the Holy Spirit* [book I, chapter 3]:

“If you say ‘Christ,’ you have designated God the Father, from whom the Son was anointed; the Son himself, who was anointed; and the Spirit with which he was anointed. For it is written: ‘This Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit’ (Acts 10:38). And if you say ‘Father,’ you have likewise indicated his Son and the spirit of his mouth, provided that you also grasp this with your heart. And if you say ‘Spirit,’ you have named God the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, because the Spirit is also the Son’s. The Father is not dishonored without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, nor the Holy Spirit without the Father and the Son.”

Again, in the same book [chapter 3, toward the end], blessed Ambrose says:

“Observe carefully why the Lord said: ‘Whoever blasphemes against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come’ (Mark 3:28). Is the offense against the Son one thing and that against the Holy Spirit another? For just as there is one Godhead, so there is one injury.”

And a little later:

“There can be no pleading for forgiveness where there is the fullness of sacrilege, because whoever has denied the Holy Spirit has also denied God the Father and the Son.”

And the same blessed Ambrose, praying:

“Now, Holy Spirit, be for us the one Spirit of the Father with the Son,”

“Deign, ready, to be poured into our breast.”

He rightly understood that the Holy Spirit is one God with the Father and the Son, who is not poured back into the human breast apart from the Father and the Son [Col. 0592C], because, just as there is one divinity, so also there is one will, power, and operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But Gothescalcus, filled with an evil spirit, misunderstood this, producing testimony from this hymn:

“When,” he says, “we thus pray individually and separately, we ought submissively to say to the same person to whom we have then prayed: ‘Thanks be to you, God,’ and, together with that person, equally to the other two: ‘Thanks be to you,’ lest we be ungrateful to the other two persons.”

Against this blasphemy blessed Ambrose says in the second book *On the Faith* (chapter 4, near the middle):

“We have learned that the Father and the Son have one image, one likeness, and one sanctification. We have learned that there is one operation, one glory, and likewise one divinity. Therefore there is one and only one God [Col. 0592D], because it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Matthew 4:10).”

For the testimony which Gothescalcus, in this blasphemy of his, brought forward from Genesis to confirm his own opinion, perversely interpreting the words, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” blessed Ambrose explained in the first book *On the Faith* (chapter 7) as follows:

“To whom,” he says, “does the Father say, ‘Let us make man,’ except to him whom he knew to be the true Son? In whom could he recognize his own image except in the true one? The adoptive and the true are not one; nor would the Son say, ‘We are one,’ if he were comparing himself with one who was not true. Therefore the Father says, ‘Let us make,’ who declared him true. Can he who made be not true, and can what is granted [Col. 0593A] to the one who speaks be denied to the one who makes? How, moreover, unless he knew the Son to be true, would he entrust to him the unity of his will and the truth of his work? For since the Son does the same works that the Father does, and the Son gives life to whom he wishes, as it is written, he is not different in power, and he is free in will. Thus unity is preserved, because the power of God lies in the particularity of the divinity, while freedom lies not in any difference but in the unity of the will.”

And blessed Augustine, although Gothescalcus, speaking of him, is accustomed repeatedly to insist by saying “our Augustine”—though he is a stranger to him in heart, mouth, and conduct—explained these testimonies, one from the Gospel and the other from Genesis, quite differently in the seventh book *On the Trinity* (chapter 5), saying:

“The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are not a greater essence [Col. 0593B] than the Father alone or the Son alone; but those three subsistences together—or persons, if they are to be called that—are equal to each individually, which the natural person does not perceive. For he cannot think except in terms of masses and spaces, whether small or great, flying about in his mind as images of bodies. Until he is cleansed of this uncleanness, let him believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God, alone, great, almighty, good, just, merciful, creator of all things visible and invisible, and in whatever else can rightly and truly be said according to human capacity.

“Nor, when he hears of the Father alone as God, should he separate the Son or the Holy Spirit from him. For he alone is God together with whom he is also one God; and when we hear [Col. 0593C] of the Son alone as God, we must understand him without any separation from the Father or the Holy Spirit. Let him therefore speak of one essence in such a way that he does not suppose one to be greater or lesser than another, or in any respect different. Yet this does not mean that the Father himself is the Son and the Holy Spirit, or that whatever is said individually in relation to one another is identical—for example, ‘Word,’ which is said only of the Son, or ‘gift,’ which is said only of the Holy Spirit.

“For this reason they also admit the plural number, as it is written in the Gospel: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30). He said ‘one’ and ‘are’: ‘one’ according to essence, which is the same God; ‘are’ according to relation, because the one is Father and the other Son. Sometimes the one essence is also left unmentioned, and only the relational terms are recalled in the plural [Col. 0593D]: ‘We shall come to him, I and the Father, and we shall make our dwelling with him’ (John 14:24). ‘We shall come’ and ‘we shall make our dwelling’ are plural, because what was stated above was ‘I and the Father,’ that is, the Son and the Father, who are spoken of relatively to one another.

“Sometimes this occurs altogether implicitly, as in Genesis: ‘Let us make man in our likeness’ (Genesis 1:26). ‘Let us make’ and ‘our’ are expressed in the plural, and cannot be understood except relationally. For it is not that gods should make man, or that he should be made in the image and likeness of gods; rather, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit should make him in the image of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that man might subsist as the image of God, while God is the Trinity.

“But because that image of God was not made wholly equal—as though it had been born from him rather than created by him—it is an image [Col. 0594A] for the purpose of signifying this fact, so that it is ‘according to the image’: that is, it does not equal him by parity but approaches him by a certain likeness. For one approaches God not by intervals of place but by likeness, and withdraws from him by unlikeness.”

And in the twelfth book (chapter 6):

“For God said, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’ (Genesis 1:26). Shortly afterward, however, it is said: ‘And God made man in the image of God.’ ‘Our,’ certainly, because it is plural, would not rightly have been said if man were made in the image of one person—whether the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit. But because he was made in the image of the Trinity, it was therefore said, ‘in our image.’ Again, lest we suppose that three gods are to be believed in the Trinity, although the same Trinity is one God [Col. 0594B], he says, ‘And God made man in the image of God,’ as if he had said, ‘in his own image.’”

Here blessed Augustine plainly shows that Gothescalcus lies and speaks heretically when he says:

“When we pray individually and separately to one person of the Trinity, we ought submissively to say to that same person to whom we then prayed and are praying: ‘Thanks be to you, God’; and equally to the other two persons: ‘Thanks be to you.’”

For it is written both in the Law and in the Gospel: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” Therefore Ambrose says in the second book *On the Faith* (chapter 4, near the middle):

“We have learned that the Father and the Son have one image, one likeness, and one sanctification; we have learned that there is one operation, one glory, and likewise one divinity [Col. 0594C]. Therefore there is one and only one God, because it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Matthew 4:10). One God—not so that he himself is Father and Son, as the impious Sabellius asserts, but because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one divinity. Where there is one divinity, there is also one will and one command.”

And Augustine, in his letter to Maximus (Letter 66, near the beginning):

“If worship (*latria*) is owed and rendered by us to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—of which it is said, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Deuteronomy 6:3)—then without doubt the Lord our God, whom alone we ought to serve with worship, is not the Father alone, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone, but the Trinity itself, one and only God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

“Not that the Father himself is the Son, or that the Holy Spirit himself is either the Father or the Son; [Col. 0594D] for in that Trinity the Father is the Father of the Son alone, the Son is the Son of the Father alone, while the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son. But because of the one and same nature and inseparable life, let the Trinity itself, insofar as human beings can understand it, be apprehended by faith preceding understanding as the one Lord our God, of whom it is said: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

And in the book *On Christian Doctrine* (Book 1, chapter 3):

“This Trinity is one God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things. Thus the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each individually, are full substance, and all together are one substance. The Father is neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit; the Son is neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. But the Father is Father alone, the Son is Son alone, and the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit alone. [Col. 0595A]

“The same eternity, the same unchangeableness, the same majesty, and the same power belong to all three. In the Father there is unity, in the Son equality, and in the Holy Spirit the concord of unity and equality. These three are one because of the Father, all are equal because of the Son, and all are joined together because of the Holy Spirit.”

And in the tractate on the fifth Psalm:

“And this Trinity is only one God, because when the Apostle said, ‘From him, through him, and in him are all things,’ he is believed to have indicated the Trinity itself; yet he did not add, ‘glory to them,’ but ‘glory to him.’ Therefore one worship, glory, service, and thanksgiving are owed [Col. 0595B] to the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and not separately, as Gothescalcus blasphemes.

“For, as Augustine likewise says in the fifth book and in the eighth book *On the Trinity*, whatever is said substantially of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must be said and understood not in the plural but in the singular: ‘the great, good, almighty God,’ as it is written, ‘You alone are God’ (Psalm 85:10), and ‘No one is good except one, God’ (Luke 18:19).”

Therefore one glory and one thanksgiving are owed to the one and only God, as the same Augustine shows elsewhere, saying:

“There is therefore one essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in which the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. This is shown to us especially at the very beginning of the holy Scriptures, where God says: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’ (Genesis 1:26) [Col. 0595C].

“For when he used the singular ‘image,’ he showed that there is one nature in whose image man was to be made. But when he says ‘our’ in the plural, he showed that God in whose image man was being made is not one person. For if the one essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were also one person, it would not be said, ‘in our image,’ but ‘in my image’; nor would he have said, ‘Let us make,’ but ‘Let me make.’ If, however, three substances were to be understood or believed in those three persons, it would not be said, ‘in our image,’ but ‘in our images.’ Man is said to have been made according to the one image of the one God, so that the essential divinity of the holy Trinity might be signified. [Col. 0595D]”

Concerning the Gospel example, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), Ambrose writes (Book 1 *On the Faith*, chapter 1):

“He said ‘one,’ so that no distinction of power and nature might be made; he added ‘are,’ so that you might recognize the Father and the Son, since the perfect Father is believed to have begotten a perfect Son, and the Father and Son are one—not by confusion of persons, but by unity of nature.”

And Augustine, in the book *Against Five Heresies*:

“Let the empty talkers and seducers of minds perish—the Arian and the Sabellian. For he says, ‘I and the Father are one.’ He did not say, ‘I and the Father am one,’ but ‘I and the Father are one.’ Let the Arian hear the ‘one’ that I say; let the Sabellian hear the ‘are.’ Let the Arian not divide the ‘one’; let the Sabellian not erase the ‘are.’ Rather, let both come and themselves also be one in us, just as I and the Father are one. Therefore, if the Father and the Son are—or rather, because they are undoubtedly one—not two but one God, [Col. 0596A]”

and the rest of what he develops there.

Likewise, concerning the other Gospel testimony which he cited, “That they may be one, just as we are one” (John 17:21), Augustine says:

“They are one in their own [nature?] in charity; we are one in ours, in unity of substance and glory” [the printed Latin is corrupt]. ‘I in them, and you in me.’ I in them as the head is in the members, and you in me as the Father is in the Son, ‘so that they may be perfected in one,’ that is, made perfect—something that he will accomplish who wished us to be one in him and through him—‘so that the world may know that you sent me, and loved them as you loved me’ (John 17:23). [Col. 0596B]

“‘You loved them’ so that they might become what they were not; ‘you loved me’ so that I might be what I always was. You loved me as the only-begotten one; you loved them as adoptive children. You loved them so that through me they might be in you; you loved me so that through you I might be in you.”

Against this statement of his—who alone among all heretics is reported to have said:

“Whoever says to any one person, ‘Thanks be to you, God,’ and equally to the other two persons, ‘Thanks be to you,’ is truly a Catholic and certainly a true Christian”—and who admits that he has frequently said to the Holy Spirit:

“Come, blessed God, Lord Paraclete; come, sent by the blessed God, Lord Paraclete, in the name of the blessed God and Lord Paraclete; and: May all honor, praise, and glory always be rendered to you, blessed God, Lord Paraclete, three and one, and likewise to your blessed name and divinity. [Col. 0596C] Amen.”

Saint Gregory, speaking in the sixteenth homily on the prophet Ezekiel, proves that he thought otherwise than the chosen people of God in the Old and New Testaments thought, saying:

“The spiritual Fathers believed almighty God to be a Trinity in the same way that the later Fathers openly declared this same Trinity. Isaiah heard the angelic hosts in heaven crying out: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts’ (Isaiah 6:3). For in order to show the Trinity of persons, ‘holy’ is said three times; but so that the Trinity’s one substance might appear, it is not said ‘of the Lord of hosts,’ but ‘Lord.’

“David likewise, thinking the same way, says: ‘May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us’ (Psalm 66:8). Although he had named God three times, in order to show that this is one, he added: ‘And may all the ends of the earth fear him.’

“Paul also says: ‘For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.’ ‘From him,’ namely from the Father; ‘through him,’ through the Son; ‘in him,’ however, in the Holy Spirit. Having thus named him three times [Col. 0596D], he added: ‘To him be glory forever and ever.’ For by not saying ‘to them’ but ‘to him,’ he distinguished the persons by saying ‘him’ three times, and by adding ‘to him be glory,’ he did not divide the substance.”

Against this, Gothescalcus, exalting himself as though he understood the divinity of the persons of the holy Trinity more profoundly than the angelic powers of the Seraphim in heaven—among whom no other spirits intervene between them and God—and as though surpassing in dignity even those heavenly ranks [Col. 0597A] called the fullness of knowledge, which the Seraphim themselves surpass in dignity, and as though interpreting more correctly what those hosts sang, supposedly without understanding what they were saying, than Isaiah, who heard those same heavenly powers singing a hymn worthy of God; and as though grasping the meaning of David’s psalm more deeply than David himself, who understood it beyond his elders and beyond all who taught him; and as though perceiving more profoundly in his mind what Paul uttered with his mind absent, although he had been caught up to the third heaven and heard secret words in paradise, and through whom, as he himself confesses, Christ spoke—not, as it seems to him, foolishly, as the heavenly hosts said, “The whole earth is full of his glory,” or as the Catholic Church, instructed by that utterance, sings, “The heavens and earth are full of your glory”—failing to understand how to say, “The heavens and earth are full of your [plural] glory”; and, “Let all the ends of the earth fear him,” not “Let all the ends of the earth fear you [plural]”; and, “To him be glory,” not “To you [plural] be glory,” said at the conclusion of his praise and prayer—or rather of his blasphemy:

### XVIII.

÷ “May honor, praise, and glory always be rendered to you, deservedly, blessed God, Lord Paraclete, three and one, and likewise to your blessed name and divinity. Amen.”

And after the foregoing he continues:

“Since, as is clear, each person of the Trinity is separately Lord God in himself.”

And shortly afterward:

“As also in the Psalm: ‘Will not my soul be subject to God?’ This is said of the Father, as is shown by what follows concerning the Son [Col. 0597C]: ‘For from him comes my salvation.’ For he himself is also my God and my savior—that is, my Jesus. Since it does not say, ‘For he himself is my God,’ but rather, ‘and he himself is my God,’ without doubt God the Holy Spirit has revealed and reveals that just as God the Father is God in himself, so also is the Son.

“Therefore, wherever the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are named without the word ‘God’ or ‘Lord’ being expressed, as in the statement, ‘Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,’ each person must always be understood as Lord God. The same applies to the statement: ‘The Paraclete, whom the Father will send in my name.’ For God sends, has sent, and will send God in the name of God.

“That is why I said a little earlier that to one person of the Trinity, to whom we pray individually and separately, we ought to say: ‘Thanks be to you, God’ [Col. 0597D]; and, lest we be ungrateful to the other two persons, we ought to add: ‘Thanks be to you.’ For whoever, speaking to one person, says, ‘Thanks be to you, God the Trinity,’ errs almost as much as a Jew and a Sabellian. But whoever says, ‘Thanks be to you, gods,’ is either a pagan or an Arian. Whoever, however, says to any one person, ‘Thanks be to you, God,’ and equally to the other two persons, ‘Thanks be to you,’ is truly a Catholic and certainly a true Christian.”

**CH.** Against these previously unheard-of blasphemies, Saint Ambrose says in the first book of *On the Faith*, chapter one:

> “The assertion of our faith is this: that we believe there is one God; that, unlike the nations, we do not separate the Son; that, unlike the Jews, we do not deny that he was born from the Father before the ages and later brought forth from the Virgin; that, unlike Sabellius, we do not confuse the Father and the Word by asserting that the same person is both Father and Son; that, unlike Photinus, we do not assign the beginning of the Son to the Virgin; and that, unlike Arius, by believing in many and dissimilar powers, we do not make many gods in the manner of pagan error, for it is written: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God’ (Deut. 6:4).

> “For ‘God’ and ‘Lord’ are names of magnificence, names of power, just as he himself says: ‘The Lord God is my name’ (Exod. 3:15), and as the prophet asserts elsewhere: ‘The Lord God Almighty is his name’ (Exod. 15; Isa. 42). The Lord and God, therefore, is so called either because he rules all things, or because he watches over all things and is feared by everyone. If, then, there is one God, one name, and one power, there is one Trinity. Finally, he himself says: ‘Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28:19)—‘in the name,’ certainly, not ‘in the names.’”

Saint Ambrose therefore did not teach that, when one prays separately and in isolation to one person of the Trinity, as Gothescalcus does, one ought to say, “Thanks be to you, God,” and, lest we be ungrateful to the other two persons, ought to add, “Thanks be to you all, God.” For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one name—that of the one God.

As Athanasius shows in the first book of *On the Faith*, saying:

> “This is the formula of the matter in the condemnation of heretics, and this is the victory of the title in the acquittal of Catholics, signified by God’s principal command: ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28:19). Hear in this admirable and royal decree how the whole mystery is contained together in the divinity of the Trinity. By saying ‘in the name,’ he clearly declared that one divinity subsists in the Trinity; and by adding ‘of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,’ he distinguished that individual persons are present under their individual names.”

And again, in the same book:

> “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6). Certainly he indicated the Son by ‘the Word,’ designated the Father by ‘the Lord,’ and called ‘the breath of his mouth’ the Holy Spirit. You see that in these persons the name of the Trinity is united in nature, as the Psalmist also confirms: ‘Therefore God, your God, has anointed you’ (Ps. 44:6). Here you find ‘God’ and ‘God,’ yet you will not find the persons called ‘gods’ in the plural.”

Nor did Athanasius teach that one may or ought to pray separately to one person and say, “Thanks be to you, God,” and to the other persons, “Thanks be to you all, God.”

Again, in another book *On the Trinity*, he says:

> “Did the apostles become transgressors of the Savior’s command, and, contrary to his tradition, baptize so great a multitude? For it is not written that they baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, but only in the name of the Lord Jesus. Yet they were not transgressors—far from it. For although only the name of the Son is mentioned, it nevertheless contains the Father and the Holy Spirit, as we have proved from the holy Scriptures. Thus the Holy Spirit is also called ‘Sabaoth,’ and he is worshiped with God and with the Son by the Seraphim; for this reason they say three times, ‘Holy, Holy, Holy,’ so that they might proclaim the Trinity.”

In this sense, therefore, blessed Ambrose also resolves the question.

Saint Augustine—of whom Gothescalcus repeatedly says, “our Augustine,” as though he were foreign and opposed to Gothescalcus, not his own personal or domestic authority—speaks against him in his book *Against Five Heresies*:

> “Whoever separates the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in eternity, substance, or communion, and whoever denies that the Spirit belongs both to the Father and to the Son, is full of an unclean spirit and empty of the Holy Spirit.”

Gothescalcus appears to separate the persons within the holy Trinity when he says:

> “Since each person of the Trinity is, as is evident, individually and in himself the Lord God, and since we pray separately and in isolation to one person of the Trinity, it ought to be said: ‘Thanks be to you, God’; and, lest we be ungrateful to the other persons, it ought to be added: ‘Thanks be to you all, God.’”

Accordingly, just as Augustine is called “our Augustine” by the Catholic Church—not boastfully and falsely, as Gothescalcus does, but joyfully and truthfully—so Augustine confesses in the aforementioned book that Gothescalcus, in saying these things, is full of an unclean spirit and empty of the Holy Spirit.

Against Gothescalcus’s claim that he is empty of the Holy Spirit when he says, “Since each person of the Trinity is, as is evident, individually and in isolation the Lord God, to whom we pray separately,” the Lord Jesus, God, full of the Holy Spirit, says:

> “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

And again:

> “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:9–10).

Explaining this while inspired by the same Holy Spirit, blessed Augustine says in his *Tractates on John*:

> “Why do you desire to know separately those who are inseparable?”

Then Christ speaks not only to Philip but to them all:

> “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself; but the Father who dwells in me himself does the works” (ibid.).

What does “I do not speak from myself” mean except “I am not, from myself, the one who speaks”? For he attributes the action to the one from whom the acting person derives his being. God the Father is from no one; the Son, however, is God equal to the Father, but from God the Father. Therefore the Father is God, but not God from God; and he is light, but not light from light. The Son, however, is God from God and light from light.”

Finally, Augustine adds:

> “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Otherwise, believe because of the works themselves” (ibid.). Earlier Philip alone was being reproved; now it is shown that he was not the only one who needed correction: ‘Because of the works themselves,’ he says, ‘believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me.’ For if we were separated, we could in no way work inseparably.”

And in his sermon to the people, where he explained what blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is, he says among other things (*On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 11, chapter 16):

> “These things are said in such a way that the operation of the Trinity is nevertheless understood to be inseparable: so that when the operation of the Father is mentioned, it is not understood as being performed without the Son and the Holy Spirit; when the operation of the Son is mentioned, not without the Father and the Holy Spirit; and when the operation of the Holy Spirit is mentioned, not without the Father and the Son. It is sufficiently known to those who believe rightly, and even to those who understand as they are able, that the saying concerning the Father—‘He himself does the works’—means that he is the source even of the works, since from him comes the existence of the cooperating persons. For the Son was born from him, and the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from him, from whom the Son was born and with whom the same Spirit is shared.”

Thus it is clear how Gothescalcus lies when he calls Augustine “his own,” repeatedly saying, “our Augustine.” Gothescalcus does not belong to Augustine, because he neither believes nor teaches as Augustine does; nor does Augustine belong to Gothescalcus, because he disagrees with Gothescalcus and thinks in a Catholic manner, whereas Gothescalcus does not.

Augustine says that the Father is God, but not God from God, while the Son is God and God from God. He does not say, as Gothescalcus falsely does, that each person of the Trinity is individually and in isolation the Lord God.

The testimony also misused by Gothescalcus to confirm his own position—where the Lord says, “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name”—Saint Gregory, filled with the Holy Spirit, explains in a very different way from Gothescalcus, who is filled with an unclean spirit.

Blessed Gregory says in the thirtieth homily on the Gospel:

> “‘But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and remind you of everything that I have said to you’ (John 14:26). You know, my very dear brothers, that in Greek usage *paracletus* is called in Latin *advocatus*, or ‘consoler.’ He is called an advocate because he intervenes with the Father’s justice on behalf of sinners who have fallen into error. He is said to be of one substance with the Father and the Son and to plead for sinners, because he makes those whom he fills into people who plead.

> “Concerning this Paraclete the Lord also says: ‘When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me, and you also will bear witness’ (John 15:26–27).”

On this statement, the holy and remarkable teacher Bede says in a Gospel homily, drawing on the words and understanding of Catholics:

> “The Lord testifies that the Spirit of truth is to be sent by him, and immediately adds that the same Spirit proceeds from the Father—not because the same Spirit proceeds from the Father in a different way than when he is sent by the Son, but because the Son says that he is sent by himself and proceeds from the Father in order to designate the Father as one person and himself as another, and, while distinguishing the persons in this way, to declare that his operation and will are one with the Father’s will and operation.

> “For when the grace of the same Spirit is given to human beings, the Spirit is plainly sent by the Father and sent by the Son; he proceeds from the Father and proceeds from the Son, because his sending itself is that procession by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son. He also comes of his own will; for, just as he is coequal with the Father and the Son, so he has the same will in common with the Father and the Son: ‘The Spirit breathes where he wills’ (John 3:8). And as the Apostle says after listing the heavenly gifts: ‘All these things the one and same Spirit brings about, distributing to each as he wills’ (1 Cor. 12:11).”

Thus, individually, the Lord God Almighty, uncreated, immeasurable, eternal, and whatever else is said of God in relation to himself, is the Father—but not in isolation from the Son, who was begotten from his substance, and from the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from him and from the Son.

Likewise, individually, the Lord God Almighty, uncreated, immeasurable, eternal, and whatever else is said of God in relation to himself, is the Son—but not in isolation from the Father, from whom he exists, and from the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and from him.

Likewise, individually, the Lord God Almighty, uncreated, immeasurable, eternal, and whatever else is said of God in relation to himself, is the Holy Spirit—but not in isolation from the Father and the Son, from whom he proceeds.

We speak individually and in isolation of God the Father and of whatever is said of God in relation to himself because, relatively, within this holy, undivided, and inseparable Trinity, there is individually one Father, individually one Son, and individually one Holy Spirit. Yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one divinity, deity, nature, essence, substance, equal glory, and coeternal majesty.

Although the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not different, because the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

“The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit” is not said according to substance but according to relation. Yet this relation is not an accident, because it is not changeable. Nothing in God is said according to accident, because nothing in him is changeable.

Since, as Augustine says, the Father alone, the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone is as great as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together—because of the one and same undivided, inseparable, complete, and perfect substance, that is, the deity, which is wholly present in each and wholly present in all three persons together—the individual persons nevertheless possess something proper to themselves, by which, in their inseparable equality, they display a particular property in themselves: the Father alone is Father, the Son alone is Son, and the Holy Spirit alone is Holy Spirit.

The Father has this as his proper characteristic: that he is from no other. Consequently, he alone is in the person of fatherhood, but not alone in the essence of deity.

The only-begotten Son of God has this as his proper characteristic: that he alone is begotten consubstantially and coessentially from the Father alone; and in this lies the property of his person.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, has this as his proper characteristic: that he proceeds equally from the Father and the Son and is the Spirit of both, of the same substance and eternity as the Father and the Son.

These three are truly three—ineffably three, and three in essence—possessing their own properties. Yet these three are one, truly one; and this one is three. They are not three fathers, nor three sons, nor three holy spirits, but three persons: one Father, one Son, and one Holy Spirit. These three—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are one in nature, omnipotence, and eternity.

Therefore, says Saint Athanasius, there is one God because the deity is united, as it is written concerning the individual persons. And since there is no God except one—“Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God”—he says through the individual persons that the deity is united. He does not say, as Gothescalcus does, that one ought to pray separately and in isolation to one person of the Trinity.

Again Saint Athanasius says in book one, *On the Unity of the Name of the Trinity*:

> “Do you not know that the Father is one God, the Son is one God, and the Holy Spirit is one God? Is there not one God, since the name is united in the nature of the *ousia*? So also there is one Spirit, because there is one deity of the same kind. For if, through the individual names of the persons, you have designated the one name ‘Spirit’ three times, ought you therefore to say that there are three spirits? Far from it. If that could be said, then it would also have to be introduced into the confession that three gods should be named in the plural, so that there would no longer be one nature of divinity in these persons, but each would subsist in its own or in a different nature. Far be this from us.”

> “Whatever, therefore, as blessed Augustine says, is said of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in relation to themselves—that is, whatever is said in a way that reveals their substance—is not said of one without the other. For neither is the Father God without the Son and the Holy Spirit, nor is the Son God without the Father and the Holy Spirit, nor is the Holy Spirit God without the Father and the Son, whose Spirit he is.

> “If, then, you are asked why God is called Father, answer relationally: because he has a Son. Likewise, concerning the Son, answer relationally that he is Son because he has a Father; and concerning the Holy Spirit, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, whose Spirit he is.

> “If it is also said to you concerning God, ‘How is the Father what the Son is, or the Son what the Father is?’ answer: according to substance, the Son is what the Father is, the Father is what the Son is, and the Holy Spirit is what the Father and the Son are, because there is one God and one substance—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

> “God is said substantially in relation to himself; the Son is said relatively in relation to the Father, the Father in relation to the Son, and the Holy Spirit in relation to the Father and the Son.

> “According to the property of person, the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Father, and the Holy Spirit is not the Father and the Son. According to the unity of substance, the Father is what the Son is, and the Holy Spirit is what the Father and the Son are—that is, one almighty God.

> “Whatever, therefore, God is said to be in relation to himself, whether this is said of the individual persons—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—or of the Trinity itself together, is said not in the plural but in the singular.”

Gothescalcus therefore speaks perversely, as a genuine heretic, when he says:

> “When we pray separately and in isolation to one person of the Trinity, it ought to be said: ‘Thanks be to you, God’; and, lest we be ungrateful to the other two persons, it ought to be added: ‘Thanks be to you all, God.’”

Against this, the venerable Alcuin says in the book collected from the statements of blessed Augustine and other Catholics for the emperor Charles the Great, book one, *On the Trinity*, chapter 12:

> “This must also be held with the greatest firmness: nothing said in relation to the Trinity itself ought to be expressed in the plural, because that simple nature of the supreme deity must be designated in the singular, not the plural. Therefore it is not permissible to speak in God of three gods, three almighty beings, three good beings, three great beings, or three essences.

> “Although the Father is personally one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, they nevertheless have one name of nature, which is called God, or substance, or essence, or omnipotence, along with many other things that are said substantially, not relatively, of him.

> “The Catholic faith, therefore, as Athanasius says, is this: that we venerate one God in the Trinity of persons and the Trinity of persons in the unity of the deity, neither confusing the persons so that there are not three, nor separating the substance so that it becomes threefold.

> “In this Trinity nothing is earlier or later, nothing greater or less; rather, all three persons are coeternal and coequal with one another. Thus in every respect the unity of deity in the Trinity of persons and the Trinity of persons in the unity of deity must be venerated.”

More testimonies of Catholics could be set down here, which the faithful and devout reader will readily find in their proper places, against these blasphemies of his, which the sacred canons also condemn and refute together with their author.

For the canons of the Council of Carthage under Aurelius established that no one should name the Father in place of the Son or the Son in place of the Father in prayers; that, when one assists at the altar, prayer should always be directed to the Father through the Son; and that no one should use prayers he has composed for himself unless he has first discussed them with more learned brothers.

Accordingly, at the end of the prayers, those assisting at the sacred altar, the holy Catholic Church petitions through Christ our Lord. At the end of the canon she says:

> “Through Christ our Lord, through him, and with him, and in him, to you, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, is all honor and glory, throughout all ages of ages.”

Or she says:

> “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who with you lives and reigns as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

This is certainly because of that mystery, as we read in the statements of the orthodox: the mediator between God and human beings became human, Christ Jesus, a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Through his own blood he entered into the holy places—not copies of the true things made by human hands, but heaven itself—where he is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us.

Interpreting this priestly office, the Apostle says:

> “Through him, therefore, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name” (Heb. 13:15).

Through him, therefore, we offer a sacrifice of praise and proclamation, because through his death we were reconciled when we were enemies. Through him, who graciously became a sacrifice for us, an acceptable sacrifice can be found in the sight of our God.

For this reason blessed Peter admonishes us:

> “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 2:5).

In this conclusion of the prayers many heretics are refuted: the Manichaeans, Sabellians, Arians, Nestorians, Eutychians, Macedonians, Eudoxians, and the other plagues and moths of the Catholic faith—those who have dared to think or say something different from the Catholic faith concerning the consubstantiality, coeternity, and equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and also concerning the incarnation of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ.

At the end of certain prayers, the Catholic and apostolic Church is also said to address the Lord Jesus Christ:

> “Who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages.”

This does not conflict with the aforementioned chapter of the canonical constitution, because in this conclusion the Son is not named together with the Father as though they were one person. Rather, the persons of the holy Trinity are properly distinguished, and the unity of the substance of that same holy and undivided Trinity is confessed in a Catholic manner.

Although Gothescalcus, writing to one of his associates, criticizes this, saying:

> “The ignorant speak incorrectly when they say, ‘Who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God,’ lest the Son—far be it from us—be thought to be the God of the Holy Spirit.”

Since he criticizes the Catholic Church on this point, it follows that he must also criticize its head and author, who says to the Father:

> “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true and only God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

He would then have to say that we are to understand the Father alone to be the true and only God, and that the one whom he sent is merely Jesus Christ.

The Catholic Church, however, believes and confesses that the Son, God, lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages. It understands the words,

> “Who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God,”

to mean the same as:

> “Who, with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, live and reign as God.”

Similarly, it understands the Lord’s words in the Gospel,

> “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only and true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent,”

to mean:

> “This is eternal life: that they may know that you, and Jesus Christ whom you sent, are the only and true God.”

Yet immediately afterward, in the same writing, he contradicts himself, saying:

> “For the Son, God, lives and reigns with God the Father, according to the saying, ‘The Word was with God, and the Word was God’ (John 1:1). Behold, God with God. Likewise, we believe, know, and confess that God the Holy Spirit reigns with God the Father and with God the Son. Yet there is no plurality of gods where there is unity and equality of nature, essence, substance, majesty, power, and deity.”

After this confession of unity, he immediately composes the following impious prayer:

> “Lord God my Ruler, my mercy, Jesus Christ, King of glory, I beseech you: graciously hear me according to your divinity, and ask your Father, the Lord our God, according to your humanity, so that he, our blessed God, the Lord Paraclete, in the name of our blessed God, the Lord Paraclete, may give us equally our Holy Spirit, God our Paraclete. And may all honor, praise, and glory always, deservedly, belong to you, blessed God, Lord Paraclete, three together and one together, to your blessed name and power. Amen.”

But so that what is said there in the plural may not trouble you—“all honor, praise, and glory always deservedly belong to you all, blessed God, the Paraclete, three together and one together, and to your blessed name”—understand that this is unquestionably appropriate to say. For when we speak to one person of the Trinity, we do not speak to the Trinity, but to whichever one person of the Trinity it may be.

He writes many other things in this manner. But the eloquent Paul did not pray in this way, nor did he teach us to pray in this way, as Augustine says in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 23:

> “For we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should. But the Spirit himself, the Apostle says, intercedes for us with unutterable groanings. And he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God” (Rom. 8:26).

What does “the Spirit himself intercedes” mean except that he causes us to intercede with unutterable but genuine groanings, because the Spirit is truth? He is the one of whom he says elsewhere:

> “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4:6).

And what does “crying” mean here except “causing us to cry,” in the manner in which we speak of a “joyful day” that causes people to rejoice?

He makes this clear elsewhere, where he says:

> “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15).

There he said “crying,” but here “in whom we cry,” thereby explaining how he said “crying”—that is, as I have already explained, “causing us to cry.”

Yet this Spirit, who causes us to cry, “Abba, Father,” does not make us ungrateful to the other persons, namely the Son and himself, when we say “Abba, Father” without naming the Son and the same Holy Spirit, as Gothescalcus said above.

Augustine also cites the Apostle’s testimony:

> “We receive the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’”

Blessed Ambrose saw the same thing. For he says:

> “To pray to God is also a gift of spiritual grace, as it is written: ‘No one says, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit’” (1 Cor. 12:3).

From the Apostle’s testimony, Augustine and Ambrose therefore do not teach that, when we speak in prayer to one person of the Trinity, we must afterward say to the other persons, “And we give thanks to you,” or, “And we entreat you.”

Elsewhere the Apostle says:

> “You are the temple of the living God, as God says: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people’” (2 Cor. 6:16).

Having these promises, therefore, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, completing sanctification in the fear of Christ (2 Cor. 7:1).

He was not afraid of being ungrateful to the other persons—the Father and the Holy Spirit—because he taught us to complete sanctification solely in the fear of Christ.

Saint Augustine also says in his book *Against Jews, Pagans, and Heretics*:

> “What are you doing, holy Lot? You see angels—two, not one—and you say, ‘Lord.’ You address one with the word, you pray to one, and you are not afraid that you may appear to wrong the other? Far from it.”

There are also many testimonies to this effect in the Scriptures, both Old and New Testament.

As blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Trinity*:

> “Whenever ‘God alone’ is read in holy Scripture, it is not to be understood of any one person in the holy Trinity, but of the whole holy Trinity, which works equally whatever it judges should be done.

> “Thus, where the Psalms say, ‘He alone does great wonders’ (Ps. 76:13), and, ‘He alone made the great lights’ (Ps. 133:7), and, ‘You alone are God’ (Ps. 85:10), and, ‘No one is good except God alone’ (Luke 18:19), and, ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God’ (Deut. 6:4), this is not to be understood of the Father alone, as the adversaries wish, but of the whole holy Trinity, which is the one and only God.

> “Similarly, what the Apostle says is not to be understood of the Father alone: ‘Blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see’ (1 Tim. 6:15).

> “In these words neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit is named specifically. Rather, ‘blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords’ means the one and only blessed, powerful, invisible, true God: the Trinity itself, which is equally blessed, equally powerful—indeed almighty, even possessing one single power, because the whole holy Trinity has one power.

> “Nor, because the Son himself, speaking elsewhere in the voice of Wisdom—for he is the Wisdom of God—says, ‘I alone encompassed the circuit of heaven’ (Sir. 24:8), did he separate the Father from himself. How much less, then, is it necessary to understand as referring to the Father alone, apart from the Son and the Holy Spirit, the words, ‘He alone possesses immortality’ and ‘He dwells in inaccessible light’?

> “Nor is it to be understood of the Son alone, apart from the Father and the Holy Spirit, when it is said that Wisdom has trampled the necks of the proud and exalted by her own power.

> “Nor is it to be understood of the Holy Spirit alone, apart from the Father and the Son, when it is said, ‘The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,’ and, ‘He who contains all things has knowledge of the voice’ (Wis. 1:7).

> “The same must be understood of the saying, ‘As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes’ (John 5:21). The Father does not give life to some, and the Son to others or in a different manner; rather, the Son gives life to the same persons to whom the Father gives life.

> “Likewise, the Holy Spirit must not be separated from this giving of life, because the work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, just as their substance and essence are one.

> “The Father, therefore, is living life; the Son is life living from the living one; the Holy Spirit is life and the giver of life to the living. They are not three lives, but one life.

> “The Father is also power and wisdom; and the Son, whom the Apostle calls ‘the power of God and the wisdom of God’ (1 Cor. 1:24), is likewise power and wisdom. Yet they are not three powers or three wisdoms, but one power and one wisdom: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

> “These names are substantial, not relative, just as there is one substance, one omnipotence, and the other attributes that are said of the substance of the deity.

> “The Father is true light, the Son true light from light, and the Holy Spirit true light and true illumination. They are not three lights, but one light. Thus it is written: ‘In your light we shall see light’ (Ps. 38:10).

> “There is likewise one power and one wisdom, because in the simplicity of the divine nature to know is not something other than to be, to be is not something other than to be able, and to be able is not something other than to live. There the wisdom is the same as the essence, the life the same as the essence; all these things are one, and God is one.”

Again Saint Augustine says in his *Tractate on Psalm 85*:

> “God could give human beings no greater gift than to make his Word, through whom he created all things, their head, and to join them to him as members, so that he would be the Son of God and the son of man, one God with the Father and one human being with human beings.

> “Thus, when we speak to God in prayer, we do not thereby separate the Son; and when the Son prays as the body, he does not separate his head from himself. There is one Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who prays for us as our priest, prays in us as our head, and is prayed to by us as our God.”

And in his sermon *On the Unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit Against the Arians*, he says:

> “Since, through the Lord’s ministry, you have an abundant loaf of the Lord’s word, place upon the table of your heart also the bread of the Lord’s prayer, and recall that the Lord said in the Gospel: ‘Whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will ask the Father, and it will be given to you’ (Mark 11:24).
