> “How, then, in the prayer he himself demonstrated, as though he had forgotten what he had said and left himself out, does he command us to ask the Father alone, saying: ‘This is how you shall pray: Our Father who are in heaven’ (Matt. 6:9)? Where is what he said: ‘Ask the Father in my name, and I will ask the Father’ (John 16:27)? How did he omit his own name from the prayer he himself taught, although he had commanded that he himself be sought through that name?

> “But because he had also said, ‘Whoever sees me sees the Father’ (John 14:9), he wished this mystery to be fulfilled by believers in the Lord’s Prayer, so that through this prayer the Son would also be asked for in the Father.

> “And because in the Creed he is again named separately from the Father, when we say, ‘I believe in God the Father and in Jesus Christ his Son,’ he wished that, on account of the unity of the deity, he should be separated from the Father in the Creed in such a way that he would again be joined to him in the prayer. Thus both mysteries—the Creed and the prayer—would show the Trinity in unity and again display unity in the Trinity.

> “He did not, therefore, omit himself in the prayer, but joined himself in the unity of the Father.

> “Just as, when you offer to the Father, you associate the body of the Son in the offering, so also in the Lord’s Prayer, by a reciprocal application of the mystery, when you ask the Father, you invoke the name of the Son as well.

> “And so that you may understand still more clearly that he then commanded that he and the Father be prayed to together, examine carefully what follows. At the beginning of the prayer itself he commanded that only the Father be invoked, but lower down he says, ‘Let your kingdom come’ (Luke 11:2), although it is the coming not of the Father but of the Son that is awaited, as the confession of the Creed handed down by the apostles concerning the Son also maintains: ‘He sits at the right hand of the Father; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.’

> “You see, therefore, how through this prayer he joins himself and the Father in one substance and one deity. Behold that day of future judgment, whose coming is promised through the Son’s advent, awaited from the Father’s presence: let it now be an unmistakable testimony of unity, so that what is promised when the Son’s advent is mentioned may be shown to have been fulfilled through the Father’s presence.”

And somewhat earlier:

> “If, then, you call the Father greater and the Son lesser, you introduce rank, remove unity, and, when you offer in the offering, you cannot say, ‘I offer to you, God,’ but ‘I offer to you all, gods’—which is absurd and unheard-of.

> “Or, if you offer by turns and separately—once offering to the Father and once offering to the Son—when you offer to the Father, you leave out the Son; and when you offer to the Son, you exclude the Father from the offering of the one who offers.

> “If you offer to the Son without the Father, you will no longer be able to complete the sacramental mystery through the Lord’s Prayer, so as to say, for the fullness of the perfect burnt offering, the Lord’s Prayer: ‘Our Father who are in heaven,’ because you will neither pray to the Father to whom you do not offer nor offer to him.

> “If, again, you offer to the incorporeal Father and omit the Son, the mystery of the offered bread will not be able [to pass] into the sacraments of the body—[the supplied text breaks off here].
to pass over, nor could you commemorate the Lord’s Supper in the consecration of the whole burnt offering, because what the Son, bodily, assigned to his own body and commanded to pertain to the memory of his passion could not, if separated from the Son, be assigned to the incorporeal Father, who was removed from the passion. If, therefore, you offer to the Father and the Son, you offer to one in the unity of the Godhead. Then the sacraments of the Father will also receive the mystery of the body; then, too, the Lord’s Prayer is rightly said in the offering of the Son. But if the Father is separated from the Son by those offering the sacrament of the body, he cannot provide what he does not possess; and if the Son is divided from the Father in his offering, through the Lord’s Prayer he will incongruously receive the name “Father,” which is not in him. Let us therefore confess that the Father and the Son are one God and of one substance; let the Father’s fatherhood be joined to the Son’s divinity, and let the consecrated flesh of the Son be mingled with the Father’s ever-present divinity. Then let whoever can dissolve from the unity of the Godhead these mystical forms, so joined into one, do so—when, in the one sacrifice, the Father has received in himself the whole flesh of the Son, and the Son has assumed in himself the whole name of the Father. [Col. 0608C–D]

And again in the same place:

“One indeed bears the flesh, but the flesh is consecrated in the mystery of the undivided Godhead. Therefore the flesh passes over into the sacrament of the Father and the Son, and the consecration or communion of the body confers upon the Father the honor that it also grants to the Son. And just as it is offered to the Son, so it is offered to the Father; and for the one offering or communicating at the altar, in one and the same offering, what the Son grants, the Father also grants. For if you separate the Son from the Father, then you neither offer to nor communicate with the incorporeal Father, because every offering passes over into the sacrament of the body.

“For when it is said, ‘This is my body,’ if the incorporeal Father is separated from the Son, every offering is separated outside the sacraments of the Father. For how can you say, when you offer to the Father, ‘This is my body,’ if the incorporeal divinity of the Father has no fellowship in the body of the Son? But if the incorporeal divinity of the Father is mingled with the corporeal divinity of the Son, as the truth of the mystery requires, you testify that the Father and the Son are one God under an undivided divinity. For when you offer the offering, you do not say, ‘I offer to you all,’ but, ‘I offer to you’; and thus every offering is indeed offered to the Father and the Son, but is shown to have been offered to one God under the name of both.” [Col. 0609A]

And again in the same sermon:

“The Father is God, the Son is God, yet both together are one God, without the number of two gods. The patriarch David also confesses this, saying: ‘God, my God, look upon me’ (Psalm 21:2); he does not say, ‘Look upon me, you gods.’ Again he says: ‘God, my God, from the light I keep vigil toward you’ (Psalm 62:2); he does not say, ‘Toward you all I keep vigil from the light.’ This confession of David is also confirmed by the Lord’s reply, when he answered the one praying and said, ‘I am God, your God’ (Psalm 49:7), and did not say, ‘We are.’

“Again David says: ‘You alone are God, who do wonderful things’ (Psalm 85:10). Thus, by naming God and God, the prophet confesses the Father and the Son; and when he again says, ‘You alone are God,’ he embraces both in one divinity. Thus, as ‘God and God,’ without the number of two gods, both are now joined in unity. Therefore, just as David names both in his prayer but nevertheless prays to one, so you too, when you name the Father and the Son, confess one God and one Lord in both.” [Col. 0609B]

And again in the same sermon:

“You have read, therefore, of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit; yet in this Trinity of the Godhead you have nowhere read of two or three gods, but in many ways of one God. Believe and confess what you have read; do not seek out or employ what you have not read.” [Col. 0609C]

And again:

“God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre, when he was sitting before the door of his tent at midday. Looking up with his eyes, he saw, and behold, three men were standing above him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them, worshiped, and said: ‘Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant’ (Genesis 18:1). It is therefore said that God appeared to him; and, looking upon this one, he saw three men. When he had run to meet the three and worshiped the one God, he asked, saying, ‘Lord, if I have found favor in your sight.’ No one accused him of worshiping one God and one Lord in the three men, or of saying that in one God and one Lord he had seen three men.

“But whoever does not understand this mystery in this way does not have Abraham’s eyes. Let him therefore seek heavenly eye-salve and apply it to his eyes, so that, once the darkness of ignorance has been removed, he may recognize the mystery of the Trinity in the unity of the Godhead; and, in one God, like Abraham, may see three men without distinction of merits or any diminution of power. After he has run to meet the three, let him ask not three but one God and one Lord; and through the form of this division, once displayed, let him understand that the Trinity always belongs to one Godhead.” [Col. 0609D]

And again there:

“I adjure you by these very things which, compelled, I have shown you—by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God in the Trinity of the Godhead—that, just as, through the Gospel’s designated pattern, on one road with three equal stages of a thousand units each I showed you not three journeys but one journey, so you too, following this Gospel path, may understand not three gods but always one God in the Trinity of the Godhead. Thus, when you offer the offering in the mystery of the Trinity, you offer not to three gods but to one God; for wherever in the divine Scriptures you hear of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, yet nowhere of three gods, you always read of one God, and one God is always announced to you.

“Therefore always retain these signs that I have shown you, because you cannot offer to the Father without the Son, nor to the Son without the Father. For if you offer an offering [Col. 0610B] only to the incorporeal Father, you do not reduce the offering to the sacrament of the body; you cannot say, ‘On the day before he suffered he instituted the form of the sacrifice’; nor can you say, ‘This is my body,’ because the Father neither possessed a body nor suffered. Again, if you offer to the Son without the Father, you cannot say the Lord’s Prayer to complete the perfect whole burnt offering, because in the prayer of the Son separated from the Father you cannot invoke the name ‘Father.’

“See, therefore, how utterly unconquerable these truths are; abandon such a heretical error and follow catholic truth. Otherwise, let the one who shows you a path other than the one I have demonstrated tell you how you can speak, having omitted these solemn formulas, amid the mysteries. But if, in the brightness of the light I have indicated, the darkness of error has failed, let obstinacy fail as well, lest, while you are ashamed to be overcome in error, you lose the promise of eternal life that comes from Christ’s truth.

[Col. 0610C]

“If someone therefore tells you, ‘The Father is the greater God, the Son the lesser God, and the Holy Spirit the third God,’ and that in these three there is not one substance but that they exist separately as three gods, without the unity of the Godhead, answer them first with the argument that has been set forth for you: an offering cannot be made to the Trinity separated from itself, because the Father is neither corporeal nor has suffered, and cannot reduce the offering to the sacrament of his body; nor can he, who did not suffer, make that Lord’s Supper the witness of his passion; nor can he say in the consecration of the mystery, ‘Who instituted the form of the everlasting sacrifice.’

[Col. 0610D]

“For what the Father did not institute but the Son did—the Son who had a body, suffered, and instituted the form of the sacrifice—if it is said of the Father separated from the Son, is a lie, since they falsely make the Father say what the Father did not say. Whoever therefore wishes to offer to the Father separated from the Son should betake himself to the Synagogue and its temples, to calves and the sacrifices of rams, since he has abandoned the form of sacrifice left to us, and the Church founded by Christ and the apostles. For by separating the Father from the Son in the offering of sacrifices instituted by the Son, he does not unite them.

[Col. 0611A]

“But if he offers to the Father and the Son together, let him not separate the Father and the Son from the unity of the Godhead. If he speaks of two gods, although the explanation of the sacrifice already given ought to be sufficient to put him to shame, nevertheless remind him that the Apostle said, ‘one God’ (Galatians 3:30), and that the law given through Moses says, ‘The Lord your God is one God’ (Deuteronomy 6:4), while he, blaspheming, speaks of two or three gods without the unity of the Godhead.

“If he still divides the Trinity in such a way that he does not reunite the mystery of the Trinity into one, let him at least return to the meaning of the Creed, where it says: ‘I believe in God the Father almighty, and in Christ Jesus his Son, who was born of the Holy Spirit.’ [Col. 0611B] First you testify that Christ’s Father is God almighty; then you say that Christ was born of the Holy Spirit. If therefore you separate the Trinity, you make Christ the son of two fathers, so that he is said to have been born of the almighty Father and of the Holy Spirit. Unite the Holy Spirit with the Father, therefore, so that you may rightly confess Christ to be the Son of one Father; and when through this prayer of the Creed you have joined the Father and the Holy Spirit into one, do not all the more separate the Son as well—whom you make not the third but the middle in the Trinity—from the unity of the Godhead.”

And in the third book *On the Trinity*:

“Among those angels there were certainly the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and sometimes the Father, sometimes the Son, sometimes the Holy Spirit, and sometimes God without any distinction of person, was represented through them,” together with the other matters that he develops there.

And blessed Ambrose, in the hymns that the catholic Church frequently sings, speaking now to the Father, now to the Son, and now to the Holy Spirit, does not ascribe glory in the singular number to the individual person of the holy Trinity to whom he is speaking, and then address the other persons in the plural number, as Gottschalk blasphemously claims. Rather, whatever he says substantially about God—that is, about the holy Trinity—he expresses in the singular number, as follows: [Col. 0611C]

Having refreshed our limbs with sleep, we rise, spurning our bed;

we ask you, Father, to be present while we sing. And:

Radiance of the Father’s glory, bringing forth light from light,

Light of light and fountain of brightness, day illuminating day. And:

Now, Holy Spirit, one with the Father and the Son,

deign readily to enter us, poured into our hearts.

At the conclusion of these hymns he always ascribes one and equal glory to the Holy Trinity, saying:

Grant, most merciful Father, and only-begotten Son equal to the Father,

with the Spirit, the Paraclete, reigning through every age. Or:

To God the Father be glory, and to his only Son,

[Col. 0611D] with the Spirit, the Paraclete, now and forever. Or:

Praise, honor, power, glory to God the Father and the Son,

together with the Holy Spirit, throughout everlasting ages. Or:

Glory to you, Lord, who rose from the dead,

with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout everlasting ages. Or:

Let us beseech Christ and the Father, the Spirit of Christ and of the Father,

one Trinity, powerful in all things, cherish us who pray. And addressing the Holy Trinity together, he likewise asks in the singular, saying:

O blessed light of the Trinity, and primordial unity,

now the fiery sun withdraws; pour light into our hearts.

And Saint Augustine says in the first book *On the Trinity* (ch. 8):

“Finally, because of that very inseparability, at times either the Father alone or the Son alone is sufficiently named, who will fill us with joy by his countenance; nor is the Spirit of both, that is, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, thereby separated. This Spirit is properly called the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive. For this is our complete joy, beyond which there is none greater: namely, to enjoy God the Trinity, in whose image we were made. For this reason he sometimes speaks of the Holy Spirit as though he alone were sufficient for our blessedness; and he is sufficient because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Son. In the same way, the Father alone is sufficient because he cannot be separated from the Son and the Holy Spirit; and the Son is therefore sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit.”

And again (ch. 9):

“For the purpose of revealing the Trinity, certain things are said separately even when the individual persons are named; yet they are not understood as separated from the others, because of the unity of that same Trinity, and the one substance and deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

“Furthermore, in the celebration of the singular sacrifice, as blessed Augustine also recalls in his books, we are instructed to give thanks to the Lord our God. For, with his help, we are able to lift up our hearts amid the sacred mysteries, since we are admonished to do so by his command. Therefore, especially in the sacrifice of Christ’s body, we begin with thanksgiving, rendering due praises to God the Father, who in the fullness of time sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons, according to the preaching of blessed Peter, who says: ‘You were not redeemed from your futile manner of life inherited from your fathers with perishable things, silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Jesus Christ, as of a spotless and unblemished lamb’ (1 Pet. I, 18).

“Through him the angels also praise his majesty; and we, without mentioning the Holy Spirit by a distinct name, give him thanks and ask that, formed according to catholic and apostolic institution, our voices may be admitted together with the voices of the angels. Thus, confessing the thrice-holy hymn with our mouths, we offer it, proclaiming by faith and understanding of the mind that the life-giving Trinity is one in divinity, equal in glory, and coeternal in majesty. Formed according to catholic and apostolic institution, we praise it with one glory, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; heaven and earth are full of your glory.’

“And although throughout the entire Preface we address the Father, we nevertheless do not, following Goteschalcus, add or substitute ‘We give you thanks’ and ‘Heaven and earth are full of your glory’ with the plural ‘your,’ lest we be ungrateful to the Son and the Holy Spirit. For neither Abraham, when he rejoiced to see the Lord’s day—he saw it and was glad—and faithfully received three men in faith and deed through hospitable welcome, incurred offense; rather, he carried away the merit of great faith. When he saw three, he addressed one as though one and worshiped one.

“Such prayers and Prefaces, handed down and accepted, are known to be catholic, confirmed by the Apostolic See and by the universal Church. Thus it is also read that this was decreed in the African Council (ch. 70), where it was likewise established that no other prayers, Prefaces, commendations, or laying on of hands whatsoever should be used unless they had been approved in the council, and that nothing else contrary to the faith should be uttered; rather, whatever had been discussed with the more prudent should be said.”

From this, when Goteschalcus’s prayers are compared with catholic prayers, it is plainly evident how far they are from faith and charity.

“He also wrote, addressing God, and told him that God himself had commanded him not to pray for me; and that, because the Son had first entered into him, then the Father, and afterward the Holy Spirit, the Spirit, entering into him, had scorched his beard around his mouth. He also wrote that he was unwilling to accept clothing from the wardrobe of the brothers who shared communion with me unless he bought it at a price, though he had no money to pay; rather, he wished to go as Adam went before he sinned. But as soon as the cold began to constrain him, he took care to seek, along with clothing, a fur garment and a fire.”

He wrote many other ridiculous things, which we found among his supporters, to whom he deceitfully gave them for safekeeping. They seemed frivolous not only to us but also to his own accomplices; and therefore we have judged it superfluous to insert them here as the ravings of a madman and old wives’ tales. Nevertheless, I decided that one more of his nonsensical pieces should be included, so that through it, as through those set out above in full, others might become known.

Some years ago, he wrote to certain intimates of his that it had been revealed to him that I was to die immediately after three and a half years from the time of his revelation, like the Antichrist, usurping the power of authority; that he himself was to become bishop of Rheims; and that after seven years he was to be killed by poison, and thus be made equal to the glory of the martyrs. When he did not see the prophecy inspired by his spirit fulfilled, among other things he wrote the following to one of his youthful followers, of the sort he used to love:

## XIX

“But now it is time to abandon the absent brother, and what shall I say to him, who is wholly unaware of what I say until he sees my writings? Let prayers be poured out to God, who is always present everywhere and knows all things eternally as a free giver.

“Lord our God and master Jesus Christ, crucified for the elect alone, you see that, behold, your enemies have made a noise and those who hate you have lifted up their heads, because he did not die, as was thought, once the year had ended after three years and a half, as a thief and robber. Briefly, but bowing low, I beseech you: do quickly to this Lord our God, true and living, one and triune, whatever pleases you. I want nothing more, neither sooner nor otherwise: when you wish, let him be rightly torn away from here—sated with life, adulterous, blind, shameless, stubborn, obstinate, heretical, an enemy of truth, a friend of falsehood.”

**ΧΡ.** The same Goteschalcus, as we have often mentioned, is accustomed to say very frequently, when speaking of blessed Augustine, “Our Augustine.” But even here Augustine is not his, because Augustine did not teach people to pray for enemies in the manner in which Goteschalcus prays; Goteschalcus is not Augustine’s.

For blessed Augustine says in his sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*:

“If, then, we wish to imitate Christ, we must run along the very path on which Christ deigned to walk even while hanging on the cross. For he was fixed to the cross, and, running along the way of charity, he pleaded for his persecutors. Finally, he said: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke XXIII, 34). Let us therefore continually pray this for all our enemies, that God may grant them amendment of conduct and forgiveness of sins.

“This is what I, however insignificant and unworthy a sinner, also endeavored to do for him, even if he did not believe it, while there was time, confident in the divine promise: ‘Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you’ (John XVI, 23). For even if he does not give it to those for whom we ask, nevertheless, when we mercifully intervene for the errors of others, he will restore to us the reward of our kindness.

“As for what he wrote—that God had forbidden him to pray for me—he lies, as he usually does. He who commanded his disciples, saying, ‘Pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. V, 44), and who demonstrated by praying on the cross for those crucifying him what he had taught by word, could not be contradictory to himself.

“And holy Pope Celestine (after Epistle 8) says:

“‘Let us consider the mysteries of priestly supplications, which, handed down from the apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the whole world and in the entire catholic Church, so that the rule of prayer may establish the rule of belief. For when the prelates of the holy peoples, acting as ambassadors by a mandate entrusted to them, plead before the divine mercy on behalf of the human race, and, while the whole Church groans with them, they ask and pray that faith may be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters may be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, when the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews; that heretics may come to their senses through the perfection of the catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be granted to the fallen; and finally that, when catechumens have been brought to the sacraments of regeneration, the hall of heavenly mercy may be opened to them.

“‘That these things are not asked of the Lord perfunctorily or in vain is shown by the outcome of the matters themselves, since from every kind of error God deigns to draw many whom, rescued from the power of darkness, he transfers into the kingdom of the Son of his glory and makes vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. It is so clearly perceived that all this is the work of God that thanksgiving and confession of praise are always rendered to God, who accomplishes these things, for the illumination or correction of such persons.’”

And blessed Gregory demonstrates that “just as no wicked person should be despaired of while he is in this life, so no one should despair that he may be changed from his wickedness.”

Although in the Old Testament it is written, “You shall love your friend, and hate your enemy” (Matt. V, 43), which the New Testament changed in accordance with the course of the times when it said, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (ibid. V, 44), the Lord is nevertheless read to have said to the prophet Jeremiah, “Do not pray for this people” (Jer. VII, 16).

Yet, as blessed Ambrose says in his book *On Repentance against the Novatians* (book I, ch. 8):

“The same prophet prayed for that people and obtained forgiveness. Finally, moved by the prophetic intercession and the supplication of so great a seer, the Lord says to Jerusalem: ‘Lord almighty, God of Israel, the soul in anguish and the distressed spirit cries out to you; hear, Lord, and have mercy’ (Baruch III). And he commands that the garments of mourning be put off and the groans of repentance cast aside. For thus it is written at the end of the book: ‘Strip yourself, Jerusalem, of the robe of your mourning and affliction, and put on the beauty of the glory that has been given you by God forever’ (Baruch V).”

But this pseudomonk—or whoever else, in this or some other way, adulterates sincere faith—an open heretic whose prayers charity does not commend and the catholic faith does not receive, receives from the Apostle, together with his accomplices, the following response when he makes such requests: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your passions” (James IV, 3).

Anyone who presumes to do such things against the sacred canons, if he appears to hold an ecclesiastical rank, deserves to be deprived of it or separated from ecclesiastical communion. According to the rule of Saint Benedict, the wicked, harsh, proud, or disobedient person is to be restrained by blows or bodily correction—not only when he persists in his obstinacy, but even at the very beginning of his sin—and is to be separated by ecclesiastical discipline from the healthy members of Christ, lest one sheep languishing from an incurable disease contaminate the whole flock.

I collected and wrote all these things, after the book *On Predestination*, against Goteschalcus and his accomplices, who assert that just as God predestined some to life, so he predestined others to death. I gathered them from authoritative Scriptures and the sayings of catholic writers at the very beginning of his blasphemy concerning the triune deity. Through myself and my brothers, and also through frequent letters, I often admonished him to come to his senses and withdraw his mind and mouth from his blasphemies against God, but I accomplished nothing with him.

At last, when our brothers to whom I had entrusted concern for him informed me that he was approaching death, I sent him through those same brothers the following note:

“Thus believe concerning the predestination by God of the elect and the abandonment of the reprobate, and concerning the fact that God wills all human beings to be saved, although not all are saved; that salvation is the gift of the one who saves, while perdition is the merit of those who perish; and that God and our Lord Jesus Christ suffered for all, whose blood is the price of the whole world. Those are strangers to this redemption who, delighting in captivity, were unwilling to be redeemed, or who, after redemption, by sinning and persisting in sins with an impenitent heart, returned to the same slavery.

“And concerning grace and free will, believe as Saint Augustine teaches in his books, namely, *On Rebuke and Grace*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, *On the Gift, or Good, of Perseverance*, in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, in the book *Hypomnesticon*, and in the letter to Sixtus, presbyter of the Roman Church; and as Saint Prosper, from the books of blessed Augustine, wrote in response to the objections of the Gauls, the Vincentians, and the Genoese; and as the other catholic teachers say. For the Apostolic See, the holy catholic Church, and we ourselves believe and hold this.

“Concerning the deity of the holy and inseparable Trinity, which is the unity of the Trinity, believe and confess as the holy catholic and apostolic Church believes, confesses, and proclaims, saying:

“‘The catholic faith is this: that we venerate one God in a Trinity of persons and a Trinity of persons in the unity of deity, neither confusing the persons, as Sabellius did, so that there are not three, nor separating the substance, as Arius did, so that there is a plurality. For the person of the Father is one and not another; the person of the Son is another and not another; the person of the Holy Spirit is another and not another. But the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one; their glory is equal and their majesty coeternal.

“‘In this holy and inseparable Trinity there is nothing prior or subsequent, nothing greater or lesser; rather, all three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are coeternal and equal to one another. Thus, in every respect, as has already been said, both the Trinity of persons in the unity of deity and the unity of deity in the Trinity of persons are to be venerated.

“‘If you believe this in your heart, confess it with your mouth, and sign with your own hand before witnesses that you believe and confess it, and if you remain in this belief and confession, then, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, through the episcopal ministry by which you were condemned, you may be absolved and restored to participation in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and to communion with the catholic Church.’”

When he heard this, however, he was driven into a frenzy, detested what had been commanded him, and began to blaspheme still more.

After those brothers had departed from me, reflecting on his hardness and impenitent heart, I sent our brothers at the monastery of Hautvillers, where he was staying, the page that follows. If, with the Lord’s help, he should withdraw from his perverse understanding and wicked opinion, they were to deal with him as I had already instructed them in words. Otherwise, they were to know how they ought to act toward him according to the sacred rules.

“In this way, as time permitted me, I have told you under what condition, if Goteschalcus should come to his senses before his soul departs from his body, you should show him both spiritual and bodily humanity. But so that you may lack nothing in any form of grace, I send you ecclesiastical authority on this matter from the words of orthodox writers.

“Leo says concerning such a case that, if he sincerely grieves and recognizes, even at the last moment, how rightly episcopal authority was exercised against him, or if he condemns everything that he wrongly thought, either by living voice or by an appropriate sign, and asks by voice or suitable sign for reconciliation and communion in ecclesiastical unity and peace, reconciliation and communion must not be denied him, as Celestine, Leo, and the sacred canons decreed.

“If he dies in this confession and communion, provide him, as you do for the other brothers, with common burial, the office of burial, and prayer after death. For our Lord, the true and good Shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep and came to save human souls, not to destroy them, wishes us to be imitators of his compassion, so that he may restrain sinners with justice but not reject those who have converted in mercy.

“If, however, he persists in his obstinacy until death, we must hold concerning him what Saint Leo says about those deprived of communion and dying in that state (Epistle 95 to Rusticus of Narbonne):

“‘Their case must be reserved for God’s judgment, in whose hand it lay that the deaths of such persons should be postponed until the remedy of communion. But we, who did not communicate with them while they were alive, cannot communicate with them when they are dead.’

“And again (Epistle 59 to Theodore of Fréjus):

“‘If any of those for whom we supplicate the Lord, intercepted by some obstacle, should fall away from the gift of present indulgence and, before reaching the appointed remedies, should end this temporal life according to human condition, he cannot obtain, once stripped of the flesh, what he did not receive while remaining in the body. Nor is it necessary for us to examine the merits and deeds of those who died in this way, since our Lord God, whose judgments cannot be comprehended, has reserved to his justice what the priestly ministry could not accomplish.’”

And the holy apostle John says (1 John V, 16): “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.”

“Sin,” says Gregory (*Moral Expositions*, book VI, ch. 28), “is unto death because the forgiveness of a sin that is not corrected in this life is sought in vain after death.”

A sin is said to extend unto hell when it is not amended through correction and repentance before the end of the present life. The memory of such people—those who persevere in sin until death—may not be commemorated at all amid the sacred mysteries of the altar, in which prayers are offered for those who preceded us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace, resting in Christ.

According to the catholic teachers, those who sleep in the sleep of peace are those who have not been separated from the unity and fellowship of Christ and the Church by heresies, schisms, or mortal crimes; and if they were ever involved in such things, they were healed through repentance and, through the prayer of the Church—to which it was said in Peter, “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19)—were reconciled and joined to the mystery of redemption. They died in peace, through the mercy of him who does not wish the sinner’s death, but rather that he should turn and live.

For the souls of the faithful dead are not separated from the Church, which now reigns with Christ over the living and the dead. For this reason, as the Apostle says, Christ died “so that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead” (Rom. XIV, 9).

Hence elsewhere he says (1 Thess. V, 9):

“For God has not appointed us for wrath, but for the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him.”

Those resting in Christ are the people of whom the Apostle says, “and the dead who are in Christ will rise first” (1 Thess. IV, 13), and of whom it is likewise written: “Blessed is the one who has a share in the resurrection; the second death will not harm him” (Rev. XX, 6).

Hence Judas the high priest, as we read in the Book of Maccabees (2 Macc. XII, 45), sent offerings to Jerusalem for those who had received the sleep of death in piety.

If, as I have said, he dies while persisting in his obstinacy, then, as we have learned from the authority of blessed Gregory and the sacred canons, he must not be carried to burial with psalms and hymns or buried in the common burial place of the brothers. Nevertheless, as I told you, the human kindness of private burial must not be denied him.

When his end was already approaching, the brothers who were present urged him to withdraw from his wicked understanding and perverse opinion and to receive holy communion. He replied that he could not withdraw from his understanding and opinion or receive communion by authority. Thus he ended an unworthy life by a deserved death and departed to his own place.

## EXCERPT

From a letter of Goteschalcus, which he wrote from Germany to Ratramnus, monk of Corbie.

[Col. 0618C]

At last there are many teachers, by the Lord’s gift,  
settled in this region, learned and rich in talent,  

and many of them remain in the royal palace.  
To these, and to others stationed throughout barbarian realms,  

I eagerly sent writings, bowing low, in recent days,  
earnestly asking that they deign to answer me  

as quickly as possible, for you know that I am greatly in need.  
The opinion of blessed Augustine was sent to them,  

and I asked that they explain it clearly, fitting it to its author.  
Indeed, I took care to impart its proper meaning to three of them,  

to Matcaudus, Jonah, and Lupus, radiant in speech,  
earnestly requesting that they strive to report the truth.  

A question alone was proposed to all the others.  
I certainly set forth the objection that is raised from both sides.  

But no one except one man has yet given me an answer.  
He is both cautious and shrewd, and therefore restrained.  

Thus, weighing the three answers of his little book,  
so that, once the full danger had been removed, it might agree  

with neither side completely, I have decided that both  
should be read aloud to you, while others hasten to answer  

with discerning mind. Thus, dearest, you may judge me  
more favorably than anything else, if you see something here  

that agrees with you but is not satisfactory to you.  
Yet I continually ask this of you with a twofold prayer:  

remember to pray with your whole heart and as a suppliant  
that speech may be made effective for them,  

and, together with the vigor of salt, may bring us  
the sacred pledges of peace.

[Col. 0619]

# HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, ON THE DIVORCE OF KING LOTHAIR AND QUEEN TETBERGA

## 557 INDEX OF CHAPTERS

[Col. 0619A]

**QUESTION I.** Concerning Lothair’s wife’s hidden crime and the booklet of the eight chapters of the Council of Aachen, in which she was said to have requested, through secret confession, that she be removed from the marriage.

**ANSWER.** That we cannot judge what is hidden from us, and that what is known through secret confession must be healed through secret counsel. Concerning the other booklet of seven chapters and the volume of the Council of Aachen. Having confessed to the king, she ought, according to the laws, to have been judged by laymen. Concerning the king’s alleged pain and sadness, and concerning Tetberga’s decree of repudiation and public penance.

**QUESTION II.** Whether she should be judged in the manner of Ebo’s secret confession concerning this woman.

**ANSWER.** Just as the orders are different, so the cause and law of a husband and wife are different; and they differ not only from those of a bishop but also from those of a priest and deacon. For a wife cannot be separated from her husband, whereas a bishop can lose his rank.

**QUESTION III.** Concerning the claim that Hincmar had consented to such an act through the bishops Wenilo, Hildegarius, and Adventius.

**ANSWER.** That through the aforesaid bishops he offered neither consent nor dissent, but testified in two letters to Adventius that the matter seemed rather to require discussion in a general synod.

**QUESTION IV.** How a marriage ought to be contracted.

**ANSWER.** Both the Old and the New Law teach how a marriage ought to be contracted, the Lord commanding it through Moses and confirming it in the Gospel.

**QUESTION V.** For what reasons contracted marriages may be separated, and whether after separation a man or woman ought to seek another union.

**ANSWER.** Not for every cause, but according to evangelical truth, for fornication alone, and not without the knowledge and authority of the bishop. Those who are separated cannot enter into other marriages. The judgment concerning the married couple Northildis and Agembert at Attigny.

**QUESTION VI.** What should be thought of the judgment by hot water that was carried out in Tetberga’s case, and of the cleansing by oath: whether a case cleansed in this way ought to be brought back into legal judgment.

**ANSWER.** Concerning the cleansing of judgment and oath, in accordance with the divine writings and the authorities of the canons and holy Fathers. Since this woman was cleansed, reconciled, and restored by such a judgment, the case does not seem to be capable of being reopened, especially since, if her representative had succumbed, her accuser would not have wished her to be admitted again to the hearing.

**QUESTION VII.** Whether it can be true, as some say, that, because of the secret confession which this woman herself made, as the witness who received it also testifies, her representative, when he went forth to the judgment, escaped unboiled.

**ANSWER.** While they proclaim truth through impious falsehood, they malign the fiction that supposedly wished to free this woman in such a way that it deceived those who believed in its judgment, although it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from deceit” (Wis. I), and simple truth does nothing through duplicity.

**QUESTION VIII.** Whether it can be done, as some say, that this woman’s intention concerned another brother of hers bearing the same name when she sent her representative to the judgment, and that for this reason she herself was not boiled in that same judgment.

**ANSWER.** In the Book of Kings it is written that a lying spirit said: “I will deceive Ahab,” and so forth, up to the words: “You will deceive him and prevail” (3 Kings XXII; 2 Chronicles XVIII). And Paul speaks of certain people who did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge; therefore God handed them over to a reprobate mind (Rom. I). Again, because they did not accept the love of truth so that they might be saved, for this reason God will send them a spirit of error, [Col. 0620A] so that they may believe a lie, in order that all who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity may be judged.

**QUESTION IX.** If any fraud is discovered in a judgment or oath after cleansing has been given, whether a case cleansed by judgment or oath ought to be brought back into legal judgment.

**ANSWER.** It should not seem surprising if fraud has occurred in a judgment through the operation of the devil, who, although he lost the glory of an angelic spirit, did not lose the subtlety of his nature. This happens with the Lord’s permission, either because of the unbelief of those who do not believe rightly or for the purification of the faithful. If deceit is found in a judgment or in the oath of cleansing through any device, the case should, with a doubled punishment of judgment, be brought back into question, whether on account of the admission of sin or of unbelieving deception.

**QUESTION X.** If this case, concerning which we have heard that judgment was carried out—and some of us also saw it—should be reopened, how ought the same judgment to be canonically arranged?

**ANSWER.** In every judgment four persons must always be present: namely, chosen judges, accusers and defenders, and witnesses, so that the person brought before them may, once refuted or certainly confessed, be subjected to a just sentence. But an extracted confession or compelled signature must possess no force.

[Col. 0620B]

**QUESTION XI.** Whether this woman should be judged on the basis of the secret confession, as it is called, entrusted to bishops, or on the basis of a written accusation presented in court.

**ANSWER.** Neither a husband from his wife nor a wife from her husband can be separated by secret confession, as we have stated, except for the love of a more continent life. Nor should anyone be subjected to public penance by a written accusation of secret confession. Nor can anyone be condemned through a written document sent directly or presented by another in his place. Rather, wherever someone is to be judged publicly, he must be publicly and while present either convicted or confess.

**QUESTION XII.** Whether, concerning such a sexual violation as this woman is believed to have suffered—namely, whether her brother could have conceived with her between her thighs, as males customarily commit shameful acts with males, and whether she could have remained a virgin after a miscarriage—if she is found to have committed these crimes before the marriage, she ought or may remain in the marriage.

**ANSWER.** It has never been heard from the beginning of the world, nor read in the Scripture of truth beneath this heaven, that a woman’s womb received and conceived seed without intercourse, and, with the womb closed and the vulva unopened, or with the flesh intact, gave birth to a living child or a miscarriage—except for the one singularly blessed and favored virgin Mary. Her conception was not of nature but of grace, as the archangel said to her, “Hail, full of grace” (Luke I). The Holy Spirit came upon her and, from virginal seed and virginal blood, without the will of the flesh and without the will of a man, granted her the fruitfulness of offspring without taking away her virginity. Just as she conceived with her flesh intact and her vulva unopened—that is, with her womb closed—so she gave birth without her vulva opening, with her womb closed; and she became a mother while remaining forever and always a virgin.

“Whether, however, any woman or virgin can conceive in such a manner as is alleged concerning this woman, the judges of the world, by the license of marital experience, may learn from their wives, lest they interpret the matter in court. We, who are inexperienced in this affair, say what we have read; we neither know nor wish to investigate anything more about it.

“Yet we are astonished: if our lord found the aforesaid woman to be a virgin, why did he permit her to be branded as though violated? But if he did not find her a virgin, why did he retain her for so long, or why did he accept a judicial examination concerning her?

“Therefore, as Saint Gregory writes (book XII, Epistle 1), no one should be deprived on account of the wishes of certain people when his own fault or crime has not removed him from the office he holds or from his rank. And elsewhere (book VIII, indiction 3, Epistle 30):

“‘It is very serious and improper that, in a doubtful matter, a certain sentence should be pronounced from which either manifest conviction or confession of the accused follows, when the subtlety of examination draws it out from hidden things and not severe affliction extorts it—for such affliction frequently causes even the innocent to be forced to confess themselves guilty.’

“It seems fair and reasonable, therefore, that the person who was in charge of and had power over the man who inflicted violence upon this woman or enticed her into the crime should be summoned; that the case should be investigated chiefly through him; that he himself should be prosecuted and examined according to law; and that he should either be acquitted by legal judgment or punished with his accomplice. Thus those who wish to judge justly will not be troubled by any suspicion, nor will detractors say that the woman, terrified by fear and afflictions, told a lie about herself—a lie which, once he had obtained his freedom, the alleged author of the crime could have removed from himself and from her, if law and justice had been observed for her.

“Let impartial judges read the sixth chapter of the first book of Roman law concerning violators, and the seventh concerning incestuous and shameful marriages, as well as the other matters that Christian laws set forth. Whenever a woman who has been discovered in such circumstances comes to us, we shall take care to exercise canonical judgment upon her according to those laws.”

**QUESTION XIII.** If, after hearing such things about his aforesaid wife and abstaining from marital relations with her, the same king perhaps committed adultery by using a concubine, and if this became known to many, by what medicinal judgment it ought to be healed.

**ANSWER.** If, as is reported, the king in question, after entering into a lawful marriage, engaged in intercourse with another woman, it cannot be denied that he committed adultery—even if the woman whom he took as his wife were perhaps found guilty of such things, as she is believed to have been—because, after entering a lawful marriage and before a legal decision, he presumed to do what was unlawful. As to how this ought to have been healed by medicinal judgment, the sacred canons determine: namely, by penance, and, according to the established laws and without regard to personal status, by the bishop’s discretion, the periods of penance should be determined.

**QUESTION XIV.** If it should happen that someone binds himself by an oath to do something criminal, whether, to avoid perjury, he ought to fulfill what he swore, or whether, so as not to commit the crime, he ought to annul the evil oath.

**ANSWER.** If it should happen that we have sworn something incautiously, and keeping it would lead to a worse outcome, let us know that we must freely change it according to sounder counsel. We should rather perjure ourselves when necessity requires it than, in order to avoid perjury, turn aside into another and more serious crime.

## QUESTION XV

If it can be true—as many people say—that there are women who, by their sorcery, can instill irreconcilable hatred between husband and wife, and can again sow indescribable love between a man and a woman; and that a man cannot approach the wife whom he has lawfully taken in marital intercourse, while he is able to have intercourse with other women; and that, by the same sorcery, his power of intercourse and the affection once felt can be restored through the art of sorceresses.

**ANSWER.** It can happen—often secretly, but never and nowhere unjustly—by divine judgment, as we shall demonstrate from the authority of Scripture and the teaching of our predecessors in the body of this little work.

## QUESTION XVI

What is the reason why God, as is said, often permits such things to occur within a lawful marriage?

**ANSWER.** By God’s hidden justice, permission is given to evil spirits, so that those whom they strangle in the snare of sin while willing, they may also, as punishment for sin and by the recompense of justice, drag into it against their will.

## QUESTION XVII

And if such men skilled in sorcery, or women who practice incantations, are found, what should be done concerning them?

**ANSWER.** Pastoral vigilance must watch over such people with the greatest intensity, and a public sermon must be preached before the people against men who engage in this kind of activity. They should be recalled from so great a stain of sacrilege, from the prospect of divine judgment, and from the danger of the present life by persuasive exhortation. If, however, the pastor finds that they are unwilling to reform and correct themselves from such practices, he must seize them with fervent zeal. If they are slaves, he must chastise them with blows and torments so that they may attain reformation; but if they are free, he must restrain them by worthy confinement and rigorous penance. If such people cannot be healed by ecclesiastical medicine, the king ought, by a judgment of equity, to destroy them from the land as impious persons.

## QUESTION XVIII

If the woman mentioned above should again come to judgment and be found innocent, ought her husband to return to her, or may he be joined to another woman?

**ANSWER.** It is superfluous to repeat this, because we have shown above that, if she is found to have been innocent before the lawful commencement of the marriage and to have kept faith with her husband after being lawfully married, then, according to evangelical and apostolic truth, the ecclesiastical laws, and the teaching of Catholics, a lawful marriage cannot be dissolved. If husband and wife have been separated, they must either remain unmarried or be reconciled to one another.

## QUESTION XIX

If the woman herself is found liable to the crimes of which she is accused, may the same king be joined to another woman?

**ANSWER.** If, according to the Christian laws—that is, the secular and ecclesiastical laws—it is found that that union was not lawful but rather incestuous, and is not to be counted by any designation as a marriage, then he may.

## QUESTION XX

If such causes are also attributed to the king himself, so that he ought to perform public penance, after she has been found guilty, may the king, after public penance, take a lawful wife?

**ANSWER.** If, after he has performed penance, fearing a fall into youthful incontinence, he chooses marital intercourse so as not to incur the crime of fornication, he will appear to be doing something venial, provided that he has intercourse with no woman at all apart from his wife. In this, however, we are not establishing a rule; we are judging what is more tolerable.

## QUESTION XXI

If the woman who has been accused is lawfully rejected, may the king himself, after performing penance, if he wishes, take as his wife the concubine whom he had and with whom he is said to have committed adultery after entering into marriage?

**ANSWER.** Since the law for man and woman is one, if he has been released from the law concerning his wife, then, as Paul says concerning a wife, “Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord”—that is, as Ambrose says, he should marry without suspicion of disgrace and marry a woman of his own religion; this is what it means to marry “in the Lord.” This release and lawful union are understood in the case of two people and occur in two ways: namely, among those who have either never entered into a lawful marriage or have been released from the law of marriage by the intervention of death.

Accordingly, when the man or woman with whom there had been a true marriage has died, a true marriage may, after penance, be contracted with the person with whom there had previously been adultery. Nevertheless, the utmost care must be taken that the king about whom the questioners wished to consult does not in any way seek marital intercourse with a concubine or with any other woman before the wife whom he lawfully took has been judged unworthy even of the name of wife by the lawful judgment of illustrious men and by priestly decree, or before she has departed from the body by divine judgment. Nor, before legitimate penance, may a man caught in adultery, according to the laws of the Church, join himself to his lawful wife—and still less to the same concubine in question.

## QUESTION XXII

Should one follow what certain people say—that some bishops teach that they ought to offer the protection of their defense to men or women who have confessed to them, so that no one may dare to summon such persons before the judgment of the state on account of crimes concerning which they have confessed to the bishops, even if the crimes are known to many?

**ANSWER.** How absurd this is, every sensible person recognizes, even if he is ignorant of the laws of the Church, as we shall sufficiently demonstrate from the authority of our predecessors in the work that follows.

## QUESTION XXIII

If, as some people say, a man and a woman wish to separate, not by mutual agreement for the sake of continence but because of some disagreement; or if, once separated, they are unable to remain continent; or if they do not wish to be reconciled, may bishops, on their own authority, provide for their weakness by saying that they had taken refuge in ecclesiastical mercy through secret confession, as in the case of the woman of Boso, concerning whom we were informed by an appeal made at the synod held in the city of the Leuci; and therefore should such persons be judged by no one other than the bishops to whom they had confessed?

**ANSWER.** Let all who say these things know that, in a certain sense, this was the fourth chapter of their error. For those who presumed to disparage and oppose the holy Council of Chalcedon erred in four chapters and were condemned as erroneous by the Apostolic See and by the unanimity of all the bishops of the world. Finally, we shall explain in the course of this work the seven questions, besides these, which we have received to resolve.

# PREFACE

[Column 623]

## Why he writes generally to everyone, and concerning the questions sent to him that provided the occasion for writing

To the glorious lords the kings, to our venerable fellow priests, and to all placed within the bosom of the Catholic Church: Hincmar, in name but not in merit bishop of Reims and servant of the people of God, together with my fellow bishops, the venerable lords and brothers of the diocese of Reims.

Concerning all doubtful or obscure matters that pertain to the rule of right faith or to the doctrines of piety, the holy Roman Church, as the mother, teacher, nurse, and instructress of all the Churches, must be consulted, and her salutary counsels must be followed—especially by those who live in the regions where, through her preaching, divine grace has brought into the faith and nourished with Catholic milk all whom it has predestined to eternal life.

Therefore, as blessed Innocent writes to Decentius, bishop of Eugubium (Letter 29, at the beginning):

> “It is manifest that throughout Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, and Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one established Churches except those whom the venerable Peter or his successors appointed as priests. They must follow what the Roman Church observes, since there is no doubt that they received the beginning of their institution from her, lest, while they devote themselves to foreign assertions, they appear to lose the head of their institutions.”

And because, as blessed Celestine, bishop of that same first see, says to Venerius and the other Gallic bishops (Letter 8):

> “It is not the concern of a few when the universal Church is assailed by any novelty.”

Writing to Nestorius of Constantinople (Letter 5, at the end), he likewise decrees:

> “Everyone ought to know what is being done whenever the concern of all is being treated; our humble voice is sent to all.”

For although the matter concerns a king and queen—that is, husband and wife, who according to sacred authority are no longer two but one flesh—the case concerns everyone generally, and is called by the divine Apostle “a great sacrament” in Christ and in the Church (Ephesians 5:32), in whom the salvation of all is believed to consist.

For concerning Christ the apostle Peter testifies: “There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). And just as in the Flood all perished whom the ark did not contain, so no one can be saved who does not persevere in right faith and good works within the unity of the holy Church.

But beyond this spiritual consideration, a matter of no small importance concerning the dignity of so exalted a name and such persons is being debated, so that the kings of the earth, all rulers of peoples, all judges of the earth, young men and virgins, the old together with the young, ought to attend to it: to the truth of judgment, priestly agreement, and the royal cultivation of gentleness, patience, and love toward their own honor. Hence it is written: “The honor of the king loves judgment” (Psalm 98:4); and: “His throne is strengthened by justice” (Proverbs 25:5); and again: “Justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne” (Psalm 88:13).

Although there are other virtues without which one does not attain the eternal kingdom, nevertheless, without these three that we have mentioned, one can become a tyrant, but no one can safely possess an earthly kingdom: without gentleness, because “the meek shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:4); without patience, because “the patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities” (Proverbs 16:32), and “in your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19); and without true love, concerning which it is said: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Psalm 96:10), because “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6).

Again, it is written in the psalm: “Give heed, prosper, proceed, and reign, because of truth, gentleness, and justice” (Psalm 64:5). For by pursuing truth he will preserve gentleness together with justice, so that he neither abandons zeal for uprightness under the weight of gentleness nor, conversely, disturbs the weight of gentleness by zeal for uprightness. For, as Wisdom says: “The king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters all evil with his gaze” (Proverbs 20:8); and again: “The king who judges the poor in truth—his throne shall be established forever” (Proverbs 29:14).

From the standpoint of priestly agreement and discernment, the Lord says:

> “Your mercy is before my eyes; I have pleased you in your truth. I have not sat with the council of vanity, and with those who do evil I shall not enter. I have hated the assembly of the wicked, and with the impious I shall not sit. I shall wash my hands among the innocent and surround your altar, Lord, so that I may hear the voice of your praise and recount all your wonders” (Psalm 25:3).

But, as Saint Gregory says (Moralia 29.6):

> “I see others to whom, because of the position of teaching, the duties of exhorting and reproving have been entrusted. They see something unlawful being committed, yet, while they fear offending the favor of certain powerful people, they do not dare to reprove it. Whoever this person is, what else does he do but see the wolf coming and flee? He flees because he remained silent; he remained silent because, having despised eternal grace, he loved temporal glory more. Behold, before the face of the powerful man he hides himself within the hiding places of his silence, and, just as he openly gave place to persecution, so secretly he gave place to fear. Of such people it is rightly said: ‘They loved the glory of men more than the glory of God’ (John 12:43). Therefore, whoever is such a person, if these things are strictly judged, even though public persecution was absent, nevertheless by remaining silent he denied Christ.”

Judges, however, are commanded: “If indeed you speak justice, judge rightly, sons of men” (Psalm 57:1). Thus, whenever any mortal gives a public judgment, if he speaks what is true, he must also judge truly; he must not set a snare of deception in flattering words by which he secretly destroys the innocent. He must bear in mind that a human being sees the face, but God sees the heart. If the eye—that is, the intention of the heart—is simple, the whole body—that is, every action—will be luminous. But if that intention is dark, then the darkness present in the action exceeds almost both the measure and the name of darkness.

Saint Gregory also says (Moralia 29.6):

> “For I see that some accept the person of the powerful in such a way that, when questioned by him, they do not hesitate, for his favor, to deny the truth in the case of their neighbor. And who is the truth except the one who said: ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life’ (John 14:6)? John the Baptist did not fall because of a confession of Christ, but because he was questioned about the truth of justice. Since Christ is the truth, he therefore went even to death for Christ, that is, for the truth.”

And blessed Bede says (On Luke, chapter 22):

> “Many today shudder at Judas’s crime—his having sold his Lord, teacher, and God for money—as monstrous and wicked, yet they do not avoid it. For when they give false testimony against anyone in exchange for gifts, plainly, because they deny the truth for money, they sell the Lord for money. He himself said: ‘I am the truth.’ When they defile the fellowship of brotherhood with some plague of discord, they betray the Lord, because ‘God is love’ (1 John 4:8). Even if no one gives them money, they sell the Lord for silver, because, neglecting the image of the Creator in whose image they were created, they take on the image of the prince of this world—that is, the examples of the ancient enemy.”

That person also sells the Lord who, neglecting love and fear of him, is shown to love and care more for earthly and transient things, indeed even for criminal things.

Since these matters stand thus, it is necessary that both ecclesiastical judges and judges of the public realm make their decisions in every case and concerning every person under the eyes of the heavenly Judge in such a way that their judgment contain no leaven of malice, deceit, complacency, pretense, or desire, nor hope of acquiring anything whatsoever. Instead, everything must be the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth: a judgment of justice, the equity of truth, and the purity of truth.

Otherwise, God forbid, we may incur the curse which the prophet pronounces generally upon us ourselves and upon the whole Church: “Let deceitful lips become mute” (Psalm 30:19); and: “They have spoken with a deceitful heart; may the Lord destroy all deceitful lips” (Psalm 11:3–4)—those who say one thing and conceal another in their hearts. Sometimes, it is true, they establish what is said, but they interpret what they say with a meaning different from what, as their conscience testifies, they understand.

Saint Jerome also says in his Commentary on Matthew (chapter 26): “A false witness is one who does not understand what is said in the same sense in which it is said.” Concerning such people it is again written: “The labor of their lips shall cover them” (Psalm 139:10), when they shall be covered “as with a double cloak of shame” (Psalm 118:29), that is, they shall be placed “like a furnace of fire in the time of the presence of God” (Psalm 20:10), so that they may burn within and without in the age that is to come.

We cannot be free judges before the sight of him to whom human thought confesses unless we speak the truth from heart and mouth. Then indeed we shall judge justly—and this also with fear and trembling, lest we fall into wrongdoing through ignorance. For it is said: “With what judgment you judge, you shall be judged” (Matthew 7:2); and: “If our heart does not condemn us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Therefore, even in matters that are certain among human beings, we cannot be secure, knowing, as Paul says, that “it is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:4), although we are often justified by human judgment.

For this reason we write to kings, whom God has placed in so exalted a position so that they may be seen by all their subjects and be regarded as a mirror, serving as either terror or love to the wicked and the upright. They should strive to do those things for which none of their subjects could justly reproach them, and diligently avoid those things that, in their subjects, they must correct because of the ministry entrusted to them by God. Otherwise they may hear from the Apostle who reproves them: “Therefore, O man, you who judge those who do such things and do them yourself, do you suppose that you will escape the judgment of God?” (Romans 2:3). And again it is written: “The severest judgment will be upon those who rule” (Wisdom 6:6).

The Holy Spirit also confirms through the blessed men Benedict and Cyprian that every king will render an account to God, the most just Judge, for all his judgments on the day of judgment; and he will unquestionably render an account for as many people as he has had under his care, with his own soul added to the reckoning. Just as he was placed first upon the throne of men, so, unless he has governed himself and those entrusted to him well, insofar as he was able with God’s help, he will have above him, in that future punishment, all the sinners whom he had beneath him in the present age, in the manner of a scourge.

Our discourse is addressed to our fellow priests and therefore to ourselves, so that we may teach what the Lord taught and proclaim what we are bound to preserve from him. For just as it is written: “Ask the priests about my law” (Haggai 2:12), so likewise the Lord says: “You who hear shall announce to them from me” (Ezekiel 33:7). He is to hear either through heavenly inspiration or through divine reading, concerning which it is written: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me” (Psalm 84:9); and: “Search the Scriptures” (John 5:39); and: “The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones” (Psalm 1:8).

What follows—“You shall announce to them from me”—means, he says, “from me,” not “from yourself.” The preacher must present to his hearers sincerely and steadfastly, not flattering or changeably according to human will, what he has learned from God, whether from sacred Scripture or from the teaching of holy masters.

And just as it is said to our hearers—may it not be to our condemnation—“Ask your fathers, and they shall tell you; your elders, and they shall explain it to you” (Deuteronomy 32:7), and through us they are exhorted: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 33:12), so elsewhere there is complaint against us: “The shepherds themselves have no understanding” (Isaiah 56:11), because “a good understanding belongs to all who do it”; and: “Those who held the law did not know me” (Jeremiah 2:8).

For those who do not proclaim to those entrusted to them, by faith and works, by life and conduct, by word and example, although they honor the Lord in name, do not truly know him, according to what is written: “He who is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14:38)—that is, he shall be rejected.

Therefore we have no ground for confidence except in the mercy of God. From our hands the blood of as many people will be demanded on the day of the great judgment as perish in their iniquities without our warning, as the Lord says to each bishop:

> “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, and the wicked man does not turn from his evil way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3:18).

We must also fear that the examiner of consciences—and still more of works—may say to us: “You have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those who could enter you hindered by your conduct” (Luke 11:52).

We must know and continually recall with the greatest fear and trembling that, because the episcopal ministry is more spiritual and therefore greater, it is also more dangerous than the royal ministry. For on behalf of the kings themselves we shall render an account to the King of kings and Shepherd of shepherds on the day of the dreadful examination.

We have also decided to speak from here to all who are placed within the bosom of the Catholic Church, so that they too may beware of committing such things, and, insofar as it depends on them, may neither consent to those who commit them nor favor them through flattery.

Concerning such people the Apostle speaks wonderfully: “Those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5:21); and again: “Those who do such things deserve death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Romans 1:32).

We have omitted enumerating these matters in this brief document so that we may not appear to have done an injury to our other lords and fellow priests, who know them sufficiently and are wiser and more capable than we are in explaining them to their hearers. Especially since they are impressed upon all who visit the Churches by frequent apostolic reading.

Our preceding discourse is directed toward this end because recently certain people, some from the ecclesiastical order and others from the lay order, persons not unworthy because of their office, their religious merit, and the honor of their devotion and nobility, came to us with a certain little book, whose text we have appended here, together with the questions it posed.

They humbly petitioned us through our Lord Jesus Christ, who said: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones” (Matthew 18:10); “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6:30); “Do not turn away from him who wishes to borrow from you” (Matthew 5:42); and: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return, and tomorrow I will give you,’ when you can give immediately” (Proverbs 3:28).

Through blessed Peter he also commanded the leaders of his Church to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks them for an account (1 Peter 3:15). For he who hides grain—that is, the teachings of sacred speech—is cursed among the peoples, whereas the blessing of the Lord is upon the head of those who sell it (Proverbs 11:26). The person who teaches what he has learned from the Lord who taught him will himself deserve a greater grace of teaching from his hearers, receiving the reward of faith and confession.

Therefore we were in no way to neglect or evade their petitions, or postpone them under any excuse. Rather, concealing the names of those who had submitted these questions and to whom we were to send our replies, we should endeavor to answer each question briefly, just as they had posed it, according to the authority of Scripture and the teaching of the Catholic Fathers, insofar as the Lord had granted us the ability.

We would have preferred not to write about these matters, but either to hear the teaching of wise men or merely to state orally what we think. And if writing had been necessary, we might perhaps have woven the order of our discourse more suitably, had we wished or been able to neglect the adjuration of such and so great a number of people.

Therefore, readers, when we write replies to their proposals from the holy Scriptures and the traditions of the Fathers, do not be angry with us because the order of our answers is disordered. If their questions draw us into matters that perhaps do not belong to this subject, do not reject us as excessive, and let no one turn our sincere reply into an insult against himself.

We remember the Lord’s saying: “You shall not show partiality in judgment” (Deuteronomy 1:17). We also imitate, according to our limited ability, the holy apostles whose place we occupy, though unworthy, who said: “We cannot but speak of what we have heard and seen” (Acts 4:20).

Accordingly, in response to the matters about which we were questioned, we have taken care to answer without flattery—not with our own words, but with the words either of divine Scripture or of those through whom the Lord spoke and from whom we learned these things, insofar as the brevity of time and the availability of memory permitted. We have prefaced each solution with the questions of those who asked.

For this reason we have written generally to everyone, because we recognized that the matter concerned people of every order. Moreover, we were expressly forbidden under adjuration to expose those who had sent us the questions.

May the Lord place in our mouths a well-directed, well-sounding discourse, so that we may appropriately bring forth collected words concerning the matters about which we were questioned—words of those to whom the Lord says: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

May the grace also of our Lord Jesus Christ, who desires all people to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4) and desires no one to perish, cause the excerpts from the sayings of the saints, spoken through our humble service, to please those who hear them—those to whom God says generally: “He who is of God hears the words of God” (John 8:47). He also said to his disciples: “He who hears you hears me” (Luke 10:16).

May he remove from the inward hearing of the hearts of all who hear the hardness that refuses obedience—he who commanded that the stone be removed from Lazarus’s tomb (John 11). May he take away the dullness of disobedience—he who formerly promised through the Prophet:

> “I will take from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh; and I will place my Spirit in your midst, and I will make you walk in my commandments, keep my judgments, and perform them” (Ezekiel 36:26–27).

Otherwise, God forbid, because they despise the counsels of his saints, concerning whom he said, “He who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16), he may say to them the very terrifying words: “Therefore you do not hear—that is, you do not obey—because you are not of God” (John 8:47).

No one should reproach us for speaking about the indecencies of such indecencies as modest ears shrink from hearing. For Paul, through the fear of Christ, whom he truly said was speaking in him, discussed such matters among others; and we shall in no way dare to remain silent about what we are able to understand from the questions put to us. He terrifies us by saying:

> “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty and that of his Father and of the holy angels” (Luke 9:26).

Nor should anyone be offended on hearing about the shameful aspects of infirmities that the poisonous cunning of diabolical malice inflicts upon human weakness. He should know that, according to the Apostle, he is surrounded by weakness (Hebrews 5:2), and should consider himself lest he too be tempted.

Nor should he fear, since blessed Gregory says in the Pastoral Rule (Part 2, chapter 5):

> “While he learns to recognize the temptations of others by showing compassion, he himself is also struck by the temptations he hears about. For the same water by which the multitude of the people is cleansed in the tub made at the Lord’s command through Moses is undoubtedly stained by the filth of the tub. While it receives the dirt of those whom it cleanses, it seems to lose the serenity of its own purity. But these things are by no means to be feared by the pastor, because, as God subtly weighs all things, he is delivered from his own temptation all the more easily the more mercifully he is wearied by the temptation of another.”
