The pastor must patiently hear the impurities of the infirmities of others and assist the infirm by every means with medicinal counsel, according to what he sees to be expedient for each person, all the more because he cannot fail to know that God, as he himself says through the Prophet (Jeremiah 6), bears the burden of our iniquities, sees our hidden adornments and even the impurities of our thoughts, and mercifully bears them while patiently waiting.

Hence Saint Augustine says in Book Four Against Julian:

> “Certainly, if we allow those over whom we have authority to commit crimes before our eyes, we shall be guilty together with them. Yet how innumerable are the things he permits to be done before his eyes—things that, if he had not wished them, he would in no way permit? And yet he is just and good, and by bearing patiently he gives opportunity for repentance, since he does not wish anyone to perish.”

Saint Gregory explains why this happens (Homily 13 on the Gospels), interpreting the testimony of Scripture: “The Most High is a patient giver of recompense” (Sirach 5):

> “For he both bears our evils patiently and repays them. Those whom he tolerates for a long time so that they may convert, if they do not convert he condemns more severely.”

# FIRST QUESTION

[Column 629]

They say in the first chapter:

The wife of Lord King Lothair was initially accused of fornication, as though her brother had committed a crime with her by male intercourse between the thighs, in the manner in which males ordinarily commit an indecency with males, and as though she had conceived from this. Therefore, in order to conceal the disgrace, she drank a potion and miscarried.

When she denied this, and the accuser and witnesses failed to provide proof, her representative underwent the ordeal of boiling water at the judgment of the lay nobles, with the advice of the bishops and the consent of the king himself. After he had been found unscalded, the same woman was restored by decree to the marital bed and royal marriage from which she had been suspended.

After some time, whether concerning the same matter or concerning an offense committed after the beginning of the marriage, a little book of this kind was written by certain bishops, as the one we are sending to you, and it is being circulated by the mouths of some people. It says that, through the secret confession designated by this little book, you other bishops, adopting a parable, ought to remove her completely from the marital union. If you demand anything further, she will be compelled to give you a written statement confirmed by her own hand, so that, just as Ebo, once bishop of Reims, was removed from his see and rank by a written statement of secret confession, so she too may be removed from marital society by a written statement of secret confession.

We have also been told concerning the venerable archbishop of Reims that he consents to such an action; that through the bishops—namely Wenilo, archbishop of Rouen, and Bishop Hildegarius—he fulfilled his role by word; that through Adventius, who had spoken with him at Reims concerning this matter, he sent letters expressing his consent to the king’s assembly and to the episcopal gathering; and that through the same Adventius he sent his letters concerning this matter to the Apostolic See.

Therefore we ask that you send us, in truth, what must be held concerning this matter according to the truth, which is God.

The text of the little book is recognized to consist of eight chapters of the following kind:

### CHAPTER I

> “We bishops, who were recently summoned and assembled at the palace of Aachen, are concerned to bring to the knowledge of our brothers and fellow bishops what we understood and what we discovered there, so that, lending the ear of their heart and body, they may discern and, by unanimous counsel, determine what outcome and what conclusion should be imposed upon a case of this kind.

### CHAPTER II

> “The glorious King Lothair, having a private and confidential conversation with us, humbly and with devout sincerity set forth his particular and personal needs, seeking counsel and a remedy. We, in turn, rejoicing in his good will, moved by his tears and sighs, and inclined toward compassion, gave counsel and applied medicinal treatment to him who was asking, seeking, and knocking, under the inspiration of the Lord.

### CHAPTER III

> “Then the same king, in a mournful voice—a matter that we indeed recount not without grief and sorrow—began to tell us concerning his wife, whom he had desired to have, that she herself repeatedly and continually begged to be released from the bonds of marriage, since, as she testified, she was unworthy of the marital bed, and that she might deserve to receive the sacred veil and serve Christ the Lord.

### CHAPTER IV

> “Meanwhile, the queen’s messenger summoned us, asking that we not delay in visiting her. When we approached her, she hastened to meet us and, almost falling at our feet, began to entreat us earnestly in these words:

> ‘For God’s sake, and because of your ministry, I beg you to give me true counsel.’

### CHAPTER V

> “We immediately replied to her:

> ‘May the Lord provide us with counsel that we may give you truthfully and beneficially. Only tell us, in the pure and truthful confession of your conscience, what is the reason for which you seek counsel with such emphatic appeals. For otherwise we cannot grant you what you request unless we learn the truth of the matter.

> ‘But this we warn you beforehand and carefully prohibit you, by the authority of God and of ourselves: do not, whether invited to other honors by anyone’s persuasion—or rather deception—or through fear of any punishment or death, falsely fabricate any crime for yourself and, God forbid, lead us into error. Instead, as we warned above, disclose the truth of the matter as it is, neither more nor less. With the Lord’s gift, we shall strive to provide you with counsel and assistance, so that you may in no respect be deprived of your justice.’

### CHAPTER VI

> “She said:

> ‘With God as witness, and my own conscience as witness, and also my confessor as witness, I shall say or confess nothing about myself, either to the right or to the left, other than as it truly is.

> ‘I acknowledge—and I know this about myself—that I am not worthy to remain in marital union. As a witness to this I present to you the bishop Guntharius, who heard my confession; for he knows that I am not worthy.’

> “Then, turning immediately to that bishop, she said in supplication:

> ‘I ask you, bishop, to make these fellow bishops of yours understand, as you know best, that it is so, just as I have testified concerning myself.’

> “The bishop mentioned replied:

> ‘It is good that you yourself disclose to these fellow bishops of mine what is still hidden, so that they may hear from your own mouth what they must judge.’

> “And she said:

> ‘Why is it necessary for me to speak otherwise than as you know? For God’s sake, make my need known to them, so that together with my lord you may grant me permission to do what I desire. For,’ she said, ‘I do not wish to lose my soul for the whole world. Therefore I beg you, for God’s sake and because of the ministry you have undertaken, not to deny me what I ask for the salvation of my soul.’”

## Chapter VII

[Col. 0632A]

“Then we bishops, testing her, asked whether she would thereafter raise any complaint about the matter, or devise any plots, if her request were granted. To this she replied in a clear voice: ‘By the faith which I profess,’ she said, ‘I promise you before God that henceforth I shall raise no complaint about it, either by myself or through my own contrivance.’”

## Chapter VIII

“What, finally, we learned from our aforesaid fellow-bishop, who was greatly saddened, distressed, and mourning over this matter, and who deeply repented that he had ever become privy to that woman’s confession, must be recounted aloud to the brothers and fellow bishops, in accordance with the terms of the permission granted, so that, when they have understood the evidence of the case hitherto concealed, they may all, with one and the same counsel and agreement, drive out the error and establish the truth, just as was stated at the beginning.”

## Response

[Col. 0632B]

We have judged it superfluous to discuss the contents of this petition point by point, as though responding to it, since it is itself sufficient to demonstrate what it contains and needs neither the assertion of our praise nor protection from blame. Nevertheless, in the fifth chapter we read the following concerning the woman in question:

“We forewarn you, and diligently prohibit you by the authority of God and of ourselves, that you should neither, enticed by anyone’s persuasion—or rather deception—into other honors, nor through fear of any punishment or death, falsely fabricate any crime against yourself and, God forbid, lead us into error.”

It is astonishing that, if it was not previously known what she was going to say, [Col. 0632C] such words were addressed to this woman before her confession; and if the matters she was to disclose had already been learned in advance, why they profess that what was said was received as though under a secret confession. Yet we think that this could have happened because, as we read in divinely inspired writings, the spirit of prophecy is not always present with the prophets. Thus Elisha said of the Shunammite woman to Gehazi, his servant:

“Leave her alone, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has concealed it from me and has not told me” (2 Kings 4:27).

And whenever he wills, that same spirit is again present with the prophets. Thus Ahijah, inspired by the divine Spirit, said to Jeroboam’s wife as soon as he heard the sound of her feet entering through the door:

“Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be someone else?” (1 Kings 14).

[Col. 0632D]

Therefore, if the Spirit of the Lord—since, as the Apostle testifies (Ephesians 4:11), the pastors of the Church are also prophets—revealed the ear of those addressing the woman, who perhaps had come to them deceitfully, it lies within the power of that Spirit, who breathes where he wills, to have suggested to them by hidden revelation that they should command this woman, by the authority of God and of themselves, not in any way to make a feigned disclosure to them.

We do not wish to dispute for long about uncertain matters, when we can produce certain testimony from the authority of Scripture. For concerning the exhortation to confession we read:

“Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in him” (Psalm 36:5).

Concerning the confession that follows, we likewise read:

“I said: I will declare my injustice to the Lord, [Col. 0633A] and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm 31:5).

For this confession remission, not punishment, was granted by the Lord. It was not extorted by fear, but brought forth through healing exhortation in the hope of pardon, as he likewise said:

“I will confess to him of my own will” (Psalm 27:7).

Nor was she invited to present honor, but to future blessedness, because it is written:

“It is vain for you to rise before daylight; rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Psalm 126:1–2).

The one who rises before daylight is he who, by neglecting God’s commandments, alienates himself from God’s keeping, and in this life, which resembles night, desires to be exalted and advance in honors before the day of the coming age. One must therefore first sit down through repentance, so that afterward one may rightly rise [Col. 0633B] through pardon; for whoever does not now humble himself voluntarily through repentance will certainly not be exalted by the glory that follows.

The Lord also shows in the Gospel of Luke what the penitent’s manner should be, saying:

“They would have repented long ago, sitting in ashes and sackcloth” (Luke 10:13);

and in the Psalm:

“I humbled my soul with fasting” (Psalm 34:13);

and:

“I clothed myself in sackcloth” (Psalm 29:8);

and:

“I became troubled” (Psalm 29:8);

and:

“I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101:10);

and:

“I kept vigil and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Psalm 5:8).

For this reason the sacred canons command that penitents, at the time when they seek penance, receive from the priest the imposition [Col. 0633C] of hands and sackcloth upon their heads, as has been established everywhere (Council of Agde, canon 15). And the African council says:

“Let the one whose crime has become public receive the imposition of hands before the apse; every public penitent ought to receive this from his own bishop, in whose diocese he is” (African Council, canon 10).

What generally injures the Church must be medicinally healed by a synod—that is, by an assembly of bishops. Yet, in a remarkable fashion, this petition describes an episcopal matter, which ought to be dealt with publicly, together with a secret confession, which requires a particular remedy.

Moreover, the seventh chapter, in which the already-mentioned woman is questioned by way of testing her, says:

“Whether she would thereafter remove any complaint about the matter, or devise any plots, if her request were granted.”

[Col. 0633D]

Since an oath is shown to have been elicited from this, the passage appears suspicious to our slow understanding. Therefore we have made no response to it, lest we seem to depart either from the legal path or from the path laid out by the chapter.

Concerning what is written in the eighth chapter of the aforesaid petition:

“What, finally, we learned from our aforesaid fellow-bishop, who was greatly saddened, distressed, and mourning over this matter, and who deeply repented that he had ever become privy to that woman’s confession, must be recounted aloud to the brothers and fellow bishops, in accordance with the terms of the permission granted, so that, when they have understood the evidence of the case hitherto concealed, they may all, with one and the same counsel and agreement, drive out the error and establish the truth”—

[Col. 0634A]

let all venerable bishops, glorious kings, and all who are placed in the bosom of Mother Church know that, for the reasons we shall explain, we prefer to remain ignorant rather than know this concealed matter under such a condition.

We have, namely, too much to do with our own sins: those confessed to us privately by the devotion of penitents, and those publicly and grievously committed by our subjects. Our eyes are wholly insufficient to weep for these. How much more, then, should we avoid seeking, out of curiosity—which Gregory calls a serious vice—to learn and hear about matters that are hidden and can be more suitably healed and washed away by others than by us?

Therefore, with this added burden, we mourn as that pious and holy man to whom the woman confessed: most sorrowful, distressed, and repentant [Col. 0634B] because he had become privy to her confession, as it is written there, he mourned. Yet we read that Samuel mourned for Saul because the Lord had rejected him, so that the Lord said to him:

“How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him?” (1 Samuel 16:7).

But we do not read that he disclosed to anyone for what sin he mourned for him, except to Saul himself, nor how much his tears on that account made known to the Lord’s ears.

Another reason is that, by the oracle of the Holy Spirit, it is recognized as having been established that those who sin should disclose the hidden causes of their sins to spiritual elders who know how to heal both their own wounds and those of others, not expose or publish them. Therefore it is written in the sacred canons of the African council:

“If a bishop says that someone confessed a crime to him alone, [Col. 0634C] and that person denies it, the bishop must not consider it an insult to himself that no one believes him alone; and if, because of a scruple of his own conscience, he says that he does not wish to communicate with the one who denies it, then, so long as his bishop does not communicate with the excommunicated person, no other bishops are to communicate with that bishop, so that the bishop may be more careful not to say of anyone what he cannot prove by other evidence” (canon 99).

For what is refusing to communicate with one who has confessed a crime other than publishing the confession of the crime? And to however many bishops the woman herself may have disclosed her offense in secret confession, it must be kept secret as though she had told it to one alone.

Thus Augustine, explaining the passage in Leviticus—

“If a soul sins, and hears the voice of one swearing an oath, and is a witness, whether [Col. 0634D] he himself saw it or is privy to it, and does not disclose it, he shall bear his iniquity” (Leviticus 5)—

says:

“This seems to say that a person sins when, in his hearing, someone swears falsely, and he knows that the person is swearing falsely and remains silent. He knows it when he has been a witness to the matter about which the oath is sworn, either because he saw it or was privy to it—that is, learned of it in some way, saw it with his own eyes, or the person swearing disclosed it to him; in this way he could have become privy to it.

“But between fear of this sin and fear of betraying people there is often no small temptation. We can recall someone prepared to commit perjury from so grave a sin by warning or forbidding him. But if he does not listen, and swears falsely in our presence concerning the matter he had disclosed to us, [Col. 0635A] should he be exposed, if, once exposed, he should also incur danger of death? This is an extremely difficult question.

“Yet because Scripture did not specify to whom the matter should be disclosed—whether to the one against whom the oath is sworn, or to a priest, or to someone who not only cannot persecute him by inflicting punishment but can also pray for him—it seems to me that a person frees himself from the bond of sin if he discloses it to those who can do more good than harm to the perjurer, whether by correcting him, by appeasing God on his behalf, or if he himself applies the remedy of confession, and so forth, as he continues there.””

What we have said concerning one sin must also be understood concerning others. Solomon says:

[Col. 0635B]

“Whoever walks deceitfully reveals secrets, but the faithful person conceals what has been entrusted to him” (Proverbs 11:13).

And Saint Gregory, in the *Pastoral Rule*, says:

“Those who preside should present themselves as persons to whom their subjects are not ashamed to disclose even their hidden matters, so that, when the little ones endure the waves of temptation, they may flee to the mind of their pastor as to a mother’s breast; and what they foresee will stain them with the filth of the assailing fault, they may wash away by the comfort of his exhortation and the tears of his prayer” (Part II, chapter 5).

It is evident to everyone from his own experience that there is no one who is not ashamed to disclose his sins to his superior if he thinks that he will be stripped bare or publicly exposed. The Council of Carthage likewise commands:

“A bishop shall hear no one’s case in which he will have to judge publicly without the presence of his clergy; otherwise the bishop’s sentence shall be invalid [Col. 0635C] unless it is confirmed by the presence of his clergy” (Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 23).

And in the Gospel the Lord commands that the offender be admonished with one or two others (Matthew 18), lest, when the matter has to be brought before the Church, the person who gave the admonition be judged not a corrector but, in the absence of witnesses, rather an accuser.

A third reason is that we cannot and ought not to judge hidden matters of which we are unaware. Such is this case, which is declared hidden in the aforesaid petition and which we desire never to know if it cannot be healed by private counsel.

Since we cannot judge hidden matters, blessed Innocent writes to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, who had asked why men who communicate do not associate with [Col. 0635D] adulterous wives, while wives appear to remain in the company of adulterous husbands, although Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes:

“Women,” he says, “do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and their hidden sins do not receive punishment. Men, however, more freely customarily bring adulterous wives before priests; and therefore communion is denied to women once their crime has been disclosed. But because men’s offense remains hidden, no one is readily excluded on the basis of suspicions; he will certainly be removed if his wrongdoing is exposed. Since, therefore, the case is equal, sometimes, when proof is lacking, the imposition of punishment is suspended” (Letter 11, chapter 4).

[Col. 0636A]

The text of the petition containing the seven chapters is as follows.

## Chapter I

“After our lord Lothair, the most serene and glorious king, joined Tetberg to himself in royal fashion in marriage, with the consent and will of his faithful, and complaints of discord began to arise between them, certain persons told the same prince that the aforesaid Tetberg bore within her soul or body a hidden wound resulting from some horrible and abominable crime which she had committed, by which she had gravely offended God, and on account of which she was not worthy, nor was it lawful or fitting for him, to keep her any longer in marriage.

## Chapter II

“Because of the opinion just mentioned, which was circulating about her from the mouths of certain people, the aforesaid king [Col. 0636B] often spoke privately and publicly in the presence of his faithful and discussed the matter with them. Subsequently a judgment was reached through their counsel. But divine mercy did not deign to reveal the truth of the matter. Later, when he had gone to Italy to his brother, the Emperor Louis, the crime that had been committed was disclosed to him more openly there.

## Chapter III

“Therefore, so that this suspicion and most wicked report concerning the king’s wife should not remain longer unexamined or unrefuted, and so that our same lord, having become more certain and secure concerning the case, might more freely carry out in royal fashion what he had to do, the following persons assembled at his command in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 860, in the fifth year of his reign, in the eighth indiction, [Col. 0636C] on the fifth day before the Ides of January, at the palace of Aachen: Guntharius, chief chaplain, and Teotgaudus, archbishops; Adventius and Franco, bishops; Hegil and Odelingus, abbots; together with his other faithful.

“After recounting to them everything inserted above, he ordered and instructed the aforesaid bishops and abbots, sending them to her to inquire from her about the whole truth of the matter concerning the aforementioned report, as they did. For she confessed to them, before God and his angels, everything that was in her, and the entire secret appeared fully to them in accordance with the report that had arisen. They returned and announced to the aforesaid king that it was not permissible for him to keep her as his wife.

## Chapter IV

“Guntharius was the first to speak:

‘She confessed to God and to us that she bore an inward wound, though it had not been inflicted by her own will but had been violently [Col. 0636D] imposed upon her. For this reason she judged herself wholly unworthy to approach the royal or marital bed any longer, and in no way could she, because of the aforesaid crime—which is shameful to name—continue in marriage with him or with anyone else. Therefore she begged that permission be granted her to change her secular clothing and withdraw from sexual intercourse, with no fraud arising from anger, nor any will that she might have held against the same king, but so that, once she had withdrawn, he might be comforted in mind and body, while she herself might, by God’s mercy and the prayers of those same bishops, mourn what she had done wrongfully.’

[Col. 0637A]

## Chapter V

“Adventius said:

‘This deed and what has been done until now have been hidden from me, and it is wicked that henceforth you should come together as man and woman. Yet if she were still beloved and dear to you as before, I would give you counsel according to the office entrusted to me, and I would emphatically recommend that you no longer allow her to be joined to your side as a wife, but, in accordance with her request, permit her to receive the veil and change her habit.’

## Chapter VI

“Teotgaudus, archbishop, spoke and agreed in the same manner.

## Chapter VII

“Abbot Egil, acting on behalf of the same Tetberg, advised and requested that this be done: since she had perpetrated the unspeakable deed not of her own will but under violent coercion, she should be granted the opportunity to receive the veil and a place in which the wound inflicted might be healed. What she was asking, however, she sought simply and without any fear imposed upon her, or any circumstance or desire, [Col. 0637B] but for the love of God and the salvation of her soul.”

We have chosen to remain silent about this petition rather than answer it, since, just as it resembles the preceding one in its irrationality for the most part, so it is so unlike truth and reason that it ought not to be believed to have been composed by the bishops named above.

[Col. 0637C]

There is also a certain volume which, because of its length, we have refrained from copying here in full. Its beginning is as follows:

“In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 860, in the eighth indiction, in the middle of the month of February, when the glorious kings Louis, Charles, and the younger Lothair had decreed it, a general assembly of the nobles from the kingdom of the blessed Lothair and a council of bishops was held at the palace of Aachen: Guntharius of Cologne, Teotgaudus of Trier, Wenilo of Rouen, Franco of Tongeren, Hatto of Verdun, Hildegarius of Meaux, and Hilduin of Avignon.”

## Chapter XV

Concerning the woman in question, we find the following written:

“Moreover, since she had no security that she could conceal or overcome this matter, she first recounted to the king the circumstances of the crime she had committed, as the report had stated. Then she explained the same matter in detail to certain bishops and laymen together. Afterward, at her request, a written statement of her confession was prepared; in the presence of all of us and of many laymen, she placed it in the hand of the glorious King Lothair. Immediately she spoke openly before everyone:

[Col. 0637D]

‘My lord king,’ she said, ‘for God’s sake, and for the sake of your reward, I beg you to allow me to do penance, since both in words and in writing I confess that I do not deserve conjugal union. Therefore, prostrate, I humbly entreat you not now or henceforth to deny me what can thereafter aid my salvation.’

“Thus the text of that written statement contained these words and this meaning:

‘I, Thietbrihc, whom the imprudence of the female sex and human frailty have deceived, and whom consciousness of sin bites, [Col. 0638A] for the hope of the salvation of my soul and out of fidelity toward my lord, make this true confession before God and his holy angels, and before the venerable bishops and noble laymen.

‘I confess that my blood brother Hucbert, a cleric, corrupted me when I was a young girl, and committed and perpetrated fornication upon my body contrary to natural intercourse. My conscience bears witness to this. I do not make this confession because of any malicious suggestion, nor under the compulsion of violence, but by my own simple will I declare the truth of the matter as it is.

‘So may the Lord help me, who came to save sinners and promised true pardon to those who confess their sins simply and truthfully, if I invent nothing, if I declare the truth with my own voice, and if I confirm what happened by the handwriting of this document. For it is more bearable for me, an imprudent and deceived woman, simply to confess my guilt before human beings than to blush before the tribunal of the Lord and suffer eternal woe.’”

## Chapter XVI

“When this was read aloud, horror and grief together struck the minds of those standing by, and the priests’ hearts were filled with groans at so great a license of diabolical fraud. [Col. 0638B]

Although her confession appeared credible, nevertheless, lest perhaps the woman so often mentioned were lying because of some deception or fear of someone, we again addressed the aforesaid king and bound him with strong appeals to confess to us whether he had compelled her, by persuasion or threats, falsely to accuse herself.

“In reply, he declared to us with the strongest attestations that he had persuaded her to confess only the truth of the matter and had done nothing more deliberately in that case. He also related to us at that very time how, after he first heard of the unspeakable deed and believed it true, he had grieved over it and how displeased he was by this unexpected and wholly unwanted misfortune.

“[Col. 0638C]

Finally, he said that he had wished to endure the shameful matter patiently and, had the report not already spread so far, to conceal it; and he did as much as he could. Thus, knowingly, he accepted and endured a false judgment in place of a genuine investigation, so that, if possible, the enormity of the shame might appear incredible and disappear from the world, and so that he himself might not remain before the world marked by so disgraceful a stain and ruinous offense.

“But after the exposed plague could no longer be concealed, and he himself could not bear the weight of so great a disgrace—especially when, traveling through Burgundy and Italy, he recoiled from the shame, which had been excessively defamed and spread abroad—he did not allow this matter to remain longer without episcopal examination. With tearful sighs he repeatedly said that this had been impressed upon him in many ways concerning the aforesaid woman, and that many people had affirmed the same thing in this kingdom, repeating it with groans.”

[Col. 0638D]

## Chapter XVII

“Therefore we again approached the same woman, first in secret and then in the presence of laymen. We exhorted her with many admonitions and under divine adjuration not to bring any false crime against herself in any way, and we sought to deter her from doing so by threats of eternal punishment. Again, relying on our counsel, assistance, protection, and defense, we made her secure against every plot or act of violence, asking only that she confess to us confidently whether she had been persuaded or compelled to accuse herself.

“To this she replied, rebuking us with a harsh look:

‘Do you think that I would have wished to destroy myself in this way for anything in the world? As I confessed before, so I confess now, and so I shall confess. I ask only, for the love of God, that you now grant me the mercy I desire in accordance with my prayers.’

[Col. 0639A]

“Our concern then asked whether she would thereafter raise any complaint about the matter, or ever devise any plots, if her request were granted. We immediately followed up on this undertaking with one accord:

‘Know, daughter, that if you await our judgment concerning you and your confession, so that the censure of divine and canonical authority may encompass you and the indissoluble chain of the priests may begin to bind you, then, from that point, you will no longer recover what you can still recover now—if indeed you can recover it at all.’

“The laymen also admonished her greatly, especially her relatives and friends, who sharply reproached her and urged her not to deceive herself. Yet she remained immovable in her confession, as though the secret [Col. 0639B] of her conscience were visibly exposed to the eyes of those who looked upon it.”

## Chapter XVIII

“Why should we delay longer? Once every doubt had been removed and the truth of the matter established, it seemed that a crime new in its nature, terrible because of its abominable pollution, and especially one whose stench rumor had long since spread far and wide among countless people, ought not to be treated with any light care or indulgence, lest it inflict a harmful corruption upon present and future generations unless it were uprooted with greater severity and diligence.

“For it is beyond doubt that natural intercourse between brother and sister does not merit temporary pardon or honor, and nothing remains except vengeance and penance. A condemnable crime that immediately cuts off entirely many things [Col. 0639C] that had previously been lawful has no opportunity to advance further. For this reason it has occurred so rarely in the world, since it is clear that no one has taken an example from it for himself, and it could never have been considered venial in the esteem of the world.

“But whenever some have fallen into this misery, it did not happen through the example of another; rather, it was a fresh and almost new fall arising from the ancient fraud of the devil and a similar impulse and plunge of human weakness.

“This kind of contagion, which is now beginning to be new and which was previously unheard of by us, must be guarded against, lest it generate a diseased plague and incurable corruption for the human race. Its pernicious origin must therefore be utterly uprooted, so that it leaves no example and no opportunity for the weak. [Col. 0639D]

Otherwise, God forbid, such a custom might grow up by which someone would avoid natural intercourse among blood relatives but become more freely accustomed to fornicating unnaturally within his own kin, considering this a minor evil.”

## Chapter XIX

“Having therefore considered and carefully examined these matters, we have decreed that the pollution of incest, lamentably brought into public view, must be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance.”

We shall briefly indicate here, demonstrating more fully in the course of the work, that Pope Leo expressly prohibits the preparation of a petition of this kind of confession (Letter 36, to the bishops throughout Campania); nor does sacred authority allow a wife to separate from her husband in this manner.

[Col. 0640A]

Moreover, since this woman presented the petition of her accusation not to the bishops, as it is written there, but to the king, and exposed her crimes to laymen, let the king establish a legal judgment, and let married laymen, according to law and justice, judge the married lay consort of the king. If the matter then comes from their judgment to episcopal judgment, let the bishops impose upon her a medicinal judgment according to ecclesiastical laws.

Concerning what is written there—that the king grieved over such an act and that, being saddened, he was displeased by this action—he must take care that his sadness is not a cleansing but, God forbid, a confession of the crime.

“For this,” as the teachers of the Church write, and as the venerable priest Bede says, following their judgment, “is the justice of the heavenly judgment: that often the reprobate both recognize and confess that they have erred, and undergo certain remorse for their error, yet do not cease from erring. [Col. 0640B] Thus, by that same confession and penance, they bear witness against themselves that they do not sin unknowingly, since they refuse to restrain themselves from the sin they condemn; and they perish all the more justly because they neglect to avoid the pit of perdition which they were able to foresee.

“Thus it is written of Herod that ‘the king was sorrowful because of Herodias’s request’ (Mark 6). Herod’s sorrow is of the same kind as the repentance of Pharaoh and Judas: each of them, after unwillingly disclosing his crimes under accusation from his conscience, foolishly increased them.

“Thus, when the head of John was requested, Herod displayed sorrow on his face, condemning himself and openly showing everyone that he knew the man whom he was about to deliver to death to be innocent and holy. But if we examine his wicked heart more carefully, we see that he was secretly pleased that the request concerned something which he had previously intended to do, if he could do so with an excuse. [Col. 0640C]

If the head of Herodias had been requested, there is no doubt that he would neither have wished to give it nor would he have refused it with genuine sorrow.”

Therefore, our lord king, fixing his eyes upon the heavenly observer, who sees the hearts of all and to whom human thought makes confession, must carefully weigh whether he would have received with equal grief, and looked upon with equal calmness of countenance, the person from whom he might then have heard:

“Since you absolve this woman, never again allow her, in any manner whatsoever, to approach you in such a way.”

Concerning the king’s profession that, knowingly, he accepted a false judgment in place of a genuine examination: since we know that we shall give the most exact account of all our judgments to the most just Judge and King of kings, [Col. 0640D]

we speak, compelled by truth and without regard to persons, according to what we believe.

He presumed to act against the legal decree and the evangelical truth, which says:

“You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matthew 4:7).

And because, as it is written again, “He mocks those who mock” (Proverbs 3:34), let him, as a sacrilegious person who contemptuously and mockingly acted against sacred sacraments, receive and perform worthy penance. Those who consented to him, if there were any, must be subjected to legal and ecclesiastical judgments.

As for what follows there—that the same woman was decreed, in accordance with her many petitions, to be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance: if, once placed in a legal judgment, she escaped it reasonably and justly, with equity or the mercy of pardon, the matter may in some way be acceptable. [Col. 0641A]

This must nevertheless be done so that, contrary to the Apostle, the permission for her separation does not become a stumbling block to the weak and does not cause her husband to commit adultery.

But if this was not the case, she ought to have heard, together with her supporters, the Apostle’s words:

“You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4:3).

For since she had accused herself before the king and noble laymen in writing, just as under Roman laws one person accuses another under the condition prescribed by those same laws, it does not seem proper that, without having been legally judged by them or absolved by a royal sentence of pardon, she should have been punished by the bishops with public penance. In a legally constituted judgment, even executioners do not drag the accused to torture without a judgment having been pronounced, nor do they release from bonds one who has not received a royal pardon.

[Col. 0641B]

Finally, after the strong testimonies of authorities—which confirm little or nothing of what was done concerning the aforesaid woman, and indeed contradict some of it—the following is added:

“Concerning our king, his vulnerable youth, and his unstable lack of self-restraint, lest he bring danger upon his peoples and kingdom, there remains a great necessity for us to seek counsel. Therefore we urgently implore that, through the counsel and sincere cooperation of your college, you quickly console and strengthen us in the Lord.”

The sentence seems to us, remarkably, to hang unfinished, since it does not provide the consolation being sought, nor does it show from where counsel ought to be given.

Therefore, since others have questioned us more explicitly whether this union between our lord the king and the woman often mentioned [Col. 0641C] was a marriage, we shall show in the course of this work what we think about it under the instruction of sacred authority. But if it was a concubinal union or incestuous pollution, we shall present what we have gathered concerning it from the sacred writings.

Meanwhile, with pardon, we admonish the writers of this volume that it would have been safer to await and seek the counsel of the general college concerning what had been done with the aforesaid woman, and to take counsel in that same assembly concerning our lord the king, as is now being requested, rather than—as the proverbial saying of old has it—to sound the trumpet after the storm. For it is written:

“Let your eyelids go before your steps” (Proverbs 4:26);

and:

“Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not repent” (Ecclesiasticus 32:24).

## Interrogation II

[Col. 0641D]

Concerning what has been written to us: some say that judgment should be made from the confession of the aforesaid woman concerning the evidence of this hidden case, after the manner of the secret confession once made by Bishop Ebo.

## Response
Perhaps laymen and such people say this—those who are ignorant of ecclesiastical laws and were not present at the episcopal judgment at that time, but infer from a faulty report what was done. Therefore we, who were present at that same council, can demonstrate from certain knowledge, from the episcopal proceedings themselves, and from that very document which Ebo produced before the council, signed by his own hand, that the aforesaid bishop, when accused in the synod, chose judges for himself; that he presented to the synod a written statement of his withdrawal from episcopal ministry [Col. 0642A], signed by his own hand because of the weight of his sins; that, confessing in accordance with the terms of the statement, he himself produced witnesses; and that finally, on the basis of his confession, supported by witnesses and written testimony, he received a synodal sentence from the judges he had chosen, requiring him to withdraw from episcopal ministry. He departed and withdrew.

Therefore, let those who say such things also learn from our explanation what they cannot fail to know from the use of Christian teaching: namely, that just as one order differs from another, so the cause and law of the case of a man differ from those of a woman, and the case of a bishop, no less than that of a presbyter or deacon, is different. For, as evangelical and apostolic truth teaches: “The husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does; and likewise the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does” (1 Cor. 7:4). By this authority over the body, as the commentators explain, the use of the sexual organs is designated. Married persons ought not to misuse them with others, but to use them matrimonially with one another.

Otherwise, as the Apostle also says of himself (1 Cor. 9), everyone who fears God has authority to discipline his body, subject it to servitude, and hand it over to death for Christ, as well as to move his other limbs according to their common and lawful use and to care for his body [Col. 0642B]. In this sense the same Apostle continues: “The woman is bound by the law to her husband as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband, and may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:27).

A man cannot dismiss his wife for any reason whatsoever, and for no reason other than fornication; and if he dismisses her, he cannot marry another while she is alive. Nor can she marry another while her husband is alive, because it is written: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 10:9). For God joined them by making the man and woman one flesh. No human being can separate this union, unless perhaps God alone.

A human being separates them when, because of a desire for a second wife, he dismisses the first. God separates them—the God who had joined them—when, by mutual agreement for the sake of serving God, because “the time is short,” a man possesses a wife “as though he had none.” God separates them, however, not from a marital and wifely union entered into according to God, but from carnal intercourse and the conjugal use of the body. If they cannot endure this, they should not deprive one another of their marital right, except perhaps for a time, so that they may devote themselves to prayer and then return again to the same relationship, lest they be tempted by Satan because of their lack of self-control [Col. 0642C].

Whoever among them falls into this temptation through lack of self-control by committing adultery will be able, by the antidote of salutary penance, to obtain the remedy of doing penance and, through ecclesiastical authority, to attain full restoration.

As for bishops, presbyters, or deacons who say that they have been defiled by a mortal crime, we read, according to the Council of Valentina (canon 4), that they are to be removed from the offices mentioned above, whether they are guilty because of a true confession or because of a falsehood. For one who has declared himself the cause of his own death cannot be absolved, since the act which, if attributed to another, would be punished as a cause of death makes anyone who is the cause of his own death a still greater murderer.

Saint Augustine explains this death, in his exposition of Deuteronomy, where it says: “If a man is found kidnapping one of his brothers, the children of Israel, and selling him and receiving payment, he shall be put to death, and you shall remove the evil from your midst” (Deut. 24:7). He explains it as follows [Col. 0642D]:

> “Scripture says this repeatedly when it commands that evil persons be put to death. The Apostle also used this manner of speaking when he said: ‘What have I to do with judging those who are outside? Is it not those who are inside whom you judge? Remove the evil person from among yourselves’” (1 Cor. 5:12).

From this it is evident that he intended someone to be understood who has committed an act deserving excommunication. For excommunication now does in the Church what execution did then. Likewise, what civil laws condemn to death through the agency of the state, ecclesiastical laws punish by the judgment of degradation or excommunication.

We also read in the African canons: “Let a bishop who has falsely claimed that he communicated with those who were not to be admitted to communion lose his episcopate.” A wife, however, cannot be separated from such a man on the basis of such collusion.

To this must be added what we stated above: a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has declared himself the cause of his own death—a cause which, if declared against another, would be punished—cannot be absolved. Since, as is reported, this woman does not make this charge against herself alone, but refers it still more to her brother, she cannot on account of such a statement be separated until the person against whom it rebounds is clearly shown, through him, either to have confessed it or to have been convicted of it [Col. 0643A].

Nor can a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has fallen into the devil’s snare and temptation receive the remedy of repentance by the laying on of hands in the same way as a husband and wife. Rather, as Leo writes (Letter 95, chapter 2), such fallen persons must seek private withdrawal in order to obtain God’s mercy; there, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also bear fruit. Through repentance they will not be able to attain restoration to the ecclesiastical grades, whereas a man and woman who have committed adultery may attain restoration to the fullness of communion, as Gelasius writes (Letter 6):

> “Such persons too, if they should happen to slip in this way, once detected, must be driven away—both those who have previously sinned and those who, forgetting their sacred profession, have violated their holy purpose; without doubt they must be removed.”

And Siricius writes to Himerius (Letter 1):

> “It was also our duty to provide that, just as no cleric is permitted to undertake penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layman should ever be permitted to obtain the honor of the clergy. For although they may have been cleansed from the contagion of all sins, they ought not to receive any instruments for administering the sacraments if they were formerly vessels of vices” [Col. 0643B].

Just as a person who has been mutilated in some part of the body, or who has performed public penance, cannot canonically enter an ecclesiastical grade or remain in one, so neither should we say that one who has been found [to have been so] before baptism or after baptism can enjoy the office of an ecclesiastical grade. Sacred authority teaches this, even though that same authority does not reject persons mutilated or publicly penitent in youth, or those who have contracted a second marriage while in the lay order. For just as one office belongs to the head and another to another limb according to the diversity of the body, so the case of a priest differs from that of the people, and the case of a shepherd differs from that of the flock [Col. 0643C].

According to canonical authority, a man and woman who have been separated even on account of fornication may, after penance, be reunited in marriage by mutual reconciliation. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon, however, who has been justly and according to ecclesiastical laws degraded cannot aspire again to his former grade.

Let whoever wishes read the letters of the great Leo and the decrees of Gregory. There he will find that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who, after canonical deposition, attempts to aspire to the ecclesiastical grades must be sent into exile or confined in a monastery under penance.

There is also the fact that a woman cannot give a man a writ of repudiation, whereas a man may give a woman one. Moses, not God, permitted this, as the Gospel testifies; the Lord himself prohibited it [Col. 0643D].

And, as Paul teaches, the law is written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God on the hearts of the righteous. The sacred canons, as Damasus and Leo teach, were likewise established by the same Holy Spirit, of whom it is written: “The Spirit of your Father is the one speaking in you” (Matt. 10:20); “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9); “God is Spirit,” and “he breathes where he wills”; and “he distributes to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11).

By the authority of these canons, whether because of weakness of soul or bodily illness, a bishop may, if he wishes, remove himself from the Church over which he presided and from his office by presenting a written statement signed by his own hand, just as blessed Gregory repeatedly indicates in his letters—for example, in his letters to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna; to the clergy and people of Ariminum; to the deacon Anatolius; to the bishop Aetherius; and to Queen Brunhild. This is also clearly recognized in the Gallican canons concerning Potamius, archbishop of Braga [Col. 0644A].

We do not, however, read that a woman ought to be separated from her husband by presenting a synodal statement to an assembly, or that she can be released from the marital yoke without a public judicial examination.

We often suffer women making complaints with the greatest insistence. With an oath—and even more when they present a written statement—they try to assert that the husbands who legally took them as wives cannot render them the marital debt, and they bring forward many other deceptions. The husbands, in turn, assert that they are lying, as the outcome in many cases proves. Men also commonly bring against their wives various charges which we consider it most shameful or unnecessary to insert here [Col. 0644B].

If we readily gave assent to such claims, an innumerable crowd of separated persons would violate the legal bonds of marriage established by the Lord. For if lustful men or women could be separated from the marital yoke in whatever way they wished, whether to enter other marriages or to defile themselves through secret adulteries, they would most eagerly separate from one another. We see this in young widows, who, after the release of their husbands, receive the sacred veil in order to abuse several men more freely. Sometimes men also withdraw from a lawful marriage so that they may enjoy the embraces of numerous concubines.

Foreseeing this and teaching that it must be avoided, the Apostle says, among other things, speaking of such matters: “I want younger widows to marry, bear children, and manage their households” (1 Tim. 5:14) [Col. 0644C].

Therefore the discerning discipline of ecclesiastical authority has provided, with great caution and wisdom, that ecclesiastical men may remove themselves from the office of sacred ministry when conscience bears witness against them and may devote themselves to worthy fruits of penance. In this matter there can be no opportunity for pleasure or deceit, but only devotion to humility and salvation.

A man and a woman, however, because sacred authority says that they are “no longer two, but one flesh,” cannot be separated by secret confession or by presenting a written statement, as it is written: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 10:9), nor in any other way except for a manifest cause of fornication [Col. 0644D]. Those who are separated must either remain in that state or be reconciled to one another.

Nor can they be so divided that one part of a single body—the man or the woman—practices continence while the other part remains in pollution. By mutual agreement, however, they may withdraw more closely united from marital intercourse, so that they may devote themselves to God in a perpetual love of continence.

## INTERROGATION III

Concerning what has been written to us [p. 583]: “It has also been reported to us concerning the venerable archbishop of Rheims that he consents to such an act; that through the bishops Wenilo, namely, archbishop of Rouen, and Hildegarius, bishop, he fulfilled his part by word; that through Adventius, who had spoken with him at Rheims concerning this matter, he sent letters expressing his agreement to the king’s assembly and to the episcopal gathering; and that through this same Adventius he sent his letters concerning the matter to the apostolic see”—an explanation must be given [Col. 0645A].

For if the Shepherd of the Church and first of the apostles, who performed signs and miracles in a singular manner, did not disdain, when reproached for having entered among the Gentiles, eaten with them, and received them into baptism, to give a humble account of himself, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 11:4), how much more ought we sinners, when reproved concerning some matter, to appease our reprovers by a humble explanation?

### RESPONSE

Therefore I, the servant of the Church of Rheims, satisfy all who wish to believe the truth: I fulfilled neither my agreement nor my disagreement in this matter by word or writing through the aforesaid bishops or through any other venerable bishops. I did not speak with the bishops named above after the recent Kalends of November and before the time when these events occurred. Nor is it within my authority to impose anything upon them by command, except in the same way that they may charitably command me whatever they wish [Col. 0645B].

The venerable bishop Adventius and my son Hincmarus, bishop of Laon, came to me at Rheims on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, on a visit. At the command of the lords and in the name of our fellow bishops, they urged me to go, if my bodily illness permitted, to the assembly then soon to be held at the palace of Aachen; or, if I could not go myself, to send one of our fellow bishops to take part in their deliberations.

While we were speaking about various matters, including what I had heard from the widespread reports circulating among the mouths not only of nobles but also of common people concerning the wife of Lord King Lothair, I said that, if perhaps both a royal command and a priestly summons required me to go to the assembly, it would be safer and more reasonable for the discussion and determination of this matter—whose novelty makes the ears of its hearers almost ring, or causes them altogether to fall silent—to be postponed in its entirety to a general synod.

I could not go because I was prevented by bodily illness; nor could I send a fellow bishop of our diocese without the consent of the provincial assembly; nor should a matter that concerns everyone so generally be determined by a small number of bishops [Col. 0645C].

When Lord Adventius insisted only that I should go, or send one of our fellow bishops in my place, and that the matter for which either my insignificant person or the presence of a representative of our province was requested would be disclosed there, the evening brought our conversation to an end. Although I questioned him, he neither disclosed to me the secret matter indicated by the earlier written statement nor revealed it of his own accord. I recognized, perhaps, that it was the matter I had heard about, as I stated above, and about which I had learned that many bishops had been consulted when the trial of purification had taken place, and which, as they say, even women turn over in their weaving workshops.

As midnight approached, the venerable Adventius went to his lodging, and Hincmarus, bishop of Laon, withdrew to his accustomed quarters. I, however, being ill and lying in bed, began to feel somewhat better. Since certain thoughts then occurred to me—Adventius, a religious man, had not told me why I was being summoned to the synod, and I had spoken with him at length about the case brought against the woman—I suspected, as I said above, that this very case might be the reason for the summons. I therefore thought it would be better to send him a letter concerning our conversation on the previous day. Anyone who wishes may read its copy here [Col. 0645D].

> “Hincmarus, unworthily called bishop of Rheims and servant of God’s people, sends abundant greetings in the Savior to his beloved brother and venerable bishop Adventius.
>
> “Yesterday we spoke at length, insofar as my illness permitted, in a mutual conversation about this unexpected matter which has arisen at this time, concerning which I had already heard such and so many things that I thought I would hear nothing more about it. Finally, as seemed better and more reasonable to us, we set this case aside to be reserved for a general synod.
>
> “But as I touched upon the matter only briefly yesterday evening, I now more explicitly and earnestly beg your most faithful charity, by way of reminder, to act kindly on my behalf. In accordance with the command of the lords and the summons of my fellow priests, I cannot go to your assembly because I am detained by illness; nor can I send in my place one of my fellow bishops, instructed according to canonical custom in a regular consultation and commended by accompanying letters. The urgency of the mission and the shortness of time do not permit me to consult my lords and fellow bishops in such matters. Without their advice—as you yourselves know well—the venerable rules permit me to undertake nothing except what pertains to my own parish; to presume anything against those rules is not without danger of punishment.
>
> “I fear that Lord King may think I wish to suspend my proper service to him and withdraw from his obedience; and I fear that the venerable bishops may suspect that, if they determine something according to the sacred rules, I desire to reconsider what is not fitting for me to reconsider.
>
> “Therefore, in accordance with the confidence I have in your goodness, let your affection, which has learned my devotion through face-to-face conversation, excuse me without any scruple. I have explained to your wisdom what I have judged more salutary. I am such a tiny human being in so great a matter, involving persons of such eminence, concerning which such acts have been undertaken by so many men and so many important men consulted. Without the discussion, advice, or consent of many people, and before I have reviewed the scriptural authorities and decrees of the Fathers concerning such a matter, I do not dare to pronounce a definitive judgment or give my agreement [Col. 0646A].
>
> “Accordingly, whatever is regularly determined by you, or whatever is settled by your assembly with God’s approval in a manner better and more reasonable than has seemed to me, I ought neither to praise nor to retract before I have heard it.
>
> “For this reason I think it fitting, at the end of this little document from my insignificance, to set down not my own words but those of the great Leo to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne: ‘In matters that are doubtful or obscure,’ he says (Letter 95), ‘we should recognize that we must follow what is found to be neither contrary to the evangelical commands nor opposed to the decrees of the holy Fathers.’
>
> “Finally, I ask your loving charity to join the reading of this document to the words of your wisdom in your holy council, as an excuse for me” [Col. 0646B].

In the course of time, the same Lord Adventius sent his messenger to me, through whom I again sent him the following letter [Col. 0646C]:

> “Hincmarus, bishop of Rheims, sends abundant greetings in the Savior to his beloved brother and venerable bishop Adventius.”

After some introductory remarks concerning the business for which he had sent his messenger, I wrote:

> “Moreover, although you have communicated nothing of this to me, I infer the nature of your mission. In it, as your prudence rightly teaches you, it is necessary for you to proceed with great caution and foresight, because this is a matter of such a kind, involving persons of such eminence and an order of proceedings such as this, that it will necessarily be known by everyone and must likewise be weighed by everyone.
>
> “For, as Celestine writes, the universal Church is shaken by every novelty. It concerns a matter between the King of kings and an earthly king, governed by the first law given to the first human being in paradise and confirmed in the Gospel by God and man.
>
> “There is likewise a matter hitherto unheard of by us, concerning which it will be necessary carefully to review the sacred authorities and consult the Christian laws, so that pontifical authority may proceed in its examination with a sincere and cautious step, and so that every Christian may not deviate from the right path.
>
> “You will indeed have to report such things to the apostolic see as, being truthfully spoken from heart and mouth—as I know you will do—ought to appear before the divine eyes; and so that no one may later be able to discover otherwise, you must not report to the apostolic see any claim based on the consent of bishops or of any laymen for the purpose of obtaining someone’s objective, except from those whose deliberation you know to have established the matter [Col. 0647A].
>
> “At the same time, you must carry out what has been entrusted to you in such a way that, as far as possible, you do not offend your superior, and especially so that what you undertake does not conflict with the sacred rules or—God forbid—oppose divine equity and justice.
>
> “Although this is more than necessary, I write it to your wisdom because I hold you dear. You deemed me worthy to promise that I could entrust myself securely to your faithfulness, and you wished me to make every effort to return my devotion to you” [Col. 0647B].

I have not so far sent any other letters concerning this matter either to the apostolic see or to any bishop [Col. 0647C].

## INTERROGATION IV

In the second chapter we ask that an answer be sent to us concerning whether the matter is considered an offense committed after a marriage has been contracted: how a marriage ought to be contracted, what law governs marriage, for what reasons and in what manner it may be dissolved, whether after separation the man or woman may seek another union, and whether either of them, if committing an offense within marriage, ought to be judged by the same standard [p. 586; Col. 0647D].

### RESPONSE

Since, as we have shown, the eighth chapter of the earlier written statement says that, by recognizing the argument of the case hitherto concealed, we should drive out error and establish the truth; and since we read that an argument is something which, although it does not yet exist, can nevertheless come to pass; and since the matter concerns marriage, before which people often sin through human frailty, often sin in contracting marriage itself, and often commit a graver offense after marriage has been contracted—we shall begin at the root and set out how marriage ought to be contracted. Then we shall show the law of marriage. Finally, if sin is committed within marriage, we shall demonstrate the judgment and order of judgment.

Since sin is evil, and evil is not a nature and therefore is not something substantial, but arises in a good substance as an accident, and since an accidental weakness is driven out by medicine once the rule—that is, natural soundness—and the medicine for weakness have been established, then, with the strength and accidental injury recognized more clearly, we shall be able, having grasped the argument of the case hitherto concealed, to drive out error and establish the truth more easily [Col. 0648A].

How marriage ought to be contracted is taught by both the Old and the New Law, when the Lord commands through Moses and demonstrates in the Gospel (Matt. 1:18): “When,” he says, “the mother of Jesus, Mary, had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together in the celebration of marriage.” The same is shown in the wedding that he honored by sanctifying it with his presence and illuminating it by the miracle performed there.

The holy Roman Pope Evaristus, fourth after blessed Peter, also writes as follows in his decretal (Letter 1, at the beginning) [Col. 0648B]:

> “We have likewise received and handed down the rule that a wife is to be lawfully joined to her husband. For, as we have received from the Fathers and found handed down by the holy apostles and their successors, a marriage is not legitimate unless the wife is requested from those who appear to exercise authority over that woman and by whom she is guarded; unless she is betrothed by her parents or relatives; unless she is endowed according to the laws; and unless, at the proper time, she is blessed by a priest according to custom, with prayers and offerings.
>
> “She is to be guarded and joined to her husband by the bridesmen, as custom teaches; requested by her relatives at the appropriate time; endowed according to the laws; and solemnly received. They should devote two or three days to prayer and preserve chastity, so that good offspring may be produced and they may please the Lord in their deeds.
>
> “In this way they will please the Lord and produce children who are not illegitimate, but legitimate and capable of inheriting. Therefore, dearest sons, and deservedly illustrious ones, know that marriages are legitimate when carried out in this manner, with the support of the Catholic faith.
>
> “Marriages presumed in any other way are not marriages but, rather, adulteries, unions of cohabitation, illicit sexual relations, or fornications, rather than legitimate marriages—unless personal consent has provided support and legitimate vows have come to the aid of the union. For it is a divine fruit to observe divine commands; no one can doubt that abandoning them is presumption.”

Why, then, should it be considered wrong to preserve the unity of the Church? Let us all alike think and declare the same thing. For if unions are presumed in another way, the transgressors themselves certainly destroy themselves, deceiving their own selves.

The angel also spoke concerning this kind of marriage to Joseph: “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife” (Matt. 1:20), that is, the woman betrothed to you [Col. 0648C].

Blessed Pope Siricius, in his decrees to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona (Letter 1, chapter 4), says:

> “It is not permitted to take another man’s betrothed into the rights of marriage. You have asked concerning the violation of marriage whether one man may take a girl betrothed to another in marriage. We absolutely prohibit this from being done, because among the faithful that blessing which the priest imposes upon women about to marry is comparable to a sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression” [Col. 0648D].

From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 10:

> “Concerning betrothed girls who have been violated by others: it has been decided that betrothed girls who have subsequently been abducted by others are to be rescued and restored to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that force was inflicted upon them by their abductors.”

We read this many times and in many forms in the definitions of the saints. But to demonstrate this kind of marriage, these examples are more than sufficient.

Since we do not condemn second marriages—in fact, we accept them—we also recognize another kind of marriage, taught by the Apostle and explained by holy Pope Leo in his decrees to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, where he shows how such marriages ought to be contracted. He says in chapter 18 (Letter 95) [p. 587; Col. 0649A]:

> “Not every woman joined to a man is the man’s wife, just as not every son is the heir of his father. The bonds of marriage are legitimate among free persons and among equals, and this was established by the Lord long before the beginning of Roman law came into existence.
>
> “Thus a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another. For this reason the Apostle, to make clear the distinction between these persons, adduces testimony from Genesis, where it is said to Abraham: ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac’” (Gal. 4:30; Gen. 21:10).
>
> “Since the partnership of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, beyond the union of the sexes, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage in whom the marital mystery is shown not to have existed.
>
> “Therefore, if someone gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this must not be understood as giving her to a married man, unless that other woman is found to have been made free, lawfully endowed, and honored by a public wedding.
>
> “Women joined to men by paternal decision are free from guilt if the women whom the men had kept were not wives in marriage, because a married woman is one thing and a concubine another. To cast a slave woman away from the marriage bed and take a wife of certain free birth is not a duplication of marriage but an advancement in respectability” [Col. 0649B].

Saint Ambrose also says in his book *On the Fall of a Virgin* (chapter 5):

> “A woman joined to a man after the betrothal has been completed before ten witnesses and the marriage consummated commits adultery, not without great danger.”

Moreover, because ecclesiastical order does not abandon those outside the ordinary order, but either receives those who repent or rejects those who persist in contempt, it is written concerning those who marry many times in the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 3 [Col. 0649C]:

> “Concerning those who have entered into several marriages: the appointed period is indeed clear, but their conduct and faith shorten the period.”

It also happens through the devastation of war and the gravest incursions of enemies that a wife is joined to another husband. Widows, virgins, and consecrated women are likewise abducted contrary to divine and human law. The canons prescribe remedies for these matters, which we do not consider it necessary to set out here.

These, then, are the ways in which marriages are joined or unions of cohabitation are usurped [Col. 0649D].

## INTERROGATION V

In what manner, and for what reasons, may marriages contracted according to authority be separated; without what conditions ought they not to be separated; and after separation, while both man and woman are alive, may either seek another union? Or, if either of them sins within marriage, ought each to be judged by the same standard?

### RESPONSE

First, marriage is contracted according to the evangelical admonition which blessed Augustine gives in his book *On the Good of Marriage*: it is entered into for love of eternal salvation, and a marriage is said to be all the better when it is preserved in a more spiritual manner than when it is dissolved [Col. 0650A].

Saint Augustine says in the fifth book *Against Julian*:

> “The evangelist Luke said of the Lord (Luke 3:23) that he was thought to be the son of Joseph, because he was thought to have been begotten through Joseph’s intercourse. He wished to remove this false opinion, not to deny that Mary was the wife of that man, contrary to the testimony of the angel. Indeed, you yourself admit that, on the basis of the faith of the betrothal, she received the name ‘wife,’ and that this faith certainly remained inviolate.
>
> “For when he saw her already a sacred virgin, endowed with divine fruitfulness, he did not seek another wife. He would not have sought this one either if he had not needed a wife. Yet he did not judge the bond of conjugal faith to be dissolved merely because the hope of sexual intercourse had been removed” [Col. 0650B].

Second, likewise according to evangelical truth, in the case of fornication. Hence a remedy of this kind is applied in the canons of the Council of Ancyra (canon 19, 589): “If,” it says, “someone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he must attain perfection through seven years of penance, according to the former degrees.”

Concerning their separation, the following is written in the African Council, chapter sixty-nine: “It has been decided that, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband may be joined to another; rather, they must remain as they are or be reconciled to one another. But if they disregard this, they are to be reduced to penance” [Col. 0651C]. Then the authority continues: “So that marriages lawfully contracted may be separated in any manner only with priestly knowledge, and may not be separated without legal judgment.”

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira (canon 9): “A faithful woman who has left her faithful adulterous husband and marries an adulterer is to be forbidden to marry; if she does marry, she is not to receive Communion before the man whom she left has departed from this world—unless perhaps the necessity of illness should compel Communion to be given.” The same judgment must also be maintained concerning the man, because, as Innocent wrote to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, and Augustine in the book *On the Ten Strings*, and Jerome in his letter to Oceanus on the death of Fabiola, “They are held under the same law of divine judgment if they are separated for any reason” [Col. 0651D].

Accordingly, Innocent writes to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, in chapter seven: “Your affection also inquired about those who, after a divorce had intervened, joined themselves to another marriage; it is clear that they are adulterers on both sides. Those, however, who, while their wife is still living—although the marriage may appear to have been dissolved—hasten to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers. Indeed, even the persons joined to such men appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery; likewise, whoever marries a woman who has been dismissed commits adultery’ (Matt. XIX, 9). Therefore all such persons must be kept from the communion of the faithful. Concerning their parents or relatives, however, nothing of this kind can be decreed unless they are discovered to have encouraged the unlawful union” [Col. 0652A].

Saint Ambrose likewise writes in the book *On Abraham*: “I warn you, men, especially those who are striving toward the grace of the Lord, not to join yourselves to an adulterous body. For whoever joins himself to a prostitute is one body with her. Nor should you give women this occasion for divorce. Let no one flatter himself on the basis of human laws: every act of sexual immorality is adultery, and what is not permitted to a woman is not permitted to a man. The same chastity is owed by the husband as by the wife. Whatever is committed with one who is not a legitimate wife is condemned under the charge of adultery. Therefore, consider what you must avoid, lest anyone make himself unworthy of the sacraments.”

In chapter 25 of the Council of Agde, concerning those who leave their wives without cause, it is written: “Those laymen who abandon or have abandoned the marital union without any more serious fault, and who, offering no credible reason for the separation, leave their marriages in order to presume upon either another’s marriage or an unlawful union—if, before stating the cause of the separation to the provincial bishop and before their wives have been condemned by judgment, they cast them off—are to be excluded from the communion of the Church and from the assembly of the holy people, because they stain the fidelity of marriage” [Col. 0652B].

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira: “Women who, without any preceding cause, leave their husbands and join themselves to others are not to receive Communion even at the end of their lives.”

There are also other incestuous unions, together with their separations and judgments. Since we are hastening to discuss other matters, we shall pass them over here. Let all readers understand concerning these things that the holy and apostolic men—namely, the successors of the apostles—did not establish the laws we have set out here from their tradition so that anyone might dissolve a marriage contracted according to divine authority without the knowledge of his bishop; nor did they establish them so that we might despise and wish to trample upon the laws of the world that are Christian. Indeed, the Church often asks emperors and kings to promulgate such laws even in ecclesiastical matters, and episcopal authority frequently uses their judgments in its own courts together with the judgments of the canons. It accepts them to such an extent that Damasus, Leo, and Saint Gregory made the judgments of the laws canonical, as is found in their letters; and in the memorandum addressed to John the Defender, who was going to Spain, blessed Gregory, in the twelfth book, letter 51, composed the entire account of the sacred orders from legal institutions [Col. 0652C–D].

Thus, among the other legal rights decreed over the course of time by kings and emperors, Augustus Louis of pious memory, in the synod and general assembly at Worms, while a legate of the Apostolic See and of Pope Gregory was present, together with many others, decreed the following concerning this matter, in accordance with the unanimous wishes of all—both bishops and faithful laymen—regarding what the bishops had recently and necessarily and usefully determined in synods held in the four regions of his empire:
