“Whoever, having abandoned his own wife, or having killed her without fault, marries another wife shall perform public penance after laying down his arms. If he is obstinate, he shall be seized by the count, bound in irons, and placed in custody until the matter is brought to our attention” [Col. 0653A].

Christ, moreover, the power and wisdom of God, says through Wisdom herself: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel and am present among learned thoughts; through me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just; through me princes rule, and the powerful decree justice” (Prov. VIII, 12).

For this reason those vicars of Christ and successors of the apostles established these laws, and we, however unworthy, presiding over the Church in their place, have set them out here: just as the Lord first gave that blessing in paradise to Adam and his wife, saying, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I, 28)—a blessing once given that has not been denied to this day and will not be denied until the end, not only to the faithful but also to unbelievers—so, through the mouths of priests, he bestows it individually upon the faithful and devout for sanctification, a sanctification that Christ bestowed upon marriage by his presence when he changed water into wine. Therefore, those who have been joined together through their ministry by God are not to be separated, without their knowledge, by the laws of the world, which are sanctified by the justice of God, by which every just person is made just; and if they are spiritually separated from carnal intercourse for God's sake, so that, cleaving to the Lord, they may become one spirit—as Paul speaks of many established in the Church, among whom some had been tax collectors and prostitutes, murderers and adulterers: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. II, 2)—then, with the blessing and knowledge of the priesthood, they may be joined more fully to the Lord [Col. 0653B].

If, however, in agreement with a just and holy civil law and with the Lord’s command, husbands and wives have been separated because of the sin of fornication, they should seek the medicinal counsel of episcopal care, so that the bishop may know how, according to the quality and extent of the wound, to apply the appropriate measure and strength of the remedy.

For in this way the Lord, once at the supper on the day before he was to suffer for the restoration and salvation of all who had perished in Adam, blessed with his own hands and commended with his mouth the Eucharist made from bread of flour and water, and from the chalice of the most holy altar, which is mixed with water. Every day, throughout the whole Catholic Church spread far and wide across the world, he consecrates it by the hands and mouths of priests, using the same unfailing words, for the redemption, restoration, and salvation of believers [Col. 0653C–D]. From its life-giving communion, priests cut off publicly sinful persons guilty of serious crimes that the laws publicly condemn, using a medicinal instrument; and after satisfaction has been made, they take care to restore them, as they judge appropriate, through salutary nourishment.

For the spiritual physicians of the Church—namely, the priests of the Lord—can give medicinal and salutary counsel concerning the infirmities of sins confessed privately to them. But by ecclesiastical judgment, that is, by separation from the communion of the Church, from ecclesiastical rank, or from the marital union, they cannot reasonably separate anyone unless that person has either publicly and voluntarily confessed crimes or has been openly convicted of them.

Confession or conviction has its own manner and order in ecclesiastical ranks, which is not thought necessary to set out here [Col. 0654A]. Public confession or conviction among secular persons likewise has its own manner and order, according to which they must be judged publicly. This is not because serious crimes are not forgiven through secret confession and penance as well, lest the weak in the Church be scandalized when they see the punishments of those whose causes they entirely do not know. Rather, what the knowledge of many people establishes as having been committed should be healed in the knowledge of many; the person who has sinned against the integrity of the Church should strive to offer the satisfaction owed to it; and the person who, insofar as it depended on him, has destroyed many through his example should heal many by the antidote of his humility, as Paul says of himself: “Who formerly was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (I Tim. I, 11). And again: “They saw that the one who formerly persecuted this faith now preaches it, and they glorified God in me” (Gal. I, 13).

It is also fitting that one who has offended God in the presence of many should more quickly obtain a remedy when many entreat the Lord on his behalf, as Saint Gregory writes to Felix, bishop of Sicily, in the twelfth book, letter 32:

“The wicked must be separated from the good, and the unjust from the just, so that at least through their shame they may recognize their consciences and turn from their wickedness. If they appear incorrigible, they must be separated from the faithful until satisfaction is made, according to the sentence of our Savior, who, among other instructions concerning a sinning brother, says: ‘If your brother sins against you’ (Matt. XVIII, 15), until the point at which it is said, ‘Let him be to you as a gentile and a publican.’ Therefore, by these and many other authorities of the holy Fathers, the wicked must be separated from the good, lest the just perish for the unjust, as it is written: ‘The just man perishes for the ungodly’ (Eccl. VII, 16).

“Discernment must always be made between the good and the wicked, as between goats and sheep. Manifest sins must not be cleansed by hidden correction; those who do harm openly must be rebuked publicly, so that, while they are healed by open reproof, those who have sinned by imitating them may be corrected. When one is rebuked, many are amended; and it is better that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through the license of one.

“Nor is it surprising that this principle is maintained among human beings, since we often observe it among animals as well: those that appear to have mange or scab are separated from the healthy, lest the others be condemned or perish through their disease. For it is better that the wicked be corrected openly than that the good perish on their account” [Col. 0654B–D].

These things have been said to explain why we have set out the laws: so that married persons, whether through love of God or because of the admission of sin, may be separated with the knowledge of the priests from whom they received the blessing for entering marriage.

But since the present subject is the separation of a husband and wife—not a separation undertaken out of love for perpetual continence, nor yet because of an openly established crime, but because of a certain suspicion—it is necessary that this matter be examined by men of that order, namely, by married men, and judged and brought to a conclusion according to the Christian laws arranged by God, with the most equitable examination. Wherever, in this matter, priestly compassion or the medicinal severity of ecclesiastical authority finds its proper place, it should offer itself without difficulty to the children of the Church and to the judges of justice, and should even take the initiative.

Since it is written, “Do not move the boundaries established by your fathers” (Prov. XXII, 28), and since their examples are true instruction for us, we have thought it necessary to recall the following event. Some of our number were present in the time of Louis Augustus of holy memory, at the palace of Attigny, when, in the universal synod of the whole empire, in the presence also of legates of the Roman See, and in the general assembly, a woman of no ignoble birth named Northild publicly brought before the emperor certain shameful matters between herself and her husband, whose name was Agembert [Col. 0655A–B].

The emperor sent her to the synod so that episcopal authority might determine what ought to be done. But the assembly of bishops referred the matter to the judgment of laymen and married men, so that they themselves might judge between her and her husband, since they were knowledgeable about such matters and fully equipped with the laws of the world. The woman submitted herself to their legal judgments and agreed to abide without appeal by whatever they decreed concerning her case. If there was any crime, then, after their judgment, she was to request from episcopal authority the appropriate measure of penance; and the bishops did not refuse to impose it upon her according to what the sacred canons had prescribed.

The noble laymen approved the bishops’ discernment, because judgment over their marriages was not taken away from them, nor was civil law prejudiced by the priestly order [Col. 0655C]. They issued a legal ruling concerning the woman’s complaint and brought her case to an end by legal judgment.

So let them likewise bring this case, which concerns persons of the highest rank, before their own court and judge it according to what they see to accord with an equitable judgment. Let them recognize most carefully that a marriage legally contracted cannot be dissolved by any means except, as we have said above, together with spiritual separation, or through manifest confession or open conviction of bodily fornication.

“For,” as blessed Augustine says in the book *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 15, “a man may not dismiss his wife, nor a wife her husband, even on account of sterility; nor may anyone join himself to another on account of children, for whose sake a wife is taken. If they do so, they themselves commit adultery with those to whom they have joined themselves. For the bond of marriage remains, even if the offspring for whose sake it was contracted does not follow because of manifest sterility” [Col. 0655D].

And in the same book, chapter 16: “Therefore, just as it is better to die of hunger than to eat food sacrificed to idols, so it is better to die without children than to seek offspring through an unlawful union.”

In the books addressed to Pollentius *On Adulterous Marriages*, the reader will find it repeatedly and insistently affirmed that “a husband cannot be separated from his wife, nor a wife from her husband, except for the sole reason of fornication; they may, however, be separated in such a way that they either remain unmarried or are reconciled to one another.”

Saint Jerome likewise writes in his commentary on Matthew: “His disciples,” he says, “say to the Lord: ‘If such is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not advantageous to marry’ (Matt. XIX, 10). The burden of wives is a heavy one if they may not be dismissed except for the reason of fornication. For what if she is drunk, irascible, badly behaved, extravagant, gluttonous, restless, quarrelsome, or abusive? Must such a woman be retained? Whether we wish it or not, she must be retained. For although we were free, we voluntarily subjected ourselves to servitude” [Col. 0656A].

And likewise, in his letter 147 to the presbyter Amandus: “Thus, cutting off every excuse, the Apostle defined most clearly that, while her husband is alive, a woman who marries another is an adulteress (I Cor. VII). Do not bring before me the violence of a ravisher, the persuasion of a mother, the authority of a father, crowds of relatives, the plots and contempt of servants, or the loss of household property. As long as her husband lives, even if he is an adulterer, even if he is a sodomite, even if he is covered with every disgrace, and even if she has abandoned him because of these crimes, he is still reckoned as her husband, and she may not take another man. Nor does the Apostle decree this by his own authority; rather, Christ speaks through him when he says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever takes a dismissed woman is an adulterer’ (Matt. XIX, 9)” [Col. 0656B].

To this evangelical truth and apostolic teaching, Innocent, Leo, and Gregory, the apostolic men; the African Council; Ambrose; John of Constantinople; Origen in the books corrected by blessed Jerome; the venerable presbyter Bede; and all Catholic teachers agree in this manner.

Therefore, if there were not this dominical and exceedingly clear command—so clear that Paul, when consulted about virgins, did not dare to alter anything concerning it in his advice, saying, “Concerning the married, I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she departs, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband” (I Cor. VII, 10)—or if Scripture contained a passage of such a kind that authors of differing, though not contrary, faith could draw different conclusions from it, as we find in the canons, we would follow the opinion of the many and of those possessing the greater authority. But now we cannot and must not think or agree otherwise than as we read in the divinely inspired writings.

Indeed, Saint Paul joined fornicators and adulterers with those who serve idols, saying that they will not possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. VI, 9), and he commanded that food not be taken with such persons. He also wrote: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (I Cor. V, 11; Heb. XIII, 4).

Those very men, moreover, who—as we have shown—are held before God under the same judgment of the law as women, if they commit adultery and are condemned to an even more serious punishment, insofar as they are the heads and rulers of women, that is, of the weaker sex and more fragile vessel, must not presume an improper license to condemn their adulterous wives without judgment.

For the Lord says in the Law concerning a slave who is his master's property: “Whoever strikes his male slave or his female slave with a rod, and they die under his hand, shall be guilty of a crime” (Exod. XXI, 20). Accordingly, the sacred canons prescribe that if anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of a judge, he must expiate the shedding of blood by two years of excommunication (Council of Agde, canon 62) [Col. 0656D–0657A]. And again: “If a mistress beats her female slave with whips, and the slave dies as a result, if this happened intentionally, she is to be admitted to Communion after seven years; if it happened accidentally, after five years, while the authority concerning the provision of Viaticum is preserved, for this may not be denied to anyone even at the final breath” (Council of Elvira, canon 5).

If, then, such equity and goodness must be maintained in every Christian household even toward those of servile condition, between master and slave, how much greater, richer, and fuller must it be preserved between husband and wife, between man and spouse, between head and body? For, as the Apostle teaches, “the man is the head of the woman, as Christ is the head of the Church, he himself the Savior of the body” (Eph. V, 22). Thus men ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church [Col. 0657B].

Let the Christian husband consider how much diligence, inspection, and medical judgment he would exercise if a foot, hand, genitals, or any other member of his body began to rot or to be consumed by cancer: he would either bear with it so that it might be healed, or cut it away from himself if it could not be healed. Let him act in the same way toward a member—or rather, toward the body—that is, toward his wife.

Thus the same Apostle says again: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word” (Eph. V, 25).

Certainly, the apostolic men commend such great, such distinctive, and such excellent love between husband and wife, while preserving within marriage the precedence of the man and the subjection of the woman, so that in that union, once instituted by God and lawfully joined, there neither ought nor can be anything greater.

For what is more venerable than that marriage should be a mystery of Christ and the Church? What is holier than for husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the Church, giving himself for her in order to sanctify and cleanse her? What is dearer and more closely united than for the man to be the head of the woman, as Christ is the head of the Church, he himself the Savior of the body?

He also testifies in the Gospel concerning this unity of marriage, saying: “Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. For, he says, the two shall be one flesh” (Matt. XIX, 5).

The Apostle adds further: “Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them” (Col. III, 19) [Col. 0657C–D].

If, therefore, husbands must not be bitter toward their wives, how much less may they be savage, cruel, bloodthirsty, observing no law, no reason, and no judgment toward them—things that Christian religion requires even toward slaves—but, as soon as they please, stirred up by impious anger and fury, have their wives led away to the slaughterhouse to be butchered, and command them to be killed by the swords of their cooks like rams and pigs? Or even slaughter them themselves with their own hands and swords, failing entirely to give themselves for their wives in imitation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in order to sanctify and cleanse them; instead, through the zeal of their own lust, they destroy them forever and impiously stain themselves with their blood. In such a case, legitimate judgment ought to be awaited all the more justly, since marital jealousy can so easily result in homicide [Col. 0658A].

Some of these men are found to be so savage and devoid of human feeling, possessing rather the ferocity of beasts, that after killing their former wives on suspicion of adultery—without any law, reason, or judgment, but solely from their own animosity and cruelty, or because their lust is directed toward another wife or concubine—they, still dripping with fresh blood, not only show no remorse through penance or satisfy God and the Church by any humility, but, exulting in their pride, approach the altar of Christ without hesitation and presume indiscriminately to touch the sacred mysteries.

Concerning those who receive his mysteries in this condition, Christ always says what he said about Judas: “Behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table” (Luke XXII, 21). They could have been absolved from the judgment concerning their sinful wives without endangering themselves mortally; but by refusing to await that judgment and anticipating the judgment of the divine law, they incur the judgment of condemnation [Col. 0658B].

Let such men defend themselves as much as they wish, whether by worldly laws, if any exist, or by human customs. Nevertheless, if they are Christians, they should know that on the day of judgment they will be judged neither by Roman, Salic, nor Burgundian laws, but by divine and apostolic laws.

Although, in a Christian kingdom, the public laws themselves ought also to be Christian, that is, suitable and consonant with Christianity. For the law of almighty God divides into three categories everything that human beings appear to possess or hold subject to themselves in worldly affairs, when it defines and says in the precepts of the Decalogue: “You shall not desire your neighbor’s wife, nor his male slave, nor his female slave, nor his ox, nor his sheep, nor his ass, nor anything that belongs to him” (Exod. XX, 7).

In these words, there is no doubt that the dignity of a wife must be considered in one way, the condition of male and female slaves in another, and the worthlessness of brute animals or inanimate things in yet another. Therefore, all these matters must be handled according to their respective merits and distinguished and judged according to their proper degrees [Col. 0658C].

We say this so that such men may consider that, in an improper ordering, they hold their wives in a lower condition than their servants. If a master who kills a slave without the knowledge of a judge is guilty of homicide, and cannot expiate the shedding of blood except through penance, what must be thought concerning a wife?

We do not say this in order to trample upon or prohibit due judgments. Rather, we urge that such judgments be sought and followed, knowing that the law of God—by which every Christian will be judged on the day of judgment, so as to receive according to his works—permits no guilty person, not even adulterers or adulteresses, to be punished except under lawful judges and witnesses. God even commanded such persons to be stoned publicly by the people in a public judgment.

Thus, when Susanna was falsely accused of adultery (Dan. XIII), we read that she was condemned in a public judgment and acquitted in a public judgment. The woman who was truly caught in adultery (John VIII) was first brought, according to the law, before the Pharisees, who exercised judicial authority among the people, and then also, as a test, brought before the judgment of the Lord, who did not reject judgment but commanded that it be carried out justly and by just persons [Col. 0658D–0659A].

Therefore, if any woman caught in adultery comes before episcopal judgment, whether on the basis of the Law of Moses promulgated by the Lord in the Old Testament or on the basis of the public laws of Christians, which the holy Church embraces, there is a most evident and entirely sufficient remedy, prepared by the salutary tradition of the apostolic men, through which, without any error of uncertainty, she may be healed by divine grace and ecclesiastical compassion.

## INTERROGATION VI

Third, we ask that you send us your reply concerning the charge of fornication and abortion brought against the aforesaid woman. Since judgment has now been rendered, what is your opinion of that judgment? For some say that a judgment customarily carried out by means of hot or cold water, or by means of hot iron, has no authority or credibility, but that these are inventions of human judgment, in which falsehood very often takes the place of truth through magical practices; and therefore such judgments ought not to be believed.

We also ask that you write back what you think about the purgation by oath, and what authority it possesses. We ask whether it can be true, as some say, that because of the secret confession made by the woman herself—and the man who received that confession is also a witness—her representative, when he underwent the judgment, emerged unburned. They also say that the woman’s intention concerned another brother of hers bearing the same name when she sent her representative to the judgment, and that for this reason she was not burned in that judgment.

Furthermore, if any fraud is discovered in the judgment or in the oath after the purgation has been given, should the case purged by the judgment or oath be brought back into legal judgment? [Col. 0659B–C]

## RESPONSE

But if the matter concerns fornication and abortion before the marriage was contracted—charges for which we have learned that the aforesaid woman is held responsible—we must first come to the judgment of examination, by which we heard that she had been, as it were, purged, and only then set out what we think on the basis of the other evidence. In this way, perhaps this purgation should be considered valid, and the case may come to rest without further labor; but if it is proved invalid and reasonably so, we shall return to the vast sea of the inquiry [Col. 0659D].

For, as Paul says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. XI, 1). John of Constantinople explains this as follows:

“Those things,” he says, “which are not seen and are hoped for are thought to be without substance, but faith gives them substance. Thus the resurrection has not yet occurred and does not yet exist in substance, but faith in a certain hope makes it subsist in our soul. This is the evidence—that is, the inference—of things that are not seen.”

For inference concerns matters that are especially evident. Faith, therefore, is the vision of things that do not appear, and it leads to the same assurance as those things that are seen. Nor can it be called faith unless, concerning things that are not seen, someone possesses greater assurance than concerning things that are seen [Col. 0660A].

For this reason, to investigate and establish what is doubtful or obscure, and to present it as though to the sight of the eyes—things that cannot be established or proved by the judicial procedure of the law—authority has sanctioned two means: judgment and an oath, which in common usage is called a sacrament. In it, by the eyes of faith, one perceives what cannot be seen by the eyes of the body.

Concerning judgment, it is written in the Book of Numbers (Num. 5:12):

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: If a man’s wife has gone astray and, scorning her husband, has slept with another man, while the husband has been unable to discover this, but the adultery remains concealed and cannot be proved by witnesses, because she was not found in the act; if the spirit of jealousy has stirred up the man against his wife, whether she has been defiled or is being accused under a false suspicion.”

And after describing the judgment to which she must accordingly be subjected, he adds: “But if she has not been defiled, she shall be innocent; and if she is found to have been defiled, the husband shall be without guilt, and she shall bear her iniquity” (ibid., 28).

Regarding an oath or solemn declaration, the Apostle Paul says to the Hebrews: “For when God made his promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself. For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and every dispute among them is ended by an oath for confirmation” (Heb. 6:15).

Pope Gregory the Younger likewise wrote through the presbyter Denuald to Bishop Boniface (Letter 11, chapter 3): “If a presbyter,” he says, “or any priest accused by the people has no reliable witnesses who can establish the truth of the charge brought against him, an oath shall be introduced, and he shall produce as witness to the purity of his innocence the one to whom all things are naked and open; and thus he shall remain in his own rank” (Col. 0660C).

This purgation by solemn declaration is extremely common both in ecclesiastical and in secular laws, and it is clear that it arose from the truth of faith already in the earliest centuries. Therefore, reverently passing over in silence what is said in the Old and New Testaments by the Deity himself:

“By myself I have sworn,” says the Lord (Gen. 22:16);

“And the Lord swore, and he will not repent” (Ps. 109:4);

and many other passages.

And: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” For the Lord greatly commends what he pronounces in this way, because, if one may put it so, his oath is expressed in the words “Amen, I say to you.” *Amen* means “true,” yet it has not been translated. It could have been rendered, “I tell you the truth,” but neither the Greek translator dared to do this, nor the Latin one. Thus it remained untranslated, so that it might possess the honor of a veil of secrecy—not so that it would be denied, but lest, once laid bare, it should become commonplace.

Therefore, “I tell you the truth” is spoken by Truth, who, even had he not said it, could not possibly lie; nevertheless, he commends and emphasizes it, as though awakening those who sleep, making them attentive, and refusing to be despised.

Abraham also said to his servant: “Put your hand under my thigh and swear to me by the God of heaven” (Gen. 24:2). And the king said to Abraham, “Swear to me by God,” and Abraham said, “I will swear” (Gen. 21:23). Isaac and King Abimelech also swore to one another (Gen. 26). And in Jeremiah: “I have sworn by my great name,” says the Lord (Jer. 44:26). David likewise says: “I have sworn and determined” (Ps. 118:106).

In the New Testament we read that the Apostle said: “God is my witness” (Rom. 1:9); and: “Behold, before God, I do not lie” (Gal. 1:20); and: “I die every day, by your glory, brothers” (1 Cor. 15:31). Anyone who wishes to search for such examples abundantly will find them in the letters of Leo and Gregory.

Finally, the Lord shows how greatly perjury must be avoided when he says in Exodus: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes the name of the Lord his God in vain” (Exod. 20:7). “In vain,” and “for no purpose,” does not mean that the act is nothing, but that for the one who takes the name of the Lord his God vainly and uselessly, it becomes harmful, as it is for one guilty of a crime.

Again, in Leviticus the Lord says: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God. I am the Lord” (Lev. 19:12). And holy David says in the psalm: “Who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive” (Ps. 14:4).

“To swear,” says Cassiodorus, “is for human beings to promise something under divine testimony. For *jurare* is said as though from *jure orare*, that is, ‘to speak justly.’ A person speaks justly when the things he promises are fulfilled.”

And Saint Ambrose, in his letter to the Emperor Valentinian (Letter 30), says: “What is swearing except confessing the divine power of the one whom you call upon as the guardian of your faith?”

It is likewise said in the psalm: “He has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor” (Ps. 23:4). Anyone who intends to act otherwise than he promises swears deceitfully, believing that it is not perjury to wickedly exploit the error of one who has been deceived into trusting him.

Hence Saint Jerome says: “There are many who swear deceitfully in order to deceive their neighbor; this is detested by the Father of lights, as Peter says: ‘You have not lied to human beings, but to God’” (Acts 5:4; the source text reads “Acts 54”).

And it is written in the Book of Kings that when famine had occurred in David’s days for three consecutive years, and David consulted the oracle of the Lord, the Lord said: “It is because of Saul and his house, and because he killed the Gibeonites” (2 Kings 21). The children of Israel had sworn to them, but Saul wished to strike them out of zeal, supposedly on behalf of the children of Israel and Judah, saying that Joshua had gratuitously allowed those same Gibeonites to live. From this it is evident how great the impiety of perjury is, since the Lord imposed such a punishment upon it (Col. 0661C–D).

The prophet Jeremiah likewise says: “Behold, you trust in lying words that will not benefit you: stealing, killing, committing adultery, swearing falsely” (Jer. 7:9). We must therefore consider how great a crime it is to swear falsely, since the prophet joined it with adultery, murder, and theft—acts whose perpetrators, the Apostle says, “shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9).

And Jerome, in his exposition of the same prophet, says:

“It could happen that some among the people were found who simulated the worship of God and swore by the Lord. He forestalls this by declaring that God is pleased not with empty words but with the truth of faith, and he will say: ‘I do not love those who swear by me and swear falsely, but those whose hearts and lips agree.’

“And in the prophet Zechariah: ‘For every thief, as it is written there, shall be judged, and every one who swears shall likewise be judged.’ ‘I will bring it forth,’ says the Lord of hosts, ‘and it shall enter the house of the thief and the house of the one who swears falsely by my name; it shall remain in its midst and consume it, its timbers and its stones’” (Zech. 5:3).

And in the prophet Ezekiel: “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he made void and whose covenant with him he broke, in the midst of Babylon he shall die’” (Ezek. 17:16).

“For,” says Jerome, “Zedekiah had despised the oath in order to break the treaty; and after doing all these things, he will not escape.”

Jerome also says: “Behold, he gave his hand to the king of Egypt, surrendered himself, and committed sacrilege by perjury against God.”

And again Jerome says:

“Lest we should think that the oath, treaty, and covenant belonged to the Babylonian king or to Zedekiah who had made it, the text continues: ‘In the transgression by which he despised me.’ Therefore, whoever despises an oath despises the one by whom he swore and does injury to the one whose name his adversary trusted. Whatever Nebuchadnezzar did against Zedekiah (2 Kings 25), he did not do by his own strength, but by the anger of God, in whose name the oath had been violated. For we read that Zedekiah was captured, taken to Riblah, and there, after his sons had been killed, blinded and shut up like a wild beast in a cage, and transported to Babylon.”

And Saint Cyprian, in the ninth degree of abuse, says that “it is the duty of a king to destroy the impious from the land and not permit parricides and perjurers to live.”

And Saint Gregory, in a homily on the Gospel concerning the Martyrs, says: “The sick come to their extinguished bodies and are healed; perjurers come and are tormented by a demon; those possessed by demons come and are freed.”

From this, then, we must conclude how great a sin it is to swear falsely by the name of the Lord and of his saints—a sin that, as we have already stated, Saint Jerome calls sacrilege.

We must also understand how greatly the rashness of swearing should be avoided, unless great necessity requires it, or unless the good of others who do not believe the truth requires that they be brought to believe, and peace and concord are to be served by a solemn declaration.

The Lord also teaches this in the Gospel, saying: “Do not swear” (Matt. 5:34). And James says in his letter: “Above all things, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath; but let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no,’ so that you may not fall under judgment” (James 5:12)—namely, under the judgment into which Herod fell, so that he would necessarily either perjure himself or, by avoiding perjury, perpetrate another crime.

But if it should happen that we have sworn something rashly, and its observance would plainly lead to a worse outcome, let us know that we must freely change it by wiser counsel; and, when necessity presses, it is better for us to commit perjury than, in order to avoid perjury, to turn aside into another and more serious crime (1 Sam. 25).

David, for example, swore by the Lord that he would kill Nabal, a foolish and wicked man, and destroy everything belonging to him. But at the first entreaty of Abigail, a prudent woman, he immediately withdrew his threats, returned his sword to its sheath, and did not regret that by such perjury he had incurred any guilt (Col. 0663A).

Herod swore to give the dancing girl whatever she asked of him; and, lest he should be called perjured by his guests, he stained the banquet itself with blood, making the prophet’s death the reward of the dance.

This moderation must be observed not only in swearing but in everything we do: if we should happen to fall into the snares of the crafty enemy in such a way that we cannot rise without some contamination of sin, we should seek the escape by which we see that we shall suffer the lesser danger. It is like those who, shut in by hostile walls and wishing to escape, see that every approach to the gates is barred; they must choose the place from which to leap where, since the wall is lower, they will incur the least danger in falling.

Accordingly, drawing from the holy Scriptures and the sayings of Catholics, a certain orthodox and distinguished poet wrote among other things:

> But if the cause of swearing presses and constrains you,  
> Do it with pure words; do it with a devout mind.  
>   
> Do not think that by verbal craft you can deceive the Thunderer,  
> To whom nothing is hidden, to whom your hearts lie open:  
>   
> He hears not according to how you swear, but according to how  
> The one to whom you swear thinks you have sworn,  
> And thus you are liable to both—  
> To God, whose name you seek to take in vain,  
> And to your companion, whom you prepare to deceive by dark fraud.  
>   
> If you swear in order to commit a crime, let your vows be void:  
> This is the more serious offense, though both are wounds.  
>   
> Small wounds weary less, greater wounds more;  
> Happy is the one who departs wounded by none.

But concerning judgment: after the Lord had spoken of his coming for the future judgment, which will be by fire, he recalled the judgment that took place by water: “As it happened in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man” (Luke 17:26). And when he referred to the fact that he judged Sodom by fire, he said: “Likewise, as it happened in the days of Lot.”

From ancient times Christianity, situated between judgments already accomplished and those still to come, established and frequently employed judgment by water, which had taken place under Noah (Gen. 19), by which the innocent were saved in the ark of faith and the guilty condemned; and also judgment in fiery water, as occurred under Lot by fire and will occur at the coming of the Son of Man.

Peter bears witness to this when he says: “The heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God; through these the world that then existed was destroyed, being overwhelmed by water. But the heavens and earth that now exist are reserved by the same word for fire, kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly people” (2 Pet. 3:6–7).

He teaches openly that it is not other heavens that will perish by fire than those that perished by water—that is, these empty and cloudy expanses of the windy air. For it should not be believed that the water of the Flood, which rose only fifteen cubits above the mountain peaks, reached beyond the boundaries of the air and ether. But wherever the water was able to reach, there, in accordance with the foregoing sentence of blessed Peter, the fire of judgment will also reach.

Since it is written, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. 24:35), and again, “The earth stands forever” (Eccl. 1:4), we must understand that heaven and earth pass away with respect to the appearance they now possess, while they continue forever in their essence. “The form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:31); and, it says, “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (2 Pet. 3:13). These should not be believed to be other ones, but these very ones are renewed. They pass away and remain, because they are cleansed of the form they now possess and are preserved forever in their own nature. Hence it is written: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Ps. 101:27).

Therefore, the making of fiery water for investigating these two judgments joined together as one—the judgment already accomplished by water and the judgment yet to be accomplished by fire—although they differ according to the variation of times, is one in the mystery of its operation. In both, the saints are delivered unharmed and the reprobate are punished and condemned.

Authority is believed to have handed this down to the Church, which the ark of the Flood prefigured. The same authority also established that, through the breath of the priest, the Holy Spirit should be breathed upon the baptismal waters—the Spirit who, at the very beginning of the world, was borne over the waters—so that nature might already then conceive the power of sanctifying waters; and that, in order that the rust of all sins may be burned away, a wax candle kindled with a consecrated flame should be kept immersed therein until the consecration of the same font is completed by him who, washing away through the waters the crimes of the guilty world, marked the image of regeneration in the very outpouring of the Flood. Thus, through the mystery of one and the same element, an end was made to vices and a beginning given to virtues by him who is to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

For in the same baptism, in which Moses the prophet significantly placed wood, as though into a myrrh-scented spring, and it was sweetened, and in which the cross of Christ’s blood is proclaimed by the Lord’s priest, three things are one—not in nature, but in the mystery of their operation: the blood of redemption, the spirit of sanctification, and the water of washing.

There, after the unclean spirit has been expelled and exorcised, it departs from the human being; judgment is made concerning the person; and the ruler of this world is cast out. The one who did not stand in the truth—the liar and father of lies—is separated from the truth of nature. This nature, created in the image of God and reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, is restored to its origin, cleansed inwardly and outwardly by faith, and proved innocent of every fabrication of falsehood and of every kind of wickedness.

Even if someone should decide that judgment by cold water alone, or by the fire of any element, suffices him, believing with unwavering faith in the author and governor of the elements—whom all the elements faithfully perceive when he is invoked—just as in the case of Moses’ staff, the water changed into blood, and blood again into water, the rock that gave water, and under Elisha the salt or wood thrown into the water, in accordance with the faith that is “the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1), it makes no difference.

For cold water, just as it is consecrated in baptism, raised the innocent with the ark to heaven in the Flood, while the guilty perished; and the Sodomites were punished by fire. In the Book of Numbers, the cold water in which the Lord commanded imprecations to be washed away, when drunk by the adulterous woman, is said to have caused her thigh to rot. And the Apostle John escaped unharmed from a cauldron of boiling oil.

Whoever chooses fiery water should understand that, when the terrifying Judge comes for the future judgment, storm and fire will accompany him, as it is written: “Fire shall burn before him, and a mighty storm around him” (Ps. 49:3), so that the storm may test those whom the fire will consume. But that future fire will be passable for the saints, who will be snatched up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, while it will inflame his enemies all around.

Since the discussion has turned to judgment for purification by boiling or cold water, let us report what certain people of keen intelligence add when they inquire into the matter.

“It is evident,” they say, “that in fiery water the guilty are boiled, while the innocent are released unboiled, because righteous Lot escaped unharmed from the fire of Sodom, and the future fire that will go before the terrifying Judge will be harmless to the saints but will burn the wicked, like the Babylonian furnace of old. That furnace did not touch or distress the children at all, nor cause them any harm, but, burning their bonds, it consumed the Chaldean servants of the king who had stoked it” (Col. 0665A–B).

But in the judgment of cold water it does not appear to hold that the innocent are submerged and the guilty float, since in the judgment of the Flood the innocent were raised with the ark and the guilty perished by drowning. The Egyptians pursuing the Hebrews through the Red Sea, when the Lord looked upon them during the morning watch through the pillar of fire and cloud, were submerged like lead in mighty waters, and not one of them survived. The children of Israel stood on the shore and saw the Egyptians dead.

Nor could the earth bear the unbelievers and sinners when it opened and swallowed Dathan and covered the assembly of Abiron. Yet the instability of the water supported Peter when he trusted in faith and walked upon it; but when he doubted in faith, it swallowed him when he was already almost submerged, until Christ’s right hand lifted him up.

The Catholic Fathers, explaining the statement of Peter’s letter about the figure of baptism in the ark of the Flood, say that it is not in other waters but in those very waters that heretics and evil Christians are plunged into hell, while every orthodox and just person is lifted up to the heavenly kingdoms.

But we must know, as blessed Gregory says (Homily 26 on the Gospels), “that if a divine work is comprehended by reason, it is not wonderful; nor does faith have merit when human reason provides the proof.”

And since the Apostle Paul says: “Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1), it is plainly clear that faith is the proof of those things that cannot appear; for things that appear no longer require faith but recognition.

“But these very works of our Redeemer” (Gregory, ibid.), “which cannot in any way be comprehended from themselves, must be assessed through another work of his, so that more wonderful deeds may provide faith in wonderful things.”

For this reason the Lord deigned to explain certain passages of Scripture himself, so that we might know to seek the meanings of things even in those passages that he did not wish to explain himself.

Let those who demand the proof of human reason in divine judgments and in the signs of miracles therefore receive this answer: the ark that contained the righteous, by which the Church of the faithful, built in faith in the Holy Trinity through the incarnation of Jesus Christ, was signified, and all those of whom the Lord said, “The end of all flesh has come before me, for the earth is filled with iniquity because of them; and behold, I will destroy them together with the earth” (Gen. 6:13), were covered by the overflowing water, yet not all were submerged. The innocent were saved, and the guilty were punished, as it is written:

“Noah entered, and his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives with him into the ark, because of the waters of the Flood” (Gen. 7:7).

And shortly afterward:

“All the fountains of the great deep were broken open, and the floodgates of heaven were opened, and rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights.”

And again:

“The waters increased and lifted the ark high above the earth.”

And shortly afterward:

“All flesh that moved upon the earth was destroyed; only Noah remained, and those who were with him in the ark.”

And again shortly afterward:

“The fountains of the deep and the floodgates of heaven were closed.”

A single cloud was made dark for the Egyptians and luminous for the Hebrews, as it is written again:

“And the angel of God who went before the camp of Israel moved behind them, and the pillar of cloud with him; leaving its place in front, it stood behind them, between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel” (Exod. 14:20).

“It was a dark cloud, yet it illuminated the night, so that they could not approach one another throughout the whole night.”

And one and the same staff, extended over the waters—which stood like a wall on the right and on the left—led the children of Israel across, as it is written (Wis. 10:18), “through overwhelming water,” while it overwhelmed the Egyptians in the midst of the waves, so that not one of those whom the Israelites saw dead on the shore of the sea survived.

The Lord had looked upon them, as we have said, during the morning watch through the pillar of fire and cloud. “He spread out a cloud as a covering for them, and fire to give them light by night” (Ps. 104:39): namely, Christ, who is the pillar of light, driving away the darkness of unbelief and pouring the light of truth and spiritual grace into human affections; and, through the pillar of cloud, the Holy Spirit.

In this baptism, just as in the Flood, the type of baptism was already being displayed.

Let us add further that Elijah invoked the name of the Lord his God, and fire descended from heaven. Elisha also invoked the name of the Lord, and the iron of an axe was raised from the water to its wooden handle and floated upon the waters. The nature of iron is heavier than the fluidity of water; therefore, we perceive that grace is greater than nature.

Regarding all these matters, the explanation of blessed Ambrose will suffice, so that the correspondence may be gathered and it may be understood why, in the judgment of cold water, one person is submerged and another lifted up.

For he says in the Book of the Sacraments, or Mysteries (Book 2, chapter 6):

“Nevertheless, lest the fraud or snares of the devil should prevail in this world, baptism was devised. Hear what Scripture says about this baptism—or rather, what the Son of God says: because the Pharisees, who refused to be baptized with the baptism of John, rejected the counsel of God. Therefore, baptism is the counsel of God.”

And shortly afterward:

“When you are submerged, that sentence is dissolved: ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go.’ The sentence is fulfilled, and a place is made for heavenly grace and remedy. Therefore, water comes from the earth. But the condition of our life did not permit us to be covered by earth and to rise again from earth. Moreover, it is not earth that washes, but water washes; therefore, the font is like a tomb.”

Furthermore, as the Apostle says: “All Scripture is inspired by God and useful for teaching, for refutation, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, so that the person of God may be complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Tim. 3:16).

And as we read in the sayings of the Catholic Fathers, the divine word is a pearl that may be pierced from every side. Whoever produces testimonies from the Scriptures for the instruction of the faithful is not a fabricator of falsehood, even if he has explained them differently from the understanding held by those through whom they were spoken.

With due regard for the understanding of our predecessors, I shall therefore say what, in accordance with the smallness of my talent, I suspect may be carved out by inference from their words.

The holy Apostle teaches that the Red Sea, through which our fathers passed under the leadership of Moses, was baptism reddened by the blood of Christ. Moses himself prefigured Christ the leader who, through baptism, led us from Egyptian slavery to the promised land—that is, from slavery to sin and domination by death into the freedom of the glory of the children of God and into the kingdom of eternal life.

So too the rock that followed the people through the desert prefigured him who follows us in the wilderness of this age through his mysteries.

Hence the same Apostle says concerning baptism: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death; therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. 6:3–4).

“What does ‘we were baptized into his death’ mean?” asks John Chrysostom. “It means that we too should die, just as he did. The cross is baptism. Therefore, what the cross and tomb of Christ are, baptism has become for us, although not in exactly the same way. For this reason he did not say ‘planted together with death,’ but ‘with the likeness of death’: he himself died and was buried in the flesh, whereas we died in sin in both respects.”

From these words it may be gathered that one who has been buried with Christ through baptism into death, liberated from death through that same baptism, and then returned through sin to the same slavery and death, fulfills the saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:4, 20).

Let him be planted in the likeness of death in the water, so that, whether he is proved guilty and, willingly or unwillingly—for good things are often done to the unwilling—confesses and is again freed from the death of the sin he committed through the confession of amendment and correction; or whether, shown innocent by God’s judgment, he is not held by us among the guilty of sin, having been planted in the likeness of death in the water.

For the sea, as has been shown above, signifies baptism and retains nothing dead within itself; as it is written, it cast the dead Egyptians upon the shore. Therefore, the dead Egyptian (Exod. 14:31)—that is, one subject to sin—so long as he remains in the death of his sin by denying it, is neither received nor retained by the water sanctified through the invocation of the truth, which is Christ.

But let him come forth, bound by the cords of his iniquities, from the hiding places of an evil conscience by confessing; and through confession of the truth let him be buried in the water, as though planted in the likeness of the death of the most true Truth, and liberated by that same Truth.

Let the person who is to be examined be tied with a rope and lowered into the water, because, as it is written, “each person is bound by the cords of his sins.” He appears to be bound for two reasons: so that he may be unable either to commit any fraud in the judgment, or, if the water receives him as innocent, to perish in the water, but may be withdrawn in time.

Lazarus, too, who had been dead for four days and by whom anyone buried beneath the weight of crimes is signified, is read to have been buried bound in grave cloths, and to have come forth from the tomb still bound in those same cloths when the Lord called him; at the Lord’s command, he was then unbound by the disciples.

Likewise, the person bound for examination in judgment is lowered into the water; he is drawn back while still bound; and he is either immediately acquitted by the judges once purified by the judgment, or he is examined by the judgment while bound until his purification.

We also read in sacred history that Elijah came to the Jordan with his disciple Elisha. He wrapped his cloak and struck the waters with it; they were divided, and both crossed. Afterward Elisha lifted up Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen from him, and, coming to the Jordan, struck the waters and, having invoked God, divided them as Elijah had done and crossed.

The Jordan rightly expresses the flow of our mortality, because *Jordan* in Latin is said to mean “their descent,” namely, the descent of Christians.

As Gregory says (Moralia 33, chapter 6): “Since the author of our redemption deigned to be baptized in the river Jordan, the multitude of those who are held within the sacrament of baptism is rightly expressed by the name Jordan.”

Hence it is written in Job concerning the ancient enemy of the human race: “He trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job 40:18). For after carrying off all unbelievers from the beginning of the world, he still presumes that he can receive the faithful as well. Every day he devours with the mouth of his deadly persuasion those whose evil life is at variance with their confession of faith.

Thus, as though the water were struck with Elijah’s cloak wrapped around it, it is divided and a passage is prepared through it when such people, as we have stated from the words of Saint Gregory, are bound and lowered into the water.

The water is divided, as it were, when it either receives certain people and shows them to be innocent, or rejects others and demonstrates that they are guilty. A passage is prepared when some are judged transferable from those reckoned among the guilty to the innocent, or when others, after their denial, are assigned by a declared judgment among the guilty who are liable to punishment.

For when a person who is thought guilty, as well as one who truly is guilty, is lowered into the water for examination, the Lord is invoked by those who lower him, in a certain likeness to the form of baptism, so that the truth being sought may be revealed and he may deign to enlighten the darkness of our ignorance, lest either an innocent person be unjustly condemned by us or a guilty person escape punishment through his denial or through diabolical fraud.

The person who is lowered into the water for examination also confirms by his response and devotion the invocation of those invoking the Lord, in a way according to the form preceding baptism, as Saint Ambrose says in the Book of the Sacraments (Book 2, chapter 7):

“You were asked, ‘Do you believe in God the almighty Father?’ You said, ‘I believe,’ and you were submerged—that is, you were buried. Again you were asked, ‘Do you believe in our Lord Jesus Christ and in his cross?’ You said, ‘I believe,’ and you were submerged; therefore you were also buried with Christ. For whoever is buried with Christ rises with Christ.

“A third time you were asked, ‘Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?’ You said, ‘I believe.’ A third time you were submerged, so that the threefold confession might absolve the manifold fall of your earlier life.

“Finally, to offer you an example, the holy Apostle Peter, after he appeared to have fallen during the Lord’s Passion through the human condition—he who had previously denied him—was afterward questioned three times by Christ whether he loved Christ, in order to erase and undo that fall. Then he said: ‘Lord, you know that I love you’ (John 21:17). He said it three times so that he might be absolved three times.”

Thus, if a person found guilty in judgment should happen to be suspected of several matters, he must be examined again and again until he is proved by a confession of amendment.

And for this purpose let us take up the words of Saint Ambrose:

“Finally, to offer you an example, the holy Apostle Peter, after he appeared to have fallen during the Lord’s Passion through the weakness of the human condition—he who had previously denied him—was afterward questioned three times by Christ whether he loved Christ, in order to erase and undo that fall. Then he said: ‘Lord, you know that I love you.’ He said it three times so that he might be absolved three times.”

And since, as we showed above, baptism is judgment by divine authority—for which reason *Jordan*, designating baptism, is interpreted as “the stream of judgment,” by which the prince of this world and his father, the liar, are cast out—and since baptism is also God’s counsel, holy men, investigating things unknown, discovered the judgment of cold water. In this judgment of cold water, at the invocation of Truth, who is God, the person who desires to conceal the truth by a lie cannot be submerged in the waters over which the voice of the Lord God of majesty thundered. For the pure nature of water does not recognize as pure, but rejects as alien, human nature that has been cleansed through the baptismal water of every fabrication of falsehood and then infected again by lying.

And just as in baptism the unclean spirit, that is, the prince of this world, is cast out from a human being, so also one who has been repossessed through sin by the devil, namely the prince of this world, is rejected by water consecrated through the invocation of the divine name. For it is written (Matt. 12; Luke 11): “When he has gone out from a man, he returns to him when he finds him unoccupied by good works—or rather, empty—with seven other spirits more wicked than himself.”

The water recognizes such a man not as natural, like one reborn from water and the Spirit and cleansed—not by the removal of bodily filth, but by the questioning and confession of a good conscience toward God—but rather as the kind of person of whom it is written in Leviticus (Lev. 22:3): “Every man,” it says, “who approaches from your offspring those things that have been consecrated, and which the children of Israel have offered to the Lord, and in whom there is impurity, shall perish before the Lord.” It does not say, “in whom there was impurity.” His impurity is in him, since he conceals the truth by a lie. Therefore, concerning the priestly race, it says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9); and in the Apocalypse: “You have made us a kingdom for God, and priests” (Rev. 5:10). Whoever approaches those things consecrated to the Lord, so long as his impurity is in him, cannot be immersed in waters sanctified by the invocation of God so as to appear innocent; rather, he will be shown to be destined for destruction.

“Cleanse out,” says the Apostle, “the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough, as you are unleavened” (1 Cor. 5:7). It is as though he were openly saying: “The person accused of a crime and denying it, whom you cannot establish by competent witnesses according to judicial procedure, cleanse either by an oath or by God’s judgment, lest, while the accursed thing remains among you, it be said to you: ‘The accursed thing is in your midst, O Israel; you will not be able to stand before your enemies’” (Josh. 7:13).

The Apostle also says: “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness” (Eph. 5:11). Hence Augustine:

> “Do not participate”—that is, do not consent. And because merely not consenting would be insufficient if neglect of discipline followed, he says, “but rather reprove them.” An evil person does not defile you in two ways: if you do not consent and if you reprove him. Thus the sinner must be accused; and if he denies it and cannot be established according to judicial procedure, he must be examined, so that, if proved, he may be made manifest, and, if rejected, he may not be able to remain concealed. Once discovered, let him confess and repent, and he will not be held by the cord of his sins, by which he has been bound, so that he may not be submerged. Let him be washed, drenched with the saving water and watered with tears; and let them be submerged like the Egyptians, who had been corrupted by carnal corruption before the Lord, “like lead in the mighty waters” (Exod. 15). And, according to the prophet, “Let his iniquities be cast into the depths of the sea” (Mic. 7:19).

For previously he could not be submerged with his lie so as to be cleansed, until by confession he cast it from himself into the depths and emerged cleansed. Before confession, he was pressed down by the water like Elisha’s iron, until, through the invocation of the divine name, it returned to the wood. In the same way, the denier is weighed down by the burden of sin in an anxious conscience, until, declaring the wickedness of his sin to the Lord, in whose wood of the cross, as Ambrose says, the weakness of all human beings is lifted up.

This is the flood, which is also baptism, by which all sins are washed away, while only the mind and grace of the righteous are raised again—for previously they had been dead through the denial of sin.

Let the devout reader read the book of the Dialogues of blessed Gregory (book II, chapter 23), and he will find that nuns who had not been corrected, and who had been excommunicated by Saint Benedict because of their lack of correction, came out after death from their graves in the church at the time of Communion because they did not communicate; but after their reconciliation they remained in their graves. He will also find that the body of a boy-monk could not be held by the earth (ibid., chapter 24), because he did not possess Benedict’s grace; that a glass vessel was shattered by the sign of the cross made by Benedict (book II, chapter 28); and again that a glass vessel, thrown at his command into an immense precipice strewn with masses of rock because of disobedience, was preserved unharmed (ibid., chapter 7). He will find that his disciple Maurus walked upon the waters of a lake (ibid., chapter 6), and that iron was recalled from the depths of the lake into its handle through him, after the manner of Elisha.

And just as it is recorded in the divine books (2 Macc. 1:20), sacred fire, which had been hidden, was found after the passage of many years transformed into thick water; and when that same water was poured over the sacrifice that had been offered, it was consumed by divine power as though by fire. Likewise, Gideon’s sacrifice (Judg. 6:20), though covered with broth, whose abundance ordinarily extinguishes fire, was consumed through angelic agency, with fire even licking the rock.

Thus, within the mystery of one and the same element, there is both an end to vices and an origin of virtues, through the operation of the Holy Spirit in the water of holy baptism. Let the diligent reader study these things, and he will not wonder that in the judgment of cold water the innocent are received by the water, while the guilty are not received, just as in hot water the guilty are boiled while the innocent remain uncooked. For Christ, the heavenly medicine of the Father and the true physician of human salvation, when invoked by his faithful—as bodily physicians also customarily do under his inspiration—heals opposites by opposites: hot things by cold, and cold things by hot.

In the single rebellion of the ancient synagogue, the earth swallowed some, while devouring flame consumed others. And while the innocent flesh of the Savior is dipped in cold waters, the fiery sword once set against the guilty is extinguished from paradise. Likewise, by the arrangement of the elements by their creator and ruler, the same sun hardens mud and melts wax.

Let these things have been said because the unstable element, in the act of submerging, receives some on account of the faith of those who believe, while it does not receive others. Likewise, through the heat of the same element some are boiled, while others escape uncooked.

Nor should it be passed over that we read in the Capitularies of the Augusti that the judgment of cold water was forbidden—not, however, in those synodal capitularies that we have received from specific synods. Some people also foolishly say that it was forbidden for this reason: because the person who is immersed in water in the name of the Lord is, as it were, rebaptized. But we find nothing of the sort written there. Nor are we unaware that blessed Ambrose speaks of several baptisms, that is, records several proclamations concerning baptism. And the sacred canons forbid rebaptisms to all, since they must be avoided.

Nevertheless, scarcely anyone among the faithful puts himself into water even for washing without the sign of the cross or the invocation of the divine name. The Apostle commands that everything be done in the name of the Lord, yet no one supposes that he is thereby baptized with the baptism by which he was reborn from water and the Spirit.

For the word, the work of God, and all the divine sacraments are manna, which, as it is written (Wis. 16:20), “possessed every delight and the sweetness of every taste.” And just as formerly it was made into a taste according to the desire of those who received it, so these things, according to the devotion of believers, become occasions for manifestations.

Thus the Lord’s incarnation is for the ruin and resurrection of many; his cross is foolishness to those who perish, but to believers it is the power of God for salvation; and his preaching is to some “the fragrance of death unto death,” and to others “the fragrance of life unto life.” The sacrament of baptism is mockery to unbelievers, but redemption to the faithful.

The sacraments of the altar likewise are life to those who approach them devoutly, but judgment to the undevout, just as bread strengthens the life of the strong but kills the little ones. A gentle whistle calms horses but incites puppies; the sun, which melts wax, hardens mud; and to healthy eyes it is light, but to bleary eyes darkness.

As poison is death to a human being but life to a serpent, so this judgment is a manifestation of truth to those who believe firmly and rightly. To those who hesitate and doubt, however, it is recognized as an error that envelops them. For, as Paul says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). It is therefore clear, as blessed Gregory explains, that faith is the evidence of those things that cannot appear; for things that appear no longer possess faith, but recognition.

Thus, in this divine judgment, once those matters about which we previously doubted have been displayed through divine manifestation—matters that we cannot see with bodily eyes—we ought, contemplating them with the eyes of faith, to grant our belief, just as Thomas, who had previously doubted, saw one thing and believed another when he touched the Lord. Divinity could not be seen by mortal man; therefore he saw a man and confessed him as God, saying: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:26). By seeing, then, he believed; considering him to be a true man, he exclaimed that this was the God whom he could not see.

So also, because we were unable to see with bodily eyes the truth of the matter about which we doubt, we ought, believing in the divine manifestation, to praise the truth, which is God.

We say these things not in order to reproach anyone—for it is not written there why this judgment should not be performed (Rom. 14:5), but only that it should not be performed—nor are we striving to defend our own statements as though they had been made more wisely than what others have been or are able to discover from the teachings of the saints. “Each one,” after all, “abounds in his own sense.”

Let everyone take care of this one thing: that he not depart from the Catholic faith and the tradition of the apostolic see. But while humbly expressing what we think, let us be ready, if someone shows us something more appropriate, to yield without contention to sound understanding and most willingly not only to agree, but even to learn.

[Col. 0672D] Since these matters stand as described, if, as we have heard, this kind of judgment was accepted by the emperor Charles of renowned name during his lifetime, and it is established that the aforesaid woman was cleansed of the charges brought against her through the counsel of noble laymen, with the consent of the bishops and by royal decree (for otherwise it ought not to have been done), and was restored or received into the marital bed not only with the consent of the noble laymen but, as we have heard, with the reconciliation and blessing of the bishops, we cannot see why we should bring the case into question again, since the Lord says: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matt. 4:7).

And let us hear what he heard from the Lord when he said to him: “Teacher, look upon my son; behold, a spirit has seized him, and I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they could not.” And the Lord said: “O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you and endure you?” (Luke 9:38).

He heard this because, by those words, he secretly accused the apostles of inability, although the inability to heal sometimes refers not to the weakness of those who heal, but to the faith of those who are to be healed. So we too, although not with the ears of the body but on account of the merit of our unbelief, shall hear this if without cause or proper reason we remove such things, as though God’s doubtful manifestation in this judgment had involved some fraud rather than our own unbelief.

If this woman appeared guilty in the judgment, why was she received? If she was innocent, why was the case dismissed? Especially since we must believe in every way that, if her representative—who had gone out to judgment on her behalf—had been burned, she would not have wanted her accuser to be admitted again for a hearing after she had been judged guilty.

Therefore, this too must now be held: just as in the judgment of baptism the liar and father of lies is cast out through the faith and mouths of those who carry the baptized and profess on their behalf, so in this case the false accusation against the woman was expelled by the faith and profession of the representative who acted on her behalf, through the execution of that same representative, by divine judgment; and the truth of her innocence was declared.

For if we receive human testimony, God’s testimony is greater (1 John 5:9): by the manifestation of his power, he testifies to us what we ought to believe concerning this matter, about which we had been doubtful before the manifestation.

## QUESTION VII

[Col. 0673C] Those who say that, because the same woman had made a secret confession, her representative escaped from the judgment uncooked on her behalf.

## ANSWER

Just as certain people, as we read, attempted through false piety to defend blessed Peter when he said that he did not know the man whom he knew to be God, although the Truth had said, “You will deny me” (Matt. 26:34), so these people, with even greater iniquity—for through impious falsehood they slander the truth while proclaiming piety—slander Truth as fictitious, although it wished to free this woman in such a way that it would deceive those who believed in the judgment, although it is written (Wis. 1:5): “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee what is fictitious.”

Hence Saint Peter said to Simon Magus, who thought that he could purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit, through whom miracles and signs are performed, and who flees every falsehood: “You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity” (Acts 8:23).

And, as blessed Gregory says, simple truth does nothing through duplicity. It searches hearts, tests the reins, and reaches even to the division of soul and body, of joints and marrow, and to the innermost parts of the heart. As the Truth says, “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth,” and commands that judgment be made in truth.

For who has called upon the Lord and been deceived? When faithfully invoked in a just judgment, he could deceive no one, since “the Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works.”

Catholic teachers also say concerning the purgation by oath that, just as it is accepted by the person to whom satisfaction is thereby made, so it is judged by the Lord. Paul says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). And there is no confession unless it includes both the heart and the confession of the mouth, so that our mind agrees with our voice.

Hence in baptism it is not the removal of bodily filth that cleanses, but “the questioning and confession of a good conscience toward God.” Peter knew that Christ, whom he had confessed as the Son of the living God, was Lord and believed him to be God, yet with his mouth he denied being Christ’s disciple. Christ had said: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father”; and: “Whoever denies me, I also will deny him” (Matt. 10:22).

And as we read, there is no other meaning to denying that one is his disciple—as Peter said, “I am not,” when he was accused of being one of that man’s disciples—than denying that one is a Christian.

Therefore the sacred canons also included among the fallen those who believed Christ in their hearts but denied him with their mouths when overcome by torments. It is likewise written: “How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Rom. 10:14).

How, I ask, did this woman invoke the Lord as her helper and liberator in the judgment if she did not believe in him? And if she faithfully believed in the Lord whom she invoked, she believed him to be true, not fictitious, and just and a lover of justice; she recognized that he could neither be deceived nor deceive.

But what else do these people say by speaking contrary to this except that they affirm that Truth can be deceived or can deceive? They are more obstinate than demons, who, as the Gospel says, came out from those who were possessed, confessing him because they knew that he was the Christ (Luke 4:41).

As for the statement that the very man who received that woman’s confession is also a witness to it, we are astonished whether this can in any way be true. We would not dare to believe it if we did not dare to believe such men as those who committed these matters to us, since one who reads the book of Leviticus knows that its statement must not be interpreted perversely: “The person who hears the voice of an oath and is a witness—whether he has seen something or knows of it and does not report it” (Lev. 5:1).

From this, as Origen explains, he undoubtedly incurred the other person’s sin, whether he had done something unjust or had sworn unjustly. This also instructs us according to the historical sense, so that we never pollute our consciences with another person’s sins or give consent to those who act wrongly.

By consent I mean not only acting together with them, but also concealing what has been done openly and unlawfully. If he knew and concealed it on account of the secret confession, why—God forbid—did he obtain or consent to the judgment being made on that matter, as is said, without revering equally the sentence of the Law and of the Gospel: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matt. 4:7)?

For if, contrary to canonical authority—which proceeds from the source of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel, proclaimed by the Holy Spirit through whom those writings also were spoken—he acts to the detriment of honor, he cannot escape danger if he strives to oppose the evangelical truth itself in matters of such great importance.

It is likewise written: “You shall repay your oaths to the Lord” (Matt. 5:33). If he had promised loyalty to his lord, how did he dare to consent against him to this deception? And if, then placed between two dangers, he chose to neglect his oath to the lesser degree in order to avoid the greater danger of becoming a betrayer of the confession, why has he now betrayed the confession itself?

For it is written: “Whoever walks deceitfully reveals secrets, but the faithful person conceals the entrusted matter of the heart” (Prov. 11:13)—as though it were plainly saying: “Whoever does not conceal the entrusted matter of the heart is unfaithful.” Paul says to the faithful: “What fellowship has the faithful with the unfaithful?” (2 Cor. 6:13).

More could be said on this subject, but it is not fitting for us. “Each person will bear his own burden.” We have said these things briefly, not because we wish anyone to believe or to accept as credible such a derogation against any priest, but so that, insofar as we must answer those who adjure us in the name of the Lord, we may indicate that this wickedness of betrayal and duplicity must be avoided by us with the greatest care and utterly detested in all human beings.

## QUESTION VIII

Concerning the statement that some make: that the woman’s intention was about another brother of hers with the same name when she sent her representative to judgment on her behalf, and that for this reason her representative did not boil in the judgment.

## ANSWER

As though he were the judge of everything that occurs, who knows all things even before they happen, we can compose an answer to what Peter asked blessed Gregory in the fourth book of the Dialogues:

> “What, I ask you,” he said, “is it that some people are brought out of the body, as though by mistake?”

Blessed Gregory replied by speaking of the two Stephens: it was not the same Stephen who had been brought before the judge and taken to the places of hell who had been ordered to be brought, but another Stephen, a blacksmith.
