After that man had been brought back, the blacksmith Stephen, whom it had been ordered to bring, was brought.

“Whenever this happens,” blessed Gregory says (chapter 36), “if it is carefully considered, it is not an error but a warning. For heavenly mercy, from the abundance of its great compassion, arranges that some people return suddenly to their bodies even after their departure, so that they may at least fear the punishments of hell, which they had heard about but had not believed.”

After the account of Stephen, who had been brought, returned, and afterward taken again to punishment, he added:

> “From this it is gathered that the punishments of hell themselves, when they are displayed, occur for some as assistance and for others as testimony: so that some may see the evils they ought to avoid, while others may be punished all the more because they were unwilling to avoid the punishments of hell even after seeing and recognizing them.”

So God also demonstrates to us from the Scripture of truth what may benefit us as a warning for correction or, through the retribution of justice, may grow into a greater delinquency and an accumulation of condemnation.

It is written in the Book of Kings, with the prophet Micaiah saying: “I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and all the army of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left. And the Lord said: ‘Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ One spoke one way, and another another way. Then a spirit came forth before the Lord and said: ‘I will deceive him.’ The Lord said to him: ‘By what means?’ And he said: ‘I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ And the Lord said: ‘You shall deceive him, and you shall prevail; go forth and do so’” (3 Kings 21:19).

What it means for an evil spirit to stand before the Lord; what it means that the Lord is said to have questioned the evil spirit; in what manner God speaks to the evil spirit and the evil spirit to God—blessed Gregory explains in the books of the Moralia (Moralia XI, chapter 4), which are well known to devoted readers.

The history in the Book of Kings continues: “Now therefore, behold, the Lord has given a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets who are here, and the Lord has spoken evil against you.” And shortly afterward:

> “A certain man bent his bow without aiming and shot an arrow at random, and by chance struck the king of Israel, that is, Ahab, between the lungs and the stomach.”

A little later, he died in the evening, and the word of the Lord was fulfilled in him through the hand of the prophet Micaiah. Earlier, Ahab had said to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, who was seeking a prophet of the Lord:

> “There remains one man through whom we can inquire of the Lord, but I hate him because he does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.”

This was evidently because he told him the truth, and therefore Ahab hated him, loving lying ministers and impious men for himself. Hence it is written (Prov. 29:12): “A ruler who willingly listens to words of falsehood will have all his ministers wicked.”

Therefore the king—and all who desire to believe falsehood—must fear lest they suppose that God can be deceived, or that he wishes to deceive anyone who rightly believes in him in judgment, or that he ought to show an unmerited mercy to one persisting in guilt and denying the guilt itself, since he even prohibited showing mercy to the poor in judgment under the pretext of pity, lest, because of other sins they had committed and for which they had not made satisfaction to the Lord, they should, through the retribution of justice, be led astray by a lying spirit, perish, and fall, deceived, into another snare.

Paul says of certain people: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened.” Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies, receiving in themselves the recompense of their error. And because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting.

And to the Thessalonians he says (2 Thess. 2:10): “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, therefore God will send them a spirit of error, so that they may believe falsehood, in order that all who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity may be judged.”

Hence Saint Augustine, in the third book of *On the Trinity* (chapter 7), speaking of the magical illusions performed by Pharaoh’s magicians in opposition to Moses, says:

> “It is understood that not even the transgressing angels themselves and the aerial powers—cast down from the dwelling of that lofty ethereal purity into this lowest darkness, as into a prison of their own kind, and through whom magical arts can accomplish whatever they accomplish—have any power unless power has been given from above. It is given either to deceive the deceitful, as it was given to the Egyptians and to the magicians themselves, so that they might appear admirable in the seduction of those spirits by whom they were to be condemned by God’s truth; or to warn the faithful not to desire to do such things as something great, which is why they have also been handed down to us by the authority of Scripture; or to exercise, test, and manifest the patience of the righteous.

> “For it was not by any small power of visible miracles that Job lost everything he had—his children and even the health of his body.”

Whatever evil transgressing angels do, corporeal creation does not serve them at their command, but God, from whom power is given. Nor should it be thought that this material of visible things serves these transgressing angels at their command, but rather God, from whom this power is given, insofar as he judges immutably from his lofty and spiritual seat. For even when the wicked have been condemned, water, fire, and earth serve them in metal, so that they may make from it not what they wish, but only what is determined.

## QUESTION IX AND ANSWER

Let us concede that there was fraud in the judgment through the operation of the devil. Although he lost the glory of an angelic spirit, he did not lose the subtlety of his nature. And, with the Lord permitting it—whether on account of the unbelief of those who do not believe rightly, or for the purification of the faithful—he is permitted by divine judgment to carry out hidden but never unjust operations of the greatest magnitude. Thus he strangled Judas, who, filled with an evil will, shared in Christ; and he buffeted Paul after his rapture to the third heaven. Much was also done through Pharaoh’s magicians that Moses, the prophet of the Lord, had done.

For Job’s testing, the air was stirred up, and fire from the aerial heaven consumed the sheep and the servants. The Antichrist will also perform many things through himself and his ministers, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error. And through the pythoness the appearance of Samuel was displayed.

In the book of the Dialogues, written by Saint Gregory, we read (book XI, chapter 10):

> “Because of an idol that had been found and, by chance, thrown for a time into the kitchen, fire suddenly appeared to come forth and showed itself before the eyes of all the monks as though the entire building of that kitchen were being consumed. While they made a tumult, throwing water and shouting as though they were extinguishing the fire, the man of God Benedict, disturbed by the same commotion, arrived. He observed that the fire was present in the eyes of the brothers but not in his own; immediately he bowed his head in prayer and recalled the brothers from the eyes by which they had been deceived by the imaginary fire, so that they could see the sound building of the kitchen standing and no longer see the flames that the ancient enemy had fabricated.”

In Peter’s *Itinerary*, concerning Clement’s father, we read that Simon Magus, whom he had abandoned, anointed him with ointment so that he might be killed by the faithful, and caused him to bear Simon’s likeness before everyone’s eyes. Peter alone saw him as he really was; by praying, he restored his disciples to the use of their eyes and, when the illusion of those looking upon him had been dispelled, restored his true appearance to their sight.

Likewise, in the *Life of John the Monk*, we read that the girl’s parents, through the operation of a demon, saw their daughter as a mare. In the Gospel too we read of two disciples walking with Christ and doubting, because their eyes were restrained so that they would not recognize him (Luke 24:16). We not improperly understand this impediment in their eyes to have come from Satan, so that Jesus would not be recognized. Nevertheless, Christ permitted it until the sacrament of the bread, so that, once they had shared in the unity of his body, the enemy’s impediment might be understood to have been removed and Christ might be recognized.

So it is not surprising if, because of the unbelief of those who hesitate and doubt in faith, the Lord permits such things to occur in a judgment. He displayed himself outwardly to the eyes of those who doubted in a manner corresponding to how he was regarded inwardly by them. What happened before their eyes was not the truth deceiving them, but their inability to perceive the truth and their supposition of something other than what the reality was.

Thus blessed Gregory says concerning Mary (Homily 25 on the Gospels):

> “She was seeking the Lord, whom she by no means believed to have risen. But because she loved and doubted, she saw and did not recognize him: love had shown him to her, while doubt concealed him.”

And to the two disciples walking on the road, although they did not believe, the Lord appeared, but he did not show them an appearance that they would recognize. Thus, outwardly, in the eyes of the body, the Lord did what was taking place inwardly in the eyes of their hearts. Simple Truth therefore did nothing through duplicity, but displayed himself to them in the body as he was in their minds.

And Saint Augustine, in the book *On Christian Doctrine* (book XI, chapter 10), says:

> “Whatever has been instituted by human beings for consultations and for certain agreements and covenants concerning signs with demons is superstitious, such as the devices of magical arts and the books of diviners and augurs. All amulets and remedies also belong to this category—remedies which the medical discipline itself condemns—whether in incantations, in certain signs called characters, or in anything that is hung up or tied” (ibid., chapter 24).

> “All these things have as much power as the presumption of the minds involved. They are, as it were, bound by a common language in covenant with demons; yet they are all full of a pestilential curiosity that torments anxiety with deadly servitude. It is not because they were effective that they were noticed; rather, by noticing and marking them, people made them effective. And therefore different things happen to different people according to their thoughts and presumptions. Those spirits that wish to deceive arrange such things for each person according to what they see him entangled in through his suspicions and agreements.”

And the venerable presbyter Bede, in his Commentary on the Book of Samuel, says (book IV, chapter 8):

> “If anyone is troubled by how a woman could, through demonic art, disturb and raise up a prophet after his death, let him know for certain either that the devil then showed those who were seeking it a false apparition, or that, if Samuel truly appeared, the devil was permitted to do these things only to the extent that the Lord allowed. Nor is it surprising that, for certain more hidden reasons, such things are permitted to the evil spirit, since he also set the Savior upon the pinnacle of the Temple and asked for and received permission to test Job.

> “But if we believe that what appeared was rather a phantasm of the unclean spirit, this too should not disturb us: how could such a spirit have spoken true and prophetic things? For we know that the devil can often foresee or proclaim many future things that he has learned from the holy angels. But one ought to listen to his words all the less because everything that he says or does among human beings he does with the purpose of deceiving.”

To prevent this from happening through the snares of demons, let us, as the Apostle exhorts, resist the devil, strong in faith, which conquers the world and through which the saints conquered kingdoms (Heb. 11:33). To those who believe firmly it is said: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” (Matt. 9:29). And the Apostle says: “Let him ask in faith, doubting nothing” (Jas. 1:6).

And if something should happen for the testing of our faith—for it is useful even for the saints to be examined by the flames of temptations, so that either those who are tested may be shown to be strong, or, having recognized their weakness through temptation, may learn to become stronger, and thus, once they have been tested, may themselves also receive the crown of life—let us not complain about divine judgments, which are sometimes hidden but never unjust.

Nor should it seem surprising if, in this kind of judgment, through diabolical cunning, some fraud occurs by God’s permission, since, as Ambrose says, even the baptismal water is faithful in some cases and lying water in others. Baptism does not heal the faithless; it does not cleanse but pollutes. Hence, according to the decrees of the canons and of Saint Innocent and the other Roman pontiffs, those baptized by heretics in the name of the Holy Trinity receive the grace of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands; but those who have been baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity are not ordered to be baptized.

But because fraud is found in the baptism of heretics, will the baptism of Catholics therefore not be approved? And if fraud is discovered in a judgment because of the faith of unbelievers, will the law of purgation be discarded from the practice of believers?

Just as private or public fraud must always be punished, so, as we read in Scripture, a custom that does not impede public utility must be retained as law.

Therefore, if in this judgment fraud is discovered through any device, the case must be brought back into question by reason, with the judgment’s punishment doubled—whether on account of the commission of sin or on account of the faithless deception.

“Moreover, concerning the purgation by oath, we read in Saint Gregory’s letter to Secundinus, bishop of Taormina (Book VIII, Letter 32), that the wife of Leo the Chartularius, who had left him on account of the charge of fornication and had assumed the religious habit, had returned to her husband without consulting the bishop, on the strength of an oath that he had given her, namely, that after entering marriage he had not fallen into the guilt of adultery. For this reason [Col. 0680A] she had been excommunicated, together with her household. Therefore the same holy pope decreed that her household should immediately be absolved. And if it were clearly established that the woman had been unable to say anything against her husband, and, moreover, that her suspicion had been removed by his oath, and that afterward she had returned to him of her own accord, he ordered that the rigor of the judgment against her should also be moderated, so that she would not be deprived of communion for a long time.”

And likewise, to Candidus the abbot (Book VII, Letter 17):

“Finally, so that this might be entirely sufficient for satisfaction, we arranged that, after giving a bodily oath, he should affirm that he had engaged in no fraud or concealed anything, but had disclosed everything completely. If anyone should attempt, in any way—and we do not believe this will happen—to advance an intention contrary to this, let him know that he is guilty before God, since he strives to rescind matters that have been usefully settled; for he should recognize that he derogates nothing from that decision and settlement.”

And to Praiecta (Book VII, Indiction 11, Letter 60):

“Indeed,” he says, “it is highly consonant with ecclesiastical moderation that matters once ordered or decided should not afterward be disturbed by any opposition.”

We have often heard about this purgation by oath, because many are accustomed to commit fraud in it, swearing by their ingenuity but rather perjuring themselves. For, as we read, an oath is judged by God according to the faith with which it is received by the person to whom satisfaction is customarily rendered through it. But we do not deny that fraud—or rather perjury—may also be detected in that same purgation by oath, just as it may occur in a judgment through diabolical cunning and divine permission. [Col. 0680C] And concerning a deceitful oath we find accounts in the Books of Kings and of the Maccabees, as well as in the Prophet, concerning an oath made to an unfaithful king—matters that did not go unpunished. We therefore think that we have said enough about this above.”

## QUESTION X

In the fourth chapter, we ask that you write back to us: if this case, concerning which we have heard that judgment was rendered—and some of us have even seen it—has been brought back before the court, how that judgment ought canonically to be arranged; and whether the same woman ought to be judged on the basis of a secret confession, as it is called, entrusted to bishops, or on the basis of a written petition presented in court; or, if it should happen that she presents the same petition under compulsion or signs it unwillingly, [Col. 0680D] whether she can lawfully be removed from the marital bed on the basis of such contrivances.

## RESPONSE

Even if this matter has been demonstrated in the judgment under discussion, as we said above, by evident indications, the judgment should be arranged as the holy pope and martyr Fabian established:

“Because,” he says (Letter 11), “four persons must always be present in every judgment: namely, duly chosen judges, accusers, defenders, and witnesses.”

For, as Leo writes to all the bishops established throughout Caesarea and Mauretania (Letter 91):

“We can judge no one unless, being present, he can be subjected to a just sentence either after being refuted or, certainly, after confessing.”

[Col. 0681A] And Saint Augustine, in his book *On Penance* (Homily L), says:

“Good Christians very often remain silent and endure the sins of others that they know because they are frequently abandoned by evidence and cannot prove before ecclesiastical judges what they themselves know. For although certain matters may be true, they are not easily to be believed by a judge unless they are demonstrated by definite indications. We, however, cannot exclude anyone from communion—even though such exclusion is not yet mortal but medicinal—unless that person has either confessed voluntarily or has been named and convicted in some judgment, whether secular or ecclesiastical. For who would dare assume both roles for himself, so as to be at once the accuser and the judge of another? Paul may be understood to have briefly indicated such a rule here when, after mentioning certain such crimes, he established from them the form of ecclesiastical judgment for similar cases. For he says: ‘I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators’ (1 Cor. 5:9), and so forth.

“And likewise:

“‘If any brother is named as a fornicator, or an idol-worshipper, or greedy, or reviler, or drunkard, or robber, with such a one not even to eat.’

“But it must be understood that the Apostle intended here a naming that occurs against someone when a sentence is pronounced in due judicial order and with integrity. For if mere naming were sufficient, many innocent people would have to be condemned, since people are often falsely named in connection with some crime. He did not wish a person to be judged according to the arbitrary judgment of suspicion or even according to an extraordinary judgment usurped without authority, but rather according to God’s law and the order of the Church—whether the person had confessed voluntarily or had been accused and convicted.”

And in the Council of Toledo (Council of Toledo VI, canon 11):

“It is right that the life of an innocent person should not be stained by the ruin brought by accusers. Therefore, whoever is accused by anyone, both the accused and the accuser must be presented, and the judgments of the laws and canons must be sought, so that if the person is found unworthy to accuse, no one may be judged or condemned on the basis of that person’s accusation.”

And in the Council of Carthage (African Council, chapter 95):

“In a judgment it must be investigated what sort of conduct and faith belong to the one who accuses and to the one who is accused.”

Likewise, in the same council (chapter 98):

“Witnesses who have been forbidden to be admitted for accusation must not be admitted for testimony either, nor those whom the accuser himself has brought from his own household.”

And the holy pope and martyr Cornelius, blessed Felix, Roman pontiff, and all the pontiffs of that see decreed that the judges of the Church must take care not to pronounce a sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being examined, because such a sentence will be invalid, and they will also have to give an account of their action in the presence of the brethren. Exceptions are the cases specifically designated by the laws of the Church, which express them individually, just as public laws define a fixed procedure by which absent persons are to be condemned in judgment—namely, when the crime is so notorious and the person involved in the crime so notorious that neither witnesses are necessary for conviction nor the person’s presence required. Thus Ambrose says in his letter to the Corinthians:

“It is not the judge’s role,” he says, “to condemn without an accuser, because the Lord did not cast out Judas, although he was a thief, since he had not been accused.

“‘Remove from among you the one who has done this’ (1 Cor. 5:2).

“Once this deed had been recognized, he ought to have been expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. For everyone knew his crime, but they did not rebuke him: publicly he kept his stepmother in the place of a wife. In this matter there was no need of witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.

“‘Although absent in body but present in spirit’—that is, absent in face but present by the authority of the Spirit, who is absent nowhere—‘I have already judged as present the one who has committed this’ (ibid., 3).”

Since it belongs to another place and time to demonstrate by what and how many other methods absent persons can and must be judged according to ecclesiastical laws, [Col. 0682B] let us now bring forward what is relevant here and what the Synod of Valence, following the Roman Church, demonstrated, namely, its fourth canon:

“If anyone has declared himself guilty, either by a true confession or by a falsehood—for,” it says, “he cannot be absolved who has declared in himself the cause of death which, if declared against another, would be punished, since everyone who is the cause of his own death is a greater murderer.”

This cannot be done in the Church either through a secret confession or through another person; how much less may it be done through priests, who are not permitted to make public the sins confessed to them unless the person who committed the sin himself has disclosed what he did wrong? The bishop, whose care this is known to concern, must provide as far as he can against this, so that no one, led astray by error or compelled by fear, may falsely accuse himself of something by which he would harm either himself or the Church. For this reason it was also decreed that an extracted confession or a forced signature should have no force, as the blessed Alexander, glorious martyr and the fourth pontiff of the Apostolic See after blessed Peter, judged in his letter to all the orthodox:

“If from such persons,” he says, “anything—which is entirely hostile to the Christian name—has in any way been extorted through fear, fraud, or force, or if anything has been written or confirmed by them through whatever device so that they might free themselves, we decree that this shall bring them no prejudice or harm, nor do we permit them, by the authority of the Lord, the holy apostles, and their successors, ever to suffer any disgrace, calumny, or deprivation of their property on this account.

“But in such matters confession must be voluntary, not compelled, as he himself testifies who says: ‘For out of the heart proceed murders, adulteries, fornications, blasphemies’ (Matt. 15:19), and the other things that belong to these.”

And likewise:

“God takes greater account of thoughts and voluntary intentions than of actions performed through simplicity or necessity. Confession in such matters must not be extorted, but should rather be offered spontaneously. It is exceedingly wrong to judge anyone on the basis of suspicion or an extracted confession, since the Lord is more an examiner of the heart than of the deed and seeks pure thoughts and good intentions rather than lying words.”

Such a confession must be made in the Church by the one who sinned, as it is written:

“Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified.”

“First,” I say, so that in confession you may forestall both the voice of the accusing devil and the face of the Lord, so that you may be justified, not condemned. For ecclesiastical excommunication itself is not eternal punishment but temporary and medicinal, intended only to turn the sinner toward the one who does not desire the sinner’s death but life (Ezek. 18:23).

And again it is written:

“By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Isa. 43:26).

Hence Jerome says:

“It is beyond doubt that a person is condemned by God because of evil words that he has uttered. But no one can be justified by good words unless he utters them from the depths of his heart with a right intention. Even if the words are good, if they were not spoken with a right purpose, they cannot justify the speaker, just as Caiaphas was not found righteous when he said: ‘It is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish’ (John 11:50). Those words, therefore, justify the speaker who retains in the marrow of his heart the good things he utters with his mouth and expresses them with a holy intention. For in the weight of words the working of human life consists, because, as Solomon says: ‘Death and life are in the power of the tongue’ (Prov. 18:21).”

And it is decreed in the chapters of the Augusti:

“That a person who, compelled by fear, has declared outside a judicial proceeding that he is a slave shall suffer no prejudice to his freedom until he is brought before a court, so that he may obtain his freedom in the presence of a judge if he proves it, or, if he is convicted of being a slave, may immediately be restored to his master.”

[Col. 0683C] Bishops, namely, judges of souls, must certainly exercise the greatest care and make this known to secular persons: in the business of accusing, giving testimony, or judging, they must not allow diabolical suggestion to steal upon them under the pretext of a future confession and penance. The devil says—not in words but by encouragement—to anyone who desires to follow the desire of his heart:

“Take care,” says the devil, “to fulfill what you desire, lest you be defeated by what you have begun. It is better for you to do penance afterward than to be disgraced as one who has been defeated.”

To witnesses he suggests:

“You can devise a stratagem so that what you say may appear to be true.”

To judges the devil often advises:

“How can I do otherwise? I judge according to what I hear.”

Let them therefore hear and heed what is written:

“Woe to you who justify yourselves before men, but the Lord knows your hearts” (Luke 16:15).

And:

“If your eye”—that is, your intention—“is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6:22).

And:

“With what judgment you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. 7:2).

And:

“A false witness will not go unpunished” (Prov. 19:6).

Let them also read what Saint Jerome says in his commentary on Matthew:

“He is a false witness,” he says, “who does not understand what has been said in the same sense in which it is said.”

How much more is one a false witness who says what was not said at all?

Against such a thought—which the devil proposes to those who form evil intentions, give testimony, or judge, under the pretext of obtaining penance—let them set what the same Saint Jerome says in the same book. He says concerning Judas:

“Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, moved by repentance, returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: ‘I have sinned in betraying innocent blood’ (Matt. 27:3–4). The weight of impiety outweighed the magnitude of avarice [another reading: ‘the magnitude of impiety’]. When Judas saw that the Lord had been sentenced to death, he returned the price to the priests, as though it were in his power to change the persecutors’ sentence. Thus, although he changed his intention, he did not change the outcome of his initial intention. But if the one who betrayed innocent blood sinned, how much more did those who bought innocent blood sin and, by offering the price, provoked the disciple to betrayal?

“But they said: ‘What is that to us? You see to it.’ And having thrown the silver pieces into the temple, he departed and went away and hanged himself with a noose (ibid., 5). It did him no good to have performed penance by which he could not correct his crime. When a brother sins against a brother in such a way that he can make amends for what he has done, the sin can be forgiven him. But if the deeds remain, penance is taken up in vain by words. This is what is said in the Psalm concerning that most wretched Judas: ‘Let his prayer become sin’ (Ps. 108:7), so that he was not only unable to correct the wickedness of his betrayal but also added to his earlier crime the guilt of his own murder.”

Let us all fear this true judgment and beware of this most destructive cunning of diabolical malice toward our deception, by which the devil fraudulently deceives us even under the hope of penance and, through his counsel, binds us in guilt. For when by sinning we fall from the state of justice, we often fall at the same time into the snare of despair and are utterly torn from the root of hope.

Hence the Lord, through the Prophet, censures not so much the evil of our rash actions as the pursuits of our sins, saying:

“Lest my indignation go forth like a fire, and be kindled, and there be no one to extinguish it, because of the wickedness of your pursuits” (Jer. 4:4).

Again, in anger he says:

“I will visit upon you according to the fruit of your pursuits” (Jer. 21:14).

“For, as blessed Gregory says (Pastoral Rule, Book III, chapter 33), sins committed by counsel differ from other sins. The Lord pursues not so much evil deeds as the pursuits of evil. In deeds one sins sometimes through weakness and sometimes through negligence; but in one’s pursuits one always sins through a malicious intention. He sits in the seat of pestilence who is so lifted up by the pride of iniquity that he attempts to accomplish evil even through counsel. From this, therefore, let those who bind themselves in guilt even through counsel infer with what vengeance they will one day be struck, since now they become not companions but leaders of the wicked.”

The cunning of the crafty enemy must also be avoided. When he sees that the mind he has overthrown through sin is afflicted by its downfall, he seduces it with the poisonous blandishments of false security and summons empty hopes and assurances before its eyes, so that he may deprive it of the benefit of sorrow. At one moment he presents the more serious deeds of others; at another, the shame arising from the promise it had made and wickedly undertaken to fulfill. At another, he says that what has been done is nothing; at another, he speaks of God’s mercy; at another, he places before the corrupted mind some advantage, gain, grace, or honor. At another, he points out another evil by which the lesser evil might be excluded. At another, he promises that time for penance will still remain, so that while the deceived mind is led on by these things, it may not be recalled from the evil it has begun and may be held back from the intention of doing penance. Thus it may receive no good later, because no evils trouble it now, and may then be overwhelmed more fully by punishments because now it even rejoices in its sins.

Often also, by a special evil, he perverts the hearts of the double-minded through the ingenuity of his ancient art, so that while they deceive others by their perverse and duplicitous action, they boast that they are wiser than the rest. Because they do not consider the strictness of retribution, the wretched rejoice in their own losses. Concerning them the Prophet says:

“Behold, the great and dreadful day of the Lord is coming upon all fortified cities and upon all lofty corners” (Zeph. 1:16),

because the anger of the final judgment destroys human hearts closed against the truth by their defenses and dissolves them when they are entangled in duplicity.

Let accusers of the innocent, deceitful witnesses, and judges also heed what is said to them:

“Woe to those who establish unjust laws, writing injustices” (Isa. 10:1).

And let them heed what the violent suffering inflicted by injustice says through Susanna. For it has its own voice, just as mercy does, concerning which it is written:

“Hide almsgiving”—that is, mercy—“in the bosom of the poor, and it will itself pray for you” (Ecclus. 29:15).

The violent suffering inflicted, as we have said, by injustice speaks as follows:

“Eternal God, who know the hidden things, who know all things before they happen, you know that they have borne false witness against me. And behold, I am dying, although I have done none of the things that these men have maliciously contrived against me” (Dan. 13:42–43).

The Lord heard her voice and repaid the presbyters who had been appointed judges of the people in that year and had borne false witness according to the evil they had done against their neighbor; they were put to death.

And let them consider that many die bodily in the present life, as Ananias and Sapphira did, and those who, when they receive communion, do not discern the Lord’s body, as Paul says (1 Cor. 11). Many, however, live in the body but are dead in soul because of an evil deed, like the woman of whom it is written:

“She who lives is dead” (1 Tim. 5:6).

Every soul that sins dies, and those who persist in sin will be crushed by a twofold destruction when they are placed like a furnace of fire and clothed, like a double garment, with their shame, when body and soul perish in Gehenna.

We say these things not to abolish just judgments, but fearing that we may knowingly judge unjustly; not forbidding true testimony, but rejecting lies.

Moreover, since above, and on the basis of the instruction of other learned men, we have sufficiently demonstrated from the decrees of blessed Gregory the procedure for deciding the case under discussion, we are still willing to show what method we ought to follow in investigating and deciding such a question.

For he says, if the case concerns what happened after the marriage was contracted, in his letter to Adrian the notary (Book IX, Letter 44):

“Agathosa,” he says, “the bearer of this letter, has complained that her husband was converted against her will in the monastery of the abbot Urbicius. Since this undoubtedly pertains to the guilt and disrepute of the same abbot, we instruct Your Experience to investigate carefully whether perhaps he was converted with her consent or whether she herself promised to change. If you discover this to be the case, arrange for him to remain in the monastery and compel her to change, as she promised.

“But if neither of these things is true, and you discover that the aforesaid woman did not commit some crime of fornication on account of which a man is permitted to leave his wife, we wish you, lest his conversion become an occasion of ruin for the wife left in the world, to return her husband to her without any excuse—whether or not he has already been tonsured. For, except on account of fornication, divine law in no way permits a man to leave his wife. Once, through the union of marriage, the man and woman have become one body, one cannot be converted in part while the other part remains in the world.”

And because it is clear that one law governs husband and wife, he demonstrates this in the letter cited above, to Secundinus, bishop of Taormina (Book VIII, Letter 32):

“The bearer of this letter, Leo the Chartularius, came to us and reported that his wife, who had left him on account of the charge of fornication—which, he said, had driven her with great force and on account of which she had assumed the religious habit—was in no way guilty and that he had not fallen into the guilt of fornication after entering marriage. He added that he had given his wife the strictest oaths, affirming that he had remained innocent in the matter concerning which suspicion had troubled her, and that for this reason she had returned to him of her own accord.

“But since he asserts that your fraternity deprived her of communion, together with her household, solely because she returned secretly to him after setting you aside, we wish her household to receive holy communion and not to let the guilt of the mistress keep it long under the punishment of this affliction. Concerning her herself, that is, the wife of the aforesaid bearer, you must observe the following: if it is clearly established that she could say nothing against her husband, and, moreover, that her suspicion was removed by an oath given—as we have been informed—and that afterward she returned to him of her own accord, then the rigor of judgment against her must also be moderated, so that she is not deprived of communion for a long time.”

## QUESTION XI

Since a husband cannot be separated from his wife, nor a wife from her husband, by a written secret confession, just as a bishop cannot remove himself, if he wishes, from the Church entrusted to him or from his rank, nor can anyone in the ecclesiastical order remove himself from his office—just as we have endeavored above to demonstrate on the authority of the Church—

## RESPONSE

No one should be subjected to public penance on the basis of a written secret confession presented in court, nor can anyone be condemned through a written statement sent directly or presented by another. Rather, where a person must be judged publicly, that person must be present and must either be convicted or confess.

The great Pope Leo wrote to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia:

“Being present, either refuted or certainly confessing, a person can be subjected to a just sentence, because it is contrary to reason to see people suffer penalties when it is impossible to know the grounds of their cases.”

Holy Scripture also demonstrates this order of judgment. When the accusers of the accused woman had prepared their case in court, they said:

“Send to Susanna, daughter of Helcias, wife of Joachim.”

And they sent for her. She came with her parents and children (Dan. 13:29–30). After the testimony had been given, the judges condemned her to death (ibid., 41). But when she was liberated by the truth that set her free, the false witnesses were punished according to the evil they had done against their neighbor.

Likewise, the woman caught in adultery was accused while present bodily, not through another person’s testimony or through writing, which the ecclesiastical and Roman laws prohibit. Her confession is also implied when the Lord says to her:

“Has no one condemned you?”

And she replies:

“No one, Lord” (John 8:10).

Pilate likewise, concerning the Lord, who had been seized and bound like a robber, says—after the legitimate order of authority had been maintained through the cohort, as Augustine says, and after he had been sent through the ministers of the Jews from Annas to Caiaphas and from Caiaphas to the praetorium:

“You have brought this man to me” (Luke 23:14).

When he heard that he belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him back to Herod, teaching us to expect Christian and just judgments from secular authorities in secular matters, and then to apply to the sick the ecclesiastical remedies of medicinal judgments. The Apostle demonstrates this same thing concerning the faithful while they were still living among unbelievers:

“There is altogether a fault among you,” he says, “because you are being judged before outsiders and not before the brethren. If, therefore, you have secular cases among you, appoint as judges those who are contemptible in the Church” (1 Cor. 6:1, 4).

Hence Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule*:

“That at least they may serve earthly affairs, those who are not adorned with spiritual gifts.”

And Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*:

“When such judgments are necessary, this shows that they are not forbidden but ought to be judged among the faithful.”

And Ambrose:

“Since, therefore,” he says, “there are wise brethren, let some of them be chosen to judge, whose judgment the world fears. For it is a great disgrace if, among those who are said to have known God, no one is found capable of examining a judgment. How will a repentant murderer receive the peace of the Church before he has been reconciled with those who are in dispute? How will a quarrelsome person be able to receive pardon before he has been joined by the bond of charity? How will a robber perform worthy fruits of penance before, following David’s judgment and Zacchaeus’s example, he offers the sacrifice of appeasement either by making amends or by giving satisfaction—he who has cruelly labored in robberies? Or how will a marriage be dissolved unless it is demonstrated, by Christian laws through which it was joined by the Lord’s authority, that it ought to be dissolved, or that it was not contracted but rather usurped contrary to Christian laws?”

And how can this be done in due order unless through human laws inspired by him through whom lawmakers make just decisions?

Hence Saint Gelasius writes to the emperor Anastasius (Letter 10):

“If, so far as concerns the order of public discipline, the religious leaders themselves obey your laws, recognizing that the imperial authority has been conferred upon you by heavenly disposition, lest they appear to oppose judgments from which worldly matters have been excluded, with what disposition, I ask, is it fitting for you to obey those who have been appointed to administer venerable mysteries?”

As we read elsewhere:

“Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21):

to Caesar, indeed, the coin, tribute, money, and the honor that is owed, so long as he himself faithfully honors the Lord, and the tax; but to God, tithes, firstfruits, offerings, sacrifices, and continual service. In this way he himself paid taxes for himself and Peter, and rendered to God what belongs to God, doing the will of the Father.

And Saint Augustine, in the sixth sermon on the Gospel of John:

“Do not say, ‘What have I to do with the king?’ What, then, have you to do with property? By the laws of kings, property is possessed.”

Thus, through legal judgments, since they are Christian, disputes concerning secular affairs must be settled.

Concerning a written petition or secret confession, Leo likewise decides, writing to all the bishops throughout Campania, Samnium, and Picenum (Letter 86), and greeting them:

“I am moved by great indignation and deeply grieved that I have discovered some of you to have forgotten the apostolic tradition and to be intent upon your own error.”

And after a little:

“Concerning the penance requested by the faithful, so that a written declaration of the kind of each person’s sins may not be made public in documents, since the guilt of consciences is sufficiently disclosed to priests alone by secret confession. Although the fullness of faith seems worthy of praise when, out of fear of God, it is not ashamed before human beings, nevertheless, since not everyone’s sins are of such a kind that those seeking penance are unafraid to make them public, let the reprehensible practice be removed, lest many be held back from the remedies of penance because they are ashamed or fear that their deeds will be disclosed to their enemies, by whom they could be punished under the provisions of the law.

“For that confession is sufficient which is first offered to God and then also to the priest, who approaches as an intercessor for the sins of those doing penance. More people will then be moved to penance if the conscience of the one confessing is not made public to the ears of the people.”

From this let everyone infer: if the sacred canons command that a bishop be excommunicated so long as he does not give communion to the person who says that he has secretly confessed a crime to him, should anyone either be required or dare, on the basis of a secret confession—whether entrusted through a written petition or through words—to subject anyone whatsoever to the laws of public penance? How much less should he dissolve a marriage lawfully contracted without a certain and manifest reason, since the same Leo thunders terrifyingly to all the bishops established throughout every province, saying (Letter 1):

“Our admonition therefore declares that if any of the brethren attempts to act contrary to the established rules and dares to do what is forbidden, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and will not be a participant in our communion. He who has refused to be a partner in discipline will not be our partner.”

## QUESTION XII

In the fifth chapter, write back to us, on the authority of Scripture and the tradition of the Fathers, what has been written concerning sexual misconduct and abortion, together with the names of the authors and the identification of their books, so that we may know whether a woman can conceive in the manner described and, after an abortion, remain a virgin, as is said to have happened in this case; and, if it is discovered that this woman committed these crimes before marriage, whether she ought or can remain in the marriage.

## RESPONSE
Finally, concerning fornication and abortion, which we have often heard were alleged against the woman, let us return to the pages of Holy Scripture, lest, deciding according to human conjecture, we offend the most just Judge. For the book of Deuteronomy says:

“If a man takes a wife and afterward hates her, and seeks opportunities by which he may dismiss her, bringing against her a very bad accusation, and says: ‘I took this woman as my wife, and when I approached her I did not find her a virgin,’ then her father and mother shall take her and bring with them the signs of her virginity to the elders of the city who are at the gate. And the father shall say: ‘I gave my daughter to this man as a wife; but because he hates her, he has brought against her a very bad accusation, saying: “I did not find your daughter a virgin”; yet these are the signs of my daughter’s virginity.’ And they shall spread out the garment before the elders of the city. Then the elders of that city shall seize the man and beat him, and, moreover, condemning him to pay one hundred shekels of silver, which he shall give to the girl’s father, because he has brought a very bad accusation against a virgin of Israel. He shall have her as his wife, and he shall not be permitted to dismiss her for all the days of his life.

“But if what he alleged is true, and virginity was not found in the girl, they shall cast her outside the doors of her father’s house, and the men of her city shall stone her with stones, and she shall die, because she committed a wicked act in Israel by committing fornication in her father’s house; and you shall remove the evil from your midst” (Deut. 22:13–21).

And concerning incest it is written in Leviticus:

“No man shall approach his near blood-relative, to uncover her nakedness; I am the Lord. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, whether she is your father’s daughter or your mother’s daughter, whether born at home or abroad” (Lev. 18:6, 9).

And again:

“Every soul that does any of these abominations shall perish from among his people” (ibid., 29).

And again:

“If a man takes his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees her brother’s shame, they have done a wicked thing. They shall be killed in the sight of the people, because they have uncovered one another’s nakedness; and they shall bear their iniquity” (Lev. 20:17).

Hence Saint Augustine says:

“What does ‘he saw’ mean in this passage, except that he knew her by lying with her, just as elsewhere in the Law it is said, ‘He knew his wife’ (Gen. 4:1), meaning that he was joined to her? And what does it mean when he says, ‘They shall bear their sin,’ except that he wished the punishment of sin itself to be called ‘sin’?”

And because we are compelled by necessity, as was the Apostle, who in one passage says of certain things, “What they do in secret it is shameful even to mention” (Eph. 5:12), he, constrained by necessity, openly rebukes in the Letter to the Romans males who commit indecency with males and females who exchange natural use for that which is against nature. Whether we wish it or not, we fear the threat of the Lord’s saying, which we set out at length above: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed before the angels of God” (Luke 9:26). Therefore we shall still set down, in this matter, a passage from the book of Genesis:

“Onan, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob the patriarch, entered in to the wife of his brother Er, Judah’s firstborn, who was wicked in the sight of the Lord and was killed by him; and he spilled his seed upon the ground. Therefore the Lord struck him, because he did a detestable thing” (Gen. 38:7, 9).

And it is written in the book of Leviticus:

“If a man lies with a male as with a woman, both have committed a wicked thing; they shall surely be put to death” (Lev. 20:13).

For this reason the Roman laws also decree, in their chapters concerning fornicators, what anyone who reads them will find. And if such a decree is made concerning male with male, what provision will the laws find concerning a male and a brother with a sister, through the intercourse of a male in the Sodomite manner?

Saint Augustine likewise writes in the second book addressed to Count Valerius, *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (ch. 20):

“But when the Apostle says of the wicked, ‘Abandoning the natural use of the female, males burned in their desire for one another, males committing indecency with males’ (Rom. 1:27), he did not say ‘conjugal use,’ but wished ‘natural’ to be understood as that which takes place through the members created for this purpose, so that the two sexes may be joined through them for begetting. Accordingly, when someone joins himself even to a prostitute with those same members, the use is natural, though it is not praiseworthy but blameworthy. But if anyone uses the part of the body that was not instituted for procreation, even with his wife, it is against nature and disgraceful.

“Accordingly, the same Apostle first said concerning women: ‘For their females exchanged the natural use for that use which is against nature’ (ibid., 26). Then, concerning males committing indecency with males after abandoning the natural use of the female, the name ‘natural’ does not praise conjugal intercourse, but marks out more unclean and more criminal acts—as though they were using females illicitly, but nevertheless naturally.”

And again, in the book *On the Good of Marriage* (ch. 11):

“But when a husband wishes to use the woman’s member for a purpose for which it was not granted, the wife is more disgraceful if she permits it to be done with her than if she permits it to be done with another.”

And in the second book *On Adulterous Marriages* (ch. 12):

“If he does not exercise self-control, let him marry lawfully, so that he may not beget shamefully, or, by lying shamefully with someone, fail to beget even more shamefully. Yet some who are lawfully married also do this last thing. For intercourse even with a lawful wife is illicit and shameful when conception of offspring is avoided; this is what Onan, Judah’s son, did, and the Lord killed him for it.”

Thus sometimes adultery is committed even by sight alone, when an unmarried woman is shamefully desired. “Yet this,” as Saint Gregory says in the twenty-first book of the *Moralia* (ch. 9), “is generally distinguished by the position or rank of the one who desires: for deliberate desire stains one person in the sacred order just as the guilt of adultery stains another.”

And in his letter to Sabinus, regional subdeacon:

“Since what is generally a fault among laypeople is a crime among those constituted in the sacred order, anyone who uses zeal for uprightness knows with what strictness that atoning outrage must be punished in them.”

And again, in the aforesaid book (*Moralia* XXI, ch. 9):

“Yet among persons who are not dissimilar, the same guilt of lust is distinguished. That the guilt of fornication is distinct from the guilt of adultery is attested by the tongue of the outstanding preacher, who among other things says: ‘Neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers shall possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Cor. 6:9). For by placing a sentence after distinct forms of guilt, he showed that they differ greatly from one another.”

And Augustine, in the book *On the Good of Marriage* (ch. 8):

“Fornication is evil, adultery worse; for it is worse to violate another’s marriage than to cling to a prostitute. Incest is worse still, because it is worse to lie with one’s mother than with another man’s wife. And one proceeds always from evil to worse, until one reaches those things which, as the Apostle says, ‘it is shameful even to mention’ (Eph. 5:12).”

And Saint Ambrose, in the first book of *On Abraham* (I, 6):

“Holy Lot was offering the chastity of his daughters. For although that impurity too was disgraceful, nevertheless it was less evil to have intercourse according to nature than to abandon them to what is contrary to nature.”

And again, in the *Epistle to the Corinthians* (ch. 7):

“Yet if the husband apostatizes, or seeks to invert the use of his wife, the woman may neither marry another nor return to him.”

These passages have been collected to magnify the crime, so that from them one may understand how great an evil incest between brother and sister is, even through intercourse in the Sodomite manner, if the matter is indeed as alleged; both acts, separately committed, are punished by death in the Heptateuch at the Lord’s command. They also destroy the most abominable assertion of those who maintain that the Sodomite crime exists only when someone fornicates inside the body—that is, in the bodily member of the obscene part, specifically inside the little vessel (*aqualiculum*)—and who wickedly and improperly abuse the Apostle’s testimony:

“Every sin that a man commits is outside the body, but the one who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18).

But such pollution, they say, is as if someone rubbed mud from his finger with his hand, or between his thighs, and then washed his hand with that same mud; similarly, they claim, this woman, after bathing, was completely cleansed from that pollution.

Those who say these things are to be regarded not as Catholics but as Cynics—that is, dog-like heretics on account of their shamelessness—as Saint Jerome demonstrates in his *Epistle to the Ephesians*, explaining the Apostle’s statement:

“But for a certain Cynic philosopher to have existed, who taught that every titillation of the flesh and every flow of semen arising from any kind of rubbing or touching need not be avoided at the proper time, and for some wise men of the world to have agreed with this shameful and disgraceful heresy—unless that had happened, the holy Apostle, writing to the Ephesians, would never have joined every impurity to fornication, saying, ‘as is fitting for saints.’ From this it follows that no one can be called holy who, apart from fornication, is found in any impurity or avarice of pleasures in which he delights. ‘For this you must know,’ says the Apostle, ‘that every fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person, who is a servant of idols, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God’ (ibid., 5).”

And above, in the second book:

“Who, despairing of themselves, gave themselves over to shamelessness for the working of uncleanness” (Eph. 4:19):

“All those who despair in avarice,” he says, “plunging themselves, in the manner of irrational beasts, into filth and a pit, gave themselves over to shamelessness and lust, doing whatever the body wished, whatever the mind desired, whatever lust suggested. And since they left nothing at all undone that is unclean, they did all this in avarice, since they are never satisfied by indulging in lust, nor does their pleasure have an end. Or else, beyond the union granted to man and woman, they rise to greater acts, committing indecency, males with males.”

For, as the same teacher explains in the third volume of that epistle, indecency is a hidden thought, when the senses are inflamed toward lust and the soul is kindled by the titillations of the flesh, yet is nevertheless restrained by fear of God and the judgment of the mind.

It is therefore evident that, as the same Apostle says to the Romans, whenever males with males, females with females, males with females, or any persons by themselves in any manner commit indecency, it is uncleanness, which separates the perpetrator from the kingdom of God and plunges him into hell, just as that same Apostle says: “Every fornicator or unclean person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.”

Hence Isidore says in the second book of the *Sentences*:

“Every unclean pollution is called fornication, although a person may prostitute himself to the pleasure of various kinds of indecency. For from the delight of fornication arise various crimes, by which the kingdom of God is closed and a person is separated from God.”

And Saint Prosper, in the book *On Virtues and Vices*:

“Thus that bodily discharge which occurs without guilt in those who are asleep sometimes occurs through guilt in those who are awake. In the former case the fullness of bodily fluid is naturally expelled; in the latter, desire is shamefully manifested. But this desire elicits that discharge in those who are awake for whom filthy conversation arouses a sordid appetite.”

Women also have this sordid appetite, as Ambrose says in his exposition of the Apostle, concerning females committing indecency with females (Rom. 1). They bring flesh against flesh, but do not place the genital member of one body inside the flesh of another, which nature’s prohibition prevents. Instead, they exchange the natural use of this bodily part for a use that is against nature. They are said also to employ certain devices of diabolical operation to inflame lust; nevertheless, those who fornicate sin against their own body.

Similarly, males committing indecency with males—that is, dissipating the heat of lust and satisfying the pleasure of the flesh that delights in it—are called by the Apostle “those who lie with males” and “the soft” (1 Cor. 6), those who voluptuously succumb to this indecency.

Moreover, whoever takes the members of Christ and makes them members of a prostitute, clinging to a prostitute with whom he becomes one body; whoever sins disgracefully against nature with a woman consecrated to God, or with a relative, or with one whom a relative has had, or with another man’s wife, or with an animal; whoever, by himself, with his hand or in any other way, pollutes himself while satisfying the heat of lust—fornicates, and is all the more liable to damnation and to heavier punishment if he does not repent worthily, the more criminally he sins against nature in his own body.

For, as Saint Augustine and the other teachers explain, in the fulfillment of fornication the mind is so completely absorbed together with the body into the flesh that at that moment it cannot think of anything else. This sin does not end as soon as it has polluted the body and soul. After the act has passed, the guilt remains to such a degree that even amid the groans of repentance the stimuli of the former pleasure are often miserably aroused. And the perpetrators of all such crimes, as the Apostle testifies, are excluded from the kingdom of God unless, before departing from the body, they strive to wash away the stains of such great crimes through mournful confession, abundant tears, and the distribution of alms and worthy fruits of repentance, with much affliction of the flesh and contrition of spirit.

Let no one therefore say that the Sodomite crime is not committed by one who acts indecently against nature with a male or a female and, through rubbing, touching, or an impure movement, deliberately and intentionally makes himself unclean. Such a person, as the Apostle teaches, is excluded from the kingdom of God. Moreover, other sins committed against the rights of nature are also reckoned as sins of Sodom and are called Sodomite, as the Lord says through the prophet to a city full of sins:

“This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: idleness, fullness of bread, and abundance” (Ezek. 16:49).

And the Jews, sinning before the Lord, were called by Isaiah “rulers of Sodom” and “people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:10). Among their other iniquities they placed a boy in a brothel and put the price of youths in their purses. Their rulers were effeminate men who, in place of youths, had been made eunuchs, as though for the protection of matrons; recruited and subjected to shamelessness and uncleanness, they were found, by a diabolical invention, both to serve lust—which, as is said, usually subdues even iron minds—and to rule over the lustful.

Such vices are attributed not only to sacrilege but also to idolatry, for which they are the recompense, as the Apostle shows. Thus it is written of gluttons: “Their god is their belly” (Phil. 3:19); and of the lustful: “Their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” (ibid.). Scripture calls God “glory,” for it says: “They exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats hay” (Ps. 105:20). And Scripture testifies concerning avarice, that it is “the service of idols” (Eph. 5:5). The diligent reader will find the same concerning other matters and among other passages of Scripture.

Concerning abortion, it is written in Exodus:

“If two men quarrel and strike a woman who is pregnant, and her child comes out not yet formed, he shall suffer a loss according to what the woman’s husband imposes upon him, and he shall pay with a demand for compensation. But if it was formed, he shall give life for life” (Exod. 21:22–23).

And concerning conception it is written in the Gospel: “For that which has been born in her” (Matt. 1:20), which, as Gregory explains, is certainly said of that which has been conceived. For Joseph first began to hesitate when he saw his betrothed’s womb swelling.

Let us therefore turn back to the Law and consider how conception takes place according to nature. It says:

“The woman who, having received seed, gives birth to a male or a female” (Lev. 12:1).

And concerning giving birth, whether to one formed or, as we stated above, unformed, and concerning what a woman, whether male or female, gives birth to or aborts, it is written:

“Everything that opens the womb” (Exod. 34:19).

It must be noted that Scripture declares that the woman receives seed—that is, seed introduced by male intercourse through the genital vein into the secret recess of the vulva, borne by the uterus, as we also learn from medical teaching—and not, as this invention claims, that she draws or receives seed in herself elsewhere, or emitted from elsewhere. The same Scripture also testifies that, at the expulsion of what she had conceived from the introduced seed, the vulva is opened, plainly at the first birth; it could not preserve the integrity of its closure even at the first natural intercourse.

Let us therefore believe what we read, and let us consider it wicked to assert what we do not read. From the beginning of the world it has never been heard, nor has it been read under this heaven in the Scripture of truth, that a woman’s vulva received seed and conceived without intercourse and, with the uterus closed and the vulva unopened, or with the flesh intact, gave birth to a living child or aborted one—except in the singular case of the blessed and holy Virgin Mary.

Her conception was not of nature but of grace, as the archangel said to her: “Hail, full of grace” (Luke 1:28). The Holy Spirit came upon her and, from virginal seed and virginal blood, without the will of the flesh and without the will of a man, granted her the fruitfulness of offspring without taking away her virginity. Just as she conceived with her flesh intact and her vulva unopened—that is, with the uterus closed—so she gave birth without the vulva being opened, but with the uterus closed. At the same time she became a mother and remained forever and always a virgin.

For the “virginal membrane,” as we read—the reason women whose flesh is intact are called virgins—that is, the little membrane which is ruptured in them at the first intercourse, nature does not permit to remain intact during the delivery of any child. Once that virginal membrane has been ruptured, a woman is not regarded as a virgin.

We also read in the Scripture of truth that, according to this diabolical invention concerning this woman and her brother, Onan, seeking to satisfy his lust with his wife and unwilling for children to be born, had intercourse with her; for this reason he was struck down and died by the Lord (Gen. 38). Therefore we do not believe that the woman could have conceived by such intercourse.

We say these things, bishops, not because we wish to reveal to those who know, or to insinuate to those who do not know, the virginal parts of girls or the private parts of women—matters of which we have no experience—but because it is written: “I diligently investigated the cause that I did not know” (Job 29:16). For this reason we call back before our eyes what we have read in the writings of the teachers of the Church, so that, if a woman found in such circumstances comes to us seeking penance according to the judgment of righteous judges, we may judge her without error.

Therefore we add this as well: if our lord the king found the aforesaid woman to be a virgin, why does he consent to her being branded as though she had been violated? But if he did not find her a virgin, why did he retain her for so long, or why did he receive a judicial examination concerning her?

In truth, those most noble laymen who are married, and the most equitable judges who will have to judge this matter, will be able to know this more accurately and more quickly for themselves, and, with marital permission, learn it from their wives: whether, in the manner we have heard concerning this woman, any woman can conceive.

They must investigate this more carefully and inquisitively, lest perhaps, in this judgment of justice and equity, they be able through some error to find fault with what may come to the knowledge of so many people, and lest many who will strive to take an example from the judgment find cause for reproach. As for us, since we are inexperienced in this matter, we state what we have read and neither seek nor wish to know or investigate anything further about it.

Let the judges of the laws determine whether, if what is said about this woman is found to be true—namely, that before her betrothal, while she remained under her own authority or under the authority of the man against whom the accusation is made, she committed some such indecent act, and afterward, once joined to her husband, preserved herself for him alone—they will decide that she should be condemned to death, whether under Roman law, under their own laws, under the laws to which that woman is subject, or under whatever laws they wish to judge her.

For just as peoples differ, so too do their laws; and if those laws are Christian, the holy Church does not reject them within their own spheres, decreeing what is fitting.

As for us, just as we who withdrew from the council after the Lord’s edict was issued know Balaam’s mark [*Balaae notam*, reading uncertain] and the penalty of the crime, so we decree that no one should be put to death. Rather, we desire that all be saved, since we desire no one to perish. Nor do we seek to do any violence to the holy and just laws which the holy Church and episcopal religion have both accepted and upheld until now.

But we urge that the royal road be held in seeking judgment, without regard to any person, just as the distinguished teacher Gregory writes to Domitian, metropolitan bishop (VIII, letter 50):

“We urge your fraternity to strive to investigate the truth with every care and, according to justice, to bring the disputes of the parties to an end as quickly as possible, lest either party complain that it has suffered prejudice in judgment. For just as we do not wish anyone to be condemned without judgment, so we do not permit what has been decided to be delayed under any pretext.”

He writes similarly to Constantius, bishop of Milan, from which anyone who is sound, wise, and attentive to what is right may take a suitable likeness and example in this matter. He says (ibid., letter 31):

“If the care shown in the inquiry had been matched by such precision in the examination, nothing concerning what was said about our brother would have remained ambiguous; rather, it would have become clear whether it was true or fabricated. For, as we have learned, a similar question had already been raised against him in Sicily before our brother of revered memory, Bishop Maximianus. But because his case was investigated with the utmost care, he who had been accused of the crime was found entirely innocent.

“Now, therefore, since the statements made against him were not investigated with the strictness that was required, and the records drawn up concerning the matter before your fraternity are shown to be sufficient neither for his condemnation nor for his acquittal, this is not a trivial matter to be decided carelessly or in passing. For it is exceedingly serious and improper that, in a doubtful matter, a definite sentence should be pronounced.

“These records could indeed have been adequate for a decision if the confession of the accused had followed them—provided, however, that the precision of the examination had drawn that confession out from hidden places rather than violent affliction having extorted it; for such affliction often causes even the innocent to be compelled to confess themselves guilty. Since the aforesaid bishop, as is said, asserts that he was tortured in custody and burned by hunger, you must determine, if this is so, whether it is harmful that the confession was extorted in this manner.

“When such cases receive a sentence and an appeal is made to the apostolic see, is not the person being judged also present, and is not the truth sought with the strictest investigation from every side, so that it may then be determined whether the sentence ought to stand? Therefore, since the person is absent and the records you sent us, as we have said, do not appear adequately to satisfy us, we neither ought nor can rashly decide anything concerning our brother’s person, lest—God forbid—we be found blameworthy in matters where, by the right of others, we are entitled to reconsider their judgments.”

And to Virgilius, bishop of Arles, he says (III, letter 63):

“Correction and punishment should strike the guilty, and a false report should not afflict the innocent.”

And he writes to Bishop Columbus (X, letter 8):

“For it is proven to be exceedingly perverse and contrary to ecclesiastical discipline that, merely to satisfy the wishes of certain people, someone should be deprived of his position when neither his fault nor his crime has cast him down from the rank of office he holds.”

Let the judges therefore draw this conclusion: if the woman is regarded as having been violated, the man who inflicted violence upon her or enticed her into the crime must be summoned. The case must be investigated chiefly through him, and he himself must be brought forward and examined according to law; he must either be released by legal judgment or punished.

This is especially necessary since, as we have heard, he himself, in the place of her parents, legally handed her over to her husband. According to the Lord’s command through Moses, even if she was not found to be a virgin at the first intercourse, he ought either to produce signs of certain virginity or to accept the accusation of fornication, lest suspicion of any kind trouble those who wish to judge justly, and lest those who are more eager and more able to disparage others than to establish their own conduct find an opportunity for insult, saying:

“The woman, terrified in custody by threats and afflictions, neither dares nor is able to say anything except what is commanded her.”

Let the man who is free come forward. Either, defending himself legally against what is charged to him, let him be released, or, since he is not merely a participant but also the author and executor of the crime attributed to him, let him be legally punished.

Then either, when he is released, let this woman who is in custody and who, because of fear, is lying against herself be legally freed; or, when he is punished, let her likewise be legally punished, as is prescribed in the sixth chapter of the first book of Roman law concerning fornicators, and in the seventh chapter concerning incestuous and shameful marriages, and as the just judges may read in the other provisions set forth by Christian laws.

For it is unjust that one who has been oppressed should be oppressed again, while the oppressor boasts of his freedom from crime. Saint Gregory strongly detests this, as he says to Goduinus, duke of Naples (XII, letter 5):

“We have been exceedingly astonished that, in the case of that soldier who, through the devil’s instigation, destroyed a servant of God, the strictest punishment has not yet been carried out. It was highly fitting, both in view of your character and of your goodness, that vengeance should reach us before the iniquity of the crime committed.

“We urge you, without any excuse, demonstrating what zeal you possess for the preservation of charity, to hasten to correct so great a crime with such strictness, as an example to others, that you may render propitious to yourselves the God whose injury that man committed, despising him by neglecting his fear. For we absolutely cannot tolerate so great an iniquity remaining unpunished.”

And earthly rulers ought not to hear with deaf ears what is said:

“Anathema is in your midst; you will not be able to stand before your enemies” (Josh. 7:13).

And again Saint Gregory writes to Bishop Syagrius (VII, letter 117):

“For it is exceedingly harmful and dangerous that those who ought to have been edified by the punishment of an evildoer should instead be destroyed by imitating his evil conduct. In this matter not only is the perpetrator found guilty, but also the one who did not resist. For he appears to consent to the one who errs if he does not join in cutting away what must be corrected.”

And let no one say, “Such a perverse man ought not to be summoned to judgment, but, as though already judged, should be condemned.” Let him hear what is written in the Gospel of John as having been said by Nicodemus to the rulers of the Jews concerning Jesus, whom they had asked to seize before judgment. For it is written:

[ p. 635; Col. 0698A ]

“Nicodemus, however, one of the Pharisees, who had come to the Lord by night, answered the Jews: ‘Does our law judge a man unless it first hears him himself and learns what he does?’” (John VII, 50–51.)

And the Lord says: “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment” (ibid., 24).

And Saint Gregory writes to the subdeacon Sabinus concerning a presbyter who was accused of the abominable crime of sodomy and of idolatry (Book VIII, Letter 5):

“It has been reported to us,” he says, “by the account of certain persons that Sisinnius, presbyter of the city of Regitana—which is exceedingly intolerable even to hear—is a worshipper and devotee of idols, to such an extent that he presumed to keep some idol set up in his house. And, what is no less impious, he is stained by the crime of sodomy. Therefore, because the wickedness of so great a crime must be investigated and punished by a strict and careful inquiry, we command you by this authority to investigate it with watchful zeal and wholly diligent care. If you are able to seize any evidence of this matter, place him in strict custody until you report to us, so that we may deliberate how so monstrous a crime ought to be examined and punished.”

[Col. 0698B]

And if anyone should say, “That same perverse man will not dare to come to account,” let him hear the advice of Saint Gregory concerning the heretics called Frontinianists, who could not otherwise be brought to account. He writes to Maximianus, bishop of Salona (Book VIII, Letter 36):

“Your Fraternity,” he says, “must be entirely concerned for the Frontinianists and, as you have begun, must strive to recall them to the bosom of the holy Church. If any of them should wish to come to me and accept an explanation, let them first provide an oath and promise that, even after receiving an explanation, they will not persist in their error. Afterwards let your Holiness promise them that they will suffer no violence from me; rather, I will give an account: if they recognize the truth, I shall receive them; if they do not recognize it, I shall dismiss them unharmed. But if any of them should wish to come to us against you without an oath, let your Fraternity by no means hold them back, because, when they come, they will either receive an explanation, or—know this—they will never again see that land.”

[Col. 0698C]

And it is written in the Council of Carthage (canon 30):

“It was decided,” it says, “that either the accused or the accuser, if he fears some violence from a reckless crowd in the place from which the accused comes, should choose for himself a nearby place where it will not be difficult to bring the witnesses, and where the case may be concluded.”

[Col. 0698D]
