And if anyone should say, “He cannot be brought to judgment because, supported by the patronage of other kings, he maintains a rebellion against the king,” let the king who, for this crime and for others, would send him to judgment if he could, bring the case he has to judgment. Let our lords the kings consider the truthful sentence of the King of kings, who is truth and judge of the living and the dead. He says this to the king who provides assistance against justice:

“‘You give help to the wicked,’ he says, ‘and you join friendship with those who hate me. Therefore you deserved the Lord’s anger—that is, death—but good works have been found in you’” (2 Chronicles XIX, 2–3).

For this reason, let kings fear who unjustly provide patronage to such men, lest through their protection they offend God, while churches, the poor of Christ, and humbler people are oppressed and devastated, and just judgments cannot be carried out. Otherwise, if they do not possess such and so many good qualities of their own as could resist so great an evil, they may perish without any obstacle; or they themselves may, because of another’s evil—in which they become participants—be made lost before God’s eyes, although in human judgment they may be thought sound in body.

[ p. 636; Col. 0699A ]

Let them also fear incurring the sentence of Scripture which says: “The just man perishes for the wicked.”

And lest anyone perversely interpret for them the sentence of Deuteronomy—“You shall not hand over to his master a servant who has taken refuge with you; he shall dwell with you in the place that he chooses, and he shall rest in one of your cities; you shall not distress him” (Deuteronomy XXIII, 15–16)—let them hear how blessed Augustine explains it:

“The Seventy,” he says, “say: ‘You shall not hand over the boy to his master who has been attached to you by his master.’ It does not say that his master attached him—that is, entrusted him—for it would more properly have said ‘deposited’; rather, it says that he was attached by his master, that is, joined to you after he had departed from him. It therefore prohibited fugitives from being returned, rather than from being received. This may be thought unjust unless we understand that these words are addressed to a nation and a people, not to one man. Thus, when a man fled from another nation to this nation to which the words were spoken, it prohibited him from being returned to his master—that is, to his own king.

“This was also observed by the foreign king of Gath when David fled to him from the presence of his master, that is, King Saul (1 Samuel XXVII). He explains this most clearly when he says of that fugitive: ‘He shall dwell among you in every place that pleases him.’”

[Col. 0699B]

This kingdom had, thanks be to God, been united from the hands of many into the hand of our parent kings; and one kingdom is one Church. Those who ought to be like one man and one ruler in one government must in no way divide it by their own division. Nor should it be said that, among our rulers, someone may flee from one people or one kingdom to another people or another kingdom; rather, as befits Christians, they should remain in one kingdom and in the unity of the mother Church.

[Col. 0699C]

Concerning the protection that those who flee to that Church ought to receive, Saint Gregory writes to John, bishop of the city of Caralis:

“If those concerning whom the dispute is raised should perhaps take refuge in the Church,” he says, “the case ought to be arranged in such a way that neither they themselves suffer violence nor those who are said to have been oppressed sustain losses. Therefore let it be your concern that, under oath, a promise be made to them by those whose interest it is to preserve law and justice; and let them be urged in every way to come out and give an account of their actions.”

[Col. 0699D]

Following this example, our rulers, sons of the Catholic Church, ought to obey the divine commands, remembering that, before God, they confirmed with their own hands that such men should not merely be protected, nor defended against law or reason, nor even received, except to the extent that they should be brought to render a proper account.

Some of those same kings who confirmed this are, thanks be to God, still alive in the body; others have departed to the Lord. But sons have been born in place of their father, and according to the Roman law which their predecessors—the emperors and kings—established and maintained, by which they happily governed and corrected their peoples, an action begun by its author must be completed by his heirs. Each of them ought in every respect to preserve the good ordinances of his predecessors, just as he desires his own enactments to be preserved by his successors.

[ p. 637; Col. 0700A ]

Let kings or anyone else not think it a small matter to violate what they strive to strengthen with their own hands. For, according to divine teaching and apostolic tradition, the confirmation of such a great matter by the hands has always been of the highest importance from the earliest ages. Thus, concerning the very vicars of the apostles, those same vicars of the apostles decreed by heavenly authority:

“Let whoever in any matter acts against his own subscription deprive himself of his honor.”

[Col. 0700B]

And let kings not say, “This was established concerning bishops, not concerning kings.” Rather, let them consider that, if they desire to be exalted and honored in the government of the people under the one king and priest Christ—from whose name the Lord’s anointed are called “christs”—and if, because of his honor, love, and fear, they are called lords and kings as participants in that great name, while being human beings like the rest; and if they wish to have a share in the heavenly kingdom with those who have been anointed with the sacred chrism, which received its name from Christ’s name, he who thereby anointed priests, prophets, kings, and martyrs, the one anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, and who made them kings and priests for our God in baptism, a royal race and a royal priesthood, according to the apostles John and Peter (Revelation II; 1 Peter II)—then let them understand and believe that, in God’s eyes, they are deprived of the dignity of the royal name and office when, although that which they had confirmed with their own hands was pleasing to God, they act against their own written subscription. They may indeed usurp that name before human eyes by an earthly and unstable power.

[Col. 0700C]

For just as good and just kings live under their good and just laws when through those laws the guilty are oppressed and punished while the innocent are raised up and freed, so apostolic men live under rules promulgated and confirmed by their own hands, by which those who act against them have been judged from the day on which they were established.

And just as the Apostle speaks of the woman who, while living, is dead (1 Timothy V, 6), so also such a transgressor, even if those who now hold the place of the apostles do not judge him—whether because they are ignorant of what happened or because they conceal it—will, if he has not corrected himself before the last day, be judged among those condemned for the gravest transgressions.

[Col. 0700D]

For the law was not established for the just, as the Apostle says (1 Timothy I, 9), but for transgressors and criminals, murderers and parricides, fornicators, and the rest of the violators of the law.

For it is not without reason that we read that the words of the Decalogue were written by the finger of God. He decreed that that law, which he wrote with his finger—that is, with his Spirit—would endure forever.

And concerning the elect the Lord says in the Gospel: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke XVI, 10). Concerning the rejected, however, the prophet Jeremiah says: “Those who depart from you, Lord, shall be written in the earth” (Jeremiah XVII, 13).

[ p. 638; Col. 0701A ]

We must not understand this childishly, as though God writes the good in heaven and the wicked on earth as a remedy for forgetfulness. Rather, it must be understood profitably: whether a person has performed heavenly or earthly works, through those works he is, as it were, marked by letters and eternally fixed in God’s memory.

In this law he demonstrates that whatever anyone has confirmed justly and reasonably with his hand, he must preserve inviolate and with persevering justice. Nor is it without meaning that a person who comes to baptism—if he is of age—or a sponsor on behalf of a child, and likewise a public penitent approaching reconciliation, gives his own written name according to ecclesiastical tradition. That name is placed upon the sacred altar during the celebration of the heavenly sacraments and is commended to the Lord by the priest for recitation at the proper point.

[Col. 0701B]

Likewise, in the sacred diptychs, the names of the faithful, both living and dead, are not written frivolously; and the names of unbelievers are erased from those same diptychs after death by divine judgment, if they had been entered there.

But perhaps rulers, relying as though on their princely license, say: “What great evil am I doing against God, or who will judge me for it, since I stand above everyone else, if I violate or disregard a command or edict that I confirm with my own hand?”

First, let them consider this: if they are above others, God is above them. And if they act wickedly and do not correct themselves, they will be judged more severely in proportion as they are placed higher than the others upon the throne of the kingdom.

[Col. 0701C]

Kings and priests correct the wicked actions of their subjects; but they must not forget that their own evils will be judged by the Lord himself. Nor should they hear with deaf ears what is written:

“The powerful shall suffer powerful torments, but mercy is granted to the lowly” (Wisdom VI, 7).

Next, let them read the history of the holy Abraham (Genesis XXIII), who received from the seller a deed confirming the purchase of his wife’s tomb in the presence of the sons and people of the land. He regarded it as so important that he even bowed to the people of the land—to the sons of Heth—in order to obtain it after hearing their concession; and they will be able to discover how highly such a matter ought to be valued.

[Col. 0701D]

They will also find sufficient treatment of this confirmation in the Law, which prevailed so greatly even before Christ’s coming that Pilate, instructed by ancient custom, when the Jews asked him to alter what he had written in the title of Christ, said: “What I have written, I have written” (John XIX, 22), unwilling that what he had done should be undone or changed.

This too had been confirmed long before by the Lord’s stipulation, as is written above a psalm: “Do not destroy the inscription of the title” (Psalm LXXIV).

[ p. 639; Col. 0702A ]

And how certain and stable a bond of writing ought to be believed to be—a *chirograph*, that is, something written by hand—is read in the Book of Tobit; and in the Gospel it is demonstrated by written bonds.

But certain rulers—may God keep such conduct far from our Christian rulers—perhaps fail to foresee that after them their weak confirmations remain while they themselves depart. As Saint Augustine says: “The act passes, but the guilt remains.”

They give to holy places through confirmation what belonged to them, yet seize for themselves through occupation what the poor of this world do not obtain through their requested grant. Indeed, they take it away for themselves and do not grant it to holy places; and from the very things by which they ought to have prepared a remedy for themselves, they commit sacrilege.

[Col. 0702B]

If they commit sacrilege concerning things of their own that were not rightly given, one must consider how great a danger they bring upon themselves through things given to God by others and taken away by them from God and against God.

Hence Saint Gregory, writing in a letter to the subdeacon Sabinus (Book VIII, Letter 7), says:

“It is sacrilegious and contrary to the laws if anyone attempts, through the efforts of an evil will, to retain for his own advantage what has been left to venerable places.”

And the sacred canons say (Council of Agde, canon 4):

“Clerics or laymen who presume to retain offerings of their parents, whether donated or left by testament, or who think that what they themselves have given to churches or monasteries ought to be taken away, shall, as the holy synod has established, be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor until they make restitution.”

[Col. 0702C]

Therefore let them know that, in the future judgment, they will be punished not only for their own sins but also for all the sins of those who gave those same possessions for the redemption of their souls.

And let those who perhaps rashly confirm what they give to the faithful or their friends, and take it away without judgment when they later recall what they had given in repentance, not postpone correction. They do not consider that those people depart from the world when the soul leaves the body, while the earth remains in the world and the charter of royal confirmation concerning those things is held by an empty possessor; and when their hearts sigh, their lips may perhaps be provoked to curse, not without the burden of sin.

[Col. 0702D]

Both matters ought to have been provided for: namely, that the king should give nothing rashly, that he should take nothing from anyone without a judgment of equity, and that after judgment an unbroken charter should not remain concerning things taken away.

For it is written: “The memory of the just is with praises, but the name of the wicked will rot” (Proverbs X, 6).

It would therefore be better and more reasonable if, through reason, a broken charter should rot while the praise of their equity remained, than that the charter of confirmation should remain while the name of their praise rotted.

[ p. 640; Col. 0703A ]

But perhaps rulers who read or hear these things will say: “The bishops have chastised us well. We shall give nothing by commands, lest we be criticized again.”

In response, let them hear what the prophet complains in the voice of those who chastise:

“We have healed Babylon, but she was not healed” (Jeremiah LI, 9).

Babylon is healed but not restored to health when a mind confused by wicked action hears words of correction and receives the blows of correction, yet refuses to return to the straight paths of salvation.

And through Wisdom he says:

“Like vinegar upon nitre, so is one who sings songs to a grievous heart” (Proverbs XXV, 30).

When vinegar is poured upon nitre, it immediately foams and boils over. In the same way, the hearts of the powerful, who swell with their power and do not humble themselves through humanity—as Abraham said to the Lord, humbling himself in his exalted conversation with him, “I shall speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Genesis XVIII, 27)—often burst from the swelling of their hearts into words of contradiction when they hear the correction sent by the Lord who chastises.

[Col. 0703B]

The bishops did not forbid giving to holy places or faithful men. Rather, they proclaimed to everyone:

“Vow and repay to the Lord your God” (Psalm LXXV, 12);

and:

“Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not repent” (Sirach XXXII, 24);

and:

“Do not do what is unjust, nor judge unjustly” (Leviticus XIX, 15);

and:

“Judge your neighbor justly” (ibid.).

Just as a ruler does not want a stronger person to take from him what God has granted him, so he too should not take from anyone, without a judgment of equity, either what he has given or what he has not given, because it is written:

“What you do not want done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit IV, 16).

[Col. 0703C]

Rather, the bishops proclaimed again and again:

“Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI, 9);

and:

“Whatever your hand is able to do, do it diligently, because there is neither place nor reasoning in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Ecclesiastes IX, 10).

And just as the bishops proclaimed these things, which are useful and honorable, so they also proclaim that the king should hasten to conceal from himself the shameful stain upon the royal name, and should wash it away as far as he can, every day and in every action, mindful of the sentence of Deuteronomy:

[Col. 0703D]

“You shall have a place outside the camp to which you may go for the needs of nature. Carrying a stake on your belt, when you sit down, dig around yourself and, after excreting, cover with the excavated earth what has been exposed. For the Lord your God walks in the midst of the camp, to rescue you and hand your enemies over to you; therefore your camp shall be holy, and nothing foul shall appear in it, lest he abandon you” (Deuteronomy XXIII, 12–14).

Burdened by the weight of corruptible nature, certain superfluities of thought burst forth from the womb of our mind, and from the work and governance of our actions things unworthy of leadership emerge, like the burdens of the belly.

[ p. 641; Col. 0704A ]

We who rule the people ought to carry a stake on our belt, so that, always girded for reproving ourselves, we may have around us a sharp goad of compunction. This goad should continually pierce the soil of our mind with the pain of repentance and conceal what foulness bursts forth from us.

The excrement of the belly is covered with earth dug by the stake when the superfluity of our mind or the foulness of our blameworthy action, examined by subtle reproof and corrected by honorable conduct, is hidden from God’s eyes by the goad of our compunction and the good of correction.

[Col. 0704B]

It must also be considered that ancient kings and emperors established by their laws that a charter of confirmation should stand strengthened by five, seven, or ten witnesses, as Ambrose writes.

Likewise, in civil law, when charters are written, a supplementary constitution is inserted, by which the person who attempts to violate that same charter is fined for the treasury; and the accuser, by subscribing to the written accusation, cannot withdraw from the condition he has assumed.

They wrote nothing concerning their own confirmation because the hand of the prince is counted, as we read concerning David in the Book of Kings, for ten thousand (1 Samuel XVIII).

[Col. 0704C]

And the king, established by God either for grace or because of the sins of the people, will be crowned by the King of kings for his just actions, or, judged by the judgment of equity, will be punished for unjust judgments and wicked actions.

They also inserted into those same laws, under the Cornelian law concerning wills, that anyone who knowingly and maliciously writes, suppresses, presents, designates, or erases a false will or any other document should, if of higher status, be deported to an island, while a person of lower status should be condemned to the mines or raised upon a cross, and a slave should be punished by death.

[Col. 0704D]

And, as blessed Augustine recalls in his Commentary on the Evangelist John (treatise 7):

“It belongs to forensic law that, if anyone has lied in petitions to the prince, the document he obtained should not benefit him; rather, he should even lose the benefit of the document by which he secured the document.”

They said nothing concerning the writing of their own confirmation because they regarded it as impious to violate what they had confirmed. Thus, in the Book of Esther, we read how great is the force of the king’s ring and its seal (Esther III), how great the precaution required in voiding that seal, and how much greater still the force of the royal hand’s subscription.

[ p. 642; Col. 0705A ]

Nor should royal dignity treat casually what is written in its commands:

“And so that this command of our authority,” it says, “may obtain fuller strength of firmness in the name of God”;

and:

“Given in such-and-such a year, happily, in the name of God.”

Otherwise, what is confirmed happily in the name of God might, without God—that is, without the judgment of truth—be unhappily brought to ruin. For it is written:

“Do not profane the name of the Lord your God” (Leviticus XVIII, 21);

and:

“Do not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exodus XXX, 7).

Let them also read Paul and the interpreters of that Apostle, and see how emphatically the same divine Apostle wrote in his Epistles:

“See what kind of letters I have written with my own hand” (Galatians VI, 11);

and again:

“The greeting of me, Paul” (1 Corinthians XVI, 21).

[Col. 0705B]

Therefore, let kings who confirm privileges granted by their own hand’s subscription, or privileges of the saints strengthened by their hands with an anathema, and who afterward treat their preservation as insignificant or delay it, as though they were not bound by the bond of an anathema, hear the sentence of blessed Gregory from his letter to the patrician Theoctista (Book XII, Letter 39):

“They themselves,” he says, “are witnesses against themselves that they are not Christians who think that they can dissolve the bonds of the holy Church through empty efforts. Consequently, they do not consider the absolution of the holy Church, which it grants to the faithful, to be true if they do not consider its bonds to be true and effective; and from the very point at which they believe they are deceiving the truth, they are truly bound in their sins.”

[Col. 0705C]

Therefore, if there are any who, under the Christian name, dare either to preach these things or to hold them silently within themselves, I, together with all Catholic bishops and the whole Church, anathematize them.

We say these things so that the rulers of the kingdom and the rectors of the holy Church may conduct everything according to reason and the order of law, and so that the case written above may be determined with a judgment of equity.

[Col. 0705D]

Saint Gregory himself described the order for constituting a judgment, if Hucbertus should come to a hearing concerning this matter and, having not been judged in a civil proceeding, should come to ecclesiastical judgment. In his memorandum to John the Defender, who was going to Spain, he says (Book XI, Letter 50):

“First, let the matter be arranged in an orderly way, so that some are accusers and others witnesses. Next, let the nature of the case be examined, whether it is worthy of exile or condemnation; and let testimony against him be presented under oath in his presence, or let it be inserted in the written record of the proceedings. Let him also have the opportunity to respond and defend himself.

“But the persons of the accusers and witnesses must be investigated carefully: what their status and reputation are; whether they are poor; whether perhaps they harbor some enmity against him; and whether they have given testimony from hearsay or have testified that they know the matter personally. Let the judgment be recorded in writing, and then let the sentence be read in the presence of the parties; and in this way let all these things be solemnly confirmed.”

In any event, if the woman is found guilty of a crime with her brother before entering into marriage, we have thought it appropriate to set forth, as a model for judgment, a letter of that same holy Gregory to John, bishop of Palermo, concerning a certain woman whom a man abandoned before he was ordained deacon and whom, after changing his clothing, he gave to a certain husband. He says (Book XI, Letter 60):

[ p. 643; Col. 0706A ]

“Because there are faults in which it is itself a fault to relax punishment, the truth must always be sought, so that it may be investigated whether guilt condemns the accused or whether disclosed innocence withdraws him from punishment.

“Accordingly, it has come to our attention that Fantinus, the defender, wished to exercise vengeance against Peter, the bearer of this letter, because, as is said, while he was a tenant, he gave the abandoned woman of a certain deacon to a husband.

[Col. 0706B]

“But since this man asserts that she was not the deacon’s wife, saying that the woman had not come to him as a virgin, and, finally, that she had not changed her religious clothing after he had been advanced in the sacred order, he adds also that she had lived under an evil reputation both before he reached the diaconate and afterward.

“Therefore we exhort your Fraternity in these words: let it investigate this case with the fear of God, as is fitting, and with the utmost carefulness. If it should be established that the woman in question was the deacon’s wife, let the aforesaid bearer be handed over in every way to the aforementioned defender and rector of the patrimony for punishment, and, with suitable correction, let those who have been wrongly joined be separated.”

[Col. 0706C]

These are passages we have excerpted from the words of Saint Gregory.

And, as we stated above from the words of blessed Augustine, what execution accomplished under the ancient law, and what execution now accomplishes under the laws of the state, excommunication and separation from the Church accomplish in the Church.

[Col. 0706D]

If, under the public laws, any woman entangled in such crimes as have been described above should evade forensic judgment and come to episcopal judgment, then, according to the sacred Council of Ancyra (canons 15 and 20), concerning those who fornicate unnaturally—that is, with males or animals—and concerning women who fornicate and kill their offspring, or who act upon themselves in order to expel what has been conceived in the womb, she shall, as it seems to us, be ordered to pray among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit.

[ p. 644; Col. 0707A ]

After being disciplined by a strict ten-year penance, she shall continue until the end of her life in fitting works of penitence. Nevertheless, out of ecclesiastical mercy, if fear of death should press upon her, she shall be judged worthy to receive the provision for the journey—the viaticum—reserved for her.

She shall be separated not only from the royal bed but also from all marital companionship, according to the decrees of blessed Pope Gregory addressed to Felix, bishop of Sicily. He says (Book XII, Letter 32):

“We decree,” he says, “that each person who has been faithfully instructed and now stands unshaken, planted with a firm root, should observe his offspring up to the seventh generation; and, so long as they recognize themselves as related by kinship, they are not to enter into a union of this kind.

[Col. 0707B]

“No Christian is or will be permitted to marry a woman whom someone has had as a wife from his own blood relationship, or whom he has stained by some illicit union, because such intercourse is incestuous and abominable to God and to all human beings.

“We have long read that the holy Fathers established that incestuous persons are not to be counted under any name of marriage. Nor do we leave aside this part of our concern: all incestuous persons are to be separated from the boundaries of the holy Church until, through satisfaction and the prayers of the priests, they are reconciled to that same holy Catholic Church.”

And in a canonical edict issued before the body of blessed Peter (Gregory XI, in the Roman synod):

“If anyone takes as wife a woman from his own kinship, or one whom his kinsman had as wife, let him be anathema.”

And all replied three times: “Let him be anathema.”

[Col. 0707C]

And Saint Ambrose says in his First Letter to the Corinthians:

“For the brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases” (1 Corinthians VII, 15)—that is, marital reverence is not owed to one who has recoiled from the author of marriage. For a marriage that exists without devotion to God is not valid.

And Saint Jerome, in the third book of his Commentary on Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, says:

“Therefore, just as the Church is subject to Christ, so let the wife be subject to her husband. To the same order to which Christ and the Church are bound by authority and subjection, husband and wife are also bound. But one must see that, just as there is a holy union in Christ and in the Church, so there must be a holy union between husband and woman.

“Just as not every congregation of heretics can be called the Church of Christ, nor is Christ their head, so not every marriage in which a wife is not joined to her husband according to Christ’s commandments can rightly be called marriage; rather, it is more properly adultery.”

[Col. 0707D]

From this it must be intelligently noted that what this same teacher says in his letter to the presbyter Amandus (Letter 147)—that so long as the husband lives, even if he is an adulterer, even if he is a sodomite, even if he is covered with every disgrace, and even if his wife has left him because of these crimes, he is still considered her husband, and she may not take another husband—he says concerning one who, after entering into a lawful marriage, sins within that marriage, in which husband and woman are held by an equal legal sentence.

Here, however, the matter concerns one who, before entering into a lawful marriage, by committing incest deprives himself or herself of the lawful marriage that he or she could have had.

And in the Council of Agde (canon 61):

“Concerning incestuous unions,” they say, “we reserve absolutely no pardon, unless they have healed the adultery by separation. Incestuous persons are truly not to be counted under any name of marriage; it is even a fatal thing to designate them as such.”

And Saint Augustine, in his book *On the Good of Marriage*:

“It is one thing not to have intercourse except with the sole intention of procreation, which bears no guilt; it is another thing to seek pleasure through intercourse of the flesh, but not outside one’s spouse, which bears a venial guilt. For intercourse may take place without the purpose of producing offspring, yet the production of offspring is not obstructed for the sake of this lust, whether by an evil vow or an evil act.

“Those who do this, although they are called spouses, are not spouses and retain none of the truth of marriage; rather, they use an honorable name to cover their shame. They are exposed, however, when they go so far as to expose the children born to them against their will, while they hate to nourish or possess those whom they feared to beget.

“Thus, when the dark iniquity rages against those whom it has begotten, it is brought clearly into the light by its iniquity, and hidden shame is convicted by manifest cruelty.

“Sometimes this lustful cruelty, or cruel lust, advances so far that it even procures poisons of sterility; and, if these accomplish nothing, it destroys and expels the conceived fetuses by some means within the womb, desiring that its offspring should die before living, or, if it was already alive in the womb, that it should be killed before being born.

“Absolutely, if both are such, they are not spouses; and if they were such from the beginning, they came together not through marriage but rather through fornication. But if they are not both such, I dare to say that either she is, in some manner, her husband’s prostitute, or he is his wife’s adulterer.”

## QUESTION XIII

In the sixth chapter, send us word whether the same king, after hearing such things concerning his aforementioned wife and being suspended from carnal relations with her, perhaps committed adultery by using a concubine; and, if this became known to many people, by what medicinal judgment the matter ought to be healed.

And if it should perhaps happen that any man has bound himself by an oath to do something criminal, whether, in order not to incur perjury, he ought to fulfill what he swore, or whether, in order not to commit the crime, he ought to render void what he wrongly swore.

And whether this can be true, as many people say: that there are women who, through their magic, can place irreconcilable hatred between husband and wife, and then sow an indescribable love again between a man and a woman; that a man cannot approach the wife he has lawfully taken in marital intercourse, yet can have intercourse with other women; and that, by the same magic, his power of intercourse and his ability to enjoy the affection he once possessed can be restored through the art of sorceresses.

And what the reason may be why God, as is said, often permits such things to occur within a lawful marriage.

And if such male sorcerers or female enchantresses should be discovered, what ought to be done concerning them.

## RESPONSE

[The supplied source ends here.]

We respond: if, as is reported, the king in question, after entering into a lawful marriage, engaged in intercourse with another woman, it cannot be denied that he committed adultery, even [Col. 0708A] if the woman whom he took as his wife should perhaps be found guilty of such things, as is alleged, since, after the marriage had lawfully been contracted and before a legal determination, she presumed to commit unlawful acts. For the Apostle says that a wife is bound by the law to her husband while her husband lives, but that when he has died she is released from the law concerning her husband (I Cor. VII). And, according to sacred authority, no one can doubt that a woman lawfully betrothed, endowed, and honored with a public wedding is a wife. Sacred authority likewise bears witness that there is one and the same law governing the husband and the wife in this matter. Therefore, before one is released from the heavy yoke imposed upon the children of Adam—from the day they emerge from their mother’s womb until the day they enter into the womb of the mother of all—either by one being dissolved from the other or by the lawgiver, who rightly decides according to the founders of the laws, establishing that the union entered into was not a lawful marriage, whoever among them divides one flesh into two by adultery cannot be said not to have committed adultery.

For Pope Leo the Great, writing to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, granted a rule from the secular laws for ecclesiastical use (Epistle 85): “Just as, in the case of slaves, fields, houses, possessions, and estates that have been carried into captivity, the right of return from captivity is preserved, so also marriages, if they have been joined to others, are to be restored.” We too must reason from these same laws, following his example: for if anyone presumptuously claims against the law what might lawfully belong to him, the law will compel him to make legal restitution to the person whom he had despoiled.

Therefore, if anyone lawfully married has presumed, before a judicial decision has determined the accusation, to act either publicly or secretly against the rights of marriage, it will be necessary for him, as a transgressor, to submit either secretly or publicly to the penalties established by the laws. Thus it was decreed in the Council of Africa (canon 10): “Let bishops, according to the difference among sins, determine the periods of penance at their discretion.” And in the Council of Carthage (Council of Carthage IV, canon 74): “Let a priest impose the laws of penance upon one who seeks penance, without respect of persons.” And [canon 47]: “If any member of the faithful, according to the Council of Elvira, having a wife, has committed adultery not once but repeatedly, he is to be visited at the point of death; but if he promises that he will cease, communion is to be granted him. If, after being restored to health, he again commits adultery, he is to be cut off more severely, so that he may not thereafter trifle with the communion of peace.”

And according to the Council of Ancyra (canon 19): “An adulterous wife, or a husband who commits adultery, shall attain the completion of reconciliation and communion after seven years of penance.” Likewise, according to the Council of Elvira (canon 69): “If anyone who has a wife falls once, he is to be reconciled after five years of penance; or, if the necessity of illness compels it, communion is to be granted him earlier.” Similarly, the Synod of Toledo decreed (First Council of Toledo, canon 17): “Whoever has both a wife and a concubine is to be separated from communion with the Church.”

In this separation, or in reconciliation after worthy satisfaction, the pastors of the Church, the successors and vicars of the apostles, must take the greatest care. For, as blessed Gregory says (Homily 26 on the Gospels), “when they have attained the office of governing, they possess the authority to loose and to bind, so that in loosing and binding their subjects they may follow not the impulse of their own will but the merits of the cases; otherwise they may condemn the undeserving, or release others while themselves remain bound, and deprive themselves of this power of binding and loosing when they exercise it according to their own wishes and not according to the character of their subjects. They must not be moved toward anyone by hatred or favor, because they will be unable to judge their subjects rightly if they decide to follow either their own hatred or their own favor in the cases of their subjects. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: ‘They were killing souls that should not die, and bringing to life souls that should not live’ (Ezek. XIII, 19). He kills one who should not die who condemns the just; and he tries to bring to life one who will not live who attempts to free the guilty from punishment. The cases, therefore, must be weighed, and then the power of binding and loosing must be exercised. It must be seen what fault preceded, and what penance followed the fault, so that those whom Almighty God visits through the grace of compunction may be absolved by the pastor’s sentence. For the absolution of the presiding minister is then true when it follows the judgment of the inner Judge.”

We ought therefore to loose by pastoral authority those whom we know our Creator to vivify through his life-giving grace. This vivification is recognized even before the practice of righteousness, already in the very confession of sin—not a confession made merely with words and scarcely with the lips, but one that proceeds from the innermost feeling of the heart, as David said: “I have sinned against the Lord,” and deserved to hear: “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (II Sam. XII, 13). And again he says: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Ps. XXXVII, 9); and: “I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin” (ibid., v. 19). So also, in the affliction he endured for the sin he had committed while fleeing from the presence of his son, he reflected, saying: “May the Lord look upon my affliction, and repay me good for this curse” (II Sam. XVI, 12). From these examples it is clear that satisfaction must neither be forbidden nor communion denied to those who confess in this manner.

Otherwise, those who, indiscriminately, have not been purified or absolved, but rather have been led astray and deceived by such pastors, presume upon the sacraments of the sacred body and precious blood of our Redeemer unto judgment for themselves. Of such pastors the prophet says: “Woe to those who sew pillows under every elbow of the hand, and make cushions under the head of persons of every age, to catch souls” (Ezek. XIII, 18)—that is, they encourage with flattering indulgence souls who fall from their uprightness and recline in the pleasure of this world, so that they may lie softly in error, untroubled by any harshness of contradiction. This is undoubtedly how rulers who love themselves behave toward those by whom they fear they may be harmed in their pursuit of temporal glory.

Of them it is again written: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps” (Isa. III, 12). And again: “Your prophets saw false and foolish things for you, and they did not uncover your iniquity in order to provoke you to repentance” (Lam. II, 14). For while they fear rebuking sins, they flatter sinners with an empty promise of security; and thus, whether they remain inclined to sin or usurp the divine mysteries before suitable satisfaction, they make God’s good gift their own judgment.

For, as the holy authors say—as the venerable priest Bede demonstrates in his commentary on the Gospel of Luke—when they explain the Lord’s saying, “Nevertheless, behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table,” and, “Nevertheless, woe to that man by whom he is betrayed” (Luke XXII, 21), they say that this applies today and forever: “Woe to that man who approaches the Lord’s table in wickedness, who does not fear to participate in the mysteries of Christ while harboring plots in his mind and having his heart polluted by some crime.”

For he too, as an example of Judas, betrays the Son of Man—not indeed to sinful Jews, but nevertheless to sinners, namely to his own members, whom he presumes to violate that immeasurable and inviolable body of the Lord. He sells the Lord who, neglecting love and fear of him, is shown to love and care more for earthly and passing things, indeed even for criminal things. Woe, I say, to that man concerning whom Jesus—who is not doubted to be present at the most holy altars during the offering, about to consecrate the offerings set before him, with heavenly ministers attending him—is compelled to complain, saying: “Behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table.”

And Paul says: “If anyone is named a brother and is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one not even to take food” (I Cor. V, 11). And again he says: “The unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God. Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 9–10). And again: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. XIII, 4). And again: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the fornicator sins against his own body” (I Cor. VI, 18).

Hence Ambrose shows that this is the gravest sin, because through it the whole body perishes, whereas in other sins only a portion perishes, not the whole. For the whole body is man and woman, since woman is a portion of man. Whoever commits another sin sins outside himself, but the fornicator sins against his own flesh. Although all sins make a person carnal, this sin in particular is the desire of the flesh, which delivers the soul, stained by filth, together with the body to Gehenna. For when the soul is overcome by the lust of the flesh, it becomes flesh, just as a body rightly governed is called spiritual. It is nevertheless the mind that either, overcome by enticements, makes the whole person carnal, or, remaining in the vigor of its nature, enables the flesh to be called spiritual.

Therefore the founders of the canons, with the Holy Spirit speaking through them, decreed that such people be separated from communion until they have made satisfaction. For those who are strangers to the kingdom of God must by every means be separated from the Church—which is and is called the kingdom of God—until correction and satisfaction. And since the disciples of Christ ought not to eat with such people, the priests of the Lord ought not to give them holy communion, as the Lord himself forbids in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. VII, 6).

Peter identifies such people when he says: “As a washed sow returns to wallowing in the mud, so is a dog that returns to its vomit” (II Pet. II, 22), as Solomon says: “A fool repeating his folly” (Prov. XXVI, 11). Whoever remains in sin, or presumes to eat the Lord’s Supper before correcting and making satisfaction for a grave sin, presumes upon that same Supper for his own condemnation, as we have stated, in accordance with the Apostle’s testimony: “Whoever,” he says, “eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (I Cor. XI, 27).

Therefore Saint Ambrose says: “What does it mean to be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, except to suffer the penalties of the Lord’s death? For he was killed on behalf of those who nullify his benefit.” “Let a person examine himself,” Paul says again, “and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (ibid., 28). To examine oneself means that a person must correct himself from sin, reject the sin itself, and, after worthy satisfaction, approach holy communion, so that the mind may know that it owes reverence to the one whose body it approaches to receive. For one must judge this within oneself: that the one whose body and blood one receives is the Lord.

The statement that follows—“Therefore many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep” (I Cor. XI, 30)—was added to present an image of the judgment upon those who receive the Lord’s body carelessly. For just as those people were physically weakened and died, so whoever remains in sin or retains an inclination to sin, and receives the body and blood of the Lord—whereby he could receive life if he received those sacraments after worthy penance and with worthy satisfaction—takes death for himself by receiving them unworthily.

If someone asks why those who now receive them unworthily do not become weak or die, as people then became weak and died, let him understand that the Apostle did not say that everyone becomes weak or dies, but “many,” he says, become weak, and many die. At the beginning of the Church, bodily signs were necessary; now true faith ought to suffice.

There is another explanation as well. As it is written, “At the end of the age the sun will be like a sackcloth of hair” (Rev. VI, 12)—that is, the Church will be in the bitterness of mourning, without the radiance of miracles, so that those who have been tested may be revealed. Some are corrected by communicating simply, even though afterward they sin, as Peter did. Others are tolerated while communicating wickedly, as Judas was; by existing as his own murderer and meeting a destructive end, he demonstrated what the soul suffers now without the body and what it will suffer eternally with the body, because he ate and drank the divine mysteries to his own judgment.

And what follows—“If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI, 31)—means that if we ourselves corrected our errors, we would not be judged by the Lord, that is, condemned. Therefore the sacred canons decreed that sinners be brought before priestly judgment, or be restored to the sacred altar, in accordance with the Lord’s saying to the lepers, who prefigured those now afflicted by the leprosy of sins in the Church: “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke XVII, 14). Thus, according as they see the magnitude or number of the sins in the sinners, and consider the worthiness of their satisfaction, they should establish, without respect of persons, the periods for their repentance and reconciliation, so that they may not take for judgment and condemnation what the Lord has bestowed upon believers for redemption and salvation.

But if a sinner is slow to recognize his fault, negligent in repenting of, confessing, and making satisfaction for what he has done, the episcopal care must not fail to admonish him, mindful of the sentence addressed to him: “If you have become surety for your friend, you have fastened your hand to a stranger” (Prov. VI, 1). This means: if you have taken responsibility for your brother’s soul in the danger arising from your conduct, you have already bound your mind to the care of vigilance, which was lacking before you undertook pastoral office. You have been ensnared by the words of your mouth and captured by your own speech; for, since you are compelled to speak good things by preaching to those entrusted to you, you must first keep what you have said yourself.

“Do therefore what I say, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into the hand of your neighbor; run, hasten, rouse your friend” (ibid., 3). Remember not only to keep watch by living well yourself, but also to separate by preaching the person over whom you preside from the torpor of sin. “Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” (ibid., 4). He gives sleep to his eyes who entirely neglects the care of his subjects; he slumbers who knows their blameworthy deeds but, because of weariness of mind, does not correct them with a fitting rebuke.

“Rescue yourself like a doe from the hand, and like a bird from the snare of the fowler” (ibid., 5). As a bird seeks to escape from a snare, or a doe from the hand of its captor, so strive to be freed from responsibility for the life of your hearer by instructing him healthfully, lest you be marked not as a shepherd but as a hireling. If you see someone being dragged toward lust, inflamed toward greed, raised up in pride, or divided through anger, and either you show partiality to the rich, fearing that he may angrily withdraw the gift he had been graciously offering you, or remain silent out of regard for familiarity or some temporal advantage, while you rejoice in earthly benefits as souls perish, you will be reckoned in the eyes of God not as a shepherd but as a hireling.

Rather, preach and insist “in season and out of season.” If, when you admonish him according to the Gospel, he does not listen to you, appeal to the royal power so that he may be restrained. And if even then you do not bring the matter to a conclusion, according to the divine command concerning the person admonished, “tell it to the Church”; and if he does not listen even to the Church, “let him be to you as a heathen and a publican.” Do not, by concealing or neglecting to rebuke him, perish with him as the priest Eli did with his sons when they sinned against God, lest they become hateful to men.

It is therefore clear that no one is to be spared against God, so that we may mercifully spare both ourselves and the person whom we do not spare by diligent correction. In our limited measure, insofar as the Lord grants it, we follow blessed Ambrose, who by not sparing Theodosius acquired for him both merit in heaven before the Lord and eternal remembrance on earth before men, so that what is written of him may be understood: “The memory of the just is with praises” (Prov. X, 7).

Nor should bishops, kings, or anyone endowed with human power hear only superficially the sentence of blessed Gregory addressed to Queen Brunhild, in which he says (Book IX, Epistle 64): “For,” he says, “the things we mention must not be concealed, since whoever can correct sins and neglects to do so undoubtedly makes himself a participant in the offense. Therefore take care of your own soul; take care of your grandchildren, whom you desire to reign happily; take care of the provinces; and before the Creator shakes out his hand to strike, give the most diligent thought to correcting the crime, lest he strike afterward with all the greater severity the longer he now waits.”

And if, as may happen, any person disobedient to the divine word is expelled, that person must be expelled from the Church according to the prescribed order, because the expulsion itself, through the Lord’s mercy, may become salutary for him, as blessed Augustine says in his book *On Correction and Grace* (chapter 15): “Let subject brothers be rebuked by their superiors with rebukes proceeding from charity, differing according to the diversity of their faults, whether lesser or greater. For even what is called condemnation—which is imposed by episcopal judgment, and than which there is no greater penalty in the Church—may, if God wills, lead and contribute to the most salutary correction. For we do not know what may happen on the following day, nor should anyone be despaired of before the end of this life; nor can God be resisted, so that he may not receive and grant repentance and, having accepted the sacrifice of a contrite spirit and a broken heart, absolve from guilt even one justly condemned, and himself not condemn the one who has been condemned. Nevertheless, pastoral necessity requires that the diseased sheep be separated from the healthy sheep, lest dreadful contagions spread among the many; perhaps through that very separation it may be healed by him for whom nothing is impossible.”

And if, God forbid, one should arise who, puffed up by the pride of earthly power, despises obedience and, breaking the restraint of Christianity, rushes headlong into the abyss of damnation, the bishop will have, according to the prophet Ezekiel, an iron griddle for his deliverance (Ezek. IV, 3)—that is, zeal burning with charity—and the memorable sentence of blessed Ambrose.

For he says in his Epistle to the Corinthians: “Blessed Paul so greatly humbles their pride when he says: ‘And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst’ (I Cor. V, 2).” In this way he makes them not now quarrelsome but rather straightforward. For they too were participants, since they allowed one who had committed so great a crime to meet with them without correction; they should all, with one accord, have cast him out if he refused to amend. But if someone does not have the authority to cast out one whom he knows to be guilty, or cannot prove the charge, he is free of guilt; and it is not the judge’s place to condemn without an accuser. For the Lord, although Judas was a thief, did not cast him out, since he had not been accused.”

And the Holy Spirit, speaking through a worthy instrument pleasing to him, namely blessed Benedict, says: “The ruler will likewise be free if, while every diligence has been devoted to an unruly and disobedient flock, and every care has been shown toward the diseased actions of the sheep, the shepherd of those sheep, acquitted at the Lord’s judgment, can say with the prophet to the Lord: ‘I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation. But they, despising, have rejected me’ (Ps. XXXIX, 11).” Then, finally, let death itself be the prevailing punishment for the disobedient sheep entrusted to his care.

## QUESTION XIV AND RESPONSE

Regarding the question proposed about an oath, the words of blessed Gregory are to be read from the thirty-third book of the *Moralia* (chapter 17). He says:

“Behold, a certain man, while seeking the friendships of this world, binds himself by oath to another person living a similar life, promising that he will conceal that person’s secrets in complete silence. But the person to whom he has sworn is discovered to be committing adultery, and even attempting to kill the husband of the adulteress. The one who gave the oath then returns to his right mind and is assailed by conflicting thoughts on every side. He fears to remain silent, lest by silence he become a participant in both adultery and murder; yet he hesitates to expose the matter, lest he bind himself by the guilt of perjury. He is therefore bound by the tangled cords of conflicting obligations: whichever way he turns, he fears that he will not be free from the contagion of transgression.”

And shortly afterward:

“There is nevertheless a useful course for destroying such deceits: when the mind is constrained between lesser and greater sins, if there is absolutely no way of escaping without sin, the lesser must always be chosen. For one who is enclosed on every side by the circuit of walls and cannot escape rushes away in flight wherever he finds the shorter wall.”

And the venerable priest Bede, in his homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, where Herod’s rash oath is described, says:

“How greatly we ought to avoid the recklessness of swearing, both the Lord himself in the Gospel and James in his epistle teach, saying: ‘Above all things, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven nor by earth nor by any other oath; but let your speech be, “Yes, yes,” “No, no,” so that you may not fall under judgment’ (James V, 12). This is the judgment under which Herod fell, so that he necessarily had either to commit perjury or, by avoiding perjury, to perpetrate another crime.

“But if it should happen that we have sworn something rashly, and keeping it would clearly lead to a worse outcome, we should know that we must freely change it to a sounder course; and, when necessity presses, we ought rather to commit perjury than turn aside into a more serious crime in order to avoid perjury.

“David swore by the Lord that he would kill Nabal, a foolish and wicked man, and destroy everything belonging to him. But at the first intercession of Abigail, a prudent woman, he immediately withdrew his threats and returned his sword to its sheath; nor did he regret having incurred any guilt by such perjury (I Sam. XXV). Herod swore to give the dancing girl whatever she asked of him; and, lest his guests call him a perjurer, he polluted the banquet with blood, making the prophet’s death the reward of a dance (Mark VI).

“This moderation must be observed not only in swearing but in everything we do: if we should happen to fall into the snares of the crafty enemy in such a way that we cannot rise without some contagion of sin, we should seek that avenue of escape in which we perceive that we will suffer the lesser danger. Similarly, when people enclosed by hostile walls wish to escape but see that access to every gate has been denied them, they must necessarily choose the place from which to leap where, because the wall is lower, they will incur the least danger in falling.”

And in the Council of Hilerdus [possibly an OCR form of the council’s name] it is decreed (canon 7):

“Whoever has bound himself by oath never to return to peace with someone with whom he is in dispute shall, for perjury, be separated for one year from communion of the body and blood of the Lord, and shall absolve his guilt by almsgiving, tears, and as many fasts as he is able to undertake. Let him hasten to return quickly to charity, which covers a multitude of sins.”

Since those asking wished to inquire about such matters concerning an oath, we thought it perhaps not irrelevant to write about things that commonly occur in human frailty. We do not direct what we write against anyone; but if there should be someone whom this counsel can help, remembering the Scripture that says, “Whatever more you spend, I will repay you” (Luke X, 35), we thought it should be added—even though we were not asked—so that anyone may know what ought to be chosen when faced with uncertainty between two alternatives.

For one will not easily find anyone now—indeed, one will find no one at all—who is holier than David, wiser than Solomon, or stronger than Samson; and those men, captured by love of women, since lust subdues even iron minds, fearing neither the rags of the poor nor the purple of kings, did things that were not fitting. Women often come to us complaining that young men promised them their faith and then left them mocked and abandoned.

Sometimes we have also found that men left their lawful wives and clung so closely to adulteresses, in order to keep the faith they had promised, that they could be separated from them only with great difficulty. Concerning this matter blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Good of Marriage* (chapter 4):

“To this is added the fact that, even in the very act by which spouses render to one another what is owed, although they may seek it somewhat intemperately and without restraint, they nevertheless owe one another fidelity. To this fidelity the Apostle assigns so much authority that he calls it a power, saying: ‘The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man; likewise, the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman’ (I Cor. VII, 4).

“The violation of this fidelity is called adultery, when, whether through the impulse of one’s own lust or with the consent of another, a man or woman has intercourse with someone else against the marriage covenant. Thus fidelity is broken—a fidelity that, even in bodily and inferior matters, is a great good of the mind; and therefore it is certain that it must be preferred even to bodily welfare, by which this present life is also sustained.

“For although a small piece of straw, compared with a great amount of gold, is almost nothing, fidelity is no less when it is sincerely preserved in a transaction involving straw than when it is preserved in one involving gold. But when fidelity is employed in order to admit a sin, it is surprising if it ought to be called fidelity at all. Nevertheless, whatever its character, if it is violated even against that very fidelity, the result is worse—unless it is abandoned for the purpose of returning to true and lawful fidelity, that is, so that the sin may be corrected by reforming the perverse will.

“This is like someone who, unable to rob a man by himself, finds a partner in iniquity and makes an agreement with him that they should do it together and divide the spoils. When the crime has been committed and the partner takes the whole spoil alone, the other is indeed distressed and complains that fidelity has not been kept toward him. Yet in that very complaint he ought to consider that fidelity should rather have been kept in a good life toward human society itself, so that the unjust spoil would not be taken from a human being—if he perceives how unjustly fidelity was not kept toward him in a partnership of sin.

“For the person who is faithless in both matters must be judged guilty as all the more criminal because, if he had refused to divide the spoil with his accomplice for the purpose of returning it to the man from whom it had been taken, that accomplice could not rightly call him faithless, since he himself was faithless.

“So too, if a woman, after violating marital fidelity, keeps faith with an adulterer, she is certainly bad; but if she does not keep faith with the adulterer, she is worse. Yet if she repents of the crime, returns to marital chastity, and dissolves the adulterous agreements and arrangements, I wonder whether even the adulterer himself would think he could rightly call her a violator of fidelity. The same must equally be understood of the adulterer: if he dissolves the agreement made with the adulteress, she too will not be able justly to call him a violator of fidelity.”

## QUESTION XV

Concerning what was asked: whether it can be true, as many people say, that there are women who, through their sorcery, can cast irreconcilable hatred between husband and wife and sow again an indescribable love between a man and a woman; and concerning the other matters that the questioners wished to derive from this question.

## RESPONSE

Let them reread the history in the Book of Kings after David’s sin with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah: how, through the devil’s suggestion, David’s son Amnon loved his sister Tamar, and, following the counsel of Jonadab—who represented the devil, who through Eve’s counsel of sin destroyed Adam—had intercourse with that same sister. Before the intercourse he loved her so greatly that he wasted away for her and became sick because of his love. After the intercourse, however, he held her hated and hated her with an exceedingly great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had previously loved her. This diabolical operation proceeded through fratricide to the other evils that readers find in that passage (II Sam. XIII).

And blessed Ambrose, explaining verse 92 of Psalm 118, “If your law had not been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation,” and speaking of Joseph enduring assaults sent through evil angels, says at that point:

“It is reported of a certain prophet—and many report that it was Isaiah—that when he was confined in prison and was being pressed by the weight of the impending destruction, the devil said to him: ‘Say that what you said was not spoken by the Lord, and I will change the minds and affections of everyone against you.’”

Something similar to what we are relating also happened in the parish of one of us. A young man of noble birth fell in love with a woman who was also of an honorable lineage. He properly sought her from her parents, and his request prevailed with the girl’s father; but the girl’s mother rejected the same request in every way. The father, whose consent in a young man’s petitions is something that rarely happens, nevertheless prevailed. After the betrothal, the endowment, and the celebration of the wedding, the young man took the girl into the privacy of the bedchamber but was in no way able to have intercourse with her as customary.

When they had spent two years leading a wearisome life in irreparable hatred, they went to the bishop, since no other solution could now be found. Necessity compelled them to do so, with persuasive, pleading, and threatening words; for, unless he allowed the marriage to be dissolved, the young man said that he himself would provide the sword by which homicide would be committed if the marriage could not be dissolved in any other way.

This same bishop, who had already often been sifted by encounters with many such things perpetrated by Satan, recalled what the Lord says through the prophet: “Son of man, pierce through the wall and see the abominations that these people commit here. And when I had pierced through the wall, an opening appeared” (Ezek. VIII), together with the rest that is read there. Through repeated discussions, moving from agreement to agreement and from question to determination, he induced them to investigate such matters, until, by God’s grace, the diabolical operations were dissolved.

Although intercourse with the former concubine had been possible and pleasurable, and with the woman lawfully allotted to him had been impossible, after penance and ecclesiastical treatment the young man was restored to the ability to have intercourse with his wife. When the diabolical hatred had been driven away, conjugal love was restored between the spouses, and it has continued to the present with the proper affection; they now rejoice in numerous offspring.

It is shameful to recount the tales known to us, and it would take too long to enumerate the sacrileges that we have discovered in such matters: objects composed from the bones of the dead, ashes and extinguished coals, hair and hairs from the genital regions of men and women, threads of many colors, various herbs, small shells, and pieces of snakes; these were enchanted with spells. People were freed from such things and, healed through ecclesiastical blessing, were restored to conjugal grace and the natural function owed to marriage.

Some were dressed in or covered with garments enchanted by spells; others were driven mad by sorcerers through drink, and others through food; still others were found to have been fascinated merely by the spells of witches and rendered almost powerless. Some men were weakened by lamiae, or women called geniciales. Certain women, too, were found to have endured intercourse with Dusii in the form of men, whose love had inflamed them. Divine power restored both the men and the women to health by suppressing and casting away the diabolical phantasms through exorcisms and Catholic remedies.

There are also other matters that necessity compelled us to settle and judge, matters that, because of their shameful depravity, we do not wish to mention; and there are criminal and wicked acts of such a kind that, so that they may not come to the knowledge of evil people who perhaps do not know them, we have refrained from writing them here. [655] There are moreover such monstrous portents of diabolical activity, performed through magical art, that have come to us that they exceed the bounds of credibility. But it is not surprising if in these last times such things appear, foreshadowing the coming of the Antichrist, as the Lord and his apostles described would come. Concerning these Paul also says: “For the mystery of iniquity is already at work according to the operation of Satan, with every kind of power, signs, and lying wonders” (2 Thess. 2:7); and again: “Now the Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons” (1 Tim. 4:1).

This vanity of magical arts, arising from the tradition of evil angels throughout the whole world, with Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians—whom Ninus, king of the Assyrians, killed in battle—as its originator, and Democritus as its propagator, prevailed for many centuries. [Col. 0718B] Among the Assyrians it was cultivated by many diabolical men, whose magical arts advanced so far that, as we said above, they even resisted Moses with signs very similar to his, turning rods into dragons and water into blood (Exod. 7). The same impiety of magic is established, as its arts differ, so also by the diversity of its names, as both pagan teachers and Christians report. [Col. 0718C] Therefore, passing over many things, we recall some.

Magi are those commonly called sorcerers because of the magnitude of their crimes. They shake the elements, disturb human minds, and, without anyone drinking poison, kill by the violence of a spell alone.

Necromancers are those whose incantations make the dead appear to be brought back to life, to give oracles and answer questions.

Hydromancers are those who, by gazing into water, summon the shadows of demons and claim to see their images or illusions there and to hear certain things from them.

Incantators are those who perform their art through words.

Arioli are those who utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols, offer deadly sacrifices, and through these ceremonies receive answers from demons. [Col. 0718D]

Haruspices are those who observe the hours for conducting business and carrying out works, who inspect the entrails, fibers, shoulder blades, or whatever else of animals, and from them foretell the future.

Augurs are those who attend to the flight and cries of birds. One kind belongs to the eyes—that is, the flight of birds—and the other to the ears—that is, the cry of birds.

There are also pythonesses, who are ventriloquists; and astrologers, so called because they practice augury from the stars. There are also those who consider the days of birth and observe the course of the stars in the case of the newborn; these are commonly called mathematicians. There are also horoscopes, who scrutinize the hours of birth according to a different and various fate.

There are also sortilegers, who, under the name of a fictitious religion, profess the knowledge of divination through certain things they call “the lots of the saints,” or who promise the future by examining whatever writings. [Col. 0719A]

There are also those who, when some part of their body leaps—whether their eyes or any other member—declare that some favorable or sad event is thereby signified for them.

[656] There are also tricksters, otherwise called *obstrigilli*, because they constrict or bind the sight of human eyes, such as those who are said to play with coins, which is entirely diabolical. And, as we read, the devil first disclosed this through Mercury; hence Mercury is also called its inventor. No Christian permits himself to perform such a diabolical work without sin, or, if he has authority over one who does such things, to leave it unpunished.

To all these things also belong the bindings made from accursed remedies, which the medical art condemns—whether in incantations, characters, or any objects that are hung up or tied, or in measurements of whatever kind. [Col. 0719B] Women call them *superventae* in their wool-working or textile crafts. In all these things there is the art of demons, arising from a pestilential partnership of human beings and evil angels. Therefore all such things must be avoided by every Christian and utterly rejected and condemned with every form of execration.

There are also those who say that, when they go hunting, they ought not to encounter a cleric. There are also those who make dogs bark at a stump as though at a wild animal. There are also those who observe days when setting out on a journey and when beginning to build a house. [Col. 0719C] The apostle Paul considered this such a great sin that he said: “You observe days and months and seasons and years; I fear that I may have labored over you in vain” (Gal. 4:10). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Likewise, just as it happened in the days of Lot: they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building” (Luke 17:28).

And, leaving aside that greatest and unspeakable crime of the people of Sodom, he mentions only those offenses that they could consider trivial or nonexistent, so that you may understand with what punishment unlawful things are struck, if even lawful things—things without which this life cannot be lived—when performed immoderately, are punished by fire and sulfur.

Rightly, therefore, blessed Augustine, seeing the allurements of harmful custom and moved by righteous grief, cries out: [Col. 0719D]

“Woe to the sins of human beings! We shudder only at unusual sins, but the customary ones—for the washing away of which the blood of the Son of God was poured out—even though they are so great that they entirely close the kingdom of God against those who commit them, we are often compelled, while avoiding everything, to tolerate; and while tolerating some things, often even to do them. And would that, O Lord, we did not do everything that we have been unable to prohibit!”

It must also be understood that, as we read in the words of the teachers, there are demons who, as though assigned especially to particular vices, although they delight in all vices, incite human beings in a special way toward those over which they preside. Therefore the evangelist Mark also records that the Lord cast seven demons out of Mary, who was a sinful woman in the city (ch. 16), [Col. 0720A] so that it might be shown that where sin abounded, grace abounded even more. For the number seven is customarily used mystically to signify totality. Thus she is to be understood as having been healed by seven demons—that is, liberated from all sins.

Accordingly, among the other demons who are teachers of vices, we read of Mammon, concerning whom the Lord says, “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. 6:24). Whoever serves Mammon—that is, riches—serves the one who, because of his perversity, has rightly been placed over these earthly things and is called by the Lord the ruler of this age. We also read of that class of demons who inflame people with anger; or who dissolve them into carnal pleasure through indulgence; or, rather, who cast them into the fire of adultery, by which the hearts of adulterers are kindled; and into waters that customarily extinguish charity. [Col. 0720B] This demon cannot be cast out except through prayer and fasting.

The ancient enemy first tested our forefather with gluttony, vainglory, and avarice, and by testing him overcame him, because through his consent he subjected him to himself. But by the same methods by which he struck down the first human being, he himself was defeated when he tested the second Human Being.

In the psalm also we sing of “the arrow that flies by day” (Ps. 90:6), that is, of the speech of heretics and philosophers, who are the devil’s instruments and cannot deceive unless they promise light. [Col. 0720C] This class of demons easily corrupts those who neglect their own actions while attending to the affairs of others, wandering outside their proper condition and order and involving themselves excessively in external concerns.

It leads the minds of such people, deceived by vain hopes, so far astray that they are suspended from the purpose of repentance. It shows them many people walking along the broad and spacious way, so that they perceive no good things now, just as they are troubled by no evils now, and so that they may later be overwhelmed more fully by punishments, although now they even rejoice in their sins.

There is also “the thing that walks in darkness,” namely, the spirit set over denial and falsehood; the attack of precipitateness and fear; and the noonday demon, that is, acedia, which causes the fervor of begun devotion to grow lukewarm. [Col. 0720D] It also causes heretics, through a pretense of upright intention and works of light, to burn with a desire for ambition. Concerning this class of demons it is written: “He sleeps under the shade, in the secret place of reeds, in moist places” (Job 40:16). It insinuates itself into darkened consciences under “the shade”; into hypocrites under “the reed,” which is bright on the outside but empty within; and into wanton and soft minds in “moist places.”

The class of demons that, having gone out from a person at the time of baptism or after the fruits of repentance and the grace of reconciliation, goes away and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and, returning to that house from which it had gone out, finds it empty, swept with brooms, and decorated (Luke 16:26), [Col. 0721A] signifies a house cleansed from its former vices through baptism or repentance, empty of good works through negligence, and decorated with simulated virtues through hypocrisy. The demon itself and the more wicked spirits it has taken with it enter and dwell there.

For by the seven evil spirits all vices are signified. Whoever, after baptism, is seized either by heretical depravity or by worldly desire will soon be cast down into the depths of every vice. Therefore those spirits are rightly called more wicked when they enter, because such a person will have not only the seven vices opposed to the seven spiritual virtues, but will also pretend through hypocrisy to possess those very virtues.

And just as in Isaiah (ch. 11) seven spirits of virtues are said to have descended upon the rod from the root of Jesse and the flower that rises from the root, so conversely the number of vices has been consecrated in the devil. [658]

There are also other kinds of demons whom we read were appointed by their prince over particular vices; we omit recording them here. We take care only to note the demons who preside over fornication, in order to show that there are also kinds of demons who delight so greatly in fornication alone that they even seek human intercourse. [Col. 0721B] We could recount some events of our own time concerning them, were we not passing over them for the sake of brevity.

And so that what we say may more readily be believed, let those who doubt such matters read what Saint Amphilochius, bishop of the city of Iconium—whom blessed Jerome mentions with due veneration in his book *On Illustrious Men*—writes among the miracles of Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man to be admired and adorned with every virtue:
