“Elladius, an eyewitness and minister of the miracles perfectly wrought by that man of most holy memory, and successor to the see after the death of the aforementioned apostolic Basil of blessed memory—a remarkable man adorned with every virtue—related to me that a certain faithful senator named Proterius went to the holy and venerable places, wishing there to consecrate his daughter, place her in one of the monasteries’ charitable houses, and offer a sacrifice to God. [Col. 0721C]

“But the devil, a murderer from the beginning, envying the divine will, stirred one of his servants and inflamed him with love for the girl. Since this man was unworthy of such an undertaking and did not dare approach the intended object, he went to one of the detestable enchanters, promising to give him a large quantity of gold if he should succeed in gaining power over the girl.

“The sorcerer said to him: ‘My man, I cannot accomplish this, but if you wish, I will send you to my patron, the devil, and he will fulfill your desire.’

“He replied: ‘I will do whatever you tell me.’

“The sorcerer said to him: ‘Do you renounce Christ in writing?’

“He replied: ‘Yes.’

“Then the worker of iniquity said to him: ‘If you are prepared for this, I will become your accomplice.’

“He replied: ‘I am prepared; only let me attain my desire.’

“The minister of wickedness then wrote a letter to the devil and sent the man to him with this message: [Col. 0721D]

“‘Since, my lord and patron, I must hasten to draw this man away from the religion of the Christians and bring him to your will, so that your portion may be increased, I have sent you this man who delivers my present letter. He is inflamed with desire for a girl, and I ask that he obtain this deed, so that I may glory in it and, with great eagerness, gather more worshipers for you.’

“After giving him the letter, he said: ‘Go at such-and-such an hour of the night, stand upon a pagan tomb, raise the writing into the air, and those who are to lead you to the devil will stand beside you.’

“The man eagerly did this, threw out a miserable cry, and invoked the devil’s help. Immediately the rulers of the power of darkness, the spiritual forces of wickedness, stood beside him. [Col. 0722A] They seized the wanderer with great joy, led him to where the devil was, and showed him seated on a high throne, with spirits of wickedness standing around him.

“The devil received the letter sent by the sorcerer and said to the wretched man: ‘Do you believe in me?’

“He replied: ‘I believe.’

“The devil said: ‘Do you deny your Christ?’

“He replied: ‘I deny him.’

“The devil said to him: ‘You Christians are faithless. Whenever you need my help, you come to me; whenever you obtain your desire, you deny me and return to your Christ, who is kind and most merciful and receives you. But write for me, in your own hand, a voluntary renunciation of your Christ and of baptism, and a voluntary profession of allegiance to me for ever, that you will be with me on the day of judgment, rejoicing with me in the eternal torments prepared for us—and I will immediately fulfill your desire.’

“The man wrote with his own hand the document that was demanded of him.

“Immediately the crooked dragon, the corrupter of souls, sent the demons who preside over fornication. [Col. 0722B] They inflamed the girl with love for the young man. Looking toward the ground, she began to cry out to her father:

“‘Have mercy on me, have mercy, father, for I am cruelly tormented because of this young man of ours. Have mercy on your own flesh; show me your fatherly love for your only daughter, and unite me to the young man whom I love. But if you do not wish to do this, you will soon see me dying an agonizing death, and on the day of judgment you will give an account to God for me.’

“The father, with tears, said: ‘Alas for me, a sinner! What is happening to my wretched daughter? Who has stolen my treasure? Who has ruined my daughter? Who has extinguished the sweet light of my eyes? I wanted you to marry the heavenly Bridegroom, Christ, to make you a companion of the angels, and I was hastening for you to sing to God in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. [Col. 0722C] I hoped to be saved through you, but you have become insane with lustful love. Allow me, as I wish, to betroth you to God. Do not lead my old age to hell through anguish, nor cover the nobility of your parents with disgrace.’

“But she, counting as nothing what her father said, persisted in crying out: ‘My father, either fulfill my desire, or soon you will see me dead.’

“The father, therefore, overcome by great weakness and swallowed up by immeasurable grief, and trusting the advice of his friends, who urged him either to yield to her will or to let her expose herself, ordered the girl’s desire to be carried out, lest she give herself over to a fatal death.

“He brought the young man she had requested to his own daughter, gave them all his property, and said to his daughter: ‘Farewell, truly wretched daughter; for in the end you will weep greatly in repentance, when it will profit you nothing.’ [Col. 0722D]

“After the unlawful marriage had been contracted and the devil’s wickedness completed, after a short time some people noticed that the young man did not enter the church or approach the immortal and life-giving mysteries. [659] They said to his wretched wife: ‘Do you know that your husband, whom you chose, is not a Christian, but a stranger to and alien from the faith?’

“Filled with darkness and grievous affliction, she threw herself upon the ground, began to tear herself with her fingernails, beat her breast, and cry out:

“‘No one who has disobeyed his parents has ever been saved. Who will announce my disgrace to my father? Alas for me, wretched woman! Into what depth of perdition have I descended! Why was I born—and, having been born, why was I not immediately taken away?’

“Learning of her lamentations, her utterly misguided husband ran to her, insisting that the matter was not true. [Col. 0723A] When she had been comforted by his persuasive words, she said to him:

“‘If you wish to satisfy me and my wretched soul, tomorrow let you and me go together to the church in harmony, and participate before me in the undefiled mysteries; then I shall be satisfied.’

“Then, compelled, he told her the terms of the compact.

“Immediately putting aside her womanly weakness and giving him good counsel, she ran to the shepherd and disciple of Christ, Basil, crying out against her impiety:

“‘Have mercy on me, a wretched woman, holy man of God; have mercy on me, disciple of the Lord. I have had dealings with demons; have mercy on me, who disobeyed my own father.’

“And she told him the whole sequence of events.

“The holy man of God summoned the young man and asked him whether these things were so. [Col. 0723B] He replied to the saint with tears:

“‘Yes, holy man of God. Even if I remain silent, my deeds will cry out.’ And he too recounted to him, from beginning to end, the devil’s wicked work.

“Then the saint said to him: ‘Do you wish to return to the Lord our God?’

“The young man replied: ‘Certainly I do, but I cannot.’

“He said: ‘Why?’

“The young man answered: ‘I denied Christ in writing and professed myself to the devil.’

“He said to him: ‘Do not be concerned. Our God is kind and will receive you when you repent, for he has compassion on our wickedness.’

“And the girl threw herself at the saint’s feet and entreated him in the Gospel manner, saying: ‘Disciple of Christ our God, help us as much as you can.’

“The saint said to the young man: ‘Do you believe that you can be saved?’

“He replied: ‘I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.’ [Col. 0723C]

“Immediately he took his hand, made the sign of Christ over him, and prayed. Then he shut him in an inner place of the sacred enclosure. Giving him a rule of life, he worked with him for three days.

“After that he visited him and said: ‘How are you, son?’

“He replied: ‘I am in great distress, holy man of God. I cannot bear their cries and terrors, their hurled objects and their stonings. Holding my written document, they accuse me, saying: “You came to us, not we to you.”’

“The saint said to him: ‘Do not fear, son; only believe.’ He gave him a little food, again made the sign of Christ over him, prayed, and shut him in.

“After a few days he visited him again and said: ‘How are you, son?’

“He replied: ‘Holy father, from far away I hear their cries and threats, but I do not see them.’ [Col. 0723D]

“Again he gave him food, prayed, closed the door, and departed.

“On the fortieth day he returned and said to him: ‘How are you, brother?’ [661]

“He replied: ‘I am well, holy man of God. For today I saw you in a vision fighting on my behalf and conquering the devil.’

“Then the saint, as was his custom, offered a prayer, brought him out, and led him into his own sleeping quarters.

“When morning came, he summoned the sacred clergy, the monasteries, and all the people who loved Christ, and said to them:

“‘My dearest children, give thanks to the Lord, all of you. Behold, the good shepherd must carry the lost sheep on his shoulders and offer it to the Church. [Col. 0724A] Therefore it is also our duty to keep vigil through the night and ask his kindness, so that the corrupter of souls may not prevail even in this matter.’

“And when the people had eagerly gathered together, they besought God throughout the entire night with the good shepherd, crying out with tears on his behalf: *Kyrie, eleison*—‘Lord, have mercy.’

“At dawn, with the whole multitude of the people, the saint took the young man. Holding his right hand, he led him into the holy church of God with psalms and hymns.

“And behold, the devil, who ensnares everyone for a sorrowful life, came with all his destructive power. Invisibly seizing the young man, he tried to snatch him from the saint’s hand. The young man began to cry out: ‘Holy man of God, help me!’

“And the wicked one attacked with such persistence that he even compelled the renowned man, dragging the young man away.

“The saint then turned to the devil and said:

“‘Most wicked one, corrupter of souls, father of darkness and perdition, is your own perdition—not only the perdition that has afflicted you and those under you—not enough for you, unless you also test the creature of my God?’ [Col. 0724B]

“The devil said to him: ‘You wrong me, Basil.’ Thus many of us heard the demons’ voices saying these things, while the people cried out: *Kyrie, eleison*.

“The holy man of God said to him: ‘The Lord rebukes you, devil.’

“He replied: ‘You wrong me, Basil. I did not go to him; he came to me. He denied Christ and professed himself to me. And behold, I have the written document, and on the day of judgment I shall lead him before the common Judge.’

“The holy man of God said: ‘Blessed is the Lord my God! This people will not lower their hands from the height of heaven until you return the written document.’

“Then he turned and said to the people: ‘Raise your hands to heaven, crying out with tears: “Christ, Lord, have mercy”—*Christe, Kyrie, eleison*.’ [Col. 0724C]

“When the people had stood for a long time with their hands extended toward heaven, behold, the young man’s written document was carried through the air. Seen by everyone, it came and was placed in the hands of our renowned father and shepherd.

“He received it, gave thanks to God, and rejoiced greatly. Before the whole people he said to the young man: ‘Do you recognize these letters, brother?’

“He replied: ‘Yes, holy man of God; it is my written document.’

“Saint Basil tore up the document, led him into the church, and deemed him worthy of the holy ministry and of communion in the mysteries and gifts of Christ. [Col. 0724D] He held a great reception, refreshed the whole people, and, leading and instructing the young man, or giving him a fitting rule of life, restored him to his wife, with an unstained mouth glorifying and praising God. Amen.”

And the venerable presbyter Bede, in the third book of his *Commentary on the Evangelist Luke*: [662]

“Jesus asked him, saying: ‘What is your name?’ And he said: ‘Legion,’ because many demons had entered him” (Luke 8:30). He does not inquire about the name as though he were ignorant, but so that, once the plague that the frenzied man was suffering had confessed itself, the power of the healer might shine forth more gratefully.

But the priests of our own time, who know how to cast out demons through the grace of exorcism, customarily say that sufferers cannot otherwise be healed unless, insofar as they are able to understand, they openly confess and disclose everything that they have experienced from unclean spirits—whether through sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch, or any other bodily or mental sense—while awake or asleep. [Col. 0725A]

This is especially the case when demons who appear to men in female form or to women in male form—demons whom the Gauls call *Dusii*—pretend, by an unspeakable marvel, that incorporeal spirits seek and perform intercourse with human bodies. The priests prescribe disclosure of the name by which the demon says it is called, as well as of the forms of oath by which the two parties mutually pledged their pact of love.

This matter resembles a lie, but is so true and so well known through the testimony of many people that a neighboring presbyter told me that he had begun to heal a certain consecrated woman from a demon, but, as long as the matter remained hidden, he could accomplish nothing with her. [Col. 0725B] Once she confessed the phantom by which she was troubled, he soon drove it away through prayers and the other kinds of purification that were required, and he cured the woman’s body of the ulcers that she had contracted through the demon’s touch, applying medical treatment together with blessed salt.

But when he was entirely unable to cover one of the ulcers, which he had found more deeply embedded in her side, because it continually opened again, he received from the very woman whom he wished to heal the advice by which she might be cured.

“‘If,’ she said, ‘you sprinkle upon the same medicine oil consecrated for the sick and then anoint me with it, I shall immediately be restored to health. For once, through the spirit, I saw in a distant city—a city I had never seen with bodily eyes—a girl suffering from the same affliction being healed in this way by a priest.’ [Col. 0725C]

“He did as she had suggested, and immediately the ulcer consented to receive the remedy, which previously it had rejected.

“I have explained these matters briefly against the deceits of demons, so that you may understand why the Lord did not ask in vain the name of the spirit whom he was about to expel.” [Col. 0725D]

## QUESTION XVI AND ANSWER

Regarding what was asked—why God, as is said, often permits such things to happen in a lawful marriage—it must be understood that, just as marriage instituted by God is good, every sin does not subsist by its own nature. Evil, indeed, is without substance; nevertheless, whatever comes to be in any way grows together, as we said above, within the nature of the good. And because sins demand it, evil comes to exist in the good of marriage through the operation of the devil.

The earth is the Lord’s, certainly good because it was created by the good God, and iniquities are ours. Yet often, because of our iniquities, we see and feel the Lord’s earth wasting away. He promised that, when angry, he would give us an iron earth and a bronze heaven, and, when appeased, that he would give us the early and late rain upon the earth, so that heaven would give rain and the earth would give its fruit. [Col. 0726A] This does not mean that the nature of created things is changed, but that, because of the difference in our merits, when God is angry or appeased, we experience punishment or grace from them.

And blessed Gregory says in the second book of the *Moralia* (ch. 4):

“By God’s hidden justice permission is given to evil spirits, so that those whom they willingly strangle in the snare of sin, they may also drag unwillingly into punishment for sin.”

And Augustine says in the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (ch. 23):

“Whoever wonders that God’s creature is subjected to the devil should not wonder. God’s creature is subjected to God’s creature, the lesser to the greater, because a human being is subject to an angel—not, however, on account of nature, but on account of vice, because the unclean is subject to the unclean.” [Col. 0726B]

For the devil himself is also an unclean spirit. The fact that he is a spirit is good; the fact that he is unclean is evil. Spirit is his nature; uncleanness is his vice. Of these two, the first is from God, the second from the devil himself. Therefore he does not hold human beings—whether adults or infants—because of that by which they are human, but because of that by which they are unclean.

And in the book *On Grace and Free Will* (ch. 21):

“For this must be fixed and immovable in your hearts: there is no iniquity with God. Therefore, when you read in the writings of truth that people are led astray by God, or that their hearts are dulled or hardened, do not doubt that their evil merits preceded this, so that they might justly suffer these things. Otherwise you will fall into that proverb of Solomon: ‘The folly of a man perverts his way, but in his heart he blames God.’” [Col. 0726C]

## QUESTION XVII AND ANSWER

Regarding what was asked—what should be done if such men who practice magic, or women who are enchantresses, should be found—Saint Leo, writing to bishops throughout the provinces, makes this clear (Letter 11, to the bishops in Italy):

“Some sorcerers,” he says, “had plunged themselves so deeply into such matters that no remedy capable of helping them could reach them. Subjected to the laws, according to the decrees of Christian rulers, they were sentenced by public judges to perpetual exile, so that they might not pollute the holy flock with their contagion.” [Col. 0726D]

And after a little:

“For we cannot govern those entrusted to us in any other way unless, with zeal for the Lord’s faith, we pursue those who are destroyers and destroyed, and cut them off from sound minds with whatever severity we can, lest this plague spread more widely. Therefore I exhort, entreat, and admonish your love to keep watch with the diligence that you ought and are able to exercise, in order to investigate them, lest they find anywhere an opportunity to conceal themselves.

“For just as the one who diligently carries out whatever may benefit the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive from God a great reward, so whoever refuses to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will not be able to excuse himself before the tribunal of the Lord for the guilt of negligence.” [Col. 0727A]

And Saint Gregory writes to the deacon Cyprian (Book XII, Letter 13):

> “Our most holy fellow-bishop Maximianus, desiring to purge the Church of God of wicked men, was, as you know, commendably diligent concerning the conduct of ecclesiastics. While he vigilantly attended to their actions with pastoral care, he learned that certain persons had been defiled by a magical practice commonly called *canterma*, and, as your Dilection’s letter also reported, he ordered them to be held in custody. But because, through the workings of our sins, he was overtaken by death and could not avenge that crime himself, your Dilection [Col. 0727B] must hasten to investigate the whole matter with the utmost subtlety and strive to punish them according to the enormity of their offense, in such a way that, according to the laws, you may recognize how the bishop mentioned above, moved by zeal for correction and justice, would have been able to act against them in this punishment for God’s sake, had he lived. Therefore, with every strength and every insistence, let your Dilection take care to display in this matter its zeal toward almighty God and to show His enemies a fitting hostility by inflicting punishment, so that it may fulfill what is written: ‘Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and was I not wasting away over your enemies?’ (Psalm 138:21). If, then, your Dilection is inflamed by this zeal, let punishment be shown toward those who have abandoned God and have done something against Him by magical practices. But if you cannot properly carry this out there, such men [Col. 0727C] must be sent to us—provided that it can be demonstrated here from what basis they may be convicted there without difficulty. Yet because I think this impossible, strict and vigorous correction must come there through you.”

And to Januarius, bishop of Sardinia (Book VII, indiction 11, Letter 66):

> “Against worshipers of idols, as well as against augurs and practitioners of lots, we urge your Fraternity to remain especially vigilant with pastoral care. Speak publicly among the people against men of this kind and, by persuasive exhortation, recall them from so great a stain of sacrilege, from the prospect of divine judgment, and from the danger of the present life. If, however, you find that they refuse to amend and correct themselves from such practices, we wish you to seize them with fervent zeal. If they are slaves, chastise them with beatings and tortures by which [Col. 0727D] they may be brought to amendment; but if they are free, they must be reduced to a fitting and strict confinement for penance, so that those who despise hearing salutary words that recall them from the danger of death may at least, through bodily sufferings, be brought back to the desired health of mind.”

And likewise in the Canonical Edict (Gregory II, in the Roman synod, chapter 12):

> “If anyone consults diviners, augurs, or enchanters, or uses amulets, let him be anathema.”

And they all answered a third time: “Let him be anathema.”

And in the Council of Ancyra, chapter 23:

> “Those who seek divinations and follow them according to the custom of the pagans, or who bring such persons into their houses to inquire into something by magical art or for the purpose of expiation, shall lie under the rule [Col. 0728A] for five years, according to the defined degrees of penance.”

From the Second Council of Braga, chapter 70:

> “If anyone, following pagan custom, brings diviners or practitioners of lots [p. 665] into his house, as though to drive out an evil, discover magical practices, or perform pagan lustrations, let him do penance for five years.”

And chapter 71:

> “Let Christians not be permitted to retain the traditions of the gentiles, or to observe or worship the elements, or the course of the moon or stars, or the empty deception of signs, whether for building a house, or on account of crops, or for planting trees, or for joining marriages. For it is written: ‘Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God’ (Colossians 3:17).”

[Col. 0728B]

And chapter 72:

> “When gathering herbs that are medicinal, let no one attend to any observances or incantations, except only with the divine Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, so that only God, the creator and Lord of all, may be honored.”

And chapter 73:

> “Let Christian women not observe any superstition in their weaving, but let them invoke as helper God, who has given them the wisdom to weave.”

And in the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 89:

> “Anyone serving auguries or incantations is to be separated from the assembly of the Church; likewise anyone adhering to Jewish superstitions or festivals.”

And in the first book of the *Chapters of the Emperors*, chapter 21:

> “Let no one be permitted to become a *coclearius* [perhaps a ‘spoon-diviner’], magician, or enchanter—persons who, it is established, were terribly condemned in the case of Simon Magus.”

And in the Council of Elvira, [Col. 0728C] chapter 6:

> “If anyone kills another by magic, because he could not accomplish it without idolatry, communion is not to be granted to him even at the end of his life.”

It must nevertheless be understood that this severity of strictness from the Council of Elvira is to be observed toward those who do not repent. Otherwise, in accordance with the decrees of blessed Celestine, final penance is to be denied to no one who acknowledges his fault.

Thus Pope Leo the Great also decreed (Letter 59, to Theodorus of Forum Julii):

> “For those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger, implore the help of penance and immediately afterward reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor the grace of reconciliation and communion denied, if they are shown to seek it even through the service of a voice already lost, by signs of sound understanding. But if they have been so aggravated by some force of illness [Col. 0728D] that they are unable, in the presence of the priest, to signify what they had shortly before requested, the testimony of the faithful standing around them ought to benefit them, and they should likewise receive the benefit both of penance and of reconciliation, while the rule of the fathers’ canons concerning those who sinned against God by departing from the faith is nevertheless preserved. In general, communion is not to be denied to anyone placed at the point of death who asks that the grace of communion be granted to him, as the Council of Nicaea defined (canon 13). His conversion is to be judged by his mind rather than by the passage of time, since true conversion suffers no delay of forgiveness before God, as the Prophet likewise testifies: ‘When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved.’”

And in the Council of Nicaea, canon 13: [Col. 0729A]

> “But in all these cases it is fitting to examine the purpose and appearance of the penitents. For all those who demonstrate their conversion by the facts themselves—not by pretense—through fear, tears, endurance, or good works.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Afterward, it will be permissible for the bishop to consider these matters somewhat more humanely.”

And in the Council of Ancyra, canon 4:

> “The bishops shall have the power, after examining the manner of their conversion, either to deal with them more humanely or to add a longer period.”

The reader will also find sufficient treatment of this matter in the fifth chapter of that same council and in other places.

Pope Innocent writes to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio (Letter 29):

> “Concerning penitents who are doing penance either for more serious offenses or for lesser ones, if no illness intervenes [Col. 0729B], the custom of the Roman Church shows that they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter. As for estimating the weight of sins, it belongs to the priest to judge, so that he may attend to the penitent’s confession and to the tears and weeping of the one correcting himself, and then order him to be released when he has seen suitable satisfaction. Certainly, if anyone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, he is to be released before Easter, lest he depart from this world without communion.”

## QUESTION XVIII

In the seventh chapter we ask you to write back to us whether, if the aforementioned woman should again come to trial and be found innocent, her husband ought to return [Col. 0729C] to her or whether he may be joined to another. Write back to us also whether, if she is found liable for the crimes of which she is accused, that same king may be joined to another woman. Write back as well whether, if such charges are judged to apply to the king himself, on account of which he ought to do public penance, and after she has been found guilty, he may, after public penance, take a legitimate wife. And write back whether, if she has also been legally rejected, he himself, after completing penance, may, if he wishes, take as his wife the concubine whom he had and with whom he is said to have committed adultery after entering into marriage.

## RESPONSE

As for what was asked—whether, if the aforementioned woman should again come to trial and be found innocent, [Col. 0729D] her husband ought to return to her or may be joined to another—it is unnecessary to repeat it, because above we showed that, if she is found to have been innocent before the marriage was legally contracted and to have kept faith with her husband after being legally married to him, then, according to evangelical and apostolic truth, ecclesiastical laws, and the teaching of Catholics, a legitimate marriage cannot be separated; and if the parties have been separated, they must either remain unmarried or be reconciled to one another.

But lest we leave the repeated question without an answer, concerning the woman who was accused, if she is found free from guilt, the Lord says through Moses in the book of Deuteronomy:

> “If a man finds a young woman who is a virgin…”

—and the passage continues until it says:

> “He will not be able [p. 667] to dismiss her all the days of his life.”

Explaining this sentence, blessed Augustine says:

> “It is rightly asked whether this is the punishment: that he cannot dismiss her for all time, whom he violated improperly and unlawfully. [Col. 0730A] For if we wish to understand that she cannot—that is, ought not—to be dismissed for all time because she has become his wife, we are confronted by the fact that Moses permitted a man to give a bill of divorce and dismiss her. But in the case of those who violate women unlawfully, he did not wish this to be permitted, lest the man appear to have acted in mockery and to have pretended rather than truly and deliberately taken her as his wife. The same command was given concerning the woman against whom her husband had brought an accusation that her virginity had not been found, concerning whom, as we said above, it is written: ‘He shall have her as his wife, and he shall not be able to dismiss her for all the time of his life.’”

Concerning the same sentence blessed Augustine also says: [Col. 0730B]

> “It is sufficiently clear from this how the law wished wives to be subject to their husbands and almost like servants. When a husband brings testimony against his wife on the basis of which she would be stoned if it were proved true, he himself is nevertheless not stoned in turn if it is established that the charge was false; rather, he is merely punished and fined, and he is ordered to cling forever to the woman of whom he had wished to be rid. In other cases, however, the law orders that the one who has harmed someone by false testimony—testimony which, if proved, would have caused the victim to be killed—be punished with the same penalty by which the accused person would have been punished had the testimony been true.”

## QUESTION XIX

Concerning what was asked, write back to us whether, if she is found liable for the crimes of which she is accused, [Col. 0730C] that same king may be joined to another woman.

## RESPONSE

We have partly answered this above, and it is no burden partly to repeat it now. Namely, if it is found, according to Christian laws—that is, both civil and ecclesiastical—that the union was not a legal one, let the judgment of blessed Gregory to Felix, bishop of Sicily, be retained. He says:

> “We have long read that it was established by the holy Fathers that incestuous persons are not to be reckoned under any name of marriage.”

And Saint Ambrose says in his First Letter to the Corinthians:

> “A brother or sister, he says, is not subject to bondage in such a case; that is, the reverence of marriage is not owed to one who shudders at the author of marriage. For a marriage is not valid [Col. 0730D] which exists without devotion to God. Therefore, it is not a sin for one dismissed for God’s sake to join oneself to another. The insult done to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage with regard to the one who is abandoned, lest he be accused when joined to another. But the unbeliever who departs is recognized as sinning both against God and against marriage, because he did not wish to have the marriage under devotion to God. Therefore, the faith [p. 668] of marriage is not to be kept with one who departed for this reason: that he would not hear the Christian God being the ruler of marriage. For if Ezra caused unbelieving wives or husbands to be dismissed so that God might be propitiated (Ezra 9 and 10), and was not angry if they took others from their own people—for they were not commanded in such a way that, after dismissing these, they were absolutely forbidden to marry others—how much more, if an unbeliever has departed, [Col. 0731A] will he have free choice, if he wishes to marry a man of his own law? For that is not to be considered a marriage which was contracted outside God’s decree. But when a person later recognizes this and grieves that he has sinned, he corrects himself so that he may deserve pardon. If, however, both have believed, the marriage is confirmed through knowledge of God. ‘In peace God has called us.’ It is true that one ought not to quarrel with the one who departs, because he departs out of hatred for God; and therefore he is not even to be considered worthy.”

Hence Saint Augustine says in his books to Pollentius:

> “The Israelites rightly dismissed the wives whom they had taken, when the Lord forbade them and the Lord commanded them, because everything that is not from faith is sin.”

The reader will be able to find a fuller treatment in those same books.

And in the Council of Agde it is written (canon 61): [Col. 0731B]

> “For incestuous unions we reserve absolutely no pardon, unless they have healed the adultery by separation. Incestuous persons, however, are not to be reckoned under any name of marriage; indeed, it is grievous even to designate them.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Those whose illicit union is forbidden shall certainly have the freedom to enter into a better marriage.”

## QUESTION XX

Concerning what was asked—whether, if the same charges are judged to apply to the king, on account of which he ought to do public penance, and after that woman has been found guilty, he himself may, after public penance, take a legitimate wife.

## RESPONSE

[Col. 0731C]

Pope Saint Leo responds to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 95, chapter 25), saying:

> “If a man established in adolescence, whether under the pressure of fear of death or the danger of captivity, undertook penance, and afterward, fearing a fall into youthful lack of self-control, chose marital intercourse lest he incur the crime of fornication, he appears to have done something pardonable, provided that he had known no woman at all except his wife. Yet we do not establish this as a rule; we judge what is more tolerable. For according to true understanding, nothing is more fitting for one who has done penance than persevering chastity of mind and body.”

Likewise, in the Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 8:

> “It is the judgment of the ancient and most holy Father, Pope Leo, that a man who, while in the age of adolescence, had recourse to the remedy of penance because he feared death, and who, if he happened to be married and was incontinent, returned to his former marriage lest he afterward incur a fall into adultery, should remain in it until, with the maturity of time, he is able [p. 669] [Col. 0731D] to attain a state of continence. We judge the same equally concerning women as concerning men—not as a general and legally binding command, but as something granted by us because of human frailty. This is provided only on the following condition: if the person who was not bound by the laws of penance should die before the other, from whom he had returned by mutual consent to continence, the survivor may not again pass to marital embraces. But if the life of the one who did not receive the blessing of the penitent [Col. 0732A] continues, let that person marry if he or she cannot remain continent and enjoy the companionship of another spouse. We clearly decree this concerning both sexes equally, namely, that in all these matters the priest’s decision is to be awaited, so that, according to whether he sees a person’s age to be suitable, he may grant either the law of release from continence or the law of strictness.”

## QUESTION XXI

Concerning what was added at the end of the questions, write back whether, if the aforementioned woman has been legally rejected, the king himself, after completing penance, may, if he wishes, take as his wife the concubine whom he had and with whom he is said to have committed adultery after entering into marriage.

## RESPONSE

[Col. 0732B]

Since the law for man and woman is one, as we have demonstrated above from the judgments of Scripture and of the Catholic Fathers, if he has been released from the law binding him to his wife, as Paul says concerning a wife:

> “Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39),

—that is, as Ambrose says, “let her marry without suspicion of disgrace and let her marry a man of her religion; this is to marry in the Lord”—

this release and lawful union are understood in two cases and occur in two ways. Namely, they apply to those who either never entered into a legal marriage or, through the intervention of death, have been released from the law of marriage, as Paul says:

> “But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry” (1 Corinthians 7:8).

And again:

> “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, [Col. 0732C] she has not sinned” (the same passage).

This is understood equally of male and female, for *hic virgo* and *haec virgo* both mean “this virgin”: *virgo* is common in gender. The Apostle demonstrates this in what follows, saying:

> “Yet such persons will have tribulation in the flesh” (the same passage).

Ambrose explains this sentence equally of man and woman:

> “Something that is permitted becomes illicit among those who could come to marriage without guilt but propose to undertake a greater good, and thereby make the lesser good, which was permitted, illicit.”

Hence it is written:

> “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:52 [the supplied citation; the wording is customarily located at 9:62]).

Whoever, therefore, had applied himself with stronger devotion is convicted of looking back if, after abandoning greater goods, he turns back to lesser ones.

Sometimes, too, when a matter of no small importance intervenes, something that was illicit becomes licit, when a legally contracted marriage is permitted to be dissolved [p. 670] [Col. 0732D] on account of unbelief. Hence Paul says:

> “If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not leave her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:12).

And shortly afterward:

> “But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (the same passage).

Or this occurs when a wife is left on account of fornication, concerning which Paul likewise says:

> “To those who are joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she has departed, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband, and let a husband not dismiss his wife” (1 Corinthians 7:10).

This is weighed equally in the opposite direction, so that, [Col. 0733A] if she has dismissed him, she must remain celibate.

Among believers, such separation after the beginning of marriage cannot occur except on account of fornication and through love of continence.

Something illicit also becomes licit through indulgence, as the same Paul demonstrates even concerning great matters by saying:

> “But this I say by way of indulgence, not by command” (the same passage, verse 6),

when a man and woman separated because of fornication, if they cannot remain continent, are reconciled to one another. For it was illicit that those who ought to have remained continent should return to the union of the flesh which they had shared while committing fornication—especially since Scripture says:

> “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious” (Proverbs 18:22).

But, as Saint Augustine says in the book *On the Good of Marriage*:

> “Because of the greater evil, what is less perverse is tolerated.” [Col. 0733B]

For the Lord says (Matthew 19:1) that a man and wife separated from one another on account of fornication commit adultery if they join themselves to others, and those who join themselves to others commit adultery.

Hence, in the book *On the Sermon on the Mount* and in the books of the *Retractions*, he says most clearly what Innocent also demonstrates in his letter to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, as we quoted above:

> “For it is clear,” Augustine likewise says, “that adultery is worse than fornication. Nor is fornication therefore good because adultery is worse, since it is worse to violate another person’s marriage than to cling to a prostitute. Nor is adultery good because incest is worse; for it is worse to lie with one’s mother than with another man’s wife, and until one reaches those acts which, as the Apostle says, [Col. 0733C] ‘it is shameful even to mention’ (Ephesians 5:12)…”

And blessed Gregory says:

> “When the weakness of two vices attacks us, and one presses more gently while the other perhaps presses more severely, help is more properly and more quickly brought to that vice through which a person is hastening rapidly toward destruction; and between two dangers the lesser is wisely chosen.”

Something illicit also becomes licit through pardon when a young man doing public penance, as Leo demonstrates, fearing a fall into youthful lack of self-control, chooses marital intercourse lest he incur the crime of fornication, thus doing something pardonable if he has known no woman at all except his wife. This is not established as a rule; rather, what is more tolerable is judged.

One also passes, as it were illicitly, from the illicit to the licit when, in the case of notorious incestuous unions designated by the Council of Agde [Col. 0733D] (canon 61), it is permitted, with the indulgence of penance, to pass to marital embraces.

The same must be said concerning the modes of concubinage: one passes from what is not good to what is good and honorable, from what is not good to what is good though not sufficiently honorable, and from evil to some good, though not honorable. [p. 671]

It is good and honorable for unmarried people, if they cannot remain in virginity, to seek a marital union, as we showed above from the apostolic tradition, Saint Evaristus writing on marriage.

It is also good and honorable for celibates, if they cannot remain continent, to enter into a legal marriage, as Saint Leo demonstrates.

But how one passes from what is not good to what is good and honorable—that is, from a concubine to a wife—the same Saint Leo [Col. 0734A] demonstrates in his letter to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 95, chapter 18):

> “Not every woman joined to a man is the man’s wife, just as not every son is the father’s heir. The bonds of marriage are legitimate among freeborn persons and among equals—indeed, this was established by the Lord long before the beginning of Roman law. Therefore, a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another. For this reason the Apostle, wishing to reveal the distinction between these persons, adduces testimony from Genesis, where it is said to Abraham: ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac’ (Galatians 4:30; Genesis 21:10). Since, therefore, the fellowship of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, beyond the union of the sexes, it also contained within itself [Col. 0734B] the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to a marriage in whom a nuptial mystery is not shown to have existed.”

And again:

> “To cast a slave woman or concubine from one’s bed and take a wife of certain free birth is not a doubling of marriage but an advance in honor. Women joined to men by paternal authority are free from blame if they were not married to the men who kept them, because a wife is one thing and a concubine another.”

From what is not good one may pass to something good, though not sufficiently honorable, as the same Leo demonstrates in the passage cited above, when a concubine who perhaps became free, if she had previously been a slave woman, and who was legally endowed and honored by a public wedding, appears to become a wife, just as every wife legally joined in marriage must, after betrothal, be legally endowed and honored by public [Col. 0734C] wedding.

From an evil one may tolerably hasten toward some good, though not honorable, as Saint Augustine says in the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 1:

> “Certainly, not only fertility, whose fruit is offspring, and not only chastity, whose bond is fidelity, but also a certain sacrament of marriage is commended to the married faithful. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church’ (Ephesians 5:25). The reality of this sacrament is undoubtedly that a male and female joined in marriage remain inseparably together for as long as they live, and that it is not permitted, except on account of fornication, for one spouse to be separated from the other. For this is preserved in Christ and the Church: that the living one, living with the living one, be separated by no divorce for eternity.

> “Such is the observance of this sacrament in the city of our God, on his holy mountain—that is [Col. 0734D], in the Church of Christ, among all the faithful gathered together, who are without doubt [p. 672] members of Christ—that when women marry or men take wives for the purpose of begetting children, it is not lawful to leave a barren wife in order to take a fertile one. If anyone does this, he is guilty of adultery not according to the law of this age, where, when a divorce intervenes, it is permitted without crime for one person to join another in marriage—a permission which the Lord testifies that holy Moses granted to the Israelites because of the hardness of their hearts—but according to the law of the Gospel (Matthew 19:8). The woman also is guilty of adultery if she marries another.

> “Indeed, the rights of marriage once entered into [Col. 0735A] remain among the living to such an extent that those who have been separated from one another are more truly spouses among themselves than they are with those to whom they have attached themselves. For they would not be adulterers with others unless they remained spouses to one another. Finally, when the man or woman with whom there had been a true marriage has died, a true marriage [may not] be formed with the person with whom there had previously been adultery.”

That is, provided that kinship, religious status, sexual misconduct of the gravest kind, or anything of that sort does not stand in the way.

And again, in the same passage, Augustine says:

> “A certain marital bond therefore remains even among the living, which neither separation nor union with another can take away. It remains as a cause of guilt, not as a bond of covenant. Thus an apostate soul, as though departing from the marriage of Christ, does not lose the sacrament of faith, even after losing the faith, which it received through the bath of regeneration; [Col. 0735B] for it would undoubtedly be restored to the one returning if it had been lost when he departed. But the one who has departed possesses this for an increase of punishment, not for the merit of reward.”

And in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 24:

> “The good of marriage, therefore, exists among all peoples and all human beings in the matter of begetting children and in the fidelity of chastity. But what belongs to the people of God is also found in the holiness of the sacrament, by which it is wicked even for one who has departed after a divorce to marry another while her husband lives; not even the reason of begetting children—which is the sole purpose for which marriages are formed—nor the failure of that purpose to follow, dissolves the marital bond, except the death of the spouse. It is as when clergy are ordained to gather a people: even if the gathering of the people does not follow [Col. 0735C], the sacrament of ordination nevertheless remains in those ordained; and if someone is removed from office because of some fault, he will not lack the sacrament of the Lord once it has been imposed, even though it remains for judgment.”

And again, in the aforementioned book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book I, chapter 11:

> “For those who, by mutual consent, choose to abstain forever from the use of carnal concupiscence, let it be far from us to say that the marital bond between them is broken. Rather, it will be stronger, insofar as they have entered into agreements with one another that are to be kept with greater affection and harmony—not through the pleasure-giving bonds of bodies, but through the voluntary affections of souls.”

These testimonies from Scripture and sayings of the saints make clear how he may take into marriage [Col. 0735D] the concubine with whom he is said to have committed adultery, if he wishes.

This is so if either the wife lawfully taken and found innocent toward him has died bodily, or if she is found to be so dead in spirit that his union with her is legally proved to be incestuous and not to be reckoned [p. 673] under any name of marriage.

Nevertheless, even if he takes such a concubine as his wife, that union will not appear free from reproach and the stain of offense, as blessed Augustine says in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapters 13, 14, and 15:

> “What the apostles command married people is what belongs to marriage. What they permit as pardonable, or what impedes prayers, is not imposed by marriage but tolerated. Thus, if perhaps—which I do not know whether it could happen, and rather think could not—yet if a concubine taken for a time should have sought only children from that union [Col. 0736A], that union nevertheless is not to be preferred even to marriages that perform that pardonable act. For one must consider what belongs to marriage, not what belongs to those who marry and use marriage immoderately.

> “If, for example, someone uses fields seized unjustly and improperly in such a way that he gives abundant alms from their produce, this does not justify the robbery. Nor, if another greedily occupies his paternal estate or property justly acquired, is the rule of civil law by which he became its legitimate possessor thereby to be blamed. Nor will the perversity of a tyrannical faction become praiseworthy if a king’s clemency leads the tyrant to treat his subjects well; nor is the order of royal power blameworthy if a king rages with tyrannical cruelty. It is one thing [Col. 0736B] to wish to use an unjust power justly, and another to use a just power unjustly.

> “Thus temporary concubines do not make their concubinage just by sleeping with men for the sake of children; nor do married women, if they behave wantonly with their husbands, impose a crime upon the order of marriage.

> “It is clearly possible for a marriage to arise from people improperly joined, when an honorable intention follows. But once a marriage has been entered into in the city of our God, where even from the first union of two human beings marriage bears a certain sacrament, it can in no way be dissolved except by the death of one of them. For the marital bond remains even if the offspring for whose sake it was entered into does not follow because of manifest sterility. Thus, even when the married parties already know that they will have no children, they may not separate for that very [Col. 0736C] reason and join themselves to others. If they do so, they commit adultery with those to whom they have joined themselves.”

For, as the holy Fathers define the goodness of marriage, marriage is good; and what is good is not sin. Therefore whoever acts against the good of marriage commits sin when he commits adultery. They also define marriage as good and established and blessed by God—marriage which He also consecrated by His presence—in which there are faith, offspring, and sacrament.

Faith requires that no one have intercourse with another woman or another man apart from the marriage bond. Offspring requires that children be received with love, nurtured kindly, and religiously educated; and that parents rejoice not so much because they have begotten children as that their children may be regenerated in Christ. The sacrament requires that marriage not be dissolved, and that neither the husband nor the wife who has been dismissed may be joined to another, not even on account of offspring.

This is the rule of marriage, by which either the fruitfulness of nature is adorned or the depravity of incontinence is governed, as Saint Augustine demonstrates sufficiently, at great length and with great eloquence, in his book *On the Good of Marriage* and in his books *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.

Therefore, every precaution must be taken that a king—about whom those consulting him wished to seek advice—does not in any way seek intercourse with a concubine or any other woman before his lawful wife, whom he legally took, has been declared unworthy even of the name of wife by the lawful judgment of distinguished men and the decree of the priests, or before she has departed from the body by divine judgment. For, as it is most clearly read in the Book of Esther, Queen Vashti, the wife of the most powerful king Ahasuerus, although he was exceedingly fierce, was not removed from the honor of her rank merely because she had offended his spirit by contempt and obstinacy. Rather, this was done by public judgment and the sentence of the princes and judges of the Medes and Persians. After that queen had been deposed by public judgment, girls pleasing to the king’s eyes were sought, among whom Esther shone in beauty and grace, and thus earned the royal union.

The ancient Romans also established and observed by their laws from ancient times that this too ought to be done by lawful judgment—not only after they had become Christians, but even while they were still pagans—as the law of the pagan emperor Antoninus very clearly demonstrates. Blessed Augustine recalls and commends it in his book *On Adulterous Marriages* in these words (Book II, chapter 8):

> “Those who dislike the preservation of an equal standard of chastity between husband and wife, and who prefer—especially in this matter—to be subject to the laws of the world rather than to those of Christ, because civil laws do not appear to bind men with the same bonds of chastity by which they bind women, should read what the emperor Antoninus, certainly not a Christian, decreed concerning this matter. There, a husband is not permitted to accuse his wife of adultery if he himself has not provided an example of chastity by his own conduct, so that both are condemned if the dispute itself proves both equally unchaste.
>
> “For these are the words of the aforementioned emperor, which are found in the Gregorian Code:
>
> “‘Certainly,’ he says, ‘my letter will in no respect prejudice the case. For if you were at fault in causing the marriage to be dissolved, and, under the Julian law, your wife Eupasia married another, she will not on that account be condemned for adultery because of my rescript, unless it is established that adultery was committed. They must, however, consider this first: whether, while you were living chastely, you also encouraged her to cultivate good morals. For it seems exceedingly unjust that a husband should demand chastity from a wife to whom he himself does not display it. This circumstance may also condemn the husband; it does not settle the matter between the two by balancing their mutual offenses, nor does it remove the cause of the act.’”

> “If these things must be observed for the honor of an earthly city, how much more when the heavenly homeland and the society of angels seek greater chastity.”

These are the matters that blessed Augustine recalls concerning the laws of the pagan emperor Antoninus. Thus the kings of the Medes, Persians, and Romans, and the judges of the world, although they were pagans and worshipers of idols, naturally doing what belongs to the law, taught—even in cases concerning spouses—that judgment ought to decree, define, and uphold not cruelty and savagery but equity and justice.

Therefore kings, bishops, and secular judges must fear what is said in the Gospel concerning the Ninevites and the Queen of the South: “They will rise in the judgment and condemn this most wicked generation” (Matt. XII, 41). They will condemn it, certainly, not by the power of judgment but by comparison with a better deed. If those kings and judges who were idolaters observed such an order of judgment, how much more must we, living under Christ, the judge of the living and the dead, beware of departing in any respect from the order of judgment through an insufficiently proper motive.

The Book of Numbers also commands (Num. V) that if a woman has been accused either of adultery or under a false suspicion, and her husband has been stirred against her by jealousy, he is to bring her to the priests and present her to divine judgment, either to be condemned or acquitted. Thus Susanna, when falsely accused of adultery, is read to have been condemned by public judgment and acquitted by public judgment (Dan. XIII). The woman in the Gospel who had truly been caught in adultery was first brought, according to the law, before the Pharisees, who exercised judicial power among the people, and then, also as a test, was brought before the Lord’s judgment. There, through His astonishing mercy, she deserved to be freed both from the punishment of stoning and from the guilt of the crime (John VIII).

Christian laws too were established under the inspiration of the Lord. By them marriage is lawfully entered into; and through the sanctity of priestly authority the Lord wishes, in His stead, to bestow upon lawfully united spouses the blessing which He Himself gave in paradise to our first parents, through those who are called His mouth, as the prophet says: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. I, 20). And the Lord Himself says: “When you separate the precious from the vile, you will be as my mouth” (Jer. XV, 19). Through these ministers He wishes to bestow it upon each individually and to heal the weak with the medicine of repentance.

The book of Ecclesiasticus says concerning a servant—how much more concerning a wife: “But do nothing grave without judgment” (Ecclus. XXXIII, 30).

That king must also observe another requirement: before legitimate repentance, undertaken and completed according to the laws of the Church, and before reconciliation has been obtained, he must not join himself in marriage, and still less to the very concubine in question. For even King David (II Kings XII, 15), without undergoing such a refining repentance, did not take Bathsheba, with whom he had committed adultery, as his wife. The son born from that adultery was immediately struck and killed by divine judgment, although David had pleaded for him with much fasting and weeping. Afterwards David was afflicted and tormented by the gravest tribulations and by the loss of his kingdom through his son Absalom; he was, as it were, refined and purified in a furnace of fire, so that he seems truly to have escaped only by divine clemency. The merciful Lord had already forgiven him his sin when he had been brought to the sharpest contrition of heart, repented, and confessed. But because He is just and loves justice, He deservedly and most justly avenged what the king, appointed by Him to punish crimes, had wickedly done.

## QUESTION XXII

Write back to us in the eighth chapter whether what some say certain bishops teach ought to be followed: that they should provide the protection of their defense for men or women who have confessed to them, so that no one may dare to bring such persons before the judgment of the state for crimes about which they had confessed to the bishops, even if the crimes are widely known. And if they wish to separate—not by mutual agreement for the sake of continence, but because of some disagreement—or if, once separated, they cannot remain continent because of their weakness, or are unwilling to be reconciled, whether the bishops may advise them by their own authority. They say that, because such persons have fled by secret confession to ecclesiastical mercy, they ought not to be judged by anyone other than the bishops to whom they had confessed—like the wife of Boso, about whom we were warned through an appeal made at the synod held in the city of Leucorum.

## RESPONSE

Anyone of sound judgment, even if ignorant of the laws of the Church, recognizes how absurd this is, because, as blessed Gregory writes to Leontius, the former consul (Book VIII, Letter 51):

> “Your Glory must remember,” he says, “that it has never received one of my letters on behalf of anyone except that you might, with justice favoring you, provide your protection. For it is shameful to defend what has not first been established to be just. I love people for the sake of justice; I do not set justice aside for the sake of people.”

For, as we wrote above that blessed Ambrose taught, a marriage pact cannot be made with fewer than ten witnesses; indeed, the very term *nuptiae*—marriage—which lacks singularity, shows that the knowledge of many people ought to be sought. What has been joined publicly cannot be separated in a corner. Likewise, a marriage joined according to Christian and public laws cannot be dissolved from that same marriage bond on the basis of a secret confession, which may not be made public; nor should such collusion be called a flight to ecclesiastical mercy.

Therefore, if anyone wishes to know what ecclesiastical authority moderately decrees concerning those who flee to it as to a mother’s bosom, we suggest that every diligent or inquisitive person reread, among other writings, the letters of blessed Gregory. In them, whenever the circumstances of the place required—and indeed very frequently—whether he was petitioning emperors or any other persons on behalf of all who fled to him, he always inserted in his letters the qualifications “with equity preserved,” “with reason preserved,” “with justice remaining,” or “with the judicial case brought to its conclusion,” and “without priestly envy.” They also wrote:

> “That it is necessary for the elected persons to undergo judgment with the opposing party, so that the truth may be known and what the order of equity advises may be determined.”

> “That, once delay has ceased, everyone be compelled to come to the judgment of the chosen.”

> “Whatever, after the truth has been ascertained, has been established by the holy Gospels must in every respect be carried into effect.”

> “Whatever, with justice advising, has seemed right must be decreed in writing.”

> “That no one be in any way burdened contrary to the laws or to reason, but that justice be preserved toward him in everything, as befits Christianity, so that he who has fled to ecclesiastical mercy may not, contrary to the order of equity, be burdened by that very mercy with what it promised him.”

> “Wherever it is necessary to assist one who has fled for refuge, let aid be given to him with his legal rights preserved.”

> “And likewise, let your assistance be enjoyed wherever necessity requires, with justice accompanying it.”

He also writes to Fantinus, the defensor (Book VI, indiction 2, Letter 83):

> “Provide the aforementioned woman with protection, with equity preserved, and in no way permit her to be burdened contrary to the order of reason.”

And again to Anatolius, the Constantinopolitan deacon (Book VII, indiction 51, Letter 82):

> “We wish Your Love to pay careful attention to this: that it not consent to involve itself in any case in which the poor are being burdened, lest, perhaps, being in some way oppressed by the power of persons, it be compelled to do what cannot benefit its soul. Therefore handle everything with fear of God, and consider above all the eternal reward.”

And to Sabinus, the subdeacon (Book VIII, Letter 6):

> “Let it be the concern of your diligence that they not be subjected to any expenses contrary to reason. But if someone attempts to defend himself by some excuse, it is appropriate to investigate the case carefully by means of the holy Gospels and then to determine it as justice and the order of the law advise, and to commit what has been determined to execution.”

And to Romanus, the defensor (Book VII, indiction 2, Letter 24):

> “You must provide ecclesiastical protection—whether you receive my letters or whether none have been sent—with such moderation that those involved in public thefts do not appear to be unjustly defended by us, lest we in any way transfer upon ourselves the reputation of evildoers through the audacity of indiscriminate defense. Rather, assist those whom you can by admonishing them as is fitting for the Church and by offering a word of intercession, so that you may help them without staining the reputation of the holy Church.”

Concerning those who have fled to the enclosure of a church and even to the sanctuaries themselves, he writes to Januarius, bishop of the city of Caralis (Book VIII, Letter 38):

> “If,” he says, “some of those concerning whom the dispute exists should perhaps flee into a church, the case must be arranged so that neither they themselves suffer violence nor those said to have been oppressed suffer loss. Let it therefore be your concern that an oath concerning the preservation of law and justice be promised to them by those whose interest it is, and that they be urged in every way to leave and to give an account of their actions.”

And in the first book of the capitularies of the lords Charles and Louis, emperors:

> “If anyone takes refuge in a church, let him have peace in the atrium of that church, and let it not be necessary for him to enter the church. Let no one presume to drag him away from there by force; but let him be permitted to confess what he has done, and from there let him be brought into public examination through the hands of good men.”

And in the first chapter of the Council of Orléans, concerning murderers, adulterers, and thieves, if they should flee to a church, it is written:

> “As has been established in the ecclesiastical canons and in the decrees of Roman law, it is not permitted to drag them from the atria of the church or from the bishop’s house. Rather, after oaths have been given concerning death, bodily injury, and every kind of punishment, so that they may not suffer violence before legal satisfaction, they shall leave the church, so that an agreement concerning satisfaction may be reached with the person against whom the criminal is guilty.”

And in the third chapter (canon 5):

> “If the servant of anyone should flee to a church for any fault, he must be compelled to return to his master’s service after an oath of immunity has been received. If, after the oath has been given, he refuses to return, his master may seize him when he refuses to leave. Those who do not observe what they have promised are ordered to be cut off from ecclesiastical communion.”

It is also written in the second chapter of the same council (canon 4):

> “If a ravisher should flee to a church with the woman whom he has abducted, and it is established that the woman herself suffered violence, she shall immediately be freed from the power of the ravisher. The ravisher, after immunity from death or punishment has been granted, shall either be subjected to servitude or be given the free opportunity to ransom himself. But if it is established that the abducted woman has a father and that the girl consented to the ravisher, she shall be returned, exculpated, to her father’s authority.”

And in the African Council it is written (canon 29):

> “If a cleric of whatever rank has been condemned by the judgment of bishops for any crime, it is not permitted for him to be defended, whether by the churches over which he presided or by any person, under penalty involving loss of money and honor. Thus the promulgators of the laws command that neither age nor sex is to provide an excuse.”

How much less ought bishops—who are, of course, preachers of equity—to defend anyone unjustly under the guise of mercy, especially when they read that it is written: “If you offer rightly but do not rightly divide, you have sinned”; and: “You shall carry out exactly what is just” (Deut. XVI, 20).

But if anything seems to anyone to sound contrary to the decrees of the Council of Orléans and of the Apostolic See, because the former demands oaths for the preservation of immunity, whereas the latter demands them for the preservation of equity, it must be understood that blessed Gregory speaks concerning those persons who believe that they will be justified in judgment but fear violence before judgment. The Council of Orléans, however, speaks concerning those who do not conceal their own injustice and who, moreover, fear violence together with the equity of judgment.

It does not, however, speak concerning the law of marriage, which the Lord gave specifically—or, to put it more precisely, uniquely—to our first parents in paradise. Nor did He change it in the Gospel when the apostles objected that, if the law governing a man and his wife were such, it was not advantageous to marry. Nor did Paul, who was caught up to the third heaven and into paradise, presume to write anything new or dare to say anything concerning this kind of defense.

Readers must also carefully observe that whenever a council, in view of the circumstances of the time or the necessity of danger, is read to have decreed something by way of advice that differs from the Apostolic See or from the ancient rules, but is not contrary to faith or religion, then, according to what is read in the sixth chapter of the Council of Nicaea—“Concerning that which has been approved by the reasonable common decision of all and according to ecclesiastical rule, when two or three contradict it, so that the judgment of the majority may prevail”—the following must be recognized as preferable.

As Gelasius writes (Letter 6, 6, 2), while the ancient constitutions remain in place on account of their venerability, and ought regularly to be observed wherever no pressing hardship of circumstances or times demands otherwise, that course must rather be followed which the Apostolic See has decreed is to be held irrefragably, or which more numerous or more authoritative councils have established.

That same blessed Gregory writes to Venantius, bishop of Luna, concerning one unwilling to submit to justice (Book VII, indiction 11, Letter 28):

> “Since the standard of equity advises that the greatest episcopal assistance ought, with reason preserved, to be present for those who have converted, for this reason we exhort your Fraternity by these letters to have the aforesaid mother of Adeodata summoned before you, and by calm exhortation persuade her not to cease voluntarily doing what she can legally be compelled to do, so that neither she may appear to be afflicted nor the other to suffer prejudice. If, as we do not believe, she wishes to delay your admonition, provide the aforesaid religious Adeodata with protection against her, and assist her more vigorously through your support before the judge, or wherever necessity requires. Apply yourselves to the execution of this case in such a way that, compelled by legal reason, she may be pressed, even unwillingly, to do what she voluntarily postpones.
>
> “Let Your Fraternity keep the aforesaid woman thief, with equity preserved, commended to you in every respect, so that, while you provide her protection, she may remain, with God protecting her, without any disturbance in the habit she has assumed.”

And to Januarius, bishop of Sardinia:

> “For this purpose we have sent our defensor Redemptus, the bearer of these presents, there: both to compel the parties to observe the judgment and, through his diligence in execution, to bring to effect whatever has been adjudicated.”

There are many other passages of this kind, and it would be tedious for us to enumerate them.

For to ask contrary to these principles is recognized as belonging neither to the Church nor to an ecclesiastical man, lest perhaps an undue mercy be judged impiety, as Saint Celestine writes to Nestorius:

> “For there is often such a kind of mercy from which impiety is born.”

And Saint Augustine, in Book IV *Against Julianus* (canon 3):

> “Perhaps,” he says, “you will say that a merciful will is a good one. This would rightly be said if, just as the faith of Christ—that is, the faith which works through love—is always good, mercy were always good as well. But if a bad mercy is also found, by which the person of a poor man is favored in judgment, and on account of which King Saul ultimately deserved to be condemned by the Lord, certainly mercifully, because against His command he spared the captive king through human affection (I Kings XV), consider carefully whether mercy is perhaps not good unless it belongs to this good faith.
>
> “Indeed, answer this, so that you may see it without doubt: do you consider an unfaithful mercy good? Moreover, if it is a vice to show mercy wrongly, then without doubt it is a vice to show mercy unfaithfully.”

No one can be so merciful as to be found more merciful than God, whom the Psalmist wished to call “Mercy,” saying: “My God, my mercy” (Ps. LVIII, 18). Yet He did not wish to remove just judgment from just judges concerning the woman caught in adultery and brought before Him (John VIII).

Therefore Saint Jerome, explaining the verse of the psalm, says: “Because of truth, meekness, and justice” (Ps. XLIV, 5). Truth is Christ Himself, and therefore He said concerning that woman to the Jews: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John VIII, 7). Meekness was shown when He said: “Neither will I condemn you” (John VIII, 11). Justice was shown when He said: “Go, woman, and do not sin again” (ibid.).

For what we read in the aforementioned volume concerning the aforesaid wife of Boso is written in this manner:

> “When her husband arrived, or stayed with us, or departed, after a security agreement had been made, we summoned him so that we might examine his wife in his presence. We avoid handing over to death, as unjust and cruel, a woman who has fled to us for refuge without examination. For since no particular accuser comes forward, although she has been admonished and questioned, she confesses nothing other than that, fearing death from the persecution of Hucbert alone, she is seeking to avoid it.”

Readers ought prudently to consider whether this agrees with authority or with reason. Authority demands firmness concerning the preservation of equity and justice for those who flee to a church. It does not demand that a man be entirely deprived of his lawful power over his wife, legally betrothed to him, legally endowed, and honored by public marriage, merely because he has been moved by suspicion against her.

As for what is written in the Heptateuch concerning jealousy (Num. V)—that a man, stirred by the spirit of jealousy, should bring his wife to the priests to be examined—this was commanded because it is the priest’s duty to write, as part of the ministry entrusted to him, the exorcisms to be washed into the water which the woman must drink. Hence the sacred canons also decreed (Council of Agde, canon 25) that secular men must not condemn or cast away their wives before they have stated the cause of the separation to the provincial bishop.

For the rest, divine authority does not take away from men the legal judgment concerning their own wives, as we demonstrated above from the evangelical truth.

Let us also examine more carefully what is contained in the volume cited above: “We avoid handing over to death, as unjust and cruel, a woman who has fled to us without examination.” We ought not hand over even those who have been examined to death, unless it is so that, dead to sin, they may live to God.

Let us nevertheless grant that the bishops, retaining this woman in their power, since she is said to have fled to them, may arrange to examine her before her husband if he attributes some wrongdoing to her. But what ought to be done if she is found guilty in the episcopal examination? If the bishops, by their own authority, wish to remove the legal judgment concerning her after she has been found guilty, they will appear to act against the one whose action and speech are known to be perfect authority, as it is written: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I, 1). For He did not remove judgment from the woman caught in adultery, although through Moses He had commanded that such women be stoned; rather, He commanded that legal judgment be carried out by just judges, saying: “Let him cast the first stone at her” (John VIII, 7).

But if the bishops, after examining her and finding her guilty, hand her over for punishment, they will be proved to act against ecclesiastical mercy and against the very head of the Church, the fountain of mercy, who said: “Neither will I condemn you; go, and do not sin again” (John VIII, 11).

Since these matters have been so clearly understood and most carefully weighed, let us, as bishops, follow the authority of our predecessors concerning those who flee to the mercy of the Church, and let us not be found deserving of blame.

Finally, what is written in the same place—that, since no particular accuser comes forward, she nevertheless, after being admonished and questioned, confesses nothing other than that she is avoiding death because she fears the persecution of Hucbert—leaves this as the only possibility: since she is accused by no one, if the bishops do not find any other course according to such canons, if such canons exist but have not yet been read by us, and if Christian and noble laymen do not find another course according to laws that we have not learned, then she should be restored to her husband with a firm guarantee of equity, if necessity and reason require it on account of some accusation brought against her. She should be protected by her husband’s marital defense, as is just, so that she is not killed by Hucbert. Finally, her husband should exercise over her, as a man ought over his wife, the legitimate and lawful power granted by Christian and ecclesiastical law.

## QUESTION XXIII

Concerning what some are said to teach: that if a man and a woman wish to separate—not by mutual agreement for the sake of continence but because of some disagreement—or if, once separated, they cannot remain continent because of their weakness, or are unwilling to be reconciled, the bishops may advise them by their own authority.

## RESPONSE

Let all who say these things know that, in a certain sense, this was the fourth chapter of the error of those who dared to disparage and oppose the holy Synod of Chalcedon and were condemned as being in error by the Apostolic See and by the unanimity of the bishops of the whole world.
