Saint Leo repeatedly wrote about this, and blessed Gregory also wrote to the patrician Theoctista, among other things, as follows (Book IX, Letter 39):

> “Truth itself says: ‘What God has joined, let no man separate’” (Matt. XIX, 6). “It also says: ‘It is not lawful to put away one’s wife except for the cause of fornication’” (Matt. V, 32). Who, then, would contradict this heavenly legislator? We know that it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24). If, therefore, husband and wife are one flesh, and the husband dismisses his wife for the sake of religion, or if the wife dismisses her husband, whether he remains in this world or perhaps even goes over to unlawful vows, what kind of conversion is this, in which one and the same flesh partly passes over to continence while partly remains in impurity?
>
> “But if both agree to lead a continent life, who would dare to condemn this, when it is certain that almighty God, who permitted lesser things, did not forbid greater ones? We know many holy men who first led a continent life with their wives and afterwards entered the governance of the holy Church.
>
> “Holy men customarily abstain even from what is lawful for two reasons: sometimes to increase their merit before almighty God, and sometimes to cleanse the sins of their former life. Therefore, when good spouses desire either to increase their merit or to erase the sins of their former life, they may bind themselves to continence and pursue a better life.
>
> “But if the wife does not follow the continence desired by the husband, or the husband refuses the continence desired by the wife, the marriage may not be divided, because it is written: ‘The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife’” (I Cor. VII, 4).

And in his letter to Adrianus, the notary of Palermo, he censures Urbicus the abbot because he had received Agathosa’s husband into a monastery for conversion against her will, and orders that her husband be restored to her, even if he had already been tonsured (Book IX, Letter 44):

> “Unless you discover that the aforesaid woman committed some crime of fornication, on account of which a man is permitted to leave his wife, we wish you absolutely to restore her husband to her—or, if he has already been tonsured, to return him—without allowing any excuse. For after one body has been made through the union of marriage between man and woman, it cannot be converted in part while remaining in part in the world.”

Let no one be angry with us because we propose ecclesiastical judgments for lay people also to hear. Let him read the Fathers’ solution to the question proposed: why the Lord, who forbade presenting holy things to those who bite and pearls to the irreverent, nevertheless, when questioned about the resurrection of the dead (Matt. XIX and XXII), opened the secrets of the law to unbelievers, envious people, and tempters through their objection concerning the shameful story of the woman with seven husbands.

He opened those secrets not to people who could not understand, but to those who could understand and were present at the same time—people whom it was not right to neglect on account of the impurity of others. When the tempters questioned Him and He answered them so that they had nothing with which to contradict Him, although they were wasting away in their own poisons rather than being nourished by His food, others who were capable of understanding nevertheless heard many useful things on account of their example.

Such people will accept from us, insignificant little men as we are, a sufficient explanation. Let them also kindly accept blessed Augustine speaking on our behalf in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*. He says (chapter 16):

> “There is one reason for concealing the truth and another necessity for speaking the truth. It would take too long to seek out or insert all the reasons for concealing the truth; nevertheless, one of them is this: we do not wish to make worse those who do not understand while wishing to make more learned those who do understand. When we remain silent about something of this kind, the learned do not become more learned, but neither do the others become worse.
>
> “But when the matter is such that, if we speak it, the person who cannot understand becomes worse, while if we remain silent, the person who can understand becomes worse, what do we think ought to be done? Should we not rather speak the truth, so that the one who can understand may understand, than remain silent, so that not only may neither understand it, but the more intelligent person may himself become worse? If he heard and understood, many others would also learn through him. For the more capable he is of learning, the more suitable he is for teaching others.”

## SEVEN QUESTIONS

Finally, seven questions follow. After the preceding questions, and after approximately six months had passed, we received these from the same persons from whom we had received the earlier ones, to be solved. As with the preceding questions, we shall place the text of each before its solution, answering as briefly as we can, as though drawing upon a boxwood tablet, so that an able person may understand from this outline what would enable him to depict the matter more fully. In this way we neither close the inward compassion of charity against the petitions of our brothers nor fail to provide the wise person, according to Scripture, with an opportunity to become wiser when he has diligently investigated these matters and sought to understand them more fully.

We also hope that the little hours which we extract rather than borrow from our many and varied occupations—since we have no holidays from our thoughts—may somehow suffice and not weary our readers, because the size of this volume, arising from the answers to the questions previously proposed, almost exceeds the bounds of brevity.

The beginning of these questions is as follows:

“We ask Your Love not to be displeased if we persist importunately in seeking from you matters necessary for us to know. After we recently sent you questions to solve, we discovered many matters concerning which we ask to receive individual answers, each based on the authority of Scripture, the rules, and the teaching of the ecclesiastical doctors.”

## QUESTION I

Some say that King Lothair has in his kingdom bishops, nobles, and faithful laymen, with whose consultation and advice he settled the case between himself and his wife, and that the bishops of another kingdom, or anyone else, have no right to reconsider anything concerning it.

## RESPONSE
Such people should be answered: “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matt. 22:29). When one group of the children of Israel built a mound as a witness, the other group, inflamed with divine zeal, almost took up arms, lest the Lord’s people be divided, as it was later divided by the calves manufactured by Jeroboam in the crime of idolatry (III Kings 12). And now these men, wishing to divide the Lord’s kingdom and the catholic Church, which is one dove and beloved, seem not merely to urge but even to compel us to say what certain men once said [Col. 0746D]: “You have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse; return to your tents, Israel,” attempting to impose upon our most pestilential age that condition in which there was neither king nor leader among that people, but each person did what seemed right to him. Would that he did not knowingly and deliberately do what merely seems right and pleasing to his desire, while in fact it is crooked and evil!

It is not as these men maliciously construct it. There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, through all, and in us all (Eph. 4:5). There is one kingdom, one dove of Christ—that is, the holy Church—under one law of Christianity, one kingdom, and one Church, although the government of the kingdom and of the churches is administered by several rulers and prelates.

[Col. 0747A] Moreover, the matter under discussion is such that it is recognized as concerning all who bear the Christian name. For it concerns a king and queen, a Christian man and a Christian woman; it concerns the law of marriage first given by God in Paradise to our original parents, strengthened in the Church, secured and established by divine and human laws confirmed by God, established by blessing through priestly ministry, and celebrated according to the custom of all the faithful. The question is how so excellent a good and gift has been stained by so great a fabrication of the devil that there can be no doubt that it is the work of him whom Scripture foretells would appear: “so that he may sit in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (II Thess. 2:4); and again: “For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work” (ibid., 7)—when lawful things are rejected unlawfully and unlawful things are usurped as though they were lawful.

By this, not only those bishops in whose parishes or diocesan responsibilities these matters arise, or those faithful before whose eyes such things are presumed and who are consequently moved as though they concerned them personally, are disturbed; rather, the whole order and people of every order are shaken by such monstrous novelty. Hence, as we have already said above, holy Pope Celestine of Rome says to Venetius and the other Gallic bishops (Epistle 8): “The whole Church is shaken by whatever novelty.” And to Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople (Epistle 5): “Everyone must know what is being done whenever the cause of all is being handled.”

This cause is, as it were, set before everyone as on a watchtower. Therefore it must be defined—or, once defined, recognized by everyone—in the manner in which it ought to be observed by all [Col. 0747C]. Thus the Lord also says: “What I say to you, I say to all: Watch” (Mark 13:37). The African Council also decreed (canon 95) that causes which are not common should be judged in their own provinces; but whenever a common cause requires it, a general synod should be convened, so that the common cause may be defined there.

For, as Pope Innocent writes to Victricius, bishop of Rouen (Epistle 1, chapter 1): “A judgment is complete when it is confirmed by the opinions of many.” Therefore this general cause, which concerns everyone generally, must come to the knowledge of all and be determined by a general definition, so that it may not be said by those less acquainted with it: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be exposed; but whoever does good comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been accomplished in God.” What has therefore been said in darkness, insofar as it concerns the public at large, must be said in the light; and what has been spoken in the ear and in private rooms must be proclaimed upon the housetops, so that no one may criticize those who shine for all in word and deed and are seen by all, like a lamp placed upon a lampstand and a city set upon a mountain.

## QUESTION II

[Col. 0747D]

They also say that there is neither authority nor reason for a case which has been decided by the judgment of bishops to return to judgment. For if it does so, these bishops who decided it will thereafter have no authority, and whatever they decide in the future will not be capable of standing firm, since it could be reconsidered.

## RESPONSE

This is recognized as the utterance of ignorant people who do not know the ecclesiastical rules. Read the Council of Sardica, which Pope Zosimus sent through Bishop Faustinus to the Carthaginian synod under the heading of the Council of Nicaea, and you will find sufficient evidence that those who speak in this way are mistaken.

Pope Leo of Rome and the synod held at Rome also wrote to the emperor Theodosius concerning the reconsideration of the Ephesian synod, which he seemed dangerously inclined to support (Epistle 27):

“Behold,” he says, “I, Christian and venerable emperor, together with my fellow priests, fulfilling toward Your Clemency the duty of sincere love and desiring in all things to please God, to whom the Church prays on your behalf lest we be judged guilty of silence before the tribunal of the Lord, beseech you before the inseparable Trinity of one divinity—which is offended by such an act, although it is itself the guardian and author of your imperial power—and before the holy angels of Christ, to order everything to remain in the condition in which it was before the judgment, until a greater number of priests from the whole world can be assembled. Do not permit yourselves to be burdened by another’s sin; for, in saying what it is necessary for us to say, we fear that the indignation of the one whose religion is being destroyed may be provoked.”

The same must be feared by all priests, kings, princes, and all the faithful generally in this matter, which is no small part of faith and religion, if it is treated negligently.

The sacred canons also make clear that responsibility for the whole province rests with the archbishop or primate. He ought to know the judgments of his fellow bishops, regarding which an appeal may be necessary, and in cases where the matter requires it he ought to designate chosen judges. All this demonstrates that the judgment of a synod of bishops from one province may be approved or corrected by a general synod’s adjudication of the provincial bishops’ decisions or disagreements, as is shown by the African synod, which determined that nothing needed to be amended from the Council of Hippo.

The Apostolic See, however, may reconsider, reopen, or confirm both provincial and general judgments, as the letters of Leo, Gelasius, and the other Roman pontiffs, as well as the Council of Sardica, clearly demonstrate. The authority of bishops who judge rightly is confirmed, while those who judge wrongly are corrected; and sometimes their authority is not destroyed altogether.

## QUESTION III

They also say that no archbishops, except the apostolic one, possess greater authority than those who decided this case. If the case returns to judgment and it is found that it ought not to remain as it is, these bishops who judged it will no longer be able to remain in the episcopate.

## RESPONSE

On the contrary, Saint Celestine wrote to Nestorius [Col. 0749A]: “We wish even priests to be corrected when they act contrary to what is right.”

Let those who say these things reread the Acts of the Apostles and observe that, concerning circumcision and observance of the law, certain men who came down from Jerusalem to Antioch stirred up a dispute against Paul and Barnabas. They therefore decided that, together with others, they should go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and presbyters concerning this question. After their arrival, the same issue was raised in Jerusalem by certain Pharisees. Let them consider that Peter defined and James judged the matter differently from the way those men had judged and defined it, and yet none of those men was condemned (Acts 15).

Let them also see in Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians that Peter was rebuked, reproved, and corrected by Paul for dissimulation, but was not condemned. This rebuke was so fully accepted by the first of the apostles that he honored with great praise the same letters of Paul in which he had read himself reproved (Gal. 2; II Pet. 3).

And lest anyone say that, just as according to Scripture the lesser is blessed by the greater (Heb. 7:7), so the greater cannot be judged by the lesser, let them read Paul’s Epistles to the Corinthians. There they will find that the archbishop and outstanding teacher rebuked and corrected disobedient bishops, but did not condemn them, because they permitted a fornicator to live among them without a fitting denunciation.

Paul himself clearly shows that he rebuked bishops for such an offense when he says: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled, and my spirit is present” (I Cor. 5:4).

And in the Second Epistle: “Therefore I beseech you to confirm your love toward him. For this reason I wrote to you, so that I might learn by testing you whether you are obedient in everything. Anyone to whom you have forgiven anything, I also forgive. For whatever I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I have forgiven for your sake in the person of Christ” (II Cor. 2:8–10).

By “I have forgiven” he meant “I have granted indulgence”; and, in the case of a public crime publicly cast out, this belongs to none but bishops, as those who are not ignorant of ecclesiastical rules know.

Hence it is also written in the Carthaginian Council (canon 15): “It has also pleased us that, when an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to ecclesiastical judges of greater authority, this should not harm those whose sentence has been set aside, unless they have been convicted either of judging with an inimical spirit or of having been corrupted by some desire or favor.”

As for the claim that the other archbishops are not of greater authority than these men, and that the case therefore cannot return to judgment before them, we have shown above that what an individual does not possess is obtained by a plurality. Scripture also demonstrates this when it says: “If two of you agree on earth about anything, it will be done for them”; and: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:19–20).

When the apostles, together with the other faithful and Mary the mother of Jesus, were gathered and prayed together, the place was shaken; and upon the hundred and twenty who were gathered on the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit appeared in tongues of fire (Acts 2).

Paul also demonstrates this, as we said above, when he says: “When you are assembled, and my spirit is present” (I Cor. 5:4).

And Peter, the prince of the apostles, filled with abundant grace of gifts and supported by the greatest power of miracles, entered the house of the gentile Cornelius at the prompting of the Spirit. When the faithful questioned him about why he had entered among the gentiles and eaten with them, and why he had received them in baptism, he answered the complaint not by authority but by reason. He explained the matter in order, appeased them with humble reasoning, and even called witnesses in the case of his own reproach, saying: “These six brothers also came with me” (Acts 10 and 11).

If therefore the shepherd of the Church and prince of the apostles, who performed signs and miracles individually, did not disdain humbly to give an account in the matter of his own reproach, how much more ought we sinners, when we are reproved concerning some matter, to appease our reprovers with humble reasoning, even if we are judged superior to them in some authority?

We say this not in order to reproach our brothers and fellow priests for judging anything according to the ecclesiastical rules, but to demonstrate more clearly what we ought to do—those who are said to be something when we are nothing, as the Apostle says (Gal. 6)—lest we deceive ourselves. If something worthy of correction appears in the case that has given rise to dispute, it should be changed for the better without violating charity, just as Paul held concerning the gentiles: they should not be circumcised or burdened with the yoke of the law; Peter agreed, and James adjudicated (Acts 15).

The holy Council of Nicaea also decreed (canon 5) that such questions should be examined jointly by all the bishops of the province gathered together, and that after the examination the judgment should either remain as it was enacted or be changed for the better (canon 6).

If two or three oppose a common decree of all, reasonably made and approved according to ecclesiastical rule—not because of the truth of the faith or the integrity of authority, but because of their own contentions—the judgment of the majority should prevail (canon 9).

But if, as sometimes happens, a fraternal decision appears to some people to require reconsideration for no sufficient reason, and a full account is given with faith and authority, let the judgment of the Acts of the Apostles be brought forward. Peter says concerning the gentiles: “If therefore God gave them the same grace as he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?” When they heard these things, they fell silent and glorified God, saying: “Then God has also granted repentance to the gentiles unto life” (Acts 11:17–18).

If a less necessary question should happen to arise, the agitation of the brothers’ minds should be settled for the preservation of peace and charity, as the Gospel authority demonstrates when a dispute arose among the disciples about which of them seemed to be greatest (Luke 22:24).

If anyone has acted violently or negligently toward those subject to him, or has acted in the sacred ministry otherwise than he ought, he should be corrected and amended by those concerned, according to the rules promulgated by the Holy Spirit. This is demonstrated by the Council of Nicaea (canon 5) concerning the excommunicated, by the Council of Sardica (canon 17) concerning an angry bishop—which he ought not to be—who wishes to drive out his presbyter or deacon, by the Council of Chalcedon (canon 25) concerning neglected episcopal ordination, and by the other councils and the letters of Leo and Gregory.

Finally, if anyone, God forbid, should rashly oppose or attempt to trample upon the faith, ecclesiastical doctrine, or the statutes of sacred authority, such people should first be admonished according to the Lord’s command. If—far be it from the Lord—they persist as rebellious, contentious, and contemptuous people, they must be struck down and restrained by fitting denunciations according to the sacred canons and the examples and statutes of our predecessors.

Thus Saint Leo decreed in his letter to all the provinces (Letter to the Italian Bishops):

“We command,” he says, “that everything promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons be guarded by Your Charity in such a way that, if anyone commits an offense against them, he should know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him. Whoever attempts to act against the established rules and dares to do what has been prohibited should know that he is to be removed from his office and will not be a participant in our communion, since he refused to be a companion in discipline.”

And blessed Gelasius says:

“Those who have dared to carry out these things, or even those who have hitherto remained silent about what they knew, should not doubt that they will suffer the loss of their own honor if they do not hasten with all possible speed to heal deadly wounds with appropriate medicine.”

And Saint Celestine says to Nestorius (Epistle 5):

“Since we have offered these counsels after the preceding admonition, it is necessary that we confirm a sentence of condemnation against those who abuse our salutary warning.”

And to Cyril of Alexandria:

“We say these things so that we may not seem to be lacking, perhaps, in the desire to correct. For if, while we endure the vine, he adds thorns to himself, let it be fulfilled; and while the earlier statutes remain, let him gather the fruit of his own judgment from what he has sown in the devil’s furrow. He will perish not by our counsel, but by his own agency.”

## QUESTION IV

They nevertheless say that, if this king is not permitted to take another wife or to retain his concubine as he now has her, his wife will be judged, whether she wishes it or not, to return to him; and that he will devise such a scheme concerning her that he will be rid of her and will no longer have to bring the matter to judgment.

## RESPONSE

We have not learned such a judgment from evangelical truth, apostolic authority, or the promulgation of the sacred canons. Rather, as the African synod decreed (canon 69):

“It has pleased us,” it says, “that, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband may be joined to another, but that they should either remain as they are or be reconciled to one another.”

It said “let them be reconciled,” not “let them be compelled.” Anyone who thinks soundly understands how reconciliation is to take place.

Paul likewise, recalling the one through whom we have been reconciled to God and received the ministry of reconciliation, says: “We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (II Cor. 5:18). This reconciliation takes place through the grace of the God who calls, not compels, and through the free, not forced, will of a human being.

It is written concerning the just man: “In the time of wrath he became reconciliation” (Ecclus. 44:17)—that is, so that offenses might not be counted against him. Whoever knows from what the words *concilio* and *reconcilio* are formed does not fail to understand the manner and order of reconciliation.

Different kinds of illness require different medicinal treatments. We read in sacred authority that some people are brought and compelled to repentance; some are excommunicated until they return to peace; and some are partly left to the freedom of their own will. We showed this above from the letter of Saint Gregory concerning the woman of Leo the chartularius, who had temporarily left him for the crime of fornication, having put on religious clothing, but after an oath had been given and her husband’s innocence recognized, returned to him of her own accord. Gregory writes to Bishop Secundinus of Taormina concerning what ought to be observed toward her.

In some cases, however, the freedom of the will must be awaited entirely, as in this matter. For it is granted that a man and woman may separate because of fornication, or that those who have separated may be reconciled. But it is compelled—once all freedom of will has been removed—and not granted that a man and woman separate except on account of fornication, or that those who have separated join themselves to others in any way.

Hence Saint Augustine says in the second book *On Adulterous Marriages* (chapter 13):

“There is nothing,” he says, “to which we can exhort those who fear reconciliation with adulterous spouses healed through repentance except the preservation of continence. For a woman is bound as long as her husband, whether adulterous or chaste, lives; if she marries another, she commits adultery. And a man is bound as long as his wife, whether adulterous or chaste, lives; if he takes another, he commits adultery (I Cor. 7:39).

“For this bond is not dissolved even if, through divorce, one spouse separates from a chaste spouse; much less is it dissolved if, without separation, one commits adultery. Consequently, nothing dissolves it except the death of the spouse—not the death of one who falls into adultery, but of one who departs from the body.

“Therefore, if a woman leaves an adulterous husband and does not wish to be reconciled to him, let her remain unmarried. And if a man dismisses an adulterous woman and does not wish to receive her even after repentance, let him preserve continence—if not by a voluntary choice of the better good, then certainly by the necessity of avoiding the pernicious evil.

“I would exhort him to this even if his wife were suffering from an incurable and prolonged illness, or even if she were bodily separated somewhere so that her husband could not approach her. Finally, I would exhort him to this even if the woman wished to live continently, so long as, contrary to discipline—not by mutual consent—she dismissed the chaste man while he remained chaste.

“For I think no Christian would deny that a man is an adulterer if, while his wife is suffering for a long time, absent for a long time, or wishing to live continently, he joins himself to another woman. Thus, too, when an adulteress has been dismissed, he is an adulterer with an adulteress, because it is not this or that particular man, but everyone who dismisses his wife and takes another who commits adultery” (Luke 16:18).

And again in the same work (chapter 18):

“To such men we will deny both grace—that is, baptism—and the medicine of repentance so long as they live with adulteresses, if, after dismissing their first wives for a reason other than fornication, they take other wives.

“Unless perhaps someone should say that no one can make his wife commit adultery if she is chaste. Yet the Lord says: ‘Everyone who dismisses his wife except for the reason of fornication makes her commit adultery’ (Matt. 5:33). This is certainly because, although she was chaste while living with her husband, after being dismissed she is compelled through lack of self-control, while her first husband is alive, to join herself to another; and this is adultery.

“If she does not do this, nevertheless he, insofar as it depends upon him, compelled her to do it; and God will count this as sin against him, even if she remains chaste.”

And again in the same place:

“Remember that I say this concerning both sexes.”

And again in the same place:

“Then there will be those who, while their former spouses are alive, cling not to their own spouses but to adulterers. And if they will be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, where will they be except where they will not be saved?”

It is therefore clear, as we have shown above by the authority of Scripture and the teaching of the masters, that a man and wife cannot be separated except either for the sake of marital continence, through which they remain joined more fully because more spiritually, or because of fornication, when one of them has divided the one body and one flesh.

For this reason, if they do not wish, after worthy repentance, to remain together or to be reconciled, they may separate if they wish. But they must not be compelled either to remain together or to be reconciled. They should be persuaded if that is possible, because reconciliation seeks willingness and requires love. Like faith and pure confession, it can be encouraged but cannot be extorted. A person can be compelled to pretend reconciliation, but those who have been separated because of fornication must in every way be prevented from joining themselves to others. If they disregard this, they must be brought to repentance.

Since we have touched upon pretence, if—God forbid—there should be pretence in any man who can openly reject his wife because of fornication, so as not to be joined to her again, let him receive her when she has been persuaded, but not compelled. Since he cannot take another while she is alive, unless some rationale is found that sacred authority does not contradict, he may contemplate destroying her by some means.

From such a man security must be demanded, of the kind that Saint Gregory commands to be exacted from those who, fearing the force of injustice, flee to sacred sanctuaries, while equity is preserved for them. If anyone is convicted of violating such security, he must be subject to public and ecclesiastical judgments.

If he acts secretly so that he cannot be legally convicted, after being warned by priestly admonition he will have his conscience as a witness—and also as his judge. For episcopal prudence, clear in its judgment, will say to him what Elijah wished to demonstrate to Elisha: “What was mine I have done for you” (III Kings 19:20). And to the Lord: “I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation” (Ps. 39:11).

In all this, and in every other matter, priestly authority in its teaching should always preserve that apostolic form in which it says: “Reprove, beseech, rebuke” (II Tim. 4:2). That is, by mingling times with times and encouragement with threats, let it show both the sternness of a teacher and the affection of a father. It should reprove the undisciplined and restless more harshly; it should beseech the obedient, gentle, and patient so that they may advance toward better things; and it should correct and rebuke the negligent and contemptuous. It must not conceal the sins of those who commit them, but as soon as they begin to arise, it must cut them out at the root as far as it can.

## QUESTION V

[Col. 0754B]

There is also the matter of Boso’s wife, concerning whom Boso himself lodged a complaint at Confluentes, and who later came to this king and was under his power. Some say that he is doing wrong because, although he can, he does not return her to her husband. Others say that it is not fitting for him to hand over to death his kinswoman, who came under his protection; nor is it right for him to oppress a free woman, constrain her as though she were a slave, and return her unwillingly to another. Others say that, if he wishes to return her, she will go to the Normans, and that it is better for him to permit her to live among Christians and preserve for her the life which the other man wishes to take away.

## RESPONSE

There are legal chapters of the emperors and kings who preceded him concerning what a person who receives a robber after the ban ought to suffer [Col. 0754C]. Our kings’ charter also expressly decrees this matter. It is the king’s responsibility to ensure that these provisions are observed, as Saint Ambrose writes to Valentinian:

“Let the emperor enact laws which he himself is the first to observe. If he himself breaks them, he must fear hearing from the Apostle: ‘You who preach that one should not steal, do you steal? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?’” (Rom. 2:21–22).

Therefore let him hear profitably and appropriately from the Lord: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23).

Let him also fear what is written when the Lord says to a certain king: “Because you have released a man deserving of death, your life shall be forfeit for his life, and your people for his people” (III Kings 20:42).

And again: “You have given help to the impious and joined friendship with those who hate me; therefore you deserved the wrath of the Lord” (II Chron. 19:2).

It is also written: “The accursed thing is among you; you will not be able to stand before your enemies” (Josh. 7:13).

And: “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclus. 13:1).

“No one can hide fire in his bosom without his garments being burned” (Prov. 6:27).

If the matter concerns mercy, let him read and see how Saul, through impious mercy, impiously offended: he spared Agag, but did not set him free, and he himself even lost the kingdom (I Kings 15). Saint Celestine says: “There is a kind of piety from which impiety is born.”

If the matter concerns kinship, let him hear what is written: “They said to their father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and they did not acknowledge their brothers in the cause of God; they kept your covenant, Lord” (Deut. 33:9).

And the Lord says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37), along with the other words that follow there.

If the matter concerns freedom, by the judgment of both divine and worldly law she is recognized as belonging to the man who found her, and the man against whom she is said to have committed fornication has no right to complain about the fornication.

If he retains her, as is said, for the sake of preserving her life, we have shown above what guarantee the ecclesiastical authority commands to be demanded from him for the preservation of equity.

If, as is said, he retains her so that she may not perish among the Normans, let the Apostle answer him: “If the unbelieving partner departs, let him depart” (I Cor. 7:15).

And: “Remove the evil person from among you” (I Cor. 5:13), lest one diseased sheep contaminate the whole flock.

This king is not more just than the Lord, who neither prevented Judas, unwillingly, from going to the Jews—or, as Peter says, “to his own place” (Acts 1:25)—nor by his power forbade Herod to kill the children, nor prevented the soldiers from being killed on Peter’s account in the prison from which he did not fail to rescue him on the very night when he was to be brought out (Acts 12).

The Lord, who taught everyone to love his neighbor as himself, did not ask anyone to sin so that another might be freed from sin. And he who laid down his soul—that is, the life of his body—even for his enemies, and preached that it should be laid down for his friends, taught that no one ought to perish eternally so that another might avoid eternal damnation.

Everyone who involves himself in such matters and raises such arguments must also take care for himself, lest he be judged to be seeking “excuses for sins.” For not only those who commit sins but also those who consent to them are worthy of death [Col. 0755C]. He will not be free from this consent if, while able to avert evil, he does not avert it, or if, while able to restrain evil people, he leaves them to their own freedom.

For a judge, as it is written, does not bear the sword without cause, but has been appointed for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good (Rom. 13:4).

In the Book of Deuteronomy the Lord gives him a rule for judgment and punishment:

“If a man or woman is found among you who does evil in the sight of the Lord your God and transgresses his covenant, going and serving foreign gods and worshiping them—the sun, the moon, or any of the host of heaven, which I have not commanded—and this is reported to you, then, after careful inquiry, you discover that it is true and that such an abomination has been committed in Israel, you shall bring the man or woman who has committed this most wicked deed to the gates of your city, and they shall be stoned with stones.

“By the testimony of two or three witnesses the one who is to be killed shall die. No one shall be put to death on the testimony of a single accuser. The hand of the witnesses shall be first against him in putting him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people, so that you may remove the evil from your midst” (Deut. 17:2–7).

And lest anyone say, “This sentence does not apply to Boso’s wife, because it is written concerning idolaters,” let him read the Scripture which says: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame; they set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. 3:19).

This sentence also applies to the shameful act that, as is said, is attributed to Hucbert and the king’s wife. For in the Book of Leviticus the abominations are individually designated and punished by death; the adulteress is ordered to be overwhelmed with stones [Col. 0756A]—subject to the promulgation of the laws imposed upon them by those who, with the Lord as author, established just laws.

Hence Saint Augustine says in the second book *On Adulterous Marriages*, after the admonitions by which he commands men to be persuaded to abstain from the blood of adulterous wives (chapter 15):

“Finally, I ask you whether a Christian husband is permitted, either according to the ancient law of God or according to Roman laws, to kill an adulterous wife. If it is permitted, it is better for him to abstain from both: from the permitted punishment of the woman who has sinned and from the forbidden marriage with her while she lives.

“If he persists in choosing one or the other, it is better for him to do what is permitted, so that the adulteress may be punished, than what is not permitted, so that while she lives he may commit adultery with her.

“But if, as is more truly said, a Christian man is not permitted to kill an adulterous wife but only to dismiss her, on the condition that she either live continently or be reconciled to him—for if he takes another while she lives, he will without doubt also be guilty of adultery…”

## QUESTION VI

They also say—indeed, some wise men say—that this prince is king and subject to no laws or judgments except those of God alone, who established him as king in the kingdom his father left to him. If he wishes, he will go to a public hearing or to a synod for this or another matter; if he does not wish to, he may freely and lawfully decline.

And just as he should not be excommunicated by his own bishops for anything he does, so he cannot be judged by other bishops, because he ought to be subject only to the authority of God, by whom alone he could have been established as prince. What he does, and what sort of ruler he is, is by divine will, as it is written: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God; wherever he wishes, he turns it” (Prov. 21:1).

[694] **RESPONSE**
This is not the voice of a catholic Christian, but of one who is exceedingly blasphemous and filled with a diabolical spirit. King and prophet David, when he sinned, heard even from his inferior Nathan that he was a man deserving death; and through the most profound repentance he was saved (II Samuel XII). Saul learned from Samuel that he had been cast out from the kingdom (I Samuel XIII and XV). Rehoboam likewise received from a prophet that the kingdom—which his father had held well—was to be torn from his hand (I Kings XI). When kings and the children of Israel sinned and were delivered into the hands of the nations, as Manasseh and Zedekiah were, or feared before the face of the Lord, as Hezekiah did, they received either anger from the Lord through the prophets or merited mercy.

And it is written in Deuteronomy:

> “If you perceive that a judgment is difficult and ambiguous for you, between blood and blood, case and case, leprosy and non-leprosy, and you see the words of the judges within your gates differing, arise and go up to the place which the Lord your God will have chosen. You shall come to the priests of the Levitical race and to the judge who shall be in office at that time; and, seeking from them, they shall show you the truth of the judgment. You shall do whatever those who preside over the place which the Lord has chosen shall say and teach you according to his law; you shall follow their decision and shall not turn aside to the right or to the left. But whoever grows proud and refuses to obey the command of the priest who at that time ministers to the Lord your God, and the decree of the judge—that man shall die; and you shall remove the evil from Israel. And all the people, hearing this, shall fear, so that no one thereafter may swell with pride.” (Deuteronomy XVII, 8–13)

Through the priests the Lord says:

> “And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Take hold of discipline, lest at any time the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way.” (Psalm II, 10–12)

And apostolic authority admonishes that kings also obey their superiors in the Lord, who keep watch over their souls, so that they may not do this with sorrow (Hebrews XIII).

And blessed Pope Gelasius writes to the emperor Anastasius (Letter 10):

> “Since there are two persons by whom this world is principally governed—namely, pontifical authority and royal dignity—and the burden of the pontiffs is so much greater because they will also render an account to the Lord concerning the kings themselves.”

Ambrose separated the emperor Theodosius from the Church when his offenses required it, and brought him back through repentance. In our own time, after the pious Augustus Louis had been driven from the kingdom, the unanimous body of the bishops, with sounder counsel and with the consent of the people, restored him to both Church and kingdom after his satisfaction.

The statement that a king is subject to no laws or judgments except those of God is true if the king is such as his name signifies. For “king” is derived from “to rule”; and if he rules himself according to the will of God, directs the good along the right way, and corrects the wicked from the crooked path to the straight, then he is a king and is subject to no laws or judgments except those of God. For there may be what are called decisions, but laws are only those which belong to God, through whom kings reign and lawgivers decree what is just.

And whoever is truly a king is not subject to the law, because the law was not established for the righteous but for the unrighteous and the disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the wicked and the defiled, for parricides and matricides, murderers, fornicators, male prostitutes, kidnappers, liars, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine, and for those who serve the works of the flesh. Of these the Apostle says:

> “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, lust, the service of idols, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murder, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you, that those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God.” (Galatians V, 19–21)

But whoever rules himself and others according to the fruits of the Spirit—which are charity, joy, peace, long-suffering, patience, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, and chastity—is not subject to the law, because against such things there is no law (ibid., 22–23). He is subject only to the judgment of Christ, from whom he will also receive his reward—Christ whose servant is the one who crucifies his flesh with its vices and desires.

Otherwise, any adulterer, murderer, unjust person, robber, or anyone liable to other vices will be judged, secretly or publicly, by the priests, who are the thrones of God, in whom God sits and through whom he pronounces his judgments. To them, as also to his apostles, whose place they occupy in the Church, the Lord said:

> “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others; but if he does not listen to them either, tell the Church. And if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector.” (Matthew XVIII, 15–16)

And lest anyone despise the priest in this matter, the Lord added:

> “Amen I say to you: whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” (ibid., 18)

And again he says:

> “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.” (Luke X, 16)

As for the statement that he could have been established by God alone in the kingdom which his father left him, let those who say this know that some are established by God in authority, such as Moses, Samuel, and Josiah, of whom it was written before he was born:

> “Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David; Josiah shall be his name.” (I Kings XIII, 2)

—and the rest that follows there.

Some are established by God through a human being, such as Joshua and David. Others are established through a human being, though not without divine providence, because nothing happens—as Augustine says—unless God either does it himself or permits it to happen; and whatever is done is done through the ministry of angels and human beings. Thus Solomon was established at the command of his father David through Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet (I Kings I).

Many kings are established in authority or cast down from it with the support of citizens or soldiers, and even holy men, as happened with Samuel (I Samuel VIII). Some reign by paternal succession, as is found concerning all these matters in histories and chronicles, and also in the book entitled *The Lives of the Caesars*. Some obtain authority by tyrannical usurpation, either to complete their own purposes or to avenge the sins of the people. Concerning them it is written:

> “They have made kings, but not from me; they have appointed princes, and I did not know it.” (Hosea VIII, 4)

And again:

> “He makes the hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people.” (Job XXXIV, 30)

This is like the saying, “It is necessary that scandals come, but woe to the person through whom the scandal comes.” For woe belongs to him because, although the event must occur, he makes himself by his own vice the kind of person through whom what belongs to that woe is carried out.

As for the statement that the kingdom was left to him by his father, this king ought rather to fear divine judgments and be ashamed before human judgments than perhaps glory in the acquisition of the kingdom—if, that is, he has not imitated his father’s good morals, holy life, and equitable and just rule, or if, God forbid, he has chosen to follow his father’s evil morals, unjust life—which we do not say that his father possessed—or unworthy rule.

For what did the sons of Samuel gain from their parent’s dignity, when they were not heirs of his virtue? What did the children of Moses gain from their father’s care for justice, when they did not inherit his imitation? Therefore paternal power is not transferred to those who marked him as their father in name only; rather, it passed to the one who was his son in virtue, not in lineage. This too he ought to fear.

Conversely, is Timothy thought to have been harmed because his father was a gentile? Holy Abraham also had an impious father, yet he did not thereby become heir to his impiety. Hezekiah was the son of the utterly profane Ahaz, yet he merited becoming a friend of God.

And what, by contrast, did the son of Noah gain from his father’s virtue, when from a freeborn man he became a slave? Joseph once served in the midst of Egypt, yet he wove for himself a glorious crown of chastity. The three boys and Daniel in Babylon were higher than its princes. We certainly see how paternal nobility is insufficient as a support for children. Vices overcame the privileges of nature and drove the sinner not only from his father’s nobility but even from liberty itself.

Was not Esau also the son of the holy Isaac, and strongly supported by his father’s favor? Although Isaac was eager and desirous to give him the blessing—and Esau therefore did everything his father commanded—yet because he had evil morals, he received no help at all from these things. Though first according to the order of nature and more secure in his father’s will, because he displeased God he lost everything that he already seemed to possess.

Let every king, and this king also, attend to this, and let him not gladly do everything that pleases him, because not everything that is permitted is expedient. And according to what is written:

> “Let the great men humble their heads in honor of the King of kings, whose is the kingdom and through whom kings reign.” (Ecclesiasticus IV; Proverbs VIII)

He says:

> “Those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be held of no account.” (I Samuel II, 30)

And to his priests he says:

> “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.” (Luke IX and X)

Finally, the scriptural example, “The heart of the king is in the hand of God; wherever he wishes, he will turn it” (Proverbs XXI, 1), which he interpreted to confirm that whatever the king does, and whatever sort of ruler he is among the people, occurs by divine providence—this man interpreted wrongly, just as the devil misused the words “He has commanded his angels concerning you” (Matthew IV, 6) before the Savior. He is the devil’s disciple in this interpretation.

But the heart of the king is in God’s hand because, as we showed above, he is truly a king who has governed himself and his thoughts, words, and deeds under divine direction. His heart is in God’s hand so that in this valley of tears he may set the ascent in his heart, walking from virtue to virtue until God is seen in Zion—that is, in the contemplation of eternal happiness and the divine vision.

Conversely, the heart of the person who is badly ruled by the devil as its rider is in the devil’s power, to such an extent that if he hears anything of God’s commandments, the devil himself comes and takes the word from his heart, lest, by believing or persevering in the practice of what he had believed, he should be able to be saved. Thus, having been handed over to a reprobate mind, he does what is unfitting, because although he has known God, he has not honored him with the worthy service due to God.

Concerning the statement that, because he is king, if he does not wish to come to the synod he may freely depart even when summoned, Holy Scripture and the sacred canons show that a judgment must not accept persons but must discern the quality of the case.

And Hucbertus, after being marked out by a definite crime committed against his sister and summoned to the synod by synodal letters, offered his presence in three synods through envoys and letters, so that he might render an account, provided only that he could come with the assurance that justice would be preserved for him. But the accuser and prosecutor of the crime was repeatedly absent or refused the freedom to give an account.

Therefore Pope Boniface writes to the Gallican bishops (Letter 11):

> “He proves that the things said against him are true who is wholly unwilling to be present to refute them. And no one doubts that the guilty person flees judgment in the same way that the innocent person seeks to be acquitted. For each person confesses everything when he thinks that he can evade judgment by delays. Therefore we have decreed that a synod be assembled, so that, if he wishes to be present, he may answer the charges in person if he has confidence; but if he neglects to appear, he shall gain no postponement of the sentence. For it makes no difference whether all that has been said is proved in the present examination, since his repeated absence, procured as it has been, is itself evident as a confession.” (ibid.)

## QUESTION VII

And since some learned men say what we have described, is there any danger arising from this for the bishops and for the other Christians who communicate with him while he persists in adultery? Or, if there is danger, how will they be free before the Lord from the danger of such communion?

## RESPONSE

It is written:

> “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.” (James V, 20)

Conversely, therefore, for as many people as someone destroys by the example of his depravity, he will be condemned for that many unless he repents worthily.

For this reason the person who repents publicly performs public penance—not because the Lord does not grant pardon, even for serious sins, to one who repents worthily through secret confession and private penance. David also repented before the one who rebuked him by the Lord’s authority, confessed, and merited the forgiveness of his sin, although afterward he endured its public punishment.

But whoever has destroyed many by his evil example should build up many for salvation through the penance of his humility, so that, just as it is said of Paul (Acts IX), those who had previously seen him persecuting the Church and afterward building it up might glorify the Lord in him.

A person who sins publicly and refuses to return to penance is therefore cast out from fellowship with the Church by public excommunication at the hands of the bishops—not because he is no longer excommunicated before the one who promulgated the ecclesiastical laws by speaking through his Spirit, but because the priests, successors of the apostles and apostolic men, perform their duty lest they be thought by their subjects to neglect their ministry. Just as the sinner’s guilt has become known, so also the rebuke of the one who corrects must become known to all.

Then the person who otherwise refuses to understand his sin may, because he is rejected by everyone and received by no one—since good things are often imposed even upon the unwilling—or may, compelled, return to penance; necessity may be turned into devotion; and the one who sinned through pride may, corrected through humility, merit incorporation into the Church through priestly reconciliation.

All kings and princes of the world must also attend to this: an evil prince and king, however many he rules in this world, will suffer proportionately many blows as punishment in the condemnation of the flames. It is therefore necessary that he examine his deeds without ceasing. When he destroys others by his example, he must fear, because the person who kills many through the example of his depravity does not perish alone; for them he will undoubtedly render an account to the Lord.

And he sins not only through himself but also through those who imitate him or transgress because of his example or authority; indeed, he sins more abundantly, especially when, as though he were sinning lawfully, he becomes an incentive for others to sin.

Therefore, speaking of another matter, the Apostle says:

> “Take care lest your freedom become a stumbling-block to the weak.” (I Corinthians VIII, 9)

And again:

> “The weak person will perish through your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, by sinning against your brothers and striking their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.” (ibid., 11–12)

And the Lord says:

> “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be cast into the depth of the sea.” (Matthew XVIII, 6)

For it would certainly have been better for such a person to spend his life in private than, placed in authority, to show himself to the rest as someone whose sin might be imitated, and to pay the penalties corresponding to the number of people whom, by sinning as though lawfully, he leads and authorizes into vices and error.

His guilt is all the heavier and his torment will be all the more severe the freer his power has been. No one sins more greatly against peoples than the person who acts perversely and usurps the order of authority. No one dares to rebuke him when he is sinning, and the example of his guilt is greatly extended when, out of reverence for his authority, the sinner is honored.

And so that he may grant honors and benefits to flatterers, the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, the person who acts unjustly is blessed, and the dead man is buried by the dead in the worst death, because it is written:

> “You saw a thief, and you ran with him; and you placed your portion with adulterers.” (Psalm XLIX, 18)

He runs with the thief and places his portion with him when someone joins himself to him either in adulterous praise or in pleasures shared by consent. He places in hell with him the portion which he ought to have with God and the angels. His mouth abounded in wickedness and his tongue fashioned deceit (Psalm XLIX, 19): when the other acted wickedly and deceitfully, he praised him, or gave consent to his evil deeds, because not only those who do such things but also those who consent to those who do them are worthy of death (Romans I, 32).

Thus Saint Ambrose says:

> “When he sees himself honored by those who are not such people, he grows in evil and perhaps glories in being such; therefore it is right that both should be punished with one penalty. But the person who judges and does such things, as Paul himself says, will not escape the judgment of God. He will be judged by himself, before whom flattery and partiality cease.” (Romans II)

Saint Augustine gives us the following counsel for avoiding this danger of communion (Sermon 18, *On the Words of the Lord*):

> “A wicked person does not defile you in two ways: if you do not consent and if you rebuke him—that is, do not communicate and do not consent. One communicates when one adds to his deed a partnership of will or approval. Therefore, warning us, the Apostle says: ‘Do not communicate in the unfruitful works of darkness’ (Ephesians V, 11). And because it would have been little merely not to consent if negligence of discipline followed, he adds: ‘But rather rebuke them’ (ibid.). See how he embraces both: ‘Do not communicate, but rather rebuke them.’ What does ‘do not communicate’ mean? Do not consent, do not praise, do not approve. What does ‘but rather rebuke them’ mean? Reprove, correct, restrain.
>
> “Then, in the rebuke or restraint of the sins of others, one must beware lest the person who rebukes another become exalted, and the person who thinks he stands see that he does not fall. Let rebuke resound terribly outside, but let love of gentleness be preserved within. Therefore do not be consenting to the wicked, so as to approve them; do not be negligent, so as not to rebuke them; and do not be proud, so as to rebuke them insultingly.”

And Saint Gregory, in his letter to Felix, bishop of Sicily, gives this instruction to all bishops (Book XII, Letter 32):

> “The wicked must be separated from the good, and the unjust from the just, so that at least through their shame they may recognize their consciences and turn from their depravity; and if they appear incorrigible, they must be separated from the faithful until satisfaction, according to the sentence of the Lord our Savior, who among other things commanded concerning a brother who sins against one:

> “‘If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. If he does not listen to them, tell the Church. But if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector.’” (Matthew XVIII, 15–17)

Therefore, by these and many other authorities of the holy Fathers, the wicked must be separated from the good, lest the just perish for the unjust, as it is written:

> “The just person perishes for the wicked.” (Ecclesiastes VII, 16)

There must always be discernment between good and evil, just as there is between goats and sheep. Manifest sins must not be cleansed by hidden correction; rather, those who do harm openly must be rebuked openly, so that, while they are healed by public reprimand, those who have sinned by imitating them may be corrected. When one person is rebuked, many are amended. It is better that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through the license of one.

Nor is it surprising that this rule is observed among human beings, since we know that it is often observed even among animals. Those that appear to have mange or a skin disease are separated from the healthy, lest the others be condemned or perish through their disease. It is better that the wicked be corrected openly than that the good perish because of them.

Therefore we wish you all, bishops, to assemble together, so that discussion may be held concerning cases that arise and a wholesome conference may take place concerning ecclesiastical observance. Thus, while past matters are corrected through this process and future matters receive a rule, the omnipotent Lord may everywhere be praised through the harmony of the brothers. Know that his presence is with you if you observe these things, because it is written:

> “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.” (Matthew XVIII, 20)

If, then, he deigns to be present where there are two or three, how much more will he not be absent where more priests assemble? It is certainly not unknown that the rules have established that a council of the Fathers should be held twice a year. But lest there perhaps be some excuse, we decree that they assemble once, so that, while a council is expected, nothing wicked and nothing unlawful may be presumed. For many people, even if not out of love of justice, refrain from what everyone knows can displease the judgment because they fear examination.”

And Saint Ambrose says in his letter to the emperor Theodosius:

> “I am always occupied, most blessed emperor, with duties and almost continual anxieties. But I have never been in such heat as now, when I see that I must beware lest anything be attributed to me even concerning the danger of sacrilege. Therefore I ask you to hear my speech patiently. For if I am unworthy to be heard by you, I am unworthy to offer on your behalf, to whom you entrust your vows and to whom you entrust your prayers. Will you yourself not hear the person whom you wish to be heard on your behalf? Will you not hear one acting for himself, whom you have heard on behalf of others? And do you not fear your own judgment, lest, when you consider someone unworthy to hear, you make him unworthy to be heard on your behalf?
>
> “Nor is it imperial to deny freedom of speech, nor priestly not to say what one thinks. Nothing is so popular or so beloved in you emperors as to love freedom even in those who are subject to you through military service. For this distinguishes good and bad rulers: the good love freedom, the wicked slavery.
>
> “Nothing is so dangerous for a priest before God, or so shameful before human beings, as not to proclaim freely what he thinks. For it is written: ‘I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed’ (Psalm CXVIII, 46). And elsewhere: ‘Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel.’ He says that if the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits an offense, because you did not distinguish it for him—that is, because you did not say what must be avoided—his righteousness will not be remembered, and I will require his blood from your hand. But if you warn the righteous person not to sin and he does not sin, he will live by his life because you warned him, and you will free your own soul (Ezekiel III, 17–19).
>
> “Therefore, emperor, I would rather that you be with me among the good than among the wicked. For this reason the silence of a priest ought to displease your clemency, while freedom should please you. You are endangered by the fault of my silence, but helped by the good of my freedom.
>
> “I do not intrude upon you improperly or thrust myself into matters belonging to others; rather, I obey what is owed and obey the commands of our God. I do this first out of love for you, for your sake, and with concern to preserve your salvation. If this is either not believed or forbidden to me, I speak plainly out of fear of divine displeasure. For if my danger could strip you of yours, I would offer myself patiently for you, but not gladly. I would rather that you be acceptable to God and glorious without danger to me.
>
> “But if the fault of my silence and concealment burdens me without freeing you, I would rather that you judge me too intrusive than useless or shameful. For it is written by the holy Apostle Paul, whose teaching you cannot refute: ‘Be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and teaching’ (II Timothy IV, 2).
>
> “We too have someone whom it is more dangerous to displease—especially since emperors do not dislike each person’s performing his own duty, and you patiently hear each person making suggestions according to his office; indeed, you rebuke him if he does not follow the order of his service. What you gladly accept from those who serve you—can this seem burdensome in priests, when we speak not what we wish but what we are commanded?
>
> “For you have read: ‘When you stand before kings and governors, do not think about what you will say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matthew X, 19). Yet if I speak in matters of the state, although justice must also be preserved there, I would not be bound by so great a fear if I were not heard. But in God’s cause, whom will you hear if you do not hear the priest? Whose greater danger is involved in sin?
>
> “Who will dare tell you the truth if a priest does not dare? I know that you are devout, merciful, gentle, and tranquil, and that you hold faith and fear of the Lord in your heart; but many things often deceive us. Some have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. Therefore I think we must beware lest this also creep into faithful hearts.
>
> “I know your devotion toward God and your gentleness toward human beings. I am bound by the benefits of your indulgence, and therefore I fear more. I am even more anxious lest you later condemn me by your own judgment because you did not avoid falling through my concealment or flattery. If I saw someone sinning against me, I ought not to remain silent. For it is written: ‘If your brother sins against you, rebuke him first, then rebuke him before two or three witnesses. If he does not listen to you, tell the Church’ (Matthew XVIII, 16–17). Shall I therefore be silent concerning God’s cause?”

And in another passage he says:

> “I certainly did what could be done most honorably, so that you might hear me more readily in the palace, lest, if it became necessary, you should hear me in the Church.”

And again, in another letter to the same emperor, he says:

> “I would remain silent, but—what would be the most miserable thing of all?—my conscience would be bound and my voice taken away. And where would be the saying: ‘If the priest does not declare to the one who has gone astray that he has gone astray, he will die in his own guilt, and the priest will be liable to punishment because he did not warn the one who had gone astray’?”

And again, in another passage:

> “Something happened in the city of the Thessalonians that no memory can contain, which I was unable to prevent from happening—or rather, which I considered would be most atrocious beforehand, when I pleaded so many times—and which you yourself considered a grave deed when you recalled it. I could not diminish the seriousness of this deed when it was first heard, because a synod had assembled on account of the arrival of the Gallican bishops. Everyone groaned; no one received the matter lightly.
>
> “The absolution of your deed did not lie in communion with Ambrose; rather, the odium of the deed would be increased if no one said that reconciliation with our God was necessary. Are you ashamed, emperor, to do what King David, prophet and ancestor of Christ according to the flesh, did? When he realized that he himself had been rebuked in the parable, he said: ‘I have sinned against the Lord’ (II Samuel XII, 13).
>
> “Therefore, emperor, do not bear impatiently the words spoken to you: ‘You did this,’ which the prophet spoke to King David. For if you listen carefully and say, ‘I have sinned against the Lord’; if you also say the prophetic words, ‘Come, let us adore and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us’ (Psalm XCIV, 6), then it will also be said to you: Because you repent, the Lord will forgive your sin, and you will not die.”

And again, in another passage:

> “Therefore the Lord repented and commanded the angel to spare the people, while David offered sacrifice. At that time there were sacrifices for sins, and now there are sacrifices of repentance. Thus the king became more acceptable to God through that humility. For it is not surprising that a human being sins; what is blameworthy is that he does not recognize that he has gone astray, that he does not humble himself before God.
>
> “The holy Job, himself powerful in this world, says: ‘I did not conceal my sin, but I proclaimed it before all the people’ (Job XXXI, 33).”

And again, in another passage:

> “I have written these things not to shame you, but so that the examples of kings may urge you to remove this sin from your kingdom. You will remove it by humbling your soul before God. You are a human being, and temptation has come to you; conquer it. Sin is removed only by tears and repentance. Neither an angel nor an archangel can remove it; only the Lord can, who alone can say, ‘I am he who blots out your iniquities’ (Isaiah XLIII, 25). If we sin, he does not forgive us unless we bring repentance.”

And again, in another passage:

> “Conquer the devil while you still have the means by which you can conquer. Do not add sin to sin by usurping what, when usurped, has harmed many.”

And shortly afterward:

> “I have no accusation of obstinacy against you, but I do have fear. I do not dare to offer the sacrifice if you wish to be present. Finally, I write with my own hand what you alone are to read. May the Lord free me from all tribulations, because I have clearly perceived that I was forbidden—not by a human being or through a human being, but openly.
>
> “For, when I was anxious on the very night when I was preparing to set out to you, as you had requested, you seemed to come to the Church; but I was not permitted to offer the sacrifice to you. I pass over other matters which I could have kept silent about but endured, as I think, out of love for you. May the Lord bring everything to a peaceful conclusion.”

He warns us about these matters in many ways through heavenly signs, the commands of the prophets, and even visions within our hearts. He wants us to understand that we should ask him to remove disturbances, preserve peace for you who rule, and ensure that the faith and tranquility of the Church endure—for it is beneficial that emperors be Christian and devout.

Certainly you wish to be approved by God. There is a time for everything, as it is written: “A time to act, O Lord” (Ecclesiastes III, 1); and, “It is the time of favor, O God” (Psalm CXVIII, 126). You will offer sacrifice when you have received the opportunity to offer it, when your offering is acceptable to God.

I would certainly be pleased to have the emperor’s favor, so that I might act according to your will, if the case permitted it. And a simple prayer is also a sacrifice: this brings forgiveness, while the other brings offense; for this contains humility, while the other contains contempt. It is God’s own saying that he prefers his command to be carried out rather than sacrifice to be offered. God cries this out to the people, Moses announces it, and the Apostle Paul preaches it.

Do what you understand to be more pleasing at the proper time. He says:

> “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice.” (Matthew IX, 13)

As though those who condemn their sin were not more Christian than those who think it must be defended. For the righteous person is an accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech (Proverbs XVIII, 17). Whoever accuses himself when he has sinned is righteous, not the person who praises himself.

You were forewarned, and I did not turn aside from what I ought to have guarded against. But thanks be to the Lord, because he wishes to chastise his little servants lest he destroy them. This is something I share with the prophets, and it will be something you share with the saints.

How, moreover, that same blessed emperor, publicly doing penance, obeyed these admonitions, the same blessed Ambrose demonstrates, among other things, in the Sermon on the fortieth day after his death, in the presence of his son, the Emperor Honorius. How also other Christians and faithful people of God may escape the danger of association of this kind, the Lord demonstrates in the Gospel concerning the person who, having been rebuked for his sin, refuses to amend (Matt. XVIII), and Paul says in the Epistle to the Corinthians:

“Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 9–10).

And again:

“Now I have written to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother but is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or is a slanderer, or drunkard, or robber; with such a person, not even to take food. Remove the evil person from among you” (I Cor. V, 11 and 13).

And Saint John the Evangelist and Apostle says:

“And now there are many antichrists” (I John II, 18).

And again:

“Everyone who withdraws and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in the teaching has both the Son and the Father. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house, nor say ‘Hail’ to him; for whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (II John 9–11).

And lest anyone say, “He is a king; how can I withdraw myself from association with him?” let him know that Saint John the Baptist was crowned with martyrdom for this reason: because he said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have her” (Mark VI, 18)—namely, an adulterous woman. And Paul, as we have already stated, forbade taking food with such a person; he also says elsewhere:

“Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII, 3).

And the Lord himself cries out in the Gospel:

“Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason you do not hear is that you are not of God” (John VIII, 47).

And again:

“If you love me, keep my commandments. Whoever does not love me does not keep my commandments” (John XIV, 15 and 24).

And the apostle John says:

“Whoever says, ‘I love God,’ and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (I John IV, 20).

And the Psalm says of the Lord:

“You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. V, 7).

And again the apostle John says in the Apocalypse:

“Nor will anything defiled enter it”—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem—“or anyone who practices abomination and falsehood” (Apoc. XXI, 27).

And again:

“But for the timid, the unbelieving, the accursed, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the pool burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death” (ibid., 8).

The terrible Gospel rebuke also assails those who loved the glory of men more than that of God (John XII, 43), and who rebuke and persecute those who wish to withdraw themselves from every brother who walks disorderly. Concerning such persecutors it is said in the Apocalypse:

“I have this against you: you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants to fornicate and to eat food sacrificed to idols. [Col. 0767B] And I gave her time to repent, but she does not wish to repent of her fornication. Behold, I cast her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great tribulation, unless they repent of their works; and I will strike her children with death. And all the churches will know that I am the one who searches the kidneys and hearts, and I will give to each according to his works” (Apoc. II, 20–23).

But those who rebuke iniquity because they do not consent to such things, he gently consoles, saying:

“I know your tribulation and your poverty—but you are rich—and you are blasphemed by those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan. Fear none of those things which you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, that you may be tested; and you will have tribulation for ten days. Be [Col. 0767C] faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. Whoever conquers will not be harmed by the second death” (ibid., 9–10).

But to those who, because of the authority of their rank, the dignity of their power, or the strength of their virtue, cannot resist such conduct, divine mercy gives this counsel in the same Apocalypse:

“But I say to the rest of you who are in Thyatira: whoever does not hold this teaching, who has not known the depths of Satan, as they say, I will not lay upon you any other burden. Nevertheless, hold fast what you have until I come.
