And whoever conquers and keeps my works to the end, I will give him authority over the nations, and he will rule them with an iron rod; they will be broken like a potter’s vessel, just as I too have received from my Father. And I will give him the morning star” (ibid., 24–28).

And Saint Ambrose says in his Epistle to the Corinthians:

“If anyone does not have the authority to cast out someone whom he knows to be guilty, or is unable to establish the charge, he is free from guilt. It is not the judge’s role to condemn without an accuser, because the Lord himself did not cast out Judas, although he was a thief, since he had not been accused. Priests, rulers, and the leading men of the earth will not be able to claim this excuse before God.” [Col. 0767D]

Hence the same blessed Ambrose says in the same place in the Epistle:

“And you are puffed up, and did not rather mourn, so that the one who committed this deed might be removed from your midst” (I Cor. V, 2).

“He so humbles their pride,” he says, “that he makes them no longer complainants but rather suppliants. For they too were participants, since they allowed the guilty man, responsible for so great a crime, to associate with them without correction; they should all, by common agreement, have expelled him if he refused to amend. Once this deed had become known, the Apostle says that he ought to be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. For they all knew his crime but did not rebuke him: publicly he had his stepmother in the place of a wife. In this matter there was no need of witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion. ‘Although absent in body, but present in spirit’—that is, absent in person but present by the authority of the Spirit, who is absent nowhere—‘I have already judged, as though present, the one who committed this deed’ (ibid., 3).”

Here it must be observed that whoever has committed criminal sins, for which judgment has already been concluded by those instruments of Christ who reign with him in heaven and shine forth on earth through miracles—whose bodies are dead ashes by nature but who are shown to be alive to God through the miracles of their merits, since they also live in their sayings and promulgations—has already been judged and, unless he has repented, condemned in advance. This is so even though, through our negligence, we fail to carry out, at the peril of ourselves and of those entrusted to us, the duties to which we have been ordered and appointed.

Therefore the great Pope Leo, writing to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, concerning the holy Council of Nicaea—a teaching which the Catholic faith holds should also be understood of other matters—writes (Epistle 56):

“Those holy and venerable Fathers who, in the city of Nicaea, after the sacrilegious Arius had been condemned together with his impiety, established laws of ecclesiastical canons destined to remain until the end of the world: they live among us and throughout the whole world in their constitutions. If anywhere anything is presumed contrary to what they decreed, it is cancelled without hesitation, so that what has been established generally for perpetual usefulness may not be altered by any change, nor may what has been prescribed for the common good be diverted to private advantage.” [Col. 0768C]

Having finally considered these matters, and others which, because of their length, we have omitted to set down, and having taken into account the authorities of the holy Scriptures and ecclesiastical rules, as well as each person’s own danger—and also that of the person under discussion—let each one return to himself. Let him either clearly demonstrate that his conduct agrees with reason and authority, lest, while himself sinning, he make others sin, as Scripture says of Jeroboam (III Kings XII), thereby offending God more grievously; or let him submit himself to salutary counsel and divine authority, since he cannot otherwise be saved.

Let him consider that youth and vain pleasure are fleeting, and that, for a brief and wretched delight, since the price of a prostitute is scarcely a loaf of bread (Prov. VI, 26), he should not give his honor to strangers, nor his years to the cruel one; nor should he give his flesh so as to make his soul sin, nor present his members as weapons of iniquity to sin (Rom. VI, 13). Let him groan in the end, when he has consumed his flesh and body, when he can no longer amend, since the soul will be compelled to repay everything it has done through the body.

Thus, reflecting on his ways and turning his feet toward the testimonies of the Lord, let him make satisfaction to the Lord and the Church for the wrongs he has committed through worthy fruits of repentance, and thereafter direct his steps according to the utterances of the Lord, by his grace, so that no iniquity may rule over him (Ps. CXVIII, 133). Let him imitate the converted Paul, who says of himself, “And in me they glorified God” (Acts IX), just as the Lord commands:

“Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

Finally, concerning the matters which we have said in this letter had come to our attention, we have expressed, as far as our limited ability permits, what we have understood through the inspiration of the Lord from the teaching of the holy Scriptures and the Catholic Fathers, compelled by truth and by the ministry imposed upon us. We prejudice no sound judgment, nor do we dishonor authority.

“For none of us,” as Saint Cyprian once said (Council of Carthage I), “has constituted himself bishop of bishops, or compelled his colleagues by tyrannical terror to obey, since every bishop—while in all things preserving the privilege of the holy and apostolic primatial See of Rome throughout the whole world, and of that pontiff, Lord Pope Nicholas, as well as the decree of the holy canons composed by the Holy Spirit—has, by the license of his own freedom and power, his own judgment, both in that he cannot be judged by another and in that he cannot himself singly judge another. Rather, as the Apostle says (Rom. XIV), let each one abound in his own understanding, and let us all await the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone has the power both to appoint us over the governance of his Church and to judge our conduct.” [Col. 0769B]

This alone we admonish all our lords and fellow priests, and ourselves together with them: according to the instruction of Pope Leo the Great to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Epistle 95):

“In matters that are doubtful or obscure, let us know that we must follow what is found to be contrary neither to the Gospel commandments nor to the decrees of the saints.”

Moreover, because our Redeemer, who graciously willed to become both king and priest for us—priest, namely, so that he might cleanse us from sins by the offering of his passion; king, so that he might grant us an everlasting kingdom and make us a kingdom and priests for God—and because he alone could become both in dignity and in name, essentially king and priest, he established, by his providence, two offices by which, as Saint Gelasius wrote to the Emperor Anastasius, this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power.

The burden of priests is so much heavier because they will also render an account before the divine tribunal for the kings themselves. Therefore, concerning these two persons of the most excellent dignities, we have thought it fitting to append to this little work the judgments of the blessed Cyprian, pontiff and glorious martyr, so that, attending to the form of their name, they may, insofar as human frailty permits, deviate in nothing from the rule of the dignity handed down to them by that pontiff of pontiffs and king of kings.

For in the book *On the Twelve Abuses of the World* he speaks first about the king and afterward about the bishop, since the higher the rank, the graver the fall, and the more spiritual the dignity, the higher the ascent.

“He says (chapter 9): ‘The ninth degree of abuse is an unjust king. For a king ought not to be unjust, but a corrector of the unjust; therefore he must preserve in himself the dignity of his name. For the name “king,” understood according to its meaning, signifies that he should provide the office of ruler for all his subjects. But how will he be able to correct others who does not correct his own conduct so that it may not be unjust? For the throne of the king is exalted by justice, and the government of peoples is made firm by truth.

‘The justice of a king is not to oppress anyone unjustly through power; to judge without partiality between one man and his neighbor; to be a defender of strangers, orphans, and widows; to restrain thefts; to punish adulteries; not to exalt the unjust; not to support the immodest and the actors; to destroy the impious from the land; not to permit parricides and perjurers to live; to defend churches; to nourish the poor by alms; to place just men over the affairs of the kingdom; to have as counselors old, wise, and sober men; not to heed the superstitions of magicians, diviners, and prophetesses; to postpone anger; to defend his homeland bravely and justly against its enemies; to live entirely in God; not to lift his spirit up in prosperity; to endure every adversity patiently; to have Catholic faith in God; not to permit his sons to act impiously; to devote himself to prayers at appointed hours; and not to taste food before the proper hours.

‘Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning’ (Eccl. X, 16). These things bring prosperity to the kingdom in the present life [Col. 0770C] and lead the king to the better kingdoms of heaven.

‘But whoever does not govern according to this law will certainly endure many adversities in his empire. For this reason the peace of peoples is often broken, disturbances are also stirred up against the kingdom, the fruits of the earth are diminished, and the services of the peoples are obstructed. Many afflictions also poison the prosperity of the kingdom; the deaths of dear ones and children bring sadness; attacks by enemies ravage the provinces on every side; wild beasts tear apart the herds of cattle and flocks of sheep; storms of spring and winter hinder the fertility of the land and the services of the sea; and sometimes strokes of lightning burn the crops, the blossoms of trees, and the vine-shoots.

‘Above all, the injustice of the king not only darkens the appearance of the present empire, but also obscures his sons and grandsons, so that they may not possess the inheritance of the kingdom after him. For because of Solomon’s guilt the Lord scattered the kingdom of the house of Israel from the hands of his sons, while because of the justice of King David he left a lamp from his seed always in Jerusalem (III Kings XI, 15).

‘Behold how much the justice of a king benefits the world: it is plainly evident to those who observe it. The peace of peoples is the protection of the homeland, the security of the common people, the defense of the nation, care for the sick, the joy of human beings, a temperate atmosphere, calm seas, the fertility of the land, consolation for the poor, an inheritance for children, and for themselves the hope of future blessedness.

‘Nevertheless, let the king know that, just as he has been established first on the throne of human beings, so, if he has not practiced justice, he will also hold the place of primacy in punishments. For all the sinners whom he had beneath him in the present life, he will then have above him in that future punishment, in a manner of chastisement.’” [Col. 0771A]

“Chapter 10. ‘The tenth degree of abuse is a negligent bishop, who seeks the honor of his rank among human beings but does not preserve the dignity of his ministry before God, for whom he serves as ambassador.

‘First, the bishop must inquire what the dignity of his name signifies. Since “bishop” is a Greek name, it is interpreted as “overseer.” Why, then, is an overseer appointed, and what is required of an overseer? The Lord himself discloses this when, under the person of the prophet Ezekiel, he declares the account of his office to the bishop, saying:

“I have appointed you as an overseer for the house of Israel. Hearing a word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them on my behalf. But if you see the sword coming and do not announce that the wicked should turn back from his way, that wicked man will indeed die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you announce it and he does not turn back, he will indeed die in his iniquity, but you will have saved your own soul” (Ezek. III, 17–19).

‘It is therefore fitting that the bishop, appointed as the overseer of all, attend carefully to sins. After hearing and observing, he should correct by word and deed if he can; and if he cannot, then, according to the rule of the Gospel, he should avoid workers of wickedness.

‘For the Gospel says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother. If he does not hear you, take with you one or two more, so that by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand. If he does not hear them, tell the Church. If he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. XVIII, 15–17).

‘A person who refuses to adhere to any such teacher or bishop must be expelled according to this order. And one who has been expelled according to this order must not be received by another teacher or bishop. Therefore whoever joins himself to one excommunicated by a Catholic, without that Catholic’s permission, transgresses the laws of the holy priesthood, which is the chosen race of Christians.

‘For this reason the bishop must be such toward those over whom he has been appointed as overseer. But what he ought to be in himself is written in the law concerning the priest: “He shall not take a widow or a divorced woman as wife” (Lev. XXI, 7).

‘The apostle Paul further explains that the one who comes to the rank of bishop must be sober, prudent, chaste, wise, modest, and hospitable; having children subject to him with complete chastity; having a good testimony from those outside; proclaiming the faithful word of doctrine; before becoming a bishop, having no more than one wife; not violent, not double-tongued, not drunk, and not a recent convert, so that by these qualities he may first show in his conduct what he teaches others in the word of doctrine (I Tim. III, 2–7).

‘Let negligent bishops therefore beware of what the Lord complains through the prophet at the time of vengeance: “Many shepherds have destroyed my people” (Jer. XII), and “the shepherds did not feed my flock, but fed themselves” (Ezek. XXXIV).

‘Rather, let those whom the Lord has appointed over his household provide them with food at the proper time, a measure of wheat (Luke XII)—that is, pure and approved doctrine—so that, when the Lord comes, they may deserve to hear:

“Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your lord”’ (Matt. XXV, 23).”

Finally, two other abuses follow, which cannot be separated from the negligence and danger of these men: namely, a people without discipline, which clearly belongs to the guilt of the negligent bishop; and a people without law, which unquestionably belongs to the perversity of the unjust king.

The eight abuses that precede these two principal ones—namely, a wise man and preacher without works; an old man without religion; a young man without obedience; a rich man without almsgiving; a woman without modesty; a lord without virtue; a contentious Christian; and a proud poor man—are recognized as looking toward these two chapters, by which this world is principally governed, whether with praise and glory or with reproach and judgment. [Col. 0772C]

For episcopal authority, by preaching through life and word, and royal dignity, by governing and correcting, ought to preside over and benefit all who desire to follow and observe discipline—that is, ordered correction—and the regular observance of the rules handed down by their predecessors.

But the bishop ought, with a medicinal sword, to cut away from the healthy the polluted member, and the king, with a judicial sword, to destroy the impious from the land—those who despise divine pronouncements and the statutes of the laws—so that at the future and fearsome judgment they may deserve to hear from the supreme Shepherd and King of kings, together with the sheep and subjects entrusted to them, as good and faithful servants in the ministry in which they were appointed, found faithful by the Lord who appointed them:

“Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34),

which God, who does not lie, promised to those who love him, and who lives and reigns before all things, through all things, and in all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0773]

## The Synodal Chapters of Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims

### I. Chapters Given to Priests in the Year 852

[Col. 0773A]

In the year 852, on the Kalends of November, when an assembly of priests was held in the metropolitan city of Rheims, among the many salutary admonitions discussed by Hincmar, the bishop, concerning ecclesiastical laws and affairs, the following matters were brought forward at the end, to be committed to memory and observed with the utmost care.

### Chapter I. That Priests Should Learn the Explanation of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, etc., Together with the Creed of Athanasius

Let each priest learn more fully the explanation of the Creed and of the Lord’s Prayer, according to the tradition of the orthodox Fathers, and thereafter diligently instruct the people entrusted to him by preaching. Let him also understand the preface of the canon and the canon itself, and be able to recite them from memory and distinctly; let him be able to read the prayers of the Mass, as well as the Epistle and the Gospel correctly. Let him know how to pronounce the words and divisions of the Psalms regularly and by heart, together with the customary chants.

Let each priest also commit to memory the sermon of Athanasius on the faith, which begins, “Whoever wishes to be saved,” understand its meaning, and be able to express it in ordinary words.

### Chapter II. Concerning the Examination and Order of Baptizing

Let no one be permitted to be wholly ignorant of the examination and the entire order of baptism.

### Chapter III. Concerning the Exorcisms of Catechumens and the Baptism of the Sick; Also Concerning Fonts and Vessels for Washing the Corporal and Altar Cloths

Let him carefully commit to memory the exorcisms and prayers to be performed for catechumens, the consecration of the fonts, and the other prayers over males and females, in the plural and singular, distinctly and appropriately. Likewise, let him learn the order of baptizing for assisting the sick.

Whoever is unable to have stone fonts should have a suitable vessel reserved solely for the office of baptism. Similarly, separate vessels should be provided for washing the corporal and the altar cloths, and nothing else should be done in them.

### Chapter IV. Concerning the Order of Reconciling and Anointing the Sick; Concerning the Funeral Rites of the Dead and the Blessing of Salt and Water

Let him learn by heart the order of reconciliation, according to the manner canonically reserved to him, and of anointing the sick, together with the prayers appropriate to that need. Likewise, let him learn the order and prayers for funeral rites and the duties performed for the dead, and no less the exorcisms and blessings of water and salt.

### Chapter V. Concerning the Blessing of Water Every Sunday Before Mass

Let every priest, every Sunday in his own church before the solemnities of Mass, prepare holy water in a clean vessel suitable for so great a ministry. Let the people entering the church be sprinkled with it; and whoever wishes may take some from it in clean little vessels and sprinkle it through their dwellings, fields, and vineyards, as well as over their cattle and their fodder, and also over their food and drink.

### Chapter VI. Concerning the Thurible and Incense

Let every priest have a thurible and incense, so that at the time when the Gospel is read, and when the offertory has ended, he may place incense over the offering, as at the death of the Redeemer.

### Chapter VII. Concerning the Blessing of Bread for the Eulogies

From the offerings brought by the people and remaining after the consecration, or from the loaves which the faithful bring to the church, or certainly from his own bread, let the priest have appropriately cut pieces in a clean and suitable vessel, so that after the solemnities of Mass those who were not prepared to communicate may receive eulogies from it every Sunday and on feast days.

Before distributing the portion from which the priest is to give the eulogies, let him bless it in these words, and then distribute it to those who are to receive it; let him also take care that crumbs do not fall carelessly:

“Holy Lord, [Col. 0774C] Father, almighty and eternal God, deign to bless this bread with your holy and spiritual blessing, so that for all who receive it with faith, reverence, and thanksgiving to you, it may be salvation of mind and body and a protection against all diseases and every snare of all enemies. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, the bread of life, who descended from heaven and gives life and salvation to the world, and who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

### Chapter VIII. Concerning the Homilies of Saint Gregory, and Concerning Ecclesiastical Computation and Chant

Let every priest diligently read and understand the forty homilies of Gregory. Let him recognize that he has been advanced in ecclesiastical ministry according to the pattern of the seventy-two disciples, and let him learn fully and commit to memory the sermon of the aforesaid teacher concerning the seventy-two disciples sent by the Lord to preach.

Let him also be fully instructed in the necessary computation and in chant throughout the cycle of the year.

### Chapter IX. Concerning the Morning Office and the Completion of the Hours; What the Priest Should Do After Mass Before the Midday Meal

(Ivo, p. VI, 181, from the Council of Nantes, concerning the celebration of Masses, chapter 1, from the Council of Agde.)

After completing the morning office, let him discharge the duty of his service by singing Prime, Terce, Sext, and None; nevertheless, afterward, at the appropriate hours and as circumstances permit, let these be completed publicly either by himself or by the scholars.

Then, after completing the solemnities of Mass and visiting the sick who are exhausted, let him go fasting to rural work and to whatever pertains to him, so that he may again be able to assist travelers, guests, and various passers-by in their needs, as well as the sick and the dead, until the appointed hour, according to the season and the opportunity.

### Chapter X. Concerning Care for Guests and Travelers

(Ivo, p. V, 257, from the Council of Nantes.)

Let him care for guests, especially the poor and weak, and also for orphans and travelers; let him summon them daily to his meal as circumstances permit, and provide them with suitable hospitality.

### Chapter XI. That Sacred Ministries Are Not to Be Given as Pledges

[Col. 0775C]

(Concerning Pledges and Other Securities, chapter 1, from the Council of Rheims.)

Let no priest presume to give as security to a tavern keeper, merchant, any layman, or a woman, a chalice, paten, altar cloth, priestly vestment, or ecclesiastical book. For the holiness of the sacred ministry is so great that, without prejudice to the higher understanding of the mystery, the Lord even forbade through the prophet that a priest should go forth to the people wearing the holy vestments; rather, after returning from the divine conversation, he was to leave them within the holy place (Ezek. XLIV).

If the sacred canons forbid one to enter taverns for drinking, how much less ought he to offer what has been sanctified by sacred ministry for touching by the unclean—and still less as a pledge—just as Saint Pope and Martyr Stephen taught Saint Hilary in his decretal letters (Epistle 1).

### Chapter XII. That No One Is to Be Buried in a Church Without the Bishop’s Consultation, and That Nothing Is to Be Demanded for Burials

Let no priest bury anyone in a church without consulting the bishop, except only those persons whom we have individually and privately designated at the synod. Let him demand or extort no gift for burying the dead.

If anything is freely offered by devout persons to the altar, the church, or himself, we do not forbid him to receive it kindly.

### Chapter XIII. That Priests Are Not to Accept Gifts from Public Sinners or Penitents in Their Favor

[Col. 0776A]

(Concerning Simony, chapter 14, from Alexander III.)

Let no priest accept a gift or any temporal profit—or rather, spiritual harm—from anyone who is publicly sinful or incestuous, in order to conceal his sin from us or from our ministers. Nor, out of regard for any person, relationship, or familiarity, let him refuse to make the sins of others known to us or to our ministers, thereby sharing in them.

Nor let him presume to accept grace, favor, or a gift from any penitent, so as to bring a penitent less worthily to reconciliation and give him a testimony of reconciliation, while through resentment removing another, more worthy penitent from reconciliation. For this is simoniacal and abhorrent both to God and to human beings.

### Chapter XIV. How They Should Conduct Themselves at the Feasts of the Dead and at Other Gatherings

(D. 44, “No Priest,” from the Council of Nantes.)

Let no priest who has gathered for the anniversary, thirtieth, or seventh day of any deceased person, or for any other occasion at which priests have assembled for a gathering, presume to make himself drunk. Let him not pray while drinking in honor of the saints or of the soul itself, nor compel others to drink, nor stuff himself by another’s drinking prayer.

Let him not presume there to make or sing disorderly applause and laughter, or recount empty stories. Let him not permit indecent jokes involving a bear or female dancers to be performed before him, nor consent to the exhibition there of demonic masks, commonly called *talamascas*. For this is diabolical and forbidden by the sacred canons.

Rather, let him dine with propriety and religion, and return to his own church in due time. Let everyone also take the greatest care, if he wishes to rejoice in his own status, not on any pretext to provoke his equal or anyone else by word to anger, quarrel, or contention, and still less to a fight or killing; nor, when provoked, should anyone rush into such conduct. For at such banquets and drinking parties, as irreligious people hold them, the devil always mixes himself in.

(D. 44, “When Priests,” from the Council of Nantes.)

When priests have gathered for a meal, let the dean or some senior member of them begin a verse before the table and bless the food. Then let them sit down according to their order, each bearing the honor of the other; let them bless the food and drink in turn; and let one of their clerics read something from the holy Scriptures.

After the meal, let them likewise sing a holy hymn, following the example of the Lord and his disciples, as we read that they did at the supper (Matt. XXVI). Thus let all priests conduct themselves in every place, especially in such circumstances, lest, as the Apostle says, our ministry be reviled (II Cor. VI).

### Chapter XV. What Priests Must Avoid When They Assemble Among Themselves at the Kalends

[Col. 0777A]

(D. 44, “When Priests,” from the Council of Nantes.)

When priests have gathered together at the Kalends, after completing the divine mystery and the necessary conference, let them not sit down there at the table as though for a meal and burden one another with such unsuitable little feasts, since this is dishonorable and burdensome.

For, often returning late to their churches, they incur greater harm through reproach and contract greater mutual burden than they gain any benefit. Concerning such a gathering, which was held under the pretext of religion, the apostle Paul appropriately rebuked the Corinthians (I Cor. XI), who gathered in an unsuitable manner to eat the Lord’s Supper.

Likewise, those who gather for the Lord’s Supper—that is, for a conference concerning the word—under an ostensible pretext, but in truth join together for the sake of their stomachs, are held blameworthy both before God and before human beings. Therefore, after everything has been completed, those who wish may break bread with charity and thanksgiving in the house of their fellow priest, together with their brothers, and each may receive a single drink. Above all, let them not touch the cup there more than three times, and let them return to their own churches.

### Chapter XVI. Concerning Confraternities and Their Gatherings, and How They Should Be Celebrated
That only such things be done concerning the collections which the common people call *geldonias* or confraternities, as we have already admonished by word and now expressly command in writing, as pertains to authority, usefulness, and reason. Beyond this, no one—neither priest nor any other member of the faithful—may dare to proceed in our parish. That is, let them be united in every service of religion: namely, in offerings, lights, mutual offerings, funeral rites, almsgiving, and the other works of piety. Thus, whoever wishes to offer a candle, whether for a particular person or generally, shall bring it to the altar either before Mass or during Mass, before the Gospel is read.

As for the offering, let him offer only one offering, together with the offertory for himself and all his associates and household members. If he wishes to provide more wine in a small bottle or vessel, or additional offerings, let him give these to the priest or his minister either before or after Mass, so that the people may receive *eulogiae*—blessed portions—as alms and blessing from him, or so that the priest may have some supplement. But we entirely prohibit the feasts and banquets which divine authority forbids, at which burdens, unlawful exactions, shameful and empty merriment, and quarrels often arise—and, as we have learned by experience, even homicides, hatred, and dissensions. Henceforth, whoever presumes to do this, if he is a priest or any cleric, shall be deprived of his rank; if he is a layman or woman, he shall be separated [from communion] until satisfaction is made.

If it is necessary for such confraternity members to meet together—for example, if one happens to have a dispute with his equal and must be reconciled, and this cannot be accomplished without the meeting of the priest and the others—then, after those matters have been completed which belong to God and accord with Christian religion, and after the proper admonitions, those who wish may receive *eulogiae* from the priest. They shall break bread only and each receive a single drink, and shall presume to undertake nothing further. Thus each person shall return to his own home with the Lord’s blessing.

## Chapter XVII.—That, when a priest has died, no one should seek his church or chapel without consulting the bishop

If any priest should die, let no neighboring priest obtain that church through any appeal or gift to an influential layman, since it had previously existed as an established title in its own right; nor let him obtain the chapel without consulting us. If he does so, let him accept the defined sentence pronounced against him, just as canonical authority has decreed concerning a bishop: whoever, out of ambition, seeks a greater city shall lose the one he held and shall by no means obtain the one he attempted to usurp.

## II. Chapter headings concerning the matters about which the masters and deans must inquire in each church and report to the bishop

These matters are to be investigated every year by the priestly masters and deans in each mother church and in the chapels of our parish, and are to be reported to us on the Kalends of July. Likewise, they must investigate and report to us how those regulations which we gave the priests to observe by chapters are being observed and kept.

**I.** It must be investigated in what village, or under whose saintly dedication, the priest has been appointed, and by whom he was ordained.

**II.** Whether he possesses a holding of twelve *bunnuaria*, apart from the cemetery and the courtyard containing the church and his house, or whether he has four dependents.

**III.** How many free and servile holdings he possesses in his parish, or tenant-residents from whom he receives a tithe.

**IV.** What the altar furnishings are: how many are new and how many old, and how clean they are; with what metal the reliquaries and crosses are covered; whether the relics are carefully stored in the altar; and whether the reliquaries are secured with locks.

**V.** Which books and how many he possesses, and whether they are properly read.

**VI.** What priestly vestments and how many he possesses, how clean they are, and whether they are kept in a clean place.

**VII.** Whether he has a prepared place where water may be poured out when the altar vessels are washed, or the mouth or hands after receiving holy communion. Also, whether the priest himself, with his own hands, or his deacon or subdeacon, first washes the corporal.

**VIII.** Of what metal the chalice and paten are, with what care they are guarded, and whether he has a pyx in which the consecrated offering reserved as viaticum for the sick can suitably be stored.

**IX.** That the chrism and consecrated oil be stored under lock.

**X.** Whether the priest himself visits the sick, anoints them with holy oil, and gives them communion personally rather than through someone else; and whether he himself gives communion to the people, not handing communion to any layman to carry to his own house on behalf of a sick person.

**XI.** Whether he has a cleric able to keep a school, read the Epistle, or sing, as he considers necessary.

**XII.** An investigation must likewise be made concerning the church’s lights, and how many candleholders the title itself possesses.

**XIII.** How the church is roofed, whether it is vaulted, and whether pigeons or other birds build nests there, on account of the uncleanness or troublesome disturbance they cause.

**XIV.** Of what metal the bells there are.

**XV.** Whether it has an enclosed churchyard, whether it has its own dwelling beside the church, and whether there are suspicious little doors around it.

**XVI.** That, according to canonical institution, the tithes be divided into four portions, and that these portions be carefully and diligently distributed in the presence of two or three faithful witnesses; and that an account be rendered each year of the two portions belonging to the church and the bishop, stating what benefit the church has derived from them.

**XVII.** That he have matricularii according to the character of the place—not oxherds or swineherds, but the weak and poor, and persons belonging to the same domain. Unless perhaps the priest has a weak brother or some close relative who is extremely poor and is supported from the same tithe. As for other relatives, if he wishes to keep them near him, he shall clothe and feed them from his own portion.

**XVIII.** *(Concerning the property of clerics, chapter 1; Ivo, part III, chapter 94.)* It must likewise be investigated whether a man who possessed no patrimony when he was advanced to ecclesiastical orders later purchased estates, and under whose legal title they stand. For, according to the decree of canonical authority, they ought to belong to the church to which he was promoted from a condition of possessing nothing.

**XIX.** *(Concerning the property of clerics, chapter 4.)* It must be investigated whether, on the pretext of the preceding chapter, any priest has henceforth purchased property in another person’s name from church revenues, or from the offerings and vows of the faithful; whether he has constructed buildings there or placed there anything belonging to the church; whether he has allowed women to frequent those places; or, what is more shameful, whether he has kept there women who practice their textile work and manage the household, and whether the priest has improperly gone to, frequented, or remained in those same places. For this evil is committed contrary to the decrees of the canons by those who perpetrate it. Just as a priest, or anyone under a rule, must not practice usury in his own name, so neither may he do so in another’s name; much less may he commit fraud concerning ecclesiastical resources. To do this is sacrilege, and is a crime equal to that of Ananias and Sapphira, and of the thieving Judas, who carried away and stole the sacred offerings sent for the use of the faithful and the poor.

For it is one thing, without harm to the church, to assist poor friends or relatives, or any needy persons, out of charity, with measure and discretion, or to offer them help; and quite another thing, while destroying the church or dissipating ecclesiastical resources, to devote—secretly, indeed by theft—those things which ought to belong to the church and be expended for its use and for the poor or guests to the carnal uses of carnal people, without regard for God. A priest promoted from a condition of possessing nothing must not presume to sell what he has purchased from the church’s resources, or to hand it over as though to the house of God, except to the church to which such things properly belong, and then only after consulting the bishop.

**XX.** It must be investigated whether priests abstain from taverns, banquets, and improper familiarity with women, as we have very often forbidden and continue to forbid. For, to our disgrace, laymen petition me that, if they find a priest in taverns with witnesses, in such a way that no one can deny it, they should be permitted to take from him his horse and cloak. Therefore, if priests henceforth do not guard themselves against such things because they do not fear divine judgment, we shall inflict temporal disgrace upon them and impose a secular penalty upon their incorrigibility.

## Concerning the illicit approach of clerics to women, and how they are to be accused or cleared of it

**XXI.** *(Council of Trosle, chapter 9.)* Concerning the approach, frequenting, and cohabitation of clerics with women—which, according to the sacred canons, we have expressly and specially forbidden in every synod—we and our fellow ministers must make a firm, explicit, and careful investigation.

For, just as the sacraments differ according to the times for those who preceded the Lord’s coming in the flesh and for those who came afterward, yet return to the religion of one and the same faith and salvation; and, as it is written, “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII, 4); so, with the passing of time, the precision and multiplication of precepts have increased, both through the Lord himself and through angels in the Old Testament, and likewise in the New Testament through himself and through Catholic teachers and masters of the Church, who, as the prophet testifies, are also called angels.

The Lord himself gave commands in paradise to Adam, and after the flood to Noah and Abraham concerning circumcision. But he gave the law through angels to Moses, the mediator, and to the people, as the Apostle shows. In the New Testament, having become incarnate, he himself said: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, Love your enemies” (Matt. V, 45). And: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 20). And: “It was said to the ancients, ‘Whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (ibid., 21–22).

Through his saints also, concerning whom it was said, “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 20), he taught that, as time advanced, the virtue of chastity was to increase, especially among the ministers of the Church. Thus the great Council of Nicaea mystically decreed in this way (canon 3):

> “The great synod has altogether forbidden that a bishop, a priest, a deacon, or anyone at all who belongs to the clergy should have a woman introduced into his household, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as escape suspicion.”

Thereafter Christian emperors promulgated the law in these terms *(Theodosian Code, Concerning Bishops, the Church, etc., book 44)*:

> “All who exercise the office of the clergy are forbidden to have the companionship of unrelated women. Let them know that only the assistance of mothers, sisters, or daughters within their house has been granted to them.”

But because, under the pretext of these persons, other women began to be introduced, the holy African canons decreed *(African Council, canon 5)*:

> “Neither bishops nor priests themselves may have solitary access to widows, virgins, or any women whatsoever; rather, let either clerics or some reputable Christians be present.”

Thus, as blessed Gregory wrote to the ministers of the Roman Church *(letter 39, indiction II, book VII)*, blessed Augustine did not consent even to live with his sister, saying:

> “Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.”

And Saint Gregory says concerning this:

> “The great caution of learned men ought therefore to be instruction for us. It is an unseemly presumption for one who is less strong not to fear what a strong man fears. He will wisely overcome what is unlawful who has learned not even to make use of what is permitted.”

For this reason Christian emperors enacted a law, saying *(Novel of Justinian 125, chapter 29)*:

> “We too forbid priests, deacons, subdeacons, and others enrolled in the clergy who have no wives, in accordance with the divine rules, to have a woman in their house, except a mother, daughter, sister, or other persons who avoid every ground of complaint. If anyone, contrary to this observance, keeps in his house a woman who could give rise to suspicion of immorality, and his fellow clerics tell him that he ought not to live with such a woman, but he refuses to remove her from his house, or if, when an accuser comes forward, he is proved to have behaved dishonorably with such a woman, then the bishop shall remove him from the clergy according to the ecclesiastical canons and hand him over to the civic court of the city in which he is a cleric.”

And, as Saint Innocent *(Innocent, bishop, letter 2 to Victricius)* and his predecessor Siricius write:

> “If in ancient times the priests of God did not depart from the temple during the year of their service, as we read concerning Zechariah, nor touch their own houses at all—although the use of a wife had been relaxed for them on account of the succession of offspring, since no one from another tribe, and no one except from the seed of Aaron, had been commanded to approach the priesthood—how much more ought those priests or Levites to preserve chastity whose priesthood or ministry exists without succession, and who do not let a day pass without being occupied either in divine sacrifices or in the ministry of baptism? For if Paul also writes to laymen, saying, ‘Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer’ (I Cor. VII, 5), how much more ought priests, whose constant duty is both to pray and to sacrifice, always to abstain from such companionship? If one of them has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will he perhaps presume to sacrifice? Or with what conscience, or by what merit, does he believe that he will be heard, when it is said: ‘To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure’ (Tit. I, 15)?”

And lest anyone say, “If I live with women, my conscience is sufficient for me,” since the Apostle says, “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I, 12), let him attend to what the same Apostle also says—through whom, as he himself truthfully acknowledges, Christ speaks: “Providing what is good not only before God but also before all human beings” (Rom. XII, 17). Again, he commanded that we be without offense toward everyone, lest the brother for whom Christ died perish because of our conscience, saying:

> “By sinning against the brothers and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ” (I Cor. VIII, 12).

Therefore, filled with the Holy Spirit, our holy Fathers decreed that ministers of the altar should not cohabit with women or introduce women into their household with them, lest they either burn their conscience with desire or defile it by a most evil consent, and lest they stain the consciences of the weak even through an evil suspicion.

Accordingly, we shall not labor to investigate through parishioners or neighbors whether priests have had intercourse with women. For the ancient heresy has been abolished—the one called Cynic, that is, “dog-like,” because of its shamelessness—which said that sexual intercourse was natural and therefore ought to be carried out publicly without embarrassment. Yet we read that the first human beings, immediately after the sin, felt desire in their genital members and concealed themselves from one another’s sight.

Although the blindness of the human mind in the performance of shameful acts cannot be hidden from the eyes of God, the angels, or the saints in heaven, nevertheless even any rustic who has intercourse with his own wife avoids, as far as he can, the sight of many people. How much more, then, if a priest has human understanding, will he take care to hide an evil act which, once exposed, he knows will cause him not only to lose his ecclesiastical rank but also to forfeit the possessions he has in the world?

We shall therefore not inquire immodestly into a matter which the Apostle also, using not an explicit but a veiled expression when speaking to lawfully married persons, took care to designate by saying: “Return again to the same” (I Cor. VII, 5). And: “Let no one defraud his brother in this matter” (I Thess. IV, 6).

But we shall investigate through such persons the approach, frequenting, and cohabitation of priests with women contrary to canonical prohibition, as the holy African canons command *(African Council, canons 96 and 98)*—that is, through those whom the public laws admit for accusation or testimony, whether in the public court or before the tribunal.

And if any priest, not only in our parish but in our diocese, has confessed or has been convicted by a legal and regular judgment of cohabitation, frequenting, or approach to women contrary to the canons, he shall in every way be deposed, according to the decrees of blessed Gregory, without restoration to his rank. This accords with the chapter of the great Pope Leo, which says *(letter 1 to the bishops throughout Campania)*:

> “Our admonition therefore declares that if any of the brethren attempts to act against these decrees, and dares to commit what has been forbidden, let him know that he is to be removed from his office and shall not be a participant in our communion, since he refused to be a companion in discipline.”

And lest anything be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions both of blessed memory Innocent and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons, be so carefully observed by your devotion that anyone who violates them may know that pardon will henceforth be denied him.

Blessed Augustine also wrote to his archbishop concerning Abundantius, a priest of his parish *(letter 236)*:

> “Because he did not walk in the ways of the servants of God, he began to have a bad reputation. Alarmed by this, yet not rashly believing anything, but having become altogether more concerned, I took pains to discover, if possible, some certain indications of his evil conduct. First I learned that he had diverted the money of a certain rustic whose wine had been entrusted to him, so that he could give no plausible account of it. Then he was convicted and confessed that, while he had no cleric with him, he had both dined and supped at the house of a woman of bad reputation, and had stayed nearby and in that same house. What she denied I left to God; what he was not permitted to conceal I judged.”

Therefore, as Saint Gregory decreed, a priest of bad reputation shall be investigated under oath by suitable witnesses, as we have stated above. Each of those who swear shall take the oath in these terms:

> “Concerning what you will ask me about this priest, whatever I know about it, I shall neither tell you a lie nor conceal the truth knowingly, so help me God and these holy things of God.”

After this oath, he is to be questioned in the following manner:

> “The holy canons command that a priest must not have such approach to, frequenting of, or cohabitation with women as could give rise to evil suspicion and an unsuitable reputation for a priest. Therefore tell me whether you have seen or certainly know that this priest has such access to, association with, or cohabitation with women as could give rise to evil suspicion and a bad reputation; and do so under the oath which you have just sworn, that you will neither conceal the truth nor speak a lie about it.”

Apart from the accusers, there shall be seven suitable witnesses who state the truth about the matter under oath. Six of them shall swear; and the seventh, if the condition or standing of the person permits it, shall submit to judgment whatever they have stated truthfully under oath. For many have already been discovered among us who, after being hired for payment, have perjured themselves.

If a priest is convicted in this way of improper cohabitation with women, he shall be deposed, as Pope Zosimus decreed, saying *(letter to Hesychius, chapter 2)*:

> “Let everyone know that whoever, disregarding the authority of the Fathers and of the Apostolic See, neglects it shall be judged by us with the greatest strictness, so that he should have no doubt that the security of his position will not remain his if he thinks that, after so many prohibitions, this can be attempted with impunity. Whatever is repeatedly forbidden but nevertheless usurped is done out of a spirit of insult.”

**XXII.** It has been established in the Law, and confirmed in the Gospel, that “every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matt. XVIII). The Apostle also commands Timothy *(I Tim. V)*—in whose person, as Leo says, he instructed the whole number of Christ’s priests—that an accusation against a priest is not to be received except under two or three witnesses. The holy Council of Nicaea likewise commanded *(canon 2)* that a newly ordained bishop reproved by two or three witnesses abstain from the clergy.

But because in the history of Susanna *(Dan. XIII)* we read that two witnesses who appeared reliable to the people, and in the history of Naboth *(III Kings XXI)*, as well as in the account of the Lord’s Passion *(Matt. XXVI)*, two witnesses gave false testimony—since Christ, the power and wisdom of God, says, “Through me lawmakers decree what is just” (Prov. VIII, 15); and since Saint Gregory frequently commands in his letters that the case of ecclesiastical ministers be determined legally and according to regular procedure; and since Saint Augustine, explaining the Apostle’s statement, “If anyone who is named a brother is a fornicator” *(I Cor. V, 11)*, and what follows, says:

> “The Apostle did not wish a person to be judged by another person according to the arbitrary suspicion or an extraordinary judgment unlawfully assumed. Rather, he wished the designation to be understood as one made according to God’s law and the order of the Church, whether the person had confessed voluntarily or had been accused and convicted, and as one made with a judicial sentence in due order and pronounced with integrity. For if mere designation were sufficient, many innocent people would have to be condemned, since a crime is often falsely alleged against someone.”

In accusations against priests, we have seen that the authority of the laws must be followed concerning the number of suitable witnesses: seven suitable witnesses are to be sought, as we have said above. If reason or the case requires it, fourteen or twenty-one witnesses are to be sought, so that the truth may be brought to light.

**XXIII.** *(2, question 5, “If there is a bad reputation.”)* If a bad reputation concerning a priest has spread through the parish on the basis of probability, but legal accusers and witnesses are lacking, then—lest the hearts of the weak be wounded by the priest’s bad reputation, lest our ministry be reviled, and lest priests, becoming more secure, fall more freely into sin—according to the decree of the younger Gregory, an oath shall be placed in the midst, and the priest of bad reputation shall have as witness in the oath of his purification the one whom he will also have as judge.

**XXIV.** Since we read in the letters of blessed Gregory that a priest who had often been defamed provided only an oath in the purification of his reputation, and since legal, apostolic, and canonical authority accepts the testimony of three witnesses for condemnation, it does not seem unreasonable that it should be accepted for purification as well.

In sacred history and in the letter of blessed Gregory, we also read that blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, when the faithful reproached him for entering among the Gentiles, appeased them with a humble explanation and, in the case of the reproach brought against him, also produced witnesses, saying: “These six brothers came with me” (Acts XI, 12).

The Carthaginian canons also decree *(canon 20)* that, if priests or deacons are accused, their own bishop is to be joined by the lawful number of colleagues from neighboring places—that is, six with him in the case of a priest, and three in the case of a deacon. We therefore consider it authoritative that, if a priest has been defamed and suitable accusers or witnesses are lacking, then, according to the character and seriousness of the case and of the person, and according to what is useful for the healing of the hearts of the weak, he should clear himself of the bad opinion either alone, or with two other witnesses, or with six other witnesses, by an oath.

Nor is this contrary to the decree of the younger Gregory if more witnesses are required for the purification of a defamed priest. For, writing to Bishop Boniface through the priest Denuald, the same pontiff says that, if a priest who has been defamed cannot be convicted by suitable witnesses, an oath should be placed in the midst; he did not define whether the priest should swear alone or with others.

**XXV.** Since, as it is written, wickedness was found even among the angels; since, according to the prophet Malachi and the Evangelist John, priests are called angels; and since we have learned by experience that certain men have conspired with one another so that they might assist one another in their purgation but in reality do one another harm, just as priests full of wicked intention conspired against Susanna, it does not seem inappropriate that, in the presence of a trustworthy representative of the bishop, the priests who have offered themselves to swear together with the defamed priest in his purgation should undergo such an examination by the advocate of the defamed priest, so that they do not destroy themselves before God by their oath, as we have already discovered certain persons here to have been refuted.

**XXVI.** Since, as Saint Augustine says, new kinds of illnesses compel us to seek new experiments in remedies; and since, instructed by the authorities cited above and without prejudging the opinions of those who may understand the matter more soundly, we have considered that the following procedure should be adopted, so that we may both draw priests back from the precipice of the Charybdis of lust, and in whatever way possible vindicate the prohibition of the canons, repeated so many times, against transgressors, and avoid being judged for lax correction, as the priest Eli was condemned because he corrected his sons less strictly and less severely than he ought, and his sons perished as well *(I Kings IV)*.

For, as Leo says *(Decrees, chapter 14)*:

> “The faults of those in lower orders are to be attributed to no one more than to sluggish and negligent rulers, who often nourish a great pestilence while they pretend not to apply the necessary medicine.”

And Saint Gregory says:

> “Whoever does not correct what must be cut away commits it.”

Again, Leo, writing to Bishop Januarius, says to each of us *(ibid., chapter 14)*:

> “Let your devotion have no doubt that, if—which we do not believe—the things we decree for the protection of the canons and the integrity of the faith are neglected, we shall be moved with the greatest severity. For, as Pope Hilary says: One sins no less against the sanctions of the holy traditions than one rushes forward in an assault upon the Lord himself.”

But concerning how one must deal with those who, through contempt, violate the sanctions of the holy traditions or rush forward in an assault upon the Lord himself, Saint Leo decrees to Bishop Rusticus *(Decrees, chapter 16)*:

> “For those who have fallen in this way, private withdrawal is to be sought in order to obtain God’s mercy, so that, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful. We are not permitted to depart from this rule of strictness, promulgated by the Holy Spirit, through any improper display of pity. For although compassion is owed to our neighbors, uprightness is owed toward vices. Hence sacred Scripture always joins uprightness to simplicity, because simplicity without uprightness is foolishness. Simplicity toward vices, therefore, as the Catholic teachers say, is lax and foolish; and uprightness toward one’s neighbors, without the simplicity of compassion, becomes harsh and severe.”

From this place to the end of this chapter nothing has been assigned to the priests.

## That those who have confessed a crime or been convicted of one are rightly to be deposed from ecclesiastical rank
And lest some—delighting, contrary to the Apostle, not only in novelty of words but also of ordinances and deeds—who, as we have heard, say that a presbyter or deacon who has confessed a crime or been convicted of one ought not to be deposed but only suspended, because they can make confession and perform penance as other people do, should accuse us, like the Novatians, of denying penance to anyone: we shall state, in accordance with the views and words of orthodox teachers, what we hold concerning the penance and degradation of ecclesiastical ministers.

But those who, in accordance with the Apostle, do not endure sound doctrine, possessing indeed an appearance of piety but denying its power, because—as Saint Ambrose says in his exposition of the psalm *Blessed are the undefiled*, and blessed Pope Celestine says in writing to Nestorius—“The piety from which impiety frequently arises: let them see how they may free themselves from the snare in which they entangle themselves, setting their mouth against heaven and speaking against the sacred canons,” as Leo says (*Decretals*, chap. 5), “which were established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world.” Those canons, following apostolic teaching, say that persons detected in crime ought not to approach ecclesiastical rank, remain in the clerical order, or return to the clerical order.

Therefore the great Leo, with a mighty roar from the city of Rome, that is, from the head of the world, thunders throughout the whole world, decreeing “that bishops depart from the canons established beforehand neither through negligence nor through presumption; and if any priest should attempt to act contrary to the decrees and dare to commit what has been prohibited, let him know that he must be removed from his office.” Pope Hilary also says (*Decretals*, chap. 18): “One sins no less against the sanctions of the sacred traditions than one rushes into an injury against the Lord himself.”

And Gelasius says: “We have learned that some persons established in those very orders are not excluded for grave crimes, although the Apostle cries out that hands should not be laid hastily upon anyone, nor should one share in the sins of others; and although the venerable decrees of our predecessors declare that such persons—even if they have perhaps secretly slipped in—must be expelled, both those who were previously guilty and have been detected, and those who have forgotten their sacred profession and have become transgressors of their holy purpose must unquestionably be removed” [Col. 0787B].

And Saint Gregory, writing to the subdeacon Anthemius (*Book IX, Letter 66*), says: “Because the evil of so great a wickedness ought not to pass without deserved punishment, we wish you to admonish our aforesaid brother Paschasius first to deprive Hilary of the office of subdeacon, which he unworthily exercises, and then, after having him publicly chastised with blows, to have him carried into exile, so that the punishment of one may serve as the correction of many.”

And to Bishop Columbus (*Book X, Letter 8*): “It has come to our attention that the deacon Donadeus was deposed for a carnal sin. Let Your Love investigate this carefully; and if it is so, he must be confined to penance, so that through tears he may be able to loose the bond of the crime he committed” [Col. 0787C].

And to Bishop Sabinianus (*Book VII, Letter 12*): “You should know that the presbyter concerning whom your fraternity consulted us through the bearer of this letter cannot in any way, after his fall, remain in the sacred order or be restored to it. Nevertheless, he must be treated more mildly because, it is said, he readily confessed the crime he committed.”

And to Archbishop John (*Book VII, indiction 1, Letter 62*): “The document of the proceedings which you sent us makes clear what complaint has been brought against Lucillus, bishop of the city of Melita. Therefore, since the punishment of so great a crime ought not to be delayed at all, let Your Fraternity summon three or four of our brothers and fellow priests, so that, with the truth disclosed and satisfaction rendered in their presence also, you may take care, without ambiguity, to depose the aforesaid Lucillus from the episcopal order, which the contagion of this crime has stained” [Col. 0787D].

Because Saint Gregory, in the *Pastoral Rule*, explaining the meaning of the law, shows that “he whose nose is small, or large, or crooked”—that is, he who is not suited to maintain the measure of discernment, or who confuses the correctness of his action through excessive subtlety—“ought not to approach the ministry of God or offer his loaves to God,” we must observe discernment in the penance or degradation of those who have fallen from the ecclesiastical ranks, according to the catholic tradition and the teaching of the Church’s masters.

For blessed Gregory says (*Moralia*, Book XXI, chap. 9): “Sometimes the guilt of fornication is in no way different from the guilt of adultery, since the Truth says: ‘Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart’ (Matthew 5:28). Because in Greek the word *moichos* means ‘adulterer,’ and because it is not another man’s wife but simply a woman whom one is forbidden to look upon, the Truth clearly shows that adultery is committed even by the mere sight, when an unmarried woman too is desired shamefully. Yet this is often distinguished by the position or rank of the one who desires: for just as deliberate desire stains one person in the sacred order, so the guilt of adultery stains another. In persons who are not unlike one another, the same guilt of lust is distinguished by the preacher’s tongue, which, among other things, declares: ‘Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers shall possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 6:9). By adding this judgment to distinct forms of guilt, he shows how greatly they differ from one another” [Col. 0788B].

And again the same author says: “We know that at times it is a lesser thing to fall into bodily corruption than to sin through silent thought in deliberate pride. But when pride is believed to be less shameful, it is less avoided; whereas people blush all the more at lust because everyone recognizes it as shameful. Thus it often happens that some who fall into lust through pride are ashamed, after experiencing the event, of the evil of their fall; and then they correct greater faults when, prostrate in lesser ones, they are confounded. They see themselves guilty in lesser matters who believed themselves free in more serious ones.

“Therefore, by the merciful dispensation of the Lord, the evil spirit sometimes draws a person from one fault to another; and while striking him more severely, he thereby loses the one whom he had seized. By the very means through which he appears to have conquered, he is overcome. For this reason the sins of such men—David and Peter—were recorded in sacred Scripture, so that the downfall of the great might be a warning to the lesser. For this reason also the penance and forgiveness of both are there proclaimed, so that the recovery of the lost might be the hope of those who are perishing. Therefore, let no one grow proud because David fell from his position; and let no one despair because David rose again after his fall” [Col. 0788C].

And Saint Augustine (*Letter 50*): “When it was established in the Church that no one should receive the clerical office after penance for any crime, or return to the clerical office, or remain in the clerical office, this was done not from despair of forgiveness but from the rigor of discipline. Otherwise an argument would be raised against the keys given to the Church, concerning which it was said: ‘Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matthew 16:19).

“But lest perhaps, even when their crimes had been detected, their minds should swell with the hope of ecclesiastical honor and they should perform penance arrogantly, it was most strictly decreed that after performing penance for a damnable crime no one should remain a cleric. Thus, through despair of temporal eminence, a greater and truer remedy of humility might be provided. Saint David also performed penance for deadly crimes, and nevertheless remained in his honor; and blessed Peter, when he shed the bitterest tears, certainly repented of having denied the Lord, and yet remained an apostle.

“But this does not mean that the later diligence should be considered pointless, because, where nothing was taken away from salvation, they added something to humility, by which salvation might be more securely protected. I believe that they had learned from the false penances of some people, undertaken in pursuit of the power of honors. For the experience of many illnesses compels us to discover many medicines” [Col. 0789A].

Therefore those who have been detected in crimes, whether by their own confession or by legal and canonical conviction, must not enter the ecclesiastical ranks, remain in the ecclesiastical ranks, or return to the ecclesiastical ranks, just as the sacred canons and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs’ see openly and expressly decree.

The Apostle, admonishing us concerning this, says: “Do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness” (Ephesians 5:11). And, as Saint Augustine says, since it was not enough not to consent—that is, not to share in them—if negligence of discipline followed, he adds: “Rather, rebuke them” (ibid.). What does “Do not share in them” mean? Do not consent; do not approve. What does “Rather, rebuke them” mean? Reprove, correct, restrain.

Likewise the same apostle says: “Rebuke those who sin in the presence of everyone, so that the others may have fear” (1 Timothy 5:20). Thus Peter rebuked Ananias and Sapphira, so that the others might have fear; thus he condemned Simon, whom he nevertheless invited to penance; thus Paul rebuked the fornicator and handed him over to Satan, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord.

Hence the words of the wise are compared with keys and goads, as Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven firmly into place” (Ecclesiastes 12:11), because they do not know how to flatter the faults of sinners but pierce them [Col. 0789C].

Yet in correcting or restraining the sins of others, as blessed Augustine says, one must take care that the person who corrects another does not exalt himself, and that the one who thinks he stands does not fail to see that he may fall. Let rebuke sound terribly outwardly, but let affection of kindness be maintained inwardly. We must not consent to evil people by approving them; nor be negligent by failing to rebuke them; nor be proud by rebuking them insultingly—as blessed Gregory sufficiently teaches us in the *Pastoral Rule*.

Those who have fallen while in the ecclesiastical order, but have not been detected, we commit to the judgment of God, whose mercy, as Leo says (*Letter to Theodore*), “we can neither measure nor define in time”; before whom true confession suffers no delay in receiving pardon. The Spirit of God says through the prophet: “When you groan, then you shall be saved”; and elsewhere: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified, because with the Lord there is mercy, and abundant redemption with him” (Psalm 129:7). And the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31) [Col. 0789D].

Hence the catholic teachers say: “The Lord the Savior is found at that time when, through fear of the Lord, our sin is now rebuked by ourselves.” Therefore all the elect know how never to spare their own faults, so that they may find the Judge of their faults appeased; and they truly believe that they will afterward find him as Savior whom they now fear as a strict Judge. For whoever spares himself now in guilt will not afterward be spared in punishment.

God now counts the faults of each person when he exposes us to lament individually everything we have done. He mercifully releases those faults because, while we punish ourselves for them, he does not judge them at the final examination. For the Lord would not mercifully place sins to be lamented before the eyes of those who love him if he intended to strike them severely by himself. It is clear that he wished to hide from his judgment those whom, in his mercy anticipating them, he made judges of themselves.

Hence it is written: “Let us come before his face in confession” (Psalm 49:2); and: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged.” In this self-judgment, each person ought to exercise greater severity against himself in proportion as he recognizes that he has sinned more gravely, so that, judged by himself, he may not be judged by the Lord.

This action of penance will then be perfect and acceptable to God if a person ascends the tribunal of his own mind against himself and places himself before his own face, lest what God threatens the sinner should afterward happen to him: “I shall rebuke you and set you before your own face” (Psalm 49:21). Once judgment has thus been established in the heart, let accusing thought be present as accuser, conscience as witness, reason as judge, and fear as executioner.

Then, as pain torments him, let the blood of the confessing soul pour forth through tears; and the more diligently each person examines his conscience by scrutinizing it, the broader streams of tears should he pour from the innermost spring of his heart. By a daily baptism, through the tears of his compunction, let him be cleansed from the contagion of all vices—not only criminal ones but also those daily faults that steal upon him [Col. 0790C], according to the one who says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; I shall water my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6:7), because our life is not judged unworthy when it is washed with tears.

Since we have defiled our life after baptism and cannot again be washed in the waters of baptism, let us baptize our conscience with tears and be renewed in the spirit of our mind from day to day. For the mind does not know how to grow old through the body when it strives always to begin anew through desire. Hence Paul says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:23). Hence the Psalmist, who had already reached the summit of perfection, spoke as though beginning: “I said: Now I begin” (Psalm 76:11). For if we do not wish to grow weary of the good things we have begun, it is necessary that we believe we must begin again every day.

For through the fervor of the mind, whether among spiritual enemies or among our fellow human beings in the flesh, we grow old in some manner through the very habit of living, and we are darkened by the appearance of the newness we assumed. Yet from this old age we are renewed daily, if the practices of vigilance remain watchful, through praying, reading, and living well; for our life, while washed with tears, exercised in good works, and directed toward holy meditations, is continually restored to its newness.

Sins, whether small or great, cannot remain unpunished, because they are punished either by a repentant person or by God’s judgment. Divine vengeance ceases, however, if human conversion comes first. For God loves to spare those who confess and not to judge those who judge themselves.

And Saint Gregory—just as his predecessor Saint Callistus had also written—replied to one who questioned him concerning those who had fallen in the ecclesiastical order but had not been detected (*Letter 2*): “We follow the fathers who preceded us, and, with God as author, we do not depart from their sacred teaching. Beginning therefore at the head and continuing to the fourth ministry of the altar, we know that this form must be observed: since the greater precedes the lesser, both in honor and in crime, and since the greater the fault that follows a person, the greater the punishment that must be imposed, after penance it is believed that the result may be fruitful.

“For what benefit is there in sowing wheat and not gathering its fruit? After worthy satisfaction, we believe that it is possible to return to honor, as the prophet says: ‘Will not the one who falls rise again, and will not the one who has turned away return?’ (Psalm 40:9). The same prophet says: ‘On whatever day you turn back and groan, then you shall be saved.’

“Hence the Psalmist says: ‘Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me’ (Psalm 50:12–13). When he asked not to be cast away from God after falling into sin, the king and prophet, terrified because he had together taken another man’s wife, trembled in fear; and the prophet disclosed his crime. Performing penance, he added: ‘Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit’ (ibid., 13).

“For if he had not made himself worthy of God through penance, he would certainly not have preached to others. For he says: ‘I shall teach the unjust your ways, and the impious shall be converted to you’ (ibid., 15). When the prophet saw that his sins had been cleansed through penance, he did not hesitate to cure the sins of others by preaching, and he strove to offer himself as a sacrifice to God when he said: ‘A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit’ (ibid., 19), and the rest, which a devout and diligent reader will be able to find in its proper place” [Col. 0791C].

And elsewhere the same author says: “We cannot perform penance worthily unless we also know its proper form. To perform penance is both to mourn the evils one has committed and not to commit again what must be mourned. For whoever laments some things while nevertheless committing others either does not know how to perform penance or pretends not to know.

“What does it profit someone to mourn the sins of lust while still panting with the fires of greed? Or what does it profit someone to grieve the faults of anger while still wasting away in the flames of envy? Therefore it is necessary that the person who laments sins should by no means commit what must be lamented, and that the person who mourns vices should fear to perpetrate vices.

“And if anyone has fallen into the fault of fornication—or perhaps, what is more serious, into adultery, incest, or something so shameful that it is even disgraceful to mention it—he ought to cut himself off from permitted things to the same degree that he remembers having perpetrated forbidden things, attending to the counsel of blessed John the Baptist, who says: ‘Produce fruits worthy of repentance’ (Luke 3:8).

“By this saying each person’s conscience is convicted, so that he seeks through penance greater profits of good works in proportion to the greater losses he has inflicted upon himself through guilt. Let him consider each individual offense, and while he mourns the defilement of his error in each one, let him at the same time cleanse the whole through tears.

“Hence it is rightly said through the prophet Jeremiah, when the individual sins of Judah were being reckoned: ‘My eye has poured forth divisions of waters’ (Lamentations 3:48). We pour forth divided water from our eyes when we assign separate tears to separate sins. For the mind does not grieve equally over everything at one and the same time; but as it is more sharply touched now by the memory of this fault, now by that one, it is moved in each case and thereby cleansed of all together.

“Thus, with regard to those who have fallen and been detected, we follow the severity of the sacred canons’ judgment together with the doctrine of the catholic and apostolic Church. Thus, concerning those who have fallen but have not been detected and who perfectly mourn their sins, we share with the catholic Church its belief in the almighty goodness of the Lord: for, as Gelasius says, there is no sin for which the Church either cannot pray that it be forgiven, or which, by the authority divinely granted to it, it cannot absolve those who desist from it or release those who do penance. To it is said: ‘Whatever you forgive on earth shall be forgiven in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (John 20:23; Matthew 18:18). This applies to all sins, however numerous and whatever their kind” [Col. 0792C].

Thus we understand that the evangelical sayings do not disagree with one another when they say: “You shall know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:16).
