We are commanded to judge those fruits of evil works—that is, manifest sins—such as sexual misconduct, blasphemies, thefts, drunkenness, and whatever other such things there may be.

But when it is said: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Matthew 7:1), and: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Corinthians 4:5), we understand this to have been said concerning deeds whose intention is uncertain, or deeds that are hidden from us [Col. 0792D].

And just as the evangelical sayings do not disagree with one another, so neither is the apostolic see inconsistent or opposed to itself. In accordance with the sacred canons, it orders those who have publicly confessed manifest sins or have been convicted of them to be deposed from ecclesiastical rank; but it in no way permits those who have not publicly confessed or been legally and canonically convicted to be condemned or degraded.

## III. Additional Chapters in the Twelfth Year of the Episcopate

[Col. 0793]

These chapters were added in the twelfth year of our episcopate, on the fourth day before the Ides of June, to the other chapters which we had already given to our fellow priests. Following the authority of the Fathers, we entrusted them to our brothers and fellow priests for observance.

### Chapter I — That presbyters must take care that public sinners receive penance and report to the bishop how they perform it; concerning the punishment of those who disdain to come to penance and of presbyters who do not report sinners; and that final penance must be denied to no one

[Col. 0793A]

Let every priest exercise the greatest care so that, if a public murder, adultery, perjury, or any other criminal sin should be publicly committed in his parish, he may immediately—if he can approach the perpetrator or an accomplice—exhort him to come to penance before his dean and fellow presbyters. Whatever they discover or do in the matter must be made known to our fellow ministers, their superiors, who reside in the city.

Thus, within fifteen days, the public sinner must come into our presence, if we are within our parish, and, according to canonical tradition, receive public penance with the laying on of hands. If we are farther away from our parish, the year and day of the Kalends must be carefully recorded: when each person committed the public sin, when he came to penance before the ministers, and when he came to receive the laying on of our hand [Col. 0793B].

And whenever the presbyters meet together from the deaneries, from one Kalends to the next, they must confer concerning their penitents: how each person is performing his penance. The matter must be reported to us through our fellow minister, so that in the course of the penance we may determine when each penitent ought to be reconciled.

If anyone should refuse to come to penance within fifteen days after committing the sin, despite the exhortation of the presbyter in whose parish it occurred, the diligence of the dean and his fellow presbyters, and the urgency of our fellow ministers, it shall be decreed that the person who committed the sin and disdains to return to penance be separated from the assembly of the Church until he returns to penance [Col. 0793C].

Let every presbyter know that, if it should become known to us through another person that such an offense has been committed in his parish, and the matter has been brought to our attention later than it should have been, he shall remain suspended from the ministry and excommunicated on bread and water for as many days as elapsed before the matter reached our knowledge or that of our fellow ministers, without his reporting it and without the proper and commanded admonition.

And if, through the negligence of a presbyter, a public sinner who was not admonished should die after the number of days we have established, let every presbyter know that he will lose his rank [Col. 0793D].

Nevertheless, let everyone guard against this in every way: no penitent who asks devoutly may be deprived of final penance or the final viaticum. The condition is that, if he recovers, he must perform penance according to the ecclesiastical rules and seek and await reconciliation, insofar as God grants it to him, within the order of penitents [Col. 0794A].

### Chapter II — That nothing may be demanded for a burial place, that no one may claim a place by hereditary right but must receive it from the presbyter, and concerning the violation of graves

No one may demand any gift from anyone for a burial place, as sacred and canonical authority has decreed. If someone wishes to offer something freely, we do not forbid its acceptance after the body of his dear man or dear woman has been buried.

No Christian may presume to contend for a burial place as though by hereditary right. Rather, it must be the concern of the priest that his parishioners be buried, in accordance with Christian devotion, in the places he determines. The priest himself, mindful of his rank, must provide a suitable burial for each person and take care that, insofar as possible, no scandal arise among his parishioners.

He must also provide—if he wishes to rejoice before God and the world in the exercise of his ministry—that no Christian’s body be thrown out of its grave, that graves not be broken open, and that *caminatae* [structures; reading uncertain] not be made from them, as is customary. For just as it is cruel to expel someone from his house, while it is an act of mercy, according to the Lord’s command, to receive the poor and wandering person into one’s home [Col. 0794B], so it is sacrilegious, because of greed, to cast a body irreverently and impiously from the grave where each person ought to have awaited in peace the Lord’s summons, so as to rise at the coming of the just Judge [Col. 0794C].

### Chapter III — That no one may celebrate Mass on an unconsecrated altar or without a board consecrated by the bishop

Since some presbyters, besides the church in which they hold title, also possess chapels, and some restore old churches, construct new altars because of the suitability of the location, or alter them, no presbyter may presume to sing before consecration at an altar that has not been consecrated by the bishop.

Therefore, if necessity requires it, until the church or altars have been consecrated—and also in chapels that do not merit consecration—each presbyter who needs one must have a board made of marble, black stone, or the finest suitable material, decently prepared according to his means. He must bring it to us for consecration and carry it with him whenever convenient, so that he may celebrate the sacred mysteries upon it according to ecclesiastical rite [Col. 0794D].

## IV. Chapters Given at the Synod of Rheims in the Year 874

[Col. 0795]

These chapters were given to the presbyters at the Synod of Rheims in the year 874 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the month of July.

### Chapter I — That presbyters of parishes and canons of monasteries cannot simultaneously hold both positions

[Col. 0795A]

“Since, through an assumption that is not only illicit but also harmful to themselves and to the people entrusted to them, and contrary to the sacred canons, the presbyters of our parish are said to neglect their churches and obtain a prebend in the monastery of Mont Falcon, while the canons of that monastery also occupy the churches of rural parishes, it is necessary for us not only to demonstrate what the sacred canons determine concerning this matter, but also, if they do not correct themselves, to exercise the force and severity of those same sacred canons against their despisers.

“To pass over for the moment those who, for definite reasons and according to the sacred canons, come from other parishes into ours and are regularly received by us; or those who are incardinated in vacant churches; or those who, for a reason consistent with the rules, are transferred from one church to another according to those same rules: concerning transgressors of the canons, the same sacred canons decree that each person must minister only in the church in which he was first ordained.

“If someone has already been transferred from one church to another, he must have no share in the affairs of the former church. As for those who, after the definition of this great and universal synod, dare to perpetrate any of the prohibited acts, the holy synod has decreed that they must withdraw from their own rank” [Col. 0795B].

And Saint Leo, pope of the Roman see, wrote concerning this to the archbishop of Aquileia, saying (*Letter 89, to Nicetas*): “We admonish you to restore that part of ecclesiastical discipline which was formerly and repeatedly decreed by the holy Fathers and by us: that no one may freely pass from one church to another, whether in the rank of presbyter, in the order of deacon, or in any subsequent clerical order. Let each person remain where he was ordained, not enticed by ambition, not led astray by greed, and not corrupted by human persuasion.

“Thus, if someone seeks his own interests rather than the things of Jesus Christ, neglects to return to his own people and his own church, let him be regarded as an outsider both from the privilege of honor and from the bond of communion” [Col. 0795C].

If anyone takes care to understand these words of blessed Leo attentively, he will find that every wrongful pretext has been excluded and every consideration of usefulness and necessity has been granted. For he says that each person must remain where he was ordained, not enticed by ambition, not led astray by greed, and not corrupted by human persuasion.

If someone has not been enticed by ambition, he will not seek to rise from a smaller church to a greater one. If he has not been led astray by greed, he will not seek his own interests but those of Jesus Christ. Consequently, he will not abandon his own people and flee for refuge, as it were, under the protection of a monastery; nor will a person ordained as a canon in a monastery abandon his monastic duties and, out of greed for dishonest gain and the income from tithes of rural parishes, strive to invade their churches, caring nothing if infants should die without baptism or the sick should die without Communion and reconciliation.

For it is established and certain that no one will be able to perform simultaneously both the duties of the monastery cloister and the obligations owed to the people in rural parishes. For if, in the silence of the dead of night, an infant were born in danger or a sick person requested the gift of viaticum, how could a canon leave the monastery cloister and go to the village to assist the needs of the sick? [Col. 0796A]

Seeing this, Saint Gregory, explaining the prophet Ezekiel before the people, says (*Homily 5 on Ezekiel*): “His throne”—that is, the Lord’s throne—“was a flame of fire, and its wheels were burning fire” (Daniel 7:9). He says: “Those who are guardians of souls and have undertaken the burdens of feeding the flock are by no means permitted to change places. Rather, because, placed in one location, they burn while carrying within themselves the presence of the divinity, the throne of God is called a flame of fire.

“Therefore we must not neglect but must execute with the greatest diligence what these holy men of God have decreed must be held on account of this matter” [Col. 0796B].

Accordingly Saint Leo, writing the foregoing to the archbishop of Aquileia, immediately added (*Decretals*, chap. 14): “Let Your Love have no doubt that, if—as we do not believe—the things we decree for the guardianship of the canons and for the integrity of the faith should be neglected, we shall be moved with the greatest severity; for the faults of those in lesser orders must be attributed to no one more than to sluggish and negligent rulers, who often nourish a great pestilence while pretending not to apply stricter discipline” [Col. 0796C].

Therefore, if any presbyter of our parish should feel, whether because of bodily weakness or because of a hidden sin of the soul, that he cannot benefit the people entrusted to him or ought not to preside over them, and should wish to seek the harbor of a monastery in order to perform penance according to the decrees of blessed Leo, let him, by a written declaration of his profession, divest himself—according to Gregory’s decrees—of his order, title, and governance of the people, and then enter the monastery.

Otherwise, let him retain and govern his church and the people entrusted to him according to the sacred rules. But if any presbyter of our parish should presume to act contrary to the aforesaid prohibitions of the canons, let him know that he must in every way be expelled from the order [Col. 0796D].

### Chapter II — That nothing may be demanded or received from anyone for a place among the matricularii

[Col. 0797A]

I have often admonished you concerning the matricularii: what sort of persons you ought to receive and how you ought to distribute to them their share of the tithe. But I have discovered that some have made light of our admonition—or rather, of God’s admonition through our insignificance. Therefore it is necessary for me to repeat what I know some are neglecting.

By God’s authority I forbade you to allow any presbyter to presume to demand or accept anything whatsoever from anyone for a place among the matricularii, whether a gift or service at harvest time or in any other service of his. No one may presume to sell to the matricularii the share of the tithe due to them, which the faithful offer to the Lord for the redemption of their sins.

I forbid this again now, showing you the divine authority. To pass over many passages from the sacred Scriptures and bring forward only a few familiar ones, the Holy Spirit sang through blessed David in the words that you sing: “My God, your mercy…” (Psalm 18:18). The tithe given by the faithful is mercy, and it is given to God, who is mercy. This mercy will say in the judgment to the merciful: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).

For *eleēmosynē*—Greek for “almsgiving”—is called *misericordia*, “mercy,” in Latin. Whoever sells almsgiving sells God, that is, our mercy, and is like Judas, of whom it is written in the Gospel that Judas had the money box (John 13:29). The things that were put into it—that is, what the faithful gave to the Lord, from which he and his disciples were to subsist according to the flesh, and from which the Lord gave alms—Judas carried, that is, carried away and stole [Col. 0797B].

And a presbyter who demands or accepts any gift from the redemption of sins—that is, from the tithe of the faithful—is not worthy to be called a presbyter but must be deposed, just as Judas was called one of the apostles but was cast out from the number of the apostles and eternally rejected into partnership with the devil.

Know also that any presbyter who is convicted of this theft of Judas will not only be removed from the presbyteral order but will not even deserve to receive a share of that tithe which the matricularii receive. Rather, he will have his portion with the one whose partner he preferred to become.

“Whatever,” says Saint Hilary, pope, “a person does not cut off in another, he will find in himself.” And Saint Gregory says: “Whoever does not correct what must be cut off commits it” [Col. 0797D].

### Chapter III — Concerning improper access to women and the deposition from ministry of those who do not correct themselves
I have already given you a chapter from the holy Scriptures and from the statements of Catholics concerning improper approach to women and undue familiarity with them. But I see that some of you make light of it. Therefore I wish it to be read again in your assembly, together with the judgment of Pope Zosimus, who says (in the decretal, ch. 2):

“Let anyone know that whoever neglects this, setting aside the authority of the Fathers and of the Apostolic See, will be more strictly punished by us, so that he may have no doubt that he cannot retain the standing of his office if he thinks that, after so many prohibitions, this may be attempted with impunity. For whatever is so often usurped after being forbidden is done in a spirit of contempt.”

And know for certain that I shall not inquire of every one of you about observed intercourse with women, but about the canonical prohibition concerning approach to women; for, as Pope Hilarus says (in his letter to Veranus, Leontius, and Victurinus):

“One sins no less against the sanctions of the holy traditions than one rushes into an injury against the Lord himself.”

And whoever among you prefers undue familiarity with women to the purity of the sacred ministry shall have what he has chosen, because he will not be able to possess both the purity of the sacred ministry and the impurity of an unclean association.

He shall therefore be removed from the sacred ministry if correction cannot benefit him. Thus Pope Leo decreed to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, saying (Letter 82):

“Your diligence must apply itself vigilantly, so that, where correction cannot be beneficial, excision may not be spared. For we must remember the evangelical commandment, which is prescribed by the Truth itself: if an eye, or a foot, or a right hand should cause us scandal, it must be removed from the body’s structure, because it is better to be without these members in the Church than to go with them into eternal punishments. This pestilential tolerance must be entirely removed from priestly vigor, for by sparing the sins of others it does not spare itself, just as once the priest Eli, by tolerating the offenses of his sons, deserved to experience with them the sentence of divine justice, because through sluggish indulgence he neglected to punish sinners (1 Sam. 4).”

“As Ambrose says: ‘When a priest indulges one unworthy person, he causes many to be drawn into the contagion of falling; for an easy pardon provides an incentive to sin.’”

And Saint Gregory says:

“While one is corrected, many are reformed; and it is better that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through the license of one.”

Nor is it surprising that this principle is observed among human beings, since we know that it is very often practiced among animals as well: those that appear to have mange or an eruption are separated from the healthy, lest the others be condemned or perish through their disease. For it is better that they be openly corrected than that the healthy perish because of them, as our true farmer, Christ the Lord, shows in the Gospel, saying:

“Every branch that does not bear fruit”—that is, the fruit of good works—“I shall take away” (John 15:2).

And this is what the Lord figuratively commands through Moses in Leviticus (Lev. 14): that a leprous stone in a house be inspected by the priest; and if it cannot be purified, it is to be counted among the unclean, removed from the order of clean stones—that is, from the fellowship of the Church—and another worthy stone is to be substituted in its place.

That is, once any harmful person who refused to keep what is said—“Hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown” (Rev. 3:11)—has been cast out of the heavenly, that is, ecclesiastical, building like a dead stone, [a replacement] is, according to the apostle Peter, to be built up as a living stone in the spiritual house, namely in the building of the holy Church, the heavenly Jerusalem, which consists of angels and human beings and is built as a city; the final phrase, *utilis superaedificetur*, is syntactically uncertain.

## CHAPTER IV — Concerning those who purchase allods from ecclesiastical resources and do not leave them to the Church

[Col. 0799A]

I hear that some of you neglect your churches, purchase allods, build and cultivate estates on them, maintain women’s dwellings on those estates, and do not leave the estates to the churches according to the sacred canons, but, contrary to the sacred canons, transfer them either to your relatives or to anyone else.

Know, therefore, that whenever I discover anyone doing this, I shall take care to judge him according to canonical severity. For no bishop or priest can possess an allod better or more securely than one assigned to the Church, provided that he wishes to live according to his order. But if through his own fault he loses his order, he will not even be able to retain the allod that he acquired from ecclesiastical resources from the day of his ordination.

Our fellow ministers could largely restrain this fraud against the sacred canons, the sequence of the holy Scriptures, and the preaching of our predecessors, if they would take care to consult the chapter collected by us from the sacred regulations and given to them and to you: what each priest does with the tithes; and, since I demand nothing from them during the visitation of the parish churches except what they provide each year in the churches from what we have established for the churches; and how each priest practices hospitality, according to the command of the blessed apostle Peter:

“Be hospitable to one another without grumbling, each administering to the others the grace he has received” (1 Pet. 4:9).

And Saint Paul says:

“Let brotherly love remain among you, and do not forget hospitality; for through it some, having received angels as guests, pleased God” (Heb. 13:1).

[Col. 0800A]

And the apostle James says:

“Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, and to keep oneself unspotted from this world” (Jas. 1:17).

## CHAPTER V — That rewards should not be given to patrons on behalf of churches left vacant

I have often admonished you not to give excessive gifts, contrary to the sacred regulations, on behalf of churches left vacant. But, as I have heard, you are not corrected by this; rather, you deliver yourselves and those whom you have nurtured into the curse of the Simoniac heresy. Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, condemned this heresy first, saying to Simon:

“May your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20).

For if you who do this possessed human understanding—for I am not speaking of everyone—you could have recognized that, if you lived well and nurtured those whom you have raised in a good life and a good conscience, there would be no need for you either to lose what belongs to you or to send yourselves into condemnation.

You yourselves know that no faithful person in our parish wishes to be without a priest in his church, and that without episcopal ordination he cannot have a priest there. Therefore, whenever a priest dies, each person asks for a priest in his church. When I seek a good cleric for him, he himself will seek a good cleric in order to receive the priestly order; and if he brings me a good one, I shall ordain him. If not, I shall seek another; and he will continue seeking a good cleric until he finds one suitable for the sacred order.

You see that it would not be necessary for you to seek churches with an excessive gift, because, if it were not for your fault, the faithful would seek good clerics more than your money. But you do not tolerate this; rather, by giving a reward to patrons, you send yourselves and those whom you have nurtured into condemnation, purchasing sin for yourselves and for them.

## 738 — CHAPTERS GIVEN TO ARCHDEACONS AND PRIESTS

[Col. 0799]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 877, on the fifth day before the Ides of July, Hincmar, archbishop, gave the following chapters to his fellow ministers, Guntarius and Odelhard, archdeacons and priests.

[Col. 0799D]

The blessed apostle Peter, whose place bishops occupy in the Church, and under whose direction their fellow ministers serve, admonishes them in his epistle, saying:

“Elders who are among you, I beseech—being myself a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, as well as a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed—feed the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly, according to God; not for the sake of shameful gain but eagerly; not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock and doing so wholeheartedly” (1 Pet. 5:1–3).

Following his word and example, Saint Pope Leo (Letter 88, to Anastasius of Thessalonica) restrained the man to whom he had entrusted his place—sharing responsibility, not the fullness of power—from an undue desire for presumption by means of distinct chapters and the bridle of discretion.

In accordance with their teaching, at the beginning of your entrusted ministry I openly and diligently admonish you in a few chapters. Insofar as human frailty permits, I command you, under the testimony of Christ, not to deviate from them.

### CHAPTER I — That they should not burden priests when making the rounds of the parishes

The eminent teacher of the nations says to his disciples:

“Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 12:1).

When you travel through the rural parishes entrusted to you, whether with me or on your own, do not, as I do not, burden the priests by demanding provisions. Do not unnecessarily take with you men of your own or your relatives, through whom you burden them with food and drink and fodder for horses.

Take care that your men who travel with you do not dishonor them or become burdensome to their people. Do not remain for a long time in the dwellings of those priests. If necessity arises and you must stay somewhere, arrange your provisions through the priests living nearby, so that you are burdensome to no one and do not waste ecclesiastical stipends in idleness and fruitlessness, just as I am not burdensome to the priests through whose parishes I travel.

## 739 — CHAPTER II — That they should visit parishes not for the sake of provisions but for the sake of instruction

Do not visit the parishes for the sake of provisions, so that, living on the stipends of others, you may preserve your own stipends. Instead, by word and example, instruct not only the priests but also the laypeople through your good conduct and inquiry, according to the ministry entrusted to you.

### CHAPTER III — That they should not accept gifts from priests in order to conceal their vices

Do not accept gifts from priests so that their evil reputation may be concealed. Rather, make it known to everyone by word and example that the love of God and neighbor is more valuable to you than the opportunity to acquire earthly gain; that kindness is more valuable than severity, admonition than agitation, and charity than power.

Toward the good and those who act well, be equal as brothers. Toward the wicked, be correctors of vices and lovers of brothers. Act similarly toward others who offend in the ministries entrusted to you.

### CHAPTER IV — That they should not ask priests for anything to take away when they return

When you travel through the parishes, do not burden the priests by asking for *friskingae*, or fish, cheeses, grain, or any other things, so that you may have something when you return to the city from which you can provide a meal, as it were, for brothers, and so that, while your stipends remain intact, you may have the means to support yourselves and your people.

### CHAPTER V — That they should not demand money or *eulogiae* from priests, but accept only what is freely offered

[Col. 0801D]

Do not ask priests for money for any purpose, as though in return for some assistance. Nor, when they come to the synod, or for an inquiry into their ministry, or to receive chrism, should you demand *eulogiae*—blessed gifts. But if someone happens, according to his own will and ability, to wish to offer something freely, accept it with thanksgiving.

### CHAPTER VI — That they should not burden priests by feeding their own horses or those of their friends

Do not presume to commend your horses, or those of your friends, to the priests for feeding, as though by way of a request; nor demand grain or fodder from them.

For this reason I provide you with assistance from ecclesiastical resources, in accordance with what the Apostle says concerning the Law:

“You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing” (1 Tim. 5:8),

so that you do not burden the priests.

## CHAPTER VII — That they should not presume to confuse or divide rural parishes, and that they should describe all the churches and chapels subject to them

I expressly command you in the name of Christ not to presume to confuse or divide rural parishes for the sake of anyone’s friendship, petition, or reward. Do not subject to other churches, as though in the place of chapels, those churches that from ancient times have been accustomed to have priests. Nor presume to subject chapels to churches other than those to which they were subject in antiquity.

Throughout your entire ministry, each of you is to describe all the churches and titles that from ancient times have had priests, together with the chapels anciently subject to them, and report them to me in writing.

### CHAPTER VIII — That they should not allow anyone to have a chapel at home or Mass to be celebrated in a house without the bishop’s permission, and that they should describe all such chapels

Let none of you allow anyone to have a chapel in his house without my permission, or allow Masses to be celebrated in his house without my permission.

Each of you is to describe, within his ministry, everyone who has had a chapel outside the principal church from the time of Ebo until my time, as well as every chapel made from my time onward with either my permission or that of another; and in whose priest’s parish each chapel has been made, and whose chapel it is.

### CHAPTER IX — That penitents should not be brought to reconciliation for any gift, or neglected afterward

Take careful care that neither you nor the priests negligently bring penitents to reconciliation for the sake of any gift, or neglect them after reconciliation. This is Simoniac.

### CHAPTER X — Concerning those who relapse after public penance

Take careful care that, if any people fall into public sin after public reconciliation, you report it to my attention, so that you may know how both you and the priests ought to act in the matter.

### CHAPTER XI — That unsuitable men should not be brought to ordination for the sake of any gift

[Col. 0802D]

Take careful care concerning the life and learning of the clerics whom you bring to ordination, lest you introduce for ordination, in return for any gift, men who ought not to be introduced, since this is Simoniac.

## CHAPTER XII — That they should see how the priests observe the chapters given to them

Take careful care, in accordance with the chapters we gave to the priests, concerning the church’s portion and what is provided from it in the churches. Also inquire concerning the matricularii and the other chapters given by us to the priests, and how they observe and preserve them.

## CHAPTER XIII — How a dean is to be chosen in place of one who has died or become useless

If a dean in your ministry is negligent, useless, or incorrigible, or if one of them dies, do not choose a dean thoughtlessly. If I am far away, provisionally install the dean who has been elected, until that election is reported to my attention and is either confirmed or changed by my appointment.

# THE ROYAL CORONATIONS OF HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

## I. THE CORONATION OF CHARLES THE BALD  
### When he was consecrated in the kingdom of Lothair

The order according to which King Charles was crowned in the city of Metz in the year 869, in the month of September, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, which fell on a Friday, with these bishops present: Hincmar the archbishop, Adventius, Hatto, Arnulf, Franco, Hincmar, and Odo; at the time when the former King Lothair, son of the Emperor Lothair, died in the city of Piacenza.

### Announcement of Bishop Adventius before the beginning of Mass in the church of Saint Stephen, before the king, the bishops, and many others

[Col. 0803B]

#### CHAPTER I

You know, and it is known in very many kingdoms, how many and what kinds of events, for well-known reasons, we commonly endured during the time of our former lord, whom until now we possessed, and with what grief and anguish our hearts were recently struck by his unhappy death.

Therefore, deprived and bereft of our king and ruler, we all considered our one and uniquely salutary refuge and counsel to be that we should turn through fasts and prayers to him who is a helper in times of need and in tribulation, whose is the counsel and whose is the kingdom; and, as it is written, to him “he will give it to whomever he wishes,” whose hand holds the hearts of kings, and who makes people dwell together in one house, breaking down the middle wall and making both one.

We were to implore his mercy so that he might give us a king and ruler after his own heart, who would govern, save, and defend us in judgment and righteousness, in every order and condition, according to his will; and so that he might incline and unite all our hearts unanimously toward the man whom, according to his mercy, he had foreknown, chosen, and predestined for our salvation and welfare.

#### CHAPTER II

Since, finally, in our harmonious unanimity we see the will of God—who does the will of those who fear him and hears their prayers—that this man is the legitimate heir of this kingdom, to whom we have voluntarily entrusted ourselves, namely, our present lord, King and ruler Charles, so that he may preside over us and benefit us, it seems to us, if it pleases you, that, as we shall make clear to you after his words, we should demonstrate by the surest sign that we believe him to have been chosen by God and given to us as ruler.

We should not be ungrateful to God, the giver, for his benefits, but, returning thanks to him, should pray that he preserve him for us for the salvation and defense of his holy Church and for the aid and welfare of us all, in safety, peace, and tranquility, for a long time; and that he govern us in his service under his administration, while we obey him with faithful devotion and enjoy the salvation we desire.

#### CHAPTER III

And, if it pleases him, it seems worthy of him and necessary for us that we should hear from his own mouth what a most Christian king, from a faithful and unanimous people in his service, ought to hear and receive with devout mind, each according to his order.

After this, King Charles himself announced the following to everyone listening in the same church:

Since, as these venerable bishops have said through the voice of one of them, and have demonstrated by sure signs through your unanimity, and as you have acclaimed, that I have come here by God’s election for your salvation, welfare, rule, and governance, know that, with the Lord’s help, I intend to preserve the honor and worship of God and of the holy churches; to honor and protect each one of you according to the dignity of his order and his person, as far as I know and am able, and to keep him honored and protected; and to preserve for each person, in his own order, law and justice according to the laws appropriate to him, both ecclesiastical and worldly.

This is so that each of you may render to me, according to his order, dignity, and ability, the royal honor and power, due obedience, and assistance necessary for maintaining and defending the kingdom given to me by God, just as your predecessors faithfully, justly, and reasonably rendered them to my predecessors.

### Announcement of Hincmar, archbishop, in the church of Saint Stephen

#### CHAPTER I

Lest it perhaps seem to anyone that I and the venerable fellow bishops of our province are acting improperly and presumptuously by involving ourselves, from another province, in the ordination and affairs of this province, let him know that we are not acting contrary to the sacred canons.

For the Churches of Rheims and Trier, together with the Churches entrusted to them, are regarded in this region of Belgica as sisters and fellow-provincial Churches, as ecclesiastical authority and the most ancient custom demonstrate. Accordingly, they ought by unanimous agreement to exercise synodal judgments and concordantly preserve what has been established by the holy Fathers, while this condition of the privilege is maintained: that whichever of the bishops of Rheims and Trier was ordained first is also to be regarded as senior.

#### CHAPTER II

The divinely inspired Law commands, saying:

“If you pass through the harvest of your friend, gathering ears of grain, you shall rub them in your hand and eat; but you shall not put in a sickle or reap with a sickle” (Deut. 23:25).

The harvest is the people, as the Lord shows in the Gospel, saying:

“The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” (Matt. 9:37–38).

For you ought to pray for us bishops, so that we may be able to speak to you worthily.

The harvest of a friend, however, is the people entrusted to another metropolitan. Therefore, by exhorting you, as though rubbing with the hand of work, we are able and ought to lead you across toward God’s will and your salvation, into the body of the Church’s unity. But we do not put the sickle of judgment into the parishioners of provinces entrusted to other metropolitans, because neither is there a basis for doing so nor do we consider it to belong to us.

#### CHAPTER III

There is also another reason: these venerable lords and our brothers, the bishops of this province, having no metropolitan bishop, command and admonish our humility, through fraternal charity, to act in their affairs just as in our own particular affairs.

Is this so, my lord brothers?

And the bishops answered:

It is so.

#### CHAPTER IV

In addition to what the lord bishop and our brother Adventius has said to you in his own voice and in that of his other brothers and of our brothers, the venerable bishops, you may also observe in this that it is God’s will that our present lord and king, who in the part of the kingdom that he has until now held and continues to hold has usefully governed and continues to govern us, our churches, and the people entrusted to him, and has beneficially ruled and continues to benefit them, has come from there to this place under the Lord’s guidance.

You too have gathered here through his inspiration and have voluntarily entrusted yourselves to him. Through the same prompting, all living creatures came together without compulsion into the ark signifying the unity of the Church.

For his father of holy memory, Lord Louis the Pious, Emperor Augustus, descended from Louis, the illustrious king of the Franks, who was converted with his whole people through the catholic preaching of the blessed Remigius, apostle of the Franks, and with three thousand Franks, excluding children and women, was baptized on the vigil of holy Easter in the metropolitan church of Rheims and anointed with chrism received from heaven, which we still possess, and consecrated king.

He arose through the blessed Arnulf, from whose flesh the same Louis the Pious Augustus derived his bodily origin, and was crowned emperor at Rheims by Pope Stephen of Rome before the altar of the holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary.

Later, deprived of earthly rule through the faction of certain people, he was restored to the aforesaid part of the kingdom by the unanimous agreement of the bishops and the faithful people before the tomb of Saint Denis, the distinguished martyr of the holy Church. In this church, before the altar of the protomartyr Stephen, whose name in interpretation sounds as “crowned,” he was restored to the authority of the crown of the kingdom by the priests of the Lord, with the acclamation of the faithful people, as we who were present saw.

And since, as we read in the sacred histories, when kings obtained kingdoms they placed the diadems of the individual kingdoms upon themselves, it does not seem improper to these venerable bishops, if it pleases your unanimity, that, upon obtaining the kingdom from which you have voluntarily come together to him and entrusted yourselves to him, he should be crowned by priestly ministry before this altar and consecrated to the Lord by sacred anointing.

If this pleases you, let your voices agree.

When everyone had shouted approval, the same bishop said:

“Let us therefore give unanimous thanks to God, singing: ‘We praise you, God.’”

# Blessings over King Charles before Mass and the altar of Saint Stephen

### Adventius, bishop of Metz

O God, who in your indulgence care for your peoples and rule them in love, grant this servant of yours the spirit of wisdom, to whom you have given the governance of discipline, so that, devoted to you with his whole heart, he may always remain capable in the governance of the kingdom and, persevering in good works, may under your guidance reach the eternal kingdom. Through the Lord, etc.

### Hatto of Verdun

Grant, we beseech you, Lord, the abundance of your grace to this servant of yours, so that, following your commandments while you act within him, he may receive the consolation of the present life and of the life to come. Through the Lord.

### Arnulf of Toul

We beseech you, Lord, be favorable to our times in the governance of this servant of yours, so that, directed by your gift, our security and Christian devotion may endure. Through the Lord.

## 745 — Franco of Tongeren

Grant, we beseech you, Lord, salvation of mind and body to this servant of yours, so that, clinging to good works, he may always deserve to be defended by your power. Through the Lord.

### Hincmar of Laon

May this servant of yours receive your blessing, Lord, by which, saved in body and mind, he may always offer you acceptable service and always find the benefits of your favor. Through the Lord.

### Odo of Beauvais

Preserve, we beseech you, Lord, this servant of yours, and graciously purify him through the abundance of your blessings, so that he may always increase through your instruction and gifts. Through the Lord.

# Blessing of Hincmar, archbishop

May almighty God extend the right hand of his blessing and pour out upon you the gift of his favor. May he surround you with the fortunate wall of his protective guardianship, through the intercession of holy Mary and all the saints. Amen.

May he forgive you all the evils you have committed and grant you the grace and mercy that you humbly ask of him. May he free you from every adversity and from the plots of all visible and invisible enemies. Amen.

May he place his good angels always and everywhere to guard you, going before you, accompanying you, and following after you. May he free you by his power from sin and the sword and from every danger. Amen.

May he turn your enemies toward the kindness of peace and charity and make you gracious and lovable in the eyes of those who hate you. May he clothe those who persist in persecuting and hating you with salutary confusion, while eternal sanctification blossoms over you. Amen.

At the words, “May the Lord crown you,” Archbishop Hincmar anointed him with chrism at the right ear, across the forehead to the left ear, and on the head.

[Col. 0807C]

May the Lord crown you with a crown of glory, in his mercy and compassion, and anoint you in the governance of the kingdom with the oil of the grace of his Holy Spirit, with which he anointed priests, kings, prophets, and martyrs who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, and obtained the promises. May you be made worthy by the grace of God of those same promises, so that you may deserve to enjoy their fellowship in the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

May he always make you victorious and triumphant over visible and invisible enemies. May he continually pour into your heart both fear and love of his holy name, make you steadfast in right faith and good works, and, granting peace in your days, lead you with the palm of victory to the everlasting kingdom. Amen.

And may he who wished to establish you as king over his people grant that you be happy in the present age and a sharer in eternal happiness. Amen.

May he cause you to govern happily for a long time, by his dispensation and through your administration, the clergy and people whom he wished, through his assistance, to subject to your authority. May they, obeying the divine commands, free from every adversity, abounding in every good, and serving your ministry with faithful love, enjoy the tranquility of peace in the present age and deserve, together with you, to obtain the fellowship of the eternal citizens. Amen.

May he himself deign to grant this.

At the words, “May the Lord crown you,” the bishops placed the crown upon his head.

May the Lord crown you with a crown of glory and righteousness, so that, with right faith and the abundant fruit of good works, you may reach the crown of the everlasting kingdom, granted by him whose kingdom and dominion endure forever and ever.

[Col. 0808B]

At the words, “May the Lord grant you the will,” they gave him the palm and the scepter.

May the Lord grant you the will and the ability to do what he commands, so that, making progress in the governance of the kingdom according to his will, you may reach the palm of everlasting glory with the palm of enduring victory. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives.

# Prayers in the Mass

Grant us, almighty God, that the venerable solemnity of your blessed martyr Gorgonius may increase both our devotion and our salvation. Through the Lord.

### Prayer for the king

We beseech you, almighty God, that your servant, who by your mercy has received the governance of the kingdom, may also receive from you an increase of virtues, so that, nobly adorned with them, he may avoid the monsters of vices and, graciously, reach you who are the way, the truth, and the life. You who live and reign with God.

### Prayer over the offerings

Look, Lord, upon the gifts of your people on this festive occasion, so that the testimony of your truth may benefit us for salvation. Through the Lord.

Sanctify, we beseech you, Lord, the gifts offered, so that they may become for us the body and blood of your Only-Begotten Son, and, by your gift, may benefit our king Charles in obtaining the salvation of soul and body in every way. Through the same Lord.

### Post-communion

May the communion we have received of your sacraments, Lord, save us and strengthen us in the light of your truth. Through the Lord.

## 747

May this saving communion, Lord, protect your servant from every adversity, so that he may obtain the tranquility of ecclesiastical peace and, after the course of this age, reach the eternal inheritance. Through the Lord.

# II. THE CORONATION OF LOUIS II  
### When he was consecrated king of the Franks

[Col. 0809]

The order according to which King Louis was crowned in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 877, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, by Hincmar, archbishop, in the palace of Compiègne; at which time the following petitions were made by the bishops before the king and promises were made by him to the bishops.

## Petition of the bishops

We ask you to grant us that, according to the first chapter that most recently at Quierzy your lord Emperor Charles, your father, publicly declared that he would observe, both on his own behalf and on yours, with the consent of his faithful and yours and of the legates of the Apostolic See, while Gauzlin read it, you preserve for each one of us and for the churches entrusted to us the canonical privilege, the due law and justice, and provide protection, just as a king ought rightly to provide in his kingdom for each bishop and the church entrusted to him.

## Promise of the king

I promise and grant you that, according to the first chapter that most recently at Quierzy my lord Emperor, my father, publicly declared that he would observe, both on his own behalf and on mine, with the consent of his faithful and ours and of the legates of the Apostolic See, while Gauzlin read it, I shall preserve for each one of you and for the churches entrusted to you the canonical privilege, the due law and justice, and, with the Lord’s help, I shall provide as much protection as I can, just as a king ought rightly to provide in his kingdom for each bishop and the church entrusted to him.

# 748 — Blessings made over Louis, king

O God, who in your power care for your peoples and rule them in love, grant this servant of yours the spirit of wisdom together with the governance of discipline, so that, devoted to you with his whole heart, he may always remain capable in the governance of the kingdom; and, through your gift, may the security of the Church be directed during his reign, and Christian devotion remain in tranquility. Through the Lord.

# Pouring of the sacred oil

Almighty and eternal God, creator and governor of heaven and earth, maker and disposer of angels and human beings, who made your servant Abraham triumph over his enemies, who granted manifold victory to Moses and Joshua, leaders of your people; who raised your humble servant David to the height of kingship, and freed him from the mouth of the lion, from the hand of the beast, from Goliath, and also from the evil sword of Saul and all his enemies; and who enriched Solomon with the ineffable gift of wisdom and peace:

Look, we beseech you, upon the prayers of our humility, and adorn this servant of yours with the virtues with which you adorned those faithful servants of yours already named, through a manifold blessing of honor. Exalt him in the governance of the kingdom, and anoint him with the oil of the grace of your Holy Spirit, with which you anointed priests, kings, prophets, and martyrs who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, and obtained the promises.

May its most holy anointing flow down upon his head, descend into his inward parts, and penetrate the innermost recesses of his heart. May he be made worthy by your grace of the promises obtained by the most victorious kings, so that he may reign happily in the present age and reach their fellowship in the heavenly kingdom.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, and by the power of the cross defeated the powers of the air, destroyed Tartarus, overcame the kingdom of the devil, and ascended victoriously to the heavens. In whose hand victory, all glory, and power consist, and who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# Placing of the crown
The Lord crown you with a crown of glory and honor of righteousness, and with the work of strength, so that through the office of our blessing, with right faith and the abundant fruit of good works, you may attain the crown of the everlasting kingdom, by the gift of him whose kingdom and dominion [Col. 0810C] endure for ages of ages. Amen.

### 749. PRESENTATION OF THE SCEPTER

Receive the scepter, the insignia of royal power, namely, the upright staff of the kingdom, the staff of strength, by which you may rightly govern yourself, the holy Church—that is, the Christian people entrusted to you by God—defend them by royal strength against the wicked, correct the perverse, and direct the upright, so that with your help they may keep to the straight way. Thus may you pass from a temporal kingdom to an eternal kingdom, with the help of him whose kingdom and dominion endure without end for ages of ages. Amen.

### BLESSINGS

May the Lord God almighty, who said to Moses his servant, “Speak to Aaron your brother, and to his sons, saying: Thus you shall bless my people, and I will bless them” (Num. VI, 23, 27), bless you and keep you. Amen.

May he make his face shine upon you and have mercy on you. Amen.

May he turn his countenance toward you and grant you peace. Amen.

May he extend the right hand of his blessing and pour out upon you the gift of his reconciliation; may he surround you with the happy wall of his protective guardianship, through the interceding merits of Saint Mary and all the saints. Amen. May he forgive you all the evils you have done and grant you the grace and mercy that you humbly ask of him; may he free you from every adversity and from the snares of all visible and invisible enemies [Col. 0811B]. Amen.

May he increase in you the abundance of his blessing and confirm you in the hope of the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

May he correct your deeds, amend your life, order your conduct, and lead you to the inheritance of the heavenly paradise. Amen.

May you be filled with such an intention as will please him forever. Amen.

May he appoint his good angels always and everywhere to go before you, accompany you, and follow after you, for your protection; and may he free you by his power from sin and the sword, and from the danger of every peril [Col. 0812A]. Amen.

May he turn your enemies toward the kindness of peace and charity, and make you gracious and lovable to those who hate you; may he clothe those who persist in pursuing and hating you with salutary shame; and may everlasting sanctification blossom over you. Amen.

May the Lord always make you victorious and triumphant over visible and invisible enemies; may he continually pour into your heart both fear and love of his holy name; may he make you steadfast in right faith and good works; and, having granted peace in your days, may he lead you with the crown of victory to the everlasting kingdom. Amen.

### 750

And may he who willed to establish you as king over his people grant you happiness in the present age and make you a sharer in eternal blessedness. Amen.

May he cause you, by his ordering and through your administration, to govern happily for many years the clergy and people whom he has willed, with his help, to subject to your authority; so that, obeying the divine commands, free from every adversity, abounding in every good thing, and serving faithfully with devoted love through your ministry, they may enjoy the tranquility of peace in the present age and, with you, deserve to possess the fellowship of the eternal citizens. Amen. May he himself deign to grant this.

## III. THE CORONATION OF JUDITH, DAUGHTER OF CHARLES, BETROTHED TO THE KING OF THE ANGLES

[Col. 0811]

### [Col. 0811C] BLESSING OVER THE QUEEN WHOM KING ÆTHELWULF TOOK AS HIS WIFE

May you be married in Christ, covered by a heavenly cloud, refreshed by spiritual grace, and protected from every unlawful desire. Make a covenant with your eyes, so that you do not look upon another man in order to desire him; do not commit adultery in body or in your heart; and turn your eyes away lest they see vanity. Thus may you be made alive in the way of the Lord, so that you may say with the Prophet: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens” (Ps. CXXII). And: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come” (Ps. CXX). Through the Creator, Redeemer, and Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns [Col. 0811D] for ages of ages.

Bless, O Lord, these marriage gifts, and deign to endow those who receive them with your blessing, so that, keeping the fidelity of marriage and an undefiled marriage-bed, they may deserve to share the fellowship of the holy patriarchs. Through the Lord.

Receive this ring, the sign of faith and love and the bond of marital union, so that man may not separate those whom God joins together. He lives and reigns for all ages of ages.

[Col. 0812C] I betroth you, a chaste virgin, to one man, to be a modest wife, as the holy women were to their husbands: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Esther, Judith, Anna, and Naomi, with Jesus Christ our Lord, the author and sanctifier of marriage, favoring you; he lives and reigns for ages of ages.

O God, who at the beginning of the growing world blessed the increase of offspring, be favorable to our supplications and pour the help of your blessing upon this your servant and this your handmaid, so that in the fellowship of marriage, according to your good pleasure, they may be joined in equal affection, like-mindedness, and mutual holiness. Enrich them with holy fruits and blessed works. Make them beget such offspring as may belong to the inheritance of your paradise. Open, O Lord, [Col. 0812D] the gates of heaven and visit them with peace. Water their land, so that it may produce spiritual fruit. Sanctify them, you who were given to us from a virgin; and grant them the seasons of salvation that the holy prophet John foretold before your coming, so that here they may believe faithfully and, living blessedly, attain life and the eternal kingdom, by your grace, Christ our Savior, who with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, live and reign as God, throughout all ages.

### [Col. 0813A] BLESSING OF THE QUEEN

We invoke you, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, that you may cause this your handmaid, whom by the providence of your divine ordering you have permitted to grow until this day, rejoicing in the flower of youth, enriched by the gift of your compassion, and full of truth, to advance continually toward better things before you and before human beings from day to day. Thus, rejoicing in the abundance of heavenly grace, may she receive it in her rule, and, protected on every side from adversity by the wall of your mercy, may she deserve to live in the peace of your reconciliation. Through the Lord.

### Lift up your hearts.

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, strength of the elect and exaltation of the humble, who at the beginning willed that the sins of the world be cleansed by the outpouring of the Flood [Col. 0813B], and through the dove carrying an olive branch showed that peace had been restored to the earth; you again anointed Aaron your servant as priest through the anointing of oil, and afterward, through the pouring out of his ointment, perfected priests, kings, and prophets for governing the Israelite people. By the prophetic voice of your servant David you foretold that the face of the Church would be gladdened by oil.

You also gladdened the face of your handmaid Judith with this ointment, for the liberation of your servants and the confusion of your enemies; and by this spiritual anointing of your mercy you made the face of your handmaid Esther so radiant that, through her prayers, you inclined the savage heart of the king toward mercy and toward the salvation of those who believe in you. We ask you, almighty God, that through the richness of this created oil [Col. 0813C] you may make her beautiful with the peace, simplicity, and chastity of the dove. Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, who is to come to judge.

### [Col. 0814A] CORONATION

The Lord crowns you with glory and honor, and places upon your head a crown of spiritual precious stone, so that whatever is signified by the brilliance of gold and the varied radiance of gems may always shine forth in your character and in your deeds. May he himself deign to grant this, to whom belong honor and glory for ages of ages.

### BLESSINGS

Bless, O Lord, this your handmaid, you who govern the kingdoms of kings from age to age. Amen.

Receive the work of her hands, and by your blessing may her land be filled with the fruits of the produce of heaven, with dew, and with the deep beneath. Amen.

[Col. 0814B] May she rejoice in your blessing from the summits of the ancient mountains and the everlasting hills, from the fruits of the earth and its fullness. Amen.

May the blessing of him who appeared in the bush come upon her head. Give her from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth an abundance of grain and wine, so that peoples may serve her and her offspring, and, in honor of you, tribes may worship her and her seed. Amen.

Fill her with the blessings of breasts and womb. May the blessings of the ancient fathers, strengthened, rest upon her and upon her offspring, as you promised your servant Abraham and his seed forever. Amen.

Grant, we ask, almighty and merciful God, that these gifts of yours, which your faithful have received from your hand, may, through those who give, receive, and distribute them, [Col. 0814C] contribute to the support of the present life, to the redemption of souls, and to attaining everlasting life. Through the Lord.

## IV. QUEEN HERMINTRUDIS

[Col. 0813]

### [Col. 0813C] ADDRESS OF TWO BISHOPS IN THE CHURCH OF SAINT MEDARD, WHEN HERMINTRUDIS WAS CONSECRATED QUEEN

We wish you to know, brothers, that our lord and senior, the glorious King Charles, has asked the devotion of our humility that, by the authority of the ministry conferred upon us by God, just as he himself was anointed and consecrated king by episcopal authority, with sacred anointing and blessing, as we read in Scripture that the Lord commanded kings to be anointed and consecrated to royal power, so we may bless his wife, our lady, in the name of queen, just as we know that this was previously done for others both by the Apostolic See and by our predecessors.

And lest it seem strange to you why he makes this request, we hasten to give an explanation to your brotherhood. It is because, as is known to many, almighty God by his grace wondrously gathered this kingdom into the hands of his predecessors [Col. 0814C]. They governed it nobly, and their descendants have ruled it by succession down to the present time.

God has also given children to this our lord, as you know. In their nobility, his faithful have rejoiced in the great hope they possess for the holy Church and for the kingdom that God entrusted to him to govern. Of these children, he offered some to God, so that he might offer to God an offering from the fruit of his own womb; God in his grace snatched some, while they were still of immature age, from this world, lest, as it is written, wickedness should change their hearts; and upon others, as you are not unaware, he permitted by his judgment to fall into such suffering as his faithful are known to mourn.

For this reason he asks that an episcopal blessing come upon his wife, so that the Lord may deign to give him through her such offspring as will provide the holy Church [Col. 0815A] with consolation, the kingdom with necessary defense, his faithful with desired assistance, and this Christian people with the tranquility they long for, together with law and justice, alongside the children he still has, if the Lord grants and cooperates.

We have authority for this in the holy Scriptures. For just as the Lord said to Abraham, “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18), and gave him, when he was already a hundred years old, Isaac as a son by his ninety-year-old wife, so he also caused Isaac to take a barren wife, in order that here too, as he often does in many matters, he might show the abundance of his mercy.

Therefore Scripture says that Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren (Gen. XXV, 21), and she conceived. Nor should it seem strange to you that he did not do this earlier [Col. 0815B]. For, as sacred Scripture says, at the beginning of the union of male and female the Lord said to Eve, “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III, 16).

When Abraham and Sarah were already mature in character for a lawful union and advanced in age—and, as Saint Peter says, “Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord” (I Pet. III, 6)—the Lord said to Abraham what we do not read that he had previously said either to him or to any other man: “Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice” (Gen. XXI, 12). By then Abraham was rightly called an elder, and the womanly qualities—that is, all wantonness—had ceased in Sarah. Then they received from the Lord the blessing of blessed offspring, in whom all the nations are blessed. Amen.

Supported, therefore, by these authorities [Col. 0815C], we who have been appointed ministers by him for the distribution of God’s gifts must not be difficult, nor neglect the requests of the devout—especially when we see that those requests have clearly arisen from God’s mercy.

For the manifold mercy of God has determined to aid human salvation in such a way that salvation itself should chiefly be obtained through the supplications of priests. In this work, as we read in the sacred writings, the Savior himself intervenes; nor is he ever absent from those things that he has entrusted to his ministers to perform, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

And if we complete anything through our service in good order and with a rejoicing affection, as Leo says, let us not doubt that it has been given to us through the Holy Spirit. Therefore, brothers [Col. 0815D], since our ministry for you and your united devotion toward us are such that one supplication is made before the Lord, as we read that priests were appointed to pray first for their own sins and then for those of the people—and that prayer was made without ceasing to God for Peter, that is, for the whole company of bishops—while we pray for our common need, or rather for the need and salvation of the whole Church and people, let your common prayer also accompany the common petition before him who makes the like-minded dwell in one house, and who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

### PRAYER

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who by the power of your strength made all things from nothing, and, having ordered the beginnings of the universe, created for the human being made in your image an inseparable helpmate in woman, giving the female body its beginning from male flesh, teaching that what you willed to be instituted from one person may not be separated by human beings: look favorably upon this your handmaid, joined in marital fellowship and seeking to be fortified by your protection.

May the yoke of love and peace be upon her. May she marry faithfully and chastely in Christ, and remain an imitator of holy women. May she be lovable to her husband like Rachel, wise like Rebekah, long-lived and faithful like Sarah. May the author of transgression seize nothing in her through her deeds; may she remain bound to the commands of faith, joined to one marriage-bed, and avoid unlawful contacts. May she fortify her weakness [Col. 0816B] with the strength of discipline.

May she be grave in modesty, venerable in chastity, and instructed in heavenly teachings. May she be fruitful in offspring pleasing to you; may she be approved and innocent. Through this sacred anointing with the oil of mercy, joy, and exultation, may she receive soundness of mind, bodily health, protection of salvation, security of hope, strengthening of faith, and fullness of charity.

Crown her, O Lord, with the crown of righteousness; crown her with holy fruits and blessed works. May she be queen in merit, name, and virtue, standing in this world with right faith and good works, and in the future crowned with honor and glory at the right hand of the king, clothed in good works and surrounded by a variety of virtues.

Make her beget such offspring as may belong to the inheritance of your paradise. Grant, O Lord, to this [Col. 0816C] your handmaid such affection of charity, devotion to mercy, and growth in religion that she may continually deserve your help.

Drive away from her the poisons of the crafty serpent, and defend her, clothed in the breastplate of faith, with the shield of salvation. Correct her deeds, amend her life, order her conduct, and deign to lead her in a good old age to the heavenly kingdoms. Through the same Lord.

May the Lord crown you with glory and honor and everlasting protection. He lives and reigns.

Almighty God, who blessed Adam and Eve, saying, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I, 28), and who blessed the marriages of the patriarchs, and who sent Raphael his angel with Tobias, by whose ministry he drove the demon away from Sarah his wife, may he bless you and Ill., your future wife, so that, according to the Lord’s command, you may become two in one flesh, and so that what God joins together no human being may separate. May he give you the blessing of the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth.

For we bless you in the name of the Lord. May he send his good angels to guard you always and drive away from you every phantom, wickedness, and cunning of all evil spirits and human beings; may they protect, fortify, and defend you from every defilement of adultery and from every human and diabolical snare, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

May he continually pour his love and fear into your hearts, so that you may grow old together in a good old age and see the children of your children [Col. 0817A] flourishing according to the will of the Lord. May peace remain with you. Persevering in right faith, good works, good harmony, sincere marital love, confession of the Holy Trinity, and communion with the Catholic Church [Col. 0818A], may you attain eternal life. May he himself deign to grant this, whose kingdom and dominion endure without end for ages of ages. Amen.

## [EXPLANATION OF THE LITTER OF SOLOMON]

[Col. 0817]

### ADMONITION TO THE READER CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING OPUSCULE

Hincmar, as Flodoard bears witness, had written a remarkable work in verse for King Charles, which he called *The Litter of Solomon*. It consisted of 446 verses, and he had added to it another portion in prose containing its explanation [Col. 0818A]. This is what is now being brought to light for the first time from an ancient copy. Of the first part, we have so far seen nothing except twelve verses, which we shall present in their proper place among the author’s fragments.

[Col. 0817]

### EXPLANATION OF THE LITTER OF SOLOMON BY HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS (C)

[Col. 0817B] 756

This royal litter, which the holy teachers say signifies the Church, namely, the body of Christ, into whose unity each person is incorporated through faith in that same Christ, as we showed above, is called in Scripture by many names: the kingdom of heaven, woman, bride, wife, dove, beloved, vineyard, sheep, sheepfold, city, tower, column, firmament, house, temple, body of Christ, fullness of Christ, dragnet, wedding, supper, and others that the reader may perhaps discover.

King Solomon—that is, “peaceful,” Idida—that is, “beloved of the Lord,” Coheleth—that is, “preacher”—made this litter for himself, namely, for the Church itself. Solomon was called by these three names because the whole Holy Trinity fashioned the temple of the true Solomon, namely, the body of the Mediator between God and human beings, in the womb of the blessed, glorious, ever-Virgin Mary, his own mother, our Lady and sovereign.

For the Holy Spirit came upon her, and the power of the Most High Father overshadowed her. Therefore everything born from her, from two substances and in two substances and natures, in the unity of one person, is called holy and is the Son of God. Through him glory is sung to God in the highest, and on earth there is peace among people of good will. He is the beloved Son in whom the Father was well pleased; from his face come knowledge and understanding; and by his Holy Spirit he teaches the Church all truth.

This King of kings and Lord of lords made this litter for himself from the woods of Lebanon, because he built the Church from souls strong in courage and steadfastness. The woods of Lebanon greatly excel in height, beauty, and their naturally incorruptible character. So these rational and fruitful woods excel in these and other virtues—not from themselves, but from him who arranged these same woods in the building of this litter, that is, the Church, by the gracious gift of his predestination and election, freely bestowed. He is the one who wills all people to be saved and wills no one to perish.

For just as he fashioned Eve from the rib of the sleeping Adam in paradise, so, through the grace of ineffable mercy, while sleeping on the cross and pouring water and blood from his side—by which she might be moistened with a washing and given drink—he built the Church. He cleanses her with the washing of water [757] in the word and redeems her with precious blood, namely, the blood of the spotless and undefiled Lamb, who is Christ Jesus himself. He sanctifies her with his Holy Spirit, saving in each person the whole human being—body and soul—he who suffered for all. And he did this on the Sabbath, that is, in the rest of the Church’s unity, in which the faithful advance toward everlasting rest through the hope of salvation; for we have been saved in hope.

The columns of this litter are two, because the crowds that came before and those that follow the Lord’s coming, saved and destined to be saved through faith in the Mediator himself, the peaceful king and builder of the litter, cry out with one confession of belief, saying, “Hosanna.” For Peter says: “Through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved, just as they are” (Acts XV, 11).

Or certainly the columns of the litter are two because whoever perseveres in the unity of the present Church with right faith and good works will rejoice forever in the future—that is, the eternal—Church, filled and glorified with indescribable exultation through the incorruption of both soul and body [Col. 0818D].

For God has balanced all things according to the measure in which quality is established, the number in which quantity is contained, and the weight in which reason is signified. Thus the souls of the elect receive the weight of virtue, not of burden, by the arrangement of him who, according to Job, “gave weight to the winds” (Job XXVIII, 25). Thus they no longer leap away from God’s purpose with a light movement, but stand fixed in him with the weight of steadfastness.

By these things all is established in his judgment and forever; by these things he established the world, governs it, and will judge it. He cannot be comprehended or reproved, and he has arranged all things so as to render rewards or punishments to each person.

The first column of this litter consists of thirty-three chapters, because whoever is baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit must steadfastly keep the commandments of the Decalogue together with faith in the Holy Trinity, if he wishes to attain everlasting life.

The number ten is multiplied three times in these same chapters, with the ternary number superimposed upon it, because the woman—that is, the Catholic Church—took the leaven, namely, faith in the Holy Trinity working through love, and hid it in three measures of flour when she arranged for it to be preached in Asia, Africa, and Europe, until the whole was leavened—that is, until the Gospel of the kingdom received from the Lord Jesus Christ concerning what he began both to do and to teach had been preached throughout the whole world.

On the third day mentioned in the Gospel reading, he came to the wedding. This means that in the third age of the world, through the mystery of the Incarnation, he joined the same holy Church to himself. The first age of the world, before the Law, shone through the examples of the patriarchs; the second, under the Law, through the writings of the prophets; and the third, under grace, through the proclamations of the evangelists, shining upon the world like the light of the third day. In this third age our Lord and Savior appeared incarnate for the redemption of the human race.

Moreover, the number ten, multiplied into a triangle, produces the number thirty—the age in which Christ was baptized and sanctified all the waters by his baptism. By the grace of this sanctification, Jesus came to baptism in the thirtieth year of his age, because after this baptism he was going to release the old Law.

Therefore he remained in observance of the Law until this age, which is capable of containing every sin, lest anyone should say that he abolished the Law because he was unable to fulfill it. For not every age is equally exposed to every vice. In the earliest years, ignorance and weakness of mind beset a person together; in adolescence, more ardent desire attacks him; and in later age, the craving for possession especially troubles him.

Therefore Christ waited through this entire age. In this way he fulfilled the righteousness of the Law throughout the whole period, and then at last came to baptism, as though completing the culmination of all the observances of the Law. Since, by the baptism that he began at the age of thirty, he was to cleanse the filth of the whole Church, the mystical kinship of these numbers also declares the same thing.

For thirty, when calculated by its equal parts, produces an additional twelve, the number of the patriarchs and apostles, making forty-two. Its parts are: thirtieth, one; fifteenth, two; twelfth, three; sixth, five; fifth, six; third, ten; and half, fifteen. Added together, these complete forty-two.

Mystically, as we have said, this indicates that the whole perfection of the Church consists in the faith and grace of Christ, first recognized by the patriarchs and spread more widely by the voice of the apostles. There is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved, just as in the number forty-two there is no part that is not contained among the equal parts of the number thirty.

Thus the number thirty completes the forty-second by its parts, because the Lord now protects the Church, laboring in time, through the sacraments of his baptism, and, when its labors are ended, leads it eternally to rest.

The thirty-year age of the baptized Savior can also disclose the mystery of our baptism: namely, faith in the Holy Trinity and the working of the Decalogue, with the grace of faith revealed. The more sublimely this is understood, the more widely it is proclaimed.

The number twelve, which, as we said, is produced by the parts of thirty, is the number of the apostles, that is, the whole choir of preachers. It is recognized to contain three fours or four threes, because the faith of the Holy Trinity and the four books of the holy Gospel must be preached by orthodox teachers throughout the four regions—East, West, North, and South—within the four-sided bounds of the world.

He taught that those to be baptized should have, as it were, a sacred period of three years when he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son [Col. 0820C] and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). He commanded this same three-year period to be multiplied by ten when he added: “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (ibid., 20).

For three years and six months he deigned, by his example and word, to illuminate the darkness of the world, healing bodies and souls through the love of God and neighbor; and for the salvation of the human race he died upon the cross [759].

He clearly showed that there are many righteous people in the Church, distinct from the eminent apostles, martyrs, confessors, and other men of stricter and more perfect life—whose indescribable glory from the most manifest vision of the divinity and of the eternal Trinity is known only to those who have deserved to enjoy it—who are perfected in faith in the Holy Trinity, in which the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ is also truly contained, and in hope, charity, and good works.
