The Incarnation did not introduce a quaternity; rather, in the one Son, God and human, who is in the glory of God the Father, the Trinity remains with the same Father and the Holy Spirit. After the dissolution of the flesh, such people are immediately received into the blessed rest of paradise. They await, amid great joy and great choirs of rejoicing, the time when, having received back their bodies, they will come and appear before the face of God.

The half-year indicates that some, though indeed predestined by their good works for the portion of the elect, nevertheless, because of certain evils with which they were polluted when they left the body, are after death severely chastised and received into the flames of purgatorial fire. Either they are cleansed from the stain of their vices by this long examination until the day of judgment, or, earlier, they are released from their punishments through the prayers, almsgiving, fasts, tears, and offerings of the saving sacrifice made by faithful friends, and themselves reach the rest of the blessed.

For the same number of years—that is, three and a half—the Antichrist will display the fabrications of his falsehood, showing himself as though he were God by signs and lying wonders, and employing the terrors of threats and punishments. But he will not prevail against those who persist, with the help of his grace, in the perfection of right faith and good works.

When he appeared in the flesh, made from a woman and made under the Law in order to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons, he was brought to the temple on the thirty-third day after his circumcision, and the offerings prescribed by the Law were presented for him—he who consecrates all things divinely.

The triangular number of the Decalogue, the three days, and the offering brought to the temple signify those days and the sacrifice of the Church, which is the body of Christ. Concerning them he himself says in the Gospel: “Behold, I cast out demons and accomplish healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke XIII, 32).

Demons are cast out when the nations, abandoning their ancestral superstitions, believe in him. Healings are accomplished when people live according to his commands after renouncing the devil and this world, continuing until the end of the resurrection. Through that resurrection, which is like the third day of perfection, the Church will be perfected—that is, brought to angelic fullness—even through the immortality of the body.

Therefore, by the meaning of this number, every devout person should understand that only the one will be saved from corruption of body and soul who, on the day of recompense, is found perfected in right faith, signified by the number three, and in good works, signified by the Decalogue, that is, by the number ten—found as a perfect man, according to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.

### 760

This column is also recognized to consist of 210 verses, speaking through the thoughts of the teachers against those who hold perverse opinions concerning ecclesiastical doctrines. The purpose of this calculation is that we should begin first from the lesser number, namely ten, and proceed from it thereafter.

Catholic teachers have spoken many eloquent and powerful things about the number ten, some of which I have taken care to record here briefly. They say that the number ten is consecrated in the Decalogue. God gave his servant Moses the ten commandments of this Decalogue—that is, of the ten-stringed psaltery—written on two stone tablets on the mountain.

Three commandments on one tablet pertain to God, because God is Trinity; and in the mystery of our redemption there are three who bear witness: spirit, water, and blood, and the three are one. The spirit is that of sanctification, the blood that of redemption, and the water that of baptism. These three are one and remain indivisible; nothing is separated from their connection. As blessed Ambrose sings:

> All things flourish in threes beneath the majesty of the Thunderer.  
>   
> Three are the Father, the Word, and likewise the Holy Spirit—one.  
>   
> Threefold is the saving form of the cross; one is the redeeming one.  
>   
> The third light received the Lord returning from death.  
>   
> For three days the whale held Jonah in its belly.  
>   
> Three youths believed God in the blazing furnace.  
>   
> Three times the blessing sings, proclaiming the holiness of Sabaoth.  
>   
> Three times must the one full of the grace of the washing be plunged into water.  
>   
> Every action is established and made firm by three witnesses.  
>   
> In the third month the seasons return to their limbs.  
>   
> There are three ages: the flower of youth, strength, and sickly old age.  
>   
> There are three roles in legal cases: judge, defender, and plaintiff.  
>   
> There are three stages through the ages: origin, passage, and end.

Three things that caress hope: rest, light, glory of life.

But the second tablet gave seven commandments, the first of which is, as the Apostle also shows, “Honor your father and mother” (Ephesians 6:2). Moreover, the number seven displays its perfection in sacred Scripture in many ways: namely, because, as Scripture testifies, God rested from his works after heaven and all its adornment had been perfected in that number of days [Col. 0822B] (Genesis 2); and through the Law the Sabbath was also given for rest (Exodus 16). In our Head, moreover—that is, in Christ Jesus, the Mediator between God and humanity—the prophet enumerated the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit (Isaiah 11). Sacred Scripture also mentions seven eyes, seven lampstands, seven seals, and seven thunders as symbols of perfection; and the whole age of the world revolves through seven days (Revelation 1, 5, 6, 10).

And by these two perfect numbers, namely three and seven, the number ten is constituted. It is also constituted by doubling the number five, which is perfect in the five most familiar senses of our body and in the five books of Moses. The number ten is likewise completed sequentially from one through four. [761] For one, two, three, and four taken together make ten, because the Decalogue of the Law is fulfilled through the four books of the holy Gospel. Perhaps for this reason those who are hired for the vineyard receive a denarius as their wage: multiplied by itself, it rises to one hundred, and through the number one hundred great perfection is signified.

By the doubled hundred, moreover, both the perfection of the spirit granted to the elect in this life and everlasting life are signified. Hence the Lord says to these same elect:

“Everyone who leaves house or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for my name will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29).

For no saint abandons earthly things so that he may possess them more abundantly in this world; whoever leaves the earth out of earthly ambition does not leave the earth but desires it. [Col. 0822D] Nor will the man who abandons one wife receive a hundred. Rather, perfection is signified by the number one hundred, after which eternal life is promised: whoever, for God’s name, despises temporal and earthly things receives perfection of mind even here, so that he no longer desires what he has despised, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life, which is signified by the number one hundred, transferred from the left to the right.

Therefore this couch, or this table—namely, holy Church—says of its maker, the true Solomon:

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song of Songs 2:6).

By his left hand [Col. 0823A] the present life, the sacraments of his incarnation, and the gifts of his presence are signified; by his right hand, the future life and the rewards that the elect will receive in the future are represented. Among these there is not only the vision of the divine majesty but also the glory of his glorified humanity, belonging to the one and same Mediator between God and humanity.

Accordingly, the bride rightly desires that his left hand be placed beneath her head and that she be embraced by his right hand, so that now she may rest from the disturbances of the world through his temporal assistance, and then may perpetually enjoy his manifest vision. Indeed, no storm ever interrupts the eternal rest of the saints. Hence it is rightly said, “His right hand will embrace me,” because the presence of the divine majesty will surround his own on every side in the heavenly kingdom, so that neither the memory of misery may violate any happiness worthy of God nor fear of the end constrain them. [Col. 0823B]

The doubled hundred also indicates that whoever desires to reach everlasting life must burn with love of God and neighbor, and must continually strive to hasten toward it through Catholic faith and right action. He must believe in orthodox faith concerning the holy and inseparable Trinity and concerning the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ—believing in his heart unto righteousness and confessing with his mouth unto salvation—that in this same holy Trinity there is nothing earlier or later, nothing greater or less, but that all three persons are coeternal and coequal with one another. Thus, in every respect, there is both the unity of deity in the Trinity of persons and the Trinity of persons in the unity of deity.

For from the Father alone—that is, from the substance of the Father—[762] the Son is begotten, equal and consubstantial, not made. [Col. 0823C] And from the Father together with the Son the Holy Spirit proceeds, equally coequal and consubstantial; he is worshiped equally with the Father and the Son, because he is equally God, wholly the Spirit of the Father and wholly the Spirit of the Son, since by nature he is one Spirit of both Father and Son.

Accordingly, he proceeds wholly from the Father and wholly from the Son; he remains wholly in the Father and wholly in the Son, because he remains in such a way that he proceeds, and proceeds in such a way that he remains. Hence by nature he possesses with the Father and the Son this fullness of unity and unity of fullness: he possesses the whole Father and the whole Son, and he himself is wholly possessed by the Father and wholly possessed by the Son. He is also given equally by the Father and the Son—indeed, he is given by himself as well. He is called the gift of God and the Paraclete, that is, the Comforter, because, while [Col. 0823D] distributing the gifts of the sacraments, he truly provides consolation to the soul. Through him the love of God is poured into our hearts, and through that love the entire Trinity dwells within us.

## Concerning the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ

Concerning the Incarnation also of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him hold faithfully that there is one person, from the same holy Trinity and in the same holy Trinity: namely, believing that he is God, true and perfect before all ages and without any beginning, and true and perfect man at the end of the ages, existing in one person in two natures and from two natures and substances. He who by the power of his divinity had created us to enjoy the blessedness of everlasting life restored us by the frailty of our humanity so that we might receive [Col. 0824A] the life we had lost.

According to the truth of the Creed, he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, who through his divinity was the servant of that man and through his flesh the mother of the Word. For the truth of the Gospel, together with the voice of Elizabeth, demonstrates that she was both the Lord’s servant and his mother—not the servant of one and the mother of another. For flesh was not first conceived in the Virgin’s womb and divinity only afterward come into the flesh; rather, at once the Word, the only-begotten one equal to the Father before the ages, came into the womb. At once the Word, while preserving the truth of its own nature, became flesh; and the same perfect man, truly possessing flesh and a rational soul, was born through the Virgin’s womb by the inscrutable miracle wrought by the Holy Spirit: the Son of God became the Son of man, one Christ.

He [Col. 0824B] died in the flesh alone for our sins and rose again in the flesh alone, because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, so that the soul might rise from the death of sin contracted in whatever manner. He also ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father—that is, in the glory of the Father’s majesty—and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

At his coming all human beings will rise with their bodies and will give an account of their own deeds. Those who, by the grace of God and by free will following that same grace, persevere in right faith and good works, having been foreknown and predestined by God for glory, will go into eternal life, prepared by God for the elect—that is, those chosen by grace from the mass of perdition of the entire human race, made in Adam himself when he sinned, for Eve herself also is Adam. [763] [Col. 0824C] As the Truth itself says:

“Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

Those who are not predestined by God for destruction, but are left by him in the mass of perdition as a just recompense, and who persevere in unbelief or evil works, will go into eternal fire. God predestined no one to that fire; rather, in a just recompense, he prepared that same fire for the devil and his body. As the Apostle says in the Gospel:

“The wages of sin,” he says, “are death, but the grace of God is eternal life” (Romans 6:23).

And:

“All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10).

And:

“Wrath—that is, vengeance—is in his indignation, and life is in his goodwill” (Psalm 29:6).

The other column of this table, therefore, contradicting [Col. 0824D] those who hold erroneous opinions about what will be accomplished for us in the other age, consists of thirty-eight sections. It indicates a languid man lying for thirty-eight years in the portico of the synagogue of Satan rather than in the bosom of the Catholic Church—namely, the chorus of those who hold erroneous opinions—whose number is thirty-eight, lacking two from the number forty, which is fulfilled by the Decalogue of the Law through the four books of the holy Gospel, and walking empty of love of God and neighbor, which the Scripture of both Law and Gospel commends.

Although there are many in this chorus, if they consent to submit to the truth, they will recover as one person in the unity of faith. For outside the unity of the Catholic faith no place of salvation is open to anyone. Whoever departs from that unity [Col. 0825A] can in no way attain the salvation that comes from the One.

This salvation is signified by the number one hundred, the number of verses in this side of the table: for Isaac, the son of promise, whose name means “laughter” or “joy,” was born to Abraham when he was a hundred years old, signifying the one who said to his disciples:

“Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

This salvation of eternal joy is reached through sixty, as the sixty additional verses show, a perfect number. Since six times ten make sixty, the number sixty contains the perfection signified by six in works: for just as the marvelous Creator is perfect in his nature, so he completed his works in six days; on the sixth day he created the human being perfect in soul and body, for whose sake all things were created; and in the sixth [Col. 0825B] age the Creator came to restore the human being whom he had created on the sixth day.

The number sixty also contains ten, which is consecrated in the Decalogue and, as we showed above, is brought to perfection. The perfection of sixty in this way is also demonstrated. Divide sixty by ten, and you will find that the number sixty is perfected by ten, just as six is perfected by one. For one, two, and three make six, which is a perfect number in its parts; likewise, sixty possesses a certain perfection when divided by the number ten. Once ten, twice ten, and three times ten [764] make sixty. [Col. 0825C]

The number sixty also includes the number fifty, by which the Jubilee year is expressed—that is, the remission of sins, the return to the inheritance of the eternal homeland, and everlasting rest. It also surpasses the married order by its doubling, while indicating laborious widowhood through the impression of a finger, since “she who sowed in tears will reap in joy.”

It contains thirty within itself. This number is depicted by the gentle kiss of the index finger and thumb and represents the married woman, bringing forth the fruit of faith through good works, like good earth producing from the seed of the divine word that it has received. In the same way, the number one hundred, transferred from the left to the right, makes a circle with the same fingers, though not the same hand, by which married women and widows are signified in the left hand, and expresses the crown of virginity.

The Word also produces thirtyfold fruit, which builds up faith in the holy Trinity; sixtyfold fruit, which teaches perfection of works; and hundredfold fruit, which proclaims everlasting life at the right hand of the kingdom. [Col. 0825D]

It is therefore necessary that whoever desires life and wishes to see good days should hasten, through the six days or ages of this world in which it is permitted to work, toward the Sabbath—that is, toward the rest of the seventh day or age, when it will no longer be permitted to work—by right faith and righteous works, fulfilling the commandments of the Decalogue without the admixture of evil deeds. Thus, when departing from the body, he may rest in the seventh day or age, or in the repose signified by the number fifty, until he attains the everlastingness signified by one hundred on the eighth day or age, together with the incorruption of bodies.

Hence the golden couch of this [Col. 0826A] table sings in a number of eight verses, because whoever, in the present life—that is, in these six days or ages in which it is permitted to work—has taken care to purify himself by the knife of that rock which is Christ, in imitation of the eighth day designated by the circumcision of the eighth day, which was given to the ancients in place of baptism, through faith, hope, and charity—not only in baptism but in every devout action—will happily rest on the seventh day of the Sabbath and will rise glorified on the eighth.

This is also our daily circumcision, that is, the continual cleansing of the heart, which never ceases to celebrate the sacrament of the eighth day. For it is accustomed to sanctify us in imitation of the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the Sabbath—so that, just as Christ rose [Col. 0826B] from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.

This is the eighth and complete day of our resurrection, blessed without any end of time. Then, when the true glory of complete circumcision shines forth, the corruptible body will no longer weigh down the soul, nor will an earthly dwelling any longer depress the mind occupied with many thoughts. Rather, the body, now incorruptible, will bring joy to the soul, and the heavenly dwelling will lift up the whole human being, who will cling to the vision of his Creator. Then our youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.

Our Solomon made this couch for us when he promised the faithful the hope of perpetual rest:

“Take my yoke upon you,” [765] he says, “and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:[Col. 0826C] 29).

He made this couch golden because he prepared for us eternal rest, radiant with the glory of his divine vision. Hence it is said:

“Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

Or certainly he made the couch in the table golden for the faithful because we will all rise, but not all will be changed. Christ, who suffered for all, obtained resurrection for all, but for the faithful he obtained the glory of incorruption of both soul and body. Of them it is said:

“They will rise in the resurrection of the just” (Luke 14:14),

although all will undoubtedly rise.

The ascent of this table Idida—that is, the beloved Son of the Father in whom he was well pleased—made purple. True purple is dyed with the blood of sea-shellfish [Col. 0826D], because the living and abundant redeeming blood of the immaculate and undefiled Lamb, Jesus Christ, conceived from the Holy Spirit—that is, through the working of the Holy Spirit—from virginal blood belonging to the seed-bearing nature, namely from the immaculate flesh of the Virgin, without any carnal desire and without any male touch, uniquely conceived, and wondrously born with the Virgin’s womb closed and her virginity intact, unshaken, and undefiled, washed us from our sins.

The blood of that Lamb, which takes away the sins of the world, is drawn from sea-shellfish by iron, because it proceeded through the succession of the race of sinful human beings, oppressed as though by the waves of the sea, as the Gospel genealogy shows, from the stock of Abraham and David. [Col. 0827A] Through the cutting of iron—that is, through the nails and the lance—the mysteries of our redemption flowed out to us from that most sacred body in which God was reconciling the world to himself, and in which all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

By these mysteries the same King and Lord of ours, who loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood, takes away the sins of the world and washes us from our daily sins—not only when he gave his blood for us on the cross, or when each of us is washed in the waters of baptism into the mystery of his most holy passion, but also every day, when the memory of that blessed passion is renewed at the altar, and when the created substance of bread and wine is transferred into the sacrament of his body and blood by the ineffable sanctification of the [Col. 0827B] Spirit.

Thus his body and blood are not poured out and slain by the hands of unbelievers to their destruction, but are received by the mouths of the faithful for their salvation. The ascent to this table is found to be purple for no other reason than that no one enters the Church unless imbued with the sacraments of the Lord’s passion. Hence he himself says:

“Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5).

And:

“Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood will have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6:54–55).

The purple ascent of the table is described in thirty verses because, according to the Apostle,

“Whoever of us were baptized [766] in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Romans 6:3), [Col. 0827C]

that is, into the one baptized at the age of thirty. In this number thirty, the number ten of the Decalogue is tripled, because the perfection of faith and good works is brought to completion through the sanctification of baptism. In it all righteousness is fulfilled, because in it are the redemption of Christ’s blood, the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, and the perfect cleansing of baptismal water.

In this table Solomon, truly the peaceful one who reconciled through the blood of his cross the things in heaven and the things on earth, and who, having broken down the dividing wall, made both one, joining the two in himself, spread the middle with love for the daughters of Jerusalem. [Col. 0827D] It was that very love with which he suffered for us:

“Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.”

And as the Apostle says:

“God demonstrates his own love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:8).

Indeed, he prepared this middle part of his Church like a bed, where faithful souls might rest softly, because he filled its entire interior with love of heavenly things. This is what he adds:

“For the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song of Songs 3:10),

that is, for souls burning with desire for heavenly things. The greater the love God commended to us by suffering, the more people he inflamed to love him in return and to suffer for him.

That love—or rather, our mercy, to which the Psalmist says, “My God, my mercy” [Col. 0828A] (Psalm 58:18)—namely, the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world and washed us from our sins in his blood, is depicted on the cross in two verses, with the same Lamb and, in that same Lamb, singing in one and the same letter. That cross, moreover, in four verses of one measure, with corresponding letters at the beginning or end, embraces in its complete circuit, through the four regions of the world, the sons of promise and Christ’s coheirs of the eternal inheritance—that is, the elect and those predestined to life—in the bosom of Christ’s redemption, he who suffered for all.

It proclaims to the world the measure of that cross: its length and breadth, its height and depth, in the love of God and neighbor. These two and four verses joined together complete the number six, because [Col. 0828B] on the sixth day the human being was created, and on the sixth day he was likewise restored through the mystery of the cross.

Among the sages of the world, the number six is therefore said to be perfect because it is completed when counted in its proper order: when one, two, and three are named, the number six is fulfilled. Or it is perfect because it is divided into three parts, namely a sixth, a third, and a half—that is, into one, two, and three.

Ecclesiastical teachers, however, call it perfect because on the sixth day God completed all his works, and because there are six ages of this world, distinguished by the most familiar divisions of time. In these, as in six days during which it is permitted to work, it is necessary to labor for God and to work for the attainment of everlasting rest. After the six days, the Savior showed his disciples the glory of his promised kingdom, because [767] whoever desires [Col. 0828C] to see God and to share in the glory of the blessed resurrection must perform the good works he knows throughout the six days.

There are also six stone jars in the Gospel: namely, the strong hearts of the saints, filled with faith and love of God and neighbor, and with the purest and unmixed knowledge of sacred Scripture, free from every admixture of heretical perversity. For whoever desires to be saved must not only hold faithfully what concerns the faith of the holy Trinity and the Lord’s Incarnation; he must also take the greatest care to preserve himself and his hearers in all ecclesiastical doctrines, free from every heretical plague and schismatic severance, to wash them from the filth of sins, and to give them drink from the pure fountain of divine knowledge. This applies especially to all [Col. 0828D] those whose perfection of life and faith is rightly recognized as set before others as an example of correct belief and conduct.

Finally, the preface of the table, addressing the most beloved prince, is written by way of exposition of that same table in twenty-four verses. This is because it describes one who is filled with right faith, good works, and the merit of life and learning; filled with love of God and neighbor and with pious devotion and action in every respect; and holding a right opinion concerning grace and free will. As the Lord says through the prophet to every faithful person:

“From me your fruit has been found” (Hosea 14:9);

that is, the gift of my prevenient grace, by which you act well, is from me, and fruit has been found through your subsequent free will.

Thus the Lord shows that whatever good we wish, think, say, and do belongs both to God, through prevenient grace, and to us, through the subsequent obedience of free will. [Col. 0829A] Therefore we will be rewarded, and we will sing the Lord’s mercies forever; but the disobedient will justly be condemned.

For this reason the writer desires the king to live well in this age and to reign with Christ forever. Accordingly, in the same preface the number ten is doubled, a number completed through the four books of the holy Gospel, because “without faith it is impossible to please God,” and “faith without works is dead in itself.”

In it the number two is also doubled, because knowledge puffs up, but love together with sound knowledge builds up. “Understanding is good for all who practice it”; and above love of God, to which no measure of number is assigned, since it is commanded with all our heart, all our mind, and all our strength [Col. 0829B], love of neighbor is subdivided into two commandments, when it is said (Tobit 4; Matthew 7):

“What you do not want done to you, do not do to another; and whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them.”

The completion, which presents the total number of verses, is composed in eight verses and is placed beneath the reclining table, which signifies the eighth day of the resurrection: for just as there are two deaths—the death of the body, namely, through the soul’s departure from it, and the death of the soul through the admission of sin into it—so also there are two resurrections: that of the soul, when the vivification of forgiveness is obtained by God’s grace through worthy fruits of repentance; 768 and that of the body, when at the Lord’s coming all human beings will rise with their bodies and render an account of their own deeds. Blessed is the one who will have a share in the first resurrection, for he will not be harmed by the second death, and he will receive two robes, namely, immortality and incorruption, of body and soul together.

But the signification of this first resurrection is rightly placed beneath that which is superior in dignity, in the order of precedence: just as Scripture also speaks of the kind of compunction when it says: “His father gave him, namely Caleb, the upper and lower spring for his daughter Achsah” (Judg. I, 15). The elect first weep from the lower spring of the soul, so that they may not be led to punishment, and afterward from the upper spring, because access to the kingdom is being delayed.

The total number of verses of the table—of heroic and elegiac verse—which the completion indicated, consists of four hundred and forty-six verses, and one multiplied by ten produces the number ten. Since we have already spoken sufficiently about this above, we avoid repeating it here. For ten multiplied by four rises to forty: we fulfill the commandments of the Decalogue when we keep the four books of the holy Gospel. We preserve them more humbly if we continually consider from where, to where, and in what manner we have fallen.

For we departed from our own region—that is, from paradise—to this valley of tears by pride, disobedience, pursuit of visible things, and tasting the forbidden food. But it is necessary that we return to it by weeping, obeying, despising visible things, and restraining the appetite of the flesh. And because we fell from the joys of paradise through food, let us rise again to them, insofar as we can, through abstinence. This abstinence, signifying that the whole period of our life ought to consist in restraint from evil works and in the practice of virtues, is observed through the number forty days. For just as the children of Israel, in whose place we have succeeded, after crossing the Red Sea spent forty years in misery amid the desolation of the wilderness before they came to the land of promise, so we also suffer in the hardships of this exile the punishments deserved for disobedience before we return to the joys of paradise.

In this probation, after holy baptism, we must first be given over to long struggles in the practice of virtues and afterward to the everlasting gifts of heavenly blessedness. Having received God’s law—that is, having heard the divine word—we must leave our former way of life and enter the solitude of the spiritual life. Thus, if we wish to enter the promised land, we may be daily chastened by the life of our new conduct and cleansed from every contagion of creeping vices, as though by a daily baptism in the Jordan, through tears of the most salutary compunction, according to him who said: “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI, 7).

Hence the stream of the Jordan is rightly interpreted as “judgment,” because the more carefully the elect examine their conscience by judging themselves, the more abundant are the tears they pour forth from the innermost fountain of the heart. Since they discover that they are less than perfect, they wash away the filth of their weakness in the waters of repentance.

But 769 the significance of the number forty—placed in Scripture for the sake of perfection through the outpouring of the flood, Jacob’s mourning, the discipline of the children of Israel in the wilderness, the preaching of Jonah, and many other manifestations—also indicates something else of the greatest necessity. Moses suspended for forty years in the wilderness the divinely commanded custom of circumcision, which had been observed for four hundred and six years; Joshua completed it with stone knives, because “the rock was Christ,” and “the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”

Moses himself also fasted twice for forty days in order to receive the law that he was to deliver to God’s people. Elijah abstained in the wilderness for forty days. The very author of humanity, when he came to humanity, took no food at all for forty days. Why, then, is the number forty observed in abstinence, unless because the virtue of the Decalogue is preserved through the four books of the holy Gospel? And since through carnal desires we have despised the commandments of the Decalogue, it is fitting that we afflict this same flesh four times tenfold.

And so that, through keeping the commandments of the Decalogue and through abstinence worthy of God, we may be carried to eternal life—which is signified by the number one hundred—by the Gospel quadriga and the four cardinal virtues, it is necessary that the number forty be multiplied by the ten of the Decalogue and thus raised to the number four hundred. For forty multiplied by ten makes four hundred, because all the elect will attain eternal life, which is represented by the number one hundred multiplied by four. They will attain it not only through the incorruption of soul and body together, but also through the vision of the divine majesty, with the glorified humanity of the mediator between God and humanity. Having returned without end to that for which they were created, they will rejoice in the true Jubilee, namely, the fiftieth year.

Since the holy Church, in some of its members, still labors on earth for eternal rest, while in others, all labor having ended, already reigns with Christ in heaven, our fathers established these two fitting religious solemnities in memory of both lives: namely, Lent, a time of affliction as Easter approaches, and the fifty days beginning with the very day of the Lord’s resurrection, during which the “Alleluia” is continually sung. The evangelist John testifies that he heard it sung by angels (Rev. XIX). And the venerable father Tobias, understanding from an angelic vision what the glory of the citizens above and the splendor of the heavenly Jerusalem are, said: “Through its streets Alleluia will be sung” (Tob. XIII, 22), although praise of God never ceases in the Church.

And because the celebration of this fifty-day period signifies to the faithful the perfection of rest, while the number ten expresses the fullness of perfection, ten times fifty reaches five hundred. It is plainly shown that abstinence from flesh alone in food and drink does not restore us to eternal joys unless, together with other good things, the devotion of the mind displays abstinence worthy of God and joined to right faith.

God approves that fast which raises to his eyes the hands of almsgiving, as the prophet says: “Sanctify a fast” (Joel I and II). To sanctify a fast is to demonstrate, together with other good works, abstinence of the flesh worthy of God, as we have said. For the flesh is afflicted in vain if the mind is not restrained from wicked pleasures; and our Redeemer can in no way be pleased with one without the other—whether one who does good works still does not abandon the stains of lust, or one who excels in chastity has not yet exercised himself through good works.

Nor should one who begins some good works for the sake of worldly respect remain in that intention, or seek the glory of the present world through good works; rather, he should place all his hope in the coming of his Redeemer. For there are many continent people who afflict their bodies through abstinence, but seek human approval for that very abstinence. They devote themselves to teaching and give much to those in need. But truly foolish are the virgins who seek only the reward of passing praise, because, as the Lord says, they receive the damnable recompense of their labors (Matt. VI).

Even good works performed with a simple intention are pleasing to God only if they are offered without any admixture of evil work, as it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 24). One must first turn away from evil, and then do good so that it may profit; first repent worthily of past sins, and then labor at good works so that they may be beneficial.

But we cannot perform repentance worthily unless we also understand the proper manner of repentance. To repent is both to mourn the evils one has committed and not to commit again those evils that must be mourned. For one who deplores some sins while nevertheless committing others either still does not know how to repent or pretends not to know.

What does it profit someone to weep over the sins of lust while still panting with the fever of greed? Or what does it profit someone to grieve over the faults of anger while still wasting away in the fires of envy? It is also necessary that one who remembers having committed unlawful acts strive to abstain even from certain lawful things, so that by this he may satisfy his Creator. One who committed what was forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what was permitted, and reproach himself in small matters because he remembers that he sinned in great ones.

Thus we truly perform repentance if we perfectly deplore what we have committed; and affliction through tears, washing and cleansing them by repentance, sanctifies those whom a more reformed life has made better.

And since we have spoken about the number of four hundred verses, it remains for us to complete the account of the mentioned number of forty-six verses. For this number of years most aptly corresponds to the perfection of the Lord’s body, by whose blood we were redeemed, by whose flesh we are nourished, and by whose blood we drink; through the most holy mysteries of whose Passion we will be saved, in soul and body, from sins and even from the corruptions that arose because of sins.

Writers on natural matters report that the form of the human body is perfected over this many days. In the first six days after conception it has the appearance of milk; in the following nine it is changed into blood; then, over twelve days, it becomes solid; and during the remaining eighteen it is strengthened until the complete outlines of all the limbs. After this, throughout the remaining period until birth, it increases in size.

Six, nine, twelve, and eighteen make forty-five. If we add one—the very day on which the body, now distinguished into its limbs, begins to increase—we have the same number of days in the formation of the Lord’s body as the number of years we find in the construction of the temple.

Regarding that temple, when he said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” the Jews answered: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” (John II, 19). Since that temple made by hands signified the Lord’s most holy flesh, which he assumed from the Virgin, as we learn from this passage, and since his body, which is the Church, likewise signifies the body and soul of each of the faithful, let us cleanse daily, throughout the entire time of our life, the temples of our bodies and hearts, so that the Spirit of God may deign to dwell in us.

According to the Apostle’s admonition: “Having cast off the works of darkness, let us put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in reveling and drunkenness, not in beds and sexual immorality, not in strife and jealousy; but let us put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. XIII, 12–14). He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0833A]

So that nothing of grace may be lacking for you, dear Charles,

The measure of the verses reveals, and the quantity of the periods.

The king’s rich table, likewise called a banquet,

Has brought forth sound things for you, O prince, through the dishes of teachers.

What was expressed in plain speech I have compressed according to the laws of verse,

And I have joined it to eloquent prose in various ways, so that you may understand.

Some things above I have indeed explained more fully,

While, passing over others, I have reckoned them more briefly.

[Col. 0834A]

And if you deem brief matters worthy of fuller explanation,

If leisure is perhaps granted to us, I shall be at hand for your wishes.

May the king grasp what the bishop offers and display it in his conduct,

May he make these meanings and words into deeds for all his subjects in the kingdom.

May Charles live long and happily in this age,

May he always live renowned in the blessed company of the saints.

# Various Short Works of Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims

[Col. 0833]

## I. On the Person of the King and Royal Ministry, to Charles the Bald, King

*(According to Sirmond, from a manuscript of Saint Remigius of Rheims.)*

### Preface

[Col. 0833B]

To the glorious Lord, faithfully devoted and devotedly faithful.

Obeying the Lord’s command through the prophet, who orders: “Ask the priests about my law” (Hag. II, 12), you have wished to consult me about certain chapters. Since Truth itself says concerning these matters, “Whoever speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John VII, 18), I judged it fitting not to answer you in my own bare speech, but briefly to gather together for you into one collection certain fragrant little flowers of what the Holy Spirit speaks about this subject in the sacred Scriptures and through catholic teachers—truly from a full field, namely, the field of Scripture, which the Lord has blessed.

And knowing the promise, “Whatever more you spend, when I return I will repay you” (Luke X, 35), I have added to what belongs, as I have seen, to the royal ministry entrusted to you by God, as though they were flashing sparks added to the lamp of your knowledge.

But because, as the Comic poet says (Terence, *Andria*):

> “Compliance wins friends; truth breeds hatred,”

and because it is not flattery—namely, adulation—that ought to please a prince and lord of the earth, while a priest ought by no means to follow it, if you should find in the sentences I have collected something expressed rather sharply about the person of the king and royal ministry, I ask you to think that I collected these statements not against you but for you. For either I know that you are such and act in such a way, in kindness and goodness, as the very sentences describe, or I desire you to be such and to act in such a way.

The statements of this little book are distinguished in a threefold collection. First, concerning the person of the king and royal ministry in the general affairs of the commonwealth. Next, concerning what discernment there ought to be in mercy and concerning the punishment of particular persons, who, if they cannot otherwise be corrected when acting destructively, are ordered to be punished by temporal death—something which some people say is contradicted. Finally, because, on account of his royal ministry, the king ought not, even out of ties of kinship, to spare carnally those who act criminally against God, the holy Church, or the commonwealth.

## Chapter I — That God makes good kings and permits bad ones

Since, as it is written, “The kingdom belongs to the Lord” (Ps. XXI, 19), “and he will give it to whomever he wishes” (Dan. IV, 14), and since blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance* (chapter 6): “Nothing happens except what God either does or justly permits to happen,” when good kings reign, just as they are good by God’s grace, so they reign by God’s action, as he himself says: “Through me kings reign” (Prov. VIII, 15).

And when bad kings reign, just as they are bad through their own fault, so they are permitted to reign by divine judgment—sometimes hidden, but never unjust—as it is written: “He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” (Job XXXIV, 30). “He makes” is said in the sense that he permits it as a recompense of justice, in the same manner of speech by which it is said: “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. IX, 12). “He hardened” means that, by grace, he did not soften it, but by a recompense of justice he permitted it to be hardened.

Concerning those who reign not because God makes them reign but because he permits it, the Lord complains through the prophet, saying: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. VIII, 4).

Gregory says of them (*Pastoral Care*, chapter 1):

> “They reign from themselves and not from the will of the supreme ruler who, supported by no virtues and by no means divinely called, but inflamed by their own desire, seize the height of government rather than attain it. Yet the inward Judge both raises them up and does not know them, because those whom he tolerates by permitting, he certainly rejects by a judgment of condemnation.”

Concerning them it is said to the Lord through the Psalmist: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. LXXII, 18). For the one who advances in honors but declines in character is cast down while being lifted up.

The Lord is just and merciful. In arranging the deeds of mortals, he grants some things in favor, permits others in anger, and tolerates the things he permits in such a way that he turns them to the use of his own plan.

## Chapter II — That the happiness of peoples is a good king, and their unhappiness a bad king

Concerning the name of king, and concerning the happiness of the peoples subject to him if a good king reigns over them by God’s grace, and concerning the unhappiness of the peoples subject to him if a bad king reigns over them through his own fault, Saint Cyprian shows in his book *On the Degrees of Abuses* (chapter 9):

> “The name ‘king,’” he says, “retains this meaning intellectually: that he should provide the office of a ruler for all his subjects. But how will one who does not correct his own conduct so that it may not be wicked be able to correct others? For the throne of a king will be exalted in justice, and the governance of peoples will be made firm in truth (Prov. XVI).
>
> “The justice of a king is to oppress no one unjustly through power; to judge justly, without respect of persons, between one man and his neighbor; to be a defender of strangers, orphans, and widows; to restrain thefts; to punish adulteries; not to exalt the wicked; not to maintain the shameless and stage performers; to destroy the impious from the land; not to permit murderers and perjurers to live; to defend churches; to feed the poor with alms; to appoint just men over the affairs of the kingdom; to have old, wise, and sober men as counselors; not to heed the superstitions of magicians, diviners, and prophetesses; to defer anger; to defend his country bravely and justly against adversaries; to trust in God in all things; not to lift his spirit up in prosperity; to endure all adversities patiently; to have catholic faith in God; not to allow his sons to act impiously; to devote himself to prayers at fixed hours; not to taste food before the proper hours.
>
> “For woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccles. X, 16). These things produce the prosperity of the kingdom in the present and lead the king to better heavenly kingdoms.
>
> “But whoever does not administer the kingdom according to this law will certainly endure many adversities of rule. For this reason the peace of peoples is often broken, offenses are stirred up even against the kingdom, the fruits of the earth are diminished, and the services of the peoples are obstructed. Many and various troubles infect the prosperity of the kingdom; the deaths of beloved persons and children bring sadness; the incursions of enemies devastate the provinces on every side; wild beasts tear apart the herds of cattle and flocks of sheep; storms disturb spring and winter; they also hinder the fertility of the lands and the services of the sea; and sometimes strokes of lightning burn the crops, the blossoms of trees, and the vine shoots.
>
> “Above all, the injustice of the king not only darkens the appearance of the present rule, but also obscures his sons and grandsons, so that they may not hold the inheritance of the kingdom after him. Because of Solomon’s offense, the Lord scattered the kingdom of the house of Israel from the hand of his sons; and because of the justice of King David, he always left a lamp from his offspring in Jerusalem (1 Kings XII, XVI).
>
> “Behold how much the justice of a king is worth in this world: it is plainly evident to those who observe it. For it is the peace of peoples, the protection of the homeland, the immunity of the common people, the defense of the nation, care for the sick, the joy of human beings, temperate air, calm seas, the fertility of the earth, consolation for the poor, and an inheritance for children—and, for the king himself, hope of future blessedness.
>
> “Nevertheless, let the king know that, just as he has been placed first among human beings on the throne, so he will hold first place among punishments if he has not done justice. For all the sinners whom he had beneath him in the present, he will have above him, in an implacable manner, in that future punishment.”

## Chapter III — That right administration is a sign of great power

That temporal power is recognized as great from the good administration of government:

> “Great,” says blessed Gregory in his book *Morals* (Book XXVI, chapter 19), “is the temporal power that has its merit before God from the good administration of government. Power is good in its proper order, but it requires a cautious life on the part of the ruler.
>
> “Therefore he exercises it well who knows both how to retain it and how to oppose it. He exercises it well who knows how through it to rise above faults and knows how, with it, to make himself equal to others. For the human mind is often lifted up even when supported by no power; how much more does it raise itself high when power is also joined to it? Yet it is prepared, through suitable execution, to correct the faults of others.
>
> “Hence Paul says: ‘He is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil’ (Rom. XIII, 4). Therefore, when the ministry of temporal power is undertaken, one must keep watch with the greatest care, so that each person may know how to take from it what helps and to overcome what assails him.
>
> “Let us therefore hold outwardly what we have undertaken for the benefit of others, and inwardly let us hold what we think about our own estimation. Yet, by means of certain signs appropriately breaking forth, let even those entrusted to us know that we are such within ourselves, so that they may see in our authority what they ought to fear and recognize in our humility what they ought to imitate.
>
> “Once the authority of government has been preserved, let us return without ceasing to our heart and continually consider what we have been created equally with others, not what has made us temporally superior to others. For the more power stands out externally, the more it ought to be pressed down internally, lest it overcome the mind, lest it seize the soul in the delight of itself, lest the mind, having submitted itself to the desire to dominate, be unable any longer to rule the power beneath it.
>
> “David knew well how to govern the power of the kingdom. He conquered the arrogance of that power by pressing himself down, saying: ‘Lord, my heart has not been exalted’ (Ps. CXXX, 1). In increasing this humility he added: ‘Nor have my eyes been lifted up’; and he continued: ‘Nor have I walked in great things.’ Still examining himself by the most subtle inquiry, he said: ‘Nor in wonderful things beyond me.’ And, draining all his thoughts from the depth of his heart, he added: ‘If I was not humbly minded, but lifted up my soul’ (ibid., 2).
>
> “Behold how frequently he repeats the sacrifice of humility offered from the innermost heart; by confessing again and again, he does not cease to offer it, and by speaking in many ways he displays it before the eyes of his Judge. What does this mean, and how had he come to know that this sacrifice, which he was offering to God by such repeated words, was pleasing to him? It is because pride is usually near to the powerful, and exaltation is almost always joined to abundant possessions, since an abundance of moisture often gives rise to the hardness of swelling.
>
> “It is remarkable when humility of character reigns in the hearts of the exalted. Hence one must consider that the powerful, when they are humble in their understanding, attain the summit of a virtue that seems foreign and far removed; rightly, through this virtue, they speedily please the Lord, because the powerful offer him a sacrifice that the powerful can scarcely find.
>
> “For the most subtle art of living is to hold the summit while restraining glory: to be in power but not to know oneself to be powerful; to recognize oneself as powerful for distributing good things, but to ignore everything one is powerfully able to do when it comes to demanding harmful things.
>
> “Thus it is rightly said of such people: ‘God does not reject the powerful, since he himself is powerful’ (Job XXXVI, 5). Whoever administers the height of power while intent on the usefulness of others and not elated by his own praises desires to imitate God. Whoever has been set over others ought to wish to benefit them, not to rule over them.
>
> “For it is the exaltation of swelling, not the order of power, that is a crime. God grants power, but our mind’s wickedness invents the arrogance of power. Let us therefore remove what we have added from ourselves; the things we possess by God’s generosity are good.”

## Chapter IV — What kind of counselors a king ought to employ

What kind of counselors a king ought to employ, Ambrose says in the books *On Duties* (Book II, chapter 17):

> “The one who gives counsel to another ought to be such that he presents himself to others as a pattern and example of good works—in teaching, integrity, and seriousness—so that his speech may be wholesome and blameless, his counsel useful, his life honorable, and his wisdom distinguished” (ibid.).
>
> “Such, therefore, ought the counselor to be: one who has nothing shadowy, nothing deceitful, nothing fanciful, nothing pretended that could refute his life and character; nothing wicked or malicious that could turn away those seeking counsel.
>
> “Some things are avoided, others despised. We avoid what can harm, what can creep maliciously toward injury: for example, if the person consulted is uncertain in faith and greedy for money, so that he can be changed by a price; or if he is injurious—such a person is avoided and shunned.
>
> “But one who is pleasure-loving and intemperate, even if free from deceit, yet avaricious and disgracefully eager for profit, is despised. For what evidence of diligence, what fruit of labor can one produce, or how can one receive care and concern in one’s mind, if one has surrendered oneself to sluggishness and idleness? (Chapter 12.)
>
> “We therefore observe that, in acquiring counselors, the integrity of life, the excellence of virtues, the practice of benevolence, and the grace of frugality [another reading: *facilitatis*, ‘of accessibility’] contribute greatly. For who would seek a fountain in mud? Who would ask for a drink from turbid water? Therefore, where there is luxury, intemperance, and confusion of vices, who would think that anything should be drawn from there? Who would not despise a filthy way of life? Who would judge someone useful to another’s cause whom he sees to be useless to his own life? Who would not flee again from a wicked, malicious, abusive person prepared to do harm? Who would not shun him with every effort?
>
> “Who, even if equipped to provide the help of counsel, would seek someone who is difficult of access, as though someone were blocking a spring of water? For what does it profit to possess wisdom if you refuse counsel? If you obstruct the opportunity to give advice, you have closed the fountain, so that it neither flows out to others nor benefits you.
>
> “The same is beautifully applicable to one who possesses prudence but stains it with the filth of vices, since he contaminates the outlet of the water. Life exposes degenerate minds. How can you judge someone superior to yourself in counsel when you see him inferior in character? He ought to be above me to whom I am preparing to entrust myself.
>
> “Or shall I consider someone fit who gives me advice that he does not give himself? Shall I believe that he is available to me who is not available to himself—whose mind is occupied by pleasures, conquered by lust, subjected to greed, disturbed by desire, and shaken by fear? How can there be a place for counsel where there is no tranquility?
>
> “A counselor is to me admirable and worthy of respect when the Lord, being favorable, gives him to fathers and, being offended, takes him away.” (Chapter 10.)

We entrust our cause to the most prudent person and seek counsel from him more readily than from others. Yet the faithful counsel of a just man frequently outweighs even the ingenuity of the wisest. For “the wounds of a friend are more useful than the kisses of others” (Prov. XXVII).

Moreover, the judgment belongs to the just man, while the argument belongs to the wise man: in the former there is the strictness of deliberation; in the latter, the skill of discovery. If you join the two, there will be great healthfulness in counsel, observed by all with admiration for wisdom and love of justice, so that everyone will seek to hear the wisdom of the man in whom the union of both virtues exists. (Chapter 8.)

Therefore prudence and justice are desired in each person and expected by many, so that the one who possesses them may be trusted as able to give useful and faithful counsel to anyone seeking it. For who would entrust himself to someone whom he did not think wiser than the one seeking counsel?

It is therefore necessary that the person from whom counsel is sought be superior to the one who seeks it. For why would you consult someone whom you do not believe able to discover something better than what you yourself understand?

But if you find someone who excels in quickness of intellect, strength of mind, and authority, and who additionally is more prepared through example and experience—one who resolves present dangers, foresees the future, announces what is imminent, explains the argument, brings a remedy at the proper time, and is prepared not only to give counsel but also to provide aid—such a person is trusted in such a way that the one seeking counsel says: “Even if evils have come upon me through him, I endure it” (Sirach XXII, 31).

To such a man, then, who is, as we said above, just and prudent, we entrust our safety and reputation. Justice ensures that there is no fear of fraud; prudence ensures that there is no suspicion of error. Yet we entrust ourselves more readily to a just man than to a prudent one. (Book I, chapter 30.)

It is beautiful, therefore, to wish well and to give in such a way through counsel that you benefit rather than harm. For if you think that something should be given to a pleasure-seeker for the indulgence of lust, or to an adulterer as payment for adultery, this is not beneficence, since there is no benevolence. It is to hinder, not to benefit, another.

If you give to one who conspires against his country and wishes, at your expense, to gather lost men who will attack the Church, this is not praiseworthy generosity. If you help one who brings a grave lawsuit against a widow and orphans, or attempts by force to seize their possessions, generosity is not approved if one person gives what he extorts from another, if he seeks it unjustly and thinks it should be distributed justly—unless perhaps, like that Zacchaeus (Luke XIX), you first repay fourfold the one whom you defrauded and compensate the vices of paganism through zeal for faith and through the action of one who believes.

Let your generosity, therefore, have a foundation. This is sought first: that when you give in faith, you commit no fraud against what has been offered.

A counselor ought to act similarly in giving counsel, because there is also the greatest generosity in counsel.

## Chapter V — Nothing is happier than for those who possess the knowledge of ruling to reign

Nothing is happier for human affairs than, by God’s mercy, for those who possess the knowledge of ruling to reign, from Augustine’s book *The City of God* (Book V, chapter 24):

> “If those endowed with true piety live well and possess the knowledge of governing peoples, nothing is happier for human affairs than, by God’s mercy, for them to possess power. We call Christian kings happy if they reign justly; if, amid the tongues of those who honor them in lofty language and the excessively humble services of those who greet them, they are not exalted but remember that they are human beings; if they make their power serve his majesty, chiefly so that the worship of God may be extended as widely as possible; if they fear, love, and worship God; if they love more that kingdom where they do not fear having associates; if they are slow to punish and quick to forgive; if they exercise punishment for the necessity of governing and protecting the commonwealth, not to satisfy the hatred of enmities; if they grant forgiveness not for the impunity of wickedness but in hope of correction; if they compensate what they are often compelled to decree harshly with the gentleness of mercy and the generosity of benefits; if their luxury is restrained in proportion to how much more freely it could be indulged; if they prefer to rule over their own wicked desires rather than over any peoples; and if they do all these things not because of the ardor of empty glory but because of love for eternal happiness; if they do not neglect to offer to their true God the sacrifice of humility, compassion, and prayer for their own sins.
>
> “We call such Christian kings happy—temporarily in hope, and afterward in reality, when what we await has arrived.”

## Chapter VI — That it is useful for good kings to reign for a long time and over a wide territory

That it is useful both to those who reign and to those over whom they reign, if they are good, for them to reign for a long time and over a wide territory, the same blessed Augustine demonstrates in the same book, saying (Book IV, chapter 2):

> “If the true God is worshiped, and he is served with true worship and good morals, it is useful for good men to reign for a long time over broad territories; and this is useful not so much for them as for those over whom they reign.
>
> “For as far as the rulers themselves are concerned, their piety and integrity, which are great gifts of God, are sufficient for true happiness, by which they may live well in this life and afterward receive eternal life.
>
> “In this world, therefore, the kingdom of good men is granted not so much to them as to human affairs. The kingdom of wicked men, however, harms the rulers more, since they ravage their own souls through the greater license of crimes. It harms those who are subjected to them in serving them only if their own iniquity is involved.
>
> “For whatever evils are inflicted on the just by wicked rulers are not the punishment of a crime but the testing of virtue. Therefore the good person, even if he serves, is free; but the wicked person, even if he reigns, is a slave—not of one human being but, what is more grievous, of as many masters as there are vices.
>
> “Regarding these vices, divine Scripture says: ‘By whatever anyone has been overcome, to this he has been enslaved’ (2 Pet. II, 19). Once justice is removed, therefore, what are kingdoms except great robberies?”

## Chapter VII — Only necessity impels good kings to wage war and enlarge the kingdom

[Col. 0840C]

That good kings are summoned to wage wars and enlarge their kingdom only by necessity, from Augustine’s *The City of God* (Book IV, chapter 15):

> “To wage war and enlarge one’s kingdom by conquering peoples seems happiness to the wicked and necessity to the good. But since it would be worse for the unjust to dominate the more just, this too is not improperly called happiness. Yet without doubt it is a greater happiness to have a neighboring good person in harmony with you than to subjugate a neighboring evil person who is fighting. It is an evil desire to wish to have someone whom you hate or fear, so that there may be someone whom you can conquer.”

## Chapter VIII — The king’s duty when preparing for war, and his exhortation to the soldiers

[Col. 0840D]

«The character of a king and his exhortation to the soldiers as they prepare for war, the Lord, says Augustine, sets forth through Moses in Deuteronomy, saying: “Let him not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Deut. XVII, 20). If he directs his ways and policies well before him who is King of kings, he will necessarily possess the borders of his kingdom in peace. Hence immediately afterward it is added there: “That he may reign for a long time over Israel.” Moreover, if he observes the commandment not to turn aside to the right or to the left, he will joyfully earn, through victory, the covenant of security and peace. “When you go forth,” says the Lord, “to war against your enemies, and you see cavalry and chariots and a multitude of the opposing army greater than yours [Col. 0841A], you shall not fear them, because the Lord your God is with you” (Deut. XX, 1). Necessity should bring about war, so that, discord having been quieted, peace may be recovered. Thus must a king conduct battle. When battle approaches, the king ought to bring before his army the words of Judas, in which he says: “Do not covet spoils, for the war is against us” (II Macc. XLIX, 17).»

### CHAPTER IX — Those who waged wars at God’s command did not sin

That those who waged wars at God’s command did not sin, Augustine, in the aforementioned book (Book I, chap. 21):

“Divine authority itself has made certain exceptions, so that it is permitted to kill a human being. But apart from those whom it commands to be killed, whether by a law that has been given or by an explicit command addressed to a particular person for the time being [Col. 0841B], the one who kills is not himself the killer, but performs the service owed to the one who commands, just as a sword is an instrument in the hand of its user. Therefore those who waged wars at God’s command, or who, acting in an official public capacity and according to his laws—that is, by the command of the most just reason—punished criminals with death, in no way acted against the commandment that says, ‘You shall not kill’ (Exod. XX, 15).

“And Abraham was not only not blamed under the name of cruelty; he was even praised under the name of piety, because he wished to kill his son not criminally but obediently (Gen. XXII). And it is rightly asked whether what Jephthah did should be regarded as commanded by God, when he killed the daughter who came out to meet her father, since he had vowed to sacrifice to God whatever first came out to meet him on his return victorious from battle [Col. 0841C] (Judg. XI). Nor is Samson excused in any other way for destroying himself together with his enemies in the collapse of the building, except because the Spirit, who worked miracles through him, had secretly commanded this (Judg. XVI).

“Except, therefore, for those whom either the just law in general or God himself, the source of justice, in a particular case commands to be killed, whoever kills a human being—himself or anyone else—is held guilty of murder.”

### CHAPTER X — Those who conduct wars and serve under arms do not displease God

That those who conduct wars and serve under arms do not displease God, Augustine likewise writes to Boniface (Letter 205):

“Do not suppose that no one who serves in military arms can please God. Among such men was holy David, of whom the Lord gave so great a testimony [Col. 0841D]. Among them also were many righteous men of that time. Among them was that centurion who said to the Lord: ‘I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes; and to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it.’ Of him the Lord also said: ‘Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel’ (Matt. VIII, 8–10).

“Among them was also Cornelius, to whom an angel was sent and said: ‘Cornelius, your almsgiving has been accepted, and your prayers have been heard’ (Acts X, 5). The angel instructed him to send for blessed Peter the apostle and hear from him what he ought to do; and, in order that the apostle might come to him, Cornelius sent a devout soldier [Col. 0842A].

“Among them also were those who came to holy John, the Lord’s forerunner and the bridegroom’s friend, of whom the Lord himself said: ‘Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist’ (Matt. XI, 11). When they asked John what they should do, he said to them: ‘Violently extort from no one, accuse no one falsely, and let your pay be sufficient for you’ (Luke III, 14). He certainly did not forbid them to serve under arms, since he commanded that their pay should suffice for them.

“Others fight for you through prayer against invisible enemies; you labor by fighting for them against visible barbarians. Would that there were one faith in all, because then the labor would be less and the devil with his angels would be more easily defeated.

“Therefore, when you arm yourself for battle, first consider [Col. 0842B] that even your bodily strength is a gift from God. Thus you will consider how not to use God’s gift against God. When faith is pledged, it must be kept even toward the enemy against whom war is waged—how much more toward a friend for whom one fights? The will ought to have peace; war ought to be a necessity, so that God may free us from necessity and preserve us in peace. Peace is not sought in order to stir up war; rather, war is waged in order to obtain peace.

“Therefore be peaceful even while fighting, so that by conquering you may lead those whom you overcome to the advantage of peace. ‘Blessed are the peacemakers,’ says the Lord, ‘for they shall be called children of God’ (Matt. V, 9). If human peace is so sweet for the temporal safety of mortals, how much sweeter is divine peace for the eternal salvation of angels?

“Let necessity, then, not the will, destroy the fighting enemy [Col. 0842C]. Just as violence is returned to one who rebels and resists, so mercy is now owed to the defeated or captured—especially when there is no fear that the disturbance of peace will continue.”

And Jerome says: “We read in the Book of Chronicles that the children of Israel went to battle with a peaceful mind, because they fought not out of a desire to conquer but in order to obtain peace.”

### CHAPTER XI — A soldier obedient to the authority under which he serves does not sin if he kills a human being

That a soldier who obeys the authority under which he is placed does not sin if he kills a human being, Augustine, in the book *The City of God* (Book I, chap. 26):

“When a soldier, obeying the authority under which he has been lawfully appointed, kills a human being, he is guilty of no homicide under the law of his state; indeed, if he did not do so, he would be guilty of deserting and despising his command [Col. 0842D]. But if he had done it on his own initiative and authority, he would have fallen into the crime of shedding human blood. Thus, for the very act for which he would be punished if he had done it without orders, he will be punished if he does not do it when ordered.

“If this is so at the command of a king, how much more at the command of the Creator? Therefore, let the one who hears that he may not kill do so if the one whose commands may not be despised has commanded it. Let him only see whether the divine command is wholly certain and free from doubt. We address our appeal to the conscience through the ear; we do not usurp judgment over hidden things. No one knows what is happening in a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him (I Cor. II).”

### CHAPTER XII — The Almighty gives victory in war to whomever he wills

That the Almighty gives victory in war through his angel [Col. 0843A] to whomever he wills and commands, Augustine demonstrates in *The City of God*, saying (Book IV, chap. 17):

“The Almighty sends victory, and victory, obeying him as though he were the king of the gods, comes to those whom he commands and takes its place on their side. This is truly said of that true King of the ages: he sends not victory, which is no substance, but his angel, and makes whomever he wills victorious. His purpose may be hidden, but it cannot be unjust.”

### CHAPTER XIII — When battle is fought, God is present and prepares victory for the just side

That when battle is fought God stands by with the heavens opened and grants victory to the just side, and that no one should presume on his own strength, Augustine demonstrates in his letter to Boniface, saying (Letter 205):

“I shall give you and your men useful counsel. Take up arms in your hands; let prayer strike the ears of the Author, because, when battle is fought, God looks on with the heavens opened, and to the side that he sees to be just he grants the palm [Col. 0843B]. Presume nothing on your own strength; glory in the Author of your virtues, and you will have no need to fear any enemy at all.”

### CHAPTER XIV — One should not lose confidence because of small numbers if the Lord is with the fighters

That one should not trust in numbers, nor lose confidence in war because of small numbers if the Lord is with the fighters; and that the famous war conducted through Gideon at the Lord’s direction, as well as the Books of the Maccabees and the history of Orosius, demonstrates this, in which it is written (Book XI, chap. 9):

“Xerxes, king of the Persians, is said to have had seven hundred thousand [Col. 0843C] armed men from his kingdom and three hundred thousand auxiliaries, as well as twelve hundred beaked ships and three thousand transports. It was therefore rightly said that scarcely were there rivers enough for such an army to drink from, scarcely lands enough for it to enter, and scarcely seas enough for it to sail.

“Against this army, so incredible for its time, whose number is now harder to establish than it then was to defeat, King Leonidas of the Spartans stood at Thermopylae with four thousand men. Xerxes, despising the smallness of the force opposed to him, ordered the battle to begin and the fighting to be joined; and for three continuous days it was not a battle between two peoples but the slaughter of one people.

“On the fourth day, when Leonidas saw that the enemy was surrounding him on every side, he urged the auxiliary allies to withdraw from the battle, climb to the summit of the mountain, and preserve themselves for better times. For himself [Col. 0843D] and his Spartans, he said, another fate had to be endured: he owed more to his country than to his life.

“After dismissing the allies, he reminded the Spartans that they had much glory to hope for but nothing for life, and that they should await neither the enemy nor the day. Under cover of night they were to break into the camp, join battle, and throw the ranks into confusion. Nowhere would they die more honorably than in the enemy’s camp.

“Persuaded that they preferred to die, they armed themselves to avenge their future death, as though they themselves both demanded and avenged their destruction. Wonderful to relate, six hundred men burst into the camp of six hundred thousand. Tumult arose throughout the entire camp. The Persians [Col. 0844A] themselves assisted the Spartans by slaughtering one another.

“The Spartans, searching for the king and not finding him, cut down and laid low everything; they roamed through the entire camp, and among dense heaps of bodies scarcely followed the few survivors. They were unquestionably victorious, had they not chosen to die.”

### CHAPTER XV — Offerings should be made for those who have fallen in war

That offerings of alms, prayers, and the sacred sacrifice ought confidently to be made for those who, fighting faithfully in war, have fallen, Scripture demonstrates, saying:

“The very brave Judas, having taken up a collection, sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem, to offer there for the sins of the dead, thinking rightly and religiously about the resurrection” (II Macc. XII, [Col. 0844B] 43), so that many might say that it was vain and superfluous to offer for the dead. For he considered that those who had fallen asleep in piety had an excellent grace laid up for them. “It is therefore a holy and salutary thought to offer sacrifice for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins” (ibid., 45–46).

### CHAPTER XVI — Kings serve the King of kings, the Lord, also by making laws on his behalf

That kings serve the King of kings, the Lord, not only in the matters mentioned above but also by making laws on his behalf, Augustine demonstrates in his letter to Boniface, saying (Letter 50):

“Let the kings of the earth serve Christ, even by enacting laws for Christ. How, then, do kings serve the Lord in fear, unless by religious severity [Col. 0844C] prohibiting and punishing the things that are done against the Lord’s commands?

“For one serves him in one way as a human being and in another way as a king. As a human being, one serves him by living faithfully; but as a king, one serves him by firmly enacting laws that command what is just and prohibit what is contrary to it.
