“Thus Hezekiah served him by destroying the sacred groves, the temples of idols, and the high places that had been built against God’s commands (IV Kings XVIII). Thus Josiah served him by doing the same things (IV Kings XXV). Thus the king of the Ninevites served him by compelling the entire city to appease the Lord (Jonah III). Thus Darius served him by handing over the idol to Daniel’s power so that it might be destroyed, and by throwing Daniel’s enemies to the lions (Dan. XIV). Thus Nebuchadnezzar served him by forbidding, through a terrible law, all those placed under his rule to blaspheme [Col. 0844D] God (Dan. III).

“In this way, therefore, kings serve the Lord insofar as they are kings, when they do for his service what only kings can do.”

### CHAPTER XVII — People must also be compelled to observe justice

That people must also be compelled to observe justice, Augustine demonstrates in his letter to Vincentius, saying (Letter 48):

“Do you think that no one ought to be compelled to justice, when you read that the master of the household said to his servants, ‘Compel them to enter, whoever you find’ (Luke XIV, 23)? When you read that Saul himself, later Paul, was compelled by the great force of Christ compelling him to recognize and hold the truth [Col. 0845A] (Acts IX)?

“And do you think that no force should be applied to a person in order to free him from the destruction of error, when you see the Lord himself, who loves us more beneficially than anyone, doing this through the clearest examples, and hear Christ saying: ‘No one comes to me unless the Father draws him’ (John VI, 44)? This occurs in the hearts of all who turn to God through fear of divine wrath.

“Whatever the true and legitimate mother Church does, even if it is felt to be harsh and bitter, she does not return evil for evil; rather, by driving out the evil of iniquity, she applies the good of discipline (ibid.).

“You see, therefore, that one must not consider what a person is compelled to do, but what the thing is to which he is compelled—whether it is good or evil. The purpose is not that anyone should become good against his will, but that, by fearing what he does not wish to suffer, he may either abandon the obstinacy [Col. 0845B] that obstructs his mind or be compelled to recognize a truth of which he was ignorant. Thus, through fear, he may reject the falsehood for which he contended or seek the truth he did not know, and then willingly hold what he previously did not want.

“For it is not good for a human being to conquer another human being; it is good for a human being to be conquered willingly by the truth, because it is evil for a human being to be conquered by the truth unwillingly. For the truth must conquer him, whether he denies it or confesses it.”

Concerning this salutary compulsion, blessed Gregory also speaks in his usual most sweet and abundant manner in Homily 36. Since his remarks are very well known and worn smooth by frequent reading, and since I judged that the discussion would otherwise become too long, I have decided to omit them here.

### CHAPTER XVIII — One who corrects the wicked out of love of justice serves Christ

[Col. 0845C]

That even by exercising discipline against the wicked and perverse, not through the rancor of hatred or the bitterness of personal vengeance, but through love of justice and divine vengeance, one serves Christ, the same blessed Augustine demonstrates, saying (Letter 48, to Vincentius):

“When truth is preached to those who err, admonition is useful to the thoughtful but affliction is useless to the senseless. ‘There is no authority except from God. Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it’ (Rom. XIII, 1–3).

“Whether authority, favoring the truth, corrects someone, the one who has been reformed receives praise from it; or whether, hostile to the truth, it rages against someone, the one who has been crowned victorious receives praise from it [Col. 0845D]. (Book IX of *The City of God*, chap. 5.)

“In our discipline it is not so much asked whether a devout mind becomes angry, but why it becomes angry; nor whether it is sad, but what makes it sad; nor whether it is afraid, but what it fears. To be angry at one who sins so that he may be corrected, to grieve for one who is afflicted so that he may be freed, to fear for one who is in danger lest he perish—I do not know whether anyone could rightly condemn these things.

“For it is customary to blame even the Stoics’ compassion; but how much more honorably would that Stoic be disturbed by compassion for a person to be rescued than by fear of shipwreck!”

Cicero spoke far better and more humanely [Col. 0846A], and more suitably to the feelings of the devout, in his praise of Caesar, where he says (*Oration for Quintus Ligarius*, chap. 12):

“Of your virtues, none is more admirable or more welcome than mercy. What, then, is mercy except a certain compassion for another’s misery in our own heart, by which we are compelled to help if we are able? This emotion serves reason when mercy is shown in such a way that justice is preserved, whether it is bestowed upon one in need or granted to one who repents.”

### CHAPTER XIX — On discernment in showing mercy

Likewise, concerning discernment in showing mercy, Ambrose, in his exposition of Psalm 118:

“There is a just mercy, and there is also an unjust mercy. Thus it is written in the law concerning a certain person: ‘You shall not pity him’ (Deut. XIX, 13). And in the Books of Kings you read that Saul incurred offense for this reason: he pitied [Col. 0846B] Agag, the king of the enemies, whom the divine sentence had forbidden to be spared (I Kings XIII).

“If someone, moved by the entreaties of a robber’s children and softened by the tears of his wife, thinks that a man should be released whose desire for robbery still remains, will he not hand over the innocent to destruction by freeing one who is intent on the destruction of many? Certainly, if he restrains the sword and loosens the bonds, why does he release him into exile? Why does he not, by whatever more merciful means he can, take away the opportunity for robbery, since he was unable to extort the will to rob?

“Again, when two men—the accuser and the defendant—are deciding a capital matter with equal danger, one if he fails to prove his case, the other if he is not convicted by the accuser, let the judge not follow what justice requires, but, while pitying the defendant, condemn the one who proves his case; or, while favoring an accuser who cannot prove his charge, let him condemn the innocent [Col. 0846C]. This, therefore, cannot be called just mercy.

“Even in the Church itself, where it is especially fitting to show mercy, the rule of justice must be maintained with the greatest care, lest someone excluded from communion be able, through a brief and temporarily prepared little tear—or even through more abundant weeping—to wrest from the priest’s easygoingness the communion that he ought to seek for a very long time. Does he not, by indulging one who is unworthy, provoke many others to the contagion of falling away? For an easy granting of pardon supplies an incentive to sin.

“This has been said so that we may know that, according to the word of God and according to reason, mercy is to be administered to those who owe a debt. If a physician, finding within a wound the scar of a serpent, ought to cut away the ulcer’s corruption lest it spread farther, but is nevertheless softened by the patient’s tears and, abandoning his purpose of cutting [Col. 0846D] and burning, covers with medicines what ought to have been opened with the knife, is this not useless mercy, if, because of the brief pain of incision or cauterization, the entire body wastes away and the use of life perishes?

“Therefore a priest, like a good physician, ought rightly to cut away a wound from the whole body of the Church lest it spread farther, and expose the hidden poison of the crime rather than nourish it, lest, by judging one person unworthy of exclusion, he make many others deserving of exclusion from the Church.

“Thus the Apostle rightly exhorts us by a divine example, saying: ‘Consider therefore the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you continue in goodness’ (Rom. XI, 22).”

### CHAPTER XX — Whom a ruler or judge may lawfully pardon

[Col. 0847A]

To whom, then, a ruler or judge may lawfully grant pardon under the just and merciful judge who forgives the one who converts and repents, blessed Gregory demonstrates in a homily on the Gospel (Homily 32):

“Behold: if the proud man turns to Christ and becomes humble, he has abandoned himself. If a man given to lust changes his life to one of continence, he has certainly denied what he was. If a miser has ceased to grasp after wealth and has learned to give his own possessions—he who previously seized what belonged to others—without doubt he has abandoned himself.

“He is indeed the same by nature, but he is not the same in wickedness. Hence it is written: ‘Turn the wicked, and they shall be no more’ (Prov. XII, 7). For converted wicked people shall be no more—not because they will not exist at all in their essence, but because they will no longer exist [Col. 0847B] in the guilt of wickedness.

“Then we abandon ourselves; then we deny ourselves, when we avoid what we were through our old condition and strive toward what we are called to be through renewal. Let us consider how Paul had denied himself, when he said: ‘I live, yet no longer I’ (Gal. II, 20). That savage persecutor had been extinguished, and the devout preacher had begun to live. For if he were still himself, he would certainly not be devout.

“But since he denies that he lives, let him say from where it comes that holy words proclaim through the teaching of truth. Immediately he adds: ‘But Christ lives in me.’ It is as though he said openly: ‘I have been extinguished with respect to myself, because I am not carnal; I live spiritually in Christ.’

“Let Truth therefore say: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny [Col. 0847C] himself’ (Matt. XVI, 24), because unless someone withdraws from himself, he does not draw near to the one who is above him; nor can he grasp what is beyond himself if he does not know how to put to death what he is.

“But perhaps someone may say: ‘How can I know whether the person whom I spare has corrected himself and has remained in correction?’ Let this person, he says, return to the Lord’s judgment: if someone has been reprimanded according to the Gospel a second and a third time and has not corrected himself, he is commanded to be regarded as a pagan and a tax collector; he must necessarily be compelled to endure the severity of the law from the ruler, lest one who was unwilling to care for himself be able to harm those who wish to live in peace.

“But if someone wishes to object to this chapter that the Lord commanded that offenses against us be forgiven not only seven times but seventy-seven times, let him know that this command concerns injuries committed against us, not injuries committed against God [Col. 0847D]. For, as Prosper says from the words of blessed Augustine in the *Book of Sentences* (Sentence 210): ‘Sins, whether small or great, cannot remain unpunished, because they are punished either when a human being repents or when God judges. Divine vengeance ceases if human conversion precedes it. For God loves to spare those who confess and not to judge those who judge themselves.’”

### CHAPTER XXI — Let a ruler beware lest he be deceived by the gifts or flatteries of any criminal

Let a ruler also fear what is read in the history of the Kings, lest he be enticed by anyone’s gifts or blandishments or deceived by flatteries:

“Ben-hadad, fleeing, entered the city into a chamber [Col. 0848A] within a chamber. His servants said to him: ‘Behold, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful. Let us therefore put sackcloth around our waists and cords on our heads, and go out to the king of Israel; perhaps he will save our lives.’

“They girded their waists with sackcloth, placed cords on their heads, and came to the king of Israel, namely Ahab, and said: ‘Your servant Ben-hadad says: “I beg you, let my life be spared.”’ And he said: ‘If he is still alive, he is my brother.’

“The men took this as a favorable sign, and, hastening, seized the word from his mouth and said: ‘Your brother Ben-hadad.’ And he said to them: ‘Go, bring him.’

“Ben-hadad therefore came out to him, and he raised him into his chariot. Ben-hadad said to him: ‘The cities that my father took from your father I will restore [Col. 0848B]; and you shall make streets for yourself in Damascus, just as my father made in Samaria; and I, having made a treaty, will depart from you.’ So he made a treaty with him and released him.

“Then a certain man from the sons of the prophets said to his companion by the word of the Lord: ‘Strike me.’ But he refused to strike him. He said to him: ‘Because you did not listen to the voice of the Lord, behold, when you depart from me, a lion will strike you.’ When he had withdrawn a little from him, a lion found him and struck him.

“Then he found another man and said to him: ‘Strike me.’ He struck him and wounded him. The prophet went away and met the king on the road; he disguised himself by sprinkling dust over his face and eyes.

“When the king passed by, he cried out to the king and said: ‘Your servant went out to fight in close combat. When one man had fled, someone brought him to me and said: “Guard this man. If he slips [Col. 0848C] away, your life will answer for his life, or you shall weigh out a talent of silver.” But while I, troubled, was turning this way and that, suddenly he was nowhere to be seen.’

“The king of Israel said to him: ‘That is your judgment, which you yourself have determined.’ At once he wiped the dust from his face, and the king of Israel recognized that he was one of the prophets. He said to him: ‘Thus says the Lord: Because you released from your hand a man deserving death, your life shall answer for his life, and your people for his people’ (III Kings XX, 30–42).”

### CHAPTER XXII — Rulers must beware of joining themselves to the friendships of criminals

Rulers must also beware of joining themselves to the friendships of such criminals or admitting such people into their intimacy [Col. 0848D].

“Whenever,” says blessed Gregory (*Pastoral Care*, Part III, chap. 23), “we carelessly join ourselves to the friendships of the wicked, we are bound by their faults. Thus Jehoshaphat, who is exalted by so many praises of his former life, is rebuked as nearly perishing through the friendship of King Ahab. The Lord says to him through the prophet: ‘You give help to the wicked and join yourself in friendship to those who hate the Lord; and for this reason you deserved the Lord’s wrath, but good works have been found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah’ (II Chron. XIX, 2–3).

“For by that very fact our life already differs from the one who is supremely upright, when our life agrees with the friendships of the perverse.”

Hence David, while binding himself entirely to the covenants of inward peace, testifies that he did not enter into concord with the wicked, saying:

“‘Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away [Col. 0849A] because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me’ (Ps. CXXXVIII, 21–22).”

To hate the enemies of God with perfect hatred is to love them for what they were made to be, rebuke what they do, restrain the conduct of the wicked, and benefit their life.

### CHAPTER XXIII — Holy men rightly punished the guilty with death in order to inspire fear

Because holy men not only avoided the friendships of such people but also, in order to inspire fear in the living, rightly punished the guilty with death, as blessed Augustine demonstrates in the book *On the Sermon on the Mount* (Book I, chap. 20), saying:

“Great and holy men, who already knew very well [Col. 0849B] that this death, which separates the soul from the body, was not to be feared, nevertheless, with regard to the minds of those who feared it, punished certain sins with death, so that a useful fear might be instilled in the living and so that death itself would not harm those who were punished by death, but rather the sin—which could have increased if they lived.

“They did not judge rashly, those to whom God had granted such judgment. Hence Elijah put many to death, both with his own hand (III Kings XVIII) and by fire obtained from heaven (IV Kings I), while many other great and divine men, by the same spirit, acted without rashness to bring human affairs to peace.

“When the disciples mentioned to the Lord the example of Elijah, recalling what he had done, so that he might also give them power to call down fire from heaven to consume those who would not offer them hospitality, the Lord rebuked in them not the example [Col. 0849C] of the holy prophet but their ignorance in taking vengeance. He observed that, while still inexperienced, they desired vengeance not from love of correction but from hatred (Luke IX).

“Afterward, once he had taught them what it meant to love one’s neighbor as oneself, and once the Holy Spirit had been poured out, whom, as he had promised, he sent from above after the completion of ten days following his ascension (Acts II), such acts of vengeance did not cease, although they occurred much more rarely than in the Old Testament. There, for the most part, people were restrained by fear; here, the free were nourished chiefly by love.

“For, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, Ananias and his wife fell dead at the words [Col. 0849D] of the apostle Peter and were not restored to life but buried (Acts V).

“And if the heretics who oppose the Old Testament do not wish to believe this book, let them look to the apostle Paul, whom they read together with us, saying of a certain sinner: ‘I handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his soul may be saved’ (I Cor. V, 5). If they do not wish to understand death here—for perhaps the matter is uncertain—let them at least admit that the Apostle inflicted some punishment through Satan. That he did this not from hatred but from love is shown by the addition, ‘so that his soul may be saved.’

“Or, in those books to which they themselves attribute great authority, let them observe what we are saying, where it is written that the apostle Thomas called down upon a certain man, by whom he had been struck on the face, the punishment of a most dreadful death [Col. 0850A], while nevertheless commending his soul so that he might be spared in the future age. After the man had been killed by a lion, a dog brought to the tables at which the apostle was dining the hand, torn from the rest of his body.

“We are permitted not to believe this writing, for it is not in the Catholic canon. Yet those who, through some sort of blindness, rage most fiercely against the bodily punishments found in the Old Testament both read and honor it as wholly incorrupt and true, without understanding at all with what intention and according to what distribution of times those punishments were carried out.

“Therefore, in this kind of injury, which is paid for by vengeance, Christians must observe this measure: when an injury has been received [Col. 0850B], the heart should not rise into hatred, but should be prepared, through compassion for weakness, to endure more; nor should it neglect correction, in which it can employ counsel, authority, or power.”

### CHAPTER XXIV — Killing a human being is not always criminal

That killing a human being is not always criminal, but that killing through malice and contrary to the laws is criminal; for in such matters it is not the act that is condemned—since it is sometimes rightly done—but the mind that counsels evil, Augustine demonstrates in *The City of God*, saying:

“If someone judges a thing that is evil to be good and does it because he thinks it good, he certainly sins. All sins of ignorance are of this kind, when someone thinks that something is being done well which is done badly.

“Concerning killing human beings so that no one may be killed by them, I do not approve of this course unless perhaps the person is a soldier or holds a public office, so that he does not do it for himself but for others or for the state in which he himself also lives, having received legitimate authority [Col. 0850C], if such action is appropriate to his position.

“Those who are restrained by some fear from doing evil are perhaps also benefited in some way. Hence it is said: ‘Let us not resist evil’ (Matt. V, 39), not so that we may neglect the correction of human beings, but so that we may not delight in vengeance, which feeds the mind on another’s evil.”

### CHAPTER XXV — The king ought to be a corrector of the wicked

Hence holy Cyprian says in the ninth degree of abuse (chap. 9):

“The king ought to be a corrector of the wicked. He must restrain thefts, punish adulteries, destroy the impious from the land, and not allow parricides and perjurers to live.”

The same writer likewise says [Col. 0850D] (chap. 11):

“The eleventh degree of abuse is a people without discipline, which, because it does not serve the exercises of discipline, does not escape God without the rigor of discipline. For just as a tunic covers the whole body except the head, so discipline covers the whole Church except Christ, because the Church is both protected and adorned under his discipline.

“The tunic had been woven from above throughout, because discipline is given and perfected for that same Church by the Lord from heaven. The tunic of Christ’s body is the discipline of the Church. Whoever is outside discipline is alien to the body of Christ.

“Let us therefore not tear it apart, but let us cast lots for it. Let us not loosen anything from Christ’s commandments, but let each person remain with God in the calling in which he was called.”

### XXVI — Because of the punishment of criminals, the sword has been permitted by God to the ruler

[Col. 0851A]

And concerning this, holy Innocent writes to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, in his Decretals:

“It has been asked,” he says, “about those who, after baptism, have administered authority and have either inflicted torture alone or have also issued a capital sentence. Concerning these matters we read that nothing was defined by our predecessors. For they remembered that these authorities had been granted by God, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of criminals, and that God’s minister had been appointed as an avenger in such matters.

“How, then, could they condemn an act that they saw had been permitted by the Lord as its author? Concerning these matters, therefore, we maintain the practice preserved until now, lest we seem either to overturn discipline or to act against the Lord’s authority [Col. 0851B]. Their deeds, however, will all be preserved for them when they render an account.”

### CHAPTER XXVII — Laws enacted by a just ruler must be enforced against anyone whatsoever

[The supplied source ends here.]

Also the same holy Innocent, in his Decrees, writes to the same man (Letter 11):

“You wished to inquire,” he says, “whether those who dictate petitions are permitted, after the regeneration of baptism, to ask princes for someone’s death or for bloodshed on account of guilt. Princes, however, never grant such a request unconditionally; rather, they always refer the matters or crimes committed to judges, so that, after the case has been heard, whatever has been entrusted to the investigator may be punished. Either acquittal or condemnation is pronounced according to the nature of the case; and while the authority of the laws is exercised against the impious, the one who dictated the petition will remain free from liability” [Col. 0851C].

And in this connection the holy Cyprian says in his book *On the Abuse of the World* (chapter 12):

“The twelfth degree of abuse,” he says, “is a people without law. While it despises edicts and the enactments of the laws, it proceeds along various paths of error and falls into the snare of perdition. Indeed, the many paths of perdition are trodden whenever, through negligence, the one royal way—namely, the law of God, which turns neither to the right nor to the left—is abandoned. Therefore a people without law is a people without Christ. Let us not, then, become without Christ in this transitory age, lest Christ begin to be without us in the future.”

And Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, says: “Through me kings reign, and those who establish laws decree what is just” (Prov. VIII, 15).

And Saint Augustine, in his book *On True Religion*, shows that the laws of princes must be obeyed (chapter 30):

“In these temporal laws,” he says, “although human beings judge concerning them when they establish them, nevertheless, once they have been established and confirmed, it is not permissible for a judge to judge the laws themselves, but only according to them” [Col. 0851D].

Therefore, just laws promulgated by the people must be obeyed, or they must be justly and reasonably enforced by a prince against each person.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That mercy should sometimes be shown to those who must be punished for their crimes

That mercy should also be shown to those who must be punished for their crimes if, at a time of necessity and pressing danger, or at the final moment of life, they should seek the aid of repentance and immediately afterward reconciliation—neither satisfaction should be forbidden them nor reconciliation denied—is plainly demonstrated by the sacred canons and the decrees of the apostolic see, through sacred, evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic authority. For we can neither set a limit to God’s mercy nor determine its times; with God, true confession suffers no delay in receiving pardon. The Spirit of God says through the prophet: “As soon as you have groaned, you shall be saved.” And again: “First declare your iniquities, that you may be justified,” because “with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption” (Ps. CXXIX, 7).

## CHAPTER XXIX. That a king ought not, out of carnal affection, to spare his relatives when they act perversely

That a king, on account of his royal office, ought not to spare—even those bound to him by any ties of kinship—those who act perversely against God, holy Church, and the commonwealth out of carnal affection, the blessed Gregory demonstrates in his homily on the Gospel from the words of the Lord:

“Whoever does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 26).

He says (Homily 36):

“If we weigh the force of the command, we can understand how to do both things with discernment, so that we neither fail to recognize those joined to us by fleshly kinship and known to us as close companions, nor those whom we suffer as adversaries on the way of God, by hating and fleeing them. For the person who, while thinking carnally, brings evil things upon us and is not heard is loved, as it were, through hatred. But to show that this hatred toward those close to us proceeds not from lack of affection but from charity, the Lord immediately added, ‘and even his own life.’ We are therefore commanded to hate those close to us, and to hate our own life. It is clear, then, that one ought to hate his neighbor while loving him—one who hates him as himself. For we hate our life rightly when we do not yield to its carnal desires, when we break its appetite and resist its pleasures. Thus, when it is rejected, it is led toward what is better and is loved, as it were, through hatred.

“So, certainly, we ought to show discernment in our hatred toward those close to us, so that in them we love what they are and hate what obstructs us on the way of God” (ibid.). “From this discernment of our hatred, let us derive the pattern for hating our neighbor. Let anyone who is an adversary in this world be loved; but let no one who is opposed to us on the way of God be loved, even if he is a relative. For whoever now desires eternal things must, in the cause of God that he has undertaken, become separated from father, mother, wife, children, relatives, and even himself, so that he may know God more truly because, in God’s cause, he recognizes no one.

“For it is a serious matter that carnal affections strike against the mind’s intention and obscure its vision. Yet we do not suffer them to be harmful if we hold them down by restraining them. Our neighbors, therefore, are to be loved; charity is to be shown to all, relatives and strangers alike; nevertheless, one must not be turned away from the love of God on account of that same charity” (ibid.). “Thus all the faithful ought to be within holy Church: they should sympathize with their neighbors through charity, yet they should not stray from the way of God through compassion.”

In this connection Saint John Chrysostom, in his seventeenth homily on the words of the Gospel according to Matthew—“If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you” (Matt. V, 29)—says:

“If he were speaking about bodily members, he would certainly not have spoken of one eye, or of the right eye, but indiscriminately of both. For whoever is scandalized by the right eye undoubtedly suffers the same thing from the left. Why, then, does he mention the eye on the right side? So that you might learn that the saying concerns not bodily members but rather those who are joined to us by familiarity.

“If, then, you love someone so much that you use him in place of an eye, or consider someone so useful to you that you regard him as your right hand, but such people nevertheless harm your soul, he says that even these must be cut away from you. Examine more carefully the force of the saying. For he did not say, ‘Withdraw from the companionship of such people,’ but, indicating the greatest separation, he said, ‘Tear it out and throw it away.’

“Then, because he had issued a sufficiently severe command, he showed the benefit arising from this severity on both sides, preserving the figurative sense of the word in the case of both the good and the wicked. ‘For it is better for you,’ he says, ‘that one of your members perish than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna’ (Matt. V, 29).

“Why did Paul wish to become anathema? (Rom. IX.) Certainly not so that he might gain nothing from it, but so that he might acquire others for salvation. Here understand the same thing concerning the case of the reprobate brother. He is harmful to both; and therefore he does not say merely, ‘Tear it out,’ but also, ‘Throw it away from you,’ so that you may never receive him again if he continues as he was. In this way you will both free him from a greater offense and save yourself from destruction.

“But so that you may see more clearly the benefit of this law, let us, if you please, also examine its meaning in relation to the body. If a choice were offered, and one of two things were necessary—either to fall into a pit with both eyes and perish there, or, without one eye, to save the rest of the body—do you suppose that, choosing between the two, you would not prefer the latter? This is plainly evident to everyone. For this would not be hating the eye, but loving the rest of the body.”

And Saint Jerome, in his *Commentary on Matthew*, concerning these same words of the Lord—“If your right eye or hand causes you to stumble, tear it out or cut it off and throw it away from you”—says:

“By the right eye and the right hand is indicated the affection for brothers, wives, children, relatives, and those close to us. If we see that they hinder us from contemplating the true light, we ought to cut off such actions, lest, while we wish to make others gain, we ourselves perish eternally. Hence it is also said concerning the high priest, whose soul is dedicated to the worship of the Lord: ‘He shall not defile himself for his father, mother, or children’ (Lev. XXI, 11)—that is, he shall acknowledge no affection except for the one to whose worship he has been dedicated.”

## CHAPTER XXX. To what extent he ought to spare sons or relatives if they have sinned

[Col. 0854A]

Let the prince observe, with regard to ties of kinship, what he ought also to observe in other cases: “Whoever conceals his crimes shall not prosper, but whoever confesses and abandons them shall obtain mercy” (Prov. XXVIII, 12). For it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell forever and ever” (Ps. XXXVI, 27).

For confession alone is not sufficient for one who confesses and repents unless correction of conduct also follows, so that the penitent does not do the things for which he should repent. Thus did the holy David, who, after hearing from the prophet, “Your sin has been forgiven” (II Kings XII, 13), became more humble in correcting his sin, so that he ate ashes like bread and mingled his drink with weeping (Ps. CI).

“For often,” as the blessed Gregory says (*Morals*, Book VIII, chapter 21), “the reprobate also confess their sins, but they disdain to reflect upon them. The elect, however, pursue their faults—which they disclose by words of confession—with tears of strict self-reproach. Hence, after the prophet promised that he would declare his iniquity, he added that he would also reflect upon it. It is as though he openly confessed, saying: ‘My tongue speaks of guilt in such a way that, through the other activities of the Spirit, it is in no way free from the stimulus of sorrow; in speaking of my faults, I uncover the wound, but in reflecting upon my faults for the sake of correction, I seek the wound’s healing through the medicine of sorrow.’

“Whoever reveals the evils he has committed but refuses to weep over what he has revealed is like someone who removes a garment and exposes a wound but, with an insensible mind, applies no medicine to the wound. The voice of confession must therefore be tortured by sorrow alone, lest the wound, exposed and neglected, become more rotten because it is now touched more freely through human knowledge.

“The Psalmist therefore not only uncovered the wounds of his heart but also applied the medicine of sorrow to what he had exposed, saying: ‘I declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin’ (Ps. XXXVII, 19). By declaring it, he uncovers the hidden wound; but by thinking upon it, what else does he do except apply medicine to the wound? Yet for the afflicted mind, which carefully considers its own losses, conflict arises within itself and against itself. For when it urges itself toward the laments of repentance, it tears itself apart through hidden reproach.”

In this way princes ought to spare sons or relatives who, if they have sinned, acknowledge their wrongdoing and repent; otherwise they ought to exercise vengeance against the sinners according to the measure of their guilt. For if God the Father, as the Apostle says, “did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32), and yet the Father loved the Son whom he sent to suffering—the Son who, as the Apostle likewise says, “delivered himself up for the Church” (Eph. V)—then the peace of the universal Church and the general stability must necessarily outweigh love even for a beloved person, and all the more for a degenerate son.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Whether mercy should be shown in grave and public crimes

Those who do not humble themselves from the heart concerning grave and public crimes, but instead seek to defend their sins by devising excuses for their sins, should not be shown mercy, because pardon cannot in any way be granted to them. Saint Celestine makes this clear in his letter to Nestorius, saying (Letter 5):

“I shall indeed pursue, as the faithful servant of my good Lord, his enemies, since the Prophet asserts that he hated them with perfect hatred (Ps. CXXXVIII). Remembering again the words of another, ‘Whom shall I spare here? Whom shall I regard with any honor, when the matter at hand is that the cause of all my hope should be taken away from me?’ These are the words of the Lord himself in the Gospel, in which he says that no one is to place before him father, mother, children, or any other relationship (Matt. XIX). For such affection is often of a kind from which impiety is born, when, with carnal affection prevailing, bodily affection is placed before that charity which is God.”

And Saint Gregory, in his *Pastoral Rule* (Part II, chapter 6), says:

“Because Eli, overcome by false piety, was unwilling to strike his delinquent sons, he struck himself and his sons with cruel condemnation before the strict Judge. Hence it is said by the divine voice: ‘You honored your sons more than me’ (I Kings II, 29). For it is recorded in sacred history that Eli rebuked his sons with words, but did not correct them with the severity of discernment as he ought to have done. Therefore his sons were killed in battle, the ark of God was captured, a great slaughter occurred among the people, and Eli himself fell from his seat; breaking his neck, he lost his life together with the leadership of the priesthood.”

And the blessed Augustine, in his letter to Macedonius (Letter 54), says:

“It is not without benefit that human boldness is restrained by fear of the laws, so that innocence may be safe among the wicked and, among the wicked themselves, while their capacity for wrongdoing is curbed by fear of punishment, their will may be healed by calling upon God.”

Just as there is sometimes mercy in punishing, so there is cruelty in sparing. For if the house of David could not otherwise have peace unless his son Absalom had been killed in the war he waged against his father—although David had earnestly commanded his men to preserve him alive and safe as far as they could, so that paternal affection might have someone to forgive when he repented—what remained for David except to mourn the one who was lost and to console his grief with the peace acquired for his kingdom? If this was not permitted even when preserving peace among his own flesh and blood, how much less, we think, should strangers be spared from the severity of the laws?

## CHAPTER XXXII. That it is proper to a good king to have both the rod of strictness and the manna of gentleness

The Lord waits a long time for sinners to be converted, but condemns those who are not converted more harshly. Likewise, the devout mother Church, in accordance with what is written—“Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. XXII, 4)—strikes with the rod and supports with the staff. She teaches that in the breast of a good ruler there should be both the rod of strictness and the manna of gentleness: there should be the severity of a rod that strikes, and the consolation of a staff that supports; there should be love, but not a love that makes one lax; strength, but not strength that provokes; zeal, but not zeal that rages immoderately; compassion, but not compassion that spares more than is expedient.

Following the example of Moses (Exod. XXXII), let him love devoutly and rage strictly. For when the Israelite people had incurred, in the sight of God, an almost unpardonable offense, Moses offered himself on behalf of that people. Yet when he came to the same people, he put to death by the sword the lives of a few, though he had sought the life of all, even at the cost of his own. He thus gave discerning rulers an example: they should spare those who acknowledge their wrongdoing, truly confess, and repent, but condemn the incorrigible and those who persist in sin—just as Peter did with Ananias and Sapphira, and with Simon Magus (Acts V), who perished by the breaking of his legs, as is related in the history of Hegesippus; and just as Paul handed over the public sinner to Satan (I Cor. V) and struck Elymas with blindness (Acts XIII).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. In the case of many sinners, vengeance should not be neglected or delayed because of the difficulty

And if someone should perhaps say that vengeance can suitably be carried out against one person, but that, in the case of many sinners, vengeance seems on account of the difficulty either to be neglected or delayed, Saint Innocent contradicts them in his Decrees, addressed to the bishops of Macedonia (Letter 11, chapter 6):

“Let your charity therefore clearly understand that such matters have hitherto gone unpunished, and observe that necessity, as you say, has indeed compelled this: that, once the Churches have been established in peace, they cannot presume to act. But, as often happens, whenever a people or crowd sins, because it is impossible to exact vengeance against everyone on account of their multitude, the matter commonly passes unpunished. I therefore say that the earlier offenses should be left to God’s judgment, while for the future the greatest care must be taken to prevent them.”

And likewise in the decrees of the apostolic see:

“If all the priests and the whole world consent to condemn those who deserve condemnation,” they say, “the condemnation implicates those who consent; consent does not absolve them from transgression. For a crime is not diminished but increased when a private offense becomes a general one. God judged this in the case of all, when he destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood.”

Behold the matters concerning which your loftiness of wisdom consulted my insignificance. You possess the judgments of sacred Scripture and of the Catholic teachers. Now draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior—that is, draw doctrine from their words, by which the same Savior says:

“Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

“This,” says the Evangelist, “he said concerning the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive” (John VII, 38–39). What they drew from that same Spirit’s inspiration flowed forth in writing for our knowledge.

## II. ON AVOIDING VICES AND PRACTICING VIRTUES, TO KING CHARLES THE BALD

*(From the same source, from the manuscript of Saint Michael on the Meuse.)*

### PREFACE. That the fruit of sacred reading must be sought, and that he should receive Saint Gregory’s letter as though it had been written to him and profit from it

[Col. 0857A]

To the glorious lord King Charles, Hincmar, by name but not by merit bishop of Rheims, and servant of the people of God.

As you commanded, I am sending you the letter of blessed Gregory to Reccared, king of the Visigoths. From it I recently told you certain things, among others, when at Silvanectum the subject of works of mercy arose. I have added to that letter a number of passages from the words of the same distinguished teacher, mindful of the promise that says: “Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return” (Luke X, 15).

For you will not repay me a small amount when you carefully read not only what has been given out but also what has been given beyond what was required, preserving it intelligently and guarding it by progressing daily more and more from virtue to virtue. For there are some who wish to possess much from letters divinely inspired, but either do not read them, or, passing over them, neglect them outright; or they wish to know them for this reason, so that they may acquire favor through the knowledge of an empty name.

There are indeed those who gladly read the words of God or receive them with their ears, but do not retain them in their minds; and “whoever does not retain nourishment is certainly thought to have no hope of life” (Saint Gregory, Homily 15). “For the word of God is food for the mind, and food that has been received is rejected by a weakened stomach when the word that has been heard is not held in the belly of memory.”

And concerning the hearts of such people, according to the evangelical parable, the devil takes away the word, so that they may not believe and be saved (Luke VIII, 12).

There are also those who hear or read the divine word in such a way that they are pierced by remorse over their sins, yet after their weeping return to their sins and forget what they had mourned, because they do not wish to extinguish the vices with which they burn.

And there are some who, after hearing or reading the word of God, rise up against themselves and are aroused most vehemently against the sins and vices they have committed. But those salutary emotions are suffocated by cares, pleasures, and riches, when they strangle the throat of the mind with their intrusive thoughts and either do not allow the good desire to enter the heart or drive it from the heart—things that kill the good desire as though they were blocking the entrance of vital breath.

To such people the Lord says: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God; the reason you do not hear is that you are not of God” (John VIII, 47). (Homily 18.)

“For if the person who is of God hears the words of God, and whoever is not of him cannot hear his words, let each person ask himself whether he perceives the words of God in the ear of his heart, and he will understand from where he comes. Truth commands us to desire the heavenly homeland, crush the desires of the flesh, turn away from the glory of the world, not covet what belongs to others, and give away what belongs to us.

“Let each one of you therefore weigh within himself whether this voice of God has grown strong in the ear of his heart, and recognize whether he is already of God. For there are some who do not deign to receive God’s commandments even with the ear of the body; there are some who do receive them with the ear of the body, but do not embrace them with any desire of the mind; and there are some who gladly receive the words of God, so that they are already pierced with tears, but after the time of their tears return to iniquity.

“These people plainly do not hear the words of God, because they disdain to put them into practice, and they place the love of the world before the love of God.”

To such people the Lord also says: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (Luke VI, 24). (*Morals*, Book X, chapter 30.)

“Who are designated here by the name ‘rich’ except those who love riches immoderately and have no regard for the coming Judge, while they swell with proud thoughts within themselves? For there are some whom wealth does not lift up through pride, but whom works of mercy exalt. And there are some who, when they see themselves abounding in earthly resources, do not seek the true riches of God and do not love the eternal homeland, because they think that it is enough for them to be supported by temporal possessions.”

Of such people Scripture says: “All who love gifts pursue rewards” (Isa. I, 23), and “fire will devour the tents of those who willingly accept gifts” (Job XV, 34). (Gregory, ibid.)

“Wealth itself is therefore not a crime, but the attachment to it. For everything that God created is good, and whoever uses good things badly acts in such a way that, as though through gluttonous excess, he dies because of the bread by which he could have lived.

“The poor man Lazarus had come to rest, while torments afflicted the proud rich man. Yet Abraham had been rich, and he held Lazarus in his bosom; nevertheless, speaking with his Creator, he says: ‘I shall speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes’ (Gen. XVIII, 27). How, then, did this man know how to value his riches, when he considered himself dust and ashes? Or when could possessions exalt one who thought so humbly even of himself, their possessor?” (Book X, chapter 13.)

Moreover, the wicked, whenever they suffer something sad or adverse in this life, find hiding places of escape because they immediately return to the pleasure of their carnal desires. So that poverty may not torment them, they soothe their minds with riches; so that contempt by those close to them may not oppress them, they exalt themselves through dignities. If the body is worn down by disgust, it is nourished by placing before it a variety of banquets. If the mind is cast down by some impulse of sadness, it is soon lifted up by the intervening charm of amusements.

Thus they have as many escapes here as they prepare pleasures for themselves. But eventually their escape is taken away, because, after losing everything, their mind sees only itself and its Judge. Then pleasure is removed, but the guilt of pleasure remains; and suddenly, by perishing, the wretched learn that they possessed things destined to perish. Yet, for as long as they live bodily, they do not cease to seek what will harm them.

Such people receive their soul in vain when they place care for the flesh before it: like the rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen, feasted splendidly every day, and received good things during his life, but without consolation in eternal life.

The holy king refused to have this transient consolation not only as the highest good but even as a true good. He said: “My soul refused consolation; I remembered God, and I was glad” (Ps. LXXVI, 3). Indeed, “it is good to cling to God and to place my hope in the Lord” (Ps. LXXII, 28). And: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI, 4), because “blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5)—those who “have arranged ascents in their heart in the valley of tears” (ibid., 6–7), that is, in this world, in the land of the dying, where that same king’s tears were his bread day and night, as he said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13).

(Gregory, Homily 18.)

“And there are those who, after hearing or reading the word of God, return fruit with patience like good soil, since they both do good humbly and endure the evils of their neighbors with equanimity. For the more deeply each person has advanced, the more difficult a burden he finds in this world, because, as the delight of our mind in the present age diminishes, the adversity of that same age increases.”

But you, most beloved lord, whom God has magnificently and powerfully endowed with the talent of understanding, attend diligently to him to whom you will have to render an account for it, before the sight of the whole human race, and of angels and archangels. Do not hide that talent, bound up in a cloth, in the earth [Col. 0859D], that is, do not entangle it solely in earthly activities; rather, lift your heart upward to him who wonderfully created us, freely nourished us, enriched us with the substance of reason in our constitution, called you by his grace, enlightened you with his gifts, and, through the solicitude of paternal compassion, brought you back from the pains of scourging to the joys of salvation by the medicine of mercy; who did not abandon you when you sinned, but glorified you with many gifts and with power.

Every day, settle accounts with yourself concerning what you have received from the hand of the Lord, and what you give—or have given—in return to him for those gifts; for he will enumerate the good things he has bestowed upon each person in this way, saying: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I wearied you? Answer me. For I led you through the desert for forty years [Col. 0860A]; your garments were not worn out; I rained down manna for you from heaven, and you forgot me” (Deut. XXIX; Mic. VI). And again: “What more ought I to have done for my vineyard, and did not do?” (Isa. V, 4.) And: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes” (ibid.).

To those who do good and persevere in right faith and good works, he will say at the judgment: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV, 35), and the other words that follow, which are very well known to you, up to what will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34). But to those who act evilly and persevere in evil works, he says, conversely: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (ibid., 42), up to what will be said: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil [Col. 0860B] and his angels” (ibid., 41).

Nor must we forget that shame, when the books—that is, consciences—are opened in the sight of every human being and of the angels. Nor should we greatly fear the punishment that will follow that confusion, when guilt will envelop the immortal soul in eternal death, and Gehenna will consume the flesh that perishes without end.

Finally, since you ordered that the aforementioned letter be sent to you, you should know that you ought to read and hear the divine words as though they had been spoken or written specifically to you, so that whatever you find in them that must be avoided, you may avoid; whatever must be done, you may perform diligently; whatever must be followed, you may follow; and whatever must be carried out toward others, you may carry out. For just as in a medical book the afflictions of the body and their cures [Col. 0860C] are found, so in the divine utterances the afflictions of the soul and their cures are found.

That every faithful person ought to understand the divine utterances in the manner we have described, and that they have been spoken in this way, the Lord demonstrates in the Gospel when he said to his disciples: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI, 41). And again: “What I say to you, I say to all: Watch” (Mark XIII, 37).

He watches who keeps the eyes of his mind open to the sight of the true light; he watches who preserves through his deeds what he believes; he watches who drives away from himself the darkness of sluggishness and negligence; he watches who commits no fraud in a good work. (*Moral. lib. IX, c. 34.*)

> “Fraud is committed in a good work in three ways: through it, without doubt, either the silent favor of the human heart, or the breeze of approval, or some external thing [Col. 0860D] is desired. In opposition to this, the prophet rightly says of the righteous man: ‘He who shakes his hands free from every gift will dwell on high’ (Isa. XXXIII, 15). For since fraud is not found only in the acceptance of money, a gift is plainly not one thing alone. There are, however, three kinds of acceptance of gifts, toward which one hastens through fraud. A gift from the heart is favor sought from one’s thoughts; a gift from the mouth is glory through approval; a gift from the hand is a reward through giving. But every righteous person shakes his hands free from every gift, because in what he rightly does he seeks to receive neither empty glory from the human heart, nor praise from the mouth, nor a payment from the hand. Therefore, the only person who commits no fraud in God’s work is the one who, while watching attentively over the pursuits of good action [Col. 0861A], does not pant after material rewards, words of praise, or the favor of human judgment” (cap. 25).

> “For the desire for human praise is like a bandit, who joins those walking along the right road from the side, so that, drawing a sword from concealment, he may slaughter the life of those who are walking. And when the intention of the proposed usefulness is diverted toward private pursuits, in a dreadful manner the same work that virtue began is completed by guilt. Often, from the very beginnings, thought desires one thing while action displays another. Often even thought itself does not manifest the mind’s faith, because it turns one thing before the eyes of the mind, while in intention it hastens toward something far different. For frequently some people seek earthly rewards and defend justice; they consider themselves innocent and rejoice that they are defenders of uprightness. But if the hope of money is taken away from them, they immediately cease defending justice. [Col. 0861B] Yet they imagine themselves defenders of justice and assert themselves to be upright, although they are seeking not uprightness but money. Against such people Moses rightly says: ‘You shall execute justice—justice’ (Deut. XVI, 20). For he executes justice unjustly who does not hesitate to sell the very justice he pretends to uphold. To execute justice justly, therefore, is to seek that same justice in defending justice. Often we do what is right and expect neither rewards nor praises from human beings; yet the mind, raised up in confidence in itself, disdains to please those from whom it seeks nothing, despises their judgments, and, falsely considering itself free, hurls itself along the precipices of pride [Col. 0861C]. From there it is overwhelmed by a worse vice, precisely where it boasts that, as though it had conquered its vices, it is subject to no desires.”

Therefore, even in the good things we do, we must fear with great caution lest, through what is rightly done by us, human approval or favor be sought; lest the desire for praise steal in, and what is displayed outwardly be emptied inwardly of its reward.

Thus the Psalmist also says of the holy Church of the elect: “All the glory of the daughter of the king is from within” (Ps. XLIV, 14). Those who, having received some favor, offer the radiance of glory to their own empty praises are, as it were, selling oil; concerning this oil the Psalmist says: “May the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” (Ps. CXL, 5). By the designation “head” is meant the mind, which rules the body. The oil of the sinner [Col. 0861D] therefore fattens the head when the favor of the flatterer caresses the mind.

For flatterers are smooth-tongued enemies. Whoever is deceived by their tongues in good works will be counted among the foolish and senseless at the coming of the Judge, and will not receive from God a recompense for good works, because for them they have received from human beings the praises they desired.

When the sinner is praised by the flatterer—not by the righteous—in the desires of his soul, and the wicked person is blessed, one destroys the other: the sinful flatterer destroys the sinner. While they praise one another—the flatterer for his approval, and the sinner for his evil action—they destroy one another. (*Moral. lib. IV, c. 27.*)

> “This is why our Redeemer raises a girl in the house, [Col. 0862A] a young man outside the gate, and Lazarus in the tomb. The one who lies hidden in sin is still dead in the house. The one whose wickedness is exposed even to the shame of public perpetration is already led out, as it were, beyond the gate. The one who is weighed down not only by the perpetration of wickedness but also by the burden of habitual practice is pressed beneath the mound of burial. Yet in his mercy he raises these to life, because divine grace often illuminates by the light of its visitation those who are dead not only in hidden but also in open sins, as well as those weighed down by the mass of evil habit.

> “Our Redeemer, however, recognizes a fourth dead man when a disciple announces him, but does not raise him; for it is exceedingly difficult for one whom, after the practice of an evil habit, the tongues of flatterers also receive, to be recalled from the death of his mind. [Col. 0862B] Of him it is rightly said: ‘Let the dead bury their dead’ (Luke IX, 60). The dead bury the dead when sinners overwhelm a sinner with their favors. For what else is it to bury than to conceal? But those who pursue the sinner with praises hide him, extinguished, beneath the mound of their words.

> “Lazarus too was dead, but he was not buried by the dead: faithful women had covered him, and they announced his death to the one who gives life. Hence he immediately returns to the light, because when the soul dies in sin, it is brought back to life more quickly if vigilant thoughts remain alive over it.”

Flattery is indeed a most destructive plague, and it quickly steals upon the mind unless it is removed at the very beginning. We must therefore examine what we hear about [Col. 0862C] ourselves and test whether what is said about us is true. Let us believe that it is foolish to believe what others say about us more than what we ourselves say about ourselves.

Hence Paul says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I, 12). Paul calls the testimony of his conscience his glory; he did not seek the approval of another’s mouth and did not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself.

And because it is written: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (II Pet. III, 10), we must keep watch, lest we leave unexamined the evils we now commit, or even our good deeds. Keeping watch in this way, we must always await anxiously the time when our Lord will return to judge us, so that when he comes and knocks, we may immediately open to him. (*Hom. XIII.*)

> “He comes when he hastens toward judgment [Col. 0862D]; he knocks when, through the troubles of illness, he indicates that death is already near. We open to him immediately if we receive him with love. For the one who trembles to leave the body and fears to see as Judge the one whom he remembers having despised does not wish to open to the Judge who knocks. But the one who is secure in his hope and his works opens immediately to the one who knocks, because he gladly receives the Judge; and when he recognizes that the time of approaching death is near, he rejoices in the glory of recompense.”

Since the hours flee in their successive moments, we must act so that they may be held fast in the reward of good work. Hence Solomon says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, perform it earnestly, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld [Col. 0863A], where you are hastening” (Eccl. IX, 10). Since we do not know the time of the coming death, and cannot work after death, it remains for us to seize the time granted before death.

Death itself is conquered in this way when it comes, if it is always feared before it comes. And now we must pass from the words of the aforementioned illustrious man to the words of the letter that you ordered to be sent to you.

## Letter of Saint Pope Gregory to King Rechared, which Charles had requested from Hincmar to be sent to him

Gregory to Rechared, king of the Visigoths.

“I cannot express in words, most excellent son, how much I delight in your work and in your life. . . . Etc.” See this letter among the works of Saint Gregory the Great, *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVII, col. 1052.

## CHAPTER ONE. That almsgiving should not be made from another’s possessions; who are worthy of the fruits of repentance, and what true confession and sorrow for sins are; what it means to deny oneself and hate one’s soul

[Col. 0863B]

Regarding works of mercy, of which he spoke, among other matters, in the preceding letter—how and from what they ought to be performed—and concerning the matters that follow, which I have attempted to gather for the present in a brief summary, the same blessed man says elsewhere (book VII, letter 107):

> “Often,” he says, “the adversary of souls, when he cannot secretly introduce wrongdoing into matters that are openly evil, attempts to overthrow a person by introducing a cunning appearance resembling piety. He perhaps persuades one that something ought to be received from those who have possessions, so that it may be distributed to those who lack them, provided that in this way he may pour deadly poisons through the concealed shadowing of almsgiving [Col. 0863C]. For neither would the hunter deceive a wild animal, nor the fowler a bird, nor the fisherman catch a fish, if the one were to set the snare in the open, or the other did not have the hook hidden beneath bait.

> “The cunning of the enemy must therefore be feared and avoided altogether, lest those whom he cannot overthrow through open temptation he may slaughter more cruelly with a hidden weapon. Nor should it be considered almsgiving if what has been acquired unlawfully is distributed to the poor; for the person who acquires wrongly with the intention of distributing it as though rightly is burdened rather than helped.

> “The almsgiving that pleases the eyes of our Redeemer is that which is not amassed from illicit things and iniquity, but which is given from possessions that are permitted and rightly acquired. Hence it is also certain that even if monasteries, hospices, or anything else is built from things unjustly [Col. 0863D] acquired, it does not contribute to the builder’s reward. For while a perverse purchaser of honor is sent into a holy place, and establishes others in his likeness by offering them advantage, he destroys more by arranging many things wrongly than the one who received the money for the construction is able to build.

> “Therefore, lest we endeavor to acquire anything with sin under the pretext of almsgiving, Holy Scripture openly forbids this, saying: ‘The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable, because they are offered from crime’ (Prov. XV, 8). Whatever is offered in God’s sacrifice from crime does not appease the anger of almighty God but provokes it.

> “Again it is written: ‘Honor the Lord from your just labors’ (Prov. III, 9). Whoever takes wrongfully in order to give as though rightly [Col. 0864A] plainly does not honor the Lord. Solomon also says: ‘Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is as though he were slaughtering a son in the sight of his father’ (Ecclus. XXXIV, 24). Let us consider how great a father’s grief would be if a son were slaughtered in his sight; from this we can easily understand how great a grief is aggravated before God if a sacrifice is offered to him from plunder.

> “It is exceedingly grievous, beloved brothers, that under the pretext of almsgiving the sins of simoniacal heresy should be committed. For it is one thing to give alms because of sins, and another to commit sins because of alms.” (*Moral. lib. III, c. 23.*)

> “Whenever we give alms after a fault, we give, as it were, a price for evil actions. But sometimes the proud rich oppress their inferiors, seize what belongs to others, and yet [Col. 0864B] distribute certain things to others; while they crush many people, they sometimes bring aid and defense to certain persons, and appear to pay a price for iniquities that they never abandon.

> “The price of almsgiving frees us from faults only when we mourn and renounce the sins committed. For the person who wishes always to sin and also wishes always to give alms pays a price in vain, because he does not redeem the soul that he does not restrain from vices.”

For it is written: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. III, 8). (*Hom. XX, on the Gospels.*)

> “In these words we should observe that we are admonished to produce not merely fruits of repentance, but fruits worthy of repentance. To speak, therefore, of fruits worthy of repentance, we must know that whoever has committed no illicit act is rightly permitted to use what is licit, and thus perform works of piety while, if he does not wish to do so, not abandoning the things of the world [Col. 0864C]. But if someone has fallen into the fault of fornication, or perhaps, what is more serious, into adultery, he ought to cut himself off from licit things to the degree that he remembers having committed illicit things.”

For violating another person’s marriage is worse than adhering to a prostitute. If a married man or married woman has committed adultery with another man’s wife or another woman’s husband, they sin more gravely because they commit not simple but multiple adulteries.

Incest is more serious than adultery. Although those who pursue such fornications are commonly called adulterers, incest is more serious in proportion as the relationship by blood is closer. For it is worse to have intercourse with two sisters, or two brothers, [Col. 0864D] or with father and son, or with mother and daughter, than to commit adultery with another man’s wife. Within one’s own kinship, the closer the relationship, the more serious the sin: it is worse with mother and daughter, or with a sister, or with a woman consecrated to God, or with someone ordained in the ecclesiastical orders. The higher the order, the more serious the fall, and the graver the crime, than intercourse with another man’s wife.

Human frailty commonly falls from one evil into a worse one, until it reaches those things which, as the Apostle says, are shameful even to mention (Eph. V, 12). Those who practice them—namely, men who have intercourse with males or animals—are ordered by the sacred canons to pray among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit; and the law given through Moses judges them worthy of death.

[Col. 0865A] Just as men and women who commit adultery are held equally bound by the same judgment, so by the judgment of this law men who practice unnatural shamefulness with animals, with males, or with females, and women who practice the same shamefulness with animals or with other women by any device or contrivance, or who consent to practice unnatural acts with men, are likewise bound by guilt. For the Apostle says: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (Rom. I, 32).

If someone has committed all these things, he is held liable to as many deaths and punishments of eternal death as the crimes with which he has been polluted.

Yet because the mercy of our Redeemer has tempered the severity of the law—he desires the sinner’s conversion and repentance [Col. 0865B] rather than his death—each person ought, as we have said, to cut himself off from licit things to the degree that he remembers having committed illicit things, and ought to reproach himself in lesser matters to the degree that he remembers having sinned in greater ones.

> “The mind often accuses itself of what it has committed; but because it does not abandon this through desire, it is ashamed to confess what it does. When, however, it suppresses the pleasure of the flesh with its entire judgment, it rises with bold voice in the confession of its accusation. But there are some who confess their faults with open words and yet do not know how to groan in confession; they speak of things that should be mourned with joy. But whoever speaks while detesting his faults must necessarily speak of them in the bitterness of his soul, so that through this very bitterness he may punish whatever the tongue, by the judgment [Col. 0865C] of the mind, accuses” (Hom. 31).

> “Often we see what ought to be done but do not fulfill it in action. We strive and are weakened. The judgment of the mind sees uprightness, but the strength of action collapses before it. For it is already part of the punishment of sin that the good can indeed be seen from within the house, yet the person is driven away by merit from what he sees. Habitual guilt binds the mind, so that it cannot rise to uprightness. It struggles and falls, because where it has long remained willingly, there it falls under compulsion even when it does not wish to” (*Moral. lib. VIII, c. 20.*).

> “But the righteous person does not spare his mouth, because, anticipating the anger of the strict Judge, he rages against himself with the words of his own confession. Hence the Psalmist says: ‘Let us come before his face in confession’ (Ps. XCIV, 2). Hence Solomon says: ‘He who conceals his crimes will not prosper; but he who confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy’ (Prov. XXVIII, 13). Again it is written: ‘The righteous man is his own accuser from the beginning’ (Prov. XVIII, 17). Hence through Solomon [Col. 0865D] it is said: Yet the mouth is not opened for confession unless, through consideration of the strict judgment, hope is constricted by fear” (cap. 21).

It should also be known that the reprobate often confess their sins but refuse to mourn them. The elect, however, pursue with the tears of strict correction the faults they reveal in the words of confession.

When we confess our sins through tears, we enter the gates of the narrow way; but when afterward we are led to eternal life, we enter the courts of our gates with praises [Col. 0866A] of confession, because there will then be no distress, when the joy of the eternal festival has taken us up. Because of this distress of our confession, Truth says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. VII, 13). And when the Psalmist presumed that he would be received into the height of eternal joy, he said: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. XXX, 9). (*Moral. lib. VIII, c. 21.*)

> “Whoever discloses the evils he has committed but refuses to weep over what he has disclosed is like someone who pulls away a garment and exposes a wound but does not apply medicine to the wound with an alert mind. Therefore sorrow must alone shake forth the voice of confession, lest the wound that has been revealed but neglected—now touched more freely because it is known to others—fester more seriously.

> “In contrast, the Psalmist not only uncovered the wound of his heart [Col. 0866B] but also applied the medicine of the mind to the wound he had uncovered, saying: ‘I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin’ (Ps. XXXVII, 19). By declaring it, he exposes the hidden wound; but by thinking upon it, what else does he do than apply medicine to the wound? Yet from the afflicted mind that anxiously considers its own losses a quarrel arises against itself. For when it urges itself to the lamentation of repentance, it tears itself apart with hidden reproach.”

To her the Lord says: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII, 47). (*Hom. 33.*)

> “As though it were said openly: The one who burns intensely with the fire of love completely burns away the rust of sin. For the rust of sin is consumed all the more the more the sinner’s heart is burned by the fire of great charity. [Col. 0866C]

> “Let us therefore consider the grace of the merciful God, and condemn the multitude of our guilt. Behold, he sees sinners and endures them; he tolerates those who resist, and yet every day he mercifully calls them through the Gospel. He desires our confession from a pure heart and forgives everything in which we have sinned. Therefore, let the one who did not wish to remain return; let the one who scorned standing rise at least after his fall” (ibid.).

He indicates how lovingly our Creator awaits us when he says through the Prophet: “I paid attention and listened, but no one speaks what is good; there is no one who reflects in his heart and says, ‘What have I done?’” (Jer. VIII, 6). Certainly we ought never to have thought evil things; but because we were unwilling to think what is right, behold, he still endures us so that we may reflect. He who long awaits sinners so that they may convert condemns those who do not convert more severely. [Col. 0866D]

> “Let us therefore see the sign of such great compassion and the judgment of severity. Let us consider the womb of mercy opened for us. Those whom he destroyed while they were thinking evil things, he seeks when they think rightly. Let us mourn whatever we remember having sinned in adolescence and whatever in youth; let us wipe away the stains of our conduct and works with tears; let us now love the footsteps of our Redeemer, which we despised by sinning.

> “Behold, as we have said, the embrace of heavenly compassion is opened to receive us, nor is a blemished life in us despised. Through the fact that we abhor our defilement, we are already brought into harmony with inward purity. The Lord mercifully embraces us when we return, because the life of sinners can no longer be unworthy of him when it has been washed by tears” [Col. 0867A].

Those who mourn the sins of their works must take care that complete lamentation may wash away completed evils, lest they be more tightly bound by the debt of the deed committed and pay less through the tears of satisfaction.

> “For it is written: ‘You gave us drink in tears, by measure’ (Ps. LXXIX, 6), so that each person’s mind may drink, in repentance, as many tears of compunction as it remembers having dried up through its sins” (*Moral. lib. IV, c. 17*). “For the Lord leaves no sin unpunished: either we pursue it through weeping, or he through judgment. It remains, therefore, that the mind should always watch diligently over its amendment, and that whatever it recognizes as the means by which mercy may come to its aid, it must wipe away through confession” (cap. 14 [Col. 0867B] and 16).

And because every faithful person knows that thoughts will be examined with subtlety at the judgment, as Paul attests when he says: “Their thoughts accusing or even defending one another, examining them inwardly” (Rom. II, 15), he should examine himself vehemently before the judgment, so that the strict Judge may come all the more peacefully, seeing that the guilt he intends to examine has already been punished as sin (cap. 16). By forgiving, he leaves unpunished in his judgment those things that he sees to have been punished by voluntary correction, as Paul attests when he says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged by the Lord” (II Cor. XI, 31).

The more foully the mind sees itself polluted, the more strictly it must be cleansed by the hand of repentance. For the fruit of a good work [Col. 0867C] ought not to be the same for one who has sinned less and one who has sinned more, or for one who has fallen into no crimes and one who has fallen into some. Through the words “Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III, 8), each person’s conscience is challenged to seek through repentance greater profits of good works in proportion to the greater losses he has inflicted upon himself through guilt. (*Hom. 34.*)

> “Behold, divine mercy itself promises, saying: ‘There will be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance’ (Luke XV, 7). Yet through the Prophet the Lord says: ‘On whatever day the righteous man sins, all his righteousnesses will be forgotten before me’ (Ezek. XXXIII, 13).

> “Let us consider, if we can, the dispensation of heavenly mercy. To those who stand, if they fall, he threatens punishment; to those who have fallen, if they desire to rise, he promises mercy. [Col. 0867D] He terrifies the former so that they may not presume in good things; he comforts the latter so that they may not despair in evil things. You are righteous: fear anger, lest you fall. You are a sinner: trust in mercy, so that you may rise.

> “But behold, we have already fallen; we were unable to stand; we lie in our wicked desires. Yet the one who created us upright still awaits us and urges us to rise. He opens the lap of his compassion and seeks to receive us back through repentance. But we cannot perform worthy repentance unless we also understand the nature of that repentance. To repent is both to mourn the evils committed and not to commit again the evils that should be mourned. For whoever mourns some sins while still committing others either does not know how to repent or pretends to do so. What benefit is there if someone mourns the sins of lust and still pants with the fever of avarice? Or what benefit is there if he now grieves the faults of anger and still wastes away in the flames of envy?” [Col. 0868A]
