In contrast, the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. XVI, 24). Let the proud person become humble, the lustful chaste, the avaricious devoted to works of mercy, the envious kind, and the angry patient; let each take up his cross and follow Christ.

Let him chastise his body through self-restraint, and sympathize with his neighbors through charity, keeping watch in these virtues against the vices near to them: in abstinence, against empty glory; and in compassion of spirit, against false piety. For compassion is owed to the human being, and uprightness to vices; and in one and the same person we must love the good that has [Col. 0868B] been done and pursue the evils he has committed.

Again the Lord says: “Whoever does not hate his neighbors, and even his own soul, cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 26). (*Hom. 37.*)

> “We hate our soul rightly when we do not yield to its carnal desires, when we break its appetite, and when we resist its pleasures. When it is despised and led toward what is better, it is loved, as it were, through hatred. We must likewise show discernment in our hatred toward our neighbors, so that in them we may love what they are and hate what, on the road of God, either resists them or resists us.”

Filled with love of the world and empty of the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the Apostle says: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. VIII, 9). (*Hom. 24.*)

> “The spirit of love itself is, as it were, a title deed to divine possession. Does the person have the Spirit [Col. 0868C] of Christ whose mind is torn apart by hatred, inflated by pride, embittered by anger even to the point of division of mind, tortured by envy, or weakened by lust?”

For whoever he is whom this Spirit does not now restore is certainly fasting from the nourishment of that eternal banquet. Therefore, whoever has already believed in Christ but still pursues the profits of avarice, is exalted by the pride of honor, burns with the flames of envy, defiles himself with the uncleanness of lust, and covets the prosperous things of the world, refuses to follow Jesus in whom he has believed.

## CHAPTER TWO. On fleeing avarice, pride, lust, gluttony, envy, and anger; concerning zeal; and that the devil has always lain in wait especially through these vices
For Paul says of avarice: “The love of money is the root of all evils” [Col. 0868D] “and avarice is the service of idols” (1 Tim. 6:10). Whoever gives himself over to this voice, disdaining what is his own, covets what belongs to others; and often, unable to obtain what he covets, he spends his days in idleness and his nights in anxious thoughts. He grows sluggish in useful work because he is wearied by illicit speculation. He multiplies his plans and spreads the bosom of his mind ever wider to the winds of thought. He strives to reach what he covets and seeks the most secret passages of legal or practical arguments by which to obtain it. As soon as he thinks he has discovered some subtle point in the case, he rejoices as though he had already secured what he desired; he devises what else he may add to the thing once obtained and considers how it ought to be cultivated so that it may be brought into a better condition.

Because he already seems to possess it and to be bringing it into a better condition, [Col. 0869A] he immediately considers the plots of those who envy him, weighs what quarrel may be stirred against him, and searches out what answer he should make. Though he possesses nothing, he already labors as an empty litigant in defense of the thing he desires. Although he has received nothing from the coveted object, he nevertheless already has in his heart the fruit of covetousness—the labor of quarrelsomeness—so that, like one who walks anxiously with God, he says: “The meditation of my heart is always in your sight” (Ps. 18:15).

Thus the avaricious person, or anyone subject to any vice—for whoever is conquered by a vice becomes its slave—since “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin,” says by his conduct and desire to the avarice or other vice he serves: “The meditation of my heart is always in your sight.” For, as the Lord testifies: “Where anyone’s treasure is, there also will his heart be” [Col. 0869B] (Matt. 6:21). (Morals, book XV, chapters 18–19.)

“For a heavy burden oppresses the person who is ravaged by the tumult of avarice as it incites him, since avarice is not merely one particular fault, but the fault from which all others arise. For it is written, as we have said: ‘The love of money is the root of all evils’ (1 Tim. 6:10). Whoever is said to be ruled by covetousness is therefore plainly shown to be subject to every evil.

“Of such a person it is written that, ‘because he crushed and stripped the house of the poor, he seized it and did not build it; his belly was not satisfied’ (Job 20:19–20). He crushes and strips the poor man’s house who does not blush to despoil through avarice the one whom he crushes through power. He seizes it and does not build it, as though it were plainly said: ‘The one who ought to have built this house even seizes it.’ [Col. 0869C] For when the Lord comes in judgment, he will say to the reprobate: ‘I was hungry and you did not give me food’; and, referring to this fault, he adds: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Matt. 25:42).

“If, then, such great punishment is inflicted on the one proved not to have given, what punishment must be inflicted on the one accused of having taken away? He seized it and did not build it, because he not only gave nothing of his own but also took away what belonged to another.” (Pastoral Care, book III, chapter 21.)

“And often some rich people consider how much they give, but pretend not to notice how much they seize: they count their rewards but refuse to weigh their sins. Let them hear what is written: ‘He who gathered wages put them into a bag full of holes’ (Hag. 1:6). In a bag full of holes, one sees the money when it is put in, but does not see it when it is lost. Those, therefore, who look at how much they give but do not weigh how much they seize put their wages into a bag full of holes: they gather them while looking toward them as the ground of their confidence, but lose them because they do not look at them properly (ibid.).

“And some rich people of this world, while Christ’s poor are tormented by hunger, feed actors with lavish gifts; and they kill almost as many people every day as they conceal resources from the poor who are dying. There are also some who now distribute their possessions mercifully but neglect to guard themselves from sins, and who suppose that God’s justice can be bought: they take care to give money for their sins and imagine that they may sin with impunity.

“There are also some rich people [Col. 0870A] who could possess enough of their own if they wished to put a limit on their covetousness. To them it is said: ‘Woe to you who join house to house and add field to field, until there is no more room! Will you alone dwell in the midst of the earth?’ (Isa. 5:8), as though it plainly said: ‘How far do you stretch yourselves, when you cannot bear to have companions sharing the world with you? You oppress those who are joined to you, yet you always find others against whom you can extend yourselves.’

“To them it is said again: ‘Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own—how long will he heap thick mud upon himself?’ (Hab. 2:6). For the avaricious person, to heap thick mud upon himself is to pile up earthly profits together with the weight of sin. Hence it is written again: ‘The avaricious person will not be filled with money, and whoever loves riches will gain no fruit from them’ (Eccl. 5:9). He would gain fruit from them if he wished to distribute them well, without loving them; but because he retains them by loving them, he will certainly leave them behind without fruit.

“Of such a person it is written: ‘He who hastens to become rich will not remain innocent’ (Prov. 28:20). For surely the one who longs to increase his wealth neglects to avoid sin. Like a bird caught, when he eagerly sees the bait of earthly things, he does not recognize the snare of sin by which he will be strangled. And when the greedy desire whatever profits belong to the present world, they do not perceive the losses they will suffer in the future.

“Let them therefore hear what is written: ‘What does it profit a person if he gathers everything that is outside himself, but condemns only what he himself is?’ Of the one who does not fear to condemn himself and is not filled with money, it is written again: ‘His belly was not satisfied’ (Job 20:20).” (Morals, book XV, [Col. 0870C] chapter 19.)

“The belly of the wicked person is avarice, because in it is collected whatever he swallows through perverse desire. It is clear, however, that avarice is not extinguished by the things desired but increased by them. For, like fire, when it receives wood to consume, it grows; and where the flame seems for a moment to be compressed, there it is soon seen to spread.

“Often, when almighty God is very angry with an avaricious mind, he first allows everything to be supplied according to its wishes, and afterward removes it in punishment, so that the person must endure penalties for these things (chapter 20). Hence it is added: ‘And when he has obtained what he desired, he will not be able to possess it’ (ibid.). For the anger is greater when what is wrongly desired is also granted, and sudden punishment follows, because the person has obtained what, while God was angry, he coveted.

“Divine judgments commonly appear later when they are held back, lest evil desires be fulfilled. For the sooner an evil desire is permitted to be fulfilled, the more quickly it is generally punished (chapter 22). Hence it is rightly said: ‘When he is satisfied, he will be confined’ (Job 20:22). First he pants through avarice to gather what he desires; and when he has heaped up much, as though into a certain belly of avarice, he will be confined when satisfied, because, while he is anxious about how to guard what he has acquired, his very fullness constricts him. The mind of the avaricious person, which earlier sought rest from abundance, afterward labors more heavily in guarding it (chapter 23).

“He who earlier labored in the very exhaustion of his desire—considering how he might seize what he coveted, how he might take some things by enticements and others by threats—is wearied by another pain after reaching his desire through the things he has acquired: he must guard with anxious fear what he remembers acquiring through great labor. He fears ambushes on every side and dreads suffering from others what he himself inflicted on them. He fears someone more powerful, lest he suffer violence from him; but when he sees the poor, he suspects a thief. He also takes great care that the things he has amassed should not be consumed through negligence because of their natural decay.

“In all these things, since fear itself is punishment, the wretched man suffers as much as he fears suffering. After this he is also led to Gehenna and handed over to eternal torments. Wonderful, however, is the security that comes from not seeking what belongs to others; from this security perpetual rest also arises, because through good and peaceful thought one passes to eternal joys (chapter 26).

“But the person placed in authority who harms others is called ‘lightning-bearing,’ because from the very source by which he raises himself against the good, as though from the light of glory, the life of the good is afflicted (chapter 29). It is said what punishment must strike him: ‘A fire that is not kindled will devour him’ (Job 20:26). In these few words the fire of Gehenna is expressed in a truly remarkable manner.

“For bodily fire, in order to be fire, needs bodily fuel. Since it must be preserved, it is undoubtedly nourished by piled-up wood; it cannot exist unless kindled and fed. But the fire of Gehenna, although bodily and although it burns bodily those cast into it, is neither kindled by its own activity nor nourished by wood. Created once for all, it endures unquenchably; it needs no kindling and does not lack heat. For the justice of almighty God, foreknowing future things, created the fire of Gehenna at the very origin of the world, so that it would begin to exist once for the punishment of the reprobate but would never end its burning even without wood.

“It must also be understood that all the reprobate, because they sinned with soul and body together, are tormented there in soul and body alike (chapter 30). When they receive this body in the resurrection, they will be handed over to burn with it in the fires of Gehenna. Then they will want to be separated from it; then, if they can, they will seek to escape its torments; then they will begin to wish to avoid what they loved. But because they made this same body hostile to God, God judging will bring it about that they are tormented by the fire even more through it.

“Here, then, they will not desire to leave the body, and yet they will be dragged away from it; there they will desire to leave it, and yet they will be kept in it for punishment. Thus, to increase their torment, here they are unwillingly led out of the body, and there they will unwillingly be held in the body.” Those who were ensnared by the enemy with a noose together with guilt amid earthly advantages, and with bait together with guilt—that is, with profit together with guilt and prosperity together with wickedness—will there be unable to escape the punishment of retribution that he will inflict. And though they seek escape when pain constrains them and their eyes open to prayer and wisdom, wisdom will be of no help, because here, where they ought and were able to act, they lost the time for acting; here they kept the eyes of their hearts closed by pleasure. Such is the fruit of avarice, and such is the outcome of its recompense.

Avarice is rightly restrained if the condition of the one who pursues it is carefully considered. For why should the one who gathers strive to gather, when the one who gathers cannot himself remain standing? Let each person therefore consider his course and recognize that what he has is enough for him, however little it may be. Perhaps he fears that provisions will fail on the journey of this life. But the shortness of the road rebukes our long desires: many things are carried uselessly when the destination is near.

Another person subjects himself to the tyranny of pride, and while raising his miserable heart against human beings, subordinates it to vice. He desires the insignia of exalted honors, seeks to be raised up by success, and paints in his thoughts the whole person he desires to be in his own estimation. Already [Col. 0872B] he seems to possess a tribunal; already he sees the services of his subjects obeying him; already he towers above others; already he inflicts evils on some and repays others because they have inflicted them. Already, surrounded by ranks, he goes forth publicly in his imagination; already he observes what services support him, though he repeats all these reflections while alone.

Already he tramples some down and raises others up; already he satisfies his hatred against those he has trampled, and receives favors from those he has raised. What, then, does the person who impresses so many phantoms upon his heart see other than a waking dream? Since he endures within himself so many causes of affairs that he invents, he plainly carries inwardly the disturbances born of his desires. (Morals, book XXXIV, chapter 23.)

“For when pride breaks into the mind, it seizes it as a tyrant seizes a besieged city; and the richer the person it captures, the harsher it rises in mastery, because the more widely virtue is practiced without humility, the more broadly pride dominates.

“Whoever receives its tyranny over himself with a captive mind first suffers this damage: with the eye of his heart closed, he loses the fairness of judgment. Everything done well by others displeases him, while only what he himself has done—however wrongly—pleases him. He always despises the works of others and always admires what he does, because whatever he has done he believes he alone has done. In what he displays, through his craving for glory, he favors himself in his own thoughts; and when he thinks he surpasses everyone in everything, he walks with himself through the broad spaces of his thoughts and silently proclaims his own praises.

“Sometimes the mind is led to such great elation that, in what makes it swell, it is also unrestrained in the ostentation of its speech. But the more imprudently someone exalts himself in his own estimation, the more easily ruin follows. Hence it is written: ‘The heart is exalted before ruin’ (Prov. 16:18).

“Hence Daniel says: ‘The king was walking in the hall of Babylon; he answered and said: “Is this not great Babylon, which I built as a royal house by the strength of my power and for the glory of my splendor?”’ (Dan. 4:26–27). But he immediately adds how swiftly vengeance suppressed this swelling: ‘While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: “To you it is spoken, King Nebuchadnezzar: Your kingdom shall pass from you, and they shall drive you away from human beings; your dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals; you shall eat grass like an ox, and seven periods shall pass over you”’ (Dan. 4:28–29).

“Behold: because the swelling of his mind carried him as far as open words, the patience of the Judge immediately burst forth into sentence; and the more implacably it struck him, the more immoderately his pride had raised itself. Because he considered it right to enumerate the goods in which he pleased himself, he heard the evils enumerated in which he would be struck.”

For all who swell inwardly with proud thought have clamor in speech, bitterness in silence, dissolution in cheerfulness, fury in sadness, dishonor in conduct, apparent honor in outward appearance, selectiveness in their walk, and rancor in their reply. Their life is always strong for inflicting insults but weak for enduring them; slow to obey but troublesome in provoking others; ignorant of what they ought to do and are capable of doing, yet ready for what they ought not and are not capable of doing. They are bent by no exhortations toward what they do not freely desire, but toward what they secretly desire they seek to be forced, because, fearing to become base through their desire, they wish to endure compulsion in carrying out their will. (Morals, book XXXIV, chapter 18.)

“It must be understood that this very elation of which we are speaking possesses some people through secular matters, and others through spiritual matters. One swells with gold, another with eloquence; one with low and earthly things, another with the highest and heavenly virtues. Yet the same reality is enacted before God’s eyes, although, when it enters human hearts, it is concealed from their sight under different clothing.

“For when the person who previously took pride in earthly glory later exalts himself over holiness, elation has not at all abandoned his heart. Rather, coming to him in its customary way, it has changed its clothing so that it may not be recognized.” To such people it is said: “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Sir. 10:9). (Morals, book XXXIII, chapter 3.)

“For there are two vices that rule the human race with monstrous power: one belongs to the spirit, the other to the flesh. Elation raises up the spirit, while lust corrupts the flesh. Thus the ancient enemy, pressing the human race chiefly through elation or lust, sleeps in the recesses of the reed-bed and in damp places, because he holds the condemned human being under the dominion of his condemnation either through the elation of the spirit or through the corruption of the flesh.”

As it is written: “There are two daughters of the leech, saying, ‘Give, give’” (Prov. 30:15). The devil is the leech, who, thirsting to sin, is ceaselessly inflamed by persuading people to sin. He has two daughters because there are two particular enticements of the human race that imitate the ardor of this ancient enemy: lust and avarice. For the more freely the reins of lust are loosened, the more harmfully it delights; and, as one of the poets says (Juvenal, Satire 14):

> The love of money grows as the money itself grows.

He possesses some people through all these things, because when the spirit of pride raises them into the swelling of its height, it bends them toward shameless corruption and subjects them to the insatiability of avarice.

Let those enslaved to lust therefore consider what inhabitant they have—namely, the devil—who, as Scripture says, rests in damp places, that is, in hearts devoted to wantonness and foul with lust; and who prepares such people with himself for eternal torments through lust. Of them it is written: “The garment mixed with blood shall be for burning and fuel for fire” (Isa. 9:5), because the body with which the soul is clothed, polluted by carnal works, will burn in the combustion of eternal fire unless it is washed with tears and cleansed by worthy fruits of repentance.

Scripture marks such people by saying: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17). “The beasts rotting in their dung” means carnal people ending their life in the foulness of lust. Whenever preachers rebuke the carnal mind for its sins, whenever past vices return to its memory, they are like turning a basket of manure around a fruitless tree, so that the mind may recall the memory of the evils it has committed and, as though growing rich from stench, may be sent toward the grace of remorse.

A basket of manure is sent to the root of the tree when the conscience of its wickedness is touched by the memory of thought. When the mind rouses itself through repentance to lamentation and is reformed for the grace of good action, the root of the heart, as though touched by manure, returns to fruitfulness in its work. It mourns what it remembers having done; it is displeased with what it recalls itself to have been; it directs its intention against itself and kindles its spirit toward better things.

Thus the tree comes back from stench to fruit, because the mind raises itself from consideration of sin to good works, listening to Paul, who says: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6:18), and to Solomon: “Do not give your honor to others and your years to the cruel one” (Prov. 5:9)—that is, do not subject the honor with which you were created in the image of God to the pleasures of unclean spirits, nor spend the time granted for living at the will of the adversary.

For whoever is subjected to any crime is certainly handed over in that respect to the dominion of evil spirits. Hence it is also said: “Lest strangers be filled with your strength and your labors be in the house of another” (ibid., 10)—that is, do not assist the deeds of demons by applying either the ingenuity of your mind or the strength of your body to the commission of crimes, and do not increase the house of another—that is, the number of the lost—by adding yourself to it.

“And you will groan at the end, when you have consumed your flesh and your body” (ibid.), that is, you will be compelled to groan in punishments when not only carnal enticements have passed away, but, after the body itself has been abandoned, the soul [Col. 0874D] that bore the body is compelled to repay everything.

Let those devoted to lust consider that, when the Lord determined to punish the crimes committed by those serving the flesh, he marked the stain of the crime in the very character of the punishment, when he rained sulfur and fire upon them, as sacred history reports (Gen. 19:24). For what is expressed by sulfur if not the foulness of the flesh, and what by fire if not the heat of carnal desire? Sulfur has foulness, and fire has heat. Those, therefore, who had burned toward perverse desires from the foulness of the flesh deserved to perish together with sulfur and fire, so that through a just punishment they might learn what they had done through unjust desire.

From this vengeance, which those devoted to lust endured while in the body, those who indulge in lust ought to consider what they will endure together with soul and body in the eternal fire, where “their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24), unless, abandoning evil through worthy fruits of repentance and fitting lamentation, and doing good, they diligently cleanse both the stains of the flesh and their hearts.

Yet even in this life it often happens that those who, by living luxuriously in their youth, had squandered their possessions later fail through poverty in old age. As the heat of the flesh cools and the flower of youth withers, they see others using the possessions they had sold in wantonness; and, groaning in tardy repentance, they say what follows: “Why did I hate discipline, and why did my heart not submit to rebukes?” (Prov. 5:12).” (Morals, book XXI, chapter 9.)

“For certain sins defile the soul, but crimes destroy it. Hence blessed Job, defining the crime of lust, says: ‘It is a fire devouring unto destruction’ (Job 21:12), because the guilt of a crime does not merely defile as far as participation; it devours unto destruction.

“And because, whatever other good works there may be, if the crime of lust is not washed away they are overwhelmed by the enormity of this crime, he continues by adding: ‘and consuming every produce.’ The produce is the soul’s good works. But if the flesh dominates it in perverse order with the fire of lust, everything it has brought forth well is burned up. For in the eyes of almighty God there are no works of justice or compassion that are not shown to be unclean through the contagion of corruption.”

And because the order of vices is often distributed according to the order of the bodily members: a belly distended with food and wine easily foams over into lust, just as manure soaked with moisture easily breeds worms.

Some people, ignorant of the order of the struggle, neglect to subdue gluttony and already rise up for spiritual battles. At times they do many things requiring great strength, but while the vice of gluttony rules them, they lose through the enticement of the flesh everything they have done courageously. While the belly is not restrained, all the virtues are overwhelmed together through the desire of the flesh. (Pastoral Care, 111, chapter 20.)

“Hence it is written, when Nebuchadnezzar conquered (2 Kings 25:8): ‘The chief of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem.’ The chief of the cooks is the belly, which the cooks serve with great care so that it may be filled delightfully with food. [Col. 0875D] The walls of Jerusalem are the virtues of the soul raised toward the desire for heavenly peace. The chief of the cooks therefore casts down the walls of Jerusalem, because, when the belly is stretched by gluttony, the virtues of the soul are destroyed through lust.”

In contrast, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with overeating, drunkenness, and the cares of this age” (Luke 21:34). There he adds a useful fear: “And that day come upon you suddenly. For it will come like a snare upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth.” (Pastoral Care, ibid.)

“Those devoted to gluttony must be warned not to plunge themselves through the sword of lust while they apply themselves to the pleasure of food. They should see how much loquacity and how much slackness of mind lie in wait for them through eating, lest, while they serve the belly softly, they be cruelly bound by the snares of vices.”

For the sacred authority testifies that levity of conduct immediately follows those devoted to gluttony, saying: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6). Excessive eating often drags them into lust, because, while the belly is stretched by satiety, the goads of desire are aroused.

Hence the cunning enemy, who opened the mind of the first human being to the desire for the fruit but bound it in the snare of sin, is addressed by the divine voice: “You shall crawl on your breast and belly” (Gen. 3:14); as though it were plainly said to him: “By thought and gluttony you shall rule over human hearts.” For the farther one withdraws from the second parent, namely Christ, the more, through immoderate use, the fall of the first parent—the earthly Adam—is repeated when the hand is extended toward food.

It must also be understood that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways. But why should I explain those same ways here, when among many people drunkenness is already maintained as a custom, and some miserable people even boast and glory as though it were a virtue that they can drink much and make others drunk? They do not heed what the Lord threatens through the prophet: “Woe to those who are mighty in drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 5:22); nor what he commands through the Apostle: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Eph. 5:18), because drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6:10).

Solomon likewise says: “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings”—that is, to all who, in every rank and sex, ought to rule both themselves and others—“because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest they drink and forget the judgments of justice and pervert the cause of the children of human beings” (Prov. 31:4).

Again, sacred Scripture says: “Wine was created for rejoicing, and not for drunkenness from the beginning; wine drunk moderately is the gladness of soul and heart; it is health for body and spirit, sobriety in drinking” (Sir. 31:35). “For wakefulness and choler are for the undisciplined man” (ibid., 23), and modest, temperate food is useful both to flesh and soul.

Much wine drunk produces irritation, anger, and many falls. Much wine drunk produces bitterness of spirit; the boldness of drunkenness is the offense of the imprudent, diminishing virtue and causing wounds. “At a banquet of wine do not rebuke your neighbor, and do not despise him in his enjoyment; do not speak words of reproach to him or press him” (ibid., 38). “A drunken laborer will not become rich; wine and women make the wise apostatize; they rebuke the sensible; and whoever joins himself to prostitutes will become worthless. Rot and worms will inherit him” (Sir. 19:1).

(Morals, book V, chapter 31.)

“Another person subjects himself to the dominion of envy. He must understand that, although the poison of the ancient enemy is infused into human hearts through every vice that is committed, in this wickedness the serpent shakes all his innards and sets them in motion with the plague of impressing evil. Of this it is plainly written: ‘Through the devil’s envy death entered the world’ (Wis. 2:24).

“When the rottenness of jealousy has corrupted a conquered heart, its outward features also reveal how grievously madness torments the soul. The complexion is struck with pallor, the eyes sink, the mind burns, and the limbs grow cold. There is rage in thought and gnashing in the teeth. As the hatred that grows in the hiding places of the heart is concealed, it drills the conscience with blind pain, like an enclosed wound.

“Nothing joyful in one’s own affairs is pleasant, because the mind wasting away is wounded by its own punishment, and another’s happiness torments it. The higher the edifice of another’s work is raised, the deeper the foundation of the envious mind is dug, so that the more others hurry toward better things, the more disastrously it falls. By this fall, moreover, what was thought to have risen through perfect work in other actions is also destroyed. For when envy has weakened the mind, it consumes everything good it finds accomplished.

“Hence Solomon rightly says: ‘The health of the heart is the life of the flesh, but envy is the rottenness of the bones’ (Prov. 14:30). What is signified by flesh if not something weak and tender, and what by bones if not strong deeds? Often it happens that some people appear weak in certain actions despite true innocence of heart, while others already perform certain deeds that seem strong in human eyes, yet inwardly waste away through the pestilence of envy toward the good of others.

“It is therefore rightly said: ‘The health of the heart is the life of the flesh,’ because if innocence of mind is preserved, even outward weaknesses are eventually strengthened. And rightly it is added: ‘Envy is the rottenness of the bones,’ because through the vice of jealousy even strong deeds of virtue perish before God’s eyes. For the bones rotting through envy means that even certain strong works are destroyed.

“But why do we speak of envy if we do not also explain how one is rescued from it? It is difficult for one person not to envy what another longs to obtain, because whatever temporal thing is received becomes less for each individual as it is divided among many. Therefore jealousy torments the mind of the one who desires, because another either takes away entirely what he seeks by receiving it, or restricts its quantity.

“Whoever therefore desires to be completely free from the plague of jealousy should love that inheritance which the number of co-heirs does not diminish: an inheritance that is one for all and wholly possessed by each, and that appears more abundant the more the multitude of those who receive it expands. The lessening of jealousy is therefore an affection arising from inward sweetness, while its complete death is perfect love of eternity.

“When the mind is withdrawn from desire for a thing that is divided among those who receive it, it loves its neighbor more, because it fears less that its own losses will result from the neighbor’s advancement. If it is perfectly carried away into love of the heavenly homeland, it is also made wholly firm in love of its neighbor, because when it desires nothing earthly, there is nothing to oppose its charity toward its neighbor. And what else is this charity than the eye of the mind? If it is touched by the dust of earthly love, it is immediately wounded and driven back from contemplating the inner light.”

Another man has laid himself under the dominion of anger: what does he do in his heart except carry on even quarrels that are not there? He often does not see those present, contradicts those absent, and utters and receives insults within himself; then he responds more harshly to what he has received, and, when no opponent is there, composes quarrels in his heart with loud cries. Thus he harbors a crowd within, while the heavy burden of inflamed thought presses upon him. [Col. 0878A]

Let us therefore consider how great is the guilt of anger, through which gentleness is lost and the likeness of the heavenly image is marred. Through anger wisdom is lost, so that one has no idea at all what should be done or in what order, as it is written: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Ecclesiastes 7:10), because it withdraws the light of understanding when it confuses the mind by agitating it. Through anger life is lost, even if wisdom seems to be retained, as it is written: “Anger destroys even the prudent,” because a confused mind does not accomplish what it could accomplish wisely, even if it is able to understand it. Through anger justice is abandoned, as it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James 1:20), because when the mind is disturbed, it inflames the judgment of its reason, and whatever it forcefully suggests it considers right. [Col. 0878B]

Through anger the grace of social life is lost, as it is written: “Do not be a constant companion of an angry man, lest you learn his ways and bring a stumbling-block upon your soul” (Proverbs 22:24), because one who does not restrain himself by human reason must live alone like a beast. Through anger harmony is broken, as it is written: “An impetuous man produces quarrels, and an angry man pours out sins” (Proverbs 16:21). An angry man pours out sins because he makes even the wicked whom he carelessly provokes to discord worse than they were.

Through anger the light of truth is lost, as it is written: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4:26), because when anger casts the darkness of confusion over the mind, God conceals from it the ray of his knowledge. [Col. 0878C] Through anger the splendor of the Holy Spirit is shut out. In opposition to this, according to the old translation, it is written: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, unless upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” For when he said “humble,” he immediately added “quiet.” If anger therefore removes the mind’s quiet, it closes the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit. When he departs, the mind, left empty, is quickly driven into open madness and is scattered outward, all the way to the surface, from the inner foundation of its thoughts.

For when the heart is kindled by the goads of anger, it throbs; the body trembles; the tongue stammers; the face burns; the eyes grow fierce; and familiar people are no longer recognized. The mouth indeed forms a cry, but the mind does not know what it is saying. In what respect, then, is this man far removed from those possessed, when he is not conscious of his own action? [Col. 0878D] Hence it often happens that anger leaps as far as the hands, and the farther reason withdraws, the more boldly it rises. The mind cannot restrain itself because it has become subject to another’s power; and fury thrusts the limbs outward in blows precisely to the degree that it holds captive within the mind itself, the mistress of the limbs.

Sometimes, however, it does not extend to the hands but turns the tongue into a dart of cursing. It calls down the death of a brother in its prayers and asks God to perpetrate what the perverse man himself either fears or is ashamed to do. Thus he commits murder by desire and speech even when he refrains from injuring his neighbor with his hands.

Sometimes anger, disturbing the mind, imposes silence as though by judgment; and to the degree that it does not express itself outwardly through the tongue, it burns more fiercely within. Thus an angry person withdraws his conversation from his neighbor and, by saying nothing, says how alienated he is. At times this severity of silence serves the administration of discipline, provided that the form of discretion is carefully maintained in the depths of the heart. At other times, however, while the inflamed mind is restrained from its customary speech, with the passage of time it becomes entirely separated from love of its neighbor. Sharper goads then come to the mind, causes that inflame it more heavily arise, and in the angry person’s eye the splinter becomes a beam when anger is changed into hatred. [Col. 0879A]

Very often anger, enclosed by silence within the mind, seethes more violently and forms silent, clamorous voices. It throws at itself the words by which it is provoked and, as though placed before a judicial hearing, responds more harshly when it has been inflamed. Solomon briefly indicates this when he says: “The expectation of the wicked is fury” (Proverbs 11:23). Thus it happens that the disturbed mind experiences a greater tumult in its silence, when the enclosed flame consumes it more grievously. [Col. 0879B]

Well, therefore, did a certain wise man before us say: “The thoughts of an angry person are generations of vipers; they eat their mother, the mind.”

It should be understood that anger kindles some people quickly and abandons them easily, while it moves others slowly but holds them more harshly. Some resemble reeds set alight: while they resound with their cries, they give back something like the noises of their own kindling. They produce a flame quickly, but immediately grow cold into ash. Others, not unlike heavier and harder wood, take fire slowly, but once kindled are extinguished with greater difficulty; and because they rouse themselves to harshness more slowly, they preserve the fire of their fury more stubbornly. [Col. 0879C] Others, which is worse, both receive the flames of anger more quickly and lay them down more slowly. Yet others receive these flames slowly and lose them quickly.

In these four ways the reader clearly recognizes that, with respect to the good of tranquility, the last approaches it more closely than the first, while, in the evil itself, the third surpasses the second. But what use is there in saying how anger possesses the mind if we do not also explain how it should be restrained? [Col. 0879D]

Anger, broken in two ways, ceases to possess the mind. The first is this: before beginning any action, the watchful mind should set before itself all the insults it may have to endure, so that, by thinking upon the reproaches endured by its Redeemer, it may prepare itself to tolerate adversity. It receives what comes all the more firmly because it has armed itself more cautiously through foreknowledge. Whoever is caught unprepared by adversity is found, as it were, sleeping before an enemy; the enemy kills him more quickly because he pierces one who does not resist. But whoever carefully anticipates the evils that threaten awaits the assaults of the enemy like a watchman awake in ambush, and from the very point at which he seemed likely to be caught unaware he girds himself bravely for victory. [Col. 0880A]

The mind should therefore diligently meditate upon every adversity before the beginning of its action, so that, always thinking upon these things, always protected against them by the breastplate of patience, it may overcome whatever comes with foresight and count as gain whatever does not come.

The second way of preserving gentleness is this: when we see the excesses of others, let us think upon our own sins, by which we have exceeded in the case of others. Consideration of our own weakness excuses the evils of others to us. For the person who remembers that perhaps he still has something for which he himself ought to be tolerated patiently endures an injury inflicted upon him. And as water extinguishes fire, so fury of mind is extinguished when each person’s own fault is recalled to his mind as anger rises. One is ashamed not to spare another’s sin when one remembers that one has often sinned in ways requiring pardon from God or from one’s neighbor.

But amid these matters we must carefully understand that one anger is aroused by impatience, and another is formed by zeal. The former is generated by vice, the latter by virtue. For if no anger arose from virtue, Phinehas would not have appeased the force of divine punishment by the sword. Because Eli did not possess this anger, he aroused against himself the movement of heavenly vengeance, which could not be appeased. For to the degree that he was lukewarm toward the vices of his subjects, to that degree the severity of the eternal ruler burned against him. [Col. 0880B]

Of this anger the Psalmist says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 6:3). Those who wish us to be angry only with ourselves, and not also with our offending neighbors, do not understand this correctly. For if we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves, it remains that we should be angry with their errors just as with our own vices.

Of this anger Solomon says: “Anger is better than laughter” (Ecclesiastes 7:4), because through sadness of countenance the mind of the offender is corrected. Again, the Psalmist says: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Psalm 6:8). Anger arising from vice blinds the eye of the mind, but anger arising from zeal troubles it, because when the mind is shaken by zeal for what is right, the contemplation that can be perceived only with a tranquil heart is disturbed. [Col. 0880C]

The very zeal for righteousness, because it agitates the mind with unrest, immediately darkens its vision, so that in its agitation it does not see higher things that it had previously beheld well in tranquility. Yet from the very point at which it is temporarily struck and prevented from seeing, it is more subtly led back to higher things. For zeal itself for what is right, after a little while, opens more abundantly into tranquility what for the moment it closes through agitation; and from the point at which the mind is disturbed so that it does not see, it advances so that it may see more truly and clearly.

It is like an eye that is weak: when an eye-salve is applied, its light is completely extinguished, but afterward it receives the light more truly from the very point at which it healthfully loses it for a time. [Col. 0880D] Yet contemplation is never joined to agitation, nor can a troubled mind perceive what even a tranquil mind can scarcely desire. The sun’s ray cannot be seen when disturbed clouds cover the face of heaven; nor does a troubled fountain return the image of the one who looks into it as clearly as a tranquil fountain does, because, in proportion as its water trembles, it obscures within itself the appearance of the likeness.

When the mind is moved by zeal, therefore, one must be extremely careful lest this same anger, assumed as an instrument of virtue, become master of the mind. It must not go before as a mistress, but, like a maidservant prepared for service, must never withdraw from behind reason. For anger is demanded more effectively against vices when it serves in subjection to reason. [Col. 0881A]

However much anger may arise from zeal for righteousness, if it conquers the mind immoderately, it immediately refuses to serve reason. It spreads itself more shamelessly in proportion as it regards the poison of impatience as virtue. Therefore the person moved by zeal for righteousness must attend above all to this: anger must not pass beyond the mind’s control. Rather, while considering the time and measure of punishment for sin, he must restrain the disturbance of his mind by examining it more subtly, suppress his aggressiveness, and arrange his ardent impulses according to equity. Thus he will be a more just avenger of another’s fault to the degree that he has first been victorious over himself.

He should correct the faults of offenders in such a way that he himself, who corrects them, first grows through patience; he should judge his own fervor by rising above it, lest, excited without restraint, he depart far from righteousness through the very zeal for righteousness. [Col. 0881B]

For one who does not first judge himself does not know how to judge evil rightly. Even if he has perhaps learned by hearsay that he ought to judge rightly, he cannot judge the merits of others when his own conscience provides him no rule of judgment through the experience of innocence. Those through whom the faults of others are struck must first be cleansed, so that those who hasten to correct the vices of others may already come pure to the work of punishment.

When the punishment of divine judgment against us is suspended, our own conscience should rebuke us and raise itself against itself to the lamentation of repentance. It should not be raised against the good while humble toward itself; rather, it should be stern against itself and submissive to all good people.

All these vices, therefore, must be avoided with the greatest care by everyone striving toward eternal life. Through them the devil hastens to drag the human race into eternal punishments, and he began this work at the beginning of the human race and continues to exercise it throughout the whole age of this world. [Col. 0881C]

He placed the face of pride before Eve’s mind when he incited her to despise the words of the Lord’s command. He kindled the flame of envy in Cain’s mind when he grieved over his brother’s accepted sacrifice, and through this brought him all the way to the crime of fratricide. He burned Solomon’s heart with the torches of lust, subjecting him to such love for women that, led on to the worship of idols, he forgot reverence for his Creator while pursuing the pleasure of the flesh. Greed also burned in Ahab’s mind when it drove him, with impatient desires, to covet another man’s vineyard and through this dragged him to the guilt of murder. [Col. 0881D]

This is the jar with an open mouth that the prophet Zechariah saw being carried by two women (chapter 5). They had wings like the wings of a kite, flying for plunder. In the middle of this jar sat a woman; she was thrown into the middle of the jar, and a mass of lead was placed in its mouth.

The two women with wings like the wings of a kite are the two principal vices, namely pride and vainglory. They carry a jar with an open mouth, that is, greed, gaping for profits. In the middle of it sat a woman, that is, impiety; into the mouth of this impiety the mass of lead is thrown. This impiety is weighed down by the burden of its greed, because greed makes the mind it infects so heavy that it cannot possibly be raised to desire the heights of heaven. [Col. 0882A]

Hence the Lord commands that one who bears a hump—that is, one who gapes after earthly things—must not offer loaves to his Lord. Pride and vainglory have a spirit in kite-like wings, because their actions are undoubtedly like those of the devil, who always lies in wait for the life of the little ones. They lift the jar, that is, desire, between earth and heaven, because pride and vainglory have this characteristic: they exalt above other people in his thoughts the person whom they have infected.

Sometimes through ambition for possessions, sometimes through desire for honors, they raise him whom they have once captured and hold, as though to the height of an elevated position. Through greed they raise the mind so high that, despising their neighbors, they seem to abandon them and seek lofty things in their pride.

Such people, while they grow proud, pass beyond in their minds those with whom they live and are not at all joined to the citizens above. The jar itself is said to be carried to the land of Shinar, which is interpreted as “their stench,” because desire is the root of all evils. Since every evil is engendered through greed, it is fitting that the house of greed should be built in stench. Greed compels some people to forget the fear or love of God, to abandon the reputation of a good name and the fragrance of holy religion and faith, of which it is written: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15). [Col. 0882B]

## CHAPTER III. On Oaths and Perjuries: That One Must Swear without Deceit and Keep Faith Even with an Enemy; and on Curiosity, Detraction, and Sins of Thought

Neglecting to avoid oaths often drives certain people to deceit; and, so that the deceit itself may be concealed, it drives them not only to swear but sometimes even to perjure themselves. This is apart from that swearing which has become ingrained in human practice through bad habit, although Scripture says: “A man who swears much will not be justified” (Ecclesiasticus 23:11). His habit is not good. [Col. 0882C]

The Gospel itself, and James in his epistle, teach how carefully we must avoid the rashness of swearing, saying: “Above all things, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath; but let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no,’ so that you may not fall under judgment” (Matthew 5:34; James 5:12). This is the judgment under which Herod fell, so that he was compelled either to commit perjury or, by avoiding perjury, to commit another crime. [Col. 0882D]

But if it should happen that we have sworn something incautiously, and keeping it would clearly lead to a worse outcome, let us recognize that it must be changed by the more salutary counsel. This moderation must be observed with even greater care not only in swearing but in everything we do: if we should happen to fall into the traps of the cunning enemy in such a way that we cannot rise from them without some stain of sin, let us seek that way of escape in which we see that we will suffer less danger.

It is like those who, shut in by hostile walls, wish to escape but see that access to every gate is barred. They must choose the place for leaping down where, because the wall is lower, they will incur the least danger in falling. [Col. 0883A]

Yet no one should neglect what he has sworn in the name of the Lord, whether necessity compelled him, anger drove him, or desire provoked him. According to the measure of the guilt, repentance that wipes away the guilt must follow, while the Lord thunders terribly through the prophet Ezekiel against King Zedekiah:

“As I live, says the Lord God, since he made his oath void and broke the covenant that he had made with the king of Babylon, in the midst of Babylon he shall die. For he despised the oath in order to break the covenant; and after he has done all these things, he shall not escape” (Ezekiel 17:16).

From this we learn that faith must be kept even among enemies, and that one must consider not to whom one swore but through whom one swore. For the one who trusted you because of the name of God and was deceived was found much more faithful than the one who, by invoking divine majesty, plotted treachery against your enemy—or rather, against one who had already become your friend. [Col. 0883B]

“Behold,” he says, “he gave his hand to the king of Egypt, delivered himself into his hand, and by perjury committed sacrilege against the Lord.”

There is a secular saying (Virgil, *Aeneid* 2):

> “Who would ask whether there is deceit or valor in an enemy?”

Those who say that enemies should be deceived commonly bring this saying against us. Even if we were to accept it, Zedekiah acted much worse. He did not deceive an enemy but a friend, to whom he had been bound by the covenant of the Lord.

Therefore, so long as you have not sworn and have not entered into a pact in the name of the Lord, it may be a matter of prudence and strength either to deceive or to overcome an adversary by whatever means you can. But once you have bound yourself by an oath, the person who trusted you is no longer an adversary but a friend; and under the pretext of the oath—that is, by invoking God—he has been deceived. [Col. 0883C]

For this reason Scripture now says: “The oath that he despised and the covenant that he violated, I will place upon his head” (Ezekiel 17:19). And lest we think that the oath, covenant, and pact belonged to the king of Babylon or to Zedekiah who had made it, the prophet continues: “In the violation by which he despised me” (ibid. 20).

Whoever therefore despises an oath despises the one through whom he swore, and he injures the one whose name the adversary trusted. For this reason the Lord says: “I will spread my net over him, and he will be caught in my snare; I will bring him to Babylon, and there I will judge him” (ibid.). [Col. 0883D]

Whatever Nabuchodonosor did against Zedekiah, he did not do by his own strength but by the anger of God, in whose name Zedekiah had committed perjury. For we read that Zedekiah was captured and brought to Riblah; there, after his sons had been killed before his eyes, he was blinded and carried into Babylon shut up like a wild animal in a cage (Jeremiah 52:5).

There are some who swear deceitfully by craft in order to deceive the person to whom they swear, yet do not consider themselves guilty of perjury. The Spirit of God contradicts them through the Prophet: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in his holy place? He who has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor” (Psalm 23:3). [Col. 0884A]

Whoever intends to act otherwise than he promises swears deceitfully, believing that it is not perjury to wickedly deceive the error of one who has trusted him. To swear (*jurare*) is, as it were, to pray by right (*jure orare*), that is, to speak justly. A person speaks justly when what he promises is fulfilled.

Many swear deceitfully in order to deceive their neighbor. The Father of lights, the Lord, abhors this, as Peter says: “You have not lied to men but to God” (Acts 5:4). In this matter we must also note that liars are called fabricators of lies. Just as a building is constructed with stones, so a lie is constructed with words. Where the speech is not deceitful but its meaning is truthful, a fortified structure rises, as it were, not from fabrication but from nature. Hence it is written: “The one who speaks truth in his heart and has not acted deceitfully with his tongue” (Psalm 23:4). [Col. 0884B]

An oath must therefore be avoided, but perjury much more so. If the necessity of swearing presses and constrains someone, it must be done with pure words and a devout mind. The person who swears must not think that he can deceive the Lord by verbal cunning. Nothing is hidden from him; all hearts lie open to him. He does not receive an oath according to the way someone swears, but according to what the one to whom the oath is sworn supposes him to have sworn.

Whoever therefore swears deceitfully is held guilty before both: before God, whose name he has taken in vain, and before the brother whom he has prepared to deceive and cheat by black treachery. Suitable repentance must follow for both offenses: because he took the name of God in vain, and because, against God’s commandment, he deceived his brother by fraud. [Col. 0884C]

Although a person who acts and speaks falsely may tremble inwardly, fearing that the truth’s arrows will expose him, and although, if discovered, he will lose the glory of popular favor, and although his conscience accuses him because he sins knowingly, he is nevertheless overcome by desire. Having suppressed the favor he seeks, he derives boldness from his iniquities. Often, even with vengeance set before his mind, he rises against God and resolves to endure any adversity from him, provided that, while he has the power, he may do everything he desires.

Hence Scripture says: “The Lord will abhor the bloody man and the deceitful” (Psalm 5:8). The whole Church also invokes judgment upon those who speak with a double heart, that the Lord may destroy “all deceitful lips” (Psalm 11:3–4). Again Scripture says: “Cursed is the deceitful man” (Malachi 1:14), and “Let deceitful lips become mute” (Psalm 30:19). [Col. 0884D]

Deceitful people, therefore, who swear—or rather perjure themselves—in the name of Christ and his saints ought to be afraid, because the Lord will abhor them as bloody men, that is, as those stained with human blood. For just as the latter kill, so the former deceive the living.

How immense and deadly a sin homicide is—and how distinctions are customarily made within it, as within other sins—is clearly shown by nature itself, by holy Scripture, and by divine and human judgments. Hence Leviticus says: “Whoever strikes and kills a man shall be put to death” (Leviticus 24:17). The Apostle says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in himself” (1 John 3:15).

Deceitful people are joined to such sinners. Many perjuries are committed that we do not perform by our own will; but deceitful people knowingly work another’s destruction. Therefore they are rightly abhorred by the Lord as bloodstained men. [Col. 0885A] The saints who contended for the truth even unto death, in whose name these people perjure themselves, will not be found to be their helpers but their judges and condemn­ers in the strict examination. Those saints whom they refused to have as companions in asserting truth and justice, and whom they brought forward as witnesses to their false testimony, will stand against them.

Since these saints see within themselves the glory of almighty God, it is impossible that there should be anything outside that they do not know. Nothing is done in creation that they cannot see. What they recognize as worthy of abhorrence when truth enlightens them, they abhor in adherence to that same truth.

Yet the brightness of their blessedness is not darkened by the sight of iniquity or by the punishment of the reprobate. Rather, their joy increases when they see the evils of the wicked, because they escaped them by God’s mercy. They give greater thanks to their Deliverer in proportion as they see in others what they themselves could have suffered had they been abandoned.

And when Truth declares, “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Proverbs 19:5, 9)—that is, one who knowingly testifies falsely against truth, or who recounts true things in order to pervert truth and, in an effort to escape punishment, brings them close to it [the wording is syntactically uncertain]—the saints exult over such witnesses as though they agreed with truth. [Col. 0885B]

There are some who think that they are not harmed, or are harmed less severely, if they do not themselves swear falsely or deceitfully but make others swear on their behalf and in their place. They do not understand that in this matter they are either deceived by the deceiving devil or knowingly plunge themselves into *deprecandum* [an uncertain reading, apparently denoting ruin or perdition].

Scripture says of such people: “They descend alive into hell” (Psalm 54:16), that is, they slip knowingly into sin. They sin all the more gravely because they do not die in sin alone: unless corrected by repentance, they plunge both themselves and those whom they send to perjure themselves into hell.

Although those who swear commit sin in such perjury, those who render the oaths sworn on their behalf void have the greater sin, as the Lord said to Pilate: “He who delivered me to you has the greater sin” (John 19:11). That is, those who have caused others to sin are held guilty before God for so many persons as they send into perjury, with the guilt of their own soul added. [Col. 0885C]

The Lord says through the prophet (Ezekiel 34) that just as he will require the sheep from the shepherd’s hand, so he will require from the hands of those who have caused their subjects, obedient to them, to perjure themselves through their action or to be polluted by any other crime.

We must not understand only pastors, bishops, presbyters, deacons, and superiors of monasteries to be shepherds. All the faithful who exercise guardianship over even a small household are rightly called shepherds, insofar as they preside over their household with vigilant care. Whoever is in charge of even one or two brothers in daily governance owes them the office of a shepherd, because, insofar as he is able, he must feed them with nourishment and exhort, rebuke, admonish, and correct them.

Indeed, everyone who is believed to live as a private person also holds the office of a shepherd and feeds a spiritual flock; if he gathers to himself a multitude of good actions and pure thoughts, and strives to govern it by the guidance of the righteous, nourish it with the heavenly pages of Scripture and examples of good works, and guard it with watchful diligence against the snares of unclean spirits, he keeps watch over it through the watches of the night, just as we read in the Gospel concerning the shepherds to whom the angel appeared at the Savior’s birth. [Col. 0885D]

There are also some who do not count the vice of curiosity among the more serious sins, but they are mistaken. The vice of curiosity is serious: while it leads someone’s mind outward to investigate the life of his neighbor, it always hides his own inner life from him, so that, while he knows what belongs to another, he does not know himself. The more knowledgeable the curious person becomes about another’s character, the more ignorant he becomes of his own.

Often, while a curious person investigates what belongs to others, he brings trouble upon himself, like a dog that diligently follows the tracks of a boar or a stag but dies when it catches up with it and is struck by its tooth or horn. [Col. 0886A]

Hence Solomon aptly says: “Do not apply your heart to all the words that are spoken, lest perhaps you hear your servant cursing you. For your conscience knows that you yourself have often cursed others” (Ecclesiasticus 7:22–23). When we consider what we have been like toward others, we are less grieved that others are like that toward us, because the injustice of others avenges in us what our own conscience accuses in itself.

Let the curious person examine himself; then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in the other whose life and merits he investigates. There are people who think themselves extremely powerful in this world and do not understand how contemptible they are—slaves serving the vice of curiosity. [Col. 0886B]

Concerning their powerless power, a certain Catholic philosopher, a man of great wisdom and knowledge, says in one of his books to every person who is deceitfully powerful and truly powerless (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book 3):

> For even if the distant Indian land  
> trembles at your rule,  
> and farthest Thule serves you,  
> yet if you cannot drive away  
> dark cares  
> and banish wretched complaints,  
> your power is no power.

> (*Pastoral Care*, book 3, chapter 24): “There are some who do not consider how manifoldly they sin when, by sowing discord among brothers, they extinguish love, which is truly the mother of all virtues. Since nothing is more precious to God than the virtue of love, and nothing is more desirable to the devil than the extinction of love, whoever destroys the love of neighbors by sowing quarrels serves God’s enemy more intimately. For where the enemy fell after losing it, this person, removing love from wounded hearts, cuts off their path of ascent.” [Col. 0886C]

There are also some who are accustomed to maliciously sweetened detraction, not attending to what the Lord says: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I pursued” (Psalm 106:5).

> (*Moralia*, book 14, chapter 24.) Hence Solomon also says: “Do not be among the banquets of drinkers, nor among the feasts of those who bring flesh to eat” (Proverbs 23:28).

To bring flesh for eating means, in a conversation of disparagement, to speak in turn of the faults of one’s neighbors. Their punishment is immediately added: “For those who devote themselves to drinking and give contributions will be consumed, and drowsiness will be clothed in rags” (ibid. 21).

“Contribution” is a Greek word, *symbolon*, and is interpreted as “a contribution” or “a sharing.” Here it is a sharing of words, just as at banquets there is commonly a sharing of money or of other things, as the present passage itself shows. Those who devote themselves to drinking are therefore those who intoxicate themselves with reproach of another’s life. To give a contribution means that, just as each person commonly contributes food for eating, so in a conversation of detraction they contribute words. [Col. 0886D]

But those who devote themselves to drinking and give contributions will be consumed, because it is written: “Every detractor will be uprooted” (Proverbs 15). “Drowsiness will be clothed in rags” because death will find the person despised and lacking every good work—the person whom the weakness of detraction occupied here while he searched out the crimes of another’s life.” [Col. 0887A]

Another person devotes himself to almsgiving and distributes what is his; but while he serves many injustices, or perhaps gives free rein to his tongue in detraction, it often happens that the one who had been merciful grows inflamed, toward the end of his life, with the goads of rapacity and cruelty. This happens by a very just judgment: he loses before human beings the thing by which he pleased human beings, because he never took care to correct what displeased God.

There are two circumstances in which it is permitted to speak about and recount another’s evils. The first is when it is necessary to take counsel with others who appear to be involved in the matter itself, concerning how the person who has sinned or done something wrong may be corrected. The second is when someone must be warned and cautioned lest he happen to enter into association with an evil person while believing him to be good, since the Apostle says: “Do not associate with such a one” (1 Corinthians 5:11), and Solomon says: “Do not remain with an angry man, lest you take a snare for your soul” (Proverbs 22:24). [Col. 0887B]

We find that the Apostle himself did this when he wrote to Timothy: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; you too avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words” (2 Timothy 4:14).

Apart from such necessities, whoever speaks against another in order either to disparage or malign him is committing detraction, even if what he says appears to be true.

There are some who, although they exceed only in small matters, do so frequently, without considering what kinds of things they commit but only how many. If they disregard their deeds, they ought to fear when they weigh them and be alarmed when they count them. The wounds that break out upon the limbs through an itch are small, but when their multitude occupies the body beyond counting, they destroy the body’s life just as one grievous wound inflicted upon the chest would. [Col. 0887C]

Hence it is written: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1). Whoever neglects to weep over and avoid small sins falls entirely from the state of righteousness—not suddenly, but little by little. [Col. 0887D]

And since the Lord says, “I am coming to gather their works and thoughts,” it is necessary that each person mourn not only the sins of his deeds but also the sins of his thoughts. Nor should one consider only the measure of the sin perpetrated in deed, but also that perpetrated in thought, so that, in proportion to the inward ruin each person feels within himself, the measure of his lamentation may likewise be increased. Otherwise, if evil thoughts cause too little anguish, they may lead to the commission of deeds.

Therefore, each person must vigilantly guard against every vice and sin; whoever laments sins should commit nothing that must be lamented, and whoever mourns vices should fear to perpetrate them. For one must think with the greatest care that whoever remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from certain lawful ones. In this way he may make satisfaction to his Creator: whoever has committed what was forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what was permitted, and should reproach himself in small matters, since he remembers having sinned in great ones.

What I am saying would be excessive if I did not affirm it from the testimony of sacred Scripture. Certainly, the Law of the Old Testament forbids coveting another man’s wife, but it does not prohibit a king from commanding mighty deeds to his soldiers, or from desiring water, as though these were punishable offenses. We all know that David, pierced by the sword of desire, both coveted and took another man’s wife; worthy chastisements followed his fault, and through the lamentation of repentance he corrected the evil he had committed.

Yet, long afterward, when he was sitting opposite the enemy ranks, he desired to drink water from their cistern. His chosen soldiers broke through the midst of the opposing forces and brought back unharmed the water the king had desired. But the man instructed by scourges immediately reproached himself for having desired the water at the risk of his soldiers, and, pouring it out to the Lord, offered it as a libation, as it is written there: “He poured it out as a libation to the Lord” (II Samuel 23:16). The water poured out was turned into an offering to the Lord, because through the repentance of his forgiveness he sacrificed the fault of desire.

Thus, he who once had no fear of coveting another man’s wife afterward trembled because he had coveted water. Since he remembered having committed unlawful acts, he had now become strict toward himself and abstained from what was lawful. This is how we do penance: if we mourn perfectly the things we have committed.

## CHAPTER IV

On works of mercy; on what repentance ought to be like and why it must not be neglected while it is possible; and likewise on the last judgment and the punishments of hell.

Meanwhile, it must be understood how greatly works of mercy avail, since they are prescribed above all else for producing worthy fruits of repentance. Hence Truth itself says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41). Again it says: “Give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 11:38). It is also written: “Water extinguishes a burning fire, and almsgiving resists sins” (Ecclesiasticus 3:33). Again it says: “Store up almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will plead for you” (Ecclesiasticus 29:15).

Hence a good father admonishes his innocent son, saying: “If you have much, give abundantly; if you have little, nevertheless be eager to share even the little gladly” (Tobit 4:9). And to show how great a virtue there is in self-restraint and in receiving those in need, our Redeemer said: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matthew 10:41).

In these words we must note that he did not say, “He will receive a reward from a prophet,” or “a reward from a righteous person,” but “a prophet’s reward,” or “a righteous person’s reward.” For a reward received from a prophet is one thing, and a prophet’s reward another; a reward received from a righteous person is one thing, and a righteous person’s reward another.

What does it mean to say, “He will receive a prophet’s reward,” except that the person who supports a prophet through his generosity, although he himself does not possess the gift of prophecy, will nevertheless receive the rewards of prophecy from the almighty Lord? This person may perhaps be righteous, and, the less he possesses in this world, the greater confidence he has to speak on behalf of righteousness. When someone who possesses something in this world supports him, while perhaps still lacking the courage to speak freely for righteousness, he makes the other’s freedom in righteousness his own share, and will receive the rewards of righteousness together with the one whom he helped by supporting him, so that the latter might speak that same righteousness freely.

The prophet is full of the spirit of prophecy, but nevertheless needs bodily nourishment; and if the body is not restored, it is certain that the voice will be withdrawn. Therefore, whoever provides nourishment to a prophet because he is a prophet gives strength to that prophet’s prophecy for speaking. He will thus receive a prophet’s reward together with the prophet, because, even though he was not full of the spirit of prophecy, he nevertheless displayed before God what he had assisted.

This is why John says of certain travelers to Gaius: “For they have gone out for the sake of the name of Christ, receiving nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to receive such persons, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (III John 7–8). Whoever grants temporal assistance to those who possess spiritual goods becomes a co-worker in those spiritual goods. For since few receive spiritual gifts, while many abound in bodily possessions, the rich make themselves partners in the virtues of the poor by giving comfort from their wealth to those holy poor.

Hence it is written: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none, and let the one who has food do likewise” (Luke 3:11). Because a tunic is more necessary for our use than a cloak, this pertains to the fruit of repentance: we ought to share with our neighbors not only external things and those less necessary, but also the things that are very necessary to us—namely, either the food by which we live bodily or the tunic with which we are clothed.

Since it is written in the Law, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 19:19), the person who does not share with his neighbor, in that neighbor’s need, even the things necessary to himself is shown to love his neighbor less. That is why the command is given to divide two tunics with one’s neighbor; it could not have been given concerning one tunic, because if one is divided, no one is clothed. In half a tunic, both the one who receives and the one who gives remain naked.

Those who have lost by sinning the garment of innocence that we received in baptism must labor to be clothed again through works of mercy and through the sacrifice of a contrite spirit. “A sacrifice to God,” it says, “is a contrite spirit” (Psalm 51:19). Our past sins were forgiven us when we received baptism, yet after baptism we committed many more sins, and we cannot be washed again with baptismal water. Since we have defiled ourselves after baptism, let us baptize our conscience with tears.

Perhaps someone has fallen through lack of faith: let him look to Peter, who wept bitterly over what he had denied through fear. Another has burned against his neighbor with the wickedness of cruelty: let him look to the thief, who, even at the very moment of death, reached the rewards of life through repentance. Another, panting with the fever of greed, has seized what belonged to others: let him look to Zacchaeus, who restored fourfold whatever he had taken from anyone. Another, inflamed by the fire of lust, has lost the purity of his flesh: let him look to Mary, who burned out in herself the love of the flesh with the fire of divine love.

Behold, the almighty God places before our eyes everywhere what we ought to imitate; everywhere he sets forth examples of his mercy. Let the evils we have experienced now become displeasing to us. The almighty God willingly forgets that we were guilty; he is ready to reckon our repentance to us as innocence. Though defiled after the waters of salvation, let us be born again from tears.

For through the fervor of the mind, whether among spiritual enemies or even among our fleshly neighbors, we grow old through a certain manner of living and darken the appearance of the newness we have assumed. Hence the Psalmist says: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Psalm 6:8).

*(Moralia, Book XIX, chapter 16.)* “Yet from this old age we are renewed daily, if the practices of vigilance remain watchful: by praying, reading, and living well, because our life, when washed with tears, is exercised in good works, extended toward holy meditations, and continually restored to its newness. The mind does not know how to grow old through the body when it strives always to begin anew through desire.

Hence Paul says: ‘Be renewed in the spirit of your mind’ (Ephesians 4:23). And again: ‘Our outward person is corrupted, but the inward person is renewed day by day’ (II Corinthians 4:16). Hence the Psalmist, who had already reached the summit of perfection, spoke as though beginning: ‘I said: Now I have begun’ (Psalm 77:11). For if we do not wish to grow weary of the good things we have begun, we must believe that we need to begin anew every day.”

*(Pastoral Care, Part III, chapter 31.)* “But there are those who mourn the sins they have committed, yet do not abandon them.
