Those who mourn their sins but do not abandon them must be admonished to understand carefully that they cleanse themselves uselessly with weeping while defiling themselves wickedly by their manner of life, since they wash themselves with tears for the very purpose of returning, once cleansed, to their filth.

Hence it is written: ‘The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud’ (II Peter 2:22). When a dog vomits, it certainly casts out the food that oppressed its stomach; but when it returns to its vomit, it is burdened again with what had relieved it. Those who mourn their sins certainly cast out through confession the wickedness with which they had been badly satisfied and which oppressed the inmost part of their minds; but when they repeat it after confession, they take it up again.

The sow, when washed in a wallow of mud, is made dirtier. So the person who mourns a sin but does not abandon it subjects himself to a heavier guilt: he both despises the forgiveness that he could have obtained by weeping and, as though in muddy water, rolls himself about. For by withdrawing the purity of life from his own tears, he makes even those tears themselves filthy before God’s eyes.

Again it is written: ‘Do not repeat a word in your prayer’ (Ecclesiastes 7:15). To repeat a word in prayer is to commit, after weeping, what must again be mourned. Hence Isaiah says: ‘Wash yourselves; be clean’ (Isaiah 1:16). Whoever does not preserve the innocence of life after tears neglects being clean after washing.

Thus those who do not cease to mourn their sins but commit again what must be mourned are washed, yet are by no means clean. Hence a certain wise man says: ‘Whoever is baptized because of the dead and then touches him again, what benefit is there in his washing?’ (Ecclesiasticus 34:30). He is baptized because of the dead who is cleansed from sin by tears; but after baptism he touches the dead who repeats his fault after tears.”

*(Pastoral Care, Part III, chapter 13.)* “On the other hand, those who abandon the sins they have committed but do not mourn them must be admonished not to consider their faults already forgiven. Although they do not multiply them by committing them, they nevertheless cleanse them with no tears.

For a writer who stops writing has not, merely because he adds nothing else, erased what he had written. Nor does the person who has inflicted insults make satisfaction merely by keeping silent, since it is plainly necessary for him to oppose the words of the pride previously spoken with words of humility spoken afterward. Nor is a debtor released merely because he does not increase his debt, unless he also pays what he had bound himself to pay.

So, when we sin against the Lord, we do not make adequate satisfaction merely by ceasing from wickedness. We must also pursue, with contrary lamentation, the pleasures we loved; we who departed after delighting in pleasures must return embittered by tears; we who fell by flowing into unlawful acts must also rise by restraining ourselves from lawful ones; the sound sorrow must burn the heart that diseased joy had filled; and the humble rejection of a lowly life must heal what the exaltation of pride had wounded.

Hence it is written: ‘I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly; and to the sinners: Do not exalt the horn’ (Psalm 75:5). Sinners raise up the horn when, through recognition of their iniquity, they do not humble themselves for repentance.

Again it says: ‘A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise’ (Psalm 51:19). Whoever mourns his sins but does not abandon them does indeed crush his heart, but refuses to humble it. Whoever has already abandoned his sins but does not mourn them does indeed humble himself, but refuses to crush his heart.

Hence Paul says: ‘And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified’ (I Corinthians 6:11). For a more reformed life sanctifies those whom the affliction of tears cleanses by washing them through repentance.

Hence Peter, seeing certain people terrified by consideration of their evils, admonished them, saying: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized’ (Acts 2:38). About to mention baptism, he first set forth the lamentation of repentance, so that they might first pour over themselves the water of their own affliction and afterward be washed by the sacrament of baptism.

Those who neglect to mourn their past sins therefore do not live secure in forgiveness, since the supreme shepherd of the Church himself believed that repentance must be added even to the sacrament that principally extinguishes sins.”

For how can any one of us be secure about forgiveness if he neglects to mourn his sins, when the Redeemer himself first wept even over a sinful city, as it is written: “When Jesus saw the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If you too had known’” (Luke 19:41–42)? He did this once when he announced that the city would perish; our Redeemer does not cease to do this daily through his chosen ones, when he sees that some have passed from a good life into depraved ways.

He mourns those who do not know why they are being mourned, who, in Solomon’s words, “rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs 2:14). If they had recognized the condemnation impending over them, they would mourn themselves with tears for their offenses.”

*(Homily 11.)* “The perverse soul, devoted to present things and dissolved in earthly pleasures, hides from itself the evils that follow, because it refuses to foresee the future things that disturb its present joy. While it abandons itself to the delight of the present life, what else does it do than go toward the fire with closed eyes?

To it it is said: ‘Days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a siege wall’ (Luke 19:43). Who, I ask, are greater enemies of the human soul than the evil spirits, who besiege it as it departs from the body, though they foster it, while it is set upon love of the flesh, with deceptive pleasures?

They surround it with a siege wall because, bringing back before the eyes of its mind the iniquities it has committed, they draw it into fellowship with their own damnation and hem it in. Thus, caught at the very end of life, it sees by which enemies it is surrounded, yet cannot find a way of escape, because it is no longer permitted to do good works—works that, when it was permitted, it despised.

*(Homily 11.)* The almighty Lord is accustomed to visit the perverse soul in many ways. He visits it continually through a commandment, sometimes through a scourge, and sometimes through a miracle, so that it may hear the truth it did not know and yet, still proud and contemptuous, may either return, pierced by sorrow, or, overcome by benefits, become ashamed of the evil it has done.

But because it did not recognize the time of his visitation, at the end of life it will be handed over to those enemies with whom it will be joined in the perpetual fellowship of condemnation at the eternal judgment. Through the evil spirits it is thrust back into hell until the day of judgment comes, from which point it too will be tormented together with them in the fires of hell.”

To that day of judgment will come the one who shakes the elements by his advent, before whose presence heaven and earth tremble. Hence the prophet says: “Once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Haggai 2:7). The entire human race is brought before his tribunal. For the punishment of the wicked and the reward of the good, angels, archangels, thrones, principalities, and dominions attend him.

Consider, dearest brothers, what terror there will be on that day before the presence of so great a judge, when there will already be no remedy in punishment. What shame will that be, when a person, compelled by his guilt, must blush in the assembly of all human beings and angels? What fear will seize one who cannot even apprehend in tranquility the one whom he must see in anger?

The prophet, contemplating that day well, says: “That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and storm, a day of trumpet and blast” (Zephaniah 1:15–16). Consider, dearest brothers, with what harshness the prophet saw the day of the final judgment grow bitter over the hearts of the reprobate, a day he cannot explain even by so many names.

But how great then will be the joy of the elect, who deserve to rejoice in the vision of the one at whose presence they see even the elements tremble? They will enter together with him into the wedding feast; those who rejoice at the bridegroom’s wedding are themselves the bride, because in the bridal chamber of the eternal kingdom God is joined to our vision. This vision will never again, throughout eternity, be torn away from the embraces of his love.

Then the door of the kingdom will be closed to those who mourn, though now it is opened daily to those who repent. For then there will indeed be repentance, but it will no longer be fruitful, because the one who loses the fitting time for forgiveness now will by no means find forgiveness then.

Hence Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Corinthians 6:2). Hence the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6). The person who considers the present life and sees not its use but its end truly shows himself cautious and watchful, so that from its end he may conclude that nothing which passes away is worth delighting in.

Hence Solomon says: “If a human being lives for many years and rejoices in all of them, he must remember the dark time and the many days; when they come, they will accuse the past of vanity” (Ecclesiastes 11:8). Again it is written: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus 7:40).

*(Moralia, Book IX, chapter 62.)* “Hence the holy man asked the Lord, saying: ‘Release me, so that I may mourn my sorrow a little’ (Job 10:20). Unless we are mercifully released from the guilt with which we have bound ourselves, we cannot perfectly mourn what we grieve within ourselves against ourselves. But the pain of our guilt is truly mourned when that dark retribution of hell is foreseen with focused fear.

*(Chapter 63.)* Hence it is appropriately added: ‘Before I go and do not return to the land of darkness, covered by the shadow of death.’ What is signified by the name of the dark land except the dark prison of Tartarus? The gloom of eternal death covers it, because it separates the condemned forever from the life of light.

Hell is not improperly called a land, because whoever is seized by it is held firmly. For it is written: ‘One generation passes away and another comes, but the earth stands forever’ (Ecclesiastes 1:4). The dark prisons of hell are therefore rightly called a dark land, because those whom they receive for punishment are tormented not by temporary punishment or by a phantom-like imagination, but are held by the solid retribution of eternal condemnation.

It is sometimes also indicated by the designation of a place, as the prophet testifies when he says: ‘They bore their disgrace with those who descend into the pit’ (Ezekiel 32:24). Hell is therefore also called land because it holds those whom it has received firmly; and it is called a pit because, once it has seized them, it swallows them forever, as they continually tremble and are tossed amid surrounding torments.

The holy man, whether speaking in his own voice or in that of the human race, asks to be released before he goes—not because the person who mourns his guilt is going to the dark land, but because the person who neglects to mourn is certainly going there. Just as a creditor says to his debtor: ‘Pay the debt before you are imprisoned on account of the debt’—yet the one who does not delay in paying what he owes is the one who is imprisoned.

It is rightly added: ‘I shall not return,’ because the mercy of the one who spares no longer frees those whom the justice of the judge has once condemned in places of punishment.

These places are described still more subtly when it says: ‘A land of misery and darkness’ *(chapter 64).* Misery pertains to pain; darkness to blindness. That which holds those expelled from the sight of the stern judge is called a land of misery and darkness, because pain tortures outside those whom blindness darkens within, separated from the true light.”

In its further description it is added: “Where there is the shadow of death and no order” *(chapter 65).* Just as external death separates flesh from the soul, so internal death separates the soul from God. The shadow of death is therefore the obscurity of separation, because the condemned person, when set aflame by eternal fire, is darkened away from the inward light.

The nature of fire is to give forth both light and burning from itself. But that avenging flame of past vices possesses burning and does not possess light. Hence Truth says to the reprobate: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). Again, signifying all their bodies in the person of one, he says: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matthew 22:13).

The flame of Gehenna devours those whom it blinds from the vision of the true light, so that the pain of burning torments them outwardly and the punishment of blindness darkens them inwardly. Thus those who sinned against their Creator in body and heart are punished in body and heart alike; they feel punishment in both respects, because while they lived here they served their depraved pleasures with both. Each condemned person is therefore followed by retribution according to the measure of his crime.

*(Chapter 65.)* Hence it is said in the condemnation of Babylon: “As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning” (Revelation 18:7). And the coming Judge declares that he will say to the reapers: “Gather the weeds and bind them in bundles to burn” (Matthew 13:30).

To bind bundles for burning means to join together in like groups those who are to be handed over to eternal fire, so that those whom similar guilt stains may be constrained by equal punishment, and those who have not been defiled by unequal iniquity may not be tormented by unequal suffering. Thus condemnation may crush together those whom arrogance had raised together; like affliction may constrict those whom ambition had likewise enlarged; and the same flame of punishment may torment those whom the same flame of sin had kindled in lust.

For just as in the Father’s house there are many dwelling places according to the diversity of virtue (John 14), so the diversity of crimes subjects the condemned to different punishments in the fires of Gehenna. Although Gehenna is one for all, it does not burn all with one and the same intensity. Just as we are all touched by the one sun, yet do not all grow hot beneath it in the same way—for the weight of heat is felt according to the condition of the body—so for the condemned there is one Gehenna that afflicts them, yet it does not burn all with the same intensity. What the differing strength of bodies produces here, the differing cause of merits produces there.

*(Chapter 66.)* Those handed over to eternal fires feel pain in their punishments, and in their pain they are continually struck by the fear of pressing dread, so that they endure what they fear and again fear without cessation what they endure. Of them it is written: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Mark 9:48).

These punishments both torment those plunged into them beyond their strength and preserve them while extinguishing within them every support of life. Thus the end of life punishes them in such a way that their torment lives forever without end. For it hastens toward an end through torment, yet, continually failing, endures without end.

For the wretched there will be death without death, an end without end, decay without decay: death lives, the end always begins, and decay never knows how to cease. Death destroys but does not extinguish; pain torments but in no way drives away fear; the flame burns but does not disperse the darkness. That fire does not shine for consolation, yet it shines somewhat in order to torment more severely.

For the reprobate will see their fellow followers with them in torment, illuminated by the flame—the ones whose love led them to sin. Thus those whose lives they loved carnally against the commands of the Creator will afflict them by their own destruction, increasing their condemnation.

This is gathered from the testimony of the Gospel (Luke 16), in which, according to the announcement of Truth, the rich man who descended to the torments of eternal burning is described as remembering his five brothers. He asked Abraham to send Lazarus to instruct them, lest they should someday come there and be tortured by punishment.

If he remembers absent relatives as an addition to his own pain, it is certainly clear that, to increase his punishment, he could shortly also see them present. What wonder is it if he sees the reprobate burning beside him, when, to increase his pain, he sees in Abraham’s bosom Lazarus, whom he had despised?

From this it follows that those whom the reprobate now love in a disordered way they will then see with themselves in torments, by a wondrous order of judgment, so that the carnal kinship placed before the Creator may increase the punishment of their own penalty by seeing those relations condemned to an equal retribution.

The fire that torments in darkness must therefore be believed to preserve light for torment, just as the flame of a torch shines within the darkness. Then the devouring flame will burn those whom carnal pleasure now defiles. Then the immeasurably vast abyss of hell will swallow those whom empty exaltation now raises up. Whatever vice they have here used to carry out the will of the cunning deceiver, the reprobate will then reach torment together with their leader.

Although the nature of angels and of human beings is greatly different, one punishment nevertheless entangles those whom one guilt binds in crime. The prophet aptly and briefly suggests this when he says: “There is Assyria and all her multitude, and around her are her graves” (Ezekiel 32:22).

Who is signified by Assyria, under the name of a proud king, except the ancient enemy who fell through pride and who, because he drags many into guilt, descends with his whole multitude into the prisons of hell? Graves cover the dead. And who suffered death more severely than the one who, despising his Creator, abandoned life? When human hearts receive that dead one, they unquestionably become his graves.

His graves are around him because those in whose minds he now buries himself through desires he afterward joins to himself through torments. And because the reprobate now receive evil spirits within themselves by committing unlawful acts, then they will burn as graves together with the dead.

As it is written concerning the bodies of the reprobate: “A fire not kindled will devour him” (Job 20:26), because the justice of the Almighty, foreknowing future things, created the fire of Gehenna from the very beginning of the world, so that it would begin once to exist in the punishment of the reprobate but would never cease burning even without wood.

It must also be understood that all the reprobate, because they sinned with soul and body together, will there be tormented partly in soul and partly in body.”

Behold, we have learned what punishment awaits the condemned; and with sacred Scripture instructing us, we have no doubt how great the fire in condemnation is, how great the darkness in the fire, and how great the fear in the darkness. But what does it profit to know these things beforehand if one does not escape them?

Therefore, we must take every care that, when we are given a time of respite, we may flee the final torments of evil through the zeal of living well. Hence Solomon says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it diligently, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in Sheol, where you are hastening” (Ecclesiastes 9:10).

Hence Isaiah says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6). Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Corinthians 6:2). Again he says: “While we have time, let us do good to all” (Galatians 6:10).

It is also written: “Blessed are those whose sins are covered” (Psalm 32:1). When we sin, we place good deeds over evil deeds. When, therefore, we renounce the evils we have done and choose to do the good, we are, as it were, placing a covering over the deed of which we are ashamed to be seen. Whoever abandons earlier evils and afterward does good thereby covers his past wickedness by adding the merits of good works.

As long as holy men are still in this life, however, they nevertheless have something that must be covered before God’s eyes, since it is altogether impossible that they should never sin in deed, speech, or thought.

## CHAPTER V

That sins are committed in many ways and healed by humble repentance; and on forgiving offenses against one’s neighbor.

But it must be understood that we perpetrate every wickedness of sin in three ways: namely, by suggestion, by delight, and by consent. The first is perpetrated through the enemy, the second through the flesh, and the third through the spirit. For the tempter suggests what is evil; the flesh submits itself to delight; and finally the spirit, overcome by delight, consents. Thus, by suggestion we recognize sin, by delight we are overcome, and by consent we are also bound.

Sin is perpetrated in the heart in four ways, and brought to completion in action in four ways. In the heart it is perpetrated by suggestion, delight, consent, and the audacity of self-defense; [Col. 0897B] and—what makes every sin more serious—we even grow proud of the vice we have committed. For although exaltation usually arises from virtue, sometimes the foolish mind is lifted up by the wickedness it has perpetrated. Hence the prophet says: “The demons will meet the onocentaurs” (Isa. XX, XIV, 14). (Moralium, book VII, chapter 12.)

“What, then, are signified by the name ‘onocentaurs’ except both the dissolute and the proud? In Greek, ὄνος (*onos*) means ‘ass,’ and by the designation ‘ass’ the prophet indicates lust when he says: ‘Their flesh is the flesh of asses’ (Ezek. XXIII, 20). By the word ‘bulls,’ however, the neck of pride is represented, just as the Psalmist says in the Lord’s voice concerning the proud Jews: ‘Fat bulls have surrounded me’ (Ps. XXI, 13). Onocentaurs, therefore, are those who, subjected to the vices of lust, raise their necks [Col. 0897C] from the very place where they ought to have been humbled; who, serving the pleasures of their flesh and casting shame far from them, not only do not grieve over losing moral uprightness but even rejoice in the work of disgrace. Demons meet the onocentaurs because evil spirits serve them very readily, seeing that they rejoice in those things over which they ought to have wept.” (Moralium, book IV, chapter 25.)

“And sin is brought to completion in action in the same four ways. At first, the hidden fault is committed; afterward, the guilt is openly revealed before human eyes without shame; then it is brought into habitual practice; and finally it is nourished either by the deceptions of false hope or by the wretched obstinacy of despair. Thus no sin is overcome, since one is perpetrated through another. [Col. 0897D] For theft is often joined to the deceitfulness of commerce, and the guilt of perjury is often heaped upon deceit. Hence it is written: ‘They will go and come upon him, the dreadful ones’ (Job XX, 15)—that is, the evil spirits will go and come upon such a sinner, each attending upon particular vices, because, when they abandon one vice, they seize upon another in the perverse mind.” (Moralium, book XV, chapter 16.)

“For you often see an unjust man placed in earthly power stirred by great fury, carrying out whatever anger has suggested; and when the fury has departed, lust immediately ravages his mind. When lust is interrupted for a time, pride is at once substituted in his thoughts, as though arising from continence; and he desires to appear terrifying, so that he may be feared by others. But when circumstances require him to speak in a two-faced manner, [Col. 0898A] he sets aside, as it were, the terror of pride and adopts a softened, flattering speech. When he has ceased to appear proud, he does not fear becoming deceitful. As many vices as successively depart and take their place, so many evil spirits devastate his mind, as though going and returning.”

And whoever fulfills all these things simultaneously in action silently retains within the mind all that is harmful. The more defiled the mind sees itself to be through consent, therefore, the more rigorously it must be cleansed by the hand of repentance. For every sin that is not restrained here through the discipline of repentance will be struck by the fires of Gehenna. Hence Solomon says: “If the spirit of one who has authority rises up against you, do not abandon your place” (Eccl. X, 4). As though he were plainly saying: If you perceive that the tempting [Col. 0898B] spirit is prevailing against you, do not abandon the humility of repentance. He demonstrates this in the following words: “For healing will cause the greatest sins to cease” (ibid.). (Moralium, book IX, chapter 19.)

“For what else is the humility of mourning except the medicine of sin? Concerning this humility of mourning it is written: ‘If I wash myself as with snow-water’ (Job IX, 30). The waters of snow are the mournings of humility; and this humility, because it surpasses the other virtues before the eyes of the strict Judge, shines white, as though with the color of great merit.

“For there are some who have mourning but do not have humility. They weep in affliction, yet even in their very tears they either grow proud against the lives of their neighbors or rise up against the ordering of the Creator. Such people have water, but they do not have snow-water, and they cannot become clean, because they are not washed by the tears of humility. [Col. 0898C] The one who confidently said, ‘A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise’ (Ps. L, 19), had washed himself from guilt with snow-water. Those who are afflicted by mourning but remain rebellious through murmuring indeed crush the mind, but refuse to humble themselves.” (Pastor, book III, chapter 25.)

“Therefore, through the prophet Jeremiah it is said, when the individual sins of the Jews were being weighed: ‘My eye has poured forth divisions of waters’ (Lam. III, 48). We pour divided waters from our eyes when we give separate tears for each individual sin. For the mind does not grieve equally over all things at one and the same time; but when it is now touched more sharply by the memory of this fault and now of that one, it is stirred concerning all of them at once [Col. 0898D] and is cleansed in each particular grief.” (Moralium, book II, chapter 26.)

“He quarrels with himself over the things he remembers having done wrongly, and he becomes displeasing to himself when the One who created all things has already begun to please him. He reproves himself for his thoughts, pursues himself because of his words, and punishes himself with weeping for his deeds. Hence, in the Apocalypse, the angelic voice says: ‘Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame’ (Apoc. XVI, 15). Our shame is now seen when a blameworthy life, before the eyes of the righteous at the judgment, is not covered by the garment of subsequent good works.”

But whoever diligently watches over the covering of his sins by good works must forgive from the heart whatever offenses are committed against him by his neighbors, because every sin pollutes the life of the soul, whereas preserved resentment against one’s neighbor [Col. 0899A] kills. It is fixed in the mind like a sword, and with its point it pierces the hidden parts of the inward being. If it is not first drawn out of the wounded heart, no benefit of divine assistance is obtained in prayer, because medicines of healing cannot be applied to wounded limbs unless the iron is first removed from the wound.

Hence Truth itself says: “Unless you forgive people their sins, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI, 14). Again he admonishes us, saying: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against another.” Again he says: “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI, 37). To this ordinance he attached the condition of the petition, saying: “Forgive us our debts, [Col. 0899B] as we also forgive our debtors” (Luke XI, 4). Thus the good which, moved by compunction, we ask from God, we should first do ourselves in our dealings with our neighbor. Let us therefore forgive what is owed to us, so that what is owed by us may be forgiven.

For if we do not offer our body for Christ, we do not obtain the soul’s salvation. By this sacrifice God is appeased; in the judgment of his mercy he approves the victory of our peace. He looks upon the struggle of our heart, and he who rewards those who conquer afterward now assists those who are striving. Often we conquer a reluctant mind when we pray even for our enemies. We pour out a prayer for our adversaries—but would that the heart possessed love! For often we offer prayer for our enemies, yet we pour it forth more from commandment than from charity. We ask for the lives [Col. 0899C] of our enemies, yet inwardly we wish and fear that we may not be heard.

But because the inward Judge considers the mind rather than the words, no one asks anything for an enemy who does not pray for him from charity. Consider, however: an enemy has grievously sinned against us; he has inflicted losses; he has harmed those who helped him; he has persecuted those who loved him. These things would have to be retained if the forgiveness of our sins were not required of us. Our Advocate has arranged peace for us in our case, and he himself is the Judge of that same case, though he is also its Advocate. He inserted a condition into the prayer he composed, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Luke XI, 4).

Since, therefore, the Judge himself has come as Advocate, he himself hears the prayer which he made. Either, then, we say without doing what we have promised, “Forgive us our debts, as we also [Col. 0899D] forgive our debtors,” and by saying this we bind ourselves more tightly; or perhaps we omit this condition in prayer, and our Advocate does not recognize the prayer he composed, immediately saying to himself: “I know what I instructed; this is not the prayer that I made.”

What, then, should we do, brothers, except offer genuine affection of charity to our brothers, with no malice remaining in the heart? Almighty God considers our charity toward our neighbor so that he may direct his mercy toward our iniquities.

Nor should we neglect a brother who sins against us, but, without correction, should provoke him by whatever means we can to return to satisfaction, so that he may recognize himself and, by asking forgiveness for the sin he committed against us, receive its pardon. [Col. 0900A] For we are commanded to love our neighbor as ourselves. The Lord says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him privately” (Matt. XVIII, 15), and so forth. And again: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; if he repents, forgive him” (Luke XVII, 3). And in the Law: “When,” he says, “your brother owes you anything, and you take his pledge from him, return the pledge to him before sunset” (Deut. XXIV, 13). (Moralium, book XVI, chapter 2.)

“What is meant in this passage by the name ‘pledge’ except the confession of sin? Our brother becomes our debtor when any neighbor is shown to have sinned against us. For we call sins ‘debts’; hence it is said to the sinful servant: ‘I forgave you all the debt’ (Matt. XVIII), and in the Lord’s Prayer we pray daily: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also’ (Luke XI, 4), etc. [Col. 0900B]

“We receive a pledge from our debtor when we have obtained from the one who is known to have sinned against us the confession of his sin; through this confession we are asked to release the sin committed against us. For the one who confesses the sin he committed and asks forgiveness has already given, as it were, a pledge for the debt.

“We are commanded to return this pledge before sunset because, before the sun of justice sets within us through the grief of the heart, we ought to return the confession of forgiveness to the one from whom we receive the confession of guilt, so that the one who remembers having sinned against us may immediately feel himself released by us from what he has done.”

## Chapter VI. On the intercession of the saints, the necessity of prayers and sacred offerings, the reverence due to the house of God and the divine mysteries, and the need to pray attentively, especially for heavenly things

[Col. 0900C]

It is also of the utmost importance for us to seek the help of the saints, who now reign with God in heaven and shine forth through miracles on earth. The sick come to their extinguished bodies and are healed; perjurers come and are tormented by demons; those possessed by demons come and are liberated.

How, then, do they live there where they live, if they live through so many miracles here where they are dead? We ought to make these saints our patrons in the case of our examination, which we shall undergo with the strict Judge; we ought to strive to have them as our defenders on that day of such great terror.

Certainly, if some case of ours were to be argued before a great judge tomorrow, [Col. 0900D] the whole of today would be spent in thought. We would seek a patron and plead earnestly that a defender might come on our behalf before so great a judge. Behold, the strict Judge, Jesus, is coming; the terror of that great assembly of angels and archangels is at hand; our case is examined in that gathering. Yet we do not now seek patrons whom we may then have as defenders.

Therefore, since we place no confidence in any work of our own, it is necessary for us to run to the protection of the saints, to persist in tears before their sacred bodies, and to pray that, through their intercession, we may merit forgiveness. Our defenders are present: the holy apostles, blessed martyrs, glorious confessors, holy women, and virgins. They wish to be asked—or, so to speak, they seek [Col. 0901A] to be sought.

Let us therefore seek them as helpers of our prayer and find them as protectors of our guilt. For he who judges himself wishes to be asked not to punish sinners; hence he threatens anger for so long a time and yet mercifully waits.

Let his mercy refresh us in such a way that it does not make us negligent in any respect. Let our sins trouble us in such a way that the mind does not collapse into despair. For if we fear while presuming, and hope while fearing, we shall more quickly attain the eternal kingdom, where there are the singing choirs of angels, the fellowship of the citizens above, and the sweet solemnity of those returning from the sad labor of this pilgrimage.

There are the far-seeing choirs of the prophets; there is the company of the apostles who are judges; [Col. 0901B] there is the victorious army of countless martyrs, all the happier there the more harshly afflicted here. There is the steadfastness of confessors, consoled by receiving their reward. There are faithful men whom worldly pleasure could not soften despite the strength of their manly virtue. There are holy women who conquered both the world and their sex. There are children who here surpassed their years in character. There are old men whom age here made weak but did not deprive of the strength of their works.

Let us therefore seek these pastures, in which we may rejoice with the solemn assembly of so many citizens. May the festival of those who rejoice invite us. And if any of us has a conscience polluted by the filth of avarice, pride, vainglory, indignation, anger, envy, or other vices, he surely has, like the Canaanite woman, a daughter grievously tormented by a demon; for her healing let him run suppliantly to the Lord. For the thought generated in his heart is, by the devil’s art, driven mad, [Col. 0901C] and he ought to ask the merciful Creator for its correction through frequent—indeed continual—lamentation and prayers.

If anyone has stained the good works he has done with the plague of perjury, theft, blasphemy, slander, quarrelling, bodily impurity, or other such things, he has a daughter driven mad by the frenzies of an unclean spirit. For the action he had produced through good labor he has now squandered by foolishly serving the devil’s deceits.

Therefore, once such a person has recognized his guilt, he must immediately flee to prayers and tears and seek the frequent intercessions and assistance of the saints. As they pray for the salvation of his soul, let them say to the Lord: “We beseech you, Lord, compassionate and merciful, [Col. 0901D] patient and of great mercy: forgive her, for she cries out after us; forgive the guilt and grant grace to the one who, bowed down, seeks our help with intimate affection.”

In humbled submission he must no longer consider himself worthy of the company of the sheep of Israel—that is, of pure souls—but rather judge himself comparable to Cain and unworthy of heavenly gifts. Yet he must not, through despair, cease from the urgency of prayer. With a doubtful mind, let him trust in the goodness of the supreme Giver, because the one who could make a confessor from a thief, an apostle from a persecutor, an evangelist from a publican, and children of Abraham from stones can also transform the most shameless dog into an Israelite sheep. To that person, in reward for the chastity granted, he may bestow the pastures of eternal life [Col. 0902A]—that is, he may graciously make the sinner who has turned from his evil way righteous and lead him, through the merit of good action, to the heavenly kingdom.

When the Lord sees such ardor of faith in us and such persistent perseverance in prayer, he will at last have mercy and grant that it may happen to us as we desire: that the turmoil of vicious thoughts may be expelled, the bonds of sins released, and the pure serenity of mind and perfection of good works restored to us.

Thus those who place no confidence in any work of their own run to the protection of the saints, persist in tears before their sacred bodies, and pray that through their intercession they may merit forgiveness. What, then, are such people doing in this humility except embracing stones, since they have no covering of good [Col. 0902B] action?

(Homily 37 on the Gospels.) “But we sinners, entangled in many and very great sins, with what tears ought we to hope for forgiveness, since in that terrifying examination we do not come to judgment on equal terms with our king, for the condition of our weakness and our inferior cause plainly show us to be beneath him? Perhaps we have already cut away the faults of evil action and now avoid whatever is wicked outwardly. But are we sufficient to render an account of our thoughts?

“For when the Gospel says that a king is coming to battle with twenty thousand (Luke XIV, 31), the one who comes with ten thousand is plainly insufficient against him. Ten thousand compared with twenty thousand is one against two. But if we make very great progress, we scarcely preserve our outward works in [Col. 0902C] uprightness. For even if the lust of the flesh has now been cut away, it has not yet been cut away completely from the heart.

“The one who comes to judge judges outward and inward things together; he weighs deeds and thoughts alike. Therefore he comes with an army twice as large against one half as large, since he examines us, scarcely prepared in action alone, concerning both action and thought.

“What, then, should we do, brothers, except that, while we see that we cannot withstand his double army with our single one, while he is still far away, we should send an embassy and ask for the things that make for peace? He is called ‘far away’ because he is not yet seen in the present judgment.

“Let us send our tears as an embassy to him; let us send works of mercy; let us offer on his altar sacrifices of appeasement; let us acknowledge that we cannot contend with him in [Col. 0902D] judgment; let us consider the power of his strength; let us ask for the things that make for peace. This is our embassy, which appeases the coming King.

“Consider, brothers, how gracious it is that the one who by his coming is able to overwhelm delays his coming. Let us send our embassy to him, as I have said, by weeping, giving alms, and offering sacred sacrifices. For the sacrifice of the sacred altar, offered with tears and kindness of mind, uniquely assists in our absolution, because the one who, rising from the dead in himself, no longer dies nevertheless suffers again for us through this mystery.

“For as often as we offer him the sacrifice of his passion, so often we renew his passion for our absolution. Many of you, I believe, dearest brothers, [Col. 0903A] have happened to know what I wish to recall to your memory by telling it.

“It is reported that, not long ago, a certain man was captured by enemies and taken far away. Since he was kept in chains for a long time, his wife, receiving no word that he had been recovered from captivity, believed him dead. For him, as though already dead, she arranged that offerings be made every week. As often as offerings were made by his wife for the absolution of his soul, his chains were released in captivity.

“After a long time he returned and, greatly amazed, told his wife that on certain days, every week, his chains had been released. When his wife examined those days and hours, she recognized that he had been released at the very times when she remembered that a sacrifice had been offered for him.

“From this, therefore, dearest brothers, draw with careful consideration how greatly the sacred offering [Col. 0903B] made by us can release the bondage of the heart within us, if an offering made by another could release the bonds of the body in another.”

(From the same homily, near the end.) “Let him therefore leave everything who can. But whoever cannot leave everything, while the King is still far away, should send an embassy and offer gifts of tears, almsgiving, and sacrifices. For he wishes to be appeased by prayers, knowing that, if angered, he cannot be borne. The fact that he still delays his coming means that he awaits an embassy of peace.

“He would already have come, if he wished, and slaughtered all his adversaries. Yet he indicates how terrible he will be when he comes, and nevertheless delays coming because he does not wish to find anyone whom he must punish; and he who cannot be endured in anger wishes to be appeased [Col. 0903C] by an embassy of requested peace.

“Wash away, therefore, dearest brothers, the stains of sins with tears; wipe them clean with almsgiving; expiate them with sacred sacrifices.”

(Dialogues, book IV, chapter 58.) “For this is the uniquely saving victim that preserves the soul from eternal destruction, renewing for us through the mystery that death of the Only-Begotten. Although, rising from the dead, he no longer dies, and death shall no longer rule over him, nevertheless, living immortal in himself, he is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of the sacred offering.

“For there his body is received; his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people; his blood is poured not into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful. From this, then, let us consider what kind of sacrifice it is that, for our absolution, continually imitates the passion of the Only-Begotten Son.

“For what faithful person could doubt that, at the very hour [Col. 0903D] of the offering, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened; that in the mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the highest and lowest are joined; that earthly and heavenly things are united; and that one reality is made from visible and invisible things?”

From this we must carefully consider with how much reverence, and with how much fear and trembling, we ought to attend upon the divine mysteries, and diligently take care that we do nothing inappropriate there, lest we hear from the Apostle, as did the Corinthians: “Do you not have houses in which to conduct or discuss worldly affairs, or do you despise the Church of God?” (I Cor. XI, 22). And lest we hear, together with the Jews: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jer. XI, 15).

We must also carefully consider [Col. 0904A] what the Lord would do if he found us entangled in quarrels, occupied with chatter, relaxed in laughter, or ensnared by any other crime—he who saw people buying the victims to be sacrificed to him in the temple and hastened to drive them out.

But, remembering what is written—“Zeal for your house has consumed me” (John II, 17)—we too ought to be zealous for the house of God and, as far as we are able, insist that nothing perverse be done in it. If we see a brother who belongs to the household of God swollen with pride, accustomed to slander, enslaved to drunkenness, weakened by lust, disturbed by anger, or subject to any other vice, let us strive, insofar as we have the ability, to correct him and to set right what is polluted and perverse.

If we cannot reform someone in such matters, we must not endure it without the sharpest grief [Col. 0904B] of mind—especially in the very house of prayer, where the Lord’s body is consecrated and where the presence of angels is always believed to be present—lest anything improper occur, lest anything that impedes our prayer or our brother’s prayer be done, and we must act with all our strength.

We have said these things for those who, after entering a church, not only neglect the intention of praying but even increase the matters for which they ought to have prayed. Moreover, they pursue those who rebuke them for such folly with insults and hatred, adding sins to sins and, as it were, weaving an exceedingly long rope for themselves through this careless accumulation, without fearing that they will be condemned by the examination of the strict Judge.

It is also not hidden that angels are often invisibly present with the elect, either to defend them from the snares of the cunning enemy or to lift them up through a greater desire for heavenly [Col. 0904C] things. The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. I, 14).

Nevertheless, we should believe that angelic spirits are especially present to us when we are particularly devoted to divine service—that is, when we enter a church and lend our ears to sacred readings, apply ourselves to psalmody, or devote ourselves to prayer, and especially when we celebrate the solemnities of the Mass. Hence the Apostle also admonishes us: “A woman ought to have a veil over her head because of the angels” (I Cor. XI, 10). And the prophet says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you” (Ps. CXXXVII, 1).

There can be no doubt that, wherever the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood are celebrated, the assembly of the citizens above is present—those who guard with such vigilant watch the tomb [Col. 0904D] in which that venerable body had been placed and from which it departed by rising again.

Therefore, we must diligently strive that, whenever we enter a church either to render the due offices of divine praise or to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass, we should always remember the presence of the angels and complete our heavenly service with fitting fear and reverence, following the example of the women devoted to God, who, when angels appeared at the tomb, are said to have been afraid and to have bowed their faces to the ground (Luke XXIV, 5).

They also offer us a typological example: if we desire to find the Lord and to be strengthened by the presence of angels, let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably, as in the day.

[Col. 0905A]

It is fitting for us, therefore, to seek the Lord not only shining with the light of good works but also filled with the grace of spiritual activity. Hence it is rightly reported that the women who came to the tomb at dawn brought with them the spices they had prepared (Luke XXIV, 1).

Our spices are the words of prayer by which we commend the desires of our heart to the Lord. The Apostle John bears witness to this when, mystically describing the most pure hearts of the saints, he says: “They held golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints” (Apoc. V, 8). For what is called *aromata* in Greek is called *odoramenta*, “fragrant offerings,” in Latin.

Thus we bring spices to the Lord’s tomb at dawn when, mindful of the passion and death which he underwent for us, we show the light of good works outwardly to our neighbors [Col. 0905B] and burn inwardly in our hearts with the sweetness of pure compunction.

This ought to be done at every hour, but especially when we enter a church to pray and when we approach the altar to receive the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood. For if the women sought the body of the dead Lord with such care, how much more fitting is it for us, who know that he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and is everywhere present through the power of his divine majesty, to stand before his presence with every reverence and celebrate his mysteries?

It is rightly said: “Carrying the spices they had prepared.” To prepare beforehand the spices which we carry for the Lord’s service means to cleanse the heart before the time of prayer from useless thoughts, so that at the very time of prayer we may know how to admit nothing filthy into the mind, think of none of the passing things of the world, and remember nothing [Col. 0905C] except what we are praying for and the one to whom we are praying, in accordance with the example of the one who says: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing, I will make melody to the Lord” (Luke XXIV, 1).

For whoever enters a church to worship and neglects to drive from his mind the habit of superfluous thought during the words of prayer has, as though seeking the Lord, brought spices with him that were less prepared.

We who are ministers of the holy altar must consider what is commanded by the divine voice: that the breastpiece of judgment be fastened upon Aaron’s breast with binding ribbons. This signifies that fleeting thoughts should by no means possess the priestly heart, but that reason alone should bind it, lest, while attending upon the sacred mysteries, we think anything indiscriminate [Col. 0905D] or useless. Since we are appointed as an example to others, we must always show by the gravity of our life how much reason we carry in our breast.

To this breastpiece of judgment it is also vigilantly added that the names of the twelve patriarchs should be inscribed upon it. To carry the inscribed fathers always upon the breast means to think without interruption about the life of the ancients. For the priest walks irreproachably when he continually observes the examples of the fathers who preceded him, when he constantly considers the footsteps of the saints, and suppresses illicit thoughts, lest he extend the foot of his action beyond the boundary of his order.

Since we also carry inscribed the names of the dead, we must understand that we sinners perform the works of death [Col. 0906A] and, being ourselves surrounded by weakness, must therefore pray for our own sins as well as for those of the people.

Those who attend should also consider how they ought to stand in the presence of the divinity and his angels. For the Lord, who regards the humble and knows the lofty from afar, does not look at the expensive garments and worldly finery with which men and women commonly adorn themselves, but at a contrite and humbled heart.

However greatly the flesh may be surrounded by masses of gold and silver, and however much it may be clothed in costly garments, what is it other than flesh? We should not therefore attend to what we have, but to what we are. For the prophet says: “Truly the people are grass, and all flesh is grass, and its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL, 6). The multitude of the human race, [Col. 0906B] which becomes green in the flesh through birth and dries up in the dust through death, is rightly called grass.

Saint Peter admonishes women to show, in fear, their chaste conduct to those who observe them. Their adornment should not be external—the braiding of hair, the wearing of gold, or the elegance of clothing—but “the hidden person of the heart in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit,” which is precious in the sight of God.

For in this way, in former times, the holy women who hoped in God also adorned themselves, subject to their own husbands, just as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him “lord.” They are her daughters when they do what is good and are not afraid of any disturbance (I Pet. III, 2).

There are also those who, when entering the church, do not boast of the adornment of their clothing or of any display; but, as though humbly, they prolong many psalms or prayers with carefully composed words. Yet, as blessed Gregory says, it is truly to pray to utter bitter groans in prayer, and not to make composed words resound. On the other hand, those who pray with their mouths but wander outwardly in their minds are deprived of all the fruit of prayer, imagining that their prayer is heard by God, although they themselves do not hear what they utter. Who could fail to perceive that this happens at the prompting of the ancient enemy? For, knowing the usefulness of prayer and envying human beings the grace of obtaining what they ask, he injects into prayers manifold fantasies of frivolous—and sometimes even shameful and harmful—thoughts, so as to impede prayer. Thus we sometimes endure, prostrate in prayer, such great and violent waves of wandering thoughts as we do not know how to endure even when lying flat on our backs in bed.

Therefore it is necessary that, as far as we can, we clear the mind we have recognized from such clouds as the enemy delights to scatter, making it serene, and that we continually beg the protection of our merciful defender. He is powerful enough to grant even unworthy sinners the grace both to pray purely and to obtain perfectly, if we do not cease praying, imitating that blind man of whom the Gospel says: “He cried out all the more: Son of David, have mercy on me” (Mark X, 48). For the more heavily we are oppressed by the tumult of carnal thoughts, the more ardently we ought to persist in prayer. Clearly, it is necessary that the voice of our heart, the more harshly it is repelled, should press on with greater strength, so that it may overcome the tumult of unlawful thought and burst forth, by the force of its importunity, to the merciful ears of the Lord.

For often, during the very sacrifice of our prayer, intrusive thoughts thrust themselves in, able either to snatch away or to stain what we ourselves offer to God as we weep. But if God is not sought in prayer, the mind quickly grows weary of prayer: for when someone asks for those things which God perhaps refuses to grant according to his hidden judgment, the one who does not wish to give what is loved also becomes a cause of disgust. Yet the Lord wishes himself to be loved more than the things he created, and eternal things to be requested rather than earthly things, as it is written: “Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew VI, 33). By saying not “they will be given,” but “they will be added to you,” he plainly indicates that one thing is given as the principal gift and another is added on: for eternity ought to be our object in intention, while temporality belongs to our use. The former is given by God, while the latter is added from his abundance. Yet people often, while asking for temporal goods, do not seek eternal rewards; they ask for what is added and do not desire the place where it is added. Nor do they consider it a gain from their petition if they are temporally poor here but live eternally rich in blessedness there. Intent only on visible things, they refuse, through the labor of asking, to purchase invisible things.

If they sought heavenly things, they would already receive their labor with profit. For when the mind, in prayers, longs for the vision of its Creator, inflamed by divine desires it is joined to heavenly things and separated from those below. It reveals the fervor of its love in order to receive, and in receiving, to be already ascending in the flame of love. While it gazes with great desire upon heavenly things, it mysteriously tastes the very thing it seeks to receive ( *Moralia*, Book XVI, chapter 19).

Thus Abraham (Genesis XV, 11), when he was offering sacrifice at sunset, endured birds of prey settling upon it, and diligently drove them away lest they carry off the sacrifice he had offered. In the same way, while we offer God a holocaust upon the altar of the heart, let us guard it from unclean birds, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts snatch away what our mind hopes profitably to offer to the Lord. And just as, in the case of Isaac, the Philistines—*Allophyli*—attempted to fill in the wells he had dug (Genesis XXVI), so unclean spirits, when they see us diligently digging out our heart, snatch away what our mind hopes profitably to offer to the Lord by piling upon us thoughts of temptation. Therefore the mind must be emptied and dug out without ceasing, lest, if it is left unexamined, the earth of perverse deeds and thoughts accumulate over us until it reaches the point of fear. (*Homily* 14 on Ezekiel.)

“And Jacob, who wrestled with the angel (Genesis XXXII), expresses the soul of every perfect man engaged in contemplation. For when the soul strives to contemplate the Lord, it is placed, as it were, in a kind of contest. At one moment it seems to prevail, because by understanding and feeling it tastes something of the unbounded light; at another it succumbs, because, even after tasting, it again fails. The angel seems to be overcome when God is grasped by the innermost understanding.”

Nevertheless, the soul is immediately thrown back upon itself and withdraws from that light which it had surpassed. So too, one who struggles sometimes prevails in the contest, but sometimes discovers that he is inferior to the one with whom he contends. (*Moralia*, Book XXIII, chapter 10.)

“Therefore it is also said in the psalm: ‘I heard you in the hidden place of the tempest’ (Psalm LXXX, 8). The hidden tempest is when, in a contrite heart, the waves of temporal thoughts swell, when the tumult of worldly cares strikes against the efforts of holy love. He is therefore heard in the hidden place of the tempest, because this very turmoil of tribulation is the cry of the one who prays.”

## CHAPTER VII. On wicked thoughts, purity of heart, conjugal chastity, and reconciliation with one’s neighbor; and on how the prayers of others benefit those who, during life, earned that benefit after death; and on the differing departure and condition of the dying

[Col. 0908B]

We must know that there are three kinds of evil thoughts. The first consists of those which contaminate the mind through deliberation and the intention to sin. If the strict judgment of the righteous Judge examines such thoughts, they are no longer merely thoughts of guilt but of deeds; for although delays in external circumstances postpone sins outwardly, inwardly the effect of the will has completed them through the act of deliberation. Of such thoughts it is written: “The wicked shall not be innocent when hand joins hand” (Proverbs XI, 21). For if he does not carry out in action the evil he wishes through deliberate intention, he nevertheless completes it in the deliberation of his will.

The second consists of those which disturb the mind through the pleasure of sin, though they do not draw it into consent to sin. The third consists of those which pass through the mind by natural impulse and entice it not so much to commit vices as to prevent it from thinking about the good things it ought to have considered. Such is the case when we recall to memory fantasies of things which we know to have been said or done at some time without necessity. Their frequent recollection, like the importunity of troublesome flies, usually circles around the eyes of the heart and disturbs its spiritual vision more than it rouses it.

Nothing is more fleeting than the heart, which departs from us as often as it flows away through wicked thoughts. Hence the Psalmist says: “My heart has forsaken me” (Psalm XXXIX, 13). Returning to himself, he says: “Your servant has found his heart, so that he may pray to you.” When, therefore, thought is restrained by watchfulness, the heart, which was accustomed to flee, is found.

Solomon warned us to be chastened by all these kinds of evil thoughts when he says: “Guard your heart with every care, for from it proceeds life” (Proverbs IV, 23). Following this warning, let us act carefully: if we have sinned in our mind by consenting to the perpetration of some crime, let us quickly wipe it away through confession and worthy fruits of repentance. If we perceive that we are being tempted by the pleasure of sinning, let us immediately drive that pleasure away by frequent prayers and tears, and by the continual remembrance of bitterness. If we see that we are not sufficient by ourselves to repel it, let us seek the help of our brothers, so that what we cannot accomplish by our own strength we may obtain through their counsel and intercession.

“For the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James V, 16). And, as the same apostle said beforehand: “The prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (ibid., 15).

Because we cannot be entirely free from superfluous thoughts, let us drive them away as far as we can by the introduction of good thoughts, and especially by frequent meditation on the Scriptures, following the example of the Psalmist, who says: “How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all day long” (Psalm CXVIII, 97).

Let us ask heavenly mercy—which is truly to ask in the name of the Savior—that it not permit our heart to be constricted by the harshness of hatred, but pour into us the grace of pure love; that it not allow us to perish from the poisons of unbelief, but grant us the strength of faith against the temptations of the ancient enemy; that it not permit us to look backward in despair of what is to come, but mercifully grant us hope of heavenly goods, by which we may despise both present adversity and prosperity. May it also grant us purity of heart and effectiveness in good works.

The purity of prayer is greatly aided if, in every place and at every time, we restrain ourselves from unlawful actions; if we always discipline both our hearing and our tongue by avoiding idle talk; and if we accustom ourselves to walk in the law of the Lord and to keep his testimonies with our whole heart. For whatever we habitually do, say, or hear must repeatedly return to the mind as to its familiar and proper dwelling.

Just as pigs habitually visit wallows, while doves frequent pure and clear streams, so unclean thoughts disturb an impure mind, whereas spiritual thoughts sanctify a chaste mind. And once the heart has been guarded, in accordance with what Scripture says—“Guard your heart with every care, for from it proceeds life”—we must also guard our bodies in sanctification and purity. When the body has been guarded and cleansed from the flow of lust, good works must follow, as the Lord commanded, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII, 35). [Homily 13.]

“There are two things commanded: to gird the loins and to hold lamps, so that there may be both the purity of chastity in the body and the light of truth in one’s conduct. Our Redeemer can in no way be pleased with one without the other, whether someone who does good works has not yet abandoned the defilements of lust, or someone who excels in chastity has not yet exercised himself in good works. Thus chastity is not great without good works, nor is a good work anything without chastity.”

What does it profit the person who gives himself to the devil and his possessions to God, when Scripture says: “Have pity on your soul, pleasing God”? (Sirach XXX, 24.) Everyone ought to begin the works of mercy with himself, so that he may first give himself to God and afterward his possessions to the Lord, in accordance with what Scripture commands: “Turn away from evil and do good, and then you shall dwell forever and ever in the house of the Lord, throughout the length of days” (Psalm XXXVI, 27).

We must know that chastity is found not only among virgins, widows, and those who practice continence, but that there is also conjugal chastity among those lawfully married and preserving the legitimate rights of marriage. (*Pastoral Care*, Part III, chapter 28.)

“Yet such people must know that they have been joined together for the sake of having children. When, serving immoderate intercourse, they turn the process of propagation into an occasion of pleasure, they should consider that, by serving excessive lust, they transgress the rights of marriage within marriage itself. Therefore they must erase through frequent prayers and daily almsgiving what they defile by mingling excessive pleasure with the honorable appearance of marital union.

This is why the apostle, skilled in heavenly medicine, did not so much prescribe remedies for the healthy as show medicines to the weak, saying: ‘Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband’ (1 Corinthians VII, 1). He who first mentioned the fear of fornication plainly did not give this command to those standing firm, but, lest they perhaps fall to the ground, spread a bed beneath those who were falling. Therefore he adds to those who are still weak: ‘Let the husband render to his wife her due, and likewise the wife to her husband’ (ibid., 6). When, in the great honor of marriage, he granted them something of pleasure, he added: ‘But I say this by way of concession, not by way of command.’ What is conceded is implied to be a fault; yet it is relaxed all the more quickly when no unlawful thing is done through it, provided what is lawful is kept under moderation.” (Ibid.)

Therefore, when a supplication is poured out to God, the life of such married people is not condemned. Concerning this prayer Paul also gives instruction, saying: “Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may be free for prayer” (1 Corinthians VII, 5).

Thus they should come to communion purer in heart and body, having washed their flesh and clothing with water, lest they be burdened by the very greatness of the ineffable mystery. For when the Lord was about to speak to the people on Mount Sinai, he first commanded that same people to abstain from women (Exodus XIX). And David is told by the priest concerning his young men that, if they were pure from women, they might receive the bread of the Presence (1 Samuel XXI, 4); they would certainly not have received it unless David had first declared them pure from women.

All who approach the communion of the sacred mysteries with a pure heart and a purified body must slay themselves for God in contrition of heart. For those who celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion must imitate what they perform. Then the sacrifice will truly be offered for us, when it has made us ourselves into a sacrifice.

(*Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 59.)

“But amid these things it must be known that the person rightly asks forgiveness for his own offense who first releases what has been committed against him. A gift is not accepted unless discord is first driven from the heart, as the Truth says: ‘If you are offering your gift at the altar, and there you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift’ (Matthew V, 23).

In this matter we must consider, since every guilt is removed by a gift, how grave the guilt of discord is, for which even the gift is not accepted. We must therefore go in our minds to our neighbor, even if he is far away and greatly separated from us, submit our heart to him, and appease him with humility and goodwill, so that our Creator, when he sees such a disposition of our mind, may free us from sin—the one who accepts a gift for guilt.

By the voice of the Truth we have learned that the servant who owed ten thousand talents, when he repented, received remission of the debt from his master. But because he did not forgive his fellow servant, who owed him one hundred denarii, he was ordered to repay what had already been forgiven him (Matthew XVIII). From these words it is clear that, if we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, we are again made to pay what we had rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance.

Therefore, while the interval of time granted to us permits it, while the Judge is patient, while the one who examines our sins awaits our conversion, let us melt the hardness of our mind in tears and form within ourselves the grace of kindness toward our neighbors. And I say confidently: we shall not need a saving sacrifice at death if, before death, we have ourselves become a sacrifice for God.”

We must know how the sacred Victim benefits those who have died—those who, while living here, obtained that the good works performed here by others might also help them after death. We must also truly believe that God does not free after death the person whom grace did not reform unto forgiveness before death.

Hence Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians VI, 2). Hence the Psalmist says: “For his mercy endures forever” (Psalm CXVII, 1). For the person whom his mercy does not rescue now, justice alone condemns after the present age.

Hence Solomon says: “When a tree falls, whether toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it shall remain” (Ecclesiastes XI, 3). For when, at the time of human death, either a holy or an evil spirit receives the departing soul from the prison of the flesh, it will retain that soul with itself forever, without any change: neither will the soul, if raised up to punishment, fall further, nor, if submerged in eternal punishments, rise again to the remedy of deliverance, the eternally condemned having been left behind.

We must know that there is a distinction among the elect who have departed from the body and those who are departing or about to depart. For there are some who, as soon as they have been or are released from the corruption of the flesh, reach the contemplation of God, to be joined with the angels—such as the holy apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, and the other men and women of stricter and more perfect life. One of them, conscious of his own struggles, did not hesitate to testify concerning himself, saying: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians I, 23).

There are, however, many righteous people in the Church who, after the dissolution of the flesh, are immediately received into the blessed rest of paradise. They await in great joy, amid great choirs of those rejoicing with them, the time when, having received their bodies, they will come and appear before the face of God.

Others, indeed, though predestined through their good works for the company of the elect, are received for more severe correction after death into the flames of purgatorial fire because of certain evils by which they depart polluted from the body. Either they are cleansed by a long examination from the filth of their vices until the day of judgment, or, released from their punishments through the devout prayers, almsgiving, fasts, tears, and offerings of the saving sacrifice made by faithful friends, they too reach the rest of the blessed.

Yet amid these things we must consider that the safer way is for each person to perform during life, on his own behalf, the good which he hopes others will perform for him after death. It is more blessed to depart free than to seek freedom after imprisonment.

Therefore we ought to despise the present age with our whole mind, since we already see it passing away; to offer God daily sacrifices of tears; to offer daily the sacrifices of his flesh and blood; and to persist in continual weeping and in our daily repentance.

## CHAPTER VIII. That Christ is our advocate in heaven: that he redeemed us through the mystery of his Incarnation and Passion, and left us his body and blood in the sacrament

We have a priest in heaven who intercedes for us. Concerning him John also says: “If we sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John II, 1).

Our spirit rejoices when we hear of the power of our advocate; but fear again wounds our rejoicing, because the one who is our advocate is said to be righteous. We have causes of injustice, whereas a righteous advocate in no way undertakes unjust causes or consents to speak in defense of injustice.

What then shall we do, my dearest brothers? Yet behold, the answer to what we should do comes to mind: let us both accuse and lament the evils we have committed. For it is written: “The righteous person is the first to accuse himself” (Proverbs XVIII, 17). Every converted sinner already begins to be righteous amid tears when he begins to accuse what he has done. For why should the person not be righteous who already rages against his own injustice through tears?

Our righteous advocate will therefore defend us as righteous in judgment, because we both recognize and accuse ourselves as unjust. Let us therefore place our confidence not in our tears or in our deeds, but in the pleading of our advocate, who, as the most merciful Redeemer, continually offers a holocaust for us, because without ceasing he displays his Incarnation to the Father on our behalf.

His very Incarnation is the offering of our cleansing. When he shows himself to be human, by intervening he wipes away human sins, and through the mystery of his humanity he offers an everlasting sacrifice, because what he cleanses is eternal. He has become priest, sacrifice, and altar for us.

Hence it is said to Israel: “You shall make an altar of earth for me” (Exodus XXXIII, 24). To make an altar of earth for God is to adore the Incarnation of the Mediator. Our gift is then accepted by God when, upon this altar—that is, upon the humanity of the Lord’s Incarnation—we establish the faith of our humility.

Humanity, created for life in the freedom of its own will, became liable to death by freely consenting to the devil. Such guilt therefore had to be erased. But it could not be erased except through sacrifice; and for sinful, rational humanity no rational victim could be offered for cleansing except a human being without sin, one who assumed from humanity its nature but not its guilt.

Thus he made his body a sacrifice for us and offered for sinners a victim without sin, one able to die in his humanity and cleanse injustice. The End appeared in the flesh—not an end that destroys, but one that perfected him. Having become priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, he will openly complete the new covenant, which he entrusted to us through bread and wine mixed with water, while he himself sacrifices, gives life, and blesses: the mystery of faith in his true body and blood, until he comes in visible form.

He will complete it when he openly shows to those who love him, who have been called saints according to his purpose, through the manifestation of his majesty, how he arises not unequal to the one who begets him; how the Spirit, coeternal and consubstantial with both, proceeds simultaneously from both; how the one who is begotten from the Father does not come after the one from whom he is begotten; how the one brought forth by procession does not precede those who bring him forth; how the one is three divisibly and the three are one indivisibly.

He assumed into the unity of his own person humanity consisting of true flesh animated by a rational soul, conceived in the womb of the blessed Mary ever-Virgin from the Holy Spirit and from her own flesh. He who was perfect God without any beginning, the Only-Begotten equal to the Father, was born as perfect man at the end of the ages: one Christ, the true Son of God, through the womb of that Virgin who is the servant of that same man by reason of his divinity and the mother of the Word in respect of the flesh. (*Moralia*, Book XVIII, chapter 27.)

“As it is written concerning him: ‘Topaz from Ethiopia shall not be compared with it’ (Job XXVIII, 19). For it is one thing for human beings who are born to receive the grace of adoption, and another for the one unique God to have proceeded, through the power of his divinity, from the very conception. The glory possessed by the Only-Begotten through nature cannot be equated with that received by others through grace.

The Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is not one person in his humanity and another in his divinity. He was not conceived and born as a mere man and afterward received, through merit, the status of God; but when the angel announced and the Spirit came, immediately the Word was in the womb, immediately the Word within the womb was flesh. While the unchangeable essence—which he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit and which is coeternal with them—remained, he assumed within the Virgin’s womb the nature by which the impassible could suffer, the immortal could die, and the eternal could become temporal at the end of the ages.

Thus, through an ineffable mystery, by holy conception and inviolate birth, the same Virgin was, as we have said, both the servant of the Lord and the mother. Therefore Elizabeth says to her: ‘And whence is this granted me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?’ (Luke I, 43). And the Virgin herself, conceiving, said: ‘Behold the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word’ (ibid., 38).
