Although he is one thing from the Father and another from the Virgin, he is nevertheless eternal from the Father and temporal from his mother; the same one who made and was made; the same one who is beautiful beyond the sons of men through his divinity, and of whom it was said through his humanity: ‘We saw him, and there was no appearance; he had neither form nor beauty’ (Isaiah LIII, 2).

He existed before the ages from the Father without a mother, and at the end of the ages from his mother without a father; he is himself the temple of the Creator and the Creator of the temple; himself the author of the work and the work of the author; remaining one in both and in each nature, neither confused by the union of the natures nor divided into two by their distinction.”

In the nature of his divinity he is equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit. In the nature of his humanity he was made a little lower than the angels; in that nature, rising from the dead, he was crowned with glory and honor, established over all the works of the Father’s hands, and given all power in heaven and on earth. He was glorified with the glory which he had in his divinity with the Father before the world existed, so that he might openly show to those who love him that, once death had been swallowed up in victory, this mortal nature of ours must put on immortality for participation in his eternal happiness.

Longing and sighing anxiously for the blessedness of that perpetual happiness, we groan, burdened in this tabernacle, possessing this treasure of faith, hope, and love in earthen vessels. Hence the Prophet says to us: “Establish a solemn day amid throngs, even unto the horn of the altar” (Psalm CXVII, 27).

A solemn day for the Lord is the compunction of our heart. But a solemn day is established amid throngs when the mind is continually dissolved in tears of love for him. And lest we be afflicted at death if it were not said how long we are to do these things, he immediately adds the limit up to which they must be done: “unto the horn of the altar.”

The horn of the altar is the exaltation of the inner sacrifice. When we have reached it, there will no longer be any need for us to make a solemn day for the Lord out of our lamentation. Only the righteous approaches that altar of inner sacrifice; and the one who reaches it is he who approaches the present and visible altar justified by the grace of God. There he will find his life who, approaching this altar, has discerned his cause.

From that altar the saving Victim is dispensed. Through it the written bond of our deserved condemnation and curse, which stood against us, has been erased; through it the enemy who counted our sins and sought something to bring against us has been conquered, finding nothing in the one in whom we triumph. We believe in him who, for us debtors to death, paid the debt of death which he did not owe, dissolving in his flesh the hostilities we had contracted by sinning. He is the good shepherd who lays down his life for his sheep, so that in our sacrament he might change his body and blood and satisfy the sheep he had redeemed with the nourishment of his flesh.

## CHAPTER IX. That Christ is sacrificed daily for us upon the altar, and that we must approach participation in him with faith and good works

When he entrusted the celebration of these most holy mysteries to his disciples, among other things he said: “The Son of Man goes according to what has been determined. Yet woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!” (Luke XXII, 22.)

But even today and forever, woe to that person who approaches the Lord’s table with evil intent; who, harboring plots in his mind and polluted in his heart by some crime, does not fear to participate in the hidden mysteries of Christ.

Such a person, following the example of Judas, betrays the Son of Man—not indeed to sinful Jews, but nevertheless to sinners, namely to his own members, whom he dares to violate that incomparable and inviolable body of the Lord. The person sells the Lord who, neglecting love and fear of him, is shown to love and care more for earthly and perishable things, indeed even for criminal things.

Woe, I say, to that person concerning whom Jesus—the one who, while being sacrificed upon the most holy altars, is not doubted to be present as the offering is consecrated, with heavenly ministers standing by—is compelled to complain, saying: “Behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table” (ibid., 21).

Concerning such people the Apostle says: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning—that is, not distinguishing, with the veneration due to it, the Lord’s body from other foods. Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (1 Corinthians XI, 26–28).

For, as the apostle John says: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Revelation I, 15). He washed us from sins in his blood not only when he gave his blood for us upon the cross, but also whenever each of us, in the mystery of his most holy Passion, has been washed in the waters of baptism. For Christ’s price is our burial.

Hence the field bought with the price of his blood is called *Acheldemach*, that is, “field of blood”: the field of the Jews, but our burial place. We were strangers and sojourners; we had nowhere to rest. He was crucified and died, and we were buried with him through baptism into death. For whoever has been baptized in Christ the Lord has been baptized into his death (Romans VI, 3).

He not only then, when he gave his blood for us upon the cross, or when in baptism he washed us from our sins in his blood, but also daily takes away the sins of the world and washes us from our daily sins in his blood, whenever the memory of that blessed Passion is recalled at the altar, whenever the creature of bread and wine is transferred by the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit into the sacrament of his flesh and blood. Thus his body and blood are not poured out and slain by the hands of unbelievers to their destruction, but are received by the mouths of the faithful for their salvation.

Its proper figure was shown by the paschal lamb in the Law. Having once liberated the people from Egyptian servitude, it used to sanctify that same people every year by its immolation, in commemoration of that liberation, until he himself should come to whom such a victim bore witness. Offered to the Father for us as a sacrifice and as a fragrance of sweetness, he was to transfer the mystery of his passion, with the lamb offered, into the substance of bread and wine, having been made a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

And just as those who, even after they had been led out from the land of Egypt by the blood of the lamb and had been baptized in the cloud and in the sea, were struck down because of their sins by the bites of serpents, so that from the outward order of the scourge they might recognize how great an inward destruction they were suffering through sin, looked upon the bronze serpent raised up as a sign—as the sacred history of Numbers recounts (Num. XX)—and were healed for a time from the temporal death and wound inflicted by the serpents’ bites, so also those who, believing, confessing, and sincerely imitating the mystery of the Lord’s passion, look upon it are saved forever from every death which by sin they had contracted alike in soul and body, so that everyone who believes in Christ may not perish but have eternal life (John III, 16).

The difference between that figure and this truth is that through the former temporal life was prolonged, whereas through the latter life is granted which will remain without end. But one must carefully ensure that what the understanding rightly perceives is completed by conduct worthy of it, so that, while living piously and soberly with the confession of our true faith, we may deserve to attain the perfection of the promised life. For thus God loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life (ibid.). Whoever perseveres in right faith and good works to the end will attain it, because faith without works is dead—namely, that faith which does not work through love—and without faith it is impossible to please God.

Among these things, in which the grace of God jointly consists, perseverance to the end is necessary, because no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God. In that kingdom the angels and the spirits of the saints live eternally from the tree of life, as he himself said:

“As the Father lives in me, and I live in him because of the Father, so whoever eats me will himself live because of me. I am the bread of life, and I am the bread descending from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die. I am the living bread that descended from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever, and the bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world. Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I shall raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. This is the bread that descended from heaven: whoever eats this bread will live forever” (John VI).

And on the day before he suffered, while he was dining with his disciples, on the night when he was betrayed, when he changed our old Passover into the new and eternal Passover—in which Christ himself was sacrificed—he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying:

“Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

And, taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying:

“Drink from it, all of you. This is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Luke XXII).

These things he said and says and brings to completion—he who spoke and they came to be, who commanded and they were created. By that Word which exists and through which all things were made, and through his prophets, he multiplied the jar of flour and the cruse of oil, and oil poured into many vessels. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. When the Most High sanctified his dwelling in the virgin’s womb, he could lay his hand upon both: upon the Father, namely, by equality of divinity, and upon our weakness, by assuming the substance of our nature, bearing and pitying it in the unity of his person without any contamination of sin.

He multiplied loaves and fishes by his blessing, in accordance with the truth of the Gospel; by a silent nod he changed water into wine; and he changes the natures of things as he wills. Believing without doubt in his truthful words, the Apostle says:

“The cup of blessing which we bless—is it not participation in the blood of Christ?” (I Cor. X).

“For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus Christ, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me.’ For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (I Cor. X, XI).

This communion and participation in the body and blood of the Lord, just as it becomes one from all who offer with right faith, so also returns as one to all—not corporeally, but by divine power. For although he who is always one and the same cannot be understood as being participated in part by part, he is nevertheless said to be participated in by his faithful, while no portion is admitted into his substance.

But because we cannot express him perfectly in speech, impeded by the weakness of infancy, as it were, within the measure of our human nature, we echo him to some extent by stammering. The Jews, pursuing his body, tried to extinguish it as though by consuming it; but the Gentiles, hungering in mind, desire through the daily sacrifice of immolation to satisfy themselves from his flesh. They afterward believed and drank the blood of the Redeemer himself, which his savage persecutors had poured out, and proclaimed him to be the Son of God (Moral., book XIII, chapter 8).

“Concerning this blood, it is written:

‘Earth, do not cover my blood, and let my cry find no place in you to hide’ (Job XVI, 19).

For it was said to sinful man: ‘You are earth, and into earth you shall go’ (Gen. III, 19). This earth does not conceal the blood of our Redeemer, because every sinner, receiving and confessing and praising the price of his redemption, makes it known to his neighbors as far as he is able. Earth has not covered his blood also because holy Church proclaims the mystery of her redemption throughout all the regions of the world. Nor has his cry found in the earth a place to hide. For the blood of redemption which is received is the cry of our Redeemer.

Hence Paul also says: ‘And the blood of sprinkling, speaking better than Abel’ (Hebr. XII, 24). It had been said of Abel’s blood: ‘The voice of your brother Abel’s blood cries to me from the earth’ (Gen. IV, 10). But the blood of Jesus speaks better than Abel’s, because Abel’s blood demanded the death of his brother, the murderer, whereas the Lord’s blood obtained life for his persecutors.

Therefore, so that the sacrament of the Lord’s passion may not be ineffectual in us, we ought to imitate what we receive and proclaim to others what we venerate. His cry will find a place to hide in us if the tongue is silent about what the mind has believed. But so that his cry may not remain hidden in us, it remains for each person, according to his measure, to make known to his neighbors the mystery of his vivification”—believing, confessing, and proclaiming that the blood of Christ is therefore the new covenant because it is the new love by which he loved us even unto death in the final age of the world.

This love renews us, so that we may be new human beings and heirs of the new covenant, as the Apostle also says:

“How much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself immaculate to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God? And therefore he is the mediator of the new covenant” (Hebr. IX, 14–15).

Through this blood of the new covenant, then, which was poured out for the forgiveness of sins, he will cleanse—that is, renew—the conscience of the faithful. And these same faithful, according to the same Apostle, become heirs according to the hope of eternal life, and those who have been called receive the promise of an eternal inheritance (ibid., 15). Therefore that blood is truly of the new and eternal covenant, because those whom it renews from their old condition it leads to eternal happiness.

For this reason the prophet Zechariah, as though speaking to the Lord himself, says:

“You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there was no water” (Zech. IX, 11).

For through the pouring out of this blood the ancient righteous, bound by the hope of future redemption, were led out from the prison of hell; and through the same blood all believers are rescued from the bonds of sins, from the pit of misery, and from the mire of filth.

Furthermore, what is here called “the mystery of faith” is not found in those words of the Lord by which he handed on the mystery of his body and blood. It seems to have been taken from another passage of the Gospel, where, according to John, speaking of this same sacrament to certain disciples who did not believe, he says:

“The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life, but there are some among you who did not believe” (John VI, 64).

For he showed that he had spoken of a great mystery when he said: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John VI, 65). But when he adds, “There are some among you who did not believe,” he shows that this great mystery is nothing other than of faith and for the faithful, who hear the words and for whom they are therefore spirit and life, because, understood spiritually, they give them life.

Everything, then, that is done in this offering of the Lord’s body and blood is a mystery. One thing is seen, another is understood: what is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit.

It must also be known that, according to the observance of the Catholic Church handed down to the apostles, the same cup of the Lord’s blood may not be offered unless it is mixed with water. For they become one in the mystery of our redemption, when he says: “I shall not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine” (Matt. XXVI, 29). And from his side, pierced by the spear, water came forth with blood, showing that wine had been pressed from the true vine of his flesh together with water.

These, then, are the sacraments of the Church, without which one does not enter into the life that is true life. That blood was poured out for the forgiveness of sins; that water tempers the saving cup; this sacrament supplies both washing and drink.

The Lord himself commends with what piety and love the whole mystery of the Lord’s offering should be performed, saying:

“Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me” (I Cor. XI, 25).

Explaining this, the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

“For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (ibid., 26).

The offering of that bread and cup, therefore, is a commemoration and proclamation of Christ’s death. It is performed not so much by words as by the mysteries themselves, through which that precious death is impressed more deeply and powerfully upon our minds.

For what is the commemoration of Christ’s death except the commendation of his love? The blessed Evangelist commends it to us, saying:

“Knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John XIII, 1).

That is, that love led him even unto death, because he loved them so greatly that he died for them. For he testified to this, saying:

“Greater love than this no one has, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13).

Therefore, as he was going to his passion and departing from the world through the glory of his resurrection and ascension, he handed this final sacrament to his disciples, so that he might impress more deeply upon their minds the memory of such great love, through which alone we are saved. Thus we may always remember what sort of people we are and how greatly we have been loved by him, so that we may not glory in ourselves but hope in him.

He explains and emphasizes both points still more carefully, saying:

“For while we were still weak, at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. V, 6).

And shortly afterward it is said:

“But God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us; much more, therefore, now justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him” (ibid., 8–9).

This, then, he commended to the Church to be done and repeated until he comes at the end of the age. Then there will be the rest of the saints—not yet in the sacrament of hope by which the Church is joined together in the present age, as long as what flowed from Christ’s side is drunk, but already in the very perfection of eternal salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God and the Father, so that in the clear contemplation of unchangeable truth we may have need of no bodily mysteries.

### CHAPTER X  
### How through Christ’s humility the bread of angels became our bread; how consecration is effected by Christ himself; and how, under the appearance of bread, Christ’s true flesh is to be eaten by us with repentance and a pure heart

Previously, according to the order of the Jews, there was Aaron’s sacrifice in the victims of animals, and this was in mystery. For the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood was not yet present—the sacrifice known to the faithful who have read the Gospel. That sacrifice is now spread throughout the whole world through him of whom it is written:

“The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

This was said of our Lord Jesus Christ, because he willed to be our salvation in his body and blood, which he commended to us through his humility. For if he were not humble, he could neither be eaten nor drunk.

Consider his height: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with him” (John I). Behold the eternal food. The angels eat it; the heavenly powers eat it; the celestial spirits eat it. They eat and are nourished, yet what satisfies and gladdens them remains whole.

But what human being could reach that food? Where would there be a heart suitable for such food? It was therefore necessary that that table should become milk, so that it might be available to little ones.

But how does food become milk? How is food changed into milk unless it passes through flesh? A mother does this. What the mother eats, the infant eats; but because the infant is not yet fit to eat bread, the mother makes it flesh and, through the moisture of the breast, feeds the infant with the nourishment of milk from that bread.

How, then, does the wisdom of God feed us from that bread? Because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14).

See, therefore, the humility: man ate the bread of angels, as it is written:

“He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 15).

That is, man ate the eternal Word by which the angels are nourished, which is equal to the Father, because, although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized. The angels are nourished by him, but he emptied himself so that man might eat the bread of angels. Taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and appearing in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II, 6, 8), so that from the cross the flesh and blood of the Lord might already be commended as a new sacrifice.

When our Lord Jesus Christ was speaking of his body, he said:

“Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John VI, 54, 56).

Spiritual understanding makes the believer a different person, because “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (II Cor. III, 6).

His disciples, who followed him, were frightened and terrified, not understanding the saying. They thought that our Lord Jesus Christ was saying something unbearably harsh: that they were going to eat the flesh of the one whom they saw and drink his blood. They could not tolerate it.

But when he commended that very body and blood of his, he took into his hands what the faithful know, and in a certain way he carried himself when he said:

“This is my body.”

For when he commends his body and blood, he commends his humility. Our Lord taught that very humility in his body and blood.

The wisdom of God, whom we shall see face to face—and all shall see him, and no one will be jealous—offers itself to everyone; it is whole and pure for everyone. They are changed into him, but he is not changed into them. He is the truth; he is God. The truth is the Word of God; it is the wisdom of God, through whom all things were made, who said:

“I have power to lay down my life” (John X, 18).

This is the humility of our Lord Jesus Christ. It is greatly commended to human beings, and it exhorts us to live according to it, as it is said in the Song of Songs:

“You will come and pass through.”

From the beginning of faith we shall come to see him face to face, as it is written:

“Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I John III, 2).

Before, then, we see face to face what the angels see, we need to approach this humility and cling to this humility which our Lord Jesus Christ commends when he commends the celebration of his body and blood—the humility which he deigned to assume for us when the Word became flesh.

“Come to him and be enlightened.”

The Jews approached him so as to be darkened; they approached him in order to crucify him. Let us approach him so that we may receive his body and blood. They were darkened by the one who was crucified; we are enlightened by eating the crucified one and drinking him.

Behold, Christ crucified is given to the nations. How do the nations approach him? By following him in faith, longing for him in heart, and running toward him in love. Your feet are love. Have two feet—that is, love of God and love of neighbor—so that you may not be lame, and run to God on these two feet.

But someone says: “How can I approach him? I am burdened with so many evils and so many sins; so many crimes cry out from my conscience. How dare I approach him?”

How? If you humble yourself through repentance and cleanse your heart. For:

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

Remove from there the filth of desires; remove the stain of greed; remove the decay of superstitions; remove sacrilege and evil thoughts; remove hatred—not only hatred against a friend, but also hatred against an enemy.

Remove those things which the Lord says proceed from the heart in the Gospel:

“From the heart come evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, impurities, perjuries, false testimonies, and the rest, which defile a person” (Matt. XV, 19).

And:

“Repent” (Acts VIII, 22).

Repentance and purity of heart make you approach God and receive again the former robe which the prodigal son lost when, after dissipating the substance he had received from his father, he lived luxuriously with prostitutes.

This substance of ours is everything that we live, understand, think, and burst forth in words, which has been given to us by God. In the dissipation of this substance we lost the robe—that is, the garment of the Holy Spirit, the wedding garment, the garment of innocence. Whoever does not have it cannot take part in the king’s banquet.

How well fashioned did man receive it! Persuaded by the serpent, he lost it through evil. We received it again in baptism. But even after baptism, through worthy fruits of repentance, we receive the grace of God; and the fattened calf is slaughtered for us, sacrificed for the salvation of the penitent—that is, the Savior himself, whose flesh we feed upon daily and whose blood we drink. Every day the Father receives the son; Christ is always sacrificed for believers.

Concerning this it is said:

“Go and bring the fattened calf” (Luke XV, 23);

that is, proclaim the one who has been slain, and offer him to be sacrificed in his mystery, and believe that he has died daily for you—that is, for sinners. And as often as you offer him the sacrifice of his passion, trust that his passion is renewed for your absolution each time.

Let us therefore feast—that is, let us faithfully receive his flesh and blood for the forgiveness of our sins.

Thus, as it is written:

“Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. XXXIII, 9),

he who said:

“Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself.”

But if you do not understand, as those did not understand who said, “How can he give us his flesh to eat?” (John VI, 53), then, as it is read in the title of Psalm Thirty-Three, “David,” that is, Christ, “will change his face,” and he will depart from you, leave you, and go away.

“Blessed is the man who hopes in him.”

Whoever does not hope in the Lord is wretched; and whoever hopes in himself or in any other human being is likewise wretched.

Truly great is the Lord, and great is his mercy: truly, the one who gave us his body to eat, in which he endured so much, and his blood to drink, which is the propitiation for our sins. For those who are not reconciled through him die in their sins, and all who hope in him will not offend.

This is the measure of human righteousness: however far mortal life may progress, since it cannot be without sin, let it not sin in this respect—by hoping in him in whom there is forgiveness of sins, which comes only through the blood of Christ.

For great is the majesty and great is the power of Christ’s blood, by which he loosens the hand of the devil and redeems us from the hand of that enemy.

For just as there are certain animals which hold something enclosed within themselves—and physicians and natural philosophers say that unless they are broken open, what they hold shut inside will not be separated from them, nor will they release what they keep enclosed within; but if oil is poured in, it is immediately dissolved, and what had been tightly held is scattered and divided into parts—so the blood of Christ loosens the devil’s exceedingly hard grip.

The devil did not want to release us. The Lord poured out blood like the oil of mercy and through it liberated us.

Concerning this oil of Christ’s mercy the prophet says:

“The yoke will rot before the face of the oil” (Isa. X, 27).

We were held under the yoke of the devil’s domination, but we were anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit, by which Christ was conceived and born of the immaculate Virgin; through his blood we have been redeemed from the yoke of the devil’s domination and cleansed from every sin, as the Apostle John says to us:

“The blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from every sin” (I John I, 7).

The sacrament of the Lord’s passion has released for us all our former sins in baptism, and whatever we have committed after baptism through daily weakness, the grace of that same Redeemer forgives us—especially when, amid the works of light that we perform, we humbly confess our errors to him each day; when we receive the sacraments of his blood; when, forgiving our debtors, we pray that our debts may be forgiven us; and when, remembering his passion, we willingly endure every adversity.

For God is faithful and will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear (I Cor. X). Whatever a person suffers for the name of Christ and for the hope of eternal life, and bears with perseverance, he will receive a greater reward. But if he yields to the devil, he will be condemned with him.

Works of mercy, however, together with devout humility, obtain from the Lord that he will not permit his servants to be tempted beyond what they can endure.

“Taste and see how sweet the Lord is; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Augustine, Sermon 2 on the Words of the Apostle).

“And let us hear the truthful divine Teacher, the Redeemer, commending to us our price, his blood. For he spoke to us of his body and blood, commending such food and such drink:

‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves’ (John VI, 51).

And of what life did he say this, if not of life itself? Yet for that person it will be death, not life, who considers life a lie.

Therefore, from his body and blood also he gave us salutary nourishment. Let those who eat, eat; let those who drink, drink; let them hunger and thirst; let them eat life and drink life.

When you eat that, you are refreshed, but you are refreshed in such a way that what refreshes you does not fail. What does it mean to drink that except to live? Eat life; drink life. You will have life, and life is whole.

But then this will be so—that is, the body and blood of Christ will be life for each person—if what is visibly received in the sacrament is spiritually eaten and spiritually drunk in the truth itself.”

Who invited us to this table, and what did he prepare? The Lord invited servants and prepared himself as food for them.

Who would dare both to eat his Lord? And yet he says:

“Whoever eats me will himself live because of me” (John VI, 58).

When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. He is not killed so that he may be eaten, but he gives life to the dead. When he is eaten, he refreshes, but he is not diminished.

Therefore let us not fear, brothers, eating that bread, lest perhaps we finish it and afterward find nothing to eat. Let Christ be eaten: he lives when eaten, because he rose after being killed.

Nor, when we eat him, do we divide him into parts. Indeed, this is how it happens in the sacrament, and the faithful know how they eat Christ’s flesh. Each person receives his portion. He is eaten in portions, yet the whole remains entire: he is eaten in portions in the sacrament, yet the whole remains entire in heaven and remains whole in your heart.

For the whole of him was with the Father when he came into the Virgin to fill her, and he did not depart from the Father. He came into flesh so that human beings might eat him, and he remained whole with the Father so that he might feed the angels. And when Christ became man, man ate the bread of angels.

Our mystery has been placed upon the Lord’s table. You receive our mystery, and you answer ‘Amen’ to what you are; by answering, you give your assent. You hear, ‘The body of Christ,’ and you respond, ‘Amen.’ May the heart hold what the mouth says; may faith possess what you answer in the word. Be a member of the body of Christ, so that your ‘Amen’ may be true.”

Christ consecrated the mystery of our peace and unity at his table. And who else but he himself is consecrated daily at his table?

For God is present through his evangelical words, without which the sacrament is not consecrated. He himself sanctifies his sacrament and makes himself present, as he says:

“This is my body, which will be given for you.”

For just as, at his word, when he first commanded it, the earth germinates green vegetation producing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kinds, and what he first said is fulfilled daily—“Increase and multiply” (Gen. I, 22)—and that blessing was not abolished even after human sin, so also the words of him who is wholly everywhere and always exists, even when spoken through sinners, obtain their perfect power of consecrating his body and blood at all the tables of the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world.

He said:

“Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given for you.”

And:

“Take and drink; this is my blood, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me.”

And just as, whether a heretic, a schismatic, or a criminal, anyone who baptizes in the confession of the Holy Trinity cannot cause the one so baptized to be rebaptized by good Catholics, lest the confession and invocation of so great a name appear to be annulled—because it is he, as it is written, who baptizes, who commanded his disciples, saying, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19)—so also, whatever the priest’s merit or character, if he performs the office of consecrating the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood according to the tradition, it is he himself who consecrates those same sacraments through his words, he who said:

“Take and eat: this is my body, which will be given for you.”

And:

“Take and drink: this is my blood, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me.”

But whoever receives the mystery of unity and does not hold the bond of peace does not receive the mystery for himself, but testimony against himself.

No one should doubt in any way that each of the faithful becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when, in baptism, he becomes a member of Christ’s body. Nor is he separated from fellowship in that bread and cup even if, before eating that bread and drinking the cup, he departs from this world while established in the unity of Christ’s body.

For he is not deprived of participation in and benefit from that sacrament when he is found to possess precisely that which gives life to the sacrament.

And Christ’s bread and cup become mystical for us not by just any consecration but by a definite one; they are not born (Book XX Against Faustus).

Therefore, what does not take place in this way, although it is bread and a cup, is nourishment for refreshment, not a sacrament of religion—except insofar as we bless and give thanks to the Lord in all his gifts, both spiritual and bodily.

For today also we receive visible food. But the sacrament is something different, which was prefigured in the manna. This bread was signified by the manna; this bread the altar of God has bestowed.

And he says:

“They drank from the spiritual drink that followed them; but the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4).

From there came bread; from there came drink. Christ was the rock in the sign; the true Christ was in the Word and in the flesh.

And how did they drink? The rock was struck twice with the staff. The double striking signifies the two pieces of wood of the cross.

This, then, is the bread descending from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die. Hence the Apostle says:

“The cup of blessing which we bless—is it not participation in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break—is it not participation in the body of the Lord?” (I Cor. X, 16).

“If anyone eats of this bread,” says the Lord, “he will live forever, and the bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI, 52).

This flesh is life for some and destruction for others, as it was for Judas—not because what Judas received was evil, but because evil Judas received the good wrongly.

For the unworthy person takes the sacrament of piety as judgment upon himself. What is good cannot be good for one who receives it badly.

“For my flesh,” he says, “is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.”

Since people seek in food and drink not to hunger or thirst, only this food and drink truly provides that, making those by whom it is received immortal and incorruptible.

For in this mystical distribution of spiritual nourishment, this is imparted and received: that, receiving the power of the heavenly food, we may pass into the flesh of him who became our flesh, so that, made one with him, we may not be held by the prince of the world, by whom we were seized through sin. We become one with him who said:

“The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

He says again:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

For just as our Lord Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God—not as human beings are sons by grace, but as a Son from the substance of the Father—so also the flesh that we receive is true flesh, as he himself said, and his drink is true.”

But perhaps you will say what Christ’s disciples also said at that time, when they heard him say, “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not remain in me, nor have eternal life” (John 6:54). Perhaps you will say: How is this so? I see a likeness, but I do not see the reality of blood.

First of all, I spoke to you about the word of Christ, which operates so as to be able to change and transform the kinds established by nature—for example, the rod of Moses, which was changed into a serpent and again into a rod; and the rivers of Egypt, which were changed into blood and again into water; and the many other signs that are read in the Scriptures.

Then, when Christ’s disciples could not accept his saying, but, hearing that he would give them his flesh to eat and his blood to drink, were withdrawing, Peter alone said: “You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:70), and “How could I withdraw from you?” Therefore, lest many should say this, as though there were some horror of blood, but the grace of redemption should remain, you receive the sacrament indeed in a likeness, but you obtain the grace and power of the true nature.

“I am,” he says, “the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41). But flesh did not come down from heaven. How, then, did bread come down from heaven—and living bread? Because our Lord Jesus Christ is at once a sharer in divinity and in the body; and you, who receive the flesh of his divine substance, participate in that nourishment. Whoever has eaten this body will receive the forgiveness of sins and will not die forever.

(Ambrose, *On the Mysteries and On the Sacraments.*)

“Therefore, you do not say ‘Amen’ without purpose, already trusting in spirit that you are receiving the body of Christ. When you have asked, the priest says to you, ‘The body of Christ,’ and you say, ‘Amen,’ that is, ‘It is true.’ Let the heart hold what the tongue confesses.

“What, then, are the words of consecration, and whose words are they? Those of the Lord Jesus. Before the words of the sacraments, it is bread; when the consecration has been added, from bread it becomes Christ’s flesh.

“On the day before he suffered, he took bread in his holy hands, looked toward heaven, toward you, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, giving thanks; he blessed it, broke it, and, having broken it, handed it to his disciples and apostles, saying: ‘Take and eat from this, all of you; for this is my body, which will be broken for many’ [Col. 0926D]. Likewise, after supper, he looked toward heaven, toward you, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, giving thanks; he blessed the cup and handed it to his apostles and disciples, saying: ‘Take and drink from this, all of you. For this is my blood’ (Matthew 26:28).

“Observe: all those words of the Evangelist continue up to ‘Take,’ whether body or blood; from that point onward they are the words of Christ. Before it is consecrated, it is bread and wine mixed with water; but when the words of Christ have been added, it is the body and blood of Christ. We therefore perceive that grace is greater than nature.

“If the word of Elijah had such power that it brought fire down from heaven (1 Kings 18:38), will Christ’s word not have the power to change the forms of the elements? You have read concerning the works of the whole world: ‘He spoke, and they were made’ (Psalm 148:5). Therefore, the word of Christ, which was able to make from nothing what did not exist, was it unable to change what exists into what it did not previously exist as? For it is no less to give new things than to change natures.

“But why do we use arguments? Let us use his own examples and establish the truth of the mystery of the Incarnation. Did it proceed according to the ordinary course of nature when the Lord Jesus was born from Mary? If we seek the natural order, a woman joined to a man ordinarily gives birth. It is therefore clear that the Virgin gave birth beyond the order of nature.

“And this body that we make is from the Virgin. Why do you seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus himself took flesh beyond nature from the Virgin Mary—flesh that was crucified and buried? Truly, therefore, it is the sacrament of that flesh. The Lord Jesus himself cries out: ‘This is my body’ (Matthew 26:26). Thus you have learned that Christ’s body is made from bread, and that wine mixed with water in the cup becomes blood through the consecration of the heavenly Word.”

Then the Lord Jesus himself bears witness to us that we receive his body and blood. Surely we ought not to doubt his faithfulness and testimony? The body of God is a spiritual body; Christ’s body is the body of the divine Spirit. That Spirit of Christ is, as we read, “Christ the Lord, the Spirit before your face.” And in Peter’s epistle we have: “Christ died for us” (1 Peter 3:18).

And Paul says:

“For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was handed over, took bread, and, giving thanks, blessed it, broke it, and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be handed over for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood. Do this in remembrance of me.’ For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11).

Finally, “Our heart is strengthened by that very food, and that very drink gladdens the human heart” (Psalm 103:13), as the Prophet recalled.

The figure of this spiritual food preceded us in the manna. Whoever gathered more than had been commanded did not have more, because Christ is wholly present in each and wholly present in all. The figure of this spiritual drink also preceded us when God commanded Moses to strike the rock with his rod (Numbers 20:11). He struck the rock, and the rock poured forth a great stream, as the Apostle says: “They were drinking from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

It was not an immovable rock, since it followed the people; and you too drink, so that Christ may follow you. Behold the mystery of God: Moses—that is, the priest—touches the rock with the word of God, and water flows, and the people of God drink. The priest therefore touches it; the water overflows into the cup; it will leap into eternal life; and the people of God, who have obtained God’s grace, drink.

One of the soldiers also touched his side with a lance after Christ’s death, and water flowed from his side: water to cleanse, blood to redeem. “This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ.” From the flesh of this bridegroom the Church came forth, when, from the side of the crucified one, with blood and water flowing out, she received the sacrament of redemption and regeneration.

And every day she is watered by the laver and by the people—that is, washed in the mystery of baptism—while receiving the body of the crucified one, made hot upon the altar of the cross, together with the rosy blood poured forth from the side of the crucified one.

For otherwise, in the holy Church, which is the body of Christ, neither priesthoods are valid nor sacrifices true, unless the true High Priest reconciles us in the particular reality and truth of our nature, and the true blood of the immaculate Lamb cleanses us. Although he is established at the right hand of the Father, he nevertheless performs the sacrament of propitiation in the same flesh that he assumed from the Virgin, as the Apostle says: “Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Romans 8:34).

And the Apostle John likewise says: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1). And again: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1:9).

Therefore, having, as the outstanding preacher says, “a great High Priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who was tempted in every respect according to our likeness, without sin. Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of grace, so that we may obtain his mercy and find grace for timely help” (Hebrews 4:14–16).

Therefore, doubting nothing, but believing in the heart for righteousness and confessing with the mouth for salvation, when we receive his body and blood, let us say with Peter, when others here doubted and he said to the Lord: “Lord, you have the words of eternal life, and we have believed and have known that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (John 6:70).

His flesh is the life of the faithful, if they do not neglect to be his body. Let them therefore become the body of Christ, if they wish to live from the Spirit of Christ; for no one lives from that Spirit except the body of Christ. He receives the food of life and drinks the cup of eternity who remains in Christ and in whom Christ dwells. But whoever disagrees with Christ neither eats Christ’s flesh nor drinks his blood for life, even if he daily receives the sacrament of so great a reality indiscriminately, to the judgment of his presumption.

In receiving it, we must follow the discernment which, we have learned, Aaron, the Lord’s holy one, followed. With a grieving mind, he showed us that he ought not to take the sacrifice offered for sin. Let us also say, with the confession of due humility: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matthew 8:8).

(From Augustine, Homily 50.)

“The Apostle admonishes us not to eat and drink judgment upon ourselves, so that, having judged ourselves through repentance, we may not be judged by the Lord. This act of repentance will then be perfect and acceptable to God if a person ascends the tribunal of his own mind against himself and sets himself before his own face, lest what the Lord threatens the sinner should afterward happen to him.

“When judgment has thus been established in the heart, accusatory thought must be present, conscience as witness, fear as executioner; then the soul’s blood must flow forth in tears. Finally, the mind itself must pronounce such a sentence that a person judges himself unworthy of participation in the body and blood of the Lord.

“Let the image of the future judgment be before his eyes, so that, when others approach the altar of God while he himself does not approach, he may consider how terrifying that punishment must be: while others receive eternal life, others eat and drink judgment upon themselves.

“In this work of repentance, one must carefully beware of the cunning of the ancient enemy. Often, when the mind recovers from guilt and tries to mourn what it has committed, he summons empty hopes and false securities before its eyes, so as to take away the benefit of repentance.

“Sometimes he speaks of the more serious deeds of others; sometimes he says that what was done is nothing; sometimes he speaks of God’s mercy; sometimes he promises that there will still be time afterward for repentance. Thus, while the deceived mind is led along by these things, it is suspended from the purpose of repentance, so that it may receive no good then because no evils distress it now, and may then be overwhelmed more fully by punishments because it now even rejoices in its sins.

“Remembering the vengeance suffered by those who offered strange fire in the presence of the Lord, as is read in the Heptateuch, we must take care not to approach the Lord’s altar with a desire to sin or with delight in sin, and not to incur what the Apostle points out in his Epistle to the Corinthians. ‘For this reason,’ he says, ‘many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep’ (1 Corinthians 11:30).

“When the flame of each sin and the delight of the heart have cooled from the heart, and after the satisfaction of repentance, let us follow what we read in the Gospel concerning Zacchaeus the tax collector: ‘He received the Lord joyfully into his house’ (Luke 19:6), and prepared a great banquet for him.

“Whose house are we, and to whom does human thought confess, while the remnants of thought celebrate a feast for him? Our heart’s contrition is a feast day for the Lord, when it is continually moved to tears out of love for him.

“Therefore, when we receive the body and blood of our Redeemer, we ought to afflict ourselves for our sins in tears, so that the very bitterness of repentance may wipe away from the stomach of our mind the perverse fluid of life.

“After the times of prayer and communion, let us preserve the mind in itself, as far as we can with God’s help, by its own weight and strength, lest afterward a wandering thought dissolve it, lest empty joy steal upon the mind, and lest the soul through negligence lose the gains of contrition through its wandering thoughts.

“Thus Hannah deserved to obtain what she had requested, because after her tears she preserved herself in the same firmness of mind. Concerning her it is written: ‘Her face was no longer changed in different directions’ (1 Samuel 1:18). Because she did not forget what she had asked, she was not deprived of the gift she had requested.”

These things, most illustrious and beloved king, having taken the opportunity afforded by the letter which you commanded to be sent to us, I have endeavoured, according to my measure, to gather for you and for us—and indeed for all who wish to read, understand, and observe them—as it were into one bundle: from the thought and words of the Catholic writers, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; from the sharp arrows of the Mighty One with desolating coals; from the flashing spears of God’s wrath; and especially from the sayings of that honeycomb, if we may so call him, of divine eloquence, namely blessed Gregory. He could truly say: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 118:35); for what he received with the Lord pouring it into his mouth, he most sweetly ministered to us. I have done so after the manner of those who cut branches from the trees to level the way of the Lord and Saviour.

Moreover, I have also written through which vices especially the boar from the forest and that solitary wild beast, the devil, do not cease, as far as they can, not only to swallow up the river of the human race but also to lay waste the vineyard of the Lord of hosts—that is, each of the faithful—and from which the remaining vices arise, as anyone wishing to know may read in the thirty-first book of the *Moralia*. Thus may your wisdom, once the devil’s snares are known, pursue the way to the eternal kingdom more easily; may the devotion of Christ’s simple faithful be built up, lest it stray from the way of truth; and may my unworthiness, by rendering the sound of speech in the ministry imposed upon it, somehow escape the Lord’s wrath. For this reason Moses is commanded that, when the priest enters the tabernacle, he be surrounded with bells: namely, that he may have the voices of preaching, lest by silence he offend the judgment of the heavenly inspector. For it is written: “That the sound may be heard when he enters and leaves the sanctuary in the presence of the Lord, and that he may not die” (Exodus 28:35). For a priest dies when entering or leaving if no sound is heard from him, because he incurs against himself the wrath of the hidden Judge if he proceeds without the sound of preaching. But because, unless there is one within who teaches, the teacher’s tongue labours outwardly in vain, we must beseech the divine mercy that what he speaks through us in your ears he may pour into your hearts through the instrument of the Holy Spirit—he who, with his coeternal Father, in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0929]

## III. ON THE DIVERSE AND MULTIPLE NATURE OF THE SOUL

[Note: Flodoard does not mention this book among Hincmar’s works, nor does the inscription in an old manuscript state the author’s name. It reads as follows: “A collection of some wise man from the books of Saint Augustine, on the diverse and multiple nature of the soul.” Nevertheless, many things persuade us that it is Hincmar’s, and the matters contained in the Preface fit only King Charles the Bald. Sirmond.]

### TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING

(From the same source, from a manuscript of Saint Remigius of Reims.) (G)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 0929D]

It is the opinion of ancient men, who always sought what was useful and entrusted their discoveries to posterity, that commonwealths would be happy if either wise men governed them or those who governed them devoted themselves to wisdom.

Our predecessors favorably received this opinion, approved it as usefully expressed, and, because it seemed salutary, also committed it to writing so that posterity might know it. We too support it and give thanks to God, since he has appointed you, good king, over our commonwealth and pours into your mind the rays of his love so that you may seek true wisdom.

And since both our opinion and theirs is that the mind of the wise person ought always to be engaged in the search for the highest good, as the Prophet says, “Seek the Lord, and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Psalm 104:4), we rightly rejoice that you cultivate those branches of philosophy which are known to tend toward the citadel of true and unique wisdom.

For it is always necessary for the ruler’s mind to remember what the Holy Spirit admonishes him through those same illustrious rulers who are also truly wise: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling. Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right way” (Psalm 2:10, 12). Likewise: “Love justice, you who judge the earth. Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wisdom 1:1).

We also approve the sharpness and liveliness of your intellect. Since you strive to seek the highest good, you endeavor to clear the path of inquiry by which you may reach what you desire. For God is not approached by bodily steps, nor is the divine nature and majesty of his being perceived by bodily eyes; rather, he is approached and seen by those steps and lights of which the Prophet says: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm 33:6).

God is therefore sought by the mind, God is approached by the mind, and God is seen by the mind. In his vision the entire search for the highest good is fulfilled. We rightly approve the occupation of your most noble intellect with this knowledge.

For no one can fully know what is above him who does not care to know himself. And because the human mind is near to God, though it is not itself what God is, it acts suitably when, wishing to know the highest things, it first takes care to know what is near the highest. It is altogether unworthy for someone to scrutinize divine things who does not care to know what his own human nature is.

By doing these things, you show yourself worthy of your ancestral line—the ancestors who roused mortal hearts, languishing in knowledge of divine and human matters. We speak of your grandfather and namesake, the defender of the doctrine and faith of the holy Church, and also of your father, the distinguished ornament of all goodness and piety.

You are also looking after yourself honorably and usefully. For it is dishonorable for one who presides to be disfigured in knowledge. It is useful and honorable, moreover, for a ruler both to excel in the beauty of understanding and, through wisdom and integrity of character, to look after himself and his subjects.

We have therefore carefully examined the outline of chapters brought to us and considered it point by point. With the help of God, and adding also the examples of holy teachers, we intend to respond to each item according to the capacity of our small intellect—not relying on our own understanding, but trusting in God, who will not deny what is worthy to one who seeks him, and who, as we trust, will open the paths of our sluggishness so that we may satisfy your desire.

## CHAPTER ONE. WHETHER THE SOUL IS CORPOREAL

The first proposition of those same chapters is: whether the soul is corporeal.

For us, the soul appears less corporeal to the extent that it is recognized as being less compounded from those elements of which all bodies consist. We do not believe that it consists of air, fire, water, or earth; rather, we say that it was created by God. In relation to the body, which subsists from these elements, it is simple; but in comparison with the Creator, it is multiple.

It is simple insofar as bodily quality is concerned, because, as has been said, its creation subsists from no elements. Yet, in comparison with God, it is multiple, because it is subject to various passions: at one time desiring, at another rejecting what it had desired; at one time joyful, at another sorrowful; at one time wise, at another foolish.

A sober understanding, attentive to the Holy Spirit’s distinction between creature and Creator, grasps that none of this can in any way apply to God. Through the Psalmist he says to God: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same” (Psalm 102:27). And again, speaking in his own person: “I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Malachi 3:6).

Meanwhile, if the creation of the human being is considered, it is easily perceived that the soul is not a body. For after God had formed the body from clay, Scripture says: “God breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7).

If one body were joined to another body, what would cause one of the two bodies to live? But when it is said that God breathed into the face of the formed human being the breath of life, whatever that breathing may have been, that breath of life was not a body but a spirit, more powerful and better than earth and than any body. Through its union, and through the joining of the previously sluggish limbs, the human being became a living soul.

We therefore do not call it a body, but the breath—or rather, the spirit—of life, and, relying on the authority of the Scriptures, we declare it to be a soul. For the Prophet says: “I am the Lord, stretching out the heavens, founding the earth, and forming the spirit of the human being within him” (Zechariah 12:1).

Hence the Psalmist, when he saw all human beings dissolved in death once their souls had been taken away, and living again at the end of the age when their souls had been restored, says: “Take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. Send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 104:29–30).

Again, the same Prophet says concerning certain rulers passing through this life: “His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth” (Psalm 146:4).

Nevertheless, we do not say that the soul is properly called “spirit,” since God is called spirit, as we find in the Gospel: “God is spirit” (John 4:24), and the holy angels are called spirits, as in: “He makes his angels spirits” (Psalm 104:4). This name is also customarily applied to evil spirits.

The soul is also called the human spirit. Hence Solomon says: “Until the dust returns to its earth from which it was taken, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

Air stirred by wind is also called spirit, as it is written: “Stormy winds, which do his word” (Psalm 148:8).

But that same substance, attributed by the Creator’s gift to vivify and govern the body, is properly called “soul”—as though *anaema*, that is, far removed from blood. This is because, unlike other living creatures, when blood fails, the soul does not also fail, although Scripture says: “The soul of all flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11). Rather, when the body fails—the body whose support is blood—the soul does not perish at all.

Some also say that the soul received its name from the fact that it animates, that is, gives life to, the substance of the body.

To explain more fully what we think about it, let us believe not our own words but those of the Creator, who, separating the soul from the body by calling it spirit, distinguished its nature, dignity, and power from the body when he said: “It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:63). Likewise: “What is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from spirit is spirit” (John 3:6).

Although the soul does not see or become visible together with the body, it does so with a bodily likeness: either when it withdraws and removes itself from the bodily senses—as happens in sleep, when it is occupied with manifold visions—or when, through ecstasy, that is, an excess of mind, it is led away into different things; or when it is entirely separated from the body, as happens in death, and is transferred either to everlasting punishments or to eternal glory.

In these conditions, although the body—which the soul itself is not—is not seen, it is nevertheless believed to possess a bodily likeness.

## CHAPTER TWO. WHETHER THE SOUL IS LOCALLY CONFINED IN THE BODY

The second chapter is: whether the soul is locally confined in the body.

As we answered in the preceding chapter, we say and firmly maintain that the soul is not a body but a spirit, and that a spirit is not bounded locally, as bodies ordinarily are, so that it is greater in one place and smaller in another.

Yet, although the soul is a spirit, we know by the authority of the sacred Scriptures that it is contained in the body in a wondrous and ineffable manner. Thus we read in Job: “Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast, and he found perversity in his angels. How much more will those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is earthly, be consumed as by a moth?” (Job 4:18–19).

Likewise, in Elijah’s prayer: “Lord God, I ask that the soul of this child return into his inward parts” (1 Kings 17:21); and shortly afterward: “The soul of the child returned within him, and he revived.”

Paul also speaks of himself and those like him: “Although our outward human being is corrupted, yet the inward human being is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). And again: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have an building from God, a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).

Likewise: “For we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (ibid., 5:4). And shortly afterward: “We are confident, and we have the good will rather to be absent from the body and present with God” (ibid., 5:8).

Again, he himself says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

The Evangelist also demonstrates that at the time of death the soul goes forth from the body when he says concerning the Lord: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 19:30). Explaining this passage, Father Augustine says: “By this the death of the body, with the soul going forth, was signified.”

On this matter, it is better to believe the authority of the Fathers than our own assertion. Blessed Ambrose says in the fourth book of the *Hexameron* (chapter 6):

“For what is flesh without the governance of the soul, without the vigor of the mind? Flesh is taken up today and laid aside tomorrow; flesh is temporary, the soul enduring. Flesh is the soul’s garment, and the soul clothes itself in a kind of bodily vesture. You are therefore not the garment, but the one who uses the garment.”

The same author says in his Letter to Orontianus (Letter 31):

“Each soul, seeing itself enclosed in this bodily hovel, yet not degraded by fellowship with this earthly dwelling, groans under the burden of its union with the body, because the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling inclines the mind toward many thoughts.”

Behold what a great and distinguished man calls the body the soul’s garment and asserts that the soul is enclosed within the body as in a kind of hovel.

Blessed Augustine, a most careful and eloquent man, expressed the soul’s definition with remarkable brevity and truth in his book *On the Quantity of the Soul*, saying (chapter 13):

“For it seems to me”—with “soul” understood—“to be a certain substance participating in reason, adapted to govern the body.”

And shortly afterward (chapter 14):

“What is surprising if the soul is neither corporeal nor extended by any length, spread out by any breadth, or solidified by any height, and yet has such power in the body that the governance of all the limbs belongs to it, and it is, as it were, a certain pivot in the activity of all bodily movements?”

Earlier, knowing that God had arranged all things in measure, number, and weight, he distinguished the soul’s space—which God knows in himself—from bodily space, saying in the same work:

“For certainly, since it is not a body—for otherwise it could not perceive anything in the body, as the preceding reasoning demonstrated—it undoubtedly lacks the space by which bodies are measured; and its quantity cannot rightly be believed, thought, or understood in this way.”

The same most learned man develops this meaning much more clearly in the sixth book of *On the Trinity*, saying (chapter 6):

“Therefore the soul”—with “soul” understood—“is simpler than the body, because it is not spread through space by mass, but in each body it is wholly present in the whole, and it is wholly present in each part of it. Thus, when something occurs in any small part of the body that the soul perceives, although it does not occur in the whole body, the soul nevertheless perceives it wholly, because nothing of it is hidden from the whole soul.”

The same author says in the twenty-first book of *The City of God* (chapter 3):

“The first death drives the unwilling soul from the body; the second death holds the unwilling soul in the body. Both deaths have this in common: the soul suffers from its own body what it does not wish.”

The same author says in the same work:

“This other manner in which spirits cling to bodies and become living creatures is wholly wondrous; it cannot be comprehended by human beings. And this is the human being himself.”

In the twenty-second book (chapter 6), he says:

“For if we were souls alone—that is, spirits without any body—and, dwelling in heaven, did not know earthly animals, and if we were told that in the future we would be joined by some wondrous bond to earthly bodies in order to give them life, would we not argue much more forcefully against believing it and say that nature does not permit an incorporeal thing to be bound by a bodily bond? And yet the earth is full of living souls, with these earthly limbs joined and interwoven with them in some wondrous manner.”

In the same book (chapter 11), he says:

“What does it”—with “soul” understood—“do in an earthly body? What does the more subtle thing of all do in this mass? What does the lightest thing of all do in this weight? What does the swiftest thing of all do in this sluggishness? Will it not be possible, through the merit of this most excellent nature, for its body to be raised into heaven? And if earthly bodies now have the natural power to press souls downward, will souls at some time not also be able to raise earthly bodies upward?”

In the seventh book of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* (chapter 24), he says:

“Let it therefore be believed, if no authority of Scripture or reasoning based on truth contradicts it, that the human being was made on the sixth day in such a way that the causal principle of the human body was already present in the elements of the world, while the soul itself was created, just as the day was first created, and lay hidden in God’s works until, at the proper time, he inserted it by breathing—that is, by inspiring it—into the body formed from clay.”

Jerome, a man of the greatest authority, also says in his consolatory letter to Paula (Letter 25, on the death of Blaesilla):

“But after the burden of flesh had been cast off, the soul flew back to its own author and, after long wandering, ascended into its ancient possession; according to custom, the funeral rites are prepared.”

The same author says in the *Epitaph of Nepotianus* (Letter 3 to Heliodorus):

“Where now is that beautiful face? Where is the dignity of the whole body, in which, as in a beautiful garment, the soul’s beauty was clothed? Alas, the lily withered as the south wind blew, and the purple of the violet gradually passed into pallor.”

Blessed Gregory likewise says in the fifth book of the *Moralia* (chapter 25):

“When the mind abandons bodily images and comes into itself, it rises to no small degree. But although the soul is incorporeal, because it clings to the body, it is recognized as local according to its own condition, since it is held in bodily places. When it forgets what it has learned, it recognizes what it did not know; it remembers what it had consigned to oblivion; it becomes joyful after sadness; it is cast down after joy. By this very diversity it shows how far it is from the substance of the eternal and immutable nature, which is always the same as it is: everywhere present, everywhere invisible, everywhere wholly present, everywhere incomprehensible.”

The same author continues (chapter 28):

“We inhabit houses of clay because we subsist in earthly bodies. Considering this well, Paul says: ‘We have this treasure in earthen vessels’ (2 Corinthians 4:7).”

And shortly afterward (in the same work):

“A moth is born from a garment and, by being born, corrupts the very garment from which it arises. In a certain sense, flesh is the soul’s garment. But this garment certainly has its own moth, because carnal temptation arises from it, and by it the garment is torn.”

Cassiodorus, a man of exceptionally keen intellect and distinguished learning, also shows in the book he wrote *On the Soul* that he follows the teachers of the holy Church in this matter, as in others, when he says, among other things (chapter 6):

“It also seems wondrous that an incorporeal thing should be bound to the most solid limbs, and that such different natures should have been brought into one harmony, so that the soul can neither separate itself when it wishes nor retain itself when it recognizes the Creator’s command. Everything is closed to it when it is ordered to remain within; everything is opened when it is commanded to depart.

“For if the harsh pain of a wound is inflicted, the soul is not lost without the Creator’s command, just as it is not preserved without his gift. Hence we frequently see those who have been gravely wounded escape death, and again others perish from slight causes.”

Behold by how many and how authoritative testimonies—not arguments but demonstrations—it is shown to us that souls are either clothed with bodies, joined to them, or bound to them. It seems dangerous for us to resist the authority of such men.

It therefore remains that, if these authorities are not believed, much must be cut away from the divine books and, with them mutilated, the teaching of so many great men must be undermined—or, what is more appropriate, the person who contradicts them must be separated from the fellowship of the Church.

## CHAPTER THREE. WHETHER THE SOUL MOVES THROUGH PLACES WITH THE BODY
## Chapter III. Whether the Soul Moves Through Places Together with the Body

The third chapter asks: whether the soul moves through places together with the body.

This chapter seems somewhat obscure, since it does not clearly show whether it inquires if the soul departs from the body it bears together with some other body, or whether it moves through places together with this body that has been divinely assigned to it. But if the question is whether the soul leaves the body together with some body, blessed Augustine answers this in his letter to Evodius (Letter 100):

> “But if you wish to hear briefly what I think, I by no means believe that the soul leaves the body together with a body, and [Col. 0936D] the rest that is contained in the same letter.”

If, however, the question is whether it moves through places together with the body—that is, with this body that it bears—it is strange how it can be said to move, since it is not moved by the body but itself moves the body. For anyone who considers the foregoing clearly understands that bodies cannot move in any way without its presence or inclination. If it should happen to depart, then what is written will occur: “The dust will return to its earth, and the spirit will return to God who gave it” (Eccles. XII, 7).

Nevertheless, just as we call its union with the body incomprehensible, so also we call spiritual, and therefore incomprehensible to us, the power and inclination by which the body is given life, vitality, and direction. Let someone nevertheless consider whether, when it departs from one place and arrives at another, it has left behind somewhere the soul that gives it vitality and life, without whose presence, as has been said, the body could not move.

That the soul is bounded by limits is established by the authority of the Fathers, as is also the case with angelic spirits. These are certainly now of greater dignity, and are frequently sent for human ministry, as Paul says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebr. I, 14.) Hence blessed Pope Gregory says in the second book of the *Moralia* (chapter 2):

> “In this, then, the angelic nature is now distinguished from the condition of our nature: we are confined by place and restricted by the ignorance of blindness, whereas the spirits of the angels are indeed confined by place, but their knowledge is nevertheless extended far beyond ours, incomparably.”

Nor are we unaware that blessed Augustine, by certain arguments, came almost to the point of saying that souls move in time and not in place. Yet, as it seems to us, considering that many objections could be raised against this view, he carefully moderated what he appeared to assert, in his usual manner, when he said in the eighth book of *On Genesis* (chapter 22):

> “As I had begun to say, if anyone is unwilling to believe this about the soul, he should not be pressed too hard.”

Moreover, concerning what the soul accomplishes in the body’s senses, and the fact that among other things it also takes pleasure in movement, the same blessed Augustine bears witness in *On the Quantity of the Soul* (chapter 33):

> “Now attend to what I had undertaken to explain: what power the soul possesses in the senses, and how it is more clearly manifested in the movement of a living creature itself, with which we can have no communion in the case of things fixed by roots. The soul applies itself to touch, and by it senses and distinguishes what is hot, cold, rough, smooth, hard, soft, light, and heavy. Then, by tasting, smelling, hearing, and seeing, it judges innumerable differences of flavors, odors, sounds, and forms. In all these things it takes up and desires whatever accords with the nature of its body, while it rejects and flees what is contrary.

> “It withdraws from these senses for a definite interval of time, and, as though restoring their movements by certain periods of rest, turns over within itself, in crowds and in manifold ways, the images of things that it has drawn in through them. This whole process is sleep and dreams. Often, too, it takes pleasure in the ease of movement, whether leaping about or wandering, and without effort arranges the harmony of the limbs. For the union of the sexes it does what it can, and in the fellowship and love of two natures it strives to make one.
