In offspring it cooperates not only in generating but also in cherishing and nourishing them. With the things among which the body acts, and by which the body is sustained, it becomes entangled through habit and is separated from them with difficulty, as though they were its limbs.”

## Chapter IV. Whether Every Creature Is Corporeal and God Alone Is Incorporeal

The fourth place is occupied by the question whether every creature is corporeal and God alone incorporeal. [Col. 0938A] In the preceding discussions, as we thought, it has already been shown sufficiently and more than sufficiently that God is not corporeal, nor is the angelic dignity, nor is the substance of human souls. This is especially clear since the Son of God himself, who is God, says of God the Father and the Holy Spirit: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John IV, 24)—that is, not in a temple or on a mountain, which are bodies, but in spirit and truth, that is, in the mind, and not in some image that the human soul is accustomed to fabricate for itself concerning God.

That the holy angels are spirits and not bodies is testified by the Holy Spirit speaking through the Psalmist, who says of God: “Who makes his angels spirits” (Ps. CIII, 4). He evidently shows that those whom God always has as spirits in his service he makes angels—that is, messengers—by sending them. For “angels” is the name of an office, not of a nature.

Paul also testifies that the substance of human souls is not a body but a spirit, saying: “For who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit that is in him?” (I Cor. II, 11.) Thus we say that the substance of God, of angels, and of human souls is not body but spirit. Yet we call God Spirit as Creator, whereas we call angels and souls spirits as creatures created by God.

But it is rightly asked how blessed Paul the Apostle, praising God, calls God alone immortal and invisible, when he says: “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen” (I Tim. I, 17), since it is evident that angels and human souls were created immortal [Col. 0938C] and, insofar as their nature is concerned, invisible.

Likewise, in the same letter to Timothy (I Tim. VI, 15), he says: “Whom the blessed and only Sovereign will reveal at his proper time, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality, dwelling in inaccessible light.”

For how is he alone blessed, when it is said: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked” (Ps. I, 1), and elsewhere: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Ps. III, 1), and: “Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he will find watching” (Matt. XXIV, 46)?

How is he alone powerful, if “the seed of the blessed man will be powerful upon the earth” (Ps. III, 2), which we understand as referring to the living?

How does he alone possess immortality, when angels cannot die and human souls were created immortal [Col. 0938D]?

We understand this as follows: insofar as their nature and substance are concerned, and also those of the lower creatures, which are certainly corporeal, they are invisible, wise, blessed, powerful, and immortal through the gift of the Creator. Yet, in comparison with the Creator, because of his surpassing greatness, they are considered to possess none of these qualities. For he alone possesses these things in the true sense, since he received them from no one. Angelic spirits and human souls, however, received them from his source like streams, so that this current of dignity might flow into them.

In the Letter to the Hebrews he likewise says:

> “For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, penetrating to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and no creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebr. IV, 12). [Col. 0939A]

These testimonies, taken together, completely resolve the difficulty posed by the question. For of the one who alone is invisible, who alone dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen and cannot see (I John IV), and who surpasses all understanding (Phil. IV), it is likewise said that no creature is invisible in his sight and that all things are naked and open to his eyes.

Since, then, as has already been said, he himself is called invisible, while all invisible things are naked and open to his eyes—that is, since he sees all things as though they were naked, but no creature sees him except insofar as he permits it by his gracious gift—it is certain that things which are incorporeal by nature are regarded as corporeal in comparison with him.

Hence blessed Pope Gregory, speaking of these matters in the second book of the *Moralia* (chapter 2), says:

> “The knowledge of the angels is therefore greatly expanded in comparison with our knowledge, but it is narrow in comparison with divine knowledge. Likewise, their spirits are spirits in comparison with our bodies, but in comparison with the supreme and unbounded Spirit they are bodies. Thus they are both sent forth and stand present: because, insofar as they are bounded, they go out, and insofar as they are also present within, they never depart.”

We could indeed provide more examples in which the holy Fathers customarily call angelic spirits bodies; but, intent on brevity, we have chosen to omit them, since we think these examples alone sufficient.

## Chapter V. Whether the Nature of the Soul Exceeds Bodily Limits

Next, in its proper order, comes the chapter: whether the nature of the soul exceeds bodily limits.

In this matter our uncertain understanding fluctuates over what bodily limits are meant: whether those by which it is surrounded, namely the members of flesh, or all bodies, such as heaven and earth and the things contained within them. We answer concerning both according to the measure of our ability.

The soul exceeds the limits of its own body when it sees farther through the bodily eyes than the body itself extends, hears farther, smells farther, and stretches touch beyond itself. Since, then, it extends these senses beyond the body, and at times takes pleasure in things that please them or is troubled by things that offend them, it is evident that it exceeds these bodily limits.

But if the question concerns every body—namely, whether it exceeds everything corporeal—it is clear that it accomplishes this not through the bodily senses subject to it, but through its own faculties: thought, memory, and conjecture.

Hence blessed Ambrose says in the sixth book of the *Hexameron* (chapter 8):

> “The flesh, therefore, cannot be in the image of God, but our soul can, since it is free and wanders here and there through its diffuse thoughts and deliberations, contemplating everything. Here we are now in Italy, yet we think about what appears to be located in the eastern or western regions [Col. 0940A], and we seem to be among those who are situated in Persia, while we see what those in Africa are doing. If that land has received people known to us, we follow them as they depart, cling to them as they travel, unite ourselves with them though they are absent, and speak with those who are separated from us.

> “We even summon the dead to conversation, embrace and hold them as though they were alive, and render to them the services and usages of life. That, therefore, is in the image of God which is not judged corporeal, but is so through the vigor of the mind: it sees those who are absent, crosses the seas in vision, traverses them in its gaze, searches out hidden things, and in a single moment carries its senses through the boundaries of the whole world and the hidden places of the universe. It is joined to God and clings to Christ. It descends into hell and ascends; free, it moves about in heaven. Finally, hear the one who says: [Col. 0940B] ‘Our citizenship is in heaven’ (Phil. III, 20).”

Augustine says in his letter to Evodius (Letter 100):

> “As for those visions and predictions of future things, let the person who knows by what power such things are produced in each soul through thought attempt to explain how they occur. For we see, and plainly perceive, that innumerable images of many visible things, and of things belonging to the other bodily senses, arise in it. It does not matter how orderly or confusedly they arise, but only that they arise—which is evident. Whoever can explain by what power and in what manner all these things occur—things that are certainly daily and continuous—may dare to assume and define something even about those exceedingly rare visions.

> “But I dare this all the less because I am even less capable of explaining how that which we experience within ourselves throughout our continual waking and sleeping takes place. When I was dictating this letter to you, I was contemplating you in my mind, although you were absent and unaware; and, according to the knowledge of you that I possess, I imagined how you might be moved by these words. Yet I was unable to grasp or investigate how this occurred in my mind, although I was certain that it did not occur through corporeal masses or corporeal qualities, even though it took place in a manner very similar to the body.”

From the fifteenth book of *The City of God*:

> “We know, and are completely certain, that these things occur in the mind or are produced by our mind. But how they occur: the more attentively we are able to consider this, the more both our speech fails and our very concentration falters, so that our understanding may reach something clearly, even if our tongue cannot. And do we suppose that, in such great weakness of mind, we can comprehend whether God’s providence is the same as memory and understanding—he who does not contemplate things individually in thought, but embraces all that he knows in one eternal, unchanging, and ineffable vision?

> “In this difficulty and confinement, I am moved to cry out to the living God: ‘Your knowledge has been made wonderful from me; it has prevailed, and I shall not attain to it’ (Ps. CXXXVIII, 6). ‘From myself,’ he says, ‘I understand how wonderful and incomprehensible is your knowledge by which you made me, since I cannot comprehend even myself, whom you made.’ And yet in my meditation a fire is kindled, so that I may always seek your face.”

## Chapter VI. Whether God Moves Through Times and Places

[Col. 0941A]

The sixth chapter follows: whether God moves through times and places.

It is astonishing, and exceedingly astonishing, if anyone so foolish is found as to think that God, the creator of times, moves through times. For how can he move through times who created times, which are subject to change?

The prophet David, considering that God has neither a beginning nor a limit, says:

> “In the beginning you founded the earth, O Lord, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and all things will grow old like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. CI, 26–28).

Whoever, therefore, considers in these words that the Lord founded the earth and heaven in the beginning—that is, when times were beginning—and that, when these things are changed, he himself remains the same, easily sees that he neither began with time nor will receive an end with times. When times began, he already existed; when they pass away, he remains the same and unchanging.

He commanded creation to move through times: he established certain stars in motion, commanded times themselves to succeed one another, willed the quality of the air to vary, ordained that the face of the earth should change in different and alternating ways, and decreed that human beings should pass through various ages until the final moment of life. Yet he did not subject himself to any law of change.

Hence he said to Moses: “I am who I am,” and: “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III, 14).

Things that were created with time move through times. But he alone cannot move with time whom we know to be bound by no law of change.

Why, moreover, should anyone think that God moves through places, when he says of himself: “Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jer. XXIII, 24.) And again:

> “What house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what place will be my resting-place? Did not my hand make all these things?” (Isa. LXVI, 1.)

Likewise, the most wise Solomon says, speaking to God:

> “If heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built?” (III Kings VIII, 27.)

And again it is written concerning Wisdom, which is God:

> “It reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII, 1).

If, then, his power penetrates all things, and creation, which was made through him, is too narrow for the greatness of the Creator, since the Psalmist says: “There is no end to his greatness” (Ps. CXLIV, 3), who could believe that he moves through place when no place is open for him to withdraw elsewhere? For if he fills all things, no empty place remains. Thus it is evident that he fills all things who created the universe.

Augustine says in the eighth book of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* (chapter 19):

> “We therefore say that the supreme, true, one, and only God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, that is, God, his Word, and the Spirit of both; the Trinity itself, neither confused nor separated; God, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see—is contained neither by a finite nor by an infinite spatial extent, nor is he altered by either a finite or an infinite succession of times.

> “For in his substance, insofar as he is God, there is not something that is shorter in a part than in the whole, as must be the case with things that exist in places; nor was there in his substance something that is no longer, or will there be something that is not yet, as occurs in natures capable of undergoing temporal change (chapter 10).

> “Living, therefore, in unchanging eternity, he created all things simultaneously, from which times would flow, places would be filled, and the ages would pass through the temporal and spatial movements of things. Among these things he created some spiritual and some corporeal, forming matter which neither another nor no one at all, but he himself, established as unformed yet formable, so that its formation would be preceded not by time but by origin.”

Isidore says in the first book of the *Sentences*, concerning the fact that no succession of times is attributed to God (book I, chapter 8):

> “Divine eternity precedes all times. In God there is believed to be nothing past, present, or future; rather, all things are called present in him because in his eternity he embraces everything. Otherwise God must be believed mutable if successions of times are attributed to him. If there were always some times with God, it would not be time but eternity; nor would times change, but they would stand still.”

## Chapter VII. Whether the Soul Alone Moves Through Time

The seventh place in the order of the chapters is occupied by the question whether the soul alone moves through time. The preceding chapter contains a discussion of this matter. Yet we are astonished that it should be asked whether the soul alone moves through time, since everything that lives through sap and vitality, as well as everything that lives through a soul but lacks reason, is subject to movement through time.

It is therefore pointless to ask whether the soul alone moves through time, since it is proven to share this condition with many creatures. It differs from them only in this: the mutability of time that occurs in many others through increase and diminution—certainly in bodily ways—occurs in the soul spiritually, as in being wise or being foolish.

For the soul is said to increase and decrease only in these respects. It moves temporally, as has already been stated, when it passes from one thing to another—not by increase or diminution, as is the case with many creatures that move through bodily change, [Col. 0942D] but chiefly through the alteration of morals and will.

Yet, occupying the pivotal place, since it is spirit, it gives life to the body and moves it locally by its own inclinations. Father Augustine excellently indicates its proper movement, in his exposition of Psalm 145, saying:

> “Behold, a man is standing and singing to God for a somewhat extended time; often his lips are moving in song, but his thought flies away through I know not what desires. Our mind, then, was standing in a certain way for the praise of God, while our soul was flowing here and there through various desires or the cares of business.

> “The mind itself, as though attending from above to the soul flowing here and there, addresses it in its troubled restlessness: ‘Bless the Lord, my soul. Why are you concerned with other things? Why are you occupied with care for earthly and mortal matters? Stand with me; bless the Lord.’

> “And the soul, as though weighed down and unable to remain as it ought, replies to the mind: ‘I will bless the Lord in my life.’ What does ‘in my life’ mean? It means that for the moment I am in my death. First, therefore, exhort yourself and say: ‘Bless the Lord, my soul.’ Your soul replies to you: ‘I bless him as much as I can—weakly, faintly, feebly.’ Why? ‘Because while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord.’

> “Why do you bless the Lord in this way—not perfectly, not steadfastly? Ask Scripture: ‘The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks of many things’ (Wis. IX, 15).

> “Take away from me the body that weighs down the soul, and I will bless the Lord. Take away from me the earthly dwelling that burdens the mind thinking of many things, and I will flow together from many things into one, so that I may bless the Lord. But as long as I am thus burdened, I cannot. What, then? Will you be silent and not bless the Lord perfectly? ‘I will bless the Lord in my life.’”

## Chapter VIII. Whether the Substance of Divinity Is Seen by Bodily Eyes after the Resurrection of Bodies
## Chapter Eight

The eighth chapter, which is also the last, asks whether the substance of the divinity will be seen by bodily eyes after the resurrection of bodies.

We know, indeed, that the desires of the saints who live in this life chiefly yearn for this: that they may be deemed worthy to see God. This is the whole reason why here they mortify the flesh with fasts and vigils and other kinds of affliction, as the apostle Paul says; and why, as far as possible, they despise all temporal gains; and, if necessity demands it, even surrender their own bodies to manifold suffering. Since, while placed here—that is, weighed down by the burden of the flesh—they cannot see him, as the Lord says to Moses, “For no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:30), they strive here to cleanse their hearts and purify them as far as possible for this purpose, so that they may deserve to attain to his vision: here, meanwhile, “through a mirror in an enigma,” and afterward “face to face.” They say to God with their inmost sighs:

“Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. 25:8).

And again:

“To you my heart has said, ‘My face has sought you’; your face, Lord, I shall seek. Do not turn your face away from me; do not withdraw in anger from your servant” (Ps. 26:8).

And also:

“My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of my God?” (Ps. 42:3.)

For they know with complete certainty that the reward of their labors is the vision of their Creator. The Psalmist shows this when he says to the Lord:

“I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 17:15).

The Lord himself also demonstrates that the supreme blessedness consists in the sight of the divine vision, saying:

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

And promising them:

“Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

He promises that not only himself but also the Father and the Holy Spirit—the inseparable triune God—will be present with those who love him, when he says:

“Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (ibid., 23).

He also promises concerning the Holy Spirit that he will remain with them and be in them.

But whether this vision takes place through bodily eyes or incorporeal ones has been investigated with much questioning, and so great a matter, because it is exceedingly obscure, has been debated at length by the holy Fathers. Some say that the invisible God cannot be seen through a visible and bodily creature; rather, what the Apostle says, “Now through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12), is equivalent to his statement, “Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (ibid.).

Others, however, appropriately assert that this gift may be attributed to the spiritual body: although it is a body, because it is endowed with spiritual dignity it may deserve to behold the very glory of its Redeemer, for whose love it did not hesitate in this world to endure various torments and labors.

On this subject we set down one of the statements of blessed Augustine, reading through the opinions of his predecessors so that we may see what he thought:

“Therefore, when I am asked,” he says (*City of God*, book 22, chapter 9), “what the saints will do in that spiritual body, I do not say what I already see, but what I believe, according to what I read in the Psalm: ‘I believed, therefore I spoke’ (Ps. 116:1). I say, then, that they will see God in that very body. But whether they will see him through it, as through the body we now see the sun, moon, stars, sea, and earth and the things that are in it, is no small question.

“For it is difficult to say that the saints will then have bodies of such a kind that they cannot close and open their eyes whenever they wish; but it is still more difficult to say that whoever closes his eyes there will not see God. For if the prophet Elisha, while bodily absent, saw his servant Gehazi receiving the gifts given him by Naaman the Syrian—whom the prophet had cleansed from the deformity of leprosy—and which the wicked servant had secretly thought he could take without his master seeing him (2 Kings 5), how much more will the saints in that spiritual body see all things, not only if they close their eyes, but even from places where they are bodily absent?

“Then that perfection will exist of which the Apostle speaks: ‘For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when perfection comes, what is in part will be abolished’ (1 Cor. 13:9). Then, to show by some likeness how far this present life is from the life that is to come—not merely the life of ordinary people, but even of those endowed here with outstanding holiness—he says: ‘When I was a child, I thought as a child, I spoke as a child, I reasoned as a child. When I became a man, I put away childish things. Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known’ (1 Cor. 13:11).

“If, therefore, in this life—where the prophecy of remarkable human beings is related to that life as childhood is to youth—Elisha nevertheless saw his servant receiving gifts where he himself was not present, when perfection comes, and the corruptible body no longer weighs down the soul, but the incorruptible body hinders nothing, will those saints need bodily eyes in order to see what Elisha, while absent, did not need bodily eyes to see in his servant?

“For according to the interpreters of the Seventy, the prophet’s words to Gehazi are these: ‘Was not my heart with you when the man turned from his chariot to meet you, and you received money?’ etc. But according to the translation from the Hebrew by the presbyter Jerome: ‘Was not my heart,’ he says, ‘present when the man turned back from his course to meet you?’ (2 Kings 5:26).

“Thus the prophet said that he had seen this with his heart, aided, without doubt, wondrously by divine power. But how much more will all then abound in this gift, when God will be all in all?

“Nevertheless, those bodily eyes will also have their proper function and will occupy their proper place, and the spirit will use them through the spiritual body. For neither did that prophet, because he did not need them in order to see someone absent, fail to use them to see things present—things which the spirit could nevertheless see even if he closed them, just as it saw absent things where the prophet himself was not present with his eyes.

“Therefore, far be it from us to say that the saints in that life will not see God with closed eyes, whom they will always see in spirit. But whether they will also see him through the eyes of the body when they keep those eyes open—that is the question.

“For if the eyes in the spiritual body will have only as much power as these eyes of ours now possess, then certainly God cannot be seen through them. They will therefore have a power of an altogether different kind, if through them that incorporeal nature will be seen which is not contained in any place but is wholly everywhere.

“For when we say that God is in heaven and on earth—for he himself says through the prophet, ‘I fill heaven and earth’ (Jer. 23:24)—we are not saying that he has one part in heaven and another on earth. He is wholly in heaven and wholly on earth, not at different times, but in both places simultaneously; something no bodily nature can do.

“The power of those eyes will therefore be exceedingly great—not so that they see more sharply than certain creatures, such as serpents and eagles, are said to see, for however great the keenness with which such animals see, they can see nothing but bodies—but so that they may see incorporeal things as well.

“And perhaps this great power of sight was granted for a time even in this mortal body to the eyes of the holy man Job, when he said to God: ‘I heard you before by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. Therefore I despise myself, and I waste away, and I regard myself as earth and ashes’ (Job 42:5).

“Although nothing prevents this from being understood as the eye of the heart, concerning which the Apostle says: ‘Having the eyes of your heart enlightened’ (Eph. 1:18). No Christian doubts that God is seen by these eyes when he faithfully accepts what that divine Teacher says: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matt. 5:8).

“But whether he will also be seen there by bodily eyes is what we are examining in this question.

“For what is written, ‘All flesh shall see the salvation of God’ (Luke 3:6), can without any difficulty be understood as though it had been said: ‘Every human being shall see Christ, the salvation of God’—Christ who was certainly seen in the body and will be seen in the body when he judges the living and the dead.

“That he is himself the salvation of God is also made clear by many other testimonies of Scripture, but most evidently by the words of that venerable old man Simeon. When he had received the infant Christ into his hands, he said: ‘Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace. For my eyes have seen your salvation’ (Luke 2:29–30).

“Likewise, what the aforementioned Job says, as it is found in the copies that are in Hebrew, ‘And in my flesh I shall see God’ (Job 19:26), undoubtedly prophesied the resurrection of the flesh; yet he did not say, ‘Through my flesh.’ If he had said that, Christ God could be understood, who will be seen through the flesh and in the flesh.

“But as it stands, it can also be understood in this way: ‘In my flesh I shall see God,’ as though he had said, ‘In my flesh I shall be when I see God.’

“Nor does what the Apostle says, ‘Face to face’ (1 Cor. 13:11), compel us to believe that we shall see God through this bodily face where the bodily eyes are, since we shall see him without interruption in spirit. For unless there were also a face of the inner person, the same Apostle would not say: ‘But we, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord’ (2 Cor. 3:18).

“Nor do we understand otherwise what is sung in the Psalm: ‘Draw near to him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed’ (Ps. 34:5). For one draws near to God by faith, which plainly belongs to the heart, not to the body.

“But since we do not know how many powers of access the spiritual body will possess—for we are speaking of a matter that we have not experienced, in which the authority of the divine Scriptures provides no passage that cannot be understood in some other way—we must experience in ourselves what is written in the Book of Wisdom: ‘The thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our plans are uncertain’ (Wis. 9:14).

“For if the reasoning of the philosophers were certain, by which they argue that intelligible things are seen by the mind’s vision and sensible things—that is, bodily things—by bodily sensation, so that the mind cannot behold intelligible things through the body, nor bodily things by themselves, then it would certainly follow that God could in no way be seen through bodily eyes, even spiritual ones.

“But true reason and prophetic authority alike mock this reasoning. For who is so alienated from truth as to dare to say that God does not know these bodily things? Does he therefore have a body through whose eyes he can learn them?

“Moreover, what we said shortly before about the prophet Elisha sufficiently indicates that bodily things can be seen by the spirit, not through the body. When that servant received the gifts, the event certainly took place bodily; yet the prophet saw it not through the body but through the spirit.

“Therefore, just as it is established that bodies are seen by the spirit, what if the power of the spiritual body will be so great that spirit too may be seen through the body? For God is spirit.

“Furthermore, each person knows his own life—by which he now lives in the body and animates these earthly limbs, making them living—not through bodily eyes but by an inner sense. Yet he sees the lives of others, although they are invisible, through the body.

“For how do we distinguish living bodies from those that are not living unless we see both the bodies and the lives together—lives which we cannot see except through bodies? We do not see lives without bodies with bodily eyes.

“Therefore it can happen, and it is highly credible, that we shall then see the bodies of the new heaven and the new earth in such a way that, through the bodies we shall bear and through which we shall look in every direction, we shall see with the clearest vision God present everywhere and governing all bodily things as well.

“Not as now, when the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made, as through a mirror in an enigma and in part, where the faith by which we believe has greater force in us than the appearance of bodily things that we see with bodily eyes; but as, among human beings with whom we live and who move and exercise vital functions, as soon as we look at them we do not believe that they live but see that they live. We cannot see their life apart from their bodies, yet through their bodies we plainly perceive it without any ambiguity.

“In the same way, wherever we direct those spiritual lights of our bodies, we shall behold the incorporeal God who governs all things, even through bodies.

“Either God will therefore be seen through those eyes in such a way that, in their great excellence, they will possess something like the mind, by which an incorporeal nature may also be perceived—a claim that is difficult or impossible to demonstrate by any examples without the testimonies of the divine Scriptures—or, what is easier to understand, God will be known and visible to us in such a way that he will be seen in spirit by each of us and within each of us; he will be seen by one person in another, seen in himself, seen in the new heaven and new earth and in every creature that will then exist; and he will be seen through bodies in every body wherever the gaze of the spiritual body’s eyes is directed.

“Our thoughts will also be open to one another. Then will be fulfilled what the Apostle said after declaring, ‘Do not judge anything before the time’: ‘until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the thoughts of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God’ (1 Cor. 4:5).”

We have thought the authority of so great and such a man sufficient for this chapter, taking care to avoid the length of an epistolary memorandum. Since we feared that your mind, occupied with many matters, might be wearied by the material of our answers, we have tried to balance our course between the two, so that the truth concerning the questions might be evident without the length becoming burdensome to a preoccupied mind.

We have not wished at this time to touch upon other works of this man, and the subject already introduced has prevented us from setting forth the brief works of other teachers. We preferred to stimulate the appetite of one desiring spiritual food rather than produce weariness through excess on our part.

There are therefore very many teachings on these matters in the holy books, which may both exercise the seeker and refresh the finder at a generous banquet. We have thus sampled these few things, as has been said, in order to encourage a mind eager to learn toward greater things.

## What Follows

What follows was appended to the preceding material in an old manuscript.

## That the Soul Is in the Body

Augustine, in Sermon 8 on the Gospel of John:

“Is it not this—the soul, and not the body, that acts, that is, the inhabitant of the body? Yet it does not see with the eyes, and from the things it does it arouses wonder. Consider how much it does through the body: when it is withdrawn from the body, the corpse lies there.”

[Col. 0948B] Likewise, in Sermon 18:

“There is the image of God; Christ dwells in the inner person; in the inner person you are renewed according to the image of God. In his image recognize its author. See how all the bodily senses report to the heart what they have sensed outside. See how many ministers one inner emperor possesses. The eyes report to the heart white and black and the other things that follow there.”

In Sermon 19:

“It is therefore itself, even if it is foolish, unjust, and impious, the life of the body. But since God is its life, how, when it is in the body, does he provide it with vigor?” And so forth.

In Sermon 29:

“There is an inner person, and there is also an outer person. The inner person is invisible, whereas the outer person is visible; but the inner is better than the outer.”

In Sermon 43:

“What is this death? The abandonment of the body, the laying down of a heavy burden—but only if another burden is not taken up, by which a person may be hurled into Gehenna.”

Likewise there:

“The body is present, but there is no sensation; the dwelling lies there, but the inhabitant has departed.”

Likewise there:

“When they were taking up stones to throw at him, what great thing would it have been if the earth had immediately opened and swallowed them, and instead of stones they had found the underworld?”

In Sermon 44:

“That rich man was burning in that night and was asking for a drop of water from the poor man’s finger. He suffered, he was tormented, he confessed, and no help was given him; and he attempted to do something good, saying: ‘Let him tell them, lest they too come into this place of torment’ (Luke 16:28).”

In Sermon 47:

“To die to your flesh is to lose your life; to die to your soul is to lose its life. The life of your flesh is your soul; the life of your soul is your God. As the flesh dies when it loses the soul, which is its life, so the soul dies when it loses God, who is its life.

“Surely, then, the soul is immortal? Certainly immortal, because it lives and is dead. For what the Apostle said about the pleasure-loving widow can also be said of the soul if it has lost its God: ‘While living, she is dead’ (1 Tim. 5:6).”

Likewise, after other material:

“He died for us on the cross; without doubt his flesh breathed out his soul. For a brief time the soul abandoned the flesh, with the soul about to return in the resurrection.”

And a little later:

“All human beings, when they die, lay down the soul, but not all lay it down in Christ, and no one has the power to take up what he has laid down. Christ, however, laid it down for us; he laid it down when he wished, and he took it up when he wished. To lay down the soul, therefore, is to die. The flesh lays down its soul by breathing it out.”

And shortly afterward:

“What does it mean, ‘The flesh handed him over’? The flesh sent him forth; the flesh breathed him out. For *exspirare* means to be made outside the spirit. Just as *exsultare* means to be made outside the ground, and *exorbitare* to be made outside the orbit, so *exspirare* means to be made outside the spirit, which is the soul. Therefore, when the soul leaves the flesh and the flesh remains without the soul, a person is said to lay down his soul.”

And after some further material:

“Ask where the Apostle Paul is now. If someone answers, ‘At rest with Christ,’ he speaks the truth. If someone else answers, ‘In Rome in the tomb,’ he too speaks the truth. The former answered me concerning his soul; the latter concerning his flesh. Yet for that reason we do not say that there are two apostles Paul, one resting in Christ and the other placed in the tomb.”

And shortly afterward:

“From the time when the partnership of flesh and soul received the name ‘human being,’ each of them individually and separately has also retained the name ‘human being.’”

In Sermon 48:

“We entered by believing; we shall depart by dying. But just as we entered through the door of faith, so let us, as believers, depart from the body.”

In Sermon 49:

“Every dead person sleeps, both good and wicked. But just as, among those who sleep and rise each day, it matters what each person sees in dreams—for some experience everything joyful, while others experience torment, so that on waking they fear to sleep lest they return to the same things—so each human being sleeps with his own cause and rises with his own cause. It matters into what sort of custody each person is received, to be brought afterward before the judge.

“For custodial receptions are also assigned according to the merits of the cases. Some are ordered to be guarded by lictors, in a humane, mild, and civil service; others are handed over to officers; others are sent to prison; and even in prison not all are thrust into its lowest depths, but only according to the merits of the more serious cases.

“Therefore, just as there are different custodial arrangements for those carrying out official duties, so there are different custodial arrangements for the dead and different merits among those who will rise.

“The poor man was received, and the rich man was received: the one in Abraham’s bosom, the other where he thirsted and could find no drop of water (Luke 16).

“All souls, then—to instruct your charity by this occasion—when they depart from the world have their various places of reception. The good have joy, the wicked torments. But when the resurrection has taken place, the joy of the good will be greater and the torments of the wicked more severe, when they are tormented together with the body.

“The holy patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and faithful believers have been received into peace; yet all will receive at the end what God promised. The resurrection of the flesh, the destruction of death, and eternal life with the angels have also been promised. We shall all receive these things together.

“For each person receives the rest that is granted immediately after death, if he is worthy of it, at the time when he dies. The patriarchs received it first—consider how long ago they have been at rest; afterward the prophets; more recently the apostles; much more recently the holy martyrs; and every day the faithful. Some have already been in this rest for a long time, others not so long, others for fewer years, and others only recently.

“But when they awaken from this sleep, they will all receive together what has been promised.”

In Sermon 57:

“But concerning those who have already departed from the body and have been stripped of the garment of flesh—for they have not been separated from it forever—the Church replies: ‘I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again?’ (Song 5:3). That tunic will indeed be received again, and the Church will once more be clothed in flesh in those who have already been stripped of it.”

[Col. 0949D] In Sermon 65:

“For if death occurs when the soul leaves the body, how is it not death when our love leaves the world? ‘Love is strong as death’ (Song 8:6).”

In Sermon 119:

“He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 19:17). Who, then, puts off his garment whenever he wishes, just as he stripped himself of flesh when he wished?”

Augustine, in the fourth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter 13:

“The devil does not know how the supreme wisdom of God, while he plots and rages, uses him for the salvation of his faithful—from the higher end, which is the beginning of spiritual creation, all the way to the lower end, which is the death of the body—extending powerfully and ordering all things sweetly.

“For through his purity he reaches everywhere, and nothing unclean enters into him. But from the death of the flesh, from which the devil is alien—for this is the source of his excessive pride—a death of another kind is prepared in the eternal fire of Tartarus, in which spirits may be tormented not only with earthly bodies but also with aerial bodies.”

The same, in *On True Religion*, chapter 28:

“What, then, remains by which the soul could not remember the first beauty that it abandoned, when it can remember even its own vices? For the wisdom of God ‘reaches powerfully from end to end’ (Wis. 8:1).

“Thus, through it, that supreme craftsman joined together his works, ordered toward one end of beauty. Thus that goodness, from the highest to the lowest, envied no beauty that could exist from him alone, so that no one is cast down from truth without being received by some likeness of truth.

“Therefore, when you ask what holds the soul in bodily pleasure, you will find nothing other than harmony. For if resistance produces pain, harmony produces pleasure.

“Recognize, then, what supreme harmony is. Do not go outside yourself; return into yourself. In the inner person truth dwells.”

The same, in the same work, chapter 51:

“If the wonders of spectacles and beauty delight us, let us desire to see that wisdom which ‘reaches powerfully from end to end and orders all things sweetly’ (Wis. 8:1). For what is more marvelous than an incorporeal power making and governing a bodily world, or what is more beautiful than its ordering and adorning it?”

The same, in *On the Quantity of the Soul*, chapter 30:

“That which the eye cannot undergo unless the soul is present—that is, what it undergoes by seeing—suffers only where it is not. From this, who could fail to see that the soul is contained in no place?”

The same, in the same work, chapter 31:

“Why, then, when so many arguments have been brought forward above and firmly confirmed by you, has it not become clear to you that the soul is not contained in a place and therefore has none of the kind of quantity that we perceive in bodies?”

The same, in the same work, chapter 34:

“The nature of the soul is neither earth, nor seas, nor stars, nor moon, nor sun, nor anything at all that can be touched or seen with the eyes.”

Augustine, in the thirteenth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter 12:

“This manner in which the human being was handed over to the power of the devil should not be understood as though God did this or commanded it to be done, but as though he merely permitted it, though justly.

“For when he abandoned the sinner, the author of sin immediately invaded him. Yet God did not abandon his creature in such a way that he ceased to show himself to it as the God who creates and gives life, and who even amid punitive evils grants many good things to the wicked.

“For he did not restrain his mercies in his anger, nor did he lose the human being from the law of his power when he permitted him to be in the devil’s power.”

The same, in book 1, chapter 3:

“I believe that some slower readers will suppose in certain passages of my books that I thought what I did not think, or did not think what I did think. Who does not know that their error ought not to be attributed to me if, following me as though they understood me but failing to grasp my meaning, they have strayed into some falsehood while I am forced to make my way through certain dense and obscure places?

“For no one would rightly attribute to the sacred authorities of the divine books the many and various errors of heretics, although all heretics attempt to defend their false and deceptive opinions from those same Scriptures.”

The same, in the same work, chapter 10:

“So that, insofar as he is God, he may subject us to him, and insofar as he is priest, he may be subject to him with us.

“Therefore, since the Son is both God and human being, with one substance as God and another as human being, the human being is rather in the Son than the Son in the Father—just as my flesh is a substance different from my soul, although both are in one human being, whereas another human being’s soul is different from my soul.”

Likewise, the same, in the same work, chapter 12:

“The Son often says, ‘The Father gave to me.’ By this he wishes it to be understood that the Father begot him—not as though he gave something to one who already existed but did not possess it, but that he gave it so that he might have it; to beget him was to make him exist.

“For the Son of God is not like a creature. Before the incarnation and before the assumption of the creature, the Only-begotten through whom all things were made is not one thing and the possessor of another thing; rather, he himself is what he is, and is himself what he possesses.”

The same, in book 3 (*On the Trinity*, chapter 1):

“We must now consider whether the angels were then acting, producing those appearances of bodies visible to human eyes and those sounds audible to human ears, when the sensible creature itself, serving at the Creator’s command, was changed for the occasion into whatever the situation required.

“As it is said in the Book of Wisdom: ‘For creation, serving you its Maker, is stretched out for punishment against the unjust, and becomes gentler in doing good to those who trust in you. Therefore, at that time also, transforming itself into all things, it served your grace, the nourisher of all, according to the will of those who desired you’ (Wis. 16:24–25).

“For the power of God’s will reaches through spiritual creation to the visible and sensible effects of bodily creation. Where does the wisdom of almighty God not work, since it ‘reaches powerfully from end to end’?” And so forth.

## In Leviticus, chapter 3

“The soul that swears and utters with its lips an oath either to do something evil or to do something good, and confirms the matter by oath and speech, but afterward, having forgotten it, recognizes its guilt, shall do penance for its sin and offer a ewe-lamb from the flocks or a she-goat; and the priest shall pray for it and for its sin” (Lev. 5:4–6).

In the same, chapter 4:

“The soul that sins and, having despised the Lord, denies to its neighbor a deposit entrusted to its keeping, or forcibly extorts something, or brings a false accusation; or finds something lost and, moreover, denies it under oath, or does any other of the many things by which human beings commonly sin—when convicted of the offense, it shall restore intact everything it sought to obtain through fraud, and shall also give a fifth part to the owner whom it injured.

“For its sin it shall offer an unblemished ram from the flock and give it to the priest according to the valuation and measure of the offense. He shall pray for him before the Lord, and it shall be forgiven him for each of the things he sinned in doing” (Lev. 6:2–7).

In the same, chapter 36:

“You shall not steal. You shall not lie, nor shall anyone deceive his neighbor. You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of your God: I am the Lord” (Lev. 19:11–12).

In Deuteronomy, chapter 3:

“You shall not use the name of your Lord in vain, for whoever takes up his name over a vain matter shall not go unpunished” (Deut. 5:11).

In the second book of Kings, chapter 21:

“There was also a famine in the days of David for three consecutive years. David consulted the oracle of the Lord, and the Lord said: ‘It is because of Saul and his house, and because he killed the Gibeonites.’

“So the Gibeonites were summoned, and the king said to them—for the Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel but remnants of the Amorites; the children of Israel had sworn an oath to them, and Saul sought to strike them in his zeal, as though for the children of Israel and Judah—David said to the Gibeonites: ‘What shall I do for you, and what shall be your atonement, so that you may bless the inheritance of the Lord?’

“The Gibeonites said to him: ‘We have no dispute concerning silver or gold, but against Saul and against his house; nor do we wish that any man of Israel be killed.’

“The king said to them: ‘What, then, do you wish me to do for you?’

“They said to the king: ‘We must destroy the man who crushed and unjustly oppressed us in such a way that not even one of his descendants remains within all the borders of Israel. Let seven men of his sons be given to us, so that we may crucify them at Gibeah of Saul, once the Lord’s chosen one.’

“The king said: ‘I will give them.’

“But the king spared Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, son of Saul, because of the oath of the Lord that had been between David and Jonathan, son of Saul” (2 Sam. 21:1–7).

At the end of this statement it is said:

“And after these things the Lord was appeased toward the land” (2 Sam. 21:14).

Solomon, in Proverbs:

“Lest, driven by poverty, I go mad and forswear the name of my God” (Prov. 30:9).

## Jerome on the Prophet Jeremiah, Book 1

“‘And you shall swear: “The Lord lives,” in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness; and the nations shall bless him and praise him’ (Jer. 4:2). How, then, does the Gospel prohibit us from swearing?

“Here, however, ‘you shall swear’ is understood as a confession and as a condemnation of the idols by which Israel used to swear. Thus the stumbling blocks are removed, and he swears by the Lord.

“Furthermore, when it says ‘the Lord lives,’ in the Old Testament this is an oath for the condemnation of the dead, by whom all idolatry swears. At the same time, it must be noted that an oath has these companions: truth, judgment, and righteousness. If these are absent, it will not be an oath but perjury.”

Book 2:

“‘Behold, you trust in yourselves upon lying words that will not profit you: stealing, killing, committing adultery, swearing falsely’ (Jer. 7:8). The sins that follow show how useless it is for them to place their confidence in the temple.

“For what benefit is there in entering boldly across the threshold of God’s house, standing with raised neck, and having not only the heart but also the hands polluted by theft, murder, adultery, perjury, and sacrilege?”

Jerome on Ezekiel, volume 1, book 5:

“‘Will he prosper or obtain salvation who has done these things? And shall he escape who has broken the covenant? As I live,’ says the Lord God, ‘surely in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he annulled and whose covenant with him he broke, in the midst of Babylon he shall die’ (Ezek. 17:16).

“‘He who has broken the covenant,’ he says, ‘shall he escape?’ From this we learn that faith must be kept even among enemies, and that one must consider not for whom but through whom one has sworn.

“For much more faithful was the one who, because of the name of God, trusted you and was deceived than you, who under cover of the divine majesty plotted against your enemy—indeed, against one who had already become your friend.

“‘Behold,’ he says, ‘he gave his hand to the king of Egypt, and surrendered himself, and committed sacrilege by perjury against God. Will it profit him? And after doing all these things, shall he escape?’

“It is a secular maxim:

> ‘Fraud or valor—which would one seek in an enemy?’

“This is commonly brought against us by those who say that enemies should be deceived by fraud. Even if we grant the point, Zedekiah did something much worse. He did not deceive an enemy, but a friend to whom he had been bound by the covenant of the Lord.

“Therefore, as long as you have not sworn and entered into a covenant under the name of God, it is a matter of prudence and courage either to deceive or to overcome your opponent by whatever means you can. Once you have bound yourself by an oath, however, the person who trusted you is no longer an adversary but a friend, and he has been deceived under the pretext of the oath—that is, by the invocation of God.

“Therefore Scripture now says: ‘The oath that he despised and the covenant that he violated, I will place upon his head’ (Ezek. 17:19).

“And lest we think that the oath, covenant, and agreement belonged to the king of Babylon or to Zedekiah who had made it, it continues: ‘In the violation by which he despised me’ (ibid., 20). Therefore, whoever despises an oath despises him.”

## IV. On Restraining the Plunderings of Soldiers

To King Charles the Bald, when he was preparing for war in order to repel the attack of his brother Louis, in the year 859.

(From the same author, from the manuscript of Saint-Remi of Reims.)

To the glorious lord, health and life.

I know that you grieve over these evils, which occur in your kingdom not only at the hands of pagans but—what is more to be feared and lamented—at the hands of Christians; and what is incomparably more horrible, detestable, and reprehensible, they occur in your palace, which ought to be called and to be sacred, and in the places where you are and through which you walk. For your heart cannot pass without dread over what the Lord says through Isaiah: “The plundering of the poor is in your house” (Isa. 3:14). And: “The widow’s case does not come before them” (Isa. 1:23). And: “From the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in it”—that is, in this kingdom (Isa. 1:6). And again: “Adultery, murder, and plundering have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:2), that is, crime has been joined to crime. And it is manifest that where such things exist, God can be present only for judgment.

He also says through the prophet to those who were in the midst of such things: “Therefore, come out from among them, and do not touch what is unclean; and I will receive you, and I will dwell among you, and I will be your God, and you shall be my sons and daughters” (2 Cor. 6:16–18). For these people do nothing other than serve as the forerunner of the army of Antichrist, whose voice says: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil” (Ps. 10:6)—that is, “I shall inflict such great evils in one place that, before I come to another place, those who live there will fear my coming, just as they will afterward experience it.”

Thus I know that you fear what the whole Church prays for on this account: “Arise, Lord God; let your hand be exalted” (ibid., 12)—that is, “Do not forget the poor people when vengeance is required.” And the Lord, who does not lie, promises, saying: “Because of the mercy shown to the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I shall arise, says the Lord” (Ps. 11:6)—that is, “Very soon I shall exercise vengeance.”

Knowing that such matters and similar ones distress you, I sympathize and groan together with your groans, along with my sins and the afflictions of the people entrusted to me, unworthy as I am. But I cannot find how to console myself—so deeply anxious for your danger, my own danger, and the destruction and affliction of the whole people—except that, since I cannot admonish you with my living voice, I may warn you by letter, terrified by the Shepherd of shepherds, who says: “The hireling, and he who is not the shepherd, sees the wolf coming, and abandons the sheep and flees” (John 10:12). He flees because he saw iniquity and kept silent: he saw robbers and plunderings, and the other miseries raging among the people entrusted to him, and he remained silent instead of admonishing them.

Therefore, Lord, I do what alone I can do in this matter: I ask God’s mercy concerning it, and I warn you about it; and through the estates where not only mounted men but even the horse-dealers themselves commit plunder, I send admonitions to the priests, so that they may read them to the plunderers. I am sending a copy of these admonitions to Your Lordship, so that you may keep it privately and command your faithful men to come on some day, saying that you wish to speak to them about whatever matter you choose. Before they return from your presence to their residences, admonish them according to the wisdom given you by God.

Have your uncle Rudolf, who fears God and hates evil and holds you and your kingdom dear, informed about this, so that he may assist you; and do the same with other such faithful men of yours, as you know. With gentleness interwoven—as the present time requires—use warnings rarely and not too harshly, if it seems appropriate to you, making no other threats except insofar as you will see in this who is faithful to God, who holds you dear, and who wishes you and your kingdom to prosper. You should endeavor that such a man deserve this [reward], if he proves your helper toward the common preservation, so that these evils may depart from this kingdom.

But whoever is not God’s helper in such matters, nor your friend and his, you will not be able to take pleasure in him, so as to do him the good you would do if you truly knew him to be your friend. Or do this in this way, or in another way that you know better than I can tell you. You know the qualities of your faithful men better than I do, and therefore, according to what you know suits each one, temper your speech.

For we know that a gentle whistle, which calms the ferocity of horses, stirs the sagacity of dogs. To such men—whom at present you do not need to keep with you, and who therefore move from their residences with almost their entire households in order to live off the labor of others—commend what you deem pleasing and necessary, and let them return to their homes, or remain with you with only a few companions, so that they may live justly. You should dwell in a more secure part of your kingdom until the full number of your faithful, at the place you have appointed, comes to you whenever you wish to go to some necessity.

But I greatly fear that such a people, who offend God in this way and do not correct themselves, will be able to help neither you nor themselves when necessity arises. Send men, according to the custom of your predecessors, who will travel farther afield concerning the fodrarii (royal provisioning exactions) and undertake responsibility for the peace. Send men who are not among those of whom the Apostle says: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. 2:21).

As I said, I am sending you a copy of our admonition, which I distributed through the estates, so that, if it pleases you, after your own admonition you may order it to be read to your faithful men in your presence. Preach to them that these are God’s words and that those who carry them are God’s messengers, and that they must not neglect these words either in themselves or in their own people.

Guard what I suggest and send you in such a way that they learn nothing about it except through you. For if they learn of it beforehand, it may happen that you will not have them fully under your authority. Nevertheless, you ought to take counsel about this and order someone to admonish them daily in your place. Thus, if there are men who did not previously hear this admonition, he may read it to them each day when they come into your presence, so that they may be without excuse and you may have some defense before God, if you do as much as you reasonably can.

Do not neglect those chapters which the synod of Quierzy sent through Wenilo and Erchanra to this Attigny last year for your brother Louis, and which, when I sent them, my son Hincmar gave you when he was with you in Burgundy. Read them carefully; for, believe me, they were made more for your sake than for his. I believed that God’s mercy ought to have recalled you, and that this admonition would be necessary and useful to you.

Moreover, Lord, three matters have come to me which I intended to conceal from you, lest your mind be disturbed still further by them among the other matters. But I reconsidered and thought it better to tell you about them, because you cannot correct what does not come to your knowledge. And however much divine judgment may be involved—for we have been punished for ignorance even in matters that were not insignificant—if you do not know what your subjects commit in a matter of general concern, you cannot escape judgment. Since I know what it is useful for you to know, if I do not bring it to your attention, I unquestionably incur danger.

Of the three things I heard, I did not want to believe two, while I believed the third only with great reluctance.

The first is that it is being spread by the mouths of many that you say you ought not to concern yourself with these plunderings and depredations, but that each person should defend what is his as best he can. Although I know this to be a lie, I did not want to conceal it from you, so that by your deeds you may demonstrate that what the malicious or the aggrieved spread by rumor is false.

Since the duty of a king is always to direct himself and those of his subjects who act well toward what is better, and to correct the wicked from their evil ways, it is impious to demand gifts and services from subjects throughout the kingdom subject to him, while failing to provide that they have the means to render what is owed and demanded of them; it is impious to command and arrange what pleases them while failing to prohibit and remove what displeases God.

I venture to suggest this to Your Lordship because, with the kingdom of your father and grandfather divided in many places, many of the principal estates of your kingdom are suffering loss. For the sake of the royal dignity that befits you, it is necessary that nothing be diminished from what your predecessors were accustomed to receive from those same places, while pagans and false Christians usurp the greater part of the portion of your kingdom that has been consumed.

And if the small portion in which your faithful men ought to live with you continues to be so destroyed, neither you nor they will be able to maintain yourselves there.

The second matter is that I was told that the complainants who come to your palace receive there no consolation, not even a kind reply. I likewise did not want to believe this, knowing that you retain in your heart what the Lord says: “He who closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard” (Prov. 21:13).

The Gospel shows when such petitioners will not be heard: “They will come saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us’; and he will answer and say, ‘Amen I say to you, I do not know you’” (Matt. 25:11). For God’s not knowing—God from whom nothing is hidden—is his rejection. The one who would not hear here what God commanded can no longer earn from God there what he asks; and the one who has wasted the appropriate time for repentance comes in vain with prayers before the gate of the kingdom.

The third is what I believed only with great reluctance: that, after receiving everything necessary for food and drink, plunderers either demand ransom from churches or violate them. Therefore, with a heavy groan, I ask what can become of Christians of this kind.

Paul brings forward as testimony what he considered among the gravest sins, and judged to be even graver, saying: “You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?” (Rom. 2:22). Yet these men heap sacrilege upon all their other offenses and do not abhor idols, because the same holy Paul says: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Eph. 5:5).

May almighty God, according to that same Apostle, grant you both the will and the accomplishment, in accordance with his good will, of what is necessary for you, for us, and for the kingdom entrusted to you.

[Col. 0957]

## V. ON THE WORDS OF THE PSALM: “THE HOUSE OF THE HERON IS THEIR GUIDE,” TO LOUIS, KING OF GERMANIA

*(In the same author, from the manuscript of Saint-Remi of Reims.)*

[Col. 0957A]

To the glorious King Louis, Hincmar, in name but not in merit bishop of Reims, servant of God’s people.

Recently, when you spoke at Tusiacum with my lord King Charles, your only brother, as you can well remember, you summoned the venerable Bishop Altfrid one day to my humble dwelling and, according to the wisdom God has given you, began to ask and carefully investigate certain hidden and more difficult statements of Sacred Scripture. As the Lord granted and the opportunity of time and place allowed, I undertook to answer you.

But your inquiry proceeded so far that we also discussed how, according to the truth of Scripture, all God’s works in Genesis are “very good” (Gen. 1), which the Apostle also confirms by saying: “All things are clean to the clean” (Tit. 1:15), and: “Nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4:4). Why, then, does the Law (Lev. 11) describe certain things as unclean and not to be eaten by God’s people?

When the question had been resolved according to Catholic tradition, you asked what was meant by what is sung in the Psalm: “The house of the heron is their guide” (Ps. 103:18).

Before I could answer, the venerable Bishop Altfrid—Saxon by origin and therefore, as it were, naturally readier in speech [the reading *suatim* is uncertain]—said that the translation of the Seventy Interpreters read: “The house of the coot is theirs.”

After him, when I began to answer that there are two kinds of herons, just as there are two kinds of pelicans—hence in Psalm 101 the verse is sung with an added qualification, “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness” (Ps. 101:7), since there is also another kind, namely the river pelican—my lord King Charles, your only brother, arrived. When he reminded you that you had come to announce something to your faithful men, you proceeded with him. As we went, you were pleased to impose upon my service your good wishes, and I remember that I promised to commit to writing what I should then have answered about the matter and to send it to Your Lordship.

Since I previously lacked the opportunity to carry this out, I have now endeavored briefly to make known to your wisdom what I have learned from the tradition of great authorities on this subject and to discharge the debt of my promise.

Concerning the matter at hand, the Hebrew truth, as translated by blessed Jerome, reads as follows: “The trees of the field will be satisfied, the cedars of Lebanon which you planted; there the birds will nest; the kite—the fir tree is its house” (Ps. 103:16).

The translation of the Seventy Interpreters, which blessed Jerome corrected three times after many had corrupted it—first at Rome, secondly at Bethlehem for Paula and Eustochium at their request, and then in writing to Sunnias and Fretela, as is found in his letters, and which he himself expounded, and which the Jerusalem and Eastern Churches, as well as the Gauls today, use—reads as follows:

“The trees of the field will be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted; there the sparrows will nest; the heron is their guide.”

The common translation, also called the Vulgate, reads:

“All the trees of the field will be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon which you planted; there the sparrows will nest; the house of the coot is their guide.”

Concerning this translation, blessed Jerome says in the aforementioned letter to Sunnias and Fretela (Epistle 135):

“Briefly I admonish you, so that you may know that there is one edition which Origen, Eusebius of Caesarea, and all the Greek commentators call κοινή—that is, common and widespread—and which by many is now called the edition of Lucian; and another edition of the Seventy Interpreters, which is found in the Hexapla manuscripts, faithfully translated by us into Latin, and sung in Jerusalem and in the Churches of the East.”

The same man says again in the same letter:

“This κοινή, that is, common edition, is itself also the edition of the Seventy. But the difference between them is that the κοινή, according to places and times and the will of copyists, is an ancient corrupted edition; whereas the edition preserved in the Hexapla, which we translated, is the one that remains in the books of the learned as the uncorrupted and immaculate translation of the Seventy Interpreters. Whatever differs from it, therefore, unquestionably also disagrees with the authority of the Hebrews.”

Blessed Augustine expounded this common edition, which says, “The house of the coot is their guide,” and which at that time nearly all Latins used; after him did Prosper, and then Cassiodorus.

Concerning this bird blessed Augustine says:

“As we all know, the coot is a sea bird; it is found either in ponds or in the sea. It has a certain house, not easily—or rather never—on the shore of the land, but in places situated in the middle of the water, usually on rocks surrounded by water.”

Saint Prosper likewise says:

“The house of the coot, which is a sea bird, is not in holes in the earth nor in the branches of trees, but on a rock surrounded by water; and the rock is understood as Christ.”

Cassiodorus, drawing on blessed Augustine and Prosper, says in his exposition “On Meanings”:

“The coot is a gentle and black bird, smaller than a duck but similar in bodily form, which dwells with pleasure in ponds. It is rightly referred to those who are baptized, who persevere in the grace of the most sacred font. Their dwellings—that is, perseverance in baptism—are therefore the guide of the sparrows that nest in the cedars, since the sacred font of all Christians is their guide while it leads them to the kingdoms of heaven.”

Finally, in the books of the *Physica*, which discuss the natures of birds, animals, serpents, trees, and herbs, I read the following about this same bird:

“They say that the coot (*fulica*) was so called because its flesh tastes like hare. For *lagōos* means ‘hare’; hence among the Greeks it is called λαγωός (*lagōos*). It is a marsh bird, having its nest in the middle of the water or on rocks surrounded by water, and it always delights in the depths of the sea. When it senses a storm, it flees and plays in shallow water.”

In the same books I also read what I shall now add. From this, I think you too may infer that Symmachus translated *fulica* for *herodius*.

The same natural philosophers write that the Diomedean birds were named after the companions of Diomedes, whom fables say were transformed into these birds. They resemble coots in form, are as large as lambs, white in color, and have hard, large beaks. They fly around the shores and rocks near Apulia, on the island of Diomedia. They distinguish between their own people and strangers. If a man is Greek, they approach more closely and flatter him; if he is foreign, they attack and wound him with their bites, grieving in voices almost like weeping, either over their own transformation or over the death of their king. For Diomedes was killed by the Illyrians.

These birds are called *Diomedeae* in Latin; the Greeks call them *herodioi*. Hence blessed Jerome says in the aforementioned letter to Sunnias and Fretela:

“For *herodius*, which in Hebrew is called *asida*, Symmachus translated ἰκτίνος (*iktinos*), that is, ‘kite.’ Accordingly, we too translated it into Latin in this way: ‘There the birds will nest; the kite—the fir tree is its house,’ since it is accustomed always to make its nests in lofty and steep trees. Hence the sixth edition translated it more clearly: ‘The cypress is for the kite as a place for nesting.’ Instead of fir trees and cypresses, however, the Hebrew has *barusim*, which signifies fir trees more than cypresses.”

And because, as I told you then, there are two kinds of herons, blessed Jerome and Saint Gregory demonstrate this.

One is the larger kind, which I have now shown from the words of the natural philosophers, and of which blessed Jerome says in his exposition of this verse:

“There the sparrows will nest; the wise will build [for] the heron [the wording is materially awkward as printed]—that is, ‘the house of the heron is their guide.’ For it is the largest of all flying creatures, and it defeats and eats the eagle.”

The other is the smaller kind, concerning which it is written in the book of Job: “The feather of the ostrich is like the feathers of the heron and the hawk” (Job 39:13).

Hence blessed Gregory says (*Moralia*, Book 31, chapter 5):

“Who does not know how greatly the heron and the hawk surpass the other birds in the speed of their flight? The ostrich, however, has feathers resembling theirs, but it does not possess the speed of their flight. It cannot rise from the earth; it raises its wings as though for flight, in outward appearance only, yet it never lifts itself from the earth by flying.”

And again:

“The bodies of the hawk and the heron are small, but they are supported by denser feathers; and therefore they fly across the air swiftly, because there is little in them that weighs them down and much that lifts them. The ostrich, by contrast, is clothed in sparse feathers and burdened by an enormous body, so that even if it wishes to fly, the very scantiness of its feathers cannot suspend in the air the mass of so great a body. The feather of the ostrich itself also resembles the feathers of the heron and the hawk in color, but not in power. Their feathers are compact and stronger, and by the force of their solidity they can press against the air in flight; whereas the feathers of the ostrich are loose and cannot take flight, and so they are surpassed by the very air which they ought to have pressed down.”

Thus, according to the literal sense, I have endeavored, at your command, to write to Your Lordship about the coot and the kinds of herons, drawing on the writings of the great authorities.

Since you neither commanded nor need me to write more fully about the typical or moral interpretation which Catholic teachers have drawn from this passage—for the Lord teaches him who teaches human knowledge, and from whose presence come wisdom and understanding—I have not presumed to do so, lest that poetic saying be applied to me:

“Do not, traveler, perhaps carry wood into the forest.”

But lest I should seem to have entirely passed over the mystical sense, I have judged it better to indicate certain things than to expound them.

“The trees,” says the Psalm, “will be satisfied”—that is, the peoples of the nations—with spiritual grace; and “the cedars of Lebanon”—that is, the noble and exalted of the world—whom the Lord planted (Ps. 103:17). From the wealthy and illustrious also he justified many who say: “He made us, and not we ourselves,” because, just as he made us human and illustrious, so likewise he made us just.

“There the sparrows will nest”—that is, in these cedars of Lebanon, which God’s grace plants and satisfies. The sparrows will nest there: those, namely, who have chosen humility and, having abandoned or sold what they possessed, have reserved nothing for themselves in this age. They are supported by necessary assistance received from the homes and estates of wealthy Christians.

Although they rest in the height of the cedars, they do not use the cedars themselves as their guides; rather, the house of the heron is their guide. For the heron of the larger kind, as we said in Jerome’s words, is the largest of all flying creatures. It defeats and eats the eagle, which is king among flying creatures just as the lion is among beasts.

Often in Scripture the devil is signified by the eagle. According to evangelical truth, the strong man armed who guards his courtyard and possesses his goods in peace—that is, the strong devil, who held the world, which lies in wickedness, under his ill-omened peaceful rule until the Savior’s coming—was defeated by Christ when one stronger came upon him. Christ took away all his armor in which he trusted and distributed his spoils, which are the insignia of the triumphant, because he destroyed his cunning and, leading captive the captivity of those deceived by him and saved by Christ, distributed gifts (Luke 11)—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the Apostle enumerates, he granted according to each person’s capacity.

The house of this heron—that is, the rulers of the Church, since Paul says that we are a house—is known to be the guide of the sparrows, namely those who despise the world, understand the needy and the poor, and are sustained by support.

Nor is this interpretation inconsistent with the lesser kind of heron when it is said: “The house of the heron is their guide.” For, according to the Apostle, Christ, although he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might be enriched (2 Cor. 8:9). And the prophet says of him: “We saw him, and he had no appearance,” and so forth, “until we did not esteem him” (Isa. 53:3). He left us an example so that we might follow in his footsteps.

The house of this heron is the guide of the sparrows—that is, of those who despise the world. For often even among secular men, in whose hearts Christ dwells through faith and in whose works his examples shine, not only ecclesiastics or monks, nor merely prelates among their subjects or men exalted by royal power in private life, may find something to imitate; they may also find something by which to correct and humble themselves. For sometimes those who are lesser in merit are greater in name, and are more praiseworthy for holiness than for fruitless honor.

Hence the prophet says: “Be ashamed, Sidon.” For the sea says, “The strength of the sea says this” (Isa. 23:4). By Sidon are understood those who are fortified and adorned, as though by a certain strength, in the name of religion; by the sea are understood secular men.
