As the true heron, through the speed of its flight and the greatness of its virtue, restrains and crushes birds as though it were catching the birds that eat the seed beside the road—that is, demons who take the word from the hearts of those who hear it, lest they believe and be saved—so does it restrain them from being able to tempt human beings so greatly.

As he teaches: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). Such people are small in their own estimation and in the praise of others. And although, weighed down by the care of their households and by earthly frailty, they cannot remain in this life without some contamination of sin, nevertheless, when they possess something that depresses them, they also possess much virtue of good action that can lift them toward heaven.

Therefore, with the greatest fear and trembling, and with the utmost continual concern, we must consider and fear that we who are seen to have received more than others in this world may on that account be judged more severely by the author of the world. For when gifts increase, the accounts demanded for those gifts also increase. Therefore, the more each person recognizes that he is bound to render an account, the more humble and ready to serve he ought to be because of the gift he has received. He knows that “to whom more has been entrusted, more will be required from him,” and according to the saying of Scripture: “The mighty will be mightily tested; mercy will be granted to the lowly” (Wis. 6:7).

Receive these things in abbreviated form. But if you command me, I shall gladly endeavor, as far as he himself grants—the one who promises the faithful servant, “Open your mouth, and I shall fill it” (Ps. 80:11)—to discuss and explain to you, by word and letter, this and other statements of Sacred Scripture, both for the ministry imposed upon me and out of the obedience owed to you. For apostolic authority commends that we obey in Christ and be subject to the king. Scripture says to you: “Ask the priests about my law” (Hag. 2:12); and to us: “Hearing a word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me” (Ezek. 33:7). I shall do this insofar as it may contribute to the salvation and instruction of your learning.

May Christ, king of this kingdom and of the eternal kingdom, grant you happy times,

Dear to me as you are.

May wisdom flourish with you through eternal gifts,

So that praise, honor, and salvation may remain with you.

May the right hand of Christ always defend you everywhere.

Live happily for God, and farewell without end.

[Col. 0961]

## VI. TO THE BISHOPS AND NOBLES OF THE PROVINCE OF REIMS, ON KEEPING FAITH WITH KING CHARLES, WHEN LOUIS AGAIN SOUGHT THE KINGDOM OF HIS BROTHER CHARLES IN HIS ABSENCE, IN THE YEAR 875

*(In the same author, from the Mainz edition of J. Busaeus.)*

[Col. 0961C] Hincmar, bishop and servant of God’s people, to his beloved brothers, the venerable bishops of the diocese of Reims.

### Chapter I

Concerning our common anxiety, about which your charity consulted my humility, putting before me the words of the holy Pope Boniface, in which, expounding to Hilary, archbishop of Narbonne, the canon of the Council of Nicaea concerning the privileges of the individual provinces, he says: “Let your charity observe that we so preserve the precepts of the canons that our own ordinance likewise determines that every province shall in all matters always await the direction of its own metropolitan.” By the Lord’s gift, I reply in writing to your charity what I understand from the teaching of our Fathers.

Saint Ambrose says among other things in his letter to the Emperor Theodosius (Epistle 29): “It is not imperial to deny freedom of speech, nor priestly not to say what you think. For nothing in you emperors is so popular and so lovable as to cherish freedom even in those who are subject to you by the obedience of service. Indeed, this is the difference between good and bad rulers: the good love freedom, the wicked slavery. Nor is anything in a priest so dangerous before God, so shameful before men, as not freely to declare what he thinks. For it is written: ‘I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and was not ashamed’ (Ps. 118:46). And elsewhere: ‘Son of man, I have set you as a watchman over the house of Israel’ (Ezek. 3:17). In this respect,” he says, “if the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits an offense because you did not distinguish it for him—that is, did not tell him what he must beware of—the memory of his righteousness shall not be retained, and I shall require his blood from your hand. But if you tell the righteous man not to sin, and he does not sin, the righteous man shall live because you told him, and you shall deliver your own soul.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man shall be ashamed when he comes in his own majesty, and that of his Father and of the holy angels” (Luke 9:26).

### Chapter II

Therefore let us, priests of the Lord, speak freely of the notable and blameworthy things said about our king, and of the praiseworthy promises said of his brother, Lord King Louis, who is asserted to be coming into the kingdom of his brother so that he may correct what his brother has wrongly done there, and by diligence endeavor to amend what his brother has allowed through negligence. Thus, if our king reads what is said of him, let him correct it if it is true; but if it is not true, let him beware henceforth of allowing it. And if his brother, Lord Louis, reads what is said of his brother as notable, let him beware of it, and let him strive to carry out the praiseworthy things promised of himself. But let us bishops and chief men of the kingdom, according to our ranks, discern from the teaching and examples of our elders what we ought to follow and what we ought to avoid.

### Chapter III

Passing over the other reversals in the disputes over the kingdom which took place among our princes in our time: sixteen years ago, when our lord King Charles and Lord Louis met near the place called Breona, with bodies of armed men prepared on both sides and standards raised, the greater part of the people who were with Lord Charles deserted him, and so compelled King Charles himself to depart thence on the day before the Ides of November. But in the third month, when Charles returned, those who were with Lord Louis separated from him and, leaving him almost alone, compelled him by their desertion to return from the district of Laon to his own lands, while Charles pursued him.

Now, however, because Lord Charles has voluntarily left us and this kingdom and gone to Italy, our lord Louis is declared, by many voices, to be coming hostilely to seize this kingdom. And Lord Charles is said to have bodies of warriors, which in the common speech we call *scarae*, deployed, and chiefs assigned to these bodies to resist his brother, lest he be able to occupy his kingdom. By his wife’s command, together with his son Louis, they are to defend his kingdom against all enemies, both Christian and pagan, with the counsel and help of the bishops and his other counselors, until he returns in peace, with the Lord’s help, having obtained the kingdom which he went to acquire.

### Chapter IV

For this reason we bishops must take sufficient care that, in the counsel which the ministers of the commonwealth may seek from us according to our lord king’s command, we do not fall away from our ministry; and that we do not withdraw from giving such assistance as God has granted each of us power to give, following the Lord’s saying: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21).

In giving assistance, therefore, let us provide spiritual weapons: fasts, prayers, tears, invocations of the aid of the saints, and divine help through ourselves and our parishes, so that Christian blood may not be shed in a seditious conflict among brothers, kinsmen, and relatives, as we lament has already happened at Fontenoy. And may the Lord, through the merits and intercessions of the saints, graciously grant peace in our days from all enemies, both Christian and pagan, so that, aided by his merciful help, we may always be free from sin and secure from every disturbance.

### Chapter V

For if war against pagans threatened, we would give counsel to our warriors and exhort them with the exhortations which we read in ecclesiastical writings. But now, because we think that a civil war, indeed a war worse than civil, threatens among Christians, let us, relying on the footsteps of the Fathers, see what we ought to do in these circumstances.

Saint Ambrose, recounting in a letter to his sister the history of his persecutions, says among other things (Epistle 33): “On the Lord’s day, after the readings and sermon, when the catechumens had been dismissed, I was delivering the creed to certain candidates for baptism in the baptisteries of the basilica. There it was announced to me that, when it had been learned that decurions had been sent from the palace to the Portian basilica to hang curtains, part of the people were going there. I nevertheless remained at my duty and began to celebrate Mass. While I was making the offering, I learned that a certain Castulus, whom the Arians called a presbyter, had been seized by the people. They had encountered him passing through the street. In the very offering I began to weep most bitterly and to pray to God that he might intervene, lest anyone’s blood be shed in the cause of the Church—or at least that my blood might be shed for the salvation not only of the people but also of the impious themselves. Why say more? By sending priests and deacons I rescued the man from violence.”

[Cols. 0964D–0965A]

## Chapter VI

We read that blessed Augustine thought the same concerning the Donatists, persecutors of the faithful. And Saint Gregory, in his homily on the Gospel (Homily 27 on the Gospels), says:

> “There is one and supreme proof of love: if the one who opposes us is also loved. Hence it is that Truth itself both endures the punishment of the cross and nevertheless bestows the affection of love upon its persecutors, saying: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23:34). What wonder, then, if they love their enemies while they are alive, when the Teacher also loved his enemies as he was being killed?”

Likewise, we read in the account of his deeds that Stephen, pontiff of the Roman see, acted in this way when he came to Pippin in Francia to obtain the rights of Saint Peter against Haistulf, the most wicked king. For when the renowned King Pippin could obtain nothing from the aforementioned king concerning Saint Peter’s rights, either by prayers or by offering gifts, he moved an army against him. But the holy pope, lest Christian blood be shed, presented apostolic admonitions and entreaties, and prevailed with Lord Pippin.

But Haistulf, puffed up with pride against the Franks who had come to guard their own fortified places according to Pippin’s order, trusting in his own ferocity, suddenly opened the fortifications and at dawn fell upon them with very numerous armies. But the righteous Judge, the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, granted victory to those very few Franks; they defeated and slaughtered that multitude of Lombards, and Haistulf took flight and, having been overcome by Pippin, was defeated with God’s aid.

[Col. 0965B]

## Chapter VII

Let each of us also, according to his strength, provide from our churches soldiers against all the enemies of the holy Church and of our prince. Let them fight together with the leaders appointed for this purpose, insofar as the Lord grants assistance and deigns to cooperate, so that, just as there is a will in heaven, so may it be done.

But if the commanders of the battle lines ask us for counsel in such an encounter—for it is written, “The Lord brings the counsels of the nations to nothing, but he rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and he rejects the counsels of princes; but the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Psalm 32:10)—we cannot find any counsel that we could give them more salutary than that which the Lord sets forth in the Gospel. He says:

> “What king, going to engage in war against another king, does not first sit down and calculate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for the things that make for peace” (Luke 14:31).

[Cols. 0965C–0965D]

## Chapter VIII

Because, long before us, we read that among nations there was a proverb well known in common speech concerning those who are oppressed by anxieties and immense evils: “They are between the hammer and the anvil,” let us also, concerning the frequent attacks of the pagans and the other anxieties by which we have long been oppressed, refrain from speaking in words and cry out with groans and sighs.

We bishops are between two kings who are brothers by blood, each striving over this kingdom in which we dwell, as between the hammer and the anvil. For if, because our king has withdrawn farther away into another kingdom, we flee and depart at the arrival of the king who is about to come, leaving our churches in every direction when no one is persecuting them or attempting, as the saying goes, to inflict harm, and if we do not place ourselves under the protection of the king who is about to arrive—especially since, as is reported, the coming king says that he is not coming to invade the kingdom but to restore and defend what has been abandoned, to establish peace and justice in it, and to provide the holy Church and its priests with the honor and defense due to them—then both we and the sheep entrusted to us will appear to be in danger.

We, indeed, will be judged before God and human beings as not shepherds but hirelings. The sheep entrusted to us will wander or be scattered without a shepherd, and the ecclesiastical possessions by which they ought to be supported, left as though without guardians, will be seized and devastated if the power of the prince who should defend them is lacking, or if there are no guardians to make representations to the prince, defender and protector of the Church, on behalf of the sheep and their sustenance.

[Cols. 0966A–0966B]

## Chapter IX

But if our king returns, he will accuse us of disloyalty, as he did certain others when, departing from Breona and not leaving them desolate, he returned after some time—although our situation is sufficiently different from that of those whom he then rebuked.

For we, led by whatever desire or enticed by shameful profit, did not, as they did, invite another king into this kingdom; nor did we abandon our own king and, without necessity, place ourselves under another. Rather, having been abandoned by our king and exposed to the power of another, we have committed ourselves, awaiting the judgment of the King of kings.

But amid all this, anxieties surround us on every side. If, abandoned by our king, we place ourselves under the power of the king who is coming, it is death for us. But if we do not act in this way, we shall be unable to attend to the guardianship of our churches and of the sheep entrusted to us, and we shall fall either now into the hands of the king who is coming, or, if our own king returns, into his hands.

[Cols. 0966B–0966C]

## Chapter X

And what shall we answer to the words of the apostle John, who says, “He who says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked” (1 John 2:6), and who says, “Just as the Father knows me, so I know the Father; and I lay down my life for my sheep” (John 10:15)?

As Gregory says, as though he were speaking plainly (Homily 14 on the Gospels):

> “By this it is established that I both know the Father and am known by the Father: that I lay down my life for my sheep. That is, by the love with which I die for the sheep, I show how greatly I love the Father.”

And the same aforementioned apostle John says (1 John 2): “He who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar.”

It is therefore better for us to fall into the hands of human beings, if God so permits, than to abandon the law—that is, the commandment of God—so that we may not desert the sheep entrusted to us by God, who laid down his life for his sheep.

In this, the way we should follow has been shown to us, and a pattern has been set in which we should be formed. Therefore, if necessary, we too ought to lay down our lives for our brothers and not desert our sheep.

[Cols. 0966C–0966D]

## Chapter XI

But now, since this kingdom is surrounded on every side by pagans and false Christians, namely Britons, and, so to speak, has been disturbed by an internal upheaval concerning those who for some time had appeared to be faithful and useful within it; and since the terms concerning the kingdoms of their nephews have been confirmed by an oath between that king and his brother—would that either these terms were unknown, or that the terms themselves were observed between them, and that neither the prelates of the churches nor the male and female servants of the Lord were disturbed, nor the Christian people afflicted, nor an internal war arise among the leaders of the kingdom, nor the seizure and plundering of ecclesiastical property, whether belonging to the rich or the poor, break out in flames.

But if, on account of these words—which we speak not out of disloyalty to our princes for the purpose of insulting them, but out of concern and with grief and groaning for their danger—any force is inflicted upon us priests by anyone whatsoever, let us, as a certain Wise Man said, bear it with an even spirit and make use of the courts, until unconquered happiness puts an end to our evils.

[Cols. 0967A–0967B]

## Chapter XII

For we know, as the Apostle says, that “all who desire to live piously will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12). But “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). And the Lord calls blessed those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness (Matthew 5:10).

For there should be no doubt that blessed John the Baptist, who endured prison and chains as a testimony on behalf of our Redeemer whom he preceded, also laid down his life for him. His persecutor did not command him to deny Christ, but to keep silent about the truth; nevertheless, he fell for Christ.

Because Christ himself says, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), he certainly suffered for Christ because he shed his blood for the truth, steadfastly saying to the king, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s living wife” (Mark 6:18).

And if, because we say what we also hear the common people complain—namely, that our king ought not rashly to have abandoned this kingdom, surrounded on every side by pagans and internally disturbed and unstable, nor to have left and deserted those whom, by God’s judgment, he undertook to govern and defend, and who entrusted themselves to him for this purpose; and because we say that his brother ought not to invade his kingdom after the oaths sworn between them, which our king says that, for his part, he wishes to keep—if we suffer some harm on this account, let us patiently endure what is inflicted upon us for Christ, because we shall endure it for the truth.

In our own limited way, let us imitate those who went away rejoicing because they had been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41).

[Cols. 0967C–0967D]

## Chapter XIII

But since, as we said above, we have been placed between the hammer and the anvil, and since what is placed between the hammer and the anvil is either broken and crushed, or stretched out and formed—as we read in the Book of Numbers that the Lord commanded Moses to make silver trumpets “between the hammer and the anvil,” capable of being extended, which by their sound would summon the people of God to his solemnities and kindle the minds of those who heard them for battle (Numbers 10:1)—and Saint David says, “Sing praises to the Lord on extended trumpets” (Psalm 98:6); and the Apostle says, “Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through perseverance and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15:4); and again, “Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; contemplating the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13:7)—let us seek the silver trumpets extended between the hammer and the anvil, that is, the words of the Lord, which are silver tested by fire and purified sevenfold (Psalm 12:7), shining and strong in virtue.

From their teaching, let us learn what we must do in the anguish of our disturbance, in the necessary and imminent battle, so that we may not be broken or crushed between the hammer and the anvil, but may be extended and formed, walking without stumbling in their footsteps and not going astray.

[Cols. 0968A–0969B]

## Chapter XIV

Saint Ambrose, in the little book that he presented to the Emperor Valentinian against Auxentius, says the following, among other things (Letter 32):

> “Would that, Emperor, you had not announced that I might go wherever I wished. Every day I went out, and no one kept watch over me. You ought to have sent me wherever you wished, since I offered myself to everyone. Now the priests tell me that it makes little difference whether you voluntarily abandon or betray the altar of Christ; for once you have abandoned it, you will betray it.”

And in his address to the people in the church (*Oration against Auxentius*, Book V of the Letters):

> “I see that you have suddenly become more disturbed than usual and are watching me closely. I wonder what this means, unless perhaps it is because you have seen or heard through the tribunes that, by imperial command, it was announced that I might leave here wherever I wished, and that anyone who wished would have the power to follow me. Were you therefore afraid that I would desert the Church and, while fearing for my own safety, leave you?
>
> “But you could also have noticed what I myself commanded: that no intention of abandoning the Church could exist in me, because I feared the Lord of the world more than the emperor of this age. Certainly, if some force were to drag me away from the Church, it could drive away my body, but not my mind. I am ready that, if he does what belongs to royal power, I should undergo what is customary for a priest.
>
> “Why, then, are you disturbed? I will never desert you willingly; under compulsion, I do not know how to resist. I shall be able to grieve, to weep, to groan. Against weapons, soldiers, and even Goths, my tears are weapons; such are the defenses of a priest. Otherwise I neither ought nor can resist.
>
> “But I am not accustomed to flee and abandon the Church, lest someone interpret the deed as arising from fear of a heavier punishment. You yourselves know that I am accustomed to show deference to emperors, not to yield to them; to offer myself willingly to punishments.”

And a little later:

> “The apostle Peter also gave you an example of both courses of action (Acts 12). When Herod sought him and seized him, he placed him in prison. The servant of God had not withdrawn but had stood firm, ignorant of fear. The Church prayed for him, but the Apostle rested in prison, which is evidence that he was not afraid. An angel was sent to awaken him as he slept, and through the angel Peter was led out of prison and escaped death for a time.
>
> “Later, after defeating Simon, when Peter was sowing God’s commandments among the people and teaching chastity, he stirred up the minds of the pagans. When they sought him, Christian souls begged him to withdraw for a little while. Although he desired martyrdom, he was nevertheless moved by the consideration of the praying people. He was asked to preserve himself in order to instruct and strengthen the people.
>
> “What more need be said? At night he began to leave by the wall, and when he saw Christ meeting him at the gate and entering the city, he said: ‘Lord, where are you going?’ Christ replied: ‘I am going to Rome to be crucified again.’
>
> “Peter understood that this divine answer concerned his own cross. For Christ could not be crucified again, since by the suffering of the death he had endured he had laid aside the flesh. ‘For in that he died, he died to sin once for all; but in that he lives, he lives to God’ (Romans 6:10).
>
> “Peter therefore understood that Christ was to be crucified again in his servant. Thus he voluntarily returned. When the Christians asked him, he gave them his answer, and immediately being seized, he glorified the Lord Jesus through his own cross. You see, therefore, that Christ wishes to suffer in his servants.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Did I myself not go out every day for visits, or go to the martyrs? Did I not pass before the royal palace as I went and returned? Yet no one detained me, although afterward they revealed their intention of driving me out, saying: ‘Leave the city and go wherever you wish.’
>
> “I confess that I was expecting something great: either a sword for the name of Christ or a fire. But they offered me comforts instead of sufferings. The athlete of Christ demands not comforts but his sufferings.
>
> “Let no one, therefore, disturb you because they had prepared either a carriage or the harsh words, as it seemed to him, uttered by Auxentius himself, who calls himself a bishop. Many were saying that assassins had been sent ahead and that the death penalty had been decreed. I fear neither the one nor abandon the other. For where shall I go, when everything is full of groans and tears?”

In the history of Theodoret (Book IX, chapter 20), we read that when Ambrose was ordered to leave the Church, he said:

> “I am not doing this willingly, lest I appear to hand the sheepfold over to wolves or to those who blaspheme God. If it pleases you, kill me here. In this place I willingly receive death with eager resolve.”

[Cols. 0969B–0969D]

## Chapter XV

Therefore, for the sake of faith and truth, if it should happen, we must not merely follow but also embrace what blessed Ambrose says about himself when speaking to his own Church (*Oration against Auxentius*):

> “I will never desert you willingly; under compulsion, I do not know how to resist. I shall be able to grieve, to weep, to groan; otherwise I neither ought nor can resist. But I am not accustomed to flee and abandon the Church.”

For this is how our holy predecessors acted, as we read in ecclesiastical histories: blessed Hilary of Poitiers, Paulinus of Trier, Dionysius of Milan, Eusebius of Vercelli, John of Constantinople, and many others. Their words and examples flourish in the holy Church to this day. In accordance with Paul’s saying, we ought to contemplate the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith and examples (Hebrews 13:7).

And concerning bishops expelled from their sees for the sake of faith and truth, just as the holy bishops mentioned above were expelled by imperial cruelty, the sacred canons of Sardica say (Canon 21):

> “If any bishop has suffered violence and has been unjustly expelled for discipline and the catholic confession, or for the defense of the truth, and, fleeing danger, innocent and devoted, has come to another city, he must not be forbidden to remain there for as long as he may either return or obtain a remedy for his injury. Even abundant kindness and humane treatment must be shown to him.”

[Cols. 0969D–0970D]

## Chapter XVI

Hence Saint Gregory also writes to all the bishops throughout Illyricum (Book I, Letter 43):

> “Brothers and our fellow bishops, whom the distress of captivity and various necessities oppresses, you ought willingly to receive them among you, to be consoled and to live with you on ecclesiastical support—not indeed so that the dignity of the episcopal throne may be divided through their sharing in communion, but so that, according to the possibility of sufficient means, they may receive sustenance from the Church.
>
> “For in this way we are shown to love both our neighbor in God and God in our neighbor. We grant them no authority whatsoever in your churches, but nevertheless we earnestly urge you to keep them among you.”

How, and for what reasons, bishops may temporarily leave their churches without harm to their office and soul, Saint Augustine also explains in his letter to Bishop Honoratus (Letter 180, at the beginning), saying, among other things:

> “It remains for us, whose ministry is so necessary to the small people of God who remain where we are that they ought not to be left without it, to say to the Lord: ‘Be for us a protecting God and a fortified place’ (Psalm 31:3).
>
> “But, as you write, this counsel does not suffice for you, lest we attempt to act contrary to the Lord’s command or example, where he instructs that one should flee from city to city. For we remember the words of the one who says: ‘When they persecute you in this city, flee into another’ (Matthew 10:23).
>
> “Who, however, could believe that the Lord wished this to be done in such a way that the flocks he acquired with his own blood should be abandoned in a necessary ministry without which they cannot live? Did he do this when, carried by his parents into Egypt, he fled as a child (Matthew 2)—when he had not yet gathered churches that we could say had been deserted by him? Or when the apostle Paul, so that the enemy might not seize him, was lowered in a basket through a window and escaped his hands (Acts 9)—was the church that was there, in its necessary ministry, abandoned, or was what was required not fulfilled by other brothers established there (2 Corinthians 11)?
>
> “The Apostle had done this with their consent, so that he might preserve himself for the Church, since that persecutor was seeking him personally. Let those who are specifically sought by persecutors flee from city to city, so that the Church may not be deserted by others who are not similarly sought. Rather, let them provide provisions for their fellow servants whom they know cannot live otherwise.
>
> “But when there is a common danger for all—that is, for bishops and clergy—those who need others must not be deserted by those whom they need. Either let all move to fortified places, or let those who have the necessity of remaining not be abandoned by those through whom their ecclesiastical need must be supplied, so that they may either live together or endure together whatever the master of the household wishes them to suffer.
>
> “If it should happen that some suffer more and others less, or that all suffer equally, it becomes apparent which of them suffer for the sake of others: namely, those who, although they could have rescued themselves from such evils by fleeing, preferred to remain rather than abandon the needs of others.
>
> “This especially proves the love that the apostle John commends, saying: ‘Just as Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers’ (1 John 3:15). For those who flee—or who cannot flee because they are bound by their own necessities—if they are seized and suffer, certainly suffer for themselves, not for their brothers.
>
> “But those who suffer because they did not wish to desert the brothers who needed them for Christian salvation undoubtedly lay down their lives for their brothers.”

[Cols. 0971A–0971C]

## Chapter XVII

Thus acted Saint Nicasius, bishop of Rheims, who in the time of the Vandals, during the general persecution, did not desert his city and within the walls of the church deserved to be crowned with martyrdom.

So also, at the same time, did Saint Anianus, as is read in the sacred histories. So did blessed Lupus, as is sung in his hymn:

> “When all the wars were destroying everything, by prayer he fortified Troyes.”

So did Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims. When the pagan Franks arrived in the Belgian province of his diocese, he did not desert his Church. Rather, through prayers and holy examples, he subdued the ferocity of the people, and by his words calmed the monsters. He not only rescued his province from the pagan sword but also, with grace cooperating, converted the pagan people to the faith of Christ. Together with their king, he brought three thousand pagans to the grace of baptism on the vigil of Holy Easter.

He rightly observed what Saint Gregory says in his homily on Ezekiel the prophet, explaining Daniel’s statement (Homily 5 on Ezekiel): “His throne was a flame of fire; its wheels were burning fire.”

> “For those who are guardians of souls and have undertaken the burdens of feeding the flock are by no means permitted to change their places. Rather, because, being placed in one location, they carry within themselves the presence of the divinity and burn, the throne of God is called a flame of fire.”

Hence Saint Augustine, in the aforementioned letter to Bishop Honoratus (Letter 180), says at the relevant point:

> “Why do they think they must obey indiscriminately the command in which they read that one should flee from city to city, and do they not dread the hireling who sees the wolf coming and flees because he has no concern for the sheep?”

And shortly afterward:

> “The Apostle fled when he himself was specifically sought by the persecutor, while others who did not have a similar necessity remained there; God forbid that the Church’s ministry should have been deserted by them. So Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, fled when the Emperor Constantius was especially eager to seize him.”

[Cols. 0971C–0972A]

## Chapter XVIII

We also read in the letters of the great Pope Leo that, when the Eutychian heresy was raging in the eastern regions, that same apostolic pontiff, as well as the bishops of the western regions, was summoned by the emperor to a universal synod.

Therefore Saint Leo, to reproduce his own words, wrote the following among other things to the Emperor Theodosius Augustus (Letter 17):

> “Although no consideration permits me to attend on the day of the episcopal council that Your Piety has appointed, since no precedents of this kind have come before and temporal necessity does not allow me to abandon the city.”

And to Augusta Pulcheria (Letter 13):

> “For that which the emperor’s piety believed even I ought to attend the council, although some preceding example might have demanded it, could nevertheless not now be fulfilled, because the exceedingly uncertain condition of present affairs would not permit me to be absent from the people of so great a city. They would be thrown into a kind of despair if, under the pretext of an ecclesiastical matter, I appeared willing to abandon my homeland and the apostolic see.
>
> “Since you therefore recognize that it belonged to the public good that, with pardon granted by Your Clemency, I should not refuse myself to the affection and prayers of the citizens, etc.”

And in his letter to Emperor Marcian (Letter 44):

> “The necessity of the present time in no way permits the priests of all the provinces to assemble, because the provinces from which they especially ought to be summoned, disturbed by war, do not allow them to depart from their churches.”

And in the Canons of the Province of Africa (chapter 57, concerning the bishops of Numidia), we read that the bishops of the province of Numidia were justly and reasonably excused because they did not send legates to the universal council even concerning common and ecclesiastical affairs, since, amid the tumult of the recruits, they remained in their own cities, either hindered by their necessities or excused by them.

[Cols. 0972B–0972D]

## Chapter XIX

From this, therefore, we must conclude that if the affection of the citizens ought to be placed before the cause of the faith and the general business of ecclesiastical definitions—as the words of Saint Leo and the sacred canons demonstrate, and as the Apostle testifies that love is greater than faith (1 Corinthians 13)—we must ask whether, for any other cause whatsoever, we can safely leave the churches and sheep entrusted to us and withdraw to whatever other regions.

Finally, when Maximus usurped part of the Empire against Theodosius and Valentinian and compelled bishops either to act against the faith, to abandon their churches, or to suffer persecution in some other way, Saint Martin did not avoid the presence or conversation of that same Maximus, but he did not abandon his own Church.

When, however, many bishops from various regions had gathered before Maximus, a man of fierce character exalted by victory in civil wars, and disgraceful universal flattery toward the ruler was being displayed, apostolic authority remained in Martin alone.

For even when it was necessary to make petitions to the king on certain matters, he commanded rather than begged; and, although frequently invited, he abstained from his banquet, saying that he could not share the table of one who had expelled one emperor from his kingdom and another from life.

At last, when Maximus asserted that he had not taken the imperial power willingly but had defended with arms the necessity of kingship imposed upon him by the soldiers through divine direction, and that God’s will did not seem foreign to him, since victory had been granted to him through such an incredible event, and none of his opponents had fallen except in battle, Martin, overcome at last either by reason or by entreaty, came to the banquet.

[Cols. 0973A–0973B]

## Chapter XX

It is likewise written in his life as follows (Severus, *Dialogue* II, chapter 6):

> “At the time when he was first appointed bishop, it became necessary for him to visit the imperial court. Valentinian then held supreme power. When he learned that Martin was asking for things he did not wish to grant, he ordered that Martin be kept away from the palace doors.
>
> “For an Arian wife had approached that harsh and proud man’s mind and turned him entirely away from the holy man, so that he would not show him the reverence due to him. Thus Martin, after attempting once and again in vain to approach the proud ruler, returned to his familiar defenses. He wrapped himself in sackcloth, sprinkled himself with ashes, abstained from food and drink, and continued in prayer day and night.”

And a little later:

> “Without waiting for Martin’s prayers, he granted everything before being asked. He frequently invited him to conversation and to his table.”

And shortly afterward (chapter 8):

> “The Emperor Maximus governed the state, a man worthy of praise for every merit of his life, if only he had been permitted either to reject the diadem unlawfully imposed upon him by soldiers in revolt or to abstain from civil arms. But a great empire could neither be refused without danger nor held without arms.
>
> “He repeatedly summoned Martin and, after receiving him within the palace, honored him reverently. All their conversation concerned present matters, future matters, the glory of the faithful, and the eternity of the saints. Meanwhile, day and night, the queen hung upon Martin’s lips. Following that Gospel example, she was no inferior: she drenched the holy man’s feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.
>
> “Martin, whom no woman had ever touched, could not escape her constant attentiveness—or rather, her servitude. She thought neither of the wealth of the kingdom, nor of the dignity of the empire, nor of the diadem, nor of the purple. Lying prostrate at Martin’s feet, she could not be torn away from them.
>
> “Finally, she asked this of her husband, and then both of them urged Martin to let her prepare a banquet for him alone, with all attendants removed. The blessed man could not resist more stubbornly.
>
> “A chaste meal was arranged by the queen’s hands. She herself spread the little seat, brought up the table, supplied water with her hands, and set before him the food she herself had cooked.”

The rest the reader will be able to find more fully in its proper places.

[Cols. 0973C–0973D]

## Chapter XXI

Saint Ambrose was engaged with his emperors, Theodosius and Valentinian, and he undertook an embassy to Maximus from his own emperor Valentinian (Letter 27). Whoever wishes to know how vigorously he carried it out, and how he rebuked Maximus while nevertheless not avoiding his conversation, should read Ambrose’s own book, which he wrote to that same Valentinian concerning the embassy he had completed.

However, as is read in the life of blessed Ambrose written later by Saint Paulinus, afterward bishop of Nola, when Theodosius had departed from Italy and was established at Constantinople, while Augustus Valentinian was stationed within Gaul, Eugenius usurped the empire tyrannically. He restored the altar of Victory and the funding of the ceremonies, which Valentinian, of blessed memory, had refused when, still a minor, he was petitioned for them. Eugenius, forgetful of his faith, granted them.

When Ambrose learned this, he left the city of Milan, toward which Eugenius was hastening, and withdrew as far as Tuscany, avoiding the sight of the sacrilegious man more than fearing the injury of the ruler. He also sent him a letter in which he confronted his conscience concerning the sacrilege. He did not avoid Eugenius’s sight and conversation because of his usurped imperial power, but because of the sacrilege he had committed.

[Cols. 0974A–0974B]

## Chapter XXII

Thus blessed Martin and Saint Ambrose followed the teaching of the apostle Paul: “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, rebuke them” (Ephesians 5:11).

Hence blessed Augustine says (*On the Words of the Lord*, Sermon 18):

> “A wicked person does not defile you in two ways: if you do not consent to him and if you rebuke him. This is not to participate: not to consent.
>
> “Participation occurs when an association of will or approval is added to his deed. See how the Apostle embraced both matters: ‘Do not participate; rather, rebuke them’ (1 Corinthians 10). What does ‘Do not participate’ mean? Do not consent, do not praise, do not approve. What does ‘rather, rebuke them’ mean? Reprove, correct, restrain.
>
> “Furthermore, in the rebuke or restraint of the sins of others, one must beware that the person who rebukes another does not exalt himself. One must keep in mind that apostolic sentence: ‘Therefore, let anyone who thinks that he stands take care lest he fall.’
>
> “Let rebuke sound terribly outwardly, but let an affection of gentleness be maintained inwardly. Let us neither consent to evil people so as to approve them, nor become proud so as to rebuke them insultingly.”

These are the things that our holy predecessors and patrons did according to the path of the holy Scriptures and in keeping with their episcopal ministry; they left them to us, their successors, as things to be done and followed when we are placed in such anxieties.

[Cols. 0974B–0974D]

## Chapter XXIII

Moreover, the true histories show how, and by whom, one ought to act toward those who invade the kingdom of a king (Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* in three parts, Book IX, chapter 21).

For Theodoret says:

> “When Maximus heard what was again being done against Ambrose, the eloquent preacher of truth, he wrote to Valentinian that the war being waged against the churches should be brought to an end. He warned him not to abandon his fatherly piety, and he also added threats of war, saying that, unless he ceased, he would fulfill his words by deeds.
>
> “For this reason, taking an army, he came to Milan, where Valentinian was then living. Valentinian, recognizing his invasion, fled to Illyricum, learning by experience what evils he was suffering through his mother’s counsel.
>
> “Theodosius, hearing what Justina had done and what the tyrant had written, replied to the fleeing Valentinian that it was not surprising if terror increased for the emperor but power for the tyrant, since the emperor had proved hostile to impiety while the tyrant was lending it assistance. Therefore the former fled naked, while the latter armed himself against the naked man.”

And Socrates says in the same work (chapter 23):

> “But when the Emperor Theodosius attacked the tyrant, the soldiers of Maximus recognized the presence of the imperial army and the arrival of his standards. They were unable to withstand even the force of his reputation. Seizing the tyrant and binding him, they immediately presented him to Theodosius, and he was killed during their consulship on the twenty-seventh day of the month of August.”

[Cols. 0974D–0975A]

## Chapter XXIV

And in the history of the life of blessed Ambrose, written by Saint Paulinus, we read:

> “Thus the priest departed from the regions of Tuscany and returned to Milan. Eugenius had already gone out from there against the Emperor Theodosius, and Ambrose awaited the arrival of the Christian emperor there, confident in God’s power: that God would not hand over one who believed in him to unjust men, nor leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity.
>
> “For Argobastes, then a count, and Fabianus, the prefect, had promised that, as they departed from Milan, if they returned as victors they would turn the church of Milan into a stable and put the clergy to the test under arms. But those pitiable men, wickedly trusting demons and opening their mouths in blasphemy against God, deprived themselves of hope of victory.
>
> “The cause of the conflict was this: the gifts of the emperor, who had involved himself in sacrilege, were rejected by the Church, and he was not granted fellowship in prayer with the Church. But the Lord, who is accustomed to protect his Church, hurled judgment from heaven and transferred every victory to the religious Emperor Theodosius.”

## CHAPTER XXV

If, finally, anyone asks why Saint Martin and Blessed Ambrose did not excommunicate Maximus, who drove two emperors—one from life and the other from the throne—from the body and blood of the Lord, but merely rebuked him; and why Blessed Ambrose did not excommunicate Eugenius, a tyrant and sacrilegious man, as he excommunicated the religious and Christian emperor Theodosius for his notorious offense, let him accept the answer given to him from the teaching of Catholic and most renowned men.

For Blessed Ambrose says, among other things, concerning the death of Theodosius:

> “I loved,” he said, “a man who approved one who rebuked rather than one who flattered. He laid aside every royal insignia that he used; he publicly mourned his sin in the Church, a sin that had crept upon him through the deceit of others; with groaning and tears he sought forgiveness. What private persons are ashamed of, the emperor was not ashamed to do publicly: to perform penance. Nor did a day afterward pass on which he did not grieve that error. What more? Although he had obtained a glorious victory, because enemies had fallen in battle, he nevertheless abstained from communion in the sacraments until, by the arrival of his sons, he might experience the Lord’s grace toward him.”

## CHAPTER XXVI

From this the reason plainly satisfies the questioner: namely, that penance benefits the penitent when it is voluntary rather than compelled, as it is written: “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Psalm 53:8); and, “I will praise him of my own free will” (Psalm 27:7).

And in Exodus we read (Exodus 25) that men, together with women, voluntarily offered whatever was necessary for the worship and adornment of the tabernacle; among the offerings, goat hair is also counted. Through goat hair, from which haircloth is made, penance is signified, as the Lord demonstrates in the Gospel when he says to the rejected city:

> “If the miracles that have been done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have done penance in haircloth and ashes” (Matthew 12:21).

In haircloth, indeed, the harshness and piercing of sins are shown; in ashes, the dust of the dead. Therefore both are customarily applied to penance, so that in the piercing of haircloth we may recognize what we have done through guilt, and in the ash’s dust consider what we have become through judgment.

Let the piercing vices therefore be considered in the haircloth; let the just punishment of the vices that follows by the sentence of death be considered in the ashes. Since shame arose after fleshly sin, let a person see in the harshness of haircloth what he did through pride; let him see in the ashes how far he reached by sinning.

## CHAPTER XXVII

But why did Saint Martin and Saint Ambrose not excommunicate the aforementioned usurpers of the empire from the body and blood of the Lord, and take common food with them? Let Saint Augustine answer in his book *On Penance* (homily 50):

> “We cannot,” he says, “prohibit anyone from communion, although this prohibition is not yet mortal but medicinal, unless that person has either confessed voluntarily, or has been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical judgment. For who would dare assume both roles for himself, so as to be another’s accuser and judge?
>
> “The Apostle Paul is also understood to have briefly indicated this rule in his Epistle to the Corinthians, when, after mentioning certain such crimes, he gave the form of ecclesiastical judgment for all similar cases. For he says: ‘I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators—not, of course, with the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or robbers, or idolaters; otherwise you would have had to leave this world’ (1 Corinthians 5:9–10).
>
> “For people living in this world cannot live except among such persons; nor can they win them for Christ if they avoid their conversation and fellowship. Hence, too, when the Lord was eating with tax collectors and sinners, he said: ‘Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners’ (Matthew 9:12).
>
> “And therefore the Apostle continues and adds: ‘Now I have written to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is a fornicator, or an idolater, or a greedy person, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber; with such a person, not even to take food together’ (1 Corinthians 5:11). For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are within? But God will judge those who are outside. ‘Remove the evil person from among yourselves.’
>
> “By these words he sufficiently shows that the wicked are not to be removed from the Church’s communion rashly or arbitrarily, but through judgment. Thus, if they cannot be removed through judgment, they should rather be tolerated, lest someone, perversely avoiding the wicked, depart from the Church himself and bind to Gehenna those whom he appears to flee.
>
> “For examples of this have also been set before us in the holy Scriptures: in the harvest, the chaff is to be endured until the final winnowing; and within those nets, good fish are to be tolerated together with bad until the separation that will take place on the shore—that is, at the end of the age.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

And in the seventh book of *On Baptism* (chapter 45):

> “John says that ‘Hail’ is not to be said to those who belong to an alien doctrine (2 John 1:10); but the Apostle Paul says more forcefully: ‘If anyone who bears the name of brother among you is greedy or drunk, and so forth, with such a person not even to take food together’ (1 Corinthians 5:11). Yet Cyprian shared not a private table but God’s altar with colleagues who were usurers, schemers, fraudsters, and robbers.”

And in the *Treatise on the Psalm* (on Psalm 54):

> “Let us love our enemies, rebuke them, chastise them, and excommunicate them with love; let us also separate them from ourselves. See what the Apostle says: ‘If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him and do not associate with him’ (2 Thessalonians 3:14). But lest anger seize you because of this and disturb your eye, he says: ‘Do not regard him as an enemy, but rebuke him as a brother, so that he may be ashamed.’ From him he ordered separation, but he did not cut off love.”

And elsewhere (Psalm 100:5; Augustine on Psalm 100):

> “The proud in eye and the insatiable in heart—I did not eat with him,” he says; that is, I did not eat together with him. How does he set this before us when he himself did not do it? He urges us to imitate him. We see that he dined with the proud; how does he forbid us to dine with them?
>
> “We, brothers, sometimes withhold ourselves even from our brothers for the sake of correction, and do not dine with them, so that they may be corrected. We dine instead with outsiders and with pagans rather than with those who were with us and attached to us, if we see them living badly, so that they may be ashamed and corrected, as the Apostle says: ‘If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him and do not associate with him—not so as to regard him as an enemy, but rebuke him as a brother’ (1 Corinthians 5:11). We do this often for the sake of healing, and yet we frequently eat with many outsiders and with impious people.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

And again in the *Treatise on the Psalm* (on Psalm 100, sermon 2):

> “Consider the gifts of the Church herself: the gift of the sacraments in baptism, in the Eucharist, and in the other holy sacraments. What sort of gift is it? The magician Simon also obtained this gift. What sort of gift is prophecy? The evil king Saul prophesied, and he prophesied at the very time when he was persecuting the holy David.”

And again in the sermon on the Gospel of John (sermon 50, on John):

> “Such was Judas, and yet he entered and went out with the eleven holy disciples. He approached the Lord’s supper together with them; he was able to associate with them, but he could not defile them. Peter received from one bread, and Judas also; and yet, what portion does the believer have with the unbeliever? Peter received it for life, Judas for death.
>
> “As the fragrance is good, so the food is good. Just as the good fragrance gives life to the good and kills the wicked, so also the good food gives life to the good and kills the wicked. For whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself—not judgment upon you. If judgment is upon himself and not upon you, tolerate the evil person, you who are good, so that you may come to the reward of the good and not be sent into the punishment of the wicked.”

## CHAPTER XXX

And in the *Treatise on the Psalm* (Augustine on Psalm 47):

> “How many does Satan fill like Judas, receiving morsels unworthily to their own judgment? For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Corinthians 11:29). What is given is not evil, but something good is given badly, to the recipient’s judgment. What is good cannot be good for one who receives it badly.”

And in the sermon *On the Words of the Apostle* (*On the Spirit of Blasphemy*):

> “How are we to understand what he also says: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’ (John 6:57)? Can we perhaps include here even those of whom the Apostle says that they eat and drink judgment upon themselves—so that they eat that very flesh and drink that very blood?
>
> “Did Judas, the seller and betrayer of his master, although he ate and drank with the other disciples the sacrament of his flesh and blood, which had first been prepared by his own hands—as the evangelist Luke more clearly declares—remain in Christ, and Christ in him?
>
> “Finally, many who eat that flesh and drink that blood either with a false heart or become apostates after eating and drinking: do they remain in Christ, or Christ in them? Certainly there is a particular manner of eating that flesh and drinking that blood, such that whoever eats and drinks in that manner remains in Christ, and Christ in him.
>
> “Therefore, not everyone who eats Christ’s flesh and drinks Christ’s blood, in whatever manner, remains in Christ and Christ in him, but only in a certain manner—the manner he himself evidently had in mind when he said these things.”

## CHAPTER XXXI

And in the letter of the council to the Donatists (volume 7 of Saint Augustine’s letters, letter 152):

> “Whoever lives well in this Church is not harmed by the sins of others, because each person will bear his own burden in it, as the Apostle says: ‘Whoever eats the body of Christ unworthily in it eats and drinks judgment upon himself.’ For the Apostle himself also wrote this.
>
> “When he says, ‘He eats judgment upon himself,’ he sufficiently shows that he does not eat judgment upon another, but upon himself, because association with the wicked does not defile anyone through participation in the sacraments, but through consent to their deeds.
>
> “For if someone does not consent to them in their evil deeds, the wicked person bears his own case and his own person and does not prejudice another whom he does not have as a partner in the consent to the evil deed.”

## CHAPTER XXXII

Nevertheless, we read in the life of Blessed Ambrose, written by Blessed Paulinus, that he separated Maximus from participation in communion and warned him to do penance for the blood poured out by his lord—and, what is more serious, for innocent blood—if he wished to secure his well-being before God.

But when he rejected penance with a proud spirit, he lost not only future salvation but also his present salvation, and he laid down the kingdom that he had seized unjustly, confessing that he had presided over the republic in the capacity of a procurator.

And Blessed Ambrose is said to have written to Eugenius in the same Life:

> “How am I bound,” he says, “by my words, both before God and before all human beings? I understood that one thing was not permitted to me and another ought not to be done, unless I took thought for myself, because I was unable to take thought for you.”

Following these most decisive and salutary words, we bishops of our lord Charles, if it should happen that we cannot take thought for him as we desire—in the temporal defense and protection of his kingdom—will nevertheless take thought for him in the observance of the faith that is owed, and take thought also for ourselves, by God’s cooperation, in the observance of the faith owed to him, in continual devotion of mind, and in supplication for him before God and his saints.

Let us take thought for ourselves also, so that, for any desire or temporal advantage, we do not depart from the faith owed to him by inviting anyone into his kingdom through envoys, whether bishops or other intermediaries; nor do we sell ourselves for abbeys, temporal honors, possessions, or resources, becoming like Judas, who went to the Jews and said: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matthew 26:15).

## CHAPTER XXXIII

Moreover, since we cannot and ought not reasonably to be trusted by anyone else if, while preserving our faith in God, we do not keep faith with our lord because of some earthly profit or injury inflicted upon us.

For in the ancient people, the prophet Samuel, whose place in the Church is now occupied by bishops, so greatly mourned Saul, whom the Lord had rejected as king on account of his sins—as sacred history records—that God said to him:

> “How long will you mourn Saul, since I have rejected him?” (1 Samuel 16:1).

And David, a warlike man, one of Saul’s leading men, and also his son-in-law, who in many ways benefited not only the king but also the kingdom, and who not only fought battles against Saul’s adversaries and against those of his kingdom but also soothed the king himself, when tormented by an evil spirit, with pleasing services—although the king repeatedly sought to have him killed—faithfully preserving what he had said concerning the appointed king and lord, “You have placed men over our heads” (Psalm 65:12), called his own persecutor lord and king.

Although he often had the opportunity to kill him, he not only did not kill him but also restrained his companions from killing him, saying:

> “Far be it from me to lay my hand upon the Lord’s anointed, for he is the Lord’s anointed” (1 Samuel 24:11).

And, so that he might be able to show by a sign what opportunity he had had to kill him, he cut off the edge of his cloak. Then, coming to his senses, he struck his own heart because he had damaged the garment of his lord.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Hence Blessed Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part 3, chapter 5):

> “Subjects must be admonished not to become bolder against their superiors when they consider their faults. Instead, if their superiors have anything very wrong, they should judge it within themselves, yet, constrained by fear of God, they must not refuse to bear the yoke of reverence under them.
>
> “We demonstrate this more clearly if we bring forward David’s deed. When Saul the persecutor entered a cave to relieve himself, David was there inside with his men. He had already endured the evils of Saul’s persecution for a very long time. When his men urged him to strike Saul, he restrained them with his reply, because he ought not to lay his hand upon the Lord’s anointed. Yet he secretly rose and cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak.
>
> “What, then, is signified by Saul except wicked rulers, and by David except good subjects? Saul’s relieving himself therefore signifies wicked superiors extending the evil conceived in their hearts into deeds of foul odor, and displaying in outward actions the harmful things they have contemplated within themselves. They silently cut, as it were, the edge of their superior’s cloak, because, when they detract from the aforesaid dignity at least harmlessly and secretly, they are, as it were, cutting the garment of the king placed over them.
>
> “For when we sin against superiors, we oppose the ordering of the one who placed them over us.”

## CHAPTER XXXV

Let us also, as far as we can with the Lord’s help, take thought for our associates and fellow soldiers, exhorting them to observe the faith owed to him.

If there are any who, as we hear, say that he holds the entire kingdom in his own hand and in the hands of his special favorites, so that no one can obtain anything through service, defense, or benefit to the kingdom except by payment, nor retain anything obtained except by payment; and that no one can have confidence in him either concerning honors or concerning intimacy, since he has dishonored and cast away all whom he has treated as favorites and intimates; and if there are those who reproach ecclesiastical men, saying that no one has oppressed and stripped the Churches through such varied devices, although he has transferred certain possessions after receiving payment, and has thus sold the entire kingdom—we should, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, set before those who inquire about such matters the following:

If God causes him to return with prosperity, he will complete what he has begun and carried out well. And because there is no human being on earth who does good and does not sin (Ecclesiastes 7:21), he will be changed into another man, and this will be “the change of the right hand of the Most High.”

For it is written: “Turn the wicked, and they will be no more” (Proverbs 12:7)—not because they will cease to exist in essence, but because they will no longer remain in the guilt of wickedness. Thus the Apostle Paul says of himself:

> “I live, yet it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

That savage persecutor had been extinguished, and the devout preacher had begun to live.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

Let us also take thought for him if there should be someone who, during his absence, is plotting to seize his kingdom. Let us remind him of the oaths made between him and our lord, which our king acknowledges that he wishes to preserve.

Let us set before him the sentence of the Lord delivered through the prophet Jeremiah against Zedekiah, who had sworn to Nebuchadnezzar, a pagan king, in the name of the Lord:

> “Therefore,” says Scripture, “because he despised the oath and violated the covenant, I will place it upon his head” (Ezekiel 17:19).

Hence Jerome says:

> “Lest we think that the oath, covenant, and agreement belonged to the Babylonian king or to Zedekiah who had made them, what follows says: ‘In his violation by which he despised me.’ Therefore, whoever despises the oath despises the one by whom he swore; and he does injury to the one whose name the adversary trusted.
>
> “For this reason he says: ‘I will spread my net over him, and he will be caught in my snare; I will bring him to Babylon, and there I will judge him.’ Whatever Nebuchadnezzar therefore did against Zedekiah, he did not do by his own strength but by the anger of God, in whose name the oath had been violated.”

For we read that Zedekiah was captured and led to Riblah (2 Kings 25), where, after his sons had been killed, he was blinded and carried to Babylon shut up like a wild beast in a cage. From this most severe vengeance for perjury it is clear that perjury is a most serious sin, as Saint Augustine also demonstrates in his book *To Hilary’s Questions* (letter 99, at the end).

## CHAPTER XXXVII

But if we are unable to take thought for those acting against their own superior, let us, according to the words of Blessed Ambrose, take thought for ourselves, so that we do not do anything through desire, flattery, deception, or association by which our ministry may be blamed and we may lose the good reputation that apostolic teaching commands a bishop to possess, even among those who are outside (1 Timothy 3:7).

That is, if another king should come upon the kingdom of our lord, and there were no military force to resist him, let us bishops follow the footsteps of our fathers: in the ordering of our rank, in preserving faith toward our superior, in receiving the king, and in all other matters, let us offer the service of conciliation toward the king who has arrived—namely, in receiving him.

For we read that Saint Basil, together with his clergy, honorably received even Julian the Apostate when he arrived, and that for this reason he did not deviate from the rule of orthodox faith, but rendered to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s.

We have also sufficiently demonstrated above, from the sayings of the Fathers, what concerns the solemnities of Masses and the sacred communion of the altar, as well as participation in the common table, the altar, and the sacraments.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Concerning military service and taxes, which according to ancient and customary practice he is accustomed to demand in proportion to the size and character of the Churches entrusted to us, we think that we ought to use the words of Blessed Ambrose and follow his actions. In the sermon that he began before the people concerning his persecution (*Oration against Auxentius on the Basilicas*), he says:

> “See how much worse the Arians are than the Jews. The Jews asked whether he thought the tribute owed to Caesar should be paid; these men wish to give the Emperor the rights of the Church.
>
> “But just as the faithless follow their author, so let us also answer what the Lord and our author taught us. For Jesus, considering the Jews’ deceit, said to them: ‘Why do you tempt me? Show me a denarius.’ When they had given one, he said: ‘Whose image and inscription does it have?’ They answered: ‘Caesar’s.’ And Jesus said to them: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s’ (Matthew 22:21).
>
> “Therefore I also say to those who object to me: ‘Show me a denarius.’ Jesus saw Caesar’s denarius and said: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.’ Can they offer Caesar’s denarius for taking possession of the basilicas of the Church?
>
> “But in the Church I know one image, namely, the image of the invisible God, concerning which God said: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’ (Genesis 1:26); that image of which it is written: ‘Because Christ is the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance’ (Hebrews 1:3).
>
> “In this image I see the Father, as the Lord Jesus himself said: ‘Whoever has seen me has seen the Father’ (John 14:9). For this image is not separated from the Father; it taught me the unity of the Trinity when it said: ‘I and the Father are one.’ And further: ‘Everything that the Father has is mine’ (John 10:30; 16:15).
>
> “And concerning the Holy Spirit, he says that he is the Spirit of Christ and received from Christ, as it is written: ‘He will take from what is mine and declare it to you’ (John 16:14).
>
> “What then? Was not our answer humble? If he demands tribute, we do not refuse it: the fields of the Church pay tribute.”

And Saint Augustine, in his book *On Instructing Beginners in the Faith* (chapter 21):

> “The apostolic teaching also says,” he says, “that every soul must be subject to higher powers, and that everything must be rendered to everyone—to whom tribute, tribute, and so forth—which, while preserving the worship of our God, we render to the rulers of human government. The Lord himself, in order to provide us an example of this sound teaching, did not disdain to pay tribute for the human head with which he was clothed (Matthew 17:26).
>
> “Christian servants and good believers are also commanded to serve their temporal masters with patience and faithfulness (Ephesians 6:5)—masters whom they will judge if they find them enemies to the end, or with whom they will reign equally if those masters too are converted to the true Lord.
>
> “Nevertheless, everyone is commanded to serve human and earthly powers until, after the appointed period signified by the seventy years, the Church is liberated from the confusion of this age as from Babylonian captivity, like Jerusalem.”

And Saint Ambrose, in a sermon to the people (letter 13 to Marcellina):

> “It is alleged,” he says, “that everything is permitted to the emperor and that everything belongs to him. I reply: Do not burden yourself, emperor, by thinking that you possess any imperial right over divine things. Do not exalt yourself; but if you wish to rule for a longer time, be subject to God.
>
> “It is written: ‘The things that are God’s to God, and the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar’ (Matthew 22:21). Palaces belong to the emperor; churches belong to the priest. You have been entrusted with authority over public walls, not over sacred things.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX

And Saint Gelasius, in his letter (letter 10) to the emperor Anastasius:

> “There are,” he says, “two powers, august emperor, by which this world is principally ruled: the sacred authority of priests and royal power. Among these, the burden of priests is all the heavier, since they will give an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves.
>
> “For you know, most merciful son, that although by your dignity you preside over the human race, nevertheless you devoutly bow your neck to the leaders of divine matters and seek from them the causes of your salvation. In receiving the heavenly sacraments and in arranging them as is fitting, you recognize that you ought to be subject to them by the order of religion rather than preside over them.
>
> “You therefore know that in these matters you depend upon their judgment, not that they wish to be reduced to your will.”

And Saint Ambrose, in his sermon to the people concerning his persecution (letter 13):

> “I myself was summoned by counts and tribunes so that the basilica might be handed over promptly. They said that the emperor was exercising his right because everything was in his power.
>
> “I replied that if he sought what was mine—that is, my estate, my silver, or any such right of mine—I would not resist, although everything that is mine belongs to the poor. But divine things are not subject to imperial power.”

And in another sermon (*Oration against Auxentius*):

> “If anything of mine were demanded—an estate, a house, gold, silver, anything within my right—I would gladly offer it. But from the temple of God I can take away nothing, nor hand over what I received to guard, not to surrender.
>
> “Moreover, I am taking thought for the emperor’s welfare, because it would benefit neither me to hand it over nor him to receive it. Let him hear the voice of a free priest: if he wishes his own welfare, let him withdraw from injury to Christ.
>
> “These words are full of humility and, as I judge, full of the affection that a priest owes the emperor.”

## CHAPTER XL

In these statements of Blessed Ambrose, the canonical distinction concerning the possessions both of the bishop and of the Church must be observed.

For the sacred canons say that the things belonging to the Church are to be preserved with every care, a good conscience, and faith in God, who considers and judges all things. They are also to be administered according to the judgment and authority of the bishop to whom the people and the souls gathered within the Church have been entrusted.

What appears to belong to the Church must be made clear with the knowledge of the priests and deacons who are around the bishop himself, so that they know and are not ignorant of what belongs specifically to the Church, and so that nothing is hidden from them. Thus, if it should happen that the bishop departs from this world, the Church’s possessions, being clearly identified, will neither perish through neglect nor be seized under the pretext of Church property when they are proved to belong to the bishop personally.

For it is just and acceptable before God and human beings that a bishop leave his own possessions to whomever he wishes, while the things belonging to the Church are preserved for the Church itself, so that neither the Church suffers any disadvantage nor the bishop is proscribed under the pretext of Church property.

## CHAPTER XLI

And just as a bishop has the authority during his life to administer both his own possessions and those of the Church with proper discernment, so the possessions of a Church left vacant after the bishop’s death are ordered to be preserved intact by the steward for his episcopal successor.

For ecclesiastical property and resources are not in the power of emperors and kings to distribute, seize, or plunder, but to defend and protect. They are sanctuaries and the Lord’s inheritance, as we read in the pages of the sacred Scriptures of both the Old and the New Testament.

They are the vows of the faithful, the price of sins, and the patrimony of the poor. We are commanded to serve kings not only through the taxes and military payments owed by the Churches, but also through prayers, as Saint Augustine demonstrates in his book *The City of God* (book 19, chapters 26–27):

> “As long as the two cities remain mixed together”—namely, Jerusalem, which is the Church, and Babylon, which is worldly power—“we too make use of Babylon’s peace. Through it, the people of God are liberated by faith in such a way that for the time being they remain pilgrims among them.
>
> “For this reason the Apostle also admonished the Church to pray for its kings and for those in high positions, adding that we should lead a quiet and peaceful life with all piety and chastity.
>
> “And when the prophet Jeremiah foretold to the ancient people of God the captivity that was to come and divinely commanded them to go obediently into Babylon, serving their God even through this patience, he also urged them to pray for Babylon, saying: ‘In its peace shall be your peace’ (Jeremiah 29:7)—the temporal peace, of course, which is common to the good and the wicked.
>
> “But our own peace is here with God through faith, and forever it will be with him through sight.”

For this reason the Apostle Paul commands that prayers be offered even when rulers persecute the Church. For he says:

> “I urge, then, first of all, that supplications be made for all people, for kings, and for all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity” (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

Thus peace was given to the Church through them, although human weakness of thought might judge that prayer should not be made for those by whom the Church was suffering persecution, since the members of Christ were to be gathered from every kind of human being.

Therefore he adds and says:

> “For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:3–4).

## CHAPTER XLII

Finally, if our king, with God’s consent, returns, let us receive him with joy; let us episcopally admonish him afterward to attend to what is necessary for himself, the Church, and the kingdom; and let us rejoice together with him in his prosperity.

But if, which we do not wish, something else should occur by God’s judgment, while sincerely preserving devotion and the faith owed to him, let us say in our hearts and with our mouths to the Lord, as it is written:

> “The daughters of Judah rejoiced”—that is, of the most humble confession—“in all your judgments, Lord” (Psalm 96:8).

---

## VII. TO KING LOUIS THE STAMMERER

### Instruction of a New King for the Right Administration of the Kingdom

*(With the same author, from the Mainz edition of J. Busaeus.)*

To the glorious lord King Louis, perpetual salvation and life.

## CHAPTER I

Your Lordship commanded me to hurry to come to you because you wished to discuss with me matters concerning your own interests, the holy Church, and the kingdom. Therefore I offer you a humble and certain answer.

The holy Apostle says (Romans 15:4):

> “Whatever was written was written for our instruction.”

We read in ancient histories that often, when kings were established, discord arose among the leading men of the kingdom because some wished to claim the king’s appointment for themselves without the counsel of the others. This discord was not settled without difficulty.

We read that good kings, once established, appointed good counselors; and through good kings and good counselors the peoples of kingdoms possessed many benefits, while through bad kings and bad counselors the peoples of kingdoms suffered many evils.

## CHAPTER II

To offer you examples from more recent histories: when your great-great-grandfather Pippin fell ill with the illness from which he also died, he summoned the leading men of his kingdom to the monastery of Saint Denis and, with their counsel, arranged how, after him, his sons Carloman and Charles, who were with him, should govern his kingdom peacefully.

After he died and was buried with great devotion, Carloman came to Soissons and Charles to Noyon. On the fifteenth day after his death, they were raised to the kingship by the counsel and assistance of the leading men of the kingdom, and each of the kingdom’s leading men went to his own king without any dispute.

About three years later, when Carloman died at Salmontiacum, Charles came to Corbeny, and the leading men of the kingdom who had been with Carloman gathered there to him, except for a few, about whom there is no need to speak now.

## CHAPTER III

When the emperor Charles died and was buried at the palace of Aachen, the leading men of the kingdom who had been with him sent to your grandfather Louis, who was in Teutwald.
