On the thirtieth day after his father’s death he came to Aachen and, with the counsel of the leading men of the kingdom, peacefully arranged the kingdom, until, when a matter arose that ought not now to be mentioned, discord arose between him and his sons. Because of it, a large part of the kingdom’s leading men went with Lothair into Lombardy.

## CHAPTER IV

When the emperor Louis, your grandfather, died, certain leading men of this kingdom summoned Lothair and the leading men who were with him from Lombardy into this kingdom.

Some of the kingdom’s leading men were with Charles, your father, and some with Louis, your uncle. Meanwhile, the leading men of the kingdom who were with the three brothers began to compete individually for honors, each seeking to obtain greater and more numerous advantages.

They disregarded the oaths made concerning the division of the kingdom and competed more for their own greed than for the safety of their lords and themselves, or for the peace of the holy Church and the people. Those who were with Lothair induced him to disinherit his brothers and to reduce to nothing the leading men of the kingdom who were with them, because he was the firstborn and bore the imperial title.

Those who were with Charles and Louis, however, said that their lords were Lothair’s brothers, that the kingdom had been divided among them by oath, and that they were neither inferior in birth nor in power to those who were with Lothair. Therefore they should not yield to them.

From this, many and great evils increased in the land, until among men related by blood and Christians there came to pass at Fontenoy such a great evil and danger as had not occurred among Christians since the time when Charles first fought with Ragenfred at Vincy.

Yet peace did not come to the kingdom because of the slaughter that took place at Fontenoy. That misery remained among the Christian people and their blood relatives until, whether they wished it or not, both the lords and the leading men of the kingdom divided the kingdom into three parts and confirmed by oath that this division should be permanent.

## Chapter V

After Lothar’s death, his sons divided his kingdom among themselves. While they were still alive, an agreement had therefore been made by oath between your father and your uncle Louis. But after Lothar’s son Lothar had died, following many disputes a division was made between your father and your uncle Louis concerning Lothar’s portion of the kingdom. After Louis, Lothar’s brother, had died in Lombardy, your father was asked by his brother and by his brother’s sons to surrender a portion of that kingdom. As a result, while Louis was still alive, and also in the preceding year, such miseries arose as are known to you; and this year there has occurred such a grievous disaster that throughout almost the whole world, and in times to come, it will rightly be a reproach.

## Chapter VI

For this reason it seems to my insignificance that it is your responsibility to attend, as far as you can, to the histories of former times, lest at the beginning of your reign discord should arise among the leading men of the kingdom concerning your rule, a discord that could not be settled without serious hindrance. Let the leading men of the kingdom who are with you so moderate themselves and their desires that they do not, through their greed or negligence, provoke the other leading men of this kingdom to scandal. This is especially important since you have no brother to whom the people might divide themselves, just as they did not divide themselves after the death of Emperor Charles, but united themselves with Louis, his only son.

For if those good barons, after Pippin’s death, acted with such sound counsel toward the two brothers that peace might exist between the royal brothers, the leading men of the kingdom, and the people, then much more easily, unless envy and greed intervene, will they be able, with God’s help, to come with you to God’s will and to their own salvation. They should bear in mind how great a misery arose from the discord that occurred among the three brothers after the death of Emperor Louis.

## Chapter VII

You know that your father first made arrangements at Rheims with the leading men of his kingdom concerning your establishment after him in the government of the kingdom. As I recall, almost all the leading men of the kingdom were present there, except the venerable Abbot Hugh and Bernard, Count of Auvergne; and all consented, according to your father’s arrangement, to your royal establishment.

When he most recently made arrangements concerning this matter at Quierzy and gave you a written list of the men by whose counsel and assistance you were to conduct the affairs of the kingdom—including Boso, who was also entered on the list—all were present except Boso himself, Abbot Hugh, and Bernard, Count of Auvergne. All who were present consented to your royal establishment, as did those who departed with your father.

Therefore send without delay to Abbots Hugh and Gozlin, and to Boso, Conrad, and Bernard, and likewise to Bernard, the counts; and ask them to arrange a place, wherever they may think most convenient, for you and for those who are in these regions, as well as for those who are in the other regions, and to inform you that you are to come there with the leading men who are in these regions.

Let each of them assemble in such a way that the kingdom is neither plundered nor devastated, so that by common counsel you may deliberate about the common necessity and advantage: namely, how those articles which your father recently announced at Quierzy may be brought to completion. In the meantime, reread them yourselves and those who are with you, and store them in your minds.

## Chapter VIII

I also believe that your father, after learning that he could not recover from his illness, did not fail to give you particular instructions concerning the government of the kingdom—matters which he knew to be in accordance with God’s will, the condition of the holy Church, your honor and that of the leading men of the kingdom, and the need and advantage of the people.

Therefore it is necessary, and it seems good, that those who were with him should also be present, and that all should deliberate together about the common need and advantage. I too, although the least among them, and weak and infirm, will gladly assemble, with the Lord’s assent, in the service of God and of you, and in their service; and if I am able to contribute anything useful, I shall do so willingly, because it is necessary for you to deliberate and make arrangements together with God’s and your faithful servants.

First, you must determine how you may remain in the government of the kingdom with honor and safety, and with provision for what is necessary, together with your kingdom and household.

Second, how the article recently proclaimed by your father at Quierzy concerning the honor of the holy Church and the rightful privilege of priests and servants of God may be brought to completion; and how the churches in this kingdom may not be oppressed by irregular *circadae* and by unlawful customary exactions, which did not exist in the time of Pippin, Charles, and Louis and which were imposed twenty years ago.

Third, how the leading men of the kingdom may remain with due security and honor toward you, and how the other noblemen in the kingdom may have security, so that by various devices they are not stripped of whatever resources they may have been able to possess. For after greed—the root of all evils—blazed up in this kingdom, so that no one, or almost no one, could acquire, retain, or securely possess honor or any good without payment, peace and counsel, justice and judgment did not have their proper place in this kingdom.

Fourth, you must discover with God’s and your faithful servants how these acts of robbery and plunder may cease in this kingdom, and how this wretched people—who for many years have been afflicted by diverse and continual plundering and by exactions for repelling the Northmen—may obtain some remedy; and how justice and judgment, which among us are almost dead, may revive, so that God may restore strength to us against the pagans. For until now, for many years, defense has had no place in this kingdom, but only ransom and tribute; and not only poor men, but also churches once rich, have been emptied.

Fifth, you must strive, as far as you can, to establish and preserve among God’s faithful and your own faithful servants the concord that is according to God, of which your father recently spoke at Quierzy, and prepare yourself toward them in such a way that they may be able and willing to give you true counsel. For, as I have heard from many people, much of the kingdom’s welfare has been lost because counselors did not dare to say what they knew to be good and useful, nor had an opportunity to say it.

No one is so wise that he does not need another’s counsel, as it is written: “The wise man who listens will become wiser, and the intelligent man will possess the means of governance; but he who trusts in his own thoughts will act wickedly” (Prov. 1:5; 12:2).

Sixth, you must discover with God’s and your faithful servants how you may have peace and friendship according to God with your cousins, the sons of your uncle, and how you may provide one another mutual assistance in accordance with God’s will, for the honor of the holy Church and of yourselves, and for the common salvation of your faithful servants.

## Chapter IX

But how these matters may be brought to completion, and how the other necessities may be found and attained, must be sought from God, who promises every devout person: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask it of God, and it will be given him” (James 1:5). He also says: “I will show you, O man, what is good and what God requires of you: namely, to do judgment and justice, and to walk carefully with your God” (Mic. 6:8).

Justice must be done, not for any earthly profit, but for the very reason that it is justice, as it is written: “You shall faithfully carry out what is just and right” (Deut. 16:20). Judgment must be rendered for the correction of the wicked and for the setting right of those who suffer injury, not for the revenge of ill will, nor for the oppression of those who have a just cause.

For those who judge unjustly do not render judgment—that is, something spoken according to law and right—but prejudice. Hence, as the Lord says, those who judge unjustly will be condemned by a just judgment.

Everyone must walk carefully with his God, and especially a king, who in the future age will be subjected to punishments as great as the number of those over whom he was powerful in this age, if he has been wicked, has not corrected himself from evil, has not done judgment and justice, and has not walked carefully with his God.

Just as a subject walks carefully with his lord, so that he may do what pleases that lord according to God for salvation, and according to the world for honor and advancement—and, if he does anything displeasing to his lord, hastens at once to correct it so that he may return to the lord’s favor—so it is necessary for you to walk carefully with your lord, the King of kings. Concerning past actions that you have done against his will, you must make satisfaction to him through confession, contrition of heart, and good works, and henceforth you must not turn away from his commands.

And if through frailty you should fall in some matter, then, like one who slips with one foot and supports himself with the other foot or with his hand in order to recover, strive again through devotion and good works to return to the favor of your lord, God. For the Lord tolerates sinners who do not repent for a long time, so that they may convert, but he condemns those who do not convert more harshly.

You can also hear and see this in your own time; you must fear and beware lest similar things happen to you. Present yourselves toward divine worship, the holy Church, priests and servants of God, and all your other faithful servants who remain in every condition, and toward the people entrusted to you by God, in such a way that they love you and are pleased to offer you their due service wherever it is necessary for you to receive it, both in spiritual service and in temporal assistance.

Let the Christian religion and humility of heart please you more than empty pomp and the pleasures of the flesh. For no matter how many masses of silver and gold surround the flesh, and no matter what precious garments clothe it, what else is it than flesh—that is, corruption, the worm, son of man, dust, and ashes?

Do not take as much pleasure in hunting wild beasts as in fighting against the pleasures of the flesh and against the enemies of God and of his holy Church, both bodily and spiritual. For as the Lord says through the Apostle: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). And: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual wickedness” (Eph. 6:12).

Do not let the riches of possessions—gold, silver, and gems—delight you so much that you are counted among those who worship idols, since, as the Apostle says, “Greed is the service of idols” (Col. 3:5); rather, let faith, hope, and charity, justice, truth, and righteous judgment delight you, for these lead the person who perseveres in them to the eternal kingdom and the fellowship of the angels.

## Chapter X

What I would now say in person to your lordship, if I were physically present, I suggest in writing. Concerning general matters of the Church and the affairs of the kingdom, I do not know how to give particular counsel, nor am I able or presume to deliberate about consent, without the general counsel and agreement of the leading men of the kingdom.

Therefore, since I am already worn down by age, illness, and weakness, it is not necessary for your lordship to impose upon me that I labor without cause before God’s faithful servants and yours assemble at your pleasure. Then, with the Lord’s favor, I shall come, in whatever way I am able, as I have said, in the service of God and of you, and in their service.

But if, God forbid, some cause of disturbance should arise in the meantime, and it should please your lordship to inform me of it, I shall faithfully labor in your service, to the best of my knowledge and ability, with counsel and assistance.

[Col. 0989]

# VIII. To Emperor Charles III: That He Establish Suitable Tutors and Counselors for the Sons of His Cousin Louis the Stammerer, the Kings

*(In the same author, from the same source.)*

[Col. 0989C]

Hincmar, bishop and servant of God’s people, wishes to the glorious lord Emperor Charles present and future prosperity and glory.

Having heard of your laudable faith and kindness toward the sons of your cousin Louis, formerly our lord, I rendered thanks to God, asking that he who gave you the will may grant you to complete what you have begun according to his good pleasure. Through me, and through the servants and subjects entrusted to me, I also ask the mercy of the Lord that your power and prosperity may be strengthened in accordance with his will, and that, having persevered in right faith and good works, he may one day lead you from the temporal kingdom to the eternal one.

## Chapter I

We ask, dearest lord, that, with regard to God, your helper and protector in government, you restore by your wise counsel and the assistance of your power the Church of this kingdom, which Christ acquired with his blood and which is spread throughout the whole world but has fallen into ruin among us in many respects. Consolidate the division of the kingdom, join its leading men together, and have removed the wrongful acts that are carried out in this kingdom because of dissensions.

Treat these young men, our kings, your relatives, and fatherless wards, as sons. Through the advice of the leading men of this kingdom, administer to them the kingdom handed down to them by succession from their ancestors, and appoint from among the leading men those who are suitable for each of them.

If there should perhaps be some among our own people who prefer to do what accords with their own will rather than what concerns the honor and defense of the holy Church and its ministers, and the peace and tranquility of the kings and the kingdom, recall them by your wisdom and power—or, if necessary, restrain them. Toward foreigners who oppose these sons of yours and all of us who are faithful to your lordship, provide the protection of your support, so that you may receive from God the reward due for this and possess a distinguished name in this world.

## Chapter II

We read of Alexander the Great, whose tutor was named Leonides, that in his childhood Alexander had a hasty character and an improper gait, and from that tutor he acquired the same faults, which, when he had grown up, he wished to correct in himself. Although he conquered all kingdoms, he could not conquer himself in this respect, because, as a certain wise man wrote:

> Whatever scent a newly made vessel has once absorbed,  
> it will long preserve.  
> *(Horace, Book I, Epistle 2.)*

And we read concerning the son of King Solomon (1 Kings 12) that, rejecting the counsel of the elders and following that of the young men, he lost a large part of the kingdom; and the Lord preserved a small part of the kingdom for him, not on account of his own merit but on account of his grandfather David.

Therefore appoint for these faithful young sons of yours, our kings, mature, prudent, and sober tutors, one for each of them. Let them hate greed and teach the young men by word and example to love justice, according to Scripture: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. 1:1), since “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6).

[Col. 0991B]

## Chapter III

Let them teach them by word and example to honor the holy Church and its ministers, as Scripture says: “Humble your soul before the priests, and bow your head before the great” (Ecclus. 4:7). The Lord says to them: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). And: “Those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be insignificant” (1 Sam. 2:30).

Let them teach them by word and example to preserve the privileges due to the rulers and ministers of the holy Church, privileges established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, as Scripture teaches: “The law of the Lord is blameless, restoring souls; the testimony of the Lord is trustworthy, giving wisdom to the simple” (Ps. 19:7).

And in the Gospel the Lord says: “He who loves me keeps my commandments” (John 14:15). And: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (1 John 4—reference as printed). And the Apostle says: “He who says, ‘I love God,’ and does not keep his commandments, is a liar” (John 8:47—reference as printed).

Again, the Lord says in the Gospel to those who despise his commandments: “He who is from God hears the words of God. For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God.”

## Chapter IV

Let them teach them by word and example to preserve for the leading men of the kingdom, the other faithful of the kingdom, and the defenders of the holy Church the law and justice appropriate to each person in his own order, as Scripture says: “The justice of the king will exalt his throne, and the foundations of peoples are made firm by truth” (Prov. 1:16).

Let them guard them and teach them to live chastely, soberly, and devoutly, because, as Scripture says: “The holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding, and will not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1:5).

## Chapter V

Let them frequently set before them the words of Saint Cyprian, who clearly explains the king’s office in the ninth grade of abuses:

> “The king,” he says, “ought not to be an unjust man, but a corrector of the unjust. Therefore he must preserve in himself the dignity of his name. For the name ‘king’ intellectually retains this meaning: that he should provide the office of a ruler for all his subjects. But how will he be able to correct others if he does not correct his own conduct, so that it may not be unjust?
>
> “The justice of a king is not to oppress anyone unjustly through power; to judge without respect of persons between one man and his neighbor; to be a defender of strangers, orphans, and widows; to restrain thefts; to punish adulteries; not to exalt the wicked; not to support the shameless and the performers; to destroy the impious from the land; not to allow parricides and perjurers to live; to defend the churches; to nourish the poor with alms; to appoint just men over the affairs of the kingdom; to have as counselors old, wise, and sober men; not to heed the superstitions of magicians, diviners, and prophetesses; to postpone anger; to defend his country bravely and justly against adversaries; to live entirely in God; not to let prosperity lift up his spirit; to bear every adversity patiently; to have Catholic faith in God; not to allow his sons to act impiously; to devote himself to prayers at appointed hours; and not to taste food before the proper hours.
>
> “Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccles. 10). These things bring prosperity to the kingdom in the present and lead the king to better heavenly kingdoms. But whoever does not administer the kingdom according to this law will certainly endure many adversities of the empire.”

If a king thinks or acts contrary to what has been prescribed, and persists in these contrary ways, then, just as he has been placed first among men on the throne, so he will have all the sinners whom he had beneath him in this present life above him in that future punishment, in a manner that cannot be appeased.

Not only a king, but everyone who possesses ruling power, must necessarily have three things: fear, order, and love. For unless the lord is loved and feared, his order cannot stand at all. Therefore, through benefits and affability, let him ensure that he is loved; and through just vengeance—not vengeance for a personal injury, but for the law of God—let him strive to be feared.

In these matters and in all others, let the ruler always think of God and cling to him. For unless he clings steadfastly to his creator, both he and all who consent to him will quickly perish.

Therefore let everyone who rules first strive with the whole intention of his heart not to doubt God’s assistance in anything. For if he begins to have the Lord as his helper in his actions, no human being will be able to hold his rule in contempt. “There is no authority except from God.” He raises the needy from the dung heap and makes him sit with the princes of his people. He casts down the powerful from their seat and exalts the humble.

## Chapter VI

The tutors themselves must take great care not to exalt themselves above their companions, but, according to Scripture: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclus. 3:20).

And we read concerning Jehoiada that he raised up the child King Joash and anointed him king (2 Kings 12:2), placing a diadem on him and giving the law into his hand, so that he might live according to it and rule the people. He taught the young king until he reached adulthood. It is written of him that Joash reigned well for as long as Jehoiada taught him.

Saint Gregory also (Book VI, Letter 23) admonishes the tutors of the sons of the Greek emperors to speak to them of those things that will unite their minds in love toward one another and in gentleness toward their subjects, lest, if the boys conceive hatred toward one another, it later burst forth openly.

“Let the words of those who nurture them,” he says, “be either milk, if they are good, or poison, if they are bad. Therefore let them suggest to the boys in childhood such things as will later show how good were the things they drank in from the mouths of their tutors.”

## Chapter VII

They must also take care that such persons are not joined to them in intimacy that, through their suggestions, the boys’ hearts may be drawn toward wicked works or toward discord among themselves and with their subjects, because it is written: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33).

Their tutors must persuade them not to envy or provoke one another, but to be joined by mutual love and ready to assist one another, because, as it is written: “Let brother help brother, and both will be comforted” (Prov. 18:19).

If, my lord king, the Church of this kingdom, its ministers, and its people obtain these things through you, you can judge from the words of the Apostle what great reward and recompense you will have with God, and what a good name you will have in this world. He says: “He who converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:20).

If, then, the Apostle, filled with the Spirit of God, promises so great a reward for one sinner converted, let your wisdom calculate how great a reward you will have with God for the salvation and advancement of so many.

[Col. 0993]

# IX. To the Leading Men of the Kingdom, for the Instruction of King Carloman, and Concerning the Order of the Palace

*(From Adalard, in the same author.)*

[Col. 0993B]

Hincmar, bishop and servant of God’s people.

## Chapter I

Because of my seniority in age and sacred order, you good and wise men, who come later in time, ask my insignificance to demonstrate, for the instruction of this young man and our present king, and for the restoration of the honor and peace of the Church and kingdom, the ecclesiastical order and the arrangement of the royal household in the sacred palace, as I have heard and seen them.

I took part in ecclesiastical and palatine affairs when they were being conducted successfully in the greatness and unity of the kingdom. I heard the counsels and teaching of those who ruled the holy Church in holiness and justice, as well as of those who in an earlier period arranged the stability of the kingdom more successfully. Through their instruction I learned the tradition of their ancestors. After the death of our lord Emperor Louis, I also labored, according to my limited ability, through frequent journeys, words, and writings, in the service of those who at that time worked for concord among his sons, our kings.

I have been asked to set these matters forth so that, at the beginning of his reign, this young man may be imbued with such instruction that he may please God in governing the kingdom, reign happily in this world, and be able to pass from the present kingdom to the eternal one.

Experience teaches us that a new vessel will long retain the taste and smell with which it was first imbued, as a certain wise man says:

> Whatever scent a newly made vessel has once absorbed,  
> it will long preserve.  
> *(Horace, Book I, Epistle 2.)*

We also read (Quintilian, Book I, chapter 1) that Alexander in his childhood had a tutor named Leonides, notable for hasty manners and an undisciplined gait, and that, like a boy drinking adulterated milk, he absorbed these traits from him. Therefore, when he had grown up, he reproached himself as a wise and powerful king and wished to avoid them; but, as we read, although he conquered every kingdom, he could not conquer himself in this matter.

[Col. 0994B]

## Chapter II

Let the lord king understand to what office he has been elevated, and let him obey the admonition and warning of the King of kings, who says to him, together with the other kings:

> “And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling. Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right way.”

We read, hear, and even know from our own time that many who neglected this admonition and warning have perished.

Let him also obey holy Scripture, which commands him: “Love justice, you who judge the earth. Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart; for wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1:1).

[Col. 0994C]

## Chapter III

For the ministry imposed upon me, and in obedience to your good and reasonable command, I shall undertake to carry out what you ask—not according to my own judgment or in my own words, but, as I stated above, according to the tradition of our ancestors, attending to what the Lord says to the prophet:

> “But you, after hearing, shall announce to them from me” (Ezek. 3:17).

“From me,” he says, “and not from yourself,” because, as he himself says: “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John 7:18).

Holy Scripture commands every administrator, in every order and profession, to understand all that he says. For if he understands from where the administration he holds began, he will strive more diligently, knowing that he will have to render an account of the talent entrusted to him: “For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may report what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (Rom. 14:10).

Let him not hear from the just judge what the Lord declares in the Gospel that he will say to the wicked and lazy servant. Rather, let him deserve to hear:

> “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25:21).

[Col. 0995A]

## Chapter IV

We read in the sacred Scripture of the Old Testament that King David, who was also a prophet and prefigured our Lord Jesus Christ—the only one who could be both king and priest—established two orders among the priests: namely, the highest pontiffs and the priests of the lesser order, who now perform the office of presbyters.

He made this provision so that, whenever any pontiff departed this life, whichever priest was considered the best might succeed him in the pontificate.

In the New Testament, our Lord Jesus Christ chose twelve from the multitude of his disciples, as we read in the Gospel, and called them Apostles. Bishops hold their place in the Church, as sacred Scripture and Catholic teachers show.

[Col. 0995B]

He also appointed seventy-two others (Luke 6:13), who under the twelve Apostles prefigured the presbyters—that is, the priests of the second order. Thus, when bishops depart this life, men from among these priests of the second and lower order may, according to the sacred canons established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, be raised to the summit of the high priesthood in place of the deceased bishops.

Sacred Scripture plainly shows this in the Acts of the Apostles. Peter said to his fellow disciples when Judas, who had been numbered among the Apostles and had received his share in the ministry of apostleship, went to his own place:

> “Therefore, of the men who have accompanied us during the whole time in which the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, one of these must become with us a witness of his resurrection” (Acts 1:21).

And divine election fell upon Matthias, who was numbered with the eleven Apostles.

## Chapter V

In the sacred history of Kings we also read that, when the chief priests consecrated kings to the kingdom with sacred anointing, they placed upon their heads a crown signifying victory and gave the law into the king’s hand, so that he might know how he ought to govern himself, correct the wicked, and direct the good in the right way.

Therefore, as Blessed Pope Gelasius demonstrates from the sacred Scriptures to the Emperor Anastasius (Letter 10), and as is contained in the matters recently conducted at the synod by the shrine of Saint Macra, there are two principal powers by which this world is governed, together with the particular care of those subject to each: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and royal power.

Just as the names of the orders are divided between these persons, so the duties of governance are divided within each order and profession. Therefore each person must carefully attend to the name by which he is designated in his order and profession, and must take great care not to differ in conduct from his name.

“For first,” as Blessed Cyprian says (*On Abuses*, chapter 10), “the bishop must inquire what the dignity of his name signifies, since *bishop*, being a Greek name, is interpreted as ‘watchman.’ Why, however, is he appointed as a watchman, and what is required of a watchman? The Lord himself discloses this when, under the person of the prophet Ezekiel, he announces to the bishop the account of his office, saying: ‘I have appointed you as a watchman over the house of Israel’ (Ezek. 3:17).”

The duty of a watchman is to announce continually to the people entrusted to him, by example and word, how they ought to live. Thus it is written of Christ, who commands that people follow him—that is, imitate him: “The things that Jesus began to do and teach” (Acts 1:1).

He must therefore watch attentively over the life and conduct of those entrusted to him; and after observing them, correct them by speech, if he can, and by action. If he cannot, then, according to the evangelical rule, he must avoid the workers of wickedness.

## Chapter VI

The king must also preserve in himself the dignity of his name. For the name “king” intellectually retains this meaning: that he should provide the office of a ruler for all his subjects. But how will he be able to correct others if he does not correct his own conduct so that it may not be unjust? For “the justice of the king exalts his throne, and peoples’ foundations are made firm by truth.”

Blessed Cyprian, in the ninth grade of abuses, shows sufficiently what the king’s justice is.

## Chapter VII

The priestly order has laws promulgated by God concerning how each person ought to come to the summit of government, namely the episcopate; how, after reaching it correctly, he ought to live; how, after living well, he ought to teach; and how, after teaching correctly, he ought daily and with what degree of reflection to recognize his own weakness.

These laws also prescribe how he ought to govern the ministers placed beneath him; with what purity of intention he ought to administer the sacred ecclesiastical orders; and with what discretion he ought to bind or loose his subjects.

Concerning these laws it is written in the same source (Celestine, Letter 3):

> “No priest is permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers. For one does not offend against the sanctions of sacred traditions less than one rushes into an injury against the Lord himself.”

This is so because, as sacred authority demonstrates, schism and heresy are related—as if it were said in other words: the schismatic who, through contempt and transgression of the sacred rules, separates himself from the unity of the holy Church, which is the body of Christ, sins no less than the heretic who thinks wrongly about God, the head of that Church.

## Chapter VIII

And just as it was said concerning ecclesiastical laws that no priest is permitted to be ignorant of his canons or to do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers, so sacred laws decree that no one may be ignorant of the laws or despise what has been established.

When it is said that no one may be ignorant of the laws or despise what has been established, no person in any worldly order is exempt from being bound by this sentence.

Kings and ministers of the commonwealth have laws by which they must govern those living in whatever province. They have the Capitularies of Christian kings and of their ancestors, which they have legally promulgated with the general consent of their faithful subjects and ordered to be observed.

Concerning these laws Blessed Augustine says (*On True Religion*, chapter 31): although people judge concerning them when they establish them, once they have been established and confirmed, judges are no longer permitted to judge the laws themselves, but must judge according to them.

## Chapter IX

Much less, however, is it permitted to a king or to anyone in any station to act contemptuously against the divine laws. Therefore the ruler of the land must take the greatest care and precaution lest God be offended in those through whom the Christian religion ought to stand firm and the others be preserved from offense. And since he has undertaken, by divine judgment, to protect and defend ecclesiastical property, with his consent, through the election of the clergy and people and the approval of the bishops of the province, each person is to be advanced to ecclesiastical government without any buying or selling; for, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1).

He must favor the ecclesiastical regulations in every way and without difficulty, if he does not wish to offend the King of kings. And just as the bishops and the king must ensure that no bishop is chosen for any consideration except God alone—that is, neither for any monetary gift, nor for any human service, nor because of blood relationship, friendship, temporal service, or any circumstance that could be contrary to the truth or to divine authority—so the king must guard himself, as Saint Augustine demonstrates (*City of God*, book V, chapter 24), lest he be enticed by the gifts or flatteries of any criminal person and deceived by adulation. Nor should he spare, out of carnal affection, those joined to him by any ties of kinship who act perversely against God, holy Church, and the commonwealth, since the Spirit of God says through the prophet David:

“Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and do I not waste away over your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me” (Psalm 138:21–22).

To hate the enemies of God with perfect hatred means to love in them what they were made for, and to rebuke what they do; to restrain the conduct of the wicked and to benefit their life.

## Chapter X

He must also appoint as counts and subordinate judges men who hate greed and love justice, and they must carry out their administration under this condition; they must likewise appoint subordinate officials of this kind.

“And all who are placed in authority in every rank and profession, and are called lords, must hold the virtue of authority with the Lord as its author and co-worker, as Saint Cyprian demonstrates in the sixth degree of the Book of Abuses (chapter 6). For it is of no benefit to possess the power of ruling if the lord himself does not also possess the firmness of virtue.

“But this firmness of virtue does not so much require outward strength—which is itself necessary for secular lords—as it must be exercised through the inner strength of the soul and good morals. For often the strength of ruling is lost through negligence of the soul. Those who rule must therefore have three things: namely, fear, order, and love. Unless a lord is both loved and feared, his order can scarcely endure.

“Through benefits and affability, therefore, he should arrange to be loved; and through just punishments—not for personal injury, but for the law of God—he should strive to be feared. Moreover, since many depend upon him, he must cling to God, who appointed him to leadership and made him, as the stronger one, firm enough to bear the burdens of many. For unless a stake is securely fixed and attached to something stronger, everything hanging upon it quickly slips away; and the stake itself, loosened from the firmness of its stability, falls to the ground together with its burdens. So also, unless a ruler clings steadfastly to his Creator, both he himself and everything he contains quickly perish.”

And let him know that just as he has been placed first in the government of men, so, unless he corrects both himself and those sinners whom he has under him in the present life, he will have them above him in an implacable manner in the punishment of the future.

## Chapter XI

In the acts previously mentioned, held at the shrine of Saint Macra, there is contained, in brief and beneficial chapters, material gathered from Catholic promulgations according to the course of the sacred Scriptures and from the constitutions of Christian kings. It concerns what relates to the honor and strength of holy Church and its rulers, what relates to the stability and care of the king and kingdom, and also the arrangement of the royal household—provided that these things are observed and carried out.

Nevertheless, because the Samaritan—the true guardian of the human race—gave two denarii, namely the Old and New Testaments, to the innkeeper, that is, to the priestly order, to whose care he had entrusted the wounded man for healing, and said, “Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return” (Luke 10:35), I strive to add to those same acts, as though from surplus labor, the matters set forth above in this little work and those that will follow.

## Chapter XII

In my youth I saw the old and wise Adalhard, a relative of the Emperor Charles the Great and abbot of the monastery of Corbie, among the foremost of the chief counselors. I read and copied his little book on the order of the palace, in which, among other things, it is stated that the condition of the entire kingdom consisted principally in two divisions, with the judgment of almighty God always and everywhere placed first.

He said that the first division was that by which the king’s palace was continually and unfailingly governed and ordered; the second was that by which the condition of the entire kingdom was preserved with the greatest diligence, each matter being considered according to its nature.

## Chapter XIII

In the first arrangement, therefore, the king’s palace was ordered as an ornament of the whole palace in this manner. With the king and queen, together with their most noble offspring, placed first in spiritual, secular, and bodily matters, it was governed at all times by these officials:

namely, by the *apocrisiarius*, that is, the respondent for ecclesiastical affairs. His office began at the time when the great emperor Constantine, having become a Christian, out of love and honor for the holy apostles Peter and Paul—through whose teaching and ministry he attained the grace of Christ in the sacrament of baptism—handed over his place and seat, namely the city of Rome, to Pope Sylvester by an edict of privilege, and built his own seat in his city, formerly called Byzantium, enlarging it as the city of his own name.

Thus representatives of both the Roman see and the other principal sees kept watch in the palace over ecclesiastical affairs.

## Chapter XIV

At times the apostolic see carried out this office through bishops, and at times through deacons. Saint Gregory held this office in the order of deacons; and from the other principal sees the office was likewise carried out through deacons, as the sacred canons command.

In these regions on this side of the Alps, after Clovis had been converted to Christ through the preaching of Saint Remigius and had been baptized by him, together with three thousand Franks, on the vigil of Holy Easter, holy bishops from their own sees, through successive generations of kings and at the appropriate time, visited the palace and in turn organized this administration.

From the time of Pippin and Charles, however, this office was sometimes carried out by presbyters and sometimes by bishops; by royal decision and episcopal consent, it was performed by deacons or presbyters rather than by bishops. For bishops must continually keep watch over their flock by example and word, and according to the sacred canons they must not remain away from their parishes for too long.

## Chapter XV

Nor, according to the decrees promulgated from the sacred canons of Saint Gregory, should the praetoria—now called royal residences, and more commonly palaces—be attended uselessly, lest they incur judgment and, by acting contrary to the canonical provisions handed down to them at their ordination, deprive themselves of ecclesiastical honor.

To give examples of what is lawful, and not remain silent about what has been unlawfully usurped: in the time of Pippin and Charles this office was carried out, with the consent of the bishops, by the presbyter Fulrad; in Charles’s time by the bishops Engelramn and Hildibald; and finally, in Louis’s time, by the presbyter Hilduin, after him by another presbyter, Fulco, and then by the bishop Drogo.

## Chapter XVI

The *apocrisiarius*, whom our people call the chaplain or guardian of the palace, governed all the palace clergy under his care and direction. Associated with him was the chief chancellor, formerly called the keeper of secrets. Subject to him were prudent, intelligent, and faithful men who wrote the royal commands without the corrupting sale of excessive greed and faithfully guarded the secrets entrusted to them.

After these, the sacred palace was arranged through the following officials: the chamberlain, the count of the palace, the *seneschal*, the cupbearer, the count of the stable, the keeper of lodgings, four chief huntsmen, and one falconer.

## Chapter XVII

Although there were other officials under them and alongside them—such as the doorkeeper, treasurer, steward, *scapoardus*, and whatever younger men or deans belonged to these offices, as well as others serving alongside them, such as huntsmen, dog-keepers, beaver-keepers, or any who still remained—nevertheless, although each of these men was attentive to his own responsibility according to his rank, the entire association of the kingdom was not joined to the palace through them, as it was through the principal officials, in the greater and lesser daily necessities, as is set out below.

Nor could all the higher officials contribute equally, because of the diversity, nature, or suitability of their offices. Yet no one could or would withdraw himself, for the sake of preserving fidelity to the king and kingdom, as was stated above. Although many things could be said about their persons and offices, the following were especially observed.

## Chapter XVIII

First of all, according to the nature and extent of each office, a minister was to be chosen who was steadfast in noble heart and body, reasonable, discerning, and sober.

Nor was there any lack of concern that, if possible, since this kingdom by God’s authority consisted of many regions, the same ministers should be chosen from the various regions—whether for the first, second, or any other position—so that the several regions might approach the palace more familiarly when they knew that members of their own lineage or region held positions there.

## Chapter XIX

Having briefly discussed the selection and appointment of the aforementioned officials, we must now turn to the order in which those officials and their offices functioned.

Although the officials mentioned above, each in his own office, looked to no one as head except the king alone, and did so not under or through another but through himself—or, insofar as the queen or the king’s glorious offspring were concerned, looked to them—not all of them approached the king equally regarding other matters or the needs of others. Each was content with his own measure, and wherever reason required it, sought the assistance of another.

Among them, two in particular—the *apocrisiarius*, whom we call the chaplain or guardian of the palace, for all ecclesiastical affairs and ministers of the Church, and the count of the palace, for all secular cases and judgments—were especially responsible for receiving and handling such matters. Thus neither ecclesiastical nor secular persons needed to trouble the lord king without their advice, until they had considered whether the necessity was such that the case deserved to come before the king.

If the matter was secret, and it was more appropriate to tell it first to the king than to anyone else, they prepared for that person a place in which to speak. The king was first brought in, so that he might receive the matter according to the character of the person—honorably, patiently, or even mercifully.

## Chapter XX

The *apocrisiarius* was responsible for all ecclesiastical religion and order, as well as for canonical or monastic disputes and for whatever persons came to the palace on ecclesiastical business. From outsiders he was to bring before the king only those matters that could not be fully settled without him.

Moreover, not only in matters that specifically concerned the ecclesiastical ornament or office to be performed within the palace, but also in every kind of spiritual consolation or counsel that anyone in the palace might seek, he was to ensure that they found faithful assistance with him as necessity required. If someone did not seek such help, but he himself perceived that the person needed it, he was to strive, according to that person’s rank, both to withdraw him from wicked thought or action and to turn him toward the way of salvation.

All other spiritual matters that needed to be provided for and anticipated in the palace—whether for those who were constantly present or for newcomers, whether according to God or according to worldly affairs—belonged especially to his care. To enumerate them would be lengthy.

This did not mean that no palace resident or outside visitor, illuminated by God’s grace with wisdom and true devotion, should undertake such a matter independently. Rather, it was chiefly customary that a person act either together with the *apocrisiarius* himself or on the basis of his advice concerning what ought to be done, lest he unwittingly impose upon the king something less useful or unworthy.

## Chapter XXI

Among the count of the palace’s almost innumerable duties, his chief concern was to determine justly and reasonably all royal disputes that had arisen elsewhere and had reached the palace for a judgment of equity, or to restore wrongly decided cases to the path of equity, so that he might please everyone before God on account of justice and before men on account of observance of the laws.

If something arose for which the worldly laws had no established provision in their definitions, or if it had been sanctioned more harshly according to the custom of the pagans than Christian rectitude or holy authority rightly permitted, the matter was brought before the king for moderation. He was then to decide and establish it together with those who knew both laws and feared the statutes of God more than human laws, so that wherever both could be preserved, both would be preserved. But if that was impossible, the law of the world was rightly restrained and the justice of God preserved.

## Chapter XXII

Responsibility for the propriety of the palace, especially its royal adornment, and also for the annual gifts to the soldiers—apart from food, drink, and horses—belonged chiefly to the queen and, under her, to the chamberlain.

According to the nature of each matter, it was their concern always to foresee future needs at the proper time, so that nothing would be lacking when required or fail to be available at the appropriate moment.

The gifts from the various embassies belonged to the chamberlain, unless, by order of the king, there was something that it was appropriate for the queen to discuss with him.

All these matters and similar ones had this purpose: that, freed as far as reasonably and honorably possible from every domestic or palatial concern, the lord king—continually entrusting his hope to almighty God—might always have his mind ready to order and preserve the condition of the entire kingdom.

## Chapter XXIII

It belonged to the three officials—the *seneschal*, the cupbearer, and the count of the stable—according to the nature and extent of each office, and with their common agreement, to ensure that they were not slow to give the necessary warnings concerning their respective responsibilities.

As quickly as possible, all the king’s agents were to know where and at what time the king would have to remain, and for how long, so that they could make the necessary arrangements and preparations. Otherwise, learning of it too late, when things were demanded at an unsuitable time or with excessive haste, the royal household might be oppressed through negligence and without necessity.

Although this concern belonged to the cupbearer and the count of the stable, it fell chiefly upon the *seneschal*, since everything else, apart from drink and the feeding of the horses, belonged to him.

The keeper of lodgings also took part in this. As his name indicates, it was especially his concern to ensure that both the aforementioned agents and the hosts knew in advance when and where the king would arrive, so that lodging preparations could be made at the proper time. Otherwise, by learning of it too late, either the household might incur offense through affliction at an unsuitable time, or the hosts might incur offense because of an inadequate reception, as though they had been unwilling to receive him properly, when in fact they had lacked the ability to do so.

## Chapter XXIV

Similarly, the four huntsmen and the fifth, the falconer, with the same unanimity, strove to give warnings according to the nature of the season, so that matters belonging to the care of their respective offices might be considered at the appropriate time and not too late: when so many or so many, when all or none, should be kept in the palace; when they should be sent outside, according to custom, to be reared until the proper time; or when they should be assigned for hunting and rearing at suitable times in designated places.

Both the matters within the palace and those outside it were always to be ordered with such measure and reason that whatever was useful would be present and whatever was not useful would not be present. For in these offices it is not easy to establish a fixed number of men, dogs, or birds. Therefore it remained to their judgment how many there should be and of what kinds.

The principle in all these matters was that the palace should never lack such officials, or such numbers of them, especially for the following needs and proprieties.

## Chapter XXV

First, so that whenever the greater officials in general, or the lesser officials individually, departed, the palace would always remain adorned with a suitable number of people, without which it could not reasonably and honorably exist, and would never be deprived of worthy counselors.

Also, so that whenever any embassy arrived, whether for reconnaissance or even for submission, all its members could be received honorably.

Second, so that one person’s counsel might report rectitude; a second might offer the consolation of mercy and kindness; and a third might provide a remedy through speech against cunning or rashness.

And so that, from every part of the kingdom, anyone who was desolate, bereaved, oppressed by another’s debt, suffocated by someone’s unjust accusation, or afflicted by anything similar—matters too lengthy now to enumerate, especially widows and orphans, whether of the higher or middle ranks—might always have someone at hand who could bring each case, according to the person’s need and condition and according to the mercy and compassion of the lords, before the ruler’s merciful ears.

## Chapter XXVI

Likewise, those who, because of long service, deserved to be rewarded, and a suitable opportunity arose in which none of the needy mentioned above would be deprived of assistance beyond measure, were to be recalled to the minds of the rulers according to their condition.

This was to be done not so much because the deserving persons themselves pressed their claims, but because those mentioned above required faithfulness and the fulfillment of what was owed, so that in them the first consideration would be to do what pleased God through justice and mercy.

In addition, those remaining in military service were thereby to be given the most certain assurance and steadfastness of faithful service. Finally, those living far away throughout the kingdom were to be shown joy and gladness.

If any official or counselor died, a suitable and useful replacement was to be appointed in his place.

## Chapter XXVII

So that the multitude that ought always to be present in the palace could persist without failing, it was supported by three orders.

The first consisted of soldiers free from official duties. With the kindness and care of their lords placed first—now by provisions, now by clothing, now by gold, now by silver, sometimes by horses or other adornments, frequently bestowed either specially or according to what time, reason, and order granted as a suitable power—they always received unfailing consolation and a mind more ardently inflamed for royal service.

The aforementioned chief officials competed in calling them, day after day, now one and now another, to their residences. They strove to provide for them not so much out of gluttonous appetite as out of genuine familiarity and affection, as far as each was able. Thus scarcely anyone remained for a week without being invited by someone for such a purpose.

## Chapter XXVIII

The second order consisted of assistants assigned appropriately to the individual offices. Each adhered to his own master; they honored and were honored, and, in their respective places, whenever opportunity arose, they received consolation by seeing or speaking with the Lord.

The third order likewise consisted, among both the greater and the lesser men, of boys or vassals. Each diligently sought to keep as many of these as he could govern and support without sin—that is, without robbery or theft.

Within these designated orders, apart from those who were constantly going to and returning from the palace, there was this pleasing advantage: they could always suffice even for an unexpected need if one suddenly arose. Nevertheless, as stated, the greater part of them always remained ready and willing, with joy and cheerfulness, because of the kindnesses mentioned above.

## Chapter XXIX

The second division, by which the condition of the entire kingdom was preserved—again with the judgment of almighty God placed first, as always and everywhere, insofar as human reason was concerned—was as follows.

The custom at that time was that two assemblies were held each year, not more frequently. One was held when the condition of the entire kingdom was ordered for the period of the coming year. Once arranged, it was changed by no event except the greatest necessity, which likewise affected the whole kingdom.

At this assembly the entire body of the greater men, both clergy and laymen, came together: the elders to arrange the counsel; the lesser men to receive that same counsel and sometimes to deliberate jointly, confirming it not by authority but through their own understanding or judgment.

## Chapter XXX

There was another assembly, held only with the elders and chief counselors, for the gifts that were to be distributed generally. At it they began to discuss the condition of the coming year, in case circumstances presented themselves that required advance planning; or in case, immediately after the preceding year had ended, some matter arose for which it was necessary to establish or provide something in advance.

For example, if truces had been pledged among the margraves in any part of the kingdom for a later date, they considered what should be done once those pledged terms had elapsed, whether the truces should be renewed or ended. They likewise considered the quarrels and peace threatening in the other regions, so that, according to what reason then required, if unrest necessarily had to be undertaken or endured in one place or another, tranquility could be arranged in the remaining regions.

When, through the counsel of these elders, they had considered from afar what action or order of action the future required, and when their decision had been reached, that decision was kept so completely unknown to all outsiders and under such silence until the next general assembly that it was as though it had neither been discovered nor discussed by anyone.

This was so that, if something had to be arranged within or outside the kingdom, no one who had foreknowledge of it could destroy it, render it useless, or turn it through some contrary stratagem into something more difficult to accomplish.

At the assembly itself, if circumstances required it—whether for the satisfaction of the other elders or not merely to calm but even to arouse the spirit of the peoples—the matter was presented as though nothing had previously been considered about it. It was then discovered anew through the counsel and agreement of those men, and, with God as guide, the plan was carried out with courage.

When the preceding year had thus been concluded, the second year was likewise arranged in the manner described.

## Chapter XXXI

As far as possible, counselors, both clerical and lay, were chosen who, first, according to their respective rank or office, feared God; and second, possessed such fidelity that, except for eternal life, they placed nothing before the king and kingdom—not friends, enemies, relatives, gift-givers, flatterers, irritators, sophists, or schemers, nor those who were wise only according to the wisdom of this age, which is hostile to God.

They were to know instead that wisdom and understanding by which they could not merely restrain, but utterly crush through just and upright wisdom, those who placed their confidence in the human cunning mentioned above.

The chosen counselors, together with the king, had established this principal rule among themselves: whatever they had discussed familiarly among themselves, whether concerning the condition of the kingdom or concerning any particular person, no one was to disclose without their consent to any member of his household or to anyone else.

The matter was to remain concealed or silent for as long as necessary—whether for one day, two days, or longer, for a year, or even permanently. For often, in such deliberations concerning some person, speech arises about something that must be done or avoided for the common good. If the person comes to know of it, he may be greatly disturbed, or—what is worse—driven to despair, or—most serious of all—turned toward disloyalty and rendered useless for every benefit that he might perhaps have performed in many ways. Yet it would have caused him no harm not to know that discussion.

What can happen in the case of one person can likewise happen with two, with a hundred, with a larger number, or even with one lineage or an entire province, if the matter is not handled with great caution.

## Chapter XXXII

The *apocrisiarius*, that is, the chaplain or guardian of the palace, and the chamberlain were always present. For this reason men were chosen or instructed with the greatest care, so that they would be worthy of attending.

Among the other officials, anyone who showed himself capable of being substituted honorably in this role, either immediately or in the future—now learning, and later giving counsel—was ordered, with the utmost concentration of mind, to attend to everything that was done: preserving what had been entrusted, learning what was unknown, and retaining what had been ordered and established.

Thus, if something arose outside or within the kingdom, or if something unexpected and therefore not previously considered was reported—and although it would less often be necessary to conduct a matter at a higher level of counsel, the appropriate time might nevertheless not be available for summoning the aforementioned counselors—the palace officials themselves, through God’s mercy and as a result of their continual familiarity with these matters, both in public councils and through domestic conversation, response, and consultation on this point, would be able, according to the nature of the matter or the time, either to give full advice about what should be done or at least to determine how the matter could be awaited or sustained until the appointed times with counsel and without any harm.

So much for the greater matters.

## Chapter XXXIII

With regard to lesser matters, or matters proper to the palace—that is, matters not generally pertaining to the kingdom, as we have said, but specifically concerning particular persons and especially affecting the palace—the lord of affairs could arrange them with those persons so clearly that not only would no harm arise from them, but any harm that had arisen or was threatening could usefully be mitigated, completely extinguished, or even rooted out.

If the matter was such that it called for speed, yet it could in some way be sustained until the general assembly, either without sin or without insult, they would know from the previously mentioned, greater practice how to advise its being sustained. They could meanwhile provide, pleasing to God and beneficial to the kingdom, an imitation of the wisdom of their predecessors.

When the aforementioned counselors were summoned to the palace, their chief concern was not to arrange particular or individual cases, nor even the cases of those who came because of disputes over property or laws, until, by the Lord’s mercy, they had arranged those matters that generally concerned the salvation or condition of the king and kingdom.

Only then, if the lord king ordered that something be reserved, would it be dealt with—something that could not have been determined by the count of the palace or by the others to whom it properly belonged without the counselors’ careful consideration.

## Chapter XXXIV

The aforementioned nobles, whether at one assembly or the other, and indeed the kingdom’s first senators, were not to appear to have been summoned without reason. Therefore, immediately by royal authority, the principal chapters that had either been discovered by the king through divine inspiration or had been reported to him from every direction after the nobles’ departure were disclosed to them for discussion and consideration.

After receiving these matters, they were given one day, two days, three days, or more, according to the weight of the affairs. Through messengers sent back and forth from the palace household, they asked about whatever seemed appropriate and received answers.

They continued in this way, with no outsider approaching, until the individual matters had been brought to completion and laid before the glorious ruler’s hearing and sacred presence. Whatever his God-given wisdom chose, they all followed.

Thus, whether one chapter, two, or however many were involved, the process continued until, by God’s mercy, everything necessary for that time had been brought to completion.

## Chapter XXXV

While these matters were being conducted in the king’s absence, the ruler himself was occupied with the remainder of the multitude: receiving gifts, greeting the nobles, speaking with those whom he saw less frequently, showing compassion to the elders, rejoicing with the younger men, and attending to other similar matters, both spiritual and secular.

Nevertheless, whenever the separated group wished it, he came to them; and likewise, he remained with them for as long as they desired. With complete familiarity they reported to him how they had found each matter, and they recounted more openly how they had debated, disputed, or contended amicably with one another.

Nor should we omit how, when the weather was clear, separate places were arranged outside, and when it was not, inside, so that the separated group could sit apart in abundance and the rest of the multitude separately. The lower-ranking persons, however, could not initially be present.

These two reception areas for the elders were divided in such a way that first all the bishops, abbots, and other more honored clergy were gathered without any mixture of laymen. Likewise, the counts and other such leaders were honorably separated from the remaining multitude early in the morning, until the appropriate time arrived, whether the king was present or absent.

Then the elders mentioned above were summoned in the customary manner: the clergy to their designated court and the laymen to theirs, with benches likewise honorably prepared.

Once separated from the others, it remained in their power to decide when they would sit together and when separately, according to what the nature of the matter under discussion taught them, whether it concerned spiritual affairs, secular affairs, or both.

Similarly, if they wished to summon anyone for any reason of eating or investigation, and that person departed after the matter had been discovered, the decision remained in their hands.

This is what may be said for the time being about the matters proposed to them by the king for discussion.

## Chapter XXXVI

The king’s second procedure was to ask what each person brought with him from the part of the kingdom from which he had come that was worthy of being reported or reconsidered. They were not merely permitted but more strictly charged to investigate this with the greatest diligence until their return, both within and outside the kingdom.

Each person was to investigate whether there was anything of this kind not only among his own people or outsiders, but among friends as well as enemies, without meanwhile asking too closely from whom he had learned the information.

If the people in any part, region, or corner of the kingdom were disturbed, they were to discover the cause of the disturbance. If the murmur of the people was growing loud, or if some irregular matter was being reported from which it was necessary to deliberate in a general council, they were to investigate that and similar matters.

Outside the kingdom, they were to inquire whether any subject people wished to rebel, whether rebels might be brought back into submission, whether those not yet confronted were plotting against the kingdom, or whether anything of this kind was threatening to arise.

In all these matters, whatever dangers threatened anyone, the chief question was what circumstance had caused such things to arise.

### Chapter XXXVII

After those matters which had been collected at the synod held at the shrine of Saint Macra concerning the constitutions of our forebears and had recently been sent to the recently deceased King Louis, I have now respectfully presented to you, in obedience to your command, these matters concerning the ordering of the palace and the arrangement of the kingdom, for the instruction of this king of ours, his ministers, and the kingdom’s administrators, just as I learned them from the writings and words of the elders and myself saw them while still a young man.

As for the persons, characters, and qualities of the men through whom anything that has fallen into disrepair may be restored, your prudence will provide for them. For of those whom I saw as administrators of the palace and prefects of the kingdom in the time of Lord Emperor Louis, I know no one to have survived. I do know, however, that sons born of their nobility have succeeded their fathers, although I do not know their character or qualities. Let them themselves take care that in character and virtue, and in proportion to their age and the circumstances of the time, they are not degenerate in wisdom and good endeavors, so that they may worthily fill their fathers’ places and offices and carefully guard themselves in that very succession, lest, as Saint Gregory says, those placed at the summit of honor be changed by the use of glory, like Saul, who was at first humble when chosen for honor but later deserved to be rejected because of his swelling pride.

[Col. 1007]

## X. A SECOND ADMONITION TO THE BISHOPS OF THE KINGDOM

Made on behalf of King Carloman at Sparnacum.

(From the same author, on the same subject.)

[Col. 1007C] HINCMAR, bishop and servant of the people of God.

### Chapter I

Christian teaching, according to the course of the holy Scriptures and the preaching of our forebears, is that, as blessed Pope Gelasius says to the Emperor Anastasius (Letter 10), and as is partly contained in the acts recently transacted at the synod held at the shrine of Saint Macra, this world is chiefly governed, under the ordering of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, our creator and redeemer—who alone could become at once king and priest, and at whose name every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings bends—by two powers, together with those specially subject to the care of each: the sacred authority of bishops and royal power.

In these persons, just as the names are divided according to their order, so too the duties of their powers are divided within each order and profession. For although the members of the true King and High Priest are said, by participation in his nature, to have magnificently received both dignities in sacred nobility, so that royal and priestly stock might subsist together, Christ nevertheless, remembering human frailty and magnificently tempering what was suitable for the salvation of his own, distinguished the functions of the two powers by their proper activities and separate dignities. He wished his people to be saved by medicinal humility, not once again to be destroyed by human pride—as happened before his coming in the flesh with the pagan emperors, who were also called supreme pontiffs.

Thus Christian kings would need bishops for eternal life, while bishops would use imperial arrangements for the course of temporal affairs, so that spiritual action might remain separate from carnal incursions and that the one who serves God might not become entangled in secular business (II Tim. II). Conversely, the person who was entangled in secular business would not appear to preside over divine matters. In this way the modesty of both orders would be preserved, so that no one supported by both might become exalted, and each profession would be suitably adapted to the qualities of its particular activities.

[Col. 1008C]

### Chapter II

Yet the burden of priests is all the heavier because, in the divine tribunal, they will also have to render an account for the kings themselves. The dignity of bishops is therefore greater than that of kings, because kings are consecrated to royal eminence by bishops, whereas bishops cannot be consecrated by kings. But in human affairs the care of kings is more extensive than that of priests, since the King of kings has imposed upon them the burden of caring for the honor, defense, and peace of the holy Church and of its rulers and ministers, both by promulgating laws and by waging war.

### Chapter III

Therefore each person must diligently attend to the name by which he is classified in his order and profession, and take the greatest care not to disagree with that name in his office. For, as we read in sacred history, King Uzziah, presuming to offer incense—which was a priestly, not a royal, ministry—was struck by God with leprosy, expelled from the temple by the priests, and confined in his own house until his death (IV Reg. XV; II Par. XXVI).

Saint Cyprian, in the tenth degree of Abuses—through which the wheel of the world is deceived if that degree is present, and by which it is rolled toward the darkness of hell by God’s just judgment without any aid of justice to hinder it—speaks of a negligent bishop as follows (chapter 10):

> “If a bishop is negligent, seeking the honor of his rank among human beings but not guarding the dignity of his ministry before God, for whom he serves as an ambassador, then the dignity contained in his name must first be examined. For since *bishop* is a Greek name, it is interpreted as ‘watchman.’ Why is a watchman appointed, and what is required of a watchman? The Lord himself reveals this when, in the person of the prophet Ezekiel, he announces to the bishop the accountability of his office, saying: ‘I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel’ (Ezek. III).”

And the rest—which those who are called by this name must read and meditate upon neither casually nor rarely.

### Chapter IV

In the Old Testament (I Par. XXIV), King David, who was also a prophet and prefigured our Lord Jesus Christ—who, as we have said, alone could become both king and priest—established two orders among the priests: namely, the high priests and the priests of the lower order, who now perform the office of presbyter. He made this provision so that whenever one of the bishops died, whichever priest was considered the best would succeed him in the episcopate.

In the New Testament (Luke VI and X), our Lord Jesus Christ, as we read in the Gospel, chose twelve from the multitude of his disciples and called them apostles. Bishops hold their place in the Church, as Saint Gregory and the other Catholic teachers demonstrate. He also appointed seventy-two others. For just as no one doubts that the twelve apostles both represent and foreshadow the form of bishops, so it must be understood that these seventy-two bore the figure of presbyters, that is, priests of the second order.

Nevertheless, in the earliest times of the Church, as apostolic Scripture testifies (Phil. I; Titus I; I Tim. III; Acts XX), both groups were called presbyters and both were called bishops. In the one designation the maturity of wisdom was signified, and in the other the diligence of pastoral care; although their offices and dignities are distinguished in certain respects, sacred discipline embraces them under one name.

> “Let no priest,” they say (Celestine, Letter 2 to the bishops throughout Apulia and Calabria), “be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, or to do anything that could conflict with the regulations of the Fathers,”

because one sins no less against the sanctions of holy tradition than one openly attacks the Lord himself. That is, schismatics who violate the sanctions of holy tradition must be separated from the same Church until they convert and are incorporated into the unity of the holy Church, just as heretics who depart from the true faith must be separated from it.

For in bishops, as blessed Ambrose says, all the orders are present, because the bishop is the first priest—that is, the chief of priests—and is also prophet and evangelist, containing within himself the offices of the other ministers so as to fulfill them in the ministry of the faithful.

### Chapter V

How, with the agreement of the ruler of the land—who, by divine judgment, has undertaken the protection and defense of ecclesiastical property—each person ought to be advanced to ecclesiastical governance by the election of clergy and people, without any act of venality, is clearly demonstrated both by the Lord in the Gospel and by the sacred canons. The Lord says:

> “He who does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John X).

The apostolic and canonical authority also determines what sort of men ought to be promoted to the episcopate (II Tim. III). Therefore the ruler of the land must take the greatest care and precaution that God is not offended in those through whom the Christian religion is to stand and the rest are to be protected from offense.
