No bishop is to be chosen for any consideration except God alone: not for any gift, whether in hope of present or future repayment; not for any human service, relationship by blood, friendship, temporal service, or any circumstance that could be contrary to truth or divine authority. The same applies to presbyters, as sacred authority demonstrates (John II; Acts VIII).

### Chapter VI

How those who have been ordained should govern the ministers placed under them is plainly shown by the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See, as well as by the sixteenth book of the Laws, by which the holy Church is governed together with the sacred canons.

With what pure intention they ought to administer the sacred ecclesiastical orders, blessed Gregory clearly shows in his homily on the Gospel, *Jesus sent his twelve disciples, commanding them and saying: Do not go on the road of the Gentiles*, and in his homily on the Gospel, *The Lord appointed seventy-two others*, and in his homily on the Gospel, *Jesus saw the city and wept over it*. With what discernment they ought to bind or loose those subject to them, he demonstrates lucidly in his homily on the Gospel, *When it was evening on the first day of the week* (homilies 4, 17, 39, 26).

How each person comes to the summit of governance—namely, the episcopate—and, having reached it rightly, how he should live; how, living well, he should teach; and how, teaching rightly, he should recognize each day, with what degree of reflection, his own weakness: blessed Gregory teaches sufficiently and most eloquently in his *Pastoral Rule*.

### Chapter VII

What sort of king a king ought finally to be, blessed Cyprian demonstrates in the ninth degree of Abuses, teaching as follows (chapter 9):

> “A king ought to be not an unjust man but a corrector of the unjust. Therefore he must preserve in himself the dignity of his name. For the name ‘king’ intellectually retains this meaning: that he should provide the office of ruler for all his subjects. But how will he be able to correct others if he does not correct his own behavior so that it may not be unjust? For the throne of the king is exalted by justice, and the government of peoples is made firm by the king’s truth.
>
> “The justice of a king is not to oppress anyone unjustly through power; to judge justly between one man and his neighbor without respect of persons; to be a defender of strangers, orphans, and widows; to restrain thefts; to punish adulteries; not to exalt the wicked; not to maintain the immodest or actors; to destroy the impious from the land; not to allow parricides and perjurers to live; to defend the churches; to feed the poor with alms; to appoint just men over the affairs of the kingdom; to have elders, wise men, and sober counselors; not to heed the superstitions of magicians, diviners, and spirit-mediums; to defer anger; to defend his homeland bravely and justly against adversaries; to trust God in all things; not to raise his mind in prosperity; to endure every adversity patiently; to hold the Catholic faith in God; not to allow his sons to act impiously; to devote himself to prayers at appointed hours; and not to taste food before the proper hours.
>
> “For woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning (Eccles. X, 16). These things produce the prosperity of the kingdom in the present life and lead the king to the better kingdoms of heaven.
>
> “But whoever does not administer the kingdom according to this law will undoubtedly endure many adversities of rule. For this reason the peace of peoples is often broken, offenses are also stirred up against the kingdom, the fruits of the earth diminish, and the services of peoples are obstructed. Many and varied sorrows stain the prosperity of the kingdom; the deaths of dear ones and children bring grief; the incursions of enemies devastate the provinces on every side; beasts tear apart the herds of cattle and flocks of sheep; storms of air and winter, disturbing the fertility of things, hinder the works of the sea; and at times flashes of lightning burn the crops, the flowers of trees, and every vine shoot.
>
> “Above all, the injustice of the king not only darkens the appearance of the present realm but also obscures his sons and grandsons, so that they may not hold the inheritance of the kingdom after him. Because of Solomon’s sin, the Lord scattered the kingdom of the house of Israel from the hands of his sons; because of the justice of King David, he always left a lamp from his seed in Jerusalem.
>
> “Behold how much the justice of a king is worth in this world: it is plainly evident to those who observe it. For it is the peace of peoples, the protection of the homeland, the security of the people, the defense of the nation, care for the sick, the joy of human beings, temperate weather, calm seas, the fertility of the earth, consolation for the poor, and an inheritance for children; and for the king himself, hope of future blessedness.
>
> “Nevertheless, let the king know that just as he has been established first upon the throne of human beings, so also, if he does not practice justice, he will hold first place in punishments. For all the sinners whom he had beneath him in the present life he will have above him, without possibility of appeasement, in that future punishment.”

### Chapter VIII

> “The sixth degree of Abuses is ‘a lord without virtue.’ This applies not only to a king but to all who are reckoned by the name of lords, because it accomplishes nothing to possess the power of ruling if the lord himself does not possess the strength of virtue.
>
> “This strength of virtue does not require so much external fortitude—which is itself necessary for secular lords—as the inward strength of mind that must be exercised through good morals. For the strength of ruling is often lost through negligence of mind, as is shown to have happened with the priest Eli (I Reg. II). Since he did not restrain his sinful sons with the severity of judgment, the Lord fiercely did not spare him in their punishment, as though he had consented to them.
>
> “Therefore those who rule must have three necessary qualities: fear, order, and love. Unless a lord is both loved and feared, his rule cannot remain firmly established. Through benefits and affability, therefore, he should arrange to be loved; and through just punishments—not for personal injury but for the sake of God’s law—he should strive to be feared.
>
> “Moreover, since many depend upon him, he must cling to God, who appointed him to leadership and strengthened him as though he were the stronger man, so that he might bear the burdens of many. For unless a stake is firmly secured and clings to something stronger, everything hanging upon it quickly falls; and once loosened from the strength of its firmness, it descends to the ground together with its burdens.
>
> “So too, unless a ruler clings steadfastly to his Creator, both he himself and everything he contains quickly perish. Some, through the office of ruling, draw closer to God; others become worse because the honor of dignity has been imposed upon them.
>
> “After Moses received leadership of the people, he used the speech of God more familiarly (Exod. XXXIII). Saul, son of Kish, however, after he had received the scepter of the kingdom, offended God through the pride of disobedience (I Reg. XV). After King Solomon had obtained the seat of his father David, God enriched him with the gift of wisdom beyond all mortals, as suited to the governance of a numerous people (III Reg. III).
>
> “By contrast, Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, after he had seized part of the kingdom of the house of David, drew the ten tribes of Israel that were in the region of Samaria into the worship of idols (III Reg. XII). These examples clearly show that some people grow toward greater perfection in a higher state, while others descend into worse things through the arrogance of domination.
>
> “From both cases it is understood that those who stoop toward better things can do so through strength of mind and God’s help, while those who turn toward worse things go astray through weakness of mind and negligence alike.
>
> “Therefore it is not fitting for a lord to be without virtue, since no one has virtue without God’s help. For whoever protects many things, if he does not possess strength of mind, cannot accomplish this, because great matters are accustomed to labor under great assaults and adversities.
>
> “Let everyone who presides therefore first and foremost take care, with his whole mind, not to doubt God’s help in anything. For if he begins to have the Lord of lords as his helper in his actions, no human being will be able to hold his rule in contempt: ‘There is no authority except from God’ (Rom. XIII, 1).
>
> “He raises the needy from the refuse and makes him sit with the princes of his people; he casts down the powerful from their seat and exalts the humble (Psal. CXII; Luke I), so that the whole world may become subject to God and all may be in need of the glory of God (I Cor. II).”

### Chapter IX

What sort of counselors a king ought to employ, and likewise those who, placed in positions of authority, are called lords, Ambrose shows in his book *On Duties* (Book II, chapter 17):

> “The person who gives counsel to another,” he says, “ought to be such that he offers himself to others as a model and example of good works, in teaching, integrity, and dignity. His speech should be wholesome and blameless, his counsel useful, his life honorable, and his judgment worthy.
>
> “Such, then, should be the counselor who has nothing obscure, nothing deceitful, nothing fictitious, nothing pretended that could refute his life and character; nothing wicked or malicious that could turn away those seeking counsel.
>
> “Some things are avoided, while others are despised. We avoid those that can harm, that can maliciously creep toward injury—for example, if the person consulted is of doubtful faith and greedy for money, so that he can be changed by a payment, or if he is injurious: such a man is avoided and shunned.
>
> “But if he is pleasure-loving and intemperate, and, although free from fraud, nevertheless greedy and shamefully desirous of profit, he is despised. (Chapter 11.) For who would seek a spring in the mud? Who would ask for a drink from troubled water? Therefore, where there is luxury, intemperance, and confusion of vices, who would think that anything should be drawn from there? Who would not despise the filth of character? Who would judge someone useful to another’s cause whom he sees to be useless to his own life?
>
> “Who, again, would not avoid a wicked, malicious, abusive person, ready to do harm? Who would not shun him with every effort? But who would seek access, even with difficulty, to a man equipped to provide counsel, if that man were inaccessible—as though someone were blocking a spring of water?
>
> “What good is it to possess wisdom if you deny counsel? If you block access to counsel, you have closed the spring, so that it flows neither to others nor benefits you.
>
> “The counselor whom the gracious Lord gave to our fathers and, when offended, took away is worthy of my admiration and respect. Nevertheless, we entrust ourselves more readily to a just man than to a prudent one. It is beautiful, therefore, to wish well and to offer counsel in such a way that you may benefit, not harm.”

### Chapter X

Against what evils a king ought to guard himself, together with other forms of wickedness, and what sort of companions and judges he ought to appoint, Saint Augustine demonstrates, saying:

> “Let the ruler beware lest he be enticed by the gifts or flatteries of any criminal or deceived by adulation, because there is a gift from what is given, a gift from favor, and a gift from service. Therefore every judge must beware lest he sell a just judgment, or a witness the truth of his testimony, or an advocate just protection, or a jurist true counsel, lest he become a companion of Judas, who sold Christ, who is truth and justice.
>
> “And so that no one placed in any position of authority may be deceived by adulation, let him carefully attend to what is read in the history of the Kings: ‘Ben-hadad, fleeing, entered the city into a chamber within a chamber, and his servants said: “Behold, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful. Let us therefore put sackcloth around our loins and ropes on our heads, and go out to the king of Israel; perhaps he will save our lives”’ (III Reg. XX, 30–31).
>
> “When this had been done, they said to the king of Israel: ‘Your servant Ben-hadad says: “I beg you, let my life be spared.”’ And he replied: ‘If he is still alive, he is my brother.’ The men took this as a favorable omen, quickly seized the word from his mouth, and said: ‘Ben-hadad is your brother.’ The king of Israel said to them: ‘Go and bring him to me’ (ibid., 32–33). When he came, he made a treaty with him and released him.
>
> “Therefore he heard from the prophet: ‘Because you have released from your hand a man deserving death, your life shall be in place of his life, and your people in place of his people’ (ibid., 42).”

### Chapter XI

Rulers must also beware of joining themselves to the friendships of criminals or receiving such men into their intimacy.

> “When we carelessly join ourselves in friendship to the wicked,” says blessed Gregory (*Pastoral Rule*, Book III, chapter 23), “we are bound by their faults. Thus Jehoshaphat, who is extolled with so many praises for his former life, is rebuked because he nearly perished through friendship with King Ahab. The Lord says to him through the prophet: ‘You give help to the impious and join yourself in friendship with those who hate the Lord; therefore you deserved the Lord’s wrath, but good works have been found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah’ (II Par. XIX).
>
> “Our life already departs from him who is supremely upright precisely insofar as it agrees with the friendships of the perverse. Hence David, while binding his whole self to the covenants of inward peace, testifies that he held no harmony with the wicked, saying: ‘Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me’ (Psal. CXXXVIII, 21–22).
>
> “To hate the enemies of God with perfect hatred means loving them for what they were made to be, reproving what they do, restraining the conduct of the wicked, and benefiting their lives.”

### Chapter XII

That a king, because of his royal ministry, and no ruler, even when joined to anyone by the closest ties of kinship, ought to spare with carnal affection those who act perversely against God, the holy Church, and the commonwealth, Saint Gregory demonstrates from the words of the Lord:

> “Whoever does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 26).

In his homily on the Gospel he says (homily 37):

> “If we weigh the force of the command, we can act in both ways through discernment: loving those who are joined to us by bodily kinship and whom we know to be close to us, while refusing to recognize as loved ones those whom we suffer as adversaries on the way of God, by hating and avoiding them.
>
> “The person who is wise according to the flesh, when he imposes wicked things upon us and is not heard, is loved as though through hatred. Let every adversary in this world be loved; but on the way of God let no opponent be loved, even if he is a relative, so that a person may know God more truly by recognizing no one in God’s cause.”

### Chapter XIII

Just as it was stated above that no priest is permitted to be ignorant of his canons or to do anything that could conflict with the regulations of the Fathers, so sacred laws decree that no one is permitted to be ignorant of the laws or to despise what has been established.

When it is said that no one may be ignorant of the laws or despise what has been established, no person in any order is exempted from the force of this judgment. For the person who is judge of judges ought to permit the poor to enter before him and diligently inquire whether perhaps those whom he has appointed and who ought to act in his place among the people are unjustly or negligently permitting the poor to suffer oppression. His fear should restrain the unjust, while his authority should raise up the benevolent and needy.

It is dangerous for anyone to carry out his office through others to such an extent that he withdraws himself from it for too long. We read that in ancient times judges sat at the gate to judge, so that no one would have difficulty approaching them.

Hence blessed Jerome, commenting on the prophet Zechariah (chapter 8), says:

> “‘Judge truth and the judgment of peace in your gates.’ In judgment, let truth and justice come first; then let mercy follow. What comes next—‘in your gates’—agrees with the prophetic word: ‘They hated the one who reproved at the gate and abhorred the holy word’ (Amos V). And elsewhere: ‘They shall not be confounded when they speak with their enemies at the gate’ (Psal. CXXIX).
>
> “David also judged at the gates when Absalom, promising the justice of judgment, was laying snares for his father (II Reg. XIX).
>
> “The question is why, among the Jews, the place of judgment was at the gates. So that farmers would not be forced to enter the cities and incur some expense, judges sat at the gates, hearing both townspeople and country people, both as they went out and as they entered the city. When the case was finished, each person could immediately return to his own dwelling.”

### Chapter XIV

Those who are to govern the people after the king—that is, dukes and counts—must be appointed as men who understand how to govern justly and equitably those under them without endangering the person who appointed them, and who strive to fulfill with good will what they understand.

They must know that they have been placed in office to save and govern the people, not to dominate and oppress them; nor to regard the people of God as their own, or to subject them to themselves for their own glory, which belongs to tyranny and unjust power.

Necessity demands this most strongly, because the king will have to render an account before the most equitable Judge for the ministry entrusted to him. Therefore he must also diligently investigate each of the ministers under him and appoint such men that he himself will not incur divine judgment on their account.

Care must be taken concerning the oppression of the poor, because God is offended by their affliction, as the Psalmist said: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” (Psal. XI, 6).

Care must also be taken that they are not oppressed by superfluous building projects or by military exactions, if God in his mercy grants peace. This must not occur contrary to the chapter of Lord Emperor Charles, which states that no one is to be compelled to come to the *mallus* or court hearing except the *scabini*, the person who seeks his own case, and the person against whom the case is sought.

### Chapter XV

Counts and vicars, and even heads of ten-man districts, should establish many court hearings; and if the parties do not come there, they should compel them to pay the composition due.

Since previously people came through *manninae*, some devised a way for them to come to the hearings through bans, as though this were better because they would not have to pay those *manninae* to one another. They did this so that they themselves might receive the ban-payment, and they oppressed the poor to such an extent that, whereas previously many could go on military service, now scarcely anyone is able to do so.

In all these matters they not only fail to loosen, according to Isaiah, the bundles that weigh people down (Isa. L), but also add burdens upon the wretched and those engaged in labor. When they hope to gain something, they turn to the law; when they do not think they can acquire anything through the law, they take refuge in the capitularies. Thus it sometimes happens that neither are the capitularies fully preserved—they are treated as worthless—nor is the law.

For the law of the Old Testament condemns every evil. But the Lord said to his disciples concerning all Christians: “Amen, I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

### Chapter XVI

Concerning laws wrongly established by some emperors and rightly established by others, Saint Augustine says to Boniface (Letter 50):

> “When emperors establish bad laws in favor of falsehood against the truth, those who believe rightly are tested and those who persevere are crowned. But when they establish good laws in favor of the truth against falsehood, the violent are terrified and the intelligent are corrected.”

To Marcellinus, concerning the good character of rulers and the enlargement of the commonwealth, he says (Letter 5):

> “From a small and poor commonwealth, those made it great and wealthy who, having received an injury, preferred to forgive rather than pursue it. In what way Cicero, praising Caesar as an administrator of the commonwealth, extolled his character, saying that he was accustomed to forget nothing except injuries (Speech for Ligarius). He said this either as a great praiser or as a great flatterer. If he was a praiser, he knew Caesar to be such; but if a flatterer, he showed that the ruler of the state ought to be such as he falsely praised Caesar as being.”

Among the ancients there was this proverb:

> “You will be king if you act rightly; if you do not act rightly, you will not be king.”

### Chapter XVII

There are especially two royal virtues: justice and piety. Nevertheless, piety is praised more highly in kings, for justice by itself, without piety, is severe.

Concerning the restraint of plunder, the restoration of peace, the sacred Scriptures, the definitions of ecclesiastical laws, and the constitutions of the sacred laws, we recently sent to the deceased brother of this king of ours, through the bishops, material sufficiently collected from the synodal assembly recently held at the shrine of blessed Macra. We have judged it unnecessary, indeed superfluous, to repeat it here.

[Col. 1017]

## XI. IN THE COMMON NAME OF THE BISHOPS, TO THE KING

Concerning the restraint and eradication of the abduction of widows, girls, and consecrated women.

(From the same author, from the *Paralipomena* of John Buseus.)

[Col. 1017B] To the most Christian, glorious, and most pious lord and ruler: the humble servants of Christ, the bishops of Gaul and Germany, for the worship and sanctity of the house of the Lord, which is the Church of the true God, the pillar and foundation of truth.

### Chapter I

We are all compelled by the greatest and most serious necessity—we who, in these last and most dangerous times, have received, although unworthy and least of all, the episcopal ministry and governance of the Churches of God—to watch carefully and energetically over the Lord’s flock, which is in peril and is suffering more miserably from day to day under the new ambushes and attacks of the ancient enemy, with common purpose and diligence, insofar as God grants us the ability.

Although the power of temporal rule in this Christian kingdom presently appears, by divine judgment, to be divided, there is nevertheless one Church in all and from all, under the protection of Christ the Lord: one Lord, one faith, one chosen race, a royal priesthood, one holy nation, one people belonging to God. The Lord and Savior himself called this people from darkness into his marvelous light. For its acquisition and perpetual union he also deigned to taste death, as the Gospel says:

> “Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John XI, 51–52).

Therefore he himself also speaks with marvelous condescension, saying:

> “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father; and I lay down my life for my sheep. I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John X, 15–16).

Since, then, the entire people of God—redeemed and united at so great a price—is one flock under one shepherd, and all the shepherds of this flock ought, through unity of faith and unanimity of care, to exist as one shepherd under and within one supreme Shepherd, they must necessarily be united by such charity and joined by such fellowship of spirit that they willingly share and bear one another’s burdens.

Their daily concern must be the care of all the Churches, so that if one member suffers, all the members may suffer with it, and if one member rejoices, all the members may rejoice with it.

This concern has always caused the blessed apostles, and the successors of the blessed apostles—that is, the rulers of the Churches of God—to love the one flock of the Lord, the one guardianship of religion, and the one mother Church with one mind, and to preserve them with unanimous devotion.

## Chapter II

Therefore we beseech your most Christian piety and glorious sublimity to hear, with reverence and fear of divine judgment, those recommendations for correction that are offered for the salvation of the faithful and the preservation and tranquility of the Christian kingdom—since you have been appointed ministers of God’s kingdom, governors of the Christian people, and preservers and defenders of divine religion and ecclesiastical holiness—and, having heard them, to examine them in just judgment and, once examined, to cut away what requires removal with appropriate severity. For nothing so provokes the anger of almighty God and disturbs the peace of the kingdom as contempt for divine law, trampling upon paternal authority, and profanation of ecclesiastical purity and holiness.

Therefore God himself speaks against the impious despisers of his law, saying: “You have forgotten the law of your God; I also will forget your children” (Hos. 4:6). Of such people it is also written elsewhere: “But they mocked the messengers of God and despised his words, until the wrath of the Lord rose against his people, and there was no remedy” (2 Chron. 36:16).

Let the law of God, therefore, always return to your memory, and let the messengers of God—notably the holy fathers of old—not be despised or mocked. Concerning them the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

Let holy mother Church have you as devoted guardians and defenders of chastity and purity. Almighty God demands these things from her to such a degree that the Apostle solemnly testifies and says: “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord” (Heb. 12:14). And again: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you? But if anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3:16).

And again: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take Christ’s members and make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not” (1 Cor. 6:15). And again: “You are not your own, for you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear the Lord in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20).

This is God’s temple and the house of the living God, concerning which it is written: “Holiness befits your house, O Lord, for length of days” (Ps. 92:5). Concerning this, too, the blessed patriarch Jacob, who was called Israel, says in mystical praise: “This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 18:27). For it has the Lord as its inhabitant now, and after the present life it sends him from the world to heaven.

## Chapter III

For the sake of this holiness and purity from demonic contagion, the Church, beloved by Christ, purchased by his Passion, and cleansed and purified by the washing of baptism, was cleansed and expiated, as the Apostle testifies, saying:

“Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, so that he might present the glorious Church to himself, having no spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but so that she might be holy and immaculate” (Eph. 5:25–27).

Whoever, therefore, truly desires to be a son of this mother, a member of this body, and a portion of this temple, should hear and faithfully obey the same Apostle, who admonishes and says:

“For you are the temple of the living God, as God says: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they will be my people’” (2 Cor. 6:16).

And shortly afterward:

“Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God” (2 Cor. 7:1).

From such members and living stones is composed that city of the great King, the new bride and spouse of the Lamb, concerning which we read in the Apocalypse:

“Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter the city by the gates. Outside are dogs, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood” (Rev. 22:14–15).

Not only bishops and priests in their sees, but also kings in their kingdoms and palaces, the counts of kings in their cities, the deputies of the counts among their peoples, and every head of a household in his home ought most faithfully to love and zealously protect the beauty of this glorious house of God and the place of his glorious dwelling—in a single unity of rich and poor, in mind and in deeds.

The Apostle especially exercised this zeal and commended it to us for imitation by his example, saying: “I am jealous for you with a divine jealousy, for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2). Concerning this the Lord himself also speaks in the Psalm: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Ps. 69:9). He exercised this zeal so terribly that, not with the word by which he also drove out demons, but with his hand and a whip, he expelled the profaners of God’s house together with their offerings and sacrifices, which they appeared to be preparing (John 2).

## Chapter IV

We beseech you, therefore, that your piety, born from this holy mother and made an imitator of the Savior himself, whose mercy has established and exalted her in safety, may take up zeal for the house of God and be jealous with a divine jealousy, restraining, uprooting, and driving out with the whip of just severity the utterly shameless audacity of certain men who, having trampled upon God’s laws and having scorned the authority of the most holy Fathers, do not fear—without any reverence for divine or human modesty, like brute and irrational beasts—to violate the temple of God, which is the holiness of the faithful, and to attempt, as far as lies within them, to destroy and overturn the very altar of the Lord, which is the priestly ministry dedicated to him and set apart for his worship.

For in certain parts of this kingdom, because of their public violence, pitiable widows are not permitted to enjoy legitimate freedom, nor are daughters of marriageable age, living in their parents’ homes, allowed to be honorably joined in marriage according to divine and human laws, with the consent and authority of those same parents. Even the devoted dedication of nuns consecrated to God is dissolved and profaned, contrary to their profession of holiness and the reverence due to their divine consecration.

Thus that ancient enemy of the human race once polluted, through the impious and sacrilegious king Belshazzar, the golden and silver vessels of God’s house (Dan. 5); now, through the profane insolence and impiety of these men, he does not cease to defile things far more precious and dearer to God and to subject them to the mockery and derision of demons.

These are public robbers and plunderers, together with the accomplices and associates of their impiety. They are not ravaging the external possessions or property of some human being, but laying waste the household of almighty God himself. With such men one ought certainly not even to eat, as apostolic authority prescribes concerning all the rapacious (1 Cor. 5).

These men occupy the first place among them: robbers of widows, girls, and nuns; despisers of priests; violators of God’s temple; and people who do not fear the apostolic declaration: “If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:17).

If they burned or destroyed some temple of God made by human hand from wood and stones, they would rightly be judged by everyone to be sacrilegious and deserving of punishment. How much more so are those who do not fear to overturn and devastate the temple of the living God, while imagining that a marriage can arise from abduction and a legitimate matrimonial union from an unlawful cohabitation—something that no law and no custom of humanity has ever permitted?

For at the beginning of the world God made male and female for the propagation of the human race, and joined them by his blessing, saying: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:28).

## Chapter V

In imitation of this, holy Church also from ancient times solemnly and reverently observed the practice of joining by divine blessing and the celebration of Mass those who were to be united in marriage within her, as though in the paradise of God.

This honorable and religious union, begun with God as its author and confirmed by his blessing, was also preserved according to legitimate order and natural law among peoples who had received no law and possessed no knowledge of God. It was never lawful to accomplish a matter of peace, charity, and concord through discord, violence, and impiety.

The public laws of the Romans testify to this—laws by which they established the whole world under their rule. Those laws plainly prescribe that male abductors and abducted women, if the women have given them consent either before or after the abduction, are to be punished with the ultimate penalties; that the abductors’ helpers and agents are to be burned; and that the mouths of the arrangers and mediators of so great a crime are to be condemned with molten, burning lead.

Nor can the woman who complains that she was abducted in any way be excused if she did not take care to guard herself even while asleep, or call upon her neighbors for assistance and aid.

This wonderfully accords with divine law, where it is commanded that a betrothed girl, if she has been assaulted by someone in the city, be stoned because she did not cry out when she was in the city, where she could have been rescued either by the gathering of the citizens or by the assistance of her household (Deut. 22:23–24).

Hence that blessed Susanna is also praised. Her parents, being righteous, had instructed her according to the law of Moses. When she was bathing alone in her husband’s garden, she not only refused the wicked elders’ consent to adultery but also cried out in a loud voice so that the household servants might hear and come to her aid; thus she was protected from the impiety of the wicked, as indeed happened (Dan. 13:24).

## Chapter VI

The law of God also intended the covenant and bond of marriage, begun with parental authority and legitimate petition, to be so holy and inviolable that it confirms a betrothed girl as the wife of the man to whom she is betrothed, even before the marital union, saying:

“If a man betroths a virgin, and someone finds her in the city and lies with her, you shall lead both of them out to the gate of that city, and they shall be stoned: the girl because she did not cry out when she was in the city, and the man because he humbled his neighbor’s wife” (Deut. 22:23–24).

This is why the Gospel also says concerning the blessed and glorious mother of God, Mary, when she was betrothed to Joseph, that the angel said to him: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife” (Matt. 1:20).

And in the prophet Hosea, when betrothed girls have been violated by others, they are called adulteresses, the Lord saying: “I will not punish your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery” (Hos. 4:14).

The law of God compares these abductors, oppressors, and violators with thieves and murderers, and commands that they be killed. Speaking of a girl who has been violently assaulted in the field, it says:

“But if a man finds a betrothed girl in the field, and seizes her and lies with her, the man alone shall die. The girl shall suffer nothing, nor is she guilty of death. For just as a thief rises against his brother to kill him, so also is the girl’s case: she was alone in the field, she cried out, and there was no one to rescue her” (Deut. 22:25–27).

## Chapter VII

Let those who are such, therefore, recognize that they are thieves, murderers, killers of souls, and deserving of death.

There is no difference between those who perpetrate such violence in the field and those who commit similar acts in cities, on roads, or in houses, even with a crowd and weapons—except that the former resemble thieves who secretly lie in wait in forests and deserted places, while the latter resemble the most savage and openly violent plunderers, who are hostile and destructive to citizens either in the silence of night or in broad daylight.

Since they have obtained no marital union through the order of divine law, the authority of parental will, or the holiness of the Church—but have instead earned public excommunication by the authority of the canons in place of priestly blessing—with what face do they wish sacrilege to be regarded as marriage, robbery as matrimony, and violence as piety?

An edifice cannot stand without a foundation, and once the root of a tree has been torn out, green branches cannot sprout. Nor can it be said of such a union—not a legitimate marriage but an adulterous cohabitation—that which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6). Rather: “What a human being has impiously and wickedly joined, may God in his justice separate.”

These are the men who, through violence and their power, after despising almighty God, also despise the Church of God and the priests of God. They show no reverence for Christ’s excommunication, although he granted this authority to the ministers and governors of his Church, saying:

“If someone does not listen to the Church”—that is, any presumptuous and stubborn person—“let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector” (Matt. 18:17).

He immediately added:

“Amen I say to you: whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (ibid., 18).

These men, however, in opposition to this, disobedient to the Church and therefore to be regarded as pagans and tax collectors, and excommunicated by temporal judgment, forcibly enter churches and do not fear to insult the divine mysteries. They attempt to join themselves to Christian worship not with humility, piety, and obedience, but with defiance and wickedness, not reflecting upon what is written, with the Lord Christ himself saying:

“He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house, and I hate those who commit transgressions” (Ps. 101:7).

And again: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). And: “For the Lord is exalted, and he regards the lowly, but he knows the proud from afar” (Ps. 138:6).

If they would deign to consider these things, they would lay aside their pride and strive through pious humility to obtain what Scripture promises elsewhere, saying:

“The Lord is near to those who are brokenhearted, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. 34:18).

The Apostle James likewise admonishes how each person may become distant from the devil and draw near to God:

“Therefore submit yourselves to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your sinful hands and purify your double-minded hearts. Be miserable, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you” (Jas. 4:7–10).

## Chapter VIII

But now, when they violently rush into churches; when they mix themselves, undisciplined and wickedly, among crowds of the faithful; when they threaten the priests themselves with destruction unless the divine mysteries are celebrated in their presence—what else are they doing but piercing themselves twice with their own sword, by despising ecclesiastical judgment and profaning the mysteries of the sacred altar?

These mysteries, just as they bring healing to the faithful, humble, and devout, bring judgment and torment to the despisers and shameless.

To these men must also be joined those foolish and wicked people who, having been excommunicated by other churches and priests, imagine that they can fraudulently receive communion in other churches and from other priests.

It ought to be perfectly clear to all the faithful that throughout the whole world, in cities and among peoples, there is only one Church of Christ, one altar of Christ, and one sacrifice, established and offered everywhere to the one God in the one religion.

Therefore no one can be excommunicated in one place and receive communion in another. From the place where someone deserved to be separated, he cannot be joined anywhere at all except through legitimate satisfaction—just as a bodily member cut off from its place cannot thereafter be fitted to any other part of the body, unless perhaps, by a miracle of divine power, it can be restored to the place from which it was torn.

Among these people some are found to be so pitiless and devoid of human feeling, possessing instead the savagery of beasts, that they kill their former wives on mere suspicion of adultery, without any law, reason, or judgment, solely through their own rage and cruelty. Still bloody and dripping with blood, they are not only untouched by any repentance and make no satisfaction to God or the Church through humility, but, exulting in their pride, approach the Lord’s altar without hesitation and presume indifferently to touch the sacred mysteries.

Even if those most wretched women had truly committed adultery and therefore appeared to have been justly punished, nevertheless God’s law—the law by which every Christian will be judged on the day of judgment, to receive according to his deeds—does not permit any guilty person, whether adulterer or adulteress, to be punished except under legitimate judges and witnesses. It even commands that such persons be stoned publicly by the people.

Thus that remarkable Susanna, when falsely accused of adultery, is recorded as having been condemned by public judgment and acquitted by public judgment (Dan. 13).

And the woman in the Gospel who had truly been caught in adultery was first brought, according to the law, to the Pharisees who exercised judicial authority over the people, and then, also as a means of testing him, to the judgment of the Lord. There, through his remarkable mercy, she deserved to be freed both from the punishment of stoning and from guilt for the offense (John 8).

The Book of Numbers also commands that if a woman is accused either of adultery or by false suspicion, and her husband is stirred against her by jealousy, he is to bring her to the priest and present her to be condemned or acquitted by divine judgment (Num. 5).

## Chapter IX

The ancient Romans also established and observed in their laws that this matter should be handled through legitimate marriage—not only after they had become Christians, but even while they were still pagans. This is most clearly shown by the law of the pagan emperor Antoninus, which the blessed Augustine recalls and commends in one place as follows (*To Pollentius*, book II, chapter 8):

“Those who dislike the maintenance of an equal standard of chastity between husband and wife, and who prefer—especially in this matter—to be subject to the laws of the world rather than to those of Christ, because the civil laws appear not to bind men with the same bonds of chastity as women, should read what the emperor Antoninus, certainly not a Christian, established concerning this matter. He decreed that a husband could not accuse his wife of adultery if he had not offered an example of chastity in his own conduct, so that both would be condemned if the same trial convicted both of equal immorality.

“For these are the words of the aforementioned emperor, as they are found in Gregorianus:

“‘Certainly, my letter will in no way prejudice the case. For if the fault lay with you, so that the marriage was dissolved and, under the Julian law, your wife Euphrasia married another, she will not on that account be condemned for adultery by my rescript unless it is established that the act was committed. Those who investigate the matter should keep before their eyes whether, while you were living chastely, you also encouraged her to cultivate good morals. For it seems utterly unjust to me that a husband should demand chastity from a wife whom he himself does not display. This circumstance can also condemn the husband; it cannot settle the matter between the two by balancing mutual offenses or remove the cause of the act. If these things must be observed for the honor of an earthly city, how much greater chastity does the heavenly homeland and the fellowship of angels require?’”

These are the things that the blessed Augustine writes about the laws of the pagan emperor Antoninus.

In the Book of Esther it is plainly recorded (chapter 1) that Vashti, the wife of the most powerful and fierce king Ahasuerus, when she had offended his spirit by contempt and defiance, was not removed from her royal position merely through his indignation and rage, but by public judgment and the decision of the nobles and judges of the Medes and Persians.

Thus, although they were pagans and worshipers of idols, by naturally doing what belongs to the law, even in matrimonial cases they taught that justice and equity, not cruelty and savagery, ought to be decreed and established.

## Chapter X

Divine law certainly also commanded that justice and judgment be preserved between master and male or female slave. Although it commands that, by public judgment, retaliation be rendered—eye for eye and tooth for tooth—nevertheless, if a master in private indignation and fury tore out the eye of his male or female slave or knocked out a tooth, it immediately condemned him to the loss of that same slave.

For thus it is written:

“If anyone strikes the eye of his male or female slave and makes him or her one-eyed, he shall set them free in exchange for the eye he removed. Likewise, if he knocks out a tooth of his male or female slave, he shall set them free” (Exod. 21:26–27).

The very just and merciful law of God therefore did not wish any impairment or disfigurement to be inflicted upon slaves by their masters without judgment. If anyone presumed to do this, he was punished by the just loss of the same slave whose subjection he had unjustly abused.

Much less did it permit a slave to be killed through the private indignation and rage of his master. If he did so, he was condemned as guilty of murder, as the same law says:

“Whoever strikes his male or female slave with a rod, and the slave dies at his hands, shall be guilty of the crime” (Exod. 21:20).

## Chapter XI

The blessed Job maintained this equity of judgment and justice toward his household by divine inspiration and natural reflection even before that law was given through Moses, as he himself testifies, saying:

“If I have rejected judgment with my male or female servant when they contended against me, what shall I do when God rises to judge, and when he asks, what shall I answer him? Did not he who made me in the womb make him also? Did not one [God] form us in the womb?” (Job 31:13–15).

For this reason our holy Fathers also established the following in the sacred canons concerning such guilt (Council of Agde, canon 62):

“If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of the judge, he shall expiate the shedding of blood by two years of excommunication.”

The Book of Ecclesiasticus, speaking about the discipline of master and slave, likewise prescribes this very thing, saying:

“Nevertheless, do nothing serious without judgment” (Ecclus. 33:30).

The Apostle especially admonishes this, saying:

“Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and fair, abandoning threats, knowing that you too have a master in heaven” (Col. 4:1).

If, therefore, such equity and goodness must be maintained in every Christian household even toward the condition of slaves, between master and slave, how much greater, richer, and fuller must they be preserved between husband and wife, between man and spouse, between head and body?

For, as the Apostle teaches:

“The husband is the head of the woman, as Christ is the head of the Church; he himself is the Savior of the body. In the same way husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies” (Eph. 5:23, 28). “He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.”

Accordingly, the same Apostle says again:

“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word” (ibid., 25).

Certainly these apostolic words commend such great, such extraordinary and surpassing love between husband and wife—while preserving within marriage the precedence of the husband and the subjection of the woman—that, once this union has been instituted by God and lawfully arranged, nothing greater ought or can exist.

For what is more venerable than for marriage to be a mystery of Christ and the Church? What is holier than for husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the Church, giving himself for her in order to sanctify and cleanse her? What is dearer and more closely joined than for the husband to be the head of the woman, as Christ is the head of the Church, himself the Savior of the body?

In the Gospel he also bears witness concerning this union of marriage, saying:

“Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. For,” he says, “the two will be one flesh” (Matt. 19:6).

The Apostle adds further, saying:

“Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them” (Col. 3:19).

If, therefore, husbands ought not to be bitter toward their wives, how much less ought they to be savage, cruel, and bloodthirsty toward them, observing no law, reason, or judgment—things that Christian religion requires even toward slaves? Yet as soon as it pleases them, stirred by impious indignation and rage, they have their wives led away to be butchered as though to a slaughterhouse, order them to be cut down by the swords of their cooks like rams and pigs, or even slaughter them themselves with their own hands and blades.

They do not at all hand themselves over for their wives in imitation of the Lord Jesus Christ, to sanctify and cleanse them. Rather, driven by zeal for their own lust, they destroy those women forever and impiously stain themselves with their blood—although in such a case legitimate judgment ought to be awaited all the more justly, because marital jealousy can so easily lead to murder.

## Chapter XII

Let those who are such defend themselves as much as they wish, whether by worldly laws, if any exist, or by human customs. Nevertheless, if they are Christians, they should know that on the day of judgment they will be judged not by Roman, Salian, or Gundobad laws, but by divine and apostolic laws.

Indeed, in a Christian kingdom even the public laws ought to be Christian—namely, compatible and consonant with Christianity.

For the law of almighty God divides into three categories everything that human beings appear to have subject to or possess in worldly affairs, when it defines and says in the commandments of the Decalogue:

“You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor male slave, nor female slave, nor ox, nor sheep, nor donkey, nor anything that belongs to him” (Exod. 20:17).

In these words, without doubt, the dignity of a wife must be considered in one way, the condition of male and female slaves in another, and the lowliness of brute animals or inanimate things in yet another. Therefore all these things must be treated within their own limits and distinguished and divided according to their proper degrees.

We say this so that those who are such may consider that they regard the condition of wives as inferior to that of little slaves.

If a master who kills a slave without the knowledge of the judge is guilty of murder, and cannot expiate the shedding of blood except through penance, what ought to be decreed concerning a spouse?

Such men even erupt into such great foolishness and blindness that they do not fear to join to themselves by violence and abduction women whom they first take contrary to every divine and human law and contrary to the very rights of humanity; nor do they fear sacrilegiously to defile women who have made a profession and assumed the habit of religious consecration.

Afterward, having softened the women with flattering words and appeased their parents by calculated—indeed, shameful—flattery, they imagine that they have escaped both divine and human judgment. They wish such an illicit and wicked cohabitation to appear like a legitimate and honorable marriage.

Yet, as has already been shown, the ancient laws of the Romans judge and punish with equal severity both the women who consent to their abductors and their parents, if the parents did not protest.

Through ecclesiastical judgment, moreover, all who are such are either to be excommunicated or anathematized, even to the point of separation; after separation they are to be excluded from all public sight and, under the strictest penance, ordered to be confined in prison until the day of death.

Indeed, even if, out of fear of public consequences, an abductor takes refuge with the abducted woman in a church, the woman who suffered the violence, excused through the intervention of the Church, is to be restored to her parents; but the abductor, because he clearly inflicted violence, is likewise, out of reverence for the sanctuary and under the protection of legal immunity, to be reduced to servitude under the parents of the woman whom he abducted—unless perhaps he is allowed to redeem himself from them.

## Chapter XIII

Now, with all these divine and human laws despised and trampled underfoot, the Church suffers public assault, public injury, and public defiance at their hands, to such an extent that they do not fear to plot against her priests and incite revolts, although those priests forbid such wicked and destructive acts.

If anyone is so insane as to think that this profane and violent cohabitation can thereby become a legitimate marriage because Scripture reports that the just and holy king David, although he sinned in certain matters as a human being, committed adultery with the wife of Uriah the Hittite and afterward, when Uriah himself had been cruelly killed, took her in marriage (2 Sam. 11), let him consider how gravely and terribly almighty God rebuked, condemned, and denounced the whole affair through his prophet, saying:

“You killed Uriah the Hittite and took his wife as your wife, and you killed him with the sword of the sons of Ammon. Therefore the sword shall not depart from your house forever, because you despised me and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife” (2 Sam. 12:9–10).

When David was immediately pierced with profound grief, repented, and humbly confessed, the guilt of so great an iniquity was forgiven him. For in a brief statement, with a great and deep groaning of the heart, he said:

“I have sinned against the Lord.”

And at once he deserved to hear through the prophet:

“The Lord has also taken away your sin; you shall not die” (ibid., 13).

Nevertheless, his sin was forgiven in such a way that he did not escape the temporal punishment that had been announced to him. The son who was born from that union was immediately struck by divine judgment and died. Later David himself was afflicted and tormented by the gravest tribulations and by the loss of his kingdom through his son Absalom, and was so chastened and purified as though in a furnace of fire that he appears truly to have escaped only through divine clemency.

The fact that this marriage, so gravely rebuked, condemned, and punished, was nevertheless permitted to remain clearly does not offer it to anyone as an example for imitation, so that anyone might believe himself to have a just marriage within an unjust arrangement.

Rather, it was a divine miracle or sacrament: that man was so cleansed through true and extraordinary repentance and healed of every adulterous usurpation that even from such a union a chaste and legitimate marriage could exist.

The same is shown at the end of his life by the extraordinary and unique virtue with which he had the most beautiful virgin Abishag the Shunammite, chosen from all the territories of the kingdom of Israel, continually ministering to him and continually lying and sleeping beside him—although he never knew her sexually (1 Kings 1).

## Chapter XIV

These matters, therefore, must either be regarded as so extraordinary that they cannot be imitated at all; or as concessions made to that period of the Mosaic law, so that, with the coming of the evangelical grace of our Lord and Savior, they must be entirely removed; or, since the Apostle says that “all these things happened to them figuratively” (1 Cor. 10:11), they must be applied to divine mysteries.

Nevertheless, if adultery had not preceded in the case of that woman, and the killing of her husband had not been added, who would not see that, after her own husband had died and had been mourned with the due rites, she could have been joined to whomever she wished in an honorable and legitimate marriage?

Likewise, since the king was not forbidden by the circumstances of that time to have several wives, could he not legitimately have taken the wife of any deceased man?

But this is clearly magnificent and highly worthy of imitation in his conduct: the wives or concubines whom he had left behind when fleeing, to guard the house, and whom his impious son had violated and polluted (2 Sam. 16), he never afterward knew sexually. Rather, as women who had suffered violence, he treated them mercifully, merely providing for them, and caused them to live enclosed in widowhood until the day of his death.

Nor is the following in any way contrary to the order and observance of religion. While David still reigned at Hebron over the tribe of Judah alone, and Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, held the kingdom of Israel, David sent to Abner, commander of the army and governor of the royal household, asking him to restore to him Michal, the daughter of Saul, who had been his wife and whom he had betrothed to himself with one hundred Philistine foreskins, but whom Saul, her father, after driving David out in hostility even beyond the borders of his kingdom, had given in marriage to another man (2 Sam. 3).

For once that persecution and expulsion had ended, it was just that David, having returned to his homeland, should recover what belonged to him by right, even in the case of any earthly possession—how much more in the fellowship of marriage, as the sacred canons likewise decree should be observed through a similar deliberation of equity?

## CHAPTER XV

Can men of this kind, and likewise their supporters and deceivers, also take as a supposedly just and lawful precedent the account given in the Book of Judges concerning the men of the tribe of Benjamin (Judges 20–21)? Because, when they had wickedly and impiously dared to defend against God and the judgment of the entire people the detestable and monstrous crime of their fellow citizens—defending it out of pride and perversity—and had fought with rebellious obstinacy against the whole kingdom, they fell in battle by divine judgment and were almost annihilated. Only six hundred men remained from the entire tribe, together with all their wives and children.

Therefore the whole people of Israel, who had advanced against them in that conflict and struck them down with the sword, were moved, in accordance with the divine command, by intense and religious grief to avenge the unspeakable crime. They grieved because, from the twelve tribes of that same people—as they had been established from the beginning, liberated from Egypt, led into the promised land, and given an inheritance by the distribution of lots—one tribe, so noble and distinguished, appeared to have been entirely removed.

Accordingly, grieving, weeping, and wailing excessively because that most sacred mystery of the twelve tribes—which was borne upon the shoulders of the high priest entering the Holy of Holies, in the two precious stones upon his breast, and also in twelve other precious stones, and which was continually offered upon the table in twelve loaves, while all these things were also being prepared for the future and most glorious choir of the apostles—appeared, through so sudden a disaster and mournful calamity, to have been shortened and mutilated, they erected an altar, appeased the Lord for themselves and for them with sacrifices and offerings, and, through the mercy and cooperation of divine grace, acted with every care and immense diligence so that neither the fullness of the people of God nor the sign of so great a mystery among them should in any way perish.

This was later accomplished wonderfully also in the New Testament, through the blessed apostles and the action of the Holy Spirit, so that the sacramental significance of that same number twelve, which had seemed to be mutilated through the destruction of Judas, might remain restored and complete through the election and appointment of Matthias (Acts 1).

And since, as has already been said, only six hundred men had survived from that entire tribe, they provided four hundred of them with four hundred virgins and gave them in marriage. But for the remaining two hundred, since they could neither give them their own daughters nor find others whom they could freely give them—as they had done with the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead, who had not taken part in that oath and had subsequently neglected to attend so public and religious a war, and therefore had been ordered to be lawfully killed, with only four hundred virgins from among them being spared to be brought for the restoration of the tribe of Benjamin—there remained the inhabitants of Shiloh, where the tabernacle of God had then been established.

These inhabitants are to be understood as having taken part neither in that oath nor in that battle, perhaps because of the immunity of the sanctuary, which, by reason of its proximity, they served more familiarly or even continually. For that reason they could lawfully give their daughters in marriage, but, because of a certain harshness and abhorrence of the crime committed by the tribe of Benjamin, they were unwilling to do so.

## CHAPTER XVI

It therefore remained that, since the parents could not lawfully be compelled to give their daughters against their will and thus turn an act of free choice into one of necessity, and since the daughters themselves could not be taken away by force, the two hundred men should suddenly meet the virgins as they proceeded on the most solemn day to the Lord’s sanctuary and led their dances. Acting on the deliberation, counsel, and authority of the people and the elders, for the restoration of that same people and the preservation of the divine mystery, the men, each without a wife, were to take one woman each from among them.

In this matter there was no longer any fear of divine anger, since everything was being done for the love and honor of God and for God’s cause. In the past war he had already rendered that tribe, almost annihilated, what it deserved; and in the present deliberation he was showing it mercy through hidden inspiration and providence.

Justice having therefore been preserved everywhere—and since the girls had been taken away not through any wantonness or defiance of their own, but solely through necessity and under the direction of their parents, while those who seized them had acted not according to their own inclination or rashness, but by the command and authority of the people and the elders—the only remaining matter was to quiet the parents’ complaint by a reasonable satisfaction. The elders said to them:

“When their parents come and begin to complain and quarrel against you, we shall answer them: ‘Have mercy on them. For they did not take them by the right of combatants and victors; rather, they asked you to give them, and you did not give them. The fault is therefore on your side’” (Judges 21:22).

Everything in this affair was thus reasonably provided for, reasonably carried out, and reasonably concluded, for the public good, by public authority and intervention. It is so singular and in no way to be imitated—or rather, so mystical—that it is recorded as having happened once and never repeated thereafter.

## CHAPTER XVII

Therefore, what Scripture records for the remembrance of piety or the commendation of a spiritual mystery must not, through the foolish and shameless wantonness of reckless men, be permitted to be seized as a precedent or defense for their own insolence. They must not suppose that this example gives them permission, whenever they do not easily obtain what they want from parents, to abduct whichever women they choose and afterward, once the parents have been appeased, retain them as though in a lawful marriage.

As has already been said, this was not written as an example, and therefore was never afterward adopted as a practice. Rather, it commemorates admirable devotion and commends a profound mystery. In that case, after the almighty God had been appeased and propitiated—for everything had been done in his worship and honor—only the parents’ mercy was implored, so that they might spare the two hundred men and divine justice might not find in them, even in this matter, something to condemn.

Although the parents too appear truly to have sinned, because in advising about so great and public a necessity they were too harsh, to the extent that they had initially been unwilling to give their daughters even when asked, here, however, God has been provoked and angered: his law is despised, his Church and priests are trampled underfoot, and his holy temple is violated by sacrilegious and impious presumption.

With what folly and madness do such people suppose that, once the parents have been appeased and pacified, they can have the Church of God pacified toward them? How can they trust that, by the parents’ authority, what is destroyed by the authority of divine law and the holy Fathers can stand? The evil of so great a transgression and impiety, committed against God and his Church, cannot be corrected by any reasoning or arguments except through the judgment of almighty God and the Church, and through satisfaction rendered to them.

The correction of so great a crime must therefore be displayed there; forgiveness must there be humbly sought; satisfaction must there be carefully offered—that is, in the Church of God and before the priests of God, where alone both remission of sin and the propitiation of the offended almighty God can truly be obtained.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Such men add to their evils an exceedingly audacious and punishable presumption: they seek and implore the authority or mediation of religious princes for their adulterous and execrable unions—which are not marriages but contaminations.

May it be far from the faithful princes and ministers of the kingdom of Christ that anyone’s wickedness should be aided by their prohibitions or interventions. For the Roman laws and the most Christian emperors of those times have most clearly and justly decreed that those who have disturbed the ears of rulers with unjust and fraudulent petitions, especially in such a matter, should both lose the benefit granted to them and, in addition, be deported into exile; and that children born from such shameful and adulterous unions should in no way be regarded as legitimate or admitted to an honorable succession of inheritance.

We therefore beseech your most gentle Serenity, most Christian and glorious prince, that you graciously hear and readily receive our prayers and supplications, which we bring on behalf of the Church of God and for the sanctification and honor of the body of Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior; and that, with the religious affection and zeal inherent in you, you vigorously and diligently bring them to effect.

Nor should you judge our care and diligence, despite our lowliness, worthy of reproach because, under God’s protection, these deadly contagions are spreading not everywhere but in many parts of this kingdom. For, although unworthy and insignificant, we are nevertheless bound by apostolic example to care for all the Churches, and these matters must be vigilantly admonished and proclaimed even where they do not occur. An antidote must be applied before the poison; and a wound, while it is still growing and worsening, must either be cut away or treated.

We therefore pray and implore your help—help which you undoubtedly owe to him by whose favor you flourish and possess power—so that the three orders of the Church, or rather the threefold fruit of God’s field, namely the thirtyfold, the sixtyfold, and the hundredfold, may, through your fear and protection, be guarded whole and undefiled as though by a hedge and a fortification, and may grow and prosper:

- the thirtyfold in the union of marriage;
- the sixtyfold in widowly continence;
- the hundredfold in the chastity and integrity of nuns.

Thus, whoever lies in wait for these fruits like savage and destructive beasts may be driven back by your protection and corrected by your severity.

## CHAPTER XIX

Let what the holy Fathers define concerning the good of marriage be heard and held fast. They say as follows (Augustine, *Book IX of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 7):

> “The good that marriage possesses can never be a sin. This good, however, has three parts: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. Fidelity requires that no one have intercourse with another man or woman outside the marriage bond. Offspring requires that children be lovingly received, kindly nourished, and religiously educated. Sacrament requires that the marriage not be dissolved, and that neither the man nor the woman who has been dismissed be joined to another, even for the sake of having children. This is, as it were, the rule of marriage, because either nature adorns fertility or innocence governs depravity.”

Let us also hear what they say again concerning the other two orders and the great holiness and reverence with which they must be regarded:

David, it is said, entered secretly into the wife of his soldier, to his great shame, and yet could not escape punishment. You, who have entered shamelessly into the chamber of the Lord of lords to violate the bride of the King Christ—how can you remain unpunished?

And if perhaps she is a widow, or whoever she may be, and has not yet professed continence and chastity, whoever she may be, she cannot be called a wife once prostituted. An everlasting mark of infamy will be branded upon both of you, and the stain of so great a crime cannot otherwise be removed unless either adultery is expiated by death under the savage force of public secular laws, or, at least, while life continues, it is washed away by fountains of tears through the deep sighs of a contrite heart and continual true repentance.

Let someone come forward, then, and say that this crime ought to be corrected by marriage, and that what is a crime should immediately be judged to be called a marriage. He will hear from me, unwilling though I am to say it, the truth: adultery can in no way be called marriage. For “marriage” (*conjugium*) is a term belonging to a religious designation.

## CHAPTER XX

To these words and judgments of the holy Fathers we shall add a few further sentences from the sacred canons. We ask that you hear them with religious devotion, in contemplation of our Lord Jesus Christ and in honor and reverence for holy mother Church—from whose womb you were born to God, by whose honors you have been glorified, and through whose honors you trust that you will be eternally glorified—and that, with the most informed care and diligence, you cause them to be recognized, revered, and observed among the Christian people entrusted to you, with the Lord protecting and cooperating in all things.

The matter for which we labor and supplicate is so great—namely, the preservation of chastity and holiness—that we ought willingly to offer even ourselves for its commendation and defense, following the example of the blessed and glorious Baptist John. Among the other proclamations of his preaching, he rebuked and reproved King Herod himself with such steadfastness because of this kind of adulterous union. He persistently announced and said to him concerning Herodias, the wife of his brother—whom Herod had obtained and retained not merely as a ravisher but also by the force and power of royal authority:

> “It is not lawful for you to have her” (Matthew 14:4).

For this cause John endured both bonds and imprisonment with equanimity, and finally preferred to be beheaded rather than cease preaching truth and justice. Thus he was truly a martyr of Christ, because he was a martyr of truth and justice itself.

# EXCERPTS

## From the Sacred Canons and the Deeds of the Holy Fathers Concerning the Cultivation of Chastity and Steadfastness in Proclaiming the Truth

### From the Decrees of Pope Siricius, Chapter 4: That It Is Not Lawful to Take Another Man’s Betrothed into Marriage

When inquiry was made concerning the violation of marriage—whether one man might take into marriage a girl betrothed to another—we absolutely prohibit this from being done. For among the faithful the blessing which the priest bestows upon those about to marry is comparable to a sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.

### At the Council of Ancyra, Chapter 10: Concerning Betrothed Girls Who Have Been Violated by Others

It was decided that betrothed girls who were afterward carried off by others should be freed and restored to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it were established that violence had been inflicted upon them by their abductors.

### From the Decrees of Pope Innocent, Chapter 20: Concerning Unveiled Virgins Who Have Gone Astray

Those who, although not yet covered with the sacred veil, have nevertheless always represented themselves as remaining steadfast in their intention of virginity—if they should perhaps marry despite not having been veiled—must undergo penance for a considerable period, because their promise was held by the Lord.

For if among human beings a contract made in good faith is ordinarily dissolved on no grounds, how much more must this promise, which they made with God, not be dissolved without punishment? For if the apostle Paul said that women who had departed from their purpose of widowhood incurred condemnation because they had made their first faith void, how much more do virgins incur it when they have attempted to break faith with their earlier promise?

### From the Decrees of Pope Leo, Chapter 27: That Those Who Adopted the Purpose of Virginity Not Under Compulsion but by Their Own Will Sin if They Marry, Even If They Have Not Yet Been Consecrated

Girls who, not compelled by the authority of their parents but by their own voluntary judgment, have adopted the purpose and habit of virginity are transgressors if they afterward choose marriage, even if the grace of consecration has not yet been added to them. They would certainly not have been deprived of that gift if they had remained in their purpose.

### Likewise from the Same Pope Leo to Rusticus: Concerning Girls Who Have Already Been Consecrated and Marry Thereafter, Thus Committing a Double Crime against Their Purpose and Their Consecration

Concerning those who have already been consecrated and afterward marry, there can be no doubt that a great crime has been committed, since both the purpose is abandoned and the consecration violated. For if human agreements cannot be violated with impunity, what will await those who have broken faith with the divine sacrament?

### From the Decrees of Pope Gelasius, Chapter 20: That Those Who Join Themselves to Sacred Virgins and Enter into Incestuous Unions Cannot Receive Communion Unless They Have Performed Public Penance

We have learned that certain men rashly join themselves to sacred virgins and, after a purpose dedicated to God, enter into incestuous and sacrilegious unions. It is immediately just that they be expelled from holy communion and not received at all unless they have performed public and approved penance. At least, however, communion as viaticum should not be denied them when they are departing from this world, provided that they have repented.

### From the Decrees of Pope Siricius, Chapter 6: Concerning Monks and Virgins Who Do Not Keep Their Purpose

Furthermore, you attest that certain monks and nuns, having abandoned their purpose of holiness, have sunk into such great wantonness that first, secretly and under the pretext of monasteries, they joined themselves in unlawful and sacrilegious intercourse; afterward, driven into the abyss by despair of conscience, they openly produced children from those unlawful embraces. Both public laws and ecclesiastical rights condemn this.

We therefore command that these shameless and detestable persons be expelled from the community of monasteries and from the assemblies of the Churches, so that, shut away in their own prisons, they may lament such a great crime with continual mourning and, through the purifying fire of repentance, be refined; thus, at least at the time of death, indulgence may come to their aid through the grace of communion, solely by reason of mercy.

### Likewise from the Council of Blessed Pope Gregory

Gregory, apostolic pope, pronounced the following sentence before the venerable body of the chief of the apostles:

“If anyone takes a nun—whom they call a servant of God—in marriage, let him be anathema.”

And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone takes his spiritual godmother in marriage, let him be anathema.”

And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone takes his brother’s wife in marriage, let him be anathema.”

And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone takes his cousin in marriage, let him be anathema.”

And all answered: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone takes a wife from his own kin, or one whom a kinsman has had, let him be anathema.”

And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone abducts a widow as a wife, or consents to her doing so, let him be anathema.”
