And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone abducts a virgin whom he has not betrothed as a wife, or consents to her doing so, let him be anathema.”

And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

“I, Gregory, bishop of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, have subscribed to this decree promulgated by us.”

Twenty-two other bishops, fourteen priests, and five deacons also subscribed.

### From the First Council of Orléans, Chapter 2

Concerning abductors, we have judged that the following must be established: if an abductor should flee to a church with the woman he has abducted, and it is established that the woman herself suffered violence, she must immediately be released from the abductor’s power; and the abductor, having been granted immunity from death or other punishments, must be subjected to the condition of servitude, or be given the opportunity to redeem himself and obtain freedom.

But if it is established that the abducted woman has a father, and the girl consented to the abductor, she is to be returned to her father’s authority, exonerated; and the abductor must be held liable to the father for compensation appropriate to his higher rank.

### From the Council of Valence, Chapter 2: Concerning Girls Dedicated to God Who Have Turned to Earthly Marriage and Are to Be Assigned Penance

Concerning girls who have vowed themselves to God, if they voluntarily turn to earthly marriage, we have decreed that this rule must be observed: penance must not be granted to them immediately; and when it has been granted, their communion must be deferred until they have fully satisfied God, to the extent required by reason.

### From the Council of Elvira, Chapter 13: Concerning Virgins Consecrated to God Who Commit Adultery

It was decided that virgins who have dedicated themselves to God, if they lose the covenant of their virginity and continue to serve that same lust, not understanding what they have lost, should not be given communion even at the end of life.

But if, after being persuaded only once, or having been violated through the weakness of the body, such women perform penance throughout their entire lives and abstain from intercourse, since they appear rather to have fallen through weakness, it was decided that they ought to receive communion at the end of life.

### From the First Council of Toledo, Chapter 16: If a Dedicated Woman Commits Adultery, Let Her Do Penance for Ten Years; If She Marries a Husband, She Is Not to Be Admitted to Penance Unless the Husband Dies

A dedicated woman who sins is not to be received into the Church unless she has ceased to sin. If, after ceasing, she performs suitable penance for ten years, she may then receive communion.

Before she is admitted into the Church for prayer, however, she must not attend the banquet of any Christian woman. If she is admitted, the woman who received her is also to be regarded as having incurred exclusion.

The corruptor is likewise to be bound by the same punishment.

But a woman who has taken a husband is not to be admitted to penance unless, while that husband is still alive, she begins to live chastely, or unless he has died—

### From the Fourth Council of Toledo, Chapter 56: Concerning the Distinction between Secular Widows and Nuns

There are two kinds of widows: secular and religious.

Secular widows are those who, while still intending to marry, have not laid aside secular clothing. Nuns are those who, after changing their secular clothing, have appeared in religious dress before a priest or the Church.

If these women turn to marriage, they will, according to the Apostle, not be without condemnation, because after first vowing themselves to God they afterward abandoned their purpose of chastity.

### From the Tenth Council of Toledo, Chapter 5

For all women who are proved to have previously been clothed in the garment of religion, no objection whatever may serve as an excuse, even if they wish to conceal themselves behind various or cunning arguments of deceit. Rather, the stricter discipline must hold and subject them by the most sacred decrees.

Let them be moved by the authority of the priest to return voluntarily. If they refuse to return, let them be brought back to the religious habit at the priest’s urging; and once restored to the monasteries, let them be struck with a sentence of appropriate excommunication.

## In the Edicts of the Pious Emperors

If anyone enters a holy church for the celebration of the divine mysteries or other sacred rites and inflicts an injury upon the bishop, clergy, or other ministers of the Church, we order that he be subjected to torture and die in exile.

If anyone disturbs holy oratories or the divine mysteries in any way, let him be punished by capital punishment.

The same rule is to be observed concerning litanies, in which bishops or clergy are present. If anyone offers an insult, let him be taken away to torture and exile; but if he disturbs the litany, let him be subject to capital danger.

For we wish not only that all places dedicated to God be entirely free from attack, but much more that all bishops and their clergy be completely secure from every danger. Thus, if any governor, judge, or military officer dares to lay hands upon them or insult them, he may expiate it in no other way than by perpetual exile or by blood.

### At the Council of Turin or Aquileia, Chapters 9 and 15

If, through the agency of sins, it should happen after the death of a holy bishop that a year passes before another bishop is appointed in the very city from which the bishop departed—although metropolitans ought to foresee this, so that the city should not remain vacant and without a shepherd for more than a month, or at most three months—we have decided that from now on the metropolitan is to be blamed for such negligence, and the clergy and people for failing to remember their salvation and hasten to the metropolitan to request a bishop.

Afterward a bishop is to be ordained for them. But if they do not have a suitable person among themselves, or if, when ordered by their metropolitan, they neglect to provide for themselves and make a choice, then, by his own judgment and authority, the metropolitan, after choosing a suitable person, shall ordain and appoint him bishop together with the other bishops, so that the people of God may not remain without a shepherd and the Church’s resources perish.

If the priests or leading men of the city do not agree to this, let them be anathematized as rebels.

## In the Edicts of the Most Pious Emperors

Let the leading men of the city swear upon the Gospels concerning the person elected to the episcopate that he has had neither a lawful wife nor a concubine, that he is neither a town councillor nor a *taxeota*, but holy and learned, understanding the canonical laws, and trained in the clergy or a monastery. Only then is he to be ordained.

But if those who ought to elect a bishop have not carried out such a confidential inquiry within six months, then the metropolitan, for the sake of the danger to his soul, after investigating all the matters we have mentioned, shall by his own authority ordain and consecrate a bishop for the clergy and people.

[Col. 1035]

# XII. EXPOSITIONS OF HINCMAR OF RHEIMS TO KING CHARLES

## For the Defense of the Liberties of the Church

*(From the Acts of the provincial Church of Rheims.)*

# FIRST EXPOSITION, ENTITLED “QUIRES” (*Quaterniones*)

[Col. 1035C]

Although, before I recently came to Rheims, from where I immediately sent a letter to Your Lordship, I had learned by hearsay some of the matters about which I am going to write, I afterward learned their history more fully from a reliable account.

If the case of Ariulf and Amalbert—which began reasonably, that is, in a manner not contrary to the sacred laws, and proceeded for some time because it began to be examined in an episcopal hearing, not in a public place but in a private and familiar inquiry—had ended with the same character, I would not occupy my discourse with it. I shall speak of what grieves me more deeply.

I have heard that, while you were seated with your faithful followers before our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar, the son of Liudo complained to Your Lordship because that same brother of ours had received from him an *exenium*—a gift or present—and had granted him his father’s benefice, and afterward had irrationally taken it away from him.

For this reason, perhaps through a vigilance in severity that was less necessary—although moderation in severity is no small adornment in a bishop—the spirit of Your Serenity was so moved that, before everyone and in a public voice, you heaped many insults upon that same bishop. No one ought to attack the priestly order in this way, least of all a king, upon whom, as upon a bishop, the eyes of all are fixed.

with reverence for God kept before your eyes and preserved—God who says what Saint Paul interpreted concerning a priest:

> “You shall not curse the prince of your people” (Acts 23:5).

And:

> “You shall not speak evil of the gods” (Exodus 22:28),

that is, of priests. For the one who inflicts insults upon priests also speaks evil of them.

The Lord likewise says concerning them:

> “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Psalm 104:15).

And:

> “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zechariah 2:8).

And:

> “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever rejects you rejects me; but whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me” (Luke 10:16).

And:

> “Those who honor me I will honor; and those who despise me will be held in contempt” (1 Samuel 2:30).

Afterward you ordered the aforesaid bishop to come on the appointed day and to the appointed place to answer your cases—that is, to secular courts—and to appoint his own advocate from his own person, namely, from the matter he himself had handled, which he had conducted without the knowledge of any fellow bishop.

He sent word to Your Lordship and conveyed an excuse for his inability to come there. An *exonia*—the term we use in the local language for this inability to come—was demanded, although this has until now been unheard of.

When his advocate was demanded and not found—an advocate who, on the basis of the aforesaid case, would answer for him personally—everything he had received, apart from the church, the bishop’s house, and the clergy’s cloister, from the ecclesiastical property and resources entrusted to him at his episcopal ordination by the gift of the Holy Spirit for governance and administration, was, by your order and through the viscount of that district, placed under the ban. In Latin law this is called *proscriptio*, confiscation.

And afterward, as I have heard, through the chancellor of your palace you instructed the vicedominus and the provost of that church, with no slight threat, to ensure that the bishop himself could receive no service from any of the church’s people and no support from the ecclesiastical resources, whether through clergy or laity. The vicedominus was to bring the laymen here with carts and workmen, and the provost was to bring the clerics who held benefices.

What was once foretold has been fulfilled:

> “And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest” (Isaiah 24:2).

There is no rule of distinction separating him from the common people.

Likewise, we see with our unhappy eyes what the blessed apostle John foretold, using, as Scripture often does, the past tense for the future. To him, together with the other apostles, it was said:

> “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke 10:23).

And he says:

> “The sun became black like a sackcloth garment” (Revelation 6:12).

At the end of this age the sun is shown as a sackcloth garment, because the shining life of preachers—of the bishops who preceded us—is displayed before the eyes of secular people, in us miserable men, as harsh and contemptible.

Although it must be believed, given the religious character of your Christianity, that you did this for the correction of the bishop himself, your wisdom is nevertheless astonishing: you so compounded the medicine for his wound that the medicine itself became wounded.

For the Lord establishes the measure of love for one’s neighbor in such a way that we are to love our neighbor as ourselves, not more than ourselves.

This fame—or rather infamy—will penetrate Burgundy and Provence and Italy, and reach Rome. Through the kingdom of your nephew it will travel not only as far as the nearer Germany but even as far as farther Germany, and, flying through Neustria, it will seize Aquitaine and Septimania.

Who, knowing nothing of the single eye—that is, the right intention—that is in you, will be able to judge otherwise? Here an act contrary to the Lord and hostile to the sacred canons has been committed, although, as blessed Leo writes, those canons were composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world. Their authors reign with the Lord in heaven and shine through miracles on earth, yet continue to live among us in their constitutions. It is also clear that the laws by which the Church is governed together with those sacred canons stand opposed to what has been done.

What will those who have heard of your former abhorrence say about you? You condemned those who did not venerate God’s churches and did not show priests the honor due to them, especially to the Roman pontiff and the holy Roman Church, the mother of all Churches. What will they say when they hear that you have proscribed her daughter—and therefore the Roman Church itself, indeed the universal Church—more by the prejudice of laymen than by judgment?

We do not read that any Christian ruler has ever done such a thing, either in the laws or in ecclesiastical books.

This action, it is said, was also undertaken and carried out because of the prejudice of certain persons who are marked as infamous persons both in the laws and in the sacred canons. If ecclesiastical vigor were as strong now as it was in the time of your predecessors and our forefathers, they would be excluded from the Church’s thresholds among criminals, since, as many say, they are criminals.

But now, through our dissolution—as some say—those themselves rush into the Church who ought to have been separated from it. We rightly attribute this to our sins, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Corinthians 10:11). To our disgrace, not to the glory of the Church, we are called priests, while we are trampled underfoot by such men; and they themselves pass judgment upon the heads of priests, although laymen of free and legally sound status would not legally accept the judgment or accusation of such persons in a public court if they wished to reject it.

In this action, as Saint Celestine writes:

> “It is not the case of the agents alone; the universal Church is shaken by every novelty.”

What has now been done is new, because under this heaven it has never been heard of that a bishop together with his Church should, under the title of proscription, be confiscated by any religious prince through the judgment of laymen.

This is especially so after the great emperor Constantine gave a law to all clergy, saying:

> “Constantine sends greetings to the clergy. In accordance with the sanction which you are said to have long ago earned, no one shall subject your estates and slaves to new levies; rather, you shall enjoy exemption.”

When he says “no one,” no one is excluded; indeed, by this comprehensive wording the imperial power itself is included.

Constantius also, although he was an Arian, and Constans granted this immunity to the Church, saying:

> “In whatever city, town, village, fortress, or municipality, anyone publicly proclaims the merit of the Christian law and of an exceptional and singular virtue, let him enjoy perpetual security. For we always wish our state to rejoice and glory in faith, knowing that our commonwealth is sustained more by religious observances than by official duties and bodily labor or sweat.”

Valentinian and Valens likewise decreed:

> “We decree that all who are established as guardians of churches or holy places and who serve religious observances are to suffer no harassment of any kind.”

Arcadius and Honorius likewise declared:

“Whatever has been established at different times by our parents, we order to remain inviolable and unaltered with regard to the holy Churches. Therefore let nothing be changed in their privileges, and let protection be extended to all who serve the churches. For in our time we desire rather that reverence be increased than that anything granted in former times be altered.”

And again the same emperors:

“We have not so much commanded anything new by the present enactment as confirmed those things that appear to have been granted long ago. Therefore we prohibit, even under threat of punishment, the mutilation of privileges that religious reverence formerly obtained, so that those also who obey the Church may enjoy its benefits.”

And again the same Augusti:

“If anyone should break out into this kind of sacrilege, so as to burst into Catholic churches and inflict any injury upon priests, ministers, the worship itself, or the place, let what has been done be reported to the authorities through letters from the ranks of officials, magistrates, and curators, and through the notaries of the apparitors whom they call stationarii, so that the names of those who can be identified may be made known. And if it is said that the offense was committed by a crowd, although not all can be identified, some may nevertheless be known, and through their confession the names of their associates may be made public.

“Thus let the governor of the province know that the injury done to priests and ministers of the Catholic Church, to the place itself, and to divine worship is to be punished by a capital sentence against those convicted or confessing. Nor should he wait for the bishop to demand vengeance for his own injury, since holiness has left to him only the glory of forgiving. Let it be not merely lawful but praiseworthy for everyone to prosecute as a public crime atrocious injuries inflicted upon priests or ministers and to obtain vengeance against such offenders. But if the violent crowd cannot be brought before the court by the execution of the civil apparitors, with the assistance of the officials or landholders, because it protects itself with weapons or by the difficulty of the terrain, let the judges request the protection of an armed force, sending letters to the illustrious count of Africa and setting forth the substance of this law, so that the perpetrators of such crimes may not escape.”

The same Augusti likewise declared:

“If anyone’s privileges belonging to the venerable Church have been violated through recklessness or neglected through negligence, let the offense be punished by a condemnation of five pounds of gold, just as was previously established.”

Many other provisions could also be set down here, provisions that have been beneficially preserved for a long time by all rulers who governed well and judged justly. But I know that your wisdom ought, from the matters cited from the sixteenth book of the Theodosian law, to understand still more.

Imitating the piety of these emperors, the ancient and modern kings of the Franks likewise have been accustomed to grant immunities to churches and to the servants of God. Those who do not preserve them accumulate their sins through the almsgiving of those kings. Therefore, when we speak of other memorable emperors and kings, the memory of your grandfather, the great Emperor Charles, must not be passed over.

When, as commonly happens, something had been insinuated into him by the tongues of flatterers, so that he might inflict some prejudice upon the churches in their possessions, the bishops opposed him, and especially Paulinus the patriarch. As I know is well known to you, he so recognized his error and made satisfaction to the Church and to the bishops that his present confession by word of mouth did not suffice him; rather, he transmitted to his descendants, who were to arise from his stock, a document of his confession and correction, confirmed by his own hand.

Part of that decree is written in your book called the *Book of Imperial Capitularies*, chapter 67, where it says:

“Because, in accordance with the tradition of the holy Fathers, we know that the possessions of the Church are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor, we desire, with God’s help, not only to preserve what each person has possessed but also to contribute many things. Nevertheless, in order completely to remove the long-conceived suspicion among churchmen that those possessions would be divided, we decree that neither in our time nor in the time of our sons, and—God directing things—in the time of our successors who may wish to imitate our will or that of our ancestors, shall they suffer any division or loss whatsoever.”

For Pope Symmachus wrote to Aeonius:

“No one may, under any necessity, transgress the arrangement of his predecessors; rather, by strengthening what his predecessors have done well, he ought to make what he himself has done valid.”

Therefore it is your duty not only to give firmness to the good provisions made by your predecessors and forefathers by preserving them, but also to recall before the eyes of your mind and body those things that you yourself have done, subscribed with your own hand, and, promising with the greatest solemnity that you would perpetually observe them, entrusted into the hands of the priests in God’s place.

A considerable obligation also rests upon you: if in any respect you have acted against those provisions, you must take the greatest care to correct it as quickly as possible and thereafter to guard diligently against acting contrary to them. For after that anointing by which, together with the other faithful, you were worthy to attain what the blessed Apostle Peter says—“You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (*I Peter* II)—you received royal dignity through episcopal and spiritual anointing and blessing, rather than through earthly power.

You must therefore attend with subtle understanding to the fact that you are not exempt from the definition of the Holy Spirit promulgated with synodal authority:

“If anyone,” it says, “acts against his profession or subscription, he himself shall deprive himself of his honor.”

[Note: [Col. 1039D] Council of Africa, canon 13.]

Although this does not happen in the sight of human beings, as often occurs, it nevertheless always happens in the sight of the Lord.

David, for example, acting proudly—“For pride is the beginning of every sin” (*Ecclesiasticus* X)—acted against his profession, which he had professed when he said, “As the Lord lives, I will play before the Lord, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (*II Samuel* VI). Having lost through sin the grace of prophecy and royal dignity, he recovered them by confessing and repenting before Nathan.

Peter likewise acted against his profession, which he had made when he said, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (*Matthew* XXV). Because he had denied the Lord three times, he confessed three times before all the apostles, as the blessed Gregory shows. He wept bitterly; what he had denied, he washed away with his tears; and the apostleship that he had lost by denying, he received again by confessing and weeping.

In the same way, anyone who confesses, repents, and corrects what he has wrongly done against his profession and subscription can, by the Lord’s mercy, return to honor and remain honorably established in it. Otherwise there will be argument against the keys given to the Church, concerning which it is said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (*Matthew* XVIII).

Christ Jesus, as the Catholic Church holds and teaches, entrusted this authority to the rulers of that same Church, so that they might impose an act of penance upon those who confess and, once those same persons had been cleansed by salutary satisfaction—which satisfaction is already understood in the confession of sin itself—restore them through the grace of reconciliation. The brevity of this work and the pressure of time have not permitted me here to set out how this restoration through reconciliation is not contrary to the sacred rules.

For these provisions, together with the other matters contained there, you promised with the greatest solemnity that you would observe them throughout all the days of your life, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 845, in April, in the sixth year of your reign, in the city of Beauvais [*Belgivacum*]. You made this promise to the bishops who were present, to the other bishops of your kingdom who were not bodily present, to all their successors, and to all bishops residing in your kingdom; at their request, you placed it in the hands of those same bishops:

I. “That you preserve ecclesiastical right and canonical law for us in the same way as your predecessors who observed these matters well and reasonably, insofar as you are able to know and as the Lord grants you the power, preserved them for our predecessors.”

II. “That, concerning my person and my order, unless—which God forbid—I should henceforth openly do something against the Lord and against you for which I ought canonically to be condemned, you shall not condemn me and my order in so damnable a manner for any past cause that condemnation or dishonor should come upon me.”

III. “That you immediately restore and preserve the possessions belonging to the church entrusted to me that were taken away during your rule, just as they were in the time of your grandfather and father; excepting what has been added and has been consumed for the use of the possessors or in buildings, as it then was, insofar as it is established—as regards what we customarily call ‘property’—that you took them thence.”

[Col. 1042A]

IV. “That the unlawful orders made by you concerning the possessions of the church entrusted to me be rescinded, and that you take care that such orders are not made in the future.”

V. “That henceforth you exact from the church entrusted to me no undue customary payments or unjust exactions, but preserve them as they were preserved in the time of your grandfather and father.”

VI. “That against the plunderers and oppressors of our churches and of the possessions belonging to them, you provide protection according to your office, insofar as God grants you the ability.”

VII. “That the orders which your grandfather and father made for the churches entrusted to us, confirmed, and preserved as secure—and which you too have preserved—you henceforth preserve as valid.”

VIII. “If you, contrary to these articles, or we—which God forbid—not through malice or perverse zeal, but through human frailty, ignorance, or deception, should act in a manner not deserving condemnation, let us correct this together by mutual counsel, and let the agreement established thereafter remain firm.”

You also confirmed the following with your own hand at the palace of Quierzy, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 858, in the eighteenth year of your reign, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, promising to observe them before the bishops and your other faithful:

“To the extent that I know and can reasonably do so, with the Lord’s help I shall honor and protect each one of you according to his order, and shall preserve each one, honored and protected, without any deceit, condemnation, or deception. I shall preserve for each person the law and justice appropriate to him.

“And to anyone who needs it and reasonably requests it, I shall show reasonable mercy, just as a faithful king ought to honor and protect his faithful by right, preserve for each person the law and justice appropriate to each order, and extend reasonable mercy to those in need who reasonably request it. I shall not, for the sake of any person, depart from this—so far as human frailty permits—through zeal, ill will, or the improper urging of anyone, to the extent that God grants me understanding and ability.

“And if, through frailty, I should be led to act against this, once I recognize it I shall voluntarily take care to correct it.”

You also confirmed other matters arising from this, which I have not set down here.

After all this and the other promises that you often made to your faithful—and also at Quierzy, when, seeking pardon, you received the laying-on of hands from the bishops who were present, and likewise in the villa of Breona—the Church of Laon, indeed the whole Church in it, now suffers such a loss that it bears, something previously unheard of, the title of proscription, contrary to the decrees of all the holy bishops who have presided over the Apostolic See. It would be too lengthy to insert all their decrees here. Therefore, for the sake of brevity, I have undertaken to set down some of them.

For Saint Urban, pope and martyr, says, among other things:

“Every effort must be made, and these matters must be faithfully guarded, and the insult of every usurpation must be driven away, lest estates dedicated to the uses of heavenly mysteries be harassed by certain intruders. If anyone should do this, then, after the severity of the deserved vengeance that by right must be imposed upon sacrilegious persons, let him be condemned to perpetual disgrace and handed over to prison, or deported into exile under perpetual condemnation. For, according to the Apostle, such a person must be handed over to Satan, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”

Saint Lucius likewise wrote to all the bishops established in the western regions, both in Gaul and in Spain, saying:

“The possessions of your churches and the offerings of the faithful, which you have indicated are being harassed by certain intruders and taken away from you and your churches, are undoubtedly a very great sin.”

And shortly afterward:

“One who seizes his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but one who takes ecclesiastical money or possessions commits sacrilege. Thus Judas, who defrauded the money that, by the Savior’s command, was being distributed for the uses of the Church—that is, for the poor whom the Church ought to feed, and whose place the bishops hold—not only became a thief but a sacrilegious thief.”

And again, after a little:

“The decrees of the prophets, the apostles, their successors, and all Catholic Fathers forbid these things, and judge such presumptions to be sacrileges. Following their examples, we, together with you and by apostolic authority, expel from the threshold of holy Mother Church and condemn as anathematized all such presumptuous persons, plunderers of the Church, and alienators of their possessions, and judge them to be sacrilegious.

“And not only them, but also all who consent to them, since not only those who commit an act are judged guilty, but also those who consent to its perpetrators. An equal punishment encompasses both those who act and those who consent.”

And Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, says:

“Whatever is done unjustly against things consecrated to God and against bishops shall be regarded as sacrilege.”

Since it is written, “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (*Matthew* XVIII), we think that these three lights, representing the decrees of all the pontiffs of the Apostolic See who have decreed similarly, ought to suffice to illuminate the hearts of those who believe in God and desire to keep his commands and orders.

All the pontiffs of that holy and principal See have entrusted ecclesiastical possessions and resources to bishops by the tradition of the Lord and his apostles. Because of the length of the work, the brevity of the time, and the urgency of the matter, I have omitted connecting their decrees here in this collection sent to you; you can read them in full in their proper places, if you wish.

The canons of Antioch likewise prescribe:

“Let the possessions of the Church be preserved with every care, a good conscience, and the faith that is in God, who considers and judges all things. They are to be administered according to the judgment and authority of the bishop to whom the people and the souls gathered within the Church have been entrusted.”

And again:

“Let the bishop have authority over ecclesiastical possessions, to distribute them to all who are in need, with the greatest reverence and fear of God. He himself may also share in whatever he needs—if indeed he needs anything—provided it contributes to the necessary uses of himself and of the brethren received by him.”

And so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1043D] Council of Antioch, A.D. 341, canons 24 and 25.]

The canons of Gangra say:

“If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, and does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.”

And again:

“If anyone gives or receives offerings apart from the bishop or the person appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, let both the giver and the receiver be anathema.”

[Note: [Col. 1043D] Council of Gangra, A.D. 325, canons 7 and 8.]

So completely are the possessions and resources of the Church entrusted to the bishop’s authority by the decree of the Holy Spirit that the great Synod of Chalcedon ordered that, even after the death of a bishop, the revenues of the widowed church be preserved intact by its steward for the future bishop.

[Note: [Col. 1044D] Council of Chalcedon, canon 25.]

Whether the bishop is living or dead, those who by any device demand from the Church, to its burden, services or undue payments cannot be without fear that they are committing sacrilege—even if they do not seize them violently but take them unjustly under the appearance of prudent ingenuity. Their conscience accuses them before the Lord, who sees the heart, whatever sinister intention they may have.

Especially since John says: “If our heart does not condemn us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things” (*I John* III). And Paul says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified. It is the Lord who judges me” (*I Corinthians* IV). For when Paul says, “You tolerate it if someone takes from you” (*II Corinthians* XI), “to take,” as Gregory explains, is sometimes understood as “to seize”; hence those birds that are eager to seize other birds are called *accipitres*, hawks.

It is clear from the laws approved by the Church—laws promulgated by his inspiration, through whom the lawmakers establish what is just—and from the sacred canons, that it is contrary to divine commands for a bishop, who possesses this authority divinely through the sacred canons, to be condemned together with the possessions and resources of his church under a title of proscription. The canons decree:

“If anyone among the powerful has despoiled a cleric, or any poorer person, or a religious person, and the bishop has ordered him to hear the case, but he has refused, let written notices immediately circulate among all the bishops of the province and among as many as he can reach, so that he may be regarded as excommunicated until he hears the case and restores what belongs to another.”

[Note: [Col. 1044D] Council of Toledo, A.D. 400, canon 11.]

As for any bishop or any member of the ecclesiastical clergy, the Apostle Paul, possessing the Spirit of the Lord and with Christ speaking through him, firmly asserts that he must not leave ecclesiastical judgment and go to public courts. With this authority, the canons of Carthage prescribe:

“Whenever a charge has been brought in the Church against any bishop, priest, deacon, or cleric, or a civil case has been initiated, if, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, he wishes to clear himself before public courts, even if a judgment has been pronounced in his favor, let him lose his place. This applies in a criminal case; in a civil case, if he prefers to retain his place, let him lose what he has won.”

[Note: [Col. 1045D] Council of Africa, canon 15.]

And the African Council says:

“Whoever—that is, any member of the clergy—has requested from the emperor a hearing before public courts shall be deprived of his own rank. But if he has requested episcopal judgment from the emperor, this shall do him no harm.”

[Note: [Col. 1046D] Ibid., canon 104. See also the Council of Rheims, A.D. 630, canon 18.]

The laws, by which the holy Church is governed together with the sacred canons, likewise confirm this in the sixteenth book of the Theodosian law. Constantine enacted:

“By the law of our clemency,” he says, “we prohibit bishops from being accused in courts, lest, while impunity is expected for the benefit they will receive in the future, free opportunity should be given to furious minds to accuse them. Therefore, if anyone brings forward any complaint, it is most fitting that it be investigated before other bishops, so that a suitable and convenient hearing may be provided for the inquiries of all.”

The interpretation of the same law says:

“It is specifically prohibited that anyone dare accuse a bishop before public judges. Rather, he must not delay bringing before the bishops whatever he thinks may properly concern him according to the nature of the case, so that what he asserts against the bishop may be decided in the judgment of other bishops.”

Valens, Gratian, and Valentinian likewise declared:

“The same procedure that is customary in civil cases is to be maintained in ecclesiastical matters, so that if there are matters arising from certain disagreements or minor offenses and pertaining to the observance of religion, they may be heard in their proper places and by the synods of their own dioceses.”

And so forth.

The interpretation of the same law says:

“Whenever a dispute concerning any matter pertaining to religion has arisen among clerics, this must especially be observed: the diocesan priests are to be summoned by the bishop, and the matters that have become subjects of dispute are to be settled by judgment.”

And so forth.

The most Christian Emperor Theodosius, the most humble hearer of the blessed Ambrose—or rather, through him, of God—addressed Optatus the Augustal in a promulgated law, at the passage that says:

“By an immediate law we enact that the names of bishops, or of those who serve the needs of the Church, are not to be dragged before the courts of either ordinary or extraordinary judges. They have their own judges, and have nothing in common with these public laws.”

And so forth.

The same emperor likewise declared:

“Clerics ought to be accused only before bishops. Therefore, if a bishop, priest, deacon, or any minister of the Christian law of lower rank has been accused before bishops—since he ought not to be accused elsewhere—by any person, whether that person is a man of high rank or of any other dignity, let the person who undertakes this kind of blameworthy accusation know that he must establish his charge by proofs and demonstrate it by documents.

“If anyone therefore brings an unprovable charge against such persons, let him understand, by the authority of this enactment, that he is subject to the loss of his own reputation. Thus, through damage to his honor and loss of standing, he may learn that, at least henceforth, he is not permitted to lie in wait for another’s shame with impunity.”

What constitutes the loss of one’s reputation, and who are infamous persons, is explained by the Roman laws and canons, as well as by the decrees of the Roman See, whose pontiffs have often addressed this matter.

Among them, the blessed Stephen, writing to Saint Hilary, says:

“As for what you have asked of the Apostolic See—who are infamous, or who are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical orders—we believe that you know, and we do not refuse to instruct you on the authority of the Apostolic See.

“We call those persons infamous who are marked with infamy for some fault: that is, all who reject the rule of the Christian law and despise ecclesiastical statutes. Likewise, thieves, sacrilegious persons, all entangled in capital crimes, violators of tombs, and those who willingly violate the statutes of the apostles, their successors, and the other holy Fathers; all who take up arms against the Fathers, who are marked with infamy throughout the whole world.

“Likewise, incestuous persons, murderers, perjurers, plunderers, sorcerers, poisoners, adulterers, those who flee from battle, those who seek to hold offices unworthy of them, and those who unjustly seize the resources of the Church; those who slander or accuse their brethren and do not prove the accusation; those who provoke the minds of princes to anger against the innocent; all who have been anathematized or expelled from the Church for their crimes; and all whom ecclesiastical or secular laws pronounce infamous.

“These persons may not be promoted to sacred orders. Nor may slaves before lawful emancipation, penitents, digamists, those who serve in the curia, those who are not sound in body, those who do not possess a sound mind or understanding, those who are disobedient to the decrees of the saints, or those who are plainly insane.

“None of these may be advanced to the sacred ranks. Neither they, nor freedmen, nor persons under suspicion, nor those who do not possess right faith or a worthy way of life, may accuse high priests.”

According to the canons of Africa, criminals—whom the Lord says are defiled by the things that proceed from the heart and whom the Apostle teaches are excluded from the kingdom of God—excommunicated persons, all marked by stains of infamy, and all whom the public laws do not admit to the public accusation of crimes cannot accuse ecclesiastical clerics except in their own cases, nor may they be admitted as witnesses against them.

Since Christian and religious princes, as we have shown above, neither wished nor permitted the clerics of the Church to be dragged or summoned before public courts, this is demonstrated with complete clarity in the edict of Honorius and Theodosius. In the same edict they show how they regarded the person who dared to act in this way against the Lord:

“We restore with willing devotion all the privileges of the churches that the tyrant had begrudged in our age, namely, that whatever has been established by deified emperors, or whatever individual bishops have obtained for ecclesiastical causes, shall be preserved with perpetual and unbroken force under threat of sacrilege.

“We also reserve for episcopal judgment those clerics whom an unfortunate presumptuous person had ordered to be indiscriminately brought before secular judges. For it is not right that ministers of a divine office should be subjected to the discretion of temporal powers.”

Therefore Saint Leo, after a synod held at Rome, wrote to Sermatio and the other bishops, saying:

“The powers of this world wished such great reverence to prevail toward the priestly order—even those whom divine power has commanded to preside over the earth under the imperial name—that, in accordance with imperial constitutions, they permitted holy bishops to exercise jurisdiction in the settlement of cases. Although this has been confirmed both by the edicts of ancient law and by laws frequently enacted, we find that in the present time it has been trampled upon by many. For, bypassing priestly judgment, they have indiscriminately passed over to the examination of secular authorities.

“Therefore it seemed good to us that this insult to the sacred laws and to our order should, for the present, be punished by full severity, and that a rule to be observed in the future should be established. We decree, therefore, that whoever, bypassing the priest of his own church, comes before secular authorities for judgment shall be expelled from the sacred thresholds and excluded from the heavenly altar.”

And so forth, as he continues there on this subject.

According to apostolic teaching, the sacred canons, and the laws—much of whose meaning is contained in those same canons and also in the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See concerning the conduct of regular judgments—you may read the following provisions, among others, in the places mentioned below:

“If they are accused, the case shall be concluded in the places where they themselves are accused.”

And:

“No one who has been stripped of his possessions or resources may be summoned by anyone, on any charge whatsoever, to give an account canonically and legally until he has been restored to possession, has lawfully made use of those possessions, and has then been regularly summoned to judgment.”

And:

“They must not be judged by secular authorities, nor summoned or dragged before secular courts, either on a criminal charge or in a civil case, just as was done in those times when the name of Christ was not revered by unbelievers.”

Therefore the Apostle James wrote to the faithful:

“Do not the rich oppress you by their power, and do they themselves not drag you before the courts?” (*James* II).

Nor may a cleric, and least of all a bishop, clear himself before public courts, since he may be subjected and held to no judgment other than that of bishops and his own regular judges. Nor is anyone permitted to condemn a bishop or a cleric of any order in any way except after judgment by the canonical judgment of bishops or, if the case requires it, upon the regular petition of those bishops.

The sacred canons demonstrate how and in what ways a bishop who has transgressed is to be corrected or judged by other bishops. Anyone who carefully considers them will understand this in those same rules. I would also set them down here if I thought it necessary.

As for the possessions and bondsmen of the church entrusted to him, although they may legally—and otherwise they ought not—be placed under a ban, nevertheless, as you know better than anyone, just as the possessions of free persons cannot be reduced into the treasury, so things dedicated to God require that the bishop, according to the laws that the Church receives and venerably approves, and according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See, appoint an advocate for public courts.

For his own person, whether in a criminal or civil case, he must give an account either before judges chosen according to the determination of the sacred laws, or he himself must give an account in a synod before the bishops. Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius decreed this in their edict:

“We decree by this sacred enactment that the privileges which the authority of the laws grants to churches and clerics remain permanent and inviolable. We also grant them this special and singular privilege: whatever has been specially obtained from us concerning matters belonging solely to the Church shall be brought to the attention of the judges and receive effect, not through persons wearing the crown but through advocates, at their discretion.

“Let the priests of the province be vigilant, however, lest under cover of this privilege some disadvantage be inflicted upon these persons, even against their own interests.”

This chapter clearly shows that, in matters belonging to the Church—matters conferred upon it by emperors, that is, by their generosity and through their laws—ecclesiastical clerics must provide advocates to the judges, not themselves. When it says, “whatever has been specially obtained from us concerning matters belonging solely to the Church,” it does not include ecclesiastical clerics, and least of all the bishop himself, to whom it entrusts the care of protecting the clerics.

And in the first book of the capitularies of our emperors, who are your forefathers, it is prescribed:

“That suffragan bishops look to the metropolitan.”

It is also prescribed that if ecclesiastical clerics incur blame or have some dispute among themselves, they are to be judged by ecclesiastical persons, not by secular authorities.

Saint Pope Gelasius likewise writes in his decrees to bishops who were making light of the afflictions of their brethren, rebuking them with suitable severity:

“Why have you not shown compassion to so many of your brethren? Why have you not approached the emperor? Why have you not, with continual appeals, lamented the cause of the Church and the pitiable disfigurement of the priests, declaring that no one has ever judged pontiffs except the Church?

“It does not belong to human laws to pronounce judgment concerning such persons without the pontiffs principally established by the Church. Christian princes are accustomed to obey the decrees of the Church, not to place their own power above them; the prince is accustomed to subject his head to the bishops, not to judge their heads.

“Therefore it is clear that, if it is not permitted to a prince, neither is it permitted to anyone else except bishops to judge the heads of bishops. Indeed, the public laws themselves, obeying ecclesiastical rules, have decreed that such persons are to be judged only by bishops.”

And again Gelasius, to the Emperor Anastasius:

“There are two things, Emperor Augustus, by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and the royal power. Among these, the burden of the priests is the greater, because they must render an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves.

“For you know, most merciful son, that although you preside over the human race by the dignity of worldly affairs, nevertheless, out of reverence for the divine, you devoutly bow your neck to the prelates and seek from them the causes of your salvation. In receiving the heavenly sacraments and in arranging them as is fitting, you recognize that you must be subject to them, and not preside over them, by the order of religion.

“Therefore, in these matters, you should depend upon their judgment rather than wish to reduce them to your will. For if, insofar as it concerns the order of public discipline, the bishops of religion themselves obey your laws, recognizing that empire has been conferred upon you by heavenly disposition, lest they should appear even in worldly matters to resist the judgment of the authorities, with what feeling, I ask, is it fitting and proper for you to obey those who have been appointed to confer the venerable mysteries?

“Accordingly, just as a grave danger rests upon pontiffs if they remain silent concerning what is appropriate for divine worship, so, God forbid, a serious danger rests upon those who, when they ought to obey, despise them.”

Therefore, most beloved and most venerable head, I shall address your most devout Christian piety in the words of Blessed Gregory from a homily on the Gospel, saying:

> “Even if you perhaps rightly despise us, unworthy and insignificant priests as we are, nevertheless preserve in your mind reverence for the Lord, who through our unworthiness calls you to the heavenly kingdom. For what I say often happens: a powerful person may regard a servant with contempt; yet when, perhaps through him, he sends some reply to his own people or to strangers, the person of the speaking servant is not despised, because the reverence owed to the lord who sent him is preserved in the heart. Those who hear do not consider through whom they hear, but what they hear, or from whom they hear.” [Col. 1049C]

Even if you discern in us our character, conduct, and the dignity of our merits, you must nevertheless attend to, and in honor of God not only venerate but also revere, the one most holy priesthood that exists through all bishops. For, as Pope Saint Symmachus writes:

> “In the likeness of the Trinity, whose power is one and indivisible, there is one priesthood through the various bishops,” [Col. 1049D]

neither holier in the just person nor less holy in the sinner.

So too, when this visible sun shines upon gold, it is not itself more beautiful, but makes the gold more splendid. When it sends its rays upon dung, the dung appears more clearly for what it is. Yet when the sun withdraws its rays from it, it contracts no impurity from it.

Whether, therefore, a holy person or a sinner administers the heavenly sacraments to you, the sacraments themselves are inviolable and perfect in themselves. For whoever baptizes in the name of the Holy Trinity—as the evangelical truth shows—the one whom John the Baptist saw as having the Spirit descend upon him and remain in him, he is the one who baptizes. Whoever, moreover, catholicly consecrates the heavenly sacraments—the one who said, “Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me”—he is the one who consecrates. [Col. 1050A]

Therefore do not despise us if you see things in us that are reprehensible, for you do not know what the one terrible in his counsels, God, has secretly ordained concerning us or concerning you.

Finally, you can remember that you told me that, just as I had explained to you the procedure of inquiry—when someone appealed to you concerning a benefice taken away by a bishop, how you ought to order that matter itself to be investigated—so afterward you happened to read that your predecessors and ancestors had observed this procedure, and that you wished to observe it as well.

If you observe that procedure, you will neither offend the Lord in your command nor violate ecclesiastical authority; you will honor your own dignity and carry out equity and justice both toward the person against whom the complaint is made and toward the person who has lodged it. Your holy and illustrious ancestors recognized this and observed it. You must certainly not readily lend your assent, against your own salvation—which God forbid—to the tongues of flatterers or of those who perhaps advise you otherwise than severity requires.

Moreover, after the bishop has arranged what belongs to the church and to himself, as well as the provisions for churchmen, the poor, and guests, when he grants a benefice from church property for military service, or to the sons of fathers who have served that same church and who could usefully succeed their fathers—for, as someone wrote, “unless the calf is nourished, the ox is not yoked to the plow”—he ought to give it to persons capable of rendering to Caesar what is Caesar’s [Col. 1050B] and to God what is God’s.

This excludes such benefices as must be granted to the ministers of the church and to those necessary to him, without whom we neither ought nor are able to exist, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing” (I Cor. 9).

Those who serve in the military ought to take care that, in proportion to the benefice, they serve the bishop faithfully and usefully, and thereby serve the church, so that through royal service they may be able to contribute generally to the defense of God’s holy Church.

If a bishop has taken a benefice away from a person who has long benefited the church, and especially that particular church and its needs, who has been useful to the commonwealth and to military service, but who, worn out by illness or age, can no longer perform these duties himself—especially if he has a son serving him who is able to perform them in his place—and if he has been unable to obtain justice through the admonitions and requests of a neighboring bishop or of anyone else, it is not unreasonable for him to appeal not by accusing the bishop before public judges, which is not permitted, but by lodging a complaint with you. [Col. 1050C]

The military benefice is like the pay and donative that formerly—and, as is still done elsewhere today—were given publicly to soldiers. Through the increased devotion of the faithful among our people, the Church grants benefices from ecclesiastical property, which consists of the vows of the faithful, the prices paid for sins, the patrimonies of the poor, and the sustenance of the Lord’s male and female servants, together with other gifts to be distributed to the prince’s attendants, for the sake of its defense. In this way the Church provides the king and the commonwealth with the revenues that we call annual gifts, observing what the Apostle commands: “To whom honor, honor; to whom tribute, tribute” (Rom. 13)—that is, provide it to the king and to your defenders.

Therefore, whoever receives the Church’s pay, whatever his order, place, or rank, if he does not diligently and to the best of his ability labor for its safety, peaceful honor, and defense, he receives it unworthily—indeed, he usurps it to his own condemnation. For just as the church’s property and resources have been entrusted to the bishop to arrange and distribute, so they have been entrusted to royal power to defend and protect.

And through the laws of kings the Church possesses its holdings, as Saint Augustine says in his sermon on the Gospel of John:

> “The laws are read openly,” he says, “in which the emperors commanded that those who usurp for themselves the name Christian apart from communion with the Catholic Church, and who are unwilling to worship in peace the author of peace, should dare to possess nothing in the name of the Church. But they say to us, ‘What have we to do with the emperor?’ But I have already said: this concerns human law. Nevertheless, the Apostle wished kings to be honored, and said, ‘Honor the king.’ Do not say, ‘What have I to do with the king?’ What, then, have you to do with property? Possessions are held through the laws of kings. You have said, ‘What have I to do with the king?’ Do not call the possessions yours, since in that very statement you have renounced the human laws through which possessions are held.” [Col. 1051B]

And in the law given to the Church by the emperors Honorius and Theodosius it is prescribed that, when priests, deacons, or other clerics have been accused before a bishop, the bishop should hear such cases with many witnesses attesting to the proceedings, so that, if they are proved innocent, this may become known to many. The Apostle also says: “A bishop must have a good testimony from those who are outside” (I Tim. 3). [Col. 1051C]

Since it has been spread in the palace by the complainant that the bishop acted unjustly, it is good that, if he acted justly, his innocence should also become known to secular persons.

And since the canons of Sardica command that a bishop be summoned to the imperial court on behalf of those who are oppressed by unjust force, and a man serving the commonwealth complains before you that he has been despoiled by a bishop, the sacred laws command that both parties—that is, the complainant and the person against whom the complaint is made—as Gregory also decreed concerning cases established by the laws, should, without delay, not merely be summoned but compelled to appear before the judgment of chosen judges.

If a layperson has refused to choose episcopal judgment—a judgment which a bishop may not refuse—it is reasonable, and does not conflict with authority, that the bishop against whom someone has lodged a complaint before you concerning a benefice unjustly taken from him should appear with his fellow bishops. It is unworthy that you should labor over the matter yourself. You should send your envoys, either requested from him or appointed by you, to hear the account of both parties and to decide according to divine and human laws, lest the church suffer loss through an unjust complainant and an unworthy man, and lest a useful man and complainant seeking justice suffer injustice and harm to his military service.

This should be done not in public but in a private place, so that, as the sacred canons say, a great man, if he has perhaps transgressed, may not suffer disgrace. [Col. 1051D] For, as Solomon says, “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccli. 7); and the Apostle says, “We all offend in many things” (Jas. 3). The bishop should obey his brothers and his judges, in accordance with the sacred canons, which say: “Let the case be concluded through episcopal judges.”

In this way, according to the justly established laws of your military service, since it is written through Wisdom, who is God, “Lawgivers decree what is just” (Prov. 8), if he has a just complaint, let him obtain his justice. If he has complained unjustly, let his mouth be legally closed by the decision of your envoys.

For, as Saint Augustine says in his sermon on the Gospel of John:

> “It belongs to judicial procedure that someone who has lied in his petitions should not benefit from what he obtained. But this is among human beings. For a human being can be deceived, and the emperor could have been deceived when you sent your petition. You said what you wished, and the person to whom you said it does not know whether it is true. He dismissed you to be convicted by your adversary; and if you are convicted before the judge of lying, since he could not fail to grant it, not knowing whether you had lied, there you should lose the very benefit that you obtained.” [Col. 1052B]

I have not found the law itself, which was explained by so great a man, set down here. It is therefore clear that, if a person ought to lose what he obtained through a lie, it is safer for the truth to be investigated before he obtains anything through falsehood, except perhaps the opportunity for inquiry. As the holy and prudent king says: “The case that I did not know I investigated most diligently” (Job 29).

And if a bishop refuses to obey the judgment of bishops chosen by himself or appointed by his primate, or the canonical judgments of a synod, so that he may correct what he has done otherwise than he ought, we have a judgment prescribed for this in the sacred canons, which he must undergo.

And if a man belonging to your military service scorns obedience to your envoys and to the laws of the world, so that he may desist from an unjust complaint, there is a judgment established in the capitularies concerning those who either unjustly bring accusations through calumny against others or bring again a case already judged.

Therefore, most Christian and most wise lord, take care for your salvation; take care for your honor; take care for your good reputation, which extends far and wide; and take care for the enrichment of the churches and for the veneration of priests and God’s servants. Do not stain that glorious reputation of yours because of anyone’s negligence. [Col. 1052D] Nor, for the sake of anyone’s expulsion, should you pretend to a cruelty in action that you do not possess in mind, doing or commanding what is unworthy of the dignity of your name.

We read in the Book of Maccabees what Eleazarus replied when his companions urged him to do something unworthy of his reputation:

> “It is not fitting,” he said, “for our age to pretend, lest many of the young, thinking that Eleazarus at ninety years of age had passed over to the life of foreigners, should themselves be deceived because of my pretense and because of the brief period of corruptible life, and I should thereby bring upon my old age stain and execration” (II Macc. 4).

What he says concerning bodily old age, you must understand as applying to the dignity of your office, name, and wisdom, as the Lord says to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people” (Num. 11). Hence Saint Gregory says:

> “Just as those who are not weighed down by any seriousness of counsel are often called young, so Sacred Scripture customarily calls old those who are mature not only in the number of their years but also in the greatness of their character.”

Hence it is said by a certain wise man: “Old age is venerable, not measured by length of time or counted by number of years. The gray hairs of a person are understanding, and an unstained life is the age of old age.”

This is why the Lord says to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people.” What else is sought in them than old age of heart, since those are commanded to be chosen who are known to be old? If bodily old age were being sought in them, they could be known by as many people as could see them. But when it is said, “whom you know to be elders of the people,” it is plainly declared that old age of mind, not of body, is to be chosen. [Col. 1053B]

Because, lord, your most dear and venerable lordship—or rather, divine command—has ordered me, and I am thereby a willing debtor, not to remain silent about what I know pertains to your salvation and to the dignity of your name and office, I humbly request and admonish you: let your wisdom reflect, and let it put in order what has been disordered, so that this irreverence toward God’s Church may not continue longer and so that the scandal stirred up against the bishops may as quickly as possible be settled by an appropriate satisfaction.

For this reason I write so insistently: because I do not dare to remain silent, for the sake of the King of kings, about what I know to be necessary for your salvation and welfare. Before his judgment you and I will come in the presence of the whole human race and of all angels and archangels. There we shall render an account not only of the actions, words, and thoughts of our individual persons, but also of the duties of the offices we have undertaken—how in them we have carried out, with sincere heart and just deeds, what pertains to those offices. For he himself says: “You shall carry out precisely what is just” (Deut. 16).

To carry out precisely what is just means, in asserting justice, to seek justice alone. For if I remain silent about what I must say and you must hear, I fear incurring that woe which the Lord, through the prophet, threatens against us wretched priests, saying: “Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow and make pillows beneath the head of people of every age, to capture souls” (Ezek. 13). [Col. 1053D]

To place cushions under every elbow is to support with flattering consolation souls that have fallen from their uprightness and reclined in love of this world. The elbow of one lying down is received, as it were, by a cushion, and his head by pillows, when the harshness of correction is withdrawn from a sinner and the softness of favor is applied to him, so that he may lie comfortably in error, untouched by any harshness of contradiction.

Rulers who love themselves undoubtedly provide such comforts to those by whom they fear they may be harmed in their pursuit of temporal glory.

The same Lord also commands through Moses that, when the priest enters the tabernacle, he be surrounded by little bells, so that he may have the sound of preaching and not offend the judgment of the heavenly inspector through silence. For it is written: “So that the sound may be heard when he enters and leaves the sanctuary in the presence of the Lord” (Exod. 28). [Col. 1054A]

A priest entering or leaving dies if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes the anger of the hidden judge against himself if he walks without the sound of preaching.

Concerning such priests the Lord says: “Mute dogs unable to bark” (Isa. 14). And through the prophet Ezekiel he threatens them collectively, saying: “If the priest does not distinguish for the people, the people themselves will die in their sin; nevertheless I will require their soul from the hand of the priest.”

He does not say that, because the people are free from sin, they will not die; rather, he says that they will die in their sin. The people therefore die for themselves alone, but the priest also dies for the people.

And because, if we remain silent about what, as I have said, we must say and you must hear, we incur sin; and because, if you do not heed what you have heard—which God forbid—you cannot be free from the death of sin, therefore let your devotion receive with attentive ear of heart what the thunder of divine threat resounds with terror:

> “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be sunk into the depths of the sea” (Matt. 18).

At that time this punishment was considered more severe than the others. [Col. 1054B]

How many, my most dear lord, do you think have been scandalized, are being scandalized, and will be scandalized when they hear of the prejudice inflicted upon one church and one bishop contrary to ecclesiastical rules? For, as Saint Paul the Apostle says: “When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (I Cor. 12).

What do you think a person can infer concerning himself and the church entrusted to him from what he sees happening to a brother and to the church entrusted to that brother, or from what he hears concerning that brother and his church, if it should happen by divine providence that he and the church entrusted to him come under your power?

Those who hear are not struck in the heart by a light matter. For the bishop was not accused of a crime before the primate of the province by legitimate accusers, as the canons prescribe; he was not regularly summoned to a synod; he was not present at a trial; he did not refuse a regular judgment; no other accusers and other witnesses were brought against him in a regular trial; no inquiry was made, through the testimony of witnesses, whether they testified from hearsay or from knowledge; no legal and canonical investigation was made concerning the persons of the accusers and witnesses, what their character, rank, or standing might be; the grounds of the proceedings were not entered in writing; permission to respond and defend himself was not granted to him; he did not confess to the crime or to the cause of his exile; he was not regularly convicted; with the parties present, the judgment reached by his judges was not read out in a written sentence; and he was not deposed from the episcopal order by a canonical and episcopal judgment.

Nevertheless, with his property confiscated, and with the property and resources of his church—which, whether the bishop had completed his office or died, ought to be preserved by the steward for the future bishop—he has been condemned by the prejudice of secular persons, contrary to all laws and all rights, both divine and human. [Col. 1055A]

Yet not only bishops of erroneous opinion, persons accused of treason, or persons accused of crimes, but also the presbyters Arius and Eutyches are recorded as having been stripped of their rank only by the judgment of councils, and as having been proscribed and sent into exile by the decree of emperors.

I cannot express in words the extent of the anguish that constrains my mind, since I hear it flying from the mouths of many that people of every nation—even Jews, enemies of Christian law—are everywhere judged according to the judgment of their own laws; that even the ox-herder, swineherd, and shepherd have a law; and that, contrary to every custom of Christian princes and to the commands of the Lord of lords, who says through the prophet, in the Gospel, and through the Apostle, “You shall not do what is unjust, and you shall not judge unjustly. Judge your neighbor justly” (Lev. 15), and, “If indeed you speak justice, judge justly, sons of men” (Ps. 17):

> “With the judgment by which you judge, you shall be judged” (Matt. 17).

You will either be condemned by a just judgment for having condemned your brother by an unjust judgment, or justice will answer you because you judged justly.

Therefore, speak in this way and act in this way, as those beginning to be judged by the law of liberty—that is, by the law of liberty, namely the Gospel, by which you are to judge.

A bishop, whatever his character, together with his church, has been ignominiously proscribed by you through the action of laypersons and certain disreputable individuals—not by judgment, but by collusion and mockery—and could not have been subjected to ecclesiastical law in this way.

Therefore, the legal sentence which Blessed Gregory, in the memorandum given to John, decreed to be canonical, just as it had been decreed by his predecessors, says: “It is necessary that what has been done contrary to the laws have no force.”

And Saint Augustine says in his book *On True Religion*:

> “In these temporal laws, although people judge concerning them when they establish them, nevertheless, once they have been established and confirmed, it is not permitted for a judge to judge concerning the laws themselves, but only according to them. Yet the maker of temporal laws, if he is a good and wise man, consults that eternal law concerning which no soul has been given the right to judge, so that according to its unchanging rules he may discern what should be commanded or forbidden for a particular time. It is therefore permitted for pure souls to know the eternal law; it is not permitted to judge it.” [Col. 1055D]

Concerning this Blessed Prosper says:

> The eternal law of God rules all things by his steadfast will;  
> nor does it change its purpose with changing time.

For if the Roman emperors called their own law eternal or everlasting, much more is that law eternal which was promulgated by the Holy Spirit.

Concerning this Saint Leo, after demonstrating the discernment contained in it, says:

> “In matters that are either doubtful or obscure, we know that we must follow what is found to be neither contrary to the Gospel commands nor opposed to the decrees of the saints.”

Saint Celestine says:

> “What matter worthy of preservation will remain among us if the standard of decretal constitutions is broken according to the whim of certain persons, once permission has been granted to the peoples?” [Col. 1056A]

And the sacred Council of Carthage under Bishop Gratus says:

> “Concerning matters on which divine Scripture has most clearly pronounced, judgment must not be postponed but rather carried out. No one acts against the prophets, no one against the Gospels, no one against the apostles without danger. We must preserve what has been set forth above in deeds or words, or what has been written by other councils and is found to accord with the law. But if anyone transgresses and corrupts the statutes, or thinks they should be treated as nothing, if he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if he is a cleric, let him be deprived of his honor.”

For, as Pope Saint Hilary decrees:

> “One sins no less against the sanctions of sacred traditions than one rises up in injury against the Lord himself.” [Col. 1056B]

For this reason I say while weeping, and declare with a grieving heart, that in our unhappy and most perilous times the law of the Lord, which is beyond reproach, does not possess such force through reverence for divinity as the Roman laws once possessed through fear of the emperor, before the name of Christ came to be honored throughout the whole world.

We read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when Paul and Silas had been beaten and thrown into prison, the magistrates sent word that they should be released. But Paul said to them:

> “They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and now they are secretly sending us away. No indeed! Let them come and release us themselves.”

The lictors reported these words to the magistrates. When they heard that the men were Romans, they were afraid, and they came and appealed to them; after bringing them out, they asked them to leave the city (Acts 16).

And again in the same sacred history:

> “For it is not customary among the Romans to condemn any person before the accused has his accusers present and is given an opportunity to defend himself, so as to clear himself of the charges” (Acts 25).

And again, when he was about to be tortured, he declared that he was a Roman and was released.

Therefore you must not hear casually what the heavenly trumpet, the Apostle Paul, says:

> “When you sin in this way against your brothers and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ” (I Cor. 8).

And in the sacred history of the Kings it is written:

> “If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased on his behalf; but if a man sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” (I Kings 2.) [Col. 1056D]

Remember the memorable deed of Theodosius and of the memorable man Ambrose. Theodosius transgressed as a human being; Ambrose corrected him as a true priest; and Theodosius patiently and humbly received divine correction through him.

For this reason he was exalted, both in merit and in name, and became distinguished for holiness above all Roman emperors after Constantine.

Happy was that emperor who in his time had such a priest—one who, after he had made him give fitting satisfaction for his transgression, caused him to establish and confirm a law that, if any prince, moved by anger, decided to take unusually severe vengeance against someone, the ministers of the commonwealth would not dare to execute that sentence for thirty days, until the prince’s anger had cooled and he had returned to himself, seen what was true, and decided to carry out what was just. [Col. 1057A]

For anger prevents a man from discerning the truth. As a certain wise man said, the thoughts of an angry person are of a viperous generation: they first consume the mind, their mother.

And the Apostle says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (Jas. 1).

Happy also was God’s priest Ambrose, who lived in the time of such an emperor. For it is written: “Blessed is the one who declares justice to an attentive ear” (Eccli. 24).

Both were happy, priest and emperor alike. For, lest the wrath of God descend upon the emperor because of his transgression, he had in his time a priest concerning whom the Lord did not complain, as he now complains concerning us, saying:

> “I sought someone who would set up a hedge and stand in the breach before me, so that I would not destroy him, and I found no one” (Ezek. 22).

This is why Isaiah, taking upon himself the role of our misery and calamity, laments grievously before God, saying:

> “We have all fallen like a leaf, and our iniquities have carried us away like the wind; and there is no one who calls upon your name, who rises up and holds you back” (Isa. 64). [Col. 1057B]

For how can we hold him back and appease him when he is angry, when, as Saint Gregory laments:

> “We have slipped into external affairs and have accepted one thing in title while displaying another in the work of our office. We have abandoned the ministry of preaching and, to our punishment, as I see it, are called bishops, though we hold the name of the office, not its virtue.”

And again:

> “Those entrusted to us abandon the Lord, and we remain silent; they lie in wicked deeds, and we do not extend the hand of correction; daily they perish through many iniquities, and we negligently watch them heading toward hell. But how can we correct another’s life when we neglect our own? For, intent upon worldly cares, we become inwardly more insensible the more diligently we appear to attend to outward affairs. Through habitual concern for earthly matters the mind grows hard toward heavenly desire, and, becoming hardened through the practice of worldly action, it cannot be softened toward the things that belong to the love of God.”

And so forth, as that same saint continues there concerning negligent priests.
