Therefore, the less worthy we are to hold the Lord back from you if he should become angry, the more carefully you must not only correct your actions, but also take care that in your commands—whether those that you decree or have decreed, or may decree, in word or in writing—there be no injustice, presumption, or lack of discernment.

You must fear the threat of the eternal Judge, who says:

> “Woe to those who establish unjust laws and, when writing, write injustice, to oppress the poor in judgment and to do violence to the cause of the humble among my people, so that widows may become their prey and they may deceive orphans. What will you do on the day of visitation and calamity from afar? To whose help will you flee, and where will you leave your glory, lest you bend beneath the chains and fall with the slain? In all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still extended” (Isa. 10). [Col. 1057D]

And since I have already shown from the words of Blessed Gelasius that there are two things by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power, in which the burden of priests is so much heavier because they must render an account before the divine tribunal even for kings themselves, you must carefully take care not to extend beyond your office—as, thanks be to God, you have so far refrained from doing—any harm against the priestly order or against the matters entrusted to that order by the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Frequently read, and commit to memory, what is written in the Second Book of Chronicles:

> “King Uzziah did what was right in the eyes of the Lord and sought the Lord. And while he sought the Lord, he directed him in everything and helped him against the Philistines, against the Arabs who dwelt in Gurbaal, and against the Ammonites; and his name became renowned as far as the entrance of Egypt because of his frequent victories. He possessed many flocks, both in the plains and in the wilderness. He also had vineyards and vinedressers in the mountains and on Carmel, for he was devoted to agriculture. The whole number of his army was three hundred ten thousand and one hundred men.

> “But when he had grown strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction, and he neglected the Lord his God. He entered the temple of the Lord and wished to burn incense upon the altar of incense. Immediately Azariah the priest entered after him, together with eighty priests of the Lord, very brave men. They resisted the king and said: ‘It is not your office, Uzziah, to burn incense to the Lord. It belongs to the priests, that is, to the sons of Aaron who have been consecrated for such ministry. Leave the sanctuary, and do not despise this, for it will not be counted to your glory by the Lord God.’

> “Uzziah became angry, and while holding the censer in his hand to burn incense, he threatened the priests. At once leprosy appeared on his forehead before the priests in the house of the Lord, above the altar of incense. When Azariah the high priest and all the other priests looked at him, they saw the leprosy on his forehead, and they hurriedly expelled him. He himself, terrified, hastened to leave, because he immediately felt the Lord’s blow. Thus King Uzziah remained a leper until the day of his death, and he lived in a separate house, full of leprosy, because of which he had also been expelled from the house of the Lord” (II Chron. 26). [Col. 1058C]

In this event, since Scripture says, “These things happened to them as a figure, but they were written for us” (I Cor. 10), we must carefully observe how long Uzziah worshiped the Lord, held his kingdom in peace, and won frequent victories against neighboring and foreign peoples.

But after he presumed upon an office that was not his, and unlawfully extended the hand of presumption against the priestly ministry, he remained full of leprosy in a separate house until the day of his death and achieved no victory. Nor, covered with leprosy—that is, struck and overwhelmed by grave sin—was he able to dwell with the others who fought the Lord’s battles against the enemies of Israel, the people who prefigured the Church. [Col. 1058D]

Thus, according to the judgment of those to whom the Lord says, “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10), and through whom the canons were promulgated by that same Spirit, whoever voluntarily and deliberately violates and tears apart the divine constitutions—since, as Peter teaches, “God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts 10)—will be separated from the body of the Church and, unless he is reunited to that Church through repentance and reconciliation by priestly indulgence, will remain separated from the eternal Church.

Hence the Apostle also commands: “With such a person, do not even take food” (I Cor. 5).

And again he declares to all, with Christ speaking through him:

> “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness” (Eph. 5).

Explaining this sentence, Blessed Augustine says:

> “The evil person does not defile you in two ways: if you do not consent and if you rebuke him. This is what it means not to participate: not to consent. One participates when companionship of will or approval is joined to his deed.

> “Thus the Apostle admonishes us when he says: ‘Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness.’ And because it was not enough merely not to consent, if negligence of discipline were to follow, he adds: ‘But rather rebuke them.’ See how he embraces both: do not participate; do not consent; do not praise; do not approve.

> “What does ‘but rather rebuke them’ mean? Reprove, correct, restrain.

> “Then, in reproving or restraining the sins of others, one must beware that the person who corrects another does not exalt himself; and whoever thinks he is standing must see that he does not fall. Let rebuke resound outwardly with terror, but inwardly let the love of gentleness be preserved.

> “Therefore, do not consent to evil persons by approving them; do not be negligent by failing to rebuke them; and do not be arrogant by rebuking them insultingly.”

[Col. 1059C] And do not suppose, most dear and most gracious lord, that I have written these things because I was moved by any affection of bodily kinship, or because these things were done only in the case of the bishop of the province of Rheims entrusted to my unworthiness. Rather, I wrote out of zeal, concerning which it is written both in the Psalm and in the Gospel: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68)—that is, zeal for the universal Church, which is God’s house; for the sacred priestly order, which is one and the same in all bishops; and for the duty of my own littleness. For I read that God’s chosen ones, because of the laws of their fathers, even desired bodily death, and that the Catholic Church sings in the divine praises: “He contended for the law of his God unto death” (2 Maccabees 6 and 7).

Nevertheless, I wrote these things out of zeal for your salvation and for the prosperity we desire for you. Finally, I ask that in [Col. 1059D] this service of mine you discern more carefully that, if certain expressions there sound somewhat biting, the words are not my meaning. Even if they were, your gentleness ought to weigh them calmly, since a flattering friend is an enemy. Scripture says: “The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy who hates” (Proverbs 27).

For your mind is not possessed, as the minds of some are captivated, by the saying—well known to you—which declares: “Obsequiousness,” that is, assent, or rather flattery, wins friends; truth breeds hatred. Since, as a friend of truth, you love truth, remember what was spoken by Truth: “You shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free” (John 8). Let what blessed Augustine says remain fixed in your mind: it is the mark of a deceitful or incompetent physician to apply a plaster to a wound in such a way that it either harms or does no good. The truths set forth above, which truthful men have spoken for your salvation without flattery, will therefore not displease you.

## SECOND EXPOSITION, ENTITLED “THE ROLL”

The sacred Council of Carthage says: “Whoever accuses one of the bishops shall bring the case before the primate of that church [Note: [Col. 1059D] African Council, canon 19].”

And again: “If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or other cleric, when a criminal charge has been brought against him in the Church [Col. 1060B] or a civil case has arisen, wishes to be cleared by public courts after abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, even if a judgment has been pronounced in his favor, let him lose his position—and this applies in a criminal case. In a civil case, however, let him lose what he has won if he prefers to retain his position [Note: [Col. 1059D] Ibid., canon 15].”

And the African Council says: “Whoever among the clergy seeks from the emperor a hearing before the public courts shall be deprived of his own dignity; but if he seeks an episcopal judgment, this shall cause him no harm [Note: [Col. 1060D] Ibid., canon 104].”

And, to set down here a few points from Roman laws and many other sources, Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodoric established: “Let no one dare to accuse a bishop before public judges, but let him not delay to bring before the bishops’ hearing whatever he thinks he can claim according to the nature of the case, so that what he alleges against the bishop may be determined in the judgment of other bishops.” The emperors also established that this procedure should be observed in private cases of this kind, so that no litigant should be bound by a judgment not pronounced by his own judge.

And Saint Leo, pontiff of the holy Roman Church, in a synod held at Rome, decreed as follows: “The powers of this world wished such reverence to prevail toward the priestly order that even those whom divine power has commanded to rule the earth under the imperial name permitted holy bishops, in accordance with imperial constitutions, to exercise jurisdiction in the determination of cases. Although this has been established both by the edicts of ancient law and by the frequent laws enacted thereafter, we find that in the present time it has been trampled upon by many [Col. 1060D]. For, neglecting priestly judgment, they have indiscriminately transferred cases to secular examination. Accordingly, it has seemed good to us that this insult to the sacred laws and to our order should both now be punished by full severity and that a rule to be observed in the future should be established. We therefore decree that whoever, neglecting the priest of his own church, comes to a dispute before secular authorities shall be expelled from the sacred thresholds and barred from the heavenly altar.”

And in the first book of the Imperial Capitularies of Lord Charles and Lord Louis it is written, chapter 8: “Let suffragan bishops look to the metropolitan bishop, and let them dare to undertake nothing new in their parishes without the knowledge and counsel of their metropolitan; nor let the metropolitan act without their counsel [Col. 1061A].”

And again, in the same book, chapter 28: “If clerics or monks have any case among themselves, let them be judged by their own bishop, not before secular authorities.”

And again, in the same book, chapter 38: “If clerics of the ecclesiastical order incur guilt, let them be judged before ecclesiastical authorities, not secular ones.”

These enactments concern offenses committed by a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, whether criminal or civil—that is, involving pecuniary matters. As for property, slaves, and offenses committed by slaves, or the property of clerics, we do not refuse, according to custom, to provide advocates to bishops in matters concerning the Churches entrusted to us [Col. 1061B].

Where, however, the offenses committed by bishops or clerics in criminal or civil matters are to be corrected, the laws clearly show, as many emperors have decreed. Among these we shall set down here the law of Valentinian and Valens, who decreed: “Let the permission to accuse be prohibited beyond the boundaries of the province.”

Accordingly, the sacred Council of Carthage decreed: “Let the accused and the accuser choose for themselves, in the place from which the accused comes, a nearby location where it will not be difficult to bring witnesses, and where the case may be concluded [Note: [Col. 1061D] African Council, canon 30].”

And the laws likewise say: “If anyone brings an action against an adversary, whether by a claim for restitution or by an accusation of crime, let him bring forward his actions in the province where the person sued resides; let him not suppose that his adversary may be dragged elsewhere, or farther away, for judgment. If the person sued considers the judge suspect, let him be permitted to appeal [Col. 1061C].”

And Saint Innocent writes to Bishop Victricius: “If any cases or disputes arise among clerics, whether of higher or lower rank, let the quarrel be brought to an end, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea, by assembling the bishops of the same province. No one may, however—without prejudice to the Roman Church, whose reverence must be preserved in every case—abandon those priests who by divine will govern the Church of God in the same province and flee to other provinces. If anyone should presume to do so, let him be judged both removed from the clerical office and guilty of injury. But if greater cases have arisen [Col. 1061D], let them, as the synod decreed and ancient custom requires, be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment.”

Hence the Council of Carthage says: “If an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges possessing greater authority, this shall not prejudice those whose judgment has been set aside, unless they can be convicted either of having judged with an inimical disposition or of having been corrupted by some greed or favor. But if the judges were chosen by agreement of the parties, it shall not be permitted to appeal even from what was decided by the smaller number [Note: [Col. 1061D] Council of Carthage, 397, canon 10].”

The laws and sacred canons show how judgment should be brought to an end: either in a synod or through judges, whether those whom the primates assign to litigants or those whom the parties themselves choose by agreement from among their neighbors [Col. 1062A].

As for the bishops appointed as judges, the African Council says: “They are to be appointed by the primate in whose province the case is being heard. But if the litigants, by common agreement, choose neighboring judges, let either one be chosen or three; and if they choose three, let them follow either the judgment of all or that of two.”

The Council of Chalcedon says: “If a cleric has a case against another cleric, let him not abandon his own bishop and run to secular tribunals. Rather, let the case first be heard before his own bishop; or, certainly, with the counsel of that bishop, let them conduct the trial before whichever judges both parties choose [Col. 1062B]. If anyone acts otherwise, let him be subject to the corrections of the canon [Note: [Col. 1062D] Council of Chalcedon, canon 9].”

And Saint Gregory, drawing upon the laws and sacred canons, established the following when writing to Boniface, defender of Corsica and acting representative of the apostolic see—offices which the primates of the provinces hold in those regions: “If anyone has a case against a cleric, let him approach the cleric’s bishop. If that bishop should happen to be suspect, an executor is to be appointed either by him or, if the plaintiff also refuses this, by Your Experience. That executor shall compel the parties, by mutual agreement, to choose judges, and whatever those judges determine shall, by your diligence or that of the bishop, be brought to completion in every respect, with the law observed, so that no occasion remains for them to be wearied by litigation.”

And if a layman has a civil—that is, pecuniary—case against a bishop [Col. 1062C], the bishop must be admonished or compelled by those whose interest is involved. Likewise, the layman must be admonished or compelled by the authority of the state to come to arbitration—that is, to the judgment of judges chosen by both parties—and the case must be concluded by their judgment.

Saint Gregory demonstrates the same in a letter written to Bishop Malchus from the laws and sacred rules: “Moreover,” he says, “we have taken care by this present command to admonish Your Fraternity that you compel Bishop Stephen to come to the appointment of judges; and whatever judgment is determined by the chosen judges between the aforesaid John, a magnificent man, and the aforementioned bishop, let him not fail to bring into effect.”

[Col. 1062D] The laws observed by the Church also say—and judges must observe this especially: “In every case, let the judgment that has been deliberated be read out in the presence of the parties duly summoned, so that those by whom the case was heard may know the judgment in its entirety; and whatever has been ordered in a case in the presence of the parties shall possess the fullest validity and cannot be altered.”

Since emperors, in their own time, appointed both an ecclesiastical minister and an administrator of the state as judges for a case involving an accused bishop, concerning pecuniary matters, as the laws and canons command, blessed Gregory demonstrates this in a decretal letter to John, bishop of Larissa, saying: “When the appeal submitted by the men of Bishop Hadrian, together with the other matters conducted before you, had been conveyed to the most devout rulers, and, as we have said, the deacon Honoratus of the apostolic see and Sebastianus, the illustrious *antigrapheus*, had been appointed, after everything had been carefully examined, the most serene rulers absolved them from all the commands.”

Hence the laws approved by the Church say: “Cases are considered judged by those who possess imperial power and authority, or by those appointed between the parties by authority of such persons.”

It should be noted, as we have already stated, that the emperors, while preserving the secular and ecclesiastical laws, appointed, for the investigation and determination of a pecuniary—that is, civil—case between a bishop and secular persons, an ecclesiastical minister together with an administrator of the state [Col. 1063B]. If a bishop should claim that he cannot come to a synod or to the judgment of judges chosen against the person bringing a case against him, whether genuinely, through feigned illness, or for any other reason, let him choose judges for himself or accept those appointed, as we have shown above from the laws and sacred rules. Let him send in his place an instructed representative to the appointed place and on the appointed day; that representative shall pursue the execution and determination of the case legally and regularly, in accordance with his principal’s instructions, before the chosen judges. Whatever is executed and determined, let him accept as binding and observe, just as the rules and decrees of the holy see of the Roman pontiffs—and Saint Gregory most frequently demonstrates in his letters from the laws and sacred rules—show must be done [Col. 1063C].

Among many such texts, I have decided to set down here one decree of blessed Gregory, which he wrote to Bishop Fortunatus: “We exhort Your Fraternity in these words to send here without delay, all excuses set aside, an instructed representative who can, in the judgment either of the chosen judges or certainly of those appointed by us, conduct whatever case exists on behalf of your side and answer in every respect the intentions and objections of your adversaries, so that, once the truth has been ascertained, a salutary conclusion may be reached here.”

And in a letter to Sergius, defender of Sipontum: “By the authority of this present command we instruct Your Experience to take care to admonish Fruniscendus that, if he knows of anything that he is bound to restore to the Church, he should not cease to make satisfaction without postponement. Otherwise, once delay has ceased, let him come, under compulsion from you, to the judgment of the chosen judges; and whatever, after the truth has been ascertained, has been determined by the sacred Gospels, let your insistence bring fully into effect, so that a complaint concerning this matter may not return to us again.”

Here the Roman laws do not employ torture in a pecuniary case, except when an inquiry concerns hereditary property. Other matters are clarified by oath or by witnesses. If a bishop refuses to obey his fellow bishops and judges chosen by himself or appointed by the primates [Col. 1064A], he shall undergo the judgment of the African Council, which says: “It shall not be permitted to appeal from judges chosen by common agreement; and whoever is proved, through contumacy, unwilling to obey the judges, once this has been established before the bishop of the first see, let him receive letters ordering that no bishop communicate with him until he obeys [Note: [Col. 1063D] African Council, canon 122].”

And if a layman bringing a claim against a bishop refuses to obey the judges, by the prince of the state, the guardian and defender of the Church, and the protector through royal benevolence [lacuna]

In the Imperial Capitularies, book two, it is written: “Concerning those who unjustly bring complaints against others: if they are convicted on that account, let them render justice for that calumny according to law and equity.”

[Col. 1064B] And in book three it is written: “Concerning those who presume to reopen a case already judged, and also concerning those who disdain to observe the law: let them be brought before the king’s presence by sureties.”

Concerning those judged according to Roman laws, it has been decreed: “Whoever, through calumny, institutes an action for injury shall be punished extraordinarily; for it has been decided that all calumniators shall be punished by exile, relegation to an island, or loss of rank.”

Royal vigilance, therefore, established by the King of kings and by God, the most righteous judge, so that judgment may be judged according to the uprightness of the heart, ought to provide carefully and diligently that it choose and appoint as judges, together with the bishops, for settling a case between ecclesiastical and secular persons, men who are religious and fear the Lord [Col. 1064C]. They must not receive a person in judgment for the reward of a gift, or out of favor, kinship, or friendship; not out of the service of an undue subjection; and not out of hatred for the other party. Rather, without contention or spite, they must judge—as Truth itself says—not according to appearance, but with righteous judgment (John 7).

And this must not occur in a public place of judgment but in private, since bishops neither ought nor can, according to the rule, be judged in the council chamber of kings, in the praetorium of judges, or anywhere except by bishops: in a synod, or in a private place, by the judgment of primates’ appointees or of judges chosen by the parties themselves.

We have learned that the ancient emperors and your predecessors [Col. 1064D] and ancestors decreed that the laws mentioned above, both public and ecclesiastical, should be observed in their own times by bishops and ecclesiastical men. Your most beloved and gracious lordship also promised us at Quierzy, by word and subscription, that you would observe them. There you composed this chapter, with the advice and counsel of your faithful men, both bishops and laymen, and subscribed to it, saying:

“As much as I shall know and reasonably be able, with the Lord’s help, I shall honor and protect each one of you according to his order and person; I shall preserve him honored and protected, without any deceit, condemnation, or deception. I shall preserve for each one the law and justice appropriate to him. To whoever needs it and reasonably requests it, I shall show reasonable mercy, as a faithful king ought, by right, to honor and protect his faithful, to preserve for each order the law and justice appropriate to it, and to extend reasonable mercy to those in need and to those who reasonably request it. For no person shall I, insofar as human frailty allows, deviate from this through zeal, ill will, or anyone’s undue urging, to the extent that God grants me understanding and ability. And if, through frailty, anything contrary to this should be stolen from me, when I recognize it I shall take care to correct it.”

[Col. 1065A] We, your faithful men—the bishops and the other members of the lay order who were present—composed this chapter together with you [Col. 1065B] and subscribed to it, each making this profession:

“As much as I shall know and be able, with the Lord’s help, without any deceit or deception, and with counsel and assistance, according to my ministry and my person, I shall be your faithful helper, so that you may be able to hold and govern, with due honor and vigor, according to God’s will and for the salvation of yourself and your faithful, the power which God has granted you in the royal name and kingdom.”

## THIRD EXPOSITION, ENTITLED “ADMONITION”

Your predecessors and ancestors, the kings, observed this law of the Church. If it was violated in any way, whether through the excesses of rulers or through the negligence of bishops, it was nevertheless corrected, as is shown in their capitularies. You too, following your predecessors, promised God and us that you would observe this ecclesiastical law, as is contained here.

In the first book of the Imperial Capitularies of Lord Charles, your grandfather, and Lord Louis, your father, in the law confirmed by them, it is written for the Church and all bishops, chapter 8: “Let suffragans look to the metropolitan bishop, and let them dare to undertake nothing new in their parishes without the knowledge and counsel of their metropolitan; nor let the metropolitan act without their counsel.”

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 28: “If clerics or monks have any case among themselves, let them be judged by their own bishop, not by secular authorities.”

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 38: “If clerics of the ecclesiastical order incur guilt, let them be judged before ecclesiastical authorities, not secular ones.”

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 77: “Since, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, we know that the property of the Church is the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimony of the poor, we desire, with God’s assistance, not only to preserve what it possesses but also to confer many things upon it. Nevertheless, in order to remove from ecclesiastical persons the suspicion concerning the non-division of its property which they have long entertained, we decree that neither in our time nor in the time of our sons—and, God disposing, of our successors who may wish to imitate our will or the example of our ancestors—shall the Church suffer any division or loss whatsoever [Col. 1066A].”

Together with other chapters, you yourself confirmed the following chapter with your own hand in the villa called Cologne, with the agreement of the bishops, Warinus, and your other leading men, in the fourth year of your reign, and sent it through Ricuinus to your brother Louis:

“Concerning the honor and worship of God, and of the holy churches which, by God’s authority, remain under the dominion and protection of our government, we jointly decree, with the Lord’s help, that just as they were cultivated, honored, and enriched in the time of blessed memory, our lord and father, so they shall remain, with due regard for equity. Whatever is honored and enriched by our generosity shall henceforth be preserved in its entirety [Col. 1066B]. Let priests and servants of God receive ecclesiastical vigor and their due privileges according to venerable authority. Let the royal power, the strength of illustrious men, and the administrators of the state likewise cooperate with them in all things reasonably and justly, so that they may competently perform their ministry.”

Together with other chapters, you confirmed the following chapter in the city of Beauvais, in the sixth year of your reign, swearing before God and his angels, on your faith and your right hand, by your sword [Note: [Col. 1065D] *Spatam*, “sword”], as the bishops who were present had requested. You promised that you would observe it for them, for all the other bishops of your kingdom, for their churches, and for all the days of your life:

“That you preserve ecclesiastical right and canonical law for us just as your predecessors, who observed these things well and reasonably, preserved them for our predecessors, insofar as this can be known and God has granted you the ability.”

Together with other chapters, you jointly confirmed the following chapter with your brothers Waltharius [Lothair] and Louis, with your own hand, at the place called Marsana, in the year 851 from the Lord’s incarnation, with the counsel and agreement of your common faithful:

“That each of our faithful may truly be secure in us, each according to his order and status, because from this time forward we shall neither condemn, dishonor, oppress, nor afflict anyone contrary to law and justice, authority, or right reason, by any improper schemes. And, with the common counsel of those who are truly faithful to us, according to God’s will and the common welfare, we give our assent to whatever pertains to the restoration of the holy Church of God, the condition of the kingdom, royal honor, and the peace of the people entrusted to us [Col. 1066D]. This is so that none of them shall not merely refrain from opposing or resisting us in carrying these things out, but shall also be faithful and obedient to us, true helpers and co-workers, with sound counsel and sincere assistance, in accomplishing the things we have stated, just as each person in his own order and status ought by right to be to his prince and lord.”

[Col. 1067A] Together with other chapters, you professed that you would observe the following chapter in the synod at the city of Soissons, in the monastery of Saint Medard, in the year 853 from the Lord’s incarnation:

“It must be announced to everyone and ordered by our envoys that all the priests of the Church remain under the immunity, privilege, ordering, and disposition of the bishops of the individual churches in which they reside, according to canonical authority and the capitularies of Lord Charles, our grandfather and emperor, and of the pious Augustus Louis, our lord and father.”

And in the year 858 from the Lord’s incarnation, in the seventeenth year of your reign, you willingly confirmed the following with your own hand in the palace at Quierzy, with the agreement of the bishops and your other faithful men [Col. 1067B]:

“As much as I shall know and reasonably be able, with the Lord’s help, I shall honor and protect each one of you according to his order, and I shall preserve him honored and protected, without any deceit, condemnation, or deception. I shall preserve for each one the law and justice appropriate to him. To whoever needs it and reasonably requests it, I shall show reasonable mercy, as a faithful king ought, by right, to honor and protect his faithful and to preserve for each order the law and justice appropriate to it, and to extend reasonable mercy to those in need and to those who reasonably request it. For no person shall I, insofar as human frailty allows, deviate from this through zeal, ill will, or anyone’s undue urging, to the extent that God grants me understanding and ability. And if, through frailty, anything contrary to this should be stolen from me, when I recognize it I shall voluntarily take care to correct it.”

Afterward, at the villa of Breona, in the year 858 from the Lord’s incarnation, when you sent us to excommunicate your brother and the people who had come against you with him, so that they might refrain from the invasion of your kingdom and from shedding your blood and that of your faithful, you publicly professed with tears before God and his angels that you would observe many such provisions for all the days of your life, for us and for all the bishops of your kingdom, for the churches entrusted to us, and for all your faithful [Col. 1067D], preserving law and justice for them.

Moreover, at Confluentes, in the year 860 from the Lord’s incarnation, the following compact was made between you, your brother, and your nephews. I have placed it here for this reason: God’s will, the condition of his holy Church, its honor and defense, and the salvation, peace, and preservation of law, justice, and right reason of the Christian people entrusted to us—where no sex, dignity, or order is excepted—as well as your common salvation and honor, must not, through forgetfulness, be taken from you by anyone in matters pertaining to them, nor may anything pertaining to you be taken from you by anyone contrary to the compact.

The compact is as follows:

“From now on, and for as long as I live, I shall be a true helper to this brother of mine by nature and to my nephews by nature, for the will of God and the condition, honor, and defense of his holy Church; for our common salvation and honor; for the safety and peace of the Christian people entrusted to us; and for the preservation of law, justice, and right reason, insofar as God grants me knowledge and ability, provided that they obey me and seek my assistance. I shall help them with true counsel and, insofar as it is reasonably and beneficially possible for me, with sincere assistance.” And the rest [Note: [Col. 1067D] Council held at Confluentes, 860].

The laws of ecclesiastical right, established by the Spirit of God and decreed by the wisdom by which the legislators themselves determine what is just, by which the holy Church is governed, and which, as Saint Leo says, have been consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, are clear. You have vowed and promised to observe them for the bishops of your kingdom and for the churches entrusted to them. Whoever does not observe them undoubtedly acts against God’s will, against the condition, honor, and defense of his holy Church, and against his own salvation, justice, and right reason. Concerning these laws, I have taken care to recall a few points relevant to the case at hand to your memory [Col. 1068B].

“If,” says the sacred Council of Carthage, “any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or other cleric, when a criminal charge has been brought against him in the Church [Col. 1068C] or a civil case has arisen, wishes to be cleared by public courts after abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, even if a judgment has been pronounced in his favor, let him lose his position—and this in a criminal case. In a civil case, however, let him lose what he has won if he prefers to retain his position [Note: [Col. 1067D] African Council, canon 15].”

And in the decretals of blessed Gregory, made canonical from the Roman laws, it was established for John the defender that, in any civil or criminal case, no judge may summon, produce, or bring an unwilling bishop before a public court. But if a cleric or anyone else brings a dispute against a bishop for any reason, the case must be judged before the metropolitan or the primate of the province according to the sacred rules. And if the bishop contradicts anything that has been judged, the case must be referred to the most blessed pontiff of the Roman see. He must bring the case to an end according to the canons and laws.

The sacred Council of Carthage decreed: “Whoever accuses one of the bishops shall bring the case before the primate of that province [Note: [Col. 1068D] Ibid., canon 19].”

And the enactment of the law of Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius expressly prohibits the following: “Let no one dare to accuse a bishop before public judges; rather, let him not delay to bring before the bishops’ hearing whatever he thinks he can claim according to the nature of the case, so that what he alleges against the bishop may be determined in the judgment of other bishops [Col. 1069A].”

And in the decretals of blessed Gregory to John, from the law of Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius: “In private cases,” he says, “let this form also be observed, so that no litigant may be bound by a judgment not pronounced by his own judge.” And again there: “What has been done contrary to the laws must have no validity.”

The Council of Carthage also decreed: “Let the accused or the accuser choose for himself, in the place from which the accused comes, a nearby location where it will not be difficult to produce witnesses and where the case may be concluded [Note: [Col. 1069C] African Council, canon 30].” The law of Valentinian and Valens likewise decrees that the permission to accuse be prohibited beyond the boundaries of the province.

And the African Council says: “Let the case be concluded through episcopal judges, whether those whom the primates assign to the litigants [Col. 1069B] or those whom the parties themselves choose by agreement from among their neighbors [Note: [Col. 1069C] Ibid., canon 120].”

As is said in the following article, the provisions established in the laws concerning cases are to be observed in the manner indicated by their proper places, as Saint Gregory decreed. The sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see likewise command that councils be held twice every year in each province, so that the questions of the province may be discussed in common with all the bishops assembled together and all controversies resolved.

The sacred canons of Antioch and Gangra, as well as the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see, likewise command that “the possessions of the Church be preserved with all care, a good conscience, and faith in God, who observes and judges all things. They are also to be administered according to the judgment and power of the pontiff to whom the people and the souls gathered within the Church [Col. 1070A] have been entrusted.”

And: “Let the bishop have authority over ecclesiastical property, in order to distribute it to all who are in need, with the greatest reverence and fear of God. Let him also partake of what he needs—if indeed he is in need—of whatever is useful for necessary purposes, both for himself and for the brothers who are received by him [Note: [Col. 1069C] Council of Antioch, canons 24 and 25].”

And: “If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, and does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.”

And: “If anyone gives or receives offerings apart from the bishop or the person appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, let both the giver and the receiver be anathema [Note: [Col. 1070C] Council of Gangra, canons 7 and 8].”

The Council of Chalcedon decreed: “Let ecclesiastical property be distributed according to the bishop’s judgment, and let the revenues of a church deprived of its bishop be preserved intact in the keeping of its steward [Note: [Col. 1070C] Council of Chalcedon, canon 25].”

And Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, says: “Whatever is unjustly done concerning the sacred things of God and the bishops shall be counted as sacrilege.”

The Council of Carthage under Bishop Gratus judged that “if anyone transgresses and violates the statutes, or considers them worthless, if he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if he is a cleric, let him be deprived of his honor [Note: [Col. 1070C] Council of Carthage, 348, canon 14].”

For, as the holy Pope Hilary says in his decree: “One sins no less against the sanctions of the holy traditions than one rushes into an injury against the Lord.”

Therefore, it is necessary that you preserve what you have justly and reasonably vowed and promised to the Lord, as the Spirit of God commands through the prophet: “Vow and pay your vows to the Lord your God” (Psalm 75).

[Col. 1069]

## XIII. CHAPTERS PROMULGATED BY HINCMAR IN THE SYNOD HELD AT SAINT MACRA

*(In Labbe, Councils, volume VIII.)*

[Col. 1069] The synod that was held at Saint Macra, in the place called Finibus of the parish of Rheims [Note: [Col. 1069D] Today they call it Fismes, a celebrated town because of the martyrdom and veneration of Saint Macra the virgin. Formerly it was called Fines because it lay on the boundaries of the district of Rheims and that of Soissons. [Col. 1070D] The old itinerary: Augusta Suessorum. Fines. Durocortum Rhemorum. SIRM.], in the time of King Louis, son of Louis, son of Charles, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the year of Christ 881, in the ninth year of Pope John VIII, and in the eleventh year of the same King Louis [rather, only the second, as Sirmond correctly states].

## PREFACE

[Col. 1069D]

The bishops of various provinces, whose names are written below, who previously could not come together because they were hindered by various occupations—both the incursions of pagans and the attacks of wicked Christians—have now, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 881, [Col. 1070D] in the fourteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, compelled by the greatest necessity, assembled in Christ’s name at the martyr-shrine of Saint Macra, in the place called Fismes, in the parish of Rheims. With the Lord’s assistance, we decree that the following provisions be observed by all who wish to live justly and piously in the communion of the Catholic Church, which is Christ’s body. We are not establishing anything new, but are recalling provisions established by our forefathers according to the course of the Holy Scriptures, promulgated by Christian emperors and kings, and preserved down to these perilous times of our misery as lights amid the darkness of wicked deeds, which blinds the sons of distrust. Thus, by the sickle of the Holy Spirit, through the divine ministry of our office and through the power of royal concern and the ministers of the commonwealth, what is growing wickedly may be cut away, and what is fruitful may be planted in Christian minds.

## CHAPTERS

### I. That royal power and the authority of the bishops are distinct.

[Col. 1071B] These, then, are the matters belonging to priestly office and royal ministry. For, as we read in the sacred writings, there are two principal powers by which this world is governed: the sacred authority of the bishops and royal power. Our Lord Jesus Christ alone could truly become both king and priest. After his incarnation, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, however, neither did the king presume to usurp the dignity of the bishop, nor the bishop royal power. Their functions and dignities were distinguished by him in such a way that Christian kings needed bishops for eternal life, while bishops used the arrangements of kings for the conduct of temporal affairs. Thus spiritual action might remain separate from carnal incursions, and therefore the one serving God might not entangle himself in secular business; and, conversely, he who was involved in secular business might not appear to preside over divine matters.

The dignity of bishops is so much greater than that of kings because kings are consecrated to the royal summit by bishops, whereas bishops cannot be consecrated by kings. The burden of priests is so much heavier than that of kings because, in the divine judgment, they will also render an account for the kings themselves. Yet the care of kings in human affairs is so much greater than that of priests because, for the honor, defense, and peace of the holy Church and of its rulers and ministers, the King of kings has imposed upon them the burden of care through promulgating laws and waging war.

We read in the sacred histories (Deut. XVII) that when priests anointed kings in the governance of the kingdom and placed diadems upon their heads, they put the law into their hands so that they might learn and know how they ought to govern themselves and their subjects and honor the priests of the Lord. We also read in sacred history that King Uzziah presumed to offer incense, which belonged not to royal but to priestly ministry. He was struck by God with leprosy, expelled from the temple by the priests, and confined in his own house until his death (II Chron. XXVI).

### II. Rebuke of the torpor and negligence of priests; from Saint Gregory.

Finally, if in the course of what follows we say anything concerning the salvation of the king, the ministers of the commonwealth, and the ministry entrusted to our unworthiness that may displease carnal minds [Col. 1072A]—for a physician often restores to the joy of health those whom he cannot cure with a gentle ointment by means of a bitter medicinal draught—let them not say of us what we read was said of those sitting in Moses’ seat: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with a finger” (Matt. XIII).

We first accuse ourselves in the words of Saint Gregory, from the homily he delivered on the Gospel at the time of a synod of bishops:

“For we have drifted into external business, partly through the necessity of barbarian fear and partly through the negligence of our own age; we have assumed one thing from our dignity, yet display something else in the exercise of our office. We abandon the ministry of preaching and, as I see, to our punishment we are called bishops, although we possess the name of the dignity but not its virtue.

“For those entrusted to us abandon God, and we remain silent. They lie in wicked deeds, and we do not extend the hand of correction. Every day they perish through many evils, and we negligently watch them heading toward hell. But when will we be able to correct another’s life, when we neglect our own? For, occupied with secular cares, we become inwardly more insensitive in proportion as we appear more diligent in outward matters.

“By habitual concern for earthly things, the mind grows hardened against heavenly desire; and while it becomes hard through its very habit by secular activity, it cannot be softened toward the things that belong to the love of God. For while we are entangled in unfamiliar activities, we neglect the ministry of our own work. We abandon God’s cause and devote ourselves to earthly business. We receive a place of holiness and become entangled in earthly activities.

“Surely what is written has been fulfilled in us: ‘And it shall be: as the people, so the priest’ (Isa. XXIV; Hos. IV). For the priest does not differ from the people when, by no merit of his life, he surpasses the activity of the common crowd.

“Behold, now scarcely any activity of the world remains that priests do not administer. We see by what sword the world is struck; we see by what daily blows the people perish. Whose doing is this, if not chiefly our sin? Behold, cities have been depopulated, strongholds overthrown, churches and monasteries destroyed, and fields reduced to solitude. Yet we who ought to have been guides to life are authors of death for the perishing people. For the multitude of the people has been struck down through our sin, because, through our negligence, it has not been instructed toward life.

“Let us therefore consider who has ever been converted from his wicked work through our tongue and, rebuked by our correction, has done penance; who has abandoned lust through our instruction; who avarice; who pride. Here we have been called shepherds, yet when we come before the eyes of the eternal Shepherd, we shall not lead with us a flock converted by our preaching. But would that, if we are not sufficient for the power of preaching, we might at least preserve the duty of our office in the innocence of our lives.”

### III. On the honor and worship of God and of the churches.

Concerning the honor and worship of God and of the holy churches, which by God’s authority stand under the rule of our king’s government [Col. 1073A], we jointly admonish our lord the king in the words of him who spoke to his disciples and apostles, whose place in the Church redeemed by Christ’s blood we occupy, unworthy though we are: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Luke X).

Just as these churches were cultivated, honored, and enlarged in their possessions in the time of his imperial and royal predecessors, so, without prejudice to equity, let them remain. Whatever has been honored and enriched by his generosity must henceforth be preserved in its entirety. Priests and the men and women who serve God must receive ecclesiastical protection and their due privileges according to the venerable authority. Royal power, the vigor of illustrious men, and the administrators of the commonwealth must reasonably and justly assist them in every way, so that they may competently carry out their ministry.

### IV. On undertaking responsibility for monasteries.

Let the royal envoys, throughout the cities and in each individual monastery—whether of canons, monks, or nuns—together with the bishop of whatever parish they belong to, and also with the advice and consent of the person who holds the monastery, investigate the life and conduct of those living there. Where necessary, let them correct them; where suitable offices are lacking, let them order them to be built; and where buildings have been constructed but destroyed through negligence, let them order them to be restored.

Let them arrange food, drink, clothing, and the other necessities according to the character and resources of the place and the needs of its inhabitants. Let them establish and organize hospitality for arriving guests and the reception of the poor there. Let them carefully inventory the treasure, vestments, and books, and bring the inventories back to the king.

Let them record what each ecclesiastical prelate found there when he assumed the church’s prelatehood, what is now lacking from it, and what and how much has been added. Let them also record the number of canons, monks, or nuns at each place and report it to the king. According to the character of the place, and with the counsel of the bishops and his faithful men, the number should be increased by royal authority wherever it is too small; but wherever it has become excessive through the indiscretion of prelates, it should be reduced to proper measure.

Let them diligently and item by item ensure that the prelates of abbeys and those living in sacred places report to the king how they have obeyed the orders given by the royal envoys.

### V. On restraining plunder and restoring peace.

We admonish plunderers—not in our own words, but by the authority of Christ and his saints, who reign with him in heaven and shine forth through miracles on earth—by the authority of him who said to us, unworthy though we are, in his apostles: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). We impress upon them the words of the Lord himself, which they will hear at the final judgment unless they correct themselves: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and the rest, where he says: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXIX).

From this, therefore, it must be understood how great a condemnation awaits those who seize what belongs to others, if those who have indiscriminately retained what belongs to themselves are struck with such severity. Let them weigh by what guilt the stolen thing binds them, if the thing not handed over subjects a person to such punishment. Let them consider what injustice inflicted deserves, if kindness not shown is worthy of so great a blow.

Let the plunderers hear: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own—how long?—and weighs himself down with thick mud against himself” (Hab. II). To weigh oneself down with thick mud against oneself is to heap up earthly profits together with the burden of sin.

Let them hear what Christ says: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI). That is, what does it profit a person if he gathers everything outside himself, if he condemns only what he himself is?

Let them hear that the things they seize will fail in this age or will leave them in this age, but that they will carry with them to judgment the causes of their plunder—that is, condemnation. Let them hear what the prophet Isaiah says: “The plunder of the poor is in your houses” (Isa. III). And: “The widow’s case does not come before them” (Isa. I). And: “The Lord will not disregard the prayers of the orphan, nor the widow if she pours out a speech of groaning. Do not the widow’s tears descend upon her cheek, and does not her cry rise against the one who causes them to flow? For from her cheek they rise up to heaven, and the Lord who hears will not be pleased with them” (Ecclus. XXXV).

Let them hear that in whose house plunder exists—whether in the house of the body or in the house of a dwelling—the Holy Spirit does not dwell in that house, but an evil spirit. And if such a person approaches communion of the body and blood of Christ before making worthy satisfaction, he is not cleansed from sin through that communion; rather, more completely, like Judas, when at the supper, full of plunder and iniquity, he presumed to communicate from Christ’s hand, he is possessed by the devil.

Therefore, he was hanged and burst open in the middle and went to his own place—that is, the place acquired by his merits, namely eternal fire. For when the holy bread entered a belly full of iniquity, the ancient enemy, called the devil and Satan, entered a cruel and impious mind.

For just as Judas handed Christ over to the sinful Jews, so the person full of plunder and iniquity hands Christ over to his sinful members, presuming to violate that inestimable body of the Lord. Woe also to the person who approaches the Lord’s table in wickedness, who does not fear to participate in the mysteries of Christ with traps hidden in his mind and with a heart polluted by plunder or some other crime.

Woe to the person of whom Jesus—who, while the holy altars are being used for sacrifice, is believed to be present as the one who will consecrate the offerings set before him, attended by heavenly ministers—is compelled to complain in the words he spoke at the supper concerning Judas: “Behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table” (Luke XXII).

And woe to the person concerning whom the apostle Paul says, as we read was given as a special warning at the Lord’s supper: “Whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning—that is, not distinguishing—the Lord’s body from other foods” (I Cor. XI). Such a person approaches the Lord’s table without reverence or fear of his sins, just as a cheerful person approaches when his companion feeds him at a full table with the proceeds of his plunder.

The same Apostle also says: “For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep,” that is, die (ibid.). This is shown in the example of the bodily illnesses and deaths of certain people, which takes place in the soul in the spiritual illnesses and deaths of all who show irreverence.

We celebrate this Passover, which the Lord then enacted as a new mystery, every day whenever we celebrate Mass. For, just as he then said in his apostles to all the bishops, priests, and other faithful who celebrate and stand present at this fearful sacrament: “Whenever you do this, you will do it in remembrance of me” (ibid).

It may happen that some, hearing that it is so dangerous to communicate in the body and blood of the Lord, and unwilling to withdraw from evil or do penance for past deeds, say: “We will abstain from that communion, since we are not withdrawing from evil conduct.” Therefore, let those to whom the devil whispers such things hear that, just as the Lord says concerning baptism that no one can be saved unless he has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, so concerning this holy communion he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI).

And just as he said: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI)—that is, just as he promised in baptism that, by renouncing the devil and his works and believing in God through faith working by love, a person should remain in faith and good works; and if he sins after baptism, should make confession and worthy penance, forgive those who have sinned against him, persist in good works, and amend what he has done wrongly—so also concerning this holy communion he said (John VI): “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” And: “If anyone eats from this bread, he will live forever, and I will raise him up on the last day.” And: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father.” And: “Whoever eats me will also live because of me.”

Let the rapacious and plundering hear what the Lord again says through the prophet: “You who plunder, will you not yourself be plundered?” (Isa. XXXIII). This means that the property of the poor, churches, and servants of God plundered by the plunderer is plundered by the devil and becomes his prey.

Let them hear what Saint Paul the Apostle says, through whom Christ spoke, who was caught up to the third heaven, who was caught up into paradise, and heard secret words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak. For he says that neither plunderers, nor murderers, nor adulterers will possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. VI). Let them therefore understand what a great sin plunder is, which the holy Apostle compared with adultery and murder.

He says again: “If anyone is a fornicator, adulterer, plunderer, or murderer, with such a person the disciple of Christ—that is, a Christian—may not even eat” (I Cor. V), before satisfaction—that is, correction, amendment, and worthy penance.

Let them hear that Saint John the Apostle, Christ’s chosen and beloved disciple, who reclined upon his breast at the supper, forbids greeting such a person, saying: “Do not even say ‘Hail’ to him, nor receive him into your house” (II John X).

Let them hear what the Lord says through the prophet to those who dwell among such people: “Come out from their midst,” he says, “and do not touch what is unclean; and I will receive you, and I will dwell among you, and I will be your God, and you will be my sons and daughters” (II Cor. VI; Jer. XXXI).

For these plunderers do nothing else but act as the vanguard of the army of Antichrist, of whom it is said: “I will not be moved from generation to generation without evil” (Ps. X). That is: “I will do so many evils in one place that, before I come to another place, those living there will fear my arrival; and afterward they will also experience it.” The Apostle John says: “Now there are many antichrists” (I John II).

Therefore we must fear what the whole Church prays for on this account: “Arise, Lord God; let your hand be exalted”—that is, for vengeance—“do not forget the poor people” (Ps. X). And the Lord, who does not lie, promises, saying: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” (Ps. XI)—that is, “I will exercise vengeance immediately, very soon.”

Let the plunderers hear what the sacred canons decree concerning such people (Council of Toledo I, can. 11):

“If anyone among the powerful strips a cleric, or any poor person, or a religious person, and the bishop sends word to him that he should hear the man, and he refuses, let letters immediately circulate among all the bishops of the province and to as many as can be reached, so that he may be held excommunicated until he hears the case and restores what belongs to another.”

This concerns plunderers of the poor.

Let plunderers and despoilers of ecclesiastical property hear what Saint Anacletus, pope, ordained presbyter by blessed Peter the Apostle himself, judged together with the priests of the whole world. He says (Epistle 1):

“Whoever takes anything from father or mother is a partner of a murderer.” Our father is undoubtedly God, who created us; our mother is the Church, which spiritually regenerated us in baptism. Therefore whoever plunders, takes away, or defrauds Christ’s money and the Church’s property is a murderer and will be counted a murderer before the sight of the just Judge.

“Whoever plunders his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but whoever takes away the Church’s money or property commits sacrilege and must be judged as a sacrilegious person.”

And Saint Urban, pope and martyr, says:

“Ecclesiastical property and resources are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord; they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimony of the poor. If anyone plunders them, he is guilty of the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira, and such a person must be handed over to Satan, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”

And Saint Lucius, pope, says:

“By apostolic authority we expel and condemn as anathematized from the thresholds of the holy Church the plunderers of ecclesiastical property and resources, and we judge them to be sacrilegious; and not only them, but also all who consent to them. For not only those who commit the acts are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those committing them. Equal punishment encompasses both the perpetrators and those who consent.”

And Saint Augustine says in his exposition of the holy Gospel of John (Tractate 50 on John):

“Judas is the sacrilegious thief of the sacred and Lord’s purses, and whoever steals or plunders anything from the Church is compared with the lost Judas.”

Again, in the sacred canons dictated by the Holy Spirit and confirmed by Christ’s blood, it is written (Council of Gangra, can. 7):

“If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, and does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.”

The bishop ought to say before all who hear him what “anathema” means: namely, alienation from Christ and from his body, which is the holy Church.

And lest such people despair and remain in sin, the bishop ought to show how long the anathema lasts—that is, as long as a person does not correct his error and amend it through worthy satisfaction, so that he may be able to merit reconciliation and pardon. But if anyone dies before satisfaction and the pardon of reconciliation, while persisting in his sins, the anathema will then be perpetual for him, and it will be a sin unto death, concerning which the Apostle does not say that one should pray (I John V).

### VI. Admonition to the king and the ministers of the commonwealth.

[Col. 1077C] We admonish the royal dignity, the ministers of the commonwealth, and the associates of the royal ministry, by episcopal authority and by the word of the Lord, to present themselves before God and before human beings in such a way that they may deserve to become God’s helpers and to be helped by him both in the present age and in the future. Let no cause whatsoever—whether the acceptance of gifts, anyone’s friendship, hatred, fear, or favor—compel them to deviate from the state of uprightness, so that they do not judge justly between one neighbor and another.

Let them become, according to their ability, helpers and defenders of orphans, widows, and all other poor people, and honorers of the holy Church and its servants. Let them also restrain by their diligence and correction, as is fitting, those who attempt through recklessness and violence, by theft, brigandage, or plunder, to disturb the common peace of the people.

Therefore we have thought it worthwhile to append, collected into one body, certain capitularies established by preceding emperors and kings. They read as follows.

#### From the capitularies of emperors and kings.

**(Book II, chapters 14–15.)** Concerning preserving peace on a military journey as far as the march: We wish this to be made known to all, that whoever knows by name the perpetrator of damage inflicted upon him in the previous year may seek and obtain justice from him. Henceforth, however, we wish to announce to everyone that each person must know all those who travel on such a journey in his service, whether they are his own men or others, so that he may know that he will have to render an account for their deeds. Whatever they commit in violation of the peace must be attributed to his peril.

The condition is that the violator of the peace must first pay a fitting penalty according to the character of his crime, whether before us or before our envoy. The lord who has taken such a person with him—one whom he either did not wish or was unable to compel to obey our order, and who moreover did not fear to commit plunder in our kingdom—shall, for his negligence, be deprived of his honor if he did not warn us about him beforehand and, after the contemptuous man’s negligence became known to him, neglected to correct him as was fitting. Thus neither of them may remain without just vengeance.

**(Book V, chapter 189.)** If anyone in the army within the kingdom, without the Lord’s command, wishes by hostile force to plunder anything, or to take hay or grain, or large or small cattle, or to break into or burn houses, we altogether prohibit such acts. If anything of this kind is done by a presumptuous person, he shall be liable to sixty solidi if he is free, and shall restore all the goods, or clear himself with twelve witnesses. If a slave does this, he shall be subject to capital punishment, and his master shall restore all the goods because he neither corrected nor guarded his slave so that he would not commit such acts. For if we consume ourselves, we will quickly perish. Nevertheless, each person must guard his army so that no plundering takes place within the kingdom.

**(Book III, chapter 65.)** If anyone breaks into another person’s house, whatever he forcibly takes away from it, plunders, or steals, he shall pay threefold according to the law of the person whose house was broken into and despoiled, and shall additionally pay the royal fine. If a slave does this, he shall receive the foregoing sentence and, in addition, shall make compensation according to his own law. If a free man causes someone such damage that he is unable to make full compensation, he should strive to give himself as a pledge for a slave until he completes the full compensation.

**(Book III, chapter 1.)** Concerning peace, we admonish that all who are rebels through any crimes be restrained.

**(The same, chapter 66.)** If anyone plunders, consumes, or steals crops or provisions on campaign in violation of the royal ban, or devastates them with horses, he shall pay threefold for the assessed damage according to the law. If a free man does this, he shall be compelled to pay the royal fine for it. A slave shall restore threefold compensation for the damage according to the law and, for the damage, shall be subjected to corporal discipline.

**(Book VI, chapter 96.)** If anyone commits plunder within the kingdom, or forcibly takes anything from any of our faithful or from one of his men, he shall make legal compensation threefold to the person from whom he took something and shall additionally pay us our fine, namely sixty solidi. Afterward he shall be brought before us by the count, so that, confined in the *bastonico* [a detention cell], he may undergo punishment until it pleases us.

If the act was committed publicly, he shall perform public penance for it according to the sanction of the sacred canons. If secretly, he shall perform penance for it on the advice of the priests, since, as the Apostle says, plunderers will not possess the kingdom of God unless they perform true penance (I Cor. VI).

Those who have taken anything from churches shall be judged more severely for it, because the removal of sacred property is sacrilege, and anyone who takes or plunders anything from it is called sacrilegious. Such persons are to be held as exiles from the thresholds of the holy mother Church until they make satisfaction to the church they have injured, and are to be firmly marked as such.

**(Charles the Bald, title XII, chapter 12.)** Let each envoy in his district take care that, if any of our faithful passes through his district, or resides or remains there, and commits plunder, devastation, or other unlawful acts by which God is customarily offended and the people are made to groan under oppression, he investigate the matter carefully and truthfully and report to us how we should arrange it so that neither that person nor anyone else will take pleasure in doing such things.

**(Charles the Bald, title XII, chapter 13.)** Let the envoys take care in their districts that our men, or anyone else, do not plunder their neighbors, great or small, in summer, when they send their horses out to pasture, or in winter, when they send their marshals to obtain fodder for them. If they do so, let our envoys investigate the matter truthfully, as we stated above, and report to us, so that we may correct the lord in such a way that he keeps his men under control, that they remain content with what is due, and that they do not unjustly desire what is not due.

**(Louis the Stammerer, title III, chapters 7 and 8.)** We wish the property of churches, in whatever kingdom they are located, both of bishoprics and of abbeys, to be possessed without any contradiction by the rulers of those churches, just as they possessed it in the time of our lord and father.

And because peace and quiet are customarily disturbed by wandering and irreverent men through tyrannical custom, we wish that, whenever such a person comes to any one of us so that he might evade an account and justice for what he has done, none of us should receive or retain him for any other purpose than to bring him to a proper account and due correction. If he evades a proper account, let everyone together, in whatever kingdom he has entered, pursue him until either he is brought to account or he is removed from the kingdom.

**(Charles the Bald, title XXVI, chapter 5.)** The same must be done with a person who is rebuked or excommunicated by any bishop for a capital and public crime, or who, after committing a crime before excommunication, changes his kingdom and the king’s government so as not to undertake the required penance or to complete lawfully the penance he has undertaken.

**(Charles the Bald, title IX, chapter 4.)** It must be announced to everyone and ordered by our envoys that all churches and priests remain under the immunity, privilege, regulation, and disposition of the bishops of the individual parishes in which they are located, according to canonical authority and the capitularies of the lord Emperor Charles and the pious Augustus Louis.

**(The same, chapter 5.)** Let our envoys, together with the bishop and the prelates of the monasteries, and through faithful and vigorous men in each parish, diligently investigate ecclesiastical properties granted as allods. According to clear and true evidence and authoritative records, let them carefully establish by whom and to whom these properties were given, record how much there is of them, and report to us, so that with the counsel of our faithful we may undertake to correct this sacrilege.

**(The same, chapter 6.)** Let our envoys, explicitly and with every diligence, together with the bishop and the prelates of the monasteries, investigate throughout each parish those ecclesiastical properties from which ninths and tithes ought to be paid but are not being paid, and compel the holders of those properties to pay them. If any contradiction arises that appears reasonable, let it be recorded. Let the prelate of the house of God from which the properties are known to derive, together with the person who holds them and refuses to pay the ninth and tithe, be ordered to come before our presence with our envoys. Then, once the truth has been discovered and a definition established, let us order whatever we find reasonable.

We also wish our envoys to investigate how those who hold the same ecclesiastical properties, from which tithes are paid or not paid, keep them safe—whether in fortified places and guarded woods—and whether lands or dependents belonging to them have been lost, or anything of this kind has occurred, or whether the household has been oppressed contrary to law. Let our envoys report everything in written inventories.

**(The same, chapter 7.)** Let our envoys throughout each parish order the counts and ministers of the commonwealth, by our ban, not to presume to hold assemblies or public pleas at the exits and courtyards of churches or at the dwellings of priests, nor on the Lord’s Day or feast days. Instead, let the count consider and find a suitable place where he may establish a station for holding the assembly. For it is unlawful for the guilty to be punished in the place where, out of respect for divine reverence, they obtain mercy by the agreement of the faithful and the decree of our predecessors.

**(The same, chapter 8.)** Let our envoys firmly announce and order, in our name, to the counts and to all ministers of the commonwealth that, from the Wednesday before the beginning of Lent—and not on that Wednesday itself—until after the octave of Easter, they must not presume to hold a public assembly or plea, except for the reconciliation and pacification of those in disagreement. Likewise, from the Wednesday before the Nativity of the Lord until after the consecrated days, let them observe the same rule. They must also make every effort to honor the days set aside during the four seasonal fasts and the Rogation days with the same observance.

**(The same, chapter 9.)** Let our envoys announce to everyone throughout each parish that if a bishop or the bishop’s ministers have flogged peasants with rods for crimes, out of fear for others and so that the criminals themselves may be corrected, with the discretion determined in the synod and without any improper pretext, and have compelled them, even unwillingly, to perform temporal and bodily penance lest they perish eternally, and if the lords of those peasants take this badly and wish to exact vengeance for it, or presume to restrain those same peasants so that they are not disciplined, let them know that they will both pay our fine and, together with ecclesiastical excommunication, endure our royal punishment.

**(The same, chapter 10.)** Let our envoys announce to all ministers of the commonwealth that the count or the ministers of the commonwealth must be present with the bishop of each parish in the bishop’s duties whenever that bishop travels through his parish, once the bishop has notified them. Those whom the bishop cannot bring to penance, account, or satisfaction by excommunication, let them bring by royal authority and power.

**(The same, chapter 11.)** Let our faithful also know that at the synod we granted the venerable bishops that, concerning ecclesiastical benefices or leases—even if any prelate of the monasteries should ask unreasonably—we will in no way issue instruments confirming them. Therefore let each person restrain himself from making an unreasonable petition.

**(Charles the Bald, title XXXII, chapter 2.)** Concerning one mansus given to a church according to the capitulary of the Augusti and our predecessors: no census or provision of fodder for horses is to be demanded by the lords from priests, as is contained in the aforesaid capitulary. Nor is anything to be demanded for small plots of land or little vineyards given to the same churches for burial, nor for tithes, as is contained in the canons and in the aforesaid capitularies.

And wherever our envoys discover that lords, without the knowledge of the bishops, eject priests from churches or install them in churches, let our envoys act in that matter as is contained in the aforesaid capitularies; and let the bishops deal with the clerics of our men as is contained in those same capitularies.

Let our envoys make this known to the counts and the people: that every week we wish to sit for one day to hear and judge cases. Let the counts and our envoys take great care lest, through their negligence, the poor be afflicted and we suffer weariness because of their complaints, if they wish to have our favor. The people, however, should be told to refrain from appealing to us concerning other cases, except those in which either our envoys or the counts have been unwilling to render them justice.

*(Charles the Bald, title XXXIV, chap. 2; title XLIII, toward the end of chap. 2.)* So that our faithful, each person in his own order and condition, may truly be secure concerning us: henceforth we shall neither condemn, dishonor, oppress, nor afflict anyone contrary to law and justice, or against authority [Col. 1081A] and just reason, by any unjust devices. Rather, with the common counsel of those who are truly faithful to us, in accordance with God’s will and the common welfare, we shall give our assent to whatever concerns the restoration of God’s holy Church, the condition of the kingdom, royal honor, and the peace of the people entrusted to us. In this, they must not merely refrain from opposing and resisting us in carrying these matters out; they must also be faithful and obedient to us, true helpers and fellow workers through sound counsel and sincere assistance, both for our due honor and for accomplishing the matters mentioned above, just as each person, in his own order and condition, ought rightly to be toward his prince and his lord.

## VII. On the correction to be rendered through penance

Behold what the Holy Spirit, through worthy instruments, has threatened and decreed concerning acts of robbery and robbers. Behold what your predecessors, emperors and kings, established concerning this in various synods and assemblies, with the counsel of the bishops and their other faithful men. Anyone who reads understands how these provisions concerning the correction of wrongful acts accord with the Law given through Moses.

In the Gospel we read that Zacchaeus said to the Lord: “Half of my possessions, Lord, I give to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold” (Luke 19). For this purpose he kept the other half of his possessions. Hence Saint Augustine says in his letter to Macedonius (Letter 54):

> “When you say,” he says, “that people wish the guilt of their crime to be forgiven them while retaining the thing on account of which the crime was committed, you describe the worst kind of people, for whom the remedy of repentance is altogether of no benefit. For if the property needed for the restitution, on account of which the sin was committed, can be returned but is not returned, repentance is not being performed but pretended. If repentance is genuinely performed, the sin will not be forgiven unless what was taken is restored—provided that it can be restored.
