Often, however, the person who takes something loses it, either by suffering other evils or by living wickedly himself, and has nothing else from which to make restitution. To such a person we certainly cannot say, ‘Return what you took,’ unless we believe that he has it and is denying it. If such a person suddenly undergoes some suffering while he is thought to possess what he could return, there is no injustice: for even if he has no means by which to return the money he took, he nevertheless rightly pays the penalty for the sin by which he took it, since he is compelled to repay it through bodily afflictions. Yet it is not inhuman to intercede even for such people, as for those guilty of crimes—not so that what belongs to others may not be restored, but so that one human being may not rage against another without cause.

> “I would say with complete confidence that anyone who intervenes on behalf of another so that he may not restore what he wickedly took, and anyone who does not compel a person who has fled to him to make restitution as far as he honestly can, is a partner in fraud and crime. For toward such people we withhold our assistance more mercifully than we offer it. One who helps another to sin does not provide assistance; rather, he overthrows and oppresses him.

> “Those whom we know both to have taken things wickedly and to possess the means of returning them, yet who are unwilling to do so, we accuse, rebuke, and detest—some secretly, some openly—as the differences among persons seem to allow different remedies, lest they be driven into greater madness to the ruin of others. Sometimes also, if a matter requiring greater care does not prevent it, we deprive them of communion at the holy altar.

> “I would not dare say that anyone should intervene so that he may possess with impunity what he took by crime; rather, one should intervene so that, once the injury has been forgiven, he may return what he wrongfully took—provided that he has either what he took or something else with which to restore it.

> “But concerning anyone who has taken property contrary to the law of human society through thefts, robberies, false accusations, oppression, or seizures, we judge that it ought to be returned rather than given away, following the Gospel example of Zacchaeus the tax collector. When he had received the Lord as a guest and had suddenly been changed to a holy life, he said: ‘Half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have taken anything from anyone, I restore fourfold’” (Luke 19).

What shall I say about interest, which even the laws and judges themselves order to be repaid? Is the person who takes or snatches something from a rich man more cruel than the one who slaughters a poor man through usury?

Let all of us, therefore—you, we, and the people of the entire kingdom—return to our consciences. Whatever we have thought, said, and done against God’s will and command, let us cleanse ourselves from the leaven of malice and wickedness through sincere confession, toward fruits worthy of penance and priestly reconciliation. As the Holy Spirit exhorts us through the Psalmist: “Let us come before his face with confession; let us fall down and weep before the Lord who made us, for he is the Lord our God, and we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Psalm 94).

For we read in the history of the Maccabees (2 Maccabees 12) that the very brave Judas fought against the enemies of the Church, which then existed, and that many of his own men fell in that war. After the adversaries had been routed, Judas himself returned with his army to bury the bodies of his men who had fallen in battle. Under the tunics of the slain, however, objects dedicated to idols were found, and God’s judgment was made manifest, because this was why they had fallen in battle.

Therefore, if under our tunics—that is, within our bodies—we have an evil conscience concerning robbery, greed, which is the worship of idols, debauchery, envy, hatred of our brothers, murder, sacrilege, incest, and other crimes and sins, let us cleanse those evils through sincere confession, devout commitment, tears, almsgiving, and fitting acts of satisfaction. As soon as the time permits, let us all together perform public penance for our past sins, whether manifest or hidden, and a three-day fast. Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, completing our sanctification in the fear of God.

For, as Saint Augustine says in explaining the Apostle’s statement, sins, whether small or great, cannot remain unpunished: they are punished either by the repentant person or by God the Judge. Divine vengeance ceases if human conversion comes first. God loves to spare those who repent and confess, and not to judge those who judge themselves.

After the fast, fruits worthy of penance, and a declaration that henceforth we must abstain from the evils in which we have until now been involved—for truly to perform penance is to mourn what has been committed and thereafter avoid what must be mourned, changing wickedness in the mind into goodness—let us receive the body and blood of Christ for the forgiveness of our sins, so that God may dwell in us and we in God, and so that neither invisible nor visible enemies may have power against us. Otherwise we shall be able to possess neither strength against wicked Christians nor victory over the pagans.

Let no one despair because of the enormity of his sins; let him only turn to the Lord with his whole heart. For a three-day penance wiped away the long-standing sins of the Ninevites (Jonah 4), and the repentant thief earned the rewards of life even at the sentence of his death (Luke 23).

Let us therefore change our hearts and presume that we have already received what we ask. The Judge is more quickly moved by a prayer when the petitioner is corrected from his wickedness. For the persistence that ordinarily displeases human beings pleases the judgment of truth: the merciful and compassionate God wishes forgiveness to be demanded from him, although he does not wish to become angry to the extent that we deserve.

Thus he says through the Prophet: “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, and I will rescue you, and you shall glorify me” (Psalm 46). He is therefore his own witness: he desires to show mercy to those who call upon him, and he urges them to call upon him. As another prophet admonishes: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God” (Lamentations 3). To lift our hearts with our hands to God means to raise the devotion of prayer together with the merit of good works.

Indeed, he gives—he gives confidence to our fear—when he cries out through the Prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 33). And this is a certain judgment: those whom God long awaits, so that they may turn, he condemns more severely if they do not turn.

After we and you have thus cleansed ourselves from our sins, as we have said, let us henceforth restrain ourselves from those and from other sins, lest that proverb happen to us which blessed Peter the Apostle applies to those who return to sin after penance: “The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (2 Peter 2).

For the power of penance against sin is great—provided that someone perseveres in that penance. For it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10).

Hence it is written: “Whoever is baptized from the dead and again touches him, what benefit does his washing provide?” (Sirach 34). Every perverse work that drags a person to death, in which the life of righteousness does not live, is dead. Therefore, the one who bewails the wicked deeds he remembers having committed is baptized from the dead and again touches him if, after his tears, he becomes entangled in those same deeds once more. The washing from that same dead work is therefore of no benefit to any soul if, by doing again what it had lamented, it does not rise through the lamentation of penance and the uprightness of justice.

Whoever, during the time of penance, declares that he will not return to his former sins—that is, anathematizes his past sins, since otherwise he can neither be absolved by God nor reconciled through priestly ministry—should carefully heed what Saint Gregory says in one of his letters (Book XI, Letter 45, to Theoctista):

> “If there are some,” he says, “who claim that, if someone anathematizes under compulsion of necessity, he is not held by the bond of the anathema, they are witnesses against themselves that they are not Christians, because they think that they can dissolve the bonds of the holy Church by futile efforts. Consequently, they do not consider the absolution of the holy Church, which she grants to the faithful, to be genuine, if they do not consider her bindings effective. There is no need to dispute at length against such people, for they must be utterly despised and anathematized. By the very means through which they think they deceive the truth, they are truly bound in their sins. Therefore, if there are any who, under the Christian name, dare either to preach these things we have mentioned or silently retain them within themselves, without a doubt I, together with all Catholic bishops and the entire Church, anathematize them, because they think and speak things contrary to the truth.”

There is, nevertheless, a very great difference between those who, after penance and a declaration, return through contempt to criminal and public sins, and delight in persisting in them, and those who, through weakness, relapse into former criminal or public sins and again seek penance.

For, as Saint Augustine says (Letter 54), human wickedness sometimes advances so far that people, even after having performed penance and after reconciliation at the altar, commit similar or more serious offenses. Yet God causes his sun to rise even upon such people and bestows upon them no less generously than before the gifts of life and salvation. And although a place for the most humble penance is not granted to them in the Church, God nevertheless does not forget his own penance concerning them.

Although, therefore, it has wisely and beneficially been provided that the place of that most humble penance be granted only once in the Church, lest a medicine become less useful to the sick because it is cheap—for it is all the more health-giving the less contemptible it is—who would nevertheless dare say to God: “Why do you still spare this person, who after his first penance has again bound himself in the snares of iniquity?” Who would dare say that what the Apostle says does not apply to them: “Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance?” (Romans 2). Or that the statement written, “Blessed are all who trust in him” (Psalm 2), has been defined with these people excluded? Or that what is said, “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Psalm 26), does not pertain to them?

## VIII. To the king, that he should love good counselors

At last we turn our speech to you, most beloved lord king, because we desire both that you prosper in this temporal kingdom and that after this kingdom you reach the eternal one.

As one of our number heard from those who were present, the Emperor Charles the Great, who nobly enlarged the Frankish kingdom and ruled it successfully for forty-six years, and who surpassed the kings of the Franks in wisdom both in the sacred Scriptures and in ecclesiastical and human laws, never at any time allowed himself to be without three of his wiser and more distinguished counselors. Rather, he kept them with him in rotation and succession, as it was possible for them to do so. At the head of his bed he kept writing tablets and a stylus, and whatever he reflected upon, whether by day or by night, concerning the welfare of holy Church and the advancement and stability of the kingdom, he recorded on those tablets. He discussed these matters with the same counselors whom he kept with him. When he came to his assembly, he carefully presented everything that had been considered to the full body of his counselors and took care to bring those matters to completion by common counsel.

If that man—so wise and strong, so wealthy in the extent of his kingdom, and peaceful ruler of many kingdoms—made this his practice, following the scriptural sayings, “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it” (Sirach 32), and, “A wise person who hears will become wiser, and one who understands will possess the helm” (Proverbs 1), and, “Where there is no governor, the people will fall; but there is safety where there is much counsel” (Proverbs 11), then consider what you ought to do. You are still immature in age and have so many fellow sharers and rivals in this small portion of the kingdom that you reign more in name than in power.

We ask you, with the counsel and assistance of your faithful, to choose men from both orders who will remain with you as counselors for each month. To them you should willingly lend the ear of your heart and body. Let them teach you to fear God, to honor holy Church and its rulers according to the sacred laws, to govern the kingdom and your faithful according to the Lord’s will, and to organize your household for you as it was organized in the time of your predecessors, when it was well ordered. In this way necessity will not draw you where your will ought not to lead you.

Thus the churches in this kingdom will not be afflicted by occasional *circadae* [circuit-obligations?] and unlawful customary exactions—impositions that did not exist in the time of Pippin, Charles, and Louis but were introduced in our own time. The leading men of the kingdom will be able to remain in your presence with due security and honor, and the other noblemen in the kingdom will have security, so that by various devices they are not stripped of the wealth they have been able to possess.

For after greed, the root of all evils, flared up in the kingdom, so that no one, or scarcely anyone, could acquire or retain honor or any good thing without payment, or possess security, peace, counsel, justice, and judgment did not have their proper place in this kingdom.

Take care, therefore, that these robberies and depredations cease in this kingdom, and that this wretched people, who for many years have been afflicted by various and continual plundering and by exactions for the Northmen, may have some remedy. Let justice and judgment, which among us are almost dead, revive. Let God restore strength to us against the pagans, because until now, for many years, defense has had no place in this kingdom; instead, ransom and tribute have emptied not only the poor but also churches that were once wealthy.

For this reason the royal name has fallen into such disgrace and such diminishment, as is known to many. This kingdom, once noble and extensive, has been divided against itself. But, as the Lord says, “A kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste” (Matthew 11)—that is, it falls from its own ground, from the earth, as though sliding from ice—so that there is no immediate prospect unless, as the Psalm says, we are converted: the Lord has already brandished his sword, stretched it out, and prepared it, and has made it instruments of death (Psalm 7).

Fear the judgment that Scripture, which does not lie, declares: “Woe to the land whose king is a boy and whose princes eat in the morning” (Ecclesiastes 10). Understand that Scripture does not condemn youth in age but in conduct, life, and folly—things that are not restrained by the weight of counsel.

Elsewhere the sayings of sacred Scripture show this by declaring: “Old age is honorable, not because of long duration, nor reckoned by the number of years. The understanding of a person is gray hair, and an undefiled life is the age of old age” (Wisdom 4).

For this reason the Lord says to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people” (Numbers 11). In them nothing other than old age of mind is sought, since those are ordered to be chosen who are known to be elders. For if bodily old age were being sought in them, they could be recognized by as many people as could see them. But when he says, “whom you know to be elders of the people,” it is plainly evident that the old age of the mind, not of the body, is being required.

As Scripture shows (1 Kings 12), Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, rejected the counsel of such old men. Following the counsel of young men of this kind, through his negligence he lost the greater part of his father’s kingdom. Because of the merits of his grandfather David, the Lord reserved for him a small portion of the kingdom.

Concerning the statement, “Woe to the land whose princes eat in the morning” (Ecclesiastes 10), Scripture speaks not of necessary but of pleasurable eating, as the Apostle shows when he says: “Do not make provision for the flesh in desires or lusts” (Romans 13). Those whom he restrains from caring for the flesh in lusts, he permits to care for it in what is necessary.

May almighty God, who speaks these things through us in your ears, speak them himself in your hearts.

[Col. 1087]

## XIV. What the bishop ought to carry out, and with what care he ought to protect ecclesiastical possessions and resources

*(In Sirmond, from the Verdun manuscript.)*
[Col. 1087A] The bishop must carry out the following duties in particular, in accordance with the sacred regulations: celebrate public Masses; regularly consecrate the sacred chrism; administer holy baptism according to ecclesiastical tradition, and ensure that it is administered by priests. At the appointed times, and as the regulations prescribe, he must ordain priests, deacons, and the other ecclesiastical ministers, without accepting any payment.

He must hold synods of priests according to the sacred canons, without venality. When summoned to the provincial synod of bishops or to the ordination of a bishop, he must attend, or send in his stead a priest or deacon with a *tractoria* setting out the reasons for his inability to attend, or with his canonical consent. He must govern the clergy according to the regulations and, as Saint Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule*, provide that clergy with what is necessary both for their interior and their bodily needs. [Col. 1087B]

He must care for the church’s lights and ornaments, its buildings, and its roofing repairs. He must receive guests and the poor individually in the hospitals established for them; and, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, “Whoever does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8), he must take care to provide the necessities of life for those of his household who serve him.

He must diligently care, according to the sacred regulations, for the monasteries in his diocese, the rural parish churches, and the *matricularii*—those enrolled on the Church’s poor-roll. He must announce the word of the Lord to the people of his diocese, teach those subject to him by word and example, and assist them by prayer.

In the signing of those who have not yet been signed on the forehead through the episcopal ministry, he must act diligently according to the regulations; and in making the rounds for this purpose, he must not burden the priests of the diocese beyond what is due and necessary, as Saint Gregory decreed. He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside the Church.

To sinners and penitents he must impose penance according to the measure of their offenses and, after satisfaction has been made, reconcile them according to the regulations. He must exercise oversight over every possession under his authority. He must provide military service for the defense of the holy Church, according to the extent of his ability and in accordance with the ancient custom, for the king’s disposition; and, in accordance with the Lord’s command, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21), he must render each its due.

For, as the most eloquent holy pope Gelasius says in his decrees, writing to the Emperor Anastasius (Epistle 10):

> “There are two powers by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of pontiffs and the royal power. But the burden of priests is the heavier, inasmuch as they must render an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves.” [Col. 1087D]

And the care of kings in human affairs is proportionately more extensive than that of priests, because, for the honor, defense, and peace of the holy Church, and of its rulers and ministers, the King of kings has imposed upon them the burden of responsibility: by promulgating laws and by waging war. Thus their actions and dignities are distinguished, so that Christian kings need pontiffs for eternal life, while pontiffs use the disposition of kings for the course of temporal affairs; so that spiritual action may remain separate from carnal interference, and the one who serves God may not involve himself in secular business, while, conversely, one who is occupied with secular business may not appear to preside over divine matters.

For the Holy Spirit, through those who reign with Christ in heaven and shine forth on earth through miracles, spoke and caused these words to reach us in writing, saying (Urban, Epistle 1):

> “Ecclesiastical possessions and resources are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord; they are the vows of the faithful, the penitential payments of sinners, and the patrimonies of the poor. Whoever steals them is guilty of the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira, and such a person must be handed over to Satan, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

> “Our glorious emperors Charles and Louis inserted the following in the first book of their *Capitularies* (ch. 83): ‘Because, in accordance with the tradition of the holy Fathers, we know that the possessions of the Church are the vows of the faithful, the penitential payments of sinners, and the patrimonies of the poor, we desire not only to preserve its existing possessions, but also, with God’s help, to confer many more. Nevertheless, so that we might entirely remove from ecclesiastical persons the suspicion formerly conceived concerning the non-division of Church property, we decree that neither during our times, nor during the times of our sons and, with God’s dispensation, of our successors who may wish to imitate our will or the example of our ancestors, shall it suffer any division or loss whatsoever.’” [Col. 1088C]

Holy Pope Anacletus, ordained a priest by the blessed Apostle Peter himself and afterward made his successor as bishop in the Roman see, judged together with the priests of the whole world (Epistle 1):

> “Whoever takes anything away from a father or mother is a participant in homicide. Without doubt our father is God, who created us; but our mother is the Church, which spiritually regenerated us in baptism. Therefore whoever steals, takes away, or plunders the money of Christ and of the Church is a homicide, and before the sight of the just Judge will be counted a homicide. Whoever steals his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but whoever takes away Church money or property commits sacrilege and must be judged as a sacrilegious person.” [Col. 1088D]

Likewise holy Pope Urban and martyr (Epistle 1):

> “Ecclesiastical possessions and resources are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord; they are the vows of the faithful, the penitential payments of sinners, and the patrimonies of the poor. Whoever steals them is guilty of the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira, and such a person must be handed over to Satan, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”

And holy Pope Lucius (Epistle 11):

> “By apostolic authority we expel and condemn from the thresholds of the holy Church those who plunder ecclesiastical possessions and resources, and we judge them to be sacrilegious. We condemn not only them but also all who consent to them, because not only those who do these things are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those who do them. The same punishment encompasses both the perpetrators and those who consent. Those whose ministry it is to prevent, restrain, and correct such things cannot be free from this punishment if they do not strive to correct them.” [Col. 1089B]

And Saint Gregory, in his letter to the subdeacon Sabinus (Book VIII, Epistle 7), says:

> “It is sacrilegious and contrary to the laws if anyone attempts, through the efforts of an evil will, to retain for his own advantage anything that has been left to venerable places.”

Saint Augustine likewise says in his sermon on the holy Gospel of John:

> “The sacrilegious thief of sacred and the Lord’s treasuries is Judas; and whoever steals or snatches anything from the Church is compared with the lost Judas.”

Again, in the sacred canons dictated by the Holy Spirit and confirmed by the blood of Christ, it is written (Council of Toledo I, canon 11):

> “If any powerful person strips a cleric, or anyone poorer, or a religious person, and the bishop sends word to him that he should hear the case, but he refuses, let writings immediately circulate among all the bishops of the province, and among as many others as can be reached; and let him be held excommunicated until he hears the case and restores what belongs to another.” [Col. 1089C]

It is also written (Council of Agde, canon 4):

> “Clerics and laypeople who presume to retain parental offerings, offerings donated or left by will, or who think that what they themselves have donated to churches or monasteries may be taken away, shall, as the holy synod has decreed, be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor until they make restitution.”

Therefore let all powerful persons be exceedingly careful, each according to his own rank and dignity, not to presume to take ecclesiastical possessions for themselves, to their own condemnation, nor to weary or afflict God’s churches and the places of the saints with unprecedented customs. Let them know that, as we have stated above, ecclesiastical possessions are the vows of the faithful, the patrimonies of the poor, and the penitential payments of sinners, and that they rest under the protection and defense of Christ, who entrusted them to the rulers and nobles of the earth to defend and preserve—not to afflict, usurp, or seize.

For whatever pretext of utility or necessity anyone may put forward, he who sees all hearts, who knows human thoughts, rewards actions, and will in no way disregard even thoughts that have gone unrewarded, sees everything. Therefore everyone who wishes to be saved, liberated from eternal death, and brought to eternal life must listen with the utmost attention of the heart to what the Holy Spirit has spoken through those to whom the Lord said:

> “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20);

> “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20);

> “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 18:18);

> “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:22);

> “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16).

For those who reign in heaven and shine forth on earth through miracles—and who, even to this day, live with us and will live forever with our successors, since their reward is with God—say:

> “If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, and does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema” (Council of Ancyra, canon 7). [Col. 1090B]

Anathema is translated in the Roman language as “alienation,” because everyone who does such things, so long as he remains in those sins, is already excommunicated and condemned by the sacred canons. This remains so even if we bishops—who, in the apostles and with the apostles, have received the power of binding and loosing not through our own merit but by divine grace—sometimes delay, sometimes lack understanding of divine matters, sometimes remain unaware of what is entrusted to us, and sometimes are unable to correct what has been committed even when correction would be beneficial, and therefore pretend or neglect to carry out what has been established, so that we fail to separate such a person from the Church and from the fellowship of the faithful by excommunication.

He remains excommunicated and already condemned by the sacred canons until he abandons that sin and, through ecclesiastical satisfaction and priestly reconciliation, receives again the grace of the Lord and the fellowship of the faithful. Whoever, entangled in his sins and in such crimes, ends this life before making the necessary satisfaction will in no way be able to have communion and fellowship with the elect in the kingdom of God, nor will he ever be able to escape the punishments of hell and the fellowship of demons.

Finally, the two chapters that follow were taken from the edict collected by Ansegisus [Col. 1090D], abbot and compiler of the imperial capitularies from various synods and judgments. For the sake of brevity, they are found in the first book of the *Capitularies*, chapters 77 and 78, concerning the non-division of ecclesiastical possessions and the election of bishops, excerpted from the material written above.

The Emperor Charles the Great sent this edict in its entirety, together with a question concerning chorepiscopi, through Archbishop Arno to Pope Leo. At the latter’s advice he issued another edict concerning the non-division of ecclesiastical possessions and the affairs of bishops, confirmed it by the authority of the apostolic see and by his own authority, and sent it to be observed perpetually throughout all the metropolitan churches of his empire.

The aforementioned chapters therefore read as follows (Book I, chapter 83):

> “Because, in accordance with the tradition of the holy Fathers, we know that the possessions of the Church are the vows of the faithful, the penitential payments of sinners, and the patrimonies of the poor, we desire not only to preserve its existing possessions, but also, with God’s help, to confer many more. Nevertheless, so that we might entirely remove from ecclesiastical persons the suspicion formerly conceived concerning the non-division of those possessions, we decree that neither during our times, nor during the times of our sons and, with God’s dispensation, of our successors who may wish to imitate our will or the example of our ancestors, shall it suffer any division or loss whatsoever.

> “We are also not ignorant of the sacred canons. Therefore, so that the holy Church may more freely enjoy its honor in the name of God, we grant our assent to the ecclesiastical order, namely, that bishops be chosen by the election of the clergy and the people, from their own diocese and according to the provisions of the canons, without regard to persons or payments, on account of the merit of their life and the gift of wisdom, so that they may everywhere benefit those subject to them by example and word” (chapter 84). [Col. 1091B]

And in the same edict, from which these passages were taken, the following continues:

> “We also command all who are subject to our authority that no one attempt to plunder the privileges of churches or monasteries, or the churches themselves, because, as we have been instructed by the holy Fathers, this is recognized as a most serious sin,”

and so forth in what follows.

And in the privilege of the Church of Beauvais, confirmed with the consent of the bishops of four provinces by the recently deceased lord Charles, the following is contained at the relevant place:

> “Let secular power, whether it has been endowed with some exalted rank or has been established in a lowly position, exercise no dominion over these things, either at present or in the future, contrary to the sacred regulations—neither by violently invading them nor by receiving the offerings. If any king, priest, judge, or secular person, knowing the text of this constitution, attempts to act against it, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, and let him know that he is guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity he has committed. Unless he either restores what he has unjustly taken from it or mourns the unlawful acts through worthy penance, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and let him be subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment. But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just for that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.” [Col. 1091D]

And in the privilege of the same Church, confirmed by Pope Nicholas, the following is contained at the relevant place (Nicholas [to] Bishop Odo):

> “Therefore no king, no judge, and no one supported by the dignity of any secular power shall have authority over or dominion over the possessions of the aforesaid monasteries, their estates, fields, slaves, or anything else that has been given to those monasteries—whether to rule, receive, or take it away—except the bishop of the Church of Beauvais who shall at that time preside over that Church. Whatever has today been assigned to those monasteries in gold, silver, or any kind of movable property, or in the substance of their entire resources, or whatever may be given to them in future times, shall be subject to the distribution and administration of the bishop of Beauvais. No right or dominion of any other power shall exercise any authority over them, except insofar as divine authority, law, and justice permit.

> “If anyone, whether a great or a small person, presumes in reckless boldness to act against this apostolic decree of ours, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the ungodly to the punishment of eternal fire. But whoever proves himself an observer of this command may deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most merciful Lord God.” [Col. 1092A]

And Saint Gregory, in a decretal letter sent to the regions of Greece concerning certain disturbances, says at the relevant place:

> “If there are some who say that, if someone has been compelled by necessity to pronounce an anathema, he is not held by the bond of anathema, they are witnesses against themselves that they are not Christians, because they think that they can dissolve the bonds of the holy Church by futile efforts; and consequently they do not regard the absolution of the holy Church, which it grants to the faithful, as genuine if they do not consider its bonds effective. There is no need to argue at length against them, because they must be utterly despised and anathematized; and by the very means through which they think they deceive the truth, they are truly bound in their sins. Both I and all Catholic bishops, together with the universal Church, anathematize them, because they hold and speak opinions contrary to the truth.” [Col. 1092C]

Therefore our most beloved lord king must take the greatest care not to act against these decrees of the Holy Spirit at the suggestion or request of any persons, nor consent to their being violated with regard to ecclesiastical possessions—especially after this visitation of God, through which we believe that he has been corrected by confession, penance, and priestly reconciliation. For penance has great power against sin, but only for the person who perseveres in that same penance, since it is written: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 18:22). It is also written: “What benefit is there for one who is baptized by a dead person and then touches him again?” (Sir. 34:30).

Every perverse work that leads to death and does not live for righteousness is dead. Therefore a person is baptized by a dead person and then touches him again when he laments the evil works he remembers having committed but, after his tears, becomes entangled in the same works again. The washing of that dead person benefits no soul that, by doing again what it has lamented, does not rise through the tears of penance to the uprightness of justice. For truly to do penance is to lament what has been committed and thereafter avoid again what is to be lamented.

Our dearest lord king must therefore take heed of what the Lord of lords and King of kings says both to him and to each one of us—and indeed to every human being without exception, since Scripture says, “God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34). He says what he had said long before to someone in the Gospel: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

Nor should he heed those who suggest evil to him, since the Apostle says: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (Rom. 1:32). He must not command the bishop who has recently been ordained to do such things or consent to such persons, lest he destroy himself by this and lose ecclesiastical grace before God.

Before his ordination, he made the strictest profession before all, including his electors and ordainers, and subscribed with his own hand to the sacred regulations of the holy councils, promising to observe them insofar as he knew and was able. The sacred canons, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, decree the following:

> “If anyone violates his own profession or his own written undertaking in any respect, he will deprive himself of his honor.”

Let those who have presumed, with his consent or favor, to destroy the possessions and resources of the Church of Beauvais—although he had no authority to grant or consent to their being given to them—be exceedingly careful lest they incur the judgments of the sacred canons written above, which all of us bishops, to whose knowledge their sacrileges have come, have invoked against them, and lest they be separated in every way from the fellowship of Christians.

[Col. 1093]

## XV. Concerning Criminal Priests Whose Guilt Has Not Been Proven

*(In the same source, from the Mainz edition of John Busaeus.)*

[Col. 1093B] **Chapter I.** What is to be done concerning criminal priests whose guilt has not been proven, and who always deny it, is written in the first book of the *Capitularies* of the lord Emperor Charles Augustus, chapter 34 (Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 33):

> “We must reconsider with great care what should be done concerning those criminal priests whose guilt has not been proven and who always deny it. For this matter has very often been debated by us and by our predecessors, but until now it has not been definitively settled. Therefore we have sent our priests to consult our father, Pope Leo, and whatever we learn from him or from his representatives, we shall not delay reporting to you together with those whom we sent.

> “In the meantime, deliberate among yourselves more attentively about what we should establish with you concerning these matters, together with the instructions of the aforesaid holy Father, so that the people’s murmuring may cease and we, while favoring these men, may remain unharmed, with the Lord’s help, by both sides.”

The previously mentioned confirmation concerning the purgation of priests follows, in chapter 35 of the same book.

**Chapter II.** *(Capitularies, Book V, chapter 34.)*

> “We do not doubt that it is known to all of you, by sight or hearing, that various crimes are very often brought against priests at the prompting of the ancient enemy. But although the manner in which reasonable examination and satisfaction are to be made concerning these matters has very often been debated—both in the time of my father, the lord Pippin, of blessed memory, and in ancient times by the holy Fathers and other persons of good devotion—we have been entirely unable to find it definitively and clearly settled.

> “In our own times this same matter has very often been debated by the holy bishops, the other priests, and the remaining ministers of ecclesiastical rank, living in our kingdoms or elsewhere and acting together with us, because many and excessive complaints concerning this matter have reached us from various regions. But we wish all ministers of both orders to know what has been determined after consultation with our lord and father Leo, the apostolic pope, the other bishops of the Roman Church, and the remaining priests, as well as the patriarchs of the East and of the Greeks, many holy bishops and priests, all our bishops, the other priests and Levites, and, with their authority and consent, after consultation with our other faithful men and all our counselors.

> “It has therefore been established, on the basis of the reason, necessity, and authority stated above and after consultation with all, that whenever a crime is brought against any priest, if the accuser himself is such a person as ought to be admitted—for the canons have fully specified what sort of persons may be admitted to accuse priests—and if that accuser, who is to be received canonically, can prove the charge against him before the bishops with the legitimate number of true and good witnesses, then judgment shall be rendered canonically, and, if he is found guilty, he shall be condemned canonically. But if the accuser cannot prove it under the conditions stated above, and this is determined canonically—”

**Chapter III.** *(The same source.)*

> “If that priest is therefore suspected or deemed untrustworthy by his bishop and by his fellow priests, or by good and upright men of his people or congregation, then, so that he may not remain under the charge or the suspicion mentioned above, his bishop shall restore him purged to the Church after he has taken an oath before the people over the four Gospels, together with three, five, or seven good priests from the neighborhood, following the example of Pope Leo, who had twelve bishops for his own purgation—or with even more, if it seems appropriate to his bishop or if he recognizes that it is necessary because of the people’s tumult—together with other good and upright men.” [Col. 1094D]

**Chapter IV.** *(The same source.)*

> “If anyone wishes to know what sort of accusers and witnesses ought to be admitted to accuse priests, and what is to be done concerning the accuser, he can find it stated fully in the canons and laws by which the holy Church is governed together with the sacred canons. Namely, those whom the public laws admit to accusation or testimony are to be admitted, and those whom the public laws do not admit are not to be received.

> “That is, persons covered with the stains of infamy are not admitted to make an accusation. Nevertheless, no one who is denied the right of accusation is to be denied the permission to accuse in his own cases. Witnesses suspected of partiality, especially those whom the accuser has produced from his own household, or whom the lowliness of their life has brought into disrepute, or who are under fourteen years of age, are not to be admitted.”

**Chapter V.**

The witnesses, as the law of Theodosius commands, must first be bound by an oath before they are questioned about the case, so that they swear that they will say nothing false [Col. 1095B]; and greater credence should be given to witnesses of honorable rather than lowly standing. The testimony of one person, however distinguished and suitable that person may appear, is in no way to be heard.

The law of Valentinian and Theodosius also commands (Book 15 of the Theodosian Code, *On Accusations*) that in criminal cases or charges no one may accuse by proxy, even if he has been able to obtain this through an imperial rescript; rather, the person who brings the charge must himself be present and accuse in person, with a written accusation submitted beforehand. Judges are to be punished, and their office condemned, if they have remained silent or have thought that an innocent person should be subjected to examination without the prior written accusation.

But if clerics give testimony before ecclesiastical authorities in ecclesiastical cases, they are not to be brought before episcopal judgment through the bond of a compromise; this was abolished by the law of Majorian.

**Chapter VI.**

Since, according to the sacred laws, a sentence pronounced without writing will not deserve even to bear the name of a sentence, and since, according to the law of Valentinian and Valens (the same Code, Book 11, *Interrogations*):

> “Unless an accusation has been formally written, no one is to be made a defendant or brought to judgment, because just as punishment binds the convicted person, so it also binds the accuser if he has not proved what he charged,”

and since the laws establish that the person bringing forward a written accusation must affirm it, and, if he does not establish its truth, must be held guilty of falsehood, informers who have been unable to prove the crime are to be condemned as perjurers and guilty of falsehood, as the law of Honorius and Theodosius decreed (Book 41 of the Theodosian Code, *On Bishops*, and elsewhere):

> “Clerics ought to be accused only before bishops.”

Therefore, if a bishop, priest, deacon, or any minister of the Christian law of a lower rank is accused before bishops—for elsewhere this ought not to occur—by any person, whether that person is a man of high rank or of any other dignity, whoever undertakes this sort of disreputable accusation must know that he must bring forward matters to be proved by evidence and demonstrated by documents. [Col. 1095D]

**Chapter VII.**

If anyone therefore brings forward against such persons charges that cannot be proved, let him understand by the authority of this sanction that he will suffer damage to his own reputation. Through the loss of his honor and the impairment of his good name, he will learn that thereafter he may not with impunity lie in wait for another person’s shame.

For just as it is right that bishops, priests, deacons, and others, if the charges brought against them can be proved, should be removed from the Church as disgraced, so that afterward, despised and bowed down by the contempt of miserable humiliation, they may have no action for injuries, so it should likewise appear consistent with justice that we have ordered a measured punishment to be imposed on those who attack innocence.

Therefore bishops must hear such cases only in the presence of many witnesses. The sacred canons of Carthage also clearly define the procedure between those who accuse clerics and the clerics who are accused, and how the condemnation of excommunication or the examination for purgation is to be carried out. Specifically:

> “When a priest or cleric of a lower rank has been accused before his own bishop, the accuser must choose for himself a place in that same location, namely in the same diocese from which the accused comes, a nearby place where it will not be difficult to produce witnesses, and where the case may be concluded.”

The laws likewise say (the same Code, Book 10):

> “The investigation of crimes must be conducted where the crime was committed. For elsewhere the accused person is forbidden to be heard.”

But if the person against whom the charge has been brought regards his judge—that is, his own bishop—as suspect, he is permitted to appeal, namely to the neighboring bishops of that province, as the canons of Sardica and Carthage decreed; or to the metropolitan bishop, in accordance with the Council of Antioch; or to provincial councils, as the sacred canons of Nicaea and Antioch established and as the African council demonstrated in its letter to Pope Celestine; or from the bishops’ decision to a number determined according to the Council of Carthage; or from the judges, whether those whom the chief bishop appointed according to the African canons or those whom he himself selected with the consent of his bishop. He must be judged according to the regulations by those from whom no appeal is permitted. [Col. 1096C]

**Chapter VIII.**

It is therefore established that, if the perfect council is the one in which the metropolitan bishop has been present, in accordance with the Council of Antioch, favorably received and commended by the universal great Council of Chalcedon in its twelfth session, then the preceding chapter concerning the proving or purgation of priests is much more perfect, binding, and deserving of observance and adherence, since it was confirmed through consultation with the apostolic see, so many bishops, and the other ecclesiastical ministers, and by the consent of the faithful of God. We read this attested by the voice of the great and orthodox emperor, and it has been strengthened by the practice and custom of succeeding bishops over so many years.

The Cisalpine Catholic Church has generally followed this authority in the deposition of criminal priests or the purgation of those accused of crimes, according to customary practice, for seventy years and more.

**Chapter IX.**

Concerning custom, Saint Augustine, counted among the Church’s best teachers by the apostolic see, when Saint Celestine was writing, says in Book IV *On Baptism* (chapter 5):

> “It is plainly true that reason and truth must be preferred to custom; but when truth supports custom, nothing ought to be held more firmly.”

It must therefore be shown whether reason, truth, and authority support this custom. It is written in the mystical Synod of Nicaea (canon 3):

> “The great synod absolutely forbade a bishop, a priest, a deacon, or anyone at all who belongs to the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, or aunt, or one of those persons alone who escape suspicion.” [Col. 1097A]

From this Valens, Gratian, and Valentinian, Augusti and Christian emperors, enacted a law (Book 44 of the Theodosian Code, *On Bishops*, and elsewhere), whose interpretation is as follows:

> “All who exercise the office of the clergy are forbidden to have the familiarity of unrelated women. They should know that only the companionship of mothers, sisters, or daughters within their household has been granted to them.”

**Chapter X.**

But because, under the pretext of these persons, other women began to be introduced, the holy African canons decreed (canon 5) that bishops and priests themselves should not visit widows, virgins, or any women alone, but only where either clerics or some serious-minded Christians are present. Therefore, as the blessed Gregory wrote to the ministers of the Roman Church (Book VII, Epistle 39), blessed Augustine did not even consent to live with his sister, saying:

> “Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.”

From this Saint Gregory says:

> “The caution of learned men ought therefore to be a great instruction for us. For it is the presumption of the unwary that what a strong person fears, a weaker person does not fear. One wisely overcomes unlawful things who has learned not even to make use of what is permitted.”

For this reason it was also decreed in the law of Justinian, chapter 475, that if anyone has in his house a woman who could give rise to suspicion of immorality, and he is told by his fellow clerics that he ought not to live with such a woman, but refuses to remove her from his house—or if an accuser proves that he has behaved dishonorably with such a woman—then the bishop is to remove him from the clergy according to the ecclesiastical canons.

## CHAPTER XI

At the Roman synods of Eugenius and Leo IV it was decreed:

“If any member of the priesthood—that is, a bishop, presbyter, or even subdeacon—is suspected of the crime of fornication with any woman, and after the first, second, and third admonition of the metropolitan, or of another bishop, or of the one to whom he appears subject, he is found to be serving her or associating with her in any way, he shall be judged canonically. Therefore every bishop ought in such a matter to exercise careful and diligent oversight, lest the Church of Christ be defiled by its own ministers, since, when a man is not permitted to have his own wife, he must especially abstain from every woman.” [Col. 1097D]

Accordingly, we should not make it our task to investigate, through the parishioners or neighbors of any presbyter, the presbyters’ intercourse with women. For the ancient heresy called Cynic—that is, “canine,” on account of its shamelessness—which maintained that sexual intercourse is natural and therefore should be practiced publicly without embarrassment, has been abolished. We read that the first human beings, immediately after the sin of disobedience, perceived desire in their sexual members and covered them from one another’s sight.

Although the blindness of the human mind in the performance of shameful acts cannot be hidden from the eyes of God, the angels, or the saints who are in heaven, nevertheless even any rustic, when having intercourse with his own wife, avoids the sight of many people as far as he can. How much more, then, will a presbyter, if he possesses human understanding, take care to conceal an evil deed, since he knows that, once it is exposed, he will lose not only his ecclesiastical rank but also whatever possessions he has from the resources of the Church. Therefore we shall not inquire immodestly into what even the Apostle, speaking not under a naked but under a veiled name among those lawfully married, took care to designate, saying: “And that no one defraud his brother in the matter” (1 Thess. 4:6).

Only concerning presbyters’ access to, association with, and cohabitation with women contrary to the canonical prohibition, if they have been accused on that account, is an inquiry to be made. For, as Saint Ambrose says (Epistle 11): “It is not the judge’s duty to condemn without an accuser, since the Lord did not cast Judas out, although he was a thief, because he had not been accused.”

## CHAPTER XII

What the procedure in accusation and judgment ought to be, Saint Augustine explains when expounding the Apostle’s statement, “If any brother is named a fornicator,” and so forth (On Penance, *The Remedy*, chapter 3):

“The Apostle,” he says, “did not wish a man to be judged by another according to the discretion of suspicion, or even according to an extraordinary judgment usurped outside the proper procedure, but rather according to the law of God—whether according to the order of the Church, or by voluntary confession, or by accusation and conviction. He intended that ‘being named’ to be understood as what is done against anyone when a sentence is pronounced in judicial order and with integrity. For if mere naming is sufficient, many innocent people must be condemned, because a crime is often falsely alleged against someone.” [Col. 1098B–C]

As for how a sentence is to be pronounced in judicial order and with integrity, the sacred canons, as stated above, and Saint Gregory—who frequently commands in his letters that the cases of ecclesiastical ministers be determined lawfully and regularly—demonstrate this in the memorandum given to John the Defender when he was going to Spain. He says (Book XI, Epistle 50):

“It must first be carefully investigated whether the trial was conducted in due order, or whether some were accusers and others witnesses. Next, the nature of the charges must be examined: whether they were serious enough to warrant exile or deposition; whether, in his presence, testimony was given against him under oath; whether the proceedings were committed to writing; and whether the accused himself had permission to answer and defend himself. The persons of the accusers and witnesses must also be examined closely: what sort of life they lead, what their status and reputation are; whether they are poor; whether perhaps they had some hostility toward the aforesaid bishop; and whether they gave testimony from hearsay or explicitly testified that they themselves knew the matter. It must also be determined whether the judgment was written down and whether the sentence was read in the presence of the parties.” [Col. 1098D]

The laws likewise define that no one may accuse another through an intermediary, nor may anyone be accused in this manner, except perhaps that a patron may accuse an ungrateful freedman; and that in a capital case no one who is absent may be condemned, unless, having been summoned to appear after an inquiry delegated according to the canons, he has neglected to do so, so that he may not gain a postponement of the sentence by his absence. [Col. 1099A]

## CHAPTER XIII

From whom accusation or testimony ought to be received, the African canons plainly show: namely, from those whom the public laws admit for accusation or testimony, as we have explained more fully and at greater length above, from the same council and from the laws, concerning secular persons.

Concerning the sacred orders, Saint Gelasius says in his decrees:

“Let no cleric believe that he will be immune from this offense if, when he sees either a bishop, presbyter, or deacon transgressing in those matters that we have set forth as salutary to follow, he does not immediately take care to bring the matter to our ears, provided that suitable proofs are duly presented, so that punishment may be inflicted upon the transgressor and the others may be forbidden to offend.” [Col. 1099A–B]

The canons of the African province and the Justinianic law also decree that clerics are not to be compelled to give testimony publicly concerning a matter belonging to the knowledge of their own judgment; they are not, however, forbidden to give testimony in an ecclesiastical court. We read the same concerning bishops in the Council of Chalcedon.

Accordingly, at the Roman synods celebrated by Eugenius and Leo IV it was decreed:

“Although the testimony of priests is considered credible, they are nevertheless not to be requested to give testimony in secular affairs or to draw up documents, because it is not fitting for them to be involved in such matters. If, however, by some occurrence they were present at a case and saw or heard something, where no suitable secular persons can be found for that purpose, then, lest the truth be concealed and an evil person be considered good, it shall be the responsibility of his own bishop to have them testify honorably, either before himself and competent judges or in some other manner.” [Col. 1099B–C]

The Justinianic law agrees with this judgment.

## CHAPTER XIV

The law establishes the number of witnesses, and this is confirmed in the Gospel: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand.” The Apostle commands Timothy—in whose person, as blessed Leo says, the whole number of Christ’s priests is instructed—not to receive an accusation against a presbyter except under two or three witnesses (1 Tim. 5:19).

The sacred Council of Nicaea (canon 11) likewise commands that a neophyte bishop who has been reproved by two or three witnesses abstain from the clergy.

But because in the story of Susanna we read that the two witnesses who appeared credible to the people, and likewise in the story of Naboth and in the account of the Lord’s Passion, gave false testimony, our predecessors wished the authority of the laws to be followed concerning the number of suitable witnesses, apart from the accusers in accusations against presbyters. Thus seven suitable witnesses are to be required; and, if reason or the case demands it, fourteen or twenty-one witnesses are to be sought, so that the truth may be brought to light.

These witnesses are to be examined after the example of Daniel, as the laws also command, since the prophet’s examination is already known to some. Witnesses have often been found to have been hired for money and to have conspired to speak lies; and often certain people, driven by envy or hatred, arise to accuse a presbyter and produce lying witnesses, because, as Saint Augustine says, new kinds of illnesses compel the search for new experiments in remedies. [Col. 1099D–1100A]

## CHAPTER XV

We have received from our predecessors the rule that, apart from the accusers, there should be seven suitable witnesses who confirm under oath that their testimony is true. Six of them shall swear, and the seventh, if the reason for the case or the status of the person permits it, shall come forward for judgment and declare that those six have spoken the truth under oath.

And thus, once the presbyter has been proved guilty, the Apostle’s sentence is to be followed: “If anyone does not obey our word by this letter or by our word, take note of that person and have no association with him” (2 Thess. 3:14), and what follows.

Pope Saint Leo also says in his decrees to all the bishops established throughout all the provinces (Epistle 1):

“Our admonition declares that if any of the brethren acts against these constitutions, or attempts to do so, and dares to admit what has been prohibited, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and that he will not be a participant in our communion, since he refused to be a partner in discipline,” and so forth. [Col. 1100A–B]

Blessed Augustine likewise wrote to his archbishop Xantippus concerning Abundantius, a presbyter of his parish, as follows (Epistle 236, to Xantippus):

“Since he had not walked in the ways of the servants of God, he had begun to acquire a bad reputation. Alarmed by this, though I did not rashly believe anything, I nevertheless became more concerned and took pains, if in any way I could, to obtain some certain indications of his bad conduct. First I discovered that he had appropriated money belonging to a certain peasant, money entrusted to him for God’s sake, so that he could give no plausible account of it. Then he was convicted and confessed that, although he had no cleric with him, he had both eaten lunch and dinner with a woman of bad reputation and had stayed in one and the same house with her. What she denied, I left to God; what he was not permitted to conceal, I judged.” [Col. 1100B–C]

Once the truth had thus been established, a presbyter convicted of prohibited cohabitation with women is legally and regularly deprived of his priestly office in these Gallic regions, as Pope Zosimus decreed, saying (Epistle 1, to Hesychius):

“Let anyone who, setting aside the authority of the Fathers and of the apostolic see, neglects this know that it will be punished by us with the greatest severity. He must not doubt that he will be unable to retain the status of his position if he thinks that, after so many prohibitions, this may be attempted with impunity. For whatever is repeatedly usurped despite prohibition is done out of a desire to insult.” [Col. 1100D]

## CHAPTER XVI

If, however, a bad reputation founded on probability of truth spreads through our parishes concerning a presbyter, and the accusers and legal witnesses are discovered not to be legitimate, or are convicted of falsehood, then, after they have been legally and regularly punished, an oath is to be administered, according to the decree of Gregory the Younger (Epistle 11, to Boniface), so that the hearts of the weak may not be troubled by the presbyter’s bad reputation, the ministry entrusted to us may not be dishonored, and presbyters, made more secure, may not fall more freely into sin. Thus the presbyter of bad reputation is to have, in the sacrament of his purgation, as a witness the person whom he will also have as judge. [Col. 1100D–1101A]

Since frequent experience has demonstrated that a presbyter persuaded by the devil into fornication or adultery is inclined to perjury, and since legal, evangelical, apostolic, and canonical authority accepts the testimony of three witnesses for condemnation (Matt. 18), it did not seem unreasonable to our fathers that such testimony should also be accepted for acquittal.

In sacred history and in the letter of blessed Gregory to the patrician Theoctista, we read (Book IX, Epistle 39) that blessed Peter, first of the apostles, when believers reproached him for entering among the Gentiles, appeased them with a humble explanation and also introduced witnesses in the case of his own reproach, saying: “These six brothers also came with me” (Acts 11:12).

The Carthaginian canons also decree (canon 10) that, if presbyters or deacons are accused, their own bishop, together with a legitimate number of colleagues from neighboring places—that is, six presbyters including himself in the case of a presbyter, and three in the case of a deacon—should be joined to them.

Our predecessors judged this authoritative, as we showed above in the chapter issued in the time of the lord Charles, Emperor Augustus, by the authority of the apostolic see and the bishops: if a presbyter has been defamed and suitable accusers or witnesses are lacking, then, according to the nature and seriousness of the case and the person, and for the benefit and healing of the hearts of the weak, he is to purge himself by an oath, either with two other witnesses or with six other witnesses. [Col. 1101A–B]

## CHAPTER XVII

Nor is it contrary to the decree of Gregory the Younger if several witnesses are required for the purgation of a defamed presbyter. For the same pontiff, writing to Boniface, bishop of Mainz, through the presbyter Denuald, says (Epistle IX, chapter 3):

“If the defamed presbyter cannot be proved guilty by suitable witnesses, an oath is to be administered; but he did not determine whether he should swear alone or with others. For if the most blessed Peter, first of the apostles, purged his reputation with six witnesses (Acts 11), as though he had acted contrary to the Lord’s command, ‘Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans’ (Matt. 10), since the command of Christ ordering, ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them’ (Matt. 28), had not yet been made known by God to many, it does not appear contrary to authority if a presbyter endeavors to purge his reputation with as many fellow witnesses as these. For by the sacred canons the bishops who are judges are commanded to judge this, the Apostle ordering that we be without offense to all and that our brother, for whom Christ died, not perish through our conscience (1 Cor. 10). And again: ‘By thus sinning against the brethren and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ’ (1 Cor. 8).” [Col. 1101C–D]

Therefore, filled with the Holy Spirit, our holy fathers established that ministers of the altar should neither cohabit with women nor bring women into their company, lest they either burn their consciences with desire or pollute them by an evil consent, and lest they stain the consciences of the weak even by creating a bad suspicion.

For, as Augustine teaches, the conduct of the saints to whom the Lord says, “Be holy” (Lev. 11), ought to be not only holy but also cautious, lest, although it is not evil through wantonness, it become evil through negligence. [Col. 1101D–1102A]

## CHAPTER XVIII

Concerning the canonical prohibition against a presbyter, the witnesses are to be questioned, and the presbyter, once convicted or having confessed, is to be judged.

Since we have learned by experience that certain presbyters have conspired with one another so that they might mutually assist each other in their purgation—though in fact they do harm—it seemed not inappropriate to our predecessors and forebears that the presbyters who, in the purgation of the defamed priest, had offered themselves with him for the oath should, before a trustworthy envoy of the bishop, undergo such an examination through the representative of the defamed presbyter that they might not destroy themselves before God by their oath. We have already found some of them convicted and degraded for perjury.

Or, as the canons decree: “A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed, but is not thereby to be deprived of communion.” For Scripture says: “The Lord will not avenge the same thing twice” (Nahum 1:9).

Concerning witnesses, whether for proving or for purging a presbyter, our predecessors judged that these principles, according to the course of Scripture and the teaching of the elders, were to be upheld, and they left them to us, their descendants, to follow, in accordance with the words of blessed Gelasius (Epistle 11, to the bishops of Dardania):

“Whatever our fathers—that is, the Catholic and learned pontiffs—once established, after assembling together, concerning the faith, the truth, and Catholic and apostolic communion, according to the course of Scripture and the teaching of the elders, they wished thereafter to remain unshaken and firm. Nor did they permit what had been laid down in this same matter to be reconsidered by any recent presumption, wisely providing that, if salutary decrees could be revisited by anyone, no stable ecclesiastical constitution would remain at all against the various errors of individuals, and every complete definition would be disturbed by the recurrence of the same madness.” [Col. 1102B–C]

## CHAPTER XIX

Some say that parishioners and subjects of a presbyter or bishop cannot regularly accuse him, as it is written: “The shadows of others protect their own shadow” (Job 40), lest what they attempt to defend in others reach them.

This defense is refuted by authority and by reason. Its authority is expressed in the words of the holy man:

“If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep together; if I have eaten its produce without payment and afflicted the souls of its cultivators, let thistles grow for me instead of wheat, and thorns instead of barley” (Job 31).

“Saint Gregory says,” [Col. 1102D–1103A] “the land cries out against its possessor if, against the one who governs it, either a private household or the holy Church murmurs concerning some injustice. For the land cries out when subjects reasonably grieve over the injustice of their ruler” (Book XXII of the *Moralia*, chapter 33).

Therefore, whenever one who rules exercises perversity among his subjects, the land cries out against him and the furrows weep. For against his injustice the uneducated populace breaks out in voices of complaint, while all the more perfect persons afflict themselves with tears because of his evil conduct. For the land to cry out while the furrows weep means that, through the matter by which the multitude of the faithful justly complains against its ruler, people of more abundant life are moved to lamentation, and so forth—what the reader can find more fully in its proper place.

Long before this, Saint Boniface sent letters to the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces (Epistle 11, to the Gallic bishops, and elsewhere) concerning Maximus, who had been accused by his fellow provincials and subjects. Saint Gregory likewise wrote to Sabinus and several bishops concerning Boniface of the Church of Regia, who had similarly been accused by his own clerics and subjects, so that the case might be diligently investigated. He also ordered a regular inquiry into the accusation of Bishop Lucillus, as the reader will find in his *Register* (Book VII, indiction 2, Epistles 46 and 62).

If such proceedings were admitted concerning bishops, they must not be set aside concerning presbyters, who are men of the second order. [Col. 1103A–B]

## CHAPTER XX

Since we find certain matters to be determined by contrast not only in the doctrines of secular learned writings but also in the Holy Scriptures—just as darkness is judged more obscure by comparison with light—the ecclesiastical case must be assessed by comparing it with divine pronouncements.

The Lord says to the disciples: “You will bear witness to me, because you have been with me from the beginning” (John 15), since without any ambiguity they were able to proclaim what they had seen and heard with him.

Therefore, when Peter wished to appoint another apostle in place of Judas, he rightly wanted to choose one who had been with them from the time when the Lord Jesus entered and departed among them, and no other (Acts 1).

Conversely, accusers and witnesses concerning the life and conduct of a presbyter ought to be heard who have known his life and conduct throughout the entire period from the time when the presbyter entered and departed among them after being ordained their superior.

These testimonies, so weighty and so numerous, should suffice to refute the empty opinion of those who say that a prelate cannot regularly be accused by his own sheep or subjects.

## CHAPTER XXI

Since some, as though possessing authority, put forward certain things said to have been decreed by Pope Saint Sylvester—things that the Catholic Church does not count among its synodal decrees, but which our predecessors left to us, their descendants, to be observed—we have thought it necessary to set them out here.

For it is written in a certain sermon, extracted from the deeds of Saint Sylvester without the name of the compiler—one that Bishop Isidore of Seville compiled together with the letters of the pontiffs of the Roman see from Saint Clement to blessed Gregory—that Saint Sylvester decreed:

“No layman shall dare to bring a charge against a cleric; and a presbyter shall not bring an accusation against a bishop, nor a deacon against a presbyter, nor a subdeacon against a deacon, nor an acolyte against a subdeacon, nor an exorcist against an acolyte, nor a lector against an exorcist, nor a doorkeeper against a lector. Let no accusation whatsoever be brought by any of them. Let no prelate be condemned except by seventy-two [witnesses]. Nor shall the supreme prelate be judged by anyone, as it is written: ‘The disciple is not above his master’ (Matt. 10).

“A cardinal presbyter shall not be condemned except by forty-four witnesses. A cardinal deacon appointed in the city of Rome shall not be condemned except by twenty-six. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, lector, or doorkeeper shall not be condemned except, as it is written, by seven witnesses.

“The witnesses and accusers, moreover, must be without any infamy, have wives and children, and altogether preach Christ. No one shall receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman.” [Col. 1103D–1104A]

## CHAPTER XXII

No one can doubt how contradictory these statements are to one another and how different they are from the holy canons and sacred laws, provided that he considers these statements rationally and reads the sacred regulations and laws more carefully.

First it is written that no layman may dare to bring a charge against a cleric. Then it says that no cleric may bring accusatory testimony against a cleric. Immediately afterward, however, it proceeds to state by how many witnesses a presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, lector, or doorkeeper may be condemned, and requires that the witnesses and accusers be without infamy, have wives and children, and preach Christ.

How absurd it is to require that those who have wives and children should rather be admitted as witnesses than those who are continent and religious is shown by plain reasoning. And contrary to the subsequent statement—that those who have wives and children and preach Christ should become witnesses—Pope Saint Leo decreed in his letter to Maximus, bishop of Antioch (Epistle 66):

“It is fitting that Your Affection take care to prevent anyone except the priests of the Lord from daring to claim for himself the right to teach and preach, whether he is a monk or a layman who boasts in the name of some learning. For although it is desirable that all the children of the Church should understand what is right and sound, it must not nevertheless be permitted that anyone established outside the priestly order assume for himself the rank of preacher, since everything in the Church of God ought to be ordered so that, in the one body of Christ, the superior members fulfill their own office and the inferior members do not rebel against the superior.” [Col. 1104B–C]

The same text also says that no one should receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman. But, as we showed above, the sacred regulations, the decision of the apostolic see, and the laws of the Christian rulers of the Roman Empire nullify this. [Col. 1104C–D]

## CHAPTER XXIII

It must also be understood that some people take the constitution mentioned above, under the name of Pope Saint Sylvester, as authority for the proposition that no cleric may be judged. They do this because blessed Gelasius placed the *Acts of Blessed Sylvester* among the works to be received, without noticing what Saint Gelasius wrote in that same catalogue.

Among other things, he says:

“We know that the Acts of blessed Sylvester, the prelate of the apostolic see, although the name of the person who wrote them is unknown, are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome, and that many Churches imitate them because of their ancient usage. Likewise, the writing concerning the discovery of the Lord’s cross and another writing concerning the discovery of the head of John the Baptist are recent accounts, and some Catholics read them. But when these writings have come into the hands of Catholics, the statement of the blessed Apostle Paul must take precedence: ‘Test everything; hold fast what is good’ (1 Thess. 5).”

Blessed Gelasius permitted these Acts to be read, but he did not command that they be held as authoritative in the manner of the Holy Scriptures and the writings of the saints.

In those Acts of Sylvester we read nothing concerning constitutions of this kind. In the book entitled *The Deeds of the Pontiffs*, however, we read that Saint Sylvester established that no layman should dare to bring a charge against a cleric. But the remaining provisions that follow, as we have set them out above, we do not read in his register as having been established by him.

Therefore we must not believe that this same holy man established the provisions written in the aforementioned sermon. Even if, perhaps, he issued such directives because of the heretics and pagans who were then persecuting Catholics, the judgment of later authorities must be followed. Saint Augustine—rightly counted by the apostolic see among the Church’s finest teachers—demonstrates this in the second book *On Baptism* (chapter 3):

“Who,” he says, “does not know that the canonical Holy Scripture, both of the Old and of the New Testament, is contained within its own fixed boundaries, and that it is placed above all later writings of bishops in such a way that there can be no doubt or dispute concerning it as to whether whatever is established as written in it is true or right?

“But the writings of bishops that were written or are being written after the canon was confirmed may be criticized if anything in them has perhaps deviated from the truth—by the more learned speech of someone more skilled in that matter, by the weightier authority and more learned judgment of other bishops, and by councils.
