The councils themselves that are held in the several regions or provinces must yield without hesitation to the authority of plenary councils held from throughout the Christian world; and these plenary councils themselves may often be corrected by later ones when some experience of events reveals what had been closed and makes known what had been hidden—all without the arrogance of sacrilegious pride, without an inflated neck of self-importance, and without the contentiousness of envious hostility, but with holy humility, Catholic peace, and Christian charity.” [Col. 1105B–D]

## CHAPTER XXIV

Otherwise, if no layman may bring an accusation against a cleric and no cleric against a layman, according to what is said in the aforementioned sermon in the words of Saint Sylvester, how will anyone be judged either by the holy Church or by judges of the public laws? No one ought to be judged either in an ecclesiastical or civil court regularly and legally except by a sentence issued in judicial order and with integrity.

For if a presbyter cannot be proved guilty except by as many suitable witnesses as are written there, he will never be proved guilty. There are presbyters among us who do not have as many parishioners—holding mansi (rural holdings), and having wives and children—as that sermon requires suitable witnesses to prove a presbyter.

The sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see would therefore have promulgated explicit judgments concerning each rank for manifest offenses in vain, and the laws would have enacted decrees uselessly for restraining or punishing the wicked, if these measures were not to be carried out.

This is especially so since Saint Leo says concerning the sacred canons (Epistle 88, to Anastasius):

“Therefore, according to the canons of the holy Fathers, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces retain inviolate the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them, so that they depart from the prescribed regulations through neither negligence nor presumption.” [Col. 1105D–1106A]

In the statement that they must not depart from the prescribed regulations through negligence, our teachers taught us to understand that bishops must not be sluggish in carrying out the statutes. In the statement that they must not depart from the prescribed regulations through presumption, they taught that bishops must not exceed them by going beyond the statutes.

Hence blessed Leo, in other words, expressed the scriptural sentence: “Do not turn to the right or to the left” (Prov. 4). [Col. 1106B]

## CHAPTER XXV

Concerning the laws, Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius decreed as follows (Book II of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Constitutions*):

“We do not permit anyone either to be ignorant of the constitutions considered by our Serenity after long deliberation or to disregard them.

“Interpretation: No one may be ignorant of the laws or despise what has been enacted.” [Col. 1106B–C]

Saint Celestine says something similar concerning the sacred canons (Epistle 3):

“No priest,” he says, “may be permitted to be ignorant of his canons or to do anything that could conflict with the regulations of the Fathers. For what matter worthy of protection will remain for us if the rule of decretal constitutions is broken at the discretion of some people and permission is granted to the populace?” [Col. 1106C]

The ecclesiastical regulations and sacred laws have therefore not been promulgated uselessly or in vain; they are to be carried out according to a regular and legal procedure.

For, as Saint Augustine and the other Catholic teachers demonstrate from the authority of the Gospel, concerning manifest offenses committed against those entrusted to us, we possess not only the power but also the command to judge so that the offenders may be corrected. Such offenses include sexual violations, blasphemies, thefts, adulteries, homicides, drunkenness, robbery, and similar acts, concerning which the Lord says: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7), and the Apostle: “The works of the flesh are manifest” (Gal. 5).

But concerning the hidden matters of a brother’s conscience—and especially concerning doubtful matters and the intention or necessity with which they are undertaken—when we cannot see into them, we must avoid the rashness of judgment.

We are also commanded to reserve ambiguous actions, which can be interpreted in either direction, rather for divine examination. The same applies to kinds of food that may be consumed indifferently with a good disposition and a simple heart, without the fault of desire, and which should be approached as one approaches medicines.

Therefore, following the teaching of the apostles and of our Savior, they judged those who sinned in manifest matters: Peter judged Simon, Ananias, and Sapphira, and Paul judged Elymas and the fornicator among the Corinthians (Acts 5; 1 Cor. 5). [Col. 1106D–1107A]

## CHAPTER XXVI

Following in their footsteps, the successors of the apostles both promulgated judgments concerning manifest sins and rebuked and judged sinners before everyone.

How, and according to what procedure, the sons born to the Church in place of the apostolic fathers—namely, the bishops—ought to issue judgments against sinners, the holy pontiffs Leo and Gregory plainly demonstrate when expounding the Lord’s statement to the apostles, and through them to their successors (Matt. 13):

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”

“Christ says to the most blessed Peter,” Leo says (*Sermon 3 on the Anniversary of the Assumption), “‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.’

“The force of this power indeed passed also to the other apostles, and the establishment of this decree was transmitted to all the rulers of the Church; yet it is not without reason that what is intimated to all is entrusted to one alone. For this is entrusted particularly to Peter because Peter’s form is set before all the rulers of the Church. Peter’s privilege therefore remains wherever judgment is issued according to his equity. There is neither excessive severity nor excessive leniency where nothing is bound and nothing loosed except what blessed Peter has bound or loosed.” [Col. 1107A–B]

Saint Gregory likewise says (*Homily 26 on the Gospels):

“It often happens that one who does not know how to control his own life becomes the judge of another’s life, so that he either condemns those who do not deserve it or, himself bound, releases others, following the movement of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. Thus the one who exercises this power of binding and loosing according to his own wishes and not according to the conduct of his subjects deprives himself of that power.

“Those who follow either their own hatred or their favor in the cases of their subjects cannot rightly judge their subjects. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: ‘They put to death souls that should not die, and they gave life to souls that should not live’ (Ezek. 13). He puts to death one who should not die when he condemns the just; and he attempts to give life to one who should not live when he seeks to absolve the guilty from punishment.

“The cases must therefore be weighed, and then the power of binding and loosing must be exercised.” [Col. 1107B–C]

## CHAPTER XXVII

At the Roman synods of the apostolic Eugenius and Leo IV, it was established where a priest ought to be placed after condemnation: if a priest, or anyone else advanced into an ecclesiastical order, is found guilty of a crime for which he ought to be rejected, he is to be deposed and, through the bishop’s care, placed in a suitable location where he may mourn his sins and commit them no further. [Col. 1107D]

Long before this, the great Pope Leo, by the authority of sacred Scripture, decreed to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne (Epistle 92, to Rusticus):

“Presbyters or deacons who have fallen are to seek private withdrawal in order to obtain God’s mercy, where, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful.” [Col. 1107D–1108A]

These are the things we have received from our predecessors concerning the deposition of a defamed presbyter, or the purgation appropriate to the case, to be carried out in these Cisalpine regions according to reason, authority, and custom.

### CHAPTER XXVIII

But if a priest or deacon, accused on specific charges and lawfully and canonically summoned to judgment, evades the regular trial, the sacred laws—whose authority is confirmed by the Evangelical tradition through the threefold agreement of the First Council of Ephesus, the great Council of Chalcedon, and Saint Celestine in his letter to Nestorius, as well as by Saint Gregory in his letters (Epistle 54)—decree that, if anyone summoned three times by letters or edicts refuses to come to his judge, before whom he has been regularly summoned on specific charges, he shall receive the sentence imposed upon the contumacious.

Hence Pope Saint Boniface also decreed to the Gallic bishops (Epistle 1 to the Gallic Bishops):

> Let anyone who has been summoned appear in person, if he wishes, and, if he has confidence, answer the charges brought against him. If he neglects to appear, he shall not gain a postponement of the sentence through his absence. For it is manifest that a person confesses the crime when, despite the trial granted and so often assigned to him, he does not use the opportunity to clear himself. Indeed, it makes no difference whether, in the present inquiry, everything said concerning him is proved, since his very absence, procured so many times, is itself established as a confession.

For, as Saint Gelasius says, a person is summoned to judgment for a specific matter so that he may either confess the charges or be convicted by them. And against the sentence issued against the contumacious there can be neither appeal nor restoration through a second hearing, as the laws define and Saint Gregory promulgated in his letters on the basis of those same laws.  
[Col. 1108B–C]

### CHAPTER XXIX

Furthermore, if priests or deacons are summoned to judgment in a pecuniary case—which in another terminology is called a civil case in the sacred regulations—for the seizure of someone’s property, or for any serious injuries, although in criminal cases no one may answer through another person, the sacred laws nevertheless grant bishops and priests permission in such cases to answer through a procurator—that is, through an advocate appointed to act on their behalf—provided, without doubt, that the judgment pronounced returns to them. In other criminal cases, however, where a person must be convicted of a crime, they should arrange to appear personally in court. If, after being summoned a third time by the executor, they refuse to come to judgment, they shall receive, as stated above, the sentence imposed upon the contumacious.  
[Col. 1108D]

### CHAPTER XXX

As for the seizure of property, whenever any member of the clergy, abandoning or disregarding the laws, seizes another person’s possessions, he is ordered, according to the decree of blessed Pope Gregory issued before the body of Saint Peter, to be bound by the bond of anathema. He plainly demonstrates this in that decree and also in other letters of his—not merely once or twice, but even a third time: no member of the clergy, if he thinks that any possessions ought to belong to his church, is to seize them unlawfully; rather, he must acquire them lawfully.

In the Roman synods of the apostolic Eugenius and Leo IV, a decree was issued concerning seizure supposedly carried out on behalf of the Church: if someone proved to be an invader claims that he acted on behalf of the Church, the invasion is to be made good from private property belonging to him and his heir. Finally, if a priest is found to be poor in such an offense, he is to be canonically judged by his own bishop, so that the church entrusted to him does not suffer loss. We decree that it must remain unharmed by the recklessness of this persuasion.

It was also decreed in that synod that bishops and all priests should have advocates, since bishops and all priests are appointed solely for the praise of God and the performance of good works. Therefore each of them ought to have an advocate, both for ecclesiastical actions and for his own affairs, except, that is, in a public criminal case—an advocate who is not under bad suspicion but is known for good reputation and commendable skill—lest, while they pursue human profits, they lose eternal rewards.  
[Col. 1109A]

The same synod also states concerning those who cannot find advocates:

> If any priest is found unable to bring an advocate before the court, his bishop ought to examine that priest before his own people: whether he is of good or bad conduct, or for what reason he is unable to have an advocate when one is required. If he is found blameworthy, care must be taken to correct him according to the nature of his fault and the rule of the canons.  
> [Col. 1109B]

### CHAPTER XXXI

But if any priest or other cleric, concerning a charge brought against him or a civil case initiated against him, wishes, after abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, to clear himself in the public courts, the Carthaginian canons decree in chapter nine—and Leo and the Roman synod, following those same canons, decreed uniformly—that, in a criminal case, even if a judgment has been rendered in his favor, he shall lose his position; in a civil case, he shall lose what he has won if he prefers to retain his position.  
[Col. 1109C]

### CHAPTER XXXII

Concerning possessions that priests had either before ordination or acquired in any manner after ordination, the Carthaginian canons establish in chapter thirty-two that bishops, priests, deacons, and any clerics who are ordained with nothing, and who during their episcopate or clerical office purchase fields or any estates in their own name, are to be held guilty of seizing the Lord’s property, unless, after being admonished, they transfer those very possessions to the church.

If something comes to them as their own through another person’s generosity or through inheritance from their family, they should dispose of it in whatever way is consistent with their profession. But if they depart from their profession and turn aside from it, they are to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, as reprobates. The same was also established by the law of Justinian, Constitution 427, chapter 453 and chapter 522. Saint Gregory likewise promulgated and established this in his letters, on the basis of the same sacred canons and laws.  
[Col. 1109D]

### CHAPTER XXXIII

But because, through the negligence or improper favoritism of episcopal officials, who attend insufficiently to what is necessary, and through the growing greed and wantonness of priests, a vice commonly increases throughout the parishes which must be cut away with greater diligence, namely this: certain priests purchase property after their ordination from church revenues, or from the offerings and vows of the faithful; they build structures on those properties; they place there what belongs to the church; and in those estates they receive women who may practice their weaving and manage the household.

On this account they neglect their churches, return to those same estates, and live there in violation of the decrees of the canons, committing fraud concerning ecclesiastical resources. For this is sacrilegious, and is the equal of the crime of Ananias and Sapphira, and of the thief Judas, who carried away and stole the sacred offerings sent for the use of the faithful and the poor.

They also customarily transfer those same estates—not leaving them to the churches, as the sacred canons require—but, contrary to the canons, to their relatives or to any others. Yet a bishop or priest can possess no property more suitably or securely than property assigned to the church, if he wishes to live according to his order.

But if he loses his order through his own fault, he will not be able to retain even the allodial estate (*alod*) which he acquired from ecclesiastical resources from the day of his ordination; according to the decrees of Saint Leo, he must seek secluded withdrawal in order to perform penance.  
[Col. 1110A–B]

### CHAPTER XXXIV

Therefore it is necessary that, every year, the bishops’ officials inquire what is found in each church concerning the portion of the tithe which, according to the sacred canons, belongs to the church.

They should also attend to the matricularii in each church, according to the resources and capacity of the place, so that priests do not accept gifts from the matricularii in return for their positions; so that they do not place their own healthy and robust relatives in the same matricula; and so that they do not demand labor from the matricularii themselves. They are not to make herdsmen or swineherds out of the matricularii, but are to appoint poor and weak persons, and to make matricularii of people from the same village from which they receive the tithe.

If the priest himself has a weak brother or some other relative, or someone extremely poor, who ought to be supported from that same tithe, the apostolic statement must be followed, which says: “Anyone who does not care for his own, and especially for the members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5).

If he wishes to keep other relatives near him, he should clothe and feed them from his own portion, without expense to the church. For it is one thing to assist poor friends or relatives, or any incestuous persons, out of charity, with moderation and reason, or to offer them support without expense to the church; it is another thing to squander improperly, with the destruction of the church or the dissipation of ecclesiastical resources, what belongs to the church.

It must also be ensured that priests promoted from a condition of having nothing do not presume to sell what they have purchased from the church’s resources, or to hand it over as though to the house of God, except to the church, to which such property ought properly to belong.  
[Col. 1110C–D]

[Col. 1111]

## XVI. THE CASE OF THE PRIEST TEUTFRID: HOW IT IS TO BE CONDUCTED OR DECIDED

*(In the same author, from the Mainz edition of John Busaeus.)*

[Col. 1111A]

### CHAPTER I

Pope Saint Gregory repeatedly decrees in his Register of Decrees that ecclesiastical affairs and the cases of ecclesiastical persons must be decided lawfully and according to canonical procedure.

Where, and by whom, the case concerning the priest Teutfrid is to be conducted or decided:

*(Theodosian Code, Book 10, On Accusations):*

> The laws decree that the right of accusation must not extend beyond the boundaries of the province. For criminal trials ought to be conducted there where the crime is said to have been committed. We restrain proceedings in foreign courts by the present laws.

And the Carthaginian canons, in chapter thirty, state:

> It has been determined, they say, that an accused person or an accuser should choose, in the place from which the accused comes, a nearby location—if he fears some violence from a rash crowd—where it will not be difficult to produce witnesses and where the case may be concluded.

[Col. 1111B]

And the synod of the province of Africa, in its letter to Pope Celestine, says:

> The Fathers acted with the greatest prudence and justice in providing that every case should be concluded in the places where it arose.

### CHAPTER II

A priest who has confessed or been convicted must be judged by his own bishop; if he is contentious, he must be judged by the bishops of his province, as the canons of Nicaea, Antioch, Sardica, Chalcedon, and the African Carthaginians decree.

Hence the Antiochene canons say in chapter sixteen:

> That is a complete council at which the metropolitan bishop is present.

And in chapter twenty, concerning episcopal councils:

> Priests and deacons, and all who consider themselves injured, should be present at those councils, and should submit themselves to the examination of the synod.

And in chapter nine:

> A bishop must attempt nothing apart from the metropolitan bishop, except what pertains to his own parish; nor may the metropolitan act without the counsel of the other priests.

[Col. 1111C]

### CHAPTER III

Since Teutfrid is said to have confessed or been convicted of secretly or sacrilegiously disposing of ecclesiastical property—namely, three chasubles, Queen Imma’s tunic, a golden belt with jewels, an ivory purse, one pound of gold, and various other objects—the laws say:

> Debtors who have confessed are regarded as condemned; therefore, from the day of confession, the appointed periods for payment are to be calculated.

And the Apostolic Canons say in chapter twenty-five:

> A bishop, priest, or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed, but is not thereby to be deprived of communion. For Scripture says: “The Lord will not punish twice for the same thing” (Nahum 1).

For if he swore fidelity to the house of God, he has been caught in perjury. But because he disposed of resources consecrated to God, he committed sacrilege, as Pope Saint Anacletus—ordained priest by the blessed apostle Peter himself and later made his successor as bishop in the Roman See—judged together with many priests:

> Whoever steals, takes away, or defrauds Christ’s money and the Church’s property is a murderer, and will be reckoned a murderer before the sight of the just Judge. Whoever steals his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but whoever takes away money or property belonging to the Church commits sacrilege and must be judged as a sacrilegious person.

And Pope Saint Urbanus and martyr says:

> Ecclesiastical possessions and resources are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord; they are the vows of the faithful and the prices of sins. If anyone steals them, he is guilty of the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira; and such a person must be handed over to Satan, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

And Pope Saint Lucius says:

> By apostolic authority we expel from the thresholds of the holy Church, anathematize, and condemn as sacrilegious those who steal ecclesiastical property and resources. The same penalty encompasses both those who act and those who consent.

And Pope Saint Gregory says:

> It is sacrilegious and contrary to the laws if anyone attempts, through the efforts of a perverse will, to retain for his own advantage what has been left to venerable places.

And Saint Augustine, rightly counted among the Church’s foremost teachers by the apostolic see through the blessed Celestine, says in his sermon on the Gospel of blessed John:

> Behold, Judas is among the saints; behold, Judas is a thief. And do not dismiss this: he is a sacrilegious thief—not an ordinary thief, but a thief of the Lord’s money-boxes, money-boxes that were sacred. If crimes are distinguished in the forum, he is not an ordinary thief but a peculator. Peculation means theft from the republic. Theft of private property is not judged in the same way as theft of public property. How much more severely, then, must the sacrilegious thief be judged, who dared to take not from just anywhere, but from the Church? Whoever steals or snatches anything from the Church is compared with the lost Judas.

And for this reason the sacred canons say (Council of Agde, canon 4):

> Clerics, or even laypeople, who presume to retain offerings of their parents, whether donated or left by testament, or who believe that what they themselves have donated to churches or monasteries may be taken away, are to be excluded from the churches, as the holy Synod has established, as murderers of the poor, until they make restitution. Those who are excluded from the churches are not to be permitted to remain in the ecclesiastical order.

[Col. 1112C–1113A]

### CHAPTER IV

If Teutfrid is found to have confessed or been convicted of seeking the palace, after abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, for his defense or purification, the eleventh chapter of the Council of Antioch must be applied to him:

> If any bishop, priest, or anyone subject to an ecclesiastical rule approaches the emperor or king without the counsel or letters of the bishops of the province, and especially of the metropolitan, he ought to be rejected and deposed—not only from communion but also from the honor in which he appears to share—because he has attempted to trouble the ears of the venerable ruler concerning the laws of the Church. If a necessary cause therefore demands approaching the ruler, this must be done with the deliberation and counsel of the metropolitan and of the other bishops who reside in the same province; they too should support the person departing with their letters.

[Col. 1113A–B]

And the Carthaginian canons say in chapter nine (Council of Carthage III, canon 9):

> Whoever among the bishops, priests, deacons, or clerics, when a crime has been brought against him in the church or a civil case has been initiated, wishes, after abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, to clear himself in the public courts—even if a judgment has been issued in his favor—shall lose his position; and this applies in criminal cases. In a civil case, he shall lose what he has won if he wishes to retain his position.

And Pope Saint Leo (Epistle 96) and the Roman synod say:

> We decree that whoever, bypassing the priest of his own church, comes to a dispute before secular authorities shall be expelled from the sacred thresholds and excluded from the heavenly altar.

[Col. 1113B–C]

### CHAPTER V

If Teutfrid is convicted or confesses that he openly or craftily led his neighbors into perjury, it must be understood that he is guilty of as many perjuries as there are people whom he maliciously led into perjury. His own sin in this matter is greater than that of those who swore at his request, just as the Lord makes clear when speaking to Pilate: “The one who handed me over to you has the greater sin” (John 19).

And Saint Gregory says concerning such matters in the Pastoral Rule (Part III, chapter 5):

> Superiors must understand that, if they ever commit perverse deeds, they are worthy of as many deaths as the examples of destruction they transmit to their subjects. Therefore they must guard themselves from fault with correspondingly greater care, since through the evil things they do they do not die alone but are guilty of the souls of others, whom they have destroyed by their evil examples.

And insofar as a priest is higher in any rank than a Christian layperson, his fault is correspondingly more serious. Whoever is implicated in their perjury is caught in their perjury, and therefore, according to chapter twenty-five of the Apostolic Canons, must be judged for perjury.

Hence Saint Jerome, explaining the prophet Ezekiel’s statement concerning King Zedekiah’s violation of an oath, says:

> For the one who trusted you because of the name of God and was deceived proved far more faithful than you, who under the pretext of divine majesty plotted treachery against your enemy—indeed, against one who had already become your friend.

Therefore Scripture says:

> “The oath that he despised and the covenant that he violated, I will place upon his head” (Ezekiel 17).

For we read that Zedekiah was captured and brought to Riblah, where, after his sons had been killed, he was blinded and, like a wild beast shut in a cage, was carried away to Babylon (2 Kings 25).

The king of Babylon, as blessed Gregory explains (Moralia, Book VII, chapter 13), is the ancient enemy, the possessor of deepest confusion. He first slays the sons before the eyes of the one who sees, because he often destroys good works in such a way that the captive himself painfully sees that he has lost them. For the mind often produces good things, yet, overcome by the pleasures of its flesh, it loses with love the good things it produced, considers the losses it suffers, and nevertheless does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon.

But while he is struck by the sight of his perpetrated wickedness, he is sometimes brought by continued practice of sin to the point that he too is deprived of the light of reason. Therefore the king of Babylon first extinguished Zedekiah’s sons and afterward tore out Zedekiah’s eyes, because the evil spirit, having first removed good works, later also takes away the light of understanding.

Zedekiah rightly suffers this at Riblah. For Riblah is interpreted as “many things.” At times the light of reason is also closed to the person who, through the multitude of his iniquity, is weighed down by evil practice.

He suffers all this by God’s just judgment because he violated an oath in the Lord’s name. For, as blessed Jerome says, whoever despises an oath despises the one by whom he swore and injures the one whose name the adversary trusted—that is, the person to whom the oath was sworn in the name of the one who says: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, nor profane it” (Exodus 20). And: “You shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord” (Matthew 5). And the Psalm says that the person who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive him will dwell in the holy place (Psalm 14).

[Col. 1113C–1114C]

### CHAPTER VI

But if he wishes to claim that necessity forced him to order the oath to be taken, although he could and ought to have kept it, and therefore that he should not be held guilty of perjury, let him hear what Saint Gregory says concerning one who swears or anathematizes:

> Whoever ought to swear or anathematize, and assures you that he will not be held guilty if he violates what he swore or anathematized because he did it unwillingly—if there are people who say that, when someone anathematizes under compulsion of necessity, he is not bound by the bond of anathema—they themselves bear witness against themselves by saying this. For they are not Christians, since they think that they can dissolve the bonds of the holy Church through empty efforts; and consequently they do not even regard the absolution of the holy Church, which it grants to the faithful, as genuine, if they do not think that its bindings have force.

> There is no need to argue at length against them, since in every respect they must be despised and anathematized. By the very means through which they think they deceive the truth, they are truly bound in their sins. Both I and all Catholic bishops, together with the universal Church, anathematize them, because they think and speak contrary to the truth.

[Col. 1114C–D]

### CHAPTER VII

But if he says what many are accustomed to say—that he ordered others to swear by means of a trick—he must not think that, through verbal artifice, he can deceive the Lord, to whom nothing is hidden. The Lord does not consider merely how a person swears, but how the person to whom the oath was sworn understood it and trusted the neighbor’s oath.

Whoever swears deceitfully is, as the Catholic teachers say, first guilty before God, whose name he takes in vain contrary to the commandment of the law; then he is guilty before his neighbor, whom he thinks to deceive through dark fraud. The Psalmist says that the innocent of hands and pure of heart—the one who does not swear deceitfully to his neighbor—will receive blessing from the Lord (Psalm 23).

He is also guilty before himself, since “he who accepts his soul in vain” is condemned by the Psalmist (the same passage).

[Col. 1115A–1116A]

[Col. 1115]

## XVII. THE VISION OF THE PRIEST BERNOLD

*(In the same author, from the manuscript of the monastery of Herivallis.)*

[Col. 1115B]

HINCMAR, bishop and servant of the people of God, to the beloved brethren and religious men to whose notice the matters that follow shall come.

(Flodoard, Book III, chapters 3 and 18.)

Recently, in our parish, a certain man known to me, named Bernold, fell ill. After confession, reconciliation, anointing with holy oil, and communion of the body and blood of Christ, his illness grew worse and nearly brought him to death. For four days he could neither take food or drink nor speak, except rarely to make a sign that water should be given to him. On the fourth day, at the ninth hour, he lay as if lifeless, so that no breath could be detected in him except intermittently; whoever put his hand to his mouth or upon his chest could scarcely sense that he still had breath [Col. 1115C]. Yet his face was deeply flushed, and he remained lying thus until midnight.

Around midnight, opening his eyes, he said with manly vigor to his wife and those standing around that they should run as quickly as possible and ask his confessor to come to him without delay, because if he did not come soon, Bernold would not be able to live. When the priest had been summoned, but before he reached the room where the sick man lay, as the priest entered the outer house, the man who was lying there said: “Put a chair here, because the priest will now enter this house.”

As soon as that priest entered the room where Bernold lay, he began to say prayers for him: “The Lord be with you.” Bernold replied in a clear voice: “And with your spirit.” After the prayers had been said, he told the priest to sit beside him and said:

“Listen attentively to what I am going to tell you, so that, if I remain in the body and cannot announce what I have been commanded, you may announce it. ”

He began to weep very bitterly and, amid sobs, said:

“Having been led from this world into another world, I came to a certain place and found forty-one bishops there. Among them I recognized Ebo, Leopardellus, and Aeneas, clothed in rags and blackened as if they had been burned, filthy like the others. At times they trembled horribly from extreme cold, with weeping and the gnashing of teeth; at other times they were tormented by intense heat.

“Bishop Ebo called me by name and said: ‘Because you will be granted permission to return to your body, I and these fellow bishops of ours beg you to help us.’

“I replied: ‘How can I help you?’

“He answered: ‘Go to our clerical and lay dependants, to whom we have done good, and tell them to give alms and offer prayers for us, and to obtain that sacred offerings be presented for us.’

“I replied that I did not know where their people were.

“He answered: ‘We shall give you a guide who will lead you to them.’

“They gave me a man who went ahead of me and led me to a very large palace, where there was a multitude of the people of those bishops. They were speaking about those bishops, and I conveyed to them on the bishops’ behalf what I had been commanded to say.

“From there, returning with my guide, I came back to the place where the bishops were. It was as though what they had asked for had already been done for them: they had cheerful faces, as if they had just been shaved and bathed, and they wore albs, stoles, and sandals on their feet, but they did not have chasubles. The aforementioned Ebo said to me: ‘Do you see how much your mission has helped us? Until now we had a very harsh guardian and a severe custody, as you saw; now we have Lord Ambrose as our guardian and a light custody.’

“From there I came to a dark place, toward which, from another side, light shone from a neighboring place that was exceedingly bright, very beautiful, full of flowers, and fragrant. I saw our lord King Charles lying there in mud made from the foul discharge of his own putrefaction. Worms were eating him; they had already consumed his flesh, and nothing remained in his body except sinews and bones [Col. 1116D].

“He called me by my name and said: ‘Why do you not help me?’

“I replied: ‘Lord, how can I help you?’

“He said: ‘Take that stone which is beside you and, lifting my head, place it beneath my head’—which I did.

“Then he said to me: ‘Go to Bishop Hincmar and tell him that I did not heed his good counsels or those of my other faithful men; therefore I am suffering these things that you see for my sins. Tell him that I always trusted in him, so that he might help me to be freed from this punishment, and that, on my behalf, he should ask all those who were faithful to me to help me. For if they undertake that struggle, I shall soon be freed from this punishment.’

“I asked him what the place was from which that light shone and such fragrance breathed forth.

“He said: ‘It is the rest of the saints.’

“Desiring to draw nearer to that place, I saw such brilliance, such sweetness, and such beauty as no human tongue can express. I saw there a multitude of people of different orders, rejoicing in white garments, and certain shining seats on which no one yet sat, but which had been prepared for them.

“On that journey I saw a certain church. When I entered it, I found Bishop Hincmar prepared, with clergy vested for singing Mass. I told him what our lord King Charles had commanded.

“Immediately I returned in spirit to the place where our lord Charles had been lying, and I found him in a bright place, sound in body, and clothed in royal [Col. 1117B] garments. He said to me: ‘Do you see how much your mission has helped me?’

“From there I came to a great and lofty rock, and found a man planted in that same rock up to his armpits. He called me and said: ‘I am Jesse. Go to my friends and tell them to help me, so that I may be freed from this rock.’

“I replied that I did not know where those men were.

“He said: ‘When you proceed from here, you will find them on the road.’

“I saw beside that great and lofty rock a deep valley and a most dreadful pit, containing black water as though it were pitch. I asked the man who called himself Jesse what that pit was.

“He replied: ‘Wait here a little, and you yourself will see what it is. For I am not so greatly burdened by the punishment I am suffering as by fear of what you are about to see.’

“Suddenly flame and smoke came forth from the pit almost up to heaven. When the flame sank back into the pit and the smoke vanished, there were four demons driving a multitude of souls, divided into four groups, through the pit toward a certain extremely cold water, just as animals are driven to be watered.

“Jesse himself said: ‘These demons do this every day, and these wretched souls endure it once each day, because none of their friends labor on their behalf. For if some had labored for them, they would not endure this punishment.’

“Proceeding from there, I met men speaking about the aforementioned Jesse, and I told them what Jesse had ordered me to tell them.

“From there I returned to the aforementioned rock and found the same man clothed in white garments and seated on an honorable seat. He gave me many thanks for the mission he had entrusted to me.

“From there I came to a certain place and found Count Otharius, who had hair and a beard, but whose entire body was infected and black with misery and filth. He tried to hide himself so that I would not see him.

“I said to him: ‘My lord count, what are you doing here?’

“He replied: ‘I am here because of my sins, and I am suffering what you see. This guardian of mine, who encouraged me during my life to do the evil things I did, was still encouraging me to hide myself so that you would not see me. But I beg you, for the love of God: go to my wife, to my people, and to my friends, and tell them to give alms for me and to obtain that prayers be offered, so that I may be freed from this punishment. I entrusted my gold and silver to one of my men; no one knew of it except me and him, and he has not yet given even a single denarius from it for me.’

“It seemed to me that I was immediately at Vongus, at the public assembly, and I told his men and the others who were there what he had ordered me to say.

“Immediately I was in spirit at the place where Otharius was, and he was as if newly shaved and bathed, sound in body and clothed in white garments. His harsh guardian was no longer there. He said to me: ‘Do you see how much your mission has helped me? My guardian no longer has power over me.’

“There was also a very dignified man there who said to me: ‘You will go from this world back to your body. Take care, through almsgiving and other good works and through a good life, that when you return here you may have a good dwelling.’ He told me how I should feed and clothe the poor according to my means.

“Another man, with a rustic face and a grim expression, was there. He said: ‘He will not go from here.’

“The dignified man replied: ‘He will do so, and he will remain in the body for fourteen more years, after which he will come here.’

“The rustic man answered: ‘The fourteen years you mention I shall make fourteen days, and he will not live any longer before returning here.’

“The dignified man said: ‘It will be as I say, not as you say, because here is his advocate and guarantor, and you will be there with me.’

“Thus he sought holy communion. After receiving it, he drank about half a staup of wine and said: ‘Now I could eat, if I had something.’

“Food was given to him, and he ate [Col. 1118C], and from that time he recovered.

“When I heard these things being spread by certain people, and since the man who had returned to life could not come to me, I summoned the aforementioned priest, a man of sound understanding and good life, to whom Bernold had related these events, and had him tell me in order everything that has been written down. I believed these things to be true, because I had read accounts of this kind both in Saint Gregory’s *Book of Dialogues*, in the history of the English, and in the writings of Saint Boniface, bishop and martyr; I had also read of such things being revealed, in our own time during the reign of Lord Emperor Louis, to a certain religious man named Witinus.

“Therefore, dearest brothers, as we read these things, let us remain always fearful and always watchful. While we are in this body, let us think about the dwellings we shall have after laying aside our bodies, and let us not neglect the remedies revealed and granted to us by God. Let us also urge those entrusted to us, and everyone whom we can reach, not to neglect them, because death is conquered in this way: if it is always feared before it comes.

“Let us also earnestly implore the Lord on behalf of our former lord King Charles, that he may grant him eternal blessings, since through his power he granted us temporal benefits.

“In this vision we can discern two judgments of the Lord. First, while enduring the punishments he suffered, Charles was also tormented by the sight of the rest of the saints, which shone from afar like light: he could have merited it while in the body, but had not yet merited it. Yet future hope somewhat refreshed him. In the same way, the Scriptures exhort us to let our sins trouble us so that our mind does not collapse into despair, but to let God’s mercy refresh us so that it does not make us negligent in any way.

“Let us also entreat the Lord’s mercy with the deepest affection on behalf of our brothers who preceded us with the sign of faith in the unity of holy Church, so that, by the consolation we provide them, we may console one another through fraternal charity, as it is written: ‘A brother helps a brother’ (Prov. XVIII), ‘and let both be consoled.’ Those who preceded us should be consoled by the comfort of charity that we provide them, and we should be consoled by the merit of brotherly love that God will return to us.

“As for what that man who returned to life said—that he had first seen certain people in punishments and afterward as though freed—I think it should be understood in this way: if what they requested has been done for them, liberation will follow, and this is shown outwardly. For in Scripture we often read of future things spoken in the past tense as though they had already happened, as a sign of certainty; and we know that the visions of prophets and other saints were shown through various forms.

“For we have not yet reached what is written: ‘beholding the glory of the Lord face to face’ (1 Cor. XIII). For it has not yet appeared what we shall be; and although what we shall be has not yet appeared, we have nevertheless been saved in hope.

“But because death is certain and the hour of our departure is uncertain, we ought with attentive minds to meditate on the saying of blessed Prosper, recorded from the words of Saint Augustine in accordance with the course of Scripture. It runs as follows (chapter 20):

> ‘Sins, whether small or great, cannot remain unpunished, because they are punished either by the repentant human being or by God the judge. Divine vengeance ceases if human conversion comes first. For God loves to spare those who confess, and not to judge those who judge themselves.’”

[Col. 1119]

## XVIII. HINCMAR’S COUNSEL CONCERNING THE PENANCE OF KING PIPPIN

(From the same author, from the manuscript of Saint Lawrence of Liège.)

[Col. 1119B] Saint Pope Gregory defined the matter in his decrees to Felix, bishop of Sicily, saying (Book XII, Letter 32):

> “We decree that each person who has been faithfully instructed and, having already put down a firm root, stands unshaken, must observe his own lineage through the seventh generation; and, so long as they recognize themselves as related by affinity, they must not enter into such a union. Nor is it permitted, or ever will be permitted, to any Christian to take as a wife one whom someone related to him by blood had as a wife, or whom he had defiled by any unlawful pollution, because such intercourse is incestuous and abominable to God and to all human beings. We read that the holy Fathers long ago established that incestuous persons are not to be counted under any name of marriage.”

Again, Pope Gregory defined the matter among other things in a synodal decree before the body of blessed Peter, in these words (Gregory II, canon 9):

> “If anyone takes as a wife a woman from his own kinship, or one whom a relative had as a wife, let him be anathema.” And all replied three times: “Let him be anathema.”

The sacred canons likewise say (Council of Epao, canon 30):

> “For incestuous unions we reserve absolutely no pardon, except when they have remedied the adultery by separation. Incestuous persons are not to be counted under any name of marriage; indeed, it is a deadly thing even to identify them. Those to whom an unlawful union is forbidden shall have the freedom to enter into a better marriage.”

Saint Siricius, in his decrees concerning apostate monks, says (chapter 6):

> “We command that these immodest and detestable persons be expelled from the assembly of monasteries and from the gatherings of churches, so that, shut away in their prisons and lamenting such a great crime in continual mourning, they may be able to purge it in the cleansing fire of repentance, and so that, at least at the hour of death, forgiveness may be granted them through the grace of communion, solely out of regard for mercy.”

Pippin now stands under this chapter, and also under another chapter in which the same Siricius decreed concerning apostates (chapter 3):

> “Since he now says that he repents of his past evils, because he abandoned his habit and profession, gravely violated the sacrament by which he bound himself, joined himself to pagans, and professes that he wishes to return to his profession and habit: since judgment concerning him was established by synodal definition and judgment, it ought to have been altered by synodal judgment if time and place permitted. But now, since judgment concerns this matter and mercy surrounds us here, instead of synodal judgment we must follow what has been defined by the apostolic see and through synodal judgments.

> “Blessed Leo says (Letter 59 to Theodore) that, in distributing God’s gifts, we ought not to be difficult, nor disregard the groans and tears of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very disposition to repent has been conceived through God’s inspiration. The Apostle says: ‘Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will’ (2 Tim. I).”

The same man also says in his decrees (Letter 95, chapter 13):

> “The monastic vocation, undertaken by one’s own judgment or will, cannot be abandoned without sin. For what one has vowed to God, one must render to him. Therefore whoever, having abandoned the profession of solitude, has fallen into military service or marriage must be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance. For although military service may be innocent and marriage honorable, abandoning the choice of what is better is a transgression.”

And because Pippin joined himself to pagans, from whose association many evils arose in Christendom, we must apply to him Leo’s chapter in which he says (Letter 95, chapter 16):

> “If they have only taken part in the banquets of the gentiles and eaten sacrificial foods, they can be cleansed through fasting and the laying on of hands, so that thereafter, abstaining from idol offerings, they may be able to participate in the sacraments of Christ. But if they worshiped idols, or were polluted by murder or fornication, they ought not to be admitted to communion except through public penance.”

The Nicene canons state how those who transgressed without necessity should do penance (canon 11; Letter 59 to Theodore).

Since, as I have learned, Pippin is accustomed to be struck by paralysis, we must apply to him the judgment of the great Leo, who says concerning those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger, implore the help of penance and immediate reconciliation:

> “Neither satisfaction should be forbidden nor reconciliation denied, because we can impose neither measures nor times upon God’s mercy. With him true confession suffers no delay in pardon, as the Spirit of God says through the prophet: ‘When you groan, then you shall be saved’ (Isa. XLIII). And again: ‘For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption’ (Ps. CXXIII).”

Innocent said (Letter 29 to Decentius):

> “Concerning penitents who do penance either for more serious offenses or for lesser ones, if no illness intervenes, the custom of the Roman Church shows that they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter. As for assessing the gravity of offenses, it belongs to the priest to judge, so that he may attend to the penitent’s confession and to the weeping and tears of the one who is correcting himself, and then order him to be released when he sees that appropriate satisfaction has been made. Certainly, if someone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, he is to be released before Easter, lest he depart from this world without communion.”

There are many other things that we could gather from this, unless we believed that these might suffice. Therefore, as it seems to me—not prejudging the synodal sentence decreed concerning Pippin, but trusting in God’s mercy, who says through his Apostle, “so that mercy may triumph over judgment” (John II), and trusting in the charity of our fellow brothers and in the authority of the sacred canons and of the Roman pontiffs—Pippin should be exhorted to make a pure confession privately concerning all his sins committed from his earliest age, because perhaps he committed sins that it would be shameful even to mention publicly.

Concerning the fact that he abandoned his habit and perjured himself, and that he joined himself to pagans, from whose association many evils were perpetrated, he should accuse himself tearfully before the Church among the public penitents, humbly seek penance and reconciliation, and, for all that he has either confessed privately or accused himself of publicly, be publicly reconciled through the laying on of the hands of episcopal authority. After reconciliation, he should receive the clerical tonsure, resume the monastic habit, and profess that henceforth he will observe what he seeks and what is fitting; then he should receive communion at the sacred altar.

After reconciliation, he should be treated kindly and mercifully kept in a suitable place under free custody, with monks and good canons as his guardians. They should exhort him, so that by their teaching and example he may learn henceforth to live well and to lament his past sins. Through their care and the suitability of the place, he should be guarded in such a way that he cannot return to his former vomit, even if, persuaded by the devil, he should wish to do so, and that a renewed scandal through him cannot arise in holy Church and in this Christian people.

“Receive, brother and son, this document, and also the other one concerning the prohibition of marriage within kinship. Carry them to the lord king and read them before him. Concerning this document, act according to his counsel and recommendation; and concerning the one sent to you about the prohibition of marriage within kinship, follow, with his counsel and help, the sacred authorities directed to you.

“Care for Pippin must not be neglected, and sufficient care must be taken to provide trustworthy and faithful guardians. Nor should we forget what happened to him in the monastery of Saint Medard, or what happened to Carloman at Corbie. For what has happened once may happen again.”

[Col. 1121]

## XIX. CONCERNING THE ESTATE OF NOVILIACUM

What follows concerns how Lord Hincmar obtained the estate of Noviliacum from Lord Emperor Charles, son of Emperor Louis.

(From the same author, from the Appendix to Flodoard.)

[Col. 1121D] When King Pippin died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October in the monastery of Saint Denis, his sons Carloman and Charles, according to their father’s arrangement and the counsel of the leading men of the realm, divided their paternal kingdom between them. They were raised to kingship on the seventh day before the Ides of October: Carloman at Soissons and Charles at Noyon, as we have it written in the *Annals of the Kings*.

In the fourth year of his reign, Carloman fell ill with the illness from which he died at Salmuntiacum. Before his death, by a command of his royal authority that we possess, in the time of Archbishop Tilpin, he granted the estate of Noviliacum, with everything belonging to it, for the remedy of his soul and as a place of burial, to the Church of Rheims of Saint Mary and to the basilica of Saint Remigius, in which he was also buried. After his death, his brother Charles confirmed that grant by a command of his authority, which we possess.

After Archbishop Tilpin died, in the twenty-third year after Carloman had granted the estate of Noviliacum to the Church of Rheims, Lord King Charles held the bishopric of Rheims as part of his royal domain. He gave the estate of Noviliacum as a benefice to Anscher the Saxon, who paid the nones and tithes from that estate to the Church of Rheims until his death. After Lord Charles and Anscher himself had died, the Church continued to possess the investiture of that estate for thirty-seven years, as has been stated, after Carloman had granted the entire estate, in its entirety, to the Church of Rheims.

After Lord Charles’s death and Anscher’s death, Lord Emperor Louis gave the estate of Noviliacum as a benefice to Donatus. With the intervention of Bigo, Donatus deceitfully obtained certain farms from that estate as his property, almost as if from the king’s treasury, by a command of Lord Emperor Louis.

When Lothair, the son of Lord Emperor Louis, came to Chalon and captured it, Donatus defected from the emperor at the estate above the Marne called Pomarius. He deceived him and fled to Lothair. When Emperor Louis came hostilely to the estate called Calciacus, Lothair came to him under constraint with his men, and he and his men swore to the emperor the oath that had been demanded of them.

Among them, Donatus, whose infidelity had been proven, swore to the emperor the oath that had been demanded. The emperor took from him the county of Meaux and the estate of Noviliacum with its dependencies, and gave them as a benefice to Ato, who had been the doorkeeper of Emperor Charles.

During Emperor Louis’s lifetime, Donatus received neither the county nor any confirmation of his property. After Lord Emperor Louis died, the kingdom was divided among the brothers, peace was made between them, and Ato died. Charles gave Noviliacum as a benefice to Donatus.

After some time, Donatus entrusted his son Gotselin to King Charles. Charles gave him the estate of Noviliacum with its dependencies as a benefice.

Later, when King Charles went to besiege the Normans who were settled on the island called Oscellus, Donatus’s wife Landrada and their sons, together with others, defected. It was judged that their honors and properties should be taken away by the Franks and reduced to the royal treasury. For this reason Landrada and her sons did not thereafter obtain the authority of King Charles.

Concerning these matters, in the twentieth year of his reign Charles gave the royal estate to the monastery of Orbais by a command of his authority, which we possess.

In the thirty-second year of his reign, the glorious Lord King Charles came to the basilica of Saint Remigius. There I showed him the tomb of King Carloman, the commands of Carloman himself and of his grandfather Charles concerning the estate of Noviliacum, and the authorities of the sacred canons, which condemn by the judgment of the Holy Spirit those who retain the alms of the dead and delay handing them over to the churches. Such people are judged to be rejected from the Church as unfaithful and to be regarded as killers of the needy, because they do not believe in God’s judgment.

He therefore returned, by a command of his authority that we possess, the estate itself, with everything belonging to it, to the Church of Rheims. At that time Bernaus held it as a benefice after his brother Rothaus.

Later it came to his attention that certain men from that estate of Noviliacum had deceitfully obtained and retained as their property goods and dependants, both from his father and from himself: namely, Landrada, once the wife of Donatus; Guntharius; Hugo; Waltrudis and her son Elampodus; Rotbertus; and Boso.

He sent his agents to investigate this. When the inquiry had been conducted and the truth had been found as it had been reported to him, and since the persons mentioned had not appeared to answer the charge as they had been summoned, he ordered that the commands of Carloman and Charles, as well as his own command, be read before his faithful men at his general assembly at Douzy, in the palatine court.

Accordingly, his faithful men—both counts and royal vassals, whose names we possess in writing, as well as all the others who were present—having reread those commands, judged that anyone who, by anyone’s command or in any manner, had obtained as property any of the goods or dependants of the estate of Noviliacum after Carloman’s grant—by which he had granted the estate of Noviliacum, with all its dependencies or in its entirety, as it then stood in the royal treasury, to the Church of Rheims—and after the confirmation of his brother Charles, must restore those goods and dependants to that house of God.

This applied unless the person could produce evidence of an exchange showing how those goods and dependants had been justly and reasonably exchanged from that house of God, since they had been obtained not from the royal treasury but, through the grant, from ecclesiastical goods and dependants. This is more fully contained in the command of restoration of Lord Charles himself, which we possess.

But when Lord Charles went to Rome and his brother Lord Louis came to Attigny, certain men from our side obtained from Queen Richildis and from Lord Louis, son of Lord King Charles, that the estate of Noviliacum with its dependencies should be handed over to the sons of Donatus and Landrada. They did not consider that, as it is written in the chapters of the emperors, such people are to be judged unfaithful with respect to royal property, and according to ecclesiastical laws are judged sacrilegious concerning ecclesiastical property.

When Lord Emperor Charles returned and came to Rheims, he heard of this action and was deeply displeased. He sent his agents, who restored the said estate to the Church of Rheims and to our advocate, as we have more fully recorded in writing.

[Col. 1125]

## XX. THE OATH WHICH ARCHBISHOP HINCMAR WAS ORDERED TO ISSUE AT PONTIGNY

(From Sirmond, from the manuscripts of Beauvais and Liège.)

[Col. 1125A] “Thus I promise: from this day forward, for as long as I live, I shall be faithful, obedient, and helpful to this my lord, to the fullest extent and in the best way that I know and can, and according to my ministry I shall provide counsel and assistance in all things, without fraud or evil contrivance, without any deceit or deception, and without regard to any person.

“Neither by myself, nor through a messenger, nor by letters, nor through any person sent out or introduced, nor in any manner or by any sign, shall I plot or consent to anyone plotting against his honor, or against the peace, tranquility, and security of him, of the Church, or of the kingdom entrusted to him. Nor shall I ever raise any scandal that could be contrary or harmful to his present or future salvation.

“So may God and these holy relics help me.”

Observations of Hincmar concerning the same oath.

What is stated absolutely in this oath—“Thus I promise”—is contradicted by the Apostle James, who says: “You do not know what tomorrow will bring”; instead, you should say: “If the Lord wills, we shall do this or that” (James 4:14). Moreover, it is more reasonably said “to this emperor” than “to this lord of mine,” who is younger in age, although superior in the nobility of his person and in worldly imperial power, but not in the dignity of the sacred order, as Saint Pope Gelasius demonstrates when writing to the Emperor Anastasius (Letter 11):

> “There are two things, Emperor Augustus, by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and the royal power. Of these, the burden of the priests is so much heavier, inasmuch as they will render an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves.”

Regarding what follows in this oath—“As long as I live, I shall be faithful, obedient, and an assistant in all things”—Saint Gelasius, writing to the Emperor Anastasius, says (Letter 11):

> “You know, most gracious son, that although you preside over the human race in dignity, nevertheless you submit your neck devotedly to the prelates of divine things, and seek from them the causes of your salvation. Thus, in receiving the heavenly sacraments and administering them as is proper, you recognize that you ought rather to submit to them in the order of religion than preside over them. Accordingly, in these matters you depend upon their judgment, not they upon your will.”

And a little later:

> “With what devotion, I ask you, ought one to obey those who have been appointed to dispense the venerable mysteries? Therefore, just as a grave danger rests upon pontiffs if they remain silent about what is fitting for the worship of God, so—God forbid—a no less serious peril awaits those who, although they ought to obey, disdain to do so.”

What is written here—“however much and however well I shall know and be able”—is not consistent with the Apostle’s saying: “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly” (Romans 12:13), that is, with moderation. And when Saint Peter was asked by the Lord, “Do you love me more than these?” (John 21:16), because he remembered that, when the Lord’s passion was imminent, he had attributed to himself more steadfastness than he possessed, having been more cautiously instructed by his own weakness, he did not answer, “I love you more than these,” but simply, “I love you.” It is therefore more correctly said, “According to my knowledge and ability,” than, “However much and however well I shall know and be able.”

But what has been added—“with counsel and assistance”—is superfluous. For in what I said, “according to my knowledge,” counsel is included; and in what I said, “according to my ability,” assistance is included.

What the learned scribe wrote—“According to my ministry, I shall be faithful, obedient, and an assistant in all things”—he added, contrary to the customary oath by which princes and lords command their subjects and even their slaves to swear. For as Scripture says: “There is no one on earth who does good and does not sin” (Psalm 13:1, 3); and James says: “For we all offend in many things” (James 3:2), although the Apostle adds concerning Christ: “If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (ibid.).

If, perchance, our lord—God forbid—should through deception order or do something that was not fitting for episcopal ministry, this most perceptive writer ought to have considered whether the bishop should be obedient and an assistant to him in such a matter. Nor do I think there is any human being who can be altogether faithful, obedient, and an assistant to another human being in all things.

Unless, perhaps, we understand the opinion of that learned man according to the same kind of expression in which the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 3:17); and: “In everything we commend ourselves as God’s ministers” (2 Corinthians 6:4). That is, we should desire him always to command and always to do those things which we ought and are able to obey, and in which we ought and are able to be his assistants.

But when he says, “so that I may be faithful, obedient, and an assistant to him in all things,” the Apostle understood human capacity differently, since we cannot all do everything. After enumerating the gifts of grace, he says: “As God has distributed to each the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3).

And what he added—“without fraud, evil intent, any deceitfulness, seduction, or deception, and without regard to any person”—which he uttered superfluously from the abundance of an envious heart, is comprehended by the sincerity of my heart when I say: “To this emperor, according to my knowledge and ability, and in accordance with my ministry, I shall be faithful.”

For between what is called an assistant and what is called a harmful agent there is no middle position. Whoever is faithful is, insofar as it depends upon him, an assistant to the one to whom he is faithful; and whoever is unfaithful is, insofar as it depends upon him, harmful to the one to whom he is unfaithful. Everyone who is faithful toward the one to whom he is faithful will neither commit nor consent to any fraud, evil intent, deceitfulness, seduction, or deception, whether by counsel or by assistance, out of regard for any person. If he does so, he will not be faithful but unfaithful.

But when, as though he had forgotten what he had already said, he added:

> “Neither by myself, nor through an envoy, nor by letters, nor through a person sent out or brought in, nor in any way or by any indication, shall I plot against his honor, or against the peace, tranquillity, and stability of himself, the Church, and the kingdom entrusted to him, nor shall I consent to one who plots,”

he judged the bishop most foolishly—indeed, miserably—for he spoke with the gall of bitterness.

For what is an envoy except a person sent out or brought in? And what is any indication except something conveyed either by words, letters, or any other means? And what is acting against his honor or against the peace of the Church and of the kingdom entrusted to him except acting unfaithfully? And what is peace except tranquillity? And what is stability except sincerity?

And when he said that he would not plot against these things—namely, those he had mentioned above—nor consent to one who plotted, he considered the bishop exceedingly stupid: the bishop who, from his very cradle into old age, had learned and repeatedly read the sacred writings, so that he would not know the Apostle’s saying: “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (Romans 1:32); nor the statement of Saint Pope Leo, that just as one sins through evil persuasion, so one also sins through evil consent.

And Saint Gelasius wrote to the Emperor Anastasius (Letter 10):

> “Certainly your laws subject accomplices in crimes and receivers of robbers to an equal penalty in the courts; nor is one considered free from the crime who, although he did not commit it himself, nevertheless admitted those who committed it into familiarity and alliance.”

Therefore, let us all return to our consciences and heed the Lord saying: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23).

Finally, what he placed at the end, because he could find nothing further to add—“Nor shall I ever cause any scandal that could be contrary or harmful to his present or future salvation”—is, just as the composition is contrary to art, so the judgment is alien to reason.

For as the Apostle says, “Love of neighbor does no evil”; “Love is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13:10); “He who loves has fulfilled the law”; and, “If there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying” (Romans 13:9). Thus everything that this writer, being of unsound mind because devoid of charity, composed is contained in the statement: “According to my knowledge and ability, and in accordance with my ministry, I shall be faithful,” just as an archbishop ought rightly to be faithful to an emperor.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “But I say to you: Do not swear at all; let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; anything more than this is from evil” (Matthew 5:37)—that is, either from the evil of one who swears wickedly and rashly, or from the evil of one who wickedly and without cause compels another to swear, as the Catholic teachers say.

And the Apostle James says: “Above all things, my brothers, do not swear any oath” (James 5:14).

The holy Fathers of the Council of Nicaea decreed that bishops who had consented to the Arian perfidy should be received without an oath. Saint Pope Leo and the Council of Chalcedon likewise decreed that bishops who had supported the Eutychian perversity, and Saint Gregory that Nestorians cast out by the Synod of Constantinople, should be received into their orders by a profession and subscription, or by profession alone, without another oath. This was especially so since the sacred canons determine that if anyone violates in any respect the profession or subscription he has made, he will deprive himself of his honor.

And your father, of blessed memory, demanded no other oath from the bishops who, willingly or unwillingly, had consented to his deposition—not even from Ebo himself, who among the bishops had been the author and instigator of that deposition—than the libelli of profession signed by them. These I possess. Nor ought another oath now to have been demanded from me, who, before my profession and subscription, and after my profession and subscription, have kept what I professed and subscribed for so many years, from youth to this old age.

But it is not surprising if, through the bearers of envy—for, as it is written, “Death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24)—the mind of your benevolence has now been moved without cause to demand from me what neither your father, during his lifetime, demanded, although for approximately eight years he entrusted his secrets to me without hesitation, nor have you until now demanded during these thirty-six years. For the Lord said to the author of envy concerning his faithful servant Job: “You have moved me against him without cause” (Job 2:3). And in paradise he said to him: “You shall lie in wait for his heel” (Genesis 3:15), that is, the heel of the human being.

He sees my heel—that is, my approaching end—and strives to lie in wait for it, so that what I have preserved toward you freely and sincerely until now, if it cannot prevail through infidelity, may prevail through the rancor of sadness.

The Apostle warns those who do good to guard carefully against this in their work, saying: “Let them not act out of sadness or compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). He also says: “So that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Corinthians 2:11).

What I now feel I had already heard promised to me by those against whom I acted together with you, with sound reasoning and sacred authority, for the sake of vengeance. But I know in whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to guard my deposit until that day—the just Judge.

[Col. 1129]

## XXI. LIFE OF SAINT REMIGIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, WRITTEN BY HINCMAR, ALSO ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

*(In Surius, Acts of the Saints, 13 January.)*

[Col. 1129A] Hincmar, a bishop in name, not in merit, and servant of the people of God, to our beloved brothers and fellow ministers, sons of this holy Church of Rheims.

As I learned by faithful report from religious men, elders already advanced in age, who were still living from the time of Tilpin, bishop of this city, when, by God’s authorship, I was chosen and advanced to the service of this holy Church—and who lived for some years afterwards—they had heard from their elders that they had seen a book of very great size, written in an ancient hand, concerning the birth, life, virtues, and death of blessed Remigius, our most holy patron.

It perished on this occasion. Aegidius, fourth bishop of this city after blessed Remigius, asked a certain religious man named Fortunatus, distinguished in metrical verse, who was then invited to various places in these Gallic and Belgian regions by many powerful and honorable men on account of his life and learning, to extract from that same book, composed in the Gallic manner, some miracles in plain speech which might be read aloud to the people, so that they could hear them without weariness, store them in their minds, and through them be stirred to love, honor, and devotion toward God and their protector himself. The reader may observe this in that very extract, where it is written: “Let us strive to recount a few things and pass over very many.” When the extract itself began to be frequently read among the people and copied by many because its brevity made it easy to use, the great codex itself began to be treated ever more negligently by negligent persons. [Col. 1129C] Until the time of Prince Charles [Note: [Col. 1129C] He means Charles Martel.], when, because of the discord and struggle for the principate between him and Raganfrid, and the frequent civil—indeed more than civil, because domestic and fratricidal—wars in the German, Belgian, and Gallic provinces, the Christian religion was almost abolished: so that, with bishops remaining in only a few places, bishoprics were granted to laymen and their possessions divided among them. Thus a certain Milo, a cleric by tonsure but an irreligious layman in morals, dress, and conduct, usurped together the bishoprics of Rheims and Trier and ruined them for about forty years.

In his unhappy time, not only were all precious things removed from this Church of Rheims, but churches and houses of religious persons were destroyed, and the possessions of the bishopric [Col. 1130A] were divided. The few clerics who remained earned their living by trade, and sometimes wrapped in parchments and leaves of books the coins they acquired by merchandising. Thus the aforesaid book, together with others, partly rotted by dripping water, partly gnawed by mice, and partly dispersed by the cutting away of leaves, perished so completely that only a few scattered leaves from it were found.

But in the time of King Pippin, son of the aforesaid Prince Charles, when a revelation had been shown to Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, concerning the eternal damnation of that same Charles, who had divided the property of the churches, Pippin restored to this bishopric of Rheims a portion of ecclesiastical property, as he did to the bishoprics of other churches, and consented that Tilpin be ordained bishop in this city of Rheims.

[Col. 1130B] For in these latter times of the age this happened in this Church of Rheims to the book mentioned, and to others besides, as Saint John Chrysostom relates in Homily 9 on the Gospel according to Matthew to have happened in ancient times to the authentic Scriptures, saying: “Many records of the prophets have perished, as may be proved from the history of Paralipomenon. For the Jews, being indolent—not merely indolent but impious as well—lost some things through negligence, while at other times they burned and profanely cut up others. Jeremiah reports such profanation (Jer. 36); and in the Fourth Book of Kings we read of negligence (4 Kings 22), how after much time the volume of Deuteronomy was scarcely found, buried in a certain place and almost obliterated.”

[Col. 1130C] We also read in the Scriptures we possess mention of many writings which we do not possess: for example, the Book of the Just, mentioned in the books of Kings (2 Kings 1); and the Book of the Wars of the Lord, mentioned in the Book of Numbers (Num. 21). Nor do we possess Solomon’s songs, or his most wise discussions of the nature of trees and of every herb, likewise of beasts of burden and birds, creeping things and fish (3 Kings 4); or what is said in the book *Words of the Days*: “The rest of the earlier and later deeds of Solomon are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the vision of Addo the seer against Jeroboam son of Nabath” (2 Chronicles 9), and many volumes of this kind, which are proved to have been written but are known not to exist today.

[Col. 1131A] For when Judaea was devastated by the Chaldeans, as we read in the writings of the Fathers, the library assembled in ancient times was also consumed by hostile fire among the other riches of the province. From it, the few books now contained in Holy Scripture were afterwards restored through the industry of Ezra, priest and prophet. Hence it is written of him: “Ezra went up from Babylon, and he was a swift scribe in the law of Moses” (1 Ezra 7)—swift, that is, because he discovered forms of letters readier than those the Hebrews had until then. And in the letter of the king of Persia: “Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, most learned scribe of the law of the God of heaven, greeting” (ibid.).

Conversely, although many other things have perished, we have many matters concerning the birth [Col. 1131B] and life, virtues, and death of our lord, most holy father, and protector Remigius, preserved for posterity in certain histories, diverse little documents, and customary report from predecessors, which are not contained in the aforementioned extract. Accordingly, your good desires have approved that my service should collect these things into one work for the knowledge of the ignorant and of those to come after. I would have done this long ago, had vain hope not deceived me through people saying that in this place and that I could find a great book concerning the virtues and life of our same lord and patron. Sending to those places, I found what had been promised to me wholly false.
