Now, however, with the help of the Lord—who promises one who trusts in him and wishes to speak of his works, he who is wonderful and glorious in his saints (Ps. 67): “Open your mouth,” he says, “and I will fill it” (Ps. 80)—aided by the merits of that apostle and patron of the Franks and by your prayers, I shall undertake what I long postponed. I shall begin with his ancestors and birth, and then arrange both what I have found concerning him in histories published by earlier writers and what I have discovered scattered in various papers; and I shall also set in order what I have learned by common report. For it was said not long before our time, and is found also in the Holy Scriptures and in Gospel truth: it is a true law of history simply to commit to writing for the instruction of posterity those things gathered through public report. Let diversity of style in all this not disturb the reader, since I shall set down as I find them both those things taken from the histories of earlier writers and those found in ancient papers.

[Col. 1131D] But the things I have learned from ancient common report, and those which I shall add for the instruction of readers or hearers, I shall either take care to set down in the words of those from whose sayings I borrow, or compose in my own speech; wishing, by offering something of my bounden service in praise which he does not need, to repay my benefactor for all that he has bestowed freely upon me, unworthy as I am, rather than rendered in return for any merits. Finally, in describing his virtues I shall not be able to preserve the order in which the Lord deigned to perform them through him; but I shall describe them as I have received them by writing or hearing. Thus Saint Jerome says that, saving the loftier mystery of prophetic inspiration divinely bestowed, the Psalms too are arranged in order [Col. 1132A] not as they were composed, but as Ezra found them at different times. Nevertheless, insofar as I find knowledge of dates or see deeds suitable to their sequence, I shall endeavor to arrange them.

In the matters concerning miracles of virtues wrought by the Lord through our most blessed patron, I shall endeavor to add sayings of Catholic writers, according to the measure of my understanding, for the exhortation of readers and hearers, attempting, though unable, to follow the footsteps of blessed Gregory. In describing the deeds of saints and the falls of the wicked, he inserted, drawing exhortation from them and according to the wisdom given him by God, many things necessary and useful for readers and hearers. Nor do I think anyone should regard it as an irrelevant undertaking if I restore things concerning the birth, conduct, and death of our lord, patron, and protector that were found nearly effaced by age in old papers, bringing them from hiddenness into light, and endeavor to entrust to writing what I have known by the certain report of the ancients. For, as I have said, we know that the Holy Scriptures, abolished through the negligence and profanation of impious Jews, were restored through the zeal of Saint Ezra the priest; and that not only was Gospel and apostolic history most sacredly composed by the Evangelists, but that many masters of the Church described the deeds of many saints for the instruction of many, and even historians recorded the struggles of secular persons for the remembrance of posterity; while we read that pagan poets also strove to display their fragments in resounding measures.

[Col. 1132C] I. After the Lord’s vengeance for crimes had been accomplished through the slaughter of Gaul, while the cruelty of the Vandals continued, heavenly mercy distilled down. For, in order to mitigate the vengeance of divine judgment, impending upon the world because of persevering iniquities, together with the barbaric ferocity of the Frankish people that was to come upon it, heaven brought forth in this order Remigius the bishop, a prelate predestined by God.

II. There was a certain venerable monk, Montanus, worthy of his profession and name. Living a solitary life in seclusion, he continually devoted himself to fasts, vigils, and prayers, and rendered himself so acceptable to God by the distinction of his other virtues that he often enjoyed angelic conversations and frequently participated in heavenly visions and revelations.

[Col. 1132D] While he was keeping vigil in prayer for the peace of the holy Church, which was being afflicted by many and diverse troubles in the Gallic and Belgian provinces, and was tirelessly beseeching the mercy of almighty God with unwearied prayers, one night he prolonged his prayer beyond his custom and remained in contemplation until the dawn twilight. Then, compelled by fatigue and the frailty of the flesh, he gave his limbs a little to sleep; suddenly, by divine grace, he was present among choirs of angels and assemblies of the souls of most blessed persons, already reigning with God but still awaiting the immortality of their bodies, and began to hear a most intimate [Col. 1133A] conversation.

Among other things that he heard in that heavenly assembly, those holy spirits, eager for human salvation, began to inquire concerning the ruin of the Gallican Church and repeatedly to discuss what ought to be done in such circumstances, saying that the time had come for mercy upon her. For she had received double for all her sins, although her dregs had not been emptied. As they thus conferred among themselves, there suddenly came a voice, resounding most healthfully and sweetly from higher and more secret courts. It comforted the sadness of the spirits present and joyfully proclaimed what was to come, saying: “The Lord looked down from his holy height; from heaven the Lord looked upon the earth, that he might hear the groaning of those in chains, that he might free the children of the slain, that his name might be proclaimed among the nations, when peoples are gathered together as one and kings serve him” (Ps. 101). “Cilinia, conceiving in her womb, shall bear a son named Remigius, to whom I shall entrust the people to be saved.”

Blessed Cilinia, indeed, though occupied with pious works and held in body in the world, dwelt in mind in heaven. In the flower of youth she had borne to her only husband Aemilius Principius, afterwards holy bishop of the city of Soissons, and his brother, father of blessed Lupus, bishop and successor of that same Principius, who exercised the priesthood until the final days of glorious Remigius and then died.

III. That venerable man [Note: [Col. 1133D] See Flodoard, ibid.] made known to Cilinia the divine oracle which he had received through God’s grace, amid the countless dangers of that time and with such consolation received. [Col. 1133C] But she said to Montanus: “How can it be that an old woman should nurse a son, since my womanly functions failed me long ago, and my husband Aemilius is old; in his aged body the blood about his heart is cold, and the works of pleasure have utterly withered in him?” For both were noble by birth and highly renowned for grace among their own people. Since they had become parents of children in many days, exhausted and now infertile in the flesh, they did not seek marital intercourse, nor had they any longer hope or desire of begetting offspring.

Blessed Montanus replied: “Know that when you have weaned the boy Remigius, you shall anoint my eyes with your milk, and I shall receive sight.” For, that his merits might be increased, as in the case of Saint Tobias (Tob. 2), according to the divine saying, “Let the just man be justified still” (Rev. 22), blessed Montanus himself had lost the sight of his bodily eyes. [Col. 1133D] At last, when the parents believed the words of the man of God, there was joy that they were to receive such offspring, in whose conception there would be no heat of satisfying lust but love for begetting a child according to the divine prediction.

Thus the future bishop of Christ was conceived; and, with Christ’s mercy helping, his most blessed mother happily bore as a son the one whom, under God’s auspices, she had conceived, and caused the name Remigius, according to the Lord’s word, to be given him in baptism. Once weaned, as his foreteller had predicted, he anointed the eyes of his seer with his mother’s milk, his mother acting as midwife, and divine grace restored his sight.

[Col. 1134A] Nor should it seem incredible that this child worked miracles by divine gift before, because of bodily age, he knew how to call his father and mother. Though as a man he was conceived in iniquities, nevertheless, contrary to the manner of the human condition, his mother bore him not in the sins of transgression but in the grace of remission. For there can be no doubt that the Holy Spirit, who foretold what he would be and by whose gift he was conceived, also absolved him from sins. The truthful judgment of the Fathers firmly establishes that the gift of the Holy Spirit is not bound by law. Therefore he who consecrated Cornelius and his household by his grace before they received baptism (Acts 10), surely also poured the gift of the same grace upon blessed Remigius not only before baptism but even before birth.

This holy man was born by promise from an old woman and an old man, long sterile, like Isaac (Gen. 17) and John (Luke 1), designated by name before he was born and, before he was known to the world, born in the district of Laon from parents of high lineage, so that his birth might show what he would be in action.

IV. [Col. 1134B] A sign of singular merit is given whenever a name is either imposed upon or changed for human beings by God. Thus Abram, because he was to be father of many nations, was called Abraham (Gen. 17). Thus Jacob, because he saw God, deserved to be called Israel (Gen. 32). Thus King Josiah, because of the height of his exceptional virtue, was named by God long before he was born (3 Kings 13). Thus John, because through the assistance of divine grace he deserved to be more than a prophet, and because no one greater than he arose among those born of women (Luke 1; Matt. 5); and Peter took his surname from the firmness and stability of a rock (Matt. 16).

And he who was first Saul was afterwards named Paul (Acts 13), because, raised up against Christ by zeal for the law, he was thrown from heaven to earth by him whom he persecuted in his members and became Paul in himself—that is, small, slight, and humble; then he became a great defender of God’s grace, a vessel of election, and the outstanding teacher and preacher of the whole Church (Acts 9). The sons of Zebedee, because they thundered terribly to the sinful world the word of God, took the surname sons of thunder [Col. 1134D] (Mark 3). And our Lord and Redeemer Jesus—that is, Savior—was surnamed before he was born in the flesh because he was to save his people from their sins (Matt. 1).

So too blessed Remigius received from God the surname Remigius because he was to steer through the winding, wave-tossed courses of the world the Church entrusted to him. For it is characteristic of servants of God to be known by name to God. Thus one of them is told: “I know you by name” (Exod. 33); and blessed Jeremiah, about to go to preach the divine word, is told: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in your mother’s womb [Col. 1135A] I sanctified you” (Jer. 1).

Jeremiah, who was to recall the people from idol worship, is sanctified in the womb; John, who was to illuminate the people by his speech, received prophetic grace in his mother’s womb (Luke 1); and blessed Remigius, who was to lead the Frankish people from the darkness of ignorance to the light of the Gospel, was likewise endowed with divine grace, so that what he was to accomplish in ministry might shine forth through an equal gift together with his companions. And he who, as has been said, was by God’s predestination to guide the Church of God—and with special care the city and province of Rheims—by the oarage of holy wings, namely word and example, merits and prayers, and who after completing his contest was to seek the heavenly kingdoms in spirit, borne up by the help of angels, was rightly called Remigius by God’s command.

V. Nor should this be passed over: in documents made in recent times after his death, and even after the lapse of many years, concerning property granted to the Church of Rheims, we read that he was named Remedius. Whoever considers his merits and deeds understands that he was fittingly called by this name. He became a mitigator of the Lord’s wrath, reconciliation in a time of anger, and was magnified by the Lord before kings; by his words, as we shall show below, he pacified monsters—that is, fierce pagans. We would therefore believe that he was called Remedius in baptism, unless in more corrected accounts of his deeds we knew that by the divine oracle through Saint Montanus he ought to be called Remigius.

[Col. 1135C] We also read the following in verses composed by him and, at his command, engraved on a certain vessel consecrated by him:

> From here let the people draw life from the sacred blood,
>
> Which Christ poured forth when the wound was inflicted eternally.
>
> Remigius the priest renders his vows to the Lord.

That vessel lasted until our times, when it was melted down and given for the ransom of Christians, so that the price of the silver chalice might ransom from the ministers of the devil, the Northmen, those whom the shed blood of the chalice—that is, of Christ’s passion—had redeemed from the power of darkness.

VI. Given over by his parents to the school to be instructed in letters, in a short time he became more excellent in learning than his contemporaries and even than those older than he. He also strove [Col. 1135D] to surpass his tender years by maturity of conduct, sweeten the benevolence of his heart with the honey of charity, avoid the crowds of thronging peoples, and serve the Lord in solitary life and seclusion, as he had learned that his forerunner had done. The place is still indicated and reverently honored in the fortress of Laon. In that seclusion, the righteous youth served the Lord, rivaling himself in the pursuits of holy conduct with successes following upon successes.

When he reached the twenty-second year of his age, Bennadius [variant: Benagius; Baronius [Col. 1136A] reads Gennadius], archbishop in this city of Rheims, died, and he is known to have been carried to the summit of the episcopate by the universal desire of all rather than elected. Thus there was a gathering of people of differing sex, condition, rank, and age; but all, with one and the same judgment, acclaimed this man as truly worthy of God and fit to be set over the people.

But the most blessed man, oppressed by these pressures, was afflicted with excessive anguish, because no way of flight lay open to him, nor could he in any way satisfy the people so that they might abandon their undertaking. For it was the divine will that he who was to provide for the salvation of all should be chosen by the acclamations of all, and that he who was to provide for unity of faith among those already faithful and those yet to become faithful should be raised to the seat [Col. 1136B] of priestly honor by the union of the whole people.

When the most holy man saw himself pressed by these acclamations, he began to complain publicly of the weakness and time of his age, declaring that the ecclesiastical order did not admit weak age to this dignity. He feared that immature age, assailed by the devices of the crafty enemy, might incur some evil. But divine grace both caused the people’s voice to persist most steadfastly in his election and protected the holy man from the malignity of the ancient enemy.

And while the multitude of the people cried out and the most holy man resisted with great constancy, it pleased almighty God to show him by the clearest signs what judgment he held concerning him.

VII. For while he was attempting to resist in the manner described, suddenly, in the sight of all present, a ray of new light descended upon the head of that holy man, as though the sun itself had moved from heaven and fallen upon him. Because he was being prepared as a light for the illumination of souls, he too, when called to this work, had to be made known by visible light. [Col. 1136C] For he was the lamp to be placed not beneath the bushel of bodily care but upon the lampstand of most pure conduct beloved by God, so that he might provide the light of the best instruction to those who would be in the house of the holy Church.

[Note: [Col. 1135D] With respect to Saint Remigius’s age, it is sometimes known to have happened that, because of the very eminent virtue and learning of someone—as we see happened in the case of Saint John Chrysostom, who could not avoid being ordained bishop at that age except by taking refuge in flight—his lesser age was not taken into account.]

### VIII

It also pleased divine omnipotence to add another sign to this miracle, for the manifestation of the blessed man’s merits. Indeed, while the aforementioned ray was illuminating him, he felt a liquid of sacred unction poured upon his head [Col. 1136D], and his entire head was drenched with it. And rightly so: since he was to anoint the peoples with spiritual oil—with a chrism invisible, that is, with the grace of the same Holy Spirit, by which their heads would be anointed visibly, but their minds through his preaching, with the Holy Spirit speaking within him—he himself was first to be marked by such an anointing.

After receiving such great and such significant omens, he feared to oppose the divine decrees. For it could not seem safe to him to contradict the divine command when so many signs had gone before, especially [Col. 1137A] since he had learned that, inwardly illumined and anointed by the light and unction of the Holy Spirit—which is signified by visible oil—he ought rather to offer himself for divine ministry than to excuse himself, just as Saint Isaiah did.

### IX

Thus, setting aside every doubt and removing his wavering judgment, he was clothed with priestly vestments by the unanimous agreement of the bishops of the province of Reims, consecrated with episcopal blessing, and placed upon the episcopal seat of this city of Reims.

There he immediately appeared so suitable and devoted, as though he had continually presided over the office to which he had newly ascended. He was generous in almsgiving, diligent in vigils, devoted in prayer, lavish in kindness, outstanding in teaching, perfect in charity, ready in speech [Col. 1137B], and most holy in conduct. He displayed the sincerity of his mind in the serenity of his face, and revealed the piety of his most merciful heart in the gentleness of his speech. Whatever could pertain to eternal salvation, the blessed man fulfilled no less in deed than he taught by the preaching of his words.

O man wholly worthy of God! The beauty of his soul shone forth in his very bearing; in the appearance of the outward man, one would have thought that the image of holiness itself was expressed. To the irreverent he was terrifying in his look, worthy of reverence in his bearing, fearsome in his severity, and venerable in his kindness. The discipline of authority was tempered by the gentleness of humility. A stern brow threatened those who did wrong, but the serenity of his heart offered them kindness.

Toward those who acted well, Peter appeared in his face; toward those who did wrong, Paul appeared in his spirit [Col. 1137C]. It was as though, in the fitting diversity of graces united in one man, he imitated the former’s compassion and the latter’s strictness—so that although scarcely anyone could endure his presence, no one could bear his absence.

As no one could fully behold the forms and appearances of his inner virtues, so no one is capable of adequately describing them. Just as he strove to cultivate them, he also labored to conceal them; and although he wished them to increase, he did not wish them to be recognized. But this is the nature of righteousness: the more diligently it desires to be hidden, the more clearly it becomes known, and concealment itself becomes proclamation. Thus the fame of such great virtues flew among the peoples.

He stood out in everyone’s admiration like a city set upon the summit of a mountain, and the lamp could no longer remain hidden beneath a bushel. That glorious soul opened the hidden riches of heavenly gifts within itself [Col. 1137D] and, from the cabinet of sweet-smelling virtues, poured the spices of sanctification and its graces over the whole Church.

He neglected rest, fled pleasure, sought labor, endured humiliation, was impatient of honor, poor in money, rich in conscience, humble in regard to his merits, and proud in opposition to vices. He cultivated within himself such varied virtues of grace that, although scarcely a few people possessed them individually, he seemed to possess them all. Always engaged in active work, always moved by compunction, he had no concern more dominant than either speaking about God in reading and discourse or speaking with God in prayer.

By continual fasting he sought to break his bones and, through a long martyrdom, triumph over the persecuting enemy, continually chewing over these words as his food and drink:

“My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm 41).

“My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord. My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Psalm 83).

“My soul has failed in longing for your salvation” (Psalm 118).

“My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh thirsted for you” (Psalm 62).

“My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41.)

And, consoling himself, he said:

“Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess him: the salvation of my countenance and my God” (ibid.).

“I shall be satisfied when his glory is revealed” (Psalm 16).

### X

Because he was not yet satisfied with the sight of his Creator, for which he longed [Col. 1138B], he desired him with continual sighs and groans and with tears by day and night. Lifted toward the joys above by loving grief, his holy soul nourished itself through weeping. Within, it endured the groaning of its sorrow, but received nourishment and refreshment from the very fact that the force of its love flowed forth in tears.

Apart from life, he hungered for nothing; apart from righteousness, he thirsted delightfully for nothing. He regarded present things as empty and already passed away, as though his spirit were absent from them, while he longed for what was reserved for the future as though it lay beneath his eyes.

Indeed, the earth that gave birth to such a man could scarcely bear him, and from its fosterling sent forth to us a patron, an angel, and a teacher. Therefore, rightly and appropriately, let us say of him according to the Prophet:

“The righteous man shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psalm 3).

He is worthily held in human memory who has passed to the joys of the angels. He found the grace of God glorified because, aided by God’s grace, he did not seek the glory of the world. Holding firmly and manfully to the rudder of faith, he had already secured the anchor of hope in a tranquil harbor. Against the assault of the devil, he held the shield of God so tirelessly that he reached victory.

In him we have a physician from heaven, with whom holiness—or rather, the very author of holiness—entered our city. How many blind people, straying from the way of truth, did he enable to see the sight by which Christ is seen? Into how many ears did he pour the precious hearing of heavenly commandments through his words? How many inwardly wounded people did he heal through the skill of his angelic mouth and the power of his prayer? How many souls, already dead in the body through sins, did he call back to amendment as though to light [Col. 1138D] and so restore to life?

Every day he taught his children not to covet the possessions of others, not to find the wives of strangers beautiful, and not to allow the poison of sin to enter the soul through the eyes. From how many hearts—hearts possessed by iniquity and impiety—did he drive out lust, remove anger, and restrain envy, bringing faith, chastity, and mercy back into them?

How many did that apostolic man restore from the death of sins through the medicines of repentance, as guardian of souls, cutting away desires, restraining anger, and uprooting wickedness? That man had been especially necessary in those times when such great iniquity, daily gathering strength as righteousness declined, was growing powerful.

Indeed, although he was established in this worldly pilgrimage in body alone, in thought he dwelt in that eternal homeland. Crucified and dead to this world, whatever he labored for, he transferred from this life to that one; he continually moved it from the left hand to the right, and stored his sweat in heaven.

Amid all this, the blessed man sought to flee the vainglory of virtues, although exalted grace could not remain hidden in him. Thus God’s faithful and prudent servant not only tamed human hearts, savage with bestial ferocity, into the gentleness of Christ, knowing how to give his fellow servants their measure of wheat at the proper time—that is, to provide the nourishment of the divine word in measured and timely fashion according to the capacity of his hearers—but also tamed birds, so that in this holy man the innocence and power of the first Adam, before he sinned, might be understood as restored through the second Adam, our Lord Jesus Christ. For, as Scripture shows, all irrational creatures had been subjected to him (Genesis 1; Psalm 8) [Col. 1139B].

### XI

When it happened that he was having a more private meal among his household and taking pleasure in the cheerfulness of his dear companions, fearless sparrows would come down to him and gather the remains of the meal in his hand. Some departed satisfied, while others came to be satisfied. Thus the wildness of the birds was tamed through the exercise of virtue.

His pleasure in the cheerfulness of his dear companions was like what we read about blessed Job: “The light of my face did not fall to the ground” (Job 29). He was accustomed to maintain such gravity in his expression that he was never relaxed into contemptible merriment. Whenever he presented himself as more cheerful to those around him, he always did so for a definite useful purpose.

So too this holy man, disciplined in all things by religious gravity, did not act from vain display or frivolity. Rather, he did so so that the grace granted him by God might be shown, and so that the hearts of his people might be stirred to love and faith in him who is wondrous in his saints, who deigns to console and glorify his servants in many ways, and might devote themselves more earnestly to his service.

Nor should we pass over without consideration why this holy man, in the cheerfulness of his loved ones, took greater pleasure in the tameness and feeding of sparrows than of other birds. To put the matter simply at first: people commonly keep other birds as domestic creatures in their houses, but sparrows, although they usually live on roofs—as we read and know from observation—and delight in human proximity, are not ordinarily kept as household pets inside people’s houses.

Therefore, if he had fed birds that were normally kept domestically in houses, it would not have been regarded as a miracle, nor would there have been anything to delight the diners. Moreover, there was no opportunity to gather in a more private room with other birds that are not ordinarily kept inside domestic chambers, except sparrows, which customarily live on roofs and delight in human proximity, in order to demonstrate the divine grace granted to God’s servant.

### XII

But if we wish to investigate something deeper in this act of the holy man, we can understand that no birds are commended so frequently in Scripture as the sparrow, the dove, and the turtledove. The dove and the turtledove, which are accustomed to produce lamentation instead of song, signify the mourning of the saints in the present age and their heavenly desires through the hidden tears of prayer and the public songs of the Church [Note: [Col. 1139D] This seems to be the correct reading; the word had been obliterated.]

The sparrow, however, is a bird small in body but greatly watchful in its cleverness. It is not easily caught in snares, nor is it deceived by greed for food through the gluttony of its belly. Because of its weakness, and so that either it itself may not be caught by its ambusher or its young may not be devoured by serpentine plots, it hastens to the lofty tops of houses.

A prudent and humble person is rightly compared to it: fleeing the deceits of diabolical cunning, such a person hastens to fortify himself within the enclosure of the holy Church through vigils, prayers, and tears of repentance [Col. 1140B].

Our Redeemer and Savior also deigned to be represented as a sparrow, as the Psalmist testifies:

“For even the sparrow has found a house for itself” (Psalm 83).

The sparrow has indeed found a house for itself, because our Redeemer entered the dwelling of eternal heaven, where he became “like a sparrow alone upon the roof” (Psalm 101): alone among the dead, free, he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high, made so much superior to the angels as he has inherited a name more distinguished than theirs (Hebrews 1), so that he is and is called the Son of God. “This is the true God and eternal life” (John 5).

While established in this pilgrimage, the soul of every faithful person sighs for him and rejoices in this way: through right faith, holy desires, and good works, it senses that its dwelling in the kingdom of heaven is being prepared, just as a sparrow rejoices in a hole in the wall. That is, the truly faithful person rejoices in the hole of the material substance, namely, in the unity of the Church, which is watered with a bath and a drink from the pierced side of Christ on the cross. Protected from the malignity of the evil spirit and his members, the faithful person rejoices there.

Although born from bloods, from the will of the flesh, and from the will of man, the faithful person has been redeemed by the blood of Jesus, the Son of God, from the power of darkness; born of water and the Spirit, by which the same Lord our God was born from the glorious ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, the faithful person himself has been reborn from the virginal mother Church in the immaculate womb of the divine font, incorporated into Christ, and rejoices with indescribable joy and exultation.

### XIII

There are other things that we can draw from this deed of the blessed apostle of the Franks for the increase of our usefulness—for the Franks are the signs of his apostleship, as we shall show in due course—by comparing it with the deed of the apostle John.

It is reported by the account of our elders that when a bird called a partridge had been presented alive and healthy to the blessed apostle John by someone, he began gently to stroke and handle it. Seeing this, one of the young men laughingly said to his companions:

“Look how that old man plays with the little bird like a child.”

The blessed apostle, perceiving this through the Spirit [Col. 1141A], called the young man to him and asked what he was holding in his hand.

“A bow,” the young man replied.

“And what is the function of what you are holding in your hand?” asked blessed John.

“We shoot beasts, birds, or anything else with it,” he answered.

“And how, or in what manner?” John asked.

The young man bent the bow, drew it, and held it drawn in his hand. But when blessed John said nothing further to him, after some time the young man relaxed the bow.

“Why did you relax the bow?” John asked.

“Because,” the young man replied, “if it were held drawn for too long, it would shoot the arrow with less force.”

“Thus,” the holy apostle said, “human frailty, if it always remains rigid in contemplation and does not condescend to itself, is necessarily lifted less effectively on the wing of contemplation [Col. 1141B].”

This is brought about by the kindly providence of our Creator and Savior, so that through the grace bestowed upon us we may grow in the progress of virtue, and through knowledge of our weakness learn to preserve the virtue of humility. By this deed and discourse he provided great edification for instruction to those who heard him and were present, and left it likewise to those who would come afterward.

So too, from this deed of the blessed Remigius, we can derive the greatest edification for instruction: both in the dear love of our loved ones and in the prudent condescension appropriate to our weakness. He supplied the sparrows with food, although they neither sow nor gather into barns, but God feeds them. When some had been satisfied and he had received others to be satisfied, we too—having received possessions and resources either by inheritance from our kin or through the gifts of the faithful—should joyfully provide whatever good we can to brothers who have not prepared anything for themselves, since “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9).

We should welcome others to whom we may distribute our goods, rejoicing more in good works than in good possessions, so that God too may rejoice in our good work, since he foretold that he would say to those who labor in mercy at the judgment:

“What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25).

### XIV

It happened at a certain time, while he was customarily traveling around the parishes with pastoral skill, so that if anything were being done negligently in divine worship the faithful servant of Christ might recognize it and, like a good farmer, cultivate what was untilled so that it might produce the fruits of good works, that he came to a village called Calmacianus [Calmicianus].

There, while a certain blind man, possessed at intervals by the invasion of a demon that concealed itself, had asked him for the help of mercy—for the demon could not remain hidden before the presence of this holy man; it belonged to the kind of which the Lord says in the Gospel, “This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Mark 9)—the same blind man began to be tormented by bodily suffering through the demon’s assault by which he had earlier been seized.

Then blessed Remigius, in prayer, by which he always directed his mind toward the Lord, humbly prostrated on the ground the body that he continually afflicted with fasts and the exercise of good works. Immediately he restored the former light to the blind man’s eyes, drove the plague of the unclean spirit away from him, and commanded it in the name of Christ never again to presume to torment him. He also granted the poor man the assistance of sustenance that he had requested.

O ineffable grace of mercy, by which, although only one substance was requested, a threefold remedy was obtained! He fed the needy man, endowed the blind man with sight, and restored the captive to freedom. Thus, through this remarkable miracle, the mystery of the Holy Trinity came about: when One appeared in the poor man, the Trinity revealed itself in his salvation.

### XV

Whoever feels himself oppressed by the assaults of the ancient enemy—whether hidden in the mind or manifest in the body—should earnestly ask for the help of Remigius’s intercession. If he asks faithfully, he should have no doubt that, through the merits and prayers of this holy man, he will be freed by God’s grace from the assault of the unclean spirit.

Whoever is ignorant of the light of heavenly contemplation, whoever is weighed down by the darkness of the present life and, because he does not lovingly behold the life to come, does not know where to direct the step of his conduct, should ask through Remigius’s intercession before the Lord’s mercy for the light of understanding and contemplation and for the necessary compunction of heart, without any hesitation, because he will certainly receive it.

Whoever recognizes that he is constrained by spiritual poverty in food and clothing—that is, by poverty of faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues—or feels himself afflicted by temporal necessities and tribulations, should seek the comfort of Remigius’s intercession with groans and tears, and should trust that he will obtain the consolation that the poor, the blind, and the demon-possessed man obtained through him.

Yet if the Lord should delay answering the prayers of this intercessor of ours at the first tears of the petitioner—that is, if he should delay granting soundness of mind to one who has gone astray or bringing help to one suffering need—even then one must not cease asking, seeking, and knocking, nor must one fall into despair of obtaining the request. Rather, one must persevere with such insistence and approach the Savior with such obstinate persistence, together with the intercessions of this protector and helper of ours, and with such a cry, until he himself pleads from heaven before the Lord for his petitioner.

Thus, if the petitioner does not change his mind from the intention he has adopted, he will by no means be deprived of the fruit of his pious request. And if someone intercedes either for his own weakness or on behalf of others, he will obtain the desired result—unless the heart of the petitioner should reproach him in his petition because he remembers that he is resisting his commands. For it is certainly fitting that anyone should be excluded from his benefits who does not wish to be subject to his commands [Col. 1142D].

The salutary remedy in this matter is that, whenever the mind reproaches itself from the memory of its fault, it should first mourn in prayer that it has gone astray. Then, when the stain of error is covered with tears, the face of the heart may appear clean before its creator in its petition.

One must also take care not to fall again into what one rejoices to have cleansed with tears, lest, when the wept-for sin is committed again, even the lament itself be made light of in the sight of the just Judge, and the heart again reproach the past while making its petition. For everyone is deeply ashamed when, whether reading or hearing, he encounters the commandments of God, which he has despised in his life; and, confused by this, he turns to pray to God.

Hence John says:

“If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God; and whatever we ask, we shall receive from him” (1 John 3).

As though he were saying: If we do what he commands, we obtain what we ask. For before God these two things necessarily correspond with one another: prayer must be supported by conduct, and conduct by prayer.

Therefore Jeremiah says:

“Let us examine our ways and seek, and let us return to the Lord. Let us lift our hearts with our hands to God in heaven” (Lamentations 3).

To examine our ways is to investigate the inner workings of our thoughts. A person lifts the heart with the hands when he strengthens his prayer with works. Whoever prays but refuses to act lifts his heart but does not lift his hands. Whoever acts but does not pray lifts his hands but does not lift his heart.

According to the voice of the laborer, the heart receives confidence in prayer when no perversity of life contradicts it [Col. 1143B].

### XVI

This most blessed bishop did not lessen his concern for inner things amid his outward occupations, nor did he abandon care for outward things amid his concern for the inner life.

As he traveled around the parish with pastoral care, he passed through Condumum, a village of the bishopric called Tudiniacus. There he saw reapers cutting the harvest. Approaching them, he encouraged them with a word of preaching and gave them food and drink to console them in their labor.

While this was taking place, it happened that his cousin, named Celsa, consecrated to God, was passing by and going to her property called Celtum. When she learned that Saint Remigius was beside the road along which she was traveling [Col. 1143C], she came to him. Kindly received by him, as was fitting, she asked the holy man to deign to visit her house together with her, since that was where she was going.

As he was gracious toward worthy requests, the holy man agreed to the petition of his cousin. When they had reached the house together and were engaged in familiar and spiritual conversation, Celsa’s steward came to her ear and said that her bailiff had already sold the wine that had been in that estate, except for a small quantity that he had reserved for preserving the vessel.

When Saint Remigius saw her face suffused with blushes, he asked what her steward had whispered in her ear. She promptly replied that she was embarrassed not so much because of the news itself as because of those who had arrived with him [Col. 1143D].

When he learned the reason, blessed Remigius consoled her with a cheerful expression, saying:

“Do not grieve over this, daughter. The Lord will, through the generosity of his mercy, provide his customary consolation from it; through his Prophet he promised that those who fear him would lack nothing” (Psalm 38).

He told his cousin, in the hearing of those who were present, to attend to her other concerns, while he wished meanwhile to go around her garden, orchard, and buildings and see how they were situated.

Thus, deliberately going around the other places first, he came to the cellar door. When he asked what the building contained, the steward replied that it was a cellar. The holy man said that he wished to enter.

Since no one dared to oppose him, he asked the cellarer whether any of those vessels contained anything, or whether any wine remained in them. When the vessel in which some wine remained had been pointed out, he said:

“Close the door, and remain on this side until I return to you.”

He went to the other end of the vessel, which stood beside the wall, made the sign of the cross over the vessel—which was of no small size—and, bending his knees in prayer, prayed for a long time. Then the wine began to overflow through the upper opening through which it had been poured into the vessel, so abundantly that it flooded the floor of the house.

While the holy man was still lying in prayer, the cellarer, struck with fear, cried out:

“In the name of Christ, who has ever seen such a thing?”

When Saint Remigius heard this, he rose from prayer and ordered him to tell no one about it, but to tell his mistress’s servants that he had obtained enough wine for them to distribute [Col. 1144B].

The saint of the Lord then returned to his aforementioned cousin and consoled her, saying:

“Daughter, do not grieve, but hope in the Lord, do good, and you shall be fed with his riches” (Psalm 36). “You now have wine; let us rejoice and exult in the Lord.”

When she and her people had learned of the event through the cellar—for it is written, “It is honorable to recount the works of the Lord” (Tobit 12)—his cousin said to him:

“Now I know, holy Father, that by divine inspiration I called you to this house today. Therefore I shall make you and your Church perpetual heirs of this estate.”

And immediately she transferred that estate itself to the Church of Reims, and made a charter and formal legal conveyance of it to the same holy bishop according to legal custom [Col. 1144C].

### XVII

We marvel that, according to the word of Elisha (2 Kings 4), large vessels were filled with oil from a small quantity of oil. Let us marvel that, through the blessing and prayer of the Lord and of our father and patron Remigius, a vessel of no small size overflowed with wine from the small amount of liquid that was in it, so that the wine even ran over onto the floor of the cellar.

And we, who are drunk with the desires [perhaps: pleasures] of the flesh, who have made others sin as well, and who have intoxicated them with sins, enticing them to sin either by our example or by our word—emptied of Christ and vessels empty of spiritual gifts—if, in memory of this blessed bishop, we vomit out from the depths of our hearts, through pure confession with contrition and groaning of heart, the poison of our iniquities, which we have greedily swallowed with delight like wine; if we empty ourselves of the gall of sins with which we have been filled; and if we wash ourselves with tears, lifting our hearts with pure hands, without anger or dispute, toward God, let us believe that through his merits and prayers we can obtain the grace of being filled with the abundant grace of God, so that a fountain of life may come to be in us and, in his light, we may see light.

### XVIII

Then let us believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation that the Son is wholly in the Father, and the Father wholly in the Word; that the Holy Spirit is wholly in the Father and in the Son; and that the same Holy Spirit proceeds wholly from the Father and the Son.

We shall see this in form in the future, when, according to his promise [Col. 1145A], our Lord Jesus Christ will openly announce to us the Father. Then, through the revealed appearance of his majesty, he will show both how he is born from the one who begets him without being unequal to him, and how the Spirit of both proceeds from both, who are coeternal.

Then we shall plainly see how that which exists by being born does not follow after the one from whom it is born, and how he who is produced by procession is not preceded by those who bring him forth. Then we shall plainly see how the Three are indivisibly One and the One indivisibly Three.

Let us therefore believe and confess that the holy and inseparable Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is coeternal, consubstantial, and coequal with itself, possessing one divinity, essence, omnipotence, glory, greatness, majesty, and everything that is said of it substantially, that is, in relation to itself.

Relationally, however, there are three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The unity of the inseparable nature cannot have separable persons. This is also shown by the fact that the persons cannot be divided in the Trinity, since the name of any one person always refers to another person. If you say “Father,” you indicate the Son. If you name the Son, you proclaim the Father. If you call upon the Holy Spirit, you must understand that he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

The following rule must also be observed: every name of nature or essence, when spoken of one person, must likewise always be expressed in the singular when spoken of the three. Nothing in God is to be spoken of according to accident, because nothing in him is changeable.

Whatever the Father is in quality and greatness, such also is the Son, and such also is the Holy Spirit. The three persons spoken of together are not in any respect greater than each person individually, because the same greatness exists in each person when named individually as exists in the three persons when named together [Col. 1145C].

### XIX

Only one person of that same holy Trinity—the person of the Son, through whom all things were made—through the operation of the Holy Spirit, assumed from the immaculate flesh of the perpetual Virgin Mary the substance of our flesh, animated by a rational and intellectual soul of our nature. Through the incomprehensible operation of his power, he assumed the whole human being in the unity of his divine person, so that he might save the whole human being.

The Lord’s birth according to the flesh, although it possesses certain characteristics by which it transcends the beginnings of human existence—whether because he alone was conceived and born from an inviolate Virgin without concupiscence, or because he was brought forth from his mother’s womb in such a way that fertility gave birth while virginity remained—nevertheless had flesh of no other nature than ours. Nor was another kind of soul breathed into him at the beginning, one that excelled not through difference of origin but through sublimity of virtue.

He had nothing opposed within his flesh, nor did discord among desires produce conflict among wills. His bodily senses were vigorous without the law of sin, and the truth of his affections was under the governance of divinity and mind: he was neither tempted by enticements nor overcome by injuries.

The true man was truly united to God, but, according to the soul that already existed, he was brought down from heaven; he was not created from nothing according to the flesh [Col. 1146A]. He retained the same person of the Word’s divinity while possessing in body and soul the nature common to us. For he would not be the mediator of God and human beings unless he were both the same God and the same human being, one and true in both.

This servile form, assumed by the Son of God alone, was fashioned by the whole Holy Trinity—whose will and operation are one—in the womb of the glorious and ever-Virgin Mary, just as the archangel announced to her:

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the Holy One who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

This whole Holy Trinity—that is, God the Father, designated by the title “Most High”; and his power and wisdom, which built a house for itself (Proverbs 9)—namely, the only-begotten Son himself, the author of the work and the work of the author, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, formed the humanity of our Savior, namely, his body and soul, in the Virgin’s womb. Through divinity she became the servant of man, and through the flesh the mother of the Word [Col. 1146B].

The flesh was not first conceived in the Virgin’s womb and divinity later come into the flesh. Rather, as soon as the Word came into the womb, the Word, while preserving the truth of his own nature, became flesh. A perfect human being—that is, one possessing the truth of flesh and a rational soul—was born through the Virgin’s womb: the Son of God, anointed with the oil of gladness, that is, with the gift of the Holy Spirit, above his companions (Psalm 44), namely, above the other human beings.

We first become sinful human beings and afterward are sanctified through the anointing of the Holy Spirit. He, however, existing as God before the ages, was conceived as a human being in the Virgin’s womb through the Holy Spirit at the end of the ages. There he was anointed by the same Spirit where he was conceived; he was not conceived first and anointed afterward. Rather, the very act of being conceived from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin’s flesh caused him to be anointed by the Holy Spirit.

In him it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell bodily (Colossians 2), that is, substantially, because the Word, through his omnipotence, willed that this perfect human being whom he assumed should become in time what he himself had always been outside time: namely, the proper Son of God. Thus two Sons of God cannot be spoken of—one begotten before the ages and another made in time—lest, God forbid, a quaternity be asserted in the Holy Trinity on account of his incarnation [Col. 1146D].

For God the Son of God assumed human nature, not a human person, assuming the temporal substance of humanity into the eternal person of divinity. The human being passed into God, not through a changeability of nature, but because of the unity of the divine person.

For just as in the Holy Trinity the person of the Father is one, the person of the Son another, and the person of the Holy Spirit another, but the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, so in the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, the divinity is one thing, the soul another, and the body another; yet the person of divinity is not one and the person of humanity another. Rather, there is one and the same person.

Therefore there are not two Christs or two Sons, but one Christ and one Son, God and human being, according to the Evangelist, “full of grace” (John 1) [Col. 1147A]. He is full of truth because, in the fullness of his humanity, the fullness of divinity dwells.

Blessed Mary the Virgin, preserving the integrity of her body, gave birth to him as one Son, God and human being, just as she conceived him while preserving her virginity: the creator of human bodies and souls, which are incorporated by the same God their maker and did not exist before they were breathed into their bodies.

But because the whole offspring of the human race was corrupted through the transgression of the first human being, no one can be freed from the condition of the old human being except through the sacrament of Christ’s baptism. In it there is no distinction among those reborn: although sex in the body and age in time distinguish people, grace gives birth to all alike into one infancy, as the Apostle says:

“For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female: for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3).

After assuming Christ’s humanity, the divinity did not abandon it in any property of its operations that distinguishes the natures in him, not even in the Passion itself, although the divinity always remains impassible in its own nature.

### XX

And since John the Baptist said that the abundance of the Spirit had been given uniquely and without measure to that same Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells (John 3), whose soul and flesh are one Christ with the Word, and one only Son, his soul has always possessed—and possesses—the full knowledge of divinity within itself, with which it is believed naturally to have one person. For he is the one who gives the Spirit to the saints; he is the one who receives it. He is equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity. And because he is powerful enough to give according to measure, he ought not therefore to receive according to measure. Remaining in the form of God, he gives the Spirit; receiving the form of a servant, he received the Spirit. For he received whole the very Spirit whom he gives according to measure.

The same one is both priest and sacrifice: coming to us to offer on our behalf what he assumed from us, so that he might take away from us what he found in us—that is, sin—the mediator between God and human beings, possessing with the Father the same nature of divinity and, with his mother, the same substance of humanity. From us he possessed, even unto death, the penalty for our iniquity; from God the Father he possessed unchangeable justice. Temporarily dead on account of our iniquity, he is himself always living on account of his justice. The same one who is Lord and King of glory (Psalm 23) was crucified in our weakness, but lives by his own power.

The same God who, made human, hung upon the cross, and the same God who, made human, lay in the tomb: yet in the tomb the same God lay according to the flesh alone, and into the underworld he descended according to the soul alone; and he rose on the third day in the flesh, because he committed no sin from which the soul would have had to rise (1 Corinthians 15). The same God and human being ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, coming to judge the living and the dead. For whatever is read as having been done in Christ was accomplished by the one Christ and by the one Son of God. The whole Christ personally deigned to perform this. Indeed, he is found to have brought about his own sufferings, since he had nothing that he suffered unwillingly.

His soul possesses such holiness and justification that all the souls of those who believe in him can be sanctified and justified through it. His flesh possesses such purity and freedom from sin that all the flesh of those who trust in him can, through the divine grace working in him, be cleansed and liberated. For the blood that flowed from that same flesh, wounded by the soldier’s spear (John 19), is the price of human salvation.

Through its outpouring, that flame guarding Paradise was extinguished, and the way was opened for the faithful to the tree of life, which was planted beside the channels of living waters (Psalm 1). The wisest Solomon, when he had said much in praise of wisdom, remembered this tree and spoke as follows: “Blessed is the man who has found wisdom and who abounds in prudence” (Proverbs 3). And shortly afterward: “Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceful” (Proverbs 3). “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her, and blessed is the one who holds her.”

John the Baptist, seeing Christ—the power of God and the wisdom of God—and his own precursor coming toward him, pointed him out with his finger to the people to whom he had long preached him, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). Behold the Lamb of God; behold the innocent one, free from every sin, for he has bone from Adam’s bones and flesh from Adam’s flesh, but he drew no stain of guilt from sinful flesh. Behold him who takes away the sin of the world; behold the one who, just among sinners and gentle among the impious—that is, appearing like a lamb among wolves—also possesses the power to justify sinners and the impious.

### XXI

But how he takes away the sin of the world, and by what order he justifies the impious, the apostle Peter shows when he says: “You were not redeemed with corruptible silver or gold from your futile way of life inherited from your ancestors, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1). And in the Apocalypse the apostle John says: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Revelation 1).

He not only washed us from our sins in his blood when he gave his blood for us upon the cross, or when each one of us was washed in the waters of baptism into the mystery of his most holy passion; rather, he also takes away the sins of the world daily and washes us from our daily sins in his blood, when the memory of that blessed passion is renewed at the altar, when the creation of bread and wine is transformed into the sacrament of his body and blood by the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit. Thus his body and blood are not poured out and slain by the hands of unbelievers to their destruction, but are received by the mouths of the faithful for salvation.

The paschal lamb in the Law rightly displayed a figure of this. Having once freed the people from Egyptian slavery, it used to sanctify that same people every year by its sacrifice, in memory of that liberation (Exodus 12), until the one to whom such a victim bore witness should come. Offered to the Father for us as a sacrifice and as an odor of sweetness, he transferred the mystery of his passion, through the offering of the lamb, into the creation of bread and wine. He became a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek; through his own blood he entered once for all into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption (Hebrews 5 and 6).

For the Word who was in the beginning, God with God, the everlasting food of the holy angels, on which the heavenly powers live, became flesh—that is, the same Word of God who was with God became human, as has been said and must always be believed and proclaimed. By his authorship and redemption, the blessed spirits now live in heaven on everlasting food, and the entire Church of the saints will live forever.

We are nourished by his true flesh from the cross and drink his true and living blood, which flowed from his side upon the cross. When eaten and drunk, he remains whole and alive, because he rose after being slain. In this mystical distribution of spiritual nourishment, this is imparted and this is received: that, receiving the power of the heavenly food, we may pass into the flesh of him who became our flesh, and that, having been crucified in him, having died with him, been buried with him, and raised with him, we may bear him in every respect in flesh and spirit.

For otherwise, in the holy Church, which is his body, neither priesthoods are valid nor sacrifices true, unless the true high priest reconciles us in the reality of our nature, and the true blood of the immaculate Lamb cleanses us. Although he is seated at the Father’s right hand, in that same flesh which he assumed from the Virgin he continues to carry out the sacrament of propitiation, as the Apostle says: “Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Romans 8).

### XXII

Since we have been filled with this grace and persevere in it until the end of life, let us ask that we may be multiplied through the merits and prayers of this father of ours, by the fruit of God’s grain, wine, and oil—that is, by holy teaching, heavenly wisdom, and the mercy of divine grace. Thus, inebriated by the abundance of his house and by its richness—namely, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, with which the Catholic Church, which is his house and body, is filled—may rivers of living water flow from our belly, that is, from our minds, spiritual teachings which are the life of the soul.

And those whom he cleansed through baptism from all the filth of sins, may he preserve in the purity of life, washed from every crime through the tears of repentance, and bring them pure to eternal life.

### XXIII

The adversary of the human race does not cease to display the power of his wickedness by inflicting harm. By his sending forth suddenly arising globes of flame, he set this city of Rheims on fire. When an immense devastation had arisen, the conflagration had already consumed nearly a third of the city, with the ashes still remaining, and the victorious flame was licking what remained.

When news of this reached the hearing of the most blessed bishop Remigius, he immediately prostrated himself in prayer in the basilica of the blessed Nicasius, bishop and martyr of this city—for he was then staying there. Rising from prayer, he looked up to heaven, groaned, and said: “God, my God, attend to my voice.” Then he ran swiftly down the stone steps laid before that very church and made for the city. His footprints were impressed upon those stones as though upon soft mud; they are still shown there today in memory of the divine miracle.

He ran swiftly in this way and placed himself before the fire. As soon as he extended his right hand toward the fire and made the sign of the holy cross while invoking the name of Christ, the whole conflagration, as though it had recognized some accusation against itself, its power broken and shattered and beaten back upon itself, began to flee before the presence of the man of God.

The man of God continually pursued it and, between the fire and what still remained untouched, opposed himself to it with the sign of the holy cross and the invocation of Christ. Thus, through divine power, he drove the entire mass of flame—which was fleeing before him—through the open gate. It was then called this because, while the other gates were closed for the city’s protection, it stood open during the day for the convenience of those going out and coming in.

He then closed that gate with another gate assigned for this purpose and prohibited anyone from ever opening it, threatening punishment against whoever should presume to open it, just as Joshua invoked vengeance upon the one who would rebuild the walls of Jericho, which had been thrown down by God’s power (Joshua 6).

After some years, a certain citizen named Fercintus, who lived beside that gate, made a hole in the masonry with which the same gate had been blocked, through which he might throw out the manure from his yard. Such vengeance immediately followed him that, when disaster came upon that house, neither human being nor animal remained there.

In this miracle God’s grace declared to everyone that the man of God, full of faith, had honored the fire of divine love more greatly: by his holy merits he conquered, drove out, and extinguished the fury of such great indignation. For in this event, because Remigius’s footprints were impressed upon flint and the blessed Peter’s customary steps were made to stand upon an unstable element at the Lord’s command, although in a different manner, we nevertheless behold the work of Christ with the same faith and grace.

For we also read in true histories that in the holy city of Jerusalem there is preserved an extremely hard stone on which the pious footprints of the Redeemer are shown, from the time when he stood before Pilate the judge. Yet his words could not be impressed upon Pilate’s heart, harder than stone, because his sins demanded this.

### XXIV

By displaying the footprints of his servant Remigius impressed upon flint, destined to fight against the malice of the devil, whose member Pilate was, Christ deigned to show that he had given Remigius, just as he had said to his disciples while present in the flesh, the power to tread upon every power of the enemy (Luke 10).

Indeed, in this deed he also wished to demonstrate the grace of his power: how precious are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things (Isaiah 52). Through Remigius he was taking something away from the hard-hearted [the object is not specified in the supplied text], and was going to take away stony hearts from the unbelieving Franks; he was giving, and was going to give, soft hearts to the obstinate and unbelieving, so that they might receive the seeds of the divine word and produce fruit in due season through perseverance.

The Lord himself, moreover, who built the Church by the water and blood poured forth from his side pierced upon the cross—by which the same Church is watered through the laver and through the cup—also wished, through this servant of his to whom he entrusted the governance of his Church, to demonstrate uniquely what he had foretold concerning that same Church, figured beforehand by Moses, when footprints were impressed upon stone, so that footprints stronger than rocks and rocks softer than footprints were displayed: “Iron and bronze shall be your shoe” (Deuteronomy 33).

In holy Scripture, a shoe signifies the protection of preaching, as it is written: “With your feet shod in the preaching of the gospel of peace” (Ephesians 6). Since strength is expressed through iron and perseverance through bronze, it is said that “iron and bronze shall be his shoe,” when his preaching is fortified at once by sharpness and steadfastness. Through iron he pierces opposing evils; through bronze he patiently preserves the good things he has proposed.

In the fact that this holy man, standing between the fire and what the blaze had not yet touched, with the sign of the cross and the invocation of Christ’s name, prevented the flames from passing beyond him—and who, with his companions, could say, “We are the good odor of Christ for God” (2 Corinthians 2) in every place—the miracle of God was represented, as when Aaron the high priest, in order to appease the Lord’s anger, took a censer with fragrant incense and stood between the dead and the living (Numbers 16).

By his merits and prayers, let us ask that the flames of vices may be extinguished within us and that we may be freed from the everlasting fire of intolerable torments.

Concerning the fact that the citizen mentioned above presumed to open, contrary to the prohibition of the blessed Remigius, the gate which he had closed, and did not escape vengeance, let us also fear to disregard the words and commands of the saints. For, with God speaking through them, the speech of those who pass away expresses judgments that remain without change.

### XXV

A certain girl, born in the city of Toulouse to distinguished parents, had been held captive under the siege of an evil spirit from childhood. Her most devout parents loved her tenderly and brought her with a great multitude and much devotion to the tomb of Saint Peter in the city of Rome.

At that time there was in those regions a man of memorable life, Benedict by grace and by name, resplendent with many virtues.

[Note: Here Baronius, in volume VI of the *Annals*, charges Hincmar with an error: that, in place of Benedict, the girl’s father, a very wealthy man in the province, he wove this account from the history of Saint Benedict. He proves this from the testament of Saint Remigius, found in Briss. and in Flod., *History of Rheims*, book V, chapter 18. See Baronius, year 507.]

When the girl’s parents heard of his reputation, they brought her to that same servant of God. He labored for her correction from the most hostile demon and earnestly sought to entreat the Lord’s power through many fasts and prayers.

When he could cure her by no intercession, nor drive out the cunning demon’s poison from her, the ancient enemy, adjured by many and most powerful exorcisms and constrained by an oath invoking the divine name, gave this answer: he could never be expelled from that dwelling by anyone other than through the prayers of this most blessed bishop Remigius.

Then her parents, carrying letters from that man of God Benedict, began to make their way to the city of Rheims. Since the girl’s parents were highly honored and close to Alaric, king of the Goths, who had established his seat in the city of Toulouse and possessed, together with the Gothic kingdom, a large part of Gaul—and since they were reported to be his blood relatives—they came to this city with his letters and envoys, bringing the girl bound with them to the blessed Remigius, so that they might recognize through him the power of Christ in the purification of their child, whose condition they had already learned from the confession of the demon.

The blessed Remigius, after long resistance, insisted that he was not worthy of so great a work and opposed the request with his customary patience. But he was overcome by the prayers of the supplicant people, so that he might pour out a prayer for her and sympathize with her parents’ tears.

Then, armed with the merits of holiness, he commanded by the authority of his word that the wicked robber should depart by the way through which he had entered and release Christ’s maidservant. Accordingly, he came out through the mouth by which he had entered, with immense vomiting and an obscene stench.

But shortly afterward, when the bishop had departed, within that same hour, while the girl, exhausted by immense suffering, nodded and was deceived by the loss of bodily warmth, she lost the breath of life.

The crowd of supplicants therefore returned to the physician with repeated prayers. The holy man accused himself rather of having caused her death than of having granted the reward of health, and of having become guilty of homicide rather than having supplied a remedy.

He therefore returned, prevailed upon by the people’s entreaty, to the basilica of Saint John the Baptist, where the lifeless body lay. There the holy Remigius prostrated himself in prayer with tears upon the pavement of the saints and urged the others to do the same.

Then, after pouring out a flood of tears, he rose and raised the dead girl, whom he had previously healed while she was sick. Taking her hand, he said: “Girl, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, arise.” Immediately she rose with complete bodily health, as she herself later acknowledged, from the very enclosures of hell, and happily returned to her own people.

### XXVI

Having been stripped of the frailty of the flesh and joined to the angelic choirs, he can rescue his own people and anyone who asks with faith from the fall of any impending danger by his merits and prayers. He can restore anyone turned from evil to good from the death of any sin, and also free that person from future everlasting death—the one who, while still placed in the prison of corruptible flesh, was able to restore life to a dead woman.

For this reason, since there are two deaths in each of us—one of the soul through sin, and the other of the body because of sin, as punishment for sin—there is death of the soul when God abandons it on account of the magnitude of its sins, and death of the body when it is abandoned by the soul.

There are also two resurrections: now, the resurrection of the soul in the Church through the Son, the Word of God, when by his grace it rises from the death of iniquity; this is the first resurrection. Whoever possesses it will also rise happily in the second resurrection, which is that of the body, to eternal life, through the Word of God made flesh, the Son of Man, who received authority to execute judgment. This judgment will take place at the end of the age; there will be no resurrection of souls there, but of bodies.

Let us therefore ask with contrite heart and tears, with good works assisting us, through the intercession of this patron of ours, that we may be raised from the death of the soul in the present life, so that we may live in Christ; and that, rising in the body at the end of the age, we may live eternally with Christ.

Let us firmly believe that through his intercession this can be obtained for us from the Lord’s mercy, if we ask faithfully. For in the girl’s first healing from the demon and afterward in the resurrection of her body from death, we have received the surest pledge of his merits.

### XXVII

Let us carefully keep before the eyes of our minds the hour of our departure from the body. Let us go before the face of the Lord in confession of our sins, with tears and good works, forgiving those who have sinned against us, so that we may be able to obtain forgiveness of our sins from the Lord’s mercy. Let us not neglect the good things that we are now able to do.

For the things we have done in this world, we shall receive a fitting reward in that world from him who, as it is written, “will repay each one according to his works” (Romans 12).

To say nothing of the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and other men of stricter and more perfect life, who, as soon as they are released from the corruption of the flesh, penetrate the heavens and can already see as equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit in the nature of divinity the one whom they knew as mortal in their own flesh—one of them, conscious of his own struggles, did not hesitate to testify concerning himself: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1).

There are many righteous people in the Church who, after the dissolution of the flesh, are immediately received into the blessed rest of Paradise. They await, in great joy and amid the great choirs of those rejoicing with them, the time when, having received their bodies again, they will come and appear before the face of God.

Yet some, although predestined on account of their good works to the lot of the elect, because they departed from the body stained by certain evils are received after death to be severely chastised in the flames of purgatorial fire. Either they are cleansed from the filth of vices through the long examination that continues until the day of judgment, or, previously released from their punishments through the prayers, almsgiving, fasts, tears, and offerings of the saving sacrifice made by faithful friends, they themselves reach the rest of the blessed.

Hence it must be considered that the safer way is for each person, while alive, to do personally the good that he hopes will be done for him by others after his death. It is indeed more blessed to depart free than to seek freedom after imprisonment.

### XXVIII

Finally, when a certain sick man of a family of no mean standing, still unbaptized, asked that Saint Remigius visit him, and, already as if at the last breath, confessed that he believed and requested baptism, the sick man renounced the devil and the holy water was blessed. Saint Remigius then asked the presbyter of that place for exorcised oil and chrism.

The presbyter replied that he had ordinary oil, but that the exorcised oil and chrism in the ampoules in which they had been kept had entirely run out. Saint Remigius ordered those very ampoules to be brought to him. He placed the empty ampoules upon the altar and prostrated himself in prayer.

When he rose from prayer, he found full the ampoule that had contained a small amount of exorcised oil and the other ampoule that had contained a small amount of sacred chrism.

Thus he anointed with exorcised oil the sick man who had previously renounced the devil, after his renunciation; then, after baptizing him, he anointed him with sacred chrism according to ecclesiastical tradition. Immediately, having recovered the health of his soul, the man also obtained bodily health.

Whom, dearest brothers, should we recognize as imitated and followed by the blessed Remigius in this miracle, if not the one who, at the wedding to which he deigned to come and to signify it by his presence, ordered empty jars to be filled with water and by his command changed that same water into wine? (John 2.)

Certainly the Lord could have filled the empty jars with wine, since at the beginning of the world’s creation he created all things from nothing. But he preferred that the jars be filled with water and that he make wine from that water: so that, through the service of the attendants, the jars might be filled with water, and through the command of his blessing the water might be changed into wine. In this way he clearly showed that, just as he made all things from nothing, so he also changes the natures of things by his sanctification, as he wills.

And the blessed Remigius, servant and friend of the Bridegroom of the Church, could, by the solemn words of the divine mysteries through which he joined the believer to the same body, have exorcised ordinary oil and consecrated sacred chrism, just as he consecrated the font. But he preferred that the Lord should separately fill the ampoules in which the sanctified sacraments had been kept with the power of his blessing, and should show himself faithful in his words—“Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 16)—in order to confirm the faith of the believing neophyte through the service of his servant.

It is certain that he who at the beginning of creation blessed each of his creatures, and by that blessing always caused them to grow and multiply for human use, also continually makes good things from the creatures of bread and wine mixed with water, and from oil, according to his tradition, at the invocation of the priest—not making what they already were, but causing the sacred mysteries to exist as what they had not yet been, namely, his body and blood and the chrism of eternal salvation.

That same one filled each ampoule with oil and, at the invocation of his priest, infused into each the blessing of sanctification.

### XXIX

As histories report, when the Greeks were attacking and conquering the city of Troy, one part of the Frankish people went with Aeneas to Italy; another part of them, namely twelve thousand men, reached the neighboring regions of Pannonia beside the Maeotian marshes. Arriving there, they built a city, which they called Sicambria in memory of themselves. They lived there for many years and grew into a great people until the time of the emperor Valentinian.

[Note: See book 1 of Paulus Aemilius, *On the Deeds of the Franks*.]
