Thus, under long-haired princes succeeding one another according to the custom of the people, they advanced through the region of Thuringia in Germany, from the fortress of Dispargum, where they had long lived, toward the cities of Tournai and Cambrai in the province of Belgica. They therefore occupied part of the province of Belgica along the upper river, where they lived for a very long time under King Clodoveus and the useful king Meroveus. From the latter’s celebrated name the Franks were called Merovingians. In the Attic language, they were called *Franci* by the emperor Valentinian—that is, “fierce.”

Childeric succeeded Meroveus in the principate. From Basina [variant: Bissina], queen of the Thuringians, he had a son named Clodoveus, who was a great king, greater than all the Frankish kings before him, and an exceptionally brave and distinguished warrior.

In those days or at that time the Franks captured the city of Agrippina on the Rhine, which they called Cologne. They also captured the city of Trier on the Moselle, which had previously been destroyed and afflicted by the Huns, taking it after the Huns’ departure.

At that time Romans lived in these regions, around the Rhine as far as the Loire River, and their prince was Aegidius. Beyond the Loire the Goths ruled, and their prince was Alaric. The Burgundians, who were Arians, lived, like the Goths, beside the Rhône River as far as the city of Lyon and the neighboring cities; their prince was Gundobad.

At that time Aegidius died, and his son Syagrius succeeded him as prince of the Romans who lived in Gaul. After Childeric died—he had occupied and devastated the cities of Orléans and Angers with his Frankish army—his son Clodoveus sagaciously assumed the kingdom of the Franks.

In the fifth year of Clodoveus’s reign, Syagrius, the son of Aegidius and commander of the Romans living in Gaul, resided in the city of Soissons, which his father had held. Clodoveus came against him with his army and defeated him. Syagrius had fled to Alaric and lived for some time with him at Toulouse; Clodoveus received him when Alaric sent him over, ordered him to be killed, and subjected everything that had belonged to him to his own power.

### XXX

At that time many churches were plundered by Clodoveus’s army. The soldiers were fanatical and pagan, as was their king. Nevertheless, when they heard of the miracles performed through the blessed Remigius, they revered him. Although they were pagans, they loved the one in whom the heavenly light of grace shone forth for all, and their king willingly listened to him. After hearing him, the king did many things and restrained himself from many wicked acts.

For Saint Remigius was a wise and most holy man, an outstanding rhetorician, renowned for his virtues, restoring sight to the blind, restoring life to the dead, driving out demons, and providing a remedy for the sicknesses of every infirmity.

### XXXI

As the king was passing near the city of Rheims along the road that is called Barbarian to this day because of the Barbarians’ passage along it, he did not wish to enter the city, lest any harm be done there by his army.

Without his will or knowledge, however, a certain group of undisciplined men entered the city, since there was no temporal authority among its inhabitants capable of resisting them. They seized and carried away certain ornaments and sacred vessels, as robbers do. Among these they seized and carried away a pitcher of extraordinary size and beauty.

Saint Remigius sent his messengers to King Clodoveus, asking that, if he did not deserve to receive any other of the Church’s sacred vessels, he would at least order that pitcher to be returned to his messengers.

When the king heard this, he said to the ecclesiastical messengers: “Follow us as far as the city of Soissons, for there all the things that have been acquired will be divided. If that pitcher should fall to me as my share, I will fulfill what the bishop asks.”

When he reached the city of Soissons, he ordered all the plunder that had been carried away or acquired to be brought into the center. When everything had been brought before the king, he said: “I ask you, bravest warriors, not to refuse to give me this pitcher.”

When the king had said this, those Franks who were well disposed replied: “Glorious king, everything you see is yours, and we are subject to your authority. Do what seems good to you, for no one dares resist your power.”

After they had said this to him courteously, one frivolous Frank, raising his battle-axe—which is also called a *francisca*—with a loud shout, struck the pitcher and said: “You will receive nothing from here, king, except what the true lot grants you.”

When everyone was stunned, the king patiently endured this insult and returned the pitcher he had received to the ecclesiastical messenger, concealing his anger in his heart.

After a year had passed, King Clodoveus, wishing to inspect the polish of all the weapons, ordered the entire army to come with its weapons and equipment, according to custom, onto the Field of Mars. They called that assembly by the name of Mars, whom the pagans believed to be the god of war; from him they also named the month of March and the third weekday, the day of Mars.

Later Franks instituted that assembly to be called the Field of May, when kings customarily set out for war.

When the king had gone around the entire army, he came to the man who the previous year had struck the pitcher with his battle-axe and said to him: “No one here has weapons as unkempt and filthy as yours, for neither your shield, nor your spear, nor your battle-axe is serviceable.”

The king took his *francisca*, that is, his battle-axe, and threw it to the ground. When the man bent down to pick it up, the king immediately raised his hand, drove his battle-axe into the man’s head, and said: “Just as you did to that pitcher in the city of Soissons last year, so I do to you.”

After the man had died, the king ordered the army to depart from that field peacefully for their homes. Great panic and fear arose among the Frankish people because of this deed.

### XXXII

In the tenth year of his reign, Clodoveus mobilized his army and subjected the province of Thuringia to himself. Then, through the counsel and agency of Aurelianus, and by divine will, he took as his wife Clotildis, the niece of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians—namely, the daughter of his brother Chilperic, whom Gundobad had killed with the sword—a sufficiently beautiful girl and truly most Christian.

The reader may read the fuller account in its proper place. In those days King Clodoveus extended his kingdom as far as the Seine.

[Note: See Aimo, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, book 1, chapter 13; Gregory of Tours, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, book 2, chapters 28–29.]

At a later time he occupied the territory as far as the Loire River. Aurelianus also received the fortress of Milidunum, which he held as a duchy.

### XXXIII

At last Clotildis conceived and bore a son. When she wished him to be consecrated in holy baptism, the king did not agree with her, for he did not yet believe in the Lord, the God of heaven. The queen preached him to the king every day, but he was unwilling to listen to her.

Meanwhile the queen prepared her son for baptism and adorned the church with veils and curtains, so that she might pierce the king’s heart and move him to believe. The boy was baptized, and she called him Ingomir; he died in the white garments of baptism.

The king was greatly saddened by this and attributed the matter to the queen, rebuking her with these words: “If the boy had been dedicated in the name of my gods, he would certainly have lived a long time in good health. But because he was baptized in the name of your God, he could not live.”

The queen replied: “I give thanks to God, who did not consider me unworthy, but deigned to receive my firstborn from my womb into his kingdom. I retain no sorrow in my heart on this account.”

Afterward she bore another son, whom she named Clodomir at baptism. When he too began to fall ill, the king said: “Nothing else can happen except that this should happen to him as it did to his brother: baptized in the name of your Christ, he will quickly die.”

But when the queen prayed, and the Lord’s mercy went before her, he recovered his health.

The queen also did not cease preaching to the king that he should worship the true God and abandon as worthless the idols he worshiped. Yet she could in no way move his mind to believe, until at last he made war against the Alemanni and the Suevi and was compelled to confess the God whom he had previously denied.

[Col. 1157D] **XXXIV.** It happened—[Note: [Col. 1158D] In the year 499. See Gregory of Tours, *On the History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 30; Flodoard, in the same place.]—that, while the Franks, Alemanni, and Suevi were fighting among themselves, Clovis’s army was suffering severe losses. Aurelianus, his counsellor, observing the king, said: “My lord king, now believe in the God of heaven, whom my lady the queen proclaims; and he himself, the King of kings and God of heaven and earth, will give you victory.”

But he raised his eyes to heaven, was moved to tears, and said: “Jesus Christ, whom my queen Clotildis proclaims to be the Son of the living God, who comes to the aid of those in tribulation, who gives help to those who hope in you, I devoutly ask your assistance: if you give me victory over these enemies, and I experience that power which the peoples proclaim to be yours, I will believe in you and be baptized in your name. For I have invoked my gods and, as I now discover, they have withdrawn from my aid. Therefore I believe that they possess no power, since they do not come to the aid of those who believe in them. I invoke you, the true God, and desire to believe in you—only deliver me from my adversaries.”

While he was crying out these words in prayer, the Alemanni were put to flight and turned their backs. When they saw that their king had been killed, they submitted to Clovis’s power, saying: “Spare us, we beg you, lord king, lest any more of the people perish; we are now yours.” Then the king ordered the slaughter that threatened them to cease, and he took the Alemanni captive, placing them under a tributary yoke in their own land.

After this victory he returned to Francia, to his queen, and told her how, through invoking the name of Jesus Christ, he had deserved to obtain victory. [Col. 1158B] These things took place in the fifteenth year of Clovis’s reign.

**XXXV.** Then the queen, so that the Apostle’s saying might be fulfilled, “The unbelieving husband is saved through the believing wife” (1 Cor. 7), summoned Saint Remigius, bishop of this city of Rheims, and begged him to proclaim to the king the way of salvation. The holy priest preached to him at length about the teaching of a life that leads to salvation and urged him to come to baptism.

He replied: “I will gladly listen to you, most blessed Father; but one obstacle remains: the people who follow me do not wish to abandon their gods. I shall go and exhort them according to your word.”

The king then went to the people and began to urge them to believe in the God who had given them victory, since their gods [Col. 1158C] had been unable to help them at all in their tribulation. But all of them cried out, as the mercy and power of God went before them: “We abandon mortal gods, glorious king, and we are ready to believe in the true and immortal God whom Remigius proclaims.”

This was reported to Saint Remigius. He too, filled with great joy, instructed the king and the people, in clear and concise words, how they ought to renounce the devil and his works and pomps and believe in God. Since the holy day of Easter was approaching, he also imposed upon them a fast according to Christian custom.

**XXXVI.** On the day of the Lord’s Passion, which ecclesiastical usage calls Parasceve—that is, the day before the king and his people were to receive the grace of baptism—Saint Remigius and Clotildis, the venerable wife of the king, spent the night in prayer for the salvation of the king and his people. The bishop poured out many tears before the altar of Saint Mary, while the queen prayed in the oratory of Saint Peter beside the royal residence.

When his prayer was completed, the bishop went to knock at the door of the king’s bedchamber, so that, in the deep silence of night, when the king was free from other concerns, he might more freely entrust to him the sacred mysteries of the word. The king’s chamberlains reverently received him when the doors were opened and, with due honour, escorted him into the king’s inner chambers.

The king himself eagerly sprang forward to meet him, embraced him, and proceeded with him and his venerable wife into the oratory of the most blessed [Col. 1159A] Peter, prince of the apostles, which, as we have said, adjoined the king’s chamber.

When the three of them—the bishop, the king, and the queen—had taken their seats, with certain clerics who had come with the bishop and the king’s and queen’s attendants standing around them, and when the holy bishop was instructing the king with salutary admonitions and filling him with evangelical teaching, the Lord also wished visibly to demonstrate, in confirmation of the preaching of the true faith delivered by the holy bishop, what he had promised to all believers: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18).

Suddenly a light so abundant filled the whole church that it surpassed the brightness of the sun. With the light a voice was heard: “Peace be with you; I am he. [Col. 1159B] Do not be afraid; remain in my love.”

After these words the light that had come withdrew, but an odour of incredible sweetness remained in the same house, plainly showing that the author of light, peace, and sweetness had come there. None of those present, terrified by the brilliance of the light, was able to look upon him except the bishop. Such a glory of brightness flooded the holy bishop that a splendour proceeding from him made the house in which they were sitting more luminous than the lamps burning there.

**XXXVII.** The king and queen therefore prostrated themselves at the feet of the holy priest. With great fear and groaning they sought his consolation and, with great devotion, asked what they ought to do for their benefit and salvation, ready to hear and carry out in practice whatever they learned from the holy bishop. For the light that had shone upon them outwardly also illuminated them inwardly and moved them to seek salutary counsel.

They delighted in the words they had heard, although they had been terrified by the brilliance of the light. But the holy man, filled with sacred wisdom, began to instruct them that it was the customary character of a divine and angelic vision that, at its coming, it terrifies the hearts of mortals, but that, through the consolation that follows, it soothes their preceding fear. He instructed them from the authority of the Holy Scriptures, explaining how, in the case of each person to whom they had appeared, such visions had at the beginning of their appearance instilled fear in those who saw them, but afterwards, through the grace of consolation, had supplied their hearts with most welcome joy. [Col. 1159D]

When the holy man had sufficiently instructed them on these matters, filled with the prophetic spirit he foretold everything that was to happen to them and their descendants: how their posterity, succeeding them, would nobly extend and govern the kingdom; exalt the holy Church; possess all Roman dignity and rule; and win victories against the attacks of other peoples—unless, degenerating from the good, they abandoned the way of truth and followed the various winding paths of vice, by which ecclesiastical discipline is customarily neglected and God offended. For this reason kingdoms are commonly overthrown and transferred from one people to another.

We read that this was written concerning Moses: “His face became radiant when the Lord looked upon him” (Exod. 34). We have heard that the same thing occurred with blessed Remigius, who was illumined by a brilliant light. For just as Moses, the lawgiver of the ancient people, had been appointed by the Lord, so blessed Remigius, the bearer of evangelical grace to the people who were soon to be renewed through the baptismal font, had been chosen by Christ for this ministry.

**XXXVIII.** Meanwhile, the route from the royal residence to the baptistery was prepared. It was extended on both sides with painted hangings and curtains and shaded above; the streets were spread with coverings; and the baptistery was adorned and sprinkled with balsam and other perfumes. The Lord supplied such grace among the people that they thought themselves refreshed by the fragrances of paradise.

Thus, with the sacred Gospels carried before them, and with everyone singing hymns, spiritual songs, and litanies and acclaiming the names of the saints, the holy bishop, holding the king’s hand, proceeded from the royal residence to the baptistery, followed by the queen and the people.

As they proceeded together, the king asked the bishop: “Patron, is this the kingdom of God that you promise me?”

The bishop replied: “This is not that kingdom, but the beginning of the road by which one comes to it.”

When they reached the baptistery, the cleric carrying the chrism was detained by the crowd and could not reach the font. After the font had been sanctified, the chrism was lacking by divine dispensation. Since, because of the press of the crowd, no one could leave or enter the church, the holy bishop, stretching his eyes and hands toward heaven, began to pray silently with tears.

And suddenly a dove, whiter than snow, brought in its beak a small flask full of holy chrism. Its wondrous fragrance surpassed all the scents they had previously experienced in the baptistery, and everyone present was filled with incomparable sweetness. When the holy bishop received the little flask, the form of the dove disappeared. The venerable bishop poured this chrism upon the sacred forehead.

**XXXIX.** When the king had witnessed so great a miracle, he renounced the pomps and works of the devil and asked to be baptized by the holy bishop.

The new Constantine proceeded to the saving bath, in which the leprosy of the ancient disease was to be removed and the filthy stains of former sins washed away. Blessed Remigius assisted in this divine gift; in him apostolic teaching and the grace of virtues seemed to present another Silvester.

When Clovis had entered the life-giving font, the holy bishop said with eloquent speech: “Bend your neck gently, Sicamber; adore what you burned, and burn what you adored.” By these salutary commands he instructed him, in humble devotion, to venerate the churches built for religious worship: to adore God in those churches which he had been accustomed to burn with harsh profanation, and, inflamed with the fervour of faith, to cast down and burn the idols that he had been accustomed to adore as gods in his sanctuaries.

His wisdom is admirable in the brevity of his words, by which he showed the distinction between that adoration and service which, as we learn from the reading of Holy Scripture, is owed to God alone as the worship due to divinity, according to his command (Deut. 6), and is not to be offered to any creature.

After confessing the orthodox faith, and in response to the holy bishop’s questioning according to ecclesiastical custom, he was baptized by threefold immersion in the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Received from the holy font by that bishop, he was anointed with sacred chrism, with the sign of the holy cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Three thousand men from his army were baptized, apart from children and women. His sisters Albofledis and Landehildis were baptized. There was great joy on that day among the holy angels in heaven and devout men on earth.

Finally, many of the Frankish army who had not yet been converted to the faith remained for some time with Raganarius beyond the River Somme. At last, with the grace of Christ cooperating, after winning glorious victories, King Ludovicus had that same Raganarius—who was devoted to shameful vices—bound by the Franks and handed over to him, put to death. Through blessed Remigius he obtained the conversion and baptism of the entire Frankish people.

**XL.** Concerning the miracle that the Lord deigned to display through the appearance of the dove in the bringing of the chrism, as also concerning other matters, the authoritative judgment of the Catholic Fathers is to be followed. It says: “If a divine action can be comprehended by reason, it is not miraculous; nor does faith possess merit when human reason supplies proof.”

**XLI.** After the king had been baptized with his entire people, both he and powerful Franks gave blessed Remigius many estates in various provinces. He distributed them among different churches, lest the Franks should think that he was greedy for temporal possessions and had therefore summoned them to Christianity, and lest they should despise the faith of Christ and the holy priesthood.

**XLII.** From these possessions, at the request of the donors, he added a certain portion in the eastern regions of Francia to the bishopric of Rheims. From what had been given to him in the province of Rheims, he gave a considerable portion to the church of Saint Mary in the castle of Laon, [*clavati*—uncertain reading] of the parish of Rheims, where he had been raised.

There he ordained as bishop Genebaldus [Genebaudus], a man noble by birth and learned both in the Holy Scriptures and in secular literature. He had abandoned his wife—who was the niece of blessed Remigius—and sought a religious life. He subjected the parish of the county of Laon to the aforesaid castle.

Genebaldus, however, trusting more than was necessary in his former life and the eminence of his rank, ought to have considered that he was neither holier than David nor wiser than Solomon, both of whom had been endangered by the blandishments of women. Carelessly he allowed his wife, whom he had left and transformed into a sister, to visit him frequently, ostensibly for salutary instruction, forgetting the Scripture that says: “The waters wear away stones, the earth is consumed by floods, and the rock is removed from its place” (Job 14).

Thus it happened that the woman’s frequent visits and affectionate, repeated conversations softened the bishop’s hard heart against the softness of lust, and, as though it were a rocky crag, moved it from the place of its sanctity to the stains of lust. This was also contrary to the Scripture that says: “Who can bind fire in his bosom without burning his garments?” (Prov. 6).

When straw was brought near the fire—that is, the substance of female flesh—the fire of lust, stirred by diabolical persuasion as by a violent wind, burst into flames. When he lay with the woman, formerly his wife, she conceived. After giving birth, she sent word to the bishop that she had borne a son.

Genebaldus, ashamed and grieving, said to the messenger: “Because he was begotten through theft, so that what could not be hidden from God might be hidden from men, he shall rightly be called Latro [‘Thief’]. Let that be his name.”

Since the sin had not become known to people, and lest suspicion arise if the woman withdrew from her customary visits, she began to frequent the bishop’s house as before. Thus it came about that the guilt was hidden from men, while the fire of lust remained concealed in the hearts of both the bishop and the woman. For, as is well known, the more a concealed fire is covered, the more fiercely it burns.

The bishop, pierced by remorse for his guilt, returned to it after weeping and forgot what he had mourned, since he did not wish to extinguish what was burning through desire. He repeated the sin he had committed. The woman conceived again and, sending a messenger, informed the bishop that she had borne a girl. He ordered that she be called Vulpecula [“Little Vixen”].

Anyone who knows the deceptions and meanings associated in Scripture with that animal, which are related to the tricks and cunning of the deceiving devil and to the enticements and winding paths of wanton flesh, can readily understand why he wished her to be given this name.

At last, when the Lord who had looked upon blessed Peter and caused him to weep bitterly over his denial (Matt. 26) looked upon Genebaldus, he came to his senses and sent to Saint Remigius, asking him to come to Laon, because matters had arisen there that he could not settle by himself.

Blessed Remigius came to Laon as Genebaldus had requested. He was received with due reverence, asked to enter a private chamber, and questioned Genebaldus about why he had summoned him.

Genebaldus, with the greatest weeping and lamentation, wished to remove the stole from his neck and proceed to the feet of Saint Remigius, but blessed Remigius restrained him with great force so that he would not remove the stole from his neck.

After they had both wept for a long time—for blessed Remigius understood that Genebaldus had committed the crime for which he wished to lay aside the stole—Genebaldus, amid sobs and tears, scarcely managed to recount everything he had done in order.

When Saint Remigius saw him contrite and almost despairing, he gently consoled him, saying: “I do not grieve so much over the crime you have committed as over the fact that you think so wrongly of the Lord’s goodness. According to the truth of the Gospel, no word is impossible for him (Luke 1). He made all things from nothing; and by grace he saved our first parent, in whom all sinned. He despises no sinner who returns to him, for he came to redeem sinners by his blood.

“He wept in compassion over Lazarus, who had lain four days and stank, through the tears of his sisters, which signify the anxious and tearful thoughts of penitents, and he raised him from the dead; after raising him, he admitted him to his banquet (John 11). He did not refuse to have his most holy feet touched by the hands of that woman who had been a sinner in the city, whose hands were stained by iniquity—he who sits at the right hand of the Father above the summit of all the angels (John 12).

“He never denies the grace of resurrection from sins to anyone who is dead through sins of whatever magnitude or kind, or buried beneath the mass and enormity of crimes. When a person duly repents and mourns his sins, he restores him through the door of reconciliation to communion at the holy altar.”

**XLIII.** Since he was extremely learned and most eloquent in speech, he gathered together testimonies from the breadth of Holy Scripture and examples concerning penitents and presented them to Genebaldus for his encouragement; and, having exhorted him, he imposed penance upon him.

He had a small dwelling constructed, with a bed in the form of a tomb, very small windows, and an oratory. These still remain beside the church of Saint Julian. He shut Genebaldus inside it and for seven years governed the clergy and people of his parish, while also governing his own parish and celebrating one Sunday at Rheims and the next at Laon.

How great was Genebaldus’s contrition and continence during this confinement of penance, divine mercy demonstrated.

**XLIV.** In the seventh year, on the vigil of the Lord’s Supper, while Genebaldus was spending the night in prayer and mourning for himself—for he had been ordained to reconcile penitents to God on that day, yet because of his crimes he did not deserve even to stand among the penitents in the church—about midnight an angel of the Lord came to him with a great light in the oratory where he was lying prostrate and said to him:

“Genebaldus, the prayers of your father Remigius have been heard on your behalf. The Lord has also accepted your penance, and your sin has been forgiven. Rise, go out from here, perform the office of episcopal ministry, and reconcile to the Lord those who repent of their crimes.”

Genebaldus, struck by excessive terror, could not reply. Then the angel of the Lord strengthened him and urged him not to be afraid but to rejoice in the mercy of the Lord bestowed upon him.

Encouraged, he said to the angel: “I cannot go out from here, because my lord and father Remigius has the key to this door with him, and he has also sealed it with his seal.”

The angel replied: “So that you may not doubt that I have been sent by the Lord, just as heaven is open before you, so this door will be opened.”

Immediately the door opened, with its seal and bolt intact.

Then Genebaldus threw himself across the threshold in the form of a cross and said: “Even if the Lord Jesus Christ himself should deign to come to me, a sinner, I will not go out from here until he comes who established me in this confinement in his name.”

Immediately the angel of the Lord departed from him.

**V.** Blessed Remigius, meanwhile, was spending the night in prayer in the crypt behind the sanctuary of the church of Saint Mary at Rheims. As though sleeping, he was carried into an ecstasy. He saw an angel standing beside him, who recounted everything to him just as it had been said and done, and ordered him to go to Laon as quickly as possible, restore Genebaldus to his see, and persuade him to perform the episcopal ministry in his presence.

At once Saint Remigius, without any hesitation, went to Laon with the utmost speed. At the threshold of the door, which had been opened while its seal and bolt remained intact, he found Genebaldus lying there. With outstretched arms, praising the Lord’s mercy amid joy and tears, he raised him up and hastened to restore him to his see and episcopal office, just as the angel of the Lord had commanded. Then he returned joyfully to Rheims.

After this Genebaldus spent all the remaining days of his life in holiness and righteousness by the grace of God, proclaiming to everyone how greatly the Lord had acted on his behalf.

**XLVI.** King Ludovicus established his seat in the city of Soissons, from which he had expelled Syagrius, and delighted in the presence and conversation of blessed Remigius.

But since the king and the Franks had given him estates in the districts of Soissons and Laon, as stated above, and he had donated them to the bishopric of Laon and to other houses of God, he possessed near the city of Soissons only one small estate, which had been given to Saint Nicasius.

Therefore, at the urging of the most religious queen and at the request of the inhabitants of the places—who were burdened by numerous gifts offered to strangers, so that they might pay to the church of Rheims what they owed the king—the king granted Saint Remigius whatever territory he could walk around while the king rested at midday.

Saint Remigius proceeded along boundaries that are still plainly visible and sent signs of his journey.

At one boundary a man who owned a mill drove Saint Remigius away, so that the mill would not be included within those boundaries. Blessed Remigius gently addressed him: “Friend, do not be troubled if we possess this mill together.” But the man rejected him.

Immediately the mill wheel began to turn backward. The man then called after blessed Remigius, saying: “Servant of God, come, and let us possess this mill together.”

Saint Remigius replied: “Neither for me nor for you.”

Thus a ditch came to exist at that place, so that from then until forever the mill could not remain there.

Since certain men also drove him away to prevent him from including a small wood within his boundaries, he declared that not even a leaf from that wood should ever fly within his boundaries, although it was adjacent, nor should a branch fall from it toward those boundaries. This was observed for as long as the wood remained.

Proceeding from there, he came to a village called Caviniacum. Wishing to include it within those boundaries, he was rejected by the men of the village. Then, with a cheerful face, at one moment rejected and at another drawing near again, he marked his route, as the places still show: the points from which he was rejected and those by which he approached.

At last, when he was rejected, he said to them: “Always labour and suffer want.” The force of these words is shown by the sentence, which remains to this day.

Meanwhile the king arose from his midday sleep. Saint Remigius returned to him, and the king, by the command of his authority, granted him everything encompassed by the circuit of his boundary-walk. To this day the church of Rheims possesses it by undisturbed right; its principal places are Judiacus and Ociliacus [Codiciacus].

**XLVII.** We read in sacred and ancient history that holy David cursed the mountains of Gilboa, so that neither dew nor rain should fall upon them and they should not be fields of firstfruits (2 Sam. 1).

We have holy Remigius, with prophetic speech, cursing inanimate creatures, so that their possessors might be struck, in retributive punishment, by the loss caused by barrenness.

**XLVIII.** A certain powerful man named Eulogius, convicted before King Ludovicus of the crime of treason against the king’s majesty, was unable to clear himself and fled for refuge to the church of Saint Mary and to the intercession of blessed Remigius.

Saint Remigius obtained for him from the king both his life and possession of his property. In return, Eulogius wished to give his estate of Sparnacum to Saint Remigius as his own property.

Saint Remigius, however, refused to accept temporal compensation for the benefit of his intercession. But since Eulogius, bound by a confession of shame, did not wish to remain in secular dress because he had deserved to be spared from death through another’s indulgence, Saint Remigius told him that, if he wished to be perfect, he should sell all that he had, give it to the poor, and follow Christ.

Accordingly, from the church treasury he gave Eulogius the assessed price—namely, five thousand pounds of silver—and purchased that same estate for the possession of the church. By this he left a good example to all bishops, both those living in the flesh in his own time and those who would succeed him in the order after his death: that, when assisting the poor, widows, orphans, those who flee to the mercy of the Church because they suffer injury, or those who, having sinned, are condemned to exile or to islands, or who receive any other sentence, they should act according to the sacred canons and not do good deeds for temporal repayment.

Rather, according to the Lord’s word, “You have received freely; give freely” (Matt. 10), they should freely—that is, without temporal compensation—bestow upon their neighbours what they have received through God’s grace, that is, what was freely given (Matt. 20). Hence, when the prophet was describing a righteous man, he appropriately said: “He shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. 33).

For he did not say merely “from a gift,” but added “from every gift,” because one gift comes from service, another from the hand, and another from the tongue. A gift from service is an improperly rendered submission; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favour.

Therefore, whoever confers sacred orders or performs any good deed from which he hopes that God will repay him in the future age shakes his hand free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no favour.

**XLIX.** He also purchased a very large part of the forest in the Vosges for a price and established settlements there. They are called Cossa and Gleni after the waters beside which they were established. He arranged for people from the nearby episcopal estate called Berna, which had been given to him by the Franks, to live in those settlements, so that they might supply pitch annually to the religious establishments of the church of Rheims. He also gave them a payment, which the inhabitants of those places still possess and with which they discharge their obligation.

He so carefully marked out the boundaries of this purchase all around that the demarcation is plain to everyone who sees it, and, from generation to generation, the boundaries he established have continued to be called and designated by name.

At one of these boundaries he placed a stone with his own hand in a hollowed-out post. Anyone who wishes can put his hand into the cavity in which the stone was placed and turn the stone, but no one is able by any means to remove it from the cavity.

After some time, a certain envious man, displeased that many people regarded this object as a religious memorial to the honour of Saint Remigius, tried to remove the stone from the cavity with his hand. When he failed, he attempted to enlarge the hole with an axe. As he raised the axe to strike the post, his right hand withered and he lost the sight of his eyes. He who had wished to extinguish the memorial of Saint Remigius instead increased the reverence paid to his glory.

In this concern that Saint Remigius took, in his own time and that of his successors, to provide pitch for the religious establishments of the church of Rheims, he clearly showed the rulers of the Church that, without abandoning concern for inner things, they ought not to diminish their provision for external things. Otherwise, those devoted to external matters may fall away from what is inward, while those occupied solely with interior matters may fail to provide their neighbours with what they owe them externally.

They should therefore devote themselves to spiritual matters in such a way that they do not abandon the administration of external affairs, lest, by completely neglecting bodily needs, they fail to come to the aid of their subjects’ necessities. If they do not give them what is necessary for the present life, their subjects do not listen to them willingly; the word of instruction does not penetrate the mind of one in need unless the hand of mercy commends it to that person’s heart. The seed of the word then germinates easily when the preacher’s compassion waters it in the hearer’s breast.

Therefore, if a ruler is to pour inward things into others, he must also provide for outward things with an innocent mind. Paul arouses this concern in pastors, saying: “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5).

How pleasing this concern of blessed Remigius was to the Lord, he clearly demonstrated by the miracle shown in the case of the man who had envied his good works.

**L.** King Ludovicus, having received God’s blessing through Saint Remigius, confident in the victory that Remigius had foretold for him, and having received the instruction that he should continue to fight for as long as the blessed wine given him by Remigius sufficed for his daily use, set out against Gundebaldus and his brother Godeglissus with a very large army.

The Burgundians, with an immense multitude, came against him at the River Ouche near the fortress called Dijon. There they engaged in fierce battle; Gundebaldus and Godeglissus with the Burgundians turned their backs and escaped only by slipping away in flight.

Ludovicus, as usual, emerged victorious. Gundebaldus shut himself up in Avignon and sought peace from Ludovicus through his counsellor Aredius. Ludovicus, however, took away the treasures and returned home with great spoils and the Frankish army.

He sent an able man named Paternus as envoy to Alaric, king of the Goths, to convey terms concerning friendship between them. But when Alaric wished to deceive Ludovicus through Paternus, Paternus investigated what was happening around him and, by his ingenuity, diverted his treasures; thus Alaric was himself deceived.

[Col. 1167B] **LI.** In those days, when King Ludovicus had come to Paris, where he established his seat, he said to the queen and his people: “It is very displeasing to me that the Arian Goths hold the best part of Gaul. Let us go, with God’s help, and drive them from this land and subject it to our rule, for it is exceedingly good. We have justice against Alaric, to whom we sent an envoy concerning the terms of friendship, and through whom he tried to deceive us.”

This plan pleased the Frankish nobles. Then, at the counsel of his queen, he built a church in the city of Paris in honour of the apostles Peter and Paul. At the counsel of blessed Remigius, he convened a synod of bishops in the city of Orléans. Many useful provisions were established at that assembly.

The most devout king, proceeding against Alaric the Arian, sought a blessing from Saint Remigius. Remigius gave him a blessing and promised him victory in the word of Christ. He also gave him a full vessel, which common usage calls a flask, of wine that he had blessed, just as he had done when Ludovicus had proceeded against Gundebaldus after the baptism. He instructed him to advance to war as far as that wine from the aforesaid flask should last for him and for his men to whom he wished to give it.

The king drank from it, as did the royal household and a large crowd of people, and they were abundantly satisfied. The vessel did not diminish in its wine, but, through the blessing of God imparted by Saint Remigius, it was replenished with an overflowing like that of a spring.

The king moved his entire army, drawn from the Frankish people, toward the city of Poitiers. King Alaric of the Goths was then staying there. Proceeding through the district of Tours and showing reverence to Saint Martin and blessed Hilary—as the reader will find in their proper places—he engaged King Alaric of the Goths in battle on the plain of Moglotinse [Aemilius has *in campis Vogladensibus*], above the River Clain, ten miles from the city of Poitiers.

When they clashed with one another, the Goths, badly struck down together with their king, turned their backs. Ludovicus, as usual, emerged victorious.

**LII.** As Alaric was being killed, two Goths struck him from opposite sides with spears. But because of the coat of mail he was wearing, they could not wound him. Rather, the Lord aided him through the prayer of Saint Remigius, his father and patron, and clothed him more securely in the armour of faith.

After achieving victory and subjugating many cities to his rule, he advanced as far as Toulouse. Having taken Alaric’s treasures, he returned home with glorious victory over many cities, passing through the city of Angoulême, whose walls collapsed at the sight of him, after the Arian Goths who were there had been killed.

**LIII.** At the same time, King Ludovicus received from the emperor Anastasius letters of appointment to the consulship. With those letters Anastasius also sent him a golden crown set with gems and a purple tunic. From that day he was called consul and Augustus.

Hormisdas, pontiff of the Roman see, likewise entrusted his authority to Saint Remigius, bishop of the ancient metropolis, which at that time had twelve cities and as many bishops presiding over them, within the kingdom of King Ludovicus, who had recently been converted to the faith with his entire people through Remigius’s holy preaching, with the Lord cooperating and confirming his word by the accompanying signs, in the following manner:

### LIV. To the Most Beloved Brother Remigius, Hormisdas

Having received with complete fraternal joy the communications in which the report of your genuine bodily well-being, supported by your spiritual duties, has gladdened us, we have judged it fitting to express in words this joy that we carry in our hearts. For you are fulfilling the teaching of the supreme pontiff, since you both perform what deserves proclamation and do not delay in making it known.

We have therefore taken a special satisfaction from our judgment when we learned that you had done what we impose upon others as an obligation: that, in provinces separated by such great distances, you should strive to apply both the authority of the apostolic see and careful observance of the rules of the Fathers.

Accordingly, with the present authority we entrust to you our vicariate throughout the entire kingdom of our beloved spiritual son, King Louis, whom, with the assistance of heavenly grace, you recently converted with his whole people and consecrated with the gift of holy baptism, accompanied by a saving proclamation and by many miracles of signs comparable to those of the apostles. This is done without prejudice to the privileges that antiquity has decreed for metropolitans. By sharing in this responsibility, we increase the dignity of your ministry and lighten, through this arrangement, the vigilance that we ourselves must exercise.

Although you do not need to be instructed about individual matters, since we have already proved that you preserve everything with exceptional discernment, it is nevertheless more welcome when a road is shown to those who are about to travel and the form of the task assigned is made clear to those who must labor.

We therefore command that the paternal rules and decrees established by the most holy councils be observed by all. In these matters we display your vigilance, your care, and the admonitions of fraternal exhortation. When these are guarded with the reverence they deserve, no obstacle to holy observance leaves room for guilt. There what is lawful and unlawful has been prescribed; there what is forbidden is identified, which no one may dare to seek; there what is permitted is established, which a mind intent on pleasing God ought to undertake.

Whenever the cause of religion requires a universal council, let all the brothers assemble when summoned by you. If any of them is troubled by the concern of a particular matter, restrain the quarrels that have arisen among them, resolving their disputes after examining them according to sacred law. Whatever is established there for the faith and the truth, whether prescribed through prudent administration or confirmed by the authority of our person, must all reach our knowledge through a report furnished with testimony.

Thus it comes about that both our spirit enjoys the charity of the duty entrusted and yours enjoys the security of what you have received. May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

### LV

During the pontificate of this holy Hormisdas, the often-mentioned glorious King Louis, at Saint Remigius’s urging, sent Blessed Peter a golden crown set with gems, which is customarily called a royal crown. This blessed Pope Hormisdas sent Germanus, Bishop of Capua, to Constantinople on an embassy to the Emperor Justin. Saint Benedict saw the soul of this Germanus carried into heaven by angels; Germanus had sent his letters to Blessed Remigius concerning the healing of a demon-possessed girl.

### LVI

After all these events, King Louis died in peace and was buried in the basilica of the holy Apostle Peter, which he and his queen had built. He died in the fifth year after he had fought against Alaric, king of the Goths. He had also reigned for thirty years in all.

At the very moment when Louis died at Paris, Blessed Remigius, who was at Rheims, learned by revelation of the Holy Spirit that he had died, and announced it to those attending him.

After these events, Clodoaldus, son of Clodomir, son of King Louis, had his brothers killed; Queen Clotildis had been raising them together with him after their father’s death. He then had himself tonsured as a cleric and, in the course of time, by the merit of his life and religion, obtained from his royal uncles the inheritance that belonged to his father. From this inheritance he gave the estate of Duziacum in the district of Mosomagus, with its dependencies, to Saint Remigius and the church of Rheims; and he assigned the estate of Riviliacum in the district of Berry to Saint Denis.

He also donated the estate of Noviantum in the district of Paris, with everything belonging to it, to the mother church of the city of Paris, where he had been ordained a priest. In that estate, full of virtues, he departed to the Lord and was buried in peace in the church that he himself had built.

### LVII

When at last the bishops of the provinces of Gaul and Belgica assembled in council for the sake of the faith, they asked Blessed Remigius, who was learned above all others and most thoroughly instructed in the holy Scriptures and practiced in ecclesiastical doctrines, to come to that same council.

An Arian heretic was present at the council, a most vigorous disputant who relied upon dialectical propositions and conclusions and was consequently excessively proud. When Saint Remigius entered the assembly of the bishops, all the multitude of brothers who were awaiting him rose and received him reverently, as though he were an angel of God.

But the proud heretic, thinking ill of the man of God, disdainfully refused to rise for him. Immediately, when the saint passed before him, he became so speechless that he could not utter even a single word. While everyone waited for the heretic to say something after Saint Remigius’s address, he was unable to speak at all. But he fell prostrate at Saint Remigius’s feet and asked forgiveness by gestures.

Saint Remigius said to him: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of the living God, if you hold this correct opinion of Him, speak; and believe and confess concerning Him as the Catholic Church believes.”

At these words, the formerly proud heretic, now humble and Catholic, confessed to him the Catholic faith concerning the holy and indivisible Trinity and confessed in a Catholic manner concerning the incarnation of Christ. He declared that he would remain in the faith of this confession.

Thus, although his soul had been lost through unbelief and his bodily voice had been condemned because of his pride, Saint Remigius, by divine power, restored health to both soul and body. He plainly showed to all the priests who were present or would hear of this how they ought to act toward those who sin against Christ—who, through His humanity, deigned to become near to us and our brother—and toward those who sin against themselves or against the Church, and toward rebels who afterward acknowledge their fault and repent.

### LVIII

As Saint Remigius grew old, the Spirit of God revealing to him that famine would follow upon the abundance of that year, he imitated the foresight of holy Joseph. From the grain that had been produced on the estates of the bishopric, or that he had purchased from others, he made heaps, which we call “mounds,” so that he might later assist the people when they suffered from famine.

Accordingly, he ordered several mounds to be made on the estate called Celtus. The people of Celtus, however, had always been rebellious and seditious. One Sunday, having become drunk, they began saying to one another: “What does that Jubilaeus”—for Saint Remigius was so called because of his advanced age—“intend to do with those mounds that he has gathered? Does he intend to make a city from them? For just as towers stand around the walls of a city, so the mounds stood around the enclosure.”

At the devil’s persuasion, they encouraged one another to set fire to them. When this was reported by a swift messenger to Saint Remigius, who was staying at a nearby estate called Basilicae Court, he mounted a horse so that he might come to Celtus and restrain such presumption.

When he arrived, the mounds were already burning. Blessed Remigius, chilled both by age and by the evening cold, as commonly happens in autumn, dismounted from his horse and began warming himself from a distance. With a calm heart and voice he said: “A fire is always good, provided it does not get out of control. Nevertheless, may all who have done this, and all who shall be born from their stock, become heavy-throated men and goitrous women.”

And this was fulfilled. For until the time of the Emperor Charlemagne, who expelled these same people from Celtus because they had killed the vicedominus of that estate with the most savage violence—and who, after killing the instigators, caused those who had consented to be scattered through various provinces and condemned to perpetual exile, while ordering that the estate be restored from the other estates of the bishopric of Rheims—the men and women remained punished just as the holy man’s sentence had declared.

We ourselves saw certain people from their lineage who, having fled at that time while the others were being scattered, remained and later returned to the same estate, bearing this sentence of vengeance, just as Gehazi, together with his household, was punished with leprosy by the curse of Elisha (IV Kings 1).

### LIX

The sentence of the man of God, filled with the Spirit, was fitting. Just as by that Spirit he saw those who were present, so he foresaw that their descendants would be rebellious and seditious. Those who presumed in this way incurred vengeance not only upon themselves but also upon their stock.

Just as, through the transmission of seed, all who were born from the first parent inherited his sin and the death of the body inflicted because of sin, so those born from the offspring of these presumptuous people would suffer the vengeance inflicted upon their ancestors.

And because there was no corresponding place in the female sex where a similar vengeance might be displayed upon similar members, just as through the throat of the first mother the illicit taste passed and transmitted guilt to the offspring of the transgressor, so an ignominious inheritance would be propagated among the women born from this stock. As it is said to the Lord through Moses: “You who repay the iniquity of fathers to sons and grandsons” (Exodus XXXIV).

### LX

After the virtues mentioned above and many others, which the Lord deigned to perform through this holy servant of His, He heard his groans and sighs, in which he said: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm XLI); and: “I shall be satisfied when Your glory is revealed” (Psalm XVI).

The Lord revealed to him, consoling him, that the day of his death was approaching. Therefore, in accordance with the sacred canons, he made a testament concerning his possessions, hastening toward that inheritance of which the Prophet says: “When He gives sleep to His beloved, this is the inheritance of the Lord” (Psalm CXXVI).

Everyone who sleeps in death loses the inheritance. But when He gives sleep to His beloved, this is the inheritance of the Lord, because God’s elect, after they have arrived at death, then find the inheritance.

Thus Saint Remigius, abandoning an earthly inheritance, received an eternal one, because he was like a fruitful olive tree in the house—that is, the Church of God—through the shining works of mercy. Therefore he rightly hoped in the mercy of his God, truly saying: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm XLI). For just as the body is nourished by bread, so the soul is refreshed by tears, since through them it hopes to obtain the forgiveness of sins.

“Day” and “night” are understood according to the changing conditions of the world, because whether in prosperous circumstances or in adversity, the soul that desires God pours out the tears of its longing, knowing what is written: “It is vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Psalm CXVI).

To rise before the light is to rejoice in the night of the present life before the brightness of eternal light and reward appears. One must first sit down so that one may afterward rise rightly, because whoever now humbles himself voluntarily is afterward exalted by the glory that follows.

He eats the bread of sorrow who groans in this pilgrimage and longs with heavenly desire for the eternal homeland.

After making his testament and arranging everything, because, as it is written, “the true farmer cleanses every fruitful branch of the true vine so that it may bear more fruit” (John XV), he was deprived for a time of the light of his bodily eyes, so that with the eyes of his mind he might more intently contemplate the things above, for which he yearned with all his desire.

During this trial of his probation, he always strove to give thanks, devoting himself day and night to hymns and praises of God and understanding with faithful mind that those who humbly receive chastisement are afterward received sublimely into rest.

The Lord wished to show this in him even in the present life and, as a pledge of eternal light, restored his sight before he died. Thus, just as he had blessed the Lord’s name when he lost his sight, so he blessed it when his sight was restored.

Knowing after no long interval that the day of his departure had arrived, he bade farewell and gave peace to his sons through the celebration of Masses and the distribution of holy Communion. After he had served the Lord as a faithful and prudent servant for twenty-two years in the clerical order and, in the episcopate, for seventy-four [74] years, with the greatest continence and devotion, in the ninety-sixth year of his age, on the Ides of January, he completed the course of his holy contest, having preserved the faith, with abundant fruit of good works and gain of souls.

As he had long desired, his soul penetrated the heavens, while his body was returned to the earth. He received a white robe—that is, everlasting blessedness of soul—until at the resurrection he receives another blessed robe, namely, the immortality of the glorified body, taken up again together with the soul.

[Note: Concerning the year in which he died and the length of time he occupied the see, see Baronius, year 511, where he accuses Hincmar of error for assigning seventy-four years to the episcopate of Saint Remigius, and proves him wrong from the Acts of the Council of Clermont, held in the year 541, where Flavius, Bishop of Rheims, is recorded as subscribing ninth; Romanus, the first successor of Saint Remigius, preceded him.]

### LXI

This blessed athlete of God was a confessor by his office and also a martyr by his zeal. Invincible in the contest, he sought the palm through blood. Because he was permitted to live long in the body, he necessarily had to endure the prolonged torments of the flesh, the devil, and wicked men.

Since, with the Lord’s help, he strove bravely to preserve the virtue of patience, he lived in the peace of the Church and nevertheless obtained the palm of martyrdom.

Having therefore happily completed his course, the precious confessor of the Lord, Remigius, gloriously entered after the death of his body into the fellowship of the holy apostles and martyrs. This is attested by the apostolic grace bestowed upon him: namely, the Frankish people, converted through him to the faith of Christ and consecrated by the grace of baptism; the palm of martyrdom, namely, the long endurance of patience throughout the length of his life; and the glory of a confessor, namely, the preaching of orthodox faith and the splendid manifestation of virtues both during his bodily life and after his death.

### LXII

When the most holy funeral was being carried toward burial in the direction of the church of the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris, beside the church of Saint Christopher the martyr, at the place where a cross is now and was thereafter erected, and where God later displayed many miracles through Saint Remigius, the bier became so heavy that it could not be moved in any way, by any device, or by any number of people.

Everyone was astonished and implored the omnipotence of God to reveal the place where He wished the body of this holy servant to be laid. They designated the basilica of the aforesaid martyrs, but the bier could not be moved. They proposed carrying it to the church of Saint Nicasius, but it could not be moved. They proposed carrying it to the church of Saints Sixtus and Sinicius, but even then it could not be moved.

At last, compelled by the circumstances, they turned to a small church in honor of Blessed Christopher the martyr. No body of that saint lay there, but the church and the surrounding courtyards had from ancient times been a cemetery of the church of Rheims. They asked the Lord to make known whether He wished that most holy body to be placed in that church.

The bier was then moved with such ease that those carrying it felt no burden. The venerable body was buried in that little church, where there is an altar in honor of Saint Genevieve, who had been especially close to Blessed Remigius.

It is clear that this happened by divine disposition and according to Remigius’s own will: just as the possessions acquired in his name had, according to sacred laws, been united to the bishopric of the church of Rheims, so whatever was thereafter acquired through his merits was to be united to the Church of Rheims, in whose territory he lay.

### LXIII

After his death, when the groin plague was devastating the people of Lower Germany and all the inhabitants of the province of Rheims were terrified by reports of this calamity, the people of Rheims hastened to the saint’s tomb to seek an appropriate remedy for the affliction.

They lit candles and many lamps and kept vigil throughout the night with heavenly hymns and psalms. When morning came, they considered what might still be lacking in their prayer.

For God revealed to them—He who wished to glorify His saint among human beings, whom He held glorious with Himself—how, after the prayer already offered, they might fortify the defenses of the city with an even greater protection.

They took a cloth from Blessed Remigius’s tomb and arranged it in the form of a bier. After lighting candles upon crosses and upon the candle-bearing stands, they raised their voices in song and went around the city through its streets, passing no lodging without including it in this procession.

What more need be said? After not many days, the plague mentioned above attacked the territory of the city of Rheims. Yet when it reached the place to which the pledge of the blessed man had come, it seemed to recognize an appointed boundary and did not dare to enter at all. It even abandoned, driven back by the force of this protection, the places it had initially invaded.

This most blessed bishop, both during his bodily life and after his death, just as he restored the grace of health to the sick, so also often acted as an avenger against those who attacked others.

[Note: See Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 79; Baronius, year 565.]

### LXIV

Not far from the basilica there was a field of fertile soil—for the inhabitants call such fields *oleae*—and it had been given to the saint’s basilica. One of the citizens seized it, despising the man who had transferred it to the holy place.

Although the bishop and the administrator of the place repeatedly admonished him to return what he had unjustly seized, he paid no attention to their words and stubbornly defended what he had taken.

At last, it was necessity, not devotion, that caused him to hurry to the saint’s basilica. The administrator of the place again accused him of seizing the field, but he gave no reasonable answer.

When the business had been concluded, he mounted his horse and prepared to return home. But the insult against the priest obstructed his effort. For, stricken by a flow of blood, he fell to the ground. His tongue, which had spoken of taking the field, was bound; his eyes, which had coveted it, were closed; his hands, which had seized it, were contracted.

### LXV

Then, stammering and scarcely able to articulate his speech, he said: “Carry me to the saint’s basilica, and throw upon his tomb as much gold as I have with me. For I have sinned by taking his property.”

When the donor of the field saw him being carried with gifts, he said: “Do not accept, I beg you, holy man of God, his gifts, which you were never accustomed to accept greedily. Do not, I beseech you, become his helper, since, inflamed by greed, he has become the wicked possessor of your property.”

The saint did not delay in hearing the voice of his poor man. For although that man had ordered gifts to be given, the saint showed that he had not accepted them.

Thus the usurper returned home, lost his spirit, and the Church recovered its property.

### LXVI

After the body of Blessed Remigius had been buried, as we have said, in the church of Saint Christopher, many astonishing miracles were performed in that church through his merits by the grace of the Lord, and the church itself was enlarged and elevated.

A crypt was made behind the altar, into which the most holy body was to be transferred. The tomb was dug up from the place where it stood so that it might be placed in the pit made in the aforementioned crypt, but it could not be moved in any way.

When night came, and the brothers had spent the night in hymns and songs with many lights burning, sleep overcame everyone around midnight. When they awoke, on the Kalends of October they found the tomb with the most holy body placed in the pit of the crypt behind the altar, as though by angelic hands.

All who were present were so filled with the sweetness of the fragrance that they could not express it in human language. The fragrance remained in that church throughout the entire day and the following day.

On the day of his translation, relics were taken from his body amid divine praises—namely, some of his hair, his chasuble, and his tunic. His body was found whole but dried, wrapped in a red cloth.

### LXVII

In the course of time, King Pippin, father of Charlemagne, wishing to take the estate of the bishopric of Laon called Anisiacus under a rent arrangement, as he had done with certain others, came to stay there.

While he was sleeping, Saint Remigius came to him and said: “What are you doing here? Why have you entered this estate, which a man more devoted to me than you gave me, and which I gave to my mistress, the holy Mother of God?”

He beat him quite severely, so that bruises afterward appeared on his body. When Blessed Remigius disappeared, Pippin rose and, seized by a violent fever, withdrew from the estate as quickly as possible. He suffered from that fever for a considerable time.

From then onward, no ruler of the kingdom stayed there until recent times, nor at Codiciacum or Juliacum—except King Louis of Germany, who stayed at Juliacum when he invaded the kingdom of his brother Charles. On the following day, fleeing shamefully before that same brother, he barely escaped.

### LXVIII

In our own time, a certain tenant of an estate of the bishopric of Rheims called Plumbea Fontana lived beside a royal fisc called Rosetus. Because of the harassment of the fiscal officials, he could not peacefully retain either his property, his harvest, or his meadow.

He often sought justice from the royal officials but could not obtain it. At last he found a salutary plan. He baked bread and cooked meat and took as much beer as he could in small vessels. He placed everything in a container commonly called a *benna*, set it on a cart, yoked oxen to it, and, holding a candle in his hand, hurried to the basilica of Saint Remigius.

When he arrived, he fed the servants of the matricularium with bread, meat, and beer, placed the candle at the saint’s tomb, and sought his help against the fiscal officials who were oppressing him.

He also gathered as much dust as he could from the church floor and tied it in a cloth. He placed it in the aforesaid *benna* and spread a linen cloth over it, as is customary over the body of a dead person. Then he returned home with his cart.

Whenever people he met asked him what he was carrying in the cart, he answered that he was carrying Saint Remigius. Everyone marveled at his words and actions, thinking him insane.

When he reached his meadow with the same cart, he found shepherds there grazing various kinds of animals belonging to the fisc of Rosetus. He invoked Saint Remigius, asking him to help him against his oppressors. Immediately the oxen and cows began attacking one another with their horns and bellowing loudly; the he-goats attacked the he-goats and the she-goats the she-goats with their horns; the pigs fought with the pigs; the rams collided with the rams; and the shepherds struck one another with sticks and fists.

Then a great whirlwind arose, and the shepherds, howling, together with the animals of each kind, began to flee toward Rosetus with such noise and tumult that it seemed as though a great multitude of pursuers were chasing them with whips.

When the fiscal officials saw and heard this, they were struck with such terror that they thought they could not live even for an hour. Corrected by this from their presumption, they ceased oppressing the poor man of Saint Remigius so completely that afterward the same poor man possessed his property peacefully and without disturbance.

Because he lived beside the river Saram in a muddy place, he also suffered great annoyance from snakes in his dwellings. He took the dust that he had gathered from the floor of Saint Remigius’s church and carried home with him, and scattered it throughout his dwellings. Afterward no snake appeared in those places where the dust had been scattered.

From these miracles we can gather with certainty that, if in our tribulations we ask from the heart for the help of Saint Remigius without hesitation in faith, we shall be freed through his merits and intercessions both from the attacks of the angels of Satan—who, in the form of a serpent, addressed and deceived the mother of the human race (Genesis III)—and from the wickedness of evil men.

### LXIX

In the time of the Emperor Louis, two Frankish foresters of his invaded part of the forest that Saint Remigius had purchased during his lifetime, as we showed above, in the Vosges woodland, claiming that the forest belonged more properly to the emperor’s fisc than to the portion belonging to Saint Remigius.

While the people under the authority of the church of Rheims were contradicting them, one of the brothers, arguing with them, went to his pigs, which he had sent into the same forest for pasture, and found a wolf among them. Mounting his horse, he pursued it swiftly.

When he wished to strike it, his horse became frightened, and he struck his head against a club from that forest, so violently that his brains flowed onto the ground; and he died.

His brother, hurrying to the other side, reached a certain rock and said: “Let everyone know that this forest belongs to the emperor as far as this rock.” When he struck the rock with the axe that he carried in his hand, fragments flew from it into his eyes, and he was blinded.

Thus both received the reward of their presumption and falsehood.

### LXX

A certain nobleman from the territory of Nevers, having obtained relics of Blessed Remigius, built an oratory in his honor on his own property. There the Lord displayed many miracles through the merits of His saint.

After the death of the Emperor Louis, when the Aquitanians, with the customary instability of their people, began to cast off the ruler’s yoke as each was able, fight among themselves, and rage through the neighboring districts, poor people tried to deposit their small possessions in churches.

Because of the reputation of the miracles performed there, they eagerly placed whatever they could in that same oratory for safekeeping. When the plunderers heard that the oratory was filled with the possessions of many people, they attacked it in order to seize them.

One of them kicked the locked door to break the bolt. Immediately his foot became attached to the door, and the presumptuous man fell backward onto the ground.

When the others saw this, they fled. But the wretched man, compelled by his torment, began with loud cries to confess his guilt and, with bitterest tears, to declare that if God, through the merits of Saint Remigius, would release his foot from that fetter, he would never again take anything from that church or any other church, nor, to the extent of his power, consent in any way to its being taken.

He also donated his horse, together with its saddle and whatever else he could, to the same church. After his confession, tears, declaration, and vow, his foot was released from the door to which it had adhered.

Nevertheless, he remained lame afterward with that withered foot until, after a long illness, his leg and thigh rotted and he died.

### LXXI

When the three royal brothers, Clothar, Louis, and Charles, divided the kingdom among themselves after their father’s death, Charles divided the bishopric of Rheims, which the priest Fulk held, among his own men and gave the estate of Juliacum to Richuvinus as a benefice.

While Richuvinus’s wife, named Berta, was lying in the chamber of that estate, Saint Remigius came to her and said: “This is not your place to lie. The person who is to possess this estate and lie in this chamber must have another merit and office. Rise immediately and depart from here.”

She paid no attention, thinking that she had seen an empty vision.

A second time Saint Remigius came to her and said: “Why have you not departed from here, as I commanded you? Take care that I do not find you here again.”

As before, she regarded it as nothing.

When Saint Remigius came to her a third time, he said: “Have I not already commanded you once and twice to depart from here? But because you have refused to leave, you will depart through the removal of others.” And he struck her with the staff that he held in his hand.

Her entire body turned into a great swelling. She told her husband Richuvinus and many others what she had seen, and, after being tormented most severely for several days, she died.

Her husband had her body carried to the church of Saint Remigius and buried there.

Some people wonder why, after expelling her from the aforesaid estate by a deadly punishment, he received her body to be buried in his church. No one will wonder at this if he considers with what intention the saints exercise vengeance upon wrongdoers: namely, so that, if they recognize their fault, they may receive here what they deserve and not be tormented after death by eternal punishments.

Thus we read in the Book of Kings about the prophet who was disobedient to the word of the Lord and died after being struck by a lion; yet after the punishment had been inflicted, his body remained untouched by the lion (III Kings XIII).

But if those against whom vengeance proceeds do not amend themselves, the punishment is inflicted so that others may be corrected by their scourges and may reform through fear, as it is written: “When the pestilent man is punished, the simple will become wiser” (Proverbs XXI).

Some also complain that Saint Remigius now does not avenge himself upon those who invade his property and oppress his household, as he did in earlier times, applying to themselves the verse of the Psalm: “We do not see our signs; there is now no prophet, and he will know us no more” (Psalm LXXIII).

But this should not be a cause for complaint; rather, it should be a cause for grief and fear, because what was foretold in ancient times is being fulfilled in our own.

For it is written in the Apocalypse: “The sun became like a sackcloth garment” (Revelation VI). In the last age of our time, the sun is displayed as though it were sackcloth, because the shining life of preachers appears harsh and despicable before the eyes of the reprobate, and the miracles of the saints are justly withheld from sinners through contempt, as it is written: “Lest they should be converted and I should heal them” (Isaiah XLI).

This is so that those who now rejoice even in their sins may be more completely overwhelmed by punishments.

Nevertheless, this holy imitator of his Lord does not avenge everything, so that His patience may be shown; nor does he leave everything unpunished, so that His providence may be demonstrated. Although he exercises vengeance against the wicked less frequently, he does not entirely leave the offenses of presumptuous people in our own time unpunished.

### LXXII

[Note: Flodoard, in the passage cited, reports that this occurred in the time of Archbishop Hincmar, the writer of this Life.]

For a certain Blithgarius recently obtained, for a price from Bernard the custodian, a holding from the church treasury at the estate of Tenoilum. From there he expelled the servants of Saint Remigius with whips.

When they cried out to Saint Remigius to help them, Blithgarius replied to them mockingly: “Now it will become clear how Saint Remigius will help you. See how he comes to your aid.”

While he was saying these words, he groaned with a tremendous cry, swelled up by inflating himself incredibly, and then burst open in the middle and died.

When we hear this, let us fear divine vengeance upon ourselves and take great care to avoid blasphemy against God and His saints. Let us strive not to treat the ecclesiastical household cruelly; not to be drawn by our neighbor’s wrongs into repaying evil with evil or into the resentment of hatred; not, through the devil’s temptations, to be drawn into the enjoyment of or consent to sin; and not, in response to the chastisements of the supreme Maker, to rush into excessive murmuring.

Although miracles through this servant of His may not be performed for us with such frequency and reverence, we must nevertheless be certain that he does not withdraw from his city and from us, its citizens, the continual assistance of his intercession, just as we read concerning Jeremiah: “This is the lover of the brothers and of the people of Israel; this is the one who prays greatly for the people and for the whole holy city of Jerusalem” (II Maccabees XV).

### LXXIII

In the year 852 from the Lord’s Incarnation, when the church itself had recently been enlarged, the tomb, together with the body of blessed Remigius, was transferred from the site of the earlier crypt into a crypt constructed on a larger and more beautiful plan. The most holy body itself was found intact by the bishops of the diocese of Rheims, just as at the earlier translation, and wrapped in a red cloth. When it was transferred from that tomb into a little silver shrine, a portion of the cloth, together with the cloth that had been over his head, was taken into a small ivory reliquary and is venerated with due honor beside the altar of Saint Mary in the city. [Col. 1178D]

The silver shrine, containing the body of that saint, was placed upon the marble tomb in which it had previously lain. The relics that had been found outside the tomb at his head were placed by the aforesaid bishops in the tomb in which he had lain, on the Kalends of October; on that same calendar day his earlier translation had been celebrated many years before.

When his most holy body was transferred from the tomb into the aforesaid silver shrine, Rado, then a subdeacon of the Church of Soissons, who had come there with his bishop Rothad, had already been tormented for a full year, day and night, by toothache, so severely that he feared losing his senses from the excessive pain. While the bishops were occupied with arranging the saint’s body, he placed the jaw in which he suffered pain against the spot where the holy body had lain. Immediately freed from that pain, he thereafter felt no toothache, as he later took care to report, twenty-five years afterward.
