On that same day, in a certain oratory where the memory of blessed Remigius is honored, in the district of Ribuarie, two crippled persons were healed. From the time of the first and second translations, as also before them, many remarkable miracles have been performed in that same place, through the merits of this saint, for people suffering from various illnesses. We have these miracles written down, but here we have omitted them because of their number and because they are displayed there so frequently. [Col. 1179A–B]

### LXXIV

Since the miracles just recounted make it abundantly clear with what distinguished glory and honor the Lord deemed him worthy to crown, and how he showed him to humanity as one who had been marvelous in His sight, let us, dearest brothers, recall a few things in a brief summary. Let us contemplate how this most blessed patron and protector of ours, while living in the body, was filled with the spirit of the fathers of both the Old and the New Testament—that is, with the diversity of their works, received from one and the same Spirit—and how after his death he shone as a sharer in miracles.

In that he was foretold from heaven and designated by name, we see Isaac the patriarch and John the Baptist represented in him (Gen. XVII; Luke I). In that he was sanctified before birth and, from adolescence, avoided the presence of the people in seclusion, we see Jeremiah and John the Baptist likewise (Jer. I; Luke I). In that he was elected by the bishops of the province of Rheims, together with the clergy and people, and was ordained bishop after divine signs had been shown over him, we see Matthias, who was elected by the apostles and the other faithful, offered to the Lord, and appointed an apostle by divine lot (Acts I).

In that, amid the bitterest waves of this world, he guided the holy Church toward the harbor of eternal light by the oarage of merits and virtues, prayers and preaching, we see Noah, who raised the ark prefiguring the Church amid the Flood (Gen. VII). In that his face became radiant through the presence of Christ, we see Moses (Exod. XXXIV). In that he stood amid flames and the remnants that the fire had not yet devoured, and prevented the conflagration from crossing over, we see Aaron (Num. XVI). In that, by cursing senseless objects, he condemned their worshipers to barrenness, we see David (II Sam. I).

In that he baptized three thousand men converted by his preaching during the vigil of holy Easter, and raised a young girl from death, we see blessed Peter, who at holy Pentecost converted an equal number of Jews to the faith and had them baptized, and who raised Dorcas from death (Acts II and IX). In that he subdued the fiercest barbarians from their savagery and shut them up at Rheims for baptism, afterward giving them the bread of heaven and spiritual drink, we see Elisha, who shut up enemies arriving in Samaria and ordered food and drink to be given them (IV Kings VI).

In that he caused very small quantities of liquid to overflow, we see Elijah and likewise Elisha (III Kings XVII; IV Kings IV). In that by prophetic inspiration he foretold to King Louis what was to come upon him and his descendants, we see Isaiah, who foretold to King Hezekiah what was to come upon him and his descendants (IV Kings XX). In that, though bodily far away, he was present in spirit and learned of the king’s death, we see Elisha likewise, whose heart was present when Naaman descended from his chariot to meet Gehazi (IV Kings V).

In that, having foreknown through the revelation of the Holy Spirit the famine that was to come, he provided for how he might assist the people who would suffer hunger, we see Joseph (Gen. XLI). In that, so that he might be justified as a just man still further, he temporarily lost the light of his bodily eyes and afterward recovered his sight, we see Tobit (Tob. II and XI).

But since he was also a branch of the true vine bearing fruit, pruned so that he might bear more fruit, and since, while retaining the light of the mind that he had not lost, he endured in temptation the loss of the light of his bodily eyes, which he had lost for a time, and offered praise, while after the temptation, once proved, he recovered the light of his bodily eyes, so that he blessed the Lord in his very loss, we recognize Job: patient in temptation, he blessed the name of the Lord, and after being proved in temptation he possessed twice as much as before (Job II and XLII).

In that, having learned the day of his departure, he bade farewell to his people through the celebration of Masses and died, we see blessed John the apostle and evangelist. In that, by the pall of his tomb, he restrained and repelled a groin affliction, we see the distinguished Paul, by whose handkerchiefs and aprons the sick were healed (Acts XIX). In that, both while living in the body and after death, he exercised punishments through zeal for justice upon those who sinned, we see Moses, Phinehas, Joshua, and Elijah; Peter, who struck down Simon Magus, Ananias, and Sapphira; and Paul, who blinded Elymas the magician.

In that his most holy body was first buried in the church designated by divine will and afterward carried from place to place by angelic ministry, we see the prophet Habakkuk, who was carried by an angel’s hand from Judea to Babylon, over the pit, and was brought back from there to Judea (Dan. XIV). We also see Moses, who was buried by the Lord, certainly through angelic ministry. Just as no one to the present day knows his tomb, so no one knows by what manner this saint’s tomb was transferred (Deut. XXXIV). [Col. 1179C–1180D]

### Verses inscribed on the tomb of Saint Remigius

Here Hincmar, servant of the Lord, placed the sacred limbs  
of gentle Remigius, led by devoted love.

He was holy before he was created in the world by his mother,  
and was called great by the mouth of God from heaven.

Happily bearing twice ten and two years,  
by God’s decree he assumed pontifical dignity.

For sixty years together with twice seven  
he had remained the honor of this city, bishop and beloved of the world.

Restoring life to the dead and light to the blind,  
even while living he had performed very many miracles.

[Col. 1181A]

For he subdued savage hearts, pious in spirit and overflowing in speech,  
consecrating the royal scepters of the Sicambrian people.

When he had completed ninety-six years,  
the splendid light departed from our darkness.

When January had already reached its full Ides,  
the veteran soldier received worthy rewards.

That same Hincmar, formerly a priest in this see,  
after thirty years took his place and office here;

as the sixteenth under this radiant lamp,  
he rendered to Remigius at Rheims his cherished services.

For seven years and five months  
he exercised the care of a shepherd, accomplishing these things worthy of remembrance.

In the eight-hundred-and-fifty-second year,  
the year in which God was born human from a Virgin,

and the third Charles was arranging the affairs of his reign,  
when October gave its first day,

and the three-hundred-and-eighth year was being reached,

[Col. 1181B]

this righteous man of the Lord sought the stars of heaven.

Three hundred and forty-three years had passed  
when he joyfully washed the Franks in the stream of life.

May he be placed in the heavenly dwelling through his prayers,  
whom the true lover honored on earth. Amen.

### LXXV

Afterward, however, because the merits of sinners demanded it, in the year 882 from the Lord’s Incarnation, while Carlomann was reigning and the aforesaid lord Hincmar, archbishop, was laboring earnestly, the venerable pledge of the body of this most sacred Father and our lord Remigius was transferred, because of the attacks of the pagans, to the estate already mentioned above, called Sparnacum, since at that time the city of Rheims had no wall enclosing it. [Col. 1181C]

Through his protection, the safety of the entire district to which this most beloved gift was brought is then shown to have been secured against invasion by barbarians or attacks by robbers.

Finally, after the death of Bishop Hincmar, this desirable treasure of the sacred limbs was brought to the monastery of Orbais. Here too, through the intercession of this most blessed patron of ours, every benefit of the atmosphere, together with unusual fertility of the soil, is granted to the inhabitants living throughout the surrounding region.

### LXXVI

After the death of the oft-mentioned bishop Hincmar, when Fulco had assumed the honor of the episcopate, in the first year of his episcopate he resolved to bring back the sacred bones of our most blessed Father. When he undertook this, having already arrived with his fellow bishops and many members of the clergy at the place where the precious relic was kept, the sky was perfectly clear but the drought exceedingly severe. Suddenly such a great rain poured forth that it seemed to have abundantly watered the whole surface of the earth. [Col. 1181D]

On the following day, while they proceeded to carry back the sacred gifts, everything became bright, joyful, and pleasant in worldly appearance. Advancing prosperously, with people flocking from every direction, they came to the village of Calminiacum, in which this distinguished Father is known to have displayed some mighty works of virtue while still enclosed in the flesh. There they laid down the venerable limbs in a church dedicated in his name and refreshed their bodies, wearied by the night’s rest.

### LXXVII

After the support of rest, when the sun’s radiance was already illuminating the earth, voices blessing God resounded everywhere, as did the voices of those praising Him because He was restoring to them bodily their own shepherd, patron, and protector, whom they trusted always to have as their intercessor before the divine mercy and as their constant advocate.

Meanwhile, after the aforesaid bishop had duly celebrated the sacraments of the heavenly mysteries, he ascended the slopes of the approaching mountain with praises, surrounded on every side by crowds of people accompanying him. There, when he had poured out prayer to the Lord for the people’s sins and for the mitigation of heavenly wrath, and they had proceeded a little farther, Christ—who was preparing to glorify, make wondrous, and magnify on earth this most blessed Father of ours, whom He had chosen to magnify with the angels in heaven—determined to reveal to the assembled multitude how great was his merit with Him. [Col. 1182A–B]

### LXXVIII

A blind woman named Doda then approached, leaning upon the hand of one who guided her steps. As soon as she came near, she obtained the restoration of her sight before everyone. When the bishop heard this, filled with great joy, he celebrated with the people a hymn of praise to God.

They had not yet finished their songs, filling heaven with rejoicing, when suddenly a certain man who had been lame for many days proceeded in complete health, rejoicing.

### LXXIX

After proceeding a little way from there with praises, a certain woman who had received the use of her hands followed. The accompanying crowds therefore doubled and tripled their acts of thanksgiving. Astonished by the magnitude of the miracles, those nearest deliberated for a while about withdrawing from such lofty holiness. The reciprocal voice of the praisers had not yet ceased from their mouths when a boy named Grimoldus, long deprived of sight, with his mouth also pitifully twisted from its proper position and troubled by a repulsive deformity, was carried to meet them by his parents. He recovered the sight he had lost some time before and, through the miraculous help of this most holy Father, was restored to his proper form.

After an interval of approximately one hour, another boy, who had been crippled in body, was happily raised upright through the intercession of the same patron. The devout company, quite unable to echo David’s songs sufficiently in melody, was moved by the greatest affection of heart. Amid voices of praise, joy drew tears from them, and they drenched their faces with abundant weeping and formed sighs and sobs in place of songs. [Col. 1182C]

The excessive crowding of the throngs who gathered, eager to kiss the shrine bearing the sacred gift, began to impede its progress, as they pressed forward with determined insistence. The report of the miracles being performed spread widely, and both the healthy and those afflicted by various calamities hastened eagerly, desiring to behold the mighty works that the almighty Lord had determined to multiply in glorifying His saint. Each person considered it a great loss—or rather counted it a sin—not only not to proceed, but even to come last.

As the citizens hurried out to meet them, when they saw the welcome gift being carried, they prostrated themselves and kissed the bare earth. Looking upward, when they saw the shrine bearing the precious jewel of the divine diadem, they shed many tears amid extraordinary joy, begging that they might not be judged to suffer any longer from the absence of that Father, but might deserve to rejoice in his perpetual presence. [Col. 1182D–1183A]

Meanwhile, the most blessed Father, favoring the devotion of his children with splendid signs, continued to gladden his people in many ways with divine miracles. While the clergy with the priests resounded with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, and the people also echoed with voices of immense jubilation, so that they might proclaim the wondrous God in His saints with still more joyful hearts, the multitude of the sick was visibly seen to recover its former health, as many were raised up from various bodily diseases. Indeed, heavenly miracles were disclosed at almost every moment, so that the intervals of places and times could scarcely be considered sufficient to enumerate them. [Col. 1183B]

### LXXX

Then a certain woman named Osanna deserved, amid the wonder of those rejoicing, to receive her sight again with swift recovery. Shortly afterward, a certain lame man obtained the use of his legs as a happy gift. A woman named Deodata, with the doors of her ears opened, gained hearing. A certain man named Teuto received the desired gift of illumination. Another woman likewise rejoiced, delighted by the same benefit. Ansoldus too, with a faithful heart, as he believed, enjoyed through the most holy intercession of this Father the sight that he longed for with intense desire. A certain Gerbertus was healed of paralysis. Another man likewise rejoiced, having been granted the benefit of the same gift.

### LXXXI

As everyone strove eagerly to go out to meet them in rivalry of pious devotion, and brought not only the intention of a kindly heart but also offerings of temporal goods, as each person’s means allowed, a certain poor woman hurried from the city to meet them, carrying in her hand a candle that had never been lit.

Wonderful to relate, suddenly, by a divine sign from heaven, the candle was lit in the hand of its bearer. As she carried it along the entire road, confessing God’s miracle, it did not lose the benefit of the heavenly light until the relics of the wondrous Father had been carried to their proper station, and the bishop had celebrated the solemn Masses. Then the woman handed the candle, burning with light, to the custodian of the basilica. Because of his joy at what had happened through heavenly grace, he ordered all the lamps that could be seen burning throughout the church to be extinguished and then relit by the divinely given light. He decreed that part of the candle be preserved as testimony to the miracle granted by heaven. [Col. 1183C–D]

### LXXXII

A woman named Rotgardis, from the district of Castricum, who had lost the ability to walk, rejoiced in the gift of her former health. She had been brought in a cart, but afterward she was able to return home on her own feet.

Moreover, a certain woman brought with her a little daughter of about six years, named Wulfidis. One day, while playing with her peers, the girl had been struck on the head by some passing woman. Injured by that blow, the back of her head seemed to have been bent backward and fixed to her neck, so that she could not incline her head in any other direction. She was able to take no nourishment except liquids, and had spent nearly an entire year under such severe suffering. [Col. 1184A]

Her mother, tenderly devoted to her and anxious for her recovery, took care to lead her out to meet the procession. Since she could not approach closely because of the density of the crowd, she arranged to go a little ahead of the people. Then, on the road along which the journey was to be made, she prostrated herself together with her child and, supported by strong faith, directed prayers to God with a devout mind.

She had not yet ceased praying when, behold, her daughter began to cry out. The mother rose to console her with maternal caresses and saw that the girl’s head had returned from its bent position to its proper straight alignment. Then, filled with immense joy and confident in her child’s recovery, she examined the place of the injury and saw it wet with blood, while the nerves that had long been contracted were stretched out as though they were cords. Having received the blessing of mercy that she had sought, she returned home joyfully with thanksgiving. [Col. 1184B]

### LXXXIII

Thus, surrounded by the dignity of this glorification and by wonder at the deeds performed, and filled with a vow of thanksgiving, the company strove to complete the whole journey with songs and hymns, exerting all the fervor of its zeal. The bishop had gone ahead, but then returned and, accompanied by the choirs of the clergy, took the most precious treasure upon his own shoulders. In this way he carried it with great glory and jubilation to the house of the most blessed Father himself.

When they reached the church, everything that seemed appropriate was properly arranged. As the sacrifice of the spiritual victim had already begun, a certain woman from the district of Troyes, afflicted by agitation of all her limbs, came and fell upon the pavement before the altar. After being miserably tormented there for a long time, she rose healed through the mercy of this most holy comforter. When questioned about the cause of such a great calamity, she confessed that she had committed the murder of her own mother.

After the solemn Masses had been completed according to custom, each person returned to his own dwelling, intending to come back early the following day in order to carry this protection of their city to its appointed place.

When morning had come, as people eagerly hurried to the agreed meeting place, a certain woman named Erluidis, living not far from the city, prepared to go out to witness such a great procession, hoping to obtain the gift of the health she desired. For she had been afflicted by illness for five years and carried the right side of her body almost dead and nearly useless. With whatever effort she could make, she endeavored to approach and advance toward the shrine of this sacred gift. [Col. 1184C–D]

When, by such exertion, she had traversed nearly half the distance, she could go no farther and fell down, exhausted by severe labor. She thought of returning home, but was entirely unable to accomplish this. After lying there for some time, wavering in this uncertainty, she finally resumed the attempt and tried to see whether she could still come somewhat nearer.

Immediately, through the mercy of divine clemency, strength was added to her sick efforts. Her powers returned together with her health, and she hurried forward freely and swiftly, rejoicing with excessive happiness. The sick woman, who had intended to drag herself to the destination, began joyfully to approach with an agile step.

She completed the appointed journey carrying a staff as a support for her illness—not because she would need its help any longer, but so that it might serve as testimony to the health granted to her. When she reached the place she desired, she gave devoted thanks in praise to her intercessor. Then she left behind the staff, the support of her former calamity, and, now vigorous and needing no such aid, retraced the journey she had completed, joyfully recounting the aid of divine consolation that she had obtained. [Col. 1185A]

### LXXXIV

The bishop then arrived, surrounded by a company of clergy and nobles. After offering the sacrifice of salvation and putting on white garments, he brought the most welcome treasure to the walls of the city, accompanied by choirs of psalm-singers.

As they proceeded happily and made their way joyfully toward the appointed place, almighty God graciously poured out in abundance the fountain of His kindness and generosity in glorifying this beloved one of His. Indeed, scarcely could any tongue express what was then accomplished during the almost moment-by-moment intervals of that journey.

For on that day the Lord performed such a multitude of mighty miracles that four men and nine women deserved to recover their sight, while two men recovered the use of their legs. Thus, with wonder at this splendid thanksgiving, they arrived at the church of the Mother of God in the city with the greatest rejoicing. The lamp that shines and burns eternally was then set upon the altar step.

As the bishop approached to consecrate the life-giving sacrament, who had a breast so iron or a heart so stony that he would not groan, beat his breast, and shed tears when he saw such astonishing divine gifts of grace? Who could enumerate the abundance of miracles poured out from heaven here on that day? Truly, no one could explain in speech how many sick people were healed, how many faltering people were raised up, and how many were freed here that day from various afflictions. [Col. 1185B–C]

### LXXXV

After the sacred rites of the mysteries had been completed, everyone hurried to depart and return to his own home. But as they were leaving, a threatening terror arose: exceedingly dark clouds and dreadful storm clouds began to gather, to cover the sky with savage darkness, to flash lightning, to make thunder roar, and to beat the earth with a considerable hailstorm.

Struck by this terror, many turned back, begging the mercy of the Most High, so that through the intercession of this most blessed Father they might deserve to be rescued from the dangers that threatened. In a marvelous manner, the disturbance that had inspired terror began to change: the darkness of the clouds grew bright, the lightning ceased, the thunder was quieted, and the entire storm began to calm and disperse. The storm, transformed from something savage into a desired rain, beneficially refreshed with fertile moisture the surface of the earth, which had been parched and heated by the excessive burning of the sun.

Thus it was plainly made known that indignation, stirred up for a time, had been changed into the assistance of salvation. Finally, through the consolation of this most kindly Father, the corruption of the dreadful plague appears to have been driven from our borders: the air became healthful, suitable rain was given, and the fear that had invaded the realm was gradually transformed into hope of security through the tranquility of peace. [Col. 1185D–1186A]

### LXXXVI

On that same day, namely the day when the sacred body was brought into the city, while the burning wheel of the sun was already hastening toward the ocean, a certain man named Nivolus, from an estate called Dominica situated on the slope of the mountain of Rheims, deaf and mute, and also weak in his hands and feet for nine years, crawled nearly five thousand paces from the light of the rising dawn and, scarcely able to make the journey by any effort throughout the day, reached the doors of the church containing the tomb at about the tenth hour.

When he arrived and discovered that the sacred body was not there, and saw that the doors of the church were carefully closed and secured with locks, he fell face down upon the ground. With a certain importunate presumption, he began secretly to strike at the ears of the saint’s holiness with a cry, complaining that he had been wearied by such great labor and had not even been permitted to see the shrine bearing the sacred relic, although he did not doubt that it possessed the exalted power to help him.

While he silently turned such thoughts over in his mind, the strength of health gradually began to enter his limbs. At once he was astonished to recover all the powers of his senses. When news of this event, reported by certain people, struck the ears of many, everyone rushed forward in rivalry. Rejoicing, they gazed upon God’s marvelous works, brought the man triumphantly to the place of the venerable tomb, rang the bells, and proclaimed praises to God with joyful voices. [Col. 1186B–C]

Moved by the fame of this miracle, very many people hurried to the church, desiring to see the mighty works of God. Seeing the signs of divine powers as they had heard, they raised their hands gratefully to heaven and blessed the Lord.

This miracle of divine kindness is then recognized as having greatly benefited, for their consolation, those who complained that they had been bodily deprived of so great a patron. Yet by this evidence of compassion he showed especially that he was not absent from them.

### LXXXVII

In the church of the blessed Mother of God, where the venerable relic of this Father was kept, several other sick people were meanwhile healed of various ailments. A certain man named Natalis of Burdenacum, a woman named Teutberga, and another woman named Guntildis deserved, through the patronage of this Father, to recover their sight. Another woman also recovered in that same house the sight she had lost in one eye. [Col. 1186D]

Moreover, a certain girl named Florgildis, from an estate called Caucella situated beside the stream of the Libra, about four years old, slipped and fell and weakened both her knees. She became so lame that she could neither set foot to the ground nor stand upon her feet at all. Although her parents were poor, they were concerned for her recovery and arranged to carry her through various churches of the saints.

After she had been afflicted by the severity of this illness for nearly twelve years and could find no remedy for her pain, she learned from reports of the sacred body and its miraculous works. She began to crawl forward with whatever effort she could make. She refused to be placed in a cart and instead desired to make the journey by being dragged along as best she could.

When she reached the church where she had heard that the precious gift of salvation was present, she poured out prayers and begged the Lord’s mercy for her liberation. She is also said to have moistened the pavement with her own tears. After she had done this for three days, while she again devoted herself to prayer, divine grace came upon her. Hardly able to bear the force of the cure, she began to cry out loudly and utter bitter wails. Then, when the knots of her nerves had been loosened and the contraction of all her knees relaxed, she lay exhausted for nearly an hour, as though dead. [Col. 1187A]

But the one who bestowed the help of release also granted strength and vigor. Immediately, as though awakening from a deep sleep, she sensed that the heavenly gift had come to her. She sought the shrine of the holy relic, not doubting that her healing had been granted through its power.

Afterward, giving thanks there and deciding gratefully to remain in that place, and persisting in frequent prayers, she celebrated due vigils for her healer and daily offered offerings of saving sacrifice.

### LXXXVIII

That most sacred body of our most blessed patron Remigius remained at Rheims in the aforesaid church of the Mother of God while the previously mentioned bishop, lord Fulco, exercised the office of bishop, namely until the episcopate of the venerable Archbishop Heriveus. When the persecution of the Normans had ceased and peace had been recovered through God’s mercy alone, he resolved to bring back the same heavenly gift to its own burial place within the walls.

As he hastened to accomplish this after summoning certain nobles of the kingdom, the Lord did not delay adding to the glorification of the one who was seeking to restore his bones to their place.

It happened that, after they had gone out of the city and were surrounded by a great crowd of people flowing together, a certain lame man named Abraham, whose knees were contracted by the dryness of his nerves, was dragging himself across the ground as best he could, clinging to little stools. When, having come near the city, he began to direct his journey toward the basilica of the saint, he was touched by divine power. The stiffness of his joints was loosened, and he began to be extended toward the remedies of health. [Col. 1188A–B]

After he had recovered his health, we saw him for many years standing upright and unharmed, walking and rejoicing in the prosperity granted to him. At the place where this gift of healing occurred, a column was later erected, bearing a cross and preserving memorials of this glorification.

The church of his tomb was adorned both earlier, very frequently, and afterward, by many splendid and manifold miracles, which have by no means been contained in writing; for they are of many kinds.

[Col. 1187]

## XXII. Eulogy of the same Saint Remigius, by Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims

*(In Surius, in the same place.)*

### I

Let us also see how this blessed Father and our shepherd, through the blessings given him by God the lawgiver, arranged within his heart, with God’s help, ascents through this world’s valley of tears, and, advancing by God’s grace from virtue to virtue, grew until he deserved to see face to face the One whom he had always desired in spirit.

The same Lord says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV). The Apostle, as though explaining this, says: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. For star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. III). For in that life of eternal blessedness, which is not unequal, each person receives a distinct place according to distinct merit. Yet he does not feel the loss arising from that difference, because what he receives is sufficient for him.

And Catholic teaching has taught us that the distinct ways of life of individual human beings correspond to the orders of the heavenly hosts, and that, by similarity of conduct, they are assigned to their lot.

### II

For there are many who grasp only small things, yet do not cease piously announcing these same small things to their brothers. Such people therefore proceed among the number of the angels.

Blessed Remigius, although through God’s gift there was in him a manifold knowledge of God, as a faithful and wise servant supplied his fellow servants with their measure of wheat—that is, according to the capacity of his hearers (Luke XII)—and, following the Apostle, first gave milk as drink to the barbarians, not solid food (I Cor. III).

And since, as Malachi testifies, “the priest is the angel of the Lord” (Mal. II), holy Remigius, a great priest, deserved the fellowship of the angels. [Col. 1188C]

### III

There are some who, filled with the gift of divine generosity, are able both to grasp and to announce the highest mysteries of heaven. To what group, then, are such people assigned, if not to the number of the archangels?

Blessed Remigius, speaking wisdom among the perfect, deserved to be assigned to the number of the archangels when, in a synod of Catholic bishops, he converted a heretic who held an evil opinion about the true Son of God. [Col. 1188D]

### IV

There are some who perform wonders and powerfully work signs. To what group, then, do such people correspond, if not to the number and lot of the heavenly Virtues?

Blessed Remigius, both while he was in the body and after his death, performed wonders and powerfully worked signs, as we have shown above. He therefore corresponds to the lot and number of the heavenly Virtues. [Col. 1189A]

### V

There are some who also drive evil spirits from possessed bodies and cast them out through the power of prayer and the force of the authority they have received. To what lot, then, do such people attain their merit, if not among the number of the heavenly Powers?

Holy Remigius, through the power of prayer and the force of the authority he had received, drove evil spirits from possessed bodies, as we have shown above. Therefore he received his lot among the number of the heavenly Powers.

### VI

There are some who, through the virtues they have received, even surpass the merits of elect human beings. Since they are better than the good, they also rule over their elect brothers. To what lot, then, have such people received their place, if not among the ranks of the Principalities?

Blessed Remigius, archbishop of this city of Rheims, ruled over holy brothers: Vedastus, whom he ordained at Arras; Medardus at Vermandois; Lupus at Soissons; Genebaldus at Laon; and the other elect brothers in the cities subject to him. Thus he received his lot among the ranks of the Principalities. [Col. 1189B]

### VII

There are some who so rule over all vices and every desire within themselves that, by the very right of purity, they are called gods among human beings. Hence it is said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you god over Pharaoh” (Exod. VII). To what group, then, do such people belong—people in comparison with whom other human beings are, so to speak, servants—if not to the ranks of the Dominations?

Blessed Remigius, having ruled within himself over every vice and every desire, was able, by the right of purity, to see the face of Christ when, as has been shown above, Christ came to him, to King Louis, to the queen, and to the other people present in the oratory of Saint Peter. And, exercising authority, he commanded the king, his subject servant, to be baptized, saying: “Lower your neck, Sicamber.” He also scourged King Pippin when the latter attempted to take the estate of Anisy from the Church of Laon.

Therefore he received his lot among the ranks of the Principalities. [Col. 1189C]

VIII. There are also some who, while ruling themselves with vigilant care, while examining themselves with attentive concern and always clinging to divine fear, receive this as the reward of virtue: that they are able rightly to judge others as well. Since divine contemplation is present to their minds, the Lord, presiding in them as upon his throne, examines the deeds of others and wondrously dispenses all things from his seat. What, then, are these people other than thrones of their Creator, and to what number are they assigned if not to the number of the heavenly thrones? Through them, while the holy Church is governed, even the elect are often judged for certain of their weak actions.

We read that this was also accomplished through Saint Remigius, when he judged the elect of God, Bishop Genebald, for his weak actions; and afterward, with the Lord presiding in his heart, he restored him to the episcopal order at the Lord’s command. It is therefore certain that blessed Remigius has been enrolled among the number of the heavenly thrones.

IX. There are also some who are so filled with love of God and neighbor [Col. 1190A] that they are rightly called Cherubim. For since *Cherubim* is said to mean “fullness of knowledge,” and since we have learned from Paul’s teaching that “love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. XIII), all who are more abundantly filled than others with love of God and neighbor have received the lot of their merits among the number of the Cherubim.

Anyone who gives careful attention to what has been read above about him clearly understands how full of love he was; and from his words and deeds, as well as from the testimony of Saint Pope Hormisdas cited earlier, perceives how greatly he was filled with knowledge. Therefore Saint Remigius strove to receive the lot of his merits among the number of the Cherubim.

X. There are also some who, kindled by the torches of love for heavenly contemplation, pant with desire for their Creator; they desire nothing more in this world and are nourished solely by love of eternity. They cast away everything earthly and transcend all temporal things in their minds. They love and burn, and in their very burning they find rest. In loving they burn, and by speaking they kindle others as well. Those whom they touch with their word they immediately cause to burn with love of God.

What, then, should I call such people except Seraphim? Their heart, transformed into fire, both shines and burns: for they illuminate the eyes of minds toward heavenly things and, piercing them with compunction and tears, cleanse away the rust of vices. Since, therefore, they have been inflamed with love of their Creator, where else could they have received the lot of their vocation except among the number of the Seraphim?

The whole people of the Franks testifies to how blessed Remigius burned with love of his Creator and kindled others by his speech, since, through his preaching, the king and the nation were converted to the Catholic faith [Col. 1190C]. His words also testify to how he cast away all earthly things, transcended all temporal matters in his mind, was nourished solely by the love of eternity, and was inflamed with love of his Creator. Set ablaze by desire for his Creator, he said almost continually with his lips, and always in his heart:

“My tears have been my bread day and night. My soul thirsted for the living God: when shall I come and appear before the face of God? I shall be satisfied when his glory is revealed” (Ps. XLI and XVI).

Among the number of the Seraphim, therefore, he received the lot of his vocation. With them, the holy soul of that apostolic man now rejoices in heavenly glory together with his companions.

XI. But then, certainly, he and those who share in his glory will rejoice much more perfectly, when they have received immortal bodies and, in that same blessedness, all their fellow servants and brothers whom they now see struggling on earth. They will no longer have any reason to turn the gaze of their thought outward, even for a little while, since they will have God within them, and will rejoice in the heavenly vision of him.

There the first and greatest commandment of the Lord will be fulfilled in its entirety, toward whose perfection the righteous in this life gird themselves, each according to his strength:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII; Mark XII).

For the more closely they behold the present face of the Lord, the more ardently they devote themselves wholly to his love, because they recognize that all their neighbors are elect and beloved by God [Col. 1191A]. The more they see that their neighbors’ hearts, no less than their own, are filled with sincere love, the more they delight in loving them no less than themselves.

For the saints pray to God for those who labor faithfully in the struggle of this life, and they sympathize with them. They also pray, as was said above, for those who, although predestined because of their good works to the lot of the elect, are nevertheless received after death into punishments proportionate to their deeds, because they leave the body stained by certain evils; once purified, they attain the repose of the blessed.

As for those who have already been deprived of their bodies and delivered over to eternal punishments, although they possess mercy in the goodness of their nature, once joined to the justice of their Creator they are bound by such strict rectitude—for they agree with the Judge to whom they cling—that they neither rescue those whom they cannot rescue nor condescend to them out of mercy. They see them as so alien to themselves as they behold them rejected by the Creator whom they love. Already exalted by the justice of judgment, they do not pity them in any way out of compassion.

Before the final judgment and its retribution, however, the unrighteous see certain righteous people in repose, so that, when they behold them in joy, they are tormented not only by their own punishment but also by the blessedness of the righteous. The righteous, for their part, continually behold the unrighteous in torment, so that their joy increases when they see the evils from which they mercifully escaped. They give greater thanks to their Deliverer the more they see in others what they themselves might have suffered had they been abandoned.

Nor will the sight of the punishment of the rejected darken such great blessedness in the minds of the righteous [Col. 1191C], because where compassion for misery no longer exists, it certainly cannot diminish the joy of the blessed. Although their own joys are fully sufficient for their delight, they nevertheless always behold the evils of the rejected. For those who see the glory of their Creator can see nothing that takes place in creation which they cannot perceive.

XII. Therefore, just as, having heard of the glory of the saints, the misery of the rejected, and the merits of this most holy patron of ours, and having heard of the benefits that believers and devout people have merited through his patronage, by the gift of grace, in the working of miracles and the granting of healings, we desire that such things likewise be granted to us through his intercession, so, having also heard of the punishments of vengeance [Col. 1191D] endured by sinners and rebels, through the retribution of justice, because of his merits, let us fear remaining rebellious in sins—and, what is even more serious, in obstinacy toward sins—lest we be overwhelmed by similar or worse punishments. For if, after learning of such great and such examples, we are neither moved by benefits to do good nor restrained from evil by fear of punishments, then the vengeance of scourges inflicted upon us is the end of our preceding sins only if it recalls us from sinning, summons us to repentance, and, after repentance, prevents crimes from staining us again. Otherwise, it is the beginning of subsequent torments.

Knowing, therefore, that this patron and protector of ours is one of those of whom it is written, “They follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. XIV), let us fear to sin in God’s presence and before his eyes. When we sin, however, let us not be ashamed to confess our sins to God, who knows them, with a contrite and humbled heart and through tears; and let us ask for pardon with fruits worthy of repentance.

Let no one, confounded by the number or enormity of his crimes, despair of obtaining salvation and fall into the abyss of despair, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “When the wicked comes into the depths of evils, he despises them” (Prov. XVIII). For, when we confess our sins and ask forgiveness, we have an anchor of faith and hope for obtaining pardon, drawn out for us through the Apostle John:

“If we confess our sins,” he says, “God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” [Col. 1192B] (1 John II).

And because we cannot be without sin in this life, confession is the first hope of salvation, lest anyone consider himself righteous and lift up his neck before God’s eyes. Then comes love, because “love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV).

The Apostle beautifully teaches us both things together: that we ought to pray for our sins and that, when we pray, we obtain forgiveness from God. Therefore he called the Lord faithful in forgiving sins, as one who keeps the promise of his faithfulness: for he who taught us to pray concerning our debts and sins promised, in paternal mercy, that forgiveness would follow. He also affirms that God is just, because he justly forgives true confession.

Our former sins were forgiven us when we received baptism. Nevertheless, after baptism we have committed many sins [Col. 1192C], and we cannot be washed again in baptismal water. Since, therefore, we have stained our lives after baptism, let us baptize our conscience with tears; and, as though by a daily baptism in the Jordan, let us cleanse our conscience with tears of compunction from every contagion of creeping vices, according to the one who says:

“I shall wash my bed every night; I shall water my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI).

Hence the stream of the Jordan is rightly interpreted as “judgment.” For the more carefully each of the elect examines his conscience by scrutinizing it, the broader are the rivers of tears that pour forth from the inner spring of the heart. And because they discover themselves to be less than perfect, they wash away the filth of their weakness in the waters of repentance, and dash their little thoughts against the rock—that is, Christ. Armed with the spiritual Rock, they strive to circumcise every sense of mind and body.

“The Rock,” he says, “was Christ” (1 Cor. X).

Through faith, hope, and love in him, the devoted hearts of the good are purified not only in baptism but in every action whatsoever. If this lord and patron of ours sees us laboring faithfully in this exercise of devotion, he will assist our course by extending the hand of his intercession, so that we may be able to reach the harbor of eternal salvation.

For, standing with the most blessed spirits of glory before his Creator, he reads in the unbounded light that almighty God gladly forgets that we were guilty and is ready to count our repentance as innocence. On the day of baptism we promised to renounce all the works of the ancient enemy and all his pomps, but we scarcely keep what we promised. We have slipped into performing evil deeds and desiring the pomps of the world.

Having therefore been defiled after the water of salvation, let us be reborn from tears. For before the merciful Judge even the one who returns to the truth after lying will not be regarded as deceitful. Since almighty God willingly receives our repentance, by his own judgment he hides what we have done wrong [Col. 1193A] …

XIII. Moreover, let none of the faithful doubt the power of this patron of ours’ merits in heaven. While he still dwelt on earth in mortal flesh, the Lord gave him power to bind and loose, to raise the dead, and to heal every disease and every infirmity [Col. 1193B] (Matt. XVIII). At the tomb of his body, as has frequently been demonstrated by many signs, living sick people come and are healed. Perjurers come and are tormented by demons. The possessed come and are delivered.

How, then, does he live there, where he lives, if he lives here through so many miracles, where his dead body lies? Let us therefore make him our patron in the case of our examination before the strict Judge. Let us call upon him as our defender on that day of such great terror.

Certainly, if some case of ours were to be argued tomorrow before a great judge, we would spend the entire present day in thought, seeking some patron and entreating him with great prayers to come as our defender before so great a judge. Behold, Christ the strict Judge is coming; the terror of that great assembly of angels and archangels is brought before us. In that gathering our case will be examined, and yet we do not now seek the patron whom we may have as our defender then.

Our defender, blessed Remigius, is present. He wishes to be asked—and, so to speak, seeks to be sought. Let us therefore seek him as the helper of our prayer, so that then we may find him the protector of our guilt. For he who judges himself wishes to be entreated that he should not punish sinners. Hence he threatens wrath for so long a time, and yet mercifully waits.

May his mercy sustain us in such a way that it does not make us negligent. May our sins disturb us in such a way that our mind does not collapse into despair. For if, although presumptuous, we fear; and although fearful, we hope, we shall obtain the eternal kingdom more quickly through the merits and God-worthy prayers of this father and patron of ours [Col. 1193D].

Let us therefore run with the swiftest feet of faith, with the hands of our minds outstretched, to his protection, and let us remain before his most sacred body with tears. Let us pray that, through his interceding merits, we may deserve his pardon, so that, since we cannot obtain it through our own merits, we may obtain forgiveness from the Lord through his merits.

Since we do not possess a covering of good works with which to conceal our sins, let us, through his merits and intercessions, through pure confessions and abundant tears, fall prostrate before his holy memorial, wash away our crimes, and wipe them away with good works.

And wherever we faithfully invoke him for the help of our salvation [Col. 1194A], he will not be absent from our being heard, clinging to Christ, just as do his other more exalted members, who is present everywhere in majesty. While he endures as the strict Judge and still does not stretch out his hand to strike, while some temporal security is indicated before the retribution of inner vengeance, we ought to reckon the evil that follows—namely, the eternal, intolerable, and unceasing punishments of fire; reckoning them, we should groan; groaning, avoid what we have committed; continually look upon our sins; looking upon them, weep; and weeping, wipe them away.

Let us strive to wash away with the bitterest tears, not superficially but daily and, if possible, continually, the crimes in which we long lay with delight; let us wipe them away through almsgiving and expiate them through sacred offerings. This is the embassy by which we seek our peace [Col. 1194B], and which appeases the King who comes to examine and judge us. Let no joy in passing prosperity dissolve us, nor let transient things block the eyes of our mind, lest they lead the blind to the fire.

XIV. We must also take the greatest care, and think upon it daily with great weeping, how fierce and terrifying the prince of this world will come at the hour of our departure, demanding his works from us, since he came even to God dying in the flesh and sought something in him in whom he could find nothing.

What will we wretches say, what will we do, who have committed countless evils? What shall we say to the adversary when he demands and discovers many things belonging to him in us, except that which is our only certain refuge and solid hope: that, concerning the sins we committed after baptism, we have been washed by tears through confession, cleansed through fruits worthy of repentance, reconciled to Christ by the merits and prayers of the saints, and, by receiving his body and blood, remaining steadfast in the right faith, have become one with him, incorporated into him—in him in whom the prince of this world sought something of his own and could find nothing [Col. 1194D]?

For he alone is “free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII), and through him we are released from the service of sin by true freedom, because through receiving his body and blood we are united to the one who is truly free. For just as Christ truly assumed the flesh of our body, and that man Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary, is truly the Son of God—not as other human beings are sons by grace, but by nature, the Son from the substance of the Father—so his flesh is true flesh and his blood true blood, which we receive in mystery to eat and drink, as he himself testifies.

And we, who truly receive the flesh and blood of his body under the mystery, are naturally made one with him through them. In them, after consecration, the likeness of bread and wine remains, lest there be any horror of bloodshed, but the grace of redemption remains in them.

Concerning the natural reality of Christ in us, he himself says:

“My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John VI).

No room for doubt has been left concerning the reality of his flesh and blood. Now, both by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood [Col. 1195A]. When these are received and consumed, they bring it about that we are in Christ and Christ in us.

He himself is therefore in us through the flesh, and we are in him, while through him what we are is in God. That we are in him through the sacrament of communion in his flesh and blood, he himself testifies, saying:

“The world no longer sees me; but you will see me, because I live and you will live, because I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you” (John XIV).

Thus, while he is in the Father through the nature of his divinity, we are in him through his bodily birth, and he is again believed to be in us through the mystery of the sacraments.

He himself testified to how natural this union in us is:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

For no one will be in him unless Christ himself is in that person, who has received into himself the flesh of him who took his own flesh.

He teaches the sacrament of this perfect union by saying:

“As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me—that is, my flesh—will live because of me” (John VI).

He therefore lives because of the Father; and, just as he lives because of the Father, so we live because of his flesh. Every comparison is introduced according to a form of understanding, so that the matter under discussion may be grasped according to the example proposed.

XV. This, then, is the cause of our life: that, in our fleshly selves, we have Christ remaining through the flesh, and that we shall live through him on the condition that he lives through the Father. If, therefore, we naturally live through him according to the flesh—that is, having attained the nature of his flesh—how can he not naturally have the Father in himself according to the Spirit, since he lives through the Father?

He lives through the Father because his birth did not introduce a foreign and different nature; because what he is is also from the Father, yet he is not separated from him through any intervening dissimilarity of nature; and because, through his birth, he has the Father in himself by the power of nature. To this Father we are truly united through the mystery of his incarnation.

This is celebrated daily in the Catholic Church, just as it is read as prefigured in sacred history:

“Elijah came to the Jordan, and, taking off his mantle, struck the waters and divided them” (2 Kings II).

The Lord came to the river of death, into which the human race was accustomed to be submerged; and, temporarily removing the garment of flesh that he had assumed, he struck death by dying and opened for us the way of life by rising again.

The Jordan rightly expresses the flow and decline of our mortality, because *Jordan* is called in Latin “their descent,” and because that river, flowing into the Dead Sea, loses its once-praiseworthy waters there.

Elijah crosses the divided Jordan on dry ground, and Elisha crosses as well. So the Savior, rising from the dead, grants his faithful hope of rising again. After crossing the Jordan, Elijah gave Elisha the choice of asking for whatever he wished. And the Lord, having completed the glory of his resurrection, more fully implanted in the minds of the disciples what he had previously promised:

“Whatever you ask in my name, I will do” (John XIII and XV).

Elisha asked that a double spirit of Elijah might be in him. The disciples, taught by the Lord, desired to receive the promised grace of the Spirit, so that they would be sufficient to preach not only to the one Jewish nation that he himself had taught while present in the flesh, but also to all the nations throughout the world.

Did he not promise a double grace of his Spirit when he said:

“Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John XIV)?

XVI. While Elijah and Elisha were speaking, suddenly a chariot and horses of fire carried Elijah away, as though to heaven. Those chariot and horses must certainly be understood as angelic powers. Of them it is written:

“The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, multiplied; the Lord is among thousands of rejoicing ones” (Ps. LXVII);

and again:

“He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. CIII).

Elijah, being a mere human being, was borne up with the help of these, so that he might be lifted from the earth [Col. 1196B]. When the Lord was speaking with the apostles, he was suddenly lifted up while they watched; and, although he was not supported by angelic aid, he was accompanied by angelic service. He was truly taken up into heaven, as the angels themselves testified when they said to them:

“This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way” (Acts I).

When Elijah was lifted up to heaven, he left Elisha the mantle with which he had been clothed. When the Lord ascended into heaven, he left his disciples—and indeed the Church—the sacraments of the humanity he had assumed, by which they might be sanctified through the power of love and warmed.

Elisha took Elijah’s mantle, struck the waters of the Jordan with it, invoked the God of Elijah, and the waters were divided, so that he crossed. The apostles received, and the whole Church established through them received, the sacraments of its Redeemer [Col. 1196C]. Spiritually instructed, washed, and consecrated by them, the Church itself, having invoked the name of God the Father, learned to overcome the force of death and, scorning its obstacle, to pass over into eternal life, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel:

“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John III).

Whoever believes in Christ and, by believing, confessing, and sincerely imitating his passion, faithfully receives its sacrament is saved forever from every death that he contracted through sin in soul and body alike. He will not merely escape the destruction of punishments but will also receive eternal life.

XVII. May he deign to lead us, persevering in right faith and good works through the merits and intercessions of his blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mother and our Lady Mary, and of this patron of ours, blessed Remigius; and, having been made one with him through receiving his body and blood, may he lead us through those same sacraments of his humility to the contemplation of the glory of his divinity, which he himself faithfully promises to his faithful servants, saying:

“Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV).

“I will manifest myself,” he says—that is, not as all may behold me, nor as even the envious were able to crucify me, but as the eyes of the pure saints alone can see me: the King of the ages in his splendor. Such will I show myself, in return for their love, to those who love me [Col. 1197A].

May Christ Jesus, God and Lord, our Creator and Redeemer and Savior from every death and corruption, bring us to that end. With God the Father and the Holy Spirit, he lives and reigns, coeternal, consubstantial, and coequal, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1197]

XXIII. THE RESPONSE OF LORD HINCMAR TO CERTAIN QUESTIONS: Why he placed the mystical Council of Nicaea in one of his writings on his humility

[According to Sirmond, from a codex of Saint Lawrence of Liège.]

[Col. 1197B] It has been asked, as certain people have told me, why I placed the mystical Council of Nicaea in one of my writings on my humility. Therefore, just as the teaching of the Catholics has handed down to us, I give the explanation: namely, because it was prefigured in ancient history, designated through the number by the sign of the passion and name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and consecrated by foreknowledge.

The name of the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, who created us through his divinity and redeemed us by assuming humanity into the unity of his divine person, is Hebrew. Among the Greeks—who, like the Hebrews in the interpretation of names, are said to glory in the numerical values of letters—it is written in Greek letters as ΙΗΣΟΥΣ, which in Greek is said to be ΣΩΤΗΡ and is translated into Latin as *SALVATOR*, “Savior,” or “saving one.”

The numerical value of the letters of this Hebrew name among the Greeks is as follows: Ι, 10; Η, 8; Σ, 200; Ο, 70; Σ, 200. When this number is added together, it amounts to 488.

For the one, which cannot be divided, multiplied by ten produces ten; ten multiplied by four rises to forty; and forty multiplied by ten produces four hundred. This is because, in Paul’s words:

“There is one God, one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for all” (1 Tim. II, 5).

By his grace, all the elect will attain eternal life, which is signified by the number one hundred and by that number multiplied fourfold. They will rejoice not only in the incorruption of soul and body together, but also in the vision of the divine majesty, together with the glory of the mediator between God and human beings, whose humanity has been glorified [Col. 1197D].

By the number eight and the number eighty, which consists of eight decades, it is plainly indicated that, just as Christ rose from the dead on the eighth day through the glory of the Father, so we too should walk in newness of life. Our daily circumcision, which in the Old Testament was performed on the eighth day—that is, the daily cleansing of our heart—must never cease to celebrate the mystery of the eighth day, until we receive the twofold garment, namely the immortality and incorruption of body and soul together, which, as we have said, is designated by the number eight and eighty.

But as we have learned from the tradition of our predecessors, in Greek books, and, as we have discovered, also in Latin books, names are written by signs. Sometimes the first and last letters are marked, with a bar placed above them extending equally to the right from the left, as in DS. N̄. V̄. Sometimes the first, middle, and last letters are marked, with a bar placed above them extending equally to the right from the left, as in ΧΡS. DNS.

Thus, when this name is written in the nominative case as ΙΗΣ, the numerical value of these letters is Ι, 10; Η, 8; Σ, 200. Added together, this number makes 218.

The number one hundred, which consists of ten decades and passes from left to right, is a perfect number. Σ, *sigma*, the final letter in the sign of the name “Jesus” in the nominative case, expresses two hundred, because God was perfect before the ages and became perfect man at the end of the ages [Col. 1198C].

Ten is likewise a perfect number in the Decalogue, containing within itself the mystery of the fourfold Gospel. Count in order from one through four, and you will find ten.

The number eight is also taught to be perfect in Jesus’ resurrection on the eighth day. Although he died through our weakness, he lives through the power of God. Through the sign of his passion, which the letter Τ, *tau*, signifies and which contains the number three hundred, he struck down the devil, killed death, and triumphed over hell. If what is on the cross were added to it by a transverse line above it, it would no longer be merely the shape of a cross but the cross itself.

Add together the number of the sign of the Lord’s passion and the number of his name, and you will find 418.

Five hundred is completed by the number fifty multiplied tenfold. Through the grace of the Lord Jesus, crucified, raised from the dead, and seated at the right hand of God, we fulfill not only the Decalogue of the Law but also the four books of the holy Gospels. Raised on the eighth day of resurrection, we shall reach eternal rest, which is designated by the jubilee, that is, by the number fifty, and eternal life, which is shown by the number one hundred, through right faith and good works.

The sacred Council of Nicaea is rightly called mystical, because not through human endeavor or any arrangement did 318 bishops arrive at that council [Col. 1199A], in order to conquer the firstborn of Satan, namely Arius, another Judas, through the treachery of unbelief, the wickedness of betrayal, and the punishment of vengeance.

Although some of them are read to have faltered for a time, nevertheless, just as the number of the apostles—the twelve—did not perish through Judas’s betrayal, so this number of bishops, chosen by Christ, did not perish through the hesitation of those who faltered.

This number, 318, is holy. In it Abraham, victorious over impious kings, was blessed by the one who is the figure of the eternal priest.

The Lord Jesus, to whom it is said uniquely and specially, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3), and, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (ibid., 4), proved himself present at this mystical council through the sign of his passion and name, as we have already explained, in the numerical value of the letters [Col. 1199B].

The cross is represented by the three hundred. Hence Gideon went to battle with three hundred. Concerning him, the prophet, foreseeing that the Lord Jesus would triumph through the cross over the powers of the air, says:

“You have overcome as on the day of Midian” (Isa. IX, 4).

ΙΗ, the name, is represented by eighteen priests. Note that here the name “Jesus” is expressed in the genitive case, not the nominative; therefore the letter C, *sigma*, is not added, but the two letters ΙΗ are written with a line above them, and together they complete the number eighteen.

Whether, in this genitive case of this most sacred name, some other letter is added before these two letters among the Greeks, or not; or whether, as in the shape of the cross—which the letter Τ, *tau*, presents, without adding above it by a transverse line what belongs to the cross, so that the figure of the cross may represent not merely its shape but the cross itself—the name of the Lord Jesus is represented in Greek usage by only these same two letters with a line above them, to designate the number eighteen bishops, it is not necessary for us to conjecture. Blessed Ambrose, most learned in both languages, Greek and Latin, should be sufficient for our knowledge and authority when he says:

“The cross is in the three hundred; the name of Jesus is in the eighteen priests.”

And, as Hilary says in his book *On Synods*, speaking of the 318 priests:

“That number itself is holy, in which Abraham, victor over impious kings, is blessed by him who is the figure of the eternal priesthood.”

Ambrose also says in Book I of *On the Faith*, where he gives the words that we cited above, in the prologue:

“Abraham led 318 men into battle and carried away trophies from countless enemies; having subdued the strength of five kings and victorious troops through the sign of the Lord’s cross and name, he avenged his kinsman and earned both a son and a triumph.”

And in Book I, chapter 9:

“Not through human endeavor, not through any arrangement, did the 318 come to the Council, namely the Council of Nicaea; but so that, in their number, through the sign of his passion and name, the Lord Jesus might prove himself present at the council: the cross is in the three hundred, the name of Jesus in the eighteen priests.”

I considered it worthy to place here, in full, the words of such great teachers, together with what I learned through the tradition of my teachers, because the Lord says, “Whoever speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John VII, 18). I did not wish to appear to defraud God’s gift by presenting as my own what belongs to others [Col. 1200C].

[Col. 1199]

XXIV. HINCMAR’S PROFESSION OF FAITH, SENT TO THE ROMAN PONTIFF

[According to Marlot, *History of the Metropolitan Church of Rheims*, p. 388.]

[Col. 1199D] I, Hincmar, to be ordained archbishop of this see and about to undertake the office of preaching in your sacred ministry, holy Fathers, confess:

I confess that the holy and ineffable Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is naturally one God, of one substance, one nature, one majesty, and one power.

I also believe that our Lord Jesus Christ was begotten from God the Father before the ages, and that he was conceived in time from the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. He suffered for the redemption of the human race, descended to the underworld, rose victorious from there, ascended into heaven, and will come at the end of the age to repay each person according to what they did while placed in the body, whether good or evil.

Moreover, I confess that I wish to receive, hold, and preach the constitutions of the four principal councils—the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—as well as the canons of the synods and the decrees that orthodox faith accepts and embraces.

The heresies and schisms that the Catholic Church anathematizes, and everything contrary to sound faith, I condemn, reject, and anathematize.

I declare that I shall offer due submission and obedience to blessed Peter and his vicar, and assistance to our suffragan bishops. Before God and his angels, and under the testimony of the present Church, I subscribe to this profession of mine.

[Col. 1201]

XXV. SEVERAL POEMS OF HINCMAR

I. Epitaph in honor of Bishop Tilpin.

[In Flodoard, *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, Book III.]

### [Column 1201A]

Here in this earth rests Tilpinus, bishop of honor,  
For whom Christ was both Life in living and in dying.  
The blessed martyr Dionysius sent him  
To the people of Rheims as a vigilant shepherd and father.  
After feeding them for forty years and more,  
He departs, stripped of the garment of old age.  
When the month of September had reached its fourth day before the Nones,  
At the time when he died, death remains life for him.  
And because place and rank had joined this man to Hincmar,  
Hincmar made this tomb for him and composed its inscription.

### II. Epitaph of Saint Remigius

(See above, in his Life.)

### III. On the Tomb of Saint Remigius

[In Flodoard, in the same place.]

Hincmar, the bishop, built this great tomb  
For you, Remigius, moved by love for you,  
So that the Lord might grant me rest through your prayer, O holy one,  
And through your worthy merits, my revered father.

### IV. On the Restored Altar of the Blessed Virgin

[In Marlot, *History of the Metropolitan Church of Rheims*, Book III.]

### [Column 1201B]

This border, consecrated in honor of the Lord’s mother,  
Was adorned everywhere by her worshipper, Bishop Hincmar,  
With sacred gifts, when he had served as priest in this see  
For eight hundred years already fully completed,  
While the forty-fifth year was running in addition to them,  
While the young Charles ruled the kingdom’s diadems,  
When the city’s people asked this man to be their shepherd.

### V. To the Image of the Mother of God Placed on That Altar

The Virgin Mary holds the man, the king, and God,  
Born from her own womb through the Holy Spirit.

### VI. Verse Inscribed in the Gospel Book That Hincmar Gave for the Use of the Altar of Blessed Mary

Holy Mother of God, and ever-virgin Mary,  
I, Hincmar the bishop, bring these gifts to you.  
These pious deeds that Christ Jesus performed  
He taught us, having been born from your chaste womb, O maiden.

### VII. From the *Dish of Solomon*

[Note: Flodoard, Book III, chapter 15, while listing the books composed by Hincmar, says: “He also wrote for King Charles an excellent work in verse concerning the grace and predestination of God, and also concerning the sacraments of the Body and Blood of Christ, the vision of God, and the origin of the soul, together with the faith of the Holy Trinity. He called this work the *Dish of Solomon*. From this work Abbot Durandus quotes twelve verses in his book *Against Berengar, On the Body and Blood of the Lord*.”]

[In Sirmund.]

Lamb of God, light of the world, feeding us with your own body,  
May you remain in us and become our dwelling.  
Lamb of God, fountain of life, giving us drink from your own blood,  
May you always, according to your custom, make us drunk and govern us.

Here is almighty God, through whom the Father made all things;  
He changes the natures of things as he himself wills.  
Here, by the cross and by his own Words, he creates our offerings,  
And in bread and wine becomes his own flesh and blood.

For on the cross the body was fixed, and the blood was also poured out—  
The blood of Christ, which he had already given to his own at the supper.  
When we, unworthy as we are, commemorate these commands,  
The Redeemer makes our gifts the price of those who were redeemed.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF HINCMAR OF RHEIMS

## [Column 1203]

# HINCMAR’S ANNALS, OR THE THIRD PART OF THE ANNALS OF SAINT-BERTIN, FROM THE YEAR 861 TO THE YEAR 882

(According to Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, volume I.)

## 861

### [Column 1203A]

Galindo, surnamed Prudentius, bishop of the city of Troyes, a Spaniard by birth and exceptionally learned in literature, who a few years earlier had resisted Gottschalk the predestinarian, later, inflamed with bitterness against certain bishops who opposed him in heresy, became a very fierce defender of that same heresy. From then on he continually wrote many things differing among themselves and contrary to the faith, and died; thus, although he had been worn down by a long illness, he brought an end both to his life and to his writing.

Carloman, son of Louis, king of Germany, enters into an alliance with Resticius, prince of the Wends; he rebels against his father and, with Resticius’s help, lays claim to a large part of his father’s kingdom as far as the River Inn.

[Note: See this editor’s prefatory notice to the second part of the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*, printed in volume CXV of the *Patrologia* among the works of Prudentius, where the third part of these Annals is attributed to Hincmar of Rheims. Some, however, including the authors of *Gallia Litteraria*, deny Hincmar’s authorship of this book. — Editor of the *Patrologia*.]

Louis deprives Arnulf, the father-in-law of his son Carloman, of his honors and expels Arnulf’s grandsons from his kingdom. They go to Charles together with Adalard, maternal uncle of Queen Irmintrudis and their own kinsman, whom Lothair was persecuting through the influence of his uncle Louis. Charles receives them kindly and consoles them with honors. Nearly all those who had recently defected from Charles to Louis also return to Charles, and he restores them to his familiarity and honors.

The Danes [Note: Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Normans*.], who had earlier burned the city of the Morini [Note: Hunfrid, bishop of the Morini, or Thérouanne, driven from his city by the Northmen, resolved to renounce the episcopate permanently and consulted Pope Nicholas about the matter. He replied: “Know, dearest brother, that if it is harmful for a helmsman to abandon a ship in calm weather, how much more so in the midst of the waves.”], return from England under the leadership of Weland, with more than two hundred ships. They sail up the Seine and besiege a fort constructed by the Northmen on an island called Oscellus, together with the Northmen themselves.

For the price of the siege [Note: The price of the hire], namely five thousand pounds of silver, together with a considerable quantity of animals and provisions from his kingdom, Charles ordered payment so that his land would not be plundered. Crossing the Seine, he goes to Meidunum [Note: Meun, below Orléans.] on the Loire and receives Robert [Note: This is Robert, surnamed the Strong, from whom the kings of the third dynasty of France derive their origin.] with the honors due to him.

On this occasion Guntfrid and Gozfrid, on whose advice Charles had received the aforementioned Robert, together with their accomplices, according to their people’s fickle character and their longstanding custom, defect from Charles to Solomon, duke of the Bretons [Note: The reading is *Brittonum* in manuscript Ch.; likewise frequently below.].

Meanwhile another division of the Danes, with sixty ships, sails up the Seine into the River Tellas [Note: The Ière in Normandy, in the district of Tellau. See Valesius, *Notitia*, pp. 547–548.]. From there they reach those who were besieging the fort and join their company.

The besieged, driven by hunger, starvation, and every kind of miserable squalor [Note: Manuscript Ch. and B. read “by every kind of misery”; the present reading is retained here.], give six thousand pounds in gold and silver to the besiegers and join them. Thus they descend by the Seine to the sea. The approaching winter prevented them from putting out to sea; therefore they divide themselves among the various ports from that place to Paris, according to their separate companies.

Weland, however, sails up the Seine with his companions as far as the fortress of Milidunum. The men of the fortress, together with Weland’s son [Note: Manuscripts Ch. and B. read *Weland*], occupy the monastery of Fossatis [Note: Saint-Maur-des-Fossés.].

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims [Note: For eight years Hincmar had sought an opportunity to depose Rothad from the episcopate, and at last found one. Rothad had canonically deposed a priest of his diocese who had been caught in fornication. The priest fled to the metropolitan, whom he knew to be hostile to the bishop. Hincmar ordered the priest to exercise the priesthood after three years, claiming that he had been unjustly deposed, although the judgment of thirty-two bishops had decreed his removal from office. In addition, Hincmar deprived of communion another priest whom Rothad had appointed in place of the deposed man; but he restored to the church over which he had previously presided the man who had been deposed for fornication. Rothad opposed so irregular a judgment. In this year, 861, Hincmar therefore convened a synod in the suburb of Soissons and deprived him of episcopal communion as guilty of contumacy.], deprives Rothad, bishop of that city, of episcopal communion according to the canonical decrees because he refuses to obey the ecclesiastical rules, until he obeys. The synod is held in the province at the monastery of Saints Crispinus and Crispinianus near the city of Soissons [Note: The text has been corrected in this way; manuscripts Ch. and B. read *martyrium*. The manuscript apparently had the abbreviation *mrium*.].

Charles, leaving his son Louis under the guardianship of Adalard, maternal uncle of Queen Irmintrudis, to protect the kingdom against the Northmen, is invited by certain people as though he were about to acquire the kingdom of Provence. Since Charles, son of the former Emperor Lothair, was regarded as useless and unsuitable to royal dignity and name, Charles travels with his wife through Burgundy as far as the city of Mâcon [Note: Mâcon.].

After affairs have gone rather badly there, and the people of the land have suffered extensive plundering, he returns to the palace of Pontigon. There he hears a delegation sent by his brother Louis and his nephew Lothair, delivered by Adventius, bishop of Metz, and Count Leutard. He releases them and celebrates the day of the Lord’s Nativity festively, as is customary.

## 862
