Charles comes through the city of Rheims to Soissons. There, from a reliable report, he learns that his daughter Judith—specifically the widow of Æthelbald, king of the English—who had sold the possessions she had held in the kingdom of the English and returned to her father, was being kept in the city of Senlis [Note: Senlis] with the honor due to a queen, under paternal, royal, and episcopal protection, until, if she could not remain continent, she might marry suitably and lawfully, according to the Apostle.

She followed Count Baldwin, who had acted as her procurer, after changing her clothing, with the consent of her brother Louis [Note: That is, Judith’s brother]. And because Louis, his son, had been solicited by the aforementioned Guntfrid and Gozfrid, he fled by night with a few companions, abandoning his father’s loyal men, and went as a deserter to those who had solicited him.

Therefore King Charles, after consulting the bishops and other leading men of his kingdom, sought from the bishops a sentence, following the judgment of secular law and the canons, against the aforesaid Baldwin and Judith, who “ran away with a thief and made herself a partner in adultery,” according to the decrees of blessed Gregory: “If anyone has stolen a widow as his wife, and those who consent to him, let them be accursed.”

He also gave the abbey of Saint Martin, which he had imprudently granted to his son Louis in accordance with the earlier arrangement, to Hucbert, a cleric who was married, with insufficient prudence.

From there he proceeded to Senlis. While he was staying there, waiting for the people to gather to him so that, after arranging forces on both banks, the rivers Oise [Note: Oise], Marne, and Seine might each be guarded and the Northmen prevented from going on a plundering expedition, he received word that selected Danes from among those who had settled at Fossatis were approaching the city of Meaux [Note: Meaux] in small ships.

He hastened there with those whom he had with him. Since the bridges had been destroyed by the Northmen and the ships had been seized, he could not approach them. Accordingly, he repaired a bridge to the island near Trejectum [Note: Called Trejectum of Baldwin, commonly Tribaldou. An old author who composed the *Life of Saint Faro* explains the matter differently.] and blocked the Northmen’s route of descent. Nevertheless, he stationed ladders on both banks of the Marne for guard duty.

The Northmen, greatly constrained by this, selected hostages and sent them to Charles, offering them on the condition that they immediately return all the captives they had taken after entering the Marne; and that either, on the appointed day of the assembly, they withdraw from the Seine with the other Northmen and seek the sea, or, if the others did not wish to return with them, that they go with Charles’s army and seek battle against them. Thus, after giving ten hostages, they were permitted to return to their own people.

About twenty days later Weland himself came to Charles, commended himself to him, and immediately gave oaths of loyalty, together with those whom he had with him. From there he returned to the ships and sailed down with the entire Danish fleet as far as Jumièges [Note: Jumièges], where they decided to repair their ships and await the spring equinox.

After the ships had been repaired, the Danes, making for the sea, divided themselves into several fleets and sailed in different directions, as each group thought best. Most of them made for the Bretons, who lived in Neustria under the leadership of Solomon. Those who had been in Spain also joined them.

Robert captured twelve ships in the Loire which Solomon had hired under a contract of lease to oppose him, and he killed everyone who was in that fleet except a few who escaped by flight and went into hiding.

Robert, unable to withstand Solomon, made an agreement against that same Solomon with the aforementioned Northmen who had come out of the Seine before Solomon had enlisted them against him. Hostages were given on both sides, and the agreement was for six thousand silver pieces.

Weland came to Charles with his wife and sons and became a Christian together with his people.

Carloman, son of Louis, king of Germany, makes peace with his father after his father grants him the portion of the kingdom that he had earlier invaded, and after he gives an oath not to invade it again without his father’s permission [Note: B. reads “escape” instead of “invade.”].

Louis, son of King Charles, then approaches Solomon on the advice of Guntfrid and Gozfrid, obtains a strong force of Bretons, and with them attacks Robert, his father’s loyal man. He devastates Angers and the other districts he could reach with slaughter, fire, and plundering.

Robert attacks the returning Bretons, who are carrying off an enormous amount of plunder, kills more than two hundred Breton leaders, and takes away the booty. Louis again seeks battle with him, is put to flight by him, and barely escapes after his companions have been scattered.

Charles, king of the Aquitanians and son of King Charles, not yet completing his fifteenth year, takes as his wife, at the persuasion of Stephen [Note: Count of Auvergne], the widow of Count Humbert, without his father’s permission or knowledge.

The aforementioned Louis, his brother, likewise, at the very beginning of holy Lent, takes as his wife the daughter of the former Count Harduin, namely the sister of Odo, whom he greatly favored.

Charles, their father, orders all the leading men of his kingdom to assemble around the Kalends of June at a place called Pistis [Note: Pistis, commonly Pistres, a place in the diocese of Rouen near the confluence of the Andelle and Seine, close to Pont-de-l’Arche. The Andelle, or Indelle, commonly Andelle, rises in the territory of the Veliocasses; the Audura, or Autura, commonly Eure, in the territory of the Carnutes.], where the Andelle flows into the Seine on one side and the Audura on the other, with many laborers and carts. He constructs fortifications on the Seine and blocks the passage of ships upstream or downstream because of the Northmen [Note: Manuscript Ch. omits *in*].

He himself, with his wife, speaks with his son Charles on the Loire at a place called Maidunus [Note: Maidunus, also Magdunum and Maudunum, in the territory of Orléans, commonly Mehun-sur-Loire.], after his men have given oaths. When Charles, as though suddenly but with lowered voice and a defiant spirit held high, returns to Aquitaine, he himself returns to Pistis, where he had previously arranged both an assembly and a synod [Note: Compare Baluze, *Capitularia*, Chiniac edition, volume II, p. 153]. While the work is in progress, he discusses with his faithful men the affairs of the holy Church and of the kingdom.

There Rothad, bishop of Soissons, a man of extraordinary madness [Note: Our author is unfair to Rothad, who in the preceding year had been deprived of episcopal communion at the council of Soissons contrary to all the rules, and in this year, 862, was expelled from his see at another council held there. Pope Nicholas I rescinded the acts of this last council in his letter to the bishops assembled at Senlis; “Soissons” should therefore be corrected there.], having been regularly deprived of communion with the bishops at a provincial synod, presented himself with his contumacy before the council of four provinces. The brotherly assembly decided to preserve him completely under appeal to the Apostolic See, so that he would not be deposed.

But afterward he pressed for the execution of the judgment of that same council from which he had appealed. Twelve judges were appointed by that synod to carry out the judgment. Because of the hardness of his heart, he became a new Pharaoh, representing ancient times, a man changed into a beast [Note: Ch. reads *beluam*, “beast”], and because of the offenses specified in the record of proceedings [Note: Ch. omits *qui in*; Ch. reads *siriae* instead of *serie*], since he refused correction, he was deposed in the suburb of the city of Soissons.

[Note: Hincmar sent three bishops to Rothad to summon him lawfully to the synod. He replied that it was not lawful for him to undergo the judgment of the synod while his appeal to the Roman See was pending. Summoned a second and a third time, Rothad gave the same reply. Then those who supported Hincmar, after giving him their pledge, persuaded him to meet the king at a place near the synod so that he could speak with the king; the clergy of Soissons also encouraged him to do this. When Rothad came forward, the king received him kindly and heard him petition that the permission previously granted to him to go to Rome not be withdrawn. The king replied that the matter belonged to the synod and to the archbishop of Rheims, his metropolitan; he himself would carry out the bishops’ decrees. When the king had returned to the synod, the three bishops again approached Rothad, urging him to appear before the synod. When they found him steadfast in his appeal, they ordered him confined in a cell until he should receive the synod’s judgment. Hincmar deposed Rothad as though he were contumacious. Three bishops announced the sentence of his removal from office to Rothad, and he was immediately thrown into prison, with Hincmar offering him the hope of an abbey if he would abandon his appeal. A bishop was ordained in his place. We learn these things from Rothad’s own petition to Pope Nicholas. — Bouquet.]

Meanwhile a miracle occurred in the city of the Morini [Note: Thérouanne]. A citizen’s servant in that city began early in the morning on the day of the Assumption of holy Mary to smooth a linen garment, commonly called a shirt, so that his master could carry it prepared when he went to Mass. At the very first stroke, when he pressed the smoothing iron onto it and drew it across, the garment became bloody. Each time the same servant drew the iron across it, blood followed, until the whole garment was stained with the blood that spread over it.

Hunfrid, bishop of that city, had the garment brought to him and preserved in the same church as a testimony. Since the inhabitants of that parish did not observe the same feast as a holiday, he ordered that everyone celebrate and keep it as a day of rest, with the honor due to the solemnity.

Louis, who had earlier rebelled against his father, returns to him. He asks forgiveness from his father and from the bishops for his offenses and binds himself by very strict oaths to remain faithful to his father thereafter. His father gives him the county of Meaux and the abbey of Saint Crispinus, and orders him to come to him from Neustria with his wife.

When Warengaud had sent an accusation of infidelity against Hunfrid [Note: That is, had accused him of infidelity], his loyal men asked that he not fight a war. Charles granted their request and reconciled Hunfrid and Warengaud.

Louis, king of Germany, summons his nephew Lothair to Mainz and asks him to go with him against the Wends [Note: Ch. reads *Winedos*], who are called [lacuna] [Note: Abodrites.], against their prince [lacuna] [Note: Tabomiuzlem; compare the *Annals of Fulda*.], with military equipment. Lothair first promised that he would go, but afterward withdrew from his promise.

Louis, however, leaving his son Charles in his homeland because he had recently taken as his wife the daughter of Count Erchangar, takes his son Louis with him and attacks the Wends [Note: Ch. reads *Winedos*]. After losing certain leaders and accomplishing nothing successfully, he returns under the pretext of hostages to the palace at Frankfurt on the Main [Note: Ch. lacks *apud*; B. reads *pergit*, “proceeds”].

The Danes ravage and plunder a large part of his kingdom with slaughter and fire. Enemies previously unknown to those peoples, who are called the Hungarians [Note: It is worth noting that in this very year, 862, the Hungarians invaded Germany], also devastate the same kingdom.

Lothair, driven mad, as was said, by Waldrada’s magic arts and drawn by blind love for that mistress for whom he had rejected his wife Theutberga, with the support of Liutfrid, his uncle, and Walthar, who were especially intimate with him for this very reason, and with certain bishops of his kingdom also consenting [Note: Three synods concerning the marriage of Lothair and Theutberga were held at Aachen. The first two were held in 860. At one of them the bishops declared to the king that he could not retain an adulterous woman as his wife; at the other they decreed a public penance for Theutberga. At the third, convened in this year, 862, they permitted Lothair to enter another marriage. The beginning of this third synod was as follows: “In the year 862, indiction 10, on the third day before the Kalends of May, at the summons of the lord Lothair, most glorious king, the archbishops and their fellow bishops assembled at Aachen: namely Gunthar, archbishop of Cologne and archchaplain of the sacred palace; also Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier; Adventius, bishop of Metz; Atto, bishop of Verdun; Franco, bishop of Tongeren; Hungar, bishop of Utrecht; and Ratold, bishop of Strasbourg, so that, with divine mercy assisting, they might faithfully and beneficially intervene by pastoral care for the welfare and needs of Mother Church before the most serene prince mentioned above.”], crowns Waldrada and joins her to himself as wife and queen, although his friends grieved and protested.

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, when King Charles came to that city, summoned the bishops of his province and reverently dedicated the mother church of that province in honor of Saint Mary, just as it had been consecrated in ancient times.

Louis, king of Germany, sends flattering messengers to his brother Charles and asks him to come to meet him in the territory of Toul [Note: Ch. reads *Tullensem*, “of Toul”]. Because Charles did not wish to confer with Lothair before explaining to his brother the reasons why he disapproved of Lothair, the matter was disputed in conversation with no little complaint.

At last Charles, together with the bishops who were with him, showed in writing, point by point, the reasons why he did not wish to communicate with Lothair unless Lothair declared that he would either give a definite account of the matter or show an appropriate correction according to authoritative precedent.

After this declaration, under the agreed conditions, Charles and the bishops who were with him received Lothair into communion. They had prepared written announcements, which had been read to their counselors and which they were supposed to announce to the people concerning their meeting. But Louis and Lothair, especially on the advice of Chuonrad, Lothair’s counselor and Charles’s uncle, rejected them completely. Chuonrad relied, as was his custom, on an arrogant but futile knowledge that was useful neither to himself nor to many others, so that the reasons Charles held against Lothair would not become known to the people [Note: Ch. reads *sueta*, “customary”].

Charles, however, contrary to their wishes, made everything fully known: he did not wish to communicate with Lothair before the aforementioned declaration because Lothair had abandoned his wife contrary to evangelical and apostolic authority and taken another woman; and because Lothair had communicated with the excommunicated Ingeldrud, the wife of Boso [Note: Ingeldrud], and with Baldwin, who had stolen her daughter as his wife.

Thus, after announcing that their assembly would take place in the following month of October on the boundary between the counties of Mouzon [Note: Around Mouzon on the Meuse] and Vouzy [Note: In the diocese of Rheims, around Vouzy or Vouziers, between the districts of Rheims and Stadin. Compare Valesius, *Notitia*, p. 621], they withdrew from one another.

Louis went to Bavaria to reconcile with or resist his son Carloman, who, with the help of Resticius [Note: Ch. reads *refeccio*], prince of the Wends, had rebelled against his father.

Charles returned from the territory of Toul through Pontigon and then along the banks of the Marne to Quierzy, where he celebrated the day of the Lord’s Nativity with the greatest reverence.

## 863

The Danes sail up the Rhine toward Cologne in January. They plunder the trading settlement called Dorestad and also a considerable village [Note: Ch. and B. read *villam Nonmodocam*, “the village of Nonmodoca,” which certainly required correction] to which the Frisians had fled. After killing many Frisian merchants [Note: Ch. reads *negociatoribus*] and capturing a considerable number of the people, they reach an island near the fortress of Neuss [Note: Neuss on the Rhine].

Lothair attacks them on one bank of the Rhine with his men, while the Saxons attack them on the other, and they remain encamped until about the Kalends of April. From there the same Danes, on the advice of Roric, withdraw by the route through which they had come.

Charles, son of Emperor Lothair and king of Provence, dies after being afflicted for a long time by an epileptic illness.

Louis, his brother, having been summoned from Italy as emperor, comes to Provence and wins over to himself as many of the leading men of that kingdom as he can. When Lothair hears this, he goes there. Through the mediation of their household officers and friends, an agreement is reached that they will return together and discuss that kingdom among themselves. Louis returns to Italy, and Lothair to his own kingdom.

King Charles goes to the city of Le Mans [Note: Ch. reads *Cenomannis*], and from there proceeds to the monastery called Interamnis [Note: Commonly Entrammes; it was a monastery of nuns in the deanery of Sablé, now a cell or priory of the abbey of Évron].

There Solomon, duke of the Bretons, comes to meet him with the leading men of his people, commends himself to him, and swears loyalty. He also makes all the leading men of Brittany swear loyalty and pays Charles the tribute of that land according to ancient custom.

For the merit of his loyalty Charles gives him as a benefice the region called Inter-duas-aquas and the abbey of Saint Albin [Note: At Angers, Saint-Aubin]. He receives Gozfrid, Roric, Heriveus, and the others who had recently, as often before, defected from him, and grants them honors with pardon. From there he returns to Le Mans and celebrates the Lord’s Easter.

Hunfrid, marquis of Gothia [Note: Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, Book XXXV, no. 105, thinks this Hunfrid is the same as Anafred, count of the district of Narbonne, whose agents Imbert and Adaulf held a hearing at Narbonne in 862 concerning the monastery of Montolieu, situated in the district of Carcassonne, by the River Durenus. The judgment was given and confirmed on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the twenty-third year of King Charles’s reign.], without the knowledge of King Charles, by the customary conspiracy of the people of Toulouse, who are accustomed to dispossess their counts of that city, takes Toulouse away from Raymond and usurps it for himself.

King Charles, returning from the regions beyond the Seine, receives Lutard, bishop of Pavia, from the side of Louis, emperor of Italy; Gebhard, bishop of Speyer, from the side of Louis, his brother, king of Germany; and Count Nanthar, from the side of Lothair, his nephew. They come to ask for peace, which Charles always wished to preserve insofar as the harassment of his opponents allowed him.

He also receives another envoy of his brother Louis, named Blitgar, who asks that Charles not receive Carloman, his son, who had abandoned Resticius the Wend and had been driven away by him, if Carloman should come to him. Not long afterward, when Carloman had been deceived and abandoned by his own men, his father Louis received him under the condition of an oath and kept him with him in honorable custody.

Charles receives the envoys of the lord apostolic Nicholas at Soissons in the monastery of Saint Medard with ample honor: namely Rodoald [Note: Ch. reads *Raduoldus*], bishop of Porto, and John, bishop of Ficodense [Note: Ch. and B. read *Ficoclense*. The letters *cl* and *d* are sometimes difficult to distinguish in the manuscripts of that age] [Note: That is, Cervia. Cervia is a suffragan church of Ravenna].

He keeps them with him for some time. He grants Baldwin [Note: This seems to have been before the eyes of the author of the genealogy of the counts of Flanders, written in the twelfth century and found in Martène, volume III, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*], who had fled to the threshold of the Apostles, the pardon for which they had come; then he dismisses them, furnished with letters, to return to the Apostolic See.

Those envoys of the Apostolic See go to Metz to hold a synod by apostolic delegation around the middle of June concerning the divorce that had occurred between Lothair and his wife Theutberga, and concerning the introduction of the concubine Waldrada, whom he had taken as his wife contrary to ecclesiastical and secular laws.

At that synod the aforesaid envoys, corrupted by gifts and concealing the letters of the lord apostolic, did nothing according to sacred authority concerning the matters entrusted to them. Yet, so that they might appear to have done something, they ordered Gunthar, archbishop of Cologne, and Theutgaud, likewise archbishop of Trier, to go to Rome with the acts [Note: The reading appears to require *cum gestis*, “with the acts,”] which the bishops of Lothair’s kingdom had signed at that synod, so that the case might be decided by the judgment of the lord apostolic. This was done through the faction of Haganon, a cunning and exceedingly greedy bishop of the Italian region [Note: The words “of Lothair’s kingdom … bishop” are absent in Ch.].

The lord apostolic, fully learning what had been done, and wishing likewise to condemn Rodoald, who had recently been corrupted at Constantinople through similar greed together with his associate, the bishop Zacharias [Note: Perhaps “a similar greed”], summoned a synod. When Rodoald learned this, he fled by night and disappeared.

Gunthar and Theutgaud, however, arriving in Rome, were condemned by the apostolic bishop, first in the synod and afterward in the church of Saint Peter, as is related below [Note: Compare the *Annals of Fulda*].

“Bishop Nicholas, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy fellow brothers Hincmar of Rheims and Wanilo of Rouen, and to all our fellow brothers, archbishops and bishops residing in the kingdom of Charles, the glorious king.

“The crime that King Lothair—if indeed he can truthfully be called a king, since he restrains no appetite of the body by any wholesome discipline but rather yields to its unlawful impulses through slippery weakness—committed with the two women Theutberga and Waldrada is known to everyone.

“Nearly the whole world, coming from every direction to the threshold or see of the Apostles, also reported to us that he had long had Theutgaud and Gunthar as the authors and agents of such an act. Even those who were absent wrote the same thing to our apostolate.

“We refused to believe this all the more firmly because we could not at all expect to hear such a thing about bishops. But when they themselves came to Rome at the time of the council, they were found before us and the holy synod to be such as many had repeatedly proclaimed them to be. They were caught by the written statement that they had confirmed with their own hands and had wished us to ratify with our own signature; and while they sought to set a trap for the innocent, they were entangled in their own snares.

“Thus was fulfilled, by God’s authority, what is written in Proverbs: ‘In vain is the net spread before the eyes of the winged’ (Proverbs 1:17). They themselves were bound and fell; but we, who were falsely said to have fallen into this disgrace, rose and stood upright with the defenders of justice, by the Lord’s action.

“Therefore, by the decision of the holy synod together with us, they undoubtedly stand deposed in our presence, excommunicated from priestly office, and removed from the governance of the episcopate.

“Accordingly, let your fraternity, preserving the rule of the canons and observing the sanctions of the decrees, take care not to presume to receive those whom we have rejected [Note: Ch. omits *nos*] into the catalogue of priests.

“The sentence of deposition that we pronounced against the aforementioned Theutgaud and Gunthar, together with the other chapters that we promulgated with the holy council’s approval, will be shown appended below.

“CAP. I. On the Complete Abolition of the Synod Convened in the City of Metz by the Archbishops Theutgaud and Gunthar
“We judge that the synod recently assembled—that is, under the most pious Emperor Hludowicus, in the eleventh indiction, in the month of June, in the city of Metz, by the bishops who had anticipated our judgment and rashly violated the institutions of the Apostolic See—is, from that time, now, and forever, annulled and to be reckoned with the Robber Synod of Ephesus; and by apostolic authority we decree that it is perpetually condemned. We further decree that it is not to be called a synod, but, as one favoring adulterers, is to be called a brothel.

**Chapter II. Deposition [Col. 1213: *deposito*, Ch.] of the archbishops Theotgaud and Guntharius.**

[Col. 1213C]

“We judge Theotgaud of Trier, primate of the province of Belgica, and Guntharius, bishop of Cologne, now before us and the holy synod, to be wholly excluded from every priestly office. They presented a written account, authenticated by their own hands, explaining how they had investigated and judged the case of King Lotharius and his two women, namely Theotberga and Waldrada; they affirmed with their own mouths, before many persons, that they had done nothing more or less, or otherwise, than what was contained therein; and they publicly confessed that they had violated the sentence which our most holy brother, the archbishop of Milan, together with Tado and our other co-bishops, had requested from the Apostolic See against Ingildrud, wife of Bozo, and which we, inflamed by divine zeal, had canonically pronounced under threat of anathema. In all these matters we have found that they transgressed apostolic and canonical sanctions in many respects and wickedly violated the rule of equity. We therefore define, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by the authority of blessed Peter exercised through us, that they stand deprived of all episcopal jurisdiction.

“But if, following their former custom as though they were bishops, they dare to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry, they are in no way to be allowed either to hope for restoration or to find a place for satisfaction in another synod. All who communicate with them are likewise to be cast out of the Church—especially if, after learning that the sentence had been pronounced against the aforesaid men, they should attempt to communicate with them.

[Note: Ch. reads *agrippinae*.]

[Note: B. reads *abjici*; Ch. reads *abici*. The editor adds: “Nor do I deny that I was persuaded that I had read it thus in the manuscript; for in books of the Middle Ages one very rarely finds *abjicere*, *rejicere*, *trajicere*, and other words of this kind.”]

[Note: Ch. reads *didicerant*.]

[Note: Ch. reads *tentaverunt*.]

**Chapter III. Concerning the other bishops.**

[The headings are absent in Ch.]

“As for the other bishops who are said to be accomplices or followers of these men, namely Theotgaud and Guntharius: if, joined with them, they have made seditions, conspiracies, or plots, or if they have dissented from the head—that is, from the See of blessed Peter—by adhering to them, they are to be held bound by an equal condemnation. But if thereafter they show themselves willing to think in agreement with the Apostolic See, from which it is manifest that they received the beginning of their episcopate, either on their own or by sending envoys to us with their written statements, they should know that we will not deny them pardon, nor should they in any way fear that we will deprive them of their honors on account of their former presumptions or subscriptions made in secular proceedings.

[Note: Col. 1213 reads *beati*; the word is absent in Ch.]

[Note: Ch. reads *ne*.]

**Chapter IV. Concerning Ingildrud.**

“We recently anathematized Ingildrud, daughter of the late Count Mactifred, who, having abandoned her own husband Bozo, has now for about seven years wandered about here and there, together with her supporters, in accordance with the rule. But because of her contumacy, we have judged that she must again be bound with the chains of anathema.

“Let her therefore be anathema, utterly and completely, from the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the one true God; from all the holy Fathers; from the entire holy catholic and apostolic Church of God; and from us, together with all her accomplices, communicants, and helpers. Thus, as we have already decreed, if anyone should presume to communicate with her or favor her in any way, then, if he is a cleric, bound by the same chain he shall lose his clerical office; while monks and laypeople, if they are disobedient to this decree, shall likewise be anathematized.

“Nevertheless, if this woman returns to her husband or hastens to Rome and comes to the Apostolic See of blessed Peter, we shall without doubt not deny her pardon after worthy satisfaction. Yet meanwhile she is to remain bound under the former bond of anathema by which we previously and now have bound her.

“If anyone, without knowing it, communicates with the same Ingildrud while she is specifically hastening to or meeting the Apostolic See of blessed Peter at Rome, or knowingly provides her assistance in coming, he shall not on this account be held bound by the anathema.

[Note: Ch. reads *factoribus*.]

[Note: Ch. reads *propter contumaces eam iterato*.]

[Note: Ch. reads *decernimus*.]

[Note: Ch. reads *ingeldrudi*.]

**Chapter V. Concerning the sentences and prohibitions of the Apostolic See.**

“If anyone despises the doctrines, commands, prohibitions, sanctions, or decrees salutarily promulgated by the bishop of the Apostolic See for the Catholic faith, for ecclesiastical discipline, for the correction of the faithful, for the amendment of criminals, or for preventing impending or future evils, let him be anathema.

“We desire your holiness to be well in Christ.”

Charles held a synod on 8 Kalends of November at the palace of Vermeria. There he legally vindicated the abbey of Saint Carilephus [Saint-Calais. BOUQ.] against Rotbert, bishop of the city of Le Mans, who wished to hold it as attached by apostolic commendation to the jurisdiction of his bishopric. He sent to Rome Rothad, recently deposed, as the lord pope had commanded him, together with his own letters, those of the bishops, and his vicars.

He solemnly received his daughter Judith, restored to peace through the intercession of the lord apostolic, and the envoy of Mahomet, king of the Saracens, with many rich gifts and letters speaking of peace and an amicable treaty.

[Note: Ch. reads *litteris*.] He arranged for him to await a suitable time in the city of Senlis, with honor, due protection, and the necessary assistance, so that he could be honorably sent back to his king.

[Note: Ch. reads *operiri*.]

From there he set out with a strong force toward Aquitaine, intending to receive his son Charles by force if he would not come otherwise, and reached the city of Auxerre. There he allowed his daughter Judith, as the lord apostolic had requested, to be legally joined in marriage to Baldwin, whom she had followed, with the counsel of his faithful men.

From there he proceeded to the city of Nevers, where he received his son Charles as he came to him. He ordered him to promise fidelity and due submission by oath, and once again made all the leading men of Aquitaine swear allegiance to him.

Two Northmen who had recently come out of their ships, ostensibly seeking baptism with Weland—as was then said and later became clear—turned against him in treachery. One of them, contending with him in arms before the king, as was customary among his people, killed him in the combat after Weland had denied the charge. [That is, Weland.]

Meanwhile Charles learned through a sorrowful report that the Northmen had come to Poitiers and, after preserving the city by means of a ransom, had burned the church of Saint Hilary, the great confessor.

[Note: Ch. reads *incenderint*.]

He celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in the same place, near the city of Nevers, where he had received his son.

## 864

[Col. 1215D]

Charles ordered the Aquitanians to march with a prepared army against the Northmen who had burned the church of Saint Hilary, taking with him his son and namesake Charles.

[Note: Ch. reads *incenderunt*.] He returned to Compiegne and sent his envoys into Gothia to receive the cities and castles.

The Northmen attacked the city of Clermont, where they killed Stephen, son of Hugh, together with a few of his men, and returned unpunished to their ships.

Pippin, son of Pippin, having become a layman and apostate from a monk, joined the Northmen and observed their customs.

The young Charles, whom his father had recently brought from Aquitaine and taken with him to Compiegne, was returning at night from hunting in the Cotia forest. Thinking that he was playing with other young men and his companions of the same age, he was struck on the head with a sword by the young Albuinus, through the agency of the devil, almost to the brain. The wound extended from the left temple to the right cheekbone.

[Note: Ch. reads *malum*.]

Lotharius, son of Lotharius, collected four denarii from every manse throughout his kingdom. He gave the total sum of money, together with a large payment of flour, livestock, wine, and cider, to the Northman Rodulf, son of Heriold, and his men as a rent.

[Col. 1216B]

Hludowicus, styled emperor of Italy, attributing to his own injury the fact that, as we have shown above, the apostolic bishop had degraded the envoys of his brother Lotharius who had been sent to Rome through his confidence and intervention, and unable to contain himself in his fury, set out for Rome with his wife, accompanied by the same envoys, Theutgaud and Guntharius.

[Note: For an oration by a certain anonymous bishop delivered on this occasion at the Roman synod, see Muratori, *Scriptores rerum Italicarum*, vol. II, part II, p. 135. It survives in a manuscript codex of the Ambrosian Library.] His intention was either that the Roman pope should restore these bishops or that, if he refused to do so, he should in some way lay a criminal hand upon him.

When the apostolic bishop heard this, he imposed a general fast upon himself and the Romans, with litanies, so that God, through the intercession of the apostles, might grant the aforesaid emperor a good disposition and reverence toward divine worship and the authority of the Apostolic See.

When the emperor reached Rome and stayed near the basilica of blessed Peter, the Roman clergy and people, celebrating a fast with crosses and litanies, went to the memorial of blessed Peter. As they began to climb the steps before the basilica of blessed Peter, the emperor’s men threw them to the ground and beat them with various blows. Those who were able to escape were driven away, while the crosses and banners were broken.

In this tumult, even the marvelous and venerable cross most beautifully made by Saint Helena of blessed memory was broken and thrown into the mud. She had placed in it a piece of the miraculous cross and presented it to Saint Peter as a most magnificent gift. It was afterward collected, as is reported, by certain men of the English people and returned to its custodians.

When the apostolic bishop, residing in the Lateran palace, learned of these crimes, and shortly afterward received reliable news that the emperor was to be captured, he secretly boarded a ship and went by way of the Tiber to the church of Saint Peter, where he remained for two days and nights without food or drink.

Meanwhile the man through whose presumption the venerable cross had been broken died, and the emperor was seized by a fever. Therefore he sent his wife to the apostolic bishop. On the security of her word, the apostolic bishop came to the emperor; and after they had spoken together, as they agreed between themselves, the apostolic bishop returned to Rome, to the Lateran palace.

Then the emperor ordered Guntharius and Theutgaud, degraded as they were when they had come with him, to return to Francia.

At that time Guntharius sent these diabolical and previously unheard-of chapters to the bishops of Lotharius’s kingdom through his brother Hilduinus, a cleric, together with his own men. He sent them to the apostolic bishop when he returned to Hludowicus’s service, as we have said, on his journey to Rome, instructing Hilduinus that, if the apostolic bishop refused to receive them, he should throw them upon the body of blessed Peter.

(We have already given Guntharius’s chapters, which are here being discussed, among his writings in volume 121 of the *Patrologia*. The reader may consult it.)

The apostolic bishop, having learned of this beforehand, refused to receive them.

The aforementioned Hilduinus entered the church of the apostle blessed Peter armed and accompanied by Guntharius’s men, without any reverence. As his brother Guntharius had commanded him, he wished to throw the diabolical document upon the body of blessed Peter if the apostolic bishop refused to receive it. When the custodians prevented him, both he and his accomplices began beating those custodians with clubs, so violently that one of them was killed there.

Hilduinus then threw the document upon the body of blessed Peter. Protecting themselves and those who had come with them with drawn swords, they left the church and returned to Guntharius after completing this mournful deed.

After a few days, the emperor left Rome and came to Ravenna, while his retinue had committed many plunderings, destroyed dwellings, violated nuns and other women, killed people, and broken into churches. There he celebrated the Lord’s Pasch with such grace from God and the apostles as he deserved.

Guntharius, arriving in Cologne on the very Lord’s Supper, presumed, as a man without God, to celebrate Masses and prepare the sacred chrism. Theutgaud, however, reverently abstained from the ministry, as he had been commanded.

Finally, while the other bishops with Lotharius were working toward this end, Lotharius took the episcopate away from Guntharius and bestowed it, solely on his own counsel, upon Hugh, son of Conrad—uncle of King Charles and son of Lotharius’s maternal aunt—a cleric by tonsure only and merely a subdeacon by ordination, but in conduct and life unlike a faithful layman.

Moved by this, Guntharius took away whatever remained of the ecclesiastical treasury in that city and returned again to Rome, so that he might set forth to the apostolic bishop, in due order, all Lotharius’s and his own fabrications concerning Theutberga and Waldrada.

The bishops of Lotharius’s kingdom also sent their envoys to the apostolic bishop with booklets of repentance and canonical professions, since in the case of Theutberga and Waldrada they had deviated not a little from evangelical truth, apostolic authority, and the sacred rules.

Lotharius, after sending Ratold, bishop of the city of Strasbourg, with writings speaking falsely, in his customary manner, about his excuse and voluntary correction, himself went by way of Gundulf’s estate [Gondreville near Toul.] and Mount Romericus [Remiremont.] to meet his brother at a place called Urba [Orbe.].

Charles sent Rothad to Rome through Rodbert, bishop of the city of Le Mans, as the apostolic bishop had commanded. But the bishops of his kingdom also sent their vicars to the Apostolic See with synodal letters concerning the case of Rothad; Hludowicus denied them passage.

[Note: Ch. reads *rothardum*, though below it writes *rothadi*.]

The envoys of both the king and the bishops secretly informed the pope of the reasons preventing them from coming to Rome.

Rothad, pretending illness at Besançon, remained behind while the others returned home.

[Note: Ch. reads *vesoncio*.] After their return, he went by way of Curiam, with the support of the partisans of Lotharius and Hludowicus, king of Germany, to the emperor of Italy, Hludowicus, in order that through his assistance he might be able to reach Rome.

[Note: Rothad obtained free passage from Emperor Ludovicus and reached Rome alone in June of this year, 864. BOUQ.]

The envoys of King Charles, having accomplished little of what they had been sent to accomplish, returned from their mission.

When Huntfrid, having abandoned Toulouse and Gothia, passed through Provence into the regions of Italy, Charles again sent other envoys to Toulouse and Gothia to receive the cities and castles.

[Note: Col. 1217 reads *negocio*; Ch. reads *negotio*.]

[Note: Col. 1217 reads *dimisso*; Ch. and B. read *dimissa*.]

Hludowicus, king of Germany, went out in hostility to meet the Bulgar khagan … named … who had promised that he wished to become a Christian. From there he intended to proceed, if he saw that matters prospered, to organize the march of the Wends.

[Note: It is clear that either the name of the khagan or the word *Bulgarorum* has fallen out after this point.]

The Northmen who had landed in Flanders with a very large fleet, when the country people resisted them, sailed up the Rhine and ravaged the neighboring kingdoms of Lotharius and Hludowicus on both banks of that river.

On the Kalends of June Charles held a general assembly at a place called Pistis. There he received, according to the custom of his predecessors, the annual gifts and also the tribute sent to him from Brittany by Salomon, duke of the Bretons—namely fifty pounds of silver—and ordered fortifications to be built there on the Seine so that the Northmen could not ascend that river.

He also established thirty-seven chapters, with the counsel of his faithful men, according to the custom of his predecessors and forefathers who were kings, and ordered that they be observed as laws throughout his entire kingdom.

[Note: The Edict of Pistis was issued on 7 Kalends of July. See Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. II.]

Pippin, the apostate, was captured by the Aquitanians through a stratagem from the company of the Northmen. He was brought before the same assembly and, as a traitor to the leading men of the kingdom, to his country, and to Christianity, was finally condemned to death by everyone in general and confined under the strictest custody at Senlis.

[Note: Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, says the following in his council concerning Pippin’s repentance:

“Therefore, as it seems to me—not prejudging the synodal sentence decreed concerning Pippin, but trusting in God’s mercy, which through his apostle says that mercy triumphs over judgment, and trusting in the charity of our brothers—Pippin should be exhorted to make secretly a pure confession of all his sins, which he committed from the beginning of his life, since perhaps he has done things that it is shameful even to mention publicly.

“He should also confess publicly before the Church, among the public penitents, with tears, that he abandoned his habit, perjured himself, and joined himself to the pagans—a union through which many evils were committed. He should humbly seek penance and reconciliation.

“For everything that he has confessed either secretly or publicly accused himself of, he should be publicly reconciled through the laying on of the hand of episcopal authority. After reconciliation, he should receive the clerical tonsure, resume the monastic habit, and promise henceforth to observe what he ought and what is required of him. Thus he may receive communion at the sacred altar.

“After reconciliation, he should be treated kindly, so that he may be mercifully guarded under free custody in a suitable place. Monks and good canons should be assigned as his custodians, to exhort him and teach him by their instruction and example to live well thereafter and mourn his past sins.

“Through their care and the suitability of the place, he should be guarded so that he cannot return to his former vomit, even if he should wish to do so at the devil’s persuasion, and so that scandal cannot again arise through him in the holy Church and in this Christian community.

“Receive, father and son, this little document, and also that one concerning the prohibition of marriage between relatives; carry them to the lord king and read them aloud before him. Concerning this one, act according to his counsel and recommendation; and concerning the other, on marriages between relatives, follow, with his counsel and assistance, the sacred authorities sent to you.

“Care for Pippin must not be neglected. Every effort must be made to provide him with trustworthy and faithful custodians. Nor must we forget what happened to him in the monastery of Saint Medard and what happened to Karloman at Corbie. For what has happened can happen again.” BOUQ.]

Bernard, son in flesh and character of the former tyrant Bernard, having received permission from the king and appearing to be going from that assembly to recover his honors, returned during the night with an armed force. Hiding in a forest [Note: Ch. reads *sylva*.], he awaited, as some said, a time and place to kill the king, who had ordered his father to be killed by the judgment of the Franks; or, as others said, to kill Rodbert and Ramnulf, the king’s faithful men.

[Note: Ch. reads *maliciis*; the present text reads *malitiis*.]

This became known to the king. He sent men to capture Bernard and bring him before him, but Bernard saved himself by flight. Therefore, by the judgment of his faithful men, the king took back the honors he had given him and granted them to his faithful man Rodbert.

[Col. 1219B]

Egfridus, who in former times had withdrawn Stephen and the king’s son and namesake from obedience to their father, was captured by Rodbert and brought before the king at the same assembly. At the request of Rodbert and his other faithful men, the king forgave him what he had committed against him, and, after he had confirmed it by oath and had been rewarded with the king’s favor, allowed him to depart unharmed.

[Note: Egfridus seems to be the same as Acfridus, to whom Charles the Bald, when he already held the abbey of Saint Hilary, gave the county of Berry in 867. BOUQ.]

Returning from the place called Pistis, Charles entered Compiegne around the Kalends of July. He sent back Mahometh, envoy of the king of the Saracens, who had come to him before winter, richly endowed with many and very great gifts, through his own envoys to that same king.

Carolomannus, son of Hludowicus, king of Germany, who had been staying in free custody with his father, pretending that he was going hunting, escaped from his father and, with the agreement of the margraves who had betrayed him, recovered the marches his father had taken from him.

His father immediately pursued him and made him come to him under terms of security, then granted him honors. [Note: Ch. and B. read *conditionem*.] Returning from there toward the palace at Frankfurt, he fell from his horse while hunting a stag in a certain park. [Note: Our *Brühl*, a wood.] Injured in the ribs, he lay in a nearby monastery and sent his son Hludowicus ahead to the aforesaid palace, where his wife was; he himself soon recovered and followed.

Pope Nicholas again sent letters to all the archbishops and bishops of Gaul, Germany, and the province of Belgica, for confirmation of the deposition of Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier, and Guntharius, archbishop of Cologne.

He also granted indulgence to the other bishops who, from Lotharius’s kingdom, had agreed to Theutberga’s divorce and the introduction of the concubine Waldrada, and who had sent him their letters with their profession, just as he had promised in the document mentioned above.

[Note: Ch. reads *divorcio*.]

He summoned a synod at Rome around the Kalends of November, announcing that there he would again confirm the deposition of the aforementioned archbishops and deal with the case of Lotharius and Ignatius, bishop of Constantinople, who had been deposed the preceding year and in whose place a certain layman was tonsured and immediately ordained bishop.

[Note: Ignatius was deposed in 861 at the false synod of Constantinople. Photius was ordained bishop on 25 December 857 and had already been intruded into Ignatius’s place in 858. BOUQ.]

The aforementioned Theutgaud and Guntharius went voluntarily to this synod, thinking that through the intervention of Emperor Hludowicus they might be restored by the apostolic bishop.

Hludowicus, styled emperor of Italy, was gravely wounded by a stag which he wished to shoot while it was in rut.

[Note: In French, *rut*.]

Nicholas, pontiff of the Roman See, asked through Arsenius, his apocrisiarius, that he be permitted to send his envoys to Charles for certain ecclesiastical matters. But Hludowicus, believing that the pope wished to send them into Francia against him with an insincere intention, refused.

Hugbertus, a married cleric and abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, who held the abbey of Saint Maurice and other honors belonging to Hludowicus, emperor of Italy, against Hludowicus’s will, was killed by his men.

His sister Theotberga, abandoned by Lotharius, came to Charles’s allegiance. Charles gave her the monastery of Avenniacum [Avenay in the diocese of Reims. BOUQ.] and entrusted the abbey of Saint Martin to Ingelwinus, a deacon of his palace.

Rodbert, count of Angers, attacked two bands of Northmen who were staying on the Loire. He killed one of them, except for a few who escaped, but was wounded when the larger second band arrived from behind. Having lost a few of his men, he secured his retreat and recovered after a few days.

[Note: Ch. reads *rediens*; the present text reads *aggrediens*.]

## 865

King Charles celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at the palace of Quierzy.

Coming to the estate of Ver, around the middle of February, he received his brother Hludowicus, who was arriving at the estate of Toussy with his sons, with considerable honor.

[Note: Ch. reads *cum omnibus*.] After deliberation with all their faithful men, they sent a royal commission through the bishops Altfrid [of Hildesheim.] and Erchanratus [Apparently the bishop of Châlons, who below appears as Erkanraus.] to their nephew Lotharius.

They instructed him that, since he often said he intended to go to Rome, he should first, according to the exhortation of the lord apostolic and of themselves, correct what he had committed in the Church against divine and human laws, a Church which he had scandalized by his presumption. Then, after arranging his kingdom, he could, if he wished, hasten to the thresholds of the apostles to seek and obtain pardon.

Lotharius, however, thinking that they wished to steal his kingdom from him and divide it between themselves, sent Liutfrid, his maternal uncle, to his brother and the emperor of Italy, asking him to obtain from the apostolic bishop that he send letters on his behalf to his uncles, so that, while maintaining peace, they would cause him no impediment concerning his kingdom. Emperor Hludowicus obtained this.

Meanwhile the Northmen staying on the Loire, with great violence and by divine judgment, sailed with a favorable wind up that same river as far as the monastery of Saint Benedict called Fleury. They burned the monastery; and on their return they burned the city of Orléans and the monasteries situated there and around it, except for the church of the Holy Cross, which the flames could not consume, although the Northmen labored greatly at it.

Thus, descending by the river’s channel and plundering everything nearby, they returned to their station.

[Note: Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Northmen*.]

From Toussy, Hludowicus went to Bavaria. Having been familiarly reconciled with his son Carolomannus, he returned the marches he had taken from him and went back to the palace at Frankfurt.

Charles, coming through Attigny to Silviacum [The village of Servais, half a league from the town of Fara, which is situated on the Isère. See Book IV of *De Re Diplomatica*, p. 325. BOUQ.], celebrated the holy Lent and the Lord’s Pasch there.

[Note: Ch. reads *sacrum quadragesima*, “the holy Lent.”]

He sent into Gothia Bernard, born of a certain Bernard and the daughter of Count Rorigonus, and entrusted to him part of that march.

[Note: This Bernard, father of Bernard, margrave of Gothia, is the same Bernard who, according to Ademar of Chabannes, together with his brother Emmo, count of Poitiers, incurred the displeasure of Louis the Pious in 839, and who was killed fighting Count Lambert of Nantes in 844. His wife was named Blichildis, daughter of Rorico, count of Le Mans, who restored the monastery of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés in 824. Bessius, in the *History of the Bishops of Poitiers*, prints a charter of Count Rorico naming his father Gauzlin, mother Aldetrude, brother Gauzbert, monk of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, and son Gauzlin, monk of Glanfeuil. Gauzbert was abbot of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés and died about 845; Gauzlin was abbot of Glanfeuil. Bernard, margrave of Gothia, was deprived of his honors in 878 at the council of Troyes. BOUQ.]

[Note: At that time the march of Gothia, which had been held whole by Hunfrid, was divided into two. For Charles separated Septimania properly so called, together with first Narbonensis, from the Spanish March. BOUQ.]

Finally, coming to the estate of Ver, he received there the bishops and other leading men of Aquitaine, who had come to meet him. At their earnest request, he allowed his son Charles, who had not yet been properly disciplined—that is, corrected; compare Italian *spazzare* and French *espousseter*, “to dust” or “brush clean”—to return to Aquitaine with royal name and authority.

[Col. 1222B]

Pope Nicholas sent Arsenius, bishop of Orte and his counselor, with letters to the brothers Hludowicus and Charles, and also to the bishops and leading men of their kingdoms, containing what Lotharius had requested through his brother.

[Note: Col. 1221: Ch. reads *continentes*; the present text reads *continentibus*.]

Arsenius conveyed them not with apostolic gentleness and the customary honor with which Roman bishops were accustomed to honor kings in their letters, but with malicious threats.

Arsenius came through Curiam and Alamannia to Hludowicus, king of Germany, at the palace of Frankfurt, and delivered the apostolic bishop’s letters to him. From there he went to Gundulf’s estate and came to Lotharius.

To Lotharius, and to the bishops and leading men of his kingdom, he gave the pope’s letters, stating that, unless he received his wife Theutberga and dismissed Waldrada, Arsenius was to reject him from the entire fellowship of Christians. In many earlier letters the pope had repeatedly declared him excommunicated and expelled from the company of Christians.

Then, coming from Lotharius to Charles around the middle of July at the palace of Attigny, Arsenius delivered letters to him, sufficiently honorably, identical with those he had given to the kings Hludowicus and Lotharius. He brought with him Rothad, canonically deposed by the bishops of five provinces but restored by Pope Nicholas not according to the rules but by force, and presented him to Charles.

And although the sacred canons say that, if a bishop deposed from his rank by the bishops of his province flees to the Roman bishop, the Roman bishop should write to the bishops of a neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may carefully investigate the case in every respect and decide it according to the truth; and that, if the deposed man should again appeal to the Roman bishop, he should either send one of his representatives, who, possessing the authority of the one by whom he was sent, should judge together with the bishops, or trust the bishops sufficiently to bring the case to an end—the apostolic bishop did none of these things.

[Note: The following passage, through the words “we were unable in every respect,” is absent from Ch. It was first added by Bouquet from “a parchment fragment attached to the Bertinian manuscript.” A folio had therefore fallen out of the manuscript, and, because those who found it did not know where it belonged, it was placed at the end.]

Instead, setting aside the judgment of the bishops, who, according to the sacred rules, after the judgment had been rendered had reported everything decided to the Apostolic See in the form of official records, he restored Rothad by his own authority.

He therefore sent the restored man to Charles with letters stating that, without any exception, whoever contradicted Rothad in anything concerning either his rank or the property of his bishopric would be anathema.

Thus, without the questioning or consent of the bishops who had deposed him, Rothad was returned to his see through the envoy Arsenius.

After this Arsenius went to Duciacum to meet Hlotharius, bringing Theotberga, who had lived honorably for some time in the kingdom of Charles. Having received an oath from twelve men on Hlotharius’s behalf, he restored that same Theotberga to him in marriage, without requiring any ecclesiastical satisfaction for the public adultery committed by him, according to the sacred canons.

The oath sworn on behalf of Theotberga was as follows, as dictated and brought from Rome [Col. 1223C] by Arsenius himself:

“I, such-and-such, swearing, promise by these four holy Gospels of Christ, which I touch with my hands, and by these relics of the saints, that my lord Hlotharius, king, son of the late most serene emperor Hlotharius of pious memory, will henceforth and forever accept Theotberga as his wife and lawful consort, and will treat her in every respect as a king ought to treat his queen and wife. And because of the dissensions already mentioned, neither in her life nor in her limbs, neither from my aforesaid lord Hlotharius nor from any person instigating, assisting, or even consenting with him, will she suffer any harm; but he will treat her as a king ought to treat his lawful wife. She must, however, henceforth conduct herself in every respect as a wife ought to honor her lord.

“These are the names of those who swore this oath:

“Of the counts: Milo, Ratharius, Erlandus, Theutmarus, Weremboldus, and Count Rocolfus.

“Of the vassals: Erleboldus, Vulfridus, Eidulfus, Bertmundus, Nithardus, and Arnostus.

“This was sworn upon the four Gospels of God, the most precious wood of the holy Lord’s cross, and other relics of the saints, at the place called Vindonissa [Note: Vindonissa is a village in the pagus of Rheims, mentioned by Flodoard in his Chronicle and History, commonly called Venderesse; it lies between Reiteste and Sedan and formerly belonged to the church of Rheims. BOUQUET.], on the third day of the month of August, in the thirteenth indiction.

“This was done in the time of the lord Nicholas, thrice most blessed and co-angelic apostolic, through the agency and appointment of Arsenius, the venerable bishop, envoy and apocrisiary of the supreme holy Catholic and Apostolic See, possessing apostolic authority and acting as legate of that same lord Nicholas the apostolic.

“The names of the bishops in whose presence this occurred, and who were present, are these: Harduicus, archbishop of Besançon [Note: Vesontiensis.]; Remedius, archbishop of Laon [Note: Lugdunensis.]; Ado, archbishop of Vienne [Note: Viennensis.]; Rodlandus, archbishop of Arles; Adventius, bishop of Metz; Atto, bishop of Verdun [Note: Virdunensis.]; Franco, bishop of Saint Lambert [Note: Liège.]; Rotaldus, bishop of Strasbourg; and Fulcricus, chaplain and imperial envoy.

“From the kingdom of Charles, Isaac, bishop of Langres [Note: Lingonensis.], and Erkanraus, bishop of Châlons. From their hands, on behalf of King Charles, Theotberga was received by Arsenius, the venerable bishop and legate of the Apostolic See, together with the archbishops and bishops named above. Noblemen from various kingdoms were standing there at the same place, along with a multitude of people, publicly seeing and hearing these things; we have not been able to insert all their names in this page [Note: Should this read *inserere*?].”

[Col. 1224C] On the same day Arsenius, bishop and legate of the Apostolic See, together with all the archbishops named above [Note: From these words, “together with all the archbishops named above,” and from what follows, it is clear that the material now added had been wrongly omitted from the printed edition and necessarily had to be restored. BOUQ.], returned and delivered Theotberga herself, the queen, into the hands of King Lotharius. They did so not only under the same solemn warning as above, but also under adjuration and excommunication: if he did not observe and fulfill everything as stated above, he would have to render an account not only in the present life but also at the terrifying eternal judgment of God before blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; at that judgment he would be condemned eternally by Peter himself and consumed in everlasting fire.

Meanwhile Lotharius sent envoys to Charles, wishing and requesting that their friendship be bound by a mutual treaty. He obtained this through the intervention of Queen Irmentrude. Coming to Attiniacum, he was received by Charles in a friendly and honorable manner and admitted into the requested alliance.

When Arsenius returned with him, he brought a letter from Pope Nicholas filled with terrible curses, previously unheard of from the moderation of the Apostolic See, against those who several years earlier had plundered and carried away a large sum from Arsenius’s treasure, unless they took steps to restore what they had taken by making satisfaction. When this letter had been reread [Note: *relicta* in B.; perhaps a typographical error?], as well as another concerning the excommunication of Ingiltrude, who had abandoned her husband Bozo and fled with a certain adulterer into Lotharius’s kingdom, Ingiltrude had received, under Charles’s protection, a villa called Vendopera [Note: Vendeuvre, a village in the territory of Langres. BOUQUET.], which the emperor Hludowicus of pious memory had given to Saint Peter and which a certain Count Wido had held for many years.

Having obtained from Charles the things for which he had come to him, Bishop Arsenius went with Lotharius to the villa of Gundulfus [Col. 1225B], where Theotberga had preceded him. He stayed there for several days because of Waldrada, who was to be brought there to him and taken by him into Italy [Note: *deduci* in C.]. After Lotharius and Theotberga had been prepared and crowned in royal attire, he celebrated Mass on the day of the Assumption of Saint Mary. From there he set out with the aforementioned Waldrada toward Urba, where Hludowicus, emperor of Italy, was said to be going to come to meet Lotharius. He then returned to Rome through Alamannia and Bavaria to recover the patrimonies of the church of Saint Peter situated in those regions.

Charles set out from Attiniacum in a hostile manner against the Northmen, who had come up the Seine with fifty ships. On this journey, through the negligence of the guards, he lost three excellent crowns, very valuable bracelets, and other precious objects [Note: *preciosa* in C.]; after not many days he found everything again except for a few gems, which had been lost in a disorderly plundering.

The Northmen, meanwhile, remaining on the Loire [Note: Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Normans*.], freely proceeded on foot toward the city of Poitiers, set the city on fire, and returned to their ships without punishment. Robert killed more than five hundred of those same Northmen who were stationed on the Loire, without loss to his own men and sent their Northmen banners and weapons to Charles.

When Charles reached the place called Pistis, where the Northmen were staying, he arranged, on the advice of his faithful men, for the bridges over the Isara and the Marne to be repaired at the places called Alvernis [Note: Auvers.] and Carenton [Note: Charenton, at the confluence of the Seine and the Marne.], since the local inhabitants, who had originally built those bridges, were unable to repair them because of the Northmen’s attacks.

He therefore ordered those assigned from more distant regions to carry out the works on the Seine to repair those bridges immediately, because of the pressing necessity, with the condition that in future no one who had now repaired them should suffer loss while working on this task. Having appointed guards to watch both banks, he went to the villa of Odriaca [Note: Below, in the years 867, 871, and 873, this is called *villa Audriaca*, Orreville, with an adjoining forest still bearing the same name. It lies on the right bank of the Alteia, at an equal distance of two thousand paces between Donincum, or Dulengium, to the west, and the village of Alteia, from which the river Alteia took its name, toward the east. See Book IV of *De re diplomatica*, p. 306. BOUQ.] in the middle of September for the purpose of hunting.

The Northmen, however, since the guards had not yet arrived on this side of the Seine, sent about two hundred of their number to Paris. When they did not find the wine they had sought, they returned unharmed to those who had sent them. More than five hundred then planned to cross the Seine and go as far as Chartres to plunder, but the guards of the riverbank attacked them. After losing some of their men and suffering injuries among others, they returned to their ships.

[Col. 1226B] Charles sent his son Hludowicus into Neustria. He did not give him or forbid him the royal title, but granted him only the county of Anjou, the abbey of Marmoutier [Note: Near Tours. BOUQ.], and certain villas.

To Robert, who had been margrave in Anjou, he granted, in addition to the other honors he possessed, the county of Auxerre and the county of Nevers. Hludowicus, king of the Germans, received his army, which had been sent against the Wends [Note: *winedos* in C.] and was proceeding successfully. His son and namesake, against his father’s will, betrothed the daughter of Adalard, thereby greatly offending his father.

Charles went to Cologne to meet his brother Hludowicus and enjoy his conversation. Among the other matters discussed, he reconciled the father and son concerning the presumption just mentioned, on the condition that the son should no longer be joined in marriage to Adalard’s daughter. Hludowicus returned to Worms, and Charles to Carisiacum.

On the way Charles was informed that on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November the Northmen had entered the monastery of Saint Denis. They remained there for about twenty days, carrying booty from it to their ships every day, and after extensive plundering returned unopposed to their camp, not far from the monastery.

Meanwhile the Northmen stationed on the Loire, joined by Britons, went toward the city of Le Mans. After plundering it without punishment, they returned to their ships. The Aquitanians engaged the Northmen stationed at Carentono [Note: This should be read *Carentono*, the Charente. BOUQ.], under their leader Sigefridus, and killed about four hundred of them. The rest fled and returned to their ships.

[Col. 1226D] Charles received at Compiegne his envoys whom he had sent the previous year to Muhammad at Córdoba, bringing many gifts: camels carrying coverings or bedding [Note: This appears to be the same as *lectus*, “covering” or “blanket.”] and tents, along with cloths of various kinds and many perfumes.

From there he came to the villa of Rofiacum [Note: There are several villas of this name; this one must have been in Neustria. BOUQ.]. He removed the honors he had granted to Adalard, whom he had entrusted with the defense against the Northmen, and also to his relatives Hugh and Berengar, because they had accomplished nothing useful against the Northmen; he distributed those honors among various persons.

The Northmen who had plundered the aforementioned monastery fell ill in various ways. Some became delirious, others were afflicted with scabies, and others died after discharging their intestines together with the *aqualiculus* through the anus [Note: That is, the stomach.].

Charles, leaving guards behind against those same Northmen, returned to Senlis to celebrate the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity. There he was informed that Lotharius, his son and abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus, had died.

## 866

[Col. 1227B] On the fourth day before the Kalends of January, part of the Northmen stationed on the Loire went out to plunder in Neustria and encountered the counts Gauzfridus, Heriveus, and Rorigus [Note: Rorigus, or Rorico, had as his father Rorico, count of Maine; as his brother, Gozfridus, count of Maine; as another brother, Gozlinus, abbot; and as his sister, Blichildis, who was the mother of Bernard, count of Gothia. The ancient parchment documents of the monastery of Juvignac mention Gozlinus the abbot and his brother Gozfridus, under whose guardianship the city of Maine had been placed, as Mabillon reports in Book XXXVII, no. 55, of the *Benedictine Annals*. BOUQ.]. In the encounter Rorigus, the brother of Gauzfridus, fell, and after losing very many of their men, the Northmen fled back to their ships.

Rudolf, the uncle of King Charles, died of colic.

The Northmen, ascending the channel of the Seine as far as the fortress of Melun, proceeded toward Charles’s fleet on both sides of the river. When they came out from their ships against the fleet that appeared larger and stronger, commanded by Robert and Odo, they put it to flight without a battle and returned to their own people with their ships loaded with booty.

Charles made a treaty with those same Northmen for four thousand pounds of silver according to their standard [Note: Compare the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Normans*, under the year 869]. Having imposed a levy throughout his kingdom to pay this tribute, he exacted six denarii from each freeholding estate, three from each servile estate, one from each tenant, and one denarius from every two hospitia [Note: *hospites* in the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Normans*.] [Note: An *hospitium* was a house inhabited by mansionarii in return for an annual rent. The tribute was therefore imposed on: (a) allodial property; (b) the possessions of merchants; (c) the clergy; and (d) the Franks, that is, the king’s *leudes*, both lesser and greater.].

A tithe was also taken from everything that merchants appeared to possess [Note: *negociatores* in C.], and from the priests a tax was exacted according to what each possessed; military fines were also collected from all the Franks.

Then one denarius was taken from each estate, both free and servile. Finally, on two occasions, according to the honors possessed by each of the kingdom’s leading men, a contribution was gathered, both in silver and in wine, and applied toward the amount agreed upon with the Northmen.

Furthermore, slaves captured by the Northmen who had escaped from them after the treaty were either returned or redeemed according to the Northmen’s pleasure. If any Northman had been killed, the price demanded for him was paid [Note: *precium* in C.].

Hludowicus, emperor of Italy, marched with his wife Ingelberga into Benevento against the Saracens.

Lotharius—through the intervention, as some maintain, of Emperor Hludowicus and his brother—entrusted the bishopric of Cologne, which he had received from Hugh, to Hilduinus, the brother of Guntharius, under the pretext of providing for it. In reality, its administration, apart from the episcopal ministry, remained in Guntharius’s hands. That metropolitan church, and also the church of Trier, remained vacant for a long time, contrary to the sacred canons and at great danger to many.

Charles gave Count Robert the abbey of Saint Martin, taken from Engilwinus, and on his advice divided the honors beyond the Seine among his accomplices. He also entrusted to his son Hludowicus, on Robert’s advice, the county of Autun, which Bernard, son of Bernard, had seized from Robert, so that it might enrich him.

In July the Northmen moved from the island beside the monastery of Saint Denis. Descending the Seine, they reached a place suitable for repairing their ships and building new ones, and there awaited what was owed to them [Note: Perhaps *tributum*, “tribute,” has fallen out.].

Charles marched in a hostile manner to the place called Pistis with workers and carts to complete the works, so that the Northmen might not again be able to sail upstream.

Hludowicus, king of Germany, marched against certain of his own men who were plotting rebellion in the march against the Wends. He subdued the rebellion that had preceded him in a short time without a battle and ordered his army, which had scarcely begun its advance, to remain at home.

In July the Northmen entered the sea. Some of them settled for a time in the pagus of Italia [Note: I believe this should be corrected to *in pago Isalae* or *Isalcae*, that is, Isalgau; C. and B. read *in pago Italiae*. The *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Normans*, which often abridges and corrupts the sense of the annals, reads here as well: “and part of them returned to Italy.”] [Note: The pagus of Isala, or Islegau, was largely swallowed by the waves of the sea in the thirteenth century; the remainder, together with its chief town Stavanger, is now counted as part of West Frisia.], and enjoyed their pleasures, except for the public alliance with Lotharius.

Charles went with his wife to the villa of the abbey of Saint Quentin called Orti-vineas to meet Lotharius. In return for certain agreements, as was said, by which guarantees had been established between them, he accepted from Lotharius the abbey of Saint Vaast, which Lotharius granted to him.

In August Charles went to the city of Soissons [Note: Pope Nicholas ordered a synod to be held at Soissons on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September of this year, as is clear from his letter to Hincmar published by Labbe, volume VIII of the *Councils*, p. 808. BOUQ.] and took his seat at the synod convened by Pope Nicholas.

There, in accordance with the recommendation of the aforesaid apostolic, the question concerning Vulfadus and his colleagues, who had been ordained by Ebo, formerly archbishop of Rheims, after Ebo’s deposition, was resolved. Since the sacred canons could not openly be overturned out of reverence for themselves and out of regard for certain persons, and since, with the king and some others exerting themselves excessively on Vulfadus’s behalf, schism [Note: *scisma* in C.] and scandal could not otherwise be avoided, the following solution was found.

Because the regular decision of the bishops of five provinces concerning the deposition of those men had been confirmed by the signatures of Pope Benedict and Pope Nicholas [Note: *ex* added from C. and B.], they would be received in their clerical orders according to the indulgence of the Council of Nicaea concerning those whom Meletius, after his condemnation, had ordained, and according to the tradition of the African council concerning the Donatists—provided that Pope Nicholas was willing to alter the sentence he had confirmed.

The synod then assembled, sending letters to Pope Nicholas through Egilo, archbishop of Sens, and the others for whom he had gone, under the stated condition [Note: Labbe published the synodal letter of the Council of Soissons to Pope Nicholas in the place cited, p. 833. BOUQ.]. It was dissolved without disagreement among the priests.

Although, according to the decrees of Innocent, what the necessity of the times had once discovered in such a matter ought certainly to cease when the necessity ceased, because one thing is the legitimate order and another the usurpation that present circumstances compel, nevertheless, since the sole object being pursued with the utmost zeal was that Vulfadus should somehow become a bishop, some thought it more tolerable, to avoid sedition, to bring this necessity—which now pressed just as it had then—forward again, and, following the counsel of James and the elders of Jerusalem, to practice the ceremonies of the Law with Paul even after the Law had been abolished, as Timothy had been circumcised, rather than provoke tumult in the Church and in the royal power.

With these matters arranged, Charles, on his own authority, entrusted to the aforementioned Vulfadus the metropolitan see of Bourges, whose archbishop Rodulfus had recently died, before the case had been decided.

Before those same bishops departed from the city, Charles asked them to consecrate his wife Hirmintrude as queen. They did so, as he himself attests, in the basilica of Saint Medard, and together with him placed the crown upon her.

From that place the king went with the queen to the palace of Attiniacum to meet Lotharius. There they recalled Theotberga, who was queen of Lotharius in name only and had received permission to go to Rome. They jointly appointed an embassy: Charles entrusted to Egilo, archbishop of Sens, and Lotharius to Ado, archbishop of Vienne, and to Walter, his domestic secretary, the confidential messages they wished to send to Pope Nicholas.

After this Charles sent his son Carolomannus, abbot of Saint Medard, to install Vulfadus in the metropolitan see of Bourges.

After they had arrived, following the dissolution of the synod as mentioned above and the dispatch through Archbishop Egilo of the synodal letters to Pope Nicholas, the aforementioned Vulfadus, in the month of September, was ordained bishop contrary to all ecclesiastical law by certain bishops who were insufficiently versed in the canons, procured by a faction of Vulfadus and bent by threats from Carolomannus, acting with his father’s authority.

For this episcopal ordination Vulfadus was clothed in a curse as in a garment [Note: Vulfadus had been ordained by Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, but deposed from his clerical rank at the Second Synod of Soissons in 853. Pope Nicholas, petitioned by Charles the Bald, who desired Vulfadus’s restoration and had designated him bishop of Bourges, ordered that Vulfadus be restored; for this reason he convened a synod at Soissons. Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, opposed Vulfadus’s restoration with all his strength, submitting four documents or booklets to the synod in succession. The bishops of seven provinces assembled at the Synod of Soissons wrote to Pope Nicholas that Hincmar had not dared, on the authority of himself and his comprovincials, to restore Vulfadus and his associates, who had been deposed at the synod of five provinces. Although they agreed to their restoration, they thought it appropriate to reserve the entire matter for completion by the pontiff who had initiated it. The following year, after Pope Nicholas died, Vulfadus was restored at the Council of Troyes, and Pope Adrian confirmed his restoration. BOUQ.]. Aldo, bishop of Limoges, who was his *exordinator* rather than his ordinator, was seized by a fever during the ordination and soon died.
