Charles’s son, named Charles and king of the Aquitanians, had suffered a blow to the head several years earlier. His brain having been affected, he was afflicted for a long time by an epileptic seizure [Note: *Epelevtica*, that is, epileptic.]. He died on the third day before the Kalends of October in a certain villa near Bosentiacas [Note: Buzançais, in the pagus of Bourges. BOUQ.] and was buried by his brother Carolomannus and by Vulfadus in the church of Saint Sulpicius at Bourges.

Charles had his nephew Wilhelm, son of the late Count Odo of Orléans, who had been captured by some of Charles’s men in Burgundy as though acting against the public interest, beheaded near the city of Senlis.

The Northmen, joined by Britons, about four hundred of them coming out from the Loire with horses, approached the city of Le Mans. After plundering it, they reached on their return as far as the place called Brieserta [Note: Bria or Briva Sartae, that is, the Bridge of the Sarthe, commonly Brisserte. BOUQ.], where they encountered Counts Rotbertus, Ramnulfus, Godtfridus, and Heriveus [Note: “Henricum … Henrico” in the Norman chronicle.], with a strong force of armed men, if God were with them.

When battle was joined, Rotbertus was killed; Ramnulfus was wounded and put to flight, later dying from his wound. Heriveus was wounded, some others were killed, and the rest withdrew, each to his own place.

Since Ramnulfus and Rodbertus had refused to be corrected for the revenge of their predecessors—one having unlawfully seized the abbey of Saint Hilary and the other the abbey of Saint Martin—they deserved to experience vengeance upon themselves.

Hludowicus, son of Hludowicus, king of Germany, acting on the advice of Warnarius and the others from whom his father had taken their honors because of their infidelity, began a quarrel against his father. He incited the Wend Resticius [Note: *restitio* in C., as in several other places.] to come and plunder as far as Bavaria, so that while his father or his father’s faithful men were occupied in those regions, he might pursue more freely what he had begun.

But Carolomannus, to whom his father had given that march, exerted himself, and Resticius confined himself within his own territory.

The elder Hludowicus, wise through experience in such matters, hastened quickly to the palace called Frankfurt. After they had exchanged pledges by clasping right hands, he summoned that same son to come to him. They promised one another that those pledges would remain in force until the fifth day before the Kalends of November.

Hludowicus then quickly returned to confirm his march against Resticius, intending to return on the eighth day before the feast of Saint Martin to meet his brother Charles and his nephew Lotharius near the city of Metz.

Charles announced to his men that he would march in a hostile manner with such an army—as he could then judge, composed chiefly of bishops—and gave Hugh the cleric, son of his maternal uncle Conrad, the county of Tours and the county of Anjou [Note: “The county of Tours and the county of Anjou” is absent in C.], together with the abbey of Saint Martin and also other abbeys. He sent him into Neustria in place of Robert.

From the abbey of Saint Vaast, as he had previously done from the abbey of Saint Quentin, he retained the head and the choicer villas for himself, dividing the rest among his various men—not so much to their advantage as to the detriment of his own soul.

Thus completing the hostile expedition he had announced, he proceeded with his wife through the city of Rheims toward Metz and reached Verdun.

There he met envoys of his brother Hludowicus, who announced that it was not necessary for him to go to his brother with an army for any reason, since Hludowicus had received his son as he himself had arranged and the revolt that had arisen against him had been completely quelled. Nor was it convenient for Hludowicus then to come to meet him as far as Metz, because he was hastening to Bavaria on account of certain necessities of his kingdom.

Charles remained at Verdun for about twenty days, plundering the city and its vicinity in the manner of an enemy. He awaited the arrival of Lotharius, who was at Trier working with the bishops of his kingdom to make Theotberga again accuse herself falsely and receive the veil; but he could not achieve this.

At last Charles returned by the road along which he had come, while his men plundered the places through which they passed. He again reached the city of Rheims [Note: “Romanam” in C.] [Note: That is, the city of Rheims.], and from there came to Compiegne, where he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord.

[Col. 1232B] The king of the Bulgarians [Note: Pagi proves at length, under the year 866, no. 1 and following, that the baptism of Boris, king of the Bulgarians, and the Bulgarian revolt against him occurred in 861, and that the Bertinian annalist’s error arose because he had learned that in 866 the Bulgarian king sent his envoys to Rome. But those envoys were sent by the same king to Rome five years after his conversion, to ask the Roman pontiff what it would be more salutary for him to do and what should be done concerning the remaining Bulgarian people, who still lacked baptism, so that they might receive the sacraments of the faith, as Baronius relates from Anastasius, who was then living at Rome. BOUQ.], who in the preceding year, inspired by God and instructed by signs and afflictions among the people of his kingdom, had planned to become a Christian, received holy baptism.

His nobles took this badly and stirred up the people against him to kill him. All those within ten counties therefore gathered around his palace. He, invoking the name of Christ, went out against that entire multitude with only forty-eight men who, burning with Christian devotion, had remained with him.

As soon as he left the city gates, seven clerics appeared to him and those who were with him. Each held a burning candle in his hand, and they went before the king and his companions.

To those who had risen against him it appeared that a great burning house was falling upon them. Their horses, as it seemed to those opposing him, walked upright and struck them with their forefeet. Such fear seized them that they prepared neither to flee nor to defend themselves, but lay prostrate on the ground, unable to move.

The king killed fifty-two of the nobles who had especially incited the people against him, but allowed the rest of the people to depart unharmed. He sent to Hludowicus, king of Germany, with whom he was joined by a peace treaty, requesting a bishop and priests. Hludowicus sent them, and the Bulgarian king received them with due reverence.

Hludowicus then sent to his brother Charles and requested sacred vessels, holy vestments, and books for the service of the clergy. Charles, receiving a considerable quantity from the bishops of his kingdom, sent it to him for delivery to the king [Note: This is the reading of Chesnius; Bouquet indicates a lacuna between *accipiens* and *ei*, followed by “of the Bulgarians.”].

The king of the Bulgarians sent his son and several of the nobles of his kingdom to Rome. He also sent Saint Peter the arms he had worn when, in the name of Christ, he triumphed over his adversaries, together with other gifts. He sent Pope Nicholas a number of questions concerning the sacraments of the faith and asked him to send bishops and priests, which he obtained.

When Hludowicus, emperor of Italy, heard this, he sent to Pope Nicholas ordering him to forward to him the arms and other things that the king of the Bulgarians had sent to Saint Peter. Nicholas sent some of them to him through Arsenius, who was staying in the region of Benevento, and sent an explanation concerning certain others.

## 867

[Col. 1233B] In the year of the Lord 867, Hludowicus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis and grandson of the emperor Charles through his eldest daughter Rotrude, died on the fifth day before the Ides of January. King Charles retained the abbey of that monastery for himself.

He arranged for the affairs and administration of the monastery to be conducted through the provost, dean, and treasurer, and for military affairs to be managed through the chief of his household, under his charge [Note: *Conlaboratio* means administration or management.].

Around the middle of Lent he went across the Loire to a villa called Bellus-Pauliacus. There he summoned the leading men of Aquitaine to meet him and appointed his son Hludowicus king over them, assigning him officials from his palace [Note: Charles’s son Ludovicus, later called the Bald, succeeded his brother Charles as king of Aquitaine in 866, as is proved by a charter of Bellus, in which Count Godofredus transfers certain properties of his own to the monastery of Bellus. This transfer was made in October, in the twenty-seventh year of King Charles and the first year of his son Ludovicus as king of the region of Aquitaine. BOUQ.].

Returning from there, he celebrated Easter at the monastery of Saint Denis. He then proceeded to Metz for a meeting with his brother, King Hludowicus of Germany. On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the palace of Salmuntiacum, he encountered Egilo, archbishop of Sens, with letters from Pope Nicholas concerning the restoration of the clerics of the church of Rheims, namely Vulfadus and his colleagues.

Striving intensely to have them restored to their offices, he charged Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, in those same letters with many things that were demonstrably untrue.

The aforementioned archbishop also brought to the lord Charles letters from the aforesaid pope to Lotharius and the bishops of his kingdom concerning the case of Lotharius’s wives, namely Theotberga and Waldrada, ordering that Waldrada be sent to Rome. Charles gave these letters to Lotharius when Lotharius came to meet him at the palace of Attiniacum.

From there Charles went to meet his brother, and on his return he came back through Lotharius, who was staying in the Ardennes forest.

Having proclaimed a general levy throughout his entire kingdom, he set his assembly for the Kalends of August at the city of Chartres, intending to march into Brittany against Salomon, duke of the Britons.

Meanwhile, through the exchange of envoys, the negotiations for peace were brought to this condition: after Charles had given hostages, Paswithen, Salomon’s son-in-law, who made extensive use of his counsel, would come to Charles at Compiegne around the aforesaid Kalends of August. Whatever was then agreed and mutually confirmed there would remain in force.

The people, however, who had been summoned to the army, were to remain prepared at home until, if necessary and if the king ordered it, they came in a hostile manner to Chartres on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.

Hludowicus, king of Germany, sent his son Hludowicus with Saxons and Thuringians in a hostile expedition against the Abodrites. He ordered the rest of the people of his kingdom to be ready, so that as soon as he commanded, they might be prepared to march in a hostile manner.

Lotharius, suspecting Charles as he was returning from Louis [Note: [Col. 1233] “to Louis,” Ch.], proceeded from the city of Metz toward Frankfurt, and made peace with the man who had long been sufficiently hostile to him. He granted to his son by Waldrada, Hugh, the duchy of Alsace, commended him to Louis, and entrusted to him the remainder of his kingdom, as though he were about to proceed to Rome and send Waldrada ahead. On his return from there, he proclaimed a levy throughout his kingdom for the defense of the country, as though against the Northmen, supposing that Rorik, whom the inhabitants—who are called by the new name “Conkingi”—had driven out of Frisia, would return with Danish auxiliaries.

Charles, having given hostages, received Paswithen, Solomon’s envoy, at Compiègne on the Kalends of August [Col. 1234C]. To him, Solomon’s representative, he granted the county of Cotentin [Note: [Col. 1233] “of Constantine,” Ch.] [Note: [Col. 1234D] Around the city of Coutances in Normandy.], with all the royal fisc-lands and villages and the abbeys situated in that county, together with whatever possessions belonging to him existed anywhere, except the bishopric; and he confirmed the grant by the oath of his leading men. From the aforesaid representative, on Solomon’s behalf, he received an oath of fidelity and peace and of providing assistance against Charles’s enemies, on the condition that Solomon and his son should retain both what they had previously possessed and this grant, and should remain faithful to Charles and his son.

When this business had been accomplished [Note: [Col. 1233] “business,” Ch.], Charles announced a synod at Troyes for the eighth day before the Kalends of November, by the authority of Pope Nicholas. He decided to remain at the abbey of Saint Vedast, at the villa of Audriaca, and in the surrounding region, for the purpose of hunting and passing the autumn [Col. 1234D] [Note: [Col. 1233] “of remaining,” Ch.].

The synod [Note: [Col. 1233] What follows has been copied word for word by Flodoard in his *History of Reims*, book III, ch. 17; I have noted his readings from Colvenerius’s edition.] of the provinces of Reims, Rouen, Tours, Sens [Note: [Col. 1233] “of Sens,” Ch.], Bordeaux, and Bourges assembled at Troyes on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [Col. 1235A]. There certain bishops, as is customary, favoring Wulfad through regard for King Charles, began to contrive certain measures against Hincmar, contrary to the truth and to the sacred authority of the canons [Note: [Col. 1235] “and,” Flod.]. But Hincmar himself, opposing their machinations with reason and authority, prevailed as the judgment of the majority carried the day. The order of the events under discussion was written down by common agreement in a letter, and the bishops who had assembled sent it to Pope Nicholas through Actard, the venerable bishop of Nantes. The contents of this letter were identical with those of the letter of Hincmar, bishop of Reims, which he had sent to Rome through his clerics in the preceding month of July, disguised as pilgrims in order to avoid the ambushes of his opponents.

Actard accepted the letter composed at the aforesaid synod and sealed with the seals of the archbishops who had assembled, to carry it to Rome; and, together with certain bishops, he returned to Charles, as Charles himself had ordered. Charles, however, forgetful of the fidelity and labors that the aforementioned Hincmar had endured for many years on his behalf, for the sake of his honor and kingdom, demanded that Actard give him the same letter [Note: [Col. 1235] “give him the letter,” Flod.]. Breaking the seals of the archbishops, he reread the acts of the synod. And because Hincmar had not been refuted at that synod as Charles had wished, he had a letter dictated in his own name to Pope Nicholas in opposition to Hincmar. He sealed it with a bull bearing his own name and sent it to Rome through Actard himself, together with the synodal letter.

The aforesaid clerics of Hincmar, arriving at Rome in the month of August, found Pope Nicholas already very ill and laboring greatly in the dispute that he was maintaining against the Greek emperors Michael and Basil [Note: [Col. 1235] “that is, the Greeks,” Flod.], as well as against the Eastern bishops. For this reason they remained there until the month of October. Pope Nicholas, however, gladly receiving what Hincmar had written, replied to him that he had been satisfied with everything [Note: [Col. 1235] “he had written to him,” Flod.]. He also sent another letter to him and to the other archbishops established in Charles’s kingdom, making known that the aforesaid Greek emperors and the Eastern bishops were slandering the holy Roman Church—or rather, the whole Church that uses the Latin language—because we fast on Saturdays; because we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; because we prohibit priests from taking wives; and because we prohibit those same priests from anointing [Note: [Col. 1235] “and because up to ‘we prohibit,’” omitted by Ch. and B.; inserted from Flodoard.] the foreheads of the baptized with chrism [Col. 1235D]. The Greeks themselves said that we Latins made chrism from river water. They reproached us Latins because, according to our custom, we do not abstain for eight weeks before Easter from eating meat and for seven weeks from eating cheese and eggs [Col. 1236A]. They also said that at Easter, following the custom of the Jews, we bless and offer a lamb upon the altar together with the Lord’s body. They further reproached us because our clerics shave their beards, saying [Note: [Col. 1235] “and they say,” Flod.] that among us a deacon, without having received the office of the priesthood, is ordained bishop.

Concerning all these matters, he ordered the metropolitans of each province, together with their fellow bishops, to write back to him. At the end of the letter he addressed Hincmar in this manner [Note: [Col. 1235D] This letter is recited in full by Baronius under the year 867, no. 46 ff. BOUQ.]:

“Your charity, brother Hincmar [Note: [Col. 1235] Absent in Flod.], when it has read this letter, should take the greatest care, as soon as it has also been delivered to the archbishops who are established in the kingdom of our son Charles, the glorious king [Note: [Col. 1235] “to the others also,” a. Flod.], to urge them not to neglect to arrange that each of them, in his own diocese together with his suffragans, regardless of whose kingdom they are established in [Col. 1236B], discuss these matters suitably and report to us what they discover. Thus you should be an energetic executor there of all that the circumstances of our present letter contain [Note: [Col. 1235] “the circumstance contains,” Flod.], and you should be found among us a truthful and prudent reporter through the sequence of your written communications. Dated on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the first indiction [Note: [Col. 1235] From “dated” through “indiction” absent in Flod.].”

Hincmar received this letter on the Ides of December [Note: [Col. 1235] “on the Ides” onward is absent in Flod.] of the first indiction. He reread it to King Charles, who was staying in the palace at Corbonac [Note: [Col. 1235D] This was a royal villa in the district of Laon, one league distant from the gate of the Aisne, commonly called Corbeny or Saint-Marcou because the relics of Saint Marculf had been brought there. BOUQ.], together with several bishops, and endeavored to send it through the other archbishops, as he had been instructed.

Pope Nicholas died on the Ides of the preceding month of December [Note: [Col. 1235] “to whom Adrian succeeded … in the pontificate,” Flod.]. Adrian succeeded him in the pontificate through the election of the clergy and the consent of the emperor Louis. When Actard came to Rome with the letters mentioned above, he found him already ordained in the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1235] Up to this point, Flodoard.].

Arsenius, a man of great cunning and excessive greed, deceived Theutgaud and Guntharius with the false hope of their restoration, and had them come to Rome so that he might receive gifts from them. After remaining there for a long time, they lost almost all their possessions. At last Theutgaud died there, while Guntharius barely escaped bodily death.

Lotharius sent his wife Theutberga to Rome so that she might accuse herself, in order that he might be able to separate from her marriage. But Pope Adrian and the Romans, not believing such empty tales, ordered her to return to her husband.

With the consent of his brother Louis, Charles ordered certain bishops to assemble at Auxerre on the coming Kalends of February, to discuss certain matters concerning Lotharius.

Finally, because Charles had received, as some said, a considerable gift from Acfrid, who possessed the abbey of Saint Hilary together with many other honorable benefices, he took the county of Bourges from Count Gerard without the latter’s presence or any imputation of guilt, and gave it to the aforesaid Acfrid. But Acfrid himself was unable to establish his claim to that county against Gerard. Therefore Charles, passing through the city of Reims, came to Troyes and from there went to Auxerre, where he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord.

## 868

In the year 868, Charles proceeded from Auxerre to the villa called Bellus-Pauliacus on the river Loire. Meanwhile, the men of Count Gerard encountered Acfrid’s men in battle at a certain villa. Because Acfrid refused to leave the very strong house into which he had shut himself, they set fire to the house, drove Acfrid out of it, cut off his head, and threw his body into the fire [Col. 1237B].

Charles then went to the district of Bourges, as if to avenge this outrage. Such evils had been committed there—in the breaking into churches, the oppression of the poor, the perpetration of every kind of outrage, and the devastation of the land—that they cannot be expressed in words, as the testimony of many thousands of people who died of hunger because of that depopulation clearly demonstrates. Yet no vengeance at all was taken against Gerard and his counts; indeed, they were not expelled by anyone from the district of Bourges.

Finally, after taking from Rotbert’s son the honors that Charles had granted him after his father’s death and distributing them among others, and after the paternal honors had also been taken from the sons of Ramnulf [Note: [Col. 1237D] That is, brought or taken away.], and after giving the abbey of Saint Hilary, which the same man had possessed, to Frotarius, archbishop of Bordeaux, Charles returned to the monastery of Saint-Denis before the beginning of the fast [Note: [Col. 1237] Perhaps it should read: “before the beginning of the fast of the holy Quadragesima.” BOUQ.] and from there proceeded to Senlis [Note: [Col. 1237] “proceeded,” Ch.].

The Northmen, however, ascending the Loire, reached Orléans. After taking booty, they returned unharmed to their encampment. Charles returned to the monastery of Saint-Denis on the Saturday before Palm Sunday and celebrated Easter there.

Before going to Silvacum, on the second day of the Rogations, he received from Adventius, bishop of Metz, and Grimland [Note: [Col. 1237D] Grimland, or Grimbland, occurs in Lotharius’s charter for Theutberga, dated 866 or 867, in Muratori, Antiquitates Italicae.], Lotharius’s chancellor, who brought letters from Pope Adrian, one letter addressed to him [Note: [Col. 1237D] This letter is not among those published. Adrian’s letter to Louis, king of Germany, on the same subject was published by Labbe, volume VIII of the Councils, p. 907. BOUQ.]. In it the same apostolic authority ordered him not to inflict any harm upon the kingdom of the emperor Louis or upon the kingdom of Lotharius. They brought another letter concerning Waldrada’s absolution to the bishops of Charles’s kingdom [Col. 1238A], saying that similar letters had been sent to the bishops of the kingdom of Louis and of Lotharius. Waldrada’s absolution, however, was granted on the condition that she should not live with Lotharius in any way.

When Charles reached Silvacum, he received Actard, bishop of Nantes, who was returning from Rome and bringing him letters. One of them gave a response concerning the matters that Charles had sent to Nicholas in opposition to Hincmar, urging him among other things that thereafter and forever such a useless question should remain settled. He brought another letter to Hincmar, filled with praise and expressions of faithful affection [Note: [Col. 1237] “directions,” Ch.], appointing him to act in these regions in Adrian’s place [Note: [Col. 1237D] This letter is said to have been given on the eighth day before the Ides of March, first indiction; it was published by Labbe, volume VIII of the Councils, p. 905. BOUQ.]. He brought a third letter to the archbishops and other bishops on this side of the Alps, stating that because Actard himself could not remain in his own city on account of the attacks of the pagans [Col. 1238B] and the oppression of the Britons, if an opportunity arose, even in a metropolitan church, the same Actard should, in a vacant city lacking a pastor, be incardinated by the bishops of that province by apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 1238D] This letter was published by Labbe, volume VIII of the Councils, p. 901. There is also there, p. 906, Adrian’s letter to Actard himself, granting him the pallium as consolation. BOUQ.] [Note: [Col. 1238D] Concerning Actard, see Hincmar of Reims, archbishop, Letter 45.].

On the fourth day after the beginning of Quadragesima, through the agency of Arsenius, his son Eleutherius deceitfully deceived and abducted Adrian’s daughter, who had been betrothed to another, and took her as his own wife. The pope was consequently greatly saddened.

Arsenius, traveling to the emperor Louis at Benevento, was struck by illness. Entrusting his treasure to the hands of the empress Engelberga and, as was said, conversing with demons, he departed without communion to his own place [Note: [Col. 1238D] That is, to hell.]. After his death, Pope Adrian obtained from the emperor envoys who would judge the aforesaid Eleutherius according to Roman laws.

The same Eleutherius, reportedly on the advice of his brother Anastasius, whom Adrian had appointed librarian [Note: [Col. 1238D] This Anastasius is different from Anastasius the Librarian, to whom the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs are attributed. BOUQ.] of the Roman Church at the beginning of his pontificate, killed Stephania, the wife of that pontiff, and the daughter whom he had abducted for himself. The same Eleutherius was then killed by the emperor’s envoys.

Pope Adrian, however, convened a synod and condemned the aforesaid Anastasius a second time in the following manner, after the condemnations that had been pronounced against him:

The following is written on the image on the right-hand side.

“While our lords Lotharius and Louis, Augusti, were reigning, on the sixteenth day of the month of December, in the fourteenth indiction [Col. 1238D].”

### Excommunication pronounced by Bishop Leo against Anastasius the presbyter, and afterward by Adrian

“Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God. Anastasius, presbyter of our cardinal clergy, whom we ordained at the title of the blessed Marcellus, and who, withdrawing from it, departed into foreign parishes without our pontifical knowledge; whom we summoned through our envoys and letters, and for whom we petitioned the lords emperors through our envoys that they order him to return to his own parish; who, now hiding here and there [Note: [Col. 1239] ‘now here and there’ is absent in Ch. and B., though the former considers it properly supplied.], has remained in that departure for two years; and who, summoned to two of our councils, did not come at all and was not even found—for, as we have said, like a wandering sheep, at the devil’s urging, he was secretly dwelling in foreign regions—is from today deprived of communion according to the canonical institutions, by the authority of almighty God, the blessed apostle Peter, and our own apostolic authority together, until he has been presented before my special presence in a canonical judgment; and if he does not come, let him never communicate.”

After the Roman pontiff, the archbishops of Ravenna and Milan and seventy-five others consented to this excommunication.

The following is written on the image on the left-hand side.

“Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops, presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, all clerics, and the entire Christian people. You know, dearly beloved brothers, that we are well and fully with you. Now again, for the sake of caution and the memory of future times, we wish it to be known to your affection how, at the instigation and persuasion of the devil, Anastasius, presbyter of our cardinal clergy, whom we ordained at the title of the blessed Marcellus, abandoning his province and church contrary to the statutes of the Fathers, has now for five years [Note: [Col. 1239] “a period of five years,” Ch.] wandered through foreign parishes like a lost sheep. Supported by canonical authority, we summoned him by apostolic letters a third and fourth time. But when he delayed returning, we convened two councils of bishops on his account. Since at their gathering we could neither see nor have his personal presence, by common decree we deprived him of holy communion, wishing by the censure of this excommunication to bring the man back to the bosom of the holy mother Church from which he had departed.

“But, treating the apostolic admonitions and the decision of the holy council as nothing, ensnared in the darkness of error, he was utterly unwilling to return. Therefore, just as we proclaimed concerning him with our own mouth while staying at Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1239] “Ravenna,” Ch.], in the church of the blessed martyr Vitalis, on the twenty-ninth day of the month of May, in the first indiction [Note: [Col. 1239] Absent in Ch.], so now again we have proclaimed it in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, on the nineteenth day of the month of June, in the indiction noted above: let him be anathema from the holy Fathers and from us; and let all who wish to offer him assistance or any kind of support, whether in his election—which God forbid—or in the honor of the pontificate, be subjected to a similar anathema [Note: [Col. 1239] ‘anathema,’ Ch.].”

After the Roman pontiff, John, archbishop of Ravenna, Notting [Note: [Col. 1239D] Bishop of Brescia.], and Sigilfred [Note: [Col. 1239D] He appears to be Sigisfred, bishop of Reggio.], the emperor’s bishops, consented to this anathema, together with six bishops belonging to the aforesaid archbishop, whose names we do not recall, and fifty-six others from the city of Rome and elsewhere, excluding the presbyters and deacons of the holy Roman Church.

### The following is written above the silver doors:

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Here begins the holy and venerable synod, which by the grace of the Lord and by his divine counsel was convened in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, namely in the seventh year of the pontificate of the most holy, coangelic, and universal fourth pope, Leo, and in the forty-second year of the imperial reign of the unconquered emperors Lotharius and Louis [Note: [Col. 1239D] Here the years of the imperial reigns of Lotharius and Louis are joined together. For Lotharius’s thirty-seventh year combined with Louis’s fifth year produces the forty-second year of their imperial reign [Col. 1240D]. Moreover, this Roman council is said in its preface to have been held ‘in the fifth and thirty-seventh years of the imperial reign of the emperors Lotharius and Louis, on the third day of December, in the second indiction.’ BOUQ.], on the eighth day of the month of December, in the second indiction.

“In this holy and venerable synod, nobly celebrated with the assistance of the Lord’s grace, after various pious and salutary admonitions and exhortations had been given by bishops, priests, clerics, and all Christians, Anastasius, presbyter of the title of Saint Marcellus, was justly and canonically deposed [Col. 1240C], because he had abandoned his own parish contrary to canonical authority for five years and had remained in another up to the present day. Although he had been summoned, excommunicated, and finally anathematized, as the truthful depiction concerning him in this synod demonstrates, he refused to come to the two councils of bishops convened on his account. Therefore, both by the supreme pontiff and by all the bishops presiding at that synod, numbering sixty-seven, he was deservedly deposed, as we have said, on account of his foolish audacity, and deprived of priestly honor, in the year, month, day, and indiction stated above.”

Up to this point Pope Leo ordered the inscription to be written. After the death of the aforementioned Leo, the anathematized and deposed Anastasius, returning by secular power from the hidden places where he had lurked like a thief, ensnared by diabolical fraud and darkness, invaded like a pagan and barbarian this church, which he ought not to have entered, to the destruction of his own soul and the peril of this venerable synod. Together with his utterly wicked accomplices and followers, he destroyed the picture and cast down the image [Note: [Col. 1241] Thus I have emended it; Ch. and B. read “imaque.”], which the most blessed Pope Benedict had restored and adorned with shining colors.

“Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God. It is known to the whole Church of God what Anastasius did in the time of our predecessors the pontiffs, and it is also clear to all how, on that account, Leo and Benedict, prelates of holy memory, instituted proceedings against him. One of them deposed, excommunicated, and anathematized him; the other, stripping him of his priestly vestments, received him into communion among the laity.

“Our predecessor, the most holy Pope Nicholas, would afterward have received him in the same manner into the bosom of the Church, if he had conducted himself faithfully toward the holy Roman Church. But his faithlessness has now appeared to such an extent that, after plundering our patriarchate and removing the synodal documents that he had found decreed at various times both against him and against such conduct by the most holy prelates [Note: [Col. 1241] ‘had found,’ Ch.], he also caused the institution of the venerable synod established by those holy pontiffs and renewed under the threat of anathema to be violated, by secretly appropriating it. He compelled men to go out through the walls of this city, like a thief, in order to sow discord between the most pious princes and the Church of God, and he suggested that a certain Adalgrim, who had taken refuge in a church, be deprived of his eyes and tongue.

“Now, as many of you heard with me from a certain presbyter related to him, named Ado, and as has also been revealed to us in other ways, forgetful of our benefactions as well, he sent a man to Eleutherius, urging the perpetration of murders—which, as you know, alas, were committed. Therefore, for all these things and for the many others by which he has struck and injured the Church of God, which he has not ceased to assail until now by deceitful schemes, by the authority of almighty God, of all the holy Fathers, of the venerable councils, and of the aforesaid pontiffs, and by the sentence of our own judgment, we decree that the same Anastasius is to be held precisely as the same lords pontiffs Leo and Benedict solemnly and synodically established concerning him. We add or subtract absolutely nothing from his anathema or his case, except that he is to remain deprived of all ecclesiastical communion until he gives us an account before the synod concerning all the charges brought against him. Whoever communicates with him in speech, food, or drink is likewise to be bound by the same excommunication with him, because, on account of his rash usurpation of what was higher than himself—what had so often been forbidden him—and because he climbed into the forbidden place, our Church has murmured and continues to murmur sufficiently.

“Certainly, if he should withdraw even for a short time from the city of Rome, or presume to seek or receive the priesthood, any clerical order, or any ministry whatsoever, since he will thereby appear to act contrary to the statutes of the aforesaid prelates and contrary to the oath that he swore—that he would never withdraw more than forty miles from the city, nor seek the priesthood or any clerical rank [Note: [Col. 1241] ‘because,’ Ch.] [Note: [Col. 1241] ‘nor’ is absent in Ch.]—let him, together with all his accomplices and followers, be subjected to perpetual anathema [Note: [Col. 1241] ‘perpetual anathema,’ Ch.].

“Pronounced in the presence of the whole holy Roman Church, before this same Anastasius, who was placed at Saint Praxedes, in the first year of the pontificate of our lord Adrian, supreme pontiff and universal pope, on the fourth day before the Ides of October, in the second indiction [Col. 1242B].”

Lotharius, suspecting Charles, again went to Louis and obtained from him an oath on his behalf that he would cause him no harm if he took Waldrada as his wife. Thus he came to the palace at Attigny for a conference with Charles, and there received an agreement that they would meet again together after the coming Kalends of October.

Charles, however, traveling through the royal estates situated in the district of Laon, ordered Hincmar, bishop of Laon, without the knowledge of any bishop of his province, to appoint an advocate on his behalf for his cases—that is, for secular judgment—because he had taken benefices away from certain of his men.

The same bishop protested that, having abandoned ecclesiastical judgment, he did not dare to approach secular judgment. As he had been ordered, he did not come to the designated place of secular judgment, but sent the king an account of his inability. King Charles nevertheless ordered certain infamous persons to judge the matter, because the aforesaid bishop had not sent a representative who would swear that he could not come, and because he had not provided his advocate for himself in secular court. By the judgment of the aforesaid persons, whatever the same bishop specifically possessed from ecclesiastical property and resources for the uses of the bishopric was proscribed.

Thus the same king came to Pîtres in the middle of August, received his annual gifts there, measured out the fortress, and assigned pediturae to each person from his kingdom [Note: [Col. 1241D] Peditura or pedatura: any space defined by a fixed number of feet.] [Col. 1242D].

Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, bringing Hincmar, bishop of Laon, with him, approached the king at Pîtres together with other bishops, in writing and in speech [Note: [Col. 1241D] See Hincmar of Reims’s letter to Charles the Bald, written in 868, in Labbe, Councils, volume VIII, p. 1735.]. He showed how greatly both episcopal authority and the universal Church suffered prejudice from such an act, and obtained an agreement that, after the bishop had been restored to the possessions of which he had been deprived, as the sacred laws prescribe, the matter would be settled in the province where it was to be judged, by the judgment of chosen men, and, if necessary, afterward by synodal examination.

By the same agreement the king also received the margraves—namely, Bernard of Toulouse and Bernard of Gothia, and likewise another Bernard [Note: [Col. 1243D] Bernard, duke of Toulouse, was the son of Raymond I; Bernard, duke of Gothia, was the son of another Bernard, count of Le Mans; the third Bernard, who had been deprived of his honors in 864 at the assembly of Pîtres, was the son of Bernard, duke of Septimania, who was killed by Charles the Bald in 844. BOUQ.].

He also encountered there an envoy of Solomon, duke of the Britons, through whom Solomon sent word that Charles himself should not proceed to attack the Northmen who were staying on the Loire, because Solomon was prepared to attack them with a strong force of Britons, provided only that he received assistance from Charles.

Charles sent to him Engelramnus, his chamberlain, master of the doorkeepers, and confidential counsellor, with a crown decorated with gold and jewels and with all the royal regalia splendidly adorned. He also sent his son Carloman, deacon and abbot, with a military contingent immediately behind him, just as Solomon had requested.

The contingent sent across the Seine with Carloman by King Charles devastated the land but achieved no useful result against the Northmen, against whom it had been sent to resist. At King Charles’s command it returned, and each man went back to his own place.

The people of Poitiers, however, making vows to God and Saint Hilary, attacked those same Northmen for the third time. They killed many of them, put the rest to flight, and presented a tithe of all the booty, except for voluntary offerings, to Saint Hilary.

On the Kalends of December, King Charles came to Quierzy and summoned certain leading men, both bishops and others from his kingdom, to meet him [Col. 1243C]. He was angered against Hincmar, bishop of Laon, because Hincmar had sent to Rome without his knowledge [Note: [Col. 1243D] See the synod of Douzy and Hincmar of Reims, On the Matter, chapter 55. BOUQ.] and had obtained letters on matters for which he had not reached agreement. He was also extremely hostile to that bishop because the bishop stubbornly resisted him.

Therefore the same bishop, without the king’s permission, went to his see, although he had often been summoned by him and had delayed coming to him; by doing so he provoked the king against himself beyond what episcopal dignity permits. Charles came to Compiègne, where he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord.

## 869

Because the same bishop, even when summoned through other bishops to come to him, refused to fulfill his command [Col. 1243D], Charles sent a military force composed of very many counts of his kingdom to Laon, so that they might bring the bishop to him by force.

The same bishop sat with his clerics beside the altar [Col. 1244A]. After certain bishops had worked on the matter, it was arranged that those who had been sent would not drag him out of the church. They returned to Charles without him, and Charles had all the free men of the bishopric swear oaths to him.

Charles, however, greatly angered, announced a synod of all the bishops of his kingdom for the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction, at Verberie [Note: [Col. 1244D] At this synod the royal grants made to the monastery of Charroux were confirmed. Labbe, volume I of the Councils, p. 1527, reproduces this confirmation.]. He ordered the same bishop Hincmar to be summoned there [Note: [Col. 1244D] See Hincmar’s Letter 35.].

He himself went to the village of Conada [Note: [Col. 1244D] Cosne. BOUQ.], most inappropriately both for the season and because of the extreme famine. There he encountered certain Aquitanians. But, not finding the margraves—namely, the three Bernards—whom he expected to meet, he returned to Senlis, not without anxiety and without achieving anything useful.

From there, on the Wednesday before the beginning of Quadragesima, he went to the monastery of Saint-Denis, where he completed the holy fast of Quadragesima and celebrated the Lord’s Easter. He also began to construct a fortress around that monastery out of wood and stone [Col. 1244B].

Before going to Conada, he sent letters throughout his kingdom ordering bishops, abbots, and abbesses to bring, by the coming Kalends of May, written statements of their honors, specifying how many manses each possessed [Note: [Col. 1243] “to,” absent in Ch.]. He ordered the royal vassals to record the benefices of the counts, and the counts to record the benefices of the vassals, and to bring written statements of the houses to the aforesaid assembly. He further ordered that from every hundred manses one haistaldus [Note: [Col. 1244D] A haistaldus was a free cultivator who did not hold an inheritance from the court. See Hontheim, History of Trier, vol. I, p. 664.] and from every thousand manses one cart with two oxen be sent to the aforesaid assembly [Note: [Col. 1243] “to the aforesaid assembly,” absent in Ch.], together with other gifts that greatly burdened his kingdom, and that they be sent to Pîtres [Col. 1244C], so that these haistaldi might cultivate and guard the fortress that he had ordered to be built there of wood and stone.

Lotharius sent to Charles and also to Louis, asking them not to cause him any hindrance in his kingdom until he returned from Rome. He received no assurance from Charles, but, as is said, received such an assurance from Louis and proceeded to Rome. First he intended to confer with his brother, the emperor Louis, so that, if possible, through him he might obtain from Pope Adrian permission to reject Theutberga and take Waldrada back. He also ordered Theutberga to travel to Rome after him.

But, as was said, Emperor Louis ought not to have withdrawn from the siege of the Saracens for the sake of his brother’s request, since the Greek king was hastily sending him more than two hundred ships to assist against those same Saracens [Col. 1244D].

Lotharius endeavored to complete the journey to Rome that he had begun at an unsuitable time—namely, in the month of June—and for the sake of his wives. He reached Ravenna, where he encountered envoys of his brother. Through them his brother forbade him to proceed any farther or to remain longer in that kingdom, ordering him to return to his own kingdom; they would meet together at a suitable time and in an appropriate place and discuss whatever matters he wished with him.

Lotharius, returning toward Rome, went as far as Benevento to his brother. Through Engelberga, with many petitions, gifts, and improper dealings, he obtained from him that Engelberga herself would return with him as far as the monastery of Saint Benedict, situated on Mount Cassino.

At the emperor’s command he also had Pope Adrian come to the same place to Engelberga and himself. There, after giving the pope many gifts, he obtained through Engelberga that the same pope would celebrate Mass for him and grant him holy communion on this agreement: that, after Pope Nicholas had excommunicated Waldrada, he had had with her neither cohabitation nor any intercourse of carnal union, nor even any conversation.

But that wretched man, like a Jew, with a feigned good conscience and shameless face, did not fear or refuse to receive the same holy communion under this agreement. His supporters also received communion from the pope together with him. Among them was Guntharius, the author and instigator of this public adultery, who received communion among the laity from Pope Adrian himself, after first making before everyone the profession that follows:

“ I, Guntharius, profess before God and his saints [Col. 1245C], to you, my lord Adrian, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and to the venerable bishops subject to you and the rest of the assembly, that I do not criticize the judgment of deposition canonically pronounced against me by Lord Nicholas, but humbly bear it. Therefore I do not presume to touch the sacred ministry any longer, unless you are willing to assist me through mercy; nor do I wish ever to stir up any scandal or adversity against the holy Roman Church or its pontiff. Rather, I protest that I will present myself as devoted to that same holy mother Church and to its prelate, and will remain obedient. I, Guntharius, have subscribed this profession made by me with my own hand. Given on the Kalends of July, in the second indiction, in the church of Saint Salvator [Note: [Col. 1245D] In the village of San Germano; in the same church, in the year 1230, Emperor Frederick II was reconciled with Pope Gregory IX.], which is in the monastery of Saint Benedict [Col. 1245D] at Cassino.”

When that same pope received this profession from Guntharius, who was standing among the laymen, and had it publicly reread among the laymen before everyone, he said to him: [Col. 1246A] “And I grant you lay communion, on the condition that, for as long as you live, you observe it in the manner in which you have just professed.”

Finally, when Engelberga returned to her [Note: [Col. 1245] Her husband, Hludowicus, seems to be missing.] emperor, Pope Adrian returned to Rome, and Lotharius followed him immediately. When Pope Adrian entered Rome, Lotharius came to the church of Saint Peter, where he encountered no cleric, but reached the tomb of Saint Peter with his men alone. From there he entered a lodging beside the church of Saint Peter, intending to stay there; he did not even find it swept. He thought that on the following day—namely Sunday, since he had reached the basilica of Saint Peter on Saturday—a Mass ought to be sung for him; but he could not obtain this from the aforesaid pontiff. Then, entering Rome on Monday, he dined with the pope himself in the Lateran palace and, having given him gifts in gold and silver vessels, obtained from him a *laena* [Note: [Col. 1245] Ch. *leena*, Bq. *leaena*; easily emended.] [Note: [Col. 1246D] *Laena*, Greek *λαΐνα*, *χλαΐνα*, a thick cloak.] and a palm and a rod, as he indeed did. He and his supporters interpreted these gifts as follows: by the cloak he was to be reclothed with Waldrada; by the palm he was to demonstrate that he was victorious in what he had begun; and by the rod he was to discipline the bishops who resisted his will by opposing them.

But they had been arranged differently by that same pope and the Romans. For the pontiff decided to send Bishop Formosus and another bishop with him to these parts of Gaul, so that they might deliberate with a plurality of bishops concerning the matters Lotharius was requesting, and report at a synod on the Kalends of March whatever they found. He announced this synod at Rome for the very Kalends of March. He also ordered four bishops from the kingdom of Hludowicus, king of Germany, with his envoys; four bishops from the kingdom of Charles, with his envoys [Note: [Col. 1245] “And four bishops from the kingdom of Charles with his envoys” is absent from Ch.]; and certain bishops from the kingdom of Lotharius to come with his letters [Note: [Col. 1245] Ch.: “of Lotharius with letters”], on the condition that they confirm through the persons of others whatever was to be examined or undertaken at the synod, both from the western and from the eastern regions. For this reason he kept separate the envoys whom he had recently sent to Constantinople concerning the dispute that the Easterners had with Pope Nicholas, intending that they should come later.

But Lotharius [Note: [Col. 1245] We have compared what follows with Royal Codex 8394 (1), which contains only what is found in the continuation of Aimoinus. BOUQUET. I compared it with the continuation of Aimoinus, book V, chapters 21–40 (in Freher, *Corpus historiae Francicae*, vol. II, pp. 477–506), and marked the more important readings by the letter A, incorporating many of them into the text.] journeying joyfully from Rome came as far as the city of Lucca, where he was seized by a fever. As the plague ravaged his men, whom he saw dying in heaps before his eyes [Note: [Col. 1245] A: “under his eyes”], yet refusing to understand the judgment of God, he reached Piacenza on the eighth day before the Ides of August. There, remaining over Sunday, around the ninth hour he unexpectedly became almost lifeless and lost his speech [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “becoming speechless”]. On the following day [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “the following morning”], at the second hour of the day, he died, and a few of his men who had survived the plague buried him in a small monastery beside the city.

When Charles, residing at the city of Senlis [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “of Senlis”]—where he and his wife, having distributed through holy places as alms the treasures they had possessed in every kind of property, returned from Pistes and gave them back to the Lord, from whose hand they had received them—learned of this through a reliable messenger, he departed from that city and came to Attigny. There he received envoys sent by certain bishops and also by some leading men of the kingdom formerly belonging to Lotharius [Note: [Col. 1247] A frequently uses the words “legates” and “messenger” where Ch. and B. have *missus*]. They asked him to remain there and not enter the kingdom that had belonged to Lotharius until his brother Hludowicus, [Col. 1247B] king of Germany, returned from his hostile expedition against the Wends [Note: [Col. 1247] Ch.: “Wineds”]. In the present and the preceding year, his men had often engaged them at close quarters, accomplishing little or nothing useful and suffering very great losses [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “and losses”]. [Note: [Col. 1247] A adds: “and in the palace of Ingelheim.”]

They therefore asked him to reside in the palace at Ingelheim, send his envoys to Hludowicus, and inform him where [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “that”] and when they should meet and discuss the division of his kingdom. Others, however, with sounder counsel, advised him to hasten as soon as conveniently possible [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “by whatever means”] to Metz [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “Mettos”], and said that they would hurry to meet him both on the road and at the city itself. Understanding that their advice was more acceptable and more salutary for him [Aimoinus: “for himself”], Charles hastened to act according to their suggestion.

Coming to Verdun, he received many men from that same kingdom, including Hatto [Note: [Col. 1247] Ch.: “Hato”; A: “Haidon”], bishop of that city, and Arnulf, bishop of Toul, who commended themselves to him. From there, coming to Metz on the Nones of September, he received Adventius, bishop of that city, and Franco, bishop of Tongeren, with many others who commended themselves to him. Thus, on the fifth day before the Ides of that month, the bishops who were present having assembled in the basilica of Saint Stephen, the following matters were publicly announced and enacted in this manner:

“ In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 869 [Note: [Col. 1247] Other copies have 868 or 859; A has 868.], in the second indiction [Note: [Col. 1247] This is the second Constantinopolitan indiction, which began on 24 September of the year 868. BOUQUET.] [Col. 1247D], on the Ides of September, in the city of Metz, in the church of Saint Stephen the Martyr, Adventius, bishop of that city, publicly announced the following chapters, in writing and orally, before the king, the bishops who were present, and the people [Aimoinus adds: “and”]:

“ You know, brothers [Aimoinus adds: “brothers”], and it is known in very many kingdoms, how great and what manner of events we collectively endured during the time of our former lord, whom until now we have had, for reasons well known to all; and with how much grief and anguish our hearts have recently been struck by his unfortunate death. Therefore, deprived and bereft of our king and prince, we have all considered our sole refuge and singularly healthful counsel [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “singularly salutary”] to be that we should turn, through fasts and prayers, to him who is a helper in times of need and in tribulation, whose is the counsel and whose is the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “whose are the counsel and kingdom”]; and, as it is written, ‘he will give it to whomever he wishes’; and to him in whose hand are the hearts of kings, who makes them dwell together in unity, breaking down the dividing wall [Col. 1248B] and making both one.

“We beseech his mercy to give us a king and prince after his own heart, who would govern, save, and defend us in judgment and justice, in every kind of order and protection [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “in every order and profession”], according to his will; and who would incline and unite all our hearts unanimously toward him. Let us beseech his mercy to give us a king and prince after his own heart, who would govern, save, and defend us in judgment and justice, in every kind of order and protection [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “in every order and profession”], according to his will; and who would incline and unite all our hearts unanimously toward him—him whom God, according to his mercy, had foreknown, chosen, and predestined for our salvation and advancement [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “for the salvation of the whole Church and people”; other copies: “may have”]. Since, moreover, in our concordant unanimity we see the will of God—who fulfills the will of those who fear him and hears their prayers—that this man is the lawful heir of this kingdom, we have voluntarily entrusted ourselves to him, namely to the lord and present king and prince, our Charles, so that he may preside over us and benefit us.

“It seems to us, if it pleases you, that, as we shall make clear to you after his speech [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “after these things”], we should demonstrate by a most certain sign that we believe him to have been chosen by God and given to us as prince [Note: [Col. 1247] Absent in A.]. And so that we may not be ungrateful to God, the generous giver, for his gifts, but may return thanks to him, let us pray [Note: [Col. 1247] Absent in A.] that he may preserve him among us for a long time—him whom he has given us as prince [Aimoinus adds: “given as prince”—for the salvation and defense of his holy Church, and for the assistance and advancement of us all, with salvation and [Note: [Col. 1247] “with salvation and” is absent] peace and tranquility—and that, obedient to him with faithful devotion and enjoying the salvation we desire [Col. 1248D] [Note: [Col. 1247] A: “and observance”], he may govern us under his administration in his service.

“And if it pleases him, it seems worthy of him and necessary for us [Note: [Col. 1247] Ch.: “to be”] that we hear from his own mouth what it is fitting for each person in his order to hear and receive with devoted mind from a most Christian king and from a people faithful and united in his service [Col. 1249A] [Note: [Col. 1249] Royal Codex: “united”; Bouquet: “this people united”; A: “this united people”].”

After this, King Charles himself publicly announced the following matters in the same church to all who were present, saying [Note: [Col. 1249] Absent in A.]:

“Since, as these venerable bishops have said through the voice of one of their number, and have demonstrated by clear signs through your [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “your and our”] unanimity, and since you have acclaimed that I have come here by God’s choice for your salvation, protection, advancement [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “advancement”], government, and administration, know that, with the Lord’s help, I will preserve the honor and worship of God and of the holy churches. I will, according to my knowledge and ability, honor and save each one of you according to the dignity of his order and person, and I wish to keep you honored and saved [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “honorably saved”; A adds: “and”]. I will preserve law and justice for each person in his order according to the laws appropriate to him, both ecclesiastical and secular [Note: [Col. 1249] Absent in A].

“In this way, may royal honor and power, due obedience, and assistance for maintaining and defending the kingdom given to me by God [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “defending”] be offered to me by each of you according to his order, dignity, and ability, just as your predecessors faithfully, justly, and reasonably offered them to my predecessors.”

But after this [Note: [Col. 1249] Ch.: “And after”] [Note: [Col. 1249] Absent in A.], Hincmar, bishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “archbishop”], publicly announced the following chapters, at the command and request of Adventius, bishop of that city, and of the other bishops of the province of Trier—namely Hatto, bishop of the church of Verdun, and Arnulf, bishop of the city of Toul [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “bishop of the church of Toul”—the words “and bishop of the city” are absent]—with the bishops of the province of Reims concurring [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “agreeing”], before the remaining bishops [Note: [Col. 1249] Absent in A.] and the king, and before all who were present in the same church:

“Lest it perhaps seem to anyone that I and the venerable fellow bishops of our province are acting improperly and presumptuously by involving ourselves, from another province, in the ordination and affairs of this province, let him know that we are not acting against the sacred canons. For the churches of Reims and Trier in this Belgian region, together with the churches entrusted to them, are regarded as sisters and fellow-provincial churches, as ecclesiastical authority and very ancient custom demonstrate. Accordingly, they ought, by unanimous agreement, to exercise synodal judgments and concordantly preserve what has been established by the holy Fathers, while observing this privilege: that whichever of the bishops of Reims and Trier was ordained first is also to be regarded as senior.

“And the law inspired by God [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “the law instituted and commanded”] gives this command, saying: ‘If you pass through the harvest of your friend, gathering ears with your hand, you shall rub them in order to eat. But you shall not put in the sickle, or reap with the sickle’ [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “but you shall not cut with the sickle”] [Note: [Col. 1249D] Deuteronomy 23:25.]. The harvest is the people, as the Lord demonstrates in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1249D] Matthew 9:37.], saying: ‘The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the workers are few; therefore ask the lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest.’

“You ought to pray for your bishops [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “for us as bishops”], so that we may be able to speak what is worthy of you [Note: [Col. 1249] Absent in Ch.]. The harvest of a friend is the people entrusted to another metropolitan. Therefore, by exhorting you, as though rubbing the hand of labor, we can and ought to lead you, for the will of God and your [Aimoinus adds: “salvation”], into the body of the Church’s unity. But we do not cast the sickle of judgment upon the parishioners of provinces entrusted to other metropolitans, since there is no basis for doing so, nor do we consider it to belong to us [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “nor do we consider it to be ours”].

“There is also another reason: these venerable lords and our brothers, the bishops of this province, having no metropolitan bishop, command and admonish our insignificance, in fraternal charity, to act in their affairs just as in our own particular affairs. Is this so, my lords and brothers?” And the bishops themselves answered: “It is so.”

“Besides what the lord bishop and our brother Adventius has said to you in his own voice and in that of his other and our brothers, the venerable bishops, you may also observe here that it is God’s will that our present lord and king—who, in the part of the kingdom which he now holds and has hitherto held, beneficially presides and has presided over us, our churches, and the people entrusted to him, and profitably benefits and has benefited them—has come from there to this place, guided by the Lord, to which you too have flowed together through his inspiration [Col. 1250C], and to him you have voluntarily commended yourselves.

“All the animals signifying the unity of the Church in Noah’s ark came together without compulsion, animated by his prompting [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “animated by the instinct of the animals signifying Noah’s ark”]. For his father, of holy memory, Lord Hludowicus, the pious emperor Augustus [Note: [Col. 1249] Absent in A.], was descended from the line of Ludoicus [Note: [Col. 1249] A: “Clodoveus”], the illustrious king of the Franks, converted with his whole people through the apostolic and catholic preaching of blessed Remigius, baptized with three thousand Franks, excluding children and women [Aimoinus adds: “in”], on the vigil of holy Easter in the metropolitan church of Reims [Note: [Col. 1249] A lacks “in the metropolitan church”], anointed with chrism received from heaven, of which we still possess some, and consecrated king. This pious Augustus Hludowicus arose through blessed Arnulf, from whose flesh he derived his bodily origin. He was crowned emperor by Stephen, Roman pope, at Reims before the altar of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin [Note: [Col. 1249] A lacks “and ever-virgin”] [Col. 1250D] [Note: [Col. 1249] Ch.: “at Reims”].

“Finally, after being deprived of his earthly empire through the faction of certain men, he was restored to the aforesaid part of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1249] A lacks “to the aforesaid part of the kingdom”] through the unanimity of the bishops and faithful people before the tomb of Saint Denis, the eminent martyr [Note: [Col. 1249] A lacks “the eminent martyr”] [Col. 1251A]. In this church, before this altar of the protomartyr Stephen—whose name, when interpreted, means ‘crowned’—he was restored to the crown of the kingdom and to imperial authority [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “to imperial authority,” without “and”] by the priests of God amid the acclamation of the faithful people, as we who were present saw.

“And since, as we read in sacred histories, when kings obtained kingdoms they placed upon themselves the diadems of each kingdom, it does not seem inappropriate to the venerable bishops [Note: [Col. 1251] A lacks “to the venerable bishops”], if it pleases your unanimity, that, upon obtaining the kingdom from which you have come together to him [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “to which you have voluntarily come”] and have commended yourselves to him [Note: [Col. 1251] A lacks “and have commended yourselves to him”], he should be crowned by priestly ministry before this altar and consecrated to God by sacred anointing. If this pleases you, let your voices agree.”

When everyone shouted agreement to this, the same bishop said: [Col. 1251B] “Let us therefore unanimously give thanks to the Lord, singing: *Te Deum laudamus*.”

After this, the same king was crowned by the bishops with a priestly blessing [Note: [Col. 1251] A lacks “by the bishops”]. From there he came to Florinkengas [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “Florikingas”] [Note: [Col. 1251D] Florenges, half an hour distant from Thionville], where he arranged what seemed necessary to him. From there he went into the Ardennes forest to occupy himself with the autumn hunt [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “the Ardennes, a place for hunting animals”].

Hludowicus, his brother, arranged to obtain peace with the Wends under a certain condition. To confirm it, he had sent his sons with the local margraves; he himself, being ill, remained in the city of Regensburg. He sent his envoys to Charles and informed him of the agreements made between them, and also concerning a portion of the kingdom formerly belonging to Lotharius. Charles therefore sent him an appropriate reply [Col. 1251C].

Meanwhile Basil, whom Michael, emperor of the Greeks, had admitted as his associate in the empire [Note: [Col. 1251] Ch. and B.: “as an associate”; A: “as a partner”], treacherously killed that same Michael and claimed the empire for himself. He had sent his patrician to Bari [Note: [Col. 1251] Read “Bari”; A: “his patrician Abbaras”] with four hundred ships [Note: [Col. 1251] A and the Chronicle of Saint-Denis: “with three hundred ships”], both to bring assistance to Hludowicus against the Saracens and to receive from Hludowicus his daughter, who had been betrothed to him, and take her to be joined to him in marriage [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “and to himself”; “to him in marriage” is absent in A.].

But when an occasion arose, Hludowicus was unwilling to give his daughter to the patrician [Note: [Col. 1251] Another reading: “it was disagreed with that Hludowicus should give his daughter to the patrician”]. Therefore the same patrician, displeased, returned to Corinth. As Hludowicus was returning from the siege of the Saracens in the region of Benevento, those same Saracens, coming out of Bari [Note: [Col. 1251] Read “Bari”; Ch.: “Barra”] and following the army of Hludowicus from behind, plundered more than two thousand of his army’s horses. Forming two wedges from among themselves with those same horses, they proceeded to the church of Saint Michael on Mount Gargano. There they plundered many of the clergy of that church, as well as many others who had gathered there for prayer, and returned to their own land with much booty [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “plunder”]. This deed greatly disturbed the emperor and the pope, as well as the Romans [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “This greatly disturbed the emperor and the pope, and also the Romans”].

Hludowicus, son of Hludowicus, king of Germany, waged war with the Saxons against the Wends who live in the regions of the Saxons. With much slaughter on both sides, he somehow gained the victory [Note: [Col. 1251D] Either something is missing here, or the account of Hludowicus’s expedition has been inserted after what had already been written.] and then returned [Aimoinus, A: “returned successfully”].

Rotlandus, archbishop of Arles, having obtained the abbey of Saint Caesarius [Note: [Col. 1252D] “Of Arles”] from Emperor Hludowicus and Engelberga, not empty-handed, built a hastily constructed fortress of bare earth on the island of Camaria, which was exceedingly rich in every respect [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “most renowned”], where many properties of the abbey lay and where the Saracens had formerly kept a harbor. When he heard of the Saracens’ arrival, he entered it rather imprudently. When the Saracens approached the fortress [Note: [Col. 1251] Ch.: “approached”; A: “drew up alongside”], after more than three hundred of his men had been killed, he was captured by those same Saracens and taken away and bound in their ship [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “ships”].

Accordingly, after one hundred fifty pounds of silver, one hundred fifty cloaks, one hundred fifty swords, and one hundred fifty slaves had been granted for his ransom, besides those things [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “those”] that were given in the settlement [Note: [Col. 1251] Ch. and B.: “were granted in the meantime”], the same bishop died aboard the ships on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October. The Saracens, cleverly hastening the matter of his ransom and claiming that they could not remain there longer if they wished to receive it, announced that his redeemers should hurry to pay the ransom for him [Col. 1252C]. And this was done.

After receiving the entire ransom, the Saracens placed the same bishop seated [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “sitting”] in a chair, dressed in the priestly garments in which he had been captured, and, as though in his honor, carried him from the ships onto the land. His redeemers, wishing to speak with him [Note: [Col. 1251] A: “to address him”] and congratulate him, found him dead. Carrying him away with the greatest mourning, they buried him [Note: [Col. 1251] A lacks this] on the tenth day before the Kalends of October in the tomb that he himself had prepared.

Solomon, duke of the Bretons, made peace with the Northmen residing on the Loire, and gathered the wine belonging to his portion of the territory of Anjou with his Bretons. Abbot Hugh and Gauzfrid, with the men from beyond the Seine, fought the Northmen residing on the Loire and killed approximately sixty of them [Col. 1252D]. They captured a certain apostate monk who, having abandoned Christianity, had gone over to the Northmen [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “to the Northmen”] and was exceedingly hostile to Christians, and had him beheaded [Note: [Col. 1253] The Royal Codex adds: “At that time, in a second incursion, the Northmen came to Paris, plundered the monastery of Saint Germanus, set fire to the brothers’ cellar, and returned with much booty acquired from every quarter.” The continuation of Aimoinus has the same account. BOUQUET.].

Charles asked the inhabitants to fortify the cities beyond the Seine—namely Le Mans and Tours—so that they might be able to serve the populations as protection against the Northmen. When the Northmen heard this, they demanded from the inhabitants of that territory a large quantity of silver, as well as grain, wine, and animals, in order to make peace with them.

While at the villa of Duciacus on the sixth day before the Ides of October, Charles learned for certain that his wife, Hirmentrudis, had died on the second day before the Nones of October in the monastery of Saint Denis, where she was also buried. While Boso, son of the late Count Buvinus, was carrying out this mission with his mother and maternal aunt Theutberga, widow of King Lotharius, he immediately had Boso’s sister, Richildis, brought to him and took her as a concubine. For this reason he gave Boso the abbey of Saint Maurice together with other honors. He himself hurried to Aachen, taking that concubine with him, so that there he might receive under his authority the remaining men of that region who had belonged to Lotharius, as they had instructed him. He announced that from there he would come to the palace called Gundulfi-villa at the Mass of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “for the feast”], in order to receive those coming to him from Provence and from the upper regions of Burgundy.

When he arrived at Aachen, he obtained no one whom he had not possessed before. Then, as he had announced, he reached Gundulfi-villa, where he received envoys of Pope Adrian, Paul and Leo, bishops, together with letters [Note: [Col. 1253D] Baronius, under the year 869, recites both letters of Pope Adrian, both that addressed to the leading men of Charles’s kingdom [Col. 1254D] and that addressed to the bishops established in his kingdom. BOUQUET.], which had been sent to him and to the bishops and leading men of the kingdom residing in these regions of Gaul [Col. 1253C].

They stated that no mortal should invade, disturb, or attempt to bend to himself the kingdom formerly belonging to King Lotharius, which by hereditary right was owed to Emperor Hludowicus, his spiritual son [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “was owed”], and which returned to him after Lotharius’s death, nor should anyone disturb the people living there. If anyone should presume to do so, he would not only be weakened through the ministry of the pope’s authority, but would also be bound by the chains of anathema, deprived of the name of Christian, and placed with the devil [Aimoinus adds: “entirely”].

And if any bishop should evade the author of such a wicked presumption by silence [Note: [Col. 1253] These words are expressed in the same way by Baronius.] or consent by failing to resist, he should know that he would be judged no longer a shepherd but a hireling; and since the sheep would no longer belong to him [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “that he would have no authority over anything concerning the sheep”], consequently neither would the pastoral dignities belong to him [Col. 1254A] [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “pastoral dignity would no longer belong to him”].

With these bishops came an envoy of Emperor Hludowicus, named Boderadus, likewise attending to these matters. After dismissing the pope’s and the emperor’s envoys, Charles, deceived by the empty persuasions of false envoys who told him that his brother Hludowicus was very near death [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “very close to death”], set out for the region of Alsace [Note: [Col. 1253] Ch.: “Elysian regions”] to secure Hugh, son of Liutfrid, and Bernard, son of Bernard [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “and Bernard, son of Bernard”; another reading repeats “Bernard”], as he indeed did. From there, returning to Aachen [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “returning”], he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there.

### 870

From there he went to meet the Northman Roricus at the palace of Nijmegen and joined him to himself by treaty. On the day of the feast of Septuagesima he took his aforesaid concubine Richildis, betrothed and endowed, as his wife [Col. 1254B]. Unexpectedly [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “contrary to hope”], he received envoys from his brother Hludowicus, king of Germany, announcing that, unless he left Aachen as quickly as possible [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “as soon as possible”] and did not entirely abandon the kingdom formerly belonging to Lotharius, and did not permit them to possess peacefully that same kingdom as Lotharius’s men had held it at the time of his death, he would attack him in war without any hesitation.

Accordingly, as envoys passed between them, the matter was brought to the point that the following oaths were made between them:

“Thus I promise on behalf of my lord, that man [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “Charles”] [Note: [Col. 1254D] “That man,” “his,” and similar expressions are used in place of the name of an unspecified person.] that my lord, that man [Note: [Col. 1253] Absent in A.], agrees that his brother, that man [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “Ludovicus”], the king, shall have such a portion of the kingdom of King Lotharius as either he himself, or their faithful men jointly, shall find to be more just and equitable [Note: [Col. 1253] Another reading: “more equal”] among themselves [Col. 1254C] [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “jointly”]. He will not deceive him in that portion, or in the kingdom he formerly held, through any fraud or covert maneuver, nor will he *forsconsiliate* [Note: [Col. 1253] Ch. and B.: *forsconciliabit*; the precise force of the rare term is uncertain.] him, provided that his brother, that man [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “Ludovicus”], observes inviolably toward my lord, for as long as he lives, the same firmness and fidelity that I have promised on behalf of my lord, that man [Note: [Col. 1253] A: “Charles”].”

After this firm agreement had been completed, Charles left Aachen and came by a single journey to Compiègne [Note: [Col. 1253] “Came as far as” is inserted from Aimoinus; it is absent from Ch. and B.], where he celebrated the Lord’s Pasch. From there, in the month of May, he came to the palace of Attigny, where he received twelve envoys from his brother Hludowicus concerning the division of the kingdom. They, elated beyond what was proper both by Hludowicus’s bodily health and by his prosperity—because he had captured and defeated, by both guile and warfare, Restitius the Wend, who had been hostile to him for a long time [Col. 1254D–1255A]—considered the oaths made between them less binding than they ought [Note: [Col. 1255] Another reading: “elevated”].

This division, debated in many ways and by numerous means on both sides, and communicated back and forth through various envoys, reached the following conclusion at Charles’s command: they should come together peacefully concerning the kingdom that was to be divided between them according to the oaths that had been given, and, as they should determine with the consent and unanimity of their common faithful men, they should divide that kingdom according to the oaths made between them.

Meanwhile, after Hincmar, bishop of Laon, had been accused on many charges [Note: [Col. 1255] Absent in A.], especially concerning subjection to royal power [Note: [Col. 1255] A: “insubjection”] and disobedience toward his archbishop, he presented at a synod of bishops from ten provinces a document bearing his own signature in order to clear himself of the accusations [Note: [Col. 1255D] This synod was held at Attigny. There Hincmar of Reims gave Hincmar of Laon the *Book of Fifty-Five Chapters*, by which he refuted at length and lucidly the collection sent to him through Wenilo, archbishop of Rouen. At that synod the king complained of rebellion; Hincmar of Reims, of contumacy; Count Nortmannus, of open violence; and the clerics of Laon, of unjust excommunication against Hincmar of Laon. By making a new profession of fidelity to the king and his metropolitan, the bishop of Laon somewhat quieted the storm that had arisen against him. But before the synod’s decision, he escaped by flight and sent a short petition requesting permission to go to Rome. Hincmar of Reims relates what he did afterward in letter 35 among those published. After the Attigny synod was broken off, Hincmar of Laon found Pope Hadrian favorable to him; the pope wrote serious and harsh letters to Charles the Bald and to Hincmar of Reims.
