Charles replied to the pontiff’s letters in a still harsher style; Hincmar of Reims composed the reply at the king’s command. BOUQUET.] It contained the following:

“ I, Hincmar, bishop of the church of Laon, from now and henceforth shall be faithful and obedient to my lord, King Charles [Aimoinus adds: “thus”], according to my ministry, as a man ought to be to his lord, and as every bishop ought to be to his king [Note: [Col. 1255] The Royal Codex reads: “a bishop, in direct relation to his king”; the continuation of Aimoinus: “a bishop, in direct relation to his king”]. In accordance with the privilege of Hincmar, metropolitan of the province of the church of Reims, and according to the sacred canons and the decrees promulgated by the Apostolic See [Aimoinus, A: “from the sacred canons”], I profess that I wish to obey to the best of my knowledge and ability [Note: [Col. 1255] Another reading: “that I will obey”].”

Carolomannus also, son of King Charles and reputed father of numerous monasteries, because he was treacherously plotting an ambush against his father, was deprived of his abbeys and confined in the city of Senlis [Col. 1255C].

[Col. 1256A] Charles [the same adds “the king”], sending his envoys—namely Odo, bishop of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 1255] “of the Belgians” in Ch.], and Odo and Harduin, counts—to his brother Louis at Frankfurt, requested that they meet together to divide the kingdom of Lothair. He himself, proceeding to Pontigon, received there [Note: [Col. 1255] “thereupon he received those envoys” in A.] the envoys of his brother, who announced to him that he should go to Heristal, while his brother Louis would come to Marsna, and that on the Kalends of August they should confer midway between those places; each of them was to bring to that conference only four bishops and ten counsellors, together with thirty ministerials and vassals.

While Louis was proceeding there, he came to Flamereshem in the Ribuarian district and fell, together with some of his men, through a wooden structure in a dilapidated upper chamber, beneath broken timbers [Note: [Col. 1255] I have inserted “through broken timbers, together with some of his men” from A.; these words are absent from Ch. and B.]. Having been somewhat injured [Note: [Col. 1255] “having been endangered” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1255D] That is, wounded.], he recovered shortly afterward; and from there he reached Aachen.

As envoys passed back and forth between the two brothers and kings, at last they came together at the place of conference on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 1255] Correct to “the sixth day before the Ides of August,” as it is read in the capitularies, letter 43, where this entire division is recited. BOUQ.], and in this manner divided the kingdom of Lothair between them. This is the division which Louis took for himself:

Cologne [Note: [Col. 1255D] That is, the dioceses of Cologne, Trier, and so forth.], Trier, Utrecht, Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 1255] “Stratburg” in Ch.; “Strasburg, Basel” in A.], Basel; the abbeys of Susteren [Note: [Col. 1255] “Sivestre” in Ch.] [Note: [Col. 1255D] Mabillon designates these monasteries in *Benedictine Annals*, vol. III, appendix, p. 678. Susteren, commonly Susteren, on the Meuse; Berch near Roermond.], Berch, Neumünster [Note: [Col. 1256C] Perhaps Nuss on the Rhine above Cologne.], Kessel [Note: [Col. 1256C] Kessel on the Meuse.], Inda [Note: [Col. 1256C] Cornelimünster near Aachen.], Saint Maximin [Note: [Col. 1256C] Near Trier.], Echternach [Note: [Col. 1256C] Echternach in the duchy of Luxembourg.], Horrea [Note: [Col. 1256C] Formerly outside, now within, the walls of Trier.], Saint Gangulf [Note: [Col. 1256C] Unknown to Mabillon; Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, p. 738, identifies it with the abbey of Saint-Gengoul in the town of Varenne, diocese of Langres; I have doubts about this.], Faverney [Note: [Col. 1256C] Faverney in the county of Burgundy.], Poligny [Note: [Col. 1256C] Poligny in the same region.], Luxeuil [Note: [Col. 1256D] Luxeuil in the same region.], Lure [Note: [Col. 1255] “Litera” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1256D] Lure in the diocese of Besançon.], Baume [Note: [Col. 1256D] Baume in the same district.], the village of Offon [Note: [Col. 1256D] Vellefaux in the same region, or Offonville in the diocese of Toul (Calmet, p. 738).], the monastery of Moyen [Note: [Col. 1256D] Moyenmoutier in the Vosges.], Saint Dié [Note: [Col. 1256D] Near the preceding.], the monastery of Bodo [Note: [Col. 1256D] Bonmoutier formerly in the Vosges, near Saint-Sauveur.], Étival [Note: [Col. 1256D] Estival, in the same region.], Remiremont [Note: [Col. 1256D] The mountain of Romeric.], Murbach [Note: [Col. 1256D] In Alsace; on these places see Schoepflin’s *Alsatia illustrata*.], Saint Gregory, the monastery of Saint Maur [Note: [Col. 1256D] In Alsace; on these places see Schoepflin’s *Alsatia illustrata*.], Ebersheim [Note: [Col. 1256D] In Alsace; on these places see Schoepflin’s *Alsatia illustrata*.] [Note: [Col. 1255] “Eboreshem” in Ch.]; Hoinowa [Note: [Col. 1257] “Homowa” in Ch. and B., “Hoinowa” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1257B] Formerly on an island of the Rhine below Strasbourg.], the monastery of Mason [Note: [Col. 1257B] Maesmünster.], Hohenburg [Note: [Col. 1257] “Hombroch” in Ch. and Bq.] [Note: [Col. 1257B] Odilienberg.], Saint Stephen [Note: [Col. 1257] “Saint Stapni” in Ch. and B.; “Saint Stamphim” in A.] at Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 1257B] Strasbourg.], Erenstein [Note: [Col. 1257] “Erenstem” in Ch.; “Erostein” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1257B] In Alsace.], Saint Ursus at Solothurn [Note: [Col. 1257B] Solothurn.], Grandval [Note: [Col. 1257B] Granfelt, in the diocese of Basel.], Altenberg [Note: [Col. 1257B] In the Vosges, near Moyenmoutier.], Lustenau [Note: [Col. 1257] Sirmond has “Justina,” Baluze “Justena,” A. “Justiniani.”] [Note: [Col. 1257B] Unknown to Mabillon and Bouquet; it does not seem that Justina or Gusten near Jülich is intended. The estate of Lustenau lies on the right bank of the Rhine, in the territory of Hohenems.], the valley of Cluse [Note: [Col. 1257B] Vaucluse, in the diocese of Besançon.], the castle of Charnon [Note: [Col. 1257B] Châtel-Chalon in Burgundy.] [Note: [Col. 1257] “Carnones” in Ch.; “the valley of Cluse, the castle of Carnones” in A.], Heribodesheim [Note: [Col. 1257B] Unknown to Mabillon and Bouquet; perhaps Herbitzheim in the western part of the Vosges, formerly in the county of Saarwerden.] [Note: [Col. 1257] “Heribodeshem” in Ch.], the abbey at Aachen [Note: [Col. 1257B] The royal basilica at Aachen.], Hohen­kirche [Note: [Col. 1257C] Unknown.], Augstkirche [Note: [Col. 1257C] Unknown]; the counties of Testrabant [Note: [Col. 1257] “Testebrant” in A.; “Commentestabant” in Ch. and B.], Batua [Note: [Col. 1257] “Baviam, Harmarias” in A.], Hattuaria [Note: [Col. 1257C] Along the Niers between the Meuse and Rhine, including Gelderland.], the lower Maasgau [Note: [Col. 1257] “Masiau” in Ch.; “the Meuse … the Meuse” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1257C] That is, Maasgau.], and likewise the upper Maasgau, which lies on the other side; Liège, which lies on this side; the Aachen district; the district of Maastricht [Note: [Col. 1257C] Maastricht.]; five counties in Ribuaria [Note: [Col. 1257C] Namely the districts of Jülich, Cologne, Zülpich, Bonn or Ahrgau, and Eifelgau. Compare Kremer’s special dissertation on this subject in the *Commentaries of the Electoral Palatine Academy*, vol. IV, historical section, p. 178 ff.], the Mejen district [Note: [Col. 1257C] Mejengau, including Andernach.], Bedagau [Note: [Col. 1257C] Along the Moselle, including Bitburg and Echternach.], Nitachau [Note: [Col. 1257C] Along the Nitt, which flows into the Saar below Saarlouis.], the lower Sarachau [Note: [Col. 1257C] Along the Saar. Compare Schoepflin’s *Alsatia illustrata*, vol. I, p. 672.], Bliestgau [Note: [Col. 1257C] Along the river Blies, where Blieskastel lies.], Selme [Note: [Col. 1257C] Valesius identifies this with the county of Salm; Schoepflin, *Alsatia illustrata*, vol. I, pp. 671–672, places it along the Saar near Selming, close to Finstingen. [Col. 1257D] It is nevertheless the Saulnois along the river Seille, which flows into the Moselle near Metz.], Albegau [Note: [Col. 1257D] Valesius places it on the river Alba, which flows into the Saar near Sarreguemines; Schoepflin, on the contrary, places it along the river Vezouze, since the monastery of Bodo was situated there. *Alsatia illustrata* I, p. 671.], Swentisgau [Note: [Col. 1258B] See above, under the year 839, p. 435.], Calmont [Note: [Col. 1258B] See above, under the year 839, p. 435.], the upper Sarachau [Note: [Col. 1258B] Along the Saar. Compare Schoepflin’s *Alsatia illustrata*, vol. I, p. 672.], Odorn [Note: [Col. 1258B] In Austrasia, along the river Orn, which flows into the Moselle between Thionville and Metz. Valesius, *Notitia*, pp. 389–390.], which Bernard held, the Soulossois [Note: [Col. 1258B] Le Soulossois, north of the Portois district, extending from the sources of the Meuse and the Mouzon.], Bassigny [Note: [Col. 1258B] Le Bassigny at the sources of the Marne, including Chaumont; it is part of the district of Langres. Compare Valesius, *Notitia*, p. 76.], Elischgau [Note: [Col. 1257] “Esischowe” in Ch.; “Eliscowe” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1258B] Valesius, pp. 13–14, places it along the Eltz, which flows into the Moselle above Trier; I regard it instead as Alsace’s Albegau, south of the Alsatian Sundgau. Schoepflin, cited work, p. 336.], Warasch [Note: [Col. 1257] “Warachstudingum” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1258B] Around Salins.], Scudingum [Note: [Col. 1258B] Along both banks of the Doubs, near Besançon.], Emaus [Note: [Col. 1258B] Valesius, *Notitia of Gaul*, p. 481, thinks this should be corrected to Amans; the district of Amans is mentioned by the monk Hericus in his book *On the Miracles of Saint Germanus*, from whose words it is clear that it was not far from the rivers Saône, Ouche, Vingeanne, and Tille.], Baslechgau [Note: [Col. 1257] “Basalclowa” in Ch.] [Note: [Col. 1258C] The Basel district. Schoepflin, cited work, p. 640.], in Alsace two counties [Note: [Col. 1258C] Namely Nordgau and Sundgau.], and of Frisia [Col. 1258A] two parts [Note: [Col. 1258C] It is understood from the laws of the Frisians that Frisia consisted of three parts: between the Weser and the Lauwers, between the Lauwers and the Fli, and between the Fli and Sinkfal. The last therefore was left to Charles.], of the kingdom which Lothair held.

For the preservation of peace and charity, we add this supplementary provision to this division: the city of Metz, with the abbeys of Saint Peter and Saint Martin and the county of Moselle [Note: [Col. 1258C] Along both banks of the Moselle, from Metz to Trier.], with all the villages situated within it, both royal estates and those of vassals; in the Ardennes, from where the river Ourte [Note: [Col. 1257] “Urca … twice Bislave” in A.] rises between Bislanc [Note: [Col. 1258C] Calmet interprets this as Bastogne; it nevertheless appears to be different. In 770, a charter of Carloman mentions the centena of Belslango within the wilderness of the Ardennes.] and Tumbas and flows down into the Meuse, and along the straight road [Note: [Col. 1258C] Namely from the source of the Ourte. Miraeus reports that the Heer- or Heiden-Strasse—that is, the military or pagan road—still exists there.] extending into the Bedan district, according to what our joint envoys may more accurately determine—except that the portion of Condroz [Note: [Col. 1258C] Between the Meuse and the Ourte, around Huy.] lies eastward, across the Ourte—and the abbeys of Prüm and Stavelot, together with all the royal estates and those of vassals.

This is the division which Charles took for himself from the same kingdom: Lyon, Besançon, Vienne, Tongeren, [Col. 1258B] Toul, Verdun, Cambrai, Viviers [Note: [Col. 1258D] Viviers. Valesius, pp. 244–245.], Uzès [Note: [Col. 1257] “Uceria” in Ch.; “Uzotias” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1258D] Uzès.], Montfaucon [Note: [Col. 1258D] The abbey of Montfaucon, four leagues from the Meuse and from the city of Verdun. Valesius, *Notitia*, p. 348.], Saint Michael [Note: [Col. 1258D] Saint-Mihiel in the Verdun region, on the Meuse.], [Col. 1259A] the monastery of Gillin [Note: [Col. 1259] “Suldum” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1259C] Perhaps the monastery of Saint Ghislain in Hainaut? In the capitularies it is the monastery of Culdini, Colmoustier.], Saint Mary at Besançon, Saint Martin in the same place, Saint Oyend [Note: [Col. 1259C] Commonly Eugendus, now Saint-Claude in the Jura department.], Saint Marcel [Note: [Col. 1259C] Near Chalon.], Saint Lawrence of Liège [Note: [Col. 1259] “Lendensis” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1259C] The monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège?], Senones [Note: [Col. 1259C] Senones in the Vosges according to Mabillon, but it seems rather to be sought in Belgium.], the abbey of Nivelles [Note: [Col. 1259C] Nivelles.], Maubeuge [Note: [Col. 1259] “Molbarium” in Baluze; “Melbarium” in Sirmond.] [Note: [Col. 1259C] Maubeuge.], Lobbes [Note: [Col. 1259C] Lobbes on the Sambre.], Saint Gaugericus [Note: [Col. 1259C] Near Cambrai.], Saint Salvius [Note: [Col. 1259C] Near Valenciennes, on the Scheldt.], Crespin [Note: [Col. 1259C] Near Valenciennes, on the Scheldt.], Fosses [Note: [Col. 1259C] In Hainaut.], Maroilles [Note: [Col. 1259C] Maroilles in the Cambrai district.], Honcourt [Note: [Col. 1259] “Hunulfcurt” in Ch.] [Note: [Col. 1259C] Honcourt near Cambrai.], Saint Servatius [Note: [Col. 1259C] The church at Maastricht on the Meuse.], Mechelen [Note: [Col. 1259C] Mechelen.], Lier [Note: [Col. 1259C] Lier in Brabant.], Soigny [Note: [Col. 1259C] Soigny.], Antoing [Note: [Col. 1259D] Antoing on the Scheldt near Tournai.], Condé [Note: [Col. 1259D] Condé.], Merbech [Note: [Col. 1259] “Merrelecchi” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1259D] Merbech, not far from Ninove, a town of Flanders.], Dickelvenne [Note: [Col. 1259] “Ticlivinni” in Baluze; “Ticlivium” in A.; “Tichvinni” in Mabillon.] [Note: [Col. 1259D] Dickelvenne, near Gerard’s Mount in Hainaut.], Leuse [Note: [Col. 1259D] Leuze in Hainaut.], Calmont [Note: [Col. 1259D] Calmont in the diocese of Liège. Compare *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, p. 935.], Saint Mary at Dinant [Note: [Col. 1259D] Dinant.], Eich [Note: [Col. 1259D] Eich on the Meuse near Maaseik, opposite Susteren.], Andenne [Note: [Col. 1259D] Andenne on the Meuse.], Wasloi [Note: [Col. 1259D] Wasler in the Faigne forest near Maubeuge.], Haumont [Note: [Col. 1259D] Haumont in Hainaut.]; the county of Toxandria [Note: [Col. 1259D] Between the mouths of the Scheldt and Meuse and the Demer, including, for example, Bergen op Zoom and ’s-Hertogenbosch.]; in Brabant, four counties [Note: [Col. 1260C] Ghent, perhaps Tournai, and two others unknown to me, among which may perhaps be Mansuaria.], Cambrai [Note: [Col. 1259] “Camatensis” in Ch.] [Note: [Col. 1260C] Le Cambrésis.], Hainaut [Note: [Col. 1260C] Hennegau.], and the county of Lomme [Note: [Col. 1260C] At the confluence of the Sambre and Meuse.]; in Hasbania, four counties [Note: [Col. 1260C] They are Haspengau, the county of Loon, and two unknown ones, one of which may perhaps be the county of Tongeren.]; the upper Maasgau on this side of the Meuse, the lower Maasgau on this side [Note: [Col. 1259] “On that side” in Ch. and B.], Liège, which is on this side of the Meuse and belongs to Visé [Note: [Col. 1260C] Visé between Maastricht and Liège.], the Scarponnais [Note: [Col. 1260C] Along the Chiers; it takes its name from the castle of Scarponna, now Sanponne or Charpeigne, between Metz and Toul.], the Verdun district [Note: [Col. 1260C] Around Verdun.], the Dormois [Note: [Col. 1260C] Le Dormois in the diocese of Rheims, “where lies the famous village of Sindunum on the Aisne, called Senuc.”], Arlon [Note: [Col. 1260C] West of the city of Luxembourg.], two counties of Wavre [Note: [Col. 1260C] Along the banks of the Alzette, Ornain, and Chiers rivers (the Eltz, Orne, and Chiers).], Mosom [Note: [Col. 1260D] Around Mouzon, on the Meuse.], Castricius [Note: [Col. 1260D] Along the Meuse and Bar rivers, including Donchery.], Condroz; in the Ardennes, from where the river Ourte rises between Bislanc and Tumbas and flows from this side into the Meuse, and along the straight road on this western side extending into the Bedan district, according to what our envoys may more accurately determine; Toul; another Odorn [Note: [Col. 1260D] Along the Orn, which flows into the Marne.], which Tetmar held [Note: [Col. 1259] “Tremarus” in Bq.] [Note: [Col. 1260D] Including Bar at the Alba.]; Bar, Portois [Note: [Col. 1260D] Le Portois.], Salmoring [Note: [Col. 1260D] Unknown to Valesius and Bouquet. Calmet places it along the Seille; but since the county of Seline or Selme was given to Louis, this may perhaps refer to the land at the sources of the Saulx, which flows into the Marne together with the Orn. I have no better suggestion at present.], Lyon, Vienne, Viviers, the district of Uzès [Note: [Col. 1260D] That is, the district of Uzès.], and one-third of Frisia.

On the following day, namely the fourth day before the Ides of the same month, [Col. 1260A] they met together; and, taking leave of one another, they departed from each other: Louis returned to Aachen, while Charles ordered his wife to come to meet him at Lestines. He divided the portion of that kingdom which he had received as he saw fit, and from there, passing through the monastery of Saint Quentin to Silvacum, and from there through Carisiacum to Compiègne, he engaged in the autumn hunt in the forest of Cotia.

Louis, having endured insufficient medical treatment for the injury caused by the blow which he had suffered in the aforesaid fall from the upper chamber, had the rotting flesh cut away by the same physicians [Note: [Col. 1259] “The rotting flesh” is absent from A.]. Consequently, he remained bedridden at Aachen for a longer time than he had expected; there, having nearly been given up for dead, he barely escaped death.

There he received the envoys of the apostolic lord Adrian, John and Peter, cardinal bishops [Note: [Col. 1259] Ch. has “cardinal bishops”; A. has “John and Peter, and likewise John the bishops, and Peter, cardinal priest of the Roman Church.”] [Col. 1260B], and likewise John, a priest of the Roman Church, as well as the envoys of the emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 1260D] Wibod was not an envoy of the emperor Louis but of Pope Adrian, as is established by letters of that same pope to King Charles, to the bishops of his kingdom, and to Louis, king of Germany, dated on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction. BOUQ.], namely Bishop Wibod [Note: [Col. 1259] “Winebod” in A.] and Count Bernard. They declared to him that he should not presume [Aimon. “should not interfere”] in the kingdom of his nephew Lothair, which was owed to his brother, the emperor Louis.

He soon sent them, having been dismissed, to his brother Charles. As soon as he had recovered somewhat, he himself set out for Regensburg and ordered Restitius, the prince of the Wends, who had been captured by Carloman through the treachery of his nephew Restitius and had been held in custody for some time, to be blinded and sent to a monastery after a sentence of death [Note: [Col. 1261] “After a sentence of death” is absent from A.]. He also ordered his sons Louis and Charles to come to him.

When they learned, through the efforts of their mother, that their father’s will was more favorably disposed toward Carloman than toward themselves, they refused to come to him. Louis came before the beginning of Lent to the assembly which he had arranged at Frankfurt. Through the efforts of the envoys, guarantees were made on both sides between him and his sons: until the coming month of May, they were to be able to remain secure on their father’s side, while the sons were to abandon the devastation of the kingdom which they had begun and live peacefully until that same assembly. When this business had thus been completed, Louis returned to Regensburg.

Charles, after completing the autumn hunt, went to the monastery [Col. 1261B] of Saint Denis to celebrate the feast of that saint. On that very day, during the solemn celebration of Mass, he received with displeasure the aforesaid envoys of the apostolic lord, who had been sent to him and to the bishops of his kingdom with letters sternly forbidding him the kingdom formerly belonging to Lothair, which was owed to his brother the emperor.

When those same envoys, together with some of his faithful men, pleaded with him, he released his son Carloman from custody in the city of Senlis and ordered him to remain with him. He had the envoys of the apostolic lord and of the emperor escorted as far as Rheims. Then, summoning a great many of his faithful men from every side and remaining there for eight days, he released those envoys.

Afterward he sent his envoys, Ansegisil [Note: [Col. 1261D] He is none other than Ansegis, the abbot who in the following year was appointed in place of Egil or Egilo, archbishop of Sens, whose death occurred in this year, 871. There is considerable dispute about which monastery of Saint Michael Ansegis was abbot of, as Mabillon notes in book XXXVII, no. 11, of the *Benedictine Annals*. Some think it was the church of Saint Michael near Beauvais, which later became collegiate after having been a monastery. Others object that no monument of that church is found before the twelfth century. Hence Hincmar, in Frodoard, book III, chapter 23, calls Ansegis a monk of the diocese—that is, province—of Rheims. In the decree of the clergy and people of Sens to the provincial bishops, Ansegis is called a priest of the diocese of Rheims, but of the church of Beauvais, and abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael. BOUQ.], namely the priest and abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael, and Lothair [Note: [Col. 1261] “Etharius” in A.; “Lietharz” in the Chronicle of Saint Denis.] [Col. 1261C], a layman [Note: [Col. 1261] “A Roman layman” in A.], with letters to the apostolic lord. He also sent an altar cloth made from his golden vestments, with two golden crowns adorned with gems, to the altar of Saint Peter. He himself proceeded as far as Lyon.

From there Carloman [Note: [Col. 1261] “Charles” in Ch.] fled from his father by night and came into the Belgian province. Gathering many henchmen and sons of Belial around him, he inflicted such cruelty and devastation, following the work of Satan, that it cannot be believed except by those who saw and endured that same ravaging.

Charles took this extremely badly; nevertheless, he did not abandon his expedition but hastened to Vienne to besiege it, where Berta, the wife of Gerard, was staying. Gerard himself was residing in another castle. During that siege the surrounding regions were devastated very severely.

Charles, however, acting with ingenuity [Note: [Col. 1261] A adds: “ingeniously sowing discord among those who were in Vienne guarding it”], won over to himself a large part of those who were in Vienne. When Berta realized this, she sent for Gerard. When he came, he surrendered the city to Charles [Note: [Col. 1261] “Restored it” in A.]. The same king entered it on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there.

## 871

After Charles had taken Vienne under his control, he compelled Gerard to give hostages in exchange for the surrender of his other castles. Having given Gerard three ships, he allowed him to depart from Vienne by the Rhône with his wife Berta and his movable possessions, and entrusted Vienne itself to Boson, his wife’s brother. He himself hastened as quickly as he could through Auxerre and Sens to the monastery of Saint Denis.

When Carloman heard this, he went with his accomplices [Col. 1262B] to Mouzon and devastated the castle itself and the surrounding villages. From there he deceitfully sent four envoys to his father, saying that he should come to him without ceremony, trusting in his loyalty, and that he wished to make satisfaction to God and to him for the offenses he had committed, provided only that he would treat mercifully those who were with him, so that they might remain safe. Nevertheless, he did not abandon, even in the slightest, the evil undertaking which he had begun.

King Charles sent to that same son of his, Carloman, Abbot Gauzlin [Note: [Col. 1261] “Gauzlium, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Germain” in A.] and Count Baldwin, Carloman’s brother-in-law, together with two of Carloman’s envoys—for he retained the other two with himself. He sent word of the arrangement by which Carloman could come safely to him, if he wished.

Carloman, however, pretending deceitfully that he would come to his father, sent the other envoys to him, demanding impossible things [Col. 1262C], and himself went into the region of Toul.

Charles, seeking judgment against such men, who had stolen from him his son—namely, a deacon and minister of Holy Church, entrusted to him by the Lord—and who had committed such and so many crimes, offenses, and devastations in his kingdom, after a sentence of death [Note: [Col. 1261] Absent from A.] ordered all their possessions to be confiscated. He organized military companies to drive that same Carloman and his accomplices from the kingdom, and sought episcopal judgment against them.

Since the Apostle commands that one should not even eat with such people, the bishops in whose parishes they had committed such evils deprived them of communion according to the sacred canons [Note: [Col. 1262D] Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, excommunicated them and sent the formula of the censure for signature to the archbishops of the other provinces and to his nephew Hincmar, bishop of Laon. Hincmar, after being admonished three or four times, refused to sign, whether from hatred of the king and archbishop, from solidarity in a similar cause, or from a desire to gain ever greater favor with Adrian the pope. For Carloman, following the example—and perhaps the advice—of Hincmar of Laon, tried to escape excommunication by sending envoys to Rome and appealing to the judgment of the pontiff. Adrian, aroused by the appeal, deceived by the embassy of the impious prince, and also hostile to Charles because he had occupied the kingdom of Austrasia, eagerly undertook Carloman’s defense and severely rebuked his father for the vengeance he had planned against his son in a letter sent to him on the third day before the Ides of July, in the fourth indiction—that is, in the year 871. He also wrote to the bishops in letters marked with the same superscription and forbade them to hurl excommunication against Carloman. On the same day he wrote to the nobles of the kingdom, ordering them not to advance to arms against the son when summoned by the father. BOUQ.]—as is contained in the letters which they accordingly sent to the other bishops in accordance with the sacred regulations [Col. 1263A].

As for Carloman, since he was a deacon of the diocese of Sens [Note: [Col. 1263] “Sennensis” in Ch.], and since he had twice taken oaths concerning which he had proved perjured [Note: [Col. 1263] “Concerning which” is absent from A.], his father took care to make known by public proclamation to all who were present that he had committed such a great rebellion and disloyalty against him, together with such crimes in his kingdom; and he decreed that the judgment of the bishops of that province should be sought against him.

Then Charles returned to the monastery of Saint Denis, as the season of Lent approached, intending to remain there until Holy Easter [Note: [Col. 1263] In the continuation of Aimoin, the entire year is omitted here, so that the narrative resumes only with the words of the year 872 and “on the Saturday before Palm Sunday.”], where he celebrated the Lord’s Easter.

Carloman, while a military force sent by his father pursued him, crossed the Jura [Note: [Col. 1263] “Juram” in Bq.; “Jurum” in Ch. several times; I fear that Bouquet removed this reading, which is also accepted by Regino, solely on his own authority.], and, as he had done in the Belgian and Gallic regions, did not cease carrying out the evil deeds he had begun. [Note: [Col. 1263] “Did not send forth” in Ch.]

Hincmar of Laon, a bishop in name only, a man of singular insolence, rebelling against the king and acting against evangelical truth and apostolic and ecclesiastical authority, raging without any reverence against his neighbors and those entrusted to him, both clerics and laymen, and scorning obedience to his metropolitan when he regularly admonished him concerning these matters, so stirred up the king, his archbishop, and all the bishops of the kingdom against himself that the king summoned a synod for the month of August at Douzy, so that a canonical judgment might there be undertaken concerning his wickedness.

King Charles himself, at the request of his nephews, Louis and Charles, the sons of his brother Louis, went through Verdun to meet them and speak with them. From there he returned to the synod at Douzy [Col. 1263C] [Note: [Col. 1264D] Douzy, or Dusiacum, was a villa situated in the district of Mouzon on the river Chiers. It is mentioned by Flodoard in his *Chronicle* and in his *History of Rheims*, and is now called Douzy-le-Pré. The Council of Douzy was held in this villa in the year 871; its acts were published by Labbe, vol. VIII of the *Councils*, p. 1547. BOUQ.].

Meanwhile Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, and Gozfrid, together with the other men from across the Seine, imprudently approached the island of the Loire, where the Northmen had their stronghold. With great loss and the death of many, they barely escaped.

Hincmar, however, eventually came to the synod with great arrogance. There, after a petition had been presented by King Charles according to ecclesiastical regulations, and after Hincmar had been canonically accused and convicted on the clearest charges, he received the canonical judgment of deposition, as is contained in the acts of that synod, which the same synod sent to the apostolic see through the venerable Bishop Actard [Note: [Col. 1264D] Of Nantes, and now also of Tours. Compare Adrian II’s letters for this year.].

[Col. 1264A] The king’s aforesaid nephews also came to him at Douzy, asking him to reconcile them with their father. Envoys of his brother Louis likewise came to him, requesting that he come to meet him near the town of Maastricht for a conference, as he did. He brought with him the envoys of his nephews, who reported to their father, in their name, what they had requested.

There also King Charles received the envoys of his son Carloman, with his brother Louis intervening, and, as before, invited Carloman to return to him on condition that he correct himself. This invitation accomplished nothing.

Louis and Charles remained for some time in that conference but accomplished little or nothing. Thus, at the beginning of September, they separated from one another, and each took care to return to his own affairs. Louis [Col. 1264B], namely, proceeded to Regensburg [Note: [Col. 1263] “Rainisburg” in Ch.], because he had suffered enormous loss from the nephew of Restitius, who had assumed the leadership of the Wends after him; indeed, he had lost margraves together with a very large number of his men, and disastrously lost the land which he had possessed in previous years.

Charles, however, returned through Lestines toward the villa of Audriaca for the sake of hunting. On this journey he received many envoys from Italy, who invited him to go to Italy, since his nephew Louis had been killed by the people of Benevento in the city of Benevento, together with his wife and daughter. Proceeding through the city of Rheims [Note: [Col. 1263] “Rheitium” in Ch.], he reached the city of Besançon.

When Carloman learned that his father was pursuing him, at the urging of his men he came to him with feigned humility. His father received him and ordered him to remain with him until he reached his faithful men in Belgium and, on their advice, determined how he ought to honor him.

Louis, king of Germany, also, when he heard that his aforementioned nephew, the emperor Louis, had died, sent his son Charles into the territory which he held beyond the Jura, so that he might bind as many men as he could by oath to loyalty to him; and he did so.

While Charles was staying at Besançon, his envoys whom he had sent ahead to Italy announced to him that the emperor Louis himself was alive and physically well. Adalgisus, together with other men of Benevento, had conspired against the emperor because that same emperor was planning, through the influence of his wife, to send him into perpetual exile.

When Adalgisus had planned to attack the emperor himself by night, the latter, with his wife and those whom he had with him, climbed a very high and strongly fortified tower, where he defended himself with his men for three days. At last the bishop of that city obtained from the Beneventans that, after receiving oaths from the emperor, they would allow him to depart alive and unharmed.

The emperor, his wife, his daughter, and all his men who were with him swore that never, nowhere, and on no occasion would he seek vengeance—either personally or through anyone else—for what had been done against him in this affair, and that he would never enter Beneventan territory with an army.

Having thus departed, he set out through Spoleto toward Ravenna, sending word to the apostolic lord [Col. 1265B] Adrian that he should come to meet him along the route of his journey, so that he might absolve him and his men from that oath.

Meanwhile Lambert and another Lambert, believing that the emperor held them responsible for what had been done against him, withdrew from him and went into the territory of Benevento, because the aforementioned Adalgisus was associated with them. The emperor pursued them; he sent his wife to Ravenna, where he intended to hold his assembly, and ordered the leading men of the Italian kingdom to come to her, so that they might deliberate concerning the orders he had given until he himself returned from that expedition.

But since the emperor could not overtake the Lamberts whom he was pursuing, he made haste to return to the place where he had intended to go.

Charles, hearing of the circumstance in which it had been thought that the emperor Louis had been killed, and learning that he was alive, set out from Besançon by a direct route through Pontigon and then through Attigny to Silvacum. There he held an assembly with his counsellors, and on their advice he once again committed Carloman to custody at Senlis. He ordered Carloman’s accomplices to be bound by oaths of loyalty to him, each in his own county.

Thus, allowing those who wished to receive whatever lordship they chose from among his faithful men and who wished to live in peace to remain in his kingdom, he proceeded from Silvacum to Compiègne, where he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in the year of the Lord 872.

## 872
Finally, setting out from Compendium, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February he began his journey to the Monastery [Note: Mabillon understands this as the Monastery of Saint Lambert at Liège, Book XXXVII of the Benedictine Annals, no. 32. BOUQ.], intending to speak with Rorico and Rodulfus the Northmen, and planning to return to Compendium at the beginning of Lent. On the Saturday before Palm Sunday [Note: “Saturday”; Ch.] he came to the monastery of Saint-Denis [Col. 1266A] and celebrated the Lord’s Pascha there. After Pascha, he went to meet the empress Ingelberga, as he had ordered her through his envoys [Note: “and”; Ch. B.], proceeding to Saint Maurice. But, having learned from a reliable messenger [Note: “not”; Ch. omits it, but A. has it certainly.] that the same Ingelberga was going to confer with Hludowic, king of Germany, at Trent in the month of May [Note: A. omits “in”; likewise below before Silvacum, Reginisburg, and elsewhere], he turned aside from the agreed route and came to Silvacum.

There Adalardus, coming on behalf of his brother Hludowic, asked him to come near Utrecht to speak with that same brother Hludowic, since Hludowic, after sending out the army with his son Carolomannus against the Wends, was returning to Regensburg and Aachen. Charles, however, appointed for his son Hludowic Boso, his wife’s brother, chamberlain and master of the doorkeepers, and gave him the honors of Gerard, count of Bourges [Note: This Gerard seems to be none other than Gerard, duke of Provence. BOUQ. Compare above, year 871; but we have no witness that Gerard, after losing the duchy of Provence, obtained the county of Bourges.]. He sent him into Aquitaine with Bernard [Note: This Bernard, son of Bernard, duke of Septimania, was count of Auvergne; he was also margrave of Gothia in the year 879. BOUQ.], and likewise with another Bernard, the margrave, entrusting him with the administration of that kingdom.

To Bernard, count of Toulouse, after he had sworn the required oaths, he granted Carcassonne and Razès [Note: Le Razès, between Carcassonne and Narbonne. Vales., p. 467.] and sent him back to Toulouse.

The aforementioned Hludowic, king of Germany, summoned his sons Hludowic and Charles to him in order to reconcile them with Carolomannus, and deceitfully caused them to be threatened [Note: “to swear”; Ch. B.]. His sons and their men likewise deceitfully offered oaths to Hludowic. Since that same father Hludowic wished his sons to march with their brother Carolomannus against the Wends, but could not prevail, he sent out with Carolomannus as large an army as he could. He himself, as has been said, met with Ingelberga at Trent and, disregarding the oaths agreed between them, secretly returned to her the portion of Lothair’s kingdom that he had received against Charles, without the consent or knowledge of Lothair’s former men who had commended themselves to him [Note: “who had commended themselves”; Ch. and B.]. Consequently, oaths were exchanged between them—different from and contrary to the earlier oaths that he had sworn with his brother.

After these events, Ingelberga sent her envoy to Charles, telling him, as before, to meet her at Saint Maurice. But Charles, having learned what had been done between her [Note: “him”; Ch.] and his brother, did not wish to go there. Instead, he sent his own messengers to her, who reported nothing definite back to him.

Pope Adrian, in accordance with the arrangements made by his predecessor Nicholas [Note: “predecessor”; A.], sent his envoys—namely Donatus, bishop of Ostia, and Stephen, bishop of Nepi, together with Marinus [Note: “Martin”; A.], a deacon of the holy Roman Church—to the emperor Basil and his sons, the Augusti Constantine and Leo, at Constantinople. Anastasius, librarian of the Roman See, who was skilled in both languages, Greek [Aimon adds “namely”] and Latin, also went with them.

After a synod had been convened, which those who assembled there called the Eighth Universal Synod, they suppressed the schism that had arisen over the deposition of Ignatius and the ordination of Photius [Note: “Photius … Photius”; Ch. reads “Photios … Photios”], anathematizing Photius and restoring Ignatius. At this synod they defined matters concerning the veneration of images differently from the way the orthodox teachers had previously defined them, and, partly out of favor toward the Roman pontiff, who agreed with their wishes concerning the veneration of images, and partly against the ancient canons and even against their own synod, they established certain decrees, as anyone who reads that same synod will plainly discover [Note: “and they established certain things”; the same source, d.].

Emperor Hludowic came to Rome on the eve of Pentecost [the same source adds “at Saint Peter’s”]. On the following day [Note: “the next day”; another reading in Bq.] he was crowned by Pope Adrian. After celebrating the solemn Masses, he rode with the pope in a ceremonial procession to the Lateran palace, crowned. Having gathered his army, he again proceeded from Rome toward the territories of Benevento.

Because the leading men of Italy hated Ingelberga for her arrogance [Note: “held her”; A.], and had substituted for her the daughter of Winigis as the emperor’s consort, they persuaded that same emperor to send his envoy to Ingelberga, ordering her to remain in Italy and not follow him, but to await his return there. She, however, refusing to obey his command [Note: “mandate”; A.; “that order”; Ch.], hastened to follow him. She sent Bishop Wibod to Charles, ostensibly as a gesture of friendship, thinking that Charles did not know what agreements had been made between her and Hludowic, king of Germany [Note: “agreements”; Ch. reads “deeds”; B.].

Wibod came to Charles at the Liudi Bridge [Note: “Liadi”; A.; “Pont-Liart,” in the Chronicle of Saint-Denis.], for Charles had gone there to settle certain matters in Burgundy. There he was informed by the men of Bernard [Note: This Bernard seems to be none other than Bernard, count of Auvergne, son of Bernard, duke of Septimania; but it is uncertain with what honors he was endowed. BOUQ.], son of Bernard, that Bernard called Vitellus had been killed and that his honors had been given to the aforementioned Bernard.

Charles returned from Burgundy to Gondulf’s estate, where he intended to hold a previously arranged assembly, on the Kalends of September. After remaining there for some time and arranging what seemed right to him [Note: “and, together with the things which he had arranged”; A.], he went to the Ardennes for the sake of hunting. In October, traveling by boat along the Meuse as far as Utrecht [Col. 1268A], to speak with Rorico and Rodulfus the Northmen, who had come by boat to meet him [Note: “having spoken”; Ch.], he received Rorico kindly as a loyal man, but sent Rodulfus away empty-handed, since he was plotting treachery and demanding excessive things. Against Rodulfus’s ambushes he prepared his faithful men for defense. From there he returned by horse through Attigny and celebrated the Lord’s Nativity in the monastery of Saint Medard.

Pope Adrian died, and John [Note: “Joannes”; Ch.], archdeacon of the Roman Church, was substituted in his place nineteen days before the Kalends of January.

## 873

[Note: A. gives 874.]

Since there were many in Charles’s kingdom [the same source adds “and in other kingdoms”] who were waiting for further evils to be revived through Carolomannus [the same source adds “his son”] in the holy Church of God [the same source adds “in his kingdom”] and in other kingdoms, Charles promulgated, through the royal administration and with the counsel of his faithful men, laws appropriate to the peace [Note: “of peace”; Ch. B.] of the Church and the stability of the kingdom, according to the custom of his predecessors and ancestors [the same source adds “the kings”], and decreed that all should observe them.

He therefore ordered the bishops of his kingdom to be summoned to the city of Senlis [Note: The acts of the Synod of Senlis have perished; nevertheless, the titles of the individual sections of the synod, divided into five chapters, are reported in Volume IX of the Councils, p. 258. BOUQ.], where that same Carolomannus was staying, so that, according to the sacred canons [Note: Ch. omits this], from which, as Leo says, they may depart neither through negligence nor presumption, they might exercise episcopal judgment concerning him. And so they did: according to the sacred rules, they deposed him from every ecclesiastical rank, while preserving for him lay communion [Note: “This is indeed what they did”; A.].

When this had been done [Note: “After this deed”; A.], the ancient and crafty adversary stirred him and his accomplices to another scheme: namely, that he might more freely rise to royal title and power [Note: “royal authority”; A.], and that, since he no longer possessed an ecclesiastical order and had lost his ecclesiastical rank by the judgment of the bishops [Note: “He lost it”; Ch. B.], he could also more freely cast off his ecclesiastical tonsure. Therefore, after his deposition, his accomplices began more fervently to reunite themselves with him and to draw into their association as many others as they could, so that, as soon as they found an opportunity [Note: Aimon adds: “and even others from other kingdoms, wherever they could find an opportunity”], they might remove him from the custody in which he was being held [the same source adds: “until it could be seen whether he wished to turn away from his evils”] and establish him as their king.

For this reason it was necessary to bring forward even those matters for which he had not been judged by the bishops and, according to the decrees of the sacred laws, to condemn him to death for his offenses. But a milder sentence was imposed, so that he might have a place and time for repentance and might not have the opportunity to commit more serious offenses, as he was planning [Note: “a place”; another reading in Bq.; “so that a place and time for repentance would not be given”; A.]. By the acclamation of all who were present, he was blinded, so that the destructive hope of those who hated peace might be frustrated in him and so that the Church of God and Christendom in his kingdom could not be disturbed by a fatal uprising amid the attacks of the pagans.

Hludowic, king of Germany, came to the palace at Frankfurt before the Lord’s Nativity and celebrated the Nativity there. He arranged to hold his assembly there around the Kalends of February and ordered his sons Hludowic and Charles to assemble with his other faithful men, as well as the men from the former kingdom of Lothair who had commended themselves to him.

While he was staying there, the devil, disguising himself as an angel of light, came to Charles, his son, and told him that his father, who was seeking to destroy him because of Carolomannus, his brother, had offended God and would soon lose the kingdom; that God had destined that kingdom for Charles to possess [Note: The royal manuscript reads: “that he would have it,” which Bq. gives as “that he would soon have it”]; and that Charles would soon obtain it.

Charles himself, terrified by fear [Note: A. adds: “he entered the church that adjoined the house in which he was lying”], because the church adjoined the house in which he was hiding, entered the church. The devil followed him there and said again: “Why are you afraid and fleeing? For unless I had come from God, announcing to you what is soon to happen, I would not follow you into this house of the Lord.” By these and other flatteries he persuaded Charles to receive from his hand the communion sent to him by God [Note: “as he claimed, to receive”; A.]. Charles did so; and after the morsel, Satan himself entered into him.

Charles came to his father and sat in council with him, with his brother and the other faithful men—both bishops and laymen [Note: “and laymen”; Ch.; the same source adds “of his father”]. Suddenly seized, he rose and said that he wished to renounce the world and that he would no longer have sexual relations with his wife [Note: “would not touch his wife in carnal intercourse”; A.]. Unbuckling his sword [Note: “cutting loose”; Ch.], he allowed it to fall to the ground [Note: A. omits “to the ground”]. As he wished to unbuckle his belt and remove his clothing, he began to be tormented.

The bishops and other men seized him. His father and all who were present were thrown into confusion and struck with intense astonishment, and Charles was led into the church. Archbishop Lintbertus put on his priestly vestments and began to sing Mass. When the reading of the Gospel was reached, Charles began to shout in a loud voice, in the language of his country, “Woe!” [Col. 1269D] [Note: Ch. omits the word. Note: In German; it is written here as *weh*!]. He continued to cry “Woe!” repeatedly until the Mass had been celebrated.

His father entrusted him to the bishops and his other faithful men [the same source adds “his own”] and ordered him to be led through the holy places of the martyr saints, so that, freed from the demon by their merits and prayers, he might, by the Lord’s mercy, be able to return to a sound mind [Col. 1270A]. He then planned to send him to Rome, but because certain matters intervened, he abandoned that journey.

Hludowic, emperor of Italy, was staying at Capua. Landbertus the Bald had already died, and the patrician of the Greek emperor had arrived with an army at the city called Hydruntum [Note: “Hydruntum”; Ch.] to aid the Beneventans, who promised that they would pay him the tribute that they had until then paid to the Frankish emperors, since Hludowic could not otherwise secure Adalgisus.

He sent word to Pope John [Note: “John”; Ch.], Adalgisus’s kinsman, asking him to come to Campania [Note: “to Capua”; A.] and reconcile Adalgisus to him. He wished to display that he was receiving Adalgisus as though through the intercession of Saint Peter’s vicar, although he had sworn that he would never return from those regions before capturing him—a feat he plainly could not accomplish by his own power.

Charles announced an expedition against Brittany, so that the Northmen who had occupied the city of Angers would not suppose that he was going there to fight them and therefore flee to other places where they could not be so tightly constrained.

While he was proceeding there, he was informed on the journey that, through the faction of his brother Hludowic, king of Germany, the blind Carolomannus had been removed from the monastery of Corbie by some of his former men, with the cooperation of two false monks, and had been brought to Hludowic, through the support and intervention of Adalardus, for the purpose of opposing Charles [Note: “was to be restrained”; A.].

Charles was not greatly disturbed by this. He continued the journey he had begun and, after gathering his army, besieged the city of Angers [Col. 1270C]. The Northmen had long been residing there, having ravaged certain cities, destroyed castles, burned monasteries and churches, and reduced the fields to desolation. Charles surrounded the city with a very strong fortification. Solomon, duke of the Bretons, was stationed beyond the river Mayenne [Note: Mayenne.] with an army of Bretons to aid him.

While King Charles was occupied with this undertaking, Solomon sent his son, named Wigon, to him with the leading men of Brittany. His son commended himself to Charles and swore fidelity to him before his faithful men.

Meanwhile, the Northman Rodulfus, who had inflicted many evils on Charles’s kingdom, was killed in Hludowic’s kingdom with five hundred or more of his accomplices. Charles was staying near the city of Angers when this was reported to him through a reliable account [Note: “While he was staying”; Ch.]: a multitude of locusts had spread through Germany into Gaul, and especially into Spain, to such an extent that it could be compared with the plague of Egypt [Note: “spread”; Ch.].

Hludowic, king of Germany, was planning to hold his assembly at the city of Metz when he received word that, unless he came very quickly to aid his son Carolomannus in the march against the Wends, he would not see him again. He immediately turned back [Note: “having turned back”; A.], went to Regensburg [Note: “Renisburg”; Ch.], and entrusted the blind Carolomannus to Archbishop Liutbertus to be maintained in the monastery of Saint Alban at Mainz. By this clear indication he showed how displeased he was with the evils that Carolomannus had perpetrated against the holy Church of God [Note: “the holy Church of God”; Ch.], against the Christian people, and against his father whenever and wherever he had prevailed.

When he reached Regensburg [Note: “Renisburg”; Ch.], he reconciled through his envoys, as best he could, the Wends who had been placed under different princes. But when envoys from those who are called the Behemi [Note: It should be pronounced *Rechin*. The Behemi perhaps took their name from their duke Bech, who was killed in 805.] came to him deceitfully, he received them and sent them to prison.

Charles carried out the siege of the Northmen around the city of Angers [Note: “of Angers”; A.] with manly vigor and determination. He subdued the Northmen so completely that their leading men came to him, commended themselves to him, performed whatever oaths he ordered, and gave him as many hostages as he requested [Note: “as many”; A.; Ch. and B. likewise read “as many”], so that on the appointed day they would leave the city of Angers and, for as long as they lived in his kingdom [Note: Perhaps it should read “for as long as he lived”?], neither make plunder nor consent to its being made.

They asked that they be permitted to remain on a certain island in the Loire until the month of February and to maintain a market there. In February, those among them who had already been baptized and genuinely wished thereafter to maintain Christianity were to come to him; those who were still pagans but wished to become Christians were to be baptized according to his arrangement; the rest were to depart from his kingdom and, as stated, never again return to it to do harm.

After this, together with the bishops and the people, and with the greatest religious devotion, Charles restored to their proper places the bodies of Saints Albinus and Licinius [Note: “Lizinius”; A.], which had been dug up from their tombs out of fear of the Northmen, giving them rich gifts. Thus, after expelling the Northmen from the city of Angers and receiving hostages, Charles arrived in November at Amiens by way of the city of Le Mans, the town of Évreux [Note: Évreux], and the vicinity of the new castle near Pîtres [Note: “at Pîtres”; Bq.].

From there he hunted at the estate of Audriaca and in the surrounding region, then reached the monastery of Saint Vedast and celebrated the Lord’s Nativity there in the year of the Lord 874.

## 874

The winter was long and severe, and so much snow fell in such abundance that no one remembered having seen anything like it [Note: “of snow”; A.].

On the Purification of Saint Mary, Charles held an assembly with his counselors in the monastery of Saint Quentin. He observed the Lenten fast in the monastery of Saint Dionysius [Note: Ch. omits “from the monastery of Saint Quentin up to the monastery of Saint…”] and celebrated the Lord’s Pascha there.

He also held a general assembly on the Ides of June at the estate of Douzy [Note: This assembly, or council, was held against incestuous marriages and the invasions of ecclesiastical property, as his synodal letter to the bishops of Aquitaine attests. It begins as follows: “The holy synod of many provinces, summoned by divine will and by the decree of the lord Charles, glorious king, at Douzy, near the township of Mouzon in the diocese of Reims, in the name of God, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 874, in the seventh indiction, on the Ides of June, to our beloved brothers and venerable fellow priests governing the holy churches of God in the provinces of the region of Aquitaine, abundant greetings in the Savior.” It survives complete in Labbe, Volume IX of the Councils, p. 258. BOUQ.], where he also received his annual gifts. From there he went through Attigny and the customary lodging places [Note: “lodging places”; Ch. B.] [Note: That is, inns or royal estates where he was accustomed to stay.] to Compendium. A long summer produced a drought and a shortage of hay and crops.

Solomon, duke of the Bretons, who in the meantime had been reported by uncertain messengers sometimes ill and sometimes dead [Note: “messengers”; Ch.], was reported to Charles at Compendium as dead through a reliable account, in the following manner.

He had been pursued by the leading men of Brittany—Pascuitan, Vurnahat [Note: Ch. reads “and Vurnahat”; others read “Vurfandus”; Vurfandus of Regino comes closer to Pascuitanus and Urbanus. A.]—and by Wigon, son of Rivilin [Note: “Ruilni”; A.], as well as by the Frankish men whom he had greatly oppressed. After his son Wigon had been captured and committed to custody, Solomon escaped and withdrew to Paucher. He entered a certain little monastery [Note: Perhaps Plebelan, which he had founded and which the author calls the Monastery of Solomon, Moutier-Salaün], seeking to secure his release. But his own men, who had been assured that he should suffer no harm from any Breton, betrayed him to the Frankish men, Fulcoaldus and others.

They blinded him, and on the following day he was found dead, receiving a fitting return for having killed his lord Herispogius on the altar while Herispogius was fleeing from persecution in Solomon’s church and calling upon the Lord.

Hludowic, king of Germany, sent his brother Charles his son Charles together with other envoys, asking that they confer together near the Moselle. When Charles was traveling to that assembly, he was detained by a discharge of the bowels and could not reach the appointed meeting as agreed. Therefore their conference—namely, between Hludowic and Charles—took place near the Meuse at Heristal around the Kalends of December.

After this conference, Charles returned through the monastery of Saint Quentin and celebrated the Lord’s Nativity at Compendium [Col. 1273A]. Hludowic celebrated the same solemnity at Aachen and then returned across the Rhine to the palace at Frankfurt.

## 875

Around the beginning of Lent, Charles went to the monastery of Saint Dionysius, where he also celebrated the Lord’s Pascha. His wife Richildis miscarried a son at night, before Wednesday of Pascha; he was baptized and immediately died [Note: “abortion”; Ch. reads “miscarriage”; A.]. While she awaited in the same monastery the day of her purification after childbirth [Aimon adds “her own”], Charles went to Baisieu [Note: “Barivum”; A.] [Note: Baisieu, two leagues from Corbie and the village of Buissi, toward the west. BOUQUET.]. From there he returned to the monastery of Saint Dionysius before the Ascension of the Lord to celebrate the litanies, and on the eve of Pentecost he came to Compendium.

Hludowic, king of Germany [Note: A. reads “Hludowic from Germany”], held his assembly at Tribur in May. Since he could not accomplish there what he had planned, he announced another assembly at the same place in August.

In August Charles reached Douzy near the Ardennes, where he learned through a reliable messenger that his nephew Hludowic, emperor of Italy, had died. Therefore, setting out immediately [Note: A. omits this], he reached Pontigon [Note: another reading: Pontion; A.] and ordered as many neighboring counselors [Note: “his own neighboring counselors”; A.] as he could to come out to meet him. He received provisions for his journey from all those from whom he was able to obtain them.

From there he reached Langres and equipped those whom he had decided to lead with him into Italy [Note: “he equipped them, and thus began his journey on the Kalends of February; the middle is missing in the codex of Saint-Bertin.”]. He sent his wife Richildis back through the city of Reims [Note: “Rheims”; others in Bq.] to Silvacum, and sent his son Hludowic into the portion of the kingdom that he had taken against his brother after the death of his nephew Lothair. He began his journey on the Kalends of September, proceeded through the monastery of Saint Maurice, crossed Mount Jovis, and entered Italy.

His brother Hludowic, king of Germany, sent his son Charles into Italy to oppose his brother. King Charles forced him to flee [Note: “to accept”; Ch. B.] and depart from there. Hludowic, king of Germany, then sent his other son Carolomannus into Italy with as many men as he could gather, to oppose his brother.

King Charles, learning this beforehand, went out to meet him with a stronger force. Since Carolomannus realized that he could not resist his uncle, he asked for peace and conferred with him. After the oaths had been confirmed on both sides, he returned home.

Hludowic, however, persuaded by Engelramnus [Note: another reading: Engilramnus; Bq.], formerly chamberlain and domesticus of King Charles [Note: “chief domesticus”; A.], who had been deprived of his offices and expelled from the queen Richildis’s circle through her influence, came with his army and his son and namesake Hludowic [Note: “and his son and namesake”; A.] as far as Attigny.

At Queen Richildis’s command, the leading men of Charles’s kingdom swore to oppose him. But they did not honor their oath; instead, ravaging Charles’s kingdom on their own side, they devastated it like an enemy army. Hludowic likewise devastated that kingdom with his army.

Thus, after celebrating the Lord’s Nativity at Attigny, and after the kingdom of Charles had been plundered through the arrangements of its leading men, Hludowic returned with certain counts from Charles’s kingdom who had come over to him. Passing through the city of Trier, he reached the palace of Frankfurt beyond the Rhine and there celebrated Lent and the Lord’s Pascha [Note: “he celebrated it. Charles”; this appears in certain codices of Saint-Bertin.].

There he learned from a reliable messenger that his wife Emma had recently died at the palace of Regensburg, shortly after the Lord’s Nativity.

Charles, although some of the leading men from Italy did not come to him, received many others and proceeded to Rome at the invitation of Pope John [Note: “John”; Ch., and likewise frequently elsewhere]. Sixteen days before the Kalends of January, he was received by the pope with great honor in the Church of Saint Peter.

## 876

In the year of the Lord 876, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity [Note: “the same Charles offered [gifts] to blessed Peter”; A.], he offered many precious gifts to blessed Peter, was anointed and crowned emperor, and was called emperor of the Romans. On the Nones of January he left Rome and returned to Pavia, where he held his assembly.

There he appointed Boso, his wife’s brother, duke of that land and invested him with the ducal crown [Note: “and with a crown”; A.]. He left with him the associates whom that duke had requested [Col. 1274C] and then hastened his journey, returning by Mount Jovis and through the monastery of Saint Maurice [Note: A. adds “returning as far as …”; from that point through “with which the emperor is inserted here”; Ch. and B. omit the passage], so that he might celebrate the Lord’s Pascha at the monastery of Saint Dionysius.

When Richildis, who was staying at Silvacum, heard this, she immediately set out to meet him on the day before the Nones of March. With the greatest speed she came on the day before the Ides of March by way of Reims, Châlons, and Langres, beyond Besançon, to a place called Warnarius-Fontana.

The emperor traveled with her through the cities of Besançon, Langres, Châlons, and Reims, and through the palace of Compendium, and reached the monastery of Saint Dionysius, where he celebrated the Lord’s Pascha.

There he summoned the envoys of the apostolic see: John of Tuscany, John of Arezzo, and Ansegisus of Sens [Note: “of Senonensis”; Ch. and A. read “of Senensis”]. With apostolic authority, their counsel, and his own sanction, he announced a synod to be held in the coming month of June [Note: Ch. and A. read “July”] at Pontigon. He reached it by way of the cities of Reims and Châlons.

After the emperor had returned from Italy to Francia, Boso, through the faction of Berengar, son of Everardus, took in marriage, by an unlawful conspiracy, Hirmengard, the daughter of Emperor Hludowic, who was staying with him [Col. 1275A].

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth indiction, the bishops and all the other clergy [Note: “and all the other clergy”; A.] having put on ecclesiastical vestments, the house and seats spread with coverings, and the holy Gospels placed upon a lectern in the midst of the synod and in view of the imperial throne [Note: “the holy Gospels at Pontigon”; this appears in a historical fragment reported in two royal codices and one codex of Saint-Germain. BOUQ.; Ch. and B. omit the words], the lord Emperor Charles came to the synod at Pontigon [Note: A. omits “at Pontigon”] in a golden garment and Frankish attire, together with the envoys of the apostolic see.

While the cantors sang the antiphon *Exaudi nos, Domine*—“Hear us, Lord”—with its verses and the *Gloria*, after the *Kyrie eleison*, and after John, bishop of Tuscany, had given the prayer [Note: “and after the prayer”; Ch. and A.], the lord emperor took his seat in the synod.

John, bishop of Tuscany, read letters sent by the lord apostolic. Among them he also read a letter concerning the primacy of Ansegisus, bishop of Sens [Note: “of Senensis”; Ch. and A.], granting him that whenever ecclesiastical necessity should dictate it—whether in convening a synod or conducting other business—he might exercise the apostolic office throughout Gaul and Germany; that the decrees of the apostolic see might be made known to the bishops through him; that, in turn, whatever had been done might, if necessary, be disclosed to the apostolic see through his report; and that greater and more difficult matters might, on his recommendation, be referred to the apostolic see for arrangement and clarification.

When the bishops asked that they be allowed to have the letter read to those to whom it had been addressed [Note: “to read it”; A.; “that the letter itself be read”; Ch.], the emperor did not agree. Instead, he sought their response concerning what they would say about these instructions of the apostolic envoy [Note: “these orders”; Ch.; “these apostolic orders”; A.].

Their response was that, while the privilege of each metropolitan’s rights was preserved according to the sacred canons and according to the decrees of the Roman pontiffs promulgated from those same sacred canons, they would obey the commands of the lord John, the apostolic pope.

Although the emperor and the apostolic envoys pressed them strongly to respond openly that they would obey the apostolic instruction concerning the primacy of Ansegisus [Note: In other acts of the same synod, quoted by Odorannus in his Chronicle, Ansegisus’s primacy is said to have been unanimously recognized and accepted. BOUQ.], they could extract no other answer from them than the one already stated [Note: “they could not”; Ch.], except that Frotarius, bishop of Bordeaux, because he had gone from Bordeaux to Poitiers and from there to Bourges against the rules through the prince’s favor, replied flatteringly [Note: “through flattery”; Ch.] with what he knew would please the emperor.

Then the emperor, moved to anger, said that the lord pope had entrusted his own authority to him in the synod and that he would strive to carry out what the pope had commanded.

He took the letter, still folded, together with John of Tuscany and John of Arezzo, and gave it to Ansegisus. He ordered that a folding chair be placed before all the bishops of his cisalpine kingdom beside John of Tuscany, who was seated at the emperor’s right hand. He ordered Ansegisus to pass over all those ordained before him and sit in that same chair.

The archbishop of Reims protested, in the hearing of everyone, that this act violated the sacred rules. The emperor nevertheless remained firm in his decision. When the bishops asked permission at least to take a copy of the letter addressed to them, they could in no way obtain this either. Thus the synod was dissolved on that day.

On the tenth day before the Kalends of the aforementioned month, the bishops assembled again. At this meeting letters sent by the lord apostolic to laymen were read. The election of the lord emperor, confirmed by the bishops and the other men of the Italian kingdom, was also read, as were the articles that he had established in the palace at Pavia and ordered to be confirmed by all. He likewise ordered these to be confirmed by the cisalpine bishops. Thus the synod was dissolved on that day.

On the fifth day before the Nones of July, the bishops assembled again [Aimon adds “again”] without the emperor. Disputes were held concerning priests from various dioceses who were appealing to the apostolic envoys. Thus the synod was dissolved on that day.

On the fourth day before the Nones of the same month, the bishops assembled again. The emperor, seated in the synod, heard the envoys of his brother King Hludowic: Willebert, archbishop of Cologne, and the counts Adalard and Meingaud [Note: A reads *Menigardum*]. Through them Hludowic requested a share of the kingdom of the emperor Hludowic, the son of their brother Lothar, asserting that it belonged to him by inheritance and had been confirmed to him by oath. John of Tusculum read a letter from Pope John addressed to the bishops of King Hludowic’s realm [Col. 1276C], and gave a copy to Archbishop Willebert [Note: Ch reads *Wiliberto*], so that he might deliver it to the aforesaid bishops. Thus the synod was dissolved that day [Note: The letters mentioned here were published by Labbe, volume IX of the Councils. BOUQ.; the same source adds *praefata*, “aforesaid,” to “the synod”].

On 10 July (the sixth day before the Ides of July), the bishops assembled. About the ninth hour, the envoys of the apostolic lord arrived: Leo, bishop, apocrisiarius, and nephew of the apostolic lord, and Peter, bishop of Foro-Simpronium. They brought letters for the emperor and empress, together with greetings from the apostolic lord to the bishops. Thus the synod was dissolved that day.

On 11 July (the fifth day before the Ides of July), when the bishops had assembled, the apostolic lord’s letter concerning the condemnation of Formosus the bishop, Gregory the nomenclator, and those who had agreed with them was read. The gifts sent by the apostolic lord were presented to the emperor [Col. 1276D]; among them the principal items were a scepter and a golden staff. Gifts were also sent by him to the empress: cloaks and bracelets set with gems. Thus the synod was dissolved that day.

On 14 July, the eve of the Ides of July, the bishops assembled, and the emperor sent the apostolic lord’s vicars to rebuke more harshly the archbishops and the other bishops who had not assembled the previous day as he had ordered. They, however, gave a canonically reasonable explanation [Note: A reads, “giving an account to them”], and the rebuke was quieted. At the emperor’s command, John of Tusculum again read the letter concerning Ansegisus’s primacy, and the bishops were once more asked for their response.

Each archbishop replied that, just as his predecessors had regularly obeyed the predecessors of Ansegisus’s predecessor, so they wished to obey Ansegisus’s decrees. Their response was more readily accepted than it had been in the emperor’s presence. Thus, after many further disputes concerning priests from various parishes who were appealing to the apostolic envoys, the petition of Frotarius, archbishop of Bordeaux, was read. He said that, because he could not remain in his city owing to the attacks of the pagans [Col. 1277B], he ought to be permitted to occupy the metropolitan see of Bourges. The unanimity of the bishops did not in any way grant his request [Note: A reads, “did not grant it at all”].

At the command of the apostolic legates, the bishops were to assemble on 16 July. In the morning, about the ninth hour, the emperor came, dressed and crowned in Greek fashion. The apostolic legates, clothed in Roman attire [Note: Ch omits this], and the bishops, wearing ecclesiastical vestments, escorted him; the others were prepared according to the arrangement of the first day, when the synod had begun [Note: another reading has “of the first hour”]. As before, the antiphon “Hear us, O Lord” was sung with its verses and the *Gloria* after the *Kyrie eleison*. After Leo the bishop had pronounced the prayer, everyone sat down.

John of Arezzo then read a certain document lacking reason and authority [Note: Ch and A read simply “a document”]. Afterward Odo, bishop of Belvagio, read certain capitularies dictated by the apostolic envoys, by Ansegisus [Note: Ch reads *Ansigisius*; so frequently], and [Note: Ch and A omit “by”] by Odo himself, without the knowledge of the synod. They disagreed with one another [Note: A reads “discordant”] and had no usefulness; indeed, they lacked both reason and authority. For that reason they are not included here.

The question of Ansegisus’s primacy was raised again [Note: A omits “again”]. After many complaints had been made by the emperor and the apostolic legates against the bishops, Ansegisus obtained as much from this matter on the final day as he had on the first day of the synod.

After this, Peter, bishop of Foro-Simpronium, and John of Tusculum went to the emperor’s chamber and brought the crowned empress Richildis into the synod. When she stood beside the emperor, everyone rose, each standing in his proper rank. Then Bishop Leo and John, bishop of Tusculum, began the acclamations. After the acclamations had been completed for the apostolic lord, the emperor, the empress, and the others according to custom, and after Leo had pronounced the prayer, the synod was dissolved by the bishop of Gavinia [Note: A reads *Gaumensi*, that is, Savinensis or Sabinensis. The same spelling is found in the acts of the synod of Douzy and in Anastasius at the beginning of the Life of Hadrian II, chapter 9. It is remarkable—and clear evidence that even very learned men can go wrong in an obvious matter—that Cardinal Baronius and Vignolius, the editor of Anastasius, who ought to have known Roman affairs well, interpreted that passage in the Life of Hadrian as referring not to the bishop of Sabina but to the bishop of Cava, in the kingdom of Naples. Yet the subject was the consecration of the supreme pontiff, which properly concerned the cardinal bishops. Nor was Muratori certain about this bishop in his geographical index, volume XXV. I have mentioned this so that my own less suitable or learned statements in so large a work may be more readily forgiven].

Afterward the emperor, having rewarded the apostolic envoys Leo and Peter, sent them back to Rome, together with Ansegisus [Note: A adds “of Siena”] and Bishop Adalgarius [Note: Ch reads “Adalard”], bishop of Autun. Meanwhile certain Northmen, who had been brought to the emperor for this purpose, were baptized by Hugh, abbot and marquis; after receiving gifts, they returned to their own people. Both before and afterward, however, the Northmen acted according to pagan custom.

On 28 July the emperor departed from Pontigon, and on 30 July he came to Châlons. There, because of a bodily ailment, he remained until 13 August. On 14 August [Note: Aimon adds “the emperor”] he came to Rheims, and from there proceeded directly to Silvacum. On 28 August he sent the apostolic legates John, another John, and Bishop Odo, together with other envoys, to his brother Hludowic, his sons, and the bishops and leading men of his kingdom.

While these envoys were on the road, the emperor was informed at Carisiacum that the aforesaid King Hludowic had died at the palace of Frankfurt on 28 August and had been buried at the monastery of Saint Nazarius on 29 August. The emperor, after sending his envoys to the leading men of his late brother’s kingdom, departed from Carisiacum and came to the estate of Satanacum [Note: Stenay]. He intended to go to the city of Metz and receive the bishops and leading men of his late brother’s kingdom when they came to him.

But suddenly changing his plan, he went to Aachen and from there to Cologne, accompanied by the apostolic legates. While all who travelled with him were plundering without any regard for God [Note: A reads, “while he was plundering and they were going”; A continues, “the Northmen, however…”], the Northmen, with about one hundred large ships, which our people call *bargas* [Note: A reads *harcas*; German *barken*], entered the Seine on 16 September. When this was reported to the emperor at Cologne, he changed nothing in the undertaking he had begun.

Hludowic, his nephew, came against him from the opposite bank of the Rhine with the Saxons and Thuringians. He sent envoys to his uncle the emperor and sought his goodwill, but did not obtain it. Then he and his counts sought the Lord’s mercy with fasts and litanies, while those who were with the emperor mocked them.

Hludowic [Note: A adds “however”], the son of King Hludowic, sent before those who were with him ten men to undergo the ordeal by hot water, ten by hot iron, and ten by cold water. All requested that God declare through that judgment whether, by right and *drictum*—that is, justice—he ought to possess the portion of the kingdom that his father had left him: the portion which his father had received together with his brother Charles, with Charles’s consent and by oath. All of them were found unharmed.

Then Hludowic himself crossed the Rhine with his men at the fortress of Andernach [Note: Andernach]. When this was reported to the emperor, he sent the pregnant empress Richildis [Note: A omits “pregnant”], together with Abbot Hilduwin and Bishop Franco [Note: of Liège], to Heristal. The emperor himself proceeded along the Rhine in a hostile manner against his nephew. He first sent envoys to him, asking him to send some of his counsellors to meet the emperor’s counsellors and negotiate peace between them. Hludowic received this humbly and obediently and remained secure, since he believed that he would not be attacked in war until that agreement [Note: A reads “convention”] had been completed.

On 7 October the emperor arranged his troops, rose during the night, and, with standards raised, advanced by narrow and difficult—indeed, impassable—roads, intending to fall suddenly upon his nephew and those with him. He reached the vicinity of Andernach, while the men and horses were exhausted by the difficult, narrow route and by the rain that had poured over them throughout the night.

Suddenly Hludowic and his men were informed that the emperor was coming against them in a hostile manner with a strong force. He himself stood opposite with those whom he had with him. When the emperor’s divisions attacked them and they resisted vigorously, the emperor’s enemy turned his back and, fleeing [Note: Ch and B read “putting to flight”], came upon the emperor. The emperor himself, with only a few men, scarcely escaped by flight.

Many who could have escaped were hindered because all the emperor’s baggage animals [Note: A reads *sauginae*], and those of the others who were with him, as well as the merchants and those selling shields who were following the emperor and the enemy, blocked the road for the fugitives in the narrow passage [Note: Ch and B read “the merchants and shields” and “and in the narrow road”].

In that engagement Counts Ragenarius and Jerome were killed, along with many others. Captured in the same field and in the neighboring forest were Bishop Ottulf [Note: of Troyes], Abbot Gauzlenus, and the counts Aledramnus, Adalardus, Bernard, and Everwinus [Note: A reads *Ebroinus*], together with many others. The enemy, Hludowic’s army, took all the baggage animals and everything the merchants were carrying.

The prophetic saying was fulfilled: “You who plunder, shall you not yourself be plundered?” [Note: Isaiah 33:1].
