Everything that the plunderers who were with the emperor possessed, and even the plunderers themselves, became the spoils of Hludowic’s army [Note: Ch and B omit “even the plunderers themselves”], so that those who were able to escape with the help of horses counted their lives as their only spoils. The rest were so stripped by the villagers that, wrapped in hay and straw, they concealed their private parts [Note: Ch and B read “shameful parts”] and fled naked; those pursuing them nevertheless did not wish to kill them. A great calamity therefore befell the plundering people.

When Richildis heard on 9 October of the flight of the imperial army and of the emperor himself, she departed from Heristal [Note: Ch and B read “she departs”]. Fleeing, she gave birth to a son on the road at cockcrow the following night. After the birth, her servant carried the child before him and, fleeing, brought him as far as Antennacum [Note: According to Abbot Lebeuf, Antennacum was a village called Antenai near the monastery of Hautvillers in the diocese of Rheims. Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, mentions Antennacum in a letter published by Eckard, *Scriptores medii aevi*, volume II, page 408. BOUQ.].

On the evening of 9 October the emperor reached the monastery of Saint Lambert [Col. 1280B]. Franco and Abbot Hilduwin returned from Richildis to him on 10 October and remained with him until he reached Antennacum after Richildis. From there he went to Douzy, then returned to Antennacum, and fixed his assembly at Salmontiacum for the fifteenth day after the feast of Saint Martin.

Hludowic, the son of the late King Hludowic, returned from Andernach through Sinciacum to Aachen. He remained there for three days, and then went to meet his brother Charles at Confluentes. After they spoke together there, Charles returned ill toward Metz and from there into Alamannia, while Hludowic proceeded beyond the Rhine. Their brother Carloman came neither to them nor to his uncle, the emperor Charles, as he had been instructed, because he was occupied in warfare against the Slavs.

Emperor Charles sent Chuonrad and other leading men to the Northmen who had entered the Seine, instructing them to make peace with them by whatever means they could and to report to him at the appointed assembly [Note: A reads “to strike an agreement”].

The emperor Charles came to his assembly at Salmontiacum [Note: Ch reads *Salmontiaco*], as he had arranged. There he received the men from that portion of the former kingdom of Lothar which his brother Hludowic had taken against him, when they came to him after the flight from Andernach. He gave certain abbeys intact as they stood [Note: A reads “to certain people”], and granted benefices from the abbey of Martianas [Note: Marchiennes in Belgium] which he had divided [Note: A reads “small benefices”]. Thus he allowed them to depart from him [Note: A reads “to come to him”].

He also arranged the troops that were to be stationed against the Northmen along the Seine. He himself came to the estate of Virzinniacum [Note: Ch reads *Vinzinniacum*]. Abbot Lebeuf interprets Virziniacum as the place called Verzenay, near the monastery of Saint Basolus in the diocese of Rheims. Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, book XXXVII, no. 79, thinks it was a place called Visignicourt, near Prémontré. There is also the estate of Virciniacum, commonly called Versigny, about three leagues from Crépy-en-Valois [Note: BOUQ.].

There he was seriously afflicted with pleurisy, so that his life was despaired of. There he celebrated Christmas in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 877.

## 877

Having recovered, he came through Carisiacum to Compendium. While he was staying there, his son—the child who had been born on the road before Richildis reached Antennacum—fell ill. He was taken from the font by his uncle Boso, was named Charles, died, and was carried to the monastery of Saint Denis for burial.

[Note: From this point the continuator of Aimoin adds more concerning the monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris, material not found in the annals. It is also omitted from the royal manuscript. CHESN.]

The emperor Charles spent Lent at Compendium and celebrated Easter there. He received the apostolic envoys of John: Peter, bishop of Foro-Simpronium, and another Peter, bishop of Senogallia. Through them the apostolic lord John summoned him to Rome by word and letter, so that, as he had promised, he might rescue and defend the holy Roman Church from the pagans who were attacking it.

On 1 May he summoned to Compendium the bishops of the province of Rheims and of the other provinces. He caused the church that he had built in the same oratory to be consecrated by those bishops with elaborate ceremony, in his presence and that of the envoys [Note: alternatively, “the messengers”; BOUQ.] of the apostolic see. From there he held his general assembly on the Kalends of July [Note: A reads “of June.” Bouquet considers this should be corrected to the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, that is, 14 June, but I cannot agree. I have observed that in manuscript calendars, when the words Kalends, Nones, and Ides were written with capital letters, this did not mean the actual Kalends, Nones, or Ides of each month, but the day to which the first of those dates referred. Thus KALEND. IVL is assigned not to the Kalends of July but to 14 June; the entire interval from 14 June to 1 July is called the Kalends of July. Hincmar therefore seems here to mean the beginning of the Kalends of July, namely 14 June, on which the synod was held].

There he arranged, by capitularies [Note: These survive in the capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 53, where they are said to have been established at Carisiacum on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the tenth indiction. BOUQ.], how his son Hludowic should govern the kingdom of France with his faithful men and the leading men of the kingdom until Charles returned from Rome. He also arranged how tribute should be collected from the portion of the kingdom of France that he had possessed before Lothar’s death, and from Burgundy.

The arrangement was as follows: from each royal estate—cultivated by the lord himself—one solidus; from each free man’s holding [Note: A reads “free holding”], four denarii from the lord’s census and four from the resources of the holder; from each servile holding, two denarii from the lord’s census and two from the resources of the holder. Each bishop was also to collect from the priests of his parish according to what each could afford—some bishops receiving as much as five solidi from each priest, others as little as four denarii—and return it to the royal envoys. A contribution was also taken from the treasures of the churches according to the wealth of each place, for payment of the same tribute.

The total tribute amounted to five thousand pounds of silver by weight. Those—both bishops and others—who were from Neustria beyond the Seine arranged to pay, from whatever sources they could, the tribute imposed upon them by the Northmen who were in the Loire.

The emperor Charles went from Carisiacum to Compendium, and from there through Soissons to the city of Rheims. Continuing his journey through Châlons, Pontigon, and Langres [The Annals of Saint-Vaast add: “against the wishes of his men”], he set out from France for Italy with his wife and a very large quantity of gold and silver, horses, and other possessions.

When he had crossed the Jura [Note: the manuscripts of Aimoin read “Lirim and Jurim”] and reached Urb, he met Bishop Adalgarius [Col. 1282B], whom he had sent to Rome in February to conduct a synod with Pope John. Adalgarius brought the emperor a copy of the synod’s acts as a great gift.

The substance of that synod, after many and repeated praises of the emperor, was this: the election and elevation to the imperial scepter celebrated at Rome in the previous year would remain firm and stable from that time forward and forever. Anyone who attempted to disturb or violate it—whatever his order, dignity, or profession—was to remain bound by anathema until satisfaction had been made [Note: A reads “subject to anathema”]. The perpetrators and instigators of this plan, if clerics, were to be deposed; if laymen or monks, they were to be struck with perpetual anathema. Since the synod held the previous year at Pontigon near Andernach [Note: A reads *Antennacum*, which should be corrected to *Andernach*] had accomplished nothing, this one was to prevail everywhere.

Adalgarius also informed the emperor that Pope John would come to meet him at Pavia. Therefore the emperor sent ahead Odacer, notary of the second bureau [Note: that is, *secundiscrinium*, second among the chancellors], Count Goiramnus, Pippin, and Heribert [Note: Pippin and Heribert were the sons of the Pippin mentioned above under the year 834, and grandsons of Bernard, king of Italy], to arrange the pope’s necessities.

He himself hastened to meet the pope and encountered him at the city of Vercelli. After receiving him with the highest honor, they proceeded together to Pavia. There they were reliably informed that Carloman, the son of his brother Hludowic, was coming against them with a very large number of warriors. Therefore, leaving Pavia, they came to Tortona [Note: Dertona or Tortona]. Pope John consecrated Richildis empress, and she immediately took flight backward with the treasury toward Moriana.

The emperor, remaining for some time in those regions together with Pope John, awaited the leading men of his kingdom whom he had ordered to accompany him: Hugh the abbot, Boso, Bernard count of Auvergne, and Bernard marquis of Gothia. They had conspired against him and sworn an oath together with the other leading men of the kingdom, except a few, and with the bishops. When he learned that they would not come, and when he and Pope John heard that Carloman was approaching, the emperor fled after Richildis, while Pope John hurried rapidly toward Rome.

Through him Emperor Charles sent to the holy apostle Peter an image of the Savior fixed upon a cross, made of a large weight of gold and adorned with precious gems.

Carloman, hearing through a false messenger that the emperor and Pope John were coming against him with a very large army, also fled by the road he had come [Note: A reads “by which he had come”]. Thus God, according to his merciful custom, dissolved that gathering.

Charles, having been seized by fever [Note: Ch reads “having seized him”], drank a powder sent to him by his excessively beloved and credulous physician, a Jew named Sedechias [Note: Ch, B, and the *History of the Kings of the Franks*, in Bouquet VII, p. 259, read “thus”; Aimoin reads “trusted”]. The physician sent it so that Charles might be freed from the fever by drinking it. But he swallowed an incurable poison and, while being carried across Mount Cenis, reached a place called Brios [Note: A village unknown to the editors; perhaps Briançon—not the well-known town, but a small village on the bank of the Isère, somewhat below Moûtiers in Tarentaise].

There he sent for Richildis, who was at Moriana, asking her to come to him, which she did. On the eleventh day after taking the poison, he died in a most wretched hut [Note: A omits “in a most wretched hut”] on 6 October.

Those who were with him opened the body, removed the intestines, poured in wine and whatever spices they could obtain, placed it in a small coffin, and began to carry it toward the monastery of Saint Denis, where he had requested to be buried. Unable to carry it because of the stench, they placed it in a cask pitched inside and out, wrapped it in hides, and found that this did nothing to remove the odor.

They could scarcely reach a certain cell of monks belonging to the bishopric of Lyon, called Nantua [Note: The royal manuscript and the continuator of Aimoin say: “They buried him in the basilica of Saint Eusebius the martyr in the city of Vercelli, where he rested for seven years. Afterward, in a vision, his body was brought to France and honorably buried in the basilica of Saint Denis the martyr at Paris.” BOUQ.]. There they buried the body, together with the cask, in the earth.

Carloman, having been sick almost to the point of death and carried back to his own lands on a litter, lay ill for a year, so that many despaired of him.

When Ludovicus received news at the estate of Audriaca that his father Charles had died, he reconciled to himself as many people as he could, giving them abbeys, counties, and estates according to each person’s request. Traveling through Carisiacum and Compendium to Vernum [Note: A reads “to Arvernum”], he intended, as he thought, to reach his father’s burial at the monastery of Saint Denis [Note: A reads “Saint Denis the martyr”].

There he heard that his father had been buried at Vercelli [Note: A reads “his father at Vercelli”], and that the leading men of the kingdom, both abbots and counts, were angry because he had granted honors to certain people without their consent and had therefore caused them to conspire against him [Note: A reads “to have conspired”]. He returned to Compendium.

The leading men themselves, together with Richildis, plundering everything that lay along their route [Note: Bouquet reads “everything that was theirs”], reached the monastery of Avennacum [Note: Avenay in the diocese of Rheims]. They arranged their assembly at Mount Witmar [Note: A reads *Witmarium*], and from there sent their envoys to Ludovicus. Ludovicus likewise sent his envoys to them.

As envoys travelled back and forth between them, it was eventually agreed that Richildis and the leading men themselves should come to him at Compendium. They arranged their assembly at Casnum [Note: A reads *Casinum*; Chesne-Herbelot places it outside the Cotian forest. BOUQ.].

Richildis came to Ludovicus at Compendium and, at the mass of Saint Andrew, brought him the document by which his father had transferred the kingdom to him before his death, together with the sword called Saint Peter’s sword, by which he was to reinvest him in the kingdom [Note: A reads “invest him”], as well as royal clothing, a crown, and a staff of gold and gems.

As envoys travelled between Ludovicus and the leading men of the kingdom, and as the honors requested by each were agreed upon, Ludovicus was consecrated and crowned king on 8 December (the sixth day before the Ides of December), with the consent of everyone—bishops and abbots, the other leading men of the kingdom, and all the rest who were present—by Hincmar, bishop of Rheims.

The bishops commended themselves and their churches to him for due defense and the preservation of canonical privileges [Note: A reads “due privileges.”] They professed that, according to their knowledge and ability and in accordance with their ministry, they would be faithful to him in counsel and assistance. The abbots, the leading men of the kingdom, and the royal vassals [Note: A reads *vassi*] commended themselves to him and promised loyalty by oath according to custom.

When Ludovicus, son of Emperor Charles, was crowned at Compendium, the bishops made the following request of him [Note: The continuator of Aimoin omits what follows down to the year 878. It is also omitted in the royal manuscript. BOUQUET.]:”

“We ask you to grant us this: that you may preserve for each one of us and for the churches entrusted to us, according to the first capitulary which most recently at Carisiacum the emperor, your father, declared—while his faithful men, yours, and the legates of the apostolic see consented, and Gozlenus read it—that he would preserve it himself and that you would preserve it [Note: In Sirmond and Baluze’s capitularies: ‘my father declared that he would preserve it himself and that I would preserve it’; Note: that is, ‘that it should be preserved’]—canonical privilege, the due law and justice, and defense, just as a king ought rightly to provide each bishop and church entrusted to him within his kingdom.”

Ludovicus himself made this promise to those bishops:

“I promise and grant you this: for each one of you and for the churches entrusted to you, according to the first capitulary which most recently at Carisiacum the emperor, my father, declared that he would preserve, while his faithful men, ours, and the legates of the apostolic see consented and Gozlenus read it, I shall preserve canonical privilege and the due law and justice, and, with the Lord’s help, I shall provide as much defense as I can, just as a king is bound to provide each bishop and church entrusted to him within his kingdom.”

This is the capitulary referred to:

“Concerning also the honor and worship of God and of the holy churches which, by God’s authority, remain under the rule and protection of our government, we decree, with the Lord’s help, that just as they were cultivated, honored, and enriched during the time of our lord father of blessed memory, and, having been honored and enriched by our liberality, so they shall henceforth be preserved in the entirety of their condition. The priests and servants of God shall possess ecclesiastical authority and their due privileges according to the venerable authority. The princely power, the vigor of illustrious men, and the administrators of the commonwealth shall all cooperate with them reasonably and justly in every matter, so that they may competently carry out their ministry. With God’s help, our son shall likewise preserve these things stated above.”

### Commendation of Ansegisus the Bishop and the Other Bishops Who Were Present at Compendium When They Blessed Ludovicus, Son of Emperor Charles

“I commend myself and the church entrusted to me to you, so that you may preserve due law and justice and provide defense, just as a king ought by just judgment to preserve and provide these things to the bishops [Note: Ch reads “to preserve and provide them to the bishops”] of his church.”

### Their Profession

“I, the same person, profess as follows: From this day forward I shall be faithful and helpful to this lord and my king Ludovicus, son of Charles and Hermentrudis, according to my knowledge and ability and my ministry, in counsel and assistance, just as a bishop rightly owes this to his lord, in my faith and my priesthood.”

In response to the bishops’ petition written above, King Ludovicus made the following profession to the bishops and, at Compendium, gave them this very document of donation in his own hand, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 877, on the eve of the Kalends of December.

### Profession of This Ludovicus, Son of Charles

“I, Ludovicus, established as king by the mercy of our Lord God and by the election of the people, promise before the Church of God, to all orders—namely bishops, priests, monks, canons, and nuns—that from this time forward I shall preserve in their entirety the rules written by the Fathers and confirmed by apostolic testimonies.

I also promise that I shall preserve the laws and statutes for the people who, by God’s mercy, are entrusted to me to govern, according to the common counsel of our faithful men and in accordance with what my predecessors, emperors and kings, inserted into their acts and decreed must be held and observed inviolate.

Therefore I, Ludovicus, rereading this spontaneous promise of mine for love of uprightness and justice, have confirmed it with my own hand [Note: The letter of Hincmar to Gozlenus, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, mentioned by Flodoard, book III, chapter 24, seems to belong to the end of this year, 877. Gozlenus had as his father Rorico, count of Maine; his brother was Gozfridus, and his sister Blichildis, who was the mother of Bernard, marquis of Gothia. BOUQ.].”

## 878

In the year 878 [Note: B omits “in the year 878”], King Ludovicus celebrated Christmas near Soissons, at the monastery of Saint Medard. From there he proceeded to the estate of Audriaca and celebrated Easter at the monastery of Saint Denis.

At the urging of Hugh, abbot and marquis [Note: Hugh, abbot and marquis, was the son of Conrad, count of Auxerre; the brother of Conrad, count of Paris; and, according to some, of Robert the Strong. BOUQ.], he crossed the Seine, both to assist Hugh against the Northmen and because the sons of Gozfrid had invaded the fortress and honors of the son of Odo, formerly a count. Moreover, Imino [Note: A reads “rather, because his brother”; Emeno, count of Poitiers, was the brother of Bernard, father of the rebellious Bernard. BOUQ.], the brother of Marquis Bernard, had usurped the city of Évreux and was carrying out many plunderings throughout those regions. In addition, he had dared to plunder Eiricus [Note: The place is unknown; the text may perhaps read *Rotomagum*, “Rouen,” but this is uncertain].

When Ludovicus came as far as Tours, he fell ill to the point of despairing for his life. But through the Lord’s mercy he recovered somewhat. As certain of his counsellors and friends of Gozfrid worked to bring this about, Gozfrid himself came to him, bringing his sons with him on the condition that they would restore to King Ludovicus the fortress and honors they had invaded, and afterward hold them by his grant.

Then Gozfrid turned some of the Bretons to loyalty to the king. But afterward they acted as the Bretons do.

Pope John, enraged against Counts Landbert and Adalbert because they had plundered his estates and city [Note: [Col. 1287] Ch. B.: “plundered.”], excommunicated them with terrible severity and left Rome. He reached Arles by ship on the holy day of Pentecost and sent his messengers [Note: [Col. 1287] Alternatively, “envoys,” Bq.] to Count Boso [Aimon., “he left, carrying with him the most precious relics, and together with Formosus, bishop of Porto,” n.]. With Boso’s assistance he came as far as Lyons, and from there sent his messengers [Note: [Col. 1287] Alternatively, “envoys,” Bq.] to King Louis at Tours, instructing him to come to meet him wherever it would be convenient for him. Louis, however, sent certain bishops to meet him and asked him to come as far as Troyes; and he had provisions supplied to him there by the bishops of that kingdom [Col. 1287B]. Since he had previously been unable to do so because of his illness, he came to him at Troyes on the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 1287D] From a letter of Pope John VIII it is evident that Louis had already arrived at Troyes—or had been at Troyes—on 18 August. BOUQ. Perhaps, as above under the year 877, the beginning of the Kalends, that is, 14 August, should be understood.].

Meanwhile, Pope John [Note: [Col. 1287D] Pope John himself speaks as follows in a privilege for the monastery of Tournus: “In the year 878 of the Lord’s incarnation, indiction 2, during the reign of the most pious and most glorious King Louis, son of Charles, most serene Augustus, … I, John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, and the aforesaid glorious King Louis, our son, established an assembly of venerable archbishops and bishops of the whole kingdom in the city of Troyes; the aforesaid most pious king attended it. And in that assembly the aforesaid glorious emperor asked us, together with our sons and brothers the bishops, to confirm by the privilege of our authority the monastery of Tournus, … in the county of Chalon, above the river Saône, ….” It should be observed that Louis is called emperor here, although he had previously been called king three times. Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 277. BOUQ.] [Note: [Col. 1287D] In a historical fragment reported in two royal manuscripts and one manuscript of Saint-Germain: “Pope John came into Gaul and stayed for a long time at the city of Troyes; and he held a synod of bishops, at which Hincmar, bishop of Laon, after the tearing out of his eyes, was restored to his bishopric.” BOUQ.] held a general synod with the bishops of the provinces of Gaul and Belgium. He had read out in the synod how he had excommunicated Landbert and Adalbert, as well as Formosus and Gregory the nomenclator and their associates at Rome, and he sought the bishops’ agreement in that same excommunication.

The bishops who were present therefore asked that, just as he had ordered the excommunication he had pronounced to be recited in the synod through the reading of the written document, so he should also allow them to express their agreement in writing. When Pope John granted this, on the following day the bishops presented the document that follows [Note: [Col. 1287] “Would present,” A.] in the synod:

> “Most holy and most reverend lord, father of fathers, John, pope of the catholic and apostolic Church, that is, of the holy Roman Church, the first see. We, your sons [Note: [Col. 1287] Absent in Ch. B.], servants [Note: [Col. 1287] Absent in A.] and disciples of your authority, the bishops of Gaul and Belgium, sympathize with the wounds of your sorrows, which wicked men and ministers of the devil have inflicted upon our holy mother and mistress of all churches by adding to your grievous wounds; we share your sorrow and mourn with you, confessing our grief.  
>
> We approve, by our vote, voice, and unanimity, and by the authority of the Holy Spirit, by whose grace we have been consecrated in the episcopal order, the judgment of your authority which, by the privilege of blessed Peter and of the apostolic see, you have pronounced against them and their associates according to the sacred canons, composed by the Spirit of God, consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, and according to the decrees of the pontiffs of that same holy Roman see, your predecessors. With the sword of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1287] Absent in Ch. B.], which is the word of God, we destroy and pursue them [Note: [Col. 1287] Ch. B.: “we prosecute them.”].  
>
> Namely, those whom, as we said above, you have excommunicated [Note: [Col. 1287] Ch. B.: “excommunicated.”], we hold to be excommunicated; those whom you have cast out from the Church, we cast out; those whom you have anathematized, we declare to be anathematized; and those whom your authority [Note: Aimon.: adds “and.”] and the apostolic see receive after they have made regular satisfaction, we too shall receive.  
>
> Moreover, as we read in sacred history concerning the plague of Egypt, rightly inflicted by God, that there was no house in which a dead person did not lie and no one who could console another, since each person had in his own house something to mourn, so in our churches also we mourn things worthy of mourning. Therefore, with all humility of mind, we beg that your authority come to our aid, asking you to promulgate a decree of your authority concerning how we ought to act toward the invaders of our churches, so that, strengthened by the censure of the apostolic see, we and our successors may thereafter, with the Lord’s help, stand more firmly and readily, in unanimous judgment, against the perverse plunderers and devastators of ecclesiastical property and resources and the despisers of the episcopal sacred ministry.  
>
> Thus, according to the statement of the outstanding preacher and the promulgation of your authority, those delivered to Satan may be saved in spirit on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1287] The passage following this point in John’s document is absent from the royal codex and from the continuation of Aimoinus, down to “What follows.”].”

### Excommunication of John the Apostolic and of the Other Bishops Who Assembled at Troyes, Concerning the Invaders of Ecclesiastical Property

> “Concerning the invaders of ecclesiastical property, whom the sacred canons, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, and the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see have established must remain under anathema until they have made regular satisfaction; and concerning the plunderers whom the Apostle, with Christ speaking through him, testifies will not possess the kingdom of God: by the power of Christ and by the judgment of the Holy Spirit we decree that, if before the next Kalends of November each of the usurpers has not restored to their churches, while making regular satisfaction, the same property which they unjustly invaded, they shall be held alien from communion in the body and blood of Christ until the ecclesiastical property has been restored and satisfaction has been made for the wrong done.  
>
> The despisers of the sacred episcopal ministry and of ecclesiastical excommunication, after they have been admonished by the bishops concerned according to evangelical and apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 1289] Ch.: “communion.”], if they do not repent after making regular satisfaction, shall remain bound by the bond of anathema until satisfaction. If they die while persisting in that obstinacy, let no one bury their bodies with hymns and psalms, nor let their memory be held at the sacred altar among the faithful dead, since the Apostle and Evangelist John says: ‘Is there a sin unto death? I do not say that anyone should pray for it.’ [Note: [Col. 1289D] 1 John 5:16, 13.]  
>
> For a sin unto death is perseverance in sin until death. And if the canons of the ancient fathers, inspired by the Holy Spirit, decreed concerning those who voluntarily inflict death upon themselves and those who are punished for their crimes that their bodies should not be carried to burial with hymns and psalms, then, following their decrees, we likewise decree by the judgment of the Holy Spirit what we have set forth concerning the invaders and plunderers of ecclesiastical property and resources, if they do not repent, just as blessed Gregory decreed, saying: ‘For such persons are not Christians; and I and all catholic bishops, indeed the universal Church, anathematize them.’”

Pope John had this document added to his excommunication, confirmed it with his own hand, and had it subscribed by all the bishops in the synod. Then, at his command, the canons of the Council of Sardica and Pope Leo’s decree concerning bishops who change their sees were read in the synod, as were the African canons and the decree that translations of bishops should not take place, any more than rebaptisms or reordinations. This was done on behalf of Frotarius, bishop of Bordeaux, who was said to have gone into exile from Bordeaux to Poitiers and then from there to the city of Bourges [Note: [Col. 1289] Ch. B.: “gone into exile.”].

And King Louis was crowned by Pope John on the seventh day before the Ides of September [Note: [Col. 1289D] This coronation of Louis the Stammerer was solely a royal, not an imperial, coronation, as many have thought with Baronius. Although Pope John endeavored to transfer the empire to him, he was harassed by the Romans for this reason and forced to leave the City that year, as Sigebert reports in his Chronicle. BOUQ.]. He invited that same pope to his home, entertained him lavishly, and honored him with many gifts, both he and his wife; then he sent him back to the city of Troyes. Later, through his envoys, he asked the same pope to crown his wife queen, but he could not obtain this [Note: [Col. 1289D] Louis could not obtain that John crown his wife queen because she had been brought in as a second wife after he had rejected his first wife. Mabillon, book 38 of the Benedictine Annals, no. 4. Compare the Chronicle of Regino, under the year 878.].

Bishops Frotarius and Adalgarius brought before Pope John’s assembly of bishops the writ by which Louis’s father had handed the kingdom over to Louis, asking on Louis’s behalf that the pope confirm that writ by his privilege. Then Pope John produced what purported to be a writ of Emperor Charles concerning the gift of the abbey of Saint-Denis to the Roman Church [Aimon.: “to be given”]. Many believed that it had been compiled at the advice of the aforementioned bishops and other counselors of King Louis, so that he might take the abbey away from Gozlenus as though by right [Note: [Col. 1289] A.: “take it away”] and keep it for himself. Pope John said that, if King Louis wished him to make a privilege concerning Louis’s writ, Louis should confirm by his own writ the writ of his father. This argument, being a contrivance rather than a justification, remained unfinished.

Finally, on the fourth day before the Ides of the aforesaid month, King Louis, compelled by the requests of certain leading men, came to the residence of the pope. After speaking with him familiarly, he returned together with him to the assembly of bishops, into a chamber beside the pope’s residence. After the excommunication of Hugh, son of Lothair, and of Imino [Note: [Col. 1289] Ch.: “Immon”; A.: “Limnon.”] and their associates, certain bishops using force and the king consenting, Pope John said that Hedenulfus, a bishop ordained by his authority [Note: [Col. 1289D] Bishop of Laon.], should retain his see and exercise the episcopal ministry, and that, if the blind Hincmar wished, he should celebrate Mass and have a portion of the property of the bishopric of Laon.

When Hedenulfus asked the same pope to release him from that see, saying that he was ill and wished to enter a monastery [Note: [Col. 1289] Absent in Ch.], he could not obtain this. Instead, with the king and the bishops who supported Hincmar consenting, the pope ordered him to retain his see and exercise the episcopal ministry.

When those supporters of Hincmar heard that Pope John had said that, if the blind Hincmar wished, he should celebrate Mass, and that the king had consented [Note: [Col. 1289] Ch. B.: “would consent.”] that he should have a portion of the bishopric of Laon, the bishops of other provinces, and also the metropolitans of other regions, unexpectedly brought Hincmar, dressed in priestly garments, into the presence of the pope without any order from him. They then lifted him up and carried him singing into the church, and had him give the sign of blessing over the people [Note: [Col. 1290D] Hincmar, dishonored in that priestly capacity of his, died not long afterward [Col. 1291D]. He was then commended by his uncle Hincmar, who is said to have written to Abbot Hugh, as reported by Flodoard, book 3, chapter 24: “He also informs him of the death of Hincmar, his nephew, bishop of Laon, asking him to strive to implore the mercy of the Lord through his subjects and familiars for the remedy of his soul.” Hincmar of Rheims himself, having received many honors from Pope John at that council, satisfied all his adversaries with a general apology; Flodoard discusses this there in chapters 21 and 29. BOUQ.]. Thus that synod was dissolved.

On the following day [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “on the following day.”] King Louis, invited by Boso, went to his home with certain of his leading counselors. Boso and his wife entertained and honored him, and he betrothed Boso’s daughter to his son Carolomannus. With the advice of those counselors, he divided the honors of Bernard, marquis of Gothia, among Theoderic the chamberlain [Note: [Col. 1291] Ch.: “Theodoroticus.”], Bernard, count of Auvergne, and others, who had been appointed secretly [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “secretly”; it seems that “by decree” should be read.].

Pope John, leaving Troyes [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “from Troyes.”], headed for Chalon [Note: [Col. 1291] Ch.: “Cavillon.”]. From there, traveling through the Maurienne, he entered Italy through the gates [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “passes.”] of Mount Cenis, escorted by Boso and his wife.

King Louis, returning from Troyes to Compiègne [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “King Louis from Troyes.”], after hearing the report of his envoys, whom he had sent to his cousin Louis to obtain peace between them, came with certain counselors as far as Herstal. On the Kalends of November they met at Marsna, and peace was firmly established between them on both sides. They agreed to meet again at the Purification of Saint Mary: Louis, son of Charles, at Gundulf’s estate, and Louis, son of Louis, near the same place, wherever it should suit him.

At that meeting they agreed, with the consent of their faithful men, to observe the following:

### Agreement Made Between the Glorious Kings Louis, Son of Emperor Charles, and Louis, Son of King Louis, at the Place Called Furonis [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “Furoni.”] [Note: [Col. 1292D] Foron, equidistant from Maastricht and Aachen. It is said that ditches, embankments, and the ruins of the foundations of an ancient castle still survive on the nearby hill called Opdesaele; as Miraeus says, I believe these are the remains of the old palace of Furon. Valesius, *Notitia Galliae*, p. 212.], on the Kalends of November, with Their Common Faithful Supporting and Consenting, in the Year of the Lord’s Incarnation 878 [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: 879, indiction twelve. Sirm. Baluz.], in the Eleventh Indiction, King Louis, Son of Charles, Speaking:

> “Just as the kingdom of Lothair was divided between my father Charles and your father Louis, so we wish it to remain. If any of our faithful has taken anything from the kingdom of his equal [Note: [Col. 1291] Ch. Bq.: “from the kingdom of his father.”] by encroachment [Note: [Col. 1291] *Purprisum* appears in Sirmond, Baluze, the continuation of Aimoinus, and the royal codex; Ch. B.: *usurpatum*, ‘usurped’], let him relinquish it at our command.  
>
> “As for the kingdom which Emperor Louis possessed in Italy [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “in Italy,”], since no division has yet been made from it, whoever now holds it shall hold it in this way until, if God wills, we come together again with our common faithful and determine what seems better and more just to us concerning it.  
>
> “Concerning the kingdom of Italy, since at present no settlement is possible, let everyone know that we have both demanded and do demand our share of that kingdom, and, with the Lord’s help, shall continue to demand it.”

The following provisions were established on the next day:

### Chapter I

> “Since the firmness of our friendship and union cannot at present exist because of certain obstructing circumstances, let such friendship remain between us until the meeting that we have arranged to hold together [Note: [Col. 1291] Absent in Ch.]. For, with the Lord’s help, this friendship will remain between us with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith, so that neither of us shall desire or perhaps advise anything against his equal’s life, kingdom, or faithful men, or anything pertaining to the safety, prosperity, or honor of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1291] Ch. B.: “anything pertaining to the safety, prosperity, or honor of the kingdom, he shall neither desire nor perhaps advise.”].”

### Chapter II

> “If pagans or pseudo-Christians rise up in the kingdom of either of us [Note: [Col. 1291] Absent in Ch.], each of us shall truthfully assist his equal wherever there is need and wherever he himself can reasonably do so, either personally or through his faithful men, with counsel and aid, as best he can [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “as well as possible.”].”

### Chapter III

> “If I survive you, I shall assist your son Louis, who is still a child, and your other sons whom the Lord may grant you, with counsel and aid, as best I can, so that they may peacefully hold their father’s kingdom by hereditary right. But if you survive me, I ask that you likewise assist my sons Louis and Carolomannus, and the others whom divine mercy may grant me, with counsel and aid, as best you can, so that they may peacefully hold their father’s kingdom [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “You shall assist.”].”

### Chapter IV

> “If certain whisperers and detractors, who envy our peace and do not allow the kingdom to be quiet, wish to sow quarrels, disputes, and dissensions between us, neither of us shall accept or willingly receive this, unless perhaps he wishes to bring the matter to a proper hearing before both of us and our common faithful. If he does not wish to do so, let him have no association with either of us [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “neither.”]; rather, let us both [Note: [Col. 1291] A.: “each of us.”] cast him out together as a lying falsifier [Note: [Col. 1291] Bq.: “false accuser.”] who wishes to sow dissension between brothers, so that no one thereafter may dare to insert such lies into our ears [Note: [Col. 1291] Ch. B.: “bring such lies to our ears.”].”

### Chapter V

> “Let us jointly, as soon as we can, send our envoys to Carolomannus and Charles, glorious kings, to invite them to the meeting that we have arranged for the eighth day before the Ides of February, and to urge them not to delay coming [Note: [Col. 1293] Ch. B.: “who are to be invited to the meeting . . . and urged not to delay coming.”]. If they are willing to come as we desire [Note: [Col. 1293] Ch. B.: “if they are able to come,”], then, with God cooperating, let us join ourselves together for the will of God, the salvation of Holy Church, our common honor and advancement, and the safety of the whole Christian people entrusted to us, so that thereafter, in the One who is one, we may be one and desire one thing, and may all say and do the same thing, according to the Apostle, and that there be no schisms among us [Note: [Col. 1293] Ch. A.: “schisms.”].”

### Chapter VI

> “If, summoned and invited by our entreaty, they or their envoys delay coming to the aforesaid meeting, let us nevertheless not fail in any way to come there, as we have arranged, and to unite ourselves according to God’s will, unless perhaps some unavoidable necessity should arise that makes this entirely impossible. If this happens, let each of us inform his equal of it in due time [Note: [Col. 1293] A.: “each of them.”]. For this reason let our friendship neither diminish nor change until, at the Lord’s command, it is perfectly confirmed at a suitable time.”

### Chapter VII

> “Let the property of the churches, wherever it is located in the kingdom of either of us, whether belonging to bishoprics or abbeys, be possessed without any contradiction by the rectors of those churches. If anything wrong has been done there [Note: [Col. 1293] Sirm. and Baluz.: “if anything unjust has been done there”; A.: “wrongdoing.”], let him in whose kingdom that property lies ensure that justice is rendered concerning it according to law [Note: [Col. 1293] Ch. B.: “according to the rule.”].”

### Chapter VIII

> “Since the peace and quiet of the kingdom are usually disturbed by vagrant and irreverent men acting according to tyrannical custom, if such a person comes to either of us in order to evade an accounting and justice for what he has done, let neither of us [Note: [Col. 1293] A.: “neither of us.”] receive or retain him for any other purpose than to bring him to a proper accounting and due correction. If he evades a proper accounting, let us both pursue him together in whichever kingdom he has entered until he is either brought to account or expelled from the kingdom or destroyed.”

### Chapter IX

> “Let those who have rightly lost their property in our kingdom be judged according to what was found to have been the practice in the times of our predecessors [Note: [Col. 1293] Ch. A.: “who have lost.”]. But those who say that they have unjustly lost their property [Note: [Col. 1293] Ch.: “their own property.”] shall come into our presence; let judgment be rendered concerning them as justice requires, and let them receive back what is theirs [Note: [Col. 1293] Ch.: “let judgment concerning them be rendered accordingly.”].”

Having said this, Louis, son of Louis, returned to his own territories, while Louis, son of Charles, came through the Ardennes and,

## 879

in the year of the Lord’s incarnation, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Longlier. After remaining for some time in the Ardennes and then setting out, he came around the Purification of Saint Mary to Pontigon. Wishing to go from there into the region of Autun to suppress the rebellion of Bernard, marquis of Gothia [Note: [Col. 1293D] This Bernard, son of another Bernard and of Blichildis, daughter of Rorico, count of Maine, had been granted the marquisate of Gothia in 865 after Humfrid. In 878 he was struck with anathema at the synod of Troyes and deprived of his honors. BOUQ.], he proceeded as far as Troyes.

But because his illness was growing worse—for it was said that he had been poisoned—he could go no farther [Col. 1294B]. He specifically entrusted his son and namesake Louis to the guardianship of Bernard, count of Auvergne [Note: [Col. 1293D] Bernard, count of Auvergne, was the son of Bernard, duke of Septimania, and Dodana. He was the father of William the Pious. He was granted the marquisate of Gothia in 878 and died in 886. BOUQ.]. He sent Abbot Hugh [Note: [Col. 1293D] Abbot Hugh, son of Count Conrad, died in 886. Boso was duke of Provence; Theoderic, chamberlain of Louis the Stammerer, was count of Autun. BOUQ.], Boso, and the aforementioned Bernard with his son, as well as Theoderic with his associates, to Autun, so that they might claim that county for Theoderic, to whom he had previously given it [Note: [Col. 1293] Ch. A.: “that county.”].

He himself, with great difficulty, came through the monastery of Jodrum [Note: [Col. 1293] A.: “through Adiodrum.”] [Note: [Col. 1294D] Commonly Jouarre, in the county of Meaux. BOUQ.] to Compiègne. Realizing that he could not escape death [Note: [Col. 1293] A.: “that he could not be freed from his illness.”], he sent his son Louis, through Odo, bishop of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 1293] Ch. A.: “bishop of Belvacum.”], and Count Albuinus, the crown, sword, and remaining royal regalia, instructing those who were with him to have him anointed and crowned king.

He himself died on the fourth day before the Ides of April, on Good Friday, already toward evening [Col. 1294C]. On the following day, namely the vigil of holy Easter, he was buried in the church of Saint Mary.

When Odo and Albuinus heard that he had died, they gave to the chamberlain Theoderic what they had brought and returned in haste. Those who were with Louis [Note: [Col. 1293] Absent in Ch. B.], the king’s son, having heard of the death of the child’s father, sent word to the leading men who were in those regions to meet them at Meaux and there deliberate what they ought to do thereafter [Note: [Col. 1293] Ch. B.: “in those regions”; A.: “so that they might.”].

Meanwhile, through the mediation of Abbot Hugh, an agreement was reached between Boso and Theoderic: Boso was to have the county of Autun, while Theoderic was to receive in exchange the abbeys that Boso had held in those regions.

Finally, Abbot Gozlenus [Note: [Col. 1294D] Goslinus, who was abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and Saint-Denis and later bishop of Paris, was the son of Rorico, count of Maine, and brother of Blichildis, mother of Bernard, marquis of Gothia, mentioned above. BOUQ.], mindful of the injuries and plots that he had previously suffered from his rivals, relying on the familiarity he had obtained with Louis, king of Germany, with his wife, and with the leading men of that land when he had been captured in battle at Andruacum and led across the Rhine, began to consider how he might repay his opponents in kind.

He joined himself to Conrad, count of Paris [Note: [Col. 1295D] Conrad, count of Paris, was the son of Conrad, count of Auxerre, and brother of Abbot Hugh. BOUQ.], deceiving him with a false hope of eminent power and describing certain schemes [Note: [Col. 1295] A.: “certain subtle means.”] by which he might accomplish this. Before those who were with the king’s son came to the agreed meeting at Meaux, Gozlenus and Conrad hastened to summon as many bishops, abbots, and powerful men as they could to an assembly where the Thara [Note: [Col. 1295D] The Tairin, which flows into the Oise at Creil. BOUQ.] flows into the Oise [Note: [Col. 1295] A.: “Nara.”]. They did this under the pretext that, since the king had died, they should unanimously deliberate concerning the peace and welfare of the kingdom.

They persuaded those who had assembled to summon Louis, king of Germany, to this kingdom, so that through his generosity they might obtain without hesitation the honors that they had hitherto been unable to secure. They sent their envoys [Note: [Col. 1295] Bq.: alternatively, “messengers.”] to the aforesaid Louis and his wife, instructing them to hasten as far as Metz, so that they might bring all the bishops, abbots, and leading men of that kingdom to him [Note: [Col. 1295] A.: “bring them to meet him.”].

Thus, committing many plunderings and robberies through Silvacum [Note: [Col. 1295D] Servais near La Fère. BOUQ.] and along the Aisne, they came as far as Verdun. When Louis arrived at Metz, they again sent envoys to him, asking him to come as far as Verdun so that they might more conveniently bring the people of that kingdom to him.

When Louis came as far as Verdun, his army committed such great evils in every kind of wickedness that their deeds seemed to surpass the deeds of pagans [Note: [Col. 1295] A.: “Saracens.”].

When Hugh, Boso, Theoderic, and their associates heard what Gozlenus and Conrad were plotting with their accomplices, they sent Walter [Note: [Col. 1295] A.: “Gualterus.”], bishop of Orléans, and Counts Goiramnus and Anscherus to Louis at Verdun. They were to offer him a portion of the kingdom of the younger Lothair, which Charles had taken from his brother Louis, Louis’s father, so that, having accepted that portion of the kingdom, he would return to his own kingdom and consent that Louis’s sons possess what remained of the kingdom of their father Charles [Note: [Col. 1295D] A.: “consent that his sons possess it.”].

Louis and his men, however, accepting this offer, rejected Gozlenus, Conrad, and their associates with disgrace. After accepting the portion of the kingdom offered to him, Louis returned to his palace at Frankfurt.

When his wife heard this, she was greatly displeased, saying that, if she had come with him, she would have had the whole kingdom. In distress, Gozlenus and Conrad took refuge with the queen, complaining about how they had been deceived. They accepted messengers [The same adds: “to their associates”] who were to encourage them on Louis’s behalf, as well as others, almost as hostages, and then returned, committing robberies and plunder wherever they were able to go. They announced to their associates that Louis would come as soon as possible with a great army, since he could not come at present: an unambiguous report had reached him that his brother Carolomannus, struck by paralysis and already near death, had died while departing [Note: [Col. 1295] Ch. B. lacks “when he departed.”], and that his son by a concubine, named Arnulfus, had seized a portion of his kingdom. For that reason he was hastening toward that region, as he indeed did.

After calming the disturbance in those regions as best he could, he returned to his wife.

When Abbot Hugh and the other leading men who were acting with the sons of their former lord Louis—namely Louis and Carolomannus—heard that Louis was coming into those regions with his wife, they sent certain bishops, Ansegisus [Note: [Col. 1295] A. omits “Ansegisus and other.”] [Note: [Col. 1295D] Ivo, bishop of Chartres, says in letter 189 that this was done without any metropolitan present, where he mentions only Louis and his wife. Yet Carolomannus himself, three years later, when he was crowned again at Quierzy after his brother’s death, recalls a document that he then granted at the monastery of Ferrières before the altar of Saint Peter, promising that he would preserve for each of the bishops and the churches entrusted to them their canonical privilege, due law, and justice, and would provide protection. Mabillon, book 38 of the Benedictine Annals, no. 21. BOUQ.], and others, to the monastery of Ferrières, and there had them consecrated and crowned as kings.

Meanwhile Boso, persuaded by his wife, who said that she did not wish to live if she could not make her husband king—she was the daughter of the emperor of Italy and betrothed to the Greek emperor [Note: [Col. 1296D] Constantine, son of Emperor Basil. BOUQ.]—persuaded the bishops of those regions to anoint and crown him king. Some were constrained by threats, others enticed by the abbeys and estates promised and later given to them [Note: [Col. 1296D] They actually performed this at the council of Mantala. BOUQ.].

Hugh, the younger Lothair’s son by Waldrada, also gathered a multitude of brigands and attempted to invade his father’s kingdom.

Charles, son of Louis, formerly king of Germany, went into Lombardy [Note: [Col. 1295] Ch.: “Lombardia.”] and took possession of that kingdom. Louis and Carolomannus went to speak with him at Orbe before he crossed Mount Jupiter. While he was going into Lombardy and they were returning from the same journey, they were informed that the Northmen who were in the Loire were plundering those lands by land [Col. 1296D] [Note: [Col. 1295] Ch. B.: “were plundering.”].

They immediately moved into those regions and, finding them there on the day of the Mass of Saint Andrew, killed many of them and drowned more in the river Vienne [Note: [Col. 1297D] The Vienne, which joins the Loire below Chinon.] [Note: [Col. 1297] A.: “They perished, swallowed up.”]. By God’s will, the Frankish army returned unharmed with victory.

### Additional textual apparatus for the agreement

[Note: [Col. 1291] In the preamble, A. omits “King Louis, son of Charles, speaking.”]

[Note: [Col. 1291] Chapter I: Ch. omits *ut* (“so that”) in “so that we may meet together.” Sirmond, Baluze, the continuation of Aimoinus, and the royal codex read: “such friendship shall remain between us.”]

[Note: [Col. 1291] Chapter II: Ch. omits “in”; A. reads *alterutrius* (“either of the two”) for *cuiuscumque* (“whichever”), *uterque* (“each of the two”) for *unusquisque* (“each one”), and “wherever necessity is for him” for “wherever there is need.”]

[Note: [Col. 1291] Chapter III: A. reads “as well as possible” for “as best I can” and again for “as best you can.”]

[Note: [Col. 1291] Chapter IV: A. reads *neuter* (“neither of the two”) for *nullus* (“no one”), *neutro* (“neither of the two”) for *nullo* (“no one”), and *uterque* (“each of the two”) for *omnes* (“all”).]

[Note: [Col. 1293] Chapter V: Ch. B. has the fragmentary reading “who are to be invited … and urged in no way …”; Sirmond and Baluze read: “who may invite them to the meeting … and urge them in no way to delay coming.” Ch. omits “and” before “say the same thing,” and reads “all, so that there be no schisms among us.”]

[Note: [Col. 1293] Chapter VIII: P. reads *neuter nostrum* (“neither of us”); A. reads *uterque* (“each of the two”) for *omnes* (“all”).]

## 880
In the year 880 of the Incarnation of the Word, Louis, king of Germany, set out from Aachen with his wife toward these regions and came as far as Douzy [Note: [Col. 1297] “Cluziacum” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1297D] Douzy-les-Prés, in the district of Mouzon, on the River Chiers. BOUQ.], where Gozlin and Conrad came to meet him, after many of their associates had already been withdrawn from their alliance. From there Louis and his wife went to Attigny, then to Ercury [Note: [Col. 1297] “Hercury” in A.] [Note: [Col. 1297D] Écry on the Aisne … Ribemont on the Oise. BOUQ.], and thus reached Ribemont. Seeing that Gozlin and Conrad could not fulfill what they had promised him, and that he and his wife could not obtain what they had hoped for, they made agreements of friendship [Note: [Col. 1297] “After the agreements had been concluded” in Ch. and B.] [Col. 1297B] with the sons of Louis [Note: [Col. 1297] “Of the king of the Franks” in A.] and arranged a court for the following month of June at Gundulf’s estate; then they returned to their own country.

When Louis encountered the Northmen on the way, with the Lord providing assistance, his army killed a large part of them; but in Saxony he suffered great losses among his faithful at the hands of the Northmen. The sons of the former king Louis [“of the Franks” added in the same source] returned to the city of Amiens and, having found their faithful men as they wished, divided their father’s kingdom among themselves: namely, that Louis should have whatever remained of [Note: [Col. 1297] “de” (“of”) is absent in Ch. and B.] France from his father’s kingdom, as well as Neustria with its marches [Note: [Col. 1297] Or “marks” in Bq.] [Note: [Col. 1297D] That is, the county of Toulouse, Septimania, the Spanish March, and the whole part of Lothair’s kingdom which Duke Boso had invaded. BOUQ.], while Carloman should have Burgundy and Aquitaine with their marches; and that each of the nobles, according to the agreement, should commend himself to the brother in whose division he held his honors. [Col. 1297C]

Returning from there to Compiègne [Note: [Col. 1297] “Returning” in Ch.; “coming back” in A.], they celebrated the Lord’s Easter there. Afterward, passing through the cities of Rheims and Châlons, they came in mid-June to the appointed court at Gundulf’s estate to meet their cousins [Note: [Col. 1297] “Kinsmen” in Ch. and B.] [Note: [Col. 1297D] Charles, Louis, and Carloman, the sons of Louis, king of Germany. BOUQ.]. Louis, detained by illness, could not come to that court, but sent representatives in his place. Charles, returning from Lombardy, came there.

At that court it was agreed by common consent that the kings themselves [Note: [Col. 1298D] Louis and Carloman, the sons of Louis the Stammerer. BOUQUET.], the sons of the former Louis, should return to Attigny with the army of Louis, king of Germany, and attack Hugh, the son of the younger Lothair. When they arrived there and did not find Hugh, they attacked his brother-in-law Theobald in battle and, after killing many, put him to flight. From there, with the army from their kingdoms and with the aforementioned army of Louis, king of Germany, the said kings appointed men to defend their kingdom against the Northmen residing at Ghent [Note: [Col. 1298D] Ghent.] and in July marched from the city of Troyes into Burgundy against Boso, while King Charles was coming there with his army [Note: [Col. 1297] “Coming with his army against Boso” in the other manuscript.].

On this march they expelled [Note: [Col. 1297] “Selected” in Ch.] Boso’s men from the fortress of Mâcon [Note: [Col. 1298D] Mâcon.] and seized the fortress itself; they gave the county to Bernard, surnamed “Planta-pilosa.” [Note: [Col. 1298D] Baluz has wrongly confused this Bernard with Bernard, marquis of Gothia and count of Auvergne, father of William the Pious. BOUQ.] Charles, Louis, and Carloman then proceeded together to besiege Vienne. Boso, leaving his wife and daughter and a large part of his men there, fled toward certain mountain regions.

But Charles, who had promised to besiege Vienne together with his cousins [Note: [Col. 1297] “Kinsmen” in Ch. and B.], withdrew from the siege as soon as certain oaths had been exchanged between them [Aimon adds: “bidding them farewell”], and went to Italy. From there, coming by a rapid route to Rome, he obtained from Pope John that he be consecrated emperor on the day of the Lord’s Nativity [Note: [Col. 1297] “Anointed” in A.].

## 881

In the year 881 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1297] These words are absent in Ba.], while Carloman remained with his men against Boso’s rebellion, his brother Louis returned to his part of the kingdom against the Northmen. They ravaged everything along their route, occupied the monastery of Corbie and the city of Amiens, as well as other holy places, killed no small number of those within them and drove out the rest. Louis himself, with his men, took flight backward, with no enemy pursuing him, thereby making divine judgment manifest: what had been done by the Northmen had been accomplished not by human but by divine power.

When the Northmen again returned to his part of the kingdom, the same Louis marched out to meet them with whatever forces he could muster [the other source adds: “with his troops”]. At the urging of certain of his counselors he enclosed a wooden fortress at a place called Stromus [Note: [Col. 1297] “Stromus” in the Codex Bertinianus; “Stroms” in Ch. and B.]. It had been constructed more as a defense for the pagans than as an aid to Christians, since King Louis himself could not find anyone to whom he could entrust the guarding of the fortress.

Returning from there, in the year 882 of the Lord’s Incarnation he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Compiègne, as well as Holy Easter.

## 882

It was announced to him [Note: [Col. 1297] “Announced” in Ch.] that his cousin [Note: [Col. 1297] “Kinsman” in Ch. and B.] Louis, son of Louis, king of Germany, having lived uselessly for himself, the Church, and the kingdom, had succumbed to death. The leading men of that part of the kingdom which had been given to that Louis in Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 1299] “In Lotharingia” in A.] came and wished to commend themselves to him, provided that he would grant them what their father and grandfather had possessed [Note: [Col. 1299] “Concede” in A.]. But, on the advice of the leading men, because of the oaths that had been exchanged between him and Charles, he did not accept them into his commendation; instead, he dispatched an armed force under Count Theodoric as though to assist them against the Northmen.

He himself crossed beyond the Seine, as though to receive the Breton princes and wage war against the Northmen, and went as far as Tours [Note: [Col. 1299] A. adds: “He, a man full of every impurity and vanity, fell ill.”]. There he fell ill in body and was carried in a litter to the monastery of Saint-Denis. He died and was buried there in August.

[Col. 1299B] The leading men of the kingdom sent a swift messenger to Carloman, instructing him that, leaving those who were besieging Vienne and resisting Boso’s rebellion, he should hasten to come to them as quickly as possible [Note: [Col. 1299] “As speedily as possible” in A.]. They themselves had been prepared for battle against the Northmen, who had already burned the cities of Cologne and Trier with their adjoining monasteries, the monastery of Saint Lambert at Liège, Prüm [Note: [Col. 1299] A. reads: “and nearby, and thence Aachen”], Inda [Note: [Col. 1299] Ch. and B. read: “and thence Aachen.” I think I have correctly emended the text.], Aachen itself with its palace, and all the monasteries of the dioceses of Tongeren, Arras [Note: [Col. 1299] A. reads “Amiens”], and Cambrai, as well as part of the diocese of Rheims. They had brought these under their authority and had in part burned them together with the fortress of Mouzon [Note: [Col. 1299] Bq. has “Mouzon”; A. has “Mosovia”]. They had also killed Wala, bishop of Metz, armed and fighting against sacred authority and the episcopal ministry, and had put his companions to flight.

[Note: [Col. 1299D] Here it is useful to include what Folcuin, abbot of Lobbes, relates about the Northmen in his book *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, quoted in volume VI of the *Spicilegium*, chapter 16:

“Some northern people, of whom perhaps it was said, ‘From the north every evil shall be opened’ (Jeremiah 1:14)—whom many call Nortalbingi, while others more commonly call Northmen—engaged in piracy and attacked France in a new and previously unheard-of manner. First occupying the seas, they then entered the mouths of the rivers that flow through France, now stopping, now advancing; wherever they saw no one resisting, they moved in whatever direction seemed good to them.

“These Normans entered France through four most famous rivers: the Rhine and the Scheldt from the east, and the Seine and the Loire from the west. They devastated everything by fire and plunder, sparing neither sex nor age; they carried people away captive and even profaned the altars with pagan hands. Because of fear of them, many bodies of saints and the finest possessions were transported to safer places. But it was not necessary to carry our patrons farther away, since the neighboring fortress of Thudinicum, which belongs to us and is very strongly fortified, ensured that those who entered could remain unharmed. The distant villages, however, were left in the desolation of widespread destruction.”

Folcuin died in the year 990. BOUQ.]

The leading men were prepared to receive him and commend themselves to him, as they indeed did. While he remained in that military expedition, in September he was informed by a reliable messenger that Vienne had been captured and that Richard, Boso’s brother, had brought Boso’s wife and daughter to his county of Autun [Note: [Col. 1299] “Augustodunum” in Ch.].

Hasting and his fellow Northmen, having emerged from the Loire, also turned toward the coastal regions. Charles, bearing the title of emperor, came against the Northmen with a large army and advanced as far as their stronghold. When he arrived there, his heart failed him, and by an agreement, through the intervention of certain men, he obtained that Godfrey and his men should receive baptism and recover Frisia and the other honors that Roric had possessed [Note: [Col. 1299] Ch. and B. read: “and with a peaceful mind”].

He also gave Sigefrid, Vurmōn, and their associates many thousands of silver and gold, which he seized from the treasury of Saint Stephen of Metz and from the sites of other saints, and allowed them to remain in order to devastate, as they had done before, part of his kingdom and part of that of his cousin.

[Note: [Col. 1300B] “This same Sigefrid, with forty thousand Northmen, had besieged the city of Paris. But when the aforementioned Gozlin, bishop of that city and abbot of the monastery of Saint-Germain, resisted, together with Odo [Note: [Col. 1299] A. reads “Hugh”], then count and afterward king of the Franks, and when the said leaders brought assistance through the merits of holy Mary, Mother of God, and the blessed Germanus, they were unable to capture the city and withdrew. At that time the body of the most blessed Germanus was carried by the monks into the *arcisterium* (*asceterium*) of that holy bishop, situated in the aforementioned city. The pagans, filling his church, situated in the suburb, with every kind of defilement, devastated it; and after many of them had been destroyed by the power of the holy bishop, they withdrew in confusion.

“Therefore the aforementioned Odo, rejoicing in the miracles he had seen performed by Saint Germanus during that siege, after attaining the royal dignity, had the vessel in which, by God’s providence, the holy remains of the bishop now rest honorably adorned with gold and gems. Aimoin’s continuator likewise relates this; but the passage has been inserted here incorrectly and belongs to the year 886. BOUQUET.”]

As for Hugh, son of the younger Lothair, he sent him the ecclesiastical resources of the bishopric of Metz for consumption [Note: [Col. 1299] “Entrusted” in A.], although the sacred canons command that they be reserved for the future bishop. He sent Engelberga, wife of Louis, king of Italy, whom the emperor had brought into Alamannia, to Pope John in Rome through Leutward, bishop of Vercelli, as she had requested [Col. 1300B]. Then, turning toward Worms [Note: [Col. 1299] A. reads “returning”], where he intended to hold his court on the Kalends of November, he withdrew from the Northmen.

For that court Abbot Hugh set out with certain companions [Note: [Col. 1299] The Codex Bertinianus reads: “he set out with companions on account of the petition”] and approached Charles to petition him concerning the part of the kingdom which his brother Louis had received as a temporary possession, asking that Charles restore it to Carloman, as Charles himself had once promised. He obtained nothing definite from him. His absence, however, caused the greatest damage in this kingdom, because Carloman lacked the means to resist the Northmen, and certain leading men of the kingdom withdrew their assistance from him.

For this reason the Northmen came as far as the fortress near Laon, plundered and burned what they found around it, and planned to come to Rheims, then to proceed through Soissons and Noyon, return to attack the aforementioned fortress, and subject the kingdom to themselves.

When Bishop Hincmar heard this with certainty—his men from the territory of the bishopric of Rheims being with Carloman—he scarcely escaped by night. Carrying the body of Saint Remigius and the ornaments of the church of Rheims, he was borne in a carrying chair as the weakness of his body required. The canons, monks, and nuns having been scattered in various directions, he barely reached a certain village beyond the Marne called Épernay [Note: [Col. 1301C] Épernay.] by flight [Note: [Col. 1301] A. reads “a certain village”].

[Col. 1301B] An armed force of Northmen, anticipating the main body of them [Note: [Col. 1301] A. reads: “anticipating the full army of the Northmen”], reached the gate of Rheims [Note: [Col. 1301] Ch. reads “of Rheims”; A. “of the Rheims district”]. They plundered what they found outside the city and burned certain small villages. But God’s power and the merits of the saints defended the city—which neither wall nor human hand defended—so that they could not enter it.

When Carloman heard of the Northmen’s arrival, he attacked them with whatever forces he could muster [Aimoin adds: “with his troops”]. He killed a large part of those who were carrying off the plunder, and some were killed in the Aisne. He especially stripped of their plunder those who had gone to Rheims [Note: [Col. 1301] A. reads “who had approached Rheims”] when they wished to return to their companions.

But the larger and stronger part of the Northmen shut themselves inside a village called Avaux [Note: [Col. 1301C] Avaux is not far from the city of Rheims and still bears the name; it is called Avaux and is distinguished by the title of a county. Valesius, *Notitia Galliae*, p. 549.]. Those who were with Carloman could not approach them without danger to themselves. Therefore, toward evening, they gradually withdrew and settled in the neighboring villages.

As soon as the moon shone upon them [Note: [Col. 1301] A. reads “shone upon”], the Northmen emerged from the village and returned by the route along which they had come.

[Note: [Col. 1302A] “Odelricus [Note: [Col. 1302C] Odelricus served as bishop of Rheims from 962 to 969.], bishop; Rodulfus, archdeacon; and all the clergy of the church of Rheims, to all the children of the Church of God.

“Certain perverse and wicked men, entering the temple of God with criminal intent, although they ought to implore God’s mercy and devote themselves to prayer, do not fear to pursue thefts and sacrileges at the devil’s prompting. Some of these men, whom we do not yet know, entered this basilica of blessed Mary, Mother of God, and did not fear to remove the pallium from above the altar of the holy cross. Other things have also recently been stolen from there: namely, linens from the bed of Frederick, the church’s custodian. From the chapel of Saint Peter within the cloister, a priestly vestment has also recently been taken, and in the previous year a missal.

“We excommunicate and anathematize the perpetrators and sacrilegious thieves of all these things, by the power and authority of God the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; by the power of the holy cross; by the virginity of blessed Mary, Mother of God; and by the authority of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of all the saints. Let them be excommunicated and separated from participation in the body and blood of Christ, from entry into the church, and from all fellowship with Christians, until they come to amendment and satisfaction or return to this church the things mentioned above which they have taken.

“So the Codex Bertinianus.”]
