# HINCMARUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS
# Contents of This Volume

## Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims

**Prolegomena.** — Historical Notice, 9. Second Historical Notice, 11. Bibliographical Notice, 17. Testimonies of Ancient Writers, 43. Sirmond’s Preface, 45.

**On Predestination, against Gottschalk**, 49. Letter to King Charles, 49. Preface to the following work, 55.

**On the Predestination of God and Free Will**, 65. Letter to the king, 65.

**Chapter I.** — When, where, and from what source this predestinarian heresy first arose, and by whom and how it was refuted and suppressed, 69.

**Chapter II.** — By whom and how this same heresy, like bastard shoots sprouting again from the trunk of bitterness, has in our time grown afresh, 84.

**Chapter III.** — On Fulgentius, from whose books the predestinarians produce examples to confirm their own position, 86.

**Chapter IV.** — On following the apostolic see, upon whose teaching we must rely and whose authority we must follow, 88.

**Chapter V.** — On the practice of Gottschalk and his associates, and on their books, from which certain passages are excerpted here, 89.

**Chapter VI.** — The origin of the chapters under discussion: from where their compiler attempted to assemble them, 90.

**Chapter VII.** — On the apostolic example which the compiler of the chapters adduces to confirm his own position, 93.

**Chapter VIII.** — Why the predestinarians’ authority—or rather, their interpretation of this kind of apostolic passage—cannot benefit them, since they have derived it from falsehood, 95.

**Chapter IX.** — How they also bring Isidore forward as a witness to confirm their own position, and produce certain passages from the books of blessed Augustine; from these the distinguished man himself refutes them, and Fulgentius himself clearly dissolves the authority which they take from him, 96.

**Chapter X.** — On the testimonies of Scripture which Gottschalk and his associates, with the meaning alien to the Catholic faith and the teaching of the orthodox, most irreverently misuse, 106.

**Chapter XI.** — On examining the remaining portions of the following chapter, 108.

**Chapter XII.** — Saint Augustine’s definition of what the predestination of the saints is. The compiler of these chapters is known to disagree with it in every respect; by evasions he weakens and perverts faith in divine predestination and bends the words of truth toward falsehood as far as he can. Catholic teaching therefore refutes him with open truth and, even if it does not turn him back from his obstinate adherence, nevertheless proves him, in his falsehood, to be opposed to the truth, 110.

**Chapter XIII.** — On what Fulgentius wrote in his book to Monimus: that God’s predestination is spoken of not only with respect to good but also with respect to evil, 122.

**Chapter XIV.** — From this follows an exhortation to Gottschalk’s disorderly school, 125.

**Chapter XV.** — From whose words and scriptural statements the four chapters which we once excerpted against the resurgent predestinarians were collected and excerpted; and what the ancient predestinarians said from them, and what the modern heretics, raving on the basis of these passages, say, 126.

**Chapter XVI.** — From this point the text of the first chapter excerpted by us is set out, with each part identified and its source indicated, 129.

**Chapter XVII.** — On the fact that Gottschalk used, to confirm his own position, a copy of a book of blessed Augustine, which his associates deny to be by that author; and on other statements of the saints proposed by us concerning the substance of the chapter excerpted, 159.

**Chapter XVIII.** — On the definite number of the predestined, 169.

**Chapter XIX.** — How God’s one predestination may faithfully be called twofold; concerning this Gottschalk and his synagogue [Col. 1314] of sinners labor anxiously and disastrously through their false thinking and interpretation, 170.

**Chapter XX.** — How one ought to understand the fact that blessed Gregory used the plural number and spoke of “predestinations,” 178.

**Chapter XXI.** — How the ancient predestinarians understood the second chapter, which we excerpted against the predestinarians, concerning grace and free will; from whose words we took what we set out there; and concerning the reversal of its order, which some are recognized to have made improperly, 182.

**Chapter XXII.** — On the man who composed, without disclosing his name, a little book criticizing these chapters; and on the synodal statements which the compiler of the chapters given to us by royal eminence collected, wishing to show that we had disagreed with them, 195.

**Chapter XXIII.** — The compiler himself is then refuted from the words of blessed Augustine and the other teachers, 207.

**Chapter XXIV.** — The account concerning the third chapter excerpted by us begins. The compiler of the chapters given to us by royal eminence vehemently criticizes it, together with what the predestinarians say they derive from it to confirm their own position, and with an explanation of how Catholics, from the statements of Scripture, contradict their perverse assertions, 210.

**Chapter XXV.** — The words of the orthodox follow, by which it may be known how the Catholic teachers of the holy Church understood the matter, 225.

**Chapter XXVI.** — Recapitulation of the account given, after the names of the saints have been identified, concerning the third chapter, 268.

**Chapter XXVII.** — The account concerning the fourth chapter begins. We excerpted it against the predestinarians, but the compiler of the chapters which you gave us marked it with excessive error. To magnify the stigma of our criticism, he brings forward the Antichrist and the impious who died in their impiety and were condemned to eternal fire before Christ’s coming, 275.

**Chapter XXVIII.** — How Catholics understood the impious who died in their impiety: that the Lord also suffered for them, although they were not redeemed for everlasting salvation through the mystery of his Passion, 283.

**Chapter XXIX.** — The explanation of the two matters which, compelled by necessity, we inserted in this fourth chapter in the words of blessed Prosper, 288.

**Chapter XXX.** — Apart from these two almost syllabic statements, we have placed nothing in this chapter except what we excerpted from the words of blessed Prosper, 294.

**Chapter XXXI.** — On the nineteen chapters which the compiler of the chapters given to us by royal authority mentions in disparagement of us, and on other matters, whether those which we found written here and there or those which we heard had been discovered by certain frivolous inquirers, 296.

**Chapter XXXII.** — On the compiler’s closing statement, and on the three matters which we took care to append to this chapter. One of them is that the crowds which preceded the Lord’s coming and those which followed it proclaim “Hosanna” with one and the same faith, because we believe that by God’s grace we are saved just as they were, 298.

**Chapter XXXIII.** — From this point follows an account of how Catholic men teach, on the authority of the holy Scriptures, that Christ suffered generally for all, 311.

**Chapter XXXIV.** — Now follows the third matter mentioned above: how orthodox and ancient teachers demonstrate from authoritative Scriptures that this must be understood with discernment. Although Christ suffered for all, nevertheless not all have been redeemed unto eternal salvation by the price of the world—namely, by the mystery of his Passion. Those are excluded from this price who, delighting in captivity, refused to be redeemed, or who after redemption returned to the same slavery of captivity, 349.

**Chapter XXXV.** — The explanation concerning the fifth chapter follows. Our harshest critic, as though adding to the pain of our wounds, wished to spit upon us in order to insult us, 369.

**Chapter XXXVI.** — An apology for our designation follows, since the son of Ephraim, bending his bow against us, shot arrows; but perhaps he will find that his bow is crooked. His own sword, turned against him, will not come to his aid on the day of battle, 382.

**Chapter XXXVII.** — Since this recently removed heresy, as we have shown, was once refuted in the ancient heretics, we have taken care to append to the preceding material, in twelve chapters, what ecclesiastical authority decrees concerning those who think perversely in this way, 393.

**Chapter XXXVIII.** — Finally there follows a brief epilogue summarizing the entire matter set out from the four chapters, since the fifth chapter, concerning baptism, is contained here in the fourth, on the Redemption of Christ. It has been composed so that it should not weary readers, being freed from the prolix reply of those who contradict the true faith. It wishes to heal the one whom it displays in the thirty-eighth chapter as though he had lain sick for thirty-eight years: namely, the company of those who think perversely, deficient by two from the number forty, which is fulfilled by the four books of the holy Gospel in the Decalogue of the Law, and walking empty of the love of God and neighbor, which the writing of both Law and Gospel commends. Although they are several in the company, if they consent to yield to the truth, they will recover health as one body in the unity of faith. For apart from the unity of the Catholic faith no place of salvation is open to anyone; whoever departs from that unity can in no way attain the salvation which comes from the One, 418.

**Chapter I of the Epilogue**, 418.

**Chapter II of the Epilogue.** — What is the distinction between grace and predestination, and between foreknowledge and predestination, 421.

**Chapter III of the Epilogue.** — What the predestination of the saints is; that those chosen by God for life are predestined; and that eternal life is predestined for them. The reprobate, however, are not predestined by God, but foreknown and left for punishment; and eternal punishment is predestined for them in accordance with the retribution of justice, 425.

**Chapter IV of the Epilogue.** — How the Catholic Church holds the doctrine of grace and free will, 438.

**Chapter V of the Epilogue.** — That God wishes all human beings to be saved, although not all are saved; that the fact that some are saved is the gift of the One who saves, while the fact that some perish is the merit of those who perish, 442.

**Chapter VI of the Epilogue.** — That Christ suffered for all human beings, although not all are redeemed for eternal salvation through the mystery of his Passion; and that, since not all are redeemed through the mystery of his Passion, this is attributable not to the power of the sacrament but to the part of unbelievers. For the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world; excluded from this price are those who, delighting in captivity, refused to be redeemed, or who after redemption returned, through persistent unbelief or wickedness, to the same slavery, 454.
